''' PLAY: A Comedy of Errors '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A hall in DUKE SOLINUS'S palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE SOLINUS, AEGEON, Gaoler, Officers, and other Attendants
AEGEON: Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall
AEGEON: And by the doom of death end woes and all.
DUKE SOLINUS: Merchant of Syracuse, plead no more,
DUKE SOLINUS: I am not partial to infringe our laws:
DUKE SOLINUS: The enmity and discord which of late
DUKE SOLINUS: Sprung from the rancorous outrage of your duke
DUKE SOLINUS: To merchants, our well-dealing countrymen,
DUKE SOLINUS: Who wanting guilders to redeem their lives
DUKE SOLINUS: Have seal'd his rigorous statutes with their bloods,
DUKE SOLINUS: Excludes all pity from our threatening looks.
DUKE SOLINUS: For, since the mortal and intestine jars
DUKE SOLINUS: 'Twixt thy seditious countrymen and us,
DUKE SOLINUS: It hath in solemn synods been decreed
DUKE SOLINUS: Both by the Syracusians and ourselves,
DUKE SOLINUS: To admit no traffic to our adverse towns Nay, more,
DUKE SOLINUS: If any born at Ephesus be seen
DUKE SOLINUS: At any Syracusian marts and fairs,
DUKE SOLINUS: Again: if any Syracusian born
DUKE SOLINUS: Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies,
DUKE SOLINUS: His goods confiscate to the duke's dispose,
DUKE SOLINUS: Unless a thousand marks be levied,
DUKE SOLINUS: To quit the penalty and to ransom him.
DUKE SOLINUS: Thy substance, valued at the highest rate,
DUKE SOLINUS: Cannot amount unto a hundred marks,
DUKE SOLINUS: Therefore by law thou art condemned to die.
AEGEON: Yet this my comfort: when your words are done,
AEGEON: My woes end likewise with the evening sun.
DUKE SOLINUS: Well, Syracusian, say in brief the cause
DUKE SOLINUS: Why thou departed'st from thy native home
DUKE SOLINUS: And for what cause thou camest to Ephesus.
AEGEON: A heavier task could not have been imposed
AEGEON: Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable:
AEGEON: Yet, that the world may witness that my end
AEGEON: Was wrought by nature, not by vile offence,
AEGEON: I'll utter what my sorrows give me leave.
AEGEON: In Syracusa was I born, and wed
AEGEON: Unto a woman, happy but for me,
AEGEON: And by me, had not our hap been bad.
AEGEON: With her I lived in joy, our wealth increased
AEGEON: By prosperous voyages I often made
AEGEON: To Epidamnum, till my factor's death
AEGEON: And the great care of goods at random left
AEGEON: Drew me from kind embracements of my spouse:
AEGEON: From whom my absence was not six months old
AEGEON: Before herself, almost at fainting under
AEGEON: The pleasing punishment that women bear,
AEGEON: Had made provision for her following me
AEGEON: And soon and safe arrived where I was.
AEGEON: There had she not been long, but she became
AEGEON: A joyful mother of two goodly sons,
AEGEON: And, which was strange, the one so like the other,
AEGEON: As could not be distinguish'd but by names.
AEGEON: That very hour, and in the self-same inn,
AEGEON: A meaner woman was delivered
AEGEON: Of such a burden, male twins, both alike:
AEGEON: Those,--for their parents were exceeding poor,--
AEGEON: I bought and brought up to attend my sons.
AEGEON: My wife, not meanly proud of two such boys,
AEGEON: Made daily motions for our home return:
AEGEON: Unwilling I agreed. Alas! too soon,
AEGEON: We came aboard.
AEGEON: A league from Epidamnum had we sail'd,
AEGEON: Before the always wind-obeying deep
AEGEON: Gave any tragic instance of our harm:
AEGEON: But longer did we not retain much hope,
AEGEON: For what obscured light the heavens did grant
AEGEON: Did but convey unto our fearful minds
AEGEON: A doubtful warrant of immediate death,
AEGEON: Which though myself would gladly have embraced,
AEGEON: Yet the incessant weepings of my wife,
AEGEON: Weeping before for what she saw must come,
AEGEON: And piteous plainings of the pretty babes,
AEGEON: That mourn'd for fashion, ignorant what to fear,
AEGEON: Forced me to seek delays for them and me.
AEGEON: And this it was, for other means was none:
AEGEON: The sailors sought for safety by our boat,
AEGEON: And left the ship, then sinking-ripe, to us:
AEGEON: My wife, more careful for the latter-born,
AEGEON: Had fasten'd him unto a small spare mast,
AEGEON: Such as seafaring men provide for storms,
AEGEON: To him one of the other twins was bound,
AEGEON: Whilst I had been like heedful of the other:
AEGEON: The children thus disposed, my wife and I,
AEGEON: Fixing our eyes on whom our care was fix'd,
AEGEON: Fasten'd ourselves at either end the mast,
AEGEON: And floating straight, obedient to the stream,
AEGEON: Was carried towards Corinth, as we thought.
AEGEON: At length the sun, gazing upon the earth,
AEGEON: Dispersed those vapours that offended us,
AEGEON: And by the benefit of his wished light,
AEGEON: The seas wax'd calm, and we discovered
AEGEON: Two ships from far making amain to us,
AEGEON: Of Corinth that, of Epidaurus this:
AEGEON: But ere they came,--O, let me say no more!
AEGEON: Gather the sequel by that went before.
DUKE SOLINUS: Nay, forward, old man, do not break off so,
DUKE SOLINUS: For we may pity, though not pardon thee.
AEGEON: O, had the gods done so, I had not now
AEGEON: Worthily term'd them merciless to us!
AEGEON: For, ere the ships could meet by twice five leagues,
AEGEON: We were encounterd by a mighty rock,
AEGEON: Which being violently borne upon,
AEGEON: Our helpful ship was splitted in the midst,
AEGEON: So that, in this unjust divorce of us,
AEGEON: Fortune had left to both of us alike
AEGEON: What to delight in, what to sorrow for.
AEGEON: Her part, poor soul! seeming as burdened
AEGEON: With lesser weight but not with lesser woe,
AEGEON: Was carried with more speed before the wind,
AEGEON: And in our sight they three were taken up
AEGEON: By fishermen of Corinth, as we thought.
AEGEON: At length, another ship had seized on us,
AEGEON: And, knowing whom it was their hap to save,
AEGEON: Gave healthful welcome to their shipwreck'd guests,
AEGEON: And would have reft the fishers of their prey,
AEGEON: Had not their bark been very slow of sail,
AEGEON: And therefore homeward did they bend their course.
AEGEON: Thus have you heard me sever'd from my bliss,
AEGEON: That by misfortunes was my life prolong'd,
AEGEON: To tell sad stories of my own mishaps.
DUKE SOLINUS: And for the sake of them thou sorrowest for,
DUKE SOLINUS: Do me the favour to dilate at full
DUKE SOLINUS: What hath befall'n of them and thee till now.
AEGEON: My youngest boy, and yet my eldest care,
AEGEON: At eighteen years became inquisitive
AEGEON: After his brother: and importuned me
AEGEON: That his attendant--so his case was like,
AEGEON: Reft of his brother, but retain'd his name--
AEGEON: Might bear him company in the quest of him:
AEGEON: Whom whilst I labour'd of a love to see,
AEGEON: I hazarded the loss of whom I loved.
AEGEON: Five summers have I spent in furthest Greece,
AEGEON: Roaming clean through the bounds of Asia,
AEGEON: And, coasting homeward, came to Ephesus,
AEGEON: Hopeless to find, yet loath to leave unsought
AEGEON: Or that or any place that harbours men.
AEGEON: But here must end the story of my life,
AEGEON: And happy were I in my timely death,
AEGEON: Could all my travels warrant me they live.
DUKE SOLINUS: Hapless AEgeon, whom the fates have mark'd
DUKE SOLINUS: To bear the extremity of dire mishap!
DUKE SOLINUS: Now, trust me, were it not against our laws,
DUKE SOLINUS: Against my crown, my oath, my dignity,
DUKE SOLINUS: Which princes, would they, may not disannul,
DUKE SOLINUS: My soul would sue as advocate for thee.
DUKE SOLINUS: But, though thou art adjudged to the death
DUKE SOLINUS: And passed sentence may not be recall'd
DUKE SOLINUS: But to our honour's great disparagement,
DUKE SOLINUS: Yet I will favour thee in what I can.
DUKE SOLINUS: Therefore, merchant, I'll limit thee this day
DUKE SOLINUS: To seek thy life by beneficial help:
DUKE SOLINUS: Try all the friends thou hast in Ephesus,
DUKE SOLINUS: Beg thou, or borrow, to make up the sum,
DUKE SOLINUS: And live, if no, then thou art doom'd to die.
DUKE SOLINUS: Gaoler, take him to thy custody.
Gaoler: I will, my lord.
AEGEON: Hopeless and helpless doth AEgeon wend,
AEGEON: But to procrastinate his lifeless end.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The Mart.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse, DROMIO of Syracuse, and First Merchant
First Merchant: Therefore give out you are of Epidamnum,
First Merchant: Lest that your goods too soon be confiscate.
First Merchant: This very day a Syracusian merchant
First Merchant: Is apprehended for arrival here,
First Merchant: And not being able to buy out his life
First Merchant: According to the statute of the town,
First Merchant: Dies ere the weary sun set in the west.
First Merchant: There is your money that I had to keep.
First Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Go bear it to the Centaur, where we host,
OF SYRACUSE: And stay there, Dromio, till I come to thee.
OF SYRACUSE: Within this hour it will be dinner-time:
OF SYRACUSE: Till that, I'll view the manners of the town,
OF SYRACUSE: Peruse the traders, gaze upon the buildings,
OF SYRACUSE: And then return and sleep within mine inn,
OF SYRACUSE: For with long travel I am stiff and weary.
OF SYRACUSE: Get thee away.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Many a man would take you at your word,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: And go indeed, having so good a mean.
NARRATOR: Exit
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: A trusty villain, sir, that very oft,
OF SYRACUSE: When I am dull with care and melancholy,
OF SYRACUSE: Lightens my humour with his merry jests.
OF SYRACUSE: What, will you walk with me about the town,
OF SYRACUSE: And then go to my inn and dine with me?
First Merchant: I am invited, sir, to certain merchants,
First Merchant: Of whom I hope to make much benefit,
First Merchant: I crave your pardon. Soon at five o'clock,
First Merchant: Please you, I'll meet with you upon the mart
First Merchant: And afterward consort you till bed-time:
First Merchant: My present business calls me from you now.
First Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Farewell till then: I will go lose myself
OF SYRACUSE: And wander up and down to view the city.
First Merchant: Sir, I commend you to your own content.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: He that commends me to mine own content
OF SYRACUSE: Commends me to the thing I cannot get.
OF SYRACUSE: I to the world am like a drop of water
OF SYRACUSE: That in the ocean seeks another drop,
OF SYRACUSE: Who, falling there to find his fellow forth,
OF SYRACUSE: Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself:
OF SYRACUSE: So I, to find a mother and a brother,
OF SYRACUSE: In quest of them, unhappy, lose myself.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Ephesus
OF SYRACUSE: Here comes the almanac of my true date.
OF SYRACUSE: What now? how chance thou art return'd so soon?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Return'd so soon! rather approach'd too late:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: The capon burns, the pig falls from the spit,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: The clock hath strucken twelve upon the bell,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: My mistress made it one upon my cheek:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: She is so hot because the meat is cold,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: The meat is cold because you come not home,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You come not home because you have no stomach,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You have no stomach having broke your fast,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But we that know what 'tis to fast and pray
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Are penitent for your default to-day.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Stop in your wind, sir: tell me this, I pray:
OF SYRACUSE: Where have you left the money that I gave you?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: O,--sixpence, that I had o' Wednesday last
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: To pay the saddler for my mistress' crupper?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: The saddler had it, sir, I kept it not.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I am not in a sportive humour now:
OF SYRACUSE: Tell me, and dally not, where is the money?
OF SYRACUSE: We being strangers here, how darest thou trust
OF SYRACUSE: So great a charge from thine own custody?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I pray you, air, as you sit at dinner:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I from my mistress come to you in post,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If I return, I shall be post indeed,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: For she will score your fault upon my pate.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Methinks your maw, like mine, should be your clock,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And strike you home without a messenger.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Come, Dromio, come, these jests are out of season,
OF SYRACUSE: Reserve them till a merrier hour than this.
OF SYRACUSE: Where is the gold I gave in charge to thee?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: To me, sir? why, you gave no gold to me.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Come on, sir knave, have done your foolishness,
OF SYRACUSE: And tell me how thou hast disposed thy charge.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: My charge was but to fetch you from the mart
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Home to your house, the Phoenix, sir, to dinner:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: My mistress and her sister stays for you.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: In what safe place you have bestow'd my money,
OF SYRACUSE: Or I shall break that merry sconce of yours
OF SYRACUSE: That stands on tricks when I am undisposed:
OF SYRACUSE: Where is the thousand marks thou hadst of me?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I have some marks of yours upon my pate,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Some of my mistress' marks upon my shoulders,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But not a thousand marks between you both.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If I should pay your worship those again,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Perchance you will not bear them patiently.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thy mistress' marks? what mistress, slave, hast thou?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Your worship's wife, my mistress at the Phoenix,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: She that doth fast till you come home to dinner,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And prays that you will hie you home to dinner.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What, wilt thou flout me thus unto my face,
OF SYRACUSE: Being forbid? There, take you that, sir knave.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: What mean you, sir? for God's sake, hold your hands!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, and you will not, sir, I'll take my heels.
NARRATOR: Exit
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Upon my life, by some device or other
OF SYRACUSE: The villain is o'er-raught of all my money.
OF SYRACUSE: They say this town is full of cozenage,
OF SYRACUSE: As, nimble jugglers that deceive the eye,
OF SYRACUSE: Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind,
OF SYRACUSE: Soul-killing witches that deform the body,
OF SYRACUSE: Disguised cheaters, prating mountebanks,
OF SYRACUSE: And many such-like liberties of sin:
OF SYRACUSE: If it prove so, I will be gone the sooner.
OF SYRACUSE: I'll to the Centaur, to go seek this slave:
OF SYRACUSE: I greatly fear my money is not safe.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The house of ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus.
NARRATOR: Enter ADRIANA and LUCIANA
ADRIANA: Neither my husband nor the slave return'd,
ADRIANA: That in such haste I sent to seek his master!
ADRIANA: Sure, Luciana, it is two o'clock.
LUCIANA: Perhaps some merchant hath invited him,
LUCIANA: And from the mart he's somewhere gone to dinner.
LUCIANA: Good sister, let us dine and never fret:
LUCIANA: A man is master of his liberty:
LUCIANA: Time is their master, and, when they see time,
LUCIANA: They'll go or come: if so, be patient, sister.
ADRIANA: Why should their liberty than ours be more?
LUCIANA: Because their business still lies out o' door.
ADRIANA: Look, when I serve him so, he takes it ill.
LUCIANA: O, know he is the bridle of your will.
ADRIANA: There's none but asses will be bridled so.
LUCIANA: Why, headstrong liberty is lash'd with woe.
LUCIANA: There's nothing situate under heaven's eye
LUCIANA: But hath his bound, in earth, in sea, in sky:
LUCIANA: The beasts, the fishes, and the winged fowls,
LUCIANA: Are their males' subjects and at their controls:
LUCIANA: Men, more divine, the masters of all these,
LUCIANA: Lords of the wide world and wild watery seas,
LUCIANA: Indued with intellectual sense and souls,
LUCIANA: Of more preeminence than fish and fowls,
LUCIANA: Are masters to their females, and their lords:
LUCIANA: Then let your will attend on their accords.
ADRIANA: This servitude makes you to keep unwed.
LUCIANA: Not this, but troubles of the marriage-bed.
ADRIANA: But, were you wedded, you would bear some sway.
LUCIANA: Ere I learn love, I'll practise to obey.
ADRIANA: How if your husband start some other where?
LUCIANA: Till he come home again, I would forbear.
ADRIANA: Patience unmoved! no marvel though she pause,
ADRIANA: They can be meek that have no other cause.
ADRIANA: A wretched soul, bruised with adversity,
ADRIANA: We bid be quiet when we hear it cry,
ADRIANA: But were we burdened with like weight of pain,
ADRIANA: As much or more would we ourselves complain:
ADRIANA: So thou, that hast no unkind mate to grieve thee,
ADRIANA: With urging helpless patience wouldst relieve me,
ADRIANA: But, if thou live to see like right bereft,
ADRIANA: This fool-begg'd patience in thee will be left.
LUCIANA: Well, I will marry one day, but to try.
LUCIANA: Here comes your man, now is your husband nigh.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Ephesus
ADRIANA: Say, is your tardy master now at hand?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, he's at two hands with me, and that my two ears
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: can witness.
ADRIANA: Say, didst thou speak with him? know'st thou his mind?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Ay, ay, he told his mind upon mine ear:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Beshrew his hand, I scarce could understand it.
LUCIANA: Spake he so doubtfully, thou couldst not feel his meaning?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, he struck so plainly, I could too well feel his
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: blows, and withal so doubtfully that I could scarce
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: understand them.
ADRIANA: But say, I prithee, is he coming home? It seems he
ADRIANA: hath great care to please his wife.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Why, mistress, sure my master is horn-mad.
ADRIANA: Horn-mad, thou villain!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I mean not cuckold-mad,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But, sure, he is stark mad.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: When I desired him to come home to dinner,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: He ask'd me for a thousand marks in gold:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ''Tis dinner-time,' quoth I, 'My gold!' quoth he,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'Your meat doth burn,' quoth I, 'My gold!' quoth he:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'Will you come home?' quoth I, 'My gold!' quoth he.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'Where is the thousand marks I gave thee, villain?'
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'The pig,' quoth I, 'is burn'd,' 'My gold!' quoth he:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'My mistress, sir' quoth I, 'Hang up thy mistress!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I know not thy mistress, out on thy mistress!'
LUCIANA: Quoth who?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Quoth my master:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: 'I know,' quoth he, 'no house, no wife, no mistress.'
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: So that my errand, due unto my tongue,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I thank him, I bare home upon my shoulders,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: For, in conclusion, he did beat me there.
ADRIANA: Go back again, thou slave, and fetch him home.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Go back again, and be new beaten home?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: For God's sake, send some other messenger.
ADRIANA: Back, slave, or I will break thy pate across.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And he will bless that cross with other beating:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Between you I shall have a holy head.
ADRIANA: Hence, prating peasant! fetch thy master home.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Am I so round with you as you with me,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: That like a football you do spurn me thus?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You spurn me hence, and he will spurn me hither:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If I last in this service, you must case me in leather.
NARRATOR: Exit
LUCIANA: Fie, how impatience loureth in your face!
ADRIANA: His company must do his minions grace,
ADRIANA: Whilst I at home starve for a merry look.
ADRIANA: Hath homely age the alluring beauty took
ADRIANA: From my poor cheek? then he hath wasted it:
ADRIANA: Are my discourses dull? barren my wit?
ADRIANA: If voluble and sharp discourse be marr'd,
ADRIANA: Unkindness blunts it more than marble hard:
ADRIANA: Do their gay vestments his affections bait?
ADRIANA: That's not my fault: he's master of my state:
ADRIANA: What ruins are in me that can be found,
ADRIANA: By him not ruin'd? then is he the ground
ADRIANA: Of my defeatures. My decayed fair
ADRIANA: A sunny look of his would soon repair
ADRIANA: But, too unruly deer, he breaks the pale
ADRIANA: And feeds from home, poor I am but his stale.
LUCIANA: Self-harming jealousy! fie, beat it hence!
ADRIANA: Unfeeling fools can with such wrongs dispense.
ADRIANA: I know his eye doth homage otherwhere,
ADRIANA: Or else what lets it but he would be here?
ADRIANA: Sister, you know he promised me a chain,
ADRIANA: Would that alone, alone he would detain,
ADRIANA: So he would keep fair quarter with his bed!
ADRIANA: I see the jewel best enamelled
ADRIANA: Will lose his beauty, yet the gold bides still,
ADRIANA: That others touch, and often touching will
ADRIANA: Wear gold: and no man that hath a name,
ADRIANA: By falsehood and corruption doth it shame.
ADRIANA: Since that my beauty cannot please his eye,
ADRIANA: I'll weep what's left away, and weeping die.
LUCIANA: How many fond fools serve mad jealousy!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: The gold I gave to Dromio is laid up
OF SYRACUSE: Safe at the Centaur, and the heedful slave
OF SYRACUSE: Is wander'd forth, in care to seek me out
OF SYRACUSE: By computation and mine host's report.
OF SYRACUSE: I could not speak with Dromio since at first
OF SYRACUSE: I sent him from the mart. See, here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Syracuse
OF SYRACUSE: How now sir! is your merry humour alter'd?
OF SYRACUSE: As you love strokes, so jest with me again.
OF SYRACUSE: You know no Centaur? you received no gold?
OF SYRACUSE: Your mistress sent to have me home to dinner?
OF SYRACUSE: My house was at the Phoenix? Wast thou mad,
OF SYRACUSE: That thus so madly thou didst answer me?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: What answer, sir? when spake I such a word?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Even now, even here, not half an hour since.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I did not see you since you sent me hence,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Home to the Centaur, with the gold you gave me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Villain, thou didst deny the gold's receipt,
OF SYRACUSE: And told'st me of a mistress and a dinner,
OF SYRACUSE: For which, I hope, thou felt'st I was displeased.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I am glad to see you in this merry vein:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: What means this jest? I pray you, master, tell me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Yea, dost thou jeer and flout me in the teeth?
OF SYRACUSE: Think'st thou I jest? Hold, take thou that, and that.
NARRATOR: Beating him
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Hold, sir, for God's sake! now your jest is earnest:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Upon what bargain do you give it me?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Because that I familiarly sometimes
OF SYRACUSE: Do use you for my fool and chat with you,
OF SYRACUSE: Your sauciness will jest upon my love
OF SYRACUSE: And make a common of my serious hours.
OF SYRACUSE: When the sun shines let foolish gnats make sport,
OF SYRACUSE: But creep in crannies when he hides his beams.
OF SYRACUSE: If you will jest with me, know my aspect,
OF SYRACUSE: And fashion your demeanor to my looks,
OF SYRACUSE: Or I will beat this method in your sconce.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Sconce call you it? so you would leave battering, I
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: had rather have it a head: an you use these blows
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: long, I must get a sconce for my head and ensconce
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: it too, or else I shall seek my wit in my shoulders.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: But, I pray, sir why am I beaten?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Dost thou not know?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Nothing, sir, but that I am beaten.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Shall I tell you why?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Ay, sir, and wherefore, for they say every why hath
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: a wherefore.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why, first,--for flouting me, and then, wherefore--
OF SYRACUSE: For urging it the second time to me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Was there ever any man thus beaten out of season,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: When in the why and the wherefore is neither rhyme
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: nor reason?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Well, sir, I thank you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thank me, sir, for what?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, sir, for this something that you gave me for nothing.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I'll make you amends next, to give you nothing for
OF SYRACUSE: something. But say, sir, is it dinner-time?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No, sir, I think the meat wants that I have.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: In good time, sir, what's that?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Basting.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Well, sir, then 'twill be dry.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: If it be, sir, I pray you, eat none of it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Your reason?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Lest it make you choleric and purchase me another
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: dry basting.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Well, sir, learn to jest in good time: there's a
OF SYRACUSE: time for all things.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I durst have denied that, before you were so choleric.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: By what rule, sir?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, sir, by a rule as plain as the plain bald
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: pate of father Time himself.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Let's hear it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: There's no time for a man to recover his hair that
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: grows bald by nature.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: May he not do it by fine and recovery?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Yes, to pay a fine for a periwig and recover the
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: lost hair of another man.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why is Time such a niggard of hair, being, as it is,
OF SYRACUSE: so plentiful an excrement?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Because it is a blessing that he bestows on beasts,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: and what he hath scanted men in hair he hath given them in wit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why, but there's many a man hath more hair than wit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Not a man of those but he hath the wit to lose his hair.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why, thou didst conclude hairy men plain dealers without wit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The plainer dealer, the sooner lost: yet he loseth
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: it in a kind of jollity.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: For what reason?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: For two, and sound ones too.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Nay, not sound, I pray you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Sure ones, then.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Nay, not sure, in a thing falsing.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Certain ones then.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Name them.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The one, to save the money that he spends in
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: trimming, the other, that at dinner they should not
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: drop in his porridge.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: You would all this time have proved there is no
OF SYRACUSE: time for all things.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, and did, sir, namely, no time to recover hair
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: lost by nature.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: But your reason was not substantial, why there is no
OF SYRACUSE: time to recover.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Thus I mend it: Time himself is bald and therefore
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: to the world's end will have bald followers.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I knew 'twould be a bald conclusion:
OF SYRACUSE: But, soft! who wafts us yonder?
NARRATOR: Enter ADRIANA and LUCIANA
ADRIANA: Ay, ay, Antipholus, look strange and frown:
ADRIANA: Some other mistress hath thy sweet aspects,
ADRIANA: I am not Adriana nor thy wife.
ADRIANA: The time was once when thou unurged wouldst vow
ADRIANA: That never words were music to thine ear,
ADRIANA: That never object pleasing in thine eye,
ADRIANA: That never touch well welcome to thy hand,
ADRIANA: That never meat sweet-savor'd in thy taste,
ADRIANA: Unless I spake, or look'd, or touch'd, or carved to thee.
ADRIANA: How comes it now, my husband, O, how comes it,
ADRIANA: That thou art thus estranged from thyself?
ADRIANA: Thyself I call it, being strange to me,
ADRIANA: That, undividable, incorporate,
ADRIANA: Am better than thy dear self's better part.
ADRIANA: Ah, do not tear away thyself from me!
ADRIANA: For know, my love, as easy mayest thou fall
ADRIANA: A drop of water in the breaking gulf,
ADRIANA: And take unmingled that same drop again,
ADRIANA: Without addition or diminishing,
ADRIANA: As take from me thyself and not me too.
ADRIANA: How dearly would it touch me to the quick,
ADRIANA: Shouldst thou but hear I were licentious
ADRIANA: And that this body, consecrate to thee,
ADRIANA: By ruffian lust should be contaminate!
ADRIANA: Wouldst thou not spit at me and spurn at me
ADRIANA: And hurl the name of husband in my face
ADRIANA: And tear the stain'd skin off my harlot-brow
ADRIANA: And from my false hand cut the wedding-ring
ADRIANA: And break it with a deep-divorcing vow?
ADRIANA: I know thou canst, and therefore see thou do it.
ADRIANA: I am possess'd with an adulterate blot,
ADRIANA: My blood is mingled with the crime of lust:
ADRIANA: For if we too be one and thou play false,
ADRIANA: I do digest the poison of thy flesh,
ADRIANA: Being strumpeted by thy contagion.
ADRIANA: Keep then far league and truce with thy true bed,
ADRIANA: I live unstain'd, thou undishonoured.
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Plead you to me, fair dame? I know you not:
OF SYRACUSE: In Ephesus I am but two hours old,
OF SYRACUSE: As strange unto your town as to your talk,
OF SYRACUSE: Who, every word by all my wit being scann'd,
OF SYRACUSE: Want wit in all one word to understand.
LUCIANA: Fie, brother! how the world is changed with you!
LUCIANA: When were you wont to use my sister thus?
LUCIANA: She sent for you by Dromio home to dinner.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: By Dromio?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: By me?
ADRIANA: By thee, and this thou didst return from him,
ADRIANA: That he did buffet thee, and, in his blows,
ADRIANA: Denied my house for his, me for his wife.
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Did you converse, sir, with this gentlewoman?
OF SYRACUSE: What is the course and drift of your compact?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I, sir? I never saw her till this time.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Villain, thou liest, for even her very words
OF SYRACUSE: Didst thou deliver to me on the mart.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I never spake with her in all my life.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: How can she thus then call us by our names,
OF SYRACUSE: Unless it be by inspiration.
ADRIANA: How ill agrees it with your gravity
ADRIANA: To counterfeit thus grossly with your slave,
ADRIANA: Abetting him to thwart me in my mood!
ADRIANA: Be it my wrong you are from me exempt,
ADRIANA: But wrong not that wrong with a more contempt.
ADRIANA: Come, I will fasten on this sleeve of thine:
ADRIANA: Thou art an elm, my husband, I a vine,
ADRIANA: Whose weakness, married to thy stronger state,
ADRIANA: Makes me with thy strength to communicate:
ADRIANA: If aught possess thee from me, it is dross,
ADRIANA: Usurping ivy, brier, or idle moss,
ADRIANA: Who, all for want of pruning, with intrusion
ADRIANA: Infect thy sap and live on thy confusion.
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: To me she speaks, she moves me for her theme:
OF SYRACUSE: What, was I married to her in my dream?
OF SYRACUSE: Or sleep I now and think I hear all this?
OF SYRACUSE: What error drives our eyes and ears amiss?
OF SYRACUSE: Until I know this sure uncertainty,
OF SYRACUSE: I'll entertain the offer'd fallacy.
LUCIANA: Dromio, go bid the servants spread for dinner.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: O, for my beads! I cross me for a sinner.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: This is the fairy land: O spite of spites!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: We talk with goblins, owls and sprites:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: If we obey them not, this will ensue,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: They'll suck our breath, or pinch us black and blue.
LUCIANA: Why pratest thou to thyself and answer'st not?
LUCIANA: Dromio, thou drone, thou snail, thou slug, thou sot!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I am transformed, master, am I not?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I think thou art in mind, and so am I.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Nay, master, both in mind and in my shape.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thou hast thine own form.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No, I am an ape.
LUCIANA: If thou art changed to aught, 'tis to an ass.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: 'Tis true, she rides me and I long for grass.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: 'Tis so, I am an ass, else it could never be
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: But I should know her as well as she knows me.
ADRIANA: Come, come, no longer will I be a fool,
ADRIANA: To put the finger in the eye and weep,
ADRIANA: Whilst man and master laugh my woes to scorn.
ADRIANA: Come, sir, to dinner. Dromio, keep the gate.
ADRIANA: Husband, I'll dine above with you to-day
ADRIANA: And shrive you of a thousand idle pranks.
ADRIANA: Sirrah, if any ask you for your master,
ADRIANA: Say he dines forth, and let no creature enter.
ADRIANA: Come, sister. Dromio, play the porter well.
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell?
OF SYRACUSE: Sleeping or waking? mad or well-advised?
OF SYRACUSE: Known unto these, and to myself disguised!
OF SYRACUSE: I'll say as they say and persever so,
OF SYRACUSE: And in this mist at all adventures go.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, shall I be porter at the gate?
ADRIANA: Ay, and let none enter, lest I break your pate.
LUCIANA: Come, come, Antipholus, we dine too late.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before the house of ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus, DROMIO of Ephesus, ANGELO, and BALTHAZAR
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Good Signior Angelo, you must excuse us all,
OF EPHESUS: My wife is shrewish when I keep not hours:
OF EPHESUS: Say that I linger'd with you at your shop
OF EPHESUS: To see the making of her carcanet,
OF EPHESUS: And that to-morrow you will bring it home.
OF EPHESUS: But here's a villain that would face me down
OF EPHESUS: He met me on the mart, and that I beat him,
OF EPHESUS: And charged him with a thousand marks in gold,
OF EPHESUS: And that I did deny my wife and house.
OF EPHESUS: Thou drunkard, thou, what didst thou mean by this?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Say what you will, sir, but I know what I know,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: That you beat me at the mart, I have your hand to show:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I think thou art an ass.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Marry, so it doth appear
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: By the wrongs I suffer and the blows I bear.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I should kick, being kick'd, and, being at that pass,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You would keep from my heels and beware of an ass.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: You're sad, Signior Balthazar: pray God our cheer
OF EPHESUS: May answer my good will and your good welcome here.
BALTHAZAR: I hold your dainties cheap, sir, and your
BALTHAZAR: welcome dear.
BALTHAZAR: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: O, Signior Balthazar, either at flesh or fish,
OF EPHESUS: A table full of welcome make scarce one dainty dish.
BALTHAZAR: Good meat, sir, is common, that every churl affords.
BALTHAZAR: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: And welcome more common, for that's nothing but words.
BALTHAZAR: Small cheer and great welcome makes a merry feast.
BALTHAZAR: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Ay, to a niggardly host, and more sparing guest:
OF EPHESUS: But though my cates be mean, take them in good part,
OF EPHESUS: Better cheer may you have, but not with better heart.
OF EPHESUS: But, soft! my door is lock'd. Go bid them let us in.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cicel, Gillian, Ginn!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Mome, malt-horse, capon, coxcomb,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: idiot, patch!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Either get thee from the door, or sit down at the hatch.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Dost thou conjure for wenches, that thou call'st
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: for such store,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: When one is one too many? Go, get thee from the door.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: What patch is made our porter? My master stays in
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: the street.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Let him walk from whence he came, lest he
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: catch cold on's feet.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Who talks within there? ho, open the door!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Right, sir, I'll tell you when, an you tell
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: me wherefore.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Wherefore? for my dinner: I have not dined to-day.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Nor to-day here you must not, come again
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: when you may.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: What art thou that keepest me out from the house I owe?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  The porter for this time, sir, and my name
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: is Dromio.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: O villain! thou hast stolen both mine office and my name.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: The one ne'er got me credit, the other mickle blame.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If thou hadst been Dromio to-day in my place,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Thou wouldst have changed thy face for a name or thy
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: name for an ass.
LUCE: [Within]  What a coil is there, Dromio? who are those
LUCE: at the gate?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Let my master in, Luce.
LUCE: [Within]  Faith, no, he comes too late,
LUCE: And so tell your master.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: O Lord, I must laugh!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Have at you with a proverb--Shall I set in my staff?
LUCE: [Within]  Have at you with another, that's--When?
LUCE: can you tell?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  If thy name be call'd Luce--Luce, thou hast
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: answered him well.
ANTIPHOLUS: Do you hear, you minion? you'll let us in, I hope?
ANTIPHOLUS: OF EPHESUS
LUCE: [Within]  I thought to have asked you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  And you said no.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: So, come, help: well struck! there was blow for blow.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Thou baggage, let me in.
LUCE: [Within]  Can you tell for whose sake?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Master, knock the door hard.
LUCE: [Within]  Let him knock till it ache.
LUCE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: You'll cry for this, minion, if I beat the door down.
LUCE: [Within]  What needs all that, and a pair of stocks in the town?
ADRIANA: [Within]  Who is that at the door that keeps all
ADRIANA: this noise?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  By my troth, your town is troubled with
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: unruly boys.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Are you there, wife? you might have come before.
ADRIANA: [Within]  Your wife, sir knave! go get you from the door.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If you went in pain, master, this 'knave' would go sore.
ANGELO: Here is neither cheer, sir, nor welcome: we would
ANGELO: fain have either.
BALTHAZAR: In debating which was best, we shall part with neither.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: They stand at the door, master, bid them welcome hither.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: There is something in the wind, that we cannot get in.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You would say so, master, if your garments were thin.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Your cake there is warm within, you stand here in the cold:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: It would make a man mad as a buck, to be so bought and sold.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Go fetch me something: I'll break ope the gate.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Break any breaking here, and I'll break your
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: knave's pate.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: A man may break a word with you, sir, and words are but wind,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Ay, and break it in your face, so he break it not behind.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  It seems thou want'st breaking: out upon
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: thee, hind!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Here's too much 'out upon thee!' I pray thee,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: let me in.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: [Within]  Ay, when fowls have no feathers and fish have no fin.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Well, I'll break in: go borrow me a crow.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: A crow without feather? Master, mean you so?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: For a fish without a fin, there's a fowl without a feather,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: If a crow help us in, sirrah, we'll pluck a crow together.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Go get thee gone, fetch me an iron crow.
BALTHAZAR: Have patience, sir, O, let it not be so!
BALTHAZAR: Herein you war against your reputation
BALTHAZAR: And draw within the compass of suspect
BALTHAZAR: The unviolated honour of your wife.
BALTHAZAR: Once this,--your long experience of her wisdom,
BALTHAZAR: Her sober virtue, years and modesty,
BALTHAZAR: Plead on her part some cause to you unknown:
BALTHAZAR: And doubt not, sir, but she will well excuse
BALTHAZAR: Why at this time the doors are made against you.
BALTHAZAR: Be ruled by me: depart in patience,
BALTHAZAR: And let us to the Tiger all to dinner,
BALTHAZAR: And about evening come yourself alone
BALTHAZAR: To know the reason of this strange restraint.
BALTHAZAR: If by strong hand you offer to break in
BALTHAZAR: Now in the stirring passage of the day,
BALTHAZAR: A vulgar comment will be made of it,
BALTHAZAR: And that supposed by the common rout
BALTHAZAR: Against your yet ungalled estimation
BALTHAZAR: That may with foul intrusion enter in
BALTHAZAR: And dwell upon your grave when you are dead,
BALTHAZAR: For slander lives upon succession,
BALTHAZAR: For ever housed where it gets possession.
BALTHAZAR: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: You have prevailed: I will depart in quiet,
OF EPHESUS: And, in despite of mirth, mean to be merry.
OF EPHESUS: I know a wench of excellent discourse,
OF EPHESUS: Pretty and witty, wild, and yet, too, gentle:
OF EPHESUS: There will we dine. This woman that I mean,
OF EPHESUS: My wife--but, I protest, without desert--
OF EPHESUS: Hath oftentimes upbraided me withal:
OF EPHESUS: To her will we to dinner.
NARRATOR: To Angelo
OF EPHESUS: Get you home
OF EPHESUS: And fetch the chain, by this I know 'tis made:
OF EPHESUS: Bring it, I pray you, to the Porpentine,
OF EPHESUS: For there's the house: that chain will I bestow--
OF EPHESUS: Be it for nothing but to spite my wife--
OF EPHESUS: Upon mine hostess there: good sir, make haste.
OF EPHESUS: Since mine own doors refuse to entertain me,
OF EPHESUS: I'll knock elsewhere, to see if they'll disdain me.
ANGELO: I'll meet you at that place some hour hence.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Do so. This jest shall cost me some expense.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIANA and ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse
LUCIANA: And may it be that you have quite forgot
LUCIANA: A husband's office? shall, Antipholus.
LUCIANA: Even in the spring of love, thy love-springs rot?
LUCIANA: Shall love, in building, grow so ruinous?
LUCIANA: If you did wed my sister for her wealth,
LUCIANA: Then for her wealth's sake use her with more kindness:
LUCIANA: Or if you like elsewhere, do it by stealth,
LUCIANA: Muffle your false love with some show of blindness:
LUCIANA: Let not my sister read it in your eye,
LUCIANA: Be not thy tongue thy own shame's orator,
LUCIANA: Look sweet, be fair, become disloyalty,
LUCIANA: Apparel vice like virtue's harbinger,
LUCIANA: Bear a fair presence, though your heart be tainted,
LUCIANA: Teach sin the carriage of a holy saint,
LUCIANA: Be secret-false: what need she be acquainted?
LUCIANA: What simple thief brags of his own attaint?
LUCIANA: 'Tis double wrong, to truant with your bed
LUCIANA: And let her read it in thy looks at board:
LUCIANA: Shame hath a bastard fame, well managed,
LUCIANA: Ill d eeds are doubled with an evil word.
LUCIANA: Alas, poor women! make us but believe,
LUCIANA: Being compact of credit, that you love us,
LUCIANA: Though others have the arm, show us the sleeve,
LUCIANA: We in your motion turn and you may move us.
LUCIANA: Then, gentle brother, get you in again,
LUCIANA: Comfort my sister, cheer her, call her wife:
LUCIANA: 'Tis holy sport to be a little vain,
LUCIANA: When the sweet breath of flattery conquers strife.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Sweet mistress--what your name is else, I know not,
OF SYRACUSE: Nor by what wonder you do hit of mine,--
OF SYRACUSE: Less in your knowledge and your grace you show not
OF SYRACUSE: Than our earth's wonder, more than earth divine.
OF SYRACUSE: Teach me, dear creature, how to think and speak,
OF SYRACUSE: Lay open to my earthy-gross conceit,
OF SYRACUSE: Smother'd in errors, feeble, shallow, weak,
OF SYRACUSE: The folded meaning of your words' deceit.
OF SYRACUSE: Against my soul's pure truth why labour you
OF SYRACUSE: To make it wander in an unknown field?
OF SYRACUSE: Are you a god? would you create me new?
OF SYRACUSE: Transform me then, and to your power I'll yield.
OF SYRACUSE: But if that I am I, then well I know
OF SYRACUSE: Your weeping sister is no wife of mine,
OF SYRACUSE: Nor to her bed no homage do I owe
OF SYRACUSE: Far more, far more to you do I decline.
OF SYRACUSE: O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note,
OF SYRACUSE: To drown me in thy sister's flood of tears:
OF SYRACUSE: Sing, siren, for thyself and I will dote:
OF SYRACUSE: Spread o'er the silver waves thy golden hairs,
OF SYRACUSE: And as a bed I'll take them and there lie,
OF SYRACUSE: And in that glorious supposition think
OF SYRACUSE: He gains by death that hath such means to die:
OF SYRACUSE: Let Love, being light, be drowned if she sink!
LUCIANA: What, are you mad, that you do reason so?
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Not mad, but mated, how, I do not know.
LUCIANA: It is a fault that springeth from your eye.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: For gazing on your beams, fair sun, being by.
LUCIANA: Gaze where you should, and that will clear your sight.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: As good to wink, sweet love, as look on night.
LUCIANA: Why call you me love? call my sister so.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thy sister's sister.
LUCIANA: That's my sister.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: No,
OF SYRACUSE: It is thyself, mine own self's better part,
OF SYRACUSE: Mine eye's clear eye, my dear heart's dearer heart,
OF SYRACUSE: My food, my fortune and my sweet hope's aim,
OF SYRACUSE: My sole earth's heaven and my heaven's claim.
LUCIANA: All this my sister is, or else should be.
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Call thyself sister, sweet, for I am thee.
OF SYRACUSE: Thee will I love and with thee lead my life:
OF SYRACUSE: Thou hast no husband yet nor I no wife.
OF SYRACUSE: Give me thy hand.
LUCIANA: O, soft, air! hold you still:
LUCIANA: I'll fetch my sister, to get her good will.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Syracuse
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why, how now, Dromio! where runn'st thou so fast?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Do you know me, sir? am I Dromio? am I your man?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: am I myself?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thou art Dromio, thou art my man, thou art thyself.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I am an ass, I am a woman's man and besides myself.
ANTIPHOLUS: What woman's man? and how besides thyself? besides thyself?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, sir, besides myself, I am due to a woman, one
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: that claims me, one that haunts me, one that will have me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What claim lays she to thee?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry sir, such claim as you would lay to your
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: horse, and she would have me as a beast: not that, I
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: being a beast, she would have me, but that she,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: being a very beastly creature, lays claim to me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What is she?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A very reverent body, ay, such a one as a man may
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: not speak of without he say 'Sir-reverence.' I have
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: but lean luck in the match, and yet is she a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: wondrous fat marriage.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: How dost thou mean a fat marriage?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, sir, she's the kitchen wench and all grease,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: and I know not what use to put her to but to make a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: lamp of her and run from her by her own light. I
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: warrant, her rags and the tallow in them will burn a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Poland winter: if she lives till doomsday,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: she'll burn a week longer than the whole world.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What complexion is she of?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Swart, like my shoe, but her face nothing half so
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: clean kept: for why, she sweats, a man may go over
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: shoes in the grime of it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: That's a fault that water will mend.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No, sir, 'tis in grain, Noah's flood could not do it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What's her name?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Nell, sir, but her name and three quarters, that's
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: an ell and three quarters, will not measure her from
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: hip to hip.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Then she bears some breadth?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No longer from head to foot than from hip to hip:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: she is spherical, like a globe, I could find out
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: countries in her.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: In what part of her body stands Ireland?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, in her buttocks: I found it out by the bogs.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where Scotland?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I found it by the barrenness, hard in the palm of the hand.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where France?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: In her forehead, armed and reverted, making war
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: against her heir.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where England?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I looked for the chalky cliffs, but I could find no
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: whiteness in them, but I guess it stood in her chin,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: by the salt rheum that ran between France and it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where Spain?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Faith, I saw it not, but I felt it hot in her breath.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where America, the Indies?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Oh, sir, upon her nose all o'er embellished with
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: rubies, carbuncles, sapphires, declining their rich
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: aspect to the hot breath of Spain, who sent whole
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: armadoes of caracks to be ballast at her nose.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Where stood Belgia, the Netherlands?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Oh, sir, I did not look so low. To conclude, this
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: drudge, or diviner, laid claim to me, call'd me
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Dromio, swore I was assured to her, told me what
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: privy marks I had about me, as, the mark of my
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: shoulder, the mole in my neck, the great wart on my
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: left arm, that I amazed ran from her as a witch:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: And, I think, if my breast had not been made of
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: faith and my heart of steel,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: She had transform'd me to a curtal dog and made
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: me turn i' the wheel.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Go hie thee presently, post to the road:
OF SYRACUSE: An if the wind blow any way from shore,
OF SYRACUSE: I will not harbour in this town to-night:
OF SYRACUSE: If any bark put forth, come to the mart,
OF SYRACUSE: Where I will walk till thou return to me.
OF SYRACUSE: If every one knows us and we know none,
OF SYRACUSE: 'Tis time, I think, to trudge, pack and be gone.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: As from a bear a man would run for life,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: So fly I from her that would be my wife.
NARRATOR: Exit
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: There's none but witches do inhabit here,
OF SYRACUSE: And therefore 'tis high time that I were hence.
OF SYRACUSE: She that doth call me husband, even my soul
OF SYRACUSE: Doth for a wife abhor. But her fair sister,
OF SYRACUSE: Possess'd with such a gentle sovereign grace,
OF SYRACUSE: Of such enchanting presence and discourse,
OF SYRACUSE: Hath almost made me traitor to myself:
OF SYRACUSE: But, lest myself be guilty to self-wrong,
OF SYRACUSE: I'll stop mine ears against the mermaid's song.
NARRATOR: Enter ANGELO with the chain
ANGELO: Master Antipholus,--
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Ay, that's my name.
ANGELO: I know it well, sir, lo, here is the chain.
ANGELO: I thought to have ta'en you at the Porpentine:
ANGELO: The chain unfinish'd made me stay thus long.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What is your will that I shall do with this?
ANGELO: What please yourself, sir: I have made it for you.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Made it for me, sir! I bespoke it not.
ANGELO: Not once, nor twice, but twenty times you have.
ANGELO: Go home with it and please your wife withal,
ANGELO: And soon at supper-time I'll visit you
ANGELO: And then receive my money for the chain.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I pray you, sir, receive the money now,
OF SYRACUSE: For fear you ne'er see chain nor money more.
ANGELO: You are a merry man, sir: fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What I should think of this, I cannot tell:
OF SYRACUSE: But this I think, there's no man is so vain
OF SYRACUSE: That would refuse so fair an offer'd chain.
OF SYRACUSE: I see a man here needs not live by shifts,
OF SYRACUSE: When in the streets he meets such golden gifts.
OF SYRACUSE: I'll to the mart, and there for Dromio stay
OF SYRACUSE: If any ship put out, then straight away.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter Second Merchant, ANGELO, and an Officer
Second Merchant: You know since Pentecost the sum is due,
Second Merchant: And since I have not much importuned you,
Second Merchant: Nor now I had not, but that I am bound
Second Merchant: To Persia, and want guilders for my voyage:
Second Merchant: Therefore make present satisfaction,
Second Merchant: Or I'll attach you by this officer.
ANGELO: Even just the sum that I do owe to you
ANGELO: Is growing to me by Antipholus,
ANGELO: And in the instant that I met with you
ANGELO: He had of me a chain: at five o'clock
ANGELO: I shall receive the money for the same.
ANGELO: Pleaseth you walk with me down to his house,
ANGELO: I will discharge my bond and thank you too.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus and DROMIO of Ephesus from the courtezan's
Officer: That labour may you save: see where he comes.
Officer: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: While I go to the goldsmith's house, go thou
OF EPHESUS: And buy a rope's end: that will I bestow
OF EPHESUS: Among my wife and her confederates,
OF EPHESUS: For locking me out of my doors by day.
OF EPHESUS: But, soft! I see the goldsmith. Get thee gone,
OF EPHESUS: Buy thou a rope and bring it home to me.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I buy a thousand pound a year: I buy a rope.
NARRATOR: Exit
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: A man is well holp up that trusts to you:
OF EPHESUS: I promised your presence and the chain,
OF EPHESUS: But neither chain nor goldsmith came to me.
OF EPHESUS: Belike you thought our love would last too long,
OF EPHESUS: If it were chain'd together, and therefore came not.
ANGELO: Saving your merry humour, here's the note
ANGELO: How much your chain weighs to the utmost carat,
ANGELO: The fineness of the gold and chargeful fashion.
ANGELO: Which doth amount to three odd ducats more
ANGELO: Than I stand debted to this gentleman:
ANGELO: I pray you, see him presently discharged,
ANGELO: For he is bound to sea and stays but for it.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I am not furnish'd with the present money,
OF EPHESUS: Besides, I have some business in the town.
OF EPHESUS: Good signior, take the stranger to my house
OF EPHESUS: And with you take the chain and bid my wife
OF EPHESUS: Disburse the sum on the receipt thereof:
OF EPHESUS: Perchance I will be there as soon as you.
ANGELO: Then you will bring the chain to her yourself?
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: No, bear it with you, lest I come not time enough.
ANGELO: Well, sir, I will. Have you the chain about you?
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: An if I have not, sir, I hope you have,
OF EPHESUS: Or else you may return without your money.
ANGELO: Nay, come, I pray you, sir, give me the chain:
ANGELO: Both wind and tide stays for this gentleman,
ANGELO: And I, to blame, have held him here too long.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Good Lord! you use this dalliance to excuse
OF EPHESUS: Your breach of promise to the Porpentine.
OF EPHESUS: I should have chid you for not bringing it,
OF EPHESUS: But, like a shrew, you first begin to brawl.
Second Merchant: The hour steals on, I pray you, sir, dispatch.
ANGELO: You hear how he importunes me,--the chain!
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Why, give it to my wife and fetch your money.
ANGELO: Come, come, you know I gave it you even now.
ANGELO: Either send the chain or send me by some token.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Fie, now you run this humour out of breath,
OF EPHESUS: where's the chain? I pray you, let me see it.
Second Merchant: My business cannot brook this dalliance.
Second Merchant: Good sir, say whether you'll answer me or no:
Second Merchant: If not, I'll leave him to the officer.
Second Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I answer you! what should I answer you?
ANGELO: The money that you owe me for the chain.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I owe you none till I receive the chain.
ANGELO: You know I gave it you half an hour since.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: You gave me none: you wrong me much to say so.
ANGELO: You wrong me more, sir, in denying it:
ANGELO: Consider how it stands upon my credit.
Second Merchant: Well, officer, arrest him at my suit.
Officer: I do, and charge you in the duke's name to obey me.
ANGELO: This touches me in reputation.
ANGELO: Either consent to pay this sum for me
ANGELO: Or I attach you by this officer.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Consent to pay thee that I never had!
OF EPHESUS: Arrest me, foolish fellow, if thou darest.
ANGELO: Here is thy fee, arrest him, officer,
ANGELO: I would not spare my brother in this case,
ANGELO: If he should scorn me so apparently.
Officer: I do arrest you, sir: you hear the suit.
Officer: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I do obey thee till I give thee bail.
OF EPHESUS: But, sirrah, you shall buy this sport as dear
OF EPHESUS: As all the metal in your shop will answer.
ANGELO: Sir, sir, I will have law in Ephesus,
ANGELO: To your notorious shame, I doubt it not.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Syracuse, from the bay
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, there is a bark of Epidamnum
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: That stays but till her owner comes aboard,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: And then, sir, she bears away. Our fraughtage, sir,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I have convey'd aboard, and I have bought
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The oil, the balsamum and aqua-vitae.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The ship is in her trim, the merry wind
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Blows fair from land: they stay for nought at all
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: But for their owner, master, and yourself.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: How now! a madman! Why, thou peevish sheep,
OF EPHESUS: What ship of Epidamnum stays for me?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A ship you sent me to, to hire waftage.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Thou drunken slave, I sent thee for a rope,
OF EPHESUS: And told thee to what purpose and what end.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: You sent me for a rope's end as soon:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: You sent me to the bay, sir, for a bark.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I will debate this matter at more leisure
OF EPHESUS: And teach your ears to list me with more heed.
OF EPHESUS: To Adriana, villain, hie thee straight:
OF EPHESUS: Give her this key, and tell her, in the desk
OF EPHESUS: That's cover'd o'er with Turkish tapestry,
OF EPHESUS: There is a purse of ducats, let her send it:
OF EPHESUS: Tell her I am arrested in the street
OF EPHESUS: And that shall bail me, hie thee, slave, be gone!
OF EPHESUS: On, officer, to prison till it come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Second Merchant, Angelo, Officer, and Antipholus of Ephesus
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: To Adriana! that is where we dined,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Where Dowsabel did claim me for her husband:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: She is too big, I hope, for me to compass.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Thither I must, although against my will,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: For servants must their masters' minds fulfil.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The house of ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus.
NARRATOR: Enter ADRIANA and LUCIANA
ADRIANA: Ah, Luciana, did he tempt thee so?
ADRIANA: Mightst thou perceive austerely in his eye
ADRIANA: That he did plead in earnest? yea or no?
ADRIANA: Look'd he or red or pale, or sad or merrily?
ADRIANA: What observation madest thou in this case
ADRIANA: Of his heart's meteors tilting in his face?
LUCIANA: First he denied you had in him no right.
ADRIANA: He meant he did me none, the more my spite.
LUCIANA: Then swore he that he was a stranger here.
ADRIANA: And true he swore, though yet forsworn he were.
LUCIANA: Then pleaded I for you.
ADRIANA: And what said he?
LUCIANA: That love I begg'd for you he begg'd of me.
ADRIANA: With what persuasion did he tempt thy love?
LUCIANA: With words that in an honest suit might move.
LUCIANA: First he did praise my beauty, then my speech.
ADRIANA: Didst speak him fair?
LUCIANA: Have patience, I beseech.
ADRIANA: I cannot, nor I will not, hold me still,
ADRIANA: My tongue, though not my heart, shall have his will.
ADRIANA: He is deformed, crooked, old and sere,
ADRIANA: Ill-faced, worse bodied, shapeless everywhere,
ADRIANA: Vicious, ungentle, foolish, blunt, unkind,
ADRIANA: Stigmatical in making, worse in mind.
LUCIANA: Who would be jealous then of such a one?
LUCIANA: No evil lost is wail'd when it is gone.
ADRIANA: Ah, but I think him better than I say,
ADRIANA: And yet would herein others' eyes were worse.
ADRIANA: Far from her nest the lapwing cries away:
ADRIANA: My heart prays for him, though my tongue do curse.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Syracuse
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Here! go, the desk, the purse! sweet, now, make haste.
LUCIANA: How hast thou lost thy breath?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: By running fast.
ADRIANA: Where is thy master, Dromio? is he well?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No, he's in Tartar limbo, worse than hell.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A devil in an everlasting garment hath him,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: One whose hard heart is button'd up with steel,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A fiend, a fury, pitiless and rough,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A wolf, nay, worse, a fellow all in buff,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A back-friend, a shoulder-clapper, one that
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: countermands
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The passages of alleys, creeks and narrow lands,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A hound that runs counter and yet draws dryfoot well,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: One that before the judgement carries poor souls to hell.
ADRIANA: Why, man, what is the matter?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I do not know the matter: he is 'rested on the case.
ADRIANA: What, is he arrested? Tell me at whose suit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I know not at whose suit he is arrested well,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: But he's in a suit of buff which 'rested him, that can I tell.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Will you send him, mistress, redemption, the money in his desk?
ADRIANA: Go fetch it, sister.
NARRATOR: Exit Luciana
ADRIANA: This I wonder at,
ADRIANA: That he, unknown to me, should be in debt.
ADRIANA: Tell me, was he arrested on a band?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Not on a band, but on a stronger thing,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A chain, a chain! Do you not hear it ring?
ADRIANA: What, the chain?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No, no, the bell: 'tis time that I were gone:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: It was two ere I left him, and now the clock
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: strikes one.
ADRIANA: The hours come back! that did I never hear.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: O, yes, if any hour meet a sergeant, a' turns back for
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: very fear.
ADRIANA: As if Time were in debt! how fondly dost thou reason!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: worth, to season.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Nay, he's a thief too: have you not heard men say
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: That Time comes stealing on by night and day?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: If Time be in debt and theft, and a sergeant in the way,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Hath he not reason to turn back an hour in a day?
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIANA with a purse
ADRIANA: Go, Dromio, there's the money, bear it straight,
ADRIANA: And bring thy master home immediately.
ADRIANA: Come, sister: I am press'd down with conceit--
ADRIANA: Conceit, my comfort and my injury.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: There's not a man I meet but doth salute me
OF SYRACUSE: As if I were their well-acquainted friend,
OF SYRACUSE: And every one doth call me by my name.
OF SYRACUSE: Some tender money to me, some invite me,
OF SYRACUSE: Some other give me thanks for kindnesses,
OF SYRACUSE: Some offer me commodities to buy:
OF SYRACUSE: Even now a tailor call'd me in his shop
OF SYRACUSE: And show'd me silks that he had bought for me,
OF SYRACUSE: And therewithal took measure of my body.
OF SYRACUSE: Sure, these are but imaginary wiles
OF SYRACUSE: And Lapland sorcerers inhabit here.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO OF SYRACUSE
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, here's the gold you sent me for. What, have
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: you got the picture of old Adam new-apparelled?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What gold is this? what Adam dost thou mean?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Not that Adam that kept the Paradise but that Adam
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: that keeps the prison: he that goes in the calf's
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: skin that was killed for the Prodigal, he that came
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: behind you, sir, like an evil angel, and bid you
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: forsake your liberty.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I understand thee not.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: No? why, 'tis a plain case: he that went, like a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: bass-viol, in a case of leather, the man, sir,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: that, when gentlemen are tired, gives them a sob
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: and 'rests them, he, sir, that takes pity on decayed
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: men and gives them suits of durance, he that sets up
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: his rest to do more exploits with his mace than a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: morris-pike.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: What, thou meanest an officer?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Ay, sir, the sergeant of the band, he that brings
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: any man to answer it that breaks his band, one that
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: thinks a man always going to bed, and says, 'God
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: give you good rest!'
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Well, sir, there rest in your foolery. Is there any
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Why, sir, I brought you word an hour since that the
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: bark Expedition put forth to-night, and then were
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: you hindered by the sergeant, to tarry for the hoy
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Delay. Here are the angels that you sent for to
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: deliver you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: The fellow is distract, and so am I,
OF SYRACUSE: And here we wander in illusions:
OF SYRACUSE: Some blessed power deliver us from hence!
NARRATOR: Enter a Courtezan
Courtezan: Well met, well met, Master Antipholus.
Courtezan: I see, sir, you have found the goldsmith now:
Courtezan: Is that the chain you promised me to-day?
Courtezan: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Satan, avoid! I charge thee, tempt me not.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, is this Mistress Satan?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: It is the devil.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Nay, she is worse, she is the devil's dam, and here
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: she comes in the habit of a light wench: and thereof
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: comes that the wenches say 'God damn me,' that's as
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: much to say 'God make me a light wench.' It is
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: written, they appear to men like angels of light:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: light is an effect of fire, and fire will burn,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ergo, light wenches will burn. Come not near her.
Courtezan: Your man and you are marvellous merry, sir.
Courtezan: Will you go with me? We'll mend our dinner here?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, if you do, expect spoon-meat, or bespeak a
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: long spoon.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Why, Dromio?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: the devil.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Avoid then, fiend! what tell'st thou me of supping?
OF SYRACUSE: Thou art, as you are all, a sorceress:
OF SYRACUSE: I conjure thee to leave me and be gone.
Courtezan: Give me the ring of mine you had at dinner,
Courtezan: Or, for my diamond, the chain you promised,
Courtezan: And I'll be gone, sir, and not trouble you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Some devils ask but the parings of one's nail,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A rush, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: A nut, a cherry-stone,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: But she, more covetous, would have a chain.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, be wise: an if you give it her,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: The devil will shake her chain and fright us with it.
Courtezan: I pray you, sir, my ring, or else the chain:
Courtezan: I hope you do not mean to cheat me so.
Courtezan: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Avaunt, thou witch! Come, Dromio, let us go.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: 'Fly pride,' says the peacock: mistress, that you know.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse
Courtezan: Now, out of doubt Antipholus is mad,
Courtezan: Else would he never so demean himself.
Courtezan: A ring he hath of mine worth forty ducats,
Courtezan: And for the same he promised me a chain:
Courtezan: Both one and other he denies me now.
Courtezan: The reason that I gather he is mad,
Courtezan: Besides this present instance of his rage,
Courtezan: Is a mad tale he told to-day at dinner,
Courtezan: Of his own doors being shut against his entrance.
Courtezan: Belike his wife, acquainted with his fits,
Courtezan: On purpose shut the doors against his way.
Courtezan: My way is now to hie home to his house,
Courtezan: And tell his wife that, being lunatic,
Courtezan: He rush'd into my house and took perforce
Courtezan: My ring away. This course I fittest choose,
Courtezan: For forty ducats is too much to lose.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus and the Officer
Courtezan: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Fear me not, man, I will not break away:
OF EPHESUS: I'll give thee, ere I leave thee, so much money,
OF EPHESUS: To warrant thee, as I am 'rested for.
OF EPHESUS: My wife is in a wayward mood to-day,
OF EPHESUS: And will not lightly trust the messenger
OF EPHESUS: That I should be attach'd in Ephesus,
OF EPHESUS: I tell you, 'twill sound harshly in her ears.
NARRATOR: Enter DROMIO of Ephesus with a rope's-end
OF EPHESUS: Here comes my man, I think he brings the money.
OF EPHESUS: How now, sir! have you that I sent you for?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Here's that, I warrant you, will pay them all.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: But where's the money?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Why, sir, I gave the money for the rope.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Five hundred ducats, villain, for a rope?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I'll serve you, sir, five hundred at the rate.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: To what end did I bid thee hie thee home?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: To a rope's-end, sir, and to that end am I returned.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: And to that end, sir, I will welcome you.
NARRATOR: Beating him
Officer: Good sir, be patient.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, 'tis for me to be patient, I am in adversity.
Officer: Good, now, hold thy tongue.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, rather persuade him to hold his hands.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Thou whoreson, senseless villain!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I would I were senseless, sir, that I might not feel
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: your blows.
ANTIPHOLUS: Thou art sensible in nothing but blows, and so is an
ANTIPHOLUS: ass.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I am an ass, indeed, you may prove it by my long
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ears. I have served him from the hour of my
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: nativity to this instant, and have nothing at his
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: hands for my service but blows. When I am cold, he
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: heats me with beating, when I am warm, he cools me
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: with beating, I am waked with it when I sleep,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: raised with it when I sit, driven out of doors with
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: it when I go from home, welcomed home with it when
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I return, nay, I bear it on my shoulders, as a
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: beggar wont her brat, and, I think when he hath
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: lamed me, I shall beg with it from door to door.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Come, go along, my wife is coming yonder.
NARRATOR: Enter ADRIANA, LUCIANA, the Courtezan, and PINCH
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Mistress, 'respice finem,' respect your end, or
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: rather, the prophecy like the parrot, 'beware the
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: rope's-end.'
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Wilt thou still talk?
NARRATOR: Beating him
Courtezan: How say you now? is not your husband mad?
ADRIANA: His incivility confirms no less.
ADRIANA: Good Doctor Pinch, you are a conjurer,
ADRIANA: Establish him in his true sense again,
ADRIANA: And I will please you what you will demand.
LUCIANA: Alas, how fiery and how sharp he looks!
Courtezan: Mark how he trembles in his ecstasy!
PINCH: Give me your hand and let me feel your pulse.
PINCH: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: There is my hand, and let it feel your ear.
NARRATOR: Striking him
PINCH: I charge thee, Satan, housed within this man,
PINCH: To yield possession to my holy prayers
PINCH: And to thy state of darkness hie thee straight:
PINCH: I conjure thee by all the saints in heaven!
PINCH: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Peace, doting wizard, peace! I am not mad.
ADRIANA: O, that thou wert not, poor distressed soul!
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: You minion, you, are these your customers?
OF EPHESUS: Did this companion with the saffron face
OF EPHESUS: Revel and feast it at my house to-day,
OF EPHESUS: Whilst upon me the guilty doors were shut
OF EPHESUS: And I denied to enter in my house?
ADRIANA: O husband, God doth know you dined at home,
ADRIANA: Where would you had remain'd until this time,
ADRIANA: Free from these slanders and this open shame!
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Dined at home! Thou villain, what sayest thou?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Sir, sooth to say, you did not dine at home.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Were not my doors lock'd up and I shut out?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Perdie, your doors were lock'd and you shut out.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: And did not she herself revile me there?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Sans fable, she herself reviled you there.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Did not her kitchen-maid rail, taunt, and scorn me?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Certes, she did, the kitchen-vestal scorn'd you.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: And did not I in rage depart from thence?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: In verity you did, my bones bear witness,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: That since have felt the vigour of his rage.
ADRIANA: Is't good to soothe him in these contraries?
PINCH: It is no shame: the fellow finds his vein,
PINCH: And yielding to him humours well his frenzy.
PINCH: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Thou hast suborn'd the goldsmith to arrest me.
ADRIANA: Alas, I sent you money to redeem you,
ADRIANA: By Dromio here, who came in haste for it.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Money by me! heart and goodwill you might,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But surely master, not a rag of money.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Went'st not thou to her for a purse of ducats?
ADRIANA: He came to me and I deliver'd it.
LUCIANA: And I am witness with her that she did.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: God and the rope-maker bear me witness
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: That I was sent for nothing but a rope!
PINCH: Mistress, both man and master is possess'd,
PINCH: I know it by their pale and deadly looks:
PINCH: They must be bound and laid in some dark room.
PINCH: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Say, wherefore didst thou lock me forth to-day?
OF EPHESUS: And why dost thou deny the bag of gold?
ADRIANA: I did not, gentle husband, lock thee forth.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And, gentle master, I received no gold,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But I confess, sir, that we were lock'd out.
ADRIANA: Dissembling villain, thou speak'st false in both.
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Dissembling harlot, thou art false in all,
OF EPHESUS: And art confederate with a damned pack
OF EPHESUS: To make a loathsome abject scorn of me:
OF EPHESUS: But with these nails I'll pluck out these false eyes
OF EPHESUS: That would behold in me this shameful sport.
NARRATOR: Enter three or four, and offer to bind him. He strives
ADRIANA: O, bind him, bind him! let him not come near me.
PINCH: More company! The fiend is strong within him.
LUCIANA: Ay me, poor man, how pale and wan he looks!
LUCIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: What, will you murder me? Thou gaoler, thou,
OF EPHESUS: I am thy prisoner: wilt thou suffer them
OF EPHESUS: To make a rescue?
Officer: Masters, let him go
Officer: He is my prisoner, and you shall not have him.
PINCH: Go bind this man, for he is frantic too.
NARRATOR: They offer to bind Dromio of Ephesus
ADRIANA: What wilt thou do, thou peevish officer?
ADRIANA: Hast thou delight to see a wretched man
ADRIANA: Do outrage and displeasure to himself?
Officer: He is my prisoner: if I let him go,
Officer: The debt he owes will be required of me.
ADRIANA: I will discharge thee ere I go from thee:
ADRIANA: Bear me forthwith unto his creditor,
ADRIANA: And, knowing how the debt grows, I will pay it.
ADRIANA: Good master doctor, see him safe convey'd
ADRIANA: Home to my house. O most unhappy day!
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: O most unhappy strumpet!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Master, I am here entered in bond for you.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Out on thee, villain! wherefore dost thou mad me?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Will you be bound for nothing? be mad, good master:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: cry 'The devil!'
LUCIANA: God help, poor souls, how idly do they talk!
ADRIANA: Go bear him hence. Sister, go you with me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but Adriana, Luciana, Officer and Courtezan
ADRIANA: Say now, whose suit is he arrested at?
Officer: One Angelo, a goldsmith: do you know him?
ADRIANA: I know the man. What is the sum he owes?
Officer: Two hundred ducats.
ADRIANA: Say, how grows it due?
Officer: Due for a chain your husband had of him.
ADRIANA: He did bespeak a chain for me, but had it not.
Courtezan: When as your husband all in rage to-day
Courtezan: Came to my house and took away my ring--
Courtezan: The ring I saw upon his finger now--
Courtezan: Straight after did I meet him with a chain.
ADRIANA: It may be so, but I did never see it.
ADRIANA: Come, gaoler, bring me where the goldsmith is:
ADRIANA: I long to know the truth hereof at large.
