NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse with his rapier drawn, and DROMIO of Syracuse
LUCIANA: God, for thy mercy! they are loose again.
ADRIANA: And come with naked swords.
ADRIANA: Let's call more help to have them bound again.
Officer: Away! they'll kill us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse
Officer: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I see these witches are afraid of swords.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: She that would be your wife now ran from you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Come to the Centaur, fetch our stuff from thence:
OF SYRACUSE: I long that we were safe and sound aboard.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Faith, stay here this night, they will surely do us
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: no harm: you saw they speak us fair, give us gold:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: methinks they are such a gentle nation that, but for
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: the mountain of mad flesh that claims marriage of
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: me, I could find in my heart to stay here still and
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: turn witch.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I will not stay to-night for all the town,
OF SYRACUSE: Therefore away, to get our stuff aboard.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A street before a Priory.
NARRATOR: Enter Second Merchant and ANGELO
ANGELO: I am sorry, sir, that I have hinder'd you,
ANGELO: But, I protest, he had the chain of me,
ANGELO: Though most dishonestly he doth deny it.
Second Merchant: How is the man esteemed here in the city?
ANGELO: Of very reverend reputation, sir,
ANGELO: Of credit infinite, highly beloved,
ANGELO: Second to none that lives here in the city:
ANGELO: His word might bear my wealth at any time.
Second Merchant: Speak softly, yonder, as I think, he walks.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse and DROMIO of Syracuse
ANGELO: 'Tis so, and that self chain about his neck
ANGELO: Which he forswore most monstrously to have.
ANGELO: Good sir, draw near to me, I'll speak to him.
ANGELO: Signior Antipholus, I wonder much
ANGELO: That you would put me to this shame and trouble,
ANGELO: And, not without some scandal to yourself,
ANGELO: With circumstance and oaths so to deny
ANGELO: This chain which now you wear so openly:
ANGELO: Beside the charge, the shame, imprisonment,
ANGELO: You have done wrong to this my honest friend,
ANGELO: Who, but for staying on our controversy,
ANGELO: Had hoisted sail and put to sea to-day:
ANGELO: This chain you had of me, can you deny it?
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I think I had, I never did deny it.
Second Merchant: Yes, that you did, sir, and forswore it too.
Second Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Who heard me to deny it or forswear it?
Second Merchant: These ears of mine, thou know'st did hear thee.
Second Merchant: Fie on thee, wretch! 'tis pity that thou livest
Second Merchant: To walk where any honest man resort.
Second Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: Thou art a villain to impeach me thus:
OF SYRACUSE: I'll prove mine honour and mine honesty
OF SYRACUSE: Against thee presently, if thou darest stand.
Second Merchant: I dare, and do defy thee for a villain.
NARRATOR: They draw
NARRATOR: Enter ADRIANA, LUCIANA, the Courtezan, and others
ADRIANA: Hold, hurt him not, for God's sake! he is mad.
ADRIANA: Some get within him, take his sword away:
ADRIANA: Bind Dromio too, and bear them to my house.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Run, master, run, for God's sake, take a house!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: This is some priory. In, or we are spoil'd!
NARRATOR: Exeunt Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse to the Priory
NARRATOR: Enter the Lady Abbess, AEMILIA
AEMELIA: Be quiet, people. Wherefore throng you hither?
ADRIANA: To fetch my poor distracted husband hence.
ADRIANA: Let us come in, that we may bind him fast
ADRIANA: And bear him home for his recovery.
ANGELO: I knew he was not in his perfect wits.
Second Merchant: I am sorry now that I did draw on him.
AEMELIA: How long hath this possession held the man?
ADRIANA: This week he hath been heavy, sour, sad,
ADRIANA: And much different from the man he was,
ADRIANA: But till this afternoon his passion
ADRIANA: Ne'er brake into extremity of rage.
AEMELIA: Hath he not lost much wealth by wreck of sea?
AEMELIA: Buried some dear friend? Hath not else his eye
AEMELIA: Stray'd his affection in unlawful love?
AEMELIA: A sin prevailing much in youthful men,
AEMELIA: Who give their eyes the liberty of gazing.
AEMELIA: Which of these sorrows is he subject to?
ADRIANA: To none of these, except it be the last,
ADRIANA: Namely, some love that drew him oft from home.
AEMELIA: You should for that have reprehended him.
ADRIANA: Why, so I did.
AEMELIA: Ay, but not rough enough.
ADRIANA: As roughly as my modesty would let me.
AEMELIA: Haply, in private.
ADRIANA: And in assemblies too.
AEMELIA: Ay, but not enough.
ADRIANA: It was the copy of our conference:
ADRIANA: In bed he slept not for my urging it,
ADRIANA: At board he fed not for my urging it,
ADRIANA: Alone, it was the subject of my theme,
ADRIANA: In company I often glanced it,
ADRIANA: Still did I tell him it was vile and bad.
AEMELIA: And thereof came it that the man was mad.
AEMELIA: The venom clamours of a jealous woman
AEMELIA: Poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth.
AEMELIA: It seems his sleeps were hinder'd by thy railing,
AEMELIA: And therefore comes it that his head is light.
AEMELIA: Thou say'st his meat was sauced with thy upbraidings:
AEMELIA: Unquiet meals make ill digestions,
AEMELIA: Thereof the raging fire of fever bred,
AEMELIA: And what's a fever but a fit of madness?
AEMELIA: Thou say'st his sports were hinderd by thy brawls:
AEMELIA: Sweet recreation barr'd, what doth ensue
AEMELIA: But moody and dull melancholy,
AEMELIA: Kinsman to grim and comfortless despair,
AEMELIA: And at her heels a huge infectious troop
AEMELIA: Of pale distemperatures and foes to life?
AEMELIA: In food, in sport and life-preserving rest
AEMELIA: To be disturb'd, would mad or man or beast:
AEMELIA: The consequence is then thy jealous fits
AEMELIA: Have scared thy husband from the use of wits.
LUCIANA: She never reprehended him but mildly,
LUCIANA: When he demean'd himself rough, rude and wildly.
LUCIANA: Why bear you these rebukes and answer not?
ADRIANA: She did betray me to my own reproof.
ADRIANA: Good people enter and lay hold on him.
AEMELIA: No, not a creature enters in my house.
ADRIANA: Then let your servants bring my husband forth.
AEMELIA: Neither: he took this place for sanctuary,
AEMELIA: And it shall privilege him from your hands
AEMELIA: Till I have brought him to his wits again,
AEMELIA: Or lose my labour in assaying it.
ADRIANA: I will attend my husband, be his nurse,
ADRIANA: Diet his sickness, for it is my office,
ADRIANA: And will have no attorney but myself,
ADRIANA: And therefore let me have him home with me.
AEMELIA: Be patient, for I will not let him stir
AEMELIA: Till I have used the approved means I have,
AEMELIA: With wholesome syrups, drugs and holy prayers,
AEMELIA: To make of him a formal man again:
AEMELIA: It is a branch and parcel of mine oath,
AEMELIA: A charitable duty of my order.
AEMELIA: Therefore depart and leave him here with me.
ADRIANA: I will not hence and leave my husband here:
ADRIANA: And ill it doth beseem your holiness
ADRIANA: To separate the husband and the wife.
AEMELIA: Be quiet and depart: thou shalt not have him.
NARRATOR: Exit
LUCIANA: Complain unto the duke of this indignity.
ADRIANA: Come, go: I will fall prostrate at his feet
ADRIANA: And never rise until my tears and prayers
ADRIANA: Have won his grace to come in person hither
ADRIANA: And take perforce my husband from the abbess.
Second Merchant: By this, I think, the dial points at five:
Second Merchant: Anon, I'm sure, the duke himself in person
Second Merchant: Comes this way to the melancholy vale,
Second Merchant: The place of death and sorry execution,
Second Merchant: Behind the ditches of the abbey here.
ANGELO: Upon what cause?
Second Merchant: To see a reverend Syracusian merchant,
Second Merchant: Who put unluckily into this bay
Second Merchant: Against the laws and statutes of this town,
Second Merchant: Beheaded publicly for his offence.
ANGELO: See where they come: we will behold his death.
LUCIANA: Kneel to the duke before he pass the abbey.
LUCIANA: Enter DUKE SOLINUS, attended, AEGEON bareheaded, with the Headsman and other Officers
DUKE SOLINUS: Yet once again proclaim it publicly,
DUKE SOLINUS: If any friend will pay the sum for him,
DUKE SOLINUS: He shall not die, so much we tender him.
ADRIANA: Justice, most sacred duke, against the abbess!
DUKE SOLINUS: She is a virtuous and a reverend lady:
DUKE SOLINUS: It cannot be that she hath done thee wrong.
ADRIANA: May it please your grace, Antipholus, my husband,
ADRIANA: Whom I made lord of me and all I had,
ADRIANA: At your important letters,--this ill day
ADRIANA: A most outrageous fit of madness took him,
ADRIANA: That desperately he hurried through the street,
ADRIANA: With him his bondman, all as mad as he--
ADRIANA: Doing displeasure to the citizens
ADRIANA: By rushing in their houses, bearing thence
ADRIANA: Rings, jewels, any thing his rage did like.
ADRIANA: Once did I get him bound and sent him home,
ADRIANA: Whilst to take order for the wrongs I went,
ADRIANA: That here and there his fury had committed.
ADRIANA: Anon, I wot not by what strong escape,
ADRIANA: He broke from those that had the guard of him,
ADRIANA: And with his mad attendant and himself,
ADRIANA: Each one with ireful passion, with drawn swords,
ADRIANA: Met us again and madly bent on us,
ADRIANA: Chased us away, till, raising of more aid,
ADRIANA: We came again to bind them. Then they fled
ADRIANA: Into this abbey, whither we pursued them:
ADRIANA: And here the abbess shuts the gates on us
ADRIANA: And will not suffer us to fetch him out,
ADRIANA: Nor send him forth that we may bear him hence.
ADRIANA: Therefore, most gracious duke, with thy command
ADRIANA: Let him be brought forth and borne hence for help.
DUKE SOLINUS: Long since thy husband served me in my wars,
DUKE SOLINUS: And I to thee engaged a prince's word,
DUKE SOLINUS: When thou didst make him master of thy bed,
DUKE SOLINUS: To do him all the grace and good I could.
DUKE SOLINUS: Go, some of you, knock at the abbey-gate
DUKE SOLINUS: And bid the lady abbess come to me.
DUKE SOLINUS: I will determine this before I stir.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: O mistress, mistress, shift and save yourself!
Servant: My master and his man are both broke loose,
Servant: Beaten the maids a-row and bound the doctor
Servant: Whose beard they have singed off with brands of fire,
Servant: And ever, as it blazed, they threw on him
Servant: Great pails of puddled mire to quench the hair:
Servant: My master preaches patience to him and the while
Servant: His man with scissors nicks him like a fool,
Servant: And sure, unless you send some present help,
Servant: Between them they will kill the conjurer.
ADRIANA: Peace, fool! thy master and his man are here,
ADRIANA: And that is false thou dost report to us.
Servant: Mistress, upon my life, I tell you true,
Servant: I have not breathed almost since I did see it.
Servant: He cries for you, and vows, if he can take you,
Servant: To scorch your face and to disfigure you.
NARRATOR: Cry within
Servant: Hark, hark! I hear him, mistress. fly, be gone!
DUKE SOLINUS: Come, stand by me, fear nothing. Guard with halberds!
ADRIANA: Ay me, it is my husband! Witness you,
ADRIANA: That he is borne about invisible:
ADRIANA: Even now we housed him in the abbey here,
ADRIANA: And now he's there, past thought of human reason.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIPHOLUS of Ephesus and DROMIO of Ephesus
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Justice, most gracious duke, O, grant me justice!
OF EPHESUS: Even for the service that long since I did thee,
OF EPHESUS: When I bestrid thee in the wars and took
OF EPHESUS: Deep scars to save thy life, even for the blood
OF EPHESUS: That then I lost for thee, now grant me justice.
AEGEON: Unless the fear of death doth make me dote,
AEGEON: I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.
AEGEON: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Justice, sweet prince, against that woman there!
OF EPHESUS: She whom thou gavest to me to be my wife,
OF EPHESUS: That hath abused and dishonour'd me
OF EPHESUS: Even in the strength and height of injury!
OF EPHESUS: Beyond imagination is the wrong
OF EPHESUS: That she this day hath shameless thrown on me.
DUKE SOLINUS: Discover how, and thou shalt find me just.
DUKE SOLINUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: This day, great duke, she shut the doors upon me,
OF EPHESUS: While she with harlots feasted in my house.
DUKE SOLINUS: A grievous fault! Say, woman, didst thou so?
ADRIANA: No, my good lord: myself, he and my sister
ADRIANA: To-day did dine together. So befall my soul
ADRIANA: As this is false he burdens me withal!
LUCIANA: Ne'er may I look on day, nor sleep on night,
LUCIANA: But she tells to your highness simple truth!
ANGELO: O perjured woman! They are both forsworn:
ANGELO: In this the madman justly chargeth them.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: My liege, I am advised what I say,
OF EPHESUS: Neither disturbed with the effect of wine,
OF EPHESUS: Nor heady-rash, provoked with raging ire,
OF EPHESUS: Albeit my wrongs might make one wiser mad.
OF EPHESUS: This woman lock'd me out this day from dinner:
OF EPHESUS: That goldsmith there, were he not pack'd with her,
OF EPHESUS: Could witness it, for he was with me then,
OF EPHESUS: Who parted with me to go fetch a chain,
OF EPHESUS: Promising to bring it to the Porpentine,
OF EPHESUS: Where Balthazar and I did dine together.
OF EPHESUS: Our dinner done, and he not coming thither,
OF EPHESUS: I went to seek him: in the street I met him
OF EPHESUS: And in his company that gentleman.
OF EPHESUS: There did this perjured goldsmith swear me down
OF EPHESUS: That I this day of him received the chain,
OF EPHESUS: Which, God he knows, I saw not: for the which
OF EPHESUS: He did arrest me with an officer.
OF EPHESUS: I did obey, and sent my peasant home
OF EPHESUS: For certain ducats: he with none return'd
OF EPHESUS: Then fairly I bespoke the officer
OF EPHESUS: To go in person with me to my house.
OF EPHESUS: By the way we met
OF EPHESUS: My wife, her sister, and a rabble more
OF EPHESUS: Of vile confederates. Along with them
OF EPHESUS: They brought one Pinch, a hungry lean-faced villain,
OF EPHESUS: A mere anatomy, a mountebank,
OF EPHESUS: A threadbare juggler and a fortune-teller,
OF EPHESUS: A needy, hollow-eyed, sharp-looking wretch,
OF EPHESUS: A dead-looking man: this pernicious slave,
OF EPHESUS: Forsooth, took on him as a conjurer,
OF EPHESUS: And, gazing in mine eyes, feeling my pulse,
OF EPHESUS: And with no face, as 'twere, outfacing me,
OF EPHESUS: Cries out, I was possess'd. Then all together
OF EPHESUS: They fell upon me, bound me, bore me thence
OF EPHESUS: And in a dark and dankish vault at home
OF EPHESUS: There left me and my man, both bound together,
OF EPHESUS: Till, gnawing with my teeth my bonds in sunder,
OF EPHESUS: I gain'd my freedom, and immediately
OF EPHESUS: Ran hither to your grace, whom I beseech
OF EPHESUS: To give me ample satisfaction
OF EPHESUS: For these deep shames and great indignities.
ANGELO: My lord, in truth, thus far I witness with him,
ANGELO: That he dined not at home, but was lock'd out.
DUKE SOLINUS: But had he such a chain of thee or no?
ANGELO: He had, my lord: and when he ran in here,
ANGELO: These people saw the chain about his neck.
Second Merchant: Besides, I will be sworn these ears of mine
Second Merchant: Heard you confess you had the chain of him
Second Merchant: After you first forswore it on the mart:
Second Merchant: And thereupon I drew my sword on you,
Second Merchant: And then you fled into this abbey here,
Second Merchant: From whence, I think, you are come by miracle.
Second Merchant: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I never came within these abbey-walls,
OF EPHESUS: Nor ever didst thou draw thy sword on me:
OF EPHESUS: I never saw the chain, so help me Heaven!
OF EPHESUS: And this is false you burden me withal.
DUKE SOLINUS: Why, what an intricate impeach is this!
DUKE SOLINUS: I think you all have drunk of Circe's cup.
DUKE SOLINUS: If here you housed him, here he would have been,
DUKE SOLINUS: If he were mad, he would not plead so coldly:
DUKE SOLINUS: You say he dined at home, the goldsmith here
DUKE SOLINUS: Denies that saying. Sirrah, what say you?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Sir, he dined with her there, at the Porpentine.
Courtezan: He did, and from my finger snatch'd that ring.
Courtezan: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: 'Tis true, my liege, this ring I had of her.
DUKE SOLINUS: Saw'st thou him enter at the abbey here?
Courtezan: As sure, my liege, as I do see your grace.
DUKE SOLINUS: Why, this is strange. Go call the abbess hither.
DUKE SOLINUS: I think you are all mated or stark mad.
NARRATOR: Exit one to Abbess
AEGEON: Most mighty duke, vouchsafe me speak a word:
AEGEON: Haply I see a friend will save my life
AEGEON: And pay the sum that may deliver me.
DUKE SOLINUS: Speak freely, Syracusian, what thou wilt.
AEGEON: Is not your name, sir, call'd Antipholus?
AEGEON: And is not that your bondman, Dromio?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Within this hour I was his bondman sir,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: But he, I thank him, gnaw'd in two my cords:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Now am I Dromio and his man unbound.
AEGEON: I am sure you both of you remember me.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Ourselves we do remember, sir, by you,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: For lately we were bound, as you are now
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: You are not Pinch's patient, are you, sir?
AEGEON: Why look you strange on me? you know me well.
ANTIPHOLUS: I never saw you in my life till now.
AEGEON: O, grief hath changed me since you saw me last,
AEGEON: And careful hours with time's deformed hand
AEGEON: Have written strange defeatures in my face:
AEGEON: But tell me yet, dost thou not know my voice?
AEGEON: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Neither.
AEGEON: Dromio, nor thou?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: No, trust me, sir, nor I.
AEGEON: I am sure thou dost.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Ay, sir, but I am sure I do not, and whatsoever a
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: man denies, you are now bound to believe him.
AEGEON: Not know my voice! O time's extremity,
AEGEON: Hast thou so crack'd and splitted my poor tongue
AEGEON: In seven short years, that here my only son
AEGEON: Knows not my feeble key of untuned cares?
AEGEON: Though now this grained face of mine be hid
AEGEON: In sap-consuming winter's drizzled snow,
AEGEON: And all the conduits of my blood froze up,
AEGEON: Yet hath my night of life some memory,
AEGEON: My wasting lamps some fading glimmer left,
AEGEON: My dull deaf ears a little use to hear:
AEGEON: All these old witnesses--I cannot err--
AEGEON: Tell me thou art my son Antipholus.
AEGEON: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I never saw my father in my life.
AEGEON: But seven years since, in Syracusa, boy,
AEGEON: Thou know'st we parted: but perhaps, my son,
AEGEON: Thou shamest to acknowledge me in misery.
AEGEON: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: The duke and all that know me in the city
OF EPHESUS: Can witness with me that it is not so
OF EPHESUS: I ne'er saw Syracusa in my life.
DUKE SOLINUS: I tell thee, Syracusian, twenty years
DUKE SOLINUS: Have I been patron to Antipholus,
DUKE SOLINUS: During which time he ne'er saw Syracusa:
DUKE SOLINUS: I see thy age and dangers make thee dote.
NARRATOR: Re-enter AEMILIA, with ANTIPHOLUS of Syracuse and DROMIO of Syracuse
AEMELIA: Most mighty duke, behold a man much wrong'd.
NARRATOR: All gather to see them
ADRIANA: I see two husbands, or mine eyes deceive me.
DUKE SOLINUS: One of these men is Genius to the other,
DUKE SOLINUS: And so of these. Which is the natural man,
DUKE SOLINUS: And which the spirit? who deciphers them?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: I, sir, am Dromio, command him away.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I, sir, am Dromio, pray, let me stay.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: AEgeon art thou not? or else his ghost?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: O, my old master! who hath bound him here?
AEMELIA: Whoever bound him, I will loose his bonds
AEMELIA: And gain a husband by his liberty.
AEMELIA: Speak, old AEgeon, if thou be'st the man
AEMELIA: That hadst a wife once call'd AEmilia
AEMELIA: That bore thee at a burden two fair sons:
AEMELIA: O, if thou be'st the same AEgeon, speak,
AEMELIA: And speak unto the same AEmilia!
AEGEON: If I dream not, thou art AEmilia:
AEGEON: If thou art she, tell me where is that son
AEGEON: That floated with thee on the fatal raft?
AEMELIA: By men of Epidamnum he and I
AEMELIA: And the twin Dromio all were taken up,
AEMELIA: But by and by rude fishermen of Corinth
AEMELIA: By force took Dromio and my son from them
AEMELIA: And me they left with those of Epidamnum.
AEMELIA: What then became of them I cannot tell
AEMELIA: I to this fortune that you see me in.
DUKE SOLINUS: Why, here begins his morning story right,
DUKE SOLINUS: These two Antipholuses, these two so like,
DUKE SOLINUS: And these two Dromios, one in semblance,--
DUKE SOLINUS: Besides her urging of her wreck at sea,--
DUKE SOLINUS: These are the parents to these children,
DUKE SOLINUS: Which accidentally are met together.
DUKE SOLINUS: Antipholus, thou camest from Corinth first?
DUKE SOLINUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: No, sir, not I, I came from Syracuse.
DUKE SOLINUS: Stay, stand apart, I know not which is which.
DUKE SOLINUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: I came from Corinth, my most gracious lord,--
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And I with him.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Brought to this town by that most famous warrior,
OF EPHESUS: Duke Menaphon, your most renowned uncle.
ADRIANA: Which of you two did dine with me to-day?
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I, gentle mistress.
ADRIANA: And are not you my husband?
ADRIANA: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: No, I say nay to that.
OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: And so do I, yet did she call me so:
OF SYRACUSE: And this fair gentlewoman, her sister here,
OF SYRACUSE: Did call me brother.
NARRATOR: To Luciana
OF SYRACUSE: What I told you then,
OF SYRACUSE: I hope I shall have leisure to make good,
OF SYRACUSE: If this be not a dream I see and hear.
ANGELO: That is the chain, sir, which you had of me.
ANGELO: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: I think it be, sir, I deny it not.
OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: And you, sir, for this chain arrested me.
ANGELO: I think I did, sir, I deny it not.
ADRIANA: I sent you money, sir, to be your bail,
ADRIANA: By Dromio, but I think he brought it not.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: No, none by me.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: This purse of ducats I received from you,
OF SYRACUSE: And Dromio, my man, did bring them me.
OF SYRACUSE: I see we still did meet each other's man,
OF SYRACUSE: And I was ta'en for him, and he for me,
OF SYRACUSE: And thereupon these errors are arose.
OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: These ducats pawn I for my father here.
DUKE SOLINUS: It shall not need, thy father hath his life.
Courtezan: Sir, I must have that diamond from you.
Courtezan: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: There, take it, and much thanks for my good cheer.
AEMELIA: Renowned duke, vouchsafe to take the pains
AEMELIA: To go with us into the abbey here
AEMELIA: And hear at large discoursed all our fortunes:
AEMELIA: And all that are assembled in this place,
AEMELIA: That by this sympathized one day's error
AEMELIA: Have suffer'd wrong, go keep us company,
AEMELIA: And we shall make full satisfaction.
AEMELIA: Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail
AEMELIA: Of you, my sons, and till this present hour
AEMELIA: My heavy burden ne'er delivered.
AEMELIA: The duke, my husband and my children both,
AEMELIA: And you the calendars of their nativity,
AEMELIA: Go to a gossips' feast and go with me,
AEMELIA: After so long grief, such festivity!
DUKE SOLINUS: With all my heart, I'll gossip at this feast.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but Antipholus of Syracuse, Antipholus of Ephesus, Dromio of Syracuse and Dromio of Ephesus
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Master, shall I fetch your stuff from shipboard?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF EPHESUS: Dromio, what stuff of mine hast thou embark'd?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Your goods that lay at host, sir, in the Centaur.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: ANTIPHOLUS
OF SYRACUSE: He speaks to me. I am your master, Dromio:
OF SYRACUSE: Come, go with us, we'll look to that anon:
OF SYRACUSE: Embrace thy brother there, rejoice with him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Antipholus of Syracuse and Antipholus of Ephesus
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: There is a fat friend at your master's house,
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: That kitchen'd me for you to-day at dinner:
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: She now shall be my sister, not my wife.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Methinks you are my glass, and not my brother:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: I see by you I am a sweet-faced youth.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Will you walk in to see their gossiping?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: Not I, sir, you are my elder.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: That's a question: how shall we try it?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE: We'll draw cuts for the senior: till then lead thou first.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: Nay, then, thus:
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: We came into the world like brother and brother,
DROMIO OF EPHESUS: And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: A Midsummer nights dream '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Athens. The palace of THESEUS.
NARRATOR: Enter THESEUS, HIPPOLYTA, PHILOSTRATE, and Attendants
THESEUS: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour
THESEUS: Draws on apace, four happy days bring in
THESEUS: Another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow
THESEUS: This old moon wanes! she lingers my desires,
THESEUS: Like to a step-dame or a dowager
THESEUS: Long withering out a young man revenue.
HIPPOLYTA: Four days will quickly steep themselves in night,
HIPPOLYTA: Four nights will quickly dream away the time,
HIPPOLYTA: And then the moon, like to a silver bow
HIPPOLYTA: New-bent in heaven, shall behold the night
HIPPOLYTA: Of our solemnities.
THESEUS: Go, Philostrate,
THESEUS: Stir up the Athenian youth to merriments,
THESEUS: Awake the pert and nimble spirit of mirth,
THESEUS: Turn melancholy forth to funerals,
THESEUS: The pale companion is not for our pomp.
NARRATOR: Exit PHILOSTRATE
THESEUS: Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword,
THESEUS: And won thy love, doing thee injuries,
THESEUS: But I will wed thee in another key,
THESEUS: With pomp, with triumph and with revelling.
NARRATOR: Enter EGEUS, HERMIA, LYSANDER, and DEMETRIUS
EGEUS: Happy be Theseus, our renowned duke!
THESEUS: Thanks, good Egeus: what's the news with thee?
EGEUS: Full of vexation come I, with complaint
EGEUS: Against my child, my daughter Hermia.
EGEUS: Stand forth, Demetrius. My noble lord,
EGEUS: This man hath my consent to marry her.
EGEUS: Stand forth, Lysander: and my gracious duke,
EGEUS: This man hath bewitch'd the bosom of my child,
EGEUS: Thou, thou, Lysander, thou hast given her rhymes,
EGEUS: And interchanged love-tokens with my child:
EGEUS: Thou hast by moonlight at her window sung,
EGEUS: With feigning voice verses of feigning love,
EGEUS: And stolen the impression of her fantasy
EGEUS: With bracelets of thy hair, rings, gawds, conceits,
EGEUS: Knacks, trifles, nosegays, sweetmeats, messengers
EGEUS: Of strong prevailment in unharden'd youth:
EGEUS: With cunning hast thou filch'd my daughter's heart,
EGEUS: Turn'd her obedience, which is due to me,
EGEUS: To stubborn harshness: and, my gracious duke,
EGEUS: Be it so she, will not here before your grace
EGEUS: Consent to marry with Demetrius,
EGEUS: I beg the ancient privilege of Athens,
EGEUS: As she is mine, I may dispose of her:
EGEUS: Which shall be either to this gentleman
EGEUS: Or to her death, according to our law
EGEUS: Immediately provided in that case.
THESEUS: What say you, Hermia? be advised fair maid:
THESEUS: To you your father should be as a god,
THESEUS: One that composed your beauties, yea, and one
THESEUS: To whom you are but as a form in wax
THESEUS: By him imprinted and within his power
THESEUS: To leave the figure or disfigure it.
THESEUS: Demetrius is a worthy gentleman.
HERMIA: So is Lysander.
THESEUS: In himself he is,
THESEUS: But in this kind, wanting your father's voice,
THESEUS: The other must be held the worthier.
HERMIA: I would my father look'd but with my eyes.
THESEUS: Rather your eyes must with his judgment look.
HERMIA: I do entreat your grace to pardon me.
HERMIA: I know not by what power I am made bold,
HERMIA: Nor how it may concern my modesty,
HERMIA: In such a presence here to plead my thoughts,
HERMIA: But I beseech your grace that I may know
HERMIA: The worst that may befall me in this case,
HERMIA: If I refuse to wed Demetrius.
THESEUS: Either to die the death or to abjure
THESEUS: For ever the society of men.
THESEUS: Therefore, fair Hermia, question your desires,
THESEUS: Know of your youth, examine well your blood,
THESEUS: Whether, if you yield not to your father's choice,
THESEUS: You can endure the livery of a nun,
THESEUS: For aye to be in shady cloister mew'd,
THESEUS: To live a barren sister all your life,
THESEUS: Chanting faint hymns to the cold fruitless moon.
THESEUS: Thrice-blessed they that master so their blood,
THESEUS: To undergo such maiden pilgrimage,
THESEUS: But earthlier happy is the rose distill'd,
THESEUS: Than that which withering on the virgin thorn
THESEUS: Grows, lives and dies in single blessedness.
HERMIA: So will I grow, so live, so die, my lord,
HERMIA: Ere I will my virgin patent up
HERMIA: Unto his lordship, whose unwished yoke
HERMIA: My soul consents not to give sovereignty.
THESEUS: Take time to pause, and, by the nest new moon--
THESEUS: The sealing-day betwixt my love and me,
THESEUS: For everlasting bond of fellowship--
THESEUS: Upon that day either prepare to die
THESEUS: For disobedience to your father's will,
THESEUS: Or else to wed Demetrius, as he would,
THESEUS: Or on Diana's altar to protest
THESEUS: For aye austerity and single life.
DEMETRIUS: Relent, sweet Hermia: and, Lysander, yield
DEMETRIUS: Thy crazed title to my certain right.
LYSANDER: You have her father's love, Demetrius,
LYSANDER: Let me have Hermia's: do you marry him.
EGEUS: Scornful Lysander! true, he hath my love,
EGEUS: And what is mine my love shall render him.
EGEUS: And she is mine, and all my right of her
EGEUS: I do estate unto Demetrius.
LYSANDER: I am, my lord, as well derived as he,
LYSANDER: As well possess'd, my love is more than his,
LYSANDER: My fortunes every way as fairly rank'd,
LYSANDER: If not with vantage, as Demetrius',
LYSANDER: And, which is more than all these boasts can be,
LYSANDER: I am beloved of beauteous Hermia:
LYSANDER: Why should not I then prosecute my right?
LYSANDER: Demetrius, I'll avouch it to his head,
LYSANDER: Made love to Nedar's daughter, Helena,
LYSANDER: And won her soul, and she, sweet lady, dotes,
LYSANDER: Devoutly dotes, dotes in idolatry,
LYSANDER: Upon this spotted and inconstant man.
THESEUS: I must confess that I have heard so much,
THESEUS: And with Demetrius thought to have spoke thereof,
THESEUS: But, being over-full of self-affairs,
THESEUS: My mind did lose it. But, Demetrius, come,
THESEUS: And come, Egeus, you shall go with me,
THESEUS: I have some private schooling for you both.
THESEUS: For you, fair Hermia, look you arm yourself
THESEUS: To fit your fancies to your father's will,
THESEUS: Or else the law of Athens yields you up--
THESEUS: Which by no means we may extenuate--
THESEUS: To death, or to a vow of single life.
THESEUS: Come, my Hippolyta: what cheer, my love?
THESEUS: Demetrius and Egeus, go along:
THESEUS: I must employ you in some business
THESEUS: Against our nuptial and confer with you
THESEUS: Of something nearly that concerns yourselves.
EGEUS: With duty and desire we follow you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but LYSANDER and HERMIA
LYSANDER: How now, my love! why is your cheek so pale?
LYSANDER: How chance the roses there do fade so fast?
HERMIA: Belike for want of rain, which I could well
HERMIA: Beteem them from the tempest of my eyes.
LYSANDER: Ay me! for aught that I could ever read,
LYSANDER: Could ever hear by tale or history,
LYSANDER: The course of true love never did run smooth,
LYSANDER: But, either it was different in blood,--
HERMIA: O cross! too high to be enthrall'd to low.
LYSANDER: Or else misgraffed in respect of years,--
HERMIA: O spite! too old to be engaged to young.
LYSANDER: Or else it stood upon the choice of friends,--
HERMIA: O hell! to choose love by another's eyes.
LYSANDER: Or, if there were a sympathy in choice,
LYSANDER: War, death, or sickness did lay siege to it,
LYSANDER: Making it momentany as a sound,
LYSANDER: Swift as a shadow, short as any dream,
LYSANDER: Brief as the lightning in the collied night,
LYSANDER: That, in a spleen, unfolds both heaven and earth,
LYSANDER: And ere a man hath power to say 'Behold!'
LYSANDER: The jaws of darkness do devour it up:
LYSANDER: So quick bright things come to confusion.
HERMIA: If then true lovers have been ever cross'd,
HERMIA: It stands as an edict in destiny:
HERMIA: Then let us teach our trial patience,
HERMIA: Because it is a customary cross,
HERMIA: As due to love as thoughts and dreams and sighs,
HERMIA: Wishes and tears, poor fancy's followers.
LYSANDER: A good persuasion: therefore, hear me, Hermia.
LYSANDER: I have a widow aunt, a dowager
LYSANDER: Of great revenue, and she hath no child:
LYSANDER: From Athens is her house remote seven leagues,
LYSANDER: And she respects me as her only son.
LYSANDER: There, gentle Hermia, may I marry thee,
LYSANDER: And to that place the sharp Athenian law
LYSANDER: Cannot pursue us. If thou lovest me then,
LYSANDER: Steal forth thy father's house to-morrow night,
LYSANDER: And in the wood, a league without the town,
LYSANDER: Where I did meet thee once with Helena,
LYSANDER: To do observance to a morn of May,
LYSANDER: There will I stay for thee.
HERMIA: My good Lysander!
HERMIA: I swear to thee, by Cupid's strongest bow,
HERMIA: By his best arrow with the golden head,
HERMIA: By the simplicity of Venus' doves,
HERMIA: By that which knitteth souls and prospers loves,
HERMIA: And by that fire which burn'd the Carthage queen,
HERMIA: When the false Troyan under sail was seen,
HERMIA: By all the vows that ever men have broke,
HERMIA: In number more than ever women spoke,
HERMIA: In that same place thou hast appointed me,
HERMIA: To-morrow truly will I meet with thee.
LYSANDER: Keep promise, love. Look, here comes Helena.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA
HERMIA: God speed fair Helena! whither away?
HELENA: Call you me fair? that fair again unsay.
HELENA: Demetrius loves your fair: O happy fair!
HELENA: Your eyes are lode-stars, and your tongue's sweet air
HELENA: More tuneable than lark to shepherd's ear,
HELENA: When wheat is green, when hawthorn buds appear.
HELENA: Sickness is catching: O, were favour so,
HELENA: Yours would I catch, fair Hermia, ere I go,
HELENA: My ear should catch your voice, my eye your eye,
HELENA: My tongue should catch your tongue's sweet melody.
HELENA: Were the world mine, Demetrius being bated,
HELENA: The rest I'd give to be to you translated.
HELENA: O, teach me how you look, and with what art
HELENA: You sway the motion of Demetrius' heart.
HERMIA: I frown upon him, yet he loves me still.
HELENA: O that your frowns would teach my smiles such skill!
HERMIA: I give him curses, yet he gives me love.
HELENA: O that my prayers could such affection move!
HERMIA: The more I hate, the more he follows me.
HELENA: The more I love, the more he hateth me.
HERMIA: His folly, Helena, is no fault of mine.
HELENA: None, but your beauty: would that fault were mine!
HERMIA: Take comfort: he no more shall see my face,
HERMIA: Lysander and myself will fly this place.
HERMIA: Before the time I did Lysander see,
HERMIA: Seem'd Athens as a paradise to me:
HERMIA: O, then, what graces in my love do dwell,
HERMIA: That he hath turn'd a heaven unto a hell!
LYSANDER: Helen, to you our minds we will unfold:
LYSANDER: To-morrow night, when Phoebe doth behold
LYSANDER: Her silver visage in the watery glass,
LYSANDER: Decking with liquid pearl the bladed grass,
LYSANDER: A time that lovers' flights doth still conceal,
LYSANDER: Through Athens' gates have we devised to steal.
HERMIA: And in the wood, where often you and I
HERMIA: Upon faint primrose-beds were wont to lie,
HERMIA: Emptying our bosoms of their counsel sweet,
HERMIA: There my Lysander and myself shall meet,
HERMIA: And thence from Athens turn away our eyes,
HERMIA: To seek new friends and stranger companies.
HERMIA: Farewell, sweet playfellow: pray thou for us,
HERMIA: And good luck grant thee thy Demetrius!
HERMIA: Keep word, Lysander: we must starve our sight
HERMIA: From lovers' food till morrow deep midnight.
LYSANDER: I will, my Hermia.
NARRATOR: Exit HERMIA
LYSANDER: Helena, adieu:
LYSANDER: As you on him, Demetrius dote on you!
NARRATOR: Exit
HELENA: How happy some o'er other some can be!
HELENA: Through Athens I am thought as fair as she.
HELENA: But what of that? Demetrius thinks not so,
HELENA: He will not know what all but he do know:
HELENA: And as he errs, doting on Hermia's eyes,
HELENA: So I, admiring of his qualities:
HELENA: Things base and vile, folding no quantity,
HELENA: Love can transpose to form and dignity:
HELENA: Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind,
HELENA: And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind:
HELENA: Nor hath Love's mind of any judgement taste,
HELENA: Wings and no eyes figure unheedy haste:
HELENA: And therefore is Love said to be a child,
HELENA: Because in choice he is so oft beguiled.
HELENA: As waggish boys in game themselves forswear,
HELENA: So the boy Love is perjured every where:
HELENA: For ere Demetrius look'd on Hermia's eyne,
HELENA: He hail'd down oaths that he was only mine,
HELENA: And when this hail some heat from Hermia felt,
HELENA: So he dissolved, and showers of oaths did melt.
HELENA: I will go tell him of fair Hermia's flight:
HELENA: Then to the wood will he to-morrow night
HELENA: Pursue her, and for this intelligence
HELENA: If I have thanks, it is a dear expense:
HELENA: But herein mean I to enrich my pain,
HELENA: To have his sight thither and back again.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Athens. QUINCE'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter QUINCE, SNUG, BOTTOM, FLUTE, SNOUT, and STARVELING
QUINCE: Is all our company here?
BOTTOM: You were best to call them generally, man by man,
BOTTOM: according to the scrip.
QUINCE: Here is the scroll of every man's name, which is
QUINCE: thought fit, through all Athens, to play in our
QUINCE: interlude before the duke and the duchess, on his
QUINCE: wedding-day at night.
BOTTOM: First, good Peter Quince, say what the play treats
BOTTOM: on, then read the names of the actors, and so grow
BOTTOM: to a point.
QUINCE: Marry, our play is, The most lamentable comedy, and
QUINCE: most cruel death of Pyramus and Thisby.
BOTTOM: A very good piece of work, I assure you, and a
BOTTOM: merry. Now, good Peter Quince, call forth your
BOTTOM: actors by the scroll. Masters, spread yourselves.
QUINCE: Answer as I call you. Nick Bottom, the weaver.
BOTTOM: Ready. Name what part I am for, and proceed.
QUINCE: You, Nick Bottom, are set down for Pyramus.
BOTTOM: What is Pyramus? a lover, or a tyrant?
QUINCE: A lover, that kills himself most gallant for love.
BOTTOM: That will ask some tears in the true performing of
BOTTOM: it: if I do it, let the audience look to their
BOTTOM: eyes, I will move storms, I will condole in some
BOTTOM: measure. To the rest: yet my chief humour is for a
BOTTOM: tyrant: I could play Ercles rarely, or a part to
BOTTOM: tear a cat in, to make all split.
BOTTOM: The raging rocks
BOTTOM: And shivering shocks
BOTTOM: Shall break the locks
BOTTOM: Of prison gates,
BOTTOM: And Phibbus' car
BOTTOM: Shall shine from far
BOTTOM: And make and mar
BOTTOM: The foolish Fates.
BOTTOM: This was lofty! Now name the rest of the players.
BOTTOM: This is Ercles' vein, a tyrant's vein, a lover is
BOTTOM: more condoling.
QUINCE: Francis Flute, the bellows-mender.
FLUTE: Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE: Flute, you must take Thisby on you.
FLUTE: What is Thisby? a wandering knight?
QUINCE: It is the lady that Pyramus must love.
FLUTE: Nay, faith, let me not play a woman, I have a beard coming.
QUINCE: That's all one: you shall play it in a mask, and
QUINCE: you may speak as small as you will.
BOTTOM: An I may hide my face, let me play Thisby too, I'll
BOTTOM: speak in a monstrous little voice. 'Thisne,
BOTTOM: Thisne,' 'Ah, Pyramus, lover dear! thy Thisby dear,
BOTTOM: and lady dear!'
QUINCE: No, no, you must play Pyramus: and, Flute, you Thisby.
BOTTOM: Well, proceed.
QUINCE: Robin Starveling, the tailor.
STARVELING: Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE: Robin Starveling, you must play Thisby's mother.
QUINCE: Tom Snout, the tinker.
SNOUT: Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE: You, Pyramus' father: myself, Thisby's father:
QUINCE: Snug, the joiner, you, the lion's part: and, I
QUINCE: hope, here is a play fitted.
SNUG: Have you the lion's part written? pray you, if it
SNUG: be, give it me, for I am slow of study.
QUINCE: You may do it extempore, for it is nothing but roaring.
BOTTOM: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will
BOTTOM: do any man's heart good to hear me, I will roar,
BOTTOM: that I will make the duke say 'Let him roar again,
BOTTOM: let him roar again.'
QUINCE: An you should do it too terribly, you would fright
QUINCE: the duchess and the ladies, that they would shriek,
QUINCE: and that were enough to hang us all.
ALL: That would hang us, every mother's son.
BOTTOM: I grant you, friends, if that you should fright the
BOTTOM: ladies out of their wits, they would have no more
BOTTOM: discretion but to hang us: but I will aggravate my
BOTTOM: voice so that I will roar you as gently as any
BOTTOM: sucking dove, I will roar you an 'twere any
BOTTOM: nightingale.
QUINCE: You can play no part but Pyramus, for Pyramus is a
QUINCE: sweet-faced man, a proper man, as one shall see in a
QUINCE: summer's day, a most lovely gentleman-like man:
QUINCE: therefore you must needs play Pyramus.
BOTTOM: Well, I will undertake it. What beard were I best
BOTTOM: to play it in?
QUINCE: Why, what you will.
BOTTOM: I will discharge it in either your straw-colour
BOTTOM: beard, your orange-tawny beard, your purple-in-grain
BOTTOM: beard, or your French-crown-colour beard, your
BOTTOM: perfect yellow.
QUINCE: Some of your French crowns have no hair at all, and
QUINCE: then you will play bare-faced. But, masters, here
QUINCE: are your parts: and I am to entreat you, request
QUINCE: you and desire you, to con them by to-morrow night,
QUINCE: and meet me in the palace wood, a mile without the
QUINCE: town, by moonlight, there will we rehearse, for if
QUINCE: we meet in the city, we shall be dogged with
QUINCE: company, and our devices known. In the meantime I
QUINCE: will draw a bill of properties, such as our play
QUINCE: wants. I pray you, fail me not.
BOTTOM: We will meet, and there we may rehearse most
BOTTOM: obscenely and courageously. Take pains, be perfect: adieu.
QUINCE: At the duke's oak we meet.
BOTTOM: Enough, hold or cut bow-strings.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A wood near Athens.
NARRATOR: Enter, from opposite sides, a Fairy, and PUCK
PUCK: How now, spirit! whither wander you?
Fairy: Over hill, over dale,
Fairy: Thorough bush, thorough brier,
Fairy: Over park, over pale,
Fairy: Thorough flood, thorough fire,
Fairy: I do wander everywhere,
Fairy: Swifter than the moon's sphere,
Fairy: And I serve the fairy queen,
Fairy: To dew her orbs upon the green.
Fairy: The cowslips tall her pensioners be:
Fairy: In their gold coats spots you see,
Fairy: Those be rubies, fairy favours,
Fairy: In those freckles live their savours:
Fairy: I must go seek some dewdrops here
Fairy: And hang a pearl in every cowslip's ear.
Fairy: Farewell, thou lob of spirits, I'll be gone:
Fairy: Our queen and all our elves come here anon.
PUCK: The king doth keep his revels here to-night:
PUCK: Take heed the queen come not within his sight,
PUCK: For Oberon is passing fell and wrath,
PUCK: Because that she as her attendant hath
PUCK: A lovely boy, stolen from an Indian king,
PUCK: She never had so sweet a changeling,
PUCK: And jealous Oberon would have the child
PUCK: Knight of his train, to trace the forests wild,
PUCK: But she perforce withholds the loved boy,
PUCK: Crowns him with flowers and makes him all her joy:
PUCK: And now they never meet in grove or green,
PUCK: By fountain clear, or spangled starlight sheen,
PUCK: But, they do square, that all their elves for fear
PUCK: Creep into acorn-cups and hide them there.
Fairy: Either I mistake your shape and making quite,
Fairy: Or else you are that shrewd and knavish sprite
Fairy: Call'd Robin Goodfellow: are not you he
Fairy: That frights the maidens of the villagery,
Fairy: Skim milk, and sometimes labour in the quern
Fairy: And bootless make the breathless housewife churn,
Fairy: And sometime make the drink to bear no barm,
Fairy: Mislead night-wanderers, laughing at their harm?
Fairy: Those that Hobgoblin call you and sweet Puck,
Fairy: You do their work, and they shall have good luck:
Fairy: Are not you he?
PUCK: Thou speak'st aright,
PUCK: I am that merry wanderer of the night.
PUCK: I jest to Oberon and make him smile
PUCK: When I a fat and bean-fed horse beguile,
PUCK: Neighing in likeness of a filly foal:
PUCK: And sometime lurk I in a gossip's bowl,
PUCK: In very likeness of a roasted crab,
PUCK: And when she drinks, against her lips I bob
PUCK: And on her wither'd dewlap pour the ale.
PUCK: The wisest aunt, telling the saddest tale,
PUCK: Sometime for three-foot stool mistaketh me,
PUCK: Then slip I from her bum, down topples she,
PUCK: And 'tailor' cries, and falls into a cough,
PUCK: And then the whole quire hold their hips and laugh,
PUCK: And waxen in their mirth and neeze and swear
PUCK: A merrier hour was never wasted there.
PUCK: But, room, fairy! here comes Oberon.
Fairy: And here my mistress. Would that he were gone!
Fairy: Enter, from one side, OBERON, with his train, from the other, TITANIA, with hers
OBERON: Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
TITANIA: What, jealous Oberon! Fairies, skip hence:
TITANIA: I have forsworn his bed and company.
OBERON: Tarry, rash wanton: am not I thy lord?
TITANIA: Then I must be thy lady: but I know
TITANIA: When thou hast stolen away from fairy land,
TITANIA: And in the shape of Corin sat all day,
TITANIA: Playing on pipes of corn and versing love
TITANIA: To amorous Phillida. Why art thou here,
TITANIA: Come from the farthest Steppe of India?
TITANIA: But that, forsooth, the bouncing Amazon,
TITANIA: Your buskin'd mistress and your warrior love,
TITANIA: To Theseus must be wedded, and you come
TITANIA: To give their bed joy and prosperity.
OBERON: How canst thou thus for shame, Titania,
OBERON: Glance at my credit with Hippolyta,
OBERON: Knowing I know thy love to Theseus?
OBERON: Didst thou not lead him through the glimmering night
OBERON: From Perigenia, whom he ravished?
OBERON: And make him with fair AEgle break his faith,
OBERON: With Ariadne and Antiopa?
TITANIA: These are the forgeries of jealousy:
TITANIA: And never, since the middle summer's spring,
TITANIA: Met we on hill, in dale, forest or mead,
TITANIA: By paved fountain or by rushy brook,
TITANIA: Or in the beached margent of the sea,
TITANIA: To dance our ringlets to the whistling wind,
TITANIA: But with thy brawls thou hast disturb'd our sport.
TITANIA: Therefore the winds, piping to us in vain,
TITANIA: As in revenge, have suck'd up from the sea
TITANIA: Contagious fogs, which falling in the land
TITANIA: Have every pelting river made so proud
TITANIA: That they have overborne their continents:
TITANIA: The ox hath therefore stretch'd his yoke in vain,
TITANIA: The ploughman lost his sweat, and the green corn
TITANIA: Hath rotted ere his youth attain'd a beard,
TITANIA: The fold stands empty in the drowned field,
TITANIA: And crows are fatted with the murrion flock,
TITANIA: The nine men's morris is fill'd up with mud,
TITANIA: And the quaint mazes in the wanton green
TITANIA: For lack of tread are undistinguishable:
TITANIA: The human mortals want their winter here,
TITANIA: No night is now with hymn or carol blest:
TITANIA: Therefore the moon, the governess of floods,
TITANIA: Pale in her anger, washes all the air,
TITANIA: That rheumatic diseases do abound:
TITANIA: And thorough this distemperature we see
TITANIA: The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts
TITANIA: Far in the fresh lap of the crimson rose,
TITANIA: And on old Hiems' thin and icy crown
TITANIA: An odorous chaplet of sweet summer buds
TITANIA: Is, as in mockery, set: the spring, the summer,
TITANIA: The childing autumn, angry winter, change
TITANIA: Their wonted liveries, and the mazed world,
TITANIA: By their increase, now knows not which is which:
TITANIA: And this same progeny of evils comes
TITANIA: From our debate, from our dissension,
TITANIA: We are their parents and original.
OBERON: Do you amend it then, it lies in you:
OBERON: Why should Titania cross her Oberon?
OBERON: I do but beg a little changeling boy,
OBERON: To be my henchman.
TITANIA: Set your heart at rest:
TITANIA: The fairy land buys not the child of me.
TITANIA: His mother was a votaress of my order:
TITANIA: And, in the spiced Indian air, by night,
TITANIA: Full often hath she gossip'd by my side,
TITANIA: And sat with me on Neptune's yellow sands,
TITANIA: Marking the embarked traders on the flood,
TITANIA: When we have laugh'd to see the sails conceive
TITANIA: And grow big-bellied with the wanton wind,
TITANIA: Which she, with pretty and with swimming gait
TITANIA: Following,--her womb then rich with my young squire,--
TITANIA: Would imitate, and sail upon the land,
TITANIA: To fetch me trifles, and return again,
TITANIA: As from a voyage, rich with merchandise.
TITANIA: But she, being mortal, of that boy did die,
TITANIA: And for her sake do I rear up her boy,
TITANIA: And for her sake I will not part with him.
OBERON: How long within this wood intend you stay?
TITANIA: Perchance till after Theseus' wedding-day.
TITANIA: If you will patiently dance in our round
TITANIA: And see our moonlight revels, go with us,
TITANIA: If not, shun me, and I will spare your haunts.
OBERON: Give me that boy, and I will go with thee.
TITANIA: Not for thy fairy kingdom. Fairies, away!
TITANIA: We shall chide downright, if I longer stay.
NARRATOR: Exit TITANIA with her train
OBERON: Well, go thy way: thou shalt not from this grove
OBERON: Till I torment thee for this injury.
OBERON: My gentle Puck, come hither. Thou rememberest
OBERON: Since once I sat upon a promontory,
OBERON: And heard a mermaid on a dolphin's back
OBERON: Uttering such dulcet and harmonious breath
OBERON: That the rude sea grew civil at her song
OBERON: And certain stars shot madly from their spheres,
OBERON: To hear the sea-maid's music.
PUCK: I remember.
OBERON: That very time I saw, but thou couldst not,
OBERON: Flying between the cold moon and the earth,
OBERON: Cupid all arm'd: a certain aim he took
OBERON: At a fair vestal throned by the west,
OBERON: And loosed his love-shaft smartly from his bow,
OBERON: As it should pierce a hundred thousand hearts,
OBERON: But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft
OBERON: Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon,
OBERON: And the imperial votaress passed on,
OBERON: In maiden meditation, fancy-free.
OBERON: Yet mark'd I where the bolt of Cupid fell:
OBERON: It fell upon a little western flower,
OBERON: Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound,
OBERON: And maidens call it love-in-idleness.
OBERON: Fetch me that flower, the herb I shew'd thee once:
OBERON: The juice of it on sleeping eye-lids laid
OBERON: Will make or man or woman madly dote
OBERON: Upon the next live creature that it sees.
OBERON: Fetch me this herb, and be thou here again
OBERON: Ere the leviathan can swim a league.
PUCK: I'll put a girdle round about the earth
PUCK: In forty minutes.
NARRATOR: Exit
OBERON: Having once this juice,
OBERON: I'll watch Titania when she is asleep,
OBERON: And drop the liquor of it in her eyes.
OBERON: The next thing then she waking looks upon,
OBERON: Be it on lion, bear, or wolf, or bull,
OBERON: On meddling monkey, or on busy ape,
OBERON: She shall pursue it with the soul of love:
OBERON: And ere I take this charm from off her sight,
OBERON: As I can take it with another herb,
OBERON: I'll make her render up her page to me.
OBERON: But who comes here? I am invisible,
OBERON: And I will overhear their conference.
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS, HELENA, following him
DEMETRIUS: I love thee not, therefore pursue me not.
DEMETRIUS: Where is Lysander and fair Hermia?
DEMETRIUS: The one I'll slay, the other slayeth me.
DEMETRIUS: Thou told'st me they were stolen unto this wood,
DEMETRIUS: And here am I, and wode within this wood,
DEMETRIUS: Because I cannot meet my Hermia.
DEMETRIUS: Hence, get thee gone, and follow me no more.
HELENA: You draw me, you hard-hearted adamant,
HELENA: But yet you draw not iron, for my heart
HELENA: Is true as steel: leave you your power to draw,
HELENA: And I shall have no power to follow you.
DEMETRIUS: Do I entice you? do I speak you fair?
DEMETRIUS: Or, rather, do I not in plainest truth
DEMETRIUS: Tell you, I do not, nor I cannot love you?
HELENA: And even for that do I love you the more.
HELENA: I am your spaniel, and, Demetrius,
HELENA: The more you beat me, I will fawn on you:
HELENA: Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me,
HELENA: Neglect me, lose me, only give me leave,
HELENA: Unworthy as I am, to follow you.
HELENA: What worser place can I beg in your love,--
HELENA: And yet a place of high respect with me,--
HELENA: Than to be used as you use your dog?
DEMETRIUS: Tempt not too much the hatred of my spirit,
DEMETRIUS: For I am sick when I do look on thee.
HELENA: And I am sick when I look not on you.
DEMETRIUS: You do impeach your modesty too much,
DEMETRIUS: To leave the city and commit yourself
DEMETRIUS: Into the hands of one that loves you not,
DEMETRIUS: To trust the opportunity of night
DEMETRIUS: And the ill counsel of a desert place
DEMETRIUS: With the rich worth of your virginity.
HELENA: Your virtue is my privilege: for that
HELENA: It is not night when I do see your face,
HELENA: Therefore I think I am not in the night,
HELENA: Nor doth this wood lack worlds of company,
HELENA: For you in my respect are all the world:
HELENA: Then how can it be said I am alone,
HELENA: When all the world is here to look on me?
DEMETRIUS: I'll run from thee and hide me in the brakes,
DEMETRIUS: And leave thee to the mercy of wild beasts.
HELENA: The wildest hath not such a heart as you.
HELENA: Run when you will, the story shall be changed:
HELENA: Apollo flies, and Daphne holds the chase,
HELENA: The dove pursues the griffin, the mild hind
HELENA: Makes speed to catch the tiger, bootless speed,
HELENA: When cowardice pursues and valour flies.
DEMETRIUS: I will not stay thy questions, let me go:
DEMETRIUS: Or, if thou follow me, do not believe
DEMETRIUS: But I shall do thee mischief in the wood.
HELENA: Ay, in the temple, in the town, the field,
HELENA: You do me mischief. Fie, Demetrius!
HELENA: Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex:
HELENA: We cannot fight for love, as men may do,
HELENA: We should be wood and were not made to woo.
NARRATOR: Exit DEMETRIUS
HELENA: I'll follow thee and make a heaven of hell,
HELENA: To die upon the hand I love so well.
NARRATOR: Exit
OBERON: Fare thee well, nymph: ere he do leave this grove,
OBERON: Thou shalt fly him and he shall seek thy love.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PUCK
OBERON: Hast thou the flower there? Welcome, wanderer.
PUCK: Ay, there it is.
OBERON: I pray thee, give it me.
OBERON: I know a bank where the wild thyme blows,
OBERON: Where oxlips and the nodding violet grows,
OBERON: Quite over-canopied with luscious woodbine,
OBERON: With sweet musk-roses and with eglantine:
OBERON: There sleeps Titania sometime of the night,
OBERON: Lull'd in these flowers with dances and delight,
OBERON: And there the snake throws her enamell'd skin,
OBERON: Weed wide enough to wrap a fairy in:
OBERON: And with the juice of this I'll streak her eyes,
OBERON: And make her full of hateful fantasies.
OBERON: Take thou some of it, and seek through this grove:
OBERON: A sweet Athenian lady is in love
OBERON: With a disdainful youth: anoint his eyes,
OBERON: But do it when the next thing he espies
OBERON: May be the lady: thou shalt know the man
OBERON: By the Athenian garments he hath on.
OBERON: Effect it with some care, that he may prove
OBERON: More fond on her than she upon her love:
OBERON: And look thou meet me ere the first cock crow.
PUCK: Fear not, my lord, your servant shall do so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Another part of the wood.
NARRATOR: Enter TITANIA, with her train
TITANIA: Come, now a roundel and a fairy song,
TITANIA: Then, for the third part of a minute, hence,
TITANIA: Some to kill cankers in the musk-rose buds,
TITANIA: Some war with rere-mice for their leathern wings,
TITANIA: To make my small elves coats, and some keep back
TITANIA: The clamorous owl that nightly hoots and wonders
TITANIA: At our quaint spirits. Sing me now asleep,
TITANIA: Then to your offices and let me rest.
NARRATOR: The Fairies sing
TITANIA: You spotted snakes with double tongue,
TITANIA: Thorny hedgehogs, be not seen,
TITANIA: Newts and blind-worms, do no wrong,
TITANIA: Come not near our fairy queen.
TITANIA: Philomel, with melody
TITANIA: Sing in our sweet lullaby,
TITANIA: Lulla, lulla, lullaby, lulla, lulla, lullaby:
TITANIA: Never harm,
TITANIA: Nor spell nor charm,
TITANIA: Come our lovely lady nigh,
TITANIA: So, good night, with lullaby.
TITANIA: Weaving spiders, come not here,
TITANIA: Hence, you long-legg'd spinners, hence!
TITANIA: Beetles black, approach not near,
TITANIA: Worm nor snail, do no offence.
TITANIA: Philomel, with melody,  and c.
Fairy: Hence, away! now all is well:
Fairy: One aloof stand sentinel.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Fairies. TITANIA sleeps
NARRATOR: Enter OBERON and squeezes the flower on TITANIA's eyelids
OBERON: What thou seest when thou dost wake,
OBERON: Do it for thy true-love take,
OBERON: Love and languish for his sake:
OBERON: Be it ounce, or cat, or bear,
OBERON: Pard, or boar with bristled hair,
OBERON: In thy eye that shall appear
OBERON: When thou wakest, it is thy dear:
OBERON: Wake when some vile thing is near.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter LYSANDER and HERMIA
LYSANDER: Fair love, you faint with wandering in the wood,
LYSANDER: And to speak troth, I have forgot our way:
LYSANDER: We'll rest us, Hermia, if you think it good,
LYSANDER: And tarry for the comfort of the day.
HERMIA: Be it so, Lysander: find you out a bed,
HERMIA: For I upon this bank will rest my head.
LYSANDER: One turf shall serve as pillow for us both,
LYSANDER: One heart, one bed, two bosoms and one troth.
HERMIA: Nay, good Lysander, for my sake, my dear,
HERMIA: Lie further off yet, do not lie so near.
LYSANDER: O, take the sense, sweet, of my innocence!
LYSANDER: Love takes the meaning in love's conference.
LYSANDER: I mean, that my heart unto yours is knit
LYSANDER: So that but one heart we can make of it,
LYSANDER: Two bosoms interchained with an oath,
LYSANDER: So then two bosoms and a single troth.
LYSANDER: Then by your side no bed-room me deny,
LYSANDER: For lying so, Hermia, I do not lie.
HERMIA: Lysander riddles very prettily:
HERMIA: Now much beshrew my manners and my pride,
HERMIA: If Hermia meant to say Lysander lied.
HERMIA: But, gentle friend, for love and courtesy
HERMIA: Lie further off, in human modesty,
HERMIA: Such separation as may well be said
HERMIA: Becomes a virtuous bachelor and a maid,
HERMIA: So far be distant, and, good night, sweet friend:
HERMIA: Thy love ne'er alter till thy sweet life end!
LYSANDER: Amen, amen, to that fair prayer, say I,
LYSANDER: And then end life when I end loyalty!
LYSANDER: Here is my bed: sleep give thee all his rest!
HERMIA: With half that wish the wisher's eyes be press'd!
NARRATOR: They sleep
NARRATOR: Enter PUCK
PUCK: Through the forest have I gone.
PUCK: But Athenian found I none,
PUCK: On whose eyes I might approve
PUCK: This flower's force in stirring love.
PUCK: Night and silence.--Who is here?
PUCK: Weeds of Athens he doth wear:
PUCK: This is he, my master said,
PUCK: Despised the Athenian maid,
PUCK: And here the maiden, sleeping sound,
PUCK: On the dank and dirty ground.
PUCK: Pretty soul! she durst not lie
PUCK: Near this lack-love, this kill-courtesy.
PUCK: Churl, upon thy eyes I throw
PUCK: All the power this charm doth owe.
PUCK: When thou wakest, let love forbid
PUCK: Sleep his seat on thy eyelid:
PUCK: So awake when I am gone,
PUCK: For I must now to Oberon.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS and HELENA, running
HELENA: Stay, though thou kill me, sweet Demetrius.
DEMETRIUS: I charge thee, hence, and do not haunt me thus.
HELENA: O, wilt thou darkling leave me? do not so.
DEMETRIUS: Stay, on thy peril: I alone will go.
NARRATOR: Exit
HELENA: O, I am out of breath in this fond chase!
HELENA: The more my prayer, the lesser is my grace.
HELENA: Happy is Hermia, wheresoe'er she lies,
HELENA: For she hath blessed and attractive eyes.
HELENA: How came her eyes so bright? Not with salt tears:
HELENA: If so, my eyes are oftener wash'd than hers.
HELENA: No, no, I am as ugly as a bear,
HELENA: For beasts that meet me run away for fear:
HELENA: Therefore no marvel though Demetrius
HELENA: Do, as a monster fly my presence thus.
HELENA: What wicked and dissembling glass of mine
HELENA: Made me compare with Hermia's sphery eyne?
HELENA: But who is here? Lysander! on the ground!
HELENA: Dead? or asleep? I see no blood, no wound.
HELENA: Lysander if you live, good sir, awake.
LYSANDER: [Awaking]  And run through fire I will for thy sweet sake.
LYSANDER: Transparent Helena! Nature shows art,
LYSANDER: That through thy bosom makes me see thy heart.
LYSANDER: Where is Demetrius? O, how fit a word
LYSANDER: Is that vile name to perish on my sword!
HELENA: Do not say so, Lysander, say not so
HELENA: What though he love your Hermia? Lord, what though?
HELENA: Yet Hermia still loves you: then be content.
LYSANDER: Content with Hermia! No, I do repent
LYSANDER: The tedious minutes I with her have spent.
LYSANDER: Not Hermia but Helena I love:
LYSANDER: Who will not change a raven for a dove?
LYSANDER: The will of man is by his reason sway'd,
LYSANDER: And reason says you are the worthier maid.
LYSANDER: Things growing are not ripe until their season
LYSANDER: So I, being young, till now ripe not to reason,
LYSANDER: And touching now the point of human skill,
LYSANDER: Reason becomes the marshal to my will
LYSANDER: And leads me to your eyes, where I o'erlook
LYSANDER: Love's stories written in love's richest book.
HELENA: Wherefore was I to this keen mockery born?
HELENA: When at your hands did I deserve this scorn?
HELENA: Is't not enough, is't not enough, young man,
HELENA: That I did never, no, nor never can,
HELENA: Deserve a sweet look from Demetrius' eye,
HELENA: But you must flout my insufficiency?
HELENA: Good troth, you do me wrong, good sooth, you do,
HELENA: In such disdainful manner me to woo.
HELENA: But fare you well: perforce I must confess
HELENA: I thought you lord of more true gentleness.
HELENA: O, that a lady, of one man refused.
HELENA: Should of another therefore be abused!
NARRATOR: Exit
LYSANDER: She sees not Hermia. Hermia, sleep thou there:
LYSANDER: And never mayst thou come Lysander near!
LYSANDER: For as a surfeit of the sweetest things
LYSANDER: The deepest loathing to the stomach brings,
LYSANDER: Or as tie heresies that men do leave
LYSANDER: Are hated most of those they did deceive,
LYSANDER: So thou, my surfeit and my heresy,
LYSANDER: Of all be hated, but the most of me!
LYSANDER: And, all my powers, address your love and might
LYSANDER: To honour Helen and to be her knight!
NARRATOR: Exit
HERMIA: [Awaking]  Help me, Lysander, help me! do thy best
HERMIA: To pluck this crawling serpent from my breast!
HERMIA: Ay me, for pity! what a dream was here!
HERMIA: Lysander, look how I do quake with fear:
HERMIA: Methought a serpent eat my heart away,
HERMIA: And you sat smiling at his cruel pray.
HERMIA: Lysander! what, removed? Lysander! lord!
HERMIA: What, out of hearing? gone? no sound, no word?
HERMIA: Alack, where are you speak, an if you hear,
HERMIA: Speak, of all loves! I swoon almost with fear.
HERMIA: No? then I well perceive you all not nigh
HERMIA: Either death or you I'll find immediately.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The wood. TITANIA lying asleep.
NARRATOR: Enter QUINCE, SNUG, BOTTOM, FLUTE, SNOUT, and STARVELING
BOTTOM: Are we all met?
QUINCE: Pat, pat, and here's a marvellous convenient place
QUINCE: for our rehearsal. This green plot shall be our
QUINCE: stage, this hawthorn-brake our tiring-house, and we
QUINCE: will do it in action as we will do it before the duke.
BOTTOM: Peter Quince,--
QUINCE: What sayest thou, bully Bottom?
BOTTOM: There are things in this comedy of Pyramus and
BOTTOM: Thisby that will never please. First, Pyramus must
BOTTOM: draw a sword to kill himself, which the ladies
BOTTOM: cannot abide. How answer you that?
SNOUT: By'r lakin, a parlous fear.
STARVELING: I believe we must leave the killing out, when all is done.
BOTTOM: Not a whit: I have a device to make all well.
BOTTOM: Write me a prologue, and let the prologue seem to
BOTTOM: say, we will do no harm with our swords, and that
BOTTOM: Pyramus is not killed indeed, and, for the more
BOTTOM: better assurance, tell them that I, Pyramus, am not
BOTTOM: Pyramus, but Bottom the weaver: this will put them
BOTTOM: out of fear.
QUINCE: Well, we will have such a prologue, and it shall be
QUINCE: written in eight and six.
BOTTOM: No, make it two more, let it be written in eight and eight.
SNOUT: Will not the ladies be afeard of the lion?
STARVELING: I fear it, I promise you.
BOTTOM: Masters, you ought to consider with yourselves: to
BOTTOM: bring in--God shield us!--a lion among ladies, is a
BOTTOM: most dreadful thing, for there is not a more fearful
BOTTOM: wild-fowl than your lion living, and we ought to
BOTTOM: look to 't.
SNOUT: Therefore another prologue must tell he is not a lion.
BOTTOM: Nay, you must name his name, and half his face must
BOTTOM: be seen through the lion's neck: and he himself
BOTTOM: must speak through, saying thus, or to the same
BOTTOM: defect,--'Ladies,'--or 'Fair-ladies--I would wish
BOTTOM: You,'--or 'I would request you,'--or 'I would
BOTTOM: entreat you,--not to fear, not to tremble: my life
BOTTOM: for yours. If you think I come hither as a lion, it
BOTTOM: were pity of my life: no I am no such thing, I am a
BOTTOM: man as other men are,' and there indeed let him name
BOTTOM: his name, and tell them plainly he is Snug the joiner.
QUINCE: Well it shall be so. But there is two hard things,
QUINCE: that is, to bring the moonlight into a chamber, for,
QUINCE: you know, Pyramus and Thisby meet by moonlight.
SNOUT: Doth the moon shine that night we play our play?
BOTTOM: A calendar, a calendar! look in the almanac, find
BOTTOM: out moonshine, find out moonshine.
QUINCE: Yes, it doth shine that night.
BOTTOM: Why, then may you leave a casement of the great
BOTTOM: chamber window, where we play, open, and the moon
BOTTOM: may shine in at the casement.
QUINCE: Ay, or else one must come in with a bush of thorns
QUINCE: and a lanthorn, and say he comes to disfigure, or to
QUINCE: present, the person of Moonshine. Then, there is
QUINCE: another thing: we must have a wall in the great
QUINCE: chamber, for Pyramus and Thisby says the story, did
QUINCE: talk through the chink of a wall.
SNOUT: You can never bring in a wall. What say you, Bottom?
BOTTOM: Some man or other must present Wall: and let him
BOTTOM: have some plaster, or some loam, or some rough-cast
BOTTOM: about him, to signify wall, and let him hold his
BOTTOM: fingers thus, and through that cranny shall Pyramus
BOTTOM: and Thisby whisper.
QUINCE: If that may be, then all is well. Come, sit  down,
QUINCE: every mother's son, and rehearse your parts.
QUINCE: Pyramus, you begin: when you have spoken your
QUINCE: speech, enter into that brake: and so every one
QUINCE: according to his cue.
NARRATOR: Enter PUCK behind
PUCK: What hempen home-spuns have we swaggering here,
PUCK: So near the cradle of the fairy queen?
PUCK: What, a play toward! I'll be an auditor,
PUCK: An actor too, perhaps, if I see cause.
QUINCE: Speak, Pyramus. Thisby, stand forth.
BOTTOM: Thisby, the flowers of odious savours sweet,--
QUINCE: Odours, odours.
BOTTOM: --odours savours sweet:
BOTTOM: So hath thy breath, my dearest Thisby dear.
BOTTOM: But hark, a voice! stay thou but here awhile,
BOTTOM: And by and by I will to thee appear.
NARRATOR: Exit
PUCK: A stranger Pyramus than e'er played here.
NARRATOR: Exit
FLUTE: Must I speak now?
QUINCE: Ay, marry, must you, for you must understand he goes
QUINCE: but to see a noise that he heard, and is to come again.
FLUTE: Most radiant Pyramus, most lily-white of hue,
FLUTE: Of colour like the red rose on triumphant brier,
FLUTE: Most brisky juvenal and eke most lovely Jew,
FLUTE: As true as truest horse that yet would never tire,
FLUTE: I'll meet thee, Pyramus, at Ninny's tomb.
QUINCE: 'Ninus' tomb,' man: why, you must not speak that
QUINCE: yet, that you answer to Pyramus: you speak all your
QUINCE: part at once, cues and all Pyramus enter: your cue
QUINCE: is past, it is, 'never tire.'
FLUTE: O,--As true as truest horse, that yet would
FLUTE: never tire.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PUCK, and BOTTOM with an ass's head
BOTTOM: If I were fair, Thisby, I were only thine.
QUINCE: O monstrous! O strange! we are haunted. Pray,
QUINCE: masters! fly, masters! Help!
NARRATOR: Exeunt QUINCE, SNUG, FLUTE, SNOUT, and STARVELING
PUCK: I'll follow you, I'll lead you about a round,
PUCK: Through bog, through bush, through brake, through brier:
PUCK: Sometime a horse I'll be, sometime a hound,
PUCK: A hog, a headless bear, sometime a fire,
PUCK: And neigh, and bark, and grunt, and roar, and burn,
PUCK: Like horse, hound, hog, bear, fire, at every turn.
NARRATOR: Exit
BOTTOM: Why do they run away? this is a knavery of them to
BOTTOM: make me afeard.
NARRATOR: Re-enter SNOUT
SNOUT: O Bottom, thou art changed! what do I see on thee?
BOTTOM: What do you see? you see an asshead of your own, do
BOTTOM: you?
NARRATOR: Exit SNOUT
NARRATOR: Re-enter QUINCE
QUINCE: Bless thee, Bottom! bless thee! thou art
QUINCE: translated.
NARRATOR: Exit
BOTTOM: I see their knavery: this is to make an ass of me,
BOTTOM: to fright me, if they could. But I will not stir
BOTTOM: from this place, do what they can: I will walk up
BOTTOM: and down here, and I will sing, that they shall hear
BOTTOM: I am not afraid.
NARRATOR: Sings
BOTTOM: The ousel cock so black of hue,
BOTTOM: With orange-tawny bill,
BOTTOM: The throstle with his note so true,
BOTTOM: The wren with little quill,--
TITANIA: [Awaking]  What angel wakes me from my flowery bed?
BOTTOM: [Sings]
BOTTOM: The finch, the sparrow and the lark,
BOTTOM: The plain-song cuckoo gray,
BOTTOM: Whose note full many a man doth mark,
BOTTOM: And dares not answer nay,--
BOTTOM: for, indeed, who would set his wit to so foolish
BOTTOM: a bird? who would give a bird the lie, though he cry
BOTTOM: 'cuckoo' never so?
TITANIA: I pray thee, gentle mortal, sing again:
TITANIA: Mine ear is much enamour'd of thy note,
TITANIA: So is mine eye enthralled to thy shape,
TITANIA: And thy fair virtue's force perforce doth move me
TITANIA: On the first view to say, to swear, I love thee.
BOTTOM: Methinks, mistress, you should have little reason
BOTTOM: for that: and yet, to say the truth, reason and
BOTTOM: love keep little company together now-a-days, the
BOTTOM: more the pity that some honest neighbours will not
BOTTOM: make them friends. Nay, I can gleek upon occasion.
TITANIA: Thou art as wise as thou art beautiful.
BOTTOM: Not so, neither: but if I had wit enough to get out
BOTTOM: of this wood, I have enough to serve mine own turn.
TITANIA: Out of this wood do not desire to go:
TITANIA: Thou shalt remain here, whether thou wilt or no.
TITANIA: I am a spirit of no common rate,
TITANIA: The summer still doth tend upon my state,
TITANIA: And I do love thee: therefore, go with me,
TITANIA: I'll give thee fairies to attend on thee,
TITANIA: And they shall fetch thee jewels from the deep,
TITANIA: And sing while thou on pressed flowers dost sleep,
TITANIA: And I will purge thy mortal grossness so
TITANIA: That thou shalt like an airy spirit go.
TITANIA: Peaseblossom! Cobweb! Moth! and Mustardseed!
NARRATOR: Enter PEASEBLOSSOM, COBWEB, MOTH, and MUSTARDSEED
PEASEBLOSSOM: Ready.
COBWEB: And I.
MOTH: And I.
MUSTARDSEED: And I.
ALL: Where shall we go?
TITANIA: Be kind and courteous to this gentleman,
TITANIA: Hop in his walks and gambol in his eyes,
TITANIA: Feed him with apricocks and dewberries,
TITANIA: With purple grapes, green figs, and mulberries,
TITANIA: The honey-bags steal from the humble-bees,
TITANIA: And for night-tapers crop their waxen thighs
TITANIA: And light them at the fiery glow-worm's eyes,
TITANIA: To have my love to bed and to arise,
TITANIA: And pluck the wings from Painted butterflies
TITANIA: To fan the moonbeams from his sleeping eyes:
TITANIA: Nod to him, elves, and do him courtesies.
PEASEBLOSSOM: Hail, mortal!
COBWEB: Hail!
MOTH: Hail!
MUSTARDSEED: Hail!
BOTTOM: I cry your worship's mercy, heartily: I beseech your
BOTTOM: worship's name.
COBWEB: Cobweb.
BOTTOM: I shall desire you of more acquaintance, good Master
BOTTOM: Cobweb: if I cut my finger, I shall make bold with
BOTTOM: you. Your name, honest gentleman?
PEASEBLOSSOM: Peaseblossom.
BOTTOM: I pray you, commend me to Mistress Squash, your
BOTTOM: mother, and to Master Peascod, your father. Good
BOTTOM: Master Peaseblossom, I shall desire you of more
BOTTOM: acquaintance too. Your name, I beseech you, sir?
MUSTARDSEED: Mustardseed.
BOTTOM: Good Master Mustardseed, I know your patience well:
BOTTOM: that same cowardly, giant-like ox-beef hath
BOTTOM: devoured many a gentleman of your house: I promise
BOTTOM: you your kindred had made my eyes water ere now. I
BOTTOM: desire your more acquaintance, good Master
BOTTOM: Mustardseed.
TITANIA: Come, wait upon him, lead him to my bower.
TITANIA: The moon methinks looks with a watery eye,
TITANIA: And when she weeps, weeps every little flower,
TITANIA: Lamenting some enforced chastity.
TITANIA: Tie up my love's tongue bring him silently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Another part of the wood.
NARRATOR: Enter OBERON
OBERON: I wonder if Titania be awaked,
OBERON: Then, what it was that next came in her eye,
OBERON: Which she must dote on in extremity.
NARRATOR: Enter PUCK
OBERON: Here comes my messenger.
OBERON: How now, mad spirit!
OBERON: What night-rule now about this haunted grove?
PUCK: My mistress with a monster is in love.
PUCK: Near to her close and consecrated bower,
PUCK: While she was in her dull and sleeping hour,
PUCK: A crew of patches, rude mechanicals,
PUCK: That work for bread upon Athenian stalls,
PUCK: Were met together to rehearse a play
PUCK: Intended for great Theseus' nuptial-day.
PUCK: The shallowest thick-skin of that barren sort,
PUCK: Who Pyramus presented, in their sport
PUCK: Forsook his scene and enter'd in a brake
PUCK: When I did him at this advantage take,
PUCK: An ass's nole I fixed on his head:
PUCK: Anon his Thisbe must be answered,
PUCK: And forth my mimic comes. When they him spy,
PUCK: As wild geese that the creeping fowler eye,
PUCK: Or russet-pated choughs, many in sort,
PUCK: Rising and cawing at the gun's report,
PUCK: Sever themselves and madly sweep the sky,
PUCK: So, at his sight, away his fellows fly,
PUCK: And, at our stamp, here o'er and o'er one falls,
PUCK: He murder cries and help from Athens calls.
PUCK: Their sense thus weak, lost with their fears
PUCK: thus strong,
PUCK: Made senseless things begin to do them wrong,
PUCK: For briers and thorns at their apparel snatch,
PUCK: Some sleeves, some hats, from yielders all
PUCK: things catch.
PUCK: I led them on in this distracted fear,
PUCK: And left sweet Pyramus translated there:
PUCK: When in that moment, so it came to pass,
PUCK: Titania waked and straightway loved an ass.
OBERON: This falls out better than I could devise.
OBERON: But hast thou yet latch'd the Athenian's eyes
OBERON: With the love-juice, as I did bid thee do?
PUCK: I took him sleeping,--that is finish'd too,--
PUCK: And the Athenian woman by his side:
PUCK: That, when he waked, of force she must be eyed.
NARRATOR: Enter HERMIA and DEMETRIUS
OBERON: Stand close: this is the same Athenian.
PUCK: This is the woman, but not this the man.
DEMETRIUS: O, why rebuke you him that loves you so?
DEMETRIUS: Lay breath so bitter on your bitter foe.
HERMIA: Now I but chide, but I should use thee worse,
HERMIA: For thou, I fear, hast given me cause to curse,
HERMIA: If thou hast slain Lysander in his sleep,
HERMIA: Being o'er shoes in blood, plunge in the deep,
HERMIA: And kill me too.
HERMIA: The sun was not so true unto the day
HERMIA: As he to me: would he have stolen away
HERMIA: From sleeping Hermia? I'll believe as soon
HERMIA: This whole earth may be bored and that the moon
HERMIA: May through the centre creep and so displease
HERMIA: Her brother's noontide with Antipodes.
HERMIA: It cannot be but thou hast murder'd him,
HERMIA: So should a murderer look, so dead, so grim.
DEMETRIUS: So should the murder'd look, and so should I,
DEMETRIUS: Pierced through the heart with your stern cruelty:
DEMETRIUS: Yet you, the murderer, look as bright, as clear,
DEMETRIUS: As yonder Venus in her glimmering sphere.
HERMIA: What's this to my Lysander? where is he?
HERMIA: Ah, good Demetrius, wilt thou give him me?
DEMETRIUS: I had rather give his carcass to my hounds.
HERMIA: Out, dog! out, cur! thou drivest me past the bounds
HERMIA: Of maiden's patience. Hast thou slain him, then?
HERMIA: Henceforth be never number'd among men!
HERMIA: O, once tell true, tell true, even for my sake!
HERMIA: Durst thou have look'd upon him being awake,
HERMIA: And hast thou kill'd him sleeping? O brave touch!
HERMIA: Could not a worm, an adder, do so much?
HERMIA: An adder did it, for with doubler tongue
HERMIA: Than thine, thou serpent, never adder stung.
DEMETRIUS: You spend your passion on a misprised mood:
DEMETRIUS: I am not guilty of Lysander's blood,
DEMETRIUS: Nor is he dead, for aught that I can tell.
HERMIA: I pray thee, tell me then that he is well.
DEMETRIUS: An if I could, what should I get therefore?
HERMIA: A privilege never to see me more.
HERMIA: And from thy hated presence part I so:
HERMIA: See me no more, whether he be dead or no.
NARRATOR: Exit
DEMETRIUS: There is no following her in this fierce vein:
DEMETRIUS: Here therefore for a while I will remain.
DEMETRIUS: So sorrow's heaviness doth heavier grow
DEMETRIUS: For debt that bankrupt sleep doth sorrow owe:
DEMETRIUS: Which now in some slight measure it will pay,
DEMETRIUS: If for his tender here I make some stay.
NARRATOR: Lies down and sleeps
OBERON: What hast thou done? thou hast mistaken quite
OBERON: And laid the love-juice on some true-love's sight:
OBERON: Of thy misprision must perforce ensue
OBERON: Some true love turn'd and not a false turn'd true.
PUCK: Then fate o'er-rules, that, one man holding troth,
PUCK: A million fail, confounding oath on oath.
OBERON: About the wood go swifter than the wind,
OBERON: And Helena of Athens look thou find:
OBERON: All fancy-sick she is and pale of cheer,
OBERON: With sighs of love, that costs the fresh blood dear:
OBERON: By some illusion see thou bring her here:
OBERON: I'll charm his eyes against she do appear.
