PUCK: I go, I go, look how I go,
PUCK: Swifter than arrow from the Tartar's bow.
NARRATOR: Exit
OBERON: Flower of this purple dye,
OBERON: Hit with Cupid's archery,
OBERON: Sink in apple of his eye.
OBERON: When his love he doth espy,
OBERON: Let her shine as gloriously
OBERON: As the Venus of the sky.
OBERON: When thou wakest, if she be by,
OBERON: Beg of her for remedy.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PUCK
PUCK: Captain of our fairy band,
PUCK: Helena is here at hand,
PUCK: And the youth, mistook by me,
PUCK: Pleading for a lover's fee.
PUCK: Shall we their fond pageant see?
PUCK: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
OBERON: Stand aside: the noise they make
OBERON: Will cause Demetrius to awake.
PUCK: Then will two at once woo one,
PUCK: That must needs be sport alone,
PUCK: And those things do best please me
PUCK: That befal preposterously.
NARRATOR: Enter LYSANDER and HELENA
LYSANDER: Why should you think that I should woo in scorn?
LYSANDER: Scorn and derision never come in tears:
LYSANDER: Look, when I vow, I weep, and vows so born,
LYSANDER: In their nativity all truth appears.
LYSANDER: How can these things in me seem scorn to you,
LYSANDER: Bearing the badge of faith, to prove them true?
HELENA: You do advance your cunning more and more.
HELENA: When truth kills truth, O devilish-holy fray!
HELENA: These vows are Hermia's: will you give her o'er?
HELENA: Weigh oath with oath, and you will nothing weigh:
HELENA: Your vows to her and me, put in two scales,
HELENA: Will even weigh, and both as light as tales.
LYSANDER: I had no judgment when to her I swore.
HELENA: Nor none, in my mind, now you give her o'er.
LYSANDER: Demetrius loves her, and he loves not you.
DEMETRIUS: [Awaking]  O Helena, goddess, nymph, perfect, divine!
DEMETRIUS: To what, my love, shall I compare thine eyne?
DEMETRIUS: Crystal is muddy. O, how ripe in show
DEMETRIUS: Thy lips, those kissing cherries, tempting grow!
DEMETRIUS: That pure congealed white, high Taurus snow,
DEMETRIUS: Fann'd with the eastern wind, turns to a crow
DEMETRIUS: When thou hold'st up thy hand: O, let me kiss
DEMETRIUS: This princess of pure white, this seal of bliss!
HELENA: O spite! O hell! I see you all are bent
HELENA: To set against me for your merriment:
HELENA: If you we re civil and knew courtesy,
HELENA: You would not do me thus much injury.
HELENA: Can you not hate me, as I know you do,
HELENA: But you must join in souls to mock me too?
HELENA: If you were men, as men you are in show,
HELENA: You would not use a gentle lady so,
HELENA: To vow, and swear, and superpraise my parts,
HELENA: When I am sure you hate me with your hearts.
HELENA: You both are rivals, and love Hermia,
HELENA: And now both rivals, to mock Helena:
HELENA: A trim exploit, a manly enterprise,
HELENA: To conjure tears up in a poor maid's eyes
HELENA: With your derision! none of noble sort
HELENA: Would so offend a virgin, and extort
HELENA: A poor soul's patience, all to make you sport.
LYSANDER: You are unkind, Demetrius, be not so,
LYSANDER: For you love Hermia, this you know I know:
LYSANDER: And here, with all good will, with all my heart,
LYSANDER: In Hermia's love I yield you up my part,
LYSANDER: And yours of Helena to me bequeath,
LYSANDER: Whom I do love and will do till my death.
HELENA: Never did mockers waste more idle breath.
DEMETRIUS: Lysander, keep thy Hermia, I will none:
DEMETRIUS: If e'er I loved her, all that love is gone.
DEMETRIUS: My heart to her but as guest-wise sojourn'd,
DEMETRIUS: And now to Helen is it home return'd,
DEMETRIUS: There to remain.
LYSANDER: Helen, it is not so.
DEMETRIUS: Disparage not the faith thou dost not know,
DEMETRIUS: Lest, to thy peril, thou aby it dear.
DEMETRIUS: Look, where thy love comes, yonder is thy dear.
NARRATOR: Re-enter HERMIA
HERMIA: Dark night, that from the eye his function takes,
HERMIA: The ear more quick of apprehension makes,
HERMIA: Wherein it doth impair the seeing sense,
HERMIA: It pays the hearing double recompense.
HERMIA: Thou art not by mine eye, Lysander, found,
HERMIA: Mine ear, I thank it, brought me to thy sound
HERMIA: But why unkindly didst thou leave me so?
LYSANDER: Why should he stay, whom love doth press to go?
HERMIA: What love could press Lysander from my side?
LYSANDER: Lysander's love, that would not let him bide,
LYSANDER: Fair Helena, who more engilds the night
LYSANDER: Than all you fiery oes and eyes of light.
LYSANDER: Why seek'st thou me? could not this make thee know,
LYSANDER: The hate I bear thee made me leave thee so?
HERMIA: You speak not as you think: it cannot be.
HELENA: Lo, she is one of this confederacy!
HELENA: Now I perceive they have conjoin'd all three
HELENA: To fashion this false sport, in spite of me.
HELENA: Injurious Hermia! most ungrateful maid!
HELENA: Have you conspired, have you with these contrived
HELENA: To bait me with this foul derision?
HELENA: Is all the counsel that we two have shared,
HELENA: The sisters' vows, the hours that we have spent,
HELENA: When we have chid the hasty-footed time
HELENA: For parting us,--O, is it all forgot?
HELENA: All school-days' friendship, childhood innocence?
HELENA: We, Hermia, like two artificial gods,
HELENA: Have with our needles created both one flower,
HELENA: Both on one sampler, sitting on one cushion,
HELENA: Both warbling of one song, both in one key,
HELENA: As if our hands, our sides, voices and minds,
HELENA: Had been incorporate. So we grow together,
HELENA: Like to a double cherry, seeming parted,
HELENA: But yet an union in partition,
HELENA: Two lovely berries moulded on one stem,
HELENA: So, with two seeming bodies, but one heart,
HELENA: Two of the first, like coats in heraldry,
HELENA: Due but to one and crowned with one crest.
HELENA: And will you rent our ancient love asunder,
HELENA: To join with men in scorning your poor friend?
HELENA: It is not friendly, 'tis not maidenly:
HELENA: Our sex, as well as I, may chide you for it,
HELENA: Though I alone do feel the injury.
HERMIA: I am amazed at your passionate words.
HERMIA: I scorn you not: it seems that you scorn me.
HELENA: Have you not set Lysander, as in scorn,
HELENA: To follow me and praise my eyes and face?
HELENA: And made your other love, Demetrius,
HELENA: Who even but now did spurn me with his foot,
HELENA: To call me goddess, nymph, divine and rare,
HELENA: Precious, celestial? Wherefore speaks he this
HELENA: To her he hates? and wherefore doth Lysander
HELENA: Deny your love, so rich within his soul,
HELENA: And tender me, forsooth, affection,
HELENA: But by your setting on, by your consent?
HELENA: What thought I be not so in grace as you,
HELENA: So hung upon with love, so fortunate,
HELENA: But miserable most, to love unloved?
HELENA: This you should pity rather than despise.
HERNIA: I understand not what you mean by this.
HELENA: Ay, do, persever, counterfeit sad looks,
HELENA: Make mouths upon me when I turn my back,
HELENA: Wink each at other, hold the sweet jest up:
HELENA: This sport, well carried, shall be chronicled.
HELENA: If you have any pity, grace, or manners,
HELENA: You would not make me such an argument.
HELENA: But fare ye well: 'tis partly my own fault,
HELENA: Which death or absence soon shall remedy.
LYSANDER: Stay, gentle Helena, hear my excuse:
LYSANDER: My love, my life my soul, fair Helena!
HELENA: O excellent!
HERMIA: Sweet, do not scorn her so.
DEMETRIUS: If she cannot entreat, I can compel.
LYSANDER: Thou canst compel no more than she entreat:
LYSANDER: Thy threats have no more strength than her weak prayers.
LYSANDER: Helen, I love thee, by my life, I do:
LYSANDER: I swear by that which I will lose for thee,
LYSANDER: To prove him false that says I love thee not.
DEMETRIUS: I say I love thee more than he can do.
LYSANDER: If thou say so, withdraw, and prove it too.
DEMETRIUS: Quick, come!
HERMIA: Lysander, whereto tends all this?
LYSANDER: Away, you Ethiope!
DEMETRIUS: No, no, he'll [        ]
DEMETRIUS: Seem to break loose, take on as you would follow,
DEMETRIUS: But yet come not: you are a tame man, go!
LYSANDER: Hang off, thou cat, thou burr! vile thing, let loose,
LYSANDER: Or I will shake thee from me like a serpent!
HERMIA: Why are you grown so rude? what change is this?
HERMIA: Sweet love,--
LYSANDER: Thy love! out, tawny Tartar, out!
LYSANDER: Out, loathed medicine! hated potion, hence!
HERMIA: Do you not jest?
HELENA: Yes, sooth, and so do you.
LYSANDER: Demetrius, I will keep my word with thee.
DEMETRIUS: I would I had your bond, for I perceive
DEMETRIUS: A weak bond holds you: I'll not trust your word.
LYSANDER: What, should I hurt her, strike her, kill her dead?
LYSANDER: Although I hate her, I'll not harm her so.
HERMIA: What, can you do me greater harm than hate?
HERMIA: Hate me! wherefore? O me! what news, my love!
HERMIA: Am not I Hermia? are not you Lysander?
HERMIA: I am as fair now as I was erewhile.
HERMIA: Since night you loved me, yet since night you left
HERMIA: me:
HERMIA: Why, then you left me--O, the gods forbid!--
HERMIA: In earnest, shall I say?
LYSANDER: Ay, by my life,
LYSANDER: And never did desire to see thee more.
LYSANDER: Therefore be out of hope, of question, of doubt,
LYSANDER: Be certain, nothing truer, 'tis no jest
LYSANDER: That I do hate thee and love Helena.
HERMIA: O me! you juggler! you canker-blossom!
HERMIA: You thief of love! what, have you come by night
HERMIA: And stolen my love's heart from him?
HELENA: Fine, i'faith!
HELENA: Have you no modesty, no maiden shame,
HELENA: No touch of bashfulness? What, will you tear
HELENA: Impatient answers from my gentle tongue?
HELENA: Fie, fie! you counterfeit, you puppet, you!
HERMIA: Puppet? why so? ay, that way goes the game.
HERMIA: Now I perceive that she hath made compare
HERMIA: Between our statures, she hath urged her height,
HERMIA: And with her personage, her tall personage,
HERMIA: Her height, forsooth, she hath prevail'd with him.
HERMIA: And are you grown so high in his esteem,
HERMIA: Because I am so dwarfish and so low?
HERMIA: How low am I, thou painted maypole? speak,
HERMIA: How low am I? I am not yet so low
HERMIA: But that my nails can reach unto thine eyes.
HELENA: I pray you, though you mock me, gentlemen,
HELENA: Let her not hurt me: I was never curst,
HELENA: I have no gift at all in shrewishness,
HELENA: I am a right maid for my cowardice:
HELENA: Let her not strike me. You perhaps may think,
HELENA: Because she is something lower than myself,
HELENA: That I can match her.
HERMIA: Lower! hark, again.
HELENA: Good Hermia, do not be so bitter with me.
HELENA: I evermore did love you, Hermia,
HELENA: Did ever keep your counsels, never wrong'd you,
HELENA: Save that, in love unto Demetrius,
HELENA: I told him of your stealth unto this wood.
HELENA: He follow'd you, for love I follow'd him,
HELENA: But he hath chid me hence and threaten'd me
HELENA: To strike me, spurn me, nay, to kill me too:
HELENA: And now, so you will let me quiet go,
HELENA: To Athens will I bear my folly back
HELENA: And follow you no further: let me go:
HELENA: You see how simple and how fond I am.
HERMIA: Why, get you gone: who is't that hinders you?
HELENA: A foolish heart, that I leave here behind.
HERMIA: What, with Lysander?
HELENA: With Demetrius.
LYSANDER: Be not afraid, she shall not harm thee, Helena.
DEMETRIUS: No, sir, she shall not, though you take her part.
HELENA: O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd!
HELENA: She was a vixen when she went to school,
HELENA: And though she be but little, she is fierce.
HERMIA: 'Little' again! nothing but 'low' and 'little'!
HERMIA: Why will you suffer her to flout me thus?
HERMIA: Let me come to her.
LYSANDER: Get you gone, you dwarf,
LYSANDER: You minimus, of hindering knot-grass made,
LYSANDER: You bead, you acorn.
DEMETRIUS: You are too officious
DEMETRIUS: In her behalf that scorns your services.
DEMETRIUS: Let her alone: speak not of Helena,
DEMETRIUS: Take not her part, for, if thou dost intend
DEMETRIUS: Never so little show of love to her,
DEMETRIUS: Thou shalt aby it.
LYSANDER: Now she holds me not,
LYSANDER: Now follow, if thou darest, to try whose right,
LYSANDER: Of thine or mine, is most in Helena.
DEMETRIUS: Follow! nay, I'll go with thee, cheek by jole.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LYSANDER and DEMETRIUS
HERMIA: You, mistress, all this coil is 'long of you:
HERMIA: Nay, go not back.
HELENA: I will not trust you, I,
HELENA: Nor longer stay in your curst company.
HELENA: Your hands than mine are quicker for a fray,
HELENA: My legs are longer though, to run away.
NARRATOR: Exit
HERMIA: I am amazed, and know not what to say.
NARRATOR: Exit
OBERON: This is thy negligence: still thou mistakest,
OBERON: Or else committ'st thy knaveries wilfully.
PUCK: Believe me, king of shadows, I mistook.
PUCK: Did not you tell me I should know the man
PUCK: By the Athenian garment be had on?
PUCK: And so far blameless proves my enterprise,
PUCK: That I have 'nointed an Athenian's eyes,
PUCK: And so far am I glad it so did sort
PUCK: As this their jangling I esteem a sport.
OBERON: Thou see'st these lovers seek a place to fight:
OBERON: Hie therefore, Robin, overcast the night,
OBERON: The starry welkin cover thou anon
OBERON: With drooping fog as black as Acheron,
OBERON: And lead these testy rivals so astray
OBERON: As one come not within another's way.
OBERON: Like to Lysander sometime frame thy tongue,
OBERON: Then stir Demetrius up with bitter wrong,
OBERON: And sometime rail thou like Demetrius,
OBERON: And from each other look thou lead them thus,
OBERON: Till o'er their brows death-counterfeiting sleep
OBERON: With leaden legs and batty wings doth creep:
OBERON: Then crush this herb into Lysander's eye,
OBERON: Whose liquor hath this virtuous property,
OBERON: To take from thence all error with his might,
OBERON: And make his eyeballs roll with wonted sight.
OBERON: When they next wake, all this derision
OBERON: Shall seem a dream and fruitless vision,
OBERON: And back to Athens shall the lovers wend,
OBERON: With league whose date till death shall never end.
OBERON: Whiles I in this affair do thee employ,
OBERON: I'll to my queen and beg her Indian boy,
OBERON: And then I will her charmed eye release
OBERON: From monster's view, and all things shall be peace.
PUCK: My fairy lord, this must be done with haste,
PUCK: For night's swift dragons cut the clouds full fast,
PUCK: And yonder shines Aurora's harbinger,
PUCK: At whose approach, ghosts, wandering here and there,
PUCK: Troop home to churchyards: damned spirits all,
PUCK: That in crossways and floods have burial,
PUCK: Already to their wormy beds are gone,
PUCK: For fear lest day should look their shames upon,
PUCK: They willfully themselves exile from light
PUCK: And must for aye consort with black-brow'd night.
OBERON: But we are spirits of another sort:
OBERON: I with the morning's love have oft made sport,
OBERON: And, like a forester, the groves may tread,
OBERON: Even till the eastern gate, all fiery-red,
OBERON: Opening on Neptune with fair blessed beams,
OBERON: Turns into yellow gold his salt green streams.
OBERON: But, notwithstanding, haste, make no delay:
OBERON: We may effect this business yet ere day.
NARRATOR: Exit
PUCK: Up and down, up and down,
PUCK: I will lead them up and down:
PUCK: I am fear'd in field and town:
PUCK: Goblin, lead them up and down.
PUCK: Here comes one.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LYSANDER
LYSANDER: Where art thou, proud Demetrius? speak thou now.
PUCK: Here, villain, drawn and ready. Where art thou?
LYSANDER: I will be with thee straight.
PUCK: Follow me, then,
PUCK: To plainer ground.
NARRATOR: Exit LYSANDER, as following the voice
NARRATOR: Re-enter DEMETRIUS
DEMETRIUS: Lysander! speak again:
DEMETRIUS: Thou runaway, thou coward, art thou fled?
DEMETRIUS: Speak! In some bush? Where dost thou hide thy head?
PUCK: Thou coward, art thou bragging to the stars,
PUCK: Telling the bushes that thou look'st for wars,
PUCK: And wilt not come? Come, recreant, come, thou child,
PUCK: I'll whip thee with a rod: he is defiled
PUCK: That draws a sword on thee.
DEMETRIUS: Yea, art thou there?
PUCK: Follow my voice: we'll try no manhood here.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Re-enter LYSANDER
LYSANDER: He goes before me and still dares me on:
LYSANDER: When I come where he calls, then he is gone.
LYSANDER: The villain is much lighter-heel'd than I:
LYSANDER: I follow'd fast, but faster he did fly,
LYSANDER: That fallen am I in dark uneven way,
LYSANDER: And here will rest me.
NARRATOR: Lies down
LYSANDER: Come, thou gentle day!
LYSANDER: For if but once thou show me thy grey light,
LYSANDER: I'll find Demetrius and revenge this spite.
NARRATOR: Sleeps
NARRATOR: Re-enter PUCK and DEMETRIUS
PUCK: Ho, ho, ho! Coward, why comest thou not?
DEMETRIUS: Abide me, if thou darest, for well I wot
DEMETRIUS: Thou runn'st before me, shifting every place,
DEMETRIUS: And darest not stand, nor look me in the face.
DEMETRIUS: Where art thou now?
PUCK: Come hither: I am here.
DEMETRIUS: Nay, then, thou mock'st me. Thou shalt buy this dear,
DEMETRIUS: If ever I thy face by daylight see:
DEMETRIUS: Now, go thy way. Faintness constraineth me
DEMETRIUS: To measure out my length on this cold bed.
DEMETRIUS: By day's approach look to be visited.
NARRATOR: Lies down and sleeps
NARRATOR: Re-enter HELENA
HELENA: O weary night, O long and tedious night,
HELENA: Abate thy hour! Shine comforts from the east,
HELENA: That I may back to Athens by daylight,
HELENA: From these that my poor company detest:
HELENA: And sleep, that sometimes shuts up sorrow's eye,
HELENA: Steal me awhile from mine own company.
NARRATOR: Lies down and sleeps
PUCK: Yet but three? Come one more,
PUCK: Two of both kinds make up four.
PUCK: Here she comes, curst and sad:
PUCK: Cupid is a knavish lad,
PUCK: Thus to make poor females mad.
NARRATOR: Re-enter HERMIA
HERMIA: Never so weary, never so in woe,
HERMIA: Bedabbled with the dew and torn with briers,
HERMIA: I can no further crawl, no further go,
HERMIA: My legs can keep no pace with my desires.
HERMIA: Here will I rest me till the break of day.
HERMIA: Heavens shield Lysander, if they mean a fray!
NARRATOR: Lies down and sleeps
PUCK: On the ground
PUCK: Sleep sound:
PUCK: I'll apply
PUCK: To your eye,
PUCK: Gentle lover, remedy.
NARRATOR: Squeezing the juice on LYSANDER's eyes
PUCK: When thou wakest,
PUCK: Thou takest
PUCK: True delight
PUCK: In the sight
PUCK: Of thy former lady's eye:
PUCK: And the country proverb known,
PUCK: That every man should take his own,
PUCK: In your waking shall be shown:
PUCK: Jack shall have Jill,
PUCK: Nought shall go ill,
PUCK: The man shall have his mare again, and all shall be well.

NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The same. LYSANDER, DEMETRIUS, HELENA, and HERMIA
PUCK: lying asleep.
PUCK: Enter TITANIA and BOTTOM, PEASEBLOSSOM, COBWEB, MOTH,  MUSTARDSEED, and other Fairies attending, OBERON behind unseen
TITANIA: Come, sit thee down upon this flowery bed,
TITANIA: While I thy amiable cheeks do coy,
TITANIA: And stick musk-roses in thy sleek smooth head,
TITANIA: And kiss thy fair large ears, my gentle joy.
BOTTOM: Where's Peaseblossom?
PEASEBLOSSOM: Ready.
BOTTOM: Scratch my head Peaseblossom. Where's Mounsieur Cobweb?
COBWEB: Ready.
BOTTOM: Mounsieur Cobweb, good mounsieur, get you your
BOTTOM: weapons in your hand, and kill me a red-hipped
BOTTOM: humble-bee on the top of a thistle, and, good
BOTTOM: mounsieur, bring me the honey-bag. Do not fret
BOTTOM: yourself too much in the action, mounsieur, and,
BOTTOM: good mounsieur, have a care the honey-bag break not,
BOTTOM: I would be loath to have you overflown with a
BOTTOM: honey-bag, signior. Where's Mounsieur Mustardseed?
MUSTARDSEED: Ready.
BOTTOM: Give me your neaf, Mounsieur Mustardseed. Pray you,
BOTTOM: leave your courtesy, good mounsieur.
MUSTARDSEED: What's your Will?
BOTTOM: Nothing, good mounsieur, but to help Cavalery Cobweb
BOTTOM: to scratch. I must to the barber's, monsieur, for
BOTTOM: methinks I am marvellous hairy about the face, and I
BOTTOM: am such a tender ass, if my hair do but tickle me,
BOTTOM: I must scratch.
TITANIA: What, wilt thou hear some music,
TITANIA: my sweet love?
BOTTOM: I have a reasonable good ear in music. Let's have
BOTTOM: the tongs and the bones.
TITANIA: Or say, sweet love, what thou desirest to eat.
BOTTOM: Truly, a peck of provender: I could munch your good
BOTTOM: dry oats. Methinks I have a great desire to a bottle
BOTTOM: of hay: good hay, sweet hay, hath no fellow.
TITANIA: I have a venturous fairy that shall seek
TITANIA: The squirrel's hoard, and fetch thee new nuts.
BOTTOM: I had rather have a handful or two of dried peas.
BOTTOM: But, I pray you, let none of your people stir me: I
BOTTOM: have an exposition of sleep come upon me.
TITANIA: Sleep thou, and I will wind thee in my arms.
TITANIA: Fairies, begone, and be all ways away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt fairies
TITANIA: So doth the woodbine the sweet honeysuckle
TITANIA: Gently entwist, the female ivy so
TITANIA: Enrings the barky fingers of the elm.
TITANIA: O, how I love thee! how I dote on thee!
NARRATOR: They sleep
NARRATOR: Enter PUCK
OBERON: [Advancing]  Welcome, good Robin.
OBERON: See'st thou this sweet sight?
OBERON: Her dotage now I do begin to pity:
OBERON: For, meeting her of late behind the wood,
OBERON: Seeking sweet favours from this hateful fool,
OBERON: I did upbraid her and fall out with her,
OBERON: For she his hairy temples then had rounded
OBERON: With a coronet of fresh and fragrant flowers,
OBERON: And that same dew, which sometime on the buds
OBERON: Was wont to swell like round and orient pearls,
OBERON: Stood now within the pretty flowerets' eyes
OBERON: Like tears that did their own disgrace bewail.
OBERON: When I had at my pleasure taunted her
OBERON: And she in mild terms begg'd my patience,
OBERON: I then did ask of her her changeling child,
OBERON: Which straight she gave me, and her fairy sent
OBERON: To bear him to my bower in fairy land.
OBERON: And now I have the boy, I will undo
OBERON: This hateful imperfection of her eyes:
OBERON: And, gentle Puck, take this transformed scalp
OBERON: From off the head of this Athenian swain,
OBERON: That, he awaking when the other do,
OBERON: May all to Athens back again repair
OBERON: And think no more of this night's accidents
OBERON: But as the fierce vexation of a dream.
OBERON: But first I will release the fairy queen.
OBERON: Be as thou wast wont to be,
OBERON: See as thou wast wont to see:
OBERON: Dian's bud o'er Cupid's flower
OBERON: Hath such force and blessed power.
OBERON: Now, my Titania, wake you, my sweet queen.
TITANIA: My Oberon! what visions have I seen!
TITANIA: Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
OBERON: There lies your love.
TITANIA: How came these things to pass?
TITANIA: O, how mine eyes do loathe his visage now!
OBERON: Silence awhile. Robin, take off this head.
OBERON: Titania, music call, and strike more dead
OBERON: Than common sleep of all these five the sense.
TITANIA: Music, ho! music, such as charmeth sleep!
NARRATOR: Music, still
PUCK: Now, when thou wakest, with thine
PUCK: own fool's eyes peep.
OBERON: Sound, music! Come, my queen, take hands with me,
OBERON: And rock the ground whereon these sleepers be.
OBERON: Now thou and I are new in amity,
OBERON: And will to-morrow midnight solemnly
OBERON: Dance in Duke Theseus' house triumphantly,
OBERON: And bless it to all fair prosperity:
OBERON: There shall the pairs of faithful lovers be
OBERON: Wedded, with Theseus, all in jollity.
PUCK: Fairy king, attend, and mark:
PUCK: I do hear the morning lark.
OBERON: Then, my queen, in silence sad,
OBERON: Trip we after the night's shade:
OBERON: We the globe can compass soon,
OBERON: Swifter than the wandering moon.
TITANIA: Come, my lord, and in our flight
TITANIA: Tell me how it came this night
TITANIA: That I sleeping here was found
TITANIA: With these mortals on the ground.

NARRATOR: Horns winded within
NARRATOR: Enter THESEUS, HIPPOLYTA, EGEUS, and train
THESEUS: Go, one of you, find out the forester,
THESEUS: For now our observation is perform'd,
THESEUS: And since we have the vaward of the day,
THESEUS: My love shall hear the music of my hounds.

THESEUS: Dispatch, I say, and find the forester.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
THESEUS: We will, fair queen, up to the mountain's top,
THESEUS: And mark the musical confusion
THESEUS: Of hounds and echo in conjunction.
HIPPOLYTA: I was with Hercules and Cadmus once,
HIPPOLYTA: When in a wood of Crete they bay'd the bear
HIPPOLYTA: With hounds of Sparta: never did I hear
HIPPOLYTA: Such gallant chiding: for, besides the groves,
HIPPOLYTA: The skies, the fountains, every region near
HIPPOLYTA: Seem'd all one mutual cry: I never heard
HIPPOLYTA: So musical a discord, such sweet thunder.
THESEUS: My hounds are bred out of the Spartan kind,
THESEUS: So flew'd, so sanded, and their heads are hung
THESEUS: With ears that sweep away the morning dew,
THESEUS: Crook-knee'd, and dew-lapp'd like Thessalian bulls,
THESEUS: Slow in pursuit, but match'd in mouth like bells,
THESEUS: Each under each. A cry more tuneable
THESEUS: Was never holla'd to, nor cheer'd with horn,
THESEUS: In Crete, in Sparta, nor in Thessaly:
THESEUS: Judge when you hear. But, soft! what nymphs are these?
EGEUS: My lord, this is my daughter here asleep,
EGEUS: And this, Lysander, this Demetrius is,
EGEUS: This Helena, old Nedar's Helena:
EGEUS: I wonder of their being here together.
THESEUS: No doubt they rose up early to observe
THESEUS: The rite of May, and hearing our intent,
THESEUS: Came here in grace our solemnity.
THESEUS: But speak, Egeus, is not this the day
THESEUS: That Hermia should give answer of her choice?
EGEUS: It is, my lord.
THESEUS: Go, bid the huntsmen wake them with their horns.
NARRATOR: Horns and shout within. LYSANDER, DEMETRIUS, HELENA, and HERMIA wake and start up
THESEUS: Good morrow, friends. Saint Valentine is past:
THESEUS: Begin these wood-birds but to couple now?
LYSANDER: Pardon, my lord.
THESEUS: I pray you all, stand up.
THESEUS: I know you two are rival enemies:
THESEUS: How comes this gentle concord in the world,
THESEUS: That hatred is so far from jealousy,
THESEUS: To sleep by hate, and fear no enmity?
LYSANDER: My lord, I shall reply amazedly,
LYSANDER: Half sleep, half waking: but as yet, I swear,
LYSANDER: I cannot truly say how I came here,
LYSANDER: But, as I think,--for truly would I speak,
LYSANDER: And now do I bethink me, so it is,--
LYSANDER: I came with Hermia hither: our intent
LYSANDER: Was to be gone from Athens, where we might,
LYSANDER: Without the peril of the Athenian law.
EGEUS: Enough, enough, my lord, you have enough:
EGEUS: I beg the law, the law, upon his head.
EGEUS: They would have stolen away, they would, Demetrius,
EGEUS: Thereby to have defeated you and me,
EGEUS: You of your wife and me of my consent,
EGEUS: Of my consent that she should be your wife.
DEMETRIUS: My lord, fair Helen told me of their stealth,
DEMETRIUS: Of this their purpose hither to this wood,
DEMETRIUS: And I in fury hither follow'd them,
DEMETRIUS: Fair Helena in fancy following me.
DEMETRIUS: But, my good lord, I wot not by what power,--
DEMETRIUS: But by some power it is,--my love to Hermia,
DEMETRIUS: Melted as the snow, seems to me now
DEMETRIUS: As the remembrance of an idle gaud
DEMETRIUS: Which in my childhood I did dote upon,
DEMETRIUS: And all the faith, the virtue of my heart,
DEMETRIUS: The object and the pleasure of mine eye,
DEMETRIUS: Is only Helena. To her, my lord,
DEMETRIUS: Was I betroth'd ere I saw Hermia:
DEMETRIUS: But, like in sickness, did I loathe this food,
DEMETRIUS: But, as in health, come to my natural taste,
DEMETRIUS: Now I do wish it, love it, long for it,
DEMETRIUS: And will for evermore be true to it.
THESEUS: Fair lovers, you are fortunately met:
THESEUS: Of this discourse we more will hear anon.
THESEUS: Egeus, I will overbear your will,
THESEUS: For in the temple by and by with us
THESEUS: These couples shall eternally be knit:
THESEUS: And, for the morning now is something worn,
THESEUS: Our purposed hunting shall be set aside.
THESEUS: Away with us to Athens, three and three,
THESEUS: We'll hold a feast in great solemnity.
THESEUS: Come, Hippolyta.
NARRATOR: Exeunt THESEUS, HIPPOLYTA, EGEUS, and train
DEMETRIUS: These things seem small and undistinguishable,
HERMIA: Methinks I see these things with parted eye,
HERMIA: When every thing seems double.
HELENA: So methinks:
HELENA: And I have found Demetrius like a jewel,
HELENA: Mine own, and not mine own.
DEMETRIUS: Are you sure
DEMETRIUS: That we are awake? It seems to me
DEMETRIUS: That yet we sleep, we dream. Do not you think
DEMETRIUS: The duke was here, and bid us follow him?
HERMIA: Yea, and my father.
HELENA: And Hippolyta.
LYSANDER: And he did bid us follow to the temple.
DEMETRIUS: Why, then, we are awake: let's follow him
DEMETRIUS: And by the way let us recount our dreams.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
BOTTOM: [Awaking]  When my cue comes, call me, and I will
BOTTOM: answer: my next is, 'Most fair Pyramus.' Heigh-ho!
BOTTOM: Peter Quince! Flute, the bellows-mender! Snout,
BOTTOM: the tinker! Starveling! God's my life, stolen
BOTTOM: hence, and left me asleep! I have had a most rare
BOTTOM: vision. I have had a dream, past the wit of man to
BOTTOM: say what dream it was: man is but an ass, if he go
BOTTOM: about to expound this dream. Methought I was--there
BOTTOM: is no man can tell what. Methought I was,--and
BOTTOM: methought I had,--but man is but a patched fool, if
BOTTOM: he will offer to say what methought I had. The eye
BOTTOM: of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not
BOTTOM: seen, man's hand is not able to taste, his tongue
BOTTOM: to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream
BOTTOM: was. I will get Peter Quince to write a ballad of
BOTTOM: this dream: it shall be called Bottom's Dream,
BOTTOM: because it hath no bottom, and I will sing it in the
BOTTOM: latter end of a play, before the duke:
BOTTOM: peradventure, to make it the more gracious, I shall
BOTTOM: sing it at her death.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Athens. QUINCE'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter QUINCE, FLUTE, SNOUT, and STARVELING
QUINCE: Have you sent to Bottom's house ? is he come home yet?
STARVELING: He cannot be heard of. Out of doubt he is
STARVELING: transported.
FLUTE: If he come not, then the play is marred: it goes
FLUTE: not forward, doth it?
QUINCE: It is not possible: you have not a man in all
QUINCE: Athens able to discharge Pyramus but he.
FLUTE: No, he hath simply the best wit of any handicraft
FLUTE: man in Athens.
QUINCE: Yea and the best person too, and he is a very
QUINCE: paramour for a sweet voice.
FLUTE: You must say 'paragon:' a paramour is, God bless us,
FLUTE: a thing of naught.
NARRATOR: Enter SNUG
SNUG: Masters, the duke is coming from the temple, and
SNUG: there is two or three lords and ladies more married:
SNUG: if our sport had gone forward, we had all been made
SNUG: men.
FLUTE: O sweet bully Bottom! Thus hath he lost sixpence a
FLUTE: day during his life, he could not have 'scaped
FLUTE: sixpence a day: an the duke had not given him
FLUTE: sixpence a day for playing Pyramus, I'll be hanged,
FLUTE: he would have deserved it: sixpence a day in
FLUTE: Pyramus, or nothing.
NARRATOR: Enter BOTTOM
BOTTOM: Where are these lads? where are these hearts?
QUINCE: Bottom! O most courageous day! O most happy hour!
BOTTOM: Masters, I am to discourse wonders: but ask me not
BOTTOM: what, for if I tell you, I am no true Athenian. I
BOTTOM: will tell you every thing, right as it fell out.
QUINCE: Let us hear, sweet Bottom.
BOTTOM: Not a word of me. All that I will tell you is, that
BOTTOM: the duke hath dined. Get your apparel together,
BOTTOM: good strings to your beards, new ribbons to your
BOTTOM: pumps, meet presently at the palace, every man look
BOTTOM: o'er his part, for the short and the long is, our
BOTTOM: play is preferred. In any case, let Thisby have
BOTTOM: clean linen, and let not him that plays the lion
BOTTOM: pair his nails, for they shall hang out for the
BOTTOM: lion's claws. And, most dear actors, eat no onions
BOTTOM: nor garlic, for we are to utter sweet breath, and I
BOTTOM: do not doubt but to hear them say, it is a sweet
BOTTOM: comedy. No more words: away! go, away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Athens. The palace of THESEUS.
NARRATOR: Enter THESEUS, HIPPOLYTA, PHILOSTRATE, Lords and Attendants
HIPPOLYTA: 'Tis strange my Theseus, that these
HIPPOLYTA: lovers speak of.
THESEUS: More strange than true: I never may believe
THESEUS: These antique fables, nor these fairy toys.
THESEUS: Lovers and madmen have such seething brains,
THESEUS: Such shaping fantasies, that apprehend
THESEUS: More than cool reason ever comprehends.
THESEUS: The lunatic, the lover and the poet
THESEUS: Are of imagination all compact:
THESEUS: One sees more devils than vast hell can hold,
THESEUS: That is, the madman: the lover, all as frantic,
THESEUS: Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt:
THESEUS: The poet's eye, in fine frenzy rolling,
THESEUS: Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven,
THESEUS: And as imagination bodies forth
THESEUS: The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen
THESEUS: Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing
THESEUS: A local habitation and a name.
THESEUS: Such tricks hath strong imagination,
THESEUS: That if it would but apprehend some joy,
THESEUS: It comprehends some bringer of that joy,
THESEUS: Or in the night, imagining some fear,
THESEUS: How easy is a bush supposed a bear!
HIPPOLYTA: But all the story of the night told over,
HIPPOLYTA: And all their minds transfigured so together,
HIPPOLYTA: More witnesseth than fancy's images
HIPPOLYTA: And grows to something of great constancy,
HIPPOLYTA: But, howsoever, strange and admirable.
THESEUS: Here come the lovers, full of joy and mirth.
NARRATOR: Enter LYSANDER, DEMETRIUS, HERMIA, and HELENA
THESEUS: Joy, gentle friends! joy and fresh days of love
THESEUS: Accompany your hearts!
LYSANDER: More than to us
LYSANDER: Wait in your royal walks, your board, your bed!
THESEUS: Come now, what masques, what dances shall we have,
THESEUS: To wear away this long age of three hours
THESEUS: Between our after-supper and bed-time?
THESEUS: Where is our usual manager of mirth?
THESEUS: What revels are in hand? Is there no play,
THESEUS: To ease the anguish of a torturing hour?
THESEUS: Call Philostrate.
PHILOSTRATE: Here, mighty Theseus.
THESEUS: Say, what abridgement have you for this evening?
THESEUS: What masque? what music? How shall we beguile
THESEUS: The lazy time, if not with some delight?
PHILOSTRATE: There is a brief how many sports are ripe:
PHILOSTRATE: Make choice of which your highness will see first.
NARRATOR: Giving a paper
THESEUS: [Reads]  'The battle with the Centaurs, to be sung
THESEUS: By an Athenian eunuch to the harp.'
THESEUS: We'll none of that: that have I told my love,
THESEUS: In glory of my kinsman Hercules.
NARRATOR: Reads
THESEUS: 'The riot of the tipsy Bacchanals,
THESEUS: Tearing the Thracian singer in their rage.'
THESEUS: That is an old device, and it was play'd
THESEUS: When I from Thebes came last a conqueror.
NARRATOR: Reads
THESEUS: 'The thrice three Muses mourning for the death
THESEUS: Of Learning, late deceased in beggary.'
THESEUS: That is some satire, keen and critical,
THESEUS: Not sorting with a nuptial ceremony.
NARRATOR: Reads
THESEUS: 'A tedious brief scene of young Pyramus
THESEUS: And his love Thisbe, very tragical mirth.'
THESEUS: Merry and tragical! tedious and brief!
THESEUS: That is, hot ice and wondrous strange snow.
THESEUS: How shall we find the concord of this discord?
PHILOSTRATE: A play there is, my lord, some ten words long,
PHILOSTRATE: Which is as brief as I have known a play,
PHILOSTRATE: But by ten words, my lord, it is too long,
PHILOSTRATE: Which makes it tedious, for in all the play
PHILOSTRATE: There is not one word apt, one player fitted:
PHILOSTRATE: And tragical, my noble lord, it is,
PHILOSTRATE: For Pyramus therein doth kill himself.
PHILOSTRATE: Which, when I saw rehearsed, I must confess,
PHILOSTRATE: Made mine eyes water, but more merry tears
PHILOSTRATE: The passion of loud laughter never shed.
THESEUS: What are they that do play it?
PHILOSTRATE: Hard-handed men that work in Athens here,
PHILOSTRATE: Which never labour'd in their minds till now,
PHILOSTRATE: And now have toil'd their unbreathed memories
PHILOSTRATE: With this same play, against your nuptial.
THESEUS: And we will hear it.
PHILOSTRATE: No, my noble lord,
PHILOSTRATE: It is not for you: I have heard it over,
PHILOSTRATE: And it is nothing, nothing in the world,
PHILOSTRATE: Unless you can find sport in their intents,
PHILOSTRATE: Extremely stretch'd and conn'd with cruel pain,
PHILOSTRATE: To do you service.
THESEUS: I will hear that play,
THESEUS: For never anything can be amiss,
THESEUS: When simpleness and duty tender it.
THESEUS: Go, bring them in: and take your places, ladies.
NARRATOR: Exit PHILOSTRATE
HIPPOLYTA: I love not to see wretchedness o'er charged
HIPPOLYTA: And duty in his service perishing.
THESEUS: Why, gentle sweet, you shall see no such thing.
HIPPOLYTA: He says they can do nothing in this kind.
THESEUS: The kinder we, to give them thanks for nothing.
THESEUS: Our sport shall be to take what they mistake:
THESEUS: And what poor duty cannot do, noble respect
THESEUS: Takes it in might, not merit.
THESEUS: Where I have come, great clerks have purposed
THESEUS: To greet me with premeditated welcomes,
THESEUS: Where I have seen them shiver and look pale,
THESEUS: Make periods in the midst of sentences,
THESEUS: Throttle their practised accent in their fears
THESEUS: And in conclusion dumbly have broke off,
THESEUS: Not paying me a welcome. Trust me, sweet,
THESEUS: Out of this silence yet I pick'd a welcome,
THESEUS: And in the modesty of fearful duty
THESEUS: I read as much as from the rattling tongue
THESEUS: Of saucy and audacious eloquence.
THESEUS: Love, therefore, and tongue-tied simplicity
THESEUS: In least speak most, to my capacity.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PHILOSTRATE
PHILOSTRATE: So please your grace, the Prologue is address'd.
THESEUS: Let him approach.
NARRATOR: Flourish of trumpets
NARRATOR: Enter QUINCE for the Prologue
Prologue: If we offend, it is with our good will.
Prologue: That you should think, we come not to offend,
Prologue: But with good will. To show our simple skill,
Prologue: That is the true beginning of our end.
Prologue: Consider then we come but in despite.
Prologue: We do not come as minding to contest you,
Prologue: Our true intent is. All for your delight
Prologue: We are not here. That you should here repent you,
Prologue: The actors are at hand and by their show
Prologue: You shall know all that you are like to know.
THESEUS: This fellow doth not stand upon points.
LYSANDER: He hath rid his prologue like a rough colt, he knows
LYSANDER: not the stop. A good moral, my lord: it is not
LYSANDER: enough to speak, but to speak true.
HIPPOLYTA: Indeed he hath played on his prologue like a child
HIPPOLYTA: on a recorder, a sound, but not in government.
THESEUS: His speech, was like a tangled chain, nothing
THESEUS: impaired, but all disordered. Who is next?
NARRATOR: Enter Pyramus and Thisbe, Wall, Moonshine, and Lion
Prologue: Gentles, perchance you wonder at this show,
Prologue: But wonder on, till truth make all things plain.
Prologue: This man is Pyramus, if you would know,
Prologue: This beauteous lady Thisby is certain.
Prologue: This man, with lime and rough-cast, doth present
Prologue: Wall, that vile Wall which did these lovers sunder,
Prologue: And through Wall's chink, poor souls, they are content
Prologue: To whisper. At the which let no man wonder.
Prologue: This man, with lanthorn, dog, and bush of thorn,
Prologue: Presenteth Moonshine, for, if you will know,
Prologue: By moonshine did these lovers think no scorn
Prologue: To meet at Ninus' tomb, there, there to woo.
Prologue: This grisly beast, which Lion hight by name,
Prologue: The trusty Thisby, coming first by night,
Prologue: Did scare away, or rather did affright,
Prologue: And, as she fled, her mantle she did fall,
Prologue: Which Lion vile with bloody mouth did stain.
Prologue: Anon comes Pyramus, sweet youth and tall,
Prologue: And finds his trusty Thisby's mantle slain:
Prologue: Whereat, with blade, with bloody blameful blade,
Prologue: He bravely broach'd is boiling bloody breast,
Prologue: And Thisby, tarrying in mulberry shade,
Prologue: His dagger drew, and died. For all the rest,
Prologue: Let Lion, Moonshine, Wall, and lovers twain
Prologue: At large discourse, while here they do remain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Prologue, Thisbe, Lion, and Moonshine
THESEUS: I wonder if the lion be to speak.
DEMETRIUS: No wonder, my lord: one lion may, when many asses do.
Wall: In this same interlude it doth befall
Wall: That I, one Snout by name, present a wall,
Wall: And such a wall, as I would have you think,
Wall: That had in it a crannied hole or chink,
Wall: Through which the lovers, Pyramus and Thisby,
Wall: Did whisper often very secretly.
Wall: This loam, this rough-cast and this stone doth show
Wall: That I am that same wall, the truth is so:
Wall: And this the cranny is, right and sinister,
Wall: Through which the fearful lovers are to whisper.
THESEUS: Would you desire lime and hair to speak better?
DEMETRIUS: It is the wittiest partition that ever I heard
DEMETRIUS: discourse, my lord.
NARRATOR: Enter Pyramus
THESEUS: Pyramus draws near the wall: silence!
Pyramus: O grim-look'd night! O night with hue so black!
Pyramus: O night, which ever art when day is not!
Pyramus: O night, O night! alack, alack, alack,
Pyramus: I fear my Thisby's promise is forgot!
Pyramus: And thou, O wall, O sweet, O lovely wall,
Pyramus: That stand'st between her father's ground and mine!
Pyramus: Thou wall, O wall, O sweet and lovely wall,
Pyramus: Show me thy chink, to blink through with mine eyne!
NARRATOR: Wall holds up his fingers
Pyramus: Thanks, courteous wall: Jove shield thee well for this!
Pyramus: But what see I? No Thisby do I see.
Pyramus: O wicked wall, through whom I see no bliss!
Pyramus: Cursed be thy stones for thus deceiving me!
THESEUS: The wall, methinks, being sensible, should curse again.
Pyramus: No, in truth, sir, he should not. 'Deceiving me'
Pyramus: is Thisby's cue: she is to enter now, and I am to
Pyramus: spy her through the wall. You shall see, it will
Pyramus: fall pat as I told you. Yonder she comes.
NARRATOR: Enter Thisbe
Thisbe: O wall, full often hast thou heard my moans,
Thisbe: For parting my fair Pyramus and me!
Thisbe: My cherry lips have often kiss'd thy stones,
Thisbe: Thy stones with lime and hair knit up in thee.
Pyramus: I see a voice: now will I to the chink,
Pyramus: To spy an I can hear my Thisby's face. Thisby!
Thisbe: My love thou art, my love I think.
Pyramus: Think what thou wilt, I am thy lover's grace,
Pyramus: And, like Limander, am I trusty still.
Thisbe: And I like Helen, till the Fates me kill.
Pyramus: Not Shafalus to Procrus was so true.
Thisbe: As Shafalus to Procrus, I to you.
Pyramus: O kiss me through the hole of this vile wall!
Thisbe: I kiss the wall's hole, not your lips at all.
Pyramus: Wilt thou at Ninny's tomb meet me straightway?
Thisbe: 'Tide life, 'tide death, I come without delay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Pyramus and Thisbe
Wall: Thus have I, Wall, my part discharged so,
Wall: And, being done, thus Wall away doth go.
NARRATOR: Exit
THESEUS: Now is the mural down between the two neighbours.
DEMETRIUS: No remedy, my lord, when walls are so wilful to hear
DEMETRIUS: without warning.
HIPPOLYTA: This is the silliest stuff that ever I heard.
THESEUS: The best in this kind are but shadows, and the worst
THESEUS: are no worse, if imagination amend them.
HIPPOLYTA: It must be your imagination then, and not theirs.
THESEUS: If we imagine no worse of them than they of
THESEUS: themselves, they may pass for excellent men. Here
THESEUS: come two noble beasts in, a man and a lion.
NARRATOR: Enter Lion and Moonshine
Lion: You, ladies, you, whose gentle hearts do fear
Lion: The smallest monstrous mouse that creeps on floor,
Lion: May now perchance both quake and tremble here,
Lion: When lion rough in wildest rage doth roar.
Lion: Then know that I, one Snug the joiner, am
Lion: A lion-fell, nor else no lion's dam,
Lion: For, if I should as lion come in strife
Lion: Into this place, 'twere pity on my life.
THESEUS: A very gentle beast, of a good conscience.
DEMETRIUS: The very best at a beast, my lord, that e'er I saw.
LYSANDER: This lion is a very fox for his valour.
THESEUS: True, and a goose for his discretion.
DEMETRIUS: Not so, my lord, for his valour cannot carry his
DEMETRIUS: discretion, and the fox carries the goose.
THESEUS: His discretion, I am sure, cannot carry his valour,
THESEUS: for the goose carries not the fox. It is well:
THESEUS: leave it to his discretion, and let us listen to the moon.
Moonshine: This lanthorn doth the horned moon present,--
DEMETRIUS: He should have worn the horns on his head.
THESEUS: He is no crescent, and his horns are
THESEUS: invisible within the circumference.
Moonshine: This lanthorn doth the horned moon present,
Moonshine: Myself the man i' the moon do seem to be.
THESEUS: This is the greatest error of all the rest: the man
THESEUS: should be put into the lanthorn. How is it else the
THESEUS: man i' the moon?
DEMETRIUS: He dares not come there for the candle, for, you
DEMETRIUS: see, it is already in snuff.
HIPPOLYTA: I am aweary of this moon: would he would change!
THESEUS: It appears, by his small light of discretion, that
THESEUS: he is in the wane, but yet, in courtesy, in all
THESEUS: reason, we must stay the time.
LYSANDER: Proceed, Moon.
Moonshine: All that I have to say, is, to tell you that the
Moonshine: lanthorn is the moon, I, the man in the moon, this
Moonshine: thorn-bush, my thorn-bush, and this dog, my dog.
DEMETRIUS: Why, all these should be in the lanthorn, for all
DEMETRIUS: these are in the moon. But, silence! here comes Thisbe.
NARRATOR: Enter Thisbe
Thisbe: This is old Ninny's tomb. Where is my love?
Lion: [Roaring]  Oh--
NARRATOR: Thisbe runs off
DEMETRIUS: Well roared, Lion.
THESEUS: Well run, Thisbe.
HIPPOLYTA: Well shone, Moon. Truly, the moon shines with a
HIPPOLYTA: good grace.
NARRATOR: The Lion shakes Thisbe's mantle, and exit
THESEUS: Well moused, Lion.
LYSANDER: And so the lion vanished.
DEMETRIUS: And then came Pyramus.
NARRATOR: Enter Pyramus
Pyramus: Sweet Moon, I thank thee for thy sunny beams,
Pyramus: I thank thee, Moon, for shining now so bright,
Pyramus: For, by thy gracious, golden, glittering gleams,
Pyramus: I trust to take of truest Thisby sight.
Pyramus: But stay, O spite!
Pyramus: But mark, poor knight,
Pyramus: What dreadful dole is here!
Pyramus: Eyes, do you see?
Pyramus: How can it be?
Pyramus: O dainty duck! O dear!
Pyramus: Thy mantle good,
Pyramus: What, stain'd with blood!
Pyramus: Approach, ye Furies fell!
Pyramus: O Fates, come, come,
Pyramus: Cut thread and thrum,
Pyramus: Quail, crush, conclude, and quell!
THESEUS: This passion, and the death of a dear friend, would
THESEUS: go near to make a man look sad.
HIPPOLYTA: Beshrew my heart, but I pity the man.
Pyramus: O wherefore, Nature, didst thou lions frame?
Pyramus: Since lion vile hath here deflower'd my dear:
Pyramus: Which is--no, no--which was the fairest dame
Pyramus: That lived, that loved, that liked, that look'd
Pyramus: with cheer.
Pyramus: Come, tears, confound,
Pyramus: Out, sword, and wound
Pyramus: The pap of Pyramus,
Pyramus: Ay, that left pap,
Pyramus: Where heart doth hop:
NARRATOR: Stabs himself
Pyramus: Thus die I, thus, thus, thus.
Pyramus: Now am I dead,
Pyramus: Now am I fled,
Pyramus: My soul is in the sky:
Pyramus: Tongue, lose thy light,
Pyramus: Moon take thy flight:
NARRATOR: Exit Moonshine
Pyramus: Now die, die, die, die, die.
NARRATOR: Dies
DEMETRIUS: No die, but an ace, for him, for he is but one.
LYSANDER: Less than an ace, man, for he is dead, he is nothing.
THESEUS: With the help of a surgeon he might yet recover, and
THESEUS: prove an ass.
HIPPOLYTA: How chance Moonshine is gone before Thisbe comes
HIPPOLYTA: back and finds her lover?
THESEUS: She will find him by starlight. Here she comes, and
THESEUS: her passion ends the play.

THESEUS: The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve:

THESEUS: A fortnight hold we this solemnity,
THESEUS: In nightly revels and new jollity.

NARRATOR: Enter PUCK
PUCK: Now the hungry lion roars,
PUCK: And the wolf behowls the moon,
PUCK: Whilst the heavy ploughman snores,
PUCK: All with weary task fordone.
PUCK: Now the wasted brands do glow,
PUCK: Whilst the screech-owl, screeching loud,
PUCK: Puts the wretch that lies in woe
PUCK: In remembrance of a shroud.
PUCK: Now it is the time of night
PUCK: That the graves all gaping wide,
PUCK: Every one lets forth his sprite,
PUCK: In the church-way paths to glide:
PUCK: And we fairies, that do run
PUCK: By the triple Hecate's team,
PUCK: From the presence of the sun,
PUCK: Following darkness like a dream,
PUCK: Now are frolic: not a mouse
PUCK: Shall disturb this hallow'd house:
PUCK: I am sent with broom before,
PUCK: To sweep the dust behind the door.

OBERON: Every elf and fairy sprite
OBERON: Hop as light as bird from brier,
OBERON: And this ditty, after me,
OBERON: Sing, and dance it trippingly.
TITANIA: First, rehearse your song by rote
TITANIA: To each word a warbling note:
TITANIA: Hand in hand, with fairy grace,
TITANIA: Will we sing, and bless this place.

OBERON: Now, until the break of day,
OBERON: Through this house each fairy stray.

OBERON: Which by us shall blessed be,
OBERON: And the issue there create
OBERON: Ever shall be fortunate.
OBERON: So shall all the couples three
OBERON: Ever true in loving be,
OBERON: And the blots of Nature's hand

OBERON: Never mole, hare lip, nor scar,
OBERON: Nor mark prodigious, such as are
OBERON: Despised in nativity,

OBERON: And the owner of it blest

PUCK: If we shadows have offended,
PUCK: Think but this, and all is mended,
PUCK: That you have but slumber'd here
PUCK: While these visions did appear.
PUCK: And this weak and idle theme,
PUCK: No more yielding but a dream,

PUCK: if you pardon, we will mend:
PUCK: And, as I am an honest Puck,
PUCK: If we have unearned luck
PUCK: Now to 'scape the serpent's tongue,

PUCK: Else the Puck a liar call,
PUCK: So, good night unto you all.

PUCK: And Robin shall restore amends.

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Antechamber in LEONTES' palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CAMILLO and ARCHIDAMUS

ARCHIDAMUS: foot, you shall see, as I have said, great
ARCHIDAMUS: difference betwixt our Bohemia and your Sicilia.

ARCHIDAMUS: Wherein our entertainment shall shame us we will be
ARCHIDAMUS: justified in our loves, for indeed--

ARCHIDAMUS: not what to say. We will give you sleepy drinks,

ARCHIDAMUS: us.
CAMILLO: You pay a great deal too dear for what's given freely.

ARCHIDAMUS: and as mine honesty puts it to utterance.
CAMILLO: Sicilia cannot show himself over-kind to Bohemia.
CAMILLO: They were trained together in their childhoods, and
CAMILLO: there rooted betwixt them then such an affection,
CAMILLO: which cannot choose but branch now. Since their
CAMILLO: more mature dignities and royal necessities made
CAMILLO: separation of their society, their encounters,
CAMILLO: though not personal, have been royally attorneyed
CAMILLO: with interchange of gifts, letters, loving
CAMILLO: embassies, that they have seemed to be together,
CAMILLO: though absent, shook hands, as over a vast, and
CAMILLO: embraced, as it were, from the ends of opposed
CAMILLO: winds. The heavens continue their loves!
ARCHIDAMUS: I think there is not in the world either malice or
ARCHIDAMUS: matter to alter it. You have an unspeakable
ARCHIDAMUS: comfort of your young prince Mamillius: it is a
ARCHIDAMUS: gentleman of the greatest promise that ever came
ARCHIDAMUS: into my note.
CAMILLO: I very well agree with you in the hopes of him: it
CAMILLO: is a gallant child, one that indeed physics the
CAMILLO: subject, makes old hearts fresh: they that went on
CAMILLO: crutches ere he was born desire yet their life to
CAMILLO: see him a man.
ARCHIDAMUS: Would they else be content to die?
CAMILLO: Yes, if there were no other excuse why they should
CAMILLO: desire to live.
ARCHIDAMUS: If the king had no son, they would desire to live
ARCHIDAMUS: on crutches till he had one.
