LEONTES: Is whispering nothing?
LEONTES: Is leaning cheek to cheek? is meeting noses?
LEONTES: Kissing with inside lip? stopping the career
LEONTES: Of laughing with a sigh?--a note infallible
LEONTES: Of breaking honesty--horsing foot on foot?
LEONTES: Skulking in corners? wishing clocks more swift?
LEONTES: Hours, minutes? noon, midnight? and all eyes
LEONTES: Blind with the pin and web but theirs, theirs only,
LEONTES: That would unseen be wicked? is this nothing?
LEONTES: Why, then the world and all that's in't is nothing,
LEONTES: The covering sky is nothing, Bohemia nothing,
LEONTES: My wife is nothing, nor nothing have these nothings,
LEONTES: If this be nothing.
CAMILLO: Good my lord, be cured
CAMILLO: Of this diseased opinion, and betimes,
CAMILLO: For 'tis most dangerous.
LEONTES: Say it be, 'tis true.
CAMILLO: No, no, my lord.
LEONTES: It is, you lie, you lie:
LEONTES: I say thou liest, Camillo, and I hate thee,
LEONTES: Pronounce thee a gross lout, a mindless slave,
LEONTES: Or else a hovering temporizer, that
LEONTES: Canst with thine eyes at once see good and evil,
LEONTES: Inclining to them both: were my wife's liver
LEONTES: Infected as her life, she would not live
LEONTES: The running of one glass.
CAMILLO: Who does infect her?
LEONTES: Why, he that wears her like a medal, hanging
LEONTES: About his neck, Bohemia: who, if I
LEONTES: Had servants true about me, that bare eyes
LEONTES: To see alike mine honour as their profits,
LEONTES: Their own particular thrifts, they would do that
LEONTES: Which should undo more doing: ay, and thou,
LEONTES: His cupbearer,--whom I from meaner form
LEONTES: Have benched and reared to worship, who mayst see
LEONTES: Plainly as heaven sees earth and earth sees heaven,
LEONTES: How I am galled,--mightst bespice a cup,
LEONTES: To give mine enemy a lasting wink,
LEONTES: Which draught to me were cordial.
CAMILLO: Sir, my lord,
CAMILLO: I could do this, and that with no rash potion,
CAMILLO: But with a lingering dram that should not work
CAMILLO: Maliciously like poison: but I cannot
CAMILLO: Believe this crack to be in my dread mistress,
CAMILLO: So sovereignly being honourable.
CAMILLO: I have loved thee,--
LEONTES: Make that thy question, and go rot!
LEONTES: Dost think I am so muddy, so unsettled,
LEONTES: To appoint myself in this vexation, sully
LEONTES: The purity and whiteness of my sheets,
LEONTES: Which to preserve is sleep, which being spotted
LEONTES: Is goads, thorns, nettles, tails of wasps,
LEONTES: Give scandal to the blood o' the prince my son,
LEONTES: Who I do think is mine and love as mine,
LEONTES: Without ripe moving to't? Would I do this?
LEONTES: Could man so blench?
CAMILLO: I must believe you, sir:
CAMILLO: I do, and will fetch off Bohemia for't,
CAMILLO: Provided that, when he's removed, your highness
CAMILLO: Will take again your queen as yours at first,
CAMILLO: Even for your son's sake, and thereby for sealing
CAMILLO: The injury of tongues in courts and kingdoms
CAMILLO: Known and allied to yours.
LEONTES: Thou dost advise me
LEONTES: Even so as I mine own course have set down:
LEONTES: I'll give no blemish to her honour, none.
CAMILLO: My lord,
CAMILLO: Go then, and with a countenance as clear
CAMILLO: As friendship wears at feasts, keep with Bohemia
CAMILLO: And with your queen. I am his cupbearer:
CAMILLO: If from me he have wholesome beverage,
CAMILLO: Account me not your servant.
LEONTES: This is all:
LEONTES: Do't and thou hast the one half of my heart,
LEONTES: Do't not, thou split'st thine own.
CAMILLO: I'll do't, my lord.
LEONTES: I will seem friendly, as thou hast advised me.
NARRATOR: Exit
CAMILLO: O miserable lady! But, for me,
CAMILLO: What case stand I in? I must be the poisoner
CAMILLO: Of good Polixenes, and my ground to do't
CAMILLO: Is the obedience to a master, one
CAMILLO: Who in rebellion with himself will have
CAMILLO: All that are his so too. To do this deed,
CAMILLO: Promotion follows. If I could find example
CAMILLO: Of thousands that had struck anointed kings
CAMILLO: And flourish'd after, I'ld not do't, but since
CAMILLO: Nor brass nor stone nor parchment bears not one,
CAMILLO: Let villany itself forswear't. I must
CAMILLO: Forsake the court: to do't, or no, is certain
CAMILLO: To me a break-neck. Happy star, reign now!
CAMILLO: Here comes Bohemia.
NARRATOR: Re-enter POLIXENES
POLIXENES: This is strange: methinks
POLIXENES: My favour here begins to warp. Not speak?
POLIXENES: Good day, Camillo.
CAMILLO: Hail, most royal sir!
POLIXENES: What is the news i' the court?
CAMILLO: None rare, my lord.
POLIXENES: The king hath on him such a countenance
POLIXENES: As he had lost some province and a region
POLIXENES: Loved as he loves himself: even now I met him
POLIXENES: With customary compliment, when he,
POLIXENES: Wafting his eyes to the contrary and falling
POLIXENES: A lip of much contempt, speeds from me and
POLIXENES: So leaves me to consider what is breeding
POLIXENES: That changeth thus his manners.
CAMILLO: I dare not know, my lord.
POLIXENES: How! dare not! do not. Do you know, and dare not?
POLIXENES: Be intelligent to me: 'tis thereabouts,
POLIXENES: For, to yourself, what you do know, you must.
POLIXENES: And cannot say, you dare not. Good Camillo,
POLIXENES: Your changed complexions are to me a mirror
POLIXENES: Which shows me mine changed too, for I must be
POLIXENES: A party in this alteration, finding
POLIXENES: Myself thus alter'd with 't.
CAMILLO: There is a sickness
CAMILLO: Which puts some of us in distemper, but
CAMILLO: I cannot name the disease, and it is caught
CAMILLO: Of you that yet are well.
POLIXENES: How! caught of me!
POLIXENES: Make me not sighted like the basilisk:
POLIXENES: I have look'd on thousands, who have sped the better
POLIXENES: By my regard, but kill'd none so. Camillo,--
POLIXENES: As you are certainly a gentleman, thereto
POLIXENES: Clerk-like experienced, which no less adorns
POLIXENES: Our gentry than our parents' noble names,
POLIXENES: In whose success we are gentle,--I beseech you,
POLIXENES: If you know aught which does behove my knowledge
POLIXENES: Thereof to be inform'd, imprison't not
POLIXENES: In ignorant concealment.
CAMILLO: I may not answer.
POLIXENES: A sickness caught of me, and yet I well!
POLIXENES: I must be answer'd. Dost thou hear, Camillo,
POLIXENES: I conjure thee, by all the parts of man
POLIXENES: Which honour does acknowledge, whereof the least
POLIXENES: Is not this suit of mine, that thou declare
POLIXENES: What incidency thou dost guess of harm
POLIXENES: Is creeping toward me, how far off, how near,
POLIXENES: Which way to be prevented, if to be,
POLIXENES: If not, how best to bear it.
CAMILLO: Sir, I will tell you,
CAMILLO: Since I am charged in honour and by him
CAMILLO: That I think honourable: therefore mark my counsel,
CAMILLO: Which must be even as swiftly follow'd as
CAMILLO: I mean to utter it, or both yourself and me
CAMILLO: Cry lost, and so good night!
POLIXENES: On, good Camillo.
CAMILLO: I am appointed him to murder you.
POLIXENES: By whom, Camillo?
CAMILLO: By the king.
POLIXENES: For what?
CAMILLO: He thinks, nay, with all confidence he swears,
CAMILLO: As he had seen't or been an instrument
CAMILLO: To vice you to't, that you have touch'd his queen
CAMILLO: Forbiddenly.
POLIXENES: O, then my best blood turn
POLIXENES: To an infected jelly and my name
POLIXENES: Be yoked with his that did betray the Best!
POLIXENES: Turn then my freshest reputation to
POLIXENES: A savour that may strike the dullest nostril
POLIXENES: Where I arrive, and my approach be shunn'd,
POLIXENES: Nay, hated too, worse than the great'st infection
POLIXENES: That e'er was heard or read!
CAMILLO: Swear his thought over
CAMILLO: By each particular star in heaven and
CAMILLO: By all their influences, you may as well
CAMILLO: Forbid the sea for to obey the moon
CAMILLO: As or by oath remove or counsel shake
CAMILLO: The fabric of his folly, whose foundation
CAMILLO: Is piled upon his faith and will continue
CAMILLO: The standing of his body.
POLIXENES: How should this grow?
CAMILLO: I know not: but I am sure 'tis safer to
CAMILLO: Avoid what's grown than question how 'tis born.
CAMILLO: If therefore you dare trust my honesty,
CAMILLO: That lies enclosed in this trunk which you
CAMILLO: Shall bear along impawn'd, away to-night!
CAMILLO: Your followers I will whisper to the business,
CAMILLO: And will by twos and threes at several posterns
CAMILLO: Clear them o' the city. For myself, I'll put
CAMILLO: My fortunes to your service, which are here
CAMILLO: By this discovery lost. Be not uncertain,
CAMILLO: For, by the honour of my parents, I
CAMILLO: Have utter'd truth: which if you seek to prove,
CAMILLO: I dare not stand by, nor shall you be safer
CAMILLO: Than one condemn'd by the king's own mouth, thereon
CAMILLO: His execution sworn.
POLIXENES: I do believe thee:
POLIXENES: I saw his heart in 's face. Give me thy hand:
POLIXENES: Be pilot to me and thy places shall
POLIXENES: Still neighbour mine. My ships are ready and
POLIXENES: My people did expect my hence departure
POLIXENES: Two days ago. This jealousy
POLIXENES: Is for a precious creature: as she's rare,
POLIXENES: Must it be great, and as his person's mighty,
POLIXENES: Must it be violent, and as he does conceive
POLIXENES: He is dishonour'd by a man which ever
POLIXENES: Profess'd to him, why, his revenges must
POLIXENES: In that be made more bitter. Fear o'ershades me:
POLIXENES: Good expedition be my friend, and comfort
POLIXENES: The gracious queen, part of his theme, but nothing
POLIXENES: Of his ill-ta'en suspicion! Come, Camillo,
POLIXENES: I will respect thee as a father if
POLIXENES: Thou bear'st my life off hence: let us avoid.
CAMILLO: It is in mine authority to command
CAMILLO: The keys of all the posterns: please your highness
CAMILLO: To take the urgent hour. Come, sir, away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A room in LEONTES' palace.
NARRATOR: Enter HERMIONE, MAMILLIUS, and Ladies
HERMIONE: Take the boy to you: he so troubles me,
HERMIONE: 'Tis past enduring.
First Lady: Come, my gracious lord,
First Lady: Shall I be your playfellow?
MAMILLIUS: No, I'll none of you.
First Lady: Why, my sweet lord?
MAMILLIUS: You'll kiss me hard and speak to me as if
MAMILLIUS: I were a baby still. I love you better.
Second Lady: And why so, my lord?
MAMILLIUS: Not for because
MAMILLIUS: Your brows are blacker, yet black brows, they say,
MAMILLIUS: Become some women best, so that there be not
MAMILLIUS: Too much hair there, but in a semicircle
MAMILLIUS: Or a half-moon made with a pen.
Second Lady: Who taught you this?
MAMILLIUS: I learnt it out of women's faces. Pray now
MAMILLIUS: What colour are your eyebrows?
First Lady: Blue, my lord.
MAMILLIUS: Nay, that's a mock: I have seen a lady's nose
MAMILLIUS: That has been blue, but not her eyebrows.
First Lady: Hark ye,
First Lady: The queen your mother rounds apace: we shall
First Lady: Present our services to a fine new prince
First Lady: One of these days, and then you'ld wanton with us,
First Lady: If we would have you.
Second Lady: She is spread of late
Second Lady: Into a goodly bulk: good time encounter her!
HERMIONE: What wisdom stirs amongst you? Come, sir, now
HERMIONE: I am for you again: pray you, sit by us,
HERMIONE: And tell 's a tale.
MAMILLIUS: Merry or sad shall't be?
HERMIONE: As merry as you will.
MAMILLIUS: A sad tale's best for winter: I have one
MAMILLIUS: Of sprites and goblins.
HERMIONE: Let's have that, good sir.
HERMIONE: Come on, sit down: come on, and do your best
HERMIONE: To fright me with your sprites, you're powerful at it.
MAMILLIUS: There was a man--
HERMIONE: Nay, come, sit down, then on.
MAMILLIUS: Dwelt by a churchyard: I will tell it softly,
MAMILLIUS: Yond crickets shall not hear it.
HERMIONE: Come on, then,
HERMIONE: And give't me in mine ear.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONTES, with ANTIGONUS, Lords and others
LEONTES: Was he met there? his train? Camillo with him?
First Lord: Behind the tuft of pines I met them, never
First Lord: Saw I men scour so on their way: I eyed them
First Lord: Even to their ships.
LEONTES: How blest am I
LEONTES: In my just censure, in my true opinion!
LEONTES: Alack, for lesser knowledge! how accursed
LEONTES: In being so blest! There may be in the cup
LEONTES: A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart,
LEONTES: And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge
LEONTES: Is not infected: but if one present
LEONTES: The abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known
LEONTES: How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides,
LEONTES: With violent hefts. I have drunk,
LEONTES: and seen the spider.
LEONTES: Camillo was his help in this, his pander:
LEONTES: There is a plot against my life, my crown,
LEONTES: All's true that is mistrusted: that false villain
LEONTES: Whom I employ'd was pre-employ'd by him:
LEONTES: He has discover'd my design, and I
LEONTES: Remain a pinch'd thing, yea, a very trick
LEONTES: For them to play at will. How came the posterns
LEONTES: So easily open?
First Lord: By his great authority,
First Lord: Which often hath no less prevail'd than so
First Lord: On your command.
LEONTES: I know't too well.
LEONTES: Give me the boy: I am glad you did not nurse him:
LEONTES: Though he does bear some signs of me, yet you
LEONTES: Have too much blood in him.
HERMIONE: What is this? sport?
LEONTES: Bear the boy hence, he shall not come about her,
LEONTES: Away with him! and let her sport herself
LEONTES: With that she's big with, for 'tis Polixenes
LEONTES: Has made thee swell thus.
HERMIONE: But I'ld say he had not,
HERMIONE: And I'll be sworn you would believe my saying,
HERMIONE: Howe'er you lean to the nayward.
LEONTES: You, my lords,
LEONTES: Look on her, mark her well, be but about
LEONTES: To say 'she is a goodly lady,' and
LEONTES: The justice of your bearts will thereto add
LEONTES: 'Tis pity she's not honest, honourable:'
LEONTES: Praise her but for this her without-door form,
LEONTES: Which on my faith deserves high speech, and straight
LEONTES: The shrug, the hum or ha, these petty brands
LEONTES: That calumny doth use--O, I am out--
LEONTES: That mercy does, for calumny will sear
LEONTES: Virtue itself: these shrugs, these hums and ha's,
LEONTES: When you have said 'she's goodly,' come between
LEONTES: Ere you can say 'she's honest:' but be 't known,
LEONTES: From him that has most cause to grieve it should be,
LEONTES: She's an adulteress.
HERMIONE: Should a villain say so,
HERMIONE: The most replenish'd villain in the world,
HERMIONE: He were as much more villain: you, my lord,
HERMIONE: Do but mistake.
LEONTES: You have mistook, my lady,
LEONTES: Polixenes for Leontes: O thou thing!
LEONTES: Which I'll not call a creature of thy place,
LEONTES: Lest barbarism, making me the precedent,
LEONTES: Should a like language use to all degrees
LEONTES: And mannerly distinguishment leave out
LEONTES: Betwixt the prince and beggar: I have said
LEONTES: She's an adulteress, I have said with whom:
LEONTES: More, she's a traitor and Camillo is
LEONTES: A federary with her, and one that knows
LEONTES: What she should shame to know herself
LEONTES: But with her most vile principal, that she's
LEONTES: A bed-swerver, even as bad as those
LEONTES: That vulgars give bold'st titles, ay, and privy
LEONTES: To this their late escape.
HERMIONE: No, by my life.
HERMIONE: Privy to none of this. How will this grieve you,
HERMIONE: When you shall come to clearer knowledge, that
HERMIONE: You thus have publish'd me! Gentle my lord,
HERMIONE: You scarce can right me throughly then to say
HERMIONE: You did mistake.
LEONTES: No, if I mistake
LEONTES: In those foundations which I build upon,
LEONTES: The centre is not big enough to bear
LEONTES: A school-boy's top. Away with her! to prison!
LEONTES: He who shall speak for her is afar off guilty
LEONTES: But that he speaks.
HERMIONE: There's some ill planet reigns:
HERMIONE: I must be patient till the heavens look
HERMIONE: With an aspect more favourable. Good my lords,
HERMIONE: I am not prone to weeping, as our sex
HERMIONE: Commonly are, the want of which vain dew
HERMIONE: Perchance shall dry your pities: but I have
HERMIONE: That honourable grief lodged here which burns
HERMIONE: Worse than tears drown: beseech you all, my lords,
HERMIONE: With thoughts so qualified as your charities
HERMIONE: Shall best instruct you, measure me, and so
HERMIONE: The king's will be perform'd!
LEONTES: Shall I be heard?
HERMIONE: Who is't that goes with me? Beseech your highness,
HERMIONE: My women may be with me, for you see
HERMIONE: My plight requires it. Do not weep, good fools,
HERMIONE: There is no cause: when you shall know your mistress
HERMIONE: Has deserved prison, then abound in tears
HERMIONE: As I come out: this action I now go on
HERMIONE: Is for my better grace. Adieu, my lord:
HERMIONE: I never wish'd to see you sorry, now
HERMIONE: I trust I shall. My women, come, you have leave.
LEONTES: Go, do our bidding, hence!
LEONTES: Exit HERMIONE, guarded, with Ladies
First Lord: Beseech your highness, call the queen again.
ANTIGONUS: Be certain what you do, sir, lest your justice
ANTIGONUS: Prove violence, in the which three great ones suffer,
ANTIGONUS: Yourself, your queen, your son.
First Lord: For her, my lord,
First Lord: I dare my life lay down and will do't, sir,
First Lord: Please you to accept it, that the queen is spotless
First Lord: I' the eyes of heaven and to you, I mean,
First Lord: In this which you accuse her.
ANTIGONUS: If it prove
ANTIGONUS: She's otherwise, I'll keep my stables where
ANTIGONUS: I lodge my wife, I'll go in couples with her,
ANTIGONUS: Than when I feel and see her no farther trust her,
ANTIGONUS: For every inch of woman in the world,
ANTIGONUS: Ay, every dram of woman's flesh is false, If she be.
LEONTES: Hold your peaces.
First Lord: Good my lord,--
ANTIGONUS: It is for you we speak, not for ourselves:
ANTIGONUS: You are abused and by some putter-on
ANTIGONUS: That will be damn'd for't, would I knew the villain,
ANTIGONUS: I would land-damn him. Be she honour-flaw'd,
ANTIGONUS: I have three daughters, the eldest is eleven
ANTIGONUS: The second and the third, nine, and some five,
ANTIGONUS: If this prove true, they'll pay for't:
ANTIGONUS: by mine honour,
ANTIGONUS: I'll geld 'em all, fourteen they shall not see,
ANTIGONUS: To bring false generations: they are co-heirs,
ANTIGONUS: And I had rather glib myself than they
ANTIGONUS: Should not produce fair issue.
LEONTES: Cease, no more.
LEONTES: You smell this business with a sense as cold
LEONTES: As is a dead man's nose: but I do see't and feel't
LEONTES: As you feel doing thus, and see withal
LEONTES: The instruments that feel.
ANTIGONUS: If it be so,
ANTIGONUS: We need no grave to bury honesty:
ANTIGONUS: There's not a grain of it the face to sweeten
ANTIGONUS: Of the whole dungy earth.
LEONTES: What! lack I credit?
First Lord: I had rather you did lack than I, my lord,
First Lord: Upon this ground, and more it would content me
First Lord: To have her honour true than your suspicion,
First Lord: Be blamed for't how you might.
LEONTES: Why, what need we
LEONTES: Commune with you of this, but rather follow
LEONTES: Our forceful instigation? Our prerogative
LEONTES: Calls not your counsels, but our natural goodness
LEONTES: Imparts this, which if you, or stupefied
LEONTES: Or seeming so in skill, cannot or will not
LEONTES: Relish a truth like us, inform yourselves
LEONTES: We need no more of your advice: the matter,
LEONTES: The loss, the gain, the ordering on't, is all
LEONTES: Properly ours.
ANTIGONUS: And I wish, my liege,
ANTIGONUS: You had only in your silent judgment tried it,
ANTIGONUS: Without more overture.
LEONTES: How could that be?
LEONTES: Either thou art most ignorant by age,
LEONTES: Or thou wert born a fool. Camillo's flight,
LEONTES: Added to their familiarity,
LEONTES: Which was as gross as ever touch'd conjecture,
LEONTES: That lack'd sight only, nought for approbation
LEONTES: But only seeing, all other circumstances
LEONTES: Made up to the deed, doth push on this proceeding:
LEONTES: Yet, for a greater confirmation,
LEONTES: For in an act of this importance 'twere
LEONTES: Most piteous to be wild, I have dispatch'd in post
LEONTES: To sacred Delphos, to Apollo's temple,
LEONTES: Cleomenes and Dion, whom you know
LEONTES: Of stuff'd sufficiency: now from the oracle
LEONTES: They will bring all, whose spiritual counsel had,
LEONTES: Shall stop or spur me. Have I done well?
First Lord: Well done, my lord.
LEONTES: Though I am satisfied and need no more
LEONTES: Than what I know, yet shall the oracle
LEONTES: Give rest to the minds of others, such as he
LEONTES: Whose ignorant credulity will not
LEONTES: Come up to the truth. So have we thought it good
LEONTES: From our free person she should be confined,
LEONTES: Lest that the treachery of the two fled hence
LEONTES: Be left her to perform. Come, follow us,
LEONTES: We are to speak in public, for this business
LEONTES: Will raise us all.
ANTIGONUS: [Aside]
ANTIGONUS: To laughter, as I take it,
ANTIGONUS: If the good truth were known.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A prison.
NARRATOR: Enter PAULINA, a Gentleman, and Attendants
PAULINA: The keeper of the prison, call to him,
PAULINA: let him have knowledge who I am.
NARRATOR: Exit Gentleman
PAULINA: Good lady,
PAULINA: No court in Europe is too good for thee,
PAULINA: What dost thou then in prison?
NARRATOR: Re-enter Gentleman, with the Gaoler
PAULINA: Now, good sir,
PAULINA: You know me, do you not?
Gaoler: For a worthy lady
Gaoler: And one whom much I honour.
PAULINA: Pray you then,
PAULINA: Conduct me to the queen.
Gaoler: I may not, madam:
Gaoler: To the contrary I have express commandment.
PAULINA: Here's ado,
PAULINA: To lock up honesty and honour from
PAULINA: The access of gentle visitors!
PAULINA: Is't lawful, pray you,
PAULINA: To see her women? any of them? Emilia?
Gaoler: So please you, madam,
Gaoler: To put apart these your attendants, I
Gaoler: Shall bring Emilia forth.
PAULINA: I pray now, call her.
PAULINA: Withdraw yourselves.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Gentleman and Attendants
Gaoler: And, madam,
Gaoler: I must be present at your conference.
PAULINA: Well, be't so, prithee.
NARRATOR: Exit Gaoler
PAULINA: Here's such ado to make no stain a stain
PAULINA: As passes colouring.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Gaoler, with EMILIA
PAULINA: Dear gentlewoman,
PAULINA: How fares our gracious lady?
EMILIA: As well as one so great and so forlorn
EMILIA: May hold together: on her frights and griefs,
EMILIA: Which never tender lady hath born greater,
EMILIA: She is something before her time deliver'd.
PAULINA: A boy?
EMILIA: A daughter, and a goodly babe,
EMILIA: Lusty and like to live: the queen receives
EMILIA: Much comfort in't, says 'My poor prisoner,
EMILIA: I am innocent as you.'
PAULINA: I dare be sworn
PAULINA: These dangerous unsafe lunes i' the king,
PAULINA: beshrew them!
PAULINA: He must be told on't, and he shall: the office
PAULINA: Becomes a woman best, I'll take't upon me:
PAULINA: If I prove honey-mouth'd let my tongue blister
PAULINA: And never to my red-look'd anger be
PAULINA: The trumpet any more. Pray you, Emilia,
PAULINA: Commend my best obedience to the queen:
PAULINA: If she dares trust me with her little babe,
PAULINA: I'll show't the king and undertake to be
PAULINA: Her advocate to the loud'st. We do not know
PAULINA: How he may soften at the sight o' the child:
PAULINA: The silence often of pure innocence
PAULINA: Persuades when speaking fails.
EMILIA: Most worthy madam,
EMILIA: Your honour and your goodness is so evident
EMILIA: That your free undertaking cannot miss
EMILIA: A thriving issue: there is no lady living
EMILIA: So meet for this great errand. Please your ladyship
EMILIA: To visit the next room, I'll presently
EMILIA: Acquaint the queen of your most noble offer,
EMILIA: Who  but to-day hammer'd of this design,
EMILIA: But durst not tempt a minister of honour,
EMILIA: Lest she should be denied.
PAULINA: Tell her, Emilia.
PAULINA: I'll use that tongue I have: if wit flow from't
PAULINA: As boldness from my bosom, let 't not be doubted
PAULINA: I shall do good.
EMILIA: Now be you blest for it!
EMILIA: I'll to the queen: please you,
EMILIA: come something nearer.
Gaoler: Madam, if't please the queen to send the babe,
Gaoler: I know not what I shall incur to pass it,
Gaoler: Having no warrant.
PAULINA: You need not fear it, sir:
PAULINA: This child was prisoner to the womb and is
PAULINA: By law and process of great nature thence
PAULINA: Freed and enfranchised, not a party to
PAULINA: The anger of the king nor guilty of,
PAULINA: If any be, the trespass of the queen.
Gaoler: I do believe it.
PAULINA: Do not you fear: upon mine honour,
PAULINA: I will stand betwixt you and danger.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in LEONTES' palace.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONTES, ANTIGONUS, Lords, and Servants
LEONTES: Nor night nor day no rest: it is but weakness
LEONTES: To bear the matter thus, mere weakness. If
LEONTES: The cause were not in being,--part o' the cause,
LEONTES: She the adulteress, for the harlot king
LEONTES: Is quite beyond mine arm, out of the blank
LEONTES: And level of my brain, plot-proof, but she
LEONTES: I can hook to me: say that she were gone,
LEONTES: Given to the fire, a moiety of my rest
LEONTES: Might come to me again. Who's there?
First Servant: My lord?
LEONTES: How does the boy?
First Servant: He took good rest to-night,
First Servant: 'Tis hoped his sickness is discharged.
LEONTES: To see his nobleness!
LEONTES: Conceiving the dishonour of his mother,
LEONTES: He straight declined, droop'd, took it deeply,
LEONTES: Fasten'd and fix'd the shame on't in himself,
LEONTES: Threw off his spirit, his appetite, his sleep,
LEONTES: And downright languish'd. Leave me solely: go,
LEONTES: See how he fares.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
LEONTES: Fie, fie! no thought of him:
LEONTES: The thought of my revenges that way
LEONTES: Recoil upon me: in himself too mighty,
LEONTES: And in his parties, his alliance, let him be
LEONTES: Until a time may serve: for present vengeance,
LEONTES: Take it on her. Camillo and Polixenes
LEONTES: Laugh at me, make their pastime at my sorrow:
LEONTES: They should not laugh if I could reach them, nor
LEONTES: Shall she within my power.
NARRATOR: Enter PAULINA, with a child
First Lord: You must not enter.
PAULINA: Nay, rather, good my lords, be second to me:
PAULINA: Fear you his tyrannous passion more, alas,
PAULINA: Than the queen's life? a gracious innocent soul,
PAULINA: More free than he is jealous.
ANTIGONUS: That's enough.
Second Servant: Madam, he hath not slept tonight, commanded
Second Servant: None should come at him.
PAULINA: Not so hot, good sir:
PAULINA: I come to bring him sleep. 'Tis such as you,
PAULINA: That creep like shadows by him and do sigh
PAULINA: At each his needless heavings, such as you
PAULINA: Nourish the cause of his awaking: I
PAULINA: Do come with words as medicinal as true,
PAULINA: Honest as either, to purge him of that humour
PAULINA: That presses him from sleep.
LEONTES: What noise there, ho?
PAULINA: No noise, my lord, but needful conference
PAULINA: About some gossips for your highness.
LEONTES: How!
LEONTES: Away with that audacious lady! Antigonus,
LEONTES: I charged thee that she should not come about me:
LEONTES: I knew she would.
ANTIGONUS: I told her so, my lord,
ANTIGONUS: On your displeasure's peril and on mine,
ANTIGONUS: She should not visit you.
LEONTES: What, canst not rule her?
PAULINA: From all dishonesty he can: in this,
PAULINA: Unless he take the course that you have done,
PAULINA: Commit me for committing honour, trust it,
PAULINA: He shall not rule me.
ANTIGONUS: La you now, you hear:
ANTIGONUS: When she will take the rein I let her run,
ANTIGONUS: But she'll not stumble.
PAULINA: Good my liege, I come,
PAULINA: And, I beseech you, hear me, who profess
PAULINA: Myself your loyal servant, your physician,
PAULINA: Your most obedient counsellor, yet that dare
PAULINA: Less appear so in comforting your evils,
PAULINA: Than such as most seem yours: I say, I come
PAULINA: From your good queen.
LEONTES: Good queen!
PAULINA: Good queen, my lord,
PAULINA: Good queen, I say good queen,
PAULINA: And would by combat make her good, so were I
PAULINA: A man, the worst about you.
LEONTES: Force her hence.
PAULINA: Let him that makes but trifles of his eyes
PAULINA: First hand me: on mine own accord I'll off,
PAULINA: But first I'll do my errand. The good queen,
PAULINA: For she is good, hath brought you forth a daughter,
PAULINA: Here 'tis, commends it to your blessing.
NARRATOR: Laying down the child
LEONTES: Out!
LEONTES: A mankind witch! Hence with her, out o' door:
LEONTES: A most intelligencing bawd!
PAULINA: Not so:
PAULINA: I am as ignorant in that as you
PAULINA: In so entitling me, and no less honest
PAULINA: Than you are mad, which is enough, I'll warrant,
PAULINA: As this world goes, to pass for honest.
LEONTES: Traitors!
LEONTES: Will you not push her out? Give her the bastard.
LEONTES: Thou dotard! thou art woman-tired, unroosted
LEONTES: By thy dame Partlet here. Take up the bastard,
LEONTES: Take't up, I say, give't to thy crone.
PAULINA: For ever
PAULINA: Unvenerable be thy hands, if thou
PAULINA: Takest up the princess by that forced baseness
PAULINA: Which he has put upon't!
LEONTES: He dreads his wife.
PAULINA: So I would you did, then 'twere past all doubt
PAULINA: You'ld call your children yours.
LEONTES: A nest of traitors!
ANTIGONUS: I am none, by this good light.
PAULINA: Nor I, nor any
PAULINA: But one that's here, and that's himself, for he
PAULINA: The sacred honour of himself, his queen's,
PAULINA: His hopeful son's, his babe's, betrays to slander,
PAULINA: Whose sting is sharper than the sword's,
PAULINA: and will not--
PAULINA: For, as the case now stands, it is a curse
PAULINA: He cannot be compell'd to't--once remove
PAULINA: The root of his opinion, which is rotten
PAULINA: As ever oak or stone was sound.
LEONTES: A callat
LEONTES: Of boundless tongue, who late hath beat her husband
LEONTES: And now baits me! This brat is none of mine,
LEONTES: It is the issue of Polixenes:
LEONTES: Hence with it, and together with the dam
LEONTES: Commit them to the fire!
PAULINA: It is yours,
PAULINA: And, might we lay the old proverb to your charge,
PAULINA: So like you, 'tis the worse. Behold, my lords,
PAULINA: Although the print be little, the whole matter
PAULINA: And copy of the father, eye, nose, lip,
PAULINA: The trick of's frown, his forehead, nay, the valley,
PAULINA: The pretty dimples of his chin and cheek,
PAULINA: His smiles,
PAULINA: The very mould and frame of hand, nail, finger:
PAULINA: And thou, good goddess Nature, which hast made it
PAULINA: So like to him that got it, if thou hast
PAULINA: The ordering of the mind too, 'mongst all colours
PAULINA: No yellow in't, lest she suspect, as he does,
PAULINA: Her children not her husband's!
LEONTES: A gross hag
LEONTES: And, lozel, thou art worthy to be hang'd,
LEONTES: That wilt not stay her tongue.
ANTIGONUS: Hang all the husbands
ANTIGONUS: That cannot do that feat, you'll leave yourself
ANTIGONUS: Hardly one subject.
LEONTES: Once more, take her hence.
PAULINA: A most unworthy and unnatural lord
PAULINA: Can do no more.
LEONTES: I'll ha' thee burnt.
PAULINA: I care not:
PAULINA: It is an heretic that makes the fire,
PAULINA: Not she which burns in't. I'll not call you tyrant,
PAULINA: But this most cruel usage of your queen,
PAULINA: Not able to produce more accusation
PAULINA: Than your own weak-hinged fancy, something savours
PAULINA: Of tyranny and will ignoble make you,
PAULINA: Yea, scandalous to the world.
LEONTES: On your allegiance,
LEONTES: Out of the chamber with her! Were I a tyrant,
LEONTES: Where were her life? she durst not call me so,
LEONTES: If she did know me one. Away with her!
PAULINA: I pray you, do not push me, I'll be gone.
PAULINA: Look to your babe, my lord, 'tis yours:
PAULINA: Jove send her
PAULINA: A better guiding spirit! What needs these hands?
PAULINA: You, that are thus so tender o'er his follies,
PAULINA: Will never do him good, not one of you.
PAULINA: So, so: farewell, we are gone.
NARRATOR: Exit
LEONTES: Thou, traitor, hast set on thy wife to this.
LEONTES: My child? away with't! Even thou, that hast
LEONTES: A heart so tender o'er it, take it hence
LEONTES: And see it instantly consumed with fire,
LEONTES: Even thou and none but thou. Take it up straight:
LEONTES: Within this hour bring me word 'tis done,
LEONTES: And by good testimony, or I'll seize thy life,
LEONTES: With what thou else call'st thine. If thou refuse
LEONTES: And wilt encounter with my wrath, say so,
LEONTES: The bastard brains with these my proper hands
LEONTES: Shall I dash out. Go, take it to the fire,
LEONTES: For thou set'st on thy wife.
ANTIGONUS: I did not, sir:
ANTIGONUS: These lords, my noble fellows, if they please,
ANTIGONUS: Can clear me in't.
Lords: We can: my royal liege,
Lords: He is not guilty of her coming hither.
LEONTES: You're liars all.
First Lord: Beseech your highness, give us better credit:
First Lord: We have always truly served you, and beseech you
First Lord: So to esteem of us, and on our knees we beg,
First Lord: As recompense of our dear services
First Lord: Past and to come, that you do change this purpose,
First Lord: Which being so horrible, so bloody, must
First Lord: Lead on to some foul issue: we all kneel.
LEONTES: I am a feather for each wind that blows:
LEONTES: Shall I live on to see this bastard kneel
LEONTES: And call me father? better burn it now
LEONTES: Than curse it then. But be it, let it live.
LEONTES: It shall not neither. You, sir, come you hither,
LEONTES: You that have been so tenderly officious
LEONTES: With Lady Margery, your midwife there,
LEONTES: To save this bastard's life,--for 'tis a bastard,
LEONTES: So sure as this beard's grey,
LEONTES: --what will you adventure
LEONTES: To save this brat's life?
ANTIGONUS: Any thing, my lord,
ANTIGONUS: That my ability may undergo
ANTIGONUS: And nobleness impose: at least thus much:
ANTIGONUS: I'll pawn the little blood which I have left
ANTIGONUS: To save the innocent: any thing possible.
LEONTES: It shall be possible. Swear by this sword
LEONTES: Thou wilt perform my bidding.
ANTIGONUS: I will, my lord.
LEONTES: Mark and perform it, see'st thou! for the fail
LEONTES: Of any point in't shall not only be
LEONTES: Death to thyself but to thy lewd-tongued wife,
LEONTES: Whom for this time we pardon. We enjoin thee,
LEONTES: As thou art liege-man to us, that thou carry
LEONTES: This female bastard hence and that thou bear it
LEONTES: To some remote and desert place quite out
LEONTES: Of our dominions, and that there thou leave it,
LEONTES: Without more mercy, to its own protection
LEONTES: And favour of the climate. As by strange fortune
LEONTES: It came to us, I do in justice charge thee,
LEONTES: On thy soul's peril and thy body's torture,
LEONTES: That thou commend it strangely to some place
LEONTES: Where chance may nurse or end it. Take it up.
ANTIGONUS: I swear to do this, though a present death
ANTIGONUS: Had been more merciful. Come on, poor babe:
ANTIGONUS: Some powerful spirit instruct the kites and ravens
ANTIGONUS: To be thy nurses! Wolves and bears, they say
ANTIGONUS: Casting their savageness aside have done
ANTIGONUS: Like offices of pity. Sir, be prosperous
ANTIGONUS: In more than this deed does require! And blessing
ANTIGONUS: Against this cruelty fight on thy side,
ANTIGONUS: Poor thing, condemn'd to loss!
NARRATOR: Exit with the child
LEONTES: No, I'll not rear
LEONTES: Another's issue.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: Please your highness, posts
Servant: From those you sent to the oracle are come
Servant: An hour since: Cleomenes and Dion,
Servant: Being well arrived from Delphos, are both landed,
Servant: Hasting to the court.
First Lord: So please you, sir, their speed
First Lord: Hath been beyond account.
LEONTES: Twenty-three days
LEONTES: They have been absent: 'tis good speed, foretells
LEONTES: The great Apollo suddenly will have
LEONTES: The truth of this appear. Prepare you, lords,
LEONTES: Summon a session, that we may arraign
LEONTES: Our most disloyal lady, for, as she hath
LEONTES: Been publicly accused, so shall she have
LEONTES: A just and open trial. While she lives
LEONTES: My heart will be a burthen to me. Leave me,
LEONTES: And think upon my bidding.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A sea-port in Sicilia.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOMENES and DION
CLEOMENES: The climate's delicate, the air most sweet,
CLEOMENES: Fertile the isle, the temple much surpassing
CLEOMENES: The common praise it bears.
DION: I shall report,
DION: For most it caught me, the celestial habits,
DION: Methinks I so should term them, and the reverence
DION: Of the grave wearers. O, the sacrifice!
DION: How ceremonious, solemn and unearthly
DION: It was i' the offering!
CLEOMENES: But of all, the burst
CLEOMENES: And the ear-deafening voice o' the oracle,
CLEOMENES: Kin to Jove's thunder, so surprised my sense.
CLEOMENES: That I was nothing.
DION: If the event o' the journey
DION: Prove as successful to the queen,--O be't so!--
DION: As it hath been to us rare, pleasant, speedy,
DION: The time is worth the use on't.
CLEOMENES: Great Apollo
CLEOMENES: Turn all to the best! These proclamations,
CLEOMENES: So forcing faults upon Hermione,
CLEOMENES: I little like.
DION: The violent carriage of it
DION: Will clear or end the business: when the oracle,
DION: Thus by Apollo's great divine seal'd up,
DION: Shall the contents discover, something rare
DION: Even then will rush to knowledge. Go: fresh horses!
DION: And gracious be the issue!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A court of Justice.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONTES, Lords, and Officers
LEONTES: This sessions, to our great grief we pronounce,
LEONTES: Even pushes 'gainst our heart: the party tried
LEONTES: The daughter of a king, our wife, and one
LEONTES: Of us too much beloved. Let us be clear'd
LEONTES: Of being tyrannous, since we so openly
LEONTES: Proceed in justice, which shall have due course,
LEONTES: Even to the guilt or the purgation.
LEONTES: Produce the prisoner.
Officer: It is his highness' pleasure that the queen
Officer: Appear in person here in court. Silence!
Officer: Enter HERMIONE guarded, PAULINA and Ladies attending
LEONTES: Read the indictment.
Officer: [Reads]            Hermione, queen to the worthy
Officer: Leontes, king of Sicilia, thou art here accused and
Officer: arraigned of high treason, in committing adultery
Officer: with Polixenes, king of Bohemia, and conspiring
Officer: with Camillo to take away the life of our sovereign
Officer: lord the king, thy royal husband: the pretence
Officer: whereof being by circumstances partly laid open,
Officer: thou, Hermione, contrary to the faith and allegiance
Officer: of a true subject, didst counsel and aid them, for
Officer: their better safety, to fly away by night.
HERMIONE: Since what I am to say must be but that
HERMIONE: Which contradicts my accusation and
HERMIONE: The testimony on my part no other
HERMIONE: But what comes from myself, it shall scarce boot me
HERMIONE: To say 'not guilty:' mine integrity
HERMIONE: Being counted falsehood, shall, as I express it,
HERMIONE: Be so received. But thus: if powers divine
HERMIONE: Behold our human actions, as they do,
HERMIONE: I doubt not then but innocence shall make
HERMIONE: False accusation blush and tyranny
HERMIONE: Tremble at patience. You, my lord, best know,
HERMIONE: Who least will seem to do so, my past life
HERMIONE: Hath been as continent, as chaste, as true,
HERMIONE: As I am now unhappy, which is more
HERMIONE: Than history can pattern, though devised
HERMIONE: And play'd to take spectators. For behold me
HERMIONE: A fellow of the royal bed, which owe
HERMIONE: A moiety of the throne a great king's daughter,
HERMIONE: The mother to a hopeful prince, here standing
HERMIONE: To prate and talk for life and honour 'fore
HERMIONE: Who please to come and hear. For life, I prize it
HERMIONE: As I weigh grief, which I would spare: for honour,
HERMIONE: 'Tis a derivative from me to mine,
HERMIONE: And only that I stand for. I appeal
HERMIONE: To your own conscience, sir, before Polixenes
HERMIONE: Came to your court, how I was in your grace,
HERMIONE: How merited to be so, since he came,
HERMIONE: With what encounter so uncurrent I
HERMIONE: Have strain'd to appear thus: if one jot beyond
HERMIONE: The bound of honour, or in act or will
HERMIONE: That way inclining, harden'd be the hearts
HERMIONE: Of all that hear me, and my near'st of kin
HERMIONE: Cry fie upon my grave!
LEONTES: I ne'er heard yet
LEONTES: That any of these bolder vices wanted
LEONTES: Less impudence to gainsay what they did
LEONTES: Than to perform it first.
HERMIONE: That's true enough,
HERMIONE: Through 'tis a saying, sir, not due to me.
LEONTES: You will not own it.
HERMIONE: More than mistress of
HERMIONE: Which comes to me in name of fault, I must not
HERMIONE: At all acknowledge. For Polixenes,
HERMIONE: With whom I am accused, I do confess
HERMIONE: I loved him as in honour he required,
HERMIONE: With such a kind of love as might become
HERMIONE: A lady like me, with a love even such,
HERMIONE: So and no other, as yourself commanded:
HERMIONE: Which not to have done I think had been in me
HERMIONE: Both disobedience and ingratitude
HERMIONE: To you and toward your friend, whose love had spoke,
HERMIONE: Even since it could speak, from an infant, freely
HERMIONE: That it was yours. Now, for conspiracy,
HERMIONE: I know not how it tastes, though it be dish'd
HERMIONE: For me to try how: all I know of it
HERMIONE: Is that Camillo was an honest man,
HERMIONE: And why he left your court, the gods themselves,
HERMIONE: Wotting no more than I, are ignorant.
LEONTES: You knew of his departure, as you know
LEONTES: What you have underta'en to do in's absence.
HERMIONE: Sir,
HERMIONE: You speak a language that I understand not:
HERMIONE: My life stands in the level of your dreams,
HERMIONE: Which I'll lay down.
LEONTES: Your actions are my dreams,
LEONTES: You had a bastard by Polixenes,
LEONTES: And I but dream'd it. As you were past all shame,--
LEONTES: Those of your fact are so--so past all truth:
LEONTES: Which to deny concerns more than avails, for as
LEONTES: Thy brat hath been cast out, like to itself,
LEONTES: No father owning it,--which is, indeed,
LEONTES: More criminal in thee than it,--so thou
LEONTES: Shalt feel our justice, in whose easiest passage
LEONTES: Look for no less than death.
HERMIONE: Sir, spare your threats:
HERMIONE: The bug which you would fright me with I seek.
HERMIONE: To me can life be no commodity:
HERMIONE: The crown and comfort of my life, your favour,
HERMIONE: I do give lost, for I do feel it gone,
HERMIONE: But know not how it went. My second joy
HERMIONE: And first-fruits of my body, from his presence
HERMIONE: I am barr'd, like one infectious. My third comfort
HERMIONE: Starr'd most unluckily, is from my breast,
HERMIONE: The innocent milk in its most innocent mouth,
HERMIONE: Haled out to murder: myself on every post
HERMIONE: Proclaimed a strumpet: with immodest hatred
HERMIONE: The child-bed privilege denied, which 'longs
HERMIONE: To women of all fashion, lastly, hurried
HERMIONE: Here to this place, i' the open air, before
HERMIONE: I have got strength of limit. Now, my liege,
HERMIONE: Tell me what blessings I have here alive,
HERMIONE: That I should fear to die? Therefore proceed.
HERMIONE: But yet hear this: mistake me not, no life,
HERMIONE: I prize it not a straw, but for mine honour,
HERMIONE: Which I would free, if I shall be condemn'd
HERMIONE: Upon surmises, all proofs sleeping else
HERMIONE: But what your jealousies awake, I tell you
HERMIONE: 'Tis rigor and not law. Your honours all,
HERMIONE: I do refer me to the oracle:
HERMIONE: Apollo be my judge!
First Lord: This your request
First Lord: Is altogether just: therefore bring forth,
First Lord: And in Apollos name, his oracle.
NARRATOR: Exeunt certain Officers
HERMIONE: The Emperor of Russia was my father:
HERMIONE: O that he were alive, and here beholding
HERMIONE: His daughter's trial! that he did but see
HERMIONE: The flatness of my misery, yet with eyes
HERMIONE: Of pity, not revenge!
NARRATOR: Re-enter Officers, with CLEOMENES and DION
Officer: You here shall swear upon this sword of justice,
Officer: That you, Cleomenes and Dion, have
Officer: Been both at Delphos, and from thence have brought
Officer: The seal'd-up oracle, by the hand deliver'd
Officer: Of great Apollo's priest, and that, since then,
Officer: You have not dared to break the holy seal
Officer: Nor read the secrets in't.
DION: All this we swear.
LEONTES: Break up the seals and read.
Officer: [Reads]	Hermione is chaste,
Officer: Polixenes blameless, Camillo a true subject, Leontes
Officer: a jealous tyrant, his innocent babe truly begotten,
Officer: and the king shall live without an heir, if that
Officer: which is lost be not found.
Lords: Now blessed be the great Apollo!
HERMIONE: Praised!
LEONTES: Hast thou read truth?
Officer: Ay, my lord, even so
Officer: As it is here set down.
LEONTES: There is no truth at all i' the oracle:
LEONTES: The sessions shall proceed: this is mere falsehood.
NARRATOR: Enter Servant
Servant: My lord the king, the king!
LEONTES: What is the business?
Servant: O sir, I shall be hated to report it!
Servant: The prince your son, with mere conceit and fear
Servant: Of the queen's speed, is gone.
LEONTES: How! gone!
Servant: Is dead.
LEONTES: Apollo's angry, and the heavens themselves
LEONTES: Do strike at my injustice.
NARRATOR: HERMIONE swoons
LEONTES: How now there!
PAULINA: This news is mortal to the queen: look down
PAULINA: And see what death is doing.
LEONTES: Take her hence:
LEONTES: Her heart is but o'ercharged, she will recover:
LEONTES: I have too much believed mine own suspicion:
LEONTES: Beseech you, tenderly apply to her
LEONTES: Some remedies for life.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PAULINA and Ladies, with HERMIONE
LEONTES: Apollo, pardon
LEONTES: My great profaneness 'gainst thine oracle!
LEONTES: I'll reconcile me to Polixenes,
LEONTES: New woo my queen, recall the good Camillo,
LEONTES: Whom I proclaim a man of truth, of mercy,
LEONTES: For, being transported by my jealousies
LEONTES: To bloody thoughts and to revenge, I chose
LEONTES: Camillo for the minister to poison
LEONTES: My friend Polixenes: which had been done,
LEONTES: But that the good mind of Camillo tardied
LEONTES: My swift command, though I with death and with
LEONTES: Reward did threaten and encourage him,
LEONTES: Not doing 't and being done: he, most humane
LEONTES: And fill'd with honour, to my kingly guest
LEONTES: Unclasp'd my practise, quit his fortunes here,
LEONTES: Which you knew great, and to the hazard
LEONTES: Of all encertainties himself commended,
LEONTES: No richer than his honour: how he glisters
LEONTES: Thorough my rust! and how his pity
LEONTES: Does my deeds make the blacker!
NARRATOR: Re-enter PAULINA
PAULINA: Woe the while!
PAULINA: O, cut my lace, lest my heart, cracking it,
PAULINA: Break too.
First Lord: What fit is this, good lady?
PAULINA: What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me?
PAULINA: What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling?
PAULINA: In leads or oils? what old or newer torture
PAULINA: Must I receive, whose every word deserves
PAULINA: To taste of thy most worst? Thy tyranny
PAULINA: Together working with thy jealousies,
PAULINA: Fancies too weak for boys, too green and idle
PAULINA: For girls of nine, O, think what they have done
PAULINA: And then run mad indeed, stark mad! for all
PAULINA: Thy by-gone fooleries were but spices of it.
PAULINA: That thou betray'dst Polixenes,'twas nothing,
PAULINA: That did but show thee, of a fool, inconstant
PAULINA: And damnable ingrateful: nor was't much,
PAULINA: Thou wouldst have poison'd good Camillo's honour,
PAULINA: To have him kill a king: poor trespasses,
PAULINA: More monstrous standing by: whereof I reckon
PAULINA: The casting forth to crows thy baby-daughter
PAULINA: To be or none or little, though a devil
PAULINA: Would have shed water out of fire ere done't:
PAULINA: Nor is't directly laid to thee, the death
PAULINA: Of the young prince, whose honourable thoughts,
PAULINA: Thoughts high for one so tender, cleft the heart
PAULINA: That could conceive a gross and foolish sire
PAULINA: Blemish'd his gracious dam: this is not, no,
PAULINA: Laid to thy answer: but the last,--O lords,
PAULINA: When I have said, cry 'woe!' the queen, the queen,
PAULINA: The sweet'st, dear'st creature's dead,
PAULINA: and vengeance for't
PAULINA: Not dropp'd down yet.
First Lord: The higher powers forbid!
PAULINA: I say she's dead, I'll swear't. If word nor oath
PAULINA: Prevail not, go and see: if you can bring
PAULINA: Tincture or lustre in her lip, her eye,
PAULINA: Heat outwardly or breath within, I'll serve you
PAULINA: As I would do the gods. But, O thou tyrant!
PAULINA: Do not repent these things, for they are heavier
PAULINA: Than all thy woes can stir, therefore betake thee
PAULINA: To nothing but despair. A thousand knees
PAULINA: Ten thousand years together, naked, fasting,
PAULINA: Upon a barren mountain and still winter
PAULINA: In storm perpetual, could not move the gods
PAULINA: To look that way thou wert.
LEONTES: Go on, go on
LEONTES: Thou canst not speak too much, I have deserved
LEONTES: All tongues to talk their bitterest.
First Lord: Say no more:
First Lord: Howe'er the business goes, you have made fault
First Lord: I' the boldness of your speech.
PAULINA: I am sorry for't:
PAULINA: All faults I make, when I shall come to know them,
PAULINA: I do repent. Alas! I have show'd too much
PAULINA: The rashness of a woman: he is touch'd
PAULINA: To the noble heart. What's gone and what's past help
PAULINA: Should be past grief: do not receive affliction
PAULINA: At my petition, I beseech you, rather
PAULINA: Let me be punish'd, that have minded you
PAULINA: Of what you should forget. Now, good my liege
PAULINA: Sir, royal sir, forgive a foolish woman:
PAULINA: The love I bore your queen--lo, fool again!--
PAULINA: I'll speak of her no more, nor of your children,
PAULINA: I'll not remember you of my own lord,
PAULINA: Who is lost too: take your patience to you,
PAULINA: And I'll say nothing.
LEONTES: Thou didst speak but well
LEONTES: When most the truth, which I receive much better
LEONTES: Than to be pitied of thee. Prithee, bring me
LEONTES: To the dead bodies of my queen and son:
LEONTES: One grave shall be for both: upon them shall
LEONTES: The causes of their death appear, unto
LEONTES: Our shame perpetual. Once a day I'll visit
LEONTES: The chapel where they lie, and tears shed there
LEONTES: Shall be my recreation: so long as nature
LEONTES: Will bear up with this exercise, so long
LEONTES: I daily vow to use it. Come and lead me
LEONTES: Unto these sorrows.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Bohemia. A desert country near the sea.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTIGONUS with a Child, and a Mariner
ANTIGONUS: Thou art perfect then, our ship hath touch'd upon
ANTIGONUS: The deserts of Bohemia?
Mariner: Ay, my lord: and fear
Mariner: We have landed in ill time: the skies look grimly
Mariner: And threaten present blusters. In my conscience,
Mariner: The heavens with that we have in hand are angry
Mariner: And frown upon 's.
ANTIGONUS: Their sacred wills be done! Go, get aboard,
ANTIGONUS: Look to thy bark: I'll not be long before
ANTIGONUS: I call upon thee.
Mariner: Make your best haste, and go not
Mariner: Too far i' the land: 'tis like to be loud weather,
Mariner: Besides, this place is famous for the creatures
Mariner: Of prey that keep upon't.
ANTIGONUS: Go thou away:
ANTIGONUS: I'll follow instantly.
Mariner: I am glad at heart
Mariner: To be so rid o' the business.
NARRATOR: Exit
ANTIGONUS: Come, poor babe:
ANTIGONUS: I have heard, but not believed,
ANTIGONUS: the spirits o' the dead
ANTIGONUS: May walk again: if such thing be, thy mother
ANTIGONUS: Appear'd to me last night, for ne'er was dream
ANTIGONUS: So like a waking. To me comes a creature,
ANTIGONUS: Sometimes her head on one side, some another,
ANTIGONUS: I never saw a vessel of like sorrow,
ANTIGONUS: So fill'd and so becoming: in pure white robes,
ANTIGONUS: Like very sanctity, she did approach
ANTIGONUS: My cabin where I lay, thrice bow'd before me,
ANTIGONUS: And gasping to begin some speech, her eyes
ANTIGONUS: Became two spouts: the fury spent, anon
ANTIGONUS: Did this break-from her: 'Good Antigonus,
ANTIGONUS: Since fate, against thy better disposition,
ANTIGONUS: Hath made thy person for the thrower-out
ANTIGONUS: Of my poor babe, according to thine oath,
ANTIGONUS: Places remote enough are in Bohemia,
ANTIGONUS: There weep and leave it crying, and, for the babe
ANTIGONUS: Is counted lost for ever, Perdita,
ANTIGONUS: I prithee, call't. For this ungentle business
ANTIGONUS: Put on thee by my lord, thou ne'er shalt see
ANTIGONUS: Thy wife Paulina more.' And so, with shrieks
ANTIGONUS: She melted into air. Affrighted much,
ANTIGONUS: I did in time collect myself and thought
ANTIGONUS: This was so and no slumber. Dreams are toys:
ANTIGONUS: Yet for this once, yea, superstitiously,
ANTIGONUS: I will be squared by this. I do believe
ANTIGONUS: Hermione hath suffer'd death, and that
ANTIGONUS: Apollo would, this being indeed the issue
ANTIGONUS: Of King Polixenes, it should here be laid,
ANTIGONUS: Either for life or death, upon the earth
ANTIGONUS: Of its right father. Blossom, speed thee well!
ANTIGONUS: There lie, and there thy character: there these,
ANTIGONUS: Which may, if fortune please, both breed thee, pretty,
ANTIGONUS: And still rest thine. The storm begins, poor wretch,
ANTIGONUS: That for thy mother's fault art thus exposed
ANTIGONUS: To loss and what may follow! Weep I cannot,
ANTIGONUS: But my heart bleeds, and most accursed am I
ANTIGONUS: To be by oath enjoin'd to this. Farewell!
ANTIGONUS: The day frowns more and more: thou'rt like to have
ANTIGONUS: A lullaby too rough: I never saw
ANTIGONUS: The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour!
ANTIGONUS: Well may I get aboard! This is the chase:
ANTIGONUS: I am gone for ever.
NARRATOR: Exit, pursued by a bear
NARRATOR: Enter a Shepherd
Shepherd: I would there were no age between sixteen and
Shepherd: three-and-twenty, or that youth would sleep out the
Shepherd: rest, for there is nothing in the between but
Shepherd: getting wenches with child, wronging the ancientry,
Shepherd: stealing, fighting--Hark you now! Would any but
Shepherd: these boiled brains of nineteen and two-and-twenty
Shepherd: hunt this weather? They have scared away two of my
Shepherd: best sheep, which I fear the wolf will sooner find
Shepherd: than the master: if any where I have them, 'tis by
Shepherd: the seaside, browsing of ivy. Good luck, an't be thy
Shepherd: will what have we here! Mercy on 's, a barne a very
Shepherd: pretty barne! A boy or a child, I wonder? A
Shepherd: pretty one, a very pretty one: sure, some 'scape:
Shepherd: though I am not bookish, yet I can read
Shepherd: waiting-gentlewoman in the 'scape. This has been
Shepherd: some stair-work, some trunk-work, some
Shepherd: behind-door-work: they were warmer that got this
Shepherd: than the poor thing is here. I'll take it up for
Shepherd: pity: yet I'll tarry till my son come, he hallooed
Shepherd: but even now. Whoa, ho, hoa!
NARRATOR: Enter Clown
Clown: Hilloa, loa!
Shepherd: What, art so near? If thou'lt see a thing to talk
Shepherd: on when thou art dead and rotten, come hither. What
Shepherd: ailest thou, man?
Clown: I have seen two such sights, by sea and by land!
Clown: but I am not to say it is a sea, for it is now the
Clown: sky: betwixt the firmament and it you cannot thrust
Clown: a bodkin's point.
Shepherd: Why, boy, how is it?
Clown: I would you did but see how it chafes, how it rages,
Clown: how it takes up the shore! but that's not the
Clown: point. O, the most piteous cry of the poor souls!
Clown: sometimes to see 'em, and not to see 'em, now the
Clown: ship boring the moon with her main-mast, and anon
Clown: swallowed with yest and froth, as you'ld thrust a
Clown: cork into a hogshead. And then for the
Clown: land-service, to see how the bear tore out his
Clown: shoulder-bone, how he cried to me for help and said
Clown: his name was Antigonus, a nobleman. But to make an
Clown: end of the ship, to see how the sea flap-dragoned
Clown: it: but, first, how the poor souls roared, and the
Clown: sea mocked them, and how the poor gentleman roared
Clown: and the bear mocked him, both roaring louder than
Clown: the sea or weather.
Shepherd: Name of mercy, when was this, boy?
Clown: Now, now: I have not winked since I saw these
Clown: sights: the men are not yet cold under water, nor
Clown: the bear half dined on the gentleman: he's at it
Clown: now.
Shepherd: Would I had been by, to have helped the old man!
Clown: I would you had been by the ship side, to have
Clown: helped her: there your charity would have lacked footing.
Shepherd: Heavy matters! heavy matters! but look thee here,
Shepherd: boy. Now bless thyself: thou mettest with things
Shepherd: dying, I with things newborn. Here's a sight for
Shepherd: thee, look thee, a bearing-cloth for a squire's
Shepherd: child! look thee here, take up, take up, boy,
Shepherd: open't. So, let's see: it was told me I should be
Shepherd: rich by the fairies. This is some changeling:
Shepherd: open't. What's within, boy?
Clown: You're a made old man: if the sins of your youth
Clown: are forgiven you, you're well to live. Gold! all gold!
Shepherd: This is fairy gold, boy, and 'twill prove so: up
Shepherd: with't, keep it close: home, home, the next way.
Shepherd: We are lucky, boy, and to be so still requires
Shepherd: nothing but secrecy. Let my sheep go: come, good
Shepherd: boy, the next way home.
Clown: Go you the next way with your findings. I'll go see
Clown: if the bear be gone from the gentleman and how much
Clown: he hath eaten: they are never curst but when they
Clown: are hungry: if there be any of him left, I'll bury
Clown: it.
Shepherd: That's a good deed. If thou mayest discern by that
Shepherd: which is left of him what he is, fetch me to the
Shepherd: sight of him.
Clown: Marry, will I, and you shall help to put him i' the ground.
Shepherd: 'Tis a lucky day, boy, and we'll do good deeds on't.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
Shepherd: SCENE I:
NARRATOR: Enter Time, the Chorus
Time: I, that please some, try all, both joy and terror
Time: Of good and bad, that makes and unfolds error,
Time: Now take upon me, in the name of Time,
Time: To use my wings. Impute it not a crime
Time: To me or my swift passage, that I slide
Time: O'er sixteen years and leave the growth untried
Time: Of that wide gap, since it is in my power
Time: To o'erthrow law and in one self-born hour
Time: To plant and o'erwhelm custom. Let me pass
Time: The same I am, ere ancient'st order was
Time: Or what is now received: I witness to
Time: The times that brought them in, so shall I do
Time: To the freshest things now reigning and make stale
Time: The glistering of this present, as my tale
Time: Now seems to it. Your patience this allowing,
Time: I turn my glass and give my scene such growing
Time: As you had slept between: Leontes leaving,
Time: The effects of his fond jealousies so grieving
Time: That he shuts up himself, imagine me,
Time: Gentle spectators, that I now may be
Time: In fair Bohemia, and remember well,
Time: I mentioned a son o' the king's, which Florizel
Time: I now name to you, and with speed so pace
Time: To speak of Perdita, now grown in grace
Time: Equal with wondering: what of her ensues
Time: I list not prophecy, but let Time's news
Time: Be known when 'tis brought forth.
Time: A shepherd's daughter,
Time: And what to her adheres, which follows after,
Time: Is the argument of Time. Of this allow,
Time: If ever you have spent time worse ere now,
Time: If never, yet that Time himself doth say
Time: He wishes earnestly you never may.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Bohemia. The palace of POLIXENES.
NARRATOR: Enter POLIXENES and CAMILLO
POLIXENES: I pray thee, good Camillo, be no more importunate:
POLIXENES: 'tis a sickness denying thee any thing, a death to
POLIXENES: grant this.
CAMILLO: It is fifteen years since I saw my country: though
CAMILLO: I have for the most part been aired abroad, I
CAMILLO: desire to lay my bones there. Besides, the penitent
CAMILLO: king, my master, hath sent for me, to whose feeling
CAMILLO: sorrows I might be some allay, or I o'erween to
CAMILLO: think so, which is another spur to my departure.
POLIXENES: As thou lovest me, Camillo, wipe not out the rest of
POLIXENES: thy services by leaving me now: the need I have of
POLIXENES: thee thine own goodness hath made, better not to
POLIXENES: have had thee than thus to want thee: thou, having
POLIXENES: made me businesses which none without thee can
POLIXENES: sufficiently manage, must either stay to execute
POLIXENES: them thyself or take away with thee the very
POLIXENES: services thou hast done, which if I have not enough
POLIXENES: considered, as too much I cannot, to be more
POLIXENES: thankful to thee shall be my study, and my profit
POLIXENES: therein the heaping friendships. Of that fatal
POLIXENES: country, Sicilia, prithee speak no more, whose very
POLIXENES: naming punishes me with the remembrance of that
POLIXENES: penitent, as thou callest him, and reconciled king,
POLIXENES: my brother, whose loss of his most precious queen
POLIXENES: and children are even now to be afresh lamented.
POLIXENES: Say to me, when sawest thou the Prince Florizel, my
POLIXENES: son? Kings are no less unhappy, their issue not
POLIXENES: being gracious, than they are in losing them when
POLIXENES: they have approved their virtues.
CAMILLO: Sir, it is three days since I saw the prince. What
CAMILLO: his happier affairs may be, are to me unknown: but I
CAMILLO: have missingly noted, he is of late much retired
CAMILLO: from court and is less frequent to his princely
CAMILLO: exercises than formerly he hath appeared.
POLIXENES: I have considered so much, Camillo, and with some
POLIXENES: care, so far that I have eyes under my service which
POLIXENES: look upon his removedness, from whom I have this
POLIXENES: intelligence, that he is seldom from the house of a
POLIXENES: most homely shepherd, a man, they say, that from
POLIXENES: very nothing, and beyond the imagination of his
POLIXENES: neighbours, is grown into an unspeakable estate.
CAMILLO: I have heard, sir, of such a man, who hath a
CAMILLO: daughter of most rare note: the report of her is
CAMILLO: extended more than can be thought to begin from such a cottage.
POLIXENES: That's likewise part of my intelligence, but, I
POLIXENES: fear, the angle that plucks our son thither. Thou
POLIXENES: shalt accompany us to the place, where we will, not
POLIXENES: appearing what we are, have some question with the
POLIXENES: shepherd, from whose simplicity I think it not
POLIXENES: uneasy to get the cause of my son's resort thither.
POLIXENES: Prithee, be my present partner in this business, and
POLIXENES: lay aside the thoughts of Sicilia.
CAMILLO: I willingly obey your command.
POLIXENES: My best Camillo! We must disguise ourselves.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A road near the Shepherd's cottage.
NARRATOR: Enter AUTOLYCUS, singing
AUTOLYCUS: When daffodils begin to peer,
AUTOLYCUS: With heigh! the doxy over the dale,
AUTOLYCUS: Why, then comes in the sweet o' the year,
AUTOLYCUS: For the red blood reigns in the winter's pale.
AUTOLYCUS: The white sheet bleaching on the hedge,
AUTOLYCUS: With heigh! the sweet birds, O, how they sing!
AUTOLYCUS: Doth set my pugging tooth on edge,
AUTOLYCUS: For a quart of ale is a dish for a king.
AUTOLYCUS: The lark, that tirra-lyra chants,
AUTOLYCUS: With heigh! with heigh! the thrush and the jay,
AUTOLYCUS: Are summer songs for me and my aunts,
AUTOLYCUS: While we lie tumbling in the hay.
AUTOLYCUS: I have served Prince Florizel and in my time
AUTOLYCUS: wore three-pile, but now I am out of service:
AUTOLYCUS: But shall I go mourn for that, my dear?
AUTOLYCUS: The pale moon shines by night:
AUTOLYCUS: And when I wander here and there,
AUTOLYCUS: I then do most go right.
AUTOLYCUS: If tinkers may have leave to live,
AUTOLYCUS: And bear the sow-skin budget,
AUTOLYCUS: Then my account I well may, give,
AUTOLYCUS: And in the stocks avouch it.
AUTOLYCUS: My traffic is sheets, when the kite builds, look to
AUTOLYCUS: lesser linen. My father named me Autolycus, who
AUTOLYCUS: being, as I am, littered under Mercury, was likewise
AUTOLYCUS: a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles. With die and
AUTOLYCUS: drab I purchased this caparison, and my revenue is
AUTOLYCUS: the silly cheat. Gallows and knock are too powerful
AUTOLYCUS: on the highway: beating and hanging are terrors to
AUTOLYCUS: me: for the life to come, I sleep out the thought
AUTOLYCUS: of it. A prize! a prize!
NARRATOR: Enter Clown
Clown: Let me see: every 'leven wether tods, every tod
Clown: yields pound and odd shilling, fifteen hundred
Clown: shorn. what comes the wool to?
AUTOLYCUS: [Aside]
AUTOLYCUS: If the springe hold, the cock's mine.
Clown: I cannot do't without counters. Let me see, what am
Clown: I to buy for our sheep-shearing feast? Three pound
Clown: of sugar, five pound of currants, rice,--what will
Clown: this sister of mine do with rice? But my father
Clown: hath made her mistress of the feast, and she lays it
Clown: on. She hath made me four and twenty nose-gays for
Clown: the shearers, three-man-song-men all, and very good
Clown: ones, but they are most of them means and bases, but
Clown: one puritan amongst them, and he sings psalms to
Clown: horn-pipes. I must have saffron to colour the warden
Clown: pies, mace, dates?--none, that's out of my note,
Clown: nutmegs, seven, a race or two of ginger, but that I
Clown: may beg, four pound of prunes, and as many of
Clown: raisins o' the sun.
AUTOLYCUS: O that ever I was born!
NARRATOR: Grovelling on the ground
Clown: I' the name of me--
AUTOLYCUS: O, help me, help me! pluck but off these rags, and
AUTOLYCUS: then, death, death!
Clown: Alack, poor soul! thou hast need of more rags to lay
Clown: on thee, rather than have these off.
AUTOLYCUS: O sir, the loathsomeness of them offends me more
AUTOLYCUS: than the stripes I have received, which are mighty
AUTOLYCUS: ones and millions.
Clown: Alas, poor man! a million of beating may come to a
Clown: great matter.
AUTOLYCUS: I am robbed, sir, and beaten, my money and apparel
AUTOLYCUS: ta'en from me, and these detestable things put upon
AUTOLYCUS: me.
Clown: What, by a horseman, or a footman?
AUTOLYCUS: A footman, sweet sir, a footman.
Clown: Indeed, he should be a footman by the garments he
Clown: has left with thee: if this be a horseman's coat,
Clown: it hath seen very hot service. Lend me thy hand,
Clown: I'll help thee: come, lend me thy hand.
AUTOLYCUS: O, good sir, tenderly, O!
Clown: Alas, poor soul!
AUTOLYCUS: O, good sir, softly, good sir! I fear, sir, my
AUTOLYCUS: shoulder-blade is out.
Clown: How now! canst stand?
AUTOLYCUS: [Picking his pocket]
AUTOLYCUS: Softly, dear sir, good sir, softly. You ha' done me
AUTOLYCUS: a charitable office.
Clown: Dost lack any money? I have a little money for thee.
AUTOLYCUS: No, good sweet sir, no, I beseech you, sir: I have
AUTOLYCUS: a kinsman not past three quarters of a mile hence,
AUTOLYCUS: unto whom I was going, I shall there have money, or
AUTOLYCUS: any thing I want: offer me no money, I pray you,
AUTOLYCUS: that kills my heart.
Clown: What manner of fellow was he that robbed you?
AUTOLYCUS: A fellow, sir, that I have known to go about with
AUTOLYCUS: troll-my-dames, I knew him once a servant of the
AUTOLYCUS: prince: I cannot tell, good sir, for which of his
AUTOLYCUS: virtues it was, but he was certainly whipped out of the court.
Clown: His vices, you would say, there's no virtue whipped
Clown: out of the court: they cherish it to make it stay
Clown: there, and yet it will no more but abide.
AUTOLYCUS: Vices, I would say, sir. I know this man well: he
AUTOLYCUS: hath been since an ape-bearer, then a
AUTOLYCUS: process-server, a bailiff, then he compassed a
AUTOLYCUS: motion of the Prodigal Son, and married a tinker's
AUTOLYCUS: wife within a mile where my land and living lies,
AUTOLYCUS: and, having flown over many knavish professions, he
AUTOLYCUS: settled only in rogue: some call him Autolycus.
Clown: Out upon him! prig, for my life, prig: he haunts
Clown: wakes, fairs and bear-baitings.
AUTOLYCUS: Very true, sir, he, sir, he, that's the rogue that
AUTOLYCUS: put me into this apparel.
Clown: Not a more cowardly rogue in all Bohemia: if you had
Clown: but looked big and spit at him, he'ld have run.
AUTOLYCUS: I must confess to you, sir, I am no fighter: I am
AUTOLYCUS: false of heart that way, and that he knew, I warrant
AUTOLYCUS: him.
Clown: How do you now?
AUTOLYCUS: Sweet sir, much better than I was, I can stand and
AUTOLYCUS: walk: I will even take my leave of you, and pace
AUTOLYCUS: softly towards my kinsman's.
Clown: Shall I bring thee on the way?
AUTOLYCUS: No, good-faced sir, no, sweet sir.
Clown: Then fare thee well: I must go buy spices for our
Clown: sheep-shearing.
AUTOLYCUS: Prosper you, sweet sir!
NARRATOR: Exit Clown
AUTOLYCUS: Your purse is not hot enough to purchase your spice.
AUTOLYCUS: I'll be with you at your sheep-shearing too: if I
AUTOLYCUS: make not this cheat bring out another and the
AUTOLYCUS: shearers prove sheep, let me be unrolled and my name
AUTOLYCUS: put in the book of virtue!
NARRATOR: Sings
AUTOLYCUS: Jog on, jog on, the foot-path way,
AUTOLYCUS: And merrily hent the stile-a:
AUTOLYCUS: A merry heart goes all the day,
AUTOLYCUS: Your sad tires in a mile-a.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The Shepherd's cottage.
NARRATOR: Enter FLORIZEL and PERDITA
FLORIZEL: These your unusual weeds to each part of you
FLORIZEL: Do give a life: no shepherdess, but Flora
FLORIZEL: Peering in April's front. This your sheep-shearing
FLORIZEL: Is as a meeting of the petty gods,
FLORIZEL: And you the queen on't.
PERDITA: Sir, my gracious lord,
PERDITA: To chide at your extremes it not becomes me:
PERDITA: O, pardon, that I name them! Your high self,
PERDITA: The gracious mark o' the land, you have obscured
PERDITA: With a swain's wearing, and me, poor lowly maid,
PERDITA: Most goddess-like prank'd up: but that our feasts
PERDITA: In every mess have folly and the feeders
PERDITA: Digest it with a custom, I should blush
PERDITA: To see you so attired, sworn, I think,
PERDITA: To show myself a glass.
FLORIZEL: I bless the time
FLORIZEL: When my good falcon made her flight across
FLORIZEL: Thy father's ground.
PERDITA: Now Jove afford you cause!
PERDITA: To me the difference forges dread, your greatness
PERDITA: Hath not been used to fear. Even now I tremble
PERDITA: To think your father, by some accident,
PERDITA: Should pass this way as you did: O, the Fates!
PERDITA: How would he look, to see his work so noble
PERDITA: Vilely bound up? What would he say? Or how
PERDITA: Should I, in these my borrow'd flaunts, behold
PERDITA: The sternness of his presence?
FLORIZEL: Apprehend
FLORIZEL: Nothing but jollity. The gods themselves,
FLORIZEL: Humbling their deities to love, have taken
FLORIZEL: The shapes of beasts upon them: Jupiter
FLORIZEL: Became a bull, and bellow'd, the green Neptune
FLORIZEL: A ram, and bleated, and the fire-robed god,
FLORIZEL: Golden Apollo, a poor humble swain,
FLORIZEL: As I seem now. Their transformations
FLORIZEL: Were never for a piece of beauty rarer,
FLORIZEL: Nor in a way so chaste, since my desires
FLORIZEL: Run not before mine honour, nor my lusts
FLORIZEL: Burn hotter than my faith.
PERDITA: O, but, sir,
PERDITA: Your resolution cannot hold, when 'tis
PERDITA: Opposed, as it must be, by the power of the king:
PERDITA: One of these two must be necessities,
PERDITA: Which then will speak, that you must
PERDITA: change this purpose,
PERDITA: Or I my life.
FLORIZEL: Thou dearest Perdita,
FLORIZEL: With these forced thoughts, I prithee, darken not
FLORIZEL: The mirth o' the feast. Or I'll be thine, my fair,
FLORIZEL: Or not my father's. For I cannot be
FLORIZEL: Mine own, nor any thing to any, if
FLORIZEL: I be not thine. To this I am most constant,
FLORIZEL: Though destiny say no. Be merry, gentle,
FLORIZEL: Strangle such thoughts as these with any thing

FLORIZEL: Shall nothing benefit your knowledge, nor
FLORIZEL: Concern me the reporting.

CAMILLO: Or stronger for your need.
FLORIZEL: Hark, Perdita
NARRATOR: Drawing her aside

FLORIZEL: Worthy Camillo,

FLORIZEL: Hold up before him?
CAMILLO: Sent by the king your father

FLORIZEL: There is some sap in this.

AUTOLYCUS: hallowed and brought a benediction to the buyer:
AUTOLYCUS: by which means I saw whose purse was best in
AUTOLYCUS: picture, and what I saw, to my good use I
AUTOLYCUS: remembered. My clown, who wants but something to
AUTOLYCUS: be a reasonable man, grew so in love with the
AUTOLYCUS: wenches' song, that he would not stir his pettitoes
AUTOLYCUS: till he had both tune and words, which so drew the
AUTOLYCUS: rest of the herd to me that all their other senses
AUTOLYCUS: stuck in ears: you might have pinched a placket, it
AUTOLYCUS: was senseless, 'twas nothing to geld a codpiece of a
AUTOLYCUS: purse, I could have filed keys off that hung in
AUTOLYCUS: chains: no hearing, no feeling, but my sir's song,
AUTOLYCUS: and admiring the nothing of it. So that in this
AUTOLYCUS: time of lethargy I picked and cut most of their
AUTOLYCUS: festival purses, and had not the old man come in
AUTOLYCUS: with a whoo-bub against his daughter and the king's
AUTOLYCUS: son and scared my choughs from the chaff, I had not
AUTOLYCUS: left a purse alive in the whole army.
NARRATOR: CAMILLO, FLORIZEL, and PERDITA come forward
CAMILLO: Nay, but my letters, by this means being there

CAMILLO: Shall satisfy your father.

PERDITA: All that you speak shows fair.

NARRATOR: Seeing AUTOLYCUS

CAMILLO: Nothing may give us aid.

AUTOLYCUS: I am a poor fellow, sir.

Clown: have none.

AUTOLYCUS: Therefore I will not disdain.
Clown: This cannot be but a great courtier.
Shepherd: His garments are rich, but he wears
Shepherd: them not handsomely.
Clown: He seems to be the more noble in being fantastical:
Clown: a great man, I'll warrant, I know by the picking
Clown: on's teeth.
AUTOLYCUS: The fardel there? what's i' the fardel?

AUTOLYCUS: Age, thou hast lost thy labour.

AUTOLYCUS: The king is not at the palace, he is gone aboard a

Shepard: married a shepherd's daughter.

AUTOLYCUS: the curses he shall have, the tortures he shall

AUTOLYCUS: sheep-cote! all deaths are too few, the sharpest too easy.

NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A room in LEONTES' palace.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONTES, CLEOMENES, DION, PAULINA, and Servants
CLEOMENES: Sir, you have done enough, and have perform'd
CLEOMENES: A saint-like sorrow: no fault could you make,
CLEOMENES: Which you have not redeem'd, indeed, paid down
CLEOMENES: More penitence than done trespass: at the last,
CLEOMENES: Do as the heavens have done, forget your evil,
CLEOMENES: With them forgive yourself.
LEONTES: Whilst I remember
LEONTES: Her and her virtues, I cannot forget
LEONTES: My blemishes in them, and so still think of
LEONTES: The wrong I did myself, which was so much,
LEONTES: That heirless it hath made my kingdom and
LEONTES: Destroy'd the sweet'st companion that e'er man
LEONTES: Bred his hopes out of.
PAULINA: True, too true, my lord:
PAULINA: If, one by one, you wedded all the world,
PAULINA: Or from the all that are took something good,
PAULINA: To make a perfect woman, she you kill'd
PAULINA: Would be unparallel'd.
LEONTES: I think so. Kill'd!
LEONTES: She I kill'd! I did so: but thou strikest me
LEONTES: Sorely, to say I did, it is as bitter
LEONTES: Upon thy tongue as in my thought: now, good now,
LEONTES: Say so but seldom.
CLEOMENES: Not at all, good lady:
CLEOMENES: You might have spoken a thousand things that would
CLEOMENES: Have done the time more benefit and graced
CLEOMENES: Your kindness better.
PAULINA: You are one of those
PAULINA: Would have him wed again.
DION: If you would not so,
DION: You pity not the state, nor the remembrance
DION: Of his most sovereign name, consider little
DION: What dangers, by his highness' fail of issue,
DION: May drop upon his kingdom and devour
DION: Incertain lookers on. What were more holy
DION: Than to rejoice the former queen is well?
DION: What holier than, for royalty's repair,
DION: For present comfort and for future good,
DION: To bless the bed of majesty again
DION: With a sweet fellow to't?
PAULINA: There is none worthy,
PAULINA: Respecting her that's gone. Besides, the gods
PAULINA: Will have fulfill'd their secret purposes,
PAULINA: For has not the divine Apollo said,
PAULINA: Is't not the tenor of his oracle,
PAULINA: That King Leontes shall not have an heir
PAULINA: Till his lost child be found? which that it shall,
PAULINA: Is all as monstrous to our human reason
PAULINA: As my Antigonus to break his grave
PAULINA: And come again to me, who, on my life,
PAULINA: Did perish with the infant. 'Tis your counsel
PAULINA: My lord should to the heavens be contrary,
PAULINA: Oppose against their wills.
NARRATOR: To LEONTES
PAULINA: Care not for issue,
PAULINA: The crown will find an heir: great Alexander
PAULINA: Left his to the worthiest, so his successor
PAULINA: Was like to be the best.
LEONTES: Good Paulina,
LEONTES: Who hast the memory of Hermione,
LEONTES: I know, in honour, O, that ever I
LEONTES: Had squared me to thy counsel! then, even now,
LEONTES: I might have look'd upon my queen's full eyes,
LEONTES: Have taken treasure from her lips--
PAULINA: And left them
PAULINA: More rich for what they yielded.
LEONTES: Thou speak'st truth.
LEONTES: No more such wives, therefore, no wife: one worse,
LEONTES: And better used, would make her sainted spirit
LEONTES: Again possess her corpse, and on this stage,
LEONTES: Where we're offenders now, appear soul-vex'd,
LEONTES: And begin, 'Why to me?'
PAULINA: Had she such power,
PAULINA: She had just cause.
LEONTES: She had, and would incense me
LEONTES: To murder her I married.
PAULINA: I should so.
PAULINA: Were I the ghost that walk'd, I'ld bid you mark
PAULINA: Her eye, and tell me for what dull part in't
PAULINA: You chose her, then I'ld shriek, that even your ears
PAULINA: Should rift to hear me, and the words that follow'd
PAULINA: Should be 'Remember mine.'
LEONTES: Stars, stars,
LEONTES: And all eyes else dead coals! Fear thou no wife,
LEONTES: I'll have no wife, Paulina.
PAULINA: Will you swear
PAULINA: Never to marry but by my free leave?
LEONTES: Never, Paulina, so be blest my spirit!
PAULINA: Then, good my lords, bear witness to his oath.
CLEOMENES: You tempt him over-much.
PAULINA: Unless another,
PAULINA: As like Hermione as is her picture,
PAULINA: Affront his eye.
CLEOMENES: Good madam,--
PAULINA: I have done.
PAULINA: Yet, if my lord will marry,--if you will, sir,
