PAULINA: And pray your mother's blessing. Turn, good lady,
PAULINA: Our Perdita is found.
HERMIONE: You gods, look down
HERMIONE: And from your sacred vials pour your graces
HERMIONE: Upon my daughter's head! Tell me, mine own.
HERMIONE: Where hast thou been preserved? where lived? how found
HERMIONE: Thy father's court? for thou shalt hear that I,
HERMIONE: Knowing by Paulina that the oracle
HERMIONE: Gave hope thou wast in being, have preserved
HERMIONE: Myself to see the issue.
PAULINA: There's time enough for that,
PAULINA: Lest they desire upon this push to trouble
PAULINA: Your joys with like relation. Go together,
PAULINA: You precious winners all, your exultation
PAULINA: Partake to every one. I, an old turtle,
PAULINA: Will wing me to some wither'd bough and there
PAULINA: My mate, that's never to be found again,
PAULINA: Lament till I am lost.
LEONTES: O, peace, Paulina!
LEONTES: Thou shouldst a husband take by my consent,
LEONTES: As I by thine a wife: this is a match,
LEONTES: And made between's by vows. Thou hast found mine,
LEONTES: But how, is to be question'd, for I saw her,
LEONTES: As I thought, dead, and have in vain said many
LEONTES: A prayer upon her grave. I'll not seek far--
LEONTES: For him, I partly know his mind--to find thee
LEONTES: An honourable husband. Come, Camillo,
LEONTES: And take her by the hand, whose worth and honesty
LEONTES: Is richly noted and here justified
LEONTES: By us, a pair of kings. Let's from this place.
LEONTES: What! look upon my brother: both your pardons,
LEONTES: That e'er I put between your holy looks
LEONTES: My ill suspicion. This is your son-in-law,
LEONTES: And son unto the king, who, heavens directing,
LEONTES: Is troth-plight to your daughter. Good Paulina,
LEONTES: Lead us from hence, where we may leisurely
LEONTES: Each one demand an answer to his part
LEONTES: Perform'd in this wide gap of time since first
LEONTES: We were dissever'd: hastily lead away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM, the COUNTESS of Rousillon, HELENA, and LAFEU, all in black
COUNTESS: In delivering my son from me, I bury a second husband.
BERTRAM: And I in going, madam, weep o'er my father's death
BERTRAM: anew: but I must attend his majesty's command, to
BERTRAM: whom I am now in ward, evermore in subjection.
LAFEU: You shall find of the king a husband, madam, you,
LAFEU: sir, a father: he that so generally is at all times
LAFEU: good must of necessity hold his virtue to you, whose
LAFEU: worthiness would stir it up where it wanted rather
LAFEU: than lack it where there is such abundance.
COUNTESS: What hope is there of his majesty's amendment?
LAFEU: He hath abandoned his physicians, madam, under whose
LAFEU: practises he hath persecuted time with hope, and
LAFEU: finds no other advantage in the process but only the
LAFEU: losing of hope by time.
COUNTESS: This young gentlewoman had a father,--O, that
COUNTESS: 'had'! how sad a passage 'tis!--whose skill was
COUNTESS: almost as great as his honesty, had it stretched so
COUNTESS: far, would have made nature immortal, and death
COUNTESS: should have play for lack of work. Would, for the
COUNTESS: king's sake, he were living! I think it would be
COUNTESS: the death of the king's disease.
LAFEU: How called you the man you speak of, madam?
COUNTESS: He was famous, sir, in his profession, and it was
COUNTESS: his great right to be so: Gerard de Narbon.
LAFEU: He was excellent indeed, madam: the king very
LAFEU: lately spoke of him admiringly and mourningly: he
LAFEU: was skilful enough to have lived still, if knowledge
LAFEU: could be set up against mortality.
BERTRAM: What is it, my good lord, the king languishes of?
LAFEU: A fistula, my lord.
BERTRAM: I heard not of it before.
LAFEU: I would it were not notorious. Was this gentlewoman
LAFEU: the daughter of Gerard de Narbon?
COUNTESS: His sole child, my lord, and bequeathed to my
COUNTESS: overlooking. I have those hopes of her good that
COUNTESS: her education promises, her dispositions she
COUNTESS: inherits, which makes fair gifts fairer, for where
COUNTESS: an unclean mind carries virtuous qualities, there
COUNTESS: commendations go with pity, they are virtues and
COUNTESS: traitors too, in her they are the better for their
COUNTESS: simpleness, she derives her honesty and achieves her goodness.
LAFEU: Your commendations, madam, get from her tears.
COUNTESS: 'Tis the best brine a maiden can season her praise
COUNTESS: in. The remembrance of her father never approaches
COUNTESS: her heart but the tyranny of her sorrows takes all
COUNTESS: livelihood from her cheek. No more of this, Helena,
COUNTESS: go to, no more, lest it be rather thought you affect
COUNTESS: a sorrow than have it.
HELENA: I do affect a sorrow indeed, but I have it too.
LAFEU: Moderate lamentation is the right of the dead,
LAFEU: excessive grief the enemy to the living.
COUNTESS: If the living be enemy to the grief, the excess
COUNTESS: makes it soon mortal.
BERTRAM: Madam, I desire your holy wishes.
LAFEU: How understand we that?
COUNTESS: Be thou blest, Bertram, and succeed thy father
COUNTESS: In manners, as in shape! thy blood and virtue
COUNTESS: Contend for empire in thee, and thy goodness
COUNTESS: Share with thy birthright! Love all, trust a few,
COUNTESS: Do wrong to none: be able for thine enemy
COUNTESS: Rather in power than use, and keep thy friend
COUNTESS: Under thy own life's key: be cheque'd for silence,
COUNTESS: But never tax'd for speech. What heaven more will,
COUNTESS: That thee may furnish and my prayers pluck down,
COUNTESS: Fall on thy head! Farewell, my lord,
COUNTESS: 'Tis an unseason'd courtier, good my lord,
COUNTESS: Advise him.
LAFEU: He cannot want the best
LAFEU: That shall attend his love.
COUNTESS: Heaven bless him! Farewell, Bertram.
NARRATOR: Exit
BERTRAM: [To HELENA]  The best wishes that can be forged in
BERTRAM: your thoughts be servants to you! Be comfortable
BERTRAM: to my mother, your mistress, and make much of her.
LAFEU: Farewell, pretty lady: you must hold the credit of
LAFEU: your father.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BERTRAM and LAFEU
HELENA: O, were that all! I think not on my father,
HELENA: And these great tears grace his remembrance more
HELENA: Than those I shed for him. What was he like?
HELENA: I have forgot him: my imagination
HELENA: Carries no favour in't but Bertram's.
HELENA: I am undone: there is no living, none,
HELENA: If Bertram be away. 'Twere all one
HELENA: That I should love a bright particular star
HELENA: And think to wed it, he is so above me:
HELENA: In his bright radiance and collateral light
HELENA: Must I be comforted, not in his sphere.
HELENA: The ambition in my love thus plagues itself:
HELENA: The hind that would be mated by the lion
HELENA: Must die for love. 'Twas pretty, though plague,
HELENA: To see him every hour, to sit and draw
HELENA: His arched brows, his hawking eye, his curls,
HELENA: In our heart's table, heart too capable
HELENA: Of every line and trick of his sweet favour:
HELENA: But now he's gone, and my idolatrous fancy
HELENA: Must sanctify his reliques. Who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES
NARRATOR: Aside
HELENA: One that goes with him: I love him for his sake,
HELENA: And yet I know him a notorious liar,
HELENA: Think him a great way fool, solely a coward,
HELENA: Yet these fixed evils sit so fit in him,
HELENA: That they take place, when virtue's steely bones
HELENA: Look bleak i' the cold wind: withal, full oft we see
HELENA: Cold wisdom waiting on superfluous folly.
PAROLLES: Save you, fair queen!
HELENA: And you, monarch!
PAROLLES: No.
HELENA: And no.
PAROLLES: Are you meditating on virginity?
HELENA: Ay. You have some stain of soldier in you: let me
HELENA: ask you a question. Man is enemy to virginity, how
HELENA: may we barricado it against him?
PAROLLES: Keep him out.
HELENA: But he assails, and our virginity, though valiant,
HELENA: in the defence yet is weak: unfold to us some
HELENA: warlike resistance.
PAROLLES: There is none: man, sitting down before you, will
PAROLLES: undermine you and blow you up.
HELENA: Bless our poor virginity from underminers and
HELENA: blowers up! Is there no military policy, how
HELENA: virgins might blow up men?
PAROLLES: Virginity being blown down, man will quicklier be
PAROLLES: blown up: marry, in blowing him down again, with
PAROLLES: the breach yourselves made, you lose your city. It
PAROLLES: is not politic in the commonwealth of nature to
PAROLLES: preserve virginity. Loss of virginity is rational
PAROLLES: increase and there was never virgin got till
PAROLLES: virginity was first lost. That you were made of is
PAROLLES: metal to make virgins. Virginity by being once lost
PAROLLES: may be ten times found, by being ever kept, it is
PAROLLES: ever lost: 'tis too cold a companion, away with 't!
HELENA: I will stand for 't a little, though therefore I die a virgin.
PAROLLES: There's little can be said in 't, 'tis against the
PAROLLES: rule of nature. To speak on the part of virginity,
PAROLLES: is to accuse your mothers, which is most infallible
PAROLLES: disobedience. He that hangs himself is a virgin:
PAROLLES: virginity murders itself and should be buried in
PAROLLES: highways out of all sanctified limit, as a desperate
PAROLLES: offendress against nature. Virginity breeds mites,
PAROLLES: much like a cheese, consumes itself to the very
PAROLLES: paring, and so dies with feeding his own stomach.
PAROLLES: Besides, virginity is peevish, proud, idle, made of
PAROLLES: self-love, which is the most inhibited sin in the
PAROLLES: canon. Keep it not, you cannot choose but loose

PAROLLES: itself ten, which is a goodly increase, and the
PAROLLES: principal itself not much the worse: away with 't!
HELENA: How might one do, sir, to lose it to her own liking?
PAROLLES: Let me see: marry, ill, to like him that ne'er it
PAROLLES: likes. 'Tis a commodity will lose the gloss with
PAROLLES: lying, the longer kept, the less worth: off with 't
PAROLLES: while 'tis vendible, answer the time of request.
PAROLLES: Virginity, like an old courtier, wears her cap out
PAROLLES: of fashion: richly suited, but unsuitable: just
PAROLLES: like the brooch and the tooth-pick, which wear not
PAROLLES: now. Your date is better in your pie and your
PAROLLES: porridge than in your cheek, and your virginity,
PAROLLES: your old virginity, is like one of our French
PAROLLES: withered pears, it looks ill, it eats drily, marry,
PAROLLES: 'tis a withered pear, it was formerly better,
PAROLLES: marry, yet 'tis a withered pear: will you anything with it?
HELENA: Not my virginity yet [         ]
HELENA: There shall your master have a thousand loves,
HELENA: A mother and a mistress and a friend,
HELENA: A phoenix, captain and an enemy,
HELENA: A guide, a goddess, and a sovereign,
HELENA: A counsellor, a traitress, and a dear,

HELENA: His jarring concord, and his discord dulcet,

HELENA: That blinking Cupid gossips. Now shall he--
HELENA: I know not what he shall. God send him well!
HELENA: The court's a learning place, and he is one--
PAROLLES: What one, i' faith?
HELENA: That I wish well. 'Tis pity--
PAROLLES: What's pity?
HELENA: That wishing well had not a body in't,
HELENA: Which might be felt, that we, the poorer born,
HELENA: Whose baser stars do shut us up in wishes,
HELENA: Might with effects of them follow our friends,
HELENA: And show what we alone must think, which never
HELENA: Return us thanks.

PAROLLES: Little Helen, farewell, if I can remember thee, I
PAROLLES: will think of thee at court.
HELENA: Monsieur Parolles, you were born under a charitable star.
PAROLLES: Under Mars, I.
HELENA: I especially think, under Mars.
PAROLLES: Why under Mars?
HELENA: The wars have so kept you under that you must needs
HELENA: be born under Mars.
PAROLLES: When he was predominant.
HELENA: When he was retrograde, I think, rather.
PAROLLES: Why think you so?
HELENA: You go so much backward when you fight.
PAROLLES: That's for advantage.
HELENA: So is running away, when fear proposes the safety,
HELENA: but the composition that your valour and fear makes

PAROLLES: thee, so thou wilt be capable of a courtier's

HELENA: Our remedies oft in ourselves do lie,
HELENA: Which we ascribe to heaven: the fated sky
HELENA: Gives us free scope, only doth backward pull
HELENA: Our slow designs when we ourselves are dull.
HELENA: What power is it which mounts my love so high,

HELENA: The mightiest space in fortune nature brings

NARRATOR: SCENE II. Paris. The KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Enter the KING of France, with letters, and divers Attendants
KING: The Florentines and Senoys are by the ears,
KING: Have fought with equal fortune and continue
KING: A braving war.
First Lord: So 'tis reported, sir.
KING: Nay, 'tis most credible, we here received it
KING: A certainty, vouch'd from our cousin Austria,
KING: With caution that the Florentine will move us
KING: For speedy aid, wherein our dearest friend
KING: Prejudicates the business and would seem
KING: To have us make denial.
First Lord: His love and wisdom,
First Lord: Approved so to your majesty, may plead
First Lord: For amplest credence.
KING: He hath arm'd our answer,
KING: And Florence is denied before he comes:
KING: Yet, for our gentlemen that mean to see
KING: The Tuscan service, freely have they leave
KING: To stand on either part.
Second Lord: It well may serve
Second Lord: A nursery to our gentry, who are sick
Second Lord: For breathing and exploit.
KING: What's he comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM, LAFEU, and PAROLLES
First Lord: It is the Count Rousillon, my good lord,
First Lord: Young Bertram.
KING: Youth, thou bear'st thy father's face,
KING: Frank nature, rather curious than in haste,
KING: Hath well composed thee. Thy father's moral parts
KING: Mayst thou inherit too! Welcome to Paris.
BERTRAM: My thanks and duty are your majesty's.
KING: I would I had that corporal soundness now,
KING: As when thy father and myself in friendship
KING: First tried our soldiership! He did look far
KING: Into the service of the time and was
KING: Discipled of the bravest: he lasted long,
KING: But on us both did haggish age steal on
KING: And wore us out of act. It much repairs me
KING: To talk of your good father. In his youth
KING: He had the wit which I can well observe
KING: To-day in our young lords, but they may jest
KING: Till their own scorn return to them unnoted
KING: Ere they can hide their levity in honour,
KING: So like a courtier, contempt nor bitterness
KING: Were in his pride or sharpness, if they were,
KING: His equal had awaked them, and his honour,
KING: Clock to itself, knew the true minute when
KING: Exception bid him speak, and at this time
KING: His tongue obey'd his hand: who were below him
KING: He used as creatures of another place
KING: And bow'd his eminent top to their low ranks,
KING: Making them proud of his humility,
KING: In their poor praise he humbled. Such a man
KING: Might be a copy to these younger times,
KING: Which, follow'd well, would demonstrate them now
KING: But goers backward.
BERTRAM: His good remembrance, sir,
BERTRAM: Lies richer in your thoughts than on his tomb,
BERTRAM: So in approof lives not his epitaph
BERTRAM: As in your royal speech.
KING: Would I were with him! He would always say--
KING: Methinks I hear him now, his plausive words
KING: He scatter'd not in ears, but grafted them,
KING: To grow there and to bear,--'Let me not live,'--
KING: This his good melancholy oft began,
KING: On the catastrophe and heel of pastime,
KING: When it was out,--'Let me not live,' quoth he,
KING: 'After my flame lacks oil, to be the snuff
KING: Of younger spirits, whose apprehensive senses
KING: All but new things disdain, whose judgments are
KING: Mere fathers of their garments, whose constancies
KING: Expire before their fashions.' This he wish'd,
KING: I after him do after him wish too,
KING: Since I nor wax nor honey can bring home,
KING: I quickly were dissolved from my hive,
KING: To give some labourers room.
Second Lord: You are loved, sir:
Second Lord: They that least lend it you shall lack you first.
KING: I fill a place, I know't. How long is't, count,
KING: Since the physician at your father's died?
KING: He was much famed.
BERTRAM: Some six months since, my lord.
KING: If he were living, I would try him yet.
KING: Lend me an arm, the rest have worn me out
KING: With several applications, nature and sickness
KING: Debate it at their leisure. Welcome, count,
KING: My son's no dearer.
BERTRAM: Thank your majesty.

NARRATOR: SCENE III. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter COUNTESS, Steward, and Clown
COUNTESS: I will now hear, what say you of this gentlewoman?
Steward: Madam, the care I have had to even your content, I
Steward: wish might be found in the calendar of my past
Steward: endeavours, for then we wound our modesty and make
Steward: foul the clearness of our deservings, when of
Steward: ourselves we publish them.

COUNTESS: the complaints I have heard of you I do not all
COUNTESS: believe: 'tis my slowness that I do not, for I know
COUNTESS: you lack not folly to commit them, and have ability
COUNTESS: enough to make such knaveries yours.
Clown: 'Tis not unknown to you, madam, I am a poor fellow.
COUNTESS: Well, sir.
Clown: No, madam, 'tis not so well that I am poor, though
Clown: many of the rich are damned: but, if I may have
Clown: your ladyship's good will to go to the world, Isbel
Clown: the woman and I will do as we may.
COUNTESS: Wilt thou needs be a beggar?
Clown: I do beg your good will in this case.
COUNTESS: In what case?
Clown: In Isbel's case and mine own. Service is no
Clown: heritage: and I think I shall never have the
Clown: blessing of God till I have issue o' my body, for
Clown: they say barnes are blessings.
COUNTESS: Tell me thy reason why thou wilt marry.
Clown: My poor body, madam, requires it: I am driven on
Clown: by the flesh, and he must needs go that the devil drives.
COUNTESS: Is this all your worship's reason?
Clown: Faith, madam, I have other holy reasons such as they
Clown: are.
COUNTESS: May the world know them?
Clown: I have been, madam, a wicked creature, as you and
Clown: all flesh and blood are, and, indeed, I do marry
Clown: that I may repent.
COUNTESS: Thy marriage, sooner than thy wickedness.
Clown: I am out o' friends, madam, and I hope to have
Clown: friends for my wife's sake.
COUNTESS: Such friends are thine enemies, knave.
Clown: You're shallow, madam, in great friends, for the
Clown: knaves come to do that for me which I am aweary of.
Clown: He that ears my land spares my team and gives me
Clown: leave to in the crop, if I be his cuckold, he's my
Clown: drudge: he that comforts my wife is the cherisher
Clown: of my flesh and blood, he that cherishes my flesh
Clown: and blood loves my flesh and blood, he that loves my
Clown: flesh and blood is my friend: ergo, he that kisses
Clown: my wife is my friend. If men could be contented to
Clown: be what they are, there were no fear in marriage,
Clown: for young Charbon the Puritan and old Poysam the
Clown: Papist, howsome'er their hearts are severed in
Clown: religion, their heads are both one, they may jowl
Clown: horns together, like any deer i' the herd.
COUNTESS: Wilt thou ever be a foul-mouthed and calumnious knave?
Clown: A prophet I, madam, and I speak the truth the next
Clown: way:
Clown: For I the ballad will repeat,
Clown: Which men full true shall find,
Clown: Your marriage comes by destiny,
Clown: Your cuckoo sings by kind.
COUNTESS: Get you gone, sir, I'll talk with you more anon.
Steward: May it please you, madam, that he bid Helen come to
Steward: you: of her I am to speak.
COUNTESS: Sirrah, tell my gentlewoman I would speak with her,
COUNTESS: Helen, I mean.
Clown: Was this fair face the cause, quoth she,
Clown: Why the Grecians sacked Troy?
Clown: Fond done, done fond,
Clown: Was this King Priam's joy?
Clown: With that she sighed as she stood,
Clown: With that she sighed as she stood,
Clown: And gave this sentence then,
Clown: Among nine bad if one be good,
Clown: Among nine bad if one be good,
Clown: There's yet one good in ten.
COUNTESS: What, one good in ten? you corrupt the song, sirrah.
Clown: One good woman in ten, madam, which is a purifying
Clown: o' the song: would God would serve the world so all
Clown: the year! we'ld find no fault with the tithe-woman,
Clown: if I were the parson. One in ten, quoth a'! An we
Clown: might have a good woman born but one every blazing
Clown: star, or at an earthquake, 'twould mend the lottery
Clown: well: a man may draw his heart out, ere a' pluck
Clown: one.
COUNTESS: You'll be gone, sir knave, and do as I command you.
Clown: That man should be at woman's command, and yet no
Clown: hurt done! Though honesty be no puritan, yet it
Clown: will do no hurt, it will wear the surplice of
Clown: humility over the black gown of a big heart. I am
Clown: going, forsooth: the business is for Helen to come hither.
NARRATOR: Exit
COUNTESS: Well, now.
Steward: I know, madam, you love your gentlewoman entirely.
COUNTESS: Faith, I do: her father bequeathed her to me, and
COUNTESS: she herself, without other advantage, may lawfully
COUNTESS: make title to as much love as she finds: there is
COUNTESS: more owing her than is paid, and more shall be paid
COUNTESS: her than she'll demand.
Steward: Madam, I was very late more near her than I think
Steward: she wished me: alone she was, and did communicate
Steward: to herself her own words to her own ears, she
Steward: thought, I dare vow for her, they touched not any
Steward: stranger sense. Her matter was, she loved your son:
Steward: Fortune, she said, was no goddess, that had put
Steward: such difference betwixt their two estates, Love no
Steward: god, that would not extend his might, only where
Steward: qualities were level, Dian no queen of virgins, that
Steward: would suffer her poor knight surprised, without
Steward: rescue in the first assault or ransom afterward.
Steward: This she delivered in the most bitter touch of
Steward: sorrow that e'er I heard virgin exclaim in: which I
Steward: held my duty speedily to acquaint you withal,
Steward: sithence, in the loss that may happen, it concerns
Steward: you something to know it.
COUNTESS: You have discharged this honestly, keep it to
COUNTESS: yourself: many likelihoods informed me of this
COUNTESS: before, which hung so tottering in the balance that
COUNTESS: I could neither believe nor misdoubt. Pray you,
COUNTESS: leave me: stall this in your bosom, and I thank you
COUNTESS: for your honest care: I will speak with you further anon.

NARRATOR: Enter HELENA
COUNTESS: Even so it was with me when I was young:
COUNTESS: If ever we are nature's, these are ours, this thorn
COUNTESS: Doth to our rose of youth rightly belong,
COUNTESS: Our blood to us, this to our blood is born,

COUNTESS: The many-colour'd Iris, rounds thine eye?
COUNTESS: Why? that you are my daughter?
HELENA: That I am not.
COUNTESS: I say, I am your mother.
HELENA: Pardon, madam,
HELENA: The Count Rousillon cannot be my brother:
HELENA: I am from humble, he from honour'd name,
HELENA: No note upon my parents, his all noble:
HELENA: My master, my dear lord he is, and I
HELENA: His servant live, and will his vassal die:
HELENA: He must not be my brother.
COUNTESS: Nor I your mother?
HELENA: You are my mother, madam, would you were,--
HELENA: So that my lord your son were not my brother,--
HELENA: Indeed my mother! or were you both our mothers,
HELENA: I care no more for than I do for heaven,
HELENA: So I were not his sister. Can't no other,
HELENA: But, I your daughter, he must be my brother?
COUNTESS: Yes, Helen, you might be my daughter-in-law:
COUNTESS: God shield you mean it not! daughter and mother
COUNTESS: So strive upon your pulse. What, pale again?
COUNTESS: My fear hath catch'd your fondness: now I see
COUNTESS: The mystery of your loneliness, and find
COUNTESS: Your salt tears' head: now to all sense 'tis gross
COUNTESS: You love my son, invention is ashamed,
COUNTESS: Against the proclamation of thy passion,
COUNTESS: To say thou dost not: therefore tell me true,
COUNTESS: But tell me then, 'tis so, for, look thy cheeks
COUNTESS: Confess it, th' one to th' other, and thine eyes
COUNTESS: See it so grossly shown in thy behaviors
COUNTESS: That in their kind they speak it: only sin
COUNTESS: And hellish obstinacy tie thy tongue,
COUNTESS: That truth should be suspected. Speak, is't so?
COUNTESS: If it be so, you have wound a goodly clew,
COUNTESS: If it be not, forswear't: howe'er, I charge thee,
COUNTESS: As heaven shall work in me for thine avail,
COUNTESS: Tell me truly.
HELENA: Good madam, pardon me!
COUNTESS: Do you love my son?
HELENA: Your pardon, noble mistress!
COUNTESS: Love you my son?
HELENA: Do not you love him, madam?
COUNTESS: Go not about, my love hath in't a bond,
COUNTESS: Whereof the world takes note: come, come, disclose
COUNTESS: The state of your affection, for your passions
COUNTESS: Have to the full appeach'd.
HELENA: Then, I confess,
HELENA: Here on my knee, before high heaven and you,
HELENA: That before you, and next unto high heaven,
HELENA: I love your son.
HELENA: My friends were poor, but honest, so's my love:
HELENA: Be not offended, for it hurts not him
HELENA: That he is loved of me: I follow him not
HELENA: By any token of presumptuous suit,
HELENA: Nor would I have him till I do deserve him,
HELENA: Yet never know how that desert should be.
HELENA: I know I love in vain, strive against hope,
HELENA: Yet in this captious and intenible sieve
HELENA: I still pour in the waters of my love
HELENA: And lack not to lose still: thus, Indian-like,
HELENA: Religious in mine error, I adore
HELENA: The sun, that looks upon his worshipper,
HELENA: But knows of him no more. My dearest madam,
HELENA: Let not your hate encounter with my love
HELENA: For loving where you do: but if yourself,
HELENA: Whose aged honour cites a virtuous youth,
HELENA: Did ever in so true a flame of liking
HELENA: Wish chastely and love dearly, that your Dian
HELENA: Was both herself and love: O, then, give pity
HELENA: To her, whose state is such that cannot choose
HELENA: But lend and give where she is sure to lose,
HELENA: That seeks not to find that her search implies,
HELENA: But riddle-like lives sweetly where she dies!
COUNTESS: Had you not lately an intent,--speak truly,--
COUNTESS: To go to Paris?
HELENA: Madam, I had.
COUNTESS: Wherefore? tell true.
HELENA: I will tell truth, by grace itself I swear.
HELENA: You know my father left me some prescriptions
HELENA: Of rare and proved effects, such as his reading
HELENA: And manifest experience had collected
HELENA: For general sovereignty, and that he will'd me
HELENA: In heedfull'st reservation to bestow them,
HELENA: As notes whose faculties inclusive were
HELENA: More than they were in note: amongst the rest,
HELENA: There is a remedy, approved, set down,
HELENA: To cure the desperate languishings whereof
HELENA: The king is render'd lost.
COUNTESS: This was your motive
COUNTESS: For Paris, was it? speak.
HELENA: My lord your son made me to think of this,
HELENA: Else Paris and the medicine and the king
HELENA: Had from the conversation of my thoughts
HELENA: Haply been absent then.
COUNTESS: But think you, Helen,
COUNTESS: If you should tender your supposed aid,
COUNTESS: He would receive it? he and his physicians
COUNTESS: Are of a mind, he, that they cannot help him,
COUNTESS: They, that they cannot help: how shall they credit
COUNTESS: A poor unlearned virgin, when the schools,
COUNTESS: Embowell'd of their doctrine, have left off
COUNTESS: The danger to itself?
HELENA: There's something in't,
HELENA: More than my father's skill, which was the greatest
HELENA: Of his profession, that his good receipt
HELENA: Shall for my legacy be sanctified
HELENA: By the luckiest stars in heaven: and, would your honour
HELENA: But give me leave to try success, I'ld venture
HELENA: The well-lost life of mine on his grace's cure
HELENA: By such a day and hour.
COUNTESS: Dost thou believe't?
HELENA: Ay, madam, knowingly.
COUNTESS: Why, Helen, thou shalt have my leave and love,
COUNTESS: Means and attendants and my loving greetings
COUNTESS: To those of mine in court: I'll stay at home
COUNTESS: And pray God's blessing into thy attempt:
COUNTESS: Be gone to-morrow, and be sure of this,
COUNTESS: What I can help thee to thou shalt not miss.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Paris. The KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Enter the KING, attended  with divers young Lords taking leave for the Florentine war, BERTRAM, and PAROLLES
KING: Farewell, young lords, these warlike principles
KING: Do not throw from you: and you, my lords, farewell:
KING: Share the advice betwixt you, if both gain, all
KING: The gift doth stretch itself as 'tis received,
KING: And is enough for both.
First Lord: 'Tis our hope, sir,
First Lord: After well enter'd soldiers, to return
First Lord: And find your grace in health.
KING: No, no, it cannot be, and yet my heart
KING: Will not confess he owes the malady
KING: That doth my life besiege. Farewell, young lords,
KING: Whether I live or die, be you the sons
KING: Of worthy Frenchmen: let higher Italy,--
KING: Those bated that inherit but the fall
KING: Of the last monarchy,--see that you come
KING: Not to woo honour, but to wed it, when
KING: The bravest questant shrinks, find what you seek,
KING: That fame may cry you loud: I say, farewell.
Second Lord: Health, at your bidding, serve your majesty!
KING: Those girls of Italy, take heed of them:
KING: They say, our French lack language to deny,
KING: If they demand: beware of being captives,
KING: Before you serve.
Both: Our hearts receive your warnings.
KING: Farewell. Come hither to me.
NARRATOR: Exit, attended
First Lord: O, my sweet lord, that you will stay behind us!
PAROLLES: 'Tis not his fault, the spark.
Second Lord: O, 'tis brave wars!
PAROLLES: Most admirable: I have seen those wars.
BERTRAM: I am commanded here, and kept a coil with
BERTRAM: 'Too young' and 'the next year' and ''tis too early.'
PAROLLES: An thy mind stand to't, boy, steal away bravely.
BERTRAM: I shall stay here the forehorse to a smock,
BERTRAM: Creaking my shoes on the plain masonry,
BERTRAM: Till honour be bought up and no sword worn
BERTRAM: But one to dance with! By heaven, I'll steal away.
First Lord: There's honour in the theft.
PAROLLES: Commit it, count.
Second Lord: I am your accessary, and so, farewell.
BERTRAM: I grow to you, and our parting is a tortured body.
First Lord: Farewell, captain.
Second Lord: Sweet Monsieur Parolles!
PAROLLES: Noble heroes, my sword and yours are kin. Good
PAROLLES: sparks and lustrous, a word, good metals: you shall
PAROLLES: find in the regiment of the Spinii one Captain
PAROLLES: Spurio, with his cicatrice, an emblem of war, here
PAROLLES: on his sinister cheek, it was this very sword
PAROLLES: entrenched it: say to him, I live, and observe his
PAROLLES: reports for me.
First Lord: We shall, noble captain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Lords
PAROLLES: Mars dote on you for his novices! what will ye do?
BERTRAM: Stay: the king.
NARRATOR: Re-enter KING. BERTRAM and PAROLLES retire
PAROLLES: [To BERTRAM]  Use a more spacious ceremony to the
PAROLLES: noble lords, you have restrained yourself within the
PAROLLES: list of too cold an adieu: be more expressive to
PAROLLES: them: for they wear themselves in the cap of the
PAROLLES: time, there do muster true gait, eat, speak, and
PAROLLES: move under the influence of the most received star,
PAROLLES: and though the devil lead the measure, such are to
PAROLLES: be followed: after them, and take a more dilated farewell.
BERTRAM: And I will do so.
PAROLLES: Worthy fellows, and like to prove most sinewy sword-men.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BERTRAM and PAROLLES
NARRATOR: Enter LAFEU
LAFEU: [Kneeling]  Pardon, my lord, for me and for my tidings.
KING: I'll fee thee to stand up.
LAFEU: Then here's a man stands, that has brought his pardon.
LAFEU: I would you had kneel'd, my lord, to ask me mercy,
LAFEU: And that at my bidding you could so stand up.
KING: I would I had, so I had broke thy pate,
KING: And ask'd thee mercy for't.
LAFEU: Good faith, across: but, my good lord 'tis thus,
LAFEU: Will you be cured of your infirmity?
KING: No.
LAFEU: O, will you eat no grapes, my royal fox?
LAFEU: Yes, but you will my noble grapes, an if
LAFEU: My royal fox could reach them: I have seen a medicine
LAFEU: That's able to breathe life into a stone,
LAFEU: Quicken a rock, and make you dance canary
LAFEU: With spritely fire and motion, whose simple touch,
LAFEU: Is powerful to araise King Pepin, nay,
LAFEU: To give great Charlemain a pen in's hand,
LAFEU: And write to her a love-line.
KING: What 'her' is this?
LAFEU: Why, Doctor She: my lord, there's one arrived,
LAFEU: If you will see her: now, by my faith and honour,
LAFEU: If seriously I may convey my thoughts
LAFEU: In this my light deliverance, I have spoke
LAFEU: With one that, in her sex, her years, profession,
LAFEU: Wisdom and constancy, hath amazed me more
LAFEU: Than I dare blame my weakness: will you see her
LAFEU: For that is her demand, and know her business?
LAFEU: That done, laugh well at me.
KING: Now, good Lafeu,
KING: Bring in the admiration, that we with thee
KING: May spend our wonder too, or take off thine
KING: By wondering how thou took'st it.
LAFEU: Nay, I'll fit you,
LAFEU: And not be all day neither.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING: Thus he his special nothing ever prologues.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LAFEU, with HELENA
LAFEU: Nay, come your ways.
KING: This haste hath wings indeed.
LAFEU: Nay, come your ways:
LAFEU: This is his majesty, say your mind to him:
LAFEU: A traitor you do look like, but such traitors
LAFEU: His majesty seldom fears: I am Cressid's uncle,
LAFEU: That dare leave two together, fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING: Now, fair one, does your business follow us?
HELENA: Ay, my good lord.
HELENA: Gerard de Narbon was my father,
HELENA: In what he did profess, well found.
KING: I knew him.
HELENA: The rather will I spare my praises towards him:
HELENA: Knowing him is enough. On's bed of death
HELENA: Many receipts he gave me: chiefly one.
HELENA: Which, as the dearest issue of his practise,
HELENA: And of his old experience the oily darling,
HELENA: He bade me store up, as a triple eye,
HELENA: Safer than mine own two, more dear, I have so,
HELENA: And hearing your high majesty is touch'd
HELENA: With that malignant cause wherein the honour
HELENA: Of my dear father's gift stands chief in power,
HELENA: I come to tender it and my appliance
HELENA: With all bound humbleness.
KING: We thank you, maiden,
KING: But may not be so credulous of cure,
KING: When our most learned doctors leave us and
KING: The congregated college have concluded
KING: That labouring art can never ransom nature
KING: From her inaidible estate, I say we must not
KING: So stain our judgment, or corrupt our hope,
KING: To prostitute our past-cure malady
KING: To empirics, or to dissever so
KING: Our great self and our credit, to esteem
KING: A senseless help when help past sense we deem.
HELENA: My duty then shall pay me for my pains:
HELENA: I will no more enforce mine office on you.
HELENA: Humbly entreating from your royal thoughts
HELENA: A modest one, to bear me back again.
KING: I cannot give thee less, to be call'd grateful:
KING: Thou thought'st to help me, and such thanks I give
KING: As one near death to those that wish him live:
KING: But what at full I know, thou know'st no part,
KING: I knowing all my peril, thou no art.
HELENA: What I can do can do no hurt to try,
HELENA: Since you set up your rest 'gainst remedy.
HELENA: He that of greatest works is finisher
HELENA: Oft does them by the weakest minister:
HELENA: So holy writ in babes hath judgment shown,
HELENA: When judges have been babes, great floods have flown
HELENA: From simple sources, and great seas have dried
HELENA: When miracles have by the greatest been denied.
HELENA: Oft expectation fails and most oft there
HELENA: Where most it promises, and oft it hits
HELENA: Where hope is coldest and despair most fits.
KING: I must not hear thee, fare thee well, kind maid,
KING: Thy pains not used must by thyself be paid:
KING: Proffers not took reap thanks for their reward.
HELENA: Inspired merit so by breath is barr'd:
HELENA: It is not so with Him that all things knows
HELENA: As 'tis with us that square our guess by shows,
HELENA: But most it is presumption in us when
HELENA: The help of heaven we count the act of men.
HELENA: Dear sir, to my endeavours give consent,
HELENA: Of heaven, not me, make an experiment.
HELENA: I am not an impostor that proclaim
HELENA: Myself against the level of mine aim,
HELENA: But know I think and think I know most sure
HELENA: My art is not past power nor you past cure.
KING: Are thou so confident? within what space
KING: Hopest thou my cure?
HELENA: The great'st grace lending grace
HELENA: Ere twice the horses of the sun shall bring
HELENA: Their fiery torcher his diurnal ring,
HELENA: Ere twice in murk and occidental damp
HELENA: Moist Hesperus hath quench'd his sleepy lamp,
HELENA: Or four and twenty times the pilot's glass
HELENA: Hath told the thievish minutes how they pass,
HELENA: What is infirm from your sound parts shall fly,
HELENA: Health shall live free and sickness freely die.
KING: Upon thy certainty and confidence
KING: What darest thou venture?
HELENA: Tax of impudence,
HELENA: A strumpet's boldness, a divulged shame
HELENA: Traduced by odious ballads: my maiden's name
HELENA: Sear'd otherwise, nay, worse--if worse--extended
HELENA: With vilest torture let my life be ended.
KING: Methinks in thee some blessed spirit doth speak
KING: His powerful sound within an organ weak:
KING: And what impossibility would slay
KING: In common sense, sense saves another way.
KING: Thy life is dear, for all that life can rate
KING: Worth name of life in thee hath estimate,
KING: Youth, beauty, wisdom, courage, all
KING: That happiness and prime can happy call:
KING: Thou this to hazard needs must intimate
KING: Skill infinite or monstrous desperate.
KING: Sweet practiser, thy physic I will try,
KING: That ministers thine own death if I die.
HELENA: If I break time, or flinch in property
HELENA: Of what I spoke, unpitied let me die,
HELENA: And well deserved: not helping, death's my fee,
HELENA: But, if I help, what do you promise me?
KING: Make thy demand.
HELENA: But will you make it even?
KING: Ay, by my sceptre and my hopes of heaven.
HELENA: Then shalt thou give me with thy kingly hand
HELENA: What husband in thy power I will command:
HELENA: Exempted be from me the arrogance
HELENA: To choose from forth the royal blood of France,
HELENA: My low and humble name to propagate
HELENA: With any branch or image of thy state,
HELENA: But such a one, thy vassal, whom I know
HELENA: Is free for me to ask, thee to bestow.
KING: Here is my hand, the premises observed,
KING: Thy will by my performance shall be served:
KING: So make the choice of thy own time, for I,
KING: Thy resolved patient, on thee still rely.
KING: More should I question thee, and more I must,
KING: Though more to know could not be more to trust,
KING: From whence thou camest, how tended on: but rest
KING: Unquestion'd welcome and undoubted blest.
KING: Give me some help here, ho! If thou proceed
KING: As high as word, my deed shall match thy meed.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter COUNTESS and Clown
COUNTESS: Come on, sir, I shall now put you to the height of
COUNTESS: your breeding.
Clown: I will show myself highly fed and lowly taught: I
Clown: know my business is but to the court.
COUNTESS: To the court! why, what place make you special,
COUNTESS: when you put off that with such contempt? But to the court!
Clown: Truly, madam, if God have lent a man any manners, he
Clown: may easily put it off at court: he that cannot make
Clown: a leg, put off's cap, kiss his hand and say nothing,
Clown: has neither leg, hands, lip, nor cap, and indeed
Clown: such a fellow, to say precisely, were not for the
Clown: court, but for me, I have an answer will serve all
Clown: men.
COUNTESS: Marry, that's a bountiful answer that fits all
COUNTESS: questions.
Clown: It is like a barber's chair that fits all buttocks,
Clown: the pin-buttock, the quatch-buttock, the brawn
Clown: buttock, or any buttock.
COUNTESS: Will your answer serve fit to all questions?
Clown: As fit as ten groats is for the hand of an attorney,
Clown: as your French crown for your taffeta punk, as Tib's
Clown: rush for Tom's forefinger, as a pancake for Shrove
Clown: Tuesday, a morris for May-day, as the nail to his
Clown: hole, the cuckold to his horn, as a scolding queen
Clown: to a wrangling knave, as the nun's lip to the
Clown: friar's mouth, nay, as the pudding to his skin.
COUNTESS: Have you, I say, an answer of such fitness for all
COUNTESS: questions?
Clown: From below your duke to beneath your constable, it
Clown: will fit any question.
COUNTESS: It must be an answer of most monstrous size that
COUNTESS: must fit all demands.
Clown: But a trifle neither, in good faith, if the learned
Clown: should speak truth of it: here it is, and all that
Clown: belongs to't. Ask me if I am a courtier: it shall
Clown: do you no harm to learn.
COUNTESS: To be young again, if we could: I will be a fool in
COUNTESS: question, hoping to be the wiser by your answer. I
COUNTESS: pray you, sir, are you a courtier?
Clown: O Lord, sir! There's a simple putting off. More,
Clown: more, a hundred of them.
COUNTESS: Sir, I am a poor friend of yours, that loves you.
Clown: O Lord, sir! Thick, thick, spare not me.
COUNTESS: I think, sir, you can eat none of this homely meat.
Clown: O Lord, sir! Nay, put me to't, I warrant you.
COUNTESS: You were lately whipped, sir, as I think.
Clown: O Lord, sir! spare not me.
COUNTESS: Do you cry, 'O Lord, sir!' at your whipping, and
COUNTESS: 'spare not me?' Indeed your 'O Lord, sir!' is very
COUNTESS: sequent to your whipping: you would answer very well
COUNTESS: to a whipping, if you were but bound to't.
Clown: I ne'er had worse luck in my life in my 'O Lord,
Clown: sir!' I see things may serve long, but not serve ever.
COUNTESS: I play the noble housewife with the time
COUNTESS: To entertain't so merrily with a fool.
Clown: O Lord, sir! why, there't serves well again.
COUNTESS: An end, sir, to your business. Give Helen this,
COUNTESS: And urge her to a present answer back:
COUNTESS: Commend me to my kinsmen and my son:
COUNTESS: This is not much.
Clown: Not much commendation to them.
COUNTESS: Not much employment for you: you understand me?
Clown: Most fruitfully: I am there before my legs.
COUNTESS: Haste you again.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Paris. The KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM, LAFEU, and PAROLLES
LAFEU: They say miracles are past, and we have our
LAFEU: philosophical persons, to make modern and familiar,
LAFEU: things supernatural and causeless. Hence is it that
LAFEU: we make trifles of terrors, ensconcing ourselves
LAFEU: into seeming knowledge, when we should submit
LAFEU: ourselves to an unknown fear.
PAROLLES: Why, 'tis the rarest argument of wonder that hath
PAROLLES: shot out in our latter times.
BERTRAM: And so 'tis.
LAFEU: To be relinquish'd of the artists,--
PAROLLES: So I say.
LAFEU: Both of Galen and Paracelsus.
PAROLLES: So I say.
LAFEU: Of all the learned and authentic fellows,--
PAROLLES: Right, so I say.
LAFEU: That gave him out incurable,--
PAROLLES: Why, there 'tis, so say I too.
LAFEU: Not to be helped,--
PAROLLES: Right, as 'twere, a man assured of a--
LAFEU: Uncertain life, and sure death.
PAROLLES: Just, you say well, so would I have said.
LAFEU: I may truly say, it is a novelty to the world.
PAROLLES: It is, indeed: if you will have it in showing, you
PAROLLES: shall read it in--what do you call there?
LAFEU: A showing of a heavenly effect in an earthly actor.
PAROLLES: That's it, I would have said the very same.
LAFEU: Why, your dolphin is not lustier: 'fore me,
LAFEU: I speak in respect--
PAROLLES: Nay, 'tis strange, 'tis very strange, that is the
PAROLLES: brief and the tedious of it, and he's of a most
PAROLLES: facinerious spirit that will not acknowledge it to be the--
LAFEU: Very hand of heaven.
PAROLLES: Ay, so I say.
LAFEU: In a most weak--
NARRATOR: pausing
LAFEU: and debile minister, great power, great
LAFEU: transcendence: which should, indeed, give us a
LAFEU: further use to be made than alone the recovery of
LAFEU: the king, as to be--
NARRATOR: pausing
LAFEU: generally thankful.
PAROLLES: I would have said it, you say well. Here comes the king.
NARRATOR: Enter KING, HELENA, and Attendants. LAFEU and PAROLLES retire
LAFEU: Lustig, as the Dutchman says: I'll like a maid the
LAFEU: better, whilst I have a tooth in my head: why, he's
LAFEU: able to lead her a coranto.
PAROLLES: Mort du vinaigre! is not this Helen?
LAFEU: 'Fore God, I think so.
KING: Go, call before me all the lords in court.
KING: Sit, my preserver, by thy patient's side,
KING: And with this healthful hand, whose banish'd sense
KING: Thou hast repeal'd, a second time receive
KING: The confirmation of my promised gift,
KING: Which but attends thy naming.
NARRATOR: Enter three or four Lords
KING: Fair maid, send forth thine eye: this youthful parcel
KING: Of noble bachelors stand at my bestowing,
KING: O'er whom both sovereign power and father's voice
KING: I have to use: thy frank election make,
KING: Thou hast power to choose, and they none to forsake.
HELENA: To each of you one fair and virtuous mistress
HELENA: Fall, when Love please! marry, to each, but one!
LAFEU: I'ld give bay Curtal and his furniture,
LAFEU: My mouth no more were broken than these boys',
LAFEU: And writ as little beard.
KING: Peruse them well:
KING: Not one of those but had a noble father.
HELENA: Gentlemen,
HELENA: Heaven hath through me restored the king to health.
All: We understand it, and thank heaven for you.
HELENA: I am a simple maid, and therein wealthiest,
HELENA: That I protest I simply am a maid.
HELENA: Please it your majesty, I have done already:
HELENA: The blushes in my cheeks thus whisper me,
HELENA: 'We blush that thou shouldst choose, but, be refused,
HELENA: Let the white death sit on thy cheek for ever,
HELENA: We'll ne'er come there again.'
KING: Make choice, and, see,
KING: Who shuns thy love shuns all his love in me.
HELENA: Now, Dian, from thy altar do I fly,
HELENA: And to imperial Love, that god most high,
HELENA: Do my sighs stream. Sir, will you hear my suit?
First Lord: And grant it.
HELENA: Thanks, sir, all the rest is mute.
LAFEU: I had rather be in this choice than throw ames-ace
LAFEU: for my life.
HELENA: The honour, sir, that flames in your fair eyes,
HELENA: Before I speak, too threateningly replies:
HELENA: Love make your fortunes twenty times above
HELENA: Her that so wishes and her humble love!
Second Lord: No better, if you please.
HELENA: My wish receive,
HELENA: Which great Love grant! and so, I take my leave.
LAFEU: Do all they deny her? An they were sons of mine,
LAFEU: I'd have them whipped, or I would send them to the
LAFEU: Turk, to make eunuchs of.
HELENA: Be not afraid that I your hand should take,
HELENA: I'll never do you wrong for your own sake:
HELENA: Blessing upon your vows! and in your bed
HELENA: Find fairer fortune, if you ever wed!
LAFEU: These boys are boys of ice, they'll none have her:
LAFEU: sure, they are bastards to the English, the French
LAFEU: ne'er got 'em.
HELENA: You are too young, too happy, and too good,
HELENA: To make yourself a son out of my blood.
Fourth Lord: Fair one, I think not so.
LAFEU: There's one grape yet, I am sure thy father drunk
LAFEU: wine: but if thou be'st not an ass, I am a youth
LAFEU: of fourteen, I have known thee already.
HELENA: [To BERTRAM]  I dare not say I take you, but I give
HELENA: Me and my service, ever whilst I live,
HELENA: Into your guiding power. This is the man.
KING: Why, then, young Bertram, take her, she's thy wife.
BERTRAM: My wife, my liege! I shall beseech your highness,
BERTRAM: In such a business give me leave to use
BERTRAM: The help of mine own eyes.
KING: Know'st thou not, Bertram,
KING: What she has done for me?
BERTRAM: Yes, my good lord,
BERTRAM: But never hope to know why I should marry her.
KING: Thou know'st she has raised me from my sickly bed.
BERTRAM: But follows it, my lord, to bring me down
BERTRAM: Must answer for your raising? I know her well:
BERTRAM: She had her breeding at my father's charge.
BERTRAM: A poor physician's daughter my wife! Disdain
BERTRAM: Rather corrupt me ever!
KING: 'Tis only title thou disdain'st in her, the which
KING: I can build up. Strange is it that our bloods,
KING: Of colour, weight, and heat, pour'd all together,
KING: Would quite confound distinction, yet stand off
KING: In differences so mighty. If she be
KING: All that is virtuous, save what thou dislikest,
KING: A poor physician's daughter, thou dislikest
KING: Of virtue for the name: but do not so:
KING: From lowest place when virtuous things proceed,
KING: The place is dignified by the doer's deed:
KING: Where great additions swell's, and virtue none,
KING: It is a dropsied honour. Good alone
KING: Is good without a name. Vileness is so:
KING: The property by what it is should go,
KING: Not by the title. She is young, wise, fair,
KING: In these to nature she's immediate heir,
KING: And these breed honour: that is honour's scorn,
KING: Which challenges itself as honour's born
KING: And is not like the sire: honours thrive,
KING: When rather from our acts we them derive
KING: Than our foregoers: the mere word's a slave
KING: Debosh'd on every tomb, on every grave
KING: A lying trophy, and as oft is dumb
KING: Where dust and damn'd oblivion is the tomb
KING: Of honour'd bones indeed. What should be said?
KING: If thou canst like this creature as a maid,
KING: I can create the rest: virtue and she
KING: Is her own dower, honour and wealth from me.
BERTRAM: I cannot love her, nor will strive to do't.
KING: Thou wrong'st thyself, if thou shouldst strive to choose.
HELENA: That you are well restored, my lord, I'm glad:
HELENA: Let the rest go.
KING: My honour's at the stake, which to defeat,
KING: I must produce my power. Here, take her hand,
KING: Proud scornful boy, unworthy this good gift,
KING: That dost in vile misprision shackle up
KING: My love and her desert, that canst not dream,
KING: We, poising us in her defective scale,
KING: Shall weigh thee to the beam, that wilt not know,
KING: It is in us to plant thine honour where
KING: We please to have it grow. Cheque thy contempt:
KING: Obey our will, which travails in thy good:
KING: Believe not thy disdain, but presently
KING: Do thine own fortunes that obedient right
KING: Which both thy duty owes and our power claims,
KING: Or I will throw thee from my care for ever
KING: Into the staggers and the careless lapse
KING: Of youth and ignorance, both my revenge and hate
KING: Loosing upon thee, in the name of justice,
KING: Without all terms of pity. Speak, thine answer.
BERTRAM: Pardon, my gracious lord, for I submit
BERTRAM: My fancy to your eyes: when I consider
BERTRAM: What great creation and what dole of honour
BERTRAM: Flies where you bid it, I find that she, which late
BERTRAM: Was in my nobler thoughts most base, is now
BERTRAM: The praised of the king, who, so ennobled,
BERTRAM: Is as 'twere born so.
KING: Take her by the hand,
KING: And tell her she is thine: to whom I promise
KING: A counterpoise, if not to thy estate
KING: A balance more replete.
BERTRAM: I take her hand.
KING: Good fortune and the favour of the king
KING: Smile upon this contract, whose ceremony
KING: Shall seem expedient on the now-born brief,
KING: And be perform'd to-night: the solemn feast
KING: Shall more attend upon the coming space,
KING: Expecting absent friends. As thou lovest her,
KING: Thy love's to me religious, else, does err.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but LAFEU and PAROLLES
LAFEU: [Advancing]  Do you hear, monsieur? a word with you.
PAROLLES: Your pleasure, sir?
LAFEU: Your lord and master did well to make his
LAFEU: recantation.
PAROLLES: Recantation! My lord! my master!
LAFEU: Ay, is it not a language I speak?
PAROLLES: A most harsh one, and not to be understood without
PAROLLES: bloody succeeding. My master!
LAFEU: Are you companion to the Count Rousillon?
PAROLLES: To any count, to all counts, to what is man.
LAFEU: To what is count's man: count's master is of
LAFEU: another style.
PAROLLES: You are too old, sir, let it satisfy you, you are too old.
LAFEU: I must tell thee, sirrah, I write man, to which
LAFEU: title age cannot bring thee.
PAROLLES: What I dare too well do, I dare not do.
LAFEU: I did think thee, for two ordinaries, to be a pretty
LAFEU: wise fellow, thou didst make tolerable vent of thy
LAFEU: travel, it might pass: yet the scarfs and the
LAFEU: bannerets about thee did manifoldly dissuade me from
LAFEU: believing thee a vessel of too great a burthen. I
LAFEU: have now found thee, when I lose thee again, I care
LAFEU: not: yet art thou good for nothing but taking up, and
LAFEU: that thou't scarce worth.
PAROLLES: Hadst thou not the privilege of antiquity upon thee,--
LAFEU: Do not plunge thyself too far in anger, lest thou
LAFEU: hasten thy trial, which if--Lord have mercy on thee
LAFEU: for a hen! So, my good window of lattice, fare thee
LAFEU: well: thy casement I need not open, for I look
LAFEU: through thee. Give me thy hand.
PAROLLES: My lord, you give me most egregious indignity.
LAFEU: Ay, with all my heart, and thou art worthy of it.
PAROLLES: I have not, my lord, deserved it.
LAFEU: Yes, good faith, every dram of it, and I will not
LAFEU: bate thee a scruple.
PAROLLES: Well, I shall be wiser.
LAFEU: Even as soon as thou canst, for thou hast to pull at
LAFEU: a smack o' the contrary. If ever thou be'st bound
LAFEU: in thy scarf and beaten, thou shalt find what it is
LAFEU: to be proud of thy bondage. I have a desire to hold
LAFEU: my acquaintance with thee, or rather my knowledge,
LAFEU: that I may say in the default, he is a man I know.
PAROLLES: My lord, you do me most insupportable vexation.
LAFEU: I would it were hell-pains for thy sake, and my poor
LAFEU: doing eternal: for doing I am past: as I will by
LAFEU: thee, in what motion age will give me leave.
NARRATOR: Exit
PAROLLES: Well, thou hast a son shall take this disgrace off
PAROLLES: me, scurvy, old, filthy, scurvy lord! Well, I must
PAROLLES: be patient, there is no fettering of authority.
PAROLLES: I'll beat him, by my life, if I can meet him with
PAROLLES: any convenience, an he were double and double a
PAROLLES: lord. I'll have no more pity of his age than I
PAROLLES: would of--I'll beat him, an if I could but meet him again.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LAFEU
LAFEU: Sirrah, your lord and master's married, there's news
LAFEU: for you: you have a new mistress.
PAROLLES: I most unfeignedly beseech your lordship to make
PAROLLES: some reservation of your wrongs: he is my good
PAROLLES: lord: whom I serve above is my master.
LAFEU: Who? God?
PAROLLES: Ay, sir.
LAFEU: The devil it is that's thy master. Why dost thou
LAFEU: garter up thy arms o' this fashion? dost make hose of
LAFEU: sleeves? do other servants so? Thou wert best set
LAFEU: thy lower part where thy nose stands. By mine
LAFEU: honour, if I were but two hours younger, I'ld beat
LAFEU: thee: methinks, thou art a general offence, and
LAFEU: every man should beat thee: I think thou wast
LAFEU: created for men to breathe themselves upon thee.
PAROLLES: This is hard and undeserved measure, my lord.
LAFEU: Go to, sir, you were beaten in Italy for picking a
LAFEU: kernel out of a pomegranate, you are a vagabond and
LAFEU: no true traveller: you are more saucy with lords
LAFEU: and honourable personages than the commission of your
LAFEU: birth and virtue gives you heraldry. You are not
LAFEU: worth another word, else I'ld call you knave. I leave you.
NARRATOR: Exit
PAROLLES: Good, very good, it is so then: good, very good,
PAROLLES: let it be concealed awhile.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BERTRAM
BERTRAM: Undone, and forfeited to cares for ever!
PAROLLES: What's the matter, sweet-heart?
BERTRAM: Although before the solemn priest I have sworn,
BERTRAM: I will not bed her.
PAROLLES: What, what, sweet-heart?
BERTRAM: O my Parolles, they have married me!
BERTRAM: I'll to the Tuscan wars, and never bed her.
PAROLLES: France is a dog-hole, and it no more merits
PAROLLES: The tread of a man's foot: to the wars!
BERTRAM: There's letters from my mother: what the import is,
BERTRAM: I know not yet.
PAROLLES: Ay, that would be known. To the wars, my boy, to the wars!
PAROLLES: He wears his honour in a box unseen,
PAROLLES: That hugs his kicky-wicky here at home,
PAROLLES: Spending his manly marrow in her arms,
PAROLLES: Which should sustain the bound and high curvet
PAROLLES: Of Mars's fiery steed. To other regions
PAROLLES: France is a stable, we that dwell in't jades,
PAROLLES: Therefore, to the war!
BERTRAM: It shall be so: I'll send her to my house,
BERTRAM: Acquaint my mother with my hate to her,
BERTRAM: And wherefore I am fled, write to the king
BERTRAM: That which I durst not speak, his present gift
BERTRAM: Shall furnish me to those Italian fields,
BERTRAM: Where noble fellows strike: war is no strife
BERTRAM: To the dark house and the detested wife.
PAROLLES: Will this capriccio hold in thee? art sure?
BERTRAM: Go with me to my chamber, and advise me.
BERTRAM: I'll send her straight away: to-morrow
BERTRAM: I'll to the wars, she to her single sorrow.
PAROLLES: Why, these balls bound, there's noise in it. 'Tis hard:
PAROLLES: A young man married is a man that's marr'd:
PAROLLES: Therefore away, and leave her bravely, go:
PAROLLES: The king has done you wrong: but, hush, 'tis so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Paris. The KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA and Clown
HELENA: My mother greets me kindly, is she well?
Clown: She is not well, but yet she has her health: she's
Clown: very merry, but yet she is not well: but thanks be
Clown: given, she's very well and wants nothing i', the
Clown: world, but yet she is not well.
HELENA: If she be very well, what does she ail, that she's
HELENA: not very well?
Clown: Truly, she's very well indeed, but for two things.
HELENA: What two things?
Clown: One, that she's not in heaven, whither God send her
Clown: quickly! the other that she's in earth, from whence
Clown: God send her quickly!
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES
PAROLLES: Bless you, my fortunate lady!
HELENA: I hope, sir, I have your good will to have mine own
HELENA: good fortunes.
PAROLLES: You had my prayers to lead them on, and to keep them
PAROLLES: on, have them still. O, my knave, how does my old lady?
Clown: So that you had her wrinkles and I her money,
Clown: I would she did as you say.
PAROLLES: Why, I say nothing.
Clown: Marry, you are the wiser man, for many a man's
Clown: tongue shakes out his master's undoing: to say
Clown: nothing, to do nothing, to know nothing, and to have
Clown: nothing, is to be a great part of your title, which
Clown: is within a very little of nothing.
PAROLLES: Away! thou'rt a knave.
Clown: You should have said, sir, before a knave thou'rt a
Clown: knave, that's, before me thou'rt a knave: this had
Clown: been truth, sir.
PAROLLES: Go to, thou art a witty fool, I have found thee.
Clown: Did you find me in yourself, sir? or were you
Clown: taught to find me? The search, sir, was profitable,
Clown: and much fool may you find in you, even to the
Clown: world's pleasure and the increase of laughter.
PAROLLES: A good knave, i' faith, and well fed.
PAROLLES: Madam, my lord will go away to-night,
PAROLLES: A very serious business calls on him.
PAROLLES: The great prerogative and rite of love,
PAROLLES: Which, as your due, time claims, he does acknowledge,
PAROLLES: But puts it off to a compell'd restraint,
PAROLLES: Whose want, and whose delay, is strew'd with sweets,
PAROLLES: Which they distil now in the curbed time,
PAROLLES: To make the coming hour o'erflow with joy
PAROLLES: And pleasure drown the brim.
HELENA: What's his will else?
PAROLLES: That you will take your instant leave o' the king
PAROLLES: And make this haste as your own good proceeding,
PAROLLES: Strengthen'd with what apology you think
PAROLLES: May make it probable need.
HELENA: What more commands he?
PAROLLES: That, having this obtain'd, you presently
PAROLLES: Attend his further pleasure.
HELENA: In every thing I wait upon his will.
PAROLLES: I shall report it so.
HELENA: I pray you.
NARRATOR: Exit PAROLLES
HELENA: Come, sirrah.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Paris. The KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter LAFEU and BERTRAM
LAFEU: But I hope your lordship thinks not him a soldier.
BERTRAM: Yes, my lord, and of very valiant approof.
LAFEU: You have it from his own deliverance.
BERTRAM: And by other warranted testimony.
LAFEU: Then my dial goes not true: I took this lark for a bunting.
BERTRAM: I do assure you, my lord, he is very great in
BERTRAM: knowledge and accordingly valiant.
LAFEU: I have then sinned against his experience and
LAFEU: transgressed against his valour, and my state that
LAFEU: way is dangerous, since I cannot yet find in my
LAFEU: heart to repent. Here he comes: I pray you, make
LAFEU: us friends, I will pursue the amity.
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES
PAROLLES: [To BERTRAM]  These things shall be done, sir.
LAFEU: Pray you, sir, who's his tailor?
PAROLLES: Sir?
LAFEU: O, I know him well, I, sir, he, sir, 's a good
LAFEU: workman, a very good tailor.
BERTRAM: [Aside to PAROLLES]  Is she gone to the king?
PAROLLES: She is.
BERTRAM: Will she away to-night?
PAROLLES: As you'll have her.
BERTRAM: I have writ my letters, casketed my treasure,
BERTRAM: Given order for our horses, and to-night,
BERTRAM: When I should take possession of the bride,
BERTRAM: End ere I do begin.
LAFEU: A good traveller is something at the latter end of a
LAFEU: dinner, but one that lies three thirds and uses a
LAFEU: known truth to pass a thousand nothings with, should
LAFEU: be once heard and thrice beaten. God save you, captain.
BERTRAM: Is there any unkindness between my lord and you, monsieur?
PAROLLES: I know not how I have deserved to run into my lord's
PAROLLES: displeasure.
LAFEU: You have made shift to run into 't, boots and spurs
LAFEU: and all, like him that leaped into the custard, and
LAFEU: out of it you'll run again, rather than suffer
LAFEU: question for your residence.
BERTRAM: It may be you have mistaken him, my lord.
LAFEU: And shall do so ever, though I took him at 's
LAFEU: prayers. Fare you well, my lord, and believe this
LAFEU: of me, there can be no kernel in this light nut, the
LAFEU: soul of this man is his clothes. Trust him not in
LAFEU: matter of heavy consequence, I have kept of them
LAFEU: tame, and know their natures. Farewell, monsieur:
LAFEU: I have spoken better of you than you have or will to
LAFEU: deserve at my hand, but we must do good against evil.
NARRATOR: Exit
PAROLLES: An idle lord. I swear.
BERTRAM: I think so.
PAROLLES: Why, do you not know him?
BERTRAM: Yes, I do know him well, and common speech
BERTRAM: Gives him a worthy pass. Here comes my clog.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA
HELENA: I have, sir, as I was commanded from you,
HELENA: Spoke with the king and have procured his leave
HELENA: For present parting, only he desires
HELENA: Some private speech with you.
BERTRAM: I shall obey his will.
BERTRAM: You must not marvel, Helen, at my course,
BERTRAM: Which holds not colour with the time, nor does
BERTRAM: The ministration and required office
BERTRAM: On my particular. Prepared I was not
BERTRAM: For such a business, therefore am I found
BERTRAM: So much unsettled: this drives me to entreat you
BERTRAM: That presently you take our way for home,
BERTRAM: And rather muse than ask why I entreat you,
BERTRAM: For my respects are better than they seem
BERTRAM: And my appointments have in them a need
BERTRAM: Greater than shows itself at the first view
BERTRAM: To you that know them not. This to my mother:
NARRATOR: Giving a letter
BERTRAM: 'Twill be two days ere I shall see you, so
BERTRAM: I leave you to your wisdom.
HELENA: Sir, I can nothing say,
HELENA: But that I am your most obedient servant.
BERTRAM: Come, come, no more of that.
HELENA: And ever shall
HELENA: With true observance seek to eke out that
HELENA: Wherein toward me my homely stars have fail'd
HELENA: To equal my great fortune.
BERTRAM: Let that go:
BERTRAM: My haste is very great: farewell, hie home.
HELENA: Pray, sir, your pardon.
BERTRAM: Well, what would you say?
HELENA: I am not worthy of the wealth I owe,
HELENA: Nor dare I say 'tis mine, and yet it is,
HELENA: But, like a timorous thief, most fain would steal
HELENA: What law does vouch mine own.
BERTRAM: What would you have?
HELENA: Something, and scarce so much: nothing, indeed.
HELENA: I would not tell you what I would, my lord:
HELENA: Faith yes,
HELENA: Strangers and foes do sunder, and not kiss.
BERTRAM: I pray you, stay not, but in haste to horse.
HELENA: I shall not break your bidding, good my lord.
BERTRAM: Where are my other men, monsieur? Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit HELENA
BERTRAM: Go thou toward home, where I will never come
BERTRAM: Whilst I can shake my sword or hear the drum.
BERTRAM: Away, and for our flight.
PAROLLES: Bravely, coragio!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Florence. The DUKE's palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter the DUKE of Florence attended, the two Frenchmen, with a troop of soldiers.
DUKE: So that from point to point now have you heard
DUKE: The fundamental reasons of this war,
DUKE: Whose great decision hath much blood let forth
DUKE: And more thirsts after.
First Lord: Holy seems the quarrel
First Lord: Upon your grace's part, black and fearful
First Lord: On the opposer.
DUKE: Therefore we marvel much our cousin France
DUKE: Would in so just a business shut his bosom
DUKE: Against our borrowing prayers.
Second Lord: Good my lord,
Second Lord: The reasons of our state I cannot yield,
Second Lord: But like a common and an outward man,
Second Lord: That the great figure of a council frames
Second Lord: By self-unable motion: therefore dare not
Second Lord: Say what I think of it, since I have found
Second Lord: Myself in my incertain grounds to fail
Second Lord: As often as I guess'd.
DUKE: Be it his pleasure.
First Lord: But I am sure the younger of our nature,
First Lord: That surfeit on their ease, will day by day
First Lord: Come here for physic.
DUKE: Welcome shall they be,
DUKE: And all the honours that can fly from us
DUKE: Shall on them settle. You know your places well,
DUKE: When better fall, for your avails they fell:
DUKE: To-morrow to the field.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter COUNTESS and Clown
COUNTESS: It hath happened all as I would have had it, save
COUNTESS: that he comes not along with her.
Clown: By my troth, I take my young lord to be a very
Clown: melancholy man.
COUNTESS: By what observance, I pray you?
Clown: Why, he will look upon his boot and sing, mend the
Clown: ruff and sing, ask questions and sing, pick his
Clown: teeth and sing. I know a man that had this trick of
Clown: melancholy sold a goodly manor for a song.
COUNTESS: Let me see what he writes, and when he means to come.
NARRATOR: Opening a letter
Clown: I have no mind to Isbel since I was at court: our
Clown: old ling and our Isbels o' the country are nothing
Clown: like your old ling and your Isbels o' the court:
Clown: the brains of my Cupid's knocked out, and I begin to
Clown: love, as an old man loves money, with no stomach.
COUNTESS: What have we here?
Clown: E'en that you have there.
NARRATOR: Exit
COUNTESS: [Reads]  I have sent you a daughter-in-law: she hath
COUNTESS: recovered the king, and undone me. I have wedded
COUNTESS: her, not bedded her, and sworn to make the 'not'
COUNTESS: eternal. You shall hear I am run away: know it
COUNTESS: before the report come. If there be breadth enough
COUNTESS: in the world, I will hold a long distance. My duty
COUNTESS: to you.	Your unfortunate son,
COUNTESS: BERTRAM.
COUNTESS: This is not well, rash and unbridled boy.
COUNTESS: To fly the favours of so good a king,
COUNTESS: To pluck his indignation on thy head
COUNTESS: By the misprising of a maid too virtuous
COUNTESS: For the contempt of empire.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Clown
Clown: O madam, yonder is heavy news within between two
Clown: soldiers and my young lady!
COUNTESS: What is the matter?
Clown: Nay, there is some comfort in the news, some
Clown: comfort, your son will not be killed so soon as I
Clown: thought he would.
COUNTESS: Why should he be killed?
Clown: So say I, madam, if he run away, as I hear he does:
Clown: the danger is in standing to't, that's the loss of
Clown: men, though it be the getting of children. Here
Clown: they come will tell you more: for my part, I only
Clown: hear your son was run away.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA, and two Gentlemen
First Gentleman: Save you, good madam.
HELENA: Madam, my lord is gone, for ever gone.
Second Gentleman: Do not say so.
COUNTESS: Think upon patience. Pray you, gentlemen,
COUNTESS: I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief,
COUNTESS: That the first face of neither, on the start,
COUNTESS: Can woman me unto't: where is my son, I pray you?
Second Gentleman: Madam, he's gone to serve the duke of Florence:
Second Gentleman: We met him thitherward, for thence we came,
Second Gentleman: And, after some dispatch in hand at court,
Second Gentleman: Thither we bend again.
HELENA: Look on his letter, madam, here's my passport.
NARRATOR: Reads
HELENA: When thou canst get the ring upon my finger which
HELENA: never shall come off, and show me a child begotten
HELENA: of thy body that I am father to, then call me
HELENA: husband: but in such a 'then' I write a 'never.'
HELENA: This is a dreadful sentence.
COUNTESS: Brought you this letter, gentlemen?
First Gentleman: Ay, madam,
First Gentleman: And for the contents' sake are sorry for our pain.
COUNTESS: I prithee, lady, have a better cheer,
COUNTESS: If thou engrossest all the griefs are thine,
COUNTESS: Thou robb'st me of a moiety: he was my son,
COUNTESS: But I do wash his name out of my blood,
COUNTESS: And thou art all my child. Towards Florence is he?
Second Gentleman: Ay, madam.
COUNTESS: And to be a soldier?
Second Gentleman: Such is his noble purpose, and believe 't,
Second Gentleman: The duke will lay upon him all the honour
Second Gentleman: That good convenience claims.
COUNTESS: Return you thither?
First Gentleman: Ay, madam, with the swiftest wing of speed.
HELENA: [Reads]  Till I have no wife I have nothing in France.
HELENA: 'Tis bitter.
COUNTESS: Find you that there?
HELENA: Ay, madam.
First Gentleman: 'Tis but the boldness of his hand, haply, which his
First Gentleman: heart was not consenting to.
COUNTESS: Nothing in France, until he have no wife!
COUNTESS: There's nothing here that is too good for him
COUNTESS: But only she, and she deserves a lord
COUNTESS: That twenty such rude boys might tend upon
COUNTESS: And call her hourly mistress. Who was with him?
First Gentleman: A servant only, and a gentleman
First Gentleman: Which I have sometime known.
COUNTESS: Parolles, was it not?
First Gentleman: Ay, my good lady, he.
COUNTESS: A very tainted fellow, and full of wickedness.
COUNTESS: My son corrupts a well-derived nature
COUNTESS: With his inducement.
First Gentleman: Indeed, good lady,
First Gentleman: The fellow has a deal of that too much,
First Gentleman: Which holds him much to have.
COUNTESS: You're welcome, gentlemen.
COUNTESS: I will entreat you, when you see my son,
COUNTESS: To tell him that his sword can never win
COUNTESS: The honour that he loses: more I'll entreat you
COUNTESS: Written to bear along.
Second Gentleman: We serve you, madam,
Second Gentleman: In that and all your worthiest affairs.
COUNTESS: Not so, but as we change our courtesies.
COUNTESS: Will you draw near!
NARRATOR: Exeunt COUNTESS and Gentlemen
HELENA: 'Till I have no wife, I have nothing in France.'
HELENA: Nothing in France, until he has no wife!
HELENA: Thou shalt have none, Rousillon, none in France,
HELENA: Then hast thou all again. Poor lord! is't I
HELENA: That chase thee from thy country and expose
HELENA: Those tender limbs of thine to the event
HELENA: Of the none-sparing war? and is it I
HELENA: That drive thee from the sportive court, where thou
HELENA: Wast shot at with fair eyes, to be the mark
HELENA: Of smoky muskets? O you leaden messengers,
HELENA: That ride upon the violent speed of fire,
HELENA: Fly with false aim, move the still-peering air,
HELENA: That sings with piercing, do not touch my lord.
HELENA: Whoever shoots at him, I set him there,
HELENA: Whoever charges on his forward breast,
HELENA: I am the caitiff that do hold him to't,
HELENA: And, though I kill him not, I am the cause
HELENA: His death was so effected: better 'twere
HELENA: I met the ravin lion when he roar'd
HELENA: With sharp constraint of hunger, better 'twere
HELENA: That all the miseries which nature owes
HELENA: Were mine at once. No, come thou home, Rousillon,
HELENA: Whence honour but of danger wins a scar,
HELENA: As oft it loses all: I will be gone,
HELENA: My being here it is that holds thee hence:
HELENA: Shall I stay here to do't?  no, no, although
HELENA: The air of paradise did fan the house
HELENA: And angels officed all: I will be gone,
HELENA: That pitiful rumour may report my flight,
HELENA: To consolate thine ear. Come, night, end, day!
HELENA: For with the dark, poor thief, I'll steal away.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Florence. Before the DUKE's palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter the DUKE of Florence, BERTRAM, PAROLLES, Soldiers, Drum, and Trumpets
DUKE: The general of our horse thou art, and we,
DUKE: Great in our hope, lay our best love and credence
DUKE: Upon thy promising fortune.
BERTRAM: Sir, it is
BERTRAM: A charge too heavy for my strength, but yet
BERTRAM: We'll strive to bear it for your worthy sake
BERTRAM: To the extreme edge of hazard.
DUKE: Then go thou forth,
DUKE: And fortune play upon thy prosperous helm,
DUKE: As thy auspicious mistress!
BERTRAM: This very day,
BERTRAM: Great Mars, I put myself into thy file:
BERTRAM: Make me but like my thoughts, and I shall prove
BERTRAM: A lover of thy drum, hater of love.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter COUNTESS and Steward
COUNTESS: Alas! and would you take the letter of her?
COUNTESS: Might you not know she would do as she has done,
COUNTESS: By sending me a letter? Read it again.
Steward: [Reads]
Steward: I am Saint Jaques' pilgrim, thither gone:
Steward: Ambitious love hath so in me offended,
Steward: That barefoot plod I the cold ground upon,
Steward: With sainted vow my faults to have amended.
Steward: Write, write, that from the bloody course of war
Steward: My dearest master, your dear son, may hie:
Steward: Bless him at home in peace, whilst I from far
Steward: His name with zealous fervor sanctify:
Steward: His taken labours bid him me forgive,
Steward: I, his despiteful Juno, sent him forth
Steward: From courtly friends, with camping foes to live,
Steward: Where death and danger dogs the heels of worth:
Steward: He is too good and fair for death and me:
Steward: Whom I myself embrace, to set him free.
COUNTESS: Ah, what sharp stings are in her mildest words!
COUNTESS: Rinaldo, you did never lack advice so much,
COUNTESS: As letting her pass so: had I spoke with her,
COUNTESS: I could have well diverted her intents,
COUNTESS: Which thus she hath prevented.
Steward: Pardon me, madam:
Steward: If I had given you this at over-night,
Steward: She might have been o'erta'en, and yet she writes,
Steward: Pursuit would be but vain.
COUNTESS: What angel shall
COUNTESS: Bless this unworthy husband? he cannot thrive,
COUNTESS: Unless her prayers, whom heaven delights to hear
COUNTESS: And loves to grant, reprieve him from the wrath
COUNTESS: Of greatest justice. Write, write, Rinaldo,
COUNTESS: To this unworthy husband of his wife,
COUNTESS: Let every word weigh heavy of her worth
COUNTESS: That he does weigh too light: my greatest grief.
COUNTESS: Though little he do feel it, set down sharply.
COUNTESS: Dispatch the most convenient messenger:
COUNTESS: When haply he shall hear that she is gone,
COUNTESS: He will return, and hope I may that she,
COUNTESS: Hearing so much, will speed her foot again,
COUNTESS: Led hither by pure love: which of them both
COUNTESS: Is dearest to me. I have no skill in sense
COUNTESS: To make distinction: provide this messenger:
COUNTESS: My heart is heavy and mine age is weak,
COUNTESS: Grief would have tears, and sorrow bids me speak.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Florence. Without the walls. A tucket afar off.
NARRATOR: Enter an old Widow of Florence, DIANA, VIOLENTA, and MARIANA, with other Citizens
Widow: Nay, come, for if they do approach the city, we
Widow: shall lose all the sight.
DIANA: They say the French count has done most honourable service.
Widow: It is reported that he has taken their greatest
Widow: commander, and that with his own hand he slew the
Widow: duke's brother.
NARRATOR: Tucket
Widow: We have lost our labour, they are gone a contrary
Widow: way: hark! you may know by their trumpets.
MARIANA: Come, let's return again, and suffice ourselves with
MARIANA: the report of it. Well, Diana, take heed of this
MARIANA: French earl: the honour of a maid is her name, and
MARIANA: no legacy is so rich as honesty.
Widow: I have told my neighbour how you have been solicited
Widow: by a gentleman his companion.
MARIANA: I know that knave, hang him! one Parolles: a
MARIANA: filthy officer he is in those suggestions for the
MARIANA: young earl. Beware of them, Diana, their promises,
MARIANA: enticements, oaths, tokens, and all these engines of
MARIANA: lust, are not the things they go under: many a maid
MARIANA: hath been seduced by them, and the misery is,
MARIANA: example, that so terrible shows in the wreck of
MARIANA: maidenhood, cannot for all that dissuade succession,
MARIANA: but that they are limed with the twigs that threaten
MARIANA: them. I hope I need not to advise you further, but
MARIANA: I hope your own grace will keep you where you are,
MARIANA: though there were no further danger known but the
MARIANA: modesty which is so lost.
DIANA: You shall not need to fear me.
Widow: I hope so.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA, disguised like a Pilgrim
Widow: Look, here comes a pilgrim: I know she will lie at
Widow: my house, thither they send one another: I'll
Widow: question her. God save you, pilgrim! whither are you bound?
HELENA: To Saint Jaques le Grand.
HELENA: Where do the palmers lodge, I do beseech you?
Widow: At the Saint Francis here beside the port.
HELENA: Is this the way?
Widow: Ay, marry, is't.
NARRATOR: A march afar
Widow: Hark you! they come this way.
Widow: If you will tarry, holy pilgrim,
Widow: But till the troops come by,
Widow: I will conduct you where you shall be lodged,
Widow: The rather, for I think I know your hostess
Widow: As ample as myself.
HELENA: Is it yourself?
Widow: If you shall please so, pilgrim.
HELENA: I thank you, and will stay upon your leisure.
Widow: You came, I think, from France?
HELENA: I did so.
Widow: Here you shall see a countryman of yours
Widow: That has done worthy service.
HELENA: His name, I pray you.
DIANA: The Count Rousillon: know you such a one?
HELENA: But by the ear, that hears most nobly of him:
HELENA: His face I know not.
DIANA: Whatsome'er he is,
DIANA: He's bravely taken here. He stole from France,
