DIANA: As 'tis reported, for the king had married him
DIANA: Against his liking: think you it is so?
HELENA: Ay, surely, mere the truth: I know his lady.
DIANA: There is a gentleman that serves the count
DIANA: Reports but coarsely of her.
HELENA: What's his name?
DIANA: Monsieur Parolles.
HELENA: O, I believe with him,
HELENA: In argument of praise, or to the worth
HELENA: Of the great count himself, she is too mean
HELENA: To have her name repeated: all her deserving
HELENA: Is a reserved honesty, and that
HELENA: I have not heard examined.
DIANA: Alas, poor lady!
DIANA: 'Tis a hard bondage to become the wife
DIANA: Of a detesting lord.
Widow: I warrant, good creature, wheresoe'er she is,
Widow: Her heart weighs sadly: this young maid might do her
Widow: A shrewd turn, if she pleased.
HELENA: How do you mean?
HELENA: May be the amorous count solicits her
HELENA: In the unlawful purpose.
Widow: He does indeed,
Widow: And brokes with all that can in such a suit
Widow: Corrupt the tender honour of a maid:
Widow: But she is arm'd for him and keeps her guard
Widow: In honestest defence.
MARIANA: The gods forbid else!
Widow: So, now they come:
NARRATOR: Drum and Colours
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM, PAROLLES, and the whole army
Widow: That is Antonio, the duke's eldest son,
Widow: That, Escalus.
HELENA: Which is the Frenchman?
DIANA: He,
DIANA: That with the plume: 'tis a most gallant fellow.
DIANA: I would he loved his wife: if he were honester
DIANA: He were much goodlier: is't not a handsome gentleman?
HELENA: I like him well.
DIANA: 'Tis pity he is not honest: yond's that same knave
DIANA: That leads him to these places: were I his lady,
DIANA: I would Poison that vile rascal.
HELENA: Which is he?
DIANA: That jack-an-apes with scarfs: why is he melancholy?
HELENA: Perchance he's hurt i' the battle.
PAROLLES: Lose our drum! well.
MARIANA: He's shrewdly vexed at something: look, he has spied us.
Widow: Marry, hang you!
MARIANA: And your courtesy, for a ring-carrier!
NARRATOR: Exeunt BERTRAM, PAROLLES, and army
Widow: The troop is past. Come, pilgrim, I will bring you
Widow: Where you shall host: of enjoin'd penitents
Widow: There's four or five, to great Saint Jaques bound,
Widow: Already at my house.
HELENA: I humbly thank you:
HELENA: Please it this matron and this gentle maid
HELENA: To eat with us to-night, the charge and thanking
HELENA: Shall be for me, and, to requite you further,
HELENA: I will bestow some precepts of this virgin
HELENA: Worthy the note.
BOTH: We'll take your offer kindly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Camp before Florence.
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM and the two French Lords
Second Lord: Nay, good my lord, put him to't, let him have his
Second Lord: way.
First Lord: If your lordship find him not a hilding, hold me no
First Lord: more in your respect.
Second Lord: On my life, my lord, a bubble.
BERTRAM: Do you think I am so far deceived in him?
Second Lord: Believe it, my lord, in mine own direct knowledge,
Second Lord: without any malice, but to speak of him as my
Second Lord: kinsman, he's a most notable coward, an infinite and
Second Lord: endless liar, an hourly promise-breaker, the owner
Second Lord: of no one good quality worthy your lordship's
Second Lord: entertainment.
First Lord: It were fit you knew him, lest, reposing too far in
First Lord: his virtue, which he hath not, he might at some
First Lord: great and trusty business in a main danger fail you.
BERTRAM: I would I knew in what particular action to try him.
First Lord: None better than to let him fetch off his drum,
First Lord: which you hear him so confidently undertake to do.
Second Lord: I, with a troop of Florentines, will suddenly
Second Lord: surprise him, such I will have, whom I am sure he
Second Lord: knows not from the enemy: we will bind and hoodwink
Second Lord: him so, that he shall suppose no other but that he
Second Lord: is carried into the leaguer of the adversaries, when
Second Lord: we bring him to our own tents. Be but your lordship
Second Lord: present at his examination: if he do not, for the
Second Lord: promise of his life and in the highest compulsion of
Second Lord: base fear, offer to betray you and deliver all the
Second Lord: intelligence in his power against you, and that with
Second Lord: the divine forfeit of his soul upon oath, never
Second Lord: trust my judgment in any thing.
First Lord: O, for the love of laughter, let him fetch his drum,
First Lord: he says he has a stratagem for't: when your
First Lord: lordship sees the bottom of his success in't, and to
First Lord: what metal this counterfeit lump of ore will be
First Lord: melted, if you give him not John Drum's
First Lord: entertainment, your inclining cannot be removed.
First Lord: Here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES
Second Lord: [Aside to BERTRAM]  O, for the love of laughter,
Second Lord: hinder not the honour of his design: let him fetch
Second Lord: off his drum in any hand.
BERTRAM: How now, monsieur! this drum sticks sorely in your
BERTRAM: disposition.
First Lord: A pox on't, let it go, 'tis but a drum.
PAROLLES: 'But a drum'! is't 'but a drum'? A drum so lost!
PAROLLES: There was excellent command,--to charge in with our
PAROLLES: horse upon our own wings, and to rend our own soldiers!
First Lord: That was not to be blamed in the command of the
First Lord: service: it was a disaster of war that Caesar
First Lord: himself could not have prevented, if he had been
First Lord: there to command.
BERTRAM: Well, we cannot greatly condemn our success: some
BERTRAM: dishonour we had in the loss of that drum, but it is
BERTRAM: not to be recovered.
PAROLLES: It might have been recovered.
BERTRAM: It might, but it is not now.
PAROLLES: It is to be recovered: but that the merit of
PAROLLES: service is seldom attributed to the true and exact
PAROLLES: performer, I would have that drum or another, or
PAROLLES: 'hic jacet.'
BERTRAM: Why, if you have a stomach, to't, monsieur: if you
BERTRAM: think your mystery in stratagem can bring this
BERTRAM: instrument of honour again into his native quarter,
BERTRAM: be magnanimous in the enterprise and go on, I will
BERTRAM: grace the attempt for a worthy exploit: if you
BERTRAM: speed well in it, the duke shall both speak of it.
BERTRAM: and extend to you what further becomes his
BERTRAM: greatness, even to the utmost syllable of your
BERTRAM: worthiness.
PAROLLES: By the hand of a soldier, I will undertake it.
BERTRAM: But you must not now slumber in it.
PAROLLES: I'll about it this evening: and I will presently
PAROLLES: pen down my dilemmas, encourage myself in my
PAROLLES: certainty, put myself into my mortal preparation,
PAROLLES: and by midnight look to hear further from me.
BERTRAM: May I be bold to acquaint his grace you are gone about it?
PAROLLES: I know not what the success will be, my lord, but
PAROLLES: the attempt I vow.
BERTRAM: I know thou'rt valiant, and, to the possibility of
BERTRAM: thy soldiership, will subscribe for thee. Farewell.
PAROLLES: I love not many words.
NARRATOR: Exit
Second Lord: No more than a fish loves water. Is not this a
Second Lord: strange fellow, my lord, that so confidently seems
Second Lord: to undertake this business, which he knows is not to
Second Lord: be done, damns himself to do and dares better be
Second Lord: damned than to do't?
First Lord: You do not know him, my lord, as we do: certain it
First Lord: is that he will steal himself into a man's favour and
First Lord: for a week escape a great deal of discoveries, but
First Lord: when you find him out, you have him ever after.
BERTRAM: Why, do you think he will make no deed at all of
BERTRAM: this that so seriously he does address himself unto?
Second Lord: None in the world, but return with an invention and
Second Lord: clap upon you two or three probable lies: but we
Second Lord: have almost embossed him, you shall see his fall
Second Lord: to-night, for indeed he is not for your lordship's respect.
First Lord: We'll make you some sport with the fox ere we case
First Lord: him. He was first smoked by the old lord Lafeu:
First Lord: when his disguise and he is parted, tell me what a
First Lord: sprat you shall find him, which you shall see this
First Lord: very night.
Second Lord: I must go look my twigs: he shall be caught.
BERTRAM: Your brother he shall go along with me.
Second Lord: As't please your lordship: I'll leave you.
NARRATOR: Exit
BERTRAM: Now will I lead you to the house, and show you
BERTRAM: The lass I spoke of.
First Lord: But you say she's honest.
BERTRAM: That's all the fault: I spoke with her but once
BERTRAM: And found her wondrous cold, but I sent to her,
BERTRAM: By this same coxcomb that we have i' the wind,
BERTRAM: Tokens and letters which she did re-send,
BERTRAM: And this is all I have done. She's a fair creature:
BERTRAM: Will you go see her?
First Lord: With all my heart, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Florence. The Widow's house.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA and Widow
HELENA: If you misdoubt me that I am not she,
HELENA: I know not how I shall assure you further,
HELENA: But I shall lose the grounds I work upon.
Widow: Though my estate be fallen, I was well born,
Widow: Nothing acquainted with these businesses,
Widow: And would not put my reputation now
Widow: In any staining act.
HELENA: Nor would I wish you.
HELENA: First, give me trust, the count he is my husband,
HELENA: And what to your sworn counsel I have spoken
HELENA: Is so from word to word, and then you cannot,
HELENA: By the good aid that I of you shall borrow,
HELENA: Err in bestowing it.
Widow: I should believe you:
Widow: For you have show'd me that which well approves
Widow: You're great in fortune.
HELENA: Take this purse of gold,
HELENA: And let me buy your friendly help thus far,
HELENA: Which I will over-pay and pay again
HELENA: When I have found it. The count he wooes your daughter,
HELENA: Lays down his wanton siege before her beauty,
HELENA: Resolved to carry her: let her in fine consent,
HELENA: As we'll direct her how 'tis best to bear it.
HELENA: Now his important blood will nought deny
HELENA: That she'll demand: a ring the county wears,
HELENA: That downward hath succeeded in his house
HELENA: From son to son, some four or five descents
HELENA: Since the first father wore it: this ring he holds
HELENA: In most rich choice, yet in his idle fire,
HELENA: To buy his will, it would not seem too dear,
HELENA: Howe'er repented after.
Widow: Now I see
Widow: The bottom of your purpose.
HELENA: You see it lawful, then: it is no more,
HELENA: But that your daughter, ere she seems as won,
HELENA: Desires this ring, appoints him an encounter,
HELENA: In fine, delivers me to fill the time,
HELENA: Herself most chastely absent: after this,
HELENA: To marry her, I'll add three thousand crowns
HELENA: To what is passed already.
Widow: I have yielded:
Widow: Instruct my daughter how she shall persever,
Widow: That time and place with this deceit so lawful
Widow: May prove coherent. Every night he comes
Widow: With musics of all sorts and songs composed
Widow: To her unworthiness: it nothing steads us
Widow: To chide him from our eaves, for he persists
Widow: As if his life lay on't.
HELENA: Why then to-night
HELENA: Let us assay our plot, which, if it speed,
HELENA: Is wicked meaning in a lawful deed
HELENA: And lawful meaning in a lawful act,
HELENA: Where both not sin, and yet a sinful fact:
HELENA: But let's about it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Without the Florentine camp.
NARRATOR: Enter Second French Lord, with five or six other Soldiers in ambush
Second Lord: He can come no other way but by this hedge-corner.
Second Lord: When you sally upon him, speak what terrible
Second Lord: language you will: though you understand it not
Second Lord: yourselves, no matter, for we must not seem to
Second Lord: understand him, unless some one among us whom we
Second Lord: must produce for an interpreter.
First Soldier: Good captain, let me be the interpreter.
Second Lord: Art not acquainted with him? knows he not thy voice?
First Soldier: No, sir, I warrant you.
Second Lord: But what linsey-woolsey hast thou to speak to us again?
First Soldier: E'en such as you speak to me.
Second Lord: He must think us some band of strangers i' the
Second Lord: adversary's entertainment. Now he hath a smack of
Second Lord: all neighbouring languages, therefore we must every
Second Lord: one be a man of his own fancy, not to know what we
Second Lord: speak one to another, so we seem to know, is to
Second Lord: know straight our purpose: choughs' language,
Second Lord: gabble enough, and good enough. As for you,
Second Lord: interpreter, you must seem very politic. But couch,
Second Lord: ho! here he comes, to beguile two hours in a sleep,
Second Lord: and then to return and swear the lies he forges.
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES
PAROLLES: Ten o'clock: within these three hours 'twill be
PAROLLES: time enough to go home. What shall I say I have
PAROLLES: done? It must be a very plausive invention that
PAROLLES: carries it: they begin to smoke me, and disgraces
PAROLLES: have of late knocked too often at my door. I find
PAROLLES: my tongue is too foolhardy, but my heart hath the
PAROLLES: fear of Mars before it and of his creatures, not
PAROLLES: daring the reports of my tongue.
Second Lord: This is the first truth that e'er thine own tongue
Second Lord: was guilty of.
PAROLLES: What the devil should move me to undertake the
PAROLLES: recovery of this drum, being not ignorant of the
PAROLLES: impossibility, and knowing I had no such purpose? I
PAROLLES: must give myself some hurts, and say I got them in
PAROLLES: exploit: yet slight ones will not carry it, they
PAROLLES: will say, 'Came you off with so little?' and great
PAROLLES: ones I dare not give. Wherefore, what's the
PAROLLES: instance? Tongue, I must put you into a
PAROLLES: butter-woman's mouth and buy myself another of
PAROLLES: Bajazet's mule, if you prattle me into these perils.
Second Lord: Is it possible he should know what he is, and be
Second Lord: that he is?
PAROLLES: I would the cutting of my garments would serve the
PAROLLES: turn, or the breaking of my Spanish sword.
Second Lord: We cannot afford you so.
PAROLLES: Or the baring of my beard, and to say it was in
PAROLLES: stratagem.
Second Lord: 'Twould not do.
PAROLLES: Or to drown my clothes, and say I was stripped.
Second Lord: Hardly serve.
PAROLLES: Though I swore I leaped from the window of the citadel.
Second Lord: How deep?
PAROLLES: Thirty fathom.
Second Lord: Three great oaths would scarce make that be believed.
PAROLLES: I would I had any drum of the enemy's: I would swear
PAROLLES: I recovered it.
Second Lord: You shall hear one anon.
PAROLLES: A drum now of the enemy's,--
NARRATOR: Alarum within
Second Lord: Throca movousus, cargo, cargo, cargo.
All: Cargo, cargo, cargo, villiando par corbo, cargo.
PAROLLES: O, ransom, ransom! do not hide mine eyes.
NARRATOR: They seize and blindfold him
First Soldier: Boskos thromuldo boskos.
PAROLLES: I know you are the Muskos' regiment:
PAROLLES: And I shall lose my life for want of language,
PAROLLES: If there be here German, or Dane, low Dutch,
PAROLLES: Italian, or French, let him speak to me, I'll
PAROLLES: Discover that which shall undo the Florentine.
First Soldier: Boskos vauvado: I understand thee, and can speak
First Soldier: thy tongue. Kerely bonto, sir, betake thee to thy
First Soldier: faith, for seventeen poniards are at thy bosom.
PAROLLES: O!
First Soldier: O, pray, pray, pray! Manka revania dulche.
Second Lord: Oscorbidulchos volivorco.
First Soldier: The general is content to spare thee yet,
First Soldier: And, hoodwink'd as thou art, will lead thee on
First Soldier: To gather from thee: haply thou mayst inform
First Soldier: Something to save thy life.
PAROLLES: O, let me live!
PAROLLES: And all the secrets of our camp I'll show,
PAROLLES: Their force, their purposes, nay, I'll speak that
PAROLLES: Which you will wonder at.
First Soldier: But wilt thou faithfully?
PAROLLES: If I do not, damn me.
First Soldier: Acordo linta.
First Soldier: Come on, thou art granted space.
NARRATOR: Exit, with PAROLLES guarded. A short alarum within
Second Lord: Go, tell the Count Rousillon, and my brother,
Second Lord: We have caught the woodcock, and will keep him muffled
Second Lord: Till we do hear from them.
Second Soldier: Captain, I will.
Second Lord: A' will betray us all unto ourselves:
Second Lord: Inform on that.
Second Soldier: So I will, sir.
Second Lord: Till then I'll keep him dark and safely lock'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Florence. The Widow's house.
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM and DIANA
BERTRAM: They told me that your name was Fontibell.
DIANA: No, my good lord, Diana.
BERTRAM: Titled goddess,
BERTRAM: And worth it, with addition! But, fair soul,
BERTRAM: In your fine frame hath love no quality?
BERTRAM: If quick fire of youth light not your mind,
BERTRAM: You are no maiden, but a monument:
BERTRAM: When you are dead, you should be such a one
BERTRAM: As you are now, for you are cold and stem,
BERTRAM: And now you should be as your mother was
BERTRAM: When your sweet self was got.
DIANA: She then was honest.
BERTRAM: So should you be.
DIANA: No:
DIANA: My mother did but duty, such, my lord,
DIANA: As you owe to your wife.
BERTRAM: No more o' that,
BERTRAM: I prithee, do not strive against my vows:
BERTRAM: I was compell'd to her, but I love thee
BERTRAM: By love's own sweet constraint, and will for ever
BERTRAM: Do thee all rights of service.
DIANA: Ay, so you serve us
DIANA: Till we serve you, but when you have our roses,
DIANA: You barely leave our thorns to prick ourselves
DIANA: And mock us with our bareness.
BERTRAM: How have I sworn!
DIANA: 'Tis not the many oaths that makes the truth,
DIANA: But the plain single vow that is vow'd true.
DIANA: What is not holy, that we swear not by,
DIANA: But take the High'st to witness: then, pray you, tell me,
DIANA: If I should swear by God's great attributes,
DIANA: I loved you dearly, would you believe my oaths,
DIANA: When I did love you ill? This has no holding,
DIANA: To swear by him whom I protest to love,
DIANA: That I will work against him: therefore your oaths
DIANA: Are words and poor conditions, but unseal'd,
DIANA: At least in my opinion.
BERTRAM: Change it, change it,
BERTRAM: Be not so holy-cruel: love is holy,
BERTRAM: And my integrity ne'er knew the crafts
BERTRAM: That you do charge men with. Stand no more off,
BERTRAM: But give thyself unto my sick desires,
BERTRAM: Who then recover: say thou art mine, and ever
BERTRAM: My love as it begins shall so persever.
DIANA: I see that men make ropes in such a scarre
DIANA: That we'll forsake ourselves. Give me that ring.
BERTRAM: I'll lend it thee, my dear, but have no power
BERTRAM: To give it from me.
DIANA: Will you not, my lord?
BERTRAM: It is an honour 'longing to our house,
BERTRAM: Bequeathed down from many ancestors,
BERTRAM: Which were the greatest obloquy i' the world
BERTRAM: In me to lose.
DIANA: Mine honour's such a ring:
DIANA: My chastity's the jewel of our house,
DIANA: Bequeathed down from many ancestors,
DIANA: Which were the greatest obloquy i' the world
DIANA: In me to lose: thus your own proper wisdom
DIANA: Brings in the champion Honour on my part,
DIANA: Against your vain assault.
BERTRAM: Here, take my ring:
BERTRAM: My house, mine honour, yea, my life, be thine,
BERTRAM: And I'll be bid by thee.
DIANA: When midnight comes, knock at my chamber-window:
DIANA: I'll order take my mother shall not hear.
DIANA: Now will I charge you in the band of truth,
DIANA: When you have conquer'd my yet maiden bed,
DIANA: Remain there but an hour, nor speak to me:
DIANA: My reasons are most strong, and you shall know them
DIANA: When back again this ring shall be deliver'd:
DIANA: And on your finger in the night I'll put
DIANA: Another ring, that what in time proceeds
DIANA: May token to the future our past deeds.
DIANA: Adieu, till then, then, fail not. You have won
DIANA: A wife of me, though there my hope be done.
BERTRAM: A heaven on earth I have won by wooing thee.
NARRATOR: Exit
DIANA: For which live long to thank both heaven and me!
DIANA: You may so in the end.
DIANA: My mother told me just how he would woo,
DIANA: As if she sat in 's heart, she says all men
DIANA: Have the like oaths: he had sworn to marry me
DIANA: When his wife's dead, therefore I'll lie with him
DIANA: When I am buried. Since Frenchmen are so braid,
DIANA: Marry that will, I live and die a maid:
DIANA: Only in this disguise I think't no sin
DIANA: To cozen him that would unjustly win.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Florentine camp.
NARRATOR: Enter the two French Lords and some two or three Soldiers
First Lord: You have not given him his mother's letter?
Second Lord: I have delivered it an hour since: there is
Second Lord: something in't that stings his nature, for on the
Second Lord: reading it he changed almost into another man.
First Lord: He has much worthy blame laid upon him for shaking
First Lord: off so good a wife and so sweet a lady.
Second Lord: Especially he hath incurred the everlasting
Second Lord: displeasure of the king, who had even tuned his
Second Lord: bounty to sing happiness to him. I will tell you a
Second Lord: thing, but you shall let it dwell darkly with you.
First Lord: When you have spoken it, 'tis dead, and I am the
First Lord: grave of it.
Second Lord: He hath perverted a young gentlewoman here in
Second Lord: Florence, of a most chaste renown, and this night he
Second Lord: fleshes his will in the spoil of her honour: he hath
Second Lord: given her his monumental ring, and thinks himself
Second Lord: made in the unchaste composition.
First Lord: Now, God delay our rebellion! as we are ourselves,
First Lord: what things are we!
Second Lord: Merely our own traitors. And as in the common course
Second Lord: of all treasons, we still see them reveal
Second Lord: themselves, till they attain to their abhorred ends,
Second Lord: so he that in this action contrives against his own
Second Lord: nobility, in his proper stream o'erflows himself.
First Lord: Is it not meant damnable in us, to be trumpeters of
First Lord: our unlawful intents? We shall not then have his
First Lord: company to-night?
Second Lord: Not till after midnight, for he is dieted to his hour.
First Lord: That approaches apace, I would gladly have him see
First Lord: his company anatomized, that he might take a measure
First Lord: of his own judgments, wherein so curiously he had
First Lord: set this counterfeit.
Second Lord: We will not meddle with him till he come, for his
Second Lord: presence must be the whip of the other.
First Lord: In the mean time, what hear you of these wars?
Second Lord: I hear there is an overture of peace.
First Lord: Nay, I assure you, a peace concluded.
Second Lord: What will Count Rousillon do then? will he travel
Second Lord: higher, or return again into France?
First Lord: I perceive, by this demand, you are not altogether
First Lord: of his council.
Second Lord: Let it be forbid, sir, so should I be a great deal
Second Lord: of his act.
First Lord: Sir, his wife some two months since fled from his
First Lord: house: her pretence is a pilgrimage to Saint Jaques
First Lord: le Grand, which holy undertaking with most austere
First Lord: sanctimony she accomplished, and, there residing the
First Lord: tenderness of her nature became as a prey to her
First Lord: grief, in fine, made a groan of her last breath, and
First Lord: now she sings in heaven.
Second Lord: How is this justified?
First Lord: The stronger part of it by her own letters, which
First Lord: makes her story true, even to the point of her
First Lord: death: her death itself, which could not be her
First Lord: office to say is come, was faithfully confirmed by
First Lord: the rector of the place.
Second Lord: Hath the count all this intelligence?
First Lord: Ay, and the particular confirmations, point from
First Lord: point, so to the full arming of the verity.
Second Lord: I am heartily sorry that he'll be glad of this.
First Lord: How mightily sometimes we make us comforts of our losses!
Second Lord: And how mightily some other times we drown our gain
Second Lord: in tears! The great dignity that his valour hath
Second Lord: here acquired for him shall at home be encountered
Second Lord: with a shame as ample.
First Lord: The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and
First Lord: ill together: our virtues would be proud, if our
First Lord: faults whipped them not, and our crimes would
First Lord: despair, if they were not cherished by our virtues.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
First Lord: How now! where's your master?
Servant: He met the duke in the street, sir, of whom he hath
Servant: taken a solemn leave: his lordship will next
Servant: morning for France. The duke hath offered him
Servant: letters of commendations to the king.
Second Lord: They shall be no more than needful there, if they
Second Lord: were more than they can commend.
First Lord: They cannot be too sweet for the king's tartness.
First Lord: Here's his lordship now.
NARRATOR: Enter BERTRAM
First Lord: How now, my lord! is't not after midnight?
BERTRAM: I have to-night dispatched sixteen businesses, a
BERTRAM: month's length a-piece, by an abstract of success:
BERTRAM: I have congied with the duke, done my adieu with his
BERTRAM: nearest, buried a wife, mourned for her, writ to my
BERTRAM: lady mother I am returning, entertained my convoy,
BERTRAM: and between these main parcels of dispatch effected
BERTRAM: many nicer needs, the last was the greatest, but
BERTRAM: that I have not ended yet.
Second Lord: If the business be of any difficulty, and this
Second Lord: morning your departure hence, it requires haste of
Second Lord: your lordship.
BERTRAM: I mean, the business is not ended, as fearing to
BERTRAM: hear of it hereafter. But shall we have this
BERTRAM: dialogue between the fool and the soldier? Come,
BERTRAM: bring forth this counterfeit module, he has deceived
BERTRAM: me, like a double-meaning prophesier.
Second Lord: Bring him forth: has sat i' the stocks all night,
Second Lord: poor gallant knave.
BERTRAM: No matter: his heels have deserved it, in usurping
BERTRAM: his spurs so long. How does he carry himself?
Second Lord: I have told your lordship already, the stocks carry
Second Lord: him. But to answer you as you would be understood,
Second Lord: he weeps like a wench that had shed her milk: he
Second Lord: hath confessed himself to Morgan, whom he supposes
Second Lord: to be a friar, from the time of his remembrance to
Second Lord: this very instant disaster of his setting i' the
Second Lord: stocks: and what think you he hath confessed?
BERTRAM: Nothing of me, has a'?
Second Lord: His confession is taken, and it shall be read to his
Second Lord: face: if your lordship be in't, as I believe you
Second Lord: are, you must have the patience to hear it.
NARRATOR: Enter PAROLLES guarded, and First Soldier
BERTRAM: A plague upon him! muffled! he can say nothing of
BERTRAM: me: hush, hush!
First Lord: Hoodman comes! Portotartarosa
First Soldier: He calls for the tortures: what will you say
First Soldier: without 'em?
PAROLLES: I will confess what I know without constraint: if
PAROLLES: ye pinch me like a pasty, I can say no more.
First Soldier: Bosko chimurcho.
First Lord: Boblibindo chicurmurco.
First Soldier: You are a merciful general. Our general bids you
First Soldier: answer to what I shall ask you out of a note.
PAROLLES: And truly, as I hope to live.
First Soldier: [Reads]  'First demand of him how many horse the
First Soldier: duke is strong.' What say you to that?
PAROLLES: Five or six thousand, but very weak and
PAROLLES: unserviceable: the troops are all scattered, and
PAROLLES: the commanders very poor rogues, upon my reputation
PAROLLES: and credit and as I hope to live.
First Soldier: Shall I set down your answer so?
PAROLLES: Do: I'll take the sacrament on't, how and which way you will.
BERTRAM: All's one to him. What a past-saving slave is this!
First Lord: You're deceived, my lord: this is Monsieur
First Lord: Parolles, the gallant militarist,--that was his own
First Lord: phrase,--that had the whole theoric of war in the
First Lord: knot of his scarf, and the practise in the chape of
First Lord: his dagger.
Second Lord: I will never trust a man again for keeping his sword
Second Lord: clean. nor believe he can have every thing in him
Second Lord: by wearing his apparel neatly.
First Soldier: Well, that's set down.
PAROLLES: Five or six thousand horse, I said,-- I will say
PAROLLES: true,--or thereabouts, set down, for I'll speak truth.
First Lord: He's very near the truth in this.
BERTRAM: But I con him no thanks for't, in the nature he
BERTRAM: delivers it.
PAROLLES: Poor rogues, I pray you, say.
First Soldier: Well, that's set down.
PAROLLES: I humbly thank you, sir: a truth's a truth, the
PAROLLES: rogues are marvellous poor.
First Soldier: [Reads]  'Demand of him, of what strength they are
First Soldier: a-foot.' What say you to that?
PAROLLES: By my troth, sir, if I were to live this present
PAROLLES: hour, I will tell true. Let me see: Spurio, a
PAROLLES: hundred and fifty, Sebastian, so many, Corambus, so
PAROLLES: many, Jaques, so many, Guiltian, Cosmo, Lodowick,
PAROLLES: and Gratii, two hundred and fifty each, mine own
PAROLLES: company, Chitopher, Vaumond, Bentii, two hundred and
PAROLLES: fifty each: so that the muster-file, rotten and
PAROLLES: sound, upon my life, amounts not to fifteen thousand
PAROLLES: poll, half of the which dare not shake snow from off
PAROLLES: their cassocks, lest they shake themselves to pieces.
BERTRAM: What shall be done to him?
First Lord: Nothing, but let him have thanks. Demand of him my
First Lord: condition, and what credit I have with the duke.
First Soldier: Well, that's set down.
NARRATOR: Reads
First Soldier: 'You shall demand of him, whether one Captain Dumain
First Soldier: be i' the camp, a Frenchman, what his reputation is
First Soldier: with the duke, what his valour, honesty, and
First Soldier: expertness in wars, or whether he thinks it were not
First Soldier: possible, with well-weighing sums of gold, to
First Soldier: corrupt him to revolt.' What say you to this? what
First Soldier: do you know of it?

PAROLLES: the inter'gatories: demand them singly.

BERTRAM: Nay, by your leave, hold your hands, though I know
BERTRAM: his brains are forfeit to the next tile that falls.

PAROLLES: Upon my knowledge, he is, and lousy.
First Lord: Nay look not so upon me, we shall hear of your
First Lord: lordship anon.
First Soldier: What is his reputation with the duke?

PAROLLES: of mine, and writ to me this other day to turn him
PAROLLES: out o' the band: I think I have his letter in my pocket.
First Soldier: Marry, we'll search.
PAROLLES: In good sadness, I do not know, either it is there,
PAROLLES: or it is upon a file with the duke's other letters
PAROLLES: in my tent.
First Soldier: Here 'tis, here's a paper: shall I read it to you?
PAROLLES: I do not know if it be it or no.
BERTRAM: Our interpreter does it well.
First Lord: Excellently.
First Soldier: [Reads]  'Dian, the count's a fool, and full of gold,'--
PAROLLES: That is not the duke's letter, sir, that is an
PAROLLES: advertisement to a proper maid in Florence, one
PAROLLES: Diana, to take heed of the allurement of one Count

First Soldier: Nay, I'll read it first, by your favour.

PAROLLES: behalf of the maid, for I knew the young count to be
PAROLLES: a dangerous and lascivious boy, who is a whale to
PAROLLES: virginity and devours up all the fry it finds.
BERTRAM: Damnable both-sides rogue!
First Soldier: [Reads]  'When he swears oaths, bid him drop gold, and take it,
First Soldier: After he scores, he never pays the score:
First Soldier: Half won is match well made, match, and well make it,
First Soldier: He ne'er pays after-debts, take it before,
First Soldier: And say a soldier, Dian, told thee this,
First Soldier: Men are to mell with, boys are not to kiss:
First Soldier: For count of this, the count's a fool, I know it,
First Soldier: Who pays before, but not when he does owe it.
First Soldier: Thine, as he vowed to thee in thine ear,
First Soldier: PAROLLES.'
BERTRAM: He shall be whipped through the army with this rhyme
BERTRAM: in's forehead.
Second Lord: This is your devoted friend, sir, the manifold
Second Lord: linguist and the armipotent soldier.
BERTRAM: I could endure any thing before but a cat, and now
BERTRAM: he's a cat to me.
First Soldier: I perceive, sir, by the general's looks, we shall be
First Soldier: fain to hang you.
PAROLLES: My life, sir, in any case: not that I am afraid to
PAROLLES: die, but that, my offences being many, I would
PAROLLES: repent out the remainder of nature: let me live,
PAROLLES: sir, in a dungeon, i' the stocks, or any where, so I may live.
First Soldier: We'll see what may be done, so you confess freely,

First Soldier: have answered to his reputation with the duke and to

PAROLLES: He will steal, sir, an egg out of a cloister: for
PAROLLES: rapes and ravishments he parallels Nessus: he
PAROLLES: professes not keeping of oaths, in breaking 'em he
PAROLLES: is stronger than Hercules: he will lie, sir, with
PAROLLES: such volubility, that you would think truth were a
PAROLLES: fool: drunkenness is his best virtue, for he will
PAROLLES: be swine-drunk, and in his sleep he does little
PAROLLES: harm, save to his bed-clothes about him, but they

PAROLLES: every thing that an honest man should not have, what
PAROLLES: an honest man should have, he has nothing.
First Lord: I begin to love him for this.
BERTRAM: For this description of thine honesty? A pox upon
BERTRAM: him for me, he's more and more a cat.
First Soldier: What say you to his expertness in war?
PAROLLES: Faith, sir, he has led the drum before the English
PAROLLES: tragedians, to belie him, I will not, and more of
PAROLLES: his soldiership I know not, except, in that country
PAROLLES: he had the honour to be the officer at a place there
PAROLLES: called Mile-end, to instruct for the doubling of
PAROLLES: files: I would do the man what honour I can, but of
PAROLLES: this I am not certain.
First Lord: He hath out-villained villany so far, that the
First Lord: rarity redeems him.
BERTRAM: A pox on him, he's a cat still.
First Soldier: His qualities being at this poor price, I need not
First Soldier: to ask you if gold will corrupt him to revolt.
PAROLLES: Sir, for a quart d'ecu he will sell the fee-simple
PAROLLES: of his salvation, the inheritance of it, and cut the
PAROLLES: entail from all remainders, and a perpetual
PAROLLES: succession for it perpetually.
First Soldier: What's his brother, the other Captain Dumain?
Second Lord: Why does be ask him of me?
First Soldier: What's he?
PAROLLES: E'en a crow o' the same nest, not altogether so
PAROLLES: great as the first in goodness, but greater a great
PAROLLES: deal in evil: he excels his brother for a coward,
PAROLLES: yet his brother is reputed one of the best that is:
PAROLLES: in a retreat he outruns any lackey, marry, in coming
PAROLLES: on he has the cramp.
First Soldier: If your life be saved, will you undertake to betray
First Soldier: the Florentine?
PAROLLES: Ay, and the captain of his horse, Count Rousillon.
First Soldier: I'll whisper with the general, and know his pleasure.
PAROLLES: [Aside]  I'll no more drumming, a plague of all
PAROLLES: drums! Only to seem to deserve well, and to
PAROLLES: beguile the supposition of that lascivious young boy

First Soldier: discovered the secrets of your army and made such

NARRATOR: Unblinding him
First Lord: So, look about you: know you any here?
BERTRAM: Good morrow, noble captain.
Second Lord: God bless you, Captain Parolles.
First Lord: God save you, noble captain.
Second Lord: Captain, what greeting will you to my Lord Lafeu?

NARRATOR: Exeunt BERTRAM and Lords

First Soldier: has a knot on't yet
PAROLLES: Who cannot be crushed with a plot?

NARRATOR: Exit with Soldiers
PAROLLES: Yet am I thankful: if my heart were great,
PAROLLES: 'Twould burst at this. Captain I'll be no more,
PAROLLES: But I will eat and drink, and sleep as soft
PAROLLES: As captain shall: simply the thing I am
PAROLLES: Shall make me live. Who knows himself a braggart,
PAROLLES: Let him fear this, for it will come to pass
PAROLLES: that every braggart shall be found an ass.
PAROLLES: Rust, sword? cool, blushes! and, Parolles, live
PAROLLES: Safest in shame! being fool'd, by foolery thrive!
PAROLLES: There's place and means for every man alive.
PAROLLES: I'll after them.

NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Florence. The Widow's house.
NARRATOR: Enter HELENA, Widow, and DIANA
HELENA: That you may well perceive I have not wrong'd you,
HELENA: One of the greatest in the Christian world
HELENA: Shall be my surety, 'fore whose throne 'tis needful,
HELENA: Ere I can perfect mine intents, to kneel:
HELENA: Time was, I did him a desired office,
HELENA: Dear almost as his life, which gratitude
HELENA: Through flinty Tartar's bosom would peep forth,
HELENA: And answer, thanks: I duly am inform'd
HELENA: His grace is at Marseilles, to which place
HELENA: We have convenient convoy. You must know
HELENA: I am supposed dead: the army breaking,
HELENA: My husband hies him home, where, heaven aiding,
HELENA: And by the leave of my good lord the king,
HELENA: We'll be before our welcome.
Widow: Gentle madam,
Widow: You never had a servant to whose trust
Widow: Your business was more welcome.
HELENA: Nor you, mistress,
HELENA: Ever a friend whose thoughts more truly labour
HELENA: To recompense your love: doubt not but heaven
HELENA: Hath brought me up to be your daughter's dower,
HELENA: As it hath fated her to be my motive
HELENA: And helper to a husband. But, O strange men!
HELENA: That can such sweet use make of what they hate,
HELENA: When saucy trusting of the cozen'd thoughts
HELENA: Defiles the pitchy night: so lust doth play
HELENA: With what it loathes for that which is away.
HELENA: But more of this hereafter. You, Diana,
HELENA: Under my poor instructions yet must suffer
HELENA: Something in my behalf.
DIANA: Let death and honesty
DIANA: Go with your impositions, I am yours
DIANA: Upon your will to suffer.
HELENA: Yet, I pray you:
HELENA: But with the word the time will bring on summer,
HELENA: When briers shall have leaves as well as thorns,
HELENA: And be as sweet as sharp. We must away,
HELENA: Our wagon is prepared, and time revives us:
HELENA: All's well that ends well, still the fine's the crown,
HELENA: Whate'er the course, the end is the renown.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Rousillon. The COUNT's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter COUNTESS, LAFEU, and Clown
LAFEU: No, no, no, your son was misled with a snipt-taffeta
LAFEU: fellow there, whose villanous saffron would have
LAFEU: made all the unbaked and doughy youth of a nation in
LAFEU: his colour: your daughter-in-law had been alive at
LAFEU: this hour, and your son here at home, more advanced
LAFEU: by the king than by that red-tailed humble-bee I speak of.
COUNTESS: I would I had not known him, it was the death of the
COUNTESS: most virtuous gentlewoman that ever nature had
COUNTESS: praise for creating. If she had partaken of my
COUNTESS: flesh, and cost me the dearest groans of a mother, I
COUNTESS: could not have owed her a more rooted love.
LAFEU: 'Twas a good lady, 'twas a good lady: we may pick a
LAFEU: thousand salads ere we light on such another herb.
Clown: Indeed, sir, she was the sweet marjoram of the
Clown: salad, or rather, the herb of grace.
LAFEU: They are not herbs, you knave, they are nose-herbs.
Clown: I am no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir, I have not much
Clown: skill in grass.
LAFEU: Whether dost thou profess thyself, a knave or a fool?
Clown: A fool, sir, at a woman's service, and a knave at a man's.
LAFEU: Your distinction?
Clown: I would cozen the man of his wife and do his service.
LAFEU: So you were a knave at his service, indeed.
Clown: And I would give his wife my bauble, sir, to do her service.
LAFEU: I will subscribe for thee, thou art both knave and fool.
Clown: At your service.
LAFEU: No, no, no.
Clown: Why, sir, if I cannot serve you, I can serve as
Clown: great a prince as you are.
LAFEU: Who's that? a Frenchman?
Clown: Faith, sir, a' has an English name, but his fisnomy
Clown: is more hotter in France than there.
LAFEU: What prince is that?
Clown: The black prince, sir, alias, the prince of
Clown: darkness, alias, the devil.
LAFEU: Hold thee, there's my purse: I give thee not this
LAFEU: to suggest thee from thy master thou talkest of,
LAFEU: serve him still.
Clown: I am a woodland fellow, sir, that always loved a
Clown: great fire, and the master I speak of ever keeps a
Clown: good fire. But, sure, he is the prince of the
Clown: world, let his nobility remain in's court. I am for
Clown: the house with the narrow gate, which I take to be
Clown: too little for pomp to enter: some that humble
Clown: themselves may, but the many will be too chill and
Clown: tender, and they'll be for the flowery way that
Clown: leads to the broad gate and the great fire.
LAFEU: Go thy ways, I begin to be aweary of thee, and I
LAFEU: tell thee so before, because I would not fall out
LAFEU: with thee. Go thy ways: let my horses be well
LAFEU: looked to, without any tricks.
Clown: If I put any tricks upon 'em, sir, they shall be
Clown: jades' tricks, which are their own right by the law of nature.

LAFEU: A shrewd knave and an unhappy.
COUNTESS: So he is. My lord that's gone made himself much
COUNTESS: sport out of him: by his authority he remains here,
COUNTESS: which he thinks is a patent for his sauciness, and,
COUNTESS: indeed, he has no pace, but runs where he will.

LAFEU: tell you, since I heard of the good lady's death and

LAFEU: moved the king my master to speak in the behalf of

LAFEU: conceived against your son, there is no fitter
LAFEU: matter. How does your ladyship like it?

COUNTESS: happily effected.
LAFEU: His highness comes post from Marseilles, of as able
LAFEU: body as when he numbered thirty: he will be here
LAFEU: to-morrow, or I am deceived by him that in such
LAFEU: intelligence hath seldom failed.

COUNTESS: die. I have letters that my son will be here
COUNTESS: to-night: I shall beseech your lordship to remain
COUNTESS: with me till they meet together.
LAFEU: Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might
LAFEU: safely be admitted.
COUNTESS: You need but plead your honourable privilege.
LAFEU: Lady, of that I have made a bold charter, but I
LAFEU: thank my God it holds yet.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Clown
Clown: O madam, yonder's my lord your son with a patch of
Clown: velvet on's face: whether there be a scar under't
Clown: or no, the velvet knows, but 'tis a goodly patch of
Clown: velvet: his left cheek is a cheek of two pile and a
Clown: half, but his right cheek is worn bare.
LAFEU: A scar nobly got, or a noble scar, is a good livery
LAFEU: of honour, so belike is that.
Clown: But it is your carbonadoed face.
LAFEU: Let us go see your son, I pray you: I long to talk
LAFEU: with the young noble soldier.
Clown: Faith there's a dozen of 'em, with delicate fine
Clown: hats and most courteous feathers, which bow the head
Clown: and nod at every man.

NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Marseilles. A street.

Gentleman: Whither I am going.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. Rousillon. Before the COUNT's palace.

PAROLLES: mood, and smell somewhat strong of her strong
PAROLLES: displeasure.

Clown: smell so strongly as thou speakest of: I will
Clown: henceforth eat no fish of fortune's buttering.
Clown: Prithee, allow the wind.
PAROLLES: Nay, you need not to stop your nose, sir, I spake
PAROLLES: but by a metaphor.
Clown: Indeed, sir, if your metaphor stink, I will stop my
Clown: nose, or against any man's metaphor. Prithee, get
Clown: thee further.
PAROLLES: Pray you, sir, deliver me this paper.
Clown: Foh! prithee, stand away: a paper from fortune's
Clown: close-stool to give to a nobleman! Look, here he
Clown: comes himself.
NARRATOR: Enter LAFEU
Clown: Here is a purr of fortune's, sir, or of fortune's
Clown: cat,--but not a musk-cat,--that has fallen into the
Clown: unclean fishpond of her displeasure, and, as he
Clown: says, is muddied withal: pray you, sir, use the
Clown: carp as you may, for he looks like a poor, decayed,

PAROLLES: My lord, I am a man whom fortune hath cruelly
PAROLLES: scratched.
LAFEU: And what would you have me to do? 'Tis too late to
LAFEU: pare her nails now. Wherein have you played the
LAFEU: knave with fortune, that she should scratch you, who
LAFEU: of herself is a good lady and would not have knaves
LAFEU: thrive long under her? There's a quart d'ecu for
LAFEU: you: let the justices make you and fortune friends:
LAFEU: I am for other business.
PAROLLES: I beseech your honour to hear me one single word.
LAFEU: You beg a single penny more: come, you shall ha't,
LAFEU: save your word.
PAROLLES: My name, my good lord, is Parolles.
LAFEU: You beg more than 'word,' then. Cox my passion!
LAFEU: give me your hand. How does your drum?
PAROLLES: O my good lord, you were the first that found me!
LAFEU: Was I, in sooth? and I was the first that lost thee.
PAROLLES: It lies in you, my lord, to bring me in some grace,
PAROLLES: for you did bring me out.
LAFEU: Out upon thee, knave! dost thou put upon me at once
LAFEU: both the office of God and the devil? One brings
LAFEU: thee in grace and the other brings thee out.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound

LAFEU: inquire further after me, I had talk of you last
LAFEU: night: though you are a fool and a knave, you shall
LAFEU: eat, go to, follow.
PAROLLES: I praise God for you.

LAFEU: Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkercher: so,
LAFEU: I thank thee: wait on me home, I'll make sport with thee:
LAFEU: Let thy courtesies alone, they are scurvy ones.
KING: Let us from point to point this story know,
KING: To make the even truth in pleasure flow.
NARRATOR: To DIANA
KING: If thou be'st yet a fresh uncropped flower,
KING: Choose thou thy husband, and I'll pay thy dower,
KING: For I can guess that by thy honest aid
KING: Thou keep'st a wife herself, thyself a maid.
KING: Of that and all the progress, more or less,
KING: Resolvedly more leisure shall express:
KING: All yet seems well, and if it end so meet,
KING: The bitter past, more welcome is the sweet.
NARRATOR: Flourish
KING: EPILOGUE
KING: The king's a beggar, now the play is done:
KING: All is well ended, if this suit be won,
KING: That you express content, which we will pay,
KING: With strife to please you, day exceeding day:
KING: Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts,
KING: Your gentle hands lend us, and take our hearts.
NARRATOR: Exeunt

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Alexandria. A room in CLEOPATRA's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS and PHILO
PHILO: Nay, but this dotage of our general's

NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. Another room.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and ALEXAS
CLEOPATRA: Where is he?

CLEOPATRA: See where he is, who's with him, what he does:

CLEOPATRA: Say I am dancing, if in mirth, report

NARRATOR: Exit ALEXAS

NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY

MARK ANTONY: My precious queen, forbear,

CLEOPATRA: I prithee, turn aside and weep for her,

MARK ANTONY: You'll heat my blood: no more.
CLEOPATRA: You can do better yet, but this is meetly.
MARK ANTONY: Now, by my sword,--
CLEOPATRA: And target. Still he mends,
CLEOPATRA: But this is not the best. Look, prithee, Charmian,
CLEOPATRA: How this Herculean Roman does become
CLEOPATRA: The carriage of his chafe.
MARK ANTONY: I'll leave you, lady.
CLEOPATRA: Courteous lord, one word.
CLEOPATRA: Sir, you and I must part, but that's not it:
CLEOPATRA: Sir, you and I have loved, but there's not it,
CLEOPATRA: That you know well: something it is I would,
CLEOPATRA: O, my oblivion is a very Antony,
CLEOPATRA: And I am all forgotten.
MARK ANTONY: But that your royalty
MARK ANTONY: Holds idleness your subject, I should take you
MARK ANTONY: For idleness itself.
CLEOPATRA: 'Tis sweating labour
CLEOPATRA: To bear such idleness so near the heart
CLEOPATRA: As Cleopatra this. But, sir, forgive me,
CLEOPATRA: Since my becomings kill me, when they do not
CLEOPATRA: Eye well to you: your honour calls you hence,
CLEOPATRA: Therefore be deaf to my unpitied folly.
CLEOPATRA: And all the gods go with you! upon your sword
CLEOPATRA: Sit laurel victory! and smooth success
CLEOPATRA: Be strew'd before your feet!
MARK ANTONY: Let us go. Come,
MARK ANTONY: Our separation so abides, and flies,
MARK ANTONY: That thou, residing here, go'st yet with me,
MARK ANTONY: And I, hence fleeting, here remain with thee. Away!

NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Rome. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's house.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, reading a letter, LEPIDUS, and their Train
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: You may see, Lepidus, and henceforth know,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: It is not Caesar's natural vice to hate
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Our great competitor: from Alexandria
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: This is the news: he fishes, drinks, and wastes
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The lamps of night in revel, is not more man-like
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Than Cleopatra, nor the queen of Ptolemy
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: More womanly than he, hardly gave audience, or

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: A man who is the abstract of all faults

LEPIDUS: His faults in him seem as the spots of heaven,

LEPIDUS: Rather than purchased, what he cannot change,

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Amiss to tumble on the bed of Ptolemy,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To give a kingdom for a mirth, to sit

LEPIDUS: Here's more news.
Messenger: Thy biddings have been done, and every hour,
Messenger: Most noble Caesar, shalt thou have report
Messenger: How 'tis abroad. Pompey is strong at sea,
Messenger: And it appears he is beloved of those
Messenger: That only have fear'd Caesar: to the ports
Messenger: The discontents repair, and men's reports
Messenger: Give him much wrong'd.

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: That he which is was wish'd until he were,

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Comes dear'd by being lack'd. This common body,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To rot itself with motion.

Messenger: Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates,
Messenger: Make the sea serve them, which they ear and wound
Messenger: With keels of every kind: many hot inroads
Messenger: They make in Italy, the borders maritime
Messenger: Lack blood to think on't, and flush youth revolt:
Messenger: No vessel can peep forth, but 'tis as soon
Messenger: Taken as seen, for Pompey's name strikes more
Messenger: Than could his war resisted.

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Yea, like the stag, when snow the pasture sheets,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The barks of trees thou browsed'st, on the Alps

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Which some did die to look on: and all this--
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: It wounds thine honour that I speak it now--
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Was borne so like a soldier, that thy cheek
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: So much as lank'd not.
LEPIDUS: 'Tis pity of him.

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Till which encounter,

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Doubt not, sir,

NARRATOR: SCENE V. Alexandria. CLEOPATRA's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and MARDIAN

NARRATOR: Enter ALEXAS, from OCTAVIUS CAESAR

CLEOPATRA: Yet, coming from him, that great medicine hath
CLEOPATRA: With his tinct gilded thee.

ALEXAS: He kiss'd,--the last of many doubled kisses,--
ALEXAS: This orient pearl. His speech sticks in my heart.
CLEOPATRA: Mine ear must pluck it thence.
ALEXAS: 'Good friend,' quoth he,
ALEXAS: 'Say, the firm Roman to great Egypt sends
ALEXAS: This treasure of an oyster, at whose foot,
ALEXAS: To mend the petty present, I will piece

ALEXAS: Who neigh'd so high, that what I would have spoke
ALEXAS: Was beastly dumb'd by him.
CLEOPATRA: What, was he sad or merry?
ALEXAS: Like to the time o' the year between the extremes

CLEOPATRA: O well-divided disposition! Note him,
CLEOPATRA: Note him good Charmian, 'tis the man, but note him:
CLEOPATRA: He was not sad, for he would shine on those
CLEOPATRA: That make their looks by his, he was not merry,
CLEOPATRA: Which seem'd to tell them his remembrance lay
CLEOPATRA: In Egypt with his joy, but between both:
CLEOPATRA: O heavenly mingle! Be'st thou sad or merry,
CLEOPATRA: The violence of either thee becomes,
CLEOPATRA: So does it no man else. Met'st thou my posts?
ALEXAS: Ay, madam, twenty several messengers:
ALEXAS: Why do you send so thick?
CLEOPATRA: Who's born that day
CLEOPATRA: When I forget to send to Antony,
CLEOPATRA: Shall die a beggar. Ink and paper, Charmian.
CLEOPATRA: Welcome, my good Alexas. Did I, Charmian,
CLEOPATRA: Ever love Caesar so?
CHARMIAN: O that brave Caesar!
CLEOPATRA: Be choked with such another emphasis!
CLEOPATRA: Say, the brave Antony.
CHARMIAN: The valiant Caesar!
CLEOPATRA: By Isis, I will give thee bloody teeth,
CLEOPATRA: If thou with Caesar paragon again
CLEOPATRA: My man of men.
CHARMIAN: By your most gracious pardon,
CHARMIAN: I sing but after you.
CLEOPATRA: My salad days,
CLEOPATRA: When I was green in judgment: cold in blood,
CLEOPATRA: To say as I said then! But, come, away,
CLEOPATRA: Get me ink and paper:
CLEOPATRA: He shall have every day a several greeting,
CLEOPATRA: Or I'll unpeople Egypt.

NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Messina. POMPEY's house.
NARRATOR: Enter POMPEY, MENECRATES, and MENAS, in warlike manner
POMPEY: If the great gods be just, they shall assist
POMPEY: The deeds of justest men.

POMPEY: Nor either cares for him.

POMPEY: Let witchcraft join with beauty, lust with both!

POMPEY: How now, Varrius!

POMPEY: themselves,
POMPEY: For they have entertained cause enough
POMPEY: To draw their swords: but how the fear of us

POMPEY: Be't as our gods will have't! It only stands

NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A plain in Syria.

SILIUS: that
SILIUS: Without the which a soldier, and his sword,

VENTIDIUS: The ne'er-yet-beaten horse of Parthia

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: No, my most wronged sister, Cleopatra
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Hath nodded him to her. He hath given his empire
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Up to a whore, who now are levying
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The kings o' the earth for war, he hath assembled
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Bocchus, the king of Libya, Archelaus,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of Cappadocia, Philadelphos, king
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of Paphlagonia, the Thracian king, Adallas,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: King Malchus of Arabia, King of Pont,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Herod of Jewry, Mithridates, king
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of Comagene, Polemon and Amyntas,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The kings of Mede and Lycaonia,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: With a more larger list of sceptres.
OCTAVIA: Ay me, most wretched,
OCTAVIA: That have my heart parted betwixt two friends
OCTAVIA: That do afflict each other!
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Welcome hither:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Your letters did withhold our breaking forth,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Till we perceived, both how you were wrong led,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And we in negligent danger. Cheer your heart,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Be you not troubled with the time, which drives
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: O'er your content these strong necessities,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: But let determined things to destiny
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Hold unbewail'd their way. Welcome to Rome,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Nothing more dear to me. You are abused
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Beyond the mark of thought: and the high gods,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To do you justice, make them ministers
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of us and those that love you. Best of comfort,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And ever welcome to us.
AGRIPPA: Welcome, lady.
MECAENAS: Welcome, dear madam.
MECAENAS: Each heart in Rome does love and pity you:
MECAENAS: Only the adulterous Antony, most large
MECAENAS: In his abominations, turns you off,
MECAENAS: And gives his potent regiment to a trull,
MECAENAS: That noises it against us.
OCTAVIA: Is it so, sir?
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Most certain. Sister, welcome: pray you,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Be ever known to patience: my dear'st sister!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Near Actium. MARK ANTONY's camp.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA and DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
CLEOPATRA: I will be even with thee, doubt it not.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: But why, why, why?
CLEOPATRA: Thou hast forspoke my being in these wars,
CLEOPATRA: And say'st it is not fit.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Well, is it, is it?
CLEOPATRA: If not denounced against us, why should not we
CLEOPATRA: Be there in person?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]  Well, I could reply:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: If we should serve with horse and mares together,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The horse were merely lost, the mares would bear
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: A soldier and his horse.
CLEOPATRA: What is't you say?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Your presence needs must puzzle Antony,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Take from his heart, take from his brain,

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: What should not then be spared. He is already
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Traduced for levity, and 'tis said in Rome

CLEOPATRA: And, as the president of my kingdom, will
CLEOPATRA: Appear there for a man. Speak not against it:
CLEOPATRA: I will not stay behind.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Nay, I have done.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Here comes the emperor.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and CANIDIUS
MARK ANTONY: Is it not strange, Canidius,

MARK ANTONY: He could so quickly cut the Ionian sea,
MARK ANTONY: And take in Toryne? You have heard on't, sweet?
CLEOPATRA: Celerity is never more admired

MARK ANTONY: A good rebuke,
MARK ANTONY: Which might have well becomed the best of men,
MARK ANTONY: To taunt at slackness. Canidius, we
MARK ANTONY: Will fight with him by sea.
CLEOPATRA: By sea! what else?
CANIDIUS: Why will my lord do so?
MARK ANTONY: For that he dares us to't.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: So hath my lord dared him to single fight.

CANIDIUS: Where Caesar fought with Pompey: but these offers,
CANIDIUS: Which serve not for his vantage, be shakes off,
CANIDIUS: And so should you.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Your ships are not well mann'd,

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Ingross'd by swift impress, in Caesar's fleet
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Are those that often have 'gainst Pompey fought:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Their ships are yare, yours, heavy: no disgrace
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Shall fall you for refusing him at sea,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Being prepared for land.
MARK ANTONY: By sea, by sea.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Most worthy sir, you therein throw away

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Distract your army, which doth most consist
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Of war-mark'd footmen, leave unexecuted
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Your own renowned knowledge, quite forego
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The way which promises assurance, and
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Give up yourself merely to chance and hazard,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: From firm security.
MARK ANTONY: I'll fight at sea.
CLEOPATRA: I have sixty sails, Caesar none better.
MARK ANTONY: Our overplus of shipping will we burn,
MARK ANTONY: And, with the rest full-mann'd, from the head of Actium
MARK ANTONY: Beat the approaching Caesar. But if we fail,
MARK ANTONY: We then can do't at land.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
MARK ANTONY: Thy business?
Messenger: The news is true, my lord, he is descried,
Messenger: Caesar has taken Toryne.
MARK ANTONY: Can he be there in person? 'tis impossible,
MARK ANTONY: Strange that power should be. Canidius,
MARK ANTONY: Our nineteen legions thou shalt hold by land,
MARK ANTONY: And our twelve thousand horse. We'll to our ship:
MARK ANTONY: Away, my Thetis!
NARRATOR: Enter a Soldier
MARK ANTONY: How now, worthy soldier?
Soldier: O noble emperor, do not fight by sea,
Soldier: Trust not to rotten planks: do you misdoubt
Soldier: This sword and these my wounds? Let the Egyptians
Soldier: And the Phoenicians go a-ducking, we
Soldier: Have used to conquer, standing on the earth,
Soldier: And fighting foot to foot.
MARK ANTONY: Well, well: away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt MARK ANTONY, QUEEN CLEOPATRA, and DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
Soldier: By Hercules, I think I am i' the right.
CANIDIUS: Soldier, thou art: but his whole action grows
CANIDIUS: Not in the power on't: so our leader's led,
CANIDIUS: And we are women's men.
Soldier: You keep by land
Soldier: The legions and the horse whole, do you not?
CANIDIUS: Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius,
CANIDIUS: Publicola, and Caelius, are for sea:
CANIDIUS: But we keep whole by land. This speed of Caesar's
CANIDIUS: Carries beyond belief.
Soldier: While he was yet in Rome,
Soldier: His power went out in such distractions as
Soldier: Beguiled all spies.
CANIDIUS: Who's his lieutenant, hear you?
Soldier: They say, one Taurus.
CANIDIUS: Well I know the man.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: The emperor calls Canidius.
CANIDIUS: With news the time's with labour, and throes forth,
CANIDIUS: Each minute, some.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. A plain near Actium.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, and TAURUS, with his army, marching
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Taurus!
TAURUS: My lord?
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Strike not by land, keep whole: provoke not battle,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Till we have done at sea. Do not exceed
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The prescript of this scroll: our fortune lies
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Upon this jump.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. Another part of the plain.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
MARK ANTONY: Set we our squadrons on yond side o' the hill,
MARK ANTONY: In eye of Caesar's battle, from which place
MARK ANTONY: We may the number of the ships behold,
MARK ANTONY: And so proceed accordingly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE X. Another part of the plain.
NARRATOR: CANIDIUS marcheth with his land army one way over  the stage, and TAURUS, the lieutenant of OCTAVIUS  CAESAR, the other way. After their going in, is heard the noise of a sea-fight
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Naught, naught all, naught! I can behold no longer:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The Antoniad, the Egyptian admiral,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: With all their sixty, fly and turn the rudder:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: To see't mine eyes are blasted.
NARRATOR: Enter SCARUS
SCARUS: Gods and goddesses,
SCARUS: All the whole synod of them!
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: What's thy passion!
SCARUS: The greater cantle of the world is lost
SCARUS: With very ignorance, we have kiss'd away
SCARUS: Kingdoms and provinces.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: How appears the fight?
SCARUS: On our side like the token'd pestilence,
SCARUS: Where death is sure. Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt,--
SCARUS: Whom leprosy o'ertake!--i' the midst o' the fight,
SCARUS: When vantage like a pair of twins appear'd,
SCARUS: Both as the same, or rather ours the elder,
SCARUS: The breese upon her, like a cow in June,
SCARUS: Hoists sails and flies.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: That I beheld:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Mine eyes did sicken at the sight, and could not
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Endure a further view.
SCARUS: She once being loof'd,
SCARUS: The noble ruin of her magic, Antony,
SCARUS: Claps on his sea-wing, and, like a doting mallard,
SCARUS: Leaving the fight in height, flies after her:
SCARUS: I never saw an action of such shame,
SCARUS: Experience, manhood, honour, ne'er before
SCARUS: Did violate so itself.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Alack, alack!
NARRATOR: Enter CANIDIUS
CANIDIUS: Our fortune on the sea is out of breath,
CANIDIUS: And sinks most lamentably. Had our general
CANIDIUS: Been what he knew himself, it had gone well:
CANIDIUS: O, he has given example for our flight,
CANIDIUS: Most grossly, by his own!
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Ay, are you thereabouts?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Why, then, good night indeed.
CANIDIUS: Toward Peloponnesus are they fled.
SCARUS: 'Tis easy to't, and there I will attend
SCARUS: What further comes.
CANIDIUS: To Caesar will I render
CANIDIUS: My legions and my horse: six kings already
CANIDIUS: Show me the way of yielding.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: I'll yet follow
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The wounded chance of Antony, though my reason
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Sits in the wind against me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XI. Alexandria. CLEOPATRA's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY with Attendants
MARK ANTONY: Hark! the land bids me tread no more upon't,
MARK ANTONY: It is ashamed to bear me! Friends, come hither:
MARK ANTONY: I am so lated in the world, that I
MARK ANTONY: Have lost my way for ever: I have a ship
MARK ANTONY: Laden with gold, take that, divide it, fly,
MARK ANTONY: And make your peace with Caesar.
All: Fly! not we.
MARK ANTONY: I have fled myself, and have instructed cowards
MARK ANTONY: To run and show their shoulders. Friends, be gone,
MARK ANTONY: I have myself resolved upon a course
MARK ANTONY: Which has no need of you, be gone:
MARK ANTONY: My treasure's in the harbour, take it. O,
MARK ANTONY: I follow'd that I blush to look upon:
MARK ANTONY: My very hairs do mutiny, for the white
MARK ANTONY: Reprove the brown for rashness, and they them
MARK ANTONY: For fear and doting. Friends, be gone: you shall
MARK ANTONY: Have letters from me to some friends that will
MARK ANTONY: Sweep your way for you. Pray you, look not sad,
MARK ANTONY: Nor make replies of loathness: take the hint

MARK ANTONY: Which leaves itself: to the sea-side straightway:
MARK ANTONY: I will possess you of that ship and treasure.
MARK ANTONY: Leave me, I pray, a little: pray you now:
MARK ANTONY: Nay, do so, for, indeed, I have lost command,
MARK ANTONY: Therefore I pray you: I'll see you by and by.
NARRATOR: Sits down
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA led by CHARMIAN and IRAS, EROS following
EROS: Nay, gentle madam, to him, comfort him.
IRAS: Do, most dear queen.
CHARMIAN: Do! why: what else?
CLEOPATRA: Let me sit down. O Juno!
MARK ANTONY: No, no, no, no, no.
EROS: See you here, sir?
MARK ANTONY: O fie, fie, fie!
CHARMIAN: Madam!
IRAS: Madam, O good empress!
EROS: Sir, sir,--
MARK ANTONY: Yes, my lord, yes, he at Philippi kept
MARK ANTONY: His sword e'en like a dancer, while I struck
MARK ANTONY: The lean and wrinkled Cassius, and 'twas I
MARK ANTONY: That the mad Brutus ended: he alone
MARK ANTONY: Dealt on lieutenantry, and no practise had

CLEOPATRA: Ah, stand by.
EROS: The queen, my lord, the queen.
IRAS: Go to him, madam, speak to him:
IRAS: He is unqualitied with very shame.
CLEOPATRA: Well then, sustain him: O!
EROS: Most noble sir, arise, the queen approaches:
EROS: Her head's declined, and death will seize her, but
EROS: Your comfort makes the rescue.
MARK ANTONY: I have offended reputation,
MARK ANTONY: A most unnoble swerving.
EROS: Sir, the queen.
MARK ANTONY: O, whither hast thou led me, Egypt? See,
MARK ANTONY: How I convey my shame out of thine eyes
MARK ANTONY: By looking back what I have left behind
MARK ANTONY: 'Stroy'd in dishonour.
CLEOPATRA: O my lord, my lord,
CLEOPATRA: Forgive my fearful sails! I little thought
CLEOPATRA: You would have follow'd.
MARK ANTONY: Egypt, thou knew'st too well
MARK ANTONY: My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings,
MARK ANTONY: And thou shouldst tow me after: o'er my spirit
MARK ANTONY: Thy full supremacy thou knew'st, and that
MARK ANTONY: Thy beck might from the bidding of the gods

CLEOPATRA: O, my pardon!
MARK ANTONY: Now I must
MARK ANTONY: To the young man send humble treaties, dodge
MARK ANTONY: And palter in the shifts of lowness, who
MARK ANTONY: With half the bulk o' the world play'd as I pleased,
MARK ANTONY: Making and marring fortunes. You did know

MARK ANTONY: My sword, made weak by my affection, would

MARK ANTONY: Fall not a tear, I say, one of them rates

NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XII. Egypt. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's camp.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, DOLABELLA, THYREUS, with others
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Let him appear that's come from Antony.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Know you him?
DOLABELLA: Caesar, 'tis his schoolmaster:
DOLABELLA: An argument that he is pluck'd, when hither
DOLABELLA: He sends so poor a pinion off his wing,
DOLABELLA: Which had superfluous kings for messengers
DOLABELLA: Not many moons gone by.
NARRATOR: Enter EUPHRONIUS, ambassador from MARK ANTONY
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Approach, and speak.
EUPHRONIUS: Such as I am, I come from Antony:
EUPHRONIUS: I was of late as petty to his ends
EUPHRONIUS: As is the morn-dew on the myrtle-leaf
EUPHRONIUS: To his grand sea.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Be't so: declare thine office.
EUPHRONIUS: Lord of his fortunes he salutes thee, and
EUPHRONIUS: Requires to live in Egypt: which not granted,
EUPHRONIUS: He lessens his requests, and to thee sues
EUPHRONIUS: To let him breathe between the heavens and earth,
EUPHRONIUS: A private man in Athens: this for him.
EUPHRONIUS: Next, Cleopatra does confess thy greatness,
EUPHRONIUS: Submits her to thy might, and of thee craves
EUPHRONIUS: The circle of the Ptolemies for her heirs,
EUPHRONIUS: Now hazarded to thy grace.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: For Antony,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: I have no ears to his request. The queen
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of audience nor desire shall fail, so she
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: From Egypt drive her all-disgraced friend,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Or take his life there: this if she perform,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: She shall not sue unheard. So to them both.
EUPHRONIUS: Fortune pursue thee!
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Bring him through the bands.
NARRATOR: Exit EUPHRONIUS
NARRATOR: To THYREUS
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: From Antony win Cleopatra: promise,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And in our name, what she requires, add more,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: From thine invention, offers: women are not
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: In their best fortunes strong, but want will perjure
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The ne'er touch'd vestal: try thy cunning, Thyreus,

OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Will answer as a law.
THYREUS: Caesar, I go.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Observe how Antony becomes his flaw,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And what thou think'st his very action speaks
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: In every power that moves.
THYREUS: Caesar, I shall.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XIII. Alexandria. CLEOPATRA's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA, DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS, CHARMIAN, and IRAS
CLEOPATRA: What shall we do, Enobarbus?

NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY with EUPHRONIUS, the Ambassador

EUPHRONIUS: Ay, my lord.
MARK ANTONY: The queen shall then have courtesy, so she

EUPHRONIUS: He says so.
MARK ANTONY: Let her know't.

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]  Yes, like enough, high-battled Caesar will

NARRATOR: Enter an Attendant
Attendant: A messenger from CAESAR.
CLEOPATRA: What, no more ceremony? See, my women!
CLEOPATRA: Against the blown rose may they stop their nose

NARRATOR: Exit Attendant
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]  Mine honesty and I begin to square.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The loyalty well held to fools does make
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Our faith mere folly: yet he that can endure
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: To follow with allegiance a fall'n lord
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Does conquer him that did his master conquer
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: And earns a place i' the story.
NARRATOR: Enter THYREUS
CLEOPATRA: Caesar's will?
THYREUS: Hear it apart.
CLEOPATRA: None but friends: say boldly.
THYREUS: So, haply, are they friends to Antony.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: He needs as many, sir, as Caesar has,

THYREUS: Thus then, thou most renown'd: Caesar entreats,
THYREUS: Not to consider in what case thou stand'st,
THYREUS: Further than he is Caesar.
CLEOPATRA: Go on: right royal.
THYREUS: He knows that you embrace not Antony
THYREUS: As you did love, but as you fear'd him.
CLEOPATRA: O!
THYREUS: The scars upon your honour, therefore, he
THYREUS: Does pity, as constrained blemishes,
THYREUS: Not as deserved.
CLEOPATRA: He is a god, and knows

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]             To be sure of that,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: I will ask Antony. Sir, sir, thou art so leaky,

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Thy dearest quit thee.

THYREUS: Shall I say to Caesar
THYREUS: What you require of him? for he partly begs
THYREUS: To be desired to give. It much would please him,
THYREUS: That of his fortunes you should make a staff
THYREUS: To lean upon: but it would warm his spirits,
THYREUS: To hear from me you had left Antony,
THYREUS: And put yourself under his shrowd,
THYREUS: The universal landlord.
CLEOPATRA: What's your name?
THYREUS: My name is Thyreus.
CLEOPATRA: Most kind messenger,
CLEOPATRA: Say to great Caesar this: in deputation
CLEOPATRA: I kiss his conquering hand: tell him, I am prompt
CLEOPATRA: To lay my crown at 's feet, and there to kneel:

THYREUS: 'Tis your noblest course.
THYREUS: Wisdom and fortune combating together,
THYREUS: If that the former dare but what it can,
THYREUS: No chance may shake it. Give me grace to lay
THYREUS: My duty on your hand.
CLEOPATRA: Your Caesar's father oft,
CLEOPATRA: When he hath mused of taking kingdoms in,
CLEOPATRA: Bestow'd his lips on that unworthy place,
CLEOPATRA: As it rain'd kisses.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARK ANTONY and DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
MARK ANTONY: Favours, by Jove that thunders!
MARK ANTONY: What art thou, fellow?
THYREUS: One that but performs
THYREUS: The bidding of the fullest man, and worthiest
THYREUS: To have command obey'd.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]               You will be whipp'd.
MARK ANTONY: Approach, there! Ah, you kite! Now, gods
MARK ANTONY: and devils!
MARK ANTONY: Authority melts from me: of late, when I cried 'Ho!'
MARK ANTONY: Like boys unto a muss, kings would start forth,
