MARK ANTONY: Antony yet.
NARRATOR: Enter Attendants
MARK ANTONY: Take hence this Jack, and whip him.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside]  'Tis better playing with a lion's whelp
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Than with an old one dying.
MARK ANTONY: Moon and stars!
MARK ANTONY: Whip him. Were't twenty of the greatest tributaries
MARK ANTONY: That do acknowledge Caesar, should I find them
MARK ANTONY: So saucy with the hand of she here,--what's her name,
MARK ANTONY: Since she was Cleopatra? Whip him, fellows,
MARK ANTONY: Till, like a boy, you see him cringe his face,
MARK ANTONY: And whine aloud for mercy: take him hence.
THYREUS: Mark Antony!
MARK ANTONY: Tug him away: being whipp'd,
MARK ANTONY: Bring him again: this Jack of Caesar's shall
MARK ANTONY: Bear us an errand to him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Attendants with THYREUS
MARK ANTONY: You were half blasted ere I knew you: ha!
MARK ANTONY: Have I my pillow left unpress'd in Rome,
MARK ANTONY: Forborne the getting of a lawful race,
MARK ANTONY: And by a gem of women, to be abused
MARK ANTONY: By one that looks on feeders?
CLEOPATRA: Good my lord,--
MARK ANTONY: You have been a boggler ever:
MARK ANTONY: But when we in our viciousness grow hard--
MARK ANTONY: O misery on't!--the wise gods seel our eyes,
MARK ANTONY: In our own filth drop our clear judgments, make us
MARK ANTONY: Adore our errors, laugh at's, while we strut
MARK ANTONY: To our confusion.
CLEOPATRA: O, is't come to this?
MARK ANTONY: I found you as a morsel cold upon
MARK ANTONY: Dead Caesar's trencher, nay, you were a fragment
MARK ANTONY: Of Cneius Pompey's, besides what hotter hours,
MARK ANTONY: Unregister'd in vulgar fame, you have
MARK ANTONY: Luxuriously pick'd out: for, I am sure,
MARK ANTONY: Though you can guess what temperance should be,
MARK ANTONY: You know not what it is.
CLEOPATRA: Wherefore is this?
MARK ANTONY: To let a fellow that will take rewards
MARK ANTONY: And say 'God quit you!' be familiar with
MARK ANTONY: My playfellow, your hand, this kingly seal
MARK ANTONY: And plighter of high hearts! O, that I were
MARK ANTONY: Upon the hill of Basan, to outroar
MARK ANTONY: The horned herd! for I have savage cause,
MARK ANTONY: And to proclaim it civilly, were like
MARK ANTONY: A halter'd neck which does the hangman thank
MARK ANTONY: For being yare about him.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Attendants with THYREUS
MARK ANTONY: Is he whipp'd?
First Attendant: Soundly, my lord.
MARK ANTONY: Cried he? and begg'd a' pardon?
First Attendant: He did ask favour.
MARK ANTONY: If that thy father live, let him repent
MARK ANTONY: Thou wast not made his daughter, and be thou sorry
MARK ANTONY: To follow Caesar in his triumph, since
MARK ANTONY: Thou hast been whipp'd for following him: henceforth
MARK ANTONY: The white hand of a lady fever thee,
MARK ANTONY: Shake thou to look on 't. Get thee back to Caesar,
MARK ANTONY: Tell him thy entertainment: look, thou say
MARK ANTONY: He makes me angry with him, for he seems
MARK ANTONY: Proud and disdainful, harping on what I am,
MARK ANTONY: Not what he knew I was: he makes me angry,
MARK ANTONY: And at this time most easy 'tis to do't,
MARK ANTONY: When my good stars, that were my former guides,
MARK ANTONY: Have empty left their orbs, and shot their fires
MARK ANTONY: Into the abysm of hell. If he mislike
MARK ANTONY: My speech and what is done, tell him he has
MARK ANTONY: Hipparchus, my enfranched bondman, whom
MARK ANTONY: He may at pleasure whip, or hang, or torture,
MARK ANTONY: As he shall like, to quit me: urge it thou:
MARK ANTONY: Hence with thy stripes, begone!
NARRATOR: Exit THYREUS
CLEOPATRA: Have you done yet?
MARK ANTONY: Alack, our terrene moon
MARK ANTONY: Is now eclipsed, and it portends alone
MARK ANTONY: The fall of Antony!
CLEOPATRA: I must stay his time.
MARK ANTONY: To flatter Caesar, would you mingle eyes
MARK ANTONY: With one that ties his points?
CLEOPATRA: Not know me yet?
MARK ANTONY: Cold-hearted toward me?
CLEOPATRA: Ah, dear, if I be so,
CLEOPATRA: From my cold heart let heaven engender hail,
CLEOPATRA: And poison it in the source, and the first stone
CLEOPATRA: Drop in my neck: as it determines, so
CLEOPATRA: Dissolve my life! The next Caesarion smite!
CLEOPATRA: Till by degrees the memory of my womb,
CLEOPATRA: Together with my brave Egyptians all,
CLEOPATRA: By the discandying of this pelleted storm,
CLEOPATRA: Lie graveless, till the flies and gnats of Nile
CLEOPATRA: Have buried them for prey!
MARK ANTONY: I am satisfied.
MARK ANTONY: Caesar sits down in Alexandria, where
MARK ANTONY: I will oppose his fate. Our force by land
MARK ANTONY: Hath nobly held, our sever'd navy too
MARK ANTONY: Have knit again, and fleet, threatening most sea-like.
MARK ANTONY: Where hast thou been, my heart? Dost thou hear, lady?
MARK ANTONY: If from the field I shall return once more
MARK ANTONY: To kiss these lips, I will appear in blood,
MARK ANTONY: I and my sword will earn our chronicle:
MARK ANTONY: There's hope in't yet.
CLEOPATRA: That's my brave lord!
MARK ANTONY: I will be treble-sinew'd, hearted, breathed,
MARK ANTONY: And fight maliciously: for when mine hours
MARK ANTONY: Were nice and lucky, men did ransom lives
MARK ANTONY: Of me for jests, but now I'll set my teeth,
MARK ANTONY: And send to darkness all that stop me. Come,
MARK ANTONY: Let's have one other gaudy night: call to me
MARK ANTONY: All my sad captains, fill our bowls once more,
MARK ANTONY: Let's mock the midnight bell.
CLEOPATRA: It is my birth-day:
CLEOPATRA: I had thought to have held it poor: but, since my lord
CLEOPATRA: Is Antony again, I will be Cleopatra.
MARK ANTONY: We will yet do well.
CLEOPATRA: Call all his noble captains to my lord.
MARK ANTONY: Do so, we'll speak to them, and to-night I'll force
MARK ANTONY: The wine peep through their scars. Come on, my queen,
MARK ANTONY: There's sap in't yet. The next time I do fight,
MARK ANTONY: I'll make death love me, for I will contend
MARK ANTONY: Even with his pestilent scythe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Now he'll outstare the lightning. To be furious,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Is to be frighted out of fear, and in that mood
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: The dove will peck the estridge, and I see still,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: A diminution in our captain's brain
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Restores his heart: when valour preys on reason,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: It eats the sword it fights with. I will seek
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Some way to leave him.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before Alexandria. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's camp.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, AGRIPPA, and MECAENAS, with his Army, OCTAVIUS CAESAR reading a letter
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: He calls me boy, and chides, as he had power
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To beat me out of Egypt, my messenger
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: He hath whipp'd with rods, dares me to personal combat,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Caesar to Antony: let the old ruffian know
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: I have many other ways to die, meantime
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Laugh at his challenge.
MECAENAS: Caesar must think,
MECAENAS: When one so great begins to rage, he's hunted
MECAENAS: Even to falling. Give him no breath, but now
MECAENAS: Make boot of his distraction: never anger
MECAENAS: Made good guard for itself.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Let our best heads
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Know, that to-morrow the last of many battles
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: We mean to fight: within our files there are,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Of those that served Mark Antony but late,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Enough to fetch him in. See it done:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And feast the army, we have store to do't,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And they have earn'd the waste. Poor Antony!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Alexandria. CLEOPATRA's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY, CLEOPATRA, DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS, CHARMIAN, IRAS, ALEXAS, with others
MARK ANTONY: He will not fight with me, Domitius.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: No.
MARK ANTONY: Why should he not?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: He thinks, being twenty times of better fortune,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: He is twenty men to one.
MARK ANTONY: To-morrow, soldier,
MARK ANTONY: By sea and land I'll fight: or I will live,
MARK ANTONY: Or bathe my dying honour in the blood
MARK ANTONY: Shall make it live again. Woo't thou fight well?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: I'll strike, and cry 'Take all.'
MARK ANTONY: Well said, come on.
MARK ANTONY: Call forth my household servants: let's to-night
MARK ANTONY: Be bounteous at our meal.
NARRATOR: Enter three or four Servitors
MARK ANTONY: Give me thy hand,
MARK ANTONY: Thou hast been rightly honest,--so hast thou,--
MARK ANTONY: Thou,--and thou,--and thou:--you have served me well,
MARK ANTONY: And kings have been your fellows.
CLEOPATRA: [Aside to DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS]  What means this?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside to CLEOPATRA]  'Tis one of those odd
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: tricks which sorrow shoots
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Out of the mind.
MARK ANTONY: And thou art honest too.
MARK ANTONY: I wish I could be made so many men,
MARK ANTONY: And all of you clapp'd up together in
MARK ANTONY: An Antony, that I might do you service
MARK ANTONY: So good as you have done.
All: The gods forbid!
MARK ANTONY: Well, my good fellows, wait on me to-night:
MARK ANTONY: Scant not my cups, and make as much of me
MARK ANTONY: As when mine empire was your fellow too,
MARK ANTONY: And suffer'd my command.
CLEOPATRA: [Aside to DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS]  What does he mean?
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: [Aside to CLEOPATRA]  To make his followers weep.
MARK ANTONY: Tend me to-night,
MARK ANTONY: May be it is the period of your duty:
MARK ANTONY: Haply you shall not see me more, or if,
MARK ANTONY: A mangled shadow: perchance to-morrow
MARK ANTONY: You'll serve another master. I look on you
MARK ANTONY: As one that takes his leave. Mine honest friends,
MARK ANTONY: I turn you not away, but, like a master
MARK ANTONY: Married to your good service, stay till death:
MARK ANTONY: Tend me to-night two hours, I ask no more,
MARK ANTONY: And the gods yield you for't!
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: What mean you, sir,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: To give them this discomfort? Look, they weep,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: And I, an ass, am onion-eyed: for shame,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Transform us not to women.
MARK ANTONY: Ho, ho, ho!
MARK ANTONY: Now the witch take me, if I meant it thus!
MARK ANTONY: Grace grow where those drops fall!
MARK ANTONY: My hearty friends,
MARK ANTONY: You take me in too dolorous a sense,
MARK ANTONY: For I spake to you for your comfort, did desire you
MARK ANTONY: To burn this night with torches: know, my hearts,
MARK ANTONY: I hope well of to-morrow, and will lead you
MARK ANTONY: Where rather I'll expect victorious life
MARK ANTONY: Than death and honour. Let's to supper, come,
MARK ANTONY: And drown consideration.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. Before the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter two Soldiers to their guard
First Soldier: Brother, good night: to-morrow is the day.
Second Soldier: It will determine one way: fare you well.
Second Soldier: Heard you of nothing strange about the streets?
First Soldier: Nothing. What news?
Second Soldier: Belike 'tis but a rumour. Good night to you.
First Soldier: Well, sir, good night.
NARRATOR: Enter two other Soldiers
Second Soldier: Soldiers, have careful watch.
Third Soldier: And you. Good night, good night.
NARRATOR: They place themselves in every corner of the stage
Fourth Soldier: Here we: and if to-morrow
Fourth Soldier: Our navy thrive, I have an absolute hope
Fourth Soldier: Our landmen will stand up.
Third Soldier: 'Tis a brave army,
Third Soldier: And full of purpose.
NARRATOR: Music of the hautboys as under the stage
Fourth Soldier: Peace! what noise?
First Soldier: List, list!
Second Soldier: Hark!
First Soldier: Music i' the air.
Third Soldier: Under the earth.
Fourth Soldier: It signs well, does it not?
Third Soldier: No.
First Soldier: Peace, I say!
First Soldier: What should this mean?
Second Soldier: 'Tis the god Hercules, whom Antony loved,
Second Soldier: Now leaves him.
First Soldier: Walk, let's see if other watchmen
First Soldier: Do hear what we do?
NARRATOR: They advance to another post
Second Soldier: How now, masters!
All: [Speaking together]  How now!
All: How now! do you hear this?
First Soldier: Ay, is't not strange?
Third Soldier: Do you hear, masters? do you hear?
First Soldier: Follow the noise so far as we have quarter,
First Soldier: Let's see how it will give off.
All: Content. 'Tis strange.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same. A room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, and others attending
MARK ANTONY: Eros! mine armour, Eros!
CLEOPATRA: Sleep a little.
MARK ANTONY: No, my chuck. Eros, come, mine armour, Eros!

CLEOPATRA: Nay, I'll help too.
CLEOPATRA: What's this for?

MARK ANTONY: Well, well,

EROS: Briefly, sir.

MARK ANTONY: Good morrow to thee, welcome:
MARK ANTONY: Thou look'st like him that knows a warlike charge:
MARK ANTONY: To business that we love we rise betime,
MARK ANTONY: And go to't with delight.
Soldier: A thousand, sir,
Soldier: Early though't be, have on their riveted trim,
Soldier: And at the port expect you.
NARRATOR: Shout. Trumpets flourish
NARRATOR: Enter Captains and Soldiers
Captain: The morn is fair. Good morrow, general.
All: Good morrow, general.
MARK ANTONY: 'Tis well blown, lads:
MARK ANTONY: This morning, like the spirit of a youth
MARK ANTONY: That means to be of note, begins betimes.
MARK ANTONY: So, so, come, give me that: this way, well said.
MARK ANTONY: Fare thee well, dame, whate'er becomes of me:
MARK ANTONY: This is a soldier's kiss: rebukeable
NARRATOR: Kisses her
MARK ANTONY: And worthy shameful cheque it were, to stand
MARK ANTONY: On more mechanic compliment, I'll leave thee
MARK ANTONY: Now, like a man of steel. You that will fight,
MARK ANTONY: Follow me close, I'll bring you to't. Adieu.
NARRATOR: Exeunt MARK ANTONY, EROS, Captains, and Soldiers
CHARMIAN: Please you, retire to your chamber.
CLEOPATRA: Lead me.
CLEOPATRA: He goes forth gallantly. That he and Caesar might
CLEOPATRA: Determine this great war in single fight!
CLEOPATRA: Then Antony,--but now--Well, on.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Alexandria. MARK ANTONY's camp.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound. Enter MARK ANTONY and EROS, a Soldier meeting them
Soldier: The gods make this a happy day to Antony!

MARK ANTONY: To make me fight at land!
Soldier: Hadst thou done so,
Soldier: The kings that have revolted, and the soldier
Soldier: That has this morning left thee, would have still
Soldier: Follow'd thy heels.
MARK ANTONY: Who's gone this morning?
Soldier: Who!
Soldier: One ever near thee: call for Enobarbus,
Soldier: He shall not hear thee, or from Caesar's camp
Soldier: Say 'I am none of thine.'
MARK ANTONY: What say'st thou?
Soldier: Sir,
Soldier: He is with Caesar.
EROS: Sir, his chests and treasure

MARK ANTONY: Is he gone?
Soldier: Most certain.
MARK ANTONY: Go, Eros, send his treasure after, do it,

MARK ANTONY: I will subscribe--gentle adieus and greetings,
MARK ANTONY: Say that I wish he never find more cause
MARK ANTONY: To change a master. O, my fortunes have
MARK ANTONY: Corrupted honest men! Dispatch.--Enobarbus!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Alexandria. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's camp.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, AGRIPPA, with DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS, and others
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Go forth, Agrippa, and begin the fight:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Our will is Antony be took alive,

AGRIPPA: Caesar, I shall.
NARRATOR: Exit
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The time of universal peace is near:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Prove this a prosperous day, the three-nook'd world

NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Antony
Messenger: Is come into the field.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Go charge Agrippa
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Plant those that have revolted in the van,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: That Antony may seem to spend his fury

NARRATOR: Exeunt all but DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Alexas did revolt, and went to Jewry on
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Affairs of Antony, there did persuade

Soldier: I tell you true: best you safed the bringer

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: I am alone the villain of the earth,

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Thou mine of bounty, how wouldst thou have paid

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Shall outstrike thought: but thought will do't, I feel.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: I fight against thee! No: I will go seek
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Some ditch wherein to die, the foul'st best fits

NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Field of battle between the camps.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Drums and trumpets. Enter AGRIPPA and others
AGRIPPA: Retire, we have engaged ourselves too far:
AGRIPPA: Caesar himself has work, and our oppression
AGRIPPA: Exceeds what we expected.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter MARK ANTONY and SCARUS wounded
SCARUS: O my brave emperor, this is fought indeed!
SCARUS: Had we done so at first, we had droven them home
SCARUS: With clouts about their heads.
MARK ANTONY: Thou bleed'st apace.
SCARUS: I had a wound here that was like a T,
SCARUS: But now 'tis made an H.
MARK ANTONY: They do retire.
SCARUS: We'll beat 'em into bench-holes: I have yet
SCARUS: Room for six scotches more.
NARRATOR: Enter EROS
EROS: They are beaten, sir, and our advantage serves
EROS: For a fair victory.
SCARUS: Let us score their backs,
SCARUS: And snatch 'em up, as we take hares, behind:
SCARUS: 'Tis sport to maul a runner.
MARK ANTONY: I will reward thee
MARK ANTONY: Once for thy spritely comfort, and ten-fold
MARK ANTONY: For thy good valour. Come thee on.
SCARUS: I'll halt after.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. Under the walls of Alexandria.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter MARK ANTONY, in a march, SCARUS, with others
MARK ANTONY: We have beat him to his camp: run one before,

MARK ANTONY: The honour'd gashes whole.
NARRATOR: To SCARUS
MARK ANTONY: Give me thy hand
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA, attended
MARK ANTONY: To this great fairy I'll commend thy acts,

NARRATOR: To CLEOPATRA

CLEOPATRA: Lord of lords!
CLEOPATRA: O infinite virtue, comest thou smiling from
CLEOPATRA: The world's great snare uncaught?
MARK ANTONY: My nightingale,
MARK ANTONY: We have beat them to their beds. What, girl!
MARK ANTONY: though grey
MARK ANTONY: Do something mingle with our younger brown, yet ha' we
MARK ANTONY: A brain that nourishes our nerves, and can
MARK ANTONY: Get goal for goal of youth. Behold this man,

MARK ANTONY: Destroy'd in such a shape.
CLEOPATRA: I'll give thee, friend,

MARK ANTONY: He has deserved it, were it carbuncled

MARK ANTONY: Through Alexandria make a jolly march,
MARK ANTONY: Bear our hack'd targets like the men that owe them:
MARK ANTONY: Had our great palace the capacity
MARK ANTONY: To camp this host, we all would sup together,
MARK ANTONY: And drink carouses to the next day's fate,
MARK ANTONY: Which promises royal peril. Trumpeters,
MARK ANTONY: With brazen din blast you the city's ear,
MARK ANTONY: Make mingle with rattling tabourines,
MARK ANTONY: That heaven and earth may strike their sounds together,
MARK ANTONY: Applauding our approach.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's camp.
NARRATOR: Sentinels at their post
First Soldier: If we be not relieved within this hour,
First Soldier: We must return to the court of guard: the night
First Soldier: Is shiny, and they say we shall embattle
First Soldier: By the second hour i' the morn.
Second Soldier: This last day was
Second Soldier: A shrewd one to's.
NARRATOR: Enter DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: O, bear me witness, night,--
Third Soldier: What man is this?
Second Soldier: Stand close, and list him.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Be witness to me, O thou blessed moon,

First Soldier: Enobarbus!
Third Soldier: Peace!
Third Soldier: Hark further.
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: O sovereign mistress of true melancholy,

DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: That life, a very rebel to my will,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: May hang no longer on me: throw my heart
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Against the flint and hardness of my fault:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Which, being dried with grief, will break to powder,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: And finish all foul thoughts. O Antony,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Nobler than my revolt is infamous,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: Forgive me in thine own particular,
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: But let the world rank me in register
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: A master-leaver and a fugitive:
DOMITIUS ENOBARBUS: O Antony! O Antony!
NARRATOR: Dies
Second Soldier: Let's speak To him.
First Soldier: Let's hear him, for the things he speaks
First Soldier: May concern Caesar.
Third Soldier: Let's do so. But he sleeps.
First Soldier: Swoons rather, for so bad a prayer as his
First Soldier: Was never yet for sleep.
Second Soldier: Go we to him.
Third Soldier: Awake, sir, awake, speak to us.
Second Soldier: Hear you, sir?
First Soldier: The hand of death hath raught him.
NARRATOR: Drums afar off
First Soldier: Hark! the drums
First Soldier: Demurely wake the sleepers. Let us bear him
First Soldier: To the court of guard, he is of note: our hour
First Soldier: Is fully out.
Third Soldier: Come on, then,
Third Soldier: He may recover yet.
NARRATOR: Exeunt with the body
NARRATOR: SCENE X. Between the two camps.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and SCARUS, with their Army
MARK ANTONY: Their preparation is to-day by sea,
MARK ANTONY: We please them not by land.
SCARUS: For both, my lord.
MARK ANTONY: I would they'ld fight i' the fire or i' the air,
MARK ANTONY: We'ld fight there too. But this it is, our foot
MARK ANTONY: Upon the hills adjoining to the city
MARK ANTONY: Shall stay with us: order for sea is given,
MARK ANTONY: They have put forth the haven
MARK ANTONY: Where their appointment we may best discover,
MARK ANTONY: And look on their endeavour.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XI. Another part of the same.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, and his Army
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: But being charged, we will be still by land,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Which, as I take't, we shall, for his best force
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Is forth to man his galleys. To the vales,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And hold our best advantage.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XII. Another part of the same.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and SCARUS
MARK ANTONY: Yet they are not join'd: where yond pine
MARK ANTONY: does stand,
MARK ANTONY: I shall discover all: I'll bring thee word
MARK ANTONY: Straight, how 'tis like to go.
NARRATOR: Exit
SCARUS: Swallows have built
SCARUS: In Cleopatra's sails their nests: the augurers
SCARUS: Say they know not, they cannot tell, look grimly,
SCARUS: And dare not speak their knowledge. Antony
SCARUS: Is valiant, and dejected, and, by starts,
SCARUS: His fretted fortunes give him hope, and fear,
SCARUS: Of what he has, and has not.
NARRATOR: Alarum afar off, as at a sea-fight
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARK ANTONY
MARK ANTONY: All is lost,
MARK ANTONY: This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me:
MARK ANTONY: My fleet hath yielded to the foe, and yonder
MARK ANTONY: They cast their caps up and carouse together
MARK ANTONY: Like friends long lost. Triple-turn'd whore!
MARK ANTONY: 'tis thou
MARK ANTONY: Hast sold me to this novice, and my heart
MARK ANTONY: Makes only wars on thee. Bid them all fly,
MARK ANTONY: For when I am revenged upon my charm,
MARK ANTONY: I have done all. Bid them all fly, begone.
NARRATOR: Exit SCARUS
MARK ANTONY: O sun, thy uprise shall I see no more:
MARK ANTONY: Fortune and Antony part here, even here
MARK ANTONY: Do we shake hands. All come to this? The hearts
MARK ANTONY: That spaniel'd me at heels, to whom I gave
MARK ANTONY: Their wishes, do discandy, melt their sweets
MARK ANTONY: On blossoming Caesar, and this pine is bark'd,
MARK ANTONY: That overtopp'd them all. Betray'd I am:
MARK ANTONY: O this false soul of Egypt! this grave charm,--
MARK ANTONY: Whose eye beck'd forth my wars, and call'd them home,
MARK ANTONY: Whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end,--
MARK ANTONY: Like a right gipsy, hath, at fast and loose,
MARK ANTONY: Beguiled me to the very heart of loss.
MARK ANTONY: What, Eros, Eros!
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA
MARK ANTONY: Ah, thou spell! Avaunt!
CLEOPATRA: Why is my lord enraged against his love?
MARK ANTONY: Vanish, or I shall give thee thy deserving,
MARK ANTONY: And blemish Caesar's triumph. Let him take thee,
MARK ANTONY: And hoist thee up to the shouting plebeians:
MARK ANTONY: Follow his chariot, like the greatest spot
MARK ANTONY: Of all thy sex, most monster-like, be shown
MARK ANTONY: For poor'st diminutives, for doits, and let
MARK ANTONY: Patient Octavia plough thy visage up
MARK ANTONY: With her prepared nails.
NARRATOR: Exit CLEOPATRA
MARK ANTONY: 'Tis well thou'rt gone,
MARK ANTONY: If it be well to live, but better 'twere
MARK ANTONY: Thou fell'st into my fury, for one death
MARK ANTONY: Might have prevented many. Eros, ho!
MARK ANTONY: The shirt of Nessus is upon me: teach me,
MARK ANTONY: Alcides, thou mine ancestor, thy rage:
MARK ANTONY: Let me lodge Lichas on the horns o' the moon,
MARK ANTONY: And with those hands, that grasp'd the heaviest club,
MARK ANTONY: Subdue my worthiest self. The witch shall die:
MARK ANTONY: To the young Roman boy she hath sold me, and I fall
MARK ANTONY: Under this plot, she dies for't. Eros, ho!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE XIII. Alexandria. Cleopatra's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMIAN, IRAS, and MARDIAN
CLEOPATRA: Help me, my women! O, he is more mad
CLEOPATRA: Than Telamon for his shield, the boar of Thessaly
CLEOPATRA: Was never so emboss'd.
CHARMIAN: To the monument!
CHARMIAN: There lock yourself, and send him word you are dead.
CHARMIAN: The soul and body rive not more in parting
CHARMIAN: Than greatness going off.
CLEOPATRA: To the monument!
CLEOPATRA: Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself,
CLEOPATRA: Say, that the last I spoke was 'Antony,'
CLEOPATRA: And word it, prithee, piteously: hence, Mardian,
CLEOPATRA: And bring me how he takes my death.
CLEOPATRA: To the monument!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE XIV. The same. Another room.
NARRATOR: Enter MARK ANTONY and EROS
MARK ANTONY: Eros, thou yet behold'st me?
EROS: Ay, noble lord.
MARK ANTONY: Sometimes we see a cloud that's dragonish,
MARK ANTONY: A vapour sometime like a bear or lion,
MARK ANTONY: A tower'd citadel, a pendent rock,
MARK ANTONY: A forked mountain, or blue promontory
MARK ANTONY: With trees upon't, that nod unto the world,
MARK ANTONY: And mock our eyes with air: thou hast seen
MARK ANTONY: these signs,
MARK ANTONY: They are black vesper's pageants.
EROS: Ay, my lord,
MARK ANTONY: That which is now a horse, even with a thought
MARK ANTONY: The rack dislimns, and makes it indistinct,
MARK ANTONY: As water is in water.
EROS: It does, my lord.
MARK ANTONY: My good knave Eros, now thy captain is
MARK ANTONY: Even such a body: here I am Antony:
MARK ANTONY: Yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave.
MARK ANTONY: I made these wars for Egypt: and the queen,--
MARK ANTONY: Whose heart I thought I had, for she had mine,
MARK ANTONY: Which whilst it was mine had annex'd unto't
MARK ANTONY: A million more, now lost,--she, Eros, has
MARK ANTONY: Pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory
MARK ANTONY: Unto an enemy's triumph.
MARK ANTONY: Nay, weep not, gentle Eros, there is left us
MARK ANTONY: Ourselves to end ourselves.
NARRATOR: Enter MARDIAN
MARK ANTONY: O! thy vile lady!
MARK ANTONY: She has robb'd me of my sword.
MARDIAN: No, Antony,
MARDIAN: My mistress loved thee, and her fortunes mingled
MARDIAN: With thine entirely.
MARK ANTONY: Hence, saucy eunuch, peace!
MARK ANTONY: She hath betray'd me and shall die the death.
MARDIAN: Death of one person can be paid but once,
MARDIAN: And that she has discharged: what thou wouldst do
MARDIAN: Is done unto thy hand: the last she spake
MARDIAN: Was 'Antony! most noble Antony!'
MARDIAN: Then in the midst a tearing groan did break
MARDIAN: The name of Antony, it was divided
MARDIAN: Between her heart and lips: she render'd life,
MARDIAN: Thy name so buried in her.
MARK ANTONY: Dead, then?
MARDIAN: Dead.
MARK ANTONY: Unarm, Eros, the long day's task is done,
MARK ANTONY: And we must sleep.
NARRATOR: To MARDIAN
MARK ANTONY: That thou depart'st hence safe,
MARK ANTONY: Does pay thy labour richly, go.
NARRATOR: Exit MARDIAN
MARK ANTONY: Off, pluck off:
MARK ANTONY: The seven-fold shield of Ajax cannot keep
MARK ANTONY: The battery from my heart. O, cleave, my sides!
MARK ANTONY: Heart, once be stronger than thy continent,
MARK ANTONY: Crack thy frail case! Apace, Eros, apace.
MARK ANTONY: No more a soldier: bruised pieces, go,
MARK ANTONY: You have been nobly borne. From me awhile.
NARRATOR: Exit EROS
MARK ANTONY: I will o'ertake thee, Cleopatra, and
MARK ANTONY: Weep for my pardon. So it must be, for now
MARK ANTONY: All length is torture: since the torch is out,
MARK ANTONY: Lie down, and stray no farther: now all labour
MARK ANTONY: Mars what it does, yea, very force entangles
MARK ANTONY: Itself with strength: seal then, and all is done.
MARK ANTONY: Eros!--I come, my queen:--Eros!--Stay for me:
MARK ANTONY: Where souls do couch on flowers, we'll hand in hand,
MARK ANTONY: And with our sprightly port make the ghosts gaze:
MARK ANTONY: Dido and her AEneas shall want troops,
MARK ANTONY: And all the haunt be ours. Come, Eros, Eros!
NARRATOR: Re-enter EROS
EROS: What would my lord?
MARK ANTONY: Since Cleopatra died,
MARK ANTONY: I have lived in such dishonour, that the gods
MARK ANTONY: Detest my baseness. I, that with my sword
MARK ANTONY: Quarter'd the world, and o'er green Neptune's back
MARK ANTONY: With ships made cities, condemn myself to lack
MARK ANTONY: The courage of a woman, less noble mind
MARK ANTONY: Than she which by her death our Caesar tells
MARK ANTONY: 'I am conqueror of myself.' Thou art sworn, Eros,
MARK ANTONY: That, when the exigent should come, which now
MARK ANTONY: Is come indeed, when I should see behind me
MARK ANTONY: The inevitable prosecution of
MARK ANTONY: Disgrace and horror, that, on my command,
MARK ANTONY: Thou then wouldst kill me: do't, the time is come:
MARK ANTONY: Thou strikest not me, 'tis Caesar thou defeat'st.
MARK ANTONY: Put colour in thy cheek.
EROS: The gods withhold me!
EROS: Shall I do that which all the Parthian darts,
EROS: Though enemy, lost aim, and could not?
MARK ANTONY: Eros,
MARK ANTONY: Wouldst thou be window'd in great Rome and see
MARK ANTONY: Thy master thus with pleach'd arms, bending down
MARK ANTONY: His corrigible neck, his face subdued
MARK ANTONY: To penetrative shame, whilst the wheel'd seat
MARK ANTONY: Of fortunate Caesar, drawn before him, branded
MARK ANTONY: His baseness that ensued?
EROS: I would not see't.
MARK ANTONY: Come, then, for with a wound I must be cured.
MARK ANTONY: Draw that thy honest sword, which thou hast worn
MARK ANTONY: Most useful for thy country.
EROS: O, sir, pardon me!
MARK ANTONY: When I did make thee free, sworest thou not then
MARK ANTONY: To do this when I bade thee? Do it at once,
MARK ANTONY: Or thy precedent services are all
MARK ANTONY: But accidents unpurposed. Draw, and come.
EROS: Turn from me, then, that noble countenance,
EROS: Wherein the worship of the whole world lies.
MARK ANTONY: Lo thee!
NARRATOR: Turning from him
EROS: My sword is drawn.
MARK ANTONY: Then let it do at once
MARK ANTONY: The thing why thou hast drawn it.
EROS: My dear master,
EROS: My captain, and my emperor, let me say,
EROS: Before I strike this bloody stroke, farewell.
MARK ANTONY: 'Tis said, man, and farewell.
EROS: Farewell, great chief. Shall I strike now?
MARK ANTONY: Now, Eros.
EROS: Why, there then: thus I do escape the sorrow
EROS: Of Antony's death.
NARRATOR: Kills himself
MARK ANTONY: Thrice-nobler than myself!
MARK ANTONY: Thou teachest me, O valiant Eros, what
MARK ANTONY: I should, and thou couldst not. My queen and Eros
MARK ANTONY: Have by their brave instruction got upon me
MARK ANTONY: A nobleness in record: but I will be
MARK ANTONY: A bridegroom in my death, and run into't
MARK ANTONY: As to a lover's bed. Come, then, and, Eros,
MARK ANTONY: Thy master dies thy scholar: to do thus
NARRATOR: Falling on his sword
MARK ANTONY: I learn'd of thee. How! not dead? not dead?
MARK ANTONY: The guard, ho! O, dispatch me!
NARRATOR: Enter DERCETAS and Guard
First Guard: What's the noise?
MARK ANTONY: I have done my work in, friends: O, make an end
MARK ANTONY: Of what I have begun.
Second Guard: The star is fall'n.
First Guard: And time is at his period.
All: Alas, and woe!
MARK ANTONY: Let him that loves me strike me dead.
First Guard: Not I.
Second Guard: Nor I.
Third Guard: Nor any one.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Guard
DERCETAS: Thy death and fortunes bid thy followers fly.
DERCETAS: This sword but shown to Caesar, with this tidings,
DERCETAS: Shall enter me with him.
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES
DIOMEDES: Where's Antony?
DERCETAS: There, Diomed there.
DIOMEDES: Lives he?
DIOMEDES: Wilt thou not answer, man?
NARRATOR: Exit DERCETAS
MARK ANTONY: Art thou there, Diomed? Draw thy sword, and give me
MARK ANTONY: Sufficing strokes for death.
DIOMEDES: Most absolute lord,
DIOMEDES: My mistress Cleopatra sent me to thee.
MARK ANTONY: When did she send thee?
DIOMEDES: Now, my lord.
MARK ANTONY: Where is she?
DIOMEDES: Lock'd in her monument. She had a prophesying fear
DIOMEDES: Of what hath come to pass: for when she saw--
DIOMEDES: Which never shall be found--you did suspect
DIOMEDES: She had disposed with Caesar, and that your rage
DIOMEDES: Would not be purged, she sent you word she was dead,
DIOMEDES: But, fearing since how it might work, hath sent
DIOMEDES: Me to proclaim the truth, and I am come,
DIOMEDES: I dread, too late.
MARK ANTONY: Too late, good Diomed: call my guard, I prithee.
DIOMEDES: What, ho, the emperor's guard! The guard, what, ho!
DIOMEDES: Come, your lord calls!
NARRATOR: Enter four or five of the Guard of MARK ANTONY
MARK ANTONY: Bear me, good friends, where Cleopatra bides,
MARK ANTONY: 'Tis the last service that I shall command you.
First Guard: Woe, woe are we, sir, you may not live to wear
First Guard: All your true followers out.
All: Most heavy day!
MARK ANTONY: Nay, good my fellows, do not please sharp fate
MARK ANTONY: To grace it with your sorrows: bid that welcome
MARK ANTONY: Which comes to punish us, and we punish it
MARK ANTONY: Seeming to bear it lightly. Take me up:
MARK ANTONY: I have led you oft: carry me now, good friends,
MARK ANTONY: And have my thanks for all.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, bearing MARK ANTONY
NARRATOR: SCENE XV. The same. A monument.
NARRATOR: Enter CLEOPATRA and her maids aloft, with CHARMIAN and IRAS
CLEOPATRA: O Charmian, I will never go from hence.
CHARMIAN: Be comforted, dear madam.
CLEOPATRA: No, I will not:
CLEOPATRA: All strange and terrible events are welcome,
CLEOPATRA: But comforts we despise, our size of sorrow,
CLEOPATRA: Proportion'd to our cause, must be as great
CLEOPATRA: As that which makes it.
NARRATOR: Enter, below, DIOMEDES
CLEOPATRA: How now! is he dead?
DIOMEDES: His death's upon him, but not dead.
DIOMEDES: Look out o' the other side your monument,
DIOMEDES: His guard have brought him thither.
NARRATOR: Enter, below, MARK ANTONY, borne by the Guard
CLEOPATRA: O sun,
CLEOPATRA: Burn the great sphere thou movest in!
CLEOPATRA: darkling stand
CLEOPATRA: The varying shore o' the world. O Antony,
CLEOPATRA: Antony, Antony! Help, Charmian, help, Iras, help,
CLEOPATRA: Help, friends below, let's draw him hither.
MARK ANTONY: Peace!
MARK ANTONY: Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony,
MARK ANTONY: But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself.
CLEOPATRA: So it should be, that none but Antony
CLEOPATRA: Should conquer Antony, but woe 'tis so!
MARK ANTONY: I am dying, Egypt, dying, only
MARK ANTONY: I here importune death awhile, until
MARK ANTONY: Of many thousand kisses the poor last
MARK ANTONY: I lay up thy lips.
CLEOPATRA: I dare not, dear,--
CLEOPATRA: Dear my lord, pardon,--I dare not,
CLEOPATRA: Lest I be taken: not the imperious show
CLEOPATRA: Of the full-fortuned Caesar ever shall
CLEOPATRA: Be brooch'd with me, if knife, drugs,
CLEOPATRA: serpents, have
CLEOPATRA: Edge, sting, or operation, I am safe:
CLEOPATRA: Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes
CLEOPATRA: And still conclusion, shall acquire no honour
CLEOPATRA: Demuring upon me. But come, come, Antony,--
CLEOPATRA: Help me, my women,--we must draw thee up:
CLEOPATRA: Assist, good friends.
MARK ANTONY: O, quick, or I am gone.
CLEOPATRA: Here's sport indeed! How heavy weighs my lord!
CLEOPATRA: Our strength is all gone into heaviness,
CLEOPATRA: That makes the weight: had I great Juno's power,
CLEOPATRA: The strong-wing'd Mercury should fetch thee up,
CLEOPATRA: And set thee by Jove's side. Yet come a little,--
CLEOPATRA: Wishes were ever fools,--O, come, come, come,
NARRATOR: They heave MARK ANTONY aloft to CLEOPATRA
CLEOPATRA: And welcome, welcome! die where thou hast lived:
CLEOPATRA: Quicken with kissing: had my lips that power,
CLEOPATRA: Thus would I wear them out.
All: A heavy sight!
MARK ANTONY: I am dying, Egypt, dying:
MARK ANTONY: Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.
CLEOPATRA: No, let me speak, and let me rail so high,
CLEOPATRA: That the false housewife Fortune break her wheel,
CLEOPATRA: Provoked by my offence.
MARK ANTONY: One word, sweet queen:
MARK ANTONY: Of Caesar seek your honour, with your safety. O!
CLEOPATRA: They do not go together.
MARK ANTONY: Gentle, hear me:
MARK ANTONY: None about Caesar trust but Proculeius.
CLEOPATRA: My resolution and my hands I'll trust,
CLEOPATRA: None about Caesar.
MARK ANTONY: The miserable change now at my end
MARK ANTONY: Lament nor sorrow at, but please your thoughts
MARK ANTONY: In feeding them with those my former fortunes
MARK ANTONY: Wherein I lived, the greatest prince o' the world,
MARK ANTONY: The noblest, and do now not basely die,
MARK ANTONY: Not cowardly put off my helmet to
MARK ANTONY: My countryman,--a Roman by a Roman
MARK ANTONY: Valiantly vanquish'd. Now my spirit is going,
MARK ANTONY: I can no more.
CLEOPATRA: Noblest of men, woo't die?
CLEOPATRA: Hast thou no care of me? shall I abide
CLEOPATRA: In this dull world, which in thy absence is
CLEOPATRA: No better than a sty? O, see, my women,
NARRATOR: MARK ANTONY dies
CLEOPATRA: The crown o' the earth doth melt. My lord!
CLEOPATRA: O, wither'd is the garland of the war,
CLEOPATRA: The soldier's pole is fall'n: young boys and girls
CLEOPATRA: Are level now with men, the odds is gone,
CLEOPATRA: And there is nothing left remarkable
CLEOPATRA: Beneath the visiting moon.
NARRATOR: Faints
CHARMIAN: O, quietness, lady!
IRAS: She is dead too, our sovereign.
CHARMIAN: Lady!
IRAS: Madam!
CHARMIAN: O madam, madam, madam!
IRAS: Royal Egypt, Empress!
CHARMIAN: Peace, peace, Iras!
CLEOPATRA: No more, but e'en a woman, and commanded
CLEOPATRA: By such poor passion as the maid that milks
CLEOPATRA: And does the meanest chares. It were for me
CLEOPATRA: To throw my sceptre at the injurious gods,
CLEOPATRA: To tell them that this world did equal theirs
CLEOPATRA: Till they had stol'n our jewel. All's but naught,
CLEOPATRA: Patience is scottish, and impatience does
CLEOPATRA: Become a dog that's mad: then is it sin
CLEOPATRA: To rush into the secret house of death,
CLEOPATRA: Ere death dare come to us? How do you, women?
CLEOPATRA: What, what! good cheer! Why, how now, Charmian!
CLEOPATRA: My noble girls! Ah, women, women, look,
CLEOPATRA: Our lamp is spent, it's out! Good sirs, take heart:
CLEOPATRA: We'll bury him, and then, what's brave,
CLEOPATRA: what's noble,
CLEOPATRA: Let's do it after the high Roman fashion,
CLEOPATRA: And make death proud to take us. Come, away:
CLEOPATRA: This case of that huge spirit now is cold:
CLEOPATRA: Ah, women, women! come, we have no friend
CLEOPATRA: But resolution, and the briefest end.
CLEOPATRA: Exeunt, those above bearing off MARK ANTONY's body
CLEOPATRA: ACT V
CLEOPATRA: SCENE I. Alexandria. OCTAVIUS CAESAR's camp.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS CAESAR, AGRIPPA, DOLABELLA, MECAENAS, GALLUS, PROCULEIUS, and others, his council of war
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Go to him, Dolabella, bid him yield,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Being so frustrate, tell him he mocks
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The pauses that he makes.
DOLABELLA: Caesar, I shall.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter DERCETAS, with the sword of MARK ANTONY
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Wherefore is that? and what art thou that darest
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Appear thus to us?
DERCETAS: I am call'd Dercetas,
DERCETAS: Mark Antony I served, who best was worthy
DERCETAS: Best to be served: whilst he stood up and spoke,
DERCETAS: He was my master, and I wore my life
DERCETAS: To spend upon his haters. If thou please
DERCETAS: To take me to thee, as I was to him
DERCETAS: I'll be to Caesar, if thou pleasest not,
DERCETAS: I yield thee up my life.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: What is't thou say'st?
DERCETAS: I say, O Caesar, Antony is dead.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The breaking of so great a thing should make
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: A greater crack: the round world
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Should have shook lions into civil streets,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: And citizens to their dens: the death of Antony
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Is not a single doom, in the name lay
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: A moiety of the world.
DERCETAS: He is dead, Caesar:
DERCETAS: Not by a public minister of justice,
DERCETAS: Nor by a hired knife, but that self hand,
DERCETAS: Which writ his honour in the acts it did,
DERCETAS: Hath, with the courage which the heart did lend it,
DERCETAS: Splitted the heart. This is his sword,
DERCETAS: I robb'd his wound of it, behold it stain'd
DERCETAS: With his most noble blood.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Look you sad, friends?
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The gods rebuke me, but it is tidings
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To wash the eyes of kings.
AGRIPPA: And strange it is,
AGRIPPA: That nature must compel us to lament
AGRIPPA: Our most persisted deeds.
MECAENAS: His taints and honours
MECAENAS: Waged equal with him.
AGRIPPA: A rarer spirit never
AGRIPPA: Did steer humanity: but you, gods, will give us
AGRIPPA: Some faults to make us men. Caesar is touch'd.
MECAENAS: When such a spacious mirror's set before him,
MECAENAS: He needs must see himself.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: O Antony!
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: I have follow'd thee to this, but we do lance
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Diseases in our bodies: I must perforce
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Have shown to thee such a declining day,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Or look on thine, we could not stall together
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: In the whole world: but yet let me lament,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: With tears as sovereign as the blood of hearts,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: That thou, my brother, my competitor
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: In top of all design, my mate in empire,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Friend and companion in the front of war,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The arm of mine own body, and the heart
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Where mine his thoughts did kindle,--that our stars,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Unreconciliable, should divide
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Our equalness to this. Hear me, good friends--
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: But I will tell you at some meeter season:
NARRATOR: Enter an Egyptian
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: The business of this man looks out of him,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: We'll hear him what he says. Whence are you?
Egyptian: A poor Egyptian yet. The queen my mistress,
Egyptian: Confined in all she has, her monument,
Egyptian: Of thy intents desires instruction,
Egyptian: That she preparedly may frame herself
Egyptian: To the way she's forced to.
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Bid her have good heart:
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: She soon shall know of us, by some of ours,
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: How honourable and how kindly we
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: Determine for her, for Caesar cannot live
OCTAVIUS CAESAR: To be ungentle.
Egyptian: So the gods preserve thee!

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Orchard of Oliver's house.
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO and ADAM
ORLANDO: As I remember, Adam, it was upon this fashion
ORLANDO: bequeathed me by will but poor a thousand crowns,
ORLANDO: and, as thou sayest, charged my brother, on his
ORLANDO: blessing, to breed me well: and there begins my
ORLANDO: sadness. My brother Jaques he keeps at school, and
ORLANDO: report speaks goldenly of his profit: for my part,
ORLANDO: he keeps me rustically at home, or, to speak more
ORLANDO: properly, stays me here at home unkept, for call you
ORLANDO: that keeping for a gentleman of my birth, that
ORLANDO: differs not from the stalling of an ox? His horses
ORLANDO: are bred better, for, besides that they are fair
ORLANDO: with their feeding, they are taught their manage,
ORLANDO: and to that end riders dearly hired: but I, his
ORLANDO: brother, gain nothing under him but growth, for the
ORLANDO: which his animals on his dunghills are as much
ORLANDO: bound to him as I. Besides this nothing that he so
ORLANDO: plentifully gives me, the something that nature gave
ORLANDO: me his countenance seems to take from me: he lets
ORLANDO: me feed with his hinds, bars me the place of a
ORLANDO: brother, and, as much as in him lies, mines my
ORLANDO: gentility with my education. This is it, Adam, that
ORLANDO: grieves me, and the spirit of my father, which I
ORLANDO: think is within me, begins to mutiny against this
ORLANDO: servitude: I will no longer endure it, though yet I
ORLANDO: know no wise remedy how to avoid it.
ADAM: Yonder comes my master, your brother.
ORLANDO: Go apart, Adam, and thou shalt hear how he will
ORLANDO: shake me up.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVER
OLIVER: Now, sir! what make you here?
ORLANDO: Nothing: I am not taught to make any thing.
OLIVER: What mar you then, sir?
ORLANDO: Marry, sir, I am helping you to mar that which God
ORLANDO: made, a poor unworthy brother of yours, with idleness.
OLIVER: Marry, sir, be better employed, and be naught awhile.
ORLANDO: Shall I keep your hogs and eat husks with them?
ORLANDO: What prodigal portion have I spent, that I should
ORLANDO: come to such penury?
OLIVER: Know you where your are, sir?
ORLANDO: O, sir, very well, here in your orchard.
OLIVER: Know you before whom, sir?
ORLANDO: Ay, better than him I am before knows me. I know
ORLANDO: you are my eldest brother, and, in the gentle
ORLANDO: condition of blood, you should so know me. The
ORLANDO: courtesy of nations allows you my better, in that
ORLANDO: you are the first-born, but the same tradition
ORLANDO: takes not away my blood, were there twenty brothers
ORLANDO: betwixt us: I have as much of my father in me as
ORLANDO: you, albeit, I confess, your coming before me is
ORLANDO: nearer to his reverence.
OLIVER: What, boy!
ORLANDO: Come, come, elder brother, you are too young in this.
OLIVER: Wilt thou lay hands on me, villain?
ORLANDO: I am no villain, I am the youngest son of Sir
ORLANDO: Rowland de Boys, he was my father, and he is thrice
ORLANDO: a villain that says such a father begot villains.
ORLANDO: Wert thou not my brother, I would not take this hand
ORLANDO: from thy throat till this other had pulled out thy
ORLANDO: tongue for saying so: thou hast railed on thyself.
ADAM: Sweet masters, be patient: for your father's
ADAM: remembrance, be at accord.
OLIVER: Let me go, I say.
ORLANDO: I will not, till I please: you shall hear me. My
ORLANDO: father charged you in his will to give me good
ORLANDO: education: you have trained me like a peasant,
ORLANDO: obscuring and hiding from me all gentleman-like
ORLANDO: qualities. The spirit of my father grows strong in
ORLANDO: me, and I will no longer endure it: therefore allow
ORLANDO: me such exercises as may become a gentleman, or
ORLANDO: give me the poor allottery my father left me by
ORLANDO: testament, with that I will go buy my fortunes.
OLIVER: And what wilt thou do? beg, when that is spent?
OLIVER: Well, sir, get you in: I will not long be troubled
OLIVER: with you, you shall have some part of your will: I
OLIVER: pray you, leave me.
ORLANDO: I will no further offend you than becomes me for my good.
OLIVER: Get you with him, you old dog.
ADAM: Is 'old dog' my reward? Most true, I have lost my
ADAM: teeth in your service. God be with my old master!
ADAM: he would not have spoke such a word.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ORLANDO and ADAM
OLIVER: Is it even so? begin you to grow upon me? I will
OLIVER: physic your rankness, and yet give no thousand
OLIVER: crowns neither. Holla, Dennis!
NARRATOR: Enter DENNIS
DENNIS: Calls your worship?
OLIVER: Was not Charles, the duke's wrestler, here to speak with me?
DENNIS: So please you, he is here at the door and importunes
DENNIS: access to you.
OLIVER: Call him in.
NARRATOR: Exit DENNIS
OLIVER: 'Twill be a good way, and to-morrow the wrestling is.
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES
CHARLES: Good morrow to your worship.
OLIVER: Good Monsieur Charles, what's the new news at the
OLIVER: new court?
CHARLES: There's no news at the court, sir, but the old news:
CHARLES: that is, the old duke is banished by his younger
CHARLES: brother the new duke, and three or four loving lords
CHARLES: have put themselves into voluntary exile with him,
CHARLES: whose lands and revenues enrich the new duke,
CHARLES: therefore he gives them good leave to wander.
OLIVER: Can you tell if Rosalind, the duke's daughter, be
OLIVER: banished with her father?
CHARLES: O, no, for the duke's daughter, her cousin, so loves
CHARLES: her, being ever from their cradles bred together,
CHARLES: that she would have followed her exile, or have died
CHARLES: to stay behind her. She is at the court, and no
CHARLES: less beloved of her uncle than his own daughter, and
CHARLES: never two ladies loved as they do.
OLIVER: Where will the old duke live?
CHARLES: They say he is already in the forest of Arden, and
CHARLES: a many merry men with him, and there they live like
CHARLES: the old Robin Hood of England: they say many young
CHARLES: gentlemen flock to him every day, and fleet the time
CHARLES: carelessly, as they did in the golden world.
OLIVER: What, you wrestle to-morrow before the new duke?
CHARLES: Marry, do I, sir, and I came to acquaint you with a
CHARLES: matter. I am given, sir, secretly to understand
CHARLES: that your younger brother Orlando hath a disposition
CHARLES: to come in disguised against me to try a fall.
CHARLES: To-morrow, sir, I wrestle for my credit, and he that
CHARLES: escapes me without some broken limb shall acquit him
CHARLES: well. Your brother is but young and tender, and,
CHARLES: for your love, I would be loath to foil him, as I
CHARLES: must, for my own honour, if he come in: therefore,
CHARLES: out of my love to you, I came hither to acquaint you
CHARLES: withal, that either you might stay him from his
CHARLES: intendment or brook such disgrace well as he shall
CHARLES: run into, in that it is a thing of his own search
CHARLES: and altogether against my will.
OLIVER: Charles, I thank thee for thy love to me, which
OLIVER: thou shalt find I will most kindly requite. I had
OLIVER: myself notice of my brother's purpose herein and
OLIVER: have by underhand means laboured to dissuade him from
OLIVER: it, but he is resolute. I'll tell thee, Charles:
OLIVER: it is the stubbornest young fellow of France, full
OLIVER: of ambition, an envious emulator of every man's
OLIVER: good parts, a secret and villanous contriver against
OLIVER: me his natural brother: therefore use thy
OLIVER: discretion, I had as lief thou didst break his neck
OLIVER: as his finger. And thou wert best look to't, for if
OLIVER: thou dost him any slight disgrace or if he do not
OLIVER: mightily grace himself on thee, he will practise
OLIVER: against thee by poison, entrap thee by some
OLIVER: treacherous device and never leave thee till he
OLIVER: hath ta'en thy life by some indirect means or other,
OLIVER: for, I assure thee, and almost with tears I speak
OLIVER: it, there is not one so young and so villanous this
OLIVER: day living. I speak but brotherly of him, but
OLIVER: should I anatomize him to thee as he is, I must
OLIVER: blush and weep and thou must look pale and wonder.
CHARLES: I am heartily glad I came hither to you. If he come
CHARLES: to-morrow, I'll give him his payment: if ever he go
CHARLES: alone again, I'll never wrestle for prize more: and
CHARLES: so God keep your worship!
OLIVER: Farewell, good Charles.
NARRATOR: Exit CHARLES
OLIVER: Now will I stir this gamester: I hope I shall see
OLIVER: an end of him, for my soul, yet I know not why,
OLIVER: hates nothing more than he. Yet he's gentle, never
OLIVER: schooled and yet learned, full of noble device, of
OLIVER: all sorts enchantingly beloved, and indeed so much
OLIVER: in the heart of the world, and especially of my own
OLIVER: people, who best know him, that I am altogether
OLIVER: misprised: but it shall not be so long, this
OLIVER: wrestler shall clear all: nothing remains but that
OLIVER: I kindle the boy thither, which now I'll go about.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Lawn before the Duke's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CELIA and ROSALIND
CELIA: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my coz, be merry.
ROSALIND: Dear Celia, I show more mirth than I am mistress of,
ROSALIND: and would you yet I were merrier? Unless you could
ROSALIND: teach me to forget a banished father, you must not
ROSALIND: learn me how to remember any extraordinary pleasure.
CELIA: Herein I see thou lovest me not with the full weight
CELIA: that I love thee. If my uncle, thy banished father,
CELIA: had banished thy uncle, the duke my father, so thou
CELIA: hadst been still with me, I could have taught my
CELIA: love to take thy father for mine: so wouldst thou,
CELIA: if the truth of thy love to me were so righteously
CELIA: tempered as mine is to thee.
ROSALIND: Well, I will forget the condition of my estate, to
ROSALIND: rejoice in yours.
CELIA: You know my father hath no child but I, nor none is
CELIA: like to have: and, truly, when he dies, thou shalt
CELIA: be his heir, for what he hath taken away from thy
CELIA: father perforce, I will render thee again in
CELIA: affection, by mine honour, I will, and when I break
CELIA: that oath, let me turn monster: therefore, my
CELIA: sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be merry.
ROSALIND: From henceforth I will, coz, and devise sports. Let
ROSALIND: me see, what think you of falling in love?
CELIA: Marry, I prithee, do, to make sport withal: but
CELIA: love no man in good earnest, nor no further in sport
CELIA: neither than with safety of a pure blush thou mayst
CELIA: in honour come off again.
ROSALIND: What shall be our sport, then?
CELIA: Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune from
CELIA: her wheel, that her gifts may henceforth be bestowed equally.
ROSALIND: I would we could do so, for her benefits are
ROSALIND: mightily misplaced, and the bountiful blind woman
ROSALIND: doth most mistake in her gifts to women.
CELIA: 'Tis true, for those that she makes fair she scarce
CELIA: makes honest, and those that she makes honest she
CELIA: makes very ill-favouredly.
ROSALIND: Nay, now thou goest from Fortune's office to
ROSALIND: Nature's: Fortune reigns in gifts of the world,
ROSALIND: not in the lineaments of Nature.
NARRATOR: Enter TOUCHSTONE
CELIA: No? when Nature hath made a fair creature, may she
CELIA: not by Fortune fall into the fire? Though Nature
CELIA: hath given us wit to flout at Fortune, hath not
CELIA: Fortune sent in this fool to cut off the argument?
ROSALIND: Indeed, there is Fortune too hard for Nature, when
ROSALIND: Fortune makes Nature's natural the cutter-off of
ROSALIND: Nature's wit.
CELIA: Peradventure this is not Fortune's work neither, but
CELIA: Nature's, who perceiveth our natural wits too dull
CELIA: to reason of such goddesses and hath sent this
CELIA: natural for our whetstone, for always the dulness of
CELIA: the fool is the whetstone of the wits. How now,
CELIA: wit! whither wander you?
TOUCHSTONE: Mistress, you must come away to your father.
CELIA: Were you made the messenger?
TOUCHSTONE: No, by mine honour, but I was bid to come for you.
ROSALIND: Where learned you that oath, fool?
TOUCHSTONE: Of a certain knight that swore by his honour they
TOUCHSTONE: were good pancakes and swore by his honour the
TOUCHSTONE: mustard was naught: now I'll stand to it, the
TOUCHSTONE: pancakes were naught and the mustard was good, and
TOUCHSTONE: yet was not the knight forsworn.
CELIA: How prove you that, in the great heap of your
CELIA: knowledge?
ROSALIND: Ay, marry, now unmuzzle your wisdom.
TOUCHSTONE: Stand you both forth now: stroke your chins, and
TOUCHSTONE: swear by your beards that I am a knave.
CELIA: By our beards, if we had them, thou art.
TOUCHSTONE: By my knavery, if I had it, then I were, but if you
TOUCHSTONE: swear by that that is not, you are not forsworn: no
TOUCHSTONE: more was this knight swearing by his honour, for he
TOUCHSTONE: never had any, or if he had, he had sworn it away
TOUCHSTONE: before ever he saw those pancakes or that mustard.
CELIA: Prithee, who is't that thou meanest?
TOUCHSTONE: One that old Frederick, your father, loves.
CELIA: My father's love is enough to honour him: enough!
CELIA: speak no more of him, you'll be whipped for taxation
CELIA: one of these days.
TOUCHSTONE: The more pity, that fools may not speak wisely what
TOUCHSTONE: wise men do foolishly.
CELIA: By my troth, thou sayest true, for since the little
CELIA: wit that fools have was silenced, the little foolery
CELIA: that wise men have makes a great show. Here comes
CELIA: Monsieur Le Beau.
ROSALIND: With his mouth full of news.
CELIA: Which he will put on us, as pigeons feed their young.
ROSALIND: Then shall we be news-crammed.
CELIA: All the better, we shall be the more marketable.
NARRATOR: Enter LE BEAU
CELIA: Bon jour, Monsieur Le Beau: what's the news?
LE BEAU: Fair princess, you have lost much good sport.
CELIA: Sport! of what colour?
LE BEAU: What colour, madam! how shall I answer you?
ROSALIND: As wit and fortune will.
TOUCHSTONE: Or as the Destinies decree.
CELIA: Well said: that was laid on with a trowel.
TOUCHSTONE: Nay, if I keep not my rank,--
ROSALIND: Thou losest thy old smell.
LE BEAU: You amaze me, ladies: I would have told you of good
LE BEAU: wrestling, which you have lost the sight of.
ROSALIND: You tell us the manner of the wrestling.
LE BEAU: I will tell you the beginning, and, if it please
LE BEAU: your ladyships, you may see the end, for the best is
LE BEAU: yet to do, and here, where you are, they are coming
LE BEAU: to perform it.
CELIA: Well, the beginning, that is dead and buried.
LE BEAU: There comes an old man and his three sons,--
CELIA: I could match this beginning with an old tale.
LE BEAU: Three proper young men, of excellent growth and presence.
ROSALIND: With bills on their necks, 'Be it known unto all men
ROSALIND: by these presents.'
LE BEAU: The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the
LE BEAU: duke's wrestler, which Charles in a moment threw him
LE BEAU: and broke three of his ribs, that there is little
LE BEAU: hope of life in him: so he served the second, and
LE BEAU: so the third. Yonder they lie, the poor old man,
LE BEAU: their father, making such pitiful dole over them
LE BEAU: that all the beholders take his part with weeping.
ROSALIND: Alas!
TOUCHSTONE: But what is the sport, monsieur, that the ladies
TOUCHSTONE: have lost?
LE BEAU: Why, this that I speak of.
TOUCHSTONE: Thus men may grow wiser every day: it is the first
TOUCHSTONE: time that ever I heard breaking of ribs was sport
TOUCHSTONE: for ladies.
CELIA: Or I, I promise thee.
ROSALIND: But is there any else longs to see this broken music
ROSALIND: in his sides? is there yet another dotes upon
ROSALIND: rib-breaking? Shall we see this wrestling, cousin?
LE BEAU: You must, if you stay here, for here is the place
LE BEAU: appointed for the wrestling, and they are ready to
LE BEAU: perform it.
CELIA: Yonder, sure, they are coming: let us now stay and see it.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter DUKE FREDERICK, Lords, ORLANDO, CHARLES, and Attendants
DUKE FREDERICK: Come on: since the youth will not be entreated, his
DUKE FREDERICK: own peril on his forwardness.
ROSALIND: Is yonder the man?
LE BEAU: Even he, madam.
CELIA: Alas, he is too young! yet he looks successfully.
DUKE FREDERICK: How now, daughter and cousin! are you crept hither
DUKE FREDERICK: to see the wrestling?
ROSALIND: Ay, my liege, so please you give us leave.
DUKE FREDERICK: You will take little delight in it, I can tell you,
DUKE FREDERICK: there is such odds in the man. In pity of the
DUKE FREDERICK: challenger's youth I would fain dissuade him, but he
DUKE FREDERICK: will not be entreated. Speak to him, ladies, see if
DUKE FREDERICK: you can move him.
CELIA: Call him hither, good Monsieur Le Beau.
DUKE FREDERICK: Do so: I'll not be by.
LE BEAU: Monsieur the challenger, the princesses call for you.
ORLANDO: I attend them with all respect and duty.
ROSALIND: Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?
ORLANDO: No, fair princess, he is the general challenger: I
ORLANDO: come but in, as others do, to try with him the
ORLANDO: strength of my youth.
CELIA: Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your
CELIA: years. You have seen cruel proof of this man's
CELIA: strength: if you saw yourself with your eyes or
CELIA: knew yourself with your judgment, the fear of your
CELIA: adventure would counsel you to a more equal
CELIA: enterprise. We pray you, for your own sake, to
CELIA: embrace your own safety and give over this attempt.
ROSALIND: Do, young sir, your reputation shall not therefore
ROSALIND: be misprised: we will make it our suit to the duke
ROSALIND: that the wrestling might not go forward.
ORLANDO: I beseech you, punish me not with your hard
ORLANDO: thoughts, wherein I confess me much guilty, to deny
ORLANDO: so fair and excellent ladies any thing. But let
ORLANDO: your fair eyes and gentle wishes go with me to my
ORLANDO: trial: wherein if I be foiled, there is but one
ORLANDO: shamed that was never gracious, if killed, but one
ORLANDO: dead that was willing to be so: I shall do my
ORLANDO: friends no wrong, for I have none to lament me, the
ORLANDO: world no injury, for in it I have nothing, only in
ORLANDO: the world I fill up a place, which may be better
ORLANDO: supplied when I have made it empty.
ROSALIND: The little strength that I have, I would it were with you.
CELIA: And mine, to eke out hers.
ROSALIND: Fare you well: pray heaven I be deceived in you!
CELIA: Your heart's desires be with you!
CHARLES: Come, where is this young gallant that is so
CHARLES: desirous to lie with his mother earth?
ORLANDO: Ready, sir, but his will hath in it a more modest working.
DUKE FREDERICK: You shall try but one fall.
CHARLES: No, I warrant your grace, you shall not entreat him
CHARLES: to a second, that have so mightily persuaded him
CHARLES: from a first.
ORLANDO: An you mean to mock me after, you should not have
ORLANDO: mocked me before: but come your ways.
ROSALIND: Now Hercules be thy speed, young man!
CELIA: I would I were invisible, to catch the strong
CELIA: fellow by the leg.
NARRATOR: They wrestle
ROSALIND: O excellent young man!
CELIA: If I had a thunderbolt in mine eye, I can tell who
CELIA: should down.
NARRATOR: Shout. CHARLES is thrown
DUKE FREDERICK: No more, no more.
ORLANDO: Yes, I beseech your grace: I am not yet well breathed.
DUKE FREDERICK: How dost thou, Charles?
LE BEAU: He cannot speak, my lord.
DUKE FREDERICK: Bear him away. What is thy name, young man?
ORLANDO: Orlando, my liege, the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.
DUKE FREDERICK: I would thou hadst been son to some man else:
DUKE FREDERICK: The world esteem'd thy father honourable,
DUKE FREDERICK: But I did find him still mine enemy:
DUKE FREDERICK: Thou shouldst have better pleased me with this deed,
DUKE FREDERICK: Hadst thou descended from another house.
DUKE FREDERICK: But fare thee well, thou art a gallant youth:
DUKE FREDERICK: I would thou hadst told me of another father.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DUKE FREDERICK, train, and LE BEAU
CELIA: Were I my father, coz, would I do this?
ORLANDO: I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son,
ORLANDO: His youngest son, and would not change that calling,
ORLANDO: To be adopted heir to Frederick.
ROSALIND: My father loved Sir Rowland as his soul,
ROSALIND: And all the world was of my father's mind:
ROSALIND: Had I before known this young man his son,
ROSALIND: I should have given him tears unto entreaties,
ROSALIND: Ere he should thus have ventured.
CELIA: Gentle cousin,
CELIA: Let us go thank him and encourage him:
CELIA: My father's rough and envious disposition
CELIA: Sticks me at heart. Sir, you have well deserved:
CELIA: If you do keep your promises in love
CELIA: But justly, as you have exceeded all promise,
CELIA: Your mistress shall be happy.
ROSALIND: Gentleman,
NARRATOR: Giving him a chain from her neck
ROSALIND: Wear this for me, one out of suits with fortune,
ROSALIND: That could give more, but that her hand lacks means.
ROSALIND: Shall we go, coz?
CELIA: Ay. Fare you well, fair gentleman.
ORLANDO: Can I not say, I thank you? My better parts
ORLANDO: Are all thrown down, and that which here stands up
ORLANDO: Is but a quintain, a mere lifeless block.
ROSALIND: He calls us back: my pride fell with my fortunes,
ROSALIND: I'll ask him what he would. Did you call, sir?
ROSALIND: Sir, you have wrestled well and overthrown
ROSALIND: More than your enemies.
CELIA: Will you go, coz?
ROSALIND: Have with you. Fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA
ORLANDO: What passion hangs these weights upon my tongue?
ORLANDO: I cannot speak to her, yet she urged conference.
ORLANDO: O poor Orlando, thou art overthrown!
ORLANDO: Or Charles or something weaker masters thee.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LE BEAU
LE BEAU: Good sir, I do in friendship counsel you
LE BEAU: To leave this place. Albeit you have deserved
LE BEAU: High commendation, true applause and love,
LE BEAU: Yet such is now the duke's condition
LE BEAU: That he misconstrues all that you have done.
LE BEAU: The duke is humorous, what he is indeed,
LE BEAU: More suits you to conceive than I to speak of.
ORLANDO: I thank you, sir: and, pray you, tell me this:
ORLANDO: Which of the two was daughter of the duke
ORLANDO: That here was at the wrestling?
LE BEAU: Neither his daughter, if we judge by manners,
LE BEAU: But yet indeed the lesser is his daughter
LE BEAU: The other is daughter to the banish'd duke,
LE BEAU: And here detain'd by her usurping uncle,
LE BEAU: To keep his daughter company, whose loves
LE BEAU: Are dearer than the natural bond of sisters.
LE BEAU: But I can tell you that of late this duke
LE BEAU: Hath ta'en displeasure 'gainst his gentle niece,
LE BEAU: Grounded upon no other argument
LE BEAU: But that the people praise her for her virtues
LE BEAU: And pity her for her good father's sake,
LE BEAU: And, on my life, his malice 'gainst the lady
LE BEAU: Will suddenly break forth. Sir, fare you well:
LE BEAU: Hereafter, in a better world than this,
LE BEAU: I shall desire more love and knowledge of you.
ORLANDO: I rest much bounden to you: fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit LE BEAU
ORLANDO: Thus must I from the smoke into the smother,
ORLANDO: From tyrant duke unto a tyrant brother:
ORLANDO: But heavenly Rosalind!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CELIA and ROSALIND
CELIA: Why, cousin! why, Rosalind! Cupid have mercy! not a word?
ROSALIND: Not one to throw at a dog.
CELIA: No, thy words are too precious to be cast away upon
CELIA: curs, throw some of them at me, come, lame me with reasons.
ROSALIND: Then there were two cousins laid up, when the one
ROSALIND: should be lamed with reasons and the other mad
ROSALIND: without any.
CELIA: But is all this for your father?
ROSALIND: No, some of it is for my child's father. O, how
ROSALIND: full of briers is this working-day world!
CELIA: They are but burs, cousin, thrown upon thee in
CELIA: holiday foolery: if we walk not in the trodden
CELIA: paths our very petticoats will catch them.
ROSALIND: I could shake them off my coat: these burs are in my heart.
CELIA: Hem them away.
ROSALIND: I would try, if I could cry 'hem' and have him.
CELIA: Come, come, wrestle with thy affections.
ROSALIND: O, they take the part of a better wrestler than myself!
CELIA: O, a good wish upon you! you will try in time, in
CELIA: despite of a fall. But, turning these jests out of
CELIA: service, let us talk in good earnest: is it
CELIA: possible, on such a sudden, you should fall into so
CELIA: strong a liking with old Sir Rowland's youngest son?
ROSALIND: The duke my father loved his father dearly.
CELIA: Doth it therefore ensue that you should love his son
CELIA: dearly? By this kind of chase, I should hate him,
CELIA: for my father hated his father dearly, yet I hate
CELIA: not Orlando.
ROSALIND: No, faith, hate him not, for my sake.
CELIA: Why should I not? doth he not deserve well?
ROSALIND: Let me love him for that, and do you love him
ROSALIND: because I do. Look, here comes the duke.
CELIA: With his eyes full of anger.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE FREDERICK, with Lords
DUKE FREDERICK: Mistress, dispatch you with your safest haste
DUKE FREDERICK: And get you from our court.
ROSALIND: Me, uncle?
DUKE FREDERICK: You, cousin
DUKE FREDERICK: Within these ten days if that thou be'st found
DUKE FREDERICK: So near our public court as twenty miles,
DUKE FREDERICK: Thou diest for it.
ROSALIND: I do beseech your grace,
ROSALIND: Let me the knowledge of my fault bear with me:
ROSALIND: If with myself I hold intelligence
ROSALIND: Or have acquaintance with mine own desires,
ROSALIND: If that I do not dream or be not frantic,--
ROSALIND: As I do trust I am not--then, dear uncle,
ROSALIND: Never so much as in a thought unborn
ROSALIND: Did I offend your highness.
DUKE FREDERICK: Thus do all traitors:
DUKE FREDERICK: If their purgation did consist in words,
DUKE FREDERICK: They are as innocent as grace itself:
DUKE FREDERICK: Let it suffice thee that I trust thee not.
ROSALIND: Yet your mistrust cannot make me a traitor:
ROSALIND: Tell me whereon the likelihood depends.
DUKE FREDERICK: Thou art thy father's daughter, there's enough.
ROSALIND: So was I when your highness took his dukedom,
ROSALIND: So was I when your highness banish'd him:
ROSALIND: Treason is not inherited, my lord,
ROSALIND: Or, if we did derive it from our friends,
ROSALIND: What's that to me? my father was no traitor:
ROSALIND: Then, good my liege, mistake me not so much
ROSALIND: To think my poverty is treacherous.
CELIA: Dear sovereign, hear me speak.
DUKE FREDERICK: Ay, Celia, we stay'd her for your sake,
DUKE FREDERICK: Else had she with her father ranged along.
CELIA: I did not then entreat to have her stay,
CELIA: It was your pleasure and your own remorse:
CELIA: I was too young that time to value her,
CELIA: But now I know her: if she be a traitor,
CELIA: Why so am I, we still have slept together,
CELIA: Rose at an instant, learn'd, play'd, eat together,
CELIA: And wheresoever we went, like Juno's swans,
CELIA: Still we went coupled and inseparable.
DUKE FREDERICK: She is too subtle for thee, and her smoothness,
DUKE FREDERICK: Her very silence and her patience
DUKE FREDERICK: Speak to the people, and they pity her.
DUKE FREDERICK: Thou art a fool: she robs thee of thy name,
DUKE FREDERICK: And thou wilt show more bright and seem more virtuous
DUKE FREDERICK: When she is gone. Then open not thy lips:
DUKE FREDERICK: Firm and irrevocable is my doom
DUKE FREDERICK: Which I have pass'd upon her, she is banish'd.
CELIA: Pronounce that sentence then on me, my liege:
CELIA: I cannot live out of her company.
DUKE FREDERICK: You are a fool. You, niece, provide yourself:
DUKE FREDERICK: If you outstay the time, upon mine honour,
DUKE FREDERICK: And in the greatness of my word, you die.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DUKE FREDERICK and Lords
CELIA: O my poor Rosalind, whither wilt thou go?
CELIA: Wilt thou change fathers? I will give thee mine.
CELIA: I charge thee, be not thou more grieved than I am.
ROSALIND: I have more cause.
CELIA: Thou hast not, cousin,
CELIA: Prithee be cheerful: know'st thou not, the duke
CELIA: Hath banish'd me, his daughter?
ROSALIND: That he hath not.
CELIA: No, hath not? Rosalind lacks then the love
CELIA: Which teacheth thee that thou and I am one:
CELIA: Shall we be sunder'd? shall we part, sweet girl?
CELIA: No: let my father seek another heir.
CELIA: Therefore devise with me how we may fly,
CELIA: Whither to go and what to bear with us,
CELIA: And do not seek to take your change upon you,
CELIA: To bear your griefs yourself and leave me out,
CELIA: For, by this heaven, now at our sorrows pale,
CELIA: Say what thou canst, I'll go along with thee.
ROSALIND: Why, whither shall we go?
CELIA: To seek my uncle in the forest of Arden.
ROSALIND: Alas, what danger will it be to us,
ROSALIND: Maids as we are, to travel forth so far!
ROSALIND: Beauty provoketh thieves sooner than gold.
CELIA: I'll put myself in poor and mean attire
CELIA: And with a kind of umber smirch my face,
CELIA: The like do you: so shall we pass along
CELIA: And never stir assailants.
ROSALIND: Were it not better,
ROSALIND: Because that I am more than common tall,
ROSALIND: That I did suit me all points like a man?
ROSALIND: A gallant curtle-axe upon my thigh,
ROSALIND: A boar-spear in my hand, and--in my heart
ROSALIND: Lie there what hidden woman's fear there will--
ROSALIND: We'll have a swashing and a martial outside,
ROSALIND: As many other mannish cowards have
ROSALIND: That do outface it with their semblances.
CELIA: What shall I call thee when thou art a man?
ROSALIND: I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page,
ROSALIND: And therefore look you call me Ganymede.
ROSALIND: But what will you be call'd?
CELIA: Something that hath a reference to my state
CELIA: No longer Celia, but Aliena.
ROSALIND: But, cousin, what if we assay'd to steal
ROSALIND: The clownish fool out of your father's court?
ROSALIND: Would he not be a comfort to our travel?
CELIA: He'll go along o'er the wide world with me,
CELIA: Leave me alone to woo him. Let's away,
CELIA: And get our jewels and our wealth together,
CELIA: Devise the fittest time and safest way
CELIA: To hide us from pursuit that will be made
CELIA: After my flight. Now go we in content
CELIA: To liberty and not to banishment.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The Forest of Arden.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and two or three Lords, like foresters
DUKE SENIOR: Now, my co-mates and brothers in exile,
DUKE SENIOR: Hath not old custom made this life more sweet
DUKE SENIOR: Than that of painted pomp? Are not these woods
DUKE SENIOR: More free from peril than the envious court?
DUKE SENIOR: Here feel we but the penalty of Adam,
DUKE SENIOR: The seasons' difference, as the icy fang
DUKE SENIOR: And churlish chiding of the winter's wind,
DUKE SENIOR: Which, when it bites and blows upon my body,
DUKE SENIOR: Even till I shrink with cold, I smile and say
DUKE SENIOR: 'This is no flattery: these are counsellors
DUKE SENIOR: That feelingly persuade me what I am.'
DUKE SENIOR: Sweet are the uses of adversity,
DUKE SENIOR: Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous,
DUKE SENIOR: Wears yet a precious jewel in his head,
DUKE SENIOR: And this our life exempt from public haunt
DUKE SENIOR: Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks,
DUKE SENIOR: Sermons in stones and good in every thing.
DUKE SENIOR: I would not change it.
AMIENS: Happy is your grace,
AMIENS: That can translate the stubbornness of fortune
AMIENS: Into so quiet and so sweet a style.
DUKE SENIOR: Come, shall we go and kill us venison?
DUKE SENIOR: And yet it irks me the poor dappled fools,
DUKE SENIOR: Being native burghers of this desert city,
DUKE SENIOR: Should in their own confines with forked heads
DUKE SENIOR: Have their round haunches gored.
First Lord: Indeed, my lord,
First Lord: The melancholy Jaques grieves at that,
First Lord: And, in that kind, swears you do more usurp
First Lord: Than doth your brother that hath banish'd you.
First Lord: To-day my Lord of Amiens and myself
First Lord: Did steal behind him as he lay along
First Lord: Under an oak whose antique root peeps out
First Lord: Upon the brook that brawls along this wood:
First Lord: To the which place a poor sequester'd stag,
First Lord: That from the hunter's aim had ta'en a hurt,
First Lord: Did come to languish, and indeed, my lord,
First Lord: The wretched animal heaved forth such groans
First Lord: That their discharge did stretch his leathern coat
First Lord: Almost to bursting, and the big round tears
First Lord: Coursed one another down his innocent nose
First Lord: In piteous chase, and thus the hairy fool
First Lord: Much marked of the melancholy Jaques,
First Lord: Stood on the extremest verge of the swift brook,
First Lord: Augmenting it with tears.
DUKE SENIOR: But what said Jaques?
DUKE SENIOR: Did he not moralize this spectacle?
First Lord: O, yes, into a thousand similes.
First Lord: First, for his weeping into the needless stream,
First Lord: 'Poor deer,' quoth he, 'thou makest a testament
First Lord: As worldlings do, giving thy sum of more
First Lord: To that which had too much:' then, being there alone,
First Lord: Left and abandon'd of his velvet friends,
First Lord: ''Tis right:' quoth he, 'thus misery doth part
First Lord: The flux of company:' anon a careless herd,
First Lord: Full of the pasture, jumps along by him
First Lord: And never stays to greet him, 'Ay' quoth Jaques,
First Lord: 'Sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens,
First Lord: 'Tis just the fashion: wherefore do you look
First Lord: Upon that poor and broken bankrupt there?'
First Lord: Thus most invectively he pierceth through
First Lord: The body of the country, city, court,
First Lord: Yea, and of this our life, swearing that we
First Lord: Are mere usurpers, tyrants and what's worse,
First Lord: To fright the animals and to kill them up
First Lord: In their assign'd and native dwelling-place.
DUKE SENIOR: And did you leave him in this contemplation?
Second Lord: We did, my lord, weeping and commenting
Second Lord: Upon the sobbing deer.
DUKE SENIOR: Show me the place:
DUKE SENIOR: I love to cope him in these sullen fits,
DUKE SENIOR: For then he's full of matter.
First Lord: I'll bring you to him straight.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE FREDERICK, with Lords
DUKE FREDERICK: Can it be possible that no man saw them?
DUKE FREDERICK: It cannot be: some villains of my court
DUKE FREDERICK: Are of consent and sufferance in this.
First Lord: I cannot hear of any that did see her.
First Lord: The ladies, her attendants of her chamber,
First Lord: Saw her abed, and in the morning early
First Lord: They found the bed untreasured of their mistress.
Second Lord: My lord, the roynish clown, at whom so oft
Second Lord: Your grace was wont to laugh, is also missing.
Second Lord: Hisperia, the princess' gentlewoman,
Second Lord: Confesses that she secretly o'erheard
Second Lord: Your daughter and her cousin much commend
Second Lord: The parts and graces of the wrestler
Second Lord: That did but lately foil the sinewy Charles,
Second Lord: And she believes, wherever they are gone,
Second Lord: That youth is surely in their company.
DUKE FREDERICK: Send to his brother, fetch that gallant hither,
DUKE FREDERICK: If he be absent, bring his brother to me,
DUKE FREDERICK: I'll make him find him: do this suddenly,
DUKE FREDERICK: And let not search and inquisition quail
DUKE FREDERICK: To bring again these foolish runaways.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Before OLIVER'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO and ADAM, meeting
ORLANDO: Who's there?
ADAM: What, my young master? O, my gentle master!
ADAM: O my sweet master! O you memory
ADAM: Of old Sir Rowland! why, what make you here?
ADAM: Why are you virtuous? why do people love you?
ADAM: And wherefore are you gentle, strong and valiant?
ADAM: Why would you be so fond to overcome
ADAM: The bonny priser of the humorous duke?
ADAM: Your praise is come too swiftly home before you.
ADAM: Know you not, master, to some kind of men
ADAM: Their graces serve them but as enemies?
ADAM: No more do yours: your virtues, gentle master,
ADAM: Are sanctified and holy traitors to you.
ADAM: O, what a world is this, when what is comely
ADAM: Envenoms him that bears it!
