ORLANDO: Why, what's the matter?
ADAM: O unhappy youth!
ADAM: Come not within these doors, within this roof
ADAM: The enemy of all your graces lives:
ADAM: Your brother--no, no brother, yet the son--
ADAM: Yet not the son, I will not call him son
ADAM: Of him I was about to call his father--
ADAM: Hath heard your praises, and this night he means
ADAM: To burn the lodging where you use to lie
ADAM: And you within it: if he fail of that,
ADAM: He will have other means to cut you off.
ADAM: I overheard him and his practises.
ADAM: This is no place, this house is but a butchery:
ADAM: Abhor it, fear it, do not enter it.
ORLANDO: Why, whither, Adam, wouldst thou have me go?
ADAM: No matter whither, so you come not here.
ORLANDO: What, wouldst thou have me go and beg my food?
ORLANDO: Or with a base and boisterous sword enforce
ORLANDO: A thievish living on the common road?
ORLANDO: This I must do, or know not what to do:
ORLANDO: Yet this I will not do, do how I can,
ORLANDO: I rather will subject me to the malice
ORLANDO: Of a diverted blood and bloody brother.
ADAM: But do not so. I have five hundred crowns,
ADAM: The thrifty hire I saved under your father,
ADAM: Which I did store to be my foster-nurse
ADAM: When service should in my old limbs lie lame
ADAM: And unregarded age in corners thrown:
ADAM: Take that, and He that doth the ravens feed,
ADAM: Yea, providently caters for the sparrow,
ADAM: Be comfort to my age! Here is the gold,
ADAM: And all this I give you. Let me be your servant:
ADAM: Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty,
ADAM: For in my youth I never did apply
ADAM: Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood,
ADAM: Nor did not with unbashful forehead woo
ADAM: The means of weakness and debility,
ADAM: Therefore my age is as a lusty winter,
ADAM: Frosty, but kindly: let me go with you,
ADAM: I'll do the service of a younger man
ADAM: In all your business and necessities.
ORLANDO: O good old man, how well in thee appears
ORLANDO: The constant service of the antique world,
ORLANDO: When service sweat for duty, not for meed!
ORLANDO: Thou art not for the fashion of these times,
ORLANDO: Where none will sweat but for promotion,
ORLANDO: And having that, do choke their service up
ORLANDO: Even with the having: it is not so with thee.
ORLANDO: But, poor old man, thou prunest a rotten tree,
ORLANDO: That cannot so much as a blossom yield
ORLANDO: In lieu of all thy pains and husbandry
ORLANDO: But come thy ways, well go along together,
ORLANDO: And ere we have thy youthful wages spent,
ORLANDO: We'll light upon some settled low content.
ADAM: Master, go on, and I will follow thee,
ADAM: To the last gasp, with truth and loyalty.
ADAM: From seventeen years till now almost fourscore
ADAM: Here lived I, but now live here no more.
ADAM: At seventeen years many their fortunes seek,
ADAM: But at fourscore it is too late a week:
ADAM: Yet fortune cannot recompense me better
ADAM: Than to die well and not my master's debtor.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The Forest of Arden.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND for Ganymede, CELIA for Aliena, and TOUCHSTONE
ROSALIND: O Jupiter, how weary are my spirits!
TOUCHSTONE: I care not for my spirits, if my legs were not weary.
ROSALIND: I could find in my heart to disgrace my man's
ROSALIND: apparel and to cry like a woman, but I must comfort
ROSALIND: the weaker vessel, as doublet and hose ought to show
ROSALIND: itself courageous to petticoat: therefore courage,
ROSALIND: good Aliena!
CELIA: I pray you, bear with me, I cannot go no further.
TOUCHSTONE: For my part, I had rather bear with you than bear
TOUCHSTONE: you, yet I should bear no cross if I did bear you,
TOUCHSTONE: for I think you have no money in your purse.
ROSALIND: Well, this is the forest of Arden.
TOUCHSTONE: Ay, now am I in Arden, the more fool I, when I was
TOUCHSTONE: at home, I was in a better place: but travellers
TOUCHSTONE: must be content.
ROSALIND: Ay, be so, good Touchstone.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIN and SILVIUS
ROSALIND: Look you, who comes here, a young man and an old in
ROSALIND: solemn talk.
CORIN: That is the way to make her scorn you still.
SILVIUS: O Corin, that thou knew'st how I do love her!
CORIN: I partly guess, for I have loved ere now.
SILVIUS: No, Corin, being old, thou canst not guess,
SILVIUS: Though in thy youth thou wast as true a lover
SILVIUS: As ever sigh'd upon a midnight pillow:
SILVIUS: But if thy love were ever like to mine--
SILVIUS: As sure I think did never man love so--
SILVIUS: How many actions most ridiculous
SILVIUS: Hast thou been drawn to by thy fantasy?
CORIN: Into a thousand that I have forgotten.
SILVIUS: O, thou didst then ne'er love so heartily!
SILVIUS: If thou remember'st not the slightest folly
SILVIUS: That ever love did make thee run into,
SILVIUS: Thou hast not loved:
SILVIUS: Or if thou hast not sat as I do now,
SILVIUS: Wearying thy hearer in thy mistress' praise,
SILVIUS: Thou hast not loved:
SILVIUS: Or if thou hast not broke from company
SILVIUS: Abruptly, as my passion now makes me,
SILVIUS: Thou hast not loved.
SILVIUS: O Phebe, Phebe, Phebe!
NARRATOR: Exit
ROSALIND: Alas, poor shepherd! searching of thy wound,
ROSALIND: I have by hard adventure found mine own.
TOUCHSTONE: And I mine. I remember, when I was in love I broke
TOUCHSTONE: my sword upon a stone and bid him take that for
TOUCHSTONE: coming a-night to Jane Smile, and I remember the
TOUCHSTONE: kissing of her batlet and the cow's dugs that her
TOUCHSTONE: pretty chopt hands had milked, and I remember the
TOUCHSTONE: wooing of a peascod instead of her, from whom I took
TOUCHSTONE: two cods and, giving her them again, said with
TOUCHSTONE: weeping tears 'Wear these for my sake.' We that are
TOUCHSTONE: true lovers run into strange capers, but as all is
TOUCHSTONE: mortal in nature, so is all nature in love mortal in folly.
ROSALIND: Thou speakest wiser than thou art ware of.
TOUCHSTONE: Nay, I shall ne'er be ware of mine own wit till I
TOUCHSTONE: break my shins against it.
ROSALIND: Jove, Jove! this shepherd's passion
ROSALIND: Is much upon my fashion.
TOUCHSTONE: And mine, but it grows something stale with me.
CELIA: I pray you, one of you question yond man
CELIA: If he for gold will give us any food:
CELIA: I faint almost to death.
TOUCHSTONE: Holla, you clown!
ROSALIND: Peace, fool: he's not thy kinsman.
CORIN: Who calls?
TOUCHSTONE: Your betters, sir.
CORIN: Else are they very wretched.
ROSALIND: Peace, I say. Good even to you, friend.
CORIN: And to you, gentle sir, and to you all.
ROSALIND: I prithee, shepherd, if that love or gold
ROSALIND: Can in this desert place buy entertainment,
ROSALIND: Bring us where we may rest ourselves and feed:
ROSALIND: Here's a young maid with travel much oppress'd
ROSALIND: And faints for succor.
CORIN: Fair sir, I pity her
CORIN: And wish, for her sake more than for mine own,
CORIN: My fortunes were more able to relieve her,
CORIN: But I am shepherd to another man
CORIN: And do not shear the fleeces that I graze:
CORIN: My master is of churlish disposition
CORIN: And little recks to find the way to heaven
CORIN: By doing deeds of hospitality:
CORIN: Besides, his cote, his flocks and bounds of feed
CORIN: Are now on sale, and at our sheepcote now,
CORIN: By reason of his absence, there is nothing
CORIN: That you will feed on, but what is, come see.
CORIN: And in my voice most welcome shall you be.
ROSALIND: What is he that shall buy his flock and pasture?
CORIN: That young swain that you saw here but erewhile,
CORIN: That little cares for buying any thing.
ROSALIND: I pray thee, if it stand with honesty,
ROSALIND: Buy thou the cottage, pasture and the flock,
ROSALIND: And thou shalt have to pay for it of us.
CELIA: And we will mend thy wages. I like this place.
CELIA: And willingly could waste my time in it.
CORIN: Assuredly the thing is to be sold:
CORIN: Go with me: if you like upon report
CORIN: The soil, the profit and this kind of life,
CORIN: I will your very faithful feeder be
CORIN: And buy it with your gold right suddenly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The Forest.
NARRATOR: Enter AMIENS, JAQUES, and others
CORIN: SONG.
AMIENS: Under the greenwood tree
AMIENS: Who loves to lie with me,
AMIENS: And turn his merry note
AMIENS: Unto the sweet bird's throat,
AMIENS: Come hither, come hither, come hither:
AMIENS: Here shall he see No enemy
AMIENS: But winter and rough weather.
JAQUES: More, more, I prithee, more.
AMIENS: It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
JAQUES: I thank it. More, I prithee, more. I can suck
JAQUES: melancholy out of a song, as a weasel sucks eggs.
JAQUES: More, I prithee, more.
AMIENS: My voice is ragged: I know I cannot please you.
JAQUES: I do not desire you to please me, I do desire you to
JAQUES: sing. Come, more, another stanzo: call you 'em stanzos?
AMIENS: What you will, Monsieur Jaques.
JAQUES: Nay, I care not for their names, they owe me
JAQUES: nothing. Will you sing?
AMIENS: More at your request than to please myself.
JAQUES: Well then, if ever I thank any man, I'll thank you,
JAQUES: but that they call compliment is like the encounter
JAQUES: of two dog-apes, and when a man thanks me heartily,
JAQUES: methinks I have given him a penny and he renders me
JAQUES: the beggarly thanks. Come, sing, and you that will
JAQUES: not, hold your tongues.
AMIENS: Well, I'll end the song. Sirs, cover the while, the
AMIENS: duke will drink under this tree. He hath been all
AMIENS: this day to look you.
JAQUES: And I have been all this day to avoid him. He is
JAQUES: too disputable for my company: I think of as many
JAQUES: matters as he, but I give heaven thanks and make no
JAQUES: boast of them. Come, warble, come.
JAQUES: SONG.
JAQUES: Who doth ambition shun
NARRATOR: All together here
JAQUES: And loves to live i' the sun,
JAQUES: Seeking the food he eats
JAQUES: And pleased with what he gets,
JAQUES: Come hither, come hither, come hither:
JAQUES: Here shall he see No enemy
JAQUES: But winter and rough weather.
JAQUES: I'll give you a verse to this note that I made
JAQUES: yesterday in despite of my invention.
AMIENS: And I'll sing it.
JAQUES: Thus it goes:--
JAQUES: If it do come to pass
JAQUES: That any man turn ass,
JAQUES: Leaving his wealth and ease,
JAQUES: A stubborn will to please,
JAQUES: Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame:
JAQUES: Here shall he see
JAQUES: Gross fools as he,
JAQUES: An if he will come to me.
AMIENS: What's that 'ducdame'?
JAQUES: 'Tis a Greek invocation, to call fools into a
JAQUES: circle. I'll go sleep, if I can, if I cannot, I'll
JAQUES: rail against all the first-born of Egypt.
AMIENS: And I'll go seek the duke: his banquet is prepared.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO and ADAM
ADAM: Dear master, I can go no further. O, I die for food!
ADAM: Here lie I down, and measure out my grave. Farewell,
ADAM: kind master.
ORLANDO: Why, how now, Adam! no greater heart in thee? Live
ORLANDO: a little, comfort a little, cheer thyself a little.
ORLANDO: If this uncouth forest yield any thing savage, I
ORLANDO: will either be food for it or bring it for food to
ORLANDO: thee. Thy conceit is nearer death than thy powers.
ORLANDO: For my sake be comfortable, hold death awhile at
ORLANDO: the arm's end: I will here be with thee presently,
ORLANDO: and if I bring thee not something to eat, I will
ORLANDO: give thee leave to die: but if thou diest before I
ORLANDO: come, thou art a mocker of my labour. Well said!
ORLANDO: thou lookest cheerly, and I'll be with thee quickly.
ORLANDO: Yet thou liest in the bleak air: come, I will bear
ORLANDO: thee to some shelter, and thou shalt not die for
ORLANDO: lack of a dinner, if there live any thing in this
ORLANDO: desert. Cheerly, good Adam!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. The forest.
NARRATOR: A table set out. Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and Lords like outlaws
DUKE SENIOR: I think he be transform'd into a beast,
DUKE SENIOR: For I can no where find him like a man.
First Lord: My lord, he is but even now gone hence:
First Lord: Here was he merry, hearing of a song.
DUKE SENIOR: If he, compact of jars, grow musical,
DUKE SENIOR: We shall have shortly discord in the spheres.
DUKE SENIOR: Go, seek him: tell him I would speak with him.
NARRATOR: Enter JAQUES
First Lord: He saves my labour by his own approach.
DUKE SENIOR: Why, how now, monsieur! what a life is this,
DUKE SENIOR: That your poor friends must woo your company?
DUKE SENIOR: What, you look merrily!
JAQUES: A fool, a fool! I met a fool i' the forest,
JAQUES: A motley fool, a miserable world!
JAQUES: As I do live by food, I met a fool
JAQUES: Who laid him down and bask'd him in the sun,
JAQUES: And rail'd on Lady Fortune in good terms,
JAQUES: In good set terms and yet a motley fool.
JAQUES: 'Good morrow, fool,' quoth I. 'No, sir,' quoth he,
JAQUES: 'Call me not fool till heaven hath sent me fortune:'
JAQUES: And then he drew a dial from his poke,
JAQUES: And, looking on it with lack-lustre eye,
JAQUES: Says very wisely, 'It is ten o'clock:
JAQUES: Thus we may see,' quoth he, 'how the world wags:
JAQUES: 'Tis but an hour ago since it was nine,
JAQUES: And after one hour more 'twill be eleven,
JAQUES: And so, from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe,
JAQUES: And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot,
JAQUES: And thereby hangs a tale.' When I did hear
JAQUES: The motley fool thus moral on the time,
JAQUES: My lungs began to crow like chanticleer,
JAQUES: That fools should be so deep-contemplative,
JAQUES: And I did laugh sans intermission
JAQUES: An hour by his dial. O noble fool!
JAQUES: A worthy fool! Motley's the only wear.
DUKE SENIOR: What fool is this?
JAQUES: O worthy fool! One that hath been a courtier,
JAQUES: And says, if ladies be but young and fair,
JAQUES: They have the gift to know it: and in his brain,
JAQUES: Which is as dry as the remainder biscuit
JAQUES: After a voyage, he hath strange places cramm'd
JAQUES: With observation, the which he vents
JAQUES: In mangled forms. O that I were a fool!
JAQUES: I am ambitious for a motley coat.
DUKE SENIOR: Thou shalt have one.
JAQUES: It is my only suit,
JAQUES: Provided that you weed your better judgments
JAQUES: Of all opinion that grows rank in them
JAQUES: That I am wise. I must have liberty
JAQUES: Withal, as large a charter as the wind,
JAQUES: To blow on whom I please, for so fools have,
JAQUES: And they that are most galled with my folly,
JAQUES: They most must laugh. And why, sir, must they so?
JAQUES: The 'why' is plain as way to parish church:
JAQUES: He that a fool doth very wisely hit
JAQUES: Doth very foolishly, although he smart,
JAQUES: Not to seem senseless of the bob: if not,
JAQUES: The wise man's folly is anatomized
JAQUES: Even by the squandering glances of the fool.
JAQUES: Invest me in my motley, give me leave
JAQUES: To speak my mind, and I will through and through
JAQUES: Cleanse the foul body of the infected world,
JAQUES: If they will patiently receive my medicine.
DUKE SENIOR: Fie on thee! I can tell what thou wouldst do.
JAQUES: What, for a counter, would I do but good?
DUKE SENIOR: Most mischievous foul sin, in chiding sin:
DUKE SENIOR: For thou thyself hast been a libertine,
DUKE SENIOR: As sensual as the brutish sting itself,
DUKE SENIOR: And all the embossed sores and headed evils,
DUKE SENIOR: That thou with licence of free foot hast caught,
DUKE SENIOR: Wouldst thou disgorge into the general world.
JAQUES: Why, who cries out on pride,
JAQUES: That can therein tax any private party?
JAQUES: Doth it not flow as hugely as the sea,
JAQUES: Till that the weary very means do ebb?
JAQUES: What woman in the city do I name,
JAQUES: When that I say the city-woman bears
JAQUES: The cost of princes on unworthy shoulders?
JAQUES: Who can come in and say that I mean her,
JAQUES: When such a one as she such is her neighbour?
JAQUES: Or what is he of basest function
JAQUES: That says his bravery is not of my cost,
JAQUES: Thinking that I mean him, but therein suits
JAQUES: His folly to the mettle of my speech?
JAQUES: There then, how then? what then? Let me see wherein
JAQUES: My tongue hath wrong'd him: if it do him right,
JAQUES: Then he hath wrong'd himself, if he be free,
JAQUES: Why then my taxing like a wild-goose flies,
JAQUES: Unclaim'd of any man. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO, with his sword drawn
ORLANDO: Forbear, and eat no more.
JAQUES: Why, I have eat none yet.
ORLANDO: Nor shalt not, till necessity be served.
JAQUES: Of what kind should this cock come of?
DUKE SENIOR: Art thou thus bolden'd, man, by thy distress,
DUKE SENIOR: Or else a rude despiser of good manners,
DUKE SENIOR: That in civility thou seem'st so empty?
ORLANDO: You touch'd my vein at first: the thorny point
ORLANDO: Of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show
ORLANDO: Of smooth civility: yet am I inland bred
ORLANDO: And know some nurture. But forbear, I say:
ORLANDO: He dies that touches any of this fruit
ORLANDO: Till I and my affairs are answered.
JAQUES: An you will not be answered with reason, I must die.
DUKE SENIOR: What would you have? Your gentleness shall force
DUKE SENIOR: More than your force move us to gentleness.
ORLANDO: I almost die for food, and let me have it.
DUKE SENIOR: Sit down and feed, and welcome to our table.
ORLANDO: Speak you so gently? Pardon me, I pray you:
ORLANDO: I thought that all things had been savage here,
ORLANDO: And therefore put I on the countenance
ORLANDO: Of stern commandment. But whate'er you are
ORLANDO: That in this desert inaccessible,
ORLANDO: Under the shade of melancholy boughs,
ORLANDO: Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time
ORLANDO: If ever you have look'd on better days,
ORLANDO: If ever been where bells have knoll'd to church,
ORLANDO: If ever sat at any good man's feast,
ORLANDO: If ever from your eyelids wiped a tear
ORLANDO: And know what 'tis to pity and be pitied,
ORLANDO: Let gentleness my strong enforcement be:
ORLANDO: In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword.
DUKE SENIOR: True is it that we have seen better days,
DUKE SENIOR: And have with holy bell been knoll'd to church
DUKE SENIOR: And sat at good men's feasts and wiped our eyes
DUKE SENIOR: Of drops that sacred pity hath engender'd:
DUKE SENIOR: And therefore sit you down in gentleness
DUKE SENIOR: And take upon command what help we have
DUKE SENIOR: That to your wanting may be minister'd.
ORLANDO: Then but forbear your food a little while,
ORLANDO: Whiles, like a doe, I go to find my fawn
ORLANDO: And give it food. There is an old poor man,
ORLANDO: Who after me hath many a weary step
ORLANDO: Limp'd in pure love: till he be first sufficed,
ORLANDO: Oppress'd with two weak evils, age and hunger,
ORLANDO: I will not touch a bit.
DUKE SENIOR: Go find him out,
DUKE SENIOR: And we will nothing waste till you return.
ORLANDO: I thank ye, and be blest for your good comfort!
NARRATOR: Exit
DUKE SENIOR: Thou seest we are not all alone unhappy:
DUKE SENIOR: This wide and universal theatre
DUKE SENIOR: Presents more woeful pageants than the scene
DUKE SENIOR: Wherein we play in.
JAQUES: All the world's a stage,
JAQUES: And all the men and women merely players:
JAQUES: They have their exits and their entrances,
JAQUES: And one man in his time plays many parts,
JAQUES: His acts being seven ages. At first the infant,
JAQUES: Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms.
JAQUES: And then the whining school-boy, with his satchel
JAQUES: And shining morning face, creeping like snail
JAQUES: Unwillingly to school. And then the lover,
JAQUES: Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad
JAQUES: Made to his mistress' eyebrow. Then a soldier,
JAQUES: Full of strange oaths and bearded like the pard,
JAQUES: Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel,
JAQUES: Seeking the bubble reputation
JAQUES: Even in the cannon's mouth. And then the justice,
JAQUES: In fair round belly with good capon lined,
JAQUES: With eyes severe and beard of formal cut,
JAQUES: Full of wise saws and modern instances,
JAQUES: And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts
JAQUES: Into the lean and slipper'd pantaloon,
JAQUES: With spectacles on nose and pouch on side,
JAQUES: His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide
JAQUES: For his shrunk shank, and his big manly voice,
JAQUES: Turning again toward childish treble, pipes
JAQUES: And whistles in his sound. Last scene of all,
JAQUES: That ends this strange eventful history,
JAQUES: Is second childishness and mere oblivion,
JAQUES: Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
NARRATOR: Re-enter ORLANDO, with ADAM
DUKE SENIOR: Welcome. Set down your venerable burthen,
DUKE SENIOR: And let him feed.
ORLANDO: I thank you most for him.
ADAM: So had you need:
ADAM: I scarce can speak to thank you for myself.
DUKE SENIOR: Welcome, fall to: I will not trouble you
DUKE SENIOR: As yet, to question you about your fortunes.
DUKE SENIOR: Give us some music, and, good cousin, sing.
DUKE SENIOR: SONG.
AMIENS: Blow, blow, thou winter wind.
AMIENS: Thou art not so unkind
AMIENS: As man's ingratitude,
AMIENS: Thy tooth is not so keen,
AMIENS: Because thou art not seen,
AMIENS: Although thy breath be rude.
AMIENS: Heigh-ho! sing, heigh-ho! unto the green holly:
AMIENS: Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly:
AMIENS: Then, heigh-ho, the holly!
AMIENS: This life is most jolly.
AMIENS: Freeze, freeze, thou bitter sky,
AMIENS: That dost not bite so nigh
AMIENS: As benefits forgot:
AMIENS: Though thou the waters warp,
AMIENS: Thy sting is not so sharp
AMIENS: As friend remember'd not.
AMIENS: Heigh-ho! sing,  and c.
DUKE SENIOR: If that you were the good Sir Rowland's son,
DUKE SENIOR: As you have whisper'd faithfully you were,
DUKE SENIOR: And as mine eye doth his effigies witness
DUKE SENIOR: Most truly limn'd and living in your face,
DUKE SENIOR: Be truly welcome hither: I am the duke
DUKE SENIOR: That loved your father: the residue of your fortune,
DUKE SENIOR: Go to my cave and tell me. Good old man,
DUKE SENIOR: Thou art right welcome as thy master is.
DUKE SENIOR: Support him by the arm. Give me your hand,
DUKE SENIOR: And let me all your fortunes understand.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE FREDERICK, Lords, and OLIVER
DUKE FREDERICK: Not see him since? Sir, sir, that cannot be:
DUKE FREDERICK: But were I not the better part made mercy,
DUKE FREDERICK: I should not seek an absent argument
DUKE FREDERICK: Of my revenge, thou present. But look to it:
DUKE FREDERICK: Find out thy brother, wheresoe'er he is,
DUKE FREDERICK: Seek him with candle, bring him dead or living
DUKE FREDERICK: Within this twelvemonth, or turn thou no more
DUKE FREDERICK: To seek a living in our territory.
DUKE FREDERICK: Thy lands and all things that thou dost call thine
DUKE FREDERICK: Worth seizure do we seize into our hands,
DUKE FREDERICK: Till thou canst quit thee by thy brothers mouth
DUKE FREDERICK: Of what we think against thee.
OLIVER: O that your highness knew my heart in this!
OLIVER: I never loved my brother in my life.
DUKE FREDERICK: More villain thou. Well, push him out of doors,
DUKE FREDERICK: And let my officers of such a nature
DUKE FREDERICK: Make an extent upon his house and lands:
DUKE FREDERICK: Do this expediently and turn him going.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO, with a paper
ORLANDO: Hang there, my verse, in witness of my love:
ORLANDO: And thou, thrice-crowned queen of night, survey
ORLANDO: With thy chaste eye, from thy pale sphere above,
ORLANDO: Thy huntress' name that my full life doth sway.
ORLANDO: O Rosalind! these trees shall be my books
ORLANDO: And in their barks my thoughts I'll character,
ORLANDO: That every eye which in this forest looks
ORLANDO: Shall see thy virtue witness'd every where.
ORLANDO: Run, run, Orlando, carve on every tree
ORLANDO: The fair, the chaste and unexpressive she.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter CORIN and TOUCHSTONE
CORIN: And how like you this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?
TOUCHSTONE: Truly, shepherd, in respect of itself, it is a good
TOUCHSTONE: life, but in respect that it is a shepherd's life,
TOUCHSTONE: it is naught. In respect that it is solitary, I
TOUCHSTONE: like it very well, but in respect that it is
TOUCHSTONE: private, it is a very vile life. Now, in respect it
TOUCHSTONE: is in the fields, it pleaseth me well, but in
TOUCHSTONE: respect it is not in the court, it is tedious. As
TOUCHSTONE: is it a spare life, look you, it fits my humour well,
TOUCHSTONE: but as there is no more plenty in it, it goes much
TOUCHSTONE: against my stomach. Hast any philosophy in thee, shepherd?
CORIN: No more but that I know the more one sickens the
CORIN: worse at ease he is, and that he that wants money,
CORIN: means and content is without three good friends,
CORIN: that the property of rain is to wet and fire to
CORIN: burn, that good pasture makes fat sheep, and that a
CORIN: great cause of the night is lack of the sun, that
CORIN: he that hath learned no wit by nature nor art may
CORIN: complain of good breeding or comes of a very dull kindred.
TOUCHSTONE: Such a one is a natural philosopher. Wast ever in
TOUCHSTONE: court, shepherd?
CORIN: No, truly.
TOUCHSTONE: Then thou art damned.
CORIN: Nay, I hope.
TOUCHSTONE: Truly, thou art damned like an ill-roasted egg, all
TOUCHSTONE: on one side.
CORIN: For not being at court? Your reason.
TOUCHSTONE: Why, if thou never wast at court, thou never sawest
TOUCHSTONE: good manners, if thou never sawest good manners,
TOUCHSTONE: then thy manners must be wicked, and wickedness is
TOUCHSTONE: sin, and sin is damnation. Thou art in a parlous
TOUCHSTONE: state, shepherd.
CORIN: Not a whit, Touchstone: those that are good manners
CORIN: at the court are as ridiculous in the country as the
CORIN: behavior of the country is most mockable at the
CORIN: court. You told me you salute not at the court, but
CORIN: you kiss your hands: that courtesy would be
CORIN: uncleanly, if courtiers were shepherds.
TOUCHSTONE: Instance, briefly, come, instance.
CORIN: Why, we are still handling our ewes, and their
CORIN: fells, you know, are greasy.
TOUCHSTONE: Why, do not your courtier's hands sweat? and is not
TOUCHSTONE: the grease of a mutton as wholesome as the sweat of
TOUCHSTONE: a man? Shallow, shallow. A better instance, I say, come.
CORIN: Besides, our hands are hard.
TOUCHSTONE: Your lips will feel them the sooner. Shallow again.
TOUCHSTONE: A more sounder instance, come.
CORIN: And they are often tarred over with the surgery of
CORIN: our sheep: and would you have us kiss tar? The
CORIN: courtier's hands are perfumed with civet.
TOUCHSTONE: Most shallow man! thou worms-meat, in respect of a
TOUCHSTONE: good piece of flesh indeed! Learn of the wise, and
TOUCHSTONE: perpend: civet is of a baser birth than tar, the
TOUCHSTONE: very uncleanly flux of a cat. Mend the instance, shepherd.
CORIN: You have too courtly a wit for me: I'll rest.
TOUCHSTONE: Wilt thou rest damned? God help thee, shallow man!
TOUCHSTONE: God make incision in thee! thou art raw.
CORIN: Sir, I am a true labourer: I earn that I eat, get
CORIN: that I wear, owe no man hate, envy no man's
CORIN: happiness, glad of other men's good, content with my
CORIN: harm, and the greatest of my pride is to see my ewes
CORIN: graze and my lambs suck.
TOUCHSTONE: That is another simple sin in you, to bring the ewes
TOUCHSTONE: and the rams together and to offer to get your
TOUCHSTONE: living by the copulation of cattle, to be bawd to a
TOUCHSTONE: bell-wether, and to betray a she-lamb of a
TOUCHSTONE: twelvemonth to a crooked-pated, old, cuckoldly ram,
TOUCHSTONE: out of all reasonable match. If thou beest not
TOUCHSTONE: damned for this, the devil himself will have no
TOUCHSTONE: shepherds, I cannot see else how thou shouldst
TOUCHSTONE: 'scape.
CORIN: Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress's brother.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND, with a paper, reading
ROSALIND: From the east to western Ind,
ROSALIND: No jewel is like Rosalind.
ROSALIND: Her worth, being mounted on the wind,
ROSALIND: Through all the world bears Rosalind.
ROSALIND: All the pictures fairest lined
ROSALIND: Are but black to Rosalind.
ROSALIND: Let no fair be kept in mind
ROSALIND: But the fair of Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: I'll rhyme you so eight years together, dinners and
TOUCHSTONE: suppers and sleeping-hours excepted: it is the
TOUCHSTONE: right butter-women's rank to market.
ROSALIND: Out, fool!
TOUCHSTONE: For a taste:
TOUCHSTONE: If a hart do lack a hind,
TOUCHSTONE: Let him seek out Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: If the cat will after kind,
TOUCHSTONE: So be sure will Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: Winter garments must be lined,
TOUCHSTONE: So must slender Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: They that reap must sheaf and bind,
TOUCHSTONE: Then to cart with Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: Sweetest nut hath sourest rind,
TOUCHSTONE: Such a nut is Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: He that sweetest rose will find
TOUCHSTONE: Must find love's prick and Rosalind.
TOUCHSTONE: This is the very false gallop of verses: why do you
TOUCHSTONE: infect yourself with them?
ROSALIND: Peace, you dull fool! I found them on a tree.
TOUCHSTONE: Truly, the tree yields bad fruit.
ROSALIND: I'll graff it with you, and then I shall graff it
ROSALIND: with a medlar: then it will be the earliest fruit
ROSALIND: i' the country, for you'll be rotten ere you be half
ROSALIND: ripe, and that's the right virtue of the medlar.
TOUCHSTONE: You have said, but whether wisely or no, let the
TOUCHSTONE: forest judge.
NARRATOR: Enter CELIA, with a writing
ROSALIND: Peace! Here comes my sister, reading: stand aside.
CELIA: [Reads]
CELIA: Why should this a desert be?
CELIA: For it is unpeopled? No:
CELIA: Tongues I'll hang on every tree,
CELIA: That shall civil sayings show:
CELIA: Some, how brief the life of man
CELIA: Runs his erring pilgrimage,
CELIA: That the stretching of a span
CELIA: Buckles in his sum of age,
CELIA: Some, of violated vows
CELIA: 'Twixt the souls of friend and friend:
CELIA: But upon the fairest boughs,
CELIA: Or at every sentence end,
CELIA: Will I Rosalinda write,
CELIA: Teaching all that read to know
CELIA: The quintessence of every sprite
CELIA: Heaven would in little show.
CELIA: Therefore Heaven Nature charged
CELIA: That one body should be fill'd
CELIA: With all graces wide-enlarged:
CELIA: Nature presently distill'd
CELIA: Helen's cheek, but not her heart,
CELIA: Cleopatra's majesty,
CELIA: Atalanta's better part,
CELIA: Sad Lucretia's modesty.
CELIA: Thus Rosalind of many parts
CELIA: By heavenly synod was devised,
CELIA: Of many faces, eyes and hearts,
CELIA: To have the touches dearest prized.
CELIA: Heaven would that she these gifts should have,
CELIA: And I to live and die her slave.
ROSALIND: O most gentle pulpiter! what tedious homily of love
ROSALIND: have you wearied your parishioners withal, and never
ROSALIND: cried 'Have patience, good people!'
CELIA: How now! back, friends! Shepherd, go off a little.
CELIA: Go with him, sirrah.
TOUCHSTONE: Come, shepherd, let us make an honourable retreat,
TOUCHSTONE: though not with bag and baggage, yet with scrip and scrippage.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CORIN and TOUCHSTONE
CELIA: Didst thou hear these verses?
ROSALIND: O, yes, I heard them all, and more too, for some of
ROSALIND: them had in them more feet than the verses would bear.
CELIA: That's no matter: the feet might bear the verses.
ROSALIND: Ay, but the feet were lame and could not bear
ROSALIND: themselves without the verse and therefore stood
ROSALIND: lamely in the verse.
CELIA: But didst thou hear without wondering how thy name
CELIA: should be hanged and carved upon these trees?
ROSALIND: I was seven of the nine days out of the wonder
ROSALIND: before you came, for look here what I found on a
ROSALIND: palm-tree. I was never so be-rhymed since
ROSALIND: Pythagoras' time, that I was an Irish rat, which I
ROSALIND: can hardly remember.
CELIA: Trow you who hath done this?
ROSALIND: Is it a man?
CELIA: And a chain, that you once wore, about his neck.
CELIA: Change you colour?
ROSALIND: I prithee, who?
CELIA: O Lord, Lord! it is a hard matter for friends to
CELIA: meet, but mountains may be removed with earthquakes
CELIA: and so encounter.
ROSALIND: Nay, but who is it?
CELIA: Is it possible?
ROSALIND: Nay, I prithee now with most petitionary vehemence,
ROSALIND: tell me who it is.
CELIA: O wonderful, wonderful, and most wonderful
CELIA: wonderful! and yet again wonderful, and after that,
CELIA: out of all hooping!
ROSALIND: Good my complexion! dost thou think, though I am
ROSALIND: caparisoned like a man, I have a doublet and hose in
ROSALIND: my disposition? One inch of delay more is a
ROSALIND: South-sea of discovery, I prithee, tell me who is it
ROSALIND: quickly, and speak apace. I would thou couldst
ROSALIND: stammer, that thou mightst pour this concealed man
ROSALIND: out of thy mouth, as wine comes out of a narrow-
ROSALIND: mouthed bottle, either too much at once, or none at
ROSALIND: all. I prithee, take the cork out of thy mouth that
ROSALIND: may drink thy tidings.
CELIA: So you may put a man in your belly.
ROSALIND: Is he of God's making? What manner of man? Is his
ROSALIND: head worth a hat, or his chin worth a beard?
CELIA: Nay, he hath but a little beard.
ROSALIND: Why, God will send more, if the man will be
ROSALIND: thankful: let me stay the growth of his beard, if
ROSALIND: thou delay me not the knowledge of his chin.
CELIA: It is young Orlando, that tripped up the wrestler's
CELIA: heels and your heart both in an instant.
ROSALIND: Nay, but the devil take mocking: speak, sad brow and
ROSALIND: true maid.
CELIA: I' faith, coz, 'tis he.
ROSALIND: Orlando?
CELIA: Orlando.
ROSALIND: Alas the day! what shall I do with my doublet and
ROSALIND: hose? What did he when thou sawest him? What said
ROSALIND: he? How looked he? Wherein went he? What makes
ROSALIND: him here? Did he ask for me? Where remains he?
ROSALIND: How parted he with thee? and when shalt thou see
ROSALIND: him again? Answer me in one word.
CELIA: You must borrow me Gargantua's mouth first: 'tis a
CELIA: word too great for any mouth of this age's size. To
CELIA: say ay and no to these particulars is more than to
CELIA: answer in a catechism.
ROSALIND: But doth he know that I am in this forest and in
ROSALIND: man's apparel? Looks he as freshly as he did the
ROSALIND: day he wrestled?
CELIA: It is as easy to count atomies as to resolve the
CELIA: propositions of a lover, but take a taste of my
CELIA: finding him, and relish it with good observance.
CELIA: I found him under a tree, like a dropped acorn.
ROSALIND: It may well be called Jove's tree, when it drops
ROSALIND: forth such fruit.
CELIA: Give me audience, good madam.
ROSALIND: Proceed.
CELIA: There lay he, stretched along, like a wounded knight.
ROSALIND: Though it be pity to see such a sight, it well
ROSALIND: becomes the ground.
CELIA: Cry 'holla' to thy tongue, I prithee, it curvets
CELIA: unseasonably. He was furnished like a hunter.
ROSALIND: O, ominous! he comes to kill my heart.
CELIA: I would sing my song without a burden: thou bringest
CELIA: me out of tune.
ROSALIND: Do you not know I am a woman? when I think, I must
ROSALIND: speak. Sweet, say on.
CELIA: You bring me out. Soft! comes he not here?
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO and JAQUES
ROSALIND: 'Tis he: slink by, and note him.
JAQUES: I thank you for your company, but, good faith, I had
JAQUES: as lief have been myself alone.
ORLANDO: And so had I, but yet, for fashion sake, I thank you
ORLANDO: too for your society.
JAQUES: God be wi' you: let's meet as little as we can.
ORLANDO: I do desire we may be better strangers.
JAQUES: I pray you, mar no more trees with writing
JAQUES: love-songs in their barks.
ORLANDO: I pray you, mar no more of my verses with reading
ORLANDO: them ill-favouredly.
JAQUES: Rosalind is your love's name?
ORLANDO: Yes, just.
JAQUES: I do not like her name.
ORLANDO: There was no thought of pleasing you when she was
ORLANDO: christened.
JAQUES: What stature is she of?
ORLANDO: Just as high as my heart.
JAQUES: You are full of pretty answers. Have you not been
JAQUES: acquainted with goldsmiths' wives, and conned them
JAQUES: out of rings?
ORLANDO: Not so, but I answer you right painted cloth, from
ORLANDO: whence you have studied your questions.
JAQUES: You have a nimble wit: I think 'twas made of
JAQUES: Atalanta's heels. Will you sit down with me? and
JAQUES: we two will rail against our mistress the world and
JAQUES: all our misery.
ORLANDO: I will chide no breather in the world but myself,
ORLANDO: against whom I know most faults.
JAQUES: The worst fault you have is to be in love.
ORLANDO: 'Tis a fault I will not change for your best virtue.
ORLANDO: I am weary of you.
JAQUES: By my troth, I was seeking for a fool when I found
JAQUES: you.
ORLANDO: He is drowned in the brook: look but in, and you
ORLANDO: shall see him.
JAQUES: There I shall see mine own figure.
ORLANDO: Which I take to be either a fool or a cipher.
JAQUES: I'll tarry no longer with you: farewell, good
JAQUES: Signior Love.
ORLANDO: I am glad of your departure: adieu, good Monsieur
ORLANDO: Melancholy.
NARRATOR: Exit JAQUES
ROSALIND: [Aside to CELIA]  I will speak to him, like a saucy
ROSALIND: lackey and under that habit play the knave with him.
ROSALIND: Do you hear, forester?
ORLANDO: Very well: what would you?
ROSALIND: I pray you, what is't o'clock?
ORLANDO: You should ask me what time o' day: there's no clock
ORLANDO: in the forest.
ROSALIND: Then there is no true lover in the forest, else
ROSALIND: sighing every minute and groaning every hour would
ROSALIND: detect the lazy foot of Time as well as a clock.
ORLANDO: And why not the swift foot of Time? had not that
ORLANDO: been as proper?
ROSALIND: By no means, sir: Time travels in divers paces with
ROSALIND: divers persons. I'll tell you who Time ambles
ROSALIND: withal, who Time trots withal, who Time gallops
ROSALIND: withal and who he stands still withal.
ORLANDO: I prithee, who doth he trot withal?
ROSALIND: Marry, he trots hard with a young maid between the
ROSALIND: contract of her marriage and the day it is
ROSALIND: solemnized: if the interim be but a se'nnight,
ROSALIND: Time's pace is so hard that it seems the length of
ROSALIND: seven year.
ORLANDO: Who ambles Time withal?
ROSALIND: With a priest that lacks Latin and a rich man that
ROSALIND: hath not the gout, for the one sleeps easily because
ROSALIND: he cannot study, and the other lives merrily because
ROSALIND: he feels no pain, the one lacking the burden of lean
ROSALIND: and wasteful learning, the other knowing no burden
ROSALIND: of heavy tedious penury, these Time ambles withal.
ORLANDO: Who doth he gallop withal?
ROSALIND: With a thief to the gallows, for though he go as
ROSALIND: softly as foot can fall, he thinks himself too soon there.
ORLANDO: Who stays it still withal?
ROSALIND: With lawyers in the vacation, for they sleep between
ROSALIND: term and term and then they perceive not how Time moves.
ORLANDO: Where dwell you, pretty youth?
ROSALIND: With this shepherdess, my sister, here in the
ROSALIND: skirts of the forest, like fringe upon a petticoat.
ORLANDO: Are you native of this place?
ROSALIND: As the cony that you see dwell where she is kindled.
ORLANDO: Your accent is something finer than you could
ORLANDO: purchase in so removed a dwelling.
ROSALIND: I have been told so of many: but indeed an old
ROSALIND: religious uncle of mine taught me to speak, who was
ROSALIND: in his youth an inland man, one that knew courtship
ROSALIND: too well, for there he fell in love. I have heard
ROSALIND: him read many lectures against it, and I thank God
ROSALIND: I am not a woman, to be touched with so many
ROSALIND: giddy offences as he hath generally taxed their
ROSALIND: whole sex withal.
ORLANDO: Can you remember any of the principal evils that he
ORLANDO: laid to the charge of women?
ROSALIND: There were none principal, they were all like one
ROSALIND: another as half-pence are, every one fault seeming
ROSALIND: monstrous till his fellow fault came to match it.
ORLANDO: I prithee, recount some of them.
ROSALIND: No, I will not cast away my physic but on those that
ROSALIND: are sick. There is a man haunts the forest, that
ROSALIND: abuses our young plants with carving 'Rosalind' on
ROSALIND: their barks, hangs odes upon hawthorns and elegies
ROSALIND: on brambles, all, forsooth, deifying the name of
ROSALIND: Rosalind: if I could meet that fancy-monger I would
ROSALIND: give him some good counsel, for he seems to have the
ROSALIND: quotidian of love upon him.
ORLANDO: I am he that is so love-shaked: I pray you tell me
ORLANDO: your remedy.
ROSALIND: There is none of my uncle's marks upon you: he
ROSALIND: taught me how to know a man in love, in which cage
ROSALIND: of rushes I am sure you are not prisoner.
ORLANDO: What were his marks?
ROSALIND: A lean cheek, which you have not, a blue eye and
ROSALIND: sunken, which you have not, an unquestionable
ROSALIND: spirit, which you have not, a beard neglected,
ROSALIND: which you have not, but I pardon you for that, for
ROSALIND: simply your having in beard is a younger brother's
ROSALIND: revenue: then your hose should be ungartered, your
ROSALIND: bonnet unbanded, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe
ROSALIND: untied and every thing about you demonstrating a
ROSALIND: careless desolation, but you are no such man, you
ROSALIND: are rather point-device in your accoutrements as
ROSALIND: loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other.
ORLANDO: Fair youth, I would I could make thee believe I love.
ROSALIND: Me believe it! you may as soon make her that you
ROSALIND: love believe it, which, I warrant, she is apter to
ROSALIND: do than to confess she does: that is one of the
ROSALIND: points in the which women still give the lie to
ROSALIND: their consciences. But, in good sooth, are you he
ROSALIND: that hangs the verses on the trees, wherein Rosalind
ROSALIND: is so admired?
ORLANDO: I swear to thee, youth, by the white hand of
ORLANDO: Rosalind, I am that he, that unfortunate he.
ROSALIND: But are you so much in love as your rhymes speak?
ORLANDO: Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.
ROSALIND: Love is merely a madness, and, I tell you, deserves
ROSALIND: as well a dark house and a whip as madmen do: and
ROSALIND: the reason why they are not so punished and cured
ROSALIND: is, that the lunacy is so ordinary that the whippers
ROSALIND: are in love too. Yet I profess curing it by counsel.
ORLANDO: Did you ever cure any so?
ROSALIND: Yes, one, and in this manner. He was to imagine me
ROSALIND: his love, his mistress, and I set him every day to
ROSALIND: woo me: at which time would I, being but a moonish
ROSALIND: youth, grieve, be effeminate, changeable, longing
ROSALIND: and liking, proud, fantastical, apish, shallow,
ROSALIND: inconstant, full of tears, full of smiles, for every
ROSALIND: passion something and for no passion truly any
ROSALIND: thing, as boys and women are for the most part
ROSALIND: cattle of this colour, would now like him, now loathe
ROSALIND: him, then entertain him, then forswear him, now weep
ROSALIND: for him, then spit at him, that I drave my suitor
ROSALIND: from his mad humour of love to a living humour of
ROSALIND: madness, which was, to forswear the full stream of
ROSALIND: the world, and to live in a nook merely monastic.
ROSALIND: And thus I cured him, and this way will I take upon
ROSALIND: me to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep's
ROSALIND: heart, that there shall not be one spot of love in't.
ORLANDO: I would not be cured, youth.
ROSALIND: I would cure you, if you would but call me Rosalind
ROSALIND: and come every day to my cote and woo me.
ORLANDO: Now, by the faith of my love, I will: tell me
ORLANDO: where it is.
ROSALIND: Go with me to it and I'll show it you and by the way
ROSALIND: you shall tell me where in the forest you live.
ROSALIND: Will you go?
ORLANDO: With all my heart, good youth.
ROSALIND: Nay you must call me Rosalind. Come, sister, will you go?
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY, JAQUES behind
TOUCHSTONE: Come apace, good Audrey: I will fetch up your
TOUCHSTONE: goats, Audrey. And how, Audrey? am I the man yet?
TOUCHSTONE: doth my simple feature content you?
AUDREY: Your features! Lord warrant us! what features!
TOUCHSTONE: I am here with thee and thy goats, as the most
TOUCHSTONE: capricious poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths.
JAQUES: [Aside]  O knowledge ill-inhabited, worse than Jove
JAQUES: in a thatched house!
TOUCHSTONE: When a man's verses cannot be understood, nor a
TOUCHSTONE: man's good wit seconded with the forward child
TOUCHSTONE: Understanding, it strikes a man more dead than a
TOUCHSTONE: great reckoning in a little room. Truly, I would
TOUCHSTONE: the gods had made thee poetical.
AUDREY: I do not know what 'poetical' is: is it honest in
AUDREY: deed and word? is it a true thing?
TOUCHSTONE: No, truly, for the truest poetry is the most
TOUCHSTONE: feigning, and lovers are given to poetry, and what
TOUCHSTONE: they swear in poetry may be said as lovers they do feign.
AUDREY: Do you wish then that the gods had made me poetical?
TOUCHSTONE: I do, truly, for thou swearest to me thou art
TOUCHSTONE: honest: now, if thou wert a poet, I might have some
TOUCHSTONE: hope thou didst feign.
AUDREY: Would you not have me honest?
TOUCHSTONE: No, truly, unless thou wert hard-favoured, for
TOUCHSTONE: honesty coupled to beauty is to have honey a sauce to sugar.
JAQUES: [Aside]  A material fool!
AUDREY: Well, I am not fair, and therefore I pray the gods
AUDREY: make me honest.
TOUCHSTONE: Truly, and to cast away honesty upon a foul slut
TOUCHSTONE: were to put good meat into an unclean dish.
AUDREY: I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.
TOUCHSTONE: Well, praised be the gods for thy foulness!
TOUCHSTONE: sluttishness may come hereafter. But be it as it may
TOUCHSTONE: be, I will marry thee, and to that end I have been
TOUCHSTONE: with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next
TOUCHSTONE: village, who hath promised to meet me in this place
TOUCHSTONE: of the forest and to couple us.
JAQUES: [Aside]  I would fain see this meeting.
AUDREY: Well, the gods give us joy!
TOUCHSTONE: Amen. A man may, if he were of a fearful heart,
TOUCHSTONE: stagger in this attempt, for here we have no temple
TOUCHSTONE: but the wood, no assembly but horn-beasts. But what
TOUCHSTONE: though? C ourage! As horns are odious, they are
TOUCHSTONE: necessary. It is said, 'many a man knows no end of
TOUCHSTONE: his goods:' right, many a man has good horns, and
TOUCHSTONE: knows no end of them. Well, that is the dowry of
TOUCHSTONE: his wife, 'tis none of his own getting. Horns?
TOUCHSTONE: Even so. Poor men alone? No, no, the noblest deer
TOUCHSTONE: hath them as huge as the rascal. Is the single man
TOUCHSTONE: therefore blessed? No: as a walled town is more
TOUCHSTONE: worthier than a village, so is the forehead of a
TOUCHSTONE: married man more honourable than the bare brow of a
TOUCHSTONE: bachelor, and by how much defence is better than no
TOUCHSTONE: skill, by so much is a horn more precious than to
TOUCHSTONE: want. Here comes Sir Oliver.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR OLIVER MARTEXT
TOUCHSTONE: Sir Oliver Martext, you are well met: will you
TOUCHSTONE: dispatch us here under this tree, or shall we go
TOUCHSTONE: with you to your chapel?
SIR OLIVER MARTEXT: Is there none here to give the woman?
TOUCHSTONE: I will not take her on gift of any man.
SIR OLIVER MARTEXT: Truly, she must be given, or the marriage is not lawful.
JAQUES: [Advancing]
JAQUES: Proceed, proceed	I'll give her.
TOUCHSTONE: Good even, good Master What-ye-call't: how do you,
TOUCHSTONE: sir? You are very well met: God 'ild you for your
TOUCHSTONE: last company: I am very glad to see you: even a
TOUCHSTONE: toy in hand here, sir: nay, pray be covered.
JAQUES: Will you be married, motley?
TOUCHSTONE: As the ox hath his bow, sir, the horse his curb and
TOUCHSTONE: the falcon her bells, so man hath his desires, and
TOUCHSTONE: as pigeons bill, so wedlock would be nibbling.
JAQUES: And will you, being a man of your breeding, be
JAQUES: married under a bush like a beggar? Get you to
JAQUES: church, and have a good priest that can tell you
JAQUES: what marriage is: this fellow will but join you
JAQUES: together as they join wainscot, then one of you will
JAQUES: prove a shrunk panel and, like green timber, warp, warp.
TOUCHSTONE: [Aside]  I am not in the mind but I were better to be
TOUCHSTONE: married of him than of another: for he is not like
TOUCHSTONE: to marry me well, and not being well married, it
TOUCHSTONE: will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife.
JAQUES: Go thou with me, and let me counsel thee.
TOUCHSTONE: 'Come, sweet Audrey:
TOUCHSTONE: We must be married, or we must live in bawdry.
TOUCHSTONE: Farewell, good Master Oliver: not,--
TOUCHSTONE: O sweet Oliver,
TOUCHSTONE: O brave Oliver,
TOUCHSTONE: Leave me not behind thee: but,--
TOUCHSTONE: Wind away,
TOUCHSTONE: Begone, I say,
TOUCHSTONE: I will not to wedding with thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt JAQUES, TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
SIR OLIVER MARTEXT: 'Tis no matter: ne'er a fantastical knave of them
SIR OLIVER MARTEXT: all shall flout me out of my calling.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND and CELIA
ROSALIND: Never talk to me, I will weep.
CELIA: Do, I prithee, but yet have the grace to consider
CELIA: that tears do not become a man.
ROSALIND: But have I not cause to weep?
CELIA: As good cause as one would desire, therefore weep.
ROSALIND: His very hair is of the dissembling colour.
CELIA: Something browner than Judas's marry, his kisses are
CELIA: Judas's own children.
ROSALIND: I' faith, his hair is of a good colour.
CELIA: An excellent colour: your chestnut was ever the only colour.
ROSALIND: And his kissing is as full of sanctity as the touch
ROSALIND: of holy bread.
CELIA: He hath bought a pair of cast lips of Diana: a nun
CELIA: of winter's sisterhood kisses not more religiously,
CELIA: the very ice of chastity is in them.
ROSALIND: But why did he swear he would come this morning, and
ROSALIND: comes not?
CELIA: Nay, certainly, there is no truth in him.
ROSALIND: Do you think so?
CELIA: Yes, I think he is not a pick-purse nor a
CELIA: horse-stealer, but for his verity in love, I do
CELIA: think him as concave as a covered goblet or a
CELIA: worm-eaten nut.
ROSALIND: Not true in love?
CELIA: Yes, when he is in, but I think he is not in.
ROSALIND: You have heard him swear downright he was.
CELIA: 'Was' is not 'is:' besides, the oath of a lover is
CELIA: no stronger than the word of a tapster, they are
CELIA: both the confirmer of false reckonings. He attends
CELIA: here in the forest on the duke your father.
ROSALIND: I met the duke yesterday and had much question with
ROSALIND: him: he asked me of what parentage I was, I told
ROSALIND: him, of as good as he, so he laughed and let me go.
ROSALIND: But what talk we of fathers, when there is such a
ROSALIND: man as Orlando?
CELIA: O, that's a brave man! he writes brave verses,
CELIA: speaks brave words, swears brave oaths and breaks
CELIA: them bravely, quite traverse, athwart the heart of
CELIA: his lover, as a puisny tilter, that spurs his horse
CELIA: but on one side, breaks his staff like a noble
CELIA: goose: but all's brave that youth mounts and folly
CELIA: guides. Who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter CORIN
CORIN: Mistress and master, you have oft inquired
CORIN: After the shepherd that complain'd of love,
CORIN: Who you saw sitting by me on the turf,
CORIN: Praising the proud disdainful shepherdess
CORIN: That was his mistress.
CELIA: Well, and what of him?
CORIN: If you will see a pageant truly play'd,
CORIN: Between the pale complexion of true love
CORIN: And the red glow of scorn and proud disdain,
CORIN: Go hence a little and I shall conduct you,
CORIN: If you will mark it.
ROSALIND: O, come, let us remove:
ROSALIND: The sight of lovers feedeth those in love.
ROSALIND: Bring us to this sight, and you shall say
ROSALIND: I'll prove a busy actor in their play.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the forest.
NARRATOR: Enter SILVIUS and PHEBE
SILVIUS: Sweet Phebe, do not scorn me, do not, Phebe,
SILVIUS: Say that you love me not, but say not so
SILVIUS: In bitterness. The common executioner,
SILVIUS: Whose heart the accustom'd sight of death makes hard,
SILVIUS: Falls not the axe upon the humbled neck
SILVIUS: But first begs pardon: will you sterner be
SILVIUS: Than he that dies and lives by bloody drops?
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND, CELIA, and CORIN, behind
PHEBE: I would not be thy executioner:
PHEBE: I fly thee, for I would not injure thee.
PHEBE: Thou tell'st me there is murder in mine eye:
PHEBE: 'Tis pretty, sure, and very probable,
PHEBE: That eyes, that are the frail'st and softest things,
PHEBE: Who shut their coward gates on atomies,
PHEBE: Should be call'd tyrants, butchers, murderers!
PHEBE: Now I do frown on thee with all my heart,
PHEBE: And if mine eyes can wound, now let them kill thee:
PHEBE: Now counterfeit to swoon, why now fall down,
PHEBE: Or if thou canst not, O, for shame, for shame,
PHEBE: Lie not, to say mine eyes are murderers!
PHEBE: Now show the wound mine eye hath made in thee:
PHEBE: Scratch thee but with a pin, and there remains
PHEBE: Some scar of it, lean but upon a rush,
PHEBE: The cicatrice and capable impressure
PHEBE: Thy palm some moment keeps, but now mine eyes,
PHEBE: Which I have darted at thee, hurt thee not,
PHEBE: Nor, I am sure, there is no force in eyes
PHEBE: That can do hurt.
SILVIUS: O dear Phebe,
SILVIUS: If ever,--as that ever may be near,--
SILVIUS: You meet in some fresh cheek the power of fancy,
SILVIUS: Then shall you know the wounds invisible
SILVIUS: That love's keen arrows make.
PHEBE: But till that time
PHEBE: Come not thou near me: and when that time comes,
PHEBE: Afflict me with thy mocks, pity me not,
PHEBE: As till that time I shall not pity thee.
ROSALIND: And why, I pray you? Who might be your mother,
ROSALIND: That you insult, exult, and all at once,
ROSALIND: Over the wretched? What though you have no beauty,--
ROSALIND: As, by my faith, I see no more in you
ROSALIND: Than without candle may go dark to bed--
ROSALIND: Must you be therefore proud and pitiless?
ROSALIND: Why, what means this? Why do you look on me?
ROSALIND: I see no more in you than in the ordinary
ROSALIND: Of nature's sale-work. 'Od's my little life,
ROSALIND: I think she means to tangle my eyes too!
ROSALIND: No, faith, proud mistress, hope not after it:
ROSALIND: 'Tis not your inky brows, your black silk hair,
ROSALIND: Your bugle eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream,
ROSALIND: That can entame my spirits to your worship.
ROSALIND: You foolish shepherd, wherefore do you follow her,
ROSALIND: Like foggy south puffing with wind and rain?
ROSALIND: You are a thousand times a properer man
ROSALIND: Than she a woman: 'tis such fools as you
ROSALIND: That makes the world full of ill-favour'd children:
ROSALIND: 'Tis not her glass, but you, that flatters her,
ROSALIND: And out of you she sees herself more proper
ROSALIND: Than any of her lineaments can show her.
ROSALIND: But, mistress, know yourself: down on your knees,
ROSALIND: And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man's love:
ROSALIND: For I must tell you friendly in your ear,
ROSALIND: Sell when you can: you are not for all markets:
ROSALIND: Cry the man mercy, love him, take his offer:
ROSALIND: Foul is most foul, being foul to be a scoffer.
ROSALIND: So take her to thee, shepherd: fare you well.
PHEBE: Sweet youth, I pray you, chide a year together:
PHEBE: I had rather hear you chide than this man woo.
ROSALIND: He's fallen in love with your foulness and she'll
ROSALIND: fall in love with my anger. If it be so, as fast as
ROSALIND: she answers thee with frowning looks, I'll sauce her
ROSALIND: with bitter words. Why look you so upon me?
PHEBE: For no ill will I bear you.
ROSALIND: I pray you, do not fall in love with me,
ROSALIND: For I am falser than vows made in wine:
ROSALIND: Besides, I like you not. If you will know my house,
ROSALIND: 'Tis at the tuft of olives here hard by.
ROSALIND: Will you go, sister? Shepherd, ply her hard.
ROSALIND: Come, sister. Shepherdess, look on him better,
ROSALIND: And be not proud: though all the world could see,
ROSALIND: None could be so abused in sight as he.
ROSALIND: Come, to our flock.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ROSALIND, CELIA and CORIN
PHEBE: Dead Shepherd, now I find thy saw of might,
PHEBE: 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'
SILVIUS: Sweet Phebe,--
PHEBE: Ha, what say'st thou, Silvius?
SILVIUS: Sweet Phebe, pity me.
PHEBE: Why, I am sorry for thee, gentle Silvius.
SILVIUS: Wherever sorrow is, relief would be:
SILVIUS: If you do sorrow at my grief in love,
SILVIUS: By giving love your sorrow and my grief
SILVIUS: Were both extermined.
PHEBE: Thou hast my love: is not that neighbourly?
SILVIUS: I would have you.
PHEBE: Why, that were covetousness.
PHEBE: Silvius, the time was that I hated thee,
PHEBE: And yet it is not that I bear thee love,
PHEBE: But since that thou canst talk of love so well,
PHEBE: Thy company, which erst was irksome to me,
PHEBE: I will endure, and I'll employ thee too:
PHEBE: But do not look for further recompense
PHEBE: Than thine own gladness that thou art employ'd.
SILVIUS: So holy and so perfect is my love,
SILVIUS: And I in such a poverty of grace,
SILVIUS: That I shall think it a most plenteous crop
SILVIUS: To glean the broken ears after the man
SILVIUS: That the main harvest reaps: loose now and then
SILVIUS: A scatter'd smile, and that I'll live upon.
PHEBE: Know'st now the youth that spoke to me erewhile?
SILVIUS: Not very well, but I have met him oft,
SILVIUS: And he hath bought the cottage and the bounds
SILVIUS: That the old carlot once was master of.
PHEBE: Think not I love him, though I ask for him:
PHEBE: 'Tis but a peevish boy, yet he talks well,
PHEBE: But what care I for words? yet words do well
PHEBE: When he that speaks them pleases those that hear.
PHEBE: It is a pretty youth: not very pretty:
PHEBE: But, sure, he's proud, and yet his pride becomes him:
PHEBE: He'll make a proper man: the best thing in him
PHEBE: Is his complexion, and faster than his tongue
PHEBE: Did make offence his eye did heal it up.
PHEBE: He is not very tall, yet for his years he's tall:
PHEBE: His leg is but so so, and yet 'tis well:
PHEBE: There was a pretty redness in his lip,
PHEBE: A little riper and more lusty red
PHEBE: Than that mix'd in his cheek, 'twas just the difference
PHEBE: Between the constant red and mingled damask.
PHEBE: There be some women, Silvius, had they mark'd him
PHEBE: In parcels as I did, would have gone near
PHEBE: To fall in love with him, but, for my part,
PHEBE: I love him not nor hate him not, and yet
PHEBE: I have more cause to hate him than to love him:
PHEBE: For what had he to do to chide at me?
PHEBE: He said mine eyes were black and my hair black:
PHEBE: And, now I am remember'd, scorn'd at me:
PHEBE: I marvel why I answer'd not again:
PHEBE: But that's all one, omittance is no quittance.
PHEBE: I'll write to him a very taunting letter,
PHEBE: And thou shalt bear it: wilt thou, Silvius?
SILVIUS: Phebe, with all my heart.
PHEBE: I'll write it straight,
PHEBE: The matter's in my head and in my heart:
PHEBE: I will be bitter with him and passing short.
PHEBE: Go with me, Silvius.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND, CELIA, and JAQUES
JAQUES: I prithee, pretty youth, let me be better acquainted
JAQUES: with thee.
ROSALIND: They say you are a melancholy fellow.
JAQUES: I am so, I do love it better than laughing.
ROSALIND: Those that are in extremity of either are abominable
ROSALIND: fellows and betray themselves to every modern
ROSALIND: censure worse than drunkards.
JAQUES: Why, 'tis good to be sad and say nothing.
ROSALIND: Why then, 'tis good to be a post.
JAQUES: I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is
JAQUES: emulation, nor the musician's, which is fantastical,
JAQUES: nor the courtier's, which is proud, nor the
JAQUES: soldier's, which is ambitious, nor the lawyer's,
JAQUES: which is politic, nor the lady's, which is nice, nor
JAQUES: the lover's, which is all these: but it is a
JAQUES: melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples,
JAQUES: extracted from many objects, and indeed the sundry's
JAQUES: contemplation of my travels, in which my often
JAQUES: rumination wraps me m a most humorous sadness.
ROSALIND: A traveller! By my faith, you have great reason to
ROSALIND: be sad: I fear you have sold your own lands to see
ROSALIND: other men's, then, to have seen much and to have
ROSALIND: nothing, is to have rich eyes and poor hands.
JAQUES: Yes, I have gained my experience.
ROSALIND: And your experience makes you sad: I had rather have
ROSALIND: a fool to make me merry than experience to make me
ROSALIND: sad, and to travel for it too!
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO
ORLANDO: Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind!
JAQUES: Nay, then, God be wi' you, an you talk in blank verse.
NARRATOR: Exit
ROSALIND: Farewell, Monsieur Traveller: look you lisp and
ROSALIND: wear strange suits, disable all the benefits of your
ROSALIND: own country, be out of love with your nativity and
ROSALIND: almost chide God for making you that countenance you
ROSALIND: are, or I will scarce think you have swam in a
ROSALIND: gondola. Why, how now, Orlando! where have you been
ROSALIND: all this while? You a lover! An you serve me such
ROSALIND: another trick, never come in my sight more.
ORLANDO: My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.
ROSALIND: Break an hour's promise in love! He that will
ROSALIND: divide a minute into a thousand parts and break but
ROSALIND: a part of the thousandth part of a minute in the
ROSALIND: affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid
ROSALIND: hath clapped him o' the shoulder, but I'll warrant
ROSALIND: him heart-whole.
ORLANDO: Pardon me, dear Rosalind.
ROSALIND: Nay, an you be so tardy, come no more in my sight: I
ROSALIND: had as lief be wooed of a snail.
ORLANDO: Of a snail?
ROSALIND: Ay, of a snail, for though he comes slowly, he
ROSALIND: carries his house on his head, a better jointure,
ROSALIND: I think, than you make a woman: besides he brings
ROSALIND: his destiny with him.
ORLANDO: What's that?
ROSALIND: Why, horns, which such as you are fain to be
ROSALIND: beholding to your wives for: but he comes armed in
ROSALIND: his fortune and prevents the slander of his wife.
ORLANDO: Virtue is no horn-maker, and my Rosalind is virtuous.
ROSALIND: And I am your Rosalind.
CELIA: It pleases him to call you so, but he hath a
CELIA: Rosalind of a better leer than you.
ROSALIND: Come, woo me, woo me, for now I am in a holiday
ROSALIND: humour and like enough to consent. What would you
ROSALIND: say to me now, an I were your very very Rosalind?
ORLANDO: I would kiss before I spoke.
ROSALIND: Nay, you were better speak first, and when you were
ROSALIND: gravelled for lack of matter, you might take
ROSALIND: occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when they are
ROSALIND: out, they will spit, and for lovers lacking--God
ROSALIND: warn us!--matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.
ORLANDO: How if the kiss be denied?
ROSALIND: Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.
ORLANDO: Who could be out, being before his beloved mistress?
ROSALIND: Marry, that should you, if I were your mistress, or
ROSALIND: I should think my honesty ranker than my wit.
ORLANDO: What, of my suit?
ROSALIND: Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit.
ROSALIND: Am not I your Rosalind?
ORLANDO: I take some joy to say you are, because I would be
ORLANDO: talking of her.
ROSALIND: Well in her person I say I will not have you.
ORLANDO: Then in mine own person I die.
ROSALIND: No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is
ROSALIND: almost six thousand years old, and in all this time
ROSALIND: there was not any man died in his own person,
ROSALIND: videlicit, in a love-cause. Troilus had his brains
ROSALIND: dashed out with a Grecian club, yet he did what he
ROSALIND: could to die before, and he is one of the patterns
ROSALIND: of love. Leander, he would have lived many a fair
ROSALIND: year, though Hero had turned nun, if it had not been
ROSALIND: for a hot midsummer night, for, good youth, he went
ROSALIND: but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and being
ROSALIND: taken with the cramp was drowned and the foolish
ROSALIND: coroners of that age found it was 'Hero of Sestos.'
ROSALIND: But these are all lies: men have died from time to
ROSALIND: time and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
ORLANDO: I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind,
ORLANDO: for, I protest, her frown might kill me.
ROSALIND: By this hand, it will not kill a fly. But come, now
ROSALIND: I will be your Rosalind in a more coming-on
ROSALIND: disposition, and ask me what you will. I will grant
ROSALIND: it.
ORLANDO: Then love me, Rosalind.
ROSALIND: Yes, faith, will I, Fridays and Saturdays and all.
ORLANDO: And wilt thou have me?
ROSALIND: Ay, and twenty such.
ORLANDO: What sayest thou?
ROSALIND: Are you not good?
ORLANDO: I hope so.
ROSALIND: Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?
ROSALIND: Come, sister, you shall be the priest and marry us.
ROSALIND: Give me your hand, Orlando. What do you say, sister?
ORLANDO: Pray thee, marry us.
CELIA: I cannot say the words.
ROSALIND: You must begin, 'Will you, Orlando--'
CELIA: Go to. Will you, Orlando, have to wife this Rosalind?
ORLANDO: I will.
ROSALIND: Ay, but when?
ORLANDO: Why now, as fast as she can marry us.
ROSALIND: Then you must say 'I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.'
ORLANDO: I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.
ROSALIND: I might ask you for your commission, but I do take
ROSALIND: thee, Orlando, for my husband: there's a girl goes
ROSALIND: before the priest, and certainly a woman's thought
ROSALIND: runs before her actions.
ORLANDO: So do all thoughts, they are winged.
ROSALIND: Now tell me how long you would have her after you
ROSALIND: have possessed her.
ORLANDO: For ever and a day.
ROSALIND: Say 'a day,' without the 'ever.' No, no, Orlando,
ROSALIND: men are April when they woo, December when they wed:
ROSALIND: maids are May when they are maids, but the sky
ROSALIND: changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous
ROSALIND: of thee than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen,
ROSALIND: more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more
ROSALIND: new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires
ROSALIND: than a monkey: I will weep for nothing, like Diana
ROSALIND: in the fountain, and I will do that when you are
ROSALIND: disposed to be merry, I will laugh like a hyen, and
ROSALIND: that when thou art inclined to sleep.
ORLANDO: But will my Rosalind do so?
ROSALIND: By my life, she will do as I do.
ORLANDO: O, but she is wise.
ROSALIND: Or else she could not have the wit to do this: the
ROSALIND: wiser, the waywarder: make the doors upon a woman's
ROSALIND: wit and it will out at the casement, shut that and
ROSALIND: 'twill out at the key-hole, stop that, 'twill fly
ROSALIND: with the smoke out at the chimney.
ORLANDO: A man that had a wife with such a wit, he might say
ORLANDO: 'Wit, whither wilt?'
ROSALIND: Nay, you might keep that cheque for it till you met
ROSALIND: your wife's wit going to your neighbour's bed.
ORLANDO: And what wit could wit have to excuse that?
ROSALIND: Marry, to say she came to seek you there. You shall
ROSALIND: never take her without her answer, unless you take
ROSALIND: her without her tongue. O, that woman that cannot
ROSALIND: make her fault her husband's occasion, let her
ROSALIND: never nurse her child herself, for she will breed
ROSALIND: it like a fool!
ORLANDO: For these two hours, Rosalind, I will leave thee.
ROSALIND: Alas! dear love, I cannot lack thee two hours.
ORLANDO: I must attend the duke at dinner: by two o'clock I
ORLANDO: will be with thee again.
ROSALIND: Ay, go your ways, go your ways, I knew what you
ROSALIND: would prove: my friends told me as much, and I
ROSALIND: thought no less: that flattering tongue of yours
ROSALIND: won me: 'tis but one cast away, and so, come,
ROSALIND: death! Two o'clock is your hour?
ORLANDO: Ay, sweet Rosalind.
ROSALIND: By my troth, and in good earnest, and so God mend
ROSALIND: me, and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous,
ROSALIND: if you break one jot of your promise or come one
ROSALIND: minute behind your hour, I will think you the most
ROSALIND: pathetical break-promise and the most hollow lover
ROSALIND: and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind that
ROSALIND: may be chosen out of the gross band of the
ROSALIND: unfaithful: therefore beware my censure and keep
ROSALIND: your promise.
ORLANDO: With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my
ORLANDO: Rosalind: so adieu.
ROSALIND: Well, Time is the old justice that examines all such
ROSALIND: offenders, and let Time try: adieu.
NARRATOR: Exit ORLANDO
CELIA: You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate:
CELIA: we must have your doublet and hose plucked over your
CELIA: head, and show the world what the bird hath done to
CELIA: her own nest.
ROSALIND: O coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz, that thou
ROSALIND: didst know how many fathom deep I am in love! But
ROSALIND: it cannot be sounded: my affection hath an unknown
ROSALIND: bottom, like the bay of Portugal.
CELIA: Or rather, bottomless, that as fast as you pour
CELIA: affection in, it runs out.
ROSALIND: No, that same wicked bastard of Venus that was begot
ROSALIND: of thought, conceived of spleen and born of madness,
ROSALIND: that blind rascally boy that abuses every one's eyes
ROSALIND: because his own are out, let him be judge how deep I
ROSALIND: am in love. I'll tell thee, Aliena, I cannot be out
ROSALIND: of the sight of Orlando: I'll go find a shadow and
ROSALIND: sigh till he come.
CELIA: And I'll sleep.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter JAQUES, Lords, and Foresters
JAQUES: Which is he that killed the deer?
A Lord: Sir, it was I.
JAQUES: Let's present him to the duke, like a Roman
JAQUES: conqueror, and it would do well to set the deer's
JAQUES: horns upon his head, for a branch of victory. Have
JAQUES: you no song, forester, for this purpose?
Forester: Yes, sir.
JAQUES: Sing it: 'tis no matter how it be in tune, so it
JAQUES: make noise enough.
JAQUES: SONG.
Forester: What shall he have that kill'd the deer?
Forester: His leather skin and horns to wear.
Forester: Then sing him home,
NARRATOR: The rest shall bear this burden
Forester: Take thou no scorn to wear the horn,
Forester: It was a crest ere thou wast born:
Forester: Thy father's father wore it,
Forester: And thy father bore it:
Forester: The horn, the horn, the lusty horn
Forester: Is not a thing to laugh to scorn.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND and CELIA
ROSALIND: How say you now? Is it not past two o'clock? and
ROSALIND: here much Orlando!
CELIA: I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain, he
CELIA: hath ta'en his bow and arrows and is gone forth to
CELIA: sleep. Look, who comes here.
NARRATOR: Enter SILVIUS
SILVIUS: My errand is to you, fair youth,
SILVIUS: My gentle Phebe bid me give you this:
SILVIUS: I know not the contents, but, as I guess
SILVIUS: By the stern brow and waspish action
SILVIUS: Which she did use as she was writing of it,
SILVIUS: It bears an angry tenor: pardon me:
SILVIUS: I am but as a guiltless messenger.
ROSALIND: Patience herself would startle at this letter
ROSALIND: And play the swaggerer, bear this, bear all:
ROSALIND: She says I am not fair, that I lack manners,
ROSALIND: She calls me proud, and that she could not love me,
ROSALIND: Were man as rare as phoenix. 'Od's my will!
ROSALIND: Her love is not the hare that I do hunt:
ROSALIND: Why writes she so to me? Well, shepherd, well,
ROSALIND: This is a letter of your own device.
SILVIUS: No, I protest, I know not the contents:
SILVIUS: Phebe did write it.
ROSALIND: Come, come, you are a fool
ROSALIND: And turn'd into the extremity of love.
ROSALIND: I saw her hand: she has a leathern hand.
ROSALIND: A freestone-colour'd hand, I verily did think
ROSALIND: That her old gloves were on, but 'twas her hands:
ROSALIND: She has a huswife's hand, but that's no matter:
ROSALIND: I say she never did invent this letter,
ROSALIND: This is a man's invention and his hand.
SILVIUS: Sure, it is hers.
ROSALIND: Why, 'tis a boisterous and a cruel style.
ROSALIND: A style for-challengers, why, she defies me,
ROSALIND: Like Turk to Christian: women's gentle brain
ROSALIND: Could not drop forth such giant-rude invention
ROSALIND: Such Ethiope words, blacker in their effect
ROSALIND: Than in their countenance. Will you hear the letter?
SILVIUS: So please you, for I never heard it yet,
SILVIUS: Yet heard too much of Phebe's cruelty.
ROSALIND: She Phebes me: mark how the tyrant writes.
NARRATOR: Reads
ROSALIND: Art thou god to shepherd turn'd,
ROSALIND: That a maiden's heart hath burn'd?
ROSALIND: Can a woman rail thus?
SILVIUS: Call you this railing?
ROSALIND: [Reads]
ROSALIND: Why, thy godhead laid apart,
ROSALIND: Warr'st thou with a woman's heart?
ROSALIND: Did you ever hear such railing?
ROSALIND: Whiles the eye of man did woo me,
ROSALIND: That could do no vengeance to me.
ROSALIND: Meaning me a beast.
ROSALIND: If the scorn of your bright eyne
ROSALIND: Have power to raise such love in mine,
ROSALIND: Alack, in me what strange effect
ROSALIND: Would they work in mild aspect!
ROSALIND: Whiles you chid me, I did love,
ROSALIND: How then might your prayers move!
ROSALIND: He that brings this love to thee
ROSALIND: Little knows this love in me:
ROSALIND: And by him seal up thy mind,
ROSALIND: Whether that thy youth and kind
ROSALIND: Will the faithful offer take
ROSALIND: Of me and all that I can make,
ROSALIND: Or else by him my love deny,
ROSALIND: And then I'll study how to die.
SILVIUS: Call you this chiding?
CELIA: Alas, poor shepherd!
ROSALIND: Do you pity him? no, he deserves no pity. Wilt
ROSALIND: thou love such a woman? What, to make thee an
ROSALIND: instrument and play false strains upon thee! not to
ROSALIND: be endured! Well, go your way to her, for I see
ROSALIND: love hath made thee a tame snake, and say this to
ROSALIND: her: that if she love me, I charge her to love
ROSALIND: thee, if she will not, I will never have her unless
ROSALIND: thou entreat for her. If you be a true lover,
ROSALIND: hence, and not a word, for here comes more company.
NARRATOR: Exit SILVIUS
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVER
OLIVER: Good morrow, fair ones: pray you, if you know,
OLIVER: Where in the purlieus of this forest stands
OLIVER: A sheep-cote fenced about with olive trees?
CELIA: West of this place, down in the neighbour bottom:
CELIA: The rank of osiers by the murmuring stream
CELIA: Left on your right hand brings you to the place.
CELIA: But at this hour the house doth keep itself,
CELIA: There's none within.
OLIVER: If that an eye may profit by a tongue,
OLIVER: Then should I know you by description,
OLIVER: Such garments and such years: 'The boy is fair,
OLIVER: Of female favour, and bestows himself
OLIVER: Like a ripe sister: the woman low
OLIVER: And browner than her brother.' Are not you
OLIVER: The owner of the house I did inquire for?
CELIA: It is no boast, being ask'd, to say we are.
OLIVER: Orlando doth commend him to you both,
OLIVER: And to that youth he calls his Rosalind
OLIVER: He sends this bloody napkin. Are you he?
ROSALIND: I am: what must we understand by this?
OLIVER: Some of my shame, if you will know of me
OLIVER: What man I am, and how, and why, and where
OLIVER: This handkercher was stain'd.
CELIA: I pray you, tell it.
OLIVER: When last the young Orlando parted from you
OLIVER: He left a promise to return again
OLIVER: Within an hour, and pacing through the forest,
OLIVER: Chewing the food of sweet and bitter fancy,
OLIVER: Lo, what befell! he threw his eye aside,
OLIVER: And mark what object did present itself:
OLIVER: Under an oak, whose boughs were moss'd with age
OLIVER: And high top bald with dry antiquity,
OLIVER: A wretched ragged man, o'ergrown with hair,
OLIVER: Lay sleeping on his back: about his neck
OLIVER: A green and gilded snake had wreathed itself,
OLIVER: Who with her head nimble in threats approach'd
OLIVER: The opening of his mouth, but suddenly,
OLIVER: Seeing Orlando, it unlink'd itself,
OLIVER: And with indented glides did slip away
OLIVER: Into a bush: under which bush's shade
OLIVER: A lioness, with udders all drawn dry,
OLIVER: Lay couching, head on ground, with catlike watch,
OLIVER: When that the sleeping man should stir, for 'tis
OLIVER: The royal disposition of that beast
OLIVER: To prey on nothing that doth seem as dead:
OLIVER: This seen, Orlando did approach the man
OLIVER: And found it was his brother, his elder brother.
CELIA: O, I have heard him speak of that same brother,
CELIA: And he did render him the most unnatural
CELIA: That lived amongst men.
OLIVER: And well he might so do,
OLIVER: For well I know he was unnatural.
ROSALIND: But, to Orlando: did he leave him there,
ROSALIND: Food to the suck'd and hungry lioness?
OLIVER: Twice did he turn his back and purposed so,
OLIVER: But kindness, nobler ever than revenge,
OLIVER: And nature, stronger than his just occasion,
OLIVER: Made him give battle to the lioness,
OLIVER: Who quickly fell before him: in which hurtling
OLIVER: From miserable slumber I awaked.
CELIA: Are you his brother?
ROSALIND: Wast you he rescued?
CELIA: Was't you that did so oft contrive to kill him?
OLIVER: 'Twas I, but 'tis not I	I do not shame
OLIVER: To tell you what I was, since my conversion
OLIVER: So sweetly tastes, being the thing I am.
ROSALIND: But, for the bloody napkin?
OLIVER: By and by.
OLIVER: When from the first to last betwixt us two
OLIVER: Tears our recountments had most kindly bathed,
OLIVER: As how I came into that desert place:--
OLIVER: In brief, he led me to the gentle duke,
OLIVER: Who gave me fresh array and entertainment,
OLIVER: Committing me unto my brother's love,
OLIVER: Who led me instantly unto his cave,
OLIVER: There stripp'd himself, and here upon his arm
OLIVER: The lioness had torn some flesh away,
OLIVER: Which all this while had bled, and now he fainted
OLIVER: And cried, in fainting, upon Rosalind.
OLIVER: Brief, I recover'd him, bound up his wound,
OLIVER: And, after some small space, being strong at heart,
OLIVER: He sent me hither, stranger as I am,
OLIVER: To tell this story, that you might excuse
OLIVER: His broken promise, and to give this napkin
OLIVER: Dyed in his blood unto the shepherd youth
OLIVER: That he in sport doth call his Rosalind.
NARRATOR: ROSALIND swoons
CELIA: Why, how now, Ganymede! sweet Ganymede!
OLIVER: Many will swoon when they do look on blood.
CELIA: There is more in it. Cousin Ganymede!
OLIVER: Look, he recovers.
ROSALIND: I would I were at home.
CELIA: We'll lead you thither.
CELIA: I pray you, will you take him by the arm?
OLIVER: Be of good cheer, youth: you a man! you lack a
OLIVER: man's heart.
ROSALIND: I do so, I confess it. Ah, sirrah, a body would
ROSALIND: think this was well counterfeited! I pray you, tell
ROSALIND: your brother how well I counterfeited. Heigh-ho!
OLIVER: This was not counterfeit: there is too great
OLIVER: testimony in your complexion that it was a passion
OLIVER: of earnest.
ROSALIND: Counterfeit, I assure you.
OLIVER: Well then, take a good heart and counterfeit to be a man.
ROSALIND: So I do: but, i' faith, I should have been a woman by right.
CELIA: Come, you look paler and paler: pray you, draw
CELIA: homewards. Good sir, go with us.
OLIVER: That will I, for I must bear answer back
