OLIVER: How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.
ROSALIND: I shall devise something: but, I pray you, commend
ROSALIND: my counterfeiting to him. Will you go?
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
TOUCHSTONE: We shall find a time, Audrey, patience, gentle Audrey.
AUDREY: Faith, the priest was good enough, for all the old
AUDREY: gentleman's saying.
TOUCHSTONE: A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile
TOUCHSTONE: Martext. But, Audrey, there is a youth here in the
TOUCHSTONE: forest lays claim to you.
AUDREY: Ay, I know who 'tis, he hath no interest in me in
AUDREY: the world: here comes the man you mean.
TOUCHSTONE: It is meat and drink to me to see a clown: by my
TOUCHSTONE: troth, we that have good wits have much to answer
TOUCHSTONE: for, we shall be flouting, we cannot hold.
NARRATOR: Enter WILLIAM
WILLIAM: Good even, Audrey.
AUDREY: God ye good even, William.
WILLIAM: And good even to you, sir.
TOUCHSTONE: Good even, gentle friend. Cover thy head, cover thy
TOUCHSTONE: head, nay, prithee, be covered. How old are you, friend?
WILLIAM: Five and twenty, sir.
TOUCHSTONE: A ripe age. Is thy name William?
WILLIAM: William, sir.
TOUCHSTONE: A fair name. Wast born i' the forest here?
WILLIAM: Ay, sir, I thank God.
TOUCHSTONE: 'Thank God,' a good answer. Art rich?
WILLIAM: Faith, sir, so so.
TOUCHSTONE: 'So so' is good, very good, very excellent good, and
TOUCHSTONE: yet it is not, it is but so so. Art thou wise?
WILLIAM: Ay, sir, I have a pretty wit.
TOUCHSTONE: Why, thou sayest well. I do now remember a saying,
TOUCHSTONE: 'The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man
TOUCHSTONE: knows himself to be a fool.' The heathen
TOUCHSTONE: philosopher, when he had a desire to eat a grape,
TOUCHSTONE: would open his lips when he put it into his mouth,
TOUCHSTONE: meaning thereby that grapes were made to eat and
TOUCHSTONE: lips to open. You do love this maid?
WILLIAM: I do, sir.
TOUCHSTONE: Give me your hand. Art thou learned?
WILLIAM: No, sir.
TOUCHSTONE: Then learn this of me: to have, is to have, for it
TOUCHSTONE: is a figure in rhetoric that drink, being poured out
TOUCHSTONE: of a cup into a glass, by filling the one doth empty
TOUCHSTONE: the other, for all your writers do consent that ipse
TOUCHSTONE: is he: now, you are not ipse, for I am he.
WILLIAM: Which he, sir?
TOUCHSTONE: He, sir, that must marry this woman. Therefore, you
TOUCHSTONE: clown, abandon,--which is in the vulgar leave,--the
TOUCHSTONE: society,--which in the boorish is company,--of this
TOUCHSTONE: female,--which in the common is woman, which
TOUCHSTONE: together is, abandon the society of this female, or,
TOUCHSTONE: clown, thou perishest, or, to thy better
TOUCHSTONE: understanding, diest, or, to wit I kill thee, make
TOUCHSTONE: thee away, translate thy life into death, thy
TOUCHSTONE: liberty into bondage: I will deal in poison with
TOUCHSTONE: thee, or in bastinado, or in steel, I will bandy
TOUCHSTONE: with thee in faction, I will o'errun thee with
TOUCHSTONE: policy, I will kill thee a hundred and fifty ways:
TOUCHSTONE: therefore tremble and depart.
AUDREY: Do, good William.
WILLIAM: God rest you merry, sir.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter CORIN
CORIN: Our master and mistress seeks you, come, away, away!
TOUCHSTONE: Trip, Audrey! trip, Audrey! I attend, I attend.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter ORLANDO and OLIVER
ORLANDO: Is't possible that on so little acquaintance you
ORLANDO: should like her? that but seeing you should love
ORLANDO: her? and loving woo? and, wooing, she should
ORLANDO: grant? and will you persever to enjoy her?
OLIVER: Neither call the giddiness of it in question, the
OLIVER: poverty of her, the small acquaintance, my sudden
OLIVER: wooing, nor her sudden consenting, but say with me,
OLIVER: I love Aliena, say with her that she loves me,
OLIVER: consent with both that we may enjoy each other: it
OLIVER: shall be to your good, for my father's house and all
OLIVER: the revenue that was old Sir Rowland's will I
OLIVER: estate upon you, and here live and die a shepherd.
ORLANDO: You have my consent. Let your wedding be to-morrow:
ORLANDO: thither will I invite the duke and all's contented
ORLANDO: followers. Go you and prepare Aliena, for look
ORLANDO: you, here comes my Rosalind.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND
ROSALIND: God save you, brother.
OLIVER: And you, fair sister.
NARRATOR: Exit
ROSALIND: O, my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see thee
ROSALIND: wear thy heart in a scarf!
ORLANDO: It is my arm.
ROSALIND: I thought thy heart had been wounded with the claws
ROSALIND: of a lion.
ORLANDO: Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.
ROSALIND: Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited to
ROSALIND: swoon when he showed me your handkerchief?
ORLANDO: Ay, and greater wonders than that.
ROSALIND: O, I know where you are: nay, 'tis true: there was
ROSALIND: never any thing so sudden but the fight of two rams
ROSALIND: and Caesar's thrasonical brag of 'I came, saw, and
ROSALIND: overcame:' for your brother and my sister no sooner
ROSALIND: met but they looked, no sooner looked but they
ROSALIND: loved, no sooner loved but they sighed, no sooner
ROSALIND: sighed but they asked one another the reason, no
ROSALIND: sooner knew the reason but they sought the remedy,
ROSALIND: and in these degrees have they made a pair of stairs
ROSALIND: to marriage which they will climb incontinent, or
ROSALIND: else be incontinent before marriage: they are in
ROSALIND: the very wrath of love and they will together, clubs
ROSALIND: cannot part them.
ORLANDO: They shall be married to-morrow, and I will bid the
ORLANDO: duke to the nuptial. But, O, how bitter a thing it
ORLANDO: is to look into happiness through another man's
ORLANDO: eyes! By so much the more shall I to-morrow be at
ORLANDO: the height of heart-heaviness, by how much I shall
ORLANDO: think my brother happy in having what he wishes for.
ROSALIND: Why then, to-morrow I cannot serve your turn for Rosalind?
ORLANDO: I can live no longer by thinking.
ROSALIND: I will weary you then no longer with idle talking.
ROSALIND: Know of me then, for now I speak to some purpose,
ROSALIND: that I know you are a gentleman of good conceit: I
ROSALIND: speak not this that you should bear a good opinion
ROSALIND: of my knowledge, insomuch I say I know you are,
ROSALIND: neither do I labour for a greater esteem than may in
ROSALIND: some little measure draw a belief from you, to do
ROSALIND: yourself good and not to grace me. Believe then, if
ROSALIND: you please, that I can do strange things: I have,
ROSALIND: since I was three year old, conversed with a
ROSALIND: magician, most profound in his art and yet not
ROSALIND: damnable. If you do love Rosalind so near the heart
ROSALIND: as your gesture cries it out, when your brother
ROSALIND: marries Aliena, shall you marry her: I know into
ROSALIND: what straits of fortune she is driven, and it is
ROSALIND: not impossible to me, if it appear not inconvenient
ROSALIND: to you, to set her before your eyes tomorrow human
ROSALIND: as she is and without any danger.
ORLANDO: Speakest thou in sober meanings?
ROSALIND: By my life, I do, which I tender dearly, though I
ROSALIND: say I am a magician. Therefore, put you in your
ROSALIND: best array: bid your friends, for if you will be
ROSALIND: married to-morrow, you shall, and to Rosalind, if you will.
NARRATOR: Enter SILVIUS and PHEBE
ROSALIND: Look, here comes a lover of mine and a lover of hers.
PHEBE: Youth, you have done me much ungentleness,
PHEBE: To show the letter that I writ to you.
ROSALIND: I care not if I have: it is my study
ROSALIND: To seem despiteful and ungentle to you:
ROSALIND: You are there followed by a faithful shepherd,
ROSALIND: Look upon him, love him, he worships you.
PHEBE: Good shepherd, tell this youth what 'tis to love.
SILVIUS: It is to be all made of sighs and tears,
SILVIUS: And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE: And I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO: And I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND: And I for no woman.
SILVIUS: It is to be all made of faith and service,
SILVIUS: And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE: And I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO: And I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND: And I for no woman.
SILVIUS: It is to be all made of fantasy,
SILVIUS: All made of passion and all made of wishes,
SILVIUS: All adoration, duty, and observance,
SILVIUS: All humbleness, all patience and impatience,
SILVIUS: All purity, all trial, all observance,
SILVIUS: And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE: And so am I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO: And so am I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND: And so am I for no woman.
PHEBE: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
SILVIUS: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
ORLANDO: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
ROSALIND: Who do you speak to, 'Why blame you me to love you?'
ORLANDO: To her that is not here, nor doth not hear.
ROSALIND: Pray you, no more of this, 'tis like the howling
ROSALIND: of Irish wolves against the moon.
NARRATOR: To SILVIUS
ROSALIND: I will help you, if I can:
NARRATOR: To PHEBE
ROSALIND: I would love you, if I could. To-morrow meet me all together.
NARRATOR: To PHEBE
ROSALIND: I will marry you, if ever I marry woman, and I'll be
ROSALIND: married to-morrow:
NARRATOR: To ORLANDO
ROSALIND: I will satisfy you, if ever I satisfied man, and you
ROSALIND: shall be married to-morrow:
NARRATOR: To SILVIUS
ROSALIND: I will content you, if what pleases you contents
ROSALIND: you, and you shall be married to-morrow.
NARRATOR: To ORLANDO
ROSALIND: As you love Rosalind, meet:
NARRATOR: To SILVIUS
ROSALIND: as you love Phebe, meet: and as I love no woman,
ROSALIND: I'll meet. So fare you well: I have left you commands.
SILVIUS: I'll not fail, if I live.
PHEBE: Nor I.
ORLANDO: Nor I.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
TOUCHSTONE: To-morrow is the joyful day, Audrey, to-morrow will
TOUCHSTONE: we be married.
AUDREY: I do desire it with all my heart, and I hope it is
AUDREY: no dishonest desire to desire to be a woman of the
AUDREY: world. Here comes two of the banished duke's pages.
NARRATOR: Enter two Pages
First Page: Well met, honest gentleman.
TOUCHSTONE: By my troth, well met. Come, sit, sit, and a song.
Second Page: We are for you: sit i' the middle.
First Page: Shall we clap into't roundly, without hawking or
First Page: spitting or saying we are hoarse, which are the only
First Page: prologues to a bad voice?
Second Page: I'faith, i'faith, and both in a tune, like two
Second Page: gipsies on a horse.
Second Page: SONG.
Second Page: It was a lover and his lass,
Second Page: With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino,
Second Page: That o'er the green corn-field did pass
Second Page: In the spring time, the only pretty ring time,
Second Page: When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding:
Second Page: Sweet lovers love the spring.
Second Page: Between the acres of the rye,
Second Page: With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino
Second Page: These pretty country folks would lie,
Second Page: In spring time,  and c.
Second Page: This carol they began that hour,
Second Page: With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino,
Second Page: How that a life was but a flower
Second Page: In spring time,  and c.
Second Page: And therefore take the present time,
Second Page: With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino,
Second Page: For love is crowned with the prime
Second Page: In spring time,  and c.
TOUCHSTONE: Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great
TOUCHSTONE: matter in the ditty, yet the note was very
TOUCHSTONE: untuneable.
First Page: You are deceived, sir: we kept time, we lost not our time.
TOUCHSTONE: By my troth, yes, I count it but time lost to hear
TOUCHSTONE: such a foolish song. God be wi' you, and God mend
TOUCHSTONE: your voices! Come, Audrey.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The forest.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, JAQUES, ORLANDO, OLIVER, and CELIA
DUKE SENIOR: Dost thou believe, Orlando, that the boy
DUKE SENIOR: Can do all this that he hath promised?
ORLANDO: I sometimes do believe, and sometimes do not,
ORLANDO: As those that fear they hope, and know they fear.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSALIND, SILVIUS, and PHEBE
ROSALIND: Patience once more, whiles our compact is urged:
ROSALIND: You say, if I bring in your Rosalind,
ROSALIND: You will bestow her on Orlando here?
DUKE SENIOR: That would I, had I kingdoms to give with her.
ROSALIND: And you say, you will have her, when I bring her?
ORLANDO: That would I, were I of all kingdoms king.
ROSALIND: You say, you'll marry me, if I be willing?
PHEBE: That will I, should I die the hour after.
ROSALIND: But if you do refuse to marry me,
ROSALIND: You'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?
PHEBE: So is the bargain.
ROSALIND: You say, that you'll have Phebe, if she will?
SILVIUS: Though to have her and death were both one thing.
ROSALIND: I have promised to make all this matter even.
ROSALIND: Keep you your word, O duke, to give your daughter,
ROSALIND: You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter:
ROSALIND: Keep your word, Phebe, that you'll marry me,
ROSALIND: Or else refusing me, to wed this shepherd:
ROSALIND: Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her.
ROSALIND: If she refuse me: and from hence I go,
ROSALIND: To make these doubts all even.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA
DUKE SENIOR: I do remember in this shepherd boy
DUKE SENIOR: Some lively touches of my daughter's favour.
ORLANDO: My lord, the first time that I ever saw him
ORLANDO: Methought he was a brother to your daughter:
ORLANDO: But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born,
ORLANDO: And hath been tutor'd in the rudiments
ORLANDO: Of many desperate studies by his uncle,
ORLANDO: Whom he reports to be a great magician,
ORLANDO: Obscured in the circle of this forest.
NARRATOR: Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
JAQUES: There is, sure, another flood toward, and these
JAQUES: couples are coming to the ark. Here comes a pair of
JAQUES: very strange beasts, which in all tongues are called fools.
TOUCHSTONE: Salutation and greeting to you all!
JAQUES: Good my lord, bid him welcome: this is the
JAQUES: motley-minded gentleman that I have so often met in
JAQUES: the forest: he hath been a courtier, he swears.
TOUCHSTONE: If any man doubt that, let him put me to my
TOUCHSTONE: purgation. I have trod a measure, I have flattered
TOUCHSTONE: a lady, I have been politic with my friend, smooth
TOUCHSTONE: with mine enemy, I have undone three tailors, I have
TOUCHSTONE: had four quarrels, and like to have fought one.
JAQUES: And how was that ta'en up?
TOUCHSTONE: Faith, we met, and found the quarrel was upon the
TOUCHSTONE: seventh cause.
JAQUES: How seventh cause? Good my lord, like this fellow.
DUKE SENIOR: I like him very well.
TOUCHSTONE: God 'ild you, sir, I desire you of the like. I
TOUCHSTONE: press in here, sir, amongst the rest of the country
TOUCHSTONE: copulatives, to swear and to forswear: according as
TOUCHSTONE: marriage binds and blood breaks: a poor virgin,
TOUCHSTONE: sir, an ill-favoured thing, sir, but mine own, a poor
TOUCHSTONE: humour of mine, sir, to take that that no man else
TOUCHSTONE: will: rich honesty dwells like a miser, sir, in a
TOUCHSTONE: poor house, as your pearl in your foul oyster.
DUKE SENIOR: By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.
TOUCHSTONE: According to the fool's bolt, sir, and such dulcet diseases.
JAQUES: But, for the seventh cause, how did you find the
JAQUES: quarrel on the seventh cause?
TOUCHSTONE: Upon a lie seven times removed:--bear your body more
TOUCHSTONE: seeming, Audrey:--as thus, sir. I did dislike the
TOUCHSTONE: cut of a certain courtier's beard: he sent me word,
TOUCHSTONE: if I said his beard was not cut well, he was in the
TOUCHSTONE: mind it was: this is called the Retort Courteous.
TOUCHSTONE: If I sent him word again 'it was not well cut,' he
TOUCHSTONE: would send me word, he cut it to please himself:
TOUCHSTONE: this is called the Quip Modest. If again 'it was
TOUCHSTONE: not well cut,' he disabled my judgment: this is
TOUCHSTONE: called the Reply Churlish. If again 'it was not
TOUCHSTONE: well cut,' he would answer, I spake not true: this
TOUCHSTONE: is called the Reproof Valiant. If again 'it was not
TOUCHSTONE: well cut,' he would say I lied: this is called the
TOUCHSTONE: Counter-cheque Quarrelsome: and so to the Lie
TOUCHSTONE: Circumstantial and the Lie Direct.
JAQUES: And how oft did you say his beard was not well cut?
TOUCHSTONE: I durst go no further than the Lie Circumstantial,
TOUCHSTONE: nor he durst not give me the Lie Direct, and so we
TOUCHSTONE: measured swords and parted.
JAQUES: Can you nominate in order now the degrees of the lie?
TOUCHSTONE: O sir, we quarrel in print, by the book, as you have
TOUCHSTONE: books for good manners: I will name you the degrees.
TOUCHSTONE: The first, the Retort Courteous, the second, the
TOUCHSTONE: Quip Modest, the third, the Reply Churlish, the
TOUCHSTONE: fourth, the Reproof Valiant, the fifth, the
TOUCHSTONE: Countercheque Quarrelsome, the sixth, the Lie with
TOUCHSTONE: Circumstance, the seventh, the Lie Direct. All
TOUCHSTONE: these you may avoid but the Lie Direct, and you may
TOUCHSTONE: avoid that too, with an If. I knew when seven
TOUCHSTONE: justices could not take up a quarrel, but when the
TOUCHSTONE: parties were met themselves, one of them thought but
TOUCHSTONE: of an If, as, 'If you said so, then I said so,' and
TOUCHSTONE: they shook hands and swore brothers. Your If is the
TOUCHSTONE: only peacemaker, much virtue in If.
JAQUES: Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? he's as good at
JAQUES: any thing and yet a fool.
DUKE SENIOR: He uses his folly like a stalking-horse and under
DUKE SENIOR: the presentation of that he shoots his wit.
NARRATOR: Enter HYMEN, ROSALIND, and CELIA
NARRATOR: Still Music
HYMEN: Then is there mirth in heaven,
HYMEN: When earthly things made even
HYMEN: Atone together.
HYMEN: Good duke, receive thy daughter
HYMEN: Hymen from heaven brought her,
HYMEN: Yea, brought her hither,
HYMEN: That thou mightst join her hand with his
HYMEN: Whose heart within his bosom is.

PHEBE: If sight and shape be true,
PHEBE: Why then, my love adieu!
ROSALIND: I'll have no father, if you be not he:
ROSALIND: I'll have no husband, if you be not he:
ROSALIND: Nor ne'er wed woman, if you be not she.
HYMEN: Peace, ho! I bar confusion:
HYMEN: 'Tis I must make conclusion
HYMEN: Of these most strange events:
HYMEN: Here's eight that must take hands
HYMEN: To join in Hymen's bands,
HYMEN: If truth holds true contents.
HYMEN: You and you no cross shall part:
HYMEN: You and you are heart in heart
HYMEN: You to his love must accord,
HYMEN: Or have a woman to your lord:
HYMEN: You and you are sure together,
HYMEN: As the winter to foul weather.
HYMEN: Whiles a wedlock-hymn we sing,
HYMEN: Feed yourselves with questioning,
HYMEN: That reason wonder may diminish,
HYMEN: How thus we met, and these things finish.

HYMEN: Wedding is great Juno's crown:
HYMEN: O blessed bond of board and bed!
HYMEN: 'Tis Hymen peoples every town,
HYMEN: High wedlock then be honoured:
HYMEN: Honour, high honour and renown,
HYMEN: To Hymen, god of every town!
DUKE SENIOR: O my dear niece, welcome thou art to me!

PHEBE: Thy faith my fancy to thee doth combine.
NARRATOR: Enter JAQUES DE BOYS
JAQUES DE BOYS: Let me have audience for a word or two:
JAQUES DE BOYS: I am the second son of old Sir Rowland,
JAQUES DE BOYS: That bring these tidings to this fair assembly.

JAQUES DE BOYS: His brother here and put him to the sword:

DUKE SENIOR: EPILOGUE
ROSALIND: It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue,
ROSALIND: but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord
ROSALIND: the prologue. If it be true that good wine needs
ROSALIND: no bush, 'tis true that a good play needs no
ROSALIND: epilogue, yet to good wine they do use good bushes,
ROSALIND: and good plays prove the better by the help of good
ROSALIND: epilogues. What a case am I in then, that am
ROSALIND: neither a good epilogue nor cannot insinuate with
ROSALIND: you in the behalf of a good play! I am not
ROSALIND: furnished like a beggar, therefore to beg will not
ROSALIND: become me: my way is to conjure you, and I'll begin
ROSALIND: with the women. I charge you, O women, for the love
ROSALIND: you bear to men, to like as much of this play as
ROSALIND: please you: and I charge you, O men, for the love
ROSALIND: you bear to women--as I perceive by your simpering,
ROSALIND: none of you hates them--that between you and the
ROSALIND: women the play may please. If I were a woman I
ROSALIND: would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased
ROSALIND: me, complexions that liked me and breaths that I
ROSALIND: defied not: and, I am sure, as many as have good
ROSALIND: beards or good faces or sweet breaths will, for my
ROSALIND: kind offer, when I make curtsy, bid me farewell.
