''' PLAY: Coriolanus '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter a company of mutinous Citizens, with staves, clubs, and other weapons
First Citizen: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
All: Speak, speak.
First Citizen: You are all resolved rather to die than to famish?
All: Resolved. resolved.
First Citizen: First, you know Caius Marcius is chief enemy to the people.
All: We know't, we know't.
First Citizen: Let us kill him, and we'll have corn at our own price.
First Citizen: Is't a verdict?
All: No more talking on't, let it be done: away, away!
Second Citizen: One word, good citizens.
First Citizen: We are accounted poor citizens, the patricians good.
First Citizen: What authority surfeits on would relieve us: if they
First Citizen: would yield us but the superfluity, while it were
First Citizen: wholesome, we might guess they relieved us humanely,
First Citizen: but they think we are too dear: the leanness that
First Citizen: afflicts us, the object of our misery, is as an
First Citizen: inventory to particularise their abundance, our
First Citizen: sufferance is a gain to them Let us revenge this with
First Citizen: our pikes, ere we become rakes: for the gods know I
First Citizen: speak this in hunger for bread, not in thirst for revenge.
Second Citizen: Would you proceed especially against Caius Marcius?
All: Against him first: he's a very dog to the commonalty.
Second Citizen: Consider you what services he has done for his country?
First Citizen: Very well, and could be content to give him good
First Citizen: report fort, but that he pays himself with being proud.
Second Citizen: Nay, but speak not maliciously.
First Citizen: I say unto you, what he hath done famously, he did
First Citizen: it to that end: though soft-conscienced men can be
First Citizen: content to say it was for his country he did it to
First Citizen: please his mother and to be partly proud, which he
First Citizen: is, even till the altitude of his virtue.
Second Citizen: What he cannot help in his nature, you account a
Second Citizen: vice in him. You must in no way say he is covetous.
First Citizen: If I must not, I need not be barren of accusations,
First Citizen: he hath faults, with surplus, to tire in repetition.
NARRATOR: Shouts within
First Citizen: What shouts are these? The other side o' the city
First Citizen: is risen: why stay we prating here? to the Capitol!
All: Come, come.
First Citizen: Soft! who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter MENENIUS AGRIPPA
Second Citizen: Worthy Menenius Agrippa, one that hath always loved
Second Citizen: the people.
First Citizen: He's one honest enough: would all the rest were so!
MENENIUS: What work's, my countrymen, in hand? where go you
MENENIUS: With bats and clubs? The matter? speak, I pray you.
First Citizen: Our business is not unknown to the senate, they have
First Citizen: had inkling this fortnight what we intend to do,
First Citizen: which now we'll show 'em in deeds. They say poor
First Citizen: suitors have strong breaths: they shall know we
First Citizen: have strong arms too.
MENENIUS: Why, masters, my good friends, mine honest neighbours,
MENENIUS: Will you undo yourselves?
First Citizen: We cannot, sir, we are undone already.
MENENIUS: I tell you, friends, most charitable care
MENENIUS: Have the patricians of you. For your wants,
MENENIUS: Your suffering in this dearth, you may as well
MENENIUS: Strike at the heaven with your staves as lift them
MENENIUS: Against the Roman state, whose course will on
MENENIUS: The way it takes, cracking ten thousand curbs
MENENIUS: Of more strong link asunder than can ever
MENENIUS: Appear in your impediment. For the dearth,
MENENIUS: The gods, not the patricians, make it, and
MENENIUS: Your knees to them, not arms, must help. Alack,
MENENIUS: You are transported by calamity
MENENIUS: Thither where more attends you, and you slander
MENENIUS: The helms o' the state, who care for you like fathers,
MENENIUS: When you curse them as enemies.
First Citizen: Care for us! True, indeed! They ne'er cared for us
First Citizen: yet: suffer us to famish, and their store-houses
First Citizen: crammed with grain, make edicts for usury, to
First Citizen: support usurers, repeal daily any wholesome act
First Citizen: established against the rich, and provide more
First Citizen: piercing statutes daily, to chain up and restrain
First Citizen: the poor. If the wars eat us not up, they will, and
First Citizen: there's all the love they bear us.
MENENIUS: Either you must
MENENIUS: Confess yourselves wondrous malicious,
MENENIUS: Or be accused of folly. I shall tell you
MENENIUS: A pretty tale: it may be you have heard it,
MENENIUS: But, since it serves my purpose, I will venture
MENENIUS: To stale 't a little more.
First Citizen: Well, I'll hear it, sir: yet you must not think to
First Citizen: fob off our disgrace with a tale: but, an 't please
First Citizen: you, deliver.
MENENIUS: There was a time when all the body's members
MENENIUS: Rebell'd against the belly, thus accused it:
MENENIUS: That only like a gulf it did remain
MENENIUS: I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive,
MENENIUS: Still cupboarding the viand, never bearing
MENENIUS: Like labour with the rest, where the other instruments
MENENIUS: Did see and hear, devise, instruct, walk, feel,
MENENIUS: And, mutually participate, did minister
MENENIUS: Unto the appetite and affection common
MENENIUS: Of the whole body. The belly answer'd--
First Citizen: Well, sir, what answer made the belly?
MENENIUS: Sir, I shall tell you. With a kind of smile,
MENENIUS: Which ne'er came from the lungs, but even thus--
MENENIUS: For, look you, I may make the belly smile
MENENIUS: As well as speak--it tauntingly replied
MENENIUS: To the discontented members, the mutinous parts
MENENIUS: That envied his receipt, even so most fitly
MENENIUS: As you malign our senators for that
MENENIUS: They are not such as you.
First Citizen: Your belly's answer? What!
First Citizen: The kingly-crowned head, the vigilant eye,
First Citizen: The counsellor heart, the arm our soldier,
First Citizen: Our steed the leg, the tongue our trumpeter.
First Citizen: With other muniments and petty helps
First Citizen: In this our fabric, if that they--
MENENIUS: What then?
MENENIUS: 'Fore me, this fellow speaks! What then? what then?
First Citizen: Should by the cormorant belly be restrain'd,
First Citizen: Who is the sink o' the body,--
MENENIUS: Well, what then?
First Citizen: The former agents, if they did complain,
First Citizen: What could the belly answer?
MENENIUS: I will tell you
MENENIUS: If you'll bestow a small--of what you have little--
MENENIUS: Patience awhile, you'll hear the belly's answer.
First Citizen: Ye're long about it.
MENENIUS: Note me this, good friend,
MENENIUS: Your most grave belly was deliberate,
MENENIUS: Not rash like his accusers, and thus answer'd:
MENENIUS: 'True is it, my incorporate friends,' quoth he,
MENENIUS: 'That I receive the general food at first,
MENENIUS: Which you do live upon, and fit it is,
MENENIUS: Because I am the store-house and the shop
MENENIUS: Of the whole body: but, if you do remember,
MENENIUS: I send it through the rivers of your blood,
MENENIUS: Even to the court, the heart, to the seat o' the brain,
MENENIUS: And, through the cranks and offices of man,
MENENIUS: The strongest nerves and small inferior veins
MENENIUS: From me receive that natural competency
MENENIUS: Whereby they live: and though that all at once,
MENENIUS: You, my good friends,'--this says the belly, mark me,--
First Citizen: Ay, sir, well, well.
MENENIUS: 'Though all at once cannot
MENENIUS: See what I do deliver out to each,
MENENIUS: Yet I can make my audit up, that all
MENENIUS: From me do back receive the flour of all,
MENENIUS: And leave me but the bran.' What say you to't?
First Citizen: It was an answer: how apply you this?
MENENIUS: The senators of Rome are this good belly,
MENENIUS: And you the mutinous members, for examine
MENENIUS: Their counsels and their cares, digest things rightly
MENENIUS: Touching the weal o' the common, you shall find
MENENIUS: No public benefit which you receive
MENENIUS: But it proceeds or comes from them to you
MENENIUS: And no way from yourselves. What do you think,
MENENIUS: You, the great toe of this assembly?
First Citizen: I the great toe! why the great toe?
MENENIUS: For that, being one o' the lowest, basest, poorest,
MENENIUS: Of this most wise rebellion, thou go'st foremost:
MENENIUS: Thou rascal, that art worst in blood to run,
MENENIUS: Lead'st first to win some vantage.
MENENIUS: But make you ready your stiff bats and clubs:
MENENIUS: Rome and her rats are at the point of battle,
MENENIUS: The one side must have bale.
NARRATOR: Enter CAIUS MARCIUS
MENENIUS: Hail, noble Marcius!
MARCIUS: Thanks. What's the matter, you dissentious rogues,
MARCIUS: That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion,
MARCIUS: Make yourselves scabs?
First Citizen: We have ever your good word.
MARCIUS: He that will give good words to thee will flatter
MARCIUS: Beneath abhorring. What would you have, you curs,
MARCIUS: That like nor peace nor war? the one affrights you,
MARCIUS: The other makes you proud. He that trusts to you,
MARCIUS: Where he should find you lions, finds you hares,
MARCIUS: Where foxes, geese: you are no surer, no,
MARCIUS: Than is the coal of fire upon the ice,
MARCIUS: Or hailstone in the sun. Your virtue is
MARCIUS: To make him worthy whose offence subdues him
MARCIUS: And curse that justice did it.
MARCIUS: Who deserves greatness
MARCIUS: Deserves your hate, and your affections are
MARCIUS: A sick man's appetite, who desires most that
MARCIUS: Which would increase his evil. He that depends
MARCIUS: Upon your favours swims with fins of lead
MARCIUS: And hews down oaks with rushes. Hang ye! Trust Ye?
MARCIUS: With every minute you do change a mind,
MARCIUS: And call him noble that was now your hate,
MARCIUS: Him vile that was your garland. What's the matter,
MARCIUS: That in these several places of the city
MARCIUS: You cry against the noble senate, who,
MARCIUS: Under the gods, keep you in awe, which else
MARCIUS: Would feed on one another? What's their seeking?
MENENIUS: For corn at their own rates, whereof, they say,
MENENIUS: The city is well stored.
MARCIUS: Hang 'em! They say!
MARCIUS: They'll sit by the fire, and presume to know
MARCIUS: What's done i' the Capitol, who's like to rise,
MARCIUS: Who thrives and who declines, side factions
MARCIUS: and give out
MARCIUS: Conjectural marriages, making parties strong
MARCIUS: And feebling such as stand not in their liking
MARCIUS: Below their cobbled shoes. They say there's
MARCIUS: grain enough!
MARCIUS: Would the nobility lay aside their ruth,
MARCIUS: And let me use my sword, I'll make a quarry
MARCIUS: With thousands of these quarter'd slaves, as high
MARCIUS: As I could pick my lance.
MENENIUS: Nay, these are almost thoroughly persuaded,
MENENIUS: For though abundantly they lack discretion,
MENENIUS: Yet are they passing cowardly. But, I beseech you,
MENENIUS: What says the other troop?
MARCIUS: They are dissolved: hang 'em!
MARCIUS: They said they were an-hungry, sigh'd forth proverbs,
MARCIUS: That hunger broke stone walls, that dogs must eat,
MARCIUS: That meat was made for mouths, that the gods sent not
MARCIUS: Corn for the rich men only: with these shreds
MARCIUS: They vented their complainings, which being answer'd,
MARCIUS: And a petition granted them, a strange one--
MARCIUS: To break the heart of generosity,
MARCIUS: And make bold power look pale--they threw their caps
MARCIUS: As they would hang them on the horns o' the moon,
MARCIUS: Shouting their emulation.
MENENIUS: What is granted them?
MARCIUS: Five tribunes to defend their vulgar wisdoms,
MARCIUS: Of their own choice: one's Junius Brutus,
MARCIUS: Sicinius Velutus, and I know not--'Sdeath!
MARCIUS: The rabble should have first unroof'd the city,
MARCIUS: Ere so prevail'd with me: it will in time
MARCIUS: Win upon power and throw forth greater themes
MARCIUS: For insurrection's arguing.
MENENIUS: This is strange.
MARCIUS: Go, get you home, you fragments!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger, hastily
Messenger: Where's Caius Marcius?
MARCIUS: Here: what's the matter?
Messenger: The news is, sir, the Volsces are in arms.
MARCIUS: I am glad on 't: then we shall ha' means to vent
MARCIUS: Our musty superfluity. See, our best elders.
MARCIUS: Enter COMINIUS, TITUS LARTIUS, and other Senators, JUNIUS BRUTUS and SICINIUS VELUTUS
First Senator: Marcius, 'tis true that you have lately told us,
First Senator: The Volsces are in arms.
MARCIUS: They have a leader,
MARCIUS: Tullus Aufidius, that will put you to 't.
MARCIUS: I sin in envying his nobility,
MARCIUS: And were I any thing but what I am,
MARCIUS: I would wish me only he.
COMINIUS: You have fought together.
MARCIUS: Were half to half the world by the ears and he.
MARCIUS: Upon my party, I'ld revolt to make
MARCIUS: Only my wars with him: he is a lion
MARCIUS: That I am proud to hunt.
First Senator: Then, worthy Marcius,
First Senator: Attend upon Cominius to these wars.
COMINIUS: It is your former promise.
MARCIUS: Sir, it is,
MARCIUS: And I am constant. Titus Lartius, thou
MARCIUS: Shalt see me once more strike at Tullus' face.
MARCIUS: What, art thou stiff? stand'st out?
TITUS: No, Caius Marcius,
TITUS: I'll lean upon one crutch and fight with t'other,
TITUS: Ere stay behind this business.
MENENIUS: O, true-bred!
First Senator: Your company to the Capitol, where, I know,
First Senator: Our greatest friends attend us.
TITUS: [To COMINIUS]                Lead you on.
NARRATOR: To MARCIUS
TITUS: Right worthy you priority.
COMINIUS: Noble Marcius!
First Senator: [To the Citizens]  Hence to your homes, be gone!
MARCIUS: Nay, let them follow:
MARCIUS: The Volsces have much corn, take these rats thither
MARCIUS: To gnaw their garners. Worshipful mutiners,
MARCIUS: Your valour puts well forth: pray, follow.
NARRATOR: Citizens steal away. Exeunt all but SICINIUS and BRUTUS
SICINIUS: Was ever man so proud as is this Marcius?
BRUTUS: He has no equal.
SICINIUS: When we were chosen tribunes for the people,--
BRUTUS: Mark'd you his lip and eyes?
SICINIUS: Nay. but his taunts.
BRUTUS: Being moved, he will not spare to gird the gods.
SICINIUS: Be-mock the modest moon.
BRUTUS: The present wars devour him: he is grown
BRUTUS: Too proud to be so valiant.
SICINIUS: Such a nature,
SICINIUS: Tickled with good success, disdains the shadow
SICINIUS: Which he treads on at noon: but I do wonder
SICINIUS: His insolence can brook to be commanded
SICINIUS: Under Cominius.
BRUTUS: Fame, at the which he aims,
BRUTUS: In whom already he's well graced, can not
BRUTUS: Better be held nor more attain'd than by
BRUTUS: A place below the first: for what miscarries
BRUTUS: Shall be the general's fault, though he perform
BRUTUS: To the utmost of a man, and giddy censure
BRUTUS: Will then cry out of Marcius 'O if he
BRUTUS: Had borne the business!'
SICINIUS: Besides, if things go well,
SICINIUS: Opinion that so sticks on Marcius shall
SICINIUS: Of his demerits rob Cominius.
BRUTUS: Come:
BRUTUS: Half all Cominius' honours are to Marcius.
BRUTUS: Though Marcius earned them not, and all his faults
BRUTUS: To Marcius shall be honours, though indeed
BRUTUS: In aught he merit not.
SICINIUS: Let's hence, and hear
SICINIUS: How the dispatch is made, and in what fashion,
SICINIUS: More than his singularity, he goes
SICINIUS: Upon this present action.
BRUTUS: Lets along.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Corioli. The Senate-house.
NARRATOR: Enter TULLUS AUFIDIUS and certain Senators
First Senator: So, your opinion is, Aufidius,
First Senator: That they of Rome are entered in our counsels
First Senator: And know how we proceed.
AUFIDIUS: Is it not yours?
AUFIDIUS: What ever have been thought on in this state,
AUFIDIUS: That could be brought to bodily act ere Rome
AUFIDIUS: Had circumvention? 'Tis not four days gone
AUFIDIUS: Since I heard thence, these are the words: I think
AUFIDIUS: I have the letter here, yes, here it is.
NARRATOR: Reads
AUFIDIUS: 'They have press'd a power, but it is not known
AUFIDIUS: Whether for east or west: the dearth is great,
AUFIDIUS: The people mutinous, and it is rumour'd,
AUFIDIUS: Cominius, Marcius your old enemy,
AUFIDIUS: Who is of Rome worse hated than of you,
AUFIDIUS: And Titus Lartius, a most valiant Roman,
AUFIDIUS: These three lead on this preparation
AUFIDIUS: Whither 'tis bent: most likely 'tis for you:
AUFIDIUS: Consider of it.'
First Senator: Our army's in the field
First Senator: We never yet made doubt but Rome was ready
First Senator: To answer us.
AUFIDIUS: Nor did you think it folly
AUFIDIUS: To keep your great pretences veil'd till when
AUFIDIUS: They needs must show themselves, which
AUFIDIUS: in the hatching,
AUFIDIUS: It seem'd, appear'd to Rome. By the discovery.
AUFIDIUS: We shall be shorten'd in our aim, which was
AUFIDIUS: To take in many towns ere almost Rome
AUFIDIUS: Should know we were afoot.
Second Senator: Noble Aufidius,
Second Senator: Take your commission, hie you to your bands:
Second Senator: Let us alone to guard Corioli:
Second Senator: If they set down before 's, for the remove
Second Senator: Bring your army, but, I think, you'll find
Second Senator: They've not prepared for us.
AUFIDIUS: O, doubt not that,
AUFIDIUS: I speak from certainties. Nay, more,
AUFIDIUS: Some parcels of their power are forth already,
AUFIDIUS: And only hitherward. I leave your honours.
AUFIDIUS: If we and Caius Marcius chance to meet,
AUFIDIUS: 'Tis sworn between us we shall ever strike
AUFIDIUS: Till one can do no more.
All: The gods assist you!
AUFIDIUS: And keep your honours safe!
First Senator: Farewell.
Second Senator: Farewell.
All: Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Rome. A room in Marcius' house.
NARRATOR: Enter VOLUMNIA and VIRGILIA	they set them down on two low stools, and sew
VOLUMNIA: I pray you, daughter, sing, or express yourself in a
VOLUMNIA: more comfortable sort: if my son were my husband, I
VOLUMNIA: should freelier rejoice in that absence wherein he
VOLUMNIA: won honour than in the embracements of his bed where
VOLUMNIA: he would show most love. When yet he was but
VOLUMNIA: tender-bodied and the only son of my womb, when
VOLUMNIA: youth with comeliness plucked all gaze his way, when
VOLUMNIA: for a day of kings' entreaties a mother should not
VOLUMNIA: sell him an hour from her beholding, I, considering
VOLUMNIA: how honour would become such a person. that it was
VOLUMNIA: no better than picture-like to hang by the wall, if
VOLUMNIA: renown made it not stir, was pleased to let him seek
VOLUMNIA: danger where he was like to find fame. To a cruel
VOLUMNIA: war I sent him, from whence he returned, his brows
VOLUMNIA: bound with oak. I tell thee, daughter, I sprang not
VOLUMNIA: more in joy at first hearing he was a man-child
VOLUMNIA: than now in first seeing he had proved himself a
VOLUMNIA: man.
VIRGILIA: But had he died in the business, madam, how then?
VOLUMNIA: Then his good report should have been my son, I
VOLUMNIA: therein would have found issue. Hear me profess
VOLUMNIA: sincerely: had I a dozen sons, each in my love
VOLUMNIA: alike and none less dear than thine and my good
VOLUMNIA: Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their
VOLUMNIA: country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.
NARRATOR: Enter a Gentlewoman
Gentlewoman: Madam, the Lady Valeria is come to visit you.
VIRGILIA: Beseech you, give me leave to retire myself.
VOLUMNIA: Indeed, you shall not.
VOLUMNIA: Methinks I hear hither your husband's drum,
VOLUMNIA: See him pluck Aufidius down by the hair,
VOLUMNIA: As children from a bear, the Volsces shunning him:
VOLUMNIA: Methinks I see him stamp thus, and call thus:
VOLUMNIA: 'Come on, you cowards! you were got in fear,
VOLUMNIA: Though you were born in Rome:' his bloody brow
VOLUMNIA: With his mail'd hand then wiping, forth he goes,
VOLUMNIA: Like to a harvest-man that's task'd to mow
VOLUMNIA: Or all or lose his hire.
VIRGILIA: His bloody brow! O Jupiter, no blood!
VOLUMNIA: Away, you fool! it more becomes a man
VOLUMNIA: Than gilt his trophy: the breasts of Hecuba,
VOLUMNIA: When she did suckle Hector, look'd not lovelier
VOLUMNIA: Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood
VOLUMNIA: At Grecian sword, contemning. Tell Valeria,
VOLUMNIA: We are fit to bid her welcome.
NARRATOR: Exit Gentlewoman
VIRGILIA: Heavens bless my lord from fell Aufidius!
VOLUMNIA: He'll beat Aufidius 'head below his knee
VOLUMNIA: And tread upon his neck.
NARRATOR: Enter VALERIA, with an Usher and Gentlewoman
VALERIA: My ladies both, good day to you.
VOLUMNIA: Sweet madam.
VIRGILIA: I am glad to see your ladyship.
VALERIA: How do you both? you are manifest house-keepers.
VALERIA: What are you sewing here? A fine spot, in good
VALERIA: faith. How does your little son?
VIRGILIA: I thank your ladyship, well, good madam.
VOLUMNIA: He had rather see the swords, and hear a drum, than
VOLUMNIA: look upon his school-master.
VALERIA: O' my word, the father's son: I'll swear,'tis a
VALERIA: very pretty boy. O' my troth, I looked upon him o'
VALERIA: Wednesday half an hour together: has such a
VALERIA: confirmed countenance. I saw him run after a gilded
VALERIA: butterfly: and when he caught it, he let it go
VALERIA: again, and after it again, and over and over he
VALERIA: comes, and again, catched it again, or whether his
VALERIA: fall enraged him, or how 'twas, he did so set his
VALERIA: teeth and tear it, O, I warrant it, how he mammocked
VALERIA: it!
VOLUMNIA: One on 's father's moods.
VALERIA: Indeed, la, 'tis a noble child.
VIRGILIA: A crack, madam.
VALERIA: Come, lay aside your stitchery, I must have you play
VALERIA: the idle husewife with me this afternoon.
VIRGILIA: No, good madam, I will not out of doors.
VALERIA: Not out of doors!
VOLUMNIA: She shall, she shall.
VIRGILIA: Indeed, no, by your patience, I'll not over the
VIRGILIA: threshold till my lord return from the wars.
VALERIA: Fie, you confine yourself most unreasonably: come,
VALERIA: you must go visit the good lady that lies in.
VIRGILIA: I will wish her speedy strength, and visit her with
VIRGILIA: my prayers, but I cannot go thither.
VOLUMNIA: Why, I pray you?
VIRGILIA: 'Tis not to save labour, nor that I want love.
VALERIA: You would be another Penelope: yet, they say, all
VALERIA: the yarn she spun in Ulysses' absence did but fill
VALERIA: Ithaca full of moths. Come, I would your cambric
VALERIA: were sensible as your finger, that you might leave
VALERIA: pricking it for pity. Come, you shall go with us.
VIRGILIA: No, good madam, pardon me, indeed, I will not forth.
VALERIA: In truth, la, go with me, and I'll tell you
VALERIA: excellent news of your husband.
VIRGILIA: O, good madam, there can be none yet.
VALERIA: Verily, I do not jest with you, there came news from
VALERIA: him last night.
VIRGILIA: Indeed, madam?
VALERIA: In earnest, it's true, I heard a senator speak it.
VALERIA: Thus it is: the Volsces have an army forth, against
VALERIA: whom Cominius the general is gone, with one part of
VALERIA: our Roman power: your lord and Titus Lartius are set
VALERIA: down before their city Corioli, they nothing doubt
VALERIA: prevailing and to make it brief wars. This is true,
VALERIA: on mine honour, and so, I pray, go with us.
VIRGILIA: Give me excuse, good madam, I will obey you in every
VIRGILIA: thing hereafter.
VOLUMNIA: Let her alone, lady: as she is now, she will but
VOLUMNIA: disease our better mirth.
VALERIA: In troth, I think she would. Fare you well, then.
VALERIA: Come, good sweet lady. Prithee, Virgilia, turn thy
VALERIA: solemness out o' door. and go along with us.
VIRGILIA: No, at a word, madam, indeed, I must not. I wish
VIRGILIA: you much mirth.
VALERIA: Well, then, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Before Corioli.
NARRATOR: Enter, with drum and colours, MARCIUS, TITUS  LARTIUS, Captains and Soldiers. To them a Messenger
MARCIUS: Yonder comes news. A wager they have met.
LARTIUS: My horse to yours, no.
MARCIUS: 'Tis done.
LARTIUS: Agreed.
MARCIUS: Say, has our general met the enemy?
Messenger: They lie in view, but have not spoke as yet.
LARTIUS: So, the good horse is mine.
MARCIUS: I'll buy him of you.
LARTIUS: No, I'll nor sell nor give him: lend you him I will
LARTIUS: For half a hundred years. Summon the town.
MARCIUS: How far off lie these armies?
Messenger: Within this mile and half.
MARCIUS: Then shall we hear their 'larum, and they ours.
MARCIUS: Now, Mars, I prithee, make us quick in work,
MARCIUS: That we with smoking swords may march from hence,
MARCIUS: To help our fielded friends! Come, blow thy blast.
NARRATOR: They sound a parley. Enter two Senators with others on the walls
MARCIUS: Tutus Aufidius, is he within your walls?
First Senator: No, nor a man that fears you less than he,
First Senator: That's lesser than a little.
NARRATOR: Drums afar off
First Senator: Hark! our drums
First Senator: Are bringing forth our youth. We'll break our walls,
First Senator: Rather than they shall pound us up: our gates,
First Senator: Which yet seem shut, we, have but pinn'd with rushes,
First Senator: They'll open of themselves.
NARRATOR: Alarum afar off
First Senator: Hark you. far off!
First Senator: There is Aufidius, list, what work he makes
First Senator: Amongst your cloven army.
MARCIUS: O, they are at it!
LARTIUS: Their noise be our instruction. Ladders, ho!
NARRATOR: Enter the army of the Volsces
MARCIUS: They fear us not, but issue forth their city.
MARCIUS: Now put your shields before your hearts, and fight
MARCIUS: With hearts more proof than shields. Advance,
MARCIUS: brave Titus:
MARCIUS: They do disdain us much beyond our thoughts,
MARCIUS: Which makes me sweat with wrath. Come on, my fellows:
MARCIUS: He that retires I'll take him for a Volsce,
MARCIUS: And he shall feel mine edge.
NARRATOR: Alarum. The Romans are beat back to their trenches. Re-enter MARCIUS cursing
MARCIUS: All the contagion of the south light on you,
MARCIUS: You shames of Rome! you herd of--Boils and plagues
MARCIUS: Plaster you o'er, that you may be abhorr'd
MARCIUS: Further than seen and one infect another
MARCIUS: Against the wind a mile! You souls of geese,
MARCIUS: That bear the shapes of men, how have you run
MARCIUS: From slaves that apes would beat! Pluto and hell!
MARCIUS: All hurt behind, backs red, and faces pale
MARCIUS: With flight and agued fear! Mend and charge home,
MARCIUS: Or, by the fires of heaven, I'll leave the foe
MARCIUS: And make my wars on you: look to't: come on,
MARCIUS: If you'll stand fast, we'll beat them to their wives,
MARCIUS: As they us to our trenches followed.
NARRATOR: Another alarum. The Volsces fly, and MARCIUS follows them to the gates
MARCIUS: So, now the gates are ope: now prove good seconds:
MARCIUS: 'Tis for the followers fortune widens them,
MARCIUS: Not for the fliers: mark me, and do the like.
NARRATOR: Enters the gates
First Soldier: Fool-hardiness, not I.
Second Soldier: Nor I.
NARRATOR: MARCIUS is shut in
First Soldier: See, they have shut him in.
All: To the pot, I warrant him.
NARRATOR: Alarum continues
NARRATOR: Re-enter TITUS LARTIUS
LARTIUS: What is become of Marcius?
All: Slain, sir, doubtless.
First Soldier: Following the fliers at the very heels,
First Soldier: With them he enters, who, upon the sudden,
First Soldier: Clapp'd to their gates: he is himself alone,
First Soldier: To answer all the city.
LARTIUS: O noble fellow!
LARTIUS: Who sensibly outdares his senseless sword,
LARTIUS: And, when it bows, stands up. Thou art left, Marcius:
LARTIUS: A carbuncle entire, as big as thou art,
LARTIUS: Were not so rich a jewel. Thou wast a soldier
LARTIUS: Even to Cato's wish, not fierce and terrible
LARTIUS: Only in strokes, but, with thy grim looks and
LARTIUS: The thunder-like percussion of thy sounds,
LARTIUS: Thou madst thine enemies shake, as if the world
LARTIUS: Were feverous and did tremble.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARCIUS, bleeding, assaulted by the enemy
First Soldier: Look, sir.
LARTIUS: O,'tis Marcius!
LARTIUS: Let's fetch him off, or make remain alike.
NARRATOR: They fight, and all enter the city
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Corioli. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter certain Romans, with spoils
First Roman: This will I carry to Rome.
Second Roman: And I this.
Third Roman: A murrain on't! I took this for silver.
NARRATOR: Alarum continues still afar off
NARRATOR: Enter MARCIUS and TITUS LARTIUS with a trumpet
MARCIUS: See here these movers that do prize their hours
MARCIUS: At a crack'd drachm! Cushions, leaden spoons,
MARCIUS: Irons of a doit, doublets that hangmen would
MARCIUS: Bury with those that wore them, these base slaves,
MARCIUS: Ere yet the fight be done, pack up: down with them!
MARCIUS: And hark, what noise the general makes! To him!
MARCIUS: There is the man of my soul's hate, Aufidius,
MARCIUS: Piercing our Romans: then, valiant Titus, take
MARCIUS: Convenient numbers to make good the city,
MARCIUS: Whilst I, with those that have the spirit, will haste
MARCIUS: To help Cominius.
LARTIUS: Worthy sir, thou bleed'st,
LARTIUS: Thy exercise hath been too violent for
LARTIUS: A second course of fight.
MARCIUS: Sir, praise me not,
MARCIUS: My work hath yet not warm'd me: fare you well:
MARCIUS: The blood I drop is rather physical
MARCIUS: Than dangerous to me: to Aufidius thus
MARCIUS: I will appear, and fight.
LARTIUS: Now the fair goddess, Fortune,
LARTIUS: Fall deep in love with thee, and her great charms
LARTIUS: Misguide thy opposers' swords! Bold gentleman,
LARTIUS: Prosperity be thy page!
MARCIUS: Thy friend no less
MARCIUS: Than those she placeth highest! So, farewell.
LARTIUS: Thou worthiest Marcius!
NARRATOR: Exit MARCIUS
LARTIUS: Go, sound thy trumpet in the market-place,
LARTIUS: Call thither all the officers o' the town,
LARTIUS: Where they shall know our mind: away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Near the camp of Cominius.
NARRATOR: Enter COMINIUS, as it were in retire, with soldiers
COMINIUS: Breathe you, my friends: well fought,
COMINIUS: we are come off
COMINIUS: Like Romans, neither foolish in our stands,
COMINIUS: Nor cowardly in retire: believe me, sirs,
COMINIUS: We shall be charged again. Whiles we have struck,
COMINIUS: By interims and conveying gusts we have heard
COMINIUS: The charges of our friends. Ye Roman gods!
COMINIUS: Lead their successes as we wish our own,
COMINIUS: That both our powers, with smiling
COMINIUS: fronts encountering,
COMINIUS: May give you thankful sacrifice.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
COMINIUS: Thy news?
Messenger: The citizens of Corioli have issued,
Messenger: And given to Lartius and to Marcius battle:
Messenger: I saw our party to their trenches driven,
Messenger: And then I came away.
COMINIUS: Though thou speak'st truth,
COMINIUS: Methinks thou speak'st not well.
COMINIUS: How long is't since?
Messenger: Above an hour, my lord.
COMINIUS: 'Tis not a mile, briefly we heard their drums:
COMINIUS: How couldst thou in a mile confound an hour,
COMINIUS: And bring thy news so late?
Messenger: Spies of the Volsces
Messenger: Held me in chase, that I was forced to wheel
Messenger: Three or four miles about, else had I, sir,
Messenger: Half an hour since brought my report.
COMINIUS: Who's yonder,
COMINIUS: That does appear as he were flay'd? O gods
COMINIUS: He has the stamp of Marcius, and I have
COMINIUS: Before-time seen him thus.
MARCIUS: [Within]                 Come I too late?
COMINIUS: The shepherd knows not thunder from a tabour
COMINIUS: More than I know the sound of Marcius' tongue
COMINIUS: From every meaner man.
NARRATOR: Enter MARCIUS
MARCIUS: Come I too late?
COMINIUS: Ay, if you come not in the blood of others,
COMINIUS: But mantled in your own.
MARCIUS: O, let me clip ye
MARCIUS: In arms as sound as when I woo'd, in heart
MARCIUS: As merry as when our nuptial day was done,
MARCIUS: And tapers burn'd to bedward!
COMINIUS: Flower of warriors,
COMINIUS: How is it with Titus Lartius?
MARCIUS: As with a man busied about decrees:
MARCIUS: Condemning some to death, and some to exile,
MARCIUS: Ransoming him, or pitying, threatening the other,
MARCIUS: Holding Corioli in the name of Rome,
MARCIUS: Even like a fawning greyhound in the leash,
MARCIUS: To let him slip at will.
COMINIUS: Where is that slave
COMINIUS: Which told me they had beat you to your trenches?
COMINIUS: Where is he? call him hither.
MARCIUS: Let him alone,
MARCIUS: He did inform the truth: but for our gentlemen,
MARCIUS: The common file--a plague! tribunes for them!--
MARCIUS: The mouse ne'er shunn'd the cat as they did budge
MARCIUS: From rascals worse than they.
COMINIUS: But how prevail'd you?
MARCIUS: Will the time serve to tell? I do not think.
MARCIUS: Where is the enemy? are you lords o' the field?
MARCIUS: If not, why cease you till you are so?
COMINIUS: Marcius,
COMINIUS: We have at disadvantage fought and did
COMINIUS: Retire to win our purpose.
MARCIUS: How lies their battle? know you on which side
MARCIUS: They have placed their men of trust?
COMINIUS: As I guess, Marcius,
COMINIUS: Their bands i' the vaward are the Antiates,
COMINIUS: Of their best trust, o'er them Aufidius,
COMINIUS: Their very heart of hope.
MARCIUS: I do beseech you,
MARCIUS: By all the battles wherein we have fought,
MARCIUS: By the blood we have shed together, by the vows
MARCIUS: We have made to endure friends, that you directly
MARCIUS: Set me against Aufidius and his Antiates,
MARCIUS: And that you not delay the present, but,
MARCIUS: Filling the air with swords advanced and darts,
MARCIUS: We prove this very hour.
COMINIUS: Though I could wish
COMINIUS: You were conducted to a gentle bath
COMINIUS: And balms applied to, you, yet dare I never
COMINIUS: Deny your asking: take your choice of those
COMINIUS: That best can aid your action.
MARCIUS: Those are they
MARCIUS: That most are willing. If any such be here--
MARCIUS: As it were sin to doubt--that love this painting
MARCIUS: Wherein you see me smear'd, if any fear
MARCIUS: Lesser his person than an ill report,
MARCIUS: If any think brave death outweighs bad life
MARCIUS: And that his country's dearer than himself,
MARCIUS: Let him alone, or so many so minded,
MARCIUS: Wave thus, to express his disposition,
MARCIUS: And follow Marcius.
NARRATOR: They all shout and wave their swords, take him up in their arms, and cast up their caps
MARCIUS: O, me alone! make you a sword of me?
MARCIUS: If these shows be not outward, which of you
MARCIUS: But is four Volsces? none of you but is
MARCIUS: Able to bear against the great Aufidius
MARCIUS: A shield as hard as his. A certain number,
MARCIUS: Though thanks to all, must I select
MARCIUS: from all: the rest
MARCIUS: Shall bear the business in some other fight,
MARCIUS: As cause will be obey'd. Please you to march,
MARCIUS: And four shall quickly draw out my command,
MARCIUS: Which men are best inclined.
COMINIUS: March on, my fellows:
COMINIUS: Make good this ostentation, and you shall
COMINIUS: Divide in all with us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. The gates of Corioli.
NARRATOR: TITUS LARTIUS, having set a guard upon  Corioli, going with drum and trumpet toward  COMINIUS and CAIUS MARCIUS, enters with Lieutenant, other Soldiers, and a Scout
LARTIUS: So, let the ports be guarded: keep your duties,
LARTIUS: As I have set them down. If I do send, dispatch
LARTIUS: Those centuries to our aid: the rest will serve
LARTIUS: For a short holding: if we lose the field,
LARTIUS: We cannot keep the town.
Lieutenant: Fear not our care, sir.
LARTIUS: Hence, and shut your gates upon's.
LARTIUS: Our guider, come, to the Roman camp conduct us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. A field of battle.
NARRATOR: Alarum as in battle. Enter, from opposite sides, MARCIUS and AUFIDIUS
MARCIUS: I'll fight with none but thee, for I do hate thee
MARCIUS: Worse than a promise-breaker.
AUFIDIUS: We hate alike:
AUFIDIUS: Not Afric owns a serpent I abhor
AUFIDIUS: More than thy fame and envy. Fix thy foot.
MARCIUS: Let the first budger die the other's slave,
MARCIUS: And the gods doom him after!
AUFIDIUS: If I fly, Marcius,
AUFIDIUS: Holloa me like a hare.
MARCIUS: Within these three hours, Tullus,
MARCIUS: Alone I fought in your Corioli walls,
MARCIUS: And made what work I pleased: 'tis not my blood
MARCIUS: Wherein thou seest me mask'd, for thy revenge
MARCIUS: Wrench up thy power to the highest.
AUFIDIUS: Wert thou the Hector
AUFIDIUS: That was the whip of your bragg'd progeny,
AUFIDIUS: Thou shouldst not scape me here.
NARRATOR: They fight, and certain Volsces come to the aid of  AUFIDIUS. MARCIUS fights till they be driven in breathless
AUFIDIUS: Officious, and not valiant, you have shamed me
AUFIDIUS: In your condemned seconds.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. The Roman camp.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Alarum. A retreat is sounded. Flourish.  Enter, from one side, COMINIUS with the Romans, from the other side, MARCIUS, with his arm in a scarf
COMINIUS: If I should tell thee o'er this thy day's work,
COMINIUS: Thou'ldst not believe thy deeds: but I'll report it
COMINIUS: Where senators shall mingle tears with smiles,
COMINIUS: Where great patricians shall attend and shrug,
COMINIUS: I' the end admire, where ladies shall be frighted,
COMINIUS: And, gladly quaked, hear more, where the
COMINIUS: dull tribunes,
COMINIUS: That, with the fusty plebeians, hate thine honours,
COMINIUS: Shall say against their hearts 'We thank the gods
COMINIUS: Our Rome hath such a soldier.'
COMINIUS: Yet camest thou to a morsel of this feast,
COMINIUS: Having fully dined before.
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS LARTIUS, with his power, from the pursuit
LARTIUS: O general,
LARTIUS: Here is the steed, we the caparison:
LARTIUS: Hadst thou beheld--
MARCIUS: Pray now, no more: my mother,
MARCIUS: Who has a charter to extol her blood,
MARCIUS: When she does praise me grieves me. I have done
MARCIUS: As you have done, that's what I can, induced
MARCIUS: As you have been, that's for my country:
MARCIUS: He that has but effected his good will
MARCIUS: Hath overta'en mine act.
COMINIUS: You shall not be
COMINIUS: The grave of your deserving, Rome must know
COMINIUS: The value of her own: 'twere a concealment
COMINIUS: Worse than a theft, no less than a traducement,
COMINIUS: To hide your doings, and to silence that,
COMINIUS: Which, to the spire and top of praises vouch'd,
COMINIUS: Would seem but modest: therefore, I beseech you
COMINIUS: In sign of what you are, not to reward
COMINIUS: What you have done--before our army hear me.
MARCIUS: I have some wounds upon me, and they smart
MARCIUS: To hear themselves remember'd.
COMINIUS: Should they not,
COMINIUS: Well might they fester 'gainst ingratitude,
COMINIUS: And tent themselves with death. Of all the horses,
COMINIUS: Whereof we have ta'en good and good store, of all
COMINIUS: The treasure in this field achieved and city,
COMINIUS: We render you the tenth, to be ta'en forth,
COMINIUS: Before the common distribution, at
COMINIUS: Your only choice.
MARCIUS: I thank you, general,
MARCIUS: But cannot make my heart consent to take
MARCIUS: A bribe to pay my sword: I do refuse it,
MARCIUS: And stand upon my common part with those
MARCIUS: That have beheld the doing.
MARCIUS: A long flourish. They all cry 'Marcius! Marcius!'  cast up their caps and lances: COMINIUS and LARTIUS stand bare
MARCIUS: May these same instruments, which you profane,
MARCIUS: Never sound more! when drums and trumpets shall
MARCIUS: I' the field prove flatterers, let courts and cities be
MARCIUS: Made all of false-faced soothing!
MARCIUS: When steel grows soft as the parasite's silk,
MARCIUS: Let him be made a coverture for the wars!
MARCIUS: No more, I say! For that I have not wash'd
MARCIUS: My nose that bled, or foil'd some debile wretch.--
MARCIUS: Which, without note, here's many else have done,--
MARCIUS: You shout me forth
MARCIUS: In acclamations hyperbolical,
MARCIUS: As if I loved my little should be dieted
MARCIUS: In praises sauced with lies.
COMINIUS: Too modest are you,
COMINIUS: More cruel to your good report than grateful
COMINIUS: To us that give you truly: by your patience,
COMINIUS: If 'gainst yourself you be incensed, we'll put you,
COMINIUS: Like one that means his proper harm, in manacles,
COMINIUS: Then reason safely with you. Therefore, be it known,
COMINIUS: As to us, to all the world, that Caius Marcius
COMINIUS: Wears this war's garland: in token of the which,
COMINIUS: My noble steed, known to the camp, I give him,
COMINIUS: With all his trim belonging, and from this time,
COMINIUS: For what he did before Corioli, call him,
COMINIUS: With all the applause and clamour of the host,
COMINIUS: CAIUS MARCIUS CORIOLANUS! Bear
COMINIUS: The addition nobly ever!
NARRATOR: Flourish. Trumpets sound, and drums
All: Caius Marcius Coriolanus!
CORIOLANUS: I will go wash,
CORIOLANUS: And when my face is fair, you shall perceive
CORIOLANUS: Whether I blush or no: howbeit, I thank you.
CORIOLANUS: I mean to stride your steed, and at all times
CORIOLANUS: To undercrest your good addition
CORIOLANUS: To the fairness of my power.
COMINIUS: So, to our tent,
COMINIUS: Where, ere we do repose us, we will write
COMINIUS: To Rome of our success. You, Titus Lartius,
COMINIUS: Must to Corioli back: send us to Rome
COMINIUS: The best, with whom we may articulate,
COMINIUS: For their own good and ours.
LARTIUS: I shall, my lord.
CORIOLANUS: The gods begin to mock me. I, that now
CORIOLANUS: Refused most princely gifts, am bound to beg
CORIOLANUS: Of my lord general.
COMINIUS: Take't, 'tis yours. What is't?
CORIOLANUS: I sometime lay here in Corioli
CORIOLANUS: At a poor man's house, he used me kindly:
CORIOLANUS: He cried to me, I saw him prisoner,
CORIOLANUS: But then Aufidius was with in my view,
CORIOLANUS: And wrath o'erwhelm'd my pity: I request you
CORIOLANUS: To give my poor host freedom.
COMINIUS: O, well begg'd!
COMINIUS: Were he the butcher of my son, he should
COMINIUS: Be free as is the wind. Deliver him, Titus.
LARTIUS: Marcius, his name?
CORIOLANUS: By Jupiter! forgot.
CORIOLANUS: I am weary, yea, my memory is tired.
CORIOLANUS: Have we no wine here?
COMINIUS: Go we to our tent:
COMINIUS: The blood upon your visage dries, 'tis time
COMINIUS: It should be look'd to: come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE X. The camp of the Volsces.
NARRATOR: A flourish. Cornets. Enter TULLUS AUFIDIUS, bloody, with two or three Soldiers
AUFIDIUS: The town is ta'en!
First Soldier: 'Twill be deliver'd back on good condition.
AUFIDIUS: Condition!
AUFIDIUS: I would I were a Roman, for I cannot,
AUFIDIUS: Being a Volsce, be that I am. Condition!
AUFIDIUS: What good condition can a treaty find
AUFIDIUS: I' the part that is at mercy? Five times, Marcius,
AUFIDIUS: I have fought with thee: so often hast thou beat me,
AUFIDIUS: And wouldst do so, I think, should we encounter
AUFIDIUS: As often as we eat. By the elements,
AUFIDIUS: If e'er again I meet him beard to beard,
AUFIDIUS: He's mine, or I am his: mine emulation
AUFIDIUS: Hath not that honour in't it had, for where
AUFIDIUS: I thought to crush him in an equal force,
AUFIDIUS: True sword to sword, I'll potch at him some way
AUFIDIUS: Or wrath or craft may get him.
First Soldier: He's the devil.
AUFIDIUS: Bolder, though not so subtle. My valour's poison'd
AUFIDIUS: With only suffering stain by him, for him
AUFIDIUS: Shall fly out of itself: nor sleep nor sanctuary,
AUFIDIUS: Being naked, sick, nor fane nor Capitol,
AUFIDIUS: The prayers of priests nor times of sacrifice,
AUFIDIUS: Embarquements all of fury, shall lift up
AUFIDIUS: Their rotten privilege and custom 'gainst
AUFIDIUS: My hate to Marcius: where I find him, were it
AUFIDIUS: At home, upon my brother's guard, even there,
AUFIDIUS: Against the hospitable canon, would I
AUFIDIUS: Wash my fierce hand in's heart. Go you to the city,
AUFIDIUS: Learn how 'tis held, and what they are that must
AUFIDIUS: Be hostages for Rome.
First Soldier: Will not you go?
AUFIDIUS: I am attended at the cypress grove: I pray you--
AUFIDIUS: 'Tis south the city mills--bring me word thither
AUFIDIUS: How the world goes, that to the pace of it
AUFIDIUS: I may spur on my journey.
First Soldier: I shall, sir.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter MENENIUS with the two Tribunes of the people, SICINIUS and BRUTUS.
MENENIUS: The augurer tells me we shall have news to-night.
BRUTUS: Good or bad?
MENENIUS: Not according to the prayer of the people, for they
MENENIUS: love not Marcius.
SICINIUS: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
MENENIUS: Pray you, who does the wolf love?
SICINIUS: The lamb.
MENENIUS: Ay, to devour him, as the hungry plebeians would the
MENENIUS: noble Marcius.
BRUTUS: He's a lamb indeed, that baes like a bear.
MENENIUS: He's a bear indeed, that lives like a lamb. You two
MENENIUS: are old men: tell me one thing that I shall ask you.
Both: Well, sir.
MENENIUS: In what enormity is Marcius poor in, that you two
MENENIUS: have not in abundance?
BRUTUS: He's poor in no one fault, but stored with all.
SICINIUS: Especially in pride.
BRUTUS: And topping all others in boasting.
MENENIUS: This is strange now: do you two know how you are
MENENIUS: censured here in the city, I mean of us o' the
MENENIUS: right-hand file? do you?
Both: Why, how are we censured?
MENENIUS: Because you talk of pride now,--will you not be angry?
Both: Well, well, sir, well.
MENENIUS: Why, 'tis no great matter, for a very little thief of
MENENIUS: occasion will rob you of a great deal of patience:
MENENIUS: give your dispositions the reins, and be angry at
MENENIUS: your pleasures, at the least if you take it as a
MENENIUS: pleasure to you in being so. You blame Marcius for
MENENIUS: being proud?
BRUTUS: We do it not alone, sir.
MENENIUS: I know you can do very little alone, for your helps
MENENIUS: are many, or else your actions would grow wondrous
MENENIUS: single: your abilities are too infant-like for
MENENIUS: doing much alone. You talk of pride: O that you
MENENIUS: could turn your eyes toward the napes of your necks,
MENENIUS: and make but an interior survey of your good selves!
MENENIUS: O that you could!
BRUTUS: What then, sir?
MENENIUS: Why, then you should discover a brace of unmeriting,
MENENIUS: proud, violent, testy magistrates, alias fools, as
MENENIUS: any in Rome.
SICINIUS: Menenius, you are known well enough too.
MENENIUS: I am known to be a humorous patrician, and one that
MENENIUS: loves a cup of hot wine with not a drop of allaying
MENENIUS: Tiber in't, said to be something imperfect in
MENENIUS: favouring the first complaint, hasty and tinder-like
MENENIUS: upon too trivial motion, one that converses more
MENENIUS: with the buttock of the night than with the forehead
MENENIUS: of the morning: what I think I utter, and spend my
MENENIUS: malice in my breath. Meeting two such wealsmen as
MENENIUS: you are--I cannot call you Lycurguses--if the drink
MENENIUS: you give me touch my palate adversely, I make a
MENENIUS: crooked face at it. I can't say your worships have
MENENIUS: delivered the matter well, when I find the ass in
MENENIUS: compound with the major part of your syllables: and
MENENIUS: though I must be content to bear with those that say
MENENIUS: you are reverend grave men, yet they lie deadly that
MENENIUS: tell you you have good faces. If you see this in
MENENIUS: the map of my microcosm, follows it that I am known
MENENIUS: well enough too? what barm can your bisson
MENENIUS: conspectuities glean out of this character, if I be
MENENIUS: known well enough too?
BRUTUS: Come, sir, come, we know you well enough.
MENENIUS: You know neither me, yourselves nor any thing. You
MENENIUS: are ambitious for poor knaves' caps and legs: you
MENENIUS: wear out a good wholesome forenoon in hearing a
MENENIUS: cause between an orange wife and a fosset-seller,
MENENIUS: and then rejourn the controversy of three pence to a
MENENIUS: second day of audience. When you are hearing a
MENENIUS: matter between party and party, if you chance to be
MENENIUS: pinched with the colic, you make faces like
MENENIUS: mummers, set up the bloody flag against all
MENENIUS: patience, and, in roaring for a chamber-pot,
MENENIUS: dismiss the controversy bleeding the more entangled
MENENIUS: by your hearing: all the peace you make in their
MENENIUS: cause is, calling both the parties knaves. You are
MENENIUS: a pair of strange ones.
BRUTUS: Come, come, you are well understood to be a
BRUTUS: perfecter giber for the table than a necessary
BRUTUS: bencher in the Capitol.
MENENIUS: Our very priests must become mockers, if they shall
MENENIUS: encounter such ridiculous subjects as you are. When
MENENIUS: you speak best unto the purpose, it is not worth the
MENENIUS: wagging of your beards, and your beards deserve not
MENENIUS: so honourable a grave as to stuff a botcher's
MENENIUS: cushion, or to be entombed in an ass's pack-
MENENIUS: saddle. Yet you must be saying, Marcius is proud,
MENENIUS: who in a cheap estimation, is worth predecessors
MENENIUS: since Deucalion, though peradventure some of the
MENENIUS: best of 'em were hereditary hangmen. God-den to
MENENIUS: your worships: more of your conversation would
MENENIUS: infect my brain, being the herdsmen of the beastly
MENENIUS: plebeians: I will be bold to take my leave of you.
NARRATOR: BRUTUS and SICINIUS go aside
NARRATOR: Enter VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA, and VALERIA
MENENIUS: How now, my as fair as noble ladies,--and the moon,
MENENIUS: were she earthly, no nobler,--whither do you follow
MENENIUS: your eyes so fast?
VOLUMNIA: Honourable Menenius, my boy Marcius approaches, for
VOLUMNIA: the love of Juno, let's go.
MENENIUS: Ha! Marcius coming home!
VOLUMNIA: Ay, worthy Menenius, and with most prosperous
VOLUMNIA: approbation.
MENENIUS: Take my cap, Jupiter, and I thank thee. Hoo!
MENENIUS: Marcius coming home!
VIRGILIA: Nay,'tis true.
VOLUMNIA: Look, here's a letter from him: the state hath
VOLUMNIA: another, his wife another, and, I think, there's one
VOLUMNIA: at home for you.
MENENIUS: I will make my very house reel tonight: a letter for
MENENIUS: me!
VIRGILIA: Yes, certain, there's a letter for you, I saw't.
MENENIUS: A letter for me! it gives me an estate of seven
MENENIUS: years' health, in which time I will make a lip at
MENENIUS: the physician: the most sovereign prescription in
MENENIUS: Galen is but empiricutic, and, to this preservative,
MENENIUS: of no better report than a horse-drench. Is he
MENENIUS: not wounded? he was wont to come home wounded.
VIRGILIA: O, no, no, no.
VOLUMNIA: O, he is wounded, I thank the gods for't.
MENENIUS: So do I too, if it be not too much: brings a'
MENENIUS: victory in his pocket? the wounds become him.
VOLUMNIA: On's brows: Menenius, he comes the third time home
VOLUMNIA: with the oaken garland.
MENENIUS: Has he disciplined Aufidius soundly?
VOLUMNIA: Titus Lartius writes, they fought together, but
VOLUMNIA: Aufidius got off.
MENENIUS: And 'twas time for him too, I'll warrant him that:
MENENIUS: an he had stayed by him, I would not have been so
MENENIUS: fidiused for all the chests in Corioli, and the gold
MENENIUS: that's in them. Is the senate possessed of this?
VOLUMNIA: Good ladies, let's go. Yes, yes, yes, the senate
VOLUMNIA: has letters from the general, wherein he gives my
VOLUMNIA: son the whole name of the war: he hath in this
VOLUMNIA: action outdone his former deeds doubly
VALERIA: In troth, there's wondrous things spoke of him.
MENENIUS: Wondrous! ay, I warrant you, and not without his
MENENIUS: true purchasing.
VIRGILIA: The gods grant them true!
VOLUMNIA: True! pow, wow.
MENENIUS: True! I'll be sworn they are true.
MENENIUS: Where is he wounded?
NARRATOR: To the Tribunes
MENENIUS: God save your good worships! Marcius is coming
MENENIUS: home: he has more cause to be proud. Where is he wounded?
VOLUMNIA: I' the shoulder and i' the left arm there will be
VOLUMNIA: large cicatrices to show the people, when he shall
VOLUMNIA: stand for his place. He received in the repulse of
VOLUMNIA: Tarquin seven hurts i' the body.
MENENIUS: One i' the neck, and two i' the thigh,--there's
MENENIUS: nine that I know.
VOLUMNIA: He had, before this last expedition, twenty-five
VOLUMNIA: wounds upon him.
MENENIUS: Now it's twenty-seven: every gash was an enemy's grave.
NARRATOR: A shout and flourish
MENENIUS: Hark! the trumpets.
VOLUMNIA: These are the ushers of Marcius: before him he
VOLUMNIA: carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears:
VOLUMNIA: Death, that dark spirit, in 's nervy arm doth lie,
VOLUMNIA: Which, being advanced, declines, and then men die.
VOLUMNIA: A sennet. Trumpets sound. Enter COMINIUS the  general, and TITUS LARTIUS, between them, CORIOLANUS,  crowned with an oaken garland, with Captains and Soldiers, and a Herald
Herald: Know, Rome, that all alone Marcius did fight
Herald: Within Corioli gates: where he hath won,
Herald: With fame, a name to Caius Marcius, these
Herald: In honour follows Coriolanus.
Herald: Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
NARRATOR: Flourish
All: Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
CORIOLANUS: No more of this, it does offend my heart:
CORIOLANUS: Pray now, no more.
COMINIUS: Look, sir, your mother!
CORIOLANUS: O,
CORIOLANUS: You have, I know, petition'd all the gods
CORIOLANUS: For my prosperity!
NARRATOR: Kneels
VOLUMNIA: Nay, my good soldier, up,
VOLUMNIA: My gentle Marcius, worthy Caius, and
VOLUMNIA: By deed-achieving honour newly named,--
VOLUMNIA: What is it?--Coriolanus must I call thee?--
VOLUMNIA: But O, thy wife!
CORIOLANUS: My gracious silence, hail!
CORIOLANUS: Wouldst thou have laugh'd had I come coffin'd home,
CORIOLANUS: That weep'st to see me triumph? Ay, my dear,
CORIOLANUS: Such eyes the widows in Corioli wear,
CORIOLANUS: And mothers that lack sons.
MENENIUS: Now, the gods crown thee!
CORIOLANUS: And live you yet?
NARRATOR: To VALERIA
CORIOLANUS: O my sweet lady, pardon.
VOLUMNIA: I know not where to turn: O, welcome home:
VOLUMNIA: And welcome, general: and ye're welcome all.
MENENIUS: A hundred thousand welcomes. I could weep
MENENIUS: And I could laugh, I am light and heavy. Welcome.
MENENIUS: A curse begin at very root on's heart,
MENENIUS: That is not glad to see thee! You are three
MENENIUS: That Rome should dote on: yet, by the faith of men,
MENENIUS: We have some old crab-trees here
MENENIUS: at home that will not
MENENIUS: Be grafted to your relish. Yet welcome, warriors:
MENENIUS: We call a nettle but a nettle and
MENENIUS: The faults of fools but folly.
COMINIUS: Ever right.
CORIOLANUS: Menenius ever, ever.
Herald: Give way there, and go on!
CORIOLANUS: [To VOLUMNIA and VIRGILIA]  Your hand, and yours:
CORIOLANUS: Ere in our own house I do shade my head,
CORIOLANUS: The good patricians must be visited,
CORIOLANUS: From whom I have received not only greetings,
CORIOLANUS: But with them change of honours.
VOLUMNIA: I have lived
VOLUMNIA: To see inherited my very wishes
VOLUMNIA: And the buildings of my fancy: only
VOLUMNIA: There's one thing wanting, which I doubt not but
VOLUMNIA: Our Rome will cast upon thee.
CORIOLANUS: Know, good mother,
CORIOLANUS: I had rather be their servant in my way,
CORIOLANUS: Than sway with them in theirs.
COMINIUS: On, to the Capitol!
NARRATOR: Flourish. Cornets. Exeunt in state, as before. BRUTUS and SICINIUS come forward
BRUTUS: All tongues speak of him, and the bleared sights
BRUTUS: Are spectacled to see him: your prattling nurse
BRUTUS: Into a rapture lets her baby cry
BRUTUS: While she chats him: the kitchen malkin pins
BRUTUS: Her richest lockram 'bout her reechy neck,
BRUTUS: Clambering the walls to eye him: stalls, bulks, windows,
BRUTUS: Are smother'd up, leads fill'd, and ridges horsed
BRUTUS: With variable complexions, all agreeing
BRUTUS: In earnestness to see him: seld-shown flamens
BRUTUS: Do press among the popular throngs and puff
BRUTUS: To win a vulgar station: or veil'd dames
BRUTUS: Commit the war of white and damask in
BRUTUS: Their nicely-gawded cheeks to the wanton spoil
BRUTUS: Of Phoebus' burning kisses: such a pother
BRUTUS: As if that whatsoever god who leads him
BRUTUS: Were slily crept into his human powers
BRUTUS: And gave him graceful posture.
SICINIUS: On the sudden,
SICINIUS: I warrant him consul.
BRUTUS: Then our office may,
BRUTUS: During his power, go sleep.
SICINIUS: He cannot temperately transport his honours
SICINIUS: From where he should begin and end, but will
SICINIUS: Lose those he hath won.
BRUTUS: In that there's comfort.
SICINIUS: Doubt not
SICINIUS: The commoners, for whom we stand, but they
SICINIUS: Upon their ancient malice will forget
SICINIUS: With the least cause these his new honours, which
SICINIUS: That he will give them make I as little question
SICINIUS: As he is proud to do't.
BRUTUS: I heard him swear,
BRUTUS: Were he to stand for consul, never would he
BRUTUS: Appear i' the market-place nor on him put
BRUTUS: The napless vesture of humility,
BRUTUS: Nor showing, as the manner is, his wounds
BRUTUS: To the people, beg their stinking breaths.
SICINIUS: 'Tis right.
BRUTUS: It was his word: O, he would miss it rather
BRUTUS: Than carry it but by the suit of the gentry to him,
BRUTUS: And the desire of the nobles.
SICINIUS: I wish no better
SICINIUS: Than have him hold that purpose and to put it
SICINIUS: In execution.
BRUTUS: 'Tis most like he will.
SICINIUS: It shall be to him then as our good wills,
SICINIUS: A sure destruction.
BRUTUS: So it must fall out
BRUTUS: To him or our authorities. For an end,
BRUTUS: We must suggest the people in what hatred
BRUTUS: He still hath held them, that to's power he would
BRUTUS: Have made them mules, silenced their pleaders and
BRUTUS: Dispropertied their freedoms, holding them,
BRUTUS: In human action and capacity,
BRUTUS: Of no more soul nor fitness for the world
BRUTUS: Than camels in the war, who have their provand
BRUTUS: Only for bearing burdens, and sore blows
BRUTUS: For sinking under them.
SICINIUS: This, as you say, suggested
SICINIUS: At some time when his soaring insolence
SICINIUS: Shall touch the people--which time shall not want,
SICINIUS: If he be put upon 't, and that's as easy
SICINIUS: As to set dogs on sheep--will be his fire
SICINIUS: To kindle their dry stubble, and their blaze
SICINIUS: Shall darken him for ever.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
BRUTUS: What's the matter?
Messenger: You are sent for to the Capitol. 'Tis thought
Messenger: That Marcius shall be consul:
Messenger: I have seen the dumb men throng to see him and
Messenger: The blind to bear him speak: matrons flung gloves,
Messenger: Ladies and maids their scarfs and handkerchers,
Messenger: Upon him as he pass'd: the nobles bended,
Messenger: As to Jove's statue, and the commons made
Messenger: A shower and thunder with their caps and shouts:
Messenger: I never saw the like.
BRUTUS: Let's to the Capitol,
BRUTUS: And carry with us ears and eyes for the time,
BRUTUS: But hearts for the event.
SICINIUS: Have with you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. The Capitol.
NARRATOR: Enter two Officers, to lay cushions
First Officer: Come, come, they are almost here. How many stand
First Officer: for consulships?
Second Officer: Three, they say: but 'tis thought of every one
Second Officer: Coriolanus will carry it.
First Officer: That's a brave fellow, but he's vengeance proud, and
First Officer: loves not the common people.
Second Officer: Faith, there had been many great men that have
Second Officer: flattered the people, who ne'er loved them, and there
Second Officer: be many that they have loved, they know not
Second Officer: wherefore: so that, if they love they know not why,
Second Officer: they hate upon no better a ground: therefore, for
Second Officer: Coriolanus neither to care whether they love or hate
Second Officer: him manifests the true knowledge he has in their
Second Officer: disposition, and out of his noble carelessness lets
Second Officer: them plainly see't.
First Officer: If he did not care whether he had their love or no,
First Officer: he waved indifferently 'twixt doing them neither
First Officer: good nor harm: but he seeks their hate with greater
First Officer: devotion than can render it him, and leaves
First Officer: nothing undone that may fully discover him their
First Officer: opposite. Now, to seem to affect the malice and
First Officer: displeasure of the people is as bad as that which he
First Officer: dislikes, to flatter them for their love.
Second Officer: He hath deserved worthily of his country: and his
Second Officer: ascent is not by such easy degrees as those who,
Second Officer: having been supple and courteous to the people,
Second Officer: bonneted, without any further deed to have them at
Second Officer: an into their estimation and report: but he hath so
Second Officer: planted his honours in their eyes, and his actions
Second Officer: in their hearts, that for their tongues to be
Second Officer: silent, and not confess so much, were a kind of
Second Officer: ingrateful injury, to report otherwise, were a
Second Officer: malice, that, giving itself the lie, would pluck
Second Officer: reproof and rebuke from every ear that heard it.
First Officer: No more of him, he is a worthy man: make way, they
First Officer: are coming.
First Officer: A sennet. Enter, with actors before them, COMINIUS  the consul, MENENIUS, CORIOLANUS, Senators,  SICINIUS and BRUTUS. The Senators take their  places, the Tribunes take their Places by themselves. CORIOLANUS stands
MENENIUS: Having determined of the Volsces and
MENENIUS: To send for Titus Lartius, it remains,
MENENIUS: As the main point of this our after-meeting,
MENENIUS: To gratify his noble service that
MENENIUS: Hath thus stood for his country: therefore,
MENENIUS: please you,
MENENIUS: Most reverend and grave elders, to desire
MENENIUS: The present consul, and last general
MENENIUS: In our well-found successes, to report
MENENIUS: A little of that worthy work perform'd
MENENIUS: By Caius Marcius Coriolanus, whom
MENENIUS: We met here both to thank and to remember
MENENIUS: With honours like himself.
First Senator: Speak, good Cominius:
First Senator: Leave nothing out for length, and make us think
First Senator: Rather our state's defective for requital
First Senator: Than we to stretch it out.
NARRATOR: To the Tribunes
First Senator: Masters o' the people,
First Senator: We do request your kindest ears, and after,
First Senator: Your loving motion toward the common body,
First Senator: To yield what passes here.
SICINIUS: We are convented
SICINIUS: Upon a pleasing treaty, and have hearts
SICINIUS: Inclinable to honour and advance
SICINIUS: The theme of our assembly.
BRUTUS: Which the rather
BRUTUS: We shall be blest to do, if he remember
BRUTUS: A kinder value of the people than
BRUTUS: He hath hereto prized them at.
MENENIUS: That's off, that's off,
MENENIUS: I would you rather had been silent. Please you
MENENIUS: To hear Cominius speak?
BRUTUS: Most willingly,
BRUTUS: But yet my caution was more pertinent
BRUTUS: Than the rebuke you give it.
MENENIUS: He loves your people
MENENIUS: But tie him not to be their bedfellow.
MENENIUS: Worthy Cominius, speak.
NARRATOR: CORIOLANUS offers to go away
MENENIUS: Nay, keep your place.
First Senator: Sit, Coriolanus, never shame to hear
First Senator: What you have nobly done.
CORIOLANUS: Your horror's pardon:
CORIOLANUS: I had rather have my wounds to heal again
CORIOLANUS: Than hear say how I got them.
BRUTUS: Sir, I hope
BRUTUS: My words disbench'd you not.
CORIOLANUS: No, sir: yet oft,
CORIOLANUS: When blows have made me stay, I fled from words.
CORIOLANUS: You soothed not, therefore hurt not: but
CORIOLANUS: your people,
CORIOLANUS: I love them as they weigh.
MENENIUS: Pray now, sit down.
CORIOLANUS: I had rather have one scratch my head i' the sun
CORIOLANUS: When the alarum were struck than idly sit
CORIOLANUS: To hear my nothings monster'd.
NARRATOR: Exit
MENENIUS: Masters of the people,
MENENIUS: Your multiplying spawn how can he flatter--
MENENIUS: That's thousand to one good one--when you now see
MENENIUS: He had rather venture all his limbs for honour
MENENIUS: Than one on's ears to hear it? Proceed, Cominius.
COMINIUS: I shall lack voice: the deeds of Coriolanus
COMINIUS: Should not be utter'd feebly. It is held
COMINIUS: That valour is the chiefest virtue, and
COMINIUS: Most dignifies the haver: if it be,
COMINIUS: The man I speak of cannot in the world
COMINIUS: Be singly counterpoised. At sixteen years,
COMINIUS: When Tarquin made a head for Rome, he fought
COMINIUS: Beyond the mark of others: our then dictator,
COMINIUS: Whom with all praise I point at, saw him fight,
COMINIUS: When with his Amazonian chin he drove
COMINIUS: The bristled lips before him: be bestrid
COMINIUS: An o'er-press'd Roman and i' the consul's view
COMINIUS: Slew three opposers: Tarquin's self he met,
COMINIUS: And struck him on his knee: in that day's feats,
COMINIUS: When he might act the woman in the scene,
COMINIUS: He proved best man i' the field, and for his meed
COMINIUS: Was brow-bound with the oak. His pupil age
COMINIUS: Man-enter'd thus, he waxed like a sea,
COMINIUS: And in the brunt of seventeen battles since
COMINIUS: He lurch'd all swords of the garland. For this last,
COMINIUS: Before and in Corioli, let me say,
COMINIUS: I cannot speak him home: he stopp'd the fliers,
COMINIUS: And by his rare example made the coward
COMINIUS: Turn terror into sport: as weeds before
COMINIUS: A vessel under sail, so men obey'd
COMINIUS: And fell below his stem: his sword, death's stamp,
COMINIUS: Where it did mark, it took, from face to foot
COMINIUS: He was a thing of blood, whose every motion
COMINIUS: Was timed with dying cries: alone he enter'd
COMINIUS: The mortal gate of the city, which he painted
COMINIUS: With shunless destiny, aidless came off,
COMINIUS: And with a sudden reinforcement struck
COMINIUS: Corioli like a planet: now all's his:
COMINIUS: When, by and by, the din of war gan pierce
COMINIUS: His ready sense, then straight his doubled spirit
COMINIUS: Re-quicken'd what in flesh was fatigate,
COMINIUS: And to the battle came he, where he did
COMINIUS: Run reeking o'er the lives of men, as if
COMINIUS: 'Twere a perpetual spoil: and till we call'd
COMINIUS: Both field and city ours, he never stood
COMINIUS: To ease his breast with panting.
MENENIUS: Worthy man!
First Senator: He cannot but with measure fit the honours
First Senator: Which we devise him.
COMINIUS: Our spoils he kick'd at,
COMINIUS: And look'd upon things precious as they were
COMINIUS: The common muck of the world: he covets less
COMINIUS: Than misery itself would give, rewards
COMINIUS: His deeds with doing them, and is content
COMINIUS: To spend the time to end it.
MENENIUS: He's right noble:
MENENIUS: Let him be call'd for.
First Senator: Call Coriolanus.
Officer: He doth appear.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CORIOLANUS
MENENIUS: The senate, Coriolanus, are well pleased
MENENIUS: To make thee consul.
CORIOLANUS: I do owe them still
CORIOLANUS: My life and services.
MENENIUS: It then remains
MENENIUS: That you do speak to the people.
CORIOLANUS: I do beseech you,
CORIOLANUS: Let me o'erleap that custom, for I cannot
CORIOLANUS: Put on the gown, stand naked and entreat them,
CORIOLANUS: For my wounds' sake, to give their suffrage: please you
CORIOLANUS: That I may pass this doing.
SICINIUS: Sir, the people
SICINIUS: Must have their voices, neither will they bate
SICINIUS: One jot of ceremony.
MENENIUS: Put them not to't:
MENENIUS: Pray you, go fit you to the custom and
MENENIUS: Take to you, as your predecessors have,
MENENIUS: Your honour with your form.
CORIOLANUS: It is apart
CORIOLANUS: That I shall blush in acting, and might well
CORIOLANUS: Be taken from the people.
BRUTUS: Mark you that?
CORIOLANUS: To brag unto them, thus I did, and thus,
CORIOLANUS: Show them the unaching scars which I should hide,
CORIOLANUS: As if I had received them for the hire
CORIOLANUS: Of their breath only!
MENENIUS: Do not stand upon't.
MENENIUS: We recommend to you, tribunes of the people,
MENENIUS: Our purpose to them: and to our noble consul
MENENIUS: Wish we all joy and honour.
Senators: To Coriolanus come all joy and honour!
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Exeunt all but SICINIUS and BRUTUS
BRUTUS: You see how he intends to use the people.
SICINIUS: May they perceive's intent! He will require them,
SICINIUS: As if he did contemn what he requested
SICINIUS: Should be in them to give.
BRUTUS: Come, we'll inform them
BRUTUS: Of our proceedings here: on the marketplace,
BRUTUS: I know, they do attend us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. The Forum.
NARRATOR: Enter seven or eight Citizens
First Citizen: Once, if he do require our voices, we ought not to deny him.
Second Citizen: We may, sir, if we will.
Third Citizen: We have power in ourselves to do it, but it is a
Third Citizen: power that we have no power to do, for if he show us
Third Citizen: his wounds and tell us his deeds, we are to put our
Third Citizen: tongues into those wounds and speak for them, so, if
Third Citizen: he tell us his noble deeds, we must also tell him
Third Citizen: our noble acceptance of them. Ingratitude is
Third Citizen: monstrous, and for the multitude to be ingrateful,
Third Citizen: were to make a monster of the multitude: of the
Third Citizen: which we being members, should bring ourselves to be
Third Citizen: monstrous members.
First Citizen: And to make us no better thought of, a little help
First Citizen: will serve, for once we stood up about the corn, he
First Citizen: himself stuck not to call us the many-headed multitude.
Third Citizen: We have been called so of many, not that our heads
Third Citizen: are some brown, some black, some auburn, some bald,
Third Citizen: but that our wits are so diversely coloured: and
Third Citizen: truly I think if all our wits were to issue out of
Third Citizen: one skull, they would fly east, west, north, south,
Third Citizen: and their consent of one direct way should be at
Third Citizen: once to all the points o' the compass.
Second Citizen: Think you so? Which way do you judge my wit would
Second Citizen: fly?
Third Citizen: Nay, your wit will not so soon out as another man's
Third Citizen: will,'tis strongly wedged up in a block-head, but
Third Citizen: if it were at liberty, 'twould, sure, southward.
Second Citizen: Why that way?
Third Citizen: To lose itself in a fog, where being three parts
Third Citizen: melted away with rotten dews, the fourth would return
Third Citizen: for conscience sake, to help to get thee a wife.
Second Citizen: You are never without your tricks: you may, you may.
Third Citizen: Are you all resolved to give your voices? But
Third Citizen: that's no matter, the greater part carries it. I
Third Citizen: say, if he would incline to the people, there was
Third Citizen: never a worthier man.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS in a gown of humility, with MENENIUS
Third Citizen: Here he comes, and in the gown of humility: mark his
Third Citizen: behavior. We are not to stay all together, but to
Third Citizen: come by him where he stands, by ones, by twos, and
Third Citizen: by threes. He's to make his requests by
Third Citizen: particulars, wherein every one of us has a single
Third Citizen: honour, in giving him our own voices with our own
Third Citizen: tongues: therefore follow me, and I direct you how
Third Citizen: you shall go by him.
All: Content, content.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Citizens
MENENIUS: O sir, you are not right: have you not known
MENENIUS: The worthiest men have done't?
CORIOLANUS: What must I say?
CORIOLANUS: 'I Pray, sir'--Plague upon't! I cannot bring
CORIOLANUS: My tongue to such a pace:--'Look, sir, my wounds!
CORIOLANUS: I got them in my country's service, when
CORIOLANUS: Some certain of your brethren roar'd and ran
CORIOLANUS: From the noise of our own drums.'
MENENIUS: O me, the gods!
MENENIUS: You must not speak of that: you must desire them
MENENIUS: To think upon you.
CORIOLANUS: Think upon me! hang 'em!
CORIOLANUS: I would they would forget me, like the virtues
CORIOLANUS: Which our divines lose by 'em.
MENENIUS: You'll mar all:
MENENIUS: I'll leave you: pray you, speak to 'em, I pray you,
MENENIUS: In wholesome manner.
NARRATOR: Exit
CORIOLANUS: Bid them wash their faces
CORIOLANUS: And keep their teeth clean.
NARRATOR: Re-enter two of the Citizens
CORIOLANUS: So, here comes a brace.
NARRATOR: Re-enter a third Citizen
CORIOLANUS: You know the cause, air, of my standing here.
Third Citizen: We do, sir, tell us what hath brought you to't.
CORIOLANUS: Mine own desert.
Second Citizen: Your own desert!
CORIOLANUS: Ay, but not mine own desire.
Third Citizen: How not your own desire?
CORIOLANUS: No, sir,'twas never my desire yet to trouble the
CORIOLANUS: poor with begging.
Third Citizen: You must think, if we give you any thing, we hope to
Third Citizen: gain by you.
CORIOLANUS: Well then, I pray, your price o' the consulship?
First Citizen: The price is to ask it kindly.
CORIOLANUS: Kindly! Sir, I pray, let me ha't: I have wounds to
CORIOLANUS: show you, which shall be yours in private. Your
CORIOLANUS: good voice, sir, what say you?
Second Citizen: You shall ha' it, worthy sir.
CORIOLANUS: A match, sir. There's in all two worthy voices
CORIOLANUS: begged. I have your alms: adieu.
Third Citizen: But this is something odd.
Second Citizen: An 'twere to give again,--but 'tis no matter.
NARRATOR: Exeunt the three Citizens
NARRATOR: Re-enter two other Citizens
CORIOLANUS: Pray you now, if it may stand with the tune of your
CORIOLANUS: voices that I may be consul, I have here the
CORIOLANUS: customary gown.
Fourth Citizen: You have deserved nobly of your country, and you
Fourth Citizen: have not deserved nobly.
CORIOLANUS: Your enigma?
Fourth Citizen: You have been a scourge to her enemies, you have
Fourth Citizen: been a rod to her friends, you have not indeed loved
Fourth Citizen: the common people.
CORIOLANUS: You should account me the more virtuous that I have
CORIOLANUS: not been common in my love. I will, sir, flatter my
CORIOLANUS: sworn brother, the people, to earn a dearer
CORIOLANUS: estimation of them, 'tis a condition they account
CORIOLANUS: gentle: and since the wisdom of their choice is
CORIOLANUS: rather to have my hat than my heart, I will practise
CORIOLANUS: the insinuating nod and be off to them most
CORIOLANUS: counterfeitly, that is, sir, I will counterfeit the
CORIOLANUS: bewitchment of some popular man and give it
CORIOLANUS: bountiful to the desirers. Therefore, beseech you,
CORIOLANUS: I may be consul.
Fifth Citizen: We hope to find you our friend, and therefore give
Fifth Citizen: you our voices heartily.
Fourth Citizen: You have received many wounds for your country.
CORIOLANUS: I will not seal your knowledge with showing them. I
CORIOLANUS: will make much of your voices, and so trouble you no further.
Both Citizens: The gods give you joy, sir, heartily!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
CORIOLANUS: Most sweet voices!
CORIOLANUS: Better it is to die, better to starve,
CORIOLANUS: Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
CORIOLANUS: Why in this woolvish toge should I stand here,
CORIOLANUS: To beg of Hob and Dick, that do appear,
CORIOLANUS: Their needless vouches? Custom calls me to't:
CORIOLANUS: What custom wills, in all things should we do't,
CORIOLANUS: The dust on antique time would lie unswept,
CORIOLANUS: And mountainous error be too highly heapt
CORIOLANUS: For truth to o'er-peer. Rather than fool it so,
CORIOLANUS: Let the high office and the honour go
CORIOLANUS: To one that would do thus. I am half through,
CORIOLANUS: The one part suffer'd, the other will I do.
NARRATOR: Re-enter three Citizens more
CORIOLANUS: Here come more voices.
CORIOLANUS: Your voices: for your voices I have fought,
CORIOLANUS: Watch'd for your voices, for Your voices bear
CORIOLANUS: Of wounds two dozen odd, battles thrice six
CORIOLANUS: I have seen and heard of, for your voices have
CORIOLANUS: Done many things, some less, some more your voices:
CORIOLANUS: Indeed I would be consul.
Sixth Citizen: He has done nobly, and cannot go without any honest
Sixth Citizen: man's voice.
Seventh Citizen: Therefore let him be consul: the gods give him joy,
Seventh Citizen: and make him good friend to the people!
All Citizens: Amen, amen. God save thee, noble consul!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
CORIOLANUS: Worthy voices!
NARRATOR: Re-enter MENENIUS, with BRUTUS and SICINIUS
MENENIUS: You have stood your limitation, and the tribunes
