MENENIUS: That, in the official marks invested, you
MENENIUS: Anon do meet the senate.
CORIOLANUS: Is this done?
SICINIUS: The custom of request you have discharged:
SICINIUS: The people do admit you, and are summon'd
SICINIUS: To meet anon, upon your approbation.
CORIOLANUS: Where? at the senate-house?
SICINIUS: There, Coriolanus.
CORIOLANUS: May I change these garments?
SICINIUS: You may, sir.
CORIOLANUS: That I'll straight do, and, knowing myself again,
CORIOLANUS: Repair to the senate-house.
MENENIUS: I'll keep you company. Will you along?
BRUTUS: We stay here for the people.
SICINIUS: Fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CORIOLANUS and MENENIUS
SICINIUS: He has it now, and by his looks methink
SICINIUS: 'Tis warm at 's heart.
BRUTUS: With a proud heart he wore his humble weeds.
BRUTUS: will you dismiss the people?
NARRATOR: Re-enter Citizens
SICINIUS: How now, my masters! have you chose this man?
First Citizen: He has our voices, sir.
BRUTUS: We pray the gods he may deserve your loves.
Second Citizen: Amen, sir: to my poor unworthy notice,
Second Citizen: He mock'd us when he begg'd our voices.
Third Citizen: Certainly
Third Citizen: He flouted us downright.
First Citizen: No,'tis his kind of speech: he did not mock us.
Second Citizen: Not one amongst us, save yourself, but says
Second Citizen: He used us scornfully: he should have show'd us
Second Citizen: His marks of merit, wounds received for's country.
SICINIUS: Why, so he did, I am sure.
Citizens: No, no, no man saw 'em.
Third Citizen: He said he had wounds, which he could show
Third Citizen: in private,
Third Citizen: And with his hat, thus waving it in scorn,
Third Citizen: 'I would be consul,' says he: 'aged custom,
Third Citizen: But by your voices, will not so permit me,
Third Citizen: Your voices therefore.' When we granted that,
Third Citizen: Here was 'I thank you for your voices: thank you:
Third Citizen: Your most sweet voices: now you have left
Third Citizen: your voices,
Third Citizen: I have no further with you.' Was not this mockery?
SICINIUS: Why either were you ignorant to see't,
SICINIUS: Or, seeing it, of such childish friendliness
SICINIUS: To yield your voices?
BRUTUS: Could you not have told him
BRUTUS: As you were lesson'd, when he had no power,
BRUTUS: But was a petty servant to the state,
BRUTUS: He was your enemy, ever spake against
BRUTUS: Your liberties and the charters that you bear
BRUTUS: I' the body of the weal, and now, arriving
BRUTUS: A place of potency and sway o' the state,
BRUTUS: If he should still malignantly remain
BRUTUS: Fast foe to the plebeii, your voices might
BRUTUS: Be curses to yourselves? You should have said
BRUTUS: That as his worthy deeds did claim no less
BRUTUS: Than what he stood for, so his gracious nature
BRUTUS: Would think upon you for your voices and
BRUTUS: Translate his malice towards you into love,
BRUTUS: Standing your friendly lord.
SICINIUS: Thus to have said,
SICINIUS: As you were fore-advised, had touch'd his spirit
SICINIUS: And tried his inclination, from him pluck'd
SICINIUS: Either his gracious promise, which you might,
SICINIUS: As cause had call'd you up, have held him to
SICINIUS: Or else it would have gall'd his surly nature,
SICINIUS: Which easily endures not article
SICINIUS: Tying him to aught, so putting him to rage,
SICINIUS: You should have ta'en the advantage of his choler
SICINIUS: And pass'd him unelected.
BRUTUS: Did you perceive
BRUTUS: He did solicit you in free contempt
BRUTUS: When he did need your loves, and do you think
BRUTUS: That his contempt shall not be bruising to you,
BRUTUS: When he hath power to crush? Why, had your bodies
BRUTUS: No heart among you? or had you tongues to cry
BRUTUS: Against the rectorship of judgment?
SICINIUS: Have you
SICINIUS: Ere now denied the asker? and now again
SICINIUS: Of him that did not ask, but mock, bestow
SICINIUS: Your sued-for tongues?
Third Citizen: He's not confirm'd, we may deny him yet.
Second Citizen: And will deny him:
Second Citizen: I'll have five hundred voices of that sound.
First Citizen: I twice five hundred and their friends to piece 'em.
BRUTUS: Get you hence instantly, and tell those friends,
BRUTUS: They have chose a consul that will from them take
BRUTUS: Their liberties, make them of no more voice
BRUTUS: Than dogs that are as often beat for barking
BRUTUS: As therefore kept to do so.
SICINIUS: Let them assemble,
SICINIUS: And on a safer judgment all revoke
SICINIUS: Your ignorant election, enforce his pride,
SICINIUS: And his old hate unto you, besides, forget not
SICINIUS: With what contempt he wore the humble weed,
SICINIUS: How in his suit he scorn'd you, but your loves,
SICINIUS: Thinking upon his services, took from you
SICINIUS: The apprehension of his present portance,
SICINIUS: Which most gibingly, ungravely, he did fashion
SICINIUS: After the inveterate hate he bears you.
BRUTUS: Lay
BRUTUS: A fault on us, your tribunes, that we laboured,
BRUTUS: No impediment between, but that you must
BRUTUS: Cast your election on him.
SICINIUS: Say, you chose him
SICINIUS: More after our commandment than as guided
SICINIUS: By your own true affections, and that your minds,
SICINIUS: Preoccupied with what you rather must do
SICINIUS: Than what you should, made you against the grain
SICINIUS: To voice him consul: lay the fault on us.
BRUTUS: Ay, spare us not. Say we read lectures to you.
BRUTUS: How youngly he began to serve his country,
BRUTUS: How long continued, and what stock he springs of,
BRUTUS: The noble house o' the Marcians, from whence came
BRUTUS: That Ancus Marcius, Numa's daughter's son,
BRUTUS: Who, after great Hostilius, here was king,
BRUTUS: Of the same house Publius and Quintus were,
BRUTUS: That our beat water brought by conduits hither,
BRUTUS: And  [Censorinus,]  nobly named so,
BRUTUS: Twice being  [by the people chosen]  censor,
BRUTUS: Was his great ancestor.
SICINIUS: One thus descended,
SICINIUS: That hath beside well in his person wrought
SICINIUS: To be set high in place, we did commend
SICINIUS: To your remembrances: but you have found,
SICINIUS: Scaling his present bearing with his past,
SICINIUS: That he's your fixed enemy, and revoke
SICINIUS: Your sudden approbation.
BRUTUS: Say, you ne'er had done't--
BRUTUS: Harp on that still--but by our putting on,
BRUTUS: And presently, when you have drawn your number,
BRUTUS: Repair to the Capitol.
All: We will so: almost all
All: Repent in their election.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Citizens
BRUTUS: Let them go on,
BRUTUS: This mutiny were better put in hazard,
BRUTUS: Than stay, past doubt, for greater:
BRUTUS: If, as his nature is, he fall in rage
BRUTUS: With their refusal, both observe and answer
BRUTUS: The vantage of his anger.
SICINIUS: To the Capitol, come:
SICINIUS: We will be there before the stream o' the people,
SICINIUS: And this shall seem, as partly 'tis, their own,
SICINIUS: Which we have goaded onward.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A street.
NARRATOR: Cornets. Enter CORIOLANUS, MENENIUS, all the Gentry, COMINIUS, TITUS LARTIUS, and other Senators
CORIOLANUS: Tullus Aufidius then had made new head?

LARTIUS: Our swifter composition.
CORIOLANUS: So then the Volsces stand but as at first,
CORIOLANUS: Ready, when time shall prompt them, to make road.
CORIOLANUS: Upon's again.

MENENIUS: The harm of unscann'd swiftness, will too late
MENENIUS: Tie leaden pounds to's heels. Proceed by process,
MENENIUS: Lest parties, as he is beloved, break out,
MENENIUS: And sack great Rome with Romans.
BRUTUS: If it were so,--
SICINIUS: What do ye talk?
SICINIUS: Have we not had a taste of his obedience?
SICINIUS: Our aediles smote? ourselves resisted? Come.
MENENIUS: Consider this: he has been bred i' the wars
MENENIUS: Since he could draw a sword, and is ill school'd
MENENIUS: In bolted language, meal and bran together
MENENIUS: He throws without distinction. Give me leave,
MENENIUS: I'll go to him, and undertake to bring him
MENENIUS: Where he shall answer, by a lawful form,
MENENIUS: In peace, to his utmost peril.
First Senator: Noble tribunes,
First Senator: It is the humane way: the other course
First Senator: Will prove too bloody, and the end of it
First Senator: Unknown to the beginning.
SICINIUS: Noble Menenius,
SICINIUS: Be you then as the people's officer.
SICINIUS: Masters, lay down your weapons.
BRUTUS: Go not home.
SICINIUS: Meet on the market-place. We'll attend you there:
SICINIUS: Where, if you bring not Marcius, we'll proceed
SICINIUS: In our first way.
MENENIUS: I'll bring him to you.
NARRATOR: To the Senators
MENENIUS: Let me desire your company: he must come,
MENENIUS: Or what is worst will follow.
First Senator: Pray you, let's to him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in CORIOLANUS'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS with Patricians
CORIOLANUS: Let them puff all about mine ears, present me
CORIOLANUS: Death on the wheel or at wild horses' heels,
CORIOLANUS: Or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock,
CORIOLANUS: That the precipitation might down stretch
CORIOLANUS: Below the beam of sight, yet will I still
CORIOLANUS: Be thus to them.
A Patrician: You do the nobler.
CORIOLANUS: I muse my mother
CORIOLANUS: Does not approve me further, who was wont
CORIOLANUS: To call them woollen vassals, things created
CORIOLANUS: To buy and sell with groats, to show bare heads
CORIOLANUS: In congregations, to yawn, be still and wonder,
CORIOLANUS: When one but of my ordinance stood up
CORIOLANUS: To speak of peace or war.
NARRATOR: Enter VOLUMNIA
CORIOLANUS: I talk of you:
CORIOLANUS: Why did you wish me milder? would you have me
CORIOLANUS: False to my nature? Rather say I play
CORIOLANUS: The man I am.
VOLUMNIA: O, sir, sir, sir,
VOLUMNIA: I would have had you put your power well on,
VOLUMNIA: Before you had worn it out.
CORIOLANUS: Let go.
VOLUMNIA: You might have been enough the man you are,
VOLUMNIA: With striving less to be so, lesser had been
VOLUMNIA: The thwartings of your dispositions, if
VOLUMNIA: You had not show'd them how ye were disposed
VOLUMNIA: Ere they lack'd power to cross you.
CORIOLANUS: Let them hang.
A Patrician: Ay, and burn too.
NARRATOR: Enter MENENIUS and Senators
MENENIUS: Come, come, you have been too rough, something
MENENIUS: too rough,
MENENIUS: You must return and mend it.
First Senator: There's no remedy,
First Senator: Unless, by not so doing, our good city
First Senator: Cleave in the midst, and perish.
VOLUMNIA: Pray, be counsell'd:
VOLUMNIA: I have a heart as little apt as yours,
VOLUMNIA: But yet a brain that leads my use of anger
VOLUMNIA: To better vantage.
MENENIUS: Well said, noble woman?
MENENIUS: Before he should thus stoop to the herd, but that
MENENIUS: The violent fit o' the time craves it as physic
MENENIUS: For the whole state, I would put mine armour on,
MENENIUS: Which I can scarcely bear.
CORIOLANUS: What must I do?
MENENIUS: Return to the tribunes.
CORIOLANUS: Well, what then? what then?
MENENIUS: Repent what you have spoke.
CORIOLANUS: For them! I cannot do it to the gods,
CORIOLANUS: Must I then do't to them?
VOLUMNIA: You are too absolute,
VOLUMNIA: Though therein you can never be too noble,
VOLUMNIA: But when extremities speak. I have heard you say,
VOLUMNIA: Honour and policy, like unsever'd friends,
VOLUMNIA: I' the war do grow together: grant that, and tell me,
VOLUMNIA: In peace what each of them by the other lose,
VOLUMNIA: That they combine not there.
CORIOLANUS: Tush, tush!
MENENIUS: A good demand.
VOLUMNIA: If it be honour in your wars to seem
VOLUMNIA: The same you are not, which, for your best ends,
VOLUMNIA: You adopt your policy, how is it less or worse,
VOLUMNIA: That it shall hold companionship in peace
VOLUMNIA: With honour, as in war, since that to both
VOLUMNIA: It stands in like request?
CORIOLANUS: Why force you this?
VOLUMNIA: Because that now it lies you on to speak
VOLUMNIA: To the people, not by your own instruction,
VOLUMNIA: Nor by the matter which your heart prompts you,
VOLUMNIA: But with such words that are but rooted in
VOLUMNIA: Your tongue, though but bastards and syllables
VOLUMNIA: Of no allowance to your bosom's truth.
VOLUMNIA: Now, this no more dishonours you at all
VOLUMNIA: Than to take in a town with gentle words,
VOLUMNIA: Which else would put you to your fortune and
VOLUMNIA: The hazard of much blood.
VOLUMNIA: I would dissemble with my nature where
VOLUMNIA: My fortunes and my friends at stake required
VOLUMNIA: I should do so in honour: I am in this,
VOLUMNIA: Your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles,
VOLUMNIA: And you will rather show our general louts
VOLUMNIA: How you can frown than spend a fawn upon 'em,
VOLUMNIA: For the inheritance of their loves and safeguard
VOLUMNIA: Of what that want might ruin.
MENENIUS: Noble lady!
MENENIUS: Come, go with us, speak fair: you may salve so,
MENENIUS: Not what is dangerous present, but the loss
MENENIUS: Of what is past.
VOLUMNIA: I prithee now, my son,
VOLUMNIA: Go to them, with this bonnet in thy hand,
VOLUMNIA: And thus far having stretch'd it--here be with them--
VOLUMNIA: Thy knee bussing the stones--for in such business
VOLUMNIA: Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant
VOLUMNIA: More learned than the ears--waving thy head,
VOLUMNIA: Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,
VOLUMNIA: Now humble as the ripest mulberry
VOLUMNIA: That will not hold the handling: or say to them,
VOLUMNIA: Thou art their soldier, and being bred in broils
VOLUMNIA: Hast not the soft way which, thou dost confess,
VOLUMNIA: Were fit for thee to use as they to claim,
VOLUMNIA: In asking their good loves, but thou wilt frame
VOLUMNIA: Thyself, forsooth, hereafter theirs, so far
VOLUMNIA: As thou hast power and person.
MENENIUS: This but done,
MENENIUS: Even as she speaks, why, their hearts were yours,
MENENIUS: For they have pardons, being ask'd, as free
MENENIUS: As words to little purpose.
VOLUMNIA: Prithee now,
VOLUMNIA: Go, and be ruled: although I know thou hadst rather
VOLUMNIA: Follow thine enemy in a fiery gulf
VOLUMNIA: Than flatter him in a bower. Here is Cominius.
NARRATOR: Enter COMINIUS
COMINIUS: I have been i' the market-place, and, sir,'tis fit
COMINIUS: You make strong party, or defend yourself
COMINIUS: By calmness or by absence: all's in anger.
MENENIUS: Only fair speech.
COMINIUS: I think 'twill serve, if he
COMINIUS: Can thereto frame his spirit.
VOLUMNIA: He must, and will
VOLUMNIA: Prithee now, say you will, and go about it.
CORIOLANUS: Must I go show them my unbarbed sconce?
CORIOLANUS: Must I with base tongue give my noble heart
CORIOLANUS: A lie that it must bear? Well, I will do't:
CORIOLANUS: Yet, were there but this single plot to lose,
CORIOLANUS: This mould of Marcius, they to dust should grind it
CORIOLANUS: And throw't against the wind. To the market-place!
CORIOLANUS: You have put me now to such a part which never
CORIOLANUS: I shall discharge to the life.
COMINIUS: Come, come, we'll prompt you.
VOLUMNIA: I prithee now, sweet son, as thou hast said
VOLUMNIA: My praises made thee first a soldier, so,
VOLUMNIA: To have my praise for this, perform a part
VOLUMNIA: Thou hast not done before.
CORIOLANUS: Well, I must do't:
CORIOLANUS: Away, my disposition, and possess me
CORIOLANUS: Some harlot's spirit! my throat of war be turn'd,
CORIOLANUS: Which quired with my drum, into a pipe
CORIOLANUS: Small as an eunuch, or the virgin voice
CORIOLANUS: That babies lulls asleep! the smiles of knaves
CORIOLANUS: Tent in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears take up
CORIOLANUS: The glasses of my sight! a beggar's tongue
CORIOLANUS: Make motion through my lips, and my arm'd knees,
CORIOLANUS: Who bow'd but in my stirrup, bend like his
CORIOLANUS: That hath received an alms! I will not do't,
CORIOLANUS: Lest I surcease to honour mine own truth
CORIOLANUS: And by my body's action teach my mind
CORIOLANUS: A most inherent baseness.
VOLUMNIA: At thy choice, then:
VOLUMNIA: To beg of thee, it is my more dishonour
VOLUMNIA: Than thou of them. Come all to ruin, let
VOLUMNIA: Thy mother rather feel thy pride than fear
VOLUMNIA: Thy dangerous stoutness, for I mock at death
VOLUMNIA: With as big heart as thou. Do as thou list
VOLUMNIA: Thy valiantness was mine, thou suck'dst it from me,
VOLUMNIA: But owe thy pride thyself.
CORIOLANUS: Pray, be content:
CORIOLANUS: Mother, I am going to the market-place,
CORIOLANUS: Chide me no more. I'll mountebank their loves,
CORIOLANUS: Cog their hearts from them, and come home beloved
CORIOLANUS: Of all the trades in Rome. Look, I am going:
CORIOLANUS: Commend me to my wife. I'll return consul,
CORIOLANUS: Or never trust to what my tongue can do
CORIOLANUS: I' the way of flattery further.
VOLUMNIA: Do your will.
NARRATOR: Exit
COMINIUS: Away! the tribunes do attend you: arm yourself
COMINIUS: To answer mildly, for they are prepared
COMINIUS: With accusations, as I hear, more strong
COMINIUS: Than are upon you yet.
CORIOLANUS: The word is 'mildly.' Pray you, let us go:
CORIOLANUS: Let them accuse me by invention, I
CORIOLANUS: Will answer in mine honour.
MENENIUS: Ay, but mildly.
CORIOLANUS: Well, mildly be it then. Mildly!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. The Forum.
NARRATOR: Enter SICINIUS and BRUTUS
BRUTUS: In this point charge him home, that he affects
BRUTUS: Tyrannical power: if he evade us there,
BRUTUS: Enforce him with his envy to the people,
BRUTUS: And that the spoil got on the Antiates
BRUTUS: Was ne'er distributed.
NARRATOR: Enter an AEdile
BRUTUS: What, will he come?
AEdile: He's coming.
BRUTUS: How accompanied?
AEdile: With old Menenius, and those senators
AEdile: That always favour'd him.
SICINIUS: Have you a catalogue
SICINIUS: Of all the voices that we have procured
SICINIUS: Set down by the poll?
AEdile: I have, 'tis ready.
SICINIUS: Have you collected them by tribes?
AEdile: I have.
SICINIUS: Assemble presently the people hither,
SICINIUS: And when they bear me say 'It shall be so
SICINIUS: I' the right and strength o' the commons,' be it either
SICINIUS: For death, for fine, or banishment, then let them
SICINIUS: If I say fine, cry 'Fine,' if death, cry 'Death.'
SICINIUS: Insisting on the old prerogative
SICINIUS: And power i' the truth o' the cause.
AEdile: I shall inform them.
BRUTUS: And when such time they have begun to cry,
BRUTUS: Let them not cease, but with a din confused
BRUTUS: Enforce the present execution
BRUTUS: Of what we chance to sentence.
AEdile: Very well.
SICINIUS: Make them be strong and ready for this hint,
SICINIUS: When we shall hap to give 't them.
BRUTUS: Go about it.
NARRATOR: Exit AEdile
BRUTUS: Put him to choler straight: he hath been used
BRUTUS: Ever to conquer, and to have his worth
BRUTUS: Of contradiction: being once chafed, he cannot
BRUTUS: Be rein'd again to temperance, then he speaks
BRUTUS: What's in his heart, and that is there which looks
BRUTUS: With us to break his neck.
SICINIUS: Well, here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS, MENENIUS, and COMINIUS, with Senators and Patricians
MENENIUS: Calmly, I do beseech you.
CORIOLANUS: Ay, as an ostler, that for the poorest piece
CORIOLANUS: Will bear the knave by the volume. The honour'd gods
CORIOLANUS: Keep Rome in safety, and the chairs of justice
CORIOLANUS: Supplied with worthy men! plant love among 's!
CORIOLANUS: Throng our large temples with the shows of peace,
CORIOLANUS: And not our streets with war!
First Senator: Amen, amen.
MENENIUS: A noble wish.
NARRATOR: Re-enter AEdile, with Citizens
SICINIUS: Draw near, ye people.
AEdile: List to your tribunes. Audience: peace, I say!
CORIOLANUS: First, hear me speak.
Both Tribunes: Well, say. Peace, ho!
CORIOLANUS: Shall I be charged no further than this present?
CORIOLANUS: Must all determine here?
SICINIUS: I do demand,
SICINIUS: If you submit you to the people's voices,
SICINIUS: Allow their officers and are content
SICINIUS: To suffer lawful censure for such faults
SICINIUS: As shall be proved upon you?
CORIOLANUS: I am content.
MENENIUS: Lo, citizens, he says he is content:
MENENIUS: The warlike service he has done, consider, think
MENENIUS: Upon the wounds his body bears, which show
MENENIUS: Like graves i' the holy churchyard.
CORIOLANUS: Scratches with briers,
CORIOLANUS: Scars to move laughter only.
MENENIUS: Consider further,
MENENIUS: That when he speaks not like a citizen,
MENENIUS: You find him like a soldier: do not take
MENENIUS: His rougher accents for malicious sounds,
MENENIUS: But, as I say, such as become a soldier,
MENENIUS: Rather than envy you.
COMINIUS: Well, well, no more.
CORIOLANUS: What is the matter
CORIOLANUS: That being pass'd for consul with full voice,
CORIOLANUS: I am so dishonour'd that the very hour
CORIOLANUS: You take it off again?
SICINIUS: Answer to us.
CORIOLANUS: Say, then: 'tis true, I ought so.
SICINIUS: We charge you, that you have contrived to take
SICINIUS: From Rome all season'd office and to wind
SICINIUS: Yourself into a power tyrannical,
SICINIUS: For which you are a traitor to the people.
CORIOLANUS: How! traitor!
MENENIUS: Nay, temperately, your promise.
CORIOLANUS: The fires i' the lowest hell fold-in the people!
CORIOLANUS: Call me their traitor! Thou injurious tribune!
CORIOLANUS: Within thine eyes sat twenty thousand deaths,
CORIOLANUS: In thy hand clutch'd as many millions, in
CORIOLANUS: Thy lying tongue both numbers, I would say
CORIOLANUS: 'Thou liest' unto thee with a voice as free
CORIOLANUS: As I do pray the gods.
SICINIUS: Mark you this, people?
Citizens: To the rock, to the rock with him!
SICINIUS: Peace!
SICINIUS: We need not put new matter to his charge:
SICINIUS: What you have seen him do and heard him speak,
SICINIUS: Beating your officers, cursing yourselves,
SICINIUS: Opposing laws with strokes and here defying
SICINIUS: Those whose great power must try him, even this,
SICINIUS: So criminal and in such capital kind,
SICINIUS: Deserves the extremest death.
BRUTUS: But since he hath
BRUTUS: Served well for Rome,--
CORIOLANUS: What do you prate of service?
BRUTUS: I talk of that, that know it.
CORIOLANUS: You?
MENENIUS: Is this the promise that you made your mother?
COMINIUS: Know, I pray you,--
CORIOLANUS: I know no further:
CORIOLANUS: Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death,
CORIOLANUS: Vagabond exile, raying, pent to linger
CORIOLANUS: But with a grain a day, I would not buy
CORIOLANUS: Their mercy at the price of one fair word,
CORIOLANUS: Nor cheque my courage for what they can give,
CORIOLANUS: To have't with saying 'Good morrow.'
SICINIUS: For that he has,
SICINIUS: As much as in him lies, from time to time
SICINIUS: Envied against the people, seeking means
SICINIUS: To pluck away their power, as now at last
SICINIUS: Given hostile strokes, and that not in the presence
SICINIUS: Of dreaded justice, but on the ministers
SICINIUS: That do distribute it, in the name o' the people
SICINIUS: And in the power of us the tribunes, we,
SICINIUS: Even from this instant, banish him our city,
SICINIUS: In peril of precipitation
SICINIUS: From off the rock Tarpeian never more
SICINIUS: To enter our Rome gates: i' the people's name,
SICINIUS: I say it shall be so.
Citizens: It shall be so, it shall be so, let him away:
Citizens: He's banish'd, and it shall be so.
COMINIUS: Hear me, my masters, and my common friends,--
SICINIUS: He's sentenced, no more hearing.
COMINIUS: Let me speak:
COMINIUS: I have been consul, and can show for Rome
COMINIUS: Her enemies' marks upon me. I do love
COMINIUS: My country's good with a respect more tender,
COMINIUS: More holy and profound, than mine own life,
COMINIUS: My dear wife's estimate, her womb's increase,
COMINIUS: And treasure of my loins, then if I would
COMINIUS: Speak that,--
SICINIUS: We know your drift: speak what?
BRUTUS: There's no more to be said, but he is banish'd,
BRUTUS: As enemy to the people and his country:
BRUTUS: It shall be so.
Citizens: It shall be so, it shall be so.
CORIOLANUS: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate
CORIOLANUS: As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize
CORIOLANUS: As the dead carcasses of unburied men
CORIOLANUS: That do corrupt my air, I banish you,
CORIOLANUS: And here remain with your uncertainty!
CORIOLANUS: Let every feeble rumour shake your hearts!
CORIOLANUS: Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes,
CORIOLANUS: Fan you into despair! Have the power still
CORIOLANUS: To banish your defenders, till at length
CORIOLANUS: Your ignorance, which finds not till it feels,
CORIOLANUS: Making not reservation of yourselves,
CORIOLANUS: Still your own foes, deliver you as most
CORIOLANUS: Abated captives to some nation
CORIOLANUS: That won you without blows! Despising,
CORIOLANUS: For you, the city, thus I turn my back:
CORIOLANUS: There is a world elsewhere.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CORIOLANUS, COMINIUS, MENENIUS, Senators, and Patricians
AEdile: The people's enemy is gone, is gone!
Citizens: Our enemy is banish'd! he is gone! Hoo! hoo!
NARRATOR: Shouting, and throwing up their caps
SICINIUS: Go, see him out at gates, and follow him,
SICINIUS: As he hath followed you, with all despite,
SICINIUS: Give him deserved vexation. Let a guard
SICINIUS: Attend us through the city.
Citizens: Come, come, let's see him out at gates, come.
Citizens: The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. Before a gate of the city.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS, VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA, MENENIUS, COMINIUS, with the young Nobility of Rome
CORIOLANUS: Come, leave your tears: a brief farewell: the beast
CORIOLANUS: With many heads butts me away. Nay, mother,
CORIOLANUS: Where is your ancient courage? you were used
CORIOLANUS: To say extremity was the trier of spirits,
CORIOLANUS: That common chances common men could bear,
CORIOLANUS: That when the sea was calm all boats alike
CORIOLANUS: Show'd mastership in floating, fortune's blows,
CORIOLANUS: When most struck home, being gentle wounded, craves
CORIOLANUS: A noble cunning: you were used to load me
CORIOLANUS: With precepts that would make invincible
CORIOLANUS: The heart that conn'd them.
VIRGILIA: O heavens! O heavens!
CORIOLANUS: Nay! prithee, woman,--
VOLUMNIA: Now the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome,
VOLUMNIA: And occupations perish!
CORIOLANUS: What, what, what!
CORIOLANUS: I shall be loved when I am lack'd. Nay, mother.
CORIOLANUS: Resume that spirit, when you were wont to say,
CORIOLANUS: If you had been the wife of Hercules,
CORIOLANUS: Six of his labours you'ld have done, and saved
CORIOLANUS: Your husband so much sweat. Cominius,
CORIOLANUS: Droop not, adieu. Farewell, my wife, my mother:
CORIOLANUS: I'll do well yet. Thou old and true Menenius,
CORIOLANUS: Thy tears are salter than a younger man's,
CORIOLANUS: And venomous to thine eyes. My sometime general,
CORIOLANUS: I have seen thee stem, and thou hast oft beheld
CORIOLANUS: Heart-hardening spectacles, tell these sad women
CORIOLANUS: 'Tis fond to wail inevitable strokes,
CORIOLANUS: As 'tis to laugh at 'em. My mother, you wot well
CORIOLANUS: My hazards still have been your solace: and
CORIOLANUS: Believe't not lightly--though I go alone,
CORIOLANUS: Like to a lonely dragon, that his fen
CORIOLANUS: Makes fear'd and talk'd of more than seen--your son
CORIOLANUS: Will or exceed the common or be caught
CORIOLANUS: With cautelous baits and practise.
VOLUMNIA: My first son.
VOLUMNIA: Whither wilt thou go? Take good Cominius
VOLUMNIA: With thee awhile: determine on some course,
VOLUMNIA: More than a wild exposture to each chance
VOLUMNIA: That starts i' the way before thee.
CORIOLANUS: O the gods!
COMINIUS: I'll follow thee a month, devise with thee
COMINIUS: Where thou shalt rest, that thou mayst hear of us
COMINIUS: And we of thee: so if the time thrust forth
COMINIUS: A cause for thy repeal, we shall not send
COMINIUS: O'er the vast world to seek a single man,
COMINIUS: And lose advantage, which doth ever cool
COMINIUS: I' the absence of the needer.
CORIOLANUS: Fare ye well:
CORIOLANUS: Thou hast years upon thee, and thou art too full
CORIOLANUS: Of the wars' surfeits, to go rove with one
CORIOLANUS: That's yet unbruised: bring me but out at gate.
CORIOLANUS: Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and
CORIOLANUS: My friends of noble touch, when I am forth,
CORIOLANUS: Bid me farewell, and smile. I pray you, come.
CORIOLANUS: While I remain above the ground, you shall
CORIOLANUS: Hear from me still, and never of me aught
CORIOLANUS: But what is like me formerly.
MENENIUS: That's worthily
MENENIUS: As any ear can hear. Come, let's not weep.
MENENIUS: If I could shake off but one seven years
MENENIUS: From these old arms and legs, by the good gods,
MENENIUS: I'ld with thee every foot.
CORIOLANUS: Give me thy hand: Come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. A  street near the gate.
NARRATOR: Enter SICINIUS, BRUTUS, and an AEdile
SICINIUS: Bid them all home, he's gone, and we'll no further.
SICINIUS: The nobility are vex'd, whom we see have sided
SICINIUS: In his behalf.
BRUTUS: Now we have shown our power,
BRUTUS: Let us seem humbler after it is done
BRUTUS: Than when it was a-doing.
SICINIUS: Bid them home:
SICINIUS: Say their great enemy is gone, and they
SICINIUS: Stand in their ancient strength.
BRUTUS: Dismiss them home.
NARRATOR: Exit AEdile
BRUTUS: Here comes his mother.
SICINIUS: Let's not meet her.
BRUTUS: Why?
SICINIUS: They say she's mad.
BRUTUS: They have ta'en note of us: keep on your way.
NARRATOR: Enter VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA, and MENENIUS
VOLUMNIA: O, ye're well met: the hoarded plague o' the gods
VOLUMNIA: Requite your love!
MENENIUS: Peace, peace, be not so loud.
VOLUMNIA: If that I could for weeping, you should hear,--
VOLUMNIA: Nay, and you shall hear some.
NARRATOR: To BRUTUS
VOLUMNIA: Will you be gone?
VIRGILIA: [To SICINIUS]  You shall stay too: I would I had the power
VIRGILIA: To say so to my husband.
SICINIUS: Are  you mankind?
VOLUMNIA: Ay, fool, is that a shame? Note but this fool.
VOLUMNIA: Was not a man my father? Hadst thou foxship
VOLUMNIA: To banish him that struck more blows for Rome
VOLUMNIA: Than thou hast spoken words?
SICINIUS: O blessed heavens!
VOLUMNIA: More noble blows than ever thou wise words,
VOLUMNIA: And for Rome's good. I'll tell thee what, yet go:
VOLUMNIA: Nay, but thou shalt stay too: I would my son
VOLUMNIA: Were in Arabia, and thy tribe before him,
VOLUMNIA: His good sword in his hand.
SICINIUS: What then?
VIRGILIA: What then!
VIRGILIA: He'ld make an end of thy posterity.
VOLUMNIA: Bastards and all.
VOLUMNIA: Good man, the wounds that he does bear for Rome!
MENENIUS: Come, come, peace.
SICINIUS: I would he had continued to his country
SICINIUS: As he began, and not unknit himself
SICINIUS: The noble knot he made.
BRUTUS: I would he had.
VOLUMNIA: 'I would he had'! 'Twas you incensed the rabble:
VOLUMNIA: Cats, that can judge as fitly of his worth
VOLUMNIA: As I can of those mysteries which heaven
VOLUMNIA: Will not have earth to know.
BRUTUS: Pray, let us go.
VOLUMNIA: Now, pray, sir, get you gone:
VOLUMNIA: You have done a brave deed. Ere you go, hear this:--
VOLUMNIA: As far as doth the Capitol exceed
VOLUMNIA: The meanest house in Rome, so far my son--
VOLUMNIA: This lady's husband here, this, do you see--
VOLUMNIA: Whom you have banish'd, does exceed you all.
BRUTUS: Well, well, we'll leave you.
SICINIUS: Why stay we to be baited
SICINIUS: With one that wants her wits?
VOLUMNIA: Take my prayers with you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Tribunes
VOLUMNIA: I would the gods had nothing else to do
VOLUMNIA: But to confirm my curses! Could I meet 'em
VOLUMNIA: But once a-day, it would unclog my heart
VOLUMNIA: Of what lies heavy to't.
MENENIUS: You have told them home,
MENENIUS: And, by my troth, you have cause. You'll sup with me?
VOLUMNIA: Anger's my meat, I sup upon myself,
VOLUMNIA: And so shall starve with feeding. Come, let's go:
VOLUMNIA: Leave this faint puling and lament as I do,
VOLUMNIA: In anger, Juno-like. Come, come, come.
MENENIUS: Fie, fie, fie!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A highway between Rome and Antium.
NARRATOR: Enter a Roman and a Volsce, meeting
Roman: I know you well, sir, and you know
Roman: me: your name, I think, is Adrian.
Volsce: It is so, sir: truly, I have forgot you.
Roman: I am a Roman, and my services are,
Roman: as you are, against 'em: know you me yet?
Volsce: Nicanor? no.
Roman: The same, sir.
Volsce: You had more beard when I last saw you, but your
Volsce: favour is well approved by your tongue. What's the
Volsce: news in Rome? I have a note from the Volscian state,
Volsce: to find you out there: you have well saved me a
Volsce: day's journey.
Roman: There hath been in Rome strange insurrections, the
Roman: people against the senators, patricians, and nobles.
Volsce: Hath been! is it ended, then? Our state thinks not
Volsce: so: they are in a most warlike preparation, and
Volsce: hope to come upon them in the heat of their division.
Roman: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing
Roman: would make it flame again: for the nobles receive
Roman: so to heart the banishment of that worthy
Roman: Coriolanus, that they are in a ripe aptness to take
Roman: all power from the people and to pluck from them
Roman: their tribunes for ever. This lies glowing, I can
Roman: tell you, and is almost mature for the violent
Roman: breaking out.
Volsce: Coriolanus banished!
Roman: Banished, sir.
Volsce: You will be welcome with this intelligence, Nicanor.
Roman: The day serves well for them now. I have heard it
Roman: said, the fittest time to corrupt a man's wife is
Roman: when she's fallen out with her husband. Your noble
Roman: Tullus Aufidius will appear well in these wars, his
Roman: great opposer, Coriolanus, being now in no request
Roman: of his country.
Volsce: He cannot choose. I am most fortunate, thus
Volsce: accidentally to encounter you: you have ended my
Volsce: business, and I will merrily accompany you home.
Roman: I shall, between this and supper, tell you most
Roman: strange things from Rome, all tending to the good of
Roman: their adversaries. Have you an army ready, say you?
Volsce: A most royal one, the centurions and their charges,
Volsce: distinctly billeted, already in the entertainment,
Volsce: and to be on foot at an hour's warning.
Roman: I am joyful to hear of their readiness, and am the
Roman: man, I think, that shall set them in present action.
Roman: So, sir, heartily well met, and most glad of your company.
Volsce: You take my part from me, sir, I have the most cause
Volsce: to be glad of yours.
Roman: Well, let us go together.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Antium. Before Aufidius's house.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS in mean apparel, disguised and muffled
CORIOLANUS: A goodly city is this Antium. City,
CORIOLANUS: 'Tis I that made thy widows: many an heir

CORIOLANUS: Have I heard groan and drop: then know me not,

CORIOLANUS: Save you, sir.
Citizen: And you.
CORIOLANUS: Direct me, if it be your will,

Citizen: He is, and feasts the nobles of the state
Citizen: At his house this night.
CORIOLANUS: Which is his house, beseech you?
Citizen: This, here before you.
CORIOLANUS: Thank you, sir: farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit Citizen
CORIOLANUS: O world, thy slippery turns! Friends now fast sworn,
CORIOLANUS: Whose double bosoms seem to wear one heart,
CORIOLANUS: Whose house, whose bed, whose meal, and exercise,
CORIOLANUS: Are still together, who twin, as 'twere, in love
CORIOLANUS: Unseparable, shall within this hour,
CORIOLANUS: On a dissension of a doit, break out
CORIOLANUS: To bitterest enmity: so, fellest foes,
CORIOLANUS: Whose passions and whose plots have broke their sleep,
CORIOLANUS: To take the one the other, by some chance,
CORIOLANUS: Some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear friends
CORIOLANUS: And interjoin their issues. So with me:
CORIOLANUS: My birth-place hate I, and my love's upon
CORIOLANUS: This enemy town. I'll enter: if he slay me,
CORIOLANUS: He does fair justice, if he give me way,
CORIOLANUS: I'll do his country service.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same. A hall in Aufidius's house.

Third Servingman: Under the canopy!
CORIOLANUS: Ay.

Second Servingman: disturbing the lords within.

CORIOLANUS: If, Tullus,
NARRATOR: Unmuffling

AUFIDIUS: O Marcius, Marcius!

AUFIDIUS: I loved the maid I married, never man

AUFIDIUS: Though not for Rome itself.
CORIOLANUS: You bless me, gods!

AUFIDIUS: And more a friend than e'er an enemy,

MENENIUS: What news? what news?
COMINIUS: You have holp to ravish your own daughters and
COMINIUS: To melt the city leads upon your pates,
COMINIUS: To see your wives dishonour'd to your noses,--
MENENIUS: What's the news? what's the news?
COMINIUS: Your temples burned in their cement, and
COMINIUS: Your franchises, whereon you stood, confined
COMINIUS: Into an auger's bore.
MENENIUS: Pray now, your news?
MENENIUS: You have made fair work, I fear me.--Pray, your news?--
MENENIUS: If Marcius should be join'd with Volscians,--
COMINIUS: If!
COMINIUS: He is their god: he leads them like a thing
COMINIUS: Made by some other deity than nature,
COMINIUS: That shapes man better, and they follow him,
COMINIUS: Against us brats, with no less confidence
COMINIUS: Than boys pursuing summer butterflies,
COMINIUS: Or butchers killing flies.
MENENIUS: You have made good work,
MENENIUS: You and your apron-men, you that stood so up much
MENENIUS: on the voice of occupation and
MENENIUS: The breath of garlic-eaters!
COMINIUS: He will shake
COMINIUS: Your Rome about your ears.
MENENIUS: As Hercules
MENENIUS: Did shake down mellow fruit.
MENENIUS: You have made fair work!
BRUTUS: But is this true, sir?
COMINIUS: Ay, and you'll look pale
COMINIUS: Before you find it other. All the regions
COMINIUS: Do smilingly revolt, and who resist
COMINIUS: Are mock'd for valiant ignorance,
COMINIUS: And perish constant fools. Who is't can blame him?
COMINIUS: Your enemies and his find something in him.
MENENIUS: We are all undone, unless
MENENIUS: The noble man have mercy.
COMINIUS: Who shall ask it?
COMINIUS: The tribunes cannot do't for shame, the people
COMINIUS: Deserve such pity of him as the wolf
COMINIUS: Does of the shepherds: for his best friends, if they
COMINIUS: Should say 'Be good to Rome,' they charged him even
COMINIUS: As those should do that had deserved his hate,
COMINIUS: And therein show'd like enemies.
MENENIUS: 'Tis true:
MENENIUS: If he were putting to my house the brand
MENENIUS: That should consume it, I have not the face
MENENIUS: To say 'Beseech you, cease.' You have made fair hands,
MENENIUS: You and your crafts! you have crafted fair!
COMINIUS: You have brought
COMINIUS: A trembling upon Rome, such as was never
COMINIUS: So incapable of help.
Both Tribunes: Say not we brought it.
MENENIUS: How! Was it we? we loved him but, like beasts
MENENIUS: And cowardly nobles, gave way unto your clusters,
MENENIUS: Who did hoot him out o' the city.
COMINIUS: But I fear
COMINIUS: They'll roar him in again. Tullus Aufidius,
COMINIUS: The second name of men, obeys his points
COMINIUS: As if he were his officer: desperation
COMINIUS: Is all the policy, strength and defence,
COMINIUS: That Rome can make against them.
NARRATOR: Enter a troop of Citizens
MENENIUS: Here come the clusters.
MENENIUS: And is Aufidius with him? You are they
MENENIUS: That made the air unwholesome, when you cast
MENENIUS: Your stinking greasy caps in hooting at
MENENIUS: Coriolanus' exile. Now he's coming,
MENENIUS: And not a hair upon a soldier's head
MENENIUS: Which will not prove a whip: as many coxcombs
MENENIUS: As you threw caps up will he tumble down,
MENENIUS: And pay you for your voices. 'Tis no matter,
MENENIUS: if he could burn us all into one coal,
MENENIUS: We have deserved it.
Citizens: Faith, we hear fearful news.
First Citizen: For mine own part,
First Citizen: When I said, banish him, I said 'twas pity.
Second Citizen: And so did I.
Third Citizen: And so did I, and, to say the truth, so did very
Third Citizen: many of us: that we did, we did for the best, and
Third Citizen: though we willingly consented to his banishment, yet
Third Citizen: it was against our will.
COMINIUS: Ye re goodly things, you voices!
MENENIUS: You have made
MENENIUS: Good work, you and your cry! Shall's to the Capitol?
COMINIUS: O, ay, what else?
NARRATOR: Exeunt COMINIUS and MENENIUS
SICINIUS: Go, masters, get you home, be not dismay'd:
SICINIUS: These are a side that would be glad to have
SICINIUS: This true which they so seem to fear. Go home,
SICINIUS: And show no sign of fear.
First Citizen: The gods be good to us! Come, masters, let's home.
First Citizen: I ever said we were i' the wrong when we banished
First Citizen: him.
Second Citizen: So did we all. But, come, let's home.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Citizens
BRUTUS: I do not like this news.
SICINIUS: Nor I.
BRUTUS: Let's to the Capitol. Would half my wealth
BRUTUS: Would buy this for a lie!
SICINIUS: Pray, let us go.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. A camp, at a small distance from Rome.
NARRATOR: Enter AUFIDIUS and his Lieutenant
AUFIDIUS: Do they still fly to the Roman?
Lieutenant: I do not know what witchcraft's in him, but
Lieutenant: Your soldiers use him as the grace 'fore meat,
Lieutenant: Their talk at table, and their thanks at end,
Lieutenant: And you are darken'd in this action, sir,
Lieutenant: Even by your own.
AUFIDIUS: I cannot help it now,
AUFIDIUS: Unless, by using means, I lame the foot
AUFIDIUS: Of our design. He bears himself more proudlier,
AUFIDIUS: Even to my person, than I thought he would
AUFIDIUS: When first I did embrace him: yet his nature
AUFIDIUS: In that's no changeling, and I must excuse
AUFIDIUS: What cannot be amended.
Lieutenant: Yet I wish, sir,--
Lieutenant: I mean for your particular,--you had not
Lieutenant: Join'd in commission with him, but either
Lieutenant: Had borne the action of yourself, or else
Lieutenant: To him had left it solely.
AUFIDIUS: I understand thee well, and be thou sure,
AUFIDIUS: when he shall come to his account, he knows not
AUFIDIUS: What I can urge against him. Although it seems,
AUFIDIUS: And so he thinks, and is no less apparent
AUFIDIUS: To the vulgar eye, that he bears all things fairly.
AUFIDIUS: And shows good husbandry for the Volscian state,
AUFIDIUS: Fights dragon-like, and does achieve as soon
AUFIDIUS: As draw his sword, yet he hath left undone
AUFIDIUS: That which shall break his neck or hazard mine,
AUFIDIUS: Whene'er we come to our account.
Lieutenant: Sir, I beseech you, think you he'll carry Rome?
AUFIDIUS: All places yield to him ere he sits down,
AUFIDIUS: And the nobility of Rome are his:
AUFIDIUS: The senators and patricians love him too:
AUFIDIUS: The tribunes are no soldiers, and their people
AUFIDIUS: Will be as rash in the repeal, as hasty
AUFIDIUS: To expel him thence. I think he'll be to Rome
AUFIDIUS: As is the osprey to the fish, who takes it
AUFIDIUS: By sovereignty of nature. First he was
AUFIDIUS: A noble servant to them, but he could not
AUFIDIUS: Carry his honours even: whether 'twas pride,
AUFIDIUS: Which out of daily fortune ever taints
AUFIDIUS: The happy man, whether defect of judgment,
AUFIDIUS: To fail in the disposing of those chances
AUFIDIUS: Which he was lord of, or whether nature,
AUFIDIUS: Not to be other than one thing, not moving
AUFIDIUS: From the casque to the cushion, but commanding peace
AUFIDIUS: Even with the same austerity and garb
AUFIDIUS: As he controll'd the war, but one of these--
AUFIDIUS: As he hath spices of them all, not all,
AUFIDIUS: For I dare so far free him--made him fear'd,
AUFIDIUS: So hated, and so banish'd: but he has a merit,
AUFIDIUS: To choke it in the utterance. So our virtues
AUFIDIUS: Lie in the interpretation of the time:
AUFIDIUS: And power, unto itself most commendable,
AUFIDIUS: Hath not a tomb so evident as a chair
AUFIDIUS: To extol what it hath done.
AUFIDIUS: One fire drives out one fire, one nail, one nail,
AUFIDIUS: Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail.
AUFIDIUS: Come, let's away. When, Caius, Rome is thine,
AUFIDIUS: Thou art poor'st of all, then shortly art thou mine.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter MENENIUS, COMINIUS, SICINIUS, BRUTUS, and others
MENENIUS: No, I'll not go: you hear what he hath said
MENENIUS: Which was sometime his general, who loved him
MENENIUS: In a most dear particular. He call'd me father:
MENENIUS: But what o' that? Go, you that banish'd him,
MENENIUS: A mile before his tent fall down, and knee
MENENIUS: The way into his mercy: nay, if he coy'd
MENENIUS: To hear Cominius speak, I'll keep at home.
COMINIUS: He would not seem to know me.
MENENIUS: Do you hear?
COMINIUS: Yet one time he did call me by my name:
COMINIUS: I urged our old acquaintance, and the drops
COMINIUS: That we have bled together. Coriolanus
COMINIUS: He would not answer to: forbad all names,
COMINIUS: He was a kind of nothing, titleless,
COMINIUS: Till he had forged himself a name o' the fire
COMINIUS: Of burning Rome.
MENENIUS: Why, so: you have made good work!
MENENIUS: A pair of tribunes that have rack'd for Rome,
MENENIUS: To make coals cheap,--a noble memory!
COMINIUS: I minded him how royal 'twas to pardon
COMINIUS: When it was less expected: he replied,
COMINIUS: It was a bare petition of a state
COMINIUS: To one whom they had punish'd.
MENENIUS: Very well:
MENENIUS: Could he say less?
COMINIUS: I offer'd to awaken his regard
COMINIUS: For's private friends: his answer to me was,
COMINIUS: He could not stay to pick them in a pile
COMINIUS: Of noisome musty chaff: he said 'twas folly,
COMINIUS: For one poor grain or two, to leave unburnt,
COMINIUS: And still to nose the offence.
MENENIUS: For one poor grain or two!
MENENIUS: I am one of those, his mother, wife, his child,
MENENIUS: And this brave fellow too, we are the grains:
MENENIUS: You are the musty chaff, and you are smelt
MENENIUS: Above the moon: we must be burnt for you.
SICINIUS: Nay, pray, be patient: if you refuse your aid
SICINIUS: In this so never-needed help, yet do not
SICINIUS: Upbraid's with our distress. But, sure, if you
SICINIUS: Would be your country's pleader, your good tongue,
SICINIUS: More than the instant army we can make,
SICINIUS: Might stop our countryman.
MENENIUS: No, I'll not meddle.
SICINIUS: Pray you, go to him.
MENENIUS: What should I do?
BRUTUS: Only make trial what your love can do
BRUTUS: For Rome, towards Marcius.
MENENIUS: Well, and say that Marcius
MENENIUS: Return me, as Cominius is return'd,
MENENIUS: Unheard, what then?
MENENIUS: But as a discontented friend, grief-shot
MENENIUS: With his unkindness? say't be so?
SICINIUS: Yet your good will
SICINIUS: must have that thanks from Rome, after the measure
SICINIUS: As you intended well.
MENENIUS: I'll undertake 't:
MENENIUS: I think he'll hear me. Yet, to bite his lip
MENENIUS: And hum at good Cominius, much unhearts me.
MENENIUS: He was not taken well, he had not dined:
MENENIUS: The veins unfill'd, our blood is cold, and then
MENENIUS: We pout upon the morning, are unapt
MENENIUS: To give or to forgive, but when we have stuff'd
MENENIUS: These and these conveyances of our blood
MENENIUS: With wine and feeding, we have suppler souls
MENENIUS: Than in our priest-like fasts: therefore I'll watch him
MENENIUS: Till he be dieted to my request,
MENENIUS: And then I'll set upon him.
BRUTUS: You know the very road into his kindness,
BRUTUS: And cannot lose your way.
MENENIUS: Good faith, I'll prove him,
MENENIUS: Speed how it will. I shall ere long have knowledge
MENENIUS: Of my success.
NARRATOR: Exit
COMINIUS: He'll never hear him.
SICINIUS: Not?
COMINIUS: I tell you, he does sit in gold, his eye
COMINIUS: Red as 'twould burn Rome, and his injury
COMINIUS: The gaoler to his pity. I kneel'd before him,
COMINIUS: 'Twas very faintly he said 'Rise,' dismiss'd me
COMINIUS: Thus, with his speechless hand: what he would do,
COMINIUS: He sent in writing after me, what he would not,
COMINIUS: Bound with an oath to yield to his conditions:
COMINIUS: So that all hope is vain.
COMINIUS: Unless his noble mother, and his wife,
COMINIUS: Who, as I hear, mean to solicit him
COMINIUS: For mercy to his country. Therefore, let's hence,
COMINIUS: And with our fair entreaties haste them on.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Entrance of the Volscian camp before Rome.
COMINIUS: Two Sentinels on guard.
NARRATOR: Enter to them, MENENIUS
First Senator: Stay: whence are you?
Second Senator: Stand, and go back.
MENENIUS: You guard like men, 'tis well: but, by your leave,
MENENIUS: I am an officer of state, and come
MENENIUS: To speak with Coriolanus.
First Senator: From whence?
MENENIUS: From Rome.
First Senator: You may not pass, you must return: our general
First Senator: Will no more hear from thence.
Second Senator: You'll see your Rome embraced with fire before
Second Senator: You'll speak with Coriolanus.
MENENIUS: Good my friends,
MENENIUS: If you have heard your general talk of Rome,
MENENIUS: And of his friends there, it is lots to blanks,
MENENIUS: My name hath touch'd your ears it is Menenius.
First Senator: Be it so, go back: the virtue of your name
First Senator: Is not here passable.
MENENIUS: I tell thee, fellow,
MENENIUS: The general is my lover: I have been
MENENIUS: The book of his good acts, whence men have read
MENENIUS: His name unparallel'd, haply amplified,
MENENIUS: For I have ever verified my friends,
MENENIUS: Of whom he's chief, with all the size that verity
MENENIUS: Would without lapsing suffer: nay, sometimes,
MENENIUS: Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground,
MENENIUS: I have tumbled past the throw, and in his praise
MENENIUS: Have almost stamp'd the leasing: therefore, fellow,
MENENIUS: I must have leave to pass.
First Senator: Faith, sir, if you had told as many lies in his
First Senator: behalf as you have uttered words in your own, you
First Senator: should not pass here, no, though it were as virtuous
First Senator: to lie as to live chastely. Therefore, go back.
MENENIUS: Prithee, fellow, remember my name is Menenius,
MENENIUS: always factionary on the party of your general.
Second Senator: Howsoever you have been his liar, as you say you
Second Senator: have, I am one that, telling true under him, must
Second Senator: say, you cannot pass. Therefore, go back.
MENENIUS: Has he dined, canst thou tell? for I would not
MENENIUS: speak with him till after dinner.
First Senator: You are a Roman, are you?
MENENIUS: I am, as thy general is.
First Senator: Then you should hate Rome, as he does. Can you,
First Senator: when you have pushed out your gates the very
First Senator: defender of them, and, in a violent popular
First Senator: ignorance, given your enemy your shield, think to
First Senator: front his revenges with the easy groans of old
First Senator: women, the virginal palms of your daughters, or with
First Senator: the palsied intercession of such a decayed dotant as
First Senator: you seem to be? Can you think to blow out the
First Senator: intended fire your city is ready to flame in, with
First Senator: such weak breath as this? No, you are deceived,
First Senator: therefore, back to Rome, and prepare for your
First Senator: execution: you are condemned, our general has sworn
First Senator: you out of reprieve and pardon.
MENENIUS: Sirrah, if thy captain knew I were here, he would
MENENIUS: use me with estimation.
Second Senator: Come, my captain knows you not.
MENENIUS: I mean, thy general.
First Senator: My general cares not for you. Back, I say, go, lest
First Senator: I let forth your half-pint of blood, back,--that's
First Senator: the utmost of your having: back.
MENENIUS: Nay, but, fellow, fellow,--
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS and AUFIDIUS
CORIOLANUS: What's the matter?
MENENIUS: Now, you companion, I'll say an errand for you:
MENENIUS: You shall know now that I am in estimation, you shall
MENENIUS: perceive that a Jack guardant cannot office me from
MENENIUS: my son Coriolanus: guess, but by my entertainment
MENENIUS: with him, if thou standest not i' the state of
MENENIUS: hanging, or of some death more long in
MENENIUS: spectatorship, and crueller in suffering, behold now
MENENIUS: presently, and swoon for what's to come upon thee.
NARRATOR: To CORIOLANUS
MENENIUS: The glorious gods sit in hourly synod about thy
MENENIUS: particular prosperity, and love thee no worse than
MENENIUS: thy old father Menenius does! O my son, my son!
MENENIUS: thou art preparing fire for us, look thee, here's
MENENIUS: water to quench it. I was hardly moved to come to
MENENIUS: thee, but being assured none but myself could move
MENENIUS: thee, I have been blown out of your gates with
MENENIUS: sighs, and conjure thee to pardon Rome, and thy
MENENIUS: petitionary countrymen. The good gods assuage thy
MENENIUS: wrath, and turn the dregs of it upon this varlet
MENENIUS: here,--this, who, like a block, hath denied my
MENENIUS: access to thee.
CORIOLANUS: Away!
MENENIUS: How! away!
CORIOLANUS: Wife, mother, child, I know not. My affairs
CORIOLANUS: Are servanted to others: though I owe
CORIOLANUS: My revenge properly, my remission lies
CORIOLANUS: In Volscian breasts. That we have been familiar,
CORIOLANUS: Ingrate forgetfulness shall poison, rather
CORIOLANUS: Than pity note how much. Therefore, be gone.
CORIOLANUS: Mine ears against your suits are stronger than
CORIOLANUS: Your gates against my force. Yet, for I loved thee,
CORIOLANUS: Take this along, I writ it for thy sake
NARRATOR: Gives a letter
CORIOLANUS: And would have rent it. Another word, Menenius,
CORIOLANUS: I will not hear thee speak. This man, Aufidius,
CORIOLANUS: Was my beloved in Rome: yet thou behold'st!
AUFIDIUS: You keep a constant temper.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CORIOLANUS and AUFIDIUS
First Senator: Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
Second Senator: 'Tis a spell, you see, of much  power: you know the
Second Senator: way home again.
First Senator: Do you hear how we are shent for keeping your
First Senator: greatness back?
Second Senator: What cause, do you think, I have to swoon?
MENENIUS: I neither care for the world nor your general: for
MENENIUS: such things as you, I can scarce think there's any,
MENENIUS: ye're so slight. He that hath a will to die by
MENENIUS: himself fears it not from another: let your general
MENENIUS: do his worst. For you, be that you are, long, and
MENENIUS: your misery increase with your age! I say to you,
MENENIUS: as I was said to, Away!
NARRATOR: Exit
First Senator: A noble fellow, I warrant him.
Second Senator: The worthy fellow is our general: he's the rock, the
Second Senator: oak not to be wind-shaken.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The tent of Coriolanus.
NARRATOR: Enter CORIOLANUS, AUFIDIUS, and others
CORIOLANUS: We will before the walls of Rome tomorrow
CORIOLANUS: Set down our host. My partner in this action,
CORIOLANUS: You must report to the Volscian lords, how plainly
CORIOLANUS: I have borne this business.
AUFIDIUS: Only their ends
AUFIDIUS: You have respected, stopp'd your ears against
AUFIDIUS: The general suit of Rome, never admitted
AUFIDIUS: A private whisper, no, not with such friends
AUFIDIUS: That thought them sure of you.
CORIOLANUS: This last old man,
CORIOLANUS: Whom with a crack'd heart I have sent to Rome,
CORIOLANUS: Loved me above the measure of a father,
CORIOLANUS: Nay, godded me, indeed. Their latest refuge
CORIOLANUS: Was to send him, for whose old love I have,
CORIOLANUS: Though I show'd sourly to him, once more offer'd

CORIOLANUS: Will I lend ear to. Ha! what shout is this?
NARRATOR: Shout within
CORIOLANUS: Shall I be tempted to infringe my vow
CORIOLANUS: In the same time 'tis made? I will not.
NARRATOR: Enter in mourning habits, VIRGILIA, VOLUMNIA, leading young MARCIUS, VALERIA, and Attendants
CORIOLANUS: My wife comes foremost, then the honour'd mould
CORIOLANUS: Wherein this trunk was framed, and in her hand

CORIOLANUS: All bond and privilege of nature, break!
CORIOLANUS: Let it be virtuous to be obstinate.
CORIOLANUS: What is that curt'sy worth? or those doves' eyes,
CORIOLANUS: Which can make gods forsworn? I melt, and am not
CORIOLANUS: Of stronger earth than others. My mother bows,

CORIOLANUS: Hath an aspect of intercession, which
CORIOLANUS: Great nature cries 'Deny not.' let the Volsces

CORIOLANUS: As if a man were author of himself
CORIOLANUS: And knew no other kin.
VIRGILIA: My lord and husband!
CORIOLANUS: These eyes are not the same I wore in Rome.
VIRGILIA: The sorrow that delivers us thus changed

CORIOLANUS: Like a dull actor now,
CORIOLANUS: I have forgot my part, and I am out,
CORIOLANUS: Even to a full disgrace. Best of my flesh,
CORIOLANUS: Forgive my tyranny, but do not say
CORIOLANUS: For that 'Forgive our Romans.' O, a kiss

CORIOLANUS: Now, by the jealous queen of heaven, that kiss
CORIOLANUS: I carried from thee, dear, and my true lip
CORIOLANUS: Hath virgin'd it e'er since. You gods! I prate,
CORIOLANUS: And the most noble mother of the world
CORIOLANUS: Leave unsaluted: sink, my knee, i' the earth,
NARRATOR: Kneels
CORIOLANUS: Of thy deep duty more impression show
CORIOLANUS: Than that of common sons.
VOLUMNIA: O, stand up blest!
VOLUMNIA: Whilst, with no softer cushion than the flint,
VOLUMNIA: I kneel before thee, and unproperly
VOLUMNIA: Show duty, as mistaken all this while
VOLUMNIA: Between the child and parent.
NARRATOR: Kneels
CORIOLANUS: What is this?
CORIOLANUS: Your knees to me? to your corrected son?
CORIOLANUS: Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach
CORIOLANUS: Fillip the stars, then let the mutinous winds

CORIOLANUS: What cannot be, slight work.
VOLUMNIA: Thou art my warrior,
VOLUMNIA: I holp to frame thee. Do you know this lady?

CORIOLANUS: The moon of Rome, chaste as the icicle

VOLUMNIA: This is a poor epitome of yours,
VOLUMNIA: Which by the interpretation of full time
VOLUMNIA: May show like all yourself.
CORIOLANUS: The god of soldiers,
CORIOLANUS: With the consent of supreme Jove, inform
CORIOLANUS: Thy thoughts with nobleness, that thou mayst prove

VOLUMNIA: Your knee, sirrah.
CORIOLANUS: That's my brave boy!
VOLUMNIA: Even he, your wife, this lady, and myself,
VOLUMNIA: Are suitors to you.
CORIOLANUS: I beseech you, peace:
CORIOLANUS: Or, if you'ld ask, remember this before:
CORIOLANUS: The thing I have forsworn to grant may never
CORIOLANUS: Be held by you denials. Do not bid me
CORIOLANUS: Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate

CORIOLANUS: To ally my rages and revenges with
CORIOLANUS: Your colder reasons.
VOLUMNIA: O, no more, no more!
VOLUMNIA: You have said you will not grant us any thing,

CORIOLANUS: Aufidius, and you Volsces, mark, for we'll

VOLUMNIA: And state of bodies would bewray what life
VOLUMNIA: We have led since thy exile. Think with thyself
VOLUMNIA: How more unfortunate than all living women
VOLUMNIA: Are we come hither: since that thy sight,
VOLUMNIA: which should
VOLUMNIA: Make our eyes flow with joy, hearts dance
VOLUMNIA: with comforts,
VOLUMNIA: Constrains them weep and shake with fear and sorrow,
VOLUMNIA: Making the mother, wife and child to see
VOLUMNIA: The son, the husband and the father tearing
VOLUMNIA: His country's bowels out. And to poor we
VOLUMNIA: Thine enmity's most capital: thou barr'st us
VOLUMNIA: Our prayers to the gods, which is a comfort
VOLUMNIA: That all but we enjoy, for how can we,
VOLUMNIA: Alas, how can we for our country pray.
VOLUMNIA: Whereto we are bound, together with thy victory,
VOLUMNIA: Whereto we are bound? alack, or we must lose
VOLUMNIA: The country, our dear nurse, or else thy person,
VOLUMNIA: Our comfort in the country. We must find
VOLUMNIA: An evident calamity, though we had
VOLUMNIA: Our wish, which side should win: for either thou
VOLUMNIA: Must, as a foreign recreant, be led
VOLUMNIA: With manacles thorough our streets, or else
VOLUMNIA: triumphantly tread on thy country's ruin,
VOLUMNIA: And bear the palm for having bravely shed
VOLUMNIA: Thy wife and children's blood. For myself, son,
VOLUMNIA: I purpose not to wait on fortune till
VOLUMNIA: These wars determine: if I cannot persuade thee
VOLUMNIA: Rather to show a noble grace to both parts
VOLUMNIA: Than seek the end of one, thou shalt no sooner
VOLUMNIA: March to assault thy country than to tread--
VOLUMNIA: Trust to't, thou shalt not--on thy mother's womb,
VOLUMNIA: That brought thee to this world.
VIRGILIA: Ay, and mine,
VIRGILIA: That brought you forth this boy, to keep your name
VIRGILIA: Living to time.
Young MARCIUS: A' shall not tread on me,
Young MARCIUS: I'll run away till I am bigger, but then I'll fight.
CORIOLANUS: Not of a woman's tenderness to be,
CORIOLANUS: Requires nor child nor woman's face to see.
CORIOLANUS: I have sat too long.
NARRATOR: Rising
VOLUMNIA: Nay, go not from us thus.
VOLUMNIA: If it were so that our request did tend
VOLUMNIA: To save the Romans, thereby to destroy
VOLUMNIA: The Volsces whom you serve, you might condemn us,
VOLUMNIA: As poisonous of your honour: no, our suit
VOLUMNIA: Is that you reconcile them: while the Volsces
VOLUMNIA: May say 'This mercy we have show'd,' the Romans,
VOLUMNIA: 'This we received,' and each in either side
VOLUMNIA: Give the all-hail to thee and cry 'Be blest
VOLUMNIA: For making up this peace!' Thou know'st, great son,
VOLUMNIA: The end of war's uncertain, but this certain,
VOLUMNIA: That, if thou conquer Rome, the benefit
VOLUMNIA: Which thou shalt thereby reap is such a name,
VOLUMNIA: Whose repetition will be dogg'd with curses,
VOLUMNIA: Whose chronicle thus writ: 'The man was noble,
VOLUMNIA: But with his last attempt he wiped it out,
VOLUMNIA: Destroy'd his country, and his name remains
VOLUMNIA: To the ensuing age abhorr'd.' Speak to me, son:
VOLUMNIA: Thou hast affected the fine strains of honour,
VOLUMNIA: To imitate the graces of the gods,
VOLUMNIA: To tear with thunder the wide cheeks o' the air,
VOLUMNIA: And yet to charge thy sulphur with a bolt
VOLUMNIA: That should but rive an oak. Why dost not speak?
VOLUMNIA: Think'st thou it honourable for a noble man
VOLUMNIA: Still to remember wrongs? Daughter, speak you:
VOLUMNIA: He cares not for your weeping. Speak thou, boy:
VOLUMNIA: Perhaps thy childishness will move him more
VOLUMNIA: Than can our reasons. There's no man in the world
VOLUMNIA: More bound to 's mother, yet here he lets me prate
VOLUMNIA: Like one i' the stocks. Thou hast never in thy life
VOLUMNIA: Show'd thy dear mother any courtesy,
VOLUMNIA: When she, poor hen, fond of no second brood,
VOLUMNIA: Has cluck'd thee to the wars and safely home,
VOLUMNIA: Loaden with honour. Say my request's unjust,
VOLUMNIA: And spurn me back: but if it be not so,
VOLUMNIA: Thou art not honest, and the gods will plague thee,
VOLUMNIA: That thou restrain'st from me the duty which
VOLUMNIA: To a mother's part belongs. He turns away:
VOLUMNIA: Down, ladies, let us shame him with our knees.
VOLUMNIA: To his surname Coriolanus 'longs more pride
VOLUMNIA: Than pity to our prayers. Down: an end,
VOLUMNIA: This is the last: so we will home to Rome,
VOLUMNIA: And die among our neighbours. Nay, behold 's:
VOLUMNIA: This boy, that cannot tell what he would have
VOLUMNIA: But kneels and holds up bands for fellowship,
VOLUMNIA: Does reason our petition with more strength
VOLUMNIA: Than thou hast to deny 't. Come, let us go:
VOLUMNIA: This fellow had a Volscian to his mother,
VOLUMNIA: His wife is in Corioli and his child
VOLUMNIA: Like him by chance. Yet give us our dispatch:
VOLUMNIA: I am hush'd until our city be a-fire,
VOLUMNIA: And then I'll speak a little.
NARRATOR: He holds her by the hand, silent
CORIOLANUS: O mother, mother!
CORIOLANUS: What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope,
CORIOLANUS: The gods look down, and this unnatural scene
CORIOLANUS: They laugh at. O my mother, mother! O!
CORIOLANUS: You have won a happy victory to Rome,
CORIOLANUS: But, for your son,--believe it, O, believe it,
CORIOLANUS: Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd,
CORIOLANUS: If not most mortal to him. But, let it come.
CORIOLANUS: Aufidius, though I cannot make true wars,
CORIOLANUS: I'll frame convenient peace. Now, good Aufidius,
CORIOLANUS: Were you in my stead, would you have heard
CORIOLANUS: A mother less? or granted less, Aufidius?
AUFIDIUS: I was moved withal.
CORIOLANUS: I dare be sworn you were:
CORIOLANUS: And, sir, it is no little thing to make
CORIOLANUS: Mine eyes to sweat compassion. But, good sir,
CORIOLANUS: What peace you'll make, advise me: for my part,
CORIOLANUS: I'll not to Rome, I'll back with you, and pray you,
CORIOLANUS: Stand to me in this cause. O mother! wife!
AUFIDIUS: [Aside]  I am glad thou hast set thy mercy and
AUFIDIUS: thy honour
AUFIDIUS: At difference in thee: out of that I'll work
AUFIDIUS: Myself a former fortune.
NARRATOR: The Ladies make signs to CORIOLANUS
CORIOLANUS: Ay, by and by,
CORIOLANUS: To VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA,  and c
CORIOLANUS: But we will drink together, and you shall bear
CORIOLANUS: A better witness back than words, which we,
CORIOLANUS: On like conditions, will have counter-seal'd.
CORIOLANUS: Come, enter with us. Ladies, you deserve
CORIOLANUS: To have a temple built you: all the swords
CORIOLANUS: In Italy, and her confederate arms,
CORIOLANUS: Could not have made this peace.

NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Rome. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter MENENIUS and SICINIUS
MENENIUS: See you yond coign o' the Capitol, yond
MENENIUS: corner-stone?
SICINIUS: Why, what of that?

MENENIUS: little finger, there is some hope the ladies of
MENENIUS: Rome, especially his mother, may prevail with him.
MENENIUS: But I say there is no hope in't: our throats are
MENENIUS: sentenced and stay upon execution.
SICINIUS: Is't possible that so short a time can alter the
SICINIUS: condition of a man!
MENENIUS: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly,
MENENIUS: yet your butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown
MENENIUS: from man to dragon: he has wings, he's more than a
MENENIUS: creeping thing.
SICINIUS: He loved his mother dearly.
MENENIUS: So did he me: and he no more remembers his mother
MENENIUS: now than an eight-year-old horse. The tartness
MENENIUS: of his face sours ripe grapes: when he walks, he
MENENIUS: moves like an engine, and the ground shrinks before
MENENIUS: his treading: he is able to pierce a corslet with
MENENIUS: his eye, talks like a knell, and his hum is a
MENENIUS: battery. He sits in his state, as a thing made for
MENENIUS: Alexander. What he bids be done is finished with
MENENIUS: his bidding. He wants nothing of a god but eternity
MENENIUS: and a heaven to throne in.
SICINIUS: Yes, mercy, if you report him truly.
MENENIUS: I paint him in the character. Mark what mercy his
MENENIUS: mother shall bring from him: there is no more mercy
MENENIUS: in him than there is milk in a male tiger, that
MENENIUS: shall our poor city find: and all this is long of
MENENIUS: you.
SICINIUS: The gods be good unto us!
MENENIUS: No, in such a case the gods will not be good unto
MENENIUS: us. When we banished him, we respected not them,
MENENIUS: and, he returning to break our necks, they respect not us.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Sir, if you'ld save your life, fly to your house:
Messenger: The plebeians have got your fellow-tribune
Messenger: And hale him up and down, all swearing, if
Messenger: The Roman ladies bring not comfort home,
Messenger: They'll give him death by inches.
NARRATOR: Enter a second Messenger
SICINIUS: What's the news?

Second Messenger: The Volscians are dislodged, and Marcius gone:
Second Messenger: A merrier day did never yet greet Rome,
Second Messenger: No, not the expulsion of the Tarquins.
SICINIUS: Friend,

Second Messenger: As certain as I know the sun is fire:
Second Messenger: Where have you lurk'd, that you make doubt of it?
Second Messenger: Ne'er through an arch so hurried the blown tide,
Second Messenger: As the recomforted through the gates. Why, hark you!
Second Messenger: Trumpets, hautboys, drums beat, all together
Second Messenger: The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries and fifes,
Second Messenger: Tabours and cymbals and the shouting Romans,

NARRATOR: A shout within
MENENIUS: This is good news:
MENENIUS: I will go meet the ladies. This Volumnia
MENENIUS: Is worth of consuls, senators, patricians,
MENENIUS: A city full, of tribunes, such as you,
MENENIUS: A sea and land full. You have pray'd well to-day:
MENENIUS: This morning for ten thousand of your throats
MENENIUS: I'd not have given a doit. Hark, how they joy!
NARRATOR: Music still, with shouts
SICINIUS: First, the gods bless you for your tidings, next,
SICINIUS: Accept my thankfulness.
Second Messenger: Sir, we have all
Second Messenger: Great cause to give great thanks.
SICINIUS: They are near the city?
Second Messenger: Almost at point to enter.
SICINIUS: We will meet them,
SICINIUS: And help the joy.

NARRATOR: Enter three or four Conspirators of AUFIDIUS' faction

Third Conspirator: The people will remain uncertain whilst
Third Conspirator: 'Twixt you there's difference, but the fall of either

AUFIDIUS: And my pretext to strike at him admits
AUFIDIUS: A good construction. I raised him, and I pawn'd

AUFIDIUS: He bow'd his nature, never known before

Third Conspirator: Sir, his stoutness
Third Conspirator: When he did stand for consul, which he lost

AUFIDIUS: Being banish'd for't, he came unto my hearth,

AUFIDIUS: My best and freshest men, served his designments
AUFIDIUS: In mine own person, holp to reap the fame

AUFIDIUS: To do myself this wrong: till, at the last,
AUFIDIUS: I seem'd his follower, not partner, and
AUFIDIUS: He waged me with his countenance, as if
AUFIDIUS: I had been mercenary.
First Conspirator: So he did, my lord:
First Conspirator: The army marvell'd at it, and, in the last,
First Conspirator: When he had carried Rome and that we look'd
First Conspirator: For no less spoil than glory,--
AUFIDIUS: There was it:
AUFIDIUS: For which my sinews shall be stretch'd upon him.
AUFIDIUS: At a few drops of women's rheum, which are
AUFIDIUS: As cheap as lies, he sold the blood and labour

NARRATOR: Drums and trumpets sound, with great shouts of the People

First Conspirator: Splitting the air with noise.

First Lord: Where he was to begin and give away

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Britain. The garden of Cymbeline's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter two Gentlemen
First Gentleman: You do not meet a man but frowns: our bloods
First Gentleman: No more obey the heavens than our courtiers
First Gentleman: Still seem as does the king.
Second Gentleman: But what's the matter?
First Gentleman: His daughter, and the heir of's kingdom, whom
First Gentleman: He purposed to his wife's sole son--a widow
First Gentleman: That late he married--hath referr'd herself
First Gentleman: Unto a poor but worthy gentleman: she's wedded,
First Gentleman: Her husband banish'd, she imprison'd: all
First Gentleman: Is outward sorrow, though I think the king
First Gentleman: Be touch'd at very heart.
Second Gentleman: None but the king?
First Gentleman: He that hath lost her too, so is the queen,
First Gentleman: That most desired the match, but not a courtier,
First Gentleman: Although they wear their faces to the bent
First Gentleman: Of the king's look's, hath a heart that is not
First Gentleman: Glad at the thing they scowl at.
Second Gentleman: And why so?
First Gentleman: He that hath miss'd the princess is a thing
First Gentleman: Too bad for bad report: and he that hath her--
First Gentleman: I mean, that married her, alack, good man!
First Gentleman: And therefore banish'd--is a creature such
First Gentleman: As, to seek through the regions of the earth
First Gentleman: For one his like, there would be something failing
First Gentleman: In him that should compare. I do not think
First Gentleman: So fair an outward and such stuff within
First Gentleman: Endows a man but he.
Second Gentleman: You speak him far.
First Gentleman: I do extend him, sir, within himself,
First Gentleman: Crush him together rather than unfold
First Gentleman: His measure duly.
Second Gentleman: What's his name and birth?
First Gentleman: I cannot delve him to the root: his father
First Gentleman: Was call'd Sicilius, who did join his honour
First Gentleman: Against the Romans with Cassibelan,
First Gentleman: But had his titles by Tenantius whom
First Gentleman: He served with glory and admired success,
First Gentleman: So gain'd the sur-addition Leonatus,
First Gentleman: And had, besides this gentleman in question,
First Gentleman: Two other sons, who in the wars o' the time
First Gentleman: Died with their swords in hand, for which
First Gentleman: their father,
First Gentleman: Then old and fond of issue, took such sorrow
First Gentleman: That he quit being, and his gentle lady,
First Gentleman: Big of this gentleman our theme, deceased
First Gentleman: As he was born. The king he takes the babe
First Gentleman: To his protection, calls him Posthumus Leonatus,
First Gentleman: Breeds him and makes him of his bed-chamber,
First Gentleman: Puts to him all the learnings that his time
First Gentleman: Could make him the receiver of, which he took,
First Gentleman: As we do air, fast as 'twas minister'd,
First Gentleman: And in's spring became a harvest, lived in court--
First Gentleman: Which rare it is to do--most praised, most loved,
First Gentleman: A sample to the youngest, to the more mature
First Gentleman: A glass that feated them, and to the graver
First Gentleman: A child that guided dotards, to his mistress,
First Gentleman: For whom he now is banish'd, her own price
First Gentleman: Proclaims how she esteem'd him and his virtue,
First Gentleman: By her election may be truly read
First Gentleman: What kind of man he is.
Second Gentleman: I honour him
Second Gentleman: Even out of your report. But, pray you, tell me,
Second Gentleman: Is she sole child to the king?
First Gentleman: His only child.
First Gentleman: He had two sons: if this be worth your hearing,
First Gentleman: Mark it: the eldest of them at three years old,
First Gentleman: I' the swathing-clothes the other, from their nursery
First Gentleman: Were stol'n, and to this hour no guess in knowledge
First Gentleman: Which way they went.
Second Gentleman: How long is this ago?
First Gentleman: Some twenty years.
Second Gentleman: That a king's children should be so convey'd,
Second Gentleman: So slackly guarded, and the search so slow,
Second Gentleman: That could not trace them!
First Gentleman: Howsoe'er 'tis strange,
First Gentleman: Or that the negligence may well be laugh'd at,
First Gentleman: Yet is it true, sir.
Second Gentleman: I do well believe you.
First Gentleman: We must forbear: here comes the gentleman,
First Gentleman: The queen, and princess.
