QUEEN: That I mean to thee. Tell thy mistress how
QUEEN: The case stands with her, do't as from thyself.
QUEEN: Think what a chance thou changest on, but think
QUEEN: Thou hast thy mistress still, to boot, my son,
QUEEN: Who shall take notice of thee: I'll move the king
QUEEN: To any shape of thy preferment such
QUEEN: As thou'lt desire, and then myself, I chiefly,
QUEEN: That set thee on to this desert, am bound
QUEEN: To load thy merit richly. Call my women:
QUEEN: Think on my words.
NARRATOR: Exit PISANIO
QUEEN: A sly and constant knave,
QUEEN: Not to be shaked, the agent for his master
QUEEN: And the remembrancer of her to hold
QUEEN: The hand-fast to her lord. I have given him that
QUEEN: Which, if he take, shall quite unpeople her
QUEEN: Of liegers for her sweet, and which she after,
QUEEN: Except she bend her humour, shall be assured
QUEEN: To taste of too.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PISANIO and Ladies
QUEEN: So, so: well done, well done:
QUEEN: The violets, cowslips, and the primroses,
QUEEN: Bear to my closet. Fare thee well, Pisanio,
QUEEN: Think on my words.
NARRATOR: Exeunt QUEEN and Ladies
PISANIO: And shall do:
PISANIO: But when to my good lord I prove untrue,
PISANIO: I'll choke myself: there's all I'll do for you.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The same. Another room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter IMOGEN
IMOGEN: A father cruel, and a step-dame false,
IMOGEN: A foolish suitor to a wedded lady,
IMOGEN: That hath her husband banish'd,--O, that husband!
IMOGEN: My supreme crown of grief! and those repeated
IMOGEN: Vexations of it! Had I been thief-stol'n,
IMOGEN: As my two brothers, happy! but most miserable
IMOGEN: Is the desire that's glorious: blest be those,
IMOGEN: How mean soe'er, that have their honest wills,
IMOGEN: Which seasons comfort. Who may this be? Fie!
NARRATOR: Enter PISANIO and IACHIMO
PISANIO: Madam, a noble gentleman of Rome,
PISANIO: Comes from my lord with letters.
IACHIMO: Change you, madam?
IACHIMO: The worthy Leonatus is in safety
IACHIMO: And greets your highness dearly.
NARRATOR: Presents a letter
IMOGEN: Thanks, good sir:
IMOGEN: You're kindly welcome.
IACHIMO: [Aside]  All of her that is out of door most rich!
IACHIMO: If she be furnish'd with a mind so rare,
IACHIMO: She is alone the Arabian bird, and I
IACHIMO: Have lost the wager. Boldness be my friend!
IACHIMO: Arm me, audacity, from head to foot!
IACHIMO: Or, like the Parthian, I shall flying fight,
IACHIMO: Rather directly fly.
IMOGEN: [Reads]  'He is one of the noblest note, to whose
IMOGEN: kindnesses I am most infinitely tied. Reflect upon
IMOGEN: him accordingly, as you value your trust--
IMOGEN: LEONATUS.'
IMOGEN: So far I read aloud:
IMOGEN: But even the very middle of my heart
IMOGEN: Is warm'd by the rest, and takes it thankfully.
IMOGEN: You are as welcome, worthy sir, as I
IMOGEN: Have words to bid you, and shall find it so
IMOGEN: In all that I can do.
IACHIMO: Thanks, fairest lady.
IACHIMO: What, are men mad? Hath nature given them eyes
IACHIMO: To see this vaulted arch, and the rich crop
IACHIMO: Of sea and land, which can distinguish 'twixt
IACHIMO: The fiery orbs above and the twinn'd stones
IACHIMO: Upon the number'd beach? and can we not
IACHIMO: Partition make with spectacles so precious
IACHIMO: 'Twixt fair and foul?
IMOGEN: What makes your admiration?
IACHIMO: It cannot be i' the eye, for apes and monkeys
IACHIMO: 'Twixt two such shes would chatter this way and
IACHIMO: Contemn with mows the other, nor i' the judgment,
IACHIMO: For idiots in this case of favour would
IACHIMO: Be wisely definite, nor i' the appetite,
IACHIMO: Sluttery to such neat excellence opposed
IACHIMO: Should make desire vomit emptiness,
IACHIMO: Not so allured to feed.
IMOGEN: What is the matter, trow?
IACHIMO: The cloyed will,
IACHIMO: That satiate yet unsatisfied desire, that tub
IACHIMO: Both fill'd and running, ravening first the lamb
IACHIMO: Longs after for the garbage.
IMOGEN: What, dear sir,
IMOGEN: Thus raps you? Are you well?
IACHIMO: Thanks, madam, well.
NARRATOR: To PISANIO
IACHIMO: Beseech you, sir, desire
IACHIMO: My man's abode where I did leave him: he
IACHIMO: Is strange and peevish.
PISANIO: I was going, sir,
PISANIO: To give him welcome.
NARRATOR: Exit
IMOGEN: Continues well my lord? His health, beseech you?
IACHIMO: Well, madam.
IMOGEN: Is he disposed to mirth? I hope he is.
IACHIMO: Exceeding pleasant, none a stranger there
IACHIMO: So merry and so gamesome: he is call'd
IACHIMO: The Briton reveller.
IMOGEN: When he was here,
IMOGEN: He did incline to sadness, and oft-times
IMOGEN: Not knowing why.
IACHIMO: I never saw him sad.
IACHIMO: There is a Frenchman his companion, one
IACHIMO: An eminent monsieur, that, it seems, much loves
IACHIMO: A Gallian girl at home, he furnaces
IACHIMO: The thick sighs from him, whiles the jolly Briton--
IACHIMO: Your lord, I mean--laughs from's free lungs, cries 'O,
IACHIMO: Can my sides hold, to think that man, who knows
IACHIMO: By history, report, or his own proof,
IACHIMO: What woman is, yea, what she cannot choose
IACHIMO: But must be, will his free hours languish for
IACHIMO: Assured bondage?'
IMOGEN: Will my lord say so?
IACHIMO: Ay, madam, with his eyes in flood with laughter:
IACHIMO: It is a recreation to be by
IACHIMO: And hear him mock the Frenchman. But, heavens know,
IACHIMO: Some men are much to blame.
IMOGEN: Not he, I hope.
IACHIMO: Not he: but yet heaven's bounty towards him might
IACHIMO: Be used more thankfully. In himself, 'tis much,
IACHIMO: In you, which I account his beyond all talents,
IACHIMO: Whilst I am bound to wonder, I am bound
IACHIMO: To pity too.
IMOGEN: What do you pity, sir?
IACHIMO: Two creatures heartily.
IMOGEN: Am I one, sir?
IMOGEN: You look on me: what wreck discern you in me
IMOGEN: Deserves your pity?
IACHIMO: Lamentable! What,
IACHIMO: To hide me from the radiant sun and solace
IACHIMO: I' the dungeon by a snuff?
IMOGEN: I pray you, sir,
IMOGEN: Deliver with more openness your answers
IMOGEN: To my demands. Why do you pity me?
IACHIMO: That others do--
IACHIMO: I was about to say--enjoy your--But
IACHIMO: It is an office of the gods to venge it,
IACHIMO: Not mine to speak on 't.
IMOGEN: You do seem to know
IMOGEN: Something of me, or what concerns me: pray you,--
IMOGEN: Since doubling things go ill often hurts more
IMOGEN: Than to be sure they do, for certainties
IMOGEN: Either are past remedies, or, timely knowing,
IMOGEN: The remedy then born--discover to me
IMOGEN: What both you spur and stop.
IACHIMO: Had I this cheek
IACHIMO: To bathe my lips upon, this hand, whose touch,
IACHIMO: Whose every touch, would force the feeler's soul
IACHIMO: To the oath of loyalty, this object, which
IACHIMO: Takes prisoner the wild motion of mine eye,
IACHIMO: Fixing it only here, should I, damn'd then,
IACHIMO: Slaver with lips as common as the stairs
IACHIMO: That mount the Capitol, join gripes with hands
IACHIMO: Made hard with hourly falsehood--falsehood, as
IACHIMO: With labour, then by-peeping in an eye
IACHIMO: Base and unlustrous as the smoky light
IACHIMO: That's fed with stinking tallow, it were fit
IACHIMO: That all the plagues of hell should at one time
IACHIMO: Encounter such revolt.
IMOGEN: My lord, I fear,
IMOGEN: Has forgot Britain.
IACHIMO: And himself. Not I,
IACHIMO: Inclined to this intelligence, pronounce
IACHIMO: The beggary of his change, but 'tis your graces
IACHIMO: That from pay mutest conscience to my tongue
IACHIMO: Charms this report out.
IMOGEN: Let me hear no more.
IACHIMO: O dearest soul! your cause doth strike my heart
IACHIMO: With pity, that doth make me sick. A lady
IACHIMO: So fair, and fasten'd to an empery,
IACHIMO: Would make the great'st king double,--to be partner'd
IACHIMO: With tomboys hired with that self-exhibition
IACHIMO: Which your own coffers yield! with diseased ventures
IACHIMO: That play with all infirmities for gold
IACHIMO: Which rottenness can lend nature! such boil'd stuff
IACHIMO: As well might poison poison! Be revenged,
IACHIMO: Or she that bore you was no queen, and you
IACHIMO: Recoil from your great stock.
IMOGEN: Revenged!
IMOGEN: How should I be revenged? If this be true,--
IMOGEN: As I have such a heart that both mine ears
IMOGEN: Must not in haste abuse--if it be true,
IMOGEN: How should I be revenged?
IACHIMO: Should he make me
IACHIMO: Live, like Diana's priest, betwixt cold sheets,
IACHIMO: Whiles he is vaulting variable ramps,
IACHIMO: In your despite, upon your purse? Revenge it.
IACHIMO: I dedicate myself to your sweet pleasure,
IACHIMO: More noble than that runagate to your bed,
IACHIMO: And will continue fast to your affection,
IACHIMO: Still close as sure.
IMOGEN: What, ho, Pisanio!
IACHIMO: Let me my service tender on your lips.
IMOGEN: Away! I do condemn mine ears that have
IMOGEN: So long attended thee. If thou wert honourable,
IMOGEN: Thou wouldst have told this tale for virtue, not
IMOGEN: For such an end thou seek'st,--as base as strange.
IMOGEN: Thou wrong'st a gentleman, who is as far
IMOGEN: From thy report as thou from honour, and
IMOGEN: Solicit'st here a lady that disdains
IMOGEN: Thee and the devil alike. What ho, Pisanio!
IMOGEN: The king my father shall be made acquainted
IMOGEN: Of thy assault: if he shall think it fit,
IMOGEN: A saucy stranger in his court to mart
IMOGEN: As in a Romish stew and to expound
IMOGEN: His beastly mind to us, he hath a court
IMOGEN: He little cares for and a daughter who
IMOGEN: He not respects at all. What, ho, Pisanio!
IACHIMO: O happy Leonatus! I may say
IACHIMO: The credit that thy lady hath of thee
IACHIMO: Deserves thy trust, and thy most perfect goodness
IACHIMO: Her assured credit. Blessed live you long!
IACHIMO: A lady to the worthiest sir that ever
IACHIMO: Country call'd his! and you his mistress, only
IACHIMO: For the most worthiest fit! Give me your pardon.
IACHIMO: I have spoke this, to know if your affiance
IACHIMO: Were deeply rooted, and shall make your lord,
IACHIMO: That which he is, new o'er: and he is one
IACHIMO: The truest manner'd, such a holy witch
IACHIMO: That he enchants societies into him,
IACHIMO: Half all men's hearts are his.
IMOGEN: You make amends.
IACHIMO: He sits 'mongst men like a descended god:
IACHIMO: He hath a kind of honour sets him off,
IACHIMO: More than a mortal seeming. Be not angry,
IACHIMO: Most mighty princess, that I have adventured
IACHIMO: To try your taking a false report, which hath
IACHIMO: Honour'd with confirmation your great judgment
IACHIMO: In the election of a sir so rare,
IACHIMO: Which you know cannot err: the love I bear him
IACHIMO: Made me to fan you thus, but the gods made you,
IACHIMO: Unlike all others, chaffless. Pray, your pardon.
IMOGEN: All's well, sir: take my power i' the court
IMOGEN: for yours.
IACHIMO: My humble thanks. I had almost forgot
IACHIMO: To entreat your grace but in a small request,
IACHIMO: And yet of moment to, for it concerns
IACHIMO: Your lord, myself and other noble friends,
IACHIMO: Are partners in the business.
IMOGEN: Pray, what is't?
IACHIMO: Some dozen Romans of us and your lord--
IACHIMO: The best feather of our wing--have mingled sums
IACHIMO: To buy a present for the emperor
IACHIMO: Which I, the factor for the rest, have done
IACHIMO: In France: 'tis plate of rare device, and jewels
IACHIMO: Of rich and exquisite form, their values great,
IACHIMO: And I am something curious, being strange,
IACHIMO: To have them in safe stowage: may it please you
IACHIMO: To take them in protection?
IMOGEN: Willingly,
IMOGEN: And pawn mine honour for their safety: since
IMOGEN: My lord hath interest in them, I will keep them
IMOGEN: In my bedchamber.
IACHIMO: They are in a trunk,
IACHIMO: Attended by my men: I will make bold
IACHIMO: To send them to you, only for this night,
IACHIMO: I must aboard to-morrow.
IMOGEN: O, no, no.
IACHIMO: Yes, I beseech, or I shall short my word
IACHIMO: By lengthening my return. From Gallia
IACHIMO: I cross'd the seas on purpose and on promise
IACHIMO: To see your grace.
IMOGEN: I thank you for your pains:
IMOGEN: But not away to-morrow!
IACHIMO: O, I must, madam:
IACHIMO: Therefore I shall beseech you, if you please
IACHIMO: To greet your lord with writing, do't to-night:
IACHIMO: I have outstood my time, which is material
IACHIMO: To the tender of our present.
IMOGEN: I will write.
IMOGEN: Send your trunk to me, it shall safe be kept,
IMOGEN: And truly yielded you. You're very welcome.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Britain. Before Cymbeline's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CLOTEN and two Lords
CLOTEN: Was there ever man had such luck! when I kissed the
CLOTEN: jack, upon an up-cast to be hit away! I had a
CLOTEN: hundred pound on't: and then a whoreson jackanapes
CLOTEN: must take me up for swearing, as if I borrowed mine
CLOTEN: oaths of him and might not spend them at my pleasure.
First Lord: What got he by that? You have broke his pate with
First Lord: your bowl.
Second Lord: [Aside]  If his wit had been like him that broke it,
Second Lord: it would have run all out.
CLOTEN: When a gentleman is disposed to swear, it is not for
CLOTEN: any standers-by to curtail his oaths, ha?
Second Lord: No my lord,
NARRATOR: Aside
Second Lord: nor crop the ears of them.
CLOTEN: Whoreson dog! I give him satisfaction?
CLOTEN: Would he had been one of my rank!
Second Lord: [Aside]  To have smelt like a fool.
CLOTEN: I am not vexed more at any thing in the earth: a
CLOTEN: pox on't! I had rather not be so noble as I am,
CLOTEN: they dare not fight with me, because of the queen my
CLOTEN: mother: every Jack-slave hath his bellyful of
CLOTEN: fighting, and I must go up and down like a cock that
CLOTEN: nobody can match.
Second Lord: [Aside]  You are cock and capon too, and you crow,
Second Lord: cock, with your comb on.
CLOTEN: Sayest thou?
Second Lord: It is not fit your lordship should undertake every
Second Lord: companion that you give offence to.
CLOTEN: No, I know that: but it is fit I should commit
CLOTEN: offence to my inferiors.
Second Lord: Ay, it is fit for your lordship only.
CLOTEN: Why, so I say.
First Lord: Did you hear of a stranger that's come to court to-night?
CLOTEN: A stranger, and I not know on't!
Second Lord: [Aside]  He's a strange fellow himself, and knows it
Second Lord: not.
First Lord: There's an Italian come, and, 'tis thought, one of
First Lord: Leonatus' friends.
CLOTEN: Leonatus! a banished rascal, and he's another,
CLOTEN: whatsoever he be. Who told you of this stranger?
First Lord: One of your lordship's pages.
CLOTEN: Is it fit I went to look upon him? is there no
CLOTEN: derogation in't?
Second Lord: You cannot derogate, my lord.
CLOTEN: Not easily, I think.
Second Lord: [Aside]  You are a fool granted, therefore your
Second Lord: issues, being foolish, do not derogate.
CLOTEN: Come, I'll go see this Italian: what I have lost
CLOTEN: to-day at bowls I'll win to-night of him. Come, go.
Second Lord: I'll attend your lordship.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CLOTEN and First Lord
Second Lord: That such a crafty devil as is his mother
Second Lord: Should yield the world this ass! a woman that
Second Lord: Bears all down with her brain, and this her son
Second Lord: Cannot take two from twenty, for his heart,
Second Lord: And leave eighteen. Alas, poor princess,
Second Lord: Thou divine Imogen, what thou endurest,
Second Lord: Betwixt a father by thy step-dame govern'd,
Second Lord: A mother hourly coining plots, a wooer
Second Lord: More hateful than the foul expulsion is
Second Lord: Of thy dear husband, than that horrid act
Second Lord: Of the divorce he'ld make! The heavens hold firm
Second Lord: The walls of thy dear honour, keep unshaked
Second Lord: That temple, thy fair mind, that thou mayst stand,
Second Lord: To enjoy thy banish'd lord and this great land!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Imogen's bedchamber in Cymbeline's palace:
Second Lord: a trunk in one corner of it.
Second Lord: IMOGEN in bed, reading, a Lady attending
IMOGEN: Who's there? my woman Helen?
Lady: Please you, madam
IMOGEN: What hour is it?
Lady: Almost midnight, madam.
IMOGEN: I have read three hours then: mine eyes are weak:
IMOGEN: Fold down the leaf where I have left: to bed:
IMOGEN: Take not away the taper, leave it burning,
IMOGEN: And if thou canst awake by four o' the clock,
IMOGEN: I prithee, call me. Sleep hath seized me wholly
NARRATOR: Exit Lady
IMOGEN: To your protection I commend me, gods.
IMOGEN: From fairies and the tempters of the night
IMOGEN: Guard me, beseech ye.
NARRATOR: Sleeps. IACHIMO comes from the trunk
IACHIMO: The crickets sing, and man's o'er-labour'd sense
IACHIMO: Repairs itself by rest. Our Tarquin thus
IACHIMO: Did softly press the rushes, ere he waken'd
IACHIMO: The chastity he wounded. Cytherea,
IACHIMO: How bravely thou becomest thy bed, fresh lily,
IACHIMO: And whiter than the sheets! That I might touch!
IACHIMO: But kiss, one kiss! Rubies unparagon'd,
IACHIMO: How dearly they do't! 'Tis her breathing that
IACHIMO: Perfumes the chamber thus: the flame o' the taper
IACHIMO: Bows toward her, and would under-peep her lids,
IACHIMO: To see the enclosed lights, now canopied
IACHIMO: Under these windows, white and azure laced
IACHIMO: With blue of heaven's own tinct. But my design,
IACHIMO: To note the chamber: I will write all down:
IACHIMO: Such and such pictures, there the window, such
IACHIMO: The adornment of her bed, the arras, figures,
IACHIMO: Why, such and such, and the contents o' the story.
IACHIMO: Ah, but some natural notes about her body,
IACHIMO: Above ten thousand meaner moveables
IACHIMO: Would testify, to enrich mine inventory.
IACHIMO: O sleep, thou ape of death, lie dull upon her!
IACHIMO: And be her sense but as a monument,
IACHIMO: Thus in a chapel lying! Come off, come off:
NARRATOR: Taking off her bracelet
IACHIMO: As slippery as the Gordian knot was hard!
IACHIMO: 'Tis mine, and this will witness outwardly,
IACHIMO: As strongly as the conscience does within,
IACHIMO: To the madding of her lord. On her left breast
IACHIMO: A mole cinque-spotted, like the crimson drops
IACHIMO: I' the bottom of a cowslip: here's a voucher,
IACHIMO: Stronger than ever law could make: this secret
IACHIMO: Will force him think I have pick'd the lock and ta'en
IACHIMO: The treasure of her honour. No more. To what end?
IACHIMO: Why should I write this down, that's riveted,
IACHIMO: Screw'd to my memory? She hath been reading late
IACHIMO: The tale of Tereus, here the leaf's turn'd down
IACHIMO: Where Philomel gave up. I have enough:
IACHIMO: To the trunk again, and shut the spring of it.
IACHIMO: Swift, swift, you dragons of the night, that dawning
IACHIMO: May bare the raven's eye! I lodge in fear,
IACHIMO: Though this a heavenly angel, hell is here.
NARRATOR: Clock strikes
IACHIMO: One, two, three: time, time!
NARRATOR: Goes into the trunk. The scene closes
nan: An ante-chamber adjoining Imogen's apartments.
NARRATOR: Enter CLOTEN and Lords
First Lord: Your lordship is the most patient man in loss, the
First Lord: most coldest that ever turned up ace.
CLOTEN: It would make any man cold to lose.
First Lord: But not every man patient after the noble temper of
First Lord: your lordship. You are most hot and furious when you win.
CLOTEN: Winning will put any man into courage. If I could
CLOTEN: get this foolish Imogen, I should have gold enough.
CLOTEN: It's almost morning, is't not?
First Lord: Day, my lord.
CLOTEN: I would this music would come: I am advised to give
CLOTEN: her music o' mornings, they say it will penetrate.
NARRATOR: Enter Musicians
CLOTEN: Come on, tune: if you can penetrate her with your
CLOTEN: fingering, so, we'll try with tongue too: if none
CLOTEN: will do, let her remain, but I'll never give o'er.
CLOTEN: First, a very excellent good-conceited thing,
CLOTEN: after, a wonderful sweet air, with admirable rich
CLOTEN: words to it: and then let her consider.
NARRATOR: SONG
CLOTEN: Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings,
CLOTEN: And Phoebus 'gins arise,
CLOTEN: His steeds to water at those springs
CLOTEN: On chaliced flowers that lies,
CLOTEN: And winking Mary-buds begin
CLOTEN: To ope their golden eyes:
CLOTEN: With every thing that pretty is,
CLOTEN: My lady sweet, arise:
CLOTEN: Arise, arise.
CLOTEN: So, get you gone. If this penetrate, I will
CLOTEN: consider your music the better: if it do not, it is
CLOTEN: a vice in her ears, which horse-hairs and
CLOTEN: calves'-guts, nor the voice of unpaved eunuch to
CLOTEN: boot, can never amend.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Musicians
Second Lord: Here comes the king.
CLOTEN: I am glad I was up so late, for that's the reason I
CLOTEN: was up so early: he cannot choose but take this
CLOTEN: service I have done fatherly.
NARRATOR: Enter CYMBELINE and QUEEN
CLOTEN: Good morrow to your majesty and to my gracious mother.
CYMBELINE: Attend you here the door of our stern daughter?
CYMBELINE: Will she not forth?
CLOTEN: I have assailed her with music, but she vouchsafes no notice.
CYMBELINE: The exile of her minion is too new,
CYMBELINE: She hath not yet forgot him: some more time
CYMBELINE: Must wear the print of his remembrance out,
CYMBELINE: And then she's yours.
QUEEN: You are most bound to the king,
QUEEN: Who lets go by no vantages that may
QUEEN: Prefer you to his daughter. Frame yourself
QUEEN: To orderly soliciting, and be friended
QUEEN: With aptness of the season, make denials
QUEEN: Increase your services, so seem as if
QUEEN: You were inspired to do those duties which
QUEEN: You tender to her, that you in all obey her,
QUEEN: Save when command to your dismission tends,
QUEEN: And therein you are senseless.
CLOTEN: Senseless! not so.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: So like you, sir, ambassadors from Rome,
Messenger: The one is Caius Lucius.
CYMBELINE: A worthy fellow,
CYMBELINE: Albeit he comes on angry purpose now,
CYMBELINE: But that's no fault of his: we must receive him
CYMBELINE: According to the honour of his sender,
CYMBELINE: And towards himself, his goodness forespent on us,
CYMBELINE: We must extend our notice. Our dear son,
CYMBELINE: When you have given good morning to your mistress,
CYMBELINE: Attend the queen and us, we shall have need
CYMBELINE: To employ you towards this Roman. Come, our queen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but CLOTEN
CLOTEN: If she be up, I'll speak with her, if not,
CLOTEN: Let her lie still and dream.
NARRATOR: Knocks
CLOTEN: By your leave, ho!
CLOTEN: I Know her women are about her: what
CLOTEN: If I do line one of their hands? 'Tis gold
CLOTEN: Which buys admittance, oft it doth, yea, and makes
CLOTEN: Diana's rangers false themselves, yield up
CLOTEN: Their deer to the stand o' the stealer, and 'tis gold
CLOTEN: Which makes the true man kill'd and saves the thief,
CLOTEN: Nay, sometime hangs both thief and true man: what
CLOTEN: Can it not do and undo? I will make
CLOTEN: One of her women lawyer to me, for
CLOTEN: I yet not understand the case myself.
NARRATOR: Knocks
CLOTEN: By your leave.
NARRATOR: Enter a Lady
Lady: Who's there that knocks?
CLOTEN: A gentleman.
Lady: No more?
CLOTEN: Yes, and a gentlewoman's son.
Lady: That's more
Lady: Than some, whose tailors are as dear as yours,
Lady: Can justly boast of. What's your lordship's pleasure?
CLOTEN: Your lady's person: is she ready?
Lady: Ay,
Lady: To keep her chamber.
CLOTEN: There is gold for you,
CLOTEN: Sell me your good report.
Lady: How! my good name? or to report of you
Lady: What I shall think is good?--The princess!
NARRATOR: Enter IMOGEN
CLOTEN: Good morrow, fairest: sister, your sweet hand.
NARRATOR: Exit Lady
IMOGEN: Good morrow, sir. You lay out too much pains
IMOGEN: For purchasing but trouble, the thanks I give
IMOGEN: Is telling you that I am poor of thanks
IMOGEN: And scarce can spare them.
CLOTEN: Still, I swear I love you.
IMOGEN: If you but said so, 'twere as deep with me:
IMOGEN: If you swear still, your recompense is still
IMOGEN: That I regard it not.
CLOTEN: This is no answer.
IMOGEN: But that you shall not say I yield being silent,
IMOGEN: I would not speak. I pray you, spare me: 'faith,
IMOGEN: I shall unfold equal discourtesy
IMOGEN: To your best kindness: one of your great knowing
IMOGEN: Should learn, being taught, forbearance.
CLOTEN: To leave you in your madness, 'twere my sin:
CLOTEN: I will not.
IMOGEN: Fools are not mad folks.
CLOTEN: Do you call me fool?
IMOGEN: As I am mad, I do:
IMOGEN: If you'll be patient, I'll no more be mad,
IMOGEN: That cures us both. I am much sorry, sir,
IMOGEN: You put me to forget a lady's manners,
IMOGEN: By being so verbal: and learn now, for all,
IMOGEN: That I, which know my heart, do here pronounce,
IMOGEN: By the very truth of it, I care not for you,
IMOGEN: And am so near the lack of charity--
IMOGEN: To accuse myself--I hate you, which I had rather
IMOGEN: You felt than make't my boast.
CLOTEN: You sin against
CLOTEN: Obedience, which you owe your father. For
CLOTEN: The contract you pretend with that base wretch,
CLOTEN: One bred of alms and foster'd with cold dishes,
CLOTEN: With scraps o' the court, it is no contract, none:
CLOTEN: And though it be allow'd in meaner parties--
CLOTEN: Yet who than he more mean?--to knit their souls,
CLOTEN: On whom there is no more dependency
CLOTEN: But brats and beggary, in self-figured knot,
CLOTEN: Yet you are curb'd from that enlargement by
CLOTEN: The consequence o' the crown, and must not soil
CLOTEN: The precious note of it with a base slave.
CLOTEN: A hilding for a livery, a squire's cloth,
CLOTEN: A pantler, not so eminent.
IMOGEN: Profane fellow
IMOGEN: Wert thou the son of Jupiter and no more
IMOGEN: But what thou art besides, thou wert too base
IMOGEN: To be his groom: thou wert dignified enough,
IMOGEN: Even to the point of envy, if 'twere made
IMOGEN: Comparative for your virtues, to be styled
IMOGEN: The under-hangman of his kingdom, and hated
IMOGEN: For being preferred so well.
CLOTEN: The south-fog rot him!
IMOGEN: He never can meet more mischance than come
IMOGEN: To be but named of thee. His meanest garment,
IMOGEN: That ever hath but clipp'd his body, is dearer
IMOGEN: In my respect than all the hairs above thee,
IMOGEN: Were they all made such men. How now, Pisanio!
NARRATOR: Enter PISANIO
CLOTEN: 'His garment!' Now the devil--
IMOGEN: To Dorothy my woman hie thee presently--
CLOTEN: 'His garment!'
IMOGEN: I am sprited with a fool.
IMOGEN: Frighted, and anger'd worse: go bid my woman
IMOGEN: Search for a jewel that too casually
IMOGEN: Hath left mine arm: it was thy master's: 'shrew me,
IMOGEN: If I would lose it for a revenue
IMOGEN: Of any king's in Europe. I do think
IMOGEN: I saw't this morning: confident I am
IMOGEN: Last night 'twas on mine arm, I kiss'd it:
IMOGEN: I hope it be not gone to tell my lord
IMOGEN: That I kiss aught but he.
PISANIO: 'Twill not be lost.
IMOGEN: I hope so: go and search.
NARRATOR: Exit PISANIO
CLOTEN: You have abused me:
CLOTEN: 'His meanest garment!'
IMOGEN: Ay, I said so, sir:
IMOGEN: If you will make't an action, call witness to't.
CLOTEN: I will inform your father.
IMOGEN: Your mother too:
IMOGEN: She's my good lady, and will conceive, I hope,
IMOGEN: But the worst of me. So, I leave you, sir,
IMOGEN: To the worst of discontent.
NARRATOR: Exit
CLOTEN: I'll be revenged:
CLOTEN: 'His meanest garment!' Well.
NARRATOR: Exit
CLOTEN: CYMBELINE
CLOTEN: SCENE IV. Rome. Philario's house.
NARRATOR: Enter POSTHUMUS and PHILARIO
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Fear it not, sir: I would I were so sure
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To win the king as I am bold her honour
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Will remain hers.
PHILARIO: What means do you make to him?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Not any, but abide the change of time,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Quake in the present winter's state and wish
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That warmer days would come: in these sear'd hopes,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I barely gratify your love, they failing,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I must die much your debtor.
PHILARIO: Your very goodness and your company
PHILARIO: O'erpays all I can do. By this, your king
PHILARIO: Hath heard of great Augustus: Caius Lucius
PHILARIO: Will do's commission throughly: and I think
PHILARIO: He'll grant the tribute, send the arrearages,
PHILARIO: Or look upon our Romans, whose remembrance
PHILARIO: Is yet fresh in their grief.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I do believe,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Statist though I am none, nor like to be,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That this will prove a war, and you shall hear
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The legions now in Gallia sooner landed
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: In our not-fearing Britain than have tidings
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of any penny tribute paid. Our countrymen
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Are men more order'd than when Julius Caesar
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Smiled at their lack of skill, but found
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: their courage
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Worthy his frowning at: their discipline,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Now mingled with their courages, will make known
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To their approvers they are people such
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That mend upon the world.
NARRATOR: Enter IACHIMO
PHILARIO: See! Iachimo!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The swiftest harts have posted you by land,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And winds of all the comers kiss'd your sails,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To make your vessel nimble.
PHILARIO: Welcome, sir.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I hope the briefness of your answer made
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The speediness of your return.
IACHIMO: Your lady
IACHIMO: Is one of the fairest that I have look'd upon.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And therewithal the best, or let her beauty
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Look through a casement to allure false hearts
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And be false with them.
IACHIMO: Here are letters for you.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Their tenor good, I trust.
IACHIMO: 'Tis very like.
PHILARIO: Was Caius Lucius in the Britain court
PHILARIO: When you were there?
IACHIMO: He was expected then,
IACHIMO: But not approach'd.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: All is well yet.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Sparkles this stone as it was wont? or is't not
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Too dull for your good wearing?
IACHIMO: If I had lost it,
IACHIMO: I should have lost the worth of it in gold.
IACHIMO: I'll make a journey twice as far, to enjoy
IACHIMO: A second night of such sweet shortness which
IACHIMO: Was mine in Britain, for the ring is won.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The stone's too hard to come by.
IACHIMO: Not a whit,
IACHIMO: Your lady being so easy.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Make not, sir,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Your loss your sport: I hope you know that we
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Must not continue friends.
IACHIMO: Good sir, we must,
IACHIMO: If you keep covenant. Had I not brought
IACHIMO: The knowledge of your mistress home, I grant
IACHIMO: We were to question further: but I now
IACHIMO: Profess myself the winner of her honour,
IACHIMO: Together with your ring, and not the wronger
IACHIMO: Of her or you, having proceeded but
IACHIMO: By both your wills.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: If you can make't apparent
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That you have tasted her in bed, my hand
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And ring is yours, if not, the foul opinion
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: You had of her pure honour gains or loses
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Your sword or mine, or masterless leaves both
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To who shall find them.
IACHIMO: Sir, my circumstances,
IACHIMO: Being so near the truth as I will make them,
IACHIMO: Must first induce you to believe: whose strength
IACHIMO: I will confirm with oath, which, I doubt not,
IACHIMO: You'll give me leave to spare, when you shall find
IACHIMO: You need it not.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Proceed.
IACHIMO: First, her bedchamber,--
IACHIMO: Where, I confess, I slept not, but profess
IACHIMO: Had that was well worth watching--it was hang'd
IACHIMO: With tapesty of silk and silver, the story
IACHIMO: Proud Cleopatra, when she met her Roman,
IACHIMO: And Cydnus swell'd above the banks, or for
IACHIMO: The press of boats or pride: a piece of work
IACHIMO: So bravely done, so rich, that it did strive
IACHIMO: In workmanship and value, which I wonder'd
IACHIMO: Could be so rarely and exactly wrought,
IACHIMO: Since the true life on't was--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: This is true,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And this you might have heard of here, by me,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Or by some other.
IACHIMO: More particulars
IACHIMO: Must justify my knowledge.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: So they must,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Or do your honour injury.
IACHIMO: The chimney
IACHIMO: Is south the chamber, and the chimney-piece

IACHIMO: So likely to report themselves: the cutter
IACHIMO: Was as another nature, dumb, outwent her,
IACHIMO: Motion and breath left out.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: This is a thing
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Which you might from relation likewise reap,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Being, as it is, much spoke of.
IACHIMO: The roof o' the chamber
IACHIMO: With golden cherubins is fretted: her andirons--
IACHIMO: I had forgot them--were two winking Cupids
IACHIMO: Of silver, each on one foot standing, nicely
IACHIMO: Depending on their brands.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: This is her honour!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Let it be granted you have seen all this--and praise
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Be given to your remembrance--the description
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of what is in her chamber nothing saves
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The wager you have laid.
IACHIMO: Then, if you can,
NARRATOR: Showing the bracelet
IACHIMO: Be pale: I beg but leave to air this jewel, see!
IACHIMO: And now 'tis up again: it must be married
IACHIMO: To that your diamond, I'll keep them.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Jove!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Once more let me behold it: is it that
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Which I left with her?
IACHIMO: Sir--I thank her--that:
IACHIMO: She stripp'd it from her arm, I see her yet,
IACHIMO: Her pretty action did outsell her gift,
IACHIMO: And yet enrich'd it too: she gave it me, and said
IACHIMO: She prized it once.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: May be she pluck'd it off
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To send it me.
IACHIMO: She writes so to you, doth she?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: O, no, no, no! 'tis true. Here, take this too,
NARRATOR: Gives the ring
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: It is a basilisk unto mine eye,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Kills me to look on't. Let there be no honour
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Where there is beauty, truth, where semblance, love,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Where there's another man: the vows of women
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of no more bondage be, to where they are made,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Than they are to their virtues, which is nothing.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: O, above measure false!
PHILARIO: Have patience, sir,
PHILARIO: And take your ring again, 'tis not yet won:
PHILARIO: It may be probable she lost it, or
PHILARIO: Who knows if one of her women, being corrupted,
PHILARIO: Hath stol'n it from her?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Very true,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And so, I hope, he came by't. Back my ring:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Render to me some corporal sign about her,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: More evident than this, for this was stolen.
IACHIMO: By Jupiter, I had it from her arm.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Hark you, he swears, by Jupiter he swears.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Tis true:--nay, keep the ring--'tis true: I am sure
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: She would not lose it: her attendants are
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: All sworn and honourable:--they induced to steal it!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And by a stranger!--No, he hath enjoyed her:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The cognizance of her incontinency
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Is this: she hath bought the name of whore
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: thus dearly.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: There, take thy hire, and all the fiends of hell
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Divide themselves between you!
PHILARIO: Sir, be patient:
PHILARIO: This is not strong enough to be believed
PHILARIO: Of one persuaded well of--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Never talk on't,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: She hath been colted by him.
IACHIMO: If you seek
IACHIMO: For further satisfying, under her breast--
IACHIMO: Worthy the pressing--lies a mole, right proud
IACHIMO: Of that most delicate lodging: by my life,
IACHIMO: I kiss'd it, and it gave me present hunger
IACHIMO: To feed again, though full. You do remember
IACHIMO: This stain upon her?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Ay, and it doth confirm
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Another stain, as big as hell can hold,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Were there no more but it.
IACHIMO: Will you hear more?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Spare your arithmetic: never count the turns,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Once, and a million!
IACHIMO: I'll be sworn--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: No swearing.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: If you will swear you have not done't, you lie,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And I will kill thee, if thou dost deny
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Thou'st made me cuckold.
IACHIMO: I'll deny nothing.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: O, that I had her here, to tear her limb-meal!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I will go there and do't, i' the court, before
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Her father. I'll do something--
NARRATOR: Exit
PHILARIO: Quite besides
PHILARIO: The government of patience! You have won:
PHILARIO: Let's follow him, and pervert the present wrath
PHILARIO: He hath against himself.
IACHIMO: With an my heart.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another room in Philario's house.
NARRATOR: Enter POSTHUMUS LEONATUS
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Is there no way for men to be but women
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Must be half-workers? We are all bastards,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And that most venerable man which I
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Did call my father, was I know not where
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: When I was stamp'd, some coiner with his tools
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Made me a counterfeit: yet my mother seem'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The Dian of that time so doth my wife
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The nonpareil of this. O, vengeance, vengeance!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Me of my lawful pleasure she restrain'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And pray'd me oft forbearance, did it with
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A pudency so rosy the sweet view on't
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Might well have warm'd old Saturn, that I thought her
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: As chaste as unsunn'd snow. O, all the devils!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: This yellow Iachimo, in an hour,--wast not?--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Or less,--at first?--perchance he spoke not, but,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Like a full-acorn'd boar, a German one,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Cried 'O!' and mounted, found no opposition
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But what he look'd for should oppose and she
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Should from encounter guard. Could I find out
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The woman's part in me! For there's no motion
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That tends to vice in man, but I affirm
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: It is the woman's part: be it lying, note it,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The woman's, flattering, hers, deceiving, hers,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Lust and rank thoughts, hers, hers, revenges, hers,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Ambitions, covetings, change of prides, disdain,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Nice longing, slanders, mutability,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: All faults that may be named, nay, that hell knows,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Why, hers, in part or all, but rather, all,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For even to vice
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: They are not constant but are changing still
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: One vice, but of a minute old, for one
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Not half so old as that. I'll write against them,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Detest them, curse them: yet 'tis greater skill
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: In a true hate, to pray they have their will:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The very devils cannot plague them better.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Britain. A hall in Cymbeline's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter in state, CYMBELINE, QUEEN, CLOTEN,  and Lords at one door, and at another, CAIUS LUCIUS and Attendants
CYMBELINE: Now say, what would Augustus Caesar with us?
CAIUS LUCIUS: When Julius Caesar, whose remembrance yet
CAIUS LUCIUS: Lives in men's eyes and will to ears and tongues
CAIUS LUCIUS: Be theme and hearing ever, was in this Britain
CAIUS LUCIUS: And conquer'd it, Cassibelan, thine uncle,--
CAIUS LUCIUS: Famous in Caesar's praises, no whit less
CAIUS LUCIUS: Than in his feats deserving it--for him
CAIUS LUCIUS: And his succession granted Rome a tribute,
CAIUS LUCIUS: Yearly three thousand pounds, which by thee lately
CAIUS LUCIUS: Is left untender'd.
QUEEN: And, to kill the marvel,
QUEEN: Shall be so ever.
CLOTEN: There be many Caesars,
CLOTEN: Ere such another Julius. Britain is
CLOTEN: A world by itself, and we will nothing pay
CLOTEN: For wearing our own noses.
QUEEN: That opportunity
QUEEN: Which then they had to take from 's, to resume
QUEEN: We have again. Remember, sir, my liege,
QUEEN: The kings your ancestors, together with
QUEEN: The natural bravery of your isle, which stands
QUEEN: As Neptune's park, ribbed and paled in
QUEEN: With rocks unscalable and roaring waters,
QUEEN: With sands that will not bear your enemies' boats,
QUEEN: But suck them up to the topmast. A kind of conquest
QUEEN: Caesar made here, but made not here his brag
QUEEN: Of 'Came' and 'saw' and 'overcame: ' with shame--
QUEEN: That first that ever touch'd him--he was carried
QUEEN: From off our coast, twice beaten, and his shipping--
QUEEN: Poor ignorant baubles!-- upon our terrible seas,
QUEEN: Like egg-shells moved upon their surges, crack'd
QUEEN: As easily 'gainst our rocks: for joy whereof
QUEEN: The famed Cassibelan, who was once at point--
QUEEN: O giglot fortune!--to master Caesar's sword,
QUEEN: Made Lud's town with rejoicing fires bright
QUEEN: And Britons strut with courage.
CLOTEN: Come, there's no more tribute to be paid: our
CLOTEN: kingdom is stronger than it was at that time, and,
CLOTEN: as I said, there is no moe such Caesars: other of
CLOTEN: them may have crook'd noses, but to owe such
CLOTEN: straight arms, none.
CYMBELINE: Son, let your mother end.
CLOTEN: We have yet many among us can gripe as hard as
CLOTEN: Cassibelan: I do not say I am one, but I have a
CLOTEN: hand. Why tribute? why should we pay tribute? If
CLOTEN: Caesar can hide the sun from us with a blanket, or
CLOTEN: put the moon in his pocket, we will pay him tribute
CLOTEN: for light, else, sir, no more tribute, pray you now.
CYMBELINE: You must know,
CYMBELINE: Till the injurious Romans did extort
CYMBELINE: This tribute from us, we were free:
CYMBELINE: Caesar's ambition,
CYMBELINE: Which swell'd so much that it did almost stretch
CYMBELINE: The sides o' the world, against all colour here
CYMBELINE: Did put the yoke upon 's, which to shake off
CYMBELINE: Becomes a warlike people, whom we reckon
CYMBELINE: Ourselves to be.
Lords: We do.
CYMBELINE: Say, then, to Caesar,
CYMBELINE: Our ancestor was that Mulmutius which
CYMBELINE: Ordain'd our laws, whose use the sword of Caesar
CYMBELINE: Hath too much mangled, whose repair and franchise
CYMBELINE: Shall, by the power we hold, be our good deed,
CYMBELINE: Though Rome be therefore angry: Mulmutius made our laws,
CYMBELINE: Who was the first of Britain which did put
CYMBELINE: His brows within a golden crown and call'd
CYMBELINE: Himself a king.
CAIUS LUCIUS: I am sorry, Cymbeline,
CAIUS LUCIUS: That I am to pronounce Augustus Caesar--
CAIUS LUCIUS: Caesar, that hath more kings his servants than
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thyself domestic officers--thine enemy:
CAIUS LUCIUS: Receive it from me, then: war and confusion
CAIUS LUCIUS: In Caesar's name pronounce I 'gainst thee: look
CAIUS LUCIUS: For fury not to be resisted. Thus defied,
CAIUS LUCIUS: I thank thee for myself.
CYMBELINE: Thou art welcome, Caius.
CYMBELINE: Thy Caesar knighted me, my youth I spent
CYMBELINE: Much under him, of him I gather'd honour,
CYMBELINE: Which he to seek of me again, perforce,
CYMBELINE: Behoves me keep at utterance. I am perfect
CYMBELINE: That the Pannonians and Dalmatians for
CYMBELINE: Their liberties are now in arms, a precedent
CYMBELINE: Which not to read would show the Britons cold:
CYMBELINE: So Caesar shall not find them.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Let proof speak.
CLOTEN: His majesty bids you welcome. Make
CLOTEN: pastime with us a day or two, or longer: if
CLOTEN: you seek us afterwards in other terms, you
CLOTEN: shall find us in our salt-water girdle: if you
CLOTEN: beat us out of it, it is yours, if you fall in
CLOTEN: the adventure, our crows shall fare the better
CLOTEN: for you, and there's an end.
CAIUS LUCIUS: So, sir.
CYMBELINE: I know your master's pleasure and he mine:
CYMBELINE: All the remain is 'Welcome!'
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Another room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter PISANIO, with a letter
PISANIO: How? of adultery? Wherefore write you not
PISANIO: What monster's her accuser? Leonatus,
PISANIO: O master! what a strange infection
PISANIO: Is fall'n into thy ear! What false Italian,
PISANIO: As poisonous-tongued as handed, hath prevail'd
PISANIO: On thy too ready hearing? Disloyal! No:
PISANIO: She's punish'd for her truth, and undergoes,
PISANIO: More goddess-like than wife-like, such assaults
PISANIO: As would take in some virtue. O my master!
PISANIO: Thy mind to her is now as low as were
PISANIO: Thy fortunes. How! that I should murder her?
PISANIO: Upon the love and truth and vows which I
PISANIO: Have made to thy command? I, her? her blood?
PISANIO: If it be so to do good service, never
PISANIO: Let me be counted serviceable. How look I,
PISANIO: That I should seem to lack humanity
PISANIO: so much as this fact comes to?
NARRATOR: Reading
PISANIO: 'Do't: the letter
PISANIO: that I have sent her, by her own command
PISANIO: Shall give thee opportunity.' O damn'd paper!
PISANIO: Black as the ink that's on thee! Senseless bauble,
PISANIO: Art thou a feodary for this act, and look'st
PISANIO: So virgin-like without? Lo, here she comes.
PISANIO: I am ignorant in what I am commanded.
NARRATOR: Enter IMOGEN
IMOGEN: How now, Pisanio!
PISANIO: Madam, here is a letter from my lord.
IMOGEN: Who? thy lord? that is my lord, Leonatus!
IMOGEN: O, learn'd indeed were that astronomer
IMOGEN: That knew the stars as I his characters,
IMOGEN: He'ld lay the future open. You good gods,
IMOGEN: Let what is here contain'd relish of love,
IMOGEN: Of my lord's health, of his content, yet not
IMOGEN: That we two are asunder, let that grieve him:
IMOGEN: Some griefs are med'cinable, that is one of them,
IMOGEN: For it doth physic love: of his content,
IMOGEN: All but in that! Good wax, thy leave. Blest be
IMOGEN: You bees that make these locks of counsel! Lovers
IMOGEN: And men in dangerous bonds pray not alike:
IMOGEN: Though forfeiters you cast in prison, yet
IMOGEN: You clasp young Cupid's tables. Good news, gods!
NARRATOR: Reads
IMOGEN: 'Justice, and your father's wrath, should he take me
IMOGEN: in his dominion, could not be so cruel to me, as
IMOGEN: you, O the dearest of creatures, would even renew me
IMOGEN: with your eyes. Take notice that I am in Cambria,
IMOGEN: at Milford-Haven: what your own love will out of
IMOGEN: this advise you, follow. So he wishes you all
IMOGEN: happiness, that remains loyal to his vow, and your,
IMOGEN: increasing in love,
IMOGEN: LEONATUS POSTHUMUS.'
IMOGEN: O, for a horse with wings! Hear'st thou, Pisanio?
IMOGEN: He is at Milford-Haven: read, and tell me
IMOGEN: How far 'tis thither. If one of mean affairs
IMOGEN: May plod it in a week, why may not I
IMOGEN: Glide thither in a day? Then, true Pisanio,--
IMOGEN: Who long'st, like me, to see thy lord, who long'st,--
IMOGEN: let me bate,-but not like me--yet long'st,
IMOGEN: But in a fainter kind:--O, not like me,
IMOGEN: For mine's beyond beyond--say, and speak thick,
IMOGEN: Love's counsellor should fill the bores of hearing,
IMOGEN: To the smothering of the sense--how far it is
IMOGEN: To this same blessed Milford: and by the way
IMOGEN: Tell me how Wales was made so happy as
IMOGEN: To inherit such a haven: but first of all,
IMOGEN: How we may steal from hence, and for the gap
IMOGEN: That we shall make in time, from our hence-going
IMOGEN: And our return, to excuse: but first, how get hence:
IMOGEN: Why should excuse be born or e'er begot?
IMOGEN: We'll talk of that hereafter. Prithee, speak,
IMOGEN: How many score of miles may we well ride
IMOGEN: 'Twixt hour and hour?
PISANIO: One score 'twixt sun and sun,
PISANIO: Madam, 's enough for you:
NARRATOR: Aside
PISANIO: and too much too.
IMOGEN: Why, one that rode to's execution, man,
IMOGEN: Could never go so slow: I have heard of
IMOGEN: riding wagers,
IMOGEN: Where horses have been nimbler than the sands
IMOGEN: That run i' the clock's behalf. But this is foolery:
IMOGEN: Go bid my woman feign a sickness, say
IMOGEN: She'll home to her father: and provide me presently
IMOGEN: A riding-suit, no costlier than would fit
IMOGEN: A franklin's housewife.
PISANIO: Madam, you're best consider.
IMOGEN: I see before me, man: nor here, nor here,
IMOGEN: Nor what ensues, but have a fog in them,
IMOGEN: That I cannot look through. Away, I prithee,
IMOGEN: Do as I bid thee: there's no more to say,
IMOGEN: Accessible is none but Milford way.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Wales: a mountainous country with a cave.
NARRATOR: Enter, from the cave, BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, and ARVIRAGUS following
BELARIUS: A goodly day not to keep house, with such
BELARIUS: Whose roof's as low as ours! Stoop, boys, this gate
BELARIUS: Instructs you how to adore the heavens and bows you
BELARIUS: To a morning's holy office: the gates of monarchs
BELARIUS: Are arch'd so high that giants may jet through
BELARIUS: And keep their impious turbans on, without
BELARIUS: Good morrow to the sun. Hail, thou fair heaven!
BELARIUS: We house i' the rock, yet use thee not so hardly
BELARIUS: As prouder livers do.
GUIDERIUS: Hail, heaven!
ARVIRAGUS: Hail, heaven!
BELARIUS: Now for our mountain sport: up to yond hill,
BELARIUS: Your legs are young, I'll tread these flats. Consider,
BELARIUS: When you above perceive me like a crow,
BELARIUS: That it is place which lessens and sets off,
BELARIUS: And you may then revolve what tales I have told you
BELARIUS: Of courts, of princes, of the tricks in war:
BELARIUS: This service is not service, so being done,
BELARIUS: But being so allow'd: to apprehend thus,
BELARIUS: Draws us a profit from all things we see,
BELARIUS: And often, to our comfort, shall we find
BELARIUS: The sharded beetle in a safer hold
BELARIUS: Than is the full-wing'd eagle. O, this life
BELARIUS: Is nobler than attending for a cheque,
BELARIUS: Richer than doing nothing for a bauble,
BELARIUS: Prouder than rustling in unpaid-for silk:
BELARIUS: Such gain the cap of him that makes 'em fine,
BELARIUS: Yet keeps his book uncross'd: no life to ours.
GUIDERIUS: Out of your proof you speak: we, poor unfledged,
GUIDERIUS: Have never wing'd from view o' the nest, nor know not
GUIDERIUS: What air's from home. Haply this life is best,
GUIDERIUS: If quiet life be best, sweeter to you
GUIDERIUS: That have a sharper known, well corresponding
GUIDERIUS: With your stiff age: but unto us it is
GUIDERIUS: A cell of ignorance, travelling a-bed,
GUIDERIUS: A prison for a debtor, that not dares
GUIDERIUS: To stride a limit.
ARVIRAGUS: What should we speak of
ARVIRAGUS: When we are old as you? when we shall hear
ARVIRAGUS: The rain and wind beat dark December, how,
ARVIRAGUS: In this our pinching cave, shall we discourse
ARVIRAGUS: The freezing hours away? We have seen nothing,
ARVIRAGUS: We are beastly, subtle as the fox for prey,
ARVIRAGUS: Like warlike as the wolf for what we eat,
ARVIRAGUS: Our valour is to chase what flies, our cage
ARVIRAGUS: We make a quire, as doth the prison'd bird,
ARVIRAGUS: And sing our bondage freely.
BELARIUS: How you speak!
BELARIUS: Did you but know the city's usuries
BELARIUS: And felt them knowingly, the art o' the court
BELARIUS: As hard to leave as keep, whose top to climb
BELARIUS: Is certain falling, or so slippery that
BELARIUS: The fear's as bad as falling, the toil o' the war,
BELARIUS: A pain that only seems to seek out danger
BELARIUS: I' the name of fame and honour, which dies i'
BELARIUS: the search,
BELARIUS: And hath as oft a slanderous epitaph
BELARIUS: As record of fair act, nay, many times,
BELARIUS: Doth ill deserve by doing well, what's worse,
BELARIUS: Must court'sy at the censure:--O boys, this story
BELARIUS: The world may read in me: my body's mark'd
BELARIUS: With Roman swords, and my report was once
BELARIUS: First with the best of note: Cymbeline loved me,
BELARIUS: And when a soldier was the theme, my name
BELARIUS: Was not far off: then was I as a tree
BELARIUS: Whose boughs did bend with fruit: but in one night,
BELARIUS: A storm or robbery, call it what you will,
BELARIUS: Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves,
BELARIUS: And left me bare to weather.
GUIDERIUS: Uncertain favour!
BELARIUS: My fault being nothing--as I have told you oft--
BELARIUS: But that two villains, whose false oaths prevail'd
BELARIUS: Before my perfect honour, swore to Cymbeline
BELARIUS: I was confederate with the Romans: so
BELARIUS: Follow'd my banishment, and this twenty years
BELARIUS: This rock and these demesnes have been my world,
BELARIUS: Where I have lived at honest freedom, paid
BELARIUS: More pious debts to heaven than in all
BELARIUS: The fore-end of my time. But up to the mountains!
BELARIUS: This is not hunters' language: he that strikes
BELARIUS: The venison first shall be the lord o' the feast,
BELARIUS: To him the other two shall minister,
BELARIUS: And we will fear no poison, which attends
BELARIUS: In place of greater state. I'll meet you in the valleys.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GUIDERIUS and ARVIRAGUS
BELARIUS: How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature!
BELARIUS: These boys know little they are sons to the king,
BELARIUS: Nor Cymbeline dreams that they are alive.
BELARIUS: They think they are mine, and though train'd
BELARIUS: up thus meanly
BELARIUS: I' the cave wherein they bow, their thoughts do hit
BELARIUS: The roofs of palaces, and nature prompts them
BELARIUS: In simple and low things to prince it much
BELARIUS: Beyond the trick of others. This Polydore,
BELARIUS: The heir of Cymbeline and Britain, who
BELARIUS: The king his father call'd Guiderius,--Jove!
BELARIUS: When on my three-foot stool I sit and tell
BELARIUS: The warlike feats I have done, his spirits fly out
BELARIUS: Into my story: say 'Thus, mine enemy fell,
BELARIUS: And thus I set my foot on 's neck,' even then
BELARIUS: The princely blood flows in his cheek, he sweats,
BELARIUS: Strains his young nerves and puts himself in posture
BELARIUS: That acts my words. The younger brother, Cadwal,
BELARIUS: Once Arviragus, in as like a figure,
BELARIUS: Strikes life into my speech and shows much more
BELARIUS: His own conceiving.--Hark, the game is roused!
BELARIUS: O Cymbeline! heaven and my conscience knows
BELARIUS: Thou didst unjustly banish me: whereon,
BELARIUS: At three and two years old, I stole these babes,
BELARIUS: Thinking to bar thee of succession, as
BELARIUS: Thou reft'st me of my lands. Euriphile,
BELARIUS: Thou wast their nurse, they took thee for
BELARIUS: their mother,
BELARIUS: And every day do honour to her grave:
BELARIUS: Myself, Belarius, that am Morgan call'd,
BELARIUS: They take for natural father. The game is up.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Country near Milford-Haven.
NARRATOR: Enter PISANIO and IMOGEN
IMOGEN: Thou told'st me, when we came from horse, the place
IMOGEN: Was near at hand: ne'er long'd my mother so
IMOGEN: To see me first, as I have now. Pisanio! man!
IMOGEN: Where is Posthumus? What is in thy mind,
IMOGEN: That makes thee stare thus? Wherefore breaks that sigh
IMOGEN: From the inward of thee? One, but painted thus,
IMOGEN: Would be interpreted a thing perplex'd
IMOGEN: Beyond self-explication: put thyself
IMOGEN: Into a havior of less fear, ere wildness
IMOGEN: Vanquish my staider senses. What's the matter?
IMOGEN: Why tender'st thou that paper to me, with
IMOGEN: A look untender? If't be summer news,
IMOGEN: Smile to't before, if winterly, thou need'st
IMOGEN: But keep that countenance still. My husband's hand!
IMOGEN: That drug-damn'd Italy hath out-craftied him,
IMOGEN: And he's at some hard point. Speak, man: thy tongue
IMOGEN: May take off some extremity, which to read
IMOGEN: Would be even mortal to me.
PISANIO: Please you, read,
PISANIO: And you shall find me, wretched man, a thing
PISANIO: The most disdain'd of fortune.
IMOGEN: [Reads]  'Thy mistress, Pisanio, hath played the
IMOGEN: strumpet in my bed, the testimonies whereof lie
IMOGEN: bleeding in me. I speak not out of weak surmises,
IMOGEN: but from proof as strong as my grief and as certain
IMOGEN: as I expect my revenge. That part thou, Pisanio,
IMOGEN: must act for me, if thy faith be not tainted with
IMOGEN: the breach of hers. Let thine own hands take away
IMOGEN: her life: I shall give thee opportunity at
IMOGEN: Milford-Haven. She hath my letter for the purpose
IMOGEN: where, if thou fear to strike and to make me certain
IMOGEN: it is done, thou art the pandar to her dishonour and
IMOGEN: equally to me disloyal.'
PISANIO: What shall I need to draw my sword? the paper
PISANIO: Hath cut her throat already. No, 'tis slander,
PISANIO: Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue
PISANIO: Outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath
PISANIO: Rides on the posting winds and doth belie
PISANIO: All corners of the world: kings, queens and states,
PISANIO: Maids, matrons, nay, the secrets of the grave
PISANIO: This viperous slander enters. What cheer, madam?
IMOGEN: False to his bed! What is it to be false?
IMOGEN: To lie in watch there and to think on him?
IMOGEN: To weep 'twixt clock and clock? if sleep
IMOGEN: charge nature,
IMOGEN: To break it with a fearful dream of him
IMOGEN: And cry myself awake? that's false to's bed, is it?
PISANIO: Alas, good lady!
IMOGEN: I false! Thy conscience witness: Iachimo,
IMOGEN: Thou didst accuse him of incontinency,
IMOGEN: Thou then look'dst like a villain, now methinks
IMOGEN: Thy favour's good enough. Some jay of Italy
IMOGEN: Whose mother was her painting, hath betray'd him:
IMOGEN: Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion,
IMOGEN: And, for I am richer than to hang by the walls,
IMOGEN: I must be ripp'd:--to pieces with me!--O,
IMOGEN: Men's vows are women's traitors! All good seeming,
IMOGEN: By thy revolt, O husband, shall be thought
IMOGEN: Put on for villany, not born where't grows,
IMOGEN: But worn a bait for ladies.
PISANIO: Good madam, hear me.
IMOGEN: True honest men being heard, like false Aeneas,
IMOGEN: Were in his time thought false, and Sinon's weeping
IMOGEN: Did scandal many a holy tear, took pity
IMOGEN: From most true wretchedness: so thou, Posthumus,
IMOGEN: Wilt lay the leaven on all proper men,
IMOGEN: Goodly and gallant shall be false and perjured
IMOGEN: From thy great fall. Come, fellow, be thou honest:
IMOGEN: Do thou thy master's bidding: when thou see'st him,
IMOGEN: A little witness my obedience: look!
IMOGEN: I draw the sword myself: take it, and hit
IMOGEN: The innocent mansion of my love, my heart,
IMOGEN: Fear not, 'tis empty of all things but grief,
IMOGEN: Thy master is not there, who was indeed
IMOGEN: The riches of it: do his bidding, strike
IMOGEN: Thou mayst be valiant in a better cause,
IMOGEN: But now thou seem'st a coward.
PISANIO: Hence, vile instrument!
PISANIO: Thou shalt not damn my hand.
IMOGEN: Why, I must die,
IMOGEN: And if I do not by thy hand, thou art
IMOGEN: No servant of thy master's. Against self-slaughter
IMOGEN: There is a prohibition so divine
IMOGEN: That cravens my weak hand. Come, here's my heart.
IMOGEN: Something's afore't. Soft, soft! we'll no defence,
IMOGEN: Obedient as the scabbard. What is here?
IMOGEN: The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus,
IMOGEN: All turn'd to heresy? Away, away,
IMOGEN: Corrupters of my faith! you shall no more
IMOGEN: Be stomachers to my heart. Thus may poor fools
IMOGEN: Believe false teachers: though those that
IMOGEN: are betray'd
IMOGEN: Do feel the treason sharply, yet the traitor
IMOGEN: Stands in worse case of woe.
IMOGEN: And thou, Posthumus, thou that didst set up
IMOGEN: My disobedience 'gainst the king my father
IMOGEN: And make me put into contempt the suits
IMOGEN: Of princely fellows, shalt hereafter find
IMOGEN: It is no act of common passage, but
IMOGEN: A strain of rareness: and I grieve myself
IMOGEN: To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her
IMOGEN: That now thou tirest on, how thy memory
IMOGEN: Will then be pang'd by me. Prithee, dispatch:
IMOGEN: The lamb entreats the butcher: where's thy knife?
IMOGEN: Thou art too slow to do thy master's bidding,
IMOGEN: When I desire it too.
PISANIO: O gracious lady,
PISANIO: Since I received command to do this business
PISANIO: I have not slept one wink.
IMOGEN: Do't, and to bed then.
PISANIO: I'll wake mine eye-balls blind first.
IMOGEN: Wherefore then
IMOGEN: Didst undertake it? Why hast thou abused
IMOGEN: So many miles with a pretence? this place?
IMOGEN: Mine action and thine own? our horses' labour?
IMOGEN: The time inviting thee? the perturb'd court,
IMOGEN: For my being absent? whereunto I never
IMOGEN: Purpose return. Why hast thou gone so far,
IMOGEN: To be unbent when thou hast ta'en thy stand,
IMOGEN: The elected deer before thee?
PISANIO: But to win time
PISANIO: To lose so bad employment, in the which
PISANIO: I have consider'd of a course. Good lady,
PISANIO: Hear me with patience.
IMOGEN: Talk thy tongue weary, speak
IMOGEN: I have heard I am a strumpet, and mine ear
IMOGEN: Therein false struck, can take no greater wound,
IMOGEN: Nor tent to bottom that. But speak.
PISANIO: Then, madam,
PISANIO: I thought you would not back again.
IMOGEN: Most like,
IMOGEN: Bringing me here to kill me.
PISANIO: Not so, neither:
PISANIO: But if I were as wise as honest, then
PISANIO: My purpose would prove well. It cannot be
PISANIO: But that my master is abused:
PISANIO: Some villain, ay, and singular in his art.
PISANIO: Hath done you both this cursed injury.
IMOGEN: Some Roman courtezan.
PISANIO: No, on my life.
PISANIO: I'll give but notice you are dead and send him
PISANIO: Some bloody sign of it, for 'tis commanded
PISANIO: I should do so: you shall be miss'd at court,
PISANIO: And that will well confirm it.
IMOGEN: Why good fellow,
IMOGEN: What shall I do the where? where bide? how live?
IMOGEN: Or in my life what comfort, when I am
IMOGEN: Dead to my husband?
PISANIO: If you'll back to the court--
IMOGEN: No court, no father, nor no more ado
IMOGEN: With that harsh, noble, simple nothing,
IMOGEN: That Cloten, whose love-suit hath been to me
IMOGEN: As fearful as a siege.
PISANIO: If not at court,
PISANIO: Then not in Britain must you bide.
IMOGEN: Where then
IMOGEN: Hath Britain all the sun that shines? Day, night,
IMOGEN: Are they not but in Britain? I' the world's volume
IMOGEN: Our Britain seems as of it, but not in 't,
IMOGEN: In a great pool a swan's nest: prithee, think
IMOGEN: There's livers out of Britain.
PISANIO: I am most glad
PISANIO: You think of other place. The ambassador,
PISANIO: Lucius the Roman, comes to Milford-Haven
PISANIO: To-morrow: now, if you could wear a mind
PISANIO: Dark as your fortune is, and but disguise
PISANIO: That which, to appear itself, must not yet be
PISANIO: But by self-danger, you should tread a course
PISANIO: Pretty and full of view, yea, haply, near
PISANIO: The residence of Posthumus, so nigh at least
PISANIO: That though his actions were not visible, yet
PISANIO: Report should render him hourly to your ear
PISANIO: As truly as he moves.
IMOGEN: O, for such means!
IMOGEN: Though peril to my modesty, not death on't,
IMOGEN: I would adventure.
PISANIO: Well, then, here's the point:
PISANIO: You must forget to be a woman, change
PISANIO: Command into obedience: fear and niceness--
PISANIO: The handmaids of all women, or, more truly,
PISANIO: Woman its pretty self--into a waggish courage:
PISANIO: Ready in gibes, quick-answer'd, saucy and
PISANIO: As quarrelous as the weasel, nay, you must
PISANIO: Forget that rarest treasure of your cheek,
PISANIO: Exposing it--but, O, the harder heart!
PISANIO: Alack, no remedy!--to the greedy touch
PISANIO: Of common-kissing Titan, and forget
PISANIO: Your laboursome and dainty trims, wherein
PISANIO: You made great Juno angry.
IMOGEN: Nay, be brief
IMOGEN: I see into thy end, and am almost
IMOGEN: A man already.
PISANIO: First, make yourself but like one.
PISANIO: Fore-thinking this, I have already fit--
PISANIO: 'Tis in my cloak-bag--doublet, hat, hose, all
PISANIO: That answer to them: would you in their serving,
PISANIO: And with what imitation you can borrow
PISANIO: From youth of such a season, 'fore noble Lucius
PISANIO: Present yourself, desire his service, tell him
PISANIO: wherein you're happy,--which you'll make him know,
PISANIO: If that his head have ear in music,--doubtless
PISANIO: With joy he will embrace you, for he's honourable
PISANIO: And doubling that, most holy. Your means abroad,
PISANIO: You have me, rich, and I will never fail
PISANIO: Beginning nor supplyment.
IMOGEN: Thou art all the comfort
IMOGEN: The gods will diet me with. Prithee, away:
IMOGEN: There's more to be consider'd, but we'll even
IMOGEN: All that good time will give us: this attempt
IMOGEN: I am soldier to, and will abide it with
IMOGEN: A prince's courage. Away, I prithee.
PISANIO: Well, madam, we must take a short farewell,
PISANIO: Lest, being miss'd, I be suspected of
PISANIO: Your carriage from the court. My noble mistress,
PISANIO: Here is a box, I had it from the queen:
PISANIO: What's in't is precious, if you are sick at sea,
PISANIO: Or stomach-qualm'd at land, a dram of this
PISANIO: Will drive away distemper. To some shade,
PISANIO: And fit you to your manhood. May the gods
PISANIO: Direct you to the best!
IMOGEN: Amen: I thank thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, severally
NARRATOR: SCENE V. A room in Cymbeline's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CYMBELINE, QUEEN, CLOTEN, LUCIUS, Lords, and Attendants
CYMBELINE: Thus far, and so farewell.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thanks, royal sir.
CAIUS LUCIUS: My emperor hath wrote, I must from hence,
CAIUS LUCIUS: And am right sorry that I must report ye
CAIUS LUCIUS: My master's enemy.
CYMBELINE: Our subjects, sir,
CYMBELINE: Will not endure his yoke, and for ourself
CYMBELINE: To show less sovereignty than they, must needs
CYMBELINE: Appear unkinglike.
CAIUS LUCIUS: So, sir: I desire of you
CAIUS LUCIUS: A conduct over-land to Milford-Haven.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Madam, all joy befal your grace!
QUEEN: And you!
CYMBELINE: My lords, you are appointed for that office,
CYMBELINE: The due of honour in no point omit.
CYMBELINE: So farewell, noble Lucius.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Your hand, my lord.
CLOTEN: Receive it friendly, but from this time forth
CLOTEN: I wear it as your enemy.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Sir, the event
CAIUS LUCIUS: Is yet to name the winner: fare you well.
CYMBELINE: Leave not the worthy Lucius, good my lords,
CYMBELINE: Till he have cross'd the Severn. Happiness!
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCIUS and Lords
QUEEN: He goes hence frowning: but it honours us
QUEEN: That we have given him cause.
CLOTEN: 'Tis all the better,
CLOTEN: Your valiant Britons have their wishes in it.
CYMBELINE: Lucius hath wrote already to the emperor
CYMBELINE: How it goes here. It fits us therefore ripely
CYMBELINE: Our chariots and our horsemen be in readiness:
CYMBELINE: The powers that he already hath in Gallia
CYMBELINE: Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves
CYMBELINE: His war for Britain.
QUEEN: 'Tis not sleepy business,
QUEEN: But must be look'd to speedily and strongly.
CYMBELINE: Our expectation that it would be thus
CYMBELINE: Hath made us forward. But, my gentle queen,
CYMBELINE: Where is our daughter? She hath not appear'd
CYMBELINE: Before the Roman, nor to us hath tender'd
CYMBELINE: The duty of the day: she looks us like
CYMBELINE: A thing more made of malice than of duty:
CYMBELINE: We have noted it. Call her before us, for
CYMBELINE: We have been too slight in sufferance.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
QUEEN: Royal sir,
QUEEN: Since the exile of Posthumus, most retired
QUEEN: Hath her life been, the cure whereof, my lord,
QUEEN: 'Tis time must do. Beseech your majesty,
QUEEN: Forbear sharp speeches to her: she's a lady
QUEEN: So tender of rebukes that words are strokes
QUEEN: And strokes death to her.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Attendant
CYMBELINE: Where is she, sir? How
CYMBELINE: Can her contempt be answer'd?
Attendant: Please you, sir,
Attendant: Her chambers are all lock'd, and there's no answer
Attendant: That will be given to the loudest noise we make.
QUEEN: My lord, when last I went to visit her,
QUEEN: She pray'd me to excuse her keeping close,
QUEEN: Whereto constrain'd by her infirmity,
QUEEN: She should that duty leave unpaid to you,
QUEEN: Which daily she was bound to proffer: this
QUEEN: She wish'd me to make known, but our great court
QUEEN: Made me to blame in memory.
CYMBELINE: Her doors lock'd?
CYMBELINE: Not seen of late? Grant, heavens, that which I fear
CYMBELINE: Prove false!
NARRATOR: Exit
QUEEN: Son, I say, follow the king.
CLOTEN: That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant,
CLOTEN: have not seen these two days.
QUEEN: Go, look after.
NARRATOR: Exit CLOTEN
QUEEN: Pisanio, thou that stand'st so for Posthumus!
QUEEN: He hath a drug of mine, I pray his absence
QUEEN: Proceed by swallowing that, for he believes
QUEEN: It is a thing most precious. But for her,
QUEEN: Where is she gone? Haply, despair hath seized her,
QUEEN: Or, wing'd with fervor of her love, she's flown
QUEEN: To her desired Posthumus: gone she is
QUEEN: To death or to dishonour, and my end
QUEEN: Can make good use of either: she being down,
QUEEN: I have the placing of the British crown.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CLOTEN
QUEEN: How now, my son!
CLOTEN: 'Tis certain she is fled.
CLOTEN: Go in and cheer the king: he rages, none
CLOTEN: Dare come about him.
QUEEN: [Aside]            All the better: may
QUEEN: This night forestall him of the coming day!
NARRATOR: Exit
CLOTEN: I love and hate her: for she's fair and royal,
CLOTEN: And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite
CLOTEN: Than lady, ladies, woman, from every one
CLOTEN: The best she hath, and she, of all compounded,
CLOTEN: Outsells them all, I love her therefore: but
CLOTEN: Disdaining me and throwing favours on
CLOTEN: The low Posthumus slanders so her judgment
CLOTEN: That what's else rare is choked, and in that point
CLOTEN: I will conclude to hate her, nay, indeed,
CLOTEN: To be revenged upon her. For when fools Shall--
NARRATOR: Enter PISANIO
CLOTEN: Who is here? What, are you packing, sirrah?
CLOTEN: Come hither: ah, you precious pander! Villain,
CLOTEN: Where is thy lady? In a word, or else
CLOTEN: Thou art straightway with the fiends.
PISANIO: O, good my lord!
CLOTEN: Where is thy lady? Or, by Jupiter,--
CLOTEN: I will not ask again. Close villain,
CLOTEN: I'll have this secret from thy heart, or rip
CLOTEN: Thy heart to find it. Is she with Posthumus?
CLOTEN: From whose so many weights of baseness cannot
CLOTEN: A dram of worth be drawn.
PISANIO: Alas, my lord,
PISANIO: How can she be with him? When was she missed?
PISANIO: He is in Rome.
CLOTEN: Where is she, sir? Come nearer,
CLOTEN: No further halting: satisfy me home
CLOTEN: What is become of her.
PISANIO: O, my all-worthy lord!
CLOTEN: All-worthy villain!
CLOTEN: Discover where thy mistress is at once,
CLOTEN: At the next word: no more of 'worthy lord!'
CLOTEN: Speak, or thy silence on the instant is
CLOTEN: Thy condemnation and thy death.
PISANIO: Then, sir,
PISANIO: This paper is the history of my knowledge
PISANIO: Touching her flight.
NARRATOR: Presenting a letter
CLOTEN: Let's see't. I will pursue her
CLOTEN: Even to Augustus' throne.
PISANIO: [Aside]                 Or this, or perish.
PISANIO: She's far enough, and what he learns by this
PISANIO: May prove his travel, not her danger.
CLOTEN: Hum!
PISANIO: [Aside]  I'll write to my lord she's dead. O Imogen,
PISANIO: Safe mayst thou wander, safe return again!
CLOTEN: Sirrah, is this letter true?
PISANIO: Sir, as I think.
CLOTEN: It is Posthumus' hand, I know't. Sirrah, if thou
CLOTEN: wouldst not be a villain, but do me true service,
CLOTEN: undergo those employments wherein I should have
CLOTEN: cause to use thee with a serious industry, that is,
CLOTEN: what villany soe'er I bid thee do, to perform it
CLOTEN: directly and truly, I would think thee an honest
CLOTEN: man: thou shouldst neither want my means for thy
CLOTEN: relief nor my voice for thy preferment.
PISANIO: Well, my good lord.
CLOTEN: Wilt thou serve me? for since patiently and
CLOTEN: constantly thou hast stuck to the bare fortune of
CLOTEN: that beggar Posthumus, thou canst not, in the
CLOTEN: course of gratitude, but be a diligent follower of
CLOTEN: mine: wilt thou serve me?
PISANIO: Sir, I will.
CLOTEN: Give me thy hand, here's my purse. Hast any of thy
CLOTEN: late master's garments in thy possession?
PISANIO: I have, my lord, at my lodging, the same suit he
PISANIO: wore when he took leave of my lady and mistress.
CLOTEN: The first service thou dost me, fetch that suit
CLOTEN: hither: let it be thy lint service, go.
PISANIO: I shall, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
CLOTEN: Meet thee at Milford-Haven!--I forgot to ask him one
CLOTEN: thing, I'll remember't anon:--even there, thou
CLOTEN: villain Posthumus, will I kill thee. I would these
CLOTEN: garments were come. She said upon a time--the
CLOTEN: bitterness of it I now belch from my heart--that she
CLOTEN: held the very garment of Posthumus in more respect
CLOTEN: than my noble and natural person together with the
CLOTEN: adornment of my qualities. With that suit upon my
CLOTEN: back, will I ravish her: first kill him, and in her
CLOTEN: eyes, there shall she see my valour, which will then
CLOTEN: be a torment to her contempt. He on the ground, my
CLOTEN: speech of insultment ended on his dead body, and
CLOTEN: when my lust hath dined,--which, as I say, to vex
CLOTEN: her I will execute in the clothes that she so
CLOTEN: praised,--to the court I'll knock her back, foot
CLOTEN: her home again. She hath despised me rejoicingly,
CLOTEN: and I'll be merry in my revenge.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PISANIO, with the clothes
CLOTEN: Be those the garments?
PISANIO: Ay, my noble lord.
CLOTEN: How long is't since she went to Milford-Haven?
PISANIO: She can scarce be there yet.
CLOTEN: Bring this apparel to my chamber, that is the second
CLOTEN: thing that I have commanded thee: the third is,
CLOTEN: that thou wilt be a voluntary mute to my design. Be
CLOTEN: but duteous, and true preferment shall tender itself
CLOTEN: to thee. My revenge is now at Milford: would I had
CLOTEN: wings to follow it! Come, and be true.
NARRATOR: Exit
PISANIO: Thou bid'st me to my loss: for true to thee
PISANIO: Were to prove false, which I will never be,
PISANIO: To him that is most true. To Milford go,
PISANIO: And find not her whom thou pursuest. Flow, flow,
PISANIO: You heavenly blessings, on her! This fool's speed
PISANIO: Be cross'd with slowness, labour be his meed!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Wales. Before the cave of Belarius.
NARRATOR: Enter IMOGEN, in boy's clothes
IMOGEN: I see a man's life is a tedious one:
IMOGEN: I have tired myself, and for two nights together
IMOGEN: Have made the ground my bed. I should be sick,
IMOGEN: But that my resolution helps me. Milford,
IMOGEN: When from the mountain-top Pisanio show'd thee,
IMOGEN: Thou wast within a ken: O Jove! I think
IMOGEN: Foundations fly the wretched, such, I mean,
IMOGEN: Where they should be relieved. Two beggars told me
IMOGEN: I could not miss my way: will poor folks lie,
IMOGEN: That have afflictions on them, knowing 'tis
IMOGEN: A punishment or trial? Yes, no wonder,
IMOGEN: When rich ones scarce tell true. To lapse in fulness
IMOGEN: Is sorer than to lie for need, and falsehood
IMOGEN: Is worse in kings than beggars. My dear lord!
IMOGEN: Thou art one o' the false ones. Now I think on thee,
IMOGEN: My hunger's gone, but even before, I was
IMOGEN: At point to sink for food. But what is this?
IMOGEN: Here is a path to't: 'tis some savage hold:
IMOGEN: I were best not to call, I dare not call:
IMOGEN: yet famine,
IMOGEN: Ere clean it o'erthrow nature, makes it valiant,
IMOGEN: Plenty and peace breeds cowards: hardness ever
IMOGEN: Of hardiness is mother. Ho! who's here?
IMOGEN: If any thing that's civil, speak, if savage,
IMOGEN: Take or lend. Ho! No answer? Then I'll enter.
IMOGEN: Best draw my sword: and if mine enemy
IMOGEN: But fear the sword like me, he'll scarcely look on't.
IMOGEN: Such a foe, good heavens!
NARRATOR: Exit, to the cave
NARRATOR: Enter BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, and ARVIRAGUS
BELARIUS: You, Polydote, have proved best woodman and
BELARIUS: Are master of the feast: Cadwal and I
BELARIUS: Will play the cook and servant, 'tis our match:
BELARIUS: The sweat of industry would dry and die,
BELARIUS: But for the end it works to. Come, our stomachs
BELARIUS: Will make what's homely savoury: weariness
BELARIUS: Can snore upon the flint, when resty sloth
BELARIUS: Finds the down pillow hard. Now peace be here,
BELARIUS: Poor house, that keep'st thyself!
GUIDERIUS: I am thoroughly weary.
ARVIRAGUS: I am weak with toil, yet strong in appetite.
GUIDERIUS: There is cold meat i' the cave, we'll browse on that,
GUIDERIUS: Whilst what we have kill'd be cook'd.
BELARIUS: [Looking into the cave]
BELARIUS: Stay, come not in.
BELARIUS: But that it eats our victuals, I should think
BELARIUS: Here were a fairy.
GUIDERIUS: What's the matter, sir?
BELARIUS: By Jupiter, an angel! or, if not,
BELARIUS: An earthly paragon! Behold divineness
BELARIUS: No elder than a boy!
NARRATOR: Re-enter IMOGEN
IMOGEN: Good masters, harm me not:
IMOGEN: Before I enter'd here, I call'd, and thought
IMOGEN: To have begg'd or bought what I have took:
IMOGEN: good troth,
IMOGEN: I have stol'n nought, nor would not, though I had found
IMOGEN: Gold strew'd i' the floor. Here's money for my meat:
IMOGEN: I would have left it on the board so soon
IMOGEN: As I had made my meal, and parted
IMOGEN: With prayers for the provider.
GUIDERIUS: Money, youth?
ARVIRAGUS: All gold and silver rather turn to dirt!
ARVIRAGUS: As 'tis no better reckon'd, but of those
ARVIRAGUS: Who worship dirty gods.
IMOGEN: I see you're angry:
IMOGEN: Know, if you kill me for my fault, I should
IMOGEN: Have died had I not made it.
BELARIUS: Whither bound?
IMOGEN: To Milford-Haven.
BELARIUS: What's your name?
IMOGEN: Fidele, sir. I have a kinsman who
IMOGEN: Is bound for Italy, he embark'd at Milford,
IMOGEN: To whom being going, almost spent with hunger,
IMOGEN: I am fall'n in this offence.
BELARIUS: Prithee, fair youth,
BELARIUS: Think us no churls, nor measure our good minds
BELARIUS: By this rude place we live in. Well encounter'd!
BELARIUS: 'Tis almost night: you shall have better cheer
BELARIUS: Ere you depart: and thanks to stay and eat it.
BELARIUS: Boys, bid him welcome.
GUIDERIUS: Were you a woman, youth,
GUIDERIUS: I should woo hard but be your groom. In honesty,
GUIDERIUS: I bid for you as I'd buy.
ARVIRAGUS: I'll make't my comfort
ARVIRAGUS: He is a man, I'll love him as my brother:
ARVIRAGUS: And such a welcome as I'd give to him
ARVIRAGUS: After long absence, such is yours: most welcome!
ARVIRAGUS: Be sprightly, for you fall 'mongst friends.
IMOGEN: 'Mongst friends,
IMOGEN: If brothers.
NARRATOR: Aside
IMOGEN: Would it had been so, that they
IMOGEN: Had been my father's sons! then had my prize
IMOGEN: Been less, and so more equal ballasting
IMOGEN: To thee, Posthumus.
BELARIUS: He wrings at some distress.
GUIDERIUS: Would I could free't!
ARVIRAGUS: Or I, whate'er it be,
ARVIRAGUS: What pain it cost, what danger. God's!
BELARIUS: Hark, boys.
NARRATOR: Whispering
IMOGEN: Great men,
IMOGEN: That had a court no bigger than this cave,
IMOGEN: That did attend themselves and had the virtue
IMOGEN: Which their own conscience seal'd them--laying by
IMOGEN: That nothing-gift of differing multitudes--
IMOGEN: Could not out-peer these twain. Pardon me, gods!
IMOGEN: I'd change my sex to be companion with them,
IMOGEN: Since Leonatus's false.
BELARIUS: It shall be so.
BELARIUS: Boys, we'll go dress our hunt. Fair youth, come in:
