BELARIUS: Discourse is heavy, fasting, when we have supp'd,
BELARIUS: We'll mannerly demand thee of thy story,
BELARIUS: So far as thou wilt speak it.
GUIDERIUS: Pray, draw near.
ARVIRAGUS: The night to the owl and morn to the lark
ARVIRAGUS: less welcome.
IMOGEN: Thanks, sir.
ARVIRAGUS: I pray, draw near.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Rome. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter two Senators and Tribunes
First Senator: This is the tenor of the emperor's writ:
First Senator: That since the common men are now in action
First Senator: 'Gainst the Pannonians and Dalmatians,
First Senator: And that the legions now in Gallia are
First Senator: Full weak to undertake our wars against
First Senator: The fall'n-off Britons, that we do incite
First Senator: The gentry to this business. He creates
First Senator: Lucius preconsul: and to you the tribunes,
First Senator: For this immediate levy, he commends
First Senator: His absolute commission. Long live Caesar!
First Tribune: Is Lucius general of the forces?
Second Senator: Ay.
First Tribune: Remaining now in Gallia?
First Senator: With those legions
First Senator: Which I have spoke of, whereunto your levy
First Senator: Must be supplyant: the words of your commission
First Senator: Will tie you to the numbers and the time
First Senator: Of their dispatch.
First Tribune: We will discharge our duty.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Wales: near the cave of Belarius.
NARRATOR: Enter CLOTEN
CLOTEN: I am near to the place where they should meet, if
CLOTEN: Pisanio have mapped it truly. How fit his garments
CLOTEN: serve me! Why should his mistress, who was made by
CLOTEN: him that made the tailor, not be fit too? the
CLOTEN: rather--saving reverence of the word--for 'tis said
CLOTEN: a woman's fitness comes by fits. Therein I must
CLOTEN: play the workman. I dare speak it to myself--for it
CLOTEN: is not vain-glory for a man and his glass to confer
CLOTEN: in his own chamber--I mean, the lines of my body are
CLOTEN: as well drawn as his, no less young, more strong,
CLOTEN: not beneath him in fortunes, beyond him in the
CLOTEN: advantage of the time, above him in birth, alike
CLOTEN: conversant in general services, and more remarkable
CLOTEN: in single oppositions: yet this imperceiverant
CLOTEN: thing loves him in my despite. What mortality is!
CLOTEN: Posthumus, thy head, which now is growing upon thy
CLOTEN: shoulders, shall within this hour be off, thy
CLOTEN: mistress enforced, thy garments cut to pieces before
CLOTEN: thy face: and all this done, spurn her home to her
CLOTEN: father, who may haply be a little angry for my so
CLOTEN: rough usage, but my mother, having power of his
CLOTEN: testiness, shall turn all into my commendations. My
CLOTEN: horse is tied up safe: out, sword, and to a sore
CLOTEN: purpose! Fortune, put them into my hand! This is
CLOTEN: the very description of their meeting-place, and
CLOTEN: the fellow dares not deceive me.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before the cave of Belarius.
NARRATOR: Enter, from the cave, BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, ARVIRAGUS, and IMOGEN
BELARIUS: [To IMOGEN]  You are not well: remain here in the cave,
BELARIUS: We'll come to you after hunting.
ARVIRAGUS: [To IMOGEN]	Brother, stay here
ARVIRAGUS: Are we not brothers?
IMOGEN: So man and man should be,
IMOGEN: But clay and clay differs in dignity,
IMOGEN: Whose dust is both alike. I am very sick.
GUIDERIUS: Go you to hunting, I'll abide with him.
IMOGEN: So sick I am not, yet I am not well,
IMOGEN: But not so citizen a wanton as
IMOGEN: To seem to die ere sick: so please you, leave me,
IMOGEN: Stick to your journal course: the breach of custom
IMOGEN: Is breach of all. I am ill, but your being by me
IMOGEN: Cannot amend me, society is no comfort
IMOGEN: To one not sociable: I am not very sick,
IMOGEN: Since I can reason of it. Pray you, trust me here:
IMOGEN: I'll rob none but myself, and let me die,
IMOGEN: Stealing so poorly.
GUIDERIUS: I love thee, I have spoke it
GUIDERIUS: How much the quantity, the weight as much,
GUIDERIUS: As I do love my father.
BELARIUS: What! how! how!
ARVIRAGUS: If it be sin to say so, I yoke me
ARVIRAGUS: In my good brother's fault: I know not why
ARVIRAGUS: I love this youth, and I have heard you say,
ARVIRAGUS: Love's reason's without reason: the bier at door,
ARVIRAGUS: And a demand who is't shall die, I'd say
ARVIRAGUS: 'My father, not this youth.'
BELARIUS: [Aside]	O noble strain!
BELARIUS: O worthiness of nature! breed of greatness!
BELARIUS: Cowards father cowards and base things sire base:
BELARIUS: Nature hath meal and bran, contempt and grace.
BELARIUS: I'm not their father, yet who this should be,
BELARIUS: Doth miracle itself, loved before me.
BELARIUS: 'Tis the ninth hour o' the morn.
ARVIRAGUS: Brother, farewell.
IMOGEN: I wish ye sport.
ARVIRAGUS: You health. So please you, sir.
IMOGEN: [Aside]  These are kind creatures. Gods, what lies
IMOGEN: I have heard!
IMOGEN: Our courtiers say all's savage but at court:
IMOGEN: Experience, O, thou disprovest report!
IMOGEN: The imperious seas breed monsters, for the dish
IMOGEN: Poor tributary rivers as sweet fish.
IMOGEN: I am sick still, heart-sick. Pisanio,
IMOGEN: I'll now taste of thy drug.
NARRATOR: Swallows some
GUIDERIUS: I could not stir him:
GUIDERIUS: He said he was gentle, but unfortunate,
GUIDERIUS: Dishonestly afflicted, but yet honest.
ARVIRAGUS: Thus did he answer me: yet said, hereafter
ARVIRAGUS: I might know more.
BELARIUS: To the field, to the field!
BELARIUS: We'll leave you for this time: go in and rest.
ARVIRAGUS: We'll not be long away.
BELARIUS: Pray, be not sick,
BELARIUS: For you must be our housewife.
IMOGEN: Well or ill,
IMOGEN: I am bound to you.
BELARIUS: And shalt be ever.
NARRATOR: Exit IMOGEN, to the cave
BELARIUS: This youth, how'er distress'd, appears he hath had
BELARIUS: Good ancestors.
ARVIRAGUS: How angel-like he sings!
GUIDERIUS: But his neat cookery! he cut our roots
GUIDERIUS: In characters,
GUIDERIUS: And sauced our broths, as Juno had been sick
GUIDERIUS: And he her dieter.
ARVIRAGUS: Nobly he yokes
ARVIRAGUS: A smiling with a sigh, as if the sigh
ARVIRAGUS: Was that it was, for not being such a smile,
ARVIRAGUS: The smile mocking the sigh, that it would fly
ARVIRAGUS: From so divine a temple, to commix
ARVIRAGUS: With winds that sailors rail at.
GUIDERIUS: I do note
GUIDERIUS: That grief and patience, rooted in him both,
GUIDERIUS: Mingle their spurs together.
ARVIRAGUS: Grow, patience!
ARVIRAGUS: And let the stinking elder, grief, untwine
ARVIRAGUS: His perishing root with the increasing vine!
BELARIUS: It is great morning. Come, away!--
BELARIUS: Who's there?
NARRATOR: Enter CLOTEN
CLOTEN: I cannot find those runagates, that villain
CLOTEN: Hath mock'd me. I am faint.
BELARIUS: 'Those runagates!'
BELARIUS: Means he not us? I partly know him: 'tis
BELARIUS: Cloten, the son o' the queen. I fear some ambush.
BELARIUS: I saw him not these many years, and yet
BELARIUS: I know 'tis he. We are held as outlaws: hence!
GUIDERIUS: He is but one: you and my brother search
GUIDERIUS: What companies are near: pray you, away,
GUIDERIUS: Let me alone with him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BELARIUS and ARVIRAGUS
CLOTEN: Soft! What are you
CLOTEN: That fly me thus? some villain mountaineers?
CLOTEN: I have heard of such. What slave art thou?
GUIDERIUS: A thing
GUIDERIUS: More slavish did I ne'er than answering
GUIDERIUS: A slave without a knock.
CLOTEN: Thou art a robber,
CLOTEN: A law-breaker, a villain: yield thee, thief.
GUIDERIUS: To who? to thee? What art thou? Have not I
GUIDERIUS: An arm as big as thine? a heart as big?
GUIDERIUS: Thy words, I grant, are bigger, for I wear not
GUIDERIUS: My dagger in my mouth. Say what thou art,
GUIDERIUS: Why I should yield to thee?
CLOTEN: Thou villain base,
CLOTEN: Know'st me not by my clothes?
GUIDERIUS: No, nor thy tailor, rascal,
GUIDERIUS: Who is thy grandfather: he made those clothes,
GUIDERIUS: Which, as it seems, make thee.
CLOTEN: Thou precious varlet,
CLOTEN: My tailor made them not.
GUIDERIUS: Hence, then, and thank
GUIDERIUS: The man that gave them thee. Thou art some fool,
GUIDERIUS: I am loath to beat thee.
CLOTEN: Thou injurious thief,
CLOTEN: Hear but my name, and tremble.
GUIDERIUS: What's thy name?
CLOTEN: Cloten, thou villain.
GUIDERIUS: Cloten, thou double villain, be thy name,
GUIDERIUS: I cannot tremble at it: were it Toad, or
GUIDERIUS: Adder, Spider,
GUIDERIUS: 'Twould move me sooner.
CLOTEN: To thy further fear,
CLOTEN: Nay, to thy mere confusion, thou shalt know
CLOTEN: I am son to the queen.
GUIDERIUS: I am sorry for 't, not seeming
GUIDERIUS: So worthy as thy birth.
CLOTEN: Art not afeard?
GUIDERIUS: Those that I reverence those I fear, the wise:
GUIDERIUS: At fools I laugh, not fear them.
CLOTEN: Die the death:
CLOTEN: When I have slain thee with my proper hand,
CLOTEN: I'll follow those that even now fled hence,
CLOTEN: And on the gates of Lud's-town set your heads:
CLOTEN: Yield, rustic mountaineer.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, fighting
NARRATOR: Re-enter BELARIUS and ARVIRAGUS
BELARIUS: No companies abroad?
ARVIRAGUS: None in the world: you did mistake him, sure.
BELARIUS: I cannot tell: long is it since I saw him,
BELARIUS: But time hath nothing blurr'd those lines of favour
BELARIUS: Which then he wore, the snatches in his voice,
BELARIUS: And burst of speaking, were as his: I am absolute
BELARIUS: 'Twas very Cloten.
ARVIRAGUS: In this place we left them:
ARVIRAGUS: I wish my brother make good time with him,
ARVIRAGUS: You say he is so fell.
BELARIUS: Being scarce made up,
BELARIUS: I mean, to man, he had not apprehension
BELARIUS: Of roaring terrors, for the effect of judgment
BELARIUS: Is oft the cause of fear. But, see, thy brother.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GUIDERIUS, with CLOTEN'S head
GUIDERIUS: This Cloten was a fool, an empty purse,
GUIDERIUS: There was no money in't: not Hercules
GUIDERIUS: Could have knock'd out his brains, for he had none:
GUIDERIUS: Yet I not doing this, the fool had borne
GUIDERIUS: My head as I do his.
BELARIUS: What hast thou done?
GUIDERIUS: I am perfect what: cut off one Cloten's head,
GUIDERIUS: Son to the queen, after his own report,
GUIDERIUS: Who call'd me traitor, mountaineer, and swore
GUIDERIUS: With his own single hand he'ld take us in
GUIDERIUS: Displace our heads where--thank the gods!--they grow,
GUIDERIUS: And set them on Lud's-town.
BELARIUS: We are all undone.
GUIDERIUS: Why, worthy father, what have we to lose,
GUIDERIUS: But that he swore to take, our lives? The law
GUIDERIUS: Protects not us: then why should we be tender
GUIDERIUS: To let an arrogant piece of flesh threat us,
GUIDERIUS: Play judge and executioner all himself,
GUIDERIUS: For we do fear the law? What company
GUIDERIUS: Discover you abroad?
BELARIUS: No single soul
BELARIUS: Can we set eye on, but in all safe reason
BELARIUS: He must have some attendants. Though his humour
BELARIUS: Was nothing but mutation, ay, and that
BELARIUS: From one bad thing to worse, not frenzy, not
BELARIUS: Absolute madness could so far have raved
BELARIUS: To bring him here alone, although perhaps
BELARIUS: It may be heard at court that such as we
BELARIUS: Cave here, hunt here, are outlaws, and in time
BELARIUS: May make some stronger head, the which he hearing--
BELARIUS: As it is like him--might break out, and swear
BELARIUS: He'ld fetch us in, yet is't not probable
BELARIUS: To come alone, either he so undertaking,
BELARIUS: Or they so suffering: then on good ground we fear,
BELARIUS: If we do fear this body hath a tail
BELARIUS: More perilous than the head.
ARVIRAGUS: Let ordinance
ARVIRAGUS: Come as the gods foresay it: howsoe'er,
ARVIRAGUS: My brother hath done well.
BELARIUS: I had no mind
BELARIUS: To hunt this day: the boy Fidele's sickness
BELARIUS: Did make my way long forth.
GUIDERIUS: With his own sword,
GUIDERIUS: Which he did wave against my throat, I have ta'en
GUIDERIUS: His head from him: I'll throw't into the creek
GUIDERIUS: Behind our rock, and let it to the sea,
GUIDERIUS: And tell the fishes he's the queen's son, Cloten:
GUIDERIUS: That's all I reck.
NARRATOR: Exit
BELARIUS: I fear 'twill be revenged:
BELARIUS: Would, Polydote, thou hadst not done't! though valour
BELARIUS: Becomes thee well enough.
ARVIRAGUS: Would I had done't
ARVIRAGUS: So the revenge alone pursued me! Polydore,
ARVIRAGUS: I love thee brotherly, but envy much
ARVIRAGUS: Thou hast robb'd me of this deed: I would revenges,
ARVIRAGUS: That possible strength might meet, would seek us through
ARVIRAGUS: And put us to our answer.
BELARIUS: Well, 'tis done:
BELARIUS: We'll hunt no more to-day, nor seek for danger
BELARIUS: Where there's no profit. I prithee, to our rock,
BELARIUS: You and Fidele play the cooks: I'll stay
BELARIUS: Till hasty Polydote return, and bring him
BELARIUS: To dinner presently.
ARVIRAGUS: Poor sick Fidele!
ARVIRAGUS: I'll weringly to him: to gain his colour
ARVIRAGUS: I'ld let a parish of such Clotens' blood,
ARVIRAGUS: And praise myself for charity.
NARRATOR: Exit
BELARIUS: O thou goddess,
BELARIUS: Thou divine Nature, how thyself thou blazon'st
BELARIUS: In these two princely boys! They are as gentle
BELARIUS: As zephyrs blowing below the violet,
BELARIUS: Not wagging his sweet head, and yet as rough,
BELARIUS: Their royal blood enchafed, as the rudest wind,
BELARIUS: That by the top doth take the mountain pine,
BELARIUS: And make him stoop to the vale. 'Tis wonder
BELARIUS: That an invisible instinct should frame them
BELARIUS: To royalty unlearn'd, honour untaught,
BELARIUS: Civility not seen from other, valour
BELARIUS: That wildly grows in them, but yields a crop
BELARIUS: As if it had been sow'd. Yet still it's strange
BELARIUS: What Cloten's being here to us portends,
BELARIUS: Or what his death will bring us.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GUIDERIUS
GUIDERIUS: Where's my brother?
GUIDERIUS: I have sent Cloten's clotpoll down the stream,
GUIDERIUS: In embassy to his mother: his body's hostage
GUIDERIUS: For his return.
NARRATOR: Solemn music
BELARIUS: My ingenious instrument!
BELARIUS: Hark, Polydore, it sounds! But what occasion
BELARIUS: Hath Cadwal now to give it motion? Hark!
GUIDERIUS: Is he at home?
BELARIUS: He went hence even now.
GUIDERIUS: What does he mean? since death of my dear'st mother
GUIDERIUS: it did not speak before. All solemn things
GUIDERIUS: Should answer solemn accidents. The matter?
GUIDERIUS: Triumphs for nothing and lamenting toys
GUIDERIUS: Is jollity for apes and grief for boys.
GUIDERIUS: Is Cadwal mad?
BELARIUS: Look, here he comes,
BELARIUS: And brings the dire occasion in his arms
BELARIUS: Of what we blame him for.
NARRATOR: Re-enter ARVIRAGUS, with IMOGEN, as dead, bearing her in his arms
ARVIRAGUS: The bird is dead
ARVIRAGUS: That we have made so much on. I had rather
ARVIRAGUS: Have skipp'd from sixteen years of age to sixty,
ARVIRAGUS: To have turn'd my leaping-time into a crutch,
ARVIRAGUS: Than have seen this.
GUIDERIUS: O sweetest, fairest lily!
GUIDERIUS: My brother wears thee not the one half so well
GUIDERIUS: As when thou grew'st thyself.
BELARIUS: O melancholy!
BELARIUS: Who ever yet could sound thy bottom? find
BELARIUS: The ooze, to show what coast thy sluggish crare
BELARIUS: Might easiliest harbour in? Thou blessed thing!
BELARIUS: Jove knows what man thou mightst have made, but I,
BELARIUS: Thou diedst, a most rare boy, of melancholy.
BELARIUS: How found you him?
ARVIRAGUS: Stark, as you see:
ARVIRAGUS: Thus smiling, as some fly hid tickled slumber,
ARVIRAGUS: Not as death's dart, being laugh'd at, his
ARVIRAGUS: right cheek
ARVIRAGUS: Reposing on a cushion.
GUIDERIUS: Where?
ARVIRAGUS: O' the floor,
ARVIRAGUS: His arms thus leagued: I thought he slept, and put
ARVIRAGUS: My clouted brogues from off my feet, whose rudeness
ARVIRAGUS: Answer'd my steps too loud.
GUIDERIUS: Why, he but sleeps:
GUIDERIUS: If he be gone, he'll make his grave a bed,
GUIDERIUS: With female fairies will his tomb be haunted,
GUIDERIUS: And worms will not come to thee.
ARVIRAGUS: With fairest flowers
ARVIRAGUS: Whilst summer lasts and I live here, Fidele,
ARVIRAGUS: I'll sweeten thy sad grave: thou shalt not lack
ARVIRAGUS: The flower that's like thy face, pale primrose, nor
ARVIRAGUS: The azured harebell, like thy veins, no, nor
ARVIRAGUS: The leaf of eglantine, whom not to slander,
ARVIRAGUS: Out-sweeten'd not thy breath: the ruddock would,
ARVIRAGUS: With charitable bill,--O bill, sore-shaming
ARVIRAGUS: Those rich-left heirs that let their fathers lie
ARVIRAGUS: Without a monument!--bring thee all this,
ARVIRAGUS: Yea, and furr'd moss besides, when flowers are none,
ARVIRAGUS: To winter-ground thy corse.
GUIDERIUS: Prithee, have done,
GUIDERIUS: And do not play in wench-like words with that
GUIDERIUS: Which is so serious. Let us bury him,
GUIDERIUS: And not protract with admiration what
GUIDERIUS: Is now due debt. To the grave!
ARVIRAGUS: Say, where shall's lay him?
GUIDERIUS: By good Euriphile, our mother.
ARVIRAGUS: Be't so:
ARVIRAGUS: And let us, Polydore, though now our voices
ARVIRAGUS: Have got the mannish crack, sing him to the ground,
ARVIRAGUS: As once our mother, use like note and words,
ARVIRAGUS: Save that Euriphile must be Fidele.
GUIDERIUS: Cadwal,
GUIDERIUS: I cannot sing: I'll weep, and word it with thee,
GUIDERIUS: For notes of sorrow out of tune are worse
GUIDERIUS: Than priests and fanes that lie.
ARVIRAGUS: We'll speak it, then.
BELARIUS: Great griefs, I see, medicine the less, for Cloten
BELARIUS: Is quite forgot. He was a queen's son, boys,
BELARIUS: And though he came our enemy, remember
BELARIUS: He was paid for that: though mean and
BELARIUS: mighty, rotting
BELARIUS: Together, have one dust, yet reverence,
BELARIUS: That angel of the world, doth make distinction
BELARIUS: Of place 'tween high and low. Our foe was princely
BELARIUS: And though you took his life, as being our foe,
BELARIUS: Yet bury him as a prince.
GUIDERIUS: Pray You, fetch him hither.
GUIDERIUS: Thersites' body is as good as Ajax',
GUIDERIUS: When neither are alive.
ARVIRAGUS: If you'll go fetch him,
ARVIRAGUS: We'll say our song the whilst. Brother, begin.
NARRATOR: Exit BELARIUS
GUIDERIUS: Nay, Cadwal, we must lay his head to the east,
GUIDERIUS: My father hath a reason for't.
ARVIRAGUS: 'Tis true.
GUIDERIUS: Come on then, and remove him.
ARVIRAGUS: So. Begin.
NARRATOR: SONG
GUIDERIUS: Fear no more the heat o' the sun,
GUIDERIUS: Nor the furious winter's rages,
GUIDERIUS: Thou thy worldly task hast done,
GUIDERIUS: Home art gone, and ta'en thy wages:
GUIDERIUS: Golden lads and girls all must,
GUIDERIUS: As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.
ARVIRAGUS: Fear no more the frown o' the great,
ARVIRAGUS: Thou art past the tyrant's stroke,
ARVIRAGUS: Care no more to clothe and eat,
ARVIRAGUS: To thee the reed is as the oak:
ARVIRAGUS: The sceptre, learning, physic, must
ARVIRAGUS: All follow this, and come to dust.
GUIDERIUS: Fear no more the lightning flash,
ARVIRAGUS: Nor the all-dreaded thunder-stone,
GUIDERIUS: Fear not slander, censure rash,
ARVIRAGUS: Thou hast finish'd joy and moan:
ARVIRAGUS: All lovers young, all lovers must
ARVIRAGUS: Consign to thee, and come to dust.
GUIDERIUS: No exorciser harm thee!
ARVIRAGUS: Nor no witchcraft charm thee!
GUIDERIUS: Ghost unlaid forbear thee!
ARVIRAGUS: Nothing ill come near thee!
ARVIRAGUS: Quiet consummation have,
ARVIRAGUS: And renowned be thy grave!
NARRATOR: Re-enter BELARIUS, with the body of CLOTEN
GUIDERIUS: We have done our obsequies: come, lay him down.
BELARIUS: Here's a few flowers, but 'bout midnight, more:
BELARIUS: The herbs that have on them cold dew o' the night
BELARIUS: Are strewings fitt'st for graves. Upon their faces.
BELARIUS: You were as flowers, now wither'd: even so
BELARIUS: These herblets shall, which we upon you strew.
BELARIUS: Come on, away: apart upon our knees.
BELARIUS: The ground that gave them first has them again:
BELARIUS: Their pleasures here are past, so is their pain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, and ARVIRAGUS
IMOGEN: [Awaking]  Yes, sir, to Milford-Haven, which is
IMOGEN: the way?--
IMOGEN: I thank you.--By yond bush?--Pray, how far thither?
IMOGEN: 'Ods pittikins! can it be six mile yet?--
IMOGEN: I have gone all night. 'Faith, I'll lie down and sleep.
IMOGEN: But, soft! no bedfellow!--O god s and goddesses!
NARRATOR: Seeing the body of CLOTEN
IMOGEN: These flowers are like the pleasures of the world,
IMOGEN: This bloody man, the care on't. I hope I dream,
IMOGEN: For so I thought I was a cave-keeper,
IMOGEN: And cook to honest creatures: but 'tis not so,
IMOGEN: 'Twas but a bolt of nothing, shot at nothing,
IMOGEN: Which the brain makes of fumes: our very eyes
IMOGEN: Are sometimes like our judgments, blind. Good faith,
IMOGEN: I tremble stiff with fear: but if there be
IMOGEN: Yet left in heaven as small a drop of pity
IMOGEN: As a wren's eye, fear'd gods, a part of it!
IMOGEN: The dream's here still: even when I wake, it is
IMOGEN: Without me, as within me, not imagined, felt.
IMOGEN: A headless man! The garments of Posthumus!
IMOGEN: I know the shape of's leg: this is his hand,
IMOGEN: His foot Mercurial, his Martial thigh,
IMOGEN: The brawns of Hercules: but his Jovial face
IMOGEN: Murder in heaven?--How!--'Tis gone. Pisanio,
IMOGEN: All curses madded Hecuba gave the Greeks,
IMOGEN: And mine to boot, be darted on thee! Thou,
IMOGEN: Conspired with that irregulous devil, Cloten,
IMOGEN: Hast here cut off my lord. To write and read
IMOGEN: Be henceforth treacherous! Damn'd Pisanio
IMOGEN: Hath with his forged letters,--damn'd Pisanio--
IMOGEN: From this most bravest vessel of the world
IMOGEN: Struck the main-top! O Posthumus! alas,
IMOGEN: Where is thy head? where's that? Ay me!
IMOGEN: where's that?
IMOGEN: Pisanio might have kill'd thee at the heart,
IMOGEN: And left this head on. How should this be? Pisanio?
IMOGEN: 'Tis he and Cloten: malice and lucre in them
IMOGEN: Have laid this woe here. O, 'tis pregnant, pregnant!
IMOGEN: The drug he gave me, which he said was precious
IMOGEN: And cordial to me, have I not found it
IMOGEN: Murderous to the senses? That confirms it home:
IMOGEN: This is Pisanio's deed, and Cloten's: O!
IMOGEN: Give colour to my pale cheek with thy blood,
IMOGEN: That we the horrider may seem to those
IMOGEN: Which chance to find us: O, my lord, my lord!
NARRATOR: Falls on the body
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS, a Captain and other Officers, and a Soothsayer
Captain: To them the legions garrison'd in Gailia,
Captain: After your will, have cross'd the sea, attending
Captain: You here at Milford-Haven with your ships:
Captain: They are in readiness.
CAIUS LUCIUS: But what from Rome?
Captain: The senate hath stirr'd up the confiners
Captain: And gentlemen of Italy, most willing spirits,
Captain: That promise noble service: and they come
Captain: Under the conduct of bold Iachimo,
Captain: Syenna's brother.
CAIUS LUCIUS: When expect you them?
Captain: With the next benefit o' the wind.
CAIUS LUCIUS: This forwardness
CAIUS LUCIUS: Makes our hopes fair. Command our present numbers
CAIUS LUCIUS: Be muster'd, bid the captains look to't. Now, sir,
CAIUS LUCIUS: What have you dream'd of late of this war's purpose?
Soothsayer: Last night the very gods show'd me a vision--
Soothsayer: I fast and pray'd for their intelligence--thus:
Soothsayer: I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, wing'd
Soothsayer: From the spongy south to this part of the west,
Soothsayer: There vanish'd in the sunbeams: which portends--
Soothsayer: Unless my sins abuse my divination--
Soothsayer: Success to the Roman host.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Dream often so,
CAIUS LUCIUS: And never false. Soft, ho! what trunk is here
CAIUS LUCIUS: Without his top? The ruin speaks that sometime
CAIUS LUCIUS: It was a worthy building. How! a page!
CAIUS LUCIUS: Or dead, or sleeping on him? But dead rather,
CAIUS LUCIUS: For nature doth abhor to make his bed
CAIUS LUCIUS: With the defunct, or sleep upon the dead.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Let's see the boy's face.
Captain: He's alive, my lord.
CAIUS LUCIUS: He'll then instruct us of this body. Young one,
CAIUS LUCIUS: Inform us of thy fortunes, for it seems
CAIUS LUCIUS: They crave to be demanded. Who is this
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thou makest thy bloody pillow? Or who was he
CAIUS LUCIUS: That, otherwise than noble nature did,
CAIUS LUCIUS: Hath alter'd that good picture? What's thy interest
CAIUS LUCIUS: In this sad wreck? How came it? Who is it?
CAIUS LUCIUS: What art thou?
IMOGEN: I am nothing: or if not,
IMOGEN: Nothing to be were better. This was my master,
IMOGEN: A very valiant Briton and a good,
IMOGEN: That here by mountaineers lies slain. Alas!
IMOGEN: There is no more such masters: I may wander
IMOGEN: From east to occident, cry out for service,
IMOGEN: Try many, all good, serve truly, never
IMOGEN: Find such another master.
CAIUS LUCIUS: 'Lack, good youth!
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thou movest no less with thy complaining than
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thy master in bleeding: say his name, good friend.
IMOGEN: Richard du Champ.
NARRATOR: Aside
IMOGEN: If I do lie and do
IMOGEN: No harm by it, though the gods hear, I hope
IMOGEN: They'll pardon it.--Say you, sir?
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thy name?
IMOGEN: Fidele, sir.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thou dost approve thyself the very same:
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thy name well fits thy faith, thy faith thy name.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Wilt take thy chance with me? I will not say
CAIUS LUCIUS: Thou shalt be so well master'd, but, be sure,
CAIUS LUCIUS: No less beloved. The Roman emperor's letters,
CAIUS LUCIUS: Sent by a consul to me, should not sooner
CAIUS LUCIUS: Than thine own worth prefer thee: go with me.
IMOGEN: I'll follow, sir. But first, an't please the gods,
IMOGEN: I'll hide my master from the flies, as deep
IMOGEN: As these poor pickaxes can dig, and when
IMOGEN: With wild wood-leaves and weeds I ha' strew'd his grave,
IMOGEN: And on it said a century of prayers,
IMOGEN: Such as I can, twice o'er, I'll weep and sigh,
IMOGEN: And leaving so his service, follow you,
IMOGEN: So please you entertain me.
CAIUS LUCIUS: Ay, good youth!
CAIUS LUCIUS: And rather father thee than master thee.
CAIUS LUCIUS: My friends,
CAIUS LUCIUS: The boy hath taught us manly duties: let us
CAIUS LUCIUS: Find out the prettiest daisied plot we can,
CAIUS LUCIUS: And make him with our pikes and partisans
CAIUS LUCIUS: A grave: come, arm him. Boy, he is preferr'd
CAIUS LUCIUS: By thee to us, and he shall be interr'd
CAIUS LUCIUS: As soldiers can. Be cheerful, wipe thine eyes
CAIUS LUCIUS: Some falls are means the happier to arise.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in Cymbeline's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter CYMBELINE, Lords, PISANIO, and Attendants
CYMBELINE: Again, and bring me word how 'tis with her.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
CYMBELINE: A fever with the absence of her son,
CYMBELINE: A madness, of which her life's in danger. Heavens,
CYMBELINE: How deeply you at once do touch me! Imogen,
CYMBELINE: The great part of my comfort, gone, my queen
CYMBELINE: Upon a desperate bed, and in a time
CYMBELINE: When fearful wars point at me, her son gone,
CYMBELINE: So needful for this present: it strikes me, past
CYMBELINE: The hope of comfort. But for thee, fellow,
CYMBELINE: Who needs must know of her departure and
CYMBELINE: Dost seem so ignorant, we'll enforce it from thee
CYMBELINE: By a sharp torture.
PISANIO: Sir, my life is yours,
PISANIO: I humbly set it at your will, but, for my mistress,
PISANIO: I nothing know where she remains, why gone,
PISANIO: Nor when she purposes return. Beseech your highness,
PISANIO: Hold me your loyal servant.
First Lord: Good my liege,
First Lord: The day that she was missing he was here:
First Lord: I dare be bound he's true and shall perform
First Lord: All parts of his subjection loyally. For Cloten,
First Lord: There wants no diligence in seeking him,
First Lord: And will, no doubt, be found.
CYMBELINE: The time is troublesome.
NARRATOR: To PISANIO
CYMBELINE: We'll slip you for a season, but our jealousy
CYMBELINE: Does yet depend.
First Lord: So please your majesty,
First Lord: The Roman legions, all from Gallia drawn,
First Lord: Are landed on your coast, with a supply
First Lord: Of Roman gentlemen, by the senate sent.
CYMBELINE: Now for the counsel of my son and queen!
CYMBELINE: I am amazed with matter.
First Lord: Good my liege,
First Lord: Your preparation can affront no less
First Lord: Than what you hear of: come more, for more
First Lord: you're ready:
First Lord: The want is but to put those powers in motion
First Lord: That long to move.
CYMBELINE: I thank you. Let's withdraw,
CYMBELINE: And meet the time as it seeks us. We fear not
CYMBELINE: What can from Italy annoy us, but
CYMBELINE: We grieve at chances here. Away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but PISANIO
PISANIO: I heard no letter from my master since
PISANIO: I wrote him Imogen was slain: 'tis strange:
PISANIO: Nor hear I from my mistress who did promise
PISANIO: To yield me often tidings: neither know I
PISANIO: What is betid to Cloten, but remain
PISANIO: Perplex'd in all. The heavens still must work.
PISANIO: Wherein I am false I am honest, not true, to be true.
PISANIO: These present wars shall find I love my country,
PISANIO: Even to the note o' the king, or I'll fall in them.
PISANIO: All other doubts, by time let them be clear'd:
PISANIO: Fortune brings in some boats that are not steer'd.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Wales: before the cave of Belarius.
NARRATOR: Enter BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, and ARVIRAGUS.
GUIDERIUS: The noise is round about us.
BELARIUS: Let us from it.
ARVIRAGUS: What pleasure, sir, find we in life, to lock it
ARVIRAGUS: From action and adventure?
GUIDERIUS: Nay, what hope
GUIDERIUS: Have we in hiding us? This way, the Romans
GUIDERIUS: Must or for Britons slay us, or receive us
GUIDERIUS: For barbarous and unnatural revolts
GUIDERIUS: During their use, and slay us after.
BELARIUS: Sons,
BELARIUS: We'll higher to the mountains, there secure us.
BELARIUS: To the king's party there's no going: newness
BELARIUS: Of Cloten's death--we being not known, not muster'd
BELARIUS: Among the bands--may drive us to a render
BELARIUS: Where we have lived, and so extort from's that
BELARIUS: Which we have done, whose answer would be death
BELARIUS: Drawn on with torture.
GUIDERIUS: This is, sir, a doubt
GUIDERIUS: In such a time nothing becoming you,
GUIDERIUS: Nor satisfying us.
ARVIRAGUS: It is not likely
ARVIRAGUS: That when they hear the Roman horses neigh,
ARVIRAGUS: Behold their quarter'd fires, have both their eyes
ARVIRAGUS: And ears so cloy'd importantly as now,
ARVIRAGUS: That they will waste their time upon our note,
ARVIRAGUS: To know from whence we are.
BELARIUS: O, I am known
BELARIUS: Of many in the army: many years,
BELARIUS: Though Cloten then but young, you see, not wore him
BELARIUS: From my remembrance. And, besides, the king
BELARIUS: Hath not deserved my service nor your loves,
BELARIUS: Who find in my exile the want of breeding,
BELARIUS: The certainty of this hard life, aye hopeless
BELARIUS: To have the courtesy your cradle promised,
BELARIUS: But to be still hot summer's tamings and
BELARIUS: The shrinking slaves of winter.
GUIDERIUS: Than be so
GUIDERIUS: Better to cease to be. Pray, sir, to the army:
GUIDERIUS: I and my brother are not known, yourself
GUIDERIUS: So out of thought, and thereto so o'ergrown,
GUIDERIUS: Cannot be question'd.
ARVIRAGUS: By this sun that shines,
ARVIRAGUS: I'll thither: what thing is it that I never
ARVIRAGUS: Did see man die! scarce ever look'd on blood,
ARVIRAGUS: But that of coward hares, hot goats, and venison!
ARVIRAGUS: Never bestrid a horse, save one that had
ARVIRAGUS: A rider like myself, who ne'er wore rowel
ARVIRAGUS: Nor iron on his heel! I am ashamed
ARVIRAGUS: To look upon the holy sun, to have
ARVIRAGUS: The benefit of his blest beams, remaining
ARVIRAGUS: So long a poor unknown.
GUIDERIUS: By heavens, I'll go:
GUIDERIUS: If you will bless me, sir, and give me leave,
GUIDERIUS: I'll take the better care, but if you will not,
GUIDERIUS: The hazard therefore due fall on me by
GUIDERIUS: The hands of Romans!
ARVIRAGUS: So say I	amen.
BELARIUS: No reason I, since of your lives you set
BELARIUS: So slight a valuation, should reserve
BELARIUS: My crack'd one to more care. Have with you, boys!
BELARIUS: If in your country wars you chance to die,
BELARIUS: That is my bed too, lads, an there I'll lie:
BELARIUS: Lead, lead.
NARRATOR: Aside
BELARIUS: The time seems long, their blood
BELARIUS: thinks scorn,
BELARIUS: Till it fly out and show them princes born.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Britain. The Roman camp.
NARRATOR: Enter POSTHUMUS, with a bloody handkerchief
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Yea, bloody cloth, I'll keep thee, for I wish'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Thou shouldst be colour'd thus. You married ones,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: If each of you should take this course, how many
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Must murder wives much better than themselves
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For wrying but a little! O Pisanio!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Every good servant does not all commands:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: No bond but to do just ones. Gods! if you
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Should have ta'en vengeance on my faults, I never
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Had lived to put on this: so had you saved
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The noble Imogen to repent, and struck
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Me, wretch more worth your vengeance. But, alack,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: You snatch some hence for little faults, that's love,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To have them fall no more: you some permit
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To second ills with ills, each elder worse,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And make them dread it, to the doers' thrift.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But Imogen is your own: do your best wills,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And make me blest to obey! I am brought hither
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Among the Italian gentry, and to fight
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Against my lady's kingdom: 'tis enough
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That, Britain, I have kill'd thy mistress, peace!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I'll give no wound to thee. Therefore, good heavens,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Hear patiently my purpose: I'll disrobe me
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of these Italian weeds and suit myself
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: As does a Briton peasant: so I'll fight
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Against the part I come with, so I'll die
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For thee, O Imogen, even for whom my life
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Is every breath a death, and thus, unknown,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Pitied nor hated, to the face of peril
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Myself I'll dedicate. Let me make men know
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: More valour in me than my habits show.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Gods, put the strength o' the Leonati in me!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To shame the guise o' the world, I will begin
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The fashion, less without and more within.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Field of battle between the British and Roman camps.
NARRATOR: Enter, from one side, LUCIUS, IACHIMO, and  the Roman Army: from the other side, the  British Army, POSTHUMUS LEONATUS following,  like a poor soldier. They march over and go  out. Then enter again, in skirmish, IACHIMO  and POSTHUMUS LEONATUS he vanquisheth and disarmeth IACHIMO, and then leaves him
IACHIMO: The heaviness and guilt within my bosom
IACHIMO: Takes off my manhood: I have belied a lady,
IACHIMO: The princess of this country, and the air on't
IACHIMO: Revengingly enfeebles me, or could this carl,
IACHIMO: A very drudge of nature's, have subdued me
IACHIMO: In my profession? Knighthoods and honours, borne
IACHIMO: As I wear mine, are titles but of scorn.
IACHIMO: If that thy gentry, Britain, go before
IACHIMO: This lout as he exceeds our lords, the odds
IACHIMO: Is that we scarce are men and you are gods.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: The battle continues, the Britons fly, CYMBELINE is  taken: then enter, to his rescue, BELARIUS, GUIDERIUS, and ARVIRAGUS
BELARIUS: Stand, stand! We have the advantage of the ground,
BELARIUS: The lane is guarded: nothing routs us but
BELARIUS: The villany of our fears.
ARVIRAGUS: Stand, stand, and fight!
ARVIRAGUS: Re-enter POSTHUMUS LEONATUS, and seconds the  Britons: they rescue CYMBELINE, and exeunt. Then re-enter LUCIUS, and IACHIMO, with IMOGEN
CAIUS LUCIUS: Away, boy, from the troops, and save thyself,
CAIUS LUCIUS: For friends kill friends, and the disorder's such
CAIUS LUCIUS: As war were hoodwink'd.
IACHIMO: 'Tis their fresh supplies.
CAIUS LUCIUS: It is a day turn'd strangely: or betimes
CAIUS LUCIUS: Let's reinforce, or fly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Enter POSTHUMUS LEONATUS and a British Lord
Lord: Camest thou from where they made the stand?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I did.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Though you, it seems, come from the fliers.
Lord: I did.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: No blame be to you, sir, for all was lost,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But that the heavens fought: the king himself
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of his wings destitute, the army broken,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And but the backs of Britons seen, all flying
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Through a straight lane, the enemy full-hearted,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Lolling the tongue with slaughtering, having work
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: More plentiful than tools to do't, struck down
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Some mortally, some slightly touch'd, some falling
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Merely through fear, that the straight pass was damm'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: With dead men hurt behind, and cowards living
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To die with lengthen'd shame.
Lord: Where was this lane?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Close by the battle, ditch'd, and wall'd with turf,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Which gave advantage to an ancient soldier,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: An honest one, I warrant, who deserved
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: So long a breeding as his white beard came to,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: In doing this for's country: athwart the lane,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: He, with two striplings-lads more like to run
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The country base than to commit such slaughter
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: With faces fit for masks, or rather fairer
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Than those for preservation cased, or shame--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Made good the passage, cried to those that fled,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Our Britain s harts die flying, not our men:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To darkness fleet souls that fly backwards. Stand,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Or we are Romans and will give you that
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Like beasts which you shun beastly, and may save,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But to look back in frown: stand, stand.'
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: These three,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Three thousand confident, in act as many--
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For three performers are the file when all
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The rest do nothing--with this word 'Stand, stand,'
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Accommodated by the place, more charming
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: With their own nobleness, which could have turn'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A distaff to a lance, gilded pale looks,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Part shame, part spirit renew'd, that some,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: turn'd coward
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But by example--O, a sin in war,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Damn'd in the first beginners!--gan to look
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The way that they did, and to grin like lions
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Upon the pikes o' the hunters. Then began
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A stop i' the chaser, a retire, anon
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A rout, confusion thick, forthwith they fly
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Chickens, the way which they stoop'd eagles, slaves,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The strides they victors made: and now our cowards,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Like fragments in hard voyages, became
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The life o' the need: having found the backdoor open
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Of the unguarded hearts, heavens, how they wound!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Some slain before, some dying, some their friends
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: O'er borne i' the former wave: ten, chased by one,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Are now each one the slaughter-man of twenty:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Those that would die or ere resist are grown
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The mortal bugs o' the field.
Lord: This was strange chance
Lord: A narrow lane, an old man, and two boys.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Nay, do not wonder at it: you are made
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Rather to wonder at the things you hear
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Than to work any. Will you rhyme upon't,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And vent it for a mockery? Here is one:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Two boys, an old man twice a boy, a lane,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Preserved the Britons, was the Romans' bane.'
Lord: Nay, be not angry, sir.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Lack, to what end?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Who dares not stand his foe, I'll be his friend,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For if he'll do as he is made to do,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I know he'll quickly fly my friendship too.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: You have put me into rhyme.
Lord: Farewell, you're angry.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Still going?
NARRATOR: Exit Lord
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: This is a lord! O noble misery,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To be i' the field, and ask 'what news?' of me!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To-day how many would have given their honours
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To have saved their carcasses! took heel to do't,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And yet died too! I, in mine own woe charm'd,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Could not find death where I did hear him groan,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Nor feel him where he struck: being an ugly monster,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Tis strange he hides him in fresh cups, soft beds,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Sweet words, or hath more ministers than we
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: That draw his knives i' the war. Well, I will find him
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For being now a favourer to the Briton,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: No more a Briton, I have resumed again
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The part I came in: fight I will no more,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But yield me to the veriest hind that shall
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Once touch my shoulder. Great the slaughter is
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Here made by the Roman, great the answer be
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Britons must take. For me, my ransom's death,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: On either side I come to spend my breath,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Which neither here I'll keep nor bear again,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: But end it by some means for Imogen.
NARRATOR: Enter two British Captains and Soldiers
First Captain: Great Jupiter be praised! Lucius is taken.
First Captain: 'Tis thought the old man and his sons were angels.
Second Captain: There was a fourth man, in a silly habit,
Second Captain: That gave the affront with them.
First Captain: So 'tis reported:
First Captain: But none of 'em can be found. Stand! who's there?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A Roman,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Who had not now been drooping here, if seconds
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Had answer'd him.
Second Captain: Lay hands on him, a dog!
Second Captain: A leg of Rome shall not return to tell
Second Captain: What crows have peck'd them here. He brags
Second Captain: his service
Second Captain: As if he were of note: bring him to the king.

Second Captain: SCENE IV. A British prison.
NARRATOR: Enter POSTHUMUS LEONATUS and two Gaolers
First Gaoler: You shall not now be stol'n, you have locks upon you,
First Gaoler: So graze as you find pasture.
Second Gaoler: Ay, or a stomach.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Gaolers
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Most welcome, bondage! for thou art away,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: think, to liberty: yet am I better
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Than one that's sick o' the gout, since he had rather
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Groan so in perpetuity than be cured
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: By the sure physician, death, who is the key
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: To unbar these locks. My conscience, thou art fetter'd
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: More than my shanks and wrists: you good gods, give me
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: The penitent instrument to pick that bolt,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Then, free for ever! Is't enough I am sorry?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: So children temporal fathers do appease,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Gods are more full of mercy. Must I repent?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I cannot do it better than in gyves,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Desired more than constrain'd: to satisfy,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: If of my freedom 'tis the main part, take
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: No stricter render of me than my all.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I know you are more clement than vile men,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Who of their broken debtors take a third,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: A sixth, a tenth, letting them thrive again
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: On their abatement: that's not my desire:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: For Imogen's dear life take mine, and though
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Tis not so dear, yet 'tis a life, you coin'd it:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: 'Tween man and man they weigh not every stamp,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Though light, take pieces for the figure's sake:
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: You rather mine, being yours: and so, great powers,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: If you will take this audit, take this life,
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: And cancel these cold bonds. O Imogen!
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I'll speak to thee in silence.
NARRATOR: Sleeps
NARRATOR: Solemn music. Enter, as in an apparition,  SICILIUS LEONATUS, father to Posthumus Leonatus,  an old man, attired like a warrior, leading in  his hand an ancient matron, his wife, and mother  to Posthumus Leonatus, with music before them:  then, after other music, follow the two young  Leonati, brothers to Posthumus Leonatus, with  wounds as they died in the wars. They circle Posthumus Leonatus round, as he lies sleeping
Sicilius Leonatus: No more, thou thunder-master, show
Sicilius Leonatus: Thy spite on mortal flies:
Sicilius Leonatus: With Mars fall out, with Juno chide,
Sicilius Leonatus: That thy adulteries
Sicilius Leonatus: Rates and revenges.

Second Brother: And from thy justice fly.
Second Brother: Jupiter descends in thunder and lightning, sitting  upon an eagle: he throws a thunderbolt. The Apparitions fall on their knees
Jupiter: No more, you petty spirits of region low,
Jupiter: Offend our hearing, hush! How dare you ghosts
Jupiter: Accuse the thunderer, whose bolt, you know,
Jupiter: Sky-planted batters all rebelling coasts?
Jupiter: Poor shadows of Elysium, hence, and rest
Jupiter: Upon your never-withering banks of flowers:
Jupiter: Be not with mortal accidents opprest,
Jupiter: No care of yours it is, you know 'tis ours.
Jupiter: Whom best I love I cross, to make my gift,
Jupiter: The more delay'd, delighted. Be content,
Jupiter: Your low-laid son our godhead will uplift:
Jupiter: His comforts thrive, his trials well are spent.
Jupiter: Our Jovial star reign'd at his birth, and in
Jupiter: Our temple was he married. Rise, and fade.
Jupiter: He shall be lord of lady Imogen,
Jupiter: And happier much by his affliction made.
Jupiter: This tablet lay upon his breast, wherein
Jupiter: Our pleasure his full fortune doth confine:
Jupiter: and so, away: no further with your din
Jupiter: Express impatience, lest you stir up mine.
Jupiter: Mount, eagle, to my palace crystalline.
NARRATOR: Ascends
Sicilius Leonatus: He came in thunder, his celestial breath
Sicilius Leonatus: Was sulphurous to smell: the holy eagle
Sicilius Leonatus: Stoop'd as to foot us: his ascension is
Sicilius Leonatus: More sweet than our blest fields: his royal bird
Sicilius Leonatus: Prunes the immortal wing and cloys his beak,

Sicilius Leonatus: The marble pavement closes, he is enter'd

Posthumus Leonatus: [Waking]  Sleep, thou hast been a grandsire, and begot
Posthumus Leonatus: A father to me, and thou hast created
Posthumus Leonatus: A mother and two brothers: but, O scorn!
Posthumus Leonatus: Gone! they went hence so soon as they were born:

Posthumus Leonatus: On greatness' favour dream as I have done,
Posthumus Leonatus: Wake and find nothing. But, alas, I swerve:
Posthumus Leonatus: Many dream not to find, neither deserve,
Posthumus Leonatus: And yet are steep'd in favours: so am I,
Posthumus Leonatus: That have this golden chance and know not why.
Posthumus Leonatus: What fairies haunt this ground? A book? O rare one!
Posthumus Leonatus: Be not, as is our fangled world, a garment
Posthumus Leonatus: Nobler than that it covers: let thy effects

NARRATOR: Reads

NARRATOR: Re-enter First Gaoler
First Gaoler: Come, sir, are you ready for death?
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Over-roasted rather, ready long ago.
First Gaoler: Hanging is the word, sir: if
First Gaoler: you be ready for that, you are well cooked.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: So, if I prove a good repast to the
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: spectators, the dish pays the shot.
First Gaoler: A heavy reckoning for you, sir. But the comfort is,
First Gaoler: you shall be called to no more payments, fear no
First Gaoler: more tavern-bills, which are often the sadness of
First Gaoler: parting, as the procuring of mirth: you come in
First Gaoler: flint for want of meat, depart reeling with too
First Gaoler: much drink, sorry that you have paid too much, and
First Gaoler: sorry that you are paid too much, purse and brain
First Gaoler: both empty, the brain the heavier for being too
First Gaoler: light, the purse too light, being drawn of
First Gaoler: heaviness: of this contradiction you shall now be
First Gaoler: quit. O, the charity of a penny cord! It sums up
First Gaoler: thousands in a trice: you have no true debitor and
First Gaoler: creditor but it, of what's past, is, and to come,
First Gaoler: the discharge: your neck, sir, is pen, book and
First Gaoler: counters, so the acquittance follows.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: I am merrier to die than thou art to live.
First Gaoler: Indeed, sir, he that sleeps feels not the
First Gaoler: tooth-ache: but a man that were to sleep your
First Gaoler: sleep, and a hangman to help him to bed, I think he
First Gaoler: would change places with his officer, for, look you,
First Gaoler: sir, you know not which way you shall go.
POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: Yes, indeed do I, fellow.

POSTHUMUS LEONATUS: direct them the way I am going, but such as wink and

NARRATOR: SCENE V. Cymbeline's tent.

CORNELIUS: O'ercome you with her show, and in time,
