Soothsayer: From south to west on wing soaring aloft,
Soothsayer: Lessen'd herself, and in the beams o' the sun
Soothsayer: So vanish'd: which foreshow'd our princely eagle,
Soothsayer: The imperial Caesar, should again unite
Soothsayer: His favour with the radiant Cymbeline,
Soothsayer: Which shines here in the west.
CYMBELINE: Laud we the gods,
CYMBELINE: And let our crooked smokes climb to their nostrils
CYMBELINE: From our blest altars. Publish we this peace
CYMBELINE: To all our subjects. Set we forward: let
CYMBELINE: A Roman and a British ensign wave
CYMBELINE: Friendly together: so through Lud's-town march:
CYMBELINE: And in the temple of great Jupiter
CYMBELINE: Our peace we'll ratify, seal it with feasts.
CYMBELINE: Set on there! Never was a war did cease,
CYMBELINE: Ere bloody hands were wash'd, with such a peace.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Hamlet '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Elsinore. A platform before the castle.
NARRATOR: FRANCISCO at his post. Enter to him BERNARDO
BERNARDO: Who's there?
FRANCISCO: Nay, answer me: stand, and unfold yourself.
BERNARDO: Long live the king!
FRANCISCO: Bernardo?
BERNARDO: He.
FRANCISCO: You come most carefully upon your hour.
BERNARDO: 'Tis now struck twelve, get thee to bed, Francisco.
FRANCISCO: For this relief much thanks: 'tis bitter cold,
FRANCISCO: And I am sick at heart.
BERNARDO: Have you had quiet guard?
FRANCISCO: Not a mouse stirring.
BERNARDO: Well, good night.
BERNARDO: If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus,
BERNARDO: The rivals of my watch, bid them make haste.
FRANCISCO: I think I hear them. Stand, ho! Who's there?
NARRATOR: Enter HORATIO and MARCELLUS
HORATIO: Friends to this ground.
MARCELLUS: And liegemen to the Dane.
FRANCISCO: Give you good night.
MARCELLUS: O, farewell, honest soldier:
MARCELLUS: Who hath relieved you?
FRANCISCO: Bernardo has my place.
FRANCISCO: Give you good night.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARCELLUS: Holla! Bernardo!
BERNARDO: Say,
BERNARDO: What, is Horatio there?
HORATIO: A piece of him.
BERNARDO: Welcome, Horatio: welcome, good Marcellus.
MARCELLUS: What, has this thing appear'd again to-night?
BERNARDO: I have seen nothing.
MARCELLUS: Horatio says 'tis but our fantasy,
MARCELLUS: And will not let belief take hold of him
MARCELLUS: Touching this dreaded sight, twice seen of us:
MARCELLUS: Therefore I have entreated him along
MARCELLUS: With us to watch the minutes of this night,
MARCELLUS: That if again this apparition come,
MARCELLUS: He may approve our eyes and speak to it.
HORATIO: Tush, tush, 'twill not appear.
BERNARDO: Sit down awhile,
BERNARDO: And let us once again assail your ears,
BERNARDO: That are so fortified against our story
BERNARDO: What we have two nights seen.
HORATIO: Well, sit we down,
HORATIO: And let us hear Bernardo speak of this.
BERNARDO: Last night of all,
BERNARDO: When yond same star that's westward from the pole
BERNARDO: Had made his course to illume that part of heaven
BERNARDO: Where now it burns, Marcellus and myself,
BERNARDO: The bell then beating one,--
NARRATOR: Enter Ghost
MARCELLUS: Peace, break thee off, look, where it comes again!
BERNARDO: In the same figure, like the king that's dead.
MARCELLUS: Thou art a scholar, speak to it, Horatio.
BERNARDO: Looks it not like the king?  mark it, Horatio.
HORATIO: Most like: it harrows me with fear and wonder.
BERNARDO: It would be spoke to.
MARCELLUS: Question it, Horatio.
HORATIO: What art thou that usurp'st this time of night,
HORATIO: Together with that fair and warlike form
HORATIO: In which the majesty of buried Denmark
HORATIO: Did sometimes march? by heaven I charge thee, speak!
MARCELLUS: It is offended.
BERNARDO: See, it stalks away!
HORATIO: Stay! speak, speak! I charge thee, speak!
NARRATOR: Exit Ghost
MARCELLUS: 'Tis gone, and will not answer.
BERNARDO: How now, Horatio! you tremble and look pale:
BERNARDO: Is not this something more than fantasy?
BERNARDO: What think you on't?
HORATIO: Before my God, I might not this believe
HORATIO: Without the sensible and true avouch
HORATIO: Of mine own eyes.
MARCELLUS: Is it not like the king?
HORATIO: As thou art to thyself:
HORATIO: Such was the very armour he had on
HORATIO: When he the ambitious Norway combated,
HORATIO: So frown'd he once, when, in an angry parle,
HORATIO: He smote the sledded Polacks on the ice.
HORATIO: 'Tis strange.
MARCELLUS: Thus twice before, and jump at this dead hour,
MARCELLUS: With martial stalk hath he gone by our watch.
HORATIO: In what particular thought to work I know not,
HORATIO: But in the gross and scope of my opinion,
HORATIO: This bodes some strange eruption to our state.
MARCELLUS: Good now, sit down, and tell me, he that knows,
MARCELLUS: Why this same strict and most observant watch
MARCELLUS: So nightly toils the subject of the land,
MARCELLUS: And why such daily cast of brazen cannon,
MARCELLUS: And foreign mart for implements of war,
MARCELLUS: Why such impress of shipwrights, whose sore task
MARCELLUS: Does not divide the Sunday from the week,
MARCELLUS: What might be toward, that this sweaty haste
MARCELLUS: Doth make the night joint-labourer with the day:
MARCELLUS: Who is't that can inform me?
HORATIO: That can I,
HORATIO: At least, the whisper goes so. Our last king,
HORATIO: Whose image even but now appear'd to us,
HORATIO: Was, as you know, by Fortinbras of Norway,
HORATIO: Thereto prick'd on by a most emulate pride,
HORATIO: Dared to the combat, in which our valiant Hamlet--
HORATIO: For so this side of our known world esteem'd him--
HORATIO: Did slay this Fortinbras, who by a seal'd compact,
HORATIO: Well ratified by law and heraldry,
HORATIO: Did forfeit, with his life, all those his lands
HORATIO: Which he stood seized of, to the conqueror:
HORATIO: Against the which, a moiety competent
HORATIO: Was gaged by our king, which had return'd
HORATIO: To the inheritance of Fortinbras,
HORATIO: Had he been vanquisher, as, by the same covenant,
HORATIO: And carriage of the article design'd,
HORATIO: His fell to Hamlet. Now, sir, young Fortinbras,
HORATIO: Of unimproved mettle hot and full,
HORATIO: Hath in the skirts of Norway here and there
HORATIO: Shark'd up a list of lawless resolutes,
HORATIO: For food and diet, to some enterprise
HORATIO: That hath a stomach in't, which is no other--
HORATIO: As it doth well appear unto our state--
HORATIO: But to recover of us, by strong hand
HORATIO: And terms compulsatory, those foresaid lands
HORATIO: So by his father lost: and this, I take it,
HORATIO: Is the main motive of our preparations,
HORATIO: The source of this our watch and the chief head
HORATIO: Of this post-haste and romage in the land.
BERNARDO: I think it be no other but e'en so:
BERNARDO: Well may it sort that this portentous figure
BERNARDO: Comes armed through our watch, so like the king
BERNARDO: That was and is the question of these wars.
HORATIO: A mote it is to trouble the mind's eye.
HORATIO: In the most high and palmy state of Rome,
HORATIO: A little ere the mightiest Julius fell,
HORATIO: The graves stood tenantless and the sheeted dead
HORATIO: Did squeak and gibber in the Roman streets:
HORATIO: As stars with trains of fire and dews of blood,
HORATIO: Disasters in the sun, and the moist star
HORATIO: Upon whose influence Neptune's empire stands
HORATIO: Was sick almost to doomsday with eclipse:
HORATIO: And even the like precurse of fierce events,
HORATIO: As harbingers preceding still the fates
HORATIO: And prologue to the omen coming on,
HORATIO: Have heaven and earth together demonstrated
HORATIO: Unto our climatures and countrymen.--
HORATIO: But soft, behold! lo, where it comes again!
NARRATOR: Re-enter Ghost
HORATIO: I'll cross it, though it blast me. Stay, illusion!
HORATIO: If thou hast any sound, or use of voice,
HORATIO: Speak to me:
HORATIO: If there be any good thing to be done,
HORATIO: That may to thee do ease and grace to me,
HORATIO: Speak to me:
NARRATOR: Cock crows
HORATIO: If thou art privy to thy country's fate,
HORATIO: Which, happily, foreknowing may avoid, O, speak!
HORATIO: Or if thou hast uphoarded in thy life
HORATIO: Extorted treasure in the womb of earth,
HORATIO: For which, they say, you spirits oft walk in death,
HORATIO: Speak of it: stay, and speak! Stop it, Marcellus.
MARCELLUS: Shall I strike at it with my partisan?
HORATIO: Do, if it will not stand.
BERNARDO: 'Tis here!
HORATIO: 'Tis here!
MARCELLUS: 'Tis gone!
NARRATOR: Exit Ghost
MARCELLUS: We do it wrong, being so majestical,
MARCELLUS: To offer it the show of violence,
MARCELLUS: For it is, as the air, invulnerable,
MARCELLUS: And our vain blows malicious mockery.
BERNARDO: It was about to speak, when the cock crew.
HORATIO: And then it started like a guilty thing
HORATIO: Upon a fearful summons. I have heard,
HORATIO: The cock, that is the trumpet to the morn,
HORATIO: Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding throat
HORATIO: Awake the god of day, and, at his warning,
HORATIO: Whether in sea or fire, in earth or air,
HORATIO: The extravagant and erring spirit hies
HORATIO: To his confine: and of the truth herein
HORATIO: This present object made probation.
MARCELLUS: It faded on the crowing of the cock.
MARCELLUS: Some say that ever 'gainst that season comes
MARCELLUS: Wherein our Saviour's birth is celebrated,
MARCELLUS: The bird of dawning singeth all night long:
MARCELLUS: And then, they say, no spirit dares stir abroad,
MARCELLUS: The nights are wholesome, then no planets strike,
MARCELLUS: No fairy takes, nor witch hath power to charm,
MARCELLUS: So hallow'd and so gracious is the time.
HORATIO: So have I heard and do in part believe it.
HORATIO: But, look, the morn, in russet mantle clad,
HORATIO: Walks o'er the dew of yon high eastward hill:
HORATIO: Break we our watch up, and by my advice,
HORATIO: Let us impart what we have seen to-night
HORATIO: Unto young Hamlet, for, upon my life,
HORATIO: This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him.
HORATIO: Do you consent we shall acquaint him with it,
HORATIO: As needful in our loves, fitting our duty?
MARCELLUS: Let's do't, I pray, and I this morning know
MARCELLUS: Where we shall find him most conveniently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room of state in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter KING CLAUDIUS, QUEEN GERTRUDE, HAMLET,  POLONIUS, LAERTES, VOLTIMAND, CORNELIUS, Lords, and Attendants
KING CLAUDIUS: Though yet of Hamlet our dear brother's death
KING CLAUDIUS: The memory be green, and that it us befitted
KING CLAUDIUS: To bear our hearts in grief and our whole kingdom
KING CLAUDIUS: To be contracted in one brow of woe,
KING CLAUDIUS: Yet so far hath discretion fought with nature
KING CLAUDIUS: That we with wisest sorrow think on him,
KING CLAUDIUS: Together with remembrance of ourselves.
KING CLAUDIUS: Therefore our sometime sister, now our queen,
KING CLAUDIUS: The imperial jointress to this warlike state,
KING CLAUDIUS: Have we, as 'twere with a defeated joy,--
KING CLAUDIUS: With an auspicious and a dropping eye,
KING CLAUDIUS: With mirth in funeral and with dirge in marriage,
KING CLAUDIUS: In equal scale weighing delight and dole,--
KING CLAUDIUS: Taken to wife: nor have we herein barr'd
KING CLAUDIUS: Your better wisdoms, which have freely gone
KING CLAUDIUS: With this affair along. For all, our thanks.
KING CLAUDIUS: Now follows, that you know, young Fortinbras,
KING CLAUDIUS: Holding a weak supposal of our worth,
KING CLAUDIUS: Or thinking by our late dear brother's death
KING CLAUDIUS: Our state to be disjoint and out of frame,
KING CLAUDIUS: Colleagued with the dream of his advantage,
KING CLAUDIUS: He hath not fail'd to pester us with message,
KING CLAUDIUS: Importing the surrender of those lands
KING CLAUDIUS: Lost by his father, with all bonds of law,
KING CLAUDIUS: To our most valiant brother. So much for him.
KING CLAUDIUS: Now for ourself and for this time of meeting:
KING CLAUDIUS: Thus much the business is: we have here writ
KING CLAUDIUS: To Norway, uncle of young Fortinbras,--
KING CLAUDIUS: Who, impotent and bed-rid, scarcely hears
KING CLAUDIUS: Of this his nephew's purpose,--to suppress
KING CLAUDIUS: His further gait herein, in that the levies,
KING CLAUDIUS: The lists and full proportions, are all made
KING CLAUDIUS: Out of his subject: and we here dispatch
KING CLAUDIUS: You, good Cornelius, and you, Voltimand,
KING CLAUDIUS: For bearers of this greeting to old Norway,
KING CLAUDIUS: Giving to you no further personal power
KING CLAUDIUS: To business with the king, more than the scope
KING CLAUDIUS: Of these delated articles allow.
KING CLAUDIUS: Farewell, and let your haste commend your duty.
VOLTIMAND: In that and all things will we show our duty.
KING CLAUDIUS: We doubt it nothing: heartily farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt VOLTIMAND and CORNELIUS
KING CLAUDIUS: And now, Laertes, what's the news with you?
KING CLAUDIUS: You told us of some suit, what is't, Laertes?
KING CLAUDIUS: You cannot speak of reason to the Dane,
KING CLAUDIUS: And loose your voice: what wouldst thou beg, Laertes,
KING CLAUDIUS: That shall not be my offer, not thy asking?
KING CLAUDIUS: The head is not more native to the heart,
KING CLAUDIUS: The hand more instrumental to the mouth,
KING CLAUDIUS: Than is the throne of Denmark to thy father.
KING CLAUDIUS: What wouldst thou have, Laertes?
LAERTES: My dread lord,
LAERTES: Your leave and favour to return to France,
LAERTES: From whence though willingly I came to Denmark,
LAERTES: To show my duty in your coronation,
LAERTES: Yet now, I must confess, that duty done,
LAERTES: My thoughts and wishes bend again toward France
LAERTES: And bow them to your gracious leave and pardon.
KING CLAUDIUS: Have you your father's leave? What says Polonius?
LORD POLONIUS: He hath, my lord, wrung from me my slow leave
LORD POLONIUS: By laboursome petition, and at last
LORD POLONIUS: Upon his will I seal'd my hard consent:
LORD POLONIUS: I do beseech you, give him leave to go.
KING CLAUDIUS: Take thy fair hour, Laertes, time be thine,
KING CLAUDIUS: And thy best graces spend it at thy will!
KING CLAUDIUS: But now, my cousin Hamlet, and my son,--
HAMLET: [Aside]  A little more than kin, and less than kind.
KING CLAUDIUS: How is it that the clouds still hang on you?
HAMLET: Not so, my lord, I am too much i' the sun.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Good Hamlet, cast thy nighted colour off,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: And let thine eye look like a friend on Denmark.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Do not for ever with thy vailed lids
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Seek for thy noble father in the dust:
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Thou know'st 'tis common, all that lives must die,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Passing through nature to eternity.
HAMLET: Ay, madam, it is common.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: If it be,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Why seems it so particular with thee?
HAMLET: Seems, madam! nay it is, I know not 'seems.'
HAMLET: 'Tis not alone my inky cloak, good mother,
HAMLET: Nor customary suits of solemn black,
HAMLET: Nor windy suspiration of forced breath,
HAMLET: No, nor the fruitful river in the eye,
HAMLET: Nor the dejected 'havior of the visage,
HAMLET: Together with all forms, moods, shapes of grief,
HAMLET: That can denote me truly: these indeed seem,
HAMLET: For they are actions that a man might play:
HAMLET: But I have that within which passeth show,
HAMLET: These but the trappings and the suits of woe.
KING CLAUDIUS: 'Tis sweet and commendable in your nature, Hamlet,
KING CLAUDIUS: To give these mourning duties to your father:
KING CLAUDIUS: But, you must know, your father lost a father,
KING CLAUDIUS: That father lost, lost his, and the survivor bound
KING CLAUDIUS: In filial obligation for some term
KING CLAUDIUS: To do obsequious sorrow: but to persever
KING CLAUDIUS: In obstinate condolement is a course
KING CLAUDIUS: Of impious stubbornness, 'tis unmanly grief,
KING CLAUDIUS: It shows a will most incorrect to heaven,
KING CLAUDIUS: A heart unfortified, a mind impatient,
KING CLAUDIUS: An understanding simple and unschool'd:
KING CLAUDIUS: For what we know must be and is as common
KING CLAUDIUS: As any the most vulgar thing to sense,
KING CLAUDIUS: Why should we in our peevish opposition
KING CLAUDIUS: Take it to heart? Fie! 'tis a fault to heaven,
KING CLAUDIUS: A fault against the dead, a fault to nature,
KING CLAUDIUS: To reason most absurd: whose common theme
KING CLAUDIUS: Is death of fathers, and who still hath cried,
KING CLAUDIUS: From the first corse till he that died to-day,
KING CLAUDIUS: 'This must be so.' We pray you, throw to earth
KING CLAUDIUS: This unprevailing woe, and think of us
KING CLAUDIUS: As of a father: for let the world take note,
KING CLAUDIUS: You are the most immediate to our throne,
KING CLAUDIUS: And with no less nobility of love
KING CLAUDIUS: Than that which dearest father bears his son,
KING CLAUDIUS: Do I impart toward you. For your intent
KING CLAUDIUS: In going back to school in Wittenberg,
KING CLAUDIUS: It is most retrograde to our desire:
KING CLAUDIUS: And we beseech you, bend you to remain
KING CLAUDIUS: Here, in the cheer and comfort of our eye,
KING CLAUDIUS: Our chiefest courtier, cousin, and our son.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Let not thy mother lose her prayers, Hamlet:
QUEEN GERTRUDE: I pray thee, stay with us, go not to Wittenberg.
HAMLET: I shall in all my best obey you, madam.
KING CLAUDIUS: Why, 'tis a loving and a fair reply:
KING CLAUDIUS: Be as ourself in Denmark. Madam, come,
KING CLAUDIUS: This gentle and unforced accord of Hamlet
KING CLAUDIUS: Sits smiling to my heart: in grace whereof,
KING CLAUDIUS: No jocund health that Denmark drinks to-day,
KING CLAUDIUS: But the great cannon to the clouds shall tell,
KING CLAUDIUS: And the king's rouse the heavens all bruit again,
KING CLAUDIUS: Re-speaking earthly thunder. Come away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but HAMLET
HAMLET: O, that this too too solid flesh would melt
HAMLET: Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!
HAMLET: Or that the Everlasting had not fix'd
HAMLET: His canon 'gainst self-slaughter! O God! God!
HAMLET: How weary, stale, flat and unprofitable,
HAMLET: Seem to me all the uses of this world!
HAMLET: Fie on't! ah fie! 'tis an unweeded garden,
HAMLET: That grows to seed, things rank and gross in nature
HAMLET: Possess it merely. That it should come to this!
HAMLET: But two months dead: nay, not so much, not two:
HAMLET: So excellent a king, that was, to this,
HAMLET: Hyperion to a satyr, so loving to my mother
HAMLET: That he might not beteem the winds of heaven
HAMLET: Visit her face too roughly. Heaven and earth!
HAMLET: Must I remember? why, she would hang on him,
HAMLET: As if increase of appetite had grown
HAMLET: By what it fed on: and yet, within a month--
HAMLET: Let me not think on't--Frailty, thy name is woman!--
HAMLET: A little month, or ere those shoes were old
HAMLET: With which she follow'd my poor father's body,
HAMLET: Like Niobe, all tears:--why she, even she--
HAMLET: O, God! a beast, that wants discourse of reason,
HAMLET: Would have mourn'd longer--married with my uncle,
HAMLET: My father's brother, but no more like my father
HAMLET: Than I to Hercules: within a month:
HAMLET: Ere yet the salt of most unrighteous tears
HAMLET: Had left the flushing in her galled eyes,
HAMLET: She married. O, most wicked speed, to post
HAMLET: With such dexterity to incestuous sheets!
HAMLET: It is not nor it cannot come to good:
HAMLET: But break, my heart, for I must hold my tongue.
NARRATOR: Enter HORATIO, MARCELLUS, and BERNARDO
HORATIO: Hail to your lordship!
HAMLET: I am glad to see you well:
HAMLET: Horatio,--or I do forget myself.
HORATIO: The same, my lord, and your poor servant ever.
HAMLET: Sir, my good friend, I'll change that name with you:
HAMLET: And what make you from Wittenberg, Horatio? Marcellus?
MARCELLUS: My good lord--
HAMLET: I am very glad to see you. Good even, sir.
HAMLET: But what, in faith, make you from Wittenberg?
HORATIO: A truant disposition, good my lord.
HAMLET: I would not hear your enemy say so,
HAMLET: Nor shall you do mine ear that violence,
HAMLET: To make it truster of your own report
HAMLET: Against yourself: I know you are no truant.
HAMLET: But what is your affair in Elsinore?
HAMLET: We'll teach you to drink deep ere you depart.
HORATIO: My lord, I came to see your father's funeral.
HAMLET: I pray thee, do not mock me, fellow-student,
HAMLET: I think it was to see my mother's wedding.
HORATIO: Indeed, my lord, it follow'd hard upon.
HAMLET: Thrift, thrift, Horatio! the funeral baked meats
HAMLET: Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables.
HAMLET: Would I had met my dearest foe in heaven
HAMLET: Or ever I had seen that day, Horatio!
HAMLET: My father!--methinks I see my father.
HORATIO: Where, my lord?
HAMLET: In my mind's eye, Horatio.
HORATIO: I saw him once, he was a goodly king.
HAMLET: He was a man, take him for all in all,
HAMLET: I shall not look upon his like again.
HORATIO: My lord, I think I saw him yesternight.
HAMLET: Saw? who?
HORATIO: My lord, the king your father.
HAMLET: The king my father!
HORATIO: Season your admiration for awhile
HORATIO: With an attent ear, till I may deliver,
HORATIO: Upon the witness of these gentlemen,
HORATIO: This marvel to you.
HAMLET: For God's love, let me hear.
HORATIO: Two nights together had these gentlemen,
HORATIO: Marcellus and Bernardo, on their watch,
HORATIO: In the dead vast and middle of the night,
HORATIO: Been thus encounter'd. A figure like your father,
HORATIO: Armed at point exactly, cap-a-pe,
HORATIO: Appears before them, and with solemn march
HORATIO: Goes slow and stately by them: thrice he walk'd
HORATIO: By their oppress'd and fear-surprised eyes,
HORATIO: Within his truncheon's length, whilst they, distilled
HORATIO: Almost to jelly with the act of fear,
HORATIO: Stand dumb and speak not to him. This to me
HORATIO: In dreadful secrecy impart they did,
HORATIO: And I with them the third night kept the watch,
HORATIO: Where, as they had deliver'd, both in time,
HORATIO: Form of the thing, each word made true and good,
HORATIO: The apparition comes: I knew your father,
HORATIO: These hands are not more like.
HAMLET: But where was this?
MARCELLUS: My lord, upon the platform where we watch'd.
HAMLET: Did you not speak to it?
HORATIO: My lord, I did,
HORATIO: But answer made it none: yet once methought
HORATIO: It lifted up its head and did address
HORATIO: Itself to motion, like as it would speak,
HORATIO: But even then the morning cock crew loud,
HORATIO: And at the sound it shrunk in haste away,
HORATIO: And vanish'd from our sight.
HAMLET: 'Tis very strange.
HORATIO: As I do live, my honour'd lord, 'tis true,
HORATIO: And we did think it writ down in our duty
HORATIO: To let you know of it.
HAMLET: Indeed, indeed, sirs, but this troubles me.
HAMLET: Hold you the watch to-night?
BERNARDO: We do, my lord.
HAMLET: Arm'd, say you?
BERNARDO: Arm'd, my lord.
HAMLET: From top to toe?
BERNARDO: My lord, from head to foot.
HAMLET: Then saw you not his face?
HORATIO: O, yes, my lord, he wore his beaver up.
HAMLET: What, look'd he frowningly?
HORATIO: A countenance more in sorrow than in anger.
HAMLET: Pale or red?
HORATIO: Nay, very pale.
HAMLET: And fix'd his eyes upon you?
HORATIO: Most constantly.
HAMLET: I would I had been there.
HORATIO: It would have much amazed you.
HAMLET: Very like, very like. Stay'd it long?
HORATIO: While one with moderate haste might tell a hundred.
BERNARDO: Longer, longer.
HORATIO: Not when I saw't.
HAMLET: His beard was grizzled--no?
HORATIO: It was, as I have seen it in his life,
HORATIO: A sable silver'd.
HAMLET: I will watch to-night,
HAMLET: Perchance 'twill walk again.
HORATIO: I warrant it will.
HAMLET: If it assume my noble father's person,
HAMLET: I'll speak to it, though hell itself should gape
HAMLET: And bid me hold my peace. I pray you all,
HAMLET: If you have hitherto conceal'd this sight,
HAMLET: Let it be tenable in your silence still,
HAMLET: And whatsoever else shall hap to-night,
HAMLET: Give it an understanding, but no tongue:
HAMLET: I will requite your loves. So, fare you well:
HAMLET: Upon the platform, 'twixt eleven and twelve,
HAMLET: I'll visit you.
All: Our duty to your honour.
HAMLET: Your loves, as mine to you: farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but HAMLET
HAMLET: My father's spirit in arms! all is not well,
HAMLET: I doubt some foul play: would the night were come!
HAMLET: Till then sit still, my soul: foul deeds will rise,
HAMLET: Though all the earth o'erwhelm them, to men's eyes.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in Polonius' house.
NARRATOR: Enter LAERTES and OPHELIA
LAERTES: My necessaries are embark'd: farewell:
LAERTES: And, sister, as the winds give benefit
LAERTES: And convoy is assistant, do not sleep,
LAERTES: But let me hear from you.
OPHELIA: Do you doubt that?
LAERTES: For Hamlet and the trifling of his favour,
LAERTES: Hold it a fashion and a toy in blood,
LAERTES: A violet in the youth of primy nature,
LAERTES: Forward, not permanent, sweet, not lasting,
LAERTES: The perfume and suppliance of a minute, No more.
OPHELIA: No more but so?
LAERTES: Think it no more,
LAERTES: For nature, crescent, does not grow alone
LAERTES: In thews and bulk, but, as this temple waxes,
LAERTES: The inward service of the mind and soul
LAERTES: Grows wide withal. Perhaps he loves you now,
LAERTES: And now no soil nor cautel doth besmirch
LAERTES: The virtue of his will: but you must fear,
LAERTES: His greatness weigh'd, his will is not his own,
LAERTES: For he himself is subject to his birth:
LAERTES: He may not, as unvalued persons do,
LAERTES: Carve for himself, for on his choice depends
LAERTES: The safety and health of this whole state,
LAERTES: And therefore must his choice be circumscribed
LAERTES: Unto the voice and yielding of that body
LAERTES: Whereof he is the head. Then if he says he loves you,
LAERTES: It fits your wisdom so far to believe it
LAERTES: As he in his particular act and place
LAERTES: May give his saying deed, which is no further
LAERTES: Than the main voice of Denmark goes withal.
LAERTES: Then weigh what loss your honour may sustain,
LAERTES: If with too credent ear you list his songs,
LAERTES: Or lose your heart, or your chaste treasure open
LAERTES: To his unmaster'd importunity.
LAERTES: Fear it, Ophelia, fear it, my dear sister,
LAERTES: And keep you in the rear of your affection,
LAERTES: Out of the shot and danger of desire.
LAERTES: The chariest maid is prodigal enough,
LAERTES: If she unmask her beauty to the moon:
LAERTES: Virtue itself 'scapes not calumnious strokes:
LAERTES: The canker galls the infants of the spring,
LAERTES: Too oft before their buttons be disclosed,
LAERTES: And in the morn and liquid dew of youth
LAERTES: Contagious blastments are most imminent.
LAERTES: Be wary then, best safety lies in fear:
LAERTES: Youth to itself rebels, though none else near.
OPHELIA: I shall the effect of this good lesson keep,
OPHELIA: As watchman to my heart. But, good my brother,
OPHELIA: Do not, as some ungracious pastors do,
OPHELIA: Show me the steep and thorny way to heaven,
OPHELIA: Whiles, like a puff'd and reckless libertine,
OPHELIA: Himself the primrose path of dalliance treads,
OPHELIA: And recks not his own rede.
LAERTES: O, fear me not.
LAERTES: I stay too long: but here my father comes.
NARRATOR: Enter POLONIUS
LAERTES: A double blessing is a double grace,
LAERTES: Occasion smiles upon a second leave.
LORD POLONIUS: Yet here, Laertes! aboard, aboard, for shame!
LORD POLONIUS: The wind sits in the shoulder of your sail,
LORD POLONIUS: And you are stay'd for. There, my blessing with thee!
LORD POLONIUS: And these few precepts in thy memory
LORD POLONIUS: See thou character. Give thy thoughts no tongue,
LORD POLONIUS: Nor any unproportioned thought his act.
LORD POLONIUS: Be thou familiar, but by no means vulgar.
LORD POLONIUS: Those friends thou hast, and their adoption tried,
LORD POLONIUS: Grapple them to thy soul with hoops of steel,
LORD POLONIUS: But do not dull thy palm with entertainment
LORD POLONIUS: Of each new-hatch'd, unfledged comrade. Beware
LORD POLONIUS: Of entrance to a quarrel, but being in,
LORD POLONIUS: Bear't that the opposed may beware of thee.
LORD POLONIUS: Give every man thy ear, but few thy voice,
LORD POLONIUS: Take each man's censure, but reserve thy judgment.
LORD POLONIUS: Costly thy habit as thy purse can buy,
LORD POLONIUS: But not express'd in fancy, rich, not gaudy,
LORD POLONIUS: For the apparel oft proclaims the man,
LORD POLONIUS: And they in France of the best rank and station
LORD POLONIUS: Are of a most select and generous chief in that.
LORD POLONIUS: Neither a borrower nor a lender be,
LORD POLONIUS: For loan oft loses both itself and friend,
LORD POLONIUS: And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
LORD POLONIUS: This above all: to thine ownself be true,
LORD POLONIUS: And it must follow, as the night the day,
LORD POLONIUS: Thou canst not then be false to any man.
LORD POLONIUS: Farewell: my blessing season this in thee!
LAERTES: Most humbly do I take my leave, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: The time invites you, go, your servants tend.
LAERTES: Farewell, Ophelia, and remember well
LAERTES: What I have said to you.
OPHELIA: 'Tis in my memory lock'd,
OPHELIA: And you yourself shall keep the key of it.
LAERTES: Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
LORD POLONIUS: What is't, Ophelia, be hath said to you?
OPHELIA: So please you, something touching the Lord Hamlet.
LORD POLONIUS: Marry, well bethought:
LORD POLONIUS: 'Tis told me, he hath very oft of late
LORD POLONIUS: Given private time to you, and you yourself
LORD POLONIUS: Have of your audience been most free and bounteous:
LORD POLONIUS: If it be so, as so 'tis put on me,
LORD POLONIUS: And that in way of caution, I must tell you,
LORD POLONIUS: You do not understand yourself so clearly
LORD POLONIUS: As it behoves my daughter and your honour.
LORD POLONIUS: What is between you? give me up the truth.
OPHELIA: He hath, my lord, of late made many tenders
OPHELIA: Of his affection to me.
LORD POLONIUS: Affection! pooh! you speak like a green girl,
LORD POLONIUS: Unsifted in such perilous circumstance.
LORD POLONIUS: Do you believe his tenders, as you call them?
OPHELIA: I do not know, my lord, what I should think.
LORD POLONIUS: Marry, I'll teach you: think yourself a baby,
LORD POLONIUS: That you have ta'en these tenders for true pay,
LORD POLONIUS: Which are not sterling. Tender yourself more dearly,
LORD POLONIUS: Or--not to crack the wind of the poor phrase,
LORD POLONIUS: Running it thus--you'll tender me a fool.
OPHELIA: My lord, he hath importuned me with love
OPHELIA: In honourable fashion.
LORD POLONIUS: Ay, fashion you may call it, go to, go to.
OPHELIA: And hath given countenance to his speech, my lord,
OPHELIA: With almost all the holy vows of heaven.
LORD POLONIUS: Ay, springes to catch woodcocks. I do know,
LORD POLONIUS: When the blood burns, how prodigal the soul
LORD POLONIUS: Lends the tongue vows: these blazes, daughter,
LORD POLONIUS: Giving more light than heat, extinct in both,
LORD POLONIUS: Even in their promise, as it is a-making,
LORD POLONIUS: You must not take for fire. From this time
LORD POLONIUS: Be somewhat scanter of your maiden presence,
LORD POLONIUS: Set your entreatments at a higher rate
LORD POLONIUS: Than a command to parley. For Lord Hamlet,
LORD POLONIUS: Believe so much in him, that he is young
LORD POLONIUS: And with a larger tether may he walk
LORD POLONIUS: Than may be given you: in few, Ophelia,
LORD POLONIUS: Do not believe his vows, for they are brokers,
LORD POLONIUS: Not of that dye which their investments show,
LORD POLONIUS: But mere implorators of unholy suits,
LORD POLONIUS: Breathing like sanctified and pious bawds,
LORD POLONIUS: The better to beguile. This is for all:
LORD POLONIUS: I would not, in plain terms, from this time forth,
LORD POLONIUS: Have you so slander any moment leisure,
LORD POLONIUS: As to give words or talk with the Lord Hamlet.
LORD POLONIUS: Look to't, I charge you: come your ways.
OPHELIA: I shall obey, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The platform.
NARRATOR: Enter HAMLET, HORATIO, and MARCELLUS
HAMLET: The air bites shrewdly, it is very cold.
HORATIO: It is a nipping and an eager air.
HAMLET: What hour now?
HORATIO: I think it lacks of twelve.
HAMLET: No, it is struck.
HORATIO: Indeed? I heard it not: then it draws near the season
HORATIO: Wherein the spirit held his wont to walk.
NARRATOR: A flourish of trumpets, and ordnance shot off, within
HORATIO: What does this mean, my lord?
HAMLET: The king doth wake to-night and takes his rouse,
HAMLET: Keeps wassail, and the swaggering up-spring reels,
HAMLET: And, as he drains his draughts of Rhenish down,
HAMLET: The kettle-drum and trumpet thus bray out
HAMLET: The triumph of his pledge.
HORATIO: Is it a custom?
HAMLET: Ay, marry, is't:
HAMLET: But to my mind, though I am native here
HAMLET: And to the manner born, it is a custom
HAMLET: More honour'd in the breach than the observance.
HAMLET: This heavy-headed revel east and west
HAMLET: Makes us traduced and tax'd of other nations:
HAMLET: They clepe us drunkards, and with swinish phrase
HAMLET: Soil our addition, and indeed it takes
HAMLET: From our achievements, though perform'd at height,
HAMLET: The pith and marrow of our attribute.
HAMLET: So, oft it chances in particular men,
HAMLET: That for some vicious mole of nature in them,
HAMLET: As, in their birth--wherein they are not guilty,
HAMLET: Since nature cannot choose his origin--
HAMLET: By the o'ergrowth of some complexion,
HAMLET: Oft breaking down the pales and forts of reason,
HAMLET: Or by some habit that too much o'er-leavens
HAMLET: The form of plausive manners, that these men,
HAMLET: Carrying, I say, the stamp of one defect,
HAMLET: Being nature's livery, or fortune's star,--
HAMLET: Their virtues else--be they as pure as grace,
HAMLET: As infinite as man may undergo--
HAMLET: Shall in the general censure take corruption
HAMLET: From that particular fault: the dram of eale
HAMLET: Doth all the noble substance of a doubt
HAMLET: To his own scandal.
HORATIO: Look, my lord, it comes!
NARRATOR: Enter Ghost
HAMLET: Angels and ministers of grace defend us!
HAMLET: Be thou a spirit of health or goblin damn'd,
HAMLET: Bring with thee airs from heaven or blasts from hell,
HAMLET: Be thy intents wicked or charitable,
HAMLET: Thou comest in such a questionable shape
HAMLET: That I will speak to thee: I'll call thee Hamlet,
HAMLET: King, father, royal Dane: O, answer me!
HAMLET: Let me not burst in ignorance, but tell
HAMLET: Why thy canonized bones, hearsed in death,
HAMLET: Have burst their cerements, why the sepulchre,
HAMLET: Wherein we saw thee quietly inurn'd,
HAMLET: Hath oped his ponderous and marble jaws,
HAMLET: To cast thee up again. What may this mean,
HAMLET: That thou, dead corse, again in complete steel
HAMLET: Revisit'st thus the glimpses of the moon,
HAMLET: Making night hideous, and we fools of nature
HAMLET: So horridly to shake our disposition
HAMLET: With thoughts beyond the reaches of our souls?
HAMLET: Say, why is this? wherefore? what should we do?
NARRATOR: Ghost beckons HAMLET
HORATIO: It beckons you to go away with it,
HORATIO: As if it some impartment did desire
HORATIO: To you alone.
MARCELLUS: Look, with what courteous action
MARCELLUS: It waves you to a more removed ground:
MARCELLUS: But do not go with it.
HORATIO: No, by no means.
HAMLET: It will not speak, then I will follow it.
HORATIO: Do not, my lord.
HAMLET: Why, what should be the fear?
HAMLET: I do not set my life in a pin's fee,
HAMLET: And for my soul, what can it do to that,
HAMLET: Being a thing immortal as itself?
HAMLET: It waves me forth again: I'll follow it.
HORATIO: What if it tempt you toward the flood, my lord,
HORATIO: Or to the dreadful summit of the cliff
HORATIO: That beetles o'er his base into the sea,
HORATIO: And there assume some other horrible form,
HORATIO: Which might deprive your sovereignty of reason
HORATIO: And draw you into madness? think of it:
HORATIO: The very place puts toys of desperation,
HORATIO: Without more motive, into every brain
HORATIO: That looks so many fathoms to the sea
HORATIO: And hears it roar beneath.
HAMLET: It waves me still.
HAMLET: Go on, I'll follow thee.
MARCELLUS: You shall not go, my lord.
HAMLET: Hold off your hands.
HORATIO: Be ruled, you shall not go.
HAMLET: My fate cries out,
HAMLET: And makes each petty artery in this body
HAMLET: As hardy as the Nemean lion's nerve.
HAMLET: Still am I call'd. Unhand me, gentlemen.
HAMLET: By heaven, I'll make a ghost of him that lets me!
HAMLET: I say, away! Go on, I'll follow thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Ghost and HAMLET
HORATIO: He waxes desperate with imagination.
MARCELLUS: Let's follow, 'tis not fit thus to obey him.
HORATIO: Have after. To what issue will this come?
MARCELLUS: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
HORATIO: Heaven will direct it.
MARCELLUS: Nay, let's follow him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the platform.
NARRATOR: Enter GHOST and HAMLET
HAMLET: Where wilt thou lead me? speak, I'll go no further.
Ghost: Mark me.
HAMLET: I will.
Ghost: My hour is almost come,
Ghost: When I to sulphurous and tormenting flames
Ghost: Must render up myself.
HAMLET: Alas, poor ghost!
Ghost: Pity me not, but lend thy serious hearing
Ghost: To what I shall unfold.
HAMLET: Speak, I am bound to hear.
Ghost: So art thou to revenge, when thou shalt hear.
HAMLET: What?
Ghost: I am thy father's spirit,
Ghost: Doom'd for a certain term to walk the night,
Ghost: And for the day confined to fast in fires,
Ghost: Till the foul crimes done in my days of nature
Ghost: Are burnt and purged away. But that I am forbid
Ghost: To tell the secrets of my prison-house,
Ghost: I could a tale unfold whose lightest word
Ghost: Would harrow up thy soul, freeze thy young blood,
Ghost: Make thy two eyes, like stars, start from their spheres,
Ghost: Thy knotted and combined locks to part
Ghost: And each particular hair to stand on end,
Ghost: Like quills upon the fretful porpentine:
Ghost: But this eternal blazon must not be
Ghost: To ears of flesh and blood. List, list, O, list!
Ghost: If thou didst ever thy dear father love--
HAMLET: O God!
Ghost: Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.
HAMLET: Murder!
Ghost: Murder most foul, as in the best it is,
Ghost: But this most foul, strange and unnatural.
HAMLET: Haste me to know't, that I, with wings as swift
HAMLET: As meditation or the thoughts of love,
HAMLET: May sweep to my revenge.
Ghost: I find thee apt,
Ghost: And duller shouldst thou be than the fat weed
Ghost: That roots itself in ease on Lethe wharf,
Ghost: Wouldst thou not stir in this. Now, Hamlet, hear:
Ghost: 'Tis given out that, sleeping in my orchard,
Ghost: A serpent stung me, so the whole ear of Denmark
Ghost: Is by a forged process of my death
Ghost: Rankly abused: but know, thou noble youth,
Ghost: The serpent that did sting thy father's life
Ghost: Now wears his crown.
HAMLET: O my prophetic soul! My uncle!
Ghost: Ay, that incestuous, that adulterate beast,
Ghost: With witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts,--
Ghost: O wicked wit and gifts, that have the power
Ghost: So to seduce!--won to his shameful lust
Ghost: The will of my most seeming-virtuous queen:
Ghost: O Hamlet, what a falling-off was there!
Ghost: From me, whose love was of that dignity
Ghost: That it went hand in hand even with the vow
Ghost: I made to her in marriage, and to decline
Ghost: Upon a wretch whose natural gifts were poor
Ghost: To those of mine!
Ghost: But virtue, as it never will be moved,
Ghost: Though lewdness court it in a shape of heaven,
Ghost: So lust, though to a radiant angel link'd,
Ghost: Will sate itself in a celestial bed,
Ghost: And prey on garbage.
Ghost: But, soft! methinks I scent the morning air,
Ghost: Brief let me be. Sleeping within my orchard,
Ghost: My custom always of the afternoon,
Ghost: Upon my secure hour thy uncle stole,
Ghost: With juice of cursed hebenon in a vial,
Ghost: And in the porches of my ears did pour
Ghost: The leperous distilment, whose effect
Ghost: Holds such an enmity with blood of man
Ghost: That swift as quicksilver it courses through
Ghost: The natural gates and alleys of the body,
Ghost: And with a sudden vigour doth posset
Ghost: And curd, like eager droppings into milk,
Ghost: The thin and wholesome blood: so did it mine,
Ghost: And a most instant tetter bark'd about,
Ghost: Most lazar-like, with vile and loathsome crust,
Ghost: All my smooth body.
Ghost: Thus was I, sleeping, by a brother's hand
Ghost: Of life, of crown, of queen, at once dispatch'd:
Ghost: Cut off even in the blossoms of my sin,
Ghost: Unhousel'd, disappointed, unanel'd,
Ghost: No reckoning made, but sent to my account
Ghost: With all my imperfections on my head:
Ghost: O, horrible! O, horrible! most horrible!
Ghost: If thou hast nature in thee, bear it not,
Ghost: Let not the royal bed of Denmark be
Ghost: A couch for luxury and damned incest.
Ghost: But, howsoever thou pursuest this act,
Ghost: Taint not thy mind, nor let thy soul contrive
Ghost: Against thy mother aught: leave her to heaven
Ghost: And to those thorns that in her bosom lodge,
Ghost: To prick and sting her. Fare thee well at once!
Ghost: The glow-worm shows the matin to be near,
Ghost: And 'gins to pale his uneffectual fire:
Ghost: Adieu, adieu! Hamlet, remember me.
NARRATOR: Exit
HAMLET: O all you host of heaven! O earth! what else?
HAMLET: And shall I couple hell? O, fie! Hold, hold, my heart,
HAMLET: And you, my sinews, grow not instant old,
HAMLET: But bear me stiffly up. Remember thee!
HAMLET: Ay, thou poor ghost, while memory holds a seat
HAMLET: In this distracted globe. Remember thee!
HAMLET: Yea, from the table of my memory
HAMLET: I'll wipe away all trivial fond records,
HAMLET: All saws of books, all forms, all pressures past,
HAMLET: That youth and observation copied there,
HAMLET: And thy commandment all alone shall live
HAMLET: Within the book and volume of my brain,
HAMLET: Unmix'd with baser matter: yes, by heaven!
HAMLET: O most pernicious woman!
HAMLET: O villain, villain, smiling, damned villain!
HAMLET: My tables,--meet it is I set it down,
HAMLET: That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain,
HAMLET: At least I'm sure it may be so in Denmark:
NARRATOR: Writing
HAMLET: So, uncle, there you are. Now to my word,
HAMLET: It is 'Adieu, adieu! remember me.'
HAMLET: I have sworn 't.
HORATIO: [Within]  My lord, my lord,--
MARCELLUS: [Within]	Lord Hamlet,--
HORATIO: [Within]	Heaven secure him!
HAMLET: So be it!
HORATIO: [Within]  Hillo, ho, ho, my lord!
HAMLET: Hillo, ho, ho, boy! come, bird, come.
NARRATOR: Enter HORATIO and MARCELLUS
MARCELLUS: How is't, my noble lord?
HORATIO: What news, my lord?
HAMLET: O, wonderful!
HORATIO: Good my lord, tell it.
HAMLET: No, you'll reveal it.
HORATIO: Not I, my lord, by heaven.
MARCELLUS: Nor I, my lord.
HAMLET: How say you, then, would heart of man once think it?
HAMLET: But you'll be secret?
MARCELLUS: Ay, by heaven, my lord.
HAMLET: There's ne'er a villain dwelling in all Denmark
HAMLET: But he's an arrant knave.
HORATIO: There needs no ghost, my lord, come from the grave
HORATIO: To tell us this.
HAMLET: Why, right, you are i' the right,
HAMLET: And so, without more circumstance at all,
HAMLET: I hold it fit that we shake hands and part:
HAMLET: You, as your business and desire shall point you,
HAMLET: For every man has business and desire,
HAMLET: Such as it is, and for mine own poor part,
HAMLET: Look you, I'll go pray.
HORATIO: These are but wild and whirling words, my lord.
HAMLET: I'm sorry they offend you, heartily,
HAMLET: Yes, 'faith heartily.
HORATIO: There's no offence, my lord.
HAMLET: Yes, by Saint Patrick, but there is, Horatio,
HAMLET: And much offence too. Touching this vision here,
HAMLET: It is an honest ghost, that let me tell you:
HAMLET: For your desire to know what is between us,
HAMLET: O'ermaster 't as you may. And now, good friends,
HAMLET: As you are friends, scholars and soldiers,
HAMLET: Give me one poor request.
HORATIO: What is't, my lord? we will.
HAMLET: Never make known what you have seen to-night.
MARCELLUS: My lord, we will not.
HAMLET: Nay, but swear't.
HORATIO: In faith,
HORATIO: My lord, not I.
MARCELLUS: Nor I, my lord, in faith.
HAMLET: Upon my sword.
MARCELLUS: We have sworn, my lord, already.
HAMLET: Indeed, upon my sword, indeed.
Ghost: [Beneath]  Swear.
HAMLET: Ah, ha, boy! say'st thou so? art thou there,
HAMLET: truepenny?
HAMLET: Come on--you hear this fellow in the cellarage--
HAMLET: Consent to swear.
HORATIO: Propose the oath, my lord.
HAMLET: Never to speak of this that you have seen,
HAMLET: Swear by my sword.
Ghost: [Beneath]  Swear.
HAMLET: Hic et ubique? then we'll shift our ground.
HAMLET: Come hither, gentlemen,
HAMLET: And lay your hands again upon my sword:
HAMLET: Never to speak of this that you have heard,
HAMLET: Swear by my sword.
Ghost: [Beneath]  Swear.
HAMLET: Well said, old mole! canst work i' the earth so fast?
HAMLET: A worthy pioner! Once more remove, good friends.
HORATIO: O day and night, but this is wondrous strange!
HAMLET: And therefore as a stranger give it welcome.
HAMLET: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,
HAMLET: Than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But come,
HAMLET: Here, as before, never, so help you mercy,
HAMLET: How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself,
HAMLET: As I perchance hereafter shall think meet
HAMLET: To put an antic disposition on,
HAMLET: That you, at such times seeing me, never shall,
HAMLET: With arms encumber'd thus, or this headshake,
HAMLET: Or by pronouncing of some doubtful phrase,
HAMLET: As 'Well, well, we know,' or 'We could, an if we would,'
HAMLET: Or 'If we list to speak,' or 'There be, an if they might,'
HAMLET: Or such ambiguous giving out, to note
HAMLET: That you know aught of me: this not to do,
HAMLET: So grace and mercy at your most need help you, Swear.
Ghost: [Beneath]  Swear.
HAMLET: Rest, rest, perturbed spirit!
NARRATOR: They swear
HAMLET: So, gentlemen,
HAMLET: With all my love I do commend me to you:
HAMLET: And what so poor a man as Hamlet is
HAMLET: May do, to express his love and friending to you,
HAMLET: God willing, shall not lack. Let us go in together,
HAMLET: And still your fingers on your lips, I pray.
HAMLET: The time is out of joint: O cursed spite,
HAMLET: That ever I was born to set it right!
HAMLET: Nay, come, let's go together.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A room in POLONIUS' house.
NARRATOR: Enter POLONIUS and REYNALDO
LORD POLONIUS: Give him this money and these notes, Reynaldo.
REYNALDO: I will, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: You shall do marvellous wisely, good Reynaldo,
LORD POLONIUS: Before you visit him, to make inquire
LORD POLONIUS: Of his behavior.
REYNALDO: My lord, I did intend it.
LORD POLONIUS: Marry, well said, very well said. Look you, sir,
LORD POLONIUS: Inquire me first what Danskers are in Paris,
LORD POLONIUS: And how, and who, what means, and where they keep,
LORD POLONIUS: What company, at what expense, and finding
LORD POLONIUS: By this encompassment and drift of question
LORD POLONIUS: That they do know my son, come you more nearer
LORD POLONIUS: Than your particular demands will touch it:
LORD POLONIUS: Take you, as 'twere, some distant knowledge of him,
LORD POLONIUS: As thus, 'I know his father and his friends,
LORD POLONIUS: And in part him: ' do you mark this, Reynaldo?
REYNALDO: Ay, very well, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: 'And in part him, but' you may say 'not well:
LORD POLONIUS: But, if't be he I mean, he's very wild,
LORD POLONIUS: Addicted so and so:' and there put on him
LORD POLONIUS: What forgeries you please, marry, none so rank
LORD POLONIUS: As may dishonour him, take heed of that,
LORD POLONIUS: But, sir, such wanton, wild and usual slips
LORD POLONIUS: As are companions noted and most known
LORD POLONIUS: To youth and liberty.
REYNALDO: As gaming, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: Ay, or drinking, fencing, swearing, quarrelling,
LORD POLONIUS: Drabbing: you may go so far.
REYNALDO: My lord, that would dishonour him.
LORD POLONIUS: 'Faith, no, as you may season it in the charge
LORD POLONIUS: You must not put another scandal on him,
LORD POLONIUS: That he is open to incontinency,
LORD POLONIUS: That's not my meaning: but breathe his faults so quaintly
LORD POLONIUS: That they may seem the taints of liberty,
LORD POLONIUS: The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind,
LORD POLONIUS: A savageness in unreclaimed blood,
LORD POLONIUS: Of general assault.
REYNALDO: But, my good lord,--
LORD POLONIUS: Wherefore should you do this?
REYNALDO: Ay, my lord,
REYNALDO: I would know that.
LORD POLONIUS: Marry, sir, here's my drift,
LORD POLONIUS: And I believe, it is a fetch of wit:
LORD POLONIUS: You laying these slight sullies on my son,
LORD POLONIUS: As 'twere a thing a little soil'd i' the working, Mark you,
LORD POLONIUS: Your party in converse, him you would sound,
LORD POLONIUS: Having ever seen in the prenominate crimes
LORD POLONIUS: The youth you breathe of guilty, be assured
LORD POLONIUS: He closes with you in this consequence,
LORD POLONIUS: 'Good sir,' or so, or 'friend,' or 'gentleman,'
LORD POLONIUS: According to the phrase or the addition
LORD POLONIUS: Of man and country.
REYNALDO: Very good, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: And then, sir, does he this--he does--what was I
LORD POLONIUS: about to say? By the mass, I was about to say
LORD POLONIUS: something: where did I leave?
REYNALDO: At 'closes in the consequence,' at 'friend or so,'
REYNALDO: and 'gentleman.'
LORD POLONIUS: At 'closes in the consequence,' ay, marry,
LORD POLONIUS: He closes thus: 'I know the gentleman,
LORD POLONIUS: I saw him yesterday, or t' other day,
LORD POLONIUS: Or then, or then, with such, or such, and, as you say,
LORD POLONIUS: There was a' gaming, there o'ertook in's rouse,
LORD POLONIUS: There falling out at tennis:' or perchance,
LORD POLONIUS: 'I saw him enter such a house of sale,'
LORD POLONIUS: Videlicet, a brothel, or so forth.
LORD POLONIUS: See you now,
LORD POLONIUS: Your bait of falsehood takes this carp of truth:
LORD POLONIUS: And thus do we of wisdom and of reach,
LORD POLONIUS: With windlasses and with assays of bias,
LORD POLONIUS: By indirections find directions out:
LORD POLONIUS: So by my former lecture and advice,
LORD POLONIUS: Shall you my son. You have me, have you not?
REYNALDO: My lord, I have.
LORD POLONIUS: God be wi' you, fare you well.
REYNALDO: Good my lord!
LORD POLONIUS: Observe his inclination in yourself.
REYNALDO: I shall, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: And let him ply his music.
REYNALDO: Well, my lord.
LORD POLONIUS: Farewell!
NARRATOR: Exit REYNALDO
NARRATOR: Enter OPHELIA
LORD POLONIUS: How now, Ophelia! what's the matter?
OPHELIA: O, my lord, my lord, I have been so affrighted!
LORD POLONIUS: With what, i' the name of God?
OPHELIA: My lord, as I was sewing in my closet,
OPHELIA: Lord Hamlet, with his doublet all unbraced,
OPHELIA: No hat upon his head, his stockings foul'd,
OPHELIA: Ungarter'd, and down-gyved to his ancle,
OPHELIA: Pale as his shirt, his knees knocking each other,
OPHELIA: And with a look so piteous in purport
OPHELIA: As if he had been loosed out of hell
OPHELIA: To speak of horrors,--he comes before me.
LORD POLONIUS: Mad for thy love?
OPHELIA: My lord, I do not know,
OPHELIA: But truly, I do fear it.
LORD POLONIUS: What said he?
OPHELIA: He took me by the wrist and held me hard,
OPHELIA: Then goes he to the length of all his arm,
OPHELIA: And, with his other hand thus o'er his brow,
OPHELIA: He falls to such perusal of my face
OPHELIA: As he would draw it. Long stay'd he so,
OPHELIA: At last, a little shaking of mine arm
OPHELIA: And thrice his head thus waving up and down,
OPHELIA: He raised a sigh so piteous and profound
OPHELIA: As it did seem to shatter all his bulk
OPHELIA: And end his being: that done, he lets me go:
OPHELIA: And, with his head over his shoulder turn'd,
OPHELIA: He seem'd to find his way without his eyes,
OPHELIA: For out o' doors he went without their helps,
OPHELIA: And, to the last, bended their light on me.
LORD POLONIUS: Come, go with me: I will go seek the king.
LORD POLONIUS: This is the very ecstasy of love,
LORD POLONIUS: Whose violent property fordoes itself
LORD POLONIUS: And leads the will to desperate undertakings
LORD POLONIUS: As oft as any passion under heaven
LORD POLONIUS: That does afflict our natures. I am sorry.
LORD POLONIUS: What, have you given him any hard words of late?
OPHELIA: No, my good lord, but, as you did command,
OPHELIA: I did repel his fetters and denied
OPHELIA: His access to me.
LORD POLONIUS: That hath made him mad.
LORD POLONIUS: I am sorry that with better heed and judgment
LORD POLONIUS: I had not quoted him: I fear'd he did but trifle,
LORD POLONIUS: And meant to wreck thee, but, beshrew my jealousy!
LORD POLONIUS: By heaven, it is as proper to our age
LORD POLONIUS: To cast beyond ourselves in our opinions
LORD POLONIUS: As it is common for the younger sort
LORD POLONIUS: To lack discretion. Come, go we to the king:
LORD POLONIUS: This must be known, which, being kept close, might
LORD POLONIUS: move
LORD POLONIUS: More grief to hide than hate to utter love.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter KING CLAUDIUS, QUEEN GERTRUDE, ROSENCRANTZ, GUILDENSTERN, and Attendants
KING CLAUDIUS: Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern!
KING CLAUDIUS: Moreover that we much did long to see you,
KING CLAUDIUS: The need we have to use you did provoke
KING CLAUDIUS: Our hasty sending. Something have you heard
KING CLAUDIUS: Of Hamlet's transformation, so call it,
KING CLAUDIUS: Sith nor the exterior nor the inward man
KING CLAUDIUS: Resembles that it was. What it should be,
KING CLAUDIUS: More than his father's death, that thus hath put him
KING CLAUDIUS: So much from the understanding of himself,
KING CLAUDIUS: I cannot dream of: I entreat you both,
KING CLAUDIUS: That, being of so young days brought up with him,
KING CLAUDIUS: And sith so neighbour'd to his youth and havior,
KING CLAUDIUS: That you vouchsafe your rest here in our court
KING CLAUDIUS: Some little time: so by your companies
KING CLAUDIUS: To draw him on to pleasures, and to gather,
KING CLAUDIUS: So much as from occasion you may glean,
KING CLAUDIUS: Whether aught, to us unknown, afflicts him thus,
KING CLAUDIUS: That, open'd, lies within our remedy.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Good gentlemen, he hath much talk'd of you,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: And sure I am two men there are not living
QUEEN GERTRUDE: To whom he more adheres. If it will please you
QUEEN GERTRUDE: To show us so much gentry and good will
QUEEN GERTRUDE: As to expend your time with us awhile,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: For the supply and profit of our hope,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Your visitation shall receive such thanks
QUEEN GERTRUDE: As fits a king's remembrance.
ROSENCRANTZ: Both your majesties
ROSENCRANTZ: Might, by the sovereign power you have of us,
ROSENCRANTZ: Put your dread pleasures more into command
ROSENCRANTZ: Than to entreaty.
GUILDENSTERN: But we both obey,
GUILDENSTERN: And here give up ourselves, in the full bent
GUILDENSTERN: To lay our service freely at your feet,
GUILDENSTERN: To be commanded.
KING CLAUDIUS: Thanks, Rosencrantz and gentle Guildenstern.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Thanks, Guildenstern and gentle Rosencrantz:
QUEEN GERTRUDE: And I beseech you instantly to visit

QUEEN GERTRUDE: And bring these gentlemen where Hamlet is.
GUILDENSTERN: Heavens make our presence and our practises

QUEEN GERTRUDE: Ay, amen!
NARRATOR: Exeunt ROSENCRANTZ, GUILDENSTERN, and some Attendants
NARRATOR: Enter POLONIUS
LORD POLONIUS: The ambassadors from Norway, my good lord,
LORD POLONIUS: Are joyfully return'd.
KING CLAUDIUS: Thou still hast been the father of good news.
LORD POLONIUS: Have I, my lord? I assure my good liege,
LORD POLONIUS: I hold my duty, as I hold my soul,
LORD POLONIUS: Both to my God and to my gracious king:
LORD POLONIUS: And I do think, or else this brain of mine
LORD POLONIUS: Hunts not the trail of policy so sure
LORD POLONIUS: As it hath used to do, that I have found
LORD POLONIUS: The very cause of Hamlet's lunacy.
KING CLAUDIUS: O, speak of that, that do I long to hear.
LORD POLONIUS: Give first admittance to the ambassadors,
LORD POLONIUS: My news shall be the fruit to that great feast.
KING CLAUDIUS: Thyself do grace to them, and bring them in.
NARRATOR: Exit POLONIUS
KING CLAUDIUS: He tells me, my dear Gertrude, he hath found
KING CLAUDIUS: The head and source of all your son's distemper.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: I doubt it is no other but the main,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: His father's death, and our o'erhasty marriage.
KING CLAUDIUS: Well, we shall sift him.
NARRATOR: Re-enter POLONIUS, with VOLTIMAND and CORNELIUS
KING CLAUDIUS: Welcome, my good friends!
KING CLAUDIUS: Say, Voltimand, what from our brother Norway?
VOLTIMAND: Most fair return of greetings and desires.
VOLTIMAND: Upon our first, he sent out to suppress
VOLTIMAND: His nephew's levies, which to him appear'd
VOLTIMAND: To be a preparation 'gainst the Polack,
VOLTIMAND: But, better look'd into, he truly found
VOLTIMAND: It was against your highness: whereat grieved,
VOLTIMAND: That so his sickness, age and impotence
VOLTIMAND: Was falsely borne in hand, sends out arrests
VOLTIMAND: On Fortinbras, which he, in brief, obeys,
VOLTIMAND: Receives rebuke from Norway, and in fine
VOLTIMAND: Makes vow before his uncle never more

VOLTIMAND: Whereon old Norway, overcome with joy,
VOLTIMAND: Gives him three thousand crowns in annual fee,
VOLTIMAND: And his commission to employ those soldiers,
VOLTIMAND: So levied as before, against the Polack:
VOLTIMAND: With an entreaty, herein further shown,
NARRATOR: Giving a paper

VOLTIMAND: Through your dominions for this enterprise,
VOLTIMAND: On such regards of safety and allowance
VOLTIMAND: As therein are set down.
KING CLAUDIUS: It likes us well,
KING CLAUDIUS: And at our more consider'd time well read,
KING CLAUDIUS: Answer, and think upon this business.
KING CLAUDIUS: Meantime we thank you for your well-took labour:
KING CLAUDIUS: Go to your rest, at night we'll feast together:
KING CLAUDIUS: Most welcome home!
NARRATOR: Exeunt VOLTIMAND and CORNELIUS
LORD POLONIUS: This business is well ended.
LORD POLONIUS: My liege, and madam, to expostulate
LORD POLONIUS: What majesty should be, what duty is,
LORD POLONIUS: Why day is day, night night, and time is time,
LORD POLONIUS: Were nothing but to waste night, day and time.
LORD POLONIUS: Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit,
LORD POLONIUS: And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,

LORD POLONIUS: Mad call I it, for, to define true madness,
LORD POLONIUS: What is't but to be nothing else but mad?
LORD POLONIUS: But let that go.
QUEEN GERTRUDE: More matter, with less art.
LORD POLONIUS: Madam, I swear I use no art at all.

LORD POLONIUS: And pity 'tis 'tis true: a foolish figure,
LORD POLONIUS: But farewell it, for I will use no art.
LORD POLONIUS: Mad let us grant him, then: and now remains

LORD POLONIUS: Or rather say, the cause of this defect,
LORD POLONIUS: For this effect defective comes by cause:
LORD POLONIUS: Thus it remains, and the remainder thus. Perpend.
LORD POLONIUS: I have a daughter--have while she is mine--
LORD POLONIUS: Who, in her duty and obedience, mark,
LORD POLONIUS: Hath given me this: now gather, and surmise.
NARRATOR: Reads

LORD POLONIUS: a vile phrase: but you shall hear. Thus:
NARRATOR: Reads

NARRATOR: Reads

LORD POLONIUS: Doubt truth to be a liar,
LORD POLONIUS: But never doubt I love.

LORD POLONIUS: 'Thine evermore most dear lady, whilst

KING CLAUDIUS: But how hath she

LORD POLONIUS: What do you think of me?

LORD POLONIUS: That I have positively said 'Tis so,'
LORD POLONIUS: When it proved otherwise?
KING CLAUDIUS: Not that I know.
LORD POLONIUS: [Pointing to his head and shoulder]

LORD POLONIUS: If circumstances lead me, I will find
LORD POLONIUS: Where truth is hid, though it were hid indeed

QUEEN GERTRUDE: But, look, where sadly the poor wretch comes reading.

LORD POLONIUS: I'll board him presently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING CLAUDIUS, QUEEN GERTRUDE, and Attendants
NARRATOR: Enter HAMLET, reading
LORD POLONIUS: O, give me leave:
LORD POLONIUS: How does my good Lord Hamlet?
HAMLET: Well, God-a-mercy.
LORD POLONIUS: Do you know me, my lord?
HAMLET: Excellent well, you are a fishmonger.
LORD POLONIUS: Not I, my lord.
HAMLET: Then I would you were so honest a man.
LORD POLONIUS: Honest, my lord!
HAMLET: Ay, sir, to be honest, as this world goes, is to be
HAMLET: one man picked out of ten thousand.
LORD POLONIUS: That's very true, my lord.
HAMLET: For if the sun breed maggots in a dead dog, being a
HAMLET: god kissing carrion,--Have you a daughter?
LORD POLONIUS: I have, my lord.
HAMLET: Let her not walk i' the sun: conception is a
HAMLET: blessing: but not as your daughter may conceive.
HAMLET: Friend, look to 't.
LORD POLONIUS: [Aside]  How say you by that? Still harping on my
LORD POLONIUS: daughter: yet he knew me not at first, he said I
LORD POLONIUS: was a fishmonger: he is far gone, far gone: and
LORD POLONIUS: truly in my youth I suffered much extremity for
LORD POLONIUS: love, very near this. I'll speak to him again.
LORD POLONIUS: What do you read, my lord?
HAMLET: Words, words, words.
LORD POLONIUS: What is the matter, my lord?

LORD POLONIUS: I mean, the matter that you read, my lord.
HAMLET: Slanders, sir: for the satirical rogue says here
HAMLET: that old men have grey beards, that their faces are
HAMLET: wrinkled, their eyes purging thick amber and
HAMLET: plum-tree gum and that they have a plentiful lack of
HAMLET: wit, together with most weak hams: all which, sir,
HAMLET: though I most powerfully and potently believe, yet
HAMLET: I hold it not honesty to have it thus set down, for
HAMLET: yourself, sir, should be old as I am, if like a crab
HAMLET: you could go backward.
LORD POLONIUS: [Aside]  Though this be madness, yet there is method
LORD POLONIUS: in 't. Will you walk out of the air, my lord?
HAMLET: Into my grave.
LORD POLONIUS: Indeed, that is out o' the air.
NARRATOR: Aside
LORD POLONIUS: How pregnant sometimes his replies are! a happiness
LORD POLONIUS: that often madness hits on, which reason and sanity
LORD POLONIUS: could not so prosperously be delivered of. I will
LORD POLONIUS: leave him, and suddenly contrive the means of
LORD POLONIUS: meeting between him and my daughter.--My honourable
LORD POLONIUS: lord, I will most humbly take my leave of you.
HAMLET: You cannot, sir, take from me any thing that I will
HAMLET: more willingly part withal: except my life, except
HAMLET: my life, except my life.
LORD POLONIUS: Fare you well, my lord.
HAMLET: These tedious old fools!
NARRATOR: Enter ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN
LORD POLONIUS: You go to seek the Lord Hamlet, there he is.
ROSENCRANTZ: [To POLONIUS]  God save you, sir!
NARRATOR: Exit POLONIUS
GUILDENSTERN: My honoured lord!
ROSENCRANTZ: My most dear lord!
HAMLET: My excellent good friends! How dost thou,
HAMLET: Guildenstern? Ah, Rosencrantz! Good lads, how do ye both?
ROSENCRANTZ: As the indifferent children of the earth.
GUILDENSTERN: Happy, in that we are not over-happy,
GUILDENSTERN: On fortune's cap we are not the very button.
HAMLET: Nor the soles of her shoe?
ROSENCRANTZ: Neither, my lord.
HAMLET: Then you live about her waist, or in the middle of
HAMLET: her favours?
GUILDENSTERN: 'Faith, her privates we.
HAMLET: In the secret parts of fortune? O, most true, she
HAMLET: is a strumpet. What's the news?
ROSENCRANTZ: None, my lord, but that the world's grown honest.
HAMLET: Then is doomsday near: but your news is not true.
HAMLET: Let me question more in particular: what have you,
HAMLET: my good friends, deserved at the hands of fortune,
HAMLET: that she sends you to prison hither?
GUILDENSTERN: Prison, my lord!
HAMLET: Denmark's a prison.
ROSENCRANTZ: Then is the world one.
HAMLET: A goodly one, in which there are many confines,
HAMLET: wards and dungeons, Denmark being one o' the worst.
ROSENCRANTZ: We think not so, my lord.
HAMLET: Why, then, 'tis none to you, for there is nothing
HAMLET: either good or bad, but thinking makes it so: to me
HAMLET: it is a prison.
ROSENCRANTZ: Why then, your ambition makes it one, 'tis too
ROSENCRANTZ: narrow for your mind.
HAMLET: O God, I could be bounded in a nut shell and count
HAMLET: myself a king of infinite space, were it not that I
HAMLET: have bad dreams.
GUILDENSTERN: Which dreams indeed are ambition, for the very
GUILDENSTERN: substance of the ambitious is merely the shadow of a dream.
HAMLET: A dream itself is but a shadow.
ROSENCRANTZ: Truly, and I hold ambition of so airy and light a
ROSENCRANTZ: quality that it is but a shadow's shadow.
HAMLET: Then are our beggars bodies, and our monarchs and
HAMLET: outstretched heroes the beggars' shadows. Shall we
HAMLET: to the court? for, by my fay, I cannot reason.
GUILDENSTERN: We'll wait upon you.
HAMLET: No such matter: I will not sort you with the rest
HAMLET: of my servants, for, to speak to you like an honest
HAMLET: man, I am most dreadfully attended. But, in the
HAMLET: beaten way of friendship, what make you at Elsinore?
ROSENCRANTZ: To visit you, my lord, no other occasion.
HAMLET: Beggar that I am, I am even poor in thanks, but I
HAMLET: thank you: and sure, dear friends, my thanks are
HAMLET: too dear a halfpenny. Were you not sent for? Is it
HAMLET: your own inclining? Is it a free visitation? Come,
HAMLET: deal justly with me: come, come, nay, speak.
GUILDENSTERN: What should we say, my lord?

HAMLET: for, and there is a kind of confession in your looks
HAMLET: which your modesties have not craft enough to colour:
HAMLET: I know the good king and queen have sent for you.
ROSENCRANTZ: To what end, my lord?
HAMLET: That you must teach me. But let me conjure you, by
HAMLET: the rights of our fellowship, by the consonancy of
HAMLET: our youth, by the obligation of our ever-preserved
HAMLET: love, and by what more dear a better proposer could
HAMLET: charge you withal, be even and direct with me,
HAMLET: whether you were sent for, or no?
ROSENCRANTZ: [Aside to GUILDENSTERN]  What say you?
HAMLET: [Aside]  Nay, then, I have an eye of you.--If you
HAMLET: love me, hold not off.
GUILDENSTERN: My lord, we were sent for.
HAMLET: I will tell you why, so shall my anticipation
HAMLET: prevent your discovery, and your secrecy to the king
HAMLET: and queen moult no feather. I have of late--but
HAMLET: wherefore I know not--lost all my mirth, forgone all
HAMLET: custom of exercises, and indeed it goes so heavily
HAMLET: with my disposition that this goodly frame, the
HAMLET: earth, seems to me a sterile promontory, this most
HAMLET: excellent canopy, the air, look you, this brave
HAMLET: o'erhanging firmament, this majestical roof fretted
