NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Another room in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter KING CLAUDIUS and LAERTES
KING CLAUDIUS: Now must your conscience my acquaintance seal,
KING CLAUDIUS: And you must put me in your heart for friend,
KING CLAUDIUS: Sith you have heard, and with a knowing ear,
KING CLAUDIUS: That he which hath your noble father slain
KING CLAUDIUS: Pursued my life.
LAERTES: It well appears: but tell me
LAERTES: Why you proceeded not against these feats,
LAERTES: So crimeful and so capital in nature,
LAERTES: As by your safety, wisdom, all things else,
LAERTES: You mainly were stirr'd up.
KING CLAUDIUS: O, for two special reasons,
KING CLAUDIUS: Which may to you, perhaps, seem much unsinew'd,
KING CLAUDIUS: But yet to me they are strong. The queen his mother
KING CLAUDIUS: Lives almost by his looks, and for myself--
KING CLAUDIUS: My virtue or my plague, be it either which--
KING CLAUDIUS: She's so conjunctive to my life and soul,
KING CLAUDIUS: That, as the star moves not but in his sphere,
KING CLAUDIUS: I could not but by her. The other motive,
KING CLAUDIUS: Why to a public count I might not go,
KING CLAUDIUS: Is the great love the general gender bear him,
KING CLAUDIUS: Who, dipping all his faults in their affection,
KING CLAUDIUS: Would, like the spring that turneth wood to stone,
KING CLAUDIUS: Convert his gyves to graces, so that my arrows,
KING CLAUDIUS: Too slightly timber'd for so loud a wind,
KING CLAUDIUS: Would have reverted to my bow again,
KING CLAUDIUS: And not where I had aim'd them.
LAERTES: And so have I a noble father lost,
LAERTES: A sister driven into desperate terms,
LAERTES: Whose worth, if praises may go back again,
LAERTES: Stood challenger on mount of all the age
LAERTES: For her perfections: but my revenge will come.
KING CLAUDIUS: Break not your sleeps for that: you must not think
KING CLAUDIUS: That we are made of stuff so flat and dull
KING CLAUDIUS: That we can let our beard be shook with danger
KING CLAUDIUS: And think it pastime. You shortly shall hear more:
KING CLAUDIUS: I loved your father, and we love ourself,
KING CLAUDIUS: And that, I hope, will teach you to imagine--
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
KING CLAUDIUS: How now! what news?
Messenger: Letters, my lord, from Hamlet:
Messenger: This to your majesty, this to the queen.
KING CLAUDIUS: From Hamlet! who brought them?
Messenger: Sailors, my lord, they say, I saw them not:
Messenger: They were given me by Claudio, he received them
Messenger: Of him that brought them.
KING CLAUDIUS: Laertes, you shall hear them. Leave us.
NARRATOR: Exit Messenger
NARRATOR: Reads
KING CLAUDIUS: 'High and mighty, You shall know I am set naked on
KING CLAUDIUS: your kingdom. To-morrow shall I beg leave to see
KING CLAUDIUS: your kingly eyes: when I shall, first asking your
KING CLAUDIUS: pardon thereunto, recount the occasion of my sudden
KING CLAUDIUS: and more strange return.                  'HAMLET.'
KING CLAUDIUS: What should this mean? Are all the rest come back?
KING CLAUDIUS: Or is it some abuse, and no such thing?
LAERTES: Know you the hand?
KING CLAUDIUS: 'Tis Hamlets character. 'Naked!
KING CLAUDIUS: And in a postscript here, he says 'alone.'
KING CLAUDIUS: Can you advise me?
LAERTES: I'm lost in it, my lord. But let him come,
LAERTES: It warms the very sickness in my heart,
LAERTES: That I shall live and tell him to his teeth,
LAERTES: 'Thus didest thou.'
KING CLAUDIUS: If it be so, Laertes--
KING CLAUDIUS: As how should it be so? how otherwise?--
KING CLAUDIUS: Will you be ruled by me?
LAERTES: Ay, my lord,
LAERTES: So you will not o'errule me to a peace.
KING CLAUDIUS: To thine own peace. If he be now return'd,
KING CLAUDIUS: As checking at his voyage, and that he means
KING CLAUDIUS: No more to undertake it, I will work him
KING CLAUDIUS: To an exploit, now ripe in my device,
KING CLAUDIUS: Under the which he shall not choose but fall:
KING CLAUDIUS: And for his death no wind of blame shall breathe,
KING CLAUDIUS: But even his mother shall uncharge the practise
KING CLAUDIUS: And call it accident.
LAERTES: My lord, I will be ruled,
LAERTES: The rather, if you could devise it so
LAERTES: That I might be the organ.
KING CLAUDIUS: It falls right.
KING CLAUDIUS: You have been talk'd of since your travel much,
KING CLAUDIUS: And that in Hamlet's hearing, for a quality
KING CLAUDIUS: Wherein, they say, you shine: your sum of parts
KING CLAUDIUS: Did not together pluck such envy from him
KING CLAUDIUS: As did that one, and that, in my regard,
KING CLAUDIUS: Of the unworthiest siege.
LAERTES: What part is that, my lord?
KING CLAUDIUS: A very riband in the cap of youth,
KING CLAUDIUS: Yet needful too, for youth no less becomes
KING CLAUDIUS: The light and careless livery that it wears
KING CLAUDIUS: Than settled age his sables and his weeds,
KING CLAUDIUS: Importing health and graveness. Two months since,
KING CLAUDIUS: Here was a gentleman of Normandy:--
KING CLAUDIUS: I've seen myself, and served against, the French,
KING CLAUDIUS: And they can well on horseback: but this gallant
KING CLAUDIUS: Had witchcraft in't, he grew unto his seat,
KING CLAUDIUS: And to such wondrous doing brought his horse,
KING CLAUDIUS: As he had been incorpsed and demi-natured
KING CLAUDIUS: With the brave beast: so far he topp'd my thought,
KING CLAUDIUS: That I, in forgery of shapes and tricks,
KING CLAUDIUS: Come short of what he did.
LAERTES: A Norman was't?
KING CLAUDIUS: A Norman.
LAERTES: Upon my life, Lamond.
KING CLAUDIUS: The very same.
LAERTES: I know him well: he is the brooch indeed
LAERTES: And gem of all the nation.
KING CLAUDIUS: He made confession of you,
KING CLAUDIUS: And gave you such a masterly report
KING CLAUDIUS: For art and exercise in your defence
KING CLAUDIUS: And for your rapier most especially,
KING CLAUDIUS: That he cried out, 'twould be a sight indeed,
KING CLAUDIUS: If one could match you: the scrimers of their nation,
KING CLAUDIUS: He swore, had had neither motion, guard, nor eye,
KING CLAUDIUS: If you opposed them. Sir, this report of his
KING CLAUDIUS: Did Hamlet so envenom with his envy
KING CLAUDIUS: That he could nothing do but wish and beg
KING CLAUDIUS: Your sudden coming o'er, to play with him.
KING CLAUDIUS: Now, out of this,--
LAERTES: What out of this, my lord?
KING CLAUDIUS: Laertes, was your father dear to you?
KING CLAUDIUS: Or are you like the painting of a sorrow,
KING CLAUDIUS: A face without a heart?
LAERTES: Why ask you this?
KING CLAUDIUS: Not that I think you did not love your father,
KING CLAUDIUS: But that I know love is begun by time,
KING CLAUDIUS: And that I see, in passages of proof,
KING CLAUDIUS: Time qualifies the spark and fire of it.
KING CLAUDIUS: There lives within the very flame of love
KING CLAUDIUS: A kind of wick or snuff that will abate it,
KING CLAUDIUS: And nothing is at a like goodness still,
KING CLAUDIUS: For goodness, growing to a plurisy,
KING CLAUDIUS: Dies in his own too much: that we would do
KING CLAUDIUS: We should do when we would, for this 'would' changes
KING CLAUDIUS: And hath abatements and delays as many
KING CLAUDIUS: As there are tongues, are hands, are accidents,
KING CLAUDIUS: And then this 'should' is like a spendthrift sigh,
KING CLAUDIUS: That hurts by easing. But, to the quick o' the ulcer:--
KING CLAUDIUS: Hamlet comes back: what would you undertake,
KING CLAUDIUS: To show yourself your father's son in deed
KING CLAUDIUS: More than in words?
LAERTES: To cut his throat i' the church.
KING CLAUDIUS: No place, indeed, should murder sanctuarize,
KING CLAUDIUS: Revenge should have no bounds. But, good Laertes,
KING CLAUDIUS: Will you do this, keep close within your chamber.
KING CLAUDIUS: Hamlet return'd shall know you are come home:
KING CLAUDIUS: We'll put on those shall praise your excellence
KING CLAUDIUS: And set a double varnish on the fame
KING CLAUDIUS: The Frenchman gave you, bring you in fine together
KING CLAUDIUS: And wager on your heads: he, being remiss,
KING CLAUDIUS: Most generous and free from all contriving,
KING CLAUDIUS: Will not peruse the foils, so that, with ease,
KING CLAUDIUS: Or with a little shuffling, you may choose
KING CLAUDIUS: A sword unbated, and in a pass of practise
KING CLAUDIUS: Requite him for your father.
LAERTES: I will do't:
LAERTES: And, for that purpose, I'll anoint my sword.
LAERTES: I bought an unction of a mountebank,
LAERTES: So mortal that, but dip a knife in it,
LAERTES: Where it draws blood no cataplasm so rare,
LAERTES: Collected from all simples that have virtue
LAERTES: Under the moon, can save the thing from death
LAERTES: That is but scratch'd withal: I'll touch my point
LAERTES: With this contagion, that, if I gall him slightly,
LAERTES: It may be death.
KING CLAUDIUS: Let's further think of this,
KING CLAUDIUS: Weigh what convenience both of time and means
KING CLAUDIUS: May fit us to our shape: if this should fail,
KING CLAUDIUS: And that our drift look through our bad performance,
KING CLAUDIUS: 'Twere better not assay'd: therefore this project
KING CLAUDIUS: Should have a back or second, that might hold,
KING CLAUDIUS: If this should blast in proof. Soft! let me see:
KING CLAUDIUS: We'll make a solemn wager on your cunnings: I ha't.
KING CLAUDIUS: When in your motion you are hot and dry--
KING CLAUDIUS: As make your bouts more violent to that end--
KING CLAUDIUS: And that he calls for drink, I'll have prepared him
KING CLAUDIUS: A chalice for the nonce, whereon but sipping,
KING CLAUDIUS: If he by chance escape your venom'd stuck,
KING CLAUDIUS: Our purpose may hold there.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN GERTRUDE
KING CLAUDIUS: How now, sweet queen!
QUEEN GERTRUDE: One woe doth tread upon another's heel,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: So fast they follow, your sister's drown'd, Laertes.
LAERTES: Drown'd! O, where?
QUEEN GERTRUDE: There is a willow grows aslant a brook,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: That shows his hoar leaves in the glassy stream,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: There with fantastic garlands did she come
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Of crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples
QUEEN GERTRUDE: That liberal shepherds give a grosser name,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: But our cold maids do dead men's fingers call them:
QUEEN GERTRUDE: There, on the pendent boughs her coronet weeds
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: When down her weedy trophies and herself
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Fell in the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: And, mermaid-like, awhile they bore her up:
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Which time she chanted snatches of old tunes,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: As one incapable of her own distress,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Or like a creature native and indued
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Unto that element: but long it could not be
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Till that her garments, heavy with their drink,
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Pull'd the poor wretch from her melodious lay
QUEEN GERTRUDE: To muddy death.
LAERTES: Alas, then, she is drown'd?
QUEEN GERTRUDE: Drown'd, drown'd.
LAERTES: Too much of water hast thou, poor Ophelia,
LAERTES: And therefore I forbid my tears: but yet
LAERTES: It is our trick, nature her custom holds,
LAERTES: Let shame say what it will: when these are gone,
LAERTES: The woman will be out. Adieu, my lord:
LAERTES: I have a speech of fire, that fain would blaze,
LAERTES: But that this folly douts it.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING CLAUDIUS: Let's follow, Gertrude:
KING CLAUDIUS: How much I had to do to calm his rage!
KING CLAUDIUS: Now fear I this will give it start again,
KING CLAUDIUS: Therefore let's follow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A churchyard.
NARRATOR: Enter two Clowns, with spades,  and c
First Clown: Is she to be buried in Christian burial that
First Clown: wilfully seeks her own salvation?
Second Clown: I tell thee she is: and therefore make her grave
Second Clown: straight: the crowner hath sat on her, and finds it
Second Clown: Christian burial.
First Clown: How can that be, unless she drowned herself in her
First Clown: own defence?
Second Clown: Why, 'tis found so.
First Clown: It must be 'se offendendo,' it cannot be else. For
First Clown: here lies the point:  if I drown myself wittingly,
First Clown: it argues an act: and an act hath three branches: it
First Clown: is, to act, to do, to perform: argal, she drowned
First Clown: herself wittingly.
Second Clown: Nay, but hear you, goodman delver,--
First Clown: Give me leave. Here lies the water, good: here
First Clown: stands the man, good, if the man go to this water,
First Clown: and drown himself, it is, will he, nill he, he
First Clown: goes,--mark you that, but if the water come to him
First Clown: and drown him, he drowns not himself: argal, he
First Clown: that is not guilty of his own death shortens not his own life.
Second Clown: But is this law?
First Clown: Ay, marry, is't, crowner's quest law.
Second Clown: Will you ha' the truth on't? If this had not been
Second Clown: a gentlewoman, she should have been buried out o'
Second Clown: Christian burial.
First Clown: Why, there thou say'st: and the more pity that
First Clown: great folk should have countenance in this world to
First Clown: drown or hang themselves, more than their even
First Clown: Christian. Come, my spade. There is no ancient
First Clown: gentleman but gardeners, ditchers, and grave-makers:
First Clown: they hold up Adam's profession.
Second Clown: Was he a gentleman?
First Clown: He was the first that ever bore arms.
Second Clown: Why, he had none.
First Clown: What, art a heathen? How dost thou understand the
First Clown: Scripture? The Scripture says 'Adam digged:'
First Clown: could he dig without arms? I'll put another
First Clown: question to thee: if thou answerest me not to the
First Clown: purpose, confess thyself--
Second Clown: Go to.
First Clown: What is he that builds stronger than either the
First Clown: mason, the shipwright, or the carpenter?
Second Clown: The gallows-maker, for that frame outlives a
Second Clown: thousand tenants.
First Clown: I like thy wit well, in good faith: the gallows
First Clown: does well, but how does it well? it does well to
First Clown: those that do in: now thou dost ill to say the
First Clown: gallows is built stronger than the church: argal,
First Clown: the gallows may do well to thee. To't again, come.
Second Clown: 'Who builds stronger than a mason, a shipwright, or
Second Clown: a carpenter?'
First Clown: Ay, tell me that, and unyoke.
Second Clown: Marry, now I can tell.
First Clown: To't.
Second Clown: Mass, I cannot tell.

First Clown: grave-maker: 'the houses that he makes last till
First Clown: doomsday. Go, get thee to Yaughan: fetch me a

First Clown: Hath claw'd me in his clutch,
First Clown: And hath shipped me intil the land,

First Clown: A pestilence on him for a mad rogue! a' poured a

First Clown: E'en that.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. A hall in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter HAMLET and HORATIO
HAMLET: So much for this, sir: now shall you see the other,

HAMLET: There's a divinity that shapes our ends,

HAMLET: Ere I could make a prologue to my brains,
HAMLET: They had begun the play--I sat me down,
HAMLET: Devised a new commission, wrote it fair:
HAMLET: I once did hold it, as our statists do,
HAMLET: A baseness to write fair and labour'd much

HAMLET: It did me yeoman's service: wilt thou know

HORATIO: Ay, good my lord.
HAMLET: An earnest conjuration from the king,
HAMLET: As England was his faithful tributary,
HAMLET: As love between them like the palm might flourish,
HAMLET: As peace should stiff her wheaten garland wear

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY, LORD JOHN OF LANCASTER, the EARL of WESTMORELAND, SIR WALTER BLUNT, and others
KING HENRY IV: So shaken as we are, so wan with care,
KING HENRY IV: Find we a time for frighted peace to pant,
KING HENRY IV: And breathe short-winded accents of new broils
KING HENRY IV: To be commenced in strands afar remote.
KING HENRY IV: No more the thirsty entrance of this soil

KING HENRY IV: In envy that my Lord Northumberland
KING HENRY IV: Should be the father to so blest a son,
KING HENRY IV: A son who is the theme of honour's tongue,
KING HENRY IV: Amongst a grove, the very straightest plant,
KING HENRY IV: Who is sweet Fortune's minion and her pride:
KING HENRY IV: Whilst I, by looking on the praise of him,
KING HENRY IV: See riot and dishonour stain the brow
KING HENRY IV: Of my young Harry. O that it could be proved
KING HENRY IV: That some night-tripping fairy had exchanged
KING HENRY IV: In cradle-clothes our children where they lay,
KING HENRY IV: And call'd mine Percy, his Plantagenet!
KING HENRY IV: Then would I have his Harry, and he mine.
KING HENRY IV: But let him from my thoughts. What think you, coz,
KING HENRY IV: Of this young Percy's pride? the prisoners,
KING HENRY IV: Which he in this adventure hath surprised,
KING HENRY IV: To his own use he keeps, and sends me word,
KING HENRY IV: I shall have none but Mordake Earl of Fife.
WESTMORELAND: This is his uncle's teaching, this is Worcester,
WESTMORELAND: Malevolent to you in all aspects,
WESTMORELAND: Which makes him prune himself, and bristle up
WESTMORELAND: The crest of youth against your dignity.
KING HENRY IV: But I have sent for him to answer this,
KING HENRY IV: And for this cause awhile we must neglect
KING HENRY IV: Our holy purpose to Jerusalem.
KING HENRY IV: Cousin, on Wednesday next our council we
KING HENRY IV: Will hold at Windsor, so inform the lords:
KING HENRY IV: But come yourself with speed to us again,
KING HENRY IV: For more is to be said and to be done
KING HENRY IV: Than out of anger can be uttered.
WESTMORELAND: I will, my liege.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. London. An apartment of the Prince's.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCE OF WALES and FALSTAFF
FALSTAFF: Now, Hal, what time of day is it, lad?
PRINCE HENRY: Thou art so fat-witted, with drinking of old sack
PRINCE HENRY: and unbuttoning thee after supper and sleeping upon
PRINCE HENRY: benches after noon, that thou hast forgotten to
PRINCE HENRY: demand that truly which thou wouldst truly know.
PRINCE HENRY: What a devil hast thou to do with the time of the
PRINCE HENRY: day? Unless hours were cups of sack and minutes
PRINCE HENRY: capons and clocks the tongues of bawds and dials the
PRINCE HENRY: signs of leaping-houses and the blessed sun himself
PRINCE HENRY: a fair hot wench in flame-coloured taffeta, I see no
PRINCE HENRY: reason why thou shouldst be so superfluous to demand
PRINCE HENRY: the time of the day.
FALSTAFF: Indeed, you come near me now, Hal, for we that take
FALSTAFF: purses go by the moon and the seven stars, and not
FALSTAFF: by Phoebus, he,'that wandering knight so fair.' And,
FALSTAFF: I prithee, sweet wag, when thou art king, as, God
FALSTAFF: save thy grace,--majesty I should say, for grace
FALSTAFF: thou wilt have none,--
PRINCE HENRY: What, none?
FALSTAFF: No, by my troth, not so much as will serve to
FALSTAFF: prologue to an egg and butter.
PRINCE HENRY: Well, how then? come, roundly, roundly.
FALSTAFF: Marry, then, sweet wag, when thou art king, let not
FALSTAFF: us that are squires of the night's body be called
FALSTAFF: thieves of the day's beauty: let us be Diana's
FALSTAFF: foresters, gentlemen of the shade, minions of the
FALSTAFF: moon, and let men say we be men of good government,
FALSTAFF: being governed, as the sea is, by our noble and
FALSTAFF: chaste mistress the moon, under whose countenance we steal.
PRINCE HENRY: Thou sayest well, and it holds well too, for the
PRINCE HENRY: fortune of us that are the moon's men doth ebb and
PRINCE HENRY: flow like the sea, being governed, as the sea is,
PRINCE HENRY: by the moon. As, for proof, now: a purse of gold
PRINCE HENRY: most resolutely snatched on Monday night and most
PRINCE HENRY: dissolutely spent on Tuesday morning, got with
PRINCE HENRY: swearing 'Lay by' and spent with crying 'Bring in,'
PRINCE HENRY: now in as low an ebb as the foot of the ladder
PRINCE HENRY: and by and by in as high a flow as the ridge of the gallows.
FALSTAFF: By the Lord, thou sayest true, lad. And is not my
FALSTAFF: hostess of the tavern a most sweet wench?
PRINCE HENRY: As the honey of Hybla, my old lad of the castle. And
PRINCE HENRY: is not a buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance?
FALSTAFF: How now, how now, mad wag! what, in thy quips and
FALSTAFF: thy quiddities? what a plague have I to do with a
FALSTAFF: buff jerkin?
PRINCE HENRY: Why, what a pox have I to do with my hostess of the tavern?
FALSTAFF: Well, thou hast called her to a reckoning many a
FALSTAFF: time and oft.
PRINCE HENRY: Did I ever call for thee to pay thy part?
FALSTAFF: No, I'll give thee thy due, thou hast paid all there.
PRINCE HENRY: Yea, and elsewhere, so far as my coin would stretch,
PRINCE HENRY: and where it would not, I have used my credit.
FALSTAFF: Yea, and so used it that were it not here apparent
FALSTAFF: that thou art heir apparent--But, I prithee, sweet
FALSTAFF: wag, shall there be gallows standing in England when
FALSTAFF: thou art king? and resolution thus fobbed as it is
FALSTAFF: with the rusty curb of old father antic the law? Do
FALSTAFF: not thou, when thou art king, hang a thief.
PRINCE HENRY: No, thou shalt.
FALSTAFF: Shall I? O rare! By the Lord, I'll be a brave judge.
PRINCE HENRY: Thou judgest false already: I mean, thou shalt have
PRINCE HENRY: the hanging of the thieves and so become a rare hangman.
FALSTAFF: Well, Hal, well, and in some sort it jumps with my
FALSTAFF: humour as well as waiting in the court, I can tell
FALSTAFF: you.
PRINCE HENRY: For obtaining of suits?
FALSTAFF: Yea, for obtaining of suits, whereof the hangman
FALSTAFF: hath no lean wardrobe. 'Sblood, I am as melancholy
FALSTAFF: as a gib cat or a lugged bear.
PRINCE HENRY: Or an old lion, or a lover's lute.
FALSTAFF: Yea, or the drone of a Lincolnshire bagpipe.
PRINCE HENRY: What sayest thou to a hare, or the melancholy of
PRINCE HENRY: Moor-ditch?
FALSTAFF: Thou hast the most unsavoury similes and art indeed
FALSTAFF: the most comparative, rascalliest, sweet young
FALSTAFF: prince. But, Hal, I prithee, trouble me no more
FALSTAFF: with vanity. I would to God thou and I knew where a
FALSTAFF: commodity of good names were to be bought. An old
FALSTAFF: lord of the council rated me the other day in the
FALSTAFF: street about you, sir, but I marked him not, and yet
FALSTAFF: he talked very wisely, but I regarded him not, and
FALSTAFF: yet he talked wisely, and in the street too.
PRINCE HENRY: Thou didst well, for wisdom cries out in the
PRINCE HENRY: streets, and no man regards it.
FALSTAFF: O, thou hast damnable iteration and art indeed able
FALSTAFF: to corrupt a saint. Thou hast done much harm upon
FALSTAFF: me, Hal, God forgive thee for it! Before I knew
FALSTAFF: thee, Hal, I knew nothing, and now am I, if a man
FALSTAFF: should speak truly, little better than one of the
FALSTAFF: wicked. I must give over this life, and I will give
FALSTAFF: it over: by the Lord, and I do not, I am a villain:
FALSTAFF: I'll be damned for never a king's son in
FALSTAFF: Christendom.
PRINCE HENRY: Where shall we take a purse tomorrow, Jack?
FALSTAFF: 'Zounds, where thou wilt, lad, I'll make one, an I
FALSTAFF: do not, call me villain and baffle me.
PRINCE HENRY: I see a good amendment of life in thee, from praying
PRINCE HENRY: to purse-taking.
FALSTAFF: Why, Hal, 'tis my vocation, Hal, 'tis no sin for a
FALSTAFF: man to labour in his vocation.
NARRATOR: Enter POINS
FALSTAFF: Poins! Now shall we know if Gadshill have set a
FALSTAFF: match. O, if men were to be saved by merit, what
FALSTAFF: hole in hell were hot enough for him? This is the
FALSTAFF: most omnipotent villain that ever cried 'Stand' to
FALSTAFF: a true man.
PRINCE HENRY: Good morrow, Ned.
POINS: Good morrow, sweet Hal. What says Monsieur Remorse?
POINS: what says Sir John Sack and Sugar? Jack! how
POINS: agrees the devil and thee about thy soul, that thou
POINS: soldest him on Good-Friday last for a cup of Madeira
POINS: and a cold capon's leg?
PRINCE HENRY: Sir John stands to his word, the devil shall have
PRINCE HENRY: his bargain, for he was never yet a breaker of
PRINCE HENRY: proverbs: he will give the devil his due.
POINS: Then art thou damned for keeping thy word with the devil.
PRINCE HENRY: Else he had been damned for cozening the devil.
POINS: But, my lads, my lads, to-morrow morning, by four
POINS: o'clock, early at Gadshill! there are pilgrims going
POINS: to Canterbury with rich offerings, and traders
POINS: riding to London with fat purses: I have vizards
POINS: for you all, you have horses for yourselves:
POINS: Gadshill lies to-night in Rochester: I have bespoke
POINS: supper to-morrow night in Eastcheap: we may do it
POINS: as secure as sleep. If you will go, I will stuff
POINS: your purses full of crowns, if you will not, tarry
POINS: at home and be hanged.
FALSTAFF: Hear ye, Yedward, if I tarry at home and go not,
FALSTAFF: I'll hang you for going.
POINS: You will, chops?
FALSTAFF: Hal, wilt thou make one?
PRINCE HENRY: Who, I rob? I a thief? not I, by my faith.
FALSTAFF: There's neither honesty, manhood, nor good
FALSTAFF: fellowship in thee, nor thou camest not of the blood
FALSTAFF: royal, if thou darest not stand for ten shillings.
PRINCE HENRY: Well then, once in my days I'll be a madcap.
FALSTAFF: Why, that's well said.
PRINCE HENRY: Well, come what will, I'll tarry at home.
FALSTAFF: By the Lord, I'll be a traitor then, when thou art king.
PRINCE HENRY: I care not.
POINS: Sir John, I prithee, leave the prince and me alone:
POINS: I will lay him down such reasons for this adventure
POINS: that he shall go.
FALSTAFF: Well, God give thee the spirit of persuasion and him
FALSTAFF: the ears of profiting, that what thou speakest may
FALSTAFF: move and what he hears may be believed, that the
FALSTAFF: true prince may, for recreation sake, prove a false
FALSTAFF: thief, for the poor abuses of the time want
FALSTAFF: countenance. Farewell: you shall find me in Eastcheap.
PRINCE HENRY: Farewell, thou latter spring! farewell, All-hallown summer!
NARRATOR: Exit Falstaff
POINS: Now, my good sweet honey lord, ride with us
POINS: to-morrow: I have a jest to execute that I cannot
POINS: manage alone. Falstaff, Bardolph, Peto and Gadshill
POINS: shall rob those men that we have already waylaid:
POINS: yourself and I will not be there, and when they
POINS: have the booty, if you and I do not rob them, cut
POINS: this head off from my shoulders.
PRINCE HENRY: How shall we part with them in setting forth?
POINS: Why, we will set forth before or after them, and
POINS: appoint them a place of meeting, wherein it is at
POINS: our pleasure to fail, and then will they adventure
POINS: upon the exploit themselves, which they shall have
POINS: no sooner achieved, but we'll set upon them.
PRINCE HENRY: Yea, but 'tis like that they will know us by our
PRINCE HENRY: horses, by our habits and by every other
PRINCE HENRY: appointment, to be ourselves.
POINS: Tut! our horses they shall not see: I'll tie them
POINS: in the wood, our vizards we will change after we
POINS: leave them: and, sirrah, I have cases of buckram
POINS: for the nonce, to immask our noted outward garments.
PRINCE HENRY: Yea, but I doubt they will be too hard for us.
POINS: Well, for two of them, I know them to be as
POINS: true-bred cowards as ever turned back, and for the
POINS: third, if he fight longer than he sees reason, I'll
POINS: forswear arms. The virtue of this jest will be, the
POINS: incomprehensible lies that this same fat rogue will
POINS: tell us when we meet at supper: how thirty, at
POINS: least, he fought with, what wards, what blows, what
POINS: extremities he endured, and in the reproof of this
POINS: lies the jest.
PRINCE HENRY: Well, I'll go with thee: provide us all things
PRINCE HENRY: necessary and meet me to-morrow night in Eastcheap,
PRINCE HENRY: there I'll sup. Farewell.
POINS: Farewell, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit Poins
PRINCE HENRY: I know you all, and will awhile uphold
PRINCE HENRY: The unyoked humour of your idleness:
PRINCE HENRY: Yet herein will I imitate the sun,
PRINCE HENRY: Who doth permit the base contagious clouds
PRINCE HENRY: To smother up his beauty from the world,
PRINCE HENRY: That, when he please again to be himself,
PRINCE HENRY: Being wanted, he may be more wonder'd at,
PRINCE HENRY: By breaking through the foul and ugly mists
PRINCE HENRY: Of vapours that did seem to strangle him.
PRINCE HENRY: If all the year were playing holidays,
PRINCE HENRY: To sport would be as tedious as to work,
PRINCE HENRY: But when they seldom come, they wish'd for come,
PRINCE HENRY: And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents.
PRINCE HENRY: So, when this loose behavior I throw off
PRINCE HENRY: And pay the debt I never promised,
PRINCE HENRY: By how much better than my word I am,
PRINCE HENRY: By so much shall I falsify men's hopes,
PRINCE HENRY: And like bright metal on a sullen ground,
PRINCE HENRY: My reformation, glittering o'er my fault,
PRINCE HENRY: Shall show more goodly and attract more eyes
PRINCE HENRY: Than that which hath no foil to set it off.
PRINCE HENRY: I'll so offend, to make offence a skill,
PRINCE HENRY: Redeeming time when men think least I will.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter the KING, NORTHUMBERLAND, WORCESTER, HOTSPUR, SIR WALTER BLUNT, with others
KING HENRY IV: My blood hath been too cold and temperate,
KING HENRY IV: Unapt to stir at these indignities,
KING HENRY IV: And you have found me, for accordingly
KING HENRY IV: You tread upon my patience: but be sure
KING HENRY IV: I will from henceforth rather be myself,
KING HENRY IV: Mighty and to be fear'd, than my condition,
KING HENRY IV: Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down,
KING HENRY IV: And therefore lost that title of respect
KING HENRY IV: Which the proud soul ne'er pays but to the proud.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Our house, my sovereign liege, little deserves
EARL OF WORCESTER: The scourge of greatness to be used on it,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And that same greatness too which our own hands
EARL OF WORCESTER: Have holp to make so portly.

KING HENRY IV: Danger and disobedience in thine eye:

KING HENRY IV: The moody frontier of a servant brow.

KING HENRY IV: Your use and counsel, we shall send for you.

NORTHUMBERLAND: Is guilty of this fault and not my son.

HOTSPUR: But I remember, when the fight was done,
HOTSPUR: When I was dry with rage and extreme toil,
HOTSPUR: Breathless and faint, leaning upon my sword,
HOTSPUR: Came there a certain lord, neat, and trimly dress'd,
HOTSPUR: Fresh as a bridegroom, and his chin new reap'd
HOTSPUR: Show'd like a stubble-land at harvest-home,
HOTSPUR: He was perfumed like a milliner,
HOTSPUR: And 'twixt his finger and his thumb he held
HOTSPUR: A pouncet-box, which ever and anon
HOTSPUR: He gave his nose and took't away again,
HOTSPUR: Who therewith angry, when it next came there,
HOTSPUR: Took it in snuff, and still he smiled and talk'd,
HOTSPUR: And as the soldiers bore dead bodies by,
HOTSPUR: He call'd them untaught knaves, unmannerly,
HOTSPUR: To bring a slovenly unhandsome corse
HOTSPUR: Betwixt the wind and his nobility.
HOTSPUR: With many holiday and lady terms
HOTSPUR: He question'd me, amongst the rest, demanded
HOTSPUR: My prisoners in your majesty's behalf.
HOTSPUR: I then, all smarting with my wounds being cold,
HOTSPUR: To be so pester'd with a popinjay,
HOTSPUR: Out of my grief and my impatience,
HOTSPUR: Answer'd neglectingly I know not what,
HOTSPUR: He should or he should not, for he made me mad
HOTSPUR: To see him shine so brisk and smell so sweet

HOTSPUR: And telling me the sovereign'st thing on earth
HOTSPUR: Was parmaceti for an inward bruise,
HOTSPUR: And that it was great pity, so it was,
HOTSPUR: This villanous salt-petre should be digg'd
HOTSPUR: Out of the bowels of the harmless earth,
HOTSPUR: Which many a good tall fellow had destroy'd
HOTSPUR: So cowardly, and but for these vile guns,

HOTSPUR: I answer'd indirectly, as I said,
HOTSPUR: And I beseech you, let not his report
HOTSPUR: Come current for an accusation
HOTSPUR: Betwixt my love and your high majesty.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: The circumstance consider'd, good my lord,

SIR WALTER BLUNT: At such a time, with all the rest retold,

HOTSPUR: An if the devil come and roar for them,

HOTSPUR: So honour cross it from the north to south,
HOTSPUR: And let them grapple: O, the blood more stirs
HOTSPUR: To rouse a lion than to start a hare!
NORTHUMBERLAND: Imagination of some great exploit
NORTHUMBERLAND: Drives him beyond the bounds of patience.
HOTSPUR: By heaven, methinks it were an easy leap,
HOTSPUR: To pluck bright honour from the pale-faced moon,
HOTSPUR: Or dive into the bottom of the deep,
HOTSPUR: Where fathom-line could never touch the ground,
HOTSPUR: And pluck up drowned honour by the locks,
HOTSPUR: So he that doth redeem her thence might wear
HOTSPUR: Without corrival, all her dignities:
HOTSPUR: But out upon this half-faced fellowship!
EARL OF WORCESTER: He apprehends a world of figures here,
EARL OF WORCESTER: But not the form of what he should attend.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Good cousin, give me audience for a while.
HOTSPUR: I cry you mercy.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Those same noble Scots
EARL OF WORCESTER: That are your prisoners,--
HOTSPUR: I'll keep them all,
HOTSPUR: By God, he shall not have a Scot of them,
HOTSPUR: No, if a Scot would save his soul, he shall not:
HOTSPUR: I'll keep them, by this hand.
EARL OF WORCESTER: You start away
EARL OF WORCESTER: And lend no ear unto my purposes.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Those prisoners you shall keep.
HOTSPUR: Nay, I will, that's flat:
HOTSPUR: He said he would not ransom Mortimer,
HOTSPUR: Forbad my tongue to speak of Mortimer,
HOTSPUR: But I will find him when he lies asleep,
HOTSPUR: And in his ear I'll holla 'Mortimer!'
HOTSPUR: Nay,
HOTSPUR: I'll have a starling shall be taught to speak
HOTSPUR: Nothing but 'Mortimer,' and give it him
HOTSPUR: To keep his anger still in motion.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Hear you, cousin, a word.
HOTSPUR: All studies here I solemnly defy,
HOTSPUR: Save how to gall and pinch this Bolingbroke:
HOTSPUR: And that same sword-and-buckler Prince of Wales,
HOTSPUR: But that I think his father loves him not
HOTSPUR: And would be glad he met with some mischance,
HOTSPUR: I would have him poison'd with a pot of ale.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Farewell, kinsman: I'll talk to you
EARL OF WORCESTER: When you are better temper'd to attend.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Why, what a wasp-stung and impatient fool
NORTHUMBERLAND: Art thou to break into this woman's mood,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Tying thine ear to no tongue but thine own!
HOTSPUR: Why, look you, I am whipp'd and scourged with rods,
HOTSPUR: Nettled and stung with pismires, when I hear
HOTSPUR: Of this vile politician, Bolingbroke.
HOTSPUR: In Richard's time,--what do you call the place?--
HOTSPUR: A plague upon it, it is in Gloucestershire,
HOTSPUR: 'Twas where the madcap duke his uncle kept,
HOTSPUR: His uncle York, where I first bow'd my knee
HOTSPUR: Unto this king of smiles, this Bolingbroke,--
HOTSPUR: 'Sblood!--
HOTSPUR: When you and he came back from Ravenspurgh.
NORTHUMBERLAND: At Berkley castle.
HOTSPUR: You say true:
HOTSPUR: Why, what a candy deal of courtesy
HOTSPUR: This fawning greyhound then did proffer me!
HOTSPUR: Look,'when his infant fortune came to age,'
HOTSPUR: And 'gentle Harry Percy,' and 'kind cousin,'
HOTSPUR: O, the devil take such cozeners! God forgive me!
HOTSPUR: Good uncle, tell your tale, I have done.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Nay, if you have not, to it again,
EARL OF WORCESTER: We will stay your leisure.
HOTSPUR: I have done, i' faith.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Then once more to your Scottish prisoners.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Deliver them up without their ransom straight,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And make the Douglas' son your only mean
EARL OF WORCESTER: For powers in Scotland, which, for divers reasons
EARL OF WORCESTER: Which I shall send you written, be assured,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Will easily be granted. You, my lord,
NARRATOR: To Northumberland
EARL OF WORCESTER: Your son in Scotland being thus employ'd,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Shall secretly into the bosom creep
EARL OF WORCESTER: Of that same noble prelate, well beloved,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The archbishop.
HOTSPUR: Of York, is it not?
EARL OF WORCESTER: True, who bears hard
EARL OF WORCESTER: His brother's death at Bristol, the Lord Scroop.
EARL OF WORCESTER: I speak not this in estimation,
EARL OF WORCESTER: As what I think might be, but what I know
EARL OF WORCESTER: Is ruminated, plotted and set down,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And only stays but to behold the face
EARL OF WORCESTER: Of that occasion that shall bring it on.
HOTSPUR: I smell it: upon my life, it will do well.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Before the game is afoot, thou still let'st slip.
HOTSPUR: Why, it cannot choose but be a noble plot,
HOTSPUR: And then the power of Scotland and of York,
HOTSPUR: To join with Mortimer, ha?
EARL OF WORCESTER: And so they shall.
HOTSPUR: In faith, it is exceedingly well aim'd.
EARL OF WORCESTER: And 'tis no little reason bids us speed,
EARL OF WORCESTER: To save our heads by raising of a head,
EARL OF WORCESTER: For, bear ourselves as even as we can,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The king will always think him in our debt,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And think we think ourselves unsatisfied,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Till he hath found a time to pay us home:
EARL OF WORCESTER: And see already how he doth begin
EARL OF WORCESTER: To make us strangers to his looks of love.
HOTSPUR: He does, he does: we'll be revenged on him.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Cousin, farewell: no further go in this
EARL OF WORCESTER: Than I by letters shall direct your course.
EARL OF WORCESTER: When time is ripe, which will be suddenly,
EARL OF WORCESTER: I'll steal to Glendower and Lord Mortimer,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Where you and Douglas and our powers at once,
EARL OF WORCESTER: As I will fashion it, shall happily meet,
EARL OF WORCESTER: To bear our fortunes in our own strong arms,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Which now we hold at much uncertainty.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Farewell, good brother: we shall thrive, I trust.
HOTSPUR: Uncle, Adieu: O, let the hours be short
HOTSPUR: Till fields and blows and groans applaud our sport!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rochester. An inn yard.
NARRATOR: Enter a Carrier with a lantern in his hand
First Carrier: Heigh-ho! an it be not four by the day, I'll be
First Carrier: hanged: Charles' wain is over the new chimney, and
First Carrier: yet our horse not packed. What, ostler!
Ostler: [Within]   Anon, anon.
First Carrier: I prithee, Tom, beat Cut's saddle, put a few flocks
First Carrier: in the point, poor jade, is wrung in the withers out
First Carrier: of all cess.
NARRATOR: Enter another Carrier
Second Carrier: Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog, and that
Second Carrier: is the next way to give poor jades the bots: this
Second Carrier: house is turned upside down since Robin Ostler died.
First Carrier: Poor fellow, never joyed since the price of oats
First Carrier: rose, it was the death of him.
Second Carrier: I think this be the most villanous house in all
Second Carrier: London road for fleas: I am stung like a tench.
First Carrier: Like a tench! by the mass, there is ne'er a king
First Carrier: christen could be better bit than I have been since
First Carrier: the first cock.
Second Carrier: Why, they will allow us ne'er a jordan, and then we
Second Carrier: leak in your chimney, and your chamber-lie breeds
Second Carrier: fleas like a loach.
First Carrier: What, ostler! come away and be hanged!
Second Carrier: I have a gammon of bacon and two razors of ginger,
Second Carrier: to be delivered as far as Charing-cross.
First Carrier: God's body! the turkeys in my pannier are quite
First Carrier: starved. What, ostler! A plague on thee! hast thou
First Carrier: never an eye in thy head? canst not hear? An
First Carrier: 'twere not as good deed as drink, to break the pate
First Carrier: on thee, I am a very villain. Come, and be hanged!
First Carrier: hast thou no faith in thee?
NARRATOR: Enter GADSHILL
GADSHILL: Good morrow, carriers. What's o'clock?
First Carrier: I think it be two o'clock.
GADSHILL: I pray thee lend me thy lantern, to see my gelding
GADSHILL: in the stable.
First Carrier: Nay, by God, soft, I know a trick worth two of that, i' faith.
GADSHILL: I pray thee, lend me thine.
Second Carrier: Ay, when? can'st tell? Lend me thy lantern, quoth
Second Carrier: he? marry, I'll see thee hanged first.
GADSHILL: Sirrah carrier, what time do you mean to come to London?
Second Carrier: Time enough to go to bed with a candle, I warrant
Second Carrier: thee. Come, neighbour Mugs, we'll call up the
Second Carrier: gentleman: they will along with company, for they
Second Carrier: have great charge.
NARRATOR: Exeunt carriers
GADSHILL: What, ho! chamberlain!
Chamberlain: [Within]  At hand, quoth pick-purse.
GADSHILL: That's even as fair as--at hand, quoth the
GADSHILL: chamberlain, for thou variest no more from picking
GADSHILL: of purses than giving direction doth from labouring,
GADSHILL: thou layest the plot how.
NARRATOR: Enter Chamberlain
Chamberlain: Good morrow, Master Gadshill. It holds current that
Chamberlain: I told you yesternight: there's a franklin in the
Chamberlain: wild of Kent hath brought three hundred marks with
Chamberlain: him in gold: I heard him tell it to one of his
Chamberlain: company last night at supper, a kind of auditor, one
Chamberlain: that hath abundance of charge too, God knows what.
Chamberlain: They are up already, and call for eggs and butter,
Chamberlain: they will away presently.
GADSHILL: Sirrah, if they meet not with Saint Nicholas'
GADSHILL: clerks, I'll give thee this neck.
Chamberlain: No, I'll none of it: I pray thee keep that for the
Chamberlain: hangman, for I know thou worshippest St. Nicholas
Chamberlain: as truly as a man of falsehood may.
GADSHILL: What talkest thou to me of the hangman? if I hang,
GADSHILL: I'll make a fat pair of gallows, for if I hang, old
GADSHILL: Sir John hangs with me, and thou knowest he is no
GADSHILL: starveling. Tut! there are other Trojans that thou
GADSHILL: dreamest not of, the which for sport sake are
GADSHILL: content to do the profession some grace, that would,
GADSHILL: if matters should be looked into, for their own
GADSHILL: credit sake, make all whole. I am joined with no
GADSHILL: foot-land rakers, no long-staff sixpenny strikers,
GADSHILL: none of these mad mustachio purple-hued malt-worms,
GADSHILL: but with nobility and tranquillity, burgomasters and
GADSHILL: great oneyers, such as can hold in, such as will
GADSHILL: strike sooner than speak, and speak sooner than
GADSHILL: drink, and drink sooner than pray: and yet, zounds,
GADSHILL: I lie, for they pray continually to their saint, the
GADSHILL: commonwealth, or rather, not pray to her, but prey
GADSHILL: on her, for they ride up and down on her and make
GADSHILL: her their boots.
Chamberlain: What, the commonwealth their boots? will she hold
Chamberlain: out water in foul way?
GADSHILL: She will, she will, justice hath liquored her. We
GADSHILL: steal as in a castle, cocksure, we have the receipt
GADSHILL: of fern-seed, we walk invisible.
Chamberlain: Nay, by my faith, I think you are more beholding to
Chamberlain: the night than to fern-seed for your walking invisible.
GADSHILL: Give me thy hand: thou shalt have a share in our
GADSHILL: purchase, as I am a true man.
Chamberlain: Nay, rather let me have it, as you are a false thief.
GADSHILL: Go to, 'homo' is a common name to all men. Bid the
GADSHILL: ostler bring my gelding out of the stable. Farewell,
GADSHILL: you muddy knave.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The highway, near Gadshill.
NARRATOR: Enter PRINCE HENRY and POINS
POINS: Come, shelter, shelter: I have removed Falstaff's
POINS: horse, and he frets like a gummed velvet.
PRINCE HENRY: Stand close.
NARRATOR: Enter FALSTAFF
FALSTAFF: Poins! Poins, and be hanged! Poins!
PRINCE HENRY: Peace, ye fat-kidneyed rascal! what a brawling dost
PRINCE HENRY: thou keep!
FALSTAFF: Where's Poins, Hal?
PRINCE HENRY: He is walked up to the top of the hill: I'll go seek him.
FALSTAFF: I am accursed to rob in that thief's company: the
FALSTAFF: rascal hath removed my horse, and tied him I know
FALSTAFF: not where. If I travel but four foot by the squier
FALSTAFF: further afoot, I shall break my wind. Well, I doubt
FALSTAFF: not but to die a fair death for all this, if I
FALSTAFF: 'scape hanging for killing that rogue. I have
FALSTAFF: forsworn his company hourly any time this two and
FALSTAFF: twenty years, and yet I am bewitched with the
FALSTAFF: rogue's company. If the rascal hath not given me
FALSTAFF: medicines to make me love him, I'll be hanged, it
FALSTAFF: could not be else: I have drunk medicines. Poins!
FALSTAFF: Hal! a plague upon you both! Bardolph! Peto!
FALSTAFF: I'll starve ere I'll rob a foot further. An 'twere
FALSTAFF: not as good a deed as drink, to turn true man and to
FALSTAFF: leave these rogues, I am the veriest varlet that
FALSTAFF: ever chewed with a tooth. Eight yards of uneven
FALSTAFF: ground is threescore and ten miles afoot with me,
FALSTAFF: and the stony-hearted villains know it well enough:
FALSTAFF: a plague upon it when thieves cannot be true one to another!
NARRATOR: They whistle
FALSTAFF: Whew! A plague upon you all! Give me my horse, you
FALSTAFF: rogues, give me my horse, and be hanged!
PRINCE HENRY: Peace, ye fat-guts! lie down, lay thine ear close
PRINCE HENRY: to the ground and list if thou canst hear the tread
PRINCE HENRY: of travellers.
FALSTAFF: Have you any levers to lift me up again, being down?
FALSTAFF: 'Sblood, I'll not bear mine own flesh so far afoot
FALSTAFF: again for all the coin in thy father's exchequer.
FALSTAFF: What a plague mean ye to colt me thus?
PRINCE HENRY: Thou liest, thou art not colted, thou art uncolted.
FALSTAFF: I prithee, good Prince Hal, help me to my horse,
FALSTAFF: good king's son.
PRINCE HENRY: Out, ye rogue! shall I be your ostler?
FALSTAFF: Go, hang thyself in thine own heir-apparent
FALSTAFF: garters! If I be ta'en, I'll peach for this. An I
FALSTAFF: have not ballads made on you all and sung to filthy
FALSTAFF: tunes, let a cup of sack be my poison: when a jest
FALSTAFF: is so forward, and afoot too! I hate it.
NARRATOR: Enter GADSHILL, BARDOLPH and PETO
GADSHILL: Stand.
FALSTAFF: So I do, against my will.
POINS: O, 'tis our setter: I know his voice. Bardolph,
POINS: what news?
BARDOLPH: Case ye, case ye, on with your vizards: there 's
BARDOLPH: money of the king's coming down the hill, 'tis going
BARDOLPH: to the king's exchequer.
FALSTAFF: You lie, ye rogue, 'tis going to the king's tavern.
GADSHILL: There's enough to make us all.
FALSTAFF: To be hanged.
PRINCE HENRY: Sirs, you four shall front them in the narrow lane,
PRINCE HENRY: Ned Poins and I will walk lower: if they 'scape
PRINCE HENRY: from your encounter, then they light on us.
PETO: How many be there of them?
GADSHILL: Some eight or ten.
FALSTAFF: 'Zounds, will they not rob us?
PRINCE HENRY: What, a coward, Sir John Paunch?
FALSTAFF: Indeed, I am not John of Gaunt, your grandfather,
FALSTAFF: but yet no coward, Hal.
PRINCE HENRY: Well, we leave that to the proof.
POINS: Sirrah Jack, thy horse stands behind the hedge:
POINS: when thou needest him, there thou shalt find him.
POINS: Farewell, and stand fast.
FALSTAFF: Now cannot I strike him, if I should be hanged.
PRINCE HENRY: Ned, where are our disguises?
POINS: Here, hard by: stand close.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PRINCE HENRY and POINS
FALSTAFF: Now, my masters, happy man be his dole, say I:
FALSTAFF: every man to his business.
NARRATOR: Enter the Travellers
First Traveller: Come, neighbour: the boy shall lead our horses down
First Traveller: the hill, we'll walk afoot awhile, and ease our legs.
Thieves: Stand!
Travellers: Jesus bless us!
FALSTAFF: Strike, down with them, cut the villains' throats:
FALSTAFF: ah! whoreson caterpillars! bacon-fed knaves! they
FALSTAFF: hate us youth: down with them: fleece them.
Travellers: O, we are undone, both we and ours for ever!
FALSTAFF: Hang ye, gorbellied knaves, are ye undone? No, ye
FALSTAFF: fat chuffs: I would your store were here! On,
FALSTAFF: bacons, on! What, ye knaves! young men must live.
FALSTAFF: You are Grand-jurors, are ye? we'll jure ye, 'faith.
NARRATOR: Here they rob them and bind them. Exeunt
NARRATOR: Re-enter PRINCE HENRY and POINS
PRINCE HENRY: The thieves have bound the true men. Now could thou
PRINCE HENRY: and I rob the thieves and go merrily to London, it
PRINCE HENRY: would be argument for a week, laughter for a month
PRINCE HENRY: and a good jest for ever.
POINS: Stand close, I hear them coming.
NARRATOR: Enter the Thieves again
FALSTAFF: Come, my masters, let us share, and then to  horse
FALSTAFF: before day. An the Prince and Poins be not two
FALSTAFF: arrant cowards, there's no equity stirring: there's
FALSTAFF: no more valour in that Poins than in a wild-duck.
PRINCE HENRY: Your money!
POINS: Villains!
POINS: As they are sharing, the Prince and Poins set upon  them, they all run away, and Falstaff, after a blow or two, runs away too, leaving the booty behind them
PRINCE HENRY: Got with much ease. Now merrily to horse:
PRINCE HENRY: The thieves are all scatter'd and possess'd with fear
PRINCE HENRY: So strongly that they dare not meet each other,
PRINCE HENRY: Each takes his fellow for an officer.
PRINCE HENRY: Away, good Ned. Falstaff sweats to death,
PRINCE HENRY: And lards the lean earth as he walks along:
PRINCE HENRY: Were 't not for laughing, I should pity him.
POINS: How the rogue roar'd!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Warkworth castle
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR, solus, reading a letter
HOTSPUR: 'But for mine own part, my lord, I could be well
HOTSPUR: contented to be there, in respect of the love I bear
HOTSPUR: your house.' He could be contented: why is he not,
HOTSPUR: then? In respect of the love he bears our house:
HOTSPUR: he shows in this, he loves his own barn better than
HOTSPUR: he loves our house. Let me see some more. 'The
HOTSPUR: purpose you undertake is dangerous,'--why, that's
HOTSPUR: certain: 'tis dangerous to take a cold, to sleep, to
HOTSPUR: drink, but I tell you, my lord fool, out of this
HOTSPUR: nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, safety. 'The
HOTSPUR: purpose you undertake is dangerous, the friends you
HOTSPUR: have named uncertain, the time itself unsorted, and
HOTSPUR: your whole plot too light for the counterpoise of so
HOTSPUR: great an opposition.' Say you so, say you so? I say
HOTSPUR: unto you again, you are a shallow cowardly hind, and
HOTSPUR: you lie.  What a lack-brain is this! By the Lord,
HOTSPUR: our plot is a good plot as ever was laid, our
HOTSPUR: friends true and constant: a good plot, good
HOTSPUR: friends, and full of expectation, an excellent plot,
HOTSPUR: very good friends. What a frosty-spirited rogue is
HOTSPUR: this! Why, my lord of York commends the plot and the
HOTSPUR: general course of action. 'Zounds, an I were now by
HOTSPUR: this rascal, I could brain him with his lady's fan.
HOTSPUR: Is there not my father, my uncle and myself? lord
HOTSPUR: Edmund Mortimer, My lord of York and Owen Glendower?
HOTSPUR: is there not besides the Douglas? have I not all
HOTSPUR: their letters to meet me in arms by the ninth of the
HOTSPUR: next month? and are they not some of them set
HOTSPUR: forward already? What a pagan rascal is this! an
HOTSPUR: infidel! Ha! you shall see now in very sincerity
HOTSPUR: of fear and cold heart, will he to the king and lay
HOTSPUR: open all our proceedings. O, I could divide myself
HOTSPUR: and go to buffets, for moving such a dish of
HOTSPUR: skim milk with so honourable an action! Hang him!
HOTSPUR: let him tell the king: we are prepared. I will set
HOTSPUR: forward to-night.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY PERCY
HOTSPUR: How now, Kate! I must leave you within these two hours.
LADY PERCY: O, my good lord, why are you thus alone?
LADY PERCY: For what offence have I this fortnight been
LADY PERCY: A banish'd woman from my Harry's bed?
LADY PERCY: Tell me, sweet lord, what is't that takes from thee
LADY PERCY: Thy stomach, pleasure and thy golden sleep?
LADY PERCY: Why dost thou bend thine eyes upon the earth,
LADY PERCY: And start so often when thou sit'st alone?
LADY PERCY: Why hast thou lost the fresh blood in thy cheeks,
LADY PERCY: And given my treasures and my rights of thee
LADY PERCY: To thick-eyed musing and cursed melancholy?
LADY PERCY: In thy faint slumbers I by thee have watch'd,
LADY PERCY: And heard thee murmur tales of iron wars,
LADY PERCY: Speak terms of manage to thy bounding steed,
LADY PERCY: Cry 'Courage! to the field!' And thou hast talk'd
LADY PERCY: Of sallies and retires, of trenches, tents,
LADY PERCY: Of palisadoes, frontiers, parapets,
LADY PERCY: Of basilisks, of cannon, culverin,
LADY PERCY: Of prisoners' ransom and of soldiers slain,
LADY PERCY: And all the currents of a heady fight.
LADY PERCY: Thy spirit within thee hath been so at war
LADY PERCY: And thus hath so bestirr'd thee in thy sleep,
LADY PERCY: That beads of sweat have stood upon thy brow
LADY PERCY: Like bubbles in a late-disturbed stream,
LADY PERCY: And in thy face strange motions have appear'd,
LADY PERCY: Such as we see when men restrain their breath
LADY PERCY: On some great sudden hest. O, what portents are these?
LADY PERCY: Some heavy business hath my lord in hand,
LADY PERCY: And I must know it, else he loves me not.
HOTSPUR: What, ho!
NARRATOR: Enter Servant
HOTSPUR: Is Gilliams with the packet gone?
Servant: He is, my lord, an hour ago.
HOTSPUR: Hath Butler brought those horses from the sheriff?
Servant: One horse, my lord, he brought even now.
HOTSPUR: What horse? a roan, a crop-ear, is it not?
Servant: It is, my lord.
HOTSPUR: That roan shall by my throne.
HOTSPUR: Well, I will back him straight: O esperance!
HOTSPUR: Bid Butler lead him forth into the park.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
LADY PERCY: But hear you, my lord.
HOTSPUR: What say'st thou, my lady?
LADY PERCY: What is it carries you away?
HOTSPUR: Why, my horse, my love, my horse.
LADY PERCY: Out, you mad-headed ape!
LADY PERCY: A weasel hath not such a deal of spleen
LADY PERCY: As you are toss'd with. In faith,
LADY PERCY: I'll know your business, Harry, that I will.
LADY PERCY: I fear my brother Mortimer doth stir
LADY PERCY: About his title, and hath sent for you
LADY PERCY: To line his enterprise: but if you go,--
HOTSPUR: So far afoot, I shall be weary, love.
LADY PERCY: Come, come, you paraquito, answer me
LADY PERCY: Directly unto this question that I ask:
LADY PERCY: In faith, I'll break thy little finger, Harry,
LADY PERCY: An if thou wilt not tell me all things true.
HOTSPUR: Away,
HOTSPUR: Away, you trifler! Love! I love thee not,
HOTSPUR: I care not for thee, Kate: this is no world
HOTSPUR: To play with mammets and to tilt with lips:
HOTSPUR: We must have bloody noses and crack'd crowns,
HOTSPUR: And pass them current too. God's me, my horse!
HOTSPUR: What say'st thou, Kate? what would'st thou
HOTSPUR: have with me?
LADY PERCY: Do you not love me? do you not, indeed?
LADY PERCY: Well, do not then, for since you love me not,
LADY PERCY: I will not love myself. Do you not love me?
LADY PERCY: Nay, tell me if you speak in jest or no.
HOTSPUR: Come, wilt thou see me ride?
HOTSPUR: And when I am on horseback, I will swear
HOTSPUR: I love thee infinitely. But hark you, Kate,
HOTSPUR: I must not have you henceforth question me
HOTSPUR: Whither I go, nor reason whereabout:
HOTSPUR: Whither I must, I must, and, to conclude,
HOTSPUR: This evening must I leave you, gentle Kate.
HOTSPUR: I know you wise, but yet no farther wise
HOTSPUR: Than Harry Percy's wife: constant you are,
HOTSPUR: But yet a woman: and for secrecy,
HOTSPUR: No lady closer, for I well believe
HOTSPUR: Thou wilt not utter what thou dost not know,

FALSTAFF: carriage, and, as I think, his age some fifty, or,
FALSTAFF: by'r lady, inclining to three score, and now I
FALSTAFF: remember me, his name is Falstaff: if that man
FALSTAFF: should be lewdly given, he deceiveth me, for, Harry,
FALSTAFF: I see virtue in his looks. If then the tree may be
FALSTAFF: known by the fruit, as the fruit by the tree, then,
FALSTAFF: peremptorily I speak it, there is virtue in that
FALSTAFF: Falstaff: him keep with, the rest banish. And tell
FALSTAFF: me now, thou naughty varlet, tell me, where hast
FALSTAFF: thou been this month?
PRINCE HENRY: Dost thou speak like a king? Do thou stand for me,
PRINCE HENRY: and I'll play my father.
FALSTAFF: Depose me? if thou dost it half so gravely, so
FALSTAFF: majestically, both in word and matter, hang me up by
FALSTAFF: the heels for a rabbit-sucker or a poulter's hare.
PRINCE HENRY: Well, here I am set.
FALSTAFF: And here I stand: judge, my masters.
PRINCE HENRY: Now, Harry, whence come you?
FALSTAFF: My noble lord, from Eastcheap.
PRINCE HENRY: The complaints I hear of thee are grievous.
FALSTAFF: 'Sblood, my lord, they are false: nay, I'll tickle
FALSTAFF: ye for a young prince, i' faith.
PRINCE HENRY: Swearest thou, ungracious boy? henceforth ne'er look
PRINCE HENRY: on me. Thou art violently carried away from grace:
PRINCE HENRY: there is a devil haunts thee in the likeness of an
PRINCE HENRY: old fat man, a tun of man is thy companion. Why
PRINCE HENRY: dost thou converse with that trunk of humours, that
PRINCE HENRY: bolting-hutch of beastliness, that swollen parcel
PRINCE HENRY: of dropsies, that huge bombard of sack, that stuffed
PRINCE HENRY: cloak-bag of guts, that roasted Manningtree ox with
PRINCE HENRY: the pudding in his belly, that reverend vice, that
PRINCE HENRY: grey iniquity, that father ruffian, that vanity in
PRINCE HENRY: years? Wherein is he good, but to taste sack and
PRINCE HENRY: drink it? wherein neat and cleanly, but to carve a
PRINCE HENRY: capon and eat it? wherein cunning, but in craft?
PRINCE HENRY: wherein crafty, but in villany? wherein villanous,
PRINCE HENRY: but in all things? wherein worthy, but in nothing?
FALSTAFF: I would your grace would take me with you: whom
FALSTAFF: means your grace?
PRINCE HENRY: That villanous abominable misleader of youth,
PRINCE HENRY: Falstaff, that old white-bearded Satan.
FALSTAFF: My lord, the man I know.
PRINCE HENRY: I know thou dost.
FALSTAFF: But to say I know more harm in him than in myself,
FALSTAFF: were to say more than I know. That he is old, the
FALSTAFF: more the pity, his white hairs do witness it, but
FALSTAFF: that he is, saving your reverence, a whoremaster,
FALSTAFF: that I utterly deny. If sack and sugar be a fault,
FALSTAFF: God help the wicked! if to be old and merry be a
FALSTAFF: sin, then many an old host that I know is damned: if
FALSTAFF: to be fat be to be hated, then Pharaoh's lean kine
FALSTAFF: are to be loved. No, my good lord, banish Peto,
FALSTAFF: banish Bardolph, banish Poins: but for sweet Jack
FALSTAFF: Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, true Jack Falstaff,
FALSTAFF: valiant Jack Falstaff, and therefore more valiant,
FALSTAFF: being, as he is, old Jack Falstaff, banish not him
FALSTAFF: thy Harry's company, banish not him thy Harry's
FALSTAFF: company: banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.
PRINCE HENRY: I do, I will.
NARRATOR: A knocking heard
NARRATOR: Exeunt Hostess, FRANCIS, and BARDOLPH
NARRATOR: Re-enter BARDOLPH, running
BARDOLPH: O, my lord, my lord! the sheriff with a most
BARDOLPH: monstrous watch is at the door.
FALSTAFF: Out, ye rogue! Play out the play: I have much to
FALSTAFF: say in the behalf of that Falstaff.
NARRATOR: Re-enter the Hostess
Hostess: O Jesu, my lord, my lord!
PRINCE HENRY: Heigh, heigh! the devil rides upon a fiddlestick:
PRINCE HENRY: what's the matter?
Hostess: The sheriff and all the watch are at the door: they
Hostess: are come to search the house. Shall I let them in?
FALSTAFF: Dost thou hear, Hal? never call a true piece of
FALSTAFF: gold a counterfeit: thou art essentially mad,
FALSTAFF: without seeming so.
PRINCE HENRY: And thou a natural coward, without instinct.
FALSTAFF: I deny your major: if you will deny the sheriff,
FALSTAFF: so, if not, let him enter: if I become not a cart
FALSTAFF: as well as another man, a plague on my bringing up!
FALSTAFF: I hope I shall as soon be strangled with a halter as another.
PRINCE HENRY: Go, hide thee behind the arras: the rest walk up
PRINCE HENRY: above. Now, my masters, for a true face and good
PRINCE HENRY: conscience.
FALSTAFF: Both which I have had: but their date is out, and
FALSTAFF: therefore I'll hide me.
PRINCE HENRY: Call in the sheriff.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all except PRINCE HENRY and PETO
NARRATOR: Enter Sheriff and the Carrier
PRINCE HENRY: Now, master sheriff, what is your will with me?
Sheriff: First, pardon me, my lord. A hue and cry
Sheriff: Hath follow'd certain men unto this house.
PRINCE HENRY: What men?
Sheriff: One of them is well known, my gracious lord,
Sheriff: A gross fat man.
Carrier: As fat as butter.
PRINCE HENRY: The man, I do assure you, is not here,
PRINCE HENRY: For I myself at this time have employ'd him.
PRINCE HENRY: And, sheriff, I will engage my word to thee
PRINCE HENRY: That I will, by to-morrow dinner-time,
PRINCE HENRY: Send him to answer thee, or any man,
PRINCE HENRY: For any thing he shall be charged withal:
PRINCE HENRY: And so let me entreat you leave the house.
Sheriff: I will, my lord. There are two gentlemen
Sheriff: Have in this robbery lost three hundred marks.
PRINCE HENRY: It may be so: if he have robb'd these men,
PRINCE HENRY: He shall be answerable, and so farewell.
Sheriff: Good night, my noble lord.
PRINCE HENRY: I think it is good morrow, is it not?
Sheriff: Indeed, my lord, I think it be two o'clock.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Sheriff and Carrier
PRINCE HENRY: This oily rascal is known as well as Paul's. Go,
PRINCE HENRY: call him forth.
PETO: Falstaff!--Fast asleep behind the arras, and
PETO: snorting like a horse.
PRINCE HENRY: Hark, how hard he fetches breath. Search his pockets.
NARRATOR: He searcheth his pockets, and findeth certain papers
PRINCE HENRY: What hast thou found?
PETO: Nothing but papers, my lord.
PRINCE HENRY: Let's see what they be: read them.
PETO: [Reads]  Item, A capon,. . 2s. 2d.
PETO: Item, Sauce,. . . 4d.
PETO: Item, Sack, two gallons, 5s. 8d.
PETO: Item, Anchovies and sack after supper, 2s. 6d.
PETO: Item, Bread,        ob.
PRINCE HENRY: O monstrous! but one half-penny-worth of bread to
PRINCE HENRY: this intolerable deal of sack! What there is else,
PRINCE HENRY: keep close, we'll read it at more advantage: there
PRINCE HENRY: let him sleep till day. I'll to the court in the
PRINCE HENRY: morning. We must all to the wars, and thy place
PRINCE HENRY: shall be honourable. I'll procure this fat rogue a
PRINCE HENRY: charge of foot, and I know his death will be a
PRINCE HENRY: march of twelve-score. The money shall be paid
PRINCE HENRY: back again with advantage. Be with me betimes in
PRINCE HENRY: the morning, and so, good morrow, Peto.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
PETO: Good morrow, good my lord.
PETO: ACT III
PETO: SCENE I. Bangor. The Archdeacon's house.
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR, WORCESTER, MORTIMER, and GLENDOWER
MORTIMER: These promises are fair, the parties sure,
MORTIMER: And our induction full of prosperous hope.
HOTSPUR: Lord Mortimer, and cousin Glendower,
HOTSPUR: Will you sit down?
HOTSPUR: And uncle Worcester: a plague upon it!
HOTSPUR: I have forgot the map.
GLENDOWER: No, here it is.
GLENDOWER: Sit, cousin Percy, sit, good cousin Hotspur,
GLENDOWER: For by that name as oft as Lancaster
GLENDOWER: Doth speak of you, his cheek looks pale and with
GLENDOWER: A rising sigh he wisheth you in heaven.
HOTSPUR: And you in hell, as oft as he hears Owen Glendower spoke of.
GLENDOWER: I cannot blame him: at my nativity
GLENDOWER: The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes,
GLENDOWER: Of burning cressets, and at my birth
GLENDOWER: The frame and huge foundation of the earth
GLENDOWER: Shaked like a coward.
HOTSPUR: Why, so it would have done at the same season, if
HOTSPUR: your mother's cat had but kittened, though yourself
HOTSPUR: had never been born.
GLENDOWER: I say the earth did shake when I was born.
HOTSPUR: And I say the earth was not of my mind,
HOTSPUR: If you suppose as fearing you it shook.
GLENDOWER: The heavens were all on fire, the earth did tremble.
HOTSPUR: O, then the earth shook to see the heavens on fire,
HOTSPUR: And not in fear of your nativity.
HOTSPUR: Diseased nature oftentimes breaks forth
HOTSPUR: In strange eruptions, oft the teeming earth
HOTSPUR: Is with a kind of colic pinch'd and vex'd
HOTSPUR: By the imprisoning of unruly wind
HOTSPUR: Within her womb, which, for enlargement striving,
HOTSPUR: Shakes the old beldam earth and topples down
HOTSPUR: Steeples and moss-grown towers. At your birth
HOTSPUR: Our grandam earth, having this distemperature,
HOTSPUR: In passion shook.
GLENDOWER: Cousin, of many men
GLENDOWER: I do not bear these crossings. Give me leave
GLENDOWER: To tell you once again that at my birth
GLENDOWER: The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes,
GLENDOWER: The goats ran from the mountains, and the herds
GLENDOWER: Were strangely clamorous to the frighted fields.
GLENDOWER: These signs have mark'd me extraordinary,
GLENDOWER: And all the courses of my life do show
GLENDOWER: I am not in the roll of common men.
GLENDOWER: Where is he living, clipp'd in with the sea
GLENDOWER: That chides the banks of England, Scotland, Wales,
GLENDOWER: Which calls me pupil, or hath read to me?
GLENDOWER: And bring him out that is but woman's son
GLENDOWER: Can trace me in the tedious ways of art
GLENDOWER: And hold me pace in deep experiments.
HOTSPUR: I think there's no man speaks better Welsh.
HOTSPUR: I'll to dinner.
MORTIMER: Peace, cousin Percy, you will make him mad.
GLENDOWER: I can call spirits from the vasty deep.
HOTSPUR: Why, so can I, or so can any man,
HOTSPUR: But will they come when you do call for them?
GLENDOWER: Why, I can teach you, cousin, to command
GLENDOWER: The devil.
HOTSPUR: And I can teach thee, coz, to shame the devil
HOTSPUR: By telling truth: tell truth and shame the devil.
HOTSPUR: If thou have power to raise him, bring him hither,
HOTSPUR: And I'll be sworn I have power to shame him hence.
HOTSPUR: O, while you live, tell truth and shame the devil!
MORTIMER: Come, come, no more of this unprofitable chat.
GLENDOWER: Three times hath Henry Bolingbroke made head
GLENDOWER: Against my power, thrice from the banks of Wye
GLENDOWER: And sandy-bottom'd Severn have I sent him
GLENDOWER: Bootless home and weather-beaten back.
HOTSPUR: Home without boots, and in foul weather too!
HOTSPUR: How 'scapes he agues, in the devil's name?
GLENDOWER: Come, here's the map: shall we divide our right
GLENDOWER: According to our threefold order ta'en?
MORTIMER: The archdeacon hath divided it
MORTIMER: Into three limits very equally:
MORTIMER: England, from Trent and Severn hitherto,
MORTIMER: By south and east is to my part assign'd:
MORTIMER: All westward, Wales beyond the Severn shore,
MORTIMER: And all the fertile land within that bound,
MORTIMER: To Owen Glendower: and, dear coz, to you
MORTIMER: The remnant northward, lying off from Trent.
MORTIMER: And our indentures tripartite are drawn,
MORTIMER: Which being sealed interchangeably,
MORTIMER: A business that this night may execute,
MORTIMER: To-morrow, cousin Percy, you and I
MORTIMER: And my good Lord of Worcester will set forth
MORTIMER: To meet your father and the Scottish power,
MORTIMER: As is appointed us, at Shrewsbury.
MORTIMER: My father Glendower is not ready yet,
MORTIMER: Not shall we need his help these fourteen days.
MORTIMER: Within that space you may have drawn together
MORTIMER: Your tenants, friends and neighbouring gentlemen.
GLENDOWER: A shorter time shall send me to you, lords:
GLENDOWER: And in my conduct shall your ladies come,
GLENDOWER: From whom you now must steal and take no leave,
GLENDOWER: For there will be a world of water shed
GLENDOWER: Upon the parting of your wives and you.
HOTSPUR: Methinks my moiety, north from Burton here,
HOTSPUR: In quantity equals not one of yours:
HOTSPUR: See how this river comes me cranking in,
HOTSPUR: And cuts me from the best of all my land
HOTSPUR: A huge half-moon, a monstrous cantle out.
HOTSPUR: I'll have the current in this place damm'd up,
HOTSPUR: And here the smug and silver Trent shall run
HOTSPUR: In a new channel, fair and evenly,
HOTSPUR: It shall not wind with such a deep indent,
HOTSPUR: To rob me of so rich a bottom here.
GLENDOWER: Not wind? it shall, it must, you see it doth.
MORTIMER: Yea, but
MORTIMER: Mark how he bears his course, and runs me up
MORTIMER: With like advantage on the other side,
MORTIMER: Gelding the opposed continent as much
MORTIMER: As on the other side it takes from you.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Yea, but a little charge will trench him here
EARL OF WORCESTER: And on this north side win this cape of land,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And then he runs straight and even.
HOTSPUR: I'll have it so: a little charge will do it.
GLENDOWER: I'll not have it alter'd.
HOTSPUR: Will not you?
GLENDOWER: No, nor you shall not.
HOTSPUR: Who shall say me nay?
GLENDOWER: Why, that will I.
HOTSPUR: Let me not understand you, then, speak it in Welsh.
GLENDOWER: I can speak English, lord, as well as you,
GLENDOWER: For I was train'd up in the English court,
GLENDOWER: Where, being but young, I framed to the harp
GLENDOWER: Many an English ditty lovely well
GLENDOWER: And gave the tongue a helpful ornament,
GLENDOWER: A virtue that was never seen in you.
HOTSPUR: Marry,
HOTSPUR: And I am glad of it with all my heart:
HOTSPUR: I had rather be a kitten and cry mew
HOTSPUR: Than one of these same metre ballad-mongers,
HOTSPUR: I had rather hear a brazen canstick turn'd,
HOTSPUR: Or a dry wheel grate on the axle-tree,
HOTSPUR: And that would set my teeth nothing on edge,
HOTSPUR: Nothing so much as mincing poetry:
HOTSPUR: 'Tis like the forced gait of a shuffling nag.
GLENDOWER: Come, you shall have Trent turn'd.
HOTSPUR: I do not care: I'll give thrice so much land
HOTSPUR: To any well-deserving friend,
HOTSPUR: But in the way of bargain, mark ye me,
HOTSPUR: I'll cavil on the ninth part of a hair.
HOTSPUR: Are the indentures drawn? shall we be gone?
GLENDOWER: The moon shines fair, you may away by night:
GLENDOWER: I'll haste the writer and withal
GLENDOWER: Break with your wives of your departure hence:
GLENDOWER: I am afraid my daughter will run mad,
GLENDOWER: So much she doteth on her Mortimer.
NARRATOR: Exit GLENDOWER
MORTIMER: Fie, cousin Percy! how you cross my father!
HOTSPUR: I cannot choose: sometime he angers me
HOTSPUR: With telling me of the mouldwarp and the ant,
HOTSPUR: Of the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies,
HOTSPUR: And of a dragon and a finless fish,
HOTSPUR: A clip-wing'd griffin and a moulten raven,
HOTSPUR: A couching lion and a ramping cat,
HOTSPUR: And such a deal of skimble-skamble stuff
HOTSPUR: As puts me from my faith. I tell you what,
HOTSPUR: He held me last night at least nine hours
HOTSPUR: In reckoning up the several devils' names
HOTSPUR: That were his lackeys: I cried 'hum,' and 'well, go to,'
HOTSPUR: But mark'd him not a word. O, he is as tedious
HOTSPUR: As a tired horse, a railing wife,
HOTSPUR: Worse than a smoky house: I had rather live
HOTSPUR: With cheese and garlic in a windmill, far,
HOTSPUR: Than feed on cates and have him talk to me
HOTSPUR: In any summer-house in Christendom.
MORTIMER: In faith, he is a worthy gentleman,
MORTIMER: Exceedingly well read, and profited
MORTIMER: In strange concealments, valiant as a lion
MORTIMER: And as wondrous affable and as bountiful
MORTIMER: As mines of India. Shall I tell you, cousin?
MORTIMER: He holds your temper in a high respect
MORTIMER: And curbs himself even of his natural scope
MORTIMER: When you come 'cross his humour, faith, he does:
MORTIMER: I warrant you, that man is not alive
MORTIMER: Might so have tempted him as you have done,
MORTIMER: Without the taste of danger and reproof:
MORTIMER: But do not use it oft, let me entreat you.
EARL OF WORCESTER: In faith, my lord, you are too wilful-blame,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And since your coming hither have done enough
EARL OF WORCESTER: To put him quite beside his patience.
EARL OF WORCESTER: You must needs learn, lord, to amend this fault:
EARL OF WORCESTER: Though sometimes it show greatness, courage, blood,--
EARL OF WORCESTER: And that's the dearest grace it renders you,--
EARL OF WORCESTER: Yet oftentimes it doth present harsh rage,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Defect of manners, want of government,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Pride, haughtiness, opinion and disdain:
EARL OF WORCESTER: The least of which haunting a nobleman
EARL OF WORCESTER: Loseth men's hearts and leaves behind a stain
EARL OF WORCESTER: Upon the beauty of all parts besides,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Beguiling them of commendation.
HOTSPUR: Well, I am school'd: good manners be your speed!
HOTSPUR: Here come our wives, and let us take our leave.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GLENDOWER with the ladies
MORTIMER: This is the deadly spite that angers me,
MORTIMER: My wife can speak no English, I no Welsh.
GLENDOWER: My daughter weeps: she will not part with you,
GLENDOWER: She'll be a soldier too, she'll to the wars.
MORTIMER: Good father, tell her that she and my aunt Percy
MORTIMER: Shall follow in your conduct speedily.
NARRATOR: Glendower speaks to her in Welsh, and she answers him in the same
GLENDOWER: She is desperate here, a peevish self-wind harlotry,
GLENDOWER: one that no persuasion can do good upon.
NARRATOR: The lady speaks in Welsh
MORTIMER: I understand thy looks: that pretty Welsh
MORTIMER: Which thou pour'st down from these swelling heavens
MORTIMER: I am too perfect in, and, but for shame,
MORTIMER: In such a parley should I answer thee.
NARRATOR: The lady speaks again in Welsh
MORTIMER: I understand thy kisses and thou mine,
MORTIMER: And that's a feeling disputation:
MORTIMER: But I will never be a truant, love,
MORTIMER: Till I have learned thy language, for thy tongue
MORTIMER: Makes Welsh as sweet as ditties highly penn'd,
MORTIMER: Sung by a fair queen in a summer's bower,
MORTIMER: With ravishing division, to her lute.
GLENDOWER: Nay, if you melt, then will she run mad.
NARRATOR: The lady speaks again in Welsh
MORTIMER: O, I am ignorance itself in this!
GLENDOWER: She bids you on the wanton rushes lay you down
GLENDOWER: And rest your gentle head upon her lap,
GLENDOWER: And she will sing the song that pleaseth you
GLENDOWER: And on your eyelids crown the god of sleep.
GLENDOWER: Charming your blood with pleasing heaviness,
GLENDOWER: Making such difference 'twixt wake and sleep
GLENDOWER: As is the difference betwixt day and night
GLENDOWER: The hour before the heavenly-harness'd team
GLENDOWER: Begins his golden progress in the east.
MORTIMER: With all my heart I'll sit and hear her sing:
MORTIMER: By that time will our book, I think, be drawn
GLENDOWER: Do so,
GLENDOWER: And those musicians that shall play to you
GLENDOWER: Hang in the air a thousand leagues from hence,
GLENDOWER: And straight they shall be here: sit, and attend.
HOTSPUR: Come, Kate, thou art perfect in lying down: come,
HOTSPUR: quick, quick, that I may lay my head in thy lap.
LADY PERCY: Go, ye giddy goose.
NARRATOR: The music plays
HOTSPUR: Now I perceive the devil understands Welsh,
HOTSPUR: And 'tis no marvel he is so humorous.
HOTSPUR: By'r lady, he is a good musician.
LADY PERCY: Then should you be nothing but musical for you are
LADY PERCY: altogether governed by humours. Lie still, ye thief,
LADY PERCY: and hear the lady sing in Welsh.
HOTSPUR: I had rather hear Lady, my brach, howl in Irish.
LADY PERCY: Wouldst thou have thy head broken?
HOTSPUR: No.
LADY PERCY: Then be still.
HOTSPUR: Neither,'tis a woman's fault.
LADY PERCY: Now God help thee!
HOTSPUR: To the Welsh lady's bed.
LADY PERCY: What's that?
HOTSPUR: Peace! she sings.
NARRATOR: Here the lady sings a Welsh song
HOTSPUR: Come, Kate, I'll have your song too.
LADY PERCY: Not mine, in good sooth.
HOTSPUR: Not yours, in good sooth! Heart! you swear like a
HOTSPUR: comfit-maker's wife. 'Not you, in good sooth,' and
HOTSPUR: 'as true as I live,' and 'as God shall mend me,' and
HOTSPUR: 'as sure as day,'
HOTSPUR: And givest such sarcenet surety for thy oaths,
HOTSPUR: As if thou never walk'st further than Finsbury.
HOTSPUR: Swear me, Kate, like a lady as thou art,
HOTSPUR: A good mouth-filling oath, and leave 'in sooth,'
HOTSPUR: And such protest of pepper-gingerbread,
HOTSPUR: To velvet-guards and Sunday-citizens.
HOTSPUR: Come, sing.
LADY PERCY: I will not sing.
HOTSPUR: 'Tis the next way to turn tailor, or be red-breast
HOTSPUR: teacher. An the indentures be drawn, I'll away
HOTSPUR: within these two hours, and so, come in when ye will.
NARRATOR: Exit
GLENDOWER: Come, come, Lord Mortimer, you are as slow
GLENDOWER: As hot Lord Percy is on fire to go.
GLENDOWER: By this our book is drawn, we'll but seal,
GLENDOWER: And then to horse immediately.
MORTIMER: With all my heart.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY IV, PRINCE HENRY, and others
KING HENRY IV: Lords, give us leave, the Prince of Wales and I
KING HENRY IV: Must have some private conference, but be near at hand,
KING HENRY IV: For we shall presently have need of you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Lords
KING HENRY IV: I know not whether God will have it so,
KING HENRY IV: For some displeasing service I have done,
KING HENRY IV: That, in his secret doom, out of my blood
KING HENRY IV: He'll breed revengement and a scourge for me,
KING HENRY IV: But thou dost in thy passages of life
KING HENRY IV: Make me believe that thou art only mark'd
KING HENRY IV: For the hot vengeance and the rod of heaven
KING HENRY IV: To punish my mistreadings. Tell me else,
KING HENRY IV: Could such inordinate and low desires,
KING HENRY IV: Such poor, such bare, such lewd, such mean attempts,
KING HENRY IV: Such barren pleasures, rude society,
KING HENRY IV: As thou art match'd withal and grafted to,
KING HENRY IV: Accompany the greatness of thy blood
KING HENRY IV: And hold their level with thy princely heart?
PRINCE HENRY: So please your majesty, I would I could
PRINCE HENRY: Quit all offences with as clear excuse
PRINCE HENRY: As well as I am doubtless I can purge
PRINCE HENRY: Myself of many I am charged withal:
PRINCE HENRY: Yet such extenuation let me beg,
PRINCE HENRY: As, in reproof of many tales devised,
PRINCE HENRY: which oft the ear of greatness needs must hear,
PRINCE HENRY: By smiling pick-thanks and base news-mongers,
PRINCE HENRY: I may, for some things true, wherein my youth
PRINCE HENRY: Hath faulty wander'd and irregular,
PRINCE HENRY: Find pardon on my true submission.
KING HENRY IV: God pardon thee! yet let me wonder, Harry,
KING HENRY IV: At thy affections, which do hold a wing
KING HENRY IV: Quite from the flight of all thy ancestors.
KING HENRY IV: Thy place in council thou hast rudely lost.
KING HENRY IV: Which by thy younger brother is supplied,
KING HENRY IV: And art almost an alien to the hearts
KING HENRY IV: Of all the court and princes of my blood:
KING HENRY IV: The hope and expectation of thy time
KING HENRY IV: Is ruin'd, and the soul of every man
KING HENRY IV: Prophetically doth forethink thy fall.
KING HENRY IV: Had I so lavish of my presence been,
KING HENRY IV: So common-hackney'd in the eyes of men,
KING HENRY IV: So stale and cheap to vulgar company,
KING HENRY IV: Opinion, that did help me to the crown,
KING HENRY IV: Had still kept loyal to possession
KING HENRY IV: And left me in reputeless banishment,
KING HENRY IV: A fellow of no mark nor likelihood.
KING HENRY IV: By being seldom seen, I could not stir
KING HENRY IV: But like a comet I was wonder'd at,
KING HENRY IV: That men would tell their children 'This is he,'
