KING HENRY IV: Others would say 'Where, which is Bolingbroke?'
KING HENRY IV: And then I stole all courtesy from heaven,
KING HENRY IV: And dress'd myself in such humility
KING HENRY IV: That I did pluck allegiance from men's hearts,
KING HENRY IV: Loud shouts and salutations from their mouths,
KING HENRY IV: Even in the presence of the crowned king.
KING HENRY IV: Thus did I keep my person fresh and new,
KING HENRY IV: My presence, like a robe pontifical,
KING HENRY IV: Ne'er seen but wonder'd at: and so my state,
KING HENRY IV: Seldom but sumptuous, showed like a feast
KING HENRY IV: And won by rareness such solemnity.
KING HENRY IV: The skipping king, he ambled up and down
KING HENRY IV: With shallow jesters and rash bavin wits,
KING HENRY IV: Soon kindled and soon burnt, carded his state,
KING HENRY IV: Mingled his royalty with capering fools,
KING HENRY IV: Had his great name profaned with their scorns
KING HENRY IV: And gave his countenance, against his name,
KING HENRY IV: To laugh at gibing boys and stand the push
KING HENRY IV: Of every beardless vain comparative,
KING HENRY IV: Grew a companion to the common streets,
KING HENRY IV: Enfeoff'd himself to popularity,
KING HENRY IV: That, being daily swallow'd by men's eyes,
KING HENRY IV: They surfeited with honey and began
KING HENRY IV: To loathe the taste of sweetness, whereof a little
KING HENRY IV: More than a little is by much too much.
KING HENRY IV: So when he had occasion to be seen,
KING HENRY IV: He was but as the cuckoo is in June,
KING HENRY IV: Heard, not regarded, seen, but with such eyes
KING HENRY IV: As, sick and blunted with community,
KING HENRY IV: Afford no extraordinary gaze,
KING HENRY IV: Such as is bent on sun-like majesty
KING HENRY IV: When it shines seldom in admiring eyes,
KING HENRY IV: But rather drowzed and hung their eyelids down,
KING HENRY IV: Slept in his face and render'd such aspect
KING HENRY IV: As cloudy men use to their adversaries,
KING HENRY IV: Being with his presence glutted, gorged and full.
KING HENRY IV: And in that very line, Harry, standest thou,
KING HENRY IV: For thou has lost thy princely privilege
KING HENRY IV: With vile participation: not an eye
KING HENRY IV: But is a-weary of thy common sight,
KING HENRY IV: Save mine, which hath desired to see thee more,
KING HENRY IV: Which now doth that I would not have it do,
KING HENRY IV: Make blind itself with foolish tenderness.
PRINCE HENRY: I shall hereafter, my thrice gracious lord,
PRINCE HENRY: Be more myself.
KING HENRY IV: For all the world
KING HENRY IV: As thou art to this hour was Richard then
KING HENRY IV: When I from France set foot at Ravenspurgh,
KING HENRY IV: And even as I was then is Percy now.
KING HENRY IV: Now, by my sceptre and my soul to boot,
KING HENRY IV: He hath more worthy interest to the state
KING HENRY IV: Than thou the shadow of succession,
KING HENRY IV: For of no right, nor colour like to right,
KING HENRY IV: He doth fill fields with harness in the realm,
KING HENRY IV: Turns head against the lion's armed jaws,
KING HENRY IV: And, being no more in debt to years than thou,
KING HENRY IV: Leads ancient lords and reverend bishops on
KING HENRY IV: To bloody battles and to bruising arms.
KING HENRY IV: What never-dying honour hath he got
KING HENRY IV: Against renowned Douglas! whose high deeds,
KING HENRY IV: Whose hot incursions and great name in arms
KING HENRY IV: Holds from all soldiers chief majority
KING HENRY IV: And military title capital
KING HENRY IV: Through all the kingdoms that acknowledge Christ:
KING HENRY IV: Thrice hath this Hotspur, Mars in swathling clothes,
KING HENRY IV: This infant warrior, in his enterprises
KING HENRY IV: Discomfited great Douglas, ta'en him once,
KING HENRY IV: Enlarged him and made a friend of him,
KING HENRY IV: To fill the mouth of deep defiance up
KING HENRY IV: And shake the peace and safety of our throne.
KING HENRY IV: And what say you to this? Percy, Northumberland,
KING HENRY IV: The Archbishop's grace of York, Douglas, Mortimer,
KING HENRY IV: Capitulate against us and are up.
KING HENRY IV: But wherefore do I tell these news to thee?
KING HENRY IV: Why, Harry, do I tell thee of my foes,
KING HENRY IV: Which art my near'st and dearest enemy?
KING HENRY IV: Thou that art like enough, through vassal fear,
KING HENRY IV: Base inclination and the start of spleen
KING HENRY IV: To fight against me under Percy's pay,
KING HENRY IV: To dog his heels and curtsy at his frowns,
KING HENRY IV: To show how much thou art degenerate.
PRINCE HENRY: Do not think so, you shall not find it so:
PRINCE HENRY: And God forgive them that so much have sway'd
PRINCE HENRY: Your majesty's good thoughts away from me!
PRINCE HENRY: I will redeem all this on Percy's head
PRINCE HENRY: And in the closing of some glorious day
PRINCE HENRY: Be bold to tell you that I am your son,
PRINCE HENRY: When I will wear a garment all of blood
PRINCE HENRY: And stain my favours in a bloody mask,
PRINCE HENRY: Which, wash'd away, shall scour my shame with it:
PRINCE HENRY: And that shall be the day, whene'er it lights,
PRINCE HENRY: That this same child of honour and renown,
PRINCE HENRY: This gallant Hotspur, this all-praised knight,
PRINCE HENRY: And your unthought-of Harry chance to meet.
PRINCE HENRY: For every honour sitting on his helm,
PRINCE HENRY: Would they were multitudes, and on my head
PRINCE HENRY: My shames redoubled! for the time will come,
PRINCE HENRY: That I shall make this northern youth exchange
PRINCE HENRY: His glorious deeds for my indignities.
PRINCE HENRY: Percy is but my factor, good my lord,
PRINCE HENRY: To engross up glorious deeds on my behalf,
PRINCE HENRY: And I will call him to so strict account,
PRINCE HENRY: That he shall render every glory up,
PRINCE HENRY: Yea, even the slightest worship of his time,
PRINCE HENRY: Or I will tear the reckoning from his heart.
PRINCE HENRY: This, in the name of God, I promise here:
PRINCE HENRY: The which if He be pleased I shall perform,
PRINCE HENRY: I do beseech your majesty may salve
PRINCE HENRY: The long-grown wounds of my intemperance:
PRINCE HENRY: If not, the end of life cancels all bands,
PRINCE HENRY: And I will die a hundred thousand deaths
PRINCE HENRY: Ere break the smallest parcel of this vow.
KING HENRY IV: A hundred thousand rebels die in this:
KING HENRY IV: Thou shalt have charge and sovereign trust herein.
NARRATOR: Enter BLUNT
KING HENRY IV: How now, good Blunt? thy looks are full of speed.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: So hath the business that I come to speak of.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Lord Mortimer of Scotland hath sent word
SIR WALTER BLUNT: That Douglas and the English rebels met
SIR WALTER BLUNT: The eleventh of this month at Shrewsbury
SIR WALTER BLUNT: A mighty and a fearful head they are,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: If promises be kept on every hand,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: As ever offer'd foul play in the state.
KING HENRY IV: The Earl of Westmoreland set forth to-day,
KING HENRY IV: With him my son, Lord John of Lancaster,
KING HENRY IV: For this advertisement is five days old:
KING HENRY IV: On Wednesday next, Harry, you shall set forward,
KING HENRY IV: On Thursday we ourselves will march: our meeting
KING HENRY IV: Is Bridgenorth: and, Harry, you shall march
KING HENRY IV: Through Gloucestershire, by which account,
KING HENRY IV: Our business valued, some twelve days hence
KING HENRY IV: Our general forces at Bridgenorth shall meet.
KING HENRY IV: Our hands are full of business: let's away,
KING HENRY IV: Advantage feeds him fat, while men delay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Eastcheap. The Boar's-Head Tavern.
NARRATOR: Enter FALSTAFF and BARDOLPH
FALSTAFF: Bardolph, am I not fallen away vilely since this last
FALSTAFF: action? do I not bate? do I not dwindle? Why my
FALSTAFF: skin hangs about me like an like an old lady's loose
FALSTAFF: gown, I am withered like an old apple-john. Well,
FALSTAFF: I'll repent, and that suddenly, while I am in some
FALSTAFF: liking, I shall be out of heart shortly, and then I
FALSTAFF: shall have no strength to repent. An I have not
FALSTAFF: forgotten what the inside of a church is made of, I
FALSTAFF: am a peppercorn, a brewer's horse: the inside of a
FALSTAFF: church! Company, villanous company, hath been the
FALSTAFF: spoil of me.
BARDOLPH: Sir John, you are so fretful, you cannot live long.
FALSTAFF: Why, there is it: come sing me a bawdy song, make
FALSTAFF: me merry. I was as virtuously given as a gentleman
FALSTAFF: need to be, virtuous enough, swore little, diced not
FALSTAFF: above seven times a week, went to a bawdy-house once
FALSTAFF: in a quarter--of an hour, paid money that I
FALSTAFF: borrowed, three of four times, lived well and in
FALSTAFF: good compass: and now I live out of all order, out
FALSTAFF: of all compass.
BARDOLPH: Why, you are so fat, Sir John, that you must needs
BARDOLPH: be out of all compass, out of all reasonable
BARDOLPH: compass, Sir John.
FALSTAFF: Do thou amend thy face, and I'll amend my life:
FALSTAFF: thou art our admiral, thou bearest the lantern in
FALSTAFF: the poop, but 'tis in the nose of thee, thou art the
FALSTAFF: Knight of the Burning Lamp.
BARDOLPH: Why, Sir John, my face does you no harm.
FALSTAFF: No, I'll be sworn, I make as good use of it as many
FALSTAFF: a man doth of a Death's-head or a memento mori: I
FALSTAFF: never see thy face but I think upon hell-fire and
FALSTAFF: Dives that lived in purple, for there he is in his
FALSTAFF: robes, burning, burning. If thou wert any way
FALSTAFF: given to virtue, I would swear by thy face, my oath
FALSTAFF: should be 'By this fire, that's God's angel:' but
FALSTAFF: thou art altogether given over, and wert indeed, but
FALSTAFF: for the light in thy face, the son of utter
FALSTAFF: darkness. When thou rannest up Gadshill in the
FALSTAFF: night to catch my horse, if I did not think thou
FALSTAFF: hadst been an ignis fatuus or a ball of wildfire,
FALSTAFF: there's no purchase in money. O, thou art a
FALSTAFF: perpetual triumph, an everlasting bonfire-light!
FALSTAFF: Thou hast saved me a thousand marks in links and
FALSTAFF: torches, walking with thee in the night betwixt
FALSTAFF: tavern and tavern: but the sack that thou hast
FALSTAFF: drunk me would have bought me lights as good cheap
FALSTAFF: at the dearest chandler's in Europe. I have
FALSTAFF: maintained that salamander of yours with fire any
FALSTAFF: time this two and thirty years, God reward me for
FALSTAFF: it!
BARDOLPH: 'Sblood, I would my face were in your belly!
FALSTAFF: God-a-mercy! so should I be sure to be heart-burned.
NARRATOR: Enter Hostess
FALSTAFF: How now, Dame Partlet the hen! have you inquired
FALSTAFF: yet who picked my pocket?
Hostess: Why, Sir John, what do you think, Sir John? do you
Hostess: think I keep thieves in my house? I have searched,
Hostess: I have inquired, so has my husband, man by man, boy
Hostess: by boy, servant by servant: the tithe of a hair
Hostess: was never lost in my house before.
FALSTAFF: Ye lie, hostess: Bardolph was shaved and lost many
FALSTAFF: a hair, and I'll be sworn my pocket was picked. Go
FALSTAFF: to, you are a woman, go.
Hostess: Who, I? no, I defy thee: God's light, I was never
Hostess: called so in mine own house before.
FALSTAFF: Go to, I know you well enough.
Hostess: No, Sir John, You do not know me, Sir John. I know
Hostess: you, Sir John: you owe me money, Sir John, and now
Hostess: you pick a quarrel to beguile me of it: I bought
Hostess: you a dozen of shirts to your back.
FALSTAFF: Dowlas, filthy dowlas: I have given them away to
FALSTAFF: bakers' wives, and they have made bolters of them.
Hostess: Now, as I am a true woman, holland of eight
Hostess: shillings an ell. You owe money here besides, Sir
Hostess: John, for your diet and by-drinkings, and money lent
Hostess: you, four and twenty pound.
FALSTAFF: He had his part of it, let him pay.
Hostess: He? alas, he is poor, he hath nothing.
FALSTAFF: How! poor? look upon his face, what call you rich?
FALSTAFF: let them coin his nose, let them coin his cheeks:
FALSTAFF: Ill not pay a denier. What, will you make a younker
FALSTAFF: of me? shall I not take mine case in mine inn but I
FALSTAFF: shall have my pocket picked? I have lost a
FALSTAFF: seal-ring of my grandfather's worth forty mark.
Hostess: O Jesu, I have heard the prince tell him, I know not
Hostess: how oft, that ring was copper!
FALSTAFF: How! the prince is a Jack, a sneak-cup: 'sblood, an
FALSTAFF: he were here, I would cudgel him like a dog, if he
FALSTAFF: would say so.
NARRATOR: Enter PRINCE HENRY and PETO, marching, and FALSTAFF meets them playing on his truncheon like a life
FALSTAFF: How now, lad! is the wind in that door, i' faith?
FALSTAFF: must we all march?
BARDOLPH: Yea, two and two, Newgate fashion.
Hostess: My lord, I pray you, hear me.
PRINCE HENRY: What sayest thou, Mistress Quickly? How doth thy
PRINCE HENRY: husband? I love him well, he is an honest man.
Hostess: Good my lord, hear me.
FALSTAFF: Prithee, let her alone, and list to me.
PRINCE HENRY: What sayest thou, Jack?
FALSTAFF: The other night I fell asleep here behind the arras
FALSTAFF: and had my pocket picked: this house is turned
FALSTAFF: bawdy-house, they pick pockets.
PRINCE HENRY: What didst thou lose, Jack?
FALSTAFF: Wilt thou believe me, Hal? three or four bonds of
FALSTAFF: forty pound apiece, and a seal-ring of my
FALSTAFF: grandfather's.
PRINCE HENRY: A trifle, some eight-penny matter.
Hostess: So I told him, my lord, and I said I heard your
Hostess: grace say so: and, my lord, he speaks most vilely
Hostess: of you, like a foul-mouthed man as he is, and said
Hostess: he would cudgel you.
PRINCE HENRY: What! he did not?
Hostess: There's neither faith, truth, nor womanhood in me else.
FALSTAFF: There's no more faith in thee than in a stewed
FALSTAFF: prune, nor no more truth in thee than in a drawn
FALSTAFF: fox, and for womanhood, Maid Marian may be the
FALSTAFF: deputy's wife of the ward to thee. Go, you thing,
FALSTAFF: go
Hostess: Say, what thing? what thing?
FALSTAFF: What thing! why, a thing to thank God on.
Hostess: I am no thing to thank God on, I would thou
Hostess: shouldst know it, I am an honest man's wife: and,
Hostess: setting thy knighthood aside, thou art a knave to
Hostess: call me so.
FALSTAFF: Setting thy womanhood aside, thou art a beast to say
FALSTAFF: otherwise.
Hostess: Say, what beast, thou knave, thou?
FALSTAFF: What beast! why, an otter.
PRINCE HENRY: An otter, Sir John! Why an otter?
FALSTAFF: Why, she's neither fish nor flesh, a man knows not
FALSTAFF: where to have her.
Hostess: Thou art an unjust man in saying so: thou or any
Hostess: man knows where to have me, thou knave, thou!
PRINCE HENRY: Thou sayest true, hostess, and he slanders thee most grossly.
Hostess: So he doth you, my lord, and said this other day you
Hostess: ought him a thousand pound.
PRINCE HENRY: Sirrah, do I owe you a thousand pound?
FALSTAFF: A thousand pound, Ha! a million: thy love is worth
FALSTAFF: a million: thou owest me thy love.
Hostess: Nay, my lord, he called you Jack, and said he would
Hostess: cudgel you.
FALSTAFF: Did I, Bardolph?
BARDOLPH: Indeed, Sir John, you said so.
FALSTAFF: Yea, if he said my ring was copper.
PRINCE HENRY: I say 'tis copper: darest thou be as good as thy word now?
FALSTAFF: Why, Hal, thou knowest, as thou art but man, I dare:
FALSTAFF: but as thou art prince, I fear thee as I fear the
FALSTAFF: roaring of a lion's whelp.
PRINCE HENRY: And why not as the lion?
FALSTAFF: The king is to be feared as the lion: dost thou
FALSTAFF: think I'll fear thee as I fear thy father? nay, an
FALSTAFF: I do, I pray God my girdle break.
PRINCE HENRY: O, if it should, how would thy guts fall about thy
PRINCE HENRY: knees! But, sirrah, there's no room for faith,
PRINCE HENRY: truth, nor honesty in this bosom of thine, it is all
PRINCE HENRY: filled up with guts and midriff. Charge an honest
PRINCE HENRY: woman with picking thy pocket! why, thou whoreson,
PRINCE HENRY: impudent, embossed rascal, if there were anything in
PRINCE HENRY: thy pocket but tavern-reckonings, memorandums of
PRINCE HENRY: bawdy-houses, and one poor penny-worth of
PRINCE HENRY: sugar-candy to make thee long-winded, if thy pocket
PRINCE HENRY: were enriched with any other injuries but these, I
PRINCE HENRY: am a villain: and yet you will stand to if, you will
PRINCE HENRY: not pocket up wrong: art thou not ashamed?
FALSTAFF: Dost thou hear, Hal? thou knowest in the state of
FALSTAFF: innocency Adam fell, and what should poor Jack
FALSTAFF: Falstaff do in the days of villany? Thou seest I
FALSTAFF: have more flesh than another man, and therefore more
FALSTAFF: frailty. You confess then, you picked my pocket?
PRINCE HENRY: It appears so by the story.
FALSTAFF: Hostess, I forgive thee: go, make ready breakfast,
FALSTAFF: love thy husband, look to thy servants, cherish thy
FALSTAFF: guests: thou shalt find me tractable to any honest
FALSTAFF: reason: thou seest I am pacified still. Nay,
FALSTAFF: prithee, be gone.
NARRATOR: Exit Hostess
FALSTAFF: Now Hal, to the news at court: for the robbery,
FALSTAFF: lad, how is that answered?
PRINCE HENRY: O, my sweet beef, I must still be good angel to
PRINCE HENRY: thee: the money is paid back again.
FALSTAFF: O, I do not like that paying back, 'tis a double labour.
PRINCE HENRY: I am good friends with my father and may do any thing.
FALSTAFF: Rob me the exchequer the first thing thou doest, and
FALSTAFF: do it with unwashed hands too.
BARDOLPH: Do, my lord.
PRINCE HENRY: I have procured thee, Jack, a charge of foot.
FALSTAFF: I would it had been of horse. Where shall I find
FALSTAFF: one that can steal well? O for a fine thief, of the
FALSTAFF: age of two and twenty or thereabouts! I am
FALSTAFF: heinously unprovided. Well, God be thanked for
FALSTAFF: these rebels, they offend none but the virtuous: I
FALSTAFF: laud them, I praise them.
PRINCE HENRY: Bardolph!
BARDOLPH: My lord?
PRINCE HENRY: Go bear this letter to Lord John of Lancaster, to my
PRINCE HENRY: brother John, this to my Lord of Westmoreland.
NARRATOR: Exit Bardolph
PRINCE HENRY: Go, Peto, to horse, to horse, for thou and I have
PRINCE HENRY: thirty miles to ride yet ere dinner time.
NARRATOR: Exit Peto
PRINCE HENRY: Jack, meet me to-morrow in the temple hall at two
PRINCE HENRY: o'clock in the afternoon.
PRINCE HENRY: There shalt thou know thy charge, and there receive
PRINCE HENRY: Money and order for their furniture.
PRINCE HENRY: The land is burning, Percy stands on high,
PRINCE HENRY: And either we or they must lower lie.
NARRATOR: Exit PRINCE HENRY
FALSTAFF: Rare words! brave world! Hostess, my breakfast, come!
FALSTAFF: O, I could wish this tavern were my drum!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The rebel camp near Shrewsbury.
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR, WORCESTER, and DOUGLAS
HOTSPUR: Well said, my noble Scot: if speaking truth
HOTSPUR: In this fine age were not thought flattery,
HOTSPUR: Such attribution should the Douglas have,
HOTSPUR: As not a soldier of this season's stamp
HOTSPUR: Should go so general current through the world.
HOTSPUR: By God, I cannot flatter, I do defy
HOTSPUR: The tongues of soothers, but a braver place
HOTSPUR: In my heart's love hath no man than yourself:
HOTSPUR: Nay, task me to my word, approve me, lord.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Thou art the king of honour:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: No man so potent breathes upon the ground
EARL OF DOUGLAS: But I will beard him.
HOTSPUR: Do so, and 'tis well.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger with letters
HOTSPUR: What letters hast thou there?--I can but thank you.
Messenger: These letters come from your father.
HOTSPUR: Letters from him! why comes he not himself?
Messenger: He cannot come, my lord, he is grievous sick.
HOTSPUR: 'Zounds! how has he the leisure to be sick
HOTSPUR: In such a rustling time? Who leads his power?
HOTSPUR: Under whose government come they along?
Messenger: His letters bear his mind, not I, my lord.
EARL OF WORCESTER: I prithee, tell me, doth he keep his bed?
Messenger: He did, my lord, four days ere I set forth,
Messenger: And at the time of my departure thence
Messenger: He was much fear'd by his physicians.
EARL OF WORCESTER: I would the state of time had first been whole
EARL OF WORCESTER: Ere he by sickness had been visited:
EARL OF WORCESTER: His health was never better worth than now.
HOTSPUR: Sick now! droop now! this sickness doth infect
HOTSPUR: The very life-blood of our enterprise,
HOTSPUR: 'Tis catching hither, even to our camp.
HOTSPUR: He writes me here, that inward sickness--
HOTSPUR: And that his friends by deputation could not
HOTSPUR: So soon be drawn, nor did he think it meet
HOTSPUR: To lay so dangerous and dear a trust
HOTSPUR: On any soul removed but on his own.
HOTSPUR: Yet doth he give us bold advertisement,
HOTSPUR: That with our small conjunction we should on,
HOTSPUR: To see how fortune is disposed to us,
HOTSPUR: For, as he writes, there is no quailing now.
HOTSPUR: Because the king is certainly possess'd
HOTSPUR: Of all our purposes. What say you to it?
EARL OF WORCESTER: Your father's sickness is a maim to us.
HOTSPUR: A perilous gash, a very limb lopp'd off:
HOTSPUR: And yet, in faith, it is not, his present want
HOTSPUR: Seems more than we shall find it: were it good
HOTSPUR: To set the exact wealth of all our states
HOTSPUR: All at one cast? to set so rich a main
HOTSPUR: On the nice hazard of one doubtful hour?
HOTSPUR: It were not good, for therein should we read
HOTSPUR: The very bottom and the soul of hope,
HOTSPUR: The very list, the very utmost bound
HOTSPUR: Of all our fortunes.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: 'Faith, and so we should,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Where now remains a sweet reversion:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: We may boldly spend upon the hope of what
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Is to come in:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: A comfort of retirement lives in this.
HOTSPUR: A rendezvous, a home to fly unto.
HOTSPUR: If that the devil and mischance look big
HOTSPUR: Upon the maidenhead of our affairs.
EARL OF WORCESTER: But yet I would your father had been here.
EARL OF WORCESTER: The quality and hair of our attempt
EARL OF WORCESTER: Brooks no division: it will be thought
EARL OF WORCESTER: By some, that know not why he is away,
EARL OF WORCESTER: That wisdom, loyalty and mere dislike
EARL OF WORCESTER: Of our proceedings kept the earl from hence:
EARL OF WORCESTER: And think how such an apprehension
EARL OF WORCESTER: May turn the tide of fearful faction
EARL OF WORCESTER: And breed a kind of question in our cause,
EARL OF WORCESTER: For well you know we of the offering side
EARL OF WORCESTER: Must keep aloof from strict arbitrement,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And stop all sight-holes, every loop from whence
EARL OF WORCESTER: The eye of reason may pry in upon us:
EARL OF WORCESTER: This absence of your father's draws a curtain,
EARL OF WORCESTER: That shows the ignorant a kind of fear
EARL OF WORCESTER: Before not dreamt of.
HOTSPUR: You strain too far.
HOTSPUR: I rather of his absence make this use:
HOTSPUR: It lends a lustre and more great opinion,
HOTSPUR: A larger dare to our great enterprise,
HOTSPUR: Than if the earl were here, for men must think,
HOTSPUR: If we without his help can make a head
HOTSPUR: To push against a kingdom, with his help
HOTSPUR: We shall o'erturn it topsy-turvy down.
HOTSPUR: Yet all goes well, yet all our joints are whole.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: As heart can think: there is not such a word
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Spoke of in Scotland as this term of fear.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR RICHARD VERNON
HOTSPUR: My cousin Vernon, welcome, by my soul.
VERNON: Pray God my news be worth a welcome, lord.
VERNON: The Earl of Westmoreland, seven thousand strong,
VERNON: Is marching hitherwards, with him Prince John.
HOTSPUR: No harm: what more?
VERNON: And further, I have learn'd,
VERNON: The king himself in person is set forth,
VERNON: Or hitherwards intended speedily,
VERNON: With strong and mighty preparation.
HOTSPUR: He shall be welcome too. Where is his son,
HOTSPUR: The nimble-footed madcap Prince of Wales,
HOTSPUR: And his comrades, that daff'd the world aside,
HOTSPUR: And bid it pass?
VERNON: All furnish'd, all in arms,
VERNON: All plumed like estridges that with the wind
VERNON: Baited like eagles having lately bathed,
VERNON: Glittering in golden coats, like images,
VERNON: As full of spirit as the month of May,
VERNON: And gorgeous as the sun at midsummer,
VERNON: Wanton as youthful goats, wild as young bulls.
VERNON: I saw young Harry, with his beaver on,
VERNON: His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd
VERNON: Rise from the ground like feather'd Mercury,
VERNON: And vaulted with such ease into his seat,
VERNON: As if an angel dropp'd down from the clouds,
VERNON: To turn and wind a fiery Pegasus
VERNON: And witch the world with noble horsemanship.
HOTSPUR: No more, no more: worse than the sun in March,
HOTSPUR: This praise doth nourish agues. Let them come:
HOTSPUR: They come like sacrifices in their trim,
HOTSPUR: And to the fire-eyed maid of smoky war
HOTSPUR: All hot and bleeding will we offer them:
HOTSPUR: The mailed Mars shall on his altar sit
HOTSPUR: Up to the ears in blood. I am on fire
HOTSPUR: To hear this rich reprisal is so nigh
HOTSPUR: And yet not ours. Come, let me taste my horse,
HOTSPUR: Who is to bear me like a thunderbolt
HOTSPUR: Against the bosom of the Prince of Wales:
HOTSPUR: Harry to Harry shall, hot horse to horse,
HOTSPUR: Meet and ne'er part till one drop down a corse.
HOTSPUR: O that Glendower were come!
VERNON: There is more news:
VERNON: I learn'd in Worcester, as I rode along,
VERNON: He cannot draw his power this fourteen days.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: That's the worst tidings that I hear of yet.
WORCESTER: Ay, by my faith, that bears a frosty sound.
HOTSPUR: What may the king's whole battle reach unto?
VERNON: To thirty thousand.
HOTSPUR: Forty let it be:
HOTSPUR: My father and Glendower being both away,
HOTSPUR: The powers of us may serve so great a day
HOTSPUR: Come, let us take a muster speedily:
HOTSPUR: Doomsday is near, die all, die merrily.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Talk not of dying: I am out of fear
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Of death or death's hand for this one-half year.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A public road near Coventry.
NARRATOR: Enter FALSTAFF and BARDOLPH
FALSTAFF: Bardolph, get thee before to Coventry, fill me a
FALSTAFF: bottle of sack: our soldiers shall march through,
FALSTAFF: we'll to Sutton Co'fil' tonight.
BARDOLPH: Will you give me money, captain?
FALSTAFF: Lay out, lay out.
BARDOLPH: This bottle makes an angel.
FALSTAFF: An if it do, take it for thy labour, and if it make
FALSTAFF: twenty, take them all, I'll answer the coinage. Bid
FALSTAFF: my lieutenant Peto meet me at town's end.
BARDOLPH: I will, captain: farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
FALSTAFF: If I be not ashamed of my soldiers, I am a soused
FALSTAFF: gurnet. I have misused the king's press damnably.
FALSTAFF: I have got, in exchange of a hundred and fifty
FALSTAFF: soldiers, three hundred and odd pounds. I press me
FALSTAFF: none but good house-holders, yeoman's sons, inquire
FALSTAFF: me out contracted bachelors, such as had been asked
FALSTAFF: twice on the banns, such a commodity of warm slaves,
FALSTAFF: as had as lieve hear the devil as a drum, such as
FALSTAFF: fear the report of a caliver worse than a struck
FALSTAFF: fowl or a hurt wild-duck. I pressed me none but such
FALSTAFF: toasts-and-butter, with hearts in their bellies no
FALSTAFF: bigger than pins' heads, and they have bought out
FALSTAFF: their services, and now my whole charge consists of
FALSTAFF: ancients, corporals, lieutenants, gentlemen of
FALSTAFF: companies, slaves as ragged as Lazarus in the
FALSTAFF: painted cloth, where the glutton's dogs licked his
FALSTAFF: sores, and such as indeed were never soldiers, but
FALSTAFF: discarded unjust serving-men, younger sons to
FALSTAFF: younger brothers, revolted tapsters and ostlers
FALSTAFF: trade-fallen, the cankers of a calm world and a
FALSTAFF: long peace, ten times more dishonourable ragged than
FALSTAFF: an old faced ancient: and such have I, to fill up
FALSTAFF: the rooms of them that have bought out their
FALSTAFF: services, that you would think that I had a hundred
FALSTAFF: and fifty tattered prodigals lately come from
FALSTAFF: swine-keeping, from eating draff and husks. A mad
FALSTAFF: fellow met me on the way and told me I had unloaded
FALSTAFF: all the gibbets and pressed the dead bodies. No eye
FALSTAFF: hath seen such scarecrows. I'll not march through
FALSTAFF: Coventry with them, that's flat: nay, and the
FALSTAFF: villains march wide betwixt the legs, as if they had
FALSTAFF: gyves on, for indeed I had the most of them out of
FALSTAFF: prison. There's but a shirt and a half in all my
FALSTAFF: company, and the half shirt is two napkins tacked
FALSTAFF: together and thrown over the shoulders like an
FALSTAFF: herald's coat without sleeves, and the shirt, to say
FALSTAFF: the truth, stolen from my host at Saint Alban's, or
FALSTAFF: the red-nose innkeeper of Daventry. But that's all
FALSTAFF: one, they'll find linen enough on every hedge.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCE and WESTMORELAND
PRINCE HENRY: How now, blown Jack! how now, quilt!
FALSTAFF: What, Hal! how now, mad wag! what a devil dost thou
FALSTAFF: in Warwickshire? My good Lord of Westmoreland, I
FALSTAFF: cry you mercy: I thought your honour had already been
FALSTAFF: at Shrewsbury.
WESTMORELAND: Faith, Sir John,'tis more than time that I were
WESTMORELAND: there, and you too, but my powers are there already.
WESTMORELAND: The king, I can tell you, looks for us all: we must
WESTMORELAND: away all night.
FALSTAFF: Tut, never fear me: I am as vigilant as a cat to
FALSTAFF: steal cream.
PRINCE HENRY: I think, to steal cream indeed, for thy theft hath
PRINCE HENRY: already made thee butter. But tell me, Jack, whose
PRINCE HENRY: fellows are these that come after?
FALSTAFF: Mine, Hal, mine.
PRINCE HENRY: I did never see such pitiful rascals.
FALSTAFF: Tut, tut, good enough to toss, food for powder, food
FALSTAFF: for powder, they'll fill a pit as well as better:
FALSTAFF: tush, man, mortal men, mortal men.
WESTMORELAND: Ay, but, Sir John, methinks they are exceeding poor
WESTMORELAND: and bare, too beggarly.
FALSTAFF: 'Faith, for their poverty, I know not where they had
FALSTAFF: that, and for their bareness, I am sure they never
FALSTAFF: learned that of me.
PRINCE HENRY: No I'll be sworn, unless you call three fingers on
PRINCE HENRY: the ribs bare. But, sirrah, make haste: Percy is
PRINCE HENRY: already in the field.
FALSTAFF: What, is the king encamped?
WESTMORELAND: He is, Sir John: I fear we shall stay too long.
FALSTAFF: Well,
FALSTAFF: To the latter end of a fray and the beginning of a feast
FALSTAFF: Fits a dull fighter and a keen guest.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The rebel camp near Shrewsbury.
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR, WORCESTER, DOUGLAS, and VERNON
HOTSPUR: We'll fight with him to-night.
EARL OF WORCESTER: It may not be.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: You give him then the advantage.
VERNON: Not a whit.
HOTSPUR: Why say you so? looks he not for supply?
VERNON: So do we.
HOTSPUR: His is certain, ours is doubtful.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Good cousin, be advised, stir not tonight.
VERNON: Do not, my lord.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: You do not counsel well:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: You speak it out of fear and cold heart.
VERNON: Do me no slander, Douglas: by my life,
VERNON: And I dare well maintain it with my life,
VERNON: If well-respected honour bid me on,
VERNON: I hold as little counsel with weak fear
VERNON: As you, my lord, or any Scot that this day lives:
VERNON: Let it be seen to-morrow in the battle
VERNON: Which of us fears.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Yea, or to-night.
VERNON: Content.
HOTSPUR: To-night, say I.
VERNON: Come, come it nay not be. I wonder much,
VERNON: Being men of such great leading as you are,
VERNON: That you foresee not what impediments
VERNON: Drag back our expedition: certain horse
VERNON: Of my cousin Vernon's are not yet come up:
VERNON: Your uncle Worcester's horse came but today,
VERNON: And now their pride and mettle is asleep,
VERNON: Their courage with hard labour tame and dull,
VERNON: That not a horse is half the half of himself.
HOTSPUR: So are the horses of the enemy
HOTSPUR: In general, journey-bated and brought low:
HOTSPUR: The better part of ours are full of rest.
EARL OF WORCESTER: The number of the king exceedeth ours:
EARL OF WORCESTER: For God's sake. cousin, stay till all come in.
NARRATOR: The trumpet sounds a parley
NARRATOR: Enter SIR WALTER BLUNT
SIR WALTER BLUNT: I come with gracious offers from the king,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: if you vouchsafe me hearing and respect.
HOTSPUR: Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt, and would to God
HOTSPUR: You were of our determination!
HOTSPUR: Some of us love you well, and even those some
HOTSPUR: Envy your great deservings and good name,
HOTSPUR: Because you are not of our quality,
HOTSPUR: But stand against us like an enemy.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: And God defend but still I should stand so,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: So long as out of limit and true rule
SIR WALTER BLUNT: You stand against anointed majesty.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: But to my charge. The king hath sent to know
SIR WALTER BLUNT: The nature of your griefs, and whereupon
SIR WALTER BLUNT: You conjure from the breast of civil peace
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Such bold hostility, teaching his duteous land
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Audacious cruelty. If that the king
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Have any way your good deserts forgot,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Which he confesseth to be manifold,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: He bids you name your griefs, and with all speed
SIR WALTER BLUNT: You shall have your desires with interest
SIR WALTER BLUNT: And pardon absolute for yourself and these
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Herein misled by your suggestion.
HOTSPUR: The king is kind, and well we know the king
HOTSPUR: Knows at what time to promise, when to pay.
HOTSPUR: My father and my uncle and myself
HOTSPUR: Did give him that same royalty he wears,
HOTSPUR: And when he was not six and twenty strong,
HOTSPUR: Sick in the world's regard, wretched and low,
HOTSPUR: A poor unminded outlaw sneaking home,
HOTSPUR: My father gave him welcome to the shore,
HOTSPUR: And when he heard him swear and vow to God
HOTSPUR: He came but to be Duke of Lancaster,
HOTSPUR: To sue his livery and beg his peace,
HOTSPUR: With tears of innocency and terms of zeal,
HOTSPUR: My father, in kind heart and pity moved,
HOTSPUR: Swore him assistance and perform'd it too.
HOTSPUR: Now when the lords and barons of the realm
HOTSPUR: Perceived Northumberland did lean to him,
HOTSPUR: The more and less came in with cap and knee,
HOTSPUR: Met him in boroughs, cities, villages,
HOTSPUR: Attended him on bridges, stood in lanes,
HOTSPUR: Laid gifts before him, proffer'd him their oaths,
HOTSPUR: Gave him their heirs, as pages follow'd him
HOTSPUR: Even at the heels in golden multitudes.
HOTSPUR: He presently, as greatness knows itself,
HOTSPUR: Steps me a little higher than his vow
HOTSPUR: Made to my father, while his blood was poor,
HOTSPUR: Upon the naked shore at Ravenspurgh,
HOTSPUR: And now, forsooth, takes on him to reform
HOTSPUR: Some certain edicts and some strait decrees
HOTSPUR: That lie too heavy on the commonwealth,
HOTSPUR: Cries out upon abuses, seems to weep
HOTSPUR: Over his country's wrongs, and by this face,
HOTSPUR: This seeming brow of justice, did he win
HOTSPUR: The hearts of all that he did angle for,
HOTSPUR: Proceeded further, cut me off the heads
HOTSPUR: Of all the favourites that the absent king
HOTSPUR: In deputation left behind him here,
HOTSPUR: When he was personal in the Irish war.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Tut, I came not to hear this.
HOTSPUR: Then to the point.
HOTSPUR: In short time after, he deposed the king,
HOTSPUR: Soon after that, deprived him of his life,
HOTSPUR: And in the neck of that, task'd the whole state:
HOTSPUR: To make that worse, suffer'd his kinsman March,
HOTSPUR: Who is, if every owner were well placed,
HOTSPUR: Indeed his king, to be engaged in Wales,
HOTSPUR: There without ransom to lie forfeited,
HOTSPUR: Disgraced me in my happy victories,
HOTSPUR: Sought to entrap me by intelligence,
HOTSPUR: Rated mine uncle from the council-board,
HOTSPUR: In rage dismiss'd my father from the court,
HOTSPUR: Broke oath on oath, committed wrong on wrong,
HOTSPUR: And in conclusion drove us to seek out
HOTSPUR: This head of safety, and withal to pry
HOTSPUR: Into his title, the which we find
HOTSPUR: Too indirect for long continuance.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Shall I return this answer to the king?
HOTSPUR: Not so, Sir Walter: we'll withdraw awhile.
HOTSPUR: Go to the king, and let there be impawn'd
HOTSPUR: Some surety for a safe return again,
HOTSPUR: And in the morning early shall my uncle
HOTSPUR: Bring him our purposes: and so farewell.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: I would you would accept of grace and love.
HOTSPUR: And may be so we shall.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Pray God you do.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. York. The ARCHBISHOP'S palace.
NARRATOR: Enter the ARCHBISHOP OF YORK and SIR MICHAEL
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Hie, good Sir Michael, bear this sealed brief
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: With winged haste to the lord marshal,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: This to my cousin Scroop, and all the rest
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: To whom they are directed. If you knew
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: How much they do to import, you would make haste.
SIR MICHAEL: My good lord,
SIR MICHAEL: I guess their tenor.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Like enough you do.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: To-morrow, good Sir Michael, is a day
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Wherein the fortune of ten thousand men
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Must bide the touch, for, sir, at Shrewsbury,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: As I am truly given to understand,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: The king with mighty and quick-raised power
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Meets with Lord Harry: and, I fear, Sir Michael,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: What with the sickness of Northumberland,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Whose power was in the first proportion,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And what with Owen Glendower's absence thence,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Who with them was a rated sinew too
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And comes not in, o'er-ruled by prophecies,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: I fear the power of Percy is too weak
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: To wage an instant trial with the king.
SIR MICHAEL: Why, my good lord, you need not fear,
SIR MICHAEL: There is Douglas and Lord Mortimer.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: No, Mortimer is not there.
SIR MICHAEL: But there is Mordake, Vernon, Lord Harry Percy,
SIR MICHAEL: And there is my Lord of Worcester and a head
SIR MICHAEL: Of gallant warriors, noble gentlemen.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And so there is: but yet the king hath drawn
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: The special head of all the land together:
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: The Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: The noble Westmoreland and warlike Blunt,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And moe corrivals and dear men
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Of estimation and command in arms.
SIR MICHAEL: Doubt not, my lord, they shall be well opposed.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: I hope no less, yet needful 'tis to fear,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And, to prevent the worst, Sir Michael, speed:
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: For if Lord Percy thrive not, ere the king
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Dismiss his power, he means to visit us,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: For he hath heard of our confederacy,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And 'tis but wisdom to make strong against him:
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Therefore make haste. I must go write again
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: To other friends, and so farewell, Sir Michael.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. KING HENRY IV's camp near Shrewsbury.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY, PRINCE HENRY, Lord John of  LANCASTER, EARL OF WESTMORELAND, SIR WALTER BLUNT, and FALSTAFF
KING HENRY IV: How bloodily the sun begins to peer
KING HENRY IV: Above yon busky hill! the day looks pale
KING HENRY IV: At his distemperature.
PRINCE HENRY: The southern wind
PRINCE HENRY: Doth play the trumpet to his purposes,
PRINCE HENRY: And by his hollow whistling in the leaves
PRINCE HENRY: Foretells a tempest and a blustering day.
KING HENRY IV: Then with the losers let it sympathize,
KING HENRY IV: For nothing can seem foul to those that win.
NARRATOR: The trumpet sounds
NARRATOR: Enter WORCESTER and VERNON
KING HENRY IV: How now, my Lord of Worcester! 'tis not well
KING HENRY IV: That you and I should meet upon such terms
KING HENRY IV: As now we meet. You have deceived our trust,
KING HENRY IV: And made us doff our easy robes of peace,
KING HENRY IV: To crush our old limbs in ungentle steel:
KING HENRY IV: This is not well, my lord, this is not well.
KING HENRY IV: What say you to it? will you again unknit
KING HENRY IV: This curlish knot of all-abhorred war?
KING HENRY IV: And move in that obedient orb again
KING HENRY IV: Where you did give a fair and natural light,
KING HENRY IV: And be no more an exhaled meteor,
KING HENRY IV: A prodigy of fear and a portent
KING HENRY IV: Of broached mischief to the unborn times?
EARL OF WORCESTER: Hear me, my liege:
EARL OF WORCESTER: For mine own part, I could be well content
EARL OF WORCESTER: To entertain the lag-end of my life
EARL OF WORCESTER: With quiet hours, for I do protest,
EARL OF WORCESTER: I have not sought the day of this dislike.
KING HENRY IV: You have not sought it! how comes it, then?
FALSTAFF: Rebellion lay in his way, and he found it.
PRINCE HENRY: Peace, chewet, peace!
EARL OF WORCESTER: It pleased your majesty to turn your looks
EARL OF WORCESTER: Of favour from myself and all our house,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And yet I must remember you, my lord,
EARL OF WORCESTER: We were the first and dearest of your friends.
EARL OF WORCESTER: For you my staff of office did I break
EARL OF WORCESTER: In Richard's time, and posted day and night
EARL OF WORCESTER: to meet you on the way, and kiss your hand,
EARL OF WORCESTER: When yet you were in place and in account
EARL OF WORCESTER: Nothing so strong and fortunate as I.
EARL OF WORCESTER: It was myself, my brother and his son,
EARL OF WORCESTER: That brought you home and boldly did outdare
EARL OF WORCESTER: The dangers of the time. You swore to us,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And you did swear that oath at Doncaster,
EARL OF WORCESTER: That you did nothing purpose 'gainst the state,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Nor claim no further than your new-fall'n right,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The seat of Gaunt, dukedom of Lancaster:
EARL OF WORCESTER: To this we swore our aid. But in short space
EARL OF WORCESTER: It rain'd down fortune showering on your head,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And such a flood of greatness fell on you,
EARL OF WORCESTER: What with our help, what with the absent king,
EARL OF WORCESTER: What with the injuries of a wanton time,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The seeming sufferances that you had borne,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And the contrarious winds that held the king
EARL OF WORCESTER: So long in his unlucky Irish wars
EARL OF WORCESTER: That all in England did repute him dead:
EARL OF WORCESTER: And from this swarm of fair advantages
EARL OF WORCESTER: You took occasion to be quickly woo'd
EARL OF WORCESTER: To gripe the general sway into your hand,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Forget your oath to us at Doncaster,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And being fed by us you used us so
EARL OF WORCESTER: As that ungentle hull, the cuckoo's bird,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Useth the sparrow, did oppress our nest,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Grew by our feeding to so great a bulk
EARL OF WORCESTER: That even our love durst not come near your sight
EARL OF WORCESTER: For fear of swallowing, but with nimble wing
EARL OF WORCESTER: We were enforced, for safety sake, to fly
EARL OF WORCESTER: Out of sight and raise this present head,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Whereby we stand opposed by such means
EARL OF WORCESTER: As you yourself have forged against yourself
EARL OF WORCESTER: By unkind usage, dangerous countenance,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And violation of all faith and troth
EARL OF WORCESTER: Sworn to us in your younger enterprise.
KING HENRY IV: These things indeed you have articulate,
KING HENRY IV: Proclaim'd at market-crosses, read in churches,
KING HENRY IV: To face the garment of rebellion
KING HENRY IV: With some fine colour that may please the eye
KING HENRY IV: Of fickle changelings and poor discontents,
KING HENRY IV: Which gape and rub the elbow at the news
KING HENRY IV: Of hurlyburly innovation:
KING HENRY IV: And never yet did insurrection want
KING HENRY IV: Such water-colours to impaint his cause,
KING HENRY IV: Nor moody beggars, starving for a time
KING HENRY IV: Of pellmell havoc and confusion.
PRINCE HENRY: In both your armies there is many a soul
PRINCE HENRY: Shall pay full dearly for this encounter,
PRINCE HENRY: If once they join in trial. Tell your nephew,
PRINCE HENRY: The Prince of Wales doth join with all the world
PRINCE HENRY: In praise of Henry Percy: by my hopes,
PRINCE HENRY: This present enterprise set off his head,
PRINCE HENRY: I do not think a braver gentleman,
PRINCE HENRY: More active-valiant or more valiant-young,
PRINCE HENRY: More daring or more bold, is now alive
PRINCE HENRY: To grace this latter age with noble deeds.
PRINCE HENRY: For my part, I may speak it to my shame,
PRINCE HENRY: I have a truant been to chivalry,
PRINCE HENRY: And so I hear he doth account me too,
PRINCE HENRY: Yet this before my father's majesty--
PRINCE HENRY: I am content that he shall take the odds
PRINCE HENRY: Of his great name and estimation,
PRINCE HENRY: And will, to save the blood on either side,
PRINCE HENRY: Try fortune with him in a single fight.
KING HENRY IV: And, Prince of Wales, so dare we venture thee,
KING HENRY IV: Albeit considerations infinite
KING HENRY IV: Do make against it. No, good Worcester, no,
KING HENRY IV: We love our people well, even those we love
KING HENRY IV: That are misled upon your cousin's part,
KING HENRY IV: And, will they take the offer of our grace,
KING HENRY IV: Both he and they and you, every man
KING HENRY IV: Shall be my friend again and I'll be his:
KING HENRY IV: So tell your cousin, and bring me word
KING HENRY IV: What he will do: but if he will not yield,
KING HENRY IV: Rebuke and dread correction wait on us
KING HENRY IV: And they shall do their office. So, be gone,
KING HENRY IV: We will not now be troubled with reply:
KING HENRY IV: We offer fair, take it advisedly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt WORCESTER and VERNON
PRINCE HENRY: It will not be accepted, on my life:
PRINCE HENRY: The Douglas and the Hotspur both together
PRINCE HENRY: Are confident against the world in arms.
KING HENRY IV: Hence, therefore, every leader to his charge,
KING HENRY IV: For, on their answer, will we set on them:
KING HENRY IV: And God befriend us, as our cause is just!
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but PRINCE HENRY and FALSTAFF
FALSTAFF: Hal, if thou see me down in the battle and bestride
FALSTAFF: me, so, 'tis a point of friendship.
PRINCE HENRY: Nothing but a colossus can do thee that friendship.
PRINCE HENRY: Say thy prayers, and farewell.
FALSTAFF: I  would 'twere bed-time, Hal, and all well.
PRINCE HENRY: Why, thou owest God a death.
NARRATOR: Exit PRINCE HENRY
FALSTAFF: 'Tis not due yet, I would be loath to pay him before
FALSTAFF: his day. What need I be so forward with him that
FALSTAFF: calls not on me? Well, 'tis no matter, honour pricks
FALSTAFF: me on. Yea, but how if honour prick me off when I
FALSTAFF: come on? how then? Can honour set to a leg? no: or
FALSTAFF: an arm? no: or take away the grief of a wound? no.
FALSTAFF: Honour hath no skill in surgery, then? no. What is
FALSTAFF: honour? a word. What is in that word honour? what
FALSTAFF: is that honour? air. A trim reckoning! Who hath it?
FALSTAFF: he that died o' Wednesday. Doth he feel it? no.
FALSTAFF: Doth he hear it? no. 'Tis insensible, then. Yea,
FALSTAFF: to the dead. But will it not live with the living?
FALSTAFF: no. Why? detraction will not suffer it. Therefore
FALSTAFF: I'll none of it. Honour is a mere scutcheon: and so
FALSTAFF: ends my catechism.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The rebel camp.
NARRATOR: Enter WORCESTER and VERNON
EARL OF WORCESTER: O, no, my nephew must not know, Sir Richard,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The liberal and kind offer of the king.
VERNON: 'Twere best he did.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Then are we all undone.
EARL OF WORCESTER: It is not possible, it cannot be,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The king should keep his word in loving us,
EARL OF WORCESTER: He will suspect us still and find a time
EARL OF WORCESTER: To punish this offence in other faults:
EARL OF WORCESTER: Suspicion all our lives shall be stuck full of eyes,
EARL OF WORCESTER: For treason is but trusted like the fox,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Who, ne'er so tame, so cherish'd and lock'd up,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Will have a wild trick of his ancestors.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Look how we can, or sad or merrily,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Interpretation will misquote our looks,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And we shall feed like oxen at a stall,
EARL OF WORCESTER: The better cherish'd, still the nearer death.
EARL OF WORCESTER: My nephew's trespass may be well forgot,
EARL OF WORCESTER: it hath the excuse of youth and heat of blood,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And an adopted name of privilege,
EARL OF WORCESTER: A hair-brain'd Hotspur, govern'd by a spleen:
EARL OF WORCESTER: All his offences live upon my head
EARL OF WORCESTER: And on his father's, we did train him on,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And, his corruption being ta'en from us,
EARL OF WORCESTER: We, as the spring of all, shall pay for all.
EARL OF WORCESTER: Therefore, good cousin, let not Harry know,
EARL OF WORCESTER: In any case, the offer of the king.
VERNON: Deliver what you will, I'll say 'tis so.
VERNON: Here comes your cousin.
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR and DOUGLAS
HOTSPUR: My uncle is return'd:
HOTSPUR: Deliver up my Lord of Westmoreland.
HOTSPUR: Uncle, what news?
EARL OF WORCESTER: The king will bid you battle presently.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Defy him by the Lord of Westmoreland.
HOTSPUR: Lord Douglas, go you and tell him so.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Marry, and shall, and very willingly.
NARRATOR: Exit
EARL OF WORCESTER: There is no seeming mercy in the king.
HOTSPUR: Did you beg any? God forbid!
EARL OF WORCESTER: I told him gently of our grievances,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Of his oath-breaking, which he mended thus,
EARL OF WORCESTER: By now forswearing that he is forsworn:
EARL OF WORCESTER: He calls us rebels, traitors, and will scourge
EARL OF WORCESTER: With haughty arms this hateful name in us.
NARRATOR: Re-enter the EARL OF DOUGLAS
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Arm, gentlemen, to arms! for I have thrown
EARL OF DOUGLAS: A brave defiance in King Henry's teeth,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: And Westmoreland, that was engaged, did bear it,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Which cannot choose but bring him quickly on.
EARL OF WORCESTER: The Prince of Wales stepp'd forth before the king,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And, nephew, challenged you to single fight.
HOTSPUR: O, would the quarrel lay upon our heads,
HOTSPUR: And that no man might draw short breath today
HOTSPUR: But I and Harry Monmouth! Tell me, tell me,
HOTSPUR: How show'd his tasking? seem'd it in contempt?
VERNON: No, by my soul, I never in my life
VERNON: Did hear a challenge urged more modestly,
VERNON: Unless a brother should a brother dare
VERNON: To gentle exercise and proof of arms.
VERNON: He gave you all the duties of a man,
VERNON: Trimm'd up your praises with a princely tongue,
VERNON: Spoke to your deservings like a chronicle,
VERNON: Making you ever better than his praise
VERNON: By still dispraising praise valued in you,
VERNON: And, which became him like a prince indeed,
VERNON: He made a blushing cital of himself,
VERNON: And chid his truant youth with such a grace
VERNON: As if he master'd there a double spirit.
VERNON: Of teaching and of learning instantly.
VERNON: There did he pause: but let me tell the world,
VERNON: If he outlive the envy of this day,
VERNON: England did never owe so sweet a hope,
VERNON: So much misconstrued in his wantonness.
HOTSPUR: Cousin, I think thou art enamoured
HOTSPUR: On his follies: never did I hear
HOTSPUR: Of any prince so wild a libertine.
HOTSPUR: But be he as he will, yet once ere night
HOTSPUR: I will embrace him with a soldier's arm,
HOTSPUR: That he shall shrink under my courtesy.
HOTSPUR: Arm, arm with speed: and, fellows, soldiers, friends,
HOTSPUR: Better consider what you have to do
HOTSPUR: Than I, that have not well the gift of tongue,
HOTSPUR: Can lift your blood up with persuasion.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord, here are letters for you.
HOTSPUR: I cannot read them now.
HOTSPUR: O gentlemen, the time of life is short!
HOTSPUR: To spend that shortness basely were too long,
HOTSPUR: If life did ride upon a dial's point,
HOTSPUR: Still ending at the arrival of an hour.
HOTSPUR: An if we live, we live to tread on kings,
HOTSPUR: If die, brave death, when princes die with us!
HOTSPUR: Now, for our consciences, the arms are fair,
HOTSPUR: When the intent of bearing them is just.
NARRATOR: Enter another Messenger
Messenger: My lord, prepare, the king comes on apace.
HOTSPUR: I thank him, that he cuts me from my tale,
HOTSPUR: For I profess not talking, only this--
HOTSPUR: Let each man do his best: and here draw I
HOTSPUR: A sword, whose temper I intend to stain
HOTSPUR: With the best blood that I can meet withal
HOTSPUR: In the adventure of this perilous day.
HOTSPUR: Now, Esperance! Percy! and set on.
HOTSPUR: Sound all the lofty instruments of war,
HOTSPUR: And by that music let us all embrace,
HOTSPUR: For, heaven to earth, some of us never shall
HOTSPUR: A second time do such a courtesy.
NARRATOR: The trumpets sound. They embrace, and exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Plain between the camps.
NARRATOR: KING HENRY enters with his power. Alarum to the battle. Then enter DOUGLAS and SIR WALTER BLUNT
SIR WALTER BLUNT: What is thy name, that in the battle thus
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Thou crossest me? what honour dost thou seek
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Upon my head?
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Know then, my name is Douglas,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: And I do haunt thee in the battle thus
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Because some tell me that thou art a king.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: They tell thee true.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: The Lord of Stafford dear to-day hath bought
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Thy likeness, for instead of thee, King Harry,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: This sword hath ended him: so shall it thee,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Unless thou yield thee as my prisoner.
SIR WALTER BLUNT: I was not born a yielder, thou proud Scot,
SIR WALTER BLUNT: And thou shalt find a king that will revenge
SIR WALTER BLUNT: Lord Stafford's death.
NARRATOR: They fight. DOUGLAS kills SIR WALTER BLUNT. Enter HOTSPUR
HOTSPUR: O Douglas, hadst thou fought at Holmedon thus,
HOTSPUR: never had triumph'd upon a Scot.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: All's done, all's won, here breathless lies the king.
HOTSPUR: Where?
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Here.
HOTSPUR: This, Douglas? no: I know this face full well:
HOTSPUR: A gallant knight he was, his name was Blunt,
HOTSPUR: Semblably furnish'd like the king himself.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: A fool go with thy soul, whither it goes!
EARL OF DOUGLAS: A borrow'd title hast thou bought too dear:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Why didst thou tell me that thou wert a king?
HOTSPUR: The king hath many marching in his coats.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Now, by my sword, I will kill all his coats,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: I'll murder all his wardrobe, piece by piece,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Until I meet the king.
HOTSPUR: Up, and away!
HOTSPUR: Our soldiers stand full fairly for the day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter FALSTAFF, solus
FALSTAFF: Though I could 'scape shot-free at London, I fear
FALSTAFF: the shot here, here's no scoring but upon the pate.
FALSTAFF: Soft! who are you? Sir Walter Blunt: there's honour
FALSTAFF: for you! here's no vanity! I am as hot as moulten
FALSTAFF: lead, and as heavy too: God keep lead out of me! I
FALSTAFF: need no more weight than mine own bowels. I have
FALSTAFF: led my ragamuffins where they are peppered: there's
FALSTAFF: not three of my hundred and fifty left alive, and
FALSTAFF: they are for the town's end, to beg during life.
FALSTAFF: But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter PRINCE HENRY
PRINCE HENRY: What, stand'st thou idle here? lend me thy sword:
PRINCE HENRY: Many a nobleman lies stark and stiff
PRINCE HENRY: Under the hoofs of vaunting enemies,
PRINCE HENRY: Whose deaths are yet unrevenged: I prithee,
PRINCE HENRY: lend me thy sword.
FALSTAFF: O Hal, I prithee, give me leave to breathe awhile.
FALSTAFF: Turk Gregory never did such deeds in arms as I have
FALSTAFF: done this day. I have paid Percy, I have made him sure.
PRINCE HENRY: He is, indeed, and living to kill thee. I prithee,
PRINCE HENRY: lend me thy sword.
FALSTAFF: Nay, before God, Hal, if Percy be alive, thou get'st
FALSTAFF: not my sword, but take my pistol, if thou wilt.
PRINCE HENRY: Give it to me: what, is it in the case?
FALSTAFF: Ay, Hal, 'tis hot, 'tis hot, there's that will sack a city.
NARRATOR: PRINCE HENRY draws it out, and finds it to be a bottle of sack
PRINCE HENRY: What, is it a time to jest and dally now?
NARRATOR: He throws the bottle at him. Exit
FALSTAFF: Well, if Percy be alive, I'll pierce him. If he do
FALSTAFF: come in my way, so: if he do not, if I come in his
FALSTAFF: willingly, let him make a carbonado of me. I like
FALSTAFF: not such grinning honour as Sir Walter hath: give me
FALSTAFF: life: which if I can save, so, if not, honour comes
FALSTAFF: unlooked for, and there's an end.
NARRATOR: Exit FALSTAFF
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Excursions. Enter PRINCE HENRY, LORD JOHN OF LANCASTER, and EARL OF WESTMORELAND
KING HENRY IV: I prithee,
KING HENRY IV: Harry, withdraw thyself, thou bleed'st too much.
KING HENRY IV: Lord John of Lancaster, go you with him.
LANCASTER: Not I, my lord, unless I did bleed too.
PRINCE HENRY: I beseech your majesty, make up,
PRINCE HENRY: Lest your retirement do amaze your friends.
KING HENRY IV: I will do so.
KING HENRY IV: My Lord of Westmoreland, lead him to his tent.
WESTMORELAND: Come, my lord, I'll lead you to your tent.
PRINCE HENRY: Lead me, my lord? I do not need your help:
PRINCE HENRY: And God forbid a shallow scratch should drive
PRINCE HENRY: The Prince of Wales from such a field as this,
PRINCE HENRY: Where stain'd nobility lies trodden on,
PRINCE HENRY: and rebels' arms triumph in massacres!
LANCASTER: We breathe too long: come, cousin Westmoreland,
LANCASTER: Our duty this way lies, for God's sake come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LANCASTER and WESTMORELAND
PRINCE HENRY: By God, thou hast deceived me, Lancaster,
PRINCE HENRY: I did not think thee lord of such a spirit:
PRINCE HENRY: Before, I loved thee as a brother, John,
PRINCE HENRY: But now, I do respect thee as my soul.
KING HENRY IV: I saw him hold Lord Percy at the point
KING HENRY IV: With lustier maintenance than I did look for
KING HENRY IV: Of such an ungrown warrior.
PRINCE HENRY: O, this boy
PRINCE HENRY: Lends mettle to us all!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter DOUGLAS
EARL OF DOUGLAS: Another king! they grow like Hydra's heads:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: I am the Douglas, fatal to all those
EARL OF DOUGLAS: That wear those colours on them: what art thou,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: That counterfeit'st the person of a king?
KING HENRY IV: The king himself, who, Douglas, grieves at heart
KING HENRY IV: So many of his shadows thou hast met
KING HENRY IV: And not the very king. I have two boys
KING HENRY IV: Seek Percy and thyself about the field:
KING HENRY IV: But, seeing thou fall'st on me so luckily,
KING HENRY IV: I will assay thee: so, defend thyself.
EARL OF DOUGLAS: I fear thou art another counterfeit,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: And yet, in faith, thou bear'st thee like a king:
EARL OF DOUGLAS: But mine I am sure thou art, whoe'er thou be,
EARL OF DOUGLAS: And thus I win thee.
NARRATOR: They fight. KING HENRY being in danger, PRINCE HENRY enters
PRINCE HENRY: Hold up thy head, vile Scot, or thou art like
PRINCE HENRY: Never to hold it up again! the spirits
PRINCE HENRY: Of valiant Shirley, Stafford, Blunt, are in my arms:
PRINCE HENRY: It is the Prince of Wales that threatens thee,
PRINCE HENRY: Who never promiseth but he means to pay.
PRINCE HENRY: They fight: DOUGLAS flies
PRINCE HENRY: Cheerly, my lord	how fares your grace?
PRINCE HENRY: Sir Nicholas Gawsey hath for succor sent,
PRINCE HENRY: And so hath Clifton: I'll to Clifton straight.
KING HENRY IV: Stay, and breathe awhile:
KING HENRY IV: Thou hast redeem'd thy lost opinion,
KING HENRY IV: And show'd thou makest some tender of my life,
KING HENRY IV: In this fair rescue thou hast brought to me.
PRINCE HENRY: O God! they did me too much injury
PRINCE HENRY: That ever said I hearken'd for your death.
PRINCE HENRY: If it were so, I might have let alone
PRINCE HENRY: The insulting hand of Douglas over you,
PRINCE HENRY: Which would have been as speedy in your end
PRINCE HENRY: As all the poisonous potions in the world
PRINCE HENRY: And saved the treacherous labour of your son.
KING HENRY IV: Make up to Clifton: I'll to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter HOTSPUR
HOTSPUR: If I mistake not, thou art Harry Monmouth.
PRINCE HENRY: Thou speak'st as if I would deny my name.
HOTSPUR: My name is Harry Percy.
PRINCE HENRY: Why, then I see
PRINCE HENRY: A very valiant rebel of the name.
PRINCE HENRY: I am the Prince of Wales, and think not, Percy,
PRINCE HENRY: To share with me in glory any more:
PRINCE HENRY: Two stars keep not their motion in one sphere,
PRINCE HENRY: Nor can one England brook a double reign,
PRINCE HENRY: Of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
HOTSPUR: Nor shall it, Harry, for the hour is come
HOTSPUR: To end the one of us, and would to God
HOTSPUR: Thy name in arms were now as great as mine!
PRINCE HENRY: I'll make it greater ere I part from thee,
PRINCE HENRY: And all the budding honours on thy crest
PRINCE HENRY: I'll crop, to make a garland for my head.
HOTSPUR: I can no longer brook thy vanities.
NARRATOR: They fight
NARRATOR: Enter FALSTAFF
FALSTAFF: Well said, Hal! to it Hal! Nay, you shall find no
FALSTAFF: boy's play here, I can tell you.
FALSTAFF: Re-enter DOUGLAS, he fights with FALSTAFF,  who falls down as if he were dead, and exit DOUGLAS. HOTSPUR is wounded, and falls
HOTSPUR: O, Harry, thou hast robb'd me of my youth!
HOTSPUR: I better brook the loss of brittle life
HOTSPUR: Than those proud titles thou hast won of me,
HOTSPUR: They wound my thoughts worse than sword my flesh:
HOTSPUR: But thought's the slave of life, and life time's fool,
HOTSPUR: And time, that takes survey of all the world,
HOTSPUR: Must have a stop. O, I could prophesy,
HOTSPUR: But that the earthy and cold hand of death
HOTSPUR: Lies on my tongue: no, Percy, thou art dust
HOTSPUR: And food for--
NARRATOR: Dies
PRINCE HENRY: For worms, brave Percy: fare thee well, great heart!
PRINCE HENRY: Ill-weaved ambition, how much art thou shrunk!
PRINCE HENRY: When that this body did contain a spirit,
PRINCE HENRY: A kingdom for it was too small a bound,
PRINCE HENRY: But now two paces of the vilest earth
PRINCE HENRY: Is room enough: this earth that bears thee dead
PRINCE HENRY: Bears not alive so stout a gentleman.
PRINCE HENRY: If thou wert sensible of courtesy,
PRINCE HENRY: I should not make so dear a show of zeal:
PRINCE HENRY: But let my favours hide thy mangled face,
PRINCE HENRY: And, even in thy behalf, I'll thank myself
PRINCE HENRY: For doing these fair rites of tenderness.
PRINCE HENRY: Adieu, and take thy praise with thee to heaven!
PRINCE HENRY: Thy ignominy sleep with thee in the grave,
PRINCE HENRY: But not remember'd in thy epitaph!
NARRATOR: He spieth FALSTAFF on the ground
PRINCE HENRY: What, old acquaintance! could not all this flesh
PRINCE HENRY: Keep in a little life? Poor Jack, farewell!
PRINCE HENRY: I could have better spared a better man:
PRINCE HENRY: O, I should have a heavy miss of thee,
PRINCE HENRY: If I were much in love with vanity!
PRINCE HENRY: Death hath not struck so fat a deer to-day,
PRINCE HENRY: Though many dearer, in this bloody fray.
PRINCE HENRY: Embowell'd will I see thee by and by:
PRINCE HENRY: Till then in blood by noble Percy lie.
NARRATOR: Exit PRINCE HENRY
FALSTAFF: [Rising up]  Embowelled! if thou embowel me to-day,
FALSTAFF: I'll give you leave to powder me and eat me too
FALSTAFF: to-morrow. 'Sblood,'twas time to counterfeit, or
FALSTAFF: that hot termagant Scot had paid me scot and lot too.
FALSTAFF: Counterfeit? I lie, I am no counterfeit: to die,
FALSTAFF: is to be a counterfeit, for he is but the
FALSTAFF: counterfeit of a man who hath not the life of a man:
FALSTAFF: but to counterfeit dying, when a man thereby
FALSTAFF: liveth, is to be no counterfeit, but the true and
FALSTAFF: perfect image of life indeed. The better part of
FALSTAFF: valour is discretion, in the which better part I
FALSTAFF: have saved my life.'Zounds, I am afraid of this
FALSTAFF: gunpowder Percy, though he be dead: how, if he
FALSTAFF: should counterfeit too and rise? by my faith, I am
FALSTAFF: afraid he would prove the better counterfeit.
FALSTAFF: Therefore I'll make him sure, yea, and I'll swear I
FALSTAFF: killed him. Why may not he rise as well as I?
FALSTAFF: Nothing confutes me but eyes, and nobody sees me.
FALSTAFF: Therefore, sirrah,
NARRATOR: Stabbing him
FALSTAFF: with a new wound in your thigh, come you along with me.
NARRATOR: Takes up HOTSPUR on his back
NARRATOR: Re-enter PRINCE HENRY and LORD JOHN OF LANCASTER
PRINCE HENRY: Come, brother John, full bravely hast thou flesh'd
PRINCE HENRY: Thy maiden sword.
LANCASTER: But, soft! whom have we here?
LANCASTER: Did you not tell me this fat man was dead?
PRINCE HENRY: I did, I saw him dead,
PRINCE HENRY: Breathless and bleeding on the ground. Art
PRINCE HENRY: thou alive?
PRINCE HENRY: Or is it fantasy that plays upon our eyesight?
PRINCE HENRY: I prithee, speak, we will not trust our eyes
PRINCE HENRY: Without our ears: thou art not what thou seem'st.
FALSTAFF: No, that's certain, I am not a double man: but if I
FALSTAFF: be not Jack Falstaff, then am I a Jack. There is Percy:
NARRATOR: Throwing the body down
FALSTAFF: if your father will do me any honour, so, if not, let
FALSTAFF: him kill the next Percy himself. I look to be either
FALSTAFF: earl or duke, I can assure you.
PRINCE HENRY: Why, Percy I killed myself and saw thee dead.
FALSTAFF: Didst thou? Lord, Lord, how this world is given to
FALSTAFF: lying! I grant you I was down and out of breath,
FALSTAFF: and so was he: but we rose both at an instant and
FALSTAFF: fought a long hour by Shrewsbury clock. If I may be
FALSTAFF: believed, so, if not, let them that should reward
FALSTAFF: valour bear the sin upon their own heads. I'll take
FALSTAFF: it upon my death, I gave him this wound in the
FALSTAFF: thigh: if the man were alive and would deny it,
FALSTAFF: 'zounds, I would make him eat a piece of my sword.
LANCASTER: This is the strangest tale that ever I heard.
PRINCE HENRY: This is the strangest fellow, brother John.
PRINCE HENRY: Come, bring your luggage nobly on your back:
PRINCE HENRY: For my part, if a lie may do thee grace,
PRINCE HENRY: I'll gild it with the happiest terms I have.
NARRATOR: A retreat is sounded
PRINCE HENRY: The trumpet sounds retreat, the day is ours.
PRINCE HENRY: Come, brother, let us to the highest of the field,
PRINCE HENRY: To see what friends are living, who are dead.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PRINCE HENRY and LANCASTER
FALSTAFF: I'll follow, as they say, for reward. He that
FALSTAFF: rewards me, God reward him! If I do grow great,
FALSTAFF: I'll grow less, for I'll purge, and leave sack, and
FALSTAFF: live cleanly as a nobleman should do.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: The trumpets sound. Enter KING HENRY IV, PRINCE  HENRY, LORD JOHN LANCASTER, EARL OF WESTMORELAND, with WORCESTER and VERNON prisoners
KING HENRY IV: Thus ever did rebellion find rebuke.
KING HENRY IV: Ill-spirited Worcester! did not we send grace,
KING HENRY IV: Pardon and terms of love to all of you?
KING HENRY IV: And wouldst thou turn our offers contrary?
KING HENRY IV: Misuse the tenor of thy kinsman's trust?
KING HENRY IV: Three knights upon our party slain to-day,
KING HENRY IV: A noble earl and many a creature else
KING HENRY IV: Had been alive this hour,
KING HENRY IV: If like a Christian thou hadst truly borne
KING HENRY IV: Betwixt our armies true intelligence.
EARL OF WORCESTER: What I have done my safety urged me to,
EARL OF WORCESTER: And I embrace this fortune patiently,
EARL OF WORCESTER: Since not to be avoided it falls on me.
KING HENRY IV: Bear Worcester to the death and Vernon too:
KING HENRY IV: Other offenders we will pause upon.
NARRATOR: Exeunt WORCESTER and VERNON, guarded
KING HENRY IV: How goes the field?
PRINCE HENRY: The noble Scot, Lord Douglas, when he saw
PRINCE HENRY: The fortune of the day quite turn'd from him,
PRINCE HENRY: The noble Percy slain, and all his men
PRINCE HENRY: Upon the foot of fear, fled with the rest,
PRINCE HENRY: And falling from a hill, he was so bruised
PRINCE HENRY: That the pursuers took him. At my tent
PRINCE HENRY: The Douglas is, and I beseech your grace
PRINCE HENRY: I may dispose of him.
KING HENRY IV: With all my heart.
PRINCE HENRY: Then, brother John of Lancaster, to you
PRINCE HENRY: This honourable bounty shall belong:
PRINCE HENRY: Go to the Douglas, and deliver him
PRINCE HENRY: Up to his pleasure, ransomless and free:
PRINCE HENRY: His valour shown upon our crests to-day
PRINCE HENRY: Hath taught us how to cherish such high deeds
PRINCE HENRY: Even in the bosom of our adversaries.
LANCASTER: I thank your grace for this high courtesy,
LANCASTER: Which I shall give away immediately.
KING HENRY IV: Then this remains, that we divide our power.
KING HENRY IV: You, son John, and my cousin Westmoreland
KING HENRY IV: Towards York shall bend you with your dearest speed,
KING HENRY IV: To meet Northumberland and the prelate Scroop,
KING HENRY IV: Who, as we hear, are busily in arms:
KING HENRY IV: Myself and you, son Harry, will towards Wales,
KING HENRY IV: To fight with Glendower and the Earl of March.
KING HENRY IV: Rebellion in this land shall lose his sway,
KING HENRY IV: Meeting the cheque of such another day:
KING HENRY IV: And since this business so fair is done,
KING HENRY IV: Let us not leave till all our own be won.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Henry V '''
PRINCE FORTINBRAS: ACT I
PRINCE FORTINBRAS: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend
Chorus: The brightest heaven of invention,
Chorus: A kingdom for a stage, princes to act
Chorus: And monarchs to behold the swelling scene!
Chorus: Then should the warlike Harry, like himself,
Chorus: Assume the port of Mars, and at his heels,
Chorus: Leash'd in like hounds, should famine, sword and fire
Chorus: Crouch for employment. But pardon, and gentles all,
Chorus: The flat unraised spirits that have dared
Chorus: On this unworthy scaffold to bring forth
Chorus: So great an object: can this cockpit hold
Chorus: The vasty fields of France? or may we cram
Chorus: Within this wooden O the very casques
Chorus: That did affright the air at Agincourt?
Chorus: O, pardon! since a crooked figure may
Chorus: Attest in little place a million,
Chorus: And let us, ciphers to this great accompt,
Chorus: On your imaginary forces work.
Chorus: Suppose within the girdle of these walls
Chorus: Are now confined two mighty monarchies,
Chorus: Whose high upreared and abutting fronts
Chorus: The perilous narrow ocean parts asunder:
Chorus: Piece out our imperfections with your thoughts,
Chorus: Into a thousand parts divide on man,
Chorus: And make imaginary puissance,
Chorus: Think when we talk of horses, that you see them
Chorus: Printing their proud hoofs i' the receiving earth,
Chorus: For 'tis your thoughts that now must deck our kings,
Chorus: Carry them here and there, jumping o'er times,
Chorus: Turning the accomplishment of many years
Chorus: Into an hour-glass: for the which supply,
Chorus: Admit me Chorus to this history,
Chorus: Who prologue-like your humble patience pray,
Chorus: Gently to hear, kindly to judge, our play.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. An ante-chamber in the KING'S palace.
NARRATOR: Enter the ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, and the BISHOP OF ELY
CANTERBURY: My lord, I'll tell you, that self bill is urged,
CANTERBURY: Which in the eleventh year of the last king's reign
CANTERBURY: Was like, and had indeed against us pass'd,
CANTERBURY: But that the scambling and unquiet time
CANTERBURY: Did push it out of farther question.
ELY: But how, my lord, shall we resist it now?
CANTERBURY: It must be thought on. If it pass against us,
CANTERBURY: We lose the better half of our possession:
CANTERBURY: For all the temporal lands which men devout
CANTERBURY: By testament have given to the church
CANTERBURY: Would they strip from us, being valued thus:
CANTERBURY: As much as would maintain, to the king's honour,
CANTERBURY: Full fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights,
CANTERBURY: Six thousand and two hundred good esquires,
CANTERBURY: And, to relief of lazars and weak age,
CANTERBURY: Of indigent faint souls past corporal toil.
CANTERBURY: A hundred almshouses right well supplied,
CANTERBURY: And to the coffers of the king beside,
CANTERBURY: A thousand pounds by the year: thus runs the bill.
ELY: This would drink deep.
CANTERBURY: 'Twould drink the cup and all.
ELY: But what prevention?
CANTERBURY: The king is full of grace and fair regard.
ELY: And a true lover of the holy church.
CANTERBURY: The courses of his youth promised it not.
CANTERBURY: The breath no sooner left his father's body,
CANTERBURY: But that his wildness, mortified in him,
CANTERBURY: Seem'd to die too, yea, at that very moment
CANTERBURY: Consideration, like an angel, came
CANTERBURY: And whipp'd the offending Adam out of him,
CANTERBURY: Leaving his body as a paradise,
CANTERBURY: To envelop and contain celestial spirits.
CANTERBURY: Never was such a sudden scholar made,
CANTERBURY: Never came reformation in a flood,
CANTERBURY: With such a heady currance, scouring faults
CANTERBURY: Nor never Hydra-headed wilfulness
CANTERBURY: So soon did lose his seat and all at once
CANTERBURY: As in this king.
ELY: We are blessed in the change.
CANTERBURY: Hear him but reason in divinity,
CANTERBURY: And all-admiring with an inward wish
CANTERBURY: You would desire the king were made a prelate:
CANTERBURY: Hear him debate of commonwealth affairs,
CANTERBURY: You would say it hath been all in all his study:
CANTERBURY: List his discourse of war, and you shall hear
CANTERBURY: A fearful battle render'd you in music:
CANTERBURY: Turn him to any cause of policy,
CANTERBURY: The Gordian knot of it he will unloose,
CANTERBURY: Familiar as his garter: that, when he speaks,
CANTERBURY: The air, a charter'd libertine, is still,
CANTERBURY: And the mute wonder lurketh in men's ears,
CANTERBURY: To steal his sweet and honey'd sentences,
CANTERBURY: So that the art and practic part of life
CANTERBURY: Must be the mistress to this theoric:
CANTERBURY: Which is a wonder how his grace should glean it,
CANTERBURY: Since his addiction was to courses vain,
CANTERBURY: His companies unletter'd, rude and shallow,
CANTERBURY: His hours fill'd up with riots, banquets, sports,
CANTERBURY: And never noted in him any study,
CANTERBURY: Any retirement, any sequestration
CANTERBURY: From open haunts and popularity.
ELY: The strawberry grows underneath the nettle
ELY: And wholesome berries thrive and ripen best
ELY: Neighbour'd by fruit of baser quality:
ELY: And so the prince obscured his contemplation
ELY: Under the veil of wildness, which, no doubt,
ELY: Grew like the summer grass, fastest by night,
ELY: Unseen, yet crescive in his faculty.
CANTERBURY: It must be so, for miracles are ceased,
CANTERBURY: And therefore we must needs admit the means
CANTERBURY: How things are perfected.
ELY: But, my good lord,
ELY: How now for mitigation of this bill
ELY: Urged by the commons? Doth his majesty
ELY: Incline to it, or no?
CANTERBURY: He seems indifferent,
CANTERBURY: Or rather swaying more upon our part
CANTERBURY: Than cherishing the exhibiters against us,
CANTERBURY: For I have made an offer to his majesty,
CANTERBURY: Upon our spiritual convocation
CANTERBURY: And in regard of causes now in hand,
CANTERBURY: Which I have open'd to his grace at large,
CANTERBURY: As touching France, to give a greater sum
CANTERBURY: Than ever at one time the clergy yet
CANTERBURY: Did to his predecessors part withal.
ELY: How did this offer seem received, my lord?
CANTERBURY: With good acceptance of his majesty,
CANTERBURY: Save that there was not time enough to hear,
CANTERBURY: As I perceived his grace would fain have done,
CANTERBURY: The severals and unhidden passages
CANTERBURY: Of his true titles to some certain dukedoms
CANTERBURY: And generally to the crown and seat of France
CANTERBURY: Derived from Edward, his great-grandfather.
ELY: What was the impediment that broke this off?
CANTERBURY: The French ambassador upon that instant
CANTERBURY: Craved audience, and the hour, I think, is come
CANTERBURY: To give him hearing: is it four o'clock?
ELY: It is.
CANTERBURY: Then go we in, to know his embassy,
CANTERBURY: Which I could with a ready guess declare,
CANTERBURY: Before the Frenchman speak a word of it.
ELY: I'll wait upon you, and I long to hear it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. The Presence chamber.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY V, GLOUCESTER, BEDFORD, EXETER, WARWICK, WESTMORELAND, and Attendants
KING HENRY V: Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
EXETER: Not here in presence.
KING HENRY V: Send for him, good uncle.
WESTMORELAND: Shall we call in the ambassador, my liege?
KING HENRY V: Not yet, my cousin: we would be resolved,
KING HENRY V: Before we hear him, of some things of weight
KING HENRY V: That task our thoughts, concerning us and France.
NARRATOR: Enter the ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, and the BISHOP of ELY
CANTERBURY: God and his angels guard your sacred throne
CANTERBURY: And make you long become it!
KING HENRY V: Sure, we thank you.
KING HENRY V: My learned lord, we pray you to proceed
KING HENRY V: And justly and religiously unfold
KING HENRY V: Why the law Salique that they have in France
KING HENRY V: Or should, or should not, bar us in our claim:
KING HENRY V: And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord,
KING HENRY V: That you should fashion, wrest, or bow your reading,
KING HENRY V: Or nicely charge your understanding soul
KING HENRY V: With opening titles miscreate, whose right
KING HENRY V: Suits not in native colours with the truth,
KING HENRY V: For God doth know how many now in health
KING HENRY V: Shall drop their blood in approbation
KING HENRY V: Of what your reverence shall incite us to.
KING HENRY V: Therefore take heed how you impawn our person,
KING HENRY V: How you awake our sleeping sword of war:
KING HENRY V: We charge you, in the name of God, take heed,
KING HENRY V: For never two such kingdoms did contend
KING HENRY V: Without much fall of blood, whose guiltless drops
KING HENRY V: Are every one a woe, a sore complaint
KING HENRY V: 'Gainst him whose wrong gives edge unto the swords
KING HENRY V: That make such waste in brief mortality.
KING HENRY V: Under this conjuration, speak, my lord,
KING HENRY V: For we will hear, note and believe in heart
KING HENRY V: That what you speak is in your conscience wash'd
KING HENRY V: As pure as sin with baptism.
CANTERBURY: Then hear me, gracious sovereign, and you peers,
CANTERBURY: That owe yourselves, your lives and services
CANTERBURY: To this imperial throne. There is no bar
CANTERBURY: To make against your highness' claim to France
CANTERBURY: But this, which they produce from Pharamond,
CANTERBURY: 'In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant:'
CANTERBURY: 'No woman shall succeed in Salique land:'
