CANTERBURY: Which Salique land the French unjustly gloze
CANTERBURY: To be the realm of France, and Pharamond
CANTERBURY: The founder of this law and female bar.
CANTERBURY: Yet their own authors faithfully affirm
CANTERBURY: That the land Salique is in Germany,
CANTERBURY: Between the floods of Sala and of Elbe,
CANTERBURY: Where Charles the Great, having subdued the Saxons,
CANTERBURY: There left behind and settled certain French,
CANTERBURY: Who, holding in disdain the German women
CANTERBURY: For some dishonest manners of their life,
CANTERBURY: Establish'd then this law, to wit, no female
CANTERBURY: Should be inheritrix in Salique land:
CANTERBURY: Which Salique, as I said, 'twixt Elbe and Sala,
CANTERBURY: Is at this day in Germany call'd Meisen.
CANTERBURY: Then doth it well appear that Salique law
CANTERBURY: Was not devised for the realm of France:
CANTERBURY: Nor did the French possess the Salique land
CANTERBURY: Until four hundred one and twenty years
CANTERBURY: After defunction of King Pharamond,
CANTERBURY: Idly supposed the founder of this law,
CANTERBURY: Who died within the year of our redemption
CANTERBURY: Four hundred twenty-six, and Charles the Great
CANTERBURY: Subdued the Saxons, and did seat the French
CANTERBURY: Beyond the river Sala, in the year
CANTERBURY: Eight hundred five. Besides, their writers say,
CANTERBURY: King Pepin, which deposed Childeric,
CANTERBURY: Did, as heir general, being descended
CANTERBURY: Of Blithild, which was daughter to King Clothair,
CANTERBURY: Make claim and title to the crown of France.
CANTERBURY: Hugh Capet also, who usurped the crown
CANTERBURY: Of Charles the duke of Lorraine, sole heir male
CANTERBURY: Of the true line and stock of Charles the Great,
CANTERBURY: To find his title with some shows of truth,
CANTERBURY: 'Through, in pure truth, it was corrupt and naught,
CANTERBURY: Convey'd himself as heir to the Lady Lingare,
CANTERBURY: Daughter to Charlemain, who was the son
CANTERBURY: To Lewis the emperor, and Lewis the son
CANTERBURY: Of Charles the Great. Also King Lewis the Tenth,
CANTERBURY: Who was sole heir to the usurper Capet,
CANTERBURY: Could not keep quiet in his conscience,
CANTERBURY: Wearing the crown of France, till satisfied
CANTERBURY: That fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother,
CANTERBURY: Was lineal of the Lady Ermengare,
CANTERBURY: Daughter to Charles the foresaid duke of Lorraine:
CANTERBURY: By the which marriage the line of Charles the Great
CANTERBURY: Was re-united to the crown of France.
CANTERBURY: So that, as clear as is the summer's sun.
CANTERBURY: King Pepin's title and Hugh Capet's claim,
CANTERBURY: King Lewis his satisfaction, all appear
CANTERBURY: To hold in right and title of the female:
CANTERBURY: So do the kings of France unto this day,
CANTERBURY: Howbeit they would hold up this Salique law
CANTERBURY: To bar your highness claiming from the female,
CANTERBURY: And rather choose to hide them in a net
CANTERBURY: Than amply to imbar their crooked titles
CANTERBURY: Usurp'd from you and your progenitors.
KING HENRY V: May I with right and conscience make this claim?
CANTERBURY: The sin upon my head, dread sovereign!
CANTERBURY: For in the book of Numbers is it writ,
CANTERBURY: When the man dies, let the inheritance
CANTERBURY: Descend unto the daughter. Gracious lord,
CANTERBURY: Stand for your own, unwind your bloody flag,
CANTERBURY: Look back into your mighty ancestors:
CANTERBURY: Go, my dread lord, to your great-grandsire's tomb,
CANTERBURY: From whom you claim, invoke his warlike spirit,
CANTERBURY: And your great-uncle's, Edward the Black Prince,
CANTERBURY: Who on the French ground play'd a tragedy,
CANTERBURY: Making defeat on the full power of France,
CANTERBURY: Whiles his most mighty father on a hill
CANTERBURY: Stood smiling to behold his lion's whelp
CANTERBURY: Forage in blood of French nobility.
CANTERBURY: O noble English. that could entertain
CANTERBURY: With half their forces the full Pride of France
CANTERBURY: And let another half stand laughing by,
CANTERBURY: All out of work and cold for action!
ELY: Awake remembrance of these valiant dead
ELY: And with your puissant arm renew their feats:
ELY: You are their heir, you sit upon their throne,
ELY: The blood and courage that renowned them
ELY: Runs in your veins, and my thrice-puissant liege
ELY: Is in the very May-morn of his youth,
ELY: Ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.
EXETER: Your brother kings and monarchs of the earth
EXETER: Do all expect that you should rouse yourself,
EXETER: As did the former lions of your blood.
WESTMORELAND: They know your grace hath cause and means and might,
WESTMORELAND: So hath your highness, never king of England
WESTMORELAND: Had nobles richer and more loyal subjects,
WESTMORELAND: Whose hearts have left their bodies here in England
WESTMORELAND: And lie pavilion'd in the fields of France.
CANTERBURY: O, let their bodies follow, my dear liege,
CANTERBURY: With blood and sword and fire to win your right,
CANTERBURY: In aid whereof we of the spiritualty
CANTERBURY: Will raise your highness such a mighty sum
CANTERBURY: As never did the clergy at one time
CANTERBURY: Bring in to any of your ancestors.
KING HENRY V: We must not only arm to invade the French,
KING HENRY V: But lay down our proportions to defend
KING HENRY V: Against the Scot, who will make road upon us
KING HENRY V: With all advantages.
CANTERBURY: They of those marches, gracious sovereign,
CANTERBURY: Shall be a wall sufficient to defend
CANTERBURY: Our inland from the pilfering borderers.
KING HENRY V: We do not mean the coursing snatchers only,
KING HENRY V: But fear the main intendment of the Scot,
KING HENRY V: Who hath been still a giddy neighbour to us,
KING HENRY V: For you shall read that my great-grandfather
KING HENRY V: Never went with his forces into France
KING HENRY V: But that the Scot on his unfurnish'd kingdom
KING HENRY V: Came pouring, like the tide into a breach,
KING HENRY V: With ample and brim fulness of his force,
KING HENRY V: Galling the gleaned land with hot assays,
KING HENRY V: Girding with grievous siege castles and towns,
KING HENRY V: That England, being empty of defence,
KING HENRY V: Hath shook and trembled at the ill neighbourhood.
CANTERBURY: She hath been then more fear'd than harm'd, my liege,
CANTERBURY: For hear her but exampled by herself:
CANTERBURY: When all her chivalry hath been in France
CANTERBURY: And she a mourning widow of her nobles,
CANTERBURY: She hath herself not only well defended
CANTERBURY: But taken and impounded as a stray
CANTERBURY: The King of Scots, whom she did send to France,
CANTERBURY: To fill King Edward's fame with prisoner kings
CANTERBURY: And make her chronicle as rich with praise
CANTERBURY: As is the ooze and bottom of the sea
CANTERBURY: With sunken wreck and sunless treasuries.
WESTMORELAND: But there's a saying very old and true,
WESTMORELAND: 'If that you will France win,
WESTMORELAND: Then with Scotland first begin:'
WESTMORELAND: For once the eagle England being in prey,
WESTMORELAND: To her unguarded nest the weasel Scot
WESTMORELAND: Comes sneaking and so sucks her princely eggs,
WESTMORELAND: Playing the mouse in absence of the cat,
WESTMORELAND: To tear and havoc more than she can eat.
EXETER: It follows then the cat must stay at home:
EXETER: Yet that is but a crush'd necessity,
EXETER: Since we have locks to safeguard necessaries,
EXETER: And pretty traps to catch the petty thieves.
EXETER: While that the armed hand doth fight abroad,
EXETER: The advised head defends itself at home,
EXETER: For government, though high and low and lower,
EXETER: Put into parts, doth keep in one consent,
EXETER: Congreeing in a full and natural close,
EXETER: Like music.
CANTERBURY: Therefore doth heaven divide
CANTERBURY: The state of man in divers functions,
CANTERBURY: Setting endeavour in continual motion,
CANTERBURY: To which is fixed, as an aim or butt,
CANTERBURY: Obedience: for so work the honey-bees,
CANTERBURY: Creatures that by a rule in nature teach
CANTERBURY: The act of order to a peopled kingdom.
CANTERBURY: They have a king and officers of sorts,
CANTERBURY: Where some, like magistrates, correct at home,
CANTERBURY: Others, like merchants, venture trade abroad,
CANTERBURY: Others, like soldiers, armed in their stings,
CANTERBURY: Make boot upon the summer's velvet buds,
CANTERBURY: Which pillage they with merry march bring home
CANTERBURY: To the tent-royal of their emperor,
CANTERBURY: Who, busied in his majesty, surveys
CANTERBURY: The singing masons building roofs of gold,
CANTERBURY: The civil citizens kneading up the honey,
CANTERBURY: The poor mechanic porters crowding in
CANTERBURY: Their heavy burdens at his narrow gate,
CANTERBURY: The sad-eyed justice, with his surly hum,
CANTERBURY: Delivering o'er to executors pale
CANTERBURY: The lazy yawning drone. I this infer,
CANTERBURY: That many things, having full reference
CANTERBURY: To one consent, may work contrariously:
CANTERBURY: As many arrows, loosed several ways,
CANTERBURY: Come to one mark, as many ways meet in one town,
CANTERBURY: As many fresh streams meet in one salt sea,
CANTERBURY: As many lines close in the dial's centre,
CANTERBURY: So may a thousand actions, once afoot.
CANTERBURY: End in one purpose, and be all well borne
CANTERBURY: Without defeat. Therefore to France, my liege.
CANTERBURY: Divide your happy England into four,
CANTERBURY: Whereof take you one quarter into France,
CANTERBURY: And you withal shall make all Gallia shake.
CANTERBURY: If we, with thrice such powers left at home,
CANTERBURY: Cannot defend our own doors from the dog,
CANTERBURY: Let us be worried and our nation lose
CANTERBURY: The name of hardiness and policy.
KING HENRY V: Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some Attendants
KING HENRY V: Now are we well resolved, and, by God's help,
KING HENRY V: And yours, the noble sinews of our power,
KING HENRY V: France being ours, we'll bend it to our awe,
KING HENRY V: Or break it all to pieces: or there we'll sit,
KING HENRY V: Ruling in large and ample empery
KING HENRY V: O'er France and all her almost kingly dukedoms,
KING HENRY V: Or lay these bones in an unworthy urn,
KING HENRY V: Tombless, with no remembrance over them:
KING HENRY V: Either our history shall with full mouth
KING HENRY V: Speak freely of our acts, or else our grave,
KING HENRY V: Like Turkish mute, shall have a tongueless mouth,
KING HENRY V: Not worshipp'd with a waxen epitaph.
NARRATOR: Enter Ambassadors of France
KING HENRY V: Now are we well prepared to know the pleasure
KING HENRY V: Of our fair cousin Dauphin, for we hear
KING HENRY V: Your greeting is from him, not from the king.
First Ambassador: May't please your majesty to give us leave
First Ambassador: Freely to render what we have in charge,
First Ambassador: Or shall we sparingly show you far off
First Ambassador: The Dauphin's meaning and our embassy?
KING HENRY V: We are no tyrant, but a Christian king,
KING HENRY V: Unto whose grace our passion is as subject
KING HENRY V: As are our wretches fetter'd in our prisons:
KING HENRY V: Therefore with frank and with uncurbed plainness
KING HENRY V: Tell us the Dauphin's mind.
First Ambassador: Thus, then, in few.
First Ambassador: Your highness, lately sending into France,
First Ambassador: Did claim some certain dukedoms, in the right
First Ambassador: Of your great predecessor, King Edward the Third.
First Ambassador: In answer of which claim, the prince our master
First Ambassador: Says that you savour too much of your youth,
First Ambassador: And bids you be advised there's nought in France
First Ambassador: That can be with a nimble galliard won,
First Ambassador: You cannot revel into dukedoms there.
First Ambassador: He therefore sends you, meeter for your spirit,
First Ambassador: This tun of treasure, and, in lieu of this,
First Ambassador: Desires you let the dukedoms that you claim
First Ambassador: Hear no more of you. This the Dauphin speaks.
KING HENRY V: What treasure, uncle?
EXETER: Tennis-balls, my liege.
KING HENRY V: We are glad the Dauphin is so pleasant with us,
KING HENRY V: His present and your pains we thank you for:
KING HENRY V: When we have march'd our rackets to these balls,
KING HENRY V: We will, in France, by God's grace, play a set
KING HENRY V: Shall strike his father's crown into the hazard.
KING HENRY V: Tell him he hath made a match with such a wrangler
KING HENRY V: That all the courts of France will be disturb'd
KING HENRY V: With chaces. And we understand him well,
KING HENRY V: How he comes o'er us with our wilder days,
KING HENRY V: Not measuring what use we made of them.
KING HENRY V: We never valued this poor seat of England,
KING HENRY V: And therefore, living hence, did give ourself
KING HENRY V: To barbarous licence, as 'tis ever common
KING HENRY V: That men are merriest when they are from home.
KING HENRY V: But tell the Dauphin I will keep my state,
KING HENRY V: Be like a king and show my sail of greatness
KING HENRY V: When I do rouse me in my throne of France:
KING HENRY V: For that I have laid by my majesty
KING HENRY V: And plodded like a man for working-days,
KING HENRY V: But I will rise there with so full a glory
KING HENRY V: That I will dazzle all the eyes of France,
KING HENRY V: Yea, strike the Dauphin blind to look on us.
KING HENRY V: And tell the pleasant prince this mock of his
KING HENRY V: Hath turn'd his balls to gun-stones, and his soul
KING HENRY V: Shall stand sore charged for the wasteful vengeance
KING HENRY V: That shall fly with them: for many a thousand widows
KING HENRY V: Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands,
KING HENRY V: Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down,
KING HENRY V: And some are yet ungotten and unborn
KING HENRY V: That shall have cause to curse the Dauphin's scorn.
KING HENRY V: But this lies all within the will of God,
KING HENRY V: To whom I do appeal, and in whose name
KING HENRY V: Tell you the Dauphin I am coming on,
KING HENRY V: To venge me as I may and to put forth
KING HENRY V: My rightful hand in a well-hallow'd cause.
KING HENRY V: So get you hence in peace, and tell the Dauphin
KING HENRY V: His jest will savour but of shallow wit,
KING HENRY V: When thousands weep more than did laugh at it.
KING HENRY V: Convey them with safe conduct. Fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Ambassadors
EXETER: This was a merry message.
KING HENRY V: We hope to make the sender blush at it.
KING HENRY V: Therefore, my lords, omit no happy hour
KING HENRY V: That may give furtherance to our expedition,
KING HENRY V: For we have now no thought in us but France,
KING HENRY V: Save those to God, that run before our business.
KING HENRY V: Therefore let our proportions for these wars
KING HENRY V: Be soon collected and all things thought upon
KING HENRY V: That may with reasonable swiftness add
KING HENRY V: More feathers to our wings, for, God before,
KING HENRY V: We'll chide this Dauphin at his father's door.
KING HENRY V: Therefore let every man now task his thought,
KING HENRY V: That this fair action may on foot be brought.
NARRATOR: Exeunt. Flourish
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Now all the youth of England are on fire,
Chorus: And silken dalliance in the wardrobe lies:
Chorus: Now thrive the armourers, and honour's thought
Chorus: Reigns solely in the breast of every man:
Chorus: They sell the pasture now to buy the horse,
Chorus: Following the mirror of all Christian kings,
Chorus: With winged heels, as English Mercuries.
Chorus: For now sits Expectation in the air,
Chorus: And hides a sword from hilts unto the point
Chorus: With crowns imperial, crowns and coronets,
Chorus: Promised to Harry and his followers.
Chorus: The French, advised by good intelligence
Chorus: Of this most dreadful preparation,
Chorus: Shake in their fear and with pale policy
Chorus: Seek to divert the English purposes.
Chorus: O England! model to thy inward greatness,
Chorus: Like little body with a mighty heart,
Chorus: What mightst thou do, that honour would thee do,
Chorus: Were all thy children kind and natural!
Chorus: But see thy fault! France hath in thee found out
Chorus: A nest of hollow bosoms, which he fills
Chorus: With treacherous crowns, and three corrupted men,
Chorus: One, Richard Earl of Cambridge, and the second,
Chorus: Henry Lord Scroop of Masham, and the third,
Chorus: Sir Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland,
Chorus: Have, for the gilt of France,--O guilt indeed!
Chorus: Confirm'd conspiracy with fearful France,
Chorus: And by their hands this grace of kings must die,
Chorus: If hell and treason hold their promises,
Chorus: Ere he take ship for France, and in Southampton.
Chorus: Linger your patience on, and we'll digest
Chorus: The abuse of distance, force a play:
Chorus: The sum is paid, the traitors are agreed,
Chorus: The king is set from London, and the scene
Chorus: Is now transported, gentles, to Southampton,
Chorus: There is the playhouse now, there must you sit:
Chorus: And thence to France shall we convey you safe,
Chorus: And bring you back, charming the narrow seas
Chorus: To give you gentle pass, for, if we may,
Chorus: We'll not offend one stomach with our play.
Chorus: But, till the king come forth, and not till then,
Chorus: Unto Southampton do we shift our scene.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter Corporal NYM and Lieutenant BARDOLPH
BARDOLPH: Well met, Corporal Nym.
NYM: Good morrow, Lieutenant Bardolph.
BARDOLPH: What, are Ancient Pistol and you friends yet?
NYM: For my part, I care not: I say little, but when
NYM: time shall serve, there shall be smiles, but that
NYM: shall be as it may. I dare not fight, but I will
NYM: wink and hold out mine iron: it is a simple one, but
NYM: what though? it will toast cheese, and it will
NYM: endure cold as another man's sword will: and
NYM: there's an end.
BARDOLPH: I will bestow a breakfast to make you friends, and
BARDOLPH: we'll be all three sworn brothers to France: let it
BARDOLPH: be so, good Corporal Nym.
NYM: Faith, I will live so long as I may, that's the
NYM: certain of it, and when I cannot live any longer, I
NYM: will do as I may: that is my rest, that is the
NYM: rendezvous of it.
BARDOLPH: It is certain, corporal, that he is married to Nell
BARDOLPH: Quickly: and certainly she did you wrong, for you
BARDOLPH: were troth-plight to her.
NYM: I cannot tell: things must be as they may: men may
NYM: sleep, and they may have their throats about them at
NYM: that time, and some say knives have edges. It must
NYM: be as it may: though patience be a tired mare, yet
NYM: she will plod. There must be conclusions. Well, I
NYM: cannot tell.
NARRATOR: Enter PISTOL and Hostess
BARDOLPH: Here comes Ancient Pistol and his wife: good
BARDOLPH: corporal, be patient here. How now, mine host Pistol!
PISTOL: Base tike, call'st thou me host? Now, by this hand,
PISTOL: I swear, I scorn the term, Nor shall my Nell keep lodgers.
Hostess: No, by my troth, not long, for we cannot lodge and
Hostess: board a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen that live
Hostess: honestly by the prick of their needles, but it will
Hostess: be thought we keep a bawdy house straight.
NARRATOR: NYM and PISTOL draw
Hostess: O well a day, Lady, if he be not drawn now! we
Hostess: shall see wilful adultery and murder committed.
BARDOLPH: Good lieutenant! good corporal! offer nothing here.
NYM: Pish!
PISTOL: Pish for thee, Iceland dog! thou prick-ear'd cur of Iceland!
Hostess: Good Corporal Nym, show thy valour, and put up your sword.
NYM: Will you shog off? I would have you solus.
PISTOL: 'Solus,' egregious dog? O viper vile!
PISTOL: The 'solus' in thy most mervailous face,
PISTOL: The 'solus' in thy teeth, and in thy throat,
PISTOL: And in thy hateful lungs, yea, in thy maw, perdy,
PISTOL: And, which is worse, within thy nasty mouth!
PISTOL: I do retort the 'solus' in thy bowels,
PISTOL: For I can take, and Pistol's cock is up,
PISTOL: And flashing fire will follow.
NYM: I am not Barbason, you cannot conjure me. I have an
NYM: humour to knock you indifferently well. If you grow
NYM: foul with me, Pistol, I will scour you with my
NYM: rapier, as I may, in fair terms: if you would walk
NYM: off, I would prick your guts a little, in good
NYM: terms, as I may: and that's the humour of it.
PISTOL: O braggart vile and damned furious wight!
PISTOL: The grave doth gape, and doting death is near,
PISTOL: Therefore exhale.
BARDOLPH: Hear me, hear me what I say: he that strikes the
BARDOLPH: first stroke, I'll run him up to the hilts, as I am a soldier.
NARRATOR: Draws
PISTOL: An oath of mickle might, and fury shall abate.
PISTOL: Give me thy fist, thy fore-foot to me give:
PISTOL: Thy spirits are most tall.
NYM: I will cut thy throat, one time or other, in fair
NYM: terms: that is the humour of it.
PISTOL: 'Couple a gorge!'
PISTOL: That is the word. I thee defy again.
PISTOL: O hound of Crete, think'st thou my spouse to get?
PISTOL: No, to the spital go,
PISTOL: And from the powdering tub of infamy
PISTOL: Fetch forth the lazar kite of Cressid's kind,
PISTOL: Doll Tearsheet she by name, and her espouse:
PISTOL: I have, and I will hold, the quondam Quickly
PISTOL: For the only she, and--pauca, there's enough. Go to.
NARRATOR: Enter the Boy
Boy: Mine host Pistol, you must come to my master, and
Boy: you, hostess: he is very sick, and would to bed.
Boy: Good Bardolph, put thy face between his sheets, and
Boy: do the office of a warming-pan. Faith, he's very ill.
BARDOLPH: Away, you rogue!
Hostess: By my troth, he'll yield the crow a pudding one of
Hostess: these days. The king has killed his heart. Good
Hostess: husband, come home presently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Hostess and Boy
BARDOLPH: Come, shall I make you two friends? We must to
BARDOLPH: France together: why the devil should we keep
BARDOLPH: knives to cut one another's throats?
PISTOL: Let floods o'erswell, and fiends for food howl on!
NYM: You'll pay me the eight shillings I won of you at betting?
PISTOL: Base is the slave that pays.
NYM: That now I will have: that's the humour of it.
PISTOL: As manhood shall compound: push home.
NARRATOR: They draw
BARDOLPH: By this sword, he that makes the first thrust, I'll
BARDOLPH: kill him, by this sword, I will.
PISTOL: Sword is an oath, and oaths must have their course.
BARDOLPH: Corporal Nym, an thou wilt be friends, be friends:
BARDOLPH: an thou wilt not, why, then, be enemies with me too.
BARDOLPH: Prithee, put up.
NYM: I shall have my eight shillings I won of you at betting?
PISTOL: A noble shalt thou have, and present pay,
PISTOL: And liquor likewise will I give to thee,
PISTOL: And friendship shall combine, and brotherhood:
PISTOL: I'll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me,
PISTOL: Is not this just? for I shall sutler be
PISTOL: Unto the camp, and profits will accrue.
PISTOL: Give me thy hand.
NYM: I shall have my noble?
PISTOL: In cash most justly paid.
NYM: Well, then, that's the humour of't.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Hostess
Hostess: As ever you came of women, come in quickly to Sir
Hostess: John. Ah, poor heart! he is so shaked of a burning
Hostess: quotidian tertian, that it is most lamentable to
Hostess: behold. Sweet men, come to him.
NYM: The king hath run bad humours on the knight, that's
NYM: the even of it.
PISTOL: Nym, thou hast spoke the right,
PISTOL: His heart is fracted and corroborate.
NYM: The king is a good king: but it must be as it may,
NYM: he passes some humours and careers.
PISTOL: Let us condole the knight, for, lambkins we will live.
PISTOL: SCENE II. Southampton. A council-chamber.
NARRATOR: Enter EXETER, BEDFORD, and WESTMORELAND
BEDFORD: 'Fore God, his grace is bold, to trust these traitors.
EXETER: They shall be apprehended by and by.
WESTMORELAND: How smooth and even they do bear themselves!
WESTMORELAND: As if allegiance in their bosoms sat,
WESTMORELAND: Crowned with faith and constant loyalty.
BEDFORD: The king hath note of all that they intend,
BEDFORD: By interception which they dream not of.
EXETER: Nay, but the man that was his bedfellow,
EXETER: Whom he hath dull'd and cloy'd with gracious favours,
EXETER: That he should, for a foreign purse, so sell
EXETER: His sovereign's life to death and treachery.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound. Enter KING HENRY V, SCROOP, CAMBRIDGE, GREY, and Attendants
KING HENRY V: Now sits the wind fair, and we will aboard.
KING HENRY V: My Lord of Cambridge, and my kind Lord of Masham,
KING HENRY V: And you, my gentle knight, give me your thoughts:
KING HENRY V: Think you not that the powers we bear with us
KING HENRY V: Will cut their passage through the force of France,
KING HENRY V: Doing the execution and the act
KING HENRY V: For which we have in head assembled them?
SCROOP: No doubt, my liege, if each man do his best.
KING HENRY V: I doubt not that, since we are well persuaded
KING HENRY V: We carry not a heart with us from hence
KING HENRY V: That grows not in a fair consent with ours,
KING HENRY V: Nor leave not one behind that doth not wish
KING HENRY V: Success and conquest to attend on us.
CAMBRIDGE: Never was monarch better fear'd and loved
CAMBRIDGE: Than is your majesty: there's not, I think, a subject
CAMBRIDGE: That sits in heart-grief and uneasiness
CAMBRIDGE: Under the sweet shade of your government.
GREY: True: those that were your father's enemies
GREY: Have steep'd their galls in honey and do serve you
GREY: With hearts create of duty and of zeal.
KING HENRY V: We therefore have great cause of thankfulness,
KING HENRY V: And shall forget the office of our hand,
KING HENRY V: Sooner than quittance of desert and merit
KING HENRY V: According to the weight and worthiness.
SCROOP: So service shall with steeled sinews toil,
SCROOP: And labour shall refresh itself with hope,
SCROOP: To do your grace incessant services.
KING HENRY V: We judge no less. Uncle of Exeter,
KING HENRY V: Enlarge the man committed yesterday,
KING HENRY V: That rail'd against our person: we consider
KING HENRY V: it was excess of wine that set him on,
KING HENRY V: And on his more advice we pardon him.
SCROOP: That's mercy, but too much security:
SCROOP: Let him be punish'd, sovereign, lest example
SCROOP: Breed, by his sufferance, more of such a kind.
KING HENRY V: O, let us yet be merciful.
CAMBRIDGE: So may your highness, and yet punish too.
GREY: Sir,
GREY: You show great mercy, if you give him life,
GREY: After the taste of much correction.
KING HENRY V: Alas, your too much love and care of me
KING HENRY V: Are heavy orisons 'gainst this poor wretch!
KING HENRY V: If little faults, proceeding on distemper,
KING HENRY V: Shall not be wink'd at, how shall we stretch our eye
KING HENRY V: When capital crimes, chew'd, swallow'd and digested,
KING HENRY V: Appear before us? We'll yet enlarge that man,
KING HENRY V: Though Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, in their dear care
KING HENRY V: And tender preservation of our person,
KING HENRY V: Would have him punished. And now to our French causes:
KING HENRY V: Who are the late commissioners?
CAMBRIDGE: I one, my lord:
CAMBRIDGE: Your highness bade me ask for it to-day.
SCROOP: So did you me, my liege.
GREY: And I, my royal sovereign.
KING HENRY V: Then, Richard Earl of Cambridge, there is yours,
KING HENRY V: There yours, Lord Scroop of Masham, and, sir knight,
KING HENRY V: Grey of Northumberland, this same is yours:
KING HENRY V: Read them, and know, I know your worthiness.
KING HENRY V: My Lord of Westmoreland, and uncle Exeter,
KING HENRY V: We will aboard to night. Why, how now, gentlemen!
KING HENRY V: What see you in those papers that you lose
KING HENRY V: So much complexion? Look ye, how they change!
KING HENRY V: Their cheeks are paper. Why, what read you there
KING HENRY V: That hath so cowarded and chased your blood
KING HENRY V: Out of appearance?
CAMBRIDGE: I do confess my fault,
CAMBRIDGE: And do submit me to your highness' mercy.
SCROOP: To which we all appeal.
KING HENRY V: The mercy that was quick in us but late,
KING HENRY V: By your own counsel is suppress'd and kill'd:
KING HENRY V: You must not dare, for shame, to talk of mercy,
KING HENRY V: For your own reasons turn into your bosoms,
KING HENRY V: As dogs upon their masters, worrying you.
KING HENRY V: See you, my princes, and my noble peers,
KING HENRY V: These English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here,
KING HENRY V: You know how apt our love was to accord
KING HENRY V: To furnish him with all appertinents
KING HENRY V: Belonging to his honour, and this man
KING HENRY V: Hath, for a few light crowns, lightly conspired,
KING HENRY V: And sworn unto the practises of France,
KING HENRY V: To kill us here in Hampton: to the which
KING HENRY V: This knight, no less for bounty bound to us
KING HENRY V: Than Cambridge is, hath likewise sworn. But, O,
KING HENRY V: What shall I say to thee, Lord Scroop? thou cruel,
KING HENRY V: Ingrateful, savage and inhuman creature!
KING HENRY V: Thou that didst bear the key of all my counsels,
KING HENRY V: That knew'st the very bottom of my soul,
KING HENRY V: That almost mightst have coin'd me into gold,
KING HENRY V: Wouldst thou have practised on me for thy use,
KING HENRY V: May it be possible, that foreign hire
KING HENRY V: Could out of thee extract one spark of evil
KING HENRY V: That might annoy my finger? 'tis so strange,
KING HENRY V: That, though the truth of it stands off as gross
KING HENRY V: As black and white, my eye will scarcely see it.
KING HENRY V: Treason and murder ever kept together,
KING HENRY V: As two yoke-devils sworn to either's purpose,
KING HENRY V: Working so grossly in a natural cause,
KING HENRY V: That admiration did not whoop at them:
KING HENRY V: But thou, 'gainst all proportion, didst bring in
KING HENRY V: Wonder to wait on treason and on murder:
KING HENRY V: And whatsoever cunning fiend it was
KING HENRY V: That wrought upon thee so preposterously
KING HENRY V: Hath got the voice in hell for excellence:
KING HENRY V: All other devils that suggest by treasons
KING HENRY V: Do botch and bungle up damnation
KING HENRY V: With patches, colours, and with forms being fetch'd
KING HENRY V: From glistering semblances of piety,
KING HENRY V: But he that temper'd thee bade thee stand up,
KING HENRY V: Gave thee no instance why thou shouldst do treason,
KING HENRY V: Unless to dub thee with the name of traitor.
KING HENRY V: If that same demon that hath gull'd thee thus
KING HENRY V: Should with his lion gait walk the whole world,
KING HENRY V: He might return to vasty Tartar back,
KING HENRY V: And tell the legions 'I can never win
KING HENRY V: A soul so easy as that Englishman's.'
KING HENRY V: O, how hast thou with 'jealousy infected
KING HENRY V: The sweetness of affiance! Show men dutiful?
KING HENRY V: Why, so didst thou: seem they grave and learned?
KING HENRY V: Why, so didst thou: come they of noble family?
KING HENRY V: Why, so didst thou: seem they religious?
KING HENRY V: Why, so didst thou: or are they spare in diet,
KING HENRY V: Free from gross passion or of mirth or anger,
KING HENRY V: Constant in spirit, not swerving with the blood,
KING HENRY V: Garnish'd and deck'd in modest complement,
KING HENRY V: Not working with the eye without the ear,
KING HENRY V: And but in purged judgment trusting neither?
KING HENRY V: Such and so finely bolted didst thou seem:
KING HENRY V: And thus thy fall hath left a kind of blot,
KING HENRY V: To mark the full-fraught man and best indued
KING HENRY V: With some suspicion. I will weep for thee,
KING HENRY V: For this revolt of thine, methinks, is like
KING HENRY V: Another fall of man. Their faults are open:
KING HENRY V: Arrest them to the answer of the law,
KING HENRY V: And God acquit them of their practises!
EXETER: I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of
EXETER: Richard Earl of Cambridge.
EXETER: I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of
EXETER: Henry Lord Scroop of Masham.
EXETER: I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of
EXETER: Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.
SCROOP: Our purposes God justly hath discover'd,
SCROOP: And I repent my fault more than my death,
SCROOP: Which I beseech your highness to forgive,
SCROOP: Although my body pay the price of it.
CAMBRIDGE: For me, the gold of France did not seduce,
CAMBRIDGE: Although I did admit it as a motive
CAMBRIDGE: The sooner to effect what I intended:
CAMBRIDGE: But God be thanked for prevention,
CAMBRIDGE: Which I in sufferance heartily will rejoice,
CAMBRIDGE: Beseeching God and you to pardon me.
GREY: Never did faithful subject more rejoice
GREY: At the discovery of most dangerous treason
GREY: Than I do at this hour joy o'er myself.
GREY: Prevented from a damned enterprise:
GREY: My fault, but not my body, pardon, sovereign.
KING HENRY V: God quit you in his mercy! Hear your sentence.
KING HENRY V: You have conspired against our royal person,
KING HENRY V: Join'd with an enemy proclaim'd and from his coffers
KING HENRY V: Received the golden earnest of our death,
KING HENRY V: Wherein you would have sold your king to slaughter,
KING HENRY V: His princes and his peers to servitude,
KING HENRY V: His subjects to oppression and contempt
KING HENRY V: And his whole kingdom into desolation.
KING HENRY V: Touching our person seek we no revenge,
KING HENRY V: But we our kingdom's safety must so tender,
KING HENRY V: Whose ruin you have sought, that to her laws
KING HENRY V: We do deliver you. Get you therefore hence,
KING HENRY V: Poor miserable wretches, to your death:
KING HENRY V: The taste whereof, God of his mercy give
KING HENRY V: You patience to endure, and true repentance
KING HENRY V: Of all your dear offences! Bear them hence.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CAMBRIDGE, SCROOP and GREY, guarded
KING HENRY V: Now, lords, for France, the enterprise whereof
KING HENRY V: Shall be to you, as us, like glorious.
KING HENRY V: We doubt not of a fair and lucky war,
KING HENRY V: Since God so graciously hath brought to light
KING HENRY V: This dangerous treason lurking in our way
KING HENRY V: To hinder our beginnings. We doubt not now
KING HENRY V: But every rub is smoothed on our way.
KING HENRY V: Then forth, dear countrymen: let us deliver
KING HENRY V: Our puissance into the hand of God,
KING HENRY V: Putting it straight in expedition.
KING HENRY V: Cheerly to sea, the signs of war advance:
KING HENRY V: No king of England, if not king of France.

NARRATOR: SCENE III. London. Before a tavern.
NARRATOR: Enter PISTOL, Hostess, NYM, BARDOLPH, and Boy
Hostess: Prithee, honey-sweet husband, let me bring thee to Staines.
PISTOL: No, for my manly heart doth yearn.
PISTOL: Bardolph, be blithe: Nym, rouse thy vaunting veins:
PISTOL: Boy, bristle thy courage up, for Falstaff he is dead,
PISTOL: And we must yearn therefore.
BARDOLPH: Would I were with him, wheresome'er he is, either in
BARDOLPH: heaven or in hell!
Hostess: Nay, sure, he's not in hell: he's in Arthur's
Hostess: bosom, if ever man went to Arthur's bosom. A' made
Hostess: a finer end and went away an it had been any
Hostess: christom child, a' parted even just between twelve
Hostess: and one, even at the turning o' the tide: for after
Hostess: I saw him fumble with the sheets and play with
Hostess: flowers and smile upon his fingers' ends, I knew
Hostess: there was but one way, for his nose was as sharp as
Hostess: a pen, and a' babbled of green fields. 'How now,
Hostess: sir John!' quoth I	'what, man! be o' good
Hostess: cheer.' So a' cried out 'God, God, God!' three or
Hostess: four times. Now I, to comfort him, bid him a'
Hostess: should not think of God, I hoped there was no need
Hostess: to trouble himself with any such thoughts yet. So
Hostess: a' bade me lay more clothes on his feet: I put my
Hostess: hand into the bed and felt them, and they were as
Hostess: cold as any stone, then I felt to his knees, and
Hostess: they were as cold as any stone, and so upward and
Hostess: upward, and all was as cold as any stone.
NYM: They say he cried out of sack.
Hostess: Ay, that a' did.
BARDOLPH: And of women.
Hostess: Nay, that a' did not.
Boy: Yes, that a' did, and said they were devils
Boy: incarnate.
Hostess: A' could never abide carnation, 'twas a colour he
Hostess: never liked.
Boy: A' said once, the devil would have him about women.
Hostess: A' did in some sort, indeed, handle women, but then
Hostess: he was rheumatic, and talked of the whore of Babylon.
Boy: Do you not remember, a' saw a flea stick upon
Boy: Bardolph's nose, and a' said it was a black soul
Boy: burning in hell-fire?
BARDOLPH: Well, the fuel is gone that maintained that fire:
BARDOLPH: that's all the riches I got in his service.
NYM: Shall we shog? the king will be gone from
NYM: Southampton.
PISTOL: Come, let's away. My love, give me thy lips.
PISTOL: Look to my chattels and my movables:
PISTOL: Let senses rule, the word is 'Pitch and Pay:'
PISTOL: Trust none,
PISTOL: For oaths are straws, men's faiths are wafer-cakes,
PISTOL: And hold-fast is the only dog, my duck:
PISTOL: Therefore, Caveto be thy counsellor.
PISTOL: Go, clear thy c rystals. Yoke-fellows in arms,
PISTOL: Let us to France, like horse-leeches, my boys,
PISTOL: To suck, to suck, the very blood to suck!
Boy: And that's but unwholesome food they say.
PISTOL: Touch her soft mouth, and march.
BARDOLPH: Farewell, hostess.
NARRATOR: Kissing her
NYM: I cannot kiss, that is the humour of it, but, adieu.
PISTOL: Let housewifery appear: keep close, I thee command.
Hostess: Farewell, adieu.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. France. The KING'S palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter the FRENCH KING, the DAUPHIN, the DUKES of BERRI and BRETAGNE, the Constable, and others
KING OF FRANCE: Thus comes the English with full power upon us,
KING OF FRANCE: And more than carefully it us concerns
KING OF FRANCE: To answer royally in our defences.
KING OF FRANCE: Therefore the Dukes of Berri and of Bretagne,
KING OF FRANCE: Of Brabant and of Orleans, shall make forth,
KING OF FRANCE: And you, Prince Dauphin, with all swift dispatch,
KING OF FRANCE: To line and new repair our towns of war
KING OF FRANCE: With men of courage and with means defendant,
KING OF FRANCE: For England his approaches makes as fierce
KING OF FRANCE: As waters to the sucking of a gulf.
KING OF FRANCE: It fits us then to be as provident
KING OF FRANCE: As fear may teach us out of late examples
KING OF FRANCE: Left by the fatal and neglected English
KING OF FRANCE: Upon our fields.
DAUPHIN: My most redoubted father,
DAUPHIN: It is most meet we arm us 'gainst the foe,
DAUPHIN: For peace itself should not so dull a kingdom,
DAUPHIN: Though war nor no known quarrel were in question,
DAUPHIN: But that defences, musters, preparations,
DAUPHIN: Should be maintain'd, assembled and collected,
DAUPHIN: As were a war in expectation.
DAUPHIN: Therefore, I say 'tis meet we all go forth
DAUPHIN: To view the sick and feeble parts of France:
DAUPHIN: And let us do it with no show of fear,
DAUPHIN: No, with no more than if we heard that England
DAUPHIN: Were busied with a Whitsun morris-dance:
DAUPHIN: For, my good liege, she is so idly king'd,
DAUPHIN: Her sceptre so fantastically borne
DAUPHIN: By a vain, giddy, shallow, humorous youth,
DAUPHIN: That fear attends her not.
Constable: O peace, Prince Dauphin!
Constable: You are too much mistaken in this king:
Constable: Question your grace the late ambassadors,
Constable: With what great state he heard their embassy,
Constable: How well supplied with noble counsellors,
Constable: How modest in exception, and withal
Constable: How terrible in constant resolution,
Constable: And you shall find his vanities forespent
Constable: Were but the outside of the Roman Brutus,
Constable: Covering discretion with a coat of folly,
Constable: As gardeners do with ordure hide those roots
Constable: That shall first spring and be most delicate.
DAUPHIN: Well, 'tis not so, my lord high constable,
DAUPHIN: But though we think it so, it is no matter:
DAUPHIN: In cases of defence 'tis best to weigh
DAUPHIN: The enemy more mighty than he seems:
DAUPHIN: So the proportions of defence are fill'd,
DAUPHIN: Which of a weak or niggardly projection
DAUPHIN: Doth, like a miser, spoil his coat with scanting
DAUPHIN: A little cloth.
KING OF FRANCE: Think we King Harry strong,
KING OF FRANCE: And, princes, look you strongly arm to meet him.
KING OF FRANCE: The kindred of him hath been flesh'd upon us,
KING OF FRANCE: And he is bred out of that bloody strain
KING OF FRANCE: That haunted us in our familiar paths:
KING OF FRANCE: Witness our too much memorable shame
KING OF FRANCE: When Cressy battle fatally was struck,
KING OF FRANCE: And all our princes captiv'd by the hand
KING OF FRANCE: Of that black name, Edward, Black Prince of Wales,
KING OF FRANCE: Whiles that his mountain sire, on mountain standing,
KING OF FRANCE: Up in the air, crown'd with the golden sun,
KING OF FRANCE: Saw his heroical seed, and smiled to see him,
KING OF FRANCE: Mangle the work of nature and deface
KING OF FRANCE: The patterns that by God and by French fathers
KING OF FRANCE: Had twenty years been made. This is a stem
KING OF FRANCE: Of that victorious stock, and let us fear
KING OF FRANCE: The native mightiness and fate of him.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Ambassadors from Harry King of England
Messenger: Do crave admittance to your majesty.
KING OF FRANCE: We'll give them present audience. Go, and bring them.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Messenger and certain Lords
KING OF FRANCE: You see this chase is hotly follow'd, friends.
DAUPHIN: Turn head, and stop pursuit, for coward dogs
DAUPHIN: Most spend their mouths when what they seem to threaten
DAUPHIN: Runs far before them. Good my sovereign,
DAUPHIN: Take up the English short, and let them know
DAUPHIN: Of what a monarchy you are the head:
DAUPHIN: Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin
DAUPHIN: As self-neglecting.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Lords, with EXETER and train
KING OF FRANCE: From our brother England?
EXETER: From him, and thus he greets your majesty.
EXETER: He wills you, in the name of God Almighty,
EXETER: That you divest yourself, and lay apart
EXETER: The borrow'd glories that by gift of heaven,
EXETER: By law of nature and of nations, 'long
EXETER: To him and to his heirs, namely, the crown
EXETER: And all wide-stretched honours that pertain
EXETER: By custom and the ordinance of times
EXETER: Unto the crown of France. That you may know
EXETER: 'Tis no sinister nor no awkward claim,
EXETER: Pick'd from the worm-holes of long-vanish'd days,
EXETER: Nor from the dust of old oblivion raked,
EXETER: He sends you this most memorable line,
EXETER: In every branch truly demonstrative,
EXETER: Willing to overlook this pedigree:
EXETER: And when you find him evenly derived
EXETER: From his most famed of famous ancestors,
EXETER: Edward the Third, he bids you then resign
EXETER: Your crown and kingdom, indirectly held
EXETER: From him the native and true challenger.
KING OF FRANCE: Or else what follows?
EXETER: Bloody constraint, for if you hide the crown
EXETER: Even in your hearts, there will he rake for it:
EXETER: Therefore in fierce tempest is he coming,
EXETER: In thunder and in earthquake, like a Jove,
EXETER: That, if requiring fail, he will compel,
EXETER: And bids you, in the bowels of the Lord,
EXETER: Deliver up the crown, and to take mercy
EXETER: On the poor souls for whom this hungry war
EXETER: Opens his vasty jaws, and on your head
EXETER: Turning the widows' tears, the orphans' cries
EXETER: The dead men's blood, the pining maidens groans,
EXETER: For husbands, fathers and betrothed lovers,
EXETER: That shall be swallow'd in this controversy.
EXETER: This is his claim, his threatening and my message,
EXETER: Unless the Dauphin be in presence here,
EXETER: To whom expressly I bring greeting too.
KING OF FRANCE: For us, we will consider of this further:
KING OF FRANCE: To-morrow shall you bear our full intent
KING OF FRANCE: Back to our brother England.
DAUPHIN: For the Dauphin,
DAUPHIN: I stand here for him: what to him from England?
EXETER: Scorn and defiance, slight regard, contempt,
EXETER: And any thing that may not misbecome
EXETER: The mighty sender, doth he prize you at.
EXETER: Thus says my king, an' if your father's highness
EXETER: Do not, in grant of all demands at large,
EXETER: Sweeten the bitter mock you sent his majesty,
EXETER: He'll call you to so hot an answer of it,
EXETER: That caves and womby vaultages of France
EXETER: Shall chide your trespass and return your mock
EXETER: In second accent of his ordnance.
DAUPHIN: Say, if my father render fair return,
DAUPHIN: It is against my will, for I desire
DAUPHIN: Nothing but odds with England: to that end,
DAUPHIN: As matching to his youth and vanity,
DAUPHIN: I did present him with the Paris balls.
EXETER: He'll make your Paris Louvre shake for it,
EXETER: Were it the mistress-court of mighty Europe:
EXETER: And, be assured, you'll find a difference,
EXETER: As we his subjects have in wonder found,
EXETER: Between the promise of his greener days
EXETER: And these he masters now: now he weighs time
EXETER: Even to the utmost grain: that you shall read
EXETER: In your own losses, if he stay in France.
KING OF FRANCE: To-morrow shall you know our mind at full.
EXETER: Dispatch us with all speed, lest that our king
EXETER: Come here himself to question our delay,
EXETER: For he is footed in this land already.
KING OF FRANCE: You shall be soon dispatch's with fair conditions:
KING OF FRANCE: A night is but small breath and little pause
KING OF FRANCE: To answer matters of this consequence.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Thus with imagined wing our swift scene flies
Chorus: In motion of no less celerity
Chorus: Than that of thought. Suppose that you have seen
Chorus: The well-appointed king at Hampton pier
Chorus: Embark his royalty, and his brave fleet
Chorus: With silken streamers the young Phoebus fanning:
Chorus: Play with your fancies, and in them behold
Chorus: Upon the hempen tackle ship-boys climbing,
Chorus: Hear the shrill whistle which doth order give
Chorus: To sounds confused, behold the threaden sails,
Chorus: Borne with the invisible and creeping wind,
Chorus: Draw the huge bottoms through the furrow'd sea,
Chorus: Breasting the lofty surge: O, do but think
Chorus: You stand upon the ravage and behold
Chorus: A city on the inconstant billows dancing,
Chorus: For so appears this fleet majestical,
Chorus: Holding due course to Harfleur. Follow, follow:
Chorus: Grapple your minds to sternage of this navy,
Chorus: And leave your England, as dead midnight still,
Chorus: Guarded with grandsires, babies and old women,
Chorus: Either past or not arrived to pith and puissance,
Chorus: For who is he, whose chin is but enrich'd
Chorus: With one appearing hair, that will not follow
Chorus: These cull'd and choice-drawn cavaliers to France?
Chorus: Work, work your thoughts, and therein see a siege,
Chorus: Behold the ordnance on their carriages,
Chorus: With fatal mouths gaping on girded Harfleur.
Chorus: Suppose the ambassador from the French comes back,
Chorus: Tells Harry that the king doth offer him
Chorus: Katharine his daughter, and with her, to dowry,
Chorus: Some petty and unprofitable dukedoms.
Chorus: The offer likes not: and the nimble gunner
Chorus: With linstock now the devilish cannon touches,
NARRATOR: Alarum, and chambers go off
Chorus: And down goes all before them. Still be kind,
Chorus: And eke out our performance with your mind.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. France. Before Harfleur.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter KING HENRY, EXETER, BEDFORD, GLOUCESTER, and Soldiers, with scaling-ladders
KING HENRY V: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more,
KING HENRY V: Or close the wall up with our English dead.
KING HENRY V: In peace there's nothing so becomes a man
KING HENRY V: As modest stillness and humility:
KING HENRY V: But when the blast of war blows in our ears,
KING HENRY V: Then imitate the action of the tiger,
KING HENRY V: Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood,
KING HENRY V: Disguise fair nature with hard-favour'd rage,
KING HENRY V: Then lend the eye a terrible aspect,
KING HENRY V: Let pry through the portage of the head
KING HENRY V: Like the brass cannon, let the brow o'erwhelm it
KING HENRY V: As fearfully as doth a galled rock
KING HENRY V: O'erhang and jutty his confounded base,
KING HENRY V: Swill'd with the wild and wasteful ocean.
KING HENRY V: Now set the teeth and stretch the nostril wide,
KING HENRY V: Hold hard the breath and bend up every spirit
KING HENRY V: To his full height. On, on, you noblest English.
KING HENRY V: Whose blood is fet from fathers of war-proof!
KING HENRY V: Fathers that, like so many Alexanders,
KING HENRY V: Have in these parts from morn till even fought
KING HENRY V: And sheathed their swords for lack of argument:
KING HENRY V: Dishonour not your mothers, now attest
KING HENRY V: That those whom you call'd fathers did beget you.
KING HENRY V: Be copy now to men of grosser blood,
KING HENRY V: And teach them how to war. And you, good yeoman,
KING HENRY V: Whose limbs were made in England, show us here
KING HENRY V: The mettle of your pasture, let us swear
KING HENRY V: That you are worth your breeding, which I doubt not,
KING HENRY V: For there is none of you so mean and base,
KING HENRY V: That hath not noble lustre in your eyes.
KING HENRY V: I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips,
KING HENRY V: Straining upon the start. The game's afoot:
KING HENRY V: Follow your spirit, and upon this charge
KING HENRY V: Cry 'God for Harry, England, and Saint George!'
NARRATOR: Exeunt. Alarum, and chambers go off
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter NYM, BARDOLPH, PISTOL, and Boy
BARDOLPH: On, on, on, on, on! to the breach, to the breach!
NYM: Pray thee, corporal, stay: the knocks are too hot,
NYM: and, for mine own part, I have not a case of lives:
NYM: the humour of it is too hot, that is the very
NYM: plain-song of it.
PISTOL: The plain-song is most just: for humours do abound:
PISTOL: Knocks go and come, God's vassals drop and die,
PISTOL: And sword and shield,
PISTOL: In bloody field,
PISTOL: Doth win immortal fame.
Boy: Would I were in an alehouse in London! I would give
Boy: all my fame for a pot of ale and safety.
PISTOL: And I:
PISTOL: If wishes would prevail with me,
PISTOL: My purpose should not fail with me,
PISTOL: But thither would I hie.
Boy: As duly, but not as truly,
Boy: As bird doth sing on bough.
NARRATOR: Enter FLUELLEN
FLUELLEN: Up to the breach, you dogs! avaunt, you cullions!
NARRATOR: Driving them forward
PISTOL: Be merciful, great duke, to men of mould.
PISTOL: Abate thy rage, abate thy manly rage,
PISTOL: Abate thy rage, great duke!
PISTOL: Good bawcock, bate thy rage, use lenity, sweet chuck!
NYM: These be good humours! your honour wins bad humours.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but Boy
Boy: As young as I am, I have observed these three
Boy: swashers. I am boy to them all three: but all they
Boy: three, though they would serve me, could not be man
Boy: to me, for indeed three such antics do not amount to
Boy: a man. For Bardolph, he is white-livered and
Boy: red-faced, by the means whereof a' faces it out, but
Boy: fights not. For Pistol, he hath a killing tongue
Boy: and a quiet sword, by the means whereof a' breaks
Boy: words, and keeps whole weapons. For Nym, he hath
Boy: heard that men of few words are the best men, and
Boy: therefore he scorns to say his prayers, lest a'
Boy: should be thought a coward: but his few bad words
Boy: are matched with as few good deeds, for a' never
Boy: broke any man's head but his own, and that was
Boy: against a post when he was drunk. They will steal
Boy: any thing, and call it purchase. Bardolph stole a
Boy: lute-case, bore it twelve leagues, and sold it for
Boy: three half pence. Nym and Bardolph are sworn
Boy: brothers in filching, and in Calais they stole a
Boy: fire-shovel: I knew by that piece of service the
Boy: men would carry coals. They would have me as
Boy: familiar with men's pockets as their gloves or their
Boy: handkerchers: which makes much against my manhood,
Boy: if I should take from another's pocket to put into
Boy: mine, for it is plain pocketing up of wrongs. I
Boy: must leave them, and seek some better service:
Boy: their villany goes against my weak stomach, and
Boy: therefore I must cast it up.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter FLUELLEN, GOWER following
GOWER: Captain Fluellen, you must come presently to the
GOWER: mines, the Duke of Gloucester would speak with you.
FLUELLEN: To the mines! tell you the duke, it is not so good
FLUELLEN: to come to the mines, for, look you, the mines is
FLUELLEN: not according to the disciplines of the war: the
FLUELLEN: concavities of it is not sufficient, for, look you,
FLUELLEN: the athversary, you may discuss unto the duke, look
FLUELLEN: you, is digt himself four yard under the
FLUELLEN: countermines: by Cheshu, I think a' will plough up
FLUELLEN: all, if there is not better directions.
GOWER: The Duke of Gloucester, to whom the order of the
GOWER: siege is given, is altogether directed by an
GOWER: Irishman, a very valiant gentleman, i' faith.
FLUELLEN: It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?
GOWER: I think it be.
FLUELLEN: By Cheshu, he is an ass, as in the world: I will
FLUELLEN: verify as much in his beard: be has no more
FLUELLEN: directions in the true disciplines of the wars, look
FLUELLEN: you, of the Roman disciplines, than is a puppy-dog.
NARRATOR: Enter MACMORRIS and Captain JAMY
GOWER: Here a' comes, and the Scots captain, Captain Jamy, with him.
FLUELLEN: Captain Jamy is a marvellous falourous gentleman,
FLUELLEN: that is certain, and of great expedition and
FLUELLEN: knowledge in th' aunchient wars, upon my particular
FLUELLEN: knowledge of his directions: by Cheshu, he will
FLUELLEN: maintain his argument as well as any military man in
FLUELLEN: the world, in the disciplines of the pristine wars
FLUELLEN: of the Romans.
JAMY: I say gud-day, Captain Fluellen.
FLUELLEN: God-den to your worship, good Captain James.
GOWER: How now, Captain Macmorris! have you quit the
GOWER: mines? have the pioneers given o'er?
MACMORRIS: By Chrish, la! tish ill done: the work ish give
MACMORRIS: over, the trompet sound the retreat. By my hand, I
MACMORRIS: swear, and my father's soul, the work ish ill done,
MACMORRIS: it ish give over: I would have blowed up the town, so
MACMORRIS: Chrish save me, la! in an hour: O, tish ill done,
MACMORRIS: tish ill done, by my hand, tish ill done!
FLUELLEN: Captain Macmorris, I beseech you now, will you
FLUELLEN: voutsafe me, look you, a few disputations with you,
FLUELLEN: as partly touching or concerning the disciplines of
FLUELLEN: the war, the Roman wars, in the way of argument,
FLUELLEN: look you, and friendly communication, partly to
FLUELLEN: satisfy my opinion, and partly for the satisfaction,
FLUELLEN: look you, of my mind, as touching the direction of
FLUELLEN: the military discipline, that is the point.
JAMY: It sall be vary gud, gud feith, gud captains bath:
JAMY: and I sall quit you with gud leve, as I may pick
JAMY: occasion, that sall I, marry.
MACMORRIS: It is no time to discourse, so Chrish save me: the
MACMORRIS: day is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the
MACMORRIS: king, and the dukes: it is no time to discourse. The
MACMORRIS: town is beseeched, and the trumpet call us to the
MACMORRIS: breach, and we talk, and, be Chrish, do nothing:
MACMORRIS: 'tis shame for us all: so God sa' me, 'tis shame to
MACMORRIS: stand still, it is shame, by my hand: and there is
MACMORRIS: throats to be cut, and works to be done, and there
MACMORRIS: ish nothing done, so Chrish sa' me, la!
JAMY: By the mess, ere theise eyes of mine take themselves
JAMY: to slomber, ay'll de gud service, or ay'll lig i'
JAMY: the grund for it, ay, or go to death, and ay'll pay
JAMY: 't as valourously as I may, that sall I suerly do,
JAMY: that is the breff and the long. Marry, I wad full
JAMY: fain hear some question 'tween you tway.
FLUELLEN: Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, under your
FLUELLEN: correction, there is not many of your nation--
MACMORRIS: Of my nation! What ish my nation? Ish a villain,
MACMORRIS: and a bastard, and a knave, and a rascal. What ish
MACMORRIS: my nation? Who talks of my nation?
FLUELLEN: Look you, if you take the matter otherwise than is
FLUELLEN: meant, Captain Macmorris, peradventure I shall think
FLUELLEN: you do not use me with that affability as in
FLUELLEN: discretion you ought to use me, look you: being as
FLUELLEN: good a man as yourself, both in the disciplines of
FLUELLEN: war, and in the derivation of my birth, and in
FLUELLEN: other particularities.
MACMORRIS: I do not know you so good a man as myself: so
MACMORRIS: Chrish save me, I will cut off your head.
GOWER: Gentlemen both, you will mistake each other.
JAMY: A! that's a foul fault.
NARRATOR: A parley sounded
GOWER: The town sounds a parley.
FLUELLEN: Captain Macmorris, when there is more better
FLUELLEN: opportunity to be required, look you, I will be so
FLUELLEN: bold as to tell you I know the disciplines of war,
FLUELLEN: and there is an end.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. Before the gates.
NARRATOR: The Governor and some Citizens on the walls, the English forces below. Enter KING HENRY and his train
KING HENRY V: How yet resolves the governor of the town?
KING HENRY V: This is the latest parle we will admit,
KING HENRY V: Therefore to our best mercy give yourselves,
KING HENRY V: Or like to men proud of destruction
KING HENRY V: Defy us to our worst: for, as I am a soldier,
KING HENRY V: A name that in my thoughts becomes me best,
KING HENRY V: If I begin the battery once again,
KING HENRY V: I will not leave the half-achieved Harfleur
KING HENRY V: Till in her ashes she lie buried.
KING HENRY V: The gates of mercy shall be all shut up,
KING HENRY V: And the flesh'd soldier, rough and hard of heart,
KING HENRY V: In liberty of bloody hand shall range
KING HENRY V: With conscience wide as hell, mowing like grass
KING HENRY V: Your fresh-fair virgins and your flowering infants.
KING HENRY V: What is it then to me, if impious war,
KING HENRY V: Array'd in flames like to the prince of fiends,
KING HENRY V: Do, with his smirch'd complexion, all fell feats
KING HENRY V: Enlink'd to waste and desolation?
KING HENRY V: What is't to me, when you yourselves are cause,
KING HENRY V: If your pure maidens fall into the hand
KING HENRY V: Of hot and forcing violation?
KING HENRY V: What rein can hold licentious wickedness
KING HENRY V: When down the hill he holds his fierce career?
KING HENRY V: We may as bootless spend our vain command
KING HENRY V: Upon the enraged soldiers in their spoil
KING HENRY V: As send precepts to the leviathan
KING HENRY V: To come ashore. Therefore, you men of Harfleur,
KING HENRY V: Take pity of your town and of your people,
KING HENRY V: Whiles yet my soldiers are in my command,
KING HENRY V: Whiles yet the cool and temperate wind of grace
KING HENRY V: O'erblows the filthy and contagious clouds
KING HENRY V: Of heady murder, spoil and villany.
KING HENRY V: If not, why, in a moment look to see
KING HENRY V: The blind and bloody soldier with foul hand
KING HENRY V: Defile the locks of your shrill-shrieking daughters,
KING HENRY V: Your fathers taken by the silver beards,
KING HENRY V: And their most reverend heads dash'd to the walls,
KING HENRY V: Your naked infants spitted upon pikes,
KING HENRY V: Whiles the mad mothers with their howls confused
KING HENRY V: Do break the clouds, as did the wives of Jewry
KING HENRY V: At Herod's bloody-hunting slaughtermen.
KING HENRY V: What say you? will you yield, and this avoid,
KING HENRY V: Or, guilty in defence, be thus destroy'd?
GOVERNOR: Our expectation hath this day an end:
GOVERNOR: The Dauphin, whom of succors we entreated,
GOVERNOR: Returns us that his powers are yet not ready
GOVERNOR: To raise so great a siege. Therefore, great king,
GOVERNOR: We yield our town and lives to thy soft mercy.
GOVERNOR: Enter our gates, dispose of us and ours,
GOVERNOR: For we no longer are defensible.
KING HENRY V: Open your gates. Come, uncle Exeter,
KING HENRY V: Go you and enter Harfleur, there remain,
KING HENRY V: And fortify it strongly 'gainst the French:
KING HENRY V: Use mercy to them all. For us, dear uncle,
KING HENRY V: The winter coming on and sickness growing
KING HENRY V: Upon our soldiers, we will retire to Calais.
KING HENRY V: To-night in Harfleur we will be your guest,
KING HENRY V: To-morrow for the march are we addrest.
NARRATOR: Flourish. The King and his train enter the town
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The FRENCH KING's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KATHARINE and ALICE
KATHARINE: Alice, tu as ete en Angleterre, et tu parles bien le langage.
ALICE: Un peu, madame.
KATHARINE: Je te prie, m'enseignez: il faut que j'apprenne a
KATHARINE: parler. Comment appelez-vous la main en Anglois?
ALICE: La main? elle est appelee de hand.
KATHARINE: De hand. Et les doigts?
ALICE: Les doigts? ma foi, j'oublie les doigts, mais je me
ALICE: souviendrai. Les doigts? je pense qu'ils sont
ALICE: appeles de fingres, oui, de fingres.
KATHARINE: La main, de hand, les doigts, de fingres. Je pense
KATHARINE: que je suis le bon ecolier, j'ai gagne deux mots
KATHARINE: d'Anglois vitement. Comment appelez-vous les ongles?
ALICE: Les ongles? nous les appelons de nails.
KATHARINE: De nails. Ecoutez, dites-moi, si je parle bien: de
KATHARINE: hand, de fingres, et de nails.
ALICE: C'est bien dit, madame, il est fort bon Anglois.
KATHARINE: Dites-moi l'Anglois pour le bras.
ALICE: De arm, madame.
KATHARINE: Et le coude?
ALICE: De elbow.
KATHARINE: De elbow. Je m'en fais la repetition de tous les
KATHARINE: mots que vous m'avez appris des a present.
ALICE: Il est trop difficile, madame, comme je pense.
KATHARINE: Excusez-moi, Alice, ecoutez: de hand, de fingres,
KATHARINE: de nails, de arma, de bilbow.
ALICE: De elbow, madame.
KATHARINE: O Seigneur Dieu, je m'en oublie! de elbow. Comment
KATHARINE: appelez-vous le col?
ALICE: De neck, madame.
KATHARINE: De nick. Et le menton?
ALICE: De chin.
KATHARINE: De sin. Le col, de nick, de menton, de sin.
ALICE: Oui. Sauf votre honneur, en verite, vous prononcez
ALICE: les mots aussi droit que les natifs d'Angleterre.
KATHARINE: Je ne doute point d'apprendre, par la grace de Dieu,
KATHARINE: et en peu de temps.
ALICE: N'avez vous pas deja oublie ce que je vous ai enseigne?
KATHARINE: Non, je reciterai a vous promptement: de hand, de
KATHARINE: fingres, de mails--
ALICE: De nails, madame.
KATHARINE: De nails, de arm, de ilbow.
ALICE: Sauf votre honneur, de elbow.
KATHARINE: Ainsi dis-je, de elbow, de nick, et de sin. Comment
KATHARINE: appelez-vous le pied et la robe?
ALICE: De foot, madame, et de coun.
KATHARINE: De foot et de coun! O Seigneur Dieu! ce sont mots
KATHARINE: de son mauvais, corruptible, gros, et impudique, et
KATHARINE: non pour les dames d'honneur d'user: je ne voudrais
KATHARINE: prononcer ces mots devant les seigneurs de France
KATHARINE: pour tout le monde. Foh! le foot et le coun!
KATHARINE: Neanmoins, je reciterai une autre fois ma lecon
KATHARINE: ensemble: de hand, de fingres, de nails, de arm, de
KATHARINE: elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, de coun.
ALICE: Excellent, madame!
KATHARINE: C'est assez pour une fois: allons-nous a diner.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter the KING OF FRANCE, the DAUPHIN, the DUKE oF BOURBON, the Constable Of France, and others
KING OF FRANCE: 'Tis certain he hath pass'd the river Somme.
Constable: And if he be not fought withal, my lord,
Constable: Let us not live in France, let us quit all
Constable: And give our vineyards to a barbarous people.
DAUPHIN: O Dieu vivant! shall a few sprays of us,
DAUPHIN: The emptying of our fathers' luxury,
DAUPHIN: Our scions, put in wild and savage stock,
DAUPHIN: Spirt up so suddenly into the clouds,
DAUPHIN: And overlook their grafters?
BOURBON: Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards!
BOURBON: Mort de ma vie! if they march along
BOURBON: Unfought withal, but I will sell my dukedom,
BOURBON: To buy a slobbery and a dirty farm
BOURBON: In that nook-shotten isle of Albion.
Constable: Dieu de batailles! where have they this mettle?
Constable: Is not their climate foggy, raw and dull,
Constable: On whom, as in despite, the sun looks pale,
Constable: Killing their fruit with frowns? Can sodden water,
Constable: A drench for sur-rein'd jades, their barley-broth,
Constable: Decoct their cold blood to such valiant heat?
Constable: And shall our quick blood, spirited with wine,
Constable: Seem frosty? O, for honour of our land,
Constable: Let us not hang like roping icicles
Constable: Upon our houses' thatch, whiles a more frosty people
Constable: Sweat drops of gallant youth in our rich fields!
Constable: Poor we may call them in their native lords.
DAUPHIN: By faith and honour,
DAUPHIN: Our madams mock at us, and plainly say
DAUPHIN: Our mettle is bred out and they will give
DAUPHIN: Their bodies to the lust of English youth
DAUPHIN: To new-store France with bastard warriors.
BOURBON: They bid us to the English dancing-schools,
BOURBON: And teach lavoltas high and swift corantos,
BOURBON: Saying our grace is only in our heels,
BOURBON: And that we are most lofty runaways.
KING OF FRANCE: Where is Montjoy the herald? speed him hence:
KING OF FRANCE: Let him greet England with our sharp defiance.
KING OF FRANCE: Up, princes! and, with spirit of honour edged
KING OF FRANCE: More sharper than your swords, hie to the field:
KING OF FRANCE: Charles Delabreth, high constable of France,
KING OF FRANCE: You Dukes of Orleans, Bourbon, and of Berri,
KING OF FRANCE: Alencon, Brabant, Bar, and Burgundy,
KING OF FRANCE: Jaques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont,
KING OF FRANCE: Beaumont, Grandpre, Roussi, and Fauconberg,
KING OF FRANCE: Foix, Lestrale, Bouciqualt, and Charolois,
KING OF FRANCE: High dukes, great princes, barons, lords and knights,
KING OF FRANCE: For your great seats now quit you of great shames.
KING OF FRANCE: Bar Harry England, that sweeps through our land
KING OF FRANCE: With pennons painted in the blood of Harfleur:
KING OF FRANCE: Rush on his host, as doth the melted snow
KING OF FRANCE: Upon the valleys, whose low vassal seat
KING OF FRANCE: The Alps doth spit and void his rheum upon:
KING OF FRANCE: Go down upon him, you have power enough,
KING OF FRANCE: And in a captive chariot into Rouen
KING OF FRANCE: Bring him our prisoner.
Constable: This becomes the great.
Constable: Sorry am I his numbers are so few,
Constable: His soldiers sick and famish'd in their march,
Constable: For I am sure, when he shall see our army,
Constable: He'll drop his heart into the sink of fear
Constable: And for achievement offer us his ransom.
KING OF FRANCE: Therefore, lord constable, haste on Montjoy.
KING OF FRANCE: And let him say to England that we send
KING OF FRANCE: To know what willing ransom he will give.
KING OF FRANCE: Prince Dauphin, you shall stay with us in Rouen.
DAUPHIN: Not so, I do beseech your majesty.
KING OF FRANCE: Be patient, for you shall remain with us.
KING OF FRANCE: Now forth, lord constable and princes all,
KING OF FRANCE: And quickly bring us word of England's fall.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The English camp in Picardy.
NARRATOR: Enter GOWER and FLUELLEN, meeting
GOWER: How now, Captain Fluellen! come you from the bridge?
FLUELLEN: I assure you, there is very excellent services
FLUELLEN: committed at the bridge.
GOWER: Is the Duke of Exeter safe?
FLUELLEN: The Duke of Exeter is as magnanimous as Agamemnon,
FLUELLEN: and a man that I love and honour with my soul, and my
FLUELLEN: heart, and my duty, and my life, and my living, and
FLUELLEN: my uttermost power: he is not-God be praised and
FLUELLEN: blessed!--any hurt in the world, but keeps the
FLUELLEN: bridge most valiantly, with excellent discipline.
FLUELLEN: There is an aunchient lieutenant there at the
FLUELLEN: pridge, I think in my very conscience he is as
FLUELLEN: valiant a man as Mark Antony, and he is a man of no
FLUELLEN: estimation in the world, but did see him do as
FLUELLEN: gallant service.
GOWER: What do you call him?
FLUELLEN: He is called Aunchient Pistol.
GOWER: I know him not.
NARRATOR: Enter PISTOL
FLUELLEN: Here is the man.
PISTOL: Captain, I thee beseech to do me favours:
PISTOL: The Duke of Exeter doth love thee well.
FLUELLEN: Ay, I praise God, and I have merited some love at
FLUELLEN: his hands.
PISTOL: Bardolph, a soldier, firm and sound of heart,
PISTOL: And of buxom valour, hath, by cruel fate,
PISTOL: And giddy Fortune's furious fickle wheel,
PISTOL: That goddess blind,
PISTOL: That stands upon the rolling restless stone--
FLUELLEN: By your patience, Aunchient Pistol. Fortune is
FLUELLEN: painted blind, with a muffler afore her eyes, to
FLUELLEN: signify to you that Fortune is blind, and she is
FLUELLEN: painted also with a wheel, to signify to you, which
FLUELLEN: is the moral of it, that she is turning, and
FLUELLEN: inconstant, and mutability, and variation: and her
FLUELLEN: foot, look you, is fixed upon a spherical stone,
FLUELLEN: which rolls, and rolls, and rolls: in good truth,
FLUELLEN: the poet makes a most excellent description of it:
FLUELLEN: Fortune is an excellent moral.
PISTOL: Fortune is Bardolph's foe, and frowns on him,
PISTOL: For he hath stolen a pax, and hanged must a' be:
PISTOL: A damned death!
PISTOL: Let gallows gape for dog, let man go free
PISTOL: And let not hemp his wind-pipe suffocate:
PISTOL: But Exeter hath given the doom of death
PISTOL: For pax of little price.
PISTOL: Therefore, go speak: the duke will hear thy voice:
PISTOL: And let not Bardolph's vital thread be cut
PISTOL: With edge of penny cord and vile reproach:
PISTOL: Speak, captain, for his life, and I will thee requite.
FLUELLEN: Aunchient Pistol, I do partly understand your meaning.
PISTOL: Why then, rejoice therefore.
FLUELLEN: Certainly, aunchient, it is not a thing to rejoice
FLUELLEN: at: for if, look you, he were my brother, I would
FLUELLEN: desire the duke to use his good pleasure, and put
FLUELLEN: him to execution, for discipline ought to be used.
PISTOL: Die and be damn'd! and figo for thy friendship!
FLUELLEN: It is well.
PISTOL: The fig of Spain!
NARRATOR: Exit
FLUELLEN: Very good.
GOWER: Why, this is an arrant counterfeit rascal, I
GOWER: remember him now, a bawd, a cutpurse.
FLUELLEN: I'll assure you, a' uttered as brave words at the
FLUELLEN: bridge as you shall see in a summer's day. But it
FLUELLEN: is very well, what he has spoke to me, that is well,
FLUELLEN: I warrant you, when time is serve.
GOWER: Why, 'tis a gull, a fool, a rogue, that now and then
GOWER: goes to the wars, to grace himself at his return
GOWER: into London under the form of a soldier. And such
GOWER: fellows are perfect in the great commanders' names:
GOWER: and they will learn you by rote where services were
GOWER: done, at such and such a sconce, at such a breach,
GOWER: at such a convoy, who came off bravely, who was
GOWER: shot, who disgraced, what terms the enemy stood on,
GOWER: and this they con perfectly in the phrase of war,
GOWER: which they trick up with new-tuned oaths: and what
GOWER: a beard of the general's cut and a horrid suit of
GOWER: the camp will do among foaming bottles and
GOWER: ale-washed wits, is wonderful to be thought on. But
GOWER: you must learn to know such slanders of the age, or
GOWER: else you may be marvellously mistook.
FLUELLEN: I tell you what, Captain Gower, I do perceive he is
FLUELLEN: not the man that he would gladly make show to the
FLUELLEN: world he is: if I find a hole in his coat, I will
FLUELLEN: tell him my mind.
NARRATOR: Drum heard
FLUELLEN: Hark you, the king is coming, and I must speak with
FLUELLEN: him from the pridge.
NARRATOR: Drum and colours. Enter KING HENRY, GLOUCESTER, and Soldiers
FLUELLEN: God pless your majesty!
KING HENRY V: How now, Fluellen! camest thou from the bridge?
FLUELLEN: Ay, so please your majesty. The Duke of Exeter has
FLUELLEN: very gallantly maintained the pridge: the French is
FLUELLEN: gone off, look you, and there is gallant and most
FLUELLEN: prave passages, marry, th' athversary was have
FLUELLEN: possession of the pridge, but he is enforced to
FLUELLEN: retire, and the Duke of Exeter is master of the
FLUELLEN: pridge: I can tell your majesty, the duke is a
FLUELLEN: prave man.
KING HENRY V: What men have you lost, Fluellen?
FLUELLEN: The perdition of th' athversary hath been very
FLUELLEN: great, reasonable great: marry, for my part, I
FLUELLEN: think the duke hath lost never a man, but one that
FLUELLEN: is like to be executed for robbing a church, one
FLUELLEN: Bardolph, if your majesty know the man: his face is
FLUELLEN: all bubukles, and whelks, and knobs, and flames o'
FLUELLEN: fire: and his lips blows at his nose, and it is like
FLUELLEN: a coal of fire, sometimes plue and sometimes red,
FLUELLEN: but his nose is executed and his fire's out.
KING HENRY V: We would have all such offenders so cut off: and we
KING HENRY V: give express charge, that in our marches through the
KING HENRY V: country, there be nothing compelled from the
KING HENRY V: villages, nothing taken but paid for, none of the
KING HENRY V: French upbraided or abused in disdainful language,
KING HENRY V: for when lenity and cruelty play for a kingdom, the
KING HENRY V: gentler gamester is the soonest winner.
NARRATOR: Tucket. Enter MONTJOY
MONTJOY: You know me by my habit.
KING HENRY V: Well then I know thee: what shall I know of thee?
MONTJOY: My master's mind.
KING HENRY V: Unfold it.
MONTJOY: Thus says my king: Say thou to Harry of England:
MONTJOY: Though we seemed dead, we did but sleep: advantage
MONTJOY: is a better soldier than rashness. Tell him we
MONTJOY: could have rebuked him at Harfleur, but that we
MONTJOY: thought not good to bruise an injury till it were
MONTJOY: full ripe: now we speak upon our cue, and our voice
MONTJOY: is imperial: England shall repent his folly, see
MONTJOY: his weakness, and admire our sufferance. Bid him
MONTJOY: therefore consider of his ransom, which must
MONTJOY: proportion the losses we have borne, the subjects we
MONTJOY: have lost, the disgrace we have digested, which in
MONTJOY: weight to re-answer, his pettiness would bow under.
MONTJOY: For our losses, his exchequer is too poor, for the
MONTJOY: effusion of our blood, the muster of his kingdom too
MONTJOY: faint a number, and for our disgrace, his own
MONTJOY: person, kneeling at our feet, but a weak and
MONTJOY: worthless satisfaction. To this add defiance: and
MONTJOY: tell him, for conclusion, he hath betrayed his
MONTJOY: followers, whose condemnation is pronounced. So far
MONTJOY: my king and master, so much my office.
KING HENRY V: What is thy name? I know thy quality.
MONTJOY: Montjoy.
KING HENRY V: Thou dost thy office fairly. Turn thee back.
KING HENRY V: And tell thy king I do not seek him now,
KING HENRY V: But could be willing to march on to Calais
KING HENRY V: Without impeachment: for, to say the sooth,
KING HENRY V: Though 'tis no wisdom to confess so much
KING HENRY V: Unto an enemy of craft and vantage,
KING HENRY V: My people are with sickness much enfeebled,
KING HENRY V: My numbers lessened, and those few I have
KING HENRY V: Almost no better than so many French,
KING HENRY V: Who when they were in health, I tell thee, herald,
KING HENRY V: I thought upon one pair of English legs
KING HENRY V: Did march three Frenchmen. Yet, forgive me, God,
KING HENRY V: That I do brag thus! This your air of France
KING HENRY V: Hath blown that vice in me: I must repent.
KING HENRY V: Go therefore, tell thy master here I am,
KING HENRY V: My ransom is this frail and worthless trunk,
KING HENRY V: My army but a weak and sickly guard,
KING HENRY V: Yet, God before, tell him we will come on,
KING HENRY V: Though France himself and such another neighbour
KING HENRY V: Stand in our way. There's for thy labour, Montjoy.
KING HENRY V: Go bid thy master well advise himself:
KING HENRY V: If we may pass, we will, if we be hinder'd,
KING HENRY V: We shall your tawny ground with your red blood
KING HENRY V: Discolour: and so Montjoy, fare you well.
KING HENRY V: The sum of all our answer is but this:
KING HENRY V: We would not seek a battle, as we are,
KING HENRY V: Nor, as we are, we say we will not shun it:
KING HENRY V: So tell your master.
MONTJOY: I shall deliver so. Thanks to your highness.
NARRATOR: Exit
GLOUCESTER: I hope they will not come upon us now.
KING HENRY V: We are in God's hand, brother, not in theirs.
KING HENRY V: March to the bridge, it now draws toward night:
KING HENRY V: Beyond the river we'll encamp ourselves,
KING HENRY V: And on to-morrow, bid them march away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. The French camp, near Agincourt:
NARRATOR: Enter the Constable of France, the LORD RAMBURES, ORLEANS, DAUPHIN, with others
Constable: Tut! I have the best armour of the world. Would it were day!
ORLEANS: You have an excellent armour, but let my horse have his due.
Constable: It is the best horse of Europe.
ORLEANS: Will it never be morning?
DAUPHIN: My lord of Orleans, and my lord high constable, you
DAUPHIN: talk of horse and armour?
ORLEANS: You are as well provided of both as any prince in the world.
DAUPHIN: What a long night is this! I will not change my
DAUPHIN: horse with any that treads but on four pasterns.
DAUPHIN: Ca, ha! he bounds from the earth, as if his
DAUPHIN: entrails were hairs, le cheval volant, the Pegasus,
DAUPHIN: chez les narines de feu! When I bestride him, I
DAUPHIN: soar, I am a hawk: he trots the air, the earth
DAUPHIN: sings when he touches it, the basest horn of his
DAUPHIN: hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
ORLEANS: He's of the colour of the nutmeg.
DAUPHIN: And of the heat of the ginger. It is a beast for
DAUPHIN: Perseus: he is pure air and fire, and the dull
DAUPHIN: elements of earth and water never appear in him, but
DAUPHIN: only in Patient stillness while his rider mounts
DAUPHIN: him: he is indeed a horse, and all other jades you
DAUPHIN: may call beasts.
Constable: Indeed, my lord, it is a most absolute and excellent horse.
DAUPHIN: It is the prince of palfreys, his neigh is like the
DAUPHIN: bidding of a monarch and his countenance enforces homage.
ORLEANS: No more, cousin.
DAUPHIN: Nay, the man hath no wit that cannot, from the
DAUPHIN: rising of the lark to the lodging of the lamb, vary
DAUPHIN: deserved praise on my palfrey: it is a theme as
DAUPHIN: fluent as the sea: turn the sands into eloquent
DAUPHIN: tongues, and my horse is argument for them all:
DAUPHIN: 'tis a subject for a sovereign to reason on, and for
DAUPHIN: a sovereign's sovereign to ride on, and for the
DAUPHIN: world, familiar to us and unknown to lay apart
DAUPHIN: their particular functions and wonder at him. I
DAUPHIN: once writ a sonnet in his praise and began thus:
DAUPHIN: 'Wonder of nature,'--
ORLEANS: I have heard a sonnet begin so to one's mistress.
DAUPHIN: Then did they imitate that which I composed to my
DAUPHIN: courser, for my horse is my mistress.
ORLEANS: Your mistress bears well.
DAUPHIN: Me well, which is the prescript praise and
DAUPHIN: perfection of a good and particular mistress.
Constable: Nay, for methought yesterday your mistress shrewdly
Constable: shook your back.
DAUPHIN: So perhaps did yours.
Constable: Mine was not bridled.
DAUPHIN: O then belike she was old and gentle, and you rode,
DAUPHIN: like a kern of Ireland, your French hose off, and in
DAUPHIN: your straight strossers.
Constable: You have good judgment in horsemanship.
DAUPHIN: Be warned by me, then: they that ride so and ride
DAUPHIN: not warily, fall into foul bogs. I had rather have
