DAUPHIN: my horse to my mistress.
Constable: I had as lief have my mistress a jade.
DAUPHIN: I tell thee, constable, my mistress wears his own hair.
Constable: I could make as true a boast as that, if I had a sow
Constable: to my mistress.
DAUPHIN: 'Le chien est retourne a son propre vomissement, et
DAUPHIN: la truie lavee au bourbier,' thou makest use of any thing.
Constable: Yet do I not use my horse for my mistress, or any
Constable: such proverb so little kin to the purpose.
RAMBURES: My lord constable, the armour that I saw in your tent
RAMBURES: to-night, are those stars or suns upon it?
Constable: Stars, my lord.
DAUPHIN: Some of them will fall to-morrow, I hope.
Constable: And yet my sky shall not want.
DAUPHIN: That may be, for you bear a many superfluously, and
DAUPHIN: 'twere more honour some were away.
Constable: Even as your horse bears your praises, who would
Constable: trot as well, were some of your brags dismounted.
DAUPHIN: Would I were able to load him with his desert! Will
DAUPHIN: it never be day? I will trot to-morrow a mile, and
DAUPHIN: my way shall be paved with English faces.
Constable: I will not say so, for fear I should be faced out of
Constable: my way: but I would it were morning, for I would
Constable: fain be about the ears of the English.
RAMBURES: Who will go to hazard with me for twenty prisoners?
Constable: You must first go yourself to hazard, ere you have them.
DAUPHIN: 'Tis midnight, I'll go arm myself.
NARRATOR: Exit
ORLEANS: The Dauphin longs for morning.
RAMBURES: He longs to eat the English.
Constable: I think he will eat all he kills.
ORLEANS: By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
Constable: Swear by her foot, that she may tread out the oath.
ORLEANS: He is simply the most active gentleman of France.
Constable: Doing is activity, and he will still be doing.
ORLEANS: He never did harm, that I heard of.
Constable: Nor will do none to-morrow: he will keep that good name still.
ORLEANS: I know him to be valiant.
Constable: I was told that  by one that knows him better than
Constable: you.
ORLEANS: What's he?
Constable: Marry, he told me so himself, and he said he cared
Constable: not who knew it
ORLEANS: He needs not, it is no hidden virtue in him.
Constable: By my faith, sir, but it is, never any body saw it
Constable: but his lackey: 'tis a hooded valour, and when it
Constable: appears, it will bate.
ORLEANS: Ill will never said well.
Constable: I will cap that proverb with 'There is flattery in friendship.'
ORLEANS: And I will take up that with 'Give the devil his due.'
Constable: Well placed: there stands your friend for the
Constable: devil: have at the very eye of that proverb with 'A
Constable: pox of the devil.'
ORLEANS: You are the better at proverbs, by how much 'A
ORLEANS: fool's bolt is soon shot.'
Constable: You have shot over.
ORLEANS: 'Tis not the first time you were overshot.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord high constable, the English lie within
Messenger: fifteen hundred paces of your tents.
Constable: Who hath measured the ground?
Messenger: The Lord Grandpre.
Constable: A valiant and most expert gentleman. Would it were
Constable: day! Alas, poor Harry of England! he longs not for
Constable: the dawning as we do.
ORLEANS: What a wretched and peevish fellow is this king of
ORLEANS: England, to mope with his fat-brained followers so
ORLEANS: far out of his knowledge!
Constable: If the English had any apprehension, they would run away.
ORLEANS: That they lack, for if their heads had any
ORLEANS: intellectual armour, they could never wear such heavy
ORLEANS: head-pieces.
RAMBURES: That island of England breeds very valiant
RAMBURES: creatures, their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage.
ORLEANS: Foolish curs, that run winking into the mouth of a
ORLEANS: Russian bear and have their heads crushed like
ORLEANS: rotten apples! You may as well say, that's a
ORLEANS: valiant flea that dare eat his breakfast on the lip of a lion.
Constable: Just, just, and the men do sympathize with the
Constable: mastiffs in robustious and rough coming on, leaving
Constable: their wits with their wives: and then give them
Constable: great meals of beef and iron and steel, they will
Constable: eat like wolves and fight like devils.
ORLEANS: Ay, but these English are shrewdly out of beef.
Constable: Then shall we find to-morrow they have only stomachs
Constable: to eat and none to fight. Now is it time to arm:
Constable: come, shall we about it?
ORLEANS: It is now two o'clock: but, let me see, by ten
ORLEANS: We shall have each a hundred Englishmen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Now entertain conjecture of a time
Chorus: When creeping murmur and the poring dark
Chorus: Fills the wide vessel of the universe.
Chorus: From camp to camp through the foul womb of night
Chorus: The hum of either army stilly sounds,
Chorus: That the fixed sentinels almost receive
Chorus: The secret whispers of each other's watch:
Chorus: Fire answers fire, and through their paly flames
Chorus: Each battle sees the other's umber'd face,
Chorus: Steed threatens steed, in high and boastful neighs
Chorus: Piercing the night's dull ear, and from the tents
Chorus: The armourers, accomplishing the knights,
Chorus: With busy hammers closing rivets up,
Chorus: Give dreadful note of preparation:
Chorus: The country cocks do crow, the clocks do toll,
Chorus: And the third hour of drowsy morning name.
Chorus: Proud of their numbers and secure in soul,
Chorus: The confident and over-lusty French
Chorus: Do the low-rated English play at dice,
Chorus: And chide the cripple tardy-gaited night
Chorus: Who, like a foul and ugly witch, doth limp
Chorus: So tediously away. The poor condemned English,
Chorus: Like sacrifices, by their watchful fires
Chorus: Sit patiently and inly ruminate
Chorus: The morning's danger, and their gesture sad
Chorus: Investing lank-lean, cheeks and war-worn coats
Chorus: Presenteth them unto the gazing moon
Chorus: So many horrid ghosts. O now, who will behold
Chorus: The royal captain of this ruin'd band
Chorus: Walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent,
Chorus: Let him cry 'Praise and glory on his head!'
Chorus: For forth he goes and visits all his host.
Chorus: Bids them good morrow with a modest smile
Chorus: And calls them brothers, friends and countrymen.
Chorus: Upon his royal face there is no note
Chorus: How dread an army hath enrounded him,
Chorus: Nor doth he dedicate one jot of colour
Chorus: Unto the weary and all-watched night,
Chorus: But freshly looks and over-bears attaint
Chorus: With cheerful semblance and sweet majesty,
Chorus: That every wretch, pining and pale before,
Chorus: Beholding him, plucks comfort from his looks:
Chorus: A largess universal like the sun
Chorus: His liberal eye doth give to every one,
Chorus: Thawing cold fear, that mean and gentle all,
Chorus: Behold, as may unworthiness define,
Chorus: A little touch of Harry in the night.
Chorus: And so our scene must to the battle fly,
Chorus: Where--O for pity!--we shall much disgrace
Chorus: With four or five most vile and ragged foils,
Chorus: Right ill-disposed in brawl ridiculous,
Chorus: The name of Agincourt. Yet sit and see,
Chorus: Minding true things by what their mockeries be.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The English camp at Agincourt.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY, BEDFORD, and GLOUCESTER
KING HENRY V: Gloucester, 'tis true that we are in great danger,
KING HENRY V: The greater therefore should our courage be.
KING HENRY V: Good morrow, brother Bedford. God Almighty!
KING HENRY V: There is some soul of goodness in things evil,
KING HENRY V: Would men observingly distil it out.
KING HENRY V: For our bad neighbour makes us early stirrers,
KING HENRY V: Which is both healthful and good husbandry:
KING HENRY V: Besides, they are our outward consciences,
KING HENRY V: And preachers to us all, admonishing
KING HENRY V: That we should dress us fairly for our end.
KING HENRY V: Thus may we gather honey from the weed,
KING HENRY V: And make a moral of the devil himself.
NARRATOR: Enter ERPINGHAM
KING HENRY V: Good morrow, old Sir Thomas Erpingham:
KING HENRY V: A good soft pillow for that good white head
KING HENRY V: Were better than a churlish turf of France.
ERPINGHAM: Not so, my liege: this lodging likes me better,
ERPINGHAM: Since I may say 'Now lie I like a king.'
KING HENRY V: 'Tis good for men to love their present pains
KING HENRY V: Upon example, so the spirit is eased:
KING HENRY V: And when the mind is quicken'd, out of doubt,
KING HENRY V: The organs, though defunct and dead before,
KING HENRY V: Break up their drowsy grave and newly move,
KING HENRY V: With casted slough and fresh legerity.
KING HENRY V: Lend me thy cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both,
KING HENRY V: Commend me to the princes in our camp,
KING HENRY V: Do my good morrow to them, and anon
KING HENRY V: Desire them an to my pavilion.
GLOUCESTER: We shall, my liege.
ERPINGHAM: Shall I attend your grace?
KING HENRY V: No, my good knight,
KING HENRY V: Go with my brothers to my lords of England:
KING HENRY V: I and my bosom must debate awhile,
KING HENRY V: And then I would no other company.
ERPINGHAM: The Lord in heaven bless thee, noble Harry!
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but KING HENRY
KING HENRY V: God-a-mercy, old heart! thou speak'st cheerfully.
NARRATOR: Enter PISTOL
PISTOL: Qui va la?
KING HENRY V: A friend.
PISTOL: Discuss unto me, art thou officer?
PISTOL: Or art thou base, common and popular?
KING HENRY V: I am a gentleman of a company.
PISTOL: Trail'st thou the puissant pike?
KING HENRY V: Even so. What are you?
PISTOL: As good a gentleman as the emperor.
KING HENRY V: Then you are a better than the king.
PISTOL: The king's a bawcock, and a heart of gold,
PISTOL: A lad of life, an imp of fame,
PISTOL: Of parents good, of fist most valiant.
PISTOL: I kiss his dirty shoe, and from heart-string
PISTOL: I love the lovely bully. What is thy name?
KING HENRY V: Harry le Roy.
PISTOL: Le Roy! a Cornish name: art thou of Cornish crew?
KING HENRY V: No, I am a Welshman.
PISTOL: Know'st thou Fluellen?
KING HENRY V: Yes.
PISTOL: Tell him, I'll knock his leek about his pate
PISTOL: Upon Saint Davy's day.
KING HENRY V: Do not you wear your dagger in your cap that day,
KING HENRY V: lest he knock that about yours.
PISTOL: Art thou his friend?
KING HENRY V: And his kinsman too.
PISTOL: The figo for thee, then!
KING HENRY V: I thank you: God be with you!
PISTOL: My name is Pistol call'd.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING HENRY V: It sorts well with your fierceness.
NARRATOR: Enter FLUELLEN and GOWER
GOWER: Captain Fluellen!
FLUELLEN: So! in the name of Jesu Christ, speak lower. It is
FLUELLEN: the greatest admiration of the universal world, when
FLUELLEN: the true and aunchient prerogatifes and laws of the
FLUELLEN: wars is not kept: if you would take the pains but to
FLUELLEN: examine the wars of Pompey the Great, you shall
FLUELLEN: find, I warrant you, that there is no tiddle toddle
FLUELLEN: nor pibble pabble in Pompey's camp, I warrant you,
FLUELLEN: you shall find the ceremonies of the wars, and the
FLUELLEN: cares of it, and the forms of it, and the sobriety
FLUELLEN: of it, and the modesty of it, to be otherwise.
GOWER: Why, the enemy is loud, you hear him all night.
FLUELLEN: If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a prating
FLUELLEN: coxcomb, is it meet, think you, that we should also,
FLUELLEN: look you, be an ass and a fool and a prating
FLUELLEN: coxcomb? in your own conscience, now?
GOWER: I will speak lower.
FLUELLEN: I pray you and beseech you that you will.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GOWER and FLUELLEN
KING HENRY V: Though it appear a little out of fashion,
KING HENRY V: There is much care and valour in this Welshman.
NARRATOR: Enter three soldiers, JOHN BATES, ALEXANDER COURT, and MICHAEL WILLIAMS
COURT: Brother John Bates, is not that the morning which
COURT: breaks yonder?
BATES: I think it be: but we have no great cause to desire
BATES: the approach of day.
WILLIAMS: We see yonder the beginning of the day, but I think
WILLIAMS: we shall never see the end of it. Who goes there?
KING HENRY V: A friend.
WILLIAMS: Under what captain serve you?
KING HENRY V: Under Sir Thomas Erpingham.
WILLIAMS: A good old commander and a most kind gentleman: I
WILLIAMS: pray you, what thinks he of our estate?
KING HENRY V: Even as men wrecked upon a sand, that look to be
KING HENRY V: washed off the next tide.
BATES: He hath not told his thought to the king?
KING HENRY V: No, nor it is not meet he should. For, though I
KING HENRY V: speak it to you, I think the king is but a man, as I
KING HENRY V: am: the violet smells to him as it doth to me: the
KING HENRY V: element shows to him as it doth to me, all his
KING HENRY V: senses have but human conditions: his ceremonies
KING HENRY V: laid by, in his nakedness he appears but a man, and
KING HENRY V: though his affections are higher mounted than ours,
KING HENRY V: yet, when they stoop, they stoop with the like
KING HENRY V: wing. Therefore when he sees reason of fears, as we
KING HENRY V: do, his fears, out of doubt, be of the same relish
KING HENRY V: as ours are: yet, in reason, no man should possess
KING HENRY V: him with any appearance of fear, lest he, by showing
KING HENRY V: it, should dishearten his army.
BATES: He may show what outward courage he will, but I
BATES: believe, as cold a night as 'tis, he could wish
BATES: himself in Thames up to the neck, and so I would he
BATES: were, and I by him, at all adventures, so we were quit here.
KING HENRY V: By my troth, I will speak my conscience of the king:
KING HENRY V: I think he would not wish himself any where but
KING HENRY V: where he is.
BATES: Then I would he were here alone, so should he be
BATES: sure to be ransomed, and a many poor men's lives saved.
KING HENRY V: I dare say you love him not so ill, to wish him here
KING HENRY V: alone, howsoever you speak this to feel other men's
KING HENRY V: minds: methinks I could not die any where so
KING HENRY V: contented as in the king's company, his cause being
KING HENRY V: just and his quarrel honourable.
WILLIAMS: That's more than we know.
BATES: Ay, or more than we should seek after, for we know
BATES: enough, if we know we are the kings subjects: if
BATES: his cause be wrong, our obedience to the king wipes
BATES: the crime of it out of us.
WILLIAMS: But if the cause be not good, the king himself hath
WILLIAMS: a heavy reckoning to make, when all those legs and
WILLIAMS: arms and heads, chopped off in battle, shall join
WILLIAMS: together at the latter day and cry all 'We died at
WILLIAMS: such a place,' some swearing, some crying for a
WILLIAMS: surgeon, some upon their wives left poor behind
WILLIAMS: them, some upon the debts they owe, some upon their
WILLIAMS: children rawly left. I am afeard there are few die
WILLIAMS: well that die in a battle, for how can they
WILLIAMS: charitably dispose of any thing, when blood is their
WILLIAMS: argument? Now, if these men do not die well, it
WILLIAMS: will be a black matter for the king that led them to
WILLIAMS: it, whom to disobey were against all proportion of
WILLIAMS: subjection.
KING HENRY V: So, if a son that is by his father sent about
KING HENRY V: merchandise do sinfully miscarry upon the sea, the
KING HENRY V: imputation of his wickedness by your rule, should be
KING HENRY V: imposed upon his father that sent him: or if a
KING HENRY V: servant, under his master's command transporting a
KING HENRY V: sum of money, be assailed by robbers and die in
KING HENRY V: many irreconciled iniquities, you may call the
KING HENRY V: business of the master the author of the servant's
KING HENRY V: damnation: but this is not so: the king is not
KING HENRY V: bound to answer the particular endings of his
KING HENRY V: soldiers, the father of his son, nor the master of
KING HENRY V: his servant, for they purpose not their death, when
KING HENRY V: they purpose their services. Besides, there is no
KING HENRY V: king, be his cause never so spotless, if it come to
KING HENRY V: the arbitrement of swords, can try it out with all
KING HENRY V: unspotted soldiers: some peradventure have on them
KING HENRY V: the guilt of premeditated and contrived murder,
KING HENRY V: some, of beguiling virgins with the broken seals of
KING HENRY V: perjury, some, making the wars their bulwark, that
KING HENRY V: have before gored the gentle bosom of peace with
KING HENRY V: pillage and robbery. Now, if these men have
KING HENRY V: defeated the law and outrun native punishment,
KING HENRY V: though they can outstrip men, they have no wings to
KING HENRY V: fly from God: war is his beadle, war is vengeance,
KING HENRY V: so that here men are punished for before-breach of
KING HENRY V: the king's laws in now the king's quarrel: where
KING HENRY V: they feared the death, they have borne life away,
KING HENRY V: and where they would be safe, they perish: then if
KING HENRY V: they die unprovided, no more is the king guilty of
KING HENRY V: their damnation than he was before guilty of those
KING HENRY V: impieties for the which they are now visited. Every
KING HENRY V: subject's duty is the king's, but every subject's
KING HENRY V: soul is his own. Therefore should every soldier in
KING HENRY V: the wars do as every sick man in his bed, wash every
KING HENRY V: mote out of his conscience: and dying so, death
KING HENRY V: is to him advantage, or not dying, the time was
KING HENRY V: blessedly lost wherein such preparation was gained:
KING HENRY V: and in him that escapes, it were not sin to think
KING HENRY V: that, making God so free an offer, He let him
KING HENRY V: outlive that day to see His greatness and to teach
KING HENRY V: others how they should prepare.
WILLIAMS: 'Tis certain, every man that dies ill, the ill upon
WILLIAMS: his own head, the king is not to answer it.
BATES: But I do not desire he should answer for me, and
BATES: yet I determine to fight lustily for him.
KING HENRY V: I myself heard the king say he would not be ransomed.
WILLIAMS: Ay, he said so, to make us fight cheerfully: but
WILLIAMS: when our throats are cut, he may be ransomed, and we
WILLIAMS: ne'er the wiser.
KING HENRY V: If I live to see it, I will never trust his word after.
WILLIAMS: You pay him then. That's a perilous shot out of an
WILLIAMS: elder-gun, that a poor and private displeasure can
WILLIAMS: do against a monarch! you may as well go about to
WILLIAMS: turn the sun to ice with fanning in his face with a
WILLIAMS: peacock's feather. You'll never trust his word
WILLIAMS: after! come, 'tis a foolish saying.
KING HENRY V: Your reproof is something too round: I should be
KING HENRY V: angry with you, if the time were convenient.
WILLIAMS: Let it be a quarrel between us, if you live.
KING HENRY V: I embrace it.
WILLIAMS: How shall I know thee again?
KING HENRY V: Give me any gage of thine, and I will wear it in my
KING HENRY V: bonnet: then, if ever thou darest acknowledge it, I
KING HENRY V: will make it my quarrel.
WILLIAMS: Here's my glove: give me another of thine.
KING HENRY V: There.
WILLIAMS: This will I also wear in my cap: if ever thou come
WILLIAMS: to me and say, after to-morrow, 'This is my glove,'
WILLIAMS: by this hand, I will take thee a box on the ear.
KING HENRY V: If ever I live to see it, I will challenge it.
WILLIAMS: Thou darest as well be hanged.
KING HENRY V: Well. I will do it, though I take thee in the
KING HENRY V: king's company.
WILLIAMS: Keep thy word: fare thee well.
BATES: Be friends, you English fools, be friends: we have
BATES: French quarrels enow, if you could tell how to reckon.
KING HENRY V: Indeed, the French may lay twenty French crowns to
KING HENRY V: one, they will beat us, for they bear them on their
KING HENRY V: shoulders: but it is no English treason to cut
KING HENRY V: French crowns, and to-morrow the king himself will
KING HENRY V: be a clipper.
NARRATOR: Exeunt soldiers
KING HENRY V: Upon the king! let us our lives, our souls,
KING HENRY V: Our debts, our careful wives,
KING HENRY V: Our children and our sins lay on the king!
KING HENRY V: We must bear all. O hard condition,
KING HENRY V: Twin-born with greatness, subject to the breath
KING HENRY V: Of every fool, whose sense no more can feel
KING HENRY V: But his own wringing! What infinite heart's-ease
KING HENRY V: Must kings neglect, that private men enjoy!
KING HENRY V: And what have kings, that privates have not too,
KING HENRY V: Save ceremony, save general ceremony?
KING HENRY V: And what art thou, thou idle ceremony?
KING HENRY V: What kind of god art thou, that suffer'st more
KING HENRY V: Of mortal griefs than do thy worshippers?
KING HENRY V: What are thy rents? what are thy comings in?
KING HENRY V: O ceremony, show me but thy worth!
KING HENRY V: What is thy soul of adoration?
KING HENRY V: Art thou aught else but place, degree and form,
KING HENRY V: Creating awe and fear in other men?
KING HENRY V: Wherein thou art less happy being fear'd
KING HENRY V: Than they in fearing.
KING HENRY V: What drink'st thou oft, instead of homage sweet,
KING HENRY V: But poison'd flattery? O, be sick, great greatness,
KING HENRY V: And bid thy ceremony give thee cure!
KING HENRY V: Think'st thou the fiery fever will go out
KING HENRY V: With titles blown from adulation?
KING HENRY V: Will it give place to flexure and low bending?
KING HENRY V: Canst thou, when thou command'st the beggar's knee,
KING HENRY V: Command the health of it? No, thou proud dream,
KING HENRY V: That play'st so subtly with a king's repose,
KING HENRY V: I am a king that find thee, and I know
KING HENRY V: 'Tis not the balm, the sceptre and the ball,
KING HENRY V: The sword, the mace, the crown imperial,
KING HENRY V: The intertissued robe of gold and pearl,
KING HENRY V: The farced title running 'fore the king,
KING HENRY V: The throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp
KING HENRY V: That beats upon the high shore of this world,
KING HENRY V: No, not all these, thrice-gorgeous ceremony,
KING HENRY V: Not all these, laid in bed majestical,
KING HENRY V: Can sleep so soundly as the wretched slave,
KING HENRY V: Who with a body fill'd and vacant mind
KING HENRY V: Gets him to rest, cramm'd with distressful bread,
KING HENRY V: Never sees horrid night, the child of hell,
KING HENRY V: But, like a lackey, from the rise to set
KING HENRY V: Sweats in the eye of Phoebus and all night
KING HENRY V: Sleeps in Elysium, next day after dawn,
KING HENRY V: Doth rise and help Hyperion to his horse,
KING HENRY V: And follows so the ever-running year,
KING HENRY V: With profitable labour, to his grave:
KING HENRY V: And, but for ceremony, such a wretch,
KING HENRY V: Winding up days with toil and nights with sleep,
KING HENRY V: Had the fore-hand and vantage of a king.
KING HENRY V: The slave, a member of the country's peace,
KING HENRY V: Enjoys it, but in gross brain little wots
KING HENRY V: What watch the king keeps to maintain the peace,
KING HENRY V: Whose hours the peasant best advantages.
NARRATOR: Enter ERPINGHAM
ERPINGHAM: My lord, your nobles, jealous of your absence,
ERPINGHAM: Seek through your camp to find you.
KING HENRY V: Good old knight,
KING HENRY V: Collect them all together at my tent:
KING HENRY V: I'll be before thee.
ERPINGHAM: I shall do't, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING HENRY V: O God of battles! steel my soldiers' hearts,
KING HENRY V: Possess them not with fear, take from them now
KING HENRY V: The sense of reckoning, if the opposed numbers
KING HENRY V: Pluck their hearts from them. Not to-day, O Lord,
KING HENRY V: O, not to-day, think not upon the fault
KING HENRY V: My father made in compassing the crown!
KING HENRY V: I Richard's body have interred anew,
KING HENRY V: And on it have bestow'd more contrite tears
KING HENRY V: Than from it issued forced drops of blood:
KING HENRY V: Five hundred poor I have in yearly pay,
KING HENRY V: Who twice a-day their wither'd hands hold up
KING HENRY V: Toward heaven, to pardon blood, and I have built
KING HENRY V: Two chantries, where the sad and solemn priests
KING HENRY V: Sing still for Richard's soul. More will I do,
KING HENRY V: Though all that I can do is nothing worth,
KING HENRY V: Since that my penitence comes after all,
KING HENRY V: Imploring pardon.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: My liege!
KING HENRY V: My brother Gloucester's voice? Ay,
KING HENRY V: I know thy errand, I will go with thee:
KING HENRY V: The day, my friends and all things stay for me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The French camp.
NARRATOR: Enter the DAUPHIN, ORLEANS, RAMBURES, and others
ORLEANS: The sun doth gild our armour, up, my lords!
DAUPHIN: Montez A cheval! My horse! varlet! laquais! ha!
ORLEANS: O brave spirit!
DAUPHIN: Via! les eaux et la terre.
ORLEANS: Rien puis? L'air et la feu.
DAUPHIN: Ciel, cousin Orleans.
NARRATOR: Enter Constable
DAUPHIN: Now, my lord constable!
Constable: Hark, how our steeds for present service neigh!
DAUPHIN: Mount them, and make incision in their hides,
DAUPHIN: That their hot blood may spin in English eyes,
DAUPHIN: And dout them with superfluous courage, ha!
RAMBURES: What, will you have them weep our horses' blood?
RAMBURES: How shall we, then, behold their natural tears?
NARRATOR: Enter Messenger
Messenger: The English are embattled, you French peers.
Constable: To horse, you gallant princes! straight to horse!
Constable: Do but behold yon poor and starved band,
Constable: And your fair show shall suck away their souls,
Constable: Leaving them but the shales and husks of men.
Constable: There is not work enough for all our hands,
Constable: Scarce blood enough in all their sickly veins
Constable: To give each naked curtle-axe a stain,
Constable: That our French gallants shall to-day draw out,
Constable: And sheathe for lack of sport: let us but blow on them,
Constable: The vapour of our valour will o'erturn them.
Constable: 'Tis positive 'gainst all exceptions, lords,
Constable: That our superfluous lackeys and our peasants,
Constable: Who in unnecessary action swarm
Constable: About our squares of battle, were enow
Constable: To purge this field of such a hilding foe,
Constable: Though we upon this mountain's basis by
Constable: Took stand for idle speculation:
Constable: But that our honours must not. What's to say?
Constable: A very little little let us do.
Constable: And all is done. Then let the trumpets sound
Constable: The tucket sonance and the note to mount,
Constable: For our approach shall so much dare the field
Constable: That England shall couch down in fear and yield.
NARRATOR: Enter GRANDPRE
GRANDPRE: Why do you stay so long, my lords of France?
GRANDPRE: Yon island carrions, desperate of their bones,
GRANDPRE: Ill-favouredly become the morning field:
GRANDPRE: Their ragged curtains poorly are let loose,
GRANDPRE: And our air shakes them passing scornfully:
GRANDPRE: Big Mars seems bankrupt in their beggar'd host
GRANDPRE: And faintly through a rusty beaver peeps:
GRANDPRE: The horsemen sit like fixed candlesticks,
GRANDPRE: With torch-staves in their hand, and their poor jades
GRANDPRE: Lob down their heads, dropping the hides and hips,
GRANDPRE: The gum down-roping from their pale-dead eyes
GRANDPRE: And in their pale dull mouths the gimmal bit
GRANDPRE: Lies foul with chew'd grass, still and motionless,
GRANDPRE: And their executors, the knavish crows,
GRANDPRE: Fly o'er them, all impatient for their hour.
GRANDPRE: Description cannot suit itself in words
GRANDPRE: To demonstrate the life of such a battle
GRANDPRE: In life so lifeless as it shows itself.
Constable: They have said their prayers, and they stay for death.
DAUPHIN: Shall we go send them dinners and fresh suits
DAUPHIN: And give their fasting horses provender,
DAUPHIN: And after fight with them?
Constable: I stay but for my guidon: to the field!
Constable: I will the banner from a trumpet take,
Constable: And use it for my haste. Come, come, away!
Constable: The sun is high, and we outwear the day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The English camp.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, BEDFORD, EXETER, ERPINGHAM, with all his host: SALISBURY and WESTMORELAND
GLOUCESTER: Where is the king?
BEDFORD: The king himself is rode to view their battle.
WESTMORELAND: Of fighting men they have full three score thousand.
EXETER: There's five to one, besides, they all are fresh.
SALISBURY: God's arm strike with us! 'tis a fearful odds.
SALISBURY: God be wi' you, princes all, I'll to my charge:
SALISBURY: If we no more meet till we meet in heaven,
SALISBURY: Then, joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford,
SALISBURY: My dear Lord Gloucester, and my good Lord Exeter,
SALISBURY: And my kind kinsman, warriors all, adieu!
BEDFORD: Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with thee!
EXETER: Farewell, kind lord, fight valiantly to-day:
EXETER: And yet I do thee wrong to mind thee of it,
EXETER: For thou art framed of the firm truth of valour.
NARRATOR: Exit SALISBURY
BEDFORD: He is full of valour as of kindness,
BEDFORD: Princely in both.
NARRATOR: Enter the KING
WESTMORELAND: O that we now had here
WESTMORELAND: But one ten thousand of those men in England
WESTMORELAND: That do no work to-day!
KING HENRY V: What's he that wishes so?
KING HENRY V: My cousin Westmoreland? No, my fair cousin:
KING HENRY V: If we are mark'd to die, we are enow
KING HENRY V: To do our country loss, and if to live,
KING HENRY V: The fewer men, the greater share of honour.
KING HENRY V: God's will! I pray thee, wish not one man more.
KING HENRY V: By Jove, I am not covetous for gold,
KING HENRY V: Nor care I who doth feed upon my cost,
KING HENRY V: It yearns me not if men my garments wear,
KING HENRY V: Such outward things dwell not in my desires:
KING HENRY V: But if it be a sin to covet honour,
KING HENRY V: I am the most offending soul alive.
KING HENRY V: No, faith, my coz, wish not a man from England:
KING HENRY V: God's peace! I would not lose so great an honour
KING HENRY V: As one man more, methinks, would share from me
KING HENRY V: For the best hope I have. O, do not wish one more!
KING HENRY V: Rather proclaim it, Westmoreland, through my host,
KING HENRY V: That he which hath no stomach to this fight,
KING HENRY V: Let him depart, his passport shall be made
KING HENRY V: And crowns for convoy put into his purse:
KING HENRY V: We would not die in that man's company
KING HENRY V: That fears his fellowship to die with us.
KING HENRY V: This day is called the feast of Crispian:
KING HENRY V: He that outlives this day, and comes safe home,
KING HENRY V: Will stand a tip-toe when the day is named,
KING HENRY V: And rouse him at the name of Crispian.
KING HENRY V: He that shall live this day, and see old age,
KING HENRY V: Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbours,
KING HENRY V: And say 'To-morrow is Saint Crispian:'
KING HENRY V: Then will he strip his sleeve and show his scars.
KING HENRY V: And say 'These wounds I had on Crispin's day.'
KING HENRY V: Old men forget: yet all shall be forgot,
KING HENRY V: But he'll remember with advantages
KING HENRY V: What feats he did that day: then shall our names.
KING HENRY V: Familiar in his mouth as household words
KING HENRY V: Harry the king, Bedford and Exeter,
KING HENRY V: Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester,
KING HENRY V: Be in their flowing cups freshly remember'd.
KING HENRY V: This story shall the good man teach his son,
KING HENRY V: And Crispin Crispian shall ne'er go by,
KING HENRY V: From this day to the ending of the world,
KING HENRY V: But we in it shall be remember'd,
KING HENRY V: We few, we happy few, we band of brothers,
KING HENRY V: For he to-day that sheds his blood with me
KING HENRY V: Shall be my brother, be he ne'er so vile,
KING HENRY V: This day shall gentle his condition:
KING HENRY V: And gentlemen in England now a-bed
KING HENRY V: Shall think themselves accursed they were not here,
KING HENRY V: And hold their manhoods cheap whiles any speaks
KING HENRY V: That fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day.
NARRATOR: Re-enter SALISBURY
SALISBURY: My sovereign lord, bestow yourself with speed:
SALISBURY: The French are bravely in their battles set,
SALISBURY: And will with all expedience charge on us.
KING HENRY V: All things are ready, if our minds be so.
WESTMORELAND: Perish the man whose mind is backward now!
KING HENRY V: Thou dost not wish more help from England, coz?
WESTMORELAND: God's will! my liege, would you and I alone,
WESTMORELAND: Without more help, could fight this royal battle!
KING HENRY V: Why, now thou hast unwish'd five thousand men,
KING HENRY V: Which likes me better than to wish us one.
KING HENRY V: You know your places: God be with you all!
NARRATOR: Tucket. Enter MONTJOY
MONTJOY: Once more I come to know of thee, King Harry,
MONTJOY: If for thy ransom thou wilt now compound,
MONTJOY: Before thy most assured overthrow:
MONTJOY: For certainly thou art so near the gulf,
MONTJOY: Thou needs must be englutted. Besides, in mercy,
MONTJOY: The constable desires thee thou wilt mind
MONTJOY: Thy followers of repentance, that their souls
MONTJOY: May make a peaceful and a sweet retire
MONTJOY: From off these fields, where, wretches, their poor bodies
MONTJOY: Must lie and fester.
KING HENRY V: Who hath sent thee now?
MONTJOY: The Constable of France.
KING HENRY V: I pray thee, bear my former answer back:
KING HENRY V: Bid them achieve me and then sell my bones.
KING HENRY V: Good God! why should they mock poor fellows thus?
KING HENRY V: The man that once did sell the lion's skin
KING HENRY V: While the beast lived, was killed with hunting him.
KING HENRY V: A many of our bodies shall no doubt
KING HENRY V: Find native graves, upon the which, I trust,
KING HENRY V: Shall witness live in brass of this day's work:
KING HENRY V: And those that leave their valiant bones in France,
KING HENRY V: Dying like men, though buried in your dunghills,
KING HENRY V: They shall be famed, for there the sun shall greet them,
KING HENRY V: And draw their honours reeking up to heaven,
KING HENRY V: Leaving their earthly parts to choke your clime,
KING HENRY V: The smell whereof shall breed a plague in France.
KING HENRY V: Mark then abounding valour in our English,
KING HENRY V: That being dead, like to the bullet's grazing,
KING HENRY V: Break out into a second course of mischief,
KING HENRY V: Killing in relapse of mortality.
KING HENRY V: Let me speak proudly: tell the constable
KING HENRY V: We are but warriors for the working-day,
KING HENRY V: Our gayness and our gilt are all besmirch'd
KING HENRY V: With rainy marching in the painful field,
KING HENRY V: There's not a piece of feather in our host--
KING HENRY V: Good argument, I hope, we will not fly--
KING HENRY V: And time hath worn us into slovenry:
KING HENRY V: But, by the mass, our hearts are in the trim,
KING HENRY V: And my poor soldiers tell me, yet ere night
KING HENRY V: They'll be in fresher robes, or they will pluck
KING HENRY V: The gay new coats o'er the French soldiers' heads
KING HENRY V: And turn them out of service. If they do this,--
KING HENRY V: As, if God please, they shall,--my ransom then
KING HENRY V: Will soon be levied. Herald, save thou thy labour,

KING HENRY V: Which if they have as I will leave 'em them,
KING HENRY V: Shall yield them little, tell the constable.

MONTJOY: Thou never shalt hear herald any more.

KING HENRY V: And how thou pleasest, God, dispose the day!

NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The field of battle.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Excursions. Enter PISTOL, French Soldier, and Boy

Boy: I did never know so full a voice issue from so

Boy: vessel makes the greatest sound.' Bardolph and Nym
Boy: had ten times more valour than this roaring devil i'

NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Enter Constable, ORLEANS, BOURBON, DAUPHIN, and RAMBURES
Constable: O diable!
ORLEANS: O seigneur! le jour est perdu, tout est perdu!
DAUPHIN: Mort de ma vie! all is confounded, all!
DAUPHIN: Reproach and everlasting shame
DAUPHIN: Sits mocking in our plumes. O merchante fortune!
DAUPHIN: Do not run away.
NARRATOR: A short alarum
Constable: Why, all our ranks are broke.
DAUPHIN: O perdurable shame! let's stab ourselves.
DAUPHIN: Be these the wretches that we play'd at dice for?
ORLEANS: Is this the king we sent to for his ransom?
BOURBON: Shame and eternal shame, nothing but shame!
BOURBON: Let us die in honour: once more back again,
BOURBON: And he that will not follow Bourbon now,
BOURBON: Let him go hence, and with his cap in hand,
BOURBON: Like a base pander, hold the chamber-door
BOURBON: Whilst by a slave, no gentler than my dog,
BOURBON: His fairest daughter is contaminated.
Constable: Disorder, that hath spoil'd us, friend us now!
Constable: Let us on heaps go offer up our lives.
ORLEANS: We are enow yet living in the field
ORLEANS: To smother up the English in our throngs,
ORLEANS: If any order might be thought upon.
BOURBON: The devil take order now! I'll to the throng:
BOURBON: Let life be short, else shame will be too long.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter KING HENRY and forces, EXETER, and others
KING HENRY V: Well have we done, thrice valiant countrymen:
KING HENRY V: But all's not done, yet keep the French the field.
EXETER: The Duke of York commends him to your majesty.
KING HENRY V: Lives he, good uncle? thrice within this hour
KING HENRY V: I saw him down, thrice up again and fighting,

EXETER: Yoke-fellow to his honour-owing wounds,
EXETER: The noble Earl of Suffolk also lies.
EXETER: Suffolk first died: and York, all haggled over,
EXETER: Comes to him, where in gore he lay insteep'd,
EXETER: And takes him by the beard, kisses the gashes
EXETER: That bloodily did spawn upon his face,
EXETER: And cries aloud 'Tarry, dear cousin Suffolk!
EXETER: My soul shall thine keep company to heaven,
EXETER: Tarry, sweet soul, for mine, then fly abreast,
EXETER: As in this glorious and well-foughten field
EXETER: We kept together in our chivalry!'
EXETER: Upon these words I came and cheer'd him up:
EXETER: He smiled me in the face, raught me his hand,
EXETER: And, with a feeble gripe, says 'Dear my lord,
EXETER: Commend my service to me sovereign.'
EXETER: So did he turn and over Suffolk's neck
EXETER: He threw his wounded arm and kiss'd his lips,
EXETER: And so espoused to death, with blood he seal'd
EXETER: A testament of noble-ending love.
EXETER: The pretty and sweet manner of it forced
EXETER: Those waters from me which I would have stopp'd,
EXETER: But I had not so much of man in me,
EXETER: And all my mother came into mine eyes
EXETER: And gave me up to tears.
KING HENRY V: I blame you not,
KING HENRY V: For, hearing this, I must perforce compound
KING HENRY V: With mistful eyes, or they will issue too.
NARRATOR: Alarum
KING HENRY V: But, hark! what new alarum is this same?
KING HENRY V: The French have reinforced their scatter'd men:
KING HENRY V: Then every soldier kill his prisoners:
KING HENRY V: Give the word through.
NARRATOR: Exeunt

KING HENRY V: Here was a royal fellowship of death!
KING HENRY V: Where is the number of our English dead?
NARRATOR: Herald shews him another paper
KING HENRY V: Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk,
KING HENRY V: Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, esquire:
KING HENRY V: None else of name, and of all other men
KING HENRY V: But five and twenty. O God, thy arm was here,
KING HENRY V: And not to us, but to thy arm alone,
KING HENRY V: Ascribe we all! When, without stratagem,
KING HENRY V: But in plain shock and even play of battle,
KING HENRY V: Was ever known so great and little loss
KING HENRY V: On one part and on the other? Take it, God,
KING HENRY V: For it is none but thine!
EXETER: 'Tis wonderful!
KING HENRY V: Come, go we in procession to the village.
KING HENRY V: And be it death proclaimed through our host
KING HENRY V: To boast of this or take the praise from God
KING HENRY V: Which is his only.
FLUELLEN: Is it not lawful, an please your majesty, to tell
FLUELLEN: how many is killed?
KING HENRY V: Yes, captain, but with this acknowledgement,
KING HENRY V: That God fought for us.
FLUELLEN: Yes, my conscience, he did us great good.
KING HENRY V: Do we all holy rites,
KING HENRY V: Let there be sung 'Non nobis' and 'Te Deum,'
KING HENRY V: The dead with charity enclosed in clay:
KING HENRY V: And then to Calais, and to England then:
KING HENRY V: Where ne'er from France arrived more happy men.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Vouchsafe to those that have not read the story,
Chorus: That I may prompt them: and of such as have,
Chorus: I humbly pray them to admit the excuse
Chorus: Of time, of numbers and due course of things,
Chorus: Which cannot in their huge and proper life
Chorus: Be here presented. Now we bear the king
Chorus: Toward Calais: grant him there, there seen,
Chorus: Heave him away upon your winged thoughts
Chorus: Athwart the sea. Behold, the English beach
Chorus: Pales in the flood with men, with wives and boys,
Chorus: Whose shouts and claps out-voice the deep mouth'd sea,
Chorus: Which like a mighty whiffler 'fore the king
Chorus: Seems to prepare his way: so let him land,
Chorus: And solemnly see him set on to London.
Chorus: So swift a pace hath thought that even now
Chorus: You may imagine him upon Blackheath,
Chorus: Where that his lords desire him to have borne
Chorus: His bruised helmet and his bended sword
Chorus: Before him through the city: he forbids it,
Chorus: Being free from vainness and self-glorious pride,
Chorus: Giving full trophy, signal and ostent
Chorus: Quite from himself to God. But now behold,
Chorus: In the quick forge and working-house of thought,
Chorus: How London doth pour out her citizens!
Chorus: The mayor and all his brethren in best sort,
Chorus: Like to the senators of the antique Rome,
Chorus: With the plebeians swarming at their heels,
Chorus: Go forth and fetch their conquering Caesar in:
Chorus: As, by a lower but loving likelihood,
Chorus: Were now the general of our gracious empress,
Chorus: As in good time he may, from Ireland coming,
Chorus: Bringing rebellion broached on his sword,
Chorus: How many would the peaceful city quit,
Chorus: To welcome him! much more, and much more cause,
Chorus: Did they this Harry. Now in London place him,
Chorus: As yet the lamentation of the French
Chorus: Invites the King of England's stay at home,
Chorus: The emperor's coming in behalf of France,
Chorus: To order peace between them, and omit
Chorus: All the occurrences, whatever chanced,
Chorus: Till Harry's back-return again to France:
Chorus: There must we bring him, and myself have play'd
Chorus: The interim, by remembering you 'tis past.
Chorus: Then brook abridgment, and your eyes advance,
Chorus: After your thoughts, straight back again to France.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. France. The English camp.
NARRATOR: Enter FLUELLEN and GOWER
GOWER: Nay, that's right, but why wear you your leek today?
GOWER: Saint Davy's day is past.
FLUELLEN: There is occasions and causes why and wherefore in
FLUELLEN: all things: I will tell you, asse my friend,
FLUELLEN: Captain Gower: the rascally, scald, beggarly,
FLUELLEN: lousy, pragging knave, Pistol, which you and
FLUELLEN: yourself and all the world know to be no petter
FLUELLEN: than a fellow, look you now, of no merits, he is
FLUELLEN: come to me and prings me pread and salt yesterday,
FLUELLEN: look you, and bid me eat my leek: it was in place
FLUELLEN: where I could not breed no contention with him, but
FLUELLEN: I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see
FLUELLEN: him once again, and then I will tell him a little
FLUELLEN: piece of my desires.
NARRATOR: Enter PISTOL
GOWER: Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey-cock.
FLUELLEN: 'Tis no matter for his swellings nor his
FLUELLEN: turkey-cocks. God pless you, Aunchient Pistol! you
FLUELLEN: scurvy, lousy knave, God pless you!
PISTOL: Ha! art thou bedlam? dost thou thirst, base Trojan,
PISTOL: To have me fold up Parca's fatal web?
PISTOL: Hence! I am qualmish at the smell of leek.
FLUELLEN: I peseech you heartily, scurvy, lousy knave, at my
FLUELLEN: desires, and my requests, and my petitions, to eat,
FLUELLEN: look you, this leek: because, look you, you do not
FLUELLEN: love it, nor your affections and your appetites and
FLUELLEN: your digestions doo's not agree with it, I would
FLUELLEN: desire you to eat it.
PISTOL: Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
FLUELLEN: There is one goat for you.
NARRATOR: Strikes him
FLUELLEN: Will you be so good, scauld knave, as eat it?
PISTOL: Base Trojan, thou shalt die.
FLUELLEN: You say very true, scauld knave, when God's will is:
FLUELLEN: I will desire you to live in the mean time, and eat
FLUELLEN: your victuals: come, there is sauce for it.
NARRATOR: Strikes him
FLUELLEN: You called me yesterday mountain-squire, but I will
FLUELLEN: make you to-day a squire of low degree. I pray you,
FLUELLEN: fall to: if you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
GOWER: Enough, captain: you have astonished him.
FLUELLEN: I say, I will make him eat some part of my leek, or
FLUELLEN: I will peat his pate four days. Bite, I pray you, it
FLUELLEN: is good for your green wound and your ploody coxcomb.
PISTOL: Must I bite?
FLUELLEN: Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question
FLUELLEN: too, and ambiguities.
PISTOL: By this leek, I will most horribly revenge: I eat
PISTOL: and eat, I swear--
FLUELLEN: Eat, I pray you: will you have some more sauce to
FLUELLEN: your leek? there is not enough leek to swear by.
PISTOL: Quiet thy cudgel, thou dost see I eat.
FLUELLEN: Much good do you, scauld knave, heartily. Nay, pray
FLUELLEN: you, throw none away, the skin is good for your
FLUELLEN: broken coxcomb. When you take occasions to see leeks
FLUELLEN: hereafter, I pray you, mock at 'em, that is all.
PISTOL: Good.
FLUELLEN: Ay, leeks is good: hold you, there is a groat to
FLUELLEN: heal your pate.
PISTOL: Me a groat!
FLUELLEN: Yes, verily and in truth, you shall take it, or I
FLUELLEN: have another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
PISTOL: I take thy groat in earnest of revenge.
FLUELLEN: If I owe you any thing, I will pay you in cudgels:
FLUELLEN: you shall be a woodmonger, and buy nothing of me but
FLUELLEN: cudgels. God b' wi' you, and keep you, and heal your pate.
NARRATOR: Exit
PISTOL: All hell shall stir for this.
GOWER: Go, go, you are a counterfeit cowardly knave. Will
GOWER: you mock at an ancient tradition, begun upon an
GOWER: honourable respect, and worn as a memorable trophy of
GOWER: predeceased valour and dare not avouch in your deeds
GOWER: any of your words? I have seen you gleeking and
GOWER: galling at this gentleman twice or thrice. You
GOWER: thought, because he could not speak English in the
GOWER: native garb, he could not therefore handle an
GOWER: English cudgel: you find it otherwise, and
GOWER: henceforth let a Welsh correction teach you a good
GOWER: English condition. Fare ye well.
NARRATOR: Exit
PISTOL: Doth Fortune play the huswife with me now?
PISTOL: News have I, that my Nell is dead i' the spital
PISTOL: Of malady of France,
PISTOL: And there my rendezvous is quite cut off.
PISTOL: Old I do wax, and from my weary limbs
PISTOL: Honour is cudgelled. Well, bawd I'll turn,
PISTOL: And something lean to cutpurse of quick hand.
PISTOL: To England will I steal, and there I'll steal:
PISTOL: And patches will I get unto these cudgell'd scars,
PISTOL: And swear I got them in the Gallia wars.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. France. A royal palace.
NARRATOR: Enter, at one door KING HENRY, EXETER, BEDFORD,  GLOUCESTER, WARWICK, WESTMORELAND, and other Lords,  at another, the FRENCH KING, QUEEN ISABEL, the  PRINCESS KATHARINE, ALICE and other Ladies, the DUKE of BURGUNDY, and his train
KING HENRY V: Peace to this meeting, wherefore we are met!
KING HENRY V: Unto our brother France, and to our sister,
KING HENRY V: Health and fair time of day, joy and good wishes
KING HENRY V: To our most fair and princely cousin Katharine,
KING HENRY V: And, as a branch and member of this royalty,
KING HENRY V: By whom this great assembly is contrived,
KING HENRY V: We do salute you, Duke of Burgundy,
KING HENRY V: And, princes French, and peers, health to you all!
KING OF FRANCE: Right joyous are we to behold your face,
KING OF FRANCE: Most worthy brother England, fairly met:
KING OF FRANCE: So are you, princes English, every one.
QUEEN ISABEL: So happy be the issue, brother England,
QUEEN ISABEL: Of this good day and of this gracious meeting,
QUEEN ISABEL: As we are now glad to behold your eyes,
QUEEN ISABEL: Your eyes, which hitherto have borne in them
QUEEN ISABEL: Against the French, that met them in their bent,
QUEEN ISABEL: The fatal balls of murdering basilisks:
QUEEN ISABEL: The venom of such looks, we fairly hope,
QUEEN ISABEL: Have lost their quality, and that this day
QUEEN ISABEL: Shall change all griefs and quarrels into love.
KING HENRY V: To cry amen to that, thus we appear.
QUEEN ISABEL: You English princes all, I do salute you.
BURGUNDY: My duty to you both, on equal love,
BURGUNDY: Great Kings of France and England! That I have labour'd,
BURGUNDY: With all my wits, my pains and strong endeavours,
BURGUNDY: To bring your most imperial majesties
BURGUNDY: Unto this bar and royal interview,
BURGUNDY: Your mightiness on both parts best can witness.
BURGUNDY: Since then my office hath so far prevail'd
BURGUNDY: That, face to face and royal eye to eye,
BURGUNDY: You have congreeted, let it not disgrace me,
BURGUNDY: If I demand, before this royal view,
BURGUNDY: What rub or what impediment there is,
BURGUNDY: Why that the naked, poor and mangled Peace,
BURGUNDY: Dear nurse of arts and joyful births,
BURGUNDY: Should not in this best garden of the world
BURGUNDY: Our fertile France, put up her lovely visage?
BURGUNDY: Alas, she hath from France too long been chased,
BURGUNDY: And all her husbandry doth lie on heaps,
BURGUNDY: Corrupting in its own fertility.
BURGUNDY: Her vine, the merry cheerer of the heart,
BURGUNDY: Unpruned dies, her hedges even-pleach'd,
BURGUNDY: Like prisoners wildly overgrown with hair,
BURGUNDY: Put forth disorder'd twigs, her fallow leas
BURGUNDY: The darnel, hemlock and rank fumitory
BURGUNDY: Doth root upon, while that the coulter rusts
BURGUNDY: That should deracinate such savagery,
BURGUNDY: The even mead, that erst brought sweetly forth
BURGUNDY: The freckled cowslip, burnet and green clover,
BURGUNDY: Wanting the scythe, all uncorrected, rank,
BURGUNDY: Conceives by idleness and nothing teems
BURGUNDY: But hateful docks, rough thistles, kecksies, burs,
BURGUNDY: Losing both beauty and utility.
BURGUNDY: And as our vineyards, fallows, meads and hedges,
BURGUNDY: Defective in their natures, grow to wildness,
BURGUNDY: Even so our houses and ourselves and children
BURGUNDY: Have lost, or do not learn for want of time,
BURGUNDY: The sciences that should become our country,
BURGUNDY: But grow like savages,--as soldiers will
BURGUNDY: That nothing do but meditate on blood,--
BURGUNDY: To swearing and stern looks, diffused attire
BURGUNDY: And every thing that seems unnatural.
BURGUNDY: Which to reduce into our former favour
BURGUNDY: You are assembled: and my speech entreats
BURGUNDY: That I may know the let, why gentle Peace
BURGUNDY: Should not expel these inconveniences
BURGUNDY: And bless us with her former qualities.
KING HENRY V: If, Duke of Burgundy, you would the peace,
KING HENRY V: Whose want gives growth to the imperfections
KING HENRY V: Which you have cited, you must buy that peace
KING HENRY V: With full accord to all our just demands,
KING HENRY V: Whose tenors and particular effects
KING HENRY V: You have enscheduled briefly in your hands.
BURGUNDY: The king hath heard them, to the which as yet
BURGUNDY: There is no answer made.
KING HENRY V: Well then the peace,
KING HENRY V: Which you before so urged, lies in his answer.
KING OF FRANCE: I have but with a cursorary eye
KING OF FRANCE: O'erglanced the articles: pleaseth your grace
KING OF FRANCE: To appoint some of your council presently
KING OF FRANCE: To sit with us once more, with better heed
KING OF FRANCE: To re-survey them, we will suddenly
KING OF FRANCE: Pass our accept and peremptory answer.
KING HENRY V: Brother, we shall. Go, uncle Exeter,
KING HENRY V: And brother Clarence, and you, brother Gloucester,
KING HENRY V: Warwick and Huntingdon, go with the king,
KING HENRY V: And take with you free power to ratify,
KING HENRY V: Augment, or alter, as your wisdoms best
KING HENRY V: Shall see advantageable for our dignity,
KING HENRY V: Any thing in or out of our demands,
KING HENRY V: And we'll consign thereto. Will you, fair sister,
KING HENRY V: Go with the princes, or stay here with us?
QUEEN ISABEL: Our gracious brother, I will go with them:
QUEEN ISABEL: Haply a woman's voice may do some good,
QUEEN ISABEL: When articles too nicely urged be stood on.
KING HENRY V: Yet leave our cousin Katharine here with us:
KING HENRY V: She is our capital demand, comprised
KING HENRY V: Within the fore-rank of our articles.
QUEEN ISABEL: She hath good leave.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all except HENRY, KATHARINE, and ALICE
KING HENRY V: Fair Katharine, and most fair,
KING HENRY V: Will you vouchsafe to teach a soldier terms
KING HENRY V: Such as will enter at a lady's ear
KING HENRY V: And plead his love-suit to her gentle heart?

KATHARINE: Pardonnez-moi, I cannot tell vat is 'like me.'

KATHARINE: Que dit-il? que je suis semblable a les anges?

ALICE: Oui, dat de tongues of de mans is be full of

KING HENRY V: Marry, if you would put me to verses or to dance for

KING HENRY V: have no strength in measure, yet a reasonable

KING HENRY V: Or if I might buffet for my love, or bound my horse

KING HENRY V: nor never break for urging. If thou canst love a
KING HENRY V: fellow of this temper, Kate, whose face is not worth

KING HENRY V: uncoined constancy, for he perforce must do thee

KATHARINE: I do not know dat

KING HENRY V: Nay, it will please him well, Kate it shall please

KATHARINE: Den it sall also content me.

ALICE: France,--I cannot tell vat is baiser en Anglish.

ALICE: Your majesty entendre bettre que moi.
KING HENRY V: It is not a fashion for the maids in France to kiss
KING HENRY V: before they are married, would she say?
ALICE: Oui, vraiment.
KING HENRY V: O Kate, nice customs curtsy to great kings. Dear
KING HENRY V: Kate, you and I cannot be confined within the weak
KING HENRY V: list of a country's fashion: we are the makers of
KING HENRY V: manners, Kate, and the liberty that follows our
KING HENRY V: places stops the mouth of all find-faults, as I will
KING HENRY V: do yours, for upholding the nice fashion of your
KING HENRY V: country in denying me a kiss: therefore, patiently
KING HENRY V: and yielding.
NARRATOR: Kissing her
KING HENRY V: You have witchcraft in your lips, Kate: there is
KING HENRY V: more eloquence in a sugar touch of them than in the
KING HENRY V: tongues of the French council, and they should
KING HENRY V: sooner persuade Harry of England than a general
KING HENRY V: petition of monarchs. Here comes your father.
NARRATOR: Re-enter the FRENCH KING and his QUEEN, BURGUNDY, and other Lords
BURGUNDY: God save your majesty! my royal cousin, teach you
BURGUNDY: our princess English?
KING HENRY V: I would have her learn, my fair cousin, how
KING HENRY V: perfectly I love her, and that is good English.
BURGUNDY: Is she not apt?
KING HENRY V: Our tongue is rough, coz, and my condition is not
KING HENRY V: smooth, so that, having neither the voice nor the
KING HENRY V: heart of flattery about me, I cannot so conjure up
KING HENRY V: the spirit of love in her, that he will appear in
KING HENRY V: his true likeness.
BURGUNDY: Pardon the frankness of my mirth, if I answer you
BURGUNDY: for that. If you would conjure in her, you must
BURGUNDY: make a circle, if conjure up love in her in his true
BURGUNDY: likeness, he must appear naked and blind. Can you
BURGUNDY: blame her then, being a maid yet rosed over with the
BURGUNDY: virgin crimson of modesty, if she deny the
BURGUNDY: appearance of a naked blind boy in her naked seeing
BURGUNDY: self? It were, my lord, a hard condition for a maid
BURGUNDY: to consign to.
KING HENRY V: Yet they do wink and yield, as love is blind and enforces.
BURGUNDY: They are then excused, my lord, when they see not
BURGUNDY: what they do.
KING HENRY V: Then, good my lord, teach your cousin to consent winking.
BURGUNDY: I will wink on her to consent, my lord, if you will
BURGUNDY: teach her to know my meaning: for maids, well
BURGUNDY: summered and warm kept, are like flies at
BURGUNDY: Bartholomew-tide, blind, though they have their
BURGUNDY: eyes, and then they will endure handling, which
BURGUNDY: before would not abide looking on.
KING HENRY V: This moral ties me over to time and a hot summer,
KING HENRY V: and so I shall catch the fly, your cousin, in the
KING HENRY V: latter end and she must be blind too.
BURGUNDY: As love is, my lord, before it loves.
KING HENRY V: It is so: and you may, some of you, thank love for
KING HENRY V: my blindness, who cannot see many a fair French city
KING HENRY V: for one fair French maid that stands in my way.
FRENCH KING: Yes, my lord, you see them perspectively, the cities
FRENCH KING: turned into a maid, for they are all girdled with
FRENCH KING: maiden walls that war hath never entered.
KING HENRY V: Shall Kate be my wife?
FRENCH KING: So please you.
KING HENRY V: I am content, so the maiden cities you talk of may
KING HENRY V: wait on her: so the maid that stood in the way for
KING HENRY V: my wish shall show me the way to my will.
FRENCH KING: We have consented to all terms of reason.
KING HENRY V: Is't so, my lords of England?
WESTMORELAND: The king hath granted every article:
WESTMORELAND: His daughter first, and then in sequel all,
WESTMORELAND: According to their firm proposed natures.
EXETER: Only he hath not yet subscribed this:
EXETER: Where your majesty demands, that the King of France,
EXETER: having any occasion to write for matter of grant,
EXETER: shall name your highness in this form and with this
EXETER: addition in French, Notre trescher fils Henri, Roi
EXETER: d'Angleterre, Heritier de France, and thus in
EXETER: Latin, Praeclarissimus filius noster Henricus, Rex
EXETER: Angliae, et Haeres Franciae.
FRENCH KING: Nor this I have not, brother, so denied,
FRENCH KING: But your request shall make me let it pass.
KING HENRY V: I pray you then, in love and dear alliance,
KING HENRY V: Let that one article rank with the rest,
KING HENRY V: And thereupon give me your daughter.
FRENCH KING: Take her, fair son, and from her blood raise up
FRENCH KING: Issue to me, that the contending kingdoms
FRENCH KING: Of France and England, whose very shores look pale
FRENCH KING: With envy of each other's happiness,
FRENCH KING: May cease their hatred, and this dear conjunction
FRENCH KING: Plant neighbourhood and Christian-like accord
FRENCH KING: In their sweet bosoms, that never war advance
FRENCH KING: His bleeding sword 'twixt England and fair France.
ALL: Amen!
KING HENRY V: Now, welcome, Kate: and bear me witness all,
KING HENRY V: That here I kiss her as my sovereign queen.
NARRATOR: Flourish
QUEEN ISABEL: God, the best maker of all marriages,
QUEEN ISABEL: Combine your hearts in one, your realms in one!
QUEEN ISABEL: As man and wife, being two, are one in love,
QUEEN ISABEL: So be there 'twixt your kingdoms such a spousal,
QUEEN ISABEL: That never may ill office, or fell jealousy,
QUEEN ISABEL: Which troubles oft the bed of blessed marriage,
QUEEN ISABEL: Thrust in between the paction of these kingdoms,
QUEEN ISABEL: To make divorce of their incorporate league,
QUEEN ISABEL: That English may as French, French Englishmen,
QUEEN ISABEL: Receive each other. God speak this Amen!
ALL: Amen!
KING HENRY V: Prepare we for our marriage--on which day,
KING HENRY V: My Lord of Burgundy, we'll take your oath,
KING HENRY V: And all the peers', for surety of our leagues.
KING HENRY V: Then shall I swear to Kate, and you to me,
KING HENRY V: And may our oaths well kept and prosperous be!
NARRATOR: Sennet. Exeunt
KING HENRY V: EPILOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Thus far, with rough and all-unable pen,
Chorus: Our bending author hath pursued the story,
Chorus: In little room confining mighty men,
Chorus: Mangling by starts the full course of their glory.
Chorus: Small time, but in that small most greatly lived
Chorus: This star of England: Fortune made his sword,
Chorus: By which the world's best garden be achieved,
Chorus: And of it left his son imperial lord.
Chorus: Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crown'd King
Chorus: Of France and England, did this king succeed,
Chorus: Whose state so many had the managing,
Chorus: That they lost France and made his England bleed:
Chorus: Which oft our stage hath shown, and, for their sake,
Chorus: In your fair minds let this acceptance take.
NARRATOR: Exit
''' PLAY: Henry VI Part 1 '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Westminster Abbey.
NARRATOR: Dead March. Enter the Funeral of KING HENRY the  Fifth, attended on by Dukes of BEDFORD, Regent of  France, GLOUCESTER, Protector, and EXETER, Earl of WARWICK, the BISHOP OF WINCHESTER, Heralds,  and c
BEDFORD: Hung be the heavens with black, yield day to night!
BEDFORD: Comets, importing change of times and states,
BEDFORD: Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky,
BEDFORD: And with them scourge the bad revolting stars
BEDFORD: That have consented unto Henry's death!
BEDFORD: King Henry the Fifth, too famous to live long!
BEDFORD: England ne'er lost a king of so much worth.
GLOUCESTER: England ne'er had a king until his time.
GLOUCESTER: Virtue he had, deserving to command:
GLOUCESTER: His brandish'd sword did blind men with his beams:
GLOUCESTER: His arms spread wider than a dragon's wings,
GLOUCESTER: His sparking eyes, replete with wrathful fire,
GLOUCESTER: More dazzled and drove back his enemies
GLOUCESTER: Than mid-day sun fierce bent against their faces.
GLOUCESTER: What should I say? his deeds exceed all speech:
GLOUCESTER: He ne'er lift up his hand but conquered.
EXETER: We mourn in black: why mourn we not in blood?
EXETER: Henry is dead and never shall revive:
EXETER: Upon a wooden coffin we attend,
EXETER: And death's dishonourable victory
EXETER: We with our stately presence glorify,
EXETER: Like captives bound to a triumphant car.
EXETER: What! shall we curse the planets of mishap
EXETER: That plotted thus our glory's overthrow?
EXETER: Or shall we think the subtle-witted French
EXETER: Conjurers and sorcerers, that afraid of him
EXETER: By magic verses have contrived his end?
EXETER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: He was a king bless'd of the King of kings.
OF WINCHESTER: Unto the French the dreadful judgement-day
OF WINCHESTER: So dreadful will not be as was his sight.
OF WINCHESTER: The battles of the Lord of hosts he fought:
OF WINCHESTER: The church's prayers made him so prosperous.
GLOUCESTER: The church! where is it? Had not churchmen pray'd,
GLOUCESTER: His thread of life had not so soon decay'd:
GLOUCESTER: None do you like but an effeminate prince,
GLOUCESTER: Whom, like a school-boy, you may over-awe.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Gloucester, whate'er we like, thou art protector
OF WINCHESTER: And lookest to command the prince and realm.
OF WINCHESTER: Thy wife is proud, she holdeth thee in awe,
OF WINCHESTER: More than God or religious churchmen may.
GLOUCESTER: Name not religion, for thou lovest the flesh,
GLOUCESTER: And ne'er throughout the year to church thou go'st
GLOUCESTER: Except it be to pray against thy foes.
BEDFORD: Cease, cease these jars and rest your minds in peace:
BEDFORD: Let's to the altar: heralds, wait on us:
BEDFORD: Instead of gold, we'll offer up our arms:
BEDFORD: Since arms avail not now that Henry's dead.
BEDFORD: Posterity, await for wretched years,
BEDFORD: When at their mothers' moist eyes babes shall suck,
BEDFORD: Our isle be made a nourish of salt tears,
BEDFORD: And none but women left to wail the dead.
BEDFORD: Henry the Fifth, thy ghost I invocate:
BEDFORD: Prosper this realm, keep it from civil broils,
BEDFORD: Combat with adverse planets in the heavens!
BEDFORD: A far more glorious star thy soul will make
BEDFORD: Than Julius Caesar or bright--
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My honourable lords, health to you all!
Messenger: Sad tidings bring I to you out of France,
Messenger: Of loss, of slaughter and discomfiture:
Messenger: Guienne, Champagne, Rheims, Orleans,
Messenger: Paris, Guysors, Poictiers, are all quite lost.
BEDFORD: What say'st thou, man, before dead Henry's corse?
BEDFORD: Speak softly, or the loss of those great towns
BEDFORD: Will make him burst his lead and rise from death.
GLOUCESTER: Is Paris lost? is Rouen yielded up?
GLOUCESTER: If Henry were recall'd to life again,
GLOUCESTER: These news would cause him once more yield the ghost.
EXETER: How were they lost? what treachery was used?
Messenger: No treachery, but want of men and money.
Messenger: Amongst the soldiers this is muttered,
Messenger: That here you maintain several factions,
Messenger: And whilst a field should be dispatch'd and fought,
Messenger: You are disputing of your generals:
Messenger: One would have lingering wars with little cost,
Messenger: Another would fly swift, but wanteth wings,
Messenger: A third thinks, without expense at all,
Messenger: By guileful fair words peace may be obtain'd.
Messenger: Awake, awake, English nobility!
Messenger: Let not sloth dim your horrors new-begot:
Messenger: Cropp'd are the flower-de-luces in your arms,
Messenger: Of England's coat one half is cut away.
EXETER: Were our tears wanting to this funeral,
EXETER: These tidings would call forth their flowing tides.
BEDFORD: Me they concern, Regent I am of France.
BEDFORD: Give me my steeled coat. I'll fight for France.
BEDFORD: Away with these disgraceful wailing robes!
BEDFORD: Wounds will I lend the French instead of eyes,
BEDFORD: To weep their intermissive miseries.
NARRATOR: Enter to them another Messenger
Messenger: Lords, view these letters full of bad mischance.
Messenger: France is revolted from the English quite,
Messenger: Except some petty towns of no import:
Messenger: The Dauphin Charles is crowned king of Rheims,
Messenger: The Bastard of Orleans with him is join'd,
Messenger: Reignier, Duke of Anjou, doth take his part,
Messenger: The Duke of Alencon flieth to his side.
EXETER: The Dauphin crowned king! all fly to him!
EXETER: O, whither shall we fly from this reproach?
GLOUCESTER: We will not fly, but to our enemies' throats.
GLOUCESTER: Bedford, if thou be slack, I'll fight it out.
BEDFORD: Gloucester, why doubt'st thou of my forwardness?
BEDFORD: An army have I muster'd in my thoughts,
BEDFORD: Wherewith already France is overrun.
NARRATOR: Enter another Messenger
Messenger: My gracious lords, to add to your laments,
Messenger: Wherewith you now bedew King Henry's hearse,
Messenger: I must inform you of a dismal fight
Messenger: Betwixt the stout Lord Talbot and the French.
Messenger: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: What! wherein Talbot overcame? is't so?
Messenger: O, no, wherein Lord Talbot was o'erthrown:
Messenger: The circumstance I'll tell you more at large.
Messenger: The tenth of August last this dreadful lord,
Messenger: Retiring from the siege of Orleans,
Messenger: Having full scarce six thousand in his troop.
Messenger: By three and twenty thousand of the French
Messenger: Was round encompassed and set upon.
Messenger: No leisure had he to enrank his men,
Messenger: He wanted pikes to set before his archers,
Messenger: Instead whereof sharp stakes pluck'd out of hedges
Messenger: They pitched in the ground confusedly,
Messenger: To keep the horsemen off from breaking in.
Messenger: More than three hours the fight continued,
Messenger: Where valiant Talbot above human thought
Messenger: Enacted wonders with his sword and lance:
Messenger: Hundreds he sent to hell, and none durst stand him,
Messenger: Here, there, and every where, enraged he flew:
Messenger: The French exclaim'd, the devil was in arms,
Messenger: All the whole army stood agazed on him:
Messenger: His soldiers spying his undaunted spirit
Messenger: A Talbot! a Talbot! cried out amain
Messenger: And rush'd into the bowels of the battle.
Messenger: Here had the conquest fully been seal'd up,
Messenger: If Sir John Fastolfe had not play'd the coward:
Messenger: He, being in the vaward, placed behind
Messenger: With purpose to relieve and follow them,
Messenger: Cowardly fled, not having struck one stroke.
Messenger: Hence grew the general wreck and massacre,
Messenger: Enclosed were they with their enemies:
Messenger: A base Walloon, to win the Dauphin's grace,
Messenger: Thrust Talbot with a spear into the back,
Messenger: Whom all France with their chief assembled strength
Messenger: Durst not presume to look once in the face.
BEDFORD: Is Talbot slain? then I will slay myself,
BEDFORD: For living idly here in pomp and ease,
BEDFORD: Whilst such a worthy leader, wanting aid,
BEDFORD: Unto his dastard foemen is betray'd.
Messenger: O no, he lives, but is took prisoner,
Messenger: And Lord Scales with him and Lord Hungerford:
Messenger: Most of the rest slaughter'd or took likewise.
BEDFORD: His ransom there is none but I shall pay:
BEDFORD: I'll hale the Dauphin headlong from his throne:
BEDFORD: His crown shall be the ransom of my friend,
BEDFORD: Four of their lords I'll change for one of ours.
BEDFORD: Farewell, my masters, to my task will I,
BEDFORD: Bonfires in France forthwith I am to make,
BEDFORD: To keep our great Saint George's feast withal:
BEDFORD: Ten thousand soldiers with me I will take,
BEDFORD: Whose bloody deeds shall make all Europe quake.
Messenger: So you had need, for Orleans is besieged,
Messenger: The English army is grown weak and faint:
Messenger: The Earl of Salisbury craveth supply,
Messenger: And hardly keeps his men from mutiny,
Messenger: Since they, so few, watch such a multitude.
EXETER: Remember, lords, your oaths to Henry sworn,
EXETER: Either to quell the Dauphin utterly,
EXETER: Or bring him in obedience to your yoke.
BEDFORD: I do remember it, and here take my leave,
BEDFORD: To go about my preparation.

GLOUCESTER: To view the artillery and munition,
GLOUCESTER: And then I will proclaim young Henry king.
NARRATOR: Exit

EXETER: And for his safety there I'll best devise.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. France. Before Orleans.
NARRATOR: Sound a flourish. Enter CHARLES, ALENCON, and REIGNIER, marching with drum and Soldiers
CHARLES: Mars his true moving, even as in the heavens
CHARLES: So in the earth, to this day is not known:
CHARLES: Late did he shine upon the English side,
CHARLES: Now we are victors, upon us he smiles.
CHARLES: What towns of any moment but we have?
CHARLES: At pleasure here we lie near Orleans,
CHARLES: Otherwhiles the famish'd English, like pale ghosts,
CHARLES: Faintly besiege us one hour in a month.
ALENCON: They want their porridge and their fat bull-beeves:
ALENCON: Either they must be dieted like mules
ALENCON: And have their provender tied to their mouths
ALENCON: Or piteous they will look, like drowned mice.
REIGNIER: Let's raise the siege: why live we idly here?
REIGNIER: Talbot is taken, whom we wont to fear:
REIGNIER: Remaineth none but mad-brain'd Salisbury,
REIGNIER: And he may well in fretting spend his gall,
REIGNIER: Nor men nor money hath he to make war.
CHARLES: Sound, sound alarum! we will rush on them.
CHARLES: Now for the honour of the forlorn French!
CHARLES: Him I forgive my death that killeth me
CHARLES: When he sees me go back one foot or fly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Here alarum, they are beaten back by the English with great loss. Re-enter CHARLES, ALENCON, and REIGNIER
CHARLES: Who ever saw the like? what men have I!
CHARLES: Dogs! cowards! dastards! I would ne'er have fled,
CHARLES: But that they left me 'midst my enemies.
REIGNIER: Salisbury is a desperate homicide,
REIGNIER: He fighteth as one weary of his life.
REIGNIER: The other lords, like lions wanting food,
REIGNIER: Do rush upon us as their hungry prey.
ALENCON: Froissart, a countryman of ours, records,

ALENCON: More truly now may this be verified,
ALENCON: For none but Samsons and Goliases
ALENCON: It sendeth forth to skirmish. One to ten!

CHARLES: Of old I know them, rather with their teeth

JOAN LA PUCELLE: And in a vision full of majesty
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Will'd me to leave my base vocation
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And free my country from calamity:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Her aid she promised and assured success:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: In complete glory she reveal'd herself,

JOAN LA PUCELLE: With those clear rays which she infused on me
JOAN LA PUCELLE: That beauty am I bless'd with which you see.

JOAN LA PUCELLE: My courage try by combat, if thou darest,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And thou shalt find that I exceed my sex.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Resolve on this, thou shalt be fortunate,

CHARLES: And if thou vanquishest, thy words are true,
CHARLES: Otherwise I renounce all confidence.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I am prepared: here is my keen-edged sword,

JOAN LA PUCELLE: The which at Touraine, in Saint Katharine's
JOAN LA PUCELLE: churchyard,

CHARLES: Then come, o' God's name, I fear no woman.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And while I live, I'll ne'er fly from a man.
NARRATOR: Here they fight, and JOAN LA PUCELLE overcomes

CHARLES: And fightest with the sword of Deborah.

CHARLES: Whoe'er helps thee, 'tis thou that must help me:
CHARLES: Impatiently I burn with thy desire,

ALENCON: These women are shrewd tempters with their tongues.

JOAN LA PUCELLE: Which Caesar and his fortune bare at once.
