CHARLES: Thou with an eagle art inspired then.
CHARLES: Helen, the mother of great Constantine,
CHARLES: Nor yet Saint Philip's daughters, were like thee.
CHARLES: Bright star of Venus, fall'n down on the earth,
CHARLES: How may I reverently worship thee enough?
ALENCON: Leave off delays, and let us raise the siege.
REIGNIER: Woman, do what thou canst to save our honours,
REIGNIER: Drive them from Orleans and be immortalized.
CHARLES: Presently we'll try: come, let's away about it:
CHARLES: No prophet will I trust, if she prove false.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. London. Before the Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, with his Serving-men in blue coats
GLOUCESTER: I am come to survey the Tower this day:
GLOUCESTER: Since Henry's death, I fear, there is conveyance.
GLOUCESTER: Where be these warders, that they wait not here?
GLOUCESTER: Open the gates, 'tis Gloucester that calls.
First Warder: [Within]  Who's there that knocks so imperiously?
First Warder: First Serving-Man	It is the noble Duke of Gloucester.
Second Warder: [Within]  Whoe'er he be, you may not be let in.
Second Warder: First Serving-Man	Villains, answer you so the lord protector?
First Warder: [Within]  The Lord protect him! so we answer him:
First Warder: We do no otherwise than we are will'd.
GLOUCESTER: Who willed you? or whose will stands but mine?
GLOUCESTER: There's none protector of the realm but I.
GLOUCESTER: Break up the gates, I'll be your warrantize.
GLOUCESTER: Shall I be flouted thus by dunghill grooms?
NARRATOR: Gloucester's men rush at the Tower Gates, and WOODVILE the Lieutenant speaks within
WOODVILE: What noise is this? what traitors have we here?
GLOUCESTER: Lieutenant, is it you whose voice I hear?
GLOUCESTER: Open the gates, here's Gloucester that would enter.
WOODVILE: Have patience, noble duke, I may not open,
WOODVILE: The Cardinal of Winchester forbids:
WOODVILE: From him I have express commandment
WOODVILE: That thou nor none of thine shall be let in.
GLOUCESTER: Faint-hearted Woodvile, prizest him 'fore me?
GLOUCESTER: Arrogant Winchester, that haughty prelate,
GLOUCESTER: Whom Henry, our late sovereign, ne'er could brook?
GLOUCESTER: Thou art no friend to God or to the king:
GLOUCESTER: Open the gates, or I'll shut thee out shortly.
GLOUCESTER: Serving-Men	Open the gates unto the lord protector,
GLOUCESTER: Or we'll burst them open, if that you come not quickly.
NARRATOR: Enter to the Protector at the Tower Gates BISHOP OF WINCHESTER and his men in tawny coats
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: How now, ambitious Humphry! what means this?
GLOUCESTER: Peel'd priest, dost thou command me to be shut out?
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: I do, thou most usurping proditor,
OF WINCHESTER: And not protector, of the king or realm.
GLOUCESTER: Stand back, thou manifest conspirator,
GLOUCESTER: Thou that contrivedst to murder our dead lord,
GLOUCESTER: Thou that givest whores indulgences to sin:
GLOUCESTER: I'll canvass thee in thy broad cardinal's hat,
GLOUCESTER: If thou proceed in this thy insolence.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Nay, stand thou back, I will not budge a foot:
OF WINCHESTER: This be Damascus, be thou cursed Cain,
OF WINCHESTER: To slay thy brother Abel, if thou wilt.
GLOUCESTER: I will not slay thee, but I'll drive thee back:
GLOUCESTER: Thy scarlet robes as a child's bearing-cloth
GLOUCESTER: I'll use to carry thee out of this place.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Do what thou darest, I beard thee to thy face.
GLOUCESTER: What! am I dared and bearded to my face?
GLOUCESTER: Draw, men, for all this privileged place,
GLOUCESTER: Blue coats to tawny coats. Priest, beware your beard,
GLOUCESTER: I mean to tug it and to cuff you soundly:
GLOUCESTER: Under my feet I stamp thy cardinal's hat:
GLOUCESTER: In spite of pope or dignities of church,
GLOUCESTER: Here by the cheeks I'll drag thee up and down.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Gloucester, thou wilt answer this before the pope.
GLOUCESTER: Winchester goose, I cry, a rope! a rope!
GLOUCESTER: Now beat them hence, why do you let them stay?
GLOUCESTER: Thee I'll chase hence, thou wolf in sheep's array.
GLOUCESTER: Out, tawny coats! out, scarlet hypocrite!
NARRATOR: Here GLOUCESTER's men beat out BISHOP OF  WINCHESTER's men, and enter in the hurly- burly the Mayor of London and his Officers
Mayor: Fie, lords! that you, being supreme magistrates,
Mayor: Thus contumeliously should break the peace!
GLOUCESTER: Peace, mayor! thou know'st little of my wrongs:
GLOUCESTER: Here's Beaufort, that regards nor God nor king,
GLOUCESTER: Hath here distrain'd the Tower to his use.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Here's Gloucester, a foe to citizens,
OF WINCHESTER: One that still motions war and never peace,
OF WINCHESTER: O'ercharging your free purses with large fines,
OF WINCHESTER: That seeks to overthrow religion,
OF WINCHESTER: Because he is protector of the realm,
OF WINCHESTER: And would have armour here out of the Tower,
OF WINCHESTER: To crown himself king and suppress the prince.
GLOUCESTER: I will not answer thee with words, but blows.
NARRATOR: Here they skirmish again
Mayor: Naught rests for me in this tumultuous strife
Mayor: But to make open proclamation:
Mayor: Come, officer, as loud as e'er thou canst,
Mayor: Cry.
Officer: All manner of men assembled here in arms this day
Officer: against God's peace and the king's, we charge and
Officer: command you, in his highness' name, to repair to
Officer: your several dwelling-places, and not to wear,
Officer: handle, or use any sword, weapon, or dagger,
Officer: henceforward, upon pain of death.
GLOUCESTER: Cardinal, I'll be no breaker of the law:
GLOUCESTER: But we shall meet, and break our minds at large.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Gloucester, we will meet, to thy cost, be sure:
OF WINCHESTER: Thy heart-blood I will have for this day's work.
Mayor: I'll call for clubs, if you will not away.
Mayor: This cardinal's more haughty than the devil.
GLOUCESTER: Mayor, farewell: thou dost but what thou mayst.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Abominable Gloucester, guard thy head,
OF WINCHESTER: For I intend to have it ere long.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, severally, GLOUCESTER and BISHOP OF WINCHESTER with their Serving-men
Mayor: See the coast clear'd, and then we will depart.
Mayor: Good God, these nobles should such stomachs bear!
Mayor: I myself fight not once in forty year.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Orleans.
NARRATOR: Enter, on the walls, a Master Gunner and his Boy
Mayor: Master-Gunner	Sirrah, thou know'st how Orleans is besieged,
Mayor: And how the English have the suburbs won.
Boy: Father, I know, and oft have shot at them,
Boy: Howe'er unfortunate I miss'd my aim.
Boy: Master-Gunner	But now thou shalt not. Be thou ruled by me:
Boy: Chief master-gunner am I of this town,
Boy: Something I must do to procure me grace.
Boy: The prince's espials have informed me
Boy: How the English, in the suburbs close intrench'd,
Boy: Wont, through a secret grate of iron bars
Boy: In yonder tower, to overpeer the city,
Boy: And thence discover how with most advantage
Boy: They may vex us with shot, or with assault.
Boy: To intercept this inconvenience,
Boy: A piece of ordnance 'gainst it I have placed,
Boy: And even these three days have I watch'd,
Boy: If I could see them.
Boy: Now do thou watch, for I can stay no longer.
Boy: If thou spy'st any, run and bring me word,
Boy: And thou shalt find me at the governor's.
NARRATOR: Exit
Boy: Father, I warrant you, take you no care,
Boy: I'll never trouble you, if I may spy them.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter, on the turrets, SALISBURY and TALBOT, GLANSDALE, GARGRAVE, and others
SALISBURY: Talbot, my life, my joy, again return'd!
SALISBURY: How wert thou handled being prisoner?
SALISBURY: Or by what means got'st thou to be released?
SALISBURY: Discourse, I prithee, on this turret's top.
TALBOT: The Duke of Bedford had a prisoner
TALBOT: Call'd the brave Lord Ponton de Santrailles,
TALBOT: For him was I exchanged and ransomed.
TALBOT: But with a baser man of arms by far
TALBOT: Once in contempt they would have barter'd me:
TALBOT: Which I, disdaining, scorn'd, and craved death,
TALBOT: Rather than I would be so vile esteem'd.
TALBOT: In fine, redeem'd I was as I desired.
TALBOT: But, O! the treacherous Fastolfe wounds my heart,
TALBOT: Whom with my bare fists I would execute,
TALBOT: If I now had him brought into my power.
SALISBURY: Yet tell'st thou not how thou wert entertain'd.
TALBOT: With scoffs and scorns and contumelious taunts.
TALBOT: In open market-place produced they me,
TALBOT: To be a public spectacle to all:
TALBOT: Here, said they, is the terror of the French,
TALBOT: The scarecrow that affrights our children so.
TALBOT: Then broke I from the officers that led me,
TALBOT: And with my nails digg'd stones out of the ground,
TALBOT: To hurl at the beholders of my shame:
TALBOT: My grisly countenance made others fly,
TALBOT: None durst come near for fear of sudden death.
TALBOT: In iron walls they deem'd me not secure,
TALBOT: So great fear of my name 'mongst them was spread,
TALBOT: That they supposed I could rend bars of steel,
TALBOT: And spurn in pieces posts of adamant:
TALBOT: Wherefore a guard of chosen shot I had,
TALBOT: That walked about me every minute-while,
TALBOT: And if I did but stir out of my bed,
TALBOT: Ready they were to shoot me to the heart.
NARRATOR: Enter the Boy with a linstock
SALISBURY: I grieve to hear what torments you endured,
SALISBURY: But we will be revenged sufficiently
SALISBURY: Now it is supper-time in Orleans:
SALISBURY: Here, through this grate, I count each one
SALISBURY: and view the Frenchmen how they fortify:
SALISBURY: Let us look in, the sight will much delight thee.
SALISBURY: Sir Thomas Gargrave, and Sir William Glansdale,
SALISBURY: Let me have your express opinions
SALISBURY: Where is best place to make our battery next.
GARGRAVE: I think, at the north gate, for there stand lords.
GLANSDALE: And I, here, at the bulwark of the bridge.
TALBOT: For aught I see, this city must be famish'd,
TALBOT: Or with light skirmishes enfeebled.
NARRATOR: Here they shoot. SALISBURY and GARGRAVE fall
SALISBURY: O Lord, have mercy on us, wretched sinners!
GARGRAVE: O Lord, have mercy on me, woful man!
TALBOT: What chance is this that suddenly hath cross'd us?
TALBOT: Speak, Salisbury, at least, if thou canst speak:
TALBOT: How farest thou, mirror of all martial men?
TALBOT: One of thy eyes and thy cheek's side struck off!
TALBOT: Accursed tower! accursed fatal hand
TALBOT: That hath contrived this woful tragedy!
TALBOT: In thirteen battles Salisbury o'ercame,
TALBOT: Henry the Fifth he first train'd to the wars,
TALBOT: Whilst any trump did sound, or drum struck up,
TALBOT: His sword did ne'er leave striking in the field.
TALBOT: Yet livest thou, Salisbury? though thy speech doth fail,
TALBOT: One eye thou hast, to look to heaven for grace:
TALBOT: The sun with one eye vieweth all the world.
TALBOT: Heaven, be thou gracious to none alive,
TALBOT: If Salisbury wants mercy at thy hands!
TALBOT: Bear hence his body, I will help to bury it.
TALBOT: Sir Thomas Gargrave, hast thou any life?
TALBOT: Speak unto Talbot, nay, look up to him.
TALBOT: Salisbury, cheer thy spirit with this comfort,
TALBOT: Thou shalt not die whiles--
TALBOT: He beckons with his hand and smiles on me.
TALBOT: As who should say 'When I am dead and gone,
TALBOT: Remember to avenge me on the French.'
TALBOT: Plantagenet, I will, and like thee, Nero,
TALBOT: Play on the lute, beholding the towns burn:
TALBOT: Wretched shall France be only in my name.
NARRATOR: Here an alarum, and it thunders and lightens
TALBOT: What stir is this? what tumult's in the heavens?
TALBOT: Whence cometh this alarum and the noise?
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord, my lord, the French have gathered head:
Messenger: The Dauphin, with one Joan la Pucelle join'd,
Messenger: A holy prophetess new risen up,
Messenger: Is come with a great power to raise the siege.
NARRATOR: Here SALISBURY lifteth himself up and groans
TALBOT: Hear, hear how dying Salisbury doth groan!
TALBOT: It irks his heart he cannot be revenged.
TALBOT: Frenchmen, I'll be a Salisbury to you:
TALBOT: Pucelle or puzzel, dolphin or dogfish,
TALBOT: Your hearts I'll stamp out with my horse's heels,
TALBOT: And make a quagmire of your mingled brains.
TALBOT: Convey me Salisbury into his tent,
TALBOT: And then we'll try what these dastard Frenchmen dare.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same.
NARRATOR: Here an alarum again: and TALBOT pursueth the  DAUPHIN, and driveth him: then enter JOAN LA  PUCELLE, driving Englishmen before her, and exit after them then re-enter TALBOT
TALBOT: Where is my strength, my valour, and my force?
TALBOT: Our English troops retire, I cannot stay them:
TALBOT: A woman clad in armour chaseth them.
NARRATOR: Re-enter JOAN LA PUCELLE
TALBOT: Here, here she comes. I'll have a bout with thee,
TALBOT: Devil or devil's dam, I'll conjure thee:
TALBOT: Blood will I draw on thee, thou art a witch,
TALBOT: And straightway give thy soul to him thou servest.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Come, come, 'tis only I that must disgrace thee.
NARRATOR: Here they fight
TALBOT: Heavens, can you suffer hell so to prevail?
TALBOT: My breast I'll burst with straining of my courage
TALBOT: And from my shoulders crack my arms asunder.
TALBOT: But I will chastise this high-minded strumpet.
NARRATOR: They fight again
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Talbot, farewell, thy hour is not yet come:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I must go victual Orleans forthwith.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: A short alarum, then enter the town with soldiers
JOAN LA PUCELLE: O'ertake me, if thou canst, I scorn thy strength.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Go, go, cheer up thy hungry-starved men,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Help Salisbury to make his testament:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: This day is ours, as many more shall be.
NARRATOR: Exit
TALBOT: My thoughts are whirled like a potter's wheel,
TALBOT: I know not where I am, nor what I do,
TALBOT: A witch, by fear, not force, like Hannibal,
TALBOT: Drives back our troops and conquers as she lists:
TALBOT: So bees with smoke and doves with noisome stench
TALBOT: Are from their hives and houses driven away.
TALBOT: They call'd us for our fierceness English dogs,
TALBOT: Now, like to whelps, we crying run away.
NARRATOR: A short alarum
TALBOT: Hark, countrymen! either renew the fight,
TALBOT: Or tear the lions out of England's coat,
TALBOT: Renounce your soil, give sheep in lions' stead:
TALBOT: Sheep run not half so treacherous from the wolf,
TALBOT: Or horse or oxen from the leopard,
TALBOT: As you fly from your oft-subdued slaves.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Here another skirmish
TALBOT: It will not be: retire into your trenches:
TALBOT: You all consented unto Salisbury's death,
TALBOT: For none would strike a stroke in his revenge.
TALBOT: Pucelle is enter'd into Orleans,
TALBOT: In spite of us or aught that we could do.
TALBOT: O, would I were to die with Salisbury!
TALBOT: The shame hereof will make me hide my head.
TALBOT: Exit TALBOT. Alarum, retreat, flourish
TALBOT: SCENE VI. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter, on the walls, JOAN LA PUCELLE, CHARLES, REIGNIER, ALENCON, and Soldiers
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Advance our waving colours on the walls,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Rescued is Orleans from the English
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Thus Joan la Pucelle hath perform'd her word.
CHARLES: Divinest creature, Astraea's daughter,
CHARLES: How shall I honour thee for this success?
CHARLES: Thy promises are like Adonis' gardens
CHARLES: That one day bloom'd and fruitful were the next.
CHARLES: France, triumph in thy glorious prophetess!
CHARLES: Recover'd is the town of Orleans:
CHARLES: More blessed hap did ne'er befall our state.
REIGNIER: Why ring not out the bells aloud throughout the town?
REIGNIER: Dauphin, command the citizens make bonfires
REIGNIER: And feast and banquet in the open streets,
REIGNIER: To celebrate the joy that God hath given us.
ALENCON: All France will be replete with mirth and joy,
ALENCON: When they shall hear how we have play'd the men.
CHARLES: 'Tis Joan, not we, by whom the day is won,
CHARLES: For which I will divide my crown with her,
CHARLES: And all the priests and friars in my realm
CHARLES: Shall in procession sing her endless praise.
CHARLES: A statelier pyramis to her I'll rear
CHARLES: Than Rhodope's or Memphis' ever was:
CHARLES: In memory of her when she is dead,
CHARLES: Her ashes, in an urn more precious
CHARLES: Than the rich-jewel'd of Darius,
CHARLES: Transported shall be at high festivals
CHARLES: Before the kings and queens of France.
CHARLES: No longer on Saint Denis will we cry,
CHARLES: But Joan la Pucelle shall be France's saint.
CHARLES: Come in, and let us banquet royally,
CHARLES: After this golden day of victory.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before Orleans.
NARRATOR: Enter a Sergeant of a band with two Sentinels
Sergeant: Sirs, take your places and be vigilant:
Sergeant: If any noise or soldier you perceive
Sergeant: Near to the walls, by some apparent sign
Sergeant: Let us have knowledge at the court of guard.
First Sentinel: Sergeant, you shall.
NARRATOR: Exit Sergeant
First Sentinel: Thus are poor servitors,
First Sentinel: When others sleep upon their quiet beds,
First Sentinel: Constrain'd to watch in darkness, rain and cold.
NARRATOR: Enter TALBOT, BEDFORD, BURGUNDY, and Forces, with scaling-ladders, their drums beating a dead march
TALBOT: Lord Regent, and redoubted Burgundy,
TALBOT: By whose approach the regions of Artois,
TALBOT: Wallon and Picardy are friends to us,
TALBOT: This happy night the Frenchmen are secure,
TALBOT: Having all day caroused and banqueted:
TALBOT: Embrace we then this opportunity
TALBOT: As fitting best to quittance their deceit
TALBOT: Contrived by art and baleful sorcery.
BEDFORD: Coward of France! how much he wrongs his fame,
BEDFORD: Despairing of his own arm's fortitude,
BEDFORD: To join with witches and the help of hell!
BURGUNDY: Traitors have never other company.
BURGUNDY: But what's that Pucelle whom they term so pure?
TALBOT: A maid, they say.
BEDFORD: A maid! and be so martial!
BURGUNDY: Pray God she prove not masculine ere long,
BURGUNDY: If underneath the standard of the French
BURGUNDY: She carry armour as she hath begun.
TALBOT: Well, let them practise and converse with spirits:
TALBOT: God is our fortress, in whose conquering name
TALBOT: Let us resolve to scale their flinty bulwarks.
BEDFORD: Ascend, brave Talbot, we will follow thee.
TALBOT: Not all together: better far, I guess,
TALBOT: That we do make our entrance several ways,
TALBOT: That, if it chance the one of us do fail,
TALBOT: The other yet may rise against their force.
BEDFORD: Agreed: I'll to yond corner.
BURGUNDY: And I to this.
TALBOT: And here will Talbot mount, or make his grave.
TALBOT: Now, Salisbury, for thee, and for the right
TALBOT: Of English Henry, shall this night appear
TALBOT: How much in duty I am bound to both.
Sentinels: Arm! arm! the enemy doth make assault!
Sentinels: Cry: 'St. George,' 'A Talbot.'
NARRATOR: The French leap over the walls in their shirts.  Enter, several ways, the BASTARD OF ORLEANS, ALENCON, and REIGNIER, half ready, and half unready
ALENCON: How now, my lords! what, all unready so?
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Unready! ay, and glad we 'scaped so well.
REIGNIER: 'Twas time, I trow, to wake and leave our beds,
REIGNIER: Hearing alarums at our chamber-doors.
ALENCON: Of all exploits since first I follow'd arms,
ALENCON: Ne'er heard I of a warlike enterprise
ALENCON: More venturous or desperate than this.
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: I think this Talbot be a fiend of hell.
REIGNIER: If not of hell, the heavens, sure, favour him.
ALENCON: Here cometh Charles: I marvel how he sped.
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Tut, holy Joan was his defensive guard.
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES and JOAN LA PUCELLE
CHARLES: Is this thy cunning, thou deceitful dame?
CHARLES: Didst thou at first, to flatter us withal,
CHARLES: Make us partakers of a little gain,
CHARLES: That now our loss might be ten times so much?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Wherefore is Charles impatient with his friend!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: At all times will you have my power alike?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Sleeping or waking must I still prevail,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Or will you blame and lay the fault on me?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Improvident soldiers! had your watch been good,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: This sudden mischief never could have fall'n.
CHARLES: Duke of Alencon, this was your default,
CHARLES: That, being captain of the watch to-night,
CHARLES: Did look no better to that weighty charge.
ALENCON: Had all your quarters been as safely kept
ALENCON: As that whereof I had the government,
ALENCON: We had not been thus shamefully surprised.
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Mine was secure.
REIGNIER: And so was mine, my lord.
CHARLES: And, for myself, most part of all this night,
CHARLES: Within her quarter and mine own precinct
CHARLES: I was employ'd in passing to and fro,
CHARLES: About relieving of the sentinels:
CHARLES: Then how or which way should they first break in?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Question, my lords, no further of the case,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: How or which way: 'tis sure they found some place
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But weakly guarded, where the breach was made.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And now there rests no other shift but this,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: To gather our soldiers, scatter'd and dispersed,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And lay new platforms to endamage them.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Alarum. Enter an English Soldier, crying 'A  Talbot! a Talbot!' They fly, leaving their clothes behind
Soldier: I'll be so bold to take what they have left.
Soldier: The cry of Talbot serves me for a sword,
Soldier: For I have loaden me with many spoils,
Soldier: Using no other weapon but his name.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Orleans. Within the town.
NARRATOR: Enter TALBOT, BEDFORD, BURGUNDY, a Captain, and others
BEDFORD: The day begins to break, and night is fled,
BEDFORD: Whose pitchy mantle over-veil'd the earth.
BEDFORD: Here sound retreat, and cease our hot pursuit.
NARRATOR: Retreat sounded
TALBOT: Bring forth the body of old Salisbury,
TALBOT: And here advance it in the market-place,
TALBOT: The middle centre of this cursed town.
TALBOT: Now have I paid my vow unto his soul,
TALBOT: For every drop of blood was drawn from him,
TALBOT: There hath at least five Frenchmen died tonight.
TALBOT: And that hereafter ages may behold
TALBOT: What ruin happen'd in revenge of him,
TALBOT: Within their chiefest temple I'll erect
TALBOT: A tomb, wherein his corpse shall be interr'd:
TALBOT: Upon the which, that every one may read,
TALBOT: Shall be engraved the sack of Orleans,
TALBOT: The treacherous manner of his mournful death
TALBOT: And what a terror he had been to France.
TALBOT: But, lords, in all our bloody massacre,
TALBOT: I muse we met not with the Dauphin's grace,
TALBOT: His new-come champion, virtuous Joan of Arc,
TALBOT: Nor any of his false confederates.
BEDFORD: 'Tis thought, Lord Talbot, when the fight began,
BEDFORD: Roused on the sudden from their drowsy beds,
BEDFORD: They did amongst the troops of armed men
BEDFORD: Leap o'er the walls for refuge in the field.
BURGUNDY: Myself, as far as I could well discern
BURGUNDY: For smoke and dusky vapours of the night,
BURGUNDY: Am sure I scared the Dauphin and his trull,
BURGUNDY: When arm in arm they both came swiftly running,
BURGUNDY: Like to a pair of loving turtle-doves
BURGUNDY: That could not live asunder day or night.
BURGUNDY: After that things are set in order here,
BURGUNDY: We'll follow them with all the power we have.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: All hail, my lords! which of this princely train
Messenger: Call ye the warlike Talbot, for his acts
Messenger: So much applauded through the realm of France?
TALBOT: Here is the Talbot: who would speak with him?
Messenger: The virtuous lady, Countess of Auvergne,
Messenger: With modesty admiring thy renown,
Messenger: By me entreats, great lord, thou wouldst vouchsafe
Messenger: To visit her poor castle where she lies,
Messenger: That she may boast she hath beheld the man
Messenger: Whose glory fills the world with loud report.
BURGUNDY: Is it even so? Nay, then, I see our wars
BURGUNDY: Will turn unto a peaceful comic sport,
BURGUNDY: When ladies crave to be encounter'd with.
BURGUNDY: You may not, my lord, despise her gentle suit.
TALBOT: Ne'er trust me then, for when a world of men
TALBOT: Could not prevail with all their oratory,
TALBOT: Yet hath a woman's kindness over-ruled:
TALBOT: And therefore tell her I return great thanks,
TALBOT: And in submission will attend on her.
TALBOT: Will not your honours bear me company?
BEDFORD: No, truly, it is more than manners will:
BEDFORD: And I have heard it said, unbidden guests
BEDFORD: Are often welcomest when they are gone.
TALBOT: Well then, alone, since there's no remedy,
TALBOT: I mean to prove this lady's courtesy.
TALBOT: Come hither, captain.
NARRATOR: Whispers
TALBOT: You perceive my mind?
Captain: I do, my lord, and mean accordingly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Auvergne. The COUNTESS's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter the COUNTESS and her Porter
Captain: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Porter, remember what I gave in charge,
OF AUVERGNE: And when you have done so, bring the keys to me.
Porter: Madam, I will.
NARRATOR: Exit
Porter: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: The plot is laid: if all things fall out right,
OF AUVERGNE: I shall as famous be by this exploit
OF AUVERGNE: As Scythian Tomyris by Cyrus' death.
OF AUVERGNE: Great is the rumor of this dreadful knight,
OF AUVERGNE: And his achievements of no less account:
OF AUVERGNE: Fain would mine eyes be witness with mine ears,
OF AUVERGNE: To give their censure of these rare reports.
NARRATOR: Enter Messenger and TALBOT
Messenger: Madam,
Messenger: According as your ladyship desired,
Messenger: By message craved, so is Lord Talbot come.
Messenger: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: And he is welcome. What! is this the man?
Messenger: Madam, it is.
Messenger: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Is this the scourge of France?
OF AUVERGNE: Is this the Talbot, so much fear'd abroad
OF AUVERGNE: That with his name the mothers still their babes?
OF AUVERGNE: I see report is fabulous and false:
OF AUVERGNE: I thought I should have seen some Hercules,
OF AUVERGNE: A second Hector, for his grim aspect,
OF AUVERGNE: And large proportion of his strong-knit limbs.
OF AUVERGNE: Alas, this is a child, a silly dwarf!
OF AUVERGNE: It cannot be this weak and writhled shrimp
OF AUVERGNE: Should strike such terror to his enemies.
TALBOT: Madam, I have been bold to trouble you,
TALBOT: But since your ladyship is not at leisure,
TALBOT: I'll sort some other time to visit you.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: What means he now? Go ask him whither he goes.
Messenger: Stay, my Lord Talbot, for my lady craves
Messenger: To know the cause of your abrupt departure.
TALBOT: Marry, for that she's in a wrong belief,
TALBOT: I go to certify her Talbot's here.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Porter with keys
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: If thou be he, then art thou prisoner.
TALBOT: Prisoner! to whom?
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: To me, blood-thirsty lord,
OF AUVERGNE: And for that cause I trained thee to my house.
OF AUVERGNE: Long time thy shadow hath been thrall to me,
OF AUVERGNE: For in my gallery thy picture hangs:
OF AUVERGNE: But now the substance shall endure the like,
OF AUVERGNE: And I will chain these legs and arms of thine,
OF AUVERGNE: That hast by tyranny these many years
OF AUVERGNE: Wasted our country, slain our citizens
OF AUVERGNE: And sent our sons and husbands captivate.
TALBOT: Ha, ha, ha!
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Laughest thou, wretch? thy mirth shall turn to moan.
TALBOT: I laugh to see your ladyship so fond
TALBOT: To think that you have aught but Talbot's shadow
TALBOT: Whereon to practise your severity.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Why, art not thou the man?
TALBOT: I am indeed.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Then have I substance too.
TALBOT: No, no, I am but shadow of myself:
TALBOT: You are deceived, my substance is not here,
TALBOT: For what you see is but the smallest part
TALBOT: And least proportion of humanity:
TALBOT: I tell you, madam, were the whole frame here,
TALBOT: It is of such a spacious lofty pitch,
TALBOT: Your roof were not sufficient to contain't.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: This is a riddling merchant for the nonce,
OF AUVERGNE: He will be here, and yet he is not here:
OF AUVERGNE: How can these contrarieties agree?
TALBOT: That will I show you presently.
TALBOT: Winds his horn. Drums strike up: a peal of ordnance. Enter soldiers
TALBOT: How say you, madam? are you now persuaded
TALBOT: That Talbot is but shadow of himself?
TALBOT: These are his substance, sinews, arms and strength,
TALBOT: With which he yoketh your rebellious necks,
TALBOT: Razeth your cities and subverts your towns
TALBOT: And in a moment makes them desolate.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: Victorious Talbot! pardon my abuse:
OF AUVERGNE: I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited
OF AUVERGNE: And more than may be gather'd by thy shape.
OF AUVERGNE: Let my presumption not provoke thy wrath,
OF AUVERGNE: For I am sorry that with reverence
OF AUVERGNE: I did not entertain thee as thou art.
TALBOT: Be not dismay'd, fair lady, nor misconstrue
TALBOT: The mind of Talbot, as you did mistake
TALBOT: The outward composition of his body.
TALBOT: What you have done hath not offended me,
TALBOT: Nor other satisfaction do I crave,
TALBOT: But only, with your patience, that we may
TALBOT: Taste of your wine and see what cates you have,
TALBOT: For soldiers' stomachs always serve them well.
TALBOT: COUNTESS
OF AUVERGNE: With all my heart, and think me honoured
OF AUVERGNE: To feast so great a warrior in my house.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. London. The Temple-garden.
NARRATOR: Enter the Earls of SOMERSET, SUFFOLK, and WARWICK, RICHARD PLANTAGENET, VERNON, and another Lawyer
OF AUVERGNE: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Great lords and gentlemen, what means this silence?
PLANTAGENET: Dare no man answer in a case of truth?
SUFFOLK: Within the Temple-hall we were too loud,
SUFFOLK: The garden here is more convenient.
SUFFOLK: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Then say at once if I maintain'd the truth,
PLANTAGENET: Or else was wrangling Somerset in the error?
SUFFOLK: Faith, I have been a truant in the law,
SUFFOLK: And never yet could frame my will to it,
SUFFOLK: And therefore frame the law unto my will.
SOMERSET: Judge you, my Lord of Warwick, then, between us.
WARWICK: Between two hawks, which flies the higher pitch,
WARWICK: Between two dogs, which hath the deeper mouth,
WARWICK: Between two blades, which bears the better temper:
WARWICK: Between two horses, which doth bear him best,
WARWICK: Between two girls, which hath the merriest eye,
WARWICK: I have perhaps some shallow spirit of judgement,
WARWICK: But in these nice sharp quillets of the law,
WARWICK: Good faith, I am no wiser than a daw.
WARWICK: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Tut, tut, here is a mannerly forbearance:
PLANTAGENET: The truth appears so naked on my side
PLANTAGENET: That any purblind eye may find it out.
SOMERSET: And on my side it is so well apparell'd,
SOMERSET: So clear, so shining and so evident
SOMERSET: That it will glimmer through a blind man's eye.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Since you are tongue-tied and so loath to speak,
PLANTAGENET: In dumb significants proclaim your thoughts:
PLANTAGENET: Let him that is a true-born gentleman
PLANTAGENET: And stands upon the honour of his birth,
PLANTAGENET: If he suppose that I have pleaded truth,
PLANTAGENET: From off this brier pluck a white rose with me.
SOMERSET: Let him that is no coward nor no flatterer,
SOMERSET: But dare maintain the party of the truth,
SOMERSET: Pluck a red rose from off this thorn with me.
WARWICK: I love no colours, and without all colour
WARWICK: Of base insinuating flattery
WARWICK: I pluck this white rose with Plantagenet.
SUFFOLK: I pluck this red rose with young Somerset
SUFFOLK: And say withal I think he held the right.
VERNON: Stay, lords and gentlemen, and pluck no more,
VERNON: Till you conclude that he upon whose side
VERNON: The fewest roses are cropp'd from the tree
VERNON: Shall yield the other in the right opinion.
SOMERSET: Good Master Vernon, it is well objected:
SOMERSET: If I have fewest, I subscribe in silence.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: And I.
VERNON: Then for the truth and plainness of the case.
VERNON: I pluck this pale and maiden blossom here,
VERNON: Giving my verdict on the white rose side.
SOMERSET: Prick not your finger as you pluck it off,
SOMERSET: Lest bleeding you do paint the white rose red
SOMERSET: And fall on my side so, against your will.
VERNON: If I my lord, for my opinion bleed,
VERNON: Opinion shall be surgeon to my hurt
VERNON: And keep me on the side where still I am.
SOMERSET: Well, well, come on: who else?
Lawyer: Unless my study and my books be false,
Lawyer: The argument you held was wrong in you:
NARRATOR: To SOMERSET
Lawyer: In sign whereof I pluck a white rose too.
Lawyer: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Now, Somerset, where is your argument?
SOMERSET: Here in my scabbard, meditating that
SOMERSET: Shall dye your white rose in a bloody red.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Meantime your cheeks do counterfeit our roses,
PLANTAGENET: For pale they look with fear, as witnessing
PLANTAGENET: The truth on our side.
SOMERSET: No, Plantagenet,
SOMERSET: 'Tis not for fear but anger that thy cheeks
SOMERSET: Blush for pure shame to counterfeit our roses,
SOMERSET: And yet thy tongue will not confess thy error.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Hath not thy rose a canker, Somerset?
SOMERSET: Hath not thy rose a thorn, Plantagenet?
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Ay, sharp and piercing, to maintain his truth,
PLANTAGENET: Whiles thy consuming canker eats his falsehood.
SOMERSET: Well, I'll find friends to wear my bleeding roses,
SOMERSET: That shall maintain what I have said is true,
SOMERSET: Where false Plantagenet dare not be seen.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Now, by this maiden blossom in my hand,
PLANTAGENET: I scorn thee and thy fashion, peevish boy.
SUFFOLK: Turn not thy scorns this way, Plantagenet.
SUFFOLK: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Proud Pole, I will, and scorn both him and thee.
SUFFOLK: I'll turn my part thereof into thy throat.
SOMERSET: Away, away, good William de la Pole!
SOMERSET: We grace the yeoman by conversing with him.
WARWICK: Now, by God's will, thou wrong'st him, Somerset,
WARWICK: His grandfather was Lionel Duke of Clarence,
WARWICK: Third son to the third Edward King of England:
WARWICK: Spring crestless yeomen from so deep a root?
WARWICK: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: He bears him on the place's privilege,
PLANTAGENET: Or durst not, for his craven heart, say thus.
SOMERSET: By him that made me, I'll maintain my words
SOMERSET: On any plot of ground in Christendom.
SOMERSET: Was not thy father, Richard Earl of Cambridge,
SOMERSET: For treason executed in our late king's days?
SOMERSET: And, by his treason, stand'st not thou attainted,
SOMERSET: Corrupted, and exempt from ancient gentry?
SOMERSET: His trespass yet lives guilty in thy blood,
SOMERSET: And, till thou be restored, thou art a yeoman.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: My father was attached, not attainted,
PLANTAGENET: Condemn'd to die for treason, but no traitor,
PLANTAGENET: And that I'll prove on better men than Somerset,
PLANTAGENET: Were growing time once ripen'd to my will.
PLANTAGENET: For your partaker Pole and you yourself,
PLANTAGENET: I'll note you in my book of memory,
PLANTAGENET: To scourge you for this apprehension:
PLANTAGENET: Look to it well and say you are well warn'd.
SOMERSET: Ah, thou shalt find us ready for thee still,
SOMERSET: And know us by these colours for thy foes,
SOMERSET: For these my friends in spite of thee shall wear.
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: And, by my soul, this pale and angry rose,
PLANTAGENET: As cognizance of my blood-drinking hate,
PLANTAGENET: Will I for ever and my faction wear,
PLANTAGENET: Until it wither with me to my grave
PLANTAGENET: Or flourish to the height of my degree.
SUFFOLK: Go forward and be choked with thy ambition!
SUFFOLK: And so farewell until I meet thee next.
NARRATOR: Exit
SOMERSET: Have with thee, Pole. Farewell, ambitious Richard.
NARRATOR: Exit
SOMERSET: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: How I am braved and must perforce endure it!
WARWICK: This blot that they object against your house
WARWICK: Shall be wiped out in the next parliament
WARWICK: Call'd for the truce of Winchester and Gloucester,
WARWICK: And if thou be not then created York,
WARWICK: I will not live to be accounted Warwick.
WARWICK: Meantime, in signal of my love to thee,
WARWICK: Against proud Somerset and William Pole,
WARWICK: Will I upon thy party wear this rose:
WARWICK: And here I prophesy: this brawl to-day,
WARWICK: Grown to this faction in the Temple-garden,
WARWICK: Shall send between the red rose and the white
WARWICK: A thousand souls to death and deadly night.
WARWICK: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Good Master Vernon, I am bound to you,
PLANTAGENET: That you on my behalf would pluck a flower.
VERNON: In your behalf still will I wear the same.
Lawyer: And so will I.
Lawyer: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Thanks, gentle sir.
PLANTAGENET: Come, let us four to dinner: I dare say
PLANTAGENET: This quarrel will drink blood another day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The Tower of London.
NARRATOR: Enter MORTIMER, brought in a chair, and Gaolers
MORTIMER: Kind keepers of my weak decaying age,
MORTIMER: Let dying Mortimer here rest himself.
MORTIMER: Even like a man new haled from the rack,
MORTIMER: So fare my limbs with long imprisonment.
MORTIMER: And these grey locks, the pursuivants of death,
MORTIMER: Nestor-like aged in an age of care,
MORTIMER: Argue the end of Edmund Mortimer.
MORTIMER: These eyes, like lamps whose wasting oil is spent,
MORTIMER: Wax dim, as drawing to their exigent,
MORTIMER: Weak shoulders, overborne with burthening grief,
MORTIMER: And pithless arms, like to a wither'd vine
MORTIMER: That droops his sapless branches to the ground,
MORTIMER: Yet are these feet, whose strengthless stay is numb,
MORTIMER: Unable to support this lump of clay,
MORTIMER: Swift-winged with desire to get a grave,
MORTIMER: As witting I no other comfort have.
MORTIMER: But tell me, keeper, will my nephew come?
First Gaoler: Richard Plantagenet, my lord, will come:
First Gaoler: We sent unto the Temple, unto his chamber,
First Gaoler: And answer was return'd that he will come.
MORTIMER: Enough: my soul shall then be satisfied.
MORTIMER: Poor gentleman! his wrong doth equal mine.
MORTIMER: Since Henry Monmouth first began to reign,
MORTIMER: Before whose glory I was great in arms,
MORTIMER: This loathsome sequestration have I had:
MORTIMER: And even since then hath Richard been obscured,
MORTIMER: Deprived of honour and inheritance.
MORTIMER: But now the arbitrator of despairs,
MORTIMER: Just death, kind umpire of men's miseries,
MORTIMER: With sweet enlargement doth dismiss me hence:
MORTIMER: I would his troubles likewise were expired,
MORTIMER: That so he might recover what was lost.
NARRATOR: Enter RICHARD PLANTAGENET
First Gaoler: My lord, your loving nephew now is come.
MORTIMER: Richard Plantagenet, my friend, is he come?
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Ay, noble uncle, thus ignobly used,
PLANTAGENET: Your nephew, late despised Richard, comes.
MORTIMER: Direct mine arms I may embrace his neck,
MORTIMER: And in his bosom spend my latter gasp:
MORTIMER: O, tell me when my lips do touch his cheeks,
MORTIMER: That I may kindly give one fainting kiss.
MORTIMER: And now declare, sweet stem from York's great stock,
MORTIMER: Why didst thou say, of late thou wert despised?
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: First, lean thine aged back against mine arm,
PLANTAGENET: And, in that ease, I'll tell thee my disease.
PLANTAGENET: This day, in argument upon a case,
PLANTAGENET: Some words there grew 'twixt Somerset and me,
PLANTAGENET: Among which terms he used his lavish tongue
PLANTAGENET: And did upbraid me with my father's death:
PLANTAGENET: Which obloquy set bars before my tongue,
PLANTAGENET: Else with the like I had requited him.
PLANTAGENET: Therefore, good uncle, for my father's sake,
PLANTAGENET: In honour of a true Plantagenet
PLANTAGENET: And for alliance sake, declare the cause
PLANTAGENET: My father, Earl of Cambridge, lost his head.
MORTIMER: That cause, fair nephew, that imprison'd me
MORTIMER: And hath detain'd me all my flowering youth
MORTIMER: Within a loathsome dungeon, there to pine,
MORTIMER: Was cursed instrument of his decease.
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Discover more at large what cause that was,
PLANTAGENET: For I am ignorant and cannot guess.
MORTIMER: I will, if that my fading breath permit
MORTIMER: And death approach not ere my tale be done.
MORTIMER: Henry the Fourth, grandfather to this king,
MORTIMER: Deposed his nephew Richard, Edward's son,
MORTIMER: The first-begotten and the lawful heir,
MORTIMER: Of Edward king, the third of that descent:
MORTIMER: During whose reign the Percies of the north,
MORTIMER: Finding his usurpation most unjust,
MORTIMER: Endeavor'd my advancement to the throne:
MORTIMER: The reason moved these warlike lords to this
MORTIMER: Was, for that--young King Richard thus removed,
MORTIMER: Leaving no heir begotten of his body--
MORTIMER: I was the next by birth and parentage,
MORTIMER: For by my mother I derived am
MORTIMER: From Lionel Duke of Clarence, the third son
MORTIMER: To King Edward the Third, whereas he
MORTIMER: From John of Gaunt doth bring his pedigree,
MORTIMER: Being but fourth of that heroic line.
MORTIMER: But mark: as in this haughty attempt
MORTIMER: They laboured to plant the rightful heir,
MORTIMER: I lost my liberty and they their lives.
MORTIMER: Long after this, when Henry the Fifth,
MORTIMER: Succeeding his father Bolingbroke, did reign,
MORTIMER: Thy father, Earl of Cambridge, then derived
MORTIMER: From famous Edmund Langley, Duke of York,
MORTIMER: Marrying my sister that thy mother was,
MORTIMER: Again in pity of my hard distress
MORTIMER: Levied an army, weening to redeem
MORTIMER: And have install'd me in the diadem:
MORTIMER: But, as the rest, so fell that noble earl
MORTIMER: And was beheaded. Thus the Mortimers,
MORTIMER: In whom the tide rested, were suppress'd.
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Of which, my lord, your honour is the last.
MORTIMER: True, and thou seest that I no issue have
MORTIMER: And that my fainting words do warrant death,
MORTIMER: Thou art my heir, the rest I wish thee gather:
MORTIMER: But yet be wary in thy studious care.
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Thy grave admonishments prevail with me:
PLANTAGENET: But yet, methinks, my father's execution
PLANTAGENET: Was nothing less than bloody tyranny.
MORTIMER: With silence, nephew, be thou politic:
MORTIMER: Strong-fixed is the house of Lancaster,
MORTIMER: And like a mountain, not to be removed.
MORTIMER: But now thy uncle is removing hence:
MORTIMER: As princes do their courts, when they are cloy'd
MORTIMER: With long continuance in a settled place.
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: O, uncle, would some part of my young years
PLANTAGENET: Might but redeem the passage of your age!
MORTIMER: Thou dost then wrong me, as that slaughterer doth
MORTIMER: Which giveth many wounds when one will kill.
MORTIMER: Mourn not, except thou sorrow for my good,
MORTIMER: Only give order for my funeral:
MORTIMER: And so farewell, and fair be all thy hopes
MORTIMER: And prosperous be thy life in peace and war!
NARRATOR: Dies
MORTIMER: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: And peace, no war, befall thy parting soul!
PLANTAGENET: In prison hast thou spent a pilgrimage
PLANTAGENET: And like a hermit overpass'd thy days.
PLANTAGENET: Well, I will lock his counsel in my breast,
PLANTAGENET: And what I do imagine let that rest.
PLANTAGENET: Keepers, convey him hence, and I myself
PLANTAGENET: Will see his burial better than his life.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Gaolers, bearing out the body of MORTIMER
PLANTAGENET: Here dies the dusky torch of Mortimer,
PLANTAGENET: Choked with ambition of the meaner sort:
PLANTAGENET: And for those wrongs, those bitter injuries,
PLANTAGENET: Which Somerset hath offer'd to my house:
PLANTAGENET: I doubt not but with honour to redress,
PLANTAGENET: And therefore haste I to the parliament,
PLANTAGENET: Either to be restored to my blood,
PLANTAGENET: Or make my ill the advantage of my good.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The Parliament-house.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING HENRY VI, EXETER, GLOUCESTER,  WARWICK, SOMERSET, and SUFFOLK, the BISHOP OF  WINCHESTER, RICHARD PLANTAGENET, and others.  GLOUCESTER offers to put up a bill, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER snatches it, and tears it
PLANTAGENET: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Comest thou with deep premeditated lines,
OF WINCHESTER: With written pamphlets studiously devised,
OF WINCHESTER: Humphrey of Gloucester? If thou canst accuse,
OF WINCHESTER: Or aught intend'st to lay unto my charge,
OF WINCHESTER: Do it without invention, suddenly,
OF WINCHESTER: As I with sudden and extemporal speech
OF WINCHESTER: Purpose to answer what thou canst object.
GLOUCESTER: Presumptuous priest! this place commands my patience,
GLOUCESTER: Or thou shouldst find thou hast dishonour'd me.
GLOUCESTER: Think not, although in writing I preferr'd
GLOUCESTER: The manner of thy vile outrageous crimes,
GLOUCESTER: That therefore I have forged, or am not able
GLOUCESTER: Verbatim to rehearse the method of my pen:
GLOUCESTER: No, prelate, such is thy audacious wickedness,
GLOUCESTER: Thy lewd, pestiferous and dissentious pranks,
GLOUCESTER: As very infants prattle of thy pride.
GLOUCESTER: Thou art a most pernicious usurer,
GLOUCESTER: Forward by nature, enemy to peace,
GLOUCESTER: Lascivious, wanton, more than well beseems
GLOUCESTER: A man of thy profession and degree,
GLOUCESTER: And for thy treachery, what's more manifest?
GLOUCESTER: In that thou laid'st a trap to take my life,
GLOUCESTER: As well at London bridge as at the Tower.
GLOUCESTER: Beside, I fear me, if thy thoughts were sifted,
GLOUCESTER: The king, thy sovereign, is not quite exempt
GLOUCESTER: From envious malice of thy swelling heart.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Gloucester, I do defy thee. Lords, vouchsafe
OF WINCHESTER: To give me hearing what I shall reply.
OF WINCHESTER: If I were covetous, ambitious or perverse,
OF WINCHESTER: As he will have me, how am I so poor?
OF WINCHESTER: Or how haps it I seek not to advance
OF WINCHESTER: Or raise myself, but keep my wonted calling?
OF WINCHESTER: And for dissension, who preferreth peace
OF WINCHESTER: More than I do?--except I be provoked.
OF WINCHESTER: No, my good lords, it is not that offends,
OF WINCHESTER: It is not that that hath incensed the duke:
OF WINCHESTER: It is, because no one should sway but he,
OF WINCHESTER: No one but he should be about the king,
OF WINCHESTER: And that engenders thunder in his breast
OF WINCHESTER: And makes him roar these accusations forth.
OF WINCHESTER: But he shall know I am as good--
GLOUCESTER: As good!
GLOUCESTER: Thou bastard of my grandfather!
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Ay, lordly sir, for what are you, I pray,
OF WINCHESTER: But one imperious in another's throne?
GLOUCESTER: Am I not protector, saucy priest?
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: And am not I a prelate of the church?
GLOUCESTER: Yes, as an outlaw in a castle keeps
GLOUCESTER: And useth it to patronage his theft.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Unreverent Gloster!
GLOUCESTER: Thou art reverent
GLOUCESTER: Touching thy spiritual function, not thy life.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: Rome shall remedy this.
WARWICK: Roam thither, then.
SOMERSET: My lord, it were your duty to forbear.
WARWICK: Ay, see the bishop be not overborne.
SOMERSET: Methinks my lord should be religious
SOMERSET: And know the office that belongs to such.

WARWICK: Is not his grace protector to the king?

Mayor: The bishop and the Duke of Gloucester's men,
Mayor: Forbidden late to carry any weapon,
Mayor: Have fill'd their pockets full of pebble stones

Mayor: Do pelt so fast at one another's pate

Mayor: Our windows are broke down in every street
Mayor: And we for fear compell'd to shut our shops.

KING HENRY VI: First Serving-man	Nay, if we be forbidden stones,

KING HENRY VI: Second Serving-man	Do what ye dare, we are as resolute.

WARWICK: BISHOP

GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  Ay, but, I fear me, with a hollow heart.--

GLOUCESTER: BISHOP

KING HENRY VI: First Serving-man	Content: I'll to the surgeon's.
KING HENRY VI: Second Serving-man	And so will I.
KING HENRY VI: Third Serving-man	And I will see what physic the tavern affords.

KING HENRY VI: That Richard be restored to his blood.
WARWICK: Let Richard be restored to his blood,
WARWICK: So shall his father's wrongs be recompensed.
WARWICK: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: As will the rest, so willeth Winchester.

KING HENRY VI: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: Thy humble servant vows obedience

KING HENRY VI: I gird thee with the valiant sword of York:
KING HENRY VI: Rise Richard, like a true Plantagenet,
KING HENRY VI: And rise created princely Duke of York.
KING HENRY VI: RICHARD
PLANTAGENET: And so thrive Richard as thy foes may fall!
PLANTAGENET: And as my duty springs, so perish they
PLANTAGENET: That grudge one thought against your majesty!

SOMERSET: [Aside]  Perish, base prince, ignoble Duke of York!
GLOUCESTER: Now will it best avail your majesty
GLOUCESTER: To cross the seas and to be crown'd in France:
GLOUCESTER: The presence of a king engenders love
GLOUCESTER: Amongst his subjects and his loyal friends,
GLOUCESTER: As it disanimates his enemies.
KING HENRY VI: When Gloucester says the word, King Henry goes,
KING HENRY VI: For friendly counsel cuts off many foes.
GLOUCESTER: Your ships already are in readiness.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Flourish. Exeunt all but EXETER
EXETER: Ay, we may march in England or in France,
EXETER: Not seeing what is likely to ensue.
EXETER: This late dissension grown betwixt the peers
EXETER: Burns under feigned ashes of forged love
EXETER: And will at last break out into a flame:
EXETER: As fester'd members rot but by degree,
EXETER: Till bones and flesh and sinews fall away,
EXETER: So will this base and envious discord breed.
EXETER: And now I fear that fatal prophecy
EXETER: Which in the time of Henry named the Fifth
EXETER: Was in the mouth of every sucking babe,
EXETER: That Henry born at Monmouth should win all
EXETER: And Henry born at Windsor lose all:
EXETER: Which is so plain that Exeter doth wish
EXETER: His days may finish ere that hapless time.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. France. Before Rouen.
NARRATOR: Enter JOAN LA PUCELLE disguised, with four Soldiers with sacks upon their backs
JOAN LA PUCELLE: These are the city gates, the gates of Rouen,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Through which our policy must make a breach:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Take heed, be wary how you place your words,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Talk like the vulgar sort of market men
JOAN LA PUCELLE: That come to gather money for their corn.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: If we have entrance, as I hope we shall,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And that we find the slothful watch but weak,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I'll by a sign give notice to our friends,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: That Charles the Dauphin may encounter them.
First Soldier: Our sacks shall be a mean to sack the city,
First Soldier: And we be lords and rulers over Rouen,
First Soldier: Therefore we'll knock.
NARRATOR: Knocks
Watch: [Within]  Qui est la?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Paysans, pauvres gens de France,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Poor market folks that come to sell their corn.
Watch: Enter, go in, the market bell is rung.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Now, Rouen, I'll shake thy bulwarks to the ground.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES, the BASTARD OF ORLEANS, ALENCON, REIGNIER, and forces

NARRATOR: An alarum. Enter TALBOT in an excursion

TALBOT: That hardly we escaped the pride of France.

NARRATOR: An alarum: excursions. BEDFORD, brought in sick  in a chair. Enter TALBOT and BURGUNDY without:  within JOAN LA PUCELLE, CHARLES, BASTARD OF ORLEANS, ALENCON, and REIGNIER, on the walls

JOAN LA PUCELLE: 'Twas full of darnel, do you like the taste?

TALBOT: And I, as sure as English Henry lives

TALBOT: As sure as in this late-betrayed town

BEDFORD: Methinks I should revive the soldiers' hearts,

TALBOT: Undaunted spirit in a dying breast!
TALBOT: Then be it so: heavens keep old Bedford safe!
TALBOT: And now no more ado, brave Burgundy,
TALBOT: But gather we our forces out of hand
TALBOT: And set upon our boasting enemy.

TALBOT: Lost, and recover'd in a day again!

TALBOT: Yet heavens have glory for this victory!

BURGUNDY: Thy noble deeds as valour's monuments.

TALBOT: I think her old familiar is asleep:
TALBOT: Now where's the Bastard's braves, and Charles his gleeks?

TALBOT: That such a valiant company are fled.
TALBOT: Now will we take some order in the town,
TALBOT: Placing therein some expert officers,
TALBOT: And then depart to Paris to the king,
TALBOT: For there young Henry with his nobles lie.
BURGUNDY: What wills Lord Talbot pleaseth Burgundy.
TALBOT: But yet, before we go, let's not forget
TALBOT: The noble Duke of Bedford late deceased,
TALBOT: But see his exequies fulfill'd in Rouen:
TALBOT: A braver soldier never couched lance,
TALBOT: A gentler heart did never sway in court,
TALBOT: But kings and mightiest potentates must die,
TALBOT: For that's the end of human misery.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The plains near Rouen.
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES, the BASTARD OF ORLEANS, ALENCON, JOAN LA PUCELLE, and forces

JOAN LA PUCELLE: And was he not in England prisoner?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But when they heard he was thine enemy,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: They set him free without his ransom paid,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: In spite of Burgundy and all his friends.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: See, then, thou fight'st against thy countrymen
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And joint'st with them will be thy slaughtermen.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Come, come, return, return, thou wandering lord:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Charles and the rest will take thee in their arms.
BURGUNDY: I am vanquished, these haughty words of hers
BURGUNDY: Have batter'd me like roaring cannon-shot,
BURGUNDY: And made me almost yield upon my knees.
BURGUNDY: Forgive me, country, and sweet countrymen,
BURGUNDY: And, lords, accept this hearty kind embrace:
BURGUNDY: My forces and my power of men are yours:
BURGUNDY: So farewell, Talbot, I'll no longer trust thee.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: [Aside]  Done like a Frenchman: turn, and turn again!
CHARLES: Welcome, brave duke! thy friendship makes us fresh.
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: And doth beget new courage in our breasts.
ALENCON: Pucelle hath bravely play'd her part in this,
ALENCON: And doth deserve a coronet of gold.
CHARLES: Now let us on, my lords, and join our powers,
CHARLES: And seek how we may prejudice the foe.

NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER, BISHOP OF  WINCHESTER, YORK, SUFFOLK, SOMERSET, WARWICK,  EXETER, VERNON	BASSET, and others. To them with his Soldiers, TALBOT

KING HENRY VI: We here create you Earl of Shrewsbury,
KING HENRY VI: And in our coronation take your place.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Flourish. Exeunt all but VERNON and BASSET
VERNON: Now, sir, to you, that were so hot at sea,
VERNON: Disgracing of these colours that I wear
VERNON: In honour of my noble Lord of York:
VERNON: Darest thou maintain the former words thou spakest?
BASSET: Yes, sir, as well as you dare patronage
BASSET: The envious barking of your saucy tongue
BASSET: Against my lord the Duke of Somerset.
VERNON: Sirrah, thy lord I honour as he is.
BASSET: Why, what is he? as good a man as York.
VERNON: Hark ye, not so: in witness, take ye that.
NARRATOR: Strikes him
BASSET: Villain, thou know'st the law of arms is such
BASSET: That whoso draws a sword, 'tis present death,
BASSET: Or else this blow should broach thy dearest blood.
BASSET: But I'll unto his majesty, and crave
BASSET: I may have liberty to venge this wrong,
BASSET: When thou shalt see I'll meet thee to thy cost.
VERNON: Well, miscreant, I'll be there as soon as you,
VERNON: And, after, meet you sooner than you would.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Paris. A hall of state.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER, BISHOP OF  WINCHESTER, YORK, SUFFOLK, SOMERSET, WARWICK, TALBOT, EXETER, the Governor, of Paris, and others
GLOUCESTER: Lord bishop, set the crown upon his head.
GLOUCESTER: BISHOP
OF WINCHESTER: God save King Henry, of that name the sixth!
GLOUCESTER: Now, governor of Paris, take your oath,
GLOUCESTER: That you elect no other king but him,
GLOUCESTER: Esteem none friends but such as are his friends,
GLOUCESTER: And none your foes but such as shall pretend
GLOUCESTER: Malicious practises against his state:
GLOUCESTER: This shall ye do, so help you righteous God!
NARRATOR: Enter FASTOLFE
FASTOLFE: My gracious sovereign, as I rode from Calais,
FASTOLFE: To haste unto your coronation,
FASTOLFE: A letter was deliver'd to my hands,
FASTOLFE: Writ to your grace from the Duke of Burgundy.
TALBOT: Shame to the Duke of Burgundy and thee!
TALBOT: I vow'd, base knight, when I did meet thee next,
TALBOT: To tear the garter from thy craven's leg,
NARRATOR: Plucking it off
TALBOT: Which I have done, because unworthily
TALBOT: Thou wast installed in that high degree.
TALBOT: Pardon me, princely Henry, and the rest
TALBOT: This dastard, at the battle of Patay,
TALBOT: When but in all I was six thousand strong
TALBOT: And that the French were almost ten to one,
TALBOT: Before we met or that a stroke was given,
TALBOT: Like to a trusty squire did run away:
TALBOT: In which assault we lost twelve hundred men,
TALBOT: Myself and divers gentlemen beside
TALBOT: Were there surprised and taken prisoners.
TALBOT: Then judge, great lords, if I have done amiss,
TALBOT: Or whether that such cowards ought to wear
TALBOT: This ornament of knighthood, yea or no.
GLOUCESTER: To say the truth, this fact was infamous
GLOUCESTER: And ill beseeming any common man,
GLOUCESTER: Much more a knight, a captain and a leader.
TALBOT: When first this order was ordain'd, my lords,
TALBOT: Knights of the garter were of noble birth,
TALBOT: Valiant and virtuous, full of haughty courage,
TALBOT: Such as were grown to credit by the wars,
TALBOT: Not fearing death, nor shrinking for distress,
TALBOT: But always resolute in most extremes.
TALBOT: He then that is not furnish'd in this sort
TALBOT: Doth but usurp the sacred name of knight,
TALBOT: Profaning this most honourable order,
TALBOT: And should, if I were worthy to be judge,
TALBOT: Be quite degraded, like a hedge-born swain
TALBOT: That doth presume to boast of gentle blood.
KING HENRY VI: Stain to thy countrymen, thou hear'st thy doom!
KING HENRY VI: Be packing, therefore, thou that wast a knight:
KING HENRY VI: Henceforth we banish thee, on pain of death.
NARRATOR: Exit FASTOLFE
KING HENRY VI: And now, my lord protector, view the letter
KING HENRY VI: Sent from our uncle Duke of Burgundy.
GLOUCESTER: What means his grace, that he hath changed his style?
GLOUCESTER: No more but, plain and bluntly, 'To the king!'
GLOUCESTER: Hath he forgot he is his sovereign?
GLOUCESTER: Or doth this churlish superscription
GLOUCESTER: Pretend some alteration in good will?
GLOUCESTER: What's here?
NARRATOR: Reads
GLOUCESTER: 'I have, upon especial cause,
GLOUCESTER: Moved with compassion of my country's wreck,
GLOUCESTER: Together with the pitiful complaints
GLOUCESTER: Of such as your oppression feeds upon,
GLOUCESTER: Forsaken your pernicious faction
GLOUCESTER: And join'd with Charles, the rightful King of France.'
GLOUCESTER: O monstrous treachery! can this be so,
GLOUCESTER: That in alliance, amity and oaths,
GLOUCESTER: There should be found such false dissembling guile?
KING HENRY VI: What! doth my uncle Burgundy revolt?
GLOUCESTER: He doth, my lord, and is become your foe.
KING HENRY VI: Is that the worst this letter doth contain?
GLOUCESTER: It is the worst, and all, my lord, he writes.
KING HENRY VI: Why, then, Lord Talbot there shall talk with him
KING HENRY VI: And give him chastisement for this abuse.
KING HENRY VI: How say you, my lord? are you not content?
TALBOT: Content, my liege! yes, but that I am prevented,
TALBOT: I should have begg'd I might have been employ'd.
KING HENRY VI: Then gather strength and march unto him straight:
KING HENRY VI: Let him perceive how ill we brook his treason
KING HENRY VI: And what offence it is to flout his friends.
TALBOT: I go, my lord, in heart desiring still
TALBOT: You may behold confusion of your foes.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter VERNON and BASSET
VERNON: Grant me the combat, gracious sovereign.
BASSET: And me, my lord, grant me the combat too.
YORK: This is my servant: hear him, noble prince.
SOMERSET: And this is mine: sweet Henry, favour him.
KING HENRY VI: Be patient, lords, and give them leave to speak.
KING HENRY VI: Say, gentlemen, what makes you thus exclaim?
KING HENRY VI: And wherefore crave you combat? or with whom?
VERNON: With him, my lord, for he hath done me wrong.
BASSET: And I with him, for he hath done me wrong.
KING HENRY VI: What is that wrong whereof you both complain?
KING HENRY VI: First let me know, and then I'll answer you.
BASSET: Crossing the sea from England into France,
BASSET: This fellow here, with envious carping tongue,
BASSET: Upbraided me about the rose I wear,
BASSET: Saying, the sanguine colour of the leaves
BASSET: Did represent my master's blushing cheeks,
BASSET: When stubbornly he did repugn the truth
BASSET: About a certain question in the law
BASSET: Argued betwixt the Duke of York and him,
BASSET: With other vile and ignominious terms:
BASSET: In confutation of which rude reproach
BASSET: And in defence of my lord's worthiness,
BASSET: I crave the benefit of law of arms.
VERNON: And that is my petition, noble lord:
VERNON: For though he seem with forged quaint conceit
VERNON: To set a gloss upon his bold intent,
VERNON: Yet know, my lord, I was provoked by him,
VERNON: And he first took exceptions at this badge,
VERNON: Pronouncing that the paleness of this flower
VERNON: Bewray'd the faintness of my master's heart.
YORK: Will not this malice, Somerset, be left?
SOMERSET: Your private grudge, my Lord of York, will out,
SOMERSET: Though ne'er so cunningly you smother it.
KING HENRY VI: Good Lord, what madness rules in brainsick men,
KING HENRY VI: When for so slight and frivolous a cause
KING HENRY VI: Such factious emulations shall arise!
KING HENRY VI: Good cousins both, of York and Somerset,
KING HENRY VI: Quiet yourselves, I pray, and be at peace.
YORK: Let this dissension first be tried by fight,
YORK: And then your highness shall command a peace.
SOMERSET: The quarrel toucheth none but us alone,
SOMERSET: Betwixt ourselves let us decide it then.
YORK: There is my pledge, accept it, Somerset.
VERNON: Nay, let it rest where it began at first.
BASSET: Confirm it so, mine honourable lord.
GLOUCESTER: Confirm it so! Confounded be your strife!
GLOUCESTER: And perish ye, with your audacious prate!
GLOUCESTER: Presumptuous vassals, are you not ashamed
GLOUCESTER: With this immodest clamorous outrage
GLOUCESTER: To trouble and disturb the king and us?
GLOUCESTER: And you, my lords, methinks you do not well
GLOUCESTER: To bear with their perverse objections,
GLOUCESTER: Much less to take occasion from their mouths
GLOUCESTER: To raise a mutiny betwixt yourselves:
GLOUCESTER: Let me persuade you take a better course.
EXETER: It grieves his highness: good my lords, be friends.
KING HENRY VI: Come hither, you that would be combatants:
KING HENRY VI: Henceforth I charge you, as you love our favour,
KING HENRY VI: Quite to forget this quarrel and the cause.
KING HENRY VI: And you, my lords, remember where we are,
KING HENRY VI: In France, amongst a fickle wavering nation:
KING HENRY VI: If they perceive dissension in our looks
KING HENRY VI: And that within ourselves we disagree,
KING HENRY VI: How will their grudging stomachs be provoked
KING HENRY VI: To wilful disobedience, and rebel!
KING HENRY VI: Beside, what infamy will there arise,
KING HENRY VI: When foreign princes shall be certified
KING HENRY VI: That for a toy, a thing of no regard,
KING HENRY VI: King Henry's peers and chief nobility
KING HENRY VI: Destroy'd themselves, and lost the realm of France!
KING HENRY VI: O, think upon the conquest of my father,
KING HENRY VI: My tender years, and let us not forego
KING HENRY VI: That for a trifle that was bought with blood
KING HENRY VI: Let me be umpire in this doubtful strife.
KING HENRY VI: I see no reason, if I wear this rose,
NARRATOR: Putting on a red rose
KING HENRY VI: That any one should therefore be suspicious
KING HENRY VI: I more incline to Somerset than York:
KING HENRY VI: Both are my kinsmen, and I love them both:
KING HENRY VI: As well they may upbraid me with my crown,
KING HENRY VI: Because, forsooth, the king of Scots is crown'd.
KING HENRY VI: But your discretions better can persuade
KING HENRY VI: Than I am able to instruct or teach:
KING HENRY VI: And therefore, as we hither came in peace,
KING HENRY VI: So let us still continue peace and love.
KING HENRY VI: Cousin of York, we institute your grace
KING HENRY VI: To be our regent in these parts of France:
KING HENRY VI: And, good my Lord of Somerset, unite
KING HENRY VI: Your troops of horsemen with his bands of foot,
KING HENRY VI: And, like true subjects, sons of your progenitors,
KING HENRY VI: Go cheerfully together and digest.
KING HENRY VI: Your angry choler on your enemies.
KING HENRY VI: Ourself, my lord protector and the rest
KING HENRY VI: After some respite will return to Calais,
KING HENRY VI: From thence to England, where I hope ere long
KING HENRY VI: To be presented, by your victories,
KING HENRY VI: With Charles, Alencon and that traitorous rout.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt all but YORK, WARWICK, EXETER and VERNON
WARWICK: My Lord of York, I promise you, the king
WARWICK: Prettily, methought, did play the orator.
YORK: And so he did, but yet I like it not,
YORK: In that he wears the badge of Somerset.
WARWICK: Tush, that was but his fancy, blame him not,
WARWICK: I dare presume, sweet prince, he thought no harm.
YORK: An if I wist he did,--but let it rest,
YORK: Other affairs must now be managed.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but EXETER
EXETER: Well didst thou, Richard, to suppress thy voice,
EXETER: For, had the passions of thy heart burst out,
EXETER: I fear we should have seen decipher'd there
EXETER: More rancorous spite, more furious raging broils,
EXETER: Than yet can be imagined or supposed.
EXETER: But howsoe'er, no simple man that sees
EXETER: This jarring discord of nobility,
EXETER: This shouldering of each other in the court,
EXETER: This factious bandying of their favourites,
EXETER: But that it doth presage some ill event.
EXETER: 'Tis much when sceptres are in children's hands,
EXETER: But more when envy breeds unkind division,
EXETER: There comes the rain, there begins confusion.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before Bourdeaux.
NARRATOR: Enter TALBOT, with trump and drum
TALBOT: Go to the gates of Bourdeaux, trumpeter:
TALBOT: Summon their general unto the wall.
NARRATOR: Trumpet sounds. Enter General and others, aloft
TALBOT: English John Talbot, captains, calls you forth,
TALBOT: Servant in arms to Harry King of England,
TALBOT: And thus he would: Open your city gates,
TALBOT: Be humble to us, call my sovereign yours,
TALBOT: And do him homage as obedient subjects,
TALBOT: And I'll withdraw me and my bloody power:
TALBOT: But, if you frown upon this proffer'd peace,
TALBOT: You tempt the fury of my three attendants,
TALBOT: Lean famine, quartering steel, and climbing fire,
TALBOT: Who in a moment even with the earth
TALBOT: Shall lay your stately and air-braving towers,
TALBOT: If you forsake the offer of their love.
General: Thou ominous and fearful owl of death,
General: Our nation's terror and their bloody scourge!
General: The period of thy tyranny approacheth.
General: On us thou canst not enter but by death,
General: For, I protest, we are well fortified
General: And strong enough to issue out and fight:
General: If thou retire, the Dauphin, well appointed,
General: Stands with the snares of war to tangle thee:
General: On either hand thee there are squadrons pitch'd,
General: To wall thee from the liberty of flight,
General: And no way canst thou turn thee for redress,
General: But death doth front thee with apparent spoil
General: And pale destruction meets thee in the face.
General: Ten thousand French have ta'en the sacrament
General: To rive their dangerous artillery
General: Upon no Christian soul but English Talbot.
General: Lo, there thou stand'st, a breathing valiant man,
General: Of an invincible unconquer'd spirit!
General: This is the latest glory of thy praise
General: That I, thy enemy, due thee withal,
General: For ere the glass, that now begins to run,
General: Finish the process of his sandy hour,
General: These eyes, that see thee now well coloured,
General: Shall see thee wither'd, bloody, pale and dead.
NARRATOR: Drum afar off
General: Hark! hark! the Dauphin's drum, a warning bell,
General: Sings heavy music to thy timorous soul,
General: And mine shall ring thy dire departure out.
General: Exeunt General,  and c
TALBOT: He fables not, I hear the enemy:
TALBOT: Out, some light horsemen, and peruse their wings.
TALBOT: O, negligent and heedless discipline!
TALBOT: How are we park'd and bounded in a pale,
TALBOT: A little herd of England's timorous deer,
TALBOT: Mazed with a yelping kennel of French curs!
TALBOT: If we be English deer, be then in blood,
TALBOT: Not rascal-like, to fall down with a pinch,
TALBOT: But rather, moody-mad and desperate stags,
TALBOT: Turn on the bloody hounds with heads of steel
TALBOT: And make the cowards stand aloof at bay:
TALBOT: Sell every man his life as dear as mine,
TALBOT: And they shall find dear deer of us, my friends.
TALBOT: God and Saint George, Talbot and England's right,
TALBOT: Prosper our colours in this dangerous fight!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Plains in Gascony.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger that meets YORK. Enter YORK with trumpet and many Soldiers
YORK: Are not the speedy scouts return'd again,
YORK: That dogg'd the mighty army of the Dauphin?
Messenger: They are return'd, my lord, and give it out
Messenger: That he is march'd to Bourdeaux with his power,
Messenger: To fight with Talbot: as he march'd along,
Messenger: By your espials were discovered
Messenger: Two mightier troops than that the Dauphin led,
Messenger: Which join'd with him and made their march for Bourdeaux.
YORK: A plague upon that villain Somerset,
YORK: That thus delays my promised supply
YORK: Of horsemen, that were levied for this siege!
YORK: Renowned Talbot doth expect my aid,
YORK: And I am lowted by a traitor villain
YORK: And cannot help the noble chevalier:
YORK: God comfort him in this necessity!
YORK: If he miscarry, farewell wars in France.
NARRATOR: Enter Sir William LUCY
LUCY: Thou princely leader of our English strength,
LUCY: Never so needful on the earth of France,
LUCY: Spur to the rescue of the noble Talbot,
LUCY: Who now is girdled with a waist of iron
LUCY: And hemm'd about with grim destruction:
LUCY: To Bourdeaux, warlike duke! to Bourdeaux, York!
LUCY: Else, farewell Talbot, France, and England's honour.
YORK: O God, that Somerset, who in proud heart
YORK: Doth stop my cornets, were in Talbot's place!
YORK: So should we save a valiant gentleman
YORK: By forfeiting a traitor and a coward.
YORK: Mad ire and wrathful fury makes me weep,
YORK: That thus we die, while remiss traitors sleep.
LUCY: O, send some succor to the distress'd lord!
YORK: He dies, we lose, I break my warlike word,
YORK: We mourn, France smiles, we lose, they daily get,
YORK: All 'long of this vile traitor Somerset.
LUCY: Then God take mercy on brave Talbot's soul,
LUCY: And on his son young John, who two hours since
LUCY: I met in travel toward his warlike father!
LUCY: This seven years did not Talbot see his son,
LUCY: And now they meet where both their lives are done.
YORK: Alas, what joy shall noble Talbot have
YORK: To bid his young son welcome to his grave?
YORK: Away! vexation almost stops my breath,
YORK: That sunder'd friends greet in the hour of death.
YORK: Lucy, farewell, no more my fortune can,
YORK: But curse the cause I cannot aid the man.
YORK: Maine, Blois, Poictiers, and Tours, are won away,
YORK: 'Long all of Somerset and his delay.
NARRATOR: Exit, with his soldiers
LUCY: Thus, while the vulture of sedition
LUCY: Feeds in the bosom of such great commanders,
LUCY: Sleeping neglection doth betray to loss
LUCY: The conquest of our scarce cold conqueror,
LUCY: That ever living man of memory,
LUCY: Henry the Fifth: whiles they each other cross,
LUCY: Lives, honours, lands and all hurry to loss.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Other plains in Gascony.
NARRATOR: Enter SOMERSET, with his army, a Captain of TALBOT's with him
SOMERSET: It is too late, I cannot send them now:
SOMERSET: This expedition was by York and Talbot
SOMERSET: Too rashly plotted: all our general force
SOMERSET: Might with a sally of the very town
SOMERSET: Be buckled with: the over-daring Talbot
SOMERSET: Hath sullied all his gloss of former honour
SOMERSET: By this unheedful, desperate, wild adventure:
SOMERSET: York set him on to fight and die in shame,
SOMERSET: That, Talbot dead, great York might bear the name.
Captain: Here is Sir William Lucy, who with me
Captain: Set from our o'ermatch'd forces forth for aid.
NARRATOR: Enter Sir William LUCY
SOMERSET: How now, Sir William! whither were you sent?
LUCY: Whither, my lord? from bought and sold Lord Talbot,
LUCY: Who, ring'd about with bold adversity,
LUCY: Cries out for noble York and Somerset,
LUCY: To beat assailing death from his weak legions:
LUCY: And whiles the honourable captain there
LUCY: Drops bloody sweat from his war-wearied limbs,
LUCY: And, in advantage lingering, looks for rescue,
LUCY: You, his false hopes, the trust of England's honour,
LUCY: Keep off aloof with worthless emulation.
LUCY: Let not your private discord keep away
LUCY: The levied succors that should lend him aid,
LUCY: While he, renowned noble gentleman,
LUCY: Yields up his life unto a world of odds:
LUCY: Orleans the Bastard, Charles, Burgundy,
LUCY: Alencon, Reignier, compass him about,
LUCY: And Talbot perisheth by your default.
SOMERSET: York set him on, York should have sent him aid.
LUCY: And York as fast upon your grace exclaims,
LUCY: Swearing that you withhold his levied host,
LUCY: Collected for this expedition.
SOMERSET: York lies, he might have sent and had the horse,
SOMERSET: I owe him little duty, and less love,
SOMERSET: And take foul scorn to fawn on him by sending.
LUCY: The fraud of England, not the force of France,
LUCY: Hath now entrapp'd the noble-minded Talbot:
LUCY: Never to England shall he bear his life,
LUCY: But dies, betray'd to fortune by your strife.
SOMERSET: Come, go, I will dispatch the horsemen straight:
SOMERSET: Within six hours they will be at his aid.
LUCY: Too late comes rescue: he is ta'en or slain,
LUCY: For fly he could not, if he would have fled,
LUCY: And fly would Talbot never, though he might.
SOMERSET: If he be dead, brave Talbot, then adieu!
LUCY: His fame lives in the world, his shame in you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The English camp near Bourdeaux.
NARRATOR: Enter TALBOT and JOHN his son
TALBOT: O young John Talbot! I did send for thee
TALBOT: To tutor thee in stratagems of war,
TALBOT: That Talbot's name might be in thee revived
TALBOT: When sapless age and weak unable limbs
TALBOT: Should bring thy father to his drooping chair.
TALBOT: But, O malignant and ill-boding stars!
TALBOT: Now thou art come unto a feast of death,
TALBOT: A terrible and unavoided danger:
TALBOT: Therefore, dear boy, mount on my swiftest horse,
TALBOT: And I'll direct thee how thou shalt escape
TALBOT: By sudden flight: come, dally not, be gone.
JOHN TALBOT: Is my name Talbot? and am I your son?
JOHN TALBOT: And shall I fly? O if you love my mother,
JOHN TALBOT: Dishonour not her honourable name,
JOHN TALBOT: To make a bastard and a slave of me!
JOHN TALBOT: The world will say, he is not Talbot's blood,
JOHN TALBOT: That basely fled when noble Talbot stood.
TALBOT: Fly, to revenge my death, if I be slain.
JOHN TALBOT: He that flies so will ne'er return again.
TALBOT: If we both stay, we both are sure to die.
JOHN TALBOT: Then let me stay, and, father, do you fly:
JOHN TALBOT: Your loss is great, so your regard should be,
JOHN TALBOT: My worth unknown, no loss is known in me.
JOHN TALBOT: Upon my death the French can little boast,
JOHN TALBOT: In yours they will, in you all hopes are lost.
JOHN TALBOT: Flight cannot stain the honour you have won,
JOHN TALBOT: But mine it will, that no exploit have done:
JOHN TALBOT: You fled for vantage, everyone will swear,
JOHN TALBOT: But, if I bow, they'll say it was for fear.
JOHN TALBOT: There is no hope that ever I will stay,
JOHN TALBOT: If the first hour I shrink and run away.
JOHN TALBOT: Here on my knee I beg mortality,
JOHN TALBOT: Rather than life preserved with infamy.
TALBOT: Shall all thy mother's hopes lie in one tomb?
JOHN TALBOT: Ay, rather than I'll shame my mother's womb.
TALBOT: Upon my blessing, I command thee go.
JOHN TALBOT: To fight I will, but not to fly the foe.
TALBOT: Part of thy father may be saved in thee.
JOHN TALBOT: No part of him but will be shame in me.
TALBOT: Thou never hadst renown, nor canst not lose it.
JOHN TALBOT: Yes, your renowned name: shall flight abuse it?
TALBOT: Thy father's charge shall clear thee from that stain.
JOHN TALBOT: You cannot witness for me, being slain.
JOHN TALBOT: If death be so apparent, then both fly.
TALBOT: And leave my followers here to fight and die?
TALBOT: My age was never tainted with such shame.
JOHN TALBOT: And shall my youth be guilty of such blame?
JOHN TALBOT: No more can I be sever'd from your side,
JOHN TALBOT: Than can yourself yourself in twain divide:
JOHN TALBOT: Stay, go, do what you will, the like do I,
JOHN TALBOT: For live I will not, if my father die.
TALBOT: Then here I take my leave of thee, fair son,
TALBOT: Born to eclipse thy life this afternoon.
TALBOT: Come, side by side together live and die.
TALBOT: And soul with soul from France to heaven fly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. A field of battle.
NARRATOR: Alarum: excursions, wherein JOHN TALBOT is hemmed about, and TALBOT rescues him
TALBOT: Saint George and victory! fight, soldiers, fight.
TALBOT: The regent hath with Talbot broke his word
TALBOT: And left us to the rage of France his sword.
TALBOT: Where is John Talbot? Pause, and take thy breath,
TALBOT: I gave thee life and rescued thee from death.
JOHN TALBOT: O, twice my father, twice am I thy son!
JOHN TALBOT: The life thou gavest me first was lost and done,
JOHN TALBOT: Till with thy warlike sword, despite of late,
JOHN TALBOT: To my determined time thou gavest new date.
TALBOT: When from the Dauphin's crest thy sword struck fire,
TALBOT: It warm'd thy father's heart with proud desire
TALBOT: Of bold-faced victory. Then leaden age,
TALBOT: Quicken'd with youthful spleen and warlike rage,
TALBOT: Beat down Alencon, Orleans, Burgundy,
TALBOT: And from the pride of Gallia rescued thee.
TALBOT: The ireful bastard Orleans, that drew blood
TALBOT: From thee, my boy, and had the maidenhood
TALBOT: Of thy first fight, I soon encountered,
TALBOT: And interchanging blows I quickly shed
TALBOT: Some of his bastard blood, and in disgrace
TALBOT: Bespoke him thus, 'Contaminated, base
TALBOT: And misbegotten blood I spill of thine,
TALBOT: Mean and right poor, for that pure blood of mine
TALBOT: Which thou didst force from Talbot, my brave boy:'
