TALBOT: Here, purposing the Bastard to destroy,
TALBOT: Came in strong rescue. Speak, thy father's care,
TALBOT: Art thou not weary, John? how dost thou fare?
TALBOT: Wilt thou yet leave the battle, boy, and fly,
TALBOT: Now thou art seal'd the son of chivalry?
TALBOT: Fly, to revenge my death when I am dead:
TALBOT: The help of one stands me in little stead.
TALBOT: O, too much folly is it, well I wot,
TALBOT: To hazard all our lives in one small boat!
TALBOT: If I to-day die not with Frenchmen's rage,
TALBOT: To-morrow I shall die with mickle age:
TALBOT: By me they nothing gain an if I stay,
TALBOT: 'Tis but the shortening of my life one day:
TALBOT: In thee thy mother dies, our household's name,
TALBOT: My death's revenge, thy youth, and England's fame:
TALBOT: All these and more we hazard by thy stay,
TALBOT: All these are saved if thou wilt fly away.
JOHN TALBOT: The sword of Orleans hath not made me smart,
JOHN TALBOT: These words of yours draw life-blood from my heart:
JOHN TALBOT: On that advantage, bought with such a shame,
JOHN TALBOT: To save a paltry life and slay bright fame,
JOHN TALBOT: Before young Talbot from old Talbot fly,
JOHN TALBOT: The coward horse that bears me fail and die!
JOHN TALBOT: And like me to the peasant boys of France,
JOHN TALBOT: To be shame's scorn and subject of mischance!
JOHN TALBOT: Surely, by all the glory you have won,
JOHN TALBOT: An if I fly, I am not Talbot's son:
JOHN TALBOT: Then talk no more of flight, it is no boot,
JOHN TALBOT: If son to Talbot, die at Talbot's foot.
TALBOT: Then follow thou thy desperate sire of Crete,
TALBOT: Thou Icarus, thy life to me is sweet:
TALBOT: If thou wilt fight, fight by thy father's side,
TALBOT: And, commendable proved, let's die in pride.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum: excursions. Enter TALBOT led by a Servant
TALBOT: Where is my other life? mine own is gone,
TALBOT: O, where's young Talbot? where is valiant John?
TALBOT: Triumphant death, smear'd with captivity,
TALBOT: Young Talbot's valour makes me smile at thee:
TALBOT: When he perceived me shrink and on my knee,
TALBOT: His bloody sword he brandish'd over me,
TALBOT: And, like a hungry lion, did commence
TALBOT: Rough deeds of rage and stern impatience,
TALBOT: But when my angry guardant stood alone,
TALBOT: Tendering my ruin and assail'd of none,
TALBOT: Dizzy-eyed fury and great rage of heart
TALBOT: Suddenly made him from my side to start
TALBOT: Into the clustering battle of the French,
TALBOT: And in that sea of blood my boy did drench
TALBOT: His over-mounting spirit, and there died,
TALBOT: My Icarus, my blossom, in his pride.
Servant: O, my dear lord, lo, where your son is borne!
NARRATOR: Enter Soldiers, with the body of JOHN TALBOT
TALBOT: Thou antic death, which laugh'st us here to scorn,
TALBOT: Anon, from thy insulting tyranny,
TALBOT: Coupled in bonds of perpetuity,
TALBOT: Two Talbots, winged through the lither sky,
TALBOT: In thy despite shall 'scape mortality.
TALBOT: O, thou, whose wounds become hard-favour'd death,
TALBOT: Speak to thy father ere thou yield thy breath!
TALBOT: Brave death by speaking, whether he will or no,
TALBOT: Imagine him a Frenchman and thy foe.
TALBOT: Poor boy! he smiles, methinks, as who should say,
TALBOT: Had death been French, then death had died to-day.
TALBOT: Come, come and lay him in his father's arms:
TALBOT: My spirit can no longer bear these harms.
TALBOT: Soldiers, adieu! I have what I would have,
TALBOT: Now my old arms are young John Talbot's grave.
NARRATOR: Dies
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES, ALENCON, BURGUNDY, BASTARD OF ORLEANS, JOAN LA PUCELLE, and forces
CHARLES: Had York and Somerset brought rescue in,
CHARLES: We should have found a bloody day of this.
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: How the young whelp of Talbot's, raging-wood,
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Did flesh his puny sword in Frenchmen's blood!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Once I encounter'd him, and thus I said:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: 'Thou maiden youth, be vanquish'd by a maid:'
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But, with a proud majestical high scorn,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: He answer'd thus: 'Young Talbot was not born
JOAN LA PUCELLE: To be the pillage of a giglot wench:'
JOAN LA PUCELLE: So, rushing in the bowels of the French,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: He left me proudly, as unworthy fight.
BURGUNDY: Doubtless he would have made a noble knight,
BURGUNDY: See, where he lies inhearsed in the arms
BURGUNDY: Of the most bloody nurser of his harms!
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Hew them to pieces, hack their bones asunder
BASTARD OF ORLEANS: Whose life was England's glory, Gallia's wonder.
CHARLES: O, no, forbear! for that which we have fled
CHARLES: During the life, let us not wrong it dead.
CHARLES: Enter Sir William LUCY, attended, Herald of the French preceding
LUCY: Herald, conduct me to the Dauphin's tent,
LUCY: To know who hath obtained the glory of the day.
CHARLES: On what submissive message art thou sent?
LUCY: Submission, Dauphin! 'tis a mere French word,
LUCY: We English warriors wot not what it means.
LUCY: I come to know what prisoners thou hast ta'en
LUCY: And to survey the bodies of the dead.
CHARLES: For prisoners ask'st thou? hell our prison is.
CHARLES: But tell me whom thou seek'st.
LUCY: But where's the great Alcides of the field,
LUCY: Valiant Lord Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury,
LUCY: Created, for his rare success in arms,
LUCY: Great Earl of Washford, Waterford and Valence,
LUCY: Lord Talbot of Goodrig and Urchinfield,
LUCY: Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdun of Alton,
LUCY: Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield,
LUCY: The thrice-victorious Lord of Falconbridge,
LUCY: Knight of the noble order of Saint George,
LUCY: Worthy Saint Michael and the Golden Fleece,
LUCY: Great marshal to Henry the Sixth
LUCY: Of all his wars within the realm of France?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Here is a silly stately style indeed!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: The Turk, that two and fifty kingdoms hath,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Writes not so tedious a style as this.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Him that thou magnifiest with all these titles
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Stinking and fly-blown lies here at our feet.
LUCY: Is Talbot slain, the Frenchmen's only scourge,
LUCY: Your kingdom's terror and black Nemesis?
LUCY: O, were mine eyeballs into bullets turn'd,
LUCY: That I in rage might shoot them at your faces!
LUCY: O, that I could but call these dead to life!
LUCY: It were enough to fright the realm of France:
LUCY: Were but his picture left amongst you here,
LUCY: It would amaze the proudest of you all.
LUCY: Give me their bodies, that I may bear them hence
LUCY: And give them burial as beseems their worth.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I think this upstart is old Talbot's ghost,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: He speaks with such a proud commanding spirit.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: For God's sake let him have 'em, to keep them here,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: They would but stink, and putrefy the air.
CHARLES: Go, take their bodies hence.
LUCY: I'll bear them hence, but from their ashes shall be rear'd
LUCY: A phoenix that shall make all France afeard.
CHARLES: So we be rid of them, do with 'em what thou wilt.
CHARLES: And now to Paris, in this conquering vein:
CHARLES: All will be ours, now bloody Talbot's slain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Enter KING HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER, and EXETER
KING HENRY VI: Have you perused the letters from the pope,
KING HENRY VI: The emperor and the Earl of Armagnac?
GLOUCESTER: I have, my lord: and their intent is this:
GLOUCESTER: They humbly sue unto your excellence
GLOUCESTER: To have a godly peace concluded of
GLOUCESTER: Between the realms of England and of France.
KING HENRY VI: How doth your grace affect their motion?
GLOUCESTER: Well, my good lord, and as the only means
GLOUCESTER: To stop effusion of our Christian blood
GLOUCESTER: And 'stablish quietness on every side.
KING HENRY VI: Ay, marry, uncle, for I always thought
KING HENRY VI: It was both impious and unnatural
KING HENRY VI: That such immanity and bloody strife
KING HENRY VI: Should reign among professors of one faith.
GLOUCESTER: Beside, my lord, the sooner to effect
GLOUCESTER: And surer bind this knot of amity,
GLOUCESTER: The Earl of Armagnac, near knit to Charles,
GLOUCESTER: A man of great authority in France,
GLOUCESTER: Proffers his only daughter to your grace
GLOUCESTER: In marriage, with a large and sumptuous dowry.
KING HENRY VI: Marriage, uncle! alas, my years are young!
KING HENRY VI: And fitter is my study and my books
KING HENRY VI: Than wanton dalliance with a paramour.
KING HENRY VI: Yet call the ambassador, and, as you please,
KING HENRY VI: So let them have their answers every one:
KING HENRY VI: I shall be well content with any choice
KING HENRY VI: Tends to God's glory and my country's weal.
NARRATOR: Enter CARDINAL OF WINCHESTER in Cardinal's habit, a Legate and two Ambassadors
EXETER: What! is my Lord of Winchester install'd,
EXETER: And call'd unto a cardinal's degree?
EXETER: Then I perceive that will be verified
EXETER: Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy,
EXETER: 'If once he come to be a cardinal,
EXETER: He'll make his cap co-equal with the crown.'
KING HENRY VI: My lords ambassadors, your several suits
KING HENRY VI: Have been consider'd and debated on.
KING HENRY VI: And therefore are we certainly resolved
KING HENRY VI: To draw conditions of a friendly peace,
KING HENRY VI: Which by my Lord of Winchester we mean
KING HENRY VI: Shall be transported presently to France.
GLOUCESTER: And for the proffer of my lord your master,
GLOUCESTER: I have inform'd his highness so at large
GLOUCESTER: As liking of the lady's virtuous gifts,
GLOUCESTER: Her beauty and the value of her dower,
GLOUCESTER: He doth intend she shall be England's queen.
KING HENRY VI: In argument and proof of which contract,
KING HENRY VI: Bear her this jewel, pledge of my affection.
KING HENRY VI: And so, my lord protector, see them guarded
KING HENRY VI: And safely brought to Dover, where inshipp'd
KING HENRY VI: Commit them to the fortune of the sea.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but CARDINAL OF WINCHESTER and Legate
KING HENRY VI: CARDINAL
OF WINCHESTER: Stay, my lord legate: you shall first receive
OF WINCHESTER: The sum of money which I promised
OF WINCHESTER: Should be deliver'd to his holiness
OF WINCHESTER: For clothing me in these grave ornaments.
Legate: I will attend upon your lordship's leisure.
Legate: CARDINAL
OF WINCHESTER: [Aside]  Now Winchester will not submit, I trow,
OF WINCHESTER: Or be inferior to the proudest peer.
OF WINCHESTER: Humphrey of Gloucester, thou shalt well perceive
OF WINCHESTER: That, neither in birth or for authority,
OF WINCHESTER: The bishop will be overborne by thee:
OF WINCHESTER: I'll either make thee stoop and bend thy knee,
OF WINCHESTER: Or sack this country with a mutiny.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. France. Plains in Anjou.
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES, BURGUNDY, ALENCON, BASTARD OF ORLEANS, REIGNIER, JOAN LA PUCELLE, and forces
CHARLES: These news, my lord, may cheer our drooping spirits:
CHARLES: 'Tis said the stout Parisians do revolt
CHARLES: And turn again unto the warlike French.
ALENCON: Then march to Paris, royal Charles of France,
ALENCON: And keep not back your powers in dalliance.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Peace be amongst them, if they turn to us,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Else, ruin combat with their palaces!
NARRATOR: Enter Scout
Scout: Success unto our valiant general,
Scout: And happiness to his accomplices!
CHARLES: What tidings send our scouts? I prithee, speak.
Scout: The English army, that divided was
Scout: Into two parties, is now conjoined in one,
Scout: And means to give you battle presently.
CHARLES: Somewhat too sudden, sirs, the warning is,
CHARLES: But we will presently provide for them.
BURGUNDY: I trust the ghost of Talbot is not there:
BURGUNDY: Now he is gone, my lord, you need not fear.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Of all base passions, fear is most accursed.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Command the conquest, Charles, it shall be thine,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Let Henry fret and all the world repine.
CHARLES: Then on, my lords, and France be fortunate!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Before Angiers.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Excursions. Enter JOAN LA PUCELLE
JOAN LA PUCELLE: The regent conquers, and the Frenchmen fly.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Now help, ye charming spells and periapts,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And ye choice spirits that admonish me
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And give me signs of future accidents.
NARRATOR: Thunder
JOAN LA PUCELLE: You speedy helpers, that are substitutes
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Under the lordly monarch of the north,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Appear and aid me in this enterprise.
NARRATOR: Enter Fiends
JOAN LA PUCELLE: This speedy and quick appearance argues proof
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Of your accustom'd diligence to me.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Now, ye familiar spirits, that are cull'd
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Out of the powerful regions under earth,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Help me this once, that France may get the field.
NARRATOR: They walk, and speak not
JOAN LA PUCELLE: O, hold me not with silence over-long!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Where I was wont to feed you with my blood,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I'll lop a member off and give it you
JOAN LA PUCELLE: In earnest of further benefit,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: So you do condescend to help me now.
NARRATOR: They hang their heads
JOAN LA PUCELLE: No hope to have redress? My body shall
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Pay recompense, if you will grant my suit.
NARRATOR: They shake their heads
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Cannot my body nor blood-sacrifice
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Entreat you to your wonted furtherance?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Then take my soul, my body, soul and all,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Before that England give the French the foil.
NARRATOR: They depart
JOAN LA PUCELLE: See, they forsake me! Now the time is come
JOAN LA PUCELLE: That France must vail her lofty-plumed crest
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And let her head fall into England's lap.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: My ancient incantations are too weak,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And hell too strong for me to buckle with:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Now, France, thy glory droopeth to the dust.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Excursions. Re-enter JOAN LA PUCELLE fighting hand  to hand with YORK. JOAN LA PUCELLE is taken. The French fly.
YORK: Damsel of France, I think I have you fast:
YORK: Unchain your spirits now with spelling charms
YORK: And try if they can gain your liberty.
YORK: A goodly prize, fit for the devil's grace!
YORK: See, how the ugly wench doth bend her brows,
YORK: As if with Circe she would change my shape!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Changed to a worser shape thou canst not be.
YORK: O, Charles the Dauphin is a proper man,
YORK: No shape but his can please your dainty eye.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: A plaguing mischief light on Charles and thee!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: And may ye both be suddenly surprised
JOAN LA PUCELLE: By bloody hands, in sleeping on your beds!
YORK: Fell banning hag, enchantress, hold thy tongue!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I prithee, give me leave to curse awhile.
YORK: Curse, miscreant, when thou comest to the stake.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter SUFFOLK with MARGARET in his hand
SUFFOLK: Be what thou wilt, thou art my prisoner.
NARRATOR: Gazes on her
SUFFOLK: O fairest beauty, do not fear nor fly!
SUFFOLK: For I will touch thee but with reverent hands,
SUFFOLK: I kiss these fingers for eternal peace,
SUFFOLK: And lay them gently on thy tender side.
SUFFOLK: Who art thou? say, that I may honour thee.
MARGARET: Margaret my name, and daughter to a king,
MARGARET: The King of Naples, whosoe'er thou art.
SUFFOLK: An earl I am, and Suffolk am I call'd.
SUFFOLK: Be not offended, nature's miracle,
SUFFOLK: Thou art allotted to be ta'en by me:
SUFFOLK: So doth the swan her downy cygnets save,
SUFFOLK: Keeping them prisoner underneath her wings.
SUFFOLK: Yet, if this servile usage once offend.
SUFFOLK: Go, and be free again, as Suffolk's friend.
NARRATOR: She is going
SUFFOLK: O, stay! I have no power to let her pass,
SUFFOLK: My hand would free her, but my heart says no
SUFFOLK: As plays the sun upon the glassy streams,
SUFFOLK: Twinkling another counterfeited beam,
SUFFOLK: So seems this gorgeous beauty to mine eyes.
SUFFOLK: Fain would I woo her, yet I dare not speak:
SUFFOLK: I'll call for pen and ink, and write my mind.
SUFFOLK: Fie, de la Pole! disable not thyself,
SUFFOLK: Hast not a tongue? is she not here?
SUFFOLK: Wilt thou be daunted at a woman's sight?
SUFFOLK: Ay, beauty's princely majesty is such,
SUFFOLK: Confounds the tongue and makes the senses rough.
MARGARET: Say, Earl of Suffolk--if thy name be so--
MARGARET: What ransom must I pay before I pass?
MARGARET: For I perceive I am thy prisoner.
SUFFOLK: How canst thou tell she will deny thy suit,
SUFFOLK: Before thou make a trial of her love?
MARGARET: Why speak'st thou not? what ransom must I pay?
SUFFOLK: She's beautiful, and therefore to be woo'd,
SUFFOLK: She is a woman, therefore to be won.
MARGARET: Wilt thou accept of ransom? yea, or no.
SUFFOLK: Fond man, remember that thou hast a wife,
SUFFOLK: Then how can Margaret be thy paramour?
MARGARET: I were best to leave him, for he will not hear.
SUFFOLK: There all is marr'd, there lies a cooling card.
MARGARET: He talks at random, sure, the man is mad.
SUFFOLK: And yet a dispensation may be had.
MARGARET: And yet I would that you would answer me.
SUFFOLK: I'll win this Lady Margaret. For whom?
SUFFOLK: Why, for my king: tush, that's a wooden thing!
MARGARET: He talks of wood: it is some carpenter.
SUFFOLK: Yet so my fancy may be satisfied,
SUFFOLK: And peace established between these realms
SUFFOLK: But there remains a scruple in that too,
SUFFOLK: For though her father be the King of Naples,
SUFFOLK: Duke of Anjou and Maine, yet is he poor,
SUFFOLK: And our nobility will scorn the match.
MARGARET: Hear ye, captain, are you not at leisure?
SUFFOLK: It shall be so, disdain they ne'er so much.
SUFFOLK: Henry is youthful and will quickly yield.
SUFFOLK: Madam, I have a secret to reveal.
MARGARET: What though I be enthrall'd? he seems a knight,
MARGARET: And will not any way dishonour me.
SUFFOLK: Lady, vouchsafe to listen what I say.
MARGARET: Perhaps I shall be rescued by the French,
MARGARET: And then I need not crave his courtesy.
SUFFOLK: Sweet madam, give me a hearing in a cause--
MARGARET: Tush, women have been captivate ere now.
SUFFOLK: Lady, wherefore talk you so?
MARGARET: I cry you mercy, 'tis but Quid for Quo.
SUFFOLK: Say, gentle princess, would you not suppose
SUFFOLK: Your bondage happy, to be made a queen?
MARGARET: To be a queen in bondage is more vile
MARGARET: Than is a slave in base servility,
MARGARET: For princes should be free.
SUFFOLK: And so shall you,
SUFFOLK: If happy England's royal king be free.
MARGARET: Why, what concerns his freedom unto me?
SUFFOLK: I'll undertake to make thee Henry's queen,
SUFFOLK: To put a golden sceptre in thy hand
SUFFOLK: And set a precious crown upon thy head,
SUFFOLK: If thou wilt condescend to be my--
MARGARET: What?
SUFFOLK: His love.
MARGARET: I am unworthy to be Henry's wife.
SUFFOLK: No, gentle madam, I unworthy am
SUFFOLK: To woo so fair a dame to be his wife,
SUFFOLK: And have no portion in the choice myself.
SUFFOLK: How say you, madam, are ye so content?
MARGARET: An if my father please, I am content.
SUFFOLK: Then call our captains and our colours forth.
SUFFOLK: And, madam, at your father's castle walls
SUFFOLK: We'll crave a parley, to confer with him.
NARRATOR: A parley sounded. Enter REIGNIER on the walls
SUFFOLK: See, Reignier, see, thy daughter prisoner!
REIGNIER: To whom?
SUFFOLK: To me.
REIGNIER: Suffolk, what remedy?
REIGNIER: I am a soldier, and unapt to weep,
REIGNIER: Or to exclaim on fortune's fickleness.
SU FFOLK: Yes, there is remedy enough, my lord:
SU FFOLK: Consent, and for thy honour give consent,
SU FFOLK: Thy daughter shall be wedded to my king,
SU FFOLK: Whom I with pain have woo'd and won thereto,
SU FFOLK: And this her easy-held imprisonment
SU FFOLK: Hath gained thy daughter princely liberty.
REIGNIER: Speaks Suffolk as he thinks?
SUFFOLK: Fair Margaret knows
SUFFOLK: That Suffolk doth not flatter, face, or feign.
REIGNIER: Upon thy princely warrant, I descend
REIGNIER: To give thee answer of thy just demand.
NARRATOR: Exit from the walls
SUFFOLK: And here I will expect thy coming.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound. Enter REIGNIER, below
REIGNIER: Welcome, brave earl, into our territories:
REIGNIER: Command in Anjou what your honour pleases.
SUFFOLK: Thanks, Reignier, happy for so sweet a child,
SUFFOLK: Fit to be made companion with a king:
SUFFOLK: What answer makes your grace unto my suit?
REIGNIER: Since thou dost deign to woo her little worth
REIGNIER: To be the princely bride of such a lord,
REIGNIER: Upon condition I may quietly
REIGNIER: Enjoy mine own, the country Maine and Anjou,
REIGNIER: Free from oppression or the stroke of war,
REIGNIER: My daughter shall be Henry's, if he please.
SUFFOLK: That is her ransom, I deliver her,
SUFFOLK: And those two counties I will undertake
SUFFOLK: Your grace shall well and quietly enjoy.
REIGNIER: And I again, in Henry's royal name,
REIGNIER: As deputy unto that gracious king,
REIGNIER: Give thee her hand, for sign of plighted faith.
SUFFOLK: Reignier of France, I give thee kingly thanks,
SUFFOLK: Because this is in traffic of a king.
NARRATOR: Aside
SUFFOLK: And yet, methinks, I could be well content
SUFFOLK: To be mine own attorney in this case.
SUFFOLK: I'll over then to England with this news,
SUFFOLK: And make this marriage to be solemnized.
SUFFOLK: So farewell, Reignier: set this diamond safe
SUFFOLK: In golden palaces, as it becomes.
REIGNIER: I do embrace thee, as I would embrace
REIGNIER: The Christian prince, King Henry, were he here.
MARGARET: Farewell, my lord: good wishes, praise and prayers
MARGARET: Shall Suffolk ever have of Margaret.
NARRATOR: Going
SUFFOLK: Farewell, sweet madam: but hark you, Margaret,
SUFFOLK: No princely commendations to my king?
MARGARET: Such commendations as becomes a maid,
MARGARET: A virgin and his servant, say to him.
SUFFOLK: Words sweetly placed and modestly directed.
SUFFOLK: But madam, I must trouble you again,
SUFFOLK: No loving token to his majesty?
MARGARET: Yes, my good lord, a pure unspotted heart,
MARGARET: Never yet taint with love, I send the king.
SUFFOLK: And this withal.
NARRATOR: Kisses her
MARGARET: That for thyself: I will not so presume
MARGARET: To send such peevish tokens to a king.
NARRATOR: Exeunt REIGNIER and MARGARET
SUFFOLK: O, wert thou for myself! But, Suffolk, stay,
SUFFOLK: Thou mayst not wander in that labyrinth,
SUFFOLK: There Minotaurs and ugly treasons lurk.
SUFFOLK: Solicit Henry with her wondrous praise:
SUFFOLK: Bethink thee on her virtues that surmount,
SUFFOLK: And natural graces that extinguish art,
SUFFOLK: Repeat their semblance often on the seas,
SUFFOLK: That, when thou comest to kneel at Henry's feet,
SUFFOLK: Thou mayst bereave him of his wits with wonder.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Camp of the YORK in Anjou.
NARRATOR: Enter YORK, WARWICK, and others
YORK: Bring forth that sorceress condemn'd to burn.
NARRATOR: Enter JOAN LA PUCELLE, guarded, and a Shepherd
Shepherd: Ah, Joan, this kills thy father's heart outright!
Shepherd: Have I sought every country far and near,
Shepherd: And, now it is my chance to find thee out,
Shepherd: Must I behold thy timeless cruel death?
Shepherd: Ah, Joan, sweet daughter Joan, I'll die with thee!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Decrepit miser! base ignoble wretch!
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I am descended of a gentler blood:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Thou art no father nor no friend of mine.
Shepherd: Out, out! My lords, an please you, 'tis not so,
Shepherd: I did beget her, all the parish knows:
Shepherd: Her mother liveth yet, can testify
Shepherd: She was the first fruit of my bachelorship.
WARWICK: Graceless! wilt thou deny thy parentage?
YORK: This argues what her kind of life hath been,
YORK: Wicked and vile, and so her death concludes.
Shepherd: Fie, Joan, that thou wilt be so obstacle!
Shepherd: God knows thou art a collop of my flesh,
Shepherd: And for thy sake have I shed many a tear:
Shepherd: Deny me not, I prithee, gentle Joan.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Peasant, avaunt! You have suborn'd this man,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Of purpose to obscure my noble birth.
Shepherd: 'Tis true, I gave a noble to the priest
Shepherd: The morn that I was wedded to her mother.
Shepherd: Kneel down and take my blessing, good my girl.
Shepherd: Wilt thou not stoop? Now cursed be the time
Shepherd: Of thy nativity! I would the milk
Shepherd: Thy mother gave thee when thou suck'dst her breast,
Shepherd: Had been a little ratsbane for thy sake!
Shepherd: Or else, when thou didst keep my lambs a-field,
Shepherd: I wish some ravenous wolf had eaten thee!
Shepherd: Dost thou deny thy father, cursed drab?
Shepherd: O, burn her, burn her! hanging is too good.
NARRATOR: Exit
YORK: Take her away, for she hath lived too long,
YORK: To fill the world with vicious qualities.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: First, let me tell you whom you have condemn'd:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Not me begotten of a shepherd swain,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But issued from the progeny of kings,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Virtuous and holy, chosen from above,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: By inspiration of celestial grace,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: To work exceeding miracles on earth.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I never had to do with wicked spirits:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But you, that are polluted with your lusts,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Stain'd with the guiltless blood of innocents,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Corrupt and tainted with a thousand vices,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Because you want the grace that others have,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: You judge it straight a thing impossible
JOAN LA PUCELLE: To compass wonders but by help of devils.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: No, misconceived! Joan of Arc hath been
JOAN LA PUCELLE: A virgin from her tender infancy,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Chaste and immaculate in very thought,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Whose maiden blood, thus rigorously effused,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Will cry for vengeance at the gates of heaven.
YORK: Ay, ay: away with her to execution!
WARWICK: And hark ye, sirs, because she is a maid,
WARWICK: Spare for no faggots, let there be enow:
WARWICK: Place barrels of pitch upon the fatal stake,
WARWICK: That so her torture may be shortened.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Will nothing turn your unrelenting hearts?
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Then, Joan, discover thine infirmity,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: That warranteth by law to be thy privilege.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: I am with child, ye bloody homicides:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Murder not then the fruit within my womb,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Although ye hale me to a violent death.
YORK: Now heaven forfend! the holy maid with child!
WARWICK: The greatest miracle that e'er ye wrought:
WARWICK: Is all your strict preciseness come to this?
YORK: She and the Dauphin have been juggling:
YORK: I did imagine what would be her refuge.
WARWICK: Well, go to, we'll have no bastards live,
WARWICK: Especially since Charles must father it.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: You are deceived, my child is none of his:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: It was Alencon that enjoy'd my love.
YORK: Alencon! that notorious Machiavel!
YORK: It dies, an if it had a thousand lives.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: O, give me leave, I have deluded you:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: 'Twas neither Charles nor yet the duke I named,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But Reignier, king of Naples, that prevail'd.
WARWICK: A married man! that's most intolerable.
YORK: Why, here's a girl! I think she knows not well,
YORK: There were so many, whom she may accuse.
WARWICK: It's sign she hath been liberal and free.
YORK: And yet, forsooth, she is a virgin pure.
YORK: Strumpet, thy words condemn thy brat and thee:
YORK: Use no entreaty, for it is in vain.
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Then lead me hence, with whom I leave my curse:
JOAN LA PUCELLE: May never glorious sun reflex his beams
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Upon the country where you make abode,
JOAN LA PUCELLE: But darkness and the gloomy shade of death
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Environ you, till mischief and despair
JOAN LA PUCELLE: Drive you to break your necks or hang yourselves!
NARRATOR: Exit, guarded
YORK: Break thou in pieces and consume to ashes,
YORK: Thou foul accursed minister of hell!
NARRATOR: Enter CARDINAL OF WINCHESTER, attended
YORK: CARDINAL
OF WINCHESTER: Lord regent, I do greet your excellence
OF WINCHESTER: With letters of commission from the king.
OF WINCHESTER: For know, my lords, the states of Christendom,
OF WINCHESTER: Moved with remorse of these outrageous broils,
OF WINCHESTER: Have earnestly implored a general peace
OF WINCHESTER: Betwixt our nation and the aspiring French,
OF WINCHESTER: And here at hand the Dauphin and his train
OF WINCHESTER: Approacheth, to confer about some matter.
YORK: Is all our travail turn'd to this effect?
YORK: After the slaughter of so many peers,
YORK: So many captains, gentlemen and soldiers,
YORK: That in this quarrel have been overthrown
YORK: And sold their bodies for their country's benefit,
YORK: Shall we at last conclude effeminate peace?
YORK: Have we not lost most part of all the towns,
YORK: By treason, falsehood and by treachery,
YORK: Our great progenitors had conquered?
YORK: O Warwick, Warwick! I foresee with grief
YORK: The utter loss of all the realm of France.
WARWICK: Be patient, York: if we conclude a peace,
WARWICK: It shall be with such strict and severe covenants
WARWICK: As little shall the Frenchmen gain thereby.
NARRATOR: Enter CHARLES, ALENCON, BASTARD OF ORLEANS, REIGNIER, and others
CHARLES: Since, lords of England, it is thus agreed
CHARLES: That peaceful truce shall be proclaim'd in France,
CHARLES: We come to be informed by yourselves
CHARLES: What the conditions of that league must be.
YORK: Speak, Winchester, for boiling choler chokes
YORK: The hollow passage of my poison'd voice,
YORK: By sight of these our baleful enemies.
YORK: CARDINAL
OF WINCHESTER: Charles, and the rest, it is enacted thus:
OF WINCHESTER: That, in regard King Henry gives consent,
OF WINCHESTER: Of mere compassion and of lenity,
OF WINCHESTER: To ease your country of distressful war,
OF WINCHESTER: And suffer you to breathe in fruitful peace,
OF WINCHESTER: You shall become true liegemen to his crown:
OF WINCHESTER: And Charles, upon condition thou wilt swear
OF WINCHESTER: To pay him tribute, submit thyself,
OF WINCHESTER: Thou shalt be placed as viceroy under him,
OF WINCHESTER: And still enjoy thy regal dignity.
ALENCON: Must he be then as shadow of himself?
ALENCON: Adorn his temples with a coronet,
ALENCON: And yet, in substance and authority,
ALENCON: Retain but privilege of a private man?
ALENCON: This proffer is absurd and reasonless.
CHARLES: 'Tis known already that I am possess'd
CHARLES: With more than half the Gallian territories,
CHARLES: And therein reverenced for their lawful king:
CHARLES: Shall I, for lucre of the rest unvanquish'd,
CHARLES: Detract so much from that prerogative,
CHARLES: As to be call'd but viceroy of the whole?
CHARLES: No, lord ambassador, I'll rather keep
CHARLES: That which I have than, coveting for more,
CHARLES: Be cast from possibility of all.
YORK: Insulting Charles! hast thou by secret means
YORK: Used intercession to obtain a league,
YORK: And, now the matter grows to compromise,
YORK: Stand'st thou aloof upon comparison?
YORK: Either accept the title thou usurp'st,
YORK: Of benefit proceeding from our king
YORK: And not of any challenge of desert,
YORK: Or we will plague thee with incessant wars.
REIGNIER: My lord, you do not well in obstinacy
REIGNIER: To cavil in the course of this contract:
REIGNIER: If once it be neglected, ten to one
REIGNIER: We shall not find like opportunity.
ALENCON: To say the truth, it is your policy
ALENCON: To save your subjects from such massacre
ALENCON: And ruthless slaughters as are daily seen
ALENCON: By our proceeding in hostility,
ALENCON: And therefore take this compact of a truce,
ALENCON: Although you break it when your pleasure serves.
WARWICK: How say'st thou, Charles? shall our condition stand?
CHARLES: It shall,
CHARLES: Only reserved, you claim no interest
CHARLES: In any of our towns of garrison.
YORK: Then swear allegiance to his majesty,
YORK: As thou art knight, never to disobey
YORK: Nor be rebellious to the crown of England,
YORK: Thou, nor thy nobles, to the crown of England.
YORK: So, now dismiss your army when ye please:
YORK: Hang up your ensign, let your drums be still,
YORK: For here we entertain a solemn peace.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter SUFFOLK in conference with KING HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER and EXETER
KING HENRY VI: Your wondrous rare description, noble earl,
KING HENRY VI: Of beauteous Margaret hath astonish'd me:
KING HENRY VI: Her virtues graced with external gifts
KING HENRY VI: Do breed love's settled passions in my heart:
KING HENRY VI: And like as rigor of tempestuous gusts
KING HENRY VI: Provokes the mightiest hulk against the tide,
KING HENRY VI: So am I driven by breath of her renown
KING HENRY VI: Either to suffer shipwreck or arrive
KING HENRY VI: Where I may have fruition of her love.
SUFFOLK: Tush, my good lord, this superficial tale
SUFFOLK: Is but a preface of her worthy praise,
SUFFOLK: The chief perfections of that lovely dame
SUFFOLK: Had I sufficient skill to utter them,
SUFFOLK: Would make a volume of enticing lines,
SUFFOLK: Able to ravish any dull conceit:
SUFFOLK: And, which is more, she is not so divine,
SUFFOLK: So full-replete with choice of all delights,
SUFFOLK: But with as humble lowliness of mind
SUFFOLK: She is content to be at your command,
SUFFOLK: Command, I mean, of virtuous chaste intents,
SUFFOLK: To love and honour Henry as her lord.
KING HENRY VI: And otherwise will Henry ne'er presume.
KING HENRY VI: Therefore, my lord protector, give consent
KING HENRY VI: That Margaret may be England's royal queen.
GLOUCESTER: So should I give consent to flatter sin.
GLOUCESTER: You know, my lord, your highness is betroth'd
GLOUCESTER: Unto another lady of esteem:
GLOUCESTER: How shall we then dispense with that contract,
GLOUCESTER: And not deface your honour with reproach?
SUFFOLK: As doth a ruler with unlawful oaths,
SUFFOLK: Or one that, at a triumph having vow'd
SUFFOLK: To try his strength, forsaketh yet the lists
SUFFOLK: By reason of his adversary's odds:
SUFFOLK: A poor earl's daughter is unequal odds,
SUFFOLK: And therefore may be broke without offence.
GLOUCESTER: Why, what, I pray, is Margaret more than that?
GLOUCESTER: Her father is no better than an earl,
GLOUCESTER: Although in glorious titles he excel.
SUFFOLK: Yes, lord, her father is a king,
SUFFOLK: The King of Naples and Jerusalem,
SUFFOLK: And of such great authority in France
SUFFOLK: As his alliance will confirm our peace
SUFFOLK: And keep the Frenchmen in allegiance.
GLOUCESTER: And so the Earl of Armagnac may do,
GLOUCESTER: Because he is near kinsman unto Charles.
EXETER: Beside, his wealth doth warrant a liberal dower,
EXETER: Where Reignier sooner will receive than give.
SUFFOLK: A dower, my lords! disgrace not so your king,
SUFFOLK: That he should be so abject, base and poor,
SUFFOLK: To choose for wealth and not for perfect love.
SUFFOLK: Henry is able to enrich his queen
SUFFOLK: And not seek a queen to make him rich:
SUFFOLK: So worthless peasants bargain for their wives,
SUFFOLK: As market-men for oxen, sheep, or horse.
SUFFOLK: Marriage is a matter of more worth
SUFFOLK: Than to be dealt in by attorneyship,
SUFFOLK: Not whom we will, but whom his grace affects,
SUFFOLK: Must be companion of his nuptial bed:
SUFFOLK: And therefore, lords, since he affects her most,
SUFFOLK: It most of all these reasons bindeth us,
SUFFOLK: In our opinions she should be preferr'd.
SUFFOLK: For what is wedlock forced but a hell,
SUFFOLK: An age of discord and continual strife?
SUFFOLK: Whereas the contrary bringeth bliss,
SUFFOLK: And is a pattern of celestial peace.
SUFFOLK: Whom should we match with Henry, being a king,
SUFFOLK: But Margaret, that is daughter to a king?
SUFFOLK: Her peerless feature, joined with her birth,
SUFFOLK: Approves her fit for none but for a king:
SUFFOLK: Her valiant courage and undaunted spirit,
SUFFOLK: More than in women commonly is seen,
SUFFOLK: Will answer our hope in issue of a king,
SUFFOLK: For Henry, son unto a conqueror,
SUFFOLK: Is likely to beget more conquerors,
SUFFOLK: If with a lady of so high resolve
SUFFOLK: As is fair Margaret he be link'd in love.
SUFFOLK: Then yield, my lords, and here conclude with me
SUFFOLK: That Margaret shall be queen, and none but she.
KING HENRY VI: Whether it be through force of your report,
KING HENRY VI: My noble Lord of Suffolk, or for that
KING HENRY VI: My tender youth was never yet attaint
KING HENRY VI: With any passion of inflaming love,
KING HENRY VI: I cannot tell, but this I am assured,
KING HENRY VI: I feel such sharp dissension in my breast,
KING HENRY VI: Such fierce alarums both of hope and fear,
KING HENRY VI: As I am sick with working of my thoughts.
KING HENRY VI: Take, therefore, shipping, post, my lord, to France,
KING HENRY VI: Agree to any covenants, and procure
KING HENRY VI: That Lady Margaret do vouchsafe to come
KING HENRY VI: To cross the seas to England and be crown'd
KING HENRY VI: King Henry's faithful and anointed queen:
KING HENRY VI: For your expenses and sufficient charge,
KING HENRY VI: Among the people gather up a tenth.
KING HENRY VI: Be gone, I say, for, till you do return,
KING HENRY VI: I rest perplexed with a thousand cares.
KING HENRY VI: And you, good uncle, banish all offence:
KING HENRY VI: If you do censure me by what you were,
KING HENRY VI: Not what you are, I know it will excuse
KING HENRY VI: This sudden execution of my will.
KING HENRY VI: And so, conduct me where, from company,
KING HENRY VI: I may revolve and ruminate my grief.
NARRATOR: Exit
GLOUCESTER: Ay, grief, I fear me, both at first and last.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GLOUCESTER and EXETER
SUFFOLK: Thus Suffolk hath prevail'd, and thus he goes,
SUFFOLK: As did the youthful Paris once to Greece,
SUFFOLK: With hope to find the like event in love,
SUFFOLK: But prosper better than the Trojan did.
SUFFOLK: Margaret shall now be queen, and rule the king,
SUFFOLK: But I will rule both her, the king and realm.
NARRATOR: Exit
''' PLAY: Henry VI Part 2 '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish of trumpets: then hautboys. Enter KING  HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER, SALISBURY, WARWICK, and  CARDINAL, on the one side, QUEEN MARGARET, SUFFOLK, YORK, SOMERSET, and BUCKINGHAM, on the other
SUFFOLK: As by your high imperial majesty
SUFFOLK: I had in charge at my depart for France,
SUFFOLK: As procurator to your excellence,
SUFFOLK: To marry Princess Margaret for your grace,
SUFFOLK: So, in the famous ancient city, Tours,
SUFFOLK: In presence of the Kings of France and Sicil,
SUFFOLK: The Dukes of Orleans, Calaber, Bretagne and Alencon,
SUFFOLK: Seven earls, twelve barons and twenty reverend bishops,
SUFFOLK: I have perform'd my task and was espoused:
SUFFOLK: And humbly now upon my bended knee,
SUFFOLK: In sight of England and her lordly peers,
SUFFOLK: Deliver up my title in the queen
SUFFOLK: To your most gracious hands, that are the substance
SUFFOLK: Of that great shadow I did represent,
SUFFOLK: The happiest gift that ever marquess gave,
SUFFOLK: The fairest queen that ever king received.
KING HENRY VI: Suffolk, arise. Welcome, Queen Margaret:
KING HENRY VI: I can express no kinder sign of love
KING HENRY VI: Than this kind kiss. O Lord, that lends me life,
KING HENRY VI: Lend me a heart replete with thankfulness!
KING HENRY VI: For thou hast given me in this beauteous face
KING HENRY VI: A world of earthly blessings to my soul,
KING HENRY VI: If sympathy of love unite our thoughts.
QUEEN MARGARET: Great King of England and my gracious lord,
QUEEN MARGARET: The mutual conference that my mind hath had,
QUEEN MARGARET: By day, by night, waking and in my dreams,
QUEEN MARGARET: In courtly company or at my beads,
QUEEN MARGARET: With you, mine alder-liefest sovereign,
QUEEN MARGARET: Makes me the bolder to salute my king
QUEEN MARGARET: With ruder terms, such as my wit affords
QUEEN MARGARET: And over-joy of heart doth minister.
KING HENRY VI: Her sight did ravish, but her grace in speech,
KING HENRY VI: Her words y-clad with wisdom's majesty,
KING HENRY VI: Makes me from wondering fall to weeping joys,
KING HENRY VI: Such is the fulness of my heart's content.
KING HENRY VI: Lords, with one cheerful voice welcome my love.
ALL: [Kneeling]  Long live Queen Margaret, England's
ALL: happiness!
QUEEN MARGARET: We thank you all.
NARRATOR: Flourish
SUFFOLK: My lord protector, so it please your grace,
SUFFOLK: Here are the articles of contracted peace
SUFFOLK: Between our sovereign and the French king Charles,
SUFFOLK: For eighteen months concluded by consent.
GLOUCESTER: [Reads]  'Imprimis, it is agreed between the French
GLOUCESTER: king Charles, and William de la Pole, Marquess of
GLOUCESTER: Suffolk, ambassador for Henry King of England, that
GLOUCESTER: the said Henry shall espouse the Lady Margaret,
GLOUCESTER: daughter unto Reignier King of Naples, Sicilia and
GLOUCESTER: Jerusalem, and crown her Queen of England ere the
GLOUCESTER: thirtieth of May next ensuing. Item, that the duchy
GLOUCESTER: of Anjou and the county of Maine shall be released
GLOUCESTER: and delivered to the king her father'--
NARRATOR: Lets the paper fall
KING HENRY VI: Uncle, how now!
GLOUCESTER: Pardon me, gracious lord,
GLOUCESTER: Some sudden qualm hath struck me at the heart
GLOUCESTER: And dimm'd mine eyes, that I can read no further.
KING HENRY VI: Uncle of Winchester, I pray, read on.
CARDINAL: [Reads]  'Item, It is further agreed between them,
CARDINAL: that the duchies of Anjou and Maine shall be
CARDINAL: released and delivered over to the king her father,
CARDINAL: and she sent over of the King of England's own
CARDINAL: proper cost and charges, without having any dowry.'
KING HENRY VI: They please us well. Lord marquess, kneel down:
KING HENRY VI: We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk,
KING HENRY VI: And gird thee with the sword. Cousin of York,
KING HENRY VI: We here discharge your grace from being regent
KING HENRY VI: I' the parts of France, till term of eighteen months
KING HENRY VI: Be full expired. Thanks, uncle Winchester,
KING HENRY VI: Gloucester, York, Buckingham, Somerset,
KING HENRY VI: Salisbury, and Warwick,
KING HENRY VI: We thank you all for the great favour done,
KING HENRY VI: In entertainment to my princely queen.
KING HENRY VI: Come, let us in, and with all speed provide
KING HENRY VI: To see her coronation be perform'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET, and SUFFOLK
GLOUCESTER: Brave peers of England, pillars of the state,
GLOUCESTER: To you Duke Humphrey must unload his grief,
GLOUCESTER: Your grief, the common grief of all the land.
GLOUCESTER: What! did my brother Henry spend his youth,
GLOUCESTER: His valour, coin and people, in the wars?
GLOUCESTER: Did he so often lodge in open field,
GLOUCESTER: In winter's cold and summer's parching heat,
GLOUCESTER: To conquer France, his true inheritance?
GLOUCESTER: And did my brother Bedford toil his wits,
GLOUCESTER: To keep by policy what Henry got?
GLOUCESTER: Have you yourselves, Somerset, Buckingham,
GLOUCESTER: Brave York, Salisbury, and victorious Warwick,
GLOUCESTER: Received deep scars in France and Normandy?
GLOUCESTER: Or hath mine uncle Beaufort and myself,
GLOUCESTER: With all the learned council of the realm,
GLOUCESTER: Studied so long, sat in the council-house
GLOUCESTER: Early and late, debating to and fro
GLOUCESTER: How France and Frenchmen might be kept in awe,
GLOUCESTER: And had his highness in his infancy
GLOUCESTER: Crowned in Paris in despite of foes?
GLOUCESTER: And shall these labours and these honours die?
GLOUCESTER: Shall Henry's conquest, Bedford's vigilance,
GLOUCESTER: Your deeds of war and all our counsel die?
GLOUCESTER: O peers of England, shameful is this league!
GLOUCESTER: Fatal this marriage, cancelling your fame,
GLOUCESTER: Blotting your names from books of memory,
GLOUCESTER: Razing the characters of your renown,
GLOUCESTER: Defacing monuments of conquer'd France,
GLOUCESTER: Undoing all, as all had never been!
CARDINAL: Nephew, what means this passionate discourse,
CARDINAL: This peroration with such circumstance?
CARDINAL: For France, 'tis ours, and we will keep it still.
GLOUCESTER: Ay, uncle, we will keep it, if we can,
GLOUCESTER: But now it is impossible we should:
GLOUCESTER: Suffolk, the new-made duke that rules the roast,
GLOUCESTER: Hath given the duchy of Anjou and Maine
GLOUCESTER: Unto the poor King Reignier, whose large style
GLOUCESTER: Agrees not with the leanness of his purse.
SALISBURY: Now, by the death of Him that died for all,
SALISBURY: These counties were the keys of Normandy.
SALISBURY: But wherefore weeps Warwick, my valiant son?
WARWICK: For grief that they are past recovery:
WARWICK: For, were there hope to conquer them again,
WARWICK: My sword should shed hot blood, mine eyes no tears.
WARWICK: Anjou and Maine! myself did win them both,
WARWICK: Those provinces these arms of mine did conquer:
WARWICK: And are the cities, that I got with wounds,
WARWICK: Delivered up again with peaceful words?
WARWICK: Mort Dieu!
YORK: For Suffolk's duke, may he be suffocate,
YORK: That dims the honour of this warlike isle!
YORK: France should have torn and rent my very heart,
YORK: Before I would have yielded to this league.
YORK: I never read but England's kings have had
YORK: Large sums of gold and dowries with their wives:
YORK: And our King Henry gives away his own,
YORK: To match with her that brings no vantages.
GLOUCESTER: A proper jest, and never heard before,
GLOUCESTER: That Suffolk should demand a whole fifteenth
GLOUCESTER: For costs and charges in transporting her!
GLOUCESTER: She should have stayed in France and starved
GLOUCESTER: in France, Before--
CARDINAL: My Lord of Gloucester, now ye grow too hot:
CARDINAL: It was the pleasure of my lord the King.
GLOUCESTER: My Lord of Winchester, I know your mind,
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis not my speeches that you do mislike,
GLOUCESTER: But 'tis my presence that doth trouble ye.
GLOUCESTER: Rancour will out: proud prelate, in thy face
GLOUCESTER: I see thy fury: if I longer stay,
GLOUCESTER: We shall begin our ancient bickerings.
GLOUCESTER: Lordings, farewell, and say, when I am gone,
GLOUCESTER: I prophesied France will be lost ere long.
NARRATOR: Exit
CARDINAL: So, there goes our protector in a rage.
CARDINAL: 'Tis known to you he is mine enemy,
CARDINAL: Nay, more, an enemy unto you all,
CARDINAL: And no great friend, I fear me, to the king.
CARDINAL: Consider, lords, he is the next of blood,
CARDINAL: And heir apparent to the English crown:
CARDINAL: Had Henry got an empire by his marriage,
CARDINAL: And all the wealthy kingdoms of the west,
CARDINAL: There's reason he should be displeased at it.
CARDINAL: Look to it, lords! let not his smoothing words
CARDINAL: Bewitch your hearts, be wise and circumspect.
CARDINAL: What though the common people favour him,
CARDINAL: Calling him 'Humphrey, the good Duke of
CARDINAL: Gloucester,'
CARDINAL: Clapping their hands, and crying with loud voice,
CARDINAL: 'Jesu maintain your royal excellence!'
CARDINAL: With 'God preserve the good Duke Humphrey!'
CARDINAL: I fear me, lords, for all this flattering gloss,
CARDINAL: He will be found a dangerous protector.
BUCKINGHAM: Why should he, then, protect our sovereign,
BUCKINGHAM: He being of age to govern of himself?
BUCKINGHAM: Cousin of Somerset, join you with me,
BUCKINGHAM: And all together, with the Duke of Suffolk,
BUCKINGHAM: We'll quickly hoise Duke Humphrey from his seat.
CARDINAL: This weighty business will not brook delay:
CARDINAL: I'll to the Duke of Suffolk presently.
NARRATOR: Exit
SOMERSET: Cousin of Buckingham, though Humphrey's pride
SOMERSET: And greatness of his place be grief to us,
SOMERSET: Yet let us watch the haughty cardinal:
SOMERSET: His insolence is more intolerable
SOMERSET: Than all the princes in the land beside:
SOMERSET: If Gloucester be displaced, he'll be protector.
BUCKINGHAM: Or thou or I, Somerset, will be protector,
BUCKINGHAM: Despite Duke Humphrey or the cardinal.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BUCKINGHAM and SOMERSET
SALISBURY: Pride went before, ambition follows him.
SALISBURY: While these do labour for their own preferment,
SALISBURY: Behoves it us to labour for the realm.
SALISBURY: I never saw but Humphrey Duke of Gloucester
SALISBURY: Did bear him like a noble gentleman.
SALISBURY: Oft have I seen the haughty cardinal,
SALISBURY: More like a soldier than a man o' the church,
SALISBURY: As stout and proud as he were lord of all,
SALISBURY: Swear like a ruffian and demean himself
SALISBURY: Unlike the ruler of a commonweal.
SALISBURY: Warwick, my son, the comfort of my age,
SALISBURY: Thy deeds, thy plainness and thy housekeeping,
SALISBURY: Hath won the greatest favour of the commons,
SALISBURY: Excepting none but good Duke Humphrey:
SALISBURY: And, brother York, thy acts in Ireland,
SALISBURY: In bringing them to civil discipline,
SALISBURY: Thy late exploits done in the heart of France,
SALISBURY: When thou wert regent for our sovereign,
SALISBURY: Have made thee fear'd and honour'd of the people:
SALISBURY: Join we together, for the public good,
SALISBURY: In what we can, to bridle and suppress
SALISBURY: The pride of Suffolk and the cardinal,
SALISBURY: With Somerset's and Buckingham's ambition,
SALISBURY: And, as we may, cherish Duke Humphrey's deeds,
SALISBURY: While they do tend the profit of the land.
WARWICK: So God help Warwick, as he loves the land,
WARWICK: And common profit of his country!
YORK: [Aside]  And so says York, for he hath greatest cause.
SALISBURY: Then let's make haste away, and look unto the main.
WARWICK: Unto the main! O father, Maine is lost,
WARWICK: That Maine which by main force Warwick did win,
WARWICK: And would have kept so long as breath did last!
WARWICK: Main chance, father, you meant, but I meant Maine,
WARWICK: Which I will win from France, or else be slain,
NARRATOR: Exeunt WARWICK and SALISBURY
YORK: Anjou and Maine are given to the French,
YORK: Paris is lost, the state of Normandy
YORK: Stands on a tickle point, now they are gone:
YORK: Suffolk concluded on the articles,
YORK: The peers agreed, and Henry was well pleased
YORK: To change two dukedoms for a duke's fair daughter.
YORK: I cannot blame them all: what is't to them?
YORK: 'Tis thine they give away, and not their own.
YORK: Pirates may make cheap pennyworths of their pillage
YORK: And purchase friends and give to courtezans,
YORK: Still revelling like lords till all be gone,
YORK: While as the silly owner of the goods
YORK: Weeps over them and wrings his hapless hands
YORK: And shakes his head and trembling stands aloof,
YORK: While all is shared and all is borne away,
YORK: Ready to starve and dare not touch his own:
YORK: So York must sit and fret and bite his tongue,
YORK: While his own lands are bargain'd for and sold.
YORK: Methinks the realms of England, France and Ireland
YORK: Bear that proportion to my flesh and blood
YORK: As did the fatal brand Althaea burn'd
YORK: Unto the prince's heart of Calydon.
YORK: Anjou and Maine both given unto the French!
YORK: Cold news for me, for I had hope of France,
YORK: Even as I have of fertile England's soil.
YORK: A day will come when York shall claim his own,
YORK: And therefore I will take the Nevils' parts
YORK: And make a show of love to proud Duke Humphrey,
YORK: And, when I spy advantage, claim the crown,
YORK: For that's the golden mark I seek to hit:
YORK: Nor shall proud Lancaster usurp my right,
YORK: Nor hold the sceptre in his childish fist,
YORK: Nor wear the diadem upon his head,
YORK: Whose church-like humours fits not for a crown.
YORK: Then, York, be still awhile, till time do serve:
YORK: Watch thou and wake when others be asleep,
YORK: To pry into the secrets of the state,
YORK: Till Henry, surfeiting in joys of love,
YORK: With his new bride and England's dear-bought queen,
YORK: And Humphrey with the peers be fall'n at jars:
YORK: Then will I raise aloft the milk-white rose,
YORK: With whose sweet smell the air shall be perfumed,
YORK: And in my standard bear the arms of York
YORK: To grapple with the house of Lancaster,
YORK: And, force perforce, I'll make him yield the crown,
YORK: Whose bookish rule hath pull'd fair England down.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. GLOUCESTER'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER and his DUCHESS
DUCHESS: Why droops my lord, like over-ripen'd corn,
DUCHESS: Hanging the head at Ceres' plenteous load?
DUCHESS: Why doth the great Duke Humphrey knit his brows,
DUCHESS: As frowning at the favours of the world?
DUCHESS: Why are thine eyes fixed to the sullen earth,
DUCHESS: Gazing on that which seems to dim thy sight?
DUCHESS: What seest thou there? King Henry's diadem,
DUCHESS: Enchased with all the honours of the world?
DUCHESS: If so, gaze on, and grovel on thy face,
DUCHESS: Until thy head be circled with the same.
DUCHESS: Put forth thy hand, reach at the glorious gold.
DUCHESS: What, is't too short? I'll lengthen it with mine:
DUCHESS: And, having both together heaved it up,
DUCHESS: We'll both together lift our heads to heaven,
DUCHESS: And never more abase our sight so low
DUCHESS: As to vouchsafe one glance unto the ground.
GLOUCESTER: O Nell, sweet Nell, if thou dost love thy lord,
GLOUCESTER: Banish the canker of ambitious thoughts.
GLOUCESTER: And may that thought, when I imagine ill
GLOUCESTER: Against my king and nephew, virtuous Henry,
GLOUCESTER: Be my last breathing in this mortal world!
GLOUCESTER: My troublous dream this night doth make me sad.
DUCHESS: What dream'd my lord? tell me, and I'll requite it
DUCHESS: With sweet rehearsal of my morning's dream.
GLOUCESTER: Methought this staff, mine office-badge in court,
GLOUCESTER: Was broke in twain, by whom I have forgot,
GLOUCESTER: But, as I think, it was by the cardinal,
GLOUCESTER: And on the pieces of the broken wand
GLOUCESTER: Were placed the heads of Edmund Duke of Somerset,
GLOUCESTER: And William de la Pole, first duke of Suffolk.
GLOUCESTER: This was my dream: what it doth bode, God knows.
DUCHESS: Tut, this was nothing but an argument
DUCHESS: That he that breaks a stick of Gloucester's grove
DUCHESS: Shall lose his head for his presumption.
DUCHESS: But list to me, my Humphrey, my sweet duke:
DUCHESS: Methought I sat in seat of majesty
DUCHESS: In the cathedral church of Westminster,
DUCHESS: And in that chair where kings and queens are crown'd,
DUCHESS: Where Henry and dame Margaret kneel'd to me
DUCHESS: And on my head did set the diadem.
GLOUCESTER: Nay, Eleanor, then must I chide outright:
GLOUCESTER: Presumptuous dame, ill-nurtured Eleanor,
GLOUCESTER: Art thou not second woman in the realm,
GLOUCESTER: And the protector's wife, beloved of him?
GLOUCESTER: Hast thou not worldly pleasure at command,
GLOUCESTER: Above the reach or compass of thy thought?
GLOUCESTER: And wilt thou still be hammering treachery,
GLOUCESTER: To tumble down thy husband and thyself
GLOUCESTER: From top of honour to disgrace's feet?
GLOUCESTER: Away from me, and let me hear no more!
DUCHESS: What, what, my lord! are you so choleric
DUCHESS: With Eleanor, for telling but her dream?
DUCHESS: Next time I'll keep my dreams unto myself,
DUCHESS: And not be cheque'd.
GLOUCESTER: Nay, be not angry, I am pleased again.
NARRATOR: Enter Messenger
Messenger: My lord protector, 'tis his highness' pleasure
Messenger: You do prepare to ride unto Saint Alban's,
Messenger: Where as the king and queen do mean to hawk.
GLOUCESTER: I go. Come, Nell, thou wilt ride with us?
DUCHESS: Yes, my good lord, I'll follow presently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GLOUCESTER and Messenger
DUCHESS: Follow I must, I cannot go before,
DUCHESS: While Gloucester bears this base and humble mind.
DUCHESS: Were I a man, a duke, and next of blood,
DUCHESS: I would remove these tedious stumbling-blocks
DUCHESS: And smooth my way upon their headless necks,
DUCHESS: And, being a woman, I will not be slack
DUCHESS: To play my part in Fortune's pageant.
DUCHESS: Where are you there? Sir John! nay, fear not, man,
DUCHESS: We are alone, here's none but thee and I.
NARRATOR: Enter HUME
HUME: Jesus preserve your royal majesty!
DUCHESS: What say'st thou? majesty! I am but grace.
HUME: But, by the grace of God, and Hume's advice,
HUME: Your grace's title shall be multiplied.
DUCHESS: What say'st thou, man? hast thou as yet conferr'd
DUCHESS: With Margery Jourdain, the cunning witch,
DUCHESS: With Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer?
DUCHESS: And will they undertake to do me good?
HUME: This they have promised, to show your highness
HUME: A spirit raised from depth of under-ground,
HUME: That shall make answer to such questions
HUME: As by your grace shall be propounded him.
DUCHESS: It is enough, I'll think upon the questions:
DUCHESS: When from St. Alban's we do make return,
DUCHESS: We'll see these things effected to the full.
DUCHESS: Here, Hume, take this reward, make merry, man,
DUCHESS: With thy confederates in this weighty cause.
NARRATOR: Exit
HUME: Hume must make merry with the duchess' gold,
HUME: Marry, and shall. But how now, Sir John Hume!
HUME: Seal up your lips, and give no words but mum:
HUME: The business asketh silent secrecy.
HUME: Dame Eleanor gives gold to bring the witch:
HUME: Gold cannot come amiss, were she a devil.
HUME: Yet have I gold flies from another coast,
HUME: I dare not say, from the rich cardinal
HUME: And from the great and new-made Duke of Suffolk,
HUME: Yet I do find it so, for to be plain,
HUME: They, knowing Dame Eleanor's aspiring humour,
HUME: Have hired me to undermine the duchess
HUME: And buz these conjurations in her brain.
HUME: They say 'A crafty knave does need no broker,'
HUME: Yet am I Suffolk and the cardinal's broker.
HUME: Hume, if you take not heed, you shall go near
HUME: To call them both a pair of crafty knaves.
HUME: Well, so it stands, and thus, I fear, at last
HUME: Hume's knavery will be the duchess' wreck,
HUME: And her attainture will be Humphrey's fall:
HUME: Sort how it will, I shall have gold for all.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter three or four Petitioners, PETER, the Armourer's man, being one
First Petitioner: My masters, let's stand close: my lord protector
First Petitioner: will come this way by and by, and then we may deliver
First Petitioner: our supplications in the quill.
Second Petitioner: Marry, the Lord protect him, for he's a good man!
Second Petitioner: Jesu bless him!
NARRATOR: Enter SUFFOLK and QUEEN MARGARET
PETER: Here a' comes, methinks, and the queen with him.
PETER: I'll be the first, sure.
Second Petitioner: Come back, fool, this is the Duke of Suffolk, and
Second Petitioner: not my lord protector.
SUFFOLK: How now, fellow! would'st anything with me?
First Petitioner: I pray, my lord, pardon me, I took ye for my lord
First Petitioner: protector.
QUEEN MARGARET: [Reading]  'To my Lord Protector!' Are your
QUEEN MARGARET: supplications to his lordship? Let me see them:
QUEEN MARGARET: what is thine?
First Petitioner: Mine is, an't please your grace, against John
First Petitioner: Goodman, my lord cardinal's man, for keeping my
First Petitioner: house, and lands, and wife and all, from me.
SUFFOLK: Thy wife, too! that's some wrong, indeed. What's
SUFFOLK: yours? What's here!
NARRATOR: Reads
SUFFOLK: 'Against the Duke of Suffolk, for enclosing the
SUFFOLK: commons of Melford.' How now, sir knave!
Second Petitioner: Alas, sir, I am but a poor petitioner of our whole township.
PETER: [Giving his petition]  Against my master, Thomas
PETER: Horner, for saying that the Duke of York was rightful
PETER: heir to the crown.
QUEEN MARGARET: What sayst thou? did the Duke of York say he was
QUEEN MARGARET: rightful heir to the crown?
PETER: That my master was? no, forsooth: my master said
PETER: that he was, and that the king was an usurper.
SUFFOLK: Who is there?
NARRATOR: Enter Servant
SUFFOLK: Take this fellow in, and send for
SUFFOLK: his master with a pursuivant presently: we'll hear
SUFFOLK: more of your matter before the King.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant with PETER
QUEEN MARGARET: And as for you, that love to be protected
QUEEN MARGARET: Under the wings of our protector's grace,
QUEEN MARGARET: Begin your suits anew, and sue to him.
NARRATOR: Tears the supplication
QUEEN MARGARET: Away, base cullions! Suffolk, let them go.
ALL: Come, let's be gone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
QUEEN MARGARET: My Lord of Suffolk, say, is this the guise,
QUEEN MARGARET: Is this the fashion in the court of England?
QUEEN MARGARET: Is this the government of Britain's isle,
QUEEN MARGARET: And this the royalty of Albion's king?
QUEEN MARGARET: What shall King Henry be a pupil still
QUEEN MARGARET: Under the surly Gloucester's governance?
QUEEN MARGARET: Am I a queen in title and in style,
QUEEN MARGARET: And must be made a subject to a duke?
QUEEN MARGARET: I tell thee, Pole, when in the city Tours
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou ran'st a tilt in honour of my love
QUEEN MARGARET: And stolest away the ladies' hearts of France,
QUEEN MARGARET: I thought King Henry had resembled thee
QUEEN MARGARET: In courage, courtship and proportion:
QUEEN MARGARET: But all his mind is bent to holiness,
QUEEN MARGARET: To number Ave-Maries on his beads,
QUEEN MARGARET: His champions are the prophets and apostles,
QUEEN MARGARET: His weapons holy saws of sacred writ,
QUEEN MARGARET: His study is his tilt-yard, and his loves
QUEEN MARGARET: Are brazen images of canonized saints.
QUEEN MARGARET: I would the college of the cardinals
QUEEN MARGARET: Would choose him pope, and carry him to Rome,
QUEEN MARGARET: And set the triple crown upon his head:
QUEEN MARGARET: That were a state fit for his holiness.
SUFFOLK: Madam, be patient: as I was cause
SUFFOLK: Your highness came to England, so will I
SUFFOLK: In England work your grace's full content.
QUEEN MARGARET: Beside the haughty protector, have we Beaufort,
QUEEN MARGARET: The imperious churchman, Somerset, Buckingham,
QUEEN MARGARET: And grumbling York: and not the least of these
QUEEN MARGARET: But can do more in England than the king.
SUFFOLK: And he of these that can do most of all
SUFFOLK: Cannot do more in England than the Nevils:
SUFFOLK: Salisbury and Warwick are no simple peers.
QUEEN MARGARET: Not all these lords do vex me half so much
QUEEN MARGARET: As that proud dame, the lord protector's wife.
QUEEN MARGARET: She sweeps it through the court with troops of ladies,
QUEEN MARGARET: More like an empress than Duke Humphrey's wife:
QUEEN MARGARET: Strangers in court do take her for the queen:
QUEEN MARGARET: She bears a duke's revenues on her back,
QUEEN MARGARET: And in her heart she scorns our poverty:
QUEEN MARGARET: Shall I not live to be avenged on her?
QUEEN MARGARET: Contemptuous base-born callet as she is,
QUEEN MARGARET: She vaunted 'mongst her minions t'other day,
QUEEN MARGARET: The very train of her worst wearing gown
QUEEN MARGARET: Was better worth than all my father's lands,
QUEEN MARGARET: Till Suffolk gave two dukedoms for his daughter.
SUFFOLK: Madam, myself have limed a bush for her,
SUFFOLK: And placed a quire of such enticing birds,
SUFFOLK: That she will light to listen to the lays,
SUFFOLK: And never mount to trouble you again.
SUFFOLK: So, let her rest: and, madam, list to me,
SUFFOLK: For I am bold to counsel you in this.
SUFFOLK: Although we fancy not the cardinal,
SUFFOLK: Yet must we join with him and with the lords,
SUFFOLK: Till we have brought Duke Humphrey in disgrace.
SUFFOLK: As for the Duke of York, this late complaint
SUFFOLK: Will make but little for his benefit.
SUFFOLK: So, one by one, we'll weed them all at last,
SUFFOLK: And you yourself shall steer the happy helm.
NARRATOR: Sound a sennet. Enter KING HENRY VI, GLOUCESTER,  CARDINAL, BUCKINGHAM, YORK, SOMERSET, SALISBURY, WARWICK, and the DUCHESS
KING HENRY VI: For my part, noble lords, I care not which,
KING HENRY VI: Or Somerset or York, all's one to me.
YORK: If York have ill demean'd himself in France,
YORK: Then let him be denay'd the regentship.
SOMERSET: If Somerset be unworthy of the place,
SOMERSET: Let York be regent, I will yield to him.
WARWICK: Whether your grace be worthy, yea or no,
WARWICK: Dispute not that: York is the worthier.
CARDINAL: Ambitious Warwick, let thy betters speak.
WARWICK: The cardinal's not my better in the field.
BUCKINGHAM: All in this presence are thy betters, Warwick.
WARWICK: Warwick may live to be the best of all.
SALISBURY: Peace, son! and show some reason, Buckingham,
SALISBURY: Why Somerset should be preferred in this.
QUEEN MARGARET: Because the king, forsooth, will have it so.
GLOUCESTER: Madam, the king is old enough himself
GLOUCESTER: To give his censure: these are no women's matters.
QUEEN MARGARET: If he be old enough, what needs your grace
QUEEN MARGARET: To be protector of his excellence?
GLOUCESTER: Madam, I am protector of the realm,
GLOUCESTER: And, at his pleasure, will resign my place.
SUFFOLK: Resign it then and leave thine insolence.
SUFFOLK: Since thou wert king--as who is king but thou?--
SUFFOLK: The commonwealth hath daily run to wreck,
SUFFOLK: The Dauphin hath prevail'd beyond the seas,
SUFFOLK: And all the peers and nobles of the realm
SUFFOLK: Have been as bondmen to thy sovereignty.
CARDINAL: The commons hast thou rack'd, the clergy's bags
CARDINAL: Are lank and lean with thy extortions.
SOMERSET: Thy sumptuous buildings and thy wife's attire
SOMERSET: Have cost a mass of public treasury.
BUCKINGHAM: Thy cruelty in execution
BUCKINGHAM: Upon offenders, hath exceeded law,
BUCKINGHAM: And left thee to the mercy of the law.
QUEEN MARGARET: They sale of offices and towns in France,
QUEEN MARGARET: If they were known, as the suspect is great,
QUEEN MARGARET: Would make thee quickly hop without thy head.
NARRATOR: Exit GLOUCESTER. QUEEN MARGARET drops her fan
QUEEN MARGARET: Give me my fan: what, minion! can ye not?
NARRATOR: She gives the DUCHESS a box on the ear
QUEEN MARGARET: I cry you mercy, madam, was it you?
DUCHESS: Was't I! yea, I it was, proud Frenchwoman:
DUCHESS: Could I come near your beauty with my nails,
DUCHESS: I'd set my ten commandments in your face.
KING HENRY VI: Sweet aunt, be quiet, 'twas against her will.
DUCHESS: Against her will! good king, look to't in time,
DUCHESS: She'll hamper thee, and dandle thee like a baby:
DUCHESS: Though in this place most master wear no breeches,
DUCHESS: She shall not strike Dame Eleanor unrevenged.
NARRATOR: Exit
BUCKINGHAM: Lord cardinal, I will follow Eleanor,
BUCKINGHAM: And listen after Humphrey, how he proceeds:
BUCKINGHAM: She's tickled now, her fume needs no spurs,
BUCKINGHAM: She'll gallop far enough to her destruction.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Now, lords, my choler being over-blown
GLOUCESTER: With walking once about the quadrangle,
GLOUCESTER: I come to talk of commonwealth affairs.
GLOUCESTER: As for your spiteful false objections,
GLOUCESTER: Prove them, and I lie open to the law:
GLOUCESTER: But God in mercy so deal with my soul,
GLOUCESTER: As I in duty love my king and country!
GLOUCESTER: But, to the matter that we have in hand:
GLOUCESTER: I say, my sovereign, York is meetest man
GLOUCESTER: To be your regent in the realm of France.
SUFFOLK: Before we make election, give me leave
SUFFOLK: To show some reason, of no little force,
SUFFOLK: That York is most unmeet of any man.
YORK: I'll tell thee, Suffolk, why I am unmeet:
YORK: First, for I cannot flatter thee in pride,
YORK: Next, if I be appointed for the place,
YORK: My Lord of Somerset will keep me here,
YORK: Without discharge, money, or furniture,
YORK: Till France be won into the Dauphin's hands:
YORK: Last time, I danced attendance on his will
YORK: Till Paris was besieged, famish'd, and lost.
WARWICK: That can I witness, and a fouler fact
WARWICK: Did never traitor in the land commit.
SUFFOLK: Peace, headstrong Warwick!
WARWICK: Image of pride, why should I hold my peace?
NARRATOR: Enter HORNER, the Armourer, and his man PETER, guarded
SUFFOLK: Because here is a man accused of treason:
SUFFOLK: Pray God the Duke of York excuse himself!
YORK: Doth any one accuse York for a traitor?
KING HENRY VI: What mean'st thou, Suffolk, tell me, what are these?
SUFFOLK: Please it your majesty, this is the man
SUFFOLK: That doth accuse his master of high treason:
SUFFOLK: His words were these: that Richard, Duke of York,
SUFFOLK: Was rightful heir unto the English crown
SUFFOLK: And that your majesty was a usurper.
KING HENRY VI: Say, man, were these thy words?
HORNER: An't shall please your majesty, I never said nor
HORNER: thought any such matter: God is my witness, I am
HORNER: falsely accused by the villain.
PETER: By these ten bones, my lords, he did speak them to
PETER: me in the garret one night, as we were scouring my
PETER: Lord of York's armour.
YORK: Base dunghill villain and mechanical,
YORK: I'll have thy head for this thy traitor's speech.
YORK: I do beseech your royal majesty,
YORK: Let him have all the rigor of the law.
HORNER: Alas, my lord, hang me, if ever I spake the words.
HORNER: My accuser is my 'prentice, and when I did correct
HORNER: him for his fault the other day, he did vow upon his
HORNER: knees he would be even with me: I have good
HORNER: witness of this: therefore I beseech your majesty,
HORNER: do not cast away an honest man for a villain's
HORNER: accusation.
KING HENRY VI: Uncle, what shall we say to this in law?
GLOUCESTER: This doom, my lord, if I may judge:
GLOUCESTER: Let Somerset be regent over the French,
GLOUCESTER: Because in York this breeds suspicion:
GLOUCESTER: And let these have a day appointed them
GLOUCESTER: For single combat in convenient place,
GLOUCESTER: For he hath witness of his servant's malice:
GLOUCESTER: This is the law, and this Duke Humphrey's doom.
SOMERSET: I humbly thank your royal majesty.
HORNER: And I accept the combat willingly.
PETER: Alas, my lord, I cannot fight, for God's sake, pity
PETER: my case. The spite of man prevaileth against me. O
PETER: Lord, have mercy upon me! I shall never be able to
PETER: fight a blow. O Lord, my heart!
GLOUCESTER: Sirrah, or you must fight, or else be hang'd.
KING HENRY VI: Away with them to prison, and the day of combat
KING HENRY VI: shall be the last of the next month. Come,
KING HENRY VI: Somerset, we'll see thee sent away.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. GLOUCESTER's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter MARGARET JOURDAIN, HUME, SOUTHWELL, and BOLINGBROKE
HUME: Come, my masters, the duchess, I tell you, expects
HUME: performance of your promises.
BOLINGBROKE: Master Hume, we are therefore provided: will her
BOLINGBROKE: ladyship behold and hear our exorcisms?
HUME: Ay, what else? fear you not her courage.
BOLINGBROKE: I have heard her reported to be a woman of an
BOLINGBROKE: invincible spirit: but it shall be convenient,
BOLINGBROKE: Master Hume, that you be by her aloft, while we be
BOLINGBROKE: busy below, and so, I pray you, go, in God's name,
BOLINGBROKE: and leave us.
NARRATOR: Exit HUME
BOLINGBROKE: Mother Jourdain, be you
BOLINGBROKE: prostrate and grovel on the earth, John Southwell,
BOLINGBROKE: read you, and let us to our work.
NARRATOR: Enter the DUCHESS aloft, HUME following
DUCHESS: Well said, my masters, and welcome all. To this
DUCHESS: gear the sooner the better.
BOLINGBROKE: Patience, good lady, wizards know their times:
BOLINGBROKE: Deep night, dark night, the silent of the night,
BOLINGBROKE: The time of night when Troy was set on fire,
BOLINGBROKE: The time when screech-owls cry and ban-dogs howl,
BOLINGBROKE: And spirits walk and ghosts break up their graves,
BOLINGBROKE: That time best fits the work we have in hand.
BOLINGBROKE: Madam, sit you and fear not: whom we raise,
BOLINGBROKE: We will make fast within a hallow'd verge.
BOLINGBROKE: Here they do the ceremonies belonging, and make the  circle, BOLINGBROKE or SOUTHWELL reads, Conjuro te, and c. It thunders and lightens terribly, then the Spirit riseth
Spirit: Adsum.
MARGARET JOURDAIN: Asmath,
MARGARET JOURDAIN: By the eternal God, whose name and power
MARGARET JOURDAIN: Thou tremblest at, answer that I shall ask,
MARGARET JOURDAIN: For, till thou speak, thou shalt not pass from hence.
Spirit: Ask what thou wilt. That I had said and done!
BOLINGBROKE: 'First of the king: what shall of him become?'
NARRATOR: Reading out of a paper
Spirit: The duke yet lives that Henry shall depose,
Spirit: But him outlive, and die a violent death.
NARRATOR: As the Spirit speaks, SOUTHWELL writes the answer
BOLINGBROKE: 'What fates await the Duke of Suffolk?'
Spirit: By water shall he die, and take his end.
BOLINGBROKE: 'What shall befall the Duke of Somerset?'
Spirit: Let him shun castles,
Spirit: Safer shall he be upon the sandy plains
Spirit: Than where castles mounted stand.
Spirit: Have done, for more I hardly can endure.
BOLINGBROKE: Descend to darkness and the burning lake!
BOLINGBROKE: False fiend, avoid!
NARRATOR: Thunder and lightning. Exit Spirit

NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Saint Alban's.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET, GLOUCESTER, CARDINAL, and SUFFOLK, with Falconers halloing

QUEEN MARGARET: Yet, by your leave, the wind was very high,
QUEEN MARGARET: And, ten to one, old Joan had not gone out.

SUFFOLK: And bears his thoughts above his falcon's pitch.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. London. YORK'S garden.
NARRATOR: Enter YORK, SALISBURY, and WARWICK
YORK: Now, my good Lords of Salisbury and Warwick,

WARWICK: The Nevils are thy subjects to command.

YORK: Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons:
YORK: The first, Edward the Black Prince, Prince of Wales,
YORK: The second, William of Hatfield, and the third,

YORK: Was John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster,
YORK: The fifth was Edmund Langley, Duke of York,
YORK: The sixth was Thomas of Woodstock, Duke of Gloucester,

YORK: And left behind him Richard, his only son,

YORK: Till Henry Bolingbroke, Duke of Lancaster,
YORK: The eldest son and heir of John of Gaunt,
YORK: Crown'd by the name of Henry the Fourth,
YORK: Seized on the realm, deposed the rightful king,
YORK: Sent his poor queen to France, from whence she came,
YORK: And him to Pomfret, where, as all you know,

WARWICK: Thus got the house of Lancaster the crown.

YORK: The issue of the next son should have reign'd.

YORK: Who married Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March:
YORK: Edmund had issue, Roger Earl of March,
YORK: Roger had issue, Edmund, Anne and Eleanor.

SALISBURY: Who kept him in captivity till he died.

YORK: Married Richard Earl of Cambridge, who was son
YORK: To Edmund Langley, Edward the Third's fifth son.

YORK: To Roger Earl of March, who was the son
YORK: Of Edmund Mortimer, who married Philippe,

WARWICK: The fourth son, York claims it from the third.

WARWICK: And in thy sons, fair slips of such a stock.

YORK: We thank you, lords. But I am not your king

YORK: With heart-blood of the house of Lancaster,

YORK: Wink at the Duke of Suffolk's insolence,
YORK: At Beaufort's pride, at Somerset's ambition,

SALISBURY: Thump! then see thou thump thy master well.
HORNER: Masters, I am come hither, as it were, upon my man's
HORNER: instigation, to prove him a knave and myself an
HORNER: honest man: and touching the Duke of York, I will
HORNER: take my death, I never meant him any ill, nor the
HORNER: king, nor the queen: and therefore, Peter, have at
HORNER: thee with a downright blow!
YORK: Dispatch: this knave's tongue begins to double.
YORK: Sound, trumpets, alarum to the combatants!
NARRATOR: Alarum. They fight, and PETER strikes him down
HORNER: Hold, Peter, hold! I confess, I confess treason.
NARRATOR: Dies
YORK: Take away his weapon. Fellow, thank God, and the
YORK: good wine in thy master's way.
PETER: O God, have I overcome mine enemy in this presence?
PETER: O Peter, thou hast prevailed in right!
KING HENRY VI: Go, take hence that traitor from our sight,
KING HENRY VI: For his death we do perceive his guilt:
KING HENRY VI: And God in justice hath revealed to us
KING HENRY VI: The truth and innocence of this poor fellow,
KING HENRY VI: Which he had thought to have murder'd wrongfully.
KING HENRY VI: Come, fellow, follow us for thy reward.
NARRATOR: Sound a flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER and his Servingmen, in mourning cloaks
GLOUCESTER: Thus sometimes hath the brightest day a cloud,
GLOUCESTER: And after summer evermore succeeds
GLOUCESTER: Barren winter, with his wrathful nipping cold:
GLOUCESTER: So cares and joys abound, as seasons fleet.
GLOUCESTER: Sirs, what's o'clock?
Servants: Ten, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: Ten is the hour that was appointed me
GLOUCESTER: To watch the coming of my punish'd duchess:
GLOUCESTER: Uneath may she endure the flinty streets,
GLOUCESTER: To tread them with her tender-feeling feet.
GLOUCESTER: Sweet Nell, ill can thy noble mind abrook
GLOUCESTER: The abject people gazing on thy face,
GLOUCESTER: With envious looks, laughing at thy shame,
GLOUCESTER: That erst did follow thy proud chariot-wheels
GLOUCESTER: When thou didst ride in triumph through the streets.
GLOUCESTER: But, soft! I think she comes, and I'll prepare
GLOUCESTER: My tear-stain'd eyes to see her miseries.
GLOUCESTER: Enter the DUCHESS in a white sheet, and a taper  burning in her hand, with STANLEY, the Sheriff, and Officers
Servant: So please your grace, we'll take her from the sheriff.
GLOUCESTER: No, stir not, for your lives, let her pass by.
DUCHESS: Come you, my lord, to see my open shame?
DUCHESS: Now thou dost penance too. Look how they gaze!
DUCHESS: See how the giddy multitude do point,
DUCHESS: And nod their heads, and throw their eyes on thee!
DUCHESS: Ah, Gloucester, hide thee from their hateful looks,
DUCHESS: And, in thy closet pent up, rue my shame,
DUCHESS: And ban thine enemies, both mine and thine!
GLOUCESTER: Be patient, gentle Nell, forget this grief.
DUCHESS: Ah, Gloucester, teach me to forget myself!
DUCHESS: For whilst I think I am thy married wife
DUCHESS: And thou a prince, protector of this land,
DUCHESS: Methinks I should not thus be led along,
DUCHESS: Mail'd up in shame, with papers on my back,
DUCHESS: And followed with a rabble that rejoice
DUCHESS: To see my tears and hear my deep-fet groans.
DUCHESS: The ruthless flint doth cut my tender feet,
DUCHESS: And when I start, the envious people laugh
DUCHESS: And bid me be advised how I tread.
DUCHESS: Ah, Humphrey, can I bear this shameful yoke?
DUCHESS: Trow'st thou that e'er I'll look upon the world,
DUCHESS: Or count them happy that enjoy the sun?
DUCHESS: No, dark shall be my light and night my day,
DUCHESS: To think upon my pomp shall be my hell.
DUCHESS: Sometime I'll say, I am Duke Humphrey's wife,
DUCHESS: And he a prince and ruler of the land:
DUCHESS: Yet so he ruled and such a prince he was
DUCHESS: As he stood by whilst I, his forlorn duchess,
DUCHESS: Was made a wonder and a pointing-stock
DUCHESS: To every idle rascal follower.
DUCHESS: But be thou mild and blush not at my shame,
DUCHESS: Nor stir at nothing till the axe of death
DUCHESS: Hang over thee, as, sure, it shortly will,
DUCHESS: For Suffolk, he that can do all in all
DUCHESS: With her that hateth thee and hates us all,
DUCHESS: And York and impious Beaufort, that false priest,
DUCHESS: Have all limed bushes to betray thy wings,
DUCHESS: And, fly thou how thou canst, they'll tangle thee:
DUCHESS: But fear not thou, until thy foot be snared,
DUCHESS: Nor never seek prevention of thy foes.
GLOUCESTER: Ah, Nell, forbear! thou aimest all awry,
GLOUCESTER: I must offend before I be attainted,
GLOUCESTER: And had I twenty times so many foes,
GLOUCESTER: And each of them had twenty times their power,
GLOUCESTER: All these could not procure me any scathe,
