GLOUCESTER: So long as I am loyal, true and crimeless.
GLOUCESTER: Wouldst have me rescue thee from this reproach?
GLOUCESTER: Why, yet thy scandal were not wiped away
GLOUCESTER: But I in danger for the breach of law.
GLOUCESTER: Thy greatest help is quiet, gentle Nell:
GLOUCESTER: I pray thee, sort thy heart to patience,
GLOUCESTER: These few days' wonder will be quickly worn.
NARRATOR: Enter a Herald
Herald: I summon your grace to his majesty's parliament,
Herald: Holden at Bury the first of this next month.
GLOUCESTER: And my consent ne'er ask'd herein before!
GLOUCESTER: This is close dealing. Well, I will be there.
NARRATOR: Exit Herald
GLOUCESTER: My Nell, I take my leave: and, master sheriff,
GLOUCESTER: Let not her penance exceed the king's commission.
Sheriff: An't please your grace, here my commission stays,
Sheriff: And Sir John Stanley is appointed now
Sheriff: To take her with him to the Isle of Man.
GLOUCESTER: Must you, Sir John, protect my lady here?
STANLEY: So am I given in charge, may't please your grace.
GLOUCESTER: Entreat her not the worse in that I pray
GLOUCESTER: You use her well: the world may laugh again,
GLOUCESTER: And I may live to do you kindness if
GLOUCESTER: You do it her: and so, Sir John, farewell!
DUCHESS: What, gone, my lord, and bid me not farewell!
GLOUCESTER: Witness my tears, I cannot stay to speak.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GLOUCESTER and Servingmen
DUCHESS: Art thou gone too? all comfort go with thee!
DUCHESS: For none abides with me: my joy is death,
DUCHESS: Death, at whose name I oft have been afear'd,
DUCHESS: Because I wish'd this world's eternity.
DUCHESS: Stanley, I prithee, go, and take me hence,
DUCHESS: I care not whither, for I beg no favour,
DUCHESS: Only convey me where thou art commanded.
STANLEY: Why, madam, that is to the Isle of Man,
STANLEY: There to be used according to your state.
DUCHESS: That's bad enough, for I am but reproach:
DUCHESS: And shall I then be used reproachfully?
STANLEY: Like to a duchess, and Duke Humphrey's lady,
STANLEY: According to that state you shall be used.
DUCHESS: Sheriff, farewell, and better than I fare,
DUCHESS: Although thou hast been conduct of my shame.
Sheriff: It is my office, and, madam, pardon me.
DUCHESS: Ay, ay, farewell, thy office is discharged.
DUCHESS: Come, Stanley, shall we go?
STANLEY: Madam, your penance done, throw off this sheet,
STANLEY: And go we to attire you for our journey.
DUCHESS: My shame will not be shifted with my sheet:
DUCHESS: No, it will hang upon my richest robes
DUCHESS: And show itself, attire me how I can.
DUCHESS: Go, lead the way, I long to see my prison.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The Abbey at Bury St. Edmund's.
NARRATOR: Sound a sennet. Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN  MARGARET, CARDINAL, SUFFOLK, YORK, BUCKINGHAM, SALISBURY and WARWICK to the Parliament
KING HENRY VI: I muse my Lord of Gloucester is not come:
KING HENRY VI: 'Tis not his wont to be the hindmost man,
KING HENRY VI: Whate'er occasion keeps him from us now.
QUEEN MARGARET: Can you not see? or will ye not observe
QUEEN MARGARET: The strangeness of his alter'd countenance?
QUEEN MARGARET: With what a majesty he bears himself,
QUEEN MARGARET: How insolent of late he is become,
QUEEN MARGARET: How proud, how peremptory, and unlike himself?
QUEEN MARGARET: We know the time since he was mild and affable,
QUEEN MARGARET: And if we did but glance a far-off look,
QUEEN MARGARET: Immediately he was upon his knee,
QUEEN MARGARET: That all the court admired him for submission:
QUEEN MARGARET: But meet him now, and, be it in the morn,
QUEEN MARGARET: When every one will give the time of day,
QUEEN MARGARET: He knits his brow and shows an angry eye,
QUEEN MARGARET: And passeth by with stiff unbowed knee,
QUEEN MARGARET: Disdaining duty that to us belongs.
QUEEN MARGARET: Small curs are not regarded when they grin,
QUEEN MARGARET: But great men tremble when the lion roars,
QUEEN MARGARET: And Humphrey is no little man in England.
QUEEN MARGARET: First note that he is near you in descent,
QUEEN MARGARET: And should you fall, he as the next will mount.
QUEEN MARGARET: Me seemeth then it is no policy,
QUEEN MARGARET: Respecting what a rancorous mind he bears
QUEEN MARGARET: And his advantage following your decease,
QUEEN MARGARET: That he should come about your royal person
QUEEN MARGARET: Or be admitted to your highness' council.
QUEEN MARGARET: By flattery hath he won the commons' hearts,
QUEEN MARGARET: And when he please to make commotion,
QUEEN MARGARET: 'Tis to be fear'd they all will follow him.
QUEEN MARGARET: Now 'tis the spring, and weeds are shallow-rooted,
QUEEN MARGARET: Suffer them now, and they'll o'ergrow the garden
QUEEN MARGARET: And choke the herbs for want of husbandry.
QUEEN MARGARET: The reverent care I bear unto my lord
QUEEN MARGARET: Made me collect these dangers in the duke.
QUEEN MARGARET: If it be fond, call it a woman's fear,
QUEEN MARGARET: Which fear if better reasons can supplant,
QUEEN MARGARET: I will subscribe and say I wrong'd the duke.
QUEEN MARGARET: My Lord of Suffolk, Buckingham, and York,
QUEEN MARGARET: Reprove my allegation, if you can,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or else conclude my words effectual.
SUFFOLK: Well hath your highness seen into this duke,
SUFFOLK: And, had I first been put to speak my mind,
SUFFOLK: I think I should have told your grace's tale.
SUFFOLK: The duchess, by his subornation,
SUFFOLK: Upon my life, began her devilish practises:
SUFFOLK: Or, if he were not privy to those faults,
SUFFOLK: Yet, by reputing of his high descent,
SUFFOLK: As next the king he was successive heir,
SUFFOLK: And such high vaunts of his nobility,
SUFFOLK: Did instigate the bedlam brain-sick duchess
SUFFOLK: By wicked means to frame our sovereign's fall.
SUFFOLK: Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep,
SUFFOLK: And in his simple show he harbours treason.
SUFFOLK: The fox barks not when he would steal the lamb.
SUFFOLK: No, no, my sovereign, Gloucester is a man
SUFFOLK: Unsounded yet and full of deep deceit.
CARDINAL: Did he not, contrary to form of law,
CARDINAL: Devise strange deaths for small offences done?
YORK: And did he not, in his protectorship,
YORK: Levy great sums of money through the realm
YORK: For soldiers' pay in France, and never sent it?
YORK: By means whereof the towns each day revolted.
BUCKINGHAM: Tut, these are petty faults to faults unknown.
BUCKINGHAM: Which time will bring to light in smooth
BUCKINGHAM: Duke Humphrey.
KING HENRY VI: My lords, at once: the care you have of us,
KING HENRY VI: To mow down thorns that would annoy our foot,
KING HENRY VI: Is worthy praise: but, shall I speak my conscience,
KING HENRY VI: Our kinsman Gloucester is as innocent
KING HENRY VI: From meaning treason to our royal person
KING HENRY VI: As is the sucking lamb or harmless dove:
KING HENRY VI: The duke is virtuous, mild and too well given
KING HENRY VI: To dream on evil or to work my downfall.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, what's more dangerous than this fond affiance!
QUEEN MARGARET: Seems he a dove? his feathers are but borrowed,
QUEEN MARGARET: For he's disposed as the hateful raven:
QUEEN MARGARET: Is he a lamb? his skin is surely lent him,
QUEEN MARGARET: For he's inclined as is the ravenous wolf.
QUEEN MARGARET: Who cannot steal a shape that means deceit?
QUEEN MARGARET: Take heed, my lord, the welfare of us all
QUEEN MARGARET: Hangs on the cutting short that fraudful man.
NARRATOR: Enter SOMERSET
SOMERSET: All health unto my gracious sovereign!
KING HENRY VI: Welcome, Lord Somerset. What news from France?
SOMERSET: That all your interest in those territories
SOMERSET: Is utterly bereft you, all is lost.
KING HENRY VI: Cold news, Lord Somerset: but God's will be done!
YORK: [Aside]  Cold news for me, for I had hope of France
YORK: As firmly as I hope for fertile England.
YORK: Thus are my blossoms blasted in the bud
YORK: And caterpillars eat my leaves away,
YORK: But I will remedy this gear ere long,
YORK: Or sell my title for a glorious grave.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: All happiness unto my lord the king!
GLOUCESTER: Pardon, my liege, that I have stay'd so long.
SUFFOLK: Nay, Gloucester, know that thou art come too soon,
SUFFOLK: Unless thou wert more loyal than thou art:
SUFFOLK: I do arrest thee of high treason here.
GLOUCESTER: Well, Suffolk, thou shalt not see me blush
GLOUCESTER: Nor change my countenance for this arrest:
GLOUCESTER: A heart unspotted is not easily daunted.
GLOUCESTER: The purest spring is not so free from mud
GLOUCESTER: As I am clear from treason to my sovereign:
GLOUCESTER: Who can accuse me? wherein am I guilty?
YORK: 'Tis thought, my lord, that you took bribes of France,
YORK: And, being protector, stayed the soldiers' pay,
YORK: By means whereof his highness hath lost France.
GLOUCESTER: Is it but thought so? what are they that think it?
GLOUCESTER: I never robb'd the soldiers of their pay,
GLOUCESTER: Nor ever had one penny bribe from France.
GLOUCESTER: So help me God, as I have watch'd the night,
GLOUCESTER: Ay, night by night, in studying good for England,
GLOUCESTER: That doit that e'er I wrested from the king,
GLOUCESTER: Or any groat I hoarded to my use,
GLOUCESTER: Be brought against me at my trial-day!
GLOUCESTER: No, many a pound of mine own proper store,
GLOUCESTER: Because I would not tax the needy commons,
GLOUCESTER: Have I disbursed to the garrisons,
GLOUCESTER: And never ask'd for restitution.
CARDINAL: It serves you well, my lord, to say so much.
GLOUCESTER: I say no more than truth, so help me God!
YORK: In your protectorship you did devise
YORK: Strange tortures for offenders never heard of,
YORK: That England was defamed by tyranny.
GLOUCESTER: Why, 'tis well known that, whiles I was
GLOUCESTER: protector,
GLOUCESTER: Pity was all the fault that was in me,
GLOUCESTER: For I should melt at an offender's tears,
GLOUCESTER: And lowly words were ransom for their fault.
GLOUCESTER: Unless it were a bloody murderer,
GLOUCESTER: Or foul felonious thief that fleeced poor passengers,
GLOUCESTER: I never gave them condign punishment:
GLOUCESTER: Murder indeed, that bloody sin, I tortured
GLOUCESTER: Above the felon or what trespass else.
SUFFOLK: My lord, these faults are easy, quickly answered:
SUFFOLK: But mightier crimes are laid unto your charge,
SUFFOLK: Whereof you cannot easily purge yourself.
SUFFOLK: I do arrest you in his highness' name,
SUFFOLK: And here commit you to my lord cardinal
SUFFOLK: To keep, until your further time of trial.
KING HENRY VI: My lord of Gloucester, 'tis my special hope
KING HENRY VI: That you will clear yourself from all suspect:
KING HENRY VI: My conscience tells me you are innocent.
GLOUCESTER: Ah, gracious lord, these days are dangerous:
GLOUCESTER: Virtue is choked with foul ambition
GLOUCESTER: And charity chased hence by rancour's hand,
GLOUCESTER: Foul subornation is predominant
GLOUCESTER: And equity exiled your highness' land.
GLOUCESTER: I know their complot is to have my life,
GLOUCESTER: And if my death might make this island happy,
GLOUCESTER: And prove the period of their tyranny,
GLOUCESTER: I would expend it with all willingness:
GLOUCESTER: But mine is made the prologue to their play,
GLOUCESTER: For thousands more, that yet suspect no peril,
GLOUCESTER: Will not conclude their plotted tragedy.
GLOUCESTER: Beaufort's red sparkling eyes blab his heart's malice,
GLOUCESTER: And Suffolk's cloudy brow his stormy hate,
GLOUCESTER: Sharp Buckingham unburthens with his tongue
GLOUCESTER: The envious load that lies upon his heart,
GLOUCESTER: And dogged York, that reaches at the moon,
GLOUCESTER: Whose overweening arm I have pluck'd back,
GLOUCESTER: By false accuse doth level at my life:
GLOUCESTER: And you, my sovereign lady, with the rest,
GLOUCESTER: Causeless have laid disgraces on my head,
GLOUCESTER: And with your best endeavour have stirr'd up
GLOUCESTER: My liefest liege to be mine enemy:
GLOUCESTER: Ay, all you have laid your heads together--
GLOUCESTER: Myself had notice of your conventicles--
GLOUCESTER: And all to make away my guiltless life.
GLOUCESTER: I shall not want false witness to condemn me,
GLOUCESTER: Nor store of treasons to augment my guilt,
GLOUCESTER: The ancient proverb will be well effected:
GLOUCESTER: 'A staff is quickly found to beat a dog.'
CARDINAL: My liege, his railing is intolerable:
CARDINAL: If those that care to keep your royal person
CARDINAL: From treason's secret knife and traitors' rage
CARDINAL: Be thus upbraided, chid and rated at,
CARDINAL: And the offender granted scope of speech,
CARDINAL: 'Twill make them cool in zeal unto your grace.
SUFFOLK: Hath he not twit our sovereign lady here
SUFFOLK: With ignominious words, though clerkly couch'd,
SUFFOLK: As if she had suborned some to swear
SUFFOLK: False allegations to o'erthrow his state?
QUEEN MARGARET: But I can give the loser leave to chide.
GLOUCESTER: Far truer spoke than meant: I lose, indeed,
GLOUCESTER: Beshrew the winners, for they play'd me false!
GLOUCESTER: And well such losers may have leave to speak.
BUCKINGHAM: He'll wrest the sense and hold us here all day:
BUCKINGHAM: Lord cardinal, he is your prisoner.
CARDINAL: Sirs, take away the duke, and guard him sure.
GLOUCESTER: Ah! thus King Henry throws away his crutch
GLOUCESTER: Before his legs be firm to bear his body.
GLOUCESTER: Thus is the shepherd beaten from thy side,
GLOUCESTER: And wolves are gnarling who shall gnaw thee first.
GLOUCESTER: Ah, that my fear were false! ah, that it were!
GLOUCESTER: For, good King Henry, thy decay I fear.
NARRATOR: Exit, guarded
KING HENRY VI: My lords, what to your wisdoms seemeth best,
KING HENRY VI: Do or undo, as if ourself were here.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, will your highness leave the parliament?
KING HENRY VI: Ay, Margaret, my heart is drown'd with grief,
KING HENRY VI: Whose flood begins to flow within mine eyes,
KING HENRY VI: My body round engirt with misery,
KING HENRY VI: For what's more miserable than discontent?
KING HENRY VI: Ah, uncle Humphrey! in thy face I see
KING HENRY VI: The map of honour, truth and loyalty:
KING HENRY VI: And yet, good Humphrey, is the hour to come
KING HENRY VI: That e'er I proved thee false or fear'd thy faith.
KING HENRY VI: What louring star now envies thy estate,
KING HENRY VI: That these great lords and Margaret our queen
KING HENRY VI: Do seek subversion of thy harmless life?
KING HENRY VI: Thou never didst them wrong, nor no man wrong,
KING HENRY VI: And as the butcher takes away the calf
KING HENRY VI: And binds the wretch, and beats it when it strays,
KING HENRY VI: Bearing it to the bloody slaughter-house,
KING HENRY VI: Even so remorseless have they borne him hence,
KING HENRY VI: And as the dam runs lowing up and down,
KING HENRY VI: Looking the way her harmless young one went,
KING HENRY VI: And can do nought but wail her darling's loss,
KING HENRY VI: Even so myself bewails good Gloucester's case
KING HENRY VI: With sad unhelpful tears, and with dimm'd eyes
KING HENRY VI: Look after him and cannot do him good,
KING HENRY VI: So mighty are his vowed enemies.
KING HENRY VI: His fortunes I will weep, and, 'twixt each groan
KING HENRY VI: Say 'Who's a traitor? Gloucester he is none.'
KING HENRY VI: Exeunt all but QUEEN MARGARET, CARDINAL, SUFFOLK, and YORK, SOMERSET remains apart
QUEEN MARGARET: Free lords, cold snow melts with the sun's hot beams.
QUEEN MARGARET: Henry my lord is cold in great affairs,
QUEEN MARGARET: Too full of foolish pity, and Gloucester's show
QUEEN MARGARET: Beguiles him as the mournful crocodile
QUEEN MARGARET: With sorrow snares relenting passengers,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or as the snake roll'd in a flowering bank,
QUEEN MARGARET: With shining chequer'd slough, doth sting a child
QUEEN MARGARET: That for the beauty thinks it excellent.
QUEEN MARGARET: Believe me, lords, were none more wise than I--
QUEEN MARGARET: And yet herein I judge mine own wit good--
QUEEN MARGARET: This Gloucester should be quickly rid the world,
QUEEN MARGARET: To rid us of the fear we have of him.
CARDINAL: That he should die is worthy policy,
CARDINAL: But yet we want a colour for his death:
CARDINAL: 'Tis meet he be condemn'd by course of law.
SUFFOLK: But, in my mind, that were no policy:
SUFFOLK: The king will labour still to save his life,
SUFFOLK: The commons haply rise, to save his life,
SUFFOLK: And yet we have but trivial argument,
SUFFOLK: More than mistrust, that shows him worthy death.
YORK: So that, by this, you would not have him die.
SUFFOLK: Ah, York, no man alive so fain as I!
YORK: 'Tis York that hath more reason for his death.
YORK: But, my lord cardinal, and you, my Lord of Suffolk,
YORK: Say as you think, and speak it from your souls,
YORK: Were't not all one, an empty eagle were set
YORK: To guard the chicken from a hungry kite,
YORK: As place Duke Humphrey for the king's protector?
QUEEN MARGARET: So the poor chicken should be sure of death.
SUFFOLK: Madam, 'tis true, and were't not madness, then,
SUFFOLK: To make the fox surveyor of the fold?
SUFFOLK: Who being accused a crafty murderer,
SUFFOLK: His guilt should be but idly posted over,
SUFFOLK: Because his purpose is not executed.
SUFFOLK: No, let him die, in that he is a fox,
SUFFOLK: By nature proved an enemy to the flock,
SUFFOLK: Before his chaps be stain'd with crimson blood,
SUFFOLK: As Humphrey, proved by reasons, to my liege.
SUFFOLK: And do not stand on quillets how to slay him:
SUFFOLK: Be it by gins, by snares, by subtlety,
SUFFOLK: Sleeping or waking, 'tis no matter how,
SUFFOLK: So he be dead, for that is good deceit
SUFFOLK: Which mates him first that first intends deceit.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thrice-noble Suffolk, 'tis resolutely spoke.
SUFFOLK: Not resolute, except so much were done,
SUFFOLK: For things are often spoke and seldom meant:
SUFFOLK: But that my heart accordeth with my tongue,
SUFFOLK: Seeing the deed is meritorious,
SUFFOLK: And to preserve my sovereign from his foe,
SUFFOLK: Say but the word, and I will be his priest.
CARDINAL: But I would have him dead, my Lord of Suffolk,
CARDINAL: Ere you can take due orders for a priest:
CARDINAL: Say you consent and censure well the deed,
CARDINAL: And I'll provide his executioner,
CARDINAL: I tender so the safety of my liege.
SUFFOLK: Here is my hand, the deed is worthy doing.
QUEEN MARGARET: And so say I.
YORK: And I    and now we three have spoke it,
YORK: It skills not greatly who impugns our doom.
NARRATOR: Enter a Post
Post: Great lords, from Ireland am I come amain,
Post: To signify that rebels there are up
Post: And put the Englishmen unto the sword:
Post: Send succors, lords, and stop the rage betime,
Post: Before the wound do grow uncurable,
Post: For, being green, there is great hope of help.
CARDINAL: A breach that craves a quick expedient stop!
CARDINAL: What counsel give you in this weighty cause?
YORK: That Somerset be sent as regent thither:
YORK: 'Tis meet that lucky ruler be employ'd,
YORK: Witness the fortune he hath had in France.
SOMERSET: If York, with all his far-fet policy,
SOMERSET: Had been the regent there instead of me,
SOMERSET: He never would have stay'd in France so long.
YORK: No, not to lose it all, as thou hast done:
YORK: I rather would have lost my life betimes
YORK: Than bring a burthen of dishonour home
YORK: By staying there so long till all were lost.
YORK: Show me one scar character'd on thy skin:
YORK: Men's flesh preserved so whole do seldom win.
QUEEN MARGARET: Nay, then, this spark will prove a raging fire,
QUEEN MARGARET: If wind and fuel be brought to feed it with:
QUEEN MARGARET: No more, good York, sweet Somerset, be still:
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy fortune, York, hadst thou been regent there,
QUEEN MARGARET: Might happily have proved far worse than his.
YORK: What, worse than nought? nay, then, a shame take all!
SOMERSET: And, in the number, thee that wishest shame!
CARDINAL: My Lord of York, try what your fortune is.
CARDINAL: The uncivil kerns of Ireland are in arms
CARDINAL: And temper clay with blood of Englishmen:
CARDINAL: To Ireland will you lead a band of men,
CARDINAL: Collected choicely, from each county some,
CARDINAL: And try your hap against the Irishmen?
YORK: I will, my lord, so please his majesty.
SUFFOLK: Why, our authority is his consent,
SUFFOLK: And what we do establish he confirms:
SUFFOLK: Then, noble York, take thou this task in hand.
YORK: I am content: provide me soldiers, lords,
YORK: Whiles I take order for mine own affairs.
SUFFOLK: A charge, Lord York, that I will see perform'd.
SUFFOLK: But now return we to the false Duke Humphrey.
CARDINAL: No more of him, for I will deal with him
CARDINAL: That henceforth he shall trouble us no more.
CARDINAL: And so break off, the day is almost spent:
CARDINAL: Lord Suffolk, you and I must talk of that event.
YORK: My Lord of Suffolk, within fourteen days
YORK: At Bristol I expect my soldiers,
YORK: For there I'll ship them all for Ireland.
SUFFOLK: I'll see it truly done, my Lord of York.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but YORK
YORK: Now, York, or never, steel thy fearful thoughts,
YORK: And change misdoubt to resolution:
YORK: Be that thou hopest to be, or what thou art
YORK: Resign to death, it is not worth the enjoying:
YORK: Let pale-faced fear keep with the mean-born man,
YORK: And find no harbour in a royal heart.
YORK: Faster than spring-time showers comes thought
YORK: on thought,
YORK: And not a thought but thinks on dignity.
YORK: My brain more busy than the labouring spider
YORK: Weaves tedious snares to trap mine enemies.
YORK: Well, nobles, well, 'tis politicly done,
YORK: To send me packing with an host of men:
YORK: I fear me you but warm the starved snake,
YORK: Who, cherish'd in your breasts, will sting
YORK: your hearts.
YORK: 'Twas men I lack'd and you will give them me:
YORK: I take it kindly, and yet be well assured
YORK: You put sharp weapons in a madman's hands.
YORK: Whiles I in Ireland nourish a mighty band,
YORK: I will stir up in England some black storm
YORK: Shall blow ten thousand souls to heaven or hell,
YORK: And this fell tempest shall not cease to rage
YORK: Until the golden circuit on my head,
YORK: Like to the glorious sun's transparent beams,
YORK: Do calm the fury of this mad-bred flaw.
YORK: And, for a minister of my intent,
YORK: I have seduced a headstrong Kentishman,
YORK: John Cade of Ashford,
YORK: To make commotion, as full well he can,
YORK: Under the title of John Mortimer.
YORK: In Ireland have I seen this stubborn Cade
YORK: Oppose himself against a troop of kerns,
YORK: And fought so long, till that his thighs with darts
YORK: Were almost like a sharp-quill'd porpentine,
YORK: And, in the end being rescued, I have seen
YORK: Him caper upright like a wild Morisco,
YORK: Shaking the bloody darts as he his bells.
YORK: Full often, like a shag-hair'd crafty kern,
YORK: Hath he conversed with the enemy,
YORK: And undiscover'd come to me again
YORK: And given me notice of their villanies.
YORK: This devil here shall be my substitute,
YORK: For that John Mortimer, which now is dead,
YORK: In face, in gait, in speech, he doth resemble:
YORK: By this I shall perceive the commons' mind,
YORK: How they affect the house and claim of York.
YORK: Say he be taken, rack'd and tortured,
YORK: I know no pain they can inflict upon him
YORK: Will make him say I moved him to those arms.
YORK: Say that he thrive, as 'tis great like he will,
YORK: Why, then from Ireland come I with my strength
YORK: And reap the harvest which that rascal sow'd,
YORK: For Humphrey being dead, as he shall be,
YORK: And Henry put apart, the next for me.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Bury St. Edmund's. A room of state.
NARRATOR: Enter certain Murderers, hastily
First Murderer: Run to my Lord of Suffolk, let him know
First Murderer: We have dispatch'd the duke, as he commanded.
Second Murderer: O that it were to do! What have we done?
Second Murderer: Didst ever hear a man so penitent?
NARRATOR: Enter SUFFOLK
First Murder: Here comes my lord.
SUFFOLK: Now, sirs, have you dispatch'd this thing?
First Murderer: Ay, my good lord, he's dead.
SUFFOLK: Why, that's well said. Go, get you to my house,
SUFFOLK: I will reward you for this venturous deed.
SUFFOLK: The king and all the peers are here at hand.
SUFFOLK: Have you laid fair the bed? Is all things well,
SUFFOLK: According as I gave directions?
First Murderer: 'Tis, my good lord.
SUFFOLK: Away! be gone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Murderers
NARRATOR: Sound trumpets. Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET, CARDINAL, SOMERSET, with Attendants
KING HENRY VI: Go, call our uncle to our presence straight,
KING HENRY VI: Say we intend to try his grace to-day.
KING HENRY VI: If he be guilty, as 'tis published.
SUFFOLK: I'll call him presently, my noble lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING HENRY VI: Lords, take your places, and, I pray you all,
KING HENRY VI: Proceed no straiter 'gainst our uncle Gloucester
KING HENRY VI: Than from true evidence of good esteem
KING HENRY VI: He be approved in practise culpable.
QUEEN MARGARET: God forbid any malice should prevail,
QUEEN MARGARET: That faultless may condemn a nobleman!
QUEEN MARGARET: Pray God he may acquit him of suspicion!
KING HENRY VI: I thank thee, Meg, these words content me much.
NARRATOR: Re-enter SUFFOLK
KING HENRY VI: How now! why look'st thou pale? why tremblest thou?
KING HENRY VI: Where is our uncle? what's the matter, Suffolk?
SUFFOLK: Dead in his bed, my lord, Gloucester is dead.
QUEEN MARGARET: Marry, God forfend!
CARDINAL: God's secret judgment: I did dream to-night
CARDINAL: The duke was dumb and could not speak a word.
NARRATOR: KING HENRY VI swoons
QUEEN MARGARET: How fares my lord? Help, lords! the king is dead.
SOMERSET: Rear up his body, wring him by the nose.
QUEEN MARGARET: Run, go, help, help! O Henry, ope thine eyes!
SUFFOLK: He doth revive again: madam, be patient.
KING HENRY VI: O heavenly God!
QUEEN MARGARET: How fares my gracious lord?
SUFFOLK: Comfort, my sovereign! gracious Henry, comfort!
KING HENRY VI: What, doth my Lord of Suffolk comfort me?
KING HENRY VI: Came he right now to sing a raven's note,
KING HENRY VI: Whose dismal tune bereft my vital powers,
KING HENRY VI: And thinks he that the chirping of a wren,
KING HENRY VI: By crying comfort from a hollow breast,
KING HENRY VI: Can chase away the first-conceived sound?
KING HENRY VI: Hide not thy poison with such sugar'd words,
KING HENRY VI: Lay not thy hands on me, forbear, I say,
KING HENRY VI: Their touch affrights me as a serpent's sting.
KING HENRY VI: Thou baleful messenger, out of my sight!
KING HENRY VI: Upon thy eye-balls murderous tyranny
KING HENRY VI: Sits in grim majesty, to fright the world.
KING HENRY VI: Look not upon me, for thine eyes are wounding:
KING HENRY VI: Yet do not go away: come, basilisk,
KING HENRY VI: And kill the innocent gazer with thy sight,
KING HENRY VI: For in the shade of death I shall find joy,
KING HENRY VI: In life but double death, now Gloucester's dead.
QUEEN MARGARET: Why do you rate my Lord of Suffolk thus?
QUEEN MARGARET: Although the duke was enemy to him,
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet he most Christian-like laments his death:
QUEEN MARGARET: And for myself, foe as he was to me,
QUEEN MARGARET: Might liquid tears or heart-offending groans
QUEEN MARGARET: Or blood-consuming sighs recall his life,
QUEEN MARGARET: I would be blind with weeping, sick with groans,
QUEEN MARGARET: Look pale as primrose with blood-drinking sighs,
QUEEN MARGARET: And all to have the noble duke alive.
QUEEN MARGARET: What know I how the world may deem of me?
QUEEN MARGARET: For it is known we were but hollow friends:
QUEEN MARGARET: It may be judged I made the duke away,
QUEEN MARGARET: So shall my name with slander's tongue be wounded,
QUEEN MARGARET: And princes' courts be fill'd with my reproach.
QUEEN MARGARET: This get I by his death: ay me, unhappy!
QUEEN MARGARET: To be a queen, and crown'd with infamy!
KING HENRY VI: Ah, woe is me for Gloucester, wretched man!
QUEEN MARGARET: Be woe for me, more wretched than he is.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, dost thou turn away and hide thy face?
QUEEN MARGARET: I am no loathsome leper, look on me.
QUEEN MARGARET: What! art thou, like the adder, waxen deaf?
QUEEN MARGARET: Be poisonous too and kill thy forlorn queen.
QUEEN MARGARET: Is all thy comfort shut in Gloucester's tomb?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, then, dame Margaret was ne'er thy joy.
QUEEN MARGARET: Erect his statue and worship it,
QUEEN MARGARET: And make my image but an alehouse sign.
QUEEN MARGARET: Was I for this nigh wreck'd upon the sea
QUEEN MARGARET: And twice by awkward wind from England's bank
QUEEN MARGARET: Drove back again unto my native clime?
QUEEN MARGARET: What boded this, but well forewarning wind
QUEEN MARGARET: Did seem to say 'Seek not a scorpion's nest,
QUEEN MARGARET: Nor set no footing on this unkind shore'?
QUEEN MARGARET: What did I then, but cursed the gentle gusts
QUEEN MARGARET: And he that loosed them forth their brazen caves:
QUEEN MARGARET: And bid them blow towards England's blessed shore,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or turn our stern upon a dreadful rock
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet AEolus would not be a murderer,
QUEEN MARGARET: But left that hateful office unto thee:
QUEEN MARGARET: The pretty-vaulting sea refused to drown me,
QUEEN MARGARET: Knowing that thou wouldst have me drown'd on shore,
QUEEN MARGARET: With tears as salt as sea, through thy unkindness:
QUEEN MARGARET: The splitting rocks cower'd in the sinking sands
QUEEN MARGARET: And would not dash me with their ragged sides,
QUEEN MARGARET: Because thy flinty heart, more hard than they,
QUEEN MARGARET: Might in thy palace perish Margaret.
QUEEN MARGARET: As far as I could ken thy chalky cliffs,
QUEEN MARGARET: When from thy shore the tempest beat us back,
QUEEN MARGARET: I stood upon the hatches in the storm,
QUEEN MARGARET: And when the dusky sky began to rob
QUEEN MARGARET: My earnest-gaping sight of thy land's view,
QUEEN MARGARET: I took a costly jewel from my neck,
QUEEN MARGARET: A heart it was, bound in with diamonds,
QUEEN MARGARET: And threw it towards thy land: the sea received it,
QUEEN MARGARET: And so I wish'd thy body might my heart:
QUEEN MARGARET: And even with this I lost fair England's view
QUEEN MARGARET: And bid mine eyes be packing with my heart
QUEEN MARGARET: And call'd them blind and dusky spectacles,
QUEEN MARGARET: For losing ken of Albion's wished coast.
QUEEN MARGARET: How often have I tempted Suffolk's tongue,
QUEEN MARGARET: The agent of thy foul inconstancy,
QUEEN MARGARET: To sit and witch me, as Ascanius did
QUEEN MARGARET: When he to madding Dido would unfold
QUEEN MARGARET: His father's acts commenced in burning Troy!
QUEEN MARGARET: Am I not witch'd like her? or thou not false like him?
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay me, I can no more! die, Margaret!
QUEEN MARGARET: For Henry weeps that thou dost live so long.
NARRATOR: Noise within. Enter WARWICK, SALISBURY, and many Commons
WARWICK: It is reported, mighty sovereign,
WARWICK: That good Duke Humphrey traitorously is murder'd
WARWICK: By Suffolk and the Cardinal Beaufort's means.
WARWICK: The commons, like an angry hive of bees
WARWICK: That want their leader, scatter up and down
WARWICK: And care not who they sting in his revenge.
WARWICK: Myself have calm'd their spleenful mutiny,
WARWICK: Until they hear the order of his death.
KING HENRY VI: That he is dead, good Warwick, 'tis too true,
KING HENRY VI: But how he died God knows, not Henry:
KING HENRY VI: Enter his chamber, view his breathless corpse,
KING HENRY VI: And comment then upon his sudden death.
WARWICK: That shall I do, my liege. Stay, Salisbury,
WARWICK: With the rude multitude till I return.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING HENRY VI: O Thou that judgest all things, stay my thoughts,
KING HENRY VI: My thoughts, that labour to persuade my soul
KING HENRY VI: Some violent hands were laid on Humphrey's life!
KING HENRY VI: If my suspect be false, forgive me, God,
KING HENRY VI: For judgment only doth belong to thee.
KING HENRY VI: Fain would I go to chafe his paly lips
KING HENRY VI: With twenty thousand kisses, and to drain
KING HENRY VI: Upon his face an ocean of salt tears,
KING HENRY VI: To tell my love unto his dumb deaf trunk,
KING HENRY VI: And with my fingers feel his hand unfeeling:
KING HENRY VI: But all in vain are these mean obsequies,
KING HENRY VI: And to survey his dead and earthly image,
KING HENRY VI: What were it but to make my sorrow greater?
NARRATOR: Re-enter WARWICK and others, bearing GLOUCESTER'S body on a bed
WARWICK: Come hither, gracious sovereign, view this body.
KING HENRY VI: That is to see how deep my grave is made,
KING HENRY VI: For with his soul fled all my worldly solace,
KING HENRY VI: For seeing him I see my life in death.
WARWICK: As surely as my soul intends to live
WARWICK: With that dread King that took our state upon him
WARWICK: To free us from his father's wrathful curse,
WARWICK: I do believe that violent hands were laid
WARWICK: Upon the life of this thrice-famed duke.
SUFFOLK: A dreadful oath, sworn with a solemn tongue!
SUFFOLK: What instance gives Lord Warwick for his vow?
WARWICK: See how the blood is settled in his face.
WARWICK: Oft have I seen a timely-parted ghost,
WARWICK: Of ashy semblance, meagre, pale and bloodless,
WARWICK: Being all descended to the labouring heart,
WARWICK: Who, in the conflict that it holds with death,
WARWICK: Attracts the same for aidance 'gainst the enemy,
WARWICK: Which with the heart there cools and ne'er returneth
WARWICK: To blush and beautify the cheek again.
WARWICK: But see, his face is black and full of blood,
WARWICK: His eye-balls further out than when he lived,
WARWICK: Staring full ghastly like a strangled man,
WARWICK: His hair uprear'd, his nostrils stretched with struggling,
WARWICK: His hands abroad display'd, as one that grasp'd
WARWICK: And tugg'd for life and was by strength subdued:
WARWICK: Look, on the sheets his hair you see, is sticking,
WARWICK: His well-proportion'd beard made rough and rugged,
WARWICK: Like to the summer's corn by tempest lodged.
WARWICK: It cannot be but he was murder'd here,
WARWICK: The least of all these signs were probable.
SUFFOLK: Why, Warwick, who should do the duke to death?
SUFFOLK: Myself and Beaufort had him in protection,
SUFFOLK: And we, I hope, sir, are no murderers.
WARWICK: But both of you were vow'd Duke Humphrey's foes,
WARWICK: And you, forsooth, had the good duke to keep:
WARWICK: 'Tis like you would not feast him like a friend,
WARWICK: And 'tis well seen he found an enemy.
QUEEN MARGARET: Then you, belike, suspect these noblemen
QUEEN MARGARET: As guilty of Duke Humphrey's timeless death.
WARWICK: Who finds the heifer dead and bleeding fresh
WARWICK: And sees fast by a butcher with an axe,
WARWICK: But will suspect 'twas he that made the slaughter?
WARWICK: Who finds the partridge in the puttock's nest,
WARWICK: But may imagine how the bird was dead,
WARWICK: Although the kite soar with unbloodied beak?
WARWICK: Even so suspicious is this tragedy.
QUEEN MARGARET: Are you the butcher, Suffolk? Where's your knife?
QUEEN MARGARET: Is Beaufort term'd a kite? Where are his talons?
SUFFOLK: I wear no knife to slaughter sleeping men,
SUFFOLK: But here's a vengeful sword, rusted with ease,
SUFFOLK: That shall be scoured in his rancorous heart
SUFFOLK: That slanders me with murder's crimson badge.
SUFFOLK: Say, if thou darest, proud Lord of Warwick-shire,
SUFFOLK: That I am faulty in Duke Humphrey's death.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CARDINAL, SOMERSET, and others
WARWICK: What dares not Warwick, if false Suffolk dare him?
QUEEN MARGARET: He dares not calm his contumelious spirit
QUEEN MARGARET: Nor cease to be an arrogant controller,
QUEEN MARGARET: Though Suffolk dare him twenty thousand times.
WARWICK: Madam, be still, with reverence may I say,
WARWICK: For every word you speak in his behalf
WARWICK: Is slander to your royal dignity.
SUFFOLK: Blunt-witted lord, ignoble in demeanor!
SUFFOLK: If ever lady wrong'd her lord so much,
SUFFOLK: Thy mother took into her blameful bed
SUFFOLK: Some stern untutor'd churl, and noble stock
SUFFOLK: Was graft with crab-tree slip, whose fruit thou art,
SUFFOLK: And never of the Nevils' noble race.
WARWICK: But that the guilt of murder bucklers thee
WARWICK: And I should rob the deathsman of his fee,
WARWICK: Quitting thee thereby of ten thousand shames,
WARWICK: And that my sovereign's presence makes me mild,
WARWICK: I would, false murderous coward, on thy knee
WARWICK: Make thee beg pardon for thy passed speech,
WARWICK: And say it was thy mother that thou meant'st
WARWICK: That thou thyself was born in bastardy,
WARWICK: And after all this fearful homage done,
WARWICK: Give thee thy hire and send thy soul to hell,
WARWICK: Pernicious blood-sucker of sleeping men!
SUFFOLK: Thou shall be waking well I shed thy blood,
SUFFOLK: If from this presence thou darest go with me.
WARWICK: Away even now, or I will drag thee hence:
WARWICK: Unworthy though thou art, I'll cope with thee
WARWICK: And do some service to Duke Humphrey's ghost.
NARRATOR: Exeunt SUFFOLK and WARWICK
KING HENRY VI: What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted!
KING HENRY VI: Thrice is he armed that hath his quarrel just,
KING HENRY VI: And he but naked, though lock'd up in steel
KING HENRY VI: Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.
NARRATOR: A noise within
QUEEN MARGARET: What noise is this?
NARRATOR: Re-enter SUFFOLK and WARWICK, with their weapons drawn
KING HENRY VI: Why, how now, lords! your wrathful weapons drawn
KING HENRY VI: Here in our presence! dare you be so bold?
KING HENRY VI: Why, what tumultuous clamour have we here?
SUFFOLK: The traitorous Warwick with the men of Bury
SUFFOLK: Set all upon me, mighty sovereign.
SALISBURY: [To the Commons, entering]  Sirs, stand apart,
SALISBURY: the king shall know your mind.
SALISBURY: Dread lord, the commons send you word by me,
SALISBURY: Unless Lord Suffolk straight be done to death,
SALISBURY: Or banished fair England's territories,
SALISBURY: They will by violence tear him from your palace
SALISBURY: And torture him with grievous lingering death.
SALISBURY: They say, by him the good Duke Humphrey died,
SALISBURY: They say, in him they fear your highness' death,
SALISBURY: And mere instinct of love and loyalty,
SALISBURY: Free from a stubborn opposite intent,
SALISBURY: As being thought to contradict your liking,
SALISBURY: Makes them thus forward in his banishment.
SALISBURY: They say, in care of your most royal person,
SALISBURY: That if your highness should intend to sleep
SALISBURY: And charge that no man should disturb your rest
SALISBURY: In pain of your dislike or pain of death,
SALISBURY: Yet, notwithstanding such a strait edict,
SALISBURY: Were there a serpent seen, with forked tongue,
SALISBURY: That slily glided towards your majesty,
SALISBURY: It were but necessary you were waked,
SALISBURY: Lest, being suffer'd in that harmful slumber,
SALISBURY: The mortal worm might make the sleep eternal,
SALISBURY: And therefore do they cry, though you forbid,
SALISBURY: That they will guard you, whether you will or no,
SALISBURY: From such fell serpents as false Suffolk is,
SALISBURY: With whose envenomed and fatal sting,
SALISBURY: Your loving uncle, twenty times his worth,
SALISBURY: They say, is shamefully bereft of life.
Commons: [Within]  An answer from the king, my
Commons: Lord of Salisbury!
SUFFOLK: 'Tis like the commons, rude unpolish'd hinds,
SUFFOLK: Could send such message to their sovereign:
SUFFOLK: But you, my lord, were glad to be employ'd,
SUFFOLK: To show how quaint an orator you are:
SUFFOLK: But all the honour Salisbury hath won
SUFFOLK: Is, that he was the lord ambassador
SUFFOLK: Sent from a sort of tinkers to the king.
Commons: [Within]  An answer from the king, or we will all break in!
KING HENRY VI: Go, Salisbury, and tell them all from me.
KING HENRY VI: I thank them for their tender loving care,
KING HENRY VI: And had I not been cited so by them,
KING HENRY VI: Yet did I purpose as they do entreat,
KING HENRY VI: For, sure, my thoughts do hourly prophesy
KING HENRY VI: Mischance unto my state by Suffolk's means:
KING HENRY VI: And therefore, by His majesty I swear,
KING HENRY VI: Whose far unworthy deputy I am,
KING HENRY VI: He shall not breathe infection in this air
KING HENRY VI: But three days longer, on the pain of death.
NARRATOR: Exit SALISBURY
QUEEN MARGARET: O Henry, let me plead for gentle Suffolk!
KING HENRY VI: Ungentle queen, to call him gentle Suffolk!
KING HENRY VI: No more, I say: if thou dost plead for him,
KING HENRY VI: Thou wilt but add increase unto my wrath.
KING HENRY VI: Had I but said, I would have kept my word,
KING HENRY VI: But when I swear, it is irrevocable.
KING HENRY VI: If, after three days' space, thou here be'st found
KING HENRY VI: On any ground that I am ruler of,
KING HENRY VI: The world shall not be ransom for thy life.
KING HENRY VI: Come, Warwick, come, good Warwick, go with me,
KING HENRY VI: I have great matters to impart to thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but QUEEN MARGARET and SUFFOLK
QUEEN MARGARET: Mischance and sorrow go along with you!
QUEEN MARGARET: Heart's discontent and sour affliction
QUEEN MARGARET: Be playfellows to keep you company!
QUEEN MARGARET: There's two of you, the devil make a third!
QUEEN MARGARET: And threefold vengeance tend upon your steps!
SUFFOLK: Cease, gentle queen, these execrations,
SUFFOLK: And let thy Suffolk take his heavy leave.
QUEEN MARGARET: Fie, coward woman and soft-hearted wretch!
QUEEN MARGARET: Hast thou not spirit to curse thine enemy?
SUFFOLK: A plague upon them! wherefore should I curse them?
SUFFOLK: Would curses kill, as doth the mandrake's groan,
SUFFOLK: I would invent as bitter-searching terms,
SUFFOLK: As curst, as harsh and horrible to hear,
SUFFOLK: Deliver'd strongly through my fixed teeth,
SUFFOLK: With full as many signs of deadly hate,
SUFFOLK: As lean-faced Envy in her loathsome cave:
SUFFOLK: My tongue should stumble in mine earnest words,
SUFFOLK: Mine eyes should sparkle like the beaten flint,
SUFFOLK: Mine hair be fixed on end, as one distract,
SUFFOLK: Ay, every joint should seem to curse and ban:
SUFFOLK: And even now my burthen'd heart would break,
SUFFOLK: Should I not curse them. Poison be their drink!
SUFFOLK: Gall, worse than gall, the daintiest that they taste!
SUFFOLK: Their sweetest shade a grove of cypress trees!
SUFFOLK: Their chiefest prospect murdering basilisks!
SUFFOLK: Their softest touch as smart as lizards' sting!
SUFFOLK: Their music frightful as the serpent's hiss,
SUFFOLK: And boding screech-owls make the concert full!
SUFFOLK: All the foul terrors in dark-seated hell--
QUEEN MARGARET: Enough, sweet Suffolk, thou torment'st thyself,
QUEEN MARGARET: And these dread curses, like the sun 'gainst glass,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or like an overcharged gun, recoil,
QUEEN MARGARET: And turn the force of them upon thyself.
SUFFOLK: You bade me ban, and will you bid me leave?
SUFFOLK: Now, by the ground that I am banish'd from,
SUFFOLK: Well could I curse away a winter's night,
SUFFOLK: Though standing naked on a mountain top,
SUFFOLK: Where biting cold would never let grass grow,
SUFFOLK: And think it but a minute spent in sport.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, let me entreat thee cease. Give me thy hand,
QUEEN MARGARET: That I may dew it with my mournful tears,
QUEEN MARGARET: Nor let the rain of heaven wet this place,
QUEEN MARGARET: To wash away my woful monuments.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, could this kiss be printed in thy hand,
QUEEN MARGARET: That thou mightst think upon these by the seal,
QUEEN MARGARET: Through whom a thousand sighs are breathed for thee!
QUEEN MARGARET: So, get thee gone, that I may know my grief,
QUEEN MARGARET: 'Tis but surmised whiles thou art standing by,
QUEEN MARGARET: As one that surfeits thinking on a want.
QUEEN MARGARET: I will repeal thee, or, be well assured,
QUEEN MARGARET: Adventure to be banished myself:
QUEEN MARGARET: And banished I am, if but from thee.
QUEEN MARGARET: Go, speak not to me, even now be gone.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, go not yet! Even thus two friends condemn'd
QUEEN MARGARET: Embrace and kiss and take ten thousand leaves,
QUEEN MARGARET: Loather a hundred times to part than die.
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet now farewell, and farewell life with thee!
SUFFOLK: Thus is poor Suffolk ten times banished,
SUFFOLK: Once by the king, and three times thrice by thee.
SUFFOLK: 'Tis not the land I care for, wert thou thence,
SUFFOLK: A wilderness is populous enough,
SUFFOLK: So Suffolk had thy heavenly company:
SUFFOLK: For where thou art, there is the world itself,
SUFFOLK: With every several pleasure in the world,
SUFFOLK: And where thou art not, desolation.
SUFFOLK: I can no more: live thou to joy thy life,
SUFFOLK: Myself no joy in nought but that thou livest.
NARRATOR: Enter VAUX
QUEEN MARGARET: Wither goes Vaux so fast? what news, I prithee?
VAUX: To signify unto his majesty
VAUX: That Cardinal Beaufort is at point of death,
VAUX: For suddenly a grievous sickness took him,
VAUX: That makes him gasp and stare and catch the air,
VAUX: Blaspheming God and cursing men on earth.
VAUX: Sometimes he talks as if Duke Humphrey's ghost
VAUX: Were by his side, sometime he calls the king,
VAUX: And whispers to his pillow, as to him,
VAUX: The secrets of his overcharged soul,
VAUX: And I am sent to tell his majesty
VAUX: That even now he cries aloud for him.
QUEEN MARGARET: Go tell this heavy message to the king.
NARRATOR: Exit VAUX
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay me! what is this world! what news are these!
QUEEN MARGARET: But wherefore grieve I at an hour's poor loss,
QUEEN MARGARET: Omitting Suffolk's exile, my soul's treasure?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why only, Suffolk, mourn I not for thee,
QUEEN MARGARET: And with the southern clouds contend in tears,
QUEEN MARGARET: Theirs for the earth's increase, mine for my sorrows?
QUEEN MARGARET: Now get thee hence: the king, thou know'st, is coming,
QUEEN MARGARET: If thou be found by me, thou art but dead.
SUFFOLK: If I depart from thee, I cannot live,
SUFFOLK: And in thy sight to die, what were it else
SUFFOLK: But like a pleasant slumber in thy lap?
SUFFOLK: Here could I breathe my soul into the air,
SUFFOLK: As mild and gentle as the cradle-babe
SUFFOLK: Dying with mother's dug between its lips:
SUFFOLK: Where, from thy sight, I should be raging mad,
SUFFOLK: And cry out for thee to close up mine eyes,
SUFFOLK: To have thee with thy lips to stop my mouth,
SUFFOLK: So shouldst thou either turn my flying soul,
SUFFOLK: Or I should breathe it so into thy body,
SUFFOLK: And then it lived in sweet Elysium.
SUFFOLK: To die by thee were but to die in jest,
SUFFOLK: From thee to die were torture more than death:
SUFFOLK: O, let me stay, befall what may befall!
QUEEN MARGARET: Away! though parting be a fretful corrosive,
QUEEN MARGARET: It is applied to a deathful wound.
QUEEN MARGARET: To France, sweet Suffolk: let me hear from thee,
QUEEN MARGARET: For wheresoe'er thou art in this world's globe,
QUEEN MARGARET: I'll have an Iris that shall find thee out.
SUFFOLK: I go.
QUEEN MARGARET: And take my heart with thee.
SUFFOLK: A jewel, lock'd into the wofull'st cask
SUFFOLK: That ever did contain a thing of worth.
SUFFOLK: Even as a splitted bark, so sunder we
SUFFOLK: This way fall I to death.
QUEEN MARGARET: This way for me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A bedchamber.
NARRATOR: Enter the KING, SALISBURY, WARWICK, to the CARDINAL in bed
KING HENRY VI: How fares my lord? speak, Beaufort, to
KING HENRY VI: thy sovereign.
CARDINAL: If thou be'st death, I'll give thee England's treasure,
CARDINAL: Enough to purchase such another island,
CARDINAL: So thou wilt let me live, and feel no pain.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, what a sign it is of evil life,
KING HENRY VI: Where death's approach is seen so terrible!
WARWICK: Beaufort, it is thy sovereign speaks to thee.
CARDINAL: Bring me unto my trial when you will.
CARDINAL: Died he not in his bed? where should he die?
CARDINAL: Can I make men live, whether they will or no?
CARDINAL: O, torture me no more! I will confess.
CARDINAL: Alive again? then show me where he is:
CARDINAL: I'll give a thousand pound to look upon him.
CARDINAL: He hath no eyes, the dust hath blinded them.
CARDINAL: Comb down his hair, look, look! it stands upright,
CARDINAL: Like lime-twigs set to catch my winged soul.
CARDINAL: Give me some drink, and bid the apothecary
CARDINAL: Bring the strong poison that I bought of him.
KING HENRY VI: O thou eternal Mover of the heavens.
KING HENRY VI: Look with a gentle eye upon this wretch!
KING HENRY VI: O, beat away the busy meddling fiend
KING HENRY VI: That lays strong siege unto this wretch's soul.
KING HENRY VI: And from his bosom purge this black despair!
WARWICK: See, how the pangs of death do make him grin!
SALISBURY: Disturb him not, let him pass peaceably.
KING HENRY VI: Peace to his soul, if God's good pleasure be!
KING HENRY VI: Lord cardinal, if thou think'st on heaven's bliss,
KING HENRY VI: Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope.
KING HENRY VI: He dies, and makes no sign. O God, forgive him!
WARWICK: So bad a death argues a monstrous life.
KING HENRY VI: Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all.
KING HENRY VI: Close up his eyes and draw the curtain close,
KING HENRY VI: And let us all to meditation.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The coast of Kent.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Fight at sea. Ordnance goes off. Enter a  Captain, a Master, a Master's-mate, WALTER WHITMORE, and others, with them SUFFOLK, and others, prisoners
Captain: The gaudy, blabbing and remorseful day
Captain: Is crept into the bosom of the sea,
Captain: And now loud-howling wolves arouse the jades
Captain: That drag the tragic melancholy night,
Captain: Who, with their drowsy, slow and flagging wings,
Captain: Clip dead men's graves and from their misty jaws
Captain: Breathe foul contagious darkness in the air.
Captain: Therefore bring forth the soldiers of our prize,
Captain: For, whilst our pinnace anchors in the Downs,
Captain: Here shall they make their ransom on the sand,
Captain: Or with their blood stain this discolour'd shore.
Captain: Master, this prisoner freely give I thee,
Captain: And thou that art his mate, make boot of this,
Captain: The other, Walter Whitmore, is thy share.
First Gentleman: What is my ransom, master? let me know.
Master: A thousand crowns, or else lay down your head.
Master: Master's-Mate	And so much shall you give, or off goes yours.
Captain: What, think you much to pay two thousand crowns,
Captain: And bear the name and port of gentlemen?
Captain: Cut both the villains' throats, for die you shall:
Captain: The lives of those which we have lost in fight
Captain: Be counterpoised with such a petty sum!
First Gentleman: I'll give it, sir, and therefore spare my life.
Second Gentleman: And so will I and write home for it straight.
WHITMORE: I lost mine eye in laying the prize aboard,
WHITMORE: And therefore to revenge it, shalt thou die,
NARRATOR: To SUFFOLK
WHITMORE: And so should these, if I might have my will.
Captain: Be not so rash, take ransom, let him live.
SUFFOLK: Look on my George, I am a gentleman:
SUFFOLK: Rate me at what thou wilt, thou shalt be paid.
WHITMORE: And so am I, my name is Walter Whitmore.
WHITMORE: How now! why start'st thou? what, doth
WHITMORE: death affright?
SUFFOLK: Thy name affrights me, in whose sound is death.
SUFFOLK: A cunning man did calculate my birth
SUFFOLK: And told me that by water I should die:
SUFFOLK: Yet let not this make thee be bloody-minded,
SUFFOLK: Thy name is Gaultier, being rightly sounded.
WHITMORE: Gaultier or Walter, which it is, I care not:
WHITMORE: Never yet did base dishonour blur our name,
WHITMORE: But with our sword we wiped away the blot,
WHITMORE: Therefore, when merchant-like I sell revenge,
WHITMORE: Broke be my sword, my arms torn and defaced,
WHITMORE: And I proclaim'd a coward through the world!
SUFFOLK: Stay, Whitmore, for thy prisoner is a prince,
SUFFOLK: The Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.
WHITMORE: The Duke of Suffolk muffled up in rags!
SUFFOLK: Ay, but these rags are no part of the duke:
SUFFOLK: Jove sometimes went disguised, and why not I?
Captain: But Jove was never slain, as thou shalt be.
SUFFOLK: Obscure and lowly swain, King Henry's blood,
SUFFOLK: The honourable blood of Lancaster,
SUFFOLK: Must not be shed by such a jaded groom.
SUFFOLK: Hast thou not kiss'd thy hand and held my stirrup?
SUFFOLK: Bare-headed plodded by my foot-cloth mule
SUFFOLK: And thought thee happy when I shook my head?
SUFFOLK: How often hast thou waited at my cup,
SUFFOLK: Fed from my trencher, kneel'd down at the board.
SUFFOLK: When I have feasted with Queen Margaret?
SUFFOLK: Remember it and let it make thee crest-fall'n,
SUFFOLK: Ay, and allay this thy abortive pride,
SUFFOLK: How in our voiding lobby hast thou stood
SUFFOLK: And duly waited for my coming forth?
SUFFOLK: This hand of mine hath writ in thy behalf,
SUFFOLK: And therefore shall it charm thy riotous tongue.
WHITMORE: Speak, captain, shall I stab the forlorn swain?
Captain: First let my words stab him, as he hath me.
SUFFOLK: Base slave, thy words are blunt and so art thou.
Captain: Convey him hence and on our longboat's side
Captain: Strike off his head.
SUFFOLK: Thou darest not, for thy own.
Captain: Yes, Pole.
SUFFOLK: Pole!
Captain: Pool! Sir Pool! lord!
Captain: Ay, kennel, puddle, sink, whose filth and dirt
Captain: Troubles the silver spring where England drinks.
Captain: Now will I dam up this thy yawning mouth
Captain: For swallowing the treasure of the realm:
Captain: Thy lips that kiss'd the queen shall sweep the ground,
Captain: And thou that smiledst at good Duke Humphrey's death,
Captain: Against the senseless winds shalt grin in vain,
Captain: Who in contempt shall hiss at thee again:
Captain: And wedded be thou to the hags of hell,
Captain: For daring to affy a mighty lord
Captain: Unto the daughter of a worthless king,
Captain: Having neither subject, wealth, nor diadem.
Captain: By devilish policy art thou grown great,
Captain: And, like ambitious Sylla, overgorged
Captain: With gobbets of thy mother's bleeding heart.
Captain: By thee Anjou and Maine were sold to France,
Captain: The false revolting Normans thorough thee
Captain: Disdain to call us lord, and Picardy
Captain: Hath slain their governors, surprised our forts,
Captain: And sent the ragged soldiers wounded home.
Captain: The princely Warwick, and the Nevils all,
Captain: Whose dreadful swords were never drawn in vain,
Captain: As hating thee, are rising up in arms:
Captain: And now the house of York, thrust from the crown
Captain: By shameful murder of a guiltless king
Captain: And lofty proud encroaching tyranny,
Captain: Burns with revenging fire, whose hopeful colours
Captain: Advance our half-faced sun, striving to shine,
Captain: Under the which is writ 'Invitis nubibus.'
Captain: The commons here in Kent are up in arms:
Captain: And, to conclude, reproach and beggary
Captain: Is crept into the palace of our king.
Captain: And all by thee. Away! convey him hence.
SUFFOLK: O that I were a god, to shoot forth thunder
SUFFOLK: Upon these paltry, servile, abject drudges!
SUFFOLK: Small things make base men proud: this villain here,
SUFFOLK: Being captain of a pinnace, threatens more
SUFFOLK: Than Bargulus the strong Illyrian pirate.
SUFFOLK: Drones suck not eagles' blood but rob beehives:
SUFFOLK: It is impossible that I should die
SUFFOLK: By such a lowly vassal as thyself.
SUFFOLK: Thy words move rage and not remorse in me:
SUFFOLK: I go of message from the queen to France,
SUFFOLK: I charge thee waft me safely cross the Channel.
Captain: Walter,--
WHITMORE: Come, Suffolk, I must waft thee to thy death.
SUFFOLK: Gelidus timor occupat artus it is thee I fear.
WHITMORE: Thou shalt have cause to fear before I leave thee.
WHITMORE: What, are ye daunted now? now will ye stoop?
First Gentleman: My gracious lord, entreat him, speak him fair.
SUFFOLK: Suffolk's imperial tongue is stern and rough,
SUFFOLK: Used to command, untaught to plead for favour.
SUFFOLK: Far be it we should honour such as these
SUFFOLK: With humble suit: no, rather let my head
SUFFOLK: Stoop to the block than these knees bow to any
SUFFOLK: Save to the God of heaven and to my king,
SUFFOLK: And sooner dance upon a bloody pole
SUFFOLK: Than stand uncover'd to the vulgar groom.
SUFFOLK: True nobility is exempt from fear:
SUFFOLK: More can I bear than you dare execute.
Captain: Hale him away, and let him talk no more.
SUFFOLK: Come, soldiers, show what cruelty ye can,
SUFFOLK: That this my death may never be forgot!
SUFFOLK: Great men oft die by vile bezonians:
SUFFOLK: A Roman sworder and banditto slave
SUFFOLK: Murder'd sweet Tully, Brutus' bastard hand
SUFFOLK: Stabb'd Julius Caesar, savage islanders
SUFFOLK: Pompey the Great, and Suffolk dies by pirates.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Whitmore and others with Suffolk
Captain: And as for these whose ransom we have set,
Captain: It is our pleasure one of them depart,
Captain: Therefore come you with us and let him go.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but the First Gentleman
NARRATOR: Re-enter WHITMORE with SUFFOLK's body
WHITMORE: There let his head and lifeless body lie,
WHITMORE: Until the queen his mistress bury it.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Gentleman: O barbarous and bloody spectacle!
First Gentleman: His body will I bear unto the king:
First Gentleman: If he revenge it not, yet will his friends,
First Gentleman: So will the queen, that living held him dear.
NARRATOR: Exit with the body
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Blackheath.
NARRATOR: Enter GEORGE BEVIS and JOHN HOLLAND
BEVIS: Come, and get thee a sword, though made of a lath,
BEVIS: they have been up these two days.
HOLLAND: They have the more need to sleep now, then.
BEVIS: I tell thee, Jack Cade the clothier means to dress
BEVIS: the commonwealth, and turn it, and set a new nap upon it.
HOLLAND: So he had need, for 'tis threadbare. Well, I say it
HOLLAND: was never merry world in England since gentlemen came up.
BEVIS: O miserable age! virtue is not regarded in handicrafts-men.
HOLLAND: The nobility think scorn to go in leather aprons.
BEVIS: Nay, more, the king's council are no good workmen.
HOLLAND: True, and yet it is said, labour in thy vocation,
HOLLAND: which is as much to say as, let the magistrates be
HOLLAND: labouring men, and therefore should we be
HOLLAND: magistrates.
BEVIS: Thou hast hit it, for there's no better sign of a
BEVIS: brave mind than a hard hand.
HOLLAND: I see them! I see them! there's Best's son, the
HOLLAND: tanner of Wingham,--
BEVIS: He shall have the skin of our enemies, to make
BEVIS: dog's-leather of.
HOLLAND: And Dick the Butcher,--
BEVIS: Then is sin struck down like an ox, and iniquity's
BEVIS: throat cut like a calf.
HOLLAND: And Smith the weaver,--
BEVIS: Argo, their thread of life is spun.
HOLLAND: Come, come, let's fall in with them.
NARRATOR: Drum. Enter CADE, DICK the Butcher, SMITH the Weaver, and a Sawyer, with infinite numbers
CADE: We John Cade, so termed of our supposed father,--
DICK: [Aside]  Or rather, of stealing a cade of herrings.
CADE: For our enemies shall fall before us, inspired with
CADE: the spirit of putting down kings and princes,
CADE: --Command silence.
DICK: Silence!
CADE: My father was a Mortimer,--
DICK: [Aside]  He was an honest man, and a good
DICK: bricklayer.
CADE: My mother a Plantagenet,--
DICK: [Aside]  I knew her well, she was a midwife.
CADE: My wife descended of the Lacies,--
DICK: [Aside]  She was, indeed, a pedler's daughter, and
DICK: sold many laces.
SMITH: [Aside]  But now of late, notable to travel with her
SMITH: furred pack, she washes bucks here at home.
CADE: Therefore am I of an honourable house.
DICK: [Aside]  Ay, by my faith, the field is honourable,
DICK: and there was he borne, under a hedge, for his
DICK: father had never a house but the cage.
CADE: Valiant I am.
SMITH: [Aside]  A' must needs, for beggary is valiant.
CADE: I am able to endure much.
DICK: [Aside]  No question of that, for I have seen him
DICK: whipped three market-days together.
CADE: I fear neither sword nor fire.
SMITH: [Aside]  He need not fear the sword, for his coat is of proof.
DICK: [Aside]  But methinks he should stand in fear of
DICK: fire, being burnt i' the hand for stealing of sheep.
CADE: Be brave, then, for your captain is brave, and vows
CADE: reformation. There shall be in England seven
CADE: halfpenny loaves sold for a penny: the three-hooped
CADE: pot, shall have ten hoops and I will make it felony
CADE: to drink small beer: all the realm shall be in
CADE: common, and in Cheapside shall my palfrey go to
CADE: grass: and when I am king, as king I will be,--
ALL: God save your majesty!
CADE: I thank you, good people: there shall be no money,
CADE: all shall eat and drink on my score, and I will
CADE: apparel them all in one livery, that they may agree
CADE: like brothers and worship me their lord.
DICK: The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers.
CADE: Nay, that I mean to do. Is not this a lamentable
CADE: thing, that of the skin of an innocent lamb should
CADE: be made parchment? that parchment, being scribbled
CADE: o'er, should undo a man? Some say the bee stings:
CADE: but I say, 'tis the bee's wax, for I did but seal
CADE: once to a thing, and I was never mine own man
CADE: since. How now! who's there?
NARRATOR: Enter some, bringing forward the Clerk of Chatham
SMITH: The clerk of Chatham: he can write and read and
SMITH: cast accompt.
CADE: O monstrous!
SMITH: We took him setting of boys' copies.
CADE: Here's a villain!
SMITH: Has a book in his pocket with red letters in't.
CADE: Nay, then, he is a conjurer.
DICK: Nay, he can make obligations, and write court-hand.
CADE: I am sorry for't: the man is a proper man, of mine
CADE: honour, unless I find him guilty, he shall not die.
CADE: Come hither, sirrah, I must examine thee: what is thy name?
Clerk: Emmanuel.
DICK: They use to write it on the top of letters: 'twill
DICK: go hard with you.
CADE: Let me alone. Dost thou use to write thy name? or
CADE: hast thou a mark to thyself, like an honest
CADE: plain-dealing man?
CLERK: Sir, I thank God, I have been so well brought up
CLERK: that I can write my name.
ALL: He hath confessed: away with him! he's a villain
ALL: and a traitor.
CADE: Away with him, I say! hang him with his pen and
CADE: ink-horn about his neck.
NARRATOR: Exit one with the Clerk
NARRATOR: Enter MICHAEL
MICHAEL: Where's our general?
CADE: Here I am, thou particular fellow.
MICHAEL: Fly, fly, fly! Sir Humphrey Stafford and his
MICHAEL: brother are hard by, with the king's forces.
CADE: Stand, villain, stand, or I'll fell thee down. He
CADE: shall be encountered with a man as good as himself:
CADE: he is but a knight, is a'?
MICHAEL: No.
CADE: To equal him, I will make myself a knight presently.
NARRATOR: Kneels
CADE: Rise up Sir John Mortimer.
NARRATOR: Rises
CADE: Now have at him!
NARRATOR: Enter SIR HUMPHREY and WILLIAM STAFFORD, with drum and soldiers
SIR HUMPHREY: Rebellious hinds, the filth and scum of Kent,
SIR HUMPHREY: Mark'd for the gallows, lay your weapons down,
SIR HUMPHREY: Home to your cottages, forsake this groom:
SIR HUMPHREY: The king is merciful, if you revolt.
WILLIAM STAFFORD: But angry, wrathful, and inclined to blood,
WILLIAM STAFFORD: If you go forward, therefore yield, or die.
CADE: As for these silken-coated slaves, I pass not:
CADE: It is to you, good people, that I speak,
CADE: Over whom, in time to come, I hope to reign,
CADE: For I am rightful heir unto the crown.
SIR HUMPHREY: Villain, thy father was a plasterer,
SIR HUMPHREY: And thou thyself a shearman, art thou not?
CADE: And Adam was a gardener.
WILLIAM STAFFORD: And what of that?
CADE: Marry, this: Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March.
CADE: Married the Duke of Clarence' daughter, did he not?
SIR HUMPHREY: Ay, sir.
CADE: By her he had two children at one birth.
WILLIAM STAFFORD: That's false.
CADE: Ay, there's the question, but I say, 'tis true:
CADE: The elder of them, being put to nurse,
CADE: Was by a beggar-woman stolen away,
CADE: And, ignorant of his birth and parentage,
CADE: Became a bricklayer when he came to age:
CADE: His son am I, deny it, if you can.
DICK: Nay, 'tis too true, therefore he shall be king.
SMITH: Sir, he made a chimney in my father's house, and
SMITH: the bricks are alive at this day to testify it,
SMITH: therefore deny it not.
SIR HUMPHREY: And will you credit this base drudge's words,
SIR HUMPHREY: That speaks he knows not what?
ALL: Ay, marry, will we, therefore get ye gone.
WILLIAM STAFFORD: Jack Cade, the Duke of York hath taught you this.
CADE: [Aside]  He lies, for I invented it myself.
CADE: Go to, sirrah, tell the king from me, that, for his
CADE: father's sake, Henry the Fifth, in whose time boys
CADE: went to span-counter for French crowns, I am content
CADE: he shall reign, but I'll be protector over him.
DICK: And furthermore, well have the Lord Say's head for
DICK: selling the dukedom of Maine.
CADE: And good reason, for thereby is England mained, and
CADE: fain to go with a staff, but that my puissance holds
CADE: it up. Fellow kings, I tell you that that Lord Say
CADE: hath gelded the commonwealth, and made it an eunuch:
CADE: and more than that, he can speak French, and
CADE: therefore he is a traitor.
SIR HUMPHREY: O gross and miserable ignorance!
CADE: Nay, answer, if you can: the Frenchmen are our
CADE: enemies, go to, then, I ask but this: can he that
CADE: speaks with the tongue of an enemy be a good
CADE: counsellor, or no?
ALL: No, no, and therefore we'll have his head.
WILLIAM STAFFORD: Well, seeing gentle words will not prevail,
WILLIAM STAFFORD: Assail them with the army of the king.
SIR HUMPHREY: Herald, away, and throughout every town
SIR HUMPHREY: Proclaim them traitors that are up with Cade,
SIR HUMPHREY: That those which fly before the battle ends
SIR HUMPHREY: May, even in their wives' and children's sight,
SIR HUMPHREY: Be hang'd up for example at their doors:
SIR HUMPHREY: And you that be the king's friends, follow me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt WILLIAM STAFFORD and SIR HUMPHREY, and soldiers
CADE: And you that love the commons, follow me.
CADE: Now show yourselves men, 'tis for liberty.
CADE: We will not leave one lord, one gentleman:
CADE: Spare none but such as go in clouted shoon,
CADE: For they are thrifty honest men, and such
CADE: As would, but that they dare not, take our parts.
DICK: They are all in order and march toward us.
CADE: But then are we in order when we are most
CADE: out of order. Come, march forward.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Another part of Blackheath.
NARRATOR: Alarums to the fight, wherein SIR HUMPHREY and WILLIAM STAFFORD are slain. Enter CADE and the rest
CADE: Where's Dick, the butcher of Ashford?
DICK: Here, sir.
CADE: They fell before thee like sheep and oxen, and thou
CADE: behavedst thyself as if thou hadst been in thine own
CADE: slaughter-house: therefore thus will I reward thee,
CADE: the Lent shall be as long again as it is, and thou
CADE: shalt have a licence to kill for a hundred lacking
CADE: one.
DICK: I desire no more.
CADE: And, to speak truth, thou deservest no less. This
CADE: monument of the victory will I bear,
NARRATOR: Putting on SIR HUMPHREY'S brigandine
CADE: and the bodies shall be dragged at my horse' heels
CADE: till I do come to London, where we will have the
CADE: mayor's sword borne before us.
DICK: If we mean to thrive and do good, break open the
DICK: gaols and let out the prisoners.
CADE: Fear not that, I warrant thee. Come, let's march
CADE: towards London.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI with a supplication, and the QUEEN with SUFFOLK'S head, BUCKINGHAM and Lord SAY
QUEEN MARGARET: Oft have I heard that grief softens the mind,
QUEEN MARGARET: And makes it fearful and degenerate,
QUEEN MARGARET: Think therefore on revenge and cease to weep.
QUEEN MARGARET: But who can cease to weep and look on this?
QUEEN MARGARET: Here may his head lie on my throbbing breast:
QUEEN MARGARET: But where's the body that I should embrace?
BUCKINGHAM: What answer makes your grace to the rebels'
BUCKINGHAM: supplication?
KING HENRY VI: I'll send some holy bishop to entreat,
KING HENRY VI: For God forbid so many simple souls
KING HENRY VI: Should perish by the sword! And I myself,
KING HENRY VI: Rather than bloody war shall cut them short,
KING HENRY VI: Will parley with Jack Cade their general:
KING HENRY VI: But stay, I'll read it over once again.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, barbarous villains! hath this lovely face
QUEEN MARGARET: Ruled, like a wandering planet, over me,
QUEEN MARGARET: And could it not enforce them to relent,
QUEEN MARGARET: That were unworthy to behold the same?
KING HENRY VI: Lord Say, Jack Cade hath sworn to have thy head.
SAY: Ay, but I hope your highness shall have his.
KING HENRY VI: How now, madam!
KING HENRY VI: Still lamenting and mourning for Suffolk's death?
KING HENRY VI: I fear me, love, if that I had been dead,
KING HENRY VI: Thou wouldst not have mourn'd so much for me.
QUEEN MARGARET: No, my love, I should not mourn, but die for thee.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
KING HENRY VI: How now! what news? why comest thou in such haste?
Messenger: The rebels are in Southwark, fly, my lord!
Messenger: Jack Cade proclaims himself Lord Mortimer,
Messenger: Descended from the Duke of Clarence' house,
Messenger: And calls your grace usurper openly
Messenger: And vows to crown himself in Westminster.
Messenger: His army is a ragged multitude
Messenger: Of hinds and peasants, rude and merciless:
Messenger: Sir Humphrey Stafford and h is brother's death
Messenger: Hath given them heart and courage to proceed:
Messenger: All scholars, lawyers, courtiers, gentlemen,
Messenger: They call false caterpillars, and intend their death.
KING HENRY VI: O graceless men! they know not what they do.
BUCKINGHAM: My gracious lord, return to Killingworth,
BUCKINGHAM: Until a power be raised to put them down.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, were the Duke of Suffolk now alive,
QUEEN MARGARET: These Kentish rebels would be soon appeased!
KING HENRY VI: Lord Say, the traitors hate thee,
KING HENRY VI: Therefore away with us to Killingworth.
SAY: So might your grace's person be in danger.
SAY: The sight of me is odious in their eyes,
SAY: And therefore in this city will I stay
SAY: And live alone as secret as I may.
NARRATOR: Enter another Messenger
Messenger: Jack Cade hath gotten London bridge:
Messenger: The citizens fly and forsake their houses:
Messenger: The rascal people, thirsting after prey,
Messenger: Join with the traitor, and they jointly swear
Messenger: To spoil the city and your royal court.
BUCKINGHAM: Then linger not, my lord, away, take horse.
KING HENRY VI: Come, Margaret, God, our hope, will succor us.
QUEEN MARGARET: My hope is gone, now Suffolk is deceased.
KING HENRY VI: Farewell, my lord: trust not the Kentish rebels.
BUCKINGHAM: Trust nobody, for fear you be betray'd.
SAY: The trust I have is in mine innocence,
SAY: And therefore am I bold and resolute.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. London. The Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter SCALES upon the Tower, walking. Then enter two or three Citizens below
SCALES: How now! is Jack Cade slain?
First Citizen: No, my lord, nor likely to be slain, for they have
First Citizen: won the bridge, killing all those that withstand
First Citizen: them: the lord mayor craves aid of your honour from
First Citizen: the Tower, to defend the city from the rebels.
SCALES: Such aid as I can spare you shall command,
SCALES: But I am troubled here with them myself,
SCALES: The rebels have assay'd to win the Tower.
SCALES: But get you to Smithfield, and gather head,
SCALES: And thither I will send you Matthew Goffe,
SCALES: Fight for your king, your country and your lives,
SCALES: And so, farewell, for I must hence again.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. London. Cannon Street.
NARRATOR: Enter CADE and the rest, and strikes his staff on London-stone
CADE: Now is Mortimer lord of this city. And here, sitting
CADE: upon London-stone, I charge and command that, of the
CADE: city's cost, the pissing-conduit run nothing but
CADE: claret wine this first year of our reign. And now
CADE: henceforward it shall be treason for any that calls
CADE: me other than Lord Mortimer.
NARRATOR: Enter a Soldier, running
Soldier: Jack Cade! Jack Cade!
CADE: Knock him down there.
NARRATOR: They kill him
SMITH: If this fellow be wise, he'll never call ye Jack
SMITH: Cade more: I think he hath a very fair warning.
DICK: My lord, there's an army gathered together in
DICK: Smithfield.
CADE: Come, then, let's go fight with them, but first, go
CADE: and set London bridge on fire, and, if you can, burn
CADE: down the Tower too. Come, let's away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. London. Smithfield.
NARRATOR: Alarums. MATTHEW GOFFE is slain, and all the rest. Then enter CADE, with his company.
CADE: So, sirs: now go some and pull down the Savoy,
CADE: others to the inns of court, down with them all.
DICK: I have a suit unto your lordship.
CADE: Be it a lordship, thou shalt have it for that word.
DICK: Only that the laws of England may come out of your mouth.
HOLLAND: [Aside]  Mass, 'twill be sore law, then, for he was
HOLLAND: thrust in the mouth with a spear, and 'tis not whole
HOLLAND: yet.
SMITH: [Aside]  Nay, John, it will be stinking law for his
SMITH: breath stinks with eating toasted cheese.
CADE: I have thought upon it, it shall be so. Away, burn
CADE: all the records of the realm: my mouth shall be
CADE: the parliament of England.
HOLLAND: [Aside]  Then we are like to have biting statutes,
HOLLAND: unless his teeth be pulled out.
CADE: And henceforward all things shall be in common.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord, a prize, a prize! here's the Lord Say,
Messenger: which sold the towns in France, he that made us pay
Messenger: one and twenty fifteens, and one shilling to the
Messenger: pound, the last subsidy.
NARRATOR: Enter BEVIS, with Lord SAY
CADE: Well, he shall be beheaded for it ten times. Ah,
CADE: thou say, thou serge, nay, thou buckram lord! now
CADE: art thou within point-blank of our jurisdiction
CADE: regal. What canst thou answer to my majesty for
CADE: giving up of Normandy unto Mounsieur Basimecu, the
CADE: dauphin of France? Be it known unto thee by these
CADE: presence, even the presence of Lord Mortimer, that I
CADE: am the besom that must sweep the court clean of such
CADE: filth as thou art. Thou hast most traitorously
CADE: corrupted the youth of the realm in erecting a
CADE: grammar school, and whereas, before, our forefathers
CADE: had no other books but the score and the tally, thou
CADE: hast caused printing to be used, and, contrary to
CADE: the king, his crown and dignity, thou hast built a
CADE: paper-mill. It will be proved to thy face that thou
CADE: hast men about thee that usually talk of a noun and
CADE: a verb, and such abominable words as no Christian
CADE: ear can endure to hear. Thou hast appointed
CADE: justices of peace, to call poor men before them
CADE: about matters they were not able to answer.
CADE: Moreover, thou hast put them in prison, and because
CADE: they could not read, thou hast hanged them, when,
CADE: indeed, only for that cause they have been most
CADE: worthy to live. Thou dost ride in a foot-cloth, dost thou not?
SAY: What of that?
CADE: Marry, thou oughtest not to let thy horse wear a
CADE: cloak, when honester men than thou go in their hose
CADE: and doublets.
DICK: And work in their shirt too, as myself, for example,
DICK: that am a butcher.
SAY: You men of Kent,--
DICK: What say you of Kent?
SAY: Nothing but this, 'tis 'bona terra, mala gens.'
CADE: Away with him, away with him! he speaks Latin.
SAY: Hear me but speak, and bear me where you will.
SAY: Kent, in the Commentaries Caesar writ,
SAY: Is term'd the civil'st place of this isle:
SAY: Sweet is the country, because full of riches,
SAY: The people liberal, valiant, active, wealthy,
SAY: Which makes me hope you are not void of pity.
SAY: I sold not Maine, I lost not Normandy,
SAY: Yet, to recover them, would lose my life.
SAY: Justice with favour have I always done,
SAY: Prayers and tears have moved me, gifts could never.
SAY: When have I aught exacted at your hands,
SAY: But to maintain the king, the realm and you?
SAY: Large gifts have I bestow'd on learned clerks,
SAY: Because my book preferr'd me to the king,
SAY: And seeing ignorance is the curse of God,
SAY: Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven,
SAY: Unless you be possess'd with devilish spirits,
SAY: You cannot but forbear to murder me:
SAY: This tongue hath parley'd unto foreign kings
SAY: For your behoof,--
CADE: Tut, when struck'st thou one blow in the field?
SAY: Great men have reaching hands: oft have I struck
SAY: Those that I never saw and struck them dead.
BEVIS: O monstrous coward! what, to come behind folks?
SAY: These cheeks are pale for watching for your good.
CADE: Give him a box o' the ear and that will make 'em red again.
SAY: Long sitting to determine poor men's causes
SAY: Hath made me full of sickness and diseases.
CADE: Ye shall have a hempen caudle, then, and the help of hatchet.
DICK: Why dost thou quiver, man?
SAY: The palsy, and not fear, provokes me.
CADE: Nay, he nods at us, as who should say, I'll be even
CADE: with you: I'll see if his head will stand steadier
CADE: on a pole, or no. Take him away, and behead him.
SAY: Tell me wherein have I offended most?
SAY: Have I affected wealth or honour? speak.
SAY: Are my chests fill'd up with extorted gold?
SAY: Is my apparel sumptuous to behold?
SAY: Whom have I injured, that ye seek my death?
SAY: These hands are free from guiltless bloodshedding,
SAY: This breast from harbouring foul deceitful thoughts.
SAY: O, let me live!
CADE: [Aside]  I feel remorse in myself with his words,
CADE: but I'll bridle it: he shall die, an it be but for
CADE: pleading so well for his life. Away with him! he
CADE: has a familiar under his tongue, he speaks not o'
CADE: God's name. Go, take him away, I say, and strike
CADE: off his head presently, and then break into his
CADE: son-in-law's house, Sir James Cromer, and strike off
CADE: his head, and bring them both upon two poles hither.
ALL: It shall be done.
SAY: Ah, countrymen! if when you make your prayers,
SAY: God should be so obdurate as yourselves,
SAY: How would it fare with your departed souls?
SAY: And therefore yet relent, and save my life.
CADE: Away with him! and do as I command ye.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some with Lord SAY
CADE: The proudest peer in the realm shall not wear a head
CADE: on his shoulders, unless he pay me tribute, there
CADE: shall not a maid be married, but she shall pay to me
CADE: her maidenhead ere they have it: men shall hold of
CADE: me in capite, and we charge and command that their
CADE: wives be as free as heart can wish or tongue can tell.
DICK: My lord, when shall we go to Cheapside and take up
DICK: commodities upon our bills?
CADE: Marry, presently.
ALL: O, brave!
NARRATOR: Re-enter one with the heads
CADE: But is not this braver? Let them kiss one another,
CADE: for they loved well when they were alive. Now part
CADE: them again, lest they consult about the giving up of
CADE: some more towns in France. Soldiers, defer the
CADE: spoil of the city until night: for with these borne
CADE: before us, instead of maces, will we ride through
CADE: the streets, and at every corner have them kiss. Away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. Southwark.
NARRATOR: Alarum and retreat. Enter CADE and all his rabblement
CADE: Up Fish Street! down Saint Magnus' Corner! Kill
CADE: and knock down! throw them into Thames!
NARRATOR: Sound a parley
CADE: What noise is this I hear? Dare any be so bold to
CADE: sound retreat or parley, when I command them kill?
