NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM and CLIFFORD, attended
BUCKINGHAM: Ay, here they be that dare and will disturb thee:
BUCKINGHAM: Know, Cade, we come ambassadors from the king
BUCKINGHAM: Unto the commons whom thou hast misled,
BUCKINGHAM: And here pronounce free pardon to them all
BUCKINGHAM: That will forsake thee and go home in peace.
CLIFFORD: What say ye, countrymen? will ye relent,
CLIFFORD: And yield to mercy whilst 'tis offer'd you,
CLIFFORD: Or let a rebel lead you to your deaths?
CLIFFORD: Who loves the king and will embrace his pardon,
CLIFFORD: Fling up his cap, and say 'God save his majesty!'
CLIFFORD: Who hateth him and honours not his father,
CLIFFORD: Henry the Fifth, that made all France to quake,
CLIFFORD: Shake he his weapon at us and pass by.
ALL: God save the king! God save the king!
CADE: What, Buckingham and Clifford, are ye so brave? And
CADE: you, base peasants, do ye believe him? will you
CADE: needs be hanged with your pardons about your necks?
CADE: Hath my sword therefore broke through London gates,
CADE: that you should leave me at the White Hart in
CADE: Southwark? I thought ye would never have given out
CADE: these arms till you had recovered your ancient
CADE: freedom: but you are all recreants and dastards,
CADE: and delight to live in slavery to the nobility. Let
CADE: them break your backs with burthens, take your
CADE: houses over your heads, ravish your wives and
CADE: daughters before your faces: for me, I will make
CADE: shift for one, and so, God's curse light upon you
CADE: all!
ALL: We'll follow Cade, we'll follow Cade!
CLIFFORD: Is Cade the son of Henry the Fifth,
CLIFFORD: That thus you do exclaim you'll go with him?
CLIFFORD: Will he conduct you through the heart of France,
CLIFFORD: And make the meanest of you earls and dukes?
CLIFFORD: Alas, he hath no home, no place to fly to,
CLIFFORD: Nor knows he how to live but by the spoil,
CLIFFORD: Unless by robbing of your friends and us.
CLIFFORD: Were't not a shame, that whilst you live at jar,
CLIFFORD: The fearful French, whom you late vanquished,
CLIFFORD: Should make a start o'er seas and vanquish you?
CLIFFORD: Methinks already in this civil broil
CLIFFORD: I see them lording it in London streets,
CLIFFORD: Crying 'Villiago!' unto all they meet.
CLIFFORD: Better ten thousand base-born Cades miscarry
CLIFFORD: Than you should stoop unto a Frenchman's mercy.
CLIFFORD: To France, to France, and get what you have lost,
CLIFFORD: Spare England, for it is your native coast,
CLIFFORD: Henry hath money, you are strong and manly,
CLIFFORD: God on our side, doubt not of victory.
ALL: A Clifford! a Clifford! we'll follow the king and Clifford.
CADE: Was ever feather so lightly blown to and fro as this
CADE: multitude? The name of Henry the Fifth hales them
CADE: to an hundred mischiefs, and makes them leave me
CADE: desolate. I see them lay their heads together to
CADE: surprise me. My sword make way for me, for here is
CADE: no staying. In despite of the devils and hell, have
CADE: through the very middest of you? and heavens and
CADE: honour be witness, that no want of resolution in me.
CADE: but only my followers' base and ignominious
CADE: treasons, makes me betake me to my heels.
NARRATOR: Exit
BUCKINGHAM: What, is he fled? Go some, and follow him,
BUCKINGHAM: And he that brings his head unto the king
BUCKINGHAM: Shall have a thousand crowns for his reward.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some of them
BUCKINGHAM: Follow me, soldiers: we'll devise a mean
BUCKINGHAM: To reconcile you all unto the king.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. Kenilworth Castle.
NARRATOR: Sound Trumpets. Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET, and SOMERSET, on the terrace
KING HENRY VI: Was ever king that joy'd an earthly throne,
KING HENRY VI: And could command no more content than I?
KING HENRY VI: No sooner was I crept out of my cradle
KING HENRY VI: But I was made a king, at nine months old.
KING HENRY VI: Was never subject long'd to be a king
KING HENRY VI: As I do long and wish to be a subject.
NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM and CLIFFORD
BUCKINGHAM: Health and glad tidings to your majesty!
KING HENRY VI: Why, Buckingham, is the traitor Cade surprised?
KING HENRY VI: Or is he but retired to make him strong?
NARRATOR: Enter below, multitudes, with halters about their necks
CLIFFORD: He is fled, my lord, and all his powers do yield,
CLIFFORD: And humbly thus, with halters on their necks,
CLIFFORD: Expect your highness' doom of life or death.
KING HENRY VI: Then, heaven, set ope thy everlasting gates,
KING HENRY VI: To entertain my vows of thanks and praise!
KING HENRY VI: Soldiers, this day have you redeemed your lives,
KING HENRY VI: And show'd how well you love your prince and country:
KING HENRY VI: Continue still in this so good a mind,
KING HENRY VI: And Henry, though he be infortunate,
KING HENRY VI: Assure yourselves, will never be unkind:
KING HENRY VI: And so, with thanks and pardon to you all,
KING HENRY VI: I do dismiss you to your several countries.
ALL: God save the king! God save the king!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Please it your grace to be advertised
Messenger: The Duke of York is newly come from Ireland,
Messenger: And with a puissant and a mighty power
Messenger: Of gallowglasses and stout kerns
Messenger: Is marching hitherward in proud array,
Messenger: And still proclaimeth, as he comes along,
Messenger: His arms are only to remove from thee
Messenger: The Duke of Somerset, whom he terms traitor.
KING HENRY VI: Thus stands my state, 'twixt Cade and York distress'd.
KING HENRY VI: Like to a ship that, having 'scaped a tempest,
KING HENRY VI: Is straightway calm'd and boarded with a pirate:
KING HENRY VI: But now is Cade driven back, his men dispersed,
KING HENRY VI: And now is York in arms to second him.
KING HENRY VI: I pray thee, Buckingham, go and meet him,
KING HENRY VI: And ask him what's the reason of these arms.
KING HENRY VI: Tell him I'll send Duke Edmund to the Tower,
KING HENRY VI: And, Somerset, we'll commit thee thither,
KING HENRY VI: Until his army be dismiss'd from him.
SOMERSET: My lord,
SOMERSET: I'll yield myself to prison willingly,
SOMERSET: Or unto death, to do my country good.
KING HENRY VI: In any case, be not too rough in terms,
KING HENRY VI: For he is fierce and cannot brook hard language.
BUCKINGHAM: I will, my lord, and doubt not so to deal
BUCKINGHAM: As all things shall redound unto your good.
KING HENRY VI: Come, wife, let's in, and learn to govern better,
KING HENRY VI: For yet may England curse my wretched reign.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE X. Kent. IDEN's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter CADE
CADE: Fie on ambition! fie on myself, that have a sword,
CADE: and yet am ready to famish! These five days have I
CADE: hid me in these woods and durst not peep out, for
CADE: all the country is laid for me, but now am I so
CADE: hungry that if I might have a lease of my life for a
CADE: thousand years I could stay no longer. Wherefore,
CADE: on a brick wall have I climbed into this garden, to
CADE: see if I can eat grass, or pick a sallet another
CADE: while, which is not amiss to cool a man's stomach
CADE: this hot weather. And I think this word 'sallet'
CADE: was born to do me good: for many a time, but for a
CADE: sallet, my brainpan had been cleft with a brown
CADE: bill, and many a time, when I have been dry and
CADE: bravely marching, it hath served me instead of a
CADE: quart pot to drink in, and now the word 'sallet'
CADE: must serve me to feed on.
NARRATOR: Enter IDEN
IDEN: Lord, who would live turmoiled in the court,
IDEN: And may enjoy such quiet walks as these?
IDEN: This small inheritance my father left me
IDEN: Contenteth me, and worth a monarchy.
IDEN: I seek not to wax great by others' waning,
IDEN: Or gather wealth, I care not, with what envy:
IDEN: Sufficeth that I have maintains my state
IDEN: And sends the poor well pleased from my gate.
CADE: Here's the lord of the soil come to seize me for a
CADE: stray, for entering his fee-simple without leave.
CADE: Ah, villain, thou wilt betray me, and get a thousand
CADE: crowns of the king carrying my head to him: but
CADE: I'll make thee eat iron like an ostrich, and swallow
CADE: my sword like a great pin, ere thou and I part.
IDEN: Why, rude companion, whatsoe'er thou be,
IDEN: I know thee not, why, then, should I betray thee?
IDEN: Is't not enough to break into my garden,
IDEN: And, like a thief, to come to rob my grounds,
IDEN: Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner,
IDEN: But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms?
CADE: Brave thee! ay, by the best blood that ever was
CADE: broached, and beard thee too. Look on me well: I
CADE: have eat no meat these five days, yet, come thou and
CADE: thy five men, and if I do not leave you all as dead
CADE: as a doornail, I pray God I may never eat grass more.
IDEN: Nay, it shall ne'er be said, while England stands,
IDEN: That Alexander Iden, an esquire of Kent,
IDEN: Took odds to combat a poor famish'd man.
IDEN: Oppose thy steadfast-gazing eyes to mine,
IDEN: See if thou canst outface me with thy looks:
IDEN: Set limb to limb, and thou art far the lesser,
IDEN: Thy hand is but a finger to my fist,
IDEN: Thy leg a stick compared with this truncheon,
IDEN: My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast,
IDEN: And if mine arm be heaved in the air,
IDEN: Thy grave is digg'd already in the earth.
IDEN: As for words, whose greatness answers words,
IDEN: Let this my sword report what speech forbears.
CADE: By my valour, the most complete champion that ever I
CADE: heard! Steel, if thou turn the edge, or cut not out
CADE: the burly-boned clown in chines of beef ere thou
CADE: sleep in thy sheath, I beseech God on my knees thou
CADE: mayst be turned to hobnails.
NARRATOR: Here they fight. CADE falls
CADE: O, I am slain! famine and no other hath slain me:
CADE: let ten thousand devils come against me, and give me
CADE: but the ten meals I have lost, and I'll defy them
CADE: all. Wither, garden, and be henceforth a
CADE: burying-place to all that do dwell in this house,
CADE: because the unconquered soul of Cade is fled.
IDEN: Is't Cade that I have slain, that monstrous traitor?
IDEN: Sword, I will hollow thee for this thy deed,
IDEN: And hang thee o'er my tomb when I am dead:
IDEN: Ne'er shall this blood be wiped from thy point,
IDEN: But thou shalt wear it as a herald's coat,
IDEN: To emblaze the honour that thy master got.
CADE: Iden, farewell, and be proud of thy victory. Tell
CADE: Kent from me, she hath lost her best man, and exhort
CADE: all the world to be cowards, for I, that never
CADE: feared any, am vanquished by famine, not by valour.
NARRATOR: Dies
IDEN: How much thou wrong'st me, heaven be my judge.
IDEN: Die, damned wretch, the curse of her that bare thee,
IDEN: And as I thrust thy body in with my sword,
IDEN: So wish I, I might thrust thy soul to hell.
IDEN: Hence will I drag thee headlong by the heels
IDEN: Unto a dunghill which shall be thy grave,
IDEN: And there cut off thy most ungracious head,
IDEN: Which I will bear in triumph to the king,
IDEN: Leaving thy trunk for crows to feed upon.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Fields between Dartford and Blackheath.
NARRATOR: Enter YORK, and his army of Irish, with drum and colours
YORK: From Ireland thus comes York to claim his right,
YORK: And pluck the crown from feeble Henry's head:
YORK: Ring, bells, aloud, burn, bonfires, clear and bright,
YORK: To entertain great England's lawful king.
YORK: Ah! sancta majestas, who would not buy thee dear?
YORK: Let them obey that know not how to rule,
YORK: This hand was made to handle naught but gold.
YORK: I cannot give due action to my words,
YORK: Except a sword or sceptre balance it:
YORK: A sceptre shall it have, have I a soul,
YORK: On which I'll toss the flower-de-luce of France.
NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM
YORK: Whom have we here? Buckingham, to disturb me?
YORK: The king hath sent him, sure: I must dissemble.
BUCKINGHAM: York, if thou meanest well, I greet thee well.
YORK: Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept thy greeting.
YORK: Art thou a messenger, or come of pleasure?
BUCKINGHAM: A messenger from Henry, our dread liege,
BUCKINGHAM: To know the reason of these arms in peace,
BUCKINGHAM: Or why thou, being a subject as I am,
BUCKINGHAM: Against thy oath and true allegiance sworn,
BUCKINGHAM: Should raise so great a power without his leave,
BUCKINGHAM: Or dare to bring thy force so near the court.
YORK: [Aside]  Scarce can I speak, my choler is so great:
YORK: O, I could hew up rocks and fight with flint,
YORK: I am so angry at these abject terms,
YORK: And now, like Ajax Telamonius,
YORK: On sheep or oxen could I spend my fury.
YORK: I am far better born than is the king,
YORK: More like a king, more kingly in my thoughts:
YORK: But I must make fair weather yet a while,
YORK: Till Henry be more weak and I more strong,--
YORK: Buckingham, I prithee, pardon me,
YORK: That I have given no answer all this while,
YORK: My mind was troubled with deep melancholy.
YORK: The cause why I have brought this army hither
YORK: Is to remove proud Somerset from the king,
YORK: Seditious to his grace and to the state.
BUCKINGHAM: That is too much presumption on thy part:
BUCKINGHAM: But if thy arms be to no other end,
BUCKINGHAM: The king hath yielded unto thy demand:
BUCKINGHAM: The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.
YORK: Upon thine honour, is he prisoner?
BUCKINGHAM: Upon mine honour, he is prisoner.
YORK: Then, Buckingham, I do dismiss my powers.
YORK: Soldiers, I thank you all, disperse yourselves,
YORK: Meet me to-morrow in St. George's field,
YORK: You shall have pay and every thing you wish.
YORK: And let my sovereign, virtuous Henry,
YORK: Command my eldest son, nay, all my sons,
YORK: As pledges of my fealty and love,
YORK: I'll send them all as willing as I live:
YORK: Lands, goods, horse, armour, any thing I have,
YORK: Is his to use, so Somerset may die.
BUCKINGHAM: York, I commend this kind submission:
BUCKINGHAM: We twain will go into his highness' tent.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI and Attendants
KING HENRY VI: Buckingham, doth York intend no harm to us,
KING HENRY VI: That thus he marcheth with thee arm in arm?
YORK: In all submission and humility
YORK: York doth present himself unto your highness.
KING HENRY VI: Then what intends these forces thou dost bring?
YORK: To heave the traitor Somerset from hence,
YORK: And fight against that monstrous rebel Cade,
YORK: Who since I heard to be discomfited.
NARRATOR: Enter IDEN, with CADE'S head
IDEN: If one so rude and of so mean condition
IDEN: May pass into the presence of a king,
IDEN: Lo, I present your grace a traitor's head,
IDEN: The head of Cade, whom I in combat slew.
KING HENRY VI: The head of Cade! Great God, how just art Thou!
KING HENRY VI: O, let me view his visage, being dead,
KING HENRY VI: That living wrought me such exceeding trouble.
KING HENRY VI: Tell me, my friend, art thou the man that slew him?
IDEN: I was, an't like your majesty.
KING HENRY VI: How art thou call'd? and what is thy degree?
IDEN: Alexander Iden, that's my name,
IDEN: A poor esquire of Kent, that loves his king.
BUCKINGHAM: So please it you, my lord, 'twere not amiss
BUCKINGHAM: He were created knight for his good service.
KING HENRY VI: Iden, kneel down.
NARRATOR: He kneels
KING HENRY VI: Rise up a knight.
KING HENRY VI: We give thee for reward a thousand marks,
KING HENRY VI: And will that thou henceforth attend on us.
IDEN: May Iden live to merit such a bounty.
IDEN: And never live but true unto his liege!
NARRATOR: Rises
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN MARGARET and SOMERSET
KING HENRY VI: See, Buckingham, Somerset comes with the queen:
KING HENRY VI: Go, bid her hide him quickly from the duke.
QUEEN MARGARET: For thousand Yorks he shall not hide his head,
QUEEN MARGARET: But boldly stand and front him to his face.
YORK: How now! is Somerset at liberty?
YORK: Then, York, unloose thy long-imprison'd thoughts,
YORK: And let thy tongue be equal with thy heart.
YORK: Shall I endure the sight of Somerset?
YORK: False king! why hast thou broken faith with me,
YORK: Knowing how hardly I can brook abuse?
YORK: King did I call thee? no, thou art not king,
YORK: Not fit to govern and rule multitudes,
YORK: Which darest not, no, nor canst not rule a traitor.
YORK: That head of thine doth not become a crown,
YORK: Thy hand is made to grasp a palmer's staff,
YORK: And not to grace an awful princely sceptre.
YORK: That gold must round engirt these brows of mine,
YORK: Whose smile and frown, like to Achilles' spear,
YORK: Is able with the change to kill and cure.
YORK: Here is a hand to hold a sceptre up
YORK: And with the same to act controlling laws.
YORK: Give place: by heaven, thou shalt rule no more
YORK: O'er him whom heaven created for thy ruler.
SOMERSET: O monstrous traitor! I arrest thee, York,
SOMERSET: Of capital treason 'gainst the king and crown,
SOMERSET: Obey, audacious traitor, kneel for grace.
YORK: Wouldst have me kneel? first let me ask of these,
YORK: If they can brook I bow a knee to man.
YORK: Sirrah, call in my sons to be my bail,
NARRATOR: Exit Attendant
YORK: I know, ere they will have me go to ward,
YORK: They'll pawn their swords for my enfranchisement.
QUEEN MARGARET: Call hither Clifford! bid him come amain,
QUEEN MARGARET: To say if that the bastard boys of York
QUEEN MARGARET: Shall be the surety for their traitor father.
NARRATOR: Exit BUCKINGHAM
YORK: O blood-besotted Neapolitan,
YORK: Outcast of Naples, England's bloody scourge!
YORK: The sons of York, thy betters in their birth,
YORK: Shall be their father's bail, and bane to those
YORK: That for my surety will refuse the boys!
NARRATOR: Enter EDWARD and RICHARD
YORK: See where they come: I'll warrant they'll
YORK: make it good.
NARRATOR: Enter CLIFFORD and YOUNG CLIFFORD
QUEEN MARGARET: And here comes Clifford to deny their bail.
CLIFFORD: Health and all happiness to my lord the king!
NARRATOR: Kneels
YORK: I thank thee, Clifford: say, what news with thee?
YORK: Nay, do not fright us with an angry look,
YORK: We are thy sovereign, Clifford, kneel again,
YORK: For thy mistaking so, we pardon thee.
CLIFFORD: This is my king, York, I do not mistake,
CLIFFORD: But thou mistakest me much to think I do:
CLIFFORD: To Bedlam with him! is the man grown mad?
KING HENRY VI: Ay, Clifford, a bedlam and ambitious humour
KING HENRY VI: Makes him oppose himself against his king.
CLIFFORD: He is a traitor, let him to the Tower,
CLIFFORD: And chop away that factious pate of his.
QUEEN MARGARET: He is arrested, but will not obey,
QUEEN MARGARET: His sons, he says, shall give their words for him.
YORK: Will you not, sons?
EDWARD: Ay, noble father, if our words will serve.
RICHARD: And if words will not, then our weapons shall.
CLIFFORD: Why, what a brood of traitors have we here!
YORK: Look in a glass, and call thy image so:
YORK: I am thy king, and thou a false-heart traitor.
YORK: Call hither to the stake my two brave bears,
YORK: That with the very shaking of their chains
YORK: They may astonish these fell-lurking curs:
YORK: Bid Salisbury and Warwick come to me.
NARRATOR: Enter the WARWICK and SALISBURY
CLIFFORD: Are these thy bears? we'll bait thy bears to death.
CLIFFORD: And manacle the bear-ward in their chains,
CLIFFORD: If thou darest bring them to the baiting place.
RICHARD: Oft have I seen a hot o'erweening cur
RICHARD: Run back and bite, because he was withheld,
RICHARD: Who, being suffer'd with the bear's fell paw,
RICHARD: Hath clapp'd his tail between his legs and cried:
RICHARD: And such a piece of service will you do,
RICHARD: If you oppose yourselves to match Lord Warwick.
CLIFFORD: Hence, heap of wrath, foul indigested lump,
CLIFFORD: As crooked in thy manners as thy shape!
YORK: Nay, we shall heat you thoroughly anon.
CLIFFORD: Take heed, lest by your heat you burn yourselves.
KING HENRY VI: Why, Warwick, hath thy knee forgot to bow?
KING HENRY VI: Old Salisbury, shame to thy silver hair,
KING HENRY VI: Thou mad misleader of thy brain-sick son!
KING HENRY VI: What, wilt thou on thy death-bed play the ruffian,
KING HENRY VI: And seek for sorrow with thy spectacles?
KING HENRY VI: O, where is faith? O, where is loyalty?
KING HENRY VI: If it be banish'd from the frosty head,
KING HENRY VI: Where shall it find a harbour in the earth?
KING HENRY VI: Wilt thou go dig a grave to find out war,
KING HENRY VI: And shame thine honourable age with blood?
KING HENRY VI: Why art thou old, and want'st experience?
KING HENRY VI: Or wherefore dost abuse it, if thou hast it?
KING HENRY VI: For shame! in duty bend thy knee to me
KING HENRY VI: That bows unto the grave with mickle age.
SALISBURY: My lord, I have consider'd with myself
SALISBURY: The title of this most renowned duke,
SALISBURY: And in my conscience do repute his grace
SALISBURY: The rightful heir to England's royal seat.
KING HENRY VI: Hast thou not sworn allegiance unto me?
SALISBURY: I have.
KING HENRY VI: Canst thou dispense with heaven for such an oath?
SALISBURY: It is great sin to swear unto a sin,
SALISBURY: But greater sin to keep a sinful oath.
SALISBURY: Who can be bound by any solemn vow
SALISBURY: To do a murderous deed, to rob a man,
SALISBURY: To force a spotless virgin's chastity,
SALISBURY: To reave the orphan of his patrimony,
SALISBURY: To wring the widow from her custom'd right,
SALISBURY: And have no other reason for this wrong
SALISBURY: But that he was bound by a solemn oath?
QUEEN MARGARET: A subtle traitor needs no sophister.
KING HENRY VI: Call Buckingham, and bid him arm himself.
YORK: Call Buckingham, and all the friends thou hast,
YORK: I am resolved for death or dignity.
CLIFFORD: The first I warrant thee, if dreams prove true.
WARWICK: You were best to go to bed and dream again,
WARWICK: To keep thee from the tempest of the field.
CLIFFORD: I am resolved to bear a greater storm
CLIFFORD: Than any thou canst conjure up to-day,
CLIFFORD: And that I'll write upon thy burgonet,
CLIFFORD: Might I but know thee by thy household badge.
WARWICK: Now, by my father's badge, old Nevil's crest,
WARWICK: The rampant bear chain'd to the ragged staff,
WARWICK: This day I'll wear aloft my burgonet,
WARWICK: As on a mountain top the cedar shows
WARWICK: That keeps his leaves in spite of any storm,
WARWICK: Even to affright thee with the view thereof.
CLIFFORD: And from thy burgonet I'll rend thy bear
CLIFFORD: And tread it under foot with all contempt,
CLIFFORD: Despite the bear-ward that protects the bear.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: And so to arms, victorious father,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: To quell the rebels and their complices.
RICHARD: Fie! charity, for shame! speak not in spite,
RICHARD: For you shall sup with Jesu Christ to-night.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Foul stigmatic, that's more than thou canst tell.
RICHARD: If not in heaven, you'll surely sup in hell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Saint Alban's.
NARRATOR: Alarums to the battle. Enter WARWICK
WARWICK: Clifford of Cumberland, 'tis Warwick calls:
WARWICK: And if thou dost not hide thee from the bear,
WARWICK: Now, when the angry trumpet sounds alarum
WARWICK: And dead men's cries do fill the empty air,
WARWICK: Clifford, I say, come forth and fight with me:
WARWICK: Proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland,
WARWICK: Warwick is hoarse with calling thee to arms.
NARRATOR: Enter YORK
WARWICK: How now, my noble lord? what, all afoot?
YORK: The deadly-handed Clifford slew my steed,
YORK: But match to match I have encounter'd him
YORK: And made a prey for carrion kites and crows
YORK: Even of the bonny beast he loved so well.
NARRATOR: Enter CLIFFORD
WARWICK: Of one or both of us the time is come.
YORK: Hold, Warwick, seek thee out some other chase,
YORK: For I myself must hunt this deer to death.
WARWICK: Then, nobly, York, 'tis for a crown thou fight'st.
WARWICK: As I intend, Clifford, to thrive to-day,
WARWICK: It grieves my soul to leave thee unassail'd.
NARRATOR: Exit
CLIFFORD: What seest thou in me, York? why dost thou pause?
YORK: With thy brave bearing should I be in love,
YORK: But that thou art so fast mine enemy.
CLIFFORD: Nor should thy prowess want praise and esteem,
CLIFFORD: But that 'tis shown ignobly and in treason.
YORK: So let it help me now against thy sword
YORK: As I in justice and true right express it.
CLIFFORD: My soul and body on the action both!
YORK: A dreadful lay! Address thee instantly.
NARRATOR: They fight, and CLIFFORD falls
CLIFFORD: La fin couronne les oeuvres.
NARRATOR: Dies
YORK: Thus war hath given thee peace, for thou art still.
YORK: Peace with his soul, heaven, if it be thy will!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter YOUNG CLIFFORD
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Shame and confusion! all is on the rout,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Fear frames disorder, and disorder wounds
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Where it should guard. O war, thou son of hell,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Whom angry heavens do make their minister
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Throw in the frozen bosoms of our part
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Hot coals of vengeance! Let no soldier fly.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: He that is truly dedicate to war
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Hath no self-love, nor he that loves himself
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Hath not essentially but by circumstance
YOUNG CLIFFORD: The name of valour.
NARRATOR: Seeing his dead father
YOUNG CLIFFORD: O, let the vile world end,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: And the premised flames of the last day
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Knit earth and heaven together!
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Now let the general trumpet blow his blast,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Particularities and petty sounds
YOUNG CLIFFORD: To cease! Wast thou ordain'd, dear father,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: To lose thy youth in peace, and to achieve
YOUNG CLIFFORD: The silver livery of advised age,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: And, in thy reverence and thy chair-days, thus
YOUNG CLIFFORD: To die in ruffian battle? Even at this sight
YOUNG CLIFFORD: My heart is turn'd to stone: and while 'tis mine,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: It shall be stony. York not our old men spares,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: No more will I their babes: tears virginal
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Shall be to me even as the dew to fire,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: And beauty that the tyrant oft reclaims
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Shall to my flaming wrath be oil and flax.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Henceforth I will not have to do with pity:
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Meet I an infant of the house of York,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Into as many gobbets will I cut it
YOUNG CLIFFORD: As wild Medea young Absyrtus did:
YOUNG CLIFFORD: In cruelty will I seek out my fame.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Come, thou new ruin of old Clifford's house:
YOUNG CLIFFORD: As did AEneas old Anchises bear,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: So bear I thee upon my manly shoulders,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: But then AEneas bare a living load,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Nothing so heavy as these woes of mine.
NARRATOR: Exit, bearing off his father
NARRATOR: Enter RICHARD and SOMERSET to fight. SOMERSET is killed
RICHARD: So, lie thou there,
RICHARD: For underneath an alehouse' paltry sign,
RICHARD: The Castle in Saint Alban's, Somerset
RICHARD: Hath made the wizard famous in his death.
RICHARD: Sword, hold thy temper, heart, be wrathful still:
RICHARD: Priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Fight: excursions. Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET, and others
QUEEN MARGARET: Away, my lord! you are slow, for shame, away!
KING HENRY VI: Can we outrun the heavens? good Margaret, stay.
QUEEN MARGARET: What are you made of? you'll nor fight nor fly:
QUEEN MARGARET: Now is it manhood, wisdom and defence,
QUEEN MARGARET: To give the enemy way, and to secure us
QUEEN MARGARET: By what we can, which can no more but fly.
NARRATOR: Alarum afar off
QUEEN MARGARET: If you be ta'en, we then should see the bottom
QUEEN MARGARET: Of all our fortunes: but if we haply scape,
QUEEN MARGARET: As well we may, if not through your neglect,
QUEEN MARGARET: We shall to London get, where you are loved
QUEEN MARGARET: And where this breach now in our fortunes made
QUEEN MARGARET: May readily be stopp'd.
NARRATOR: Re-enter YOUNG CLIFFORD
YOUNG CLIFFORD: But that my heart's on future mischief set,
YOUNG CLIFFORD: I would speak blasphemy ere bid you fly:
YOUNG CLIFFORD: But fly you must, uncurable discomfit
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Reigns in the hearts of all our present parts.
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Away, for your relief! and we will live
YOUNG CLIFFORD: To see their day and them our fortune give:
YOUNG CLIFFORD: Away, my lord, away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Fields near St. Alban's.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Retreat. Enter YORK, RICHARD, WARWICK, and Soldiers, with drum and colours
YORK: Of Salisbury, who can report of him,
YORK: That winter lion, who in rage forgets
YORK: Aged contusions and all brush of time,
YORK: And, like a gallant in the brow of youth,
YORK: Repairs him with occasion? This happy day
YORK: Is not itself, nor have we won one foot,
YORK: If Salisbury be lost.
RICHARD: My noble father,
RICHARD: Three times to-day I holp him to his horse,
RICHARD: Three times bestrid him, thrice I led him off,
RICHARD: Persuaded him from any further act:
RICHARD: But still, where danger was, still there I met him,
RICHARD: And like rich hangings in a homely house,
RICHARD: So was his will in his old feeble body.
RICHARD: But, noble as he is, look where he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter SALISBURY
SALISBURY: Now, by my sword, well hast thou fought to-day,
SALISBURY: By the mass, so did we all. I thank you, Richard:
SALISBURY: God knows how long it is I have to live,
SALISBURY: And it hath pleased him that three times to-day
SALISBURY: You have defended me from imminent death.
SALISBURY: Well, lords, we have not got that which we have:
SALISBURY: 'Tis not enough our foes are this time fled,
SALISBURY: Being opposites of such repairing nature.
YORK: I know our safety is to follow them,
YORK: For, as I hear, the king is fled to London,
YORK: To call a present court of parliament.
YORK: Let us pursue him ere the writs go forth.
YORK: What says Lord Warwick? shall we after them?
WARWICK: After them! nay, before them, if we can.
WARWICK: Now, by my faith, lords, 'twas a glorious day:
WARWICK: Saint Alban's battle won by famous York
WARWICK: Shall be eternized in all age to come.
WARWICK: Sound drums and trumpets, and to London all:
WARWICK: And more such days as these to us befall!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Henry VI Part 3 '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The Parliament-house.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter YORK, EDWARD, RICHARD, NORFOLK, MONTAGUE, WARWICK, and Soldiers
WARWICK: I wonder how the king escaped our hands.
YORK: While we pursued the horsemen of the north,
YORK: He slily stole away and left his men:
YORK: Whereat the great Lord of Northumberland,
YORK: Whose warlike ears could never brook retreat,
YORK: Cheer'd up the drooping army, and himself,
YORK: Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford, all abreast,
YORK: Charged our main battle's front, and breaking in
YORK: Were by the swords of common soldiers slain.
EDWARD: Lord Stafford's father, Duke of Buckingham,
EDWARD: Is either slain or wounded dangerously,
EDWARD: I cleft his beaver with a downright blow:
EDWARD: That this is true, father, behold his blood.
MONTAGUE: And, brother, here's the Earl of Wiltshire's blood,
MONTAGUE: Whom I encounter'd as the battles join'd.
RICHARD: Speak thou for me and tell them what I did.
NARRATOR: Throwing down SOMERSET's head
YORK: Richard hath best deserved of all my sons.
YORK: But is your grace dead, my Lord of Somerset?
NORFOLK: Such hope have all the line of John of Gaunt!
RICHARD: Thus do I hope to shake King Henry's head.
WARWICK: And so do I. Victorious Prince of York,
WARWICK: Before I see thee seated in that throne
WARWICK: Which now the house of Lancaster usurps,
WARWICK: I vow by heaven these eyes shall never close.
WARWICK: This is the palace of the fearful king,
WARWICK: And this the regal seat: possess it, York,
WARWICK: For this is thine and not King Henry's heirs'
YORK: Assist me, then, sweet Warwick, and I will,
YORK: For hither we have broken in by force.
NORFOLK: We'll all assist you, he that flies shall die.
YORK: Thanks, gentle Norfolk: stay by me, my lords,
YORK: And, soldiers, stay and lodge by me this night.
NARRATOR: They go up
WARWICK: And when the king comes, offer no violence,
WARWICK: Unless he seek to thrust you out perforce.
YORK: The queen this day here holds her parliament,
YORK: But little thinks we shall be of her council:
YORK: By words or blows here let us win our right.
RICHARD: Arm'd as we are, let's stay within this house.
WARWICK: The bloody parliament shall this be call'd,
WARWICK: Unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, be king,
WARWICK: And bashful Henry deposed, whose cowardice
WARWICK: Hath made us by-words to our enemies.
YORK: Then leave me not, my lords, be resolute,
YORK: I mean to take possession of my right.
WARWICK: Neither the king, nor he that loves him best,
WARWICK: The proudest he that holds up Lancaster,
WARWICK: Dares stir a wing, if Warwick shake his bells.
WARWICK: I'll plant Plantagenet, root him up who dares:
WARWICK: Resolve thee, Richard, claim the English crown.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING HENRY VI, CLIFFORD, NORTHUMBERLAND, WESTMORELAND, EXETER, and the rest
KING HENRY VI: My lords, look where the sturdy rebel sits,
KING HENRY VI: Even in the chair of state: belike he means,
KING HENRY VI: Back'd by the power of Warwick, that false peer,
KING HENRY VI: To aspire unto the crown and reign as king.
KING HENRY VI: Earl of Northumberland, he slew thy father.
KING HENRY VI: And thine, Lord Clifford, and you both have vow'd revenge
KING HENRY VI: On him, his sons, his favourites and his friends.
NORTHUMBERLAND: If I be not, heavens be revenged on me!
CLIFFORD: The hope thereof makes Clifford mourn in steel.
WESTMORELAND: What, shall we suffer this? let's pluck him down:
WESTMORELAND: My heart for anger burns, I cannot brook it.
KING HENRY VI: Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmoreland.
CLIFFORD: Patience is for poltroons, such as he:
CLIFFORD: He durst not sit there, had your father lived.
CLIFFORD: My gracious lord, here in the parliament
CLIFFORD: Let us assail the family of York.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Well hast thou spoken, cousin: be it so.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, know you not the city favours them,
KING HENRY VI: And they have troops of soldiers at their beck?
EXETER: But when the duke is slain, they'll quickly fly.
KING HENRY VI: Far be the thought of this from Henry's heart,
KING HENRY VI: To make a shambles of the parliament-house!
KING HENRY VI: Cousin of Exeter, frowns, words and threats
KING HENRY VI: Shall be the war that Henry means to use.
KING HENRY VI: Thou factious Duke of York, descend my throne,
KING HENRY VI: and kneel for grace and mercy at my feet,
KING HENRY VI: I am thy sovereign.
YORK: I am thine.
EXETER: For shame, come down: he made thee Duke of York.
YORK: 'Twas my inheritance, as the earldom was.
EXETER: Thy father was a traitor to the crown.
WARWICK: Exeter, thou art a traitor to the crown
WARWICK: In following this usurping Henry.
CLIFFORD: Whom should he follow but his natural king?
WARWICK: True, Clifford, and that's Richard Duke of York.
KING HENRY VI: And shall I stand, and thou sit in my throne?
YORK: It must and shall be so: content thyself.
WARWICK: Be Duke of Lancaster, let him be king.
WESTMORELAND: He is both king and Duke of Lancaster,
WESTMORELAND: And that the Lord of Westmoreland shall maintain.
WARWICK: And Warwick shall disprove it. You forget
WARWICK: That we are those which chased you from the field
WARWICK: And slew your fathers, and with colours spread
WARWICK: March'd through the city to the palace gates.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Yes, Warwick, I remember it to my grief,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And, by his soul, thou and thy house shall rue it.
WESTMORELAND: Plantagenet, of thee and these thy sons,
WESTMORELAND: Thy kinsman and thy friends, I'll have more lives
WESTMORELAND: Than drops of blood were in my father's veins.
CLIFFORD: Urge it no more, lest that, instead of words,
CLIFFORD: I send thee, Warwick, such a messenger
CLIFFORD: As shall revenge his death before I stir.
WARWICK: Poor Clifford! how I scorn his worthless threats!
YORK: Will you we show our title to the crown?
YORK: If not, our swords shall plead it in the field.
KING HENRY VI: What title hast thou, traitor, to the crown?
KING HENRY VI: Thy father was, as thou art, Duke of York,
KING HENRY VI: Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March:
KING HENRY VI: I am the son of Henry the Fifth,
KING HENRY VI: Who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop
KING HENRY VI: And seized upon their towns and provinces.
WARWICK: Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all.
KING HENRY VI: The lord protector lost it, and not I:
KING HENRY VI: When I was crown'd I was but nine months old.
RICHARD: You are old enough now, and yet, methinks, you lose.
RICHARD: Father, tear the crown from the usurper's head.
EDWARD: Sweet father, do so, set it on your head.
MONTAGUE: Good brother, as thou lovest and honourest arms,
MONTAGUE: Let's fight it out and not stand cavilling thus.
RICHARD: Sound drums and trumpets, and the king will fly.
YORK: Sons, peace!
KING HENRY VI: Peace, thou! and give King Henry leave to speak.
WARWICK: Plantagenet shall speak first: hear him, lords,
WARWICK: And be you silent and attentive too,
WARWICK: For he that interrupts him shall not live.
KING HENRY VI: Think'st thou that I will leave my kingly throne,
KING HENRY VI: Wherein my grandsire and my father sat?
KING HENRY VI: No: first shall war unpeople this my realm,
KING HENRY VI: Ay, and their colours, often borne in France,
KING HENRY VI: And now in England to our heart's great sorrow,
KING HENRY VI: Shall be my winding-sheet. Why faint you, lords?
KING HENRY VI: My title's good, and better far than his.
WARWICK: Prove it, Henry, and thou shalt be king.
KING HENRY VI: Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown.
YORK: 'Twas by rebellion against his king.
KING HENRY VI: [Aside]  I know not what to say, my title's weak.--
KING HENRY VI: Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?
YORK: What then?
KING HENRY VI: An if he may, then am I lawful king,
KING HENRY VI: For Richard, in the view of many lords,
KING HENRY VI: Resign'd the crown to Henry the Fourth,
KING HENRY VI: Whose heir my father was, and I am his.
YORK: He rose against him, being his sovereign,
YORK: And made him to resign his crown perforce.
WARWICK: Suppose, my lords, he did it unconstrain'd,
WARWICK: Think you 'twere prejudicial to his crown?
EXETER: No, for he could not so resign his crown
EXETER: But that the next heir should succeed and reign.
KING HENRY VI: Art thou against us, Duke of Exeter?
EXETER: His is the right, and therefore pardon me.
YORK: Why whisper you, my lords, and answer not?
EXETER: My conscience tells me he is lawful king.
KING HENRY VI: [Aside]  All will revolt from me, and turn to him.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Plantagenet, for all the claim thou lay'st,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Think not that Henry shall be so deposed.
WARWICK: Deposed he shall be, in despite of all.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Thou art deceived: 'tis not thy southern power,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, nor of Kent,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Which makes thee thus presumptuous and proud,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Can set the duke up in despite of me.
CLIFFORD: King Henry, be thy title right or wrong,
CLIFFORD: Lord Clifford vows to fight in thy defence:
CLIFFORD: May that ground gape and swallow me alive,
CLIFFORD: Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father!
KING HENRY VI: O Clifford, how thy words revive my heart!
YORK: Henry of Lancaster, resign thy crown.
YORK: What mutter you, or what conspire you, lords?
WARWICK: Do right unto this princely Duke of York,
WARWICK: Or I will fill the house with armed men,
WARWICK: And over the chair of state, where now he sits,
WARWICK: Write up his title with usurping blood.
NARRATOR: He stamps with his foot and the soldiers show themselves
KING HENRY VI: My Lord of Warwick, hear me but one word:
KING HENRY VI: Let me for this my life-time reign as king.
YORK: Confirm the crown to me and to mine heirs,
YORK: And thou shalt reign in quiet while thou livest.
KING HENRY VI: I am content: Richard Plantagenet,
KING HENRY VI: Enjoy the kingdom after my decease.
CLIFFORD: What wrong is this unto the prince your son!
WARWICK: What good is this to England and himself!
WESTMORELAND: Base, fearful and despairing Henry!
CLIFFORD: How hast thou injured both thyself and us!
WESTMORELAND: I cannot stay to hear these articles.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Nor I.
CLIFFORD: Come, cousin, let us tell the queen these news.
WESTMORELAND: Farewell, faint-hearted and degenerate king,
WESTMORELAND: In whose cold blood no spark of honour bides.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Be thou a prey unto the house of York,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And die in bands for this unmanly deed!
CLIFFORD: In dreadful war mayst thou be overcome,
CLIFFORD: Or live in peace abandon'd and despised!
NARRATOR: Exeunt NORTHUMBERLAND, CLIFFORD, and WESTMORELAND
WARWICK: Turn this way, Henry, and regard them not.
EXETER: They seek revenge and therefore will not yield.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, Exeter!
WARWICK: Why should you sigh, my lord?
KING HENRY VI: Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son,
KING HENRY VI: Whom I unnaturally shall disinherit.
KING HENRY VI: But be it as it may: I here entail
KING HENRY VI: The crown to thee and to thine heirs for ever,
KING HENRY VI: Conditionally, that here thou take an oath
KING HENRY VI: To cease this civil war, and, whilst I live,
KING HENRY VI: To honour me as thy king and sovereign,
KING HENRY VI: And neither by treason nor hostility
KING HENRY VI: To seek to put me down and reign thyself.
YORK: This oath I willingly take and will perform.
WARWICK: Long live King Henry! Plantagenet embrace him.
KING HENRY VI: And long live thou and these thy forward sons!
YORK: Now York and Lancaster are reconciled.
EXETER: Accursed be he that seeks to make them foes!
NARRATOR: Sennet. Here they come down
YORK: Farewell, my gracious lord, I'll to my castle.
WARWICK: And I'll keep London with my soldiers.
NORFOLK: And I to Norfolk with my followers.
MONTAGUE: And I unto the sea from whence I came.
NARRATOR: Exeunt YORK, EDWARD, EDMUND, GEORGE, RICHARD,  WARWICK, NORFOLK, MONTAGUE, their Soldiers, and Attendants
KING HENRY VI: And I, with grief and sorrow, to the court.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN MARGARET and PRINCE EDWARD
EXETER: Here comes the queen, whose looks bewray her anger:
EXETER: I'll steal away.
KING HENRY VI: Exeter, so will I.
QUEEN MARGARET: Nay, go not from me, I will follow thee.
KING HENRY VI: Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.
QUEEN MARGARET: Who can be patient in such extremes?
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, wretched man! would I had died a maid
QUEEN MARGARET: And never seen thee, never borne thee son,
QUEEN MARGARET: Seeing thou hast proved so unnatural a father
QUEEN MARGARET: Hath he deserved to lose his birthright thus?
QUEEN MARGARET: Hadst thou but loved him half so well as I,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or felt that pain which I did for him once,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or nourish'd him as I did with my blood,
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou wouldst have left thy dearest heart-blood there,
QUEEN MARGARET: Rather than have that savage duke thine heir
QUEEN MARGARET: And disinherited thine only son.
PRINCE EDWARD: Father, you cannot disinherit me:
PRINCE EDWARD: If you be king, why should not I succeed?
KING HENRY VI: Pardon me, Margaret, pardon me, sweet son:
KING HENRY VI: The Earl of Warwick and the duke enforced me.
QUEEN MARGARET: Enforced thee! art thou king, and wilt be forced?
QUEEN MARGARET: I shame to hear thee speak. Ah, timorous wretch!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou hast undone thyself, thy son and me,
QUEEN MARGARET: And given unto the house of York such head
QUEEN MARGARET: As thou shalt reign but by their sufferance.
QUEEN MARGARET: To entail him and his heirs unto the crown,
QUEEN MARGARET: What is it, but to make thy sepulchre
QUEEN MARGARET: And creep into it far before thy time?
QUEEN MARGARET: Warwick is chancellor and the lord of Calais,
QUEEN MARGARET: Stern Falconbridge commands the narrow seas,
QUEEN MARGARET: The duke is made protector of the realm,
QUEEN MARGARET: And yet shalt thou be safe? such safety finds
QUEEN MARGARET: The trembling lamb environed with wolves.
QUEEN MARGARET: Had I been there, which am a silly woman,
QUEEN MARGARET: The soldiers should have toss'd me on their pikes
QUEEN MARGARET: Before I would have granted to that act.
QUEEN MARGARET: But thou preferr'st thy life before thine honour:
QUEEN MARGARET: And seeing thou dost, I here divorce myself
QUEEN MARGARET: Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed,
QUEEN MARGARET: Until that act of parliament be repeal'd
QUEEN MARGARET: Whereby my son is disinherited.
QUEEN MARGARET: The northern lords that have forsworn thy colours
QUEEN MARGARET: Will follow mine, if once they see them spread,
QUEEN MARGARET: And spread they shall be, to thy foul disgrace
QUEEN MARGARET: And utter ruin of the house of York.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thus do I leave thee. Come, son, let's away,
QUEEN MARGARET: Our army is ready, come, we'll after them.
KING HENRY VI: Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou hast spoke too much already: get thee gone.
KING HENRY VI: Gentle son Edward, thou wilt stay with me?
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, to be murder'd by his enemies.
PRINCE EDWARD: When I return with victory from the field
PRINCE EDWARD: I'll see your grace: till then I'll follow her.
QUEEN MARGARET: Come, son, away, we may not linger thus.
NARRATOR: Exeunt QUEEN MARGARET and PRINCE EDWARD
KING HENRY VI: Poor queen! how love to me and to her son
KING HENRY VI: Hath made her break out into terms of rage!
KING HENRY VI: Revenged may she be on that hateful duke,
KING HENRY VI: Whose haughty spirit, winged with desire,
KING HENRY VI: Will cost my crown, and like an empty eagle
KING HENRY VI: Tire on the flesh of me and of my son!
KING HENRY VI: The loss of those three lords torments my heart:
KING HENRY VI: I'll write unto them and entreat them fair.
KING HENRY VI: Come, cousin you shall be the messenger.
EXETER: And I, I hope, shall reconcile them all.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Sandal Castle.
NARRATOR: Enter RICHARD, EDWARD, and MONTAGUE
RICHARD: Brother, though I be youngest, give me leave.
EDWARD: No, I can better play the orator.
MONTAGUE: But I have reasons strong and forcible.
NARRATOR: Enter YORK
YORK: Why, how now, sons and brother! at a strife?
YORK: What is your quarrel? how began it first?
EDWARD: No quarrel, but a slight contention.
YORK: About what?
RICHARD: About that which concerns your grace and us,
RICHARD: The crown of England, father, which is yours.
YORK: Mine boy? not till King Henry be dead.
RICHARD: Your right depends not on his life or death.
EDWARD: Now you are heir, therefore enjoy it now:
EDWARD: By giving the house of Lancaster leave to breathe,
EDWARD: It will outrun you, father, in the end.
YORK: I took an oath that he should quietly reign.
EDWARD: But for a kingdom any oath may be broken:
EDWARD: I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year.
RICHARD: No, God forbid your grace should be forsworn.
YORK: I shall be, if I claim by open war.
RICHARD: I'll prove the contrary, if you'll hear me speak.
YORK: Thou canst not, son, it is impossible.
RICHARD: An oath is of no moment, being not took
RICHARD: Before a true and lawful magistrate,
RICHARD: That hath authority over him that swears:
RICHARD: Henry had none, but did usurp the place,
RICHARD: Then, seeing 'twas he that made you to depose,
RICHARD: Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.
RICHARD: Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think
RICHARD: How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown,
RICHARD: Within whose circuit is Elysium
RICHARD: And all that poets feign of bliss and joy.
RICHARD: Why do we finger thus? I cannot rest
RICHARD: Until the white rose that I wear be dyed
RICHARD: Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry's heart.
YORK: Richard, enough, I will be king, or die.
YORK: Brother, thou shalt to London presently,
YORK: And whet on Warwick to this enterprise.
YORK: Thou, Richard, shalt to the Duke of Norfolk,
YORK: And tell him privily of our intent.
YORK: You Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham,
YORK: With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise:
YORK: In them I trust, for they are soldiers,
YORK: Witty, courteous, liberal, full of spirit.
YORK: While you are thus employ'd, what resteth more,
YORK: But that I seek occasion how to rise,
YORK: And yet the king not privy to my drift,
YORK: Nor any of the house of Lancaster?
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
YORK: But, stay: what news? Why comest thou in such post?
Messenger: The queen with all the northern earls and lords
Messenger: Intend here to besiege you in your castle:
Messenger: She is hard by with twenty thousand men,
Messenger: And therefore fortify your hold, my lord.
YORK: Ay, with my sword. What! think'st thou that we fear them?
YORK: Edward and Richard, you shall stay with me,
YORK: My brother Montague shall post to London:
YORK: Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest,
YORK: Whom we have left protectors of the king,
YORK: With powerful policy strengthen themselves,
YORK: And trust not simple Henry nor his oaths.
MONTAGUE: Brother, I go, I'll win them, fear it not:
MONTAGUE: And thus most humbly I do take my leave.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter JOHN MORTIMER and HUGH MORTIMER
MONTAGUE: Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, mine uncles,
MONTAGUE: You are come to Sandal in a happy hour,
MONTAGUE: The army of the queen mean to besiege us.
JOHN MORTIMER: She shall not need, we'll meet her in the field.
YORK: What, with five thousand men?
RICHARD: Ay, with five hundred, father, for a need:
RICHARD: A woman's general, what should we fear?
NARRATOR: A march afar off
EDWARD: I hear their drums: let's set our men in order,
EDWARD: And issue forth and bid them battle straight.
YORK: Five men to twenty! though the odds be great,
YORK: I doubt not, uncle, of our victory.
YORK: Many a battle have I won in France,
YORK: When as the enemy hath been ten to one:
YORK: Why should I not now have the like success?
NARRATOR: Alarum. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Field of battle betwixt Sandal Castle and Wakefield.
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter RUTLAND and his Tutor
RUTLAND: Ah, whither shall I fly to 'scape their hands?
RUTLAND: Ah, tutor, look where bloody Clifford comes!
NARRATOR: Enter CLIFFORD and Soldiers
CLIFFORD: Chaplain, away! thy priesthood saves thy life.
CLIFFORD: As for the brat of this accursed duke,
CLIFFORD: Whose father slew my father, he shall die.
Tutor: And I, my lord, will bear him company.
CLIFFORD: Soldiers, away with him!
Tutor: Ah, Clifford, murder not this innocent child,
Tutor: Lest thou be hated both of God and man!
NARRATOR: Exit, dragged off by Soldiers
CLIFFORD: How now! is he dead already? or is it fear
CLIFFORD: That makes him close his eyes? I'll open them.
RUTLAND: So looks the pent-up lion o'er the wretch
RUTLAND: That trembles under his devouring paws,
RUTLAND: And so he walks, insulting o'er his prey,
RUTLAND: And so he comes, to rend his limbs asunder.
RUTLAND: Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with thy sword,
RUTLAND: And not with such a cruel threatening look.
RUTLAND: Sweet Clifford, hear me speak before I die.
RUTLAND: I am too mean a subject for thy wrath:
RUTLAND: Be thou revenged on men, and let me live.
CLIFFORD: In vain thou speak'st, poor boy, my father's blood
CLIFFORD: Hath stopp'd the passage where thy words should enter.
RUTLAND: Then let my father's blood open it again:
RUTLAND: He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him.
CLIFFORD: Had thy brethren here, their lives and thine
CLIFFORD: Were not revenge sufficient for me,
CLIFFORD: No, if I digg'd up thy forefathers' graves
CLIFFORD: And hung their rotten coffins up in chains,
CLIFFORD: It could not slake mine ire, nor ease my heart.
CLIFFORD: The sight of any of the house of York
CLIFFORD: Is as a fury to torment my soul,
CLIFFORD: And till I root out their accursed line
CLIFFORD: And leave not one alive, I live in hell.
CLIFFORD: Therefore--
NARRATOR: Lifting his hand
RUTLAND: O, let me pray before I take my death!
RUTLAND: To thee I pray, sweet Clifford, pity me!
CLIFFORD: Such pity as my rapier's point affords.
RUTLAND: I never did thee harm: why wilt thou slay me?
CLIFFORD: Thy father hath.
RUTLAND: But 'twas ere I was born.
RUTLAND: Thou hast one son, for his sake pity me,
RUTLAND: Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just,
RUTLAND: He be as miserably slain as I.
RUTLAND: Ah, let me live in prison all my days,
RUTLAND: And when I give occasion of offence,
RUTLAND: Then let me die, for now thou hast no cause.
CLIFFORD: No cause!
CLIFFORD: Thy father slew my father, therefore, die.
NARRATOR: Stabs him
RUTLAND: Di faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae!
NARRATOR: Dies
CLIFFORD: Plantagenet! I come, Plantagenet!
CLIFFORD: And this thy son's blood cleaving to my blade
CLIFFORD: Shall rust upon my weapon, till thy blood,
CLIFFORD: Congeal'd with this, do make me wipe off both.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter YORK
YORK: The army of the queen hath got the field:
YORK: My uncles both are slain in rescuing me,
YORK: And all my followers to the eager foe
YORK: Turn back and fly, like ships before the wind
YORK: Or lambs pursued by hunger-starved wolves.
YORK: My sons, God knows what hath bechanced them:
YORK: But this I know, they have demean'd themselves
YORK: Like men born to renown by life or death.
YORK: Three times did Richard make a lane to me.
YORK: And thrice cried 'Courage, father! fight it out!'
YORK: And full as oft came Edward to my side,
YORK: With purple falchion, painted to the hilt
YORK: In blood of those that had encounter'd him:
YORK: And when the hardiest warriors did retire,
YORK: Richard cried 'Charge! and give no foot of ground!'
YORK: And cried 'A crown, or else a glorious tomb!
YORK: A sceptre, or an earthly sepulchre!'
YORK: With this, we charged again: but, out, alas!
YORK: We bodged again, as I have seen a swan
YORK: With bootless labour swim against the tide
YORK: And spend her strength with over-matching waves.
NARRATOR: A short alarum within
YORK: Ah, hark! the fatal followers do pursue,
YORK: And I am faint and cannot fly their fury:
YORK: And were I strong, I would not shun their fury:
YORK: The sands are number'd that make up my life,
YORK: Here must I stay, and here my life must end.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN MARGARET, CLIFFORD, NORTHUMBERLAND, PRINCE EDWARD, and Soldiers
YORK: Come, bloody Clifford, rough Northumberland,
YORK: I dare your quenchless fury to more rage:
YORK: I am your butt, and I abide your shot.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Yield to our mercy, proud Plantagenet.
CLIFFORD: Ay, to such mercy as his ruthless arm,
CLIFFORD: With downright payment, show'd unto my father.
CLIFFORD: Now Phaethon hath tumbled from his car,
CLIFFORD: And made an evening at the noontide prick.
YORK: My ashes, as the phoenix, may bring forth
YORK: A bird that will revenge upon you all:
YORK: And in that hope I throw mine eyes to heaven,
YORK: Scorning whate'er you can afflict me with.
YORK: Why come you not? what! multitudes, and fear?
CLIFFORD: So cowards fight when they can fly no further,
CLIFFORD: So doves do peck the falcon's piercing talons,
CLIFFORD: So desperate thieves, all hopeless of their lives,
CLIFFORD: Breathe out invectives 'gainst the officers.
YORK: O Clifford, but bethink thee once again,
YORK: And in thy thought o'er-run my former time,
YORK: And, if though canst for blushing, view this face,
YORK: And bite thy tongue, that slanders him with cowardice
YORK: Whose frown hath made thee faint and fly ere this!
CLIFFORD: I will not bandy with thee word for word,
CLIFFORD: But buckle with thee blows, twice two for one.
QUEEN MARGARET: Hold, valiant Clifford! for a thousand causes
QUEEN MARGARET: I would prolong awhile the traitor's life.
QUEEN MARGARET: Wrath makes him deaf: speak thou, Northumberland.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Hold, Clifford! do not honour him so much
NORTHUMBERLAND: To prick thy finger, though to wound his heart:
NORTHUMBERLAND: What valour were it, when a cur doth grin,
NORTHUMBERLAND: For one to thrust his hand between his teeth,
NORTHUMBERLAND: When he might spurn him with his foot away?
NORTHUMBERLAND: It is war's prize to take all vantages,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And ten to one is no impeach of valour.
NARRATOR: They lay hands on YORK, who struggles
CLIFFORD: Ay, ay, so strives the woodcock with the gin.
NORTHUMBERLAND: So doth the cony struggle in the net.
YORK: So triumph thieves upon their conquer'd booty,
YORK: So true men yield, with robbers so o'ermatch'd.
NORTHUMBERLAND: What would your grace have done unto him now?
QUEEN MARGARET: Brave warriors, Clifford and Northumberland,
QUEEN MARGARET: Come, make him stand upon this molehill here,
QUEEN MARGARET: That raught at mountains with outstretched arms,
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet parted but the shadow with his hand.
QUEEN MARGARET: What! was it you that would be England's king?
QUEEN MARGARET: Was't you that revell'd in our parliament,
QUEEN MARGARET: And made a preachment of your high descent?
QUEEN MARGARET: Where are your mess of sons to back you now?
QUEEN MARGARET: The wanton Edward, and the lusty George?
QUEEN MARGARET: And where's that valiant crook-back prodigy,
QUEEN MARGARET: Dicky your boy, that with his grumbling voice
QUEEN MARGARET: Was wont to cheer his dad in mutinies?
QUEEN MARGARET: Or, with the rest, where is your darling Rutland?
QUEEN MARGARET: Look, York: I stain'd this napkin with the blood
QUEEN MARGARET: That valiant Clifford, with his rapier's point,
QUEEN MARGARET: Made issue from the bosom of the boy,
QUEEN MARGARET: And if thine eyes can water for his death,
QUEEN MARGARET: I give thee this to dry thy cheeks withal.
QUEEN MARGARET: Alas poor York! but that I hate thee deadly,
QUEEN MARGARET: I should lament thy miserable state.
QUEEN MARGARET: I prithee, grieve, to make me merry, York.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, hath thy fiery heart so parch'd thine entrails
QUEEN MARGARET: That not a tear can fall for Rutland's death?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why art thou patient, man? thou shouldst be mad,
QUEEN MARGARET: And I, to make thee mad, do mock thee thus.
QUEEN MARGARET: Stamp, rave, and fret, that I may sing and dance.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou wouldst be fee'd, I see, to make me sport:
QUEEN MARGARET: York cannot speak, unless he wear a crown.
QUEEN MARGARET: A crown for York! and, lords, bow low to him:
QUEEN MARGARET: Hold you his hands, whilst I do set it on.
NARRATOR: Putting a paper crown on his head
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, marry, sir, now looks he like a king!
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, this is he that took King Henry's chair,
QUEEN MARGARET: And this is he was his adopted heir.
QUEEN MARGARET: But how is it that great Plantagenet
QUEEN MARGARET: Is crown'd so soon, and broke his solemn oath?
QUEEN MARGARET: As I bethink me, you should not be king
QUEEN MARGARET: Till our King Henry had shook hands with death.
QUEEN MARGARET: And will you pale your head in Henry's glory,
QUEEN MARGARET: And rob his temples of the diadem,
QUEEN MARGARET: Now in his life, against your holy oath?
QUEEN MARGARET: O, 'tis a fault too too unpardonable!
QUEEN MARGARET: Off with the crown, and with the crown his head,
QUEEN MARGARET: And, whilst we breathe, take time to do him dead.
CLIFFORD: That is my office, for my father's sake.
QUEEN MARGARET: Nay, stay, lets hear the orisons he makes.
YORK: She-wolf of France, but worse than wolves of France,
YORK: Whose tongue more poisons than the adder's tooth!
YORK: How ill-beseeming is it in thy sex
YORK: To triumph, like an Amazonian trull,
YORK: Upon their woes whom fortune captivates!
YORK: But that thy face is, vizard-like, unchanging,
YORK: Made impudent with use of evil deeds,
YORK: I would assay, proud queen, to make thee blush.
YORK: To tell thee whence thou camest, of whom derived,
YORK: Were shame enough to shame thee, wert thou not shameless.
YORK: Thy father bears the type of King of Naples,
YORK: Of both the Sicils and Jerusalem,
YORK: Yet not so wealthy as an English yeoman.
YORK: Hath that poor monarch taught thee to insult?
YORK: It needs not, nor it boots thee not, proud queen,
YORK: Unless the adage must be verified,
YORK: That beggars mounted run their horse to death.
YORK: 'Tis beauty that doth oft make women proud,
YORK: But, God he knows, thy share thereof is small:
YORK: 'Tis virtue that doth make them most admired,
YORK: The contrary doth make thee wonder'd at:
YORK: 'Tis government that makes them seem divine,
YORK: The want thereof makes thee abominable:
YORK: Thou art as opposite to every good
YORK: As the Antipodes are unto us,
YORK: Or as the south to the septentrion.
YORK: O tiger's heart wrapt in a woman's hide!
YORK: How couldst thou drain the life-blood of the child,
YORK: To bid the father wipe his eyes withal,
YORK: And yet be seen to bear a woman's face?
YORK: Women are soft, mild, pitiful and flexible,
YORK: Thou stern, obdurate, flinty, rough, remorseless.
YORK: Bids't thou me rage? why, now thou hast thy wish:
YORK: Wouldst have me weep? why, now thou hast thy will:
YORK: For raging wind blows up incessant showers,
YORK: And when the rage allays, the rain begins.
YORK: These tears are my sweet Rutland's obsequies:
YORK: And every drop cries vengeance for his death,
YORK: 'Gainst thee, fell Clifford, and thee, false
YORK: Frenchwoman.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Beshrew me, but his passion moves me so
NORTHUMBERLAND: That hardly can I cheque my eyes from tears.
YORK: That face of his the hungry cannibals
YORK: Would not have touch'd, would not have stain'd with blood:
YORK: But you are more inhuman, more inexorable,
YORK: O, ten times more, than tigers of Hyrcania.
YORK: See, ruthless queen, a hapless father's tears:
YORK: This cloth thou dip'dst in blood of my sweet boy,
YORK: And I with tears do wash the blood away.
YORK: Keep thou the napkin, and go boast of this:
YORK: And if thou tell'st the heavy story right,
YORK: Upon my soul, the hearers will shed tears,
YORK: Yea even my foes will shed fast-falling tears,
YORK: And say 'Alas, it was a piteous deed!'
YORK: There, take the crown, and, with the crown, my curse,
YORK: And in thy need such comfort come to thee
YORK: As now I reap at thy too cruel hand!
YORK: Hard-hearted Clifford, take me from the world:
YORK: My soul to heaven, my blood upon your heads!
NORTHUMBERLAND: Had he been slaughter-man to all my kin,
NORTHUMBERLAND: I should not for my life but weep with him.
NORTHUMBERLAND: To see how inly sorrow gripes his soul.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, weeping-ripe, my Lord Northumberland?
QUEEN MARGARET: Think but upon the wrong he did us all,
QUEEN MARGARET: And that will quickly dry thy melting tears.
CLIFFORD: Here's for my oath, here's for my father's death.
NARRATOR: Stabbing him
QUEEN MARGARET: And here's to right our gentle-hearted king.
NARRATOR: Stabbing him
YORK: Open Thy gate of mercy, gracious God!
YORK: My soul flies through these wounds to seek out Thee.
NARRATOR: Dies
QUEEN MARGARET: Off with his head, and set it on York gates,
QUEEN MARGARET: So York may overlook the town of York.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A plain near Mortimer's Cross in Herefordshire.
NARRATOR: A march. Enter EDWARD, RICHARD, and their power
EDWARD: I wonder how our princely father 'scaped,
EDWARD: Or whether he be 'scaped away or no
EDWARD: From Clifford's and Northumberland's pursuit:
EDWARD: Had he been ta'en, we should have heard the news,
EDWARD: Had he been slain, we should have heard the news,
EDWARD: Or had he 'scaped, methinks we should have heard
EDWARD: The happy tidings of his good escape.
EDWARD: How fares my brother? why is he so sad?
RICHARD: I cannot joy, until I be resolved
RICHARD: Where our right valiant father is become.
RICHARD: I saw him in the battle range about,
RICHARD: And watch'd him how he singled Clifford forth.
RICHARD: Methought he bore him in the thickest troop
RICHARD: As doth a lion in a herd of neat,
RICHARD: Or as a bear, encompass'd round with dogs,
RICHARD: Who having pinch'd a few and made them cry,
RICHARD: The rest stand all aloof, and bark at him.
RICHARD: So fared our father with his enemies,
RICHARD: So fled his enemies my warlike father:
RICHARD: Methinks, 'tis prize enough to be his son.
RICHARD: See how the morning opes her golden gates,
RICHARD: And takes her farewell of the glorious sun!
RICHARD: How well resembles it the prime of youth,
RICHARD: Trimm'd like a younker prancing to his love!
EDWARD: Dazzle mine eyes, or do I see three suns?
RICHARD: Three glorious suns, each one a perfect sun,
RICHARD: Not separated with the racking clouds,
RICHARD: But sever'd in a pale clear-shining sky.
RICHARD: See, see! they join, embrace, and seem to kiss,
RICHARD: As if they vow'd some league inviolable:
RICHARD: Now are they but one lamp, one light, one sun.
RICHARD: In this the heaven figures some event.
EDWARD: 'Tis wondrous strange, the like yet never heard of.
EDWARD: I think it cites us, brother, to the field,
EDWARD: That we, the sons of brave Plantagenet,
EDWARD: Each one already blazing by our meeds,
EDWARD: Should notwithstanding join our lights together
EDWARD: And over-shine the earth as this the world.
EDWARD: Whate'er it bodes, henceforward will I bear
EDWARD: Upon my target three fair-shining suns.
RICHARD: Nay, bear three daughters: by your leave I speak it,
RICHARD: You love the breeder better than the male.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
RICHARD: But what art thou, whose heavy looks foretell
RICHARD: Some dreadful story hanging on thy tongue?
Messenger: Ah, one that was a woful looker-on
Messenger: When as the noble Duke of York was slain,
Messenger: Your princely father and my loving lord!
EDWARD: O, speak no more, for I have heard too much.
RICHARD: Say how he died, for I will hear it all.
Messenger: Environed he was with many foes,
Messenger: And stood against them, as the hope of Troy
Messenger: Against the Greeks that would have enter'd Troy.
Messenger: But Hercules himself must yield to odds,
Messenger: And many strokes, though with a little axe,
Messenger: Hew down and fell the hardest-timber'd oak.
Messenger: By many hands your father was subdued,
Messenger: But only slaughter'd by the ireful arm
Messenger: Of unrelenting Clifford and the queen,
Messenger: Who crown'd the gracious duke in high despite,
Messenger: Laugh'd in his face, and when with grief he wept,
Messenger: The ruthless queen gave him to dry his cheeks
Messenger: A napkin steeped in the harmless blood
Messenger: Of sweet young Rutland, by rough Clifford slain:
Messenger: And after many scorns, many foul taunts,
Messenger: They took his head, and on the gates of York
Messenger: They set the same, and there it doth remain,
Messenger: The saddest spectacle that e'er I view'd.
EDWARD: Sweet Duke of York, our prop to lean upon,
EDWARD: Now thou art gone, we have no staff, no stay.
EDWARD: O Clifford, boisterous Clifford! thou hast slain
EDWARD: The flower of Europe for his chivalry,
EDWARD: And treacherously hast thou vanquish'd him,
EDWARD: For hand to hand he would have vanquish'd thee.
EDWARD: Now my soul's palace is become a prison:
EDWARD: Ah, would she break from hence, that this my body
EDWARD: Might in the ground be closed up in rest!
EDWARD: For never henceforth shall I joy again,
EDWARD: Never, O never shall I see more joy!
RICHARD: I cannot weep, for all my body's moisture
RICHARD: Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heart:
RICHARD: Nor can my tongue unload my heart's great burthen,
RICHARD: For selfsame wind that I should speak withal
RICHARD: Is kindling coals that fires all my breast,
RICHARD: And burns me up with flames that tears would quench.
RICHARD: To weep is to make less the depth of grief:
RICHARD: Tears then for babes, blows and revenge for me
RICHARD: Richard, I bear thy name, I'll venge thy death,
RICHARD: Or die renowned by attempting it.
EDWARD: His name that valiant duke hath left with thee,
EDWARD: His dukedom and his chair with me is left.
RICHARD: Nay, if thou be that princely eagle's bird,
RICHARD: Show thy descent by gazing 'gainst the sun:
RICHARD: For chair and dukedom, throne and kingdom say,
RICHARD: Either that is thine, or else thou wert not his.
NARRATOR: March. Enter WARWICK, MONTAGUE, and their army
WARWICK: How now, fair lords! What fare? what news abroad?
RICHARD: Great Lord of Warwick, if we should recount
RICHARD: Our baleful news, and at each word's deliverance
RICHARD: Stab poniards in our flesh till all were told,
RICHARD: The words would add more anguish than the wounds.
RICHARD: O valiant lord, the Duke of York is slain!
EDWARD: O Warwick, Warwick! that Plantagenet,
EDWARD: Which held three dearly as his soul's redemption,
EDWARD: Is by the stern Lord Clifford done to death.
WARWICK: Ten days ago I drown'd these news in tears,
WARWICK: And now, to add more measure to your woes,
WARWICK: I come to tell you things sith then befall'n.
WARWICK: After the bloody fray at Wakefield fought,
WARWICK: Where your brave father breathed his latest gasp,
WARWICK: Tidings, as swiftly as the posts could run,
WARWICK: Were brought me of your loss and his depart.
WARWICK: I, then in London keeper of the king,
WARWICK: Muster'd my soldiers, gather'd flocks of friends,
WARWICK: And very well appointed, as I thought,
WARWICK: March'd toward Saint Alban's to intercept the queen,
WARWICK: Bearing the king in my behalf along,
WARWICK: For by my scouts I was advertised
WARWICK: That she was coming with a full intent
WARWICK: To dash our late decree in parliament
WARWICK: Touching King Henry's oath and your succession.
WARWICK: Short tale to make, we at Saint Alban's met
WARWICK: Our battles join'd, and both sides fiercely fought:
WARWICK: But whether 'twas the coldness of the king,
WARWICK: Who look'd full gently on his warlike queen,
WARWICK: That robb'd my soldiers of their heated spleen,
WARWICK: Or whether 'twas report of her success,
WARWICK: Or more than common fear of Clifford's rigour,
WARWICK: Who thunders to his captives blood and death,
WARWICK: I cannot judge: but to conclude with truth,
WARWICK: Their weapons like to lightning came and went,
WARWICK: Our soldiers', like the night-owl's lazy flight,
WARWICK: Or like an idle thresher with a flail,
WARWICK: Fell gently down, as if they struck their friends.
WARWICK: I cheer'd them up with justice of our cause,
WARWICK: With promise of high pay and great rewards:
WARWICK: But all in vain, they had no heart to fight,
WARWICK: And we in them no hope to win the day,
WARWICK: So that we fled, the king unto the queen,
WARWICK: Lord George your brother, Norfolk and myself,
WARWICK: In haste, post-haste, are come to join with you:
WARWICK: For in the marches here we heard you were,
WARWICK: Making another head to fight again.
EDWARD: Where is the Duke of Norfolk, gentle Warwick?
EDWARD: And when came George from Burgundy to England?
WARWICK: Some six miles off the duke is with the soldiers,
WARWICK: And for your brother, he was lately sent
WARWICK: From your kind aunt, Duchess of Burgundy,
WARWICK: With aid of soldiers to this needful war.
RICHARD: 'Twas odds, belike, when valiant Warwick fled:
RICHARD: Oft have I heard his praises in pursuit,
RICHARD: But ne'er till now his scandal of retire.
WARWICK: Nor now my scandal, Richard, dost thou hear,
WARWICK: For thou shalt know this strong right hand of mine
WARWICK: Can pluck the diadem from faint Henry's head,
WARWICK: And wring the awful sceptre from his fist,
WARWICK: Were he as famous and as bold in war
WARWICK: As he is famed for mildness, peace, and prayer.
RICHARD: I know it well, Lord Warwick, blame me not:
RICHARD: 'Tis love I bear thy glories makes me speak.
RICHARD: But in this troublous time what's to be done?
RICHARD: Shall we go throw away our coats of steel,
RICHARD: And wrap our bodies in black mourning gowns,
RICHARD: Numbering our Ave-Maries with our beads?
RICHARD: Or shall we on the helmets of our foes
RICHARD: Tell our devotion with revengeful arms?
RICHARD: If for the last, say ay, and to it, lords.
WARWICK: Why, therefore Warwick came to seek you out,
WARWICK: And therefore comes my brother Montague.
WARWICK: Attend me, lords. The proud insulting queen,
WARWICK: With Clifford and the haught Northumberland,
WARWICK: And of their feather many more proud birds,
WARWICK: Have wrought the easy-melting king like wax.
WARWICK: He swore consent to your succession,
WARWICK: His oath enrolled in the parliament,
WARWICK: And now to London all the crew are gone,
WARWICK: To frustrate both his oath and what beside
WARWICK: May make against the house of Lancaster.
WARWICK: Their power, I think, is thirty thousand strong:
WARWICK: Now, if the help of Norfolk and myself,
WARWICK: With all the friends that thou, brave Earl of March,
WARWICK: Amongst the loving Welshmen canst procure,
WARWICK: Will but amount to five and twenty thousand,
WARWICK: Why, Via! to London will we march amain,
WARWICK: And once again bestride our foaming steeds,
WARWICK: And once again cry 'Charge upon our foes!'
WARWICK: But never once again turn back and fly.
RICHARD: Ay, now methinks I hear great Warwick speak:
RICHARD: Ne'er may he live to see a sunshine day,
RICHARD: That cries 'Retire,' if Warwick bid him stay.
EDWARD: Lord Warwick, on thy shoulder will I lean,
EDWARD: And when thou fail'st--as God forbid the hour!--
EDWARD: Must Edward fall, which peril heaven forfend!
WARWICK: No longer Earl of March, but Duke of York:
WARWICK: The next degree is England's royal throne,
WARWICK: For King of England shalt thou be proclaim'd
WARWICK: In every borough as we pass along,
WARWICK: And he that throws not up his cap for joy
WARWICK: Shall for the fault make forfeit of his head.
WARWICK: King Edward, valiant Richard, Montague,
WARWICK: Stay we no longer, dreaming of renown,
WARWICK: But sound the trumpets, and about our task.
RICHARD: Then, Clifford, were thy heart as hard as steel,
RICHARD: As thou hast shown it flinty by thy deeds,
RICHARD: I come to pierce it, or to give thee mine.
EDWARD: Then strike up drums: God and Saint George for us!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
WARWICK: How now! what news?
Messenger: The Duke of Norfolk sends you word by me,
Messenger: The queen is coming with a puissant host,
Messenger: And craves your company for speedy counsel.
WARWICK: Why then it sorts, brave warriors, let's away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before York.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING HENRY VI, QUEEN MARGARET,  PRINCE EDWARD, CLIFFORD, and NORTHUMBERLAND, with drum and trumpets
QUEEN MARGARET: Welcome, my lord, to this brave town of York.
QUEEN MARGARET: Yonder's the head of that arch-enemy
QUEEN MARGARET: That sought to be encompass'd with your crown:
QUEEN MARGARET: Doth not the object cheer your heart, my lord?
KING HENRY VI: Ay, as the rocks cheer them that fear their wreck:
KING HENRY VI: To see this sight, it irks my very soul.
KING HENRY VI: Withhold revenge, dear God! 'tis not my fault,
KING HENRY VI: Nor wittingly have I infringed my vow.
CLIFFORD: My gracious liege, this too much lenity
CLIFFORD: And harmful pity must be laid aside.
CLIFFORD: To whom do lions cast their gentle looks?
CLIFFORD: Not to the beast that would usurp their den.
CLIFFORD: Whose hand is that the forest bear doth lick?
CLIFFORD: Not his that spoils her young before her face.
CLIFFORD: Who 'scapes the lurking serpent's mortal sting?
CLIFFORD: Not he that sets his foot upon her back.
CLIFFORD: The smallest worm will turn being trodden on,
CLIFFORD: And doves will peck in safeguard of their brood.
CLIFFORD: Ambitious York doth level at thy crown,
CLIFFORD: Thou smiling while he knit his angry brows:
CLIFFORD: He, but a duke, would have his son a king,
CLIFFORD: And raise his issue, like a loving sire,
CLIFFORD: Thou, being a king, blest with a goodly son,
CLIFFORD: Didst yield consent to disinherit him,
CLIFFORD: Which argued thee a most unloving father.
CLIFFORD: Unreasonable creatures feed their young,
CLIFFORD: And though man's face be fearful to their eyes,
CLIFFORD: Yet, in protection of their tender ones,
CLIFFORD: Who hath not seen them, even with those wings
CLIFFORD: Which sometime they have used with fearful flight,
CLIFFORD: Make war with him that climb'd unto their nest,
CLIFFORD: Offer their own lives in their young's defence?
CLIFFORD: For shame, my liege, make them your precedent!
CLIFFORD: Were it not pity that this goodly boy
CLIFFORD: Should lose his birthright by his father's fault,
CLIFFORD: And long hereafter say unto his child,
CLIFFORD: 'What my great-grandfather and his grandsire got
CLIFFORD: My careless father fondly gave away'?
CLIFFORD: Ah, what a shame were this! Look on the boy,
CLIFFORD: And let his manly face, which promiseth
CLIFFORD: Successful fortune, steel thy melting heart
CLIFFORD: To hold thine own and leave thine own with him.
KING HENRY VI: Full well hath Clifford play'd the orator,
KING HENRY VI: Inferring arguments of mighty force.
KING HENRY VI: But, Clifford, tell me, didst thou never hear
KING HENRY VI: That things ill-got had ever bad success?
KING HENRY VI: And happy always was it for that son
KING HENRY VI: Whose father for his hoarding went to hell?
KING HENRY VI: I'll leave my son my virtuous deeds behind,
KING HENRY VI: And would my father had left me no more!
KING HENRY VI: For all the rest is held at such a rate
KING HENRY VI: As brings a thousand-fold more care to keep
KING HENRY VI: Than in possession and jot of pleasure.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, cousin York! would thy best friends did know
KING HENRY VI: How it doth grieve me that thy head is here!
QUEEN MARGARET: My lord, cheer up your spirits: our foes are nigh,
QUEEN MARGARET: And this soft courage makes your followers faint.
QUEEN MARGARET: You promised knighthood to our forward son:
QUEEN MARGARET: Unsheathe your sword, and dub him presently.
QUEEN MARGARET: Edward, kneel down.
KING HENRY VI: Edward Plantagenet, arise a knight,
KING HENRY VI: And learn this lesson, draw thy sword in right.
PRINCE: My gracious father, by your kingly leave,
PRINCE: I'll draw it as apparent to the crown,
PRINCE: And in that quarrel use it to the death.
CLIFFORD: Why, that is spoken like a toward prince.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Royal commanders, be in readiness:
Messenger: For with a band of thirty thousand men
Messenger: Comes Warwick, backing of the Duke of York,
Messenger: And in the towns, as they do march along,
Messenger: Proclaims him king, and many fly to him:
Messenger: Darraign your battle, for they are at hand.
CLIFFORD: I would your highness would depart the field:
CLIFFORD: The queen hath best success when you are absent.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, good my lord, and leave us to our fortune.
KING HENRY VI: Why, that's my fortune too, therefore I'll stay.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Be it with resolution then to fight.
PRINCE EDWARD: My royal father, cheer these noble lords
PRINCE EDWARD: And hearten those that fight in your defence:
PRINCE EDWARD: Unsheathe your sword, good father, cry 'Saint George!'
NARRATOR: March. Enter EDWARD, GEORGE, RICHARD, WARWICK, NORFOLK, MONTAGUE, and Soldiers
EDWARD: Now, perjured Henry! wilt thou kneel for grace,
EDWARD: And set thy diadem upon my head,
EDWARD: Or bide the mortal fortune of the field?
QUEEN MARGARET: Go, rate thy minions, proud insulting boy!
QUEEN MARGARET: Becomes it thee to be thus bold in terms
QUEEN MARGARET: Before thy sovereign and thy lawful king?
EDWARD: I am his king, and he should bow his knee,
EDWARD: I was adopted heir by his consent:
EDWARD: Since when, his oath is broke, for, as I hear,
EDWARD: You, that are king, though he do wear the crown,
EDWARD: Have caused him, by new act of parliament,
EDWARD: To blot out me, and put his own son in.
CLIFFORD: And reason too:
CLIFFORD: Who should succeed the father but the son?
RICHARD: Are you there, butcher? O, I cannot speak!
CLIFFORD: Ay, crook-back, here I stand to answer thee,
CLIFFORD: Or any he the proudest of thy sort.
