RICHARD: 'Twas you that kill'd young Rutland, was it not?
CLIFFORD: Ay, and old York, and yet not satisfied.
RICHARD: For God's sake, lords, give signal to the fight.
WARWICK: What say'st thou, Henry, wilt thou yield the crown?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, how now, long-tongued Warwick! dare you speak?
QUEEN MARGARET: When you and I met at Saint Alban's last,
QUEEN MARGARET: Your legs did better service than your hands.
WARWICK: Then 'twas my turn to fly, and now 'tis thine.
CLIFFORD: You said so much before, and yet you fled.
WARWICK: 'Twas not your valour, Clifford, drove me thence.
NORTHUMBERLAND: No, nor your manhood that durst make you stay.
RICHARD: Northumberland, I hold thee reverently.
RICHARD: Break off the parley, for scarce I can refrain
RICHARD: The execution of my big-swoln heart
RICHARD: Upon that Clifford, that cruel child-killer.
CLIFFORD: I slew thy father, call'st thou him a child?
RICHARD: Ay, like a dastard and a treacherous coward,
RICHARD: As thou didst kill our tender brother Rutland,
RICHARD: But ere sunset I'll make thee curse the deed.
KING HENRY VI: Have done with words, my lords, and hear me speak.
QUEEN MARGARET: Defy them then, or else hold close thy lips.
KING HENRY VI: I prithee, give no limits to my tongue:
KING HENRY VI: I am a king, and privileged to speak.
CLIFFORD: My liege, the wound that bred this meeting here
CLIFFORD: Cannot be cured by words, therefore be still.
RICHARD: Then, executioner, unsheathe thy sword:
RICHARD: By him that made us all, I am resolved
RICHARD: that Clifford's manhood lies upon his tongue.
EDWARD: Say, Henry, shall I have my right, or no?
EDWARD: A thousand men have broke their fasts to-day,
EDWARD: That ne'er shall dine unless thou yield the crown.
WARWICK: If thou deny, their blood upon thy head,
WARWICK: For York in justice puts his armour on.
PRINCE EDWARD: If that be right which Warwick says is right,
PRINCE EDWARD: There is no wrong, but every thing is right.
RICHARD: Whoever got thee, there thy mother stands,
RICHARD: For, well I wot, thou hast thy mother's tongue.
QUEEN MARGARET: But thou art neither like thy sire nor dam,
QUEEN MARGARET: But like a foul mis-shapen stigmatic,
QUEEN MARGARET: Mark'd by the destinies to be avoided,
QUEEN MARGARET: As venom toads, or lizards' dreadful stings.
RICHARD: Iron of Naples hid with English gilt,
RICHARD: Whose father bears the title of a king,--
RICHARD: As if a channel should be call'd the sea,--
RICHARD: Shamest thou not, knowing whence thou art extraught,
RICHARD: To let thy tongue detect thy base-born heart?
EDWARD: A wisp of straw were worth a thousand crowns,
EDWARD: To make this shameless callet know herself.
EDWARD: Helen of Greece was fairer far than thou,
EDWARD: Although thy husband may be Menelaus,
EDWARD: And ne'er was Agamemnon's brother wrong'd
EDWARD: By that false woman, as this king by thee.
EDWARD: His father revell'd in the heart of France,
EDWARD: And tamed the king, and made the dauphin stoop,
EDWARD: And had he match'd according to his state,
EDWARD: He might have kept that glory to this day,
EDWARD: But when he took a beggar to his bed,
EDWARD: And graced thy poor sire with his bridal-day,
EDWARD: Even then that sunshine brew'd a shower for him,
EDWARD: That wash'd his father's fortunes forth of France,
EDWARD: And heap'd sedition on his crown at home.
EDWARD: For what hath broach'd this tumult but thy pride?
EDWARD: Hadst thou been meek, our title still had slept,
EDWARD: And we, in pity of the gentle king,
EDWARD: Had slipp'd our claim until another age.
GEORGE: But when we saw our sunshine made thy spring,
GEORGE: And that thy summer bred us no increase,
GEORGE: We set the axe to thy usurping root,
GEORGE: And though the edge hath something hit ourselves,
GEORGE: Yet, know thou, since we have begun to strike,
GEORGE: We'll never leave till we have hewn thee down,
GEORGE: Or bathed thy growing with our heated bloods.
EDWARD: And, in this resolution, I defy thee,
EDWARD: Not willing any longer conference,
EDWARD: Since thou deniest the gentle king to speak.
EDWARD: Sound trumpets! let our bloody colours wave!
EDWARD: And either victory, or else a grave.
QUEEN MARGARET: Stay, Edward.
EDWARD: No, wrangling woman, we'll no longer stay:
EDWARD: These words will cost ten thousand lives this day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A field of battle between Towton and Saxton, in
EDWARD: Yorkshire.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Excursions. Enter WARWICK
WARWICK: Forspent with toil, as runners with a race,
WARWICK: I lay me down a little while to breathe,
WARWICK: For strokes received, and many blows repaid,
WARWICK: Have robb'd my strong-knit sinews of their strength,
WARWICK: And spite of spite needs must I rest awhile.
NARRATOR: Enter EDWARD, running
EDWARD: Smile, gentle heaven! or strike, ungentle death!
EDWARD: For this world frowns, and Edward's sun is clouded.
WARWICK: How now, my lord! what hap? what hope of good?
NARRATOR: Enter GEORGE
GEORGE: Our hap is loss, our hope but sad despair,
GEORGE: Our ranks are broke, and ruin follows us:
GEORGE: What counsel give you? whither shall we fly?
EDWARD: Bootless is flight, they follow us with wings,
EDWARD: And weak we are and cannot shun pursuit.
NARRATOR: Enter RICHARD
RICHARD: Ah, Warwick, why hast thou withdrawn thyself?
RICHARD: Thy brother's blood the thirsty earth hath drunk,
RICHARD: Broach'd with the steely point of Clifford's lance,
RICHARD: And in the very pangs of death he cried,
RICHARD: Like to a dismal clangour heard from far,
RICHARD: 'Warwick, revenge! brother, revenge my death!'
RICHARD: So, underneath the belly of their steeds,
RICHARD: That stain'd their fetlocks in his smoking blood,
RICHARD: The noble gentleman gave up the ghost.
WARWICK: Then let the earth be drunken with our blood:
WARWICK: I'll kill my horse, because I will not fly.
WARWICK: Why stand we like soft-hearted women here,
WARWICK: Wailing our losses, whiles the foe doth rage,
WARWICK: And look upon, as if the tragedy
WARWICK: Were play'd in jest by counterfeiting actors?
WARWICK: Here on my knee I vow to God above,
WARWICK: I'll never pause again, never stand still,
WARWICK: Till either death hath closed these eyes of mine
WARWICK: Or fortune given me measure of revenge.
EDWARD: O Warwick, I do bend my knee with thine,
EDWARD: And in this vow do chain my soul to thine!
EDWARD: And, ere my knee rise from the earth's cold face,
EDWARD: I throw my hands, mine eyes, my heart to thee,
EDWARD: Thou setter up and plucker down of kings,
EDWARD: Beseeching thee, if with they will it stands
EDWARD: That to my foes this body must be prey,
EDWARD: Yet that thy brazen gates of heaven may ope,
EDWARD: And give sweet passage to my sinful soul!
EDWARD: Now, lords, take leave until we meet again,
EDWARD: Where'er it be, in heaven or in earth.
RICHARD: Brother, give me thy hand, and, gentle Warwick,
RICHARD: Let me embrace thee in my weary arms:
RICHARD: I, that did never weep, now melt with woe
RICHARD: That winter should cut off our spring-time so.
WARWICK: Away, away! Once more, sweet lords farewell.
GEORGE: Yet let us all together to our troops,
GEORGE: And give them leave to fly that will not stay,
GEORGE: And call them pillars that will stand to us,
GEORGE: And, if we thrive, promise them such rewards
GEORGE: As victors wear at the Olympian games:
GEORGE: This may plant courage in their quailing breasts,
GEORGE: For yet is hope of life and victory.
GEORGE: Forslow no longer, make we hence amain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Excursions. Enter RICHARD and CLIFFORD
RICHARD: Now, Clifford, I have singled thee alone:
RICHARD: Suppose this arm is for the Duke of York,
RICHARD: And this for Rutland, both bound to revenge,
RICHARD: Wert thou environ'd with a brazen wall.
CLIFFORD: Now, Richard, I am with thee here alone:
CLIFFORD: This is the hand that stabb'd thy father York,
CLIFFORD: And this the hand that slew thy brother Rutland,
CLIFFORD: And here's the heart that triumphs in their death
CLIFFORD: And cheers these hands that slew thy sire and brother
CLIFFORD: To execute the like upon thyself,
CLIFFORD: And so, have at thee!
CLIFFORD: They fight. WARWICK comes, CLIFFORD flies
RICHARD: Nay Warwick, single out some other chase,
RICHARD: For I myself will hunt this wolf to death.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter KING HENRY VI alone
KING HENRY VI: This battle fares like to the morning's war,
KING HENRY VI: When dying clouds contend with growing light,
KING HENRY VI: What time the shepherd, blowing of his nails,
KING HENRY VI: Can neither call it perfect day nor night.
KING HENRY VI: Now sways it this way, like a mighty sea
KING HENRY VI: Forced by the tide to combat with the wind,
KING HENRY VI: Now sways it that way, like the selfsame sea
KING HENRY VI: Forced to retire by fury of the wind:
KING HENRY VI: Sometime the flood prevails, and then the wind,
KING HENRY VI: Now one the better, then another best,
KING HENRY VI: Both tugging to be victors, breast to breast,
KING HENRY VI: Yet neither conqueror nor conquered:
KING HENRY VI: So is the equal of this fell war.
KING HENRY VI: Here on this molehill will I sit me down.
KING HENRY VI: To whom God will, there be the victory!
KING HENRY VI: For Margaret my queen, and Clifford too,
KING HENRY VI: Have chid me from the battle, swearing both
KING HENRY VI: They prosper best of all when I am thence.
KING HENRY VI: Would I were dead! if God's good will were so,
KING HENRY VI: For what is in this world but grief and woe?
KING HENRY VI: O God! methinks it were a happy life,
KING HENRY VI: To be no better than a homely swain,
KING HENRY VI: To sit upon a hill, as I do now,
KING HENRY VI: To carve out dials quaintly, point by point,
KING HENRY VI: Thereby to see the minutes how they run,
KING HENRY VI: How many make the hour full complete,
KING HENRY VI: How many hours bring about the day,
KING HENRY VI: How many days will finish up the year,
KING HENRY VI: How many years a mortal man may live.
KING HENRY VI: When this is known, then to divide the times:
KING HENRY VI: So many hours must I tend my flock,
KING HENRY VI: So many hours must I take my rest,
KING HENRY VI: So many hours must I contemplate,
KING HENRY VI: So many hours must I sport myself,
KING HENRY VI: So many days my ewes have been with young,
KING HENRY VI: So many weeks ere the poor fools will ean:
KING HENRY VI: So many years ere I shall shear the fleece:
KING HENRY VI: So minutes, hours, days, months, and years,
KING HENRY VI: Pass'd over to the end they were created,
KING HENRY VI: Would bring white hairs unto a quiet grave.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, what a life were this! how sweet! how lovely!
KING HENRY VI: Gives not the hawthorn-bush a sweeter shade
KING HENRY VI: To shepherds looking on their silly sheep,
KING HENRY VI: Than doth a rich embroider'd canopy
KING HENRY VI: To kings that fear their subjects' treachery?
KING HENRY VI: O, yes, it doth, a thousand-fold it doth.
KING HENRY VI: And to conclude, the shepherd's homely curds,
KING HENRY VI: His cold thin drink out of his leather bottle.
KING HENRY VI: His wonted sleep under a fresh tree's shade,
KING HENRY VI: All which secure and sweetly he enjoys,
KING HENRY VI: Is far beyond a prince's delicates,
KING HENRY VI: His viands sparkling in a golden cup,
KING HENRY VI: His body couched in a curious bed,
KING HENRY VI: When care, mistrust, and treason waits on him.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter a Son that has killed his father, dragging in the dead body
Son: Ill blows the wind that profits nobody.
Son: This man, whom hand to hand I slew in fight,
Son: May be possessed with some store of crowns,
Son: And I, that haply take them from him now,
Son: May yet ere night yield both my life and them
Son: To some man else, as this dead man doth me.
Son: Who's this? O God! it is my father's face,
Son: Whom in this conflict I unwares have kill'd.
Son: O heavy times, begetting such events!
Son: From London by the king was I press'd forth,
Son: My father, being the Earl of Warwick's man,
Son: Came on the part of York, press'd by his master,
Son: And I, who at his hands received my life, him
Son: Have by my hands of life bereaved him.
Son: Pardon me, God, I knew not what I did!
Son: And pardon, father, for I knew not thee!
Son: My tears shall wipe away these bloody marks,
Son: And no more words till they have flow'd their fill.
KING HENRY VI: O piteous spectacle! O bloody times!
KING HENRY VI: Whiles lions war and battle for their dens,
KING HENRY VI: Poor harmless lambs abide their enmity.
KING HENRY VI: Weep, wretched man, I'll aid thee tear for tear,
KING HENRY VI: And let our hearts and eyes, like civil war,
KING HENRY VI: Be blind with tears, and break o'ercharged with grief.
NARRATOR: Enter a Father that has killed his son, bringing in the body
Father: Thou that so stoutly hast resisted me,
Father: Give me thy gold, if thou hast any gold:
Father: For I have bought it with an hundred blows.
Father: But let me see: is this our foeman's face?
Father: Ah, no, no, no, it is mine only son!
Father: Ah, boy, if any life be left in thee,
Father: Throw up thine eye! see, see what showers arise,
Father: Blown with the windy tempest of my heart,
Father: Upon thy words, that kill mine eye and heart!
Father: O, pity, God, this miserable age!
Father: What stratagems, how fell, how butcherly,
Father: Erroneous, mutinous and unnatural,
Father: This deadly quarrel daily doth beget!
Father: O boy, thy father gave thee life too soon,
Father: And hath bereft thee of thy life too late!
KING HENRY VI: Woe above woe! grief more than common grief!
KING HENRY VI: O that my death would stay these ruthful deeds!
KING HENRY VI: O pity, pity, gentle heaven, pity!
KING HENRY VI: The red rose and the white are on his face,
KING HENRY VI: The fatal colours of our striving houses:
KING HENRY VI: The one his purple blood right well resembles,
KING HENRY VI: The other his pale cheeks, methinks, presenteth:
KING HENRY VI: Wither one rose, and let the other flourish,
KING HENRY VI: If you contend, a thousand lives must wither.
Son: How will my mother for a father's death
Son: Take on with me and ne'er be satisfied!
Father: How will my wife for slaughter of my son
Father: Shed seas of tears and ne'er be satisfied!
KING HENRY VI: How will the country for these woful chances
KING HENRY VI: Misthink the king and not be satisfied!
Son: Was ever son so rued a father's death?
Father: Was ever father so bemoan'd his son?
KING HENRY VI: Was ever king so grieved for subjects' woe?
KING HENRY VI: Much is your sorrow, mine ten times so much.
Son: I'll bear thee hence, where I may weep my fill.
NARRATOR: Exit with the body
Father: These arms of mine shall be thy winding-sheet,
Father: My heart, sweet boy, shall be thy sepulchre,
Father: For from my heart thine image ne'er shall go,
Father: My sighing breast shall be thy funeral bell,
Father: And so obsequious will thy father be,
Father: Even for the loss of thee, having no more,
Father: As Priam was for all his valiant sons.
Father: I'll bear thee hence, and let them fight that will,
Father: For I have murdered where I should not kill.
NARRATOR: Exit with the body
KING HENRY VI: Sad-hearted men, much overgone with care,
KING HENRY VI: Here sits a king more woful than you are.
KING HENRY VI: Alarums: excursions. Enter QUEEN MARGARET, PRINCE EDWARD, and EXETER
PRINCE EDWARD: Fly, father, fly! for all your friends are fled,
PRINCE EDWARD: And Warwick rages like a chafed bull:
PRINCE EDWARD: Away! for death doth hold us in pursuit.
QUEEN MARGARET: Mount you, my lord, towards Berwick post amain:
QUEEN MARGARET: Edward and Richard, like a brace of greyhounds
QUEEN MARGARET: Having the fearful flying hare in sight,
QUEEN MARGARET: With fiery eyes sparkling for very wrath,
QUEEN MARGARET: And bloody steel grasp'd in their ireful hands,
QUEEN MARGARET: Are at our backs, and therefore hence amain.
EXETER: Away! for vengeance comes along with them:
EXETER: Nay, stay not to expostulate, make speed,
EXETER: Or else come after: I'll away before.
KING HENRY VI: Nay, take me with thee, good sweet Exeter:
KING HENRY VI: Not that I fear to stay, but love to go
KING HENRY VI: Whither the queen intends. Forward, away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: A loud alarum. Enter CLIFFORD, wounded
CLIFFORD: Here burns my candle out, ay, here it dies,
CLIFFORD: Which, whiles it lasted, gave King Henry light.
CLIFFORD: O Lancaster, I fear thy overthrow
CLIFFORD: More than my body's parting with my soul!
CLIFFORD: My love and fear glued many friends to thee,
CLIFFORD: And, now I fall, thy tough commixture melts.
CLIFFORD: Impairing Henry, strengthening misproud York,
CLIFFORD: The common people swarm like summer flies,
CLIFFORD: And whither fly the gnats but to the sun?
CLIFFORD: And who shines now but Henry's enemies?
CLIFFORD: O Phoebus, hadst thou never given consent
CLIFFORD: That Phaethon should cheque thy fiery steeds,
CLIFFORD: Thy burning car never had scorch'd the earth!
CLIFFORD: And, Henry, hadst thou sway'd as kings should do,
CLIFFORD: Or as thy father and his father did,
CLIFFORD: Giving no ground unto the house of York,
CLIFFORD: They never then had sprung like summer flies,
CLIFFORD: I and ten thousand in this luckless realm
CLIFFORD: Had left no mourning widows for our death,
CLIFFORD: And thou this day hadst kept thy chair in peace.
CLIFFORD: For what doth cherish weeds but gentle air?
CLIFFORD: And what makes robbers bold but too much lenity?
CLIFFORD: Bootless are plaints, and cureless are my wounds,
CLIFFORD: No way to fly, nor strength to hold out flight:
CLIFFORD: The foe is merciless, and will not pity,
CLIFFORD: For at their hands I have deserved no pity.
CLIFFORD: The air hath got into my deadly wounds,
CLIFFORD: And much effuse of blood doth make me faint.
CLIFFORD: Come, York and Richard, Warwick and the rest,
CLIFFORD: I stabb'd your fathers' bosoms, split my breast.
NARRATOR: He faints
NARRATOR: Alarum and retreat. Enter EDWARD, GEORGE, RICHARD, MONTAGUE, WARWICK, and Soldiers
EDWARD: Now breathe we, lords: good fortune bids us pause,
EDWARD: And smooth the frowns of war with peaceful looks.
EDWARD: Some troops pursue the bloody-minded queen,
EDWARD: That led calm Henry, though he were a king,
EDWARD: As doth a sail, fill'd with a fretting gust,
EDWARD: Command an argosy to stem the waves.
EDWARD: But think you, lords, that Clifford fled with them?
WARWICK: No, 'tis impossible he should escape,
WARWICK: For, though before his face I speak the words
WARWICK: Your brother Richard mark'd him for the grave:
WARWICK: And wheresoe'er he is, he's surely dead.
NARRATOR: CLIFFORD groans, and dies
EDWARD: Whose soul is that which takes her heavy leave?
RICHARD: A deadly groan, like life and death's departing.
EDWARD: See who it is: and, now the battle's ended,
EDWARD: If friend or foe, let him be gently used.
RICHARD: Revoke that doom of mercy, for 'tis Clifford,
RICHARD: Who not contented that he lopp'd the branch
RICHARD: In hewing Rutland when his leaves put forth,
RICHARD: But set his murdering knife unto the root
RICHARD: From whence that tender spray did sweetly spring,
RICHARD: I mean our princely father, Duke of York.
WARWICK: From off the gates of York fetch down the head,
WARWICK: Your father's head, which Clifford placed there,
WARWICK: Instead whereof let this supply the room:
WARWICK: Measure for measure must be answered.
EDWARD: Bring forth that fatal screech-owl to our house,
EDWARD: That nothing sung but death to us and ours:
EDWARD: Now death shall stop his dismal threatening sound,
EDWARD: And his ill-boding tongue no more shall speak.
WARWICK: I think his understanding is bereft.
WARWICK: Speak, Clifford, dost thou know who speaks to thee?
WARWICK: Dark cloudy death o'ershades his beams of life,
WARWICK: And he nor sees nor hears us what we say.
RICHARD: O, would he did! and so perhaps he doth:
RICHARD: 'Tis but his policy to counterfeit,
RICHARD: Because he would avoid such bitter taunts
RICHARD: Which in the time of death he gave our father.
GEORGE: If so thou think'st, vex him with eager words.
RICHARD: Clifford, ask mercy and obtain no grace.
EDWARD: Clifford, repent in bootless penitence.
WARWICK: Clifford, devise excuses for thy faults.
GEORGE: While we devise fell tortures for thy faults.
RICHARD: Thou didst love York, and I am son to York.
EDWARD: Thou pitied'st Rutland, I will pity thee.
GEORGE: Where's Captain Margaret, to fence you now?
WARWICK: They mock thee, Clifford: swear as thou wast wont.
RICHARD: What, not an oath? nay, then the world goes hard
RICHARD: When Clifford cannot spare his friends an oath.
RICHARD: I know by that he's dead, and, by my soul,
RICHARD: If this right hand would buy two hour's life,
RICHARD: That I in all despite might rail at him,
RICHARD: This hand should chop it off, and with the
RICHARD: issuing blood
RICHARD: Stifle the villain whose unstanched thirst
RICHARD: York and young Rutland could not satisfy.
WARWICK: Ay, but he's dead: off with the traitor's head,
WARWICK: And rear it in the place your father's stands.
WARWICK: And now to London with triumphant march,
WARWICK: There to be crowned England's royal king:
WARWICK: From whence shall Warwick cut the sea to France,
WARWICK: And ask the Lady Bona for thy queen:
WARWICK: So shalt thou sinew both these lands together,
WARWICK: And, having France thy friend, thou shalt not dread
WARWICK: The scatter'd foe that hopes to rise again,
WARWICK: For though they cannot greatly sting to hurt,
WARWICK: Yet look to have them buzz to offend thine ears.
WARWICK: First will I see the coronation,
WARWICK: And then to Brittany I'll cross the sea,
WARWICK: To effect this marriage, so it please my lord.
EDWARD: Even as thou wilt, sweet Warwick, let it be,
EDWARD: For in thy shoulder do I build my seat,
EDWARD: And never will I undertake the thing
EDWARD: Wherein thy counsel and consent is wanting.
EDWARD: Richard, I will create thee Duke of Gloucester,
EDWARD: And George, of Clarence: Warwick, as ourself,
EDWARD: Shall do and undo as him pleaseth best.
RICHARD: Let me be Duke of Clarence, George of Gloucester,
RICHARD: For Gloucester's dukedom is too ominous.
WARWICK: Tut, that's a foolish observation:
WARWICK: Richard, be Duke of Gloucester. Now to London,
WARWICK: To see these honours in possession.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A forest in the north of England.
NARRATOR: Enter two Keepers, with cross-bows in their hands
First Keeper: Under this thick-grown brake we'll shroud ourselves,
First Keeper: For through this laund anon the deer will come,
First Keeper: And in this covert will we make our stand,
First Keeper: Culling the principal of all the deer.
Second Keeper: I'll stay above the hill, so both may shoot.
First Keeper: That cannot be, the noise of thy cross-bow
First Keeper: Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost.
First Keeper: Here stand we both, and aim we at the best:
First Keeper: And, for the time shall not seem tedious,
First Keeper: I'll tell thee what befell me on a day
First Keeper: In this self-place where now we mean to stand.
Second Keeper: Here comes a man, let's stay till he be past.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI, disguised, with a prayerbook
KING HENRY VI: From Scotland am I stol'n, even of pure love,
KING HENRY VI: To greet mine own land with my wishful sight.
KING HENRY VI: No, Harry, Harry, 'tis no land of thine,
KING HENRY VI: Thy place is fill'd, thy sceptre wrung from thee,
KING HENRY VI: Thy balm wash'd off wherewith thou wast anointed:
KING HENRY VI: No bending knee will call thee Caesar now,
KING HENRY VI: No humble suitors press to speak for right,
KING HENRY VI: No, not a man comes for redress of thee,
KING HENRY VI: For how can I help them, and not myself?
First Keeper: Ay, here's a deer whose skin's a keeper's fee:
First Keeper: This is the quondam king, let's seize upon him.
KING HENRY VI: Let me embrace thee, sour adversity,
KING HENRY VI: For wise men say it is the wisest course.
Second Keeper: Why linger we? let us lay hands upon him.
First Keeper: Forbear awhile, we'll hear a little more.
KING HENRY VI: My queen and son are gone to France for aid,
KING HENRY VI: And, as I hear, the great commanding Warwick
KING HENRY VI: Is thither gone, to crave the French king's sister
KING HENRY VI: To wife for Edward: if this news be true,
KING HENRY VI: Poor queen and son, your labour is but lost,
KING HENRY VI: For Warwick is a subtle orator,
KING HENRY VI: And Lewis a prince soon won with moving words.
KING HENRY VI: By this account then Margaret may win him,
KING HENRY VI: For she's a woman to be pitied much:
KING HENRY VI: Her sighs will make a battery in his breast,
KING HENRY VI: Her tears will pierce into a marble heart,
KING HENRY VI: The tiger will be mild whiles she doth mourn,
KING HENRY VI: And Nero will be tainted with remorse,
KING HENRY VI: To hear and see her plaints, her brinish tears.
KING HENRY VI: Ay, but she's come to beg, Warwick to give,
KING HENRY VI: She, on his left side, craving aid for Henry,
KING HENRY VI: He, on his right, asking a wife for Edward.
KING HENRY VI: She weeps, and says her Henry is deposed,
KING HENRY VI: He smiles, and says his Edward is install'd,
KING HENRY VI: That she, poor wretch, for grief can speak no more,
KING HENRY VI: Whiles Warwick tells his title, smooths the wrong,
KING HENRY VI: Inferreth arguments of mighty strength,
KING HENRY VI: And in conclusion wins the king from her,
KING HENRY VI: With promise of his sister, and what else,
KING HENRY VI: To strengthen and support King Edward's place.
KING HENRY VI: O Margaret, thus 'twill be, and thou, poor soul,
KING HENRY VI: Art then forsaken, as thou went'st forlorn!
Second Keeper: Say, what art thou that talk'st of kings and queens?
KING HENRY VI: More than I seem, and less than I was born to:
KING HENRY VI: A man at least, for less I should not be,
KING HENRY VI: And men may talk of kings, and why not I?
Second Keeper: Ay, but thou talk'st as if thou wert a king.
KING HENRY VI: Why, so I am, in mind, and that's enough.
Second Keeper: But, if thou be a king, where is thy crown?
KING HENRY VI: My crown is in my heart, not on my head,
KING HENRY VI: Not decked with diamonds and Indian stones,
KING HENRY VI: Nor to be seen: my crown is called content:
KING HENRY VI: A crown it is that seldom kings enjoy.
Second Keeper: Well, if you be a king crown'd with content,
Second Keeper: Your crown content and you must be contented
Second Keeper: To go along with us, for as we think,
Second Keeper: You are the king King Edward hath deposed,
Second Keeper: And we his subjects sworn in all allegiance
Second Keeper: Will apprehend you as his enemy.
KING HENRY VI: But did you never swear, and break an oath?
Second Keeper: No, never such an oath, nor will not now.
KING HENRY VI: Where did you dwell when I was King of England?
Second Keeper: Here in this country, where we now remain.
KING HENRY VI: I was anointed king at nine months old,
KING HENRY VI: My father and my grandfather were kings,
KING HENRY VI: And you were sworn true subjects unto me:
KING HENRY VI: And tell me, then, have you not broke your oaths?
First Keeper: No,
First Keeper: For we were subjects but while you were king.
KING HENRY VI: Why, am I dead? do I not breathe a man?
KING HENRY VI: Ah, simple men, you know not what you swear!
KING HENRY VI: Look, as I blow this feather from my face,
KING HENRY VI: And as the air blows it to me again,
KING HENRY VI: Obeying with my wind when I do blow,
KING HENRY VI: And yielding to another when it blows,
KING HENRY VI: Commanded always by the greater gust,
KING HENRY VI: Such is the lightness of you common men.
KING HENRY VI: But do not break your oaths, for of that sin
KING HENRY VI: My mild entreaty shall not make you guilty.
KING HENRY VI: Go where you will, the king shall be commanded,
KING HENRY VI: And be you kings, command, and I'll obey.
First Keeper: We are true subjects to the king, King Edward.
KING HENRY VI: So would you be again to Henry,
KING HENRY VI: If he were seated as King Edward is.
First Keeper: We charge you, in God's name, and the king's,
First Keeper: To go with us unto the officers.
KING HENRY VI: In God's name, lead, your king's name be obey'd:
KING HENRY VI: And what God will, that let your king perform,
KING HENRY VI: And what he will, I humbly yield unto.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, CLARENCE, and LADY GREY
KING EDWARD IV: Brother of Gloucester, at Saint Alban's field
KING EDWARD IV: This lady's husband, Sir Richard Grey, was slain,
KING EDWARD IV: His lands then seized on by the conqueror:
KING EDWARD IV: Her suit is now to repossess those lands,
KING EDWARD IV: Which we in justice cannot well deny,
KING EDWARD IV: Because in quarrel of the house of York
KING EDWARD IV: The worthy gentleman did lose his life.
GLOUCESTER: Your highness shall do well to grant her suit,
GLOUCESTER: It were dishonour to deny it her.
KING EDWARD IV: It were no less, but yet I'll make a pause.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  Yea, is it so?
GLOUCESTER: I see the lady hath a thing to grant,
GLOUCESTER: Before the king will grant her humble suit.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  He knows the game: how true
CLARENCE: he keeps the wind!
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  Silence!
KING EDWARD IV: Widow, we will consider of your suit,
KING EDWARD IV: And come some other time to know our mind.
LADY GREY: Right gracious lord, I cannot brook delay:
LADY GREY: May it please your highness to resolve me now,
LADY GREY: And what your pleasure is, shall satisfy me.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  Ay, widow? then I'll warrant
GLOUCESTER: you all your lands,
GLOUCESTER: An if what pleases him shall pleasure you.
GLOUCESTER: Fight closer, or, good faith, you'll catch a blow.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  I fear her not, unless she
CLARENCE: chance to fall.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE] God forbid that! for he'll
GLOUCESTER: take vantages.
KING EDWARD IV: How many children hast thou, widow? tell me.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  I think he means to beg a
CLARENCE: child of her.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  Nay, whip me then: he'll rather
GLOUCESTER: give her two.
LADY GREY: Three, my most gracious lord.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  You shall have four, if you'll
GLOUCESTER: be ruled by him.
KING EDWARD IV: 'Twere pity they should lose their father's lands.
LADY GREY: Be pitiful, dread lord, and grant it then.
KING EDWARD IV: Lords, give us leave: I'll try this widow's wit.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  Ay, good leave have you, for
GLOUCESTER: you will have leave,
GLOUCESTER: Till youth take leave and leave you to the crutch.
NARRATOR: GLOUCESTER and CLARENCE retire
KING EDWARD IV: Now tell me, madam, do you love your children?
LADY GREY: Ay, full as dearly as I love myself.
KING EDWARD IV: And would you not do much to do them good?
LADY GREY: To do them good, I would sustain some harm.
KING EDWARD IV: Then get your husband's lands, to do them good.
LADY GREY: Therefore I came unto your majesty.
KING EDWARD IV: I'll tell you how these lands are to be got.
LADY GREY: So shall you bind me to your highness' service.
KING EDWARD IV: What service wilt thou do me, if I give them?
LADY GREY: What you command, that rests in me to do.
KING EDWARD IV: But you will take exceptions to my boon.
LADY GREY: No, gracious lord, except I cannot do it.
KING EDWARD IV: Ay, but thou canst do what I mean to ask.
LADY GREY: Why, then I will do what your grace commands.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  He plies her hard, and much rain
GLOUCESTER: wears the marble.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  As red as fire! nay, then
CLARENCE: her wax must melt.
LADY GREY: Why stops my lord, shall I not hear my task?
KING EDWARD IV: An easy task, 'tis but to love a king.
LADY GREY: That's soon perform'd, because I am a subject.
KING EDWARD IV: Why, then, thy husband's lands I freely give thee.
LADY GREY: I take my leave with many thousand thanks.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  The match is made, she seals it
GLOUCESTER: with a curtsy.
KING EDWARD IV: But stay thee, 'tis the fruits of love I mean.
LADY GREY: The fruits of love I mean, my loving liege.
KING EDWARD IV: Ay, but, I fear me, in another sense.
KING EDWARD IV: What love, think'st thou, I sue so much to get?
LADY GREY: My love till death, my humble thanks, my prayers,
LADY GREY: That love which virtue begs and virtue grants.
KING EDWARD IV: No, by my troth, I did not mean such love.
LADY GREY: Why, then you mean not as I thought you did.
KING EDWARD IV: But now you partly may perceive my mind.
LADY GREY: My mind will never grant what I perceive
LADY GREY: Your highness aims at, if I aim aright.
KING EDWARD IV: To tell thee plain, I aim to lie with thee.
LADY GREY: To tell you plain, I had rather lie in prison.
KING EDWARD IV: Why, then thou shalt not have thy husband's lands.
LADY GREY: Why, then mine honesty shall be my dower,
LADY GREY: For by that loss I will not purchase them.
KING EDWARD IV: Therein thou wrong'st thy children mightily.
LADY GREY: Herein your highness wrongs both them and me.
LADY GREY: But, mighty lord, this merry inclination
LADY GREY: Accords not with the sadness of my suit:
LADY GREY: Please you dismiss me either with 'ay' or 'no.'
KING EDWARD IV: Ay, if thou wilt say 'ay' to my request,
KING EDWARD IV: No if thou dost say 'no' to my demand.
LADY GREY: Then, no, my lord. My suit is at an end.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  The widow likes him not, she
GLOUCESTER: knits her brows.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  He is the bluntest wooer in
CLARENCE: Christendom.
KING EDWARD IV: [Aside]  Her looks do argue her replete with modesty,
KING EDWARD IV: Her words do show her wit incomparable,
KING EDWARD IV: All her perfections challenge sovereignty:
KING EDWARD IV: One way or other, she is for a king,
KING EDWARD IV: And she shall be my love, or else my queen.--
KING EDWARD IV: Say that King Edward take thee for his queen?
LADY GREY: 'Tis better said than done, my gracious lord:
LADY GREY: I am a subject fit to jest withal,
LADY GREY: But far unfit to be a sovereign.
KING EDWARD IV: Sweet widow, by my state I swear to thee
KING EDWARD IV: I speak no more than what my soul intends,
KING EDWARD IV: And that is, to enjoy thee for my love.
LADY GREY: And that is more than I will yield unto:
LADY GREY: I know I am too mean to be your queen,
LADY GREY: And yet too good to be your concubine.
KING EDWARD IV: You cavil, widow: I did mean, my queen.
LADY GREY: 'Twill grieve your grace my sons should call you father.
KING EDWARD IV: No more than when my daughters call thee mother.
KING EDWARD IV: Thou art a widow, and thou hast some children,
KING EDWARD IV: And, by God's mother, I, being but a bachelor,
KING EDWARD IV: Have other some: why, 'tis a happy thing
KING EDWARD IV: To be the father unto many sons.
KING EDWARD IV: Answer no more, for thou shalt be my queen.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside to CLARENCE]  The ghostly father now hath done
GLOUCESTER: his shrift.
CLARENCE: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]  When he was made a shriver,
CLARENCE: 'twas for shift.
KING EDWARD IV: Brothers, you muse what chat we two have had.
GLOUCESTER: The widow likes it not, for she looks very sad.
KING EDWARD IV: You'll think it strange if I should marry her.
CLARENCE: To whom, my lord?
KING EDWARD IV: Why, Clarence, to myself.
GLOUCESTER: That would be ten days' wonder at the least.
CLARENCE: That's a day longer than a wonder lasts.
GLOUCESTER: By so much is the wonder in extremes.
KING EDWARD IV: Well, jest on, brothers: I can tell you both
KING EDWARD IV: Her suit is granted for her husband's lands.
NARRATOR: Enter a Nobleman
Nobleman: My gracious lord, Henry your foe is taken,
Nobleman: And brought your prisoner to your palace gate.
KING EDWARD IV: See that he be convey'd unto the Tower:
KING EDWARD IV: And go we, brothers, to the man that took him,
KING EDWARD IV: To question of his apprehension.
KING EDWARD IV: Widow, go you along. Lords, use her honourably.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Ay, Edward will use women honourably.
GLOUCESTER: Would he were wasted, marrow, bones and all,
GLOUCESTER: That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring,
GLOUCESTER: To cross me from the golden time I look for!
GLOUCESTER: And yet, between my soul's desire and me--
GLOUCESTER: The lustful Edward's title buried--
GLOUCESTER: Is Clarence, Henry, and his son young Edward,
GLOUCESTER: And all the unlook'd for issue of their bodies,
GLOUCESTER: To take their rooms, ere I can place myself:
GLOUCESTER: A cold premeditation for my purpose!
GLOUCESTER: Why, then, I do but dream on sovereignty,
GLOUCESTER: Like one that stands upon a promontory,
GLOUCESTER: And spies a far-off shore where he would tread,
GLOUCESTER: Wishing his foot were equal with his eye,
GLOUCESTER: And chides the sea that sunders him from thence,
GLOUCESTER: Saying, he'll lade it dry to have his way:
GLOUCESTER: So do I wish the crown, being so far off,
GLOUCESTER: And so I chide the means that keeps me from it,
GLOUCESTER: And so I say, I'll cut the causes off,
GLOUCESTER: Flattering me with impossibilities.
GLOUCESTER: My eye's too quick, my heart o'erweens too much,
GLOUCESTER: Unless my hand and strength could equal them.
GLOUCESTER: Well, say there is no kingdom then for Richard,
GLOUCESTER: What other pleasure can the world afford?
GLOUCESTER: I'll make my heaven in a lady's lap,
GLOUCESTER: And deck my body in gay ornaments,
GLOUCESTER: And witch sweet ladies with my words and looks.
GLOUCESTER: O miserable thought! and more unlikely
GLOUCESTER: Than to accomplish twenty golden crowns!
GLOUCESTER: Why, love forswore me in my  mother's womb:
GLOUCESTER: And, for I should not deal in her soft laws,
GLOUCESTER: She did corrupt frail nature with some bribe,
GLOUCESTER: To shrink mine arm up like a wither'd shrub,
GLOUCESTER: To make an envious mountain on my back,
GLOUCESTER: Where sits deformity to mock my body,
GLOUCESTER: To shape my legs of an unequal size,
GLOUCESTER: To disproportion me in every part,
GLOUCESTER: Like to a chaos, or an unlick'd bear-whelp
GLOUCESTER: That carries no impression like the dam.
GLOUCESTER: And am I then a man to be beloved?
GLOUCESTER: O monstrous fault, to harbour such a thought!
GLOUCESTER: Then, since this earth affords no joy to me,
GLOUCESTER: But to command, to cheque, to o'erbear such
GLOUCESTER: As are of better person than myself,
GLOUCESTER: I'll make my heaven to dream upon the crown,
GLOUCESTER: And, whiles I live, to account this world but hell,
GLOUCESTER: Until my mis-shaped trunk that bears this head
GLOUCESTER: Be round impaled with a glorious crown.
GLOUCESTER: And yet I know not how to get the crown,
GLOUCESTER: For many lives stand between me and home:
GLOUCESTER: And I,--like one lost in a thorny wood,
GLOUCESTER: That rends the thorns and is rent with the thorns,
GLOUCESTER: Seeking a way and straying from the way,
GLOUCESTER: Not knowing how to find the open air,
GLOUCESTER: But toiling desperately to find it out,--
GLOUCESTER: Torment myself to catch the English crown:
GLOUCESTER: And from that torment I will free myself,
GLOUCESTER: Or hew my way out with a bloody axe.
GLOUCESTER: Why, I can smile, and murder whiles I smile,
GLOUCESTER: And cry 'Content' to that which grieves my heart,
GLOUCESTER: And wet my cheeks with artificial tears,
GLOUCESTER: And frame my face to all occasions.
GLOUCESTER: I'll drown more sailors than the mermaid shall,
GLOUCESTER: I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk,
GLOUCESTER: I'll play the orator as well as Nestor,
GLOUCESTER: Deceive more slily than Ulysses could,
GLOUCESTER: And, like a Sinon, take another Troy.
GLOUCESTER: I can add colours to the chameleon,
GLOUCESTER: Change shapes with Proteus for advantages,
GLOUCESTER: And set the murderous Machiavel to school.
GLOUCESTER: Can I do this, and cannot get a crown?
GLOUCESTER: Tut, were it farther off, I'll pluck it down.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. France. KING LEWIS XI's palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING LEWIS XI, his sister BONA,  his Admiral, called BOURBON, PRINCE EDWARD, QUEEN  MARGARET, and OXFORD. KING LEWIS XI sits, and riseth up again
KING LEWIS XI: Fair Queen of England, worthy Margaret,
KING LEWIS XI: Sit down with us: it ill befits thy state
KING LEWIS XI: And birth, that thou shouldst stand while Lewis doth sit.
QUEEN MARGARET: No, mighty King of France: now Margaret
QUEEN MARGARET: Must strike her sail and learn awhile to serve
QUEEN MARGARET: Where kings command. I was, I must confess,
QUEEN MARGARET: Great Albion's queen in former golden days:
QUEEN MARGARET: But now mischance hath trod my title down,
QUEEN MARGARET: And with dishonour laid me on the ground,
QUEEN MARGARET: Where I must take like seat unto my fortune,
QUEEN MARGARET: And to my humble seat conform myself.
KING LEWIS XI: Why, say, fair queen, whence springs this deep despair?
QUEEN MARGARET: From such a cause as fills mine eyes with tears
QUEEN MARGARET: And stops my tongue, while heart is drown'd in cares.
KING LEWIS XI: Whate'er it be, be thou still like thyself,
KING LEWIS XI: And sit thee by our side:
NARRATOR: Seats her by him
KING LEWIS XI: Yield not thy neck
KING LEWIS XI: To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind
KING LEWIS XI: Still ride in triumph over all mischance.
KING LEWIS XI: Be plain, Queen Margaret, and tell thy grief,
KING LEWIS XI: It shall be eased, if France can yield relief.
QUEEN MARGARET: Those gracious words revive my drooping thoughts
QUEEN MARGARET: And give my tongue-tied sorrows leave to speak.
QUEEN MARGARET: Now, therefore, be it known to noble Lewis,
QUEEN MARGARET: That Henry, sole possessor of my love,
QUEEN MARGARET: Is of a king become a banish'd man,
QUEEN MARGARET: And forced to live in Scotland a forlorn,
QUEEN MARGARET: While proud ambitious Edward Duke of York
QUEEN MARGARET: Usurps the regal title and the seat
QUEEN MARGARET: Of England's true-anointed lawful king.
QUEEN MARGARET: This is the cause that I, poor Margaret,
QUEEN MARGARET: With this my son, Prince Edward, Henry's heir,
QUEEN MARGARET: Am come to crave thy just and lawful aid,
QUEEN MARGARET: And if thou fail us, all our hope is done:
QUEEN MARGARET: Scotland hath will to help, but cannot help,
QUEEN MARGARET: Our people and our peers are both misled,
QUEEN MARGARET: Our treasures seized, our soldiers put to flight,
QUEEN MARGARET: And, as thou seest, ourselves in heavy plight.
KING LEWIS XI: Renowned queen, with patience calm the storm,
KING LEWIS XI: While we bethink a means to break it off.
QUEEN MARGARET: The more we stay, the stronger grows our foe.
KING LEWIS XI: The more I stay, the more I'll succor thee.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, but impatience waiteth on true sorrow.
QUEEN MARGARET: And see where comes the breeder of my sorrow!
NARRATOR: Enter WARWICK
KING LEWIS XI: What's he approacheth boldly to our presence?
QUEEN MARGARET: Our Earl of Warwick, Edward's greatest friend.
KING LEWIS XI: Welcome, brave Warwick! What brings thee to France?
NARRATOR: He descends. She ariseth
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, now begins a second storm to rise,
QUEEN MARGARET: For this is he that moves both wind and tide.
WARWICK: From worthy Edward, King of Albion,
WARWICK: My lord and sovereign, and thy vowed friend,
WARWICK: I come, in kindness and unfeigned love,
WARWICK: First, to do greetings to thy royal person,
WARWICK: And then to crave a league of amity,
WARWICK: And lastly, to confirm that amity
WARWICK: With a nuptial knot, if thou vouchsafe to grant
WARWICK: That virtuous Lady Bona, thy fair sister,
WARWICK: To England's king in lawful marriage.
QUEEN MARGARET: [Aside]  If that go forward, Henry's hope is done.
WARWICK: [To BONA]  And, gracious madam, in our king's behalf,
WARWICK: I am commanded, with your leave and favour,
WARWICK: Humbly to kiss your hand, and with my tongue
WARWICK: To tell the passion of my sovereign's heart,
WARWICK: Where fame, late entering at his heedful ears,
WARWICK: Hath placed thy beauty's image and thy virtue.
QUEEN MARGARET: King Lewis and Lady Bona, hear me speak,
QUEEN MARGARET: Before you answer Warwick. His demand
QUEEN MARGARET: Springs not from Edward's well-meant honest love,
QUEEN MARGARET: But from deceit bred by necessity,
QUEEN MARGARET: For how can tyrants safely govern home,
QUEEN MARGARET: Unless abroad they purchase great alliance?
QUEEN MARGARET: To prove him tyrant this reason may suffice,
QUEEN MARGARET: That Henry liveth still: but were he dead,
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet here Prince Edward stands, King Henry's son.
QUEEN MARGARET: Look, therefore, Lewis, that by this league and marriage
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou draw not on thy danger and dishonour,
QUEEN MARGARET: For though usurpers sway the rule awhile,
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet heavens are just, and time suppresseth wrongs.
WARWICK: Injurious Margaret!
PRINCE EDWARD: And why not queen?
WARWICK: Because thy father Henry did usurp,
WARWICK: And thou no more are prince than she is queen.
OXFORD: Then Warwick disannuls great John of Gaunt,
OXFORD: Which did subdue the greatest part of Spain,
OXFORD: And, after John of Gaunt, Henry the Fourth,
OXFORD: Whose wisdom was a mirror to the wisest,
OXFORD: And, after that wise prince, Henry the Fifth,
OXFORD: Who by his prowess conquered all France:
OXFORD: From these our Henry lineally descends.
WARWICK: Oxford, how haps it, in this smooth discourse,
WARWICK: You told not how Henry the Sixth hath lost
WARWICK: All that which Henry Fifth had gotten?
WARWICK: Methinks these peers of France should smile at that.
WARWICK: But for the rest, you tell a pedigree
WARWICK: Of threescore and two years, a silly time
WARWICK: To make prescription for a kingdom's worth.
OXFORD: Why, Warwick, canst thou speak against thy liege,
OXFORD: Whom thou obeyed'st thirty and six years,
OXFORD: And not bewray thy treason with a blush?
WARWICK: Can Oxford, that did ever fence the right,
WARWICK: Now buckler falsehood with a pedigree?
WARWICK: For shame! leave Henry, and call Edward king.
OXFORD: Call him my king by whose injurious doom
OXFORD: My elder brother, the Lord Aubrey Vere,
OXFORD: Was done to death? and more than so, my father,
OXFORD: Even in the downfall of his mellow'd years,
OXFORD: When nature brought him to the door of death?
OXFORD: No, Warwick, no, while life upholds this arm,
OXFORD: This arm upholds the house of Lancaster.
WARWICK: And I the house of York.
KING LEWIS XI: Queen Margaret, Prince Edward, and Oxford,
KING LEWIS XI: Vouchsafe, at our request, to stand aside,
KING LEWIS XI: While I use further conference with Warwick.
NARRATOR: They stand aloof
QUEEN MARGARET: Heavens grant that Warwick's words bewitch him not!
KING LEWIS XI: Now Warwick, tell me, even upon thy conscience,
KING LEWIS XI: Is Edward your true king? for I were loath
KING LEWIS XI: To link with him that were not lawful chosen.
WARWICK: Thereon I pawn my credit and mine honour.
KING LEWIS XI: But is he gracious in the people's eye?
WARWICK: The more that Henry was unfortunate.
KING LEWIS XI: Then further, all dissembling set aside,
KING LEWIS XI: Tell me for truth the measure of his love
KING LEWIS XI: Unto our sister Bona.
WARWICK: Such it seems
WARWICK: As may beseem a monarch like himself.
WARWICK: Myself have often heard him say and swear
WARWICK: That this his love was an eternal plant,
WARWICK: Whereof the root was fix'd in virtue's ground,
WARWICK: The leaves and fruit maintain'd with beauty's sun,
WARWICK: Exempt from envy, but not from disdain,
WARWICK: Unless the Lady Bona quit his pain.
KING LEWIS XI: Now, sister, let us hear your firm resolve.
BONA: Your grant, or your denial, shall be mine:
NARRATOR: To WARWICK
BONA: Yet I confess that often ere this day,
BONA: When I have heard your king's desert recounted,
BONA: Mine ear hath tempted judgment to desire.
KING LEWIS XI: Then, Warwick, thus: our sister shall be Edward's,
KING LEWIS XI: And now forthwith shall articles be drawn
KING LEWIS XI: Touching the jointure that your king must make,
KING LEWIS XI: Which with her dowry shall be counterpoised.
KING LEWIS XI: Draw near, Queen Margaret, and be a witness
KING LEWIS XI: That Bona shall be wife to the English king.
PRINCE EDWARD: To Edward, but not to the English king.
QUEEN MARGARET: Deceitful Warwick! it was thy device
QUEEN MARGARET: By this alliance to make void my suit:
QUEEN MARGARET: Before thy coming Lewis was Henry's friend.
KING LEWIS XI: And still is friend to him and Margaret:
KING LEWIS XI: But if your title to the crown be weak,
KING LEWIS XI: As may appear by Edward's good success,
KING LEWIS XI: Then 'tis but reason that I be released
KING LEWIS XI: From giving aid which late I promised.
KING LEWIS XI: Yet shall you have all kindness at my hand
KING LEWIS XI: That your estate requires and mine can yield.
WARWICK: Henry now lives in Scotland at his ease,
WARWICK: Where having nothing, nothing can he lose.
WARWICK: And as for you yourself, our quondam queen,
WARWICK: You have a father able to maintain you,
WARWICK: And better 'twere you troubled him than France.
QUEEN MARGARET: Peace, impudent and shameless Warwick, peace,
QUEEN MARGARET: Proud setter up and puller down of kings!
QUEEN MARGARET: I will not hence, till, with my talk and tears,
QUEEN MARGARET: Both full of truth, I make King Lewis behold
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy sly conveyance and thy lord's false love,
QUEEN MARGARET: For both of you are birds of selfsame feather.
NARRATOR: Post blows a horn within
KING LEWIS XI: Warwick, this is some post to us or thee.
NARRATOR: Enter a Post
Post: [To WARWICK]  My lord ambassador, these letters are for you,
Post: Sent from your brother, Marquess Montague:
NARRATOR: To KING LEWIS XI
Post: These from our king unto your majesty:
NARRATOR: To QUEEN MARGARET
Post: And, madam, these for you, from whom I know not.
NARRATOR: They all read their letters
OXFORD: I like it well that our fair queen and mistress
OXFORD: Smiles at her news, while Warwick frowns at his.
PRINCE EDWARD: Nay, mark how Lewis stamps, as he were nettled:
PRINCE EDWARD: I hope all's for the best.
KING LEWIS XI: Warwick, what are thy news? and yours, fair queen?
QUEEN MARGARET: Mine, such as fill my heart with unhoped joys.
WARWICK: Mine, full of sorrow and heart's discontent.
KING LEWIS XI: What! has your king married the Lady Grey!
KING LEWIS XI: And now, to soothe your forgery and his,
KING LEWIS XI: Sends me a paper to persuade me patience?
KING LEWIS XI: Is this the alliance that he seeks with France?
KING LEWIS XI: Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?
QUEEN MARGARET: I told your majesty as much before:
QUEEN MARGARET: This proveth Edward's love and Warwick's honesty.
WARWICK: King Lewis, I here protest, in sight of heaven,
WARWICK: And by the hope I have of heavenly bliss,
WARWICK: That I am clear from this misdeed of Edward's,
WARWICK: No more my king, for he dishonours me,
WARWICK: But most himself, if he could see his shame.
WARWICK: Did I forget that by the house of York
WARWICK: My father came untimely to his death?
WARWICK: Did I let pass the abuse done to my niece?
WARWICK: Did I impale him with the regal crown?
WARWICK: Did I put Henry from his native right?
WARWICK: And am I guerdon'd at the last with shame?
WARWICK: Shame on himself! for my desert is honour:
WARWICK: And to repair my honour lost for him,
WARWICK: I here renounce him and return to Henry.
WARWICK: My noble queen, let former grudges pass,
WARWICK: And henceforth I am thy true servitor:
WARWICK: I will revenge his wrong to Lady Bona,
WARWICK: And replant Henry in his former state.
QUEEN MARGARET: Warwick, these words have turn'd my hate to love,
QUEEN MARGARET: And I forgive and quite forget old faults,
QUEEN MARGARET: And joy that thou becomest King Henry's friend.
WARWICK: So much his friend, ay, his unfeigned friend,
WARWICK: That, if King Lewis vouchsafe to furnish us
WARWICK: With some few bands of chosen soldiers,
WARWICK: I'll undertake to land them on our coast
WARWICK: And force the tyrant from his seat by war.
WARWICK: 'Tis not his new-made bride shall succor him:
WARWICK: And as for Clarence, as my letters tell me,
WARWICK: He's very likely now to fall from him,
WARWICK: For matching more for wanton lust than honour,
WARWICK: Or than for strength and safety of our country.
BONA: Dear brother, how shall Bona be revenged
BONA: But by thy help to this distressed queen?
QUEEN MARGARET: Renowned prince, how shall poor Henry live,
QUEEN MARGARET: Unless thou rescue him from foul despair?
BONA: My quarrel and this English queen's are one.
WARWICK: And mine, fair lady Bona, joins with yours.
KING LEWIS XI: And mine with hers, and thine, and Margaret's.
KING LEWIS XI: Therefore at last I firmly am resolved
KING LEWIS XI: You shall have aid.
QUEEN MARGARET: Let me give humble thanks for all at once.
KING LEWIS XI: Then, England's messenger, return in post,
KING LEWIS XI: And tell false Edward, thy supposed king,
KING LEWIS XI: That Lewis of France is sending over masquers
KING LEWIS XI: To revel it with him and his new bride:
KING LEWIS XI: Thou seest what's past, go fear thy king withal.
BONA: Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly,
BONA: I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.
QUEEN MARGARET: Tell him, my mourning weeds are laid aside,
QUEEN MARGARET: And I am ready to put armour on.
WARWICK: Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong,
WARWICK: And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long.
WARWICK: There's thy reward: be gone.
NARRATOR: Exit Post
KING LEWIS XI: But, Warwick,
KING LEWIS XI: Thou and Oxford, with five thousand men,
KING LEWIS XI: Shall cross the seas, and bid false Edward battle,
KING LEWIS XI: And, as occasion serves, this noble queen
KING LEWIS XI: And prince shall follow with a fresh supply.
KING LEWIS XI: Yet, ere thou go, but answer me one doubt,
KING LEWIS XI: What pledge have we of thy firm loyalty?
WARWICK: This shall assure my constant loyalty,
WARWICK: That if our queen and this young prince agree,
WARWICK: I'll join mine eldest daughter and my joy
WARWICK: To him forthwith in holy wedlock bands.
QUEEN MARGARET: Yes, I agree, and thank you for your motion.
QUEEN MARGARET: Son Edward, she is fair and virtuous,
QUEEN MARGARET: Therefore delay not, give thy hand to Warwick,
QUEEN MARGARET: And, with thy hand, thy faith irrevocable,
QUEEN MARGARET: That only Warwick's daughter shall be thine.
PRINCE EDWARD: Yes, I accept her, for she well deserves it,
PRINCE EDWARD: And here, to pledge my vow, I give my hand.
NARRATOR: He gives his hand to WARWICK
KING LEWIS XI: Why stay we now? These soldiers shall be levied,
KING LEWIS XI: And thou, Lord Bourbon, our high admiral,
KING LEWIS XI: Shalt waft them over with our royal fleet.
KING LEWIS XI: I long till Edward fall by war's mischance,
KING LEWIS XI: For mocking marriage with a dame of France.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but WARWICK
WARWICK: I came from Edward as ambassador,
WARWICK: But I return his sworn and mortal foe:
WARWICK: Matter of marriage was the charge he gave me,
WARWICK: But dreadful war shall answer his demand.
WARWICK: Had he none else to make a stale but me?
WARWICK: Then none but I shall turn his jest to sorrow.
WARWICK: I was the chief that raised him to the crown,
WARWICK: And I'll be chief to bring him down again:
WARWICK: Not that I pity Henry's misery,
WARWICK: But seek revenge on Edward's mockery.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, CLARENCE, SOMERSET, and MONTAGUE
GLOUCESTER: Now tell me, brother Clarence, what think you
GLOUCESTER: Of this new marriage with the Lady Grey?
GLOUCESTER: Hath not our brother made a worthy choice?
CLARENCE: Alas, you know, 'tis far from hence to France,
CLARENCE: How could he stay till Warwick made return?
SOMERSET: My lords, forbear this talk, here comes the king.
GLOUCESTER: And his well-chosen bride.
CLARENCE: I mind to tell him plainly what I think.
CLARENCE: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV, attended, QUEEN ELIZABETH, PEMBROKE, STAFFORD, HASTINGS, and others
KING EDWARD IV: Now, brother of Clarence, how like you our choice,
KING EDWARD IV: That you stand pensive, as half malcontent?
CLARENCE: As well as Lewis of France, or the Earl of Warwick,
CLARENCE: Which are so weak of courage and in judgment
CLARENCE: That they'll take no offence at our abuse.
KING EDWARD IV: Suppose they take offence without a cause,
KING EDWARD IV: They are but Lewis and Warwick: I am Edward,
KING EDWARD IV: Your king and Warwick's, and must have my will.
GLOUCESTER: And shall have your will, because our king:
GLOUCESTER: Yet hasty marriage seldom proveth well.
KING EDWARD IV: Yea, brother Richard, are you offended too?
GLOUCESTER: Not I:
GLOUCESTER: No, God forbid that I should wish them sever'd
GLOUCESTER: Whom God hath join'd together, ay, and 'twere pity
GLOUCESTER: To sunder them that yoke so well together.
KING EDWARD IV: Setting your scorns and your mislike aside,
KING EDWARD IV: Tell me some reason why the Lady Grey
KING EDWARD IV: Should not become my wife and England's queen.
KING EDWARD IV: And you too, Somerset and Montague,
KING EDWARD IV: Speak freely what you think.
CLARENCE: Then this is mine opinion: that King Lewis
CLARENCE: Becomes your enemy, for mocking him
CLARENCE: About the marriage of the Lady Bona.
GLOUCESTER: And Warwick, doing what you gave in charge,
GLOUCESTER: Is now dishonoured by this new marriage.
KING EDWARD IV: What if both Lewis and Warwick be appeased
KING EDWARD IV: By such invention as I can devise?
MONTAGUE: Yet, to have join'd with France in such alliance
MONTAGUE: Would more have strengthen'd this our commonwealth
MONTAGUE: 'Gainst foreign storms than any home-bred marriage.
HASTINGS: Why, knows not Montague that of itself
HASTINGS: England is safe, if true within itself?
MONTAGUE: But the safer when 'tis back'd with France.
HASTINGS: 'Tis better using France than trusting France:
HASTINGS: Let us be back'd with God and with the seas
HASTINGS: Which He hath given for fence impregnable,
HASTINGS: And with their helps only defend ourselves,
HASTINGS: In them and in ourselves our safety lies.
CLARENCE: For this one speech Lord Hastings well deserves
CLARENCE: To have the heir of the Lord Hungerford.
KING EDWARD IV: Ay, what of that? it was my will and grant,
KING EDWARD IV: And for this once my will shall stand for law.
GLOUCESTER: And yet methinks your grace hath not done well,
GLOUCESTER: To give the heir and daughter of Lord Scales
GLOUCESTER: Unto the brother of your loving bride,
GLOUCESTER: She better would have fitted me or Clarence:
GLOUCESTER: But in your bride you bury brotherhood.
CLARENCE: Or else you would not have bestow'd the heir
CLARENCE: Of the Lord Bonville on your new wife's son,
CLARENCE: And leave your brothers to go speed elsewhere.
KING EDWARD IV: Alas, poor Clarence! is it for a wife
KING EDWARD IV: That thou art malcontent? I will provide thee.
CLARENCE: In choosing for yourself, you show'd your judgment,
CLARENCE: Which being shallow, you give me leave
CLARENCE: To play the broker in mine own behalf,
CLARENCE: And to that end I shortly mind to leave you.
KING EDWARD IV: Leave me, or tarry, Edward will be king,
KING EDWARD IV: And not be tied unto his brother's will.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My lords, before it pleased his majesty
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To raise my state to title of a queen,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Do me but right, and you must all confess
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That I was not ignoble of descent,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And meaner than myself have had like fortune.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: But as this title honours me and mine,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: So your dislike, to whom I would be pleasing,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Doth cloud my joys with danger and with sorrow.
KING EDWARD IV: My love, forbear to fawn upon their frowns:
KING EDWARD IV: What danger or what sorrow can befall thee,
KING EDWARD IV: So long as Edward is thy constant friend,
KING EDWARD IV: And their true sovereign, whom they must obey?
KING EDWARD IV: Nay, whom they shall obey, and love thee too,
KING EDWARD IV: Unless they seek for hatred at my hands,
KING EDWARD IV: Which if they do, yet will I keep thee safe,
KING EDWARD IV: And they shall feel the vengeance of my wrath.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  I hear, yet say not much, but think the more.
NARRATOR: Enter a Post
KING EDWARD IV: Now, messenger, what letters or what news
KING EDWARD IV: From France?
Post: My sovereign liege, no letters, and few words,
Post: But such as I, without your special pardon,
Post: Dare not relate.
KING EDWARD IV: Go to, we pardon thee: therefore, in brief,
KING EDWARD IV: Tell me their words as near as thou canst guess them.
KING EDWARD IV: What answer makes King Lewis unto our letters?
Post: At my depart, these were his very words:
Post: 'Go tell false Edward, thy supposed king,
Post: That Lewis of France is sending over masquers
Post: To revel it with him and his new bride.'
KING EDWARD IV: Is Lewis so brave? belike he thinks me Henry.
KING EDWARD IV: But what said Lady Bona to my marriage?
Post: These were her words, utter'd with mad disdain:
Post: 'Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly,
Post: I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.'
KING EDWARD IV: I blame not her, she could say little less,
KING EDWARD IV: She had the wrong. But what said Henry's queen?
KING EDWARD IV: For I have heard that she was there in place.
Post: 'Tell him,' quoth she, 'my mourning weeds are done,
Post: And I am ready to put armour on.'
KING EDWARD IV: Belike she minds to play the Amazon.
KING EDWARD IV: But what said Warwick to these injuries?
Post: He, more incensed against your majesty
Post: Than all the rest, discharged me with these words:
Post: 'Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong,
Post: And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long.'
KING EDWARD IV: Ha! durst the traitor breathe out so proud words?
KING EDWARD IV: Well I will arm me, being thus forewarn'd:
KING EDWARD IV: They shall have wars and pay for their presumption.
KING EDWARD IV: But say, is Warwick friends with Margaret?
Post: Ay, gracious sovereign, they are so link'd in
Post: friendship
Post: That young Prince Edward marries Warwick's daughter.
CLARENCE: Belike the elder, Clarence will have the younger.
CLARENCE: Now, brother king, farewell, and sit you fast,
CLARENCE: For I will hence to Warwick's other daughter,
CLARENCE: That, though I want a kingdom, yet in marriage
CLARENCE: I may not prove inferior to yourself.
CLARENCE: You that love me and Warwick, follow me.
NARRATOR: Exit CLARENCE, and SOMERSET follows
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  Not I:
GLOUCESTER: My thoughts aim at a further matter, I
GLOUCESTER: Stay not for the love of Edward, but the crown.
KING EDWARD IV: Clarence and Somerset both gone to Warwick!
KING EDWARD IV: Yet am I arm'd against the worst can happen,
KING EDWARD IV: And haste is needful in this desperate case.
KING EDWARD IV: Pembroke and Stafford, you in our behalf
KING EDWARD IV: Go levy men, and make prepare for war,
KING EDWARD IV: They are already, or quickly will be landed:
KING EDWARD IV: Myself in person will straight follow you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PEMBROKE and STAFFORD
KING EDWARD IV: But, ere I go, Hastings and Montague,
KING EDWARD IV: Resolve my doubt. You twain, of all the rest,
KING EDWARD IV: Are near to Warwick by blood and by alliance:
KING EDWARD IV: Tell me if you love Warwick more than me?
KING EDWARD IV: If it be so, then both depart to him,
KING EDWARD IV: I rather wish you foes than hollow friends:
KING EDWARD IV: But if you mind to hold your true obedience,
KING EDWARD IV: Give me assurance with some friendly vow,
KING EDWARD IV: That I may never have you in suspect.
MONTAGUE: So God help Montague as he proves true!
HASTINGS: And Hastings as he favours Edward's cause!
KING EDWARD IV: Now, brother Richard, will you stand by us?
GLOUCESTER: Ay, in despite of all that shall withstand you.
KING EDWARD IV: Why, so! then am I sure of victory.
KING EDWARD IV: Now therefore let us hence, and lose no hour,
KING EDWARD IV: Till we meet Warwick with his foreign power.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A plain in Warwickshire.
NARRATOR: Enter WARWICK and OXFORD, with French soldiers
WARWICK: Trust me, my lord, all hitherto goes well,
WARWICK: The common people by numbers swarm to us.
NARRATOR: Enter CLARENCE and SOMERSET
WARWICK: But see where Somerset and Clarence come!
WARWICK: Speak suddenly, my lords, are we all friends?
CLARENCE: Fear not that, my lord.
WARWICK: Then, gentle Clarence, welcome unto Warwick,
WARWICK: And welcome, Somerset: I hold it cowardice
WARWICK: To rest mistrustful where a noble heart
WARWICK: Hath pawn'd an open hand in sign of love,
WARWICK: Else might I think that Clarence, Edward's brother,
WARWICK: Were but a feigned friend to our proceedings:
WARWICK: But welcome, sweet Clarence, my daughter shall be thine.
WARWICK: And now what rests but, in night's coverture,
WARWICK: Thy brother being carelessly encamp'd,
WARWICK: His soldiers lurking in the towns about,
WARWICK: And but attended by a simple guard,
WARWICK: We may surprise and take him at our pleasure?
WARWICK: Our scouts have found the adventure very easy:
WARWICK: That as Ulysses and stout Diomede
WARWICK: With sleight and manhood stole to Rhesus' tents,
WARWICK: And brought from thence the Thracian fatal steeds,
WARWICK: So we, well cover'd with the night's black mantle,
WARWICK: At unawares may beat down Edward's guard
WARWICK: And seize himself, I say not, slaughter him,
WARWICK: For I intend but only to surprise him.
WARWICK: You that will follow me to this attempt,
WARWICK: Applaud the name of Henry with your leader.
WARWICK: They all cry, 'Henry!'
WARWICK: Why, then, let's on our way in silent sort:
WARWICK: For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Edward's camp, near Warwick.
NARRATOR: Enter three Watchmen, to guard KING EDWARD IV's tent
First Watchman: Come on, my masters, each man take his stand:
First Watchman: The king by this is set him down to sleep.
Second Watchman: What, will he not to bed?
First Watchman: Why, no, for he hath made a solemn vow
First Watchman: Never to lie and take his natural rest
First Watchman: Till Warwick or himself be quite suppress'd.
Second Watchman: To-morrow then belike shall be the day,
Second Watchman: If Warwick be so near as men report.
Third Watchman: But say, I pray, what nobleman is that
Third Watchman: That with the king here resteth in his tent?
First Watchman: 'Tis the Lord Hastings, the king's chiefest friend.
Third Watchman: O, is it so? But why commands the king
Third Watchman: That his chief followers lodge in towns about him,
Third Watchman: While he himself keeps in the cold field?
Second Watchman: 'Tis the more honour, because more dangerous.
Third Watchman: Ay, but give me worship and quietness,
Third Watchman: I like it better than a dangerous honour.
Third Watchman: If Warwick knew in what estate he stands,
Third Watchman: 'Tis to be doubted he would waken him.
First Watchman: Unless our halberds did shut up his passage.
Second Watchman: Ay, wherefore else guard we his royal tent,
Second Watchman: But to defend his person from night-foes?
NARRATOR: Enter WARWICK, CLARENCE, OXFORD, SOMERSET, and French soldiers, silent all
WARWICK: This is his tent, and see where stand his guard.
WARWICK: Courage, my masters! honour now or never!
WARWICK: But follow me, and Edward shall be ours.
First Watchman: Who goes there?
Second Watchman: Stay, or thou diest!
Second Watchman: WARWICK and the rest cry all, 'Warwick! Warwick!'  and set upon the Guard, who fly, crying, 'Arm! arm!' WARWICK and the rest following them
NARRATOR: The drum playing and trumpet sounding, reenter  WARWICK, SOMERSET, and the rest, bringing KING  EDWARD IV out in his gown, sitting in a chair. RICHARD and HASTINGS fly over the stage
SOMERSET: What are they that fly there?
WARWICK: Richard and Hastings: let them go, here is The duke.
KING EDWARD IV: The duke! Why, Warwick, when we parted,
KING EDWARD IV: Thou call'dst me king.
WARWICK: Ay, but the case is alter'd:
WARWICK: When you disgraced me in my embassade,
WARWICK: Then I degraded you from being king,
WARWICK: And come now to create you Duke of York.
WARWICK: Alas! how should you govern any kingdom,
WARWICK: That know not how to use ambassadors,
WARWICK: Nor how to be contented with one wife,
WARWICK: Nor how to use your brothers brotherly,
WARWICK: Nor how to study for the people's welfare,
WARWICK: Nor how to shroud yourself from enemies?
KING EDWARD IV: Yea, brother of Clarence, are thou here too?
KING EDWARD IV: Nay, then I see that Edward needs must down.
KING EDWARD IV: Yet, Warwick, in despite of all mischance,
KING EDWARD IV: Of thee thyself and all thy complices,
KING EDWARD IV: Edward will always bear himself as king:
KING EDWARD IV: Though fortune's malice overthrow my state,
KING EDWARD IV: My mind exceeds the compass of her wheel.
WARWICK: Then, for his mind, be Edward England's king:
NARRATOR: Takes off his crown
WARWICK: But Henry now shall wear the English crown,
WARWICK: And be true king indeed, thou but the shadow.
WARWICK: My Lord of Somerset, at my request,
WARWICK: See that forthwith Duke Edward be convey'd
WARWICK: Unto my brother, Archbishop of York.
WARWICK: When I have fought with Pembroke and his fellows,
WARWICK: I'll follow you, and tell what answer
WARWICK: Lewis and the Lady Bona send to him.
WARWICK: Now, for a while farewell, good Duke of York.
NARRATOR: They lead him out forcibly
KING EDWARD IV: What fates impose, that men must needs abide,
KING EDWARD IV: It boots not to resist both wind and tide.
NARRATOR: Exit, guarded
OXFORD: What now remains, my lords, for us to do
OXFORD: But march to London with our soldiers?
WARWICK: Ay, that's the first thing that we have to do,
WARWICK: To free King Henry from imprisonment
WARWICK: And see him seated in the regal throne.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH and RIVERS
RIVERS: Madam, what makes you in this sudden change?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Why brother Rivers, are you yet to learn
QUEEN ELIZABETH: What late misfortune is befall'n King Edward?
RIVERS: What! loss of some pitch'd battle against Warwick?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: No, but the loss of his own royal person.
RIVERS: Then is my sovereign slain?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Ay, almost slain, for he is taken prisoner,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Either betray'd by falsehood of his guard
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Or by his foe surprised at unawares:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And, as I further have to understand,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Is new committed to the Bishop of York,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Fell Warwick's brother and by that our foe.
RIVERS: These news I must confess are full of grief,
RIVERS: Yet, gracious madam, bear it as you may:
RIVERS: Warwick may lose, that now hath won the day.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Till then fair hope must hinder life's decay.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And I the rather wean me from despair
QUEEN ELIZABETH: For love of Edward's offspring in my womb:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: This is it that makes me bridle passion
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And bear with mildness my misfortune's cross,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Ay, ay, for this I draw in many a tear
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And stop the rising of blood-sucking sighs,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Lest with my sighs or tears I blast or drown
QUEEN ELIZABETH: King Edward's fruit, true heir to the English crown.
RIVERS: But, madam, where is Warwick then become?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I am inform'd that he comes towards London,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To set the crown once more on Henry's head:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Guess thou the rest, King Edward's friends must down,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: But, to prevent the tyrant's violence,--
QUEEN ELIZABETH: For trust not him that hath once broken faith,--
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I'll hence forthwith unto the sanctuary,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To save at least the heir of Edward's right:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: There shall I rest secure from force and fraud.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Come, therefore, let us fly while we may fly:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: If Warwick take us we are sure to die.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. A park near Middleham Castle In Yorkshire.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, HASTINGS, and STANLEY
GLOUCESTER: Now, my Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley,
GLOUCESTER: Leave off to wonder why I drew you hither,
GLOUCESTER: Into this chiefest thicket of the park.
GLOUCESTER: Thus stands the case: you know our king, my brother,
GLOUCESTER: Is prisoner to the bishop here, at whose hands
GLOUCESTER: He hath good usage and great liberty,
GLOUCESTER: And, often but attended with weak guard,
GLOUCESTER: Comes hunting this way to disport himself.
GLOUCESTER: I have advertised him by secret means
GLOUCESTER: That if about this hour he make his way
GLOUCESTER: Under the colour of his usual game,
GLOUCESTER: He shall here find his friends with horse and men
GLOUCESTER: To set him free from his captivity.
NARRATOR: Enter KING EDWARD IV and a Huntsman with him
Huntsman: This way, my lord, for this way lies the game.
KING EDWARD IV: Nay, this way, man: see where the huntsmen stand.
KING EDWARD IV: Now, brother of Gloucester, Lord Hastings, and the rest,
KING EDWARD IV: Stand you thus close, to steal the bishop's deer?
GLOUCESTER: Brother, the time and case requireth haste:
GLOUCESTER: Your horse stands ready at the park-corner.
KING EDWARD IV: But whither shall we then?
HASTINGS: To Lynn, my lord,
HASTINGS: And ship from thence to Flanders.
GLOUCESTER: Well guess'd, believe me, for that was my meaning.
KING EDWARD IV: Stanley, I will requite thy forwardness.
GLOUCESTER: But wherefore stay we? 'tis no time to talk.
KING EDWARD IV: Huntsman, what say'st thou? wilt thou go along?
Huntsman: Better do so than tarry and be hang'd.
GLOUCESTER: Come then, away, let's ha' no more ado.
KING EDWARD IV: Bishop, farewell: shield thee from Warwick's frown,
KING EDWARD IV: And pray that I may repossess the crown.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. London. The Tower.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING HENRY VI, CLARENCE, WARWICK,  SOMERSET, HENRY OF RICHMOND, OXFORD, MONTAGUE, and Lieutenant of the Tower
KING HENRY VI: Master lieutenant, now that God and friends
KING HENRY VI: Have shaken Edward from the regal seat,
KING HENRY VI: And turn'd my captive state to liberty,
KING HENRY VI: My fear to hope, my sorrows unto joys,
KING HENRY VI: At our enlargement what are thy due fees?
Lieutenant: Subjects may challenge nothing of their sovereigns,
Lieutenant: But if an humble prayer may prevail,
Lieutenant: I then crave pardon of your majesty.
KING HENRY VI: For what, lieutenant? for well using me?
KING HENRY VI: Nay, be thou sure I'll well requite thy kindness,
KING HENRY VI: For that it made my imprisonment a pleasure,
KING HENRY VI: Ay, such a pleasure as incaged birds
KING HENRY VI: Conceive when after many moody thoughts
KING HENRY VI: At last by notes of household harmony
KING HENRY VI: They quite forget their loss of liberty.
KING HENRY VI: But, Warwick, after God, thou set'st me free,
KING HENRY VI: And chiefly therefore I thank God and thee,
KING HENRY VI: He was the author, thou the instrument.
KING HENRY VI: Therefore, that I may conquer fortune's spite
KING HENRY VI: By living low, where fortune cannot hurt me,
KING HENRY VI: And that the people of this blessed land
KING HENRY VI: May not be punish'd with my thwarting stars,
KING HENRY VI: Warwick, although my head still wear the crown,
KING HENRY VI: I here resign my government to thee,
KING HENRY VI: For thou art fortunate in all thy deeds.
WARWICK: Your grace hath still been famed for virtuous,
WARWICK: And now may seem as wise as virtuous,
WARWICK: By spying and avoiding fortune's malice,
WARWICK: For few men rightly temper with the stars:
WARWICK: Yet in this one thing let me blame your grace,
WARWICK: For choosing me when Clarence is in place.
CLARENCE: No, Warwick, thou art worthy of the sway,
CLARENCE: To whom the heavens in thy nativity
CLARENCE: Adjudged an olive branch and laurel crown,
CLARENCE: As likely to be blest in peace and war,
CLARENCE: And therefore I yield thee my free consent.
WARWICK: And I choose Clarence only for protector.
KING HENRY VI: Warwick and Clarence give me both your hands:
KING HENRY VI: Now join your hands, and with your hands your hearts,
KING HENRY VI: That no dissension hinder government:
KING HENRY VI: I make you both protectors of this land,
KING HENRY VI: While I myself will lead a private life
KING HENRY VI: And in devotion spend my latter days,
KING HENRY VI: To sin's rebuke and my Creator's praise.
WARWICK: What answers Clarence to his sovereign's will?
CLARENCE: That he consents, if Warwick yield consent,
CLARENCE: For on thy fortune I repose myself.
WARWICK: Why, then, though loath, yet must I be content:
WARWICK: We'll yoke together, like a double shadow
WARWICK: To Henry's body, and supply his place,
WARWICK: I mean, in bearing weight of government,
WARWICK: While he enjoys the honour and his ease.
WARWICK: And, Clarence, now then it is more than needful
WARWICK: Forthwith that Edward be pronounced a traitor,
WARWICK: And all his lands and goods be confiscate.
CLARENCE: What else? and that succession be determined.
WARWICK: Ay, therein Clarence shall not want his part.
KING HENRY VI: But, with the first of all your chief affairs,
KING HENRY VI: Let me entreat, for I command no more,
KING HENRY VI: That Margaret your queen and my son Edward
KING HENRY VI: Be sent for, to return from France with speed,
KING HENRY VI: For, till I see them here, by doubtful fear
KING HENRY VI: My joy of liberty is half eclipsed.
CLARENCE: It shall be done, my sovereign, with all speed.
KING HENRY VI: My Lord of Somerset, what youth is that,
KING HENRY VI: Of whom you seem to have so tender care?
SOMERSET: My liege, it is young Henry, earl of Richmond.
KING HENRY VI: Come hither, England's hope.
NARRATOR: Lays his hand on his head
KING HENRY VI: If secret powers
KING HENRY VI: Suggest but truth to my divining thoughts,
KING HENRY VI: This pretty lad will prove our country's bliss.
KING HENRY VI: His looks are full of peaceful majesty,
KING HENRY VI: His head by nature framed to wear a crown,
KING HENRY VI: His hand to wield a sceptre, and himself
KING HENRY VI: Likely in time to bless a regal throne.
KING HENRY VI: Make much of him, my lords, for this is he
KING HENRY VI: Must help you more than you are hurt by me.
NARRATOR: Enter a Post
WARWICK: What news, my friend?
Post: That Edward is escaped from your brother,
Post: And fled, as he hears since, to Burgundy.
WARWICK: Unsavoury news! but how made he escape?
Post: He was convey'd by Richard Duke of Gloucester
Post: And the Lord Hastings, who attended him
Post: In secret ambush on the forest side
Post: And from the bishop's huntsmen rescued him,
Post: For hunting was his daily exercise.
WARWICK: My brother was too careless of his charge.
WARWICK: But let us hence, my sovereign, to provide
WARWICK: A salve for any sore that may betide.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but SOMERSET, HENRY OF RICHMOND, and OXFORD
SOMERSET: My lord, I like not of this flight of Edward's,
SOMERSET: For doubtless Burgundy will yield him help,
SOMERSET: And we shall have more wars before 't be long.
SOMERSET: As Henry's late presaging prophecy
SOMERSET: Did glad my heart with hope of this young Richmond,
SOMERSET: So doth my heart misgive me, in these conflicts
SOMERSET: What may befall him, to his harm and ours:
SOMERSET: Therefore, Lord Oxford, to prevent the worst,
SOMERSET: Forthwith we'll send him hence to Brittany,
SOMERSET: Till storms be past of civil enmity.
OXFORD: Ay, for if Edward repossess the crown,
OXFORD: 'Tis like that Richmond with the rest shall down.
SOMERSET: It shall be so, he shall to Brittany.
SOMERSET: Come, therefore, let's about it speedily.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
