NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Before York.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, HASTINGS, and Soldiers
KING EDWARD IV: Now, brother Richard, Lord Hastings, and the rest,
KING EDWARD IV: Yet thus far fortune maketh us amends,
KING EDWARD IV: And says that once more I shall interchange
KING EDWARD IV: My waned state for Henry's regal crown.
KING EDWARD IV: Well have we pass'd and now repass'd the seas
KING EDWARD IV: And brought desired help from Burgundy:
KING EDWARD IV: What then remains, we being thus arrived
KING EDWARD IV: From Ravenspurgh haven before the gates of York,
KING EDWARD IV: But that we enter, as into our dukedom?
GLOUCESTER: The gates made fast! Brother, I like not this,
GLOUCESTER: For many men that stumble at the threshold
GLOUCESTER: Are well foretold that danger lurks within.
KING EDWARD IV: Tush, man, abodements must not now affright us:
KING EDWARD IV: By fair or foul means we must enter in,
KING EDWARD IV: For hither will our friends repair to us.
HASTINGS: My liege, I'll knock once more to summon them.
NARRATOR: Enter, on the walls, the Mayor of York, and his Brethren
Mayor: My lords, we were forewarned of your coming,
Mayor: And shut the gates for safety of ourselves,
Mayor: For now we owe allegiance unto Henry.
KING EDWARD IV: But, master mayor, if Henry be your king,
KING EDWARD IV: Yet Edward at the least is Duke of York.
Mayor: True, my good lord, I know you for no less.
KING EDWARD IV: Why, and I challenge nothing but my dukedom,
KING EDWARD IV: As being well content with that alone.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  But when the fox hath once got in his nose,
GLOUCESTER: He'll soon find means to make the body follow.
HASTINGS: Why, master mayor, why stand you in a doubt?
HASTINGS: Open the gates, we are King Henry's friends.
Mayor: Ay, say you so? the gates shall then be open'd.
NARRATOR: They descend
GLOUCESTER: A wise stout captain, and soon persuaded!
HASTINGS: The good old man would fain that all were well,
HASTINGS: So 'twere not 'long of him, but being enter'd,
HASTINGS: I doubt not, I, but we shall soon persuade
HASTINGS: Both him and all his brothers unto reason.
NARRATOR: Enter the Mayor and two Aldermen, below
KING EDWARD IV: So, master mayor: these gates must not be shut
KING EDWARD IV: But in the night or in the time of war.
KING EDWARD IV: What! fear not, man, but yield me up the keys,
NARRATOR: Takes his keys
KING EDWARD IV: For Edward will defend the town and thee,
KING EDWARD IV: And all those friends that deign to follow me.
NARRATOR: March. Enter MONTGOMERY, with drum and soldiers
GLOUCESTER: Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery,
GLOUCESTER: Our trusty friend, unless I be deceived.
KING EDWARD IV: Welcome, Sir John! But why come you in arms?
MONTAGUE: To help King Edward in his time of storm,
MONTAGUE: As every loyal subject ought to do.
KING EDWARD IV: Thanks, good Montgomery, but we now forget
KING EDWARD IV: Our title to the crown and only claim
KING EDWARD IV: Our dukedom till God please to send the rest.
MONTAGUE: Then fare you well, for I will hence again:
MONTAGUE: I came to serve a king and not a duke.
MONTAGUE: Drummer, strike up, and let us march away.
NARRATOR: The drum begins to march
KING EDWARD IV: Nay, stay, Sir John, awhi le, and we'll debate
KING EDWARD IV: By what safe means the crown may be recover'd.
MONTAGUE: What talk you of debating? in few words,
MONTAGUE: If you'll not here proclaim yourself our king,
MONTAGUE: I'll leave you to your fortune and be gone
MONTAGUE: To keep them back that come to succor you:
MONTAGUE: Why shall we fight, if you pretend no title?
GLOUCESTER: Why, brother, wherefore stand you on nice points?
KING EDWARD IV: When we grow stronger, then we'll make our claim:
KING EDWARD IV: Till then, 'tis wisdom to conceal our meaning.
HASTINGS: Away with scrupulous wit! now arms must rule.
GLOUCESTER: And fearless minds climb soonest unto crowns.
GLOUCESTER: Brother, we will proclaim you out of hand:
GLOUCESTER: The bruit thereof will bring you many friends.
KING EDWARD IV: Then be it as you will, for 'tis my right,
KING EDWARD IV: And Henry but usurps the diadem.
MONTAGUE: Ay, now my sovereign speaketh like himself,
MONTAGUE: And now will I be Edward's champion.
HASTINGS: Sound trumpet, Edward shall be here proclaim'd:
HASTINGS: Come, fellow-soldier, make thou proclamation.
NARRATOR: Flourish
Soldier: Edward the Fourth, by the grace of God, king of
Soldier: England and France, and lord of Ireland,  and c.
MONTAGUE: And whosoe'er gainsays King Edward's right,
MONTAGUE: By this I challenge him to single fight.
NARRATOR: Throws down his gauntlet
All: Long live Edward the Fourth!
KING EDWARD IV: Thanks, brave Montgomery, and thanks unto you all:
KING EDWARD IV: If fortune serve me, I'll requite this kindness.
KING EDWARD IV: Now, for this night, let's harbour here in York,
KING EDWARD IV: And when the morning sun shall raise his car
KING EDWARD IV: Above the border of this horizon,
KING EDWARD IV: We'll forward towards Warwick and his mates,
KING EDWARD IV: For well I wot that Henry is no soldier.
KING EDWARD IV: Ah, froward Clarence! how evil it beseems thee
KING EDWARD IV: To flatter Henry and forsake thy brother!
KING EDWARD IV: Yet, as we may, we'll meet both thee and Warwick.
KING EDWARD IV: Come on, brave soldiers: doubt not of the day,
KING EDWARD IV: And, that once gotten, doubt not of large pay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING HENRY VI, WARWICK, MONTAGUE, CLARENCE, EXETER, and OXFORD
WARWICK: What counsel, lords? Edward from Belgia,
WARWICK: With hasty Germans and blunt Hollanders,
WARWICK: Hath pass'd in safety through the narrow seas,
WARWICK: And with his troops doth march amain to London,
WARWICK: And many giddy people flock to him.
KING HENRY VI: Let's levy men, and beat him back again.
CLARENCE: A little fire is quickly trodden out,
CLARENCE: Which, being suffer'd, rivers cannot quench.
WARWICK: In Warwickshire I have true-hearted friends,
WARWICK: Not mutinous in peace, yet bold in war,
WARWICK: Those will I muster up: and thou, son Clarence,
WARWICK: Shalt stir up in Suffolk, Norfolk, and in Kent,
WARWICK: The knights and gentlemen to come with thee:
WARWICK: Thou, brother Montague, in Buckingham,
WARWICK: Northampton and in Leicestershire, shalt find
WARWICK: Men well inclined to hear what thou command'st:
WARWICK: And thou, brave Oxford, wondrous well beloved,
WARWICK: In Oxfordshire shalt muster up thy friends.
WARWICK: My sovereign, with the loving citizens,
WARWICK: Like to his island girt in with the ocean,
WARWICK: Or modest Dian circled with her nymphs,
WARWICK: Shall rest in London till we come to him.
WARWICK: Fair lords, take leave and stand not to reply.
WARWICK: Farewell, my sovereign.
KING HENRY VI: Farewell, my Hector, and my Troy's true hope.
CLARENCE: In sign of truth, I kiss your highness' hand.
KING HENRY VI: Well-minded Clarence, be thou fortunate!
MONTAGUE: Comfort, my lord, and so I take my leave.
OXFORD: And thus I seal my truth, and bid adieu.
KING HENRY VI: Sweet Oxford, and my loving Montague,
KING HENRY VI: And all at once, once more a happy farewell.
WARWICK: Farewell, sweet lords: let's meet at Coventry.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but KING HENRY VI and EXETER
KING HENRY VI: Here at the palace I will rest awhile.
KING HENRY VI: Cousin of Exeter, what thinks your lordship?
KING HENRY VI: Methinks the power that Edward hath in field
KING HENRY VI: Should not be able to encounter mine.
EXETER: The doubt is that he will seduce the rest.
KING HENRY VI: That's not my fear, my meed hath got me fame:
KING HENRY VI: I have not stopp'd mine ears to their demands,
KING HENRY VI: Nor posted off their suits with slow delays,
KING HENRY VI: My pity hath been balm to heal their wounds,
KING HENRY VI: My mildness hath allay'd their swelling griefs,
KING HENRY VI: My mercy dried their water-flowing tears,
KING HENRY VI: I have not been desirous of their wealth,
KING HENRY VI: Nor much oppress'd them with great subsidies.
KING HENRY VI: Nor forward of revenge, though they much err'd:
KING HENRY VI: Then why should they love Edward more than me?
KING HENRY VI: No, Exeter, these graces challenge grace:
KING HENRY VI: And when the lion fawns upon the lamb,
KING HENRY VI: The lamb will never cease to follow him.
KING HENRY VI: Shout within. 'A Lancaster! A Lancaster!'
EXETER: Hark, hark, my lord! what shouts are these?
NARRATOR: Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, and soldiers
KING EDWARD IV: Seize on the shame-faced Henry, bear him hence,
KING EDWARD IV: And once again proclaim us King of England.
KING EDWARD IV: You are the fount that makes small brooks to flow:
KING EDWARD IV: Now stops thy spring, my sea sha$l suck them dry,
KING EDWARD IV: And swell so much the higher by their ebb.
KING EDWARD IV: Hence with him to the Tower, let him not speak.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some with KING HENRY VI
KING EDWARD IV: And, lords, towards Coventry bend we our course
KING EDWARD IV: Where peremptory Warwick now remains:
KING EDWARD IV: The sun shines hot, and, if we use delay,
KING EDWARD IV: Cold biting winter mars our hoped-for hay.
GLOUCESTER: Away betimes, before his forces join,
GLOUCESTER: And take the great-grown traitor unawares:
GLOUCESTER: Brave warriors, march amain towards Coventry.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Coventry.
NARRATOR: Enter WARWICK, the Mayor of Coventry, two Messengers, and others upon the walls
WARWICK: Where is the post that came from valiant Oxford?
WARWICK: How far hence is thy lord, mine honest fellow?
First Messenger: By this at Dunsmore, marching hitherward.
WARWICK: How far off is our brother Montague?
WARWICK: Where is the post that came from Montague?
Second Messenger: By this at Daintry, with a puissant troop.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR JOHN SOMERVILLE
WARWICK: Say, Somerville, what says my loving son?
WARWICK: And, by thy guess, how nigh is Clarence now?
SOMERSET: At Southam I did leave him with his forces,
SOMERSET: And do expect him here some two hours hence.
NARRATOR: Drum heard
WARWICK: Then Clarence is at hand, I hear his drum.
SOMERSET: It is not his, my lord, here Southam lies:
SOMERSET: The drum your honour hears marcheth from Warwick.
WARWICK: Who should that be? belike, unlook'd-for friends.
SOMERSET: They are at hand, and you shall quickly know.
SOMERSET: March: flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, and soldiers
KING EDWARD IV: Go, trumpet, to the walls, and sound a parle.
GLOUCESTER: See how the surly Warwick mans the wall!
WARWICK: O unbid spite! is sportful Edward come?
WARWICK: Where slept our scouts, or how are they seduced,
WARWICK: That we could hear no news of his repair?
KING EDWARD IV: Now, Warwick, wilt thou ope the city gates,
KING EDWARD IV: Speak gentle words and humbly bend thy knee,
KING EDWARD IV: Call Edward king and at his hands beg mercy?
KING EDWARD IV: And he shall pardon thee these outrages.
WARWICK: Nay, rather, wilt thou draw thy forces hence,
WARWICK: Confess who set thee up and pluck'd thee own,
WARWICK: Call Warwick patron and be penitent?
WARWICK: And thou shalt still remain the Duke of York.
GLOUCESTER: I thought, at least, he would have said the king,
GLOUCESTER: Or did he make the jest against his will?
WARWICK: Is not a dukedom, sir, a goodly gift?
GLOUCESTER: Ay, by my faith, for a poor earl to give:
GLOUCESTER: I'll do thee service for so good a gift.
WARWICK: 'Twas I that gave the kingdom to thy brother.
KING EDWARD IV: Why then 'tis mine, if but by Warwick's gift.
WARWICK: Thou art no Atlas for so great a weight:
WARWICK: And weakling, Warwick takes his gift again,
WARWICK: And Henry is my king, Warwick his subject.
KING EDWARD IV: But Warwick's king is Edward's prisoner:
KING EDWARD IV: And, gallant Warwick, do but answer this:
KING EDWARD IV: What is the body when the head is off?
GLOUCESTER: Alas, that Warwick had no more forecast,
GLOUCESTER: But, whiles he thought to steal the single ten,
GLOUCESTER: The king was slily finger'd from the deck!
GLOUCESTER: You left poor Henry at the Bishop's palace,
GLOUCESTER: And, ten to one, you'll meet him in the Tower.
EDWARD: 'Tis even so, yet you are Warwick still.
GLOUCESTER: Come, Warwick, take the time, kneel down, kneel down:
GLOUCESTER: Nay, when? strike now, or else the iron cools.
WARWICK: I had rather chop this hand off at a blow,
WARWICK: And with the other fling it at thy face,
WARWICK: Than bear so low a sail, to strike to thee.
KING EDWARD IV: Sail how thou canst, have wind and tide thy friend,
KING EDWARD IV: This hand, fast wound about thy coal-black hair
KING EDWARD IV: Shall, whiles thy head is warm and new cut off,
KING EDWARD IV: Write in the dust this sentence with thy blood,
KING EDWARD IV: 'Wind-changing Warwick now can change no more.'
NARRATOR: Enter OXFORD, with drum and colours
WARWICK: O cheerful colours! see where Oxford comes!
OXFORD: Oxford, Oxford, for Lancaster!
NARRATOR: He and his forces enter the city
GLOUCESTER: The gates are open, let us enter too.
KING EDWARD IV: So other foes may set upon our backs.
KING EDWARD IV: Stand we in good array, for they no doubt
KING EDWARD IV: Will issue out again and bid us battle:
KING EDWARD IV: If not, the city being but of small defence,
KING EDWARD IV: We'll quickly rouse the traitors in the same.
WARWICK: O, welcome, Oxford! for we want thy help.
NARRATOR: Enter MONTAGUE with drum and colours
MONTAGUE: Montague, Montague, for Lancaster!
NARRATOR: He and his forces enter the city
GLOUCESTER: Thou and thy brother both shall buy this treason
GLOUCESTER: Even with the dearest blood your bodies bear.
KING EDWARD IV: The harder match'd, the greater victory:
KING EDWARD IV: My mind presageth happy gain and conquest.
NARRATOR: Enter SOMERSET, with drum and colours
SOMERSET: Somerset, Somerset, for Lancaster!
NARRATOR: He and his forces enter the city
GLOUCESTER: Two of thy name, both Dukes of Somerset,
GLOUCESTER: Have sold their lives unto the house of York,
GLOUCESTER: And thou shalt be the third if this sword hold.
NARRATOR: Enter CLARENCE, with drum and colours
WARWICK: And lo, where George of Clarence sweeps along,
WARWICK: Of force enough to bid his brother battle,
WARWICK: With whom an upright zeal to right prevails
WARWICK: More than the nature of a brother's love!
WARWICK: Come, Clarence, come, thou wilt, if Warwick call.
CLARENCE: Father of Warwick, know you what this means?
NARRATOR: Taking his red rose out of his hat
CLARENCE: Look here, I throw my infamy at thee
CLARENCE: I will not ruinate my father's house,
CLARENCE: Who gave his blood to lime the stones together,
CLARENCE: And set up Lancaster. Why, trow'st thou, Warwick,
CLARENCE: That Clarence is so harsh, so blunt, unnatural,
CLARENCE: To bend the fatal instruments of war
CLARENCE: Against his brother and his lawful king?
CLARENCE: Perhaps thou wilt object my holy oath:
CLARENCE: To keep that oath were more impiety
CLARENCE: Than Jephthah's, when he sacrificed his daughter.
CLARENCE: I am so sorry for my trespass made
CLARENCE: That, to deserve well at my brother's hands,
CLARENCE: I here proclaim myself thy mortal foe,
CLARENCE: With resolution, wheresoe'er I meet thee--
CLARENCE: As I will meet thee, if thou stir abroad--
CLARENCE: To plague thee for thy foul misleading me.
CLARENCE: And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy thee,
CLARENCE: And to my brother turn my blushing cheeks.
CLARENCE: Pardon me, Edward, I will make amends:
CLARENCE: And, Richard, do not frown upon my faults,
CLARENCE: For I will henceforth be no more unconstant.
KING EDWARD IV: Now welcome more, and ten times more beloved,
KING EDWARD IV: Than if thou never hadst deserved our hate.
GLOUCESTER: Welcome, good Clarence, this is brotherlike.
WARWICK: O passing traitor, perjured and unjust!
KING EDWARD IV: What, Warwick, wilt thou leave the town and fight?
KING EDWARD IV: Or shall we beat the stones about thine ears?
WARWICK: Alas, I am not coop'd here for defence!
WARWICK: I will away towards Barnet presently,
WARWICK: And bid thee battle, Edward, if thou darest.
KING EDWARD IV: Yes, Warwick, Edward dares, and leads the way.
KING EDWARD IV: Lords, to the field, Saint George and victory!
NARRATOR: Exeunt King Edward and his company. March. Warwick and his company follow
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A field of battle near Barnet.
NARRATOR: Alarum and excursions. Enter KING EDWARD IV, bringing forth WARWICK wounded
KING EDWARD IV: So, lie thou there: die thou, and die our fear,
KING EDWARD IV: For Warwick was a bug that fear'd us all.
KING EDWARD IV: Now, Montague, sit fast, I seek for thee,
KING EDWARD IV: That Warwick's bones may keep thine company.
NARRATOR: Exit
WARWICK: Ah, who is nigh? come to me, friend or foe,
WARWICK: And tell me who is victor, York or Warwick?
WARWICK: Why ask I that? my mangled body shows,
WARWICK: My blood, my want of strength, my sick heart shows.
WARWICK: That I must yield my body to the earth
WARWICK: And, by my fall, the conquest to my foe.
WARWICK: Thus yields the cedar to the axe's edge,
WARWICK: Whose arms gave shelter to the princely eagle,
WARWICK: Under whose shade the ramping lion slept,
WARWICK: Whose top-branch overpeer'd Jove's spreading tree
WARWICK: And kept low shrubs from winter's powerful wind.
WARWICK: These eyes, that now are dimm'd with death's black veil,
WARWICK: Have been as piercing as the mid-day sun,
WARWICK: To search the secret treasons of the world:
WARWICK: The wrinkles in my brows, now filled with blood,
WARWICK: Were liken'd oft to kingly sepulchres,
WARWICK: For who lived king, but I could dig his grave?
WARWICK: And who durst mine when Warwick bent his brow?
WARWICK: Lo, now my glory smear'd in dust and blood!
WARWICK: My parks, my walks, my manors that I had.
WARWICK: Even now forsake me, and of all my lands
WARWICK: Is nothing left me but my body's length.
WARWICK: Why, what is pomp, rule, reign, but earth and dust?
WARWICK: And, live we how we can, yet die we must.
NARRATOR: Enter OXFORD and SOMERSET
SOMERSET: Ah, Warwick, Warwick! wert thou as we are.
SOMERSET: We might recover all our loss again,
SOMERSET: The queen from France hath brought a puissant power:
SOMERSET: Even now we heard the news: ah, could'st thou fly!
WARWICK: Why, then I would not fly. Ah, Montague,
WARWICK: If thou be there, sweet brother, take my hand.
WARWICK: And with thy lips keep in my soul awhile!
WARWICK: Thou lovest me not, for, brother, if thou didst,
WARWICK: Thy tears would wash this cold congealed blood
WARWICK: That glues my lips and will not let me speak.
WARWICK: Come quickly, Montague, or I am dead.
SOMERSET: Ah, Warwick! Montague hath breathed his last,
SOMERSET: And to the latest gasp cried out for Warwick,
SOMERSET: And said 'Commend me to my valiant brother.'
SOMERSET: And more he would have said, and more he spoke,
SOMERSET: Which sounded like a clamour in a vault,
SOMERSET: That mought not be distinguished, but at last
SOMERSET: I well might hear, delivered with a groan,
SOMERSET: 'O, farewell, Warwick!'
WARWICK: Sweet rest his soul! Fly, lords, and save yourselves,
WARWICK: For Warwick bids you all farewell to meet in heaven.
NARRATOR: Dies
OXFORD: Away, away, to meet the queen's great power!
NARRATOR: Here they bear away his body. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV in triumph, with GLOUCESTER, CLARENCE, and the rest
KING EDWARD IV: Thus far our fortune keeps an upward course,
KING EDWARD IV: And we are graced with wreaths of victory.
KING EDWARD IV: But, in the midst of this bright-shining day,
KING EDWARD IV: I spy a black, suspicious, threatening cloud,
KING EDWARD IV: That will encounter with our glorious sun,
KING EDWARD IV: Ere he attain his easeful western bed:
KING EDWARD IV: I mean, my lords, those powers that the queen
KING EDWARD IV: Hath raised in Gallia have arrived our coast
KING EDWARD IV: And, as we hear, march on to fight with us.
CLARENCE: A little gale will soon disperse that cloud
CLARENCE: And blow it to the source from whence it came:
CLARENCE: The very beams will dry those vapours up,
CLARENCE: For every cloud engenders not a storm.
GLOUCESTER: The queen is valued thirty thousand strong,
GLOUCESTER: And Somerset, with Oxford fled to her:
GLOUCESTER: If she have time to breathe be well assured
GLOUCESTER: Her faction will be full as strong as ours.
KING EDWARD IV: We are advertised by our loving friends
KING EDWARD IV: That they do hold their course toward Tewksbury:
KING EDWARD IV: We, having now the best at Barnet field,
KING EDWARD IV: Will thither straight, for willingness rids way,
KING EDWARD IV: And, as we march, our strength will be augmented
KING EDWARD IV: In every county as we go along.
KING EDWARD IV: Strike up the drum, cry 'Courage!' and away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Plains near Tewksbury.
NARRATOR: March. Enter QUEEN MARGARET, PRINCE EDWARD, SOMERSET, OXFORD, and soldiers
QUEEN MARGARET: Great lords, wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss,
QUEEN MARGARET: But cheerly seek how to redress their harms.
QUEEN MARGARET: What though the mast be now blown overboard,
QUEEN MARGARET: The cable broke, the holding-anchor lost,
QUEEN MARGARET: And half our sailors swallow'd in the flood?
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet lives our pilot still. Is't meet that he
QUEEN MARGARET: Should leave the helm and like a fearful lad
QUEEN MARGARET: With tearful eyes add water to the sea
QUEEN MARGARET: And give more strength to that which hath too much,
QUEEN MARGARET: Whiles, in his moan, the ship splits on the rock,
QUEEN MARGARET: Which industry and courage might have saved?
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, what a shame! ah, what a fault were this!
QUEEN MARGARET: Say Warwick was our anchor, what of that?
QUEEN MARGARET: And Montague our topmost, what of him?
QUEEN MARGARET: Our slaughter'd friends the tackles, what of these?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, is not Oxford here another anchor?
QUEEN MARGARET: And Somerset another goodly mast?
QUEEN MARGARET: The friends of France our shrouds and tacklings?
QUEEN MARGARET: And, though unskilful, why not Ned and I
QUEEN MARGARET: For once allow'd the skilful pilot's charge?
QUEEN MARGARET: We will not from the helm to sit and weep,
QUEEN MARGARET: But keep our course, though the rough wind say no,
QUEEN MARGARET: From shelves and rocks that threaten us with wreck.
QUEEN MARGARET: As good to chide the waves as speak them fair.
QUEEN MARGARET: And what is Edward but ruthless sea?
QUEEN MARGARET: What Clarence but a quicksand of deceit?
QUEEN MARGARET: And Richard but a ragged fatal rock?
QUEEN MARGARET: All these the enemies to our poor bark.
QUEEN MARGARET: Say you can swim, alas, 'tis but a while!
QUEEN MARGARET: Tread on the sand, why, there you quickly sink:
QUEEN MARGARET: Bestride the rock, the tide will wash you off,
QUEEN MARGARET: Or else you famish, that's a threefold death.
QUEEN MARGARET: This speak I, lords, to let you understand,
QUEEN MARGARET: If case some one of you would fly from us,
QUEEN MARGARET: That there's no hoped-for mercy with the brothers
QUEEN MARGARET: More than with ruthless waves, with sands and rocks.
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, courage then! what cannot be avoided
QUEEN MARGARET: 'Twere childish weakness to lament or fear.
PRINCE EDWARD: Methinks a woman of this valiant spirit
PRINCE EDWARD: Should, if a coward heard her speak these words,
PRINCE EDWARD: Infuse his breast with magnanimity
PRINCE EDWARD: And make him, naked, foil a man at arms.
PRINCE EDWARD: I speak not this as doubting any here
PRINCE EDWARD: For did I but suspect a fearful man
PRINCE EDWARD: He should have leave to go away betimes,
PRINCE EDWARD: Lest in our need he might infect another
PRINCE EDWARD: And make him of like spirit to himself.
PRINCE EDWARD: If any such be here--as God forbid!--
PRINCE EDWARD: Let him depart before we need his help.
OXFORD: Women and children of so high a courage,
OXFORD: And warriors faint! why, 'twere perpetual shame.
OXFORD: O brave young prince! thy famous grandfather
OXFORD: Doth live again in thee: long mayst thou live
OXFORD: To bear his image and renew his glories!
SOMERSET: And he that will not fight for such a hope.
SOMERSET: Go home to bed, and like the owl by day,
SOMERSET: If he arise, be mock'd and wonder'd at.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thanks, gentle Somerset, sweet Oxford, thanks.
PRINCE EDWARD: And take his thanks that yet hath nothing else.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Prepare you, lords, for Edward is at hand.
Messenger: Ready to fight, therefore be resolute.
OXFORD: I thought no less: it is his policy
OXFORD: To haste thus fast, to find us unprovided.
SOMERSET: But he's deceived, we are in readiness.
QUEEN MARGARET: This cheers my heart, to see your forwardness.
OXFORD: Here pitch our battle, hence we will not budge.
NARRATOR: Flourish and march. Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, CLARENCE, and soldiers
KING EDWARD IV: Brave followers, yonder stands the thorny wood,
KING EDWARD IV: Which, by the heavens' assistance and your strength,
KING EDWARD IV: Must by the roots be hewn up yet ere night.
KING EDWARD IV: I need not add more fuel to your fire,
KING EDWARD IV: For well I wot ye blaze to burn them out
KING EDWARD IV: Give signal to the fight, and to it, lords!
QUEEN MARGARET: Lords, knights, and gentlemen, what I should say
QUEEN MARGARET: My tears gainsay, for every word I speak,
QUEEN MARGARET: Ye see, I drink the water of mine eyes.
QUEEN MARGARET: Therefore, no more but this: Henry, your sovereign,
QUEEN MARGARET: Is prisoner to the foe, his state usurp'd,
QUEEN MARGARET: His realm a slaughter-house, his subjects slain,
QUEEN MARGARET: His statutes cancell'd and his treasure spent,
QUEEN MARGARET: And yonder is the wolf that makes this spoil.
QUEEN MARGARET: You fight in justice: then, in God's name, lords,
QUEEN MARGARET: Be valiant and give signal to the fight.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Retreat. Excursions. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV, GLOUCESTER, CLARENCE,  and soldiers, with QUEEN MARGARET, OXFORD, and SOMERSET, prisoners
KING EDWARD IV: Now here a period of tumultuous broils.
KING EDWARD IV: Away with Oxford to Hames Castle straight:
KING EDWARD IV: For Somerset, off with his guilty head.
KING EDWARD IV: Go, bear them hence, I will not hear them speak.
OXFORD: For my part, I'll not trouble thee with words.
SOMERSET: Nor I, but stoop with patience to my fortune.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Oxford and Somerset, guarded
QUEEN MARGARET: So part we sadly in this troublous world,
QUEEN MARGARET: To meet with joy in sweet Jerusalem.
KING EDWARD IV: Is proclamation made, that who finds Edward
KING EDWARD IV: Shall have a high reward, and he his life?
GLOUCESTER: It is: and lo, where youthful Edward comes!
NARRATOR: Enter soldiers, with PRINCE EDWARD
KING EDWARD IV: Bring forth the gallant, let us hear him speak.
KING EDWARD IV: What! can so young a thorn begin to prick?
KING EDWARD IV: Edward, what satisfaction canst thou make
KING EDWARD IV: For bearing arms, for stirring up my subjects,
KING EDWARD IV: And all the trouble thou hast turn'd me to?
PRINCE EDWARD: Speak like a subject, proud ambitious York!
PRINCE EDWARD: Suppose that I am now my father's mouth,
PRINCE EDWARD: Resign thy chair, and where I stand kneel thou,
PRINCE EDWARD: Whilst I propose the selfsame words to thee,
PRINCE EDWARD: Which traitor, thou wouldst have me answer to.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ah, that thy father had been so resolved!
GLOUCESTER: That you might still have worn the petticoat,
GLOUCESTER: And ne'er have stol'n the breech from Lancaster.
PRINCE EDWARD: Let AEsop fable in a winter's night,
PRINCE EDWARD: His currish riddles sort not with this place.
GLOUCESTER: By heaven, brat, I'll plague ye for that word.
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, thou wast born to be a plague to men.
GLOUCESTER: For God's sake, take away this captive scold.
PRINCE EDWARD: Nay, take away this scolding crookback rather.
KING EDWARD IV: Peace, wilful boy, or I will charm your tongue.
CLARENCE: Untutor'd lad, thou art too malapert.
PRINCE EDWARD: I know my duty, you are all undutiful:
PRINCE EDWARD: Lascivious Edward, and thou perjured George,
PRINCE EDWARD: And thou mis-shapen Dick, I tell ye all
PRINCE EDWARD: I am your better, traitors as ye are:
PRINCE EDWARD: And thou usurp'st my father's right and mine.
KING EDWARD IV: Take that, thou likeness of this railer here.
NARRATOR: Stabs him
GLOUCESTER: Sprawl'st thou? take that, to end thy agony.
NARRATOR: Stabs him
CLARENCE: And there's for twitting me with perjury.
NARRATOR: Stabs him
QUEEN MARGARET: O, kill me too!
GLOUCESTER: Marry, and shall.
NARRATOR: Offers to kill her
KING EDWARD IV: Hold, Richard, hold, for we have done too much.
GLOUCESTER: Why should she live, to fill the world with words?
KING EDWARD IV: What, doth she swoon? use means for her recovery.
GLOUCESTER: Clarence, excuse me to the king my brother,
GLOUCESTER: I'll hence to London on a serious matter:
GLOUCESTER: Ere ye come there, be sure to hear some news.
CLARENCE: What? what?
GLOUCESTER: The Tower, the Tower.
NARRATOR: Exit
QUEEN MARGARET: O Ned, sweet Ned! speak to thy mother, boy!
QUEEN MARGARET: Canst thou not speak? O traitors! murderers!
QUEEN MARGARET: They that stabb'd Caesar shed no blood at all,
QUEEN MARGARET: Did not offend, nor were not worthy blame,
QUEEN MARGARET: If this foul deed were by to equal it:
QUEEN MARGARET: He was a man, this, in respect, a child:
QUEEN MARGARET: And men ne'er spend their fury on a child.
QUEEN MARGARET: What's worse than murderer, that I may name it?
QUEEN MARGARET: No, no, my heart will burst, and if I speak:
QUEEN MARGARET: And I will speak, that so my heart may burst.
QUEEN MARGARET: Butchers and villains! bloody cannibals!
QUEEN MARGARET: How sweet a plant have you untimely cropp'd!
QUEEN MARGARET: You have no children, butchers! if you had,
QUEEN MARGARET: The thought of them would have stirr'd up remorse:
QUEEN MARGARET: But if you ever chance to have a child,
QUEEN MARGARET: Look in his youth to have him so cut off
QUEEN MARGARET: As, deathmen, you have rid this sweet young prince!
KING EDWARD IV: Away with her, go, bear her hence perforce.
QUEEN MARGARET: Nay, never bear me hence, dispatch me here,
QUEEN MARGARET: Here sheathe thy sword, I'll pardon thee my death:
QUEEN MARGARET: What, wilt thou not? then, Clarence, do it thou.
CLARENCE: By heaven, I will not do thee so much ease.
QUEEN MARGARET: Good Clarence, do, sweet Clarence, do thou do it.
CLARENCE: Didst thou not hear me swear I would not do it?
QUEEN MARGARET: Ay, but thou usest to forswear thyself:
QUEEN MARGARET: 'Twas sin before, but now 'tis charity.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, wilt thou not? Where is that devil's butcher,
QUEEN MARGARET: Hard-favour'd Richard? Richard, where art thou?
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou art not here: murder is thy alms-deed,
QUEEN MARGARET: Petitioners for blood thou ne'er put'st back.
KING EDWARD IV: Away, I say, I charge ye, bear her hence.
QUEEN MARGARET: So come to you and yours, as to this Prince!
NARRATOR: Exit, led out forcibly
KING EDWARD IV: Where's Richard gone?
CLARENCE: To London, all in post, and, as I guess,
CLARENCE: To make a bloody supper in the Tower.
KING EDWARD IV: He's sudden, if a thing comes in his head.
KING EDWARD IV: Now march we hence: discharge the common sort
KING EDWARD IV: With pay and thanks, and let's away to London
KING EDWARD IV: And see our gentle queen how well she fares:
KING EDWARD IV: By this, I hope, she hath a son for me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. London. The Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VI and GLOUCESTER, with the Lieutenant, on the walls
GLOUCESTER: Good day, my lord. What, at your book so hard?
KING HENRY VI: Ay, my good lord:--my lord, I should say rather,
KING HENRY VI: 'Tis sin to flatter, 'good' was little better:
KING HENRY VI: 'Good Gloucester' and 'good devil' were alike,
KING HENRY VI: And both preposterous, therefore, not 'good lord.'
GLOUCESTER: Sirrah, leave us to ourselves: we must confer.
NARRATOR: Exit Lieutenant
KING HENRY VI: So flies the reckless shepherd from the wolf,
KING HENRY VI: So first the harmless sheep doth yield his fleece
KING HENRY VI: And next his throat unto the butcher's knife.
KING HENRY VI: What scene of death hath Roscius now to act?
GLOUCESTER: Suspicion always haunts the guilty mind,
GLOUCESTER: The thief doth fear each bush an officer.
KING HENRY VI: The bird that hath been limed in a bush,
KING HENRY VI: With trembling wings misdoubteth every bush,
KING HENRY VI: And I, the hapless male to one sweet bird,
KING HENRY VI: Have now the fatal object in my eye
KING HENRY VI: Where my poor young was limed, was caught and kill'd.
GLOUCESTER: Why, what a peevish fool was that of Crete,
GLOUCESTER: That taught his son the office of a fowl!
GLOUCESTER: An yet, for all his wings, the fool was drown'd.
KING HENRY VI: I, Daedalus, my poor boy, Icarus,
KING HENRY VI: Thy father, Minos, that denied our course,
KING HENRY VI: The sun that sear'd the wings of my sweet boy
KING HENRY VI: Thy brother Edward, and thyself the sea
KING HENRY VI: Whose envious gulf did swallow up his life.
KING HENRY VI: Ah, kill me with thy weapon, not with words!
KING HENRY VI: My breast can better brook thy dagger's point
KING HENRY VI: Than can my ears that tragic history.
KING HENRY VI: But wherefore dost thou come? is't for my life?
GLOUCESTER: Think'st thou I am an executioner?
KING HENRY VI: A persecutor, I am sure, thou art:
KING HENRY VI: If murdering innocents be executing,
KING HENRY VI: Why, then thou art an executioner.
GLOUCESTER: Thy son I kill'd for his presumption.
KING HENRY VI: Hadst thou been kill'd when first thou didst presume,
KING HENRY VI: Thou hadst not lived to kill a son of mine.
KING HENRY VI: And thus I prophesy, that many a thousand,
KING HENRY VI: Which now mistrust no parcel of my fear,
KING HENRY VI: And many an old man's sigh and many a widow's,
KING HENRY VI: And many an orphan's water-standing eye--
KING HENRY VI: Men for their sons, wives for their husbands,
KING HENRY VI: And orphans for their parents timeless death--
KING HENRY VI: Shall rue the hour that ever thou wast born.
KING HENRY VI: The owl shriek'd at thy birth,--an evil sign,
KING HENRY VI: The night-crow cried, aboding luckless time,
KING HENRY VI: Dogs howl'd, and hideous tempest shook down trees,
KING HENRY VI: The raven rook'd her on the chimney's top,
KING HENRY VI: And chattering pies in dismal discords sung.
KING HENRY VI: Thy mother felt more than a mother's pain,
KING HENRY VI: And, yet brought forth less than a mother's hope,
KING HENRY VI: To wit, an indigested and deformed lump,
KING HENRY VI: Not like the fruit of such a goodly tree.
KING HENRY VI: Teeth hadst thou in thy head when thou wast born,
KING HENRY VI: To signify thou camest to bite the world:
KING HENRY VI: And, if the rest be true which I have heard,
KING HENRY VI: Thou camest--
GLOUCESTER: I'll hear no more: die, prophet in thy speech:
NARRATOR: Stabs him
GLOUCESTER: For this amongst the rest, was I ordain'd.
KING HENRY VI: Ay, and for much more slaughter after this.
KING HENRY VI: God forgive my sins, and pardon thee!
NARRATOR: Dies
GLOUCESTER: What, will the aspiring blood of Lancaster
GLOUCESTER: Sink in the ground? I thought it would have mounted.
GLOUCESTER: See how my sword weeps for the poor king's death!
GLOUCESTER: O, may such purple tears be alway shed
GLOUCESTER: From those that wish the downfall of our house!
GLOUCESTER: If any spark of life be yet remaining,
GLOUCESTER: Down, down to hell, and say I sent thee thither:
NARRATOR: Stabs him again
GLOUCESTER: I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear.
GLOUCESTER: Indeed, 'tis true that Henry told me of,
GLOUCESTER: For I have often heard my mother say
GLOUCESTER: I came into the world with my legs forward:
GLOUCESTER: Had I not reason, think ye, to make haste,
GLOUCESTER: And seek their ruin that usurp'd our right?
GLOUCESTER: The midwife wonder'd and the women cried
GLOUCESTER: 'O, Jesus bless us, he is born with teeth!'
GLOUCESTER: And so I was, which plainly signified
GLOUCESTER: That I should snarl and bite and play the dog.
GLOUCESTER: Then, since the heavens have shaped my body so,
GLOUCESTER: Let hell make crook'd my mind to answer it.
GLOUCESTER: I have no brother, I am like no brother,
GLOUCESTER: And this word 'love,' which graybeards call divine,
GLOUCESTER: Be resident in men like one another
GLOUCESTER: And not in me: I am myself alone.
GLOUCESTER: Clarence, beware, thou keep'st me from the light:
GLOUCESTER: But I will sort a pitchy day for thee,
GLOUCESTER: For I will buz abroad such prophecies
GLOUCESTER: That Edward shall be fearful of his life,
GLOUCESTER: And then, to purge his fear, I'll be thy death.
GLOUCESTER: King Henry and the prince his son are gone:
GLOUCESTER: Clarence, thy turn is next, and then the rest,
GLOUCESTER: Counting myself but bad till I be best.
GLOUCESTER: I'll throw thy body in another room
GLOUCESTER: And triumph, Henry, in thy day of doom.
NARRATOR: Exit, with the body
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV, QUEEN ELIZABETH,  CLARENCE, GLOUCESTER, HASTINGS, a Nurse with the young Prince, and Attendants
KING EDWARD IV: Once more we sit in England's royal throne,
KING EDWARD IV: Re-purchased with the blood of enemies.
KING EDWARD IV: What valiant foemen, like to autumn's corn,
KING EDWARD IV: Have we mow'd down, in tops of all their pride!
KING EDWARD IV: Three Dukes of Somerset, threefold renown'd
KING EDWARD IV: For hardy and undoubted champions,
KING EDWARD IV: Two Cliffords, as the father and the son,
KING EDWARD IV: And two Northumberlands, two braver men
KING EDWARD IV: Ne'er spurr'd their coursers at the trumpet's sound,
KING EDWARD IV: With them, the two brave bears, Warwick and Montague,
KING EDWARD IV: That in their chains fetter'd the kingly lion
KING EDWARD IV: And made the forest tremble when they roar'd.
KING EDWARD IV: Thus have we swept suspicion from our seat
KING EDWARD IV: And made our footstool of security.
KING EDWARD IV: Come hither, Bess, and let me kiss my boy.
KING EDWARD IV: Young Ned, for thee, thine uncles and myself
KING EDWARD IV: Have in our armours watch'd the winter's night,
KING EDWARD IV: Went all afoot in summer's scalding heat,
KING EDWARD IV: That thou mightst repossess the crown in peace,
KING EDWARD IV: And of our labours thou shalt reap the gain.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  I'll blast his harvest, if your head were laid,
GLOUCESTER: For yet I am not look'd on in the world.
GLOUCESTER: This shoulder was ordain'd so thick to heave,
GLOUCESTER: And heave it shall some weight, or break my back:
GLOUCESTER: Work thou the way,--and thou shalt execute.
KING EDWARD IV: Clarence and Gloucester, love my lovely queen,
KING EDWARD IV: And kiss your princely nephew, brothers both.
CLARENCE: The duty that I owe unto your majesty
CLARENCE: I seal upon the lips of this sweet babe.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Thanks, noble Clarence, worthy brother, thanks.
GLOUCESTER: And, that I love the tree from whence thou sprang'st,
GLOUCESTER: Witness the loving kiss I give the fruit.
NARRATOR: Aside
GLOUCESTER: And cried 'all hail!' when as he meant all harm.
KING EDWARD IV: Now am I seated as my soul delights,
KING EDWARD IV: Having my country's peace and brothers' loves.
CLARENCE: What will your grace have done with Margaret?
CLARENCE: Reignier, her father, to the king of France
CLARENCE: Hath pawn'd the Sicils and Jerusalem,
CLARENCE: And hither have they sent it for her ransom.
KING EDWARD IV: Away with her, and waft her hence to France.
KING EDWARD IV: And now what rests but that we spend the time
KING EDWARD IV: With stately triumphs, mirthful comic shows,
KING EDWARD IV: Such as befits the pleasure of the court?
KING EDWARD IV: Sound drums and trumpets! farewell sour annoy!
KING EDWARD IV: For here, I hope, begins our lasting joy.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Henry VIII '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
Chorus: I come no more to make you laugh: things now,
Chorus: That bear a weighty and a serious brow,
Chorus: Sad, high, and working, full of state and woe,
Chorus: Such noble scenes as draw the eye to flow,
Chorus: We now present. Those that can pity, here
Chorus: May, if they think it well, let fall a tear,
Chorus: The subject will deserve it. Such as give
Chorus: Their money out of hope they may believe,
Chorus: May here find truth too. Those that come to see
Chorus: Only a show or two, and so agree
Chorus: The play may pass, if they be still and willing,
Chorus: I'll undertake may see away their shilling
Chorus: Richly in two short hours. Only they
Chorus: That come to hear a merry bawdy play,
Chorus: A noise of targets, or to see a fellow
Chorus: In a long motley coat guarded with yellow,
Chorus: Will be deceived, for, gentle hearers, know,
Chorus: To rank our chosen truth with such a show
Chorus: As fool and fight is, beside forfeiting
Chorus: Our own brains, and the opinion that we bring,
Chorus: To make that only true we now intend,
Chorus: Will leave us never an understanding friend.
Chorus: Therefore, for goodness' sake, and as you are known
Chorus: The first and happiest hearers of the town,
Chorus: Be sad, as we would make ye: think ye see
Chorus: The very persons of our noble story
Chorus: As they were living, think you see them great,
Chorus: And follow'd with the general throng and sweat
Chorus: Of thousand friends, then in a moment, see
Chorus: How soon this mightiness meets misery:
Chorus: And, if you can be merry then, I'll say
Chorus: A man may weep upon his wedding-day.
Chorus: SCENE I. London. An ante-chamber in the palace.
Chorus: Enter NORFOLK at one door, at the other, BUCKINGHAM and ABERGAVENNY
BUCKINGHAM: Good morrow, and well met. How have ye done
BUCKINGHAM: Since last we saw in France?
NORFOLK: I thank your grace,
NORFOLK: Healthful, and ever since a fresh admirer
NORFOLK: Of what I saw there.
BUCKINGHAM: An untimely ague
BUCKINGHAM: Stay'd me a prisoner in my chamber when
BUCKINGHAM: Those suns of glory, those two lights of men,
BUCKINGHAM: Met in the vale of Andren.
NORFOLK: 'Twixt Guynes and Arde:
NORFOLK: I was then present, saw them salute on horseback,
NORFOLK: Beheld them, when they lighted, how they clung
NORFOLK: In their embracement, as they grew together,
NORFOLK: Which had they, what four throned ones could have weigh'd
NORFOLK: Such a compounded one?
BUCKINGHAM: All the whole time
BUCKINGHAM: I was my chamber's prisoner.
NORFOLK: Then you lost
NORFOLK: The view of earthly glory: men might say,
NORFOLK: Till this time pomp was single, but now married
NORFOLK: To one above itself. Each following day
NORFOLK: Became the next day's master, till the last
NORFOLK: Made former wonders its. To-day the French,
NORFOLK: All clinquant, all in gold, like heathen gods,
NORFOLK: Shone down the English, and, to-morrow, they
NORFOLK: Made Britain India: every man that stood
NORFOLK: Show'd like a mine. Their dwarfish pages were
NORFOLK: As cherubins, all guilt: the madams too,
NORFOLK: Not used to toil, did almost sweat to bear
NORFOLK: The pride upon them, that their very labour
NORFOLK: Was to them as a painting: now this masque
NORFOLK: Was cried incomparable, and the ensuing night
NORFOLK: Made it a fool and beggar. The two kings,
NORFOLK: Equal in lustre, were now best, now worst,
NORFOLK: As presence did present them, him in eye,
NORFOLK: Still him in praise: and, being present both
NORFOLK: 'Twas said they saw but one, and no discerner
NORFOLK: Durst wag his tongue in censure. When these suns--
NORFOLK: For so they phrase 'em--by their heralds challenged
NORFOLK: The noble spirits to arms, they did perform
NORFOLK: Beyond thought's compass, that former fabulous story,
NORFOLK: Being now seen possible enough, got credit,
NORFOLK: That Bevis was believed.
BUCKINGHAM: O, you go far.
NORFOLK: As I belong to worship and affect
NORFOLK: In honour honesty, the tract of every thing
NORFOLK: Would by a good discourser lose some life,
NORFOLK: Which action's self was tongue to. All was royal,
NORFOLK: To the disposing of it nought rebell'd.
NORFOLK: Order gave each thing view, the office did
NORFOLK: Distinctly his full function.
BUCKINGHAM: Who did guide,
BUCKINGHAM: I mean, who set the body and the limbs
BUCKINGHAM: Of this great sport together, as you guess?
NORFOLK: One, certes, that promises no element
NORFOLK: In such a business.
BUCKINGHAM: I pray you, who, my lord?
NORFOLK: All this was order'd by the good discretion
NORFOLK: Of the right reverend Cardinal of York.
BUCKINGHAM: The devil speed him! no man's pie is freed
BUCKINGHAM: From his ambitious finger. What had he
BUCKINGHAM: To do in these fierce vanities? I wonder
BUCKINGHAM: That such a keech can with his very bulk
BUCKINGHAM: Take up the rays o' the beneficial sun
BUCKINGHAM: And keep it from the earth.
NORFOLK: Surely, sir,
NORFOLK: There's in him stuff that puts him to these ends,
NORFOLK: For, being not propp'd by ancestry, whose grace
NORFOLK: Chalks successors their way, nor call'd upon
NORFOLK: For high feats done to the crown, neither allied
NORFOLK: For eminent assistants, but, spider-like,
NORFOLK: Out of his self-drawing web, he gives us note,
NORFOLK: The force of his own merit makes his way
NORFOLK: A gift that heaven gives for him, which buys
NORFOLK: A place next to the king.
ABERGAVENNY: I cannot tell
ABERGAVENNY: What heaven hath given him,--let some graver eye
ABERGAVENNY: Pierce into that, but I can see his pride
ABERGAVENNY: Peep through each part of him: whence has he that,
ABERGAVENNY: If not from hell? the devil is a niggard,
ABERGAVENNY: Or has given all before, and he begins
ABERGAVENNY: A new hell in himself.
BUCKINGHAM: Why the devil,
BUCKINGHAM: Upon this French going out, took he upon him,
BUCKINGHAM: Without the privity o' the king, to appoint
BUCKINGHAM: Who should attend on him? He makes up the file
BUCKINGHAM: Of all the gentry, for the most part such
BUCKINGHAM: To whom as great a charge as little honour
BUCKINGHAM: He meant to lay upon: and his own letter,
BUCKINGHAM: The honourable board of council out,
BUCKINGHAM: Must fetch him in the papers.
ABERGAVENNY: I do know
ABERGAVENNY: Kinsmen of mine, three at the least, that have
ABERGAVENNY: By this so sickened their estates, that never
ABERGAVENNY: They shall abound as formerly.
BUCKINGHAM: O, many
BUCKINGHAM: Have broke their backs with laying manors on 'em
BUCKINGHAM: For this great journey. What did this vanity
BUCKINGHAM: But minister communication of
BUCKINGHAM: A most poor issue?
NORFOLK: Grievingly I think,
NORFOLK: The peace between the French and us not values
NORFOLK: The cost that did conclude it.
BUCKINGHAM: Every man,
BUCKINGHAM: After the hideous storm that follow'd, was
BUCKINGHAM: A thing inspired, and, not consulting, broke
BUCKINGHAM: Into a general prophecy, That this tempest,
BUCKINGHAM: Dashing the garment of this peace, aboded
BUCKINGHAM: The sudden breach on't.
NORFOLK: Which is budded out,
NORFOLK: For France hath flaw'd the league, and hath attach'd
NORFOLK: Our merchants' goods at Bourdeaux.
ABERGAVENNY: Is it therefore
ABERGAVENNY: The ambassador is silenced?
NORFOLK: Marry, is't.
ABERGAVENNY: A proper title of a peace, and purchased
ABERGAVENNY: At a superfluous rate!
BUCKINGHAM: Why, all this business
BUCKINGHAM: Our reverend cardinal carried.
NORFOLK: Like it your grace,
NORFOLK: The state takes notice of the private difference
NORFOLK: Betwixt you and the cardinal. I advise you--
NORFOLK: And take it from a heart that wishes towards you
NORFOLK: Honour and plenteous safety--that you read
NORFOLK: The cardinal's malice and his potency
NORFOLK: Together, to consider further that
NORFOLK: What his high hatred would effect wants not
NORFOLK: A minister in his power. You know his nature,
NORFOLK: That he's revengeful, and I know his sword
NORFOLK: Hath a sharp edge: it's long and, 't may be said,
NORFOLK: It reaches far, and where 'twill not extend,
NORFOLK: Thither he darts it. Bosom up my counsel,
NORFOLK: You'll find it wholesome. Lo, where comes that rock
NORFOLK: That I advise your shunning.
NARRATOR: Enter CARDINAL WOLSEY, the purse borne before him,  certain of the Guard, and two Secretaries with  papers. CARDINAL WOLSEY in his passage fixeth his  eye on BUCKINGHAM, and BUCKINGHAM on him, both full of disdain
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The Duke of Buckingham's surveyor, ha?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Where's his examination?
First Secretary: Here, so please you.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Is he in person ready?
First Secretary: Ay, please your grace.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Well, we shall then know more, and Buckingham
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Shall lessen this big look.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CARDINAL WOLSEY and his Train
BUCKINGHAM: This butcher's cur is venom-mouth'd, and I
BUCKINGHAM: Have not the power to muzzle him, therefore best
BUCKINGHAM: Not wake him in his slumber. A beggar's book
BUCKINGHAM: Outworths a noble's blood.
NORFOLK: What, are you chafed?
NORFOLK: Ask God for temperance, that's the appliance only
NORFOLK: Which your disease requires.
BUCKINGHAM: I read in's looks
BUCKINGHAM: Matter against me, and his eye reviled
BUCKINGHAM: Me, as his abject object: at this instant
BUCKINGHAM: He bores me with some trick: he's gone to the king,
BUCKINGHAM: I'll follow and outstare him.
NORFOLK: Stay, my lord,
NORFOLK: And let your reason with your choler question
NORFOLK: What 'tis you go about: to climb steep hills
NORFOLK: Requires slow pace at first: anger is like
NORFOLK: A full-hot horse, who being allow'd his way,
NORFOLK: Self-mettle tires him. Not a man in England
NORFOLK: Can advise me like you: be to yourself
NORFOLK: As you would to your friend.
BUCKINGHAM: I'll to the king,
BUCKINGHAM: And from a mouth of honour quite cry down
BUCKINGHAM: This Ipswich fellow's insolence, or proclaim
BUCKINGHAM: There's difference in no persons.
NORFOLK: Be advised,
NORFOLK: Heat not a furnace for your foe so hot
NORFOLK: That it do singe yourself: we may outrun,
NORFOLK: By violent swiftness, that which we run at,
NORFOLK: And lose by over-running. Know you not,
NORFOLK: The fire that mounts the liquor til run o'er,
NORFOLK: In seeming to augment it wastes it? Be advised:
NORFOLK: I say again, there is no English soul
NORFOLK: More stronger to direct you than yourself,
NORFOLK: If with the sap of reason you would quench,
NORFOLK: Or but allay, the fire of passion.
BUCKINGHAM: Sir,
BUCKINGHAM: I am thankful to you, and I'll go along
BUCKINGHAM: By your prescription: but this top-proud fellow,
BUCKINGHAM: Whom from the flow of gall I name not but
BUCKINGHAM: From sincere motions, by intelligence,
BUCKINGHAM: And proofs as clear as founts in July when
BUCKINGHAM: We see each grain of gravel, I do know
BUCKINGHAM: To be corrupt and treasonous.
NORFOLK: Say not 'treasonous.'
BUCKINGHAM: To the king I'll say't, and make my vouch as strong
BUCKINGHAM: As shore of rock. Attend. This holy fox,
BUCKINGHAM: Or wolf, or both,--for he is equal ravenous
BUCKINGHAM: As he is subtle, and as prone to mischief
BUCKINGHAM: As able to perform't, his mind and place
BUCKINGHAM: Infecting one another, yea, reciprocally--
BUCKINGHAM: Only to show his pomp as well in France
BUCKINGHAM: As here at home, suggests the king our master
BUCKINGHAM: To this last costly treaty, the interview,
BUCKINGHAM: That swallow'd so much treasure, and like a glass
BUCKINGHAM: Did break i' the rinsing.
NORFOLK: Faith, and so it did.
BUCKINGHAM: Pray, give me favour, sir. This cunning cardinal
BUCKINGHAM: The articles o' the combination drew
BUCKINGHAM: As himself pleased, and they were ratified
BUCKINGHAM: As he cried 'Thus let be': to as much end
BUCKINGHAM: As give a crutch to the dead: but our count-cardinal
BUCKINGHAM: Has done this, and 'tis well, for worthy Wolsey,
BUCKINGHAM: Who cannot err, he did it. Now this follows,--
BUCKINGHAM: Which, as I take it, is a kind of puppy
BUCKINGHAM: To the old dam, treason,--Charles the emperor,
BUCKINGHAM: Under pretence to see the queen his aunt--
BUCKINGHAM: For 'twas indeed his colour, but he came
BUCKINGHAM: To whisper Wolsey,--here makes visitation:
BUCKINGHAM: His fears were, that the interview betwixt
BUCKINGHAM: England and France might, through their amity,
BUCKINGHAM: Breed him some prejudice, for from this league
BUCKINGHAM: Peep'd harms that menaced him: he privily
BUCKINGHAM: Deals with our cardinal, and, as I trow,--
BUCKINGHAM: Which I do well, for I am sure the emperor
BUCKINGHAM: Paid ere he promised, whereby his suit was granted
BUCKINGHAM: Ere it was ask'd, but when the way was made,
BUCKINGHAM: And paved with gold, the emperor thus desired,
BUCKINGHAM: That he would please to alter the king's course,
BUCKINGHAM: And break the foresaid peace. Let the king know,
BUCKINGHAM: As soon he shall by me, that thus the cardinal
BUCKINGHAM: Does buy and sell his honour as he pleases,
BUCKINGHAM: And for his own advantage.
NORFOLK: I am sorry
NORFOLK: To hear this of him, and could wish he were
NORFOLK: Something mistaken in't.
BUCKINGHAM: No, not a syllable:
BUCKINGHAM: I  do pronounce him in that very shape
BUCKINGHAM: He shall appear in proof.
NARRATOR: Enter BRANDON, a Sergeant-at-arms before him, and two or three of the Guard
BRANDON: Your office, sergeant, execute it.
Sergeant: Sir,
Sergeant: My lord the Duke of Buckingham, and Earl
Sergeant: Of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton, I
Sergeant: Arrest thee of high treason, in the name
Sergeant: Of our most sovereign king.
BUCKINGHAM: Lo, you, my lord,
BUCKINGHAM: The net has fall'n upon me! I shall perish
BUCKINGHAM: Under device and practise.
BRANDON: I am sorry
BRANDON: To see you ta'en from liberty, to look on
BRANDON: The business present: 'tis his highness' pleasure
BRANDON: You shall to the Tower.
BUCKINGHAM: It will help me nothing
BUCKINGHAM: To plead mine innocence, for that dye is on me
BUCKINGHAM: Which makes my whitest part black. The will of heaven
BUCKINGHAM: Be done in this and all things! I obey.
BUCKINGHAM: O my Lord Abergavenny, fare you well!
BRANDON: Nay, he must bear you company. The king
NARRATOR: To ABERGAVENNY
BRANDON: Is pleased you shall to the Tower, till you know
BRANDON: How he determines further.
ABERGAVENNY: As the duke said,
ABERGAVENNY: The will of heaven be done, and the king's pleasure
ABERGAVENNY: By me obey'd!
BRANDON: Here is a warrant from
BRANDON: The king to attach Lord Montacute, and the bodies
BRANDON: Of the duke's confessor, John de la Car,
BRANDON: One Gilbert Peck, his chancellor--
BUCKINGHAM: So, so,
BUCKINGHAM: These are the limbs o' the plot: no more, I hope.
BRANDON: A monk o' the Chartreux.
BUCKINGHAM: O, Nicholas Hopkins?
BRANDON: He.
BUCKINGHAM: My surveyor is false, the o'er-great cardinal
BUCKINGHAM: Hath show'd him gold, my life is spann'd already:
BUCKINGHAM: I am the shadow of poor Buckingham,
BUCKINGHAM: Whose figure even this instant cloud puts on,
BUCKINGHAM: By darkening my clear sun. My lord, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. The council-chamber.
NARRATOR: Cornets. Enter KING HENRY VIII, leaning on  CARDINAL WOLSEY's shoulder, the Nobles, and LOVELL,  CARDINAL WOLSEY places himself under KING HENRY VIII's feet on his right side
KING HENRY VIII: My life itself, and the best heart of it,

KING HENRY VIII: Of a full-charged confederacy, and give thanks
KING HENRY VIII: To you that choked it. Let be call'd before us

KING HENRY VIII: The other moiety, ere you ask, is given,

QUEEN KATHARINE: escapes not

QUEEN KATHARINE: The sides of loyalty, and almost appears
QUEEN KATHARINE: In loud rebellion.
NORFOLK: Not almost appears,

NORFOLK: The clothiers all, not able to maintain

KING HENRY VIII: Wherein? and what taxation? My lord cardinal,
KING HENRY VIII: You that are blamed for it alike with us,

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Please you, sir,

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Pertains to the state, and front but in that file
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Where others tell steps with me.
QUEEN KATHARINE: No, my lord,
QUEEN KATHARINE: You know no more than others, but you frame
QUEEN KATHARINE: Things that are known alike, which are not wholesome
QUEEN KATHARINE: To those which would not know them, and yet must
QUEEN KATHARINE: Perforce be their acquaintance. These exactions,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Whereof my sovereign would have note, they are
QUEEN KATHARINE: Most pestilent to the bearing, and, to bear 'em,

QUEEN KATHARINE: Too hard an exclamation.
KING HENRY VIII: Still exaction!
KING HENRY VIII: The nature of it? in what kind, let's know,
KING HENRY VIII: Is this exaction?
QUEEN KATHARINE: I am much too venturous

QUEEN KATHARINE: Under your promised pardon. The subjects' grief

QUEEN KATHARINE: Tongues spit their duties out, and cold hearts freeze

QUEEN KATHARINE: This tractable obedience is a slave

QUEEN KATHARINE: Would give it quick consideration, for
QUEEN KATHARINE: There is no primer business.
KING HENRY VIII: By my life,
KING HENRY VIII: This is against our pleasure.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And for me,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I have no further gone in this than by
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A single voice, and that not pass'd me but
CARDINAL WOLSEY: By learned approbation of the judges. If I am
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Traduced by ignorant tongues, which neither know
CARDINAL WOLSEY: My faculties nor person, yet will be
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The chronicles of my doing, let me say
CARDINAL WOLSEY: 'Tis but the fate of place, and the rough brake
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That virtue must go through. We must not stint
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Our necessary actions, in the fear
CARDINAL WOLSEY: To cope malicious censurers, which ever,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: As ravenous fishes, do a vessel follow
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That is new-trimm'd, but benefit no further
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Than vainly longing. What we oft do best,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: By sick interpreters, once weak ones, is
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Not ours, or not allow'd, what worst, as oft,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Hitting a grosser quality, is cried up
CARDINAL WOLSEY: For our best act. If we shall stand still,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: In fear our motion will be mock'd or carp'd at,

CARDINAL WOLSEY: State-statues only.
KING HENRY VIII: Things done well,

KING HENRY VIII: We must not rend our subjects from our laws,

CARDINAL WOLSEY: A word with you.
NARRATOR: To the Secretary

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Hardly conceive of me, let it be noised

CARDINAL WOLSEY: And pardon comes: I shall anon advise you
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Further in the proceeding.
NARRATOR: Exit Secretary
NARRATOR: Enter Surveyor
QUEEN KATHARINE: I am sorry that the Duke of Buckingham

KING HENRY VIII: We cannot feel too little, hear too much.

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Most like a careful subject, have collected

Surveyor: First, it was usual with him, every day
Surveyor: It would infect his speech, that if the king
Surveyor: Should without issue die, he'll carry it so
Surveyor: To make the sceptre his: these very words
Surveyor: I've heard him utter to his son-in-law,
Surveyor: Lord Abergavenny, to whom by oath he menaced
Surveyor: Revenge upon the cardinal.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Please your highness, note
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This dangerous conception in this point.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Not friended by by his wish, to your high person
CARDINAL WOLSEY: His will is most malignant, and it stretches
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Beyond you, to your friends.
QUEEN KATHARINE: My learn'd lord cardinal,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Deliver all with charity.
KING HENRY VIII: Speak on:
KING HENRY VIII: How grounded he his title to the crown,
KING HENRY VIII: Upon our fail? to this point hast thou heard him
KING HENRY VIII: At any time speak aught?
Surveyor: He was brought to this
Surveyor: By a vain prophecy of Nicholas Hopkins.
KING HENRY VIII: What was that Hopkins?
Surveyor: Sir, a Chartreux friar,
Surveyor: His confessor, who fed him every minute
Surveyor: With words of sovereignty.
KING HENRY VIII: How know'st thou this?
Surveyor: Not long before your highness sped to France,

Surveyor: Men fear'd the French would prove perfidious,

Surveyor: 'Twould prove the verity of certain words
Surveyor: Spoke by a holy monk, 'that oft,' says he,
Surveyor: 'Hath sent to me, wishing me to permit
Surveyor: John de la Car, my chaplain, a choice hour
Surveyor: To hear from him a matter of some moment:
Surveyor: Whom after under the confession's seal
Surveyor: He solemnly had sworn, that what he spoke
Surveyor: My chaplain to no creature living, but
Surveyor: To me, should utter, with demure confidence

Surveyor: To gain the love o' the commonalty: the duke
Surveyor: Shall govern England.'

QUEEN KATHARINE: You were the duke's surveyor, and lost your office
QUEEN KATHARINE: On the complaint o' the tenants: take good heed
QUEEN KATHARINE: You charge not in your spleen a noble person
QUEEN KATHARINE: And spoil your nobler soul: I say, take heed,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Yes, heartily beseech you.
KING HENRY VIII: Let him on.
KING HENRY VIII: Go forward.
Surveyor: On my soul, I'll speak but truth.
Surveyor: I told my lord the duke, by the devil's illusions
Surveyor: The monk might be deceived, and that 'twas dangerous for him
Surveyor: To ruminate on this so far, until
Surveyor: It forged him some design, which, being believed,
Surveyor: It was much like to do: he answer'd, 'Tush,
Surveyor: It can do me no damage,' adding further,
Surveyor: That, had the king in his last sickness fail'd,
Surveyor: The cardinal's and Sir Thomas Lovell's heads
Surveyor: Should have gone off.
KING HENRY VIII: Ha! what, so rank? Ah ha!
KING HENRY VIII: There's mischief in this man: canst thou say further?
Surveyor: I can, my liege.
KING HENRY VIII: Proceed.
Surveyor: Being at Greenwich,
Surveyor: After your highness had reproved the duke
Surveyor: About Sir William Blomer,--
KING HENRY VIII: I remember
KING HENRY VIII: Of such a time: being my sworn servant,

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Now, madam, may his highness live in freedom,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: and this man out of prison?
QUEEN KATHARINE: God mend all!
KING HENRY VIII: There's something more would out of thee, what say'st?
Surveyor: After 'the duke his father,' with 'the knife,'
Surveyor: He stretch'd him, and, with one hand on his dagger,
Surveyor: Another spread on's breast, mounting his eyes
Surveyor: He did discharge a horrible oath, whose tenor
Surveyor: Was,--were he evil used, he would outgo
Surveyor: His father by as much as a performance
Surveyor: Does an irresolute purpose.
KING HENRY VIII: There's his period,
KING HENRY VIII: To sheathe his knife in us. He is attach'd,
KING HENRY VIII: Call him to present trial: if he may
KING HENRY VIII: Find mercy in the law, 'tis his: if none,
KING HENRY VIII: Let him not seek 't of us: by day and night,

NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. An ante-chamber in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter Chamberlain and SANDS
Chamberlain: Is't possible the spells of France should juggle
Chamberlain: Men into such strange mysteries?
SANDS: New customs,
SANDS: Though they be never so ridiculous,
SANDS: Nay, let 'em be unmanly, yet are follow'd.
Chamberlain: As far as I see, all the good our English
Chamberlain: Have got by the late voyage is but merely
Chamberlain: A fit or two o' the face, but they are shrewd ones,
Chamberlain: For when they hold 'em, you would swear directly
Chamberlain: Their very noses had been counsellors
Chamberlain: To Pepin or Clotharius, they keep state so.
SANDS: They have all new legs, and lame ones: one would take it,
SANDS: That never saw 'em pace before, the spavin
SANDS: Or springhalt reign'd among 'em.
Chamberlain: Death! my lord,
Chamberlain: Their clothes are after such a pagan cut too,
Chamberlain: That, sure, they've worn out Christendom.
NARRATOR: Enter LOVELL
Chamberlain: How now!
Chamberlain: What news, Sir Thomas Lovell?
LOVELL: Faith, my lord,
LOVELL: I hear of none, but the new proclamation
LOVELL: That's clapp'd upon the court-gate.
Chamberlain: What is't for?

Chamberlain: To think an English courtier may be wise,

LOVELL: Of fool and feather that they got in France,

LOVELL: Short blister'd breeches, and those types of travel,

LOVELL: They may, 'cum privilegio,' wear away
LOVELL: The lag end of their lewdness and be laugh'd at.

SANDS: Are grown so catching.

LOVELL: Ay, marry,

SANDS: An honest country lord, as I am, beaten
SANDS: A long time out of play, may bring his plainsong
SANDS: And have an hour of hearing, and, by'r lady,
SANDS: Held current music too.
Chamberlain: Well said, Lord Sands,

SANDS: No, my lord,
SANDS: Nor shall not, while I have a stump.

Chamberlain: This night he makes a supper, and a great one,

LOVELL: His dews fall every where.
