NARRATOR: Exit Chamberlain, attended. All rise, and tables removed
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You have now a broken banquet, but we'll mend it.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A good digestion to you all: and once more
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I shower a welcome on ye, welcome all.
NARRATOR: Hautboys. Enter KING HENRY VIII and others, as  masquers, habited like shepherds, ushered by the  Chamberlain. They pass directly before CARDINAL WOLSEY, and gracefully salute him
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A noble company! what are their pleasures?
Chamberlain: Because they speak no English, thus they pray'd
Chamberlain: To tell your grace, that, having heard by fame
Chamberlain: Of this so noble and so fair assembly
Chamberlain: This night to meet here, they could do no less
Chamberlain: Out of the great respect they bear to beauty,
Chamberlain: But leave their flocks, and, under your fair conduct,
Chamberlain: Crave leave to view these ladies and entreat
Chamberlain: An hour of revels with 'em.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Say, lord chamberlain,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: They have done my poor house grace, for which I pay 'em
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A thousand thanks, and pray 'em take their pleasures.
NARRATOR: They choose Ladies for the dance. KING HENRY VIII chooses ANNE
KING HENRY VIII: The fairest hand I ever touch'd! O beauty,
KING HENRY VIII: Till now I never knew thee!
NARRATOR: Music. Dance
CARDINAL WOLSEY: My lord!
Chamberlain: Your grace?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Pray, tell 'em thus much from me:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There should be one amongst 'em, by his person,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: More worthy this place than myself, to whom,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: If I but knew him, with my love and duty
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I would surrender it.
Chamberlain: I will, my lord.
NARRATOR: Whispers the Masquers
CARDINAL WOLSEY: What say they?
Chamberlain: Such a one, they all confess,
Chamberlain: There is indeed, which they would have your grace
Chamberlain: Find out, and he will take it.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Let me see, then.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: By all your good leaves, gentlemen, here I'll make
CARDINAL WOLSEY: My royal choice.
KING HENRY VIII: Ye have found him, cardinal:
NARRATOR: Unmasking
KING HENRY VIII: You hold a fair assembly, you do well, lord:
KING HENRY VIII: You are a churchman, or, I'll tell you, cardinal,
KING HENRY VIII: I should judge now unhappily.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I am glad
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Your grace is grown so pleasant.
KING HENRY VIII: My lord chamberlain,
KING HENRY VIII: Prithee, come hither: what fair lady's that?
Chamberlain: An't please your grace, Sir Thomas Bullen's daughter--
Chamberlain: The Viscount Rochford,--one of her highness' women.
KING HENRY VIII: By heaven, she is a dainty one. Sweetheart,
KING HENRY VIII: I were unmannerly, to take you out,
KING HENRY VIII: And not to kiss you. A health, gentlemen!
KING HENRY VIII: Let it go round.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Sir Thomas Lovell, is the banquet ready
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I' the privy chamber?
LOVELL: Yes, my lord.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Your grace,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I fear, with dancing is a little heated.
KING HENRY VIII: I fear, too much.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There's fresher air, my lord,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: In the next chamber.
KING HENRY VIII: Lead in your ladies, every one: sweet partner,
KING HENRY VIII: I must not yet forsake you: let's be merry:
KING HENRY VIII: Good my lord cardinal, I have half a dozen healths
KING HENRY VIII: To drink to these fair ladies, and a measure
KING HENRY VIII: To lead 'em once again, and then let's dream
KING HENRY VIII: Who's best in favour. Let the music knock it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt with trumpets
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Westminster. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter two Gentlemen, meeting
First Gentleman: Whither away so fast?
Second Gentleman: O, God save ye!
Second Gentleman: Even to the hall, to hear what shall become
Second Gentleman: Of the great Duke of Buckingham.
First Gentleman: I'll save you
First Gentleman: That labour, sir. All's now done, but the ceremony
First Gentleman: Of bringing back the prisoner.
Second Gentleman: Were you there?
First Gentleman: Yes, indeed, was I.
Second Gentleman: Pray, speak what has happen'd.
First Gentleman: You may guess quickly what.
Second Gentleman: Is he found guilty?
First Gentleman: Yes, truly is he, and condemn'd upon't.
Second Gentleman: I am sorry for't.
First Gentleman: So are a number more.
Second Gentleman: But, pray, how pass'd it?
First Gentleman: I'll tell you in a little. The great duke
First Gentleman: Came to the bar, where to his accusations
First Gentleman: He pleaded still not guilty and alleged
First Gentleman: Many sharp reasons to defeat the law.
First Gentleman: The king's attorney on the contrary
First Gentleman: Urged on the examinations, proofs, confessions
First Gentleman: Of divers witnesses, which the duke desired
First Gentleman: To have brought viva voce to his face:
First Gentleman: At which appear'd against him his surveyor,
First Gentleman: Sir Gilbert Peck his chancellor, and John Car,
First Gentleman: Confessor to him, with that devil-monk,
First Gentleman: Hopkins, that made this mischief.
Second Gentleman: That was he
Second Gentleman: That fed him with his prophecies?
First Gentleman: The same.
First Gentleman: All these accused him strongly, which he fain
First Gentleman: Would have flung from him, but, indeed, he could not:
First Gentleman: And so his peers, upon this evidence,
First Gentleman: Have found him guilty of high treason. Much
First Gentleman: He spoke, and learnedly, for life, but all
First Gentleman: Was either pitied in him or forgotten.
Second Gentleman: After all this, how did he bear himself?
First Gentleman: When he was brought again to the bar, to hear
First Gentleman: His knell rung out, his judgment, he was stirr'd
First Gentleman: With such an agony, he sweat extremely,
First Gentleman: And something spoke in choler, ill, and hasty:
First Gentleman: But he fell to himself again, and sweetly
First Gentleman: In all the rest show'd a most noble patience.
Second Gentleman: I do not think he fears death.
First Gentleman: Sure, he does not:
First Gentleman: He never was so womanish, the cause
First Gentleman: He may a little grieve at.
Second Gentleman: Certainly
Second Gentleman: The cardinal is the end of this.
First Gentleman: 'Tis likely,
First Gentleman: By all conjectures: first, Kildare's attainder,
First Gentleman: Then deputy of Ireland, who removed,
First Gentleman: Earl Surrey was sent thither, and in haste too,
First Gentleman: Lest he should help his father.
Second Gentleman: That trick of state
Second Gentleman: Was a deep envious one.
First Gentleman: At his return
First Gentleman: No doubt he will requite it. This is noted,
First Gentleman: And generally, whoever the king favours,
First Gentleman: The cardinal instantly will find employment,
First Gentleman: And far enough from court too.
Second Gentleman: All the commons
Second Gentleman: Hate him perniciously, and, o' my conscience,
Second Gentleman: Wish him ten fathom deep: this duke as much
Second Gentleman: They love and dote on, call him bounteous Buckingham,
Second Gentleman: The mirror of all courtesy,--
First Gentleman: Stay there, sir,
First Gentleman: And see the noble ruin'd man you speak of.
First Gentleman: Enter BUCKINGHAM from his arraignment, tip-staves  before him, the axe with the edge towards him,  halberds on each side: accompanied with LOVELL, VAUX, SANDS, and common people
Second Gentleman: Let's stand close, and behold him.
BUCKINGHAM: All good people,
BUCKINGHAM: You that thus far have come to pity me,
BUCKINGHAM: Hear what I say, and then go home and lose me.
BUCKINGHAM: I have this day received a traitor's judgment,
BUCKINGHAM: And by that name must die: yet, heaven bear witness,
BUCKINGHAM: And if I have a co nscience, let it sink me,
BUCKINGHAM: Even as the axe falls, if I be not faithful!
BUCKINGHAM: The law I bear no malice for my death,
BUCKINGHAM: 'T has done, upon the premises, but justice:
BUCKINGHAM: But those that sought it I could wish more Christians:
BUCKINGHAM: Be what they will, I heartily forgive 'em:
BUCKINGHAM: Yet let 'em look they glory not in mischief,
BUCKINGHAM: Nor build their evils on the graves of great men,
BUCKINGHAM: For then my guiltless blood must cry against 'em.
BUCKINGHAM: For further life in this world I ne'er hope,
BUCKINGHAM: Nor will I sue, although the king have mercies
BUCKINGHAM: More than I dare make faults. You few that loved me,
BUCKINGHAM: And dare be bold to weep for Buckingham,
BUCKINGHAM: His noble friends and fellows, whom to leave
BUCKINGHAM: Is only bitter to him, only dying,
BUCKINGHAM: Go with me, like good angels, to my end,
BUCKINGHAM: And, as the long divorce of steel falls on me,
BUCKINGHAM: Make of your prayers one sweet sacrifice,
BUCKINGHAM: And lift my soul to heaven. Lead on, o' God's name.
LOVELL: I do beseech your grace, for charity,
LOVELL: If ever any malice in your heart
LOVELL: Were hid against me, now to forgive me frankly.
BUCKINGHAM: Sir Thomas Lovell, I as free forgive you
BUCKINGHAM: As I would be forgiven: I forgive all,
BUCKINGHAM: There cannot be those numberless offences
BUCKINGHAM: 'Gainst me, that I cannot take peace with:
BUCKINGHAM: no black envy
BUCKINGHAM: Shall mark my grave. Commend me to his grace,
BUCKINGHAM: And if he speak of Buckingham, pray, tell him
BUCKINGHAM: You met him half in heaven: my vows and prayers
BUCKINGHAM: Yet are the king's, and, till my soul forsake,
BUCKINGHAM: Shall cry for blessings on him: may he live
BUCKINGHAM: Longer than I have time to tell his years!
BUCKINGHAM: Ever beloved and loving may his rule be!
BUCKINGHAM: And when old time shall lead him to his end,
BUCKINGHAM: Goodness and he fill up one monument!
LOVELL: To the water side I must conduct your grace,
LOVELL: Then give my charge up to Sir Nicholas Vaux,
LOVELL: Who undertakes you to your end.
VAUX: Prepare there,
VAUX: The duke is coming: see the barge be ready,
VAUX: And fit it with such furniture as suits
VAUX: The greatness of his person.
BUCKINGHAM: Nay, Sir Nicholas,
BUCKINGHAM: Let it alone, my state now will but mock me.
BUCKINGHAM: When I came hither, I was lord high constable
BUCKINGHAM: And Duke of Buckingham, now, poor Edward Bohun:
BUCKINGHAM: Yet I am richer than my base accusers,
BUCKINGHAM: That never knew what truth meant: I now seal it,
BUCKINGHAM: And with that blood will make 'em one day groan for't.
BUCKINGHAM: My noble father, Henry of Buckingham,
BUCKINGHAM: Who first raised head against usurping Richard,
BUCKINGHAM: Flying for succor to his servant Banister,
BUCKINGHAM: Being distress'd, was by that wretch betray'd,
BUCKINGHAM: And without trial fell, God's peace be with him!
BUCKINGHAM: Henry the Seventh succeeding, truly pitying
BUCKINGHAM: My father's loss, like a most royal prince,
BUCKINGHAM: Restored me to my honours, and, out of ruins,
BUCKINGHAM: Made my name once more noble. Now his son,
BUCKINGHAM: Henry the Eighth, life, honour, name and all
BUCKINGHAM: That made me happy at one stroke has taken
BUCKINGHAM: For ever from the world. I had my trial,
BUCKINGHAM: And, must needs say, a noble one, which makes me,
BUCKINGHAM: A little happier than my wretched father:
BUCKINGHAM: Yet thus far we are one in fortunes: both
BUCKINGHAM: Fell by our servants, by those men we loved most,
BUCKINGHAM: A most unnatural and faithless service!
BUCKINGHAM: Heaven has an end in all: yet, you that hear me,
BUCKINGHAM: This from a dying man receive as certain:
BUCKINGHAM: Where you are liberal of your loves and counsels
BUCKINGHAM: Be sure you be not loose, for those you make friends
BUCKINGHAM: And give your hearts to, when they once perceive
BUCKINGHAM: The least rub in your fortunes, fall away
BUCKINGHAM: Like water from ye, never found again
BUCKINGHAM: But where they mean to sink ye. All good people,
BUCKINGHAM: Pray for me! I must now forsake ye: the last hour
BUCKINGHAM: Of my long weary life is come upon me. Farewell:
BUCKINGHAM: And when you would say something that is sad,
BUCKINGHAM: Speak how I fell. I have done, and God forgive me!
NARRATOR: Exeunt BUCKINGHAM and Train
First Gentleman: O, this is full of pity! Sir, it calls,
First Gentleman: I fear, too many curses on their beads
First Gentleman: That were the authors.
Second Gentleman: If the duke be guiltless,
Second Gentleman: 'Tis full of woe: yet I can give you inkling
Second Gentleman: Of an ensuing evil, if it fall,
Second Gentleman: Greater than this.
First Gentleman: Good angels keep it from us!
First Gentleman: What may it be? You do not doubt my faith, sir?
Second Gentleman: This secret is so weighty, 'twill require
Second Gentleman: A strong faith to conceal it.
First Gentleman: Let me have it,
First Gentleman: I do not talk much.
Second Gentleman: I am confident,
Second Gentleman: You shall, sir: did you not of late days hear
Second Gentleman: A buzzing of a separation
Second Gentleman: Between the king and Katharine?
First Gentleman: Yes, but it held not:
First Gentleman: For when the king once heard it, out of anger
First Gentleman: He sent command to the lord mayor straight
First Gentleman: To stop the rumor, and allay those tongues
First Gentleman: That durst disperse it.
Second Gentleman: But that slander, sir,
Second Gentleman: Is found a truth now: for it grows again
Second Gentleman: Fresher than e'er it was, and held for certain
Second Gentleman: The king will venture at it. Either the cardinal,
Second Gentleman: Or some about him near, have, out of malice
Second Gentleman: To the good queen, possess'd him with a scruple
Second Gentleman: That will undo her: to confirm this too,
Second Gentleman: Cardinal Campeius is arrived, and lately,
Second Gentleman: As all think, for this business.
First Gentleman: 'Tis the cardinal,
First Gentleman: And merely to revenge him on the emperor
First Gentleman: For not bestowing on him, at his asking,
First Gentleman: The archbishopric of Toledo, this is purposed.
Second Gentleman: I think you have hit the mark: but is't not cruel
Second Gentleman: That she should feel the smart of this? The cardinal
Second Gentleman: Will have his will, and she must fall.
First Gentleman: 'Tis woful.
First Gentleman: We are too open here to argue this,
First Gentleman: Let's think in private more.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. An ante-chamber in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter Chamberlain, reading a letter
Chamberlain: 'My lord, the horses your lordship sent for, with
Chamberlain: all the care I had, I saw well chosen, ridden, and
Chamberlain: furnished. They were young and handsome, and of the
Chamberlain: best breed in the north. When they were ready to
Chamberlain: set out for London, a man of my lord cardinal's, by
Chamberlain: commission and main power, took 'em from me, with
Chamberlain: this reason: His master would be served before a
Chamberlain: subject, if not before the king, which stopped our
Chamberlain: mouths, sir.'
Chamberlain: I fear he will indeed: well, let him have them:
Chamberlain: He will have all, I think.
NARRATOR: Enter, to Chamberlain, NORFOLK and SUFFOLK
NORFOLK: Well met, my lord chamberlain.
Chamberlain: Good day to both your graces.
SUFFOLK: How is the king employ'd?
Chamberlain: I left him private,
Chamberlain: Full of sad thoughts and troubles.
NORFOLK: What's the cause?
Chamberlain: It seems the marriage with his brother's wife
Chamberlain: Has crept too near his conscience.
SUFFOLK: No, his conscience
SUFFOLK: Has crept too near another lady.
NORFOLK: 'Tis so:
NORFOLK: This is the cardinal's doing, the king-cardinal:
NORFOLK: That blind priest, like the eldest son of fortune,
NORFOLK: Turns what he list. The king will know him one day.
SUFFOLK: Pray God he do! he'll never know himself else.
NORFOLK: How holily he works in all his business!
NORFOLK: And with what zeal! for, now he has crack'd the league
NORFOLK: Between us and the emperor, the queen's great nephew,
NORFOLK: He dives into the king's soul, and there scatters
NORFOLK: Dangers, doubts, wringing of the conscience,
NORFOLK: Fears, and despairs, and all these for his marriage:
NORFOLK: And out of all these to restore the king,
NORFOLK: He counsels a divorce, a loss of her
NORFOLK: That, like a jewel, has hung twenty years
NORFOLK: About his neck, yet never lost her lustre,
NORFOLK: Of her that loves him with that excellence
NORFOLK: That angels love good men with, even of her
NORFOLK: That, when the greatest stroke of fortune falls,
NORFOLK: Will bless the king: and is not this course pious?
Chamberlain: Heaven keep me from such counsel! 'Tis most true
Chamberlain: These news are every where, every tongue speaks 'em,
Chamberlain: And every true heart weeps for't: all that dare
Chamberlain: Look into these affairs see this main end,
Chamberlain: The French king's sister. Heaven will one day open
Chamberlain: The king's eyes, that so long have slept upon
Chamberlain: This bold bad man.
SUFFOLK: And free us from his slavery.
NORFOLK: We had need pray,
NORFOLK: And heartily, for our deliverance,
NORFOLK: Or this imperious man will work us all
NORFOLK: From princes into pages: all men's honours
NORFOLK: Lie like one lump before him, to be fashion'd
NORFOLK: Into what pitch he please.
SUFFOLK: For me, my lords,
SUFFOLK: I love him not, nor fear him, there's my creed:
SUFFOLK: As I am made without him, so I'll stand,
SUFFOLK: If the king please, his curses and his blessings
SUFFOLK: Touch me alike, they're breath I not believe in.
SUFFOLK: I knew him, and I know him, so I leave him
SUFFOLK: To him that made him proud, the pope.
NORFOLK: Let's in,
NORFOLK: And with some other business put the king
NORFOLK: From these sad thoughts, that work too much upon him:
NORFOLK: My lord, you'll bear us company?
Chamberlain: Excuse me,
Chamberlain: The king has sent me otherwhere: besides,
Chamberlain: You'll find a most unfit time to disturb him:
Chamberlain: Health to your lordships.
NORFOLK: Thanks, my good lord chamberlain.
NORFOLK: Exit Chamberlain, and KING HENRY VIII draws the curtain, and sits reading pensively
SUFFOLK: How sad he looks! sure, he is much afflicted.
KING HENRY VIII: Who's there, ha?
NORFOLK: Pray God he be not angry.
KING HENRY VIII: Who's there, I say? How dare you thrust yourselves
KING HENRY VIII: Into my private meditations?
KING HENRY VIII: Who am I? ha?
NORFOLK: A gracious king that pardons all offences
NORFOLK: Malice ne'er meant: our breach of duty this way
NORFOLK: Is business of estate, in which we come
NORFOLK: To know your royal pleasure.
KING HENRY VIII: Ye are too bold:
KING HENRY VIII: Go to, I'll make ye know your times of business:
KING HENRY VIII: Is this an hour for temporal affairs, ha?
NARRATOR: Enter CARDINAL WOLSEY and CARDINAL CAMPEIUS, with a commission

KING HENRY VIII: The quiet of my wounded conscience,
KING HENRY VIII: Thou art a cure fit for a king.
NARRATOR: To CARDINAL CAMPEIUS
KING HENRY VIII: You're welcome,

KING HENRY VIII: Use us and it.
NARRATOR: To CARDINAL WOLSEY
KING HENRY VIII: My good lord, have great care

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Sir, you cannot.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I would your grace would give us but an hour

KING HENRY VIII: [To NORFOLK and SUFFOLK]
KING HENRY VIII: We are busy, go.
NORFOLK: [Aside to SUFFOLK]
NORFOLK: This priest has no pride in him?
SUFFOLK: [Aside to NORFOLK]             Not to speak of:
SUFFOLK: I would not be so sick though for his place:
SUFFOLK: But this cannot continue.
NORFOLK: [Aside to SUFFOLK]      If it do,
NORFOLK: I'll venture one have-at-him.
SUFFOLK: [Aside to NORFOLK]          I another.
NARRATOR: Exeunt NORFOLK and SUFFOLK
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Your grace has given a precedent of wisdom
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Above all princes, in committing freely
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Your scruple to the voice of Christendom:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Who can be angry now? what envy reach you?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The Spaniard, tied blood and favour to her,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Must now confess, if they have any goodness,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The trial just and noble. All the clerks,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I mean the learned ones, in Christian kingdoms
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Have their free voices: Rome, the nurse of judgment,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Invited by your noble self, hath sent
CARDINAL WOLSEY: One general tongue unto us, this good man,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This just and learned priest, Cardinal Campeius,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Whom once more I present unto your highness.
KING HENRY VIII: And once more in mine arms I bid him welcome,

KING HENRY VIII: They have sent me such a man I would have wish'd for.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Your grace must needs deserve all strangers' loves,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: You are so noble. To your highness' hand
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: I tender my commission, by whose virtue,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: The court of Rome commanding, you, my lord
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Cardinal of York, are join'd with me their servant
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: In the unpartial judging of this business.
KING HENRY VIII: Two equal men. The queen shall be acquainted
KING HENRY VIII: Forthwith for what you come. Where's Gardiner?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I know your majesty has always loved her
CARDINAL WOLSEY: So dear in heart, not to deny her that
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A woman of less place might ask by law:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Scholars allow'd freely to argue for her.
KING HENRY VIII: Ay, and the best she shall have, and my favour
KING HENRY VIII: To him that does best: God forbid else. Cardinal,
KING HENRY VIII: Prithee, call Gardiner to me, my new secretary:
KING HENRY VIII: I find him a fit fellow.
NARRATOR: Exit CARDINAL WOLSEY
NARRATOR: Re-enter CARDINAL WOLSEY, with GARDINER
CARDINAL WOLSEY: [Aside to GARDINER]  Give me your hand much joy and
CARDINAL WOLSEY: favour to you,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You are the king's now.
GARDINER: [Aside to CARDINAL WOLSEY]
GARDINER: But to be commanded
GARDINER: For ever by your grace, whose hand has raised me.
KING HENRY VIII: Come hither, Gardiner.
NARRATOR: Walks and whispers
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: My Lord of York, was not one Doctor Pace
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: In this man's place before him?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Yes, he was.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Was he not held a learned man?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Yes, surely.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Believe me, there's an ill opinion spread then
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Even of yourself, lord cardinal.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: How! of me?
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: They will not stick to say you envied him,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: And fearing he would rise, he was so virtuous,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Kept him a foreign man still, which so grieved him,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: That he ran mad and died.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Heaven's peace be with him!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That's Christian care enough: for living murmurers
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There's places of rebuke. He was a fool,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: For he would needs be virtuous: that good fellow,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: If I command him, follows my appointment:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I will have none so near else. Learn this, brother,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: We live not to be grip'd by meaner persons.
KING HENRY VIII: Deliver this with modesty to the queen.
NARRATOR: Exit GARDINER
KING HENRY VIII: The most convenient place that I can think of
KING HENRY VIII: For such receipt of learning is Black-Friars,
KING HENRY VIII: There ye shall meet about this weighty business.
KING HENRY VIII: My Wolsey, see it furnish'd. O, my lord,
KING HENRY VIII: Would it not grieve an able man to leave
KING HENRY VIII: So sweet a bedfellow? But, conscience, conscience!
KING HENRY VIII: O, 'tis a tender place, and I must leave her.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. An ante-chamber of the QUEEN'S apartments.
NARRATOR: Enter ANNE and an Old Lady
ANNE: Not for that neither: here's the pang that pinches:
ANNE: His highness having lived so long with her, and she
ANNE: So good a lady that no tongue could ever
ANNE: Pronounce dishonour of her, by my life,
ANNE: She never knew harm-doing: O, now, after
ANNE: So many courses of the sun enthroned,
ANNE: Still growing in a majesty and pomp, the which
ANNE: To leave a thousand-fold more bitter than
ANNE: 'Tis sweet at first to acquire,--after this process,
ANNE: To give her the avaunt! it is a pity
ANNE: Would move a monster.
Old Lady: Hearts of most hard temper
Old Lady: Melt and lament for her.
ANNE: O, God's will! much better
ANNE: She ne'er had known pomp: though't be temporal,
ANNE: Yet, if that quarrel, fortune, do divorce
ANNE: It from the bearer, 'tis a sufferance panging
ANNE: As soul and body's severing.
Old Lady: Alas, poor lady!
Old Lady: She's a stranger now again.
ANNE: So much the more
ANNE: Must pity drop upon her. Verily,
ANNE: I swear, 'tis better to be lowly born,
ANNE: And range with humble livers in content,
ANNE: Than to be perk'd up in a glistering grief,
ANNE: And wear a golden sorrow.
Old Lady: Our content
Old Lady: Is our best having.
ANNE: By my troth and maidenhead,
ANNE: I would not be a queen.
Old Lady: Beshrew me, I would,
Old Lady: And venture maidenhead for't, and so would you,
Old Lady: For all this spice of your hypocrisy:
Old Lady: You, that have so fair parts of woman on you,
Old Lady: Have too a woman's heart, which ever yet
Old Lady: Affected eminence, wealth, sovereignty,
Old Lady: Which, to say sooth, are blessings, and which gifts,
Old Lady: Saving your mincing, the capacity
Old Lady: Of your soft cheveril conscience would receive,
Old Lady: If you might please to stretch it.
ANNE: Nay, good troth.
Old Lady: Yes, troth, and troth, you would not be a queen?
ANNE: No, not for all the riches under heaven.
ANNE: Old Lady:	'Tis strange: a three-pence bow'd would hire me,
ANNE: Old as I am, to queen it: but, I pray you,
ANNE: What think you of a duchess? have you limbs
ANNE: To bear that load of title?
ANNE: No, in truth.
Old Lady: Then you are weakly made: pluck off a little,
Old Lady: I would not be a young count in your way,
Old Lady: For more than blushing comes to: if your back
Old Lady: Cannot vouchsafe this burthen,'tis too weak
Old Lady: Ever to get a boy.
ANNE: How you do talk!
ANNE: I swear again, I would not be a queen
ANNE: For all the world.
Old Lady: In faith, for little England
Old Lady: You'ld venture an emballing: I myself
Old Lady: Would for Carnarvonshire, although there long'd
Old Lady: No more to the crown but that. Lo, who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter Chamberlain
Chamberlain: Good morrow, ladies. What were't worth to know
Chamberlain: The secret of your conference?
ANNE: My good lord,
ANNE: Not your demand, it values not your asking:
ANNE: Our mistress' sorrows we were pitying.
Chamberlain: It was a gentle business, and becoming
Chamberlain: The action of good women: there is hope
Chamberlain: All will be well.
ANNE: Now, I pray God, amen!
Chamberlain: You bear a gentle mind, and heavenly blessings
Chamberlain: Follow such creatures. That you may, fair lady,

Chamberlain: Ta'en of your many virtues, the king's majesty
Chamberlain: Commends his good opinion of you, and
Chamberlain: Does purpose honour to you no less flowing
Chamberlain: Than Marchioness of Pembroke: to which title
Chamberlain: A thousand pound a year, annual support,
Chamberlain: Out of his grace he adds.
ANNE: I do not know
ANNE: What kind of my obedience I should tender,
ANNE: More than my all is nothing: nor my prayers
ANNE: Are not words duly hallow'd, nor my wishes
ANNE: More worth than empty vanities, yet prayers and wishes
ANNE: Are all I can return. Beseech your lordship,
ANNE: Vouchsafe to speak my thanks and my obedience,
ANNE: As from a blushing handmaid, to his highness,
ANNE: Whose health and royalty I pray for.
Chamberlain: Lady,
Chamberlain: I shall not fail to approve the fair conceit
Chamberlain: The king hath of you.
NARRATOR: Aside
Chamberlain: I have perused her well,
Chamberlain: Beauty and honour in her are so mingled
Chamberlain: That they have caught the king: and who knows yet
Chamberlain: But from this lady may proceed a gem
Chamberlain: To lighten all this isle? I'll to the king,
Chamberlain: And say I spoke with you.

ANNE: My honour'd lord.
Old Lady: Why, this it is, see, see!
Old Lady: I have been begging sixteen years in court,
Old Lady: Am yet a courtier beggarly, nor could
Old Lady: Come pat betwixt too early and too late
Old Lady: For any suit of pounds, and you, O fate!
Old Lady: A very fresh-fish here--fie, fie, fie upon
Old Lady: This compell'd fortune!--have your mouth fill'd up
Old Lady: Before you open it.
ANNE: This is strange to me.
Old Lady: How tastes it? is it bitter? forty pence, no.
Old Lady: There was a lady once, 'tis an old story,
Old Lady: That would not be a queen, that would she not,
Old Lady: For all the mud in Egypt: have you heard it?
ANNE: Come, you are pleasant.
Old Lady: With your theme, I could
Old Lady: O'ermount the lark. The Marchioness of Pembroke!
Old Lady: A thousand pounds a year for pure respect!
Old Lady: No other obligation! By my life,
Old Lady: That promises moe thousands: honour's train
Old Lady: Is longer than his foreskirt. By this time
Old Lady: I know your back will bear a duchess: say,
Old Lady: Are you not stronger than you were?
ANNE: Good lady,
ANNE: Make yourself mirth with your particular fancy,
ANNE: And leave me out on't. Would I had no being,
ANNE: If this salute my blood a jot: it faints me,
ANNE: To think what follows.
ANNE: The queen is comfortless, and we forgetful
ANNE: In our long absence: pray, do not deliver
ANNE: What here you've heard to her.
Old Lady: What do you think me?
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A hall in Black-Friars.
NARRATOR: Trumpets, sennet, and cornets. Enter two Vergers,  with short silver wands, next them, two Scribes, in  the habit of doctors, after them, CANTERBURY alone,  after him, LINCOLN, Ely, Rochester, and Saint  Asaph, next them, with some small distance, follows  a Gentleman bearing the purse, with the great seal,  and a cardinal's hat, then two Priests, bearing  each a silver cross, then a Gentleman-usher  bare-headed, accompanied with a Sergeant-at-arms  bearing a silver mace, then two Gentlemen bearing  two great silver pillars, after them, side by side,  CARDINAL WOLSEY and CARDINAL CAMPEIUS, two Noblemen  with the sword and mace. KING HENRY VIII takes  place under the cloth of state, CARDINAL WOLSEY and  CARDINAL CAMPEIUS sit under him as judges. QUEEN  KATHARINE takes place some distance from KING  HENRY VIII. The Bishops place themselves on each  side the court, in manner of a consistory, below  them, the Scribes. The Lords sit next the Bishops. NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. QUEEN KATHARINE's apartments.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN KATHARINE and her Women, as at work

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Between the king and you, and to deliver,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Like free and honest men, our just opinions
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And comforts to your cause.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Most honour'd madam,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: My Lord of York, out of his noble nature,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Zeal and obedience he still bore your grace,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Forgetting, like a good man your late censure
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Both of his truth and him, which was too far,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Offers, as I do, in a sign of peace,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: His service and his counsel.
QUEEN KATHARINE: [Aside]	To betray me.--
QUEEN KATHARINE: My lords, I thank you both for your good wills,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Ye speak like honest men, pray God, ye prove so!
QUEEN KATHARINE: But how to make ye suddenly an answer,
QUEEN KATHARINE: In such a point of weight, so near mine honour,--
QUEEN KATHARINE: More near my life, I fear,--with my weak wit,
QUEEN KATHARINE: And to such men of gravity and learning,
QUEEN KATHARINE: In truth, I know not. I was set at work
QUEEN KATHARINE: Among my maids: full little, God knows, looking
QUEEN KATHARINE: Either for such men or such business.
QUEEN KATHARINE: For her sake that I have been,--for I feel
QUEEN KATHARINE: The last fit of my greatness,--good your graces,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Let me have time and counsel for my cause:
QUEEN KATHARINE: Alas, I am a woman, friendless, hopeless!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Madam, you wrong the king's love with these fears:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Your hopes and friends are infinite.
QUEEN KATHARINE: In England
QUEEN KATHARINE: But little for my profit: can you think, lords,
QUEEN KATHARINE: That any Englishman dare give me counsel?
QUEEN KATHARINE: Or be a known friend, 'gainst his highness' pleasure,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Though he be grown so desperate to be honest,
QUEEN KATHARINE: And live a subject? Nay, forsooth, my friends,
QUEEN KATHARINE: They that must weigh out my afflictions,
QUEEN KATHARINE: They that my trust must grow to, live not here:
QUEEN KATHARINE: They are, as all my other comforts, far hence
QUEEN KATHARINE: In mine own country, lords.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: I would your grace
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Would leave your griefs, and take my counsel.
QUEEN KATHARINE: How, sir?
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Put your main cause into the king's protection,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: He's loving and most gracious: 'twill be much
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Both for your honour better and your cause,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: For if the trial of the law o'ertake ye,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: You'll part away disgraced.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: He tells you rightly.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Ye tell me what ye wish for both,--my ruin:
QUEEN KATHARINE: Is this your Christian counsel? out upon ye!
QUEEN KATHARINE: Heaven is above all yet, there sits a judge
QUEEN KATHARINE: That no king can corrupt.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Your rage mistakes us.
QUEEN KATHARINE: The more shame for ye: holy men I thought ye,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Upon my soul, two reverend cardinal virtues,
QUEEN KATHARINE: But cardinal sins and hollow hearts I fear ye:
QUEEN KATHARINE: Mend 'em, for shame, my lords. Is this your comfort?
QUEEN KATHARINE: The cordial that ye bring a wretched lady,
QUEEN KATHARINE: A woman lost among ye, laugh'd at, scorn'd?
QUEEN KATHARINE: I will not wish ye half my miseries,
QUEEN KATHARINE: I have more charity: but say, I warn'd ye,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Take heed, for heaven's sake, take heed, lest at once
QUEEN KATHARINE: The burthen of my sorrows fall upon ye.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Madam, this is a mere distraction,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You turn the good we offer into envy.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Ye turn me into nothing: woe upon ye
QUEEN KATHARINE: And all such false professors! would you have me--
QUEEN KATHARINE: If you have any justice, any pity,
QUEEN KATHARINE: If ye be any thing but churchmen's habits--
QUEEN KATHARINE: Put my sick cause into his hands that hates me?
QUEEN KATHARINE: Alas, has banish'd me his bed already,
QUEEN KATHARINE: His love, too long ago! I am old, my lords,
QUEEN KATHARINE: And all the fellowship I hold now with him
QUEEN KATHARINE: Is only my obedience. What can happen
QUEEN KATHARINE: To me above this wretchedness? all your studies
QUEEN KATHARINE: Make me a curse like this.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Your fears are worse.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Have I lived thus long--let me speak myself,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Since virtue finds no friends--a wife, a true one?
QUEEN KATHARINE: A woman, I dare say without vain-glory,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Never yet branded with suspicion?
QUEEN KATHARINE: Have I with all my full affections
QUEEN KATHARINE: Still met the king? loved him next heaven?
QUEEN KATHARINE: obey'd him?
QUEEN KATHARINE: Been, out of fondness, superstitious to him?
QUEEN KATHARINE: Almost forgot my prayers to content him?
QUEEN KATHARINE: And am I thus rewarded? 'tis not well, lords.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Bring me a constant woman to her husband,
QUEEN KATHARINE: One that ne'er dream'd a joy beyond his pleasure,
QUEEN KATHARINE: And to that woman, when she has done most,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Yet will I add an honour, a great patience.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Madam, you wander from the good we aim at.
QUEEN KATHARINE: My lord, I dare not make myself so guilty,
QUEEN KATHARINE: To give up willingly that noble title
QUEEN KATHARINE: Your master wed me to: nothing but death
QUEEN KATHARINE: Shall e'er divorce my dignities.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Pray, hear me.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Would I had never trod this English earth,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Or felt the flatteries that grow upon it!
QUEEN KATHARINE: Ye have angels' faces, but heaven knows your hearts.
QUEEN KATHARINE: What will become of me now, wretched lady!
QUEEN KATHARINE: I am the most unhappy woman living.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Alas, poor wenches, where are now your fortunes!
QUEEN KATHARINE: Shipwreck'd upon a kingdom, where no pity,
QUEEN KATHARINE: No friend, no hope, no kindred weep for me,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Almost no grave allow'd me: like the lily,
QUEEN KATHARINE: That once was mistress of the field and flourish'd,
QUEEN KATHARINE: I'll hang my head and perish.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: If your grace
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Could but be brought to know our ends are honest,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You'ld feel more comfort: why should we, good lady,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Upon what cause, wrong you? alas, our places,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The way of our profession is against it:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: We are to cure such sorrows, not to sow 'em.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: For goodness' sake, consider what you do,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: How you may hurt yourself, ay, utterly
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Grow from the king's acquaintance, by this carriage.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The hearts of princes kiss obedience,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: So much they love it, but to stubborn spirits
CARDINAL WOLSEY: They swell, and grow as terrible as storms.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I know you have a gentle, noble temper,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A soul as even as a calm: pray, think us
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Those we profess, peace-makers, friends, and servants.
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Madam, you'll find it so. You wrong your virtues
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: With these weak women's fears: a noble spirit,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: As yours was put into you, ever casts
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Such doubts, as false coin, from it. The king loves you,
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: Beware you lose it not: for us, if you please
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: To trust us in your business, we are ready
CARDINAL CAMPEIUS: To use our utmost  studies in your service.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Do what ye will, my lords: and, pray, forgive me,
QUEEN KATHARINE: If I have used myself unmannerly,
QUEEN KATHARINE: You know I am a woman, lacking wit
QUEEN KATHARINE: To make a seemly answer to such persons.
QUEEN KATHARINE: Pray, do my service to his majesty:
QUEEN KATHARINE: He has my heart yet, and shall have my prayers
QUEEN KATHARINE: While I shall have my life. Come, reverend fathers,
QUEEN KATHARINE: Bestow your counsels on me: she now begs,
QUEEN KATHARINE: That little thought, when she set footing here,
QUEEN KATHARINE: She should have bought her dignities so dear.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Ante-chamber to KING HENRY VIII's apartment.

CARDINAL WOLSEY: Ye appear in every thing may bring my ruin!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Follow your envious courses, men of malice,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You have Christian warrant for 'em, and, no doubt,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: In time will find their fit rewards. That seal,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You ask with such a violence, the king,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Mine and your master, with his own hand gave me,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Bade me enjoy it, with the place and honours,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: During my life, and, to confirm his goodness,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Tied it by letters-patents: now, who'll take it?
SURREY: The king, that gave it.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: It must be himself, then.
SURREY: Thou art a proud traitor, priest.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Proud lord, thou liest:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Within these forty hours Surrey durst better
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Have burnt that tongue than said so.
SURREY: Thy ambition,
SURREY: Thou scarlet sin, robb'd this bewailing land
SURREY: Of noble Buckingham, my father-in-law:
SURREY: The heads of all thy brother cardinals,
SURREY: With thee and all thy best parts bound together,
SURREY: Weigh'd not a hair of his. Plague of your policy!
SURREY: You sent me deputy for Ireland,
SURREY: Far from his succor, from the king, from all
SURREY: That might have mercy on the fault thou gavest him,
SURREY: Whilst your great goodness, out of holy pity,
SURREY: Absolved him with an axe.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This, and all else
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This talking lord can lay upon my credit,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I answer is most false. The duke by law
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Found his deserts: how innocent I was
CARDINAL WOLSEY: From any private malice in his end,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: His noble jury and foul cause can witness.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: If I loved many words, lord, I should tell you
CARDINAL WOLSEY: You have as little honesty as honour,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That in the way of loyalty and truth
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Toward the king, my ever royal master,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Dare mate a sounder man than Surrey can be,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And all that love his follies.
SURREY: By my soul,
SURREY: Your long coat, priest, protects you, thou
SURREY: shouldst feel
SURREY: My sword i' the life-blood of thee else. My lords,
SURREY: Can ye endure to hear this arrogance?
SURREY: And from this fellow? if we live thus tamely,
SURREY: To be thus jaded by a piece of scarlet,
SURREY: Farewell nobility, let his grace go forward,
SURREY: And dare us with his cap like larks.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: All goodness
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Is poison to thy stomach.
SURREY: Yes, that goodness
SURREY: Of gleaning all the land's wealth into one,
SURREY: Into your own hands, cardinal, by extortion,
SURREY: The goodness of your intercepted packets
SURREY: You writ to the pope against the king: your goodness,
SURREY: Since you provoke me, shall be most notorious.
SURREY: My Lord of Norfolk, as you are truly noble,
SURREY: As you respect the common good, the state
SURREY: Of our despised nobility, our issues,
SURREY: Who, if he live, will scarce be gentlemen,
SURREY: Produce the grand sum of his sins, the articles
SURREY: Collected from his life. I'll startle you
SURREY: Worse than the scaring bell, when the brown wench
SURREY: Lay kissing in your arms, lord cardinal.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: How much, methinks, I could despise this man,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: But that I am bound in charity against it!
NORFOLK: Those articles, my lord, are in the king's hand:
NORFOLK: But, thus much, they are foul ones.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: So much fairer
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And spotless shall mine innocence arise,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: When the king knows my truth.
SURREY: This cannot save you:
SURREY: I thank my memory, I yet remember
SURREY: Some of these articles, and out they shall.
SURREY: Now, if you can blush and cry 'guilty,' cardinal,
SURREY: You'll show a little honesty.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Speak on, sir,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I dare your worst objections: if I blush,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: It is to see a nobleman want manners.
SURREY: I had rather want those than my head. Have at you!
SURREY: First, that, without the king's assent or knowledge,
SURREY: You wrought to be a legate, by which power
SURREY: You maim'd the jurisdiction of all bishops.
NORFOLK: Then, that in all you writ to Rome, or else
NORFOLK: To foreign princes, 'Ego et Rex meus'
NORFOLK: Was still inscribed, in which you brought the king
NORFOLK: To be your servant.
SUFFOLK: Then that, without the knowledge
SUFFOLK: Either of king or council, when you went
SUFFOLK: Ambassador to the emperor, you made bold
SUFFOLK: To carry into Flanders the great seal.
SURREY: Item, you sent a large commission
SURREY: To Gregory de Cassado, to conclude,
SURREY: Without the king's will or the state's allowance,
SURREY: A league between his highness and Ferrara.
SUFFOLK: That, out of mere ambition, you have caused
SUFFOLK: Your holy hat to be stamp'd on the king's coin.
SURREY: Then that you have sent innumerable substance--
SURREY: By what means got, I leave to your own conscience--
SURREY: To furnish Rome, and to prepare the ways
SURREY: You have for dignities, to the mere undoing
SURREY: Of all the kingdom. Many more there are,
SURREY: Which, since they are of you, and odious,
SURREY: I will not taint my mouth with.
Chamberlain: O my lord,
Chamberlain: Press not a falling man too far! 'tis virtue:
Chamberlain: His faults lie open to the laws, let them,
Chamberlain: Not you, correct him. My heart weeps to see him
Chamberlain: So little of his great self.
SURREY: I forgive him.
SUFFOLK: Lord cardinal, the king's further pleasure is,
SUFFOLK: Because all those things you have done of late,
SUFFOLK: By your power legatine, within this kingdom,
SUFFOLK: Fall into the compass of a praemunire,
SUFFOLK: That therefore such a writ be sued against you,
SUFFOLK: To forfeit all your goods, lands, tenements,
SUFFOLK: Chattels, and whatsoever, and to be
SUFFOLK: Out of the king's protection. This is my charge.
NORFOLK: And so we'll leave you to your meditations
NORFOLK: How to live better. For your stubborn answer
NORFOLK: About the giving back the great seal to us,
NORFOLK: The king shall know it, and, no doubt, shall thank you.
NORFOLK: So fare you well, my little good lord cardinal.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but CARDINAL WOLSEY
CARDINAL WOLSEY: So farewell to the little good you bear me.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Farewell! a long farewell, to all my greatness!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This is the state of man: to-day he puts forth
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The tender leaves of hopes, to-morrow blossoms,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And bears his blushing honours thick upon him,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The third day comes a frost, a killing frost,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And, when he thinks, good easy man, full surely
CARDINAL WOLSEY: His greatness is a-ripening, nips his root,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And then he falls, as I do. I have ventured,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Like little wanton boys that swim on bladders,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: This many summers in a sea of glory,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: But far beyond my depth: my high-blown pride
CARDINAL WOLSEY: At length broke under me and now has left me,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Weary and old with service, to the mercy
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Of a rude stream, that must for ever hide me.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Vain pomp and glory of this world, I hate ye:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I feel my heart new open'd. O, how wretched
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Is that poor man that hangs on princes' favours!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There is, betwixt that smile we would aspire to,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That sweet aspect of princes, and their ruin,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: More pangs and fears than wars or women have:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And when he falls, he falls like Lucifer,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Never to hope again.
NARRATOR: Enter CROMWELL, and stands amazed
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Why, how now, Cromwell!
CROMWELL: I have no power to speak, sir.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: What, amazed
CARDINAL WOLSEY: At my misfortunes? can thy spirit wonder
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A great man should decline? Nay, an you weep,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I am fall'n indeed.
CROMWELL: How does your grace?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Why, well,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Never so truly happy, my good Cromwell.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I know myself now, and I feel within me
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A peace above all earthly dignities,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A still and quiet conscience. The king has cured me,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I humbly thank his grace, and from these shoulders,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: These ruin'd pillars, out of pity, taken
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A load would sink a navy, too much honour:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: O, 'tis a burthen, Cromwell, 'tis a burthen
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Too heavy for a man that hopes for heaven!
CROMWELL: I am glad your grace has made that right use of it.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I hope I have: I am able now, methinks,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Out of a fortitude of soul I feel,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: To endure more miseries and greater far
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Than my weak-hearted enemies dare offer.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: What news abroad?
CROMWELL: The heaviest and the worst
CROMWELL: Is your displeasure with the king.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: God bless him!
CROMWELL: The next is, that Sir Thomas More is chosen
CROMWELL: Lord chancellor in your place.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That's somewhat sudden:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: But he's a learned man. May he continue
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Long in his highness' favour, and do justice
CARDINAL WOLSEY: For truth's sake and his conscience, that his bones,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: When he has run his course and sleeps in blessings,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: May have a tomb of orphans' tears wept on em! What more?
CROMWELL: That Cranmer is return'd with welcome,
CROMWELL: Install'd lord archbishop of Canterbury.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That's news indeed.
CROMWELL: Last, that the Lady Anne,
CROMWELL: Whom the king hath in secrecy long married,
CROMWELL: This day was view'd in open as his queen,
CROMWELL: Going to chapel, and the voice is now
CROMWELL: Only about her coronation.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There was the weight that pull'd me down. O Cromwell,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The king has gone beyond me: all my glories
CARDINAL WOLSEY: In that one woman I have lost for ever:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: No sun shall ever usher forth mine honours,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Or gild again the noble troops that waited
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Upon my smiles. Go, get thee from me, Cromwell,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I am a poor fall'n man, unworthy now
CARDINAL WOLSEY: To be thy lord and master: seek the king,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: That sun, I pray, may never set! I have told him
CARDINAL WOLSEY: What and how true thou art: he will advance thee,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Some little memory of me will stir him--
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I know his noble nature--not to let
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Thy hopeful service perish too: good Cromwell,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Neglect him not, make use now, and provide
CARDINAL WOLSEY: For thine own future safety.
CROMWELL: O my lord,
CROMWELL: Must I, then, leave you? must I needs forego
CROMWELL: So good, so noble and so true a master?
CROMWELL: Bear witness, all that have not hearts of iron,
CROMWELL: With what a sorrow Cromwell leaves his lord.
CROMWELL: The king shall have my service: but my prayers
CROMWELL: For ever and for ever shall be yours.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Cromwell, I did not think to shed a tear
CARDINAL WOLSEY: In all my miseries, but thou hast forced me,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Out of thy honest truth, to play the woman.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Let's dry our eyes: and thus far hear me, Cromwell,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And, when I am forgotten, as I shall be,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And sleep in dull cold marble, where no mention
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Of me more must be heard of, say, I taught thee,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Say, Wolsey, that once trod the ways of glory,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And sounded all the depths and shoals of honour,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Found thee a way, out of his wreck, to rise in,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: A sure and safe one, though thy master miss'd it.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Mark but my fall, and that that ruin'd me.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: By that sin fell the angels, how can man, then,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The image of his Maker, hope to win by it?
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Love thyself last: cherish those hearts that hate thee,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Corruption wins not more than honesty.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Still in thy right hand carry gentle peace,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: To silence envious tongues. Be just, and fear not:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Let all the ends thou aim'st at be thy country's,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Thy God's, and truth's, then if thou fall'st,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: O Cromwell,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Thou fall'st a blessed martyr! Serve the king,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And,--prithee, lead me in:
CARDINAL WOLSEY: There take an inventory of all I have,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: To the last penny, 'tis the king's: my robe,
CARDINAL WOLSEY: And my integrity to heaven, is all
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I dare now call mine own. O Cromwell, Cromwell!
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Had I but served my God with half the zeal
CARDINAL WOLSEY: I served my king, he would not in mine age
CARDINAL WOLSEY: Have left me naked to mine enemies.
CROMWELL: Good sir, have patience.
CARDINAL WOLSEY: So I have. Farewell
CARDINAL WOLSEY: The hopes of court! my hopes in heaven do dwell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A street in Westminster.
NARRATOR: Enter two Gentlemen, meeting one another
First Gentleman: You're well met once again.
Second Gentleman: So are you.
First Gentleman: You come to take your stand here, and behold
First Gentleman: The Lady Anne pass from her coronation?
Second Gentleman: 'Tis all my business. At our last encounter,
Second Gentleman: The Duke of Buckingham came from his trial.
First Gentleman: 'Tis very true: but that time offer'd sorrow,
First Gentleman: This, general joy.
Second Gentleman: 'Tis well: the citizens,
Second Gentleman: I am sure, have shown at full their royal minds--
Second Gentleman: As, let 'em have their rights, they are ever forward--
Second Gentleman: In celebration of this day with shows,
Second Gentleman: Pageants and sights of honour.
First Gentleman: Never greater,
First Gentleman: Nor, I'll assure you, better taken, sir.
Second Gentleman: May I be bold to ask at what that contains,
Second Gentleman: That paper in your hand?
First Gentleman: Yes, 'tis the list
First Gentleman: Of those that claim their offices this day
First Gentleman: By custom of the coronation.
First Gentleman: The Duke of Suffolk is the first, and claims
First Gentleman: To be high-steward, next, the Duke of Norfolk,
First Gentleman: He to be earl marshal: you may read the rest.
Second Gentleman: I thank you, sir: had I not known those customs,
Second Gentleman: I should have been beholding to your paper.
Second Gentleman: But, I beseech you, what's become of Katharine,
Second Gentleman: The princess dowager? how goes her business?
First Gentleman: That I can tell you too. The Archbishop
First Gentleman: Of Canterbury, accompanied with other
First Gentleman: Learned and reverend fathers of his order,
First Gentleman: Held a late court at Dunstable, six miles off
First Gentleman: From Ampthill where the princess lay, to which
First Gentleman: She was often cited by them, but appear'd not:
First Gentleman: And, to be short, for not appearance and
First Gentleman: The king's late scruple, by the main assent
First Gentleman: Of all these learned men she was divorced,
First Gentleman: And the late marriage made of none effect
First Gentleman: Since which she was removed to Kimbolton,
First Gentleman: Where she remains now sick.
Second Gentleman: Alas, good lady!
NARRATOR: Trumpets
Second Gentleman: The trumpets sound: stand close, the queen is coming.
NARRATOR: Hautboys
NARRATOR: THE ORDER OF THE CORONATION
Second Gentleman: 1. A lively flourish of Trumpets.
Second Gentleman: 2. Then, two Judges.
Second Gentleman: 3. Lord Chancellor, with the purse and mace
Second Gentleman: before him.
Second Gentleman: 4. Choristers, singing.
NARRATOR: Music
Second Gentleman: 5. Mayor of London, bearing the mace. Then
Second Gentleman: Garter, in his coat of arms, and on his
Second Gentleman: head a gilt copper crown.
Second Gentleman: 6. Marquess Dorset, bearing a sceptre of gold,
Second Gentleman: on his head a demi-coronal of gold. With
Second Gentleman: him, SURREY, bearing the rod of silver with
Second Gentleman: the dove, crowned with an earl's coronet.
Second Gentleman: Collars of SS.
Second Gentleman: 7. SUFFOLK, in his robe of estate, his coronet
Second Gentleman: on his head, bearing a long white wand, as
Second Gentleman: high-steward. With him, NORFOLK, with the
Second Gentleman: rod of marshalship, a coronet on his head.
Second Gentleman: Collars of SS.
Second Gentleman: 8. A canopy borne by four of the Cinque-ports,
Second Gentleman: under it, QUEEN ANNE in her robe, in her hair
Second Gentleman: richly adorned with pearl, crowned. On each
Second Gentleman: side her, the Bishops of London and
Second Gentleman: Winchester.
Second Gentleman: 9. The old Duchess of Norfolk, in a coronal of
Second Gentleman: gold, wrought with flowers, bearing QUEEN
Second Gentleman: ANNE's train.
Second Gentleman: 10. Certain Ladies or Countesses, with plain
Second Gentleman: circlets of gold without flowers.
NARRATOR: They pass over the stage in order and state
Second Gentleman: A royal train, believe me. These I know:
Second Gentleman: Who's that that bears the sceptre?
First Gentleman: Marquess Dorset:
First Gentleman: And that the Earl of Surrey, with the rod.
Second Gentleman: A bold brave gentleman. That should be
Second Gentleman: The Duke of Suffolk?
First Gentleman: 'Tis the same: high-steward.
Second Gentleman: And that my Lord of Norfolk?
First Gentleman: Yes,
Second Gentleman: Heaven bless thee!
NARRATOR: Looking on QUEEN ANNE
Second Gentleman: Thou hast the sweetest face I ever look'd on.
Second Gentleman: Sir, as I have a soul, she is an angel,
Second Gentleman: Our king has all the Indies in his arms,
Second Gentleman: And more and richer, when he strains that lady:
Second Gentleman: I cannot blame his conscience.
First Gentleman: They that bear
First Gentleman: The cloth of honour over her, are four barons
First Gentleman: Of the Cinque-ports.
Second Gentleman: Those men are happy, and so are all are near her.
Second Gentleman: I take it, she that carries up the train
Second Gentleman: Is that old noble lady, Duchess of Norfolk.
First Gentleman: It is, and all the rest are countesses.
Second Gentleman: Their coronets say so. These are stars indeed,
Second Gentleman: And sometimes falling ones.
First Gentleman: No more of that.
NARRATOR: Exit procession, and then a great flourish of trumpets
NARRATOR: Enter a third Gentleman
First Gentleman: God save you, sir! where have you been broiling?
Third Gentleman: Among the crowd i' the Abbey, where a finger
Third Gentleman: Could not be wedged in more: I am stifled
Third Gentleman: With the mere rankness of their joy.
Second Gentleman: You saw
Second Gentleman: The ceremony?
Third Gentleman: That I did.
First Gentleman: How was it?
Third Gentleman: Well worth the seeing.
Second Gentleman: Good sir, speak it to us.
Third Gentleman: As well as I am able. The rich stream
Third Gentleman: Of lords and ladies, having brought the queen
Third Gentleman: To a prepared place in the choir, fell off
Third Gentleman: A distance from her, while her grace sat down
Third Gentleman: To rest awhile, some half an hour or so,
Third Gentleman: In a rich chair of state, opposing freely
Third Gentleman: The beauty of her person to the people.
Third Gentleman: Believe me, sir, she is the goodliest woman
Third Gentleman: That ever lay by man: which when the people
Third Gentleman: Had the full view of, such a noise arose
Third Gentleman: As the shrouds make at sea in a stiff tempest,
Third Gentleman: As loud, and to as many tunes: hats, cloaks--
Third Gentleman: Doublets, I think,--flew up, and had their faces
Third Gentleman: Been loose, this day they had been lost. Such joy
Third Gentleman: I never saw before. Great-bellied women,
Third Gentleman: That had not half a week to go, like rams
Third Gentleman: In the old time of war, would shake the press,
Third Gentleman: And make 'em reel before 'em. No man living
Third Gentleman: Could say 'This is my wife' there, all were woven
Third Gentleman: So strangely in one piece.
Second Gentleman: But, what follow'd?
Third Gentleman: At length her grace rose, and with modest paces
Third Gentleman: Came to the altar, where she kneel'd, and saint-like
Third Gentleman: Cast her fair eyes to heaven and pray'd devoutly.
Third Gentleman: Then rose again and bow'd her to the people:
Third Gentleman: When by the Archbishop of Canterbury
Third Gentleman: She had all the royal makings of a queen,
Third Gentleman: As holy oil, Edward Confessor's crown,
Third Gentleman: The rod, and bird of peace, and all such emblems
Third Gentleman: Laid nobly on her: which perform'd, the choir,
Third Gentleman: With all the choicest music of the kingdom,
Third Gentleman: Together sung 'Te Deum.' So she parted,
Third Gentleman: And with the same full state paced back again
Third Gentleman: To York-place, where the feast is held.
First Gentleman: Sir,
First Gentleman: You must no more call it York-place, that's past,
First Gentleman: For, since the cardinal fell, that title's lost:
First Gentleman: 'Tis now the king's, and call'd Whitehall.
Third Gentleman: I know it,
Third Gentleman: But 'tis so lately alter'd, that the old name
Third Gentleman: Is fresh about me.
Second Gentleman: What two reverend bishops
Second Gentleman: Were those that went on each side of the queen?
Third Gentleman: Stokesly and Gardiner, the one of Winchester,
Third Gentleman: Newly preferr'd from the king's secretary,
Third Gentleman: The other, London.
Second Gentleman: He of Winchester
Second Gentleman: Is held no great good lover of the archbishop's,
Second Gentleman: The virtuous Cranmer.
Third Gentleman: All the land knows that:
Third Gentleman: However, yet there is no great breach, when it comes,
Third Gentleman: Cranmer will find a friend will not shrink from him.
Second Gentleman: Who may that be, I pray you?
Third Gentleman: Thomas Cromwell,
Third Gentleman: A man in much esteem with the king, and truly
Third Gentleman: A worthy friend. The king has made him master
Third Gentleman: O' the jewel house,
Third Gentleman: And one, already, of the privy council.
Second Gentleman: He will deserve more.
Third Gentleman: Yes, without all doubt.
Third Gentleman: Come, gentlemen, ye shall go my way, which
Third Gentleman: Is to the court, and there ye shall be my guests:
Third Gentleman: Something I can command. As I walk thither,
Third Gentleman: I'll tell ye more.
Both: You may command us, sir.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Kimbolton.
NARRATOR: Enter KATHARINE, Dowager, sick, led between GRIFFITH, her gentleman usher, and PATIENCE, her woman
GRIFFITH: How does your grace?
KATHARINE: O Griffith, sick to death!
KATHARINE: My legs, like loaden branches, bow to the earth,
KATHARINE: Willing to leave their burthen. Reach a chair:
KATHARINE: So, now, methinks, I feel a little ease.
KATHARINE: Didst thou not tell me, Griffith, as thou led'st me,
KATHARINE: That the great child of honour, Cardinal Wolsey, Was dead?
GRIFFITH: Yes, madam, but I think your grace,
GRIFFITH: Out of the pain you suffer'd, gave no ear to't.
KATHARINE: Prithee, good Griffith, tell me how he died:
KATHARINE: If well, he stepp'd before me, happily
KATHARINE: For my example.
GRIFFITH: Well, the voice goes, madam:
GRIFFITH: For after the stout Earl Northumberland
GRIFFITH: Arrested him at York, and brought him forward,
GRIFFITH: As a man sorely tainted, to his answer,
GRIFFITH: He fell sick suddenly, and grew so ill
GRIFFITH: He could not sit his mule.
KATHARINE: Alas, poor man!
GRIFFITH: At last, with easy roads, he came to Leicester,
GRIFFITH: Lodged in the abbey, where the reverend abbot,
GRIFFITH: With all his covent, honourably received him,
GRIFFITH: To whom he gave these words, 'O, father abbot,
GRIFFITH: An old man, broken with the storms of state,
GRIFFITH: Is come to lay his weary bones among ye,
GRIFFITH: Give him a little earth for charity!'
GRIFFITH: So went to bed, where eagerly his sickness
GRIFFITH: Pursued him still: and, three nights after this,
GRIFFITH: About the hour of eight, which he himself
GRIFFITH: Foretold should be his last, full of repentance,
GRIFFITH: Continual meditations, tears, and sorrows,
GRIFFITH: He gave his honours to the world again,
GRIFFITH: His blessed part to heaven, and slept in peace.
KATHARINE: So may he rest, his faults lie gently on him!
KATHARINE: Yet thus far, Griffith, give me leave to speak him,
KATHARINE: And yet with charity. He was a man
KATHARINE: Of an unbounded stomach, ever ranking
KATHARINE: Himself with princes, one that, by suggestion,
KATHARINE: Tied all the kingdom: simony was fair-play,
KATHARINE: His own opinion was his law: i' the presence
KATHARINE: He would say untruths, and be ever double
KATHARINE: Both in his words and meaning: he was never,
KATHARINE: But where he meant to ruin, pitiful:
KATHARINE: His promises were, as he then was, mighty,
KATHARINE: But his performance, as he is now, nothing:
KATHARINE: Of his own body he was ill, and gave
KATHARINE: The clergy in example.
GRIFFITH: Noble madam,
GRIFFITH: Men's evil manners live in brass, their virtues
GRIFFITH: We write in water. May it please your highness
GRIFFITH: To hear me speak his good now?
KATHARINE: Yes, good Griffith,
KATHARINE: I were malicious else.
GRIFFITH: This cardinal,
GRIFFITH: Though from an humble stock, undoubtedly
GRIFFITH: Was fashion'd to much honour from his cradle.
GRIFFITH: He was a scholar, and a ripe and good one,
GRIFFITH: Exceeding wise, fair-spoken, and persuading:
GRIFFITH: Lofty and sour to them that loved him not,
GRIFFITH: But to those men that sought him sweet as summer.
GRIFFITH: And though he were unsatisfied in getting,
GRIFFITH: Which was a sin, yet in bestowing, madam,
GRIFFITH: He was most princely: ever witness for him
GRIFFITH: Those twins Of learning that he raised in you,
GRIFFITH: Ipswich and Oxford! one of which fell with him,
GRIFFITH: Unwilling to outlive the good that did it,
GRIFFITH: The other, though unfinish'd, yet so famous,
GRIFFITH: So excellent in art, and still so rising,
GRIFFITH: That Christendom shall ever speak his virtue.
GRIFFITH: His overthrow heap'd happiness upon him,
GRIFFITH: For then, and not till then, he felt himself,
GRIFFITH: And found the blessedness of being little:
GRIFFITH: And, to add greater honours to his age
GRIFFITH: Than man could give him, he died fearing God.
KATHARINE: After my death I wish no other herald,
KATHARINE: No other speaker of my living actions,
KATHARINE: To keep mine honour from corruption,
KATHARINE: But such an honest chronicler as Griffith.
KATHARINE: Whom I most hated living, thou hast made me,
KATHARINE: With thy religious truth and modesty,
KATHARINE: Now in his ashes honour: peace be with him!
KATHARINE: Patience, be near me still, and set me lower:
KATHARINE: I have not long to trouble thee. Good Griffith,
KATHARINE: Cause the musicians play me that sad note
KATHARINE: I named my knell, whilst I sit meditating
KATHARINE: On that celestial harmony I go to.
NARRATOR: Sad and solemn music
GRIFFITH: She is asleep: good wench, let's sit down quiet,
GRIFFITH: For fear we wake her: softly, gentle Patience.
GRIFFITH: The vision. Enter, solemnly tripping one after  another, six personages, clad in white robes,  wearing on their heads garlands of bays, and golden  vizards on their faces, branches of bays or palm in  their hands. They first congee unto her, then  dance, and, at certain changes, the first two hold  a spare garland over her head, at which the other  four make reverent curtsies, then the two that held  the garland deliver the same to the other next two,  who observe the same order in their changes, and  holding the garland over her head: which done,  they deliver the same garland to the last two, who  likewise observe the same order: at which, as it  were by inspiration, she makes in her sleep signs  of rejoicing, and holdeth up her hands to heaven:  and so in their dancing vanish, carrying the garland with them. The music continues
KATHARINE: Spirits of peace, where are ye? are ye all gone,
KATHARINE: And leave me here in wretchedness behind ye?
GRIFFITH: Madam, we are here.
KATHARINE: It is not you I call for:
KATHARINE: Saw ye none enter since I slept?
GRIFFITH: None, madam.
KATHARINE: No? Saw you not, even now, a blessed troop
KATHARINE: Invite me to a banquet, whose bright faces
KATHARINE: Cast thousand beams upon me, like the sun?
KATHARINE: They promised me eternal happiness,
KATHARINE: And brought me garlands, Griffith, which I feel
KATHARINE: I am not worthy yet to wear: I shall, assuredly.
GRIFFITH: I am most joyful, madam, such good dreams
GRIFFITH: Possess your fancy.
KATHARINE: Bid the music leave,
KATHARINE: They are harsh and heavy to me.
NARRATOR: Music ceases
PATIENCE: Do you note
PATIENCE: How much her grace is alter'd on the sudden?
PATIENCE: How long her face is drawn? how pale she looks,
PATIENCE: And of an earthy cold? Mark her eyes!
GRIFFITH: She is going, wench: pray, pray.
PATIENCE: Heaven comfort her!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: An't like your grace,--
KATHARINE: You are a saucy fellow:
KATHARINE: Deserve we no more reverence?
GRIFFITH: You are to blame,
GRIFFITH: Knowing she will not lose her wonted greatness,
GRIFFITH: To use so rude behavior, go to, kneel.
Messenger: I humbly do entreat your highness' pardon,
Messenger: My haste made me unmannerly. There is staying
Messenger: A gentleman, sent from the king, to see you.
KATHARINE: Admit him entrance, Griffith: but this fellow
KATHARINE: Let me ne'er see again.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GRIFFITH and Messenger
NARRATOR: Re-enter GRIFFITH, with CAPUCIUS
KATHARINE: If my sight fail not,
KATHARINE: You should be lord ambassador from the emperor,
KATHARINE: My royal nephew, and your name Capucius.
CAPUCIUS: Madam, the same, your servant.
KATHARINE: O, my lord,
KATHARINE: The times and titles now are alter'd strangely
KATHARINE: With me since first you knew me. But, I pray you,
KATHARINE: What is your pleasure with me?
CAPUCIUS: Noble lady,
CAPUCIUS: First mine own service to your grace, the next,
CAPUCIUS: The king's request that I would visit you,
CAPUCIUS: Who grieves much for your weakness, and by me
CAPUCIUS: Sends you his princely commendations,
CAPUCIUS: And heartily entreats you take good comfort.
KATHARINE: O my good lord, that comfort comes too late,
KATHARINE: 'Tis like a pardon after execution:
KATHARINE: That gentle physic, given in time, had cured me,
KATHARINE: But now I am past an comforts here, but prayers.
KATHARINE: How does his highness?
CAPUCIUS: Madam, in good health.
KATHARINE: So may he ever do! and ever flourish,
KATHARINE: When I shal l dwell with worms, and my poor name
KATHARINE: Banish'd the kingdom! Patience, is that letter,
KATHARINE: I caused you write, yet sent away?
PATIENCE: No, madam.
NARRATOR: Giving it to KATHARINE
KATHARINE: Sir, I most humbly pray you to deliver
KATHARINE: This to my lord the king.
CAPUCIUS: Most willing, madam.
KATHARINE: In which I have commended to his goodness
KATHARINE: The model of our chaste loves, his young daughter,
KATHARINE: The dews of heaven fall thick in blessings on her!
KATHARINE: Beseeching him to give her virtuous breeding--
KATHARINE: She is young, and of a noble modest nature,
KATHARINE: I hope she will deserve well,--and a little
KATHARINE: To love her for her mother's sake, that loved him,
KATHARINE: Heaven knows how dearly. My next poor petition
KATHARINE: Is, that his noble grace would have some pity
KATHARINE: Upon my wretched women, that so long
KATHARINE: Have follow'd both my fortunes faithfully:
KATHARINE: Of which there is not one, I dare avow,
KATHARINE: And now I should not lie, but will deserve
KATHARINE: For virtue and true beauty of the soul,
KATHARINE: For honesty and decent carriage,
KATHARINE: A right good husband, let him be a noble
KATHARINE: And, sure, those men are happy that shall have 'em.
KATHARINE: The last is, for my men, they are the poorest,
KATHARINE: But poverty could never draw 'em from me,
KATHARINE: That they may have their wages duly paid 'em,
KATHARINE: And something over to remember me by:
KATHARINE: If heaven had pleased to have given me longer life
KATHARINE: And able means, we had not parted thus.
KATHARINE: These are the whole contents: and, good my lord,
KATHARINE: By that you love the dearest in this world,
KATHARINE: As you wish Christian peace to souls departed,
KATHARINE: Stand these poor people's friend, and urge the king
KATHARINE: To do me this last right.
CAPUCIUS: By heaven, I will,
CAPUCIUS: Or let me lose the fashion of a man!
KATHARINE: I thank you, honest lord. Remember me
KATHARINE: In all humility unto his highness:
KATHARINE: Say his long trouble now is passing
KATHARINE: Out of this world, tell him, in death I bless'd him,
KATHARINE: For so I will. Mine eyes grow dim. Farewell,
KATHARINE: My lord. Griffith, farewell. Nay, Patience,
KATHARINE: You must not leave me yet: I must to bed,
KATHARINE: Call in more women. When I am dead, good wench,
KATHARINE: Let me be used with honour: strew me over
KATHARINE: With maiden flowers, that all the world may know
KATHARINE: I was a chaste wife to my grave: embalm me,
KATHARINE: Then lay me forth: although unqueen'd, yet like
KATHARINE: A queen, and daughter to a king, inter me.
KATHARINE: I can no more.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, leading KATHARINE
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. A gallery in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter GARDINER, Bishop of Winchester, a Page with a torch before him, met by LOVELL
GARDINER: It's one o'clock, boy, is't not?
Boy: It hath struck.
GARDINER: These should be hours for necessities,
GARDINER: Not for delights, times to repair our nature
GARDINER: With comforting repose, and not for us
GARDINER: To waste these times. Good hour of night, Sir Thomas!

LOVELL: Came you from the king, my lord
GARDINER: I did, Sir Thomas: and left him at primero

LOVELL: Before he go to bed. I'll take my leave.

GARDINER: No great offence belongs to't, give your friend

GARDINER: As they say spirits do, at midnight, have
GARDINER: In them a wilder nature than the business
GARDINER: That seeks dispatch by day.
LOVELL: My lord, I love you,
LOVELL: And durst commend a secret to your ear

LOVELL: They say, in great extremity, and fear'd
LOVELL: She'll with the labour end.
GARDINER: The fruit she goes with
GARDINER: I pray for heartily, that it may find
GARDINER: Good time, and live: but for the stock, Sir Thomas,
GARDINER: I wish it grubb'd up now.
LOVELL: Methinks I could

LOVELL: She's a good creature, and, sweet lady, does
LOVELL: Deserve our better wishes.
GARDINER: But, sir, sir,
GARDINER: Hear me, Sir Thomas: you're a gentleman

GARDINER: And, let me tell you, it will ne'er be well,
GARDINER: 'Twill not, Sir Thomas Lovell, take't of me,

GARDINER: Sleep in their graves.
LOVELL: Now, sir, you speak of two

LOVELL: Beside that of the jewel house, is made master

LOVELL: Is the king's hand and tongue, and who dare speak

GARDINER: Yes, yes, Sir Thomas,

GARDINER: To speak my mind of him: and indeed this day,
GARDINER: Sir, I may tell it you, I think I have
GARDINER: Incensed the lords o' the council, that he is,
GARDINER: For so I know he is, they know he is,
GARDINER: A most arch heretic, a pestilence
GARDINER: That does infect the land: with which they moved
GARDINER: Have broken with the king, who hath so far
GARDINER: Given ear to our complaint, of his great grace
GARDINER: And princely care foreseeing those fell mischiefs
GARDINER: Our reasons laid before him, hath commanded
GARDINER: To-morrow morning to the council-board
GARDINER: He be convented. He's a rank weed, Sir Thomas,
GARDINER: And we must root him out. From your affairs
GARDINER: I hinder you too long: good night, Sir Thomas.
LOVELL: Many good nights, my lord: I rest your servant.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GARDINER and Page
NARRATOR: Enter KING HENRY VIII and SUFFOLK

LOVELL: So said her woman, and that her sufferance made
LOVELL: Almost each pang a death.

SUFFOLK: God safely quit her of her burthen, and
SUFFOLK: With gentle travail, to the gladding of
SUFFOLK: Your highness with an heir!

KING HENRY VIII: Would not be friendly to.
SUFFOLK: I wish your highness
SUFFOLK: A quiet night, and my good mistress will

NARRATOR: Exit SUFFOLK

NARRATOR: LOVELL seems to stay

CRANMER: To attend your highness' pleasure.

NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Council-Chamber.
NARRATOR: Enter Chancellor, places himself at the upper end  of the table on the left hand, a seat being left  void above him, as for CRANMER's seat. SUFFOLK,  NORFOLK, SURREY, Chamberlain, GARDINER, seat  themselves in order on each side. CROMWELL at lower end, as secretary. Keeper at the door

CROMWELL: Please your honours,

''' PLAY: Julius Caesar '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter FLAVIUS, MARULLUS, and certain Commoners
FLAVIUS: Hence! home, you idle creatures get you home:
FLAVIUS: Is this a holiday? what! know you not,
FLAVIUS: Being mechanical, you ought not walk
FLAVIUS: Upon a labouring day without the sign
FLAVIUS: Of your profession? Speak, what trade art thou?
First Commoner: Why, sir, a carpenter.
MARULLUS: Where is thy leather apron and thy rule?
MARULLUS: What dost thou with thy best apparel on?
MARULLUS: You, sir, what trade are you?
Second Commoner: Truly, sir, in respect of a fine workman, I am but,
Second Commoner: as you would say, a cobbler.
MARULLUS: But what trade art thou? answer me directly.
Second Commoner: A trade, sir, that, I hope, I may use with a safe
Second Commoner: conscience, which is, indeed, sir, a mender of bad soles.
MARULLUS: What trade, thou knave? thou naughty knave, what trade?
Second Commoner: Nay, I beseech you, sir, be not out with me: yet,
Second Commoner: if you be out, sir, I can mend you.
MARULLUS: What meanest thou by that? mend me, thou saucy fellow!
Second Commoner: Why, sir, cobble you.
FLAVIUS: Thou art a cobbler, art thou?
Second Commoner: Truly, sir, all that I live by is with the awl: I
Second Commoner: meddle with no tradesman's matters, nor women's
Second Commoner: matters, but with awl. I am, indeed, sir, a surgeon
Second Commoner: to old shoes, when they are in great danger, I
Second Commoner: recover them. As proper men as ever trod upon
Second Commoner: neat's leather have gone upon my handiwork.
FLAVIUS: But wherefore art not in thy shop today?
FLAVIUS: Why dost thou lead these men about the streets?
Second Commoner: Truly, sir, to wear out their shoes, to get myself
Second Commoner: into more work. But, indeed, sir, we make holiday,
Second Commoner: to see Caesar and to rejoice in his triumph.
MARULLUS: Wherefore rejoice? What conquest brings he home?
MARULLUS: What tributaries follow him to Rome,
MARULLUS: To grace in captive bonds his chariot-wheels?
MARULLUS: You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things!
MARULLUS: O you hard hearts, you cruel men of Rome,
MARULLUS: Knew you not Pompey? Many a time and oft
MARULLUS: Have you climb'd up to walls and battlements,
MARULLUS: To towers and windows, yea, to chimney-tops,
MARULLUS: Your infants in your arms, and there have sat
MARULLUS: The livelong day, with patient expectation,
MARULLUS: To see great Pompey pass the streets of Rome:
MARULLUS: And when you saw his chariot but appear,
MARULLUS: Have you not made an universal shout,
MARULLUS: That Tiber trembled underneath her banks,
MARULLUS: To hear the replication of your sounds
MARULLUS: Made in her concave shores?
MARULLUS: And do you now put on your best attire?
MARULLUS: And do you now cull out a holiday?
MARULLUS: And do you now strew flowers in his way
MARULLUS: That comes in triumph over Pompey's blood? Be gone!
MARULLUS: Run to your houses, fall upon your knees,
MARULLUS: Pray to the gods to intermit the plague
MARULLUS: That needs must light on this ingratitude.
FLAVIUS: Go, go, good countrymen, and, for this fault,
FLAVIUS: Assemble all the poor men of your sort,
FLAVIUS: Draw them to Tiber banks, and weep your tears
FLAVIUS: Into the channel, till the lowest stream
FLAVIUS: Do kiss the most exalted shores of all.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all the Commoners
FLAVIUS: See whether their basest metal be not moved,
FLAVIUS: They vanish tongue-tied in their guiltiness.
FLAVIUS: Go you down that way towards the Capitol,
FLAVIUS: This way will I disrobe the images,
FLAVIUS: If you do find them deck'd with ceremonies.
MARULLUS: May we do so?
MARULLUS: You know it is the feast of Lupercal.
FLAVIUS: It is no matter, let no images
FLAVIUS: Be hung with Caesar's trophies. I'll about,
FLAVIUS: And drive away the vulgar from the streets:
FLAVIUS: So do you too, where you perceive them thick.
FLAVIUS: These growing feathers pluck'd from Caesar's wing
FLAVIUS: Will make him fly an ordinary pitch,
FLAVIUS: Who else would soar above the view of men
FLAVIUS: And keep us all in servile fearfulness.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A public place.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter CAESAR, ANTONY, for the course,  CALPURNIA, PORTIA, DECIUS BRUTUS, CICERO, BRUTUS,  CASSIUS, and CASCA, a great crowd following, among them a Soothsayer
CAESAR: Calpurnia!
CASCA: Peace, ho! Caesar speaks.
CAESAR: Calpurnia!
CALPURNIA: Here, my lord.
CAESAR: Stand you directly in Antonius' way,
