CAESAR: When he doth run his course. Antonius!
ANTONY: Caesar, my lord?
CAESAR: Forget not, in your speed, Antonius,
CAESAR: To touch Calpurnia, for our elders say,
CAESAR: The barren, touched in this holy chase,
CAESAR: Shake off their sterile curse.
ANTONY: I shall remember:
ANTONY: When Caesar says 'do this,' it is perform'd.
CAESAR: Set on, and leave no ceremony out.
NARRATOR: Flourish
Soothsayer: Caesar!
CAESAR: Ha! who calls?
CASCA: Bid every noise be still: peace yet again!
CAESAR: Who is it in the press that calls on me?
CAESAR: I hear a tongue, shriller than all the music,
CAESAR: Cry 'Caesar!' Speak, Caesar is turn'd to hear.
Soothsayer: Beware the ides of March.
CAESAR: What man is that?
BRUTUS: A soothsayer bids you beware the ides of March.
CAESAR: Set him before me, let me see his face.
CASSIUS: Fellow, come from the throng, look upon Caesar.
CAESAR: What say'st thou to me now? speak once again.
Soothsayer: Beware the ides of March.
CAESAR: He is a dreamer, let us leave him: pass.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Exeunt all except BRUTUS and CASSIUS
CASSIUS: Will you go see the order of the course?
BRUTUS: Not I.
CASSIUS: I pray you, do.
BRUTUS: I am not gamesome: I do lack some part
BRUTUS: Of that quick spirit that is in Antony.
BRUTUS: Let me not hinder, Cassius, your desires,
BRUTUS: I'll leave you.
CASSIUS: Brutus, I do observe you now of late:
CASSIUS: I have not from your eyes that gentleness
CASSIUS: And show of love as I was wont to have:
CASSIUS: You bear too stubborn and too strange a hand
CASSIUS: Over your friend that loves you.
BRUTUS: Cassius,
BRUTUS: Be not deceived: if I have veil'd my look,
BRUTUS: I turn the trouble of my countenance
BRUTUS: Merely upon myself. Vexed I am
BRUTUS: Of late with passions of some difference,
BRUTUS: Conceptions only proper to myself,
BRUTUS: Which give some soil perhaps to my behaviors,
BRUTUS: But let not therefore my good friends be grieved--
BRUTUS: Among which number, Cassius, be you one--
BRUTUS: Nor construe any further my neglect,
BRUTUS: Than that poor Brutus, with himself at war,
BRUTUS: Forgets the shows of love to other men.
CASSIUS: Then, Brutus, I have much mistook your passion,
CASSIUS: By means whereof this breast of mine hath buried
CASSIUS: Thoughts of great value, worthy cogitations.
CASSIUS: Tell me, good Brutus, can you see your face?
BRUTUS: No, Cassius, for the eye sees not itself,
BRUTUS: But by reflection, by some other things.
CASSIUS: 'Tis just:
CASSIUS: And it is very much lamented, Brutus,
CASSIUS: That you have no such mirrors as will turn
CASSIUS: Your hidden worthiness into your eye,
CASSIUS: That you might see your shadow. I have heard,
CASSIUS: Where many of the best respect in Rome,
CASSIUS: Except immortal Caesar, speaking of Brutus
CASSIUS: And groaning underneath this age's yoke,
CASSIUS: Have wish'd that noble Brutus had his eyes.
BRUTUS: Into what dangers would you lead me, Cassius,
BRUTUS: That you would have me seek into myself
BRUTUS: For that which is not in me?
CASSIUS: Therefore, good Brutus, be prepared to hear:
CASSIUS: And since you know you cannot see yourself
CASSIUS: So well as by reflection, I, your glass,
CASSIUS: Will modestly discover to yourself
CASSIUS: That of yourself which you yet know not of.
CASSIUS: And be not jealous on me, gentle Brutus:
CASSIUS: Were I a common laugher, or did use
CASSIUS: To stale with ordinary oaths my love
CASSIUS: To every new protester, if you know
CASSIUS: That I do fawn on men and hug them hard
CASSIUS: And after scandal them, or if you know
CASSIUS: That I profess myself in banqueting
CASSIUS: To all the rout, then hold me dangerous.
NARRATOR: Flourish, and shout
BRUTUS: What means this shouting? I do fear, the people
BRUTUS: Choose Caesar for their king.
CASSIUS: Ay, do you fear it?
CASSIUS: Then must I think you would not have it so.
BRUTUS: I would not, Cassius, yet I love him well.
BRUTUS: But wherefore do you hold me here so long?
BRUTUS: What is it that you would impart to me?
BRUTUS: If it be aught toward the general good,
BRUTUS: Set honour in one eye and death i' the other,
BRUTUS: And I will look on both indifferently,
BRUTUS: For let the gods so speed me as I love
BRUTUS: The name of honour more than I fear death.
CASSIUS: I know that virtue to be in you, Brutus,
CASSIUS: As well as I do know your outward favour.
CASSIUS: Well, honour is the subject of my story.
CASSIUS: I cannot tell what you and other men
CASSIUS: Think of this life, but, for my single self,
CASSIUS: I had as lief not be as live to be
CASSIUS: In awe of such a thing as I myself.
CASSIUS: I was born free as Caesar, so were you:
CASSIUS: We both have fed as well, and we can both
CASSIUS: Endure the winter's cold as well as he:
CASSIUS: For once, upon a raw and gusty day,
CASSIUS: The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores,
CASSIUS: Caesar said to me 'Darest thou, Cassius, now
CASSIUS: Leap in with me into this angry flood,
CASSIUS: And swim to yonder point?' Upon the word,
CASSIUS: Accoutred as I was, I plunged in
CASSIUS: And bade him follow, so indeed he did.
CASSIUS: The torrent roar'd, and we did buffet it
CASSIUS: With lusty sinews, throwing it aside
CASSIUS: And stemming it with hearts of controversy,
CASSIUS: But ere we could arrive the point proposed,
CASSIUS: Caesar cried 'Help me, Cassius, or I sink!'
CASSIUS: I, as Aeneas, our great ancestor,
CASSIUS: Did from the flames of Troy upon his shoulder
CASSIUS: The old Anchises bear, so from the waves of Tiber
CASSIUS: Did I the tired Caesar. And this man
CASSIUS: Is now become a god, and Cassius is
CASSIUS: A wretched creature and must bend his body,
CASSIUS: If Caesar carelessly but nod on him.
CASSIUS: He had a fever when he was in Spain,
CASSIUS: And when the fit was on him, I did mark
CASSIUS: How he did shake: 'tis true, this god did shake,
CASSIUS: His coward lips did from their colour fly,
CASSIUS: And that same eye whose bend doth awe the world
CASSIUS: Did lose his lustre: I did hear him groan:
CASSIUS: Ay, and that tongue of his that bade the Romans
CASSIUS: Mark him and write his speeches in their books,
CASSIUS: Alas, it cried 'Give me some drink, Titinius,'
CASSIUS: As a sick girl. Ye gods, it doth amaze me
CASSIUS: A man of such a feeble temper should
CASSIUS: So get the start of the majestic world
CASSIUS: And bear the palm alone.
NARRATOR: Shout. Flourish
BRUTUS: Another general shout!
BRUTUS: I do believe that these applauses are
BRUTUS: For some new honours that are heap'd on Caesar.
CASSIUS: Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world
CASSIUS: Like a Colossus, and we petty men
CASSIUS: Walk under his huge legs and peep about
CASSIUS: To find ourselves dishonourable graves.
CASSIUS: Men at some time are masters of their fates:
CASSIUS: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars,
CASSIUS: But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
CASSIUS: Brutus and Caesar: what should be in that 'Caesar'?
CASSIUS: Why should that name be sounded more than yours?
CASSIUS: Write them together, yours is as fair a name,
CASSIUS: Sound them, it doth become the mouth as well,
CASSIUS: Weigh them, it is as heavy, conjure with 'em,
CASSIUS: Brutus will start a spirit as soon as Caesar.
CASSIUS: Now, in the names of all the gods at once,
CASSIUS: Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed,
CASSIUS: That he is grown so great? Age, thou art shamed!
CASSIUS: Rome, thou hast lost the breed of noble bloods!
CASSIUS: When went there by an age, since the great flood,
CASSIUS: But it was famed with more than with one man?
CASSIUS: When could they say till now, that talk'd of Rome,
CASSIUS: That her wide walls encompass'd but one man?
CASSIUS: Now is it Rome indeed and room enough,
CASSIUS: When there is in it but one only man.
CASSIUS: O, you and I have heard our fathers say,
CASSIUS: There was a Brutus once that would have brook'd
CASSIUS: The eternal devil to keep his state in Rome
CASSIUS: As easily as a king.
BRUTUS: That you do love me, I am nothing jealous,
BRUTUS: What you would work me to, I have some aim:
BRUTUS: How I have thought of this and of these times,
BRUTUS: I shall recount hereafter, for this present,
BRUTUS: I would not, so with love I might entreat you,
BRUTUS: Be any further moved. What you have said
BRUTUS: I will consider, what you have to say
BRUTUS: I will with patience hear, and find a time
BRUTUS: Both meet to hear and answer such high things.
BRUTUS: Till then, my noble friend, chew upon this:
BRUTUS: Brutus had rather be a villager
BRUTUS: Than to repute himself a son of Rome
BRUTUS: Under these hard conditions as this time
BRUTUS: Is like to lay upon us.
CASSIUS: I am glad that my weak words
CASSIUS: Have struck but thus much show of fire from Brutus.
BRUTUS: The games are done and Caesar is returning.
CASSIUS: As they pass by, pluck Casca by the sleeve,
CASSIUS: And he will, after his sour fashion, tell you
CASSIUS: What hath proceeded worthy note to-day.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CAESAR and his Train
BRUTUS: I will do so. But, look you, Cassius,
BRUTUS: The angry spot doth glow on Caesar's brow,
BRUTUS: And all the rest look like a chidden train:
BRUTUS: Calpurnia's cheek is pale, and Cicero
BRUTUS: Looks with such ferret and such fiery eyes
BRUTUS: As we have seen him in the Capitol,
BRUTUS: Being cross'd in conference by some senators.
CASSIUS: Casca will tell us what the matter is.
CAESAR: Antonius!
ANTONY: Caesar?
CAESAR: Let me have men about me that are fat,
CAESAR: Sleek-headed men and such as sleep o' nights:
CAESAR: Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look,
CAESAR: He thinks too much: such men are dangerous.
ANTONY: Fear him not, Caesar, he's not dangerous,
ANTONY: He is a noble Roman and well given.
CAESAR: Would he were fatter! But I fear him not:
CAESAR: Yet if my name were liable to fear,
CAESAR: I do not know the man I should avoid
CAESAR: So soon as that spare Cassius. He reads much,
CAESAR: He is a great observer and he looks
CAESAR: Quite through the deeds of men: he loves no plays,
CAESAR: As thou dost, Antony, he hears no music,
CAESAR: Seldom he smiles, and smiles in such a sort
CAESAR: As if he mock'd himself and scorn'd his spirit
CAESAR: That could be moved to smile at any thing.
CAESAR: Such men as he be never at heart's ease
CAESAR: Whiles they behold a greater than themselves,
CAESAR: And therefore are they very dangerous.
CAESAR: I rather tell thee what is to be fear'd
CAESAR: Than what I fear, for always I am Caesar.
CAESAR: Come on my right hand, for this ear is deaf,
CAESAR: And tell me truly what thou think'st of him.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Exeunt CAESAR and all his Train, but CASCA
CASCA: You pull'd me by the cloak, would you speak with me?
BRUTUS: Ay, Casca, tell us what hath chanced to-day,
BRUTUS: That Caesar looks so sad.
CASCA: Why, you were with him, were you not?
BRUTUS: I should not then ask Casca what had chanced.
CASCA: Why, there was a crown offered him: and being
CASCA: offered him, he put it by with the back of his hand,
CASCA: thus, and then the people fell a-shouting.
BRUTUS: What was the second noise for?
CASCA: Why, for that too.
CASSIUS: They shouted thrice: what was the last cry for?
CASCA: Why, for that too.
BRUTUS: Was the crown offered him thrice?
CASCA: Ay, marry, was't, and he put it by thrice, every
CASCA: time gentler than other, and at every putting-by
CASCA: mine honest neighbours shouted.
CASSIUS: Who offered him the crown?
CASCA: Why, Antony.
BRUTUS: Tell us the manner of it, gentle Casca.
CASCA: I can as well be hanged as tell the manner of it:
CASCA: it was mere foolery, I did not mark it. I saw Mark
CASCA: Antony offer him a crown,--yet 'twas not a crown
CASCA: neither, 'twas one of these coronets,--and, as I told
CASCA: you, he put it by once: but, for all that, to my
CASCA: thinking, he would fain have had it. Then he
CASCA: offered it to him again, then he put it by again:
CASCA: but, to my thinking, he was very loath to lay his
CASCA: fingers off it. And then he offered it the third
CASCA: time, he put it the third time by: and still as he
CASCA: refused it, the rabblement hooted and clapped their
CASCA: chapped hands and threw up their sweaty night-caps
CASCA: and uttered such a deal of stinking breath because
CASCA: Caesar refused the crown that it had almost choked
CASCA: Caesar, for he swounded and fell down at it: and
CASCA: for mine own part, I durst not laugh, for fear of
CASCA: opening my lips and receiving the bad air.
CASSIUS: But, soft, I pray you: what, did Caesar swound?
CASCA: He fell down in the market-place, and foamed at
CASCA: mouth, and was speechless.
BRUTUS: 'Tis very like: he hath the failing sickness.
CASSIUS: No, Caesar hath it not, but you and I,
CASSIUS: And honest Casca, we have the falling sickness.
CASCA: I know not what you mean by that, but, I am sure,
CASCA: Caesar fell down. If the tag-rag people did not
CASCA: clap him and hiss him, according as he pleased and
CASCA: displeased them, as they use to do the players in
CASCA: the theatre, I am no true man.
BRUTUS: What said he when he came unto himself?
CASCA: Marry, before he fell down, when he perceived the
CASCA: common herd was glad he refused the crown, he
CASCA: plucked me ope his doublet and offered them his
CASCA: throat to cut. An I had been a man of any
CASCA: occupation, if I would not have taken him at a word,
CASCA: I would I might go to hell among the rogues. And so
CASCA: he fell. When he came to himself again, he said,
CASCA: If he had done or said any thing amiss, he desired
CASCA: their worships to think it was his infirmity. Three
CASCA: or four wenches, where I stood, cried 'Alas, good
CASCA: soul!' and forgave him with all their hearts: but
CASCA: there's no heed to be taken of them, if Caesar had
CASCA: stabbed their mothers, they would have done no less.
BRUTUS: And after that, he came, thus sad, away?
CASCA: Ay.
CASSIUS: Did Cicero say any thing?
CASCA: Ay, he spoke Greek.
CASSIUS: To what effect?
CASCA: Nay, an I tell you that, Ill ne'er look you i' the
CASCA: face again: but those that understood him smiled at
CASCA: one another and shook their heads, but, for mine own
CASCA: part, it was Greek to me. I could tell you more
CASCA: news too: Marullus and Flavius, for pulling scarfs
CASCA: off Caesar's images, are put to silence. Fare you
CASCA: well. There was more foolery yet, if I could
CASCA: remember it.
CASSIUS: Will you sup with me to-night, Casca?
CASCA: No, I am promised forth.
CASSIUS: Will you dine with me to-morrow?
CASCA: Ay, if I be alive and your mind hold and your dinner
CASCA: worth the eating.
CASSIUS: Good: I will expect you.
CASCA: Do so. Farewell, both.
NARRATOR: Exit
BRUTUS: What a blunt fellow is this grown to be!
BRUTUS: He was quick mettle when he went to school.
CASSIUS: So is he now in execution
CASSIUS: Of any bold or noble enterprise,
CASSIUS: However he puts on this tardy form.
CASSIUS: This rudeness is a sauce to his good wit,
CASSIUS: Which gives men stomach to digest his words
CASSIUS: With better appetite.
BRUTUS: And so it is. For this time I will leave you:
BRUTUS: To-morrow, if you please to speak with me,
BRUTUS: I will come home to you, or, if you will,
BRUTUS: Come home to me, and I will wait for you.
CASSIUS: I will do so: till then, think of the world.
NARRATOR: Exit BRUTUS
CASSIUS: Well, Brutus, thou art noble, yet, I see,
CASSIUS: Thy honourable metal may be wrought
CASSIUS: From that it is disposed: therefore it is meet
CASSIUS: That noble minds keep ever with their likes,
CASSIUS: For who so firm that cannot be seduced?
CASSIUS: Caesar doth bear me hard, but he loves Brutus:
CASSIUS: If I were Brutus now and he were Cassius,
CASSIUS: He should not humour me. I will this night,
CASSIUS: In several hands, in at his windows throw,
CASSIUS: As if they came from several citizens,
CASSIUS: Writings all tending to the great opinion
CASSIUS: That Rome holds of his name, wherein obscurely
CASSIUS: Caesar's ambition shall be glanced at:
CASSIUS: And after this let Caesar seat him sure,
CASSIUS: For we will shake him, or worse days endure.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. A street.
NARRATOR: Thunder and lightning. Enter from opposite sides, CASCA, with his sword drawn, and CICERO
CICERO: Good even, Casca: brought you Caesar home?
CICERO: Why are you breathless? and why stare you so?
CASCA: Are not you moved, when all the sway of earth
CASCA: Shakes like a thing unfirm? O Cicero,
CASCA: I have seen tempests, when the scolding winds
CASCA: Have rived the knotty oaks, and I have seen
CASCA: The ambitious ocean swell and rage and foam,
CASCA: To be exalted with the threatening clouds:
CASCA: But never till to-night, never till now,
CASCA: Did I go through a tempest dropping fire.
CASCA: Either there is a civil strife in heaven,
CASCA: Or else the world, too saucy with the gods,
CASCA: Incenses them to send destruction.
CICERO: Why, saw you any thing more wonderful?
CASCA: A common slave--you know him well by sight--
CASCA: Held up his left hand, which did flame and burn
CASCA: Like twenty torches join'd, and yet his hand,
CASCA: Not sensible of fire, remain'd unscorch'd.
CASCA: Besides--I ha' not since put up my sword--
CASCA: Against the Capitol I met a lion,
CASCA: Who glared upon me, and went surly by,
CASCA: Without annoying me: and there were drawn
CASCA: Upon a heap a hundred ghastly women,
CASCA: Transformed with their fear, who swore they saw
CASCA: Men all in fire walk up and down the streets.
CASCA: And yesterday the bird of night did sit
CASCA: Even at noon-day upon the market-place,
CASCA: Hooting and shrieking. When these prodigies
CASCA: Do so conjointly meet, let not men say
CASCA: 'These are their reasons, they are natural,'
CASCA: For, I believe, they are portentous things
CASCA: Unto the climate that they point upon.
CICERO: Indeed, it is a strange-disposed time:
CICERO: But men may construe things after their fashion,
CICERO: Clean from the purpose of the things themselves.
CICERO: Come Caesar to the Capitol to-morrow?
CASCA: He doth, for he did bid Antonius
CASCA: Send word to you he would be there to-morrow.
CICERO: Good night then, Casca: this disturbed sky
CICERO: Is not to walk in.
CASCA: Farewell, Cicero.
NARRATOR: Exit CICERO
NARRATOR: Enter CASSIUS
CASSIUS: Who's there?
CASCA: A Roman.
CASSIUS: Casca, by your voice.
CASCA: Your ear is good. Cassius, what night is this!
CASSIUS: A very pleasing night to honest men.
CASCA: Who ever knew the heavens menace so?
CASSIUS: Those that have known the earth so full of faults.
CASSIUS: For my part, I have walk'd about the streets,
CASSIUS: Submitting me unto the perilous night,
CASSIUS: And, thus unbraced, Casca, as you see,
CASSIUS: Have bared my bosom to the thunder-stone,
CASSIUS: And when the cross blue lightning seem'd to open
CASSIUS: The breast of heaven, I did present myself
CASSIUS: Even in the aim and very flash of it.
CASCA: But wherefore did you so much tempt the heavens?
CASCA: It is the part of men to fear and tremble,
CASCA: When the most mighty gods by tokens send
CASCA: Such dreadful heralds to astonish us.
CASSIUS: You are dull, Casca, and those sparks of life
CASSIUS: That should be in a Roman you do want,
CASSIUS: Or else you use not. You look pale and gaze
CASSIUS: And put on fear and cast yourself in wonder,
CASSIUS: To see the strange impatience of the heavens:
CASSIUS: But if you would consider the true cause
CASSIUS: Why all these fires, why all these gliding ghosts,
CASSIUS: Why birds and beasts from quality and kind,
CASSIUS: Why old men fool and children calculate,
CASSIUS: Why all these things change from their ordinance
CASSIUS: Their natures and preformed faculties
CASSIUS: To monstrous quality,--why, you shall find
CASSIUS: That heaven hath infused them with these spirits,
CASSIUS: To make them instruments of fear and warning
CASSIUS: Unto some monstrous state.
CASSIUS: Now could I, Casca, name to thee a man
CASSIUS: Most like this dreadful night,
CASSIUS: That thunders, lightens, opens graves, and roars
CASSIUS: As doth the lion in the Capitol,
CASSIUS: A man no mightier than thyself or me
CASSIUS: In personal action, yet prodigious grown
CASSIUS: And fearful, as these strange eruptions are.
CASCA: 'Tis Caesar that you mean, is it not, Cassius?
CASSIUS: Let it be who it is: for Romans now
CASSIUS: Have thews and limbs like to their ancestors,
CASSIUS: But, woe the while! our fathers' minds are dead,
CASSIUS: And we are govern'd with our mothers' spirits,
CASSIUS: Our yoke and sufferance show us womanish.
CASCA: Indeed, they say the senators tomorrow
CASCA: Mean to establish Caesar as a king,
CASCA: And he shall wear his crown by sea and land,
CASCA: In every place, save here in Italy.
CASSIUS: I know where I will wear this dagger then,
CASSIUS: Cassius from bondage will deliver Cassius:
CASSIUS: Therein, ye gods, you make the weak most strong,
CASSIUS: Therein, ye gods, you tyrants do defeat:
CASSIUS: Nor stony tower, nor walls of beaten brass,
CASSIUS: Nor airless dungeon, nor strong links of iron,
CASSIUS: Can be retentive to the strength of spirit,
CASSIUS: But life, being weary of these worldly bars,
CASSIUS: Never lacks power to dismiss itself.
CASSIUS: If I know this, know all the world besides,
CASSIUS: That part of tyranny that I do bear
CASSIUS: I can shake off at pleasure.
NARRATOR: Thunder still
CASCA: So can I:
CASCA: So every bondman in his own hand bears
CASCA: The power to cancel his captivity.
CASSIUS: And why should Caesar be a tyrant then?
CASSIUS: Poor man! I know he would not be a wolf,
CASSIUS: But that he sees the Romans are but sheep:
CASSIUS: He were no lion, were not Romans hinds.
CASSIUS: Those that with haste will make a mighty fire
CASSIUS: Begin it with weak straws: what trash is Rome,
CASSIUS: What rubbish and what offal, when it serves
CASSIUS: For the base matter to illuminate
CASSIUS: So vile a thing as Caesar! But, O grief,
CASSIUS: Where hast thou led me? I perhaps speak this
CASSIUS: Before a willing bondman, then I know
CASSIUS: My answer must be made. But I am arm'd,
CASSIUS: And dangers are to me indifferent.
CASCA: You speak to Casca, and to such a man
CASCA: That is no fleering tell-tale. Hold, my hand:
CASCA: Be factious for redress of all these griefs,
CASCA: And I will set this foot of mine as far
CASCA: As who goes farthest.
CASSIUS: There's a bargain made.
CASSIUS: Now know you, Casca, I have moved already
CASSIUS: Some certain of the noblest-minded Romans
CASSIUS: To undergo with me an enterprise
CASSIUS: Of honourable-dangerous consequence,
CASSIUS: And I do know, by this, they stay for me
CASSIUS: In Pompey's porch: for now, this fearful night,
CASSIUS: There is no stir or walking in the streets,
CASSIUS: And the complexion of the element
CASSIUS: In favour's like the work we have in hand,
CASSIUS: Most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.
CASCA: Stand close awhile, for here comes one in haste.
CASSIUS: 'Tis Cinna, I do know him by his gait,
CASSIUS: He is a friend.
NARRATOR: Enter CINNA
CASSIUS: Cinna, where haste you so?
CINNA: To find out you. Who's that? Metellus Cimber?
CASSIUS: No, it is Casca, one incorporate
CASSIUS: To our attempts. Am I not stay'd for, Cinna?
CINNA: I am glad on 't. What a fearful night is this!
CINNA: There's two or three of us have seen strange sights.
CASSIUS: Am I not stay'd for? tell me.
CINNA: Yes, you are.
CINNA: O Cassius, if you could
CINNA: But win the noble Brutus to our party--
CASSIUS: Be you content: good Cinna, take this paper,
CASSIUS: And look you lay it in the praetor's chair,
CASSIUS: Where Brutus may but find it, and throw this
CASSIUS: In at his window, set this up with wax
CASSIUS: Upon old Brutus' statue: all this done,
CASSIUS: Repair to Pompey's porch, where you shall find us.
CASSIUS: Is Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?
CINNA: All but Metellus Cimber, and he's gone
CINNA: To seek you at your house. Well, I will hie,
CINNA: And so bestow these papers as you bade me.
CASSIUS: That done, repair to Pompey's theatre.
NARRATOR: Exit CINNA
CASSIUS: Come, Casca, you and I will yet ere day
CASSIUS: See Brutus at his house: three parts of him
CASSIUS: Is ours already, and the man entire
CASSIUS: Upon the next encounter yields him ours.
CASCA: O, he sits high in all the people's hearts:
CASCA: And that which would appear offence in us,
CASCA: His countenance, like richest alchemy,
CASCA: Will change to virtue and to worthiness.
CASSIUS: Him and his worth and our great need of him
CASSIUS: You have right well conceited. Let us go,
CASSIUS: For it is after midnight, and ere day
CASSIUS: We will awake him and be sure of him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. BRUTUS's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter BRUTUS
BRUTUS: What, Lucius, ho!
BRUTUS: I cannot, by the progress of the stars,
BRUTUS: Give guess how near to day. Lucius, I say!
BRUTUS: I would it were my fault to sleep so soundly.
BRUTUS: When, Lucius, when? awake, I say! what, Lucius!
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS
LUCIUS: Call'd you, my lord?
BRUTUS: Get me a taper in my study, Lucius:
BRUTUS: When it is lighted, come and call me here.
LUCIUS: I will, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
BRUTUS: It must be by his death: and for my part,
BRUTUS: I know no personal cause to spurn at him,
BRUTUS: But for the general. He would be crown'd:
BRUTUS: How that might change his nature, there's the question.
BRUTUS: It is the bright day that brings forth the adder,
BRUTUS: And that craves wary walking. Crown him?--that,--
BRUTUS: And then, I grant, we put a sting in him,
BRUTUS: That at his will he may do danger with.
BRUTUS: The abuse of greatness is, when it disjoins
BRUTUS: Remorse from power: and, to speak truth of Caesar,
BRUTUS: I have not known when his affections sway'd
BRUTUS: More than his reason. But 'tis a common proof,
BRUTUS: That lowliness is young ambition's ladder,
BRUTUS: Whereto the climber-upward turns his face,
BRUTUS: But when he once attains the upmost round.
BRUTUS: He then unto the ladder turns his back,
BRUTUS: Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees
BRUTUS: By which he did ascend. So Caesar may.
BRUTUS: Then, lest he may, prevent. And, since the quarrel
BRUTUS: Will bear no colour for the thing he is,
BRUTUS: Fashion it thus, that what he is, augmented,
BRUTUS: Would run to these and these extremities:
BRUTUS: And therefore think him as a serpent's egg
BRUTUS: Which, hatch'd, would, as his kind, grow mischievous,
BRUTUS: And kill him in the shell.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS
LUCIUS: The taper burneth in your closet, sir.
LUCIUS: Searching the window for a flint, I found
LUCIUS: This paper, thus seal'd up, and, I am sure,
LUCIUS: It did not lie there when I went to bed.
NARRATOR: Gives him the letter
BRUTUS: Get you to bed again, it is not day.
BRUTUS: Is not to-morrow, boy, the ides of March?
LUCIUS: I know not, sir.
BRUTUS: Look in the calendar, and bring me word.
LUCIUS: I will, sir.
NARRATOR: Exit
BRUTUS: The exhalations whizzing in the air
BRUTUS: Give so much light that I may read by them.
NARRATOR: Opens the letter and reads
BRUTUS: 'Brutus, thou sleep'st: awake, and see thyself.
BRUTUS: Shall Rome,  and c. Speak, strike, redress!
BRUTUS: Brutus, thou sleep'st: awake!'
BRUTUS: Such instigations have been often dropp'd
BRUTUS: Where I have took them up.
BRUTUS: 'Shall Rome,  and c.' Thus must I piece it out:
BRUTUS: Shall Rome stand under one man's awe? What, Rome?
BRUTUS: My ancestors did from the streets of Rome
BRUTUS: The Tarquin drive, when he was call'd a king.
BRUTUS: 'Speak, strike, redress!' Am I entreated
BRUTUS: To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise:
BRUTUS: If the redress will follow, thou receivest
BRUTUS: Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus!
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS
LUCIUS: Sir, March is wasted fourteen days.
NARRATOR: Knocking within
BRUTUS: 'Tis good. Go to the gate, somebody knocks.
NARRATOR: Exit LUCIUS
BRUTUS: Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar,
BRUTUS: I have not slept.
BRUTUS: Between the acting of a dreadful thing
BRUTUS: And the first motion, all the interim is
BRUTUS: Like a phantasma, or a hideous dream:
BRUTUS: The Genius and the mortal instruments
BRUTUS: Are then in council, and the state of man,
BRUTUS: Like to a little kingdom, suffers then
BRUTUS: The nature of an insurrection.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS
LUCIUS: Sir, 'tis your brother Cassius at the door,
LUCIUS: Who doth desire to see you.
BRUTUS: Is he alone?
LUCIUS: No, sir, there are moe with him.
BRUTUS: Do you know them?
LUCIUS: No, sir, their hats are pluck'd about their ears,
LUCIUS: And half their faces buried in their cloaks,
LUCIUS: That by no means I may discover them
LUCIUS: By any mark of favour.
BRUTUS: Let 'em enter.
NARRATOR: Exit LUCIUS
BRUTUS: They are the faction. O conspiracy,
BRUTUS: Shamest thou to show thy dangerous brow by night,
BRUTUS: When evils are most free? O, then by day
BRUTUS: Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough
BRUTUS: To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy,
BRUTUS: Hide it in smiles and affability:
BRUTUS: For if thou path, thy native semblance on,
BRUTUS: Not Erebus itself were dim enough
BRUTUS: To hide thee from prevention.
NARRATOR: Enter the conspirators, CASSIUS, CASCA, DECIUS BRUTUS, CINNA, METELLUS CIMBER, and TREBONIUS
CASSIUS: I think we are too bold upon your rest:
CASSIUS: Good morrow, Brutus, do we trouble you?
BRUTUS: I have been up this hour, awake all night.
BRUTUS: Know I these men that come along with you?
CASSIUS: Yes, every man of them, and no man here
CASSIUS: But honours you, and every one doth wish
CASSIUS: You had but that opinion of yourself
CASSIUS: Which every noble Roman bears of you.
CASSIUS: This is Trebonius.
BRUTUS: He is welcome hither.
CASSIUS: This, Decius Brutus.
BRUTUS: He is welcome too.
CASSIUS: This, Casca, this, Cinna, and this, Metellus Cimber.
BRUTUS: They are all welcome.
BRUTUS: What watchful cares do interpose themselves
BRUTUS: Betwixt your eyes and night?
CASSIUS: Shall I entreat a word?
NARRATOR: BRUTUS and CASSIUS whisper
DECIUS BRUTUS: Here lies the east: doth not the day break here?
CASCA: No.
CINNA: O, pardon, sir, it doth, and yon gray lines
CINNA: That fret the clouds are messengers of day.
CASCA: You shall confess that you are both deceived.
CASCA: Here, as I point my sword, the sun arises,
CASCA: Which is a great way growing on the south,
CASCA: Weighing the youthful season of the year.
CASCA: Some two months hence up higher toward the north
CASCA: He first presents his fire, and the high east
CASCA: Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.
BRUTUS: Give me your hands all over, one by one.
CASSIUS: And let us swear our resolution.
BRUTUS: No, not an oath: if not the face of men,
BRUTUS: The sufferance of our souls, the time's abuse,--
BRUTUS: If these be motives weak, break off betimes,
BRUTUS: And every man hence to his idle bed,
BRUTUS: So let high-sighted tyranny range on,
BRUTUS: Till each man drop by lottery. But if these,
BRUTUS: As I am sure they do, bear fire enough
BRUTUS: To kindle cowards and to steel with valour
BRUTUS: The melting spirits of women, then, countrymen,
BRUTUS: What need we any spur but our own cause,
BRUTUS: To prick us to redress? what other bond
BRUTUS: Than secret Romans, that have spoke the word,
BRUTUS: And will not palter? and what other oath
BRUTUS: Than honesty to honesty engaged,
BRUTUS: That this shall be, or we will fall for it?
BRUTUS: Swear priests and cowards and men cautelous,
BRUTUS: Old feeble carrions and such suffering souls
BRUTUS: That welcome wrongs, unto bad causes swear
BRUTUS: Such creatures as men doubt, but do not stain
BRUTUS: The even virtue of our enterprise,
BRUTUS: Nor the insuppressive mettle of our spirits,
BRUTUS: To think that or our cause or our performance
BRUTUS: Did need an oath, when every drop of blood
BRUTUS: That every Roman bears, and nobly bears,
BRUTUS: Is guilty of a several bastardy,
BRUTUS: If he do break the smallest particle
BRUTUS: Of any promise that hath pass'd from him.
CASSIUS: But what of Cicero? shall we sound him?
CASSIUS: I think he will stand very strong with us.
CASCA: Let us not leave him out.
CINNA: No, by no means.
METELLUS CIMBER: O, let us have him, for his silver hairs
METELLUS CIMBER: Will purchase us a good opinion
METELLUS CIMBER: And buy men's voices to commend our deeds:
METELLUS CIMBER: It shall be said, his judgment ruled our hands,
METELLUS CIMBER: Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear,
METELLUS CIMBER: But all be buried in his gravity.
BRUTUS: O, name him not: let us not break with him,
BRUTUS: For he will never follow any thing
BRUTUS: That other men begin.
CASSIUS: Then leave him out.
CASCA: Indeed he is not fit.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Shall no man else be touch'd but only Caesar?
CASSIUS: Decius, well urged: I think it is not meet,
CASSIUS: Mark Antony, so well beloved of Caesar,
CASSIUS: Should outlive Caesar: we shall find of him
CASSIUS: A shrewd contriver, and, you know, his means,
CASSIUS: If he improve them, may well stretch so far
CASSIUS: As to annoy us all: which to prevent,
CASSIUS: Let Antony and Caesar fall together.
BRUTUS: Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,
BRUTUS: To cut the head off and then hack the limbs,
BRUTUS: Like wrath in death and envy afterwards,
BRUTUS: For Antony is but a limb of Caesar:
BRUTUS: Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.
BRUTUS: We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar,
BRUTUS: And in the spirit of men there is no blood:
BRUTUS: O, that we then could come by Caesar's spirit,
BRUTUS: And not dismember Caesar! But, alas,
BRUTUS: Caesar must bleed for it! And, gentle friends,
BRUTUS: Let's kill him boldly, but not wrathfully,
BRUTUS: Let's carve him as a dish fit for the gods,
BRUTUS: Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds:
BRUTUS: And let our hearts, as subtle masters do,
BRUTUS: Stir up their servants to an act of rage,
BRUTUS: And after seem to chide 'em. This shall make
BRUTUS: Our purpose necessary and not envious:
BRUTUS: Which so appearing to the common eyes,
BRUTUS: We shall be call'd purgers, not murderers.
BRUTUS: And for Mark Antony, think not of him,
BRUTUS: For he can do no more than Caesar's arm
BRUTUS: When Caesar's head is off.
CASSIUS: Yet I fear him,
CASSIUS: For in the ingrafted love he bears to Caesar--
BRUTUS: Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him:
BRUTUS: If he love Caesar, all that he can do
BRUTUS: Is to himself, take thought and die for Caesar:
BRUTUS: And that were much he should, for he is given
BRUTUS: To sports, to wildness and much company.
TREBONIUS: There is no fear in him, let him not die,
TREBONIUS: For he will live, and laugh at this hereafter.
NARRATOR: Clock strikes
BRUTUS: Peace! count the clock.
CASSIUS: The clock hath stricken three.
TREBONIUS: 'Tis time to part.
CASSIUS: But it is doubtful yet,
CASSIUS: Whether Caesar will come forth to-day, or no,
CASSIUS: For he is superstitious grown of late,
CASSIUS: Quite from the main opinion he held once
CASSIUS: Of fantasy, of dreams and ceremonies:
CASSIUS: It may be, these apparent prodigies,
CASSIUS: The unaccustom'd terror of this night,
CASSIUS: And the persuasion of his augurers,
CASSIUS: May hold him from the Capitol to-day.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Never fear that: if he be so resolved,
DECIUS BRUTUS: I can o'ersway him, for he loves to hear
DECIUS BRUTUS: That unicorns may be betray'd with trees,
DECIUS BRUTUS: And bears with glasses, elephants with holes,
DECIUS BRUTUS: Lions with toils and men with flatterers,
DECIUS BRUTUS: But when I tell him he hates flatterers,
DECIUS BRUTUS: He says he does, being then most flattered.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Let me work,
DECIUS BRUTUS: For I can give his humour the true bent,
DECIUS BRUTUS: And I will bring him to the Capitol.
CASSIUS: Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.
BRUTUS: By the eighth hour: is that the uttermost?
CINNA: Be that the uttermost, and fail not then.
METELLUS CIMBER: Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard,
METELLUS CIMBER: Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey:
METELLUS CIMBER: I wonder none of you have thought of him.
BRUTUS: Now, good Metellus, go along by him:
BRUTUS: He loves me well, and I have given him reasons,
BRUTUS: Send him but hither, and I'll fashion him.
CASSIUS: The morning comes upon 's: we'll leave you, Brutus.
CASSIUS: And, friends, disperse yourselves, but all remember
CASSIUS: What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.
BRUTUS: Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily,
BRUTUS: Let not our looks put on our purposes,
BRUTUS: But bear it as our Roman actors do,
BRUTUS: With untired spirits and formal constancy:
BRUTUS: And so good morrow to you every one.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BRUTUS
BRUTUS: Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? It is no matter,
BRUTUS: Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber:
BRUTUS: Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies,
BRUTUS: Which busy care draws in the brains of men,
BRUTUS: Therefore thou sleep'st so sound.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA
PORTIA: Brutus, my lord!
BRUTUS: Portia, what mean you? wherefore rise you now?
BRUTUS: It is not for your health thus to commit
BRUTUS: Your weak condition to the raw cold morning.
PORTIA: Nor for yours neither. You've ungently, Brutus,
PORTIA: Stole from my bed: and yesternight, at supper,
PORTIA: You suddenly arose, and walk'd about,
PORTIA: Musing and sighing, with your arms across,
PORTIA: And when I ask'd you what the matter was,
PORTIA: You stared upon me with ungentle looks,
PORTIA: I urged you further, then you scratch'd your head,
PORTIA: And too impatiently stamp'd with your foot,
PORTIA: Yet I insisted, yet you answer'd not,
PORTIA: But, with an angry wafture of your hand,
PORTIA: Gave sign for me to leave you: so I did,
PORTIA: Fearing to strengthen that impatience
PORTIA: Which seem'd too much enkindled, and withal
PORTIA: Hoping it was but an effect of humour,
PORTIA: Which sometime hath his hour with every man.
PORTIA: It will not let you eat, nor talk, nor sleep,
PORTIA: And could it work so much upon your shape
PORTIA: As it hath much prevail'd on your condition,
PORTIA: I should not know you, Brutus. Dear my lord,
PORTIA: Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.
BRUTUS: I am not well in health, and that is all.
PORTIA: Brutus is wise, and, were he not in health,
PORTIA: He would embrace the means to come by it.
BRUTUS: Why, so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.
PORTIA: Is Brutus sick? and is it physical
PORTIA: To walk unbraced and suck up the humours
PORTIA: Of the dank morning? What, is Brutus sick,
PORTIA: And will he steal out of his wholesome bed,
PORTIA: To dare the vile contagion of the night
PORTIA: And tempt the rheumy and unpurged air
PORTIA: To add unto his sickness? No, my Brutus,
PORTIA: You have some sick offence within your mind,
PORTIA: Which, by the right and virtue of my place,
PORTIA: I ought to know of: and, upon my knees,
PORTIA: I charm you, by my once-commended beauty,
PORTIA: By all your vows of love and that great vow
PORTIA: Which did incorporate and make us one,
PORTIA: That you unfold to me, yourself, your half,
PORTIA: Why you are heavy, and what men to-night
PORTIA: Have had to resort to you: for here have been
PORTIA: Some six or seven, who did hide their faces
PORTIA: Even from darkness.
BRUTUS: Kneel not, gentle Portia.
PORTIA: I should not need, if you were gentle Brutus.
PORTIA: Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus,
PORTIA: Is it excepted I should know no secrets
PORTIA: That appertain to you? Am I yourself
PORTIA: But, as it were, in sort or limitation,
PORTIA: To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed,
PORTIA: And talk to you sometimes? Dwell I but in the suburbs
PORTIA: Of your good pleasure? If it be no more,
PORTIA: Portia is Brutus' harlot, not his wife.
BRUTUS: You are my true and honourable wife,
BRUTUS: As dear to me as are the ruddy drops
BRUTUS: That visit my sad heart
PORTIA: If this were true, then should I know this secret.
PORTIA: I grant I am a woman, but withal
PORTIA: A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife:
PORTIA: I grant I am a woman, but withal
PORTIA: A woman well-reputed, Cato's daughter.
PORTIA: Think you I am no stronger than my sex,
PORTIA: Being so father'd and so husbanded?
PORTIA: Tell me your counsels, I will not disclose 'em:
PORTIA: I have made strong proof of my constancy,
PORTIA: Giving myself a voluntary wound
PORTIA: Here, in the thigh: can I bear that with patience.
PORTIA: And not my husband's secrets?
BRUTUS: O ye gods,
BRUTUS: Render me worthy of this noble wife!
NARRATOR: Knocking within
BRUTUS: Hark, hark! one knocks: Portia, go in awhile,
BRUTUS: And by and by thy bosom shall partake
BRUTUS: The secrets of my heart.
BRUTUS: All my engagements I will construe to thee,
BRUTUS: All the charactery of my sad brows:
BRUTUS: Leave me with haste.
NARRATOR: Exit PORTIA
BRUTUS: Lucius, who's that knocks?
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS with LIGARIUS
LUCIUS: He is a sick man that would speak with you.
BRUTUS: Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spake of.
BRUTUS: Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius! how?
LIGARIUS: Vouchsafe good morrow from a feeble tongue.
BRUTUS: O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius,
BRUTUS: To wear a kerchief! Would you were not sick!
LIGARIUS: I am not sick, if Brutus have in hand
LIGARIUS: Any exploit worthy the name of honour.
BRUTUS: Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius,
BRUTUS: Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.
LIGARIUS: By all the gods that Romans bow before,
LIGARIUS: I here discard my sickness! Soul of Rome!
LIGARIUS: Brave son, derived from honourable loins!
LIGARIUS: Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjured up
LIGARIUS: My mortified spirit. Now bid me run,
LIGARIUS: And I will strive with things impossible,
LIGARIUS: Yea, get the better of them. What's to do?
BRUTUS: A piece of work that will make sick men whole.
LIGARIUS: But are not some whole that we must make sick?
BRUTUS: That must we also. What it is, my Caius,
BRUTUS: I shall unfold to thee, as we are going
BRUTUS: To whom it must be done.
LIGARIUS: Set on your foot,
LIGARIUS: And with a heart new-fired I follow you,
LIGARIUS: To do I know not what: but it sufficeth
LIGARIUS: That Brutus leads me on.
BRUTUS: Follow me, then.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. CAESAR's house.
NARRATOR: Thunder and lightning. Enter CAESAR, in his night-gown
CAESAR: Nor heaven nor earth have been at peace to-night:
CAESAR: Thrice hath Calpurnia in her sleep cried out,
CAESAR: 'Help, ho! they murder Caesar!' Who's within?
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: My lord?
CAESAR: Go bid the priests do present sacrifice
CAESAR: And bring me their opinions of success.
Servant: I will, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter CALPURNIA
CALPURNIA: What mean you, Caesar? think you to walk forth?
CALPURNIA: You shall not stir out of your house to-day.
CAESAR: Caesar shall forth: the things that threaten'd me
CAESAR: Ne'er look'd but on my back, when they shall see
CAESAR: The face of Caesar, they are vanished.
CALPURNIA: Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies,
CALPURNIA: Yet now they fright me. There is one within,
CALPURNIA: Besides the things that we have heard and seen,
CALPURNIA: Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch.
CALPURNIA: A lioness hath whelped in the streets,
CALPURNIA: And graves have yawn'd, and yielded up their dead,
CALPURNIA: Fierce fiery warriors fought upon the clouds,
CALPURNIA: In ranks and squadrons and right form of war,
CALPURNIA: Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol,
CALPURNIA: The noise of battle hurtled in the air,
CALPURNIA: Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan,
CALPURNIA: And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets.
CALPURNIA: O Caesar! these things are beyond all use,
CALPURNIA: And I do fear them.
CAESAR: What can be avoided
CAESAR: Whose end is purposed by the mighty gods?
CAESAR: Yet Caesar shall go forth, for these predictions
CAESAR: Are to the world in general as to Caesar.
CALPURNIA: When beggars die, there are no comets seen,
CALPURNIA: The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.
CAESAR: Cowards die many times before their deaths,
CAESAR: The valiant never taste of death but once.
CAESAR: Of all the wonders that I yet have heard.
CAESAR: It seems to me most strange that men should fear,
CAESAR: Seeing that death, a necessary end,
CAESAR: Will come when it will come.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servant
CAESAR: What say the augurers?
Servant: They would not have you to stir forth to-day.
Servant: Plucking the entrails of an offering forth,
Servant: They could not find a heart within the beast.
CAESAR: The gods do this in shame of cowardice:
CAESAR: Caesar should be a beast without a heart,
CAESAR: If he should stay at home to-day for fear.
CAESAR: No, Caesar shall not: danger knows full well
CAESAR: That Caesar is more dangerous than he:
CAESAR: We are two lions litter'd in one day,
CAESAR: And I the elder and more terrible:
CAESAR: And Caesar shall go forth.
CALPURNIA: Alas, my lord,
CALPURNIA: Your wisdom is consumed in confidence.
CALPURNIA: Do not go forth to-day: call it my fear
CALPURNIA: That keeps you in the house, and not your own.
CALPURNIA: We'll send Mark Antony to the senate-house:
CALPURNIA: And he shall say you are not well to-day:
CALPURNIA: Let me, upon my knee, prevail in this.
CAESAR: Mark Antony shall say I am not well,
CAESAR: And, for thy humour, I will stay at home.
NARRATOR: Enter DECIUS BRUTUS
CAESAR: Here's Decius Brutus, he shall tell them so.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Caesar, all hail! good morrow, worthy Caesar:
DECIUS BRUTUS: I come to fetch you to the senate-house.
CAESAR: And you are come in very happy time,
CAESAR: To bear my greeting to the senators
CAESAR: And tell them that I will not come to-day:
CAESAR: Cannot, is false, and that I dare not, falser:
CAESAR: I will not come to-day: tell them so, Decius.
CALPURNIA: Say he is sick.
CAESAR: Shall Caesar send a lie?
CAESAR: Have I in conquest stretch'd mine arm so far,
CAESAR: To be afraid to tell graybeards the truth?
CAESAR: Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause,
DECIUS BRUTUS: Lest I be laugh'd at when I tell them so.
CAESAR: The cause is in my will: I will not come,
CAESAR: That is enough to satisfy the senate.
CAESAR: But for your private satisfaction,
CAESAR: Because I love you, I will let you know:
CAESAR: Calpurnia here, my wife, stays me at home:
CAESAR: She dreamt to-night she saw my statua,
CAESAR: Which, like a fountain with an hundred spouts,
CAESAR: Did run pure blood: and many lusty Romans
CAESAR: Came smiling, and did bathe their hands in it:
CAESAR: And these does she apply for warnings, and portents,
CAESAR: And evils imminent, and on her knee
CAESAR: Hath begg'd that I will stay at home to-day.
DECIUS BRUTUS: This dream is all amiss interpreted,
DECIUS BRUTUS: It was a vision fair and fortunate:
DECIUS BRUTUS: Your statue spouting blood in many pipes,
DECIUS BRUTUS: In which so many smiling Romans bathed,
DECIUS BRUTUS: Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck
DECIUS BRUTUS: Reviving blood, and that great men shall press
DECIUS BRUTUS: For tinctures, stains, relics and cognizance.
DECIUS BRUTUS: This by Calpurnia's dream is signified.
CAESAR: And this way have you well expounded it.
DECIUS BRUTUS: I have, when you have heard what I can say:
DECIUS BRUTUS: And know it now: the senate have concluded
DECIUS BRUTUS: To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar.
DECIUS BRUTUS: If you shall send them word you will not come,
DECIUS BRUTUS: Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock
DECIUS BRUTUS: Apt to be render'd, for some one to say
DECIUS BRUTUS: 'Break up the senate till another time,
DECIUS BRUTUS: When Caesar's wife shall meet with better dreams.'
DECIUS BRUTUS: If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper
DECIUS BRUTUS: 'Lo, Caesar is afraid'?
DECIUS BRUTUS: Pardon me, Caesar, for my dear dear love
DECIUS BRUTUS: To our proceeding bids me tell you this,
DECIUS BRUTUS: And reason to my love is liable.
CAESAR: How foolish do your fears seem now, Calpurnia!
CAESAR: I am ashamed I did yield to them.
CAESAR: Give me my robe, for I will go.
NARRATOR: Enter PUBLIUS, BRUTUS, LIGARIUS, METELLUS, CASCA, TREBONIUS, and CINNA
CAESAR: And look where Publius is come to fetch me.
PUBLIUS: Good morrow, Caesar.
CAESAR: Welcome, Publius.
CAESAR: What, Brutus, are you stirr'd so early too?
CAESAR: Good morrow, Casca. Caius Ligarius,
CAESAR: Caesar was ne'er so much your enemy
CAESAR: As that same ague which hath made you lean.
CAESAR: What is 't o'clock?
BRUTUS: Caesar, 'tis strucken eight.
CAESAR: I thank you for your pains and courtesy.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONY
CAESAR: See! Antony, that revels long o' nights,
CAESAR: Is notwithstanding up. Good morrow, Antony.
ANTONY: So to most noble Caesar.
CAESAR: Bid them prepare within:
CAESAR: I am to blame to be thus waited for.
CAESAR: Now, Cinna: now, Metellus: what, Trebonius!
CAESAR: I have an hour's talk in store for you,
CAESAR: Remember that you call on me to-day:
CAESAR: Be near me, that I may remember you.
TREBONIUS: Caesar, I will:
NARRATOR: Aside
TREBONIUS: and so near will I be,
TREBONIUS: That your best friends shall wish I had been further.
CAESAR: Good friends, go in, and taste some wine with me,
CAESAR: And we, like friends, will straightway go together.
BRUTUS: [Aside]  That every like is not the same, O Caesar,
BRUTUS: The heart of Brutus yearns to think upon!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A street near the Capitol.
NARRATOR: Enter ARTEMIDORUS, reading a paper
ARTEMIDORUS: 'Caesar, beware of Brutus, take heed of Cassius,
ARTEMIDORUS: come not near Casca, have an eye to Cinna, trust not
ARTEMIDORUS: Trebonius: mark well Metellus Cimber: Decius Brutus
ARTEMIDORUS: loves thee not: thou hast wronged Caius Ligarius.
ARTEMIDORUS: There is but one mind in all these men, and it is
ARTEMIDORUS: bent against Caesar. If thou beest not immortal,
ARTEMIDORUS: look about you: security gives way to conspiracy.
ARTEMIDORUS: The mighty gods defend thee! Thy lover,
ARTEMIDORUS: 'ARTEMIDORUS.'
ARTEMIDORUS: Here will I stand till Caesar pass along,
ARTEMIDORUS: And as a suitor will I give him this.
ARTEMIDORUS: My heart laments that virtue cannot live
ARTEMIDORUS: Out of the teeth of emulation.
ARTEMIDORUS: If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayst live,
ARTEMIDORUS: If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the same street, before the house of BRUTUS.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA and LUCIUS
PORTIA: I prithee, boy, run to the senate-house,
PORTIA: Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone:
PORTIA: Why dost thou stay?
LUCIUS: To know my errand, madam.
PORTIA: I would have had thee there, and here again,
PORTIA: Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there.
PORTIA: O constancy, be strong upon my side,
PORTIA: Set a huge mountain 'tween my heart and tongue!
PORTIA: I have a man's mind, but a woman's might.
PORTIA: How hard it is for women to keep counsel!
PORTIA: Art thou here yet?
LUCIUS: Madam, what should I do?
LUCIUS: Run to the Capitol, and nothing else?
LUCIUS: And so return to you, and nothing else?
PORTIA: Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well,
PORTIA: For he went sickly forth: and take good note
PORTIA: What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him.
PORTIA: Hark, boy! what noise is that?
LUCIUS: I hear none, madam.
PORTIA: Prithee, listen well,
PORTIA: I heard a bustling rumour, like a fray,
PORTIA: And the wind brings it from the Capitol.
LUCIUS: Sooth, madam, I hear nothing.
NARRATOR: Enter the Soothsayer
PORTIA: Come hither, fellow: which way hast thou been?
Soothsayer: At mine own house, good lady.
PORTIA: What is't o'clock?
Soothsayer: About the ninth hour, lady.
PORTIA: Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?
Soothsayer: Madam, not yet: I go to take my stand,
Soothsayer: To see him pass on to the Capitol.
PORTIA: Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?
Soothsayer: That I have, lady: if it will please Caesar
Soothsayer: To be so good to Caesar as to hear me,
Soothsayer: I shall beseech him to befriend himself.
PORTIA: Why, know'st thou any harm's intended towards him?
Soothsayer: None that I know will be, much that I fear may chance.
Soothsayer: Good morrow to you. Here the street is narrow:
Soothsayer: The throng that follows Caesar at the heels,
Soothsayer: Of senators, of praetors, common suitors,
Soothsayer: Will crowd a feeble man almost to death:
Soothsayer: I'll get me to a place more void, and there
Soothsayer: Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.
NARRATOR: Exit
PORTIA: I must go in. Ay me, how weak a thing
PORTIA: The heart of woman is! O Brutus,
PORTIA: The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise!
PORTIA: Sure, the boy heard me: Brutus hath a suit
PORTIA: That Caesar will not grant. O, I grow faint.
PORTIA: Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord,
PORTIA: Say I am merry: come to me again,
PORTIA: And bring me word what he doth say to thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. Before the Capitol, the Senate sitting above.
NARRATOR: A crowd of people, among them ARTEMIDORUS and the  Soothsayer. Flourish. Enter CAESAR, BRUTUS,  CASSIUS, CASCA, DECIUS BRUTUS, METELLUS CIMBER,  TREBONIUS, CINNA, ANTONY, LEPIDUS, POPILIUS, PUBLIUS, and others
CAESAR: [To the Soothsayer]  The ides of March are come.
Soothsayer: Ay, Caesar, but not gone.
ARTEMIDORUS: Hail, Caesar! read this schedule.
DECIUS BRUTUS: Trebonius doth desire you to o'erread,
DECIUS BRUTUS: At your best leisure, this his humble suit.
ARTEMIDORUS: O Caesar, read mine first, for mine's a suit
ARTEMIDORUS: That touches Caesar nearer: read it, great Caesar.
CAESAR: What touches us ourself shall be last served.
ARTEMIDORUS: Delay not, Caesar, read it instantly.
CAESAR: What, is the fellow mad?
PUBLIUS: Sirrah, give place.
CASSIUS: What, urge you your petitions in the street?
CASSIUS: Come to the Capitol.
NARRATOR: CAESAR goes up to the Senate-House, the rest following
POPILIUS: I wish your enterprise to-day may thrive.
CASSIUS: What enterprise, Popilius?
POPILIUS: Fare you well.
NARRATOR: Advances to CAESAR
BRUTUS: What said Popilius Lena?
CASSIUS: He wish'd to-day our enterprise might thrive.
CASSIUS: I fear our purpose is discovered.
BRUTUS: Look, how he makes to Caesar, mark him.
CASSIUS: Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention.
CASSIUS: Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known,
CASSIUS: Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back,
CASSIUS: For I will slay myself.
BRUTUS: Cassius, be constant:
BRUTUS: Popilius Lena speaks not of our purposes,
BRUTUS: For, look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.
CASSIUS: Trebonius knows his time, for, look you, Brutus.
CASSIUS: He draws Mark Antony out of the way.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ANTONY and TREBONIUS
DECIUS BRUTUS: Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go,
DECIUS BRUTUS: And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.
BRUTUS: He is address'd: press near and second him.
CINNA: Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.
CAESAR: Are we all ready? What is now amiss
CAESAR: That Caesar and his senate must redress?
METELLUS CIMBER: Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar,
METELLUS CIMBER: Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat
METELLUS CIMBER: An humble heart,--
NARRATOR: Kneeling
CAESAR: I must prevent thee, Cimber.
CAESAR: These couchings and these lowly courtesies
CAESAR: Might fire the blood of ordinary men,
CAESAR: And turn pre-ordinance and first decree
CAESAR: Into the law of children. Be not fond,
CAESAR: To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood
CAESAR: That will be thaw'd from the true quality
CAESAR: With that which melteth fools, I mean, sweet words,
CAESAR: Low-crooked court'sies and base spaniel-fawning.
CAESAR: Thy brother by decree is banished:
CAESAR: If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him,
CAESAR: I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.
CAESAR: Know, Caesar doth not wrong, nor without cause
CAESAR: Will he be satisfied.
METELLUS CIMBER: Is there no voice more worthy than my own
METELLUS CIMBER: To sound more sweetly in great Caesar's ear
METELLUS CIMBER: For the repealing of my banish'd brother?
BRUTUS: I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery, Caesar,
BRUTUS: Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may
BRUTUS: Have an immediate freedom of repeal.
CAESAR: What, Brutus!
CASSIUS: Pardon, Caesar, Caesar, pardon:
CASSIUS: As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall,
CASSIUS: To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.
CASSIUS: I could be well moved, if I were as you:
CASSIUS: If I could pray to move, prayers would move me:
CASSIUS: But I am constant as the northern star,
CASSIUS: Of whose true-fix'd and resting quality
CASSIUS: There is no fellow in the firmament.
CASSIUS: The skies are painted with unnumber'd sparks,
CASSIUS: They are all fire and every one doth shine,
CASSIUS: But there's but one in all doth hold his place:
CASSIUS: So in the world, 'tis furnish'd well with men,
CASSIUS: And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive,
CASSIUS: Yet in the number I do know but one
CASSIUS: That unassailable holds on his rank,
CASSIUS: Unshaked of motion: and that I am he,
CASSIUS: Let me a little show it, even in this,
CASSIUS: That I was constant Cimber should be banish'd,
CASSIUS: And constant do remain to keep him so.
CINNA: O Caesar,--
CAESAR: Hence! wilt thou lift up Olympus?
DECIUS BRUTUS: Great Caesar,--
CAESAR: Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?
CASCA: Speak, hands for me!
NARRATOR: CASCA first, then the other Conspirators and BRUTUS stab CAESAR
CAESAR: Et tu, Brute! Then fall, Caesar.
NARRATOR: Dies
CINNA: Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead!
CINNA: Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.
CASSIUS: Some to the common pulpits, and cry out
CASSIUS: 'Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!'
BRUTUS: People and senators, be not affrighted,
BRUTUS: Fly not, stand stiff: ambition's debt is paid.
CASCA: Go to the pulpit, Brutus.
DECIUS BRUTUS: And Cassius too.
BRUTUS: Where's Publius?
CINNA: Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.
METELLUS CIMBER: Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar's
METELLUS CIMBER: Should chance--
BRUTUS: Talk not of standing. Publius, good cheer,
BRUTUS: There is no harm intended to your person,
BRUTUS: Nor to no Roman else: so tell them, Publius.
CASSIUS: And leave us, Publius, lest that the people,
CASSIUS: Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.
BRUTUS: Do so: and let no man abide this deed,
BRUTUS: But we the doers.
NARRATOR: Re-enter TREBONIUS
CASSIUS: Where is Antony?
TREBONIUS: Fled to his house amazed:
TREBONIUS: Men, wives and children stare, cry out and run
TREBONIUS: As it were doomsday.
BRUTUS: Fates, we will know your pleasures:
BRUTUS: That we shall die, we know, 'tis but the time
BRUTUS: And drawing days out, that men stand upon.
CASSIUS: Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life
CASSIUS: Cuts off so many years of fearing death.
BRUTUS: Grant that, and then is death a benefit:
BRUTUS: So are we Caesar's friends, that have abridged
BRUTUS: His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop,
BRUTUS: And let us bathe our hands in Caesar's blood
BRUTUS: Up to the elbows, and besmear our swords:
BRUTUS: Then walk we forth, even to the market-place,
BRUTUS: And, waving our red weapons o'er our heads,
BRUTUS: Let's all cry 'Peace, freedom and liberty!'
CASSIUS: Stoop, then, and wash. How many ages hence
CASSIUS: Shall this our lofty scene be acted over
CASSIUS: In states unborn and accents yet unknown!
BRUTUS: How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport,
BRUTUS: That now on Pompey's basis lies along
BRUTUS: No worthier than the dust!
CASSIUS: So oft as that shall be,
CASSIUS: So often shall the knot of us be call'd
CASSIUS: The men that gave their country liberty.
DECIUS BRUTUS: What, shall we forth?
CASSIUS: Ay, every man away:
CASSIUS: Brutus shall lead, and we will grace his heels
CASSIUS: With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
BRUTUS: Soft! who comes here? A friend of Antony's.
Servant: Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel:
Servant: Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall down,
Servant: And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say:
Servant: Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest,
Servant: Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving:
Servant: Say I love Brutus, and I honour him,
Servant: Say I fear'd Caesar, honour'd him and loved him.
Servant: If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony
Servant: May safely come to him, and be resolved
Servant: How Caesar hath deserved to lie in death,
Servant: Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead
Servant: So well as Brutus living, but will follow
Servant: The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus
Servant: Thorough the hazards of this untrod state
Servant: With all true faith. So says my master Antony.
BRUTUS: Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman,
BRUTUS: I never thought him worse.
BRUTUS: Tell him, so please him come unto this place,
BRUTUS: He shall be satisfied, and, by my honour,
BRUTUS: Depart untouch'd.
Servant: I'll fetch him presently.
NARRATOR: Exit
BRUTUS: I know that we shall have him well to friend.
CASSIUS: I wish we may: but yet have I a mind
CASSIUS: That fears him much, and my misgiving still
CASSIUS: Falls shrewdly to the purpose.
BRUTUS: But here comes Antony.
NARRATOR: Re-enter ANTONY
BRUTUS: Welcome, Mark Antony.
ANTONY: O mighty Caesar! dost thou lie so low?
ANTONY: Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils,
ANTONY: Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well.
ANTONY: I know not, gentlemen, what you intend,
ANTONY: Who else must be let blood, who else is rank:
ANTONY: If I myself, there is no hour so fit
ANTONY: As Caesar's death hour, nor no instrument
ANTONY: Of half that worth as those your swords, made rich
ANTONY: With the most noble blood of all this world.
ANTONY: I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard,
ANTONY: Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke,
ANTONY: Fulfil your pleasure. Live a thousand years,
ANTONY: I shall not find myself so apt to die:
ANTONY: No place will please me so, no mean of death,
ANTONY: As here by Caesar, and by you cut off,
ANTONY: The choice and master spirits of this age.
BRUTUS: O Antony, beg not your death of us.
BRUTUS: Though now we must appear bloody and cruel,
BRUTUS: As, by our hands and this our present act,
BRUTUS: You see we do, yet see you but our hands
BRUTUS: And this the bleeding business they have done:
BRUTUS: Our hearts you see not, they are pitiful,
BRUTUS: And pity to the general wrong of Rome--
BRUTUS: As fire drives out fire, so pity pity--
BRUTUS: Hath done this deed on Caesar. For your part,
BRUTUS: To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony:
BRUTUS: Our arms, in strength of malice, and our hearts
BRUTUS: Of brothers' temper, do receive you in
BRUTUS: With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.
CASSIUS: Your voice shall be as strong as any man's
CASSIUS: In the disposing of new dignities.
BRUTUS: Only be patient till we have appeased
BRUTUS: The multitude, beside themselves with fear,
BRUTUS: And then we will deliver you the cause,
BRUTUS: Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him,
BRUTUS: Have thus proceeded.
ANTONY: I doubt not of your wisdom.
ANTONY: Let each man render me his bloody hand:
ANTONY: First, Marcus Brutus, will I shake with you,
ANTONY: Next, Caius Cassius, do I take your hand,
ANTONY: Now, Decius Brutus, yours: now yours, Metellus,
ANTONY: Yours, Cinna, and, my valiant Casca, yours,
ANTONY: Though last, not last in love, yours, good Trebonius.
ANTONY: Gentlemen all,--alas, what shall I say?
ANTONY: My credit now stands on such slippery ground,
ANTONY: That one of two bad ways you must conceit me,
ANTONY: Either a coward or a flatterer.
ANTONY: That I did love thee, Caesar, O, 'tis true:
ANTONY: If then thy spirit look upon us now,
ANTONY: Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death,
ANTONY: To see thy thy Anthony making his peace,
ANTONY: Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes,
ANTONY: Most noble! in the presence of thy corse?
ANTONY: Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds,
ANTONY: Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood,
ANTONY: It would become me better than to close
ANTONY: In terms of friendship with thine enemies.
ANTONY: Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bay'd, brave hart,
ANTONY: Here didst thou fall, and here thy hunters stand,
ANTONY: Sign'd in thy spoil, and crimson'd in thy lethe.
ANTONY: O world, thou wast the forest to this hart,
ANTONY: And this, indeed, O world, the heart of thee.
ANTONY: How like a deer, strucken by many princes,
ANTONY: Dost thou here lie!
CASSIUS: Mark Antony,--
ANTONY: Pardon me, Caius Cassius:
ANTONY: The enemies of Caesar shall say this,
ANTONY: Then, in a friend, it is cold modesty.
CASSIUS: I blame you not for praising Caesar so,
CASSIUS: But what compact mean you to have with us?
CASSIUS: Will you be prick'd in number of our friends,
CASSIUS: Or shall we on, and not depend on you?
ANTONY: Therefore I took your hands, but was, indeed,
ANTONY: Sway'd from the point, by looking down on Caesar.
ANTONY: Friends am I with you all and love you all,
ANTONY: Upon this hope, that you shall give me reasons
ANTONY: Why and wherein Caesar was dangerous.
BRUTUS: Or else were this a savage spectacle:
BRUTUS: Our reasons are so full of good regard
BRUTUS: That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar,
BRUTUS: You should be satisfied.
ANTONY: That's all I seek:
ANTONY: And am moreover suitor that I may
ANTONY: Produce his body to the market-place,
ANTONY: And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend,
ANTONY: Speak in the order of his funeral.
BRUTUS: You shall, Mark Antony.
CASSIUS: Brutus, a word with you.
NARRATOR: Aside to BRUTUS
CASSIUS: You know not what you do: do not consent
CASSIUS: That Antony speak in his funeral:
CASSIUS: Know you how much the people may be moved
CASSIUS: By that which he will utter?
BRUTUS: By your pardon,
BRUTUS: I will myself into the pulpit first,
BRUTUS: And show the reason of our Caesar's death:
BRUTUS: What Antony shall speak, I will protest
BRUTUS: He speaks by leave and by permission,
BRUTUS: And that we are contented Caesar shall
BRUTUS: Have all true rites and lawful ceremonies.
BRUTUS: It shall advantage more than do us wrong.
CASSIUS: I know not what may fall, I like it not.
BRUTUS: Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar's body.
BRUTUS: You shall not in your funeral speech blame us,
BRUTUS: But speak all good you can devise of Caesar,
BRUTUS: And say you do't by our permission,
BRUTUS: Else shall you not have any hand at all
BRUTUS: About his funeral: and you shall speak
BRUTUS: In the same pulpit whereto I am going,
BRUTUS: After my speech is ended.
ANTONY: Be it so.
ANTONY: I do desire no more.
BRUTUS: Prepare the body then, and follow us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but ANTONY
ANTONY: O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth,
ANTONY: That I am meek and gentle with these butchers!
ANTONY: Thou art the ruins of the noblest man
ANTONY: That ever lived in the tide of times.
ANTONY: Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood!
ANTONY: Over thy wounds now do I prophesy,--
ANTONY: Which, like dumb mouths, do ope their ruby lips,
ANTONY: To beg the voice and utterance of my tongue--
ANTONY: A curse shall light upon the limbs of men,
ANTONY: Domestic fury and fierce civil strife
ANTONY: Shall cumber all the parts of Italy,
ANTONY: Blood and destruction shall be so in use
ANTONY: And dreadful objects so familiar
ANTONY: That mothers shall but smile when they behold
ANTONY: Their infants quarter'd with the hands of war,
ANTONY: All pity choked with custom of fell deeds:
ANTONY: And Caesar's spirit, ranging for revenge,
ANTONY: With Ate by his side come hot from hell,
ANTONY: Shall in these confines with a monarch's voice
ANTONY: Cry  'Havoc,' and let slip the dogs of war,
ANTONY: That this foul deed shall smell above the earth
ANTONY: With carrion men, groaning for burial.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
ANTONY: You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?
Servant: I do, Mark Antony.
ANTONY: Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.
Servant: He did receive his letters, and is coming,
Servant: And bid me say to you by word of mouth--
Servant: O Caesar!--
NARRATOR: Seeing the body
ANTONY: Thy heart is big, get thee apart and weep.
ANTONY: Passion, I see, is catching, for mine eyes,
ANTONY: Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine,
ANTONY: Began to water. Is thy master coming?
Servant: He lies to-night within seven leagues of Rome.
ANTONY: Post back with speed, and tell him what hath chanced:
ANTONY: Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome,
ANTONY: No Rome of safety for Octavius yet,
ANTONY: Hie hence, and tell him so. Yet, stay awhile,
ANTONY: Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corse
ANTONY: Into the market-place: there shall I try
ANTONY: In my oration, how the people take
ANTONY: The cruel issue of these bloody men,
ANTONY: According to the which, thou shalt discourse
ANTONY: To young Octavius of the state of things.
ANTONY: Lend me your hand.
NARRATOR: Exeunt with CAESAR's body
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The Forum.
NARRATOR: Enter BRUTUS and CASSIUS, and a throng of Citizens
Citizens: We will be satisfied, let us be satisfied.
BRUTUS: Then follow me, and give me audience, friends.
BRUTUS: Cassius, go you into the other street,
BRUTUS: And part the numbers.
BRUTUS: Those that will hear me speak, let 'em stay here,
BRUTUS: Those that will follow Cassius, go with him,
BRUTUS: And public reasons shall be rendered
BRUTUS: Of Caesar's death.
First Citizen: I will hear Brutus speak.
Second Citizen: I will hear Cassius, and compare their reasons,
Second Citizen: When severally we hear them rendered.
NARRATOR: Exit CASSIUS, with some of the Citizens. BRUTUS goes into the pulpit
Third Citizen: The noble Brutus is ascended: silence!
BRUTUS: Be patient till the last.
BRUTUS: Romans, countrymen, and lovers! hear me for my
BRUTUS: cause, and be silent, that you may hear: believe me
BRUTUS: for mine honour, and have respect to mine honour, that
BRUTUS: you may believe: censure me in your wisdom, and
BRUTUS: awake your senses, that you may the better judge.
BRUTUS: If there be any in this assembly, any dear friend of
BRUTUS: Caesar's, to him I say, that Brutus' love to Caesar
BRUTUS: was no less than his. If then that friend demand
BRUTUS: why Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my answer:
BRUTUS: --Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved
BRUTUS: Rome more. Had you rather Caesar were living and
BRUTUS: die all slaves, than that Caesar were dead, to live
BRUTUS: all free men? As Caesar loved me, I weep for him,
BRUTUS: as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it, as he was
BRUTUS: valiant, I honour him: but, as he was ambitious, I
BRUTUS: slew him. There is tears for his love, joy for his
BRUTUS: fortune, honour for his valour, and death for his
BRUTUS: ambition. Who is here so base that would be a
BRUTUS: bondman? If any, speak, for him have I offended.
BRUTUS: Who is here so rude that would not be a Roman? If
BRUTUS: any, speak, for him have I offended. Who is here so
BRUTUS: vile that will not love his country? If any, speak,
BRUTUS: for him have I offended. I pause for a reply.
All: None, Brutus, none.
BRUTUS: Then none have I offended. I have done no more to
BRUTUS: Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The question of
BRUTUS: his death is enrolled in the Capitol, his glory not
BRUTUS: extenuated, wherein he was worthy, nor his offences
BRUTUS: enforced, for which he suffered death.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONY and others, with CAESAR's body
BRUTUS: Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony: who,
BRUTUS: though he had no hand in his death, shall receive
BRUTUS: the benefit of his dying, a place in the
BRUTUS: commonwealth, as which of you shall not? With this
BRUTUS: I depart,--that, as I slew my best lover for the
BRUTUS: good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself,
BRUTUS: when it shall please my country to need my death.
All: Live, Brutus! live, live!
First Citizen: Bring him with triumph home unto his house.
Second Citizen: Give him a statue with his ancestors.
Third Citizen: Let him be Caesar.
Fourth Citizen: Caesar's better parts
Fourth Citizen: Shall be crown'd in Brutus.
First Citizen: We'll bring him to his house
First Citizen: With shouts and clamours.
BRUTUS: My countrymen,--
Second Citizen: Peace, silence! Brutus speaks.
First Citizen: Peace, ho!
BRUTUS: Good countrymen, let me depart alone,
BRUTUS: And, for my sake, stay here with Antony:
BRUTUS: Do grace to Caesar's corpse, and grace his speech
BRUTUS: Tending to Caesar's glories, which Mark Antony,
BRUTUS: By our permission, is allow'd to make.
BRUTUS: I do entreat you, not a man depart,
BRUTUS: Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Citizen: Stay, ho! and let us hear Mark Antony.
Third Citizen: Let him go up into the public chair,
Third Citizen: We'll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.
ANTONY: For Brutus' sake, I am beholding to you.
NARRATOR: Goes into the pulpit
Fourth Citizen: What does he say of Brutus?
Third Citizen: He says, for Brutus' sake,
Third Citizen: He finds himself beholding to us all.
Fourth Citizen: 'Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here.
First Citizen: This Caesar was a tyrant.
Third Citizen: Nay, that's certain:
Third Citizen: We are blest that Rome is rid of him.
Second Citizen: Peace! let us hear what Antony can say.
ANTONY: You gentle Romans,--
Citizens: Peace, ho! let us hear him.
ANTONY: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears,
ANTONY: I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.
ANTONY: The evil that men do lives after them,
ANTONY: The good is oft interred with their bones,
ANTONY: So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus
ANTONY: Hath told you Caesar was ambitious:
ANTONY: If it were so, it was a grievous fault,
ANTONY: And grievously hath Caesar answer'd it.
ANTONY: Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest--
ANTONY: For Brutus is an honourable man,
ANTONY: So are they all, all honourable men--
ANTONY: Come I to speak in Caesar's funeral.
ANTONY: He was my friend, faithful and just to me:
ANTONY: But Brutus says he was ambitious,
ANTONY: And Brutus is an honourable man.
ANTONY: He hath brought many captives home to Rome
ANTONY: Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill:
ANTONY: Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?
ANTONY: When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept:
ANTONY: Ambition should be made of sterner stuff:
ANTONY: Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,
ANTONY: And Brutus is an honourable man.
ANTONY: You all did see that on the Lupercal
ANTONY: I thrice presented him a kingly crown,
ANTONY: Which he did thrice refuse: was this ambition?
ANTONY: Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,
ANTONY: And, sure, he is an honourable man.
ANTONY: I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke,
ANTONY: But here I am to speak what I do know.
ANTONY: You all did love him once, not without cause:
ANTONY: What cause withholds you then, to mourn for him?
ANTONY: O judgment! thou art fled to brutish beasts,
ANTONY: And men have lost their reason. Bear with me,
ANTONY: My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,
ANTONY: And I must pause till it come back to me.
First Citizen: Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.
Second Citizen: If thou consider rightly of the matter,
Second Citizen: Caesar has had great wrong.
Third Citizen: Has he, masters?
Third Citizen: I fear there will a worse come in his place.
Fourth Citizen: Mark'd ye his words? He would not take the crown,
Fourth Citizen: Therefore 'tis certain he was not ambitious.
First Citizen: If it be found so, some will dear abide it.
Second Citizen: Poor soul! his eyes are red as fire with weeping.
Third Citizen: There's not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.
Fourth Citizen: Now mark him, he begins again to speak.
ANTONY: But yesterday the word of Caesar might
ANTONY: Have stood against the world, now lies he there.
ANTONY: And none so poor to do him reverence.
ANTONY: O masters, if I were disposed to stir
ANTONY: Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage,
ANTONY: I should do Brutus wrong, and Cassius wrong,
ANTONY: Who, you all know, are honourable men:
ANTONY: I will not do them wrong, I rather choose
ANTONY: To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you,
ANTONY: Than I will wrong such honourable men.
ANTONY: But here's a parchment with the seal of Caesar,
ANTONY: I found it in his closet, 'tis his will:
ANTONY: Let but the commons hear this testament--
ANTONY: Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read--
ANTONY: And they would go and kiss dead Caesar's wounds
ANTONY: And dip their napkins in his sacred blood,
ANTONY: Yea, beg a hair of him for memory,
ANTONY: And, dying, mention it within their wills,
ANTONY: Bequeathing it as a rich legacy
ANTONY: Unto their issue.
Fourth Citizen: We'll hear the will: read it, Mark Antony.
All: The will, the will! we will hear Caesar's will.
ANTONY: Have patience, gentle friends, I must not read it,
ANTONY: It is not meet you know how Caesar loved you.
ANTONY: You are not wood, you are not stones, but men,
ANTONY: And, being men, bearing the will of Caesar,
ANTONY: It will inflame you, it will make you mad:
ANTONY: 'Tis good you know not that you are his heirs,
ANTONY: For, if you should, O, what would come of it!
Fourth Citizen: Read the will, we'll hear it, Antony,
Fourth Citizen: You shall read us the will, Caesar's will.
ANTONY: Will you be patient? will you stay awhile?
ANTONY: I have o'ershot myself to tell you of it:
ANTONY: I fear I wrong the honourable men
ANTONY: Whose daggers have stabb'd Caesar, I do fear it.
Fourth Citizen: They were traitors: honourable men!
All: The will! the testament!
Second Citizen: They were villains, murderers: the will! read the will.
ANTONY: You will compel me, then, to read the will?
ANTONY: Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar,
ANTONY: And let me show you him that made the will.
ANTONY: Shall I descend? and will you give me leave?
Several Citizens: Come down.
Second Citizen: Descend.
Third Citizen: You shall have leave.
NARRATOR: ANTONY comes down
Fourth Citizen: A ring, stand round.
First Citizen: Stand from the hearse, stand from the body.
Second Citizen: Room for Antony, most noble Antony.
ANTONY: Nay, press not so upon me, stand far off.
Several Citizens: Stand back, room, bear back.
ANTONY: If you have tears, prepare to shed them now.
ANTONY: You all do know this mantle: I remember
ANTONY: The first time ever Caesar put it on,
ANTONY: 'Twas on a summer's evening, in his tent,
ANTONY: That day he overcame the Nervii:
ANTONY: Look, in this place ran Cassius' dagger through:
ANTONY: See what a rent the envious Casca made:
ANTONY: Through this the well-beloved Brutus stabb'd,
ANTONY: And as he pluck'd his cursed steel away,
ANTONY: Mark how the blood of Caesar follow'd it,
ANTONY: As rushing out of doors, to be resolved
ANTONY: If Brutus so unkindly knock'd, or no,
ANTONY: For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar's angel:
ANTONY: Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar loved him!
ANTONY: This was the most unkindest cut of all,
ANTONY: For when the noble Caesar saw him stab,
ANTONY: Ingratitude, more strong than traitors' arms,
ANTONY: Quite vanquish'd him: then burst his mighty heart,
ANTONY: And, in his mantle muffling up his face,
ANTONY: Even at the base of Pompey's statua,
ANTONY: Which all the while ran blood, great Caesar fell.
ANTONY: O, what a fall was there, my countrymen!
ANTONY: Then I, and you, and all of us fell down,
ANTONY: Whilst bloody treason flourish'd over us.
ANTONY: O, now you weep, and, I perceive, you feel
ANTONY: The dint of pity: these are gracious drops.
ANTONY: Kind souls, what, weep you when you but behold
ANTONY: Our Caesar's vesture wounded? Look you here,
ANTONY: Here is himself, marr'd, as you see, with traitors.
First Citizen: O piteous spectacle!
Second Citizen: O noble Caesar!
Third Citizen: O woful day!
Fourth Citizen: O traitors, villains!
First Citizen: O most bloody sight!
Second Citizen: We will be revenged.
All: Revenge! About! Seek! Burn! Fire! Kill! Slay!
All: Let not a traitor live!
ANTONY: Stay, countrymen.
First Citizen: Peace there! hear the noble Antony.
Second Citizen: We'll hear him, we'll follow him, we'll die with him.
ANTONY: Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up
ANTONY: To such a sudden flood of mutiny.
ANTONY: They that have done this deed are honourable:
