ANTONY: What private griefs they have, alas, I know not,
ANTONY: That made them do it: they are wise and honourable,
ANTONY: And will, no doubt, with reasons answer you.
ANTONY: I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts:
ANTONY: I am no orator, as Brutus is,
ANTONY: But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man,
ANTONY: That love my friend, and that they know full well
ANTONY: That gave me public leave to speak of him:
ANTONY: For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth,
ANTONY: Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech,
ANTONY: To stir men's blood: I only speak right on,
ANTONY: I tell you that which you yourselves do know,
ANTONY: Show you sweet Caesar's wounds, poor poor dumb mouths,
ANTONY: And bid them speak for me: but were I Brutus,
ANTONY: And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony
ANTONY: Would ruffle up your spirits and put a tongue
ANTONY: In every wound of Caesar that should move
ANTONY: The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.
All: We'll mutiny.
First Citizen: We'll burn the house of Brutus.
Third Citizen: Away, then! come, seek the conspirators.
ANTONY: Yet hear me, countrymen, yet hear me speak.
All: Peace, ho! Hear Antony. Most noble Antony!
ANTONY: Why, friends, you go to do you know not what:
ANTONY: Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves?
ANTONY: Alas, you know not: I must tell you then:
ANTONY: You have forgot the will I told you of.
All: Most true. The will! Let's stay and hear the will.
ANTONY: Here is the will, and under Caesar's seal.
ANTONY: To every Roman citizen he gives,
ANTONY: To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.
Second Citizen: Most noble Caesar! We'll revenge his death.
Third Citizen: O royal Caesar!
ANTONY: Hear me with patience.
All: Peace, ho!
ANTONY: Moreover, he hath left you all his walks,
ANTONY: His private arbours and new-planted orchards,
ANTONY: On this side Tiber, he hath left them you,
ANTONY: And to your heirs for ever, common pleasures,
ANTONY: To walk abroad, and recreate yourselves.
ANTONY: Here was a Caesar! when comes such another?
First Citizen: Never, never. Come, away, away!
First Citizen: We'll burn his body in the holy place,
First Citizen: And with the brands fire the traitors' houses.
First Citizen: Take up the body.
Second Citizen: Go fetch fire.
Third Citizen: Pluck down benches.
Fourth Citizen: Pluck down forms, windows, any thing.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Citizens with the body
ANTONY: Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot,
ANTONY: Take thou what course thou wilt!
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
ANTONY: How now, fellow!
Servant: Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.
ANTONY: Where is he?
Servant: He and Lepidus are at Caesar's house.
ANTONY: And thither will I straight to visit him:
ANTONY: He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry,
ANTONY: And in this mood will give us any thing.
Servant: I heard him say, Brutus and Cassius
Servant: Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.
ANTONY: Belike they had some notice of the people,
ANTONY: How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter CINNA the poet
CINNA THE POET: I dreamt to-night that I did feast with Caesar,
CINNA THE POET: And things unlucky charge my fantasy:
CINNA THE POET: I have no will to wander forth of doors,
CINNA THE POET: Yet something leads me forth.
NARRATOR: Enter Citizens
First Citizen: What is your name?
Second Citizen: Whither are you going?
Third Citizen: Where do you dwell?
Fourth Citizen: Are you a married man or a bachelor?
Second Citizen: Answer every man directly.
First Citizen: Ay, and briefly.
Fourth Citizen: Ay, and wisely.
Third Citizen: Ay, and truly, you were best.
CINNA THE POET: What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I
CINNA THE POET: dwell? Am I a married man or a bachelor? Then, to
CINNA THE POET: answer every man directly and briefly, wisely and
CINNA THE POET: truly: wisely I say, I am a bachelor.
Second Citizen: That's as much as to say, they are fools that marry:
Second Citizen: you'll bear me a bang for that, I fear. Proceed, directly.
CINNA THE POET: Directly, I am going to Caesar's funeral.
First Citizen: As a friend or an enemy?
CINNA THE POET: As a friend.
Second Citizen: That matter is answered directly.
Fourth Citizen: For your dwelling,--briefly.
CINNA THE POET: Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.
Third Citizen: Your name, sir, truly.
CINNA THE POET: Truly, my name is Cinna.
First Citizen: Tear him to pieces, he's a conspirator.
CINNA THE POET: I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.
Fourth Citizen: Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses.
CINNA THE POET: I am not Cinna the conspirator.
Fourth Citizen: It is no matter, his name's Cinna, pluck but his
Fourth Citizen: name out of his heart, and turn him going.
Third Citizen: Tear him, tear him! Come, brands ho! fire-brands:
Third Citizen: to Brutus', to Cassius', burn all: some to Decius'
Third Citizen: house, and some to Casca's, some to Ligarius': away, go!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A house in Rome.
NARRATOR: ANTONY, OCTAVIUS, and LEPIDUS, seated at a table
ANTONY: These many, then, shall die, their names are prick'd.
OCTAVIUS: Your brother too must die, consent you, Lepidus?
LEPIDUS: I do consent--
OCTAVIUS: Prick him down, Antony.
LEPIDUS: Upon condition Publius shall not live,
LEPIDUS: Who is your sister's son, Mark Antony.
ANTONY: He shall not live, look, with a spot I damn him.
ANTONY: But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar's house,
ANTONY: Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine
ANTONY: How to cut off some charge in legacies.
LEPIDUS: What, shall I find you here?
OCTAVIUS: Or here, or at the Capitol.
NARRATOR: Exit LEPIDUS
ANTONY: This is a slight unmeritable man,
ANTONY: Meet to be sent on errands: is it fit,
ANTONY: The three-fold world divided, he should stand
ANTONY: One of the three to share it?
OCTAVIUS: So you thought him,
OCTAVIUS: And took his voice who should be prick'd to die,
OCTAVIUS: In our black sentence and proscription.
ANTONY: Octavius, I have seen more days than you:
ANTONY: And though we lay these honours on this man,
ANTONY: To ease ourselves of divers slanderous loads,
ANTONY: He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold,
ANTONY: To groan and sweat under the business,
ANTONY: Either led or driven, as we point the way,
ANTONY: And having brought our treasure where we will,
ANTONY: Then take we down his load, and turn him off,
ANTONY: Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears,
ANTONY: And graze in commons.
OCTAVIUS: You may do your will,
OCTAVIUS: But he's a tried and valiant soldier.
ANTONY: So is my horse, Octavius, and for that
ANTONY: I do appoint him store of provender:
ANTONY: It is a creature that I teach to fight,
ANTONY: To wind, to stop, to run directly on,
ANTONY: His corporal motion govern'd by my spirit.
ANTONY: And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so,
ANTONY: He must be taught and train'd and bid go forth,
ANTONY: A barren-spirited fellow, one that feeds
ANTONY: On abjects, orts and imitations,
ANTONY: Which, out of use and staled by other men,
ANTONY: Begin his fashion: do not talk of him,
ANTONY: But as a property. And now, Octavius,
ANTONY: Listen great things:--Brutus and Cassius
ANTONY: Are levying powers: we must straight make head:
ANTONY: Therefore let our alliance be combined,
ANTONY: Our best friends made, our means stretch'd
ANTONY: And let us presently go sit in council,
ANTONY: How covert matters may be best disclosed,
ANTONY: And open perils surest answered.
OCTAVIUS: Let us do so: for we are at the stake,
OCTAVIUS: And bay'd about with many enemies,
OCTAVIUS: And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear,
OCTAVIUS: Millions of mischiefs.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Camp near Sardis. Before BRUTUS's tent.
NARRATOR: Drum. Enter BRUTUS, LUCILIUS, LUCIUS, and Soldiers, TITINIUS and PINDARUS meeting them
BRUTUS: Stand, ho!
LUCILIUS: Give the word, ho! and stand.
BRUTUS: What now, Lucilius! is Cassius near?
LUCILIUS: He is at hand, and Pindarus is come
LUCILIUS: To do you salutation from his master.
BRUTUS: He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus,
BRUTUS: In his own change, or by ill officers,
BRUTUS: Hath given me some worthy cause to wish
BRUTUS: Things done, undone: but, if he be at hand,
BRUTUS: I shall be satisfied.
PINDARUS: I do not doubt
PINDARUS: But that my noble master will appear
PINDARUS: Such as he is, full of regard and honour.
BRUTUS: He is not doubted. A word, Lucilius,
BRUTUS: How he received you, let me be resolved.
LUCILIUS: With courtesy and with respect enough,
LUCILIUS: But not with such familiar instances,
LUCILIUS: Nor with such free and friendly conference,
LUCILIUS: As he hath used of old.
BRUTUS: Thou hast described
BRUTUS: A hot friend cooling: ever note, Lucilius,
BRUTUS: When love begins to sicken and decay,
BRUTUS: It useth an enforced ceremony.
BRUTUS: There are no tricks in plain and simple faith,
BRUTUS: But hollow men, like horses hot at hand,
BRUTUS: Make gallant show and promise of their mettle,
BRUTUS: But when they should endure the bloody spur,
BRUTUS: They fall their crests, and, like deceitful jades,
BRUTUS: Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?
LUCILIUS: They mean this night in Sardis to be quarter'd,
LUCILIUS: The greater part, the horse in general,
LUCILIUS: Are come with Cassius.
BRUTUS: Hark! he is arrived.
NARRATOR: Low march within
BRUTUS: March gently on to meet him.
NARRATOR: Enter CASSIUS and his powers
CASSIUS: Stand, ho!
BRUTUS: Stand, ho! Speak the word along.
First Soldier: Stand!
Second Soldier: Stand!
Third Soldier: Stand!
CASSIUS: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.
BRUTUS: Judge me, you gods! wrong I mine enemies?
BRUTUS: And, if not so, how should I wrong a brother?
CASSIUS: Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs,
CASSIUS: And when you do them--
BRUTUS: Cassius, be content.
BRUTUS: Speak your griefs softly: I do know you well.
BRUTUS: Before the eyes of both our armies here,
BRUTUS: Which should perceive nothing but love from us,
BRUTUS: Let us not wrangle: bid them move away,
BRUTUS: Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs,
BRUTUS: And I will give you audience.
CASSIUS: Pindarus,
CASSIUS: Bid our commanders lead their charges off
CASSIUS: A little from this ground.
BRUTUS: Lucilius, do you the like, and let no man
BRUTUS: Come to our tent till we have done our conference.
BRUTUS: Let Lucius and Titinius guard our door.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Brutus's tent.
NARRATOR: Enter BRUTUS and CASSIUS
CASSIUS: That you have wrong'd me doth appear in this:
CASSIUS: You have condemn'd and noted Lucius Pella
CASSIUS: For taking bribes here of the Sardians,
CASSIUS: Wherein my letters, praying on his side,
CASSIUS: Because I knew the man, were slighted off.
BRUTUS: You wronged yourself to write in such a case.
CASSIUS: In such a time as this it is not meet
CASSIUS: That every nice offence should bear his comment.
BRUTUS: Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself
BRUTUS: Are much condemn'd to have an itching palm,
BRUTUS: To sell and mart your offices for gold
BRUTUS: To undeservers.
CASSIUS: I an itching palm!
CASSIUS: You know that you are Brutus that speak this,
CASSIUS: Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.
BRUTUS: The name of Cassius honours this corruption,
BRUTUS: And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.
CASSIUS: Chastisement!
BRUTUS: Remember March, the ides of March remember:
BRUTUS: Did not great Julius bleed for justice' sake?
BRUTUS: What villain touch'd his body, that did stab,
BRUTUS: And not for justice? What, shall one of us
BRUTUS: That struck the foremost man of all this world
BRUTUS: But for supporting robbers, shall we now
BRUTUS: Contaminate our fingers with base bribes,
BRUTUS: And sell the mighty space of our large honours
BRUTUS: For so much trash as may be grasped thus?
BRUTUS: I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon,
BRUTUS: Than such a Roman.
CASSIUS: Brutus, bay not me,
CASSIUS: I'll not endure it: you forget yourself,
CASSIUS: To hedge me in, I am a soldier, I,
CASSIUS: Older in practise, abler than yourself
CASSIUS: To make conditions.
BRUTUS: Go to, you are not, Cassius.
CASSIUS: I am.
BRUTUS: I say you are not.
CASSIUS: Urge me no more, I shall forget myself,
CASSIUS: Have mind upon your health, tempt me no further.
BRUTUS: Away, slight man!
CASSIUS: Is't possible?
BRUTUS: Hear me, for I will speak.
BRUTUS: Must I give way and room to your rash choler?
BRUTUS: Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?
CASSIUS: O ye gods, ye gods! must I endure all this?
BRUTUS: All this! ay, more: fret till your proud heart break,
BRUTUS: Go show your slaves how choleric you are,
BRUTUS: And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge?
BRUTUS: Must I observe you? must I stand and crouch
BRUTUS: Under your testy humour? By the gods
BRUTUS: You shall digest the venom of your spleen,
BRUTUS: Though it do split you, for, from this day forth,
BRUTUS: I'll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter,
BRUTUS: When you are waspish.
CASSIUS: Is it come to this?
BRUTUS: You say you are a better soldier:
BRUTUS: Let it appear so, make your vaunting true,
BRUTUS: And it shall please me well: for mine own part,
BRUTUS: I shall be glad to learn of noble men.
CASSIUS: You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus,
CASSIUS: I said, an elder soldier, not a better:
CASSIUS: Did I say 'better'?
BRUTUS: If you did, I care not.
CASSIUS: When Caesar lived, he durst not thus have moved me.
BRUTUS: Peace, peace! you durst not so have tempted him.
CASSIUS: I durst not!
BRUTUS: No.
CASSIUS: What, durst not tempt him!
BRUTUS: For your life you durst not!
CASSIUS: Do not presume too much upon my love,
CASSIUS: I may do that I shall be sorry for.
BRUTUS: You have done that you should be sorry for.
BRUTUS: There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats,
BRUTUS: For I am arm'd so strong in honesty
BRUTUS: That they pass by me as the idle wind,
BRUTUS: Which I respect not. I did send to you
BRUTUS: For certain sums of gold, which you denied me:
BRUTUS: For I can raise no money by vile means:
BRUTUS: By heaven, I had rather coin my heart,
BRUTUS: And drop my blood for drachmas, than to wring
BRUTUS: From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash
BRUTUS: By any indirection: I did send
BRUTUS: To you for gold to pay my legions,
BRUTUS: Which you denied me: was that done like Cassius?
BRUTUS: Should I have answer'd Caius Cassius so?
BRUTUS: When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous,
BRUTUS: To lock such rascal counters from his friends,
BRUTUS: Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts,
BRUTUS: Dash him to pieces!
CASSIUS: I denied you not.
BRUTUS: You did.
CASSIUS: I did not: he was but a fool that brought
CASSIUS: My answer back. Brutus hath rived my heart:
CASSIUS: A friend should bear his friend's infirmities,
CASSIUS: But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.
BRUTUS: I do not, till you practise them on me.
CASSIUS: You love me not.
BRUTUS: I do not like your faults.
CASSIUS: A friendly eye could never see such faults.
BRUTUS: A flatterer's would not, though they do appear
BRUTUS: As huge as high Olympus.
CASSIUS: Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come,
CASSIUS: Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius,
CASSIUS: For Cassius is aweary of the world,
CASSIUS: Hated by one he loves, braved by his brother,
CASSIUS: Cheque'd like a bondman, all his faults observed,
CASSIUS: Set in a note-book, learn'd, and conn'd by rote,
CASSIUS: To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep
CASSIUS: My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger,
CASSIUS: And here my naked breast, within, a heart
CASSIUS: Dearer than Plutus' mine, richer than gold:
CASSIUS: If that thou be'st a Roman, take it forth,
CASSIUS: I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart:
CASSIUS: Strike, as thou didst at Caesar, for, I know,
CASSIUS: When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better
CASSIUS: Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.
BRUTUS: Sheathe your dagger:
BRUTUS: Be angry when you will, it shall have scope,
BRUTUS: Do what you will, dishonour shall be humour.
BRUTUS: O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb
BRUTUS: That carries anger as the flint bears fire,
BRUTUS: Who, much enforced, shows a hasty spark,
BRUTUS: And straight is cold again.
CASSIUS: Hath Cassius lived
CASSIUS: To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus,
CASSIUS: When grief, and blood ill-temper'd, vexeth him?
BRUTUS: When I spoke that, I was ill-temper'd too.
CASSIUS: Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.
BRUTUS: And my heart too.
CASSIUS: O Brutus!
BRUTUS: What's the matter?
CASSIUS: Have not you love enough to bear with me,
CASSIUS: When that rash humour which my mother gave me
CASSIUS: Makes me forgetful?
BRUTUS: Yes, Cassius, and, from henceforth,
BRUTUS: When you are over-earnest with your Brutus,
BRUTUS: He'll think your mother chides, and leave you so.
Poet: [Within]  Let me go in to see the generals,
Poet: There is some grudge between 'em, 'tis not meet
Poet: They be alone.
LUCILIUS: [Within]  You shall not come to them.
Poet: [Within]  Nothing but death shall stay me.
NARRATOR: Enter Poet, followed by LUCILIUS, TITINIUS, and LUCIUS
CASSIUS: How now! what's the matter?
Poet: For shame, you generals! what do you mean?
Poet: Love, and be friends, as two such men should be,
Poet: For I have seen more years, I'm sure, than ye.
CASSIUS: Ha, ha! how vilely doth this cynic rhyme!
BRUTUS: Get you hence, sirrah, saucy fellow, hence!
CASSIUS: Bear with him, Brutus, 'tis his fashion.
BRUTUS: I'll know his humour, when he knows his time:
BRUTUS: What should the wars do with these jigging fools?
BRUTUS: Companion, hence!
CASSIUS: Away, away, be gone.
NARRATOR: Exit Poet
BRUTUS: Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders
BRUTUS: Prepare to lodge their companies to-night.
CASSIUS: And come yourselves, and bring Messala with you
CASSIUS: Immediately to us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCILIUS and TITINIUS
BRUTUS: Lucius, a bowl of wine!
NARRATOR: Exit LUCIUS
CASSIUS: I did not think you could have been so angry.
BRUTUS: O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.
CASSIUS: Of your philosophy you make no use,
CASSIUS: If you give place to accidental evils.
BRUTUS: No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
CASSIUS: Ha! Portia!
BRUTUS: She is dead.
CASSIUS: How 'scaped I killing when I cross'd you so?
CASSIUS: O insupportable and touching loss!
CASSIUS: Upon what sickness?
BRUTUS: Impatient of my absence,
BRUTUS: And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony
BRUTUS: Have made themselves so strong:--for with her death
BRUTUS: That tidings came,--with this she fell distract,
BRUTUS: And, her attendants absent, swallow'd fire.
CASSIUS: And died so?
BRUTUS: Even so.
CASSIUS: O ye immortal gods!
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS, with wine and taper
BRUTUS: Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine.
BRUTUS: In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.
CASSIUS: My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge.
CASSIUS: Fill, Lucius, till the wine o'erswell the cup,
CASSIUS: I cannot drink too much of Brutus' love.
BRUTUS: Come in, Titinius!
NARRATOR: Exit LUCIUS
NARRATOR: Re-enter TITINIUS, with MESSALA
BRUTUS: Welcome, good Messala.
BRUTUS: Now sit we close about this taper here,
BRUTUS: And call in question our necessities.
CASSIUS: Portia, art thou gone?
BRUTUS: No more, I pray you.
BRUTUS: Messala, I have here received letters,
BRUTUS: That young Octavius and Mark Antony
BRUTUS: Come down upon us with a mighty power,
BRUTUS: Bending their expedition toward Philippi.
MESSALA: Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.
BRUTUS: With what addition?
MESSALA: That by proscription and bills of outlawry,
MESSALA: Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus,
MESSALA: Have put to death an hundred senators.
BRUTUS: Therein our letters do not well agree,
BRUTUS: Mine speak of seventy senators that died
BRUTUS: By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.
CASSIUS: Cicero one!
MESSALA: Cicero is dead,
MESSALA: And by that order of proscription.
MESSALA: Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?
BRUTUS: No, Messala.
MESSALA: Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?
BRUTUS: Nothing, Messala.
MESSALA: That, methinks, is strange.
BRUTUS: Why ask you? hear you aught of her in yours?
MESSALA: No, my lord.
BRUTUS: Now, as you are a Roman, tell me true.
MESSALA: Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell:
MESSALA: For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.
BRUTUS: Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala:
BRUTUS: With meditating that she must die once,
BRUTUS: I have the patience to endure it now.
MESSALA: Even so great men great losses should endure.
CASSIUS: I have as much of this in art as you,
CASSIUS: But yet my nature could not bear it so.
BRUTUS: Well, to our work alive. What do you think
BRUTUS: Of marching to Philippi presently?
CASSIUS: I do not think it good.
BRUTUS: Your reason?
CASSIUS: This it is:
CASSIUS: 'Tis better that the enemy seek us:
CASSIUS: So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers,
CASSIUS: Doing himself offence, whilst we, lying still,
CASSIUS: Are full of rest, defense, and nimbleness.
BRUTUS: Good reasons must, of force, give place to better.
BRUTUS: The people 'twixt Philippi and this ground
BRUTUS: Do stand but in a forced affection,
BRUTUS: For they have grudged us contribution:
BRUTUS: The enemy, marching along by them,
BRUTUS: By them shall make a fuller number up,
BRUTUS: Come on refresh'd, new-added, and encouraged,
BRUTUS: From which advantage shall we cut him off,
BRUTUS: If at Philippi we do face him there,
BRUTUS: These people at our back.
CASSIUS: Hear me, good brother.
BRUTUS: Under your pardon. You must note beside,
BRUTUS: That we have tried the utmost of our friends,
BRUTUS: Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe:
BRUTUS: The enemy increaseth every day,
BRUTUS: We, at the height, are ready to decline.
BRUTUS: There is a tide in the affairs of men,
BRUTUS: Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune,
BRUTUS: Omitted, all the voyage of their life
BRUTUS: Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
BRUTUS: On such a full sea are we now afloat,
BRUTUS: And we must take the current when it serves,
BRUTUS: Or lose our ventures.
CASSIUS: Then, with your will, go on,
CASSIUS: We'll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.
BRUTUS: The deep of night is crept upon our talk,
BRUTUS: And nature must obey necessity,
BRUTUS: Which we will niggard with a little rest.
BRUTUS: There is no more to say?
CASSIUS: No more. Good night:
CASSIUS: Early to-morrow will we rise, and hence.
BRUTUS: Lucius!
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS
BRUTUS: My gown.
NARRATOR: Exit LUCIUS
BRUTUS: Farewell, good Messala:
BRUTUS: Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius,
BRUTUS: Good night, and good repose.
CASSIUS: O my dear brother!
CASSIUS: This was an ill beginning of the night:
CASSIUS: Never come such division 'tween our souls!
CASSIUS: Let it not, Brutus.
BRUTUS: Every thing is well.
CASSIUS: Good night, my lord.
BRUTUS: Good night, good brother.
MESSALA: Good night, Lord Brutus.
BRUTUS: Farewell, every one.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BRUTUS
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS, with the gown
BRUTUS: Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?
LUCIUS: Here in the tent.
BRUTUS: What, thou speak'st drowsily?
BRUTUS: Poor knave, I blame thee not, thou art o'er-watch'd.
BRUTUS: Call Claudius and some other of my men:
BRUTUS: I'll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
LUCIUS: Varro and Claudius!
NARRATOR: Enter VARRO and CLAUDIUS
VARRO: Calls my lord?
BRUTUS: I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep,
BRUTUS: It may be I shall raise you by and by
BRUTUS: On business to my brother Cassius.
VARRO: So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.
BRUTUS: I will not have it so: lie down, good sirs,
BRUTUS: It may be I shall otherwise bethink me.
BRUTUS: Look, Lucius, here's the book I sought for so,
BRUTUS: I put it in the pocket of my gown.
NARRATOR: VARRO and CLAUDIUS lie down
LUCIUS: I was sure your lordship did not give it me.
BRUTUS: Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful.
BRUTUS: Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile,
BRUTUS: And touch thy instrument a strain or two?
LUCIUS: Ay, my lord, an't please you.
BRUTUS: It does, my boy:
BRUTUS: I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.
LUCIUS: It is my duty, sir.
BRUTUS: I should not urge thy duty past thy might,
BRUTUS: I know young bloods look for a time of rest.
LUCIUS: I have slept, my lord, already.
BRUTUS: It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again,
BRUTUS: I will not hold thee long: if I do live,
BRUTUS: I will be good to thee.
NARRATOR: Music, and a song
BRUTUS: This is a sleepy tune. O murderous slumber,
BRUTUS: Lay'st thou thy leaden mace upon my boy,
BRUTUS: That plays thee music? Gentle knave, good night,
BRUTUS: I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee:
BRUTUS: If thou dost nod, thou break'st thy instrument,
BRUTUS: I'll take it from thee, and, good boy, good night.
BRUTUS: Let me see, let me see, is not the leaf turn'd down
BRUTUS: Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of CAESAR
BRUTUS: How ill this taper burns! Ha! who comes here?
BRUTUS: I think it is the weakness of mine eyes
BRUTUS: That shapes this monstrous apparition.
BRUTUS: It comes upon me. Art thou any thing?
BRUTUS: Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil,
BRUTUS: That makest my blood cold and my hair to stare?
BRUTUS: Speak to me what thou art.
GHOST: Thy evil spirit, Brutus.
BRUTUS: Why comest thou?
GHOST: To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.
BRUTUS: Well, then I shall see thee again?
GHOST: Ay, at Philippi.
BRUTUS: Why, I will see thee at Philippi, then.
NARRATOR: Exit Ghost
BRUTUS: Now I have taken heart thou vanishest:
BRUTUS: Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee.
BRUTUS: Boy, Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, awake! Claudius!
LUCIUS: The strings, my lord, are false.
BRUTUS: He thinks he still is at his instrument.
BRUTUS: Lucius, awake!
LUCIUS: My lord?
BRUTUS: Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?
LUCIUS: My lord, I do not know that I did cry.
BRUTUS: Yes, that thou didst: didst thou see any thing?
LUCIUS: Nothing, my lord.
BRUTUS: Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius!
NARRATOR: To VARRO
BRUTUS: Fellow thou, awake!
VARRO: My lord?
CLAUDIUS: My lord?
BRUTUS: Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?
CLAUDIUS: Did we, my lord?
BRUTUS: Ay: saw you any thing?
VARRO: No, my lord, I saw nothing.
CLAUDIUS: Nor I, my lord.
BRUTUS: Go and commend me to my brother Cassius,
BRUTUS: Bid him set on his powers betimes before,
BRUTUS: And we will follow.
CLAUDIUS: It shall be done, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The plains of Philippi.
NARRATOR: Enter OCTAVIUS, ANTONY, and their army
OCTAVIUS: Now, Antony, our hopes are answered:
OCTAVIUS: You said the enemy would not come down,
OCTAVIUS: But keep the hills and upper regions,
OCTAVIUS: It proves not so: their battles are at hand,
OCTAVIUS: They mean to warn us at Philippi here,
OCTAVIUS: Answering before we do demand of them.
ANTONY: Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know
ANTONY: Wherefore they do it: they could be content
ANTONY: To visit other places, and come down
ANTONY: With fearful bravery, thinking by this face
ANTONY: To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage,
ANTONY: But 'tis not so.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Prepare you, generals:
Messenger: The enemy comes on in gallant show,
Messenger: Their bloody sign of battle is hung out,
Messenger: And something to be done immediately.
ANTONY: Octavius, lead your battle softly on,
ANTONY: Upon the left hand of the even field.
OCTAVIUS: Upon the right hand I, keep thou the left.
ANTONY: Why do you cross me in this exigent?
OCTAVIUS: I do not cross you, but I will do so.
NARRATOR: March
NARRATOR: Drum. Enter BRUTUS, CASSIUS, and their Army, LUCILIUS, TITINIUS, MESSALA, and others
BRUTUS: They stand, and would have parley.
CASSIUS: Stand fast, Titinius: we must out and talk.
OCTAVIUS: Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?
ANTONY: No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge.
ANTONY: Make forth, the generals would have some words.
OCTAVIUS: Stir not until the signal.
BRUTUS: Words before blows: is it so, countrymen?
OCTAVIUS: Not that we love words better, as you do.
BRUTUS: Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.
ANTONY: In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words:
ANTONY: Witness the hole you made in Caesar's heart,
ANTONY: Crying 'Long live! hail, Caesar!'
CASSIUS: Antony,
CASSIUS: The posture of your blows are yet unknown,
CASSIUS: But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees,
CASSIUS: And leave them honeyless.
ANTONY: Not stingless too.
BRUTUS: O, yes, and soundless too,
BRUTUS: For you have stol'n their buzzing, Antony,
BRUTUS: And very wisely threat before you sting.
ANTONY: Villains, you did not so, when your vile daggers
ANTONY: Hack'd one another in the sides of Caesar:
ANTONY: You show'd your teeth like apes, and fawn'd like hounds,
ANTONY: And bow'd like bondmen, kissing Caesar's feet,
ANTONY: Whilst damned Casca, like a cur, behind
ANTONY: Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!
CASSIUS: Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself:
CASSIUS: This tongue had not offended so to-day,
CASSIUS: If Cassius might have ruled.
OCTAVIUS: Come, come, the cause: if arguing make us sweat,
OCTAVIUS: The proof of it will turn to redder drops. Look,
OCTAVIUS: I draw a sword against conspirators,
OCTAVIUS: When think you that the sword goes up again?
OCTAVIUS: Never, till Caesar's three and thirty wounds
OCTAVIUS: Be well avenged, or till another Caesar
OCTAVIUS: Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.
BRUTUS: Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors' hands,
BRUTUS: Unless thou bring'st them with thee.
OCTAVIUS: So I hope,
OCTAVIUS: I was not born to die on Brutus' sword.
BRUTUS: O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain,
BRUTUS: Young man, thou couldst not die more honourable.
CASSIUS: A peevish schoolboy, worthless of such honour,
CASSIUS: Join'd with a masker and a reveller!
ANTONY: Old Cassius still!
OCTAVIUS: Come, Antony, away!
OCTAVIUS: Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth:
OCTAVIUS: If you dare fight to-day, come to the field,
OCTAVIUS: If not, when you have stomachs.
NARRATOR: Exeunt OCTAVIUS, ANTONY, and their army
CASSIUS: Why, now, blow wind, swell billow and swim bark!
CASSIUS: The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.
BRUTUS: Ho, Lucilius! hark, a word with you.
LUCILIUS: [Standing forth]	My lord?
NARRATOR: BRUTUS and LUCILIUS converse apart
CASSIUS: Messala!
MESSALA: [Standing forth]  What says my general?
CASSIUS: Messala,
CASSIUS: This is my birth-day, as this very day
CASSIUS: Was Cassius born. Give me thy hand, Messala:
CASSIUS: Be thou my witness that against my will,
CASSIUS: As Pompey was, am I compell'd to set
CASSIUS: Upon one battle all our liberties.
CASSIUS: You know that I held Epicurus strong
CASSIUS: And his opinion: now I change my mind,
CASSIUS: And partly credit things that do presage.
CASSIUS: Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign
CASSIUS: Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perch'd,
CASSIUS: Gorging and feeding from our soldiers' hands,
CASSIUS: Who to Philippi here consorted us:
CASSIUS: This morning are they fled away and gone,
CASSIUS: And in their steads do ravens, crows and kites,
CASSIUS: Fly o'er our heads and downward look on us,
CASSIUS: As we were sickly prey: their shadows seem
CASSIUS: A canopy most fatal, under which
CASSIUS: Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.
MESSALA: Believe not so.
CASSIUS: I but believe it partly,
CASSIUS: For I am fresh of spirit and resolved
CASSIUS: To meet all perils very constantly.
BRUTUS: Even so, Lucilius.
CASSIUS: Now, most noble Brutus,
CASSIUS: The gods to-day stand friendly, that we may,
CASSIUS: Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age!
CASSIUS: But since the affairs of men rest still incertain,
CASSIUS: Let's reason with the worst that may befall.
CASSIUS: If we do lose this battle, then is this
CASSIUS: The very last time we shall speak together:
CASSIUS: What are you then determined to do?
BRUTUS: Even by the rule of that philosophy
BRUTUS: By which I did blame Cato for the death
BRUTUS: Which he did give himself, I know not how,
BRUTUS: But I do find it cowardly and vile,
BRUTUS: For fear of what might fall, so to prevent
BRUTUS: The time of life: arming myself with patience
BRUTUS: To stay the providence of some high powers
BRUTUS: That govern us below.
CASSIUS: Then, if we lose this battle,
CASSIUS: You are contented to be led in triumph
CASSIUS: Thorough the streets of Rome?
BRUTUS: No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman,
BRUTUS: That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome,
BRUTUS: He bears too great a mind. But this same day
BRUTUS: Must end that work the ides of March begun,
BRUTUS: And whether we shall meet again I know not.
BRUTUS: Therefore our everlasting farewell take:
BRUTUS: For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius!
BRUTUS: If we do meet again, why, we shall smile,
BRUTUS: If not, why then, this parting was well made.
CASSIUS: For ever, and for ever, farewell, Brutus!
CASSIUS: If we do meet again, we'll smile indeed,
CASSIUS: If not, 'tis true this parting was well made.
BRUTUS: Why, then, lead on. O, that a man might know
BRUTUS: The end of this day's business ere it come!
BRUTUS: But it sufficeth that the day will end,
BRUTUS: And then the end is known. Come, ho! away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. The field of battle.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter BRUTUS and MESSALA
BRUTUS: Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills
BRUTUS: Unto the legions on the other side.
NARRATOR: Loud alarum
BRUTUS: Let them set on at once, for I perceive
BRUTUS: But cold demeanor in Octavius' wing,
BRUTUS: And sudden push gives them the overthrow.
BRUTUS: Ride, ride, Messala: let them all come down.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter CASSIUS and TITINIUS
CASSIUS: O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly!
CASSIUS: Myself have to mine own turn'd enemy:
CASSIUS: This ensign here of mine was turning back,
CASSIUS: I slew the coward, and did take it from him.
TITINIUS: O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early,
TITINIUS: Who, having some advantage on Octavius,
TITINIUS: Took it too eagerly: his soldiers fell to spoil,
TITINIUS: Whilst we by Antony are all enclosed.
NARRATOR: Enter PINDARUS
PINDARUS: Fly further off, my lord, fly further off,
PINDARUS: Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord
PINDARUS: Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.
CASSIUS: This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius,
CASSIUS: Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?
TITINIUS: They are, my lord.
CASSIUS: Titinius, if thou lovest me,
CASSIUS: Mount thou my horse, and hide thy spurs in him,
CASSIUS: Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops,
CASSIUS: And here again, that I may rest assured
CASSIUS: Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.
TITINIUS: I will be here again, even with a thought.
NARRATOR: Exit
CASSIUS: Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill,
CASSIUS: My sight was ever thick, regard Titinius,
CASSIUS: And tell me what thou notest about the field.
NARRATOR: PINDARUS ascends the hill
CASSIUS: This day I breathed first: time is come round,
CASSIUS: And where I did begin, there shall I end,
CASSIUS: My life is run his compass. Sirrah, what news?
PINDARUS: [Above]  O my lord!
CASSIUS: What news?
PINDARUS: [Above]  Titinius is enclosed round about
PINDARUS: With horsemen, that make to him on the spur,
PINDARUS: Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him.
PINDARUS: Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too.
PINDARUS: He's ta'en.
NARRATOR: Shout
PINDARUS: And, hark! they shout for joy.
CASSIUS: Come down, behold no more.
CASSIUS: O, coward that I am, to live so long,
CASSIUS: To see my best friend ta'en before my face!
NARRATOR: PINDARUS descends
CASSIUS: Come hither, sirrah:
CASSIUS: In Parthia did I take thee prisoner,
CASSIUS: And then I swore thee, saving of thy life,
CASSIUS: That whatsoever I did bid thee do,
CASSIUS: Thou shouldst attempt it. Come now, keep thine oath,
CASSIUS: Now be a freeman: and with this good sword,
CASSIUS: That ran through Caesar's bowels, search this bosom.
CASSIUS: Stand not to answer: here, take thou the hilts,
CASSIUS: And, when my face is cover'd, as 'tis now,
CASSIUS: Guide thou the sword.
NARRATOR: PINDARUS stabs him
CASSIUS: Caesar, thou art revenged,
CASSIUS: Even with the sword that kill'd thee.
NARRATOR: Dies
PINDARUS: So, I am free, yet would not so have been,
PINDARUS: Durst I have done my will. O Cassius,
PINDARUS: Far from this country Pindarus shall run,
PINDARUS: Where never Roman shall take note of him.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter TITINIUS with MESSALA
MESSALA: It is but change, Titinius, for Octavius
MESSALA: Is overthrown by noble Brutus' power,
MESSALA: As Cassius' legions are by Antony.
TITINIUS: These tidings will well comfort Cassius.
MESSALA: Where did you leave him?
TITINIUS: All disconsolate,
TITINIUS: With Pindarus his bondman, on this hill.
MESSALA: Is not that he t hat lies upon the ground?
TITINIUS: He lies not like the living. O my heart!
MESSALA: Is not that he?
TITINIUS: No, this was he, Messala,
TITINIUS: But Cassius is no more. O setting sun,
TITINIUS: As in thy red rays thou dost sink to-night,
TITINIUS: So in his red blood Cassius' day is set,
TITINIUS: The sun of Rome is set! Our day is gone,
TITINIUS: Clouds, dews, and dangers come, our deeds are done!
TITINIUS: Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.
MESSALA: Mistrust of good success hath done this deed.
MESSALA: O hateful error, melancholy's child,
MESSALA: Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men
MESSALA: The things that are not? O error, soon conceived,
MESSALA: Thou never comest unto a happy birth,
MESSALA: But kill'st the mother that engender'd thee!
TITINIUS: What, Pindarus! where art thou, Pindarus?
MESSALA: Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet
MESSALA: The noble Brutus, thrusting this report
MESSALA: Into his ears, I may say, thrusting it,
MESSALA: For piercing steel and darts envenomed
MESSALA: Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus
MESSALA: As tidings of this sight.
TITINIUS: Hie you, Messala,
TITINIUS: And I will seek for Pindarus the while.
NARRATOR: Exit MESSALA
TITINIUS: Why didst thou send me forth, brave Cassius?
TITINIUS: Did I not meet thy friends? and did not they
TITINIUS: Put on my brows this wreath of victory,
TITINIUS: And bid me give it thee? Didst thou not hear their shouts?
TITINIUS: Alas, thou hast misconstrued every thing!
TITINIUS: But, hold thee, take this garland on thy brow,
TITINIUS: Thy Brutus bid me give it thee, and I
TITINIUS: Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace,
TITINIUS: And see how I regarded Caius Cassius.
TITINIUS: By your leave, gods:--this is a Roman's part
TITINIUS: Come, Cassius' sword, and find Titinius' heart.
NARRATOR: Kills himself
NARRATOR: Alarum. Re-enter MESSALA, with BRUTUS, CATO, STRATO, VOLUMNIUS, and LUCILIUS
BRUTUS: Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?
MESSALA: Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.
BRUTUS: Titinius' face is upward.
CATO: He is slain.
BRUTUS: O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet!
BRUTUS: Thy spirit walks abroad and turns our swords
BRUTUS: In our own proper entrails.
NARRATOR: Low alarums
CATO: Brave Titinius!
CATO: Look, whether he have not crown'd dead Cassius!
BRUTUS: Are yet two Romans living such as these?
BRUTUS: The last of all the Romans, fare thee well!
BRUTUS: It is impossible that ever Rome
BRUTUS: Should breed thy fellow. Friends, I owe more tears
BRUTUS: To this dead man than you shall see me pay.
BRUTUS: I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time.
BRUTUS: Come, therefore, and to Thasos send his body:
BRUTUS: His funerals shall not be in our camp,
BRUTUS: Lest it discomfort us. Lucilius, come,
BRUTUS: And come, young Cato, let us to the field.
BRUTUS: Labeo and Flavius, set our battles on:
BRUTUS: 'Tis three o'clock, and, Romans, yet ere night
BRUTUS: We shall try fortune in a second fight.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter fighting, Soldiers of both armies, then BRUTUS, CATO, LUCILIUS, and others
BRUTUS: Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!
CATO: What bastard doth not? Who will go with me?
CATO: I will proclaim my name about the field:
CATO: I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
CATO: A foe to tyrants, and my country's friend,
CATO: I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
BRUTUS: And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I,
BRUTUS: Brutus, my country's friend, know me for Brutus!
NARRATOR: Exit
LUCILIUS: O young and noble Cato, art thou down?
LUCILIUS: Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius,
LUCILIUS: And mayst be honour'd, being Cato's son.
First Soldier: Yield, or thou diest.
LUCILIUS: Only I yield to die:
LUCILIUS: There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight,
NARRATOR: Offering money
LUCILIUS: Kill Brutus, and be honour'd in his death.
First Soldier: We must not. A noble prisoner!
Second Soldier: Room, ho! Tell Antony, Brutus is ta'en.
First Soldier: I'll tell the news. Here comes the general.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONY
First Soldier: Brutus is ta'en, Brutus is ta'en, my lord.
ANTONY: Where is he?
LUCILIUS: Safe, Antony, Brutus is safe enough:
LUCILIUS: I dare assure thee that no enemy
LUCILIUS: Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus:
LUCILIUS: The gods defend him from so great a shame!
LUCILIUS: When you do find him, or alive or dead,
LUCILIUS: He will be found like Brutus, like himself.
ANTONY: This is not Brutus, friend, but, I assure you,
ANTONY: A prize no less in worth: keep this man safe,
ANTONY: Give him all kindness: I had rather have
ANTONY: Such men my friends than enemies. Go on,
ANTONY: And see whether Brutus be alive or dead,
ANTONY: And bring us word unto Octavius' tent
ANTONY: How every thing is chanced.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Enter BRUTUS, DARDANIUS, CLITUS, STRATO, and VOLUMNIUS
BRUTUS: Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.
CLITUS: Statilius show'd the torch-light, but, my lord,
CLITUS: He came not back: he is or ta'en or slain.
BRUTUS: Sit thee down, Clitus: slaying is the word,
BRUTUS: It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.
NARRATOR: Whispers
CLITUS: What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.
BRUTUS: Peace then! no words.
CLITUS: I'll rather kill myself.
BRUTUS: Hark thee, Dardanius.
NARRATOR: Whispers
DARDANIUS: Shall I do such a deed?
CLITUS: O Dardanius!
DARDANIUS: O Clitus!
CLITUS: What ill request did Brutus make to thee?
DARDANIUS: To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.
CLITUS: Now is that noble vessel full of grief,
CLITUS: That it runs over even at his eyes.
BRUTUS: Come hither, good Volumnius, list a word.
VOLUMNIUS: What says my lord?
BRUTUS: Why, this, Volumnius:
BRUTUS: The ghost of Caesar hath appear'd to me
BRUTUS: Two several times by night, at Sardis once,
BRUTUS: And, this last night, here in Philippi fields:
BRUTUS: I know my hour is come.
VOLUMNIUS: Not so, my lord.
BRUTUS: Nay, I am sure it is, Volumnius.
BRUTUS: Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes,
BRUTUS: Our enemies have beat us to the pit:
NARRATOR: Low alarums
BRUTUS: It is more worthy to leap in ourselves,
BRUTUS: Than tarry till they push us. Good Volumnius,
BRUTUS: Thou know'st that we two went to school together:
BRUTUS: Even for that our love of old, I prithee,
BRUTUS: Hold thou my sword-hilts, whilst I run on it.
VOLUMNIUS: That's not an office for a friend, my lord.
NARRATOR: Alarum still
CLITUS: Fly, fly, my lord, there is no tarrying here.
BRUTUS: Farewell to you, and you, and you, Volumnius.
BRUTUS: Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep,
BRUTUS: Farewell to thee too, Strato. Countrymen,
BRUTUS: My heart doth joy that yet in all my life
BRUTUS: I found no man but he was true to me.
BRUTUS: I shall have glory by this losing day
BRUTUS: More than Octavius and Mark Antony
BRUTUS: By this vile conquest shall attain unto.
BRUTUS: So fare you well at once, for Brutus' tongue
BRUTUS: Hath almost ended his life's history:
BRUTUS: Night hangs upon mine eyes, my bones would rest,
BRUTUS: That have but labour'd to attain this hour.
BRUTUS: Alarum. Cry within, 'Fly, fly, fly!'
CLITUS: Fly, my lord, fly.
BRUTUS: Hence! I will follow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CLITUS, DARDANIUS, and VOLUMNIUS
BRUTUS: I prithee, Strato, stay thou by thy lord:
BRUTUS: Thou art a fellow of a good respect,
BRUTUS: Thy life hath had some smatch of honour in it:
BRUTUS: Hold then my sword, and turn away thy face,
BRUTUS: While I do run upon it. Wilt thou, Strato?
STRATO: Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.
BRUTUS: Farewell, good Strato.
NARRATOR: Runs on his sword
BRUTUS: Caesar, now be still:
BRUTUS: I kill'd not thee with half so good a will.
NARRATOR: Dies
NARRATOR: Alarum. Retreat. Enter OCTAVIUS, ANTONY, MESSALA, LUCILIUS, and the army
OCTAVIUS: What man is that?
MESSALA: My master's man. Strato, where is thy master?
STRATO: Free from the bondage you are in, Messala:
STRATO: The conquerors can but make a fire of him,
STRATO: For Brutus only overcame himself,
STRATO: And no man else hath honour by his death.
LUCILIUS: So Brutus should be found. I thank thee, Brutus,
LUCILIUS: That thou hast proved Lucilius' saying true.
OCTAVIUS: All that served Brutus, I will entertain them.
OCTAVIUS: Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?
STRATO: Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.
OCTAVIUS: Do so, good Messala.
MESSALA: How died my master, Strato?
STRATO: I held the sword, and he did run on it.
MESSALA: Octavius, then take him to follow thee,
MESSALA: That did the latest service to my master.
ANTONY: This was the noblest Roman of them all:
ANTONY: All the conspirators save only he
ANTONY: Did that they did in envy of great Caesar,
ANTONY: He only, in a general honest thought
ANTONY: And common good to all, made one of them.
ANTONY: His life was gentle, and the elements
ANTONY: So mix'd in him that Nature might stand up
ANTONY: And say to all the world 'This was a man!'
OCTAVIUS: According to his virtue let us use him,
OCTAVIUS: With all respect and rites of burial.
OCTAVIUS: Within my tent his bones to-night shall lie,
OCTAVIUS: Most like a soldier, order'd honourably.
OCTAVIUS: So call the field to rest, and let's away,
OCTAVIUS: To part the glories of this happy day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: King John '''
KING HENRY VIII: ACT I
KING HENRY VIII: SCENE I. KING JOHN'S palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING JOHN, QUEEN ELINOR, PEMBROKE, ESSEX, SALISBURY, and others, with CHATILLON
KING JOHN: Now, say, Chatillon, what would France with us?
CHATILLON: Thus, after greeting, speaks the King of France
CHATILLON: In my behavior to the majesty,
CHATILLON: The borrow'd majesty, of England here.
QUEEN ELINOR: A strange beginning: 'borrow'd majesty!'
KING JOHN: Silence, good mother, hear the embassy.
CHATILLON: Philip of France, in right and true behalf
CHATILLON: Of thy deceased brother Geffrey's son,
CHATILLON: Arthur Plantagenet, lays most lawful claim
CHATILLON: To this fair island and the territories,
CHATILLON: To Ireland, Poictiers, Anjou, Touraine, Maine,
CHATILLON: Desiring thee to lay aside the sword
CHATILLON: Which sways usurpingly these several titles,
CHATILLON: And put these same into young Arthur's hand,
CHATILLON: Thy nephew and right royal sovereign.
KING JOHN: What follows if we disallow of this?
CHATILLON: The proud control of fierce and bloody war,
CHATILLON: To enforce these rights so forcibly withheld.
KING JOHN: Here have we war for war and blood for blood,
KING JOHN: Controlment for controlment: so answer France.
CHATILLON: Then take my king's defiance from my mouth,
CHATILLON: The farthest limit of my embassy.
KING JOHN: Bear mine to him, and so depart in peace:
KING JOHN: Be thou as lightning in the eyes of France,
KING JOHN: For ere thou canst report I will be there,
KING JOHN: The thunder of my cannon shall be heard:
KING JOHN: So hence! Be thou the trumpet of our wrath
KING JOHN: And sullen presage of your own decay.
KING JOHN: An honourable conduct let him have:
KING JOHN: Pembroke, look to 't. Farewell, Chatillon.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CHATILLON and PEMBROKE
QUEEN ELINOR: What now, my son! have I not ever said
QUEEN ELINOR: How that ambitious Constance would not cease
QUEEN ELINOR: Till she had kindled France and all the world,
QUEEN ELINOR: Upon the right and party of her son?
QUEEN ELINOR: This might have been prevented and made whole
QUEEN ELINOR: With very easy arguments of love,
QUEEN ELINOR: Which now the manage of two kingdoms must
QUEEN ELINOR: With fearful bloody issue arbitrate.
KING JOHN: Our strong possession and our right for us.
QUEEN ELINOR: Your strong possession much more than your right,
QUEEN ELINOR: Or else it must go wrong with you and me:
QUEEN ELINOR: So much my conscience whispers in your ear,
QUEEN ELINOR: Which none but heaven and you and I shall hear.
NARRATOR: Enter a Sheriff
ESSEX: My liege, here is the strangest controversy
ESSEX: Come from country to be judged by you,
ESSEX: That e'er I heard: shall I produce the men?
KING JOHN: Let them approach.
KING JOHN: Our abbeys and our priories shall pay
KING JOHN: This expedition's charge.
NARRATOR: Enter ROBERT and the BASTARD
KING JOHN: What men are you?
BASTARD: Your faithful subject I, a gentleman
BASTARD: Born in Northamptonshire and eldest son,
BASTARD: As I suppose, to Robert Faulconbridge,
BASTARD: A soldier, by the honour-giving hand
BASTARD: Of Coeur-de-lion knighted in the field.
KING JOHN: What art thou?
ROBERT: The son and heir to that same Faulconbridge.
KING JOHN: Is that the elder, and art thou the heir?
KING JOHN: You came not of one mother then, it seems.
BASTARD: Most certain of one mother, mighty king,
BASTARD: That is well known, and, as I think, one father:
BASTARD: But for the certain knowledge of that truth
BASTARD: I put you o'er to heaven and to my mother:
BASTARD: Of that I doubt, as all men's children may.
QUEEN ELINOR: Out on thee, rude man! thou dost shame thy mother
QUEEN ELINOR: And wound her honour with this diffidence.
BASTARD: I, madam? no, I have no reason for it,
BASTARD: That is my brother's plea and none of mine,
BASTARD: The which if he can prove, a' pops me out
BASTARD: At least from fair five hundred pound a year:
BASTARD: Heaven guard my mother's honour and my land!
KING JOHN: A good blunt fellow. Why, being younger born,
KING JOHN: Doth he lay claim to thine inheritance?
BASTARD: I know not why, except to get the land.
BASTARD: But once he slander'd me with bastardy:
BASTARD: But whether I be as true begot or no,
BASTARD: That still I lay upon my mother's head,
BASTARD: But that I am as well begot, my liege,--
BASTARD: Fair fall the bones that took the pains for me!--
BASTARD: Compare our faces and be judge yourself.
BASTARD: If old sir Robert did beget us both
BASTARD: And were our father and this son like him,
BASTARD: O old sir Robert, father, on my knee
BASTARD: I give heaven thanks I was not like to thee!
KING JOHN: Why, what a madcap hath heaven lent us here!
QUEEN ELINOR: He hath a trick of Coeur-de-lion's face,
QUEEN ELINOR: The accent of his tongue affecteth him.
QUEEN ELINOR: Do you not read some tokens of my son
QUEEN ELINOR: In the large composition of this man?
KING JOHN: Mine eye hath well examined his parts
KING JOHN: And finds them perfect Richard. Sirrah, speak,
KING JOHN: What doth move you to claim your brother's land?
BASTARD: Because he hath a half-face, like my father.
BASTARD: With half that face would he have all my land:
BASTARD: A half-faced groat five hundred pound a year!
ROBERT: My gracious liege, when that my father lived,
ROBERT: Your brother did employ my father much,--
BASTARD: Well, sir, by this you cannot get my land:
BASTARD: Your tale must be how he employ'd my mother.
ROBERT: And once dispatch'd him in an embassy
ROBERT: To Germany, there with the emperor
ROBERT: To treat of high affairs touching that time.
ROBERT: The advantage of his absence took the king
ROBERT: And in the mean time sojourn'd at my father's,
ROBERT: Where how he did prevail I shame to speak,
ROBERT: But truth is truth: large lengths of seas and shores
ROBERT: Between my father and my mother lay,
ROBERT: As I have heard my father speak himself,
ROBERT: When this same lusty gentleman was got.
ROBERT: Upon his death-bed he by will bequeath'd
ROBERT: His lands to me, and took it on his death
ROBERT: That this my mother's son was none of his,
ROBERT: And if he were, he came into the world
ROBERT: Full fourteen weeks before the course of time.
ROBERT: Then, good my liege, let me have what is mine,
ROBERT: My father's land, as was my father's will.
KING JOHN: Sirrah, your brother is legitimate,
KING JOHN: Your father's wife did after wedlock bear him,
KING JOHN: And if she did play false, the fault was hers,
KING JOHN: Which fault lies on the hazards of all husbands
KING JOHN: That marry wives. Tell me, how if my brother,
KING JOHN: Who, as you say, took pains to get this son,
KING JOHN: Had of your father claim'd this son for his?
KING JOHN: In sooth, good friend, your father might have kept
KING JOHN: This calf bred from his cow from all the world,
KING JOHN: In sooth he might, then, if he were my brother's,
KING JOHN: My brother might not claim him, nor your father,
KING JOHN: Being none of his, refuse him: this concludes,
KING JOHN: My mother's son did get your father's heir,
KING JOHN: Your father's heir must have your father's land.
ROBERT: Shall then my father's will be of no force
ROBERT: To dispossess that child which is not his?
BASTARD: Of no more force to dispossess me, sir,
BASTARD: Than was his will to get me, as I think.
QUEEN ELINOR: Whether hadst thou rather be a Faulconbridge
QUEEN ELINOR: And like thy brother, to enjoy thy land,
QUEEN ELINOR: Or the reputed son of Coeur-de-lion,
QUEEN ELINOR: Lord of thy presence and no land beside?
BASTARD: Madam, an if my brother had my shape,
BASTARD: And I had his, sir Robert's his, like him,
BASTARD: And if my legs were two such riding-rods,
BASTARD: My arms such eel-skins stuff'd, my face so thin
BASTARD: That in mine ear I durst not stick a rose
BASTARD: Lest men should say 'Look, where three-farthings goes!'
BASTARD: And, to his shape, were heir to all this land,
BASTARD: Would I might never stir from off this place,
BASTARD: I would give it every foot to have this face,
BASTARD: I would not be sir Nob in any case.
QUEEN ELINOR: I like thee well: wilt thou forsake thy fortune,
QUEEN ELINOR: Bequeath thy land to him and follow me?
QUEEN ELINOR: I am a soldier and now bound to France.
BASTARD: Brother, take you my land, I'll take my chance.
BASTARD: Your face hath got five hundred pound a year,
BASTARD: Yet sell your face for five pence and 'tis dear.
BASTARD: Madam, I'll follow you unto the death.
QUEEN ELINOR: Nay, I would have you go before me thither.
BASTARD: Our country manners give our betters way.
KING JOHN: What is thy name?
BASTARD: Philip, my liege, so is my name begun,
BASTARD: Philip, good old sir Robert's wife's eldest son.
KING JOHN: From henceforth bear his name whose form thou bear'st:
KING JOHN: Kneel thou down Philip, but rise more great,
KING JOHN: Arise sir Richard and Plantagenet.
BASTARD: Brother by the mother's side, give me your hand:
BASTARD: My father gave me honour, yours gave land.
BASTARD: Now blessed by the hour, by night or day,
BASTARD: When I was got, sir Robert was away!
QUEEN ELINOR: The very spirit of Plantagenet!
QUEEN ELINOR: I am thy grandam, Richard, call me so.
BASTARD: Madam, by chance but not by truth, what though?
BASTARD: Something about, a little from the right,
BASTARD: In at the window, or else o'er the hatch:
BASTARD: Who dares not stir by day must walk by night,
BASTARD: And have is have, however men do catch:
BASTARD: Near or far off, well won is still well shot,
BASTARD: And I am I, howe'er I was begot.
KING JOHN: Go, Faulconbridge: now hast thou thy desire,
KING JOHN: A landless knight makes thee a landed squire.
KING JOHN: Come, madam, and come, Richard, we must speed
KING JOHN: For France, for France, for it is more than need.
BASTARD: Brother, adieu: good fortune come to thee!
BASTARD: For thou wast got i' the way of honesty.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BASTARD
BASTARD: A foot of honour better than I was,
BASTARD: But many a many foot of land the worse.
BASTARD: Well, now can I make any Joan a lady.
BASTARD: 'Good den, sir Richard!'--'God-a-mercy, fellow!'--
BASTARD: And if his name be George, I'll call him Peter,
BASTARD: For new-made honour doth forget men's names,
BASTARD: 'Tis too respective and too sociable
BASTARD: For your conversion. Now your traveller,
BASTARD: He and his toothpick at my worship's mess,
BASTARD: And when my knightly stomach is sufficed,
BASTARD: Why then I suck my teeth and catechise
BASTARD: My picked man of countries: 'My dear sir,'
BASTARD: Thus, leaning on mine elbow, I begin,
BASTARD: 'I shall beseech you'--that is question now,
BASTARD: And then comes answer like an Absey book:
BASTARD: 'O sir,' says answer, 'at your best command,
BASTARD: At your employment, at your service, sir,'
BASTARD: 'No, sir,' says question, 'I, sweet sir, at yours:'
BASTARD: And so, ere answer knows what question would,
BASTARD: Saving in dialogue of compliment,
BASTARD: And talking of the Alps and Apennines,
BASTARD: The Pyrenean and the river Po,
BASTARD: It draws toward supper in conclusion so.
BASTARD: But this is worshipful society
BASTARD: And fits the mounting spirit like myself,
BASTARD: For he is but a bastard to the time
BASTARD: That doth not smack of observation,
BASTARD: And so am I, whether I smack or no,
BASTARD: And not alone in habit and device,
BASTARD: Exterior form, outward accoutrement,
BASTARD: But from the inward motion to deliver
BASTARD: Sweet, sweet, sweet poison for the age's tooth:
BASTARD: Which, though I will not practise to deceive,
BASTARD: Yet, to avoid deceit, I mean to learn,
BASTARD: For it shall strew the footsteps of my rising.
BASTARD: But who comes in such haste in riding-robes?
BASTARD: What woman-post is this? hath she no husband
BASTARD: That will take pains to blow a horn before her?
NARRATOR: Enter LADY FAULCONBRIDGE and GURNEY
BASTARD: O me! it is my mother. How now, good lady!
BASTARD: What brings you here to court so hastily?
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Where is that slave, thy brother? where is he,
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: That holds in chase mine honour up and down?
BASTARD: My brother Robert? old sir Robert's son?
BASTARD: Colbrand the giant, that same mighty man?
BASTARD: Is it sir Robert's son that you seek so?
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Sir Robert's son! Ay, thou unreverend boy,
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Sir Robert's son: why scorn'st thou at sir Robert?
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: He is sir Robert's son, and so art thou.
BASTARD: James Gurney, wilt thou give us leave awhile?
GURNEY: Good leave, good Philip.
BASTARD: Philip! sparrow: James,
BASTARD: There's toys abroad: anon I'll tell thee more.
NARRATOR: Exit GURNEY
BASTARD: Madam, I was not old sir Robert's son:
BASTARD: Sir Robert might have eat his part in me
BASTARD: Upon Good-Friday and ne'er broke his fast:
BASTARD: Sir Robert could do well: marry, to confess,
BASTARD: Could he get me? Sir Robert could not do it:
BASTARD: We know his handiwork: therefore, good mother,
BASTARD: To whom am I beholding for these limbs?
BASTARD: Sir Robert never holp to make this leg.
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Hast thou conspired with thy brother too,
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: That for thine own gain shouldst defend mine honour?
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: What means this scorn, thou most untoward knave?
BASTARD: Knight, knight, good mother, Basilisco-like.
BASTARD: What! I am dubb'd! I have it on my shoulder.
BASTARD: But, mother, I am not sir Robert's son,
BASTARD: I have disclaim'd sir Robert and my land,
BASTARD: Legitimation, name and all is gone:
BASTARD: Then, good my mother, let me know my father,
BASTARD: Some proper man, I hope: who was it, mother?
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Hast thou denied thyself a Faulconbridge?
BASTARD: As faithfully as I deny the devil.
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: King Richard Coeur-de-lion was thy father:
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: By long and vehement suit I was seduced
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: To make room for him in my husband's bed:
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Heaven lay not my transgression to my charge!
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Thou art the issue of my dear offence,
LADY FAULCONBRIDGE: Which was so strongly urged past my defence.
BASTARD: Now, by this light, were I to get again,
BASTARD: Madam, I would not wish a better father.
BASTARD: Some sins do bear their privilege on earth,
BASTARD: And so doth yours, your fault was not your folly:
BASTARD: Needs must you lay your heart at his dispose,
BASTARD: Subjected tribute to commanding love,
BASTARD: Against whose fury and unmatched force
BASTARD: The aweless lion could not wage the fight,
BASTARD: Nor keep his princely heart from Richard's hand.
BASTARD: He that perforce robs lions of their hearts
BASTARD: May easily win a woman's. Ay, my mother,
BASTARD: With all my heart I thank thee for my father!
BASTARD: Who lives and dares but say thou didst not well
BASTARD: When I was got, I'll send his soul to hell.
BASTARD: Come, lady, I will show thee to my kin,
BASTARD: And they shall say, when Richard me begot,
BASTARD: If thou hadst said him nay, it had been sin:
BASTARD: Who says it was, he lies, I say 'twas not.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. France. Before Angiers.
NARRATOR: Enter AUSTRIA and forces, drums, etc. on one side:  on the other KING PHILIP and his power, LEWIS, ARTHUR, CONSTANCE and attendants
LEWIS: Before Angiers well met, brave Austria.
LEWIS: Arthur, that great forerunner of thy blood,
LEWIS: Richard, that robb'd the lion of his heart
LEWIS: And fought the holy wars in Palestine,
LEWIS: By this brave duke came early to his grave:
LEWIS: And for amends to his posterity,
LEWIS: At our importance hither is he come,
LEWIS: To spread his colours, boy, in thy behalf,
LEWIS: And to rebuke the usurpation
LEWIS: Of thy unnatural uncle, English John:
LEWIS: Embrace him, love him, give him welcome hither.
ARTHUR: God shall forgive you Coeur-de-lion's death
ARTHUR: The rather that you give his offspring life,
ARTHUR: Shadowing their right under your wings of war:
ARTHUR: I give you welcome with a powerless hand,
ARTHUR: But with a heart full of unstained love:
ARTHUR: Welcome before the gates of Angiers, duke.
LEWIS: A noble boy! Who would not do thee right?
AUSTRIA: Upon thy cheek lay I this zealous kiss,
AUSTRIA: As seal to this indenture of my love,
AUSTRIA: That to my home I will no more return,
AUSTRIA: Till Angiers and the right thou hast in France,
AUSTRIA: Together with that pale, that white-faced shore,
AUSTRIA: Whose foot spurns back the ocean's roaring tides
AUSTRIA: And coops from other lands her islanders,
AUSTRIA: Even till that England, hedged in with the main,
AUSTRIA: That water-walled bulwark, still secure
AUSTRIA: And confident from foreign purposes,
AUSTRIA: Even till that utmost corner of the west
AUSTRIA: Salute thee for her king: till then, fair boy,
AUSTRIA: Will I not think of home, but follow arms.
CONSTANCE: O, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks,
CONSTANCE: Till your strong hand shall help to give him strength
CONSTANCE: To make a more requital to your love!
AUSTRIA: The peace of heaven is theirs that lift their swords
AUSTRIA: In such a just and charitable war.
KING PHILIP: Well then, to work: our cannon shall be bent
KING PHILIP: Against the brows of this resisting town.
KING PHILIP: Call for our chiefest men of discipline,
KING PHILIP: To cull the plots of best advantages:
KING PHILIP: We'll lay before this town our royal bones,
KING PHILIP: Wade to the market-place in Frenchmen's blood,
KING PHILIP: But we will make it subject to this boy.
CONSTANCE: Stay for an answer to your embassy,
CONSTANCE: Lest unadvised you stain your swords with blood:
CONSTANCE: My Lord Chatillon may from England bring,
CONSTANCE: That right in peace which here we urge in war,
CONSTANCE: And then we shall repent each drop of blood
CONSTANCE: That hot rash haste so indirectly shed.
NARRATOR: Enter CHATILLON
KING PHILIP: A wonder, lady! lo, upon thy wish,
KING PHILIP: Our messenger Chatillon is arrived!
KING PHILIP: What England says, say briefly, gentle lord,
KING PHILIP: We coldly pause for thee, Chatillon, speak.
CHATILLON: Then turn your forces from this paltry siege
CHATILLON: And stir them up against a mightier task.
CHATILLON: England, impatient of your just demands,
CHATILLON: Hath put himself in arms: the adverse winds,
CHATILLON: Whose leisure I have stay'd, have given him time
CHATILLON: To land his legions all as soon as I,
CHATILLON: His marches are expedient to this town,
CHATILLON: His forces strong, his soldiers confident.
CHATILLON: With him along is come the mother-queen,
CHATILLON: An Ate, stirring him to blood and strife,
CHATILLON: With her her niece, the Lady Blanch of Spain,
CHATILLON: With them a bastard of the king's deceased,

CHATILLON: To do offence and scath in Christendom.

KING PHILIP: To our own vantage.
KING JOHN: We will heal up all,
KING JOHN: For we'll create young Arthur Duke of Bretagne
KING JOHN: And Earl of Richmond, and this rich fair town
KING JOHN: We make him lord of. Call the Lady Constance,
KING JOHN: Some speedy messenger bid her repair
KING JOHN: To our solemnity: I trust we shall,
KING JOHN: If not fill up the measure of her will,
KING JOHN: Yet in some measure satisfy her so
KING JOHN: That we shall stop her exclamation.
KING JOHN: Go we, as well as haste will suffer us,
KING JOHN: To this unlook'd for, unprepared pomp.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but the BASTARD
BASTARD: Mad world! mad kings! mad composition!
BASTARD: John, to stop Arthur's title in the whole,
BASTARD: Hath willingly departed with a part,
BASTARD: And France, whose armour conscience buckled on,
BASTARD: Whom zeal and charity brought to the field
BASTARD: As God's own soldier, rounded in the ear
BASTARD: With that same purpose-changer, that sly devil,
BASTARD: That broker, that still breaks the pate of faith,
BASTARD: That daily break-vow, he that wins of all,
BASTARD: Of kings, of beggars, old men, young men, maids,
BASTARD: Who, having no external thing to lose
BASTARD: But the word 'maid,' cheats the poor maid of that,
BASTARD: That smooth-faced gentleman, tickling Commodity,
BASTARD: Commodity, the bias of the world,
BASTARD: The world, who of itself is peised well,
BASTARD: Made to run even upon even ground,
BASTARD: Till this advantage, this vile-drawing bias,
BASTARD: This sway of motion, this Commodity,
BASTARD: Makes it take head from all indifferency,
BASTARD: From all direction, purpose, course, intent:
BASTARD: And this same bias, this Commodity,
BASTARD: This bawd, this broker, this all-changing word,
BASTARD: Clapp'd on the outward eye of fickle France,
BASTARD: Hath drawn him from his own determined aid,
BASTARD: From a resolved and honourable war,
BASTARD: To a most base and vile-concluded peace.
BASTARD: And why rail I on this Commodity?
BASTARD: But for because he hath not woo'd me yet:
BASTARD: Not that I have the power to clutch my hand,
BASTARD: When his fair angels would salute my palm,
BASTARD: But for my hand, as unattempted yet,
BASTARD: Like a poor beggar, raileth on the rich.
BASTARD: Well, whiles I am a beggar, I will rail
BASTARD: And say there is no sin but to be rich,
BASTARD: And being rich, my virtue then shall be
BASTARD: To say there is no vice but beggary.
BASTARD: Since kings break faith upon commodity,
BASTARD: Gain, be my lord, for I will worship thee.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The French King's pavilion.
NARRATOR: Enter CONSTANCE, ARTHUR, and SALISBURY
CONSTANCE: Gone to be married! gone to swear a peace!
CONSTANCE: False blood to false blood join'd! gone to be friends!
CONSTANCE: Shall Lewis have Blanch, and Blanch those provinces?
CONSTANCE: It is not so, thou hast misspoke, misheard:
CONSTANCE: Be well advised, tell o'er thy tale again:
CONSTANCE: It cannot be, thou dost but say 'tis so:
CONSTANCE: I trust I may not trust thee, for thy word
CONSTANCE: Is but the vain breath of a common man:
CONSTANCE: Believe me, I do not believe thee, man,
CONSTANCE: I have a king's oath to the contrary.
CONSTANCE: Thou shalt be punish'd for thus frighting me,
CONSTANCE: For I am sick and capable of fears,
CONSTANCE: Oppress'd with wrongs and therefore full of fears,
CONSTANCE: A widow, husbandless, subject to fears,
CONSTANCE: A woman, naturally born to fears,
CONSTANCE: And though thou now confess thou didst but jest,
CONSTANCE: With my vex'd spirits I cannot take a truce,
CONSTANCE: But they will quake and tremble all this day.
CONSTANCE: What dost thou mean by shaking of thy head?
CONSTANCE: Why dost thou look so sadly on my son?
CONSTANCE: What means that hand upon that breast of thine?
CONSTANCE: Why holds thine eye that lamentable rheum,
CONSTANCE: Like a proud river peering o'er his bounds?
CONSTANCE: Be these sad signs confirmers of thy words?
CONSTANCE: Then speak again, not all thy former tale,
CONSTANCE: But this one word, whether thy tale be true.
SALISBURY: As true as I believe you think them false
SALISBURY: That give you cause to prove my saying true.
CONSTANCE: O, if thou teach me to believe this sorrow,
CONSTANCE: Teach thou this sorrow how to make me die,
CONSTANCE: And let belief and life encounter so
CONSTANCE: As doth the fury of two desperate men
CONSTANCE: Which in the very meeting fall and die.
CONSTANCE: Lewis marry Blanch! O boy, then where art thou?
CONSTANCE: France friend with England, what becomes of me?
CONSTANCE: Fellow, be gone: I cannot brook thy sight:
CONSTANCE: This news hath made thee a most ugly man.
SALISBURY: What other harm have I, good lady, done,
SALISBURY: But spoke the harm that is by others done?
CONSTANCE: Which harm within itself so heinous is
CONSTANCE: As it makes harmful all that speak of it.
ARTHUR: I do beseech you, madam, be content.
CONSTANCE: If thou, that bid'st me be content, wert grim,
CONSTANCE: Ugly and slanderous to thy mother's womb,
CONSTANCE: Full of unpleasing blots and sightless stains,
CONSTANCE: Lame, foolish, crooked, swart, prodigious,
CONSTANCE: Patch'd with foul moles and eye-offending marks,
CONSTANCE: I would not care, I then would be content,
CONSTANCE: For then I should not love thee, no, nor thou
CONSTANCE: Become thy great birth nor deserve a crown.
CONSTANCE: But thou art fair, and at thy birth, dear boy,
CONSTANCE: Nature and Fortune join'd to make thee great:
CONSTANCE: Of Nature's gifts thou mayst with lilies boast,
CONSTANCE: And with the half-blown rose. But Fortune, O,
CONSTANCE: She is corrupted, changed and won from thee,
CONSTANCE: She adulterates hourly with thine uncle John,
CONSTANCE: And with her golden hand hath pluck'd on France
CONSTANCE: To tread down fair respect of sovereignty,
CONSTANCE: And made his majesty the bawd to theirs.
CONSTANCE: France is a bawd to Fortune and King John,
CONSTANCE: That strumpet Fortune, that usurping John!
CONSTANCE: Tell me, thou fellow, is not France forsworn?
CONSTANCE: Envenom him with words, or get thee gone
CONSTANCE: And leave those woes alone which I alone
CONSTANCE: Am bound to under-bear.
SALISBURY: Pardon me, madam,
SALISBURY: I may not go without you to the kings.
CONSTANCE: Thou mayst, thou shalt, I will not go with thee:
CONSTANCE: I will instruct my sorrows to be proud,
CONSTANCE: For grief is proud and makes his owner stoop.
CONSTANCE: To me and to the state of my great grief
CONSTANCE: Let kings assemble, for my grief's so great
CONSTANCE: That no supporter but the huge firm earth
CONSTANCE: Can hold it up: here I and sorrows sit,
CONSTANCE: Here is my throne, bid kings come bow to it.
NARRATOR: Seats herself on the ground
NARRATOR: Enter KING JOHN, KING PHILLIP, LEWIS, BLANCH, QUEEN ELINOR, the BASTARD, AUSTRIA, and Attendants
KING PHILIP: 'Tis true, fair daughter, and this blessed day
KING PHILIP: Ever in France shall be kept festival:
KING PHILIP: To solemnize this day the glorious sun
KING PHILIP: Stays in his course and plays the alchemist,
KING PHILIP: Turning with splendor of his precious eye
KING PHILIP: The meagre cloddy earth to glittering gold:
KING PHILIP: The yearly course that brings this day about
KING PHILIP: Shall never see it but a holiday.
CONSTANCE: A wicked day, and not a holy day!
NARRATOR: Rising
CONSTANCE: What hath this day deserved? what hath it done,
CONSTANCE: That it in golden letters should be set
CONSTANCE: Among the high tides in the calendar?
CONSTANCE: Nay, rather turn this day out of the week,
CONSTANCE: This day of shame, oppression, perjury.
CONSTANCE: Or, if it must stand still, let wives with child
CONSTANCE: Pray that their burthens may not fall this day,
CONSTANCE: Lest that their hopes prodigiously be cross'd:
CONSTANCE: But on this day let seamen fear no wreck,
CONSTANCE: No bargains break that are not this day made:
CONSTANCE: This day, all things begun come to ill end,
CONSTANCE: Yea, faith itself to hollow falsehood change!
KING PHILIP: By heaven, lady, you shall have no cause
KING PHILIP: To curse the fair proceedings of this day:
KING PHILIP: Have I not pawn'd to you my majesty?
CONSTANCE: You have beguiled me with a counterfeit
CONSTANCE: Resembling majesty, which, being touch'd and tried,
CONSTANCE: Proves valueless: you are forsworn, forsworn,
CONSTANCE: You came in arms to spill mine enemies' blood,
CONSTANCE: But now in arms you strengthen it with yours:
CONSTANCE: The grappling vigour and rough frown of war
CONSTANCE: Is cold in amity and painted peace,
CONSTANCE: And our oppression hath made up this league.
CONSTANCE: Arm, arm, you heavens, against these perjured kings!
CONSTANCE: A widow cries, be husband to me, heavens!
CONSTANCE: Let not the hours of this ungodly day
CONSTANCE: Wear out the day in peace, but, ere sunset,
CONSTANCE: Set armed discord 'twixt these perjured kings!
CONSTANCE: Hear me, O, hear me!
AUSTRIA: Lady Constance, peace!
CONSTANCE: War! war! no peace! peace is to me a war
CONSTANCE: O Lymoges! O Austria! thou dost shame
CONSTANCE: That bloody spoil: thou slave, thou wretch, thou coward!
CONSTANCE: Thou little valiant, great in villany!
CONSTANCE: Thou ever strong upon the stronger side!
CONSTANCE: Thou Fortune's champion that dost never fight
CONSTANCE: But when her humorous ladyship is by
CONSTANCE: To teach thee safety! thou art perjured too,
CONSTANCE: And soothest up greatness. What a fool art thou,
CONSTANCE: A ramping fool, to brag and stamp and swear
CONSTANCE: Upon my party! Thou cold-blooded slave,
CONSTANCE: Hast thou not spoke like thunder on my side,
CONSTANCE: Been sworn my soldier, bidding me depend
CONSTANCE: Upon thy stars, thy fortune and thy strength,
CONSTANCE: And dost thou now fall over to my fores?
CONSTANCE: Thou wear a lion's hide! doff it for shame,
CONSTANCE: And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
AUSTRIA: O, that a man should speak those words to me!
BASTARD: And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
AUSTRIA: Thou darest not say so, villain, for thy life.
BASTARD: And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
KING JOHN: We like not this, thou dost forget thyself.
NARRATOR: Enter CARDINAL PANDULPH
KING PHILIP: Here comes the holy legate of the pope.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Hail, you anointed deputies of heaven!
CARDINAL PANDULPH: To thee, King John, my holy errand is.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: I Pandulph, of fair Milan cardinal,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: And from Pope Innocent the legate here,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Do in his name religiously demand
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Why thou against the church, our holy mother,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: So wilfully dost spurn, and force perforce
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Keep Stephen Langton, chosen archbishop
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Of Canterbury, from that holy see?
CARDINAL PANDULPH: This, in our foresaid holy father's name,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Pope Innocent, I do demand of thee.
KING JOHN: What earthy name to interrogatories
KING JOHN: Can task the free breath of a sacred king?
KING JOHN: Thou canst not, cardinal, devise a name
KING JOHN: So slight, unworthy and ridiculous,
KING JOHN: To charge me to an answer, as the pope.
KING JOHN: Tell him this tale, and from the mouth of England
KING JOHN: Add thus much more, that no Italian priest
KING JOHN: Shall tithe or toll in our dominions,
KING JOHN: But as we, under heaven, are supreme head,
KING JOHN: So under Him that great supremacy,
KING JOHN: Where we do reign, we will alone uphold,
KING JOHN: Without the assistance of a mortal hand:
KING JOHN: So tell the pope, all reverence set apart
KING JOHN: To him and his usurp'd authority.
KING PHILIP: Brother of England, you blaspheme in this.
KING JOHN: Though you and all the kings of Christendom
KING JOHN: Are led so grossly by this meddling priest,
KING JOHN: Dreading the curse that money may buy out,
KING JOHN: And by the merit of vile gold, dross, dust,
KING JOHN: Purchase corrupted pardon of a man,
KING JOHN: Who in that sale sells pardon from himself,
KING JOHN: Though you and all the rest so grossly led
KING JOHN: This juggling witchcraft with revenue cherish,
KING JOHN: Yet I alone, alone do me oppose
KING JOHN: Against the pope and count his friends my foes.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Then, by the lawful power that I have,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Thou shalt stand cursed and excommunicate.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: And blessed shall he be that doth revolt
CARDINAL PANDULPH: From his allegiance to an heretic,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: And meritorious shall that hand be call'd,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Canonized and worshipped as a saint,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: That takes away by any secret course
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Thy hateful life.
CONSTANCE: O, lawful let it be
CONSTANCE: That I have room with Rome to curse awhile!
CONSTANCE: Good father cardinal, cry thou amen
CONSTANCE: To my keen curses, for without my wrong
CONSTANCE: There is no tongue hath power to curse him right.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: There's law and warrant, lady, for my curse.
CONSTANCE: And for mine too: when law can do no right,
CONSTANCE: Let it be lawful that law bar no wrong:
CONSTANCE: Law cannot give my child his kingdom here,
CONSTANCE: For he that holds his kingdom holds the law,
CONSTANCE: Therefore, since law itself is perfect wrong,
CONSTANCE: How can the law forbid my tongue to curse?
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Philip of France, on peril of a curse,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Let go the hand of that arch-heretic,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: And raise the power of France upon his head,
CARDINAL PANDULPH: Unless he do submit himself to Rome.
QUEEN ELINOR: Look'st thou pale, France? do not let go thy hand.
CONSTANCE: Look to that, devil, lest that France repent,
CONSTANCE: And by disjoining hands, hell lose a soul.
AUSTRIA: King Philip, listen to the cardinal.
BASTARD: And hang a calf's-skin on his recreant limbs.
AUSTRIA: Well, ruffian, I must pocket up these wrongs, Because--
BASTARD: Your breeches best may carry them.
KING JOHN: Philip, what say'st thou to the cardinal?
CONSTANCE: What should he say, but as the cardinal?
LEWIS: Bethink you, father, for the difference
LEWIS: Is purchase of a heavy curse from Rome,
LEWIS: Or the light loss of England for a friend:
LEWIS: Forego the easier.
BLANCH: That's the curse of Rome.
CONSTANCE: O Lewis, stand fast! the devil tempts thee here
CONSTANCE: In likeness of a new untrimmed bride.
BLANCH: The Lady Constance speaks not from her faith,
BLANCH: But from her need.
CONSTANCE: O, if thou grant my need,
CONSTANCE: Which only lives but by the death of faith,
CONSTANCE: That need must needs infer this principle,
CONSTANCE: That faith would live again by death of need.
CONSTANCE: O then, tread down my need, and faith mounts up,
CONSTANCE: Keep my need up, and faith is trodden down!
KING JOHN: The king is moved, and answers not to this.
CONSTANCE: O, be removed from him, and answer well!
AUSTRIA: Do so, King Philip, hang no more in doubt.
BASTARD: Hang nothing but a calf's-skin, most sweet lout.
KING PHILIP: I am perplex'd, and know not what to say.
CARDINAL PANDULPH: What canst thou say but will perplex thee more,
