SALISBURY: To the sea-side, and put his cause and quarrel
SALISBURY: To the disposing of the cardinal:
SALISBURY: With whom yourself, myself and other lords,
SALISBURY: If you think meet, this afternoon will post
SALISBURY: To consummate this business happily.
BASTARD: Let it be so: and you, my noble prince,
BASTARD: With other princes that may best be spared,
BASTARD: Shall wait upon your father's funeral.
PRINCE HENRY: At Worcester must his body be interr'd,
PRINCE HENRY: For so he will'd it.
BASTARD: Thither shall it then:
BASTARD: And happily may your sweet self put on
BASTARD: The lineal state and glory of the land!
BASTARD: To whom with all submission, on my knee
BASTARD: I do bequeath my faithful services
BASTARD: And true subjection everlastingly.
SALISBURY: And the like tender of our love we make,
SALISBURY: To rest without a spot for evermore.
PRINCE HENRY: I have a kind soul that would give you thanks
PRINCE HENRY: And knows not how to do it but with tears.
BASTARD: O, let us pay the time but needful woe,
BASTARD: Since it hath been beforehand with our griefs.
BASTARD: This England never did, nor never shall,
BASTARD: Lie at the proud foot of a conqueror,
BASTARD: But when it first did help to wound itself.
BASTARD: Now these her princes are come home again,
BASTARD: Come the three corners of the world in arms,
BASTARD: And we shall shock them. Nought shall make us rue,
BASTARD: If England to itself do rest but true.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: King Lear '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. King Lear's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KENT, GLOUCESTER, and EDMUND
KENT: I thought the king had more affected the Duke of
KENT: Albany than Cornwall.
GLOUCESTER: It did always seem so to us: but now, in the
GLOUCESTER: division of the kingdom, it appears not which of
GLOUCESTER: the dukes he values most, for equalities are so
GLOUCESTER: weighed, that curiosity in neither can make choice
GLOUCESTER: of either's moiety.
KENT: Is not this your son, my lord?
GLOUCESTER: His breeding, sir, hath been at my charge: I have
GLOUCESTER: so often blushed to acknowledge him, that now I am
GLOUCESTER: brazed to it.
KENT: I cannot conceive you.
GLOUCESTER: Sir, this young fellow's mother could: whereupon
GLOUCESTER: she grew round-wombed, and had, indeed, sir, a son
GLOUCESTER: for her cradle ere she had a husband for her bed.
GLOUCESTER: Do you smell a fault?
KENT: I cannot wish the fault undone, the issue of it
KENT: being so proper.
GLOUCESTER: But I have, sir, a son by order of law, some year
GLOUCESTER: elder than this, who yet is no dearer in my account:
GLOUCESTER: though this knave came something saucily into the
GLOUCESTER: world before he was sent for, yet was his mother
GLOUCESTER: fair, there was good sport at his making, and the
GLOUCESTER: whoreson must be acknowledged. Do you know this
GLOUCESTER: noble gentleman, Edmund?
EDMUND: No, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: My lord of Kent: remember him hereafter as my
GLOUCESTER: honourable friend.
EDMUND: My services to your lordship.
KENT: I must love you, and sue to know you better.
EDMUND: Sir, I shall study deserving.
GLOUCESTER: He hath been out nine years, and away he shall
GLOUCESTER: again. The king is coming.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Enter KING LEAR, CORNWALL, ALBANY, GONERIL, REGAN, CORDELIA, and Attendants
KING LEAR: Attend the lords of France and Burgundy, Gloucester.
GLOUCESTER: I shall, my liege.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GLOUCESTER and EDMUND
KING LEAR: Meantime we shall express our darker purpose.
KING LEAR: Give me the map there. Know that we have divided
KING LEAR: In three our kingdom: and 'tis our fast intent
KING LEAR: To shake all cares and business from our age,
KING LEAR: Conferring them on younger strengths, while we
KING LEAR: Unburthen'd crawl toward death. Our son of Cornwall,
KING LEAR: And you, our no less loving son of Albany,
KING LEAR: We have this hour a constant will to publish
KING LEAR: Our daughters' several dowers, that future strife
KING LEAR: May be prevented now. The princes, France and Burgundy,
KING LEAR: Great rivals in our youngest daughter's love,
KING LEAR: Long in our court have made their amorous sojourn,
KING LEAR: And here are to be answer'd. Tell me, my daughters,--
KING LEAR: Since now we will divest us both of rule,
KING LEAR: Interest of territory, cares of state,--
KING LEAR: Which of you shall we say doth love us most?
KING LEAR: That we our largest bounty may extend
KING LEAR: Where nature doth with merit challenge. Goneril,
KING LEAR: Our eldest-born, speak first.
GONERIL: Sir, I love you more than words can wield the matter,
GONERIL: Dearer than eye-sight, space, and liberty,
GONERIL: Beyond what can be valued, rich or rare,
GONERIL: No less than life, with grace, health, beauty, honour,
GONERIL: As much as child e'er loved, or father found,
GONERIL: A love that makes breath poor, and speech unable,
GONERIL: Beyond all manner of so much I love you.
CORDELIA: [Aside]  What shall Cordelia do?
CORDELIA: Love, and be silent.
LEAR: Of all these bounds, even from this line to this,
LEAR: With shadowy forests and with champains rich'd,
LEAR: With plenteous rivers and wide-skirted meads,
LEAR: We make thee lady: to thine and Albany's issue
LEAR: Be this perpetual. What says our second daughter,
LEAR: Our dearest Regan, wife to Cornwall? Speak.
REGAN: Sir, I am made
REGAN: Of the self-same metal that my sister is,
REGAN: And prize me at her worth. In my true heart
REGAN: I find she names my very deed of love,
REGAN: Only she comes too short: that I profess
REGAN: Myself an enemy to all other joys,
REGAN: Which the most precious square of sense possesses,
REGAN: And find I am alone felicitate
REGAN: In your dear highness' love.
CORDELIA: [Aside]	Then poor Cordelia!
CORDELIA: And yet not so, since, I am sure, my love's
CORDELIA: More richer than my tongue.
KING LEAR: To thee and thine hereditary ever
KING LEAR: Remain this ample third of our fair kingdom,
KING LEAR: No less in space, validity, and pleasure,
KING LEAR: Than that conferr'd on Goneril. Now, our joy,
KING LEAR: Although the last, not least, to whose young love
KING LEAR: The vines of France and milk of Burgundy
KING LEAR: Strive to be interess'd, what can you say to draw
KING LEAR: A third more opulent than your sisters? Speak.
CORDELIA: Nothing, my lord.
KING LEAR: Nothing!
CORDELIA: Nothing.
KING LEAR: Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.
CORDELIA: Unhappy that I am, I cannot heave
CORDELIA: My heart into my mouth: I love your majesty
CORDELIA: According to my bond, nor more nor less.
KING LEAR: How, how, Cordelia! mend your speech a little,
KING LEAR: Lest it may mar your fortunes.
CORDELIA: Good my lord,
CORDELIA: You have begot me, bred me, loved me: I
CORDELIA: Return those duties back as are right fit,
CORDELIA: Obey you, love you, and most honour you.
CORDELIA: Why have my sisters husbands, if they say
CORDELIA: They love you all? Haply, when I shall wed,
CORDELIA: That lord whose hand must take my plight shall carry
CORDELIA: Half my love with him, half my care and duty:
CORDELIA: Sure, I shall never marry like my sisters,
CORDELIA: To love my father all.
KING LEAR: But goes thy heart with this?
CORDELIA: Ay, good my lord.
KING LEAR: So young, and so untender?
CORDELIA: So young, my lord, and true.
KING LEAR: Let it be so, thy truth, then, be thy dower:
KING LEAR: For, by the sacred radiance of the sun,
KING LEAR: The mysteries of Hecate, and the night,
KING LEAR: By all the operation of the orbs
KING LEAR: From whom we do exist, and cease to be,
KING LEAR: Here I disclaim all my paternal care,
KING LEAR: Propinquity and property of blood,
KING LEAR: And as a stranger to my heart and me
KING LEAR: Hold thee, from this, for ever. The barbarous Scythian,
KING LEAR: Or he that makes his generation messes
KING LEAR: To gorge his appetite, shall to my bosom
KING LEAR: Be as well neighbour'd, pitied, and relieved,
KING LEAR: As thou my sometime daughter.
KENT: Good my liege,--
KING LEAR: Peace, Kent!
KING LEAR: Come not between the dragon and his wrath.
KING LEAR: I loved her most, and thought to set my rest
KING LEAR: On her kind nursery. Hence, and avoid my sight!
KING LEAR: So be my grave my peace, as here I give
KING LEAR: Her father's heart from her! Call France, who stirs?
KING LEAR: Call Burgundy. Cornwall and Albany,
KING LEAR: With my two daughters' dowers digest this third:
KING LEAR: Let pride, which she calls plainness, marry her.
KING LEAR: I do invest you jointly with my power,
KING LEAR: Pre-eminence, and all the large effects
KING LEAR: That troop with majesty. Ourself, by monthly course,
KING LEAR: With reservation of an hundred knights,
KING LEAR: By you to be sustain'd, shall our abode
KING LEAR: Make with you by due turns. Only we still retain
KING LEAR: The name, and all the additions to a king,
KING LEAR: The sway, revenue, execution of the rest,
KING LEAR: Beloved sons, be yours: which to confirm,
KING LEAR: This coronet part betwixt you.
NARRATOR: Giving the crown
KENT: Royal Lear,
KENT: Whom I have ever honour'd as my king,
KENT: Loved as my father, as my master follow'd,
KENT: As my great patron thought on in my prayers,--
KING LEAR: The bow is bent and drawn, make from the shaft.
KENT: Let it fall rather, though the fork invade
KENT: The region of my heart: be Kent unmannerly,
KENT: When Lear is mad. What wilt thou do, old man?
KENT: Think'st thou that duty shall have dread to speak,
KENT: When power to flattery bows? To plainness honour's bound,
KENT: When majesty stoops to folly. Reverse thy doom,
KENT: And, in thy best consideration, cheque
KENT: This hideous rashness: answer my life my judgment,
KENT: Thy youngest daughter does not love thee least,
KENT: Nor are those empty-hearted whose low sound
KENT: Reverbs no hollowness.
KING LEAR: Kent, on thy life, no more.
KENT: My life I never held but as a pawn
KENT: To wage against thy enemies, nor fear to lose it,
KENT: Thy safety being the motive.
KING LEAR: Out of my sight!
KENT: See better, Lear, and let me still remain
KENT: The true blank of thine eye.
KING LEAR: Now, by Apollo,--
KENT: Now, by Apollo, king,
KENT: Thou swear'st thy gods in vain.
KING LEAR: O, vassal! miscreant!
NARRATOR: Laying his hand on his sword
CORNWALL: Dear sir, forbear.
KENT: Do:
KENT: Kill thy physician, and the fee bestow
KENT: Upon thy foul disease. Revoke thy doom,
KENT: Or, whilst I can vent clamour from my throat,
KENT: I'll tell thee thou dost evil.
KING LEAR: Hear me, recreant!
KING LEAR: On thine allegiance, hear me!
KING LEAR: Since thou hast sought to make us break our vow,
KING LEAR: Which we durst never yet, and with strain'd pride
KING LEAR: To come between our sentence and our power,
KING LEAR: Which nor our nature nor our place can bear,
KING LEAR: Our potency made good, take thy reward.
KING LEAR: Five days we do allot thee, for provision
KING LEAR: To shield thee from diseases of the world,
KING LEAR: And on the sixth to turn thy hated back
KING LEAR: Upon our kingdom: if, on the tenth day following,
KING LEAR: Thy banish'd trunk be found in our dominions,
KING LEAR: The moment is thy death. Away! by Jupiter,
KING LEAR: This shall not be revoked.
KENT: Fare thee well, king: sith thus thou wilt appear,
KENT: Freedom lives hence, and banishment is here.
NARRATOR: To CORDELIA
KENT: The gods to their dear shelter take thee, maid,
KENT: That justly think'st, and hast most rightly said!
NARRATOR: To REGAN and GONERIL
KENT: And your large speeches may your deeds approve,
KENT: That good effects may spring from words of love.
KENT: Thus Kent, O princes, bids you all adieu,
KENT: He'll shape his old course in a country new.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Flourish. Re-enter GLOUCESTER, with KING OF FRANCE, BURGUNDY, and Attendants
GLOUCESTER: Here's France and Burgundy, my noble lord.
KING LEAR: My lord of Burgundy.
KING LEAR: We first address towards you, who with this king
KING LEAR: Hath rivall'd for our daughter: what, in the least,
KING LEAR: Will you require in present dower with her,
KING LEAR: Or cease your quest of love?
BURGUNDY: Most royal majesty,
BURGUNDY: I crave no more than what your highness offer'd,
BURGUNDY: Nor will you tender less.
KING LEAR: Right noble Burgundy,
KING LEAR: When she was dear to us, we did hold her so,
KING LEAR: But now her price is fall'n. Sir, there she stands:
KING LEAR: If aught within that little seeming substance,
KING LEAR: Or all of it, with our displeasure pieced,
KING LEAR: And nothing more, may fitly like your grace,
KING LEAR: She's there, and she is yours.
BURGUNDY: I know no answer.
KING LEAR: Will you, with those infirmities she owes,
KING LEAR: Unfriended, new-adopted to our hate,
KING LEAR: Dower'd with our curse, and stranger'd with our oath,
KING LEAR: Take her, or leave her?
BURGUNDY: Pardon me, royal sir,
BURGUNDY: Election makes not up on such conditions.
KING LEAR: Then leave her, sir, for, by the power that made me,
KING LEAR: I tell you all her wealth.
NARRATOR: To KING OF FRANCE
KING LEAR: For you, great king,
KING LEAR: I would not from your love make such a stray,
KING LEAR: To match you where I hate, therefore beseech you
KING LEAR: To avert your liking a more worthier way
KING LEAR: Than on a wretch whom nature is ashamed
KING LEAR: Almost to acknowledge hers.
KING OF FRANCE: This is most strange,
KING OF FRANCE: That she, that even but now was your best object,
KING OF FRANCE: The argument of your praise, balm of your age,
KING OF FRANCE: Most best, most dearest, should in this trice of time
KING OF FRANCE: Commit a thing so monstrous, to dismantle
KING OF FRANCE: So many folds of favour. Sure, her offence
KING OF FRANCE: Must be of such unnatural degree,
KING OF FRANCE: That monsters it, or your fore-vouch'd affection
KING OF FRANCE: Fall'n into taint: which to believe of her,
KING OF FRANCE: Must be a faith that reason without miracle
KING OF FRANCE: Could never plant in me.
CORDELIA: I yet beseech your majesty,--
CORDELIA: If for I want that glib and oily art,
CORDELIA: To speak and purpose not, since what I well intend,
CORDELIA: I'll do't before I speak,--that you make known
CORDELIA: It is no vicious blot, murder, or foulness,
CORDELIA: No unchaste action, or dishonour'd step,
CORDELIA: That hath deprived me of your grace and favour,
CORDELIA: But even for want of that for which I am richer,
CORDELIA: A still-soliciting eye, and such a tongue
CORDELIA: As I am glad I have not, though not to have it
CORDELIA: Hath lost me in your liking.
KING LEAR: Better thou
KING LEAR: Hadst not been born than not to have pleased me better.
KING OF FRANCE: Is it but this,--a tardiness in nature
KING OF FRANCE: Which often leaves the history unspoke
KING OF FRANCE: That it intends to do? My lord of Burgundy,
KING OF FRANCE: What say you to the lady? Love's not love
KING OF FRANCE: When it is mingled with regards that stand
KING OF FRANCE: Aloof from the entire point. Will you have her?
KING OF FRANCE: She is herself a dowry.
BURGUNDY: Royal Lear,
BURGUNDY: Give but that portion which yourself proposed,
BURGUNDY: And here I take Cordelia by the hand,
BURGUNDY: Duchess of Burgundy.
KING LEAR: Nothing: I have sworn, I am firm.
BURGUNDY: I am sorry, then, you have so lost a father
BURGUNDY: That you must lose a husband.
CORDELIA: Peace be with Burgundy!
CORDELIA: Since that respects of fortune are his love,
CORDELIA: I shall not be his wife.
KING OF FRANCE: Fairest Cordelia, that art most rich, being poor,
KING OF FRANCE: Most choice, forsaken, and most loved, despised!
KING OF FRANCE: Thee and thy virtues here I seize upon:
KING OF FRANCE: Be it lawful I take up what's cast away.
KING OF FRANCE: Gods, gods! 'tis strange that from their cold'st neglect
KING OF FRANCE: My love should kindle to inflamed respect.
KING OF FRANCE: Thy dowerless daughter, king, thrown to my chance,
KING OF FRANCE: Is queen of us, of ours, and our fair France:
KING OF FRANCE: Not all the dukes of waterish Burgundy
KING OF FRANCE: Can buy this unprized precious maid of me.
KING OF FRANCE: Bid them farewell, Cordelia, though unkind:
KING OF FRANCE: Thou losest here, a better where to find.
KING LEAR: Thou hast her, France: let her be thine, for we
KING LEAR: Have no such daughter, nor shall ever see
KING LEAR: That face of hers again. Therefore be gone
KING LEAR: Without our grace, our love, our benison.
KING LEAR: Come, noble Burgundy.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt all but KING OF FRANCE, GONERIL, REGAN, and CORDELIA
KING OF FRANCE: Bid farewell to your sisters.
CORDELIA: The jewels of our father, with wash'd eyes
CORDELIA: Cordelia leaves you: I know you what you are,
CORDELIA: And like a sister am most loath to call
CORDELIA: Your faults as they are named. Use well our father:
CORDELIA: To your professed bosoms I commit him
CORDELIA: But yet, alas, stood I within his grace,
CORDELIA: I would prefer him to a better place.
CORDELIA: So, farewell to you both.
REGAN: Prescribe not us our duties.
GONERIL: Let your study
GONERIL: Be to content your lord, who hath received you
GONERIL: At fortune's alms. You have obedience scanted,
GONERIL: And well are worth the want that you have wanted.
CORDELIA: Time shall unfold what plaited cunning hides:
CORDELIA: Who cover faults, at last shame them derides.
CORDELIA: Well may you prosper!
KING OF FRANCE: Come, my fair Cordelia.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING OF FRANCE and CORDELIA
GONERIL: Sister, it is not a little I have to say of what
GONERIL: most nearly appertains to us both. I think our
GONERIL: father will hence to-night.
REGAN: That's most certain, and with you, next month with us.
GONERIL: You see how full of changes his age is, the
GONERIL: observation we have made of it hath not been
GONERIL: little: he always loved our sister most, and
GONERIL: with what poor judgment he hath now cast her off
GONERIL: appears too grossly.
REGAN: 'Tis the infirmity of his age: yet he hath ever
REGAN: but slenderly known himself.
GONERIL: The best and soundest of his time hath been but
GONERIL: rash, then must we look to receive from his age,
GONERIL: not alone the imperfections of long-engraffed
GONERIL: condition, but therewithal the unruly waywardness
GONERIL: that infirm and choleric years bring with them.
REGAN: Such unconstant starts are we like to have from
REGAN: him as this of Kent's banishment.
GONERIL: There is further compliment of leavetaking
GONERIL: between France and him. Pray you, let's hit
GONERIL: together: if our father carry authority with
GONERIL: such dispositions as he bears, this last
GONERIL: surrender of his will but offend us.
REGAN: We shall further think on't.
GONERIL: We must do something, and i' the heat.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The Earl of Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter EDMUND, with a letter
EDMUND: Thou, nature, art my goddess, to thy law
EDMUND: My services are bound. Wherefore should I
EDMUND: Stand in the plague of custom, and permit
EDMUND: The curiosity of nations to deprive me,
EDMUND: For that I am some twelve or fourteen moon-shines
EDMUND: Lag of a brother? Why bastard? wherefore base?
EDMUND: When my dimensions are as well compact,
EDMUND: My mind as generous, and my shape as true,
EDMUND: As honest madam's issue? Why brand they us
EDMUND: With base? with baseness? bastardy? base, base?
EDMUND: Who, in the lusty stealth of nature, take
EDMUND: More composition and fierce quality
EDMUND: Than doth, within a dull, stale, tired bed,
EDMUND: Go to the creating a whole tribe of fops,
EDMUND: Got 'tween asleep and wake? Well, then,
EDMUND: Legitimate Edgar, I must have your land:
EDMUND: Our father's love is to the bastard Edmund
EDMUND: As to the legitimate: fine word,--legitimate!
EDMUND: Well, my legitimate, if this letter speed,
EDMUND: And my invention thrive, Edmund the base
EDMUND: Shall top the legitimate. I grow, I prosper:
EDMUND: Now, gods, stand up for bastards!
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Kent banish'd thus! and France in choler parted!
GLOUCESTER: And the king gone to-night! subscribed his power!
GLOUCESTER: Confined to exhibition! All this done
GLOUCESTER: Upon the gad! Edmund, how now! what news?
EDMUND: So please your lordship, none.
NARRATOR: Putting up the letter
GLOUCESTER: Why so earnestly seek you to put up that letter?
EDMUND: I know no news, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: What paper were you reading?
EDMUND: Nothing, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: No? What needed, then, that terrible dispatch of
GLOUCESTER: it into your pocket? the quality of nothing hath
GLOUCESTER: not such need to hide itself. Let's see: come,
GLOUCESTER: if it be nothing, I shall not need spectacles.
EDMUND: I beseech you, sir, pardon me: it is a letter
EDMUND: from my brother, that I have not all o'er-read,
EDMUND: and for so much as I have perused, I find it not
EDMUND: fit for your o'er-looking.
GLOUCESTER: Give me the letter, sir.
EDMUND: I shall offend, either to detain or give it. The
EDMUND: contents, as in part I understand them, are to blame.
GLOUCESTER: Let's see, let's see.
EDMUND: I hope, for my brother's justification, he wrote
EDMUND: this but as an essay or taste of my virtue.
GLOUCESTER: [Reads]  'This policy and reverence of age makes
GLOUCESTER: the world bitter to the best of our times, keeps
GLOUCESTER: our fortunes from us till our oldness cannot relish
GLOUCESTER: them. I begin to find an idle and fond bondage
GLOUCESTER: in the oppression of aged tyranny, who sways, not
GLOUCESTER: as it hath power, but as it is suffered. Come to
GLOUCESTER: me, that of this I may speak more. If our father
GLOUCESTER: would sleep till I waked him, you should half his
GLOUCESTER: revenue for ever, and live the beloved of your
GLOUCESTER: brother,	EDGAR.'
GLOUCESTER: Hum--conspiracy!--'Sleep till I waked him,--you
GLOUCESTER: should enjoy half his revenue,'--My son Edgar!
GLOUCESTER: Had he a hand to write this? a heart and brain
GLOUCESTER: to breed it in?--When came this to you? who
GLOUCESTER: brought it?
EDMUND: It was not brought me, my lord, there's the
EDMUND: cunning of it, I found it thrown in at the
EDMUND: casement of my closet.
GLOUCESTER: You know the character to be your brother's?
EDMUND: If the matter were good, my lord, I durst swear
EDMUND: it were his, but, in respect of that, I would
EDMUND: fain think it were not.
GLOUCESTER: It is his.
EDMUND: It is his hand, my lord, but I hope his heart is
EDMUND: not in the contents.
GLOUCESTER: Hath he never heretofore sounded you in this business?
EDMUND: Never, my lord: but I have heard him oft
EDMUND: maintain it to be fit, that, sons at perfect age,
EDMUND: and fathers declining, the father should be as
EDMUND: ward to the son, and the son manage his revenue.
GLOUCESTER: O villain, villain! His very opinion in the
GLOUCESTER: letter! Abhorred villain! Unnatural, detested,
GLOUCESTER: brutish villain! worse than brutish! Go, sirrah,
GLOUCESTER: seek him, I'll apprehend him: abominable villain!
GLOUCESTER: Where is he?
EDMUND: I do not well know, my lord. If it shall please
EDMUND: you to suspend your indignation against my
EDMUND: brother till you can derive from him better
EDMUND: testimony of his intent, you shall run a certain
EDMUND: course, where, if you violently proceed against
EDMUND: him, mistaking his purpose, it would make a great
EDMUND: gap in your own honour, and shake in pieces the
EDMUND: heart of his obedience. I dare pawn down my life
EDMUND: for him, that he hath wrote this to feel my
EDMUND: affection to your honour, and to no further
EDMUND: pretence of danger.
GLOUCESTER: Think you so?
EDMUND: If your honour judge it meet, I will place you
EDMUND: where you shall hear us confer of this, and by an
EDMUND: auricular assurance have your satisfaction, and
EDMUND: that without any further delay than this very evening.
GLOUCESTER: He cannot be such a monster--
EDMUND: Nor is not, sure.
GLOUCESTER: To his father, that so tenderly and entirely
GLOUCESTER: loves him. Heaven and earth! Edmund, seek him
GLOUCESTER: out: wind me into him, I pray you: frame the
GLOUCESTER: business after your own wisdom. I would unstate
GLOUCESTER: myself, to be in a due resolution.
EDMUND: I will seek him, sir, presently: convey the
EDMUND: business as I shall find means and acquaint you withal.
GLOUCESTER: These late eclipses in the sun and moon portend
GLOUCESTER: no good to us: though the wisdom of nature can
GLOUCESTER: reason it thus and thus, yet nature finds itself
GLOUCESTER: scourged by the sequent effects: love cools,
GLOUCESTER: friendship falls off, brothers divide: in
GLOUCESTER: cities, mutinies, in countries, discord, in
GLOUCESTER: palaces, treason, and the bond cracked 'twixt son
GLOUCESTER: and father. This villain of mine comes under the
GLOUCESTER: prediction, there's son against father: the king
GLOUCESTER: falls from bias of nature, there's father against
GLOUCESTER: child. We have seen the best of our time:
GLOUCESTER: machinations, hollowness, treachery, and all
GLOUCESTER: ruinous disorders, follow us disquietly to our
GLOUCESTER: graves. Find out this villain, Edmund, it shall
GLOUCESTER: lose thee nothing, do it carefully. And the
GLOUCESTER: noble and true-hearted Kent banished! his
GLOUCESTER: offence, honesty! 'Tis strange.
NARRATOR: Exit
EDMUND: This is the excellent foppery of the world, that,
EDMUND: when we are sick in fortune,--often the surfeit
EDMUND: of our own behavior,--we make guilty of our
EDMUND: disasters the sun, the moon, and the stars: as
EDMUND: if we were villains by necessity, fools by
EDMUND: heavenly compulsion, knaves, thieves, and
EDMUND: treachers, by spherical predominance, drunkards,
EDMUND: liars, and adulterers, by an enforced obedience of
EDMUND: planetary influence, and all that we are evil in,
EDMUND: by a divine thrusting on: an admirable evasion
EDMUND: of whoremaster man, to lay his goatish
EDMUND: disposition to the charge of a star! My
EDMUND: father compounded with my mother under the
EDMUND: dragon's tail, and my nativity was under Ursa
EDMUND: major, so that it follows, I am rough and
EDMUND: lecherous. Tut, I should have been that I am,
EDMUND: had the maidenliest star in the firmament
EDMUND: twinkled on my bastardizing. Edgar--
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR
EDMUND: And pat he comes like the catastrophe of the old
EDMUND: comedy: my cue is villanous melancholy, with a
EDMUND: sigh like Tom o' Bedlam. O, these eclipses do
EDMUND: portend these divisions! fa, sol, la, mi.
EDGAR: How now, brother Edmund! what serious
EDGAR: contemplation are you in?
EDMUND: I am thinking, brother, of a prediction I read
EDMUND: this other day, what should follow these eclipses.
EDGAR: Do you busy yourself about that?
EDMUND: I promise you, the effects he writes of succeed
EDMUND: unhappily, as of unnaturalness between the child
EDMUND: and the parent, death, dearth, dissolutions of
EDMUND: ancient amities, divisions in state, menaces and
EDMUND: maledictions against king and nobles, needless
EDMUND: diffidences, banishment of friends, dissipation
EDMUND: of cohorts, nuptial breaches, and I know not what.
EDGAR: How long have you been a sectary astronomical?
EDMUND: Come, come, when saw you my father last?
EDGAR: Why, the night gone by.
EDMUND: Spake you with him?
EDGAR: Ay, two hours together.
EDMUND: Parted you in good terms? Found you no
EDMUND: displeasure in him by word or countenance?
EDGAR: None at all.
EDMUND: Bethink yourself wherein you may have offended
EDMUND: him: and at my entreaty forbear his presence
EDMUND: till some little time hath qualified the heat of
EDMUND: his displeasure, which at this instant so rageth
EDMUND: in him, that with the mischief of your person it
EDMUND: would scarcely allay.
EDGAR: Some villain hath done me wrong.
EDMUND: That's my fear. I pray you, have a continent
EDMUND: forbearance till the spied of his rage goes
EDMUND: slower, and, as I say, retire with me to my
EDMUND: lodging, from whence I will fitly bring you to
EDMUND: hear my lord speak: pray ye, go, there's my key:
EDMUND: if you do stir abroad, go armed.
EDGAR: Armed, brother!
EDMUND: Brother, I advise you to the best, go armed: I
EDMUND: am no honest man if there be any good meaning
EDMUND: towards you: I have told you what I have seen
EDMUND: and heard, but faintly, nothing like the image
EDMUND: and horror of it: pray you, away.
EDGAR: Shall I hear from you anon?
EDMUND: I do serve you in this business.
NARRATOR: Exit EDGAR
EDMUND: A credulous father! and a brother noble,
EDMUND: Whose nature is so far from doing harms,
EDMUND: That he suspects none: on whose foolish honesty
EDMUND: My practises ride easy! I see the business.
EDMUND: Let me, if not by birth, have lands by wit:
EDMUND: All with me's meet that I can fashion fit.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Duke of Albany's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter GONERIL, and OSWALD, her steward
GONERIL: Did my father strike my gentleman for chiding of his fool?
OSWALD: Yes, madam.
GONERIL: By day and night he wrongs me, every hour
GONERIL: He flashes into one gross crime or other,
GONERIL: That sets us all at odds: I'll not endure it:
GONERIL: His knights grow riotous, and himself upbraids us
GONERIL: On every trifle. When he returns from hunting,
GONERIL: I will not speak with him, say I am sick:
GONERIL: If you come slack of former services,
GONERIL: You shall do well, the fault of it I'll answer.
OSWALD: He's coming, madam, I hear him.
NARRATOR: Horns within
GONERIL: Put on what weary negligence you please,
GONERIL: You and your fellows, I'll have it come to question:
GONERIL: If he dislike it, let him to our sister,
GONERIL: Whose mind and mine, I know, in that are one,
GONERIL: Not to be over-ruled. Idle old man,
GONERIL: That still would manage those authorities
GONERIL: That he hath given away! Now, by my life,
GONERIL: Old fools are babes again, and must be used
GONERIL: With cheques as flatteries,--when they are seen abused.
GONERIL: Remember what I tell you.
OSWALD: Well, madam.
GONERIL: And let his knights have colder looks among you,
GONERIL: What grows of it, no matter, advise your fellows so:
GONERIL: I would breed from hence occasions, and I shall,
GONERIL: That I may speak: I'll write straight to my sister,
GONERIL: To hold my very course. Prepare for dinner.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A hall in the same.
NARRATOR: Enter KENT, disguised
KENT: If but as well I other accents borrow,
KENT: That can my speech defuse, my good intent
KENT: May carry through itself to that full issue
KENT: For which I razed my likeness. Now, banish'd Kent,
KENT: If thou canst serve where thou dost stand condemn'd,
KENT: So may it come, thy master, whom thou lovest,
KENT: Shall find thee full of labours.
NARRATOR: Horns within. Enter KING LEAR, Knights, and Attendants
KING LEAR: Let me not stay a jot for dinner, go get it ready.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
KING LEAR: How now! what art thou?
KENT: A man, sir.
KING LEAR: What dost thou profess? what wouldst thou with us?
KENT: I do profess to be no less than I seem, to serve
KENT: him truly that will put me in trust: to love him
KENT: that is honest, to converse with him that is wise,
KENT: and says little, to fear judgment, to fight when I
KENT: cannot choose, and to eat no fish.
KING LEAR: What art thou?
KENT: A very honest-hearted fellow, and as poor as the king.
KING LEAR: If thou be as poor for a subject as he is for a
KING LEAR: king, thou art poor enough. What wouldst thou?
KENT: Service.
KING LEAR: Who wouldst thou serve?
KENT: You.
KING LEAR: Dost thou know me, fellow?
KENT: No, sir, but you have that in your countenance
KENT: which I would fain call master.
KING LEAR: What's that?
KENT: Authority.
KING LEAR: What services canst thou do?
KENT: I can keep honest counsel, ride, run, mar a curious
KENT: tale in telling it, and deliver a plain message
KENT: bluntly: that which ordinary men are fit for, I am
KENT: qualified in, and the best of me is diligence.
KING LEAR: How old art thou?
KENT: Not so young, sir, to love a woman for singing, nor
KENT: so old to dote on her for any thing: I have years
KENT: on my back forty eight.
KING LEAR: Follow me, thou shalt serve me: if I like thee no
KING LEAR: worse after dinner, I will not part from thee yet.
KING LEAR: Dinner, ho, dinner! Where's my knave? my fool?
KING LEAR: Go you, and call my fool hither.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
NARRATOR: Enter OSWALD
KING LEAR: You, you, sirrah, where's my daughter?
OSWALD: So please you,--
NARRATOR: Exit
KING LEAR: What says the fellow there? Call the clotpoll back.
NARRATOR: Exit a Knight
KING LEAR: Where's my fool, ho? I think the world's asleep.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Knight
KING LEAR: How now! where's that mongrel?
Knight: He says, my lord, your daughter is not well.
KING LEAR: Why came not the slave back to me when I called him.
Knight: Sir, he answered me in the roundest manner, he would
Knight: not.
KING LEAR: He would not!
Knight: My lord, I know not what the matter is, but, to my
Knight: judgment, your highness is not entertained with that
Knight: ceremonious affection as you were wont, there's a
Knight: great abatement of kindness appears as well in the
Knight: general dependants as in the duke himself also and
Knight: your daughter.
KING LEAR: Ha! sayest thou so?
Knight: I beseech you, pardon me, my lord, if I be mistaken,
Knight: for my duty cannot be silent when I think your
Knight: highness wronged.
KING LEAR: Thou but rememberest me of mine own conception: I
KING LEAR: have perceived a most faint neglect of late, which I
KING LEAR: have rather blamed as mine own jealous curiosity
KING LEAR: than as a very pretence and purpose of unkindness:
KING LEAR: I will look further into't. But where's my fool? I
KING LEAR: have not seen him this two days.
Knight: Since my young lady's going into France, sir, the
Knight: fool hath much pined away.
KING LEAR: No more of that, I have noted it well. Go you, and
KING LEAR: tell my daughter I would speak with her.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
KING LEAR: Go you, call hither my fool.
NARRATOR: Exit an Attendant
NARRATOR: Re-enter OSWALD
KING LEAR: O, you sir, you, come you hither, sir: who am I,
KING LEAR: sir?
OSWALD: My lady's father.
KING LEAR: 'My lady's father'! my lord's knave: your
KING LEAR: whoreson dog! you slave! you cur!
OSWALD: I am none of these, my lord, I beseech your pardon.
KING LEAR: Do you bandy looks with me, you rascal?
NARRATOR: Striking him
OSWALD: I'll not be struck, my lord.
KENT: Nor tripped neither, you base football player.
NARRATOR: Tripping up his heels
KING LEAR: I thank thee, fellow, thou servest me, and I'll
KING LEAR: love thee.
KENT: Come, sir, arise, away! I'll teach you differences:
KENT: away, away! if you will measure your lubber's
KENT: length again, tarry: but away! go to, have you
KENT: wisdom? so.
NARRATOR: Pushes OSWALD out
KING LEAR: Now, my friendly knave, I thank thee: there's
KING LEAR: earnest of thy service.
NARRATOR: Giving KENT money
NARRATOR: Enter Fool
Fool: Let me hire him too: here's my coxcomb.
NARRATOR: Offering KENT his cap
KING LEAR: How now, my pretty knave! how dost thou?
Fool: Sirrah, you were best take my coxcomb.
KENT: Why, fool?
Fool: Why, for taking one's part that's out of favour:
Fool: nay, an thou canst not smile as the wind sits,
Fool: thou'lt catch cold shortly: there, take my coxcomb:
Fool: why, this fellow has banished two on's daughters,
Fool: and did the third a blessing against his will, if
Fool: thou follow him, thou must needs wear my coxcomb.
Fool: How now, nuncle! Would I had two coxcombs and two daughters!
KING LEAR: Why, my boy?
Fool: If I gave them all my living, I'ld keep my coxcombs
Fool: myself. There's mine, beg another of thy daughters.
KING LEAR: Take heed, sirrah, the whip.
Fool: Truth's a dog must to kennel, he must be whipped
Fool: out, when Lady the brach may stand by the fire and stink.
KING LEAR: A pestilent gall to me!
Fool: Sirrah, I'll teach thee a speech.
KING LEAR: Do.
Fool: Mark it, nuncle:
Fool: Have more than thou showest,
Fool: Speak less than thou knowest,
Fool: Lend less than thou owest,
Fool: Ride more than thou goest,
Fool: Learn more than thou trowest,
Fool: Set less than thou throwest,
Fool: Leave thy drink and thy whore,
Fool: And keep in-a-door,
Fool: And thou shalt have more
Fool: Than two tens to a score.
KENT: This is nothing, fool.
Fool: Then 'tis like the breath of an unfee'd lawyer, you
Fool: gave me nothing for't. Can you make no use of
Fool: nothing, nuncle?
KING LEAR: Why, no, boy, nothing can be made out of nothing.
Fool: [To KENT]  Prithee, tell him, so much the rent of
Fool: his land comes to: he will not believe a fool.
KING LEAR: A bitter fool!
Fool: Dost thou know the difference, my boy, between a
Fool: bitter fool and a sweet fool?
KING LEAR: No, lad, teach me.
Fool: That lord that counsell'd thee
Fool: To give away thy land,
Fool: Come place him here by me,
Fool: Do thou for him stand:
Fool: The sweet and bitter fool
Fool: Will presently appear,
Fool: The one in motley here,
Fool: The other found out there.
KING LEAR: Dost thou call me fool, boy?
Fool: All thy other titles thou hast given away, that
Fool: thou wast born with.
KENT: This is not altogether fool, my lord.
Fool: No, faith, lords and great men will not let me, if
Fool: I had a monopoly out, they would have part on't:
Fool: and ladies too, they will not let me have all fool
Fool: to myself, they'll be snatching. Give me an egg,
Fool: nuncle, and I'll give thee two crowns.
KING LEAR: What two crowns shall they be?
Fool: Why, after I have cut the egg i' the middle, and eat
Fool: up the meat, the two crowns of the egg. When thou
Fool: clovest thy crown i' the middle, and gavest away
Fool: both parts, thou borest thy ass on thy back o'er
Fool: the dirt: thou hadst little wit in thy bald crown,
Fool: when thou gavest thy golden one away. If I speak
Fool: like myself in this, let him be whipped that first
Fool: finds it so.
NARRATOR: Singing
Fool: Fools had ne'er less wit in a year,
Fool: For wise men are grown foppish,
Fool: They know not how their wits to wear,
Fool: Their manners are so apish.
KING LEAR: When were you wont to be so full of songs, sirrah?
Fool: I have used it, nuncle, ever since thou madest thy
Fool: daughters thy mothers: for when thou gavest them
Fool: the rod, and put'st down thine own breeches,
NARRATOR: Singing
Fool: Then they for sudden joy did weep,
Fool: And I for sorrow sung,
Fool: That such a king should play bo-peep,
Fool: And go the fools among.
Fool: Prithee, nuncle, keep a schoolmaster that can teach
Fool: thy fool to lie: I would fain learn to lie.
KING LEAR: An you lie, sirrah, we'll have you whipped.
Fool: I marvel what kin thou and thy daughters are:
Fool: they'll have me whipped for speaking true, thou'lt
Fool: have me whipped for lying, and sometimes I am
Fool: whipped for holding my peace. I had rather be any
Fool: kind o' thing than a fool: and yet I would not be
Fool: thee, nuncle, thou hast pared thy wit o' both sides,
Fool: and left nothing i' the middle: here comes one o'
Fool: the parings.
NARRATOR: Enter GONERIL
KING LEAR: How now, daughter! what makes that frontlet on?
KING LEAR: Methinks you are too much of late i' the frown.
Fool: Thou wast a pretty fellow when thou hadst no need to
Fool: care for her frowning, now thou art an O without a
Fool: figure: I am better than thou art now, I am a fool,
Fool: thou art nothing.
NARRATOR: To GONERIL
Fool: Yes, forsooth, I will hold my tongue, so your face
Fool: bids me, though you say nothing. Mum, mum,
Fool: He that keeps nor crust nor crum,
Fool: Weary of all, shall want some.
NARRATOR: Pointing to KING LEAR
Fool: That's a shealed peascod.
GONERIL: Not only, sir, this your all-licensed fool,
GONERIL: But other of your insolent retinue
GONERIL: Do hourly carp and quarrel, breaking forth
GONERIL: In rank and not-to-be endured riots. Sir,
GONERIL: I had thought, by making this well known unto you,
GONERIL: To have found a safe redress, but now grow fearful,
GONERIL: By what yourself too late have spoke and done.
GONERIL: That you protect this course, and put it on
GONERIL: By your allowance, which if you should, the fault
GONERIL: Would not 'scape censure, nor the redresses sleep,
GONERIL: Which, in the tender of a wholesome weal,
GONERIL: Might in their working do you that offence,
GONERIL: Which else were shame, that then necessity
GONERIL: Will call discreet proceeding.
Fool: For, you trow, nuncle,
Fool: The hedge-sparrow fed the cuckoo so long,
Fool: That it's had it head bit off by it young.
Fool: So, out went the candle, and we were left darkling.
KING LEAR: Are you our daughter?
GONERIL: Come, sir,
GONERIL: I would you would make use of that good wisdom,
GONERIL: Whereof I know you are fraught, and put away
GONERIL: These dispositions, that of late transform you
GONERIL: From what you rightly are.
Fool: May not an ass know when the cart
Fool: draws the horse? Whoop, Jug! I love thee.
KING LEAR: Doth any here know me? This is not Lear:
KING LEAR: Doth Lear walk thus? speak thus? Where are his eyes?
KING LEAR: Either his notion weakens, his discernings
KING LEAR: Are lethargied--Ha! waking? 'tis not so.
KING LEAR: Who is it that can tell me who I am?
Fool: Lear's shadow.
KING LEAR: I would learn that, for, by the
KING LEAR: marks of sovereignty, knowledge, and reason,
KING LEAR: I should be false persuaded I had daughters.
Fool: Which they will make an obedient father.
KING LEAR: Your name, fair gentlewoman?
GONERIL: This admiration, sir, is much o' the savour
GONERIL: Of other your new pranks. I do beseech you
GONERIL: To understand my purposes aright:
GONERIL: As you are old and reverend, you should be wise.
GONERIL: Here do you keep a hundred knights and squires,
GONERIL: Men so disorder'd, so debosh'd and bold,
GONERIL: That this our court, infected with their manners,
GONERIL: Shows like a riotous inn: epicurism and lust
GONERIL: Make it more like a tavern or a brothel
GONERIL: Than a graced palace. The shame itself doth speak
GONERIL: For instant remedy: be then desired
GONERIL: By her, that else will take the thing she begs,
GONERIL: A little to disquantity your train,
GONERIL: And the remainder, that shall still depend,
GONERIL: To be such men as may besort your age,
GONERIL: And know themselves and you.
KING LEAR: Darkness and devils!
KING LEAR: Saddle my horses, call my train together:
KING LEAR: Degenerate bastard! I'll not trouble thee.
KING LEAR: Yet have I left a daughter.
GONERIL: You strike my people, and your disorder'd rabble
GONERIL: Make servants of their betters.
NARRATOR: Enter ALBANY
KING LEAR: Woe, that too late repents,--
NARRATOR: To ALBANY
KING LEAR: O, sir, are you come?
KING LEAR: Is it your will? Speak, sir. Prepare my horses.
KING LEAR: Ingratitude, thou marble-hearted fiend,
KING LEAR: More hideous when thou show'st thee in a child
KING LEAR: Than the sea-monster!
ALBANY: Pray, sir, be patient.
KING LEAR: [To GONERIL]  Detested kite! thou liest.
KING LEAR: My train are men of choice and rarest parts,
KING LEAR: That all particulars of duty know,
KING LEAR: And in the most exact regard support
KING LEAR: The worships of their name. O most small fault,
KING LEAR: How ugly didst thou in Cordelia show!
KING LEAR: That, like an engine, wrench'd my frame of nature
KING LEAR: From the fix'd place, drew from heart all love,
KING LEAR: And added to the gall. O Lear, Lear, Lear!
KING LEAR: Beat at this gate, that let thy folly in,
NARRATOR: Striking his head
KING LEAR: And thy dear judgment out! Go, go, my people.
ALBANY: My lord, I am guiltless, as I am ignorant
ALBANY: Of what hath moved you.
KING LEAR: It may be so, my lord.
KING LEAR: Hear, nature, hear, dear goddess, hear!
KING LEAR: Suspend thy purpose, if thou didst intend
KING LEAR: To make this creature fruitful!
KING LEAR: Into her womb convey sterility!
KING LEAR: Dry up in her the organs of increase,
KING LEAR: And from her derogate body never spring
KING LEAR: A babe to honour her! If she must teem,
KING LEAR: Create her child of spleen, that it may live,
KING LEAR: And be a thwart disnatured torment to her!
KING LEAR: Let it stamp wrinkles in her brow of youth,
KING LEAR: With cadent tears fret channels in her cheeks,
KING LEAR: Turn all her mother's pains and benefits
KING LEAR: To laughter and contempt, that she may feel
KING LEAR: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is
KING LEAR: To have a thankless child! Away, away!
NARRATOR: Exit
ALBANY: Now, gods that we adore, whereof comes this?
GONERIL: Never afflict yourself to know the cause,
GONERIL: But let his disposition have that scope
GONERIL: That dotage gives it.
NARRATOR: Re-enter KING LEAR
KING LEAR: What, fifty of my followers at a clap!
KING LEAR: Within a fortnight!
ALBANY: What's the matter, sir?
KING LEAR: I'll tell thee:
NARRATOR: To GONERIL
KING LEAR: Life and death! I am ashamed
KING LEAR: That thou hast power to shake my manhood thus,
KING LEAR: That these hot tears, which break from me perforce,
KING LEAR: Should make thee worth them. Blasts and fogs upon thee!
KING LEAR: The untented woundings of a father's curse
KING LEAR: Pierce every sense about thee! Old fond eyes,
KING LEAR: Beweep this cause again, I'll pluck ye out,
KING LEAR: And cast you, with the waters that you lose,
KING LEAR: To temper clay. Yea, it is come to this?
KING LEAR: Let is be so: yet have I left a daughter,
KING LEAR: Who, I am sure, is kind and comfortable:
KING LEAR: When she shall hear this of thee, with her nails
KING LEAR: She'll flay thy wolvish visage. Thou shalt find
KING LEAR: That I'll resume the shape which thou dost think
KING LEAR: I have cast off for ever: thou shalt,
KING LEAR: I warrant thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING LEAR, KENT, and Attendants
GONERIL: Do you mark that, my lord?
ALBANY: I cannot be so partial, Goneril,
ALBANY: To the great love I bear you,--
GONERIL: Pray you, content. What, Oswald, ho!
NARRATOR: To the Fool
GONERIL: You, sir, more knave than fool, after your master.
Fool: Nuncle Lear, nuncle Lear, tarry and take the fool
Fool: with thee.
Fool: A fox, when one has caught her,
Fool: And such a daughter,
Fool: Should sure to the slaughter,
Fool: If my cap would buy a halter:
Fool: So the fool follows after.
NARRATOR: Exit
GONERIL: This man hath had good counsel:--a hundred knights!
GONERIL: 'Tis politic and safe to let him keep
GONERIL: At point a hundred knights: yes, that, on every dream,
GONERIL: Each buzz, each fancy, each complaint, dislike,
GONERIL: He may enguard his dotage with their powers,
GONERIL: And hold our lives in mercy. Oswald, I say!
ALBANY: Well, you may fear too far.
GONERIL: Safer than trust too far:
GONERIL: Let me still take away the harms I fear,
GONERIL: Not fear still to be taken: I know his heart.
GONERIL: What he hath utter'd I have writ my sister
GONERIL: If she sustain him and his hundred knights
GONERIL: When I have show'd the unfitness,--
NARRATOR: Re-enter OSWALD
GONERIL: How now, Oswald!
GONERIL: What, have you writ that letter to my sister?
OSWALD: Yes, madam.
GONERIL: Take you some company, and away to horse:
GONERIL: Inform her full of my particular fear,
GONERIL: And thereto add such reasons of your own
GONERIL: As may compact it more. Get you gone,
GONERIL: And hasten your return.
NARRATOR: Exit OSWALD
GONERIL: No, no, my lord,
GONERIL: This milky gentleness and course of yours
GONERIL: Though I condemn not, yet, under pardon,
GONERIL: You are much more attask'd for want of wisdom
GONERIL: Than praised for harmful mildness.
ALBANY: How far your eyes may pierce I can not tell:
ALBANY: Striving to better, oft we mar what's well.
GONERIL: Nay, then--
ALBANY: Well, well, the event.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Court before the same.
NARRATOR: Enter KING LEAR, KENT, and Fool
KING LEAR: Go you before to Gloucester with these letters.
KING LEAR: Acquaint my daughter no further with any thing you
KING LEAR: know than comes from her demand out of the letter.
KING LEAR: If your diligence be not speedy, I shall be there afore you.
KENT: I will not sleep, my lord, till I have delivered
KENT: your letter.
NARRATOR: Exit
Fool: If a man's brains were in's heels, were't not in
Fool: danger of kibes?
KING LEAR: Ay, boy.
Fool: Then, I prithee, be merry, thy wit shall ne'er go
Fool: slip-shod.
KING LEAR: Ha, ha, ha!
Fool: Shalt see thy other daughter will use thee kindly,
Fool: for though she's as like this as a crab's like an
Fool: apple, yet I can tell what I can tell.
KING LEAR: Why, what canst thou tell, my boy?
Fool: She will taste as like this as a crab does to a
Fool: crab. Thou canst tell why one's nose stands i'
Fool: the middle on's face?
KING LEAR: No.
Fool: Why, to keep one's eyes of either side's nose, that
Fool: what a man cannot smell out, he may spy into.
KING LEAR: I did her wrong--
Fool: Canst tell how an oyster makes his shell?
KING LEAR: No.
Fool: Nor I neither, but I can tell why a snail has a house.
KING LEAR: Why?
Fool: Why, to put his head in, not to give it away to his
Fool: daughters, and leave his horns without a case.
KING LEAR: I will forget my nature. So kind a father! Be my
KING LEAR: horses ready?
Fool: Thy asses are gone about 'em. The reason why the
Fool: seven stars are no more than seven is a pretty reason.
KING LEAR: Because they are not eight?
Fool: Yes, indeed: thou wouldst make a good fool.
KING LEAR: To take 't again perforce! Monster ingratitude!
Fool: If thou wert my fool, nuncle, I'ld have thee beaten
Fool: for being old before thy time.
KING LEAR: How's that?
Fool: Thou shouldst not have been old till thou hadst
Fool: been wise.
KING LEAR: O, let me not be mad, not mad, sweet heaven
KING LEAR: Keep me in temper: I would not be mad!
NARRATOR: Enter Gentleman
KING LEAR: How now! are the horses ready?
Gentleman: Ready, my lord.
KING LEAR: Come, boy.
Fool: She that's a maid now, and laughs at my departure,
Fool: Shall not be a maid long, unless things be cut shorter.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. GLOUCESTER's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter EDMUND, and CURAN meets him
EDMUND: Save thee, Curan.
CURAN: And you, sir. I have been with your father, and
CURAN: given him notice that the Duke of Cornwall and Regan
CURAN: his duchess will be here with him this night.
EDMUND: How comes that?
CURAN: Nay, I know not. You have heard of the news abroad,
CURAN: I mean the whispered ones, for they are yet but
CURAN: ear-kissing arguments?
EDMUND: Not I	pray you, what are they?
CURAN: Have you heard of no likely wars toward, 'twixt the
CURAN: Dukes of Cornwall and Albany?
EDMUND: Not a word.
CURAN: You may do, then, in time. Fare you well, sir.
NARRATOR: Exit
EDMUND: The duke be here to-night? The better! best!
EDMUND: This weaves itself perforce into my business.
EDMUND: My father hath set guard to take my brother,
EDMUND: And I have one thing, of a queasy question,
EDMUND: Which I must act: briefness and fortune, work!
EDMUND: Brother, a word, descend: brother, I say!
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR
EDMUND: My father watches: O sir, fly this place,
EDMUND: Intelligence is given where you are hid,
EDMUND: You have now the good advantage of the night:
EDMUND: Have you not spoken 'gainst the Duke of Cornwall?
EDMUND: He's coming hither: now, i' the night, i' the haste,
EDMUND: And Regan with him: have you nothing said
EDMUND: Upon his party 'gainst the Duke of Albany?
EDMUND: Advise yourself.
EDGAR: I am sure on't, not a word.
EDMUND: I hear my father coming: pardon me:
EDMUND: In cunning I must draw my sword upon you
EDMUND: Draw, seem to defend yourself, now quit you well.
EDMUND: Yield: come before my father. Light, ho, here!
EDMUND: Fly, brother. Torches, torches! So, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit EDGAR
EDMUND: Some blood drawn on me would beget opinion.
NARRATOR: Wounds his arm
EDMUND: Of my more fierce endeavour: I have seen drunkards
EDMUND: Do more than this in sport. Father, father!
EDMUND: Stop, stop! No help?
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, and Servants with torches
GLOUCESTER: Now, Edmund, where's the villain?
EDMUND: Here stood he in the dark, his sharp sword out,
EDMUND: Mumbling of wicked charms, conjuring the moon
EDMUND: To stand auspicious mistress,--
GLOUCESTER: But where is he?
EDMUND: Look, sir, I bleed.
GLOUCESTER: Where is the villain, Edmund?
EDMUND: Fled this way, sir. When by no means he could--
GLOUCESTER: Pursue him, ho! Go after.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some Servants
GLOUCESTER: By no means what?
EDMUND: Persuade me to the murder of your lordship,
EDMUND: But that I told him, the revenging gods
EDMUND: 'Gainst parricides did all their thunders bend,
EDMUND: Spoke, with how manifold and strong a bond
EDMUND: The child was bound to the father, sir, in fine,
EDMUND: Seeing how loathly opposite I stood
EDMUND: To his unnatural purpose, in fell motion,
EDMUND: With his prepared sword, he charges home
EDMUND: My unprovided body, lanced mine arm:
EDMUND: But when he saw my best alarum'd spirits,
EDMUND: Bold in the quarrel's right, roused to the encounter,
EDMUND: Or whether gasted by the noise I made,
EDMUND: Full suddenly he fled.
GLOUCESTER: Let him fly far:
GLOUCESTER: Not in this land shall he remain uncaught,

GLOUCESTER: He that conceals him, death.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter KENT and OSWALD, severally

KENT: Ay.
OSWALD: Where may we set our horses?
KENT: I' the mire.

KENT: hundred-pound, filthy, worsted-stocking knave, a

NARRATOR: SCENE III. A wood.
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR
EDGAR: I heard myself proclaim'd,
EDGAR: And by the happy hollow of a tree
EDGAR: Escaped the hunt. No port is free, no place,
EDGAR: That guard, and most unusual vigilance,
EDGAR: Does not attend my taking. Whiles I may 'scape,
EDGAR: I will preserve myself: and am bethought
EDGAR: To take the basest and most poorest shape
EDGAR: That ever penury, in contempt of man,
EDGAR: Brought near to beast: my face I'll grime with filth,
EDGAR: Blanket my loins: elf all my hair in knots,
EDGAR: And with presented nakedness out-face
EDGAR: The winds and persecutions of the sky.
EDGAR: The country gives me proof and precedent
EDGAR: Of Bedlam beggars, who, with roaring voices,
EDGAR: Strike in their numb'd and mortified bare arms
EDGAR: Pins, wooden pricks, nails, sprigs of rosemary,
EDGAR: And with this horrible object, from low farms,
EDGAR: Poor pelting villages, sheep-cotes, and mills,
EDGAR: Sometime with lunatic bans, sometime with prayers,
EDGAR: Enforce their charity. Poor Turlygod! poor Tom!
EDGAR: That's something yet: Edgar I nothing am.

KING LEAR: Allow obedience, if yourselves are old,
KING LEAR: Make it your cause, send down, and take my part!
NARRATOR: To GONERIL
KING LEAR: Art not ashamed to look upon this beard?
KING LEAR: O Regan, wilt thou take her by the hand?
GONERIL: Why not by the hand, sir? How have I offended?
GONERIL: All's not offence that indiscretion finds
GONERIL: And dotage terms so.
KING LEAR: O sides, you are too tough,
KING LEAR: Will you yet hold? How came my man i' the stocks?
CORNWALL: I set him there, sir: but his own disorders
CORNWALL: Deserved much less advancement.
KING LEAR: You! did you?
REGAN: I pray you, father, being weak, seem so.
REGAN: If, till the expiration of your month,
REGAN: You will return and sojourn with my sister,
REGAN: Dismissing half your train, come then to me:
REGAN: I am now from home, and out of that provision
REGAN: Which shall be needful for your entertainment.
KING LEAR: Return to her, and fifty men dismiss'd?
KING LEAR: No, rather I abjure all roofs, and choose
KING LEAR: To wage against the enmity o' the air,
KING LEAR: To be a comrade with the wolf and owl,--
KING LEAR: Necessity's sharp pinch! Return with her?
KING LEAR: Why, the hot-blooded France, that dowerless took
KING LEAR: Our youngest born, I could as well be brought
KING LEAR: To knee his throne, and, squire-like, pension beg
KING LEAR: To keep base life afoot. Return with her?
KING LEAR: Persuade me rather to be slave and sumpter
KING LEAR: To this detested groom.
NARRATOR: Pointing at OSWALD
GONERIL: At your choice, sir.
KING LEAR: I prithee, daughter, do not make me mad:
KING LEAR: I will not trouble thee, my child, farewell:
KING LEAR: We'll no more meet, no more see one another:
KING LEAR: But yet thou art my flesh, my blood, my daughter,
KING LEAR: Or rather a disease that's in my flesh,
KING LEAR: Which I must needs call mine: thou art a boil,
KING LEAR: A plague-sore, an embossed carbuncle,
KING LEAR: In my corrupted blood. But I'll not chide thee,
KING LEAR: Let shame come when it will, I do not call it:
KING LEAR: I do not bid the thunder-bearer shoot,
KING LEAR: Nor tell tales of thee to high-judging Jove:
KING LEAR: Mend when thou canst, be better at thy leisure:
KING LEAR: I can be patient, I can stay with Regan,
KING LEAR: I and my hundred knights.
REGAN: Not altogether so:
REGAN: I look'd not for you yet, nor am provided
REGAN: For your fit welcome. Give ear, sir, to my sister,
REGAN: For those that mingle reason with your passion
REGAN: Must be content to think you old, and so--
REGAN: But she knows what she does.
KING LEAR: Is this well spoken?
REGAN: I dare avouch it, sir: what, fifty followers?
REGAN: Is it not well? What should you need of more?
REGAN: Yea, or so many, sith that both charge and danger
REGAN: Speak 'gainst so great a number? How, in one house,
REGAN: Should many people, under two commands,
REGAN: Hold amity? 'Tis hard, almost impossible.
GONERIL: Why might not you, my lord, receive attendance
GONERIL: From those that she calls servants or from mine?
REGAN: Why not, my lord? If then they chanced to slack you,
REGAN: We could control them. If you will come to me,--
REGAN: For now I spy a danger,--I entreat you
REGAN: To bring but five and twenty: to no more
REGAN: Will I give place or notice.
KING LEAR: I gave you all--
REGAN: And in good time you gave it.
KING LEAR: Made you my guardians, my depositaries,
KING LEAR: But kept a reservation to be follow'd
KING LEAR: With such a number. What, must I come to you
KING LEAR: With five and twenty, Regan? said you so?
REGAN: And speak't again, my lord, no more with me.
KING LEAR: Those wicked creatures yet do look well-favour'd,
KING LEAR: When others are more wicked: not being the worst
KING LEAR: Stands in some rank of praise.
NARRATOR: To GONERIL
KING LEAR: I'll go with thee:
KING LEAR: Thy fifty yet doth double five and twenty,
KING LEAR: And thou art twice her love.
GONERIL: Hear me, my lord,
GONERIL: What need you five and twenty, ten, or five,
GONERIL: To follow in a house where twice so many
GONERIL: Have a command to tend you?
REGAN: What need one?
KING LEAR: O, reason not the need: our basest beggars
KING LEAR: Are in the poorest thing superfluous:
KING LEAR: Allow not nature more than nature needs,
KING LEAR: Man's life's as cheap as beast's: thou art a lady,
KING LEAR: If only to go warm were gorgeous,
KING LEAR: Why, nature needs not what thou gorgeous wear'st,
KING LEAR: Which scarcely keeps thee warm. But, for true need,--
KING LEAR: You heavens, give me that patience, patience I need!
KING LEAR: You see me here, you gods, a poor old man,
KING LEAR: As full of grief as age, wretched in both!
KING LEAR: If it be you that stir these daughters' hearts
KING LEAR: Against their father, fool me not so much
KING LEAR: To bear it tamely, touch me with noble anger,
KING LEAR: And let not women's weapons, water-drops,
KING LEAR: Stain my man's cheeks! No, you unnatural hags,
KING LEAR: I will have such revenges on you both,
KING LEAR: That all the world shall--I will do such things,--
KING LEAR: What they are, yet I know not: but they shall be
KING LEAR: The terrors of the earth. You think I'll weep
KING LEAR: No, I'll not weep:
KING LEAR: I have full cause of weeping, but this heart
KING LEAR: Shall break into a hundred thousand flaws,
KING LEAR: Or ere I'll weep. O fool, I shall go mad!
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING LEAR, GLOUCESTER, KENT, and Fool
NARRATOR: Storm and tempest
CORNWALL: Let us withdraw, 'twill be a storm.
REGAN: This house is little: the old man and his people
REGAN: Cannot be well bestow'd.
GONERIL: 'Tis his own blame, hath put himself from rest,
GONERIL: And must needs taste his folly.
REGAN: For his particular, I'll receive him gladly,
REGAN: But not one follower.
GONERIL: So am I purposed.
GONERIL: Where is my lord of Gloucester?
CORNWALL: Follow'd the old man forth: he is return'd.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: The king is in high rage.
CORNWALL: Whither is he going?
GLOUCESTER: He calls to horse, but will I know not whither.
CORNWALL: 'Tis best to give him way, he leads himself.
GONERIL: My lord, entreat him by no means to stay.
GLOUCESTER: Alack, the night comes on, and the bleak winds
GLOUCESTER: Do sorely ruffle, for many miles a bout
GLOUCESTER: There's scarce a bush.
REGAN: O, sir, to wilful men,
REGAN: The injuries that they themselves procure
REGAN: Must be their schoolmasters. Shut up your doors:
REGAN: He is attended with a desperate train,
REGAN: And what they may incense him to, being apt
REGAN: To have his ear abused, wisdom bids fear.
CORNWALL: Shut up your doors, my lord, 'tis a wild night:
CORNWALL: My Regan counsels well, come out o' the storm.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A heath.
NARRATOR: Storm still. Enter KENT and a Gentleman, meeting
KENT: Who's there, besides foul weather?
Gentleman: One minded like the weather, most unquietly.
KENT: I know you. Where's the king?
Gentleman: Contending with the fretful element:
Gentleman: Bids the winds blow the earth into the sea,
Gentleman: Or swell the curled water 'bove the main,
Gentleman: That things might change or cease, tears his white hair,
Gentleman: Which the impetuous blasts, with eyeless rage,
Gentleman: Catch in their fury, and make nothing of,
Gentleman: Strives in his little world of man to out-scorn
Gentleman: The to-and-fro-conflicting wind and rain.
Gentleman: This night, wherein the cub-drawn bear would couch,
Gentleman: The lion and the belly-pinched wolf
Gentleman: Keep their fur dry, unbonneted he runs,
Gentleman: And bids what will take all.
KENT: But who is with him?
Gentleman: None but the fool, who labours to out-jest
Gentleman: His heart-struck injuries.
KENT: Sir, I do know you,
KENT: And dare, upon the warrant of my note,
KENT: Commend a dear thing to you. There is division,
KENT: Although as yet the face of it be cover'd
KENT: With mutual cunning, 'twixt Albany and Cornwall,
KENT: Who have--as who have not, that their great stars
KENT: Throned and set high?--servants, who seem no less,
KENT: Which are to France the spies and speculations
KENT: Intelligent of our state, what hath been seen,
KENT: Either in snuffs and packings of the dukes,
KENT: Or the hard rein which both of them have borne
KENT: Against the old kind king, or something deeper,
KENT: Whereof perchance these are but furnishings,
KENT: But, true it is, from France there comes a power
KENT: Into this scatter'd kingdom, who already,
KENT: Wise in our negligence, have secret feet
KENT: In some of our best ports, and are at point
KENT: To show their open banner. Now to you:
KENT: If on my credit you dare build so far
KENT: To make your speed to Dover, you shall find
KENT: Some that will thank you, making just report
KENT: Of how unnatural and bemadding sorrow
KENT: The king hath cause to plain.
KENT: I am a gentleman of blood and breeding,
KENT: And, from some knowledge and assurance, offer
KENT: This office to you.
Gentleman: I will talk further with you.
KENT: No, do not.
KENT: For confirmation that I am much more
KENT: Than my out-wall, open this purse, and take
KENT: What it contains. If you shall see Cordelia,--
KENT: As fear not but you shall,--show her this ring,
KENT: And she will tell you who your fellow is
KENT: That yet you do not know. Fie on this storm!
KENT: I will go seek the king.
Gentleman: Give me your hand: have you no more to say?
KENT: Few words, but, to effect, more than all yet,
KENT: That, when we have found the king,--in which your pain
KENT: That way, I'll this,--he that first lights on him
KENT: Holla the other.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Another part of the heath. Storm still.
NARRATOR: Enter KING LEAR and Fool
KING LEAR: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow!
KING LEAR: You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout
KING LEAR: Till you have drench'd our steeples, drown'd the cocks!
KING LEAR: You sulphurous and thought-executing fires,
KING LEAR: Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts,
KING LEAR: Singe my white head! And thou, all-shaking thunder,
KING LEAR: Smite flat the thick rotundity o' the world!
KING LEAR: Crack nature's moulds, an germens spill at once,
KING LEAR: That make ingrateful man!
Fool: O nuncle, court holy-water in a dry
Fool: house is better than this rain-water out o' door.
Fool: Good nuncle, in, and ask thy daughters' blessing:
Fool: here's a night pities neither wise man nor fool.
KING LEAR: Rumble thy bellyful! Spit, fire! spout, rain!
KING LEAR: Nor rain, wind, thunder, fire, are my daughters:
KING LEAR: I tax not you, you elements, with unkindness,
KING LEAR: I never gave you kingdom, call'd you children,
KING LEAR: You owe me no subscription: then let fall
KING LEAR: Your horrible pleasure: here I stand, your slave,
KING LEAR: A poor, infirm, weak, and despised old man:
KING LEAR: But yet I call you servile ministers,
KING LEAR: That have with two pernicious daughters join'd
KING LEAR: Your high engender'd battles 'gainst a head
KING LEAR: So old and white as this. O! O! 'tis foul!
Fool: He that has a house to put's head in has a good
Fool: head-piece.
Fool: The cod-piece that will house
Fool: Before the head has any,
Fool: The head and he shall louse,
Fool: So beggars marry many.
Fool: The man that makes his toe
Fool: What he his heart should make
Fool: Shall of a corn cry woe,
Fool: And turn his sleep to wake.
Fool: For there was never yet fair woman but she made
Fool: mouths in a glass.
KING LEAR: No, I will be the pattern of all patience,
KING LEAR: I will say nothing.
NARRATOR: Enter KENT
KENT: Who's there?
Fool: Marry, here's grace and a cod-piece, that's a wise
Fool: man and a fool.
KENT: Alas, sir, are you here? things that love night
KENT: Love not such nights as these, the wrathful skies
KENT: Gallow the very wanderers of the dark,
KENT: And make them keep their caves: since I was man,
KENT: Such sheets of fire, such bursts of horrid thunder,
KENT: Such groans of roaring wind and rain, I never
KENT: Remember to have heard: man's nature cannot carry
KENT: The affliction nor the fear.
KING LEAR: Let the great gods,
KING LEAR: That keep this dreadful pother o'er our heads,
KING LEAR: Find out their enemies now. Tremble, thou wretch,
KING LEAR: That hast within thee undivulged crimes,
KING LEAR: Unwhipp'd of justice: hide thee, thou bloody hand,
KING LEAR: Thou perjured, and thou simular man of virtue
KING LEAR: That art incestuous: caitiff, to pieces shake,
KING LEAR: That under covert and convenient seeming
KING LEAR: Hast practised on man's life: close pent-up guilts,
KING LEAR: Rive your concealing continents, and cry
KING LEAR: These dreadful summoners grace. I am a man
KING LEAR: More sinn'd against than sinning.
KENT: Alack, bare-headed!
KENT: Gracious my lord, hard by here is a hovel,
KENT: Some friendship will it lend you 'gainst the tempest:
KENT: Repose you there, while I to this hard house--
KENT: More harder than the stones whereof 'tis raised,
KENT: Which even but now, demanding after you,
KENT: Denied me to come in--return, and force
KENT: Their scanted courtesy.
KING LEAR: My wits begin to turn.
KING LEAR: Come on, my boy: how dost, my boy? art cold?
KING LEAR: I am cold myself. Where is this straw, my fellow?
KING LEAR: The art of our necessities is strange,
KING LEAR: That can make vile things precious. Come,
KING LEAR: your hovel.
KING LEAR: Poor fool and knave, I have one part in my heart
KING LEAR: That's sorry yet for thee.
Fool: [Singing]
Fool: He that has and a little tiny wit--
Fool: With hey, ho, the wind and the rain,--
Fool: Must make content with his fortunes fit,
Fool: For the rain it raineth every day.
KING LEAR: True, my good boy. Come, bring us to this hovel.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING LEAR and KENT
Fool: This is a brave night to cool a courtezan.
Fool: I'll speak a prophecy ere I go:
Fool: When priests are more in word than matter,
Fool: When brewers mar their malt with water,
Fool: When nobles are their tailors' tutors,
Fool: No heretics burn'd, but wenches' suitors,
Fool: When every case in law is right,
Fool: No squire in debt, nor no poor knight,
Fool: When slanders do not live in tongues,
Fool: Nor cutpurses come not to throngs,
Fool: When usurers tell their gold i' the field,
Fool: And bawds and whores do churches build,
Fool: Then shall the realm of Albion
Fool: Come to great confusion:
Fool: Then comes the time, who lives to see't,
Fool: That going shall be used with feet.
Fool: This prophecy Merlin shall make, for I live before his time.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER and EDMUND
GLOUCESTER: Alack, alack, Edmund, I like not this unnatural
GLOUCESTER: dealing. When I desire their leave that I might
GLOUCESTER: pity him, they took from me the use of mine own
GLOUCESTER: house, charged me, on pain of their perpetual
GLOUCESTER: displeasure, neither to speak of him, entreat for
GLOUCESTER: him, nor any way sustain him.
EDMUND: Most savage and unnatural!
GLOUCESTER: Go to, say you nothing. There's a division betwixt
GLOUCESTER: the dukes, and a worse matter than that: I have
GLOUCESTER: received a letter this night, 'tis dangerous to be
GLOUCESTER: spoken, I have locked the letter in my closet:
GLOUCESTER: these injuries the king now bears will be revenged
GLOUCESTER: home, there's part of a power already footed: we
GLOUCESTER: must incline to the king. I will seek him, and
GLOUCESTER: privily relieve him: go you and maintain talk with
GLOUCESTER: the duke, that my charity be not of him perceived:
GLOUCESTER: if he ask for me. I am ill, and gone to bed.
GLOUCESTER: Though I die for it, as no less is threatened me,
GLOUCESTER: the king my old master must be relieved. There is
GLOUCESTER: some strange thing toward, Edmund, pray you, be careful.
NARRATOR: Exit
EDMUND: This courtesy, forbid thee, shall the duke
EDMUND: Instantly know, and of that letter too:
EDMUND: This seems a fair deserving, and must draw me
EDMUND: That which my father loses, no less than all:
EDMUND: The younger rises when the old doth fall.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The heath. Before a hovel.
NARRATOR: Enter KING LEAR, KENT, and Fool
KENT: Here is the place, my lord, good my lord, enter:
KENT: The tyranny of the open night's too rough
KENT: For nature to endure.
NARRATOR: Storm still
KING LEAR: Let me alone.
KENT: Good my lord, enter here.
KING LEAR: Wilt break my heart?
KENT: I had rather break mine own. Good my lord, enter.
KING LEAR: Thou think'st 'tis much that this contentious storm
KING LEAR: Invades us to the skin: so 'tis to thee,
KING LEAR: But where the greater malady is fix'd,
KING LEAR: The lesser is scarce felt. Thou'ldst shun a bear,
KING LEAR: But if thy flight lay toward the raging sea,
KING LEAR: Thou'ldst meet the bear i' the mouth. When the
KING LEAR: mind's free,
KING LEAR: The body's delicate: the tempest in my mind
KING LEAR: Doth from my senses take all feeling else
KING LEAR: Save what beats there. Filial ingratitude!
KING LEAR: Is it not as this mouth should tear this hand
KING LEAR: For lifting food to't? But I will punish home:
KING LEAR: No, I will weep no more. In such a night
KING LEAR: To shut me out! Pour on, I will endure.
KING LEAR: In such a night as this! O Regan, Goneril!
KING LEAR: Your old kind father, whose frank heart gave all,--
KING LEAR: O, that way madness lies, let me shun that,
KING LEAR: No more of that.
KENT: Good my lord, enter here.
KING LEAR: Prithee, go in thyself: seek thine own ease:
KING LEAR: This tempest will not give me leave to ponder
KING LEAR: On things would hurt me more. But I'll go in.
NARRATOR: To the Fool
KING LEAR: In, boy, go first. You houseless poverty,--
KING LEAR: Nay, get thee in. I'll pray, and then I'll sleep.
NARRATOR: Fool goes in
KING LEAR: Poor naked wretches, whereso'er you are,
KING LEAR: That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm,
KING LEAR: How shall your houseless heads and unfed sides,
KING LEAR: Your loop'd and window'd raggedness, defend you
KING LEAR: From seasons such as these? O, I have ta'en
KING LEAR: Too little care of this! Take physic, pomp,
KING LEAR: Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel,
KING LEAR: That thou mayst shake the superflux to them,
KING LEAR: And show the heavens more just.
EDGAR: [Within]  Fathom and half, fathom and half! Poor Tom!
NARRATOR: The Fool runs out from the hovel
Fool: Come not in here, nuncle, here's a spirit
Fool: Help me, help me!
KENT: Give me thy hand. Who's there?
Fool: A spirit, a spirit: he says his name's poor Tom.
KENT: What art thou that dost grumble there i' the straw?
KENT: Come forth.
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR disguised as a mad man
EDGAR: Away! the foul fiend follows me!
EDGAR: Through the sharp hawthorn blows the cold wind.
EDGAR: Hum! go to thy cold bed, and warm thee.
KING LEAR: Hast thou given all to thy two daughters?
KING LEAR: And art thou come to this?
EDGAR: Who gives any thing to poor Tom? whom the foul
EDGAR: fiend hath led through fire and through flame, and
EDGAR: through ford and whirlipool e'er bog and quagmire,
EDGAR: that hath laid knives under his pillow, and halters
EDGAR: in his pew, set ratsbane by his porridge, made film
EDGAR: proud of heart, to ride on a bay trotting-horse over
EDGAR: four-inched bridges, to course his own shadow for a
EDGAR: traitor. Bless thy five wits! Tom's a-cold,--O, do
EDGAR: de, do de, do de. Bless thee from whirlwinds,
EDGAR: star-blasting, and taking! Do poor Tom some
EDGAR: charity, whom the foul fiend vexes: there could I
EDGAR: have him now,--and there,--and there again, and there.
NARRATOR: Storm still
KING LEAR: What, have his daughters brought him to this pass?
KING LEAR: Couldst thou save nothing? Didst thou give them all?
Fool: Nay, he reserved a blanket, else we had been all shamed.
KING LEAR: Now, all the plagues that in the pendulous air
KING LEAR: Hang fated o'er men's faults light on thy daughters!
KENT: He hath no daughters, sir.
KING LEAR: Death, traitor! nothing could have subdued nature
KING LEAR: To such a lowness but his unkind daughters.
KING LEAR: Is it the fashion, that discarded fathers
KING LEAR: Should have thus little mercy on their flesh?
KING LEAR: Judicious punishment! 'twas this flesh begot
KING LEAR: Those pelican daughters.
EDGAR: Pillicock sat on Pillicock-hill:
EDGAR: Halloo, halloo, loo, loo!
Fool: This cold night will turn us all to fools and madmen.
EDGAR: Take heed o' the foul fiend: obey thy parents,
EDGAR: keep thy word justly, swear not, commit not with
EDGAR: man's sworn spouse, set not thy sweet heart on proud
EDGAR: array. Tom's a-cold.
KING LEAR: What hast thou been?
EDGAR: A serving-man, proud in heart and mind, that curled
EDGAR: my hair, wore gloves in my cap, served the lust of
EDGAR: my mistress' heart, and did the act of darkness with
EDGAR: her, swore as many oaths as I spake words, and
EDGAR: broke them in the sweet face of heaven: one that
EDGAR: slept in the contriving of lust, and waked to do it:
EDGAR: wine loved I deeply, dice dearly: and in woman
EDGAR: out-paramoured the Turk: false of heart, light of
EDGAR: ear, bloody of hand, hog in sloth, fox in stealth,
EDGAR: wolf in greediness, dog in madness, lion in prey.
EDGAR: Let not the creaking of shoes nor the rustling of
EDGAR: silks betray thy poor heart to woman: keep thy foot
EDGAR: out of brothels, thy hand out of plackets, thy pen
EDGAR: from lenders' books, and defy the foul fiend.
EDGAR: Still through the hawthorn blows the cold wind:
EDGAR: Says suum, mun, ha, no, nonny.
EDGAR: Dolphin my boy, my boy, sessa! let him trot by.
NARRATOR: Storm still
KING LEAR: Why, thou wert better in thy grave than to answer
KING LEAR: with thy uncovered body this extremity of the skies.
KING LEAR: Is man no more than this? Consider him well. Thou
KING LEAR: owest the worm no silk, the beast no hide, the sheep
KING LEAR: no wool, the cat no perfume. Ha! here's three on
KING LEAR: 's are sophisticated! Thou art the thing itself:
KING LEAR: unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor bare,
KING LEAR: forked animal as thou art. Off, off, you lendings!
KING LEAR: come unbutton here.
NARRATOR: Tearing off his clothes
Fool: Prithee, nuncle, be contented, 'tis a naughty night
Fool: to swim in. Now a little fire in a wild field were
Fool: like an old lecher's heart, a small spark, all the
Fool: rest on's body cold. Look, here comes a walking fire.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, with a torch
EDGAR: This is the foul fiend Flibbertigibbet: he begins
EDGAR: at curfew, and walks till the first cock, he gives
EDGAR: the web and the pin, squints the eye, and makes the
EDGAR: hare-lip, mildews the white wheat, and hurts the
EDGAR: poor creature of earth.
EDGAR: S. Withold footed thrice the old,
EDGAR: He met the night-mare, and her nine-fold,
EDGAR: Bid her alight,
EDGAR: And her troth plight,
EDGAR: And, aroint thee, witch, aroint thee!
KENT: How fares your grace?
KING LEAR: What's he?
KENT: Who's there? What is't you seek?
GLOUCESTER: What are you there? Your names?
EDGAR: Poor Tom, that eats the swimming frog, the toad,
EDGAR: the tadpole, the wall-newt and the water, that in
EDGAR: the fury of his heart, when the foul fiend rages,
EDGAR: eats cow-dung for sallets, swallows the old rat and
EDGAR: the ditch-dog, drinks the green mantle of the
EDGAR: standing pool, who is whipped from tithing to
EDGAR: tithing, and stock- punished, and imprisoned, who
EDGAR: hath had three suits to his back, six shirts to his
EDGAR: body, horse to ride, and weapon to wear,
EDGAR: But mice and rats, and such small deer,
EDGAR: Have been Tom's food for seven long year.
EDGAR: Beware my follower. Peace, Smulkin, peace, thou fiend!
GLOUCESTER: What, hath your grace no better company?
EDGAR: The prince of darkness is a gentleman:
EDGAR: Modo he's call'd, and Mahu.
GLOUCESTER: Our flesh and blood is grown so vile, my lord,
GLOUCESTER: That it doth hate what gets it.
EDGAR: Poor Tom's a-cold.
GLOUCESTER: Go in with me: my duty cannot suffer
GLOUCESTER: To obey in all your daughters' hard commands:
GLOUCESTER: Though their injunction be to bar my doors,
GLOUCESTER: And let this tyrannous night take hold upon you,
GLOUCESTER: Yet have I ventured to come seek you out,
GLOUCESTER: And bring you where both fire and food is ready.
KING LEAR: First let me talk with this philosopher.
KING LEAR: What is the cause of thunder?
KENT: Good my lord, take his offer, go into the house.
KING LEAR: I'll talk a word with this same learned Theban.
KING LEAR: What is your study?
EDGAR: How to prevent the fiend, and to kill vermin.
KING LEAR: Let me ask you one word in private.
KENT: Importune him once more to go, my lord,
KENT: His wits begin to unsettle.
GLOUCESTER: Canst thou blame him?
NARRATOR: Storm still
GLOUCESTER: His daughters seek his death: ah, that good Kent!
GLOUCESTER: He said it would be thus, poor banish'd man!
GLOUCESTER: Thou say'st the king grows mad, I'll tell thee, friend,
GLOUCESTER: I am almost mad myself: I had a son,
GLOUCESTER: Now outlaw'd from my blood, he sought my life,
GLOUCESTER: But lately, very late: I loved him, friend,
GLOUCESTER: No father his son dearer: truth to tell thee,
GLOUCESTER: The grief hath crazed my wits. What a night's this!
GLOUCESTER: I do beseech your grace,--
KING LEAR: O, cry your mercy, sir.
KING LEAR: Noble philosopher, your company.
EDGAR: Tom's a-cold.
GLOUCESTER: In, fellow, there, into the hovel: keep thee warm.
KING LEAR: Come let's in all.
KENT: This way, my lord.
KING LEAR: With him,
KING LEAR: I will keep still with my philosopher.
KENT: Good my lord, soothe him, let him take the fellow.
