GLOUCESTER: Take him you on.
KENT: Sirrah, come on, go along with us.
KING LEAR: Come, good Athenian.
GLOUCESTER: No words, no words: hush.
EDGAR: Child Rowland to the dark tower came,
EDGAR: His word was still,--Fie, foh, and fum,
EDGAR: I smell the blood of a British man.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter CORNWALL and EDMUND
CORNWALL: I will have my revenge ere I depart his house.
EDMUND: How, my lord, I may be censured, that nature thus
EDMUND: gives way to loyalty, something fears me to think
EDMUND: of.
CORNWALL: I now perceive, it was not altogether your
CORNWALL: brother's evil disposition made him seek his death,
CORNWALL: but a provoking merit, set a-work by a reprovable
CORNWALL: badness in himself.
EDMUND: How malicious is my fortune, that I must repent to
EDMUND: be just! This is the letter he spoke of, which
EDMUND: approves him an intelligent party to the advantages
EDMUND: of France: O heavens! that this treason were not,
EDMUND: or not I the detector!
CORNWALL: o with me to the duchess.
EDMUND: If the matter of this paper be certain, you have
EDMUND: mighty business in hand.
CORNWALL: True or false, it hath made thee earl of
CORNWALL: Gloucester. Seek out where thy father is, that he
CORNWALL: may be ready for our apprehension.
EDMUND: [Aside]  If I find him comforting the king, it will
EDMUND: stuff his suspicion more fully.--I will persevere in
EDMUND: my course of loyalty, though the conflict be sore
EDMUND: between that and my blood.
CORNWALL: I will lay trust upon thee, and thou shalt find a
CORNWALL: dearer father in my love.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. A chamber in a farmhouse adjoining the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, KING LEAR, KENT, Fool, and EDGAR
GLOUCESTER: Here is better than the open air, take it
GLOUCESTER: thankfully. I will piece out the comfort with what
GLOUCESTER: addition I can: I will not be long from you.
KENT: All the power of his wits have given way to his
KENT: impatience: the gods reward your kindness!
NARRATOR: Exit GLOUCESTER
EDGAR: Frateretto calls me, and tells me
EDGAR: Nero is an angler in the lake of darkness.
EDGAR: Pray, innocent, and beware the foul fiend.
Fool: Prithee, nuncle, tell me whether a madman be a
Fool: gentleman or a yeoman?
KING LEAR: A king, a king!
Fool: No, he's a yeoman that has a gentleman to his son,
Fool: for he's a mad yeoman that sees his son a gentleman
Fool: before him.
KING LEAR: To have a thousand with red burning spits
KING LEAR: Come hissing in upon 'em,--
EDGAR: The foul fiend bites my back.
Fool: He's mad that trusts in the tameness of a wolf, a
Fool: horse's health, a boy's love, or a whore's oath.
KING LEAR: It shall be done, I will arraign them straight.
NARRATOR: To EDGAR
KING LEAR: Come, sit thou here, most learned justicer,
NARRATOR: To the Fool
KING LEAR: Thou, sapient sir, sit here. Now, you she foxes!
EDGAR: Look, where he stands and glares!
EDGAR: Wantest thou eyes at trial, madam?
EDGAR: Come o'er the bourn, Bessy, to me,--
Fool: Her boat hath a leak,
Fool: And she must not speak
Fool: Why she dares not come over to thee.
EDGAR: The foul fiend haunts poor Tom in the voice of a
EDGAR: nightingale. Hopdance cries in Tom's belly for two
EDGAR: white herring. Croak not, black angel, I have no
EDGAR: food for thee.
KENT: How do you, sir? Stand you not so amazed:
KENT: Will you lie down and rest upon the cushions?
KING LEAR: I'll see their trial first. Bring in the evidence.
NARRATOR: To EDGAR
KING LEAR: Thou robed man of justice, take thy place,
NARRATOR: To the Fool
KING LEAR: And thou, his yoke-fellow of equity,
KING LEAR: Bench by his side:
NARRATOR: To KENT
KING LEAR: you are o' the commission,
KING LEAR: Sit you too.
EDGAR: Let us deal justly.
EDGAR: Sleepest or wakest thou, jolly shepherd?
EDGAR: Thy sheep be in the corn,
EDGAR: And for one blast of thy minikin mouth,
EDGAR: Thy sheep shall take no harm.
EDGAR: Pur! the cat is gray.
KING LEAR: Arraign her first, 'tis Goneril. I here take my
KING LEAR: oath before this honourable assembly, she kicked the
KING LEAR: poor king her father.
Fool: Come hither, mistress. Is your name Goneril?
KING LEAR: She cannot deny it.
Fool: Cry you mercy, I took you for a joint-stool.
KING LEAR: And here's another, whose warp'd looks proclaim
KING LEAR: What store her heart is made on. Stop her there!
KING LEAR: Arms, arms, sword, fire! Corruption in the place!
KING LEAR: False justicer, why hast thou let her 'scape?
EDGAR: Bless thy five wits!
KENT: O pity! Sir, where is the patience now,
KENT: That thou so oft have boasted to retain?
EDGAR: [Aside]  My tears begin to take his part so much,
EDGAR: They'll mar my counterfeiting.
KING LEAR: The little dogs and all, Tray, Blanch, and
KING LEAR: Sweet-heart, see, they bark at me.
EDGAR: Tom will throw his head at them. Avaunt, you curs!
EDGAR: Be thy mouth or black or white,
EDGAR: Tooth that poisons if it bite,
EDGAR: Mastiff, grey-hound, mongrel grim,
EDGAR: Hound or spaniel, brach or lym,
EDGAR: Or bobtail tike or trundle-tail,
EDGAR: Tom will make them weep and wail:
EDGAR: For, with throwing thus my head,
EDGAR: Dogs leap the hatch, and all are fled.
EDGAR: Do de, de, de. Sessa! Come, march to wakes and
EDGAR: fairs and market-towns. Poor Tom, thy horn is dry.
KING LEAR: Then let them anatomize Regan, see what breeds
KING LEAR: about her heart. Is there any cause in nature that
KING LEAR: makes these hard hearts?
NARRATOR: To EDGAR
KING LEAR: You, sir, I entertain for one of my hundred, only I
KING LEAR: do not like the fashion of your garments: you will
KING LEAR: say they are Persian attire: but let them be changed.
KENT: Now, good my lord, lie here and rest awhile.
KING LEAR: Make no noise, make no noise, draw the curtains:
KING LEAR: so, so, so. We'll go to supper i' he morning. So, so, so.
Fool: And I'll go to bed at noon.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Come hither, friend: where is the king my master?
KENT: Here, sir, but trouble him not, his wits are gone.
GLOUCESTER: Good friend, I prithee, take him in thy arms,
GLOUCESTER: I have o'erheard a plot of death upon him:
GLOUCESTER: There is a litter ready, lay him in 't,
GLOUCESTER: And drive towards Dover, friend, where thou shalt meet
GLOUCESTER: Both welcome and protection. Take up thy master:
GLOUCESTER: If thou shouldst dally half an hour, his life,
GLOUCESTER: With thine, and all that offer to defend him,
GLOUCESTER: Stand in assured loss: take up, take up,
GLOUCESTER: And follow me, that will to some provision
GLOUCESTER: Give thee quick conduct.
KENT: Oppressed nature sleeps:
KENT: This rest might yet have balm'd thy broken senses,
KENT: Which, if convenience will not allow,
KENT: Stand in hard cure.
NARRATOR: To the Fool
KENT: Come, help to bear thy master,
KENT: Thou must not stay behind.
GLOUCESTER: Come, come, away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but EDGAR
EDGAR: When we our betters see bearing our woes,
EDGAR: We scarcely think our miseries our foes.
EDGAR: Who alone suffers suffers most i' the mind,
EDGAR: Leaving free things and happy shows behind:
EDGAR: But then the mind much sufferance doth o'er skip,
EDGAR: When grief hath mates, and bearing fellowship.
EDGAR: How light and portable my pain seems now,
EDGAR: When that which makes me bend makes the king bow,
EDGAR: He childed as I father'd! Tom, away!
EDGAR: Mark the high noises, and thyself bewray,
EDGAR: When false opinion, whose wrong thought defiles thee,
EDGAR: In thy just proof, repeals and reconciles thee.
EDGAR: What will hap more to-night, safe 'scape the king!
EDGAR: Lurk, lurk.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter CORNWALL, REGAN, GONERIL, EDMUND, and Servants
CORNWALL: Post speedily to my lord your husband, show him
CORNWALL: this letter: the army of France is landed. Seek
CORNWALL: out the villain Gloucester.
NARRATOR: Exeunt some of the Servants
REGAN: Hang him instantly.
GONERIL: Pluck out his eyes.
CORNWALL: Leave him to my displeasure. Edmund, keep you our
CORNWALL: sister company: the revenges we are bound to take
CORNWALL: upon your traitorous father are not fit for your
CORNWALL: beholding. Advise the duke, where you are going, to
CORNWALL: a most festinate preparation: we are bound to the
CORNWALL: like. Our posts shall be swift and intelligent
CORNWALL: betwixt us. Farewell, dear sister: farewell, my
CORNWALL: lord of Gloucester.
NARRATOR: Enter OSWALD
CORNWALL: How now! where's the king?
OSWALD: My lord of Gloucester hath convey'd him hence:
OSWALD: Some five or six and thirty of his knights,
OSWALD: Hot questrists after him, met him at gate,
OSWALD: Who, with some other of the lords dependants,
OSWALD: Are gone with him towards Dover, where they boast
OSWALD: To have well-armed friends.
CORNWALL: Get horses for your mistress.
GONERIL: Farewell, sweet lord, and sister.
CORNWALL: Edmund, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GONERIL, EDMUND, and OSWALD
CORNWALL: Go seek the traitor Gloucester,
CORNWALL: Pinion him like a thief, bring him before us.
NARRATOR: Exeunt other Servants
CORNWALL: Though well we may not pass upon his life
CORNWALL: Without the form of justice, yet our power
CORNWALL: Shall do a courtesy to our wrath, which men
CORNWALL: May blame, but not control. Who's there? the traitor?
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, brought in by two or three
REGAN: Ingrateful fox! 'tis he.
CORNWALL: Bind fast his corky arms.
GLOUCESTER: What mean your graces? Good my friends, consider
GLOUCESTER: You are my guests: do me no foul play, friends.
CORNWALL: Bind him, I say.
NARRATOR: Servants bind him
REGAN: Hard, hard. O filthy traitor!
GLOUCESTER: Unmerciful lady as you are, I'm none.
CORNWALL: To this chair bind him. Villain, thou shalt find--
NARRATOR: REGAN plucks his beard
GLOUCESTER: By the kind gods, 'tis most ignobly done
GLOUCESTER: To pluck me by the beard.
REGAN: So white, and such a traitor!
GLOUCESTER: Naughty lady,
GLOUCESTER: These hairs, which thou dost ravish from my chin,
GLOUCESTER: Will quicken, and accuse thee: I am your host:
GLOUCESTER: With robbers' hands my hospitable favours
GLOUCESTER: You should not ruffle thus. What will you do?
CORNWALL: Come, sir, what letters had you late from France?
REGAN: Be simple answerer, for we know the truth.
CORNWALL: And what confederacy have you with the traitors
CORNWALL: Late footed in the kingdom?
REGAN: To whose hands have you sent the lunatic king? Speak.
GLOUCESTER: I have a letter guessingly set down,
GLOUCESTER: Which came from one that's of a neutral heart,
GLOUCESTER: And not from one opposed.
CORNWALL: Cunning.
REGAN: And false.
CORNWALL: Where hast thou sent the king?
GLOUCESTER: To Dover.
REGAN: Wherefore to Dover? Wast thou not charged at peril--
CORNWALL: Wherefore to Dover? Let him first answer that.
GLOUCESTER: I am tied to the stake, and I must stand the course.
REGAN: Wherefore to Dover, sir?
GLOUCESTER: Because I would not see thy cruel nails
GLOUCESTER: Pluck out his poor old eyes, nor thy fierce sister
GLOUCESTER: In his anointed flesh stick boarish fangs.
GLOUCESTER: The sea, with such a storm as his bare head
GLOUCESTER: In hell-black night endured, would have buoy'd up,
GLOUCESTER: And quench'd the stelled fires:
GLOUCESTER: Yet, poor old heart, he holp the heavens to rain.
GLOUCESTER: If wolves had at thy gate howl'd that stern time,
GLOUCESTER: Thou shouldst have said 'Good porter, turn the key,'
GLOUCESTER: All cruels else subscribed: but I shall see
GLOUCESTER: The winged vengeance overtake such children.
CORNWALL: See't shalt thou never. Fellows, hold the chair.
CORNWALL: Upon these eyes of thine I'll set my foot.
GLOUCESTER: He that will think to live till he be old,
GLOUCESTER: Give me some help! O cruel! O you gods!
REGAN: One side will mock another, the other too.
CORNWALL: If you see vengeance,--
First Servant: Hold your hand, my lord:
First Servant: I have served you ever since I was a child,
First Servant: But better service have I never done you
First Servant: Than now to bid you hold.
REGAN: How now, you dog!
First Servant: If you did wear a beard upon your chin,
First Servant: I'd shake it on this quarrel. What do you mean?
CORNWALL: My villain!
NARRATOR: They draw and fight
First Servant: Nay, then, come on, and take the chance of anger.
REGAN: Give me thy sword. A peasant stand up thus!
NARRATOR: Takes a sword, and runs at him behind
First Servant: O, I am slain! My lord, you have one eye left
First Servant: To see some mischief on him. O!
NARRATOR: Dies
CORNWALL: Lest it see more, prevent it. Out, vile jelly!
CORNWALL: Where is thy lustre now?
GLOUCESTER: All dark and comfortless. Where's my son Edmund?
GLOUCESTER: Edmund, enkindle all the sparks of nature,
GLOUCESTER: To quit this horrid act.
REGAN: Out, treacherous villain!
REGAN: Thou call'st on him that hates thee: it was he
REGAN: That made the overture of thy treasons to us,
REGAN: Who is too good to pity thee.
GLOUCESTER: O my follies! then Edgar was abused.
GLOUCESTER: Kind gods, forgive me that, and prosper him!
REGAN: Go thrust him out at gates, and let him smell
REGAN: His way to Dover.
NARRATOR: Exit one with GLOUCESTER
REGAN: How is't, my lord? how look you?
CORNWALL: I have received a hurt: follow me, lady.
CORNWALL: Turn out that eyeless villain, throw this slave
CORNWALL: Upon the dunghill. Regan, I bleed apace:
CORNWALL: Untimely comes this hurt: give me your arm.
NARRATOR: Exit CORNWALL, led by REGAN
Second Servant: I'll never care what wickedness I do,
Second Servant: If this man come to good.
Third Servant: If she live long,
Third Servant: And in the end meet the old course of death,
Third Servant: Women will all turn monsters.
Second Servant: Let's follow the old earl, and get the Bedlam
Second Servant: To lead him where he would: his roguish madness
Second Servant: Allows itself to any thing.
Third Servant: Go thou: I'll fetch some flax and whites of eggs
Third Servant: To apply to his bleeding face. Now, heaven help him!
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The heath.
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR
EDGAR: Yet better thus, and known to be contemn'd,
EDGAR: Than still contemn'd and flatter'd. To be worst,
EDGAR: The lowest and most dejected thing of fortune,
EDGAR: Stands still in esperance, lives not in fear:
EDGAR: The lamentable change is from the best,
EDGAR: The worst returns to laughter. Welcome, then,
EDGAR: Thou unsubstantial air that I embrace!
EDGAR: The wretch that thou hast blown unto the worst
EDGAR: Owes nothing to thy blasts. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, led by an Old Man
EDGAR: My father, poorly led? World, world, O world!
EDGAR: But that thy strange mutations make us hate thee,
EDGAR: Lie would not yield to age.
Old Man: O, my good lord, I have been your tenant, and
Old Man: your father's tenant, these fourscore years.
GLOUCESTER: Away, get thee away, good friend, be gone:
GLOUCESTER: Thy comforts can do me no good at all,
GLOUCESTER: Thee they may hurt.
Old Man: Alack, sir, you cannot see your way.
GLOUCESTER: I have no way, and therefore want no eyes,
GLOUCESTER: I stumbled when I saw: full oft 'tis seen,
GLOUCESTER: Our means secure us, and our mere defects
GLOUCESTER: Prove our commodities. O dear son Edgar,
GLOUCESTER: The food of thy abused father's wrath!
GLOUCESTER: Might I but live to see thee in my touch,
GLOUCESTER: I'ld say I had eyes again!
Old Man: How now! Who's there?
EDGAR: [Aside]  O gods! Who is't can say 'I am at
EDGAR: the worst'?
EDGAR: I am worse than e'er I was.
Old Man: 'Tis poor mad Tom.
EDGAR: [Aside]  And worse I may be yet: the worst is not
EDGAR: So long as we can say  'This is the worst.'
Old Man: Fellow, where goest?
GLOUCESTER: Is it a beggar-man?
Old Man: Madman and beggar too.
GLOUCESTER: He has some reason, else he could not beg.
GLOUCESTER: I' the last night's storm I such a fellow saw,
GLOUCESTER: Which made me think a man a worm: my son
GLOUCESTER: Came then into my mind, and yet my mind
GLOUCESTER: Was then scarce friends with him: I have heard
GLOUCESTER: more since.
GLOUCESTER: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods.
GLOUCESTER: They kill us for their sport.
EDGAR: [Aside]	How should this be?
EDGAR: Bad is the trade that must play fool to sorrow,
EDGAR: Angering itself and others.--Bless thee, master!
GLOUCESTER: Is that the naked fellow?
Old Man: Ay, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: Then, prithee, get thee gone: if, for my sake,
GLOUCESTER: Thou wilt o'ertake us, hence a mile or twain,
GLOUCESTER: I' the way toward Dover, do it for ancient love,
GLOUCESTER: And bring some covering for this naked soul,
GLOUCESTER: Who I'll entreat to lead me.
Old Man: Alack, sir, he is mad.
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis the times' plague, when madmen lead the blind.
GLOUCESTER: Do as I bid thee, or rather do thy pleasure,
GLOUCESTER: Above the rest, be gone.
Old Man: I'll bring him the best 'parel that I have,
Old Man: Come on't what will.
NARRATOR: Exit
GLOUCESTER: Sirrah, naked fellow,--
EDGAR: Poor Tom's a-cold.
NARRATOR: Aside
EDGAR: I cannot daub it further.
GLOUCESTER: Come hither, fellow.
EDGAR: [Aside]  And yet I must.--Bless thy sweet eyes, they bleed.
GLOUCESTER: Know'st thou the way to Dover?
EDGAR: Both stile and gate, horse-way and foot-path. Poor
EDGAR: Tom hath been scared out of his good wits: bless
EDGAR: thee, good man's son, from the foul fiend! five
EDGAR: fiends have been in poor Tom at once, of lust, as
EDGAR: Obidicut, Hobbididence, prince of dumbness, Mahu, of
EDGAR: stealing, Modo, of murder, Flibbertigibbet, of
EDGAR: mopping and mowing, who since possesses chambermaids
EDGAR: and waiting-women. So, bless thee, master!
GLOUCESTER: Here, take this purse, thou whom the heavens' plagues
GLOUCESTER: Have humbled to all strokes: that I am wretched
GLOUCESTER: Makes thee the happier: heavens, deal so still!
GLOUCESTER: Let the superfluous and lust-dieted man,
GLOUCESTER: That slaves your ordinance, that will not see
GLOUCESTER: Because he doth not feel, feel your power quickly,
GLOUCESTER: So distribution should undo excess,
GLOUCESTER: And each man have enough. Dost thou know Dover?
EDGAR: Ay, master.
GLOUCESTER: There is a cliff, whose high and bending head
GLOUCESTER: Looks fearfully in the confined deep:
GLOUCESTER: Bring me but to the very brim of it,
GLOUCESTER: And I'll repair the misery thou dost bear
GLOUCESTER: With something rich about me: from that place
GLOUCESTER: I shall no leading need.
EDGAR: Give me thy arm:
EDGAR: Poor Tom shall lead thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before ALBANY's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter GONERIL and EDMUND
GONERIL: Welcome, my lord: I marvel our mild husband
GONERIL: Not met us on the way.
NARRATOR: Enter OSWALD
GONERIL: Now, where's your master'?
OSWALD: Madam, within, but never man so changed.
OSWALD: I told him of the army that was landed,
OSWALD: He smiled at it: I told him you were coming:
OSWALD: His answer was 'The worse:' of Gloucester's treachery,
OSWALD: And of the loyal service of his son,
OSWALD: When I inform'd him, then he call'd me sot,
OSWALD: And told me I had turn'd the wrong side out:
OSWALD: What most he should dislike seems pleasant to him,
OSWALD: What like, offensive.
GONERIL: [To EDMUND]  Then shall you go no further.
GONERIL: It is the cowish terror of his spirit,
GONERIL: That dares not undertake: he'll not feel wrongs
GONERIL: Which tie him to an answer. Our wishes on the way
GONERIL: May prove effects. Back, Edmund, to my brother,
GONERIL: Hasten his musters and conduct his powers:
GONERIL: I must change arms at home, and give the distaff
GONERIL: Into my husband's hands. This trusty servant
GONERIL: Shall pass between us: ere long you are like to hear,
GONERIL: If you dare venture in your own behalf,
GONERIL: A mistress's command. Wear this, spare speech,
NARRATOR: Giving a favour
GONERIL: Decline your head: this kiss, if it durst speak,
GONERIL: Would stretch thy spirits up into the air:
GONERIL: Conceive, and fare thee well.
EDMUND: Yours in the ranks of death.
GONERIL: My most dear Gloucester!
NARRATOR: Exit EDMUND
GONERIL: O, the difference of man and man!
GONERIL: To thee a woman's services are due:
GONERIL: My fool usurps my body.
OSWALD: Madam, here comes my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter ALBANY
GONERIL: I have been worth the whistle.
ALBANY: O Goneril!
ALBANY: You are not worth the dust which the rude wind
ALBANY: Blows in your face. I fear your disposition:
ALBANY: That nature, which contemns its origin,
ALBANY: Cannot be border'd certain in itself,
ALBANY: She that herself will sliver and disbranch
ALBANY: From her material sap, perforce must wither
ALBANY: And come to deadly use.
GONERIL: No more, the text is foolish.
ALBANY: Wisdom and goodness to the vile seem vile:
ALBANY: Filths savour but themselves. What have you done?
ALBANY: Tigers, not daughters, what have you perform'd?
ALBANY: A father, and a gracious aged man,
ALBANY: Whose reverence even the head-lugg'd bear would lick,
ALBANY: Most barbarous, most degenerate! have you madded.
ALBANY: Could my good brother suffer you to do it?
ALBANY: A man, a prince, by him so benefited!
ALBANY: If that the heavens do not their visible spirits
ALBANY: Send quickly down to tame these vile offences,
ALBANY: It will come,
ALBANY: Humanity must perforce prey on itself,
ALBANY: Like monsters of the deep.
GONERIL: Milk-liver'd man!
GONERIL: That bear'st a cheek for blows, a head for wrongs,
GONERIL: Who hast not in thy brows an eye discerning
GONERIL: Thine honour from thy suffering, that not know'st
GONERIL: Fools do those villains pity who are punish'd
GONERIL: Ere they have done their mischief. Where's thy drum?
GONERIL: France spreads his banners in our noiseless land,
GONERIL: With plumed helm thy slayer begins threats,
GONERIL: Whiles thou, a moral fool, sit'st still, and criest
GONERIL: 'Alack, why does he so?'
ALBANY: See thyself, devil!
ALBANY: Proper deformity seems not in the fiend
ALBANY: So horrid as in woman.
GONERIL: O vain fool!
ALBANY: Thou changed and self-cover'd thing, for shame,
ALBANY: Be-monster not thy feature. Were't my fitness
ALBANY: To let these hands obey my blood,
ALBANY: They are apt enough to dislocate and tear
ALBANY: Thy flesh and bones: howe'er thou art a fiend,
ALBANY: A woman's shape doth shield thee.
GONERIL: Marry, your manhood now--
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
ALBANY: What news?
Messenger: O, my good lord, the Duke of Cornwall's dead:
Messenger: Slain by his servant, going to put out
Messenger: The other eye of Gloucester.
ALBANY: Gloucester's eye!
Messenger: A servant that he bred, thrill'd with remorse,
Messenger: Opposed against the act, bending his sword
Messenger: To his great master, who, thereat enraged,
Messenger: Flew on him, and amongst them fell'd him dead,
Messenger: But not without that harmful stroke, which since
Messenger: Hath pluck'd him after.
ALBANY: This shows you are above,
ALBANY: You justicers, that these our nether crimes
ALBANY: So speedily can venge! But, O poor Gloucester!
ALBANY: Lost he his other eye?
Messenger: Both, both, my lord.
Messenger: This letter, madam, craves a speedy answer,
Messenger: 'Tis from your sister.
GONERIL: [Aside]              One way I like this well,
GONERIL: But being widow, and my Gloucester with her,
GONERIL: May all the building in my fancy pluck
GONERIL: Upon my hateful life: another way,
GONERIL: The news is not so tart.--I'll read, and answer.
NARRATOR: Exit
ALBANY: Where was his son when they did take his eyes?
Messenger: Come with my lady hither.
ALBANY: He is not here.
Messenger: No, my good lord, I met him back again.
ALBANY: Knows he the wickedness?
Messenger: Ay, my good lord, 'twas he inform'd against him,
Messenger: And quit the house on purpose, that their punishment
Messenger: Might have the freer course.
ALBANY: Gloucester, I live
ALBANY: To thank thee for the love thou show'dst the king,
ALBANY: And to revenge thine eyes. Come hither, friend:
ALBANY: Tell me what more thou know'st.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The French camp near Dover.
NARRATOR: Enter KENT and a Gentleman
KENT: Why the King of France is so suddenly gone back
KENT: know you the reason?
Gentleman: Something he left imperfect in the
Gentleman: state, which since his coming forth is thought
Gentleman: of, which imports to the kingdom so much
Gentleman: fear and danger, that his personal return was
Gentleman: most required and necessary.
KENT: Who hath he left behind him general?
Gentleman: The Marshal of France, Monsieur La Far.
KENT: Did your letters pierce the queen to any
KENT: demonstration of grief?
Gentleman: Ay, sir, she took them, read them in my presence,
Gentleman: And now and then an ample tear trill'd down
Gentleman: Her delicate cheek: it seem'd she was a queen
Gentleman: Over her passion, who, most rebel-like,
Gentleman: Sought to be king o'er her.
KENT: O, then it moved her.
Gentleman: Not to a rage: patience and sorrow strove
Gentleman: Who should express her goodliest. You have seen
Gentleman: Sunshine and rain at once: her smiles and tears
Gentleman: Were like a better way: those happy smilets,
Gentleman: That play'd on her ripe lip, seem'd not to know
Gentleman: What guests were in her eyes, which parted thence,
Gentleman: As pearls from diamonds dropp'd. In brief,
Gentleman: Sorrow would be a rarity most beloved,
Gentleman: If all could so become it.
KENT: Made she no verbal question?
Gentleman: 'Faith, once or twice she heaved the name of 'father'
Gentleman: Pantingly forth, as if it press'd her heart:
Gentleman: Cried 'Sisters! sisters! Shame of ladies! sisters!
Gentleman: Kent! father! sisters! What, i' the storm? i' the night?
Gentleman: Let pity not be believed!' There she shook
Gentleman: The holy water from her heavenly eyes,
Gentleman: And clamour moisten'd: then away she started
Gentleman: To deal with grief alone.
KENT: It is the stars,
KENT: The stars above us, govern our conditions,
KENT: Else one self mate and mate could not beget
KENT: Such different issues. You spoke not with her since?
Gentleman: No.
KENT: Was this before the king return'd?
Gentleman: No, since.
KENT: Well, sir, the poor distressed Lear's i' the town,
KENT: Who sometime, in his better tune, remembers
KENT: What we are come about, and by no means
KENT: Will yield to see his daughter.
Gentleman: Why, good sir?
KENT: A sovereign shame so elbows him: his own unkindness,
KENT: That stripp'd her from his benediction, turn'd her
KENT: To foreign casualties, gave her dear rights
KENT: To his dog-hearted daughters, these things sting
KENT: His mind so venomously, that burning shame
KENT: Detains him from Cordelia.
Gentleman: Alack, poor gentleman!
KENT: Of Albany's and Cornwall's powers you heard not?
Gentleman: 'Tis so, they are afoot.
KENT: Well, sir, I'll bring you to our master Lear,
KENT: And leave you to attend him: some dear cause
KENT: Will in concealment wrap me up awhile,
KENT: When I am known aright, you shall not grieve
KENT: Lending me this acquaintance. I pray you, go
KENT: Along with me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same. A tent.
NARRATOR: Enter, with drum and colours, CORDELIA, Doctor, and Soldiers
CORDELIA: Alack, 'tis he: why, he was met even now
CORDELIA: As mad as the vex'd sea, singing aloud,
CORDELIA: Crown'd with rank fumiter and furrow-weeds,
CORDELIA: With bur-docks, hemlock, nettles, cuckoo-flowers,
CORDELIA: Darnel, and all the idle weeds that grow
CORDELIA: In our sustaining corn. A century send forth,
CORDELIA: Search every acre in the high-grown field,
CORDELIA: And bring him to our eye.
NARRATOR: Exit an Officer
CORDELIA: What can man's wisdom
CORDELIA: In the restoring his bereaved sense?
CORDELIA: He that helps him take all my outward worth.
Doctor: There is means, madam:
Doctor: Our foster-nurse of nature is repose,
Doctor: The which he lacks, that to provoke in him,
Doctor: Are many simples operative, whose power
Doctor: Will close the eye of anguish.
CORDELIA: All blest secrets,
CORDELIA: All you unpublish'd virtues of the earth,
CORDELIA: Spring with my tears! be aidant and remediate
CORDELIA: In the good man's distress! Seek, seek for him,
CORDELIA: Lest his ungovern'd rage dissolve the life
CORDELIA: That wants the means to lead it.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: News, madam,
Messenger: The British powers are marching hitherward.
CORDELIA: 'Tis known before, our preparation stands
CORDELIA: In expectation of them. O dear father,
CORDELIA: It is thy business that I go about,
CORDELIA: Therefore great France
CORDELIA: My mourning and important tears hath pitied.
CORDELIA: No blown ambition doth our arms incite,
CORDELIA: But love, dear love, and our aged father's right:
CORDELIA: Soon may I hear and see him!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Gloucester's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter REGAN and OSWALD
REGAN: But are my brother's powers set forth?
OSWALD: Ay, madam.
REGAN: Himself in person there?
OSWALD: Madam, with much ado:
OSWALD: Your sister is the better soldier.
REGAN: Lord Edmund spake not with your lord at home?
OSWALD: No, madam.
REGAN: What might import my sister's letter to him?
OSWALD: I know not, lady.
REGAN: 'Faith, he is posted hence on serious matter.
REGAN: It was great ignorance, Gloucester's eyes being out,
REGAN: To let him live: where he arrives he moves
REGAN: All hearts against us: Edmund, I think, is gone,
REGAN: In pity of his misery, to dispatch
REGAN: His nighted life: moreover, to descry
REGAN: The strength o' the enemy.
OSWALD: I must needs after him, madam, with my letter.
REGAN: Our troops set forth to-morrow: stay with us,
REGAN: The ways are dangerous.
OSWALD: I may not, madam:
OSWALD: My lady charged my duty in this business.
REGAN: Why should she write to Edmund? Might not you
REGAN: Transport her purposes by word? Belike,
REGAN: Something--I know not what: I'll love thee much,
REGAN: Let me unseal the letter.
OSWALD: Madam, I had rather--
REGAN: I know your lady does not love her husband,
REGAN: I am sure of that: and at her late being here
REGAN: She gave strange oeillades and most speaking looks
REGAN: To noble Edmund. I know you are of her bosom.
OSWALD: I, madam?
REGAN: I speak in understanding, you are, I know't:
REGAN: Therefore I do advise you, take this note:
REGAN: My lord is dead, Edmund and I have talk'd,
REGAN: And more convenient is he for my hand
REGAN: Than for your lady's: you may gather more.
REGAN: If you do find him, pray you, give him this,
REGAN: And when your mistress hears thus much from you,
REGAN: I pray, desire her call her wisdom to her.
REGAN: So, fare you well.
REGAN: If you do chance to hear of that blind traitor,
REGAN: Preferment falls on him that cuts him off.
OSWALD: Would I could meet him, madam! I should show
OSWALD: What party I do follow.
REGAN: Fare thee well.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Fields near Dover.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, and EDGAR dressed like a peasant
GLOUCESTER: When shall we come to the top of that same hill?
EDGAR: You do climb up it now: look, how we labour.
GLOUCESTER: Methinks the ground is even.
EDGAR: Horrible steep.
EDGAR: Hark, do you hear the sea?
GLOUCESTER: No, truly.
EDGAR: Why, then, your other senses grow imperfect
EDGAR: By your eyes' anguish.
GLOUCESTER: So may it be, indeed:
GLOUCESTER: Methinks thy voice is alter'd, and thou speak'st
GLOUCESTER: In better phrase and matter than thou didst.
EDGAR: You're much deceived: in nothing am I changed
EDGAR: But in my garments.
GLOUCESTER: Methinks you're better spoken.
EDGAR: Come on, sir, here's the place: stand still. How fearful
EDGAR: And dizzy 'tis, to cast one's eyes so low!
EDGAR: The crows and choughs that wing the midway air
EDGAR: Show scarce so gross as beetles: half way down
EDGAR: Hangs one that gathers samphire, dreadful trade!
EDGAR: Methinks he seems no bigger than his head:
EDGAR: The fishermen, that walk upon the beach,
EDGAR: Appear like mice, and yond tall anchoring bark,
EDGAR: Diminish'd to her cock, her cock, a buoy
EDGAR: Almost too small for sight: the murmuring surge,
EDGAR: That on the unnumber'd idle pebbles chafes,
EDGAR: Cannot be heard so high. I'll look no more,
EDGAR: Lest my brain turn, and the deficient sight
EDGAR: Topple down headlong.
GLOUCESTER: Set me where you stand.
EDGAR: Give me your hand: you are now within a foot
EDGAR: Of the extreme verge: for all beneath the moon
EDGAR: Would I not leap upright.
GLOUCESTER: Let go my hand.
GLOUCESTER: Here, friend, 's another purse, in it a jewel
GLOUCESTER: Well worth a poor man's taking: fairies and gods
GLOUCESTER: Prosper it with thee! Go thou farther off,
GLOUCESTER: Bid me farewell, and let me hear thee going.
EDGAR: Now fare you well, good sir.
GLOUCESTER: With all my heart.
EDGAR: Why I do trifle thus with his despair
EDGAR: Is done to cure it.
GLOUCESTER: [Kneeling]  O you mighty gods!
GLOUCESTER: This world I do renounce, and, in your sights,
GLOUCESTER: Shake patiently my great affliction off:
GLOUCESTER: If I could bear it longer, and not fall
GLOUCESTER: To quarrel with your great opposeless wills,
GLOUCESTER: My snuff and loathed part of nature should
GLOUCESTER: Burn itself out. If Edgar live, O, bless him!
GLOUCESTER: Now, fellow, fare thee well.
NARRATOR: He falls forward
EDGAR: Gone, sir: farewell.
EDGAR: And yet I know not how conceit may rob
EDGAR: The treasury of life, when life itself
EDGAR: Yields to the theft: had he been where he thought,
EDGAR: By this, had thought been past. Alive or dead?
EDGAR: Ho, you sir! friend! Hear you, sir! speak!
EDGAR: Thus might he pass indeed: yet he revives.
EDGAR: What are you, sir?
GLOUCESTER: Away, and let me die.
EDGAR: Hadst thou been aught but gossamer, feathers, air,
EDGAR: So many fathom down precipitating,
EDGAR: Thou'dst shiver'd like an egg: but thou dost breathe,
EDGAR: Hast heavy substance, bleed'st not, speak'st, art sound.
EDGAR: Ten masts at each make not the altitude
EDGAR: Which thou hast perpendicularly fell:
EDGAR: Thy life's a miracle. Speak yet again.
GLOUCESTER: But have I fall'n, or no?
EDGAR: From the dread summit of this chalky bourn.
EDGAR: Look up a-height, the shrill-gorged lark so far
EDGAR: Cannot be seen or heard: do but look up.
GLOUCESTER: Alack, I have no eyes.
GLOUCESTER: Is wretchedness deprived that benefit,
GLOUCESTER: To end itself by death? 'Twas yet some comfort,
GLOUCESTER: When misery could beguile the tyrant's rage,
GLOUCESTER: And frustrate his proud will.
EDGAR: Give me your arm:
EDGAR: Up: so. How is 't? Feel you your legs? You stand.
GLOUCESTER: Too well, too well.
EDGAR: This is above all strangeness.
EDGAR: Upon the crown o' the cliff, what thing was that
EDGAR: Which parted from you?
GLOUCESTER: A poor unfortunate beggar.
EDGAR: As I stood here below, methought his eyes
EDGAR: Were two full moons, he had a thousand noses,
EDGAR: Horns whelk'd and waved like the enridged sea:
EDGAR: It was some fiend, therefore, thou happy father,
EDGAR: Think that the clearest gods, who make them honours
EDGAR: Of men's impossibilities, have preserved thee.
GLOUCESTER: I do remember now: henceforth I'll bear
GLOUCESTER: Affliction till it do cry out itself
GLOUCESTER: 'Enough, enough,' and die. That thing you speak of,
GLOUCESTER: I took it for a man, often 'twould say
GLOUCESTER: 'The fiend, the fiend:' he led me to that place.
EDGAR: Bear free and patient thoughts. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter KING LEAR, fantastically dressed with wild flowers
EDGAR: The safer sense will ne'er accommodate
EDGAR: His master thus.
KING LEAR: No, they cannot touch me for coining, I am the
KING LEAR: king himself.
EDGAR: O thou side-piercing sight!
KING LEAR: Nature's above art in that respect. There's your
KING LEAR: press-money. That fellow handles his bow like a
KING LEAR: crow-keeper: draw me a clothier's yard. Look,
KING LEAR: look, a mouse! Peace, peace, this piece of toasted
KING LEAR: cheese will do 't. There's my gauntlet, I'll prove
KING LEAR: it on a giant. Bring up the brown bills. O, well
KING LEAR: flown, bird! i' the clout, i' the clout: hewgh!
KING LEAR: Give the word.
EDGAR: Sweet marjoram.
KING LEAR: Pass.
GLOUCESTER: I know that voice.
KING LEAR: Ha! Goneril, with a white beard! They flattered
KING LEAR: me like a dog, and told me I had white hairs in my
KING LEAR: beard ere the black ones were there. To say 'ay'
KING LEAR: and 'no' to every thing that I said!--'Ay' and 'no'
KING LEAR: too was no good divinity. When the rain came to
KING LEAR: wet me once, and the wind to make me chatter, when
KING LEAR: the thunder would not peace at my bidding, there I
KING LEAR: found 'em, there I smelt 'em out. Go to, they are
KING LEAR: not men o' their words: they told me I was every
KING LEAR: thing, 'tis a lie, I am not ague-proof.
GLOUCESTER: The trick of that voice I do well remember:
GLOUCESTER: Is 't not the king?
KING LEAR: Ay, every inch a king:
KING LEAR: When I do stare, see how the subject quakes.
KING LEAR: I pardon that man's life. What was thy cause? Adultery?
KING LEAR: Thou shalt not die: die for adultery! No:
KING LEAR: The wren goes to 't, and the small gilded fly
KING LEAR: Does lecher in my sight.
KING LEAR: Let copulation thrive, for Gloucester's bastard son
KING LEAR: Was kinder to his father than my daughters
KING LEAR: Got 'tween the lawful sheets.
KING LEAR: To 't, luxury, pell-mell! for I lack soldiers.
KING LEAR: Behold yond simpering dame,
KING LEAR: Whose face between her forks presages snow,
KING LEAR: That minces virtue, and does shake the head
KING LEAR: To hear of pleasure's name,
KING LEAR: The fitchew, nor the soiled horse, goes to 't
KING LEAR: With a more riotous appetite.
KING LEAR: Down from the waist they are Centaurs,
KING LEAR: Though women all above:
KING LEAR: But to the girdle do the gods inherit,
KING LEAR: Beneath is all the fiends',
KING LEAR: There's hell, there's darkness, there's the
KING LEAR: sulphurous pit,
KING LEAR: Burning, scalding, stench, consumption, fie,
KING LEAR: fie, fie! pah, pah! Give me an ounce of civet,
KING LEAR: good apothecary, to sweeten my imagination:
KING LEAR: there's money for thee.
GLOUCESTER: O, let me kiss that hand!
KING LEAR: Let me wipe it first, it smells of mortality.
GLOUCESTER: O ruin'd piece of nature! This great world
GLOUCESTER: Shall so wear out to nought. Dost thou know me?
KING LEAR: I remember thine eyes well enough. Dost thou squiny
KING LEAR: at me? No, do thy worst, blind Cupid! I'll not
KING LEAR: love. Read thou this challenge, mark but the
KING LEAR: penning of it.
GLOUCESTER: Were all the letters suns, I could not see one.
EDGAR: I would not take this from report, it is,
EDGAR: And my heart breaks at it.
KING LEAR: Read.
GLOUCESTER: What, with the case of eyes?
KING LEAR: O, ho, are you there with me? No eyes in your
KING LEAR: head, nor no money in your purse? Your eyes are in
KING LEAR: a heavy case, your purse in a light, yet you see how
KING LEAR: this world goes.
GLOUCESTER: I see it feelingly.
KING LEAR: What, art mad? A man may see how this world goes
KING LEAR: with no eyes. Look with thine ears: see how yond
KING LEAR: justice rails upon yond simple thief. Hark, in
KING LEAR: thine ear: change places, and, handy-dandy, which
KING LEAR: is the justice, which is the thief? Thou hast seen
KING LEAR: a farmer's dog bark at a beggar?
GLOUCESTER: Ay, sir.
KING LEAR: And the creature run from the cur? There thou
KING LEAR: mightst behold the great image of authority: a
KING LEAR: dog's obeyed in office.
KING LEAR: Thou rascal beadle, hold thy bloody hand!
KING LEAR: Why dost thou lash that whore? Strip thine own back,
KING LEAR: Thou hotly lust'st to use her in that kind
KING LEAR: For which thou whipp'st her. The usurer hangs the cozener.
KING LEAR: Through tatter'd clothes small vices do appear,
KING LEAR: Robes and furr'd gowns hide all. Plate sin with gold,
KING LEAR: And the strong lance of justice hurtless breaks:
KING LEAR: Arm it in rags, a pigmy's straw does pierce it.
KING LEAR: None does offend, none, I say, none, I'll able 'em:
KING LEAR: Take that of me, my friend, who have the power
KING LEAR: To seal the accuser's lips. Get thee glass eyes,
KING LEAR: And like a scurvy politician, seem
KING LEAR: To see the things thou dost not. Now, now, now, now:
KING LEAR: Pull off my boots: harder, harder: so.
EDGAR: O, matter and impertinency mix'd! Reason in madness!
KING LEAR: If thou wilt weep my fortunes, take my eyes.
KING LEAR: I know thee well enough, thy name is Gloucester:
KING LEAR: Thou must be patient, we came crying hither:
KING LEAR: Thou know'st, the first time that we smell the air,
KING LEAR: We wawl and cry. I will preach to thee: mark.
GLOUCESTER: Alack, alack the day!
KING LEAR: When we are born, we cry that we are come
KING LEAR: To this great stage of fools: this a good block,
KING LEAR: It were a delicate stratagem, to shoe
KING LEAR: A troop of horse with felt: I'll put 't in proof,
KING LEAR: And when I have stol'n upon these sons-in-law,
KING LEAR: Then, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill, kill!
NARRATOR: Enter a Gentleman, with Attendants
Gentleman: O, here he is: lay hand upon him. Sir,
Gentleman: Your most dear daughter--
KING LEAR: No rescue? What, a prisoner? I am even
KING LEAR: The natural fool of fortune. Use me well,
KING LEAR: You shall have ransom. Let me have surgeons,
KING LEAR: I am cut to the brains.
Gentleman: You shall have any thing.
KING LEAR: No seconds? all myself?
KING LEAR: Why, this would make a man a man of salt,
KING LEAR: To use his eyes for garden water-pots,
KING LEAR: Ay, and laying autumn's dust.
Gentleman: Good sir,--
KING LEAR: I will die bravely, like a bridegroom. What!
KING LEAR: I will be jovial: come, come, I am a king,
KING LEAR: My masters, know you that.
Gentleman: You are a royal one, and we obey you.
KING LEAR: Then there's life in't. Nay, if you get it, you
KING LEAR: shall get it with running. Sa, sa, sa, sa.
KING LEAR: Exit running, Attendants follow
Gentleman: A sight most pitiful in the meanest wretch,
Gentleman: Past speaking of in a king! Thou hast one daughter,
Gentleman: Who redeems nature from the general curse
Gentleman: Which twain have brought her to.
EDGAR: Hail, gentle sir.
Gentleman: Sir, speed you: what's your will?
EDGAR: Do you hear aught, sir, of a battle toward?
Gentleman: Most sure and vulgar: every one hears that,
Gentleman: Which can distinguish sound.
EDGAR: But, by your favour,
EDGAR: How near's the other army?
Gentleman: Near and on speedy foot, the main descry
Gentleman: Stands on the hourly thought.
EDGAR: I thank you, sir: that's all.
Gentleman: Though that the queen on special cause is here,
Gentleman: Her army is moved on.
EDGAR: I thank you, sir.
NARRATOR: Exit Gentleman
GLOUCESTER: You ever-gentle gods, take my breath from me:
GLOUCESTER: Let not my worser spirit tempt me again
GLOUCESTER: To die before you please!
EDGAR: Well pray you, father.
GLOUCESTER: Now, good sir, what are you?
EDGAR: A most poor man, made tame to fortune's blows,
EDGAR: Who, by the art of known and feeling sorrows,
EDGAR: Am pregnant to good pity. Give me your hand,
EDGAR: I'll lead you to some biding.
GLOUCESTER: Hearty thanks:
GLOUCESTER: The bounty and the benison of heaven
GLOUCESTER: To boot, and boot!
NARRATOR: Enter OSWALD
OSWALD: A proclaim'd prize! Most happy!
OSWALD: That eyeless head of thine was first framed flesh
OSWALD: To raise my fortunes. Thou old unhappy traitor,
OSWALD: Briefly thyself remember: the sword is out
OSWALD: That must destroy thee.
GLOUCESTER: Now let thy friendly hand
GLOUCESTER: Put strength enough to't.
NARRATOR: EDGAR interposes
OSWALD: Wherefore, bold peasant,
OSWALD: Darest thou support a publish'd traitor? Hence,
OSWALD: Lest that the infection of his fortune take
OSWALD: Like hold on thee. Let go his arm.
EDGAR: Ch'ill not let go, zir, without vurther 'casion.
OSWALD: Let go, slave, or thou diest!
EDGAR: Good gentleman, go your gait, and let poor volk
EDGAR: pass. An chud ha' bin zwaggered out of my life,
EDGAR: 'twould not ha' bin zo long as 'tis by a vortnight.
EDGAR: Nay, come not near th' old man, keep out, che vor
EDGAR: ye, or ise try whether your costard or my ballow be
EDGAR: the harder: ch'ill be plain with you.
OSWALD: Out, dunghill!
EDGAR: Ch'ill pick your teeth, zir: come, no matter vor
EDGAR: your foins.
NARRATOR: They fight, and EDGAR knocks him down
OSWALD: Slave, thou hast slain me: villain, take my purse:
OSWALD: If ever thou wilt thrive, bury my body,
OSWALD: And give the letters which thou find'st about me
OSWALD: To Edmund earl of Gloucester, seek him out
OSWALD: Upon the British party: O, untimely death!
NARRATOR: Dies
EDGAR: I know thee well: a serviceable villain,
EDGAR: As duteous to the vices of thy mistress
EDGAR: As badness would desire.
GLOUCESTER: What, is he dead?
EDGAR: Sit you down, father, rest you
EDGAR: Let's see these pockets: the letters that he speaks of
EDGAR: May be my friends. He's dead, I am only sorry
EDGAR: He had no other death's-man. Let us see:
EDGAR: Leave, gentle wax, and, manners, blame us not:
EDGAR: To know our enemies' minds, we'ld rip their hearts,
EDGAR: Their papers, is more lawful.
NARRATOR: Reads
EDGAR: 'Let our reciprocal vows be remembered. You have
EDGAR: many opportunities to cut him off: if your will
EDGAR: want not, time and place will be fruitfully offered.
EDGAR: There is nothing done, if he return the conqueror:
EDGAR: then am I the prisoner, and his bed my goal, from
EDGAR: the loathed warmth whereof deliver me, and supply
EDGAR: the place for your labour.
EDGAR: 'Your--wife, so I would say--
EDGAR: 'Affectionate servant,
EDGAR: 'GONERIL.'
EDGAR: O undistinguish'd space of woman's will!
EDGAR: A plot upon her virtuous husband's life,
EDGAR: And the exchange my brother! Here, in the sands,
EDGAR: Thee I'll rake up, the post unsanctified
EDGAR: Of murderous lechers: and in the mature time
EDGAR: With this ungracious paper strike the sight
EDGAR: Of the death practised duke: for him 'tis well
EDGAR: That of thy death and business I can tell.
GLOUCESTER: The king is mad: how stiff is my vile sense,
GLOUCESTER: That I stand up, and have ingenious feeling
GLOUCESTER: Of my huge sorrows! Better I were distract:
GLOUCESTER: So should my thoughts be sever'd from my griefs,
GLOUCESTER: And woes by wrong imaginations lose
GLOUCESTER: The knowledge of themselves.
EDGAR: Give me your hand:
NARRATOR: Drum afar off
EDGAR: Far off, methinks, I hear the beaten drum:
EDGAR: Come, father, I'll bestow you with a friend.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. A tent in the French camp. LEAR on a bed asleep,
EDGAR: soft music playing, Gentleman, and others attending.
NARRATOR: Enter CORDELIA, KENT, and Doctor
CORDELIA: O thou good Kent, how shall I live and work,
CORDELIA: To match thy goodness? My life will be too short,
CORDELIA: And every measure fail me.
KENT: To be acknowledged, madam, is o'erpaid.
KENT: All my reports go with the modest truth,
KENT: Nor more nor clipp'd, but so.
CORDELIA: Be better suited:
CORDELIA: These weeds are memories of those worser hours:
CORDELIA: I prithee, put them off.
KENT: Pardon me, dear madam,
KENT: Yet to be known shortens my made intent:
KENT: My boon I make it, that you know me not
KENT: Till time and I think meet.
CORDELIA: Then be't so, my good lord.
NARRATOR: To the Doctor
CORDELIA: How does the king?
Doctor: Madam, sleeps still.
CORDELIA: O you kind gods,
CORDELIA: Cure this great breach in his abused nature!
CORDELIA: The untuned and jarring senses, O, wind up
CORDELIA: Of this child-changed father!
Doctor: So please your majesty
Doctor: That we may wake the king: he hath slept long.
CORDELIA: Be govern'd by your knowledge, and proceed
CORDELIA: I' the sway of your own will. Is he array'd?
Gentleman: Ay, madam, in the heaviness of his sleep
Gentleman: We put fresh garments on him.
Doctor: Be by, good madam, when we do awake him,
Doctor: I doubt not of his temperance.
CORDELIA: Very well.
Doctor: Please you, draw near. Louder the music there!
CORDELIA: O my dear father! Restoration hang
CORDELIA: Thy medicine on my lips, and let this kiss
CORDELIA: Repair those violent harms that my two sisters
CORDELIA: Have in thy reverence made!
KENT: Kind and dear princess!
CORDELIA: Had you not been their father, these white flakes
CORDELIA: Had challenged pity of them. Was this a face
CORDELIA: To be opposed against the warring winds?
CORDELIA: To stand against the deep dread-bolted thunder?
CORDELIA: In the most terrible and nimble stroke
CORDELIA: Of quick, cross lightning? to watch--poor perdu!--
CORDELIA: With this thin helm? Mine enemy's dog,
CORDELIA: Though he had bit me, should have stood that night
CORDELIA: Against my fire, and wast thou fain, poor father,
CORDELIA: To hovel thee with swine, and rogues forlorn,
CORDELIA: In short and musty straw? Alack, alack!
CORDELIA: 'Tis wonder that thy life and wits at once
CORDELIA: Had not concluded all. He wakes, speak to him.
Doctor: Madam, do you, 'tis fittest.
CORDELIA: How does my royal lord? How fares your majesty?
KING LEAR: You do me wrong to take me out o' the grave:
KING LEAR: Thou art a soul in bliss, but I am bound
KING LEAR: Upon a wheel of fire, that mine own tears
KING LEAR: Do scald like moulten lead.
CORDELIA: Sir, do you know me?
KING LEAR: You are a spirit, I know: when did you die?
CORDELIA: Still, still, far wide!
Doctor: He's scarce awake: let him alone awhile.
KING LEAR: Where have I been? Where am I? Fair daylight?
KING LEAR: I am mightily abused. I should e'en die with pity,
KING LEAR: To see another thus. I know not what to say.
KING LEAR: I will not swear these are my hands: let's see,
KING LEAR: I feel this pin prick. Would I were assured
KING LEAR: Of my condition!
CORDELIA: O, look upon me, sir,
CORDELIA: And hold your hands in benediction o'er me:
CORDELIA: No, sir, you must not kneel.
KING LEAR: Pray, do not mock me:
KING LEAR: I am a very foolish fond old man,
KING LEAR: Fourscore and upward, not an hour more nor less,
KING LEAR: And, to deal plainly,
KING LEAR: I fear I am not in my perfect mind.
KING LEAR: Methinks I should know you, and know this man,
KING LEAR: Yet I am doubtful for I am mainly ignorant
KING LEAR: What place this is, and all the skill I have
KING LEAR: Remembers not these garments, nor I know not
KING LEAR: Where I did lodge last night. Do not laugh at me,
KING LEAR: For, as I am a man, I think this lady
KING LEAR: To be my child Cordelia.
CORDELIA: And so I am, I am.
KING LEAR: Be your tears wet? yes, 'faith. I pray, weep not:
KING LEAR: If you have poison for me, I will drink it.
KING LEAR: I know you do not love me, for your sisters
KING LEAR: Have, as I do remember, done me wrong:
KING LEAR: You have some cause, they have not.
CORDELIA: No cause, no cause.
KING LEAR: Am I in France?
KENT: In your own kingdom, sir.
KING LEAR: Do not abuse me.
Doctor: Be comforted, good madam: the great rage,
Doctor: You see, is kill'd in him: and yet it is danger
Doctor: To make him even o'er the time he has lost.
Doctor: Desire him to go in, trouble him no more
Doctor: Till further settling.
CORDELIA: Will't please your highness walk?
KING LEAR: You must bear with me:
KING LEAR: Pray you now, forget and forgive: I am old and foolish.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but KENT and Gentleman
Gentleman: Holds it true, sir, that the Duke of Cornwall was so slain?
KENT: Most certain, sir.
Gentleman: Who is conductor of his people?
KENT: As 'tis said, the bastard son of Gloucester.
Gentleman: They say Edgar, his banished son, is with the Earl
Gentleman: of Kent in Germany.
KENT: Report is changeable. 'Tis time to look about, the
KENT: powers of the kingdom approach apace.
Gentleman: The arbitrement is like to be bloody. Fare you
Gentleman: well, sir.
NARRATOR: Exit
KENT: My point and period will be throughly wrought,
KENT: Or well or ill, as this day's battle's fought.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The British camp, near Dover.
NARRATOR: Enter, with drum and colours, EDMUND, REGAN, Gentlemen, and Soldiers.
EDMUND: Know of the duke if his last purpose hold,
EDMUND: Or whether since he is advised by aught
EDMUND: To change the course: he's full of alteration
EDMUND: And self-reproving: bring his constant pleasure.
NARRATOR: To a Gentleman, who goes out
REGAN: Our sister's man is certainly miscarried.
EDMUND: 'Tis to be doubted, madam.
REGAN: Now, sweet lord,
REGAN: You know the goodness I intend upon you:
REGAN: Tell me--but truly--but then speak the truth,
REGAN: Do you not love my sister?
EDMUND: In honour'd love.
REGAN: But have you never found my brother's way
REGAN: To the forfended place?
EDMUND: That thought abuses you.
REGAN: I am doubtful that you have been conjunct
REGAN: And bosom'd with her, as far as we call hers.
EDMUND: No, by mine honour, madam.
REGAN: I never shall endure her: dear my lord,
REGAN: Be not familiar with her.
EDMUND: Fear me not:
EDMUND: She and the duke her husband!
NARRATOR: Enter, with drum and colours, ALBANY, GONERIL, and Soldiers
GONERIL: [Aside]  I had rather lose the battle than that sister
GONERIL: Should loosen him and me.
ALBANY: Our very loving sister, well be-met.
ALBANY: Sir, this I hear, the king is come to his daughter,
ALBANY: With others whom the rigor of our state
ALBANY: Forced to cry out. Where I could not be honest,
ALBANY: I never yet was valiant: for this business,
ALBANY: It toucheth us, as France invades our land,
ALBANY: Not bolds the king, with others, whom, I fear,
ALBANY: Most just and heavy causes make oppose.
EDMUND: Sir, you speak nobly.
REGAN: Why is this reason'd?
GONERIL: Combine together 'gainst the enemy,
GONERIL: For these domestic and particular broils
GONERIL: Are not the question here.
ALBANY: Let's then determine
ALBANY: With the ancient of war on our proceedings.
EDMUND: I shall attend you presently at your tent.
REGAN: Sister, you'll go with us?
GONERIL: No.
REGAN: 'Tis most convenient, pray you, go with us.
GONERIL: [Aside]  O, ho, I know the riddle.--I will go.
NARRATOR: As they are going out, enter EDGAR disguised
EDGAR: If e'er your grace had speech with man so poor,
EDGAR: Hear me one word.
ALBANY: I'll overtake you. Speak.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but ALBANY and EDGAR
EDGAR: Before you fight the battle, ope this letter.
EDGAR: If you have victory, let the trumpet sound
EDGAR: For him that brought it: wretched though I seem,
EDGAR: I can produce a champion that will prove
EDGAR: What is avouched there. If you miscarry,
EDGAR: Your business of the world hath so an end,
EDGAR: And machination ceases. Fortune love you.
ALBANY: Stay till I have read the letter.
EDGAR: I was forbid it.
EDGAR: When time shall serve, let but the herald cry,
EDGAR: And I'll appear again.
ALBANY: Why, fare thee well: I will o'erlook thy paper.
NARRATOR: Exit EDGAR
NARRATOR: Re-enter EDMUND
EDMUND: The enemy's in view, draw up your powers.
EDMUND: Here is the guess of their true strength and forces
EDMUND: By diligent discovery, but your haste
EDMUND: Is now urged on you.
ALBANY: We will greet the time.
NARRATOR: Exit
EDMUND: To both these sisters have I sworn my love,
EDMUND: Each jealous of the other, as the stung
EDMUND: Are of the adder. Which of them shall I take?
EDMUND: Both? one? or neither? Neither can be enjoy'd,
EDMUND: If both remain alive: to take the widow
EDMUND: Exasperates, makes mad her sister Goneril,
EDMUND: And hardly shall I carry out my side,
EDMUND: Her husband being alive. Now then we'll use
EDMUND: His countenance for the battle, which being done,
EDMUND: Let her who would be rid of him devise
EDMUND: His speedy taking off. As for the mercy
EDMUND: Which he intends to Lear and to Cordelia,
EDMUND: The battle done, and they within our power,
EDMUND: Shall never see his pardon, for my state
EDMUND: Stands on me to defend, not to debate.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A field between the two camps.
NARRATOR: Alarum within. Enter, with drum and colours,  KING LEAR, CORDELIA, and Soldiers, over the stage, and exeunt
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR and GLOUCESTER
EDGAR: Here, father, take the shadow of this tree
EDGAR: For your good host, pray that the right may thrive:
EDGAR: If ever I return to you again,
EDGAR: I'll bring you comfort.
GLOUCESTER: Grace go with you, sir!
NARRATOR: Exit EDGAR
NARRATOR: Alarum and retreat within. Re-enter EDGAR
EDGAR: Away, old man, give me thy hand, away!
EDGAR: King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter ta'en:
EDGAR: Give me thy hand, come on.
GLOUCESTER: No farther, sir, a man may rot even here.
EDGAR: What, in ill thoughts again? Men must endure
EDGAR: Their going hence, even as their coming hither,
EDGAR: Ripeness is all: come on.
GLOUCESTER: And that's true too.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The British camp near Dover.
NARRATOR: Enter, in conquest, with drum and colours, EDMUND,  KING LEAR and CORDELIA, prisoners, Captain, Soldiers,  and c
EDMUND: Some officers take them away: good guard,
EDMUND: Until their greater pleasures first be known
EDMUND: That are to censure them.
CORDELIA: We are not the first
CORDELIA: Who, with best meaning, have incurr'd the worst.
CORDELIA: For thee, oppressed king, am I cast down,
CORDELIA: Myself could else out-frown false fortune's frown.
CORDELIA: Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?
KING LEAR: No, no, no, no! Come, let's away to prison:
KING LEAR: We two alone will sing like birds i' the cage:
KING LEAR: When thou dost ask me blessing, I'll kneel down,
KING LEAR: And ask of thee forgiveness: so we'll live,
KING LEAR: And pray, and sing, and tell old tales, and laugh
KING LEAR: At gilded butterflies, and hear poor rogues
KING LEAR: Talk of court news, and we'll talk with them too,
KING LEAR: Who loses and who wins, who's in, who's out,
KING LEAR: And take upon's the mystery of things,
KING LEAR: As if we were God's spies: and we'll wear out,
KING LEAR: In a wall'd prison, packs and sects of great ones,
KING LEAR: That ebb and flow by the moon.
EDMUND: Take them away.
KING LEAR: Upon such sacrifices, my Cordelia,
KING LEAR: The gods themselves throw incense. Have I caught thee?
KING LEAR: He that parts us shall bring a brand from heaven,
KING LEAR: And fire us hence like foxes. Wipe thine eyes,
KING LEAR: The good-years shall devour them, flesh and fell,
KING LEAR: Ere they shall make us weep: we'll see 'em starve
KING LEAR: first. Come.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING LEAR and CORDELIA, guarded
EDMUND: Come hither, captain, hark.
EDMUND: Take thou this note,
NARRATOR: Giving a paper
EDMUND: go follow them to prison:
EDMUND: One step I have advanced thee, if thou dost
EDMUND: As this instructs thee, thou dost make thy way
EDMUND: To noble fortunes: know thou this, that men
EDMUND: Are as the time is: to be tender-minded
EDMUND: Does not become a sword: thy great employment
EDMUND: Will not bear question, either say thou'lt do 't,
EDMUND: Or thrive by other means.
Captain: I'll do 't, my lord.
EDMUND: About it, and write happy when thou hast done.
EDMUND: Mark, I say, instantly, and carry it so
EDMUND: As I have set it down.
Captain: I cannot draw a cart, nor eat dried oats,
Captain: If it be man's work, I'll do 't.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter ALBANY, GONERIL, REGAN, another Captain, and Soldiers
ALBANY: Sir, you have shown to-day your valiant strain,
ALBANY: And fortune led you well: you have the captives
ALBANY: That were the opposites of this day's strife:
ALBANY: We do require them of you, so to use them
ALBANY: As we shall find their merits and our safety
ALBANY: May equally determine.
EDMUND: Sir, I thought it fit
EDMUND: To send the old and miserable king
EDMUND: To some retention and appointed guard,
EDMUND: Whose age has charms in it, whose title more,
EDMUND: To pluck the common bosom on his side,
EDMUND: An turn our impress'd lances in our eyes
EDMUND: Which do command them. With him I sent the queen,
EDMUND: My reason all the same, and they are ready
EDMUND: To-morrow, or at further space, to appear
EDMUND: Where you shall hold your session. At this time
EDMUND: We sweat and bleed: the friend hath lost his friend,
EDMUND: And the best quarrels, in the heat, are cursed
EDMUND: By those that feel their sharpness:
EDMUND: The question of Cordelia and her father
EDMUND: Requires a fitter place.
ALBANY: Sir, by your patience,
ALBANY: I hold you but a subject of this war,
ALBANY: Not as a brother.
REGAN: That's as we list to grace him.
REGAN: Methinks our pleasure might have been demanded,
REGAN: Ere you had spoke so far. He led our powers,
REGAN: Bore the commission of my place and person,
REGAN: The which immediacy may well stand up,
REGAN: And call itself your brother.
GONERIL: Not so hot:
GONERIL: In his own grace he doth exalt himself,
GONERIL: More than in your addition.
REGAN: In my rights,
REGAN: By me invested, he compeers the best.
GONERIL: That were the most, if he should husband you.
REGAN: Jesters do oft prove prophets.
GONERIL: Holla, holla!
GONERIL: That eye that told you so look'd but a-squint.
REGAN: Lady, I am not well, else I should answer
REGAN: From a full-flowing stomach. General,
REGAN: Take thou my soldiers, prisoners, patrimony,
REGAN: Dispose of them, of me, the walls are thine:
REGAN: Witness the world, that I create thee here
REGAN: My lord and master.
GONERIL: Mean you to enjoy him?
ALBANY: The let-alone lies not in your good will.
EDMUND: Nor in thine, lord.
ALBANY: Half-blooded fellow, yes.
REGAN: [To EDMUND]  Let the drum strike, and prove my title thine.
ALBANY: Stay yet, hear reason. Edmund, I arrest thee
ALBANY: On capital treason, and, in thine attaint,
ALBANY: This gilded serpent
NARRATOR: Pointing to Goneril
ALBANY: For your claim, fair sister,
ALBANY: I bar it in the interest of my wife:
ALBANY: 'Tis she is sub-contracted to this lord,
ALBANY: And I, her husband, contradict your bans.
ALBANY: If you will marry, make your loves to me,
ALBANY: My lady is bespoke.
GONERIL: An interlude!
ALBANY: Thou art arm'd, Gloucester: let the trumpet sound:
ALBANY: If none appear to prove upon thy head
ALBANY: Thy heinous, manifest, and many treasons,
ALBANY: There is my pledge,
NARRATOR: Throwing down a glove
ALBANY: I'll prove it on thy heart,
ALBANY: Ere I taste bread, thou art in nothing less
ALBANY: Than I have here proclaim'd thee.
REGAN: Sick, O, sick!
GONERIL: [Aside]  If not, I'll ne'er trust medicine.
EDMUND: There's my exchange:
NARRATOR: Throwing down a glove
EDMUND: what in the world he is
EDMUND: That names me traitor, villain-like he lies:
EDMUND: Call by thy trumpet: he that dares approach,
EDMUND: On him, on you, who not? I will maintain
EDMUND: My truth and honour firmly.
ALBANY: A herald, ho!
EDMUND: A herald, ho, a herald!
ALBANY: Trust to thy single virtue, for thy soldiers,
ALBANY: All levied in my name, have in my name
ALBANY: Took their discharge.
REGAN: My sickness grows upon me.
ALBANY: She is not well, convey her to  my tent.
NARRATOR: Exit Regan, led
NARRATOR: Enter a Herald
ALBANY: Come hither, herald,--Let the trumpet sound,
ALBANY: And read out this.
Captain: Sound, trumpet!
NARRATOR: A trumpet sounds
Herald: [Reads]  'If any man of quality or degree within
Herald: the lists of the army will maintain upon Edmund,
Herald: supposed Earl of Gloucester, that he is a manifold
Herald: traitor, let him appear by the third sound of the
Herald: trumpet: he is bold in his defence.'
EDMUND: Sound!
NARRATOR: First trumpet
Herald: Again!
NARRATOR: Second trumpet
Herald: Again!
NARRATOR: Third trumpet
NARRATOR: Trumpet answers within
NARRATOR: Enter EDGAR, at the third sound, armed, with a trumpet before him
ALBANY: Ask him his purposes, why he appears
ALBANY: Upon this call o' the trumpet.
Herald: What are you?
Herald: Your name, your quality? and why you answer
Herald: This present summons?
EDGAR: Know, my name is lost,
EDGAR: By treason's tooth bare-gnawn and canker-bit:
EDGAR: Yet am I noble as the adversary
EDGAR: I come to cope.
ALBANY: Which is that adversary?
EDGAR: What's he that speaks for Edmund Earl of Gloucester?
EDMUND: Himself: what say'st thou to him?

EDGAR: That, if my speech offend a noble heart,
EDGAR: Thy arm may do thee justice: here is mine.
EDGAR: Behold, it is the privilege of mine honours,
EDGAR: My oath, and my profession: I protest,
EDGAR: Maugre thy strength, youth, place, and eminence,
EDGAR: Despite thy victor sword and fire-new fortune,
EDGAR: Thy valour and thy heart, thou art a traitor,
EDGAR: False to thy gods, thy brother, and thy father,
EDGAR: Conspirant 'gainst this high-illustrious prince,
EDGAR: And, from the extremest upward of thy head
EDGAR: To the descent and dust below thy foot,
EDGAR: A most toad-spotted traitor. Say thou 'No,'

EDGAR: To prove upon thy heart, whereto I speak,
EDGAR: Thou liest.
EDMUND: In wisdom I should ask thy name,
EDMUND: But, since thy outside looks so fair and warlike,

EDMUND: What safe and nicely I might well delay
EDMUND: By rule of knighthood, I disdain and spurn:
EDMUND: Back do I toss these treasons to thy head,
EDMUND: With the hell-hated lie o'erwhelm thy heart,
EDMUND: Which, for they yet glance by and scarcely bruise,
