EDMUND: Where they shall rest for ever. Trumpets, speak!
NARRATOR: Alarums. They fight. EDMUND falls
ALBANY: Save him, save him!
GONERIL: This is practise, Gloucester:
GONERIL: By the law of arms thou wast not bound to answer
GONERIL: An unknown opposite, thou art not vanquish'd,
GONERIL: But cozen'd and beguiled.
ALBANY: Shut your mouth, dame,
ALBANY: Or with this paper shall I stop it: Hold, sir:
ALBANY: Thou worse than any name, read thine own evil:
ALBANY: No tearing, lady: I perceive you know it.
NARRATOR: Gives the letter to EDMUND
GONERIL: Say, if I do, the laws are mine, not thine:
GONERIL: Who can arraign me for't.
ALBANY: Most monstrous! oh!
ALBANY: Know'st thou this paper?
GONERIL: Ask me not what I know.
NARRATOR: Exit
ALBANY: Go after her: she's desperate, govern her.
EDMUND: What you have charged me with, that have I done,
EDMUND: And more, much more, the time will bring it out:
EDMUND: 'Tis past, and so am I. But what art thou
EDMUND: That hast this fortune on me? If thou'rt noble,
EDMUND: I do forgive thee.
EDGAR: Let's exchange charity.
EDGAR: I am no less in blood than thou art, Edmund,
EDGAR: If more, the more thou hast wrong'd me.
EDGAR: My name is Edgar, and thy father's son.
EDGAR: The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices
EDGAR: Make instruments to plague us:
EDGAR: The dark and vicious place where thee he got
EDGAR: Cost him his eyes.
EDMUND: Thou hast spoken right, 'tis true,
EDMUND: The wheel is come full circle: I am here.
ALBANY: Methought thy very gait did prophesy
ALBANY: A royal nobleness: I must embrace thee:
ALBANY: Let sorrow split my heart, if ever I
ALBANY: Did hate thee or thy father!
EDGAR: Worthy prince, I know't.
ALBANY: Where have you hid yourself?
ALBANY: How have you known the miseries of your father?
EDGAR: By nursing them, my lord. List a brief tale,
EDGAR: And when 'tis told, O, that my heart would burst!
EDGAR: The bloody proclamation to escape,
EDGAR: That follow'd me so near,--O, our lives' sweetness!
EDGAR: That we the pain of death would hourly die
EDGAR: Rather than die at once!--taught me to shift
EDGAR: Into a madman's rags, to assume a semblance
EDGAR: That very dogs disdain'd: and in this habit
EDGAR: Met I my father with his bleeding rings,
EDGAR: Their precious stones new lost: became his guide,
EDGAR: Led him, begg'd for him, saved him from despair,
EDGAR: Never,--O fault!--reveal'd myself unto him,
EDGAR: Until some half-hour past, when I was arm'd:
EDGAR: Not sure, though hoping, of this good success,
EDGAR: I ask'd his blessing, and from first to last
EDGAR: Told him my pilgrimage: but his flaw'd heart,
EDGAR: Alack, too weak the conflict to support!
EDGAR: 'Twixt two extremes of passion, joy and grief,
EDGAR: Burst smilingly.
EDMUND: This speech of yours hath moved me,
EDMUND: And shall perchance do good: but speak you on,
EDMUND: You look as you had something more to say.
ALBANY: If there be more, more woeful, hold it in,
ALBANY: For I am almost ready to dissolve,
ALBANY: Hearing of this.
EDGAR: This would have seem'd a period
EDGAR: To such as love not sorrow, but another,
EDGAR: To amplify too much, would make much more,
EDGAR: And top extremity.
EDGAR: Whilst I was big in clamour came there in a man,
EDGAR: Who, having seen me in my worst estate,
EDGAR: Shunn'd my abhorr'd society, but then, finding
EDGAR: Who 'twas that so endured, with his strong arms
EDGAR: He fastened on my neck, and bellow'd out
EDGAR: As he'ld burst heaven, threw him on my father,
EDGAR: Told the most piteous tale of Lear and him
EDGAR: That ever ear received: which in recounting
EDGAR: His grief grew puissant and the strings of life
EDGAR: Began to crack: twice then the trumpets sounded,
EDGAR: And there I left him tranced.
ALBANY: But who was this?
EDGAR: Kent, sir, the banish'd Kent, who in disguise
EDGAR: Follow'd his enemy king, and did him service
EDGAR: Improper for a slave.
NARRATOR: Enter a Gentleman, with a bloody knife
Gentleman: Help, help, O, help!
EDGAR: What kind of help?
ALBANY: Speak, man.
EDGAR: What means that bloody knife?
Gentleman: 'Tis hot, it smokes,
Gentleman: It came even from the heart of--O, she's dead!
ALBANY: Who dead? speak, man.
Gentleman: Your lady, sir, your lady: and her sister
Gentleman: By her is poisoned, she hath confess'd it.
EDMUND: I was contracted to them both: all three
EDMUND: Now marry in an instant.
EDGAR: Here comes Kent.
ALBANY: Produce their bodies, be they alive or dead:
ALBANY: This judgment of the heavens, that makes us tremble,
ALBANY: Touches us not with pity.
NARRATOR: Exit Gentleman
NARRATOR: Enter KENT
ALBANY: O, is this he?
ALBANY: The time will not allow the compliment
ALBANY: Which very manners urges.
KENT: I am come
KENT: To bid my king and master aye good night:
KENT: Is he not here?
ALBANY: Great thing of us forgot!
ALBANY: Speak, Edmund, where's the king? and where's Cordelia?
ALBANY: See'st thou this object, Kent?
NARRATOR: The bodies of GONERIL and REGAN are brought in
KENT: Alack, why thus?
EDMUND: Yet Edmund was beloved:
EDMUND: The one the other poison'd for my sake,
EDMUND: And after slew herself.
ALBANY: Even so. Cover their faces.
EDMUND: I pant for life: some good I mean to do,
EDMUND: Despite of mine own nature. Quickly send,
EDMUND: Be brief in it, to the castle, for my writ
EDMUND: Is on the life of Lear and on Cordelia:
EDMUND: Nay, send in time.
ALBANY: Run, run, O, run!
EDGAR: To who, my lord? Who hath the office? send
EDGAR: Thy token of reprieve.
EDMUND: Well thought on: take my sword,
EDMUND: Give it the captain.
ALBANY: Haste thee, for thy life.
NARRATOR: Exit EDGAR
EDMUND: He hath commission from thy wife and me
EDMUND: To hang Cordelia in the prison, and
EDMUND: To lay the blame upon her own despair,
EDMUND: That she fordid herself.
ALBANY: The gods defend her! Bear him hence awhile.
NARRATOR: EDMUND is borne off
NARRATOR: Re-enter KING LEAR, with CORDELIA dead in his arms, EDGAR, Captain, and others following
KING LEAR: Howl, howl, howl, howl! O, you are men of stones:
KING LEAR: Had I your tongues and eyes, I'ld use them so
KING LEAR: That heaven's vault should crack. She's gone for ever!
KING LEAR: I know when one is dead, and when one lives,
KING LEAR: She's dead as earth. Lend me a looking-glass,
KING LEAR: If that her breath will mist or stain the stone,
KING LEAR: Why, then she lives.
KENT: Is this the promised end
EDGAR: Or image of that horror?
ALBANY: Fall, and cease!
KING LEAR: This feather stirs, she lives! if it be so,
KING LEAR: It is a chance which does redeem all sorrows
KING LEAR: That ever I have felt.
KENT: [Kneeling]  O my good master!
KING LEAR: Prithee, away.
EDGAR: 'Tis noble Kent, your friend.
KING LEAR: A plague upon you, murderers, traitors all!
KING LEAR: I might have saved her, now she's gone for ever!
KING LEAR: Cordelia, Cordelia! stay a little. Ha!
KING LEAR: What is't thou say'st? Her voice was ever soft,
KING LEAR: Gentle, and low, an excellent thing in woman.
KING LEAR: I kill'd the slave that was a-hanging thee.
Captain: 'Tis true, my lords, he did.
KING LEAR: Did I not, fellow?
KING LEAR: I have seen the day, with my good biting falchion
KING LEAR: I would have made them skip: I am old now,
KING LEAR: And these same crosses spoil me. Who are you?
KING LEAR: Mine eyes are not o' the best: I'll tell you straight.
KENT: If fortune brag of two she loved and hated,
KENT: One of them we behold.
KING LEAR: This is a dull sight. Are you not Kent?
KENT: The same,
KENT: Your servant Kent: Where is your servant Caius?
KING LEAR: He's a good fellow, I can tell you that,
KING LEAR: He'll strike, and quickly too: he's dead and rotten.
KENT: No, my good lord, I am the very man,--
KING LEAR: I'll see that straight.
KENT: That, from your first of difference and decay,
KENT: Have follow'd your sad steps.
KING LEAR: You are welcome hither.
KENT: Nor no man else: all's cheerless, dark, and deadly.
KENT: Your eldest daughters have fordone them selves,
KENT: And desperately are dead.
KING LEAR: Ay, so I think.
ALBANY: He knows not what he says: and vain it is
ALBANY: That we present us to him.
EDGAR: Very bootless.
NARRATOR: Enter a Captain
Captain: Edmund is dead, my lord.
ALBANY: That's but a trifle here.
ALBANY: You lords and noble friends, know our intent.
ALBANY: What comfort to this great decay may come
ALBANY: Shall be applied: for us we will resign,
ALBANY: During the life of this old majesty,
ALBANY: To him our absolute power:
NARRATOR: To EDGAR and KENT
ALBANY: you, to your rights:
ALBANY: With boot, and such addition as your honours
ALBANY: Have more than merited. All friends shall taste
ALBANY: The wages of their virtue, and all foes
ALBANY: The cup of their deservings. O, see, see!
KING LEAR: And my poor fool is hang'd! No, no, no life!
KING LEAR: Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life,
KING LEAR: And thou no breath at all? Thou'lt come no more,
KING LEAR: Never, never, never, never, never!
KING LEAR: Pray you, undo this button: thank you, sir.
KING LEAR: Do you see this? Look on her, look, her lips,
KING LEAR: Look there, look there!
NARRATOR: Dies
EDGAR: He faints! My lord, my lord!
KENT: Break, heart, I prithee, break!
EDGAR: Look up, my lord.
KENT: Vex not his ghost: O, let him pass! he hates him much
KENT: That would upon the rack of this tough world
KENT: Stretch him out longer.
EDGAR: He is gone, indeed.
KENT: The wonder is, he hath endured so long:
KENT: He but usurp'd his life.
ALBANY: Bear them from hence. Our present business
ALBANY: Is general woe.
NARRATOR: To KENT and EDGAR
ALBANY: Friends of my soul, you twain
ALBANY: Rule in this realm, and the gored state sustain.
KENT: I have a journey, sir, shortly to go,
KENT: My master calls me, I must not say no.
ALBANY: The weight of this sad time we must obey,
ALBANY: Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say.
ALBANY: The oldest hath borne most: we that are young
ALBANY: Shall never see so much, nor live so long.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, with a dead march
''' PLAY: Loves Labours Lost '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The king of Navarre's park.
NARRATOR: Enter FERDINAND king of Navarre, BIRON, LONGAVILLE and DUMAIN
FERDINAND: Let fame, that all hunt after in their lives,
FERDINAND: Live register'd upon our brazen tombs
FERDINAND: And then grace us in the disgrace of death,
FERDINAND: When, spite of cormorant devouring Time,
FERDINAND: The endeavor of this present breath may buy
FERDINAND: That honour which shall bate his scythe's keen edge
FERDINAND: And make us heirs of all eternity.
FERDINAND: Therefore, brave conquerors,--for so you are,
FERDINAND: That war against your own affections
FERDINAND: And the huge army of the world's desires,--
FERDINAND: Our late edict shall strongly stand in force:
FERDINAND: Navarre shall be the wonder of the world,
FERDINAND: Our court shall be a little Academe,
FERDINAND: Still and contemplative in living art.
FERDINAND: You three, Biron, Dumain, and Longaville,
FERDINAND: Have sworn for three years' term to live with me
FERDINAND: My fellow-scholars, and to keep those statutes
FERDINAND: That are recorded in this schedule here:
FERDINAND: Your oaths are pass'd, and now subscribe your names,
FERDINAND: That his own hand may strike his honour down
FERDINAND: That violates the smallest branch herein:
FERDINAND: If you are arm'd to do as sworn to do,
FERDINAND: Subscribe to your deep oaths, and keep it too.
LONGAVILLE: I am resolved, 'tis but a three years' fast:
LONGAVILLE: The mind shall banquet, though the body pine:
LONGAVILLE: Fat paunches have lean pates, and dainty bits
LONGAVILLE: Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits.
DUMAIN: My loving lord, Dumain is mortified:
DUMAIN: The grosser manner of these world's delights
DUMAIN: He throws upon the gross world's baser slaves:
DUMAIN: To love, to wealth, to pomp, I pine and die,
DUMAIN: With all these living in philosophy.
BIRON: I can but say their protestation over,
BIRON: So much, dear liege, I have already sworn,
BIRON: That is, to live and study here three years.
BIRON: But there are other strict observances,
BIRON: As, not to see a woman in that term,
BIRON: Which I hope well is not enrolled there,
BIRON: And one day in a week to touch no food
BIRON: And but one meal on every day beside,
BIRON: The which I hope is not enrolled there,
BIRON: And then, to sleep but three hours in the night,
BIRON: And not be seen to wink of all the day--
BIRON: When I was wont to think no harm all night
BIRON: And make a dark night too of half the day--
BIRON: Which I hope well is not enrolled there:
BIRON: O, these are barren tasks, too hard to keep,
BIRON: Not to see ladies, study, fast, not sleep!
FERDINAND: Your oath is pass'd to pass away from these.
BIRON: Let me say no, my liege, an if you please:
BIRON: I only swore to study with your grace
BIRON: And stay here in your court for three years' space.
LONGAVILLE: You swore to that, Biron, and to the rest.
BIRON: By yea and nay, sir, then I swore in jest.
BIRON: What is the end of study? let me know.
FERDINAND: Why, that to know, which else we should not know.
BIRON: Things hid and barr'd, you mean, from common sense?
FERDINAND: Ay, that is study's godlike recompense.
BIRON: Come on, then, I will swear to study so,
BIRON: To know the thing I am forbid to know:
BIRON: As thus,--to study where I well may dine,
BIRON: When I to feast expressly am forbid,
BIRON: Or study where to meet some mistress fine,
BIRON: When mistresses from common sense are hid,
BIRON: Or, having sworn too hard a keeping oath,
BIRON: Study to break it and not break my troth.
BIRON: If study's gain be thus and this be so,
BIRON: Study knows that which yet it doth not know:
BIRON: Swear me to this, and I will ne'er say no.
FERDINAND: These be the stops that hinder study quite
FERDINAND: And train our intellects to vain delight.
BIRON: Why, all delights are vain, but that most vain,
BIRON: Which with pain purchased doth inherit pain:
BIRON: As, painfully to pore upon a book
BIRON: To seek the light of truth, while truth the while
BIRON: Doth falsely blind the eyesight of his look:
BIRON: Light seeking light doth light of light beguile:
BIRON: So, ere you find where light in darkness lies,
BIRON: Your light grows dark by losing of your eyes.
BIRON: Study me how to please the eye indeed
BIRON: By fixing it upon a fairer eye,
BIRON: Who dazzling so, that eye shall be his heed
BIRON: And give him light that it was blinded by.
BIRON: Study is like the heaven's glorious sun
BIRON: That will not be deep-search'd with saucy looks:
BIRON: Small have continual plodders ever won
BIRON: Save base authority from others' books
BIRON: These earthly godfathers of heaven's lights
BIRON: That give a name to every fixed star
BIRON: Have no more profit of their shining nights
BIRON: Than those that walk and wot not what they are.
BIRON: Too much to know is to know nought but fame,
BIRON: And every godfather can give a name.
FERDINAND: How well he's read, to reason against reading!
DUMAIN: Proceeded well, to stop all good proceeding!
LONGAVILLE: He weeds the corn and still lets grow the weeding.
BIRON: The spring is near when green geese are a-breeding.
DUMAIN: How follows that?
BIRON: Fit in his place and time.
DUMAIN: In reason nothing.
BIRON: Something then in rhyme.
FERDINAND: Biron is like an envious sneaping frost,
FERDINAND: That bites the first-born infants of the spring.
BIRON: Well, say I am, why should proud summer boast
BIRON: Before the birds have any cause to sing?
BIRON: Why should I joy in any abortive birth?
BIRON: At Christmas I no more desire a rose
BIRON: Than wish a snow in May's new-fangled mirth,
BIRON: But like of each thing that in season grows.
BIRON: So you, to study now it is too late,
BIRON: Climb o'er the house to unlock the little gate.
FERDINAND: Well, sit you out: go home, Biron: adieu.
BIRON: No, my good lord, I have sworn to stay with you:
BIRON: And though I have for barbarism spoke more
BIRON: Than for that angel knowledge you can say,
BIRON: Yet confident I'll keep what I have swore
BIRON: And bide the penance of each three years' day.
BIRON: Give me the paper, let me read the same,
BIRON: And to the strict'st decrees I'll write my name.
FERDINAND: How well this yielding rescues thee from shame!
BIRON: [Reads]  'Item, That no woman shall come within a
BIRON: mile of my court:' Hath this been proclaimed?
LONGAVILLE: Four days ago.
BIRON: Let's see the penalty.
NARRATOR: Reads
BIRON: 'On pain of losing her tongue.' Who devised this penalty?
LONGAVILLE: Marry, that did I.
BIRON: Sweet lord, and why?
LONGAVILLE: To fright them hence with that dread penalty.
BIRON: A dangerous law against gentility!
NARRATOR: Reads
BIRON: 'Item, If any man be seen to talk with a woman
BIRON: within the term of three years, he shall endure such
BIRON: public shame as the rest of the court can possibly devise.'
BIRON: This article, my liege, yourself must break,
BIRON: For well you know here comes in embassy
BIRON: The French king's daughter with yourself to speak--
BIRON: A maid of grace and complete majesty--
BIRON: About surrender up of Aquitaine
BIRON: To her decrepit, sick and bedrid father:
BIRON: Therefore this article is made in vain,
BIRON: Or vainly comes the admired princess hither.
FERDINAND: What say you, lords? Why, this was quite forgot.
BIRON: So study evermore is overshot:
BIRON: While it doth study to have what it would
BIRON: It doth forget to do the thing it should,
BIRON: And when it hath the thing it hunteth most,
BIRON: 'Tis won as towns with fire, so won, so lost.
FERDINAND: We must of force dispense with this decree,
FERDINAND: She must lie here on mere necessity.
BIRON: Necessity will make us all forsworn
BIRON: Three thousand times within this three years' space,
BIRON: For every man with his affects is born,
BIRON: Not by might master'd but by special grace:
BIRON: If I break faith, this word shall speak for me,
BIRON: I am forsworn on 'mere necessity.'
BIRON: So to the laws at large I write my name:
NARRATOR: Subscribes
BIRON: And he that breaks them in the least degree
BIRON: Stands in attainder of eternal shame:
BIRON: Suggestions are to other as to me,
BIRON: But I believe, although I seem so loath,
BIRON: I am the last that will last keep his oath.
BIRON: But is there no quick recreation granted?
FERDINAND: Ay, that there is. Our court, you know, is haunted
FERDINAND: With a refined traveller of Spain,
FERDINAND: A man in all the world's new fashion planted,
FERDINAND: That hath a mint of phrases in his brain,
FERDINAND: One whom the music of his own vain tongue
FERDINAND: Doth ravish like enchanting harmony,
FERDINAND: A man of complements, whom right and wrong
FERDINAND: Have chose as umpire of their mutiny:
FERDINAND: This child of fancy, that Armado hight,
FERDINAND: For interim to our studies shall relate
FERDINAND: In high-born words the worth of many a knight
FERDINAND: From tawny Spain lost in the world's debate.
FERDINAND: How you delight, my lords, I know not, I,
FERDINAND: But, I protest, I love to hear him lie
FERDINAND: And I will use him for my minstrelsy.
BIRON: Armado is a most illustrious wight,
BIRON: A man of fire-new words, fashion's own knight.
LONGAVILLE: Costard the swain and he shall be our sport,
LONGAVILLE: And so to study, three years is but short.
NARRATOR: Enter DULL with a letter, and COSTARD
DULL: Which is the duke's own person?
BIRON: This, fellow: what wouldst?
DULL: I myself reprehend his own person, for I am his
DULL: grace's tharborough: but I would see his own person
DULL: in flesh and blood.
BIRON: This is he.
DULL: Signior Arme--Arme--commends you. There's villany
DULL: abroad: this letter will tell you more.
COSTARD: Sir, the contempts thereof are as touching me.
FERDINAND: A letter from the magnificent Armado.
BIRON: How low soever the matter, I hope in God for high words.
LONGAVILLE: A high hope for a low heaven: God grant us patience!
BIRON: To hear? or forbear laughing?
LONGAVILLE: To hear meekly, sir, and to laugh moderately, or to
LONGAVILLE: forbear both.
BIRON: Well, sir, be it as the style shall give us cause to
BIRON: climb in the merriness.
COSTARD: The matter is to me, sir, as concerning Jaquenetta.
COSTARD: The manner of it is, I was taken with the manner.
BIRON: In what manner?
COSTARD: In manner and form following, sir, all those three:
COSTARD: I was seen with her in the manor-house, sitting with
COSTARD: her upon the form, and taken following her into the
COSTARD: park, which, put together, is in manner and form
COSTARD: following. Now, sir, for the manner,--it is the
COSTARD: manner of a man to speak to a woman: for the form,--
COSTARD: in some form.
BIRON: For the following, sir?
COSTARD: As it shall follow in my correction: and God defend
COSTARD: the right!
FERDINAND: Will you hear this letter with attention?
BIRON: As we would hear an oracle.
COSTARD: Such is the simplicity of man to hearken after the flesh.
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'Great deputy, the welkin's vicegerent and
FERDINAND: sole dominator of Navarre, my soul's earth's god,
FERDINAND: and body's fostering patron.'
COSTARD: Not a word of Costard yet.
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'So it is,'--
COSTARD: It may be so: but if he say it is so, he is, in
COSTARD: telling true, but so.
FERDINAND: Peace!
COSTARD: Be to me and every man that dares not fight!
FERDINAND: No words!
COSTARD: Of other men's secrets, I beseech you.
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'So it is, besieged with sable-coloured
FERDINAND: melancholy, I did commend the black-oppressing humour
FERDINAND: to the most wholesome physic of thy health-giving
FERDINAND: air, and, as I am a gentleman, betook myself to
FERDINAND: walk. The time when. About the sixth hour, when
FERDINAND: beasts most graze, birds best peck, and men sit down
FERDINAND: to that nourishment which is called supper: so much
FERDINAND: for the time when. Now for the ground which, which,
FERDINAND: I mean, I walked upon: it is y-cleped thy park. Then
FERDINAND: for the place where, where, I mean, I did encounter
FERDINAND: that obscene and preposterous event, that draweth
FERDINAND: from my snow-white pen the ebon-coloured ink, which
FERDINAND: here thou viewest, beholdest, surveyest, or seest,

FERDINAND: and by east from the west corner of thy curious-
FERDINAND: knotted garden: there did I see that low-spirited
FERDINAND: swain, that base minnow of thy mirth,'--
COSTARD: Me?
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'that unlettered small-knowing soul,'--
COSTARD: Me?
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'that shallow vassal,'--
COSTARD: Still me?
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'which, as I remember, hight Costard,'--
COSTARD: O, me!
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'sorted and consorted, contrary to thy
FERDINAND: established proclaimed edict and continent canon,

FERDINAND: wherewith,--
COSTARD: With a wench.
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'with a child of our grandmother Eve, a
FERDINAND: female, or, for thy more sweet understanding, a
FERDINAND: woman. Him I, as my ever-esteemed duty pricks me on,
FERDINAND: have sent to thee, to receive the meed of
FERDINAND: punishment, by thy sweet grace's officer, Anthony
FERDINAND: Dull, a man of good repute, carriage, bearing, and
FERDINAND: estimation.'
DULL: 'Me, an't shall please you, I am Anthony Dull.
FERDINAND: [Reads]  'For Jaquenetta,--so is the weaker vessel
FERDINAND: called which I apprehended with the aforesaid
FERDINAND: swain,--I keep her as a vessel of the law's fury,
FERDINAND: and shall, at the least of thy sweet notice, bring
FERDINAND: her to trial. Thine, in all compliments of devoted
FERDINAND: and heart-burning heat of duty.
FERDINAND: DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'
BIRON: This is not so well as I looked for, but the best
BIRON: that ever I heard.
FERDINAND: Ay, the best for the worst. But, sirrah, what say
FERDINAND: you to this?
COSTARD: Sir, I confess the wench.
FERDINAND: Did you hear the proclamation?
COSTARD: I do confess much of the hearing it but little of
COSTARD: the marking of it.
FERDINAND: It was proclaimed a year's imprisonment, to be taken
FERDINAND: with a wench.
COSTARD: I was taken with none, sir: I was taken with a damsel.
FERDINAND: Well, it was proclaimed 'damsel.'
COSTARD: This was no damsel, neither, sir, she was a virgin.
FERDINAND: It is so varied, too, for it was proclaimed 'virgin.'
COSTARD: If it were, I deny her virginity: I was taken with a maid.
FERDINAND: This maid will not serve your turn, sir.
COSTARD: This maid will serve my turn, sir.
FERDINAND: Sir, I will pronounce your sentence: you shall fast
FERDINAND: a week with bran and water.
COSTARD: I had rather pray a month with mutton and porridge.
FERDINAND: And Don Armado shall be your keeper.
FERDINAND: My Lord Biron, see him deliver'd o'er:
FERDINAND: And go we, lords, to put in practise that
FERDINAND: Which each to other hath so strongly sworn.
NARRATOR: Exeunt FERDINAND, LONGAVILLE, and DUMAIN
BIRON: I'll lay my head to any good man's hat,
BIRON: These oaths and laws will prove an idle scorn.
BIRON: Sirrah, come on.
COSTARD: I suffer for the truth, sir, for true it is, I was
COSTARD: taken with Jaquenetta, and Jaquenetta is a true
COSTARD: girl, and therefore welcome the sour cup of
COSTARD: prosperity! Affliction may one day smile again, and
COSTARD: till then, sit thee down, sorrow!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
COSTARD: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
COSTARD: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO and MOTH
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Boy, what sign is it when a man of great spirit
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: grows melancholy?
MOTH: A great sign, sir, that he will look sad.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Why, sadness is one and the self-same thing, dear imp.
MOTH: No, no, O Lord, sir, no.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: How canst thou part sadness and melancholy, my
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: tender juvenal?
MOTH: By a familiar demonstration of the working, my tough senior.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Why tough senior? why tough senior?
MOTH: Why tender juvenal? why tender juvenal?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I spoke it, tender juvenal, as a congruent epitheton
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: appertaining to thy young days, which we may
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: nominate tender.
MOTH: And I, tough senior, as an appertinent title to your
MOTH: old time, which we may name tough.
MOTH: DON ADRIANO DE
ARMADO: Pretty and apt.
MOTH: How mean you, sir? I pretty, and my saying apt? or
MOTH: I apt, and my saying pretty?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Thou pretty, because little.
MOTH: Little pretty, because little. Wherefore apt?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: And therefore apt, because quick.
MOTH: Speak you this in my praise, master?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: In thy condign praise.
MOTH: I will praise an eel with the same praise.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: What, that an eel is ingenious?
MOTH: That an eel is quick.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I do say thou art quick in answers: thou heatest my blood.
MOTH: I am answered, sir.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I love not to be crossed.
MOTH: [Aside]  He speaks the mere contrary, crosses love not him.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I have promised to study three years with the duke.
MOTH: You may do it in an hour, sir.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Impossible.
MOTH: How many is one thrice told?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I am ill at reckoning, it fitteth the spirit of a tapster.
MOTH: You are a gentleman and a gamester, sir.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I confess both: they are both the varnish of a
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: complete man.
MOTH: Then, I am sure, you know how much the gross sum of
MOTH: deuce-ace amounts to.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: It doth amount to one more than two.
MOTH: Which the base vulgar do call three.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: True.
MOTH: Why, sir, is this such a piece of study? Now here
MOTH: is three studied, ere ye'll thrice wink: and how
MOTH: easy it is to put 'years' to the word 'three,' and
MOTH: study three years in two words, the dancing horse
MOTH: will tell you.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: A most fine figure!
MOTH: To prove you a cipher.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I will hereupon confess I am in love: and as it is
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: base for a soldier to love, so am I in love with a
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: base wench. If drawing my sword against the humour
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: of affection would deliver me from the reprobate
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: thought of it, I would take Desire prisoner, and
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: ransom him to any French courtier for a new-devised
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: courtesy. I think scorn to sigh: methinks I should
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: outswear Cupid. Comfort, me, boy: what great men
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: have been in love?
MOTH: Hercules, master.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Most sweet Hercules! More authority, dear boy, name
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: more, and, sweet my child, let them be men of good
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: repute and carriage.
MOTH: Samson, master: he was a man of good carriage, great
MOTH: carriage, for he carried the town-gates on his back
MOTH: like a porter: and he was in love.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: O well-knit Samson! strong-jointed Samson! I do
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: excel thee in my rapier as much as thou didst me in
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: carrying gates. I am in love too. Who was Samson's
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: love, my dear Moth?
MOTH: A woman, master.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Of what complexion?
MOTH: Of all the four, or the three, or the two, or one of the four.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Tell me precisely of what complexion.
MOTH: Of the sea-water green, sir.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Is that one of the four complexions?
MOTH: As I have read, sir, and the best of them too.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Green indeed is the colour of lovers, but to have a
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: love of that colour, methinks Samson had small reason
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: for it. He surely affected her for her wit.
MOTH: It was so, sir, for she had a green wit.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: My love is most immaculate white and red.
MOTH: Most maculate thoughts, master, are masked under
MOTH: such colours.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Define, define, well-educated infant.
MOTH: My father's wit and my mother's tongue, assist me!
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sweet invocation of a child, most pretty and
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: pathetical!
MOTH: If she be made of white and red,
MOTH: Her faults will ne'er be known,
MOTH: For blushing cheeks by faults are bred
MOTH: And fears by pale white shown:
MOTH: Then if she fear, or be to blame,
MOTH: By this you shall not know,
MOTH: For still her cheeks possess the same
MOTH: Which native she doth owe.
MOTH: A dangerous rhyme, master, against the reason of
MOTH: white and red.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Is there not a ballad, boy, of the King and the Beggar?
MOTH: The world was very guilty of such a ballad some
MOTH: three ages since: but I think now 'tis not to be
MOTH: found, or, if it were, it would neither serve for
MOTH: the writing nor the tune.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I will have that subject newly writ o'er, that I may
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: example my digression by some mighty precedent.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Boy, I do love that country girl that I took in the
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: park with the rational hind Costard: she deserves well.
MOTH: [Aside]  To be whipped, and yet a better love than
MOTH: my master.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sing, boy, my spirit grows heavy in love.
MOTH: And that's great marvel, loving a light wench.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I say, sing.
MOTH: Forbear till this company be past.
NARRATOR: Enter DULL, COSTARD, and JAQUENETTA
DULL: Sir, the duke's pleasure is, that you keep Costard
DULL: safe: and you must suffer him to take no delight
DULL: nor no penance, but a' must fast three days a week.
DULL: For this damsel, I must keep her at the park: she
DULL: is allowed for the day-woman. Fare you well.
DULL: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I do betray myself with blushing. Maid!
JAQUENETTA: Man?
JAQUENETTA: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I will visit thee at the lodge.
JAQUENETTA: That's hereby.
JAQUENETTA: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I know where it is situate.
JAQUENETTA: Lord, how wise you are!
JAQUENETTA: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I will tell thee wonders.
JAQUENETTA: With that face?
JAQUENETTA: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I love thee.
JAQUENETTA: So I heard you say.
JAQUENETTA: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: And so, farewell.
JAQUENETTA: Fair weather after you!
DULL: Come, Jaquenetta, away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt DULL and JAQUENETTA
DULL: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Villain, thou shalt fast for thy offences ere thou
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: be pardoned.
COSTARD: Well, sir, I hope, when I do it, I shall do it on a
COSTARD: full stomach.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Thou shalt be heavily punished.
COSTARD: I am more bound to you than your fellows, for they
COSTARD: are but lightly rewarded.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Take away this villain, shut him up.
MOTH: Come, you transgressing slave, away!
COSTARD: Let me not be pent up, sir: I will fast, being loose.
MOTH: No, sir, that were fast and loose: thou shalt to prison.
COSTARD: Well, if ever I do see the merry days of desolation
COSTARD: that I have seen, some shall see.
MOTH: What shall some see?
COSTARD: Nay, nothing, Master Moth, but what they look upon.
COSTARD: It is not for prisoners to be too silent in their
COSTARD: words, and therefore I will say nothing: I thank
COSTARD: God I have as little patience as another man, and
COSTARD: therefore I can be quiet.
NARRATOR: Exeunt MOTH and COSTARD
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I do affect the very ground, which is base, where
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: her shoe, which is baser, guided by her foot, which
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: is basest, doth tread. I shall be forsworn, which
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: is a great argument of falsehood, if I love. And
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: how can that be true love which is falsely
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: attempted? Love is a familiar, Love is a devil:
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: there is no evil angel but Love. Yet was Samson so
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: tempted, and he had an excellent strength, yet was
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Solomon so seduced, and he had a very good wit.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Cupid's butt-shaft is too hard for Hercules' club,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: and therefore too much odds for a Spaniard's rapier.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The first and second cause will not serve my turn,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: the passado he respects not, the duello he regards
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: not: his disgrace is to be called boy, but his
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: glory is to subdue men. Adieu, valour! rust rapier!
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: be still, drum! for your manager is in love, yea,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: he loveth. Assist me, some extemporal god of rhyme,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: for I am sure I shall turn sonnet. Devise, wit,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: write, pen, for I am for whole volumes in folio.
NARRATOR: Exit
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: ACT II
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: SCENE I. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCESS of France, ROSALINE, MARIA, KATHARINE, BOYET, Lords, and other Attendants
BOYET: Now, madam, summon up your dearest spirits:
BOYET: Consider who the king your father sends,
BOYET: To whom he sends, and what's his embassy:
BOYET: Yourself, held precious in the world's esteem,
BOYET: To parley with the sole inheritor
BOYET: Of all perfections that a man may owe,
BOYET: Matchless Navarre, the plea of no less weight
BOYET: Than Aquitaine, a dowry for a queen.
BOYET: Be now as prodigal of all dear grace
BOYET: As Nature was in making graces dear
BOYET: When she did starve the general world beside
BOYET: And prodigally gave them all to you.
PRINCESS: Good Lord Boyet, my beauty, though but mean,
PRINCESS: Needs not the painted flourish of your praise:
PRINCESS: Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye,
PRINCESS: Not utter'd by base sale of chapmen's tongues:
PRINCESS: I am less proud to hear you tell my worth
PRINCESS: Than you much willing to be counted wise
PRINCESS: In spending your wit in the praise of mine.
PRINCESS: But now to task the tasker: good Boyet,
PRINCESS: You are not ignorant, all-telling fame
PRINCESS: Doth noise abroad, Navarre hath made a vow,
PRINCESS: Till painful study shall outwear three years,
PRINCESS: No woman may approach his silent court:
PRINCESS: Therefore to's seemeth it a needful course,
PRINCESS: Before we enter his forbidden gates,
PRINCESS: To know his pleasure, and in that behalf,
PRINCESS: Bold of your worthiness, we single you
PRINCESS: As our best-moving fair solicitor.
PRINCESS: Tell him, the daughter of the King of France,
PRINCESS: On serious business, craving quick dispatch,
PRINCESS: Importunes personal conference with his grace:
PRINCESS: Haste, signify so much, while we attend,
PRINCESS: Like humble-visaged suitors, his high will.
BOYET: Proud of employment, willingly I go.
PRINCESS: All pride is willing pride, and yours is so.
NARRATOR: Exit BOYET
PRINCESS: Who are the votaries, my loving lords,
PRINCESS: That are vow-fellows with this virtuous duke?
First Lord: Lord Longaville is one.
PRINCESS: Know you the man?
MARIA: I know him, madam: at a marriage-feast,
MARIA: Between Lord Perigort and the beauteous heir
MARIA: Of Jaques Falconbridge, solemnized
MARIA: In Normandy, saw I this Longaville:
MARIA: A man of sovereign parts he is esteem'd,
MARIA: Well fitted in arts, glorious in arms:
MARIA: Nothing becomes him ill that he would well.
MARIA: The only soil of his fair virtue's gloss,
MARIA: If virtue's gloss will stain with any soil,
MARIA: Is a sharp wit matched with too blunt a will,
MARIA: Whose edge hath power to cut, whose will still wills
MARIA: It should none spare that come within his power.
PRINCESS: Some merry mocking lord, belike, is't so?
MARIA: They say so most that most his humours know.
PRINCESS: Such short-lived wits do wither as they grow.
PRINCESS: Who are the rest?
KATHARINE: The young Dumain, a well-accomplished youth,
KATHARINE: Of all that virtue love for virtue loved:
KATHARINE: Most power to do most harm, least knowing ill,
KATHARINE: For he hath wit to make an ill shape good,
KATHARINE: And shape to win grace though he had no wit.
KATHARINE: I saw him at the Duke Alencon's once,
KATHARINE: And much too little of that good I saw
KATHARINE: Is my report to his great worthiness.
ROSALINE: Another of these students at that time
ROSALINE: Was there with him, if I have heard a truth.
ROSALINE: Biron they call him, but a merrier man,
ROSALINE: Within the limit of becoming mirth,
ROSALINE: I never spent an hour's talk withal:
ROSALINE: His eye begets occasion for his wit,
ROSALINE: For every object that the one doth catch
ROSALINE: The other turns to a mirth-moving jest,
ROSALINE: Which his fair tongue, conceit's expositor,
ROSALINE: Delivers in such apt and gracious words
ROSALINE: That aged ears play truant at his tales
ROSALINE: And younger hearings are quite ravished,
ROSALINE: So sweet and voluble is his discourse.
PRINCESS: God bless my ladies! are they all in love,
PRINCESS: That every one her own hath garnished
PRINCESS: With such bedecking ornaments of praise?
First Lord: Here comes Boyet.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BOYET
PRINCESS: Now, what admittance, lord?
BOYET: Navarre had notice of your fair approach,
BOYET: And he and his competitors in oath
BOYET: Were all address'd to meet you, gentle lady,
BOYET: Before I came. Marry, thus much I have learnt:
BOYET: He rather means to lodge you in the field,
BOYET: Like one that comes here to besiege his court,
BOYET: Than seek a dispensation for his oath,
BOYET: To let you enter his unpeopled house.
BOYET: Here comes Navarre.
NARRATOR: Enter FERDINAND, LONGAVILLE, DUMAIN, BIRON, and Attendants
FERDINAND: Fair princess, welcome to the court of Navarre.
PRINCESS: 'Fair' I give you back again, and 'welcome' I have
PRINCESS: not yet: the roof of this court is too high to be
PRINCESS: yours, and welcome to the wide fields too base to be mine.
FERDINAND: You shall be welcome, madam, to my court.
PRINCESS: I will be welcome, then: conduct me thither.
FERDINAND: Hear me, dear lady, I have sworn an oath.
PRINCESS: Our Lady help my lord! he'll be forsworn.
FERDINAND: Not for the world, fair madam, by my will.
PRINCESS: Why, will shall break it, will and nothing else.
FERDINAND: Your ladyship is ignorant what it is.
PRINCESS: Were my lord so, his ignorance were wise,
PRINCESS: Where now his knowledge must prove ignorance.
PRINCESS: I hear your grace hath sworn out house-keeping:
PRINCESS: Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord,
PRINCESS: And sin to break it.
PRINCESS: But pardon me. I am too sudden-bold:
PRINCESS: To teach a teacher ill beseemeth me.
PRINCESS: Vouchsafe to read the purpose of my coming,
PRINCESS: And suddenly resolve me in my suit.
FERDINAND: Madam, I will, if suddenly I may.
PRINCESS: You will the sooner, that I were away,
PRINCESS: For you'll prove perjured if you make me stay.
BIRON: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
ROSALINE: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
BIRON: I know you did.
ROSALINE: How needless was it then to ask the question!
BIRON: You must not be so quick.
ROSALINE: 'Tis 'long of you that spur me with such questions.
BIRON: Your wit's too hot, it speeds too fast, 'twill tire.
ROSALINE: Not till it leave the rider in the mire.
BIRON: What time o' day?
ROSALINE: The hour that fools should ask.
BIRON: Now fair befall your mask!
ROSALINE: Fair fall the face it covers!
BIRON: And send you many lovers!
ROSALINE: Amen, so you be none.
BIRON: Nay, then will I be gone.
FERDINAND: Madam, your father here doth intimate
FERDINAND: The payment of a hundred thousand crowns,
FERDINAND: Being but the one half of an entire sum
FERDINAND: Disbursed by my father in his wars.
FERDINAND: But say that he or we, as neither have,
FERDINAND: Received that sum, yet there remains unpaid
FERDINAND: A hundred thousand more, in surety of the which,
FERDINAND: One part of Aquitaine is bound to us,
FERDINAND: Although not valued to the money's worth.
FERDINAND: If then the king your father will restore
FERDINAND: But that one half which is unsatisfied,
FERDINAND: We will give up our right in Aquitaine,
FERDINAND: And hold fair friendship with his majesty.
FERDINAND: But that, it seems, he little purposeth,
FERDINAND: For here he doth demand to have repaid
FERDINAND: A hundred thousand crowns, and not demands,
FERDINAND: On payment of a hundred thousand crowns,
FERDINAND: To have his title live in Aquitaine,
FERDINAND: Which we much rather had depart withal
FERDINAND: And have the money by our father lent
FERDINAND: Than Aquitaine so gelded as it is.
FERDINAND: Dear Princess, were not his requests so far
FERDINAND: From reason's yielding, your fair self should make
FERDINAND: A yielding 'gainst some reason in my breast
FERDINAND: And go well satisfied to France again.
PRINCESS: You do the king my father too much wrong
PRINCESS: And wrong the reputation of your name,
PRINCESS: In so unseeming to confess receipt
PRINCESS: Of that which hath so faithfully been paid.
FERDINAND: I do protest I never heard of it,
FERDINAND: And if you prove it, I'll repay it back
FERDINAND: Or yield up Aquitaine.
PRINCESS: We arrest your word.
PRINCESS: Boyet, you can produce acquittances
PRINCESS: For such a sum from special officers
PRINCESS: Of Charles his father.
FERDINAND: Satisfy me so.
BOYET: So please your grace, the packet is not come
BOYET: Where that and other specialties are bound:
BOYET: To-morrow you shall have a sight of them.
FERDINAND: It shall suffice me: at which interview
FERDINAND: All liberal reason I will yield unto.
FERDINAND: Meantime receive such welcome at my hand
FERDINAND: As honour without breach of honour may
FERDINAND: Make tender of to thy true worthiness:
FERDINAND: You may not come, fair princess, in my gates,
FERDINAND: But here without you shall be so received
FERDINAND: As you shall deem yourself lodged in my heart,
FERDINAND: Though so denied fair harbour in my house.
FERDINAND: Your own good thoughts excuse me, and farewell:
FERDINAND: To-morrow shall we visit you again.
PRINCESS: Sweet health and fair desires consort your grace!
FERDINAND: Thy own wish wish I thee in every place!
NARRATOR: Exit
BIRON: Lady, I will commend you to mine own heart.
ROSALINE: Pray you, do my commendations, I would be glad to see it.
BIRON: I would you heard it groan.
ROSALINE: Is the fool sick?
BIRON: Sick at the heart.
ROSALINE: Alack, let it blood.
BIRON: Would that do it good?
ROSALINE: My physic says 'ay.'
BIRON: Will you prick't with your eye?
ROSALINE: No point, with my knife.
BIRON: Now, God save thy life!
ROSALINE: And yours from long living!
BIRON: I cannot stay thanksgiving.
NARRATOR: Retiring
DUMAIN: Sir, I pray you, a word: what lady is that same?
BOYET: The heir of Alencon, Katharine her name.
DUMAIN: A gallant lady. Monsieur, fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit
LONGAVILLE: I beseech you a word: what is she in the white?
BOYET: A woman sometimes, an you saw her in the light.
LONGAVILLE: Perchance light in the light. I desire her name.
BOYET: She hath but one for herself, to desire that were a shame.
LONGAVILLE: Pray you, sir, whose daughter?
BOYET: Her mother's, I have heard.
LONGAVILLE: God's blessing on your beard!
BOYET: Good sir, be not offended.
BOYET: She is an heir of Falconbridge.
LONGAVILLE: Nay, my choler is ended.
LONGAVILLE: She is a most sweet lady.
BOYET: Not unlike, sir, that may be.
NARRATOR: Exit LONGAVILLE
BIRON: What's her name in the cap?
BOYET: Rosaline, by good hap.
BIRON: Is she wedded or no?
BOYET: To her will, sir, or so.
BIRON: You are welcome, sir: adieu.
BOYET: Farewell to me, sir, and welcome to you.
NARRATOR: Exit BIRON
MARIA: That last is Biron, the merry madcap lord:
MARIA: Not a word with him but a jest.
BOYET: And every jest but a word.
PRINCESS: It was well done of you to take him at his word.
BOYET: I was as willing to grapple as he was to board.
MARIA: Two hot sheeps, marry.
BOYET: And wherefore not ships?
BOYET: No sheep, sweet lamb, unless we feed on your lips.
MARIA: You sheep, and I pasture: shall that finish the jest?
BOYET: So you grant pasture for me.
NARRATOR: Offering to kiss her
MARIA: Not so, gentle beast:
MARIA: My lips are no common, though several they be.
BOYET: Belonging to whom?
MARIA: To my fortunes and me.
PRINCESS: Good wits will be jangling, but, gentles, agree:
PRINCESS: This civil war of wits were much better used
PRINCESS: On Navarre and his book-men, for here 'tis abused.
BOYET: If my observation, which very seldom lies,
BOYET: By the heart's still rhetoric disclosed with eyes,
BOYET: Deceive me not now, Navarre is infected.
PRINCESS: With what?
BOYET: With that which we lovers entitle affected.
PRINCESS: Your reason?
BOYET: Why, all his behaviors did make their retire
BOYET: To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire:
BOYET: His heart, like an agate, with your print impress'd,
BOYET: Proud with his form, in his eye pride express'd:
BOYET: His tongue, all impatient to speak and not see,
BOYET: Did stumble with haste in his eyesight to be,
BOYET: All senses to that sense did make their repair,
BOYET: To feel only looking on fairest of fair:
BOYET: Methought all his senses were lock'd in his eye,
BOYET: As jewels in crystal for some prince to buy,
BOYET: Who, tendering their own worth from where they were glass'd,
BOYET: Did point you to buy them, along as you pass'd:
BOYET: His face's own margent did quote such amazes
BOYET: That all eyes saw his eyes enchanted with gazes.
BOYET: I'll give you Aquitaine and all that is his,
BOYET: An you give him for my sake but one loving kiss.
PRINCESS: Come to our pavilion: Boyet is disposed.
BOYET: But to speak that in words which his eye hath
BOYET: disclosed.
BOYET: I only have made a mouth of his eye,
BOYET: By adding a tongue which I know will not lie.
ROSALINE: Thou art an old love-monger and speakest skilfully.
MARIA: He is Cupid's grandfather and learns news of him.
ROSALINE: Then was Venus like her mother, for her father is but grim.
BOYET: Do you hear, my mad wenches?
MARIA: No.
BOYET: What then, do you see?
ROSALINE: Ay, our way to be gone.
BOYET: You are too hard for me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
BOYET: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
BOYET: ACT III
BOYET: SCENE I. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO and MOTH
BOYET: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Warble, child, make passionate my sense of hearing.
MOTH: Concolinel.
NARRATOR: Singing
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sweet air! Go, tenderness of years, take this key,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: give enlargement to the swain, bring him festinately
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: hither: I must employ him in a letter to my love.
MOTH: Master, will you win your love with a French brawl?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: How meanest thou? brawling in French?
MOTH: No, my complete master: but to jig off a tune at
MOTH: the tongue's end, canary to it with your feet, humour
MOTH: it with turning up your eyelids, sigh a note and
MOTH: sing a note, sometime through the throat, as if you
MOTH: swallowed love with singing love, sometime through
MOTH: the nose, as if you snuffed up love by smelling
MOTH: love, with your hat penthouse-like o'er the shop of
MOTH: your eyes, with your arms crossed on your thin-belly
MOTH: doublet like a rabbit on a spit, or your hands in
MOTH: your pocket like a man after the old painting, and
MOTH: keep not too long in one tune, but a snip and away.
MOTH: These are complements, these are humours, these
MOTH: betray nice wenches, that would be betrayed without
MOTH: these, and make them men of note--do you note
MOTH: me?--that most are affected to these.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: How hast thou purchased this experience?
MOTH: By my penny of observation.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: But O,--but O,--
MOTH: 'The hobby-horse is forgot.'
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Callest thou my love 'hobby-horse'?
MOTH: No, master, the hobby-horse is but a colt, and your
MOTH: love perhaps a hackney. But have you forgot your love?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Almost I had.
MOTH: Negligent student! learn her by heart.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: By heart and in heart, boy.
MOTH: And out of heart, master: all those three I will prove.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: What wilt thou prove?
MOTH: A man, if I live, and this, by, in, and without, upon
MOTH: the instant: by heart you love her, because your
MOTH: heart cannot come by her, in heart you love her,
MOTH: because your heart is in love with her, and out of
MOTH: heart you love her, being out of heart that you
MOTH: cannot enjoy her.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I am all these three.
MOTH: And three times as much more, and yet nothing at
MOTH: all.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Fetch hither the swain: he must carry me a letter.
MOTH: A message well sympathized, a horse to be ambassador
MOTH: for an ass.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Ha, ha! what sayest thou?
MOTH: Marry, sir, you must send the ass upon the horse,
MOTH: for he is very slow-gaited. But I go.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The way is but short: away!
MOTH: As swift as lead, sir.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The meaning, pretty ingenious?
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Is not lead a metal heavy, dull, and slow?
MOTH: Minime, honest master, or rather, master, no.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I say lead is slow.
MOTH: You are too swift, sir, to say so:
MOTH: Is that lead slow which is fired from a gun?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sweet smoke of rhetoric!
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: He reputes me a cannon, and the bullet, that's he:
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I shoot thee at the swain.
MOTH: Thump then and I flee.
NARRATOR: Exit
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: A most acute juvenal, voluble and free of grace!
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: By thy favour, sweet welkin, I must sigh in thy face:
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Most rude melancholy, valour gives thee place.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: My herald is return'd.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MOTH with COSTARD
MOTH: A wonder, master! here's a costard broken in a shin.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Some enigma, some riddle: come, thy l'envoy, begin.
COSTARD: No enigma, no riddle, no l'envoy, no salve in the
COSTARD: mail, sir: O, sir, plantain, a plain plantain! no
COSTARD: l'envoy, no l'envoy, no salve, sir, but a plantain!
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: By virtue, thou enforcest laughter, thy silly
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: thought my spleen, the heaving of my lungs provokes
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: me to ridiculous smiling. O, pardon me, my stars!
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Doth the inconsiderate take salve for l'envoy, and
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: the word l'envoy for a salve?
MOTH: Do the wise think them other? is not l'envoy a salve?
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: No, page: it is an epilogue or discourse, to make plain
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Some obscure precedence that hath tofore been sain.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I will example it:
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Were still at odds, being but three.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: There's the moral. Now the l'envoy.
MOTH: I will add the l'envoy. Say the moral again.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Were still at odds, being but three.
MOTH: Until the goose came out of door,
MOTH: And stay'd the odds by adding four.
MOTH: Now will I begin your moral, and do you follow with
MOTH: my l'envoy.
MOTH: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee,
MOTH: Were still at odds, being but three.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Until the goose came out of door,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Staying the odds by adding four.
MOTH: A good l'envoy, ending in the goose: would you
MOTH: desire more?
COSTARD: The boy hath sold him a bargain, a goose, that's flat.
COSTARD: Sir, your pennyworth is good, an your goose be fat.
COSTARD: To sell a bargain well is as cunning as fast and loose:
COSTARD: Let me see, a fat l'envoy, ay, that's a fat goose.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Come hither, come hither. How did this argument begin?
MOTH: By saying that a costard was broken in a shin.
MOTH: Then call'd you for the l'envoy.
COSTARD: True, and I for a plantain: thus came your
COSTARD: argument in,
COSTARD: Then the boy's fat l'envoy, the goose that you bought,
COSTARD: And he ended the market.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: But tell me, how was there a costard broken in a shin?
MOTH: I will tell you sensibly.
COSTARD: Thou hast no feeling of it, Moth: I will speak that l'envoy:
COSTARD: I Costard, running out, that was safely within,
COSTARD: Fell over the threshold and broke my shin.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: We will talk no more of this matter.
COSTARD: Till there be more matter in the shin.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sirrah Costard, I will enfranchise thee.
COSTARD: O, marry me to one Frances: I smell some l'envoy,
COSTARD: some goose, in this.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: By my sweet soul, I mean setting thee at liberty,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: enfreedoming thy person, thou wert immured,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: restrained, captivated, bound.
COSTARD: True, true, and now you will be my purgation and let me loose.
COSTARD: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I give thee thy liberty, set thee from durance, and,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: in lieu thereof, impose on thee nothing but this:
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: bear this significant
NARRATOR: Giving a letter

ADRIANO DE ARMADO: there is remuneration, for the best ward of mine
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: honour is rewarding my dependents. Moth, follow.
NARRATOR: Exit
MOTH: Like the sequel, I. Signior Costard, adieu.
COSTARD: My sweet ounce of man's flesh! my incony Jew!
NARRATOR: Exit MOTH
COSTARD: Now will I look to his remuneration. Remuneration!
COSTARD: O, that's the Latin word for three farthings: three
COSTARD: farthings--remuneration.--'What's the price of this
COSTARD: inkle?'--'One penny.'--'No, I'll give you a
COSTARD: remuneration:' why, it carries it. Remuneration!
COSTARD: why, it is a fairer name than French crown. I will
COSTARD: never buy and sell out of this word.
NARRATOR: Enter BIRON
BIRON: O, my good knave Costard! exceedingly well met.
COSTARD: Pray you, sir, how much carnation ribbon may a man
COSTARD: buy for a remuneration?
BIRON: What is a remuneration?
COSTARD: Marry, sir, halfpenny farthing.
BIRON: Why, then, three-farthing worth of silk.
COSTARD: I thank your worship: God be wi' you!
BIRON: Stay, slave, I must employ thee:
BIRON: As thou wilt win my favour, good my knave,
BIRON: Do one thing for me that I shall entreat.
COSTARD: When would you have it done, sir?
BIRON: This afternoon.
COSTARD: Well, I will do it, sir: fare you well.
BIRON: Thou knowest not what it is.
COSTARD: I shall know, sir, when I have done it.
BIRON: Why, villain, thou must know first.
COSTARD: I will come to your worship to-morrow morning.
BIRON: It must be done this afternoon.
BIRON: Hark, slave, it is but this:
BIRON: The princess comes to hunt here in the park,
BIRON: And in her train there is a gentle lady,
BIRON: When tongues speak sweetly, then they name her name,
BIRON: And Rosaline they call her: ask for her,
BIRON: And to her white hand see thou do commend
BIRON: This seal'd-up counsel. There's thy guerdon, go.
NARRATOR: Giving him a shilling
COSTARD: Gardon, O sweet gardon! better than remuneration,
COSTARD: a'leven-pence farthing better: most sweet gardon! I
COSTARD: will do it sir, in print. Gardon! Remuneration!
NARRATOR: Exit
BIRON: And I, forsooth, in love! I, that have been love's whip,
BIRON: A very beadle to a humorous sigh,
BIRON: A critic, nay, a night-watch constable,
BIRON: A domineering pedant o'er the boy,
BIRON: Than whom no mortal so magnificent!
BIRON: This whimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy,
BIRON: This senior-junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid,
BIRON: Regent of love-rhymes, lord of folded arms,
BIRON: The anointed sovereign of sighs and groans,
BIRON: Liege of all loiterers and malcontents,
BIRON: Dread prince of plackets, king of codpieces,
BIRON: Sole imperator and great general
BIRON: Of trotting 'paritors:--O my little heart:--
BIRON: And I to be a corporal of his field,
BIRON: And wear his colours like a tumbler's hoop!
BIRON: What, I! I love! I sue! I seek a wife!
BIRON: A woman, that is like a German clock,
BIRON: Still a-repairing, ever out of frame,
BIRON: And never going aright, being a watch,
BIRON: But being watch'd that it may still go right!
BIRON: Nay, to be perjured, which is worst of all,
BIRON: And, among three, to love the worst of all,
BIRON: A wightly wanton with a velvet brow,
BIRON: With two pitch-balls stuck in her face for eyes,
BIRON: Ay, and by heaven, one that will do the deed
BIRON: Though Argus were her eunuch and her guard:
BIRON: And I to sigh for her! to watch for her!
BIRON: To pray for her! Go to, it is a plague
BIRON: That Cupid will impose for my neglect
BIRON: Of his almighty dreadful little might.
BIRON: Well, I will love, write, sigh, pray, sue and groan:
BIRON: Some men must love my lady and some Joan.
NARRATOR: Exit
BIRON: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
BIRON: ACT IV
BIRON: SCENE I. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCESS, and her train, a Forester, BOYET, ROSALINE, MARIA, and KATHARINE
PRINCESS: Was that the king, that spurred his horse so hard
PRINCESS: Against the steep uprising of the hill?
BOYET: I know not, but I think it was not he.
PRINCESS: Whoe'er a' was, a' show'd a mounting mind.
PRINCESS: Well, lords, to-day we shall have our dispatch:
PRINCESS: On Saturday we will return to France.
PRINCESS: Then, forester, my friend, where is the bush
PRINCESS: That we must stand and play the murderer in?
Forester: Hereby, upon the edge of yonder coppice,
Forester: A stand where you may make the fairest shoot.
PRINCESS: I thank my beauty, I am fair that shoot,
PRINCESS: And thereupon thou speak'st the fairest shoot.
Forester: Pardon me, madam, for I meant not so.
PRINCESS: What, what? first praise me and again say no?
PRINCESS: O short-lived pride! Not fair? alack for woe!
Forester: Yes, madam, fair.
PRINCESS: Nay, never paint me now:
PRINCESS: Where fair is not, praise cannot mend the brow.
PRINCESS: Here, good my glass, take this for telling true:
PRINCESS: Fair payment for foul words is more than due.
Forester: Nothing but fair is that which you inherit.
PRINCESS: See see, my beauty will be saved by merit!
PRINCESS: O heresy in fair, fit for these days!
PRINCESS: A giving hand, though foul, shall have fair praise.
PRINCESS: But come, the bow: now mercy goes to kill,
PRINCESS: And shooting well is then accounted ill.
PRINCESS: Thus will I save my credit in the shoot:
PRINCESS: Not wounding, pity would not let me do't,
PRINCESS: If wounding, then it was to show my skill,
PRINCESS: That more for praise than purpose meant to kill.
PRINCESS: And out of question so it is sometimes,
PRINCESS: Glory grows guilty of detested crimes,
PRINCESS: When, for fame's sake, for praise, an outward part,
PRINCESS: We bend to that the working of the heart,
PRINCESS: As I for praise alone now seek to spill
PRINCESS: The poor deer's blood, that my heart means no ill.
BOYET: Do not curst wives hold that self-sovereignty
BOYET: Only for praise sake, when they strive to be
BOYET: Lords o'er their lords?
PRINCESS: Only for praise: and praise we may afford
PRINCESS: To any lady that subdues a lord.
BOYET: Here comes a member of the commonwealth.
NARRATOR: Enter COSTARD
COSTARD: God dig-you-den all! Pray you, which is the head lady?
PRINCESS: Thou shalt know her, fellow, by the rest that have no heads.
COSTARD: Which is the greatest lady, the highest?
PRINCESS: The thickest and the tallest.
COSTARD: The thickest and the tallest! it is so, truth is truth.
COSTARD: An your waist, mistress, were as slender as my wit,
COSTARD: One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should be fit.
COSTARD: Are not you the chief woman? you are the thickest here.
PRINCESS: What's your will, sir? what's your will?
COSTARD: I have a letter from Monsieur Biron to one Lady Rosaline.
PRINCESS: O, thy letter, thy letter! he's a good friend of mine:
PRINCESS: Stand aside, good bearer. Boyet, you can carve,
PRINCESS: Break up this capon.
BOYET: I am bound to serve.
BOYET: This letter is mistook, it importeth none here,
BOYET: It is writ to Jaquenetta.
PRINCESS: We will read it, I swear.
PRINCESS: Break the neck of the wax, and every one give ear.
NARRATOR: Reads
BOYET: 'By heaven, that thou art fair, is most infallible,
BOYET: true, that thou art beauteous, truth itself, that
BOYET: thou art lovely. More fairer than fair, beautiful
BOYET: than beauteous, truer than truth itself, have
BOYET: commiseration on thy heroical vassal! The
BOYET: magnanimous and most illustrate king Cophetua set
BOYET: eye upon the pernicious and indubitate beggar
BOYET: Zenelophon, and he it was that might rightly say,
BOYET: Veni, vidi, vici, which to annothanize in the
BOYET: vulgar,--O base and obscure vulgar!--videlicet, He
BOYET: came, saw, and overcame: he came, one, saw two,
BOYET: overcame, three. Who came? the king: why did he
BOYET: come? to see: why did he see? to overcome: to
BOYET: whom came he? to the beggar: what saw he? the
BOYET: beggar: who overcame he? the beggar. The
BOYET: conclusion is victory: on whose side? the king's.
BOYET: The captive is enriched: on whose side? the
BOYET: beggar's. The catastrophe is a nuptial: on whose
BOYET: side? the king's: no, on both in one, or one in
BOYET: both. I am the king, for so stands the comparison:
BOYET: thou the beggar, for so witnesseth thy lowliness.
BOYET: Shall I command thy love? I may: shall I enforce
BOYET: thy love? I could: shall I entreat thy love? I
BOYET: will. What shalt thou exchange for rags? robes,
BOYET: for tittles? titles, for thyself? me. Thus,
BOYET: expecting thy reply, I profane my lips on thy foot,
BOYET: my eyes on thy picture. and my heart on thy every
BOYET: part. Thine, in the dearest design of industry,
BOYET: DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'
BOYET: Thus dost thou hear the Nemean lion roar
BOYET: 'Gainst thee, thou lamb, that standest as his prey.
BOYET: Submissive fall his princely feet before,
BOYET: And he from forage will incline to play:
BOYET: But if thou strive, poor soul, what art thou then?
BOYET: Food for his rage, repasture for his den.
PRINCESS: What plume of feathers is he that indited this letter?
PRINCESS: What vane? what weathercock? did you ever hear better?
BOYET: I am much deceived but I remember the style.
PRINCESS: Else your memory is bad, going o'er it erewhile.

BOYET: A phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes sport

PRINCESS: Thou fellow, a word:
PRINCESS: Who gave thee this letter?
COSTARD: I told you, my lord.
PRINCESS: To whom shouldst thou give it?
COSTARD: From my lord to my lady.
PRINCESS: From which lord to which lady?
COSTARD: From my lord Biron, a good master of mine,
COSTARD: To a lady of France that he call'd Rosaline.
PRINCESS: Thou hast mistaken his letter. Come, lords, away.

BOYET: Who is the suitor? who is the suitor?
ROSALINE: Shall I teach you to know?
BOYET: Ay, my continent of beauty.
ROSALINE: Why, she that bears the bow.
ROSALINE: Finely put off!
BOYET: My lady goes to kill horns, but, if thou marry,
BOYET: Hang me by the neck, if horns that year miscarry.
BOYET: Finely put on!
ROSALINE: Well, then, I am the shooter.
BOYET: And who is your deer?
ROSALINE: If we choose by the horns, yourself come not near.
ROSALINE: Finely put on, indeed!
MARIA: You still wrangle with her, Boyet, and she strikes
MARIA: at the brow.
BOYET: But she herself is hit lower: have I hit her now?
ROSALINE: Shall I come upon thee with an old saying, that was
ROSALINE: a man when King Pepin of France was a little boy, as
ROSALINE: touching the hit it?
BOYET: So I may answer thee with one as old, that was a
BOYET: woman when Queen Guinover of Britain was a little
BOYET: wench, as touching the hit it.
ROSALINE: Thou canst not hit it, hit it, hit it,
ROSALINE: Thou canst not hit it, my good man.
BOYET: An I cannot, cannot, cannot,
BOYET: An I cannot, another can.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ROSALINE and KATHARINE
COSTARD: By my troth, most pleasant: how both did fit it!
MARIA: A mark marvellous well shot, for they both did hit it.
BOYET: A mark! O, mark but that mark! A mark, says my lady!
BOYET: Let the mark have a prick in't, to mete at, if it may be.
MARIA: Wide o' the bow hand! i' faith, your hand is out.
COSTARD: Indeed, a' must shoot nearer, or he'll ne'er hit the clout.
BOYET: An if my hand be out, then belike your hand is in.
COSTARD: Then will she get the upshoot by cleaving the pin.
MARIA: Come, come, you talk greasily, your lips grow foul.
COSTARD: She's too hard for you at pricks, sir: challenge her to bowl.
BOYET: I fear too much rubbing. Good night, my good owl.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BOYET and MARIA
COSTARD: By my soul, a swain! a most simple clown!
COSTARD: Lord, Lord, how the ladies and I have put him down!
COSTARD: O' my troth, most sweet jests! most incony
COSTARD: vulgar wit!
COSTARD: When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely, as it
COSTARD: were, so fit.
COSTARD: Armado o' th' one side,--O, a most dainty man!
COSTARD: To see him walk before a lady and to bear her fan!
COSTARD: To see him kiss his hand! and how most sweetly a'
COSTARD: will swear!
COSTARD: And his page o' t' other side, that handful of wit!
COSTARD: Ah, heavens, it is a most pathetical nit!
COSTARD: Sola, sola!
NARRATOR: Shout within
NARRATOR: Exit COSTARD, running
COSTARD: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
COSTARD: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter HOLOFERNES, SIR NATHANIEL, and DULL
SIR NATHANIEL: Very reverend sport, truly, and done in the testimony
SIR NATHANIEL: of a good conscience.
HOLOFERNES: The deer was, as you know, sanguis, in blood, ripe
HOLOFERNES: as the pomewater, who now hangeth like a jewel in
HOLOFERNES: the ear of caelo, the sky, the welkin, the heaven,
HOLOFERNES: and anon falleth like a crab on the face of terra,
HOLOFERNES: the soil, the land, the earth.
SIR NATHANIEL: Truly, Master Holofernes, the epithets are sweetly
SIR NATHANIEL: varied, like a scholar at the least: but, sir, I
SIR NATHANIEL: assure ye, it was a buck of the first head.
HOLOFERNES: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.
DULL: 'Twas not a haud credo, 'twas a pricket.
HOLOFERNES: Most barbarous intimation! yet a kind of
HOLOFERNES: insinuation, as it were, in via, in way, of
HOLOFERNES: explication, facere, as it were, replication, or
HOLOFERNES: rather, ostentare, to show, as it were, his
HOLOFERNES: inclination, after his undressed, unpolished,
HOLOFERNES: uneducated, unpruned, untrained, or rather,
HOLOFERNES: unlettered, or ratherest, unconfirmed fashion, to
HOLOFERNES: insert again my haud credo for a deer.
DULL: I said the deer was not a haud credo, twas a pricket.
HOLOFERNES: Twice-sod simplicity, his coctus!
HOLOFERNES: O thou monster Ignorance, how deformed dost thou look!
SIR NATHANIEL: Sir, he hath never fed of the dainties that are bred
SIR NATHANIEL: in a book, he hath not eat paper, as it were, he
SIR NATHANIEL: hath not drunk ink: his intellect is not
SIR NATHANIEL: replenished, he is only an animal, only sensible in
SIR NATHANIEL: the duller parts:
SIR NATHANIEL: And such barren plants are set before us, that we
SIR NATHANIEL: thankful should be,
SIR NATHANIEL: Which we of taste and feeling are, for those parts that
SIR NATHANIEL: do fructify in us more than he.
SIR NATHANIEL: For as it would ill become me to be vain, indiscreet, or a fool,
SIR NATHANIEL: So were there a patch set on learning, to see him in a school:
SIR NATHANIEL: But omne bene, say I, being of an old father's mind,
SIR NATHANIEL: Many can brook the weather that love not the wind.
DULL: You two are book-men: can you tell me by your wit
DULL: What was a month old at Cain's birth, that's not five
DULL: weeks old as yet?
HOLOFERNES: Dictynna, goodman Dull, Dictynna, goodman Dull.
DULL: What is Dictynna?
SIR NATHANIEL: A title to Phoebe, to Luna, to the moon.
HOLOFERNES: The moon was a month old when Adam was no more,
HOLOFERNES: And raught not to five weeks when he came to
HOLOFERNES: five-score.
HOLOFERNES: The allusion holds in the exchange.
DULL: 'Tis true indeed, the collusion holds in the exchange.
HOLOFERNES: God comfort thy capacity! I say, the allusion holds
HOLOFERNES: in the exchange.
DULL: And I say, the pollusion holds in the exchange, for
DULL: the moon is never but a month old: and I say beside
DULL: that, 'twas a pricket that the princess killed.
HOLOFERNES: Sir Nathaniel, will you hear an extemporal epitaph
HOLOFERNES: on the death of the deer? And, to humour the
HOLOFERNES: ignorant, call I the deer the princess killed a pricket.
SIR NATHANIEL: Perge, good Master Holofernes, perge, so it shall
SIR NATHANIEL: please you to abrogate scurrility.
HOLOFERNES: I will something affect the letter, for it argues facility.
HOLOFERNES: The preyful princess pierced and prick'd a pretty
HOLOFERNES: pleasing pricket,
HOLOFERNES: Some say a sore, but not a sore, till now made
HOLOFERNES: sore with shooting.
HOLOFERNES: The dogs did yell: put L to sore, then sorel jumps
HOLOFERNES: from thicket,
HOLOFERNES: Or pricket sore, or else sorel, the people fall a-hooting.
HOLOFERNES: If sore be sore, then L to sore makes fifty sores
HOLOFERNES: one sorel.
HOLOFERNES: Of one sore I an hundred make by adding but one more L.
SIR NATHANIEL: A rare talent!
DULL: [Aside]  If a talent be a claw, look how he claws
DULL: him with a talent.
HOLOFERNES: This is a gift that I have, simple, simple, a
HOLOFERNES: foolish extravagant spirit, full of forms, figures,
HOLOFERNES: shapes, objects, ideas, apprehensions, motions,
HOLOFERNES: revolutions: these are begot in the ventricle of
HOLOFERNES: memory, nourished in the womb of pia mater, and
HOLOFERNES: delivered upon the mellowing of occasion. But the
HOLOFERNES: gift is good in those in whom it is acute, and I am
HOLOFERNES: thankful for it.
SIR NATHANIEL: Sir, I praise the Lord for you, and so may my
SIR NATHANIEL: parishioners, for their sons are well tutored by
SIR NATHANIEL: you, and their daughters profit very greatly under
SIR NATHANIEL: you: you are a good member of the commonwealth.
HOLOFERNES: Mehercle, if their sons be ingenuous, they shall
HOLOFERNES: want no instruction, if their daughters be capable,
HOLOFERNES: I will put it to them: but vir sapit qui pauca
HOLOFERNES: loquitur, a soul feminine saluteth us.
NARRATOR: Enter JAQUENETTA and COSTARD
JAQUENETTA: God give you good morrow, master Parson.
HOLOFERNES: Master Parson, quasi pers-on. An if one should be
HOLOFERNES: pierced, which is the one?
COSTARD: Marry, master schoolmaster, he that is likest to a hogshead.
HOLOFERNES: Piercing a hogshead! a good lustre of conceit in a
HOLOFERNES: tuft of earth, fire enough for a flint, pearl enough
HOLOFERNES: for a swine: 'tis pretty, it is well.
