JAQUENETTA: letter: it was given me by Costard, and sent me
JAQUENETTA: from Don Armado: I beseech you, read it.
HOLOFERNES: Fauste, precor gelida quando pecus omne sub umbra
HOLOFERNES: Ruminat,--and so forth. Ah, good old Mantuan! I
HOLOFERNES: may speak of thee as the traveller doth of Venice,
HOLOFERNES: Venetia, Venetia,
HOLOFERNES: Chi non ti vede non ti pretia.
HOLOFERNES: Old Mantuan, old Mantuan! who understandeth thee
HOLOFERNES: not, loves thee not. Ut, re, sol, la, mi, fa.
HOLOFERNES: Under pardon, sir, what are the contents? or rather,
HOLOFERNES: as Horace says in his--What, my soul, verses?
SIR NATHANIEL: Ay, sir, and very learned.
HOLOFERNES: Let me hear a staff, a stanze, a verse, lege, domine.
SIR NATHANIEL: [Reads]
SIR NATHANIEL: If love make me forsworn, how shall I swear to love?
SIR NATHANIEL: Ah, never faith could hold, if not to beauty vow'd!
SIR NATHANIEL: Though to myself forsworn, to thee I'll faithful prove:
SIR NATHANIEL: Those thoughts to me were oaks, to thee like
SIR NATHANIEL: osiers bow'd.
SIR NATHANIEL: Study his bias leaves and makes his book thine eyes,
SIR NATHANIEL: Where all those pleasures live that art would
SIR NATHANIEL: comprehend:
SIR NATHANIEL: If knowledge be the mark, to know thee shall suffice,
SIR NATHANIEL: Well learned is that tongue that well can thee commend,
SIR NATHANIEL: All ignorant that soul that sees thee without wonder,
SIR NATHANIEL: Which is to me some praise that I thy parts admire:
SIR NATHANIEL: Thy eye Jove's lightning bears, thy voice his dreadful thunder,
SIR NATHANIEL: Which not to anger bent, is music and sweet fire.
SIR NATHANIEL: Celestial as thou art, O, pardon, love, this wrong,
SIR NATHANIEL: That sings heaven's praise with such an earthly tongue.
HOLOFERNES: You find not the apostraphas, and so miss the
HOLOFERNES: accent: let me supervise the canzonet. Here are
HOLOFERNES: only numbers ratified, but, for the elegancy,
HOLOFERNES: facility, and golden cadence of poesy, caret.
HOLOFERNES: Ovidius Naso was the man: and why, indeed, Naso,
HOLOFERNES: but for smelling out the odouriferous flowers of
HOLOFERNES: fancy, the jerks of invention? Imitari is nothing:
HOLOFERNES: so doth the hound his master, the ape his keeper,
HOLOFERNES: the tired horse his rider. But, damosella virgin,
HOLOFERNES: was this directed to you?
JAQUENETTA: Ay, sir, from one Monsieur Biron, one of the strange
JAQUENETTA: queen's lords.
HOLOFERNES: I will overglance the superscript: 'To the
HOLOFERNES: snow-white hand of the most beauteous Lady
HOLOFERNES: Rosaline.' I will look again on the intellect of
HOLOFERNES: the letter, for the nomination of the party writing
HOLOFERNES: to the person written unto: 'Your ladyship's in all
HOLOFERNES: desired employment, BIRON.' Sir Nathaniel, this
HOLOFERNES: Biron is one of the votaries with the king, and here
HOLOFERNES: he hath framed a letter to a sequent of the stranger
HOLOFERNES: queen's, which accidentally, or by the way of
HOLOFERNES: progression, hath miscarried. Trip and go, my
HOLOFERNES: sweet, deliver this paper into the royal hand of the
HOLOFERNES: king: it may concern much. Stay not thy
HOLOFERNES: compliment, I forgive thy duty, adieu.
JAQUENETTA: Good Costard, go with me. Sir, God save your life!
COSTARD: Have with thee, my girl.
NARRATOR: Exeunt COSTARD and JAQUENETTA
SIR NATHANIEL: Sir, you have done this in the fear of God, very
SIR NATHANIEL: religiously, and, as a certain father saith,--
HOLOFERNES: Sir tell me not of the father, I do fear colourable
HOLOFERNES: colours. But to return to the verses: did they
HOLOFERNES: please you, Sir Nathaniel?
SIR NATHANIEL: Marvellous well for the pen.
HOLOFERNES: I do dine to-day at the father's of a certain pupil
HOLOFERNES: of mine, where, if, before repast, it shall please
HOLOFERNES: you to gratify the table with a grace, I will, on my
HOLOFERNES: privilege I have with the parents of the foresaid
HOLOFERNES: child or pupil, undertake your ben venuto, where I
HOLOFERNES: will prove those verses to be very unlearned,
HOLOFERNES: neither savouring of poetry, wit, nor invention: I
HOLOFERNES: beseech your society.
SIR NATHANIEL: And thank you too, for society, saith the text, is
SIR NATHANIEL: the happiness of life.
HOLOFERNES: And, certes, the text most infallibly concludes it.
NARRATOR: To DULL
HOLOFERNES: Sir, I do invite you too, you shall not
HOLOFERNES: say me nay: pauca verba. Away! the gentles are at
HOLOFERNES: their game, and we will to our recreation.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
HOLOFERNES: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
HOLOFERNES: SCENE III. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter BIRON, with a paper
BIRON: The king he is hunting the deer, I am coursing
BIRON: myself: they have pitched a toil, I am toiling in
BIRON: a pitch,--pitch that defiles: defile! a foul
BIRON: word. Well, set thee down, sorrow! for so they say
BIRON: the fool said, and so say I, and I the fool: well
BIRON: proved, wit! By the Lord, this love is as mad as
BIRON: Ajax: it kills sheep, it kills me, I a sheep:
BIRON: well proved again o' my side! I will not love: if
BIRON: I do, hang me, i' faith, I will not. O, but her
BIRON: eye,--by this light, but for her eye, I would not
BIRON: love her, yes, for her two eyes. Well, I do nothing
BIRON: in the world but lie, and lie in my throat. By
BIRON: heaven, I do love: and it hath taught me to rhyme
BIRON: and to be melancholy, and here is part of my rhyme,
BIRON: and here my melancholy. Well, she hath one o' my
BIRON: sonnets already: the clown bore it, the fool sent
BIRON: it, and the lady hath it: sweet clown, sweeter
BIRON: fool, sweetest lady! By the world, I would not care
BIRON: a pin, if the other three were in. Here comes one
BIRON: with a paper: God give him grace to groan!
NARRATOR: Stands aside
NARRATOR: Enter FERDINAND, with a paper
FERDINAND: Ay me!
BIRON: [Aside]  Shot, by heaven! Proceed, sweet Cupid:
BIRON: thou hast thumped him with thy bird-bolt under the
BIRON: left pap. In faith, secrets!
FERDINAND: [Reads]
FERDINAND: So sweet a kiss the golden sun gives not
FERDINAND: To those fresh morning drops upon the rose,
FERDINAND: As thy eye-beams, when their fresh rays have smote
FERDINAND: The night of dew that on my cheeks down flows:
FERDINAND: Nor shines the silver moon one half so bright
FERDINAND: Through the transparent bosom of the deep,
FERDINAND: As doth thy face through tears of mine give light,
FERDINAND: Thou shinest in every tear that I do weep:
FERDINAND: No drop but as a coach doth carry thee,
FERDINAND: So ridest thou triumphing in my woe.
FERDINAND: Do but behold the tears that swell in me,
FERDINAND: And they thy glory through my grief will show:
FERDINAND: But do not love thyself, then thou wilt keep
FERDINAND: My tears for glasses, and still make me weep.
FERDINAND: O queen of queens! how far dost thou excel,
FERDINAND: No thought can think, nor tongue of mortal tell.
FERDINAND: How shall she know my griefs? I'll drop the paper:
FERDINAND: Sweet leaves, shade folly. Who is he comes here?
NARRATOR: Steps aside
FERDINAND: What, Longaville! and reading! listen, ear.
BIRON: Now, in thy likeness, one more fool appear!
NARRATOR: Enter LONGAVILLE, with a paper
LONGAVILLE: Ay me, I am forsworn!
BIRON: Why, he comes in like a perjure, wearing papers.
FERDINAND: In love, I hope: sweet fellowship in shame!
BIRON: One drunkard loves another of the name.
LONGAVILLE: Am I the first that have been perjured so?
BIRON: I could put thee in comfort. Not by two that I know:
BIRON: Thou makest the triumviry, the corner-cap of society,
BIRON: The shape of Love's Tyburn that hangs up simplicity.
LONGAVILLE: I fear these stubborn lines lack power to move:
LONGAVILLE: O sweet Maria, empress of my love!
LONGAVILLE: These numbers will I tear, and write in prose.
BIRON: O, rhymes are guards on wanton Cupid's hose:
BIRON: Disfigure not his slop.
LONGAVILLE: This same shall go.
NARRATOR: Reads
LONGAVILLE: Did not the heavenly rhetoric of thine eye,
LONGAVILLE: 'Gainst whom the world cannot hold argument,
LONGAVILLE: Persuade my heart to this false perjury?
LONGAVILLE: Vows for thee broke deserve not punishment.
LONGAVILLE: A woman I forswore, but I will prove,
LONGAVILLE: Thou being a goddess, I forswore not thee:
LONGAVILLE: My vow was earthly, thou a heavenly love,
LONGAVILLE: Thy grace being gain'd cures all disgrace in me.
LONGAVILLE: Vows are but breath, and breath a vapour is:
LONGAVILLE: Then thou, fair sun, which on my earth dost shine,
LONGAVILLE: Exhalest this vapour-vow, in thee it is:
LONGAVILLE: If broken then, it is no fault of mine:
LONGAVILLE: If by me broke, what fool is not so wise
LONGAVILLE: To lose an oath to win a paradise?
BIRON: This is the liver-vein, which makes flesh a deity,
BIRON: A green goose a goddess: pure, pure idolatry.
BIRON: God amend us, God amend! we are much out o' the way.
LONGAVILLE: By whom shall I send this?--Company! stay.
NARRATOR: Steps aside
BIRON: All hid, all hid, an old infant play.
BIRON: Like a demigod here sit I in the sky.
BIRON: And wretched fools' secrets heedfully o'ereye.
BIRON: More sacks to the mill! O heavens, I have my wish!
NARRATOR: Enter DUMAIN, with a paper
BIRON: Dumain transform'd! four woodcocks in a dish!
DUMAIN: O most divine Kate!
BIRON: O most profane coxcomb!
DUMAIN: By heaven, the wonder in a mortal eye!
BIRON: By earth, she is not, corporal, there you lie.
DUMAIN: Her amber hair for foul hath amber quoted.
BIRON: An amber-colour'd raven was well noted.
DUMAIN: As upright as the cedar.
BIRON: Stoop, I say,
BIRON: Her shoulder is with child.
DUMAIN: As fair as day.
BIRON: Ay, as some days, but then no sun must shine.
DUMAIN: O that I had my wish!
LONGAVILLE: And I had mine!
FERDINAND: And I mine too, good Lord!
BIRON: Amen, so I had mine: is not that a good word?
DUMAIN: I would forget her, but a fever she
DUMAIN: Reigns in my blood and will remember'd be.
BIRON: A fever in your blood! why, then incision
BIRON: Would let her out in saucers: sweet misprision!
DUMAIN: Once more I'll read the ode that I have writ.
BIRON: Once more I'll mark how love can vary wit.
DUMAIN: [Reads]
DUMAIN: On a day--alack the day!--
DUMAIN: Love, whose month is ever May,
DUMAIN: Spied a blossom passing fair
DUMAIN: Playing in the wanton air:
DUMAIN: Through the velvet leaves the wind,
DUMAIN: All unseen, can passage find,
DUMAIN: That the lover, sick to death,
DUMAIN: Wish himself the heaven's breath.
DUMAIN: Air, quoth he, thy cheeks may blow,
DUMAIN: Air, would I might triumph so!
DUMAIN: But, alack, my hand is sworn
DUMAIN: Ne'er to pluck thee from thy thorn,
DUMAIN: Vow, alack, for youth unmeet,
DUMAIN: Youth so apt to pluck a sweet!
DUMAIN: Do not call it sin in me,
DUMAIN: That I am forsworn for thee,
DUMAIN: Thou for whom Jove would swear
DUMAIN: Juno but an Ethiope were,
DUMAIN: And deny himself for Jove,
DUMAIN: Turning mortal for thy love.
DUMAIN: This will I send, and something else more plain,
DUMAIN: That shall express my true love's fasting pain.
DUMAIN: O, would the king, Biron, and Longaville,
DUMAIN: Were lovers too! Ill, to example ill,
DUMAIN: Would from my forehead wipe a perjured note,
DUMAIN: For none offend where all alike do dote.
LONGAVILLE: [Advancing]  Dumain, thy love is far from charity.
LONGAVILLE: You may look pale, but I should blush, I know,
LONGAVILLE: To be o'erheard and taken napping so.
FERDINAND: [Advancing]  Come, sir, you blush, as his your case is such,
FERDINAND: You chide at him, offending twice as much,
FERDINAND: You do not love Maria, Longaville
FERDINAND: Did never sonnet for her sake compile,
FERDINAND: Nor never lay his wreathed arms athwart
FERDINAND: His loving bosom to keep down his heart.
FERDINAND: I have been closely shrouded in this bush
FERDINAND: And mark'd you both and for you both did blush:
FERDINAND: I heard your guilty rhymes, observed your fashion,
FERDINAND: Saw sighs reek from you, noted well your passion:
FERDINAND: Ay me! says one, O Jove! the other cries,
FERDINAND: One, her hairs were gold, crystal the other's eyes:
NARRATOR: To LONGAVILLE
FERDINAND: You would for paradise break faith, and troth,
NARRATOR: To DUMAIN
FERDINAND: And Jove, for your love, would infringe an oath.
FERDINAND: What will Biron say when that he shall hear
FERDINAND: Faith so infringed, which such zeal did swear?
FERDINAND: How will he scorn! how will he spend his wit!
FERDINAND: How will he triumph, leap and laugh at it!
FERDINAND: For all the wealth that ever I did see,
FERDINAND: I would not have him know so much by me.
BIRON: Now step I forth to whip hypocrisy.
NARRATOR: Advancing
BIRON: Ah, good my liege, I pray thee, pardon me!
BIRON: Good heart, what grace hast thou, thus to reprove
BIRON: These worms for loving, that art most in love?
BIRON: Your eyes do make no coaches, in your tears
BIRON: There is no certain princess that appears,
BIRON: You'll not be perjured, 'tis a hateful thing,
BIRON: Tush, none but minstrels like of sonneting!
BIRON: But are you not ashamed? nay, are you not,
BIRON: All three of you, to be thus much o'ershot?
BIRON: You found his mote, the king your mote did see,
BIRON: But I a beam do find in each of three.
BIRON: O, what a scene of foolery have I seen,
BIRON: Of sighs, of groans, of sorrow and of teen!
BIRON: O me, with what strict patience have I sat,
BIRON: To see a king transformed to a gnat!
BIRON: To see great Hercules whipping a gig,
BIRON: And profound Solomon to tune a jig,
BIRON: And Nestor play at push-pin with the boys,
BIRON: And critic Timon laugh at idle toys!
BIRON: Where lies thy grief, O, tell me, good Dumain?
BIRON: And gentle Longaville, where lies thy pain?
BIRON: And where my liege's? all about the breast:
BIRON: A caudle, ho!
FERDINAND: Too bitter is thy jest.
FERDINAND: Are we betray'd thus to thy over-view?
BIRON: Not you to me, but I betray'd by you:
BIRON: I, that am honest, I, that hold it sin
BIRON: To break the vow I am engaged in,
BIRON: I am betray'd, by keeping company
BIRON: With men like men of inconstancy.
BIRON: When shall you see me write a thing in rhyme?
BIRON: Or groan for love? or spend a minute's time
BIRON: In pruning me? When shall you hear that I
BIRON: Will praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye,
BIRON: A gait, a state, a brow, a breast, a waist,
BIRON: A leg, a limb?
FERDINAND: Soft! whither away so fast?
FERDINAND: A true man or a thief that gallops so?
BIRON: I post from love: good lover, let me go.
NARRATOR: Enter JAQUENETTA and COSTARD
JAQUENETTA: God bless the king!
FERDINAND: What present hast thou there?
COSTARD: Some certain treason.
FERDINAND: What makes treason here?
COSTARD: Nay, it makes nothing, sir.
FERDINAND: If it mar nothing neither,
FERDINAND: The treason and you go in peace away together.
JAQUENETTA: I beseech your grace, let this letter be read:
JAQUENETTA: Our parson misdoubts it, 'twas treason, he said.
FERDINAND: Biron, read it over.
NARRATOR: Giving him the paper
FERDINAND: Where hadst thou it?
JAQUENETTA: Of Costard.
FERDINAND: Where hadst thou it?
COSTARD: Of Dun Adramadio, Dun Adramadio.
NARRATOR: BIRON tears the letter
FERDINAND: How now! what is in you? why dost thou tear it?
BIRON: A toy, my liege, a toy: your grace needs not fear it.
LONGAVILLE: It did move him to passion, and therefore let's hear it.
DUMAIN: It is Biron's writing, and here is his name.
NARRATOR: Gathering up the pieces
BIRON: [To COSTARD]  Ah, you whoreson loggerhead! you were
BIRON: born to do me shame.
BIRON: Guilty, my lord, guilty! I confess, I confess.
FERDINAND: What?
BIRON: That you three fools lack'd me fool to make up the mess:
BIRON: He, he, and you, and you, my liege, and I,
BIRON: Are pick-purses in love, and we deserve to die.
BIRON: O, dismiss this audience, and I shall tell you more.
DUMAIN: Now the number is even.
BIRON: True, true, we are four.
BIRON: Will these turtles be gone?
FERDINAND: Hence, sirs, away!
COSTARD: Walk aside the true folk, and let the traitors stay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt COSTARD and JAQUENETTA
BIRON: Sweet lords, sweet lovers, O, let us embrace!
BIRON: As true we are as flesh and blood can be:
BIRON: The sea will ebb and flow, heaven show his face,
BIRON: Young blood doth not obey an old decree:
BIRON: We cannot cross the cause why we were born,
BIRON: Therefore of all hands must we be forsworn.
FERDINAND: What, did these rent lines show some love of thine?
BIRON: Did they, quoth you? Who sees the heavenly Rosaline,
BIRON: That, like a rude and savage man of Inde,
BIRON: At the first opening of the gorgeous east,
BIRON: Bows not his vassal head and strucken blind
BIRON: Kisses the base ground with obedient breast?
BIRON: What peremptory eagle-sighted eye
BIRON: Dares look upon the heaven of her brow,
BIRON: That is not blinded by her majesty?
FERDINAND: What zeal, what fury hath inspired thee now?
FERDINAND: My love, her mistress, is a gracious moon,
FERDINAND: She an attending star, scarce seen a light.
BIRON: My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Biron:
BIRON: O, but for my love, day would turn to night!
BIRON: Of all complexions the cull'd sovereignty
BIRON: Do meet, as at a fair, in her fair cheek,
BIRON: Where several worthies make one dignity,
BIRON: Where nothing wants that want itself doth seek.
BIRON: Lend me the flourish of all gentle tongues,--
BIRON: Fie, painted rhetoric! O, she needs it not:
BIRON: To things of sale a seller's praise belongs,
BIRON: She passes praise, then praise too short doth blot.
BIRON: A wither'd hermit, five-score winters worn,
BIRON: Might shake off fifty, looking in her eye:
BIRON: Beauty doth varnish age, as if new-born,
BIRON: And gives the crutch the cradle's infancy:
BIRON: O, 'tis the sun that maketh all things shine.
FERDINAND: By heaven, thy love is black as ebony.
BIRON: Is ebony like her? O wood divine!
BIRON: A wife of such wood were felicity.
BIRON: O, who can give an oath? where is a book?
BIRON: That I may swear beauty doth beauty lack,
BIRON: If that she learn not of her eye to look:
BIRON: No face is fair that is not full so black.
FERDINAND: O paradox! Black is the badge of hell,
FERDINAND: The hue of dungeons and the suit of night,
FERDINAND: And beauty's crest becomes the heavens well.
BIRON: Devils soonest tempt, resembling spirits of light.
BIRON: O, if in black my lady's brows be deck'd,
BIRON: It mourns that painting and usurping hair
BIRON: Should ravish doters with a false aspect,
BIRON: And therefore is she born to make black fair.
BIRON: Her favour turns the fashion of the days,
BIRON: For native blood is counted painting now,
BIRON: And therefore red, that would avoid dispraise,
BIRON: Paints itself black, to imitate her brow.
DUMAIN: To look like her are chimney-sweepers black.
LONGAVILLE: And since her time are colliers counted bright.
FERDINAND: And Ethiopes of their sweet complexion crack.
DUMAIN: Dark needs no candles now, for dark is light.
BIRON: Your mistresses dare never come in rain,
BIRON: For fear their colours should be wash'd away.
FERDINAND: 'Twere good, yours did, for, sir, to tell you plain,
FERDINAND: I'll find a fairer face not wash'd to-day.
BIRON: I'll prove her fair, or talk till doomsday here.
FERDINAND: No devil will fright thee then so much as she.
DUMAIN: I never knew man hold vile stuff so dear.
LONGAVILLE: Look, here's thy love: my foot and her face see.
BIRON: O, if the streets were paved with thine eyes,
BIRON: Her feet were much too dainty for such tread!
DUMAIN: O, vile! then, as she goes, what upward lies
DUMAIN: The street should see as she walk'd overhead.
FERDINAND: But what of this? are we not all in love?
BIRON: Nothing so sure, and thereby all forsworn.
FERDINAND: Then leave this chat, and, good Biron, now prove
FERDINAND: Our loving lawful, and our faith not torn.
DUMAIN: Ay, marry, there, some flattery for this evil.
LONGAVILLE: O, some authority how to proceed,
LONGAVILLE: Some tricks, some quillets, how to cheat the devil.
DUMAIN: Some salve for perjury.
BIRON: 'Tis more than need.
BIRON: Have at you, then, affection's men at arms.
BIRON: Consider what you first did swear unto,
BIRON: To fast, to study, and to see no woman,
BIRON: Flat treason 'gainst the kingly state of youth.
BIRON: Say, can you fast? your stomachs are too young,
BIRON: And abstinence engenders maladies.
BIRON: And where that you have vow'd to study, lords,
BIRON: In that each of you have forsworn his book,
BIRON: Can you still dream and pore and thereon look?
BIRON: For when would you, my lord, or you, or you,
BIRON: Have found the ground of study's excellence
BIRON: Without the beauty of a woman's face?
BIRON: From women's eyes this doctrine I derive,  They are the ground, the books, the academes From whence doth spring the true Promethean fire
BIRON: Why, universal plodding poisons up
BIRON: The nimble spirits in the arteries,
BIRON: As motion and long-during action tires
BIRON: The sinewy vigour of the traveller.
BIRON: Now, for not looking on a woman's face,
BIRON: You have in that forsworn the use of eyes
BIRON: And study too, the causer of your vow,
BIRON: For where is any author in the world
BIRON: Teaches such beauty as a woman's eye?
BIRON: Learning is but an adjunct to ourself
BIRON: And where we are our learning likewise is:
BIRON: Then when ourselves we see in ladies' eyes,
BIRON: Do we not likewise see our learning there?
BIRON: O, we have made a vow to study, lords,
BIRON: And in that vow we have forsworn our books.
BIRON: For when would you, my liege, or you, or you,
BIRON: In leaden contemplation have found out
BIRON: Such fiery numbers as the prompting eyes
BIRON: Of beauty's tutors have enrich'd you with?
BIRON: Other slow arts entirely keep the brain,
BIRON: And therefore, finding barren practisers,
BIRON: Scarce show a harvest of their heavy toil:
BIRON: But love, first learned in a lady's eyes,
BIRON: Lives not alone immured in the brain,
BIRON: But, with the motion of all elements,
BIRON: Courses as swift as thought in every power,
BIRON: And gives to every power a double power,
BIRON: Above their functions and their offices.
BIRON: It adds a precious seeing to the eye,
BIRON: A lover's eyes will gaze an eagle blind,
BIRON: A lover's ear will hear the lowest sound,
BIRON: When the suspicious head of theft is stopp'd:
BIRON: Love's feeling is more soft and sensible
BIRON: Than are the tender horns of cockl'd snails,
BIRON: Love's tongue proves dainty Bacchus gross in taste:
BIRON: For valour, is not Love a Hercules,
BIRON: Still climbing trees in the Hesperides?
BIRON: Subtle as Sphinx, as sweet and musical
BIRON: As bright Apollo's lute, strung with his hair:
BIRON: And when Love speaks, the voice of all the gods
BIRON: Makes heaven drowsy with the harmony.
BIRON: Never durst poet touch a pen to write
BIRON: Until his ink were temper'd with Love's sighs,
BIRON: O, then his lines would ravish savage ears
BIRON: And plant in tyrants mild humility.
BIRON: From women's eyes this doctrine I derive:
BIRON: They sparkle still the right Promethean fire,
BIRON: They are the books, the arts, the academes,
BIRON: That show, contain and nourish all the world:
BIRON: Else none at all in ought proves excellent.
BIRON: Then fools you were these women to forswear,
BIRON: Or keeping what is sworn, you will prove fools.
BIRON: For wisdom's sake, a word that all men love,
BIRON: Or for love's sake, a word that loves all men,
BIRON: Or for men's sake, the authors of these women,
BIRON: Or women's sake, by whom we men are men,
BIRON: Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves,
BIRON: Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths.
BIRON: It is religion to be thus forsworn,
BIRON: For charity itself fulfills the law,
BIRON: And who can sever love from charity?
FERDINAND: Saint Cupid, then! and, soldiers, to the field!
BIRON: Advance your standards, and upon them, lords,
BIRON: Pell-mell, down with them! but be first advised,
BIRON: In conflict that you get the sun of them.
LONGAVILLE: Now to plain-dealing, lay these glozes by:
LONGAVILLE: Shall we resolve to woo these girls of France?
FERDINAND: And win them too: therefore let us devise
FERDINAND: Some entertainment for them in their tents.
BIRON: First, from the park let us conduct them thither,
BIRON: Then homeward every man attach the hand
BIRON: Of his fair mistress: in the afternoon
BIRON: We will with some strange pastime solace them,
BIRON: Such as the shortness of the time can shape,
BIRON: For revels, dances, masks and merry hours
BIRON: Forerun fair Love, strewing her way with flowers.
FERDINAND: Away, away! no time shall be omitted
FERDINAND: That will betime, and may by us be fitted.
BIRON: Allons! allons! Sow'd cockle reap'd no corn,
BIRON: And justice always whirls in equal measure:
BIRON: Light wenches may prove plagues to men forsworn,
BIRON: If so, our copper buys no better treasure.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
BIRON: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
BIRON: ACT V
BIRON: SCENE I. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter HOLOFERNES, SIR NATHANIEL, and DULL
HOLOFERNES: Satis quod sufficit.
SIR NATHANIEL: I praise God for you, sir: your reasons at dinner
SIR NATHANIEL: have been sharp and sententious, pleasant without
SIR NATHANIEL: scurrility, witty without affection, audacious without
SIR NATHANIEL: impudency, learned without opinion, and strange with-
SIR NATHANIEL: out heresy. I did converse this quondam day with
SIR NATHANIEL: a companion of the king's, who is intituled, nomi-
SIR NATHANIEL: nated, or called, Don Adriano de Armado.
HOLOFERNES: Novi hominem tanquam te: his humour is lofty, his
HOLOFERNES: discourse peremptory, his tongue filed, his eye
HOLOFERNES: ambitious, his gait majestical, and his general
HOLOFERNES: behavior vain, ridiculous, and thrasonical. He is
HOLOFERNES: too picked, too spruce, too affected, too odd, as it
HOLOFERNES: were, too peregrinate, as I may call it.
SIR NATHANIEL: A most singular and choice epithet.
NARRATOR: Draws out his table-book
HOLOFERNES: He draweth out the thread of his verbosity finer
HOLOFERNES: than the staple of his argument. I abhor such
HOLOFERNES: fanatical phantasimes, such insociable and
HOLOFERNES: point-devise companions, such rackers of
HOLOFERNES: orthography, as to speak dout, fine, when he should
HOLOFERNES: say doubt, det, when he should pronounce debt,--d,
HOLOFERNES: e, b, t, not d, e, t: he clepeth a calf, cauf,
HOLOFERNES: half, hauf, neighbour vocatur nebor, neigh
HOLOFERNES: abbreviated ne. This is abhominable,--which he
HOLOFERNES: would call abbominable: it insinuateth me of
HOLOFERNES: insanie: anne intelligis, domine? to make frantic, lunatic.
SIR NATHANIEL: Laus Deo, bene intelligo.
HOLOFERNES: Bon, bon, fort bon, Priscian! a little scratch'd,
HOLOFERNES: 'twill serve.
SIR NATHANIEL: Videsne quis venit?
HOLOFERNES: Video, et gaudeo.
NARRATOR: Enter DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO, MOTH, and COSTARD
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Chirrah!
NARRATOR: To MOTH
HOLOFERNES: Quare chirrah, not sirrah?
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Men of peace, well encountered.
HOLOFERNES: Most military sir, salutation.
MOTH: [Aside to COSTARD]  They have been at a great feast
MOTH: of languages, and stolen the scraps.
COSTARD: O, they have lived long on the alms-basket of words.
COSTARD: I marvel thy master hath not eaten thee for a word,
COSTARD: for thou art not so long by the head as
COSTARD: honorificabilitudinitatibus: thou art easier
COSTARD: swallowed than a flap-dragon.
MOTH: Peace! the peal begins.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: [To HOLOFERNES]  Monsieur, are you not lettered?
MOTH: Yes, yes, he teaches boys the hornbook. What is a,
MOTH: b, spelt backward, with the horn on his head?
HOLOFERNES: Ba, pueritia, with a horn added.
MOTH: Ba, most silly sheep with a horn. You hear his learning.
HOLOFERNES: Quis, quis, thou consonant?
MOTH: The third of the five vowels, if you repeat them, or
MOTH: the fifth, if I.
HOLOFERNES: I will repeat them,--a, e, i,--
MOTH: The sheep: the other two concludes it,--o, u.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Now, by the salt wave of the Mediterraneum, a sweet
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: touch, a quick venue of wit! snip, snap, quick and
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: home! it rejoiceth my intellect: true wit!
MOTH: Offered by a child to an old man, which is wit-old.
HOLOFERNES: What is the figure? what is the figure?
MOTH: Horns.
HOLOFERNES: Thou disputest like an infant: go, whip thy gig.
MOTH: Lend me your horn to make one, and I will whip about
MOTH: your infamy circum circa,--a gig of a cuckold's horn.
COSTARD: An I had but one penny in the world, thou shouldst
COSTARD: have it to buy gingerbread: hold, there is the very
COSTARD: remuneration I had of thy master, thou halfpenny
COSTARD: purse of wit, thou pigeon-egg of discretion. O, an
COSTARD: the heavens were so pleased that thou wert but my
COSTARD: bastard, what a joyful father wouldst thou make me!
COSTARD: Go to, thou hast it ad dunghill, at the fingers'
COSTARD: ends, as they say.
HOLOFERNES: O, I smell false Latin, dunghill for unguem.
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Arts-man, preambulate, we will be singled from the
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: barbarous. Do you not educate youth at the
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: charge-house on the top of the mountain?
HOLOFERNES: Or mons, the hill.
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: At your sweet pleasure, for the mountain.
HOLOFERNES: I do, sans question.
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sir, it is the king's most sweet pleasure and
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: affection to congratulate the princess at her
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: pavilion in the posteriors of this day, which the
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: rude multitude call the afternoon.
HOLOFERNES: The posterior of the day, most generous sir, is
HOLOFERNES: liable, congruent and measurable for the afternoon:
HOLOFERNES: the word is well culled, chose, sweet and apt, I do
HOLOFERNES: assure you, sir, I do assure.
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Sir, the king is a noble gentleman, and my familiar,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: I do assure ye, very good friend: for what is
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: inward between us, let it pass. I do beseech thee,
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: remember thy courtesy, I beseech thee, apparel thy
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: head: and among other important and most serious
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: designs, and of great import indeed, too, but let
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: that pass: for I must tell thee, it will please his
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: grace, by the world, sometime to lean upon my poor
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: shoulder, and with his royal finger, thus, dally
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: with my excrement, with my mustachio, but, sweet
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: heart, let that pass. By the world, I recount no
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: fable: some certain special honours it pleaseth his
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: greatness to impart to Armado, a soldier, a man of
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: travel, that hath seen the world, but let that pass.
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: The very all of all is,--but, sweet heart, I do
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: implore secrecy,--that the king would have me
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: present the princess, sweet chuck, with some
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: delightful ostentation, or show, or pageant, or
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: antique, or firework. Now, understanding that the
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: curate and your sweet self are good at such
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: eruptions and sudden breaking out of mirth, as it
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: were, I have acquainted you withal, to the end to
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: crave your assistance.
HOLOFERNES: Sir, you shall present before her the Nine Worthies.
HOLOFERNES: Sir, as concerning some entertainment of time, some
HOLOFERNES: show in the posterior of this day, to be rendered by
HOLOFERNES: our assistants, at the king's command, and this most
HOLOFERNES: gallant, illustrate, and learned gentleman, before
HOLOFERNES: the princess, I say none so fit as to present the
HOLOFERNES: Nine Worthies.
SIR NATHANIEL: Where will you find men worthy enough to present them?
HOLOFERNES: Joshua, yourself, myself and this gallant gentleman,
HOLOFERNES: Judas Maccabaeus, this swain, because of his great
HOLOFERNES: limb or joint, shall pass Pompey the Great, the
HOLOFERNES: page, Hercules,--
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Pardon, sir, error: he is not quantity enough for
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: that Worthy's thumb: he is not so big as the end of his club.
HOLOFERNES: Shall I have audience? he shall present Hercules in
HOLOFERNES: minority: his enter and exit shall be strangling a
HOLOFERNES: snake, and I will have an apology for that purpose.
MOTH: An excellent device! so, if any of the audience
MOTH: hiss, you may cry 'Well done, Hercules! now thou
MOTH: crushest the snake!' that is the way to make an
MOTH: offence gracious, though few have the grace to do it.
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: For the rest of the Worthies?--
HOLOFERNES: I will play three myself.
MOTH: Thrice-worthy gentleman!
MOTH: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: Shall I tell you a thing?
HOLOFERNES: We attend.
HOLOFERNES: DON
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: We will have, if this fadge not, an antique. I
ADRIANO DE ARMADO: beseech you, follow.
HOLOFERNES: Via, goodman Dull! thou hast spoken no word all this while.
DULL: Nor understood none neither, sir.
HOLOFERNES: Allons! we will employ thee.
DULL: I'll make one in a dance, or so, or I will play
DULL: On the tabour to the Worthies, and let them dance the hay.
HOLOFERNES: Most dull, honest Dull! To our sport, away!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
HOLOFERNES: LOVE'S LABOURS LOST
HOLOFERNES: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCESS, KATHARINE, ROSALINE, and MARIA
PRINCESS: Sweet hearts, we shall be rich ere we depart,
PRINCESS: If fairings come thus plentifully in:
PRINCESS: A lady wall'd about with diamonds!
PRINCESS: Look you what I have from the loving king.
ROSALINE: Madame, came nothing else along with that?
PRINCESS: Nothing but this! yes, as much love in rhyme
PRINCESS: As would be cramm'd up in a sheet of paper,
PRINCESS: Writ o' both sides the leaf, margent and all,
PRINCESS: That he was fain to seal on Cupid's name.
ROSALINE: That was the way to make his godhead wax,
ROSALINE: For he hath been five thousand years a boy.
KATHARINE: Ay, and a shrewd unhappy gallows too.
ROSALINE: You'll ne'er be friends with him, a' kill'd your sister.
KATHARINE: He made her melancholy, sad, and heavy,
KATHARINE: And so she died: had she been light, like you,
KATHARINE: Of such a merry, nimble, stirring spirit,
KATHARINE: She might ha' been a grandam ere she died:
KATHARINE: And so may you, for a light heart lives long.
ROSALINE: What's your dark meaning, mouse, of this light word?
KATHARINE: A light condition in a beauty dark.
ROSALINE: We need more light to find your meaning out.
KATHARINE: You'll mar the light by taking it in snuff,
KATHARINE: Therefore I'll darkly end the argument.
ROSALINE: Look what you do, you do it still i' the dark.
KATHARINE: So do not you, for you are a light wench.
ROSALINE: Indeed I weigh not you, and therefore light.
KATHARINE: You weigh me not? O, that's you care not for me.
ROSALINE: Great reason, for 'past cure is still past care.'
PRINCESS: Well bandied both, a set of wit well play'd.
PRINCESS: But Rosaline, you have a favour too:
PRINCESS: Who sent it? and what is it?
ROSALINE: I would you knew:
ROSALINE: An if my face were but as fair as yours,
ROSALINE: My favour were as great, be witness this.
ROSALINE: Nay, I have verses too, I thank Biron:
ROSALINE: The numbers true, and, were the numbering too,
ROSALINE: I were the fairest goddess on the ground:
ROSALINE: I am compared to twenty thousand fairs.
ROSALINE: O, he hath drawn my picture in his letter!
PRINCESS: Any thing like?
ROSALINE: Much in the letters, nothing in the praise.
PRINCESS: Beauteous as ink, a good conclusion.
KATHARINE: Fair as a text B in a copy-book.
ROSALINE: 'Ware pencils, ho! let me not die your debtor,
ROSALINE: My red dominical, my golden letter:
ROSALINE: O, that your face were not so full of O's!
KATHARINE: A pox of that jest! and I beshrew all shrows.
PRINCESS: But, Katharine, what was sent to you from fair Dumain?
KATHARINE: Madam, this glove.
PRINCESS: Did he not send you twain?
KATHARINE: Yes, madam, and moreover
KATHARINE: Some thousand verses of a faithful lover,
KATHARINE: A huge translation of hypocrisy,
KATHARINE: Vilely compiled, profound simplicity.
MARIA: This and these pearls to me sent Longaville:
MARIA: The letter is too long by half a mile.
PRINCESS: I think no less. Dost thou not wish in heart
PRINCESS: The chain were longer and the letter short?
MARIA: Ay, or I would these hands might never part.
PRINCESS: We are wise girls to mock our lovers so.
ROSALINE: They are worse fools to purchase mocking so.
ROSALINE: That same Biron I'll torture ere I go:
ROSALINE: O that I knew he were but in by the week!
ROSALINE: How I would make him fawn and beg and seek
ROSALINE: And wait the season and observe the times
ROSALINE: And spend his prodigal wits in bootless rhymes
ROSALINE: And shape his service wholly to my hests
ROSALINE: And make him proud to make me proud that jests!
ROSALINE: So perttaunt-like would I o'ersway his state
ROSALINE: That he should be my fool and I his fate.
PRINCESS: None are so surely caught, when they are catch'd,
PRINCESS: As wit turn'd fool: folly, in wisdom hatch'd,
PRINCESS: Hath wisdom's warrant and the help of school
PRINCESS: And wit's own grace to grace a learned fool.
ROSALINE: The blood of youth burns not with such excess
ROSALINE: As gravity's revolt to wantonness.
MARIA: Folly in fools bears not so strong a note
MARIA: As foolery in the wise, when wit doth dote,
MARIA: Since all the power thereof it doth apply
MARIA: To prove, by wit, worth in simplicity.
PRINCESS: Here comes Boyet, and mirth is in his face.
NARRATOR: Enter BOYET
BOYET: O, I am stabb'd with laughter! Where's her grace?
PRINCESS: Thy news Boyet?
BOYET: Prepare, madam, prepare!
BOYET: Arm, wenches, arm! encounters mounted are
BOYET: Against your peace: Love doth approach disguised,
BOYET: Armed in arguments, you'll be surprised:
BOYET: Muster your wits, stand in your own defence,
BOYET: Or hide your heads like cowards, and fly hence.
PRINCESS: Saint Denis to Saint Cupid! What are they
PRINCESS: That charge their breath against us? say, scout, say.
BOYET: Under the cool shade of a sycamore
BOYET: I thought to close mine eyes some half an hour,
BOYET: When, lo! to interrupt my purposed rest,
BOYET: Toward that shade I might behold addrest
BOYET: The king and his companions: warily
BOYET: I stole into a neighbour thicket by,
BOYET: And overheard what you shall overhear,
BOYET: That, by and by, disguised they will be here.
BOYET: Their herald is a pretty knavish page,
BOYET: That well by heart hath conn'd his embassage:
BOYET: Action and accent did they teach him there,
BOYET: 'Thus must thou speak,' and 'thus thy body bear:'
BOYET: And ever and anon they made a doubt
BOYET: Presence majestical would put him out,
BOYET: 'For,' quoth the king, 'an angel shalt thou see,
BOYET: Yet fear not thou, but speak audaciously.'
BOYET: The boy replied, 'An angel is not evil,
BOYET: I should have fear'd her had she been a devil.'
BOYET: With that, all laugh'd and clapp'd him on the shoulder,
BOYET: Making the bold wag by their praises bolder:
BOYET: One rubb'd his elbow thus, and fleer'd and swore
BOYET: A better speech was never spoke before,
BOYET: Another, with his finger and his thumb,
BOYET: Cried, 'Via! we will do't, come what will come,'
BOYET: The third he caper'd, and cried, 'All goes well,'
BOYET: The fourth turn'd on the toe, and down he fell.
BOYET: With that, they all did tumble on the ground,
BOYET: With such a zealous laughter, so profound,
BOYET: That in this spleen ridiculous appears,
BOYET: To cheque their folly, passion's solemn tears.
PRINCESS: But what, but what, come they to visit us?
BOYET: They do, they do: and are apparell'd thus.
BOYET: Like Muscovites or Russians, as I guess.
BOYET: Their purpose is to parle, to court and dance,
BOYET: And every one his love-feat will advance
BOYET: Unto his several mistress, which they'll know
BOYET: By favours several which they did bestow.
PRINCESS: And will they so? the gallants shall be task'd,
PRINCESS: For, ladies, we shall every one be mask'd,
PRINCESS: And not a man of them shall have the grace,
PRINCESS: Despite of suit, to see a lady's face.
PRINCESS: Hold, Rosaline, this favour thou shalt wear,
PRINCESS: And then the king will court thee for his dear,
PRINCESS: Hold, take thou this, my sweet, and give me thine,
PRINCESS: So shall Biron take me for Rosaline.
PRINCESS: And change your favours too, so shall your loves
PRINCESS: Woo contrary, deceived by these removes.
ROSALINE: Come on, then, wear the favours most in sight.
KATHARINE: But in this changing what is your intent?
PRINCESS: The effect of my intent is to cross theirs:
PRINCESS: They do it but in mocking merriment,
PRINCESS: And mock for mock is only my intent.
PRINCESS: Their several counsels they unbosom shall
PRINCESS: To loves mistook, and so be mock'd withal
PRINCESS: Upon the next occasion that we meet,
PRINCESS: With visages displayed, to talk and greet.
ROSALINE: But shall we dance, if they desire to't?
PRINCESS: No, to the death, we will not move a foot,
PRINCESS: Nor to their penn'd speech render we no grace,
PRINCESS: But while 'tis spoke each turn away her face.
BOYET: Why, that contempt will kill the speaker's heart,
BOYET: And quite divorce his memory from his part.
PRINCESS: Therefore I do it, and I make no doubt
PRINCESS: The rest will ne'er come in, if he be out
PRINCESS: There's no such sport as sport by sport o'erthrown,
PRINCESS: To make theirs ours and ours none but our own:
PRINCESS: So shall we stay, mocking intended game,
PRINCESS: And they, well mock'd, depart away with shame.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound within
BOYET: The trumpet sounds: be mask'd, the maskers come.
NARRATOR: The Ladies mask
NARRATOR: Enter Blackamoors with music, MOTH, FERDINAND,  BIRON, LONGAVILLE, and DUMAIN, in Russian habits, and masked
MOTH: All hail, the richest beauties on the earth!--
BOYET: Beauties no richer than rich taffeta.
MOTH: A holy parcel of the fairest dames.
NARRATOR: The Ladies turn their backs to him
MOTH: That ever turn'd their--backs--to mortal views!
BIRON: [Aside to MOTH]  Their eyes, villain, their eyes!
MOTH: That ever turn'd their eyes to mortal views!--Out--
BOYET: True, out indeed.
MOTH: Out of your favours, heavenly spirits, vouchsafe
MOTH: Not to behold--
BIRON: [Aside to MOTH]  Once to behold, rogue.
MOTH: Once to behold with your sun-beamed eyes,
MOTH: --with your sun-beamed eyes--
BOYET: They will not answer to that epithet,
BOYET: You were best call it 'daughter-beamed eyes.'
MOTH: They do not mark me, and that brings me out.
BIRON: Is this your perfectness? be gone, you rogue!
NARRATOR: Exit MOTH
ROSALINE: What would these strangers? know their minds, Boyet:
ROSALINE: If they do speak our language, 'tis our will:
ROSALINE: That some plain man recount their purposes
ROSALINE: Know what they would.
BOYET: What would you with the princess?
BIRON: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
ROSALINE: What would they, say they?
BOYET: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
ROSALINE: Why, that they have, and bid them so be gone.
BOYET: She says, you have it, and you may be gone.
FERDINAND: Say to her, we have measured many miles
FERDINAND: To tread a measure with her on this grass.
BOYET: They say, that they have measured many a mile
BOYET: To tread a measure with you on this grass.
ROSALINE: It is not so. Ask them how many inches
ROSALINE: Is in one mile: if they have measured many,
ROSALINE: The measure then of one is easily told.
BOYET: If to come hither you have measured miles,
BOYET: And many miles, the princess bids you tell
BOYET: How many inches doth fill up one mile.
BIRON: Tell her, we measure them by weary steps.
BOYET: She hears herself.
ROSALINE: How many weary steps,
ROSALINE: Of many weary miles you have o'ergone,
ROSALINE: Are number'd in the travel of one mile?
BIRON: We number nothing that we spend for you:
BIRON: Our duty is so rich, so infinite,
BIRON: That we may do it still without accompt.
BIRON: Vouchsafe to show the sunshine of your face,
BIRON: That we, like savages, may worship it.
ROSALINE: My face is but a moon, and clouded too.
FERDINAND: Blessed are clouds, to do as such clouds do!
FERDINAND: Vouchsafe, bright moon, and these thy stars, to shine,
FERDINAND: Those clouds removed, upon our watery eyne.
ROSALINE: O vain petitioner! beg a greater matter,
ROSALINE: Thou now request'st but moonshine in the water.
FERDINAND: Then, in our measure do but vouchsafe one change.
FERDINAND: Thou bid'st me beg: this begging is not strange.
ROSALINE: Play, music, then! Nay, you must do it soon.
NARRATOR: Music plays
ROSALINE: Not yet! no dance! Thus change I like the moon.
FERDINAND: Will you not dance? How come you thus estranged?
ROSALINE: You took the moon at full, but now she's changed.
FERDINAND: Yet still she is the moon, and I the man.
FERDINAND: The music plays, vouchsafe some motion to it.
ROSALINE: Our ears vouchsafe it.
FERDINAND: But your legs should do it.
ROSALINE: Since you are strangers and come here by chance,
ROSALINE: We'll not be nice: take hands. We will not dance.
FERDINAND: Why take we hands, then?
ROSALINE: Only to part friends:
ROSALINE: Curtsy, sweet hearts, and so the measure ends.
FERDINAND: More measure of this measure, be not nice.
ROSALINE: We can afford no more at such a price.
FERDINAND: Prize you yourselves: what buys your company?
ROSALINE: Your absence only.
FERDINAND: That can never be.
ROSALINE: Then cannot we be bought: and so, adieu,
ROSALINE: Twice to your visor, and half once to you.
FERDINAND: If you deny to dance, let's hold more chat.
ROSALINE: In private, then.
FERDINAND: I am best pleased with that.
NARRATOR: They converse apart
BIRON: White-handed mistress, one sweet word with thee.
PRINCESS: Honey, and milk, and sugar, there is three.
BIRON: Nay then, two treys, and if you grow so nice,
BIRON: Metheglin, wort, and malmsey: well run, dice!
BIRON: There's half-a-dozen sweets.
PRINCESS: Seventh sweet, adieu:
PRINCESS: Since you can cog, I'll play no more with you.
BIRON: One word in secret.
PRINCESS: Let it not be sweet.
BIRON: Thou grievest my gall.
PRINCESS: Gall! bitter.
BIRON: Therefore meet.
NARRATOR: They converse apart
DUMAIN: Will you vouchsafe with me to change a word?
MARIA: Name it.
DUMAIN: Fair lady,--
MARIA: Say you so? Fair lord,--
MARIA: Take that for your fair lady.
DUMAIN: Please it you,
DUMAIN: As much in private, and I'll bid adieu.
NARRATOR: They converse apart
KATHARINE: What, was your vizard made without a tongue?
LONGAVILLE: I know the reason, lady, why you ask.
KATHARINE: O for your reason! quickly, sir, I long.
LONGAVILLE: You have a double tongue within your mask,
LONGAVILLE: And would afford my speechless vizard half.
KATHARINE: Veal, quoth the Dutchman. Is not 'veal' a calf?
LONGAVILLE: A calf, fair lady!
KATHARINE: No, a fair lord calf.
LONGAVILLE: Let's part the word.
KATHARINE: No, I'll not be your half
KATHARINE: Take all, and wean it, it may prove an ox.
LONGAVILLE: Look, how you butt yourself in these sharp mocks!
LONGAVILLE: Will you give horns, chaste lady? do not so.
KATHARINE: Then die a calf, before your horns do grow.
LONGAVILLE: One word in private with you, ere I die.
KATHARINE: Bleat softly then, the butcher hears you cry.
NARRATOR: They converse apart
BOYET: The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen
BOYET: As is the razor's edge invisible,
BOYET: Cutting a smaller hair than may be seen,
BOYET: Above the sense of sense, so sensible
BOYET: Seemeth their conference, their conceits have wings
BOYET: Fleeter than arrows, bullets, wind, thought, swifter things.
ROSALINE: Not one word more, my maids, break off, break off.
BIRON: By heaven, all dry-beaten with pure scoff!
FERDINAND: Farewell, mad wenches, you have simple wits.
PRINCESS: Twenty adieus, my frozen Muscovits.
NARRATOR: Exeunt FERDINAND, Lords, and Blackamoors
PRINCESS: Are these the breed of wits so wonder'd at?
BOYET: Tapers they are, with your sweet breaths puff'd out.
ROSALINE: Well-liking wits they have, gross, gross, fat, fat.
PRINCESS: O poverty in wit, kingly-poor flout!
PRINCESS: Will they not, think you, hang themselves tonight?
PRINCESS: Or ever, but in vizards, show their faces?
PRINCESS: This pert Biron was out of countenance quite.
ROSALINE: O, they were all in lamentable cases!
ROSALINE: The king was weeping-ripe for a good word.
PRINCESS: Biron did swear himself out of all suit.
MARIA: Dumain was at my service, and his sword:
MARIA: No point, quoth I, my servant straight was mute.
KATHARINE: Lord Longaville said, I came o'er his heart,
KATHARINE: And trow you what he called me?
PRINCESS: Qualm, perhaps.
KATHARINE: Yes, in good faith.
PRINCESS: Go, sickness as thou art!
ROSALINE: Well, better wits have worn plain statute-caps.
ROSALINE: But will you hear? the king is my love sworn.
PRINCESS: And quick Biron hath plighted faith to me.
KATHARINE: And Longaville was for my service born.
MARIA: Dumain is mine, as sure as bark on tree.

BOYET: Immediately they will again be here
BOYET: In their own shapes, for it can never be
BOYET: They will digest this harsh indignity.
PRINCESS: Will they return?
BOYET: They will, they will, God knows,
BOYET: And leap for joy, though they are lame with blows:
BOYET: Therefore change favours, and, when they repair,
BOYET: Blow like sweet roses in this summer air.
PRINCESS: How blow? how blow? speak to be understood.
BOYET: Fair ladies mask'd are roses in their bud,
BOYET: Dismask'd, their damask sweet commixture shown,
BOYET: Are angels vailing clouds, or roses blown.
PRINCESS: Avaunt, perplexity! What shall we do,
PRINCESS: If they return in their own shapes to woo?

ROSALINE: Let us complain to them what fools were here,
ROSALINE: Disguised like Muscovites, in shapeless gear,
ROSALINE: And wonder what they were and to what end
ROSALINE: Their shallow shows and prologue vilely penn'd
ROSALINE: And their rough carriage so ridiculous,
ROSALINE: Should be presented at our tent to us.
BOYET: Ladies, withdraw: the gallants are at hand.
PRINCESS: Whip to our tents, as roes run o'er land.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PRINCESS, ROSALINE, KATHARINE, and MARIA

BOYET: I will, and so will she, I know, my lord.

BIRON: This fellow pecks up wit as pigeons pease,
BIRON: And utters it again when God doth please:
BIRON: He is wit's pedler, and retails his wares
BIRON: At wakes and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs,
BIRON: And we that sell by gross, the Lord doth know,
BIRON: Have not the grace to grace it with such show.
BIRON: This gallant pins the wenches on his sleeve,
BIRON: Had he been Adam, he had tempted Eve,
BIRON: A' can carve too, and lisp: why, this is he
BIRON: That kiss'd his hand away in courtesy,
BIRON: This is the ape of form, monsieur the nice,
BIRON: That, when he plays at tables, chides the dice
BIRON: In honourable terms: nay, he can sing
BIRON: A mean most meanly, and in ushering
BIRON: Mend him who can: the ladies call him sweet,
BIRON: The stairs, as he treads on them, kiss his feet:
BIRON: This is the flower that smiles on every one,
BIRON: To show his teeth as white as whale's bone,
BIRON: And consciences, that will not die in debt,
BIRON: Pay him the due of honey-tongued Boyet.
FERDINAND: A blister on his sweet tongue, with my heart,
FERDINAND: That put Armado's page out of his part!
BIRON: See where it comes! Behavior, what wert thou
BIRON: Till this madman show'd thee? and what art thou now?

PRINCESS: 'Fair' in 'all hail' is foul, as I conceive.

PRINCESS: Nor God, nor I, delights in perjured men.

PRINCESS: For virtue's office never breaks men's troth.

ROSALINE: When they are thirsty, fools would fain have drink.

ROSALINE: All the fool mine?

ROSALINE: There, then, that vizard, that superfluous case
ROSALINE: That hid the worse and show'd the better face.

BIRON: Can any face of brass hold longer out?
BIRON: lady, dart thy skill at me,
BIRON: Bruise me with scorn, confound me with a flout,
BIRON: Thrust thy sharp wit quite through my ignorance,
BIRON: Cut me to pieces with thy keen conceit,
BIRON: And I will wish thee never more to dance,
BIRON: Nor never more in Russian habit wait.
BIRON: O, never will I trust to speeches penn'd,
BIRON: Nor to the motion of a schoolboy's tongue,
BIRON: Nor never come in vizard to my friend,
BIRON: Nor woo in rhyme, like a blind harper's song!
BIRON: Taffeta phrases, silken terms precise,
BIRON: Three-piled hyperboles, spruce affectation,
BIRON: Figures pedantical, these summer-flies
BIRON: Have blown me full of maggot ostentation:

BIRON: By this white glove,--how white the hand, God knows!--

BIRON: In russet yeas and honest kersey noes:
BIRON: And, to begin, wench,--so God help me, la!--

BIRON: Yet I have a trick
BIRON: Of the old rage: bear with me, I am sick,
