ISABELLA: [Within]  Peace, ho, be here!
DUKE VINCENTIO: The tongue of Isabel. She's come to know
DUKE VINCENTIO: If yet her brother's pardon be come hither:
DUKE VINCENTIO: But I will keep her ignorant of her good,
DUKE VINCENTIO: To make her heavenly comforts of despair,
DUKE VINCENTIO: When it is least expected.
NARRATOR: Enter ISABELLA
ISABELLA: Ho, by your leave!
DUKE VINCENTIO: Good morning to you, fair and gracious daughter.
ISABELLA: The better, given me by so holy a man.
ISABELLA: Hath yet the deputy sent my brother's pardon?
DUKE VINCENTIO: He hath released him, Isabel, from the world:
DUKE VINCENTIO: His head is off and sent to Angelo.
ISABELLA: Nay, but it is not so.
DUKE VINCENTIO: It is no other: show your wisdom, daughter,
DUKE VINCENTIO: In your close patience.
ISABELLA: O, I will to him and pluck out his eyes!
DUKE VINCENTIO: You shall not be admitted to his sight.
ISABELLA: Unhappy Claudio! wretched Isabel!
ISABELLA: Injurious world! most damned Angelo!
DUKE VINCENTIO: This nor hurts him nor profits you a jot,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Forbear it therefore, give your cause to heaven.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Mark what I say, which you shall find
DUKE VINCENTIO: By every syllable a faithful verity:
DUKE VINCENTIO: The duke comes home to-morrow, nay, dry your eyes,
DUKE VINCENTIO: One of our convent, and his confessor,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Gives me this instance: already he hath carried
DUKE VINCENTIO: Notice to Escalus and Angelo,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Who do prepare to meet him at the gates,
DUKE VINCENTIO: There to give up their power. If you can, pace your wisdom
DUKE VINCENTIO: In that good path that I would wish it go,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And you shall have your bosom on this wretch,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Grace of the duke, revenges to your heart,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And general honour.
ISABELLA: I am directed by you.
DUKE VINCENTIO: This letter, then, to Friar Peter give,
DUKE VINCENTIO: 'Tis that he sent me of the duke's return:
DUKE VINCENTIO: Say, by this token, I desire his company
DUKE VINCENTIO: At Mariana's house to-night. Her cause and yours
DUKE VINCENTIO: I'll perfect him withal, and he shall bring you
DUKE VINCENTIO: Before the duke, and to the head of Angelo
DUKE VINCENTIO: Accuse him home and home. For my poor self,
DUKE VINCENTIO: I am combined by a sacred vow
DUKE VINCENTIO: And shall be absent. Wend you with this letter:
DUKE VINCENTIO: Command these fretting waters from your eyes
DUKE VINCENTIO: With a light heart, trust not my holy order,
DUKE VINCENTIO: If I pervert your course. Who's here?
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIO
LUCIO: Good even. Friar, where's the provost?
DUKE VINCENTIO: Not within, sir.
LUCIO: O pretty Isabella, I am pale at mine heart to see
LUCIO: thine eyes so red: thou must be patient. I am fain
LUCIO: to dine and sup with water and bran, I dare not for
LUCIO: my head fill my belly, one fruitful meal would set
LUCIO: me to 't. But they say the duke will be here
LUCIO: to-morrow. By my troth, Isabel, I loved thy brother:
LUCIO: if the old fantastical duke of dark corners had been
LUCIO: at home, he had lived.
NARRATOR: Exit ISABELLA
DUKE VINCENTIO: Sir, the duke is marvellous little beholding to your
DUKE VINCENTIO: reports, but the best is, he lives not in them.
LUCIO: Friar, thou knowest not the duke so well as I do:
LUCIO: he's a better woodman than thou takest him for.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Well, you'll answer this one day. Fare ye well.
LUCIO: Nay, tarry, I'll go along with thee
LUCIO: I can tell thee pretty tales of the duke.
DUKE VINCENTIO: You have told me too many of him already, sir, if
DUKE VINCENTIO: they be true, if not true, none were enough.
LUCIO: I was once before him for getting a wench with child.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Did you such a thing?
LUCIO: Yes, marry, did I	but I was fain to forswear it,
LUCIO: they would else have married me to the rotten medlar.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Sir, your company is fairer than honest. Rest you well.
LUCIO: By my troth, I'll go with thee to the lane's end:
LUCIO: if bawdy talk offend you, we'll have very little of
LUCIO: it. Nay, friar, I am a kind of burr, I shall stick.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A room in ANGELO's house.
NARRATOR: Enter ANGELO and ESCALUS
ESCALUS: Every letter he hath writ hath disvouched other.
ANGELO: In most uneven and distracted manner. His actions
ANGELO: show much like to madness: pray heaven his wisdom be
ANGELO: not tainted! And why meet him at the gates, and
ANGELO: redeliver our authorities there
ESCALUS: I guess not.
ANGELO: And why should we proclaim it in an hour before his
ANGELO: entering, that if any crave redress of injustice,
ANGELO: they should exhibit their petitions in the street?
ESCALUS: He shows his reason for that: to have a dispatch of
ESCALUS: complaints, and to deliver us from devices
ESCALUS: hereafter, which shall then have no power to stand
ESCALUS: against us.
ANGELO: Well, I beseech you, let it be proclaimed betimes
ANGELO: i' the morn, I'll call you at your house: give
ANGELO: notice to such men of sort and suit as are to meet
ANGELO: him.
ESCALUS: I shall, sir. Fare you well.
ANGELO: Good night.
NARRATOR: Exit ESCALUS
ANGELO: This deed unshapes me quite, makes me unpregnant
ANGELO: And dull to all proceedings. A deflower'd maid!
ANGELO: And by an eminent body that enforced
ANGELO: The law against it! But that her tender shame
ANGELO: Will not proclaim against her maiden loss,
ANGELO: How might she tongue me! Yet reason dares her no,
ANGELO: For my authority bears of a credent bulk,
ANGELO: That no particular scandal once can touch
ANGELO: But it confounds the breather. He should have lived,
ANGELO: Save that riotous youth, with dangerous sense,
ANGELO: Might in the times to come have ta'en revenge,
ANGELO: By so receiving a dishonour'd life
ANGELO: With ransom of such shame. Would yet he had lived!
ANGELO: A lack, when once our grace we have forgot,
ANGELO: Nothing goes right: we would, and we would not.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Fields without the town.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE VINCENTIO in his own habit, and FRIAR PETER
DUKE VINCENTIO: These letters at fit time deliver me
NARRATOR: Giving letters
DUKE VINCENTIO: The provost knows our purpose and our plot.
DUKE VINCENTIO: The matter being afoot, keep your instruction,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And hold you ever to our special drift,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Though sometimes you do blench from this to that,
DUKE VINCENTIO: As cause doth minister. Go call at Flavius' house,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And tell him where I stay: give the like notice
DUKE VINCENTIO: To Valentinus, Rowland, and to Crassus,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And bid them bring the trumpets to the gate,

FRIAR PETER: It shall be speeded well.
NARRATOR: Exit

DUKE VINCENTIO: I thank thee, Varrius, thou hast made good haste:
DUKE VINCENTIO: Come, we will walk. There's other of our friends

NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Street near the city gate.
NARRATOR: Enter ISABELLA and MARIANA
ISABELLA: To speak so indirectly I am loath:
ISABELLA: I would say the truth, but to accuse him so,
ISABELLA: That is your part: yet I am advised to do it,
ISABELLA: He says, to veil full purpose.
MARIANA: Be ruled by him.
ISABELLA: Besides, he tells me that, if peradventure
ISABELLA: He speak against me on the adverse side,
ISABELLA: I should not think it strange, for 'tis a physic
ISABELLA: That's bitter to sweet end.
MARIANA: I would Friar Peter--
ISABELLA: O, peace! the friar is come.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR PETER
FRIAR PETER: Come, I have found you out a stand most fit,
FRIAR PETER: Where you may have such vantage on the duke,
FRIAR PETER: He shall not pass you. Twice have the trumpets sounded,
FRIAR PETER: The generous and gravest citizens
FRIAR PETER: Have hent the gates, and very near upon
FRIAR PETER: The duke is entering: therefore, hence, away!

NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The city gate.
NARRATOR: MARIANA veiled, ISABELLA, and FRIAR PETER, at their  stand. Enter DUKE VINCENTIO, VARRIUS, Lords,  ANGELO, ESCALUS, LUCIO, Provost, Officers, and Citizens, at several doors
DUKE VINCENTIO: My very worthy cousin, fairly met!
DUKE VINCENTIO: Our old and faithful friend, we are glad to see you.
ESCALUS: Happy return be to your royal grace!
DUKE VINCENTIO: Many and hearty thankings to you both.
DUKE VINCENTIO: We have made inquiry of you, and we hear
DUKE VINCENTIO: Such goodness of your justice, that our soul
DUKE VINCENTIO: Cannot but yield you forth to public thanks,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Forerunning more requital.
ANGELO: You make my bonds still greater.
DUKE VINCENTIO: O, your desert speaks loud, and I should wrong it,
DUKE VINCENTIO: To lock it in the wards of covert bosom,
DUKE VINCENTIO: When it deserves, with characters of brass,
DUKE VINCENTIO: A forted residence 'gainst the tooth of time
DUKE VINCENTIO: And razure of oblivion. Give me your hand,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And let the subject see, to make them know
DUKE VINCENTIO: That outward courtesies would fain proclaim
DUKE VINCENTIO: Favours that keep within. Come, Escalus,
DUKE VINCENTIO: You must walk by us on our other hand,
DUKE VINCENTIO: And good supporters are you.
NARRATOR: FRIAR PETER and ISABELLA come forward
FRIAR PETER: Now is your time: speak loud and kneel before him.
ISABELLA: Justice, O royal duke! Vail your regard
ISABELLA: Upon a wrong'd, I would fain have said, a maid!
ISABELLA: O worthy prince, dishonour not your eye
ISABELLA: By throwing it on any other object
ISABELLA: Till you have heard me in my true complaint
ISABELLA: And given me justice, justice, justice, justice!
DUKE VINCENTIO: Relate your wrongs, in what? by whom? be brief.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Here is Lord Angelo shall give you justice:
DUKE VINCENTIO: Reveal yourself to him.
ISABELLA: O worthy duke,
ISABELLA: You bid me seek redemption of the devil:
ISABELLA: Hear me yourself, for that which I must speak
ISABELLA: Must either punish me, not being believed,
ISABELLA: Or wring redress from you. Hear me, O hear me, here!
ANGELO: My lord, her wits, I fear me, are not firm:
ANGELO: She hath been a suitor to me for her brother
ANGELO: Cut off by course of justice,--
ISABELLA: By course of justice!
ANGELO: And she will speak most bitterly and strange.
ISABELLA: Most strange, but yet most truly, will I speak:
ISABELLA: That Angelo's forsworn, is it not strange?
ISABELLA: That Angelo's a murderer, is 't not strange?
ISABELLA: That Angelo is an adulterous thief,
ISABELLA: An hypocrite, a virgin-violator,
ISABELLA: Is it not strange and strange?
DUKE VINCENTIO: Nay, it is ten times strange.
ISABELLA: It is not truer he is Angelo
ISABELLA: Than this is all as true as it is strange:
ISABELLA: Nay, it is ten times true, for truth is truth
ISABELLA: To the end of reckoning.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Away with her! Poor soul,
DUKE VINCENTIO: She speaks this in the infirmity of sense.
ISABELLA: O prince, I conjure thee, as thou believest
ISABELLA: There is another comfort than this world,
ISABELLA: That thou neglect me not, with that opinion
ISABELLA: That I am touch'd with madness! Make not impossible
ISABELLA: That which but seems unlike: 'tis not impossible
ISABELLA: But one, the wicked'st caitiff on the ground,
ISABELLA: May seem as shy, as grave, as just, as absolute
ISABELLA: As Angelo, even so may Angelo,
ISABELLA: In all his dressings, characts, titles, forms,
ISABELLA: Be an arch-villain, believe it, royal prince:
ISABELLA: If he be less, he's nothing, but he's more,
ISABELLA: Had I more name for badness.
DUKE VINCENTIO: By mine honesty,
DUKE VINCENTIO: If she be mad,--as I believe no other,--
DUKE VINCENTIO: Her madness hath the oddest frame of sense,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Such a dependency of thing on thing,
DUKE VINCENTIO: As e'er I heard in madness.
ISABELLA: O gracious duke,
ISABELLA: Harp not on that, nor do not banish reason
ISABELLA: For inequality, but let your reason serve
ISABELLA: To make the truth appear where it seems hid,
ISABELLA: And hide the false seems true.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Many that are not mad
DUKE VINCENTIO: Have, sure, more lack of reason. What would you say?
ISABELLA: I am the sister of one Claudio,
ISABELLA: Condemn'd upon the act of fornication
ISABELLA: To lose his head, condemn'd by Angelo:
ISABELLA: I, in probation of a sisterhood,
ISABELLA: Was sent to by my brother, one Lucio
ISABELLA: As then the messenger,--
LUCIO: That's I, an't like your grace:
LUCIO: I came to her from Claudio, and desired her
LUCIO: To try her gracious fortune with Lord Angelo
LUCIO: For her poor brother's pardon.
ISABELLA: That's he indeed.
DUKE VINCENTIO: You were not bid to speak.
LUCIO: No, my good lord,
LUCIO: Nor wish'd to hold my peace.
DUKE VINCENTIO: I wish you now, then,
DUKE VINCENTIO: Pray you, take note of it: and when you have
DUKE VINCENTIO: A business for yourself, pray heaven you then
DUKE VINCENTIO: Be perfect.
LUCIO: I warrant your honour.
DUKE VINCENTIO: The warrants for yourself, take heed to't.
ISABELLA: This gentleman told somewhat of my tale,--
LUCIO: Right.
DUKE VINCENTIO: It may be right, but you are i' the wrong
DUKE VINCENTIO: To speak before your time. Proceed.
ISABELLA: I went
ISABELLA: To this pernicious caitiff deputy,--
DUKE VINCENTIO: That's somewhat madly spoken.
ISABELLA: Pardon it,
ISABELLA: The phrase is to the matter.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Mended again. The matter, proceed.
ISABELLA: In brief, to set the needless process by,
ISABELLA: How I persuaded, how I pray'd, and kneel'd,

ISABELLA: For this was of much length,--the vile conclusion

ISABELLA: He would not, but by gift of my chaste body

DUKE VINCENTIO: This is most likely!
ISABELLA: O, that it were as like as it is true!

DUKE VINCENTIO: He would have weigh'd thy brother by himself

DUKE VINCENTIO: Confess the truth, and say by whose advice

ISABELLA: And is this all?
ISABELLA: Then, O you blessed ministers above,
ISABELLA: Keep me in patience, and with ripen'd time
ISABELLA: Unfold the evil which is here wrapt up
ISABELLA: In countenance! Heaven shield your grace from woe,
ISABELLA: As I, thus wrong'd, hence unbelieved go!
DUKE VINCENTIO: I know you'ld fain be gone. An officer!

DUKE VINCENTIO: A blasting and a scandalous breath to fall
DUKE VINCENTIO: On him so near us? This needs must be a practise.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Who knew of Your intent and coming hither?
ISABELLA: One that I would were here, Friar Lodowick.
DUKE VINCENTIO: A ghostly father, belike. Who knows that Lodowick?
LUCIO: My lord, I know him, 'tis a meddling friar,
LUCIO: I do not like the man: had he been lay, my lord
LUCIO: For certain words he spake against your grace
LUCIO: In your retirement, I had swinged him soundly.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Words against me? this is a good friar, belike!
DUKE VINCENTIO: And to set on this wretched woman here
DUKE VINCENTIO: Against our substitute! Let this friar be found.
LUCIO: But yesternight, my lord, she and that friar,
LUCIO: I saw them at the prison: a saucy friar,
LUCIO: A very scurvy fellow.
FRIAR PETER: Blessed be your royal grace!
FRIAR PETER: I have stood by, my lord, and I have heard
FRIAR PETER: Your royal ear abused. First, hath this woman
FRIAR PETER: Most wrongfully accused your substitute,
FRIAR PETER: Who is as free from touch or soil with her
FRIAR PETER: As she from one ungot.
DUKE VINCENTIO: We did believe no less.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Know you that Friar Lodowick that she speaks of?
FRIAR PETER: I know him for a man divine and holy,
FRIAR PETER: Not scurvy, nor a temporary meddler,
FRIAR PETER: As he's reported by this gentleman,
FRIAR PETER: And, on my trust, a man that never yet
FRIAR PETER: Did, as he vouches, misreport your grace.
LUCIO: My lord, most villanously, believe it.
FRIAR PETER: Well, he in time may come to clear himself,
FRIAR PETER: But at this instant he is sick my lord,
FRIAR PETER: Of a strange fever. Upon his mere request,
FRIAR PETER: Being come to knowledge that there was complaint
FRIAR PETER: Intended 'gainst Lord Angelo, came I hither,
FRIAR PETER: To speak, as from his mouth, what he doth know
FRIAR PETER: Is true and false, and what he with his oath
FRIAR PETER: And all probation will make up full clear,
FRIAR PETER: Whensoever he's convented. First, for this woman.
FRIAR PETER: To justify this worthy nobleman,
FRIAR PETER: So vulgarly and personally accused,
FRIAR PETER: Her shall you hear disproved to her eyes,
FRIAR PETER: Till she herself confess it.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Good friar, let's hear it.
DUKE VINCENTIO: ISABELLA is carried off guarded, and MARIANA comes forward
DUKE VINCENTIO: Do you not smile at this, Lord Angelo?
DUKE VINCENTIO: O heaven, the vanity of wretched fools!
DUKE VINCENTIO: Give us some seats. Come, cousin Angelo,
DUKE VINCENTIO: In this I'll be impartial, be you judge
DUKE VINCENTIO: Of your own cause. Is this the witness, friar?
DUKE VINCENTIO: First, let her show her face, and after speak.
MARIANA: Pardon, my lord, I will not show my face
MARIANA: Until my husband bid me.
DUKE VINCENTIO: What, are you married?
MARIANA: No, my lord.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Are you a maid?
MARIANA: No, my lord.
DUKE VINCENTIO: A widow, then?
MARIANA: Neither, my lord.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Why, you are nothing then: neither maid, widow, nor wife?
LUCIO: My lord, she may be a punk, for many of them are
LUCIO: neither maid, widow, nor wife.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Silence that fellow: I would he had some cause
DUKE VINCENTIO: To prattle for himself.
LUCIO: Well, my lord.
MARIANA: My lord, I do confess I ne'er was married,
MARIANA: And I confess besides I am no maid:
MARIANA: I have known my husband, yet my husband
MARIANA: Knows not that ever he knew me.
LUCIO: He was drunk then, my lord: it can be no better.
DUKE VINCENTIO: For the benefit of silence, would thou wert so too!
LUCIO: Well, my lord.
DUKE VINCENTIO: This is no witness for Lord Angelo.
MARIANA: Now I come to't my lord
MARIANA: She that accuses him of fornication,
MARIANA: In self-same manner doth accuse my husband,
MARIANA: And charges him my lord, with such a time
MARIANA: When I'll depose I had him in mine arms
MARIANA: With all the effect of love.
ANGELO: Charges she more than me?
MARIANA: Not that I know.
DUKE VINCENTIO: No? you say your husband.
MARIANA: Why, just, my lord, and that is Angelo,
MARIANA: Who thinks he knows that he ne'er knew my body,
MARIANA: But knows he thinks that he knows Isabel's.
ANGELO: This is a strange abuse. Let's see thy face.
MARIANA: My husband bids me, now I will unmask.
NARRATOR: Unveiling
MARIANA: This is that face, thou cruel Angelo,
MARIANA: Which once thou sworest was worth the looking on,
MARIANA: This is the hand which, with a vow'd contract,
MARIANA: Was fast belock'd in thine, this is the body
MARIANA: That took away the match from Isabel,
MARIANA: And did supply thee at thy garden-house
MARIANA: In her imagined person.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Know you this woman?
LUCIO: Carnally, she says.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Sirrah, no more!
LUCIO: Enough, my lord.
ANGELO: My lord, I must confess I know this woman:
ANGELO: And five years since there was some speech of marriage
ANGELO: Betwixt myself and her, which was broke off,
ANGELO: Partly for that her promised proportions
ANGELO: Came short of composition, but in chief
ANGELO: For that her reputation was disvalued

ANGELO: Upon my faith and honour.

MARIANA: As there is sense in truth and truth in virtue,

MARIANA: As words could make up vows: and, my good lord,
MARIANA: But Tuesday night last gone in's garden-house

MARIANA: Let me in safety raise me from my knees
MARIANA: Or else for ever be confixed here,
MARIANA: A marble monument!

ANGELO: These poor informal women are no more
ANGELO: But instruments of some more mightier member
ANGELO: That sets them on: let me have way, my lord,
ANGELO: To find this practise out.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Ay, with my heart
DUKE VINCENTIO: And punish them to your height of pleasure.
DUKE VINCENTIO: Thou foolish friar, and thou pernicious woman,

FRIAR PETER: Your provost knows the place where he abides

DUKE VINCENTIO: Upon these slanderers.

ESCALUS: notable fellow.

LUCIO: she'll be ashamed.

LUCIO: That's the way, for women are light at midnight.

ESCALUS: that you have said.

LUCIO: Mum.

''' PLAY: Merchant of Venice '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO, SALARINO, and SALANIO
ANTONIO: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
ANTONIO: It wearies me, you say it wearies you,
ANTONIO: But how I caught it, found it, or came by it,
ANTONIO: What stuff 'tis made of, whereof it is born,
ANTONIO: I am to learn,
ANTONIO: And such a want-wit sadness makes of me,
ANTONIO: That I have much ado to know myself.
SALARINO: Your mind is tossing on the ocean,
SALARINO: There, where your argosies with portly sail,
SALARINO: Like signiors and rich burghers on the flood,
SALARINO: Or, as it were, the pageants of the sea,
SALARINO: Do overpeer the petty traffickers,
SALARINO: That curtsy to them, do them reverence,
SALARINO: As they fly by them with their woven wings.
SALANIO: Believe me, sir, had I such venture forth,
SALANIO: The better part of my affections would
SALANIO: Be with my hopes abroad. I should be still
SALANIO: Plucking the grass, to know where sits the wind,
SALANIO: Peering in maps for ports and piers and roads,
SALANIO: And every object that might make me fear
SALANIO: Misfortune to my ventures, out of doubt
SALANIO: Would make me sad.
SALARINO: My wind cooling my broth
SALARINO: Would blow me to an ague, when I thought
SALARINO: What harm a wind too great at sea might do.
SALARINO: I should not see the sandy hour-glass run,
SALARINO: But I should think of shallows and of flats,
SALARINO: And see my wealthy Andrew dock'd in sand,
SALARINO: Vailing her high-top lower than her ribs
SALARINO: To kiss her burial. Should I go to church
SALARINO: And see the holy edifice of stone,
SALARINO: And not bethink me straight of dangerous rocks,
SALARINO: Which touching but my gentle vessel's side,
SALARINO: Would scatter all her spices on the stream,
SALARINO: Enrobe the roaring waters with my silks,
SALARINO: And, in a word, but even now worth this,
SALARINO: And now worth nothing? Shall I have the thought
SALARINO: To think on this, and shall I lack the thought
SALARINO: That such a thing bechanced would make me sad?
SALARINO: But tell not me, I know, Antonio
SALARINO: Is sad to think upon his merchandise.
ANTONIO: Believe me, no: I thank my fortune for it,
ANTONIO: My ventures are not in one bottom trusted,
ANTONIO: Nor to one place, nor is my whole estate
ANTONIO: Upon the fortune of this present year:
ANTONIO: Therefore my merchandise makes me not sad.
SALARINO: Why, then you are in love.
ANTONIO: Fie, fie!
SALARINO: Not in love neither? Then let us say you are sad,
SALARINO: Because you are not merry: and 'twere as easy
SALARINO: For you to laugh and leap and say you are merry,
SALARINO: Because you are not sad. Now, by two-headed Janus,
SALARINO: Nature hath framed strange fellows in her time:
SALARINO: Some that will evermore peep through their eyes
SALARINO: And laugh like parrots at a bag-piper,
SALARINO: And other of such vinegar aspect
SALARINO: That they'll not show their teeth in way of smile,
SALARINO: Though Nestor swear the jest be laughable.
NARRATOR: Enter BASSANIO, LORENZO, and GRATIANO
SALANIO: Here comes Bassanio, your most noble kinsman,
SALANIO: Gratiano and Lorenzo. Fare ye well:
SALANIO: We leave you now with better company.
SALARINO: I would have stay'd till I had made you merry,
SALARINO: If worthier friends had not prevented me.
ANTONIO: Your worth is very dear in my regard.
ANTONIO: I take it, your own business calls on you
ANTONIO: And you embrace the occasion to depart.
SALARINO: Good morrow, my good lords.
BASSANIO: Good signiors both, when shall we laugh? say, when?
BASSANIO: You grow exceeding strange: must it be so?
SALARINO: We'll make our leisures to attend on yours.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Salarino and Salanio
LORENZO: My Lord Bassanio, since you have found Antonio,
LORENZO: We two will leave you: but at dinner-time,
LORENZO: I pray you, have in mind where we must meet.
BASSANIO: I will not fail you.
GRATIANO: You look not well, Signior Antonio,
GRATIANO: You have too much respect upon the world:
GRATIANO: They lose it that do buy it with much care:
GRATIANO: Believe me, you are marvellously changed.
ANTONIO: I hold the world but as the world, Gratiano,
ANTONIO: A stage where every man must play a part,
ANTONIO: And mine a sad one.
GRATIANO: Let me play the fool:
GRATIANO: With mirth and laughter let old wrinkles come,
GRATIANO: And let my liver rather heat with wine
GRATIANO: Than my heart cool with mortifying groans.
GRATIANO: Why should a man, whose blood is warm within,
GRATIANO: Sit like his grandsire cut in alabaster?
GRATIANO: Sleep when he wakes and creep into the jaundice
GRATIANO: By being peevish? I tell thee what, Antonio--
GRATIANO: I love thee, and it is my love that speaks--
GRATIANO: There are a sort of men whose visages
GRATIANO: Do cream and mantle like a standing pond,
GRATIANO: And do a wilful stillness entertain,
GRATIANO: With purpose to be dress'd in an opinion
GRATIANO: Of wisdom, gravity, profound conceit,
GRATIANO: As who should say 'I am Sir Oracle,
GRATIANO: And when I ope my lips let no dog bark!'
GRATIANO: O my Antonio, I do know of these
GRATIANO: That therefore only are reputed wise
GRATIANO: For saying nothing, when, I am very sure,
GRATIANO: If they should speak, would almost damn those ears,
GRATIANO: Which, hearing them, would call their brothers fools.
GRATIANO: I'll tell thee more of this another time:
GRATIANO: But fish not, with this melancholy bait,
GRATIANO: For this fool gudgeon, this opinion.
GRATIANO: Come, good Lorenzo. Fare ye well awhile:
GRATIANO: I'll end my exhortation after dinner.
LORENZO: Well, we will leave you then till dinner-time:
LORENZO: I must be one of these same dumb wise men,
LORENZO: For Gratiano never lets me speak.
GRATIANO: Well, keep me company but two years moe,
GRATIANO: Thou shalt not know the sound of thine own tongue.
ANTONIO: Farewell: I'll grow a talker for this gear.
GRATIANO: Thanks, i' faith, for silence is only commendable
GRATIANO: In a neat's tongue dried and a maid not vendible.
NARRATOR: Exeunt GRATIANO and LORENZO
ANTONIO: Is that any thing now?
BASSANIO: Gratiano speaks an infinite deal of nothing, more
BASSANIO: than any man in all Venice. His reasons are as two
BASSANIO: grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff: you
BASSANIO: shall seek all day ere you find them, and when you
BASSANIO: have them, they are not worth the search.
ANTONIO: Well, tell me now what lady is the same
ANTONIO: To whom you swore a secret pilgrimage,
ANTONIO: That you to-day promised to tell me of?
BASSANIO: 'Tis not unknown to you, Antonio,
BASSANIO: How much I have disabled mine estate,
BASSANIO: By something showing a more swelling port
BASSANIO: Than my faint means would grant continuance:
BASSANIO: Nor do I now make moan to be abridged
BASSANIO: From such a noble rate, but my chief care
BASSANIO: Is to come fairly off from the great debts
BASSANIO: Wherein my time something too prodigal
BASSANIO: Hath left me gaged. To you, Antonio,
BASSANIO: I owe the most, in money and in love,
BASSANIO: And from your love I have a warranty
BASSANIO: To unburden all my plots and purposes
BASSANIO: How to get clear of all the debts I owe.
ANTONIO: I pray you, good Bassanio, let me know it,
ANTONIO: And if it stand, as you yourself still do,
ANTONIO: Within the eye of honour, be assured,
ANTONIO: My purse, my person, my extremest means,
ANTONIO: Lie all unlock'd to your occasions.
BASSANIO: In my school-days, when I had lost one shaft,
BASSANIO: I shot his fellow of the self-same flight
BASSANIO: The self-same way with more advised watch,
BASSANIO: To find the other forth, and by adventuring both
BASSANIO: I oft found both: I urge this childhood proof,
BASSANIO: Because what follows is pure innocence.
BASSANIO: I owe you much, and, like a wilful youth,
BASSANIO: That which I owe is lost, but if you please
BASSANIO: To shoot another arrow that self way
BASSANIO: Which you did shoot the first, I do not doubt,
BASSANIO: As I will watch the aim, or to find both
BASSANIO: Or bring your latter hazard back again
BASSANIO: And thankfully rest debtor for the first.
ANTONIO: You know me well, and herein spend but time
ANTONIO: To wind about my love with circumstance,
ANTONIO: And out of doubt you do me now more wrong
ANTONIO: In making question of my uttermost
ANTONIO: Than if you had made waste of all I have:
ANTONIO: Then do but say to me what I should do
ANTONIO: That in your knowledge may by me be done,
ANTONIO: And I am prest unto it: therefore, speak.
BASSANIO: In Belmont is a lady richly left,
BASSANIO: And she is fair, and, fairer than that word,
BASSANIO: Of wondrous virtues: sometimes from her eyes
BASSANIO: I did receive fair speechless messages:
BASSANIO: Her name is Portia, nothing undervalued
BASSANIO: To Cato's daughter, Brutus' Portia:
BASSANIO: Nor is the wide world ignorant of her worth,
BASSANIO: For the four winds blow in from every coast
BASSANIO: Renowned suitors, and her sunny locks
BASSANIO: Hang on her temples like a golden fleece,
BASSANIO: Which makes her seat of Belmont Colchos' strand,
BASSANIO: And many Jasons come in quest of her.
BASSANIO: O my Antonio, had I but the means
BASSANIO: To hold a rival place with one of them,
BASSANIO: I have a mind presages me such thrift,
BASSANIO: That I should questionless be fortunate!
ANTONIO: Thou know'st that all my fortunes are at sea,
ANTONIO: Neither have I money nor commodity
ANTONIO: To raise a present sum: therefore go forth,
ANTONIO: Try what my credit can in Venice do:
ANTONIO: That shall be rack'd, even to the uttermost,
ANTONIO: To furnish thee to Belmont, to fair Portia.
ANTONIO: Go, presently inquire, and so will I,
ANTONIO: Where money is, and I no question make
ANTONIO: To have it of my trust or for my sake.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
ANTONIO: SCENE II: Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA and NERISSA
PORTIA: By my troth, Nerissa, my little body is aweary of
PORTIA: this great world.
NERISSA: You would be, sweet madam, if your miseries were in
NERISSA: the same abundance as your good fortunes are: and
NERISSA: yet, for aught I see, they are as sick that surfeit
NERISSA: with too much as they that starve with nothing. It
NERISSA: is no mean happiness therefore, to be seated in the
NERISSA: mean: superfluity comes sooner by white hairs, but
NERISSA: competency lives longer.
PORTIA: Good sentences and well pronounced.
NERISSA: They would be better, if well followed.
PORTIA: If to do were as easy as to know what were good to
PORTIA: do, chapels had been churches and poor men's
PORTIA: cottages princes' palaces. It is a good divine that
PORTIA: follows his own instructions: I can easier teach
PORTIA: twenty what were good to be done, than be one of the
PORTIA: twenty to follow mine own teaching. The brain may
PORTIA: devise laws for the blood, but a hot temper leaps
PORTIA: o'er a cold decree: such a hare is madness the
PORTIA: youth, to skip o'er the meshes of good counsel the
PORTIA: cripple. But this reasoning is not in the fashion to
PORTIA: choose me a husband. O me, the word 'choose!' I may
PORTIA: neither choose whom I would nor refuse whom I
PORTIA: dislike, so is the will of a living daughter curbed
PORTIA: by the will of a dead father. Is it not hard,
PORTIA: Nerissa, that I cannot choose one nor refuse none?
NERISSA: Your father was ever virtuous, and holy men at their
NERISSA: death have good inspirations: therefore the lottery,
NERISSA: that he hath devised in these three chests of gold,
NERISSA: silver and lead, whereof who chooses his meaning
NERISSA: chooses you, will, no doubt, never be chosen by any
NERISSA: rightly but one who shall rightly love. But what
NERISSA: warmth is there in your affection towards any of
NERISSA: these princely suitors that are already come?
PORTIA: I pray thee, over-name them, and as thou namest
PORTIA: them, I will describe them, and, according to my
PORTIA: description, level at my affection.
NERISSA: First, there is the Neapolitan prince.
PORTIA: Ay, that's a colt indeed, for he doth nothing but
PORTIA: talk of his horse, and he makes it a great
PORTIA: appropriation to his own good parts, that he can
PORTIA: shoe him himself. I am much afeard my lady his
PORTIA: mother played false with a smith.
NERISSA: Then there is the County Palatine.
PORTIA: He doth nothing but frown, as who should say 'If you
PORTIA: will not have me, choose:' he hears merry tales and
PORTIA: smiles not: I fear he will prove the weeping
PORTIA: philosopher when he grows old, being so full of
PORTIA: unmannerly sadness in his youth. I had rather be
PORTIA: married to a death's-head with a bone in his mouth
PORTIA: than to either of these. God defend me from these
PORTIA: two!
NERISSA: How say you by the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?
PORTIA: God made him, and therefore let him pass for a man.
PORTIA: In truth, I know it is a sin to be a mocker: but,
PORTIA: he! why, he hath a horse better than the
PORTIA: Neapolitan's, a better bad habit of frowning than
PORTIA: the Count Palatine, he is every man in no man, if a
PORTIA: throstle sing, he falls straight a capering: he will
PORTIA: fence with his own shadow: if I should marry him, I
PORTIA: should marry twenty husbands. If he would despise me
PORTIA: I would forgive him, for if he love me to madness, I
PORTIA: shall never requite him.
NERISSA: What say you, then, to Falconbridge, the young baron
NERISSA: of England?
PORTIA: You know I say nothing to him, for he understands
PORTIA: not me, nor I him: he hath neither Latin, French,
PORTIA: nor Italian, and you will come into the court and
PORTIA: swear that I have a poor pennyworth in the English.
PORTIA: He is a proper man's picture, but, alas, who can
PORTIA: converse with a dumb-show? How oddly he is suited!
PORTIA: I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his round
PORTIA: hose in France, his bonnet in Germany and his
PORTIA: behavior every where.
NERISSA: What think you of the Scottish lord, his neighbour?
PORTIA: That he hath a neighbourly charity in him, for he
PORTIA: borrowed a box of the ear of the Englishman and
PORTIA: swore he would pay him again when he was able: I
PORTIA: think the Frenchman became his surety and sealed
PORTIA: under for another.
NERISSA: How like you the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?
PORTIA: Very vilely in the morning, when he is sober, and
PORTIA: most vilely in the afternoon, when he is drunk: when
PORTIA: he is best, he is a little worse than a man, and
PORTIA: when he is worst, he is little better than a beast:
PORTIA: and the worst fall that ever fell, I hope I shall
PORTIA: make shift to go without him.
NERISSA: If he should offer to choose, and choose the right
NERISSA: casket, you should refuse to perform your father's
NERISSA: will, if you should refuse to accept him.
PORTIA: Therefore, for fear of the worst, I pray thee, set a
PORTIA: deep glass of rhenish wine on the contrary casket,
PORTIA: for if the devil be within and that temptation
PORTIA: without, I know he will choose it. I will do any
PORTIA: thing, Nerissa, ere I'll be married to a sponge.
NERISSA: You need not fear, lady, the having any of these
NERISSA: lords: they have acquainted me with their
NERISSA: determinations, which is, indeed, to return to their
NERISSA: home and to trouble you with no more suit, unless
NERISSA: you may be won by some other sort than your father's
NERISSA: imposition depending on the caskets.
PORTIA: If I live to be as old as Sibylla, I will die as
PORTIA: chaste as Diana, unless I be obtained by the manner
PORTIA: of my father's will. I am glad this parcel of wooers
PORTIA: are so reasonable, for there is not one among them
PORTIA: but I dote on his very absence, and I pray God grant
PORTIA: them a fair departure.
NERISSA: Do you not remember, lady, in your father's time, a
NERISSA: Venetian, a scholar and a soldier, that came hither
NERISSA: in company of the Marquis of Montferrat?
PORTIA: Yes, yes, it was Bassanio, as I think, he was so called.
NERISSA: True, madam: he, of all the men that ever my foolish
NERISSA: eyes looked upon, was the best deserving a fair lady.
PORTIA: I remember him well, and I remember him worthy of
PORTIA: thy praise.
NARRATOR: Enter a Serving-man
PORTIA: How now! what news?
Servant: The four strangers seek for you, madam, to take
Servant: their leave: and there is a forerunner come from a
Servant: fifth, the Prince of Morocco, who brings word the
Servant: prince his master will be here to-night.
PORTIA: If I could bid the fifth welcome with so good a
PORTIA: heart as I can bid the other four farewell, I should
PORTIA: be glad of his approach: if he have the condition
PORTIA: of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I had
PORTIA: rather he should shrive me than wive me. Come,
PORTIA: Nerissa. Sirrah, go before.
PORTIA: Whiles we shut the gates
PORTIA: upon one wooer, another knocks at the door.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Venice. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter BASSANIO and SHYLOCK
SHYLOCK: Three thousand ducats, well.
BASSANIO: Ay, sir, for three months.
SHYLOCK: For three months, well.
BASSANIO: For the which, as I told you, Antonio shall be bound.
SHYLOCK: Antonio shall become bound, well.
BASSANIO: May you stead me? will you pleasure me? shall I
BASSANIO: know your answer?
SHYLOCK: Three thousand ducats for three months and Antonio bound.
BASSANIO: Your answer to that.
SHYLOCK: Antonio is a good man.
BASSANIO: Have you heard any imputation to the contrary?
SHYLOCK: Oh, no, no, no, no: my meaning in saying he is a
SHYLOCK: good man is to have you understand me that he is
SHYLOCK: sufficient. Yet his means are in supposition: he
SHYLOCK: hath an argosy bound to Tripolis, another to the
SHYLOCK: Indies, I understand moreover, upon the Rialto, he
SHYLOCK: hath a third at Mexico, a fourth for England, and
SHYLOCK: other ventures he hath, squandered abroad. But ships
SHYLOCK: are but boards, sailors but men: there be land-rats
SHYLOCK: and water-rats, water-thieves and land-thieves, I
SHYLOCK: mean pirates, and then there is the peril of waters,
SHYLOCK: winds and rocks. The man is, notwithstanding,
SHYLOCK: sufficient. Three thousand ducats, I think I may
SHYLOCK: take his bond.
BASSANIO: Be assured you may.
SHYLOCK: I will be assured I may, and, that I may be assured,
SHYLOCK: I will bethink me. May I speak with Antonio?
BASSANIO: If it please you to dine with us.
SHYLOCK: Yes, to smell pork, to eat of the habitation which
SHYLOCK: your prophet the Nazarite conjured the devil into. I
SHYLOCK: will buy with you, sell with you, talk with you,
SHYLOCK: walk with you, and so following, but I will not eat
SHYLOCK: with you, drink with you, nor pray with you. What
SHYLOCK: news on the Rialto? Who is he comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO
BASSANIO: This is Signior Antonio.
SHYLOCK: [Aside]  How like a fawning publican he looks!
SHYLOCK: I hate him for he is a Christian,
SHYLOCK: But more for that in low simplicity
SHYLOCK: He lends out money gratis and brings down
SHYLOCK: The rate of usance here with us in Venice.
SHYLOCK: If I can catch him once upon the hip,
SHYLOCK: I will feed fat the ancient grudge I bear him.
SHYLOCK: He hates our sacred nation, and he rails,
SHYLOCK: Even there where merchants most do congregate,
SHYLOCK: On me, my bargains and my well-won thrift,
SHYLOCK: Which he calls interest. Cursed be my tribe,
SHYLOCK: If I forgive him!
BASSANIO: Shylock, do you hear?
SHYLOCK: I am debating of my present store,
SHYLOCK: And, by the near guess of my memory,
SHYLOCK: I cannot instantly raise up the gross
SHYLOCK: Of full three thousand ducats. What of that?
SHYLOCK: Tubal, a wealthy Hebrew of my tribe,
SHYLOCK: Will furnish me. But soft! how many months
SHYLOCK: Do you desire?
NARRATOR: To ANTONIO
SHYLOCK: Rest you fair, good signior,
SHYLOCK: Your worship was the last man in our mouths.
ANTONIO: Shylock, although I neither lend nor borrow
ANTONIO: By taking nor by giving of excess,
ANTONIO: Yet, to supply the ripe wants of my friend,
ANTONIO: I'll break a custom. Is he yet possess'd
ANTONIO: How much ye would?
SHYLOCK: Ay, ay, three thousand ducats.
ANTONIO: And for three months.
SHYLOCK: I had forgot, three months, you told me so.
SHYLOCK: Well then, your bond, and let me see, but hear you,
SHYLOCK: Methought you said you neither lend nor borrow
SHYLOCK: Upon advantage.
ANTONIO: I do never use it.
SHYLOCK: When Jacob grazed his uncle Laban's sheep--
SHYLOCK: This Jacob from our holy Abram was,
SHYLOCK: As his wise mother wrought in his behalf,
SHYLOCK: The third possessor, ay, he was the third--
ANTONIO: And what of him? did he take interest?
SHYLOCK: No, not take interest, not, as you would say,
SHYLOCK: Directly interest: mark what Jacob did.
SHYLOCK: When Laban and himself were compromised
SHYLOCK: That all the eanlings which were streak'd and pied
SHYLOCK: Should fall as Jacob's hire, the ewes, being rank,
SHYLOCK: In the end of autumn turned to the rams,
SHYLOCK: And, when the work of generation was
SHYLOCK: Between these woolly breeders in the act,
SHYLOCK: The skilful shepherd peel'd me certain wands,
SHYLOCK: And, in the doing of the deed of kind,
SHYLOCK: He stuck them up before the fulsome ewes,
SHYLOCK: Who then conceiving did in eaning time
SHYLOCK: Fall parti-colour'd lambs, and those were Jacob's.
SHYLOCK: This was a way to thrive, and he was blest:
SHYLOCK: And thrift is blessing, if men steal it not.
ANTONIO: This was a venture, sir, that Jacob served for,
ANTONIO: A thing not in his power to bring to pass,
ANTONIO: But sway'd and fashion'd by the hand of heaven.
ANTONIO: Was this inserted to make interest good?
ANTONIO: Or is your gold and silver ewes and rams?
SHYLOCK: I cannot tell, I make it breed as fast:
SHYLOCK: But note me, signior.
ANTONIO: Mark you this, Bassanio,
ANTONIO: The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
ANTONIO: An evil soul producing holy witness
ANTONIO: Is like a villain with a smiling cheek,
ANTONIO: A goodly apple rotten at the heart:
ANTONIO: O, what a goodly outside falsehood hath!
SHYLOCK: Three thousand ducats, 'tis a good round sum.
SHYLOCK: Three months from twelve, then, let me see, the rate--
ANTONIO: Well, Shylock, shall we be beholding to you?
SHYLOCK: Signior Antonio, many a time and oft
SHYLOCK: In the Rialto you have rated me
SHYLOCK: About my moneys and my usances:
SHYLOCK: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug,
SHYLOCK: For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
SHYLOCK: You call me misbeliever, cut-throat dog,
SHYLOCK: And spit upon my Jewish gaberdine,
SHYLOCK: And all for use of that which is mine own.
SHYLOCK: Well then, it now appears you need my help:
SHYLOCK: Go to, then, you come to me, and you say
SHYLOCK: 'Shylock, we would have moneys:' you say so,
SHYLOCK: You, that did void your rheum upon my beard
SHYLOCK: And foot me as you spurn a stranger cur
SHYLOCK: Over your threshold: moneys is your suit
SHYLOCK: What should I say to you? Should I not say
SHYLOCK: 'Hath a dog money? is it possible
SHYLOCK: A cur can lend three thousand ducats?' Or
SHYLOCK: Shall I bend low and in a bondman's key,
SHYLOCK: With bated breath and whispering humbleness, Say this,
SHYLOCK: 'Fair sir, you spit on me on Wednesday last,
SHYLOCK: You spurn'd me such a day, another time
SHYLOCK: You call'd me dog, and for these courtesies
SHYLOCK: I'll lend you thus much moneys'?
ANTONIO: I am as like to call thee so again,
ANTONIO: To spit on thee again, to spurn thee too.
ANTONIO: If thou wilt lend this money, lend it not
ANTONIO: As to thy friends, for when did friendship take
ANTONIO: A breed for barren metal of his friend?
ANTONIO: But lend it rather to thine enemy,
ANTONIO: Who, if he break, thou mayst with better face
ANTONIO: Exact the penalty.
SHYLOCK: Why, look you, how you storm!
SHYLOCK: I would be friends with you and have your love,
SHYLOCK: Forget the shames that you have stain'd me with,
SHYLOCK: Supply your present wants and take no doit
SHYLOCK: Of usance for my moneys, and you'll not hear me:
SHYLOCK: This is kind I offer.
BASSANIO: This were kindness.
SHYLOCK: This kindness will I show.
SHYLOCK: Go with me to a notary, seal me there
SHYLOCK: Your single bond, and, in a merry sport,
SHYLOCK: If you repay me not on such a day,
SHYLOCK: In such a place, such sum or sums as are
SHYLOCK: Express'd in the condition, let the forfeit
SHYLOCK: Be nominated for an equal pound
SHYLOCK: Of your fair flesh, to be cut off and taken
SHYLOCK: In what part of your body pleaseth me.
ANTONIO: Content, i' faith: I'll seal to such a bond
ANTONIO: And say there is much kindness in the Jew.
BASSANIO: You shall not seal to such a bond for me:
BASSANIO: I'll rather dwell in my necessity.
ANTONIO: Why, fear not, man, I will not forfeit it:
ANTONIO: Within these two months, that's a month before
ANTONIO: This bond expires, I do expect return
ANTONIO: Of thrice three times the value of this bond.
SHYLOCK: O father Abram, what these Christians are,
SHYLOCK: Whose own hard dealings teaches them suspect
SHYLOCK: The thoughts of others! Pray you, tell me this,
SHYLOCK: If he should break his day, what should I gain
SHYLOCK: By the exaction of the forfeiture?
SHYLOCK: A pound of man's flesh taken from a man
SHYLOCK: Is not so estimable, profitable neither,
SHYLOCK: As flesh of muttons, beefs, or goats. I say,
SHYLOCK: To buy his favour, I extend this friendship:
SHYLOCK: If he will take it, so, if not, adieu,
SHYLOCK: And, for my love, I pray you wrong me not.
ANTONIO: Yes Shylock, I will seal unto this bond.
SHYLOCK: Then meet me forthwith at the notary's,
SHYLOCK: Give him direction for this merry bond,
SHYLOCK: And I will go and purse the ducats straight,
SHYLOCK: See to my house, left in the fearful guard
SHYLOCK: Of an unthrifty knave, and presently
SHYLOCK: I will be with you.
ANTONIO: Hie thee, gentle Jew.
NARRATOR: Exit Shylock
ANTONIO: The Hebrew will turn Christian: he grows kind.
BASSANIO: I like not fair terms and a villain's mind.
ANTONIO: Come on: in this there can be no dismay,
ANTONIO: My ships come home a month before the day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Enter the PRINCE OF MOROCCO  and his train, PORTIA, NERISSA, and others attending
MOROCCO: Mislike me not for my complexion,
MOROCCO: The shadow'd livery of the burnish'd sun,
MOROCCO: To whom I am a neighbour and near bred.
MOROCCO: Bring me the fairest creature northward born,
MOROCCO: Where Phoebus' fire scarce thaws the icicles,
MOROCCO: And let us make incision for your love,
MOROCCO: To prove whose blood is reddest, his or mine.
MOROCCO: I tell thee, lady, this aspect of mine
MOROCCO: Hath fear'd the valiant: by my love I swear
MOROCCO: The best-regarded virgins of our clime
MOROCCO: Have loved it too: I would not change this hue,
MOROCCO: Except to steal your thoughts, my gentle queen.
PORTIA: In terms of choice I am not solely led
PORTIA: By nice direction of a maiden's eyes,
PORTIA: Besides, the lottery of my destiny
PORTIA: Bars me the right of voluntary choosing:
PORTIA: But if my father had not scanted me
PORTIA: And hedged me by his wit, to yield myself
PORTIA: His wife who wins me by that means I told you,
PORTIA: Yourself, renowned prince, then stood as fair
PORTIA: As any comer I have look'd on yet
PORTIA: For my affection.
MOROCCO: Even for that I thank you:
MOROCCO: Therefore, I pray you, lead me to the caskets
MOROCCO: To try my fortune. By this scimitar
MOROCCO: That slew the Sophy and a Persian prince
MOROCCO: That won three fields of Sultan Solyman,
MOROCCO: I would outstare the sternest eyes that look,
MOROCCO: Outbrave the heart most daring on the earth,
MOROCCO: Pluck the young sucking cubs from the she-bear,
MOROCCO: Yea, mock the lion when he roars for prey,
MOROCCO: To win thee, lady. But, alas the while!
MOROCCO: If Hercules and Lichas play at dice
MOROCCO: Which is the better man, the greater throw
MOROCCO: May turn by fortune from the weaker hand:
MOROCCO: So is Alcides beaten by his page,
MOROCCO: And so may I, blind fortune leading me,
MOROCCO: Miss that which one unworthier may attain,
MOROCCO: And die with grieving.
PORTIA: You must take your chance,
PORTIA: And either not attempt to choose at all
PORTIA: Or swear before you choose, if you choose wrong
PORTIA: Never to speak to lady afterward
PORTIA: In way of marriage: therefore be advised.
MOROCCO: Nor will not. Come, bring me unto my chance.
PORTIA: First, forward to the temple: after dinner
PORTIA: Your hazard shall be made.
MOROCCO: Good fortune then!
MOROCCO: To make me blest or cursed'st among men.
NARRATOR: Cornets, and exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter LAUNCELOT
LAUNCELOT: Certainly my conscience will serve me to run from
LAUNCELOT: this Jew my master. The fiend is at mine elbow and
LAUNCELOT: tempts me saying to me 'Gobbo, Launcelot Gobbo, good
LAUNCELOT: Launcelot,' or 'good Gobbo,' or good Launcelot
LAUNCELOT: Gobbo, use your legs, take the start, run away. My
LAUNCELOT: conscience says 'No, take heed,' honest Launcelot,
LAUNCELOT: take heed, honest Gobbo, or, as aforesaid, 'honest
LAUNCELOT: Launcelot Gobbo, do not run, scorn running with thy
LAUNCELOT: heels.' Well, the most courageous fiend bids me
LAUNCELOT: pack: 'Via!' says the fiend, 'away!' says the
LAUNCELOT: fiend, 'for the heavens, rouse up a brave mind,'
LAUNCELOT: says the fiend, 'and run.' Well, my conscience,
LAUNCELOT: hanging about the neck of my heart, says very wisely
LAUNCELOT: to me 'My honest friend Launcelot, being an honest
LAUNCELOT: man's son,' or rather an honest woman's son, for,
LAUNCELOT: indeed, my father did something smack, something
LAUNCELOT: grow to, he had a kind of taste, well, my conscience
LAUNCELOT: says 'Launcelot, budge not.' 'Budge,' says the
LAUNCELOT: fiend. 'Budge not,' says my conscience.
LAUNCELOT: 'Conscience,' say I, 'you counsel well,' ' Fiend,'
LAUNCELOT: say I, 'you counsel well:' to be ruled by my
LAUNCELOT: conscience, I should stay with the Jew my master,
LAUNCELOT: who, God bless the mark, is a kind of devil, and, to
LAUNCELOT: run away from the Jew, I should be ruled by the
LAUNCELOT: fiend, who, saving your reverence, is the devil
LAUNCELOT: himself. Certainly the Jew is the very devil
LAUNCELOT: incarnal, and, in my conscience, my conscience is
LAUNCELOT: but a kind of hard conscience, to offer to counsel
LAUNCELOT: me to stay with the Jew. The fiend gives the more
LAUNCELOT: friendly counsel: I will run, fiend, my heels are
LAUNCELOT: at your command, I will run.
NARRATOR: Enter Old GOBBO, with a basket
GOBBO: Master young man, you, I pray you, which is the way
GOBBO: to master Jew's?
LAUNCELOT: [Aside]  O heavens, this is my true-begotten father!
LAUNCELOT: who, being more than sand-blind, high-gravel blind,
LAUNCELOT: knows me not: I will try confusions with him.
GOBBO: Master young gentleman, I pray you, which is the way
GOBBO: to master Jew's?
LAUNCELOT: Turn up on your right hand at the next turning, but,
LAUNCELOT: at the next turning of all, on your left, marry, at
LAUNCELOT: the very next turning, turn of no hand, but turn
LAUNCELOT: down indirectly to the Jew's house.
GOBBO: By God's sonties, 'twill be a hard way to hit. Can
GOBBO: you tell me whether one Launcelot,
GOBBO: that dwells with him, dwell with him or no?
LAUNCELOT: Talk you of young Master Launcelot?
NARRATOR: Aside
LAUNCELOT: Mark me now, now will I raise the waters. Talk you
LAUNCELOT: of young Master Launcelot?
GOBBO: No master, sir, but a poor man's son: his father,
GOBBO: though I say it, is an honest exceeding poor man
GOBBO: and, God be thanked, well to live.
LAUNCELOT: Well, let his father be what a' will, we talk of
LAUNCELOT: young Master Launcelot.
GOBBO: Your worship's friend and Launcelot, sir.
LAUNCELOT: But I pray you, ergo, old man, ergo, I beseech you,
LAUNCELOT: talk you of young Master Launcelot?
GOBBO: Of Launcelot, an't please your mastership.
LAUNCELOT: Ergo, Master Launcelot. Talk not of Master
LAUNCELOT: Launcelot, father, for the young gentleman,
LAUNCELOT: according to Fates and Destinies and such odd
LAUNCELOT: sayings, the Sisters Three and such branches of
LAUNCELOT: learning, is indeed deceased, or, as you would say
LAUNCELOT: in plain terms, gone to heaven.
GOBBO: Marry, God forbid! the boy was the very staff of my
GOBBO: age, my very prop.
LAUNCELOT: Do I look like a cudgel or a hovel-post, a staff or
LAUNCELOT: a prop? Do you know me, father?
GOBBO: Alack the day, I know you not, young gentleman:
GOBBO: but, I pray you, tell me, is my boy, God rest his
GOBBO: soul, alive or dead?
LAUNCELOT: Do you not know me, father?
GOBBO: Alack, sir, I am sand-blind, I know you not.
LAUNCELOT: Nay, indeed, if you had your eyes, you might fail of
LAUNCELOT: the knowing me: it is a wise father that knows his
LAUNCELOT: own child. Well, old man, I will tell you news of
LAUNCELOT: your son: give me your blessing: truth will come
LAUNCELOT: to light, murder cannot be hid long, a man's son
LAUNCELOT: may, but at the length truth will out.
GOBBO: Pray you, sir, stand up: I am sure you are not
GOBBO: Launcelot, my boy.
LAUNCELOT: Pray you, let's have no more fooling about it, but
LAUNCELOT: give me your blessing: I am Launcelot, your boy
LAUNCELOT: that was, your son that is, your child that shall
LAUNCELOT: be.
GOBBO: I cannot think you are my son.
LAUNCELOT: I know not what I shall think of that: but I am
LAUNCELOT: Launcelot, the Jew's man, and I am sure Margery your
LAUNCELOT: wife is my mother.
GOBBO: Her name is Margery, indeed: I'll be sworn, if thou
GOBBO: be Launcelot, thou art mine own flesh and blood.
GOBBO: Lord worshipped might he be! what a beard hast thou
GOBBO: got! thou hast got more hair on thy chin than
GOBBO: Dobbin my fill-horse has on his tail.
LAUNCELOT: It should seem, then, that Dobbin's tail grows
LAUNCELOT: backward: I am sure he had more hair of his tail
LAUNCELOT: than I have of my face when I last saw him.
GOBBO: Lord, how art thou changed! How dost thou and thy
GOBBO: master agree? I have brought him a present. How
GOBBO: 'gree you now?
LAUNCELOT: Well, well: but, for mine own part, as I have set
LAUNCELOT: up my rest to run away, so I will not rest till I
LAUNCELOT: have run some ground. My master's a very Jew: give
LAUNCELOT: him a present! give him a halter: I am famished in
LAUNCELOT: his service, you may tell every finger I have with
LAUNCELOT: my ribs. Father, I am glad you are come: give me
LAUNCELOT: your present to one Master Bassanio, who, indeed,
LAUNCELOT: gives rare new liveries: if I serve not him, I
LAUNCELOT: will run as far as God has any ground. O rare
LAUNCELOT: fortune! here comes the man: to him, father, for I
LAUNCELOT: am a Jew, if I serve the Jew any longer.
NARRATOR: Enter BASSANIO, with LEONARDO and other followers
BASSANIO: You may do so, but let it be so hasted that supper
BASSANIO: be ready at the farthest by five of the clock. See
BASSANIO: these letters delivered, put the liveries to making,
BASSANIO: and desire Gratiano to come anon to my lodging.
NARRATOR: Exit a Servant
LAUNCELOT: To him, father.
GOBBO: God bless your worship!
BASSANIO: Gramercy! wouldst thou aught with me?
GOBBO: Here's my son, sir, a poor boy,--
LAUNCELOT: Not a poor boy, sir, but the rich Jew's man, that
LAUNCELOT: would, sir, as my father shall specify--
GOBBO: He hath a great infection, sir, as one would say, to serve--
LAUNCELOT: Indeed, the short and the long is, I serve the Jew,
LAUNCELOT: and have a desire, as my father shall specify--
GOBBO: His master and he, saving your worship's reverence,
GOBBO: are scarce cater-cousins--
LAUNCELOT: To be brief, the very truth is that the Jew, having
LAUNCELOT: done me wrong, doth cause me, as my father, being, I
LAUNCELOT: hope, an old man, shall frutify unto you--
GOBBO: I have here a dish of doves that I would bestow upon
GOBBO: your worship, and my suit is--
LAUNCELOT: In very brief, the suit is impertinent to myself, as
LAUNCELOT: your worship shall know by this honest old man, and,
LAUNCELOT: though I say it, though old man, yet poor man, my father.
BASSANIO: One speak for both. What would you?
LAUNCELOT: Serve you, sir.
GOBBO: That is the very defect of the matter, sir.
BASSANIO: I know thee well, thou hast obtain'd thy suit:
BASSANIO: Shylock thy master spoke with me this day,
BASSANIO: And hath preferr'd thee, if it be preferment
BASSANIO: To leave a rich Jew's service, to become
BASSANIO: The follower of so poor a gentleman.
LAUNCELOT: The old proverb is very well parted between my
LAUNCELOT: master Shylock and you, sir: you have the grace of
LAUNCELOT: God, sir, and he hath enough.
BASSANIO: Thou speak'st it well. Go, father, with thy son.
BASSANIO: Take leave of thy old master and inquire
BASSANIO: My lodging out. Give him a livery
BASSANIO: More guarded than his fellows': see it done.
LAUNCELOT: Father, in. I cannot get a service, no, I have
LAUNCELOT: ne'er a tongue in my head. Well, if any man in
LAUNCELOT: Italy have a fairer table which doth offer to swear
LAUNCELOT: upon a book, I shall have good fortune. Go to,
LAUNCELOT: here's a simple line of life: here's a small trifle
LAUNCELOT: of wives: alas, fifteen wives is nothing! eleven
LAUNCELOT: widows and nine maids is a simple coming-in for one
LAUNCELOT: man: and then to 'scape drowning thrice, and to be
LAUNCELOT: in peril of my life with the edge of a feather-bed,
LAUNCELOT: here are simple scapes. Well, if Fortune be a
LAUNCELOT: woman, she's a good wench for this gear. Father,
LAUNCELOT: come, I'll take my leave of the Jew in the twinkling of an eye.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Launcelot and Old Gobbo
BASSANIO: I pray thee, good Leonardo, think on this:
BASSANIO: These things being bought and orderly bestow'd,
BASSANIO: Return in haste, for I do feast to-night
BASSANIO: My best-esteem'd acquaintance: hie thee, go.
LEONARDO: My best endeavours shall be done herein.
NARRATOR: Enter GRATIANO
GRATIANO: Where is your master?
LEONARDO: Yonder, sir, he walks.
NARRATOR: Exit
GRATIANO: Signior Bassanio!
BASSANIO: Gratiano!
GRATIANO: I have a suit to you.
BASSANIO: You have obtain'd it.
GRATIANO: You must not deny me: I must go with you to Belmont.
BASSANIO: Why then you must. But hear thee, Gratiano,
BASSANIO: Thou art too wild, too rude and bold of voice,
BASSANIO: Parts that become thee happily enough
BASSANIO: And in such eyes as ours appear not faults,
BASSANIO: But where thou art not known, why, there they show
BASSANIO: Something too liberal. Pray thee, take pain
BASSANIO: To allay with some cold drops of modesty
BASSANIO: Thy skipping spirit, lest through thy wild behavior
BASSANIO: I be misconstrued in the place I go to,
BASSANIO: And lose my hopes.
GRATIANO: Signior Bassanio, hear me:
GRATIANO: If I do not put on a sober habit,
GRATIANO: Talk with respect and swear but now and then,
GRATIANO: Wear prayer-books in my pocket, look demurely,
GRATIANO: Nay more, while grace is saying, hood mine eyes
GRATIANO: Thus with my hat, and sigh and say 'amen,'
GRATIANO: Use all the observance of civility,
GRATIANO: Like one well studied in a sad ostent
GRATIANO: To please his grandam, never trust me more.
BASSANIO: Well, we shall see your bearing.
GRATIANO: Nay, but I bar to-night: you shall not gauge me
GRATIANO: By what we do to-night.
BASSANIO: No, that were pity:
BASSANIO: I would entreat you rather to put on
BASSANIO: Your boldest suit of mirth, for we have friends
BASSANIO: That purpose merriment. But fare you well:
BASSANIO: I have some business.
GRATIANO: And I must to Lorenzo and the rest:
GRATIANO: But we will visit you at supper-time.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. A room in SHYLOCK'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter JESSICA and LAUNCELOT
JESSICA: I am sorry thou wilt leave my father so:
JESSICA: Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil,
JESSICA: Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
JESSICA: But fare thee well, there is a ducat for thee:
JESSICA: And, Launcelot, soon at supper shalt thou see
JESSICA: Lorenzo, who is thy new master's guest:
JESSICA: Give him this letter, do it secretly,
JESSICA: And so farewell: I would not have my father
JESSICA: See me in talk with thee.
LAUNCELOT: Adieu! tears exhibit my tongue. Most beautiful
LAUNCELOT: pagan, most sweet Jew! if a Christian did not play
LAUNCELOT: the knave and get thee, I am much deceived. But,
LAUNCELOT: adieu: these foolish drops do something drown my
LAUNCELOT: manly spirit: adieu.
JESSICA: Farewell, good Launcelot.
NARRATOR: Exit Launcelot
JESSICA: Alack, what heinous sin is it in me
JESSICA: To be ashamed to be my father's child!
JESSICA: But though I am a daughter to his blood,
JESSICA: I am not to his manners. O Lorenzo,
JESSICA: If thou keep promise, I shall end this strife,
JESSICA: Become a Christian and thy loving wife.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter GRATIANO, LORENZO, SALARINO, and SALANIO
LORENZO: Nay, we will slink away in supper-time,
LORENZO: Disguise us at my lodging and return,
LORENZO: All in an hour.
GRATIANO: We have not made good preparation.
SALARINO: We have not spoke us yet of torchbearers.
SALANIO: 'Tis vile, unless it may be quaintly order'd,
SALANIO: And better in my mind not undertook.
LORENZO: 'Tis now but four o'clock: we have two hours
LORENZO: To furnish us.
NARRATOR: Enter LAUNCELOT, with a letter
LORENZO: Friend Launcelot, what's the news?
LAUNCELOT: An it shall please you to break up
LAUNCELOT: this, it shall seem to signify.
LORENZO: I know the hand: in faith, 'tis a fair hand,
LORENZO: And whiter than the paper it writ on
LORENZO: Is the fair hand that writ.
GRATIANO: Love-news, in faith.
LAUNCELOT: By your leave, sir.
LORENZO: Whither goest thou?
LAUNCELOT: Marry, sir, to bid my old master the
LAUNCELOT: Jew to sup to-night with my new master the Christian.
LORENZO: Hold here, take this: tell gentle Jessica
LORENZO: I will not fail her, speak it privately.
LORENZO: Go, gentlemen,
NARRATOR: Exit Launcelot
LORENZO: Will you prepare you for this masque tonight?
LORENZO: I am provided of a torch-bearer.
SALANIO: Ay, marry, I'll be gone about it straight.
SALANIO: And so will I.
LORENZO: Meet me and Gratiano
LORENZO: At Gratiano's lodging some hour hence.
SALARINO: 'Tis good we do so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt SALARINO and SALANIO
GRATIANO: Was not that letter from fair Jessica?
LORENZO: I must needs tell thee all. She hath directed
LORENZO: How I shall take her from her father's house,
LORENZO: What gold and jewels she is furnish'd with,
LORENZO: What page's suit she hath in readiness.
LORENZO: If e'er the Jew her father come to heaven,
LORENZO: It will be for his gentle daughter's sake:
LORENZO: And never dare misfortune cross her foot,
LORENZO: Unless she do it under this excuse,
LORENZO: That she is issue to a faithless Jew.
LORENZO: Come, go with me, peruse this as thou goest:
LORENZO: Fair Jessica shall be my torch-beare r.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same. Before SHYLOCK'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter SHYLOCK and LAUNCELOT
SHYLOCK: Well, thou shalt see, thy eyes shall be thy judge,
SHYLOCK: The difference of old Shylock and Bassanio:--
SHYLOCK: What, Jessica!--thou shalt not gormandise,
SHYLOCK: As thou hast done with me:--What, Jessica!--
SHYLOCK: And sleep and snore, and rend apparel out,--
SHYLOCK: Why, Jessica, I say!
LAUNCELOT: Why, Jessica!
SHYLOCK: Who bids thee call? I do not bid thee call.
LAUNCELOT: Your worship was wont to tell me that
LAUNCELOT: I could do nothing without bidding.
NARRATOR: Enter Jessica
JESSICA: Call you? what is your will?
SHYLOCK: I am bid forth to supper, Jessica:
SHYLOCK: There are my keys. But wherefore should I go?
SHYLOCK: I am not bid for love, they flatter me:
SHYLOCK: But yet I'll go in hate, to feed upon
SHYLOCK: The prodigal Christian. Jessica, my girl,
SHYLOCK: Look to my house. I am right loath to go:
SHYLOCK: There is some ill a-brewing towards my rest,
SHYLOCK: For I did dream of money-bags to-night.
LAUNCELOT: I beseech you, sir, go: my young master doth expect
LAUNCELOT: your reproach.
SHYLOCK: So do I his.
LAUNCELOT: An they have conspired together, I will not say you
LAUNCELOT: shall see a masque, but if you do, then it was not
LAUNCELOT: for nothing that my nose fell a-bleeding on
LAUNCELOT: Black-Monday last at six o'clock i' the morning,
LAUNCELOT: falling out that year on Ash-Wednesday was four
LAUNCELOT: year, in the afternoon.
SHYLOCK: What, are there masques? Hear you me, Jessica:
SHYLOCK: Lock up my doors, and when you hear the drum
SHYLOCK: And the vile squealing of the wry-neck'd fife,
SHYLOCK: Clamber not you up to the casements then,
SHYLOCK: Nor thrust your head into the public street
SHYLOCK: To gaze on Christian fools with varnish'd faces,
SHYLOCK: But stop my house's ears, I mean my casements:
SHYLOCK: Let not the sound of shallow foppery enter
SHYLOCK: My sober house. By Jacob's staff, I swear,
SHYLOCK: I have no mind of feasting forth to-night:
SHYLOCK: But I will go. Go you before me, sirrah,
SHYLOCK: Say I will come.
LAUNCELOT: I will go before, sir. Mistress, look out at
LAUNCELOT: window, for all this, There will come a Christian
LAUNCELOT: boy, will be worth a Jewess' eye.
NARRATOR: Exit
SHYLOCK: What says that fool of Hagar's offspring, ha?
JESSICA: His words were 'Farewell mistress,' nothing else.
SHYLOCK: The patch is kind enough, but a huge feeder,
SHYLOCK: Snail-slow in profit, and he sleeps by day
SHYLOCK: More than the wild-cat: drones hive not with me,
SHYLOCK: Therefore I part with him, and part with him
SHYLOCK: To one that would have him help to waste
SHYLOCK: His borrow'd purse. Well, Jessica, go in,
SHYLOCK: Perhaps I will return immediately:
SHYLOCK: Do as I bid you, shut doors after you:
SHYLOCK: Fast bind, fast find,
SHYLOCK: A proverb never stale in thrifty mind.
NARRATOR: Exit
JESSICA: Farewell, and if my fortune be not crost,
JESSICA: I have a father, you a daughter, lost.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter GRATIANO and SALARINO, masqued
GRATIANO: This is the pent-house under which Lorenzo
GRATIANO: Desired us to make stand.
SALARINO: His hour is almost past.
GRATIANO: And it is marvel he out-dwells his hour,
GRATIANO: For lovers ever run before the clock.
SALARINO: O, ten times faster Venus' pigeons fly
SALARINO: To seal love's bonds new-made, than they are wont
SALARINO: To keep obliged faith unforfeited!
GRATIANO: That ever holds: who riseth from a feast
GRATIANO: With that keen appetite that he sits down?
GRATIANO: Where is the horse that doth untread again
GRATIANO: His tedious measures with the unbated fire
GRATIANO: That he did pace them first? All things that are,
GRATIANO: Are with more spirit chased than enjoy'd.
GRATIANO: How like a younker or a prodigal
GRATIANO: The scarfed bark puts from her native bay,
GRATIANO: Hugg'd and embraced by the strumpet wind!
GRATIANO: How like the prodigal doth she return,
GRATIANO: With over-weather'd ribs and ragged sails,
GRATIANO: Lean, rent and beggar'd by the strumpet wind!
SALARINO: Here comes Lorenzo: more of this hereafter.
NARRATOR: Enter LORENZO
LORENZO: Sweet friends, your patience for my long abode,
LORENZO: Not I, but my affairs, have made you wait:
LORENZO: When you shall please to play the thieves for wives,
LORENZO: I'll watch as long for you then. Approach,
LORENZO: Here dwells my father Jew. Ho! who's within?
NARRATOR: Enter JESSICA, above, in boy's clothes
JESSICA: Who are you? Tell me, for more certainty,
JESSICA: Albeit I'll swear that I do know your tongue.
LORENZO: Lorenzo, and thy love.
JESSICA: Lorenzo, certain, and my love indeed,
JESSICA: For who love I so much? And now who knows
JESSICA: But you, Lorenzo, whether I am yours?
LORENZO: Heaven and thy thoughts are witness that thou art.
JESSICA: Here, catch this casket, it is worth the pains.
JESSICA: I am glad 'tis night, you do not look on me,
JESSICA: For I am much ashamed of my exchange:
JESSICA: But love is blind and lovers cannot see
JESSICA: The pretty follies that themselves commit,
JESSICA: For if they could, Cupid himself would blush
JESSICA: To see me thus transformed to a boy.
LORENZO: Descend, for you must be my torchbearer.
JESSICA: What, must I hold a candle to my shames?
JESSICA: They in themselves, good-sooth, are too too light.
JESSICA: Why, 'tis an office of discovery, love,
JESSICA: And I should be obscured.
LORENZO: So are you, sweet,
LORENZO: Even in the lovely garnish of a boy.
LORENZO: But come at once,
LORENZO: For the close night doth play the runaway,
LORENZO: And we are stay'd for at Bassanio's feast.
JESSICA: I will make fast the doors, and gild myself
JESSICA: With some more ducats, and be with you straight.
NARRATOR: Exit above
GRATIANO: Now, by my hood, a Gentile and no Jew.
LORENZO: Beshrew me but I love her heartily,
LORENZO: For she is wise, if I can judge of her,
LORENZO: And fair she is, if that mine eyes be true,
LORENZO: And true she is, as she hath proved herself,
LORENZO: And therefore, like herself, wise, fair and true,
LORENZO: Shall she be placed in my constant soul.
NARRATOR: Enter JESSICA, below
LORENZO: What, art thou come? On, gentlemen, away!
LORENZO: Our masquing mates by this time for us stay.
NARRATOR: Exit with Jessica and Salarino
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO
ANTONIO: Who's there?
GRATIANO: Signior Antonio!
ANTONIO: Fie, fie, Gratiano! where are all the rest?
ANTONIO: 'Tis nine o'clock: our friends all stay for you.
ANTONIO: No masque to-night: the wind is come about,
ANTONIO: Bassanio presently will go aboard:
ANTONIO: I have sent twenty out to seek for you.
GRATIANO: I am glad on't: I desire no more delight
GRATIANO: Than to be under sail and gone to-night.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Enter PORTIA, with the PRINCE OF MOROCCO, and their trains
PORTIA: Go draw aside the curtains and discover
PORTIA: The several caskets to this noble prince.
PORTIA: Now make your choice.
MOROCCO: The first, of gold, who this inscription bears,
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire,'
MOROCCO: The second, silver, which this promise carries,
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves,'
MOROCCO: This third, dull lead, with warning all as blunt,
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath.'
MOROCCO: How shall I know if I do choose the right?
PORTIA: The one of them contains my picture, prince:
PORTIA: If you choose that, then I am yours withal.
MOROCCO: Some god direct my judgment! Let me see,
MOROCCO: I will survey the inscriptions back again.
MOROCCO: What says this leaden casket?
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath.'
MOROCCO: Must give: for what? for lead? hazard for lead?
MOROCCO: This casket threatens. Men that hazard all
MOROCCO: Do it in hope of fair advantages:
MOROCCO: A golden mind stoops not to shows of dross,
MOROCCO: I'll then nor give nor hazard aught for lead.
MOROCCO: What says the silver with her virgin hue?
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves.'
MOROCCO: As much as he deserves! Pause there, Morocco,
MOROCCO: And weigh thy value with an even hand:
MOROCCO: If thou be'st rated by thy estimation,
MOROCCO: Thou dost deserve enough, and yet enough
MOROCCO: May not extend so far as to the lady:
MOROCCO: And yet to be afeard of my deserving
MOROCCO: Were but a weak disabling of myself.
MOROCCO: As much as I deserve! Why, that's the lady:
MOROCCO: I do in birth deserve her, and in fortunes,
MOROCCO: In graces and in qualities of breeding,
MOROCCO: But more than these, in love I do deserve.
MOROCCO: What if I stray'd no further, but chose here?
MOROCCO: Let's see once more this saying graved in gold
MOROCCO: 'Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire.'
MOROCCO: Why, that's the lady, all the world desires her,
MOROCCO: From the four corners of the earth they come,
MOROCCO: To kiss this shrine, this mortal-breathing saint:
MOROCCO: The Hyrcanian deserts and the vasty wilds
MOROCCO: Of wide Arabia are as thoroughfares now
MOROCCO: For princes to come view fair Portia:
MOROCCO: The watery kingdom, whose ambitious head
MOROCCO: Spits in the face of heaven, is no bar
MOROCCO: To stop the foreign spirits, but they come,
MOROCCO: As o'er a brook, to see fair Portia.
MOROCCO: One of these three contains her heavenly picture.
MOROCCO: Is't like that lead contains her? 'Twere damnation
MOROCCO: To think so base a thought: it were too gross
MOROCCO: To rib her cerecloth in the obscure grave.
MOROCCO: Or shall I think in silver she's immured,
MOROCCO: Being ten times undervalued to tried gold?
MOROCCO: O sinful thought! Never so rich a gem
MOROCCO: Was set in worse than gold. They have in England
MOROCCO: A coin that bears the figure of an angel
MOROCCO: Stamped in gold, but that's insculp'd upon,
MOROCCO: But here an angel in a golden bed
MOROCCO: Lies all within. Deliver me the key:
MOROCCO: Here do I choose, and thrive I as I may!
PORTIA: There, take it, prince, and if my form lie there,
PORTIA: Then I am yours.
NARRATOR: He unlocks the golden casket
MOROCCO: O hell! what have we here?
MOROCCO: A carrion Death, within whose empty eye
MOROCCO: There is a written scroll! I'll read the writing.
NARRATOR: Reads
MOROCCO: All that glitters is not gold,
MOROCCO: Often have you heard that told:
MOROCCO: Many a man his life hath sold
MOROCCO: But my outside to behold:
MOROCCO: Gilded tombs do worms enfold.
MOROCCO: Had you been as wise as bold,
MOROCCO: Young in limbs, in judgment old,
MOROCCO: Your answer had not been inscroll'd:
MOROCCO: Fare you well, your suit is cold.
MOROCCO: Cold, indeed, and labour lost:
MOROCCO: Then, farewell, heat, and welcome, frost!
MOROCCO: Portia, adieu. I have too grieved a heart
MOROCCO: To take a tedious leave: thus losers part.
NARRATOR: Exit with his train. Flourish of cornets
PORTIA: A gentle riddance. Draw the curtains, go.
PORTIA: Let all of his complexion choose me so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter SALARINO and SALANIO
SALARINO: Why, man, I saw Bassanio under sail:
SALARINO: With him is Gratiano gone along,
SALARINO: And in their ship I am sure Lorenzo is not.
SALANIO: The villain Jew with outcries raised the duke,
SALANIO: Who went with him to search Bassanio's ship.
SALARINO: He came too late, the ship was under sail:
SALARINO: But there the duke was given to understand
SALARINO: That in a gondola were seen together
SALARINO: Lorenzo and his amorous Jessica:
SALARINO: Besides, Antonio certified the duke
SALARINO: They were not with Bassanio in his ship.
SALANIO: I never heard a passion so confused,
SALANIO: So strange, outrageous, and so variable,
SALANIO: As the dog Jew did utter in the streets:
SALANIO: 'My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!
SALANIO: Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats!
SALANIO: Justice! the law! my ducats, and my daughter!
SALANIO: A sealed bag, two sealed bags of ducats,
SALANIO: Of double ducats, stolen from me by my daughter!
SALANIO: And jewels, two stones, two rich and precious stones,
SALANIO: Stolen by my daughter! Justice! find the girl,
SALANIO: She hath the stones upon her, and the ducats.'
SALARINO: Why, all the boys in Venice follow him,
SALARINO: Crying, his stones, his daughter, and his ducats.
SALANIO: Let good Antonio look he keep his day,
SALANIO: Or he shall pay for this.
SALARINO: Marry, well remember'd.
SALARINO: I reason'd with a Frenchman yesterday,
SALARINO: Who told me, in the narrow seas that part
SALARINO: The French and English, there miscarried
SALARINO: A vessel of our country richly fraught:
SALARINO: I thought upon Antonio when he told me,
SALARINO: And wish'd in silence that it were not his.
SALANIO: You were best to tell Antonio what you hear,
SALANIO: Yet do not suddenly, for it may grieve him.
SALARINO: A kinder gentleman treads not the earth.
SALARINO: I saw Bassanio and Antonio part:
SALARINO: Bassanio told him he would make some speed
SALARINO: Of his return: he answer'd, 'Do not so,
SALARINO: Slubber not business for my sake, Bassanio
SALARINO: But stay the very riping of the time,
SALARINO: And for the Jew's bond which he hath of me,
SALARINO: Let it not enter in your mind of love:
SALARINO: Be merry, and employ your chiefest thoughts
SALARINO: To courtship and such fair ostents of love
SALARINO: As shall conveniently become you there:'
SALARINO: And even there, his eye being big with tears,
SALARINO: Turning his face, he put his hand behind him,
SALARINO: And with affection wondrous sensible
SALARINO: He wrung Bassanio's hand, and so they parted.
SALANIO: I think he only loves the world for him.
SALANIO: I pray thee, let us go and find him out
SALANIO: And quicken his embraced heaviness
SALANIO: With some delight or other.
SALARINO: Do we so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter NERISSA with a Servitor
NERISSA: Quick, quick, I pray thee, draw the curtain straight:
NERISSA: The Prince of Arragon hath ta'en his oath,
NERISSA: And comes to his election presently.
NARRATOR: Flourish of cornets. Enter the PRINCE OF ARRAGON, PORTIA, and their trains
PORTIA: Behold, there stand the caskets, noble prince:
PORTIA: If you choose that wherein I am contain'd,
PORTIA: Straight shall our nuptial rites be solemnized:
PORTIA: But if you fail, without more speech, my lord,
PORTIA: You must be gone from hence immediately.
ARRAGON: I am enjoin'd by oath to observe three things:
ARRAGON: First, never to unfold to any one
ARRAGON: Which casket 'twas I chose, next, if I fail
ARRAGON: Of the right casket, never in my life
ARRAGON: To woo a maid in way of marriage: Lastly,
ARRAGON: If I do fail in fortune of my choice,
ARRAGON: Immediately to leave you and be gone.
PORTIA: To these injunctions every one doth swear
PORTIA: That comes to hazard for my worthless self.
ARRAGON: And so have I address'd me. Fortune now
ARRAGON: To my heart's hope! Gold, silver, and base lead.
ARRAGON: 'Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath.'
ARRAGON: You shall look fairer, ere I give or hazard.
ARRAGON: What says the golden chest? ha! let me see:
ARRAGON: 'Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire.'
ARRAGON: What many men desire! that 'many' may be meant
ARRAGON: By the fool multitude, that choose by show,
ARRAGON: Not learning more than the fond eye doth teach,
ARRAGON: Which pries not to the interior, but, like the martlet,
ARRAGON: Builds in the weather on the outward wall,
ARRAGON: Even in the force and road of casualty.
ARRAGON: I will not choose what many men desire,
ARRAGON: Because I will not jump with common spirits
ARRAGON: And rank me with the barbarous multitudes.
ARRAGON: Why, then to thee, thou silver treasure-house,
ARRAGON: Tell me once more what title thou dost bear:
ARRAGON: 'Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves:'
ARRAGON: And well said too, for who shall go about
ARRAGON: To cozen fortune and be honourable
ARRAGON: Without the stamp of merit? Let none presume
ARRAGON: To wear an undeserved dignity.
ARRAGON: O, that estates, degrees and offices
ARRAGON: Were not derived corruptly, and that clear honour
ARRAGON: Were purchased by the merit of the wearer!
ARRAGON: How many then should cover that stand bare!
ARRAGON: How many be commanded that command!
ARRAGON: How much low peasantry would then be glean'd
ARRAGON: From the true seed of honour! and how much honour
ARRAGON: Pick'd from the chaff and ruin of the times
ARRAGON: To be new-varnish'd! Well, but to my choice:
ARRAGON: 'Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves.'
ARRAGON: I will assume desert. Give me a key for this,
ARRAGON: And instantly unlock my fortunes here.
NARRATOR: He opens the silver casket
PORTIA: Too long a pause for that which you find there.
ARRAGON: What's here? the portrait of a blinking idiot,
ARRAGON: Presenting me a schedule! I will read it.
ARRAGON: How much unlike art thou to Portia!
