ARRAGON: How much unlike my hopes and my deservings!
ARRAGON: 'Who chooseth me shall have as much as he deserves.'
ARRAGON: Did I deserve no more than a fool's head?
ARRAGON: Is that my prize? are my deserts no better?
PORTIA: To offend, and judge, are distinct offices
PORTIA: And of opposed natures.
ARRAGON: What is here?
NARRATOR: Reads
ARRAGON: The fire seven times tried this:
ARRAGON: Seven times tried that judgment is,
ARRAGON: That did never choose amiss.
ARRAGON: Some there be that shadows kiss,
ARRAGON: Such have but a shadow's bliss:
ARRAGON: There be fools alive, I wis,
ARRAGON: Silver'd o'er, and so was this.
ARRAGON: Take what wife you will to bed,
ARRAGON: I will ever be your head:
ARRAGON: So be gone: you are sped.
ARRAGON: Still more fool I shall appear
ARRAGON: By the time I linger here
ARRAGON: With one fool's head I came to woo,
ARRAGON: But I go away with two.
ARRAGON: Sweet, adieu. I'll keep my oath,
ARRAGON: Patiently to bear my wroth.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Arragon and train
PORTIA: Thus hath the candle singed the moth.
PORTIA: O, these deliberate fools! when they do choose,
PORTIA: They have the wisdom by their wit to lose.
NERISSA: The ancient saying is no heresy,
NERISSA: Hanging and wiving goes by destiny.
PORTIA: Come, draw the curtain, Nerissa.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: Where is my lady?
PORTIA: Here: what would my lord?
Servant: Madam, there is alighted at your gate
Servant: A young Venetian, one that comes before
Servant: To signify the approaching of his lord,
Servant: From whom he bringeth sensible regreets,
Servant: To wit, besides commends and courteous breath,
Servant: Gifts of rich value. Yet I have not seen
Servant: So likely an ambassador of love:
Servant: A day in April never came so sweet,
Servant: To show how costly summer was at hand,
Servant: As this fore-spurrer comes before his lord.
PORTIA: No more, I pray thee: I am half afeard
PORTIA: Thou wilt say anon he is some kin to thee,
PORTIA: Thou spend'st such high-day wit in praising him.
PORTIA: Come, come, Nerissa, for I long to see
PORTIA: Quick Cupid's post that comes so mannerly.
NERISSA: Bassanio, lord Love, if thy will it be!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter SALANIO and SALARINO
SALANIO: Now, what news on the Rialto?
SALARINO: Why, yet it lives there uncheck'd that Antonio hath
SALARINO: a ship of rich lading wrecked on the narrow seas,
SALARINO: the Goodwins, I think they call the place, a very
SALARINO: dangerous flat and fatal, where the carcasses of many
SALARINO: a tall ship lie buried, as they say, if my gossip
SALARINO: Report be an honest woman of her word.
SALANIO: I would she were as lying a gossip in that as ever
SALANIO: knapped ginger or made her neighbours believe she
SALANIO: wept for the death of a third husband. But it is
SALANIO: true, without any slips of prolixity or crossing the
SALANIO: plain highway of talk, that the good Antonio, the
SALANIO: honest Antonio,--O that I had a title good enough
SALANIO: to keep his name company!--
SALARINO: Come, the full stop.
SALANIO: Ha! what sayest thou? Why, the end is, he hath
SALANIO: lost a ship.
SALARINO: I would it might prove the end of his losses.
SALANIO: Let me say 'amen' betimes, lest the devil cross my
SALANIO: prayer, for here he comes in the likeness of a Jew.
NARRATOR: Enter SHYLOCK
SALANIO: How now, Shylock! what news among the merchants?
SHYLOCK: You know, none so well, none so well as you, of my
SHYLOCK: daughter's flight.
SALARINO: That's certain: I, for my part, knew the tailor
SALARINO: that made the wings she flew withal.
SALANIO: And Shylock, for his own part, knew the bird was
SALANIO: fledged, and then it is the complexion of them all
SALANIO: to leave the dam.
SHYLOCK: She is damned for it.
SALANIO: That's certain, if the devil may be her judge.
SHYLOCK: My own flesh and blood to rebel!
SALANIO: Out upon it, old carrion! rebels it at these years?
SHYLOCK: I say, my daughter is my flesh and blood.
SALARINO: There is more difference between thy flesh and hers
SALARINO: than between jet and ivory, more between your bloods
SALARINO: than there is between red wine and rhenish. But
SALARINO: tell us, do you hear whether Antonio have had any
SALARINO: loss at sea or no?
SHYLOCK: There I have another bad match: a bankrupt, a
SHYLOCK: prodigal, who dare scarce show his head on the
SHYLOCK: Rialto, a beggar, that was used to come so smug upon
SHYLOCK: the mart, let him look to his bond: he was wont to
SHYLOCK: call me usurer, let him look to his bond: he was
SHYLOCK: wont to lend money for a Christian courtesy, let him
SHYLOCK: look to his bond.
SALARINO: Why, I am sure, if he forfeit, thou wilt not take
SALARINO: his flesh: what's that good for?
SHYLOCK: To bait fish withal: if it will feed nothing else,
SHYLOCK: it will feed my revenge. He hath disgraced me, and
SHYLOCK: hindered me half a million, laughed at my losses,
SHYLOCK: mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my
SHYLOCK: bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine
SHYLOCK: enemies, and what's his reason? I am a Jew. Hath
SHYLOCK: not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs,
SHYLOCK: dimensions, senses, affections, passions? fed with
SHYLOCK: the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject
SHYLOCK: to the same diseases, healed by the same means,
SHYLOCK: warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer, as
SHYLOCK: a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed?
SHYLOCK: if you tickle us, do we not laugh? if you poison
SHYLOCK: us, do we not die? and if you wrong us, shall we not
SHYLOCK: revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will
SHYLOCK: resemble you in that. If a Jew wrong a Christian,
SHYLOCK: what is his humility? Revenge. If a Christian
SHYLOCK: wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by
SHYLOCK: Christian example? Why, revenge. The villany you
SHYLOCK: teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I
SHYLOCK: will better the instruction.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: Gentlemen, my master Antonio is at his house and
Servant: desires to speak with you both.
SALARINO: We have been up and down to seek him.
NARRATOR: Enter TUBAL
SALANIO: Here comes another of the tribe: a third cannot be
SALANIO: matched, unless the devil himself turn Jew.
NARRATOR: Exeunt SALANIO, SALARINO, and Servant
SHYLOCK: How now, Tubal! what news from Genoa? hast thou
SHYLOCK: found my daughter?
TUBAL: I often came where I did hear of her, but cannot find her.
SHYLOCK: Why, there, there, there, there! a diamond gone,
SHYLOCK: cost me two thousand ducats in Frankfort! The curse
SHYLOCK: never fell upon our nation till now, I never felt it
SHYLOCK: till now: two thousand ducats in that, and other
SHYLOCK: precious, precious jewels. I would my daughter
SHYLOCK: were dead at my foot, and the jewels in her ear!
SHYLOCK: would she were hearsed at my foot, and the ducats in
SHYLOCK: her coffin! No news of them? Why, so: and I know
SHYLOCK: not what's spent in the search: why, thou loss upon
SHYLOCK: loss! the thief gone with so much, and so much to
SHYLOCK: find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge:
SHYLOCK: nor no in luck stirring but what lights on my
SHYLOCK: shoulders, no sighs but of my breathing, no tears
SHYLOCK: but of my shedding.
TUBAL: Yes, other men have ill luck too: Antonio, as I
TUBAL: heard in Genoa,--
SHYLOCK: What, what, what? ill luck, ill luck?
TUBAL: Hath an argosy cast away, coming from Tripolis.
SHYLOCK: I thank God, I thank God. Is't true, is't true?
TUBAL: I spoke with some of the sailors that escaped the wreck.
SHYLOCK: I thank thee, good Tubal: good news, good news!
SHYLOCK: ha, ha! where? in Genoa?
TUBAL: Your daughter spent in Genoa, as I heard, in one
TUBAL: night fourscore ducats.
SHYLOCK: Thou stickest a dagger in me: I shall never see my
SHYLOCK: gold again: fourscore ducats at a sitting!
SHYLOCK: fourscore ducats!
TUBAL: There came divers of Antonio's creditors in my
TUBAL: company to Venice, that swear he cannot choose but break.
SHYLOCK: I am very glad of it: I'll plague him, I'll torture
SHYLOCK: him: I am glad of it.
TUBAL: One of them showed me a ring that he had of your
TUBAL: daughter for a monkey.
SHYLOCK: Out upon her! Thou torturest me, Tubal: it was my
SHYLOCK: turquoise, I had it of Leah when I was a bachelor:
SHYLOCK: I would not have given it for a wilderness of monkeys.
TUBAL: But Antonio is certainly undone.
SHYLOCK: Nay, that's true, that's very true. Go, Tubal, fee
SHYLOCK: me an officer, bespeak him a fortnight before. I
SHYLOCK: will have the heart of him, if he forfeit, for, were
SHYLOCK: he out of Venice, I can make what merchandise I
SHYLOCK: will. Go, go, Tubal, and meet me at our synagogue,
SHYLOCK: go, good Tubal, at our synagogue, Tubal.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter BASSANIO, PORTIA, GRATIANO, NERISSA, and Attendants
PORTIA: I pray you, tarry: pause a day or two
PORTIA: Before you hazard, for, in choosing wrong,
PORTIA: I lose your company: therefore forbear awhile.
PORTIA: There's something tells me, but it is not love,
PORTIA: I would not lose you, and you know yourself,
PORTIA: Hate counsels not in such a quality.
PORTIA: But lest you should not understand me well,--
PORTIA: And yet a maiden hath no tongue but thought,--
PORTIA: I would detain you here some month or two
PORTIA: Before you venture for me. I could teach you
PORTIA: How to choose right, but I am then forsworn,
PORTIA: So will I never be: so may you miss me,
PORTIA: But if you do, you'll make me wish a sin,
PORTIA: That I had been forsworn. Beshrew your eyes,
PORTIA: They have o'erlook'd me and divided me,
PORTIA: One half of me is yours, the other half yours,
PORTIA: Mine own, I would say, but if mine, then yours,
PORTIA: And so all yours. O, these naughty times
PORTIA: Put bars between the owners and their rights!
PORTIA: And so, though yours, not yours. Prove it so,
PORTIA: Let fortune go to hell for it, not I.
PORTIA: I speak too long, but 'tis to peize the time,
PORTIA: To eke it and to draw it out in length,
PORTIA: To stay you from election.
BASSANIO: Let me choose
BASSANIO: For as I am, I live upon the rack.
PORTIA: Upon the rack, Bassanio! then confess
PORTIA: What treason there is mingled with your love.
BASSANIO: None but that ugly treason of mistrust,
BASSANIO: Which makes me fear the enjoying of my love:
BASSANIO: There may as well be amity and life
BASSANIO: 'Tween snow and fire, as treason and my love.
PORTIA: Ay, but I fear you speak upon the rack,
PORTIA: Where men enforced do speak anything.
BASSANIO: Promise me life, and I'll confess the truth.
PORTIA: Well then, confess and live.
BASSANIO: 'Confess' and 'love'
BASSANIO: Had been the very sum of my confession:
BASSANIO: O happy torment, when my torturer
BASSANIO: Doth teach me answers for deliverance!
BASSANIO: But let me to my fortune and the caskets.
PORTIA: Away, then! I am lock'd in one of them:
PORTIA: If you do love me, you will find me out.
PORTIA: Nerissa and the rest, stand all aloof.
PORTIA: Let music sound while he doth make his choice,
PORTIA: Then, if he lose, he makes a swan-like end,
PORTIA: Fading in music: that the comparison
PORTIA: May stand more proper, my eye shall be the stream
PORTIA: And watery death-bed for him. He may win,
PORTIA: And what is music then? Then music is
PORTIA: Even as the flourish when true subjects bow
PORTIA: To a new-crowned monarch: such it is
PORTIA: As are those dulcet sounds in break of day
PORTIA: That creep into the dreaming bridegroom's ear,
PORTIA: And summon him to marriage. Now he goes,
PORTIA: With no less presence, but with much more love,
PORTIA: Than young Alcides, when he did redeem
PORTIA: The virgin tribute paid by howling Troy
PORTIA: To the sea-monster: I stand for sacrifice
PORTIA: The rest aloof are the Dardanian wives,
PORTIA: With bleared visages, come forth to view
PORTIA: The issue of the exploit. Go, Hercules!
PORTIA: Live thou, I live: with much, much more dismay
PORTIA: I view the fight than thou that makest the fray.
NARRATOR: Music, whilst BASSANIO comments on the caskets to himself
PORTIA: SONG.
PORTIA: Tell me where is fancy bred,
PORTIA: Or in the heart, or in the head?
PORTIA: How begot, how nourished?
PORTIA: Reply, reply.
PORTIA: It is engender'd in the eyes,
PORTIA: With gazing fed, and fancy dies
PORTIA: In the cradle where it lies.
PORTIA: Let us all ring fancy's knell
PORTIA: I'll begin it,--Ding, dong, bell.
ALL: Ding, dong, bell.
BASSANIO: So may the outward shows be least themselves:
BASSANIO: The world is still deceived with ornament.
BASSANIO: In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt,
BASSANIO: But, being seasoned with a gracious voice,
BASSANIO: Obscures the show of evil? In religion,
BASSANIO: What damned error, but some sober brow
BASSANIO: Will bless it and approve it with a text,
BASSANIO: Hiding the grossness with fair ornament?
BASSANIO: There is no vice so simple but assumes
BASSANIO: Some mark of virtue on his outward parts:
BASSANIO: How many cowards, whose hearts are all as false
BASSANIO: As stairs of sand, wear yet upon their chins
BASSANIO: The beards of Hercules and frowning Mars,
BASSANIO: Who, inward search'd, have livers white as milk,
BASSANIO: And these assume but valour's excrement
BASSANIO: To render them redoubted! Look on beauty,
BASSANIO: And you shall see 'tis purchased by the weight,
BASSANIO: Which therein works a miracle in nature,
BASSANIO: Making them lightest that wear most of it:
BASSANIO: So are those crisped snaky golden locks
BASSANIO: Which make such wanton gambols with the wind,
BASSANIO: Upon supposed fairness, often known
BASSANIO: To be the dowry of a second head,
BASSANIO: The skull that bred them in the sepulchre.
BASSANIO: Thus ornament is but the guiled shore
BASSANIO: To a most dangerous sea, the beauteous scarf
BASSANIO: Veiling an Indian beauty, in a word,
BASSANIO: The seeming truth which cunning times put on
BASSANIO: To entrap the wisest. Therefore, thou gaudy gold,
BASSANIO: Hard food for Midas, I will none of thee,
BASSANIO: Nor none of thee, thou pale and common drudge
BASSANIO: 'Tween man and man: but thou, thou meagre lead,
BASSANIO: Which rather threatenest than dost promise aught,
BASSANIO: Thy paleness moves me more than eloquence,
BASSANIO: And here choose I, joy be the consequence!
PORTIA: [Aside]  How all the other passions fleet to air,
PORTIA: As doubtful thoughts, and rash-embraced despair,
PORTIA: And shuddering fear, and green-eyed jealousy! O love,
PORTIA: Be moderate, allay thy ecstasy,
PORTIA: In measure rein thy joy, scant this excess.
PORTIA: I feel too much thy blessing: make it less,
PORTIA: For fear I surfeit.
BASSANIO: What find I here?
NARRATOR: Opening the leaden casket
BASSANIO: Fair Portia's counterfeit! What demi-god
BASSANIO: Hath come so near creation? Move these eyes?
BASSANIO: Or whether, riding on the balls of mine,
BASSANIO: Seem they in motion? Here are sever'd lips,
BASSANIO: Parted with sugar breath: so sweet a bar
BASSANIO: Should sunder such sweet friends. Here in her hairs
BASSANIO: The painter plays the spider and hath woven
BASSANIO: A golden mesh to entrap the hearts of men,
BASSANIO: Faster than gnats in cobwebs, but her eyes,--
BASSANIO: How could he see to do them? having made one,
BASSANIO: Methinks it should have power to steal both his
BASSANIO: And leave itself unfurnish'd. Yet look, how far
BASSANIO: The substance of my praise doth wrong this shadow
BASSANIO: In underprizing it, so far this shadow
BASSANIO: Doth limp behind the substance. Here's the scroll,
BASSANIO: The continent and summary of my fortune.
NARRATOR: Reads
BASSANIO: You that choose not by the view,
BASSANIO: Chance as fair and choose as true!
BASSANIO: Since this fortune falls to you,
BASSANIO: Be content and seek no new,
BASSANIO: If you be well pleased with this
BASSANIO: And hold your fortune for your bliss,
BASSANIO: Turn you where your lady is
BASSANIO: And claim her with a loving kiss.
BASSANIO: A gentle scroll. Fair lady, by your leave,
BASSANIO: I come by note, to give and to receive.
BASSANIO: Like one of two contending in a prize,
BASSANIO: That thinks he hath done well in people's eyes,
BASSANIO: Hearing applause and universal shout,
BASSANIO: Giddy in spirit, still gazing in a doubt
BASSANIO: Whether these pearls of praise be his or no,
BASSANIO: So, thrice fair lady, stand I, even so,
BASSANIO: As doubtful whether what I see be true,
BASSANIO: Until confirm'd, sign'd, ratified by you.
PORTIA: You see me, Lord Bassanio, where I stand,
PORTIA: Such as I am: though for myself alone
PORTIA: I would not be ambitious in my wish,
PORTIA: To wish myself much better, yet, for you
PORTIA: I would be trebled twenty times myself,
PORTIA: A thousand times more fair, ten thousand times more rich,
PORTIA: That only to stand high in your account,
PORTIA: I might in virtue, beauties, livings, friends,
PORTIA: Exceed account, but the full sum of me
PORTIA: Is sum of something, which, to term in gross,
PORTIA: Is an unlesson'd girl, unschool'd, unpractised,
PORTIA: Happy in this, she is not yet so old
PORTIA: But she may learn, happier than this,
PORTIA: She is not bred so dull but she can learn,
PORTIA: Happiest of all is that her gentle spirit
PORTIA: Commits itself to yours to be directed,
PORTIA: As from her lord, her governor, her king.
PORTIA: Myself and what is mine to you and yours
PORTIA: Is now converted: but now I was the lord
PORTIA: Of this fair mansion, master of my servants,
PORTIA: Queen o'er myself: and even now, but now,
PORTIA: This house, these servants and this same myself
PORTIA: Are yours, my lord: I give them with this ring,
PORTIA: Which when you part from, lose, or give away,
PORTIA: Let it presage the ruin of your love
PORTIA: And be my vantage to exclaim on you.
BASSANIO: Madam, you have bereft me of all words,
BASSANIO: Only my blood speaks to you in my veins,
BASSANIO: And there is such confusion in my powers,
BASSANIO: As after some oration fairly spoke
BASSANIO: By a beloved prince, there doth appear
BASSANIO: Among the buzzing pleased multitude,
BASSANIO: Where every something, being blent together,
BASSANIO: Turns to a wild of nothing, save of joy,
BASSANIO: Express'd and not express'd. But when this ring
BASSANIO: Parts from this finger, then parts life from hence:
BASSANIO: O, then be bold to say Bassanio's dead!
NERISSA: My lord and lady, it is now our time,
NERISSA: That have stood by and seen our wishes prosper,
NERISSA: To cry, good joy: good joy, my lord and lady!
GRATIANO: My lord Bassanio and my gentle lady,
GRATIANO: I wish you all the joy that you can wish,
GRATIANO: For I am sure you can wish none from me:
GRATIANO: And when your honours mean to solemnize
GRATIANO: The bargain of your faith, I do beseech you,
GRATIANO: Even at that time I may be married too.
BASSANIO: With all my heart, so thou canst get a wife.
GRATIANO: I thank your lordship, you have got me one.
GRATIANO: My eyes, my lord, can look as swift as yours:
GRATIANO: You saw the mistress, I beheld the maid,
GRATIANO: You loved, I loved for intermission.
GRATIANO: No more pertains to me, my lord, than you.
GRATIANO: Your fortune stood upon the casket there,
GRATIANO: And so did mine too, as the matter falls,
GRATIANO: For wooing here until I sweat again,
GRATIANO: And sweating until my very roof was dry
GRATIANO: With oaths of love, at last, if promise last,
GRATIANO: I got a promise of this fair one here
GRATIANO: To have her love, provided that your fortune
GRATIANO: Achieved her mistress.
PORTIA: Is this true, Nerissa?
NERISSA: Madam, it is, so you stand pleased withal.
BASSANIO: And do you, Gratiano, mean good faith?
GRATIANO: Yes, faith, my lord.
BASSANIO: Our feast shall be much honour'd in your marriage.
GRATIANO: We'll play with them the first boy for a thousand ducats.
NERISSA: What, and stake down?
GRATIANO: No, we shall ne'er win at that sport, and stake down.
GRATIANO: But who comes here? Lorenzo and his infidel? What,
GRATIANO: and my old Venetian friend Salerio?
NARRATOR: Enter LORENZO, JESSICA, and SALERIO, a Messenger from Venice
BASSANIO: Lorenzo and Salerio, welcome hither,
BASSANIO: If that the youth of my new interest here
BASSANIO: Have power to bid you welcome. By your leave,
BASSANIO: I bid my very friends and countrymen,
BASSANIO: Sweet Portia, welcome.
PORTIA: So do I, my lord:
PORTIA: They are entirely welcome.
LORENZO: I thank your honour. For my part, my lord,
LORENZO: My purpose was not to have seen you here,
LORENZO: But meeting with Salerio by the way,
LORENZO: He did entreat me, past all saying nay,
LORENZO: To come with him along.
SALERIO: I did, my lord,
SALERIO: And I have reason for it. Signior Antonio
SALERIO: Commends him to you.
NARRATOR: Gives Bassanio a letter
BASSANIO: Ere I ope his letter,
BASSANIO: I pray you, tell me how my good friend doth.
SALERIO: Not sick, my lord, unless it be in mind,
SALERIO: Nor well, unless in mind: his letter there
SALERIO: Will show you his estate.
GRATIANO: Nerissa, cheer yon stranger, bid her welcome.
GRATIANO: Your hand, Salerio: what's the news from Venice?
GRATIANO: How doth that royal merchant, good Antonio?
GRATIANO: I know he will be glad of our success,
GRATIANO: We are the Jasons, we have won the fleece.
SALERIO: I would you had won the fleece that he hath lost.
PORTIA: There are some shrewd contents in yon same paper,
PORTIA: That steals the colour from Bassanio's cheek:
PORTIA: Some dear friend dead, else nothing in the world
PORTIA: Could turn so much the constitution
PORTIA: Of any constant man. What, worse and worse!
PORTIA: With leave, Bassanio: I am half yourself,
PORTIA: And I must freely have the half of anything
PORTIA: That this same paper brings you.
BASSANIO: O sweet Portia,
BASSANIO: Here are a few of the unpleasant'st words
BASSANIO: That ever blotted paper! Gentle lady,
BASSANIO: When I did first impart my love to you,
BASSANIO: I freely told you, all the wealth I had
BASSANIO: Ran in my veins, I was a gentleman,
BASSANIO: And then I told you true: and yet, dear lady,
BASSANIO: Rating myself at nothing, you shall see
BASSANIO: How much I was a braggart. When I told you
BASSANIO: My state was nothing, I should then have told you
BASSANIO: That I was worse than nothing, for, indeed,
BASSANIO: I have engaged myself to a dear friend,
BASSANIO: Engaged my friend to his mere enemy,
BASSANIO: To feed my means. Here is a letter, lady,
BASSANIO: The paper as the body of my friend,
BASSANIO: And every word in it a gaping wound,
BASSANIO: Issuing life-blood. But is it true, Salerio?
BASSANIO: Have all his ventures fail'd? What, not one hit?
BASSANIO: From Tripolis, from Mexico and England,
BASSANIO: From Lisbon, Barbary and India?
BASSANIO: And not one vessel 'scape the dreadful touch
BASSANIO: Of merchant-marring rocks?
SALERIO: Not one, my lord.
SALERIO: Besides, it should appear, that if he had
SALERIO: The present money to discharge the Jew,
SALERIO: He would not take it. Never did I know
SALERIO: A creature, that did bear the shape of man,
SALERIO: So keen and greedy to confound a man:
SALERIO: He plies the duke at morning and at night,
SALERIO: And doth impeach the freedom of the state,
SALERIO: If they deny him justice: twenty merchants,
SALERIO: The duke himself, and the magnificoes
SALERIO: Of greatest port, have all persuaded with him,
SALERIO: But none can drive him from the envious plea
SALERIO: Of forfeiture, of justice and his bond.
JESSICA: When I was with him I have heard him swear
JESSICA: To Tubal and to Chus, his countrymen,
JESSICA: That he would rather have Antonio's flesh
JESSICA: Than twenty times the value of the sum
JESSICA: That he did owe him: and I know, my lord,
JESSICA: If law, authority and power deny not,
JESSICA: It will go hard with poor Antonio.
PORTIA: Is it your dear friend that is thus in trouble?
BASSANIO: The dearest friend to me, the kindest man,
BASSANIO: The best-condition'd and unwearied spirit
BASSANIO: In doing courtesies, and one in whom
BASSANIO: The ancient Roman honour more appears
BASSANIO: Than any that draws breath in Italy.
PORTIA: What sum owes he the Jew?
BASSANIO: For me three thousand ducats.
PORTIA: What, no more?
PORTIA: Pay him six thousand, and deface the bond,
PORTIA: Double six thousand, and then treble that,
PORTIA: Before a friend of this description
PORTIA: Shall lose a hair through Bassanio's fault.
PORTIA: First go with me to church and call me wife,
PORTIA: And then away to Venice to your friend,
PORTIA: For never shall you lie by Portia's side
PORTIA: With an unquiet soul. You shall have gold
PORTIA: To pay the petty debt twenty times over:
PORTIA: When it is paid, bring your true friend along.
PORTIA: My maid Nerissa and myself meantime
PORTIA: Will live as maids and widows. Come, away!
PORTIA: For you shall hence upon your wedding-day:
PORTIA: Bid your friends welcome, show a merry cheer:
PORTIA: Since you are dear bought, I will love you dear.
PORTIA: But let me hear the letter of your friend.
BASSANIO: [Reads]  Sweet Bassanio, my ships have all
BASSANIO: miscarried, my creditors grow cruel, my estate is
BASSANIO: very low, my bond to the Jew is forfeit, and since
BASSANIO: in paying it, it is impossible I should live, all
BASSANIO: debts are cleared between you and I, if I might but
BASSANIO: see you at my death. Notwithstanding, use your
BASSANIO: pleasure: if your love do not persuade you to come,
BASSANIO: let not my letter.
PORTIA: O love, dispatch all business, and be gone!
BASSANIO: Since I have your good leave to go away,
BASSANIO: I will make haste: but, till I come again,
BASSANIO: No bed shall e'er be guilty of my stay,
BASSANIO: No rest be interposer 'twixt us twain.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter SHYLOCK, SALARINO, ANTONIO, and Gaoler
SHYLOCK: Gaoler, look to him: tell not me of mercy,
SHYLOCK: This is the fool that lent out money gratis:
SHYLOCK: Gaoler, look to him.
ANTONIO: Hear me yet, good Shylock.
SHYLOCK: I'll have my bond, speak not against my bond:
SHYLOCK: I have sworn an oath that I will have my bond.
SHYLOCK: Thou call'dst me dog before thou hadst a cause,
SHYLOCK: But, since I am a dog, beware my fangs:
SHYLOCK: The duke shall grant me justice. I do wonder,
SHYLOCK: Thou naughty gaoler, that thou art so fond
SHYLOCK: To come abroad with him at his request.
ANTONIO: I pray thee, hear me speak.
SHYLOCK: I'll have my bond, I will not hear thee speak:
SHYLOCK: I'll have my bond, and therefore speak no more.
SHYLOCK: I'll not be made a soft and dull-eyed fool,
SHYLOCK: To shake the head, relent, and sigh, and yield
SHYLOCK: To Christian intercessors. Follow not,
SHYLOCK: I'll have no speaking: I will have my bond.
NARRATOR: Exit
SALARINO: It is the most impenetrable cur
SALARINO: That ever kept with men.
ANTONIO: Let him alone:
ANTONIO: I'll follow him no more with bootless prayers.
ANTONIO: He seeks my life, his reason well I know:
ANTONIO: I oft deliver'd from his forfeitures
ANTONIO: Many that have at times made moan to me,
ANTONIO: Therefore he hates me.
SALARINO: I am sure the duke
SALARINO: Will never grant this forfeiture to hold.
ANTONIO: The duke cannot deny the course of law:
ANTONIO: For the commodity that strangers have
ANTONIO: With us in Venice, if it be denied,
ANTONIO: Will much impeach the justice of his state,
ANTONIO: Since that the trade and profit of the city
ANTONIO: Consisteth of all nations. Therefore, go:
ANTONIO: These griefs and losses have so bated me,
ANTONIO: That I shall hardly spare a pound of flesh
ANTONIO: To-morrow to my bloody creditor.
ANTONIO: Well, gaoler, on. Pray God, Bassanio come
ANTONIO: To see me pay his debt, and then I care not!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Belmont. A room in PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA, NERISSA, LORENZO, JESSICA, and BALTHASAR
LORENZO: Madam, although I speak it in your presence,
LORENZO: You have a noble and a true conceit
LORENZO: Of godlike amity, which appears most strongly
LORENZO: In bearing thus the absence of your lord.
LORENZO: But if you  knew to whom you show this honour,
LORENZO: How true a gentleman you send relief,
LORENZO: How dear a lover of my lord your husband,
LORENZO: I know you would be prouder of the work
LORENZO: Than customary bounty can enforce you.
PORTIA: I never did repent for doing good,
PORTIA: Nor shall not now: for in companions
PORTIA: That do converse and waste the time together,
PORTIA: Whose souls do bear an equal yoke Of love,
PORTIA: There must be needs a like proportion
PORTIA: Of lineaments, of manners and of spirit,
PORTIA: Which makes me think that this Antonio,
PORTIA: Being the bosom lover of my lord,
PORTIA: Must needs be like my lord. If it be so,
PORTIA: How little is the cost I have bestow'd
PORTIA: In purchasing the semblance of my soul
PORTIA: From out the state of hellish misery!
PORTIA: This comes too near the praising of myself,
PORTIA: Therefore no more of it: hear other things.
PORTIA: Lorenzo, I commit into your hands
PORTIA: The husbandry and manage of my house
PORTIA: Until my lord's return: for mine own part,
PORTIA: I have toward heaven breathed a secret vow
PORTIA: To live in prayer and contemplation,
PORTIA: Only attended by Nerissa here,
PORTIA: Until her husband and my lord's return:
PORTIA: There is a monastery two miles off,
PORTIA: And there will we abide. I do desire you
PORTIA: Not to deny this imposition,
PORTIA: The which my love and some necessity
PORTIA: Now lays upon you.
LORENZO: Madam, with all my heart,
LORENZO: I shall obey you in all fair commands.
PORTIA: My people do already know my mind,
PORTIA: And will acknowledge you and Jessica
PORTIA: In place of Lord Bassanio and myself.
PORTIA: And so farewell, till we shall meet again.
LORENZO: Fair thoughts and happy hours attend on you!
JESSICA: I wish your ladyship all heart's content.
PORTIA: I thank you for your wish, and am well pleased
PORTIA: To wish it back on you: fare you well Jessica.
NARRATOR: Exeunt JESSICA and LORENZO
PORTIA: Now, Balthasar,
PORTIA: As I have ever found thee honest-true,
PORTIA: So let me find thee still. Take this same letter,
PORTIA: And use thou all the endeavour of a man
PORTIA: In speed to Padua: see thou render this
PORTIA: Into my cousin's hand, Doctor Bellario,
PORTIA: And, look, what notes and garments he doth give thee,
PORTIA: Bring them, I pray thee, with imagined speed
PORTIA: Unto the tranect, to the common ferry
PORTIA: Which trades to Venice. Waste no time in words,
PORTIA: But get thee gone: I shall be there before thee.
BALTHASAR: Madam, I go with all convenient speed.
NARRATOR: Exit
PORTIA: Come on, Nerissa, I have work in hand
PORTIA: That you yet know not of: we'll see our husbands
PORTIA: Before they think of us.
NERISSA: Shall they see us?
PORTIA: They shall, Nerissa, but in such a habit,
PORTIA: That they shall think we are accomplished
PORTIA: With that we lack. I'll hold thee any wager,
PORTIA: When we are both accoutred like young men,
PORTIA: I'll prove the prettier fellow of the two,
PORTIA: And wear my dagger with the braver grace,
PORTIA: And speak between the change of man and boy
PORTIA: With a reed voice, and turn two mincing steps
PORTIA: Into a manly stride, and speak of frays
PORTIA: Like a fine bragging youth, and tell quaint lies,
PORTIA: How honourable ladies sought my love,
PORTIA: Which I denying, they fell sick and died,
PORTIA: I could not do withal, then I'll repent,
PORTIA: And wish for all that, that I had not killed them,
PORTIA: And twenty of these puny lies I'll tell,
PORTIA: That men shall swear I have discontinued school
PORTIA: Above a twelvemonth. I have within my mind
PORTIA: A thousand raw tricks of these bragging Jacks,
PORTIA: Which I will practise.
NERISSA: Why, shall we turn to men?
PORTIA: Fie, what a question's that,
PORTIA: If thou wert near a lewd interpreter!
PORTIA: But come, I'll tell thee all my whole device
PORTIA: When I am in my coach, which stays for us
PORTIA: At the park gate, and therefore haste away,
PORTIA: For we must measure twenty miles to-day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same. A garden.
NARRATOR: Enter LAUNCELOT and JESSICA
LAUNCELOT: Yes, truly, for, look you, the sins of the father
LAUNCELOT: are to be laid upon the children: therefore, I
LAUNCELOT: promise ye, I fear you. I was always plain with
LAUNCELOT: you, and so now I speak my agitation of the matter:
LAUNCELOT: therefore be of good cheer, for truly I think you
LAUNCELOT: are damned. There is but one hope in it that can do
LAUNCELOT: you any good, and that is but a kind of bastard
LAUNCELOT: hope neither.
JESSICA: And what hope is that, I pray thee?
LAUNCELOT: Marry, you may partly hope that your father got you
LAUNCELOT: not, that you are not the Jew's daughter.
JESSICA: That were a kind of bastard hope, indeed: so the
JESSICA: sins of my mother should be visited upon me.
LAUNCELOT: Truly then I fear you are damned both by father and
LAUNCELOT: mother: thus when I shun Scylla, your father, I
LAUNCELOT: fall into Charybdis, your mother: well, you are
LAUNCELOT: gone both ways.
JESSICA: I shall be saved by my husband, he hath made me a
JESSICA: Christian.
LAUNCELOT: Truly, the more to blame he: we were Christians
LAUNCELOT: enow before, e'en as many as could well live, one by
LAUNCELOT: another. This making Christians will raise the
LAUNCELOT: price of hogs: if we grow all to be pork-eaters, we
LAUNCELOT: shall not shortly have a rasher on the coals for money.
NARRATOR: Enter LORENZO
JESSICA: I'll tell my husband, Launcelot, what you say: here he comes.
LORENZO: I shall grow jealous of you shortly, Launcelot, if
LORENZO: you thus get my wife into corners.
JESSICA: Nay, you need not fear us, Lorenzo: Launcelot and I
JESSICA: are out. He tells me flatly, there is no mercy for
JESSICA: me in heaven, because I am a Jew's daughter: and he
JESSICA: says, you are no good member of the commonwealth,
JESSICA: for in converting Jews to Christians, you raise the
JESSICA: price of pork.
LORENZO: I shall answer that better to the commonwealth than
LORENZO: you can the getting up of the negro's belly: the
LORENZO: Moor is with child by you, Launcelot.
LAUNCELOT: It is much that the Moor should be more than reason:
LAUNCELOT: but if she be less than an honest woman, she is
LAUNCELOT: indeed more than I took her for.
LORENZO: How every fool can play upon the word! I think the
LORENZO: best grace of wit will shortly turn into silence,
LORENZO: and discourse grow commendable in none only but
LORENZO: parrots. Go in, sirrah, bid them prepare for dinner.
LAUNCELOT: That is done, sir, they have all stomachs.
LORENZO: Goodly Lord, what a wit-snapper are you! then bid
LORENZO: them prepare dinner.
LAUNCELOT: That is done too, sir, only 'cover' is the word.
LORENZO: Will you cover then, sir?
LAUNCELOT: Not so, sir, neither, I know my duty.
LORENZO: Yet more quarrelling with occasion! Wilt thou show
LORENZO: the whole wealth of thy wit in an instant? I pray
LORENZO: tree, understand a plain man in his plain meaning:
LORENZO: go to thy fellows, bid them cover the table, serve
LORENZO: in the meat, and we will come in to dinner.
LAUNCELOT: For the table, sir, it shall be served in, for the
LAUNCELOT: meat, sir, it shall be covered, for your coming in
LAUNCELOT: to dinner, sir, why, let it be as humours and
LAUNCELOT: conceits shall govern.
NARRATOR: Exit
LORENZO: O dear discretion, how his words are suited!
LORENZO: The fool hath planted in his memory
LORENZO: An army of good words, and I do know
LORENZO: A many fools, that stand in better place,
LORENZO: Garnish'd like him, that for a tricksy word
LORENZO: Defy the matter. How cheerest thou, Jessica?
LORENZO: And now, good sweet, say thy opinion,
LORENZO: How dost thou like the Lord Bassanio's wife?
JESSICA: Past all expressing. It is very meet
JESSICA: The Lord Bassanio live an upright life,
JESSICA: For, having such a blessing in his lady,
JESSICA: He finds the joys of heaven here on earth,
JESSICA: And if on earth he do not mean it, then
JESSICA: In reason he should never come to heaven
JESSICA: Why, if two gods should play some heavenly match
JESSICA: And on the wager lay two earthly women,
JESSICA: And Portia one, there must be something else
JESSICA: Pawn'd with the other, for the poor rude world
JESSICA: Hath not her fellow.
LORENZO: Even such a husband
LORENZO: Hast thou of me as she is for a wife.
JESSICA: Nay, but ask my opinion too of that.
LORENZO: I will anon: first, let us go to dinner.
JESSICA: Nay, let me praise you while I have a stomach.
LORENZO: No, pray thee, let it serve for table-talk,
LORENZO: '	Then, howso'er thou speak'st, 'mong other things
LORENZO: I shall digest it.
JESSICA: Well, I'll set you forth.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Venice. A court of justice.
NARRATOR: Enter the DUKE, the Magnificoes, ANTONIO, BASSANIO, GRATIANO, SALERIO, and others
DUKE: What, is Antonio here?
ANTONIO: Ready, so please your grace.
DUKE: I am sorry for thee: thou art come to answer
DUKE: A stony adversary, an inhuman wretch
DUKE: uncapable of pity, void and empty
DUKE: From any dram of mercy.
ANTONIO: I have heard
ANTONIO: Your grace hath ta'en great pains to qualify
ANTONIO: His rigorous course, but since he stands obdurate
ANTONIO: And that no lawful means can carry me
ANTONIO: Out of his envy's reach, I do oppose
ANTONIO: My patience to his fury, and am arm'd
ANTONIO: To suffer, with a quietness of spirit,
ANTONIO: The very tyranny and rage of his.
DUKE: Go one, and call the Jew into the court.
SALERIO: He is ready at the door: he comes, my lord.
NARRATOR: Enter SHYLOCK
DUKE: Make room, and let him stand before our face.
DUKE: Shylock, the world thinks, and I think so too,
DUKE: That thou but lead'st this fashion of thy malice
DUKE: To the last hour of act, and then 'tis thought
DUKE: Thou'lt show thy mercy and remorse more strange
DUKE: Than is thy strange apparent cruelty,
DUKE: And where thou now exact'st the penalty,
DUKE: Which is a pound of this poor merchant's flesh,
DUKE: Thou wilt not only loose the forfeiture,
DUKE: But, touch'd with human gentleness and love,
DUKE: Forgive a moiety of the principal,
DUKE: Glancing an eye of pity on his losses,
DUKE: That have of late so huddled on his back,
DUKE: Enow to press a royal merchant down
DUKE: And pluck commiseration of his state
DUKE: From brassy bosoms and rough hearts of flint,
DUKE: From stubborn Turks and Tartars, never train'd
DUKE: To offices of tender courtesy.
DUKE: We all expect a gentle answer, Jew.
SHYLOCK: I have possess'd your grace of what I purpose,
SHYLOCK: And by our holy Sabbath have I sworn
SHYLOCK: To have the due and forfeit of my bond:
SHYLOCK: If you deny it, let the danger light
SHYLOCK: Upon your charter and your city's freedom.
SHYLOCK: You'll ask me, why I rather choose to have
SHYLOCK: A weight of carrion flesh than to receive
SHYLOCK: Three thousand ducats: I'll not answer that:
SHYLOCK: But, say, it is my humour: is it answer'd?
SHYLOCK: What if my house be troubled with a rat
SHYLOCK: And I be pleased to give ten thousand ducats
SHYLOCK: To have it baned? What, are you answer'd yet?
SHYLOCK: Some men there are love not a gaping pig,
SHYLOCK: Some, that are mad if they behold a cat,
SHYLOCK: And others, when the bagpipe sings i' the nose,
SHYLOCK: Cannot contain their urine: for affection,
SHYLOCK: Mistress of passion, sways it to the mood
SHYLOCK: Of what it likes or loathes. Now, for your answer:
SHYLOCK: As there is no firm reason to be render'd,
SHYLOCK: Why he cannot abide a gaping pig,
SHYLOCK: Why he, a harmless necessary cat,
SHYLOCK: Why he, a woollen bagpipe, but of force
SHYLOCK: Must yield to such inevitable shame
SHYLOCK: As to offend, himself being offended,
SHYLOCK: So can I give no reason, nor I will not,
SHYLOCK: More than a lodged hate and a certain loathing
SHYLOCK: I bear Antonio, that I follow thus
SHYLOCK: A losing suit against him. Are you answer'd?
BASSANIO: This is no answer, thou unfeeling man,
BASSANIO: To excuse the current of thy cruelty.
SHYLOCK: I am not bound to please thee with my answers.
BASSANIO: Do all men kill the things they do not love?
SHYLOCK: Hates any man the thing he would not kill?
BASSANIO: Every offence is not a hate at first.
SHYLOCK: What, wouldst thou have a serpent sting thee twice?
ANTONIO: I pray you, think you question with the Jew:
ANTONIO: You may as well go stand upon the beach
ANTONIO: And bid the main flood bate his usual height,
ANTONIO: You may as well use question with the wolf
ANTONIO: Why he hath made the ewe bleat for the lamb,
ANTONIO: You may as well forbid the mountain pines
ANTONIO: To wag their high tops and to make no noise,
ANTONIO: When they are fretten with the gusts of heaven,
ANTONIO: You may as well do anything most hard,
ANTONIO: As seek to soften that--than which what's harder?--
ANTONIO: His Jewish heart: therefore, I do beseech you,
ANTONIO: Make no more offers, use no farther means,
ANTONIO: But with all brief and plain conveniency
ANTONIO: Let me have judgment and the Jew his will.
BASSANIO: For thy three thousand ducats here is six.
SHYLOCK: What judgment shall I dread, doing
SHYLOCK: Were in six parts and every part a ducat,
SHYLOCK: I would not draw them, I would have my bond.
DUKE: How shalt thou hope for mercy, rendering none?
SHYLOCK: What judgment shall I dread, doing no wrong?
SHYLOCK: You have among you many a purchased slave,
SHYLOCK: Which, like your asses and your dogs and mules,
SHYLOCK: You use in abject and in slavish parts,
SHYLOCK: Because you bought them: shall I say to you,
SHYLOCK: Let them be free, marry them to your heirs?
SHYLOCK: Why sweat they under burthens? let their beds
SHYLOCK: Be made as soft as yours and let their palates
SHYLOCK: Be season'd with such viands? You will answer
SHYLOCK: 'The slaves are ours:' so do I answer you:
SHYLOCK: The pound of flesh, which I demand of him,
SHYLOCK: Is dearly bought, 'tis mine and I will have it.
SHYLOCK: If you deny me, fie upon your law!
SHYLOCK: There is no force in the decrees of Venice.
SHYLOCK: I stand for judgment: answer, shall I have it?
DUKE: Upon my power I may dismiss this court,
DUKE: Unless Bellario, a learned doctor,
DUKE: Whom I have sent for to determine this,
DUKE: Come here to-day.
SALERIO: My lord, here stays without
SALERIO: A messenger with letters from the doctor,
SALERIO: New come from Padua.
DUKE: Bring us the letter, call the messenger.
BASSANIO: Good cheer, Antonio! What, man, courage yet!
BASSANIO: The Jew shall have my flesh, blood, bones and all,
BASSANIO: Ere thou shalt lose for me one drop of blood.
ANTONIO: I am a tainted wether of the flock,
ANTONIO: Meetest for death: the weakest kind of fruit
ANTONIO: Drops earliest to the ground, and so let me
ANTONIO: You cannot better be employ'd, Bassanio,
ANTONIO: Than to live still and write mine epitaph.
NARRATOR: Enter NERISSA, dressed like a lawyer's clerk
DUKE: Came you from Padua, from Bellario?
NERISSA: From both, my lord. Bellario greets your grace.
NARRATOR: Presenting a letter
BASSANIO: Why dost thou whet thy knife so earnestly?
SHYLOCK: To cut the forfeiture from that bankrupt there.
GRATIANO: Not on thy sole, but on thy soul, harsh Jew,
GRATIANO: Thou makest thy knife keen, but no metal can,
GRATIANO: No, not the hangman's axe, bear half the keenness
GRATIANO: Of thy sharp envy. Can no prayers pierce thee?
SHYLOCK: No, none that thou hast wit enough to make.
GRATIANO: O, be thou damn'd, inexecrable dog!
GRATIANO: And for thy life let justice be accused.
GRATIANO: Thou almost makest me waver in my faith
GRATIANO: To hold opinion with Pythagoras,
GRATIANO: That souls of animals infuse themselves
GRATIANO: Into the trunks of men: thy currish spirit
GRATIANO: Govern'd a wolf, who, hang'd for human slaughter,
GRATIANO: Even from the gallows did his fell soul fleet,
GRATIANO: And, whilst thou lay'st in thy unhallow'd dam,
GRATIANO: Infused itself in thee, for thy desires
GRATIANO: Are wolvish, bloody, starved and ravenous.
SHYLOCK: Till thou canst rail the seal from off my bond,
SHYLOCK: Thou but offend'st thy lungs to speak so loud:
SHYLOCK: Repair thy wit, good youth, or it will fall
SHYLOCK: To cureless ruin. I stand here for law.
DUKE: This letter from Bellario doth commend
DUKE: A young and learned doctor to our court.
DUKE: Where is he?
NERISSA: He attendeth here hard by,
NERISSA: To know your answer, whether you'll admit him.
DUKE: With all my heart. Some three or four of you
DUKE: Go give him courteous conduct to this place.
DUKE: Meantime the court shall hear Bellario's letter.
Clerk: [Reads]
Clerk: Your grace shall understand that at the receipt of
Clerk: your letter I am very sick: but in the instant that
Clerk: your messenger came, in loving visitation was with
Clerk: me a young doctor of Rome, his name is Balthasar. I
Clerk: acquainted him with the cause in controversy between
Clerk: the Jew and Antonio the merchant: we turned o'er
Clerk: many books together: he is furnished with my
Clerk: opinion, which, bettered with his own learning, the
Clerk: greatness whereof I cannot enough commend, comes
Clerk: with him, at my importunity, to fill up your grace's
Clerk: request in my stead. I beseech you, let his lack of
Clerk: years be no impediment to let him lack a reverend
Clerk: estimation, for I never knew so young a body with so
Clerk: old a head. I leave him to your gracious
Clerk: acceptance, whose trial shall better publish his
Clerk: commendation.
DUKE: You hear the learn'd Bellario, what he writes:
DUKE: And here, I take it, is the doctor come.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA, dressed like a doctor of laws
DUKE: Give me your hand. Come you from old Bellario?
PORTIA: I did, my lord.
DUKE: You are welcome: take your place.
DUKE: Are you acquainted with the difference
DUKE: That holds this present question in the court?
PORTIA: I am informed thoroughly of the cause.
PORTIA: Which is the merchant here, and which the Jew?
DUKE: Antonio and old Shylock, both stand forth.
PORTIA: Is your name Shylock?
SHYLOCK: Shylock is my name.
PORTIA: Of a strange nature is the suit you follow,
PORTIA: Yet in such rule that the Venetian law
PORTIA: Cannot impugn you as you do proceed.
PORTIA: You stand within his danger, do you not?
ANTONIO: Ay, so he says.
PORTIA: Do you confess the bond?
ANTONIO: I do.
PORTIA: Then must the Jew be merciful.
SHYLOCK: On what compulsion must I? tell me that.
PORTIA: The quality of mercy is not strain'd,
PORTIA: It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven
PORTIA: Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest,
PORTIA: It blesseth him that gives and him that takes:
PORTIA: 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest: it becomes
PORTIA: The throned monarch better than his crown,
PORTIA: His sceptre shows the force of temporal power,
PORTIA: The attribute to awe and majesty,
PORTIA: Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings,
PORTIA: But mercy is above this sceptred sway,
PORTIA: It is enthroned in the hearts of kings,
PORTIA: It is an attribute to God himself,
PORTIA: And earthly power doth then show likest God's
PORTIA: When mercy seasons justice. Therefore, Jew,
PORTIA: Though justice be thy plea, consider this,
PORTIA: That, in the course of justice, none of us
PORTIA: Should see salvation: we do pray for mercy,
PORTIA: And that same prayer doth teach us all to render
PORTIA: The deeds of mercy. I have spoke thus much
PORTIA: To mitigate the justice of thy plea,
PORTIA: Which if thou follow, this strict court of Venice
PORTIA: Must needs give sentence 'gainst the merchant there.
SHYLOCK: My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,
SHYLOCK: The penalty and forfeit of my bond.
PORTIA: Is he not able to discharge the money?
BASSANIO: Yes, here I tender it for him in the court,
BASSANIO: Yea, twice the sum: if that will not suffice,
BASSANIO: I will be bound to pay it ten times o'er,
BASSANIO: On forfeit of my hands, my head, my heart:
BASSANIO: If this will not suffice, it must appear
BASSANIO: That malice bears down truth. And I beseech you,
BASSANIO: Wrest once the law to your authority:
BASSANIO: To do a great right, do a little wrong,
BASSANIO: And curb this cruel devil of his will.
PORTIA: It must not be, there is no power in Venice
PORTIA: Can alter a decree established:
PORTIA: 'Twill be recorded for a precedent,
PORTIA: And many an error by the same example
PORTIA: Will rush into the state: it cannot be.
SHYLOCK: A Daniel come to judgment! yea, a Daniel!
SHYLOCK: O wise young judge, how I do honour thee!
PORTIA: I pray you, let me look upon the bond.
SHYLOCK: Here 'tis, most reverend doctor, here it is.
PORTIA: Shylock, there's thrice thy money offer'd thee.
SHYLOCK: An oath, an oath, I have an oath in heaven:
SHYLOCK: Shall I lay perjury upon my soul?
SHYLOCK: No, not for Venice.
PORTIA: Why, this bond is forfeit,
PORTIA: And lawfully by this the Jew may claim
PORTIA: A pound of flesh, to be by him cut off
PORTIA: Nearest the merchant's heart. Be merciful:
PORTIA: Take thrice thy money, bid me tear the bond.
SHYLOCK: When it is paid according to the tenor.
SHYLOCK: It doth appear you are a worthy judge,
SHYLOCK: You know the law, your exposition
SHYLOCK: Hath been most sound: I charge you by the law,
SHYLOCK: Whereof you are a well-deserving pillar,
SHYLOCK: Proceed to judgment: by my soul I swear
SHYLOCK: There is no power in the tongue of man
SHYLOCK: To alter me: I stay here on my bond.
ANTONIO: Most heartily I do beseech the court
ANTONIO: To give the judgment.
PORTIA: Why then, thus it is:
PORTIA: You must prepare your bosom for his knife.
SHYLOCK: O noble judge! O excellent young man!
PORTIA: For the intent and purpose of the law
PORTIA: Hath full relation to the penalty,
PORTIA: Which here appeareth due upon the bond.
SHYLOCK: 'Tis very true: O wise and upright judge!
SHYLOCK: How much more elder art thou than thy looks!
PORTIA: Therefore lay bare your bosom.
SHYLOCK: Ay, his breast:
SHYLOCK: So says the bond: doth it not, noble judge?
SHYLOCK: 'Nearest his heart:' those are the very words.
PORTIA: It is so. Are there balance here to weigh
PORTIA: The flesh?
SHYLOCK: I have them ready.
PORTIA: Have by some surgeon, Shylock, on your charge,
PORTIA: To stop his wounds, lest he do bleed to death.
SHYLOCK: Is it so nominated in the bond?
PORTIA: It is not so express'd: but what of that?
PORTIA: 'Twere good you do so much for charity.
SHYLOCK: I cannot find it, 'tis not in the bond.
PORTIA: You, merchant, have you any thing to say?
ANTONIO: But little: I am arm'd and well prepared.
ANTONIO: Give me your hand, Bassanio: fare you well!
ANTONIO: Grieve not that I am fallen to this for you,
ANTONIO: For herein Fortune shows herself more kind
ANTONIO: Than is her custom: it is still her use
ANTONIO: To let the wretched man outlive his wealth,
ANTONIO: To view with hollow eye and wrinkled brow
ANTONIO: An age of poverty, from which lingering penance
ANTONIO: Of such misery doth she cut me off.
ANTONIO: Commend me to your honourable wife:
ANTONIO: Tell her the process of Antonio's end,
ANTONIO: Say how I loved you, speak me fair in death,
ANTONIO: And, when the tale is told, bid her be judge
ANTONIO: Whether Bassanio had not once a love.
ANTONIO: Repent but you that you shall lose your friend,
ANTONIO: And he repents not that he pays your debt,
ANTONIO: For if the Jew do cut but deep enough,
ANTONIO: I'll pay it presently with all my heart.
BASSANIO: Antonio, I am married to a wife
BASSANIO: Which is as dear to me as life itself,
BASSANIO: But life itself, my wife, and all the world,
BASSANIO: Are not with me esteem'd above thy life:
BASSANIO: I would lose all, ay, sacrifice them all
BASSANIO: Here to this devil, to deliver you.
PORTIA: Your wife would give you little thanks for that,
PORTIA: If she were by, to hear you make the offer.
GRATIANO: I have a wife, whom, I protest, I love:
GRATIANO: I would she were in heaven, so she could
GRATIANO: Entreat some power to change this currish Jew.
NERISSA: 'Tis well you offer it behind her back,
NERISSA: The wish would make else an unquiet house.
SHYLOCK: These be the Christian husbands. I have a daughter,
SHYLOCK: Would any of the stock of Barrabas
SHYLOCK: Had been her husband rather than a Christian!
NARRATOR: Aside
SHYLOCK: We trifle time: I pray thee, pursue sentence.
PORTIA: A pound of that same merchant's flesh is thine:
PORTIA: The court awards it, and the law doth give it.
SHYLOCK: Most rightful judge!
PORTIA: And you must cut this flesh from off his breast:
PORTIA: The law allows it, and the court awards it.
SHYLOCK: Most learned judge! A sentence! Come, prepare!
PORTIA: Tarry a little, there is something else.
PORTIA: This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood,
PORTIA: The words expressly are 'a pound of flesh:'
PORTIA: Take then thy bond, take thou thy pound of flesh,
PORTIA: But, in the cutting it, if thou dost shed
PORTIA: One drop of Christian blood, thy lands and goods
PORTIA: Are, by the laws of Venice, confiscate
PORTIA: Unto the state of Venice.
GRATIANO: O upright judge! Mark, Jew: O learned judge!
SHYLOCK: Is that the law?
PORTIA: Thyself shalt see the act:
PORTIA: For, as thou urgest justice, be assured
PORTIA: Thou shalt have justice, more than thou desirest.
GRATIANO: O learned judge! Mark, Jew: a learned judge!
SHYLOCK: I take this offer, then, pay the bond thrice
SHYLOCK: And let the Christian go.
BASSANIO: Here is the money.
PORTIA: Soft!
PORTIA: The Jew shall have all justice, soft! no haste:
PORTIA: He shall have nothing but the penalty.
GRATIANO: O Jew! an upright judge, a learned judge!
PORTIA: Therefore prepare thee to cut off the flesh.
PORTIA: Shed thou no blood, nor cut thou less nor more
PORTIA: But just a pound of flesh: if thou cut'st more
PORTIA: Or less than a just pound, be it but so much
PORTIA: As makes it light or heavy in the substance,
PORTIA: Or the division of the twentieth part
PORTIA: Of one poor scruple, nay, if the scale do turn
PORTIA: But in the estimation of a hair,
PORTIA: Thou diest and all thy goods are confiscate.
GRATIANO: A second Daniel, a Daniel, Jew!
GRATIANO: Now, infidel, I have you on the hip.
PORTIA: Why doth the Jew pause? take thy forfeiture.
SHYLOCK: Give me my principal, and let me go.
BASSANIO: I have it ready for thee, here it is.
PORTIA: He hath refused it in the open court:
PORTIA: He shall have merely justice and his bond.
GRATIANO: A Daniel, still say I, a second Daniel!
GRATIANO: I thank thee, Jew, for teaching me that word.
SHYLOCK: Shall I not have barely my principal?
PORTIA: Thou shalt have nothing but the forfeiture,
PORTIA: To be so taken at thy peril, Jew.
SHYLOCK: Why, then the devil give him good of it!
SHYLOCK: I'll stay no longer question.
PORTIA: Tarry, Jew:
PORTIA: The law hath yet another hold on you.
PORTIA: It is enacted in the laws of Venice,
PORTIA: If it be proved against an alien
PORTIA: That by direct or indirect attempts
PORTIA: He seek the life of any citizen,
PORTIA: The party 'gainst the which he doth contrive
PORTIA: Shall seize one half his goods, the other half
PORTIA: Comes to the privy coffer of the state,
PORTIA: And the offender's life lies in the mercy
PORTIA: Of the duke only, 'gainst all other voice.
PORTIA: In which predicament, I say, thou stand'st,
PORTIA: For it appears, by manifest proceeding,
PORTIA: That indirectly and directly too
PORTIA: Thou hast contrived against the very life
PORTIA: Of the defendant, and thou hast incurr'd
PORTIA: The danger formerly by me rehearsed.
PORTIA: Down therefore and beg mercy of the duke.
GRATIANO: Beg that thou mayst have leave to hang thyself:
GRATIANO: And yet, thy wealth being forfeit to the state,
GRATIANO: Thou hast not left the value of a cord,
GRATIANO: Therefore thou must be hang'd at the state's charge.
DUKE: That thou shalt see the difference of our spirits,
DUKE: I pardon thee thy life before thou ask it:
DUKE: For half thy wealth, it is Antonio's,
DUKE: The other half comes to the general state,
DUKE: Which humbleness may drive unto a fine.
PORTIA: Ay, for the state, not for Antonio.
SHYLOCK: Nay, take my life and all, pardon not that:
SHYLOCK: You take my house when you do take the prop
SHYLOCK: That doth sustain my house, you take my life
SHYLOCK: When you do take the means whereby I live.
PORTIA: What mercy can you render him, Antonio?
GRATIANO: A halter gratis, nothing else, for God's sake.
ANTONIO: So please my lord the duke and all the court
ANTONIO: To quit the fine for one half of his goods,
ANTONIO: I am content, so he will let me have
ANTONIO: The other half in use, to render it,
ANTONIO: Upon his death, unto the gentleman
ANTONIO: That lately stole his daughter:
ANTONIO: Two things provided more, that, for this favour,
ANTONIO: He presently become a Christian,
ANTONIO: The other, that he do record a gift,
ANTONIO: Here in the court, of all he dies possess'd,
ANTONIO: Unto his son Lorenzo and his daughter.
DUKE: He shall do this, or else I do recant
DUKE: The pardon that I late pronounced here.
PORTIA: Art thou contented, Jew? what dost thou say?
SHYLOCK: I am content.
PORTIA: Clerk, draw a deed of gift.
SHYLOCK: I pray you, give me leave to go from hence,
SHYLOCK: I am not well: send the deed after me,
SHYLOCK: And I will sign it.
DUKE: Get thee gone, but do it.
GRATIANO: In christening shalt thou have two god-fathers:
GRATIANO: Had I been judge, thou shouldst have had ten more,
GRATIANO: To bring thee to the gallows, not the font.
NARRATOR: Exit SHYLOCK
DUKE: Sir, I entreat you home with me to dinner.
PORTIA: I humbly do desire your grace of pardon:
PORTIA: I must away this night toward Padua,
PORTIA: And it is meet I presently set forth.
DUKE: I am sorry that your leisure serves you not.
DUKE: Antonio, gratify this gentleman,
DUKE: For, in my mind, you are much bound to him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Duke and his train
BASSANIO: Most worthy gentleman, I and my friend
BASSANIO: Have by your wisdom been this day acquitted
BASSANIO: Of grievous penalties, in lieu whereof,
BASSANIO: Three thousand ducats, due unto the Jew,
BASSANIO: We freely cope your courteous pains withal.
ANTONIO: And stand indebted, over and above,
ANTONIO: In love and service to you evermore.
PORTIA: He is well paid that is well satisfied,
PORTIA: And I, delivering you, am satisfied
PORTIA: And therein do account myself well paid:
PORTIA: My mind was never yet more mercenary.
PORTIA: I pray you, know me when we meet again:
PORTIA: I wish you well, and so I take my leave.
BASSANIO: Dear sir, of force I must attempt you further:
BASSANIO: Take some remembrance of us, as a tribute,
BASSANIO: Not as a fee: grant me two things, I pray you,
BASSANIO: Not to deny me, and to pardon me.
PORTIA: You press me far, and therefore I will yield.
NARRATOR: To ANTONIO
PORTIA: Give me your gloves, I'll wear them for your sake,
NARRATOR: To BASSANIO
PORTIA: And, for your love, I'll take this ring from you:
PORTIA: Do not draw back your hand, I'll take no more,
PORTIA: And you in love shall not deny me this.
BASSANIO: This ring, good sir, alas, it is a trifle!
BASSANIO: I will not shame myself to give you this.
PORTIA: I will have nothing else but only this,
PORTIA: And now methinks I have a mind to it.
BASSANIO: There's more depends on this than on the value.
BASSANIO: The dearest ring in Venice will I give you,
BASSANIO: And find it out by proclamation:
BASSANIO: Only for this, I pray you, pardon me.
PORTIA: I see, sir, you are liberal in offers
PORTIA: You taught me first to beg, and now methinks
PORTIA: You teach me how a beggar should be answer'd.
BASSANIO: Good sir, this ring was given me by my wife,
BASSANIO: And when she put it on, she made me vow
BASSANIO: That I should neither sell nor give nor lose it.
PORTIA: That 'scuse serves many men to save their gifts.
PORTIA: An if your wife be not a mad-woman,
PORTIA: And know how well I have deserved the ring,
PORTIA: She would not hold out enemy for ever,
PORTIA: For giving it to me. Well, peace be with you!
NARRATOR: Exeunt Portia and Nerissa
ANTONIO: My Lord Bassanio, let him have the ring:
ANTONIO: Let his deservings and my love withal
ANTONIO: Be valued against your wife's commandment.
BASSANIO: Go, Gratiano, run and overtake him,
BASSANIO: Give him the ring, and bring him, if thou canst,
BASSANIO: Unto Antonio's house: away! make haste.
NARRATOR: Exit Gratiano
BASSANIO: Come, you and I will thither presently,
BASSANIO: And in the morning early will we both
BASSANIO: Fly toward Belmont: come, Antonio.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA and NERISSA
PORTIA: Inquire the Jew's house out, give him this deed
PORTIA: And let him sign it: we'll away to-night
PORTIA: And be a day before our husbands home:
PORTIA: This deed will be well welcome to Lorenzo.
NARRATOR: Enter GRATIANO
GRATIANO: Fair sir, you are well o'erta'en
GRATIANO: My Lord Bassanio upon more advice
GRATIANO: Hath sent you here this ring, and doth entreat
GRATIANO: Your company at dinner.
PORTIA: That cannot be:
PORTIA: His ring I do accept most thankfully:
PORTIA: And so, I pray you, tell him: furthermore,
PORTIA: I pray you, show my youth old Shylock's house.
GRATIANO: That will I do.
NERISSA: Sir, I would speak with you.
NARRATOR: Aside to PORTIA
NERISSA: I'll see if I can get my husband's ring,
NERISSA: Which I did make him swear to keep for ever.
PORTIA: [Aside to NERISSA]  Thou mayst, I warrant.
PORTIA: We shall have old swearing
PORTIA: That they did give the rings away to men,
PORTIA: But we'll outface them, and outswear them too.
NARRATOR: Aloud
PORTIA: Away! make haste: thou knowist where I will tarry.
NERISSA: Come, good sir, will you show me to this house?
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Belmont. Avenue to PORTIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LORENZO and JESSICA
LORENZO: The moon shines bright: in such a night as this,
LORENZO: When the sweet wind did gently kiss the trees
LORENZO: And they did make no noise, in such a night
LORENZO: Troilus methinks mounted the Troyan walls
LORENZO: And sigh'd his soul toward the Grecian tents,
LORENZO: Where Cressid lay that night.
JESSICA: In such a night
JESSICA: Did Thisbe fearfully o'ertrip the dew
JESSICA: And saw the lion's shadow ere himself
JESSICA: And ran dismay'd away.
LORENZO: In such a night
LORENZO: Stood Dido with a willow in her hand
LORENZO: Upon the wild sea banks and waft her love
LORENZO: To come again to Carthage.
JESSICA: In such a night
JESSICA: Medea gather'd the enchanted herbs
JESSICA: That did renew old AEson.
LORENZO: In such a night
LORENZO: Did Jessica steal from the wealthy Jew
LORENZO: And with an unthrift love did run from Venice
LORENZO: As far as Belmont.
JESSICA: In such a night
JESSICA: Did young Lorenzo swear he loved her well,
JESSICA: Stealing her soul with many vows of faith
JESSICA: And ne'er a true one.
LORENZO: In such a night
LORENZO: Did pretty Jessica, like a little shrew,
LORENZO: Slander her love, and he forgave it her.
JESSICA: I would out-night you, did no body come,
JESSICA: But, hark, I hear the footing of a man.
NARRATOR: Enter STEPHANO
LORENZO: Who comes so fast in silence of the night?
STEPHANO: A friend.
LORENZO: A friend! what friend? your name, I pray you, friend?
STEPHANO: Stephano is my name, and I bring word
STEPHANO: My mistress will before the break of day
STEPHANO: Be here at Belmont, she doth stray about
STEPHANO: By holy crosses, where she kneels and prays
STEPHANO: For happy wedlock hours.
LORENZO: Who comes with her?
STEPHANO: None but a holy hermit and her maid.
STEPHANO: I pray you, is my master yet return'd?
LORENZO: He is not, nor we have not heard from him.
LORENZO: But go we in, I pray thee, Jessica,
LORENZO: And ceremoniously let us prepare
LORENZO: Some welcome for the mistress of the house.
NARRATOR: Enter LAUNCELOT
LAUNCELOT: Sola, sola! wo ha, ho! sola, sola!
LORENZO: Who calls?
LAUNCELOT: Sola! did you see Master Lorenzo?
LAUNCELOT: Master Lorenzo, sola, sola!
LORENZO: Leave hollaing, man: here.
LAUNCELOT: Sola! where? where?
LORENZO: Here.
LAUNCELOT: Tell him there's a post come from my master, with
LAUNCELOT: his horn full of good news: my master will be here
LAUNCELOT: ere morning.
NARRATOR: Exit
LORENZO: Sweet soul, let's in, and there expect their coming.
LORENZO: And yet no matter: why should we go in?
LORENZO: My friend Stephano, signify, I pray you,
LORENZO: Within the house, your mistress is at hand,
LORENZO: And bring your music forth into the air.
NARRATOR: Exit Stephano
LORENZO: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!
LORENZO: Here will we sit and let the sounds of music
LORENZO: Creep in our ears: soft stillness and the night
LORENZO: Become the touches of sweet harmony.
LORENZO: Sit, Jessica. Look how the floor of heaven
LORENZO: Is thick inlaid with patines of bright gold:
LORENZO: There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st
LORENZO: But in his motion like an angel sings,
LORENZO: Still quiring to the young-eyed cherubins,
LORENZO: Such harmony is in immortal souls,
LORENZO: But whilst this muddy vesture of decay
LORENZO: Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it.
NARRATOR: Enter Musicians
LORENZO: Come, ho! and wake Diana with a hymn!
LORENZO: With sweetest touches pierce your mistress' ear,
LORENZO: And draw her home with music.
NARRATOR: Music
JESSICA: I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
LORENZO: The reason is, your spirits are attentive:
LORENZO: For do but note a wild and wanton herd,
LORENZO: Or race of youthful and unhandled colts,
LORENZO: Fetching mad bounds, bellowing and neighing loud,
LORENZO: Which is the hot condition of their blood,
LORENZO: If they but hear perchance a trumpet sound,
LORENZO: Or any air of music touch their ears,
LORENZO: You shall perceive them make a mutual stand,
LORENZO: Their savage eyes turn'd to a modest gaze
LORENZO: By the sweet power of music: therefore the poet
LORENZO: Did feign that Orpheus drew trees, stones and floods,
LORENZO: Since nought so stockish, hard and full of rage,
LORENZO: But music for the time doth change his nature.
LORENZO: The man that hath no music in himself,
LORENZO: Nor is not moved with concord of sweet sounds,
LORENZO: Is fit for treasons, stratagems and spoils,
LORENZO: The motions of his spirit are dull as night
LORENZO: And his affections dark as Erebus:
LORENZO: Let no such man be trusted. Mark the music.
NARRATOR: Enter PORTIA and NERISSA
PORTIA: That light we see is burning in my hall.
PORTIA: How far that little candle throws his beams!
PORTIA: So shines a good deed in a naughty world.
NERISSA: When the moon shone, we did not see the candle.
PORTIA: So doth the greater glory dim the less:
PORTIA: A substitute shines brightly as a king
PORTIA: Unto the king be by, and then his state
PORTIA: Empties itself, as doth an inland brook
PORTIA: Into the main of waters. Music! hark!
NERISSA: It is your music, madam, of the house.
PORTIA: Nothing is good, I see, without respect:
PORTIA: Methinks it sounds much sweeter than by day.
NERISSA: Silence bestows that virtue on it, madam.
PORTIA: The crow doth sing as sweetly as the lark,
PORTIA: When neither is attended, and I think
PORTIA: The nightingale, if she should sing by day,
PORTIA: When every goose is cackling, would be thought
PORTIA: No better a musician than the wren.
PORTIA: How many things by season season'd are
PORTIA: To their right praise and true perfection!
PORTIA: Peace, ho! the moon sleeps with Endymion
PORTIA: And would not be awaked.
NARRATOR: Music ceases
LORENZO: That is the voice,
LORENZO: Or I am much deceived, of Portia.
PORTIA: He knows me as the blind man knows the cuckoo,
PORTIA: By the bad voice.
LORENZO: Dear lady, welcome home.
PORTIA: We have been praying for our husbands' healths,
PORTIA: Which speed, we hope, the better for our words.
PORTIA: Are they return'd?
LORENZO: Madam, they are not yet,
LORENZO: But there is come a messenger before,
LORENZO: To signify their coming.
PORTIA: Go in, Nerissa,
PORTIA: Give order to my servants that they take
PORTIA: No note at all of our being absent hence,
PORTIA: Nor you, Lorenzo, Jessica, nor you.
NARRATOR: A tucket sounds
LORENZO: Your husband is at hand, I hear his trumpet:
LORENZO: We are no tell-tales, madam, fear you not.
PORTIA: This night methinks is but the daylight sick,
PORTIA: It looks a little paler: 'tis a day,
PORTIA: Such as the day is when the sun is hid.
NARRATOR: Enter BASSANIO, ANTONIO, GRATIANO, and their followers
BASSANIO: We should hold day with the Antipodes,
BASSANIO: If you would walk in absence of the sun.
PORTIA: Let me give light, but let me not be light,
PORTIA: For a light wife doth make a heavy husband,
PORTIA: And never be Bassanio so for me:
PORTIA: But God sort all! You are welcome home, my lord.
BASSANIO: I thank you, madam. Give welcome to my friend.
BASSANIO: This is the man, this is Antonio,
BASSANIO: To whom I am so infinitely bound.
PORTIA: You should in all sense be much bound to him.
PORTIA: For, as I hear, he was much bound for you.
ANTONIO: No more than I am well acquitted of.
PORTIA: Sir, you are very welcome to our house:
PORTIA: It must appear in other ways than words,
PORTIA: Therefore I scant this breathing courtesy.
GRATIANO: [To NERISSA]  By yonder moon I swear you do me wrong,
GRATIANO: In faith, I gave it to the judge's clerk:
GRATIANO: Would he were gelt that had it, for my part,
GRATIANO: Since you do take it, love, so much at heart.
PORTIA: A quarrel, ho, already! what's the matter?
GRATIANO: About a hoop of gold, a paltry ring
GRATIANO: That she did give me, whose posy was
GRATIANO: For all the world like cutler's poetry
GRATIANO: Upon  a knife, 'Love me, and leave me not.'

NERISSA: That you would wear it till your hour of death
NERISSA: And that it should lie with you in your grave:

NERISSA: You should have been respective and have kept it.
NERISSA: Gave it a judge's clerk! no, God's my judge,
NERISSA: The clerk will ne'er wear hair on's face that had it.
GRATIANO: He will, an if he live to be a man.
NERISSA: Ay, if a woman live to be a man.
GRATIANO: Now, by this hand, I gave it to a youth,
GRATIANO: A kind of boy, a little scrubbed boy,
GRATIANO: No higher than thyself, the judge's clerk,
GRATIANO: A prating boy, that begg'd it as a fee:
GRATIANO: I could not for my heart deny it him.

PORTIA: To part so slightly with your wife's first gift:
PORTIA: A thing stuck on with oaths upon your finger
PORTIA: And so riveted with faith unto your flesh.
PORTIA: I gave my love a ring and made him swear
PORTIA: Never to part with it, and here he stands,
PORTIA: I dare be sworn for him he would not leave it
PORTIA: Nor pluck it from his finger, for the wealth
PORTIA: That the world masters. Now, in faith, Gratiano,
PORTIA: You give your wife too unkind a cause of grief:
PORTIA: An 'twere to me, I should be mad at it.
BASSANIO: [Aside]  Why, I were best to cut my left hand off
BASSANIO: And swear I lost the ring defending it.
GRATIANO: My Lord Bassanio gave his ring away
GRATIANO: Unto the judge that begg'd it and indeed
GRATIANO: Deserved it too, and then the boy, his clerk,
GRATIANO: That took some pains in writing, he begg'd mine,
GRATIANO: And neither man nor master would take aught
GRATIANO: But the two rings.
PORTIA: What ring gave you my lord?
PORTIA: Not that, I hope, which you received of me.
BASSANIO: If I could add a lie unto a fault,
BASSANIO: I would deny it, but you see my finger
BASSANIO: Hath not the ring upon it, it is gone.
PORTIA: Even so void is your false heart of truth.
PORTIA: By heaven, I will ne'er come in your bed
PORTIA: Until I see the ring.
NERISSA: Nor I in yours
NERISSA: Till I again see mine.
BASSANIO: Sweet Portia,
BASSANIO: If you did know to whom I gave the ring,
BASSANIO: If you did know for whom I gave the ring
BASSANIO: And would conceive for what I gave the ring
BASSANIO: And how unwillingly I left the ring,
BASSANIO: When nought would be accepted but the ring,
BASSANIO: You would abate the strength of your displeasure.
PORTIA: If you had known the virtue of the ring,
PORTIA: Or half her worthiness that gave the ring,
PORTIA: Or your own honour to contain the ring,
PORTIA: You would not then have parted with the ring.
PORTIA: What man is there so much unreasonable,
PORTIA: If you had pleased to have defended it
PORTIA: With any terms of zeal, wanted the modesty
PORTIA: To urge the thing held as a ceremony?
PORTIA: Nerissa teaches me what to believe:
PORTIA: I'll die for't but some woman had the ring.
BASSANIO: No, by my honour, madam, by my soul,
BASSANIO: No woman had it, but a civil doctor,
BASSANIO: Which did refuse three thousand ducats of me
BASSANIO: And begg'd the ring, the which I did deny him
BASSANIO: And suffer'd him to go displeased away,
BASSANIO: Even he that did uphold the very life
BASSANIO: Of my dear friend. What should I say, sweet lady?
BASSANIO: I was enforced to send it after him,
BASSANIO: I was beset with shame and courtesy,
BASSANIO: My honour would not let ingratitude
BASSANIO: So much besmear it. Pardon me, good lady,
BASSANIO: For, by these blessed candles of the night,
BASSANIO: Had you been there, I think you would have begg'd
BASSANIO: The ring of me to give the worthy doctor.
PORTIA: Let not that doctor e'er come near my house:
PORTIA: Since he hath got the jewel that I loved,
PORTIA: And that which you did swear to keep for me,
PORTIA: I will become as liberal as you,
PORTIA: I'll not deny him any thing I have,
PORTIA: No, not my body nor my husband's bed:
PORTIA: Know him I shall, I am well sure of it:
PORTIA: Lie not a night from home, watch me like Argus:
PORTIA: If you do not, if I be left alone,
PORTIA: Now, by mine honour, which is yet mine own,
PORTIA: I'll have that doctor for my bedfellow.
NERISSA: And I his clerk, therefore be well advised
NERISSA: How you do leave me to mine own protection.
GRATIANO: Well, do you so, let not me take him, then,
GRATIANO: For if I do, I'll mar the young clerk's pen.
ANTONIO: I am the unhappy subject of these quarrels.
PORTIA: Sir, grieve not you, you are welcome notwithstanding.
BASSANIO: Portia, forgive me this enforced wrong,
BASSANIO: And, in the hearing of these many friends,
BASSANIO: I swear to thee, even by thine own fair eyes,
BASSANIO: Wherein I see myself--
PORTIA: Mark you but that!
PORTIA: In both my eyes he doubly sees himself,
PORTIA: In each eye, one: swear by your double self,
PORTIA: And there's an oath of credit.
BASSANIO: Nay, but hear me:
BASSANIO: Pardon this fault, and by my soul I swear
BASSANIO: I never more will break an oath with thee.
ANTONIO: I once did lend my body for his wealth,
ANTONIO: Which, but for him that had your husband's ring,
ANTONIO: Had quite miscarried: I dare be bound again,
ANTONIO: My soul upon the forfeit, that your lord
ANTONIO: Will never more break faith advisedly.
PORTIA: Then you shall be his surety. Give him this
PORTIA: And bid him keep it better than the other.
ANTONIO: Here, Lord Bassanio, swear to keep this ring.
BASSANIO: By heaven, it is the same I gave the doctor!
PORTIA: I had it of him: pardon me, Bassanio,
PORTIA: For, by this ring, the doctor lay with me.
NERISSA: And pardon me, my gentle Gratiano,
NERISSA: For that same scrubbed boy, the doctor's clerk,
NERISSA: In lieu of this last night did lie with me.
GRATIANO: Why, this is like the mending of highways
GRATIANO: In summer, where the ways are fair enough:
GRATIANO: What, are we cuckolds ere we have deserved it?
PORTIA: Speak not so grossly. You are all amazed:
PORTIA: Here is a letter, read it at your leisure,
PORTIA: It comes from Padua, from Bellario:
PORTIA: There you shall find that Portia was the doctor,
PORTIA: Nerissa there her clerk: Lorenzo here
PORTIA: Shall witness I set forth as soon as you
PORTIA: And even but now return'd, I have not yet
PORTIA: Enter'd my house. Antonio, you are welcome,
PORTIA: And I have better news in store for you
PORTIA: Than you expect: unseal this letter soon,
PORTIA: There you shall find three of your argosies
PORTIA: Are richly come to harbour suddenly:
PORTIA: You shall not know by what strange accident
PORTIA: I chanced on this letter.
ANTONIO: I am dumb.
BASSANIO: Were you the doctor and I knew you not?
GRATIANO: Were you the clerk that is to make me cuckold?
NERISSA: Ay, but the clerk that never means to do it,
NERISSA: Unless he live until he be a man.
BASSANIO: Sweet doctor, you shall be my bed-fellow:
BASSANIO: When I am absent, then lie with my wife.
ANTONIO: Sweet lady, you have given me life and living,
ANTONIO: For here I read for certain that my ships
ANTONIO: Are safely come to road.
PORTIA: How now, Lorenzo!
PORTIA: My clerk hath some good comforts too for you.
NERISSA: Ay, and I'll give them him without a fee.
NERISSA: There do I give to you and Jessica,
NERISSA: From the rich Jew, a special deed of gift,
NERISSA: After his death, of all he dies possess'd of.
LORENZO: Fair ladies, you drop manna in the way
LORENZO: Of starved people.
PORTIA: It is almost morning,
PORTIA: And yet I am sure you are not satisfied
PORTIA: Of these events at full. Let us go in,
PORTIA: And charge us there upon inter'gatories,
PORTIA: And we will answer all things faithfully.
GRATIANO: Let it be so: the first inter'gatory
GRATIANO: That my Nerissa shall be sworn on is,
GRATIANO: Whether till the next night she had rather stay,
GRATIANO: Or go to bed now, being two hours to day:
GRATIANO: But were the day come, I should wish it dark,
GRATIANO: That I were couching with the doctor's clerk.
GRATIANO: Well, while I live I'll fear no other thing
GRATIANO: So sore as keeping safe Nerissa's ring.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
