PUCK: ACT I
PUCK: SCENE I. Before LEONATO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO, HERO, and BEATRICE, with a Messenger
LEONATO: I learn in this letter that Don Peter of Arragon
LEONATO: comes this night to Messina.
Messenger: He is very near by this: he was not three leagues off
Messenger: when I left him.
LEONATO: How many gentlemen have you lost in this action?
Messenger: But few of any sort, and none of name.
LEONATO: A victory is twice itself when the achiever brings
LEONATO: home full numbers. I find here that Don Peter hath
LEONATO: bestowed much honour on a young Florentine called Claudio.
Messenger: Much deserved on his part and equally remembered by
Messenger: Don Pedro: he hath borne himself beyond the
Messenger: promise of his age, doing, in the figure of a lamb,
Messenger: the feats of a lion: he hath indeed better
Messenger: bettered expectation than you must expect of me to
Messenger: tell you how.
LEONATO: He hath an uncle here in Messina will be very much
LEONATO: glad of it.
Messenger: I have already delivered him letters, and there
Messenger: appears much joy in him, even so much that joy could
Messenger: not show itself modest enough without a badge of
Messenger: bitterness.
LEONATO: Did he break out into tears?
Messenger: In great measure.
LEONATO: A kind overflow of kindness: there are no faces
LEONATO: truer than those that are so washed. How much
LEONATO: better is it to weep at joy than to joy at weeping!
BEATRICE: I pray you, is Signior Mountanto returned from the
BEATRICE: wars or no?
Messenger: I know none of that name, lady: there was none such
Messenger: in the army of any sort.
LEONATO: What is he that you ask for, niece?
HERO: My cousin means Signior Benedick of Padua.
Messenger: O, he's returned, and as pleasant as ever he was.
BEATRICE: He set up his bills here in Messina and challenged
BEATRICE: Cupid at the flight, and my uncle's fool, reading
BEATRICE: the challenge, subscribed for Cupid, and challenged
BEATRICE: him at the bird-bolt. I pray you, how many hath he
BEATRICE: killed and eaten in these wars? But how many hath
BEATRICE: he killed? for indeed I promised to eat all of his killing.
LEONATO: Faith, niece, you tax Signior Benedick too much,
LEONATO: but he'll be meet with you, I doubt it not.
Messenger: He hath done good service, lady, in these wars.
BEATRICE: You had musty victual, and he hath holp to eat it:
BEATRICE: he is a very valiant trencherman, he hath an
BEATRICE: excellent stomach.
Messenger: And a good soldier too, lady.
BEATRICE: And a good soldier to a lady: but what is he to a lord?
Messenger: A lord to a lord, a man to a man, stuffed with all
Messenger: honourable virtues.
BEATRICE: It is so, indeed, he is no less than a stuffed man:
BEATRICE: but for the stuffing,--well, we are all mortal.
LEONATO: You must not, sir, mistake my niece. There is a
LEONATO: kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her:
LEONATO: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit
LEONATO: between them.
BEATRICE: Alas! he gets nothing by that. In our last
BEATRICE: conflict four of his five wits went halting off, and
BEATRICE: now is the whole man governed with one: so that if
BEATRICE: he have wit enough to keep himself warm, let him
BEATRICE: bear it for a difference between himself and his
BEATRICE: horse, for it is all the wealth that he hath left,
BEATRICE: to be known a reasonable creature. Who is his
BEATRICE: companion now? He hath every month a new sworn brother.
Messenger: Is't possible?
BEATRICE: Very easily possible: he wears his faith but as
BEATRICE: the fashion of his hat, it ever changes with the
BEATRICE: next block.
Messenger: I see, lady, the gentleman is not in your books.
BEATRICE: No, an he were, I would burn my study. But, I pray
BEATRICE: you, who is his companion? Is there no young
BEATRICE: squarer now that will make a voyage with him to the devil?
Messenger: He is most in the company of the right noble Claudio.
BEATRICE: O Lord, he will hang upon him like a disease: he
BEATRICE: is sooner caught than the pestilence, and the taker
BEATRICE: runs presently mad. God help the noble Claudio! if
BEATRICE: he have caught the Benedick, it will cost him a
BEATRICE: thousand pound ere a' be cured.
Messenger: I will hold friends with you, lady.
BEATRICE: Do, good friend.
LEONATO: You will never run mad, niece.
BEATRICE: No, not till a hot January.
Messenger: Don Pedro is approached.

BENEDICK: I noted her not, but I looked on her.

BENEDICK: my simple true judgment, or would you have me speak
BENEDICK: after my custom, as being a professed tyrant to their sex?

BENEDICK: Yea, and a case to put it into. But speak you this

BENEDICK: I can see yet without spectacles and I see no such

BENEDICK: man, I would have you think so, but, on my
BENEDICK: allegiance, mark you this, on my allegiance. He is
BENEDICK: in love. With who? now that is your grace's part.
BENEDICK: Mark how short his answer is,--With Hero, Leonato's
BENEDICK: short daughter.
CLAUDIO: If this were so, so were it uttered.
BENEDICK: Like the old tale, my lord: 'it is not so, nor
BENEDICK: 'twas not so, but, indeed, God forbid it should be
BENEDICK: so.'
CLAUDIO: If my passion change not shortly, God forbid it
CLAUDIO: should be otherwise.
DON PEDRO: Amen, if you love her, for the lady is very well worthy.
CLAUDIO: You speak this to fetch me in, my lord.
DON PEDRO: By my troth, I speak my thought.
CLAUDIO: And, in faith, my lord, I spoke mine.
BENEDICK: And, by my two faiths and troths, my lord, I spoke mine.
CLAUDIO: That I love her, I feel.
DON PEDRO: That she is worthy, I know.
BENEDICK: That I neither feel how she should be loved nor
BENEDICK: know how she should be worthy, is the opinion that
BENEDICK: fire cannot melt out of me: I will die in it at the stake.
DON PEDRO: Thou wast ever an obstinate heretic in the despite
DON PEDRO: of beauty.
CLAUDIO: And never could maintain his part but in the force
CLAUDIO: of his will.
BENEDICK: That a woman conceived me, I thank her, that she
BENEDICK: brought me up, I likewise give her most humble
BENEDICK: thanks: but that I will have a recheat winded in my
BENEDICK: forehead, or hang my bugle in an invisible baldrick,
BENEDICK: all women shall pardon me. Because I will not do
BENEDICK: them the wrong to mistrust any, I will do myself the
BENEDICK: right to trust none, and the fine is, for the which
BENEDICK: I may go the finer, I will live a bachelor.
DON PEDRO: I shall see thee, ere I die, look pale with love.
BENEDICK: With anger, with sickness, or with hunger, my lord,
BENEDICK: not with love: prove that ever I lose more blood
BENEDICK: with love than I will get again with drinking, pick
BENEDICK: out mine eyes with a ballad-maker's pen and hang me
BENEDICK: up at the door of a brothel-house for the sign of
BENEDICK: blind Cupid.
DON PEDRO: Well, if ever thou dost fall from this faith, thou
DON PEDRO: wilt prove a notable argument.
BENEDICK: If I do, hang me in a bottle like a cat and shoot
BENEDICK: at me, and he that hits me, let him be clapped on
BENEDICK: the shoulder, and called Adam.
DON PEDRO: Well, as time shall try: 'In time the savage bull
DON PEDRO: doth bear the yoke.'
BENEDICK: The savage bull may, but if ever the sensible
BENEDICK: Benedick bear it, pluck off the bull's horns and set
BENEDICK: them in my forehead: and let me be vilely painted,
BENEDICK: and in such great letters as they write 'Here is
BENEDICK: good horse to hire,' let them signify under my sign
BENEDICK: 'Here you may see Benedick the married man.'
CLAUDIO: If this should ever happen, thou wouldst be horn-mad.
DON PEDRO: Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in
DON PEDRO: Venice, thou wilt quake for this shortly.
BENEDICK: I look for an earthquake too, then.
DON PEDRO: Well, you temporize with the hours. In the
DON PEDRO: meantime, good Signior Benedick, repair to
DON PEDRO: Leonato's: commend me to him and tell him I will
DON PEDRO: not fail him at supper, for indeed he hath made
DON PEDRO: great preparation.
BENEDICK: I have almost matter enough in me for such an
BENEDICK: embassage, and so I commit you--
CLAUDIO: To the tuition of God: From my house, if I had it,--
DON PEDRO: The sixth of July: Your loving friend, Benedick.
BENEDICK: Nay, mock not, mock not. The body of your
BENEDICK: discourse is sometime guarded with fragments, and
BENEDICK: the guards are but slightly basted on neither: ere
BENEDICK: you flout old ends any further, examine your
BENEDICK: conscience: and so I leave you.
NARRATOR: Exit
CLAUDIO: My liege, your highness now may do me good.
DON PEDRO: My love is thine to teach: teach it but how,
DON PEDRO: And thou shalt see how apt it is to learn
DON PEDRO: Any hard lesson that may do thee good.
CLAUDIO: Hath Leonato any son, my lord?
DON PEDRO: No child but Hero, she's his only heir.
DON PEDRO: Dost thou affect her, Claudio?
CLAUDIO: O, my lord,
CLAUDIO: When you went onward on this ended action,
CLAUDIO: I look'd upon her with a soldier's eye,
CLAUDIO: That liked, but had a rougher task in hand
CLAUDIO: Than to drive liking to the name of love:
CLAUDIO: But now I am return'd and that war-thoughts
CLAUDIO: Have left their places vacant, in their rooms
CLAUDIO: Come thronging soft and delicate desires,
CLAUDIO: All prompting me how fair young Hero is,
CLAUDIO: Saying, I liked her ere I went to wars.
DON PEDRO: Thou wilt be like a lover presently
DON PEDRO: And tire the hearer with a book of words.
DON PEDRO: If thou dost love fair Hero, cherish it,
DON PEDRO: And I will break with her and with her father,
DON PEDRO: And thou shalt have her. Was't not to this end
DON PEDRO: That thou began'st to twist so fine a story?
CLAUDIO: How sweetly you do minister to love,
CLAUDIO: That know love's grief by his complexion!
CLAUDIO: But lest my liking might too sudden seem,
CLAUDIO: I would have salved it with a longer treatise.
DON PEDRO: What need the bridge much broader than the flood?
DON PEDRO: The fairest grant is the necessity.
DON PEDRO: Look, what will serve is fit: 'tis once, thou lovest,
DON PEDRO: And I will fit thee with the remedy.
DON PEDRO: I know we shall have revelling to-night:
DON PEDRO: I will assume thy part in some disguise
DON PEDRO: And tell fair Hero I am Claudio,
DON PEDRO: And in her bosom I'll unclasp my heart
DON PEDRO: And take her hearing prisoner with the force
DON PEDRO: And strong encounter of my amorous tale:
DON PEDRO: Then after to her father will I break,
DON PEDRO: And the conclusion is, she shall be thine.
DON PEDRO: In practise let us put it presently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in LEONATO's house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO and ANTONIO, meeting
LEONATO: How now, brother! Where is my cousin, your son?
LEONATO: hath he provided this music?
ANTONIO: He is very busy about it. But, brother, I can tell
ANTONIO: you strange news that you yet dreamt not of.
LEONATO: Are they good?
ANTONIO: As the event stamps them: but they have a good
ANTONIO: cover, they show well outward. The prince and Count
ANTONIO: Claudio, walking in a thick-pleached alley in mine
ANTONIO: orchard, were thus much overheard by a man of mine:
ANTONIO: the prince discovered to Claudio that he loved my
ANTONIO: niece your daughter and meant to acknowledge it
ANTONIO: this night in a dance: and if he found her
ANTONIO: accordant, he meant to take the present time by the
ANTONIO: top and instantly break with you of it.
LEONATO: Hath the fellow any wit that told you this?
ANTONIO: A good sharp fellow: I will send for him, and
ANTONIO: question him yourself.
LEONATO: No, no, we will hold it as a dream till it appear
LEONATO: itself: but I will acquaint my daughter withal,
LEONATO: that she may be the better prepared for an answer,
LEONATO: if peradventure this be true. Go you and tell her of it.
NARRATOR: Enter Attendants
LEONATO: Cousins, you know what you have to do. O, I cry you
LEONATO: mercy, friend, go you with me, and I will use your
LEONATO: skill. Good cousin, have a care this busy time.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter DON JOHN and CONRADE
CONRADE: What the good-year, my lord! why are you thus out
CONRADE: of measure sad?
DON JOHN: There is no measure in the occasion that breeds,
DON JOHN: therefore the sadness is without limit.
CONRADE: You should hear reason.
DON JOHN: And when I have heard it, what blessing brings it?
CONRADE: If not a present remedy, at least a patient
CONRADE: sufferance.
DON JOHN: I wonder that thou, being, as thou sayest thou art,
DON JOHN: born under Saturn, goest about to apply a moral
DON JOHN: medicine to a mortifying mischief. I cannot hide
DON JOHN: what I am: I must be sad when I have cause and smile
DON JOHN: at no man's jests, eat when I have stomach and wait
DON JOHN: for no man's leisure, sleep when I am drowsy and
DON JOHN: tend on no man's business, laugh when I am merry and
DON JOHN: claw no man in his humour.
CONRADE: Yea, but you must not make the full show of this
CONRADE: till you may do it without controlment. You have of
CONRADE: late stood out against your brother, and he hath
CONRADE: ta'en you newly into his grace, where it is
CONRADE: impossible you should take true root but by the
CONRADE: fair weather that you make yourself: it is needful
CONRADE: that you frame the season for your own harvest.
DON JOHN: I had rather be a canker in a hedge than a rose in
DON JOHN: his grace, and it better fits my blood to be
DON JOHN: disdained of all than to fashion a carriage to rob
DON JOHN: love from any: in this, though I cannot be said to
DON JOHN: be a flattering honest man, it must not be denied
DON JOHN: but I am a plain-dealing villain. I am trusted with
DON JOHN: a muzzle and enfranchised with a clog, therefore I
DON JOHN: have decreed not to sing in my cage. If I had my
DON JOHN: mouth, I would bite, if I had my liberty, I would do
DON JOHN: my liking: in the meantime let me be that I am and
DON JOHN: seek not to alter me.
CONRADE: Can you make no use of your discontent?
DON JOHN: I make all use of it, for I use it only.
DON JOHN: Who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter BORACHIO
DON JOHN: What news, Borachio?
BORACHIO: I came yonder from a great supper: the prince your
BORACHIO: brother is royally entertained by Leonato: and I
BORACHIO: can give you intelligence of an intended marriage.
DON JOHN: Will it serve for any model to build mischief on?
DON JOHN: What is he for a fool that betroths himself to
DON JOHN: unquietness?
BORACHIO: Marry, it is your brother's right hand.
DON JOHN: Who? the most exquisite Claudio?
BORACHIO: Even he.
DON JOHN: A proper squire! And who, and who? which way looks
DON JOHN: he?
BORACHIO: Marry, on Hero, the daughter and heir of Leonato.
DON JOHN: A very forward March-chick! How came you to this?
BORACHIO: Being entertained for a perfumer, as I was smoking a
BORACHIO: musty room, comes me the prince and Claudio, hand
BORACHIO: in hand in sad conference: I whipt me behind the
BORACHIO: arras, and there heard it agreed upon that the
BORACHIO: prince should woo Hero for himself, and having
BORACHIO: obtained her, give her to Count Claudio.
DON JOHN: Come, come, let us thither: this may prove food to
DON JOHN: my displeasure. That young start-up hath all the
DON JOHN: glory of my overthrow: if I can cross him any way, I
DON JOHN: bless myself every way. You are both sure, and will assist me?
CONRADE: To the death, my lord.
DON JOHN: Let us to the great supper: their cheer is the
DON JOHN: greater that I am subdued. Would the cook were of
DON JOHN: my mind! Shall we go prove what's to be done?
BORACHIO: We'll wait upon your lordship.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A hall in LEONATO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO, ANTONIO, HERO, BEATRICE, and others
LEONATO: Was not Count John here at supper?
ANTONIO: I saw him not.
BEATRICE: How tartly that gentleman looks! I never can see
BEATRICE: him but I am heart-burned an hour after.
HERO: He is of a very melancholy disposition.
BEATRICE: He were an excellent man that were made just in the
BEATRICE: midway between him and Benedick: the one is too
BEATRICE: like an image and says nothing, and the other too
BEATRICE: like my lady's eldest son, evermore tattling.
LEONATO: Then half Signior Benedick's tongue in Count John's
LEONATO: mouth, and half Count John's melancholy in Signior
LEONATO: Benedick's face,--
BEATRICE: With a good leg and a good foot, uncle, and money
BEATRICE: enough in his purse, such a man would win any woman
BEATRICE: in the world, if a' could get her good-will.
LEONATO: By my troth, niece, thou wilt never get thee a
LEONATO: husband, if thou be so shrewd of thy tongue.
ANTONIO: In faith, she's too curst.
BEATRICE: Too curst is more than curst: I shall lessen God's
BEATRICE: sending that way, for it is said, 'God sends a curst
BEATRICE: cow short horns,' but to a cow too curst he sends none.
LEONATO: So, by being too curst, God will send you no horns.
BEATRICE: Just, if he send me no husband, for the which
BEATRICE: blessing I am at him upon my knees every morning and
BEATRICE: evening. Lord, I could not endure a husband with a
BEATRICE: beard on his face: I had rather lie in the woollen.
LEONATO: You may light on a husband that hath no beard.
BEATRICE: What should I do with him? dress him in my apparel
BEATRICE: and make him my waiting-gentlewoman? He that hath a
BEATRICE: beard is more than a youth, and he that hath no
BEATRICE: beard is less than a man: and he that is more than
BEATRICE: a youth is not for me, and he that is less than a
BEATRICE: man, I am not for him: therefore, I will even take
BEATRICE: sixpence in earnest of the bear-ward, and lead his
BEATRICE: apes into hell.
LEONATO: Well, then, go you into hell?
BEATRICE: No, but to the gate, and there will the devil meet
BEATRICE: me, like an old cuckold, with horns on his head, and
BEATRICE: say 'Get you to heaven, Beatrice, get you to
BEATRICE: heaven, here's no place for you maids:' so deliver
BEATRICE: I up my apes, and away to Saint Peter for the
BEATRICE: heavens, he shows me where the bachelors sit, and
BEATRICE: there live we as merry as the day is long.
ANTONIO: [To HERO]  Well, niece, I trust you will be ruled
ANTONIO: by your father.
BEATRICE: Yes, faith, it is my cousin's duty to make curtsy
BEATRICE: and say 'Father, as it please you.' But yet for all
BEATRICE: that, cousin, let him be a handsome fellow, or else
BEATRICE: make another curtsy and say 'Father, as it please
BEATRICE: me.'
LEONATO: Well, niece, I hope to see you one day fitted with a husband.
BEATRICE: Not till God make men of some other metal than
BEATRICE: earth. Would it not grieve a woman to be
BEATRICE: overmastered with a pierce of valiant dust? to make
BEATRICE: an account of her life to a clod of wayward marl?
BEATRICE: No, uncle, I'll none: Adam's sons are my brethren,
BEATRICE: and, truly, I hold it a sin to match in my kindred.
LEONATO: Daughter, remember what I told you: if the prince
LEONATO: do solicit you in that kind, you know your answer.
BEATRICE: The fault will be in the music, cousin, if you be
BEATRICE: not wooed in good time: if the prince be too
BEATRICE: important, tell him there is measure in every thing
BEATRICE: and so dance out the answer. For, hear me, Hero:
BEATRICE: wooing, wedding, and repenting, is as a Scotch jig,
BEATRICE: a measure, and a cinque pace: the first suit is hot
BEATRICE: and hasty, like a Scotch jig, and full as
BEATRICE: fantastical, the wedding, mannerly-modest, as a
BEATRICE: measure, full of state and ancientry, and then comes
BEATRICE: repentance and, with his bad legs, falls into the
BEATRICE: cinque pace faster and faster, till he sink into his grave.
LEONATO: Cousin, you apprehend passing shrewdly.
BEATRICE: I have a good eye, uncle, I can see a church by daylight.
LEONATO: The revellers are entering, brother: make good room.
NARRATOR: All put on their masks
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO, CLAUDIO, BENEDICK, BALTHASAR, DON JOHN, BORACHIO, MARGARET, URSULA and others, masked
DON PEDRO: Lady, will you walk about with your friend?
HERO: So you walk softly and look sweetly and say nothing,
HERO: I am yours for the walk, and especially when I walk away.
DON PEDRO: With me in your company?
HERO: I may say so, when I please.
DON PEDRO: And when please you to say so?
HERO: When I like your favour, for God defend the lute
HERO: should be like the case!
DON PEDRO: My visor is Philemon's roof, within the house is Jove.
HERO: Why, then, your visor should be thatched.
DON PEDRO: Speak low, if you speak love.
NARRATOR: Drawing her aside
BALTHASAR: Well, I would you did like me.
MARGARET: So would not I, for your own sake, for I have many
MARGARET: ill-qualities.
BALTHASAR: Which is one?
MARGARET: I say my prayers aloud.
BALTHASAR: I love you the better: the hearers may cry, Amen.
MARGARET: God match me with a good dancer!
BALTHASAR: Amen.
MARGARET: And God keep him out of my sight when the dance is
MARGARET: done! Answer, clerk.
BALTHASAR: No more words: the clerk is answered.
URSULA: I know you well enough, you are Signior Antonio.
ANTONIO: At a word, I am not.
URSULA: I know you by the waggling of your head.
ANTONIO: To tell you true, I counterfeit him.
URSULA: You could never do him so ill-well, unless you were
URSULA: the very man. Here's his dry hand up and down: you
URSULA: are he, you are he.
ANTONIO: At a word, I am not.
URSULA: Come, come, do you think I do not know you by your
URSULA: excellent wit? can virtue hide itself? Go to,
URSULA: mum, you are he: graces will appear, and there's an
URSULA: end.
BEATRICE: Will you not tell me who told you so?
BENEDICK: No, you shall pardon me.
BEATRICE: Nor will you not tell me who you are?
BENEDICK: Not now.
BEATRICE: That I was disdainful, and that I had my good wit
BEATRICE: out of the 'Hundred Merry Tales:'--well this was
BEATRICE: Signior Benedick that said so.
BENEDICK: What's he?
BEATRICE: I am sure you know him well enough.
BENEDICK: Not I, believe me.
BEATRICE: Did he never make you laugh?
BENEDICK: I pray you, what is he?
BEATRICE: Why, he is the prince's jester: a very dull fool,
BEATRICE: only his gift is in devising impossible slanders:
BEATRICE: none but libertines delight in him, and the
BEATRICE: commendation is not in his wit, but in his villany,
BEATRICE: for he both pleases men and angers them, and then
BEATRICE: they laugh at him and beat him. I am sure he is in
BEATRICE: the fleet: I would he had boarded me.
BENEDICK: When I know the gentleman, I'll tell him what you say.
BEATRICE: Do, do: he'll but break a comparison or two on me,
BEATRICE: which, peradventure not marked or not laughed at,
BEATRICE: strikes him into melancholy, and then there's a
BEATRICE: partridge wing saved, for the fool will eat no
BEATRICE: supper that night.
NARRATOR: Music
BEATRICE: We must follow the leaders.
BENEDICK: In every good thing.
BEATRICE: Nay, if they lead to any ill, I will leave them at
BEATRICE: the next turning.
NARRATOR: Dance. Then exeunt all except DON JOHN, BORACHIO, and CLAUDIO
DON JOHN: Sure my brother is amorous on Hero and hath
DON JOHN: withdrawn her father to break with him about it.
DON JOHN: The ladies follow her and but one visor remains.
BORACHIO: And that is Claudio: I know him by his bearing.
DON JOHN: Are not you Signior Benedick?
CLAUDIO: You know me well, I am he.
DON JOHN: Signior, you are very near my brother in his love:
DON JOHN: he is enamoured on Hero, I pray you, dissuade him
DON JOHN: from her: she is no equal for his birth: you may
DON JOHN: do the part of an honest man in it.
CLAUDIO: How know you he loves her?
DON JOHN: I heard him swear his affection.
BORACHIO: So did I too, and he swore he would marry her to-night.
DON JOHN: Come, let us to the banquet.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DON JOHN and BORACHIO
CLAUDIO: Thus answer I in the name of Benedick,
CLAUDIO: But hear these ill news with the ears of Claudio.
CLAUDIO: 'Tis certain so, the prince wooes for himself.
CLAUDIO: Friendship is constant in all other things
CLAUDIO: Save in the office and affairs of love:
CLAUDIO: Therefore, all hearts in love use their own tongues,
CLAUDIO: Let every eye negotiate for itself
CLAUDIO: And trust no agent, for beauty is a witch
CLAUDIO: Against whose charms faith melteth into blood.
CLAUDIO: This is an accident of hourly proof,
CLAUDIO: Which I mistrusted not. Farewell, therefore, Hero!
NARRATOR: Re-enter BENEDICK
BENEDICK: Count Claudio?
CLAUDIO: Yea, the same.
BENEDICK: Come, will you go with me?
CLAUDIO: Whither?
BENEDICK: Even to the next willow, about your own business,
BENEDICK: county. What fashion will you wear the garland of?
BENEDICK: about your neck, like an usurer's chain? or under
BENEDICK: your arm, like a lieutenant's scarf? You must wear
BENEDICK: it one way, for the prince hath got your Hero.
CLAUDIO: I wish him joy of her.
BENEDICK: Why, that's spoken like an honest drovier: so they
BENEDICK: sell bullocks. But did you think the prince would
BENEDICK: have served you thus?
CLAUDIO: I pray you, leave me.
BENEDICK: Ho! now you strike like the blind man: 'twas the
BENEDICK: boy that stole your meat, and you'll beat the post.
CLAUDIO: If it will not be, I'll leave you.
NARRATOR: Exit
BENEDICK: Alas, poor hurt fowl! now will he creep into sedges.
BENEDICK: But that my Lady Beatrice should know me, and not
BENEDICK: know me! The prince's fool! Ha? It may be I go
BENEDICK: under that title because I am merry. Yea, but so I
BENEDICK: am apt to do myself wrong, I am not so reputed: it
BENEDICK: is the base, though bitter, disposition of Beatrice
BENEDICK: that puts the world into her person and so gives me
BENEDICK: out. Well, I'll be revenged as I may.
NARRATOR: Re-enter DON PEDRO
DON PEDRO: Now, signior, where's the count? did you see him?
BENEDICK: Troth, my lord, I have played the part of Lady Fame.
BENEDICK: I found him here as melancholy as a lodge in a
BENEDICK: warren: I told him, and I think I told him true,
BENEDICK: that your grace had got the good will of this young
BENEDICK: lady, and I offered him my company to a willow-tree,
BENEDICK: either to make him a garland, as being forsaken, or
BENEDICK: to bind him up a rod, as being worthy to be whipped.
DON PEDRO: To be whipped! What's his fault?
BENEDICK: The flat transgression of a schoolboy, who, being
BENEDICK: overjoyed with finding a birds' nest, shows it his
BENEDICK: companion, and he steals it.
DON PEDRO: Wilt thou make a trust a transgression? The
DON PEDRO: transgression is in the stealer.
BENEDICK: Yet it had not been amiss the rod had been made,
BENEDICK: and the garland too, for the garland he might have
BENEDICK: worn himself, and the rod he might have bestowed on
BENEDICK: you, who, as I take it, have stolen his birds' nest.
DON PEDRO: I will but teach them to sing, and restore them to
DON PEDRO: the owner.
BENEDICK: If their singing answer your saying, by my faith,
BENEDICK: you say honestly.
DON PEDRO: The Lady Beatrice hath a quarrel to you: the
DON PEDRO: gentleman that danced with her told her she is much
DON PEDRO: wronged by you.
BENEDICK: O, she misused me past the endurance of a block!
BENEDICK: an oak but with one green leaf on it would have
BENEDICK: answered her, my very visor began to assume life and
BENEDICK: scold with her. She told me, not thinking I had been
BENEDICK: myself, that I was the prince's jester, that I was
BENEDICK: duller than a great thaw, huddling jest upon jest
BENEDICK: with such impossible conveyance upon me that I stood
BENEDICK: like a man at a mark, with a whole army shooting at
BENEDICK: me. She speaks poniards, and every word stabs:
BENEDICK: if her breath were as terrible as her terminations,
BENEDICK: there were no living near her, she would infect to
BENEDICK: the north star. I would not marry her, though she
BENEDICK: were endowed with all that Adam bad left him before
BENEDICK: he transgressed: she would have made Hercules have
BENEDICK: turned spit, yea, and have cleft his club to make
BENEDICK: the fire too. Come, talk not of her: you shall find
BENEDICK: her the infernal Ate in good apparel. I would to God
BENEDICK: some scholar would conjure her, for certainly, while
BENEDICK: she is here, a man may live as quiet in hell as in a
BENEDICK: sanctuary, and people sin upon purpose, because they
BENEDICK: would go thither, so, indeed, all disquiet, horror
BENEDICK: and perturbation follows her.
DON PEDRO: Look, here she comes.
NARRATOR: Enter CLAUDIO, BEATRICE, HERO, and LEONATO
BENEDICK: Will your grace command me any service to the
BENEDICK: world's end? I will go on the slightest errand now
BENEDICK: to the Antipodes that you can devise to send me on,
BENEDICK: I will fetch you a tooth-picker now from the
BENEDICK: furthest inch of Asia, bring you the length of
BENEDICK: Prester John's foot, fetch you a hair off the great
BENEDICK: Cham's beard, do you any embassage to the Pigmies,
BENEDICK: rather than hold three words' conference with this
BENEDICK: harpy. You have no employment for me?
DON PEDRO: None, but to desire your good company.
BENEDICK: O God, sir, here's a dish I love not: I cannot
BENEDICK: endure my Lady Tongue.
NARRATOR: Exit
DON PEDRO: Come, lady, come, you have lost the heart of
DON PEDRO: Signior Benedick.
BEATRICE: Indeed, my lord, he lent it me awhile, and I gave
BEATRICE: him use for it, a double heart for his single one:
BEATRICE: marry, once before he won it of me with false dice,
BEATRICE: therefore your grace may well say I have lost it.
DON PEDRO: You have put him down, lady, you have put him down.
BEATRICE: So I would not he should do me, my lord, lest I
BEATRICE: should prove the mother of fools. I have brought
BEATRICE: Count Claudio, whom you sent me to seek.
DON PEDRO: Why, how now, count! wherefore are you sad?
CLAUDIO: Not sad, my lord.
DON PEDRO: How then? sick?
CLAUDIO: Neither, my lord.
BEATRICE: The count is neither sad, nor sick, nor merry, nor
BEATRICE: well, but civil count, civil as an orange, and
BEATRICE: something of that jealous complexion.
DON PEDRO: I' faith, lady, I think your blazon to be true,
DON PEDRO: though, I'll be sworn, if he be so, his conceit is
DON PEDRO: false. Here, Claudio, I have wooed in thy name, and
DON PEDRO: fair Hero is won: I have broke with her father,
DON PEDRO: and his good will obtained: name the day of
DON PEDRO: marriage, and God give thee joy!
LEONATO: Count, take of me my daughter, and with her my
LEONATO: fortunes: his grace hath made the match, and an
LEONATO: grace say Amen to it.
BEATRICE: Speak, count, 'tis your cue.
CLAUDIO: Silence is the perfectest herald of joy: I were
CLAUDIO: but little happy, if I could say how much. Lady, as
CLAUDIO: you are mine, I am yours: I give away myself for
CLAUDIO: you and dote upon the exchange.
BEATRICE: Speak, cousin, or, if you cannot, stop his mouth
BEATRICE: with a kiss, and let not him speak neither.
DON PEDRO: In faith, lady, you have a merry heart.
BEATRICE: Yea, my lord, I thank it, poor fool, it keeps on
BEATRICE: the windy side of care. My cousin tells him in his
BEATRICE: ear that he is in her heart.
CLAUDIO: And so she doth, cousin.
BEATRICE: Good Lord, for alliance! Thus goes every one to the
BEATRICE: world but I, and I am sunburnt, I may sit in a
BEATRICE: corner and cry heigh-ho for a husband!
DON PEDRO: Lady Beatrice, I will get you one.
BEATRICE: I would rather have one of your father's getting.
BEATRICE: Hath your grace ne'er a brother like you? Your
BEATRICE: father got excellent husbands, if a maid could come by them.
DON PEDRO: Will you have me, lady?
BEATRICE: No, my lord, unless I might have another for
BEATRICE: working-days: your grace is too costly to wear
BEATRICE: every day. But, I beseech your grace, pardon me: I
BEATRICE: was born to speak all mirth and no matter.
DON PEDRO: Your silence most offends me, and to be merry best
DON PEDRO: becomes you, for, out of question, you were born in
DON PEDRO: a merry hour.
BEATRICE: No, sure, my lord, my mother cried, but then there
BEATRICE: was a star danced, and under that was I born.
BEATRICE: Cousins, God give you joy!
LEONATO: Niece, will you look to those things I told you of?
BEATRICE: I cry you mercy, uncle. By your grace's pardon.
NARRATOR: Exit
DON PEDRO: By my troth, a pleasant-spirited lady.
LEONATO: There's little of the melancholy element in her, my
LEONATO: lord: she is never sad but when she sleeps, and
LEONATO: not ever sad then, for I have heard my daughter say,
LEONATO: she hath often dreamed of unhappiness and waked
LEONATO: herself with laughing.
DON PEDRO: She cannot endure to hear tell of a husband.
LEONATO: O, by no means: she mocks all her wooers out of suit.
DON PEDRO: She were an excellent wife for Benedict.
LEONATO: O Lord, my lord, if they were but a week married,
LEONATO: they would talk themselves mad.
DON PEDRO: County Claudio, when mean you to go to church?
CLAUDIO: To-morrow, my lord: time goes on crutches till love
CLAUDIO: have all his rites.
LEONATO: Not till Monday, my dear son, which is hence a just
LEONATO: seven-night, and a time too brief, too, to have all
LEONATO: things answer my mind.
DON PEDRO: Come, you shake the head at so long a breathing:
DON PEDRO: but, I warrant thee, Claudio, the time shall not go
DON PEDRO: dully by us. I will in the interim undertake one of
DON PEDRO: Hercules' labours, which is, to bring Signior
DON PEDRO: Benedick and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of
DON PEDRO: affection the one with the other. I would fain have
DON PEDRO: it a match, and I doubt not but to fashion it, if
DON PEDRO: you three will but minister such assistance as I
DON PEDRO: shall give you direction.
LEONATO: My lord, I am for you, though it cost me ten
LEONATO: nights' watchings.
CLAUDIO: And I, my lord.
DON PEDRO: And you too, gentle Hero?
HERO: I will do any modest office, my lord, to help my
HERO: cousin to a good husband.
DON PEDRO: And Benedick is not the unhopefullest husband that
DON PEDRO: I know. Thus far can I praise him, he is of a noble
DON PEDRO: strain, of approved valour and confirmed honesty. I
DON PEDRO: will teach you how to humour your cousin, that she
DON PEDRO: shall fall in love with Benedick, and I, with your
DON PEDRO: two helps, will so practise on Benedick that, in
DON PEDRO: despite of his quick wit and his queasy stomach, he
DON PEDRO: shall fall in love with Beatrice. If we can do this,
DON PEDRO: Cupid is no longer an archer: hi s glory shall be
DON PEDRO: ours, for we are the only love-gods. Go in with me,
DON PEDRO: and I will tell you my drift.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter DON JOHN and BORACHIO
DON JOHN: It is so, the Count Claudio shall marry the
DON JOHN: daughter of Leonato.
BORACHIO: Yea, my lord, but I can cross it.
DON JOHN: Any bar, any cross, any impediment will be
DON JOHN: medicinable to me: I am sick in displeasure to him,
DON JOHN: and whatsoever comes athwart his affection ranges
DON JOHN: evenly with mine. How canst thou cross this marriage?
BORACHIO: Not honestly, my lord, but so covertly that no
BORACHIO: dishonesty shall appear in me.
DON JOHN: Show me briefly how.
BORACHIO: I think I told your lordship a year since, how much
BORACHIO: I am in the favour of Margaret, the waiting
BORACHIO: gentlewoman to Hero.
DON JOHN: I remember.
BORACHIO: I can, at any unseasonable instant of the night,
BORACHIO: appoint her to look out at her lady's chamber window.
DON JOHN: What life is in that, to be the death of this marriage?
BORACHIO: The poison of that lies in you to temper. Go you to
BORACHIO: the prince your brother, spare not to tell him that
BORACHIO: he hath wronged his honour in marrying the renowned
BORACHIO: Claudio--whose estimation do you mightily hold
BORACHIO: up--to a contaminated stale, such a one as Hero.
DON JOHN: What proof shall I make of that?
BORACHIO: Proof enough to misuse the prince, to vex Claudio,
BORACHIO: to undo Hero and kill Leonato. Look you for any
BORACHIO: other issue?
DON JOHN: Only to despite them, I will endeavour any thing.
BORACHIO: Go, then, find me a meet hour to draw Don Pedro and
BORACHIO: the Count Claudio alone: tell them that you know
BORACHIO: that Hero loves me, intend a kind of zeal both to the
BORACHIO: prince and Claudio, as,--in love of your brother's
BORACHIO: honour, who hath made this match, and his friend's
BORACHIO: reputation, who is thus like to be cozened with the
BORACHIO: semblance of a maid,--that you have discovered
BORACHIO: thus. They will scarcely believe this without trial:
BORACHIO: offer them instances, which shall bear no less
BORACHIO: likelihood than to see me at her chamber-window,
BORACHIO: hear me call Margaret Hero, hear Margaret term me
BORACHIO: Claudio, and bring them to see this the very night
BORACHIO: before the intended wedding,--for in the meantime I
BORACHIO: will so fashion the matter that Hero shall be
BORACHIO: absent,--and there shall appear such seeming truth
BORACHIO: of Hero's disloyalty that jealousy shall be called
BORACHIO: assurance and all the preparation overthrown.
DON JOHN: Grow this to what adverse issue it can, I will put
DON JOHN: it in practise. Be cunning in the working this, and
DON JOHN: thy fee is a thousand ducats.
BORACHIO: Be you constant in the accusation, and my cunning
BORACHIO: shall not shame me.
DON JOHN: I will presently go learn their day of marriage.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. LEONATO'S orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter BENEDICK
BENEDICK: Boy!
NARRATOR: Enter Boy
Boy: Signior?
BENEDICK: In my chamber-window lies a book: bring it hither
BENEDICK: to me in the orchard.
Boy: I am here already, sir.
BENEDICK: I know that, but I would have thee hence, and here again.
NARRATOR: Exit Boy
BENEDICK: I do much wonder that one man, seeing how much
BENEDICK: another man is a fool when he dedicates his
BENEDICK: behaviors to love, will, after he hath laughed at
BENEDICK: such shallow follies in others, become the argument
BENEDICK: of his own scorn by failing in love: and such a man
BENEDICK: is Claudio. I have known when there was no music
BENEDICK: with him but the drum and the fife, and now had he
BENEDICK: rather hear the tabour and the pipe: I have known
BENEDICK: when he would have walked ten mile a-foot to see a
BENEDICK: good armour, and now will he lie ten nights awake,
BENEDICK: carving the fashion of a new doublet. He was wont to
BENEDICK: speak plain and to the purpose, like an honest man
BENEDICK: and a soldier, and now is he turned orthography, his
BENEDICK: words are a very fantastical banquet, just so many
BENEDICK: strange dishes. May I be so converted and see with
BENEDICK: these eyes? I cannot tell, I think not: I will not
BENEDICK: be sworn, but love may transform me to an oyster, but
BENEDICK: I'll take my oath on it, till he have made an oyster
BENEDICK: of me, he shall never make me such a fool. One woman
BENEDICK: is fair, yet I am well, another is wise, yet I am
BENEDICK: well, another virtuous, yet I am well, but till all
BENEDICK: graces be in one woman, one woman shall not come in
BENEDICK: my grace. Rich she shall be, that's certain, wise,
BENEDICK: or I'll none, virtuous, or I'll never cheapen her,
BENEDICK: fair, or I'll   never look on her, mild, or come not
BENEDICK: near me, noble, or not I for an angel, of good
BENEDICK: discourse, an excellent musician, and her hair shall
BENEDICK: be of what colour it please God. Ha! the prince and
BENEDICK: Monsieur Love! I will hide me in the arbour.
NARRATOR: Withdraws
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO, CLAUDIO, and LEONATO
DON PEDRO: Come, shall we hear this music?
CLAUDIO: Yea, my good lord. How still the evening is,
CLAUDIO: As hush'd on purpose to grace harmony!
DON PEDRO: See you where Benedick hath hid himself?
CLAUDIO: O, very well, my lord: the music ended,
CLAUDIO: We'll fit the kid-fox with a pennyworth.
NARRATOR: Enter BALTHASAR with Music
DON PEDRO: Come, Balthasar, we'll hear that song again.
BALTHASAR: O, good my lord, tax not so bad a voice
BALTHASAR: To slander music any more than once.
DON PEDRO: It is the witness still of excellency
DON PEDRO: To put a strange face on his own perfection.
DON PEDRO: I pray thee, sing, and let me woo no more.
BALTHASAR: Because you talk of wooing, I will sing,
BALTHASAR: Since many a wooer doth commence his suit
BALTHASAR: To her he thinks not worthy, yet he wooes,
BALTHASAR: Yet will he swear he loves.
DON PEDRO: Now, pray thee, come,
DON PEDRO: Or, if thou wilt hold longer argument,
DON PEDRO: Do it in notes.
BALTHASAR: Note this before my notes,
BALTHASAR: There's not a note of mine that's worth the noting.
DON PEDRO: Why, these are very crotchets that he speaks,
DON PEDRO: Note, notes, forsooth, and nothing.
NARRATOR: Air
BENEDICK: Now, divine air! now is his soul ravished! Is it
BENEDICK: not strange that sheeps' guts should hale souls out
BENEDICK: of men's bodies? Well, a horn for my money, when
BENEDICK: all's done.
NARRATOR: The Song
BALTHASAR: Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more,
BALTHASAR: Men were deceivers ever,
BALTHASAR: One foot in sea and one on shore,
BALTHASAR: To one thing constant never:
BALTHASAR: Then sigh not so, but let them go,
BALTHASAR: And be you blithe and bonny,
BALTHASAR: Converting all your sounds of woe
BALTHASAR: Into Hey nonny, nonny.
BALTHASAR: Sing no more ditties, sing no moe,
BALTHASAR: Of dumps so dull and heavy,
BALTHASAR: The fraud of men was ever so,
BALTHASAR: Since summer first was leafy:
BALTHASAR: Then sigh not so,  and c.
DON PEDRO: By my troth, a good song.
BALTHASAR: And an ill singer, my lord.
DON PEDRO: Ha, no, no, faith, thou singest well enough for a shift.
BENEDICK: An he had been a dog that should have howled thus,
BENEDICK: they would have hanged him: and I pray God his bad
BENEDICK: voice bode no mischief. I had as lief have heard the
BENEDICK: night-raven, come what plague could have come after
BENEDICK: it.
DON PEDRO: Yea, marry, dost thou hear, Balthasar? I pray thee,
DON PEDRO: get us some excellent music, for to-morrow night we
DON PEDRO: would have it at the Lady Hero's chamber-window.
BALTHASAR: The best I can, my lord.
DON PEDRO: Do so: farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit BALTHASAR
DON PEDRO: Come hither, Leonato. What was it you told me of
DON PEDRO: to-day, that your niece Beatrice was in love with
DON PEDRO: Signior Benedick?
CLAUDIO: O, ay: stalk on. stalk on, the fowl sits. I did
CLAUDIO: never think that lady would have loved any man.
LEONATO: No, nor I neither, but most wonderful that she
LEONATO: should so dote on Signior Benedick, whom she hath in
LEONATO: all outward behaviors seemed ever to abhor.
BENEDICK: Is't possible? Sits the wind in that corner?
LEONATO: By my troth, my lord, I cannot tell what to think
LEONATO: of it but that she loves him with an enraged
LEONATO: affection: it is past the infinite of thought.
DON PEDRO: May be she doth but counterfeit.
CLAUDIO: Faith, like enough.
LEONATO: O God, counterfeit! There was never counterfeit of
LEONATO: passion came so near the life of passion as she
LEONATO: discovers it.
DON PEDRO: Why, what effects of passion shows she?
CLAUDIO: Bait the hook well, this fish will bite.
LEONATO: What effects, my lord? She will sit you, you heard
LEONATO: my daughter tell you how.
CLAUDIO: She did, indeed.
DON PEDRO: How, how, pray you? You amaze me: I would have I
DON PEDRO: thought her spirit had been invincible against all
DON PEDRO: assaults of affection.
LEONATO: I would have sworn it had, my lord, especially
LEONATO: against Benedick.
BENEDICK: I should think this a gull, but that the
BENEDICK: white-bearded fellow speaks it: knavery cannot,
BENEDICK: sure, hide himself in such reverence.
CLAUDIO: He hath ta'en the infection: hold it up.
DON PEDRO: Hath she made her affection known to Benedick?
LEONATO: No, and swears she never will: that's her torment.
CLAUDIO: 'Tis true, indeed, so your daughter says: 'Shall
CLAUDIO: I,' says she, 'that have so oft encountered him
CLAUDIO: with scorn, write to him that I love him?'
LEONATO: This says she now when she is beginning to write to
LEONATO: him, for she'll be up twenty times a night, and
LEONATO: there will she sit in her smock till she have writ a
LEONATO: sheet of paper: my daughter tells us all.
CLAUDIO: Now you talk of a sheet of paper, I remember a
CLAUDIO: pretty jest your daughter told us of.
LEONATO: O, when she had writ it and was reading it over, she
LEONATO: found Benedick and Beatrice between the sheet?
CLAUDIO: That.
LEONATO: O, she tore the letter into a thousand halfpence,
LEONATO: railed at herself, that she should be so immodest
LEONATO: to write to one that she knew would flout her, 'I
LEONATO: measure him,' says she, 'by my own spirit, for I
LEONATO: should flout him, if he writ to me, yea, though I
LEONATO: love him, I should.'
CLAUDIO: Then down upon her knees she falls, weeps, sobs,
CLAUDIO: beats her heart, tears her hair, prays, curses, 'O
CLAUDIO: sweet Benedick! God give me patience!'
LEONATO: She doth indeed, my daughter says so: and the
LEONATO: ecstasy hath so much overborne her that my daughter
LEONATO: is sometime afeared she will do a desperate outrage
LEONATO: to herself: it is very true.
DON PEDRO: It were good that Benedick knew of it by some
DON PEDRO: other, if she will not discover it.
CLAUDIO: To what end? He would make but a sport of it and
CLAUDIO: torment the poor lady worse.
DON PEDRO: An he should, it were an alms to hang him. She's an
DON PEDRO: excellent sweet lady, and, out of all suspicion,
DON PEDRO: she is virtuous.
CLAUDIO: And she is exceeding wise.
DON PEDRO: In every thing but in loving Benedick.
LEONATO: O, my lord, wisdom and blood combating in so tender
LEONATO: a body, we have ten proofs to one that blood hath
LEONATO: the victory. I am sorry for her, as I have just
LEONATO: cause, being her uncle and her guardian.
DON PEDRO: I would she had bestowed this dotage on me: I would
DON PEDRO: have daffed all other respects and made her half
DON PEDRO: myself. I pray you, tell Benedick of it, and hear
DON PEDRO: what a' will say.
LEONATO: Were it good, think you?
CLAUDIO: Hero thinks surely she will die, for she says she
CLAUDIO: will die, if he love her not, and she will die, ere
CLAUDIO: she make her love known, and she will die, if he woo
CLAUDIO: her, rather than she will bate one breath of her
CLAUDIO: accustomed crossness.
DON PEDRO: She doth well: if she should make tender of her
DON PEDRO: love, 'tis very possible he'll scorn it, for the
DON PEDRO: man, as you know all, hath a contemptible spirit.
CLAUDIO: He is a very proper man.
DON PEDRO: He hath indeed a good outward happiness.
CLAUDIO: Before God! and, in my mind, very wise.
DON PEDRO: He doth indeed show some sparks that are like wit.
CLAUDIO: And I take him to be valiant.
DON PEDRO: As Hector, I assure you: and in the managing of
DON PEDRO: quarrels you may say he is wise, for either he
DON PEDRO: avoids them with great discretion, or undertakes
DON PEDRO: them with a most Christian-like fear.
LEONATO: If he do fear God, a' must necessarily keep peace:
LEONATO: if he break the peace, he ought to enter into a
LEONATO: quarrel with fear and trembling.
DON PEDRO: And so will he do, for the man doth fear God,
DON PEDRO: howsoever it seems not in him by some large jests
DON PEDRO: he will make. Well I am sorry for your niece. Shall
DON PEDRO: we go seek Benedick, and tell him of her love?
CLAUDIO: Never tell him, my lord: let her wear it out with
CLAUDIO: good counsel.
LEONATO: Nay, that's impossible: she may wear her heart out first.
DON PEDRO: Well, we will hear further of it by your daughter:
DON PEDRO: let it cool the while. I love Benedick well, and I
DON PEDRO: could wish he would modestly examine himself, to see
DON PEDRO: how much he is unworthy so good a lady.
LEONATO: My lord, will you walk? dinner is ready.
CLAUDIO: If he do not dote on her upon this, I will never
CLAUDIO: trust my expectation.
DON PEDRO: Let there be the same net spread for her, and that
DON PEDRO: must your daughter and her gentlewomen carry. The
DON PEDRO: sport will be, when they hold one an opinion of
DON PEDRO: another's dotage, and no such matter: that's the
DON PEDRO: scene that I would see, which will be merely a
DON PEDRO: dumb-show. Let us send her to call him in to dinner.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DON PEDRO, CLAUDIO, and LEONATO
BENEDICK: [Coming forward]  This can be no trick: the
BENEDICK: conference was sadly borne. They have the truth of
BENEDICK: this from Hero. They seem to pity the lady: it
BENEDICK: seems her affections have their full bent. Love me!
BENEDICK: why, it must be requited. I hear how I am censured:
BENEDICK: they say I will bear myself proudly, if I perceive
BENEDICK: the love come from her, they say too that she will
BENEDICK: rather die than give any sign of affection. I did
BENEDICK: never think to marry: I must not seem proud: happy
BENEDICK: are they that hear their detractions and can put
BENEDICK: them to mending. They say the lady is fair, 'tis a
BENEDICK: truth, I can bear them witness, and virtuous, 'tis
BENEDICK: so, I cannot reprove it, and wise, but for loving
BENEDICK: me, by my troth, it is no addition to her wit, nor
BENEDICK: no great argument of her folly, for I will be
BENEDICK: horribly in love with her. I may chance have some
BENEDICK: odd quirks and remnants of wit broken on me,
BENEDICK: because I have railed so long against marriage: but
BENEDICK: doth not the appetite alter? a man loves the meat
BENEDICK: in his youth that he cannot endure in his age.
BENEDICK: Shall quips and sentences and these paper bullets of
BENEDICK: the brain awe a man from the career of his humour?
BENEDICK: No, the world must be peopled. When I said I would
BENEDICK: die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I
BENEDICK: were married. Here comes Beatrice. By this day!
BENEDICK: she's a fair lady: I do spy some marks of love in
BENEDICK: her.
NARRATOR: Enter BEATRICE
BEATRICE: Against my will I am sent to bid you come in to dinner.
BENEDICK: Fair Beatrice, I thank you for your pains.
BEATRICE: I took no more pains for those thanks than you take
BEATRICE: pains to thank me: if it had been painful, I would
BEATRICE: not have come.
BENEDICK: You take pleasure then in the message?
BEATRICE: Yea, just so much as you may take upon a knife's
BEATRICE: point and choke a daw withal. You have no stomach,
BEATRICE: signior: fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit
BENEDICK: Ha! 'Against my will I am sent to bid you come in
BENEDICK: to dinner,' there's a double meaning in that 'I took
BENEDICK: no more pains for those thanks than you took pains
BENEDICK: to thank me.' that's as much as to say, Any pains
BENEDICK: that I take for you is as easy as thanks. If I do
BENEDICK: not take pity of her, I am a villain, if I do not
BENEDICK: love her, I am a Jew. I will go get her picture.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. LEONATO'S garden.
NARRATOR: Enter HERO, MARGARET, and URSULA
HERO: Good Margaret, run thee to the parlor,
HERO: There shalt thou find my cousin Beatrice
HERO: Proposing with the prince and Claudio:
HERO: Whisper her ear and tell her, I and Ursula
HERO: Walk in the orchard and our whole discourse
HERO: Is all of her, say that thou overheard'st us,
HERO: And bid her steal into the pleached bower,
HERO: Where honeysuckles, ripen'd by the sun,
HERO: Forbid the sun to enter, like favourites,
HERO: Made proud by princes, that advance their pride
HERO: Against that power that bred it: there will she hide her,
HERO: To listen our purpose.  This is thy office,
HERO: Bear thee well in it and leave us alone.
MARGARET: I'll make her come, I warrant you, presently.
NARRATOR: Exit
HERO: Now, Ursula, when Beatrice doth come,
HERO: As we do trace this alley up and down,
HERO: Our talk must only be of Benedick.
HERO: When I do name him, let it be thy part
HERO: To praise him more than ever man did merit:
HERO: My talk to thee must be how Benedick
HERO: Is sick in love with Beatrice. Of this matter
HERO: Is little Cupid's crafty arrow made,
HERO: That only wounds by hearsay.
NARRATOR: Enter BEATRICE, behind
HERO: Now begin,
HERO: For look where Beatrice, like a lapwing, runs
HERO: Close by the ground, to hear our conference.
URSULA: The pleasant'st angling is to see the fish
URSULA: Cut with her golden oars the silver stream,
URSULA: And greedily devour the treacherous bait:
URSULA: So angle we for Beatrice, who even now
URSULA: Is couched in the woodbine coverture.
URSULA: Fear you not my part of the dialogue.
HERO: Then go we near her, that her ear lose nothing
HERO: Of the false sweet bait that we lay for it.
NARRATOR: Approaching the bower
HERO: No, truly, Ursula, she is too disdainful,
HERO: I know her spirits are as coy and wild
HERO: As haggerds of the rock.
URSULA: But are you sure
URSULA: That Benedick loves Beatrice so entirely?
HERO: So says the prince and my new-trothed lord.
URSULA: And did they bid you tell her of it, madam?
HERO: They did entreat me to acquaint her of it,
HERO: But I persuaded them, if they loved Benedick,
HERO: To wish him wrestle with affection,
HERO: And never to let Beatrice know of it.
URSULA: Why did you so? Doth not the gentleman
URSULA: Deserve as full as fortunate a bed
URSULA: As ever Beatrice shall couch upon?
HERO: O god of love! I know he doth deserve
HERO: As much as may be yielded to a man:
HERO: But Nature never framed a woman's heart
HERO: Of prouder stuff than that of Beatrice,
HERO: Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes,
HERO: Misprising what they look on, and her wit
HERO: Values itself so highly that to her
HERO: All matter else seems weak: she cannot love,
HERO: Nor take no shape nor project of affection,
HERO: She is so self-endeared.
URSULA: Sure, I think so,
URSULA: And therefore certainly it were not good
URSULA: She knew his love, lest she make sport at it.
HERO: Why, you speak truth. I never yet saw man,
HERO: How wise, how noble, young, how rarely featured,
HERO: But she would spell him backward: if fair-faced,
HERO: She would swear the gentleman should be her sister,
HERO: If black, why, Nature, drawing of an antique,
HERO: Made a foul blot, if tall, a lance ill-headed,
HERO: If low, an agate very vilely cut,
HERO: If speaking, why, a vane blown with all winds,
HERO: If silent, why, a block moved with none.
HERO: So turns she every man the wrong side out
HERO: And never gives to truth and virtue that
HERO: Which simpleness and merit purchaseth.
URSULA: Sure, sure, such carping is not commendable.
HERO: No, not to be so odd and from all fashions
HERO: As Beatrice is, cannot be commendable:
HERO: But who dare tell her so? If I should speak,
HERO: She would mock me into air, O, she would laugh me
HERO: Out of myself, press me to death with wit.
HERO: Therefore let Benedick, like cover'd fire,
HERO: Consume away in sighs, waste inwardly:
HERO: It were a better death than die with mocks,
HERO: Which is as bad as die with tickling.
URSULA: Yet tell her of it: hear what she will say.
HERO: No, rather I will go to Benedick
HERO: And counsel him to fight against his passion.
HERO: And, truly, I'll devise some honest slanders
HERO: To stain my cousin with: one doth not know
HERO: How much an ill word may empoison liking.
URSULA: O, do not do your cousin such a wrong.
URSULA: She cannot be so much without true judgment--
URSULA: Having so swift and excellent a wit
URSULA: As she is prized to have--as to refuse
URSULA: So rare a gentleman as Signior Benedick.
HERO: He is the only man of Italy.
HERO: Always excepted my dear Claudio.
URSULA: I pray you, be not angry with me, madam,
URSULA: Speaking my fancy: Signior Benedick,
URSULA: For shape, for bearing, argument and valour,
URSULA: Goes foremost in report through Italy.
HERO: Indeed, he hath an excellent good name.
URSULA: His excellence did earn it, ere he had it.
URSULA: When are you married, madam?
HERO: Why, every day, to-morrow. Come, go in:
HERO: I'll show thee some attires, and have thy counsel
HERO: Which is the best to furnish me to-morrow.
URSULA: She's limed, I warrant you: we have caught her, madam.
HERO: If it proves so, then loving goes by haps:
HERO: Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
NARRATOR: Exeunt HERO and URSULA
BEATRICE: [Coming forward]
BEATRICE: What fire is in mine ears? Can this be true?
BEATRICE: Stand I condemn'd for pride and scorn so much?
BEATRICE: Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu!
BEATRICE: No glory lives behind the back of such.
BEATRICE: And, Benedick, love on, I will requite thee,
BEATRICE: Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand:
BEATRICE: If thou dost love, my kindness shall incite thee
BEATRICE: To bind our loves up in a holy band,
BEATRICE: For others say thou dost deserve, and I
BEATRICE: Believe it better than reportingly.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in LEONATO'S house
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO, CLAUDIO, BENEDICK, and LEONATO
DON PEDRO: I do but stay till your marriage be consummate, and
DON PEDRO: then go I toward Arragon.
CLAUDIO: I'll bring you thither, my lord, if you'll
CLAUDIO: vouchsafe me.
DON PEDRO: Nay, that would be as great a soil in the new gloss
DON PEDRO: of your marriage as to show a child his new coat
DON PEDRO: and forbid him to wear it. I will only be bold
DON PEDRO: with Benedick for his company, for, from the crown
DON PEDRO: of his head to the sole of his foot, he is all
DON PEDRO: mirth: he hath twice or thrice cut Cupid's
DON PEDRO: bow-string and the little hangman dare not shoot at
DON PEDRO: him, he hath a heart as sound as a bell and his
DON PEDRO: tongue is the clapper, for what his heart thinks his
DON PEDRO: tongue speaks.
BENEDICK: Gallants, I am not as I have been.
LEONATO: So say I	methinks you are sadder.
CLAUDIO: I hope he be in love.
DON PEDRO: Hang him, truant! there's no true drop of blood in
DON PEDRO: him, to be truly touched with love: if he be sad,
DON PEDRO: he wants money.
BENEDICK: I have the toothache.
DON PEDRO: Draw it.
BENEDICK: Hang it!
CLAUDIO: You must hang it first, and draw it afterwards.
DON PEDRO: What! sigh for the toothache?
LEONATO: Where is but a humour or a worm.
BENEDICK: Well, every one can master a grief but he that has
BENEDICK: it.
CLAUDIO: Yet say I, he is in love.
DON PEDRO: There is no appearance of fancy in him, unless it be
DON PEDRO: a fancy that he hath to strange disguises, as, to be
DON PEDRO: a Dutchman today, a Frenchman to-morrow, or in the
DON PEDRO: shape of two countries at once, as, a German from
DON PEDRO: the waist downward, all slops, and a Spaniard from
DON PEDRO: the hip upward, no doublet. Unless he have a fancy
DON PEDRO: to this foolery, as it appears he hath, he is no
DON PEDRO: fool for fancy, as you would have it appear he is.
CLAUDIO: If he be not in love with some woman, there is no
CLAUDIO: believing old signs: a' brushes his hat o'
CLAUDIO: mornings, what should that bode?
DON PEDRO: Hath any man seen him at the barber's?
CLAUDIO: No, but the barber's man hath been seen with him,
CLAUDIO: and the old ornament of his cheek hath already
CLAUDIO: stuffed tennis-balls.
LEONATO: Indeed, he looks younger than he did, by the loss of a beard.
DON PEDRO: Nay, a' rubs himself with civet: can you smell him
DON PEDRO: out by that?
CLAUDIO: That's as much as to say, the sweet youth's in love.
DON PEDRO: The greatest note of it is his melancholy.
CLAUDIO: And when was he wont to wash his face?
DON PEDRO: Yea, or to paint himself? for the which, I hear
DON PEDRO: what they say of him.
CLAUDIO: Nay, but his jesting spirit, which is now crept into
CLAUDIO: a lute-string and now governed by stops.
DON PEDRO: Indeed, that tells a heavy tale for him: conclude,
DON PEDRO: conclude he is in love.
CLAUDIO: Nay, but I know who loves him.
DON PEDRO: That would I know too: I warrant, one that knows him not.
CLAUDIO: Yes, and his ill conditions, and, in despite of
CLAUDIO: all, dies for him.
DON PEDRO: She shall be buried with her face upwards.
BENEDICK: Yet is this no charm for the toothache. Old
BENEDICK: signior, walk aside with me: I have studied eight
BENEDICK: or nine wise words to speak to you, which these
BENEDICK: hobby-horses must not hear.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BENEDICK and LEONATO
DON PEDRO: For my life, to break with him about Beatrice.
CLAUDIO: 'Tis even so. Hero and Margaret have by this
CLAUDIO: played their parts with Beatrice, and then the two
CLAUDIO: bears will not bite one another when they meet.
NARRATOR: Enter DON JOHN
DON JOHN: My lord and brother, God save you!
DON PEDRO: Good den, brother.
DON JOHN: If your leisure served, I would speak with you.
DON PEDRO: In private?
DON JOHN: If it please you: yet Count Claudio may hear, for
DON JOHN: what I would speak of concerns him.
DON PEDRO: What's the matter?
DON JOHN: [To CLAUDIO]  Means your lordship to be married
DON JOHN: to-morrow?
DON PEDRO: You know he does.
DON JOHN: I know not that, when he knows what I know.
CLAUDIO: If there be any impediment, I pray you discover it.
DON JOHN: You may think I love you not: let that appear
DON JOHN: hereafter, and aim better at me by that I now will
DON JOHN: manifest. For my brother, I think he holds you
DON JOHN: well, and in dearness of heart hath holp to effect
DON JOHN: your ensuing marriage,--surely suit ill spent and
DON JOHN: labour ill bestowed.
DON PEDRO: Why, what's the matter?
DON JOHN: I came hither to tell you, and, circumstances
DON JOHN: shortened, for she has been too long a talking of,
DON JOHN: the lady is disloyal.
CLAUDIO: Who, Hero?
DON PEDRO: Even she, Leonato's Hero, your Hero, every man's Hero:
CLAUDIO: Disloyal?
DON JOHN: The word is too good to paint out her wickedness, I
DON JOHN: could say she were worse: think you of a worse
DON JOHN: title, and I will fit her to it. Wonder not till
DON JOHN: further warrant: go but with me to-night, you shall
DON JOHN: see her chamber-window entered, even the night
DON JOHN: before her wedding-day: if you love her then,
DON JOHN: to-morrow wed her, but it would better fit your honour
DON JOHN: to change your mind.
CLAUDIO: May this be so?
DON PEDRO: I will not think it.
DON JOHN: If you dare not trust that you see, confess not
DON JOHN: that you know: if you will follow me, I will show
DON JOHN: you enough, and when you have seen more and heard
DON JOHN: more, proceed accordingly.
CLAUDIO: If I see any thing to-night why I should not marry
CLAUDIO: her to-morrow in the congregation, where I should
CLAUDIO: wed, there will I shame her.
DON PEDRO: And, as I wooed for thee to obtain her, I will join
DON PEDRO: with thee to disgrace her.
DON JOHN: I will disparage her no farther till you are my
DON JOHN: witnesses: bear it coldly but till midnight, and
DON JOHN: let the issue show itself.
DON PEDRO: O day untowardly turned!
CLAUDIO: O mischief strangely thwarting!
DON JOHN: O plague right well prevented! so will you say when
DON JOHN: you have seen the sequel.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter DOGBERRY and VERGES with the Watch
DOGBERRY: Are you good men and true?
VERGES: Yea, or else it were pity but they should suffer
VERGES: salvation, body and soul.
DOGBERRY: Nay, that were a punishment too good for them, if
DOGBERRY: they should have any allegiance in them, being
DOGBERRY: chosen for the prince's watch.
VERGES: Well, give them their charge, neighbour Dogberry.
DOGBERRY: First, who think you the most desertless man to be
DOGBERRY: constable?
First Watchman: Hugh Otecake, sir, or George Seacole, for they can
First Watchman: write and read.
DOGBERRY: Come hither, neighbour Seacole. God hath blessed
DOGBERRY: you with a good name: to be a well-favoured man is
DOGBERRY: the gift of fortune, but to write and read comes by nature.
Second Watchman: Both which, master constable,--
DOGBERRY: You have: I knew it would be your answer. Well,
DOGBERRY: for your favour, sir, why, give God thanks, and make
DOGBERRY: no boast of it, and for your writing and reading,
DOGBERRY: let that appear when there is no need of such
DOGBERRY: vanity. You are thought here to be the most
DOGBERRY: senseless and fit man for the constable of the
DOGBERRY: watch, therefore bear you the lantern. This is your
DOGBERRY: charge: you shall comprehend all vagrom men, you are
DOGBERRY: to bid any man stand, in the prince's name.
Second Watchman: How if a' will not stand?
DOGBERRY: Why, then, take no note of him, but let him go, and
DOGBERRY: presently call the rest of the watch together and
DOGBERRY: thank God you are rid of a knave.
VERGES: If he will not stand when he is bidden, he is none
VERGES: of the prince's subjects.
DOGBERRY: True, and they are to meddle with none but the
DOGBERRY: prince's subjects. You shall also make no noise in
DOGBERRY: the streets, for, for the watch to babble and to
DOGBERRY: talk is most tolerable and not to be endured.
Watchman: We will rather sleep than talk: we know what
Watchman: belongs to a watch.
DOGBERRY: Why, you speak like an ancient and most quiet
DOGBERRY: watchman, for I cannot see how sleeping should
DOGBERRY: offend: only, have a care that your bills be not
DOGBERRY: stolen. Well, you are to call at all the
DOGBERRY: ale-houses, and bid those that are drunk get them to bed.
Watchman: How if they will not?
DOGBERRY: Why, then, let them alone till they are sober: if
DOGBERRY: they make you not then the better answer, you may
DOGBERRY: say they are not the men you took them for.
Watchman: Well, sir.
DOGBERRY: If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, by virtue
DOGBERRY: of your office, to be no true man, and, for such
DOGBERRY: kind of men, the less you meddle or make with them,
DOGBERRY: why the more is for your honesty.
Watchman: If we know him to be a thief, shall we not lay
Watchman: hands on him?
DOGBERRY: Truly, by your office, you may, but I think they
DOGBERRY: that touch pitch will be defiled: the most peaceable
DOGBERRY: way for you, if you do take a thief, is to let him
DOGBERRY: show himself what he is and steal out of your company.
VERGES: You have been always called a merciful man, partner.
DOGBERRY: Truly, I would not hang a dog by my will, much more
DOGBERRY: a man who hath any honesty in him.
VERGES: If you hear a child cry in the night, you must call
VERGES: to the nurse and bid her still it.
Watchman: How if the nurse be asleep and will not hear us?
DOGBERRY: Why, then, depart in peace, and let the child wake
DOGBERRY: her with crying, for the ewe that will not hear her
DOGBERRY: lamb when it baes will never answer a calf when he bleats.
VERGES: 'Tis very true.
DOGBERRY: This is the end of the charge:--you, constable, are
DOGBERRY: to present the prince's own person: if you meet the
DOGBERRY: prince in the night, you may stay him.
VERGES: Nay, by'r our lady, that I think a' cannot.
DOGBERRY: Five shillings to one on't, with any man that knows
DOGBERRY: the statutes, he may stay him: marry, not without
DOGBERRY: the prince be willing, for, indeed, the watch ought
DOGBERRY: to offend no man, and it is an offence to stay a
DOGBERRY: man against his will.
VERGES: By'r lady, I think it be so.
DOGBERRY: Ha, ha, ha! Well, masters, good night: an there be
DOGBERRY: any matter of weight chances, call up me: keep your
DOGBERRY: fellows' counsels and your own, and good night.
DOGBERRY: Come, neighbour.
Watchman: Well, masters, we hear our charge: let us go sit here
Watchman: upon the church-bench till two, and then all to bed.
DOGBERRY: One word more, honest neighbours. I pray you watch
DOGBERRY: about Signior Leonato's door, for the wedding being
DOGBERRY: there to-morrow, there is a great coil to-night.
DOGBERRY: Adieu: be vigitant, I beseech you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DOGBERRY and VERGES
NARRATOR: Enter BORACHIO and CONRADE
BORACHIO: What Conrade!
Watchman: [Aside]  Peace! stir not.
BORACHIO: Conrade, I say!
CONRADE: Here, man, I am at thy elbow.
BORACHIO: Mass, and my elbow itched, I thought there would a
BORACHIO: scab follow.
CONRADE: I will owe thee an answer for that: and now forward
CONRADE: with thy tale.
BORACHIO: Stand thee close, then, under this pent-house, for
BORACHIO: it drizzles rain, and I will, like a true drunkard,
BORACHIO: utter all to thee.
Watchman: [Aside]  Some treason, masters: yet stand close.
BORACHIO: Therefore know I have earned of Don John a thousand ducats.
CONRADE: Is it possible that any villany should be so dear?
BORACHIO: Thou shouldst rather ask if it were possible any
BORACHIO: villany should be so rich, for when rich villains
BORACHIO: have need of poor ones, poor ones may make what
BORACHIO: price they will.
CONRADE: I wonder at it.
BORACHIO: That shows thou art unconfirmed. Thou knowest that
BORACHIO: the fashion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloak, is
BORACHIO: nothing to a man.
CONRADE: Yes, it is apparel.
BORACHIO: I mean, the fashion.
CONRADE: Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
BORACHIO: Tush! I may as well say the fool's the fool. But
BORACHIO: seest thou not what a deformed thief this fashion
BORACHIO: is?
Watchman: [Aside]  I know that Deformed, a' has been a vile
Watchman: thief this seven year, a' goes up and down like a
Watchman: gentleman: I remember his name.
BORACHIO: Didst thou not hear somebody?
CONRADE: No, 'twas the vane on the house.
BORACHIO: Seest thou not, I say, what a deformed thief this
BORACHIO: fashion is? how giddily a' turns about all the hot
BORACHIO: bloods between fourteen and five-and-thirty?
BORACHIO: sometimes fashioning them like Pharaoh's soldiers
BORACHIO: in the reeky painting, sometime like god Bel's
BORACHIO: priests in the old church-window, sometime like the
BORACHIO: shaven Hercules in the smirched worm-eaten tapestry,
BORACHIO: where his codpiece seems as massy as his club?
CONRADE: All this I see, and I see that the fashion wears
CONRADE: out more apparel than the man. But art not thou
CONRADE: thyself giddy with the fashion too, that thou hast
CONRADE: shifted out of thy tale into telling me of the fashion?
BORACHIO: Not so, neither: but know that I have to-night
BORACHIO: wooed Margaret, the Lady Hero's gentlewoman, by the
BORACHIO: name of Hero: she leans me out at her mistress'
BORACHIO: chamber-window, bids me a thousand times good
BORACHIO: night,--I tell this tale vilely:--I should first
BORACHIO: tell thee how the prince, Claudio and my master,
BORACHIO: planted and placed and possessed by my master Don
BORACHIO: John, saw afar off in the orchard this amiable encounter.
CONRADE: And thought they Margaret was Hero?
BORACHIO: Two of them did, the prince and Claudio, but the
BORACHIO: devil my master knew she was Margaret, and partly
BORACHIO: by his oaths, which first possessed them, partly by
BORACHIO: the dark night, which did deceive them, but chiefly
BORACHIO: by my villany, which did confirm any slander that
BORACHIO: Don John had made, away went Claudio enraged, swore
BORACHIO: he would meet her, as he was appointed, next morning
BORACHIO: at the temple, and there, before the whole
BORACHIO: congregation, shame her with what he saw o'er night
BORACHIO: and send her home again without a husband.
First Watchman: We charge you, in the prince's name, stand!
Second Watchman: Call up the right master constable. We have here
Second Watchman: recovered the most dangerous piece of lechery that
Second Watchman: ever was known in the commonwealth.
First Watchman: And one Deformed is one of them: I know him, a'
First Watchman: wears a lock.
CONRADE: Masters, masters,--
Second Watchman: You'll be made bring Deformed forth, I warrant you.
CONRADE: Masters,--
First Watchman: Never speak: we charge you let us obey you to go with us.
BORACHIO: We are like to prove a goodly commodity, being taken
BORACHIO: up of these men's bills.
CONRADE: A commodity in question, I warrant you. Come, we'll obey you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. HERO's apartment.
NARRATOR: Enter HERO, MARGARET, and URSULA
HERO: Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice, and desire
HERO: her to rise.
URSULA: I will, lady.
HERO: And bid her come hither.
URSULA: Well.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARGARET: Troth, I think your other rabato were better.
HERO: No, pray thee, good Meg, I'll wear this.
MARGARET: By my troth, 's not so good, and I warrant your
MARGARET: cousin will say so.
HERO: My cousin's a fool, and thou art another: I'll wear
HERO: none but this.
MARGARET: I like the new tire within excellently, if the hair
MARGARET: were a thought browner, and your gown's a most rare
MARGARET: fashion, i' faith. I saw the Duchess of Milan's
MARGARET: gown that they praise so.
HERO: O, that exceeds, they say.
MARGARET: By my troth, 's but a night-gown in respect of
MARGARET: yours: cloth o' gold, and cuts, and laced with
MARGARET: silver, set with pearls, down sleeves, side sleeves,
MARGARET: and skirts, round underborne with a bluish tinsel:
MARGARET: but for a fine, quaint, graceful and excellent
MARGARET: fashion, yours is worth ten on 't.
HERO: God give me joy to wear it! for my heart is
HERO: exceeding heavy.
MARGARET: 'Twill be heavier soon by the weight of a man.
HERO: Fie upon thee! art not ashamed?
MARGARET: Of what, lady? of speaking honourably? Is not
MARGARET: marriage honourable in a beggar? Is not your lord
MARGARET: honourable without marriage? I think you would have
MARGARET: me say, 'saving your reverence, a husband:' and bad
MARGARET: thinking do not wrest true speaking, I'll offend
MARGARET: nobody: is there any harm in 'the heavier for a
MARGARET: husband'? None, I think, and it be the right husband
MARGARET: and the right wife, otherwise 'tis light, and not
MARGARET: heavy: ask my Lady Beatrice else, here she comes.
NARRATOR: Enter BEATRICE
HERO: Good morrow, coz.
BEATRICE: Good morrow, sweet Hero.
HERO: Why how now? do you speak in the sick tune?
BEATRICE: I am out of all other tune, methinks.
MARGARET: Clap's into 'Light o' love,' that goes without a
MARGARET: burden: do you sing it, and I'll dance it.
BEATRICE: Ye light o' love, with your heels! then, if your
BEATRICE: husband have stables enough, you'll see he shall
BEATRICE: lack no barns.
MARGARET: O illegitimate construction! I scorn that with my heels.
BEATRICE: 'Tis almost five o'clock, cousin, tis time you were
BEATRICE: ready. By my troth, I am exceeding ill: heigh-ho!
MARGARET: For a hawk, a horse, or a husband?
BEATRICE: For the letter that begins them all, H.
MARGARET: Well, and you be not turned Turk, there's no more
MARGARET: sailing by the star.
BEATRICE: What means the fool, trow?
MARGARET: Nothing I, but God send every one their heart's desire!
HERO: These gloves the count sent me, they are an
HERO: excellent perfume.
BEATRICE: I am stuffed, cousin, I cannot smell.
MARGARET: A maid, and stuffed! there's goodly catching of cold.
BEATRICE: O, God help me! God help me! how long have you
BEATRICE: professed apprehension?
MARGARET: Even since you left it. Doth not my wit become me rarely?
BEATRICE: It is not seen enough, you should wear it in your
BEATRICE: cap. By my troth, I am sick.
MARGARET: Get you some of this distilled Carduus Benedictus,
MARGARET: and lay it to your heart: it is the only thing for a qualm.
HERO: There thou prickest her with a thistle.
BEATRICE: Benedictus! why Benedictus? you have some moral in
BEATRICE: this Benedictus.
MARGARET: Moral! no, by my troth, I have no moral meaning, I
MARGARET: meant, plain holy-thistle. You may think perchance
MARGARET: that I think you are in love: nay, by'r lady, I am
MARGARET: not such a fool to think what I list, nor I list
MARGARET: not to think what I can, nor indeed I cannot think,
MARGARET: if I would think my heart out of thinking, that you
MARGARET: are in love or that you will be in love or that you
MARGARET: can be in love. Yet Benedick was such another, and
MARGARET: now is he become a man: he swore he would never
MARGARET: marry, and yet now, in despite of his heart, he eats
MARGARET: his meat without grudging: and how you may be
MARGARET: converted I know not, but methinks you look with
MARGARET: your eyes as other women do.
BEATRICE: What pace is this that thy tongue keeps?
MARGARET: Not a false gallop.
NARRATOR: Re-enter URSULA
URSULA: Madam, withdraw: the prince, the count, Signior
URSULA: Benedick, Don John, and all the gallants of the
URSULA: town, are come to fetch you to church.
HERO: Help to dress me, good coz, good Meg, good Ursula.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another room in LEONATO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO, with DOGBERRY and VERGES
LEONATO: What would you with me, honest neighbour?
DOGBERRY: Marry, sir, I would have some confidence with you
DOGBERRY: that decerns you nearly.
LEONATO: Brief, I pray you, for you see it is a busy time with me.
DOGBERRY: Marry, this it is, sir.
VERGES: Yes, in truth it is, sir.
LEONATO: What is it, my good friends?
DOGBERRY: Goodman Verges, sir, speaks a little off the
DOGBERRY: matter: an old man, sir, and his wits are not so
DOGBERRY: blunt as, God help, I would desire they were, but,
DOGBERRY: in faith, honest as the skin between his brows.
VERGES: Yes, I thank God I am as honest as any man living
VERGES: that is an old man and no honester than I.
DOGBERRY: Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbour Verges.
LEONATO: Neighbours, you are tedious.
DOGBERRY: It pleases your worship to say so, but we are the
DOGBERRY: poor duke's officers, but truly, for mine own part,
DOGBERRY: if I were as tedious as a king, I could find it in
DOGBERRY: my heart to bestow it all of your worship.
LEONATO: All thy tediousness on me, ah?
DOGBERRY: Yea, an 'twere a thousand pound more than 'tis, for
DOGBERRY: I hear as good exclamation on your worship as of any
DOGBERRY: man in the city, and though I be but a poor man, I
DOGBERRY: am glad to hear it.
VERGES: And so am I.
LEONATO: I would fain know what you have to say.
VERGES: Marry, sir, our watch to-night, excepting your
VERGES: worship's presence, ha' ta'en a couple of as arrant
VERGES: knaves as any in Messina.
DOGBERRY: A good old man, sir, he will be talking: as they
DOGBERRY: say, when the age is in, the wit is out: God help
DOGBERRY: us! it is a world to see. Well said, i' faith,
DOGBERRY: neighbour Verges: well, God's a good man, an two men
DOGBERRY: ride of a horse, one must ride behind. An honest
DOGBERRY: soul, i' faith, sir, by my troth he is, as ever
DOGBERRY: broke bread, but God is to be worshipped, all men
DOGBERRY: are not alike, alas, good neighbour!
LEONATO: Indeed, neighbour, he comes too short of you.
DOGBERRY: Gifts that God gives.
LEONATO: I must leave you.
DOGBERRY: One word, sir: our watch, sir, have indeed
DOGBERRY: comprehended two aspicious persons, and we would
DOGBERRY: have them this morning examined before your worship.
LEONATO: Take their examination yourself and bring it me: I
LEONATO: am now in great haste, as it may appear unto you.
DOGBERRY: It shall be suffigance.
LEONATO: Drink some wine ere you go: fare you well.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord, they stay for you to give your daughter to
Messenger: her husband.
LEONATO: I'll wait upon them: I am ready.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LEONATO and Messenger
DOGBERRY: Go, good partner, go, get you to Francis Seacole,
DOGBERRY: bid him bring his pen and inkhorn to the gaol: we
DOGBERRY: are now to examination these men.
VERGES: And we must do it wisely.
DOGBERRY: We will spare for no wit, I warrant you, here's
DOGBERRY: that shall drive some of them to a non-come: only
DOGBERRY: get the learned writer to set down our
DOGBERRY: excommunication and meet me at the gaol.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A church.
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO, DON JOHN, LEONATO, FRIAR FRANCIS, CLAUDIO, BENEDICK, HERO, BEATRICE, and Attendants
LEONATO: Come, Friar Francis, be brief, only to the plain
LEONATO: form of marriage, and you shall recount their
LEONATO: particular duties afterwards.
FRIAR FRANCIS: You come hither, my lord, to marry this lady.
CLAUDIO: No.
LEONATO: To be married to her: friar, you come to marry her.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Lady, you come hither to be married to this count.
HERO: I do.
FRIAR FRANCIS: If either of you know any inward impediment why you
