FRIAR FRANCIS: should not be conjoined, charge you, on your souls,
FRIAR FRANCIS: to utter it.
CLAUDIO: Know you any, Hero?
HERO: None, my lord.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Know you any, count?
LEONATO: I dare make his answer, none.
CLAUDIO: O, what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily
CLAUDIO: do, not knowing what they do!
BENEDICK: How now! interjections? Why, then, some be of
BENEDICK: laughing, as, ah, ha, he!
CLAUDIO: Stand thee by, friar. Father, by your leave:
CLAUDIO: Will you with free and unconstrained soul
CLAUDIO: Give me this maid, your daughter?
LEONATO: As freely, son, as God did give her me.
CLAUDIO: And what have I to give you back, whose worth
CLAUDIO: May counterpoise this rich and precious gift?
DON PEDRO: Nothing, unless you render her again.
CLAUDIO: Sweet prince, you learn me noble thankfulness.
CLAUDIO: There, Leonato, take her back again:
CLAUDIO: Give not this rotten orange to your friend,
CLAUDIO: She's but the sign and semblance of her honour.
CLAUDIO: Behold how like a maid she blushes here!
CLAUDIO: O, what authority and show of truth
CLAUDIO: Can cunning sin cover itself withal!
CLAUDIO: Comes not that blood as modest evidence
CLAUDIO: To witness simple virtue? Would you not swear,
CLAUDIO: All you that see her, that she were a maid,
CLAUDIO: By these exterior shows? But she is none:
CLAUDIO: She knows the heat of a luxurious bed,
CLAUDIO: Her blush is guiltiness, not modesty.
LEONATO: What do you mean, my lord?
CLAUDIO: Not to be married,
CLAUDIO: Not to knit my soul to an approved wanton.
LEONATO: Dear my lord, if you, in your own proof,
LEONATO: Have vanquish'd the resistance of her youth,
LEONATO: And made defeat of her virginity,--
CLAUDIO: I know what you would say: if I have known her,
CLAUDIO: You will say she did embrace me as a husband,
CLAUDIO: And so extenuate the 'forehand sin:
CLAUDIO: No, Leonato,
CLAUDIO: I never tempted her with word too large,
CLAUDIO: But, as a brother to his sister, show'd
CLAUDIO: Bashful sincerity and comely love.
HERO: And seem'd I ever otherwise to you?
CLAUDIO: Out on thee! Seeming! I will write against it:
CLAUDIO: You seem to me as Dian in her orb,
CLAUDIO: As chaste as is the bud ere it be blown,
CLAUDIO: But you are more intemperate in your blood
CLAUDIO: Than Venus, or those pamper'd animals
CLAUDIO: That rage in savage sensuality.
HERO: Is my lord well, that he doth speak so wide?
LEONATO: Sweet prince, why speak not you?
DON PEDRO: What should I speak?
DON PEDRO: I stand dishonour'd, that have gone about
DON PEDRO: To link my dear friend to a common stale.
LEONATO: Are these things spoken, or do I but dream?
DON JOHN: Sir, they are spoken, and these things are true.
BENEDICK: This looks not like a nuptial.
HERO: True! O God!
CLAUDIO: Leonato, stand I here?
CLAUDIO: Is this the prince? is this the prince's brother?
CLAUDIO: Is this face Hero's? are our eyes our own?
LEONATO: All this is so: but what of this, my lord?
CLAUDIO: Let me but move one question to your daughter,
CLAUDIO: And, by that fatherly and kindly power
CLAUDIO: That you have in her, bid her answer truly.
LEONATO: I charge thee do so, as thou art my child.
HERO: O, God defend me! how am I beset!
HERO: What kind of catechising call you this?
CLAUDIO: To make you answer truly to your name.
HERO: Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name
HERO: With any just reproach?
CLAUDIO: Marry, that can Hero,
CLAUDIO: Hero itself can blot out Hero's virtue.
CLAUDIO: What man was he talk'd with you yesternight
CLAUDIO: Out at your window betwixt twelve and one?
CLAUDIO: Now, if you are a maid, answer to this.
HERO: I talk'd with no man at that hour, my lord.
DON PEDRO: Why, then are you no maiden. Leonato,
DON PEDRO: I am sorry you must hear: upon mine honour,
DON PEDRO: Myself, my brother and this grieved count
DON PEDRO: Did see her, hear her, at that hour last night
DON PEDRO: Talk with a ruffian at her chamber-window
DON PEDRO: Who hath indeed, most like a liberal villain,
DON PEDRO: Confess'd the vile encounters they have had
DON PEDRO: A thousand times in secret.
DON JOHN: Fie, fie! they are not to be named, my lord,
DON JOHN: Not to be spoke of,
DON JOHN: There is not chastity enough in language
DON JOHN: Without offence to utter them. Thus, pretty lady,
DON JOHN: I am sorry for thy much misgovernment.
CLAUDIO: O Hero, what a Hero hadst thou been,
CLAUDIO: If half thy outward graces had been placed
CLAUDIO: About thy thoughts and counsels of thy heart!
CLAUDIO: But fare thee well, most foul, most fair! farewell,
CLAUDIO: Thou pure impiety and impious purity!
CLAUDIO: For thee I'll lock up all the gates of love,
CLAUDIO: And on my eyelids shall conjecture hang,
CLAUDIO: To turn all beauty into thoughts of harm,
CLAUDIO: And never shall it more be gracious.
LEONATO: Hath no man's dagger here a point for me?
NARRATOR: HERO swoons
BEATRICE: Why, how now, cousin! wherefore sink you down?
DON JOHN: Come, let us go. These things, come thus to light,
DON JOHN: Smother her spirits up.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DON PEDRO, DON JOHN, and CLAUDIO
BENEDICK: How doth the lady?
BEATRICE: Dead, I think. Help, uncle!
BEATRICE: Hero! why, Hero! Uncle! Signior Benedick! Friar!
LEONATO: O Fate! take not away thy heavy hand.
LEONATO: Death is the fairest cover for her shame
LEONATO: That may be wish'd for.
BEATRICE: How now, cousin Hero!
FRIAR FRANCIS: Have comfort, lady.
LEONATO: Dost thou look up?
FRIAR FRANCIS: Yea, wherefore should she not?
LEONATO: Wherefore! Why, doth not every earthly thing
LEONATO: Cry shame upon her? Could she here deny
LEONATO: The story that is printed in her blood?
LEONATO: Do not live, Hero, do not ope thine eyes:
LEONATO: For, did I think thou wouldst not quickly die,
LEONATO: Thought I thy spirits were stronger than thy shames,
LEONATO: Myself would, on the rearward of reproaches,
LEONATO: Strike at thy life. Grieved I, I had but one?
LEONATO: Chid I for that at frugal nature's frame?
LEONATO: O, one too much by thee! Why had I one?
LEONATO: Why ever wast thou lovely in my eyes?
LEONATO: Why had I not with charitable hand
LEONATO: Took up a beggar's issue at my gates,
LEONATO: Who smirch'd thus and mired with infamy,
LEONATO: I might have said 'No part of it is mine,
LEONATO: This shame derives itself from unknown loins'?
LEONATO: But mine and mine I loved and mine I praised
LEONATO: And mine that I was proud on, mine so much
LEONATO: That I myself was to myself not mine,
LEONATO: Valuing of her,--why, she, O, she is fallen
LEONATO: Into a pit of ink, that the wide sea
LEONATO: Hath drops too few to wash her clean again
LEONATO: And salt too little which may season give
LEONATO: To her foul-tainted flesh!
BENEDICK: Sir, sir, be patient.
BENEDICK: For my part, I am so attired in wonder,
BENEDICK: I know not what to say.
BEATRICE: O, on my soul, my cousin is belied!
BENEDICK: Lady, were you her bedfellow last night?
BEATRICE: No, truly not, although, until last night,
BEATRICE: I have this twelvemonth been her bedfellow.
LEONATO: Confirm'd, confirm'd! O, that is stronger made
LEONATO: Which was before barr'd up with ribs of iron!
LEONATO: Would the two princes lie, and Claudio lie,
LEONATO: Who loved her so, that, speaking of her foulness,
LEONATO: Wash'd it with tears? Hence from her! let her die.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Hear me a little,
FRIAR FRANCIS: For I have only been silent so long
FRIAR FRANCIS: And given way unto this course of fortune.
FRIAR FRANCIS: ...
FRIAR FRANCIS: By noting of the lady I have mark'd
FRIAR FRANCIS: A thousand blushing apparitions
FRIAR FRANCIS: To start into her face, a thousand innocent shames
FRIAR FRANCIS: In angel whiteness beat away those blushes,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And in her eye there hath appear'd a fire,
FRIAR FRANCIS: To burn the errors that these princes hold
FRIAR FRANCIS: Against her maiden truth. Call me a fool,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Trust not my reading nor my observations,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Which with experimental seal doth warrant
FRIAR FRANCIS: The tenor of my book, trust not my age,
FRIAR FRANCIS: My reverence, calling, nor divinity,
FRIAR FRANCIS: If this sweet lady lie not guiltless here
FRIAR FRANCIS: Under some biting error.
LEONATO: Friar, it cannot be.
LEONATO: Thou seest that all the grace that she hath left
LEONATO: Is that she will not add to her damnation
LEONATO: A sin of perjury, she not denies it:
LEONATO: Why seek'st thou then to cover with excuse
LEONATO: That which appears in proper nakedness?
FRIAR FRANCIS: Lady, what man is he you are accused of?
HERO: They know that do accuse me, I know none:
HERO: If I know more of any man alive
HERO: Than that which maiden modesty doth warrant,
HERO: Let all my sins lack mercy! O my father,
HERO: Prove you that any man with me conversed
HERO: At hours unmeet, or that I yesternight
HERO: Maintain'd the change of words with any creature,
HERO: Refuse me, hate me, torture me to death!
FRIAR FRANCIS: There is some strange misprision in the princes.
BENEDICK: Two of them have the very bent of honour,
BENEDICK: And if their wisdoms be misled in this,
BENEDICK: The practise of it lives in John the bastard,
BENEDICK: Whose spirits toil in frame of villanies.
LEONATO: I know not. If they speak but truth of her,
LEONATO: These hands shall tear her, if they wrong her honour,
LEONATO: The proudest of them shall well hear of it.
LEONATO: Time hath not yet so dried this blood of mine,
LEONATO: Nor age so eat up my invention,
LEONATO: Nor fortune made such havoc of my means,
LEONATO: Nor my bad life reft me so much of friends,
LEONATO: But they shall find, awaked in such a kind,
LEONATO: Both strength of limb and policy of mind,
LEONATO: Ability in means and choice of friends,
LEONATO: To quit me of them throughly.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Pause awhile,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And let my counsel sway you in this case.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Your daughter here the princes left for dead:
FRIAR FRANCIS: Let her awhile be secretly kept in,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And publish it that she is dead indeed,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Maintain a mourning ostentation
FRIAR FRANCIS: And on your family's old monument
FRIAR FRANCIS: Hang mournful epitaphs and do all rites
FRIAR FRANCIS: That appertain unto a burial.
LEONATO: What shall become of this? what will this do?
FRIAR FRANCIS: Marry, this well carried shall on her behalf
FRIAR FRANCIS: Change slander to remorse, that is some good:
FRIAR FRANCIS: But not for that dream I on this strange course,
FRIAR FRANCIS: But on this travail look for greater birth.
FRIAR FRANCIS: She dying, as it must so be maintain'd,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Upon the instant that she was accused,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Shall be lamented, pitied and excused
FRIAR FRANCIS: Of every hearer: for it so falls out
FRIAR FRANCIS: That what we have we prize not to the worth
FRIAR FRANCIS: Whiles we enjoy it, but being lack'd and lost,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Why, then we rack the value, then we find
FRIAR FRANCIS: The virtue that possession would not show us
FRIAR FRANCIS: Whiles it was ours. So will it fare with Claudio:
FRIAR FRANCIS: When he shall hear she died upon his words,
FRIAR FRANCIS: The idea of her life shall sweetly creep
FRIAR FRANCIS: Into his study of imagination,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And every lovely organ of her life
FRIAR FRANCIS: Shall come apparell'd in more precious habit,
FRIAR FRANCIS: More moving-delicate and full of life,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Into the eye and prospect of his soul,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Than when she lived indeed, then shall he mourn,
FRIAR FRANCIS: If ever love had interest in his liver,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And wish he had not so accused her,
FRIAR FRANCIS: No, though he thought his accusation true.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Let this be so, and doubt not but success
FRIAR FRANCIS: Will fashion the event in better shape
FRIAR FRANCIS: Than I can lay it down in likelihood.
FRIAR FRANCIS: But if all aim but this be levell'd false,
FRIAR FRANCIS: The supposition of the lady's death
FRIAR FRANCIS: Will quench the wonder of her infamy:
FRIAR FRANCIS: And if it sort not well, you may conceal her,
FRIAR FRANCIS: As best befits her wounded reputation,
FRIAR FRANCIS: In some reclusive and religious life,
FRIAR FRANCIS: Out of all eyes, tongues, minds and injuries.
BENEDICK: Signior Leonato, let the friar advise you:
BENEDICK: And though you know my inwardness and love
BENEDICK: Is very much unto the prince and Claudio,
BENEDICK: Yet, by mine honour, I will deal in this
BENEDICK: As secretly and justly as your soul
BENEDICK: Should with your body.
LEONATO: Being that I flow in grief,
LEONATO: The smallest twine may lead me.
FRIAR FRANCIS: 'Tis well consented: presently away,
FRIAR FRANCIS: For to strange sores strangely they strain the cure.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Come, lady, die to live: this wedding-day
FRIAR FRANCIS: Perhaps is but prolong'd: have patience and endure.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BENEDICK and BEATRICE
BENEDICK: Lady Beatrice, have you wept all this while?
BEATRICE: Yea, and I will weep a while longer.
BENEDICK: I will not desire that.
BEATRICE: You have no reason, I do it freely.
BENEDICK: Surely I do believe your fair cousin is wronged.
BEATRICE: Ah, how much might the man deserve of me that would right her!
BENEDICK: Is there any way to show such friendship?
BEATRICE: A very even way, but no such friend.
BENEDICK: May a man do it?
BEATRICE: It is a man's office, but not yours.
BENEDICK: I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is
BENEDICK: not that strange?
BEATRICE: As strange as the thing I know not. It were as
BEATRICE: possible for me to say I loved nothing so well as
BEATRICE: you: but believe me not, and yet I lie not, I
BEATRICE: confess nothing, nor I deny nothing. I am sorry for my cousin.
BENEDICK: By my sword, Beatrice, thou lovest me.
BEATRICE: Do not swear, and eat it.
BENEDICK: I will swear by it that you love me, and I will make
BENEDICK: him eat it that says I love not you.
BEATRICE: Will you not eat your word?
BENEDICK: With no sauce that can be devised to it. I protest
BENEDICK: I love thee.
BEATRICE: Why, then, God forgive me!
BENEDICK: What offence, sweet Beatrice?
BEATRICE: You have stayed me in a happy hour: I was about to
BEATRICE: protest I loved you.
BENEDICK: And do it with all thy heart.
BEATRICE: I love you with so much of my heart that none is
BEATRICE: left to protest.
BENEDICK: Come, bid me do any thing for thee.
BEATRICE: Kill Claudio.
BENEDICK: Ha! not for the wide world.
BEATRICE: You kill me to deny it. Farewell.
BENEDICK: Tarry, sweet Beatrice.
BEATRICE: I am gone, though I am here: there is no love in
BEATRICE: you: nay, I pray you, let me go.
BENEDICK: Beatrice,--
BEATRICE: In faith, I will go.
BENEDICK: We'll be friends first.
BEATRICE: You dare easier be friends with me than fight with mine enemy.
BENEDICK: Is Claudio thine enemy?
BEATRICE: Is he not approved in the height a villain, that
BEATRICE: hath slandered, scorned, dishonoured my kinswoman? O
BEATRICE: that I were a man! What, bear her in hand until they
BEATRICE: come to take hands, and then, with public
BEATRICE: accusation, uncovered slander, unmitigated rancour,
BEATRICE: --O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart
BEATRICE: in the market-place.
BENEDICK: Hear me, Beatrice,--
BEATRICE: Talk with a man out at a window! A proper saying!
BENEDICK: Nay, but, Beatrice,--
BEATRICE: Sweet Hero! She is wronged, she is slandered, she is undone.
BENEDICK: Beat--
BEATRICE: Princes and counties! Surely, a princely testimony,
BEATRICE: a goodly count, Count Comfect, a sweet gallant,
BEATRICE: surely! O that I were a man for his sake! or that I
BEATRICE: had any friend would be a man for my sake! But
BEATRICE: manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into
BEATRICE: compliment, and men are only turned into tongue, and
BEATRICE: trim ones too: he is now as valiant as Hercules
BEATRICE: that only tells a lie and swears it. I cannot be a
BEATRICE: man with wishing, therefore I will die a woman with grieving.
BENEDICK: Tarry, good Beatrice. By this hand, I love thee.
BEATRICE: Use it for my love some other way than swearing by it.
BENEDICK: Think you in your soul the Count Claudio hath wronged Hero?
BEATRICE: Yea, as sure as I have a thought or a soul.
BENEDICK: Enough, I am engaged, I will challenge him. I will
BENEDICK: kiss your hand, and so I leave you. By this hand,
BENEDICK: Claudio shall render me a dear account. As you
BENEDICK: hear of me, so think of me. Go, comfort your
BENEDICK: cousin: I must say she is dead: and so, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A prison.
NARRATOR: Enter DOGBERRY, VERGES, and Sexton, in gowns, and the Watch, with CONRADE and BORACHIO
DOGBERRY: Is our whole dissembly appeared?
VERGES: O, a stool and a cushion for the sexton.
Sexton: Which be the malefactors?
DOGBERRY: Marry, that am I and my partner.
VERGES: Nay, that's certain, we have the exhibition to examine.
Sexton: But which are the offenders that are to be
Sexton: examined? let them come before master constable.
DOGBERRY: Yea, marry, let them come before me. What is your
DOGBERRY: name, friend?
BORACHIO: Borachio.
DOGBERRY: Pray, write down, Borachio. Yours, sirrah?
CONRADE: I am a gentleman, sir, and my name is Conrade.
DOGBERRY: Write down, master gentleman Conrade. Masters, do
DOGBERRY: you serve God?
BORACHIO: Yea, sir, we hope.
DOGBERRY: Write down, that they hope they serve God: and
DOGBERRY: write God first, for God defend but God should go
DOGBERRY: before such villains! Masters, it is proved already
DOGBERRY: that you are little better than false knaves, and it
DOGBERRY: will go near to be thought so shortly. How answer
DOGBERRY: you for yourselves?
CONRADE: Marry, sir, we say we are none.
DOGBERRY: A marvellous witty fellow, I assure you: but I
DOGBERRY: will go about with him. Come you hither, sirrah, a
DOGBERRY: word in your ear: sir, I say to you, it is thought
DOGBERRY: you are false knaves.
BORACHIO: Sir, I say to you we are none.
DOGBERRY: Well, stand aside. 'Fore God, they are both in a
DOGBERRY: tale. Have you writ down, that they are none?
Sexton: Master constable, you go not the way to examine:
Sexton: you must call forth the watch that are their accusers.
DOGBERRY: Yea, marry, that's the eftest way. Let the watch
DOGBERRY: come forth. Masters, I charge you, in the prince's
DOGBERRY: name, accuse these men.
First Watchman: This man said, sir, that Don John, the prince's
First Watchman: brother, was a villain.
DOGBERRY: Write down Prince John a villain. Why, this is flat
DOGBERRY: perjury, to call a prince's brother villain.
BORACHIO: Master constable,--
DOGBERRY: Pray thee, fellow, peace: I do not like thy look,
DOGBERRY: I promise thee.
Sexton: What heard you him say else?
Second Watchman: Marry, that he had received a thousand ducats of
Second Watchman: Don John for accusing the Lady Hero wrongfully.
DOGBERRY: Flat burglary as ever was committed.
VERGES: Yea, by mass, that it is.
Sexton: What else, fellow?
First Watchman: And that Count Claudio did mean, upon his words, to
First Watchman: disgrace Hero before the whole assembly. and not marry her.
DOGBERRY: O villain! thou wilt be condemned into everlasting
DOGBERRY: redemption for this.
Sexton: What else?
Watchman: This is all.
Sexton: And this is more, masters, than you can deny.
Sexton: Prince John is this morning secretly stolen away,
Sexton: Hero was in this manner accused, in this very manner
Sexton: refused, and upon the grief of this suddenly died.
Sexton: Master constable, let these men be bound, and
Sexton: brought to Leonato's: I will go before and show
Sexton: him their examination.
NARRATOR: Exit
DOGBERRY: Come, let them be opinioned.
VERGES: Let them be in the hands--
CONRADE: Off, coxcomb!
DOGBERRY: God's my life, where's the sexton? let him write
DOGBERRY: down the prince's officer coxcomb. Come, bind them.
DOGBERRY: Thou naughty varlet!
CONRADE: Away! you are an ass, you are an ass.
DOGBERRY: Dost thou not suspect my place? dost thou not
DOGBERRY: suspect my years? O that he were here to write me
DOGBERRY: down an ass! But, masters, remember that I am an
DOGBERRY: ass, though it be not written down, yet forget not
DOGBERRY: that I am an ass. No, thou villain, thou art full of
DOGBERRY: piety, as shall be proved upon thee by good witness.
DOGBERRY: I am a wise fellow, and, which is more, an officer,
DOGBERRY: and, which is more, a householder, and, which is
DOGBERRY: more, as pretty a piece of flesh as any is in
DOGBERRY: Messina, and one that knows the law, go to, and a
DOGBERRY: rich fellow enough, go to, and a fellow that hath
DOGBERRY: had losses, and one that hath two gowns and every
DOGBERRY: thing handsome about him. Bring him away. O that
DOGBERRY: I had been writ down an ass!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before LEONATO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO and ANTONIO
ANTONIO: If you go on thus, you will kill yourself:
ANTONIO: And 'tis not wisdom thus to second grief
ANTONIO: Against yourself.
LEONATO: I pray thee, cease thy counsel,
LEONATO: Which falls into mine ears as profitless
LEONATO: As water in a sieve: give not me counsel,
LEONATO: Nor let no comforter delight mine ear
LEONATO: But such a one whose wrongs do suit with mine.
LEONATO: Bring me a father that so loved his child,
LEONATO: Whose joy of her is overwhelm'd like mine,
LEONATO: And bid him speak of patience,
LEONATO: Measure his woe the length and breadth of mine
LEONATO: And let it answer every strain for strain,
LEONATO: As thus for thus and such a grief for such,
LEONATO: In every lineament, branch, shape, and form:
LEONATO: If such a one will smile and stroke his beard,
LEONATO: Bid sorrow wag, cry 'hem!' when he should groan,
LEONATO: Patch grief with proverbs, make misfortune drunk
LEONATO: With candle-wasters, bring him yet to me,
LEONATO: And I of him will gather patience.
LEONATO: But there is no such man: for, brother, men
LEONATO: Can counsel and speak comfort to that grief
LEONATO: Which they themselves not feel, but, tasting it,
LEONATO: Their counsel turns to passion, which before
LEONATO: Would give preceptial medicine to rage,
LEONATO: Fetter strong madness in a silken thread,
LEONATO: Charm ache with air and agony with words:
LEONATO: No, no, 'tis all men's office to speak patience
LEONATO: To those that wring under the load of sorrow,
LEONATO: But no man's virtue nor sufficiency
LEONATO: To be so moral when he shall endure
LEONATO: The like himself. Therefore give me no counsel:
LEONATO: My griefs cry louder than advertisement.
ANTONIO: Therein do men from children nothing differ.
LEONATO: I pray thee, peace. I will be flesh and blood,
LEONATO: For there was never yet philosopher
LEONATO: That could endure the toothache patiently,
LEONATO: However they have writ the style of gods
LEONATO: And made a push at chance and sufferance.
ANTONIO: Yet bend not all the harm upon yourself,
ANTONIO: Make those that do offend you suffer too.
LEONATO: There thou speak'st reason: nay, I will do so.
LEONATO: My soul doth tell me Hero is belied,
LEONATO: And that shall Claudio know, so shall the prince
LEONATO: And all of them that thus dishonour her.
ANTONIO: Here comes the prince and Claudio hastily.
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO and CLAUDIO
DON PEDRO: Good den, good den.
CLAUDIO: Good day to both of you.
LEONATO: Hear you. my lords,--
DON PEDRO: We have some haste, Leonato.
LEONATO: Some haste, my lord! well, fare you well, my lord:
LEONATO: Are you so hasty now? well, all is one.
DON PEDRO: Nay, do not quarrel with us, good old man.
ANTONIO: If he could right himself with quarreling,
ANTONIO: Some of us would lie low.
CLAUDIO: Who wrongs him?
LEONATO: Marry, thou dost wrong me, thou dissembler, thou:--
LEONATO: Nay, never lay thy hand upon thy sword,
LEONATO: I fear thee not.
CLAUDIO: Marry, beshrew my hand,
CLAUDIO: If it should give your age such cause of fear:
CLAUDIO: In faith, my hand meant nothing to my sword.
LEONATO: Tush, tush, man, never fleer and jest at me:
LEONATO: I speak not like a dotard nor a fool,
LEONATO: As under privilege of age to brag
LEONATO: What I have done being young, or what would do
LEONATO: Were I not old. Know, Claudio, to thy head,
LEONATO: Thou hast so wrong'd mine innocent child and me
LEONATO: That I am forced to lay my reverence by
LEONATO: And, with grey hairs and bruise of many days,
LEONATO: Do challenge thee to trial of a man.
LEONATO: I say thou hast belied mine innocent child,
LEONATO: Thy slander hath gone through and through her heart,
LEONATO: And she lies buried with her ancestors,
LEONATO: O, in a tomb where never scandal slept,
LEONATO: Save this of hers, framed by thy villany!
CLAUDIO: My villany?
LEONATO: Thine, Claudio, thine, I say.
DON PEDRO: You say not right, old man.
LEONATO: My lord, my lord,
LEONATO: I'll prove it on his body, if he dare,
LEONATO: Despite his nice fence and his active practise,
LEONATO: His May of youth and bloom of lustihood.
CLAUDIO: Away! I will not have to do with you.
LEONATO: Canst thou so daff me? Thou hast kill'd my child:
LEONATO: If thou kill'st me, boy, thou shalt kill a man.
ANTONIO: He shall kill two of us, and men indeed:
ANTONIO: But that's no matter, let him kill one first,
ANTONIO: Win me and wear me, let him answer me.
ANTONIO: Come, follow me, boy, come, sir boy, come, follow me:
ANTONIO: Sir boy, I'll whip you from your foining fence,
ANTONIO: Nay, as I am a gentleman, I will.
LEONATO: Brother,--
ANTONIO: Content yourself. God knows I loved my niece,
ANTONIO: And she is dead, slander'd to death by villains,
ANTONIO: That dare as well answer a man indeed
ANTONIO: As I dare take a serpent by the tongue:
ANTONIO: Boys, apes, braggarts, Jacks, milksops!
LEONATO: Brother Antony,--
ANTONIO: Hold you content. What, man! I know them, yea,
ANTONIO: And what they weigh, even to the utmost scruple,--
ANTONIO: Scrambling, out-facing, fashion-monging boys,
ANTONIO: That lie and cog and flout, deprave and slander,
ANTONIO: Go anticly, show outward hideousness,
ANTONIO: And speak off half a dozen dangerous words,
ANTONIO: How they might hurt their enemies, if they durst,
ANTONIO: And this is all.
LEONATO: But, brother Antony,--
ANTONIO: Come, 'tis no matter:
ANTONIO: Do not you meddle, let me deal in this.
DON PEDRO: Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience.
DON PEDRO: My heart is sorry for your daughter's death:
DON PEDRO: But, on my honour, she was charged with nothing
DON PEDRO: But what was true and very full of proof.
LEONATO: My lord, my lord,--
DON PEDRO: I will not hear you.
LEONATO: No? Come, brother, away! I will be heard.
ANTONIO: And shall, or some of us will smart for it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LEONATO and ANTONIO
DON PEDRO: See, see, here comes the man we went to seek.
NARRATOR: Enter BENEDICK
CLAUDIO: Now, signior, what news?
BENEDICK: Good day, my lord.
DON PEDRO: Welcome, signior: you are almost come to part
DON PEDRO: almost a fray.
CLAUDIO: We had like to have had our two noses snapped off
CLAUDIO: with two old men without teeth.
DON PEDRO: Leonato and his brother. What thinkest thou? Had
DON PEDRO: we fought, I doubt we should have been too young for them.
BENEDICK: In a false quarrel there is no true valour. I came
BENEDICK: to seek you both.
CLAUDIO: We have been up and down to seek thee, for we are
CLAUDIO: high-proof melancholy and would fain have it beaten
CLAUDIO: away. Wilt thou use thy wit?
BENEDICK: It is in my scabbard: shall I draw it?
DON PEDRO: Dost thou wear thy wit by thy side?
CLAUDIO: Never any did so, though very many have been beside
CLAUDIO: their wit. I will bid thee draw, as we do the
CLAUDIO: minstrels, draw, to pleasure us.
DON PEDRO: As I am an honest man, he looks pale. Art thou
DON PEDRO: sick, or angry?
CLAUDIO: What, courage, man! What though care killed a cat,
CLAUDIO: thou hast mettle enough in thee to kill care.
BENEDICK: Sir, I shall meet your wit in the career, and you
BENEDICK: charge it against me. I pray you choose another subject.
CLAUDIO: Nay, then, give him another staff: this last was
CLAUDIO: broke cross.
DON PEDRO: By this light, he changes more and more: I think
DON PEDRO: he be angry indeed.
CLAUDIO: If he be, he knows how to turn his girdle.
BENEDICK: Shall I speak a word in your ear?
CLAUDIO: God bless me from a challenge!
BENEDICK: [Aside to CLAUDIO]  You are a villain, I jest not:
BENEDICK: I will make it good how you dare, with what you
BENEDICK: dare, and when you dare. Do me right, or I will
BENEDICK: protest your cowardice. You have killed a sweet
BENEDICK: lady, and her death shall fall heavy on you. Let me
BENEDICK: hear from you.
CLAUDIO: Well, I will meet you, so I may have good cheer.
DON PEDRO: What, a feast, a feast?
CLAUDIO: I' faith, I thank him, he hath bid me to a calf's
CLAUDIO: head and a capon, the which if I do not carve most
CLAUDIO: curiously, say my knife's naught. Shall I not find
CLAUDIO: a woodcock too?
BENEDICK: Sir, your wit ambles well, it goes easily.
DON PEDRO: I'll tell thee how Beatrice praised thy wit the
DON PEDRO: other day. I said, thou hadst a fine wit: 'True,'
DON PEDRO: said she, 'a fine little one.' 'No,' said I, 'a
DON PEDRO: great wit:' 'Right,' says she, 'a great gross one.'
DON PEDRO: 'Nay,' said I, 'a good wit:' 'Just,' said she, 'it
DON PEDRO: hurts nobody.' 'Nay,' said I, 'the gentleman
DON PEDRO: is wise:' 'Certain,' said she, 'a wise gentleman.'
DON PEDRO: 'Nay,' said I, 'he hath the tongues:' 'That I
DON PEDRO: believe,' said she, 'for he swore a thing to me on
DON PEDRO: Monday night, which he forswore on Tuesday morning,
DON PEDRO: there's a double tongue, there's two tongues.' Thus
DON PEDRO: did she, an hour together, transshape thy particular
DON PEDRO: virtues: yet at last she concluded with a sigh, thou
DON PEDRO: wast the properest man in Italy.
CLAUDIO: For the which she wept heartily and said she cared
CLAUDIO: not.
DON PEDRO: Yea, that she did: but yet, for all that, an if she
DON PEDRO: did not hate him deadly, she would love him dearly:
DON PEDRO: the old man's daughter told us all.
CLAUDIO: All, all, and, moreover, God saw him when he was
CLAUDIO: hid in the garden.
DON PEDRO: But when shall we set the savage bull's horns on
DON PEDRO: the sensible Benedick's head?
CLAUDIO: Yea, and text underneath, 'Here dwells Benedick the
CLAUDIO: married man'?
BENEDICK: Fare you well, boy: you know my mind. I will leave
BENEDICK: you now to your gossip-like humour: you break jests
BENEDICK: as braggarts do their blades, which God be thanked,
BENEDICK: hurt not. My lord, for your many courtesies I thank
BENEDICK: you: I must discontinue your company: your brother
BENEDICK: the bastard is fled from Messina: you have among
BENEDICK: you killed a sweet and innocent lady. For my Lord
BENEDICK: Lackbeard there, he and I shall meet: and, till
BENEDICK: then, peace be with him.
NARRATOR: Exit
DON PEDRO: He is in earnest.
CLAUDIO: In most profound earnest, and, I'll warrant you, for
CLAUDIO: the love of Beatrice.
DON PEDRO: And hath challenged thee.
CLAUDIO: Most sincerely.
DON PEDRO: What a pretty thing man is when he goes in his
DON PEDRO: doublet and hose and leaves off his wit!
CLAUDIO: He is then a giant to an ape, but then is an ape a
CLAUDIO: doctor to such a man.
DON PEDRO: But, soft you, let me be: pluck up, my heart, and
DON PEDRO: be sad. Did he not say, my brother was fled?
NARRATOR: Enter DOGBERRY, VERGES, and the Watch, with CONRADE and BORACHIO
DOGBERRY: Come you, sir: if justice cannot tame you, she
DOGBERRY: shall ne'er weigh more reasons in her balance: nay,
DOGBERRY: an you be a cursing hypocrite once, you must be looked to.
DON PEDRO: How now? two of my brother's men bound! Borachio
DON PEDRO: one!
CLAUDIO: Hearken after their offence, my lord.
DON PEDRO: Officers, what offence have these men done?
DOGBERRY: Marry, sir, they have committed false report,
DOGBERRY: moreover, they have spoken untruths, secondarily,
DOGBERRY: they are slanders, sixth and lastly, they have
DOGBERRY: belied a lady, thirdly, they have verified unjust
DOGBERRY: things, and, to conclude, they are lying knaves.
DON PEDRO: First, I ask thee what they have done, thirdly, I
DON PEDRO: ask thee what's their offence, sixth and lastly, why
DON PEDRO: they are committed, and, to conclude, what you lay
DON PEDRO: to their charge.
CLAUDIO: Rightly reasoned, and in his own division: and, by
CLAUDIO: my troth, there's one meaning well suited.
DON PEDRO: Who have you offended, masters, that you are thus
DON PEDRO: bound to your answer? this learned constable is
DON PEDRO: too cunning to be understood: what's your offence?
BORACHIO: Sweet prince, let me go no farther to mine answer:
BORACHIO: do you hear me, and let this count kill me. I have
BORACHIO: deceived even your very eyes: what your wisdoms
BORACHIO: could not discover, these shallow fools have brought
BORACHIO: to light: who in the night overheard me confessing
BORACHIO: to this man how Don John your brother incensed me
BORACHIO: to slander the Lady Hero, how you were brought into
BORACHIO: the orchard and saw me court Margaret in Hero's
BORACHIO: garments, how you disgraced her, when you should
BORACHIO: marry her: my villany they have upon record, which
BORACHIO: I had rather seal with my death than repeat over
BORACHIO: to my shame. The lady is dead upon mine and my
BORACHIO: master's false accusation, and, briefly, I desire
BORACHIO: nothing but the reward of a villain.
DON PEDRO: Runs not this speech like iron through your blood?
CLAUDIO: I have drunk poison whiles he utter'd it.
DON PEDRO: But did my brother set thee on to this?
BORACHIO: Yea, and paid me richly for the practise of it.
DON PEDRO: He is composed and framed of treachery:
DON PEDRO: And fled he is upon this villany.
CLAUDIO: Sweet Hero! now thy image doth appear
CLAUDIO: In the rare semblance that I loved it first.
DOGBERRY: Come, bring away the plaintiffs: by this time our
DOGBERRY: sexton hath reformed Signior Leonato of the matter:
DOGBERRY: and, masters, do not forget to specify, when time
DOGBERRY: and place shall serve, that I am an ass.
VERGES: Here, here comes master Signior Leonato, and the
VERGES: Sexton too.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LEONATO and ANTONIO, with the Sexton
LEONATO: Which is the villain? let me see his eyes,
LEONATO: That, when I note another man like him,
LEONATO: I may avoid him: which of these is he?
BORACHIO: If you would know your wronger, look on me.
LEONATO: Art thou the slave that with thy breath hast kill'd
LEONATO: Mine innocent child?
BORACHIO: Yea, even I alone.
LEONATO: No, not so, villain, thou beliest thyself:
LEONATO: Here stand a pair of honourable men,
LEONATO: A third is fled, that had a hand in it.
LEONATO: I thank you, princes, for my daughter's death:
LEONATO: Record it with your high and worthy deeds:
LEONATO: 'Twas bravely done, if you bethink you of it.
CLAUDIO: I know not how to pray your patience,
CLAUDIO: Yet I must speak. Choose your revenge yourself,
CLAUDIO: Impose me to what penance your invention
CLAUDIO: Can lay upon my sin: yet sinn'd I not
CLAUDIO: But in mistaking.
DON PEDRO: By my soul, nor I:
DON PEDRO: And yet, to satisfy this good old man,
DON PEDRO: I would bend under any heavy weight
DON PEDRO: That he'll enjoin me to.
LEONATO: I cannot bid you bid my daughter live,
LEONATO: That were impossible: but, I pray you both,
LEONATO: Possess the people in Messina here
LEONATO: How innocent she died, and if your love
LEONATO: Can labour ought in sad invention,
LEONATO: Hang her an epitaph upon her tomb
LEONATO: And sing it to her bones, sing it to-night:
LEONATO: To-morrow morning come you to my house,
LEONATO: And since you could not be my son-in-law,
LEONATO: Be yet my nephew: my brother hath a daughter,
LEONATO: Almost the copy of my child that's dead,
LEONATO: And she alone is heir to both of us:
LEONATO: Give her the right you should have given her cousin,
LEONATO: And so dies my revenge.
CLAUDIO: O noble sir,
CLAUDIO: Your over-kindness doth wring tears from me!
CLAUDIO: I do embrace your offer, and dispose
CLAUDIO: For henceforth of poor Claudio.
LEONATO: To-morrow then I will expect your coming,
LEONATO: To-night I take my leave. This naughty man
LEONATO: Shall face to face be brought to Margaret,
LEONATO: Who I believe was pack'd in all this wrong,
LEONATO: Hired to it by your brother.
BORACHIO: No, by my soul, she was not,
BORACHIO: Nor knew not what she did when she spoke to me,
BORACHIO: But always hath been just and virtuous
BORACHIO: In any thing that I do know by her.
DOGBERRY: Moreover, sir, which indeed is not under white and
DOGBERRY: black, this plaintiff here, the offender, did call
DOGBERRY: me ass: I beseech you, let it be remembered in his
DOGBERRY: punishment. And also, the watch heard them talk of
DOGBERRY: one Deformed: they say be wears a key in his ear and
DOGBERRY: a lock hanging by it, and borrows money in God's
DOGBERRY: name, the which he hath used so long and never paid
DOGBERRY: that now men grow hard-hearted and will lend nothing
DOGBERRY: for God's sake: pray you, examine him upon that point.
LEONATO: I thank thee for thy care and honest pains.
DOGBERRY: Your worship speaks like a most thankful and
DOGBERRY: reverend youth, and I praise God for you.
LEONATO: There's for thy pains.
DOGBERRY: God save the foundation!
LEONATO: Go, I discharge thee of thy prisoner, and I thank thee.
DOGBERRY: I leave an arrant knave with your worship, which I
DOGBERRY: beseech your worship to correct yourself, for the
DOGBERRY: example of others. God keep your worship! I wish
DOGBERRY: your worship well, God restore you to health! I
DOGBERRY: humbly give you leave to depart, and if a merry
DOGBERRY: meeting may be wished, God prohibit it! Come, neighbour.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DOGBERRY and VERGES
LEONATO: Until to-morrow morning, lords, farewell.
ANTONIO: Farewell, my lords: we look for you to-morrow.
DON PEDRO: We will not fail.
CLAUDIO: To-night I'll mourn with Hero.
LEONATO: [To the Watch]  Bring you these fellows on. We'll
LEONATO: talk with Margaret,
LEONATO: How her acquaintance grew with this lewd fellow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, severally
NARRATOR: SCENE II. LEONATO'S garden.
NARRATOR: Enter BENEDICK and MARGARET, meeting
BENEDICK: Pray thee, sweet Mistress Margaret, deserve well at
BENEDICK: my hands by helping me to the speech of Beatrice.
MARGARET: Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty?
BENEDICK: In so high a style, Margaret, that no man living
BENEDICK: shall come over it, for, in most comely truth, thou
BENEDICK: deservest it.
MARGARET: To have no man come over me! why, shall I always
MARGARET: keep below stairs?
BENEDICK: Thy wit is as quick as the greyhound's mouth, it catches.
MARGARET: And yours as blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit,
MARGARET: but hurt not.
BENEDICK: A most manly wit, Margaret, it will not hurt a
BENEDICK: woman: and so, I pray thee, call Beatrice: I give
BENEDICK: thee the bucklers.
MARGARET: Give us the swords, we have bucklers of our own.
BENEDICK: If you use them, Margaret, you must put in the
BENEDICK: pikes with a vice, and they are dangerous weapons for maids.
MARGARET: Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I think hath legs.
BENEDICK: And therefore will come.
NARRATOR: Exit MARGARET
NARRATOR: Sings
BENEDICK: The god of love,
BENEDICK: That sits above,
BENEDICK: And knows me, and knows me,
BENEDICK: How pitiful I deserve,--
BENEDICK: I mean in singing, but in loving, Leander the good
BENEDICK: swimmer, Troilus the first employer of panders, and
BENEDICK: a whole bookful of these quondam carpet-mangers,
BENEDICK: whose names yet run smoothly in the even road of a
BENEDICK: blank verse, why, they were never so truly turned
BENEDICK: over and over as my poor self in love. Marry, I
BENEDICK: cannot show it in rhyme, I have tried: I can find
BENEDICK: out no rhyme to 'lady' but 'baby,' an innocent
BENEDICK: rhyme, for 'scorn,' 'horn,' a hard rhyme, for,
BENEDICK: 'school,' 'fool,' a babbling rhyme, very ominous
BENEDICK: endings: no, I was not born under a rhyming planet,
BENEDICK: nor I cannot woo in festival terms.
NARRATOR: Enter BEATRICE
BENEDICK: Sweet Beatrice, wouldst thou come when I called thee?
BEATRICE: Yea, signior, and depart when you bid me.
BENEDICK: O, stay but till then!
BEATRICE: 'Then' is spoken, fare you well now: and yet, ere
BEATRICE: I go, let me go with that I came, which is, with
BEATRICE: knowing what hath passed between you and Claudio.
BENEDICK: Only foul words, and thereupon I will kiss thee.
BEATRICE: Foul words is but foul wind, and foul wind is but
BEATRICE: foul breath, and foul breath is noisome, therefore I
BEATRICE: will depart unkissed.
BENEDICK: Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sense,
BENEDICK: so forcible is thy wit. But I must tell thee
BENEDICK: plainly, Claudio undergoes my challenge, and either
BENEDICK: I must shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe
BENEDICK: him a coward. And, I pray thee now, tell me for
BENEDICK: which of my bad parts didst thou first fall in love with me?
BEATRICE: For them all together, which maintained so politic
BEATRICE: a state of evil that they will not admit any good
BEATRICE: part to intermingle with them. But for which of my
BEATRICE: good parts did you first suffer love for me?
BENEDICK: Suffer love! a good epithet! I do suffer love
BENEDICK: indeed, for I love thee against my will.
BEATRICE: In spite of your heart, I think, alas, poor heart!
BEATRICE: If you spite it for my sake, I will spite it for
BEATRICE: yours, for I will never love that which my friend hates.
BENEDICK: Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably.
BEATRICE: It appears not in this confession: there's not one
BEATRICE: wise man among twenty that will praise himself.
BENEDICK: An old, an old instance, Beatrice, that lived in
BENEDICK: the lime of good neighbours. If a man do not erect
BENEDICK: in this age his own tomb ere he dies, he shall live
BENEDICK: no longer in monument than the bell rings and the
BENEDICK: widow weeps.
BEATRICE: And how long is that, think you?
BENEDICK: Question: why, an hour in clamour and a quarter in
BENEDICK: rheum: therefore is it most expedient for the
BENEDICK: wise, if Don Worm, his conscience, find no
BENEDICK: impediment to the contrary, to be the trumpet of his
BENEDICK: own virtues, as I am to myself. So much for
BENEDICK: praising myself, who, I myself will bear witness, is
BENEDICK: praiseworthy: and now tell me, how doth your cousin?
BEATRICE: Very ill.
BENEDICK: And how do you?
BEATRICE: Very ill too.
BENEDICK: Serve God, love me and mend. There will I leave
BENEDICK: you too, for here comes one in haste.
NARRATOR: Enter URSULA
URSULA: Madam, you must come to your uncle. Yonder's old
URSULA: coil at home: it is proved my Lady Hero hath been
URSULA: falsely accused, the prince and Claudio mightily
URSULA: abused, and Don John is the author of all, who is
URSULA: fed and gone. Will you come presently?
BEATRICE: Will you go hear this news, signior?
BENEDICK: I will live in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be
BENEDICK: buried in thy eyes, and moreover I will go with
BENEDICK: thee to thy uncle's.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A church.
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO, CLAUDIO, and three or four with tapers
CLAUDIO: Is this the monument of Leonato?
Lord: It is, my lord.
CLAUDIO: [Reading out of a scroll]
CLAUDIO: Done to death by slanderous tongues
CLAUDIO: Was the Hero that here lies:
CLAUDIO: Death, in guerdon of her wrongs,
CLAUDIO: Gives her fame which never dies.
CLAUDIO: So the life that died with shame
CLAUDIO: Lives in death with glorious fame.
CLAUDIO: Hang thou there upon the tomb,
CLAUDIO: Praising her when I am dumb.
CLAUDIO: Now, music, sound, and sing your solemn hymn.
CLAUDIO: SONG.
CLAUDIO: Pardon, goddess of the night,
CLAUDIO: Those that slew thy virgin knight,
CLAUDIO: For the which, with songs of woe,
CLAUDIO: Round about her tomb they go.
CLAUDIO: Midnight, assist our moan,
CLAUDIO: Help us to sigh and groan,
CLAUDIO: Heavily, heavily:
CLAUDIO: Graves, yawn and yield your dead,
CLAUDIO: Till death be uttered,
CLAUDIO: Heavily, heavily.
CLAUDIO: Now, unto thy bones good night!
CLAUDIO: Yearly will I do this rite.
DON PEDRO: Good morrow, masters, put your torches out:
DON PEDRO: The wolves have prey'd, and look, the gentle day,
DON PEDRO: Before the wheels of Phoebus, round about
DON PEDRO: Dapples the drowsy east with spots of grey.
DON PEDRO: Thanks to you all, and leave us: fare you well.
CLAUDIO: Good morrow, masters: each his several way.
DON PEDRO: Come, let us hence, and put on other weeds,
DON PEDRO: And then to Leonato's we will go.
CLAUDIO: And Hymen now with luckier issue speed's
CLAUDIO: Than this for whom we render'd up this woe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A room in LEONATO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LEONATO, ANTONIO, BENEDICK, BEATRICE, MARGARET, URSULA, FRIAR FRANCIS, and HERO
FRIAR FRANCIS: Did I not tell you she was innocent?
LEONATO: So are the prince and Claudio, who accused her
LEONATO: Upon the error that you heard debated:
LEONATO: But Margaret was in some fault for this,
LEONATO: Although against her will, as it appears
LEONATO: In the true course of all the question.
ANTONIO: Well, I am glad that all things sort so well.
BENEDICK: And so am I, being else by faith enforced
BENEDICK: To call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.
LEONATO: Well, daughter, and you gentle-women all,
LEONATO: Withdraw into a chamber by yourselves,
LEONATO: And when I send for you, come hither mask'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Ladies
LEONATO: The prince and Claudio promised by this hour
LEONATO: To visit me. You know your office, brother:
LEONATO: You must be father to your brother's daughter
LEONATO: And give her to young Claudio.
ANTONIO: Which I will do with confirm'd countenance.
BENEDICK: Friar, I must entreat your pains, I think.
FRIAR FRANCIS: To do what, signior?
BENEDICK: To bind me, or undo me, one of them.
BENEDICK: Signior Leonato, truth it is, good signior,
BENEDICK: Your niece regards me with an eye of favour.
LEONATO: That eye my daughter lent her: 'tis most true.
BENEDICK: And I do with an eye of love requite her.
LEONATO: The sight whereof I think you had from me,
LEONATO: From Claudio and the prince: but what's your will?
BENEDICK: Your answer, sir, is enigmatical:
BENEDICK: But, for my will, my will is your good will
BENEDICK: May stand with ours, this day to be conjoin'd
BENEDICK: In the state of honourable marriage:
BENEDICK: In which, good friar, I shall desire your help.
LEONATO: My heart is with your liking.
FRIAR FRANCIS: And my help.
FRIAR FRANCIS: Here comes the prince and Claudio.
NARRATOR: Enter DON PEDRO and CLAUDIO, and two or three others
DON PEDRO: Good morrow to this fair assembly.
LEONATO: Good morrow, prince, good morrow, Claudio:
LEONATO: We here attend you. Are you yet determined
LEONATO: To-day to marry with my brother's daughter?
CLAUDIO: I'll hold my mind, were she an Ethiope.
LEONATO: Call her forth, brother, here's the friar ready.
NARRATOR: Exit ANTONIO
DON PEDRO: Good morrow, Benedick. Why, what's the matter,
DON PEDRO: That you have such a February face,
DON PEDRO: So full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?
CLAUDIO: I think he thinks upon the savage bull.
CLAUDIO: Tush, fear not, man, we'll tip thy horns with gold
CLAUDIO: And all Europa shall rejoice at thee,
CLAUDIO: As once Europa did at lusty Jove,
CLAUDIO: When he would play the noble beast in love.
BENEDICK: Bull Jove, sir, had an amiable low,
BENEDICK: And some such strange bull leap'd your father's cow,
BENEDICK: And got a calf in that same noble feat
BENEDICK: Much like to you, for you have just his bleat.
CLAUDIO: For this I owe you: here comes other reckonings.
NARRATOR: Re-enter ANTONIO, with the Ladies masked
CLAUDIO: Which is the lady I must seize upon?
ANTONIO: This same is she, and I do give you her.
CLAUDIO: Why, then she's mine. Sweet, let me see your face.
LEONATO: No, that you shall not, till you take her hand
LEONATO: Before this friar and swear to marry her.
CLAUDIO: Give me your hand: before this holy friar,
CLAUDIO: I am your husband, if you like of me.
HERO: And when I lived, I was your other wife:
NARRATOR: Unmasking
HERO: And when you loved, you were my other husband.
CLAUDIO: Another Hero!
HERO: Nothing certainer:
HERO: One Hero died defiled, but I do live,
HERO: And surely as I live, I am a maid.
DON PEDRO: The former Hero! Hero that is dead!
LEONATO: She died, my lord, but whiles her slander lived.
FRIAR FRANCIS: All this amazement can I qualify:
FRIAR FRANCIS: When after that the holy rites are ended,
FRIAR FRANCIS: I'll tell you largely of fair Hero's death:
FRIAR FRANCIS: Meantime let wonder seem familiar,
FRIAR FRANCIS: And to the chapel let us presently.
BENEDICK: Soft and fair, friar. Which is Beatrice?
BEATRICE: [Unmasking]  I answer to that name. What is your will?
BENEDICK: Do not you love me?
BEATRICE: Why, no, no more than reason.
BENEDICK: Why, then your uncle and the prince and Claudio
BENEDICK: Have been deceived, they swore you did.
BEATRICE: Do not you love me?
BENEDICK: Troth, no, no more than reason.
BEATRICE: Why, then my cousin Margaret and Ursula
BEATRICE: Are much deceived, for they did swear you did.
BENEDICK: They swore that you were almost sick for me.
BEATRICE: They swore that you were well-nigh dead for me.
BENEDICK: 'Tis no such matter. Then you do not love me?
BEATRICE: No, truly, but in friendly recompense.
LEONATO: Come, cousin, I am sure you love the gentleman.
CLAUDIO: And I'll be sworn upon't that he loves her,
CLAUDIO: For here's a paper written in his hand,
CLAUDIO: A halting sonnet of his own pure brain,
CLAUDIO: Fashion'd to Beatrice.
HERO: And here's another
HERO: Writ in my cousin's hand, stolen from her pocket,
HERO: Containing her affection unto Benedick.
BENEDICK: A miracle! here's our own hands against our hearts.
BENEDICK: Come, I will have thee, but, by this light, I take
BENEDICK: thee for pity.
BEATRICE: I would not deny you, but, by this good day, I yield
BEATRICE: upon great persuasion, and partly to save your life,
BEATRICE: for I was told you were in a consumption.
BENEDICK: Peace! I will stop your mouth.
NARRATOR: Kissing her
DON PEDRO: How dost thou, Benedick, the married man?
BENEDICK: I'll tell thee what, prince, a college of
BENEDICK: wit-crackers cannot flout me out of my humour. Dost
BENEDICK: thou think I  care for a satire or an epigram? No:
BENEDICK: if a man will be beaten with brains, a' shall wear
BENEDICK: nothing handsome about him. In brief, since I do
BENEDICK: purpose to marry, I will think nothing to any
BENEDICK: purpose that the world can say against it, and
BENEDICK: therefore never flout at me for what I have said
BENEDICK: against it, for man is a giddy thing, and this is my
BENEDICK: conclusion. For thy part, Claudio, I did think to
BENEDICK: have beaten thee, but in that thou art like to be my
BENEDICK: kinsman, live unbruised and love my cousin.
CLAUDIO: I had well hoped thou wouldst have denied Beatrice,
CLAUDIO: that I might have cudgelled thee out of thy single
CLAUDIO: life, to make thee a double-dealer, which, out of
CLAUDIO: question, thou wilt be, if my cousin do not look
CLAUDIO: exceedingly narrowly to thee.
BENEDICK: Come, come, we are friends: let's have a dance ere
BENEDICK: we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts
BENEDICK: and our wives' heels.
LEONATO: We'll have dancing afterward.
BENEDICK: First, of my word, therefore play, music. Prince,
BENEDICK: thou art sad, get thee a wife, get thee a wife:
BENEDICK: there is no staff more reverend than one tipped with horn.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: My lord, your brother John is ta'en in flight,
Messenger: And brought with armed men back to Messina.
BENEDICK: Think not on him till to-morrow:
BENEDICK: I'll devise thee brave punishments for him.
BENEDICK: Strike up, pipers.
NARRATOR: Dance
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Othello '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Venice. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter RODERIGO and IAGO
RODERIGO: Tush! never tell me, I take it much unkindly
RODERIGO: That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse
RODERIGO: As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
IAGO: 'Sblood, but you will not hear me:
IAGO: If ever I did dream of such a matter, Abhor me.
RODERIGO: Thou told'st me thou didst hold him in thy hate.
IAGO: Despise me, if I do not. Three great ones of the city,
IAGO: In personal suit to make me his lieutenant,
IAGO: Off-capp'd to him: and, by the faith of man,
IAGO: I know my price, I am worth no worse a place:
IAGO: But he, as loving his own pride and purposes,
IAGO: Evades them, with a bombast circumstance
IAGO: Horribly stuff'd with epithets of war,
IAGO: And, in conclusion,
IAGO: Nonsuits my mediators, for, 'Certes,' says he,
IAGO: 'I have already chose my officer.'
IAGO: And what was he?
IAGO: Forsooth, a great arithmetician,
IAGO: One Michael Cassio, a Florentine,
IAGO: A fellow almost damn'd in a fair wife,
IAGO: That never set a squadron in the field,
IAGO: Nor the division of a battle knows
IAGO: More than a spinster, unless the bookish theoric,
IAGO: Wherein the toged consuls can propose
IAGO: As masterly as he: mere prattle, without practise,
IAGO: Is all his soldiership. But he, sir, had the election:
IAGO: And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof
IAGO: At Rhodes, at Cyprus and on other grounds
IAGO: Christian and heathen, must be be-lee'd and calm'd
IAGO: By debitor and creditor: this counter-caster,
IAGO: He, in good time, must his lieutenant be,
IAGO: And I--God bless the mark!--his Moorship's ancient.
RODERIGO: By heaven, I rather would have been his hangman.
IAGO: Why, there's no remedy, 'tis the curse of service,
IAGO: Preferment goes by letter and affection,
IAGO: And not by old gradation, where each second
IAGO: Stood heir to the first. Now, sir, be judge yourself,
IAGO: Whether I in any just term am affined
IAGO: To love the Moor.
RODERIGO: I would not follow him then.
IAGO: O, sir, content you,
IAGO: I follow him to serve my turn upon him:
IAGO: We cannot all be masters, nor all masters
IAGO: Cannot be truly follow'd. You shall mark
IAGO: Many a duteous and knee-crooking knave,
IAGO: That, doting on his own obsequious bondage,
IAGO: Wears out his time, much like his master's ass,
IAGO: For nought but provender, and when he's old, cashier'd:
IAGO: Whip me such honest knaves. Others there are
IAGO: Who, trimm'd in forms and visages of duty,
IAGO: Keep yet their hearts attending on themselves,
IAGO: And, throwing but shows of service on their lords,
IAGO: Do well thrive by them and when they have lined
IAGO: their coats
IAGO: Do themselves homage: these fellows have some soul,
IAGO: And such a one do I profess myself. For, sir,
IAGO: It is as sure as you are Roderigo,
IAGO: Were I the Moor, I would not be Iago:
IAGO: In following him, I follow but myself,
IAGO: Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,
IAGO: But seeming so, for my peculiar end:
IAGO: For when my outward action doth demonstrate
IAGO: The native act and figure of my heart
IAGO: In compliment extern, 'tis not long after
IAGO: But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve
IAGO: For daws to peck at: I am not what I am.
RODERIGO: What a full fortune does the thicklips owe
RODERIGO: If he can carry't thus!
IAGO: Call up her father,
IAGO: Rouse him: make after him, poison his delight,
IAGO: Proclaim him in the streets, incense her kinsmen,
IAGO: And, though he in a fertile climate dwell,
IAGO: Plague him with flies: though that his joy be joy,
IAGO: Yet throw such changes of vexation on't,
IAGO: As it may lose some colour.
RODERIGO: Here is her father's house, I'll call aloud.
IAGO: Do, with like timorous accent and dire yell
IAGO: As when, by night and negligence, the fire
IAGO: Is spied in populous cities.
RODERIGO: What, ho, Brabantio! Signior Brabantio, ho!
IAGO: Awake! what, ho, Brabantio! thieves! thieves! thieves!
IAGO: Look to your house, your daughter and your bags!
IAGO: Thieves! thieves!
NARRATOR: BRABANTIO appears above, at a window
BRABANTIO: What is the reason of this terrible summons?
BRABANTIO: What is the matter there?
RODERIGO: Signior, is all your family within?
IAGO: Are your doors lock'd?
BRABANTIO: Why, wherefore ask you this?
IAGO: 'Zounds, sir, you're robb'd, for shame, put on
IAGO: your gown,
IAGO: Your heart is burst, you have lost half your soul,
IAGO: Even now, now, very now, an old black ram
IAGO: Is topping your white ewe. Arise, arise,
IAGO: Awake the snorting citizens with the bell,
IAGO: Or else the devil will make a grandsire of you:
IAGO: Arise, I say.
BRABANTIO: What, have you lost your wits?
RODERIGO: Most reverend signior, do you know my voice?
BRABANTIO: Not I	what are you?
RODERIGO: My name is Roderigo.
BRABANTIO: The worser welcome:
BRABANTIO: I have charged thee not to haunt about my doors:
BRABANTIO: In honest plainness thou hast heard me say
BRABANTIO: My daughter is not for thee, and now, in madness,
BRABANTIO: Being full of supper and distempering draughts,
BRABANTIO: Upon malicious bravery, dost thou come
BRABANTIO: To start my quiet.
RODERIGO: Sir, sir, sir,--
BRABANTIO: But thou must needs be sure
BRABANTIO: My spirit and my place have in them power
BRABANTIO: To make this bitter to thee.
RODERIGO: Patience, good sir.
BRABANTIO: What tell'st thou me of robbing? this is Venice,
BRABANTIO: My house is not a grange.
RODERIGO: Most grave Brabantio,
RODERIGO: In simple and pure soul I come to you.
IAGO: 'Zounds, sir, you are one of those that will not
IAGO: serve God, if the devil bid you. Because we come to
IAGO: do you service and you think we are ruffians, you'll
IAGO: have your daughter covered with a Barbary horse,
IAGO: you'll have your nephews neigh to you, you'll have
IAGO: coursers for cousins and gennets for germans.
BRABANTIO: What profane wretch art thou?
IAGO: I am one, sir, that comes to tell you your daughter
IAGO: and the Moor are now making the beast with two backs.
BRABANTIO: Thou art a villain.
IAGO: You are--a senator.
BRABANTIO: This thou shalt answer, I know thee, Roderigo.
RODERIGO: Sir, I will answer any thing. But, I beseech you,
RODERIGO: If't be your pleasure and most wise consent,
RODERIGO: As partly I find it is, that your fair daughter,
RODERIGO: At this odd-even and dull watch o' the night,
RODERIGO: Transported, with no worse nor better guard
RODERIGO: But with a knave of common hire, a gondolier,
RODERIGO: To the gross clasps of a lascivious Moor--
RODERIGO: If this be known to you and your allowance,
RODERIGO: We then have done you bold and saucy wrongs,
RODERIGO: But if you know not this, my manners tell me
RODERIGO: We have your wrong rebuke. Do not believe
RODERIGO: That, from the sense of all civility,
RODERIGO: I thus would play and trifle with your reverence:
RODERIGO: Your daughter, if you have not given her leave,
RODERIGO: I say again, hath made a gross revolt,
RODERIGO: Tying her duty, beauty, wit and fortunes
RODERIGO: In an extravagant and wheeling stranger
RODERIGO: Of here and every where. Straight satisfy yourself:
RODERIGO: If she be in her chamber or your house,
RODERIGO: Let loose on me the justice of the state
RODERIGO: For thus deluding you.
BRABANTIO: Strike on the tinder, ho!
BRABANTIO: Give me a taper! call up all my people!
BRABANTIO: This accident is not unlike my dream:
BRABANTIO: Belief of it oppresses me already.
BRABANTIO: Light, I say! light!
NARRATOR: Exit above
IAGO: Farewell, for I must leave you:
IAGO: It seems not meet, nor wholesome to my place,
IAGO: To be produced--as, if I stay, I shall--
IAGO: Against the Moor: for, I do know, the state,
IAGO: However this may gall him with some cheque,
IAGO: Cannot with safety cast him, for he's embark'd
IAGO: With such loud reason to the Cyprus wars,
IAGO: Which even now stand in act, that, for their souls,
IAGO: Another of his fathom they have none,
IAGO: To lead their business: in which regard,
IAGO: Though I do hate him as I do hell-pains.
IAGO: Yet, for necessity of present life,
IAGO: I must show out a flag and sign of love,
IAGO: Which is indeed but sign. That you shall surely find him,
IAGO: Lead to the Sagittary the raised search,
IAGO: And there will I be with him. So, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter, below, BRABANTIO, and Servants with torches
BRABANTIO: It is too true an evil: gone she is,
BRABANTIO: And what's to come of my despised time
BRABANTIO: Is nought but bitterness. Now, Roderigo,
BRABANTIO: Where didst thou see her? O unhappy girl!
BRABANTIO: With the Moor, say'st thou? Who would be a father!
BRABANTIO: How didst thou know 'twas she? O she deceives me
BRABANTIO: Past thought! What said she to you? Get more tapers:
BRABANTIO: Raise all my kindred. Are they married, think you?
RODERIGO: Truly, I think they are.
BRABANTIO: O heaven! How got she out? O treason of the blood!
BRABANTIO: Fathers, from hence trust not your daughters' minds
BRABANTIO: By what you see them act. Is there not charms
BRABANTIO: By which the property of youth and maidhood
BRABANTIO: May be abused? Have you not read, Roderigo,
BRABANTIO: Of some such thing?
RODERIGO: Yes, sir, I have indeed.
BRABANTIO: Call up my brother. O, would you had had her!
BRABANTIO: Some one way, some another. Do you know
BRABANTIO: Where we may apprehend her and the Moor?
RODERIGO: I think I can discover him, if you please,
RODERIGO: To get good guard and go along with me.
BRABANTIO: Pray you, lead on. At every house I'll call,
BRABANTIO: I may command at most. Get weapons, ho!
BRABANTIO: And raise some special officers of night.
BRABANTIO: On, good Roderigo: I'll deserve your pains.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Another street.
NARRATOR: Enter OTHELLO, IAGO, and Attendants with torches
IAGO: Though in the trade of war I have slain men,
IAGO: Yet do I hold it very stuff o' the conscience
IAGO: To do no contrived murder: I lack iniquity
IAGO: Sometimes to do me service: nine or ten times
IAGO: I had thought to have yerk'd him here under the ribs.
OTHELLO: 'Tis better as it is.
IAGO: Nay, but he prated,
IAGO: And spoke such scurvy and provoking terms
IAGO: Against your honour
IAGO: That, with the little godliness I have,
IAGO: I did full hard forbear him. But, I pray you, sir,
IAGO: Are you fast married? Be assured of this,
IAGO: That the magnifico is much beloved,
IAGO: And hath in his effect a voice potential
IAGO: As double as the duke's: he will divorce you,
IAGO: Or put upon you what restraint and grievance
IAGO: The law, with all his might to enforce it on,
IAGO: Will give him cable.
OTHELLO: Let him do his spite:
OTHELLO: My services which I have done the signiory
OTHELLO: Shall out-tongue his complaints. 'Tis yet to know,--
OTHELLO: Which, when I know that boasting is an honour,
OTHELLO: I shall promulgate--I fetch my life and being
OTHELLO: From men of royal siege, and my demerits
OTHELLO: May speak unbonneted to as proud a fortune
OTHELLO: As this that I have reach'd: for know, Iago,
OTHELLO: But that I love the gentle Desdemona,
OTHELLO: I would not my unhoused free condition
OTHELLO: Put into circumscription and confine
OTHELLO: For the sea's worth. But, look! what lights come yond?
IAGO: Those are the raised father and his friends:
IAGO: You were best go in.
OTHELLO: Not I	I must be found:
OTHELLO: My parts, my title and my perfect soul
OTHELLO: Shall manifest me rightly. Is it they?
IAGO: By Janus, I think no.
NARRATOR: Enter CASSIO, and certain Officers with torches
OTHELLO: The servants of the duke, and my lieutenant.
OTHELLO: The goodness of the night upon you, friends!
OTHELLO: What is the news?
CASSIO: The duke does greet you, general,
CASSIO: And he requires your haste-post-haste appearance,
CASSIO: Even on the instant.
OTHELLO: What is the matter, think you?
CASSIO: Something from Cyprus as I may divine:
CASSIO: It is a business of some heat: the galleys
CASSIO: Have sent a dozen sequent messengers
CASSIO: This very night at one another's heels,
CASSIO: And many of the consuls, raised and met,
CASSIO: Are at the duke's already: you have been
CASSIO: hotly call'd for,
CASSIO: When, being not at your lodging to be found,
CASSIO: The senate hath sent about three several guests
CASSIO: To search you out.
OTHELLO: 'Tis well I am found by you.
OTHELLO: I will but spend a word here in the house,
OTHELLO: And go with you.
NARRATOR: Exit
CASSIO: Ancient, what makes he here?
IAGO: 'Faith, he to-night hath boarded a land carack:
IAGO: If it prove lawful prize, he's made for ever.
CASSIO: I do not understand.
IAGO: He's married.
CASSIO: To who?
NARRATOR: Re-enter OTHELLO
IAGO: Marry, to--Come, captain, will you go?
OTHELLO: Have with you.
CASSIO: Here comes another troop to seek for you.
IAGO: It is Brabantio. General, be advised,
IAGO: He comes to bad intent.
NARRATOR: Enter BRABANTIO, RODERIGO, and Officers with torches and weapons
OTHELLO: Holla! stand there!
RODERIGO: Signior, it is the Moor.
BRABANTIO: Down with him, thief!
NARRATOR: They draw on both sides
IAGO: You, Roderigo! come, sir, I am for you.
OTHELLO: Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them.
OTHELLO: Good signior, you shall more command with years
OTHELLO: Than with your weapons.
BRABANTIO: O thou foul thief, where hast thou stow'd my daughter?
BRABANTIO: Damn'd as thou art, thou hast enchanted her,
BRABANTIO: For I'll refer me to all things of sense,
BRABANTIO: If she in chains of magic were not bound,
BRABANTIO: Whether a maid so tender, fair and happy,
BRABANTIO: So opposite to marriage that she shunned
BRABANTIO: The wealthy curled darlings of our nation,
BRABANTIO: Would ever have, to incur a general mock,
BRABANTIO: Run from her guardage to the sooty bosom
BRABANTIO: Of such a thing as thou, to fear, not to delight.
BRABANTIO: Judge me the world, if 'tis not gross in sense
BRABANTIO: That thou hast practised on her with foul charms,
BRABANTIO: Abused her delicate youth with drugs or minerals
BRABANTIO: That weaken motion: I'll have't disputed on,
BRABANTIO: 'Tis probable and palpable to thinking.
BRABANTIO: I therefore apprehend and do attach thee
BRABANTIO: For an abuser of the world, a practiser
BRABANTIO: Of arts inhibited and out of warrant.
BRABANTIO: Lay hold upon him: if he do resist,
BRABANTIO: Subdue him at his peril.
OTHELLO: Hold your hands,
OTHELLO: Both you of my inclining, and the rest:
OTHELLO: Were it my cue to fight, I should have known it
OTHELLO: Without a prompter. Where will you that I go
OTHELLO: To answer this your charge?
BRABANTIO: To prison, till fit time
BRABANTIO: Of law and course of direct session
BRABANTIO: Call thee to answer.
OTHELLO: What if I do obey?
OTHELLO: How may the duke be therewith satisfied,
OTHELLO: Whose messengers are here about my side,
OTHELLO: Upon some present business of the state
OTHELLO: To bring me to him?
First Officer: 'Tis true, most worthy signior,
First Officer: The duke's in council and your noble self,
First Officer: I am sure, is sent for.
BRABANTIO: How! the duke in council!
BRABANTIO: In this time of the night! Bring him away:
BRABANTIO: Mine's not an idle cause: the duke himself,
BRABANTIO: Or any of my brothers of the state,
BRABANTIO: Cannot but feel this wrong as 'twere their own,
BRABANTIO: For if such actions may have passage free,
BRABANTIO: Bond-slaves and pagans shall our statesmen be.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A council-chamber.
NARRATOR: The DUKE and Senators sitting at a table, Officers attending
DUKE OF VENICE: There is no composition in these news
DUKE OF VENICE: That gives them credit.
First Senator: Indeed, they are disproportion'd,
First Senator: My letters say a hundred and seven galleys.
DUKE OF VENICE: And mine, a hundred and forty.
Second Senator: And mine, two hundred:
Second Senator: But though they jump not on a just account,--
Second Senator: As in these cases, where the aim reports,
Second Senator: 'Tis oft with difference--yet do they all confirm
Second Senator: A Turkish fleet, and bearing up to Cyprus.
DUKE OF VENICE: Nay, it is possible enough to judgment:
DUKE OF VENICE: I do not so secure me in the error,
DUKE OF VENICE: But the main article I do approve
DUKE OF VENICE: In fearful sense.
Sailor: [Within]  What, ho! what, ho! what, ho!
First Officer: A messenger from the galleys.
NARRATOR: Enter a Sailor
DUKE OF VENICE: Now, what's the business?
Sailor: The Turkish preparation makes for Rhodes,
Sailor: So was I bid report here to the state
Sailor: By Signior Angelo.
DUKE OF VENICE: How say you by this change?
First Senator: This cannot be,
First Senator: By no assay of reason: 'tis a pageant,
First Senator: To keep us in false gaze. When we consider
First Senator: The importancy of Cyprus to the Turk,
First Senator: And let ourselves again but understand,
First Senator: That as it more concerns the Turk than Rhodes,
First Senator: So may he with more facile question bear it,
First Senator: For that it stands not in such warlike brace,
First Senator: But altogether lacks the abilities
First Senator: That Rhodes is dress'd in: if we make thought of this,
First Senator: We must not think the Turk is so unskilful
First Senator: To leave that latest which concerns him first,
First Senator: Neglecting an attempt of ease and gain,
First Senator: To wake and wage a danger profitless.
DUKE OF VENICE: Nay, in all confidence, he's not for Rhodes.
First Officer: Here is more news.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: The Ottomites, reverend and gracious,
Messenger: Steering with due course towards the isle of Rhodes,
Messenger: Have there injointed them with an after fleet.
First Senator: Ay, so I thought. How many, as you guess?
Messenger: Of thirty sail: and now they do restem
Messenger: Their backward course, bearing with frank appearance
Messenger: Their purposes toward Cyprus. Signior Montano,
Messenger: Your trusty and most valiant servitor,
Messenger: With his free duty recommends you thus,
Messenger: And prays you to believe him.
DUKE OF VENICE: 'Tis certain, then, for Cyprus.
DUKE OF VENICE: Marcus Luccicos, is not he in town?
First Senator: He's now in Florence.
DUKE OF VENICE: Write from us to him, post-post-haste dispatch.
First Senator: Here comes Brabantio and the valiant Moor.
NARRATOR: Enter BRABANTIO, OTHELLO, IAGO, RODERIGO, and Officers
DUKE OF VENICE: Valiant Othello, we must straight employ you
DUKE OF VENICE: Against the general enemy Ottoman.
NARRATOR: To BRABANTIO
DUKE OF VENICE: I did not see you, welcome, gentle signior,
DUKE OF VENICE: We lack'd your counsel and your help tonight.
BRABANTIO: So did I yours. Good your grace, pardon me,
BRABANTIO: Neither my place nor aught I heard of business
BRABANTIO: Hath raised me from my bed, nor doth the general care
BRABANTIO: Take hold on me, for my particular grief
BRABANTIO: Is of so flood-gate and o'erbearing nature
BRABANTIO: That it engluts and swallows other sorrows
BRABANTIO: And it is still itself.
DUKE OF VENICE: Why, what's the matter?
BRABANTIO: My daughter! O, my daughter!
Senator: Dead?
BRABANTIO: Ay, to me,
BRABANTIO: She is abused, stol'n from me, and corrupted
BRABANTIO: By spells and medicines bought of mountebanks,
BRABANTIO: For nature so preposterously to err,
BRABANTIO: Being not deficient, blind, or lame of sense,
BRABANTIO: Sans witchcraft could not.
DUKE OF VENICE: Whoe'er he be that in this foul proceeding
DUKE OF VENICE: Hath thus beguiled your daughter of herself
DUKE OF VENICE: And you of her, the bloody book of law
DUKE OF VENICE: You shall yourself read in the bitter letter
DUKE OF VENICE: After your own sense, yea, though our proper son
DUKE OF VENICE: Stood in your action.
BRABANTIO: Humbly I thank your grace.
BRABANTIO: Here is the man, this Moor, whom now, it seems,
BRABANTIO: Your special mandate for the state-affairs
BRABANTIO: Hath hither brought.
Senator: We are very sorry for't.
DUKE OF VENICE: [To OTHELLO]  What, in your own part, can you say to this?
BRABANTIO: Nothing, but this is so.
OTHELLO: Most potent, grave, and reverend signiors,
OTHELLO: My very noble and approved good masters,
OTHELLO: That I have ta'en away this old man's daughter,
OTHELLO: It is most true, true, I have married her:
OTHELLO: The very head and front of my offending
OTHELLO: Hath this extent, no more. Rude am I in my speech,
OTHELLO: And little bless'd with the soft phrase of peace:
OTHELLO: For since these arms of mine had seven years' pith,
OTHELLO: Till now some nine moons wasted, they have used
OTHELLO: Their dearest action in the tented field,
OTHELLO: And little of this great world can I speak,
OTHELLO: More than pertains to feats of broil and battle,
OTHELLO: And therefore little shall I grace my cause
OTHELLO: In speaking for myself. Yet, by your gracious patience,
OTHELLO: I will a round unvarnish'd tale deliver
OTHELLO: Of my whole course of love, what drugs, what charms,
OTHELLO: What conjuration and what mighty magic,
OTHELLO: For such proceeding I am charged withal,
OTHELLO: I won his daughter.
BRABANTIO: A maiden never bold,
BRABANTIO: Of spirit so still and quiet, that her motion
BRABANTIO: Blush'd at herself, and she, in spite of nature,
BRABANTIO: Of years, of country, credit, every thing,
BRABANTIO: To fall in love with what she fear'd to look on!
BRABANTIO: It is a judgment maim'd and most imperfect
BRABANTIO: That will confess perfection so could err
BRABANTIO: Against all rules of nature, and must be driven
BRABANTIO: To find out practises of cunning hell,
BRABANTIO: Why this should be. I therefore vouch again
BRABANTIO: That with some mixtures powerful o'er the blood,
BRABANTIO: Or with some dram conjured to this effect,
BRABANTIO: He wrought upon her.
DUKE OF VENICE: To vouch this, is no proof,
DUKE OF VENICE: Without more wider and more overt test
DUKE OF VENICE: Than these thin habits and poor likelihoods
DUKE OF VENICE: Of modern seeming do prefer against him.
First Senator: But, Othello, speak:
First Senator: Did you by indirect and forced courses
First Senator: Subdue and poison this young maid's affections?
First Senator: Or came it by request and such fair question
First Senator: As soul to soul affordeth?
OTHELLO: I do beseech you,
OTHELLO: Send for the lady to the Sagittary,
OTHELLO: And let her speak of me before her father:
OTHELLO: If you do find me foul in her report,
OTHELLO: The trust, the office I do hold of you,
OTHELLO: Not only take away, but let your sentence
OTHELLO: Even fall upon my life.
DUKE OF VENICE: Fetch Desdemona hither.
OTHELLO: Ancient, conduct them: you best know the place.
NARRATOR: Exeunt IAGO and Attendants
OTHELLO: And, till she come, as truly as to heaven
OTHELLO: I do confess the vices of my blood,
OTHELLO: So justly to your grave ears I'll present
OTHELLO: How I did thrive in this fair lady's love,
OTHELLO: And she in mine.
DUKE OF VENICE: Say it, Othello.
OTHELLO: Her father loved me, oft invited me,
OTHELLO: Still question'd me the story of my life,
OTHELLO: From year to year, the battles, sieges, fortunes,
OTHELLO: That I have passed.
OTHELLO: I ran it through, even from my boyish days,
OTHELLO: To the very moment that he bade me tell it,
OTHELLO: Wherein I spake of most disastrous chances,
OTHELLO: Of moving accidents by flood and field
OTHELLO: Of hair-breadth scapes i' the imminent deadly breach,
OTHELLO: Of being taken by the insolent foe
OTHELLO: And sold to slavery, of my redemption thence
OTHELLO: And portance in my travels' history:
OTHELLO: Wherein of antres vast and deserts idle,
OTHELLO: Rough quarries, rocks and hills whose heads touch heaven
OTHELLO: It was my hint to speak,--such was the process,
OTHELLO: And of the Cannibals that each other eat,
OTHELLO: The Anthropophagi and men whose heads
OTHELLO: Do grow beneath their shoulders. This to hear
OTHELLO: Would Desdemona seriously incline:
OTHELLO: But still the house-affairs would draw her thence:
OTHELLO: Which ever as she could with haste dispatch,
OTHELLO: She'ld come again, and with a greedy ear
OTHELLO: Devour up my discourse: which I observing,
OTHELLO: Took once a pliant hour, and found good means
OTHELLO: To draw from her a prayer of earnest heart
OTHELLO: That I would all my pilgrimage dilate,
OTHELLO: Whereof by parcels she had something heard,
OTHELLO: But not intentively: I did consent,
OTHELLO: And often did beguile her of her tears,
OTHELLO: When I did speak of some distressful stroke
OTHELLO: That my youth suffer'd. My story being done,
OTHELLO: She gave me for my pains a world of sighs:
OTHELLO: She swore, in faith, twas strange, 'twas passing strange,
OTHELLO: 'Twas pitiful, 'twas wondrous pitiful:
OTHELLO: She wish'd she had not heard it, yet she wish'd
OTHELLO: That heaven had made her such a man: she thank'd me,
OTHELLO: And bade me, if I had a friend that loved her,
OTHELLO: I should but teach him how to tell my story.
OTHELLO: And that would woo her. Upon this hint I spake:
OTHELLO: She loved me for the dangers I had pass'd,
OTHELLO: And I loved her that she did pity them.
OTHELLO: This only is the witchcraft I have used:
OTHELLO: Here comes the lady, let her witness it.
NARRATOR: Enter DESDEMONA, IAGO, and Attendants
DUKE OF VENICE: I think this tale would win my daughter too.
DUKE OF VENICE: Good Brabantio,
DUKE OF VENICE: Take up this mangled matter at the best:
DUKE OF VENICE: Men do their broken weapons rather use
DUKE OF VENICE: Than their bare hands.
BRABANTIO: I pray you, hear her speak:
BRABANTIO: If she confess that she was half the wooer,
BRABANTIO: Destruction on my head, if my bad blame
BRABANTIO: Light on the man! Come hither, gentle mistress:
BRABANTIO: Do you perceive in all this noble company
BRABANTIO: Where most you owe obedience?
DESDEMONA: My noble father,
DESDEMONA: I do perceive here a divided duty:
DESDEMONA: To you I am bound for life and education,
DESDEMONA: My life and education both do learn me
DESDEMONA: How to respect you, you are the lord of duty,
DESDEMONA: I am hitherto your daughter: but here's my husband,
DESDEMONA: And so much duty as my mother show'd
DESDEMONA: To you, preferring you before her father,
DESDEMONA: So much I challenge that I may profess
DESDEMONA: Due to the Moor my lord.
BRABANTIO: God be wi' you! I have done.
BRABANTIO: Please it your grace, on to the state-affairs:
BRABANTIO: I had rather to adopt a child than get it.
BRABANTIO: Come hither, Moor:
BRABANTIO: I here do give thee that with all my heart
BRABANTIO: Which, but thou hast already, with all my heart
BRABANTIO: I would keep from thee. For your sake, jewel,
BRABANTIO: I am glad at soul I have no other child:
BRABANTIO: For thy escape would teach me tyranny,
BRABANTIO: To hang clogs on them. I have done, my lord.
DUKE OF VENICE: Let me speak like yourself, and lay a sentence,
DUKE OF VENICE: Which, as a grise or step, may help these lovers
DUKE OF VENICE: Into your favour.
DUKE OF VENICE: When remedies are past, the griefs are ended
DUKE OF VENICE: By seeing the worst, which late on hopes depended.
DUKE OF VENICE: To mourn a mischief that is past and gone
DUKE OF VENICE: Is the next way to draw new mischief on.
DUKE OF VENICE: What cannot be preserved when fortune takes
DUKE OF VENICE: Patience her injury a mockery makes.
DUKE OF VENICE: The robb'd that smiles steals something from the thief,
DUKE OF VENICE: He robs himself that spends a bootless grief.
BRABANTIO: So let the Turk of Cyprus us beguile,
BRABANTIO: We lose it not, so long as we can smile.
BRABANTIO: He bears the sentence well that nothing bears
BRABANTIO: But the free comfort which from thence he hears,
BRABANTIO: But he bears both the sentence and the sorrow
BRABANTIO: That, to pay grief, must of poor patience borrow.
BRABANTIO: These sentences, to sugar, or to gall,
BRABANTIO: Being strong on both sides, are equivocal:
BRABANTIO: But words are words, I never yet did hear
BRABANTIO: That the bruised heart was pierced through the ear.
BRABANTIO: I humbly beseech you, proceed to the affairs of state.
DUKE OF VENICE: The Turk with a most mighty preparation makes for
DUKE OF VENICE: Cyprus. Othello, the fortitude of the place is best
DUKE OF VENICE: known to you, and though we have there a substitute
DUKE OF VENICE: of most allowed sufficiency, yet opinion, a
