NARRATOR: SCENE II. Mytilene. A room in a brothel.

NARRATOR: SCENE III. Tarsus. A room in CLEON's house.

NARRATOR: Enter GOWER, before the monument of MARINA at Tarsus
GOWER: Thus time we waste, and longest leagues make short,

GOWER: Making, to take your imagination,
GOWER: From bourn to bourn, region to region.

GOWER: See how belief may suffer by foul show!

GOWER: Thetis, being proud, swallow'd some part o' the earth:

GOWER: No visor does become black villany

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. KING RICHARD II's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD II, JOHN OF GAUNT, with other Nobles and Attendants
KING RICHARD II: Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster,
KING RICHARD II: Hast thou, according to thy oath and band,
KING RICHARD II: Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son,
KING RICHARD II: Here to make good the boisterous late appeal,
KING RICHARD II: Which then our leisure would not let us hear,
KING RICHARD II: Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
JOHN OF GAUNT: I have, my liege.
KING RICHARD II: Tell me, moreover, hast thou sounded him,
KING RICHARD II: If he appeal the duke on ancient malice,
KING RICHARD II: Or worthily, as a good subject should,
KING RICHARD II: On some known ground of treachery in him?
JOHN OF GAUNT: As near as I could sift him on that argument,
JOHN OF GAUNT: On some apparent danger seen in him
JOHN OF GAUNT: Aim'd at your highness, no inveterate malice.
KING RICHARD II: Then call them to our presence, face to face,
KING RICHARD II: And frowning brow to brow, ourselves will hear
KING RICHARD II: The accuser and the accused freely speak:
KING RICHARD II: High-stomach'd are they both, and full of ire,
KING RICHARD II: In rage deaf as the sea, hasty as fire.
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE and THOMAS MOWBRAY
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Many years of happy days befal
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My gracious sovereign, my most loving liege!
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Each day still better other's happiness,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Until the heavens, envying earth's good hap,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Add an immortal title to your crown!
KING RICHARD II: We thank you both: yet one but flatters us,
KING RICHARD II: As well appeareth by the cause you come,
KING RICHARD II: Namely to appeal each other of high treason.
KING RICHARD II: Cousin of Hereford, what dost thou object
KING RICHARD II: Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: First, heaven be the record to my speech!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: In the devotion of a subject's love,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Tendering the precious safety of my prince,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And free from other misbegotten hate,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Come I appellant to this princely presence.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Now, Thomas Mowbray, do I turn to thee,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And mark my greeting well, for what I speak
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My body shall make good upon this earth,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or my divine soul answer it in heaven.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Thou art a traitor and a miscreant,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Too good to be so and too bad to live,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Since the more fair and crystal is the sky,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The uglier seem the clouds that in it fly.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Once more, the more to aggravate the note,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With a foul traitor's name stuff I thy throat,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And wish, so please my sovereign, ere I move,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What my tongue speaks my right drawn sword may prove.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Let not my cold words here accuse my zeal:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: 'Tis not the trial of a woman's war,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The bitter clamour of two eager tongues,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Can arbitrate this cause betwixt us twain,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The blood is hot that must be cool'd for this:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Yet can I not of such tame patience boast
THOMAS MOWBRAY: As to be hush'd and nought at all to say:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: First, the fair reverence of your highness curbs me
THOMAS MOWBRAY: From giving reins and spurs to my free speech,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which else would post until it had return'd
THOMAS MOWBRAY: These terms of treason doubled down his throat.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Setting aside his high blood's royalty,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And let him be no kinsman to my liege,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I do defy him, and I spit at him,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Call him a slanderous coward and a villain:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which to maintain I would allow him odds,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And meet him, were I tied to run afoot
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Even to the frozen ridges of the Alps,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Or any other ground inhabitable,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Where ever Englishman durst set his foot.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Mean time let this defend my loyalty,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: By all my hopes, most falsely doth he lie.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Pale trembling coward, there I throw my gage,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Disclaiming here the kindred of the king,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And lay aside my high blood's royalty,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which fear, not reverence, makes thee to except.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: If guilty dread have left thee so much strength
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As to take up mine honour's pawn, then stoop:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By that and all the rites of knighthood else,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Will I make good against thee, arm to arm,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What I have spoke, or thou canst worse devise.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I take it up, and by that sword I swear
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which gently laid my knighthood on my shoulder,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I'll answer thee in any fair degree,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Or chivalrous design of knightly trial:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And when I mount, alive may I not light,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: If I be traitor or unjustly fight!
KING RICHARD II: What doth our cousin lay to Mowbray's charge?
KING RICHARD II: It must be great that can inherit us
KING RICHARD II: So much as of a thought of ill in him.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Look, what I speak, my life shall prove it true,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That Mowbray hath received eight thousand nobles
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: In name of lendings for your highness' soldiers,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The which he hath detain'd for lewd employments,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Like a false traitor and injurious villain.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Besides I say and will in battle prove,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or here or elsewhere to the furthest verge
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That ever was survey'd by English eye,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That all the treasons for these eighteen years
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Complotted and contrived in this land
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Fetch from false Mowbray their first head and spring.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Further I say and further will maintain
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Upon his bad life to make all this good,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That he did plot the Duke of Gloucester's death,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Suggest his soon-believing adversaries,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And consequently, like a traitor coward,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Sluiced out his innocent soul through streams of blood:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which blood, like sacrificing Abel's, cries,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Even from the tongueless caverns of the earth,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To me for justice and rough chastisement,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And, by the glorious worth of my descent,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: This arm shall do it, or this life be spent.
KING RICHARD II: How high a pitch his resolution soars!
KING RICHARD II: Thomas of Norfolk, what say'st thou to this?
THOMAS MOWBRAY: O, let my sovereign turn away his face
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And bid his ears a little while be deaf,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Till I have told this slander of his blood,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: How God and good men hate so foul a liar.
KING RICHARD II: Mowbray, impartial are our eyes and ears:
KING RICHARD II: Were he my brother, nay, my kingdom's heir,
KING RICHARD II: As he is but my father's brother's son,
KING RICHARD II: Now, by my sceptre's awe, I make a vow,
KING RICHARD II: Such neighbour nearness to our sacred blood
KING RICHARD II: Should nothing privilege him, nor partialize
KING RICHARD II: The unstooping firmness of my upright soul:
KING RICHARD II: He is our subject, Mowbray, so art thou:
KING RICHARD II: Free speech and fearless I to thee allow.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Then, Bolingbroke, as low as to thy heart,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Through the false passage of thy throat, thou liest.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Three parts of that receipt I had for Calais
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Disbursed I duly to his highness' soldiers,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The other part reserved I by consent,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: For that my sovereign liege was in my debt
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Upon remainder of a dear account,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Since last I went to France to fetch his queen:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Now swallow down that lie. For Gloucester's death,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I slew him not, but to my own disgrace
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Neglected my sworn duty in that case.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: For you, my noble Lord of Lancaster,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The honourable father to my foe
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Once did I lay an ambush for your life,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A trespass that doth vex my grieved soul
THOMAS MOWBRAY: But ere I last received the sacrament
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I did confess it, and exactly begg'd
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Your grace's pardon, and I hope I had it.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: This is my fault: as for the rest appeall'd,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: It issues from the rancour of a villain,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A recreant and most degenerate traitor
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which in myself I boldly will defend,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And interchangeably hurl down my gage
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Upon this overweening traitor's foot,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: To prove myself a loyal gentleman
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Even in the best blood chamber'd in his bosom.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: In haste whereof, most heartily I pray
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Your highness to assign our trial day.
KING RICHARD II: Wrath-kindled gentlemen, be ruled by me,
KING RICHARD II: Let's purge this choler without letting blood:
KING RICHARD II: This we prescribe, though no physician,
KING RICHARD II: Deep malice makes too deep incision,
KING RICHARD II: Forget, forgive, conclude and be agreed,
KING RICHARD II: Our doctors say this is no month to bleed.
KING RICHARD II: Good uncle, let this end where it begun,
KING RICHARD II: We'll calm the Duke of Norfolk, you your son.
JOHN OF GAUNT: To be a make-peace shall become my age:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Throw down, my son, the Duke of Norfolk's gage.
KING RICHARD II: And, Norfolk, throw down his.
JOHN OF GAUNT: When, Harry, when?
JOHN OF GAUNT: Obedience bids I should not bid again.
KING RICHARD II: Norfolk, throw down, we bid, there is no boot.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Myself I throw, dread sovereign, at thy foot.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: My life thou shalt command, but not my shame:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The one my duty owes, but my fair name,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Despite of death that lives upon my grave,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: To dark dishonour's use thou shalt not have.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I am disgraced, impeach'd and baffled here,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Pierced to the soul with slander's venom'd spear,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The which no balm can cure but his heart-blood
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which breathed this poison.
KING RICHARD II: Rage must be withstood:
KING RICHARD II: Give me his gage: lions make leopards tame.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Yea, but not change his spots: take but my shame.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And I resign my gage. My dear dear lord,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The purest treasure mortal times afford
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Is spotless reputation: that away,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Men are but gilded loam or painted clay.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A jewel in a ten-times-barr'd-up chest
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Is a bold spirit in a loyal breast.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Mine honour is my life, both grow in one:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Take honour from me, and my life is done:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Then, dear my liege, mine honour let me try,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: In that I live and for that will I die.
KING RICHARD II: Cousin, throw up your gage, do you begin.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O, God defend my soul from such deep sin!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Shall I seem crest-fall'n in my father's sight?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or with pale beggar-fear impeach my height
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Before this out-dared dastard? Ere my tongue
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Shall wound my honour with such feeble wrong,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or sound so base a parle, my teeth shall tear
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The slavish motive of recanting fear,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And spit it bleeding in his high disgrace,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Where shame doth harbour, even in Mowbray's face.
NARRATOR: Exit JOHN OF GAUNT
KING RICHARD II: We were not born to sue, but to command,
KING RICHARD II: Which since we cannot do to make you friends,
KING RICHARD II: Be ready, as your lives shall answer it,
KING RICHARD II: At Coventry, upon Saint Lambert's day:
KING RICHARD II: There shall your swords and lances arbitrate
KING RICHARD II: The swelling difference of your settled hate:
KING RICHARD II: Since we can not atone you, we shall see
KING RICHARD II: Justice design the victor's chivalry.
KING RICHARD II: Lord marshal, command our officers at arms
KING RICHARD II: Be ready to direct these home alarms.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The DUKE OF LANCASTER'S palace.
NARRATOR: Enter JOHN OF GAUNT with DUCHESS
JOHN OF GAUNT: Alas, the part I had in Woodstock's blood
JOHN OF GAUNT: Doth more solicit me than your exclaims,
JOHN OF GAUNT: To stir against the butchers of his life!
JOHN OF GAUNT: But since correction lieth in those hands
JOHN OF GAUNT: Which made the fault that we cannot correct,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Put we our quarrel to the will of heaven,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Who, when they see the hours ripe on earth,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Will rain hot vengeance on offenders' heads.
DUCHESS: Finds brotherhood in thee no sharper spur?
DUCHESS: Hath love in thy old blood no living fire?
DUCHESS: Edward's seven sons, whereof thyself art one,
DUCHESS: Were as seven vials of his sacred blood,
DUCHESS: Or seven fair branches springing from one root:
DUCHESS: Some of those seven are dried by nature's course,
DUCHESS: Some of those branches by the Destinies cut,
DUCHESS: But Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester,
DUCHESS: One vial full of Edward's sacred blood,
DUCHESS: One flourishing branch of his most royal root,
DUCHESS: Is crack'd, and all the precious liquor spilt,
DUCHESS: Is hack'd down, and his summer leaves all faded,
DUCHESS: By envy's hand and murder's bloody axe.
DUCHESS: Ah, Gaunt, his blood was thine! that bed, that womb,
DUCHESS: That metal, that self-mould, that fashion'd thee
DUCHESS: Made him a man, and though thou livest and breathest,
DUCHESS: Yet art thou slain in him: thou dost consent
DUCHESS: In some large measure to thy father's death,
DUCHESS: In that thou seest thy wretched brother die,
DUCHESS: Who was the model of thy father's life.
DUCHESS: Call it not patience, Gaunt, it is despair:
DUCHESS: In suffering thus thy brother to be slaughter'd,
DUCHESS: Thou showest the naked pathway to thy life,
DUCHESS: Teaching stern murder how to butcher thee:
DUCHESS: That which in mean men we intitle patience
DUCHESS: Is pale cold cowardice in noble breasts.
DUCHESS: What shall I say? to safeguard thine own life,
DUCHESS: The best way is to venge my Gloucester's death.
JOHN OF GAUNT: God's is the quarrel, for God's substitute,
JOHN OF GAUNT: His deputy anointed in His sight,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Hath caused his death: the which if wrongfully,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Let heaven revenge, for I may never lift
JOHN OF GAUNT: An angry arm against His minister.
DUCHESS: Where then, alas, may I complain myself?
JOHN OF GAUNT: To God, the widow's champion and defence.
DUCHESS: Why, then, I will. Farewell, old Gaunt.
DUCHESS: Thou goest to Coventry, there to behold
DUCHESS: Our cousin Hereford and fell Mowbray fight:
DUCHESS: O, sit my husband's wrongs on Hereford's spear,
DUCHESS: That it may enter butcher Mowbray's breast!
DUCHESS: Or, if misfortune miss the first career,
DUCHESS: Be Mowbray's sins so heavy in his bosom,
DUCHESS: They may break his foaming courser's back,
DUCHESS: And throw the rider headlong in the lists,
DUCHESS: A caitiff recreant to my cousin Hereford!
DUCHESS: Farewell, old Gaunt: thy sometimes brother's wife
DUCHESS: With her companion grief must end her life.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Sister, farewell, I must to Coventry:
JOHN OF GAUNT: As much good stay with thee as go with me!
DUCHESS: Yet one word more: grief boundeth where it falls,
DUCHESS: Not with the empty hollowness, but weight:
DUCHESS: I take my leave before I have begun,
DUCHESS: For sorrow ends not when it seemeth done.
DUCHESS: Commend me to thy brother, Edmund York.
DUCHESS: Lo, this is all:--nay, yet depart not so,
DUCHESS: Though this be all, do not so quickly go,
DUCHESS: I shall remember more. Bid him--ah, what?--
DUCHESS: With all good speed at Plashy visit me.
DUCHESS: Alack, and what shall good old York there see
DUCHESS: But empty lodgings and unfurnish'd walls,
DUCHESS: Unpeopled offices, untrodden stones?
DUCHESS: And what hear there for welcome but my groans?
DUCHESS: Therefore commend me, let him not come there,
DUCHESS: To seek out sorrow that dwells every where.
DUCHESS: Desolate, desolate, will I hence and die:
DUCHESS: The last leave of thee takes my weeping eye.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The lists at Coventry.
NARRATOR: Enter the Lord Marshal and the DUKE OF AUMERLE
Lord Marshal: My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford arm'd?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Yea, at all points, and longs to enter in.
Lord Marshal: The Duke of Norfolk, sprightfully and bold,
Lord Marshal: Stays but the summons of the appellant's trumpet.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Why, then, the champions are prepared, and stay
DUKE OF AUMERLE: For nothing but his majesty's approach.
NARRATOR: The trumpets sound, and KING RICHARD enters with  his nobles, JOHN OF GAUNT, BUSHY, BAGOT, GREEN, and  others. When they are set, enter THOMAS MOWBRAY in arms, defendant, with a Herald
KING RICHARD II: Marshal, demand of yonder champion
KING RICHARD II: The cause of his arrival here in arms:
KING RICHARD II: Ask him his name and orderly proceed
KING RICHARD II: To swear him in the justice of his cause.
Lord Marshal: In God's name and the king's, say who thou art
Lord Marshal: And why thou comest thus knightly clad in arms,
Lord Marshal: Against what man thou comest, and what thy quarrel:
Lord Marshal: Speak truly, on thy knighthood and thy oath,
Lord Marshal: As so defend thee heaven and thy valour!
THOMAS MOWBRAY: My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Who hither come engaged by my oath--
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which God defend a knight should violate!--
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Both to defend my loyalty and truth
THOMAS MOWBRAY: To God, my king and my succeeding issue,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Against the Duke of Hereford that appeals me
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And, by the grace of God and this mine arm,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: To prove him, in defending of myself,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A traitor to my God, my king, and me:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!
NARRATOR: The trumpets sound. Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE, appellant, in armour, with a Herald
KING RICHARD II: Marshal, ask yonder knight in arms,
KING RICHARD II: Both who he is and why he cometh hither
KING RICHARD II: Thus plated in habiliments of war,
KING RICHARD II: And formally, according to our law,
KING RICHARD II: Depose him in the justice of his cause.
Lord Marshal: What is thy name? and wherefore comest thou hither,
Lord Marshal: Before King Richard in his royal lists?
Lord Marshal: Against whom comest thou? and what's thy quarrel?
Lord Marshal: Speak like a true knight, so defend thee heaven!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Am I, who ready here do stand in arms,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To prove, by God's grace and my body's valour,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: In lists, on Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That he is a traitor, foul and dangerous,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To God of heaven, King Richard and to me,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!
Lord Marshal: On pain of death, no person be so bold
Lord Marshal: Or daring-hardy as to touch the lists,
Lord Marshal: Except the marshal and such officers
Lord Marshal: Appointed to direct these fair designs.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Lord marshal, let me kiss my sovereign's hand,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And bow my knee before his majesty:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For Mowbray and myself are like two men
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That vow a long and weary pilgrimage,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Then let us take a ceremonious leave
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And loving farewell of our several friends.
Lord Marshal: The appellant in all duty greets your highness,
Lord Marshal: And craves to kiss your hand and take his leave.
KING RICHARD II: We will descend and fold him in our arms.
KING RICHARD II: Cousin of Hereford, as thy cause is right,
KING RICHARD II: So be thy fortune in this royal fight!
KING RICHARD II: Farewell, my blood, which if to-day thou shed,
KING RICHARD II: Lament we may, but not revenge thee dead.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O let no noble eye profane a tear
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For me, if I be gored with Mowbray's spear:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As confident as is the falcon's flight
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Against a bird, do I with Mowbray fight.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My loving lord, I take my leave of you,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Of you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Not sick, although I have to do with death,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But lusty, young, and cheerly drawing breath.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Lo, as at English feasts, so I regreet
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The daintiest last, to make the end most sweet:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O thou, the earthly author of my blood,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Whose youthful spirit, in me regenerate,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Doth with a twofold vigour lift me up
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To reach at victory above my head,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Add proof unto mine armour with thy prayers,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And with thy blessings steel my lance's point,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That it may enter Mowbray's waxen coat,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And furbish new the name of John a Gaunt,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Even in the lusty havior of his son.
JOHN OF GAUNT: God in thy good cause make thee prosperous!
JOHN OF GAUNT: Be swift like lightning in the execution,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And let thy blows, doubly redoubled,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Fall like amazing thunder on the casque
JOHN OF GAUNT: Of thy adverse pernicious enemy:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Rouse up thy youthful blood, be valiant and live.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Mine innocency and Saint George to thrive!
THOMAS MOWBRAY: However God or fortune cast my lot,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: There lives or dies, true to King Richard's throne,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A loyal, just and upright gentleman:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Never did captive with a freer heart
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Cast off his chains of bondage and embrace
THOMAS MOWBRAY: His golden uncontroll'd enfranchisement,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: More than my dancing soul doth celebrate
THOMAS MOWBRAY: This feast of battle with mine adversary.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Most mighty liege, and my companion peers,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Take from my mouth the wish of happy years:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: As gentle and as jocund as to jest
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Go I to fight: truth hath a quiet breast.
KING RICHARD II: Farewell, my lord: securely I espy
KING RICHARD II: Virtue with valour couched in thine eye.
KING RICHARD II: Order the trial, marshal, and begin.
Lord Marshal: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby,
Lord Marshal: Receive thy lance, and God defend the right!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Strong as a tower in hope, I cry amen.
Lord Marshal: Go bear this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.
First Herald: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby,
First Herald: Stands here for God, his sovereign and himself,
First Herald: On pain to be found false and recreant,
First Herald: To prove the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray,
First Herald: A traitor to his God, his king and him,
First Herald: And dares him to set forward to the fight.
Second Herald: Here standeth Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,
Second Herald: On pain to be found false and recreant,
Second Herald: Both to defend himself and to approve
Second Herald: Henry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby,
Second Herald: To God, his sovereign and to him disloyal,
Second Herald: Courageously and with a free desire
Second Herald: Attending but the signal to begin.
Lord Marshal: Sound, trumpets, and set forward, combatants.
NARRATOR: A charge sounded
Lord Marshal: Stay, the king hath thrown his warder down.
KING RICHARD II: Let them lay by their helmets and their spears,
KING RICHARD II: And both return back to their chairs again:
KING RICHARD II: Withdraw with us: and let the trumpets sound
KING RICHARD II: While we return these dukes what we decree.
NARRATOR: A long flourish
KING RICHARD II: Draw near,
KING RICHARD II: And list what with our council we have done.
KING RICHARD II: For that our kingdom's earth should not be soil'd
KING RICHARD II: With that dear blood which it hath fostered,
KING RICHARD II: And for our eyes do hate the dire aspect
KING RICHARD II: Of civil wounds plough'd up with neighbours' sword,
KING RICHARD II: And for we think the eagle-winged pride
KING RICHARD II: Of sky-aspiring and ambitious thoughts,
KING RICHARD II: With rival-hating envy, set on you
KING RICHARD II: To wake our peace, which in our country's cradle
KING RICHARD II: Draws the sweet infant breath of gentle sleep,
KING RICHARD II: Which so roused up with boisterous untuned drums,
KING RICHARD II: With harsh resounding trumpets' dreadful bray,
KING RICHARD II: And grating shock of wrathful iron arms,
KING RICHARD II: Might from our quiet confines fright fair peace
KING RICHARD II: And make us wade even in our kindred's blood,
KING RICHARD II: Therefore, we banish you our territories:
KING RICHARD II: You, cousin Hereford, upon pain of life,
KING RICHARD II: Till twice five summers have enrich'd our fields
KING RICHARD II: Shall not regreet our fair dominions,
KING RICHARD II: But tread the stranger paths of banishment.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Your will be done: this must my comfort be,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Sun that warms you here shall shine on me,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And those his golden beams to you here lent
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Shall point on me and gild my banishment.
KING RICHARD II: Norfolk, for thee remains a heavier doom,
KING RICHARD II: Which I with some unwillingness pronounce:
KING RICHARD II: The sly slow hours shall not determinate
KING RICHARD II: The dateless limit of thy dear exile,
KING RICHARD II: The hopeless word of 'never to return'
KING RICHARD II: Breathe I against thee, upon pain of life.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A heavy sentence, my most sovereign liege,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And all unlook'd for from your highness' mouth:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: A dearer merit, not so deep a maim
THOMAS MOWBRAY: As to be cast forth in the common air,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Have I deserved at your highness' hands.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: The language I have learn'd these forty years,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: My native English, now I must forego:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And now my tongue's use is to me no more
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Than an unstringed viol or a harp,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Or like a cunning instrument cased up,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Or, being open, put into his hands
THOMAS MOWBRAY: That knows no touch to tune the harmony:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Within my mouth you have engaol'd my tongue,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Doubly portcullis'd with my teeth and lips,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And dull unfeeling barren ignorance
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Is made my gaoler to attend on me.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: I am too old to fawn upon a nurse,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Too far in years to be a pupil now:
THOMAS MOWBRAY: What is thy sentence then but speechless death,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Which robs my tongue from breathing native breath?
KING RICHARD II: It boots thee not to be compassionate:
KING RICHARD II: After our sentence plaining comes too late.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Then thus I turn me from my country's light,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: To dwell in solemn shades of endless night.
KING RICHARD II: Return again, and take an oath with thee.
KING RICHARD II: Lay on our royal sword your banish'd hands,
KING RICHARD II: Swear by the duty that you owe to God--
KING RICHARD II: Our part therein we banish with yourselves--
KING RICHARD II: To keep the oath that we administer:
KING RICHARD II: You never shall, so help you truth and God!
KING RICHARD II: Embrace each other's love in banishment,
KING RICHARD II: Nor never look upon each other's face,
KING RICHARD II: Nor never write, regreet, nor reconcile
KING RICHARD II: This louring tempest of your home-bred hate,
KING RICHARD II: Nor never by advised purpose meet
KING RICHARD II: To plot, contrive, or complot any ill
KING RICHARD II: 'Gainst us, our state, our subjects, or our land.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I swear.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And I, to keep all this.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Norfolk, so far as to mine enemy:--
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By this time, had the king permitted us,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: One of our souls had wander'd in the air.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Banish'd this frail sepulchre of our flesh,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As now our flesh is banish'd from this land:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Confess thy treasons ere thou fly the realm,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Since thou hast far to go, bear not along
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The clogging burthen of a guilty soul.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: No, Bolingbroke: if ever I were traitor,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: My name be blotted from the book of life,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And I from heaven banish'd as from hence!
THOMAS MOWBRAY: But what thou art, God, thou, and I do know,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: And all too soon, I fear, the king shall rue.
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Farewell, my liege. Now no way can I stray,
THOMAS MOWBRAY: Save back to England, all the world's my way.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING RICHARD II: Uncle, even in the glasses of thine eyes
KING RICHARD II: I see thy grieved heart: thy sad aspect
KING RICHARD II: Hath from the number of his banish'd years
KING RICHARD II: Pluck'd four away.
NARRATOR: To HENRY BOLINGBROKE
KING RICHARD II: Six frozen winter spent,
KING RICHARD II: Return with welcome home from banishment.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: How long a time lies in one little word!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Four lagging winters and four wanton springs
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
JOHN OF GAUNT: I thank my liege, that in regard of me
JOHN OF GAUNT: He shortens four years of my son's exile:
JOHN OF GAUNT: But little vantage shall I reap thereby,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For, ere the six years that he hath to spend
JOHN OF GAUNT: Can change their moons and bring their times about
JOHN OF GAUNT: My oil-dried lamp and time-bewasted light
JOHN OF GAUNT: Shall be extinct with age and endless night,
JOHN OF GAUNT: My inch of taper will be burnt and done,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And blindfold death not let me see my son.
KING RICHARD II: Why uncle, thou hast many years to live.
JOHN OF GAUNT: But not a minute, king, that thou canst give:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Shorten my days thou canst with sullen sorrow,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And pluck nights from me, but not lend a morrow,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Thou canst help time to furrow me with age,
JOHN OF GAUNT: But stop no wrinkle in his pilgrimage,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Thy word is current with him for my death,
JOHN OF GAUNT: But dead, thy kingdom cannot buy my breath.
KING RICHARD II: Thy son is banish'd upon good advice,
KING RICHARD II: Whereto thy tongue a party-verdict gave:
KING RICHARD II: Why at our justice seem'st thou then to lour?
JOHN OF GAUNT: Things sweet to taste prove in digestion sour.
JOHN OF GAUNT: You urged me as a judge, but I had rather
JOHN OF GAUNT: You would have bid me argue like a father.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, had it been a stranger, not my child,
JOHN OF GAUNT: To smooth his fault I should have been more mild:
JOHN OF GAUNT: A partial slander sought I to avoid,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And in the sentence my own life destroy'd.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Alas, I look'd when some of you should say,
JOHN OF GAUNT: I was too strict to make mine own away,
JOHN OF GAUNT: But you gave leave to my unwilling tongue
JOHN OF GAUNT: Against my will to do myself this wrong.
KING RICHARD II: Cousin, farewell, and, uncle, bid him so:
KING RICHARD II: Six years we banish him, and he shall go.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt KING RICHARD II and train
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Cousin, farewell: what presence must not know,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: From where you do remain let paper show.
Lord Marshal: My lord, no leave take I, for I will ride,
Lord Marshal: As far as land will let me, by your side.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, to what purpose dost thou hoard thy words,
JOHN OF GAUNT: That thou return'st no greeting to thy friends?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I have too few to take my leave of you,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: When the tongue's office should be prodigal
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To breathe the abundant dolour of the heart.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Thy grief is but thy absence for a time.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Joy absent, grief is present for that time.
JOHN OF GAUNT: What is six winters? they are quickly gone.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To men in joy, but grief makes one hour ten.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Call it a travel that thou takest for pleasure.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My heart will sigh when I miscall it so,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which finds it an inforced pilgrimage.
JOHN OF GAUNT: The sullen passage of thy weary steps
JOHN OF GAUNT: Esteem as foil wherein thou art to set
JOHN OF GAUNT: The precious jewel of thy home return.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Nay, rather, every tedious stride I make
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Will but remember me what a deal of world
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I wander from the jewels that I love.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Must I not serve a long apprenticehood
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To foreign passages, and in the end,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Having my freedom, boast of nothing else
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But that I was a journeyman to grief?
JOHN OF GAUNT: All places that the eye of heaven visits
JOHN OF GAUNT: Are to a wise man ports and happy havens.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Teach thy necessity to reason thus,
JOHN OF GAUNT: There is no virtue like necessity.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Think not the king did banish thee,
JOHN OF GAUNT: But thou the king. Woe doth the heavier sit,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Where it perceives it is but faintly borne.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Go, say I sent thee forth to purchase honour
JOHN OF GAUNT: And not the king exiled thee, or suppose
JOHN OF GAUNT: Devouring pestilence hangs in our air
JOHN OF GAUNT: And thou art flying to a fresher clime:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Look, what thy soul holds dear, imagine it
JOHN OF GAUNT: To lie that way thou go'st, not whence thou comest:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Suppose the singing birds musicians,
JOHN OF GAUNT: The grass whereon thou tread'st the presence strew'd,
JOHN OF GAUNT: The flowers fair ladies, and thy steps no more
JOHN OF GAUNT: Than a delightful measure or a dance,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For gnarling sorrow hath less power to bite
JOHN OF GAUNT: The man that mocks at it and sets it light.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O, who can hold a fire in his hand
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By thinking on the frosty Caucasus?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or cloy the hungry edge of appetite
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By bare imagination of a feast?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Or wallow naked in December snow
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By thinking on fantastic summer's heat?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O, no! the apprehension of the good
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Gives but the greater feeling to the worse:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Fell sorrow's tooth doth never rankle more
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Than when he bites, but lanceth not the sore.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Come, come, my son, I'll bring thee on thy way:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Had I thy youth and cause, I would not stay.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Then, England's ground, farewell, sweet soil, adieu,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My mother, and my nurse, that bears me yet!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Where'er I wander, boast of this I can,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Though banish'd, yet a trueborn Englishman.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The court.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD II, with BAGOT and GREEN at one door, and the DUKE OF AUMERLE at another
KING RICHARD II: We did observe. Cousin Aumerle,
KING RICHARD II: How far brought you high Hereford on his way?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: I brought high Hereford, if you call him so,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: But to the next highway, and there I left him.
KING RICHARD II: And say, what store of parting tears were shed?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Faith, none for me, except the north-east wind,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Which then blew bitterly against our faces,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Awaked the sleeping rheum, and so by chance
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Did grace our hollow parting with a tear.
KING RICHARD II: What said our cousin when you parted with him?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: 'Farewell:'
DUKE OF AUMERLE: And, for my heart disdained that my tongue
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Should so profane the word, that taught me craft
DUKE OF AUMERLE: To counterfeit oppression of such grief
DUKE OF AUMERLE: That words seem'd buried in my sorrow's grave.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Marry, would the word 'farewell' have lengthen'd hours
DUKE OF AUMERLE: And added years to his short banishment,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: He should have had a volume of farewells,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: But since it would not, he had none of me.
KING RICHARD II: He is our cousin, cousin, but 'tis doubt,
KING RICHARD II: When time shall call him home from banishment,
KING RICHARD II: Whether our kinsman come to see his friends.
KING RICHARD II: Ourself and Bushy, Bagot here and Green
KING RICHARD II: Observed his courtship to the common people,
KING RICHARD II: How he did seem to dive into their hearts
KING RICHARD II: With humble and familiar courtesy,
KING RICHARD II: What reverence he did throw away on slaves,
KING RICHARD II: Wooing poor craftsmen with the craft of smiles
KING RICHARD II: And patient underbearing of his fortune,
KING RICHARD II: As 'twere to banish their affects with him.
KING RICHARD II: Off goes his bonnet to an oyster-wench,
KING RICHARD II: A brace of draymen bid God speed him well
KING RICHARD II: And had the tribute of his supple knee,
KING RICHARD II: With 'Thanks, my countrymen, my loving friends,'
KING RICHARD II: As were our England in reversion his,
KING RICHARD II: And he our subjects' next degree in hope.
GREEN: Well, he is gone, and with him go these thoughts.
GREEN: Now for the rebels which stand out in Ireland,
GREEN: Expedient manage must be made, my liege,
GREEN: Ere further leisure yield them further means
GREEN: For their advantage and your highness' loss.
KING RICHARD II: We will ourself in person to this war:
KING RICHARD II: And, for our coffers, with too great a court
KING RICHARD II: And liberal largess, are grown somewhat light,
KING RICHARD II: We are inforced to farm our royal realm,
KING RICHARD II: The revenue whereof shall furnish us
KING RICHARD II: For our affairs in hand: if that come short,
KING RICHARD II: Our substitutes at home shall have blank charters,
KING RICHARD II: Whereto, when they shall know what men are rich,
KING RICHARD II: They shall subscribe them for large sums of gold
KING RICHARD II: And send them after to supply our wants,
KING RICHARD II: For we will make for Ireland presently.
NARRATOR: Enter BUSHY
KING RICHARD II: Bushy, what news?
BUSHY: Old John of Gaunt is grievous sick, my lord,
BUSHY: Suddenly taken, and hath sent post haste
BUSHY: To entreat your majesty to visit him.
KING RICHARD II: Where lies he?
BUSHY: At Ely House.
KING RICHARD II: Now put it, God, in the physician's mind
KING RICHARD II: To help him to his grave immediately!
KING RICHARD II: The lining of his coffers shall make coats
KING RICHARD II: To deck our soldiers for these Irish wars.
KING RICHARD II: Come, gentlemen, let's all go visit him:
KING RICHARD II: Pray God we may make haste, and come too late!
All: Amen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Ely House.
NARRATOR: Enter JOHN OF GAUNT sick, with the DUKE OF YORK, and c
JOHN OF GAUNT: Will the king come, that I may breathe my last
JOHN OF GAUNT: In wholesome counsel to his unstaid youth?
DUKE OF YORK: Vex not yourself, nor strive not with your breath,
DUKE OF YORK: For all in vain comes counsel to his ear.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, but they say the tongues of dying men
JOHN OF GAUNT: Enforce attention like deep harmony:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Where words are scarce, they are seldom spent in vain,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For they breathe truth that breathe their words in pain.
JOHN OF GAUNT: He that no more must say is listen'd more
JOHN OF GAUNT: Than they whom youth and ease have taught to glose,
JOHN OF GAUNT: More are men's ends mark'd than their lives before:
JOHN OF GAUNT: The setting sun, and music at the close,
JOHN OF GAUNT: As the last taste of sweets, is sweetest last,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Writ in remembrance more than things long past:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Though Richard my life's counsel would not hear,
JOHN OF GAUNT: My death's sad tale may yet undeaf his ear.
DUKE OF YORK: No, it is stopp'd with other flattering sounds,
DUKE OF YORK: As praises, of whose taste the wise are fond,
DUKE OF YORK: Lascivious metres, to whose venom sound
DUKE OF YORK: The open ear of youth doth always listen,
DUKE OF YORK: Report of fashions in proud Italy,
DUKE OF YORK: Whose manners still our tardy apish nation
DUKE OF YORK: Limps after in base imitation.
DUKE OF YORK: Where doth the world thrust forth a vanity--
DUKE OF YORK: So it be new, there's no respect how vile--
DUKE OF YORK: That is not quickly buzzed into his ears?
DUKE OF YORK: Then all too late comes counsel to be heard,
DUKE OF YORK: Where will doth mutiny with wit's regard.
DUKE OF YORK: Direct not him whose way himself will choose:
DUKE OF YORK: 'Tis breath thou lack'st, and that breath wilt thou lose.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired
JOHN OF GAUNT: And thus expiring do foretell of him:
JOHN OF GAUNT: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For violent fires soon burn out themselves,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Small showers last long, but sudden storms are short,
JOHN OF GAUNT: He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes,
JOHN OF GAUNT: With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Light vanity, insatiate cormorant,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Consuming means, soon preys upon itself.
JOHN OF GAUNT: This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This other Eden, demi-paradise,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This fortress built by Nature for herself
JOHN OF GAUNT: Against infection and the hand of war,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This happy breed of men, this little world,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This precious stone set in the silver sea,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Which serves it in the office of a wall,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Or as a moat defensive to a house,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Against the envy of less happier lands,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This nurse, this teeming womb of royal kings,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Fear'd by their breed and famous by their birth,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Renowned for their deeds as far from home,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For Christian service and true chivalry,
JOHN OF GAUNT: As is the sepulchre in stubborn Jewry,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Of the world's ransom, blessed Mary's Son,
JOHN OF GAUNT: This land of such dear souls, this dear dear land,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Dear for her reputation through the world,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Is now leased out, I die pronouncing it,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Like to a tenement or pelting farm:
JOHN OF GAUNT: England, bound in with the triumphant sea
JOHN OF GAUNT: Whose rocky shore beats back the envious siege
JOHN OF GAUNT: Of watery Neptune, is now bound in with shame,
JOHN OF GAUNT: With inky blots and rotten parchment bonds:
JOHN OF GAUNT: That England, that was wont to conquer others,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Ah, would the scandal vanish with my life,
JOHN OF GAUNT: How happy then were my ensuing death!
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD II and QUEEN, DUKE OF AUMERLE,  BUSHY, GREEN, BAGOT, LORD ROSS, and LORD WILLOUGHBY
DUKE OF YORK: The king is come: deal mildly with his youth,
DUKE OF YORK: For young hot colts being raged do rage the more.
QUEEN: How fares our noble uncle, Lancaster?
KING RICHARD II: What comfort, man? how is't with aged Gaunt?
JOHN OF GAUNT: O how that name befits my composition!
JOHN OF GAUNT: Old Gaunt indeed, and gaunt in being old:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Within me grief hath kept a tedious fast,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And who abstains from meat that is not gaunt?
JOHN OF GAUNT: For sleeping England long time have I watch'd,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Watching breeds leanness, leanness is all gaunt:
JOHN OF GAUNT: The pleasure that some fathers feed upon,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Is my strict fast, I mean, my children's looks,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And therein fasting, hast thou made me gaunt:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Gaunt am I for the grave, gaunt as a grave,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Whose hollow womb inherits nought but bones.
KING RICHARD II: Can sick men play so nicely with their names?
JOHN OF GAUNT: No, misery makes sport to mock itself:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Since thou dost seek to kill my name in me,
JOHN OF GAUNT: I mock my name, great king, to flatter thee.
KING RICHARD II: Should dying men flatter with those that live?
JOHN OF GAUNT: No, no, men living flatter those that die.
KING RICHARD II: Thou, now a-dying, say'st thou flatterest me.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, no! thou diest, though I the sicker be.
KING RICHARD II: I am in health, I breathe, and see thee ill.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Now He that made me knows I see thee ill,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Ill in myself to see, and in thee seeing ill.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Thy death-bed is no lesser than thy land
JOHN OF GAUNT: Wherein thou liest in reputation sick,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And thou, too careless patient as thou art,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Commit'st thy anointed body to the cure
JOHN OF GAUNT: Of those physicians that first wounded thee:
JOHN OF GAUNT: A thousand flatterers sit within thy crown,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Whose compass is no bigger than thy head,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And yet, incaged in so small a verge,
JOHN OF GAUNT: The waste is no whit lesser than thy land.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, had thy grandsire with a prophet's eye
JOHN OF GAUNT: Seen how his son's son should destroy his sons,
JOHN OF GAUNT: From forth thy reach he would have laid thy shame,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Deposing thee before thou wert possess'd,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Which art possess'd now to depose thyself.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Why, cousin, wert thou regent of the world,
JOHN OF GAUNT: It were a shame to let this land by lease,
JOHN OF GAUNT: But for thy world enjoying but this land,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Is it not more than shame to shame it so?
JOHN OF GAUNT: Landlord of England art thou now, not king:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Thy state of law is bondslave to the law, And thou--
KING RICHARD II: A lunatic lean-witted fool,
KING RICHARD II: Presuming on an ague's privilege,
KING RICHARD II: Darest with thy frozen admonition
KING RICHARD II: Make pale our cheek, chasing the royal blood
KING RICHARD II: With fury from his native residence.
KING RICHARD II: Now, by my seat's right royal majesty,
KING RICHARD II: Wert thou not brother to great Edward's son,
KING RICHARD II: This tongue that runs so roundly in thy head
KING RICHARD II: Should run thy head from thy unreverent shoulders.
JOHN OF GAUNT: O, spare me not, my brother Edward's son,
JOHN OF GAUNT: For that I was his father Edward's son,
JOHN OF GAUNT: That blood already, like the pelican,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Hast thou tapp'd out and drunkenly caroused:
JOHN OF GAUNT: My brother Gloucester, plain well-meaning soul,
JOHN OF GAUNT: Whom fair befal in heaven 'mongst happy souls!
JOHN OF GAUNT: May be a precedent and witness good
JOHN OF GAUNT: That thou respect'st not spilling Edward's blood:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Join with the present sickness that I have,
JOHN OF GAUNT: And thy unkindness be like crooked age,
JOHN OF GAUNT: To crop at once a too long wither'd flower.
JOHN OF GAUNT: Live in thy shame, but die not shame with thee!
JOHN OF GAUNT: These words hereafter thy tormentors be!
JOHN OF GAUNT: Convey me to my bed, then to my grave:
JOHN OF GAUNT: Love they to live that love and honour have.
NARRATOR: Exit, borne off by his Attendants
KING RICHARD II: And let them die that age and sullens have,
KING RICHARD II: For both hast thou, and both become the grave.
DUKE OF YORK: I do beseech your majesty, impute his words
DUKE OF YORK: To wayward sickliness and age in him:
DUKE OF YORK: He loves you, on my life, and holds you dear
DUKE OF YORK: As Harry Duke of Hereford, were he here.
KING RICHARD II: Right, you say true: as Hereford's love, so his,
KING RICHARD II: As theirs, so mine, and all be as it is.
NARRATOR: Enter NORTHUMBERLAND
NORTHUMBERLAND: My liege, old Gaunt commends him to your majesty.
KING RICHARD II: What says he?
NORTHUMBERLAND: Nay, nothing, all is said
NORTHUMBERLAND: His tongue is now a stringless instrument,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Words, life and all, old Lancaster hath spent.
DUKE OF YORK: Be York the next that must be bankrupt so!
DUKE OF YORK: Though death be poor, it ends a mortal woe.
KING RICHARD II: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he,
KING RICHARD II: His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be.
KING RICHARD II: So much for that. Now for our Irish wars:
KING RICHARD II: We must supplant those rough rug-headed kerns,
KING RICHARD II: Which live like venom where no venom else
KING RICHARD II: But only they have privilege to live.
KING RICHARD II: And for these great affairs do ask some charge,
KING RICHARD II: Towards our assistance we do seize to us
KING RICHARD II: The plate, corn, revenues and moveables,
KING RICHARD II: Whereof our uncle Gaunt did stand possess'd.
DUKE OF YORK: How long shall I be patient? ah, how long
DUKE OF YORK: Shall tender duty make me suffer wrong?
DUKE OF YORK: Not Gloucester's death, nor Hereford's banishment
DUKE OF YORK: Not Gaunt's rebukes, nor England's private wrongs,
DUKE OF YORK: Nor the prevention of poor Bolingbroke
DUKE OF YORK: About his marriage, nor my own disgrace,
DUKE OF YORK: Have ever made me sour my patient cheek,
DUKE OF YORK: Or bend one wrinkle on my sovereign's face.
DUKE OF YORK: I am the last of noble Edward's sons,
DUKE OF YORK: Of whom thy father, Prince of Wales, was first:
DUKE OF YORK: In war was never lion raged more fierce,
DUKE OF YORK: In peace was never gentle lamb more mild,
DUKE OF YORK: Than was that young and princely gentleman.
DUKE OF YORK: His face thou hast, for even so look'd he,
DUKE OF YORK: Accomplish'd with the number of thy hours,
DUKE OF YORK: But when he frown'd, it was against the French
DUKE OF YORK: And not against his friends, his noble hand
DUKE OF YORK: Did will what he did spend and spent not that
DUKE OF YORK: Which his triumphant father's hand had won,
DUKE OF YORK: His hands were guilty of no kindred blood,
DUKE OF YORK: But bloody with the enemies of his kin.
DUKE OF YORK: O Richard! York is too far gone with grief,
DUKE OF YORK: Or else he never would compare between.
KING RICHARD II: Why, uncle, what's the matter?
DUKE OF YORK: O my liege,
DUKE OF YORK: Pardon me, if you please, if n ot, I, pleased
DUKE OF YORK: Not to be pardon'd, am content withal.
DUKE OF YORK: Seek you to seize and gripe into your hands
DUKE OF YORK: The royalties and rights of banish'd Hereford?
DUKE OF YORK: Is not Gaunt dead, and doth not Hereford live?
DUKE OF YORK: Was not Gaunt just, and is not Harry true?
DUKE OF YORK: Did not the one deserve to have an heir?
DUKE OF YORK: Is not his heir a well-deserving son?
DUKE OF YORK: Take Hereford's rights away, and take from Time
DUKE OF YORK: His charters and his customary rights,
DUKE OF YORK: Let not to-morrow then ensue to-day,
DUKE OF YORK: Be not thyself, for how art thou a king
DUKE OF YORK: But by fair sequence and succession?
DUKE OF YORK: Now, afore God--God forbid I say true!--
DUKE OF YORK: If you do wrongfully seize Hereford's rights,
DUKE OF YORK: Call in the letters patent that he hath
DUKE OF YORK: By his attorneys-general to sue
DUKE OF YORK: His livery, and deny his offer'd homage,
DUKE OF YORK: You pluck a thousand dangers on your head,
DUKE OF YORK: You lose a thousand well-disposed hearts
DUKE OF YORK: And prick my tender patience, to those thoughts
DUKE OF YORK: Which honour and allegiance cannot think.
KING RICHARD II: Think what you will, we seize into our hands
KING RICHARD II: His plate, his goods, his money and his lands.
DUKE OF YORK: I'll not be by the while: my liege, farewell:
DUKE OF YORK: What will ensue hereof, there's none can tell,
DUKE OF YORK: But by bad courses may be understood
DUKE OF YORK: That their events can never fall out good.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING RICHARD II: Go, Bushy, to the Earl of Wiltshire straight:
KING RICHARD II: Bid him repair to us to Ely House
KING RICHARD II: To see this business. To-morrow next
KING RICHARD II: We will for Ireland, and 'tis time, I trow:
KING RICHARD II: And we create, in absence of ourself,
KING RICHARD II: Our uncle York lord governor of England,
KING RICHARD II: For he is just and always loved us well.
KING RICHARD II: Come on, our queen: to-morrow must we part,
KING RICHARD II: Be merry, for our time of stay is short
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt KING RICHARD II, QUEEN, DUKE OF AUMERLE, BUSHY, GREEN, and BAGOT
NORTHUMBERLAND: Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
LORD ROSS: And living too, for now his son is duke.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Barely in title, not in revenue.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Richly in both, if justice had her right.
LORD ROSS: My heart is great, but it must break with silence,
LORD ROSS: Ere't be disburden'd with a liberal tongue.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Nay, speak thy mind, and let him ne'er speak more
NORTHUMBERLAND: That speaks thy words again to do thee harm!
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Tends that thou wouldst speak to the Duke of Hereford?
LORD WILLOUGHBY: If it be so, out with it boldly, man,
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Quick is mine ear to hear of good towards him.
LORD ROSS: No good at all that I can do for him,
LORD ROSS: Unless you call it good to pity him,
LORD ROSS: Bereft and gelded of his patrimony.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Now, afore God, 'tis shame such wrongs are borne
NORTHUMBERLAND: In him, a royal prince, and many moe
NORTHUMBERLAND: Of noble blood in this declining land.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The king is not himself, but basely led
NORTHUMBERLAND: By flatterers, and what they will inform,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Merely in hate, 'gainst any of us all,
NORTHUMBERLAND: That will the king severely prosecute
NORTHUMBERLAND: 'Gainst us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.
LORD ROSS: The commons hath he pill'd with grievous taxes,
LORD ROSS: And quite lost their hearts: the nobles hath he fined
LORD ROSS: For ancient quarrels, and quite lost their hearts.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: And daily new exactions are devised,
LORD WILLOUGHBY: As blanks, benevolences, and I wot not what:
LORD WILLOUGHBY: But what, o' God's name, doth become of this?
NORTHUMBERLAND: Wars have not wasted it, for warr'd he hath not,
NORTHUMBERLAND: But basely yielded upon compromise
NORTHUMBERLAND: That which his noble ancestors achieved with blows:
NORTHUMBERLAND: More hath he spent in peace than they in wars.
LORD ROSS: The Earl of Wiltshire hath the realm in farm.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: The king's grown bankrupt, like a broken man.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Reproach and dissolution hangeth over him.
LORD ROSS: He hath not money for these Irish wars,
LORD ROSS: His burthenous taxations notwithstanding,
LORD ROSS: But by the robbing of the banish'd duke.
NORTHUMBERLAND: His noble kinsman: most degenerate king!
NORTHUMBERLAND: But, lords, we hear this fearful tempest sing,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Yet see no shelter to avoid the storm,
NORTHUMBERLAND: We see the wind sit sore upon our sails,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And yet we strike not, but securely perish.
LORD ROSS: We see the very wreck that we must suffer,
LORD ROSS: And unavoided is the danger now,
LORD ROSS: For suffering so the causes of our wreck.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Not so, even through the hollow eyes of death
NORTHUMBERLAND: I spy life peering, but I dare not say
NORTHUMBERLAND: How near the tidings of our comfort is.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Nay, let us share thy thoughts, as thou dost ours.
LORD ROSS: Be confident to speak, Northumberland:
LORD ROSS: We three are but thyself, and, speaking so,
LORD ROSS: Thy words are but as thoughts, therefore, be bold.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Then thus: I have from Port le Blanc, a bay
NORTHUMBERLAND: In Brittany, received intelligence
NORTHUMBERLAND: That Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham,
NORTHUMBERLAND: That late broke from the Duke of Exeter,
NORTHUMBERLAND: His brother, Archbishop late of Canterbury,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton and Francis Quoint,
NORTHUMBERLAND: All these well furnish'd by the Duke of Bretagne
NORTHUMBERLAND: With eight tall ships, three thousand men of war,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Are making hither with all due expedience
NORTHUMBERLAND: And shortly mean to touch our northern shore:
NORTHUMBERLAND: Perhaps they had ere this, but that they stay
NORTHUMBERLAND: The first departing of the king for Ireland.
NORTHUMBERLAND: If then we shall shake off our slavish yoke,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Imp out our drooping country's broken wing,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Redeem from broking pawn the blemish'd crown,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Wipe off the dust that hides our sceptre's gilt
NORTHUMBERLAND: And make high majesty look like itself,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Away with me in post to Ravenspurgh,
NORTHUMBERLAND: But if you faint, as fearing to do so,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Stay and be secret, and myself will go.
LORD ROSS: To horse, to horse! urge doubts to them that fear.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Hold out my horse, and I will first be there.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN, BUSHY, and BAGOT
BUSHY: Madam, your majesty is too much sad:
BUSHY: You promised, when you parted with the king,
BUSHY: To lay aside life-harming heaviness
BUSHY: And entertain a cheerful disposition.
QUEEN: To please the king I did, to please myself
QUEEN: I cannot do it, yet I know no cause
QUEEN: Why I should welcome such a guest as grief,
QUEEN: Save bidding farewell to so sweet a guest
QUEEN: As my sweet Richard: yet again, methinks,
QUEEN: Some unborn sorrow, ripe in fortune's womb,
QUEEN: Is coming towards me, and my inward soul
QUEEN: With nothing trembles: at some thing it grieves,
QUEEN: More than with parting from my lord the king.
BUSHY: Each substance of a grief hath twenty shadows,
BUSHY: Which shows like grief itself, but is not so,
BUSHY: For sorrow's eye, glazed with blinding tears,
BUSHY: Divides one thing entire to many objects,
BUSHY: Like perspectives, which rightly gazed upon
BUSHY: Show nothing but confusion, eyed awry
BUSHY: Distinguish form: so your sweet majesty,
BUSHY: Looking awry upon your lord's departure,
BUSHY: Find shapes of grief, more than himself, to wail,
BUSHY: Which, look'd on as it is, is nought but shadows
BUSHY: Of what it is not. Then, thrice-gracious queen,
BUSHY: More than your lord's departure weep not: more's not seen,
BUSHY: Or if it be, 'tis with false sorrow's eye,
BUSHY: Which for things true weeps things imaginary.
QUEEN: It may be so, but yet my inward soul
QUEEN: Persuades me it is otherwise: howe'er it be,
QUEEN: I cannot but be sad, so heavy sad
QUEEN: As, though on thinking on no thought I think,
QUEEN: Makes me with heavy nothing faint and shrink.
BUSHY: 'Tis nothing but conceit, my gracious lady.
QUEEN: 'Tis nothing less: conceit is still derived
QUEEN: From some forefather grief, mine is not so,
QUEEN: For nothing had begot my something grief,
QUEEN: Or something hath the nothing that I grieve:
QUEEN: 'Tis in reversion that I do possess,
QUEEN: But what it is, that is not yet known, what
QUEEN: I cannot name, 'tis nameless woe, I wot.
NARRATOR: Enter GREEN
GREEN: God save your majesty! and well met, gentlemen:
GREEN: I hope the king is not yet shipp'd for Ireland.
QUEEN: Why hopest thou so? 'tis better hope he is,
QUEEN: For his designs crave haste, his haste good hope:
QUEEN: Then wherefore dost thou hope he is not shipp'd?
GREEN: That he, our hope, might have retired his power,
GREEN: And driven into despair an enemy's hope,
GREEN: Who strongly hath set footing in this land:
GREEN: The banish'd Bolingbroke repeals himself,
GREEN: And with uplifted arms is safe arrived
GREEN: At Ravenspurgh.
QUEEN: Now God in heaven forbid!
GREEN: Ah, madam, 'tis too true: and that is worse,
GREEN: The Lord Northumberland, his son young Henry Percy,
GREEN: The Lords of Ross, Beaumond, and Willoughby,
GREEN: With all their powerful friends, are fled to him.
BUSHY: Why have you not proclaim'd Northumberland
BUSHY: And all the rest revolted faction traitors?
GREEN: We have: whereupon the Earl of Worcester
GREEN: Hath broke his staff, resign'd his stewardship,
GREEN: And all the household servants fled with him
GREEN: To Bolingbroke.
QUEEN: So, Green, thou art the midwife to my woe,
QUEEN: And Bolingbroke my sorrow's dismal heir:
QUEEN: Now hath my soul brought forth her prodigy,
QUEEN: And I, a gasping new-deliver'd mother,
QUEEN: Have woe to woe, sorrow to sorrow join'd.
BUSHY: Despair not, madam.
QUEEN: Who shall hinder me?
QUEEN: I will despair, and be at enmity
QUEEN: With cozening hope: he is a flatterer,
QUEEN: A parasite, a keeper back of death,
QUEEN: Who gently would dissolve the bands of life,
QUEEN: Which false hope lingers in extremity.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF YORK
GREEN: Here comes the Duke of York.
QUEEN: With signs of war about his aged neck:
QUEEN: O, full of careful business are his looks!
QUEEN: Uncle, for God's sake, speak comfortable words.
DUKE OF YORK: Should I do so, I should belie my thoughts:
DUKE OF YORK: Comfort's in heaven, and we are on the earth,
DUKE OF YORK: Where nothing lives but crosses, cares and grief.
DUKE OF YORK: Your husband, he is gone to save far off,
DUKE OF YORK: Whilst others come to make him lose at home:
DUKE OF YORK: Here am I left to underprop his land,
DUKE OF YORK: Who, weak with age, cannot support myself:
DUKE OF YORK: Now comes the sick hour that his surfeit made,
DUKE OF YORK: Now shall he try his friends that flatter'd him.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: My lord, your son was gone before I came.
DUKE OF YORK: He was? Why, so! go all which way it will!
DUKE OF YORK: The nobles they are fled, the commons they are cold,
DUKE OF YORK: And will, I fear, revolt on Hereford's side.
DUKE OF YORK: Sirrah, get thee to Plashy, to my sister Gloucester,
DUKE OF YORK: Bid her send me presently a thousand pound:
DUKE OF YORK: Hold, take my ring.
Servant: My lord, I had forgot to tell your lordship,
Servant: To-day, as I came by, I called there,
Servant: But I shall grieve you to report the rest.
DUKE OF YORK: What is't, knave?
Servant: An hour before I came, the duchess died.
DUKE OF YORK: God for his mercy! what a tide of woes
DUKE OF YORK: Comes rushing on this woeful land at once!
DUKE OF YORK: I know not what to do: I would to God,
DUKE OF YORK: So my untruth had not provoked him to it,
DUKE OF YORK: The king had cut off my head with my brother's.
DUKE OF YORK: What, are there no posts dispatch'd for Ireland?
DUKE OF YORK: How shall we do for money for these wars?
DUKE OF YORK: Come, sister,--cousin, I would say--pray, pardon me.
DUKE OF YORK: Go, fellow, get thee home, provide some carts
DUKE OF YORK: And bring away the armour that is there.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
DUKE OF YORK: Gentlemen, will you go muster men?
DUKE OF YORK: If I know how or which way to order these affairs
DUKE OF YORK: Thus thrust disorderly into my hands,
DUKE OF YORK: Never believe me. Both are my kinsmen:
DUKE OF YORK: The one is my sovereign, whom both my oath
DUKE OF YORK: And duty bids defend, the other again
DUKE OF YORK: Is my kinsman, whom the king hath wrong'd,
DUKE OF YORK: Whom conscience and my kindred bids to right.
DUKE OF YORK: Well, somewhat we must do. Come, cousin, I'll
DUKE OF YORK: Dispose of you.
DUKE OF YORK: Gentlemen, go, muster up your men,
DUKE OF YORK: And meet me presently at Berkeley.
DUKE OF YORK: I should to Plashy too,
DUKE OF YORK: But time will not permit: all is uneven,
DUKE OF YORK: And every thing is left at six and seven.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DUKE OF YORK and QUEEN
BUSHY: The wind sits fair for news to go to Ireland,
BUSHY: But none returns. For us to levy power
BUSHY: Proportionable to the enemy
BUSHY: Is all unpossible.
GREEN: Besides, our nearness to the king in love
GREEN: Is near the hate of those love not the king.
BAGOT: And that's the wavering commons: for their love
BAGOT: Lies in their purses, and whoso empties them
BAGOT: By so much fills their hearts with deadly hate.
BUSHY: Wherein the king stands generally condemn'd.
BAGOT: If judgement lie in them, then so do we,
BAGOT: Because we ever have been near the king.
GREEN: Well, I will for refuge straight to Bristol castle:
GREEN: The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
BUSHY: Thither will I with you, for little office
BUSHY: The hateful commons will perform for us,
BUSHY: Except like curs to tear us all to pieces.
BUSHY: Will you go along with us?
BAGOT: No, I will to Ireland to his majesty.
BAGOT: Farewell: if heart's presages be not vain,
BAGOT: We three here art that ne'er shall meet again.
BUSHY: That's as York thrives to beat back Bolingbroke.
GREEN: Alas, poor duke! the task he undertakes
GREEN: Is numbering sands and drinking oceans dry:
GREEN: Where one on his side fights, thousands will fly.
GREEN: Farewell at once, for once, for all, and ever.
BUSHY: Well, we may meet again.
BAGOT: I fear me, never.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Wilds in Gloucestershire.
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE and NORTHUMBERLAND, with Forces
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: How far is it, my lord, to Berkeley now?
NORTHUMBERLAND: Believe me, noble lord,
NORTHUMBERLAND: I am a stranger here in Gloucestershire:
NORTHUMBERLAND: These high wild hills and rough uneven ways
NORTHUMBERLAND: Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And yet your fair discourse hath been as sugar,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Making the hard way sweet and delectable.
NORTHUMBERLAND: But I bethink me what a weary way
NORTHUMBERLAND: From Ravenspurgh to Cotswold will be found
NORTHUMBERLAND: In Ross and Willoughby, wanting your company,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Which, I protest, hath very much beguiled
NORTHUMBERLAND: The tediousness and process of my travel:
NORTHUMBERLAND: But theirs is sweetened with the hope to have
NORTHUMBERLAND: The present benefit which I possess,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And hope to joy is little less in joy
NORTHUMBERLAND: Than hope enjoy'd: by this the weary lords
NORTHUMBERLAND: Shall make their way seem short, as mine hath done
NORTHUMBERLAND: By sight of what I have, your noble company.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Of much less value is my company
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Than your good words. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY PERCY
NORTHUMBERLAND: It is my son, young Harry Percy,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Sent from my brother Worcester, whencesoever.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Harry, how fares your uncle?
HENRY PERCY: I had thought, my lord, to have learn'd his health of you.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Why, is he not with the queen?
HENRY PERCY: No, my good Lord, he hath forsook the court,
HENRY PERCY: Broken his staff of office and dispersed
HENRY PERCY: The household of the king.
NORTHUMBERLAND: What was his reason?
NORTHUMBERLAND: He was not so resolved when last we spake together.
HENRY PERCY: Because your lordship was proclaimed traitor.
HENRY PERCY: But he, my lord, is gone to Ravenspurgh,
HENRY PERCY: To offer service to the Duke of Hereford,
HENRY PERCY: And sent me over by Berkeley, to discover
HENRY PERCY: What power the Duke of York had levied there,
HENRY PERCY: Then with directions to repair to Ravenspurgh.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Have you forgot the Duke of Hereford, boy?
HENRY PERCY: No, my good lord, for that is not forgot
HENRY PERCY: Which ne'er I did remember: to my knowledge,
HENRY PERCY: I never in my life did look on him.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Then learn to know him now, this is the duke.
HENRY PERCY: My gracious lord, I tender you my service,
HENRY PERCY: Such as it is, being tender, raw and young:
HENRY PERCY: Which elder days shall ripen and confirm
HENRY PERCY: To more approved service and desert.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I thank thee, gentle Percy, and be sure
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I count myself in nothing else so happy
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As in a soul remembering my good friends,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And, as my fortune ripens with thy love,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: It shall be still thy true love's recompense:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My heart this covenant makes, my hand thus seals it.
NORTHUMBERLAND: How far is it to Berkeley? and what stir
NORTHUMBERLAND: Keeps good old York there with his men of war?
HENRY PERCY: There stands the castle, by yon tuft of trees,
HENRY PERCY: Mann'd with three hundred men, as I have heard,
HENRY PERCY: And in it are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour,
HENRY PERCY: None else of name and noble estimate.
NARRATOR: Enter LORD ROSS and LORD WILLOUGHBY
NORTHUMBERLAND: Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Bloody with spurring, fiery-red with haste.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Welcome, my lords. I wot your love pursues
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: A banish'd traitor: all my treasury
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Is yet but unfelt thanks, which more enrich'd
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Shall be your love and labour's recompense.
LORD ROSS: Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: And far surmounts our labour to attain it.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Evermore thanks, the exchequer of the poor,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which, till my infant fortune comes to years,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Stands for my bounty. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter LORD BERKELEY
NORTHUMBERLAND: It is my Lord of Berkeley, as I guess.
LORD BERKELEY: My Lord of Hereford, my message is to you.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My lord, my answer is--to Lancaster,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And I am come to seek that name in England,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And I must find that title in your tongue,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Before I make reply to aught you say.
LORD BERKELEY: Mistake me not, my lord, 'tis not my meaning
LORD BERKELEY: To raze one title of your honour out:
LORD BERKELEY: To you, my lord, I come, what lord you will,
LORD BERKELEY: From the most gracious regent of this land,
LORD BERKELEY: The Duke of York, to know what pricks you on
LORD BERKELEY: To take advantage of the absent time
LORD BERKELEY: And fright our native peace with self-born arms.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF YORK attended
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I shall not need transport my words by you,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Here comes his grace in person. My noble uncle!
NARRATOR: Kneels
DUKE OF YORK: Show me thy humble heart, and not thy knee,
DUKE OF YORK: Whose duty is deceiveable and false.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My gracious uncle--
DUKE OF YORK: Tut, tut!
DUKE OF YORK: Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle:
DUKE OF YORK: I am no traitor's uncle, and that word 'grace.'
DUKE OF YORK: In an ungracious mouth is but profane.
DUKE OF YORK: Why have those banish'd and forbidden legs
DUKE OF YORK: Dared once to touch a dust of England's ground?
DUKE OF YORK: But then more 'why?' why have they dared to march
DUKE OF YORK: So many miles upon her peaceful bosom,
DUKE OF YORK: Frighting her pale-faced villages with war
DUKE OF YORK: And ostentation of despised arms?
DUKE OF YORK: Comest thou because the anointed king is hence?
DUKE OF YORK: Why, foolish boy, the king is left behind,
DUKE OF YORK: And in my loyal bosom lies his power.
DUKE OF YORK: Were I but now the lord of such hot youth
DUKE OF YORK: As when brave Gaunt, thy father, and myself
DUKE OF YORK: Rescued the Black Prince, that young Mars of men,
DUKE OF YORK: From forth the ranks of many thousand French,
DUKE OF YORK: O, then how quickly should this arm of mine.
DUKE OF YORK: Now prisoner to the palsy, chastise thee
DUKE OF YORK: And minister correction to thy fault!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My gracious uncle, let me know my fault:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: On what condition stands it and wherein?
DUKE OF YORK: Even in condition of the worst degree,
DUKE OF YORK: In gross rebellion and detested treason:
DUKE OF YORK: Thou art a banish'd man, and here art come
DUKE OF YORK: Before the expiration of thy time,
DUKE OF YORK: In braving arms against thy sovereign.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As I was banish'd, I was banish'd Hereford,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But as I come, I come for Lancaster.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And, noble uncle, I beseech your grace
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Look on my wrongs with an indifferent eye:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: You are my father, for methinks in you
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I see old Gaunt alive, O, then, my father,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Will you permit that I shall stand condemn'd
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: A wandering vagabond, my rights and royalties
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Pluck'd from my arms perforce and given away
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To upstart unthrifts? Wherefore was I born?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: If that my cousin king be King of England,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: It must be granted I am Duke of Lancaster.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Had you first died, and he been thus trod down,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: He should have found his uncle Gaunt a father,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To rouse his wrongs and chase them to the bay.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I am denied to sue my livery here,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And yet my letters-patents give me leave:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My father's goods are all distrain'd and sold,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And these and all are all amiss employ'd.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What would you have me do? I am a subject,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And I challenge law: attorneys are denied me,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And therefore, personally I lay my claim
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To my inheritance of free descent.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The noble duke hath been too much abused.
LORD ROSS: It stands your grace upon to do him right.
LORD WILLOUGHBY: Base men by his endowments are made great.
DUKE OF YORK: My lords of England, let me tell you this:
DUKE OF YORK: I have had feeling of my cousin's wrongs
DUKE OF YORK: And laboured all I could to do him right,
DUKE OF YORK: But in this kind to come, in braving arms,
DUKE OF YORK: Be his own carver and cut out his way,
DUKE OF YORK: To find out right with wrong, it may not be,
DUKE OF YORK: And you that do abet him in this kind
DUKE OF YORK: Cherish rebellion and are rebels all.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The noble duke hath sworn his coming is
NORTHUMBERLAND: But for his own, and for the right of that
NORTHUMBERLAND: We all have strongly sworn to give him aid,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And let him ne'er see joy that breaks that oath!
DUKE OF YORK: Well, well, I see the issue of these arms:
DUKE OF YORK: I cannot mend it, I must needs confess,
DUKE OF YORK: Because my power is weak and all ill left:
DUKE OF YORK: But if I could, by Him that gave me life,
DUKE OF YORK: I would attach you all and make you stoop
DUKE OF YORK: Unto the sovereign mercy of the king,
DUKE OF YORK: But since I cannot, be it known to you
DUKE OF YORK: I do remain as neuter. So, fare you well,
DUKE OF YORK: Unless you please to enter in the castle
DUKE OF YORK: And there repose you for this night.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: An offer, uncle, that we will accept:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But we must win your grace to go with us
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To Bristol castle, which they say is held
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By Bushy, Bagot and their complices,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The caterpillars of the commonwealth,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
DUKE OF YORK: It may be I will go with you: but yet I'll pause,
DUKE OF YORK: For I am loath to break our country's laws.
DUKE OF YORK: Nor friends nor foes, to me welcome you are:
DUKE OF YORK: Things past redress are now with me past care.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A camp in Wales.
NARRATOR: Enter EARL OF SALISBURY and a Welsh Captain
Captain: My lord of Salisbury, we have stay'd ten days,
Captain: And hardly kept our countrymen together,
Captain: And yet we hear no tidings from the king,
Captain: Therefore we will disperse ourselves: farewell.
EARL OF SALISBURY: Stay yet another day, thou trusty Welshman:
EARL OF SALISBURY: The king reposeth all his confidence in thee.
Captain: 'Tis thought the king is dead, we will not stay.
Captain: The bay-trees in our country are all wither'd
Captain: And meteors fright the fixed stars of heaven,
Captain: The pale-faced moon looks bloody on the earth
Captain: And lean-look'd prophets whisper fearful change,
Captain: Rich men look sad and ruffians dance and leap,
Captain: The one in fear to lose what they enjoy,
Captain: The other to enjoy by rage and war:
Captain: These signs forerun the death or fall of kings.
Captain: Farewell: our countrymen are gone and fled,
Captain: As well assured Richard their king is dead.
NARRATOR: Exit
EARL OF SALISBURY: Ah, Richard, with the eyes of heavy mind
EARL OF SALISBURY: I see thy glory like a shooting star
EARL OF SALISBURY: Fall to the base earth from the firmament.
EARL OF SALISBURY: Thy sun sets weeping in the lowly west,
EARL OF SALISBURY: Witnessing storms to come, woe and unrest:
EARL OF SALISBURY: Thy friends are fled to wait upon thy foes,
EARL OF SALISBURY: And crossly to thy good all fortune goes.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Bristol. Before the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE, DUKE OF YORK,  NORTHUMBERLAND, LORD ROSS, HENRY PERCY, LORD WILLOUGHBY, with BUSHY and GREEN, prisoners
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Bring forth these men.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Bushy and Green, I will not vex your souls--
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Since presently your souls must part your bodies--
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With too much urging your pernicious lives,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For 'twere no charity, yet, to wash your blood
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: From off my hands, here in the view of men
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I will unfold some causes of your deaths.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: You have misled a prince, a royal king,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: A happy gentleman in blood and lineaments,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: By you unhappied and disfigured clean:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: You have in manner with your sinful hours
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Made a divorce betwixt his queen and him,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Broke the possession of a royal bed
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And stain'd the beauty of a fair queen's cheeks
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With tears drawn from her eyes by your foul wrongs.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Myself, a prince by fortune of my birth,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Near to the king in blood, and near in love
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Till you did make him misinterpret me,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Have stoop'd my neck under your injuries,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And sigh'd my English breath in foreign clouds,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Eating the bitter bread of banishment,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Whilst you have fed upon my signories,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Dispark'd my parks and fell'd my forest woods,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: From my own windows torn my household coat,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Razed out my imprese, leaving me no sign,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Save men's opinions and my living blood,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To show the world I am a gentleman.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: This and much more, much more than twice all this,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Condemns you to the death. See them deliver'd over
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To execution and the hand of death.
BUSHY: More welcome is the stroke of death to me
BUSHY: Than Bolingbroke to England. Lords, farewell.
GREEN: My comfort is that heaven will take our souls
GREEN: And plague injustice with the pains of hell.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My Lord Northumberland, see them dispatch'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt NORTHUMBERLAND and others, with the prisoners
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Uncle, you say the queen is at your house,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For God's sake, fairly let her be entreated:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Tell her I send to her my kind commends,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Take special care my greetings be deliver'd.
DUKE OF YORK: A gentleman of mine I have dispatch'd
DUKE OF YORK: With letters of your love to her at large.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Thank, gentle uncle. Come, lords, away.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To fight with Glendower and his complices:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Awhile to work, and after holiday.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
