NARRATOR: SCENE II. The coast of Wales. A castle in view.
NARRATOR: Drums, flourish and colours. Enter KING RICHARD II, the BISHOP OF CARLISLE, DUKE OF AUMERLE, and Soldiers
KING RICHARD II: Barkloughly castle call they this at hand?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Yea, my lord. How brooks your grace the air,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: After your late tossing on the breaking seas?
KING RICHARD II: Needs must I like it well: I weep for joy
KING RICHARD II: To stand upon my kingdom once again.
KING RICHARD II: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand,
KING RICHARD II: Though rebels wound thee with their horses' hoofs:
KING RICHARD II: As a long-parted mother with her child
KING RICHARD II: Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting,
KING RICHARD II: So, weeping, smiling, greet I thee, my earth,
KING RICHARD II: And do thee favours with my royal hands.
KING RICHARD II: Feed not thy sovereign's foe, my gentle earth,
KING RICHARD II: Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense,
KING RICHARD II: But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom,
KING RICHARD II: And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way,
KING RICHARD II: Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet
KING RICHARD II: Which with usurping steps do trample thee:
KING RICHARD II: Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies,
KING RICHARD II: And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower,
KING RICHARD II: Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder
KING RICHARD II: Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch
KING RICHARD II: Throw death upon thy sovereign's enemies.
KING RICHARD II: Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords:
KING RICHARD II: This earth shall have a feeling and these stones
KING RICHARD II: Prove armed soldiers, ere her native king
KING RICHARD II: Shall falter under foul rebellion's arms.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Fear not, my lord: that Power that made you king
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Hath power to keep you king in spite of all.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: The means that heaven yields must be embraced,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And not neglected, else, if heaven would,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And we will not, heaven's offer we refuse,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: The proffer'd means of succor and redress.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: He means, my lord, that we are too remiss,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Grows strong and great in substance and in power.
KING RICHARD II: Discomfortable cousin! know'st thou not
KING RICHARD II: That when the searching eye of heaven is hid,
KING RICHARD II: Behind the globe, that lights the lower world,
KING RICHARD II: Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen
KING RICHARD II: In murders and in outrage, boldly here,
KING RICHARD II: But when from under this terrestrial ball
KING RICHARD II: He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines
KING RICHARD II: And darts his light through every guilty hole,
KING RICHARD II: Then murders, treasons and detested sins,
KING RICHARD II: The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs,
KING RICHARD II: Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves?
KING RICHARD II: So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke,
KING RICHARD II: Who all this while hath revell'd in the night
KING RICHARD II: Whilst we were wandering with the antipodes,
KING RICHARD II: Shall see us rising in our throne, the east,
KING RICHARD II: His treasons will sit blushing in his face,
KING RICHARD II: Not able to endure the sight of day,
KING RICHARD II: But self-affrighted tremble at his sin.
KING RICHARD II: Not all the water in the rough rude sea
KING RICHARD II: Can wash the balm off from an anointed king,
KING RICHARD II: The breath of worldly men cannot depose
KING RICHARD II: The deputy elected by the Lord:
KING RICHARD II: For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd
KING RICHARD II: To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown,
KING RICHARD II: God for his Richard hath in heavenly pay
KING RICHARD II: A glorious angel: then, if angels fight,
KING RICHARD II: Weak men must fall, for heaven still guards the right.
NARRATOR: Enter EARL OF SALISBURY
KING RICHARD II: Welcome, my lord	how far off lies your power?
EARL OF SALISBURY: Nor near nor farther off, my gracious lord,
EARL OF SALISBURY: Than this weak arm: discomfort guides my tongue
EARL OF SALISBURY: And bids me speak of nothing but despair.
EARL OF SALISBURY: One day too late, I fear me, noble lord,
EARL OF SALISBURY: Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth:
EARL OF SALISBURY: O, call back yesterday, bid time return,
EARL OF SALISBURY: And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men!
EARL OF SALISBURY: To-day, to-day, unhappy day, too late,
EARL OF SALISBURY: O'erthrows thy joys, friends, fortune and thy state:
EARL OF SALISBURY: For all the Welshmen, hearing thou wert dead.
EARL OF SALISBURY: Are gone to Bolingbroke, dispersed and fled.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Comfort, my liege, why looks your grace so pale?
KING RICHARD II: But now the blood of twenty thousand men
KING RICHARD II: Did triumph in my face, and they are fled,
KING RICHARD II: And, till so much blood thither come again,
KING RICHARD II: Have I not reason to look pale and dead?
KING RICHARD II: All souls that will be safe fly from my side,
KING RICHARD II: For time hath set a blot upon my pride.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Comfort, my liege, remember who you are.
KING RICHARD II: I had forgot myself, am I not king?
KING RICHARD II: Awake, thou coward majesty! thou sleepest.
KING RICHARD II: Is not the king's name twenty thousand names?
KING RICHARD II: Arm, arm, my name! a puny subject strikes
KING RICHARD II: At thy great glory. Look not to the ground,
KING RICHARD II: Ye favourites of a king: are we not high?
KING RICHARD II: High be our thoughts: I know my uncle York
KING RICHARD II: Hath power enough to serve our turn. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter SIR STEPHEN SCROOP
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: More health and happiness betide my liege
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Than can my care-tuned tongue deliver him!
KING RICHARD II: Mine ear is open and my heart prepared,
KING RICHARD II: The worst is worldly loss thou canst unfold.
KING RICHARD II: Say, is my kingdom lost? why, 'twas my care
KING RICHARD II: And what loss is it to be rid of care?
KING RICHARD II: Strives Bolingbroke to be as great as we?
KING RICHARD II: Greater he shall not be, if he serve God,
KING RICHARD II: We'll serve Him too and be his fellow so:
KING RICHARD II: Revolt our subjects? that we cannot mend,
KING RICHARD II: They break their faith to God as well as us:
KING RICHARD II: Cry woe, destruction, ruin and decay:
KING RICHARD II: The worst is death, and death will have his day.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Glad am I that your highness is so arm'd
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: To bear the tidings of calamity.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Like an unseasonable stormy day,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Which makes the silver rivers drown their shores,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: As if the world were all dissolved to tears,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: So high above his limits swells the rage
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Of Bolingbroke, covering your fearful land
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: With hard bright steel and hearts harder than steel.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Against thy majesty, boys, with women's voices,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Strive to speak big and clap their female joints
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: In stiff unwieldy arms against thy crown:
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: The very beadsmen learn to bend their bows
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Of double-fatal yew against thy state,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Yea, distaff-women manage rusty bills
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Against thy seat: both young and old rebel,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: And all goes worse than I have power to tell.
KING RICHARD II: Too well, too well thou tell'st a tale so ill.
KING RICHARD II: Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? where is Bagot?
KING RICHARD II: What is become of Bushy? where is Green?
KING RICHARD II: That they have let the dangerous enemy
KING RICHARD II: Measure our confines with such peaceful steps?
KING RICHARD II: If we prevail, their heads shall pay for it:
KING RICHARD II: I warrant they have made peace with Bolingbroke.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Peace have they made with him indeed, my lord.
KING RICHARD II: O villains, vipers, damn'd without redemption!
KING RICHARD II: Dogs, easily won to fawn on any man!
KING RICHARD II: Snakes, in my heart-blood warm'd, that sting my heart!
KING RICHARD II: Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas!
KING RICHARD II: Would they make peace? terrible hell make war
KING RICHARD II: Upon their spotted souls for this offence!
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Sweet love, I see, changing his property,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Turns to the sourest and most deadly hate:
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Again uncurse their souls, their peace is made
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: With heads, and not with hands, those whom you curse
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Have felt the worst of death's destroying wound
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: And lie full low, graved in the hollow ground.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Is Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Ay, all of them at Bristol lost their heads.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Where is the duke my father with his power?
KING RICHARD II: No matter where, of comfort no man speak:
KING RICHARD II: Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs,
KING RICHARD II: Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes
KING RICHARD II: Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth,
KING RICHARD II: Let's choose executors and talk of wills:
KING RICHARD II: And yet not so, for what can we bequeath
KING RICHARD II: Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
KING RICHARD II: Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke's,
KING RICHARD II: And nothing can we call our own but death
KING RICHARD II: And that small model of the barren earth
KING RICHARD II: Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
KING RICHARD II: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground
KING RICHARD II: And tell sad stories of the death of kings,
KING RICHARD II: How some have been deposed, some slain in war,
KING RICHARD II: Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed,
KING RICHARD II: Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd,
KING RICHARD II: All murder'd: for within the hollow crown
KING RICHARD II: That rounds the mortal temples of a king
KING RICHARD II: Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits,
KING RICHARD II: Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
KING RICHARD II: Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
KING RICHARD II: To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks,
KING RICHARD II: Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
KING RICHARD II: As if this flesh which walls about our life,
KING RICHARD II: Were brass impregnable, and humour'd thus
KING RICHARD II: Comes at the last and with a little pin
KING RICHARD II: Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!
KING RICHARD II: Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood
KING RICHARD II: With solemn reverence: throw away respect,
KING RICHARD II: Tradition, form and ceremonious duty,
KING RICHARD II: For you have but mistook me all this while:
KING RICHARD II: I live with bread like you, feel want,
KING RICHARD II: Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus,
KING RICHARD II: How can you say to me, I am a king?
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: My lord, wise men ne'er sit and wail their woes,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: But presently prevent the ways to wail.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Gives in your weakness strength unto your foe,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And so your follies fight against yourself.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Fear and be slain, no worse can come to fight:
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And fight and die is death destroying death,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: My father hath a power, inquire of him
DUKE OF AUMERLE: And learn to make a body of a limb.
KING RICHARD II: Thou chidest me well: proud Bolingbroke, I come
KING RICHARD II: To change blows with thee for our day of doom.
KING RICHARD II: This ague fit of fear is over-blown,
KING RICHARD II: An easy task it is to win our own.
KING RICHARD II: Say, Scroop, where lies our uncle with his power?
KING RICHARD II: Speak sweetly, man, although thy looks be sour.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Men judge by the complexion of the sky
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: The state and inclination of the day:
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: So may you by my dull and heavy eye,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: My tongue hath but a heavier tale to say.
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: I play the torturer, by small and small
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: To lengthen out the worst that must be spoken:
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Your uncle York is join'd with Bolingbroke,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: And all your northern castles yielded up,
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: And all your southern gentlemen in arms
SIR STEPHEN SCROOP: Upon his party.
KING RICHARD II: Thou hast said enough.
KING RICHARD II: Beshrew thee, cousin, which didst lead me forth
NARRATOR: To DUKE OF AUMERLE
KING RICHARD II: Of that sweet way I was in to despair!
KING RICHARD II: What say you now? what comfort have we now?
KING RICHARD II: By heaven, I'll hate him everlastingly
KING RICHARD II: That bids me be of comfort any more.
KING RICHARD II: Go to Flint castle: there I'll pine away,
KING RICHARD II: A king, woe's slave, shall kingly woe obey.
KING RICHARD II: That power I have, discharge, and let them go
KING RICHARD II: To ear the land that hath some hope to grow,
KING RICHARD II: For I have none: let no man speak again
KING RICHARD II: To alter this, for counsel is but vain.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: My liege, one word.
KING RICHARD II: He does me double wrong
KING RICHARD II: That wounds me with the flatteries of his tongue.
KING RICHARD II: Discharge my followers: let them hence away,
KING RICHARD II: From Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Wales. Before Flint castle.
NARRATOR: Enter, with drum and colours, HENRY BOLINGBROKE, DUKE OF YORK, NORTHUMBERLAND, Attendants, and forces
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: So that by this intelligence we learn
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The Welshmen are dispersed, and Salisbury
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Is gone to meet the king, who lately landed
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With some few private friends upon this coast.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The news is very fair and good, my lord:
NORTHUMBERLAND: Richard not far from hence hath hid his head.
DUKE OF YORK: It would beseem the Lord Northumberland
DUKE OF YORK: To say 'King Richard:' alack the heavy day
DUKE OF YORK: When such a sacred king should hide his head.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Your grace mistakes, only to be brief
NORTHUMBERLAND: Left I his title out.
DUKE OF YORK: The time hath been,
DUKE OF YORK: Would you have been so brief with him, he would
DUKE OF YORK: Have been so brief with you, to shorten you,
DUKE OF YORK: For taking so the head, your whole head's length.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Mistake not, uncle, further than you should.
DUKE OF YORK: Take not, good cousin, further than you should.
DUKE OF YORK: Lest you mistake the heavens are o'er our heads.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I know it, uncle, and oppose not myself
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Against their will. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY PERCY
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Welcome, Harry: what, will not this castle yield?
HENRY PERCY: The castle royally is mann'd, my lord,
HENRY PERCY: Against thy entrance.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Royally!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Why, it contains no king?
HENRY PERCY: Yes, my good lord,
HENRY PERCY: It doth contain a king, King Richard lies
HENRY PERCY: Within the limits of yon lime and stone:
HENRY PERCY: And with him are the Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury,
HENRY PERCY: Sir Stephen Scroop, besides a clergyman
HENRY PERCY: Of holy reverence, who, I cannot learn.
NORTHUMBERLAND: O, belike it is the Bishop of Carlisle.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Noble lords,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Go to the rude ribs of that ancient castle,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Through brazen trumpet send the breath of parley
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Into his ruin'd ears, and thus deliver:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Henry Bolingbroke
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: On both his knees doth kiss King Richard's hand
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And sends allegiance and true faith of heart
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To his most royal person, hither come
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Even at his feet to lay my arms and power,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Provided that my banishment repeal'd
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And lands restored again be freely granted:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: If not, I'll use the advantage of my power
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And lay the summer's dust with showers of blood
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Rain'd from the wounds of slaughter'd Englishmen:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The which, how far off from the mind of Bolingbroke
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: It is, such crimson tempest should bedrench
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The fresh green lap of fair King Richard's land,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My stooping duty tenderly shall show.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Go, signify as much, while here we march
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Upon the grassy carpet of this plain.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Let's march without the noise of threatening drum,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That from this castle's tatter'd battlements
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Our fair appointments may be well perused.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Methinks King Richard and myself should meet
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With no less terror than the elements
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Of fire and water, when their thundering shock
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: At meeting tears the cloudy cheeks of heaven.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Be he the fire, I'll be the yielding water:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The rage be his, whilst on the earth I rain
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My waters, on the earth, and not on him.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: March on, and mark King Richard how he looks.
NARRATOR: Parle without, and answer within. Then a flourish.  Enter on the walls, KING RICHARD II, the BISHOP OF  CARLISLE, DUKE OF AUMERLE, SIR STEPHEN SCROOP, and EARL OF SALISBURY
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: See, see, King Richard doth himself appear,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As doth the blushing discontented sun
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: From out the fiery portal of the east,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: When he perceives the envious clouds are bent
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To dim his glory and to stain the track
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Of his bright passage to the occident.
DUKE OF YORK: Yet looks he like a king: behold, his eye,
DUKE OF YORK: As bright as is the eagle's, lightens forth
DUKE OF YORK: Controlling majesty: alack, alack, for woe,
DUKE OF YORK: That any harm should stain so fair a show!
KING RICHARD II: We are amazed, and thus long have we stood
KING RICHARD II: To watch the fearful bending of thy knee,
NARRATOR: To NORTHUMBERLAND
KING RICHARD II: Because we thought ourself thy lawful king:
KING RICHARD II: And if we be, how dare thy joints forget
KING RICHARD II: To pay their awful duty to our presence?
KING RICHARD II: If we be not, show us the hand of God
KING RICHARD II: That hath dismissed us from our stewardship,
KING RICHARD II: For well we know, no hand of blood and bone
KING RICHARD II: Can gripe the sacred handle of our sceptre,
KING RICHARD II: Unless he do profane, steal, or usurp.
KING RICHARD II: And though you think that all, as you have done,
KING RICHARD II: Have torn their souls by turning them from us,
KING RICHARD II: And we are barren and bereft of friends,
KING RICHARD II: Yet know, my master, God omnipotent,
KING RICHARD II: Is mustering in his clouds on our behalf
KING RICHARD II: Armies of pestilence, and they shall strike
KING RICHARD II: Your children yet unborn and unbegot,
KING RICHARD II: That lift your vassal hands against my head
KING RICHARD II: And threat the glory of my precious crown.
KING RICHARD II: Tell Bolingbroke--for yond methinks he stands--
KING RICHARD II: That every stride he makes upon my land
KING RICHARD II: Is dangerous treason: he is come to open
KING RICHARD II: The purple testament of bleeding war,
KING RICHARD II: But ere the crown he looks for live in peace,
KING RICHARD II: Ten thousand bloody crowns of mothers' sons
KING RICHARD II: Shall ill become the flower of England's face,
KING RICHARD II: Change the complexion of her maid-pale peace
KING RICHARD II: To scarlet indignation and bedew
KING RICHARD II: Her pastures' grass with faithful English blood.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The king of heaven forbid our lord the king
NORTHUMBERLAND: Should so with civil and uncivil arms
NORTHUMBERLAND: Be rush'd upon! Thy thrice noble cousin
NORTHUMBERLAND: Harry Bolingbroke doth humbly kiss thy hand,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And by the honourable tomb he swears,
NORTHUMBERLAND: That stands upon your royal grandsire's bones,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And by the royalties of both your bloods,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Currents that spring from one most gracious head,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And by the buried hand of warlike Gaunt,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And by the worth and honour of himself,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Comprising all that may be sworn or said,
NORTHUMBERLAND: His coming hither hath no further scope
NORTHUMBERLAND: Than for his lineal royalties and to beg
NORTHUMBERLAND: Enfranchisement immediate on his kn ees:
NORTHUMBERLAND: Which on thy royal party granted once,
NORTHUMBERLAND: His glittering arms he will commend to rust,
NORTHUMBERLAND: His barbed steeds to stables, and his heart
NORTHUMBERLAND: To faithful service of your majesty.
NORTHUMBERLAND: This swears he, as he is a prince, is just,
NORTHUMBERLAND: And, as I am a gentleman, I credit him.
KING RICHARD II: Northumberland, say thus the king returns:
KING RICHARD II: His noble cousin is right welcome hither,
KING RICHARD II: And all the number of his fair demands
KING RICHARD II: Shall be accomplish'd without contradiction:
KING RICHARD II: With all the gracious utterance thou hast
KING RICHARD II: Speak to his gentle hearing kind commends.
KING RICHARD II: We do debase ourselves, cousin, do we not,
NARRATOR: To DUKE OF AUMERLE
KING RICHARD II: To look so poorly and to speak so fair?
KING RICHARD II: Shall we call back Northumberland, and send
KING RICHARD II: Defiance to the traitor, and so die?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: No, good my lord, let's fight with gentle words
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Till time lend friends and friends their helpful swords.
KING RICHARD II: O God, O God! that e'er this tongue of mine,
KING RICHARD II: That laid the sentence of dread banishment
KING RICHARD II: On yon proud man, should take it off again
KING RICHARD II: With words of sooth! O that I were as great
KING RICHARD II: As is my grief, or lesser than my name!
KING RICHARD II: Or that I could forget what I have been,
KING RICHARD II: Or not remember what I must be now!
KING RICHARD II: Swell'st thou, proud heart? I'll give thee scope to beat,
KING RICHARD II: Since foes have scope to beat both thee and me.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Northumberland comes back from Bolingbroke.
KING RICHARD II: What must the king do now? must he submit?
KING RICHARD II: The king shall do it: must he be deposed?
KING RICHARD II: The king shall be contented: must he lose
KING RICHARD II: The name of king? o' God's name, let it go:
KING RICHARD II: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads,
KING RICHARD II: My gorgeous palace for a hermitage,
KING RICHARD II: My gay apparel for an almsman's gown,
KING RICHARD II: My figured goblets for a dish of wood,
KING RICHARD II: My sceptre for a palmer's walking staff,
KING RICHARD II: My subjects for a pair of carved saints
KING RICHARD II: And my large kingdom for a little grave,
KING RICHARD II: A little little grave, an obscure grave,
KING RICHARD II: Or I'll be buried in the king's highway,
KING RICHARD II: Some way of common trade, where subjects' feet
KING RICHARD II: May hourly trample on their sovereign's head,
KING RICHARD II: For on my heart they tread now whilst I live,
KING RICHARD II: And buried once, why not upon my head?
KING RICHARD II: Aumerle, thou weep'st, my tender-hearted cousin!
KING RICHARD II: We'll make foul weather with despised tears,
KING RICHARD II: Our sighs and they shall lodge the summer corn,
KING RICHARD II: And make a dearth in this revolting land.
KING RICHARD II: Or shall we play the wantons with our woes,
KING RICHARD II: And make some pretty match with shedding tears?
KING RICHARD II: As thus, to drop them still upon one place,
KING RICHARD II: Till they have fretted us a pair of graves
KING RICHARD II: Within the earth, and, therein laid,--there lies
KING RICHARD II: Two kinsmen digg'd their graves with weeping eyes.
KING RICHARD II: Would not this ill do well? Well, well, I see
KING RICHARD II: I talk but idly, and you laugh at me.
KING RICHARD II: Most mighty prince, my Lord Northumberland,
KING RICHARD II: What says King Bolingbroke? will his majesty
KING RICHARD II: Give Richard leave to live till Richard die?
KING RICHARD II: You make a leg, and Bolingbroke says ay.
NORTHUMBERLAND: My lord, in the base court he doth attend
NORTHUMBERLAND: To speak with you, may it please you to come down.
KING RICHARD II: Down, down I come, like glistering Phaethon,
KING RICHARD II: Wanting the manage of unruly jades.
KING RICHARD II: In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base,
KING RICHARD II: To come at traitors' calls and do them grace.
KING RICHARD II: In the base court? Come down? Down, court!
KING RICHARD II: down, king!
KING RICHARD II: For night-owls shriek where mounting larks
KING RICHARD II: should sing.
NARRATOR: Exeunt from above
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What says his majesty?
NORTHUMBERLAND: Sorrow and grief of heart
NORTHUMBERLAND: Makes him speak fondly, like a frantic man
NORTHUMBERLAND: Yet he is come.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD and his attendants below
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Stand all apart,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And show fair duty to his majesty.
NARRATOR: He kneels down
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My gracious lord,--
KING RICHARD II: Fair cousin, you debase your princely knee
KING RICHARD II: To make the base earth proud with kissing it:
KING RICHARD II: Me rather had my heart might feel your love
KING RICHARD II: Than my unpleased eye see your courtesy.
KING RICHARD II: Up, cousin, up, your heart is up, I know,
KING RICHARD II: Thus high at least, although your knee be low.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My gracious lord, I come but for mine own.
KING RICHARD II: Your own is yours, and I am yours, and all.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: So far be mine, my most redoubted lord,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As my true service shall deserve your love.
KING RICHARD II: Well you deserve: they well deserve to have,
KING RICHARD II: That know the strong'st and surest way to get.
KING RICHARD II: Uncle, give me your hands: nay, dry your eyes,
KING RICHARD II: Tears show their love, but want their remedies.
KING RICHARD II: Cousin, I am too young to be your father,
KING RICHARD II: Though you are old enough to be my heir.
KING RICHARD II: What you will have, I'll give, and willing too,
KING RICHARD II: For do we must what force will have us do.
KING RICHARD II: Set on towards London, cousin, is it so?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Yea, my good lord.
KING RICHARD II: Then I must not say no.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. LANGLEY. The DUKE OF YORK's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter the QUEEN and two Ladies
QUEEN: What sport shall we devise here in this garden,
QUEEN: To drive away the heavy thought of care?
Lady: Madam, we'll play at bowls.
QUEEN: 'Twill make me think the world is full of rubs,
QUEEN: And that my fortune rubs against the bias.
Lady: Madam, we'll dance.
QUEEN: My legs can keep no measure in delight,
QUEEN: When my poor heart no measure keeps in grief:
QUEEN: Therefore, no dancing, girl, some other sport.
Lady: Madam, we'll tell tales.
QUEEN: Of sorrow or of joy?
Lady: Of either, madam.
QUEEN: Of neither, girl:
QUEEN: For of joy, being altogether wanting,
QUEEN: It doth remember me the more of sorrow,
QUEEN: Or if of grief, being altogether had,
QUEEN: It adds more sorrow to my want of joy:
QUEEN: For what I have I need not to repeat,
QUEEN: And what I want it boots not to complain.
Lady: Madam, I'll sing.
QUEEN: 'Tis well that thou hast cause
QUEEN: But thou shouldst please me better, wouldst thou weep.
Lady: I could weep, madam, would it do you good.
QUEEN: And I could sing, would weeping do me good,
QUEEN: And never borrow any tear of thee.
NARRATOR: Enter a Gardener, and two Servants
QUEEN: But stay, here come the gardeners:
QUEEN: Let's step into the shadow of these trees.
QUEEN: My wretchedness unto a row of pins,
QUEEN: They'll talk of state, for every one doth so
QUEEN: Against a change, woe is forerun with woe.
NARRATOR: QUEEN and Ladies retire
Gardener: Go, bind thou up yon dangling apricocks,
Gardener: Which, like unruly children, make their sire
Gardener: Stoop with oppression of their prodigal weight:
Gardener: Give some supportance to the bending twigs.
Gardener: Go thou, and like an executioner,
Gardener: Cut off the heads of too fast growing sprays,
Gardener: That look too lofty in our commonwealth:
Gardener: All must be even in our government.
Gardener: You thus employ'd, I will go root away
Gardener: The noisome weeds, which without profit suck
Gardener: The soil's fertility from wholesome flowers.
Servant: Why should we in the compass of a pale
Servant: Keep law and form and due proportion,
Servant: Showing, as in a model, our firm estate,
Servant: When our sea-walled garden, the whole land,
Servant: Is full of weeds, her fairest flowers choked up,
Servant: Her fruit-trees all upturned, her hedges ruin'd,
Servant: Her knots disorder'd and her wholesome herbs
Servant: Swarming with caterpillars?
Gardener: Hold thy peace:
Gardener: He that hath suffer'd this disorder'd spring
Gardener: Hath now himself met with the fall of leaf:
Gardener: The weeds which his broad-spreading leaves did shelter,
Gardener: That seem'd in eating him to hold him up,
Gardener: Are pluck'd up root and all by Bolingbroke,
Gardener: I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy, Green.
Servant: What, are they dead?
Gardener: They are, and Bolingbroke
Gardener: Hath seized the wasteful king. O, what pity is it
Gardener: That he had not so trimm'd and dress'd his land
Gardener: As we this garden! We at time of year
Gardener: Do wound the bark, the skin of our fruit-trees,
Gardener: Lest, being over-proud in sap and blood,
Gardener: With too much riches it confound itself:
Gardener: Had he done so to great and growing men,
Gardener: They might have lived to bear and he to taste
Gardener: Their fruits of duty: superfluous branches
Gardener: We lop away, that bearing boughs may live:
Gardener: Had he done so, himself had borne the crown,
Gardener: Which waste of idle hours hath quite thrown down.
Servant: What, think you then the king shall be deposed?
Gardener: Depress'd he is already, and deposed
Gardener: 'Tis doubt he will be: letters came last night
Gardener: To a dear friend of the good Duke of York's,
Gardener: That tell black tidings.
QUEEN: O, I am press'd to death through want of speaking!
NARRATOR: Coming forward
QUEEN: Thou, old Adam's likeness, set to dress this garden,
QUEEN: How dares thy harsh rude tongue sound this unpleasing news?
QUEEN: What Eve, what serpent, hath suggested thee
QUEEN: To make a second fall of cursed man?
QUEEN: Why dost thou say King Richard is deposed?
QUEEN: Darest thou, thou little better thing than earth,
QUEEN: Divine his downfall? Say, where, when, and how,
QUEEN: Camest thou by this ill tidings? speak, thou wretch.
Gardener: Pardon me, madam: little joy have I
Gardener: To breathe this news, yet what I say is true.
Gardener: King Richard, he is in the mighty hold
Gardener: Of Bolingbroke: their fortunes both are weigh'd:
Gardener: In your lord's scale is nothing but himself,
Gardener: And some few vanities that make him light,
Gardener: But in the balance of great Bolingbroke,
Gardener: Besides himself, are all the English peers,
Gardener: And with that odds he weighs King Richard down.
Gardener: Post you to London, and you will find it so,
Gardener: I speak no more than every one doth know.
QUEEN: Nimble mischance, that art so light of foot,
QUEEN: Doth not thy embassage belong to me,
QUEEN: And am I last that knows it? O, thou think'st
QUEEN: To serve me last, that I may longest keep
QUEEN: Thy sorrow in my breast. Come, ladies, go,
QUEEN: To meet at London London's king in woe.
QUEEN: What, was I born to this, that my sad look
QUEEN: Should grace the triumph of great Bolingbroke?
QUEEN: Gardener, for telling me these news of woe,
QUEEN: Pray God the plants thou graft'st may never grow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt QUEEN and Ladies
GARDENER: Poor queen! so that thy state might be no worse,
GARDENER: I would my skill were subject to thy curse.
GARDENER: Here did she fall a tear, here in this place
GARDENER: I'll set a bank of rue, sour herb of grace:
GARDENER: Rue, even for ruth, here shortly shall be seen,
GARDENER: In the remembrance of a weeping queen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Westminster Hall.
NARRATOR: Enter, as to the Parliament, HENRY BOLINGBROKE,  DUKE OF AUMERLE, NORTHUMBERLAND, HENRY PERCY, LORD  FITZWATER, DUKE OF SURREY, the BISHOP OF CARLISLE,  the Abbot Of Westminster, and another Lord, Herald, Officers, and BAGOT
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Call forth Bagot.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Now, Bagot, freely speak thy mind,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What thou dost know of noble Gloucester's death,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Who wrought it with the king, and who perform'd
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The bloody office of his timeless end.
BAGOT: Then set before my face the Lord Aumerle.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Cousin, stand forth, and look upon that man.
BAGOT: My Lord Aumerle, I know your daring tongue
BAGOT: Scorns to unsay what once it hath deliver'd.
BAGOT: In that dead time when Gloucester's death was plotted,
BAGOT: I heard you say, 'Is not my arm of length,
BAGOT: That reacheth from the restful English court
BAGOT: As far as Calais, to mine uncle's head?'
BAGOT: Amongst much other talk, that very time,
BAGOT: I heard you say that you had rather refuse
BAGOT: The offer of an hundred thousand crowns
BAGOT: Than Bolingbroke's return to England,
BAGOT: Adding withal how blest this land would be
BAGOT: In this your cousin's death.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Princes and noble lords,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: What answer shall I make to this base man?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Shall I so much dishonour my fair stars,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: On equal terms to give him chastisement?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Either I must, or have mine honour soil'd
DUKE OF AUMERLE: With the attainder of his slanderous lips.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: There is my gage, the manual seal of death,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: That marks thee out for hell: I say, thou liest,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: And will maintain what thou hast said is false
DUKE OF AUMERLE: In thy heart-blood, though being all too base
DUKE OF AUMERLE: To stain the temper of my knightly sword.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Bagot, forbear, thou shalt not take it up.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Excepting one, I would he were the best
DUKE OF AUMERLE: In all this presence that hath moved me so.
LORD FITZWATER: If that thy valour stand on sympathy,
LORD FITZWATER: There is my gage, Aumerle, in gage to thine:
LORD FITZWATER: By that fair sun which shows me where thou stand'st,
LORD FITZWATER: I heard thee say, and vauntingly thou spakest it
LORD FITZWATER: That thou wert cause of noble Gloucester's death.
LORD FITZWATER: If thou deny'st it twenty times, thou liest,
LORD FITZWATER: And I will turn thy falsehood to thy heart,
LORD FITZWATER: Where it was forged, with my rapier's point.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Thou darest not, coward, live to see that day.
LORD FITZWATER: Now by my soul, I would it were this hour.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Fitzwater, thou art damn'd to hell for this.
HENRY PERCY: Aumerle, thou liest, his honour is as true
HENRY PERCY: In this appeal as thou art all unjust,
HENRY PERCY: And that thou art so, there I throw my gage,
HENRY PERCY: To prove it on thee to the extremest point
HENRY PERCY: Of mortal breathing: seize it, if thou darest.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: An if I do not, may my hands rot off
DUKE OF AUMERLE: And never brandish more revengeful steel
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Over the glittering helmet of my foe!
Lord: I task the earth to the like, forsworn Aumerle,
Lord: And spur thee on with full as many lies
Lord: As may be holloa'd in thy treacherous ear
Lord: From sun to sun: there is my honour's pawn,
Lord: Engage it to the trial, if thou darest.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Who sets me else? by heaven, I'll throw at all:
DUKE OF AUMERLE: I have a thousand spirits in one breast,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: To answer twenty thousand such as you.
DUKE OF SURREY: My Lord Fitzwater, I do remember well
DUKE OF SURREY: The very time Aumerle and you did talk.
LORD FITZWATER: 'Tis very true: you were in presence then,
LORD FITZWATER: And you can witness with me this is true.
DUKE OF SURREY: As false, by heaven, as heaven itself is true.
LORD FITZWATER: Surrey, thou liest.
DUKE OF SURREY: Dishonourable boy!
DUKE OF SURREY: That lie shall lie so heavy on my sword,
DUKE OF SURREY: That it shall render vengeance and revenge
DUKE OF SURREY: Till thou the lie-giver and that lie do lie
DUKE OF SURREY: In earth as quiet as thy father's skull:
DUKE OF SURREY: In proof whereof, there is my honour's pawn,
DUKE OF SURREY: Engage it to the trial, if thou darest.
LORD FITZWATER: How fondly dost thou spur a forward horse!
LORD FITZWATER: If I dare eat, or drink, or breathe, or live,
LORD FITZWATER: I dare meet Surrey in a wilderness,
LORD FITZWATER: And spit upon him, whilst I say he lies,
LORD FITZWATER: And lies, and lies: there is my bond of faith,
LORD FITZWATER: To tie thee to my strong correction.
LORD FITZWATER: As I intend to thrive in this new world,
LORD FITZWATER: Aumerle is guilty of my true appeal:
LORD FITZWATER: Besides, I heard the banish'd Norfolk say
LORD FITZWATER: That thou, Aumerle, didst send two of thy men
LORD FITZWATER: To execute the noble duke at Calais.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Some honest Christian trust me with a gage
DUKE OF AUMERLE: That Norfolk lies: here do I throw down this,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: If he may be repeal'd, to try his honour.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: These differences shall all rest under gage
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Till Norfolk be repeal'd: repeal'd he shall be,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And, though mine enemy, restored again
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To all his lands and signories: when he's return'd,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Against Aumerle we will enforce his trial.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: That honourable day shall ne'er be seen.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Many a time hath banish'd Norfolk fought
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: For Jesu Christ in glorious Christian field,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Streaming the ensign of the Christian cross
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Against black pagans, Turks, and Saracens:
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And toil'd with works of war, retired himself
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: To Italy, and there at Venice gave
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: His body to that pleasant country's earth,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And his pure soul unto his captain Christ,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Under whose colours he had fought so long.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Why, bishop, is Norfolk dead?
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: As surely as I live, my lord.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Sweet peace conduct his sweet soul to the bosom
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Of good old Abraham! Lords appellants,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Your differences shall all rest under gage
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Till we assign you to your days of trial.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF YORK, attended
DUKE OF YORK: Great Duke of Lancaster, I come to thee
DUKE OF YORK: From plume-pluck'd Richard, who with willing soul
DUKE OF YORK: Adopts thee heir, and his high sceptre yields
DUKE OF YORK: To the possession of thy royal hand:
DUKE OF YORK: Ascend his throne, descending now from him,
DUKE OF YORK: And long live Henry, fourth of that name!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: In God's name, I'll ascend the regal throne.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Marry. God forbid!
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Worst in this royal presence may I speak,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Yet best beseeming me to speak the truth.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Would God that any in this noble presence
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Were enough noble to be upright judge
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Of noble Richard! then true noblesse would
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Learn him forbearance from so foul a wrong.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: What subject can give sentence on his king?
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And who sits here that is not Richard's subject?
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Thieves are not judged but they are by to hear,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Although apparent guilt be seen in them,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And shall the figure of God's majesty,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: His captain, steward, deputy-elect,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Anointed, crowned, planted many years,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Be judged by subject and inferior breath,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And he himself not present? O, forfend it, God,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: That in a Christian climate souls refined
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Should show so heinous, black, obscene a deed!
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: I speak to subjects, and a subject speaks,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Stirr'd up by God, thus boldly for his king:
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: My Lord of Hereford here, whom you call king,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Is a foul traitor to proud Hereford's king:
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And if you crown him, let me prophesy:
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: The blood of English shall manure the ground,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And future ages groan for this foul act,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Peace shall go sleep with Turks and infidels,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: And in this seat of peace tumultuous wars
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Shall kin with kin and kind with kind confound,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Disorder, horror, fear and mutiny
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Shall here inhabit, and this land be call'd
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: The field of Golgotha and dead men's skulls.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: O, if you raise this house against this house,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: It will the woefullest division prove
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: That ever fell upon this cursed earth.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Prevent it, resist it, let it not be so,
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Lest child, child's children, cry against you woe!
NORTHUMBERLAND: Well have you argued, sir, and, for your pains,
NORTHUMBERLAND: Of capital treason we arrest you here.
NORTHUMBERLAND: My Lord of Westminster, be it your charge
NORTHUMBERLAND: To keep him safely till his day of trial.
NORTHUMBERLAND: May it please you, lords, to grant the commons' suit.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Fetch hither Richard, that in common view
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: He may surrender, so we shall proceed
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Without suspicion.
DUKE OF YORK: I will be his conduct.
NARRATOR: Exit
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Lords, you that here are under our arrest,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Procure your sureties for your days of answer.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Little are we beholding to your love,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And little look'd for at your helping hands.
NARRATOR: Re-enter DUKE OF YORK, with KING RICHARD II, and Officers bearing the regalia
KING RICHARD II: Alack, why am I sent for to a king,
KING RICHARD II: Before I have shook off the regal thoughts
KING RICHARD II: Wherewith I reign'd? I hardly yet have learn'd
KING RICHARD II: To insinuate, flatter, bow, and bend my limbs:
KING RICHARD II: Give sorrow leave awhile to tutor me
KING RICHARD II: To this submission. Yet I well remember
KING RICHARD II: The favours of these men: were they not mine?
KING RICHARD II: Did they not sometime cry, 'all hail!' to me?
KING RICHARD II: So Judas did to Christ: but he, in twelve,
KING RICHARD II: Found truth in all but one: I, in twelve thousand, none.
KING RICHARD II: God save the king! Will no man say amen?
KING RICHARD II: Am I both priest and clerk? well then, amen.
KING RICHARD II: God save the king! although I be not he,
KING RICHARD II: And yet, amen, if heaven do think him me.
KING RICHARD II: To do what service am I sent for hither?
DUKE OF YORK: To do that office of thine own good will
DUKE OF YORK: Which tired majesty did make thee offer,
DUKE OF YORK: The resignation of thy state and crown
DUKE OF YORK: To Henry Bolingbroke.
KING RICHARD II: Give me the crown. Here, cousin, seize the crown,
KING RICHARD II: Here cousin:
KING RICHARD II: On this side my hand, and on that side yours.
KING RICHARD II: Now is this golden crown like a deep well
KING RICHARD II: That owes two buckets, filling one another,
KING RICHARD II: The emptier ever dancing in the air,
KING RICHARD II: The other down, unseen and full of water:
KING RICHARD II: That bucket down and full of tears am I,
KING RICHARD II: Drinking my griefs, whilst you mount up on high.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I thought you had been willing to resign.
KING RICHARD II: My crown I am, but still my griefs are mine:
KING RICHARD II: You may my glories and my state depose,
KING RICHARD II: But not my griefs, still am I king of those.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Part of your cares you give me with your crown.
KING RICHARD II: Your cares set up do not pluck my cares down.
KING RICHARD II: My care is loss of care, by old care done,
KING RICHARD II: Your care is gain of care, by new care won:
KING RICHARD II: The cares I give I have, though given away,
KING RICHARD II: They tend the crown, yet still with me they stay.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Are you contented to resign the crown?
KING RICHARD II: Ay, no, no, ay, for I must nothing be,
KING RICHARD II: Therefore no no, for I resign to thee.
KING RICHARD II: Now mark me, how I will undo myself,
KING RICHARD II: I give this heavy weight from off my head
KING RICHARD II: And this unwieldy sceptre from my hand,
KING RICHARD II: The pride of kingly sway from out my heart,
KING RICHARD II: With mine own tears I wash away my balm,
KING RICHARD II: With mine own hands I give away my crown,
KING RICHARD II: With mine own tongue deny my sacred state,
KING RICHARD II: With mine own breath release all duty's rites:
KING RICHARD II: All pomp and majesty I do forswear,
KING RICHARD II: My manors, rents, revenues I forego,
KING RICHARD II: My acts, decrees, and statutes I deny:
KING RICHARD II: God pardon all oaths that are broke to me!
KING RICHARD II: God keep all vows unbroke that swear to thee!
KING RICHARD II: Make me, that nothing have, with nothing grieved,
KING RICHARD II: And thou with all pleased, that hast all achieved!
KING RICHARD II: Long mayst thou live in Richard's seat to sit,
KING RICHARD II: And soon lie Richard in an earthly pit!
KING RICHARD II: God save King Harry, unking'd Richard says,
KING RICHARD II: And send him many years of sunshine days!
KING RICHARD II: What more remains?
NORTHUMBERLAND: No more, but that you read
NORTHUMBERLAND: These accusations and these grievous crimes
NORTHUMBERLAND: Committed by your person and your followers
NORTHUMBERLAND: Against the state and profit of this land,
NORTHUMBERLAND: That, by confessing them, the souls of men
NORTHUMBERLAND: May deem that you are worthily deposed.
KING RICHARD II: Must I do so? and must I ravel out
KING RICHARD II: My weaved-up folly? Gentle Northumberland,
KING RICHARD II: If thy offences were upon record,
KING RICHARD II: Would it not shame thee in so fair a troop
KING RICHARD II: To read a lecture of them? If thou wouldst,
KING RICHARD II: There shouldst thou find one heinous article,
KING RICHARD II: Containing the deposing of a king
KING RICHARD II: And cracking the strong warrant of an oath,
KING RICHARD II: Mark'd with a blot, damn'd in the book of heaven:
KING RICHARD II: Nay, all of you that stand and look upon,
KING RICHARD II: Whilst that my wretchedness doth bait myself,
KING RICHARD II: Though some of you with Pilate wash your hands
KING RICHARD II: Showing an outward pity, yet you Pilates
KING RICHARD II: Have here deliver'd me to my sour cross,
KING RICHARD II: And water cannot wash away your sin.
NORTHUMBERLAND: My lord, dispatch, read o'er these articles.
KING RICHARD II: Mine eyes are full of tears, I cannot see:
KING RICHARD II: And yet salt water blinds them not so much
KING RICHARD II: But they can see a sort of traitors here.
KING RICHARD II: Nay, if I turn mine eyes upon myself,
KING RICHARD II: I find myself a traitor with the rest,
KING RICHARD II: For I have given here my soul's consent
KING RICHARD II: To undeck the pompous body of a king,
KING RICHARD II: Made glory base and sovereignty a slave,
KING RICHARD II: Proud majesty a subject, state a peasant.
NORTHUMBERLAND: My lord,--
KING RICHARD II: No lord of thine, thou haught insulting man,
KING RICHARD II: Nor no man's lord, I have no name, no title,
KING RICHARD II: No, not that name was given me at the font,
KING RICHARD II: But 'tis usurp'd: alack the heavy day,
KING RICHARD II: That I have worn so many winters out,
KING RICHARD II: And know not now what name to call myself!
KING RICHARD II: O that I were a mockery king of snow,
KING RICHARD II: Standing before the sun of Bolingbroke,
KING RICHARD II: To melt myself away in water-drops!
KING RICHARD II: Good king, great king, and yet not greatly good,
KING RICHARD II: An if my word be sterling yet in England,
KING RICHARD II: Let it command a mirror hither straight,
KING RICHARD II: That it may show me what a face I have,
KING RICHARD II: Since it is bankrupt of his majesty.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Go some of you and fetch a looking-glass.
NARRATOR: Exit an attendant
NORTHUMBERLAND: Read o'er this paper while the glass doth come.
KING RICHARD II: Fiend, thou torment'st me ere I come to hell!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Urge it no more, my Lord Northumberland.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The commons will not then be satisfied.
KING RICHARD II: They shall be satisfied: I'll read enough,
KING RICHARD II: When I do see the very book indeed
KING RICHARD II: Where all my sins are writ, and that's myself.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Attendant, with a glass
KING RICHARD II: Give me the glass, and therein will I read.
KING RICHARD II: No deeper wrinkles yet? hath sorrow struck
KING RICHARD II: So many blows upon this face of mine,
KING RICHARD II: And made no deeper wounds? O flattering glass,
KING RICHARD II: Like to my followers in prosperity,
KING RICHARD II: Thou dost beguile me! Was this face the face
KING RICHARD II: That every day under his household roof
KING RICHARD II: Did keep ten thousand men? was this the face
KING RICHARD II: That, like the sun, did make beholders wink?
KING RICHARD II: Was this the face that faced so many follies,
KING RICHARD II: And was at last out-faced by Bolingbroke?
KING RICHARD II: A brittle glory shineth in this face:
KING RICHARD II: As brittle as the glory is the face,
NARRATOR: Dashes the glass against the ground
KING RICHARD II: For there it is, crack'd in a hundred shivers.
KING RICHARD II: Mark, silent king, the moral of this sport,
KING RICHARD II: How soon my sorrow hath destroy'd my face.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The shadow of your sorrow hath destroy'd
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The shadow or your face.
KING RICHARD II: Say that again.
KING RICHARD II: The shadow of my sorrow! ha! let's see:
KING RICHARD II: 'Tis very true, my grief lies all within,
KING RICHARD II: And these external manners of laments
KING RICHARD II: Are merely shadows to the unseen grief
KING RICHARD II: That swells with silence in the tortured soul,
KING RICHARD II: There lies the substance: and I thank thee, king,
KING RICHARD II: For thy great bounty, that not only givest
KING RICHARD II: Me cause to wail but teachest me the way
KING RICHARD II: How to lament the cause. I'll beg one boon,
KING RICHARD II: And then be gone and trouble you no more.
KING RICHARD II: Shall I obtain it?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Name it, fair cousin.
KING RICHARD II: 'Fair cousin'? I am greater than a king:
KING RICHARD II: For when I was a king, my flatterers
KING RICHARD II: Were then but subjects, being now a subject,
KING RICHARD II: I have a king here to my flatterer.
KING RICHARD II: Being so great, I have no need to beg.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Yet ask.
KING RICHARD II: And shall I have?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: You shall.
KING RICHARD II: Then give me leave to go.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Whither?
KING RICHARD II: Whither you will, so I were from your sights.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Go, some of you convey him to the Tower.
KING RICHARD II: O, good! convey? conveyers are you all,
KING RICHARD II: That rise thus nimbly by a true king's fall.
NARRATOR: Exeunt KING RICHARD II, some Lords, and a Guard
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: On Wednesday next we solemnly set down
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Our coronation: lords, prepare yourselves.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all except the BISHOP OF CARLISLE, the Abbot of Westminster, and DUKE OF AUMERLE
Abbot: A woeful pageant have we here beheld.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: The woe's to come, the children yet unborn.
BISHOP OF CARLISLE: Shall feel this day as sharp to them as thorn.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: You holy clergymen, is there no plot
DUKE OF AUMERLE: To rid the realm of this pernicious blot?
Abbot: My lord,
Abbot: Before I freely speak my mind herein,
Abbot: You shall not only take the sacrament
Abbot: To bury mine intents, but also to effect
Abbot: Whatever I shall happen to devise.
Abbot: I see your brows are full of discontent,
Abbot: Your hearts of sorrow and your eyes of tears:
Abbot: Come home with me to supper, and I'll lay
Abbot: A plot shall show us all a merry day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. A street leading to the Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN and Ladies
QUEEN: This way the king will come, this is the way
QUEEN: To Julius Caesar's ill-erected tower,
QUEEN: To whose flint bosom my condemned lord
QUEEN: Is doom'd a prisoner by proud Bolingbroke:
QUEEN: Here let us rest, if this rebellious earth
QUEEN: Have any resting for her true king's queen.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD II and Guard
QUEEN: But soft, but see, or rather do not see,
QUEEN: My fair rose wither: yet look up, behold,
QUEEN: That you in pity may dissolve to dew,
QUEEN: And wash him fresh again with true-love tears.
QUEEN: Ah, thou, the model where old Troy did stand,
QUEEN: Thou map of honour, thou King Richard's tomb,
QUEEN: And not King Richard, thou most beauteous inn,
QUEEN: Why should hard-favour'd grief be lodged in thee,
QUEEN: When triumph is become an alehouse guest?
KING RICHARD II: Join not with grief, fair woman, do not so,
KING RICHARD II: To make my end too sudden: learn, good soul,
KING RICHARD II: To think our former state a happy dream,
KING RICHARD II: From which awaked, the truth of what we are
KING RICHARD II: Shows us but this: I am sworn brother, sweet,
KING RICHARD II: To grim Necessity, and he and I
KING RICHARD II: Will keep a league till death. Hie thee to France
KING RICHARD II: And cloister thee in some religious house:
KING RICHARD II: Our holy lives must win a new world's crown,
KING RICHARD II: Which our profane hours here have stricken down.
QUEEN: What, is my Richard both in shape and mind
QUEEN: Transform'd and weaken'd? hath Bolingbroke deposed
QUEEN: Thine intellect? hath he been in thy heart?
QUEEN: The lion dying thrusteth forth his paw,
QUEEN: And wounds the earth, if nothing else, with rage
QUEEN: To be o'erpower'd, and wilt thou, pupil-like,
QUEEN: Take thy correction mildly, kiss the rod,
QUEEN: And fawn on rage with base humility,
QUEEN: Which art a lion and a king of beasts?
KING RICHARD II: A king of beasts, indeed, if aught but beasts,
KING RICHARD II: I had been still a happy king of men.
KING RICHARD II: Good sometime queen, prepare thee hence for France:
KING RICHARD II: Think I am dead and that even here thou takest,
KING RICHARD II: As from my death-bed, thy last living leave.
KING RICHARD II: In winter's tedious nights sit by the fire
KING RICHARD II: With good old folks and let them tell thee tales
KING RICHARD II: Of woeful ages long ago betid,
KING RICHARD II: And ere thou bid good night, to quit their griefs,
KING RICHARD II: Tell thou the lamentable tale of me
KING RICHARD II: And send the hearers weeping to their beds:
KING RICHARD II: For why, the senseless brands will sympathize
KING RICHARD II: The heavy accent of thy moving tongue
KING RICHARD II: And in compassion weep the fire out,
KING RICHARD II: And some will mourn in ashes, some coal-black,
KING RICHARD II: For the deposing of a rightful king.
NARRATOR: Enter NORTHUMBERLAND and others
NORTHUMBERLAND: My lord, the mind of Bolingbroke is changed:
NORTHUMBERLAND: You must to Pomfret, not unto the Tower.
NORTHUMBERLAND: And, madam, there is order ta'en for you,
NORTHUMBERLAND: With all swift speed you must away to France.
KING RICHARD II: Northumberland, thou ladder wherewithal
KING RICHARD II: The mounting Bolingbroke ascends my throne,
KING RICHARD II: The time shall not be many hours of age
KING RICHARD II: More than it is ere foul sin gathering head
KING RICHARD II: Shalt break into corruption: thou shalt think,
KING RICHARD II: Though he divide the realm and give thee half,
KING RICHARD II: It is too little, helping him to all,
KING RICHARD II: And he shall think that thou, which know'st the way
KING RICHARD II: To plant unrightful kings, wilt know again,
KING RICHARD II: Being ne'er so little urged, another way
KING RICHARD II: To pluck him headlong from the usurped throne.
KING RICHARD II: The love of wicked men converts to fear,
KING RICHARD II: That fear to hate, and hate turns one or both
KING RICHARD II: To worthy danger and deserved death.
NORTHUMBERLAND: My guilt be on my head, and there an end.
NORTHUMBERLAND: Take leave and part, for you must part forthwith.
KING RICHARD II: Doubly divorced! Bad men, you violate
KING RICHARD II: A twofold marriage, 'twixt my crown and me,
KING RICHARD II: And then betwixt me and my married wife.
KING RICHARD II: Let me unkiss the oath 'twixt thee and me,
KING RICHARD II: And yet not so, for with a kiss 'twas made.
KING RICHARD II: Part us, Northumberland, I toward the north,
KING RICHARD II: Where shivering cold and sickness pines the clime,
KING RICHARD II: My wife to France: from whence, set forth in pomp,
KING RICHARD II: She came adorned hither like sweet May,
KING RICHARD II: Sent back like Hallowmas or short'st of day.
QUEEN: And must we be divided? must we part?
KING RICHARD II: Ay, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
QUEEN: Banish us both and send the king with me.
NORTHUMBERLAND: That were some love but little policy.
QUEEN: Then whither he goes, thither let me go.
KING RICHARD II: So two, together weeping, make one woe.
KING RICHARD II: Weep thou for me in France, I for thee here,
KING RICHARD II: Better far off than near, be ne'er the near.
KING RICHARD II: Go, count thy way with sighs, I mine with groans.
QUEEN: So longest way shall have the longest moans.
KING RICHARD II: Twice for one step I'll groan, the way being short,
KING RICHARD II: And piece the way out with a heavy heart.
KING RICHARD II: Come, come, in wooing sorrow let's be brief,
KING RICHARD II: Since, wedding it, there is such length in grief,
KING RICHARD II: One kiss shall stop our mouths, and dumbly part,
KING RICHARD II: Thus give I mine, and thus take I thy heart.
QUEEN: Give me mine own again, 'twere no good part
QUEEN: To take on me to keep and kill thy heart.
QUEEN: So, now I have mine own again, be gone,
QUEEN: That I might strive to kill it with a groan.
KING RICHARD II: We make woe wanton with this fond delay:
KING RICHARD II: Once more, adieu, the rest let sorrow say.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The DUKE OF YORK's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF YORK and DUCHESS OF YORK
DUCHESS OF YORK: My lord, you told me you would tell the rest,
DUCHESS OF YORK: When weeping made you break the story off,
DUCHESS OF YORK: of our two cousins coming into London.
DUKE OF YORK: Where did I leave?
DUCHESS OF YORK: At that sad stop, my lord,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Where rude misgovern'd hands from windows' tops
DUCHESS OF YORK: Threw dust and rubbish on King Richard's head.
DUKE OF YORK: Then, as I said, the duke, great Bolingbroke,
DUKE OF YORK: Mounted upon a hot and fiery steed
DUKE OF YORK: Which his aspiring rider seem'd to know,
DUKE OF YORK: With slow but stately pace kept on his course,
DUKE OF YORK: Whilst all tongues cried 'God save thee,
DUKE OF YORK: Bolingbroke!'
DUKE OF YORK: You would have thought the very windows spake,
DUKE OF YORK: So many greedy looks of young and old
DUKE OF YORK: Through casements darted their desiring eyes
DUKE OF YORK: Upon his visage, and that all the walls
DUKE OF YORK: With painted imagery had said at once
DUKE OF YORK: 'Jesu preserve thee! welcome, Bolingbroke!'
DUKE OF YORK: Whilst he, from the one side to the other turning,
DUKE OF YORK: Bareheaded, lower than his proud steed's neck,
DUKE OF YORK: Bespake them thus: 'I thank you, countrymen:'
DUKE OF YORK: And thus still doing, thus he pass'd along.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Alack, poor Richard! where rode he the whilst?
DUKE OF YORK: As in a theatre, the eyes of men,
DUKE OF YORK: After a well-graced actor leaves the stage,
DUKE OF YORK: Are idly bent on him that enters next,
DUKE OF YORK: Thinking his prattle to be tedious,
DUKE OF YORK: Even so, or with much more contempt, men's eyes
DUKE OF YORK: Did scowl on gentle Richard, no man cried 'God save him!'
DUKE OF YORK: No joyful tongue gave him his welcome home:
DUKE OF YORK: But dust was thrown upon his sacred head:
DUKE OF YORK: Which with such gentle sorrow he shook off,
DUKE OF YORK: His face still combating with tears and smiles,
DUKE OF YORK: The badges of his grief and patience,
DUKE OF YORK: That had not God, for some strong purpose, steel'd
DUKE OF YORK: The hearts of men, they must perforce have melted
DUKE OF YORK: And barbarism itself have pitied him.
DUKE OF YORK: But heaven hath a hand in these events,
DUKE OF YORK: To whose high will we bound our calm contents.
DUKE OF YORK: To Bolingbroke are we sworn subjects now,
DUKE OF YORK: Whose state and honour I for aye allow.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Here comes my son Aumerle.
DUKE OF YORK: Aumerle that was,
DUKE OF YORK: But that is lost for being Richard's friend,
DUKE OF YORK: And, madam, you must call him Rutland now:
DUKE OF YORK: I am in parliament pledge for his truth
DUKE OF YORK: And lasting fealty to the new-made king.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF AUMERLE
DUCHESS OF YORK: Welcome, my son: who are the violets now
DUCHESS OF YORK: That strew the green lap of the new come spring?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Madam, I know not, nor I greatly care not:
DUKE OF AUMERLE: God knows I had as lief be none as one.
DUKE OF YORK: Well, bear you well in this new spring of time,
DUKE OF YORK: Lest you be cropp'd before you come to prime.
DUKE OF YORK: What news from Oxford? hold those justs and triumphs?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: For aught I know, my lord, they do.
DUKE OF YORK: You will be there, I know.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: If God prevent not, I purpose so.
DUKE OF YORK: What seal is that, that hangs without thy bosom?
DUKE OF YORK: Yea, look'st thou pale? let me see the writing.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: My lord, 'tis nothing.
DUKE OF YORK: No matter, then, who see it,
DUKE OF YORK: I will be satisfied, let me see the writing.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: I do beseech your grace to pardon me:
DUKE OF AUMERLE: It is a matter of small consequence,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Which for some reasons I would not have seen.
DUKE OF YORK: Which for some reasons, sir, I mean to see.
DUKE OF YORK: I fear, I fear,--
DUCHESS OF YORK: What should you fear?
DUCHESS OF YORK: 'Tis nothing but some bond, that he is enter'd into
DUCHESS OF YORK: For gay apparel 'gainst the triumph day.
DUKE OF YORK: Bound to himself! what doth he with a bond
DUKE OF YORK: That he is bound to? Wife, thou art a fool.
DUKE OF YORK: Boy, let me see the writing.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: I do beseech you, pardon me, I may not show it.
DUKE OF YORK: I will be satisfied, let me see it, I say.
NARRATOR: He plucks it out of his bosom and reads it
DUKE OF YORK: Treason! foul treason! Villain! traitor! slave!
DUCHESS OF YORK: What is the matter, my lord?
DUKE OF YORK: Ho! who is within there?
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
DUKE OF YORK: Saddle my horse.
DUKE OF YORK: God for his mercy, what treachery is here!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Why, what is it, my lord?
DUKE OF YORK: Give me my boots, I say, saddle my horse.
DUKE OF YORK: Now, by mine honour, by my life, by my troth,
DUKE OF YORK: I will appeach the villain.
DUCHESS OF YORK: What is the matter?
DUKE OF YORK: Peace, foolish woman.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I will not peace. What is the matter, Aumerle.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Good mother, be content, it is no more
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Than my poor life must answer.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Thy life answer!
DUKE OF YORK: Bring me my boots: I will unto the king.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servant with boots
DUCHESS OF YORK: Strike him, Aumerle. Poor boy, thou art amazed.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Hence, villain! never more come in my sight.
DUKE OF YORK: Give me my boots, I say.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Why, York, what wilt thou do?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Wilt thou not hide the trespass of thine own?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Have we more sons? or are we like to have?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Is not my teeming date drunk up with time?
DUCHESS OF YORK: And wilt thou pluck my fair son from mine age,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And rob me of a happy mother's name?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Is he not like thee? is he not thine own?
DUKE OF YORK: Thou fond mad woman,
DUKE OF YORK: Wilt thou conceal this dark conspiracy?
DUKE OF YORK: A dozen of them here have ta'en the sacrament,
DUKE OF YORK: And interchangeably set down their hands,
DUKE OF YORK: To kill the king at Oxford.
DUCHESS OF YORK: He shall be none,
DUCHESS OF YORK: We'll keep him here: then what is that to him?
DUKE OF YORK: Away, fond woman! were he twenty times my son,
DUKE OF YORK: I would appeach him.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Hadst thou groan'd for him
DUCHESS OF YORK: As I have done, thou wouldst be more pitiful.
DUCHESS OF YORK: But now I know thy mind, thou dost suspect
DUCHESS OF YORK: That I have been disloyal to thy bed,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And that he is a bastard, not thy son:
DUCHESS OF YORK: Sweet York, sweet husband, be not of that mind:
DUCHESS OF YORK: He is as like thee as a man may be,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Not like to me, or any of my kin,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And yet I love him.
DUKE OF YORK: Make way, unruly woman!
NARRATOR: Exit
DUCHESS OF YORK: After, Aumerle! mount thee upon his horse,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Spur post, and get before him to the king,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And beg thy pardon ere he do accuse thee.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I'll not be long behind, though I be old,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I doubt not but to ride as fast as York:
DUCHESS OF YORK: And never will I rise up from the ground
DUCHESS OF YORK: Till Bolingbroke have pardon'd thee. Away, be gone!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A royal palace.
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE, HENRY PERCY, and other Lords
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Can no man tell me of my unthrifty son?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: 'Tis full three months since I did see him last,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: If any plague hang over us, 'tis he.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I would to God, my lords, he might be found:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Inquire at London, 'mongst the taverns there,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For there, they say, he daily doth frequent,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With unrestrained loose companions,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Even such, they say, as stand in narrow lanes,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And beat our watch, and rob our passengers,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Which he, young wanton and effeminate boy,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Takes on the point of honour to support
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: So dissolute a crew.
HENRY PERCY: My lord, some two days since I saw the prince,
HENRY PERCY: And told him of those triumphs held at Oxford.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And what said the gallant?
HENRY PERCY: His answer was, he would unto the stews,
HENRY PERCY: And from the common'st creature pluck a glove,
HENRY PERCY: And wear it as a favour, and with that
HENRY PERCY: He would unhorse the lustiest challenger.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: As dissolute as desperate, yet through both
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I see some sparks of better hope, which elder years
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: May happily bring forth. But who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF AUMERLE
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Where is the king?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What means our cousin, that he stares and looks
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: So wildly?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: God save your grace! I do beseech your majesty,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: To have some conference with your grace alone.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Withdraw yourselves, and leave us here alone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt HENRY PERCY and Lords
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What is the matter with our cousin now?
DUKE OF AUMERLE: For ever may my knees grow to the earth,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: My tongue cleave to my roof within my mouth
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Unless a pardon ere I rise or speak.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Intended or committed was this fault?
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: If on the first, how heinous e'er it be,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To win thy after-love I pardon thee.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Then give me leave that I may turn the key,
DUKE OF AUMERLE: That no man enter till my tale be done.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Have thy desire.
DUKE OF YORK: [Within]  My liege, beware, look to thyself,
DUKE OF YORK: Thou hast a traitor in thy presence there.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Villain, I'll make thee safe.
NARRATOR: Drawing
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Stay thy revengeful hand, thou hast no cause to fear.
DUKE OF YORK: [Within]  Open the door, secure, foolhardy king:
DUKE OF YORK: Shall I for love speak treason to thy face?
DUKE OF YORK: Open the door, or I will break it open.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE OF YORK
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What is the matter, uncle? speak,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Recover breath, tell us how near is danger,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That we may arm us to encounter it.
DUKE OF YORK: Peruse this writing here, and thou shalt know
DUKE OF YORK: The treason that my haste forbids me show.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Remember, as thou read'st, thy promise pass'd:
DUKE OF AUMERLE: I do repent me, read not my name there
DUKE OF AUMERLE: My heart is not confederate with my hand.
DUKE OF YORK: It was, villain, ere thy hand did set it down.
DUKE OF YORK: I tore it from the traitor's bosom, king,
DUKE OF YORK: Fear, and not love, begets his penitence:
DUKE OF YORK: Forget to pity him, lest thy pity prove
DUKE OF YORK: A serpent that will sting thee to the heart.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O heinous, strong and bold conspiracy!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: O loyal father of a treacherous son!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Thou sheer, immaculate and silver fountain,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: From when this stream through muddy passages
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Hath held his current and defiled himself!
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Thy overflow of good converts to bad,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And thy abundant goodness shall excuse
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: This deadly blot in thy digressing son.
DUKE OF YORK: So shall my virtue be his vice's bawd,
DUKE OF YORK: And he shall spend mine honour with his shame,
DUKE OF YORK: As thriftless sons their scraping fathers' gold.
DUKE OF YORK: Mine honour lives when his dishonour dies,
DUKE OF YORK: Or my shamed life in his dishonour lies:
DUKE OF YORK: Thou kill'st me in his life, giving him breath,
DUKE OF YORK: The traitor lives, the true man's put to death.
DUCHESS OF YORK: [Within]  What ho, my liege! for God's sake,
DUCHESS OF YORK: let me in.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: What shrill-voiced suppliant makes this eager cry?
DUCHESS OF YORK: A woman, and thy aunt, great king, 'tis I.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Speak with me, pity me, open the door.
DUCHESS OF YORK: A beggar begs that never begg'd before.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Our scene is alter'd from a serious thing,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And now changed to 'The Beggar and the King.'
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: My dangerous cousin, let your mother in:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I know she is come to pray for your foul sin.
DUKE OF YORK: If thou do pardon, whosoever pray,
DUKE OF YORK: More sins for this forgiveness prosper may.
DUKE OF YORK: This fester'd joint cut off, the rest rest sound,
DUKE OF YORK: This let alone will all the rest confound.
NARRATOR: Enter DUCHESS OF YORK
DUCHESS OF YORK: O king, believe not this hard-hearted man!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Love loving not itself none other can.
DUKE OF YORK: Thou frantic woman, what dost thou make here?
DUKE OF YORK: Shall thy old dugs once more a traitor rear?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Sweet York, be patient. Hear me, gentle liege.
NARRATOR: Kneels
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Rise up, good aunt.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Not yet, I thee beseech:
DUCHESS OF YORK: For ever will I walk upon my knees,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And never see day that the happy sees,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Till thou give joy, until thou bid me joy,
DUCHESS OF YORK: By pardoning Rutland, my transgressing boy.
DUKE OF AUMERLE: Unto my mother's prayers I bend my knee.
DUKE OF YORK: Against them both my true joints bended be.
DUKE OF YORK: Ill mayst thou thrive, if thou grant any grace!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Pleads he in earnest? look upon his face,
DUCHESS OF YORK: His eyes do drop no tears, his prayers are in jest,
DUCHESS OF YORK: His words come from his mouth, ours from our breast:
DUCHESS OF YORK: He prays but faintly and would be denied,
DUCHESS OF YORK: We pray with heart and soul and all beside:
DUCHESS OF YORK: His weary joints would gladly rise, I know,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Our knees shall kneel till to the ground they grow:
DUCHESS OF YORK: His prayers are full of false hypocrisy,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Ours of true zeal and deep integrity.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Our prayers do out-pray his, then let them have
DUCHESS OF YORK: That mercy which true prayer ought to have.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Good aunt, stand up.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Nay, do not say, 'stand up,'
DUCHESS OF YORK: Say, 'pardon' first, and afterwards 'stand up.'
DUCHESS OF YORK: And if I were thy nurse, thy tongue to teach,
DUCHESS OF YORK: 'Pardon' should be the first word of thy speech.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I never long'd to hear a word till now,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Say 'pardon,' king, let pity teach thee how:
DUCHESS OF YORK: The word is short, but not so short as sweet,
DUCHESS OF YORK: No word like 'pardon' for kings' mouths so meet.
DUKE OF YORK: Speak it in French, king, say, 'pardonne moi.'
DUCHESS OF YORK: Dost thou teach pardon pardon to destroy?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Ah, my sour husband, my hard-hearted lord,
DUCHESS OF YORK: That set'st the word itself against the word!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Speak 'pardon' as 'tis current in our land,
DUCHESS OF YORK: The chopping French we do not understand.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Thine eye begins to speak, set thy tongue there,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Or in thy piteous heart plant thou thine ear,
DUCHESS OF YORK: That hearing how our plaints and prayers do pierce,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Pity may move thee 'pardon' to rehearse.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Good aunt, stand up.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I do not sue to stand,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Pardon is all the suit I have in hand.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I pardon him, as God shall pardon me.
DUCHESS OF YORK: O happy vantage of a kneeling knee!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Yet am I sick for fear: speak it again,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Twice saying 'pardon' doth not pardon twain,
DUCHESS OF YORK: But makes one pardon strong.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With all my heart
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I pardon him.
DUCHESS OF YORK: A god on earth thou art.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But for our trusty brother-in-law and the abbot,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With all the rest of that consorted crew,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Destruction straight shall dog them at the heels.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Good uncle, help to order several powers
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To Oxford, or where'er these traitors are:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: They shall not live within this world, I swear,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But I will have them, if I once know where.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Uncle, farewell: and, cousin too, adieu:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Your mother well hath pray'd, and prove you true.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Come, my old son: I pray God make thee new.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter EXTON and Servant
EXTON: Didst thou not mark the king, what words he spake,
EXTON: 'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?'
EXTON: Was it not so?
Servant: These were his very words.
EXTON: 'Have I no friend?' quoth he: he spake it twice,
EXTON: And urged it twice together, did he not?
Servant: He did.
EXTON: And speaking it, he wistly look'd on me,
EXTON: And who should say, 'I would thou wert the man'
EXTON: That would divorce this terror from my heart,'
EXTON: Meaning the king at Pomfret. Come, let's go:
EXTON: I am the king's friend, and will rid his foe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Pomfret castle.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD
KING RICHARD II: I have been studying how I may compare
KING RICHARD II: This prison where I live unto the world:
KING RICHARD II: And for because the world is populous
KING RICHARD II: And here is not a creature but myself,
KING RICHARD II: I cannot do it, yet I'll hammer it out.
KING RICHARD II: My brain I'll prove the female to my soul,
KING RICHARD II: My soul the father, and these two beget
KING RICHARD II: A generation of still-breeding thoughts,
KING RICHARD II: And these same thoughts people this little world,
KING RICHARD II: In humours like the people of this world,
KING RICHARD II: For no thought is contented. The better sort,
KING RICHARD II: As thoughts of things divine, are intermix'd
KING RICHARD II: With scruples and do set the word itself
KING RICHARD II: Against the word:
KING RICHARD II: As thus, 'Come, little ones,' and then again,
KING RICHARD II: 'It is as hard to come as for a camel
KING RICHARD II: To thread the postern of a small needle's eye.'
KING RICHARD II: Thoughts tending to ambition, they do plot
KING RICHARD II: Unlikely wonders, how these vain weak nails
KING RICHARD II: May tear a passage through the flinty ribs
KING RICHARD II: Of this hard world, my ragged prison walls,
KING RICHARD II: And, for they cannot, die in their own pride.
KING RICHARD II: Thoughts tending to content flatter themselves
KING RICHARD II: That they are not the first of fortune's slaves,
KING RICHARD II: Nor shall not be the last, like silly beggars
KING RICHARD II: Who sitting in the stocks refuge their shame,
KING RICHARD II: That many have and others must sit there,
KING RICHARD II: And in this thought they find a kind of ease,
KING RICHARD II: Bearing their own misfortunes on the back
KING RICHARD II: Of such as have before endured the like.
KING RICHARD II: Thus play I in one person many people,
KING RICHARD II: And none contented: sometimes am I king,
KING RICHARD II: Then treasons make me wish myself a beggar,
KING RICHARD II: And so I am: then crushing penury
KING RICHARD II: Persuades me I was better when a king,
KING RICHARD II: Then am I king'd again: and by and by
KING RICHARD II: Think that I am unking'd by Bolingbroke,
KING RICHARD II: And straight am nothing: but whate'er I be,
KING RICHARD II: Nor I nor any man that but man is
KING RICHARD II: With nothing shall be pleased, till he be eased
KING RICHARD II: With being nothing. Music do I hear?
NARRATOR: Music
KING RICHARD II: Ha, ha! keep time: how sour sweet music is,
KING RICHARD II: When time is broke and no proportion kept!
KING RICHARD II: So is it in the music of men's lives.
KING RICHARD II: And here have I the daintiness of ear
KING RICHARD II: To cheque time broke in a disorder'd string,
KING RICHARD II: But for the concord of my state and time
KING RICHARD II: Had not an ear to hear my true time broke.
KING RICHARD II: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me,
KING RICHARD II: For now hath time made me his numbering clock:
KING RICHARD II: My thoughts are minutes, and with sighs they jar
KING RICHARD II: Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch,
KING RICHARD II: Whereto my finger, like a dial's point,
KING RICHARD II: Is pointing still, in cleansing them from tears.
KING RICHARD II: Now sir, the sound that tells what hour it is
KING RICHARD II: Are clamorous groans, which strike upon my heart,
KING RICHARD II: Which is the bell: so sighs and tears and groans
KING RICHARD II: Show minutes, times, and hours: but my time
KING RICHARD II: Runs posting on in Bolingbroke's proud joy,
KING RICHARD II: While I stand fooling here, his Jack o' the clock.
KING RICHARD II: This music mads me, let it sound no more,
KING RICHARD II: For though it have holp madmen to their wits,
KING RICHARD II: In me it seems it will make wise men mad.
KING RICHARD II: Yet blessing on his heart that gives it me!
KING RICHARD II: For 'tis a sign of love, and love to Richard
