KING RICHARD II: Is a strange brooch in this all-hating world.
NARRATOR: Enter a Groom of the Stable
Groom: Hail, royal prince!
KING RICHARD II: Thanks, noble peer,
KING RICHARD II: The cheapest of us is ten groats too dear.
KING RICHARD II: What art thou? and how comest thou hither,
KING RICHARD II: Where no man never comes but that sad dog
KING RICHARD II: That brings me food to make misfortune live?
Groom: I was a poor groom of thy stable, king,
Groom: When thou wert king, who, travelling towards York,
Groom: With much ado at length have gotten leave
Groom: To look upon my sometimes royal master's face.
Groom: O, how it yearn'd my heart when I beheld
Groom: In London streets, that coronation-day,
Groom: When Bolingbroke rode on roan Barbary,
Groom: That horse that thou so often hast bestrid,
Groom: That horse that I so carefully have dress'd!
KING RICHARD II: Rode he on Barbary? Tell me, gentle friend,
KING RICHARD II: How went he under him?
Groom: So proudly as if he disdain'd the ground.
KING RICHARD II: So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back!
KING RICHARD II: That jade hath eat bread from my royal hand,
KING RICHARD II: This hand hath made him proud with clapping him.
KING RICHARD II: Would he not stumble? would he not fall down,
KING RICHARD II: Since pride must have a fall, and break the neck
KING RICHARD II: Of that proud man that did usurp his back?
KING RICHARD II: Forgiveness, horse! why do I rail on thee,
KING RICHARD II: Since thou, created to be awed by man,
KING RICHARD II: Wast born to bear? I was not made a horse,
KING RICHARD II: And yet I bear a burthen like an ass,
KING RICHARD II: Spurr'd, gall'd and tired by jouncing Bolingbroke.
NARRATOR: Enter Keeper, with a dish
Keeper: Fellow, give place, here is no longer stay.
KING RICHARD II: If thou love me, 'tis time thou wert away.
Groom: What my tongue dares not, that my heart shall say.
NARRATOR: Exit
Keeper: My lord, will't please you to fall to?
KING RICHARD II: Taste of it first, as thou art wont to do.
Keeper: My lord, I dare not: Sir Pierce of Exton, who
Keeper: lately came from the king, commands the contrary.
KING RICHARD II: The devil take Henry of Lancaster and thee!
KING RICHARD II: Patience is stale, and I am weary of it.
NARRATOR: Beats the keeper
Keeper: Help, help, help!
NARRATOR: Enter EXTON and Servants, armed
KING RICHARD II: How now! what means death in this rude assault?
KING RICHARD II: Villain, thy own hand yields thy death's instrument.
NARRATOR: Snatching an axe from a Servant and killing him
KING RICHARD II: Go thou, and fill another room in hell.
NARRATOR: He kills another. Then Exton strikes him down
KING RICHARD II: That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire
KING RICHARD II: That staggers thus my person. Exton, thy fierce hand
KING RICHARD II: Hath with the king's blood stain'd the king's own land.
KING RICHARD II: Mount, mount, my soul! thy seat is up on high,
KING RICHARD II: Whilst my gross flesh sinks downward, here to die.
NARRATOR: Dies
EXTON: As full of valour as of royal blood:
EXTON: Both have I spill'd, O would the deed were good!
EXTON: For now the devil, that told me I did well,
EXTON: Says that this deed is chronicled in hell.
EXTON: This dead king to the living king I'll bear
EXTON: Take hence the rest, and give them burial here.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Windsor castle.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter HENRY BOLINGBROKE, DUKE OF YORK, with other Lords, and Attendants
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Kind uncle York, the latest news we hear
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Is that the rebels have consumed with fire
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Our town of Cicester in Gloucestershire,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But whether they be ta'en or slain we hear not.
NARRATOR: Enter NORTHUMBERLAND
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Welcome, my lord	what is the news?
NORTHUMBERLAND: First, to thy sacred state wish I all happiness.
NORTHUMBERLAND: The next news is, I have to London sent
NORTHUMBERLAND: The heads of Oxford, Salisbury, Blunt, and Kent:
NORTHUMBERLAND: The manner of their taking may appear
NORTHUMBERLAND: At large discoursed in this paper here.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: We thank thee, gentle Percy, for thy pains,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And to thy worth will add right worthy gains.
NARRATOR: Enter LORD FITZWATER
LORD FITZWATER: My lord, I have from Oxford sent to London
LORD FITZWATER: The heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely,
LORD FITZWATER: Two of the dangerous consorted traitors
LORD FITZWATER: That sought at Oxford thy dire overthrow.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Thy pains, Fitzwater, shall not be forgot,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Right noble is thy merit, well I wot.
NARRATOR: Enter HENRY PERCY, and the BISHOP OF CARLISLE
HENRY PERCY: The grand conspirator, Abbot of Westminster,
HENRY PERCY: With clog of conscience and sour melancholy
HENRY PERCY: Hath yielded up his body to the grave,
HENRY PERCY: But here is Carlisle living, to abide
HENRY PERCY: Thy kingly doom and sentence of his pride.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Carlisle, this is your doom:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Choose out some secret place, some reverend room,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: More than thou hast, and with it joy thy life,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: So as thou livest in peace, die free from strife:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: For though mine enemy thou hast ever been,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: High sparks of honour in thee have I seen.
NARRATOR: Enter EXTON, with persons bearing a coffin
EXTON: Great king, within this coffin I present
EXTON: Thy buried fear: herein all breathless lies
EXTON: The mightiest of thy greatest enemies,
EXTON: Richard of Bordeaux, by me hither brought.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Exton, I thank thee not, for thou hast wrought
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: A deed of slander with thy fatal hand
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Upon my head and all this famous land.
EXTON: From your own mouth, my lord, did I this deed.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: They love not poison that do poison need,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Nor do I thee: though I did wish him dead,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I hate the murderer, love him murdered.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: The guilt of conscience take thou for thy labour,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: But neither my good word nor princely favour:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: With Cain go wander through shades of night,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And never show thy head by day nor light.
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Lords, I protest, my soul is full of woe,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: That blood should sprinkle me to make me grow:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: Come, mourn with me for that I do lament,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: And put on sullen black incontinent:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: To wash this blood off from my guilty hand:
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: March sadly after, grace my mournings here,
HENRY BOLINGBROKE: In weeping after this untimely bier.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Richard III '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, solus
GLOUCESTER: Now is the winter of our discontent
GLOUCESTER: Made glorious summer by this sun of York,
GLOUCESTER: And all the clouds that lour'd upon our house
GLOUCESTER: In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
GLOUCESTER: Now are our brows bound with victorious wreaths,
GLOUCESTER: Our bruised arms hung up for monuments,
GLOUCESTER: Our stern alarums changed to merry meetings,
GLOUCESTER: Our dreadful marches to delightful measures.
GLOUCESTER: Grim-visaged war hath smooth'd his wrinkled front,
GLOUCESTER: And now, instead of mounting barded steeds
GLOUCESTER: To fright the souls of fearful adversaries,
GLOUCESTER: He capers nimbly in a lady's chamber
GLOUCESTER: To the lascivious pleasing of a lute.
GLOUCESTER: But I, that am not shaped for sportive tricks,
GLOUCESTER: Nor made to court an amorous looking-glass,
GLOUCESTER: I, that am rudely stamp'd, and want love's majesty
GLOUCESTER: To strut before a wanton ambling nymph,
GLOUCESTER: I, that am curtail'd of this fair proportion,
GLOUCESTER: Cheated of feature by dissembling nature,
GLOUCESTER: Deformed, unfinish'd, sent before my time
GLOUCESTER: Into this breathing world, scarce half made up,
GLOUCESTER: And that so lamely and unfashionable
GLOUCESTER: That dogs bark at me as I halt by them,
GLOUCESTER: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace,
GLOUCESTER: Have no delight to pass away the time,
GLOUCESTER: Unless to spy my shadow in the sun
GLOUCESTER: And descant on mine own deformity:
GLOUCESTER: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover,
GLOUCESTER: To entertain these fair well-spoken days,
GLOUCESTER: I am determined to prove a villain
GLOUCESTER: And hate the idle pleasures of these days.
GLOUCESTER: Plots have I laid, inductions dangerous,
GLOUCESTER: By drunken prophecies, libels and dreams,
GLOUCESTER: To set my brother Clarence and the king
GLOUCESTER: In deadly hate the one against the other:
GLOUCESTER: And if King Edward be as true and just
GLOUCESTER: As I am subtle, false and treacherous,
GLOUCESTER: This day should Clarence closely be mew'd up,
GLOUCESTER: About a prophecy, which says that 'G'
GLOUCESTER: Of Edward's heirs the murderer shall be.
GLOUCESTER: Dive, thoughts, down to my soul: here
GLOUCESTER: Clarence comes.
NARRATOR: Enter CLARENCE, guarded, and BRAKENBURY
GLOUCESTER: Brother, good day, what means this armed guard
GLOUCESTER: That waits upon your grace?
CLARENCE: His majesty
CLARENCE: Tendering my person's safety, hath appointed
CLARENCE: This conduct to convey me to the Tower.
GLOUCESTER: Upon what cause?
CLARENCE: Because my name is George.
GLOUCESTER: Alack, my lord, that fault is none of yours,
GLOUCESTER: He should, for that, commit your godfathers:
GLOUCESTER: O, belike his majesty hath some intent
GLOUCESTER: That you shall be new-christen'd in the Tower.
GLOUCESTER: But what's the matter, Clarence?  may I know?
CLARENCE: Yea, Richard, when I know, for I protest
CLARENCE: As yet I do not: but, as I can learn,
CLARENCE: He hearkens after prophecies and dreams,
CLARENCE: And from the cross-row plucks the letter G.
CLARENCE: And says a wizard told him that by G
CLARENCE: His issue disinherited should be,
CLARENCE: And, for my name of George begins with G,
CLARENCE: It follows in his thought that I am he.
CLARENCE: These, as I learn, and such like toys as these
CLARENCE: Have moved his highness to commit me now.
GLOUCESTER: Why, this it is, when men are ruled by women:
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis not the king that sends you to the Tower:
GLOUCESTER: My Lady Grey his wife, Clarence, 'tis she
GLOUCESTER: That tempers him to this extremity.
GLOUCESTER: Was it not she and that good man of worship,
GLOUCESTER: Anthony Woodville, her brother there,
GLOUCESTER: That made him send Lord Hastings to the Tower,
GLOUCESTER: From whence this present day he is deliver'd?
GLOUCESTER: We are not safe, Clarence, we are not safe.
CLARENCE: By heaven, I think there's no man is secure
CLARENCE: But the queen's kindred and night-walking heralds
CLARENCE: That trudge betwixt the king and Mistress Shore.
CLARENCE: Heard ye not what an humble suppliant
CLARENCE: Lord hastings was to her for his delivery?
GLOUCESTER: Humbly complaining to her deity
GLOUCESTER: Got my lord chamberlain his liberty.
GLOUCESTER: I'll tell you what, I think it is our way,
GLOUCESTER: If we will keep in favour with the king,
GLOUCESTER: To be her men and wear her livery:
GLOUCESTER: The jealous o'erworn widow and herself,
GLOUCESTER: Since that our brother dubb'd them gentlewomen.
GLOUCESTER: Are mighty gossips in this monarchy.
BRAKENBURY: I beseech your graces both to pardon me,
BRAKENBURY: His majesty hath straitly given in charge
BRAKENBURY: That no man shall have private conference,
BRAKENBURY: Of what degree soever, with his brother.
GLOUCESTER: Even so, an't please your worship, Brakenbury,
GLOUCESTER: You may partake of any thing we say:
GLOUCESTER: We speak no treason, man: we say the king
GLOUCESTER: Is wise and virtuous, and his noble queen
GLOUCESTER: Well struck in years, fair, and not jealous,
GLOUCESTER: We say that Shore's wife hath a pretty foot,
GLOUCESTER: A cherry lip, a bonny eye, a passing pleasing tongue,
GLOUCESTER: And that the queen's kindred are made gentle-folks:
GLOUCESTER: How say you sir? Can you deny all this?
BRAKENBURY: With this, my lord, myself have nought to do.
GLOUCESTER: Naught to do with mistress Shore! I tell thee, fellow,
GLOUCESTER: He that doth naught with her, excepting one,
GLOUCESTER: Were best he do it secretly, alone.
BRAKENBURY: What one, my lord?
GLOUCESTER: Her husband, knave: wouldst thou betray me?
BRAKENBURY: I beseech your grace to pardon me, and withal
BRAKENBURY: Forbear your conference with the noble duke.
CLARENCE: We know thy charge, Brakenbury, and will obey.
GLOUCESTER: We are the queen's abjects, and must obey.
GLOUCESTER: Brother, farewell: I will unto the king,
GLOUCESTER: And whatsoever you will employ me in,
GLOUCESTER: Were it to call King Edward's widow sister,
GLOUCESTER: I will perform it to enfranchise you.
GLOUCESTER: Meantime, this deep disgrace in brotherhood
GLOUCESTER: Touches me deeper than you can imagine.
CLARENCE: I know it pleaseth neither of us well.
GLOUCESTER: Well, your imprisonment shall not be long,
GLOUCESTER: Meantime, have patience.
CLARENCE: I must perforce. Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CLARENCE, BRAKENBURY, and Guard
GLOUCESTER: Go, tread the path that thou shalt ne'er return.
GLOUCESTER: Simple, plain Clarence! I do love thee so,
GLOUCESTER: That I will shortly send thy soul to heaven,
GLOUCESTER: If heaven will take the present at our hands.
GLOUCESTER: But who comes here? the new-deliver'd Hastings?
NARRATOR: Enter HASTINGS
HASTINGS: Good time of day unto my gracious lord!
GLOUCESTER: As much unto my good lord chamberlain!
GLOUCESTER: Well are you welcome to the open air.
GLOUCESTER: How hath your lordship brook'd imprisonment?
HASTINGS: With patience, noble lord, as prisoners must:
HASTINGS: But I shall live, my lord, to give them thanks
HASTINGS: That were the cause of my imprisonment.
GLOUCESTER: No doubt, no doubt, and so shall Clarence too,
GLOUCESTER: For they that were your enemies are his,
GLOUCESTER: And have prevail'd as much on him as you.
HASTINGS: More pity that the eagle should be mew'd,
HASTINGS: While kites and buzzards prey at liberty.
GLOUCESTER: What news abroad?
HASTINGS: No news so bad abroad as this at home,
HASTINGS: The King is sickly, weak and melancholy,
HASTINGS: And his physicians fear him mightily.
GLOUCESTER: Now, by Saint Paul, this news is bad indeed.
GLOUCESTER: O, he hath kept an evil diet long,
GLOUCESTER: And overmuch consumed his royal person:
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis very grievous to be thought upon.
GLOUCESTER: What, is he in his bed?
HASTINGS: He is.
GLOUCESTER: Go you before, and I will follow you.
NARRATOR: Exit HASTINGS
GLOUCESTER: He cannot live, I hope, and must not die
GLOUCESTER: Till George be pack'd with post-horse up to heaven.
GLOUCESTER: I'll in, to urge his hatred more to Clarence,
GLOUCESTER: With lies well steel'd with weighty arguments,
GLOUCESTER: And, if I fall not in my deep intent,
GLOUCESTER: Clarence hath not another day to live:
GLOUCESTER: Which done, God take King Edward to his mercy,
GLOUCESTER: And leave the world for me to bustle in!
GLOUCESTER: For then I'll marry Warwick's youngest daughter.
GLOUCESTER: What though I kill'd her husband and her father?
GLOUCESTER: The readiest way to make the wench amends
GLOUCESTER: Is to become her husband and her father:
GLOUCESTER: The which will I, not all so much for love
GLOUCESTER: As for another secret close intent,
GLOUCESTER: By marrying her which I must reach unto.
GLOUCESTER: But yet I run before my horse to market:
GLOUCESTER: Clarence still breathes, Edward still lives and reigns:
GLOUCESTER: When they are gone, then must I count my gains.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. Another street.
NARRATOR: Enter the corpse of KING HENRY the Sixth, Gentlemen with halberds to guard it, LADY ANNE being the mourner
LADY ANNE: Set down, set down your honourable load,
LADY ANNE: If honour may be shrouded in a hearse,
LADY ANNE: Whilst I awhile obsequiously lament
LADY ANNE: The untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster.
LADY ANNE: Poor key-cold figure of a holy king!
LADY ANNE: Pale ashes of the house of Lancaster!
LADY ANNE: Thou bloodless remnant of that royal blood!
LADY ANNE: Be it lawful that I invocate thy ghost,
LADY ANNE: To hear the lamentations of Poor Anne,
LADY ANNE: Wife to thy Edward, to thy slaughter'd son,
LADY ANNE: Stabb'd by the selfsame hand that made these wounds!
LADY ANNE: Lo, in these windows that let forth thy life,
LADY ANNE: I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes.
LADY ANNE: Cursed be the hand that made these fatal holes!
LADY ANNE: Cursed be the heart that had the heart to do it!
LADY ANNE: Cursed the blood that let this blood from hence!
LADY ANNE: More direful hap betide that hated wretch,
LADY ANNE: That makes us wretched by the death of thee,
LADY ANNE: Than I can wish to adders, spiders, toads,
LADY ANNE: Or any creeping venom'd thing that lives!
LADY ANNE: If ever he have child, abortive be it,
LADY ANNE: Prodigious, and untimely brought to light,
LADY ANNE: Whose ugly and unnatural aspect
LADY ANNE: May fright the hopeful mother at the view,
LADY ANNE: And that be heir to his unhappiness!
LADY ANNE: If ever he have wife, let her he made
LADY ANNE: A miserable by the death of him
LADY ANNE: As I am made by my poor lord and thee!
LADY ANNE: Come, now towards Chertsey with your holy load,
LADY ANNE: Taken from Paul's to be interred there,
LADY ANNE: And still, as you are weary of the weight,
LADY ANNE: Rest you, whiles I lament King Henry's corse.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Stay, you that bear the corse, and set it down.
LADY ANNE: What black magician conjures up this fiend,
LADY ANNE: To stop devoted charitable deeds?
GLOUCESTER: Villains, set down the corse, or, by Saint Paul,
GLOUCESTER: I'll make a corse of him that disobeys.
Gentleman: My lord, stand back, and let the coffin pass.
GLOUCESTER: Unmanner'd dog! stand thou, when I command:
GLOUCESTER: Advance thy halbert higher than my breast,
GLOUCESTER: Or, by Saint Paul, I'll strike thee to my foot,
GLOUCESTER: And spurn upon thee, beggar, for thy boldness.
LADY ANNE: What, do you tremble? are you all afraid?
LADY ANNE: Alas, I blame you not, for you are mortal,
LADY ANNE: And mortal eyes cannot endure the devil.
LADY ANNE: Avaunt, thou dreadful minister of hell!
LADY ANNE: Thou hadst but power over his mortal body,
LADY ANNE: His soul thou canst not have, therefore be gone.
GLOUCESTER: Sweet saint, for charity, be not so curst.
LADY ANNE: Foul devil, for God's sake, hence, and trouble us not,
LADY ANNE: For thou hast made the happy earth thy hell,
LADY ANNE: Fill'd it with cursing cries and deep exclaims.
LADY ANNE: If thou delight to view thy heinous deeds,
LADY ANNE: Behold this pattern of thy butcheries.
LADY ANNE: O, gentlemen, see, see! dead Henry's wounds
LADY ANNE: Open their congeal'd mouths and bleed afresh!
LADY ANNE: Blush, Blush, thou lump of foul deformity,
LADY ANNE: For 'tis thy presence that exhales this blood
LADY ANNE: From cold and empty veins, where no blood dwells,
LADY ANNE: Thy deed, inhuman and unnatural,
LADY ANNE: Provokes this deluge most unnatural.
LADY ANNE: O God, which this blood madest, revenge his death!
LADY ANNE: O earth, which this blood drink'st revenge his death!
LADY ANNE: Either heaven with lightning strike the
LADY ANNE: murderer dead,
LADY ANNE: Or earth, gape open wide and eat him quick,
LADY ANNE: As thou dost swallow up this good king's blood
LADY ANNE: Which his hell-govern'd arm hath butchered!
GLOUCESTER: Lady, you know no rules of charity,
GLOUCESTER: Which renders good for bad, blessings for curses.
LADY ANNE: Villain, thou know'st no law of God nor man:
LADY ANNE: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity.
GLOUCESTER: But I know none, and therefore am no beast.
LADY ANNE: O wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
GLOUCESTER: More wonderful, when angels are so angry.
GLOUCESTER: Vouchsafe, divine perfection of a woman,
GLOUCESTER: Of these supposed-evils, to give me leave,
GLOUCESTER: By circumstance, but to acquit myself.
LADY ANNE: Vouchsafe, defused infection of a man,
LADY ANNE: For these known evils, but to give me leave,
LADY ANNE: By circumstance, to curse thy cursed self.
GLOUCESTER: Fairer than tongue can name thee, let me have
GLOUCESTER: Some patient leisure to excuse myself.
LADY ANNE: Fouler than heart can think thee, thou canst make
LADY ANNE: No excuse current, but to hang thyself.
GLOUCESTER: By such despair, I should accuse myself.
LADY ANNE: And, by despairing, shouldst thou stand excused,
LADY ANNE: For doing worthy vengeance on thyself,
LADY ANNE: Which didst unworthy slaughter upon others.
GLOUCESTER: Say that I slew them not?
LADY ANNE: Why, then they are not dead:
LADY ANNE: But dead they are, and devilish slave, by thee.
GLOUCESTER: I did not kill your husband.
LADY ANNE: Why, then he is alive.
GLOUCESTER: Nay, he is dead, and slain by Edward's hand.
LADY ANNE: In thy foul throat thou liest: Queen Margaret saw
LADY ANNE: Thy murderous falchion smoking in his blood,
LADY ANNE: The which thou once didst bend against her breast,
LADY ANNE: But that thy brothers beat aside the point.
GLOUCESTER: I was provoked by her slanderous tongue,
GLOUCESTER: which laid their guilt upon my guiltless shoulders.
LADY ANNE: Thou wast provoked by thy bloody mind.
LADY ANNE: Which never dreamt on aught but butcheries:
LADY ANNE: Didst thou not kill this king?
GLOUCESTER: I grant ye.
LADY ANNE: Dost grant me, hedgehog? then, God grant me too
LADY ANNE: Thou mayst be damned for that wicked deed!
LADY ANNE: O, he was gentle, mild, and virtuous!
GLOUCESTER: The fitter for the King of heaven, that hath him.
LADY ANNE: He is in heaven, where thou shalt never come.
GLOUCESTER: Let him thank me, that holp to send him thither,
GLOUCESTER: For he was fitter for that place than earth.
LADY ANNE: And thou unfit for any place but hell.
GLOUCESTER: Yes, one place else, if you will hear me name it.
LADY ANNE: Some dungeon.
GLOUCESTER: Your bed-chamber.
LADY ANNE: I'll rest betide the chamber where thou liest!
GLOUCESTER: So will it, madam till I lie with you.
LADY ANNE: I hope so.
GLOUCESTER: I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne,
GLOUCESTER: To leave this keen encounter of our wits,
GLOUCESTER: And fall somewhat into a slower method,
GLOUCESTER: Is not the causer of the timeless deaths
GLOUCESTER: Of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward,
GLOUCESTER: As blameful as the executioner?
LADY ANNE: Thou art the cause, and most accursed effect.
GLOUCESTER: Your beauty was the cause of that effect,
GLOUCESTER: Your beauty: which did haunt me in my sleep
GLOUCESTER: To undertake the death of all the world,
GLOUCESTER: So I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
LADY ANNE: If I thought that, I tell thee, homicide,
LADY ANNE: These nails should rend that beauty from my cheeks.
GLOUCESTER: These eyes could never endure sweet beauty's wreck,
GLOUCESTER: You should not blemish it, if I stood by:
GLOUCESTER: As all the world is cheered by the sun,
GLOUCESTER: So I by that, it is my day, my life.
LADY ANNE: Black night o'ershade thy day, and death thy life!
GLOUCESTER: Curse not thyself, fair creature thou art both.
LADY ANNE: I would I were, to be revenged on thee.
GLOUCESTER: It is a quarrel most unnatural,
GLOUCESTER: To be revenged on him that loveth you.
LADY ANNE: It is a quarrel just and reasonable,
LADY ANNE: To be revenged on him that slew my husband.
GLOUCESTER: He that bereft thee, lady, of thy husband,
GLOUCESTER: Did it to help thee to a better husband.
LADY ANNE: His better doth not breathe upon the earth.
GLOUCESTER: He lives that loves thee better than he could.
LADY ANNE: Name him.
GLOUCESTER: Plantagenet.
LADY ANNE: Why, that was he.
GLOUCESTER: The selfsame name, but one of better nature.
LADY ANNE: Where is he?
GLOUCESTER: Here.
NARRATOR: She spitteth at him
GLOUCESTER: Why dost thou spit at me?
LADY ANNE: Would it were mortal poison, for thy sake!
GLOUCESTER: Never came poison from so sweet a place.
LADY ANNE: Never hung poison on a fouler toad.
LADY ANNE: Out of my sight! thou dost infect my eyes.
GLOUCESTER: Thine eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
LADY ANNE: Would they were basilisks, to strike thee dead!
GLOUCESTER: I would they were, that I might die at once,
GLOUCESTER: For now they kill me with a living death.
GLOUCESTER: Those eyes of thine from mine have drawn salt tears,
GLOUCESTER: Shamed their aspect with store of childish drops:
GLOUCESTER: These eyes that never shed remorseful tear,
GLOUCESTER: No, when my father York and Edward wept,
GLOUCESTER: To hear the piteous moan that Rutland made
GLOUCESTER: When black-faced Clifford shook his sword at him,
GLOUCESTER: Nor when thy warlike father, like a child,
GLOUCESTER: Told the sad story of my father's death,
GLOUCESTER: And twenty times made pause to sob and weep,
GLOUCESTER: That all the standers-by had wet their cheeks
GLOUCESTER: Like trees bedash'd with rain: in that sad time
GLOUCESTER: My manly eyes did scorn an humble tear,
GLOUCESTER: And what these sorrows could not thence exhale,
GLOUCESTER: Thy beauty hath, and made them blind with weeping.
GLOUCESTER: I never sued to friend nor enemy,
GLOUCESTER: My tongue could never learn sweet smoothing word,
GLOUCESTER: But now thy beauty is proposed my fee,
GLOUCESTER: My proud heart sues, and prompts my tongue to speak.
NARRATOR: She looks scornfully at him
GLOUCESTER: Teach not thy lips such scorn, for they were made
GLOUCESTER: For kissing, lady, not for such contempt.
GLOUCESTER: If thy revengeful heart cannot forgive,
GLOUCESTER: Lo, here I lend thee this sharp-pointed sword,
GLOUCESTER: Which if thou please to hide in this true bosom.
GLOUCESTER: And let the soul forth that adoreth thee,
GLOUCESTER: I lay it naked to the deadly stroke,
GLOUCESTER: And humbly beg the death upon my knee.
GLOUCESTER: He lays his breast open: she offers at it with his sword
GLOUCESTER: Nay, do not pause, for I did kill King Henry,
GLOUCESTER: But 'twas thy beauty that provoked me.
GLOUCESTER: Nay, now dispatch, 'twas I that stabb'd young Edward,
GLOUCESTER: But 'twas thy heavenly face that set me on.
NARRATOR: Here she lets fall the sword
GLOUCESTER: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
LADY ANNE: Arise, dissembler: though I wish thy death,
LADY ANNE: I will not be the executioner.
GLOUCESTER: Then bid me kill myself, and I will do it.
LADY ANNE: I have already.
GLOUCESTER: Tush, that was in thy rage:
GLOUCESTER: Speak it again, and, even with the word,
GLOUCESTER: That hand, which, for thy love, did kill thy love,
GLOUCESTER: Shall, for thy love, kill a far truer love,
GLOUCESTER: To both their deaths thou shalt be accessary.
LADY ANNE: I would I knew thy heart.
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis figured in my tongue.
LADY ANNE: I fear me both are false.
GLOUCESTER: Then never man was true.
LADY ANNE: Well, well, put up your sword.
GLOUCESTER: Say, then, my peace is made.
LADY ANNE: That shall you know hereafter.
GLOUCESTER: But shall I live in hope?
LADY ANNE: All men, I hope, live so.
GLOUCESTER: Vouchsafe to wear this ring.
LADY ANNE: To take is not to give.
GLOUCESTER: Look, how this ring encompasseth finger.
GLOUCESTER: Even so thy breast encloseth my poor heart,
GLOUCESTER: Wear both of them, for both of them are thine.
GLOUCESTER: And if thy poor devoted suppliant may
GLOUCESTER: But beg one favour at thy gracious hand,
GLOUCESTER: Thou dost confirm his happiness for ever.
LADY ANNE: What is it?
GLOUCESTER: That it would please thee leave these sad designs
GLOUCESTER: To him that hath more cause to be a mourner,
GLOUCESTER: And presently repair to Crosby Place,
GLOUCESTER: Where, after I have solemnly interr'd
GLOUCESTER: At Chertsey monastery this noble king,
GLOUCESTER: And wet his grave with my repentant tears,
GLOUCESTER: I will with all expedient duty see you:
GLOUCESTER: For divers unknown reasons. I beseech you,
GLOUCESTER: Grant me this boon.
LADY ANNE: With all my heart, and much it joys me too,
LADY ANNE: To see you are become so penitent.
LADY ANNE: Tressel and Berkeley, go along with me.
GLOUCESTER: Bid me farewell.
LADY ANNE: 'Tis more than you deserve,
LADY ANNE: But since you teach me how to flatter you,
LADY ANNE: Imagine I have said farewell already.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LADY ANNE, TRESSEL, and BERKELEY
GLOUCESTER: Sirs, take up the corse.
GENTLEMEN: Towards Chertsey, noble lord?
GLOUCESTER: No, to White-Friars, there attend my coining.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Was ever woman in this humour woo'd?
GLOUCESTER: Was ever woman in this humour won?
GLOUCESTER: I'll have her, but I will not keep her long.
GLOUCESTER: What! I, that kill'd her husband and his father,
GLOUCESTER: To take her in her heart's extremest hate,
GLOUCESTER: With curses in her mouth, tears in her eyes,
GLOUCESTER: The bleeding witness of her hatred by,
GLOUCESTER: Having God, her conscience, and these bars
GLOUCESTER: against me,
GLOUCESTER: And I nothing to back my suit at all,
GLOUCESTER: But the plain devil and dissembling looks,
GLOUCESTER: And yet to win her, all the world to nothing!
GLOUCESTER: Ha!
GLOUCESTER: Hath she forgot already that brave prince,
GLOUCESTER: Edward, her lord, whom I, some three months since,
GLOUCESTER: Stabb'd in my angry mood at Tewksbury?
GLOUCESTER: A sweeter and a lovelier gentleman,
GLOUCESTER: Framed in the prodigality of nature,
GLOUCESTER: Young, valiant, wise, and, no doubt, right royal,
GLOUCESTER: The spacious world cannot again afford
GLOUCESTER: And will she yet debase her eyes on me,
GLOUCESTER: That cropp'd the golden prime of this sweet prince,
GLOUCESTER: And made her widow to a woful bed?
GLOUCESTER: On me, whose all not equals Edward's moiety?
GLOUCESTER: On me, that halt and am unshapen thus?
GLOUCESTER: My dukedom to a beggarly denier,
GLOUCESTER: I do mistake my person all this while:
GLOUCESTER: Upon my life, she finds, although I cannot,
GLOUCESTER: Myself to be a marvellous proper man.
GLOUCESTER: I'll be at charges for a looking-glass,
GLOUCESTER: And entertain some score or two of tailors,
GLOUCESTER: To study fashions to adorn my body:
GLOUCESTER: Since I am crept in favour with myself,
GLOUCESTER: Will maintain it with some little cost.
GLOUCESTER: But first I'll turn yon fellow in his grave,
GLOUCESTER: And then return lamenting to my love.
GLOUCESTER: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass,
GLOUCESTER: That I may see my shadow as I pass.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH, RIVERS, and GREY
RIVERS: Have patience, madam: there's no doubt his majesty
RIVERS: Will soon recover his accustom'd health.
GREY: In that you brook it in, it makes him worse:
GREY: Therefore, for God's sake, entertain good comfort,
GREY: And cheer his grace with quick and merry words.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: If he were dead, what would betide of me?
RIVERS: No other harm but loss of such a lord.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The loss of such a lord includes all harm.
GREY: The heavens have bless'd you with a goodly son,
GREY: To be your comforter when he is gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Oh, he is young and his minority
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Is put unto the trust of Richard Gloucester,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: A man that loves not me, nor none of you.
RIVERS: Is it concluded that he shall be protector?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: It is determined, not concluded yet:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: But so it must be, if the king miscarry.
NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM and DERBY
GREY: Here come the lords of Buckingham and Derby.
BUCKINGHAM: Good time of day unto your royal grace!
DERBY: God make your majesty joyful as you have been!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The Countess Richmond, good my Lord of Derby.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To your good prayers will scarcely say amen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Yet, Derby, notwithstanding she's your wife,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And loves not me, be you, good lord, assured
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I hate not you for her proud arrogance.
DERBY: I do beseech you, either not believe
DERBY: The envious slanders of her false accusers,
DERBY: Or, if she be accused in true report,
DERBY: Bear with her weakness, which, I think proceeds
DERBY: From wayward sickness, and no grounded malice.
RIVERS: Saw you the king to-day, my Lord of Derby?
DERBY: But now the Duke of Buckingham and I
DERBY: Are come from visiting his majesty.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: What likelihood of his amendment, lords?
BUCKINGHAM: Madam, good hope, his grace speaks cheerfully.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: God grant him health! Did you confer with him?
BUCKINGHAM: Madam, we did: he desires to make atonement
BUCKINGHAM: Betwixt the Duke of Gloucester and your brothers,
BUCKINGHAM: And betwixt them and my lord chamberlain,
BUCKINGHAM: And sent to warn them to his royal presence.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Would all were well! but that will never be
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I fear our happiness is at the highest.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, HASTINGS, and DORSET
GLOUCESTER: They do me wrong, and I will not endure it:
GLOUCESTER: Who are they that complain unto the king,
GLOUCESTER: That I, forsooth, am stern, and love them not?
GLOUCESTER: By holy Paul, they love his grace but lightly
GLOUCESTER: That fill his ears with such dissentious rumours.
GLOUCESTER: Because I cannot flatter and speak fair,
GLOUCESTER: Smile in men's faces, smooth, deceive and cog,
GLOUCESTER: Duck with French nods and apish courtesy,
GLOUCESTER: I must be held a rancorous enemy.
GLOUCESTER: Cannot a plain man live and think no harm,
GLOUCESTER: But thus his simple truth must be abused
GLOUCESTER: By silken, sly, insinuating Jacks?
RIVERS: To whom in all this presence speaks your grace?
GLOUCESTER: To thee, that hast nor honesty nor grace.
GLOUCESTER: When have I injured thee? when done thee wrong?
GLOUCESTER: Or thee? or thee? or any of your faction?
GLOUCESTER: A plague upon you all! His royal person,--
GLOUCESTER: Whom God preserve better than you would wish!--
GLOUCESTER: Cannot be quiet scarce a breathing-while,
GLOUCESTER: But you must trouble him with lewd complaints.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Brother of Gloucester, you mistake the matter.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The king, of his own royal disposition,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And not provoked by any suitor else,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Aiming, belike, at your interior hatred,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Which in your outward actions shows itself
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Against my kindred, brothers, and myself,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Makes him to send, that thereby he may gather
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The ground of your ill-will, and so remove it.
GLOUCESTER: I cannot tell: the world is grown so bad,
GLOUCESTER: That wrens make prey where eagles dare not perch:
GLOUCESTER: Since every Jack became a gentleman
GLOUCESTER: There's many a gentle person made a Jack.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Come, come, we know your meaning, brother
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Gloucester,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: You envy my advancement and my friends':
QUEEN ELIZABETH: God grant we never may have need of you!
GLOUCESTER: Meantime, God grants that we have need of you:
GLOUCESTER: Your brother is imprison'd by your means,
GLOUCESTER: Myself disgraced, and the nobility
GLOUCESTER: Held in contempt, whilst many fair promotions
GLOUCESTER: Are daily given to ennoble those
GLOUCESTER: That scarce, some two days since, were worth a noble.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: By Him that raised me to this careful height
QUEEN ELIZABETH: From that contented hap which I enjoy'd,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I never did incense his majesty
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Against the Duke of Clarence, but have been
QUEEN ELIZABETH: An earnest advocate to plead for him.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My lord, you do me shameful injury,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Falsely to draw me in these vile suspects.
GLOUCESTER: You may deny that you were not the cause
GLOUCESTER: Of my Lord Hastings' late imprisonment.
RIVERS: She may, my lord, for--
GLOUCESTER: She may, Lord Rivers! why, who knows not so?
GLOUCESTER: She may do more, sir, than denying that:
GLOUCESTER: She may help you to many fair preferments,
GLOUCESTER: And then deny her aiding hand therein,
GLOUCESTER: And lay those honours on your high deserts.
GLOUCESTER: What may she not? She may, yea, marry, may she--
RIVERS: What, marry, may she?
GLOUCESTER: What, marry, may she! marry with a king,
GLOUCESTER: A bachelor, a handsome stripling too:
GLOUCESTER: I wis your grandam had a worser match.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My Lord of Gloucester, I have too long borne
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Your blunt upbraidings and your bitter scoffs:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: By heaven, I will acquaint his majesty
QUEEN ELIZABETH: With those gross taunts I often have endured.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I had rather be a country servant-maid
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Than a great queen, with this condition,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To be thus taunted, scorn'd, and baited at:
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN MARGARET, behind
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Small joy have I in being England's queen.
QUEEN MARGARET: And lessen'd be that small, God, I beseech thee!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy honour, state and seat is due to me.
GLOUCESTER: What! threat you me with telling of the king?
GLOUCESTER: Tell him, and spare not: look, what I have said
GLOUCESTER: I will avouch in presence of the king:
GLOUCESTER: I dare adventure to be sent to the Tower.
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis time to speak, my pains are quite forgot.
QUEEN MARGARET: Out, devil! I remember them too well:
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou slewest my husband Henry in the Tower,
QUEEN MARGARET: And Edward, my poor son, at Tewksbury.
GLOUCESTER: Ere you were queen, yea, or your husband king,
GLOUCESTER: I was a pack-horse in his great affairs,
GLOUCESTER: A weeder-out of his proud adversaries,
GLOUCESTER: A liberal rewarder of his friends:
GLOUCESTER: To royalize his blood I spilt mine own.
QUEEN MARGARET: Yea, and much better blood than his or thine.
GLOUCESTER: In all which time you and your husband Grey
GLOUCESTER: Were factious for the house of Lancaster,
GLOUCESTER: And, Rivers, so were you. Was not your husband
GLOUCESTER: In Margaret's battle at Saint Alban's slain?
GLOUCESTER: Let me put in your minds, if you forget,
GLOUCESTER: What you have been ere now, and what you are,
GLOUCESTER: Withal, what I have been, and what I am.
QUEEN MARGARET: A murderous villain, and so still thou art.
GLOUCESTER: Poor Clarence did forsake his father, Warwick,
GLOUCESTER: Yea, and forswore himself,--which Jesu pardon!--
QUEEN MARGARET: Which God revenge!
GLOUCESTER: To fight on Edward's party for the crown,
GLOUCESTER: And for his meed, poor lord, he is mew'd up.
GLOUCESTER: I would to God my heart were flint, like Edward's,
GLOUCESTER: Or Edward's soft and pitiful, like mine
GLOUCESTER: I am too childish-foolish for this world.
QUEEN MARGARET: Hie thee to hell for shame, and leave the world,
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou cacodemon! there thy kingdom is.
RIVERS: My Lord of Gloucester, in those busy days
RIVERS: Which here you urge to prove us enemies,
RIVERS: We follow'd then our lord, our lawful king:
RIVERS: So should we you, if you should be our king.
GLOUCESTER: If I should be! I had rather be a pedlar:
GLOUCESTER: Far be it from my heart, the thought of it!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: As little joy, my lord, as you suppose
QUEEN ELIZABETH: You should enjoy, were you this country's king,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: As little joy may you suppose in me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That I enjoy, being the queen thereof.
QUEEN MARGARET: A little joy enjoys the queen thereof,
QUEEN MARGARET: For I am she, and altogether joyless.
QUEEN MARGARET: I can no longer hold me patient.
NARRATOR: Advancing
QUEEN MARGARET: Hear me, you wrangling pirates, that fall out
QUEEN MARGARET: In sharing that which you have pill'd from me!
QUEEN MARGARET: Which of you trembles not that looks on me?
QUEEN MARGARET: If not, that, I being queen, you bow like subjects,
QUEEN MARGARET: Yet that, by you deposed, you quake like rebels?
QUEEN MARGARET: O gentle villain, do not turn away!
GLOUCESTER: Foul wrinkled witch, what makest thou in my sight?
QUEEN MARGARET: But repetition of what thou hast marr'd,
QUEEN MARGARET: That will I make before I let thee go.
GLOUCESTER: Wert thou not banished on pain of death?
QUEEN MARGARET: I was, but I do find more pain in banishment
QUEEN MARGARET: Than death can yield me here by my abode.
QUEEN MARGARET: A husband and a son thou owest to me,
QUEEN MARGARET: And thou a kingdom, all of you allegiance:
QUEEN MARGARET: The sorrow that I have, by right is yours,
QUEEN MARGARET: And all the pleasures you usurp are mine.
GLOUCESTER: The curse my noble father laid on thee,
GLOUCESTER: When thou didst crown his warlike brows with paper
GLOUCESTER: And with thy scorns drew'st rivers from his eyes,
GLOUCESTER: And then, to dry them, gavest the duke a clout
GLOUCESTER: Steep'd in the faultless blood of pretty Rutland--
GLOUCESTER: His curses, then from bitterness of soul
GLOUCESTER: Denounced against thee, are all fall'n upon thee,
GLOUCESTER: And God, not we, hath plagued thy bloody deed.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: So just is God, to right the innocent.
HASTINGS: O, 'twas the foulest deed to slay that babe,
HASTINGS: And the most merciless that e'er was heard of!
RIVERS: Tyrants themselves wept when it was reported.
DORSET: No man but prophesied revenge for it.
BUCKINGHAM: Northumberland, then present, wept to see it.
QUEEN MARGARET: What were you snarling all before I came,
QUEEN MARGARET: Ready to catch each other by the throat,
QUEEN MARGARET: And turn you all your hatred now on me?
QUEEN MARGARET: Did York's dread curse prevail so much with heaven?
QUEEN MARGARET: That Henry's death, my lovely Edward's death,
QUEEN MARGARET: Their kingdom's loss, my woful banishment,
QUEEN MARGARET: Could all but answer for that peevish brat?
QUEEN MARGARET: Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven?
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, then, give way, dull clouds, to my quick curses!
QUEEN MARGARET: If not by war, by surfeit die your king,
QUEEN MARGARET: As ours by murder, to make him a king!
QUEEN MARGARET: Edward thy son, which now is Prince of Wales,
QUEEN MARGARET: For Edward my son, which was Prince of Wales,
QUEEN MARGARET: Die in his youth by like untimely violence!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thyself a queen, for me that was a queen,
QUEEN MARGARET: Outlive thy glory, like my wretched self!
QUEEN MARGARET: Long mayst thou live to wail thy children's loss,
QUEEN MARGARET: And see another, as I see thee now,
QUEEN MARGARET: Deck'd in thy rights, as thou art stall'd in mine!
QUEEN MARGARET: Long die thy happy days before thy death,
QUEEN MARGARET: And, after many lengthen'd hours of grief,
QUEEN MARGARET: Die neither mother, wife, nor England's queen!
QUEEN MARGARET: Rivers and Dorset, you were standers by,
QUEEN MARGARET: And so wast thou, Lord Hastings, when my son
QUEEN MARGARET: Was stabb'd with bloody daggers: God, I pray him,
QUEEN MARGARET: That none of you may live your natural age,
QUEEN MARGARET: But by some unlook'd accident cut off!
GLOUCESTER: Have done thy charm, thou hateful wither'd hag!
QUEEN MARGARET: And leave out thee? stay, dog, for thou shalt hear me.
QUEEN MARGARET: If heaven have any grievous plague in store
QUEEN MARGARET: Exceeding those that I can wish upon thee,
QUEEN MARGARET: O, let them keep it till thy sins be ripe,
QUEEN MARGARET: And then hurl down their indignation
QUEEN MARGARET: On thee, the troubler of the poor world's peace!
QUEEN MARGARET: The worm of conscience still begnaw thy soul!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy friends suspect for traitors while thou livest,
QUEEN MARGARET: And take deep traitors for thy dearest friends!
QUEEN MARGARET: No sleep close up that deadly eye of thine,
QUEEN MARGARET: Unless it be whilst some tormenting dream
QUEEN MARGARET: Affrights thee with a hell of ugly devils!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity
QUEEN MARGARET: The slave of nature and the son of hell!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou slander of thy mother's heavy womb!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou loathed issue of thy father's loins!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou rag of honour! thou detested--
GLOUCESTER: Margaret.
QUEEN MARGARET: Richard!
GLOUCESTER: Ha!
QUEEN MARGARET: I call thee not.
GLOUCESTER: I cry thee mercy then, for I had thought
GLOUCESTER: That thou hadst call'd me all these bitter names.
QUEEN MARGARET: Why, so I did, but look'd for no reply.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, let me make the period to my curse!
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis done by me, and ends in 'Margaret.'
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Thus have you breathed your curse against yourself.
QUEEN MARGARET: Poor painted queen, vain flourish of my fortune!
QUEEN MARGARET: Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider,
QUEEN MARGARET: Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about?
QUEEN MARGARET: Fool, fool! thou whet'st a knife to kill thyself.
QUEEN MARGARET: The time will come when thou shalt wish for me
QUEEN MARGARET: To help thee curse that poisonous bunchback'd toad.
HASTINGS: False-boding woman, end thy frantic curse,
HASTINGS: Lest to thy harm thou move our patience.
QUEEN MARGARET: Foul shame upon you! you have all moved mine.
RIVERS: Were you well served, you would be taught your duty.
QUEEN MARGARET: To serve me well, you all should do me duty,
QUEEN MARGARET: Teach me to be your queen, and you my subjects:
QUEEN MARGARET: O, serve me well, and teach yourselves that duty!
DORSET: Dispute not with her, she is lunatic.
QUEEN MARGARET: Peace, master marquess, you are malapert:
QUEEN MARGARET: Your fire-new stamp of honour is scarce current.
QUEEN MARGARET: O, that your young nobility could judge
QUEEN MARGARET: What 'twere to lose it, and be miserable!
QUEEN MARGARET: They that stand high have many blasts to shake them,
QUEEN MARGARET: And if they fall, they dash themselves to pieces.
GLOUCESTER: Good counsel, marry: learn it, learn it, marquess.
DORSET: It toucheth you, my lord, as much as me.
GLOUCESTER: Yea, and much more: but I was born so high,
GLOUCESTER: Our aery buildeth in the cedar's top,
GLOUCESTER: And dallies with the wind and scorns the sun.
QUEEN MARGARET: And turns the sun to shade, alas! alas!
QUEEN MARGARET: Witness my son, now in the shade of death,
QUEEN MARGARET: Whose bright out-shining beams thy cloudy wrath
QUEEN MARGARET: Hath in eternal darkness folded up.
QUEEN MARGARET: Your aery buildeth in our aery's nest.
QUEEN MARGARET: O God, that seest it, do not suffer it!
QUEEN MARGARET: As it was won with blood, lost be it so!
BUCKINGHAM: Have done! for shame, if not for charity.
QUEEN MARGARET: Urge neither charity nor shame to me:
QUEEN MARGARET: Uncharitably with me have you dealt,
QUEEN MARGARET: And shamefully by you my hopes are butcher'd.
QUEEN MARGARET: My charity is outrage, life my shame
QUEEN MARGARET: And in that shame still live my sorrow's rage.
BUCKINGHAM: Have done, have done.
QUEEN MARGARET: O princely Buckingham I'll kiss thy hand,
QUEEN MARGARET: In sign of league and amity with thee:
QUEEN MARGARET: Now fair befal thee and thy noble house!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy garments are not spotted with our blood,
QUEEN MARGARET: Nor thou within the compass of my curse.
BUCKINGHAM: Nor no one here, for curses never pass
BUCKINGHAM: The lips of those that breathe them in the air.
QUEEN MARGARET: I'll not believe but they ascend the sky,
QUEEN MARGARET: And there awake God's gentle-sleeping peace.
QUEEN MARGARET: O Buckingham, take heed of yonder dog!
QUEEN MARGARET: Look, when he fawns, he bites, and when he bites,
QUEEN MARGARET: His venom tooth will rankle to the death:
QUEEN MARGARET: Have not to do with him, beware of him,
QUEEN MARGARET: Sin, death, and hell have set their marks on him,
QUEEN MARGARET: And all their ministers attend on him.
GLOUCESTER: What doth she say, my Lord of Buckingham?
BUCKINGHAM: Nothing that I respect, my gracious lord.
QUEEN MARGARET: What, dost thou scorn me for my gentle counsel?
QUEEN MARGARET: And soothe the devil that I warn thee from?
QUEEN MARGARET: O, but remember this another day,
QUEEN MARGARET: When he shall split thy very heart with sorrow,
QUEEN MARGARET: And say poor Margaret was a prophetess!
QUEEN MARGARET: Live each of you the subjects to his hate,
QUEEN MARGARET: And he to yours, and all of you to God's!
NARRATOR: Exit
HASTINGS: My hair doth stand on end to hear her curses.
RIVERS: And so doth mine: I muse why she's at liberty.
GLOUCESTER: I cannot blame her: by God's holy mother,
GLOUCESTER: She hath had too much wrong, and I repent
GLOUCESTER: My part thereof that I have done to her.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I never did her any, to my knowledge.
GLOUCESTER: But you have all the vantage of her wrong.
GLOUCESTER: I was too hot to do somebody good,
GLOUCESTER: That is too cold in thinking of it now.
GLOUCESTER: Marry, as for Clarence, he is well repaid,
GLOUCESTER: He is frank'd up to fatting for his pains
GLOUCESTER: God pardon them that are the cause of it!
RIVERS: A virtuous and a Christian-like conclusion,
RIVERS: To pray for them that have done scathe to us.
GLOUCESTER: So do I ever:
NARRATOR: Aside
GLOUCESTER: being well-advised.
GLOUCESTER: For had I cursed now, I had cursed myself.
NARRATOR: Enter CATESBY
CATESBY: Madam, his majesty doth call for you,
CATESBY: And for your grace, and you, my noble lords.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Catesby, we come. Lords, will you go with us?
RIVERS: Madam, we will attend your grace.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: I do the wrong, and first begin to brawl.
GLOUCESTER: The secret mischiefs that I set abroach
GLOUCESTER: I lay unto the grievous charge of others.
GLOUCESTER: Clarence, whom I, indeed, have laid in darkness,
GLOUCESTER: I do beweep to many simple gulls
GLOUCESTER: Namely, to Hastings, Derby, Buckingham,
GLOUCESTER: And say it is the queen and her allies
GLOUCESTER: That stir the king against the duke my brother.
GLOUCESTER: Now, they believe it, and withal whet me
GLOUCESTER: To be revenged on Rivers, Vaughan, Grey:
GLOUCESTER: But then I sigh, and, with a piece of scripture,
GLOUCESTER: Tell them that God bids us do good for evil:
GLOUCESTER: And thus I clothe my naked villany
GLOUCESTER: With old odd ends stolen out of holy writ,
GLOUCESTER: And seem a saint, when most I play the devil.
NARRATOR: Enter two Murderers
GLOUCESTER: But, soft! here come my executioners.
GLOUCESTER: How now, my hardy, stout resolved mates!
GLOUCESTER: Are you now going to dispatch this deed?
First Murderer: We are, my lord, and come to have the warrant
First Murderer: That we may be admitted where he is.
GLOUCESTER: Well thought upon, I have it here about me.
NARRATOR: Gives the warrant
GLOUCESTER: When you have done, repair to Crosby Place.
GLOUCESTER: But, sirs, be sudden in the execution,
GLOUCESTER: Withal obdurate, do not hear him plead,
GLOUCESTER: For Clarence is well-spoken, and perhaps
GLOUCESTER: May move your hearts to pity if you mark him.
First Murderer: Tush!
First Murderer: Fear not, my lord, we will not stand to prate,
First Murderer: Talkers are no good doers: be assured
First Murderer: We come to use our hands and not our tongues.
GLOUCESTER: Your eyes drop millstones, when fools' eyes drop tears:
GLOUCESTER: I like you, lads, about your business straight,
GLOUCESTER: Go, go, dispatch.
First Murderer: We will, my noble lord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. London. The Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter CLARENCE and BRAKENBURY
BRAKENBURY: Why looks your grace so heavily today?
CLARENCE: O, I have pass'd a miserable night,
CLARENCE: So full of ugly sights, of ghastly dreams,
CLARENCE: That, as I am a Christian faithful man,
CLARENCE: I would not spend another such a night,
CLARENCE: Though 'twere to buy a world of happy days,
CLARENCE: So full of dismal terror was the time!
BRAKENBURY: What was your dream? I long to hear you tell it.
CLARENCE: Methoughts that I had broken from the Tower,
CLARENCE: And was embark'd to cross to Burgundy,
CLARENCE: And, in my company, my brother Gloucester,
CLARENCE: Who from my cabin tempted me to walk
CLARENCE: Upon the hatches: thence we looked toward England,
CLARENCE: And cited up a thousand fearful times,
CLARENCE: During the wars of York and Lancaster
CLARENCE: That had befall'n us. As we paced along
CLARENCE: Upon the giddy footing of the hatches,
CLARENCE: Methought that Gloucester stumbled, and, in falling,
CLARENCE: Struck me, that thought to stay him, overboard,
CLARENCE: Into the tumbling billows of the main.
CLARENCE: Lord, Lord! methought, what pain it was to drown!
CLARENCE: What dreadful noise of waters in mine ears!
CLARENCE: What ugly sights of death within mine eyes!
CLARENCE: Methought I saw a thousand fearful wrecks,
CLARENCE: Ten thousand men that fishes gnaw'd upon,
CLARENCE: Wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl,
CLARENCE: Inestimable stones, unvalued jewels,
CLARENCE: All scatter'd in the bottom of the sea:
CLARENCE: Some lay in dead men's skulls, and, in those holes
CLARENCE: Where eyes did once inhabit, there were crept,
CLARENCE: As 'twere in scorn of eyes, reflecting gems,
CLARENCE: Which woo'd the slimy bottom of the deep,
CLARENCE: And mock'd the dead bones that lay scatter'd by.
BRAKENBURY: Had you such leisure in the time of death
BRAKENBURY: To gaze upon the secrets of the deep?
CLARENCE: Methought I had, and often did I strive
CLARENCE: To yield the ghost: but still the envious flood
CLARENCE: Kept in my soul, and would not let it forth
CLARENCE: To seek the empty, vast and wandering air,
CLARENCE: But smother'd it within my panting bulk,
CLARENCE: Which almost burst to belch it in the sea.
BRAKENBURY: Awaked you not with this sore agony?
CLARENCE: O, no, my dream was lengthen'd after life,
CLARENCE: O, then began the tempest to my soul,
CLARENCE: Who pass'd, methought, the melancholy flood,
CLARENCE: With that grim ferryman which poets write of,
CLARENCE: Unto the kingdom of perpetual night.
CLARENCE: The first that there did greet my stranger soul,
CLARENCE: Was my great father-in-law, renowned Warwick,
CLARENCE: Who cried aloud, 'What scourge for perjury
CLARENCE: Can this dark monarchy afford false Clarence?'
CLARENCE: And so he vanish'd: then came wandering by
CLARENCE: A shadow like an angel, with bright hair
CLARENCE: Dabbled in blood, and he squeak'd out aloud,
CLARENCE: 'Clarence is come, false, fleeting, perjured Clarence,
CLARENCE: That stabb'd me in the field by Tewksbury,
CLARENCE: Seize on him, Furies, take him to your torments!'
CLARENCE: With that, methoughts, a legion of foul fiends
CLARENCE: Environ'd me about, and howled in mine ears
CLARENCE: Such hideous cries, that with the very noise
CLARENCE: I trembling waked, and for a season after
CLARENCE: Could not believe but that I was in hell,
CLARENCE: Such terrible impression made the dream.
BRAKENBURY: No marvel, my lord, though it affrighted you,
BRAKENBURY: I promise, I am afraid to hear you tell it.
CLARENCE: O Brakenbury, I have done those things,
CLARENCE: Which now bear evidence against my soul,
CLARENCE: For Edward's sake, and see how he requites me!
CLARENCE: O God! if my deep prayers cannot appease thee,
CLARENCE: But thou wilt be avenged on my misdeeds,
CLARENCE: Yet execute thy wrath in me alone,
CLARENCE: O, spare my guiltless wife and my poor children!
CLARENCE: I pray thee, gentle keeper, stay by me,
CLARENCE: My soul is heavy, and I fain would sleep.
BRAKENBURY: I will, my lord: God give your grace good rest!
NARRATOR: CLARENCE sleeps
BRAKENBURY: Sorrow breaks seasons and reposing hours,
BRAKENBURY: Makes the night morning, and the noon-tide night.
BRAKENBURY: Princes have but their tides for their glories,
BRAKENBURY: An outward honour for an inward toil,
BRAKENBURY: And, for unfelt imagination,
BRAKENBURY: They often feel a world of restless cares:
BRAKENBURY: So that, betwixt their tides and low names,
BRAKENBURY: There's nothing differs but the outward fame.
NARRATOR: Enter the two Murderers
First Murderer: Ho! who's here?
BRAKENBURY: In God's name what are you, and how came you hither?
First Murderer: I would speak with Clarence, and I came hither on my legs.
BRAKENBURY: Yea, are you so brief?
Second Murderer: O sir, it is better to be brief than tedious. Show
Second Murderer: him our commission, talk no more.
NARRATOR: BRAKENBURY reads it
BRAKENBURY: I am, in this, commanded to deliver
BRAKENBURY: The noble Duke of Clarence to your hands:
BRAKENBURY: I will not reason what is meant hereby,
BRAKENBURY: Because I will be guiltless of the meaning.
BRAKENBURY: Here are the keys, there sits the duke asleep:
BRAKENBURY: I'll to the king, and signify to him
BRAKENBURY: That thus I have resign'd my charge to you.
First Murderer: Do so, it is a point of wisdom: fare you well.
NARRATOR: Exit BRAKENBURY
Second Murderer: What, shall we stab him as he sleeps?
First Murderer: No, then he will say 'twas done cowardly, when he wakes.
Second Murderer: When he wakes! why, fool, he shall never wake till
Second Murderer: the judgment-day.
First Murderer: Why, then he will say we stabbed him sleeping.
Second Murderer: The urging of that word 'judgment' hath bred a kind
Second Murderer: of remorse in me.
First Murderer: What, art thou afraid?
Second Murderer: Not to kill him, having a warrant for it, but to be
Second Murderer: damned for killing him, from which no warrant can defend us.
First Murderer: I thought thou hadst been resolute.
Second Murderer: So I am, to let him live.
First Murderer: Back to the Duke of Gloucester, tell him so.
Second Murderer: I pray thee, stay a while: I hope my holy humour
Second Murderer: will change, 'twas wont to hold me but while one
Second Murderer: would tell twenty.
First Murderer: How dost thou feel thyself now?
Second Murderer: 'Faith, some certain dregs of conscience are yet
Second Murderer: within me.
First Murderer: Remember our reward, when the deed is done.
Second Murderer: 'Zounds, he dies: I had forgot the reward.
First Murderer: Where is thy conscience now?
Second Murderer: In the Duke of Gloucester's purse.
First Murderer: So when he opens his purse to give us our reward,
First Murderer: thy conscience flies out.
Second Murderer: Let it go, there's few or none will entertain it.
First Murderer: How if it come to thee again?
Second Murderer: I'll not meddle with it: it is a dangerous thing: it
Second Murderer: makes a man a coward: a man cannot steal, but it
Second Murderer: accuseth him, he cannot swear, but it cheques him,
Second Murderer: he cannot lie with his neighbour's wife, but it
Second Murderer: detects him: 'tis a blushing shamefast spirit that
Second Murderer: mutinies in a man's bosom, it fills one full of
Second Murderer: obstacles: it made me once restore a purse of gold
Second Murderer: that I found, it beggars any man that keeps it: it
Second Murderer: is turned out of all towns and cities for a
Second Murderer: dangerous thing, and every man that means to live
Second Murderer: well endeavours to trust to himself and to live
Second Murderer: without it.
First Murderer: 'Zounds, it is even now at my elbow, persuading me
First Murderer: not to kill the duke.
Second Murderer: Take the devil in thy mind, and relieve him not: he
Second Murderer: would insinuate with thee but to make thee sigh.
First Murderer: Tut, I am strong-framed, he cannot prevail with me,
First Murderer: I warrant thee.
Second Murderer: Spoke like a tail fellow that respects his
Second Murderer: reputation. Come, shall we to this gear?
First Murderer: Take him over the costard with the hilts of thy
First Murderer: sword, and then we will chop him in the malmsey-butt
First Murderer: in the next room.
Second Murderer: O excellent devise! make a sop of him.
First Murderer: Hark! he stirs: shall I strike?
Second Murderer: No, first let's reason with him.
CLARENCE: Where art thou, keeper? give me a cup of wine.
Second murderer: You shall have wine enough, my lord, anon.
CLARENCE: In God's name, what art thou?
Second Murderer: A man, as you are.
CLARENCE: But not, as I am, royal.
Second Murderer: Nor you, as we are, loyal.
CLARENCE: Thy voice is thunder, but thy looks are humble.
Second Murderer: My voice is now the king's, my looks mine own.
CLARENCE: How darkly and how deadly dost thou speak!
CLARENCE: Your eyes do menace me: why look you pale?
CLARENCE: Who sent you hither? Wherefore do you come?
Both: To, to, to--
CLARENCE: To murder me?
Both: Ay, ay.
CLARENCE: You scarcely have the hearts to tell me so,
CLARENCE: And therefore cannot have the hearts to do it.
CLARENCE: Wherein, my friends, have I offended you?
First Murderer: Offended us you have not, but the king.
CLARENCE: I shall be reconciled to him again.
Second Murderer: Never, my lord, therefore prepare to die.
CLARENCE: Are you call'd forth from out a world of men
CLARENCE: To slay the innocent? What is my offence?
CLARENCE: Where are the evidence that do accuse me?
CLARENCE: What lawful quest have given their verdict up
CLARENCE: Unto the frowning judge? or who pronounced
CLARENCE: The bitter sentence of poor Clarence' death?
CLARENCE: Before I be convict by course of law,
CLARENCE: To threaten me with death is most unlawful.
CLARENCE: I charge you, as you hope to have redemption
CLARENCE: By Christ's dear blood shed for our grievous sins,
CLARENCE: That you depart and lay no hands on me
CLARENCE: The deed you undertake is damnable.
First Murderer: What we will do, we do upon command.
Second Murderer: And he that hath commanded is the king.
CLARENCE: Erroneous vassal! the great King of kings
CLARENCE: Hath in the tables of his law commanded
CLARENCE: That thou shalt do no murder: and wilt thou, then,
CLARENCE: Spurn at his edict and fulfil a man's?
CLARENCE: Take heed, for he holds vengeance in his hands,
CLARENCE: To hurl upon their heads that break his law.
Second Murderer: And that same vengeance doth he hurl on thee,
Second Murderer: For false forswearing and for murder too:
Second Murderer: Thou didst receive the holy sacrament,
Second Murderer: To fight in quarrel of the house of Lancaster.
First Murderer: And, like a traitor to the name of God,
First Murderer: Didst break that vow, and with thy treacherous blade
First Murderer: Unrip'dst the bowels of thy sovereign's son.
Second Murderer: Whom thou wert sworn to cherish and defend.
First Murderer: How canst thou urge God's dreadful law to us,
First Murderer: When thou hast broke it in so dear degree?
CLARENCE: Alas! for whose sake did I that ill deed?
CLARENCE: For Edward, for my brother, for his sake: Why, sirs,
CLARENCE: He sends ye not to murder me for this
CLARENCE: For in this sin he is as deep as I.
CLARENCE: If God will be revenged for this deed.
CLARENCE: O, know you yet, he doth it publicly,
CLARENCE: Take not the quarrel from his powerful arm,
CLARENCE: He needs no indirect nor lawless course
CLARENCE: To cut off those that have offended him.
First Murderer: Who made thee, then, a bloody minister,
First Murderer: When gallant-springing brave Plantagenet,
First Murderer: That princely novice, was struck dead by thee?
CLARENCE: My brother's love, the devil, and my rage.
First Murderer: Thy brother's love, our duty, and thy fault,
First Murderer: Provoke us hither now to slaughter thee.
CLARENCE: Oh, if you love my brother, hate not me,
CLARENCE: I am his brother, and I love him well.
CLARENCE: If you be hired for meed, go back again,
CLARENCE: And I will send you to my brother Gloucester,
CLARENCE: Who shall reward you better for my life
CLARENCE: Than Edward will for tidings of my death.
Second Murderer: You are deceived, your brother Gloucester hates you.
CLARENCE: O, no, he loves me, and he holds me dear:
CLARENCE: Go you to him from me.
Both: Ay, so we will.
CLARENCE: Tell him, when that our princely father York
CLARENCE: Bless'd his three sons with his victorious arm,
CLARENCE: And charged us from his soul to love each other,
CLARENCE: He little thought of this divided friendship:
CLARENCE: Bid Gloucester think of this, and he will weep.
First Murderer: Ay, millstones, as be lesson'd us to weep.
CLARENCE: O, do not slander him, for he is kind.
First Murderer: Right,
First Murderer: As snow in harvest. Thou deceivest thyself:
First Murderer: 'Tis he that sent us hither now to slaughter thee.
CLARENCE: It cannot be, for when I parted with him,
CLARENCE: He hugg'd me in his arms, and swore, with sobs,
CLARENCE: That he would labour my delivery.
Second Murderer: Why, so he doth, now he delivers thee
Second Murderer: From this world's thraldom to the joys of heaven.
First Murderer: Make peace with God, for you must die, my lord.
CLARENCE: Hast thou that holy feeling in thy soul,
CLARENCE: To counsel me to make my peace with God,
CLARENCE: And art thou yet to thy own soul so blind,
CLARENCE: That thou wilt war with God by murdering me?
CLARENCE: Ah, sirs, consider, he that set you on
CLARENCE: To do this deed will hate you for the deed.
Second Murderer: What shall we do?
CLARENCE: Relent, and save your souls.
First Murderer: Relent! 'tis cowardly and womanish.
CLARENCE: Not to relent is beastly, savage, devilish.
CLARENCE: Which of you, if you were a prince's son,
CLARENCE: Being pent from liberty, as I am now,
CLARENCE: if two such murderers as yourselves came to you,
CLARENCE: Would not entreat for life?
CLARENCE: My friend, I spy some pity in thy looks:
CLARENCE: O, if thine eye be not a flatterer,
CLARENCE: Come thou on my side, and entreat for me,
CLARENCE: As you would beg, were you in my distress
CLARENCE: A begging prince what beggar pities not?
Second Murderer: Look behind you, my lord.
First Murderer: Take that, and that: if all this will not do,
NARRATOR: Stabs him
First Murderer: I'll drown you in the malmsey-butt within.
NARRATOR: Exit, with the body
Second Murderer: A bloody deed, and desperately dispatch'd!
Second Murderer: How fain, like Pilate, would I wash my hands
Second Murderer: Of this most grievous guilty murder done!
NARRATOR: Re-enter First Murderer
First Murderer: How now! what mean'st thou, that thou help'st me not?
First Murderer: By heavens, the duke shall know how slack thou art!
Second Murderer: I would he knew that I had saved his brother!
Second Murderer: Take thou the fee, and tell him what I say,
Second Murderer: For I repent me that the duke is slain.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Murderer: So do not I: go, coward as thou art.
First Murderer: Now must I hide his body in some hole,
First Murderer: Until the duke take order for his burial:
First Murderer: And when I have my meed, I must away,
First Murderer: For this will out, and here I must not stay.
First Murderer: ACT II
First Murderer: SCENE I. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Enter KING EDWARD IV sick, QUEEN  ELIZABETH, DORSET, RIVERS, HASTINGS, BUCKINGHAM, GREY, and others
KING EDWARD IV: Why, so: now have I done a good day's work:
KING EDWARD IV: You peers, continue this united league:
KING EDWARD IV: I every day expect an embassage
KING EDWARD IV: From my Redeemer to redeem me hence,
KING EDWARD IV: And now in peace my soul shall part to heaven,
KING EDWARD IV: Since I have set my friends at peace on earth.
KING EDWARD IV: Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand,
KING EDWARD IV: Dissemble not your hatred, swear your love.
RIVERS: By heaven, my heart is purged from grudging hate:
RIVERS: And with my hand I seal my true heart's love.
HASTINGS: So thrive I, as I truly swear the like!
KING EDWARD IV: Take heed you dally not before your king,
KING EDWARD IV: Lest he that is the supreme King of kings
KING EDWARD IV: Confound your hidden falsehood, and award
KING EDWARD IV: Either of you to be the other's end.
HASTINGS: So prosper I, as I swear perfect love!
RIVERS: And I, as I love Hastings with my heart!
KING EDWARD IV: Madam, yourself are not exempt in this,
KING EDWARD IV: Nor your son Dorset, Buckingham, nor you,
KING EDWARD IV: You have been factious one against the other,
KING EDWARD IV: Wife, love Lord Hastings, let him kiss your hand,
KING EDWARD IV: And what you do, do it unfeignedly.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Here, Hastings, I will never more remember
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Our former hatred, so thrive I and mine!
KING EDWARD IV: Dorset, embrace him, Hastings, love lord marquess.
DORSET: This interchange of love, I here protest,
DORSET: Upon my part shall be unviolable.
HASTINGS: And so swear I, my lord
NARRATOR: They embrace
KING EDWARD IV: Now, princely Buckingham, seal thou this league
KING EDWARD IV: With thy embracements to my wife's allies,
KING EDWARD IV: And make me happy in your unity.
BUCKINGHAM: Whenever Buckingham doth turn his hate
BUCKINGHAM: On you or yours,
NARRATOR: To the Queen
BUCKINGHAM: but with all duteous love
BUCKINGHAM: Doth cherish you and yours, God punish me
BUCKINGHAM: With hate in those where I expect most love!
BUCKINGHAM: When I have most need to employ a friend,
BUCKINGHAM: And most assured that he is a friend
BUCKINGHAM: Deep, hollow, treacherous, and full of guile,
BUCKINGHAM: Be he unto me! this do I beg of God,
BUCKINGHAM: When I am cold in zeal to yours.
KING EDWARD IV: A pleasing cordial, princely Buckingham,
KING EDWARD IV: is this thy vow unto my sickly heart.
KING EDWARD IV: There wanteth now our brother Gloucester here,
KING EDWARD IV: To make the perfect period of this peace.
BUCKINGHAM: And, in good time, here comes the noble duke.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Good morrow to my sovereign king and queen:
GLOUCESTER: And, princely peers, a happy time of day!
KING EDWARD IV: Happy, indeed, as we have spent the day.
KING EDWARD IV: Brother, we done deeds of charity,
KING EDWARD IV: Made peace enmity, fair love of hate,
KING EDWARD IV: Between these swelling wrong-incensed peers.
GLOUCESTER: A blessed labour, my most sovereign liege:
GLOUCESTER: Amongst this princely heap, if any here,
GLOUCESTER: By false intelligence, or wrong surmise,
GLOUCESTER: Hold me a foe,
GLOUCESTER: If I unwittingly, or in my rage,
GLOUCESTER: Have aught committed that is hardly borne
GLOUCESTER: By any in this presence, I desire
GLOUCESTER: To reconcile me to his friendly peace:
GLOUCESTER: 'Tis death to me to be at enmity,
GLOUCESTER: I hate it, and desire all good men's love.
GLOUCESTER: First, madam, I entreat true peace of you,
GLOUCESTER: Which I will purchase with my duteous service,
GLOUCESTER: Of you, my noble cousin Buckingham,
GLOUCESTER: If ever any grudge were lodged between us,
GLOUCESTER: Of you, Lord Rivers, and, Lord Grey, of you,
GLOUCESTER: That without desert have frown'd on me,
GLOUCESTER: Dukes, earls, lords, gentlemen, indeed, of all.
GLOUCESTER: I do not know that Englishman alive
GLOUCESTER: With whom my soul is any jot at odds
GLOUCESTER: More than the infant that is born to-night
GLOUCESTER: I thank my God for my humility.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: A holy day shall this be kept hereafter:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I would to God all strifes were well compounded.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My sovereign liege, I do beseech your majesty
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To take our brother Clarence to your grace.
GLOUCESTER: Why, madam, have I offer'd love for this
GLOUCESTER: To be so bouted in this royal presence?
GLOUCESTER: Who knows not that the noble duke is dead?
NARRATOR: They all start
GLOUCESTER: You do him injury to scorn his corse.
RIVERS: Who knows not he is dead! who knows he is?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: All seeing heaven, what a world is this!
BUCKINGHAM: Look I so pale, Lord Dorset, as the rest?
DORSET: Ay, my good lord, and no one in this presence
DORSET: But his red colour hath forsook his cheeks.
KING EDWARD IV: Is Clarence dead? the order was reversed.
GLOUCESTER: But he, poor soul, by your first order died,
GLOUCESTER: And that a winged Mercury did bear:
GLOUCESTER: Some tardy cripple bore the countermand,
GLOUCESTER: That came too lag to see him buried.
GLOUCESTER: God grant that some, less noble and less loyal,
GLOUCESTER: Nearer in bloody thoughts, but not in blood,
GLOUCESTER: Deserve not worse than wretched Clarence did,
GLOUCESTER: And yet go current from suspicion!
NARRATOR: Enter DERBY
DORSET: A boon, my sovereign, for my service done!
KING EDWARD IV: I pray thee, peace: my soul is full of sorrow.
DORSET: I will not rise, unless your highness grant.
KING EDWARD IV: Then speak at once what is it thou demand'st.
DORSET: The forfeit, sovereign, of my servant's life,
DORSET: Who slew to-day a righteous gentleman
DORSET: Lately attendant on the Duke of Norfolk.
KING EDWARD IV: Have a tongue to doom my brother's death,
KING EDWARD IV: And shall the same give pardon to a slave?
KING EDWARD IV: My brother slew no man, his fault was thought,
KING EDWARD IV: And yet his punishment was cruel death.
KING EDWARD IV: Who sued to me for him? who, in my rage,
KING EDWARD IV: Kneel'd at my feet, and bade me be advised
KING EDWARD IV: Who spake of brotherhood? who spake of love?
KING EDWARD IV: Who told me how the poor soul did forsake
KING EDWARD IV: The mighty Warwick, and did fight for me?
KING EDWARD IV: Who told me, in the field by Tewksbury
KING EDWARD IV: When Oxford had me down, he rescued me,
KING EDWARD IV: And said, 'Dear brother, live, and be a king'?
KING EDWARD IV: Who told me, when we both lay in the field
KING EDWARD IV: Frozen almost to death, how he did lap me
KING EDWARD IV: Even in his own garments, and gave himself,
KING EDWARD IV: All thin and naked, to the numb cold night?
KING EDWARD IV: All this from my remembrance brutish wrath
KING EDWARD IV: Sinfully pluck'd, and not a man of you
KING EDWARD IV: Had so much grace to put it in my mind.
KING EDWARD IV: But when your carters or your waiting-vassals
KING EDWARD IV: Have done a drunken slaughter, and defaced
KING EDWARD IV: The precious image of our dear Redeemer,
KING EDWARD IV: You straight are on your knees for pardon, pardon,
KING EDWARD IV: And I unjustly too, must grant it you
KING EDWARD IV: But for my brother not a man would speak,
KING EDWARD IV: Nor I, ungracious, speak unto myself
KING EDWARD IV: For him, poor soul. The proudest of you all
KING EDWARD IV: Have been beholding to him in his life,
KING EDWARD IV: Yet none of you would once plead for his life.
KING EDWARD IV: O God, I fear thy justice will take hold
KING EDWARD IV: On me, and you, and mine, and yours for this!
KING EDWARD IV: Come, Hastings, help me to my closet.
KING EDWARD IV: Oh, poor Clarence!
NARRATOR: Exeunt some with KING EDWARD IV and QUEEN MARGARET
GLOUCESTER: This is the fruit of rashness! Mark'd you not
GLOUCESTER: How that the guilty kindred of the queen
GLOUCESTER: Look'd pale when they did hear of Clarence' death?
GLOUCESTER: O, they did urge it still unto the king!
GLOUCESTER: God will revenge it. But come, let us in,
GLOUCESTER: To comfort Edward with our company.
BUCKINGHAM: We wait upon your grace.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter the DUCHESS OF YORK, with the two children of CLARENCE
Boy: Tell me, good grandam, is our father dead?
DUCHESS OF YORK: No, boy.
Boy: Why do you wring your hands, and beat your breast,
Boy: And cry 'O Clarence, my unhappy son!'
Girl: Why do you look on us, and shake your head,
Girl: And call us wretches, orphans, castaways
Girl: If that our noble father be alive?
DUCHESS OF YORK: My pretty cousins, you mistake me much,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I do lament the sickness of the king.
DUCHESS OF YORK: As loath to lose him, not your father's death,
DUCHESS OF YORK: It were lost sorrow to wail one that's lost.
Boy: Then, grandam, you conclude that he is dead.
Boy: The king my uncle is to blame for this:
Boy: God will revenge it, whom I will importune
Boy: With daily prayers all to that effect.
Girl: And so will I.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Peace, children, peace! the king doth love you well:
DUCHESS OF YORK: Incapable and shallow innocents,
DUCHESS OF YORK: You cannot guess who caused your father's death.
Boy: Grandam, we can, for my good uncle Gloucester
Boy: Told me, the king, provoked by the queen,
Boy: Devised impeachments to imprison him :
Boy: And when my uncle told me so, he wept,
Boy: And hugg'd me in his arm, and kindly kiss'd my cheek,
Boy: Bade me rely on him as on my father,
Boy: And he would love me dearly as his child.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Oh, that deceit should steal such gentle shapes,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And with a virtuous vizard hide foul guile!
DUCHESS OF YORK: He is my son, yea, and therein my shame,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Yet from my dugs he drew not this deceit.
Boy: Think you my uncle did dissemble, grandam?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Ay, boy.
Boy: I cannot think it. Hark! what noise is this?
Boy: Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH, with her hair about her ears, RIVERS, and DORSET after her
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Oh, who shall hinder me to wail and weep,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To chide my fortune, and torment myself?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I'll join with black despair against my soul,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And to myself become an enemy.
DUCHESS OF YORK: What means this scene of rude impatience?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To make an act of tragic violence:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Edward, my lord, your son, our king, is dead.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Why grow the branches now the root is wither'd?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Why wither not the leaves the sap being gone?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: If you will live, lament, if die, be brief,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That our swift-winged souls may catch the king's,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Or, like obedient subjects, follow him
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To his new kingdom of perpetual rest.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Ah, so much interest have I in thy sorrow
DUCHESS OF YORK: As I had title in thy noble husband!
DUCHESS OF YORK: I have bewept a worthy husband's death,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And lived by looking on his images:
DUCHESS OF YORK: But now two mirrors of his princely semblance
DUCHESS OF YORK: Are crack'd in pieces by malignant death,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And I for comfort have but one false glass,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Which grieves me when I see my shame in him.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Thou art a widow, yet thou art a mother,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And hast the comfort of thy children left thee:
DUCHESS OF YORK: But death hath snatch'd my husband from mine arms,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And pluck'd two crutches from my feeble limbs,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Edward and Clarence. O, what cause have I,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Thine being but a moiety of my grief,
DUCHESS OF YORK: To overgo thy plaints and drown thy cries!
Boy: Good aunt, you wept not for our father's death,
Boy: How can we aid you with our kindred tears?
Girl: Our fatherless distress was left unmoan'd,
Girl: Your widow-dolour likewise be unwept!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Give me no help in lamentation,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I am not barren to bring forth complaints
QUEEN ELIZABETH: All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That I, being govern'd by the watery moon,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Oh for my husband, for my dear lord Edward!
Children: Oh for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: What stay had I but Edward? and he's gone.
Children: What stay had we but Clarence? and he's gone.
DUCHESS OF YORK: What stays had I but they? and they are gone.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Was never widow had so dear a loss!
Children: Were never orphans had so dear a loss!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Was never mother had so dear a loss!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Alas, I am the mother of these moans!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Their woes are parcell'd, mine are general.
DUCHESS OF YORK: She for an Edward weeps, and so do I,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I for a Clarence weep, so doth not she:
DUCHESS OF YORK: These babes for Clarence weep and so do I,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I for an Edward weep, so do not they:
DUCHESS OF YORK: Alas, you three, on me, threefold distress'd,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Pour all your tears! I am your sorrow's nurse,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And I will pamper it with lamentations.
DORSET: Comfort, dear mother: God is much displeased
DORSET: That you take with unthankfulness, his doing:
DORSET: In common worldly things, 'tis call'd ungrateful,
DORSET: With dull unwilligness to repay a debt
DORSET: Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent,
DORSET: Much more to be thus opposite with heaven,
DORSET: For it requires the royal debt it lent you.
RIVERS: Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother,
RIVERS: Of the young prince your son: send straight for him
