RIVERS: Let him be crown'd, in him your comfort lives:
RIVERS: Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave,
RIVERS: And plant your joys in living Edward's throne.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER, BUCKINGHAM, DERBY, HASTINGS, and RATCLIFF
GLOUCESTER: Madam, have comfort: all of us have cause
GLOUCESTER: To wail the dimming of our shining star,
GLOUCESTER: But none can cure their harms by wailing them.
GLOUCESTER: Madam, my mother, I do cry you mercy,
GLOUCESTER: I did not see your grace: humbly on my knee
GLOUCESTER: I crave your blessing.
DUCHESS OF YORK: God bless thee, and put meekness in thy mind,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Love, charity, obedience, and true duty!
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  Amen, and make me die a good old man!
GLOUCESTER: That is the butt-end of a mother's blessing:
GLOUCESTER: I marvel why her grace did leave it out.
BUCKINGHAM: You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers,
BUCKINGHAM: That bear this mutual heavy load of moan,
BUCKINGHAM: Now cheer each other in each other's love
BUCKINGHAM: Though we have spent our harvest of this king,
BUCKINGHAM: We are to reap the harvest of his son.
BUCKINGHAM: The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts,
BUCKINGHAM: But lately splinter'd, knit, and join'd together,
BUCKINGHAM: Must gently be preserved, cherish'd, and kept:
BUCKINGHAM: Me seemeth good, that, with some little train,
BUCKINGHAM: Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fetch'd
BUCKINGHAM: Hither to London, to be crown'd our king.
RIVERS: Why with some little train, my Lord of Buckingham?
BUCKINGHAM: Marry, my lord, lest, by a multitude,
BUCKINGHAM: The new-heal'd wound of malice should break out,
BUCKINGHAM: Which would be so much the more dangerous
BUCKINGHAM: By how much the estate is green and yet ungovern'd:
BUCKINGHAM: Where every horse bears his commanding rein,
BUCKINGHAM: And may direct his course as please himself,
BUCKINGHAM: As well the fear of harm, as harm apparent,
BUCKINGHAM: In my opinion, ought to be prevented.
GLOUCESTER: I hope the king made peace with all of us
GLOUCESTER: And the compact is firm and true in me.
RIVERS: And so in me, and so, I think, in all:
RIVERS: Yet, since it is but green, it should be put
RIVERS: To no apparent likelihood of breach,
RIVERS: Which haply by much company might be urged:
RIVERS: Therefore I say with noble Buckingham,
RIVERS: That it is meet so few should fetch the prince.
HASTINGS: And so say I.
GLOUCESTER: Then be it so, and go we to determine
GLOUCESTER: Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow.
GLOUCESTER: Madam, and you, my mother, will you go
GLOUCESTER: To give your censures in this weighty business?
DUCHESS OF YORK: With all our harts.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BUCKINGHAM and GLOUCESTER
BUCKINGHAM: My lord, whoever journeys to the Prince,
BUCKINGHAM: For God's sake, let not us two be behind,
BUCKINGHAM: For, by the way, I'll sort occasion,
BUCKINGHAM: As index to the story we late talk'd of,
BUCKINGHAM: To part the queen's proud kindred from the king.
GLOUCESTER: My other self, my counsel's consistory,
GLOUCESTER: My oracle, my prophet! My dear cousin,
GLOUCESTER: I, like a child, will go by thy direction.
GLOUCESTER: Towards Ludlow then, for we'll not stay behind.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. London. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter two Citizens meeting
First Citizen: Neighbour, well met: whither away so fast?
Second Citizen: I promise you, I scarcely know myself:
Second Citizen: Hear you the news abroad?
First Citizen: Ay, that the king is dead.
Second Citizen: Bad news, by'r lady, seldom comes the better:
Second Citizen: I fear, I fear 'twill prove a troublous world.
NARRATOR: Enter another Citizen
Third Citizen: Neighbours, God speed!
First Citizen: Give you good morrow, sir.
Third Citizen: Doth this news hold of good King Edward's death?
Second Citizen: Ay, sir, it is too true, God help the while!
Third Citizen: Then, masters, look to see a troublous world.
First Citizen: No, no, by God's good grace his son shall reign.
Third Citizen: Woe to the land that's govern'd by a child!
Second Citizen: In him there is a hope of government,
Second Citizen: That in his nonage council under him,
Second Citizen: And in his full and ripen'd years himself,
Second Citizen: No doubt, shall then and till then govern well.
First Citizen: So stood the state when Henry the Sixth
First Citizen: Was crown'd in Paris but at nine months old.
Third Citizen: Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot,
Third Citizen: For then this land was famously enrich'd
Third Citizen: With politic grave counsel, then the king
Third Citizen: Had virtuous uncles to protect his grace.
First Citizen: Why, so hath this, both by the father and mother.
Third Citizen: Better it were they all came by the father,
Third Citizen: Or by the father there were none at all,
Third Citizen: For emulation now, who shall be nearest,
Third Citizen: Will touch us all too near, if God prevent not.
Third Citizen: O, full of danger is the Duke of Gloucester!
Third Citizen: And the queen's sons and brothers haught and proud:
Third Citizen: And were they to be ruled, and not to rule,
Third Citizen: This sickly land might solace as before.
First Citizen: Come, come, we fear the worst, all shall be well.
Third Citizen: When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks,
Third Citizen: When great leaves fall, the winter is at hand,
Third Citizen: When the sun sets, who doth not look for night?
Third Citizen: Untimely storms make men expect a dearth.
Third Citizen: All may be well, but, if God sort it so,
Third Citizen: 'Tis more than we deserve, or I expect.
Second Citizen: Truly, the souls of men are full of dread:
Second Citizen: Ye cannot reason almost with a man
Second Citizen: That looks not heavily and full of fear.
Third Citizen: Before the times of change, still is it so:
Third Citizen: By a divine instinct men's minds mistrust
Third Citizen: Ensuing dangers, as by proof, we see
Third Citizen: The waters swell before a boisterous storm.
Third Citizen: But leave it all to God. whither away?
Second Citizen: Marry, we were sent for to the justices.
Third Citizen: And so was I: I'll bear you company.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter the ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, young YORK, QUEEN ELIZABETH, and the DUCHESS OF YORK
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Last night, I hear, they lay at Northampton,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: At Stony-Stratford will they be to-night:
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: To-morrow, or next day, they will be here.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I long with all my heart to see the prince:
DUCHESS OF YORK: I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: But I hear, no, they say my son of York
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Hath almost overta'en him in his growth.
YORK: Ay, mother, but I would not have it so.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Why, my young cousin, it is good to grow.
YORK: Grandam, one night, as we did sit at supper,
YORK: My uncle Rivers talk'd how I did grow
YORK: More than my brother: 'Ay,' quoth my uncle
YORK: Gloucester,
YORK: 'Small herbs have grace, great weeds do grow apace:'
YORK: And since, methinks, I would not grow so fast,
YORK: Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold
DUCHESS OF YORK: In him that did object the same to thee,
DUCHESS OF YORK: He was the wretched'st thing when he was young,
DUCHESS OF YORK: So long a-growing and so leisurely,
DUCHESS OF YORK: That, if this rule were true, he should be gracious.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Why, madam, so, no doubt, he is.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I hope he is, but yet let mothers doubt.
YORK: Now, by my troth, if I had been remember'd,
YORK: I could have given my uncle's grace a flout,
YORK: To touch his growth nearer than he touch'd mine.
DUCHESS OF YORK: How, my pretty York? I pray thee, let me hear it.
YORK: Marry, they say my uncle grew so fast
YORK: That he could gnaw a crust at two hours old
YORK: 'Twas full two years ere I could get a tooth.
YORK: Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I pray thee, pretty York, who told thee this?
YORK: Grandam, his nurse.
DUCHESS OF YORK: His nurse! why, she was dead ere thou wert born.
YORK: If 'twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: A parlous boy: go to, you are too shrewd.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Good madam, be not angry with the child.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Pitchers have ears.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Here comes a messenger. What news?
Messenger: Such news, my lord, as grieves me to unfold.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: How fares the prince?
Messenger: Well, madam, and in health.
DUCHESS OF YORK: What is thy news then?
Messenger: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret,
Messenger: With them Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Who hath committed them?
Messenger: The mighty dukes
Messenger: Gloucester and Buckingham.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: For what offence?
Messenger: The sum of all I can, I have disclosed,
Messenger: Why or for what these nobles were committed
Messenger: Is all unknown to me, my gracious lady.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Ay me, I see the downfall of our house!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The tiger now hath seized the gentle hind,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Insulting tyranny begins to jet
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Upon the innocent and aweless throne:
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Welcome, destruction, death, and massacre!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I see, as in a map, the end of all.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Accursed and unquiet wrangling days,
DUCHESS OF YORK: How many of you have mine eyes beheld!
DUCHESS OF YORK: My husband lost his life to get the crown,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And often up and down my sons were toss'd,
DUCHESS OF YORK: For me to joy and weep their gain and loss:
DUCHESS OF YORK: And being seated, and domestic broils
DUCHESS OF YORK: Clean over-blown, themselves, the conquerors.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Make war upon themselves, blood against blood,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Self against self: O, preposterous
DUCHESS OF YORK: And frantic outrage, end thy damned spleen,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Or let me die, to look on death no more!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Come, come, my boy, we will to sanctuary.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Madam, farewell.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I'll go along with you.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: You have no cause.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: My gracious lady, go,
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: And thither bear your treasure and your goods.
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: For my part, I'll resign unto your grace
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: The seal I keep: and so betide to me
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: As well I tender you and all of yours!
ARCHBISHOP OF YORK: Come, I'll conduct you to the sanctuary.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. London. A street.
NARRATOR: The trumpets sound. Enter the young PRINCE EDWARD, GLOUCESTER, BUCKINGHAM, CARDINAL, CATESBY, and others
BUCKINGHAM: Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.
GLOUCESTER: Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts' sovereign
GLOUCESTER: The weary way hath made you melancholy.
PRINCE EDWARD: No, uncle, but our crosses on the way
PRINCE EDWARD: Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy
PRINCE EDWARD: I want more uncles here to welcome me.
GLOUCESTER: Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years
GLOUCESTER: Hath not yet dived into the world's deceit
GLOUCESTER: Nor more can you distinguish of a man
GLOUCESTER: Than of his outward show, which, God he knows,
GLOUCESTER: Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart.
GLOUCESTER: Those uncles which you want were dangerous,
GLOUCESTER: Your grace attended to their sugar'd words,
GLOUCESTER: But look'd not on the poison of their hearts :
GLOUCESTER: God keep you from them, and from such false friends!
PRINCE EDWARD: God keep me from false friends! but they were none.
GLOUCESTER: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.
NARRATOR: Enter the Lord Mayor and his train
Lord Mayor: God bless your grace with health and happy days!
PRINCE EDWARD: I thank you, good my lord, and thank you all.
PRINCE EDWARD: I thought my mother, and my brother York,
PRINCE EDWARD: Would long ere this have met us on the way
PRINCE EDWARD: Fie, what a slug is Hastings, that he comes not
PRINCE EDWARD: To tell us whether they will come or no!
NARRATOR: Enter HASTINGS
BUCKINGHAM: And, in good time, here comes the sweating lord.
PRINCE EDWARD: Welcome, my lord: what, will our mother come?
HASTINGS: On what occasion, God he knows, not I,
HASTINGS: The queen your mother, and your brother York,
HASTINGS: Have taken sanctuary: the tender prince
HASTINGS: Would fain have come with me to meet your grace,
HASTINGS: But by his mother was perforce withheld.
BUCKINGHAM: Fie, what an indirect and peevish course
BUCKINGHAM: Is this of hers! Lord cardinal, will your grace
BUCKINGHAM: Persuade the queen to send the Duke of York
BUCKINGHAM: Unto his princely brother presently?
BUCKINGHAM: If she deny, Lord Hastings, go with him,
BUCKINGHAM: And from her jealous arms pluck him perforce.
CARDINAL: My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory
CARDINAL: Can from his mother win the Duke of York,
CARDINAL: Anon expect him here, but if she be obdurate
CARDINAL: To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid
CARDINAL: We should infringe the holy privilege
CARDINAL: Of blessed sanctuary! not for all this land
CARDINAL: Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.
BUCKINGHAM: You are too senseless--obstinate, my lord,
BUCKINGHAM: Too ceremonious and traditional
BUCKINGHAM: Weigh it but with the grossness of this age,
BUCKINGHAM: You break not sanctuary in seizing him.
BUCKINGHAM: The benefit thereof is always granted
BUCKINGHAM: To those whose dealings have deserved the place,
BUCKINGHAM: And those who have the wit to claim the place:
BUCKINGHAM: This prince hath neither claim'd it nor deserved it,
BUCKINGHAM: And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it:
BUCKINGHAM: Then, taking him from thence that is not there,
BUCKINGHAM: You break no privilege nor charter there.
BUCKINGHAM: Oft have I heard of sanctuary men,
BUCKINGHAM: But sanctuary children ne'er till now.
CARDINAL: My lord, you shall o'er-rule my mind for once.
CARDINAL: Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
HASTINGS: I go, my lord.
PRINCE EDWARD: Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CARDINAL and HASTINGS
PRINCE EDWARD: Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother come,
PRINCE EDWARD: Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?
GLOUCESTER: Where it seems best unto your royal self.
GLOUCESTER: If I may counsel you, some day or two
GLOUCESTER: Your highness shall repose you at the Tower:
GLOUCESTER: Then where you please, and shall be thought most fit
GLOUCESTER: For your best health and recreation.
PRINCE EDWARD: I do not like the Tower, of any place.
PRINCE EDWARD: Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
BUCKINGHAM: He did, my gracious lord, begin that place,
BUCKINGHAM: Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.
PRINCE EDWARD: Is it upon record, or else reported
PRINCE EDWARD: Successively from age to age, he built it?
BUCKINGHAM: Upon record, my gracious lord.
PRINCE EDWARD: But say, my lord, it were not register'd,
PRINCE EDWARD: Methinks the truth should live from age to age,
PRINCE EDWARD: As 'twere retail'd to all posterity,
PRINCE EDWARD: Even to the general all-ending day.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  So wise so young, they say, do never
GLOUCESTER: live long.
PRINCE EDWARD: What say you, uncle?
GLOUCESTER: I say, without characters, fame lives long.
NARRATOR: Aside
GLOUCESTER: Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity,
GLOUCESTER: I moralize two meanings in one word.
PRINCE EDWARD: That Julius Caesar was a famous man,
PRINCE EDWARD: With what his valour did enrich his wit,
PRINCE EDWARD: His wit set down to make his valour live
PRINCE EDWARD: Death makes no conquest of this conqueror,
PRINCE EDWARD: For now he lives in fame, though not in life.
PRINCE EDWARD: I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham,--
BUCKINGHAM: What, my gracious lord?
PRINCE EDWARD: An if I live until I be a man,
PRINCE EDWARD: I'll win our ancient right in France again,
PRINCE EDWARD: Or die a soldier, as I lived a king.
GLOUCESTER: [Aside]  Short summers lightly have a forward spring.
NARRATOR: Enter young YORK, HASTINGS, and the CARDINAL
BUCKINGHAM: Now, in good time, here comes the Duke of York.
PRINCE EDWARD: Richard of York! how fares our loving brother?
YORK: Well, my dread lord, so must I call you now.
PRINCE EDWARD: Ay, brother, to our grief, as it is yours:
PRINCE EDWARD: Too late he died that might have kept that title,
PRINCE EDWARD: Which by his death hath lost much majesty.
GLOUCESTER: How fares our cousin, noble Lord of York?
YORK: I thank you, gentle uncle. O, my lord,
YORK: You said that idle weeds are fast in growth
YORK: The prince my brother hath outgrown me far.
GLOUCESTER: He hath, my lord.
YORK: And therefore is he idle?
GLOUCESTER: O, my fair cousin, I must not say so.
YORK: Then is he more beholding to you than I.
GLOUCESTER: He may command me as my sovereign,
GLOUCESTER: But you have power in me as in a kinsman.
YORK: I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.
GLOUCESTER: My dagger, little cousin? with all my heart.
PRINCE EDWARD: A beggar, brother?
YORK: Of my kind uncle, that I know will give,
YORK: And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.
GLOUCESTER: A greater gift than that I'll give my cousin.
YORK: A greater gift! O, that's the sword to it.
GLOUCESTER: A gentle cousin, were it light enough.
YORK: O, then, I see, you will part but with light gifts,
YORK: In weightier things you'll say a beggar nay.
GLOUCESTER: It is too heavy for your grace to wear.
YORK: I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.
GLOUCESTER: What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
YORK: I would, that I might thank you as you call me.
GLOUCESTER: How?
YORK: Little.
PRINCE EDWARD: My Lord of York will still be cross in talk:
PRINCE EDWARD: Uncle, your grace knows how to bear with him.
YORK: You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me:
YORK: Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me,
YORK: Because that I am little, like an ape,
YORK: He thinks that you should bear me on your shoulders.
BUCKINGHAM: With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons!
BUCKINGHAM: To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle,
BUCKINGHAM: He prettily and aptly taunts himself:
BUCKINGHAM: So cunning and so young is wonderful.
GLOUCESTER: My lord, will't please you pass along?
GLOUCESTER: Myself and my good cousin Buckingham
GLOUCESTER: Will to your mother, to entreat of her
GLOUCESTER: To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
YORK: What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?
PRINCE EDWARD: My lord protector needs will have it so.
YORK: I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.
GLOUCESTER: Why, what should you fear?
YORK: Marry, my uncle Clarence' angry ghost:
YORK: My grandam told me he was murdered there.
PRINCE EDWARD: I fear no uncles dead.
GLOUCESTER: Nor none that live, I hope.
PRINCE EDWARD: An if they live, I hope I need not fear.
PRINCE EDWARD: But come, my lord, and with a heavy heart,
PRINCE EDWARD: Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.
NARRATOR: A Sennet. Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER, BUCKINGHAM and CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: Think you, my lord, this little prating York
BUCKINGHAM: Was not incensed by his subtle mother
BUCKINGHAM: To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?
GLOUCESTER: No doubt, no doubt, O, 'tis a parlous boy,
GLOUCESTER: Bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable
GLOUCESTER: He is all the mother's, from the top to toe.
BUCKINGHAM: Well, let them rest. Come hither, Catesby.
BUCKINGHAM: Thou art sworn as deeply to effect what we intend
BUCKINGHAM: As closely to conceal what we impart:
BUCKINGHAM: Thou know'st our reasons urged upon the way,
BUCKINGHAM: What think'st thou? is it not an easy matter
BUCKINGHAM: To make William Lord Hastings of our mind,
BUCKINGHAM: For the instalment of this noble duke
BUCKINGHAM: In the seat royal of this famous isle?
CATESBY: He for his father's sake so loves the prince,
CATESBY: That he will not be won to aught against him.
BUCKINGHAM: What think'st thou, then, of Stanley? what will he?
CATESBY: He will do all in all as Hastings doth.
BUCKINGHAM: Well, then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby,
BUCKINGHAM: And, as it were far off sound thou Lord Hastings,
BUCKINGHAM: How doth he stand affected to our purpose,
BUCKINGHAM: And summon him to-morrow to the Tower,
BUCKINGHAM: To sit about the coronation.
BUCKINGHAM: If thou dost find him tractable to us,
BUCKINGHAM: Encourage him, and show him all our reasons:
BUCKINGHAM: If he be leaden, icy-cold, unwilling,
BUCKINGHAM: Be thou so too, and so break off your talk,
BUCKINGHAM: And give us notice of his inclination:
BUCKINGHAM: For we to-morrow hold divided councils,
BUCKINGHAM: Wherein thyself shalt highly be employ'd.
GLOUCESTER: Commend me to Lord William: tell him, Catesby,
GLOUCESTER: His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries
GLOUCESTER: To-morrow are let blood at Pomfret-castle,
GLOUCESTER: And bid my friend, for joy of this good news,
GLOUCESTER: Give mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.
BUCKINGHAM: Good Catesby, go, effect this business soundly.
CATESBY: My good lords both, with all the heed I may.
GLOUCESTER: Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?
CATESBY: You shall, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: At Crosby Place, there shall you find us both.
NARRATOR: Exit CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: Now, my lord, what shall we do, if we perceive
BUCKINGHAM: Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?
GLOUCESTER: Chop off his head, man, somewhat we will do:
GLOUCESTER: And, look, when I am king, claim thou of me
GLOUCESTER: The earldom of Hereford, and the moveables
GLOUCESTER: Whereof the king my brother stood possess'd.
BUCKINGHAM: I'll claim that promise at your grace's hands.
GLOUCESTER: And look to have it yielded with all willingness.
GLOUCESTER: Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards
GLOUCESTER: We may digest our complots in some form.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before Lord Hastings' house.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: What, ho! my lord!
HASTINGS: [Within]  Who knocks at the door?
Messenger: A messenger from the Lord Stanley.
NARRATOR: Enter HASTINGS
HASTINGS: What is't o'clock?
Messenger: Upon the stroke of four.
HASTINGS: Cannot thy master sleep these tedious nights?
Messenger: So it should seem by that I have to say.
Messenger: First, he commends him to your noble lordship.
HASTINGS: And then?
Messenger: And then he sends you word
Messenger: He dreamt to-night the boar had razed his helm:
Messenger: Besides, he says there are two councils held,
Messenger: And that may be determined at the one
Messenger: which may make you and him to rue at the other.
Messenger: Therefore he sends to know your lordship's pleasure,
Messenger: If presently you will take horse with him,
Messenger: And with all speed post with him toward the north,
Messenger: To shun the danger that his soul divines.
HASTINGS: Go, fellow, go, return unto thy lord,
HASTINGS: Bid him not fear the separated councils
HASTINGS: His honour and myself are at the one,
HASTINGS: And at the other is my servant Catesby
HASTINGS: Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us
HASTINGS: Whereof I shall not have intelligence.
HASTINGS: Tell him his fears are shallow, wanting instance:
HASTINGS: And for his dreams, I wonder he is so fond
HASTINGS: To trust the mockery of unquiet slumbers
HASTINGS: To fly the boar before the boar pursues,
HASTINGS: Were to incense the boar to follow us
HASTINGS: And make pursuit where he did mean no chase.
HASTINGS: Go, bid thy master rise and come to me
HASTINGS: And we will both together to the Tower,
HASTINGS: Where, he shall see, the boar will use us kindly.
Messenger: My gracious lord, I'll tell him what you say.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter CATESBY
CATESBY: Many good morrows to my noble lord!
HASTINGS: Good morrow, Catesby, you are early stirring
HASTINGS: What news, what news, in this our tottering state?
CATESBY: It is a reeling world, indeed, my lord,
CATESBY: And I believe twill never stand upright
CATESBY: Tim Richard wear the garland of the realm.
HASTINGS: How! wear the garland! dost thou mean the crown?
CATESBY: Ay, my good lord.
HASTINGS: I'll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders
HASTINGS: Ere I will see the crown so foul misplaced.
HASTINGS: But canst thou guess that he doth aim at it?
CATESBY: Ay, on my life, and hopes to find forward
CATESBY: Upon his party for the gain thereof:
CATESBY: And thereupon he sends you this good news,
CATESBY: That this same very day your enemies,
CATESBY: The kindred of the queen, must die at Pomfret.
HASTINGS: Indeed, I am no mourner for that news,
HASTINGS: Because they have been still mine enemies:
HASTINGS: But, that I'll give my voice on Richard's side,
HASTINGS: To bar my master's heirs in true descent,
HASTINGS: God knows I will not do it, to the death.
CATESBY: God keep your lordship in that gracious mind!
HASTINGS: But I shall laugh at this a twelve-month hence,
HASTINGS: That they who brought me in my master's hate
HASTINGS: I live to look upon their tragedy.
HASTINGS: I tell thee, Catesby--
CATESBY: What, my lord?
HASTINGS: Ere a fortnight make me elder,
HASTINGS: I'll send some packing that yet think not on it.
CATESBY: 'Tis a vile thing to die, my gracious lord,
CATESBY: When men are unprepared and look not for it.
HASTINGS: O monstrous, monstrous! and so falls it out
HASTINGS: With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey: and so 'twill do
HASTINGS: With some men else, who think themselves as safe
HASTINGS: As thou and I, who, as thou know'st, are dear
HASTINGS: To princely Richard and to Buckingham.
CATESBY: The princes both make high account of you,
NARRATOR: Aside
CATESBY: For they account his head upon the bridge.
HASTINGS: I know they do, and I have well deserved it.
NARRATOR: Enter STANLEY
HASTINGS: Come on, come on, where is your boar-spear, man?
HASTINGS: Fear you the boar, and go so unprovided?
STANLEY: My lord, good morrow, good morrow, Catesby:
STANLEY: You may jest on, but, by the holy rood,
STANLEY: I do not like these several councils, I.
HASTINGS: My lord,
HASTINGS: I hold my life as dear as you do yours,
HASTINGS: And never in my life, I do protest,
HASTINGS: Was it more precious to me than 'tis now:
HASTINGS: Think you, but that I know our state secure,
HASTINGS: I would be so triumphant as I am?
STANLEY: The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London,
STANLEY: Were jocund, and supposed their state was sure,
STANLEY: And they indeed had no cause to mistrust,
STANLEY: But yet, you see how soon the day o'ercast.
STANLEY: This sudden stag of rancour I misdoubt:
STANLEY: Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward!
STANLEY: What, shall we toward the Tower? the day is spent.
HASTINGS: Come, come, have with you. Wot you what, my lord?
HASTINGS: To-day the lords you talk of are beheaded.
LORD STANLEY: They, for their truth, might better wear their heads
LORD STANLEY: Than some that have accused them wear their hats.
LORD STANLEY: But come, my lord, let us away.
NARRATOR: Enter a Pursuivant
HASTINGS: Go on before, I'll talk with this good fellow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt STANLEY and CATESBY
HASTINGS: How now, sirrah! how goes the world with thee?
Pursuivant: The better that your lordship please to ask.
HASTINGS: I tell thee, man, 'tis better with me now
HASTINGS: Than when I met thee last where now we meet:
HASTINGS: Then was I going prisoner to the Tower,
HASTINGS: By the suggestion of the queen's allies,
HASTINGS: But now, I tell thee--keep it to thyself--
HASTINGS: This day those enemies are put to death,
HASTINGS: And I in better state than e'er I was.
Pursuivant: God hold it, to your honour's good content!
HASTINGS: Gramercy, fellow: there, drink that for me.
NARRATOR: Throws him his purse
Pursuivant: God save your lordship!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter a Priest
Priest: Well met, my lord, I am glad to see your honour.
HASTINGS: I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart.
HASTINGS: I am in your debt for your last exercise,
HASTINGS: Come the next Sabbath, and I will content you.
NARRATOR: He whispers in his ear
NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM
BUCKINGHAM: What, talking with a priest, lord chamberlain?
BUCKINGHAM: Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest,
BUCKINGHAM: Your honour hath no shriving work in hand.
HASTINGS: Good faith, and when I met this holy man,
HASTINGS: Those men you talk of came into my mind.
HASTINGS: What, go you toward the Tower?
BUCKINGHAM: I do, my lord, but long I shall not stay
BUCKINGHAM: I shall return before your lordship thence.
HASTINGS: 'Tis like enough, for I stay dinner there.
BUCKINGHAM: [Aside]  And supper too, although thou know'st it not.
BUCKINGHAM: Come, will you go?
HASTINGS: I'll wait upon your lordship.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Pomfret Castle.
NARRATOR: Enter RATCLIFF, with halberds, carrying RIVERS, GREY, and VAUGHAN to death
RATCLIFF: Come, bring forth the prisoners.
RIVERS: Sir Richard Ratcliff, let me tell thee this:
RIVERS: To-day shalt thou behold a subject die
RIVERS: For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
GREY: God keep the prince from all the pack of you!
GREY: A knot you are of damned blood-suckers!
VAUGHAN: You live that shall cry woe for this after.
RATCLIFF: Dispatch, the limit of your lives is out.
RIVERS: O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison,
RIVERS: Fatal and ominous to noble peers!
RIVERS: Within the guilty closure of thy walls
RIVERS: Richard the second here was hack'd to death,
RIVERS: And, for more slander to thy dismal seat,
RIVERS: We give thee up our guiltless blood to drink.
GREY: Now Margaret's curse is fall'n upon our heads,
GREY: For standing by when Richard stabb'd her son.
RIVERS: Then cursed she Hastings, then cursed she Buckingham,
RIVERS: Then cursed she Richard. O, remember, God
RIVERS: To hear her prayers for them, as now for us
RIVERS: And for my sister and her princely sons,
RIVERS: Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood,
RIVERS: Which, as thou know'st, unjustly must be spilt.
RATCLIFF: Make haste, the hour of death is expiate.
RIVERS: Come, Grey, come, Vaughan, let us all embrace:
RIVERS: And take our leave, until we meet in heaven.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The Tower of London.
NARRATOR: Enter BUCKINGHAM, DERBY, HASTINGS, the BISHOP OF  ELY, RATCLIFF, LOVEL, with others, and take their seats at a table
HASTINGS: My lords, at once: the cause why we are met
HASTINGS: Is, to determine of the coronation.
HASTINGS: In God's name, speak: when is the royal day?
BUCKINGHAM: Are all things fitting for that royal time?
DERBY: It is, and wants but nomination.
BISHOP OF ELY: To-morrow, then, I judge a happy day.
BUCKINGHAM: Who knows the lord protector's mind herein?
BUCKINGHAM: Who is most inward with the royal duke?
BISHOP OF ELY: Your grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
BUCKINGHAM: Who, I, my lord I we know each other's faces,
BUCKINGHAM: But for our hearts, he knows no more of mine,
BUCKINGHAM: Than I of yours,
BUCKINGHAM: Nor I no more of his, than you of mine.
BUCKINGHAM: Lord Hastings, you and he are near in love.
HASTINGS: I thank his grace, I know he loves me well,
HASTINGS: But, for his purpose in the coronation.
HASTINGS: I have not sounded him, nor he deliver'd
HASTINGS: His gracious pleasure any way therein:
HASTINGS: But you, my noble lords, may name the time,
HASTINGS: And in the duke's behalf I'll give my voice,
HASTINGS: Which, I presume, he'll take in gentle part.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER
BISHOP OF ELY: Now in good time, here comes the duke himself.
GLOUCESTER: My noble lords and cousins all, good morrow.
GLOUCESTER: I have been long a sleeper, but, I hope,
GLOUCESTER: My absence doth neglect no great designs,
GLOUCESTER: Which by my presence might have been concluded.
BUCKINGHAM: Had not you come upon your cue, my lord
BUCKINGHAM: William Lord Hastings had pronounced your part,--
BUCKINGHAM: I mean, your voice,--for crowning of the king.
GLOUCESTER: Than my Lord Hastings no man might be bolder,
GLOUCESTER: His lordship knows me well, and loves me well.
HASTINGS: I thank your grace.
GLOUCESTER: My lord of Ely!
BISHOP OF ELY: My lord?
GLOUCESTER: When I was last in Holborn,
GLOUCESTER: I saw good strawberries in your garden there
GLOUCESTER: I do beseech you send for some of them.
BISHOP OF ELY: Marry, and will, my lord, with all my heart.
NARRATOR: Exit
GLOUCESTER: Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you.
NARRATOR: Drawing him aside
GLOUCESTER: Catesby hath sounded Hastings in our business,
GLOUCESTER: And finds the testy gentleman so hot,
GLOUCESTER: As he will lose his head ere give consent
GLOUCESTER: His master's son, as worshipful as he terms it,
GLOUCESTER: Shall lose the royalty of England's throne.
BUCKINGHAM: Withdraw you hence, my lord, I'll follow you.
NARRATOR: Exit GLOUCESTER, BUCKINGHAM following
DERBY: We have not yet set down this day of triumph.
DERBY: To-morrow, in mine opinion, is too sudden,
DERBY: For I myself am not so well provided
DERBY: As else I would be, were the day prolong'd.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BISHOP OF ELY
BISHOP OF ELY: Where is my lord protector? I have sent for these
BISHOP OF ELY: strawberries.
HASTINGS: His grace looks cheerfully and smooth to-day,
HASTINGS: There's some conceit or other likes him well,
HASTINGS: When he doth bid good morrow with such a spirit.
HASTINGS: I think there's never a man in Christendom
HASTINGS: That can less hide his love or hate than he,
HASTINGS: For by his face straight shall you know his heart.
DERBY: What of his heart perceive you in his face
DERBY: By any likelihood he show'd to-day?
HASTINGS: Marry, that with no man here he is offended,
HASTINGS: For, were he, he had shown it in his looks.
DERBY: I pray God he be not, I say.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GLOUCESTER and BUCKINGHAM
GLOUCESTER: I pray you all, tell me what they deserve
GLOUCESTER: That do conspire my death with devilish plots
GLOUCESTER: Of damned witchcraft, and that have prevail'd
GLOUCESTER: Upon my body with their hellish charms?
HASTINGS: The tender love I bear your grace, my lord,
HASTINGS: Makes me most forward in this noble presence
HASTINGS: To doom the offenders, whatsoever they be
HASTINGS: I say, my lord, they have deserved death.
GLOUCESTER: Then be your eyes the witness of this ill:
GLOUCESTER: See how I am bewitch'd, behold mine arm
GLOUCESTER: Is, like a blasted sapling, wither'd up:
GLOUCESTER: And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch,
GLOUCESTER: Consorted with that harlot strumpet Shore,
GLOUCESTER: That by their witchcraft thus have marked me.
HASTINGS: If they have done this thing, my gracious lord--
GLOUCESTER: If I thou protector of this damned strumpet--
GLOUCESTER: Tellest thou me of 'ifs'?  Thou art a traitor:
GLOUCESTER: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear,
GLOUCESTER: I will not dine until I see the same.
GLOUCESTER: Lovel and Ratcliff, look that it be done:
GLOUCESTER: The rest, that love me, rise and follow me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but HASTINGS, RATCLIFF, and LOVEL
HASTINGS: Woe, woe for England! not a whit for me,
HASTINGS: For I, too fond, might have prevented this.
HASTINGS: Stanley did dream the boar did raze his helm,
HASTINGS: But I disdain'd it, and did scorn to fly:
HASTINGS: Three times to-day my foot-cloth horse did stumble,
HASTINGS: And startled, when he look'd upon the Tower,
HASTINGS: As loath to bear me to the slaughter-house.
HASTINGS: O, now I want the priest that spake to me:
HASTINGS: I now repent I told the pursuivant
HASTINGS: As 'twere triumphing at mine enemies,
HASTINGS: How they at Pomfret bloodily were butcher'd,
HASTINGS: And I myself secure in grace and favour.
HASTINGS: O Margaret, Margaret, now thy heavy curse
HASTINGS: Is lighted on poor Hastings' wretched head!
RATCLIFF: Dispatch, my lord, the duke would be at dinner:
RATCLIFF: Make a short shrift, he longs to see your head.
HASTINGS: O momentary grace of mortal men,
HASTINGS: Which we more hunt for than the grace of God!
HASTINGS: Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks,
HASTINGS: Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast,
HASTINGS: Ready, with every nod, to tumble down
HASTINGS: Into the fatal bowels of the deep.
LOVEL: Come, come, dispatch, 'tis bootless to exclaim.
HASTINGS: O bloody Richard! miserable England!
HASTINGS: I prophesy the fearful'st time to thee
HASTINGS: That ever wretched age hath look'd upon.
HASTINGS: Come, lead me to the block, bear him my head.
HASTINGS: They smile at me that shortly shall be dead.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The Tower-walls.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER and BUCKINGHAM, in rotten armour, marvellous ill-favoured
GLOUCESTER: Come, cousin, canst thou quake, and change thy colour,
GLOUCESTER: Murder thy breath in the middle of a word,
GLOUCESTER: And then begin again, and stop again,
GLOUCESTER: As if thou wert distraught and mad with terror?
BUCKINGHAM: Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian,
BUCKINGHAM: Speak and look back, and pry on every side,
BUCKINGHAM: Tremble and start at wagging of a straw,
BUCKINGHAM: Intending deep suspicion: ghastly looks
BUCKINGHAM: Are at my service, like enforced smiles,
BUCKINGHAM: And both are ready in their offices,
BUCKINGHAM: At any time, to grace my stratagems.
BUCKINGHAM: But what, is Catesby gone?
GLOUCESTER: He is, and, see, he brings the mayor along.
NARRATOR: Enter the Lord Mayor and CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: Lord mayor,--
GLOUCESTER: Look to the drawbridge there!
BUCKINGHAM: Hark! a drum.
GLOUCESTER: Catesby, o'erlook the walls.
BUCKINGHAM: Lord mayor, the reason we have sent--
GLOUCESTER: Look back, defend thee, here are enemies.
BUCKINGHAM: God and our innocency defend and guard us!
GLOUCESTER: Be patient, they are friends, Ratcliff and Lovel.
NARRATOR: Enter LOVEL and RATCLIFF, with HASTINGS' head
LOVEL: Here is the head of that ignoble traitor,
LOVEL: The dangerous and unsuspected Hastings.
GLOUCESTER: So dear I loved the man, that I must weep.
GLOUCESTER: I took him for the plainest harmless creature
GLOUCESTER: That breathed upon this earth a Christian,
GLOUCESTER: Made him my book wherein my soul recorded
GLOUCESTER: The history of all her secret thoughts:
GLOUCESTER: So smooth he daub'd his vice with show of virtue,
GLOUCESTER: That, his apparent open guilt omitted,
GLOUCESTER: I mean, his conversation with Shore's wife,
GLOUCESTER: He lived from all attainder of suspect.
BUCKINGHAM: Well, well, he was the covert'st shelter'd traitor
BUCKINGHAM: That ever lived.
BUCKINGHAM: Would you imagine, or almost believe,
BUCKINGHAM: Were't not that, by great preservation,
BUCKINGHAM: We live to tell it you, the subtle traitor
BUCKINGHAM: This day had plotted, in the council-house
BUCKINGHAM: To murder me and my good Lord of Gloucester?
Lord Mayor: What, had he so?
GLOUCESTER: What, think You we are Turks or infidels?
GLOUCESTER: Or that we would, against the form of law,
GLOUCESTER: Proceed thus rashly to the villain's death,
GLOUCESTER: But that the extreme peril of the case,
GLOUCESTER: The peace of England and our persons' safety,
GLOUCESTER: Enforced us to this execution?
Lord Mayor: Now, fair befall you! he deserved his death,
Lord Mayor: And you my good lords, both have well proceeded,
Lord Mayor: To warn false traitors from the like attempts.
Lord Mayor: I never look'd for better at his hands,
Lord Mayor: After he once fell in with Mistress Shore.
GLOUCESTER: Yet had not we determined he should die,
GLOUCESTER: Until your lordship came to see his death,
GLOUCESTER: Which now the loving haste of these our friends,
GLOUCESTER: Somewhat against our meaning, have prevented:
GLOUCESTER: Because, my lord, we would have had you heard
GLOUCESTER: The traitor speak, and timorously confess
GLOUCESTER: The manner and the purpose of his treason,
GLOUCESTER: That you might well have signified the same
GLOUCESTER: Unto the citizens, who haply may
GLOUCESTER: Misconstrue us in him and wail his death.
Lord Mayor: But, my good lord, your grace's word shall serve,
Lord Mayor: As well as I had seen and heard him speak
Lord Mayor: And doubt you not, right noble princes both,
Lord Mayor: But I'll acquaint our duteous citizens
Lord Mayor: With all your just proceedings in this cause.
GLOUCESTER: And to that end we wish'd your lord-ship here,
GLOUCESTER: To avoid the carping censures of the world.
BUCKINGHAM: But since you come too late of our intents,
BUCKINGHAM: Yet witness what you hear we did intend:
BUCKINGHAM: And so, my good lord mayor, we bid farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit Lord Mayor
GLOUCESTER: Go, after, after, cousin Buckingham.
GLOUCESTER: The mayor towards Guildhall hies him in all post:
GLOUCESTER: There, at your meet'st advantage of the time,
GLOUCESTER: Infer the bastardy of Edward's children:
GLOUCESTER: Tell them how Edward put to death a citizen,
GLOUCESTER: Only for saying he would make his son
GLOUCESTER: Heir to the crown, meaning indeed his house,
GLOUCESTER: Which, by the sign thereof was termed so.
GLOUCESTER: Moreover, urge his hateful luxury
GLOUCESTER: And bestial appetite in change of lust,
GLOUCESTER: Which stretched to their servants, daughters, wives,
GLOUCESTER: Even where his lustful eye or savage heart,
GLOUCESTER: Without control, listed to make his prey.
GLOUCESTER: Nay, for a need, thus far come near my person:
GLOUCESTER: Tell them, when that my mother went with child
GLOUCESTER: Of that unsatiate Edward, noble York
GLOUCESTER: My princely father then had wars in France
GLOUCESTER: And, by just computation of the time,
GLOUCESTER: Found that the issue was not his begot,
GLOUCESTER: Which well appeared in his lineaments,
GLOUCESTER: Being nothing like the noble duke my father:
GLOUCESTER: But touch this sparingly, as 'twere far off,
GLOUCESTER: Because you know, my lord, my mother lives.
BUCKINGHAM: Fear not, my lord, I'll play the orator
BUCKINGHAM: As if the golden fee for which I plead
BUCKINGHAM: Were for myself: and so, my lord, adieu.
GLOUCESTER: If you thrive well, bring them to Baynard's Castle,
GLOUCESTER: Where you shall find me well accompanied
GLOUCESTER: With reverend fathers and well-learned bishops.
BUCKINGHAM: I go: and towards three or four o'clock
BUCKINGHAM: Look for the news that the Guildhall affords.
NARRATOR: Exit BUCKINGHAM
GLOUCESTER: Go, Lovel, with all speed to Doctor Shaw,
NARRATOR: To CATESBY
GLOUCESTER: Go thou to Friar Penker, bid them both
GLOUCESTER: Meet me within this hour at Baynard's Castle.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but GLOUCESTER
GLOUCESTER: Now will I in, to take some privy order,
GLOUCESTER: To draw the brats of Clarence out of sight,
GLOUCESTER: And to give notice, that no manner of person
GLOUCESTER: At any time have recourse unto the princes.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter a Scrivener, with a paper in his hand
Scrivener: This is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings,
Scrivener: Which in a set hand fairly is engross'd,
Scrivener: That it may be this day read over in Paul's.
Scrivener: And mark how well the sequel hangs together:
Scrivener: Eleven hours I spent to write it over,
Scrivener: For yesternight by Catesby was it brought me,
Scrivener: The precedent was full as long a-doing:
Scrivener: And yet within these five hours lived Lord Hastings,
Scrivener: Untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty
Scrivener: Here's a good world the while! Why who's so gross,
Scrivener: That seeth not this palpable device?
Scrivener: Yet who's so blind, but says he sees it not?
Scrivener: Bad is the world, and all will come to nought,
Scrivener: When such bad dealings must be seen in thought.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Baynard's Castle.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER and BUCKINGHAM, at several doors
GLOUCESTER: How now, my lord, what say the citizens?
BUCKINGHAM: Now, by the holy mother of our Lord,
BUCKINGHAM: The citizens are mum and speak not a word.
GLOUCESTER: Touch'd you the bastardy of Edward's children?
BUCKINGHAM: I did, with his contract with Lady Lucy,
BUCKINGHAM: And his contract by deputy in France,
BUCKINGHAM: The insatiate greediness of his desires,
BUCKINGHAM: And his enforcement of the city wives,
BUCKINGHAM: His tyranny for trifles, his own bastardy,
BUCKINGHAM: As being got, your father then in France,
BUCKINGHAM: His resemblance, being not like the duke,
BUCKINGHAM: Withal I did infer your lineaments,
BUCKINGHAM: Being the right idea of your father,
BUCKINGHAM: Both in your form and nobleness of mind,
BUCKINGHAM: Laid open all your victories in Scotland,
BUCKINGHAM: Your dicipline in war, wisdom in peace,
BUCKINGHAM: Your bounty, virtue, fair humility:
BUCKINGHAM: Indeed, left nothing fitting for the purpose
BUCKINGHAM: Untouch'd, or slightly handled, in discourse
BUCKINGHAM: And when mine oratory grew to an end
BUCKINGHAM: I bid them that did love their country's good
BUCKINGHAM: Cry 'God save Richard, England's royal king!'
GLOUCESTER: Ah! and did they so?
BUCKINGHAM: No, so God help me, they spake not a word,
BUCKINGHAM: But, like dumb statues or breathing stones,
BUCKINGHAM: Gazed each on other, and look'd deadly pale.
BUCKINGHAM: Which when I saw, I reprehended them,
BUCKINGHAM: And ask'd the mayor what meant this wilful silence:
BUCKINGHAM: His answer was, the people were not wont
BUCKINGHAM: To be spoke to but by the recorder.
BUCKINGHAM: Then he was urged to tell my tale again,
BUCKINGHAM: 'Thus saith the duke, thus hath the duke inferr'd,'
BUCKINGHAM: But nothing spake in warrant from himself.
BUCKINGHAM: When he had done, some followers of mine own,
BUCKINGHAM: At the lower end of the hall, hurl'd up their caps,
BUCKINGHAM: And some ten voices cried 'God save King Richard!'
BUCKINGHAM: And thus I took the vantage of those few,
BUCKINGHAM: 'Thanks, gentle citizens and friends,' quoth I,
BUCKINGHAM: 'This general applause and loving shout
BUCKINGHAM: Argues your wisdoms and your love to Richard:'
BUCKINGHAM: And even here brake off, and came away.
GLOUCESTER: What tongueless blocks were they! would not they speak?
BUCKINGHAM: No, by my troth, my lord.
GLOUCESTER: Will not the mayor then and his brethren come?
BUCKINGHAM: The mayor is here at hand: intend some fear,
BUCKINGHAM: Be not you spoke with, but by mighty suit:
BUCKINGHAM: And look you get a prayer-book in your hand,
BUCKINGHAM: And stand betwixt two churchmen, good my lord,
BUCKINGHAM: For on that ground I'll build a holy descant:
BUCKINGHAM: And be not easily won to our request:
BUCKINGHAM: Play the maid's part, still answer nay, and take it.
GLOUCESTER: I go, and if you plead as well for them
GLOUCESTER: As I can say nay to thee for myself,
GLOUCESTER: No doubt well bring it to a happy issue.
BUCKINGHAM: Go, go, up to the leads, the lord mayor knocks.
NARRATOR: Exit GLOUCESTER
NARRATOR: Enter the Lord Mayor and Citizens
BUCKINGHAM: Welcome my lord, I dance attendance here,
BUCKINGHAM: I think the duke will not be spoke withal.
NARRATOR: Enter CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: Here comes his servant: how now, Catesby,
BUCKINGHAM: What says he?
CATESBY: My lord: he doth entreat your grace,
CATESBY: To visit him to-morrow or next day:
CATESBY: He is within, with two right reverend fathers,
CATESBY: Divinely bent to meditation,
CATESBY: And no worldly suit would he be moved,
CATESBY: To draw him from his holy exercise.
BUCKINGHAM: Return, good Catesby, to thy lord again,
BUCKINGHAM: Tell him, myself, the mayor and citizens,
BUCKINGHAM: In deep designs and matters of great moment,
BUCKINGHAM: No less importing than our general good,
BUCKINGHAM: Are come to have some conference with his grace.
CATESBY: I'll tell him what you say, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
BUCKINGHAM: Ah, ha, my lord, this prince is not an Edward!
BUCKINGHAM: He is not lolling on a lewd day-bed,
BUCKINGHAM: But on his knees at meditation,
BUCKINGHAM: Not dallying with a brace of courtezans,
BUCKINGHAM: But meditating with two deep divines,
BUCKINGHAM: Not sleeping, to engross his idle body,
BUCKINGHAM: But praying, to enrich his watchful soul:
BUCKINGHAM: Happy were England, would this gracious prince
BUCKINGHAM: Take on himself the sovereignty thereof:
BUCKINGHAM: But, sure, I fear, we shall ne'er win him to it.
Lord Mayor: Marry, God forbid his grace should say us nay!
BUCKINGHAM: I fear he will.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: How now, Catesby, what says your lord?
CATESBY: My lord,
CATESBY: He wonders to what end you have assembled
CATESBY: Such troops of citizens to speak with him,
CATESBY: His grace not being warn'd thereof before:
CATESBY: My lord, he fears you mean no good to him.
BUCKINGHAM: Sorry I am my noble cousin should
BUCKINGHAM: Suspect me, that I mean no good to him:
BUCKINGHAM: By heaven, I come in perfect love to him,
BUCKINGHAM: And so once more return and tell his grace.
NARRATOR: Exit CATESBY
BUCKINGHAM: When holy and devout religious men
BUCKINGHAM: Are at their beads, 'tis hard to draw them thence,
BUCKINGHAM: So sweet is zealous contemplation.
NARRATOR: Enter GLOUCESTER aloft, between two Bishops. CATESBY returns
Lord Mayor: See, where he stands between two clergymen!
BUCKINGHAM: Two props of virtue for a Christian prince,
BUCKINGHAM: To stay him from the fall of vanity:
BUCKINGHAM: And, see, a book of prayer in his hand,
BUCKINGHAM: True ornaments to know a holy man.
BUCKINGHAM: Famous Plantagenet, most gracious prince,
BUCKINGHAM: Lend favourable ears to our request,
BUCKINGHAM: And pardon us the interruption
BUCKINGHAM: Of thy devotion and right Christian zeal.
GLOUCESTER: My lord, there needs no such apology:
GLOUCESTER: I rather do beseech you pardon me,
GLOUCESTER: Who, earnest in the service of my God,
GLOUCESTER: Neglect the visitation of my friends.
GLOUCESTER: But, leaving this, what is your grace's pleasure?
BUCKINGHAM: Even that, I hope, which pleaseth God above,
BUCKINGHAM: And all good men of this ungovern'd isle.
GLOUCESTER: I do suspect I have done some offence
GLOUCESTER: That seems disgracious in the city's eyes,
GLOUCESTER: And that you come to reprehend my ignorance.
BUCKINGHAM: You have, my lord: would it might please your grace,
BUCKINGHAM: At our entreaties, to amend that fault!
GLOUCESTER: Else wherefore breathe I in a Christian land?
BUCKINGHAM: Then know, it is your fault that you resign
BUCKINGHAM: The supreme seat, the throne majestical,
BUCKINGHAM: The scepter'd office of your ancestors,
BUCKINGHAM: Your state of fortune and your due of birth,
BUCKINGHAM: The lineal glory of your royal house,
BUCKINGHAM: To the corruption of a blemished stock:
BUCKINGHAM: Whilst, in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts,
BUCKINGHAM: Which here we waken to our country's good,
BUCKINGHAM: This noble isle doth want her proper limbs,
BUCKINGHAM: Her face defaced with scars of infamy,
BUCKINGHAM: Her royal stock graft with ignoble plants,
BUCKINGHAM: And almost shoulder'd in the swallowing gulf
BUCKINGHAM: Of blind forgetfulness and dark oblivion.
BUCKINGHAM: Which to recure, we heartily solicit
BUCKINGHAM: Your gracious self to take on you the charge
BUCKINGHAM: And kingly government of this your land,
BUCKINGHAM: Not as protector, steward, substitute,
BUCKINGHAM: Or lowly factor for another's gain,
BUCKINGHAM: But as successively from blood to blood,
BUCKINGHAM: Your right of birth, your empery, your own.
BUCKINGHAM: For this, consorted with the citizens,
BUCKINGHAM: Your very worshipful and loving friends,
BUCKINGHAM: And by their vehement instigation,
BUCKINGHAM: In this just suit come I to move your grace.
GLOUCESTER: I know not whether to depart in silence,
GLOUCESTER: Or bitterly to speak in your reproof.
GLOUCESTER: Best fitteth my degree or your condition
GLOUCESTER: If not to answer, you might haply think
GLOUCESTER: Tongue-tied ambition, not replying, yielded
GLOUCESTER: To bear the golden yoke of sovereignty,
GLOUCESTER: Which fondly you would here impose on me,
GLOUCESTER: If to reprove you for this suit of yours,
GLOUCESTER: So season'd with your faithful love to me.
GLOUCESTER: Then, on the other side, I cheque'd my friends.
GLOUCESTER: Therefore, to speak, and to avoid the first,
GLOUCESTER: And then, in speaking, not to incur the last,
GLOUCESTER: Definitively thus I answer you.
GLOUCESTER: Your love deserves my thanks, but my desert
GLOUCESTER: Unmeritable shuns your high request.
GLOUCESTER: First if all obstacles were cut away,
GLOUCESTER: And that my path were even to the crown,
GLOUCESTER: As my ripe revenue and due by birth
GLOUCESTER: Yet so much is my poverty of spirit,
GLOUCESTER: So mighty and so many my defects,
GLOUCESTER: As I had rather hide me from my greatness,
GLOUCESTER: Being a bark to brook no mighty sea,
GLOUCESTER: Than in my greatness covet to be hid,
GLOUCESTER: And in the vapour of my glory smother'd.
GLOUCESTER: But, God be thank'd, there's no need of me,
GLOUCESTER: And much I need to help you, if need were,
GLOUCESTER: The royal tree hath left us royal fruit,
GLOUCESTER: Which, mellow'd by the stealing hours of time,
GLOUCESTER: Will well become the seat of majesty,
GLOUCESTER: And make, no doubt, us happy by his reign.
GLOUCESTER: On him I lay what you would lay on me,
GLOUCESTER: The right and fortune of his happy stars,
GLOUCESTER: Which God defend that I should wring from him!
BUCKINGHAM: My lord, this argues conscience in your grace,
BUCKINGHAM: But the respects thereof are nice and trivial,
BUCKINGHAM: All circumstances well considered.
BUCKINGHAM: You say that Edward is your brother's son:
BUCKINGHAM: So say we too, but not by Edward's wife,
BUCKINGHAM: For first he was contract to Lady Lucy--
BUCKINGHAM: Your mother lives a witness to that vow--
BUCKINGHAM: And afterward by substitute betroth'd
BUCKINGHAM: To Bona, sister to the King of France.
BUCKINGHAM: These both put by a poor petitioner,
BUCKINGHAM: A care-crazed mother of a many children,
BUCKINGHAM: A beauty-waning and distressed widow,
BUCKINGHAM: Even in the afternoon of her best days,
BUCKINGHAM: Made prize and purchase of his lustful eye,
BUCKINGHAM: Seduced the pitch and height of all his thoughts
BUCKINGHAM: To base declension and loathed bigamy
BUCKINGHAM: By her, in his unlawful bed, he got
BUCKINGHAM: This Edward, whom our manners term the prince.
BUCKINGHAM: More bitterly could I expostulate,
BUCKINGHAM: Save that, for reverence to some alive,
BUCKINGHAM: I give a sparing limit to my tongue.
BUCKINGHAM: Then, good my lord, take to your royal self
BUCKINGHAM: This proffer'd benefit of dignity,
BUCKINGHAM: If non to bless us and the land withal,
BUCKINGHAM: Yet to draw forth your noble ancestry
BUCKINGHAM: From the corruption of abusing times,
BUCKINGHAM: Unto a lineal true-derived course.
Lord Mayor: Do, good my lord, your citizens entreat you.
BUCKINGHAM: Refuse not, mighty lord, this proffer'd love.
CATESBY: O, make them joyful, grant their lawful suit!
GLOUCESTER: Alas, why would you heap these cares on me?
GLOUCESTER: I am unfit for state and majesty,
GLOUCESTER: I do beseech you, take it not amiss,
GLOUCESTER: I cannot nor I will not yield to you.
BUCKINGHAM: If you refuse it,--as, in love and zeal,
BUCKINGHAM: Loath to depose the child, Your brother's son,
BUCKINGHAM: As well we know your tenderness of heart
BUCKINGHAM: And gentle, kind, effeminate remorse,
BUCKINGHAM: Which we have noted in you to your kin,
BUCKINGHAM: And egally indeed to all estates,--
BUCKINGHAM: Yet whether you accept our suit or no,
BUCKINGHAM: Your brother's son shall never reign our king,
BUCKINGHAM: But we will plant some other in the throne,
BUCKINGHAM: To the disgrace and downfall of your house:
BUCKINGHAM: And in this resolution here we leave you.--
BUCKINGHAM: Come, citizens: 'zounds! I'll entreat no more.
GLOUCESTER: O, do not swear, my lord of Buckingham.
NARRATOR: Exit BUCKINGHAM with the Citizens
CATESBY: Call them again, my lord, and accept their suit.
ANOTHER: Do, good my lord, lest all the land do rue it.
GLOUCESTER: Would you enforce me to a world of care?
GLOUCESTER: Well, call them again. I am not made of stone,
GLOUCESTER: But penetrable to your. kind entreats,
GLOUCESTER: Albeit against my conscience and my soul.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BUCKINGHAM and the rest
GLOUCESTER: Cousin of Buckingham, and you sage, grave men,
GLOUCESTER: Since you will buckle fortune on my back,
GLOUCESTER: To bear her burthen, whether I will or no,
GLOUCESTER: I must have patience to endure the load:
GLOUCESTER: But if black scandal or foul-faced reproach
GLOUCESTER: Attend the sequel of your imposition,
GLOUCESTER: Your mere enforcement shall acquittance me
GLOUCESTER: From all the impure blots and stains thereof,
GLOUCESTER: For God he knows, and you may partly see,
GLOUCESTER: How far I am from the desire thereof.
Lord Mayor: God bless your grace! we see it, and will say it.
GLOUCESTER: In saying so, you shall but say the truth.
BUCKINGHAM: Then I salute you with this kingly title:
BUCKINGHAM: Long live Richard, England's royal king!
Citizens: Amen.
BUCKINGHAM: To-morrow will it please you to be crown'd?
GLOUCESTER: Even when you please, since you will have it so.
BUCKINGHAM: To-morrow, then, we will attend your grace:
BUCKINGHAM: And so most joyfully we take our leave.
GLOUCESTER: Come, let us to our holy task again.
GLOUCESTER: Farewell, good cousin, farewell, gentle friends.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before the Tower.
NARRATOR: Enter, on one side, QUEEN ELIZABETH, DUCHESS OF  YORK, and DORSET, on the other, ANNE, Duchess of  Gloucester, leading Lady Margaret Plantagenet, CLARENCE's young Daughter
DUCHESS OF YORK: Who m eets us here?  my niece Plantagenet
DUCHESS OF YORK: Led in the hand of her kind aunt of Gloucester?
DUCHESS OF YORK: Now, for my life, she's wandering to the Tower,
DUCHESS OF YORK: On pure heart's love to greet the tender princes.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Daughter, well met.
LADY ANNE: God give your graces both
LADY ANNE: A happy and a joyful time of day!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: As much to you, good sister! Whither away?
LADY ANNE: No farther than the Tower, and, as I guess,
LADY ANNE: Upon the like devotion as yourselves,
LADY ANNE: To gratulate the gentle princes there.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Kind sister, thanks: we'll enter all together.
NARRATOR: Enter BRAKENBURY
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And, in good time, here the lieutenant comes.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Master lieutenant, pray you, by your leave,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: How doth the prince, and my young son of York?
BRAKENBURY: Right well, dear madam. By your patience,
BRAKENBURY: I may not suffer you to visit them,
BRAKENBURY: The king hath straitly charged the contrary.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The king! why, who's that?
BRAKENBURY: I cry you mercy: I mean the lord protector.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: The Lord protect him from that kingly title!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Hath he set bounds betwixt their love and me?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: I am their mother, who should keep me from them?
DUCHESS OF YORK: I am their fathers mother, I will see them.
LADY ANNE: Their aunt I am in law, in love their mother:
LADY ANNE: Then bring me to their sights, I'll bear thy blame
LADY ANNE: And take thy office from thee, on my peril.
BRAKENBURY: No, madam, no, I may not leave it so:
BRAKENBURY: I am bound by oath, and therefore pardon me.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter LORD STANLEY
LORD STANLEY: Let me but meet you, ladies, one hour hence,
LORD STANLEY: And I'll salute your grace of York as mother,
LORD STANLEY: And reverend looker on, of two fair queens.
NARRATOR: To LADY ANNE
LORD STANLEY: Come, madam, you must straight to Westminster,
LORD STANLEY: There to be crowned Richard's royal queen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O, cut my lace in sunder, that my pent heart
QUEEN ELIZABETH: May have some scope to beat, or else I swoon
QUEEN ELIZABETH: With this dead-killing news!
LADY ANNE: Despiteful tidings! O unpleasing news!
DORSET: Be of good cheer: mother, how fares your grace?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O Dorset, speak not to me, get thee hence!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Death and destruction dog thee at the heels,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Thy mother's name is ominous to children.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: If thou wilt outstrip death, go cross the seas,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And live with Richmond, from the reach of hell
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Go, hie thee, hie thee from this slaughter-house,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Lest thou increase the number of the dead,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And make me die the thrall of Margaret's curse,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Nor mother, wife, nor England's counted queen.
LORD STANLEY: Full of wise care is this your counsel, madam.
LORD STANLEY: Take all the swift advantage of the hours,
LORD STANLEY: You shall have letters from me to my son
LORD STANLEY: To meet you on the way, and welcome you.
LORD STANLEY: Be not ta'en tardy by unwise delay.
DUCHESS OF YORK: O ill-dispersing wind of misery!
DUCHESS OF YORK: O my accursed womb, the bed of death!
DUCHESS OF YORK: A cockatrice hast thou hatch'd to the world,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Whose unavoided eye is murderous.
LORD STANLEY: Come, madam, come, I in all haste was sent.
LADY ANNE: And I in all unwillingness will go.
LADY ANNE: I would to God that the inclusive verge
LADY ANNE: Of golden metal that must round my brow
LADY ANNE: Were red-hot steel, to sear me to the brain!
LADY ANNE: Anointed let me be with deadly venom,
LADY ANNE: And die, ere men can say, God save the queen!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Go, go, poor soul, I envy not thy glory
QUEEN ELIZABETH: To feed my humour, wish thyself no harm.
LADY ANNE: No! why?  When he that is my husband now
LADY ANNE: Came to me, as I follow'd Henry's corse,
LADY ANNE: When scarce the blood was well wash'd from his hands
LADY ANNE: Which issued from my other angel husband
LADY ANNE: And that dead saint which then I weeping follow'd,
LADY ANNE: O, when, I say, I look'd on Richard's face,
LADY ANNE: This was my wish: 'Be thou,' quoth I, ' accursed,
LADY ANNE: For making me, so young, so old a widow!
LADY ANNE: And, when thou wed'st, let sorrow haunt thy bed,
LADY ANNE: And be thy wife--if any be so mad--
LADY ANNE: As miserable by the life of thee
LADY ANNE: As thou hast made me by my dear lord's death!
LADY ANNE: Lo, ere I can repeat this curse again,
LADY ANNE: Even in so short a space, my woman's heart
LADY ANNE: Grossly grew captive to his honey words
LADY ANNE: And proved the subject of my own soul's curse,
LADY ANNE: Which ever since hath kept my eyes from rest,
LADY ANNE: For never yet one hour in his bed
LADY ANNE: Have I enjoy'd the golden dew of sleep,
LADY ANNE: But have been waked by his timorous dreams.
LADY ANNE: Besides, he hates me for my father Warwick,
LADY ANNE: And will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Poor heart, adieu! I pity thy complaining.
LADY ANNE: No more than from my soul I mourn for yours.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Farewell, thou woful welcomer of glory!
LADY ANNE: Adieu, poor soul, that takest thy leave of it!
DUCHESS OF YORK: [To DORSET]
DUCHESS OF YORK: Go thou to Richmond, and good fortune guide thee!
NARRATOR: To LADY ANNE
DUCHESS OF YORK: Go thou to Richard, and good angels guard thee!
NARRATOR: To QUEEN ELIZABETH
DUCHESS OF YORK: Go thou to sanctuary, and good thoughts possess thee!
DUCHESS OF YORK: I to my grave, where peace and rest lie with me!
DUCHESS OF YORK: Eighty odd years of sorrow have I seen,
DUCHESS OF YORK: And each hour's joy wrecked with a week of teen.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Stay, yet look back with me unto the Tower.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Whom envy hath immured within your walls!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Rough cradle for such little pretty ones!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Rude ragged nurse, old sullen playfellow
QUEEN ELIZABETH: For tender princes, use my babies well!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: So foolish sorrow bids your stones farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. London. The palace.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Enter KING RICHARD III, in pomp, crowned, BUCKINGHAM, CATESBY, a page, and others
KING RICHARD III: Stand all apart Cousin of Buckingham!
BUCKINGHAM: My gracious sovereign?
KING RICHARD III: Give me thy hand.
NARRATOR: Here he ascendeth his throne
KING RICHARD III: Thus high, by thy advice
KING RICHARD III: And thy assistance, is King Richard seated,
KING RICHARD III: But shall we wear these honours for a day?
KING RICHARD III: Or shall they last, and we rejoice in them?
BUCKINGHAM: Still live they and for ever may they last!
KING RICHARD III: O Buckingham, now do I play the touch,
KING RICHARD III: To try if thou be current gold indeed
KING RICHARD III: Young Edward lives: think now what I would say.
BUCKINGHAM: Say on, my loving lord.
KING RICHARD III: Why, Buckingham, I say, I would be king,
BUCKINGHAM: Why, so you are, my thrice renowned liege.
KING RICHARD III: Ha! am I king? 'tis so: but Edward lives.
BUCKINGHAM: True, noble prince.
KING RICHARD III: O bitter consequence,
KING RICHARD III: That Edward still should live! 'True, noble prince!'
KING RICHARD III: Cousin, thou wert not wont to be so dull:
KING RICHARD III: Shall I be plain? I wish the bastards dead,
KING RICHARD III: And I would have it suddenly perform'd.
KING RICHARD III: What sayest thou? speak suddenly, be brief.
BUCKINGHAM: Your grace may do your pleasure.
KING RICHARD III: Tut, tut, thou art all ice, thy kindness freezeth:
KING RICHARD III: Say, have I thy consent that they shall die?
BUCKINGHAM: Give me some breath, some little pause, my lord
BUCKINGHAM: Before I positively herein:
BUCKINGHAM: I will resolve your grace immediately.
NARRATOR: Exit
CATESBY: [Aside to a stander by]
CATESBY: The king is angry: see, he bites the lip.
KING RICHARD III: I will converse with iron-witted fools
KING RICHARD III: And unrespective boys: none are for me
KING RICHARD III: That look into me with considerate eyes:
KING RICHARD III: High-reaching Buckingham grows circumspect.
KING RICHARD III: Boy!
Page: My lord?
KING RICHARD III: Know'st thou not any whom corrupting gold
KING RICHARD III: Would tempt unto a close exploit of death?
Page: My lord, I know a discontented gentleman,
Page: Whose humble means match not his haughty mind:
Page: Gold were as good as twenty orators,
Page: And will, no doubt, tempt him to any thing.
KING RICHARD III: What is his name?
Page: His name, my lord, is Tyrrel.
KING RICHARD III: I partly know the man: go, call him hither.
NARRATOR: Exit Page
KING RICHARD III: The deep-revolving witty Buckingham
KING RICHARD III: No more shall be the neighbour to my counsel:
KING RICHARD III: Hath he so long held out with me untired,
KING RICHARD III: And stops he now for breath?
NARRATOR: Enter STANLEY
KING RICHARD III: How now! what news with you?
STANLEY: My lord, I hear the Marquis Dorset's fled
STANLEY: To Richmond, in those parts beyond the sea
STANLEY: Where he abides.
NARRATOR: Stands apart
KING RICHARD III: Catesby!
CATESBY: My lord?
KING RICHARD III: Rumour it abroad
KING RICHARD III: That Anne, my wife, is sick and like to die:
KING RICHARD III: I will take order for her keeping close.
KING RICHARD III: Inquire me out some mean-born gentleman,
KING RICHARD III: Whom I will marry straight to Clarence' daughter:
KING RICHARD III: The boy is foolish, and I fear not him.
KING RICHARD III: Look, how thou dream'st! I say again, give out
KING RICHARD III: That Anne my wife is sick and like to die:
KING RICHARD III: About it, for it stands me much upon,
KING RICHARD III: To stop all hopes whose growth may damage me.
NARRATOR: Exit CATESBY
KING RICHARD III: I must be married to my brother's daughter,
KING RICHARD III: Or else my kingdom stands on brittle glass.
KING RICHARD III: Murder her brothers, and then marry her!
KING RICHARD III: Uncertain way of gain! But I am in
KING RICHARD III: So far in blood that sin will pluck on sin:
KING RICHARD III: Tear-falling pity dwells not in this eye.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Page, with TYRREL
KING RICHARD III: Is thy name Tyrrel?
TYRREL: James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
KING RICHARD III: Art thou, indeed?
TYRREL: Prove me, my gracious sovereign.
KING RICHARD III: Darest thou resolve to kill a friend of mine?
TYRREL: Ay, my lord,
TYRREL: But I had rather kill two enemies.
KING RICHARD III: Why, there thou hast it: two deep enemies,
KING RICHARD III: Foes to my rest and my sweet sleep's disturbers
KING RICHARD III: Are they that I would have thee deal upon:
KING RICHARD III: Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
TYRREL: Let me have open means to come to them,
TYRREL: And soon I'll rid you from the fear of them.
KING RICHARD III: Thou sing'st sweet music. Hark, come hither, Tyrrel
KING RICHARD III: Go, by this token: rise, and lend thine ear:
NARRATOR: Whispers
KING RICHARD III: There is no more but so: say it is done,
KING RICHARD III: And I will love thee, and prefer thee too.
TYRREL: 'Tis done, my gracious lord.
KING RICHARD III: Shall we hear from thee, Tyrrel, ere we sleep?
TYRREL: Ye shall, my Lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter BUCKINGHAM
BUCKINGHAM: My Lord, I have consider'd in my mind
BUCKINGHAM: The late demand that you did sound me in.
KING RICHARD III: Well, let that pass. Dorset is fled to Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM: I hear that news, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: Stanley, he is your wife's son well, look to it.
BUCKINGHAM: My lord, I claim your gift, my due by promise,
BUCKINGHAM: For which your honour and your faith is pawn'd,
BUCKINGHAM: The earldom of Hereford and the moveables
BUCKINGHAM: The which you promised I should possess.
KING RICHARD III: Stanley, look to your wife, if she convey
KING RICHARD III: Letters to Richmond, you shall answer it.
BUCKINGHAM: What says your highness to my just demand?
KING RICHARD III: As I remember, Henry the Sixth
KING RICHARD III: Did prophesy that Richmond should be king,
KING RICHARD III: When Richmond was a little peevish boy.
KING RICHARD III: A king, perhaps, perhaps,--
BUCKINGHAM: My lord!
KING RICHARD III: How chance the prophet could not at that time
KING RICHARD III: Have told me, I being by, that I should kill him?
BUCKINGHAM: My lord, your promise for the earldom,--
KING RICHARD III: Richmond! When last I was at Exeter,
KING RICHARD III: The mayor in courtesy show'd me the castle,
KING RICHARD III: And call'd it Rougemont: at which name I started,
KING RICHARD III: Because a bard of Ireland told me once
KING RICHARD III: I should not live long after I saw Richmond.
BUCKINGHAM: My Lord!
KING RICHARD III: Ay, what's o'clock?
BUCKINGHAM: I am thus bold to put your grace in mind
BUCKINGHAM: Of what you promised me.
KING RICHARD III: Well, but what's o'clock?
BUCKINGHAM: Upon the stroke of ten.
KING RICHARD III: Well, let it strike.
BUCKINGHAM: Why let it strike?
KING RICHARD III: Because that, like a Jack, thou keep'st the stroke
KING RICHARD III: Betwixt thy begging and my meditation.
KING RICHARD III: I am not in the giving vein to-day.
BUCKINGHAM: Why, then resolve me whether you will or no.
KING RICHARD III: Tut, tut,
KING RICHARD III: Thou troublest me, am not in the vein.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but BUCKINGHAM
BUCKINGHAM: Is it even so? rewards he my true service
BUCKINGHAM: With such deep contempt made I him king for this?
BUCKINGHAM: O, let me think on Hastings, and be gone
BUCKINGHAM: To Brecknock, while my fearful head is on!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same.
NARRATOR: Enter TYRREL
TYRREL: The tyrannous and bloody deed is done.
TYRREL: The most arch of piteous massacre
TYRREL: That ever yet this land was guilty of.
TYRREL: Dighton and Forrest, whom I did suborn
TYRREL: To do this ruthless piece of butchery,
TYRREL: Although they were flesh'd villains, bloody dogs,
TYRREL: Melting with tenderness and kind compassion
TYRREL: Wept like two children in their deaths' sad stories.
TYRREL: 'Lo, thus' quoth Dighton, 'lay those tender babes:'
TYRREL: 'Thus, thus,' quoth Forrest, 'girdling one another
TYRREL: Within their innocent alabaster arms:
TYRREL: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk,
TYRREL: Which in their summer beauty kiss'd each other.
TYRREL: A book of prayers on their pillow lay,
TYRREL: Which once,' quoth Forrest, 'almost changed my mind,
TYRREL: But O! the devil'--there the villain stopp'd
TYRREL: Whilst Dighton thus told on: 'We smothered
TYRREL: The most replenished sweet work of nature,
TYRREL: That from the prime creation e'er she framed.'
TYRREL: Thus both are gone with conscience and remorse,
TYRREL: They could not speak, and so I left them both,
TYRREL: To bring this tidings to the bloody king.
TYRREL: And here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD III
TYRREL: All hail, my sovereign liege!
KING RICHARD III: Kind Tyrrel, am I happy in thy news?
TYRREL: If to have done the thing you gave in charge
TYRREL: Beget your happiness, be happy then,
TYRREL: For it is done, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: But didst thou see them dead?
TYRREL: I did, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: And buried, gentle Tyrrel?
TYRREL: The chaplain of the Tower hath buried them,
TYRREL: But how or in what place I do not know.
KING RICHARD III: Come to me, Tyrrel, soon at after supper,
KING RICHARD III: And thou shalt tell the process of their death.
KING RICHARD III: Meantime, but think how I may do thee good,
KING RICHARD III: And be inheritor of thy desire.
KING RICHARD III: Farewell till soon.
NARRATOR: Exit TYRREL
KING RICHARD III: The son of Clarence have I pent up close,
KING RICHARD III: His daughter meanly have I match'd in marriage,
KING RICHARD III: The sons of Edward sleep in Abraham's bosom,
KING RICHARD III: And Anne my wife hath bid the world good night.
KING RICHARD III: Now, for I know the Breton Richmond aims
KING RICHARD III: At young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter,
KING RICHARD III: And, by that knot, looks proudly o'er the crown,
KING RICHARD III: To her I go, a jolly thriving wooer.
NARRATOR: Enter CATESBY
CATESBY: My lord!
KING RICHARD III: Good news or bad, that thou comest in so bluntly?
CATESBY: Bad news, my lord: Ely is fled to Richmond,
CATESBY: And Buckingham, back'd with the hardy Welshmen,
CATESBY: Is in the field, and still his power increaseth.
KING RICHARD III: Ely with Richmond troubles me more near
KING RICHARD III: Than Buckingham and his rash-levied army.
KING RICHARD III: Come, I have heard that fearful commenting
KING RICHARD III: Is leaden servitor to dull delay,
KING RICHARD III: Delay leads impotent and snail-paced beggary
KING RICHARD III: Then fiery expedition be my wing,
KING RICHARD III: Jove's Mercury, and herald for a king!
KING RICHARD III: Come, muster men: my counsel is my shield,
KING RICHARD III: We must be brief when traitors brave the field.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Before the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN MARGARET
QUEEN MARGARET: So, now prosperity begins to mellow
QUEEN MARGARET: And drop into the rotten mouth of death.
QUEEN MARGARET: Here in these confines slily have I lurk'd,
QUEEN MARGARET: To watch the waning of mine adversaries.
QUEEN MARGARET: A dire induction am I witness to,
QUEEN MARGARET: And will to France, hoping the consequence
QUEEN MARGARET: Will prove as bitter, black, and tragical.
QUEEN MARGARET: Withdraw thee, wretched Margaret: who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter QUEEN ELIZABETH and the DUCHESS OF YORK
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Ah, my young princes! ah, my tender babes!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My unblown flowers, new-appearing sweets!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: If yet your gentle souls fly in the air
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And be not fix'd in doom perpetual,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Hover about me with your airy wings
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And hear your mother's lamentation!
QUEEN MARGARET: Hover about her, say, that right for right
QUEEN MARGARET: Hath dimm'd your infant morn to aged night.
DUCHESS OF YORK: So many miseries have crazed my voice,
DUCHESS OF YORK: That my woe-wearied tongue is mute and dumb,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Edward Plantagenet, why art thou dead?
QUEEN MARGARET: Plantagenet doth quit Plantagenet.
QUEEN MARGARET: Edward for Edward pays a dying debt.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Wilt thou, O God, fly from such gentle lambs,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And throw them in the entrails of the wolf?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: When didst thou sleep when such a deed was done?
QUEEN MARGARET: When holy Harry died, and my sweet son.
DUCHESS OF YORK: Blind sight, dead life, poor mortal living ghost,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Woe's scene, world's shame, grave's due by life usurp'd,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Brief abstract and record of tedious days,
DUCHESS OF YORK: Rest thy unrest on England's lawful earth,
NARRATOR: Sitting down
DUCHESS OF YORK: Unlawfully made drunk with innocents' blood!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O, that thou wouldst as well afford a grave
QUEEN ELIZABETH: As thou canst yield a melancholy seat!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Then would I hide my bones, not rest them here.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O, who hath any cause to mourn but I?
NARRATOR: Sitting down by her
QUEEN MARGARET: If ancient sorrow be most reverend,
QUEEN MARGARET: Give mine the benefit of seniory,
QUEEN MARGARET: And let my woes frown on the upper hand.
QUEEN MARGARET: If sorrow can admit society,
NARRATOR: Sitting down with them
QUEEN MARGARET: Tell o'er your woes again by viewing mine:
QUEEN MARGARET: I had an Edward, till a Richard kill'd him,
QUEEN MARGARET: I had a Harry, till a Richard kill'd him:
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou hadst an Edward, till a Richard kill'd him,
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou hadst a Richard, till a Richard killed him,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I had a Richard too, and thou didst kill him,
DUCHESS OF YORK: I had a Rutland too, thou holp'st to kill him.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou hadst a Clarence too, and Richard kill'd him.
QUEEN MARGARET: From forth the kennel of thy womb hath crept
QUEEN MARGARET: A hell-hound that doth hunt us all to death:
QUEEN MARGARET: That dog, that had his teeth before his eyes,
QUEEN MARGARET: To worry lambs and lap their gentle blood,
QUEEN MARGARET: That foul defacer of God's handiwork,
QUEEN MARGARET: That excellent grand tyrant of the earth,
QUEEN MARGARET: That reigns in galled eyes of weeping souls,
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy womb let loose, to chase us to our graves.
QUEEN MARGARET: O upright, just, and true-disposing God,
QUEEN MARGARET: How do I thank thee, that this carnal cur
QUEEN MARGARET: Preys on the issue of his mother's body,
QUEEN MARGARET: And makes her pew-fellow with others' moan!
DUCHESS OF YORK: O Harry's wife, triumph not in my woes!
DUCHESS OF YORK: God witness with me, I have wept for thine.
QUEEN MARGARET: Bear with me, I am hungry for revenge,
QUEEN MARGARET: And now I cloy me with beholding it.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy Edward he is dead, that stabb'd my Edward:
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy other Edward dead, to quit my Edward,
QUEEN MARGARET: Young York he is but boot, because both they
QUEEN MARGARET: Match not the high perfection of my loss:
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy Clarence he is dead that kill'd my Edward,
QUEEN MARGARET: And the beholders of this tragic play,
QUEEN MARGARET: The adulterate Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey,
QUEEN MARGARET: Untimely smother'd in their dusky graves.
QUEEN MARGARET: Richard yet lives, hell's black intelligencer,
QUEEN MARGARET: Only reserved their factor, to buy souls
QUEEN MARGARET: And send them thither: but at hand, at hand,
QUEEN MARGARET: Ensues his piteous and unpitied end:
QUEEN MARGARET: Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray.
QUEEN MARGARET: To have him suddenly convey'd away.
QUEEN MARGARET: Cancel his bond of life, dear God, I prey,
QUEEN MARGARET: That I may live to say, The dog is dead!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O, thou didst prophesy the time would come
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That I should wish for thee to help me curse
QUEEN ELIZABETH: That bottled spider, that foul bunch-back'd toad!
QUEEN MARGARET: I call'd thee then vain flourish of my fortune,
QUEEN MARGARET: I call'd thee then poor shadow, painted queen,
QUEEN MARGARET: The presentation of but what I was,
QUEEN MARGARET: The flattering index of a direful pageant,
QUEEN MARGARET: One heaved a-high, to be hurl'd down below,
QUEEN MARGARET: A mother only mock'd with two sweet babes,
QUEEN MARGARET: A dream of what thou wert, a breath, a bubble,
QUEEN MARGARET: A sign of dignity, a garish flag,
QUEEN MARGARET: To be the aim of every dangerous shot,
QUEEN MARGARET: A queen in jest, only to fill the scene.
QUEEN MARGARET: Where is thy husband now? where be thy brothers?
QUEEN MARGARET: Where are thy children? wherein dost thou, joy?
QUEEN MARGARET: Who sues to thee and cries 'God save the queen'?
QUEEN MARGARET: Where be the bending peers that flatter'd thee?
