QUEEN MARGARET: Where be the thronging troops that follow'd thee?
QUEEN MARGARET: Decline all this, and see what now thou art:
QUEEN MARGARET: For happy wife, a most distressed widow,
QUEEN MARGARET: For joyful mother, one that wails the name,
QUEEN MARGARET: For queen, a very caitiff crown'd with care,
QUEEN MARGARET: For one being sued to, one that humbly sues,
QUEEN MARGARET: For one that scorn'd at me, now scorn'd of me,
QUEEN MARGARET: For one being fear'd of all, now fearing one,
QUEEN MARGARET: For one commanding all, obey'd of none.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thus hath the course of justice wheel'd about,
QUEEN MARGARET: And left thee but a very prey to time,
QUEEN MARGARET: Having no more but thought of what thou wert,
QUEEN MARGARET: To torture thee the more, being what thou art.
QUEEN MARGARET: Thou didst usurp my place, and dost thou not
QUEEN MARGARET: Usurp the just proportion of my sorrow?
QUEEN MARGARET: Now thy proud neck bears half my burthen'd yoke,
QUEEN MARGARET: From which even here I slip my weary neck,
QUEEN MARGARET: And leave the burthen of it all on thee.
QUEEN MARGARET: Farewell, York's wife, and queen of sad mischance:
QUEEN MARGARET: These English woes will make me smile in France.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: O thou well skill'd in curses, stay awhile,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: And teach me how to curse mine enemies!
QUEEN MARGARET: Forbear to sleep the nights, and fast the days,
QUEEN MARGARET: Compare dead happiness with living woe,
QUEEN MARGARET: Think that thy babes were fairer than they were,
QUEEN MARGARET: And he that slew them fouler than he is:
QUEEN MARGARET: Bettering thy loss makes the bad causer worse:
QUEEN MARGARET: Revolving this will teach thee how to curse.
QUEEN ELIZABETH: My words are dull, O, quicken them with thine!
QUEEN MARGARET: Thy woes will make them sharp, and pierce like mine.
NARRATOR: Exit
DUCHESS OF YORK: Why should calamity be full of words?
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Windy attorneys to their client woes,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Airy succeeders of intestate joys,
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Poor breathing orators of miseries!
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Let them have scope: though what they do impart
QUEEN ELIZABETH: Help not all, yet do they ease the heart.

DUCHESS OF YORK: My damned son, which thy two sweet sons smother'd.
DUCHESS OF YORK: I hear his drum: be copious in exclaims.

KING RICHARD III: Hath any well-advised friend proclaim'd
KING RICHARD III: Reward to him that brings the traitor in?
Third Messenger: Such proclamation hath been made, my liege.
NARRATOR: Enter another Messenger
Fourth Messenger: Sir Thomas Lovel and Lord Marquis Dorset,
Fourth Messenger: 'Tis said, my liege, in Yorkshire are in arms.
Fourth Messenger: Yet this good comfort bring I to your grace,
Fourth Messenger: The Breton navy is dispersed by tempest:
Fourth Messenger: Richmond, in Yorkshire, sent out a boat
Fourth Messenger: Unto the shore, to ask those on the banks
Fourth Messenger: If they were his assistants, yea or no,
Fourth Messenger: Who answer'd him, they came from Buckingham.
Fourth Messenger: Upon his party: he, mistrusting them,
Fourth Messenger: Hoisted sail and made away for Brittany.
KING RICHARD III: March on, march on, since we are up in arms,
KING RICHARD III: If not to fight with foreign enemies,
KING RICHARD III: Yet to beat down these rebels here at home.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CATESBY
CATESBY: My liege, the Duke of Buckingham is taken,
CATESBY: That is the best news: that the Earl of Richmond
CATESBY: Is with a mighty power landed at Milford,
CATESBY: Is colder tidings, yet they must be told.
KING RICHARD III: Away towards Salisbury! while we reason here,
KING RICHARD III: A royal battle might be won and lost
KING RICHARD III: Some one take order Buckingham be brought
KING RICHARD III: To Salisbury, the rest march on with me.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Lord Derby's house.
NARRATOR: Enter DERBY and SIR CHRISTOPHER URSWICK
DERBY: Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me:
DERBY: That in the sty of this most bloody boar
DERBY: My son George Stanley is frank'd up in hold:
DERBY: If I revolt, off goes young George's head,
DERBY: The fear of that withholds my present aid.
DERBY: But, tell me, where is princely Richmond now?
CHRISTOPHER: At Pembroke, or at Harford-west, in Wales.
DERBY: What men of name resort to him?
CHRISTOPHER: Sir Walter Herbert, a renowned soldier,
CHRISTOPHER: Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley,
CHRISTOPHER: Oxford, redoubted Pembroke, Sir James Blunt,
CHRISTOPHER: And Rice ap Thomas with a valiant crew,
CHRISTOPHER: And many more of noble fame and worth:
CHRISTOPHER: And towards London they do bend their course,
CHRISTOPHER: If by the way they be not fought withal.
DERBY: Return unto thy lord, commend me to him:
DERBY: Tell him the queen hath heartily consented
DERBY: He shall espouse Elizabeth her daughter.
DERBY: These letters will resolve him of my mind. Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Salisbury. An open place.
NARRATOR: Enter the Sheriff, and BUCKINGHAM, with halberds, led to execution
BUCKINGHAM: Will not King Richard let me speak with him?
Sheriff: No, my good lord, therefore be patient.
BUCKINGHAM: Hastings, and Edward's children, Rivers, Grey,
BUCKINGHAM: Holy King Henry, and thy fair son Edward,
BUCKINGHAM: Vaughan, and all that have miscarried
BUCKINGHAM: By underhand corrupted foul injustice,
BUCKINGHAM: If that your moody discontented souls
BUCKINGHAM: Do through the clouds behold this present hour,
BUCKINGHAM: Even for revenge mock my destruction!
BUCKINGHAM: This is All-Souls' day, fellows, is it not?
Sheriff: It is, my lord.
BUCKINGHAM: Why, then All-Souls' day is my body's doomsday.
BUCKINGHAM: This is the day that, in King Edward's time,
BUCKINGHAM: I wish't might fall on me, when I was found
BUCKINGHAM: False to his children or his wife's allies
BUCKINGHAM: This is the day wherein I wish'd to fall
BUCKINGHAM: By the false faith of him I trusted most,
BUCKINGHAM: This, this All-Souls' day to my fearful soul
BUCKINGHAM: Is the determined respite of my wrongs:
BUCKINGHAM: That high All-Seer that I dallied with
BUCKINGHAM: Hath turn'd my feigned prayer on my head
BUCKINGHAM: And given in earnest what I begg'd in jest.
BUCKINGHAM: Thus doth he force the swords of wicked men
BUCKINGHAM: To turn their own points on their masters' bosoms:
BUCKINGHAM: Now Margaret's curse is fallen upon my head,
BUCKINGHAM: 'When he,' quoth she, 'shall split thy heart with sorrow,
BUCKINGHAM: Remember Margaret was a prophetess.'
BUCKINGHAM: Come, sirs, convey me to the block of shame,
BUCKINGHAM: Wrong hath but wrong, and blame the due of blame.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The camp near Tamworth.
NARRATOR: Enter RICHMOND, OXFORD, BLUNT, HERBERT, and others, with drum and colours
RICHMOND: Fellows in arms, and my most loving friends,
RICHMOND: Bruised underneath the yoke of tyranny,
RICHMOND: Thus far into the bowels of the land
RICHMOND: Have we march'd on without impediment,
RICHMOND: And here receive we from our father Stanley
RICHMOND: Lines of fair comfort and encouragement.
RICHMOND: The wretched, bloody, and usurping boar,
RICHMOND: That spoil'd your summer fields and fruitful vines,
RICHMOND: Swills your warm blood like wash, and makes his trough
RICHMOND: In your embowell'd bosoms, this foul swine
RICHMOND: Lies now even in the centre of this isle,
RICHMOND: Near to the town of Leicester, as we learn
RICHMOND: From Tamworth thither is but one day's march.
RICHMOND: In God's name, cheerly on, courageous friends,
RICHMOND: To reap the harvest of perpetual peace
RICHMOND: By this one bloody trial of sharp war.
OXFORD: Every man's conscience is a thousand swords,
OXFORD: To fight against that bloody homicide.
HERBERT: I doubt not but his friends will fly to us.
BLUNT: He hath no friends but who are friends for fear.
BLUNT: Which in his greatest need will shrink from him.
RICHMOND: All for our vantage. Then, in God's name, march:
RICHMOND: True hope is swift, and flies with swallow's wings:
RICHMOND: Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Bosworth Field.
NARRATOR: Enter KING RICHARD III in arms, with NORFOLK, SURREY, and others
KING RICHARD III: Here pitch our tents, even here in Bosworth field.
KING RICHARD III: My Lord of Surrey, why look you so sad?
SURREY: My heart is ten times lighter than my looks.
KING RICHARD III: My Lord of Norfolk,--
NORFOLK: Here, most gracious liege.
KING RICHARD III: Norfolk, we must have knocks, ha! must we not?
NORFOLK: We must both give and take, my gracious lord.
KING RICHARD III: Up with my tent there! here will I lie tonight,
KING RICHARD III: But where to-morrow?  Well, all's one for that.
KING RICHARD III: Who hath descried the number of the foe?
NORFOLK: Six or seven thousand is their utmost power.
KING RICHARD III: Why, our battalion trebles that account:
KING RICHARD III: Besides, the king's name is a tower of strength,
KING RICHARD III: Which they upon the adverse party want.
KING RICHARD III: Up with my tent there! Valiant gentlemen,
KING RICHARD III: Let us survey the vantage of the field
KING RICHARD III: Call for some men of sound direction
KING RICHARD III: Let's want no discipline, make no delay,
KING RICHARD III: For, lords, to-morrow is a busy day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Enter, on the other side of the field, RICHMOND,  Sir William Brandon, OXFORD, and others. Some of the Soldiers pitch RICHMOND's tent
RICHMOND: The weary sun hath made a golden set,
RICHMOND: And by the bright track of his fiery car,
RICHMOND: Gives signal, of a goodly day to-morrow.
RICHMOND: Sir William Brandon, you shall bear my standard.
RICHMOND: Give me some ink and paper in my tent
RICHMOND: I'll draw the form and model of our battle,
RICHMOND: Limit each leader to his several charge,
RICHMOND: And part in just proportion our small strength.
RICHMOND: My Lord of Oxford, you, Sir William Brandon,
RICHMOND: And you, Sir Walter Herbert, stay with me.
RICHMOND: The Earl of Pembroke keeps his regiment:
RICHMOND: Good Captain Blunt, bear my good night to him
RICHMOND: And by the second hour in the morning
RICHMOND: Desire the earl to see me in my tent:
RICHMOND: Yet one thing more, good Blunt, before thou go'st,
RICHMOND: Where is Lord Stanley quarter'd, dost thou know?
BLUNT: Unless I have mista'en his colours much,
BLUNT: Which well I am assured I have not done,
BLUNT: His regiment lies half a mile at least
BLUNT: South from the mighty power of the king.
RICHMOND: If without peril it be possible,
RICHMOND: Good Captain Blunt, bear my good-night to him,
RICHMOND: And give him from me this most needful scroll.
BLUNT: Upon my life, my lord, I'll under-take it,
BLUNT: And so, God give you quiet rest to-night!
RICHMOND: Good night, good Captain Blunt. Come gentlemen,
RICHMOND: Let us consult upon to-morrow's business
RICHMOND: In to our tent, the air is raw and cold.
NARRATOR: They withdraw into the tent
NARRATOR: Enter, to his tent, KING RICHARD III, NORFOLK, RATCLIFF, CATESBY, and others
KING RICHARD III: What is't o'clock?
CATESBY: It's supper-time, my lord,
CATESBY: It's nine o'clock.
KING RICHARD III: I will not sup to-night.
KING RICHARD III: Give me some ink and paper.
KING RICHARD III: What, is my beaver easier than it was?
KING RICHARD III: And all my armour laid into my tent?
CATESBY: If is, my liege, and all things are in readiness.
KING RICHARD III: Good Norfolk, hie thee to thy charge,
KING RICHARD III: Use careful watch, choose trusty sentinels.
NORFOLK: I go, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: Stir with the lark to-morrow, gentle Norfolk.
NORFOLK: I warrant you, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
KING RICHARD III: Catesby!
CATESBY: My lord?
KING RICHARD III: Send out a pursuivant at arms
KING RICHARD III: To Stanley's regiment, bid him bring his power
KING RICHARD III: Before sunrising, lest his son George fall
KING RICHARD III: Into the blind cave of eternal night.
NARRATOR: Exit CATESBY
KING RICHARD III: Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a watch.
KING RICHARD III: Saddle white Surrey for the field to-morrow.
KING RICHARD III: Look that my staves be sound, and not too heavy.
KING RICHARD III: Ratcliff!
RATCLIFF: My lord?
KING RICHARD III: Saw'st thou the melancholy Lord Northumberland?
RATCLIFF: Thomas the Earl of Surrey, and himself,
RATCLIFF: Much about cock-shut time, from troop to troop
RATCLIFF: Went through the army, cheering up the soldiers.
KING RICHARD III: So, I am satisfied. Give me a bowl of wine:
KING RICHARD III: I have not that alacrity of spirit,
KING RICHARD III: Nor cheer of mind, that I was wont to have.
KING RICHARD III: Set it down. Is ink and paper ready?
RATCLIFF: It is, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: Bid my guard watch, leave me.
KING RICHARD III: Ratcliff, about the mid of night come to my tent
KING RICHARD III: And help to arm me. Leave me, I say.
NARRATOR: Exeunt RATCLIFF and the other Attendants
NARRATOR: Enter DERBY to RICHMOND in his tent, Lords and others attending
DERBY: Fortune and victory sit on thy helm!
RICHMOND: All comfort that the dark night can afford
RICHMOND: Be to thy person, noble father-in-law!
RICHMOND: Tell me, how fares our loving mother?
DERBY: I, by attorney, bless thee from thy mother
DERBY: Who prays continually for Richmond's good:
DERBY: So much for that. The silent hours steal on,
DERBY: And flaky darkness breaks within the east.
DERBY: In brief,--for so the season bids us be,--
DERBY: Prepare thy battle early in the morning,
DERBY: And put thy fortune to the arbitrement
DERBY: Of bloody strokes and mortal-staring war.
DERBY: I, as I may--that which I would I cannot,--
DERBY: With best advantage will deceive the time,
DERBY: And aid thee in this doubtful shock of arms:
DERBY: But on thy side I may not be too forward
DERBY: Lest, being seen, thy brother, tender George,
DERBY: Be executed in his father's sight.
DERBY: Farewell: the leisure and the fearful time
DERBY: Cuts off the ceremonious vows of love
DERBY: And ample interchange of sweet discourse,
DERBY: Which so long sunder'd friends should dwell upon:
DERBY: God give us leisure for these rites of love!
DERBY: Once more, adieu: be valiant, and speed well!
RICHMOND: Good lords, conduct him to his regiment:
RICHMOND: I'll strive, with troubled thoughts, to take a nap,
RICHMOND: Lest leaden slumber peise me down to-morrow,
RICHMOND: When I should mount with wings of victory:
RICHMOND: Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but RICHMOND
RICHMOND: O Thou, whose captain I account myself,
RICHMOND: Look on my forces with a gracious eye,
RICHMOND: Put in their hands thy bruising irons of wrath,
RICHMOND: That they may crush down with a heavy fall
RICHMOND: The usurping helmets of our adversaries!
RICHMOND: Make us thy ministers of chastisement,
RICHMOND: That we may praise thee in the victory!
RICHMOND: To thee I do commend my watchful soul,
RICHMOND: Ere I let fall the windows of mine eyes:
RICHMOND: Sleeping and waking, O, defend me still!
NARRATOR: Sleeps
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of Prince Edward, son to King Henry VI
RICHMOND: Ghost
of Prince Edward: [To KING RICHARD III]
of Prince Edward: Let me sit heavy on thy soul to-morrow!
of Prince Edward: Think, how thou stab'dst me in my prime of youth
of Prince Edward: At Tewksbury: despair, therefore, and die!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
of Prince Edward: Be cheerful, Richmond, for the wronged souls
of Prince Edward: Of butcher'd princes fight in thy behalf
of Prince Edward: King Henry's issue, Richmond, comforts thee.
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of King Henry VI
of Prince Edward: Ghost
of King Henry VI: [To KING RICHARD III]
of King Henry VI: When I was mortal, my anointed body
of King Henry VI: By thee was punched full of deadly holes
of King Henry VI: Think on the Tower and me: despair, and die!
of King Henry VI: Harry the Sixth bids thee despair, and die!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
of King Henry VI: Virtuous and holy, be thou conqueror!
of King Henry VI: Harry, that prophesied thou shouldst be king,
of King Henry VI: Doth comfort thee in thy sleep: live, and flourish!
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of CLARENCE
Ghost of CLARENCE: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of CLARENCE: Let me sit heavy on thy soul to-morrow!
Ghost of CLARENCE: I, that was wash'd to death with fulsome wine,
Ghost of CLARENCE: Poor Clarence, by thy guile betrayed to death!
Ghost of CLARENCE: To-morrow in the battle think on me,
Ghost of CLARENCE: And fall thy edgeless sword: despair, and die!--
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
Ghost of CLARENCE: Thou offspring of the house of Lancaster
Ghost of CLARENCE: The wronged heirs of York do pray for thee
Ghost of CLARENCE: Good angels guard thy battle! live, and flourish!
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghosts of RIVERS, GRAY, and VAUGHAN
Ghost of RIVERS: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of RIVERS: Let me sit heavy on thy soul to-morrow,
Ghost of RIVERS: Rivers. that died at Pomfret! despair, and die!
Ghost of GREY: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of GREY: Think upon Grey, and let thy soul despair!
Ghost of VAUGHAN: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of VAUGHAN: Think upon Vaughan, and, with guilty fear,
Ghost of VAUGHAN: Let fall thy lance: despair, and die!
All: [To RICHMOND]
All: Awake, and think our wrongs in Richard's bosom
All: Will conquer him! awake, and win the day!
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of HASTINGS
Ghost of HASTINGS: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of HASTINGS: Bloody and guilty, guiltily awake,
Ghost of HASTINGS: And in a bloody battle end thy days!
Ghost of HASTINGS: Think on Lord Hastings: despair, and die!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
Ghost of HASTINGS: Quiet untroubled soul, awake, awake!
Ghost of HASTINGS: Arm, fight, and conquer, for fair England's sake!
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghosts of the two young Princes
Ghost of HASTINGS: Ghosts
of young Princes: [To KING RICHARD III]
of young Princes: Dream on thy cousins smother'd in the Tower:
of young Princes: Let us be led within thy bosom, Richard,
of young Princes: And weigh thee down to ruin, shame, and death!
of young Princes: Thy nephews' souls bid thee despair and die!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
of young Princes: Sleep, Richmond, sleep in peace, and wake in joy,
of young Princes: Good angels guard thee from the boar's annoy!
of young Princes: Live, and beget a happy race of kings!
of young Princes: Edward's unhappy sons do bid thee flourish.
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of LADY ANNE
Ghost of LADY ANNE: [To KING RICHARD III]
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Richard, thy wife, that wretched Anne thy wife,
Ghost of LADY ANNE: That never slept a quiet hour with thee,
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Now fills thy sleep with perturbations
Ghost of LADY ANNE: To-morrow in the battle think on me,
Ghost of LADY ANNE: And fall thy edgeless sword: despair, and die!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Thou quiet soul, sleep thou a quiet sleep
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Dream of success and happy victory!
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Thy adversary's wife doth pray for thee.
NARRATOR: Enter the Ghost of BUCKINGHAM
Ghost of LADY ANNE: Ghost
of BUCKINGHAM: [To KING RICHARD III]
of BUCKINGHAM: The last was I that helped thee to the crown,
of BUCKINGHAM: The last was I that felt thy tyranny:
of BUCKINGHAM: O, in the battle think on Buckingham,
of BUCKINGHAM: And die in terror of thy guiltiness!
of BUCKINGHAM: Dream on, dream on, of bloody deeds and death:
of BUCKINGHAM: Fainting, despair, despairing, yield thy breath!
NARRATOR: To RICHMOND
of BUCKINGHAM: I died for hope ere I could lend thee aid:
of BUCKINGHAM: But cheer thy heart, and be thou not dismay'd:
of BUCKINGHAM: God and good angel fight on Richmond's side,
of BUCKINGHAM: And Richard falls in height of all his pride.
NARRATOR: The Ghosts vanish
NARRATOR: KING RICHARD III starts out of his dream
KING RICHARD III: Give me another horse: bind up my wounds.
KING RICHARD III: Have mercy, Jesu!--Soft! I did but dream.
KING RICHARD III: O coward conscience, how dost thou afflict me!
KING RICHARD III: The lights burn blue. It is now dead midnight.
KING RICHARD III: Cold fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh.
KING RICHARD III: What do I fear?  myself?  there's none else by:
KING RICHARD III: Richard loves Richard, that is, I am I.
KING RICHARD III: Is there a murderer here?  No. Yes, I am:
KING RICHARD III: Then fly. What, from myself?   Great reason why:
KING RICHARD III: Lest I revenge. What, myself upon myself?
KING RICHARD III: Alack. I love myself. Wherefore?  for any good
KING RICHARD III: That I myself have done unto myself?
KING RICHARD III: O, no! alas, I rather hate myself
KING RICHARD III: For hateful deeds committed by myself!
KING RICHARD III: I am a villain: yet I lie. I am not.
KING RICHARD III: Fool, of thyself speak well: fool, do not flatter.
KING RICHARD III: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues,
KING RICHARD III: And every tongue brings in a several tale,
KING RICHARD III: And every tale condemns me for a villain.
KING RICHARD III: Perjury, perjury, in the high'st degree
KING RICHARD III: Murder, stem murder, in the direst degree,
KING RICHARD III: All several sins, all used in each degree,
KING RICHARD III: Throng to the bar, crying all, Guilty! guilty!
KING RICHARD III: I shall despair. There is no creature loves me,
KING RICHARD III: And if I die, no soul shall pity me:
KING RICHARD III: Nay, wherefore should they, since that I myself
KING RICHARD III: Find in myself no pity to myself?
KING RICHARD III: Methought the souls of all that I had murder'd
KING RICHARD III: Came to my tent, and every one did threat
KING RICHARD III: To-morrow's vengeance on the head of Richard.
NARRATOR: Enter RATCLIFF
RATCLIFF: My lord!
KING RICHARD III: 'Zounds! who is there?
RATCLIFF: Ratcliff, my lord, 'tis I. The early village-cock
RATCLIFF: Hath twice done salutation to the morn,
RATCLIFF: Your friends are up, and buckle on their armour.
KING RICHARD III: O Ratcliff, I have dream'd a fearful dream!
KING RICHARD III: What thinkest thou, will our friends prove all true?
RATCLIFF: No doubt, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: O Ratcliff, I fear, I fear,--
RATCLIFF: Nay, good my lord, be not afraid of shadows.
KING RICHARD III: By the apostle Paul, shadows to-night
KING RICHARD III: Have struck more terror to the soul of Richard
KING RICHARD III: Than can the substance of ten thousand soldiers
KING RICHARD III: Armed in proof, and led by shallow Richmond.
KING RICHARD III: It is not yet near day. Come, go with me,
KING RICHARD III: Under our tents I'll play the eaves-dropper,
KING RICHARD III: To see if any mean to shrink from me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Enter the Lords to RICHMOND, sitting in his tent
LORDS: Good morrow, Richmond!
RICHMOND: Cry mercy, lords and watchful gentlemen,
RICHMOND: That you have ta'en a tardy sluggard here.
LORDS: How have you slept, my lord?
RICHMOND: The sweetest sleep, and fairest-boding dreams
RICHMOND: That ever enter'd in a drowsy head,
RICHMOND: Have I since your departure had, my lords.
RICHMOND: Methought their souls, whose bodies Richard murder'd,
RICHMOND: Came to my tent, and cried on victory:
RICHMOND: I promise you, my soul is very jocund
RICHMOND: In the remembrance of so fair a dream.
RICHMOND: How far into the morning is it, lords?
LORDS: Upon the stroke of four.
RICHMOND: Why, then 'tis time to arm and give direction.
NARRATOR: His oration to his soldiers
RICHMOND: More than I have said, loving countrymen,
RICHMOND: The leisure and enforcement of the time
RICHMOND: Forbids to dwell upon: yet remember this,
RICHMOND: God and our good cause fight upon our side,
RICHMOND: The prayers of holy saints and wronged souls,
RICHMOND: Like high-rear'd bulwarks, stand before our faces,
RICHMOND: Richard except, those whom we fight against
RICHMOND: Had rather have us win than him they follow:
RICHMOND: For what is he they follow?  truly, gentlemen,
RICHMOND: A bloody tyrant and a homicide,
RICHMOND: One raised in blood, and one in blood establish'd,
RICHMOND: One that made means to come by what he hath,
RICHMOND: And slaughter'd those that were the means to help him,
RICHMOND: Abase foul stone, made precious by the foil
RICHMOND: Of England's chair, where he is falsely set,
RICHMOND: One that hath ever been God's enemy:
RICHMOND: Then, if you fight against God's enemy,
RICHMOND: God will in justice ward you as his soldiers,
RICHMOND: If you do sweat to put a tyrant down,
RICHMOND: You sleep in peace, the tyrant being slain,
RICHMOND: If you do fight against your country's foes,
RICHMOND: Your country's fat shall pay your pains the hire,
RICHMOND: If you do fight in safeguard of your wives,
RICHMOND: Your wives shall welcome home the conquerors,
RICHMOND: If you do free your children from the sword,
RICHMOND: Your children's children quit it in your age.
RICHMOND: Then, in the name of God and all these rights,
RICHMOND: Advance your standards, draw your willing swords.
RICHMOND: For me, the ransom of my bold attempt
RICHMOND: Shall be this cold corpse on the earth's cold face,
RICHMOND: But if I thrive, the gain of my attempt
RICHMOND: The least of you shall share his part thereof.
RICHMOND: Sound drums and trumpets boldly and cheerfully,
RICHMOND: God and Saint George! Richmond and victory!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Re-enter KING RICHARD, RATCLIFF, Attendants and Forces
KING RICHARD III: What said Northumberland as touching Richmond?
RATCLIFF: That he was never trained up in arms.
KING RICHARD III: He said the truth: and what said Surrey then?
RATCLIFF: He smiled and said 'The better for our purpose.'
KING RICHARD III: He was in the right, and so indeed it is.
NARRATOR: Clock striketh
KING RICHARD III: Ten the clock there. Give me a calendar.
KING RICHARD III: Who saw the sun to-day?
RATCLIFF: Not I, my lord.
KING RICHARD III: Then he disdains to shine, for by the book
KING RICHARD III: He should have braved the east an hour ago
KING RICHARD III: A black day will it be to somebody. Ratcliff!
RATCLIFF: My lord?
KING RICHARD III: The sun will not be seen to-day,
KING RICHARD III: The sky doth frown and lour upon our army.
KING RICHARD III: I would these dewy tears were from the ground.
KING RICHARD III: Not shine to-day! Why, what is that to me
KING RICHARD III: More than to Richmond?  for the selfsame heaven
KING RICHARD III: That frowns on me looks sadly upon him.
NARRATOR: Enter NORFOLK
NORFOLK: Arm, arm, my lord, the foe vaunts in the field.
KING RICHARD III: Come, bustle, bustle, caparison my horse.
KING RICHARD III: Call up Lord Stanley, bid him bring his power:
KING RICHARD III: I will lead forth my soldiers to the plain,
KING RICHARD III: And thus my battle shall be ordered:
KING RICHARD III: My foreward shall be drawn out all in length,
KING RICHARD III: Consisting equally of horse and foot,
KING RICHARD III: Our archers shall be placed in the midst
KING RICHARD III: John Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Earl of Surrey,
KING RICHARD III: Shall have the leading of this foot and horse.
KING RICHARD III: They thus directed, we will follow
KING RICHARD III: In the main battle, whose puissance on either side
KING RICHARD III: Shall be well winged with our chiefest horse.
KING RICHARD III: This, and Saint George to boot! What think'st thou, Norfolk?
NORFOLK: A good direction, warlike sovereign.
NORFOLK: This found I on my tent this morning.
NARRATOR: He sheweth him a paper
KING RICHARD III: [Reads]
KING RICHARD III: 'Jockey of Norfolk, be not too bold,
KING RICHARD III: For Dickon thy master is bought and sold.'
KING RICHARD III: A thing devised by the enemy.
KING RICHARD III: Go, gentleman, every man unto his charge
KING RICHARD III: Let not our babbling dreams affright our souls:
KING RICHARD III: Conscience is but a word that cowards use,
KING RICHARD III: Devised at first to keep the strong in awe:
KING RICHARD III: Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law.
KING RICHARD III: March on, join bravely, let us to't pell-mell
KING RICHARD III: If not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.
NARRATOR: His oration to his Army
KING RICHARD III: What shall I say more than I have inferr'd?
KING RICHARD III: Remember whom you are to cope withal,
KING RICHARD III: A sort of vagabonds, rascals, and runaways,
KING RICHARD III: A scum of Bretons, and base lackey peasants,
KING RICHARD III: Whom their o'er-cloyed country vomits forth
KING RICHARD III: To desperate ventures and assured destruction.
KING RICHARD III: You sleeping safe, they bring to you unrest,
KING RICHARD III: You having lands, and blest with beauteous wives,
KING RICHARD III: They would restrain the one, distain the other.
KING RICHARD III: And who doth lead them but a paltry fellow,
KING RICHARD III: Long kept in Bretagne at our mother's cost?
KING RICHARD III: A milk-sop, one that never in his life
KING RICHARD III: Felt so much cold as over shoes in snow?
KING RICHARD III: Let's whip these stragglers o'er the seas again,
KING RICHARD III: Lash hence these overweening rags of France,
KING RICHARD III: These famish'd beggars, weary of their lives,
KING RICHARD III: Who, but for dreaming on this fond exploit,
KING RICHARD III: For want of means, poor rats, had hang'd themselves:
KING RICHARD III: If we be conquer'd, let men conquer us,
KING RICHARD III: And not these bastard Bretons, whom our fathers
KING RICHARD III: Have in their own land beaten, bobb'd, and thump'd,
KING RICHARD III: And in record, left them the heirs of shame.
KING RICHARD III: Shall these enjoy our lands?  lie with our wives?
KING RICHARD III: Ravish our daughters?
NARRATOR: Drum afar off
KING RICHARD III: Hark! I hear their drum.
KING RICHARD III: Fight, gentlemen of England! fight, bold yoemen!
KING RICHARD III: Draw, archers, draw your arrows to the head!
KING RICHARD III: Spur your proud horses hard, and ride in blood,
KING RICHARD III: Amaze the welkin with your broken staves!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
KING RICHARD III: What says Lord Stanley? will he bring his power?
Messenger: My lord, he doth deny to come.
KING RICHARD III: Off with his son George's head!
NORFOLK: My lord, the enemy is past the marsh
NORFOLK: After the battle let George Stanley die.
KING RICHARD III: A thousand hearts are great within my bosom:
KING RICHARD III: Advance our standards, set upon our foes
KING RICHARD III: Our ancient word of courage, fair Saint George,
KING RICHARD III: Inspire us with the spleen of fiery dragons!
KING RICHARD III: Upon them! victory sits on our helms.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum: excursions. Enter NORFOLK and forces fighting, to him CATESBY
CATESBY: Rescue, my Lord of Norfolk, rescue, rescue!
CATESBY: The king enacts more wonders than a man,
CATESBY: Daring an opposite to every danger:
CATESBY: His horse is slain, and all on foot he fights,
CATESBY: Seeking for Richmond in the throat of death.
CATESBY: Rescue, fair lord, or else the day is lost!
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter KING RICHARD III
KING RICHARD III: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
CATESBY: Withdraw, my lord, I'll help you to a horse.
KING RICHARD III: Slave, I have set my life upon a cast,
KING RICHARD III: And I will stand the hazard of the die:
KING RICHARD III: I think there be six Richmonds in the field,
KING RICHARD III: Five have I slain to-day instead of him.
KING RICHARD III: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter KING RICHARD III and RICHMOND, they  fight. KING RICHARD III is slain. Retreat and  flourish. Re-enter RICHMOND, DERBY bearing the crown, with divers other Lords
RICHMOND: God and your arms be praised, victorious friends,
RICHMOND: The day is ours, the bloody dog is dead.
DERBY: Courageous Richmond, well hast thou acquit thee.
DERBY: Lo, here, this long-usurped royalty
DERBY: From the dead temples of this bloody wretch
DERBY: Have I pluck'd off, to grace thy brows withal:
DERBY: Wear it, enjoy it, and make much of it.
RICHMOND: Great God of heaven, say Amen to all!
RICHMOND: But, tell me, is young George Stanley living?
DERBY: He is, my lord, and safe in Leicester town,
DERBY: Whither, if it please you, we may now withdraw us.
RICHMOND: What men of name are slain on either side?
DERBY: John Duke of Norfolk, Walter Lord Ferrers,
DERBY: Sir Robert Brakenbury, and Sir William Brandon.
RICHMOND: Inter their bodies as becomes their births:
RICHMOND: Proclaim a pardon to the soldiers fled
RICHMOND: That in submission will return to us:
RICHMOND: And then, as we have ta'en the sacrament,
RICHMOND: We will unite the white rose and the red:
RICHMOND: Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction,
RICHMOND: That long have frown'd upon their enmity!
RICHMOND: What traitor hears me, and says not amen?
RICHMOND: England hath long been mad, and scarr'd herself,
RICHMOND: The brother blindly shed the brother's blood,
RICHMOND: The father rashly slaughter'd his own son,
RICHMOND: The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire:
RICHMOND: All this divided York and Lancaster,
RICHMOND: Divided in their dire division,
RICHMOND: O, now, let Richmond and Elizabeth,
RICHMOND: The true succeeders of each royal house,
RICHMOND: By God's fair ordinance conjoin together!
RICHMOND: And let their heirs, God, if thy will be so.
RICHMOND: Enrich the time to come with smooth-faced peace,
RICHMOND: With smiling plenty and fair prosperous days!
RICHMOND: Abate the edge of traitors, gracious Lord,
RICHMOND: That would reduce these bloody days again,
RICHMOND: And make poor England weep in streams of blood!
RICHMOND: Let them not live to taste this land's increase
RICHMOND: That would with treason wound this fair land's peace!
RICHMOND: Now civil wounds are stopp'd, peace lives again:
RICHMOND: That she may long live here, God say amen!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Romeo and Juliet '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
RICHMOND: Two households, both alike in dignity,
RICHMOND: In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
RICHMOND: From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
RICHMOND: Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
RICHMOND: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
RICHMOND: A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life,
RICHMOND: Whose misadventured piteous overthrows
RICHMOND: Do with their death bury their parents' strife.
RICHMOND: The fearful passage of their death-mark'd love,
RICHMOND: And the continuance of their parents' rage,
RICHMOND: Which, but their children's end, nought could remove,
RICHMOND: Is now the two hours' traffic of our stage,
RICHMOND: The which if you with patient ears attend,
RICHMOND: What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.
RICHMOND: SCENE I. Verona. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter SAMPSON and GREGORY, of the house of Capulet, armed with swords and bucklers
SAMPSON: Gregory, o' my word, we'll not carry coals.
GREGORY: No, for then we should be colliers.
SAMPSON: I mean, an we be in choler, we'll draw.
GREGORY: Ay, while you live, draw your neck out o' the collar.
SAMPSON: I strike quickly, being moved.
GREGORY: But thou art not quickly moved to strike.
SAMPSON: A dog of the house of Montague moves me.
GREGORY: To move is to stir, and to be valiant is to stand:
GREGORY: therefore, if thou art moved, thou runn'st away.
SAMPSON: A dog of that house shall move me to stand: I will
SAMPSON: take the wall of any man or maid of Montague's.
GREGORY: That shows thee a weak slave, for the weakest goes
GREGORY: to the wall.
SAMPSON: True, and therefore women, being the weaker vessels,
SAMPSON: are ever thrust to the wall: therefore I will push
SAMPSON: Montague's men from the wall, and thrust his maids
SAMPSON: to the wall.
GREGORY: The quarrel is between our masters and us their men.
SAMPSON: 'Tis all one, I will show myself a tyrant: when I
SAMPSON: have fought with the men, I will be cruel with the
SAMPSON: maids, and cut off their heads.
GREGORY: The heads of the maids?
SAMPSON: Ay, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads,
SAMPSON: take it in what sense thou wilt.
GREGORY: They must take it in sense that feel it.
SAMPSON: Me they shall feel while I am able to stand: and
SAMPSON: 'tis known I am a pretty piece of flesh.
GREGORY: 'Tis well thou art not fish, if thou hadst, thou
GREGORY: hadst been poor John. Draw thy tool! here comes
GREGORY: two of the house of the Montagues.
SAMPSON: My naked weapon is out: quarrel, I will back thee.
GREGORY: How! turn thy back and run?
SAMPSON: Fear me not.
GREGORY: No, marry, I fear thee!
SAMPSON: Let us take the law of our sides, let them begin.
GREGORY: I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as
GREGORY: they list.
SAMPSON: Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them,
SAMPSON: which is a disgrace to them, if they bear it.
NARRATOR: Enter ABRAHAM and BALTHASAR
ABRAHAM: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON: I do bite my thumb, sir.
ABRAHAM: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
SAMPSON: [Aside to GREGORY]  Is the law of our side, if I say
SAMPSON: ay?
GREGORY: No.
SAMPSON: No, sir, I do not bite my thumb at you, sir, but I
SAMPSON: bite my thumb, sir.
GREGORY: Do you quarrel, sir?
ABRAHAM: Quarrel sir! no, sir.
SAMPSON: If you do, sir, I am for you: I serve as good a man as you.
ABRAHAM: No better.
SAMPSON: Well, sir.
GREGORY: Say 'better:' here comes one of my master's kinsmen.
SAMPSON: Yes, better, sir.
ABRAHAM: You lie.
SAMPSON: Draw, if you be men. Gregory, remember thy swashing blow.
NARRATOR: They fight
NARRATOR: Enter BENVOLIO
BENVOLIO: Part, fools!
BENVOLIO: Put up your swords, you know not what you do.
NARRATOR: Beats down their swords
NARRATOR: Enter TYBALT
TYBALT: What, art thou drawn among these heartless hinds?
TYBALT: Turn thee, Benvolio, look upon thy death.
BENVOLIO: I do but keep the peace: put up thy sword,
BENVOLIO: Or manage it to part these men with me.
TYBALT: What, drawn, and talk of peace! I hate the word,
TYBALT: As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee:
TYBALT: Have at thee, coward!
NARRATOR: They fight
NARRATOR: Enter, several of both houses, who join the fray, then enter Citizens, with clubs
First Citizen: Clubs, bills, and partisans! strike! beat them down!
First Citizen: Down with the Capulets! down with the Montagues!
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET in his gown, and LADY CAPULET
CAPULET: What noise is this? Give me my long sword, ho!
LADY CAPULET: A crutch, a crutch! why call you for a sword?
CAPULET: My sword, I say! Old Montague is come,
CAPULET: And flourishes his blade in spite of me.
NARRATOR: Enter MONTAGUE and LADY MONTAGUE
MONTAGUE: Thou villain Capulet,--Hold me not, let me go.
LADY MONTAGUE: Thou shalt not stir a foot to seek a foe.
NARRATOR: Enter PRINCE, with Attendants
PRINCE: Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace,
PRINCE: Profaners of this neighbour-stained steel,--
PRINCE: Will they not hear? What, ho! you men, you beasts,
PRINCE: That quench the fire of your pernicious rage
PRINCE: With purple fountains issuing from your veins,
PRINCE: On pain of torture, from those bloody hands
PRINCE: Throw your mistemper'd weapons to the ground,
PRINCE: And hear the sentence of your moved prince.
PRINCE: Three civil brawls, bred of an airy word,
PRINCE: By thee, old Capulet, and Montague,
PRINCE: Have thrice disturb'd the quiet of our streets,
PRINCE: And made Verona's ancient citizens
PRINCE: Cast by their grave beseeming ornaments,
PRINCE: To wield old partisans, in hands as old,
PRINCE: Canker'd with peace, to part your canker'd hate:
PRINCE: If ever you disturb our streets again,
PRINCE: Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace.
PRINCE: For this time, all the rest depart away:
PRINCE: You Capulet, shall go along with me:
PRINCE: And, Montague, come you this afternoon,
PRINCE: To know our further pleasure in this case,
PRINCE: To old Free-town, our common judgment-place.
PRINCE: Once more, on pain of death, all men depart.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but MONTAGUE, LADY MONTAGUE, and BENVOLIO
MONTAGUE: Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?
MONTAGUE: Speak, nephew, were you by when it began?
BENVOLIO: Here were the servants of your adversary,
BENVOLIO: And yours, close fighting ere I did approach:
BENVOLIO: I drew to part them: in the instant came
BENVOLIO: The fiery Tybalt, with his sword prepared,
BENVOLIO: Which, as he breathed defiance to my ears,
BENVOLIO: He swung about his head and cut the winds,
BENVOLIO: Who nothing hurt withal hiss'd him in scorn:
BENVOLIO: While we were interchanging thrusts and blows,
BENVOLIO: Came more and more and fought on part and part,
BENVOLIO: Till the prince came, who parted either part.
LADY MONTAGUE: O, where is Romeo? saw you him to-day?
LADY MONTAGUE: Right glad I am he was not at this fray.
BENVOLIO: Madam, an hour before the worshipp'd sun
BENVOLIO: Peer'd forth the golden window of the east,
BENVOLIO: A troubled mind drave me to walk abroad,
BENVOLIO: Where, underneath the grove of sycamore
BENVOLIO: That westward rooteth from the city's side,
BENVOLIO: So early walking did I see your son:
BENVOLIO: Towards him I made, but he was ware of me
BENVOLIO: And stole into the covert of the wood:
BENVOLIO: I, measuring his affections by my own,
BENVOLIO: That most are busied when they're most alone,
BENVOLIO: Pursued my humour not pursuing his,
BENVOLIO: And gladly shunn'd who gladly fled from me.
MONTAGUE: Many a morning hath he there been seen,
MONTAGUE: With tears augmenting the fresh morning dew.
MONTAGUE: Adding to clouds more clouds with his deep sighs,
MONTAGUE: But all so soon as the all-cheering sun
MONTAGUE: Should in the furthest east begin to draw
MONTAGUE: The shady curtains from Aurora's bed,
MONTAGUE: Away from the light steals home my heavy son,
MONTAGUE: And private in his chamber pens himself,
MONTAGUE: Shuts up his windows, locks far daylight out
MONTAGUE: And makes himself an artificial night:
MONTAGUE: Black and portentous must this humour prove,
MONTAGUE: Unless good counsel may the cause remove.
BENVOLIO: My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
MONTAGUE: I neither know it nor can learn of him.
BENVOLIO: Have you importuned him by any means?
MONTAGUE: Both by myself and many other friends:
MONTAGUE: But he, his own affections' counsellor,
MONTAGUE: Is to himself--I will not say how true--
MONTAGUE: But to himself so secret and so close,
MONTAGUE: So far from sounding and discovery,
MONTAGUE: As is the bud bit with an envious worm,
MONTAGUE: Ere he can spread his sweet leaves to the air,
MONTAGUE: Or dedicate his beauty to the sun.
MONTAGUE: Could we but learn from whence his sorrows grow.
MONTAGUE: We would as willingly give cure as know.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
BENVOLIO: See, where he comes: so please you, step aside,
BENVOLIO: I'll know his grievance, or be much denied.
MONTAGUE: I would thou wert so happy by thy stay,
MONTAGUE: To hear true shrift. Come, madam, let's away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt MONTAGUE and LADY MONTAGUE
BENVOLIO: Good-morrow, cousin.
ROMEO: Is the day so young?
BENVOLIO: But new struck nine.
ROMEO: Ay me! sad hours seem long.
ROMEO: Was that my father that went hence so fast?
BENVOLIO: It was. What sadness lengthens Romeo's hours?
ROMEO: Not having that, which, having, makes them short.
BENVOLIO: In love?
ROMEO: Out--
BENVOLIO: Of love?
ROMEO: Out of her favour, where I am in love.
BENVOLIO: Alas, that love, so gentle in his view,
BENVOLIO: Should be so tyrannous and rough in proof!
ROMEO: Alas, that love, whose view is muffled still,
ROMEO: Should, without eyes, see pathways to his will!
ROMEO: Where shall we dine? O me! What fray was here?
ROMEO: Yet tell me not, for I have heard it all.
ROMEO: Here's much to do with hate, but more with love.
ROMEO: Why, then, O brawling love! O loving hate!
ROMEO: O any thing, of nothing first create!
ROMEO: O heavy lightness! serious vanity!
ROMEO: Mis-shapen chaos of well-seeming forms!
ROMEO: Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire,
ROMEO: sick health!
ROMEO: Still-waking sleep, that is not what it is!
ROMEO: This love feel I, that feel no love in this.
ROMEO: Dost thou not laugh?
BENVOLIO: No, coz, I rather weep.
ROMEO: Good heart, at what?
BENVOLIO: At thy good heart's oppression.
ROMEO: Why, such is love's transgression.
ROMEO: Griefs of mine own lie heavy in my breast,
ROMEO: Which thou wilt propagate, to have it prest
ROMEO: With more of thine: this love that thou hast shown
ROMEO: Doth add more grief to too much of mine own.
ROMEO: Love is a smoke raised with the fume of sighs,
ROMEO: Being purged, a fire sparkling in lovers' eyes,
ROMEO: Being vex'd a sea nourish'd with lovers' tears:
ROMEO: What is it else? a madness most discreet,
ROMEO: A choking gall and a preserving sweet.
ROMEO: Farewell, my coz.
BENVOLIO: Soft! I will go along,
BENVOLIO: An if you leave me so, you do me wrong.
ROMEO: Tut, I have lost myself, I am not here,
ROMEO: This is not Romeo, he's some other where.
BENVOLIO: Tell me in sadness, who is that you love.
ROMEO: What, shall I groan and tell thee?
BENVOLIO: Groan! why, no.
BENVOLIO: But sadly tell me who.
ROMEO: Bid a sick man in sadness make his will:
ROMEO: Ah, word ill urged to one that is so ill!
ROMEO: In sadness, cousin, I do love a woman.
BENVOLIO: I aim'd so near, when I supposed you loved.
ROMEO: A right good mark-man! And she's fair I love.
BENVOLIO: A right fair mark, fair coz, is soonest hit.
ROMEO: Well, in that hit you miss: she'll not be hit
ROMEO: With Cupid's arrow, she hath Dian's wit,
ROMEO: And, in strong proof of chastity well arm'd,
ROMEO: From love's weak childish bow she lives unharm'd.
ROMEO: She will not stay the siege of loving terms,
ROMEO: Nor bide the encounter of assailing eyes,
ROMEO: Nor ope her lap to saint-seducing gold:
ROMEO: O, she is rich in beauty, only poor,
ROMEO: That when she dies with beauty dies her store.
BENVOLIO: Then she hath sworn that she will still live chaste?
ROMEO: She hath, and in that sparing makes huge waste,
ROMEO: For beauty starved with her severity
ROMEO: Cuts beauty off from all posterity.
ROMEO: She is too fair, too wise, wisely too fair,
ROMEO: To merit bliss by making me despair:
ROMEO: She hath forsworn to love, and in that vow
ROMEO: Do I live dead that live to tell it now.
BENVOLIO: Be ruled by me, forget to think of her.
ROMEO: O, teach me how I should forget to think.
BENVOLIO: By giving liberty unto thine eyes,
BENVOLIO: Examine other beauties.
ROMEO: 'Tis the way
ROMEO: To call hers exquisite, in question more:
ROMEO: These happy masks that kiss fair ladies' brows
ROMEO: Being black put us in mind they hide the fair,
ROMEO: He that is strucken blind cannot forget
ROMEO: The precious treasure of his eyesight lost:
ROMEO: Show me a mistress that is passing fair,
ROMEO: What doth her beauty serve, but as a note
ROMEO: Where I may read who pass'd that passing fair?
ROMEO: Farewell: thou canst not teach me to forget.
BENVOLIO: I'll pay that doctrine, or else die in debt.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET, PARIS, and Servant
CAPULET: But Montague is bound as well as I,
CAPULET: In penalty alike, and 'tis not hard, I think,
CAPULET: For men so old as we to keep the peace.
PARIS: Of honourable reckoning are you both,
PARIS: And pity 'tis you lived at odds so long.
PARIS: But now, my lord, what say you to my suit?
CAPULET: But saying o'er what I have said before:
CAPULET: My child is yet a stranger in the world,
CAPULET: She hath not seen the change of fourteen years,
CAPULET: Let two more summers wither in their pride,
CAPULET: Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.
PARIS: Younger than she are happy mothers made.
CAPULET: And too soon marr'd are those so early made.
CAPULET: The earth hath swallow'd all my hopes but she,
CAPULET: She is the hopeful lady of my earth:
CAPULET: But woo her, gentle Paris, get her heart,
CAPULET: My will to her consent is but a part,
CAPULET: An she agree, within her scope of choice
CAPULET: Lies my consent and fair according voice.
CAPULET: This night I hold an old accustom'd feast,
CAPULET: Whereto I have invited many a guest,
CAPULET: Such as I love, and you, among the store,
CAPULET: One more, most welcome, makes my number more.
CAPULET: At my poor house look to behold this night
CAPULET: Earth-treading stars that make dark heaven light:
CAPULET: Such comfort as do lusty young men feel
CAPULET: When well-apparell'd April on the heel
CAPULET: Of limping winter treads, even such delight
CAPULET: Among fresh female buds shall you this night
CAPULET: Inherit at my house, hear all, all see,
CAPULET: And like her most whose merit most shall be:
CAPULET: Which on more view, of many mine being one
CAPULET: May stand in number, though in reckoning none,
CAPULET: Come, go with me.
NARRATOR: To Servant, giving a paper
CAPULET: Go, sirrah, trudge about
CAPULET: Through fair Verona, find those persons out
CAPULET: Whose names are written there, and to them say,
CAPULET: My house and welcome on their pleasure stay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CAPULET and PARIS
Servant: Find them out whose names are written here! It is
Servant: written, that the shoemaker should meddle with his
Servant: yard, and the tailor with his last, the fisher with
Servant: his pencil, and the painter with his nets, but I am
Servant: sent to find those persons whose names are here
Servant: writ, and can never find what names the writing
Servant: person hath here writ. I must to the learned.--In good time.
NARRATOR: Enter BENVOLIO and ROMEO
BENVOLIO: Tut, man, one fire burns out another's burning,
BENVOLIO: One pain is lessen'd by another's anguish,
BENVOLIO: Turn giddy, and be holp by backward turning,
BENVOLIO: One desperate grief cures with another's languish:
BENVOLIO: Take thou some new infection to thy eye,
BENVOLIO: And the rank poison of the old will die.
ROMEO: Your plaintain-leaf is excellent for that.
BENVOLIO: For what, I pray thee?
ROMEO: For your broken shin.
BENVOLIO: Why, Romeo, art thou mad?
ROMEO: Not mad, but bound more than a mad-man is,
ROMEO: Shut up in prison, kept without my food,
ROMEO: Whipp'd and tormented and--God-den, good fellow.
Servant: God gi' god-den. I pray, sir, can you read?
ROMEO: Ay, mine own fortune in my misery.
Servant: Perhaps you have learned it without book: but, I
Servant: pray, can you read any thing you see?
ROMEO: Ay, if I know the letters and the language.
Servant: Ye say honestly: rest you merry!
ROMEO: Stay, fellow, I can read.
NARRATOR: Reads
ROMEO: 'Signior Martino and his wife and daughters,
ROMEO: County Anselme and his beauteous sisters, the lady
ROMEO: widow of Vitravio, Signior Placentio and his lovely
ROMEO: nieces, Mercutio and his brother Valentine, mine
ROMEO: uncle Capulet, his wife and daughters, my fair niece
ROMEO: Rosaline, Livia, Signior Valentio and his cousin
ROMEO: Tybalt, Lucio and the lively Helena.' A fair
ROMEO: assembly: whither should they come?
Servant: Up.
ROMEO: Whither?
Servant: To supper, to our house.
ROMEO: Whose house?
Servant: My master's.
ROMEO: Indeed, I should have ask'd you that before.
Servant: Now I'll tell you without asking: my master is the
Servant: great rich Capulet, and if you be not of the house
Servant: of Montagues, I pray, come and crush a cup of wine.
Servant: Rest you merry!
NARRATOR: Exit
BENVOLIO: At this same ancient feast of Capulet's
BENVOLIO: Sups the fair Rosaline whom thou so lovest,
BENVOLIO: With all the admired beauties of Verona:
BENVOLIO: Go thither, and, with unattainted eye,
BENVOLIO: Compare her face with some that I shall show,
BENVOLIO: And I will make thee think thy swan a crow.
ROMEO: When the devout religion of mine eye
ROMEO: Maintains such falsehood, then turn tears to fires,
ROMEO: And these, who often drown'd could never die,
ROMEO: Transparent heretics, be burnt for liars!
ROMEO: One fairer than my love! the all-seeing sun
ROMEO: Ne'er saw her match since first the world begun.
BENVOLIO: Tut, you saw her fair, none else being by,
BENVOLIO: Herself poised with herself in either eye:
BENVOLIO: But in that crystal scales let there be weigh'd
BENVOLIO: Your lady's love against some other maid
BENVOLIO: That I will show you shining at this feast,
BENVOLIO: And she shall scant show well that now shows best.
ROMEO: I'll go along, no such sight to be shown,
ROMEO: But to rejoice in splendor of mine own.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in Capulet's house.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY CAPULET and Nurse
LADY CAPULET: Nurse, where's my daughter? call her forth to me.
Nurse: Now, by my maidenhead, at twelve year old,
Nurse: I bade her come. What, lamb! what, ladybird!
Nurse: God forbid! Where's this girl? What, Juliet!
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
JULIET: How now! who calls?
Nurse: Your mother.
JULIET: Madam, I am here.
JULIET: What is your will?
LADY CAPULET: This is the matter:--Nurse, give leave awhile,
LADY CAPULET: We must talk in secret:--nurse, come back again,
LADY CAPULET: I have remember'd me, thou's hear our counsel.
LADY CAPULET: Thou know'st my daughter's of a pretty age.
Nurse: Faith, I can tell her age unto an hour.
LADY CAPULET: She's not fourteen.
Nurse: I'll lay fourteen of my teeth,--
Nurse: And yet, to my teeth be it spoken, I have but four--
Nurse: She is not fourteen. How long is it now
Nurse: To Lammas-tide?
LADY CAPULET: A fortnight and odd days.
Nurse: Even or odd, of all days in the year,
Nurse: Come Lammas-eve at night shall she be fourteen.
Nurse: Susan and she--God rest all Christian souls!--
Nurse: Were of an age: well, Susan is with God,
Nurse: She was too good for me: but, as I said,
Nurse: On Lammas-eve at night shall she be fourteen,
Nurse: That shall she, marry, I remember it well.
Nurse: 'Tis since the earthquake now eleven years,
Nurse: And she was wean'd,--I never shall forget it,--
Nurse: Of all the days of the year, upon that day:
Nurse: For I had then laid wormwood to my dug,
Nurse: Sitting in the sun under the dove-house wall,
Nurse: My lord and you were then at Mantua:--
Nurse: Nay, I do bear a brain:--but, as I said,
Nurse: When it did taste the wormwood on the nipple
Nurse: Of my dug and felt it bitter, pretty fool,
Nurse: To see it tetchy and fall out with the dug!
Nurse: Shake quoth the dove-house: 'twas no need, I trow,
Nurse: To bid me trudge:
Nurse: And since that time it is eleven years,
Nurse: For then she could stand alone, nay, by the rood,
Nurse: She could have run and waddled all about,
Nurse: For even the day before, she broke her brow:
Nurse: And then my husband--God be with his soul!
Nurse: A' was a merry man--took up the child:
Nurse: 'Yea,' quoth he, 'dost thou fall upon thy face?
Nurse: Thou wilt fall backward when thou hast more wit,
Nurse: Wilt thou not, Jule?' and, by my holidame,
Nurse: The pretty wretch left crying and said 'Ay.'
Nurse: To see, now, how a jest shall come about!
Nurse: I warrant, an I should live a thousand years,
Nurse: I never should forget it: 'Wilt thou not, Jule?' quoth he,
Nurse: And, pretty fool, it stinted and said 'Ay.'
LADY CAPULET: Enough of this, I pray thee, hold thy peace.
Nurse: Yes, madam: yet I cannot choose but laugh,
Nurse: To think it should leave crying and say 'Ay.'
Nurse: And yet, I warrant, it had upon its brow
Nurse: A bump as big as a young cockerel's stone,
Nurse: A parlous knock, and it cried bitterly:
Nurse: 'Yea,' quoth my husband,'fall'st upon thy face?
Nurse: Thou wilt fall backward when thou comest to age,
Nurse: Wilt thou not, Jule?' it stinted and said 'Ay.'
JULIET: And stint thou too, I pray thee, nurse, say I.
Nurse: Peace, I have done. God mark thee to his grace!
Nurse: Thou wast the prettiest babe that e'er I nursed:
Nurse: An I might live to see thee married once,
Nurse: I have my wish.
LADY CAPULET: Marry, that 'marry' is the very theme
LADY CAPULET: I came to talk of. Tell me, daughter Juliet,
LADY CAPULET: How stands your disposition to be married?
JULIET: It is an honour that I dream not of.
Nurse: An honour! were not I thine only nurse,
Nurse: I would say thou hadst suck'd wisdom from thy teat.
LADY CAPULET: Well, think of marriage now, younger than you,
LADY CAPULET: Here in Verona, ladies of esteem,
LADY CAPULET: Are made already mothers: by my count,
LADY CAPULET: I was your mother much upon these years
LADY CAPULET: That you are now a maid. Thus then in brief:
LADY CAPULET: The valiant Paris seeks you for his love.
Nurse: A man, young lady! lady, such a man
Nurse: As all the world--why, he's a man of wax.
LADY CAPULET: Verona's summer hath not such a flower.
Nurse: Nay, he's a flower, in faith, a very flower.
LADY CAPULET: What say you? can you love the gentleman?
LADY CAPULET: This night you shall behold him at our feast,
LADY CAPULET: Read o'er the volume of young Paris' face,
LADY CAPULET: And find delight writ there with beauty's pen,
LADY CAPULET: Examine every married lineament,
LADY CAPULET: And see how one another lends content
LADY CAPULET: And what obscured in this fair volume lies
LADY CAPULET: Find written in the margent of his eyes.
LADY CAPULET: This precious book of love, this unbound lover,
LADY CAPULET: To beautify him, only lacks a cover:
LADY CAPULET: The fish lives in the sea, and 'tis much pride
LADY CAPULET: For fair without the fair within to hide:
LADY CAPULET: That book in many's eyes doth share the glory,
LADY CAPULET: That in gold clasps locks in the golden story,
LADY CAPULET: So shall you share all that he doth possess,
LADY CAPULET: By having him, making yourself no less.
Nurse: No less! nay, bigger, women grow by men.
LADY CAPULET: Speak briefly, can you like of Paris' love?
JULIET: I'll look to like, if looking liking move:
JULIET: But no more deep will I endart mine eye
JULIET: Than your consent gives strength to make it fly.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: Madam, the guests are come, supper served up, you
Servant: called, my young lady asked for, the nurse cursed in
Servant: the pantry, and every thing in extremity. I must
Servant: hence to wait, I beseech you, follow straight.
LADY CAPULET: We follow thee.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
LADY CAPULET: Juliet, the county stays.
Nurse: Go, girl, seek happy nights to happy days.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO, MERCUTIO, BENVOLIO, with five or six Maskers, Torch-bearers, and others
ROMEO: What, shall this speech be spoke for our excuse?
ROMEO: Or shall we on without a apology?
BENVOLIO: The date is out of such prolixity:
BENVOLIO: We'll have no Cupid hoodwink'd with a scarf,
BENVOLIO: Bearing a Tartar's painted bow of lath,
BENVOLIO: Scaring the ladies like a crow-keeper,
BENVOLIO: Nor no without-book prologue, faintly spoke
BENVOLIO: After the prompter, for our entrance:
BENVOLIO: But let them measure us by what they will,
BENVOLIO: We'll measure them a measure, and be gone.
ROMEO: Give me a torch: I am not for this ambling,
ROMEO: Being but heavy, I will bear the light.
MERCUTIO: Nay, gentle Romeo, we must have you dance.
ROMEO: Not I, believe me: you have dancing shoes
ROMEO: With nimble soles: I have a soul of lead
ROMEO: So stakes me to the ground I cannot move.
MERCUTIO: You are a lover, borrow Cupid's wings,
MERCUTIO: And soar with them above a common bound.
ROMEO: I am too sore enpierced with his shaft
ROMEO: To soar with his light feathers, and so bound,
ROMEO: I cannot bound a pitch above dull woe:
ROMEO: Under love's heavy burden do I sink.
MERCUTIO: And, to sink in it, should you burden love,
MERCUTIO: Too great oppression for a tender thing.
ROMEO: Is love a tender thing? it is too rough,
ROMEO: Too rude, too boisterous, and it pricks like thorn.
MERCUTIO: If love be rough with you, be rough with love,
MERCUTIO: Prick love for pricking, and you beat love down.
MERCUTIO: Give me a case to put my visage in:
MERCUTIO: A visor for a visor! what care I
MERCUTIO: What curious eye doth quote deformities?
MERCUTIO: Here are the beetle brows shall blush for me.
BENVOLIO: Come, knock and enter, and no sooner in,
BENVOLIO: But every man betake him to his legs.
ROMEO: A torch for me: let wantons light of heart
ROMEO: Tickle the senseless rushes with their heels,
ROMEO: For I am proverb'd with a grandsire phrase,
ROMEO: I'll be a candle-holder, and look on.
ROMEO: The game was ne'er so fair, and I am done.
MERCUTIO: Tut, dun's the mouse, the constable's own word:
MERCUTIO: If thou art dun, we'll draw thee from the mire
MERCUTIO: Of this sir-reverence love, wherein thou stick'st
MERCUTIO: Up to the ears. Come, we burn daylight, ho!
ROMEO: Nay, that's not so.
MERCUTIO: I mean, sir, in delay
MERCUTIO: We waste our lights in vain, like lamps by day.
MERCUTIO: Take our good meaning, for our judgment sits
MERCUTIO: Five times in that ere once in our five wits.
ROMEO: And we mean well in going to this mask,
ROMEO: But 'tis no wit to go.
MERCUTIO: Why, may one ask?
ROMEO: I dream'd a dream to-night.
MERCUTIO: And so did I.
ROMEO: Well, what was yours?
MERCUTIO: That dreamers often lie.
ROMEO: In bed asleep, while they do dream things true.
MERCUTIO: O, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you.
MERCUTIO: She is the fairies' midwife, and she comes
MERCUTIO: In shape no bigger than an agate-stone
MERCUTIO: On the fore-finger of an alderman,
MERCUTIO: Drawn with a team of little atomies
MERCUTIO: Athwart men's noses as they lie asleep,
MERCUTIO: Her wagon-spokes made of long spiders' legs,
MERCUTIO: The cover of the wings of grasshoppers,
MERCUTIO: The traces of the smallest spider's web,
MERCUTIO: The collars of the moonshine's watery beams,
MERCUTIO: Her whip of cricket's bone, the lash of film,
MERCUTIO: Her wagoner a small grey-coated gnat,
MERCUTIO: Not so big as a round little worm
MERCUTIO: Prick'd from the lazy finger of a maid,
MERCUTIO: Her chariot is an empty hazel-nut
MERCUTIO: Made by the joiner squirrel or old grub,
MERCUTIO: Time out o' mind the fairies' coachmakers.
MERCUTIO: And in this state she gallops night by night
MERCUTIO: Through lovers' brains, and then they dream of love,
MERCUTIO: O'er courtiers' knees, that dream on court'sies straight,
MERCUTIO: O'er lawyers' fingers, who straight dream on fees,
MERCUTIO: O'er ladies ' lips, who straight on kisses dream,
MERCUTIO: Which oft the angry Mab with blisters plagues,
MERCUTIO: Because their breaths with sweetmeats tainted are:
MERCUTIO: Sometime she gallops o'er a courtier's nose,
MERCUTIO: And then dreams he of smelling out a suit,
MERCUTIO: And sometime comes she with a tithe-pig's tail
MERCUTIO: Tickling a parson's nose as a' lies asleep,
MERCUTIO: Then dreams, he of another benefice:
MERCUTIO: Sometime she driveth o'er a soldier's neck,
MERCUTIO: And then dreams he of cutting foreign throats,
MERCUTIO: Of breaches, ambuscadoes, Spanish blades,
MERCUTIO: Of healths five-fathom deep, and then anon
MERCUTIO: Drums in his ear, at which he starts and wakes,
MERCUTIO: And being thus frighted swears a prayer or two
MERCUTIO: And sleeps again. This is that very Mab
MERCUTIO: That plats the manes of horses in the night,
MERCUTIO: And bakes the elflocks in foul sluttish hairs,
MERCUTIO: Which once untangled, much misfortune bodes:
MERCUTIO: This is the hag, when maids lie on their backs,
MERCUTIO: That presses them and learns them first to bear,
MERCUTIO: Making them women of good carriage:
MERCUTIO: This is she--
ROMEO: Peace, peace, Mercutio, peace!
ROMEO: Thou talk'st of nothing.
MERCUTIO: True, I talk of dreams,
MERCUTIO: Which are the children of an idle brain,
MERCUTIO: Begot of nothing but vain fantasy,
MERCUTIO: Which is as thin of substance as the air
MERCUTIO: And more inconstant than the wind, who wooes
MERCUTIO: Even now the frozen bosom of the north,
MERCUTIO: And, being anger'd, puffs away from thence,
MERCUTIO: Turning his face to the dew-dropping south.
BENVOLIO: This wind, you talk of, blows us from ourselves,
BENVOLIO: Supper is done, and we shall come too late.
ROMEO: I fear, too early: for my mind misgives
ROMEO: Some consequence yet hanging in the stars
ROMEO: Shall bitterly begin his fearful date
ROMEO: With this night's revels and expire the term
ROMEO: Of a despised life closed in my breast
ROMEO: By some vile forfeit of untimely death.
ROMEO: But He, that hath the steerage of my course,
ROMEO: Direct my sail! On, lusty gentlemen.
BENVOLIO: Strike, drum.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. A hall in Capulet's house.
NARRATOR: Musicians waiting. Enter Servingmen with napkins
First Servant: Where's Potpan, that he helps not to take away? He
First Servant: shift a trencher? he scrape a trencher!
Second Servant: When good manners shall lie all in one or two men's
Second Servant: hands and they unwashed too, 'tis a foul thing.
First Servant: Away with the joint-stools, remove the
First Servant: court-cupboard, look to the plate. Good thou, save
First Servant: me a piece of marchpane, and, as thou lovest me, let
First Servant: the porter let in Susan Grindstone and Nell.
First Servant: Antony, and Potpan!
Second Servant: Ay, boy, ready.
First Servant: You are looked for and called for, asked for and
First Servant: sought for, in the great chamber.
Second Servant: We cannot be here and there too. Cheerly, boys, be
Second Servant: brisk awhile, and the longer liver take all.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET, with JULIET and others of his house, meeting the Guests and Maskers
CAPULET: Welcome, gentlemen! ladies that have their toes
CAPULET: Unplagued with corns will have a bout with you.
CAPULET: Ah ha, my mistresses! which of you all
CAPULET: Will now deny to dance? she that makes dainty,
CAPULET: She, I'll swear, hath corns, am I come near ye now?
CAPULET: Welcome, gentlemen! I have seen the day
CAPULET: That I have worn a visor and could tell
CAPULET: A whispering tale in a fair lady's ear,
CAPULET: Such as would please: 'tis gone, 'tis gone, 'tis gone:
CAPULET: You are welcome, gentlemen! come, musicians, play.
CAPULET: A hall, a hall! give room! and foot it, girls.
NARRATOR: Music plays, and they dance
CAPULET: More light, you knaves, and turn the tables up,
CAPULET: And quench the fire, the room is grown too hot.
CAPULET: Ah, sirrah, this unlook'd-for sport comes well.
CAPULET: Nay, sit, nay, sit, good cousin Capulet,
CAPULET: For you and I are past our dancing days:
CAPULET: How long is't now since last yourself and I
CAPULET: Were in a mask?
Second Capulet: By'r lady, thirty years.
CAPULET: What, man! 'tis not so much, 'tis not so much:
CAPULET: 'Tis since the nuptials of Lucentio,
CAPULET: Come pentecost as quickly as it will,
CAPULET: Some five and twenty years, and then we mask'd.
Second Capulet: 'Tis more, 'tis more, his son is elder, sir,
Second Capulet: His son is thirty.
CAPULET: Will you tell me that?
CAPULET: His son was but a ward two years ago.
ROMEO: [To a Servingman]  What lady is that, which doth
ROMEO: enrich the hand
ROMEO: Of yonder knight?
Servant: I know not, sir.
ROMEO: O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!
ROMEO: It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night
ROMEO: Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope's ear,
ROMEO: Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear!
ROMEO: So shows a snowy dove trooping with crows,
ROMEO: As yonder lady o'er her fellows shows.
ROMEO: The measure done, I'll watch her place of stand,
ROMEO: And, touching hers, make blessed my rude hand.
ROMEO: Did my heart love till now? forswear it, sight!
ROMEO: For I ne'er saw true beauty till this night.
TYBALT: This, by his voice, should be a Montague.
TYBALT: Fetch me my rapier, boy. What dares the slave
TYBALT: Come hither, cover'd with an antic face,
TYBALT: To fleer and scorn at our solemnity?
TYBALT: Now, by the stock and honour of my kin,
TYBALT: To strike him dead, I hold it not a sin.
CAPULET: Why, how now, kinsman! wherefore storm you so?
TYBALT: Uncle, this is a Montague, our foe,
TYBALT: A villain that is hither come in spite,
TYBALT: To scorn at our solemnity this night.
CAPULET: Young Romeo is it?
TYBALT: 'Tis he, that villain Romeo.
CAPULET: Content thee, gentle coz, let him alone,
CAPULET: He bears him like a portly gentleman,
CAPULET: And, to say truth, Verona brags of him
CAPULET: To be a virtuous and well-govern'd youth:
CAPULET: I would not for the wealth of all the town
CAPULET: Here in my house do him disparagement:
CAPULET: Therefore be patient, take no note of him:
CAPULET: It is my will, the which if thou respect,
CAPULET: Show a fair presence and put off these frowns,
CAPULET: And ill-beseeming semblance for a feast.
TYBALT: It fits, when such a villain is a guest:
TYBALT: I'll not endure him.
CAPULET: He shall be endured:
CAPULET: What, goodman boy! I say, he shall: go to,
CAPULET: Am I the master here, or you? go to.
CAPULET: You'll not endure him! God shall mend my soul!
CAPULET: You'll make a mutiny among my guests!
CAPULET: You will set cock-a-hoop! you'll be the man!
TYBALT: Why, uncle, 'tis a shame.
CAPULET: Go to, go to,
CAPULET: You are a saucy boy: is't so, indeed?
CAPULET: This trick may chance to scathe you, I know what:
CAPULET: You must contrary me! marry, 'tis time.
CAPULET: Well said, my hearts! You are a princox, go:
CAPULET: Be quiet, or--More light, more light! For shame!
CAPULET: I'll make you quiet. What, cheerly, my hearts!
TYBALT: Patience perforce with wilful choler meeting
TYBALT: Makes my flesh tremble in their different greeting.
TYBALT: I will withdraw: but this intrusion shall
TYBALT: Now seeming sweet convert to bitter gall.
NARRATOR: Exit
ROMEO: [To JULIET]  If I profane with my unworthiest hand
ROMEO: This holy shrine, the gentle fine is this:
ROMEO: My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand
ROMEO: To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
JULIET: Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
JULIET: Which mannerly devotion shows in this,
JULIET: For saints have hands that pilgrims' hands do touch,
JULIET: And palm to palm is holy palmers' kiss.
ROMEO: Have not saints lips, and holy palmers too?
JULIET: Ay, pilgrim, lips that they must use in prayer.
ROMEO: O, then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do,
ROMEO: They pray, grant thou, lest faith turn to despair.
JULIET: Saints do not move, though grant for prayers' sake.
ROMEO: Then move not, while my prayer's effect I take.
ROMEO: Thus from my lips, by yours, my sin is purged.
JULIET: Then have my lips the sin that they have took.
ROMEO: Sin from thy lips? O trespass sweetly urged!
ROMEO: Give me my sin again.
JULIET: You kiss by the book.
Nurse: Madam, your mother craves a word with you.
ROMEO: What is her mother?
Nurse: Marry, bachelor,
Nurse: Her mother is the lady of the house,
Nurse: And a good lady, and a wise and virtuous
Nurse: I nursed her daughter, that you talk'd withal,
Nurse: I tell you, he that can lay hold of her
Nurse: Shall have the chinks.
ROMEO: Is she a Capulet?
ROMEO: O dear account! my life is my foe's debt.
BENVOLIO: Away, begone, the sport is at the best.
ROMEO: Ay, so I fear, the more is my unrest.
CAPULET: Nay, gentlemen, prepare not to be gone,
CAPULET: We have a trifling foolish banquet towards.
CAPULET: Is it e'en so? why, then, I thank you all
CAPULET: I thank you, honest gentlemen, good night.
CAPULET: More torches here! Come on then, let's to bed.
CAPULET: Ah, sirrah, by my fay, it waxes late:
CAPULET: I'll to my rest.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but JULIET and Nurse
JULIET: Come hither, nurse. What is yond gentleman?
Nurse: The son and heir of old Tiberio.
JULIET: What's he that now is going out of door?
Nurse: Marry, that, I think, be young Petrucio.
JULIET: What's he that follows there, that would not dance?
Nurse: I know not.
JULIET: Go ask his name: if he be married.
JULIET: My grave is like to be my wedding bed.
Nurse: His name is Romeo, and a Montague,
Nurse: The only son of your great enemy.
JULIET: My only love sprung from my only hate!
JULIET: Too early seen unknown, and known too late!
JULIET: Prodigious birth of love it is to me,
JULIET: That I must love a loathed enemy.
Nurse: What's this? what's this?
JULIET: A rhyme I learn'd even now
JULIET: Of one I danced withal.
NARRATOR: One calls within 'Juliet.'
Nurse: Anon, anon!
Nurse: Come, let's away, the strangers all are gone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
NARRATOR: Enter Chorus
Chorus: Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie,
Chorus: And young affection gapes to be his heir,
Chorus: That fair for which love groan'd for and would die,
Chorus: With tender Juliet match'd, is now not fair.
Chorus: Now Romeo is beloved and loves again,
Chorus: Alike betwitched by the charm of looks,
Chorus: But to his foe supposed he must complain,
Chorus: And she steal love's sweet bait from fearful hooks:
Chorus: Being held a foe, he may not have access
Chorus: To breathe such vows as lovers use to swear,
Chorus: And she as much in love, her means much less
Chorus: To meet her new-beloved any where:
Chorus: But passion lends them power, time means, to meet
Chorus: Tempering extremities with extreme sweet.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A lane by the wall of Capulet's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
ROMEO: Can I go forward when my heart is here?
ROMEO: Turn back, dull earth, and find thy centre out.
NARRATOR: He climbs the wall, and leaps down within it
NARRATOR: Enter BENVOLIO and MERCUTIO
BENVOLIO: Romeo! my cousin Romeo!
MERCUTIO: He is wise,
MERCUTIO: And, on my lie, hath stol'n him home to bed.
BENVOLIO: He ran this way, and leap'd this orchard wall:
BENVOLIO: Call, good Mercutio.
MERCUTIO: Nay, I'll conjure too.
MERCUTIO: Romeo! humours! madman! passion! lover!
MERCUTIO: Appear thou in the likeness of a sigh:
MERCUTIO: Speak but one rhyme, and I am satisfied,
MERCUTIO: Cry but 'Ay me!' pronounce but 'love' and 'dove,'
MERCUTIO: Speak to my gossip Venus one fair word,
MERCUTIO: One nick-name for her purblind son and heir,
MERCUTIO: Young Adam Cupid, he that shot so trim,
MERCUTIO: When King Cophetua loved the beggar-maid!
MERCUTIO: He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not,
MERCUTIO: The ape is dead, and I must conjure him.
MERCUTIO: I conjure thee by Rosaline's bright eyes,
MERCUTIO: By her high forehead and her scarlet lip,
MERCUTIO: By her fine foot, straight leg and quivering thigh
MERCUTIO: And the demesnes that there adjacent lie,
MERCUTIO: That in thy likeness thou appear to us!
BENVOLIO: And if he hear thee, thou wilt anger him.
MERCUTIO: This cannot anger him: 'twould anger him
MERCUTIO: To raise a spirit in his mistress' circle
MERCUTIO: Of some strange nature, letting it there stand
MERCUTIO: Till she had laid it and conjured it down,
MERCUTIO: That were some spite: my invocation
MERCUTIO: Is fair and honest, and in his mistres s' name
MERCUTIO: I conjure only but to raise up him.
BENVOLIO: Come, he hath hid himself among these trees,
BENVOLIO: To be consorted with the humorous night:
BENVOLIO: Blind is his love and best befits the dark.
MERCUTIO: If love be blind, love cannot hit the mark.
MERCUTIO: Now will he sit under a medlar tree,
MERCUTIO: And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit
MERCUTIO: As maids call medlars, when they laugh alone.
MERCUTIO: Romeo, that she were, O, that she were
MERCUTIO: An open et caetera, thou a poperin pear!
MERCUTIO: Romeo, good night: I'll to my truckle-bed,
MERCUTIO: This field-bed is too cold for me to sleep:
MERCUTIO: Come, shall we go?
BENVOLIO: Go, then, for 'tis in vain
BENVOLIO: To seek him here that means not to be found.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Capulet's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
ROMEO: He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
NARRATOR: JULIET appears above at a window
ROMEO: But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks?
ROMEO: It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
ROMEO: Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon,
ROMEO: Who is already sick and pale with grief,
ROMEO: That thou her maid art far more fair than she:
ROMEO: Be not her maid, since she is envious,
ROMEO: Her vestal livery is but sick and green
ROMEO: And none but fools do wear it, cast it off.
ROMEO: It is my lady, O, it is my love!
ROMEO: O, that she knew she were!
ROMEO: She speaks yet she says nothing: what of that?
ROMEO: Her eye discourses, I will answer it.
ROMEO: I am too bold, 'tis not to me she speaks:
ROMEO: Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,
ROMEO: Having some business, do entreat her eyes
ROMEO: To twinkle in their spheres till they return.
ROMEO: What if her eyes were there, they in her head?
ROMEO: The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars,
ROMEO: As daylight doth a lamp, her eyes in heaven
ROMEO: Would through the airy region stream so bright
ROMEO: That birds would sing and think it were not night.
ROMEO: See, how she leans her cheek upon her hand!
ROMEO: O, that I were a glove upon that hand,
ROMEO: That I might touch that cheek!
JULIET: Ay me!
ROMEO: She speaks:
ROMEO: O, speak again, bright angel! for thou art
ROMEO: As glorious to this night, being o'er my head
ROMEO: As is a winged messenger of heaven
ROMEO: Unto the white-upturned wondering eyes
ROMEO: Of mortals that fall back to gaze on him
ROMEO: When he bestrides the lazy-pacing clouds
ROMEO: And sails upon the bosom of the air.
JULIET: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo?
JULIET: Deny thy father and refuse thy name,
JULIET: Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,
JULIET: And I'll no longer be a Capulet.
ROMEO: [Aside]  Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
JULIET: 'Tis but thy name that is my enemy,
JULIET: Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.
JULIET: What's Montague? it is nor hand, nor foot,
JULIET: Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part
JULIET: Belonging to a man. O, be some other name!
JULIET: What's in a name? that which we call a rose
JULIET: By any other name would smell as sweet,
JULIET: So Romeo would, were he not Romeo call'd,
JULIET: Retain that dear perfection which he owes
JULIET: Without that title. Romeo, doff thy name,
JULIET: And for that name which is no part of thee
JULIET: Take all myself.
ROMEO: I take thee at thy word:
ROMEO: Call me but love, and I'll be new baptized,
ROMEO: Henceforth I never will be Romeo.
JULIET: What man art thou that thus bescreen'd in night
JULIET: So stumblest on my counsel?
ROMEO: By a name
ROMEO: I know not how to tell thee who I am:
ROMEO: My name, dear saint, is hateful to myself,
ROMEO: Because it is an enemy to thee,
ROMEO: Had I it written, I would tear the word.
JULIET: My ears have not yet drunk a hundred words
JULIET: Of that tongue's utterance, yet I know the sound:
JULIET: Art thou not Romeo and a Montague?
ROMEO: Neither, fair saint, if either thee dislike.
JULIET: How camest thou hither, tell me, and wherefore?
JULIET: The orchard walls are high and hard to climb,
JULIET: And the place death, considering who thou art,
JULIET: If any of my kinsmen find thee here.
ROMEO: With love's light wings did I o'er-perch these walls,
ROMEO: For stony limits cannot hold love out,
ROMEO: And what love can do that dares love attempt,
ROMEO: Therefore thy kinsmen are no let to me.
JULIET: If they do see thee, they will murder thee.
ROMEO: Alack, there lies more peril in thine eye
ROMEO: Than twenty of their swords: look thou but sweet,
ROMEO: And I am proof against their enmity.
JULIET: I would not for the world they saw thee here.
ROMEO: I have night's cloak to hide me from their sight,
ROMEO: And but thou love me, let them find me here:
ROMEO: My life were better ended by their hate,
ROMEO: Than death prorogued, wanting of thy love.
JULIET: By whose direction found'st thou out this place?
ROMEO: By love, who first did prompt me to inquire,
ROMEO: He lent me counsel and I lent him eyes.
ROMEO: I am no pilot, yet, wert thou as far
ROMEO: As that vast shore wash'd with the farthest sea,
ROMEO: I would adventure for such merchandise.
JULIET: Thou know'st the mask of night is on my face,
JULIET: Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek
JULIET: For that which thou hast heard me speak to-night
JULIET: Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny
JULIET: What I have spoke: but farewell compliment!
JULIET: Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say 'Ay,'
JULIET: And I will take thy word: yet if thou swear'st,
JULIET: Thou mayst prove false, at lovers' perjuries
JULIET: Then say, Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo,
JULIET: If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully:
JULIET: Or if thou think'st I am too quickly won,
JULIET: I'll frown and be perverse an say thee nay,
JULIET: So thou wilt woo, but else, not for the world.
