JULIET: In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond,
JULIET: And therefore thou mayst think my 'havior light:
JULIET: But trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more true
JULIET: Than those that have more cunning to be strange.
JULIET: I should have been more strange, I must confess,
JULIET: But that thou overheard'st, ere I was ware,
JULIET: My true love's passion: therefore pardon me,
JULIET: And not impute this yielding to light love,
JULIET: Which the dark night hath so discovered.
ROMEO: Lady, by yonder blessed moon I swear
ROMEO: That tips with silver all these fruit-tree tops--
JULIET: O, swear not by the moon, the inconstant moon,
JULIET: That monthly changes in her circled orb,
JULIET: Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
ROMEO: What shall I swear by?
JULIET: Do not swear at all,
JULIET: Or, if thou wilt, swear by thy gracious self,
JULIET: Which is the god of my idolatry,
JULIET: And I'll believe thee.
ROMEO: If my heart's dear love--
JULIET: Well, do not swear: although I joy in thee,
JULIET: I have no joy of this contract to-night:
JULIET: It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden,
JULIET: Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be
JULIET: Ere one can say 'It lightens.' Sweet, good night!
JULIET: This bud of love, by summer's ripening breath,
JULIET: May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet.
JULIET: Good night, good night! as sweet repose and rest
JULIET: Come to thy heart as that within my breast!
ROMEO: O, wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?
JULIET: What satisfaction canst thou have to-night?
ROMEO: The exchange of thy love's faithful vow for mine.
JULIET: I gave thee mine before thou didst request it:
JULIET: And yet I would it were to give again.
ROMEO: Wouldst thou withdraw it? for what purpose, love?
JULIET: But to be frank, and give it thee again.
JULIET: And yet I wish but for the thing I have:
JULIET: My bounty is as boundless as the sea,
JULIET: My love as deep, the more I give to thee,
JULIET: The more I have, for both are infinite.
NARRATOR: Nurse calls within
JULIET: I hear some noise within, dear love, adieu!
JULIET: Anon, good nurse! Sweet Montague, be true.
JULIET: Stay but a little, I will come again.
NARRATOR: Exit, above
ROMEO: O blessed, blessed night! I am afeard.
ROMEO: Being in night, all this is but a dream,
ROMEO: Too flattering-sweet to be substantial.
NARRATOR: Re-enter JULIET, above
JULIET: Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed.
JULIET: If that thy bent of love be honourable,
JULIET: Thy purpose marriage, send me word to-morrow,
JULIET: By one that I'll procure to come to thee,
JULIET: Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite,
JULIET: And all my fortunes at thy foot I'll lay
JULIET: And follow thee my lord throughout the world.
Nurse: [Within]  Madam!
JULIET: I come, anon.--But if thou mean'st not well,
JULIET: I do beseech thee--
Nurse: [Within]  Madam!
JULIET: By and by, I come:--
JULIET: To cease thy suit, and leave me to my grief:
JULIET: To-morrow will I send.
ROMEO: So thrive my soul--
JULIET: A thousand times good night!
NARRATOR: Exit, above
ROMEO: A thousand times the worse, to want thy light.
ROMEO: Love goes toward love, as schoolboys from
ROMEO: their books,
ROMEO: But love from love, toward school with heavy looks.
NARRATOR: Retiring
NARRATOR: Re-enter JULIET, above
JULIET: Hist! Romeo, hist! O, for a falconer's voice,
JULIET: To lure this tassel-gentle back again!
JULIET: Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud,
JULIET: Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies,
JULIET: And make her airy tongue more hoarse than mine,
JULIET: With repetition of my Romeo's name.
ROMEO: It is my soul that calls upon my name:
ROMEO: How silver-sweet sound lovers' tongues by night,
ROMEO: Like softest music to attending ears!
JULIET: Romeo!
ROMEO: My dear?
JULIET: At what o'clock to-morrow
JULIET: Shall I send to thee?
ROMEO: At the hour of nine.
JULIET: I will not fail: 'tis twenty years till then.
JULIET: I have forgot why I did call thee back.
ROMEO: Let me stand here till thou remember it.
JULIET: I shall forget, to have thee still stand there,
JULIET: Remembering how I love thy company.
ROMEO: And I'll still stay, to have thee still forget,
ROMEO: Forgetting any other home but this.
JULIET: 'Tis almost morning, I would have thee gone:
JULIET: And yet no further than a wanton's bird,
JULIET: Who lets it hop a little from her hand,
JULIET: Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves,
JULIET: And with a silk thread plucks it back again,
JULIET: So loving-jealous of his liberty.
ROMEO: I would I were thy bird.
JULIET: Sweet, so would I:
JULIET: Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing.
JULIET: Good night, good night! parting is such
JULIET: sweet sorrow,
JULIET: That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
NARRATOR: Exit above
ROMEO: Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast!
ROMEO: Would I were sleep and peace, so sweet to rest!
ROMEO: Hence will I to my ghostly father's cell,
ROMEO: His help to crave, and my dear hap to tell.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Friar Laurence's cell.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE, with a basket
FRIAR LAURENCE: The grey-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Chequering the eastern clouds with streaks of light,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And flecked darkness like a drunkard reels
FRIAR LAURENCE: From forth day's path and Titan's fiery wheels:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Now, ere the sun advance his burning eye,
FRIAR LAURENCE: The day to cheer and night's dank dew to dry,
FRIAR LAURENCE: I must up-fill this osier cage of ours
FRIAR LAURENCE: With baleful weeds and precious-juiced flowers.
FRIAR LAURENCE: The earth that's nature's mother is her tomb,
FRIAR LAURENCE: What is her burying grave that is her womb,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And from her womb children of divers kind
FRIAR LAURENCE: We sucking on her natural bosom find,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Many for many virtues excellent,
FRIAR LAURENCE: None but for some and yet all different.
FRIAR LAURENCE: O, mickle is the powerful grace that lies
FRIAR LAURENCE: In herbs, plants, stones, and their true qualities:
FRIAR LAURENCE: For nought so vile that on the earth doth live
FRIAR LAURENCE: But to the earth some special good doth give,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Nor aught so good but strain'd from that fair use
FRIAR LAURENCE: Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Virtue itself turns vice, being misapplied,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And vice sometimes by action dignified.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Within the infant rind of this small flower
FRIAR LAURENCE: Poison hath residence and medicine power:
FRIAR LAURENCE: For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Being tasted, slays all senses with the heart.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Two such opposed kings encamp them still
FRIAR LAURENCE: In man as well as herbs, grace and rude will,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And where the worser is predominant,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Full soon the canker death eats up that plant.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
ROMEO: Good morrow, father.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Benedicite!
FRIAR LAURENCE: What early tongue so sweet saluteth me?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Young son, it argues a distemper'd head
FRIAR LAURENCE: So soon to bid good morrow to thy bed:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Care keeps his watch in every old man's eye,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And where care lodges, sleep will never lie,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But where unbruised youth with unstuff'd brain
FRIAR LAURENCE: Doth couch his limbs, there golden sleep doth reign:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Therefore thy earliness doth me assure
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou art up-roused by some distemperature,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Or if not so, then here I hit it right,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Our Romeo hath not been in bed to-night.
ROMEO: That last is true, the sweeter rest was mine.
FRIAR LAURENCE: God pardon sin! wast thou with Rosaline?
ROMEO: With Rosaline, my ghostly father? no,
ROMEO: I have forgot that name, and that name's woe.
FRIAR LAURENCE: That's my good son: but where hast thou been, then?
ROMEO: I'll tell thee, ere thou ask it me again.
ROMEO: I have been feasting with mine enemy,
ROMEO: Where on a sudden one hath wounded me,
ROMEO: That's by me wounded: both our remedies
ROMEO: Within thy help and holy physic lies:
ROMEO: I bear no hatred, blessed man, for, lo,
ROMEO: My intercession likewise steads my foe.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Riddling confession finds but riddling shrift.
ROMEO: Then plainly know my heart's dear love is set
ROMEO: On the fair daughter of rich Capulet:
ROMEO: As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine,
ROMEO: And all combined, save what thou must combine
ROMEO: By holy marriage: when and where and how
ROMEO: We met, we woo'd and made exchange of vow,
ROMEO: I'll tell thee as we pass, but this I pray,
ROMEO: That thou consent to marry us to-day.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Holy Saint Francis, what a change is here!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is Rosaline, whom thou didst love so dear,
FRIAR LAURENCE: So soon forsaken? young men's love then lies
FRIAR LAURENCE: Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hath wash'd thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline!
FRIAR LAURENCE: How much salt water thrown away in waste,
FRIAR LAURENCE: To season love, that of it doth not taste!
FRIAR LAURENCE: The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy old groans ring yet in my ancient ears,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Lo, here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit
FRIAR LAURENCE: Of an old tear that is not wash'd off yet:
FRIAR LAURENCE: If e'er thou wast thyself and these woes thine,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline:
FRIAR LAURENCE: And art thou changed? pronounce this sentence then,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Women may fall, when there's no strength in men.
ROMEO: Thou chid'st me oft for loving Rosaline.
FRIAR LAURENCE: For doting, not for loving, pupil mine.
ROMEO: And bad'st me bury love.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Not in a grave,
FRIAR LAURENCE: To lay one in, another out to have.
ROMEO: I pray thee, chide not, she whom I love now
ROMEO: Doth grace for grace and love for love allow,
ROMEO: The other did not so.
FRIAR LAURENCE: O, she knew well
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy love did read by rote and could not spell.
FRIAR LAURENCE: But come, young waverer, come, go with me,
FRIAR LAURENCE: In one respect I'll thy assistant be,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For this alliance may so happy prove,
FRIAR LAURENCE: To turn your households' rancour to pure love.
ROMEO: O, let us hence, I stand on sudden haste.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Wisely and slow, they stumble that run fast.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter BENVOLIO and MERCUTIO
MERCUTIO: Where the devil should this Romeo be?
MERCUTIO: Came he not home to-night?
BENVOLIO: Not to his father's, I spoke with his man.
MERCUTIO: Ah, that same pale hard-hearted wench, that Rosaline.
MERCUTIO: Torments him so, that he will sure run mad.
BENVOLIO: Tybalt, the kinsman of old Capulet,
BENVOLIO: Hath sent a letter to his father's house.
MERCUTIO: A challenge, on my life.
BENVOLIO: Romeo will answer it.
MERCUTIO: Any man that can write may answer a letter.
BENVOLIO: Nay, he will answer the letter's master, how he
BENVOLIO: dares, being dared.
MERCUTIO: Alas poor Romeo! he is already dead, stabbed with a
MERCUTIO: white wench's black eye, shot through the ear with a
MERCUTIO: love-song, the very pin of his heart cleft with the
MERCUTIO: blind bow-boy's butt-shaft: and is he a man to
MERCUTIO: encounter Tybalt?
BENVOLIO: Why, what is Tybalt?
MERCUTIO: More than prince of cats, I can tell you. O, he is
MERCUTIO: the courageous captain of compliments. He fights as
MERCUTIO: you sing prick-song, keeps time, distance, and
MERCUTIO: proportion, rests me his minim rest, one, two, and
MERCUTIO: the third in your bosom: the very butcher of a silk
MERCUTIO: button, a duellist, a duellist, a gentleman of the
MERCUTIO: very first house, of the first and second cause:
MERCUTIO: ah, the immortal passado! the punto reverso! the
MERCUTIO: hai!
BENVOLIO: The what?
MERCUTIO: The pox of such antic, lisping, affecting
MERCUTIO: fantasticoes, these new tuners of accents! 'By Jesu,
MERCUTIO: a very good blade! a very tall man! a very good
MERCUTIO: whore!' Why, is not this a lamentable thing,
MERCUTIO: grandsire, that we should be thus afflicted with
MERCUTIO: these strange flies, these fashion-mongers, these
MERCUTIO: perdona-mi's, who stand so much on the new form,
MERCUTIO: that they cannot at ease on the old bench? O, their
MERCUTIO: bones, their bones!
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
BENVOLIO: Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo.
MERCUTIO: Without his roe, like a dried herring: flesh, flesh,
MERCUTIO: how art thou fishified! Now is he for the numbers
MERCUTIO: that Petrarch flowed in: Laura to his lady was but a
MERCUTIO: kitchen-wench, marry, she had a better love to
MERCUTIO: be-rhyme her, Dido a dowdy, Cleopatra a gipsy,
MERCUTIO: Helen and Hero hildings and harlots, Thisbe a grey
MERCUTIO: eye or so, but not to the purpose. Signior
MERCUTIO: Romeo, bon jour! there's a French salutation
MERCUTIO: to your French slop. You gave us the counterfeit
MERCUTIO: fairly last night.
ROMEO: Good morrow to you both. What counterfeit did I give you?
MERCUTIO: The ship, sir, the slip, can you not conceive?
ROMEO: Pardon, good Mercutio, my business was great, and in
ROMEO: such a case as mine a man may strain courtesy.
MERCUTIO: That's as much as to say, such a case as yours
MERCUTIO: constrains a man to bow in the hams.
ROMEO: Meaning, to court'sy.
MERCUTIO: Thou hast most kindly hit it.
ROMEO: A most courteous exposition.
MERCUTIO: Nay, I am the very pink of courtesy.
ROMEO: Pink for flower.
MERCUTIO: Right.
ROMEO: Why, then is my pump well flowered.
MERCUTIO: Well said: follow me this jest now till thou hast
MERCUTIO: worn out thy pump, that when the single sole of it
MERCUTIO: is worn, the jest may remain after the wearing sole singular.
ROMEO: O single-soled jest, solely singular for the
ROMEO: singleness.
MERCUTIO: Come between us, good Benvolio, my wits faint.
ROMEO: Switch and spurs, switch and spurs, or I'll cry a match.
MERCUTIO: Nay, if thy wits run the wild-goose chase, I have
MERCUTIO: done, for thou hast more of the wild-goose in one of
MERCUTIO: thy wits than, I am sure, I have in my whole five:
MERCUTIO: was I with you there for the goose?
ROMEO: Thou wast never with me for any thing when thou wast
ROMEO: not there for the goose.
MERCUTIO: I will bite thee by the ear for that jest.
ROMEO: Nay, good goose, bite not.
MERCUTIO: Thy wit is a very bitter sweeting, it is a most
MERCUTIO: sharp sauce.
ROMEO: And is it not well served in to a sweet goose?
MERCUTIO: O here's a wit of cheveril, that stretches from an
MERCUTIO: inch narrow to an ell broad!
ROMEO: I stretch it out for that word 'broad,' which added
ROMEO: to the goose, proves thee far and wide a broad goose.
MERCUTIO: Why, is not this better now than groaning for love?
MERCUTIO: now art thou sociable, now art thou Romeo, now art
MERCUTIO: thou what thou art, by art as well as by nature:
MERCUTIO: for this drivelling love is like a great natural,
MERCUTIO: that runs lolling up and down to hide his bauble in a hole.
BENVOLIO: Stop there, stop there.
MERCUTIO: Thou desirest me to stop in my tale against the hair.
BENVOLIO: Thou wouldst else have made thy tale large.
MERCUTIO: O, thou art deceived, I would have made it short:
MERCUTIO: for I was come to the whole depth of my tale, and
MERCUTIO: meant, indeed, to occupy the argument no longer.
ROMEO: Here's goodly gear!
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse and PETER
MERCUTIO: A sail, a sail!
BENVOLIO: Two, two, a shirt and a smock.
Nurse: Peter!
PETER: Anon!
Nurse: My fan, Peter.
MERCUTIO: Good Peter, to hide her face, for her fan's the
MERCUTIO: fairer face.
Nurse: God ye good morrow, gentlemen.
MERCUTIO: God ye good den, fair gentlewoman.
Nurse: Is it good den?
MERCUTIO: 'Tis no less, I tell you, for the bawdy hand of the
MERCUTIO: dial is now upon the prick of noon.
Nurse: Out upon you! what a man are you!
ROMEO: One, gentlewoman, that God hath made for himself to
ROMEO: mar.
Nurse: By my troth, it is well said, 'for himself to mar,'
Nurse: quoth a'? Gentlemen, can any of you tell me where I
Nurse: may find the young Romeo?
ROMEO: I can tell you, but young Romeo will be older when
ROMEO: you have found him than he was when you sought him:
ROMEO: I am the youngest of that name, for fault of a worse.
Nurse: You say well.
MERCUTIO: Yea, is the worst well? very well took, i' faith,
MERCUTIO: wisely, wisely.
Nurse: if you be he, sir, I desire some confidence with
Nurse: you.
BENVOLIO: She will indite him to some supper.
MERCUTIO: A bawd, a bawd, a bawd! so ho!
ROMEO: What hast thou found?
MERCUTIO: No hare, sir, unless a hare, sir, in a lenten pie,
MERCUTIO: that is something stale and hoar ere it be spent.
NARRATOR: Sings
MERCUTIO: An old hare hoar,
MERCUTIO: And an old hare hoar,
MERCUTIO: Is very good meat in lent
MERCUTIO: But a hare that is hoar
MERCUTIO: Is too much for a score,
MERCUTIO: When it hoars ere it be spent.
MERCUTIO: Romeo, will you come to your father's? we'll
MERCUTIO: to dinner, thither.
ROMEO: I will follow you.
MERCUTIO: Farewell, ancient lady, farewell,
NARRATOR: Singing
MERCUTIO: 'lady, lady, lady.'
NARRATOR: Exeunt MERCUTIO and BENVOLIO
Nurse: Marry, farewell! I pray you, sir, what saucy
Nurse: merchant was this, that was so full of his ropery?
ROMEO: A gentleman, nurse, that loves to hear himself talk,
ROMEO: and will speak more in a minute than he will stand
ROMEO: to in a month.
Nurse: An a' speak any thing against me, I'll take him
Nurse: down, an a' were lustier than he is, and twenty such
Nurse: Jacks, and if I cannot, I'll find those that shall.
Nurse: Scurvy knave! I am none of his flirt-gills, I am
Nurse: none of his skains-mates. And thou must stand by
Nurse: too, and suffer every knave to use me at his pleasure?
PETER: I saw no man use you a pleasure, if I had, my weapon
PETER: should quickly have been out, I warrant you: I dare
PETER: draw as soon as another man, if I see occasion in a
PETER: good quarrel, and the law on my side.
Nurse: Now, afore God, I am so vexed, that every part about
Nurse: me quivers. Scurvy knave! Pray you, sir, a word:
Nurse: and as I told you, my young lady bade me inquire you
Nurse: out, what she bade me say, I will keep to myself:
Nurse: but first let me tell ye, if ye should lead her into
Nurse: a fool's paradise, as they say, it were a very gross
Nurse: kind of behavior, as they say: for the gentlewoman
Nurse: is young, and, therefore, if you should deal double
Nurse: with her, truly it were an ill thing to be offered
Nurse: to any gentlewoman, and very weak dealing.
ROMEO: Nurse, commend me to thy lady and mistress. I
ROMEO: protest unto thee--
Nurse: Good heart, and, i' faith, I will tell her as much:
Nurse: Lord, Lord, she will be a joyful woman.
ROMEO: What wilt thou tell her, nurse? thou dost not mark me.
Nurse: I will tell her, sir, that you do protest, which, as
Nurse: I take it, is a gentlemanlike offer.
ROMEO: Bid her devise
ROMEO: Some means to come to shrift this afternoon,
ROMEO: And there she shall at Friar Laurence' cell
ROMEO: Be shrived and married. Here is for thy pains.
Nurse: No truly sir, not a penny.
ROMEO: Go to, I say you shall.
Nurse: This afternoon, sir? well, she shall be there.
ROMEO: And stay, good nurse, behind the abbey wall:
ROMEO: Within this hour my man shall be with thee
ROMEO: And bring thee cords made like a tackled stair,
ROMEO: Which to the high top-gallant of my joy
ROMEO: Must be my convoy in the secret night.
ROMEO: Farewell, be trusty, and I'll quit thy pains:
ROMEO: Farewell, commend me to thy mistress.
Nurse: Now God in heaven bless thee! Hark you, sir.
ROMEO: What say'st thou, my dear nurse?
Nurse: Is your man secret? Did you ne'er hear say,
Nurse: Two may keep counsel, putting one away?
ROMEO: I warrant thee, my man's as true as steel.
NURSE: Well, sir, my mistress is the sweetest lady--Lord,
NURSE: Lord! when 'twas a little prating thing:--O, there
NURSE: is a nobleman in town, one Paris, that would fain
NURSE: lay knife aboard, but she, good soul, had as lief
NURSE: see a toad, a very toad, as see him. I anger her
NURSE: sometimes and tell her that Paris is the properer
NURSE: man, but, I'll warrant you, when I say so, she looks
NURSE: as pale as any clout in the versal world. Doth not
NURSE: rosemary and Romeo begin both with a letter?
ROMEO: Ay, nurse, what of that? both with an R.
Nurse: Ah. mocker! that's the dog's name, R is for
Nurse: the--No, I know it begins with some other
Nurse: letter:--and she hath the prettiest sententious of
Nurse: it, of you and rosemary, that it would do you good
Nurse: to hear it.
ROMEO: Commend me to thy lady.
Nurse: Ay, a thousand times.
NARRATOR: Exit Romeo
Nurse: Peter!
PETER: Anon!
Nurse: Peter, take my fan, and go before and apace.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Capulet's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
JULIET: The clock struck nine when I did send the nurse,
JULIET: In half an hour she promised to return.
JULIET: Perchance she cannot meet him: that's not so.
JULIET: O, she is lame! love's heralds should be thoughts,
JULIET: Which ten times faster glide than the sun's beams,
JULIET: Driving back shadows over louring hills:
JULIET: Therefore do nimble-pinion'd doves draw love,
JULIET: And therefore hath the wind-swift Cupid wings.
JULIET: Now is the sun upon the highmost hill
JULIET: Of this day's journey, and from nine till twelve
JULIET: Is three long hours, yet she is not come.
JULIET: Had she affections and warm youthful blood,
JULIET: She would be as swift in motion as a ball,
JULIET: My words would bandy her to my sweet love,
JULIET: And his to me:
JULIET: But old folks, many feign as they were dead,
JULIET: Unwieldy, slow, heavy and pale as lead.
JULIET: O God, she comes!
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse and PETER
JULIET: O honey nurse, what news?
JULIET: Hast thou met with him? Send thy man away.
Nurse: Peter, stay at the gate.
NARRATOR: Exit PETER
JULIET: Now, good sweet nurse,--O Lord, why look'st thou sad?
JULIET: Though news be sad, yet tell them merrily,
JULIET: If good, thou shamest the music of sweet news
JULIET: By playing it to me with so sour a face.
Nurse: I am a-weary, give me leave awhile:
Nurse: Fie, how my bones ache! what a jaunt have I had!
JULIET: I would thou hadst my bones, and I thy news:
JULIET: Nay, come, I pray thee, speak, good, good nurse, speak.
Nurse: Jesu, what haste? can you not stay awhile?
Nurse: Do you not see that I am out of breath?
JULIET: How art thou out of breath, when thou hast breath
JULIET: To say to me that thou art out of breath?
JULIET: The excuse that thou dost make in this delay
JULIET: Is longer than the tale thou dost excuse.
JULIET: Is thy news good, or bad? answer to that,
JULIET: Say either, and I'll stay the circumstance:
JULIET: Let me be satisfied, is't good or bad?
Nurse: Well, you have made a simple choice, you know not
Nurse: how to choose a man: Romeo! no, not he, though his
Nurse: face be better than any man's, yet his leg excels
Nurse: all men's, and for a hand, and a foot, and a body,
Nurse: though they be not to be talked on, yet they are
Nurse: past compare: he is not the flower of courtesy,
Nurse: but, I'll warrant him, as gentle as a lamb. Go thy
Nurse: ways, wench, serve God. What, have you dined at home?
JULIET: No, no: but all this did I know before.
JULIET: What says he of our marriage? what of that?
Nurse: Lord, how my head aches! what a head have I!
Nurse: It beats as it would fall in twenty pieces.
Nurse: My back o' t' other side,--O, my back, my back!
Nurse: Beshrew your heart for sending me about,
Nurse: To catch my death with jaunting up and down!
JULIET: I' faith, I am sorry that thou art not well.
JULIET: Sweet, sweet, sweet nurse, tell me, what says my love?
Nurse: Your love says, like an honest gentleman, and a
Nurse: courteous, and a kind, and a handsome, and, I
Nurse: warrant, a virtuous,--Where is your mother?
JULIET: Where is my mother! why, she is within,
JULIET: Where should she be? How oddly thou repliest!
JULIET: 'Your love says, like an honest gentleman,
JULIET: Where is your mother?'
Nurse: O God's lady dear!
Nurse: Are you so hot? marry, come up, I trow,
Nurse: Is this the poultice for my aching bones?
Nurse: Henceforward do your messages yourself.
JULIET: Here's such a coil! come, what says Romeo?
Nurse: Have you got leave to go to shrift to-day?
JULIET: I have.
Nurse: Then hie you hence to Friar Laurence' cell,
Nurse: There stays a husband to make you a wife:
Nurse: Now comes the wanton blood up in your cheeks,
Nurse: They'll be in scarlet straight at any news.
Nurse: Hie you to church, I must another way,
Nurse: To fetch a ladder, by the which your love
Nurse: Must climb a bird's nest soon when it is dark:
Nurse: I am the drudge and toil in your delight,
Nurse: But you shall bear the burden soon at night.
Nurse: Go, I'll to dinner: hie you to the cell.
JULIET: Hie to high fortune! Honest nurse, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Friar Laurence's cell.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE and ROMEO
FRIAR LAURENCE: So smile the heavens upon this holy act,
FRIAR LAURENCE: That after hours with sorrow chide us not!
ROMEO: Amen, amen! but come what sorrow can,
ROMEO: It cannot countervail the exchange of joy
ROMEO: That one short minute gives me in her sight:
ROMEO: Do thou but close our hands with holy words,
ROMEO: Then love-devouring death do what he dare,
ROMEO: It is enough I may but call her mine.
FRIAR LAURENCE: These violent delights have violent ends
FRIAR LAURENCE: And in their triumph die, like fire and powder,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Which as they kiss consume: the sweetest honey
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is loathsome in his own deliciousness
FRIAR LAURENCE: And in the taste confounds the appetite:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Therefore love moderately, long love doth so,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
FRIAR LAURENCE: Here comes the lady: O, so light a foot
FRIAR LAURENCE: Will ne'er wear out the everlasting flint:
FRIAR LAURENCE: A lover may bestride the gossamer
FRIAR LAURENCE: That idles in the wanton summer air,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And yet not fall, so light is vanity.
JULIET: Good even to my ghostly confessor.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo shall thank thee, daughter, for us both.
JULIET: As much to him, else is his thanks too much.
ROMEO: Ah, Juliet, if the measure of thy joy
ROMEO: Be heap'd like mine and that thy skill be more
ROMEO: To blazon it, then sweeten with thy breath
ROMEO: This neighbour air, and let rich music's tongue
ROMEO: Unfold the imagined happiness that both
ROMEO: Receive in either by this dear encounter.
JULIET: Conceit, more rich in matter than in words,
JULIET: Brags of his substance, not of ornament:
JULIET: They are but beggars that can count their worth,
JULIET: But my true love is grown to such excess
JULIET: I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Come, come with me, and we will make short work,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For, by your leaves, you shall not stay alone
FRIAR LAURENCE: Till holy church incorporate two in one.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter MERCUTIO, BENVOLIO, Page, and Servants
BENVOLIO: I pray thee, good Mercutio, let's retire:
BENVOLIO: The day is hot, the Capulets abroad,
BENVOLIO: And, if we meet, we shall not scape a brawl,
BENVOLIO: For now, these hot days, is the mad blood stirring.
MERCUTIO: Thou art like one of those fellows that when he
MERCUTIO: enters the confines of a tavern claps me his sword
MERCUTIO: upon the table and says 'God send me no need of
MERCUTIO: thee!' and by the operation of the second cup draws
MERCUTIO: it on the drawer, when indeed there is no need.
BENVOLIO: Am I like such a fellow?
MERCUTIO: Come, come, thou art as hot a Jack in thy mood as
MERCUTIO: any in Italy, and as soon moved to be moody, and as
MERCUTIO: soon moody to be moved.
BENVOLIO: And what to?
MERCUTIO: Nay, an there were two such, we should have none
MERCUTIO: shortly, for one would kill the other. Thou! why,
MERCUTIO: thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a hair more,
MERCUTIO: or a hair less, in his beard, than thou hast: thou
MERCUTIO: wilt quarrel with a man for cracking nuts, having no
MERCUTIO: other reason but because thou hast hazel eyes: what
MERCUTIO: eye but such an eye would spy out such a quarrel?
MERCUTIO: Thy head is as fun of quarrels as an egg is full of
MERCUTIO: meat, and yet thy head hath been beaten as addle as
MERCUTIO: an egg for quarrelling: thou hast quarrelled with a
MERCUTIO: man for coughing in the street, because he hath
MERCUTIO: wakened thy dog that hath lain asleep in the sun:
MERCUTIO: didst thou not fall out with a tailor for wearing
MERCUTIO: his new doublet before Easter? with another, for
MERCUTIO: tying his new shoes with old riband? and yet thou
MERCUTIO: wilt tutor me from quarrelling!
BENVOLIO: An I were so apt to quarrel as thou art, any man
BENVOLIO: should buy the fee-simple of my life for an hour and a quarter.
MERCUTIO: The fee-simple! O simple!
BENVOLIO: By my head, here come the Capulets.
MERCUTIO: By my heel, I care not.
NARRATOR: Enter TYBALT and others
TYBALT: Follow me close, for I will speak to them.
TYBALT: Gentlemen, good den: a word with one of you.
MERCUTIO: And but one word with one of us? couple it with
MERCUTIO: something, make it a word and a blow.
TYBALT: You shall find me apt enough to that, sir, an you
TYBALT: will give me occasion.
MERCUTIO: Could you not take some occasion without giving?
TYBALT: Mercutio, thou consort'st with Romeo,--
MERCUTIO: Consort! what, dost thou make us minstrels? an
MERCUTIO: thou make minstrels of us, look to hear nothing but
MERCUTIO: discords: here's my fiddlestick, here's that shall
MERCUTIO: make you dance. 'Zounds, consort!
BENVOLIO: We talk here in the public haunt of men:
BENVOLIO: Either withdraw unto some private place,
BENVOLIO: And reason coldly of your grievances,
BENVOLIO: Or else depart, here all eyes gaze on us.
MERCUTIO: Men's eyes were made to look, and let them gaze,
MERCUTIO: I will not budge for no man's pleasure, I.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
TYBALT: Well, peace be with you, sir: here comes my man.
MERCUTIO: But I'll be hanged, sir, if he wear your livery:
MERCUTIO: Marry, go before to field, he'll be your follower,
MERCUTIO: Your worship in that sense may call him 'man.'
TYBALT: Romeo, the hate I bear thee can afford
TYBALT: No better term than this,--thou art a villain.
ROMEO: Tybalt, the reason that I have to love thee
ROMEO: Doth much excuse the appertaining rage
ROMEO: To such a greeting: villain am I none,
ROMEO: Therefore farewell, I see thou know'st me not.
TYBALT: Boy, this shall not excuse the injuries
TYBALT: That thou hast done me, therefore turn and draw.
ROMEO: I do protest, I never injured thee,
ROMEO: But love thee better than thou canst devise,
ROMEO: Till thou shalt know the reason of my love:
ROMEO: And so, good Capulet,--which name I tender
ROMEO: As dearly as my own,--be satisfied.
MERCUTIO: O calm, dishonourable, vile submission!
MERCUTIO: Alla stoccata carries it away.
NARRATOR: Draws
MERCUTIO: Tybalt, you rat-catcher, will you walk?
TYBALT: What wouldst thou have with me?
MERCUTIO: Good king of cats, nothing but one of your nine
MERCUTIO: lives, that I mean to make bold withal, and as you
MERCUTIO: shall use me hereafter, drybeat the rest of the
MERCUTIO: eight. Will you pluck your sword out of his pitcher
MERCUTIO: by the ears? make haste, lest mine be about your
MERCUTIO: ears ere it be out.
TYBALT: I am for you.
NARRATOR: Drawing
ROMEO: Gentle Mercutio, put thy rapier up.
MERCUTIO: Come, sir, your passado.
NARRATOR: They fight
ROMEO: Draw, Benvolio, beat down their weapons.
ROMEO: Gentlemen, for shame, forbear this outrage!
ROMEO: Tybalt, Mercutio, the prince expressly hath
ROMEO: Forbidden bandying in Verona streets:
ROMEO: Hold, Tybalt! good Mercutio!
NARRATOR: TYBALT under ROMEO's arm stabs MERCUTIO, and flies with his followers
MERCUTIO: I am hurt.
MERCUTIO: A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
MERCUTIO: Is he gone, and hath nothing?
BENVOLIO: What, art thou hurt?
MERCUTIO: Ay, ay, a scratch, a scratch, marry, 'tis enough.
MERCUTIO: Where is my page? Go, villain, fetch a surgeon.
NARRATOR: Exit Page
ROMEO: Courage, man, the hurt cannot be much.
MERCUTIO: No, 'tis not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a
MERCUTIO: church-door, but 'tis enough,'twill serve: ask for
MERCUTIO: me to-morrow, and you shall find me a grave man. I
MERCUTIO: am peppered, I warrant, for this world. A plague o'
MERCUTIO: both your houses! 'Zounds, a dog, a rat, a mouse, a
MERCUTIO: cat, to scratch a man to death! a braggart, a
MERCUTIO: rogue, a villain, that fights by the book of
MERCUTIO: arithmetic! Why the devil came you between us? I
MERCUTIO: was hurt under your arm.
ROMEO: I thought all for the best.
MERCUTIO: Help me into some house, Benvolio,
MERCUTIO: Or I shall faint. A plague o' both your houses!
MERCUTIO: They have made worms' meat of me: I have it,
MERCUTIO: And soundly too: your houses!
NARRATOR: Exeunt MERCUTIO and BENVOLIO
ROMEO: This gentleman, the prince's near ally,
ROMEO: My very friend, hath got his mortal hurt
ROMEO: In my behalf, my reputation stain'd
ROMEO: With Tybalt's slander,--Tybalt, that an hour
ROMEO: Hath been my kinsman! O sweet Juliet,
ROMEO: Thy beauty hath made me effeminate
ROMEO: And in my temper soften'd valour's steel!
NARRATOR: Re-enter BENVOLIO
BENVOLIO: O Romeo, Romeo, brave Mercutio's dead!
BENVOLIO: That gallant spirit hath aspired the clouds,
BENVOLIO: Which too untimely here did scorn the earth.
ROMEO: This day's black fate on more days doth depend,
ROMEO: This but begins the woe, others must end.
BENVOLIO: Here comes the furious Tybalt back again.
ROMEO: Alive, in triumph! and Mercutio slain!
ROMEO: Away to heaven, respective lenity,
ROMEO: And fire-eyed fury be my conduct now!
NARRATOR: Re-enter TYBALT
ROMEO: Now, Tybalt, take the villain back again,
ROMEO: That late thou gavest me, for Mercutio's soul

ROMEO: Staying for thine to keep him company:
ROMEO: Either thou, or I, or both, must go with him.
TYBALT: Thou, wretched boy, that didst consort him here,
TYBALT: Shalt with him hence.
ROMEO: This shall determine that.
ROMEO: They fight, TYBALT falls
BENVOLIO: Romeo, away, be gone!
BENVOLIO: The citizens are up, and Tybalt slain.
BENVOLIO: Stand not amazed: the prince will doom thee death,
BENVOLIO: If thou art taken: hence, be gone, away!
ROMEO: O, I am fortune's fool!
BENVOLIO: Why dost thou stay?
NARRATOR: Exit ROMEO
NARRATOR: Enter Citizens,  and c
First Citizen: Which way ran he that kill'd Mercutio?
First Citizen: Tybalt, that murderer, which way ran he?
BENVOLIO: There lies that Tybalt.
First Citizen: Up, sir, go with me,
First Citizen: I charge thee in the princes name, obey.
First Citizen: Enter Prince, attended, MONTAGUE, CAPULET, their Wives, and others
PRINCE: Where are the vile beginners of this fray?
BENVOLIO: O noble prince, I can discover all
BENVOLIO: The unlucky manage of this fatal brawl:
BENVOLIO: There lies the man, slain by young Romeo,
BENVOLIO: That slew thy kinsman, brave Mercutio.
LADY CAPULET: Tybalt, my cousin! O my brother's child!
LADY CAPULET: O prince! O cousin! husband! O, the blood is spilt
LADY CAPULET: O my dear kinsman! Prince, as thou art true,

LADY CAPULET: O cousin, cousin!
PRINCE: Benvolio, who began this bloody fray?
BENVOLIO: Tybalt, here slain, whom Romeo's hand did slay,
BENVOLIO: Romeo that spoke him fair, bade him bethink
BENVOLIO: How nice the quarrel was, and urged withal
BENVOLIO: Your high displeasure: all this uttered
BENVOLIO: With gentle breath, calm look, knees humbly bow'd,
BENVOLIO: Could not take truce with the unruly spleen
BENVOLIO: Of Tybalt deaf to peace, but that he tilts
BENVOLIO: With piercing steel at bold Mercutio's breast,
BENVOLIO: Who all as hot, turns deadly point to point,
BENVOLIO: And, with a martial scorn, with one hand beats
BENVOLIO: Cold death aside, and with the other sends
BENVOLIO: It back to Tybalt, whose dexterity,
BENVOLIO: Retorts it: Romeo he cries aloud,
BENVOLIO: 'Hold, friends! friends, part!' and, swifter than
BENVOLIO: his tongue,
BENVOLIO: His agile arm beats down their fatal points,
BENVOLIO: And 'twixt them rushes, underneath whose arm
BENVOLIO: An envious thrust from Tybalt hit the life
BENVOLIO: Of stout Mercutio, and then Tybalt fled,
BENVOLIO: But by and by comes back to Romeo,
BENVOLIO: Who had but newly entertain'd revenge,
BENVOLIO: And to 't they go like lightning, for, ere I
BENVOLIO: Could draw to part them, was stout Tybalt slain.
BENVOLIO: And, as he fell, did Romeo turn and fly.
BENVOLIO: This is the truth, or let Benvolio die.
LADY CAPULET: He is a kinsman to the Montague,
LADY CAPULET: Affection makes him false, he speaks not true:
LADY CAPULET: Some twenty of them fought in this black strife,
LADY CAPULET: And all those twenty could but kill one life.
LADY CAPULET: I beg for justice, which thou, prince, must give,
LADY CAPULET: Romeo slew Tybalt, Romeo must not live.
PRINCE: Romeo slew him, he slew Mercutio,
PRINCE: Who now the price of his dear blood doth owe?
MONTAGUE: Not Romeo, prince, he was Mercutio's friend,
MONTAGUE: His fault concludes but what the law should end,
MONTAGUE: The life of Tybalt.
PRINCE: And for that offence
PRINCE: Immediately we do exile him hence:
PRINCE: I have an interest in your hate's proceeding,
PRINCE: My blood for your rude brawls doth lie a-bleeding,
PRINCE: But I'll amerce you with so strong a fine
PRINCE: That you shall all repent the loss of mine:
PRINCE: I will be deaf to pleading and excuses,
PRINCE: Nor tears nor prayers shall purchase out abuses:
PRINCE: Therefore use none: let Romeo hence in haste,
PRINCE: Else, when he's found, that hour is his last.
PRINCE: Bear hence this body and attend our will:
PRINCE: Mercy but murders, pardoning those that kill.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Capulet's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
JULIET: Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds,
JULIET: Towards Phoebus' lodging: such a wagoner
JULIET: As Phaethon would whip you to the west,
JULIET: And bring in cloudy night immediately.
JULIET: Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night,
JULIET: That runaway's eyes may wink and Romeo
JULIET: Leap to these arms, untalk'd of and unseen.
JULIET: Lovers can see to do their amorous rites
JULIET: By their own beauties, or, if love be blind,
JULIET: It best agrees with night. Come, civil night,
JULIET: Thou sober-suited matron, all in black,
JULIET: And learn me how to lose a winning match,
JULIET: Play'd for a pair of stainless maidenhoods:
JULIET: Hood my unmann'd blood, bating in my cheeks,
JULIET: With thy black mantle, till strange love, grown bold,
JULIET: Think true love acted simple modesty.
JULIET: Come, night, come, Romeo, come, thou day in night,
JULIET: For thou wilt lie upon the wings of night
JULIET: Whiter than new snow on a raven's back.
JULIET: Come, gentle night, come, loving, black-brow'd night,
JULIET: Give me my Romeo, and, when he shall die,
JULIET: Take him and cut him out in little stars,
JULIET: And he will make the face of heaven so fine
JULIET: That all the world will be in love with night
JULIET: And pay no worship to the garish sun.
JULIET: O, I have bought the mansion of a love,
JULIET: But not possess'd it, and, though I am sold,
JULIET: Not yet enjoy'd: so tedious is this day
JULIET: As is the night before some festival
JULIET: To an impatient child that hath new robes
JULIET: And may not wear them. O, here comes my nurse,
JULIET: And she brings news, and every tongue that speaks
JULIET: But Romeo's name speaks heavenly eloquence.
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse, with cords
JULIET: Now, nurse, what news? What hast thou there? the cords
JULIET: That Romeo bid thee fetch?
Nurse: Ay, ay, the cords.
NARRATOR: Throws them down
JULIET: Ay me! what news? why dost thou wring thy hands?
Nurse: Ah, well-a-day! he's dead, he's dead, he's dead!
Nurse: We are undone, lady, we are undone!
Nurse: Alack the day! he's gone, he's kill'd, he's dead!
JULIET: Can heaven be so envious?
Nurse: Romeo can,
Nurse: Though heaven cannot: O Romeo, Romeo!
Nurse: Who ever would have thought it? Romeo!
JULIET: What devil art thou, that dost torment me thus?
JULIET: This torture should be roar'd in dismal hell.
JULIET: Hath Romeo slain himself? say thou but 'I,'
JULIET: And that bare vowel 'I' shall poison more
JULIET: Than the death-darting eye of cockatrice:
JULIET: I am not I, if there be such an I,
JULIET: Or those eyes shut, that make thee answer 'I.'
JULIET: If he be slain, say 'I', or if not, no:
JULIET: Brief sounds determine of my weal or woe.
Nurse: I saw the wound, I saw it with mine eyes,--
Nurse: God save the mark!--here on his manly breast:
Nurse: A piteous corse, a bloody piteous corse,
Nurse: Pale, pale as ashes, all bedaub'd in blood,
Nurse: All in gore-blood, I swounded at the sight.
JULIET: O, break, my heart! poor bankrupt, break at once!
JULIET: To prison, eyes, ne'er look on liberty!
JULIET: Vile earth, to earth resign, end motion here,
JULIET: And thou and Romeo press one heavy bier!
Nurse: O Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had!
Nurse: O courteous Tybalt! honest gentleman!
Nurse: That ever I should live to see thee dead!
JULIET: What storm is this that blows so contrary?
JULIET: Is Romeo slaughter'd, and is Tybalt dead?
JULIET: My dear-loved cousin, and my dearer lord?
JULIET: Then, dreadful trumpet, sound the general doom!
JULIET: For who is living, if those two are gone?
Nurse: Tybalt is gone, and Romeo banished,
Nurse: Romeo that kill'd him, he is banished.
JULIET: O God! did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?
Nurse: It did, it did, alas the day, it did!
JULIET: O serpent heart, hid with a flowering face!
JULIET: Did ever dragon keep so fair a cave?
JULIET: Beautiful tyrant! fiend angelical!
JULIET: Dove-feather'd raven! wolvish-ravening lamb!
JULIET: Despised substance of divinest show!
JULIET: Just opposite to what thou justly seem'st,
JULIET: A damned saint, an honourable villain!
JULIET: O nature, what hadst thou to do in hell,
JULIET: When thou didst bower the spirit of a fiend
JULIET: In moral paradise of such sweet flesh?
JULIET: Was ever book containing such vile matter
JULIET: So fairly bound? O that deceit should dwell
JULIET: In such a gorgeous palace!
Nurse: There's no trust,
Nurse: No faith, no honesty in men, all perjured,
Nurse: All forsworn, all naught, all dissemblers.
Nurse: Ah, where's my man? give me some aqua vitae:
Nurse: These griefs, these woes, these sorrows make me old.
Nurse: Shame come to Romeo!
JULIET: Blister'd be thy tongue
JULIET: For such a wish! he was not born to shame:
JULIET: Upon his brow shame is ashamed to sit,
JULIET: For 'tis a throne where honour may be crown'd
JULIET: Sole monarch of the universal earth.
JULIET: O, what a beast was I to chide at him!
Nurse: Will you speak well of him that kill'd your cousin?
JULIET: Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband?
JULIET: Ah, poor my lord, what tongue shall smooth thy name,
JULIET: When I, thy three-hours wife, have mangled it?
JULIET: But, wherefore, villain, didst thou kill my cousin?
JULIET: That villain cousin would have kill'd my husband:
JULIET: Back, foolish tears, back to your native spring,
JULIET: Your tributary drops belong to woe,
JULIET: Which you, mistaking, offer up to joy.
JULIET: My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain,
JULIET: And Tybalt's dead, that would have slain my husband:
JULIET: All this is comfort, wherefore weep I then?
JULIET: Some word there was, worser than Tybalt's death,
JULIET: That murder'd me: I would forget it fain,
JULIET: But, O, it presses to my memory,
JULIET: Like damned guilty deeds to sinners' minds:
JULIET: 'Tybalt is dead, and Romeo--banished,'
JULIET: That 'banished,' that one word 'banished,'
JULIET: Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt's death
JULIET: Was woe enough, if it had ended there:
JULIET: Or, if sour woe delights in fellowship
JULIET: And needly will be rank'd with other griefs,
JULIET: Why follow'd not, when she said 'Tybalt's dead,'
JULIET: Thy father, or thy mother, nay, or both,
JULIET: Which modern lamentations might have moved?
JULIET: But with a rear-ward following Tybalt's death,
JULIET: 'Romeo is banished,' to speak that word,
JULIET: Is father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet,
JULIET: All slain, all dead. 'Romeo is banished!'
JULIET: There is no end, no limit, measure, bound,
JULIET: In that word's death, no words can that woe sound.
JULIET: Where is my father, and my mother, nurse?
Nurse: Weeping and wailing over Tybalt's corse:
Nurse: Will you go to them? I will bring you thither.
JULIET: Wash they his wounds with tears: mine shall be spent,
JULIET: When theirs are dry, for Romeo's banishment.
JULIET: Take up those cords: poor ropes, you are beguiled,
JULIET: Both you and I, for Romeo is exiled:
JULIET: He made you for a highway to my bed,
JULIET: But I, a maid, die maiden-widowed.
JULIET: Come, cords, come, nurse, I'll to my wedding-bed,
JULIET: And death, not Romeo, take my maidenhead!
Nurse: Hie to your chamber: I'll find Romeo
Nurse: To comfort you: I wot well where he is.
Nurse: Hark ye, your Romeo will be here at night:
Nurse: I'll to him, he is hid at Laurence' cell.
JULIET: O, find him! give this ring to my true knight,
JULIET: And bid him come to take his last farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Friar Laurence's cell.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo, come forth, come forth, thou fearful man:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Affliction is enamour'd of thy parts,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And thou art wedded to calamity.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
ROMEO: Father, what news? what is the prince's doom?
ROMEO: What sorrow craves acquaintance at my hand,
ROMEO: That I yet know not?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Too familiar
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is my dear son with such sour company:
FRIAR LAURENCE: I bring thee tidings of the prince's doom.
ROMEO: What less than dooms-day is the prince's doom?
FRIAR LAURENCE: A gentler judgment vanish'd from his lips,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Not body's death, but body's banishment.
ROMEO: Ha, banishment! be merciful, say 'death,'
ROMEO: For exile hath more terror in his look,
ROMEO: Much more than death: do not say 'banishment.'
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hence from Verona art thou banished:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Be patient, for the world is broad and wide.
ROMEO: There is no world without Verona walls,
ROMEO: But purgatory, torture, hell itself.
ROMEO: Hence-banished is banish'd from the world,
ROMEO: And world's exile is death: then banished,
ROMEO: Is death mis-term'd: calling death banishment,
ROMEO: Thou cutt'st my head off with a golden axe,
ROMEO: And smilest upon the stroke that murders me.
FRIAR LAURENCE: O deadly sin! O rude unthankfulness!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy fault our law calls death, but the kind prince,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Taking thy part, hath rush'd aside the law,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And turn'd that black word death to banishment:
FRIAR LAURENCE: This is dear mercy, and thou seest it not.
ROMEO: 'Tis torture, and not mercy: heaven is here,
ROMEO: Where Juliet lives, and every cat and dog
ROMEO: And little mouse, every unworthy thing,
ROMEO: Live here in heaven and may look on her,
ROMEO: But Romeo may not: more validity,
ROMEO: More honourable state, more courtship lives
ROMEO: In carrion-flies than Romeo: they my seize
ROMEO: On the white wonder of dear Juliet's hand
ROMEO: And steal immortal blessing from her lips,
ROMEO: Who even in pure and vestal modesty,
ROMEO: Still blush, as thinking their own kisses sin,
ROMEO: But Romeo may not, he is banished:
ROMEO: Flies may do this, but I from this must fly:
ROMEO: They are free men, but I am banished.
ROMEO: And say'st thou yet that exile is not death?
ROMEO: Hadst thou no poison mix'd, no sharp-ground knife,
ROMEO: No sudden mean of death, though ne'er so mean,
ROMEO: But 'banished' to kill me?--'banished'?
ROMEO: O friar, the damned use that word in hell,
ROMEO: Howlings attend it: how hast thou the heart,
ROMEO: Being a divine, a ghostly confessor,
ROMEO: A sin-absolver, and my friend profess'd,
ROMEO: To mangle me with that word 'banished'?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou fond mad man, hear me but speak a word.
ROMEO: O, thou wilt speak again of banishment.
FRIAR LAURENCE: I'll give thee armour to keep off that word:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Adversity's sweet milk, philosophy,
FRIAR LAURENCE: To comfort thee, though thou art banished.
ROMEO: Yet 'banished'? Hang up philosophy!
ROMEO: Unless philosophy can make a Juliet,
ROMEO: Displant a town, reverse a prince's doom,
ROMEO: It helps not, it prevails not: talk no more.
FRIAR LAURENCE: O, then I see that madmen have no ears.
ROMEO: How should they, when that wise men have no eyes?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Let me dispute with thee of thy estate.
ROMEO: Thou canst not speak of that thou dost not feel:
ROMEO: Wert thou as young as I, Juliet thy love,
ROMEO: An hour but married, Tybalt murdered,
ROMEO: Doting like me and like me banished,
ROMEO: Then mightst thou speak, then mightst thou tear thy hair,
ROMEO: And fall upon the ground, as I do now,
ROMEO: Taking the measure of an unmade grave.
NARRATOR: Knocking within
FRIAR LAURENCE: Arise, one knocks, good Romeo, hide thyself.
ROMEO: Not I, unless the breath of heartsick groans,
ROMEO: Mist-like, infold me from the search of eyes.
NARRATOR: Knocking
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hark, how they knock! Who's there? Romeo, arise,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou wilt be taken. Stay awhile! Stand up,
NARRATOR: Knocking
FRIAR LAURENCE: Run to my study. By and by! God's will,
FRIAR LAURENCE: What simpleness is this! I come, I come!
NARRATOR: Knocking
FRIAR LAURENCE: Who knocks so hard? whence come you? what's your will?
Nurse: [Within]  Let me come in, and you shall know
Nurse: my errand,
Nurse: I come from Lady Juliet.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Welcome, then.
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse
Nurse: O holy friar, O, tell me, holy friar,
Nurse: Where is my lady's lord, where's Romeo?
FRIAR LAURENCE: There on the ground, with his own tears made drunk.
Nurse: O, he is even in my mistress' case,
Nurse: Just in her case! O woful sympathy!
Nurse: Piteous predicament! Even so lies she,
Nurse: Blubbering and weeping, weeping and blubbering.
Nurse: Stand up, stand up, stand, and you be a man:
Nurse: For Juliet's sake, for her sake, rise and stand,
Nurse: Why should you fall into so deep an O?
ROMEO: Nurse!
Nurse: Ah sir! ah sir! Well, death's the end of all.
ROMEO: Spakest thou of Juliet? how is it with her?
ROMEO: Doth she not think me an old murderer,
ROMEO: Now I have stain'd the childhood of our joy
ROMEO: With blood removed but little from her own?
ROMEO: Where is she? and how doth she? and what says
ROMEO: My conceal'd lady to our cancell'd love?
Nurse: O, she says nothing, sir, but weeps and weeps,
Nurse: And now falls on her bed, and then starts up,
Nurse: And Tybalt calls, and then on Romeo cries,
Nurse: And then down falls again.
ROMEO: As if that name,
ROMEO: Shot from the deadly level of a gun,
ROMEO: Did murder her, as that name's cursed hand
ROMEO: Murder'd her kinsman. O, tell me, friar, tell me,
ROMEO: In what vile part of this anatomy
ROMEO: Doth my name lodge? tell me, that I may sack
ROMEO: The hateful mansion.
NARRATOR: Drawing his sword
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hold thy desperate hand:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Art thou a man? thy form cries out thou art:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy tears are womanish, thy wild acts denote
FRIAR LAURENCE: The unreasonable fury of a beast:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Unseemly woman in a seeming man!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Or ill-beseeming beast in seeming both!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou hast amazed me: by my holy order,
FRIAR LAURENCE: I thought thy disposition better temper'd.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hast thou slain Tybalt? wilt thou slay thyself?
FRIAR LAURENCE: And stay thy lady too that lives in thee,
FRIAR LAURENCE: By doing damned hate upon thyself?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Why rail'st thou on thy birth, the heaven, and earth?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Since birth, and heaven, and earth, all three do meet
FRIAR LAURENCE: In thee at once, which thou at once wouldst lose.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Fie, fie, thou shamest thy shape, thy love, thy wit,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Which, like a usurer, abound'st in all,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And usest none in that true use indeed
FRIAR LAURENCE: Which should bedeck thy shape, thy love, thy wit:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy noble shape is but a form of wax,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Digressing from the valour of a man,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy dear love sworn but hollow perjury,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Killing that love which thou hast vow'd to cherish,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy wit, that ornament to shape and love,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Misshapen in the conduct of them both,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Like powder in a skitless soldier's flask,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is set afire by thine own ignorance,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And thou dismember'd with thine own defence.
FRIAR LAURENCE: What, rouse thee, man! thy Juliet is alive,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For whose dear sake thou wast but lately dead,
FRIAR LAURENCE: There art thou happy: Tybalt would kill thee,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But thou slew'st Tybalt, there are thou happy too:
FRIAR LAURENCE: The law that threaten'd death becomes thy friend
FRIAR LAURENCE: And turns it to exile, there art thou happy:
FRIAR LAURENCE: A pack of blessings lights up upon thy back,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Happiness courts thee in her best array,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But, like a misbehaved and sullen wench,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou pout'st upon thy fortune and thy love:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Take heed, take heed, for such die miserable.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Go, get thee to thy love, as was decreed,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Ascend her chamber, hence and comfort her:
FRIAR LAURENCE: But look thou stay not till the watch be set,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For then thou canst not pass to Mantua,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Where thou shalt live, till we can find a time
FRIAR LAURENCE: To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Beg pardon of the prince, and call thee back
FRIAR LAURENCE: With twenty hundred thousand times more joy
FRIAR LAURENCE: Than thou went'st forth in lamentation.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Go before, nurse: commend me to thy lady,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And bid her hasten all the house to bed,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Which heavy sorrow makes them apt unto:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo is coming.
Nurse: O Lord, I could have stay'd here all the night
Nurse: To hear good counsel: O, what learning is!
Nurse: My lord, I'll tell my lady you will come.
ROMEO: Do so, and bid my sweet prepare to chide.
Nurse: Here, sir, a ring she bid me give you, sir:
Nurse: Hie you, make haste, for it grows very late.
NARRATOR: Exit
ROMEO: How well my comfort is revived by this!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Go hence, good night, and here stands all your state:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Either be gone before the watch be set,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Or by the break of day disguised from hence:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Sojourn in Mantua, I'll find out your man,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And he shall signify from time to time
FRIAR LAURENCE: Every good hap to you that chances here:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Give me thy hand, 'tis late: farewell, good night.
ROMEO: But that a joy past joy calls out on me,
ROMEO: It were a grief, so brief to part with thee: Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. A room in Capulet's house.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET, LADY CAPULET, and PARIS
CAPULET: Things have fall'n out, sir, so unluckily,
CAPULET: That we have had no time to move our daughter:
CAPULET: Look you, she loved her kinsman Tybalt dearly,
CAPULET: And so did I:--Well, we were born to die.
CAPULET: 'Tis very late, she'll not come down to-night:
CAPULET: I promise you, but for your company,
CAPULET: I would have been a-bed an hour ago.
PARIS: These times of woe afford no time to woo.
PARIS: Madam, good night: commend me to your daughter.
LADY CAPULET: I will, and know her mind early to-morrow,
LADY CAPULET: To-night she is mew'd up to her heaviness.
CAPULET: Sir Paris, I will make a desperate tender
CAPULET: Of my child's love: I think she will be ruled
CAPULET: In all respects by me, nay, more, I doubt it not.
CAPULET: Wife, go you to her ere you go to bed,
CAPULET: Acquaint her here of my son Paris' love,
CAPULET: And bid her, mark you me, on Wednesday next--
CAPULET: But, soft! what day is this?
PARIS: Monday, my lord,
CAPULET: Monday! ha, ha! Well, Wednesday is too soon,
CAPULET: O' Thursday let it be: o' Thursday, tell her,
CAPULET: She shall be married to this noble earl.
CAPULET: Will you be ready? do you like this haste?
CAPULET: We'll keep no great ado,--a friend or two,
CAPULET: For, hark you, Tybalt being slain so late,
CAPULET: It may be thought we held him carelessly,
CAPULET: Being our kinsman, if we revel much:
CAPULET: Therefore we'll have some half a dozen friends,
CAPULET: And there an end. But what say you to Thursday?
PARIS: My lord, I would that Thursday were to-morrow.
CAPULET: Well get you gone: o' Thursday be it, then.
CAPULET: Go you to Juliet ere you go to bed,
CAPULET: Prepare her, wife, against this wedding-day.
CAPULET: Farewell, my lord. Light to my chamber, ho!
CAPULET: Afore me! it is so very very late,
CAPULET: That we may call it early by and by.
CAPULET: Good night.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Capulet's orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO and JULIET above, at the window
JULIET: Wilt thou be gone? it is not yet near day:
JULIET: It was the nightingale, and not the lark,
JULIET: That pierced the fearful hollow of thine ear,
JULIET: Nightly she sings on yon pomegranate-tree:
JULIET: Believe me, love, it was the nightingale.
ROMEO: It was the lark, the herald of the morn,
ROMEO: No nightingale: look, love, what envious streaks
ROMEO: Do lace the severing clouds in yonder east:
ROMEO: Night's candles are burnt out, and jocund day
ROMEO: Stands tiptoe on the misty mountain tops.
ROMEO: I must be gone and live, or stay and die.
JULIET: Yon light is not day-light, I know it, I:
JULIET: It is some meteor that the sun exhales,
JULIET: To be to thee this night a torch-bearer,
JULIET: And light thee on thy way to Mantua:
JULIET: Therefore stay yet, thou need'st not to be gone.
ROMEO: Let me be ta'en, let me be put to death,
ROMEO: I am content, so thou wilt have it so.
ROMEO: I'll say yon grey is not the morning's eye,
ROMEO: 'Tis but the pale reflex of Cynthia's brow,
ROMEO: Nor that is not the lark, whose notes do beat
ROMEO: The vaulty heaven so high above our heads:
ROMEO: I have more care to stay than will to go:
ROMEO: Come, death, and welcome! Juliet wills it so.
ROMEO: How is't, my soul? let's talk, it is not day.
JULIET: It is, it is: hie hence, be gone, away!
JULIET: It is the lark that sings so out of tune,
JULIET: Straining harsh discords and unpleasing sharps.
JULIET: Some say the lark makes sweet division,
JULIET: This doth not so, for she divideth us:
JULIET: Some say the lark and loathed toad change eyes,
JULIET: O, now I would they had changed voices too!
JULIET: Since arm from arm that voice doth us affray,
JULIET: Hunting thee hence with hunt's-up to the day,
JULIET: O, now be gone, more light and light it grows.
ROMEO: More light and light, more dark and dark our woes!
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse, to the chamber
Nurse: Madam!
JULIET: Nurse?
Nurse: Your lady mother is coming to your chamber:
Nurse: The day is broke, be wary, look about.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: Then, window, let day in, and let life out.
ROMEO: Farewell, farewell! one kiss, and I'll descend.
NARRATOR: He goeth down
JULIET: Art thou gone so? love, lord, ay, husband, friend!
JULIET: I must hear from thee every day in the hour,
JULIET: For in a minute there are many days:
JULIET: O, by this count I shall be much in years
JULIET: Ere I again behold my Romeo!
ROMEO: Farewell!
ROMEO: I will omit no opportunity
ROMEO: That may convey my greetings, love, to thee.
JULIET: O think'st thou we shall ever meet again?
ROMEO: I doubt it not, and all these woes shall serve
ROMEO: For sweet discourses in our time to come.
JULIET: O God, I have an ill-divining soul!
JULIET: Methinks I see thee, now thou art below,
JULIET: As one dead in the bottom of a tomb:
JULIET: Either my eyesight fails, or thou look'st pale.
ROMEO: And trust me, love, in my eye so do you:
ROMEO: Dry sorrow drinks our blood. Adieu, adieu!
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: O fortune, fortune! all men call thee fickle:
JULIET: If thou art fickle, what dost thou with him.
JULIET: That is renown'd for faith? Be fickle, fortune,
JULIET: For then, I hope, thou wilt not keep him long,
JULIET: But send him back.
LADY CAPULET: [Within]         Ho, daughter! are you up?
JULIET: Who is't that calls? is it my lady mother?
JULIET: Is she not down so late, or up so early?
JULIET: What unaccustom'd cause procures her hither?
NARRATOR: Enter LADY CAPULET
LADY CAPULET: Why, how now, Juliet!
JULIET: Madam, I am not well.
LADY CAPULET: Evermore weeping for your cousin's death?
LADY CAPULET: What, wilt thou wash him from his grave with tears?
LADY CAPULET: An if thou couldst, thou couldst not make him live,
LADY CAPULET: Therefore, have done: some grief shows much of love,
LADY CAPULET: But much of grief shows still some want of wit.
JULIET: Yet let me weep for such a feeling loss.
LADY CAPULET: So shall you feel the loss, but not the friend
LADY CAPULET: Which you weep for.
JULIET: Feeling so the loss,
JULIET: Cannot choose but ever weep the friend.
LADY CAPULET: Well, girl, thou weep'st not so much for his death,
LADY CAPULET: As that the villain lives which slaughter'd him.
JULIET: What villain madam?
LADY CAPULET: That same villain, Romeo.
JULIET: [Aside]  Villain and he be many miles asunder.--
JULIET: God Pardon him! I do, with all my heart,
JULIET: And yet no man like he doth grieve my heart.
LADY CAPULET: That is, because the traitor murderer lives.
JULIET: Ay, madam, from the reach of these my hands:
JULIET: Would none but I might venge my cousin's death!
LADY CAPULET: We will have vengeance for it, fear thou not:
LADY CAPULET: Then weep no more. I'll send to one in Mantua,
LADY CAPULET: Where that same banish'd runagate doth live,
LADY CAPULET: Shall give him such an unaccustom'd dram,
LADY CAPULET: That he shall soon keep Tybalt company:
LADY CAPULET: And then, I hope, thou wilt be satisfied.
JULIET: Indeed, I never shall be satisfied
JULIET: With Romeo, till I behold him--dead--
JULIET: Is my poor heart for a kinsman vex'd.
JULIET: Madam, if you could find out but a man
JULIET: To bear a poison, I would temper it,
JULIET: That Romeo should, upon receipt thereof,
JULIET: Soon sleep in quiet. O, how my heart abhors
JULIET: To hear him named, and cannot come to him.
JULIET: To wreak the love I bore my cousin
JULIET: Upon his body that slaughter'd him!
LADY CAPULET: Find thou the means, and I'll find such a man.
LADY CAPULET: But now I'll tell thee joyful tidings, girl.
JULIET: And joy comes well in such a needy time:
JULIET: What are they, I beseech your ladyship?
LADY CAPULET: Well, well, thou hast a careful father, child,
LADY CAPULET: One who, to put thee from thy heaviness,
LADY CAPULET: Hath sorted out a sudden day of joy,
LADY CAPULET: That thou expect'st not nor I look'd not for.
JULIET: Madam, in happy time, what day is that?
LADY CAPULET: Marry, my child, early next Thursday morn,
LADY CAPULET: The gallant, young and noble gentleman,
LADY CAPULET: The County Paris, at Saint Peter's Church,
LADY CAPULET: Shall happily make thee there a joyful bride.
JULIET: Now, by Saint Peter's Church and Peter too,
JULIET: He shall not make me there a joyful bride.
JULIET: I wonder at this haste, that I must wed
JULIET: Ere he, that should be husband, comes to woo.
JULIET: I pray you, tell my lord and father, madam,
JULIET: I will not marry yet, and, when I do, I swear,
JULIET: It shall be Romeo, whom you know I hate,
JULIET: Rather than Paris. These are news indeed!
LADY CAPULET: Here comes your father, tell him so yourself,
LADY CAPULET: And see how he will take it at your hands.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET and Nurse
CAPULET: When the sun sets, the air doth drizzle dew,
CAPULET: But for the sunset of my brother's son
CAPULET: It rains downright.
CAPULET: How now! a conduit, girl? what, still in tears?
CAPULET: Evermore showering? In one little body
CAPULET: Thou counterfeit'st a bark, a sea, a wind,
CAPULET: For still thy eyes, which I may call the sea,
CAPULET: Do ebb and flow with tears, the bark thy body is,
CAPULET: Sailing in this salt flood, the winds, thy sighs,
CAPULET: Who, raging with thy tears, and they with them,
CAPULET: Without a sudden calm, will overset
CAPULET: Thy tempest-tossed body. How now, wife!
CAPULET: Have you deliver'd to her our decree?
LADY CAPULET: Ay, sir, but she will none, she gives you thanks.
LADY CAPULET: I would the fool were married to her grave!
CAPULET: Soft! take me with you, take me with you, wife.
CAPULET: How! will she none? doth she not give us thanks?
CAPULET: Is she not proud? doth she not count her blest,
CAPULET: Unworthy as she is, that we have wrought
CAPULET: So worthy a gentleman to be her bridegroom?
JULIET: Not proud, you have, but thankful, that you have:
JULIET: Proud can I never be of what I hate,
JULIET: But thankful even for hate, that is meant love.
CAPULET: How now, how now, chop-logic! What is this?
CAPULET: 'Proud,' and 'I thank you,' and 'I thank you not,'
CAPULET: And yet 'not proud,' mistress minion, you,
CAPULET: Thank me no thankings, nor, proud me no prouds,
CAPULET: But fettle your fine joints 'gainst Thursday next,
CAPULET: To go with Paris to Saint Peter's Church,
CAPULET: Or I will drag thee on a hurdle thither.
CAPULET: Out, you green-sickness carrion! out, you baggage!
CAPULET: You tallow-face!
LADY CAPULET: Fie, fie! what, are you mad?
JULIET: Good father, I beseech you on my knees,
JULIET: Hear me with patience but to speak a word.
CAPULET: Hang thee, young baggage! disobedient wretch!
CAPULET: I tell thee what: get thee to church o' Thursday,
CAPULET: Or never after look me in the face:
CAPULET: Speak not, reply not, do not answer me,
CAPULET: My fingers itch. Wife, we scarce thought us blest
CAPULET: That God had lent us but this only child,
CAPULET: But now I see this one is one too much,
CAPULET: And that we have a curse in having her:
CAPULET: Out on her, hilding!
Nurse: God in heaven bless her!
Nurse: You are to blame, my lord, to rate her so.
CAPULET: And why, my lady wisdom? hold your tongue,
CAPULET: Good prudence, smatter with your gossips, go.
Nurse: I speak no treason.
CAPULET: O, God ye god-den.
Nurse: May not one speak?
CAPULET: Peace, you mumbling fool!
CAPULET: Utter your gravity o'er a gossip's bowl,
CAPULET: For here we need it not.
LADY CAPULET: You are too hot.
CAPULET: God's bread! it makes me mad:
CAPULET: Day, night, hour, tide, time, work, play,
CAPULET: Alone, in company, still my care hath been
CAPULET: To have her match'd: and having now provided
CAPULET: A gentleman of noble parentage,
CAPULET: Of fair demesnes, youthful, and nobly train'd,
CAPULET: Stuff'd, as they say, with honourable parts,
CAPULET: Proportion'd as one's thought would wish a man,
CAPULET: And then to have a wretched puling fool,
CAPULET: A whining mammet, in her fortune's tender,
CAPULET: To answer 'I'll not wed, I cannot love,
CAPULET: I am too young, I pray you, pardon me.'
CAPULET: But, as you will not wed, I'll pardon you:
CAPULET: Graze where you will you shall not house with me:
CAPULET: Look to't, think on't, I do not use to jest.
CAPULET: Thursday is near, lay hand on heart, advise:
CAPULET: An you be mine, I'll give you to my friend,
CAPULET: And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in
CAPULET: the streets,
CAPULET: For, by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee,
CAPULET: Nor what is mine shall never do thee good:
CAPULET: Trust to't, bethink you, I'll not be forsworn.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: Is there no pity sitting in the clouds,
JULIET: That sees into the bottom of my grief?
JULIET: O, sweet my mother, cast me not away!
JULIET: Delay this marriage for a month, a week,
JULIET: Or, if you do not, make the bridal bed
JULIET: In that dim monument where Tybalt lies.
LADY CAPULET: Talk not to me, for I'll not speak a word:
LADY CAPULET: Do as thou wilt, for I have done with thee.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: O God!--O nurse, how shall this be prevented?
JULIET: My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven,
JULIET: How shall that faith return again to earth,
JULIET: Unless that husband send it me from heaven
JULIET: By leaving earth? comfort me, counsel me.
JULIET: Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems
JULIET: Upon so soft a subject as myself!
JULIET: What say'st thou? hast thou not a word of joy?
JULIET: Some comfort, nurse.
Nurse: Faith, here it is.
Nurse: Romeo is banish'd, and all the world to nothing,
Nurse: That he dares ne'er come back to challenge you,
Nurse: Or, if he do, it needs must be by stealth.
Nurse: Then, since the case so stands as now it doth,
Nurse: I think it best you married with the county.
Nurse: O, he's a lovely gentleman!
Nurse: Romeo's a dishclout to him: an eagle, madam,
Nurse: Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye
Nurse: As Paris hath. Beshrew my very heart,
Nurse: I think you are happy in this second match,
Nurse: For it excels your first: or if it did not,
Nurse: Your first is dead, or 'twere as good he were,
Nurse: As living here and you no use of him.
JULIET: Speakest thou from thy heart?
Nurse: And from my soul too,
Nurse: Or else beshrew them both.
JULIET: Amen!
Nurse: What?
JULIET: Well, thou hast comforted me marvellous much.
JULIET: Go in: and tell my lady I am gone,
JULIET: Having displeased my father, to Laurence' cell,
JULIET: To make confession and to be absolved.
Nurse: Marry, I will, and this is wisely done.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: Ancient damnation! O most wicked fiend!
JULIET: Is it more sin to wish me thus forsworn,
JULIET: Or to dispraise my lord with that same tongue
JULIET: Which she hath praised him with above compare
JULIET: So many thousand times? Go, counsellor,
JULIET: Thou and my bosom henceforth shall be twain.
JULIET: I'll to the friar, to know his remedy:
JULIET: If all else fail, myself have power to die.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Friar Laurence's cell.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE and PARIS
FRIAR LAURENCE: On Thursday, sir? the time is very short.
PARIS: My father Capulet will have it so,
PARIS: And I am nothing slow to slack his haste.
FRIAR LAURENCE: You say you do not know the lady's mind:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Uneven is the course, I like it not.
PARIS: Immoderately she weeps for Tybalt's death,
PARIS: And therefore have I little talk'd of love,
PARIS: For Venus smiles not in a house of tears.
PARIS: Now, sir, her father counts it dangerous
PARIS: That she doth give her sorrow so much sway,
PARIS: And in his wisdom hastes our marriage,
PARIS: To stop the inundation of her tears,
PARIS: Which, too much minded by herself alone,
PARIS: May be put from her by society:
PARIS: Now do you know the reason of this haste.
FRIAR LAURENCE: [Aside]  I would I knew not why it should be slow'd.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Look, sir, here comes the lady towards my cell.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
PARIS: Happily met, my lady and my wife!
JULIET: That may be, sir, when I may be a wife.
PARIS: That may be must be, love, on Thursday next.
JULIET: What must be shall be.
FRIAR LAURENCE: That's a certain text.
PARIS: Come you to make confession to this father?
JULIET: To answer that, I should confess to you.
PARIS: Do not deny to him that you love me.
JULIET: I will confess to you that I love him.
PARIS: So will ye, I am sure, that you love me.
JULIET: If I do so, it will be of more price,
JULIET: Being spoke behind your back, than to your face.
PARIS: Poor soul, thy face is much abused with tears.
JULIET: The tears have got small victory by that,
JULIET: For it was bad enough before their spite.
PARIS: Thou wrong'st it, more than tears, with that report.
JULIET: That is no slander, sir, which is a truth,
JULIET: And what I spake, I spake it to my face.
PARIS: Thy face is mine, and thou hast slander'd it.
JULIET: It may be so, for it is not mine own.
JULIET: Are you at leisure, holy father, now,
JULIET: Or shall I come to you at evening mass?
FRIAR LAURENCE: My leisure serves me, pensive daughter, now.
FRIAR LAURENCE: My lord, we must entreat the time alone.
PARIS: God shield I should disturb devotion!
PARIS: Juliet, on Thursday early will I rouse ye:
PARIS: Till then, adieu, and keep this holy kiss.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIET: O shut the door! and when thou hast done so,
JULIET: Come weep with me, past hope, past cure, past help!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Ah, Juliet, I already know thy grief,
FRIAR LAURENCE: It strains me past the compass of my wits:
FRIAR LAURENCE: I hear thou must, and nothing may prorogue it,
FRIAR LAURENCE: On Thursday next be married to this county.
JULIET: Tell me not, friar, that thou hear'st of this,
JULIET: Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it:
JULIET: If, in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help,
JULIET: Do thou but call my resolution wise,
JULIET: And with this knife I'll help it presently.
JULIET: God join'd my heart and Romeo's, thou our hands,
JULIET: And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo seal'd,
JULIET: Shall be the label to another deed,
JULIET: Or my true heart with treacherous revolt
JULIET: Turn to another, this shall slay them both:
JULIET: Therefore, out of thy long-experienced time,
JULIET: Give me some present counsel, or, behold,
JULIET: 'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife
JULIET: Shall play the umpire, arbitrating that
JULIET: Which the commission of thy years and art
JULIET: Could to no issue of true honour bring.
JULIET: Be not so long to speak, I long to die,
JULIET: If what thou speak'st speak not of remedy.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hold, daughter: I do spy a kind of hope,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Which craves as desperate an execution.
FRIAR LAURENCE: As that is desperate which we would prevent.
FRIAR LAURENCE: If, rather than to marry County Paris,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou hast the strength of will to slay thyself,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Then is it likely thou wilt undertake
FRIAR LAURENCE: A thing like death to chide away this shame,
FRIAR LAURENCE: That copest with death himself to scape from it:
FRIAR LAURENCE: And, if thou darest, I'll give thee remedy.
JULIET: O, bid me leap, rather than marry Paris,
JULIET: From off the battlements of yonder tower,
JULIET: Or walk in thievish ways, or bid me lurk
JULIET: Where serpents are, chain me with roaring bears,
JULIET: Or shut me nightly in a charnel-house,
JULIET: O'er-cover'd quite with dead men's rattling bones,
JULIET: With reeky shanks and yellow chapless skulls,
JULIET: Or bid me go into a new-made grave
JULIET: And hide me with a dead man in his shroud,
JULIET: Things that, to hear them told, have made me tremble,
JULIET: And I will do it without fear or doubt,
JULIET: To live an unstain'd wife to my sweet love.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hold, then, go home, be merry, give consent
FRIAR LAURENCE: To marry Paris: Wednesday is to-morrow:
FRIAR LAURENCE: To-morrow night look that thou lie alone,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Let not thy nurse lie with thee in thy chamber:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Take thou this vial, being then in bed,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And this distilled liquor drink thou off,
FRIAR LAURENCE: When presently through all thy veins shall run
FRIAR LAURENCE: A cold and drowsy humour, for no pulse
FRIAR LAURENCE: Shall keep his native progress, but surcease:
FRIAR LAURENCE: No warmth, no breath, shall testify thou livest,
FRIAR LAURENCE: The roses in thy lips and cheeks shall fade
FRIAR LAURENCE: To paly ashes, thy eyes' windows fall,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Like death, when he shuts up the day of life,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Each part, deprived of supple government,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Shall, stiff and stark and cold, appear like death:
FRIAR LAURENCE: And in this borrow'd likeness of shrunk death
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou shalt continue two and forty hours,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And then awake as from a pleasant sleep.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Now, when the bridegroom in the morning comes
FRIAR LAURENCE: To rouse thee from thy bed, there art thou dead:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Then, as the manner of our country is,
FRIAR LAURENCE: In thy best robes uncover'd on the bier
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thou shalt be borne to that same ancient vault
FRIAR LAURENCE: Where all the kindred of the Capulets lie.
FRIAR LAURENCE: In the mean time, against thou shalt awake,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Shall Romeo by my letters know our drift,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And hither shall he come: and he and I
FRIAR LAURENCE: Will watch thy waking, and that very night
FRIAR LAURENCE: Shall Romeo bear thee hence to Mantua.
FRIAR LAURENCE: And this shall free thee from this present shame,
FRIAR LAURENCE: If no inconstant toy, nor womanish fear,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Abate thy valour in the acting it.
JULIET: Give me, give me! O, tell not me of fear!
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hold, get you gone, be strong and prosperous
FRIAR LAURENCE: In this resolve: I'll send a friar with speed
FRIAR LAURENCE: To Mantua, with my letters to thy lord.
JULIET: Love give me strength! and strength shall help afford.
JULIET: Farewell, dear father!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Hall in Capulet's house.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET, LADY  CAPULET, Nurse, and two Servingmen
CAPULET: So many guests invite as here are writ.
NARRATOR: Exit First Servant
CAPULET: Sirrah, go hire me twenty cunning cooks.
Second Servant: You shall have none ill, sir, for I'll try if they
Second Servant: can lick their fingers.
CAPULET: How canst thou try them so?
Second Servant: Marry, sir, 'tis an ill cook that cannot lick his
Second Servant: own fingers: therefore he that cannot lick his
Second Servant: fingers goes not with me.
CAPULET: Go, be gone.
NARRATOR: Exit Second Servant
CAPULET: We shall be much unfurnished for this time.
CAPULET: What, is my daughter gone to Friar Laurence?
Nurse: Ay, forsooth.
CAPULET: Well, he may chance to do some good on her:
CAPULET: A peevish self-will'd harlotry it is.
Nurse: See where she comes from shrift with merry look.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET
CAPULET: How now, my headstrong! where have you been gadding?
JULIET: Where I have learn'd me to repent the sin
JULIET: Of disobedient opposition
JULIET: To you and your behests, and am enjoin'd
JULIET: By holy Laurence to fall prostrate here,
JULIET: And beg your pardon: pardon, I beseech you!
JULIET: Henceforward I am ever ruled by you.
CAPULET: Send for the county, go tell him of this:
CAPULET: I'll have this knot knit up to-morrow morning.
JULIET: I met the youthful lord at Laurence' cell,
JULIET: And gave him what becomed love I might,
JULIET: Not step o'er the bounds of modesty.
CAPULET: Why, I am glad on't, this is well: stand up:
CAPULET: This is as't should be. Let me see the county,
CAPULET: Ay, marry, go, I say, and fetch him hither.
CAPULET: Now, afore God! this reverend holy friar,
CAPULET: Our whole city is much bound to him.
JULIET: Nurse, will you go with me into my closet,
JULIET: To help me sort such needful ornaments
JULIET: As you think fit to furnish me to-morrow?
LADY CAPULET: No, not till Thursday, there is time enough.
CAPULET: Go, nurse, go with her: we'll to church to-morrow.
NARRATOR: Exeunt JULIET and Nurse
LADY  CAPULET: We shall be short in our provision:
LADY  CAPULET: 'Tis now near night.
CAPULET: Tush, I will stir about,
CAPULET: And all things shall be well, I warrant thee, wife:
CAPULET: Go thou to Juliet, help to deck up her,
CAPULET: I'll not to bed to-night, let me alone,
CAPULET: I'll play the housewife for this once. What, ho!
CAPULET: They are all forth. Well, I will walk myself
CAPULET: To County Paris, to prepare him up
CAPULET: Against to-morrow: my heart is wondrous light,
CAPULET: Since this same wayward girl is so reclaim'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Juliet's chamber.
NARRATOR: Enter JULIET and Nurse
JULIET: Ay, those attires are best: but, gentle nurse,
JULIET: I pray thee, leave me to my self to-night,
JULIET: For I have need of many orisons
JULIET: To move the heavens to smile upon my state,
