JULIET: Which, well thou know'st, is cross, and full of sin.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY CAPULET
LADY CAPULET: What, are you busy, ho? need you my help?
JULIET: No, madam, we have cull'd such necessaries
JULIET: As are behoveful for our state to-morrow:
JULIET: So please you, let me now be left alone,
JULIET: And let the nurse this night sit up with you,
JULIET: For, I am sure, you have your hands full all,
JULIET: In this so sudden business.
LADY CAPULET: Good night:
LADY CAPULET: Get thee to bed, and rest, for thou hast need.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LADY CAPULET and Nurse
JULIET: Farewell! God knows when we shall meet again.
JULIET: I have a faint cold fear thrills through my veins,
JULIET: That almost freezes up the heat of life:
JULIET: I'll call them back again to comfort me:
JULIET: Nurse! What should she do here?
JULIET: My dismal scene I needs must act alone.
JULIET: Come, vial.
JULIET: What if this mixture do not work at all?
JULIET: Shall I be married then to-morrow morning?
JULIET: No, no: this shall forbid it: lie thou there.
NARRATOR: Laying down her dagger
JULIET: What if it be a poison, which the friar
JULIET: Subtly hath minister'd to have me dead,
JULIET: Lest in this marriage he should be dishonour'd,
JULIET: Because he married me before to Romeo?
JULIET: I fear it is: and yet, methinks, it should not,
JULIET: For he hath still been tried a holy man.
JULIET: How if, when I am laid into the tomb,
JULIET: I wake before the time that Romeo
JULIET: Come to redeem me? there's a fearful point!
JULIET: Shall I not, then, be stifled in the vault,
JULIET: To whose foul mouth no healthsome air breathes in,
JULIET: And there die strangled ere my Romeo comes?
JULIET: Or, if I live, is it not very like,
JULIET: The horrible conceit of death and night,
JULIET: Together with the terror of the place,--
JULIET: As in a vault, an ancient receptacle,
JULIET: Where, for these many hundred years, the bones
JULIET: Of all my buried ancestors are packed:
JULIET: Where bloody Tybalt, yet but green in earth,
JULIET: Lies festering in his shroud, where, as they say,
JULIET: At some hours in the night spirits resort,--
JULIET: Alack, alack, is it not like that I,
JULIET: So early waking, what with loathsome smells,
JULIET: And shrieks like mandrakes' torn out of the earth,
JULIET: That living mortals, hearing them, run mad:--
JULIET: O, if I wake, shall I not be distraught,
JULIET: Environed with all these hideous fears?
JULIET: And madly play with my forefather's joints?
JULIET: And pluck the mangled Tybalt from his shroud?
JULIET: And, in this rage, with some great kinsman's bone,
JULIET: As with a club, dash out my desperate brains?
JULIET: O, look! methinks I see my cousin's ghost
JULIET: Seeking out Romeo, that did spit his body
JULIET: Upon a rapier's point: stay, Tybalt, stay!
JULIET: Romeo, I come! this do I drink to thee.
NARRATOR: She falls upon her bed, within the curtains
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Hall in Capulet's house.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY CAPULET and Nurse
LADY CAPULET: Hold, take these keys, and fetch more spices, nurse.
Nurse: They call for dates and quinces in the pastry.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET
CAPULET: Come, stir, stir, stir! the second cock hath crow'd,
CAPULET: The curfew-bell hath rung, 'tis three o'clock:
CAPULET: Look to the baked meats, good Angelica:
CAPULET: Spare not for the cost.
Nurse: Go, you cot-quean, go,
Nurse: Get you to bed, faith, You'll be sick to-morrow
Nurse: For this night's watching.
CAPULET: No, not a whit: what! I have watch'd ere now
CAPULET: All night for lesser cause, and ne'er been sick.
LADY CAPULET: Ay, you have been a mouse-hunt in your time,
LADY CAPULET: But I will watch you from such watching now.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LADY CAPULET and Nurse
CAPULET: A jealous hood, a jealous hood!
NARRATOR: Enter three or four Servingmen, with spits, logs, and baskets
CAPULET: Now, fellow,
CAPULET: What's there?
First Servant: Things for the cook, sir, but I know not what.
CAPULET: Make haste, make haste.
NARRATOR: Exit First Servant
CAPULET: Sirrah, fetch drier logs:
CAPULET: Call Peter, he will show thee where they are.
Second Servant: I have a head, sir, that will find out logs,
Second Servant: And never trouble Peter for the matter.
NARRATOR: Exit
CAPULET: Mass, and well said, a merry whoreson, ha!
CAPULET: Thou shalt be logger-head. Good faith, 'tis day:
CAPULET: The county will be here with music straight,
CAPULET: For so he said he would: I hear him near.
NARRATOR: Music within
CAPULET: Nurse! Wife! What, ho! What, nurse, I say!
NARRATOR: Re-enter Nurse
CAPULET: Go waken Juliet, go and trim her up,
CAPULET: I'll go and chat with Paris: hie, make haste,
CAPULET: Make haste, the bridegroom he is come already:
CAPULET: Make haste, I say.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Juliet's chamber.
NARRATOR: Enter Nurse
Nurse: Mistress! what, mistress! Juliet! fast, I warrant her, she:
Nurse: Why, lamb! why, lady! fie, you slug-a-bed!
Nurse: Why, love, I say! madam! sweet-heart! why, bride!
Nurse: What, not a word? you take your pennyworths now,
Nurse: Sleep for a week, for the next night, I warrant,
Nurse: The County Paris hath set up his rest,
Nurse: That you shall rest but little. God forgive me,
Nurse: Marry, and amen, how sound is she asleep!
Nurse: I must needs wake her. Madam, madam, madam!
Nurse: Ay, let the county take you in your bed,
Nurse: He'll fright you up, i' faith. Will it not be?
NARRATOR: Undraws the curtains
Nurse: What, dress'd! and in your clothes! and down again!
Nurse: I must needs wake you, Lady! lady! lady!
Nurse: Alas, alas! Help, help! my lady's dead!
Nurse: O, well-a-day, that ever I was born!
Nurse: Some aqua vitae, ho! My lord! my lady!
NARRATOR: Enter LADY CAPULET
LADY CAPULET: What noise is here?
Nurse: O lamentable day!
LADY CAPULET: What is the matter?
Nurse: Look, look! O heavy day!
LADY CAPULET: O me, O me! My child, my only life,
LADY CAPULET: Revive, look up, or I will die with thee!
LADY CAPULET: Help, help! Call help.
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET
CAPULET: For shame, bring Juliet forth, her lord is come.
Nurse: She's dead, deceased, she's dead, alack the day!
LADY CAPULET: Alack the day, she's dead, she's dead, she's dead!
CAPULET: Ha! let me see her: out, alas! she's cold:
CAPULET: Her blood is settled, and her joints are stiff,
CAPULET: Life and these lips have long been separated:
CAPULET: Death lies on her like an untimely frost
CAPULET: Upon the sweetest flower of all the field.
Nurse: O lamentable day!
LADY CAPULET: O woful time!
CAPULET: Death, that hath ta'en her hence to make me wail,
CAPULET: Ties up my tongue, and will not let me speak.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE and PARIS, with Musicians
FRIAR LAURENCE: Come, is the bride ready to go to church?
CAPULET: Ready to go, but never to return.
CAPULET: O son! the night before thy wedding-day
CAPULET: Hath Death lain with thy wife. There she lies,
CAPULET: Flower as she was, deflowered by him.
CAPULET: Death is my son-in-law, Death is my heir,
CAPULET: My daughter he hath wedded: I will die,
CAPULET: And leave him all, life, living, all is Death's.
PARIS: Have I thought long to see this morning's face,
PARIS: And doth it give me such a sight as this?
LADY CAPULET: Accursed, unhappy, wretched, hateful day!
LADY CAPULET: Most miserable hour that e'er time saw
LADY CAPULET: In lasting labour of his pilgrimage!
LADY CAPULET: But one, poor one, one poor and loving child,
LADY CAPULET: But one thing to rejoice and solace in,
LADY CAPULET: And cruel death hath catch'd it from my sight!
Nurse: O woe! O woful, woful, woful day!
Nurse: Most lamentable day, most woful day,
Nurse: That ever, ever, I did yet behold!
Nurse: O day! O day! O day! O hateful day!
Nurse: Never was seen so black a day as this:
Nurse: O woful day, O woful day!
PARIS: Beguiled, divorced, wronged, spited, slain!
PARIS: Most detestable death, by thee beguil'd,
PARIS: By cruel cruel thee quite overthrown!
PARIS: O love! O life! not life, but love in death!
CAPULET: Despised, distressed, hated, martyr'd, kill'd!
CAPULET: Uncomfortable time, why camest thou now
CAPULET: To murder, murder our solemnity?
CAPULET: O child! O child! my soul, and not my child!
CAPULET: Dead art thou! Alack! my child is dead,
CAPULET: And with my child my joys are buried.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Peace, ho, for shame! confusion's cure lives not
FRIAR LAURENCE: In these confusions. Heaven and yourself
FRIAR LAURENCE: Had part in this fair maid, now heaven hath all,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And all the better is it for the maid:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Your part in her you could not keep from death,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But heaven keeps his part in eternal life.
FRIAR LAURENCE: The most you sought was her promotion,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For 'twas your heaven she should be advanced:
FRIAR LAURENCE: And weep ye now, seeing she is advanced
FRIAR LAURENCE: Above the clouds, as high as heaven itself?
FRIAR LAURENCE: O, in this love, you love your child so ill,
FRIAR LAURENCE: That you run mad, seeing that she is well:
FRIAR LAURENCE: She's not well married that lives married long,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But she's best married that dies married young.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Dry up your tears, and stick your rosemary
FRIAR LAURENCE: On this fair corse, and, as the custom is,
FRIAR LAURENCE: In all her best array bear her to church:
FRIAR LAURENCE: For though fond nature bids us an lament,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Yet nature's tears are reason's merriment.
CAPULET: All things that we ordained festival,
CAPULET: Turn from their office to black funeral,
CAPULET: Our instruments to melancholy bells,
CAPULET: Our wedding cheer to a sad burial feast,
CAPULET: Our solemn hymns to sullen dirges change,
CAPULET: Our bridal flowers serve for a buried corse,
CAPULET: And all things change them to the contrary.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Sir, go you in, and, madam, go with him,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And go, Sir Paris, every one prepare
FRIAR LAURENCE: To follow this fair corse unto her grave:
FRIAR LAURENCE: The heavens do lour upon you for some ill,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Move them no more by crossing their high will.
NARRATOR: Exeunt CAPULET, LADY CAPULET, PARIS, and FRIAR LAURENCE
First Musician: Faith, we may put up our pipes, and be gone.
Nurse: Honest goodfellows, ah, put up, put up,
Nurse: For, well you know, this is a pitiful case.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Musician: Ay, by my troth, the case may be amended.
NARRATOR: Enter PETER
PETER: Musicians, O, musicians, 'Heart's ease, Heart's
PETER: ease:' O, an you will have me live, play 'Heart's ease.'
First Musician: Why 'Heart's ease?'
PETER: O, musicians, because my heart itself plays 'My
PETER: heart is full of woe:' O, play me some merry dump,
PETER: to comfort me.
First Musician: Not a dump we, 'tis no time to play now.
PETER: You will not, then?
First Musician: No.
PETER: I will then give it you soundly.
First Musician: What will you give us?
PETER: No money, on my faith, but the gleek,
PETER: I will give you the minstrel.
First Musician: Then I will give you the serving-creature.
PETER: Then will I lay the serving-creature's dagger on
PETER: your pate. I will carry no crotchets: I'll re you,
PETER: I'll fa you, do you note me?
First Musician: An you re us and fa us, you note us.
Second Musician: Pray you, put up your dagger, and put out your wit.
PETER: Then have at you with my wit! I will dry-beat you
PETER: with an iron wit, and put up my iron dagger. Answer
PETER: me like men:
PETER: 'When griping grief the heart doth wound,
PETER: And doleful dumps the mind oppress,
PETER: Then music with her silver sound'--
PETER: why 'silver sound'? why 'music with her silver
PETER: sound'? What say you, Simon Catling?
Musician: Marry, sir, because silver hath a sweet sound.
PETER: Pretty! What say you, Hugh Rebeck?
Second Musician: I say 'silver sound,' because musicians sound for silver.
PETER: Pretty too! What say you, James Soundpost?
Third Musician: Faith, I know not what to say.
PETER: O, I cry you mercy, you are the singer: I will say
PETER: for you. It is 'music with her silver sound,'
PETER: because musicians have no gold for sounding:
PETER: 'Then music with her silver sound
PETER: With speedy help doth lend redress.'
NARRATOR: Exit
First Musician: What a pestilent knave is this same!
Second Musician: Hang him, Jack! Come, we'll in here, tarry for the
Second Musician: mourners, and stay dinner.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Mantua. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO
ROMEO: If I may trust the flattering truth of sleep,
ROMEO: My dreams presage some joyful news at hand:
ROMEO: My bosom's lord sits lightly in his throne,
ROMEO: And all this day an unaccustom'd spirit
ROMEO: Lifts me above the ground with cheerful thoughts.
ROMEO: I dreamt my lady came and found me dead--
ROMEO: Strange dream, that gives a dead man leave
ROMEO: to think!--
ROMEO: And breathed such life with kisses in my lips,
ROMEO: That I revived, and was an emperor.
ROMEO: Ah me! how sweet is love itself possess'd,
ROMEO: When but love's shadows are so rich in joy!
NARRATOR: Enter BALTHASAR, booted
ROMEO: News from Verona!--How now, Balthasar!
ROMEO: Dost thou not bring me letters from the friar?
ROMEO: How doth my lady? Is my father well?
ROMEO: How fares my Juliet? that I ask again,
ROMEO: For nothing can be ill, if she be well.
BALTHASAR: Then she is well, and nothing can be ill:
BALTHASAR: Her body sleeps in Capel's monument,
BALTHASAR: And her immortal part with angels lives.
BALTHASAR: I saw her laid low in her kindred's vault,
BALTHASAR: And presently took post to tell it you:
BALTHASAR: O, pardon me for bringing these ill news,
BALTHASAR: Since you did leave it for my office, sir.
ROMEO: Is it even so? then I defy you, stars!
ROMEO: Thou know'st my lodging: get me ink and paper,
ROMEO: And hire post-horses, I will hence to-night.
BALTHASAR: I do beseech you, sir, have patience:
BALTHASAR: Your looks are pale and wild, and do import
BALTHASAR: Some misadventure.
ROMEO: Tush, thou art deceived:
ROMEO: Leave me, and do the thing I bid thee do.
ROMEO: Hast thou no letters to me from the friar?
BALTHASAR: No, my good lord.
ROMEO: No matter: get thee gone,
ROMEO: And hire those horses, I'll be with thee straight.
NARRATOR: Exit BALTHASAR
ROMEO: Well, Juliet, I will lie with thee to-night.
ROMEO: Let's see for means: O mischief, thou art swift
ROMEO: To enter in the thoughts of desperate men!
ROMEO: I do remember an apothecary,--
ROMEO: And hereabouts he dwells,--which late I noted
ROMEO: In tatter'd weeds, with overwhelming brows,
ROMEO: Culling of simples, meagre were his looks,
ROMEO: Sharp misery had worn him to the bones:
ROMEO: And in his needy shop a tortoise hung,
ROMEO: An alligator stuff'd, and other skins
ROMEO: Of ill-shaped fishes, and about his shelves
ROMEO: A beggarly account of empty boxes,
ROMEO: Green earthen pots, bladders and musty seeds,
ROMEO: Remnants of packthread and old cakes of roses,
ROMEO: Were thinly scatter'd, to make up a show.
ROMEO: Noting this penury, to myself I said
ROMEO: 'An if a man did need a poison now,
ROMEO: Whose sale is present death in Mantua,
ROMEO: Here lives a caitiff wretch would sell it him.'
ROMEO: O, this same thought did but forerun my need,
ROMEO: And this same needy man must sell it me.
ROMEO: As I remember, this should be the house.
ROMEO: Being holiday, the beggar's shop is shut.
ROMEO: What, ho! apothecary!
NARRATOR: Enter Apothecary
Apothecary: Who calls so loud?
ROMEO: Come hither, man. I see that thou art poor:
ROMEO: Hold, there is forty ducats: let me have
ROMEO: A dram of poison, such soon-speeding gear
ROMEO: As will disperse itself through all the veins
ROMEO: That the life-weary taker may fall dead
ROMEO: And that the trunk may be discharged of breath
ROMEO: As violently as hasty powder fired
ROMEO: Doth hurry from the fatal cannon's womb.
Apothecary: Such mortal drugs I have, but Mantua's law
Apothecary: Is death to any he that utters them.
ROMEO: Art thou so bare and full of wretchedness,
ROMEO: And fear'st to die? famine is in thy cheeks,
ROMEO: Need and oppression starveth in thine eyes,
ROMEO: Contempt and beggary hangs upon thy back,
ROMEO: The world is not thy friend nor the world's law,
ROMEO: The world affords no law to make thee rich,
ROMEO: Then be not poor, but break it, and take this.
Apothecary: My poverty, but not my will, consents.
ROMEO: I pay thy poverty, and not thy will.
Apothecary: Put this in any liquid thing you will,
Apothecary: And drink it off, and, if you had the strength
Apothecary: Of twenty men, it would dispatch you straight.
ROMEO: There is thy gold, worse poison to men's souls,
ROMEO: Doing more murders in this loathsome world,
ROMEO: Than these poor compounds that thou mayst not sell.
ROMEO: I sell thee poison, thou hast sold me none.
ROMEO: Farewell: buy food, and get thyself in flesh.
ROMEO: Come, cordial and not poison, go with me
ROMEO: To Juliet's grave, for there must I use thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Friar Laurence's cell.
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR JOHN
FRIAR JOHN: Holy Franciscan friar! brother, ho!
NARRATOR: Enter FRIAR LAURENCE
FRIAR LAURENCE: This same should be the voice of Friar John.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Welcome from Mantua: what says Romeo?
FRIAR LAURENCE: Or, if his mind be writ, give me his letter.
FRIAR JOHN: Going to find a bare-foot brother out
FRIAR JOHN: One of our order, to associate me,
FRIAR JOHN: Here in this city visiting the sick,
FRIAR JOHN: And finding him, the searchers of the town,
FRIAR JOHN: Suspecting that we both were in a house
FRIAR JOHN: Where the infectious pestilence did reign,
FRIAR JOHN: Seal'd up the doors, and would not let us forth,
FRIAR JOHN: So that my speed to Mantua there was stay'd.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Who bare my letter, then, to Romeo?
FRIAR JOHN: I could not send it,--here it is again,--
FRIAR JOHN: Nor get a messenger to bring it thee,
FRIAR JOHN: So fearful were they of infection.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Unhappy fortune! by my brotherhood,
FRIAR LAURENCE: The letter was not nice but full of charge
FRIAR LAURENCE: Of dear import, and the neglecting it
FRIAR LAURENCE: May do much danger. Friar John, go hence,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Get me an iron crow, and bring it straight
FRIAR LAURENCE: Unto my cell.
FRIAR JOHN: Brother, I'll go and bring it thee.
NARRATOR: Exit
FRIAR LAURENCE: Now must I to the monument alone,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Within three hours will fair Juliet wake:
FRIAR LAURENCE: She will beshrew me much that Romeo
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hath had no notice of these accidents,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But I will write again to Mantua,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And keep her at my cell till Romeo come,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Poor living corse, closed in a dead man's tomb!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A churchyard, in it a tomb belonging to the Capulets.
NARRATOR: Enter PARIS, and his Page bearing flowers and a torch
PARIS: Give me thy torch, boy: hence, and stand aloof:
PARIS: Yet put it out, for I would not be seen.
PARIS: Under yond yew-trees lay thee all along,
PARIS: Holding thine ear close to the hollow ground,
PARIS: So shall no foot upon the churchyard tread,
PARIS: Being loose, unfirm, with digging up of graves,
PARIS: But thou shalt hear it: whistle then to me,
PARIS: As signal that thou hear'st something approach.
PARIS: Give me those flowers. Do as I bid thee, go.
PAGE: [Aside]  I am almost afraid to stand alone
PAGE: Here in the churchyard, yet I will adventure.
NARRATOR: Retires
PARIS: Sweet flower, with flowers thy bridal bed I strew,--
PARIS: O woe! thy canopy is dust and stones,--
PARIS: Which with sweet water nightly I will dew,
PARIS: Or, wanting that, with tears distill'd by moans:
PARIS: The obsequies that I for thee will keep
PARIS: Nightly shall be to strew thy grave and weep.
NARRATOR: The Page whistles
PARIS: The boy gives warning something doth approach.
PARIS: What cursed foot wanders this way to-night,
PARIS: To cross my obsequies and true love's rite?
PARIS: What with a torch! muffle me, night, awhile.
NARRATOR: Retires
NARRATOR: Enter ROMEO and BALTHASAR, with a torch, mattock,  and c
ROMEO: Give me that mattock and the wrenching iron.
ROMEO: Hold, take this letter, early in the morning
ROMEO: See thou deliver it to my lord and father.
ROMEO: Give me the light: upon thy life, I charge thee,
ROMEO: Whate'er thou hear'st or seest, stand all aloof,
ROMEO: And do not interrupt me in my course.
ROMEO: Why I descend into this bed of death,
ROMEO: Is partly to behold my lady's face,
ROMEO: But chiefly to take thence from her dead finger
ROMEO: A precious ring, a ring that I must use
ROMEO: In dear employment: therefore hence, be gone:
ROMEO: But if thou, jealous, dost return to pry
ROMEO: In what I further shall intend to do,
ROMEO: By heaven, I will tear thee joint by joint
ROMEO: And strew this hungry churchyard with thy limbs:
ROMEO: The time and my intents are savage-wild,
ROMEO: More fierce and more inexorable far
ROMEO: Than empty tigers or the roaring sea.
BALTHASAR: I will be gone, sir, and not trouble you.
ROMEO: So shalt thou show me friendship. Take thou that:
ROMEO: Live, and be prosperous: and farewell, good fellow.
BALTHASAR: [Aside]  For all this same, I'll hide me hereabout:
BALTHASAR: His looks I fear, and his intents I doubt.
NARRATOR: Retires
ROMEO: Thou detestable maw, thou womb of death,
ROMEO: Gorged with the dearest morsel of the earth,
ROMEO: Thus I enforce thy rotten jaws to open,
ROMEO: And, in despite, I'll cram thee with more food!
NARRATOR: Opens the tomb
PARIS: This is that banish'd haughty Montague,
PARIS: That murder'd my love's cousin, with which grief,
PARIS: It is supposed, the fair creature died,
PARIS: And here is come to do some villanous shame
PARIS: To the dead bodies: I will apprehend him.
NARRATOR: Comes forward
PARIS: Stop thy unhallow'd toil, vile Montague!
PARIS: Can vengeance be pursued further than death?
PARIS: Condemned villain, I do apprehend thee:
PARIS: Obey, and go with me, for thou must die.
ROMEO: I must indeed, and therefore came I hither.
ROMEO: Good gentle youth, tempt not a desperate man,
ROMEO: Fly hence, and leave me: think upon these gone,
ROMEO: Let them affright thee. I beseech thee, youth,
ROMEO: Put not another sin upon my head,
ROMEO: By urging me to fury: O, be gone!
ROMEO: By heaven, I love thee better than myself,
ROMEO: For I come hither arm'd against myself:
ROMEO: Stay not, be gone, live, and hereafter say,
ROMEO: A madman's mercy bade thee run away.
PARIS: I do defy thy conjurations,
PARIS: And apprehend thee for a felon here.
ROMEO: Wilt thou provoke me? then have at thee, boy!
NARRATOR: They fight
PAGE: O Lord, they fight! I will go call the watch.
NARRATOR: Exit
PARIS: O, I am slain!
NARRATOR: Falls
PARIS: If thou be merciful,
PARIS: Open the tomb, lay me with Juliet.
NARRATOR: Dies
ROMEO: In faith, I will. Let me peruse this face.
ROMEO: Mercutio's kinsman, noble County Paris!
ROMEO: What said my man, when my betossed soul
ROMEO: Did not attend him as we rode? I think
ROMEO: He told me Paris should have married Juliet:
ROMEO: Said he not so? or did I dream it so?
ROMEO: Or am I mad, hearing him talk of Juliet,
ROMEO: To think it was so? O, give me thy hand,
ROMEO: One writ with me in sour misfortune's book!
ROMEO: I'll bury thee in a triumphant grave,
ROMEO: A grave? O no! a lantern, slaughter'd youth,
ROMEO: For here lies Juliet, and her beauty makes
ROMEO: This vault a feasting presence full of light.
ROMEO: Death, lie thou there, by a dead man interr'd.
NARRATOR: Laying PARIS in the tomb
ROMEO: How oft when men are at the point of death
ROMEO: Have they been merry! which their keepers call
ROMEO: A lightning before death: O, how may I
ROMEO: Call this a lightning? O my love! my wife!
ROMEO: Death, that hath suck'd the honey of thy breath,
ROMEO: Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty:
ROMEO: Thou art not conquer'd, beauty's ensign yet
ROMEO: Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks,
ROMEO: And death's pale flag is not advanced there.
ROMEO: Tybalt, liest thou there in thy bloody sheet?
ROMEO: O, what more favour can I do to thee,
ROMEO: Than with that hand that cut thy youth in twain
ROMEO: To sunder his that was thine enemy?
ROMEO: Forgive me, cousin! Ah, dear Juliet,
ROMEO: Why art thou yet so fair? shall I believe
ROMEO: That unsubstantial death is amorous,
ROMEO: And that the lean abhorred monster keeps
ROMEO: Thee here in dark to be his paramour?
ROMEO: For fear of that, I still will stay with thee,
ROMEO: And never from this palace of dim night
ROMEO: Depart again: here, here will I remain
ROMEO: With worms that are thy chamber-maids, O, here
ROMEO: Will I set up my everlasting rest,
ROMEO: And shake the yoke of inauspicious stars
ROMEO: From this world-wearied flesh. Eyes, look your last!
ROMEO: Arms, take your last embrace! and, lips, O you
ROMEO: The doors of breath, seal with a righteous kiss
ROMEO: A dateless bargain to engrossing death!
ROMEO: Come, bitter conduct, come, unsavoury guide!
ROMEO: Thou desperate pilot, now at once run on
ROMEO: The dashing rocks thy sea-sick weary bark!
ROMEO: Here's to my love!
NARRATOR: Drinks
ROMEO: O true apothecary!
ROMEO: Thy drugs are quick. Thus with a kiss I die.
NARRATOR: Dies
NARRATOR: Enter, at the other end of the churchyard, FRIAR LAURENCE, with a lantern, crow, and spade
FRIAR LAURENCE: Saint Francis be my speed! how oft to-night
FRIAR LAURENCE: Have my old feet stumbled at graves! Who's there?
BALTHASAR: Here's one, a friend, and one that knows you well.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Bliss be upon you! Tell me, good my friend,
FRIAR LAURENCE: What torch is yond, that vainly lends his light
FRIAR LAURENCE: To grubs and eyeless skulls? as I discern,
FRIAR LAURENCE: It burneth in the Capel's monument.
BALTHASAR: It doth so, holy sir, and there's my master,
BALTHASAR: One that you love.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Who is it?
BALTHASAR: Romeo.
FRIAR LAURENCE: How long hath he been there?
BALTHASAR: Full half an hour.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Go with me to the vault.
BALTHASAR: I dare not, sir
BALTHASAR: My master knows not but I am gone hence,
BALTHASAR: And fearfully did menace me with death,
BALTHASAR: If I did stay to look on his intents.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Stay, then, I'll go alone. Fear comes upon me:
FRIAR LAURENCE: O, much I fear some ill unlucky thing.
BALTHASAR: As I did sleep under this yew-tree here,
BALTHASAR: I dreamt my master and another fought,
BALTHASAR: And that my master slew him.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo!
NARRATOR: Advances
FRIAR LAURENCE: Alack, alack, what blood is this, which stains
FRIAR LAURENCE: The stony entrance of this sepulchre?
FRIAR LAURENCE: What mean these masterless and gory swords
FRIAR LAURENCE: To lie discolour'd by this place of peace?
NARRATOR: Enters the tomb
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo! O, pale! Who else? what, Paris too?
FRIAR LAURENCE: And steep'd in blood? Ah, what an unkind hour
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is guilty of this lamentable chance!
FRIAR LAURENCE: The lady stirs.
NARRATOR: JULIET wakes
JULIET: O comfortable friar! where is my lord?
JULIET: I do remember well where I should be,
JULIET: And there I am. Where is my Romeo?
NARRATOR: Noise within
FRIAR LAURENCE: I hear some noise. Lady, come from that nest
FRIAR LAURENCE: Of death, contagion, and unnatural sleep:
FRIAR LAURENCE: A greater power than we can contradict
FRIAR LAURENCE: Hath thwarted our intents. Come, come away.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Thy husband in thy bosom there lies dead,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And Paris too. Come, I'll dispose of thee
FRIAR LAURENCE: Among a sisterhood of holy nuns:
FRIAR LAURENCE: Stay not to question, for the watch is coming,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Come, go, good Juliet,
NARRATOR: Noise again
FRIAR LAURENCE: I dare no longer stay.
JULIET: Go, get thee hence, for I will not away.
NARRATOR: Exit FRIAR LAURENCE
JULIET: What's here? a cup, closed in my true love's hand?
JULIET: Poison, I see, hath been his timeless end:
JULIET: O churl! drunk all, and left no friendly drop
JULIET: To help me after? I will kiss thy lips,
JULIET: Haply some poison yet doth hang on them,
JULIET: To make die with a restorative.
NARRATOR: Kisses him
JULIET: Thy lips are warm.
First Watchman: [Within]  Lead, boy: which way?
JULIET: Yea, noise? then I'll be brief. O happy dagger!
NARRATOR: Snatching ROMEO's dagger
JULIET: This is thy sheath,
NARRATOR: Stabs herself
JULIET: there rust, and let me die.
NARRATOR: Falls on ROMEO's body, and dies
NARRATOR: Enter Watch, with the Page of PARIS
PAGE: This is the place, there, where the torch doth burn.
First Watchman: The ground is bloody, search about the churchyard:
First Watchman: Go, some of you, whoe'er you find attach.
First Watchman: Pitiful sight! here lies the county slain,
First Watchman: And Juliet bleeding, warm, and newly dead,
First Watchman: Who here hath lain these two days buried.
First Watchman: Go, tell the prince: run to the Capulets:
First Watchman: Raise up the Montagues: some others search:
First Watchman: We see the ground whereon these woes do lie,
First Watchman: But the true ground of all these piteous woes
First Watchman: We cannot without circumstance descry.
NARRATOR: Re-enter some of the Watch, with BALTHASAR
Second Watchman: Here's Romeo's man, we found him in the churchyard.
First Watchman: Hold him in safety, till the prince come hither.
NARRATOR: Re-enter others of the Watch, with FRIAR LAURENCE
Third Watchman: Here is a friar, that trembles, sighs and weeps:
Third Watchman: We took this mattock and this spade from him,
Third Watchman: As he was coming from this churchyard side.
First Watchman: A great suspicion: stay the friar too.
NARRATOR: Enter the PRINCE and Attendants
PRINCE: What misadventure is so early up,
PRINCE: That calls our person from our morning's rest?
NARRATOR: Enter CAPULET, LADY CAPULET, and others
CAPULET: What should it be, that they so shriek abroad?
LADY CAPULET: The people in the street cry Romeo,
LADY CAPULET: Some Juliet, and some Paris, and all run,
LADY CAPULET: With open outcry toward our monument.
PRINCE: What fear is this which startles in our ears?
First Watchman: Sovereign, here lies the County Paris slain,
First Watchman: And Romeo dead, and Juliet, dead before,
First Watchman: Warm and new kill'd.
PRINCE: Search, seek, and know how this foul murder comes.
First Watchman: Here is a friar, and slaughter'd Romeo's man,
First Watchman: With instruments upon them, fit to open
First Watchman: These dead men's tombs.
CAPULET: O heavens! O wife, look how our daughter bleeds!
CAPULET: This dagger hath mista'en--for, lo, his house
CAPULET: Is empty on the back of Montague,--
CAPULET: And it mis-sheathed in my daughter's bosom!
LADY CAPULET: O me! this sight of death is as a bell,
LADY CAPULET: That warns my old age to a sepulchre.
NARRATOR: Enter MONTAGUE and others
PRINCE: Come, Montague, for thou art early up,
PRINCE: To see thy son and heir more early down.
MONTAGUE: Alas, my liege, my wife is dead to-night,
MONTAGUE: Grief of my son's exile hath stopp'd her breath:
MONTAGUE: What further woe conspires against mine age?
PRINCE: Look, and thou shalt see.
MONTAGUE: O thou untaught! what manners is in this?
MONTAGUE: To press before thy father to a grave?
PRINCE: Seal up the mouth of outrage for a while,
PRINCE: Till we can clear these ambiguities,
PRINCE: And know their spring, their head, their
PRINCE: true descent,
PRINCE: And then will I be general of your woes,
PRINCE: And lead you even to death: meantime forbear,
PRINCE: And let mischance be slave to patience.
PRINCE: Bring forth the parties of suspicion.
FRIAR LAURENCE: I am the greatest, able to do least,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Yet most suspected, as the time and place
FRIAR LAURENCE: Doth make against me of this direful murder,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And here I stand, both to impeach and purge
FRIAR LAURENCE: Myself condemned and myself excused.
PRINCE: Then say at once what thou dost know in this.
FRIAR LAURENCE: I will be brief, for my short date of breath
FRIAR LAURENCE: Is not so long as is a tedious tale.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Romeo, there dead, was husband to that Juliet,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And she, there dead, that Romeo's faithful wife:
FRIAR LAURENCE: I married them, and their stol'n marriage-day
FRIAR LAURENCE: Was Tybalt's dooms-day, whose untimely death
FRIAR LAURENCE: Banish'd the new-made bridegroom from the city,
FRIAR LAURENCE: For whom, and not for Tybalt, Juliet pined.
FRIAR LAURENCE: You, to remove that siege of grief from her,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Betroth'd and would have married her perforce
FRIAR LAURENCE: To County Paris: then comes she to me,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And, with wild looks, bid me devise some mean
FRIAR LAURENCE: To rid her from this second marriage,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Or in my cell there would she kill herself.
FRIAR LAURENCE: Then gave I her, so tutor'd by my art,
FRIAR LAURENCE: A sleeping potion, which so took effect
FRIAR LAURENCE: As I intended, for it wrought on her
FRIAR LAURENCE: The form of death: meantime I writ to Romeo,
FRIAR LAURENCE: That he should hither come as this dire night,
FRIAR LAURENCE: To help to take her from her borrow'd grave,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Being the time the potion's force should cease.
FRIAR LAURENCE: But he which bore my letter, Friar John,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Was stay'd by accident, and yesternight
FRIAR LAURENCE: Return'd my letter back. Then all alone
FRIAR LAURENCE: At the prefixed hour of her waking,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Came I to take her from her kindred's vault,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Meaning to keep her closely at my cell,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Till I conveniently could send to Romeo:
FRIAR LAURENCE: But when I came, some minute ere the time
FRIAR LAURENCE: Of her awaking, here untimely lay
FRIAR LAURENCE: The noble Paris and true Romeo dead.
FRIAR LAURENCE: She wakes, and I entreated her come forth,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And bear this work of heaven with patience:
FRIAR LAURENCE: But then a noise did scare me from the tomb,
FRIAR LAURENCE: And she, too desperate, would not go with me,
FRIAR LAURENCE: But, as it seems, did violence on herself.
FRIAR LAURENCE: All this I know, and to the marriage
FRIAR LAURENCE: Her nurse is privy: and, if aught in this
FRIAR LAURENCE: Miscarried by my fault, let my old life
FRIAR LAURENCE: Be sacrificed, some hour before his time,
FRIAR LAURENCE: Unto the rigour of severest law.
PRINCE: We still have known thee for a holy man.
PRINCE: Where's Romeo's man? what can he say in this?
BALTHASAR: I brought my master news of Juliet's death,
BALTHASAR: And then in post he came from Mantua
BALTHASAR: To this same place, to this same monument.
BALTHASAR: This letter he early bid me give his father,
BALTHASAR: And threatened me with death, going in the vault,
BALTHASAR: I departed not and left him there.
PRINCE: Give me the letter, I will look on it.
PRINCE: Where is the county's page, that raised the watch?
PRINCE: Sirrah, what made your master in this place?
PAGE: He came with flowers to strew his lady's grave,
PAGE: And bid me stand aloof, and so I did:
PAGE: Anon comes one with light to ope the tomb,
PAGE: And by and by my master drew on him,
PAGE: And then I ran away to call the watch.
PRINCE: This letter doth make good the friar's words,
PRINCE: Their course of love, the tidings of her death:
PRINCE: And here he writes that he did buy a poison
PRINCE: Of a poor 'pothecary, and therewithal
PRINCE: Came to this vault to die, and lie with Juliet.
PRINCE: Where be these enemies? Capulet! Montague!
PRINCE: See, what a scourge is laid upon your hate,
PRINCE: That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love.
PRINCE: And I for winking at your discords too
PRINCE: Have lost a brace of kinsmen: all are punish'd.
CAPULET: O brother Montague, give me thy hand:
CAPULET: This is my daughter's jointure, for no more
CAPULET: Can I demand.
MONTAGUE: But I can give thee more:
MONTAGUE: For I will raise her statue in pure gold,
MONTAGUE: That while Verona by that name is known,
MONTAGUE: There shall no figure at such rate be set
MONTAGUE: As that of true and faithful Juliet.
CAPULET: As rich shall Romeo's by his lady's lie,
CAPULET: Poor sacrifices of our enmity!
PRINCE: A glooming peace this morning with it brings,
PRINCE: The sun, for sorrow, will not show his head:
PRINCE: Go hence, to have more talk of these sad things,
PRINCE: Some shall be pardon'd, and some punished:
PRINCE: For never was a story of more woe
PRINCE: Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.
NARRATOR: Exeunt

NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before an alehouse on a heath.
NARRATOR: Enter Hostess and SLY
SLY: I'll pheeze you, in faith.
Hostess: A pair of stocks, you rogue!
SLY: Ye are a baggage: the Slys are no rogues, look in
SLY: the chronicles, we came in with Richard Conqueror.
SLY: Therefore paucas pallabris, let the world slide: sessa!
Hostess: You will not pay for the glasses you have burst?
SLY: No, not a denier. Go by, Jeronimy: go to thy cold
SLY: bed, and warm thee.
Hostess: I know my remedy, I must go fetch the
Hostess: third--borough.
NARRATOR: Exit
SLY: Third, or fourth, or fifth borough, I'll answer him
SLY: by law: I'll not budge an inch, boy: let him come,
SLY: and kindly.
NARRATOR: Falls asleep
NARRATOR: Horns winded. Enter a Lord from hunting, with his train
Lord: Huntsman, I charge thee, tender well my hounds:
Lord: Brach Merriman, the poor cur is emboss'd,
Lord: And couple Clowder with the deep--mouth'd brach.
Lord: Saw'st thou not, boy, how Silver made it good
Lord: At the hedge-corner, in the coldest fault?
Lord: I would not lose the dog for twenty pound.
First Huntsman: Why, Belman is as good as he, my lord,
First Huntsman: He cried upon it at the merest loss
First Huntsman: And twice to-day pick'd out the dullest scent:
First Huntsman: Trust me, I take him for the better dog.
Lord: Thou art a fool: if Echo were as fleet,
Lord: I would esteem him worth a dozen such.
Lord: But sup them well and look unto them all:
Lord: To-morrow I intend to hunt again.
First Huntsman: I will, my lord.
Lord: What's here? one dead, or drunk? See, doth he breathe?
Second Huntsman: He breathes, my lord. Were he not warm'd with ale,
Second Huntsman: This were a bed but cold to sleep so soundly.
Lord: O monstrous beast! how like a swine he lies!
Lord: Grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image!
Lord: Sirs, I will practise on this drunken man.
Lord: What think you, if he were convey'd to bed,
Lord: Wrapp'd in sweet clothes, rings put upon his fingers,
Lord: A most delicious banquet by his bed,
Lord: And brave attendants near him when he wakes,
Lord: Would not the beggar then forget himself?
First Huntsman: Believe me, lord, I think he cannot choose.
Second Huntsman: It would seem strange unto him when he waked.
Lord: Even as a flattering dream or worthless fancy.
Lord: Then take him up and manage well the jest:
Lord: Carry him gently to my fairest chamber
Lord: And hang it round with all my wanton pictures:
Lord: Balm his foul head in warm distilled waters
Lord: And burn sweet wood to make the lodging sweet:
Lord: Procure me music ready when he wakes,
Lord: To make a dulcet and a heavenly sound,
Lord: And if he chance to speak, be ready straight
Lord: And with a low submissive reverence
Lord: Say 'What is it your honour will command?'
Lord: Let one attend him with a silver basin
Lord: Full of rose-water and bestrew'd with flowers,
Lord: Another bear the ewer, the third a diaper,
Lord: And say 'Will't please your lordship cool your hands?'
Lord: Some one be ready with a costly suit
Lord: And ask him what apparel he will wear,
Lord: Another tell him of his hounds and horse,
Lord: And that his lady mourns at his disease:
Lord: Persuade him that he hath been lunatic,
Lord: And when he says he is, say that he dreams,
Lord: For he is nothing but a mighty lord.
Lord: This do and do it kindly, gentle sirs:
Lord: It will be pastime passing excellent,
Lord: If it be husbanded with modesty.
First Huntsman: My lord, I warrant you we will play our part,
First Huntsman: As he shall think by our true diligence
First Huntsman: He is no less than what we say he is.
Lord: Take him up gently and to bed with him,
Lord: And each one to his office when he wakes.
NARRATOR: Some bear out SLY. A trumpet sounds
Lord: Sirrah, go see what trumpet 'tis that sounds:
NARRATOR: Exit Servingman
Lord: Belike, some noble gentleman that means,
Lord: Travelling some journey, to repose him here.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servingman
Lord: How now! who is it?
Servant: An't please your honour, players
Servant: That offer service to your lordship.
Lord: Bid them come near.
NARRATOR: Enter Players
Lord: Now, fellows, you are welcome.
Players: We thank your honour.
Lord: Do you intend to stay with me tonight?
A Player: So please your lordship to accept our duty.
Lord: With all my heart. This fellow I remember,
Lord: Since once he play'd a farmer's eldest son:
Lord: 'Twas where you woo'd the gentlewoman so well:
Lord: I have forgot your name, but, sure, that part
Lord: Was aptly fitted and naturally perform'd.
A Player: I think 'twas Soto that your honour means.
Lord: 'Tis very true: thou didst it excellent.
Lord: Well, you are come to me in a happy time,
Lord: The rather for I have some sport in hand
Lord: Wherein your cunning can assist me much.
Lord: There is a lord will hear you play to-night:
Lord: But I am doubtful of your modesties,
Lord: Lest over-eyeing of his odd behavior,--
Lord: For yet his honour never heard a play--
Lord: You break into some merry passion
Lord: And so offend him, for I tell you, sirs,
Lord: If you should smile he grows impatient.
A Player: Fear not, my lord: we can contain ourselves,
A Player: Were he the veriest antic in the world.
Lord: Go, sirrah, take them to the buttery,
Lord: And give them friendly welcome every one:
Lord: Let them want nothing that my house affords.
NARRATOR: Exit one with the Players
Lord: Sirrah, go you to Barthol'mew my page,
Lord: And see him dress'd in all suits like a lady:
Lord: That done, conduct him to the drunkard's chamber,
Lord: And call him 'madam,' do him obeisance.
Lord: Tell him from me, as he will win my love,
Lord: He bear himself with honourable action,
Lord: Such as he hath observed in noble ladies
Lord: Unto their lords, by them accomplished:
Lord: Such duty to the drunkard let him do
Lord: With soft low tongue and lowly courtesy,
Lord: And say 'What is't your honour will command,
Lord: Wherein your lady and your humble wife
Lord: May show her duty and make known her love?'
Lord: And then with kind embracements, tempting kisses,
Lord: And with declining head into his bosom,
Lord: Bid him shed tears, as being overjoy'd
Lord: To see her noble lord restored to health,
Lord: Who for this seven years hath esteem'd him
Lord: No better than a poor and loathsome beggar:
Lord: And if the boy have not a woman's gift
Lord: To rain a shower of commanded tears,
Lord: An onion will do well for such a shift,
Lord: Which in a napkin being close convey'd
Lord: Shall in despite enforce a watery eye.
Lord: See this dispatch'd with all the haste thou canst:
Lord: Anon I'll give thee more instructions.
NARRATOR: Exit a Servingman
Lord: I know the boy will well usurp the grace,
Lord: Voice, gait and action of a gentlewoman:
Lord: I long to hear him call the drunkard husband,
Lord: And how my men will stay themselves from laughter
Lord: When they do homage to this simple peasant.
Lord: I'll in to counsel them, haply my presence
Lord: May well abate the over-merry spleen
Lord: Which otherwise would grow into extremes.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. A bedchamber in the Lord's house.
NARRATOR: Enter aloft SLY, with Attendants, some with apparel, others with basin and ewer and appurtenances, and Lord
SLY: For God's sake, a pot of small ale.
First Servant: Will't please your lordship drink a cup of sack?
Second Servant: Will't please your honour taste of these conserves?
Third Servant: What raiment will your honour wear to-day?
SLY: I am Christophero Sly, call not me 'honour' nor
SLY: 'lordship:' I ne'er drank sack in my life, and if
SLY: you give me any conserves, give me conserves of
SLY: beef: ne'er ask me what raiment I'll wear, for I
SLY: have no more doublets than backs, no more stockings
SLY: than legs, nor no more shoes than feet, nay,
SLY: sometimes more feet than shoes, or such shoes as my
SLY: toes look through the over-leather.
Lord: Heaven cease this idle humour in your honour!
Lord: O, that a mighty man of such descent,
Lord: Of such possessions and so high esteem,
Lord: Should be infused with so foul a spirit!
SLY: What, would you make me mad? Am not I Christopher
SLY: Sly, old Sly's son of Burtonheath, by birth a
SLY: pedlar, by education a cardmaker, by transmutation a
SLY: bear-herd, and now by present profession a tinker?
SLY: Ask Marian Hacket, the fat ale-wife of Wincot, if
SLY: she know me not: if she say I am not fourteen pence
SLY: on the score for sheer ale, score me up for the
SLY: lyingest knave in Christendom. What! I am not
SLY: bestraught: here's--
Third Servant: O, this it is that makes your lady mourn!
Second Servant: O, this is it that makes your servants droop!
Lord: Hence comes it that your kindred shuns your house,
Lord: As beaten hence by your strange lunacy.
Lord: O noble lord, bethink thee of thy birth,
Lord: Call home thy ancient thoughts from banishment
Lord: And banish hence these abject lowly dreams.
Lord: Look how thy servants do attend on thee,
Lord: Each in his office ready at thy beck.
Lord: Wilt thou have music? hark! Apollo plays,
NARRATOR: Music
Lord: And twenty caged nightingales do sing:
Lord: Or wilt thou sleep? we'll have thee to a couch
Lord: Softer and sweeter than the lustful bed
Lord: On purpose trimm'd up for Semiramis.
Lord: Say thou wilt walk, we will bestrew the ground:
Lord: Or wilt thou ride? thy horses shall be trapp'd,
Lord: Their harness studded all with gold and pearl.
Lord: Dost thou love hawking? thou hast hawks will soar
Lord: Above the morning lark or wilt thou hunt?
Lord: Thy hounds shall make the welkin answer them
Lord: And fetch shrill echoes from the hollow earth.
First Servant: Say thou wilt course, thy greyhounds are as swift
First Servant: As breathed stags, ay, fleeter than the roe.
Second Servant: Dost thou love pictures? we will fetch thee straight
Second Servant: Adonis painted by a running brook,
Second Servant: And Cytherea all in sedges hid,
Second Servant: Which seem to move and wanton with her breath,
Second Servant: Even as the waving sedges play with wind.
Lord: We'll show thee Io as she was a maid,
Lord: And how she was beguiled and surprised,
Lord: As lively painted as the deed was done.
Third Servant: Or Daphne roaming through a thorny wood,
Third Servant: Scratching her legs that one shall swear she bleeds,
Third Servant: And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep,
Third Servant: So workmanly the blood and tears are drawn.
Lord: Thou art a lord, and nothing but a lord:
Lord: Thou hast a lady far more beautiful
Lord: Than any woman in this waning age.
First Servant: And till the tears that she hath shed for thee
First Servant: Like envious floods o'er-run her lovely face,
First Servant: She was the fairest creature in the world,
First Servant: And yet she is inferior to none.
SLY: Am I a lord? and have I such a lady?
SLY: Or do I dream? or have I dream'd till now?
SLY: I do not sleep: I see, I hear, I speak,
SLY: I smell sweet savours and I feel soft things:
SLY: Upon my life, I am a lord indeed
SLY: And not a tinker nor Christophero Sly.
SLY: Well, bring our lady hither to our sight,
SLY: And once again, a pot o' the smallest ale.
Second Servant: Will't please your mightiness to wash your hands?
Second Servant: O, how we joy to see your wit restored!
Second Servant: O, that once more you knew but what you are!
Second Servant: These fifteen years you have been in a dream,
Second Servant: Or when you waked, so waked as if you slept.
SLY: These fifteen years! by my fay, a goodly nap.
SLY: But did I never speak of all that time?
First Servant: O, yes, my lord, but very idle words:
First Servant: For though you lay here in this goodly chamber,
First Servant: Yet would you say ye were beaten out of door,
First Servant: And rail upon the hostess of the house,
First Servant: And say you would present her at the leet,
First Servant: Because she brought stone jugs and no seal'd quarts:
First Servant: Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.
SLY: Ay, the woman's maid of the house.
Third Servant: Why, sir, you know no house nor no such maid,
Third Servant: Nor no such men as you have reckon'd up,
Third Servant: As Stephen Sly and did John Naps of Greece
Third Servant: And Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell
Third Servant: And twenty more such names and men as these
Third Servant: Which never were nor no man ever saw.
SLY: Now Lord be thanked for my good amends!
ALL: Amen.
SLY: I thank thee: thou shalt not lose by it.

NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Padua. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCENTIO and his man TRANIO
LUCENTIO: Tranio, since for the great desire I had
LUCENTIO: To see fair Padua, nursery of arts,
LUCENTIO: I am arrived for fruitful Lombardy,
LUCENTIO: The pleasant garden of great Italy,
LUCENTIO: And by my father's love and leave am arm'd
LUCENTIO: With his good will and thy good company,
LUCENTIO: My trusty servant, well approved in all,
LUCENTIO: Here let us breathe and haply institute
LUCENTIO: A course of learning and ingenious studies.
LUCENTIO: Pisa renown'd for grave citizens
LUCENTIO: Gave me my being and my father first,
LUCENTIO: A merchant of great traffic through the world,
LUCENTIO: Vincetino come of Bentivolii.
LUCENTIO: Vincetino's son brought up in Florence
LUCENTIO: It shall become to serve all hopes conceived,
LUCENTIO: To deck his fortune with his virtuous deeds:
LUCENTIO: And therefore, Tranio, for the time I study,
LUCENTIO: Virtue and that part of philosophy
LUCENTIO: Will I apply that treats of happiness
LUCENTIO: By virtue specially to be achieved.
LUCENTIO: Tell me thy mind, for I have Pisa left
LUCENTIO: And am to Padua come, as he that leaves
LUCENTIO: A shallow plash to plunge him in the deep
LUCENTIO: And with satiety seeks to quench his thirst.
TRANIO: Mi perdonato, gentle master mine,
TRANIO: I am in all affected as yourself,
TRANIO: Glad that you thus continue your resolve
TRANIO: To suck the sweets of sweet philosophy.
TRANIO: Only, good master, while we do admire
TRANIO: This virtue and this moral discipline,
TRANIO: Let's be no stoics nor no stocks, I pray,
TRANIO: Or so devote to Aristotle's cheques
TRANIO: As Ovid be an outcast quite abjured:
TRANIO: Balk logic with acquaintance that you have
TRANIO: And practise rhetoric in your common talk,
TRANIO: Music and poesy use to quicken you,
TRANIO: The mathematics and the metaphysics,
TRANIO: Fall to them as you find your stomach serves you,
TRANIO: No profit grows where is no pleasure ta'en:
TRANIO: In brief, sir, study what you most affect.
LUCENTIO: Gramercies, Tranio, well dost thou advise.
LUCENTIO: If, Biondello, thou wert come ashore,
LUCENTIO: We could at once put us in readiness,
LUCENTIO: And take a lodging fit to entertain
LUCENTIO: Such friends as time in Padua shall beget.
LUCENTIO: But stay a while: what company is this?
TRANIO: Master, some show to welcome us to town.
NARRATOR: Enter BAPTISTA, KATHARINA, BIANCA, GREMIO, and HORTENSIO. LUCENTIO and TRANIO stand by
BAPTISTA: Gentlemen, importune me no farther,
BAPTISTA: For how I firmly am resolved you know,
BAPTISTA: That is, not bestow my youngest daughter
BAPTISTA: Before I have a husband for the elder:
BAPTISTA: If either of you both love Katharina,
BAPTISTA: Because I know you well and love you well,
BAPTISTA: Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure.
GREMIO: [Aside]  To cart her rather: she's too rough for me.
GREMIO: There, There, Hortensio, will you any wife?
KATHARINA: I pray you, sir, is it your will
KATHARINA: To make a stale of me amongst these mates?
HORTENSIO: Mates, maid! how mean you that? no mates for you,
HORTENSIO: Unless you were of gentler, milder mould.
KATHARINA: I'faith, sir, you shall never need to fear:
KATHARINA: I wis it is not half way to her heart,
KATHARINA: But if it were, doubt not her care should be
KATHARINA: To comb your noddle with a three-legg'd stool
KATHARINA: And paint your face and use you like a fool.
HORTENSIA: From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!
GREMIO: And me too, good Lord!
TRANIO: Hush, master! here's some good pastime toward:
TRANIO: That wench is stark mad or wonderful froward.
LUCENTIO: But in the other's silence do I see
LUCENTIO: Maid's mild behavior and sobriety.
LUCENTIO: Peace, Tranio!
TRANIO: Well said, master, mum! and gaze your fill.
BAPTISTA: Gentlemen, that I may soon make good
BAPTISTA: What I have said, Bianca, get you in:
BAPTISTA: And let it not displease thee, good Bianca,
BAPTISTA: For I will love thee ne'er the less, my girl.
KATHARINA: A pretty peat! it is best
KATHARINA: Put finger in the eye, an she knew why.
BIANCA: Sister, content you in my discontent.
BIANCA: Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe:
BIANCA: My books and instruments shall be my company,
BIANCA: On them to took and practise by myself.
LUCENTIO: Hark, Tranio! thou may'st hear Minerva speak.
HORTENSIO: Signior Baptista, will you be so strange?
HORTENSIO: Sorry am I that our good will effects
HORTENSIO: Bianca's grief.
GREMIO: Why will you mew her up,
GREMIO: Signior Baptista, for this fiend of hell,
GREMIO: And make her bear the penance of her tongue?
BAPTISTA: Gentlemen, content ye, I am resolved:
BAPTISTA: Go in, Bianca:
NARRATOR: Exit BIANCA
BAPTISTA: And for I know she taketh most delight
BAPTISTA: In music, instruments and poetry,
BAPTISTA: Schoolmasters will I keep within my house,
BAPTISTA: Fit to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio,
BAPTISTA: Or Signior Gremio, you, know any such,
BAPTISTA: Prefer them hither, for to cunning men
BAPTISTA: I will be very kind, and liberal
BAPTISTA: To mine own children in good bringing up:
BAPTISTA: And so farewell. Katharina, you may stay,
BAPTISTA: For I have more to commune with Bianca.

KATHARINA: Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not? What,
KATHARINA: shall I be appointed hours, as though, belike, I
KATHARINA: knew not what to take and what to leave, ha?

GREMIO: You may go to the devil's dam: your gifts are so
GREMIO: good, here's none will hold you. Their love is not
GREMIO: so great, Hortensio, but we may blow our nails

GREMIO: man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will
GREMIO: wish him to her father.
HORTENSIO: So will I, Signior Gremio: but a word, I pray.

HORTENSIO: that we may yet again have access to our fair
HORTENSIO: mistress and be happy rivals in Bianco's love, to
HORTENSIO: labour and effect one thing specially.
GREMIO: What's that, I pray?
HORTENSIO: Marry, sir, to get a husband for her sister.
GREMIO: A husband! a devil.
HORTENSIO: I say, a husband.
GREMIO: I say, a devil. Thinkest thou, Hortensio, though
GREMIO: her father be very rich, any man is so very a fool
GREMIO: to be married to hell?
HORTENSIO: Tush, Gremio, though it pass your patience and mine

HORTENSIO: fellows in the world, an a man could light on them,
HORTENSIO: would take her with all faults, and money enough.
GREMIO: I cannot tell, but I had as lief take her dowry with
GREMIO: this condition, to be whipped at the high cross
GREMIO: every morning.
HORTENSIO: Faith, as you say, there's small choice in rotten
HORTENSIO: apples. But come, since this bar in law makes us
HORTENSIO: friends, it shall be so far forth friendly
HORTENSIO: maintained all by helping Baptista's eldest daughter
HORTENSIO: to a husband we set his youngest free for a husband,
HORTENSIO: and then have to't a fresh. Sweet Bianca! Happy man
HORTENSIO: be his dole! He that runs fastest gets the ring.
HORTENSIO: How say you, Signior Gremio?
GREMIO: I am agreed, and would I had given him the best
GREMIO: horse in Padua to begin his wooing that would
GREMIO: thoroughly woo her, wed her and bed her and rid the
GREMIO: house of her! Come on.

TRANIO: I pray, sir, tell me, is it possible
TRANIO: That love should of a sudden take such hold?
LUCENTIO: O Tranio, till I found it to be true,
LUCENTIO: I never thought it possible or likely,
LUCENTIO: But see, while idly I stood looking on,
LUCENTIO: I found the effect of love in idleness:
LUCENTIO: And now in plainness do confess to thee,
LUCENTIO: That art to me as secret and as dear
LUCENTIO: As Anna to the queen of Carthage was,
LUCENTIO: Tranio, I burn, I pine, I perish, Tranio,
LUCENTIO: If I achieve not this young modest girl.
LUCENTIO: Counsel me, Tranio, for I know thou canst,
LUCENTIO: Assist me, Tranio, for I know thou wilt.
TRANIO: Master, it is no time to chide you now,
TRANIO: Affection is not rated from the heart:
TRANIO: If love have touch'd you, nought remains but so,
TRANIO: 'Redime te captum quam queas minimo.'
LUCENTIO: Gramercies, lad, go forward, this contents:
LUCENTIO: The rest will comfort, for thy counsel's sound.
TRANIO: Master, you look'd so longly on the maid,
TRANIO: Perhaps you mark'd not what's the pith of all.
LUCENTIO: O yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face,
LUCENTIO: Such as the daughter of Agenor had,
LUCENTIO: That made great Jove to humble him to her hand.
LUCENTIO: When with his knees he kiss'd the Cretan strand.
TRANIO: Saw you no more? mark'd you not how her sister
TRANIO: Began to scold and raise up such a storm
TRANIO: That mortal ears might hardly endure the din?
LUCENTIO: Tranio, I saw her coral lips to move
LUCENTIO: And with her breath she did perfume the air:
LUCENTIO: Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.
TRANIO: Nay, then, 'tis time to stir him from his trance.
TRANIO: I pray, awake, sir: if you love the maid,
TRANIO: Bend thoughts and wits to achieve her. Thus it stands:
TRANIO: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd
TRANIO: That till the father rid his hands of her,
TRANIO: Master, your love must live a maid at home,
TRANIO: And therefore has he closely mew'd her up,
TRANIO: Because she will not be annoy'd with suitors.
LUCENTIO: Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father's he!
LUCENTIO: But art thou not advised, he took some care
LUCENTIO: To get her cunning schoolmasters to instruct her?
TRANIO: Ay, marry, am I, sir, and now 'tis plotted.
LUCENTIO: I have it, Tranio.
TRANIO: Master, for my hand,
TRANIO: Both our inventions meet and jump in one.
LUCENTIO: Tell me thine first.
TRANIO: You will be schoolmaster
TRANIO: And undertake the teaching of the maid:
TRANIO: That's your device.
LUCENTIO: It is: may it be done?
TRANIO: Not possible, for who shall bear your part,
TRANIO: And be in Padua here Vincentio's son,
TRANIO: Keep house and ply his book, welcome his friends,
TRANIO: Visit his countrymen and banquet them?
LUCENTIO: Basta, content thee, for I have it full.
LUCENTIO: We have not yet been seen in any house,
LUCENTIO: Nor can we lie distinguish'd by our faces
LUCENTIO: For man or master, then it follows thus,
LUCENTIO: Thou shalt be master, Tranio, in my stead,
LUCENTIO: Keep house and port and servants as I should:
LUCENTIO: I will some other be, some Florentine,
LUCENTIO: Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa.
LUCENTIO: 'Tis hatch'd and shall be so: Tranio, at once
LUCENTIO: Uncase thee, take my colour'd hat and cloak:
LUCENTIO: When Biondello comes, he waits on thee,
LUCENTIO: But I will charm him first to keep his tongue.
TRANIO: So had you need.
TRANIO: In brief, sir, sith it your pleasure is,
TRANIO: And I am tied to be obedient,
TRANIO: For so your father charged me at our parting,
TRANIO: 'Be serviceable to my son,' quoth he,
TRANIO: Although I think 'twas in another sense,
TRANIO: I am content to be Lucentio,
TRANIO: Because so well I love Lucentio.
LUCENTIO: Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves:
LUCENTIO: And let me be a slave, to achieve that maid
LUCENTIO: Whose sudden sight hath thrall'd my wounded eye.
LUCENTIO: Here comes the rogue.
NARRATOR: Enter BIONDELLO
LUCENTIO: Sirrah, where have you been?
BIONDELLO: Where have I been! Nay, how now! where are you?
BIONDELLO: Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or
BIONDELLO: you stolen his? or both? pray, what's the news?
LUCENTIO: Sirrah, come hither: 'tis no time to jest,
LUCENTIO: And therefore frame your manners to the time.
LUCENTIO: Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life,
LUCENTIO: Puts my apparel and my countenance on,
LUCENTIO: And I for my escape have put on his,
LUCENTIO: For in a quarrel since I came ashore
LUCENTIO: I kill'd a man and fear I was descried:
LUCENTIO: Wait you on him, I charge you, as becomes,
LUCENTIO: While I make way from hence to save my life:
LUCENTIO: You understand me?
BIONDELLO: I, sir! ne'er a whit.
LUCENTIO: And not a jot of Tranio in your mouth:
LUCENTIO: Tranio is changed into Lucentio.
BIONDELLO: The better for him: would I were so too!
TRANIO: So could I, faith, boy, to have the next wish after,
TRANIO: That Lucentio indeed had Baptista's youngest daughter.
TRANIO: But, sirrah, not for my sake, but your master's, I advise
TRANIO: You use your manners discreetly in all kind of companies:
TRANIO: When I am alone, why, then I am Tranio,
TRANIO: But in all places else your master Lucentio.
LUCENTIO: Tranio, let's go: one thing more rests, that
LUCENTIO: thyself execute, to make one among these wooers: if

SLY: comes there any more of it?
Page: My lord, 'tis but begun.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. Padua. Before HORTENSIO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO and his man GRUMIO
PETRUCHIO: Verona, for a while I take my leave,
PETRUCHIO: To see my friends in Padua, but of all
PETRUCHIO: My best beloved and approved friend,
PETRUCHIO: Hortensio, and I trow this is his house.
PETRUCHIO: Here, sirrah Grumio, knock, I say.
GRUMIO: Knock, sir! whom should I knock? is there man has
GRUMIO: rebused your worship?
PETRUCHIO: Villain, I say, knock me here soundly.
GRUMIO: Knock you here, sir! why, sir, what am I, sir, that
GRUMIO: I should knock you here, sir?
PETRUCHIO: Villain, I say, knock me at this gate
PETRUCHIO: And rap me well, or I'll knock your knave's pate.
GRUMIO: My master is grown quarrelsome. I should knock
GRUMIO: you first,
GRUMIO: And then I know after who comes by the worst.
PETRUCHIO: Will it not be?
PETRUCHIO: Faith, sirrah, an you'll not knock, I'll ring it,
PETRUCHIO: I'll try how you can sol, fa, and sing it.
NARRATOR: He wrings him by the ears
GRUMIO: Help, masters, help! my master is mad.
PETRUCHIO: Now, knock when I bid you, sirrah villain!
NARRATOR: Enter HORTENSIO
HORTENSIO: How now! what's the matter? My old friend Grumio!
HORTENSIO: and my good friend Petruchio! How do you all at Verona?
PETRUCHIO: Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray?
PETRUCHIO: 'Con tutto il cuore, ben trovato,' may I say.
HORTENSIO: 'Alla nostra casa ben venuto, molto honorato signor

HORTENSIO: this quarrel.
GRUMIO: Nay, 'tis no matter, sir, what he 'leges in Latin.
GRUMIO: if this be not a lawful case for me to leave his
GRUMIO: service, look you, sir, he bid me knock him and rap
GRUMIO: him soundly, sir: well, was it fit for a servant to
GRUMIO: use his master so, being perhaps, for aught I see,
GRUMIO: two and thirty, a pip out? Whom would to God I had
GRUMIO: well knock'd at first, Then had not Grumio come by the worst.
PETRUCHIO: A senseless villain! Good Hortensio,
PETRUCHIO: I bade the rascal knock upon your gate
PETRUCHIO: And could not get him for my heart to do it.
GRUMIO: Knock at the gate! O heavens! Spake you not these
GRUMIO: words plain, 'Sirrah, knock me here, rap me here,
GRUMIO: knock me well, and knock me soundly'? And come you
GRUMIO: now with, 'knocking at the gate'?
PETRUCHIO: Sirrah, be gone, or talk not, I advise you.
HORTENSIO: Petruchio, patience, I am Grumio's pledge:
HORTENSIO: Why, this's a heavy chance 'twixt him and you,

HORTENSIO: And tell me now, sweet friend, what happy gale

PETRUCHIO: Such wind as scatters young men through the world,
PETRUCHIO: To seek their fortunes farther than at home
PETRUCHIO: Where small experience grows. But in a few,
PETRUCHIO: Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me:
PETRUCHIO: Antonio, my father, is deceased,
PETRUCHIO: And I have thrust myself into this maze,
PETRUCHIO: Haply to wive and thrive as best I may:
PETRUCHIO: Crowns in my purse I have and goods at home,
PETRUCHIO: And so am come abroad to see the world.
HORTENSIO: Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee

HORTENSIO: Thou'ldst thank me but a little for my counsel:
HORTENSIO: And yet I'll promise thee she shall be rich

HORTENSIO: And I'll not wish thee to her.
PETRUCHIO: Signior Hortensio, 'twixt such friends as we
PETRUCHIO: Few words suffice, and therefore, if thou know
PETRUCHIO: One rich enough to be Petruchio's wife,
PETRUCHIO: As wealth is burden of my wooing dance,
PETRUCHIO: Be she as foul as was Florentius' love,
PETRUCHIO: As old as Sibyl and as curst and shrewd
PETRUCHIO: As Socrates' Xanthippe, or a worse,
PETRUCHIO: She moves me not, or not removes, at least,

PETRUCHIO: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua,
PETRUCHIO: If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
GRUMIO: Nay, look you, sir, he tells you flatly what his

GRUMIO: so money comes withal.
HORTENSIO: Petruchio, since we are stepp'd thus far in,
HORTENSIO: I will continue that I broach'd in jest.
HORTENSIO: I can, Petruchio, help thee to a wife

HORTENSIO: Is that she is intolerable curst
HORTENSIO: And shrewd and froward, so beyond all measure
HORTENSIO: That, were my state far worser than it is,
HORTENSIO: I would not wed her for a mine of gold.
PETRUCHIO: Hortensio, peace! thou know'st not gold's effect:
PETRUCHIO: Tell me her father's name and 'tis enough,
PETRUCHIO: For I will board her, though she chide as loud

HORTENSIO: Her father is Baptista Minola,
HORTENSIO: An affable and courteous gentleman:
HORTENSIO: Her name is Katharina Minola,
HORTENSIO: Renown'd in Padua for her scolding tongue.
PETRUCHIO: I know her father, though I know not her,
PETRUCHIO: And he knew my deceased father well.
PETRUCHIO: I will not sleep, Hortensio, till I see her,
PETRUCHIO: And therefore let me be thus bold with you
PETRUCHIO: To give you over at this first encounter,
PETRUCHIO: Unless you will accompany me thither.
GRUMIO: I pray you, sir, let him go while the humour lasts.

GRUMIO: would think scolding would do little good upon him:
GRUMIO: she may perhaps call him half a score knaves or so:
GRUMIO: why, that's nothing, an he begin once, he'll rail in
GRUMIO: his rope-tricks. I'll tell you what sir, an she
GRUMIO: stand him but a little, he will throw a figure in
GRUMIO: her face and so disfigure her with it that she
GRUMIO: shall have no more eyes to see withal than a cat.
GRUMIO: You know him not, sir.
HORTENSIO: Tarry, Petruchio, I must go with thee,

HORTENSIO: He hath the jewel of my life in hold,
HORTENSIO: His youngest daughter, beautiful Binaca,

HORTENSIO: Supposing it a thing impossible,
HORTENSIO: For those defects I have before rehearsed,
HORTENSIO: That ever Katharina will be woo'd,
HORTENSIO: Therefore this order hath Baptista ta'en,
HORTENSIO: That none shall have access unto Bianca
HORTENSIO: Till Katharina the curst have got a husband.
GRUMIO: Katharina the curst!
GRUMIO: A title for a maid of all titles the worst.
HORTENSIO: Now shall my friend Petruchio do me grace,
HORTENSIO: And offer me disguised in sober robes
HORTENSIO: To old Baptista as a schoolmaster
HORTENSIO: Well seen in music, to instruct Bianca,
HORTENSIO: That so I may, by this device, at least
HORTENSIO: Have leave and leisure to make love to her
HORTENSIO: And unsuspected court her by herself.
GRUMIO: Here's no knavery! See, to beguile the old folks,
GRUMIO: how the young folks lay their heads together!
NARRATOR: Enter GREMIO, and LUCENTIO disguised

GRUMIO: A proper stripling and an amorous!
GREMIO: O, very well, I have perused the note.

GREMIO: And so we will, provided that he win her.
GRUMIO: I would I were as sure of a good dinner.

TRANIO: Baptista is a noble gentleman,
TRANIO: To whom my father is not all unknown,
TRANIO: And were his daughter fairer than she is,
TRANIO: She may more suitors have and me for one.
TRANIO: Fair Leda's daughter had a thousand wooers,
TRANIO: Then well one more may fair Bianca have:
TRANIO: And so she shall, Lucentio shall make one,

HORTENSIO: Sir, let me be so bold as ask you,

TRANIO: The one as famous for a scolding tongue

PETRUCHIO: Sir, sir, the first's for me, let her go by.

GREMIO: And let it be more than Alcides' twelve.

PETRUCHIO: The younges t daughter whom you hearken for

PETRUCHIO: And will not promise her to any man
PETRUCHIO: Until the elder sister first be wed:
PETRUCHIO: The younger then is free and not before.
TRANIO: If it be so, sir, that you are the man
TRANIO: Must stead us all and me amongst the rest,
TRANIO: And if you break the ice and do this feat,
TRANIO: Achieve the elder, set the younger free
TRANIO: For our access, whose hap shall be to have her
TRANIO: Will not so graceless be to be ingrate.
HORTENSIO: Sir, you say well and well you do conceive,
HORTENSIO: And since you do profess to be a suitor,
HORTENSIO: You must, as we do, gratify this gentleman,
HORTENSIO: To whom we all rest generally beholding.
TRANIO: Sir, I shall not be slack: in sign whereof,
TRANIO: Please ye we may contrive this afternoon,
TRANIO: And quaff carouses to our mistress' health,
TRANIO: And do as adversaries do in law,
TRANIO: Strive mightily, but eat and drink as friends.
BIONDELLO: O excellent motion! Fellows, let's be gone.
HORTENSIO: The motion's good indeed and be it so,
HORTENSIO: Petruchio, I shall be your ben venuto.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Padua. A room in BAPTISTA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter KATHARINA and BIANCA
BIANCA: Good sister, wrong me not, nor wrong yourself,
BIANCA: To make a bondmaid and a slave of me,
BIANCA: That I disdain: but for these other gawds,
BIANCA: Unbind my hands, I'll pull them off myself,
BIANCA: Yea, all my raiment, to my petticoat,
BIANCA: Or what you will command me will I do,
BIANCA: So well I know my duty to my elders.
KATHARINA: Of all thy suitors, here I charge thee, tell
KATHARINA: Whom thou lovest best: see thou dissemble not.
BIANCA: Believe me, sister, of all the men alive
BIANCA: I never yet beheld that special face
BIANCA: Which I could fancy more than any other.
KATHARINA: Minion, thou liest. Is't not Hortensio?
BIANCA: If you affect him, sister, here I swear
BIANCA: I'll plead for you myself, but you shall have
BIANCA: him.
KATHARINA: O then, belike, you fancy riches more:
KATHARINA: You will have Gremio to keep you fair.
BIANCA: Is it for him you do envy me so?
BIANCA: Nay then you jest, and now I well perceive
BIANCA: You have but jested with me all this while:
BIANCA: I prithee, sister Kate, untie my hands.
KATHARINA: If that be jest, then all the rest was so.
NARRATOR: Strikes her
NARRATOR: Enter BAPTISTA
BAPTISTA: Why, how now, dame! whence grows this insolence?
BAPTISTA: Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl! she weeps.
BAPTISTA: Go ply thy needle, meddle not with her.
BAPTISTA: For shame, thou helding of a devilish spirit,
BAPTISTA: Why dost thou wrong her that did ne'er wrong thee?
BAPTISTA: When did she cross thee with a bitter word?
KATHARINA: Her silence flouts me, and I'll be revenged.
NARRATOR: Flies after BIANCA
BAPTISTA: What, in my sight? Bianca, get thee in.
NARRATOR: Exit BIANCA
KATHARINA: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see
KATHARINA: She is your treasure, she must have a husband,
KATHARINA: I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day
KATHARINA: And for your love to her lead apes in hell.
KATHARINA: Talk not to me: I will go sit and weep
KATHARINA: Till I can find occasion of revenge.
NARRATOR: Exit
BAPTISTA: Was ever gentleman thus grieved as I?
BAPTISTA: But who comes here?
BAPTISTA: Enter GREMIO, LUCENTIO in the habit of a mean man,  PETRUCHIO, with HORTENSIO as a musician, and TRANIO, with BIONDELLO bearing a lute and books
GREMIO: Good morrow, neighbour Baptista.
BAPTISTA: Good morrow, neighbour Gremio.
BAPTISTA: God save you, gentlemen!
PETRUCHIO: And you, good sir! Pray, have you not a daughter
PETRUCHIO: Call'd Katharina, fair and virtuous?
BAPTISTA: I have a daughter, sir, called Katharina.
GREMIO: You are too blunt: go to it orderly.
PETRUCHIO: You wrong me, Signior Gremio: give me leave.
PETRUCHIO: I am a gentleman of Verona, sir,
PETRUCHIO: That, hearing of her beauty and her wit,
PETRUCHIO: Her affability and bashful modesty,
PETRUCHIO: Her wondrous qualities and mild behavior,
PETRUCHIO: Am bold to show myself a forward guest
PETRUCHIO: Within your house, to make mine eye the witness
PETRUCHIO: Of that report which I so oft have heard.
PETRUCHIO: And, for an entrance to my entertainment,
PETRUCHIO: I do present you with a man of mine,
NARRATOR: Presenting HORTENSIO
PETRUCHIO: Cunning in music and the mathematics,
PETRUCHIO: To instruct her fully in those sciences,
PETRUCHIO: Whereof I know she is not ignorant:
PETRUCHIO: Accept of him, or else you do me wrong:
PETRUCHIO: His name is Licio, born in Mantua.
BAPTISTA: You're welcome, sir, and he, for your good sake.
BAPTISTA: But for my daughter Katharina, this I know,
BAPTISTA: She is not for your turn, the more my grief.
PETRUCHIO: I see you do not mean to part with her,
PETRUCHIO: Or else you like not of my company.
BAPTISTA: Mistake me not, I speak but as I find.
BAPTISTA: Whence are you, sir? what may I call your name?
PETRUCHIO: Petruchio is my name, Antonio's son,
PETRUCHIO: A man well known throughout all Italy.
BAPTISTA: I know him well: you are welcome for his sake.
GREMIO: Saving your tale, Petruchio, I pray,
GREMIO: Let us, that are poor petitioners, speak too:
GREMIO: Baccare! you are marvellous forward.
PETRUCHIO: O, pardon me, Signior Gremio, I would fain be doing.
GREMIO: I doubt it not, sir, but you will curse your
GREMIO: wooing. Neighbour, this is a gift very grateful, I am
GREMIO: sure of it. To express the like kindness, myself,
GREMIO: that have been more kindly beholding to you than
GREMIO: any, freely give unto you this young scholar,
NARRATOR: Presenting LUCENTIO
GREMIO: that hath been long studying at Rheims, as cunning
GREMIO: in Greek, Latin, and other languages, as the other
GREMIO: in music and mathematics: his name is Cambio, pray,
GREMIO: accept his service.
BAPTISTA: A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio.
BAPTISTA: Welcome, good Cambio.
NARRATOR: To TRANIO
BAPTISTA: But, gentle sir, methinks you walk like a stranger:
BAPTISTA: may I be so bold to know the cause of your coming?
TRANIO: Pardon me, sir, the boldness is mine own,
TRANIO: That, being a stranger in this city here,
TRANIO: Do make myself a suitor to your daughter,
TRANIO: Unto Bianca, fair and virtuous.
TRANIO: Nor is your firm resolve unknown to me,
TRANIO: In the preferment of the eldest sister.
TRANIO: This liberty is all that I request,
TRANIO: That, upon knowledge of my parentage,
TRANIO: I may have welcome 'mongst the rest that woo
TRANIO: And free access and favour as the rest:
TRANIO: And, toward the education of your daughters,
TRANIO: I here bestow a simple instrument,
TRANIO: And this small packet of Greek and Latin books:
TRANIO: If you accept them, then their worth is great.
BAPTISTA: Lucentio is your name, of whence, I pray?
TRANIO: Of Pisa, sir, son to Vincentio.
BAPTISTA: A mighty man of Pisa, by report
BAPTISTA: I know him well: you are very welcome, sir,
BAPTISTA: Take you the lute, and you the set of books,
BAPTISTA: You shall go see your pupils presently.
BAPTISTA: Holla, within!
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
BAPTISTA: Sirrah, lead these gentlemen
BAPTISTA: To my daughters, and tell them both,
BAPTISTA: These are their tutors: bid them use them well.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant, with LUCENTIO and HORTENSIO, BIONDELLO following
BAPTISTA: We will go walk a little in the orchard,
BAPTISTA: And then to dinner. You are passing welcome,
BAPTISTA: And so I pray you all to think yourselves.
PETRUCHIO: Signior Baptista, my business asketh haste,
PETRUCHIO: And every day I cannot come to woo.
PETRUCHIO: You knew my father well, and in him me,
PETRUCHIO: Left solely heir to all his lands and goods,
PETRUCHIO: Which I have better'd rather than decreased:
PETRUCHIO: Then tell me, if I get your daughter's love,
PETRUCHIO: What dowry shall I have with her to wife?
BAPTISTA: After my death the one half of my lands,
BAPTISTA: And in possession twenty thousand crowns.
PETRUCHIO: And, for that dowry, I'll assure her of
PETRUCHIO: Her widowhood, be it that she survive me,
PETRUCHIO: In all my lands and leases whatsoever:
PETRUCHIO: Let specialties be therefore drawn between us,
PETRUCHIO: That covenants may be kept on either hand.
BAPTISTA: Ay, when the special thing is well obtain'd,
BAPTISTA: That is, her love, for that is all in all.
PETRUCHIO: Why, that is nothing: for I tell you, father,
PETRUCHIO: I am as peremptory as she proud-minded,
PETRUCHIO: And where two raging fires meet together
PETRUCHIO: They do consume the thing that feeds their fury:
PETRUCHIO: Though little fire grows great with little wind,
PETRUCHIO: Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all:
PETRUCHIO: So I to her and so she yields to me,
PETRUCHIO: For I am rough and woo not like a babe.
BAPTISTA: Well mayst thou woo, and happy be thy speed!
BAPTISTA: But be thou arm'd for some unhappy words.
PETRUCHIO: Ay, to the proof, as mountains are for winds,
PETRUCHIO: That shake not, though they blow perpetually.
NARRATOR: Re-enter HORTENSIO, with his head broke
BAPTISTA: How now, my friend! why dost thou look so pale?
HORTENSIO: For fear, I promise you, if I look pale.
BAPTISTA: What, will my daughter prove a good musician?
HORTENSIO: I think she'll sooner prove a soldier
HORTENSIO: Iron may hold with her, but never lutes.
BAPTISTA: Why, then thou canst not break her to the lute?
HORTENSIO: Why, no, for she hath broke the lute to me.
HORTENSIO: I did but tell her she mistook her frets,
HORTENSIO: And bow'd her hand to teach her fingering,
HORTENSIO: When, with a most impatient devilish spirit,
HORTENSIO: 'Frets, call you these?' quoth she, 'I'll fume
HORTENSIO: with them:'
HORTENSIO: And, with that word, she struck me on the head,
HORTENSIO: And through the instrument my pate made way,
HORTENSIO: And there I stood amazed for a while,
HORTENSIO: As on a pillory, looking through the lute,
HORTENSIO: While she did call me rascal fiddler
HORTENSIO: And twangling Jack, with twenty such vile terms,
HORTENSIO: As had she studied to misuse me so.
PETRUCHIO: Now, by the world, it is a lusty wench,
PETRUCHIO: I love her ten times more than e'er I did:
PETRUCHIO: O, how I long to have some chat with her!
BAPTISTA: Well, go with me and be not so discomfited:
BAPTISTA: Proceed in practise with my younger daughter,
BAPTISTA: She's apt to learn and thankful for good turns.
BAPTISTA: Signior Petruchio, will you go with us,
BAPTISTA: Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?
PETRUCHIO: I pray you do.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but PETRUCHIO
PETRUCHIO: I will attend her here,
PETRUCHIO: And woo her with some spirit when she comes.
PETRUCHIO: Say that she rail, why then I'll tell her plain
PETRUCHIO: She sings as sweetly as a nightingale:
PETRUCHIO: Say that she frown, I'll say she looks as clear
PETRUCHIO: As morning roses newly wash'd with dew:
PETRUCHIO: Say she be mute and will not speak a word,
PETRUCHIO: Then I'll commend her volubility,
PETRUCHIO: And say she uttereth piercing eloquence:
PETRUCHIO: If she do bid me pack, I'll give her thanks,
PETRUCHIO: As though she bid me stay by her a week:
PETRUCHIO: If she deny to wed, I'll crave the day
PETRUCHIO: When I shall ask the banns and when be married.
PETRUCHIO: But here she comes, and now, Petruchio, speak.
NARRATOR: Enter KATHARINA
PETRUCHIO: Good morrow, Kate, for that's your name, I hear.
KATHARINA: Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing:
KATHARINA: They call me Katharina that do talk of me.
PETRUCHIO: You lie, in faith, for you are call'd plain Kate,
PETRUCHIO: And bonny Kate and sometimes Kate the curst,
PETRUCHIO: But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom
PETRUCHIO: Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate,
PETRUCHIO: For dainties are all Kates, and therefore, Kate,
PETRUCHIO: Take this of me, Kate of my consolation,
