PETRUCHIO: Hearing thy mildness praised in every town,
PETRUCHIO: Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded,
PETRUCHIO: Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs,
PETRUCHIO: Myself am moved to woo thee for my wife.
KATHARINA: Moved! in good time: let him that moved you hither
KATHARINA: Remove you hence: I knew you at the first
KATHARINA: You were a moveable.
PETRUCHIO: Why, what's a moveable?
KATHARINA: A join'd-stool.
PETRUCHIO: Thou hast hit it: come, sit on me.
KATHARINA: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
PETRUCHIO: Women are made to bear, and so are you.
KATHARINA: No such jade as you, if me you mean.
PETRUCHIO: Alas! good Kate, I will not burden thee,
PETRUCHIO: For, knowing thee to be but young and light--
KATHARINA: Too light for such a swain as you to catch,
KATHARINA: And yet as heavy as my weight should be.
PETRUCHIO: Should be! should--buzz!
KATHARINA: Well ta'en, and like a buzzard.
PETRUCHIO: O slow-wing'd turtle! shall a buzzard take thee?
KATHARINA: Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.
PETRUCHIO: Come, come, you wasp, i' faith, you are too angry.
KATHARINA: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.
PETRUCHIO: My remedy is then, to pluck it out.
KATHARINA: Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies,
PETRUCHIO: Who knows not where a wasp does
PETRUCHIO: wear his sting? In his tail.
KATHARINA: In his tongue.
PETRUCHIO: Whose tongue?
KATHARINA: Yours, if you talk of tails: and so farewell.
PETRUCHIO: What, with my tongue in your tail? nay, come again,
PETRUCHIO: Good Kate, I am a gentleman.
KATHARINA: That I'll try.
NARRATOR: She strikes him
PETRUCHIO: I swear I'll cuff you, if you strike again.
KATHARINA: So may you lose your arms:
KATHARINA: If you strike me, you are no gentleman,
KATHARINA: And if no gentleman, why then no arms.
PETRUCHIO: A herald, Kate? O, put me in thy books!
KATHARINA: What is your crest? a coxcomb?
PETRUCHIO: A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.
KATHARINA: No cock of mine, you crow too like a craven.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, come, Kate, come, you must not look so sour.
KATHARINA: It is my fashion, when I see a crab.
PETRUCHIO: Why, here's no crab, and therefore look not sour.
KATHARINA: There is, there is.
PETRUCHIO: Then show it me.
KATHARINA: Had I a glass, I would.
PETRUCHIO: What, you mean my face?
KATHARINA: Well aim'd of such a young one.
PETRUCHIO: Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.
KATHARINA: Yet you are wither'd.
PETRUCHIO: 'Tis with cares.
KATHARINA: I care not.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, hear you, Kate: in sooth you scape not so.
KATHARINA: I chafe you, if I tarry: let me go.
PETRUCHIO: No, not a whit: I find you passing gentle.
PETRUCHIO: 'Twas told me you were rough and coy and sullen,
PETRUCHIO: And now I find report a very liar,
PETRUCHIO: For thou are pleasant, gamesome, passing courteous,
PETRUCHIO: But slow in speech, yet sweet as spring-time flowers:
PETRUCHIO: Thou canst not frown, thou canst not look askance,
PETRUCHIO: Nor bite the lip, as angry wenches will,
PETRUCHIO: Nor hast thou pleasure to be cross in talk,
PETRUCHIO: But thou with mildness entertain'st thy wooers,
PETRUCHIO: With gentle conference, soft and affable.
PETRUCHIO: Why does the world report that Kate doth limp?
PETRUCHIO: O slanderous world! Kate like the hazel-twig
PETRUCHIO: Is straight and slender and as brown in hue
PETRUCHIO: As hazel nuts and sweeter than the kernels.
PETRUCHIO: O, let me see thee walk: thou dost not halt.
KATHARINA: Go, fool, and whom thou keep'st command.
PETRUCHIO: Did ever Dian so become a grove
PETRUCHIO: As Kate this chamber with her princely gait?
PETRUCHIO: O, be thou Dian, and let her be Kate,
PETRUCHIO: And then let Kate be chaste and Dian sportful!
KATHARINA: Where did you study all this goodly speech?
PETRUCHIO: It is extempore, from my mother-wit.
KATHARINA: A witty mother! witless else her son.
PETRUCHIO: Am I not wise?
KATHARINA: Yes, keep you warm.
PETRUCHIO: Marry, so I mean, sweet Katharina, in thy bed:
PETRUCHIO: And therefore, setting all this chat aside,
PETRUCHIO: Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented
PETRUCHIO: That you shall be my wife, your dowry 'greed on,
PETRUCHIO: And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you.
PETRUCHIO: Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn,
PETRUCHIO: For, by this light, whereby I see thy beauty,
PETRUCHIO: Thy beauty, that doth make me like thee well,
PETRUCHIO: Thou must be married to no man but me,
PETRUCHIO: For I am he am born to tame you Kate,
PETRUCHIO: And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate
PETRUCHIO: Conformable as other household Kates.
PETRUCHIO: Here comes your father: never make denial,
PETRUCHIO: I must and will have Katharina to my wife.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BAPTISTA, GREMIO, and TRANIO
BAPTISTA: Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?
PETRUCHIO: How but well, sir? how but well?
PETRUCHIO: It were impossible I should speed amiss.
BAPTISTA: Why, how now, daughter Katharina! in your dumps?
KATHARINA: Call you me daughter? now, I promise you
KATHARINA: You have show'd a tender fatherly regard,
KATHARINA: To wish me wed to one half lunatic,
KATHARINA: A mad-cup ruffian and a swearing Jack,
KATHARINA: That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.
PETRUCHIO: Father, 'tis thus: yourself and all the world,
PETRUCHIO: That talk'd of her, have talk'd amiss of her:
PETRUCHIO: If she be curst, it is for policy,
PETRUCHIO: For she's not froward, but modest as the dove,
PETRUCHIO: She is not hot, but temperate as the morn,
PETRUCHIO: For patience she will prove a second Grissel,
PETRUCHIO: And Roman Lucrece for her chastity:
PETRUCHIO: And to conclude, we have 'greed so well together,
PETRUCHIO: That upon Sunday is the wedding-day.
KATHARINA: I'll see thee hang'd on Sunday first.
GREMIO: Hark, Petruchio, she says she'll see thee
GREMIO: hang'd first.
TRANIO: Is this your speeding? nay, then, good night our part!
PETRUCHIO: Be patient, gentlemen, I choose her for myself:
PETRUCHIO: If she and I be pleased, what's that to you?
PETRUCHIO: 'Tis bargain'd 'twixt us twain, being alone,
PETRUCHIO: That she shall still be curst in company.
PETRUCHIO: I tell you, 'tis incredible to believe
PETRUCHIO: How much she loves me: O, the kindest Kate!
PETRUCHIO: She hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss
PETRUCHIO: She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath,
PETRUCHIO: That in a twink she won me to her love.
PETRUCHIO: O, you are novices! 'tis a world to see,
PETRUCHIO: How tame, when men and women are alone,
PETRUCHIO: A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew.
PETRUCHIO: Give me thy hand, Kate: I will unto Venice,
PETRUCHIO: To buy apparel 'gainst the wedding-day.
PETRUCHIO: Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests,
PETRUCHIO: I will be sure my Katharina shall be fine.
BAPTISTA: I know not what to say: but give me your hands,
BAPTISTA: God send you joy, Petruchio! 'tis a match.
TRANIO: Amen, say we: we will be witnesses.
PETRUCHIO: Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu,
PETRUCHIO: I will to Venice, Sunday comes apace:
PETRUCHIO: We will have rings and things and fine array,
PETRUCHIO: And kiss me, Kate, we will be married o'Sunday.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PETRUCHIO and KATHARINA severally
GREMIO: Was ever match clapp'd up so suddenly?
BAPTISTA: Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant's part,
BAPTISTA: And venture madly on a desperate mart.
TRANIO: 'Twas a commodity lay fretting by you:
TRANIO: 'Twill bring you gain, or perish on the seas.
BAPTISTA: The gain I seek is, quiet in the match.
GREMIO: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch.
GREMIO: But now, Baptists, to your younger daughter:
GREMIO: Now is the day we long have looked for:
GREMIO: I am your neighbour, and was suitor first.
TRANIO: And I am one that love Bianca more
TRANIO: Than words can witness, or your thoughts can guess.
GREMIO: Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.
TRANIO: Graybeard, thy love doth freeze.
GREMIO: But thine doth fry.
GREMIO: Skipper, stand back: 'tis age that nourisheth.
TRANIO: But youth in ladies' eyes that flourisheth.
BAPTISTA: Content you, gentlemen: I will compound this strife:
BAPTISTA: 'Tis deeds must win the prize, and he of both
BAPTISTA: That can assure my daughter greatest dower
BAPTISTA: Shall have my Bianca's love.
BAPTISTA: Say, Signior Gremio, What can you assure her?
GREMIO: First, as you know, my house within the city
GREMIO: Is richly furnished with plate and gold,
GREMIO: Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands,
GREMIO: My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry,
GREMIO: In ivory coffers I have stuff'd my crowns,
GREMIO: In cypress chests my arras counterpoints,
GREMIO: Costly apparel, tents, and canopies,
GREMIO: Fine linen, Turkey cushions boss'd with pearl,
GREMIO: Valance of Venice gold in needlework,
GREMIO: Pewter and brass and all things that belong
GREMIO: To house or housekeeping: then, at my farm
GREMIO: I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail,
GREMIO: Sixscore fat oxen standing in my stalls,
GREMIO: And all things answerable to this portion.
GREMIO: Myself am struck in years, I must confess,
GREMIO: And if I die to-morrow, this is hers,
GREMIO: If whilst I live she will be only mine.
TRANIO: That 'only' came well in. Sir, list to me:
TRANIO: I am my father's heir and only son:
TRANIO: If I may have your daughter to my wife,
TRANIO: I'll leave her houses three or four as good,
TRANIO: Within rich Pisa walls, as any one
TRANIO: Old Signior Gremio has in Padua,
TRANIO: Besides two thousand ducats by the year
TRANIO: Of fruitful land, all which shall be her jointure.
TRANIO: What, have I pinch'd you, Signior Gremio?
GREMIO: Two thousand ducats by the year of land!
GREMIO: My land amounts not to so much in all:
GREMIO: That she shall have, besides an argosy
GREMIO: That now is lying in Marseilles' road.
GREMIO: What, have I choked you with an argosy?
TRANIO: Gremio, 'tis known my father hath no less
TRANIO: Than three great argosies, besides two galliases,
TRANIO: And twelve tight galleys: these I will assure her,
TRANIO: And twice as much, whate'er thou offer'st next.
GREMIO: Nay, I have offer'd all, I have no more,
GREMIO: And she can have no more than all I have:
GREMIO: If you like me, she shall have me and mine.
TRANIO: Why, then the maid is mine from all the world,
TRANIO: By your firm promise: Gremio is out-vied.
BAPTISTA: I must confess your offer is the best,
BAPTISTA: And, let your father make her the assurance,
BAPTISTA: She is your own, else, you must pardon me,
BAPTISTA: if you should die before him, where's her dower?
TRANIO: That's but a cavil: he is old, I young.
GREMIO: And may not young men die, as well as old?
BAPTISTA: Well, gentlemen,
BAPTISTA: I am thus resolved: on Sunday next you know
BAPTISTA: My daughter Katharina is to be married:
BAPTISTA: Now, on the Sunday following, shall Bianca
BAPTISTA: Be bride to you, if you this assurance,
BAPTISTA: If not, Signior Gremio:
BAPTISTA: And so, I take my leave, and thank you both.
GREMIO: Adieu, good neighbour.
NARRATOR: Exit BAPTISTA
GREMIO: Now I fear thee not:
GREMIO: Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool
GREMIO: To give thee all, and in his waning age
GREMIO: Set foot under thy table: tut, a toy!
GREMIO: An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.
NARRATOR: Exit
TRANIO: A vengeance on your crafty wither'd hide!
TRANIO: Yet I have faced it with a card of ten.
TRANIO: 'Tis in my head to do my master good:
TRANIO: I see no reason but supposed Lucentio
TRANIO: Must get a father, call'd 'supposed Vincentio,'
TRANIO: And that's a wonder: fathers commonly
TRANIO: Do get their children, but in this case of wooing,
TRANIO: A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Padua. BAPTISTA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCENTIO, HORTENSIO, and BIANCA
LUCENTIO: Fiddler, forbear, you grow too forward, sir:
LUCENTIO: Have you so soon forgot the entertainment
LUCENTIO: Her sister Katharina welcomed you withal?
HORTENSIO: But, wrangling pedant, this is
HORTENSIO: The patroness of heavenly harmony:
HORTENSIO: Then give me leave to have prerogative,
HORTENSIO: And when in music we have spent an hour,
HORTENSIO: Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.
LUCENTIO: Preposterous ass, that never read so far
LUCENTIO: To know the cause why music was ordain'd!
LUCENTIO: Was it not to refresh the mind of man
LUCENTIO: After his studies or his usual pain?
LUCENTIO: Then give me leave to read philosophy,
LUCENTIO: And while I pause, serve in your harmony.
HORTENSIO: Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of thine.
BIANCA: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong,
BIANCA: To strive for that which resteth in my choice:
BIANCA: I am no breeching scholar in the schools,
BIANCA: I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times,
BIANCA: But learn my lessons as I please myself.
BIANCA: And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down:
BIANCA: Take you your instrument, play you the whiles,
BIANCA: His lecture will be done ere you have tuned.
HORTENSIO: You'll leave his lecture when I am in tune?
LUCENTIO: That will be never: tune your instrument.
BIANCA: Where left we last?
LUCENTIO: Here, madam:
LUCENTIO: 'Hic ibat Simois, hic est Sigeia tellus,
LUCENTIO: Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.'
BIANCA: Construe them.
LUCENTIO: 'Hic ibat,' as I told you before, 'Simois,' I am
LUCENTIO: Lucentio, 'hic est,' son unto Vincentio of Pisa,
LUCENTIO: 'Sigeia tellus,' disguised thus to get your love,
LUCENTIO: 'Hic steterat,' and that Lucentio that comes
LUCENTIO: a-wooing, 'Priami,' is my man Tranio, 'regia,'
LUCENTIO: bearing my port, 'celsa senis,' that we might
LUCENTIO: beguile the old pantaloon.
HORTENSIO: Madam, my instrument's in tune.
BIANCA: Let's hear. O fie! the treble jars.
LUCENTIO: Spit in the hole, man, and tune again.
BIANCA: Now let me see if I can construe it: 'Hic ibat
BIANCA: Simois,' I know you not, 'hic est Sigeia tellus,' I
BIANCA: trust you not, 'Hic steterat Priami,' take heed
BIANCA: he hear us not, 'regia,' presume not, 'celsa senis,'
BIANCA: despair not.
HORTENSIO: Madam, 'tis now in tune.
LUCENTIO: All but the base.
HORTENSIO: The base is right, 'tis the base knave that jars.
NARRATOR: Aside
HORTENSIO: How fiery and forward our pedant is!
HORTENSIO: Now, for my life, the knave doth court my love:
HORTENSIO: Pedascule, I'll watch you better yet.
BIANCA: In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.
LUCENTIO: Mistrust it not: for, sure, AEacides
LUCENTIO: Was Ajax, call'd so from his grandfather.
BIANCA: I must believe my master, else, I promise you,
BIANCA: I should be arguing still upon that doubt:
BIANCA: But let it rest. Now, Licio, to you:
BIANCA: Good masters, take it not unkindly, pray,
BIANCA: That I have been thus pleasant with you both.
HORTENSIO: You may go walk, and give me leave a while:
HORTENSIO: My lessons make no music in three parts.
LUCENTIO: Are you so formal, sir? well, I must wait,
NARRATOR: Aside
LUCENTIO: And watch withal, for, but I be deceived,
LUCENTIO: Our fine musician groweth amorous.
HORTENSIO: Madam, before you touch the instrument,
HORTENSIO: To learn the order of my fingering,
HORTENSIO: I must begin with rudiments of art,
HORTENSIO: To teach you gamut in a briefer sort,
HORTENSIO: More pleasant, pithy and effectual,
HORTENSIO: Than hath been taught by any of my trade:
HORTENSIO: And there it is in writing, fairly drawn.
BIANCA: Why, I am past my gamut long ago.
HORTENSIO: Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.
BIANCA: [Reads]  ''Gamut' I am, the ground of all accord,
BIANCA: 'A re,' to Plead Hortensio's passion,
BIANCA: 'B mi,' Bianca, take him for thy lord,
BIANCA: 'C fa ut,' that loves with all affection:
BIANCA: 'D sol re,' one clef, two notes have I:
BIANCA: 'E la mi,' show pity, or I die.'
BIANCA: Call you this gamut? tut, I like it not:
BIANCA: Old fashions please me best, I am not so nice,
BIANCA: To change true rules for old inventions.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: Mistress, your father prays you leave your books
Servant: And help to dress your sister's chamber up:
Servant: You know to-morrow is the wedding-day.
BIANCA: Farewell, sweet masters both, I must be gone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BIANCA and Servant
LUCENTIO: Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to stay.
NARRATOR: Exit
HORTENSIO: But I have cause to pry into this pedant:
HORTENSIO: Methinks he looks as though he were in love:
HORTENSIO: Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble
HORTENSIO: To cast thy wandering eyes on every stale,
HORTENSIO: Seize thee that list: if once I find thee ranging,
HORTENSIO: Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Padua. Before BAPTISTA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter BAPTISTA, GREMIO, TRANIO, KATHARINA, BIANCA, LUCENTIO, and others, attendants
BAPTISTA: [To TRANIO]  Signior Lucentio, this is the
BAPTISTA: 'pointed day.
BAPTISTA: That Katharina and Petruchio should be married,
BAPTISTA: And yet we hear not of our son-in-law.
BAPTISTA: What will be said? what mockery will it be,
BAPTISTA: To want the bridegroom when the priest attends
BAPTISTA: To speak the ceremonial rites of marriage!
BAPTISTA: What says Lucentio to this shame of ours?
KATHARINA: No shame but mine: I must, forsooth, be forced
KATHARINA: To give my hand opposed against my heart
KATHARINA: Unto a mad-brain rudesby full of spleen,
KATHARINA: Who woo'd in haste and means to wed at leisure.
KATHARINA: I told you, I, he was a frantic fool,
KATHARINA: Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behavior:
KATHARINA: And, to be noted for a merry man,
KATHARINA: He'll woo a thousand, 'point the day of marriage,
KATHARINA: Make feasts, invite friends, and proclaim the banns,
KATHARINA: Yet never means to wed where he hath woo'd.
KATHARINA: Now must the world point at poor Katharina,
KATHARINA: And say, 'Lo, there is mad Petruchio's wife,
KATHARINA: If it would please him come and marry her!'
TRANIO: Patience, good Katharina, and Baptista too.
TRANIO: Upon my life, Petruchio means but well,
TRANIO: Whatever fortune stays him from his word:
TRANIO: Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise,
TRANIO: Though he be merry, yet withal he's honest.
KATHARINA: Would Katharina had never seen him though!
NARRATOR: Exit weeping, followed by BIANCA and others
BAPTISTA: Go, girl, I cannot blame thee now to weep,
BAPTISTA: For such an injury would vex a very saint,
BAPTISTA: Much more a shrew of thy impatient humour.
NARRATOR: Enter BIONDELLO
BIONDELLO: Master, master! news, old news, and such news as
BIONDELLO: you never heard of!
BAPTISTA: Is it new and old too? how may that be?
BIONDELLO: Why, is it not news, to hear of Petruchio's coming?
BAPTISTA: Is he come?
BIONDELLO: Why, no, sir.
BAPTISTA: What then?
BIONDELLO: He is coming.
BAPTISTA: When will he be here?
BIONDELLO: When he stands where I am and sees you there.
TRANIO: But say, what to thine old news?
BIONDELLO: Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old
BIONDELLO: jerkin, a pair of old breeches thrice turned, a pair
BIONDELLO: of boots that have been candle-cases, one buckled,
BIONDELLO: another laced, an old rusty sword ta'en out of the
BIONDELLO: town-armory, with a broken hilt, and chapeless,
BIONDELLO: with two broken points: his horse hipped with an
BIONDELLO: old mothy saddle and stirrups of no kindred,
BIONDELLO: besides, possessed with the glanders and like to mose
BIONDELLO: in the chine, troubled with the lampass, infected
BIONDELLO: with the fashions, full of wingdalls, sped with
BIONDELLO: spavins, rayed with yellows, past cure of the fives,
BIONDELLO: stark spoiled with the staggers, begnawn with the
BIONDELLO: bots, swayed in the back and shoulder-shotten,
BIONDELLO: near-legged before and with, a half-chequed bit
BIONDELLO: and a head-stall of sheeps leather which, being
BIONDELLO: restrained to keep him from stumbling, hath been
BIONDELLO: often burst and now repaired with knots, one girth
BIONDELLO: six time pieced and a woman's crupper of velure,
BIONDELLO: which hath two letters for her name fairly set down
BIONDELLO: in studs, and here and there pieced with packthread.
BAPTISTA: Who comes with him?
BIONDELLO: O, sir, his lackey, for all the world caparisoned
BIONDELLO: like the horse, with a linen stock on one leg and a
BIONDELLO: kersey boot-hose on the other, gartered with a red
BIONDELLO: and blue list, an old hat and 'the humour of forty
BIONDELLO: fancies' pricked in't for a feather: a monster, a
BIONDELLO: very monster in apparel, and not like a Christian
BIONDELLO: footboy or a gentleman's lackey.
TRANIO: 'Tis some odd humour pricks him to this fashion,
TRANIO: Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-apparell'd.
BAPTISTA: I am glad he's come, howsoe'er he comes.
BIONDELLO: Why, sir, he comes not.
BAPTISTA: Didst thou not say he comes?
BIONDELLO: Who? that Petruchio came?
BAPTISTA: Ay, that Petruchio came.
BIONDELLO: No, sir, I say his horse comes, with him on his back.
BAPTISTA: Why, that's all one.
BIONDELLO: Nay, by Saint Jamy,
BIONDELLO: I hold you a penny,
BIONDELLO: A horse and a man
BIONDELLO: Is more than one,
BIONDELLO: And yet not many.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO and GRUMIO
PETRUCHIO: Come, where be these gallants? who's at home?
BAPTISTA: You are welcome, sir.
PETRUCHIO: And yet I come not well.
BAPTISTA: And yet you halt not.
TRANIO: Not so well apparell'd
TRANIO: As I wish you were.
PETRUCHIO: Were it better, I should rush in thus.
PETRUCHIO: But where is Kate? where is my lovely bride?
PETRUCHIO: How does my father? Gentles, methinks you frown:
PETRUCHIO: And wherefore gaze this goodly company,
PETRUCHIO: As if they saw some wondrous monument,
PETRUCHIO: Some comet or unusual prodigy?
BAPTISTA: Why, sir, you know this is your wedding-day:
BAPTISTA: First were we sad, fearing you would not come,
BAPTISTA: Now sadder, that you come so unprovided.
BAPTISTA: Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate,
BAPTISTA: An eye-sore to our solemn festival!
TRANIO: And tells us, what occasion of import
TRANIO: Hath all so long detain'd you from your wife,
TRANIO: And sent you hither so unlike yourself?
PETRUCHIO: Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to hear:
PETRUCHIO: Sufficeth I am come to keep my word,
PETRUCHIO: Though in some part enforced to digress,
PETRUCHIO: Which, at more leisure, I will so excuse
PETRUCHIO: As you shall well be satisfied withal.
PETRUCHIO: But where is Kate? I stay too long from her:
PETRUCHIO: The morning wears, 'tis time we were at church.
TRANIO: See not your bride in these unreverent robes:
TRANIO: Go to my chamber, Put on clothes of mine.
PETRUCHIO: Not I, believe me: thus I'll visit her.
BAPTISTA: But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.
PETRUCHIO: Good sooth, even thus, therefore ha' done with words:
PETRUCHIO: To me she's married, not unto my clothes:
PETRUCHIO: Could I repair what she will wear in me,
PETRUCHIO: As I can change these poor accoutrements,
PETRUCHIO: 'Twere well for Kate and better for myself.
PETRUCHIO: But what a fool am I to chat with you,
PETRUCHIO: When I should bid good morrow to my bride,
PETRUCHIO: And seal the title with a lovely kiss!
NARRATOR: Exeunt PETRUCHIO and GRUMIO
TRANIO: He hath some meaning in his mad attire:
TRANIO: We will persuade him, be it possible,
TRANIO: To put on better ere he go to church.
BAPTISTA: I'll after him, and see the event of this.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BAPTISTA, GREMIO, and attendants
TRANIO: But to her love concerneth us to add
TRANIO: Her father's liking: which to bring to pass,
TRANIO: As I before unparted to your worship,
TRANIO: I am to get a man,--whate'er he be,
TRANIO: It skills not much. we'll fit him to our turn,--
TRANIO: And he shall be Vincentio of Pisa,
TRANIO: And make assurance here in Padua
TRANIO: Of greater sums than I have promised.
TRANIO: So shall you quietly enjoy your hope,
TRANIO: And marry sweet Bianca with consent.
LUCENTIO: Were it not that my fellow-school-master
LUCENTIO: Doth watch Bianca's steps so narrowly,
LUCENTIO: 'Twere good, methinks, to steal our marriage,
LUCENTIO: Which once perform'd, let all the world say no,
LUCENTIO: I'll keep mine own, despite of all the world.
TRANIO: That by degrees we mean to look into,
TRANIO: And watch our vantage in this business:
TRANIO: We'll over-reach the greybeard, Gremio,
TRANIO: The narrow-prying father, Minola,
TRANIO: The quaint musician, amorous Licio,
TRANIO: All for my master's sake, Lucentio.
NARRATOR: Re-enter GREMIO
TRANIO: Signior Gremio, came you from the church?
GREMIO: As willingly as e'er I came from school.
TRANIO: And is the bride and bridegroom coming home?
GREMIO: A bridegroom say you? 'tis a groom indeed,
GREMIO: A grumbling groom, and that the girl shall find.
TRANIO: Curster than she? why, 'tis impossible.
GREMIO: Why he's a devil, a devil, a very fiend.
TRANIO: Why, she's a devil, a devil, the devil's dam.
GREMIO: Tut, she's a lamb, a dove, a fool to him!
GREMIO: I'll tell you, Sir Lucentio: when the priest
GREMIO: Should ask, if Katharina should be his wife,
GREMIO: 'Ay, by gogs-wouns,' quoth he, and swore so loud,
GREMIO: That, all-amazed, the priest let fall the book,
GREMIO: And, as he stoop'd again to take it up,
GREMIO: The mad-brain'd bridegroom took him such a cuff
GREMIO: That down fell priest and book and book and priest:
GREMIO: 'Now take them up,' quoth he, 'if any list.'
TRANIO: What said the wench when he rose again?
GREMIO: Trembled and shook, for why, he stamp'd and swore,
GREMIO: As if the vicar meant to cozen him.
GREMIO: But after many ceremonies done,
GREMIO: He calls for wine: 'A health!' quoth he, as if
GREMIO: He had been aboard, carousing to his mates
GREMIO: After a storm, quaff'd off the muscadel
GREMIO: And threw the sops all in the sexton's face,
GREMIO: Having no other reason
GREMIO: But that his beard grew thin and hungerly
GREMIO: And seem'd to ask him sops as he was drinking.
GREMIO: This done, he took the bride about the neck
GREMIO: And kiss'd her lips with such a clamorous smack
GREMIO: That at the parting all the church did echo:
GREMIO: And I seeing this came thence for very shame,
GREMIO: And after me, I know, the rout is coming.
GREMIO: Such a mad marriage never was before:
GREMIO: Hark, hark! I hear the minstrels play.
NARRATOR: Music
NARRATOR: Re-enter PETRUCHIO, KATHARINA, BIANCA, BAPTISTA, HORTENSIO, GRUMIO, and Train
PETRUCHIO: Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for your pains:
PETRUCHIO: I know you think to dine with me to-day,
PETRUCHIO: And have prepared great store of wedding cheer,
PETRUCHIO: But so it is, my haste doth call me hence,
PETRUCHIO: And therefore here I mean to take my leave.
BAPTISTA: Is't possible you will away to-night?
PETRUCHIO: I must away to-day, before night come:
PETRUCHIO: Make it no wonder, if you knew my business,
PETRUCHIO: You would entreat me rather go than stay.
PETRUCHIO: And, honest company, I thank you all,
PETRUCHIO: That have beheld me give away myself
PETRUCHIO: To this most patient, sweet and virtuous wife:
PETRUCHIO: Dine with my father, drink a health to me,
PETRUCHIO: For I must hence, and farewell to you all.
TRANIO: Let us entreat you stay till after dinner.
PETRUCHIO: It may not be.
GREMIO: Let me entreat you.
PETRUCHIO: It cannot be.
KATHARINA: Let me entreat you.
PETRUCHIO: I am content.
KATHARINA: Are you content to stay?
PETRUCHIO: I am content you shall entreat me stay,
PETRUCHIO: But yet not stay, entreat me how you can.
KATHARINA: Now, if you love me, stay.
PETRUCHIO: Grumio, my horse.
GRUMIO: Ay, sir, they be ready: the oats have eaten the horses.
KATHARINA: Nay, then,
KATHARINA: Do what thou canst, I will not go to-day,
KATHARINA: No, nor to-morrow, not till I please myself.
KATHARINA: The door is open, sir, there lies your way,
KATHARINA: You may be jogging whiles your boots are green,
KATHARINA: For me, I'll not be gone till I please myself:
KATHARINA: 'Tis like you'll prove a jolly surly groom,
KATHARINA: That take it on you at the first so roundly.
PETRUCHIO: O Kate, content thee, prithee, be not angry.
KATHARINA: I will be angry: what hast thou to do?
KATHARINA: Father, be quiet, he shall stay my leisure.
GREMIO: Ay, marry, sir, now it begins to work.
KATARINA: Gentlemen, forward to the bridal dinner:
KATARINA: I see a woman may be made a fool,
KATARINA: If she had not a spirit to resist.
PETRUCHIO: They shall go forward, Kate, at thy command.
PETRUCHIO: Obey the bride, you that attend on her,
PETRUCHIO: Go to the feast, revel and domineer,
PETRUCHIO: Carouse full measure to her maidenhead,
PETRUCHIO: Be mad and merry, or go hang yourselves:
PETRUCHIO: But for my bonny Kate, she must with me.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, look not big, nor stamp, nor stare, nor fret,
PETRUCHIO: I will be master of what is mine own:
PETRUCHIO: She is my goods, my chattels, she is my house,
PETRUCHIO: My household stuff, my field, my barn,
PETRUCHIO: My horse, my ox, my ass, my any thing,
PETRUCHIO: And here she stands, touch her whoever dare,
PETRUCHIO: I'll bring mine action on the proudest he
PETRUCHIO: That stops my way in Padua. Grumio,
PETRUCHIO: Draw forth thy weapon, we are beset with thieves,
PETRUCHIO: Rescue thy mistress, if thou be a man.
PETRUCHIO: Fear not, sweet wench, they shall not touch
PETRUCHIO: thee, Kate:
PETRUCHIO: I'll buckler thee against a million.
NARRATOR: Exeunt PETRUCHIO, KATHARINA, and GRUMIO
BAPTISTA: Nay, let them go, a couple of quiet ones.
GREMIO: Went they not quickly, I should die with laughing.
TRANIO: Of all mad matches never was the like.
LUCENTIO: Mistress, what's your opinion of your sister?
BIANCA: That, being mad herself, she's madly mated.
GREMIO: I warrant him, Petruchio is Kated.
BAPTISTA: Neighbours and friends, though bride and
BAPTISTA: bridegroom wants
BAPTISTA: For to supply the places at the table,
BAPTISTA: You know there wants no junkets at the feast.
BAPTISTA: Lucentio, you shall supply the bridegroom's place:
BAPTISTA: And let Bianca take her sister's room.
TRANIO: Shall sweet Bianca practise how to bride it?
BAPTISTA: She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let's go.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. PETRUCHIO'S country house.
NARRATOR: Enter GRUMIO
GRUMIO: Fie, fie on all tired jades, on all mad masters, and
GRUMIO: all foul ways! Was ever man so beaten? was ever
GRUMIO: man so rayed? was ever man so weary? I am sent
GRUMIO: before to make a fire, and they are coming after to
GRUMIO: warm them. Now, were not I a little pot and soon
GRUMIO: hot, my very lips might freeze to my teeth, my
GRUMIO: tongue to the roof of my mouth, my heart in my
GRUMIO: belly, ere I should come by a fire to thaw me: but
GRUMIO: I, with blowing the fire, shall warm myself, for,
GRUMIO: considering the weather, a taller man than I will
GRUMIO: take cold. Holla, ho! Curtis.
NARRATOR: Enter CURTIS
CURTIS: Who is that calls so coldly?
GRUMIO: A piece of ice: if thou doubt it, thou mayst slide
GRUMIO: from my shoulder to my heel with no greater a run
GRUMIO: but my head and my neck. A fire good Curtis.
CURTIS: Is my master and his wife coming, Grumio?
GRUMIO: O, ay, Curtis, ay: and therefore fire, fire, cast
GRUMIO: on no water.
CURTIS: Is she so hot a shrew as she's reported?
GRUMIO: She was, good Curtis, before this frost: but, thou
GRUMIO: knowest, winter tames man, woman and beast, for it
GRUMIO: hath tamed my old master and my new mistress and
GRUMIO: myself, fellow Curtis.
CURTIS: Away, you three-inch fool! I am no beast.
GRUMIO: Am I but three inches? why, thy horn is a foot, and
GRUMIO: so long am I at the least. But wilt thou make a
GRUMIO: fire, or shall I complain on thee to our mistress,
GRUMIO: whose hand, she being now at hand, thou shalt soon
GRUMIO: feel, to thy cold comfort, for being slow in thy hot office?
CURTIS: I prithee, good Grumio, tell me, how goes the world?
GRUMIO: A cold world, Curtis, in every office but thine, and
GRUMIO: therefore fire: do thy duty, and have thy duty, for
GRUMIO: my master and mistress are almost frozen to death.
CURTIS: There's fire ready, and therefore, good Grumio, the news.
GRUMIO: Why, 'Jack, boy! ho! boy!' and as much news as
GRUMIO: will thaw.
CURTIS: Come, you are so full of cony-catching!
GRUMIO: Why, therefore fire, for I have caught extreme cold.
GRUMIO: Where's the cook? is supper ready, the house
GRUMIO: trimmed, rushes strewed, cobwebs swept, the
GRUMIO: serving-men in their new fustian, their white
GRUMIO: stockings, and every officer his wedding-garment on?
GRUMIO: Be the jacks fair within, the jills fair without,
GRUMIO: the carpets laid, and every thing in order?
CURTIS: All ready, and therefore, I pray thee, news.
GRUMIO: First, know, my horse is tired, my master and
GRUMIO: mistress fallen out.
CURTIS: How?
GRUMIO: Out of their saddles into the dirt, and thereby
GRUMIO: hangs a tale.
CURTIS: Let's ha't, good Grumio.
GRUMIO: Lend thine ear.
CURTIS: Here.
GRUMIO: There.
NARRATOR: Strikes him
CURTIS: This is to feel a tale, not to hear a tale.
GRUMIO: And therefore 'tis called a sensible tale: and this
GRUMIO: cuff was but to knock at your ear, and beseech
GRUMIO: listening. Now I begin: Imprimis, we came down a
GRUMIO: foul hill, my master riding behind my mistress,--
CURTIS: Both of one horse?
GRUMIO: What's that to thee?
CURTIS: Why, a horse.
GRUMIO: Tell thou the tale: but hadst thou not crossed me,
GRUMIO: thou shouldst have heard how her horse fell and she
GRUMIO: under her horse, thou shouldst have heard in how
GRUMIO: miry a place, how she was bemoiled, how he left her
GRUMIO: with the horse upon her, how he beat me because
GRUMIO: her horse stumbled, how she waded through the dirt
GRUMIO: to pluck him off me, how he swore, how she prayed,
GRUMIO: that never prayed before, how I cried, how the
GRUMIO: horses ran away, how her bridle was burst, how I
GRUMIO: lost my crupper, with many things of worthy memory,
GRUMIO: which now shall die in oblivion and thou return
GRUMIO: unexperienced to thy grave.
CURTIS: By this reckoning he is more shrew than she.
GRUMIO: Ay, and that thou and the proudest of you all shall
GRUMIO: find when he comes home. But what talk I of this?
GRUMIO: Call forth Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Philip,
GRUMIO: Walter, Sugarsop and the rest: let their heads be
GRUMIO: sleekly combed their blue coats brushed and their
GRUMIO: garters of an indifferent knit: let them curtsy
GRUMIO: with their left legs and not presume to touch a hair
GRUMIO: of my master's horse-tail till they kiss their
GRUMIO: hands. Are they all ready?
CURTIS: They are.
GRUMIO: Call them forth.
CURTIS: Do you hear, ho? you must meet my master to
CURTIS: countenance my mistress.
GRUMIO: Why, she hath a face of her own.
CURTIS: Who knows not that?
GRUMIO: Thou, it seems, that calls for company to
GRUMIO: countenance her.
CURTIS: I call them forth to credit her.
GRUMIO: Why, she comes to borrow nothing of them.
NARRATOR: Enter four or five Serving-men
NATHANIEL: Welcome home, Grumio!
PHILIP: How now, Grumio!
JOSEPH: What, Grumio!
NICHOLAS: Fellow Grumio!
NATHANIEL: How now, old lad?
GRUMIO: Welcome, you,--how now, you,-- what, you,--fellow,
GRUMIO: you,--and thus much for greeting. Now, my spruce
GRUMIO: companions, is all ready, and all things neat?
NATHANIEL: All things is ready. How near is our master?
GRUMIO: E'en at hand, alighted by this, and therefore be
GRUMIO: not--Cock's passion, silence! I hear my master.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO and KATHARINA
PETRUCHIO: Where be these knaves? What, no man at door
PETRUCHIO: To hold my stirrup nor to take my horse!
PETRUCHIO: Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?
PETRUCHIO: ALL SERVING-MEN	Here, here, sir, here, sir.
PETRUCHIO: Here, sir! here, sir! here, sir! here, sir!
PETRUCHIO: You logger-headed and unpolish'd grooms!
PETRUCHIO: What, no attendance? no regard? no duty?
PETRUCHIO: Where is the foolish knave I sent before?
GRUMIO: Here, sir, as foolish as I was before.
PETRUCHIO: You peasant swain! you whoreson malt-horse drudge!
PETRUCHIO: Did I not bid thee meet me in the park,
PETRUCHIO: And bring along these rascal knaves with thee?
GRUMIO: Nathaniel's coat, sir, was not fully made,
GRUMIO: And Gabriel's pumps were all unpink'd i' the heel,
GRUMIO: There was no link to colour Peter's hat,
GRUMIO: And Walter's dagger was not come from sheathing:
GRUMIO: There were none fine but Adam, Ralph, and Gregory,
GRUMIO: The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly,
GRUMIO: Yet, as they are, here are they come to meet you.
PETRUCHIO: Go, rascals, go, and fetch my supper in.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Servants
NARRATOR: Singing
PETRUCHIO: Where is the life that late I led--
PETRUCHIO: Where are those--Sit down, Kate, and welcome.--
PETRUCHIO: Sound, sound, sound, sound!
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servants with supper
PETRUCHIO: Why, when, I say? Nay, good sweet Kate, be merry.
PETRUCHIO: Off with my boots, you rogues! you villains, when?
NARRATOR: Sings
PETRUCHIO: It was the friar of orders grey,
PETRUCHIO: As he forth walked on his way:--
PETRUCHIO: Out, you rogue! you pluck my foot awry:
PETRUCHIO: Take that, and mend the plucking off the other.
NARRATOR: Strikes him
PETRUCHIO: Be merry, Kate. Some water, here, what, ho!
PETRUCHIO: Where's my spaniel Troilus? Sirrah, get you hence,
PETRUCHIO: And bid my cousin Ferdinand come hither:
PETRUCHIO: One, Kate, that you must kiss, and be acquainted with.
PETRUCHIO: Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water?
NARRATOR: Enter one with water
PETRUCHIO: Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome heartily.
PETRUCHIO: You whoreson villain! will you let it fall?
NARRATOR: Strikes him
KATHARINA: Patience, I pray you, 'twas a fault unwilling.
PETRUCHIO: A whoreson beetle-headed, flap-ear'd knave!
PETRUCHIO: Come, Kate, sit down, I know you have a stomach.
PETRUCHIO: Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or else shall I?
PETRUCHIO: What's this? mutton?
First Servant: Ay.
PETRUCHIO: Who brought it?
PETER: I.
PETRUCHIO: 'Tis burnt, and so is all the meat.
PETRUCHIO: What dogs are these! Where is the rascal cook?
PETRUCHIO: How durst you, villains, bring it from the dresser,
PETRUCHIO: And serve it thus to me that love it not?
PETRUCHIO: Theretake it to you, trenchers, cups, and all,
PETRUCHIO: Throws the meat,  and c. about the stage
PETRUCHIO: You heedless joltheads and unmanner'd slaves!
PETRUCHIO: What, do you grumble? I'll be with you straight.
KATHARINA: I pray you, husband, be not so disquiet:
KATHARINA: The meat was well, if you were so contented.
PETRUCHIO: I tell thee, Kate, 'twas burnt and dried away,
PETRUCHIO: And I expressly am forbid to touch it,
PETRUCHIO: For it engenders choler, planteth anger,
PETRUCHIO: And better 'twere that both of us did fast,
PETRUCHIO: Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric,
PETRUCHIO: Than feed it with such over-roasted flesh.
PETRUCHIO: Be patient, to-morrow 't shall be mended,
PETRUCHIO: And, for this night, we'll fast for company:
PETRUCHIO: Come, I will bring thee to thy bridal chamber.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servants severally
NATHANIEL: Peter, didst ever see the like?
PETER: He kills her in her own humour.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CURTIS
GRUMIO: Where is he?
CURTIS: In her chamber, making a sermon of continency to her,
CURTIS: And rails, and swears, and rates, that she, poor soul,
CURTIS: Knows not which way to stand, to look, to speak,
CURTIS: And sits as one new-risen from a dream.
CURTIS: Away, away! for he is coming hither.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Re-enter PETRUCHIO
PETRUCHIO: Thus have I politicly begun my reign,
PETRUCHIO: And 'tis my hope to end successfully.
PETRUCHIO: My falcon now is sharp and passing empty,
PETRUCHIO: And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged,
PETRUCHIO: For then she never looks upon her lure.
PETRUCHIO: Another way I have to man my haggard,
PETRUCHIO: To make her come and know her keeper's call,
PETRUCHIO: That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites
PETRUCHIO: That bate and beat and will not be obedient.
PETRUCHIO: She eat no meat to-day, nor none shall eat,
PETRUCHIO: Last night she slept not, nor to-night she shall not,
PETRUCHIO: As with the meat, some undeserved fault
PETRUCHIO: I'll find about the making of the bed,
PETRUCHIO: And here I'll fling the pillow, there the bolster,
PETRUCHIO: This way the coverlet, another way the sheets:
PETRUCHIO: Ay, and amid this hurly I intend
PETRUCHIO: That all is done in reverend care of her,
PETRUCHIO: And in conclusion she shall watch all night:
PETRUCHIO: And if she chance to nod I'll rail and brawl
PETRUCHIO: And with the clamour keep her still awake.
PETRUCHIO: This is a way to kill a wife with kindness,
PETRUCHIO: And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour.
PETRUCHIO: He that knows better how to tame a shrew,
PETRUCHIO: Now let him speak: 'tis charity to show.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Padua. Before BAPTISTA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter TRANIO and HORTENSIO
TRANIO: Is't possible, friend Licio, that Mistress Bianca
TRANIO: Doth fancy any other but Lucentio?
TRANIO: I tell you, sir, she bears me fair in hand.
HORTENSIO: Sir, to satisfy you in what I have said,
HORTENSIO: Stand by and mark the manner of his teaching.
NARRATOR: Enter BIANCA and LUCENTIO
LUCENTIO: Now, mistress, profit you in what you read?
BIANCA: What, master, read you? first resolve me that.
LUCENTIO: I read that I profess, the Art to Love.
BIANCA: And may you prove, sir, master of your art!
LUCENTIO: While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of my heart!
HORTENSIO: Quick proceeders, marry! Now, tell me, I pray,
HORTENSIO: You that durst swear at your mistress Bianca
HORTENSIO: Loved none in the world so well as Lucentio.
TRANIO: O despiteful love! unconstant womankind!
TRANIO: I tell thee, Licio, this is wonderful.
HORTENSIO: Mistake no more: I am not Licio,
HORTENSIO: Nor a musician, as I seem to be,
HORTENSIO: But one that scorn to live in this disguise,
HORTENSIO: For such a one as leaves a gentleman,
HORTENSIO: And makes a god of such a cullion:
HORTENSIO: Know, sir, that I am call'd Hortensio.
TRANIO: Signior Hortensio, I have often heard
TRANIO: Of your entire affection to Bianca,
TRANIO: And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness,
TRANIO: I will with you, if you be so contented,
TRANIO: Forswear Bianca and her love for ever.
HORTENSIO: See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio,
HORTENSIO: Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow
HORTENSIO: Never to woo her no more, but do forswear her,
HORTENSIO: As one unworthy all the former favours
HORTENSIO: That I have fondly flatter'd her withal.
TRANIO: And here I take the unfeigned oath,
TRANIO: Never to marry with her though she would entreat:
TRANIO: Fie on her! see, how beastly she doth court him!
HORTENSIO: Would all the world but he had quite forsworn!
HORTENSIO: For me, that I may surely keep mine oath,
HORTENSIO: I will be married to a wealthy widow,
HORTENSIO: Ere three days pass, which hath as long loved me
HORTENSIO: As I have loved this proud disdainful haggard.
HORTENSIO: And so farewell, Signior Lucentio.
HORTENSIO: Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks,
HORTENSIO: Shall win my love: and so I take my leave,
HORTENSIO: In resolution as I swore before.
NARRATOR: Exit
TRANIO: Mistress Bianca, bless you with such grace
TRANIO: As 'longeth to a lover's blessed case!
TRANIO: Nay, I have ta'en you napping, gentle love,
TRANIO: And have forsworn you with Hortensio.
BIANCA: Tranio, you jest: but have you both forsworn me?
TRANIO: Mistress, we have.
LUCENTIO: Then we are rid of Licio.
TRANIO: I' faith, he'll have a lusty widow now,
TRANIO: That shall be wood and wedded in a day.
BIANCA: God give him joy!
TRANIO: Ay, and he'll tame her.
BIANCA: He says so, Tranio.
TRANIO: Faith, he is gone unto the taming-school.
BIANCA: The taming-school! what, is there such a place?
TRANIO: Ay, mistress, and Petruchio is the master,
TRANIO: That teacheth tricks eleven and twenty long,
TRANIO: To tame a shrew and charm her chattering tongue.
NARRATOR: Enter BIONDELLO
BIONDELLO: O master, master, I have watch'd so long
BIONDELLO: That I am dog-weary: but at last I spied
BIONDELLO: An ancient angel coming down the hill,
BIONDELLO: Will serve the turn.
TRANIO: What is he, Biondello?
BIONDELLO: Master, a mercatante, or a pedant,
BIONDELLO: I know not what, but format in apparel,
BIONDELLO: In gait and countenance surely like a father.
LUCENTIO: And what of him, Tranio?
TRANIO: If he be credulous and trust my tale,
TRANIO: I'll make him glad to seem Vincentio,
TRANIO: And give assurance to Baptista Minola,
TRANIO: As if he were the right Vincentio
TRANIO: Take in your love, and then let me alone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCENTIO and BIANCA
NARRATOR: Enter a Pedant
Pedant: God save you, sir!
TRANIO: And you, sir! you are welcome.
TRANIO: Travel you far on, or are you at the farthest?
Pedant: Sir, at the farthest for a week or two:
Pedant: But then up farther, and as for as Rome,
Pedant: And so to Tripoli, if God lend me life.
TRANIO: What countryman, I pray?
Pedant: Of Mantua.
TRANIO: Of Mantua, sir? marry, God forbid!
TRANIO: And come to Padua, careless of your life?
Pedant: My life, sir! how, I pray? for that goes hard.
TRANIO: 'Tis death for any one in Mantua
TRANIO: To come to Padua. Know you not the cause?
TRANIO: Your ships are stay'd at Venice, and the duke,
TRANIO: For private quarrel 'twixt your duke and him,
TRANIO: Hath publish'd and proclaim'd it openly:
TRANIO: 'Tis, marvel, but that you are but newly come,
TRANIO: You might have heard it else proclaim'd about.
Pedant: Alas! sir, it is worse for me than so,
Pedant: For I have bills for money by exchange
Pedant: From Florence and must here deliver them.
TRANIO: Well, sir, to do you courtesy,
TRANIO: This will I do, and this I will advise you:
TRANIO: First, tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?
Pedant: Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been,
Pedant: Pisa renowned for grave citizens.
TRANIO: Among them know you one Vincentio?
Pedant: I know him not, but I have heard of him,
Pedant: A merchant of incomparable wealth.
TRANIO: He is my father, sir, and, sooth to say,
TRANIO: In countenance somewhat doth resemble you.
BIONDELLO: [Aside]  As much as an apple doth an oyster,
BIONDELLO: and all one.
TRANIO: To save your life in this extremity,
TRANIO: This favour will I do you for his sake,
TRANIO: And think it not the worst of an your fortunes
TRANIO: That you are like to Sir Vincentio.
TRANIO: His name and credit shall you undertake,
TRANIO: And in my house you shall be friendly lodged:
TRANIO: Look that you take upon you as you should,
TRANIO: You understand me, sir: so shall you stay
TRANIO: Till you have done your business in the city:
TRANIO: If this be courtesy, sir, accept of it.
Pedant: O sir, I do, and will repute you ever
Pedant: The patron of my life and liberty.
TRANIO: Then go with me to make the matter good.
TRANIO: This, by the way, I let you understand,
TRANIO: my father is here look'd for every day,
TRANIO: To pass assurance of a dower in marriage
TRANIO: 'Twixt me and one Baptista's daughter here:
TRANIO: In all these circumstances I'll instruct you:
TRANIO: Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A room in PETRUCHIO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter KATHARINA and GRUMIO
GRUMIO: No, no, forsooth, I dare not for my life.
KATHARINA: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears:
KATHARINA: What, did he marry me to famish me?
KATHARINA: Beggars, that come unto my father's door,
KATHARINA: Upon entreaty have a present aims,
KATHARINA: If not, elsewhere they meet with charity:
KATHARINA: But I, who never knew how to entreat,
KATHARINA: Nor never needed that I should entreat,
KATHARINA: Am starved for meat, giddy for lack of sleep,
KATHARINA: With oath kept waking and with brawling fed:
KATHARINA: And that which spites me more than all these wants,
KATHARINA: He does it under name of perfect love,
KATHARINA: As who should say, if I should sleep or eat,
KATHARINA: 'Twere deadly sickness or else present death.
KATHARINA: I prithee go and get me some repast,
KATHARINA: I care not what, so it be wholesome food.
GRUMIO: What say you to a neat's foot?
KATHARINA: 'Tis passing good: I prithee let me have it.
GRUMIO: I fear it is too choleric a meat.
GRUMIO: How say you to a fat tripe finely broil'd?
KATHARINA: I like it well: good Grumio, fetch it me.
GRUMIO: I cannot tell, I fear 'tis choleric.
GRUMIO: What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?
KATHARINA: A dish that I do love to feed upon.
GRUMIO: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.
KATHARINA: Why then, the beef, and let the mustard rest.
GRUMIO: Nay then, I will not: you shall have the mustard,
GRUMIO: Or else you get no beef of Grumio.
KATHARINA: Then both, or one, or any thing thou wilt.
GRUMIO: Why then, the mustard without the beef.
KATHARINA: Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave,
NARRATOR: Beats him
KATHARINA: That feed'st me with the very name of meat:
KATHARINA: Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you,
KATHARINA: That triumph thus upon my misery!
KATHARINA: Go, get thee gone, I say.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO and HORTENSIO with meat
PETRUCHIO: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?
HORTENSIO: Mistress, what cheer?
KATHARINA: Faith, as cold as can be.
PETRUCHIO: Pluck up thy spirits, look cheerfully upon me.
PETRUCHIO: Here love, thou see'st how diligent I am
PETRUCHIO: To dress thy meat myself and bring it thee:
PETRUCHIO: I am sure, sweet Kate, this kindness merits thanks.
PETRUCHIO: What, not a word? Nay, then thou lovest it not,
PETRUCHIO: And all my pains is sorted to no proof.
PETRUCHIO: Here, take away this dish.
KATHARINA: I pray you, let it stand.
PETRUCHIO: The poorest service is repaid with thanks,
PETRUCHIO: And so shall mine, before you touch the meat.
KATHARINA: I thank you, sir.
HORTENSIO: Signior Petruchio, fie! you are to blame.
HORTENSIO: Come, mistress Kate, I'll bear you company.
PETRUCHIO: [Aside]  Eat it up all, Hortensio, if thou lovest me.
PETRUCHIO: Much good do it unto thy gentle heart!
PETRUCHIO: Kate, eat apace: and now, my honey love,
PETRUCHIO: Will we return unto thy father's house
PETRUCHIO: And revel it as bravely as the best,
PETRUCHIO: With silken coats and caps and golden rings,
PETRUCHIO: With ruffs and cuffs and fardingales and things,
PETRUCHIO: With scarfs and fans and double change of bravery,
PETRUCHIO: With amber bracelets, beads and all this knavery.
PETRUCHIO: What, hast thou dined? The tailor stays thy leisure,
PETRUCHIO: To deck thy body with his ruffling treasure.
NARRATOR: Enter Tailor
PETRUCHIO: Come, tailor, let us see these ornaments,
PETRUCHIO: Lay forth the gown.
NARRATOR: Enter Haberdasher
PETRUCHIO: What news with you, sir?
Haberdasher: Here is the cap your worship did bespeak.
PETRUCHIO: Why, this was moulded on a porringer,
PETRUCHIO: A velvet dish: fie, fie! 'tis lewd and filthy:
PETRUCHIO: Why, 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell,
PETRUCHIO: A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap:
PETRUCHIO: Away with it! come, let me have a bigger.
KATHARINA: I'll have no bigger: this doth fit the time,
KATHARINA: And gentlewomen wear such caps as these
PETRUCHIO: When you are gentle, you shall have one too,
PETRUCHIO: And not till then.
HORTENSIO: [Aside]  That will not be in haste.
KATHARINA: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak,
KATHARINA: And speak I will, I am no child, no babe:
KATHARINA: Your betters have endured me say my mind,
KATHARINA: And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
KATHARINA: My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,
KATHARINA: Or else my heart concealing it will break,
KATHARINA: And rather than it shall, I will be free
KATHARINA: Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.
PETRUCHIO: Why, thou say'st true, it is a paltry cap,
PETRUCHIO: A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie:
PETRUCHIO: I love thee well, in that thou likest it not.
KATHARINA: Love me or love me not, I like the cap,
KATHARINA: And it I will have, or I will have none.
NARRATOR: Exit Haberdasher
PETRUCHIO: Thy gown? why, ay: come, tailor, let us see't.
PETRUCHIO: O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here?
PETRUCHIO: What's this? a sleeve? 'tis like a demi-cannon:
PETRUCHIO: What, up and down, carved like an apple-tart?
PETRUCHIO: Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash,
PETRUCHIO: Like to a censer in a barber's shop:
PETRUCHIO: Why, what, i' devil's name, tailor, call'st thou this?
HORTENSIO: [Aside]  I see she's like to have neither cap nor gown.
Tailor: You bid me make it orderly and well,
Tailor: According to the fashion and the time.
PETRUCHIO: Marry, and did, but if you be remember'd,
PETRUCHIO: I did not bid you mar it to the time.
PETRUCHIO: Go, hop me over every kennel home,
PETRUCHIO: For you shall hop without my custom, sir:
PETRUCHIO: I'll none of it: hence! make your best of it.
KATHARINA: I never saw a better-fashion'd gown,
KATHARINA: More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable:
KATHARINA: Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.
PETRUCHIO: Why, true, he means to make a puppet of thee.
Tailor: She says your worship means to make
Tailor: a puppet of her.
PETRUCHIO: O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread,
PETRUCHIO: thou thimble,
PETRUCHIO: Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail!
PETRUCHIO: Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter-cricket thou!
PETRUCHIO: Braved in mine own house with a skein of thread?
PETRUCHIO: Away, thou rag, thou quantity, thou remnant,
PETRUCHIO: Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard
PETRUCHIO: As thou shalt think on prating whilst thou livest!
PETRUCHIO: I tell thee, I, that thou hast marr'd her gown.
Tailor: Your worship is deceived, the gown is made
Tailor: Just as my master had direction:
Tailor: Grumio gave order how it should be done.
GRUMIO: I gave him no order, I gave him the stuff.
Tailor: But how did you desire it should be made?
GRUMIO: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.
Tailor: But did you not request to have it cut?
GRUMIO: Thou hast faced many things.
Tailor: I have.
GRUMIO: Face not me: thou hast braved many men, brave not
GRUMIO: me, I will neither be faced nor braved. I say unto
GRUMIO: thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown, but I did
GRUMIO: not bid him cut it to pieces: ergo, thou liest.
Tailor: Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify
PETRUCHIO: Read it.
GRUMIO: The note lies in's throat, if he say I said so.
Tailor: [Reads]  'Imprimis, a loose-bodied gown:'
GRUMIO: Master, if ever I said loose-bodied gown, sew me in
GRUMIO: the skirts of it, and beat me to death with a bottom
GRUMIO: of brown thread: I said a gown.
PETRUCHIO: Proceed.
Tailor: [Reads]  'With a small compassed cape:'
GRUMIO: I confess the cape.
Tailor: [Reads]  'With a trunk sleeve:'
GRUMIO: I confess two sleeves.
Tailor: [Reads]  'The sleeves curiously cut.'
PETRUCHIO: Ay, there's the villany.
GRUMIO: Error i' the bill, sir, error i' the bill.
GRUMIO: I commanded the sleeves should be cut out and
GRUMIO: sewed up again, and that I'll prove upon thee,
GRUMIO: though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.
Tailor: This is true that I say: an I had thee
Tailor: in place where, thou shouldst know it.
GRUMIO: I am for thee straight: take thou the
GRUMIO: bill, give me thy mete-yard, and spare not me.
HORTENSIO: God-a-mercy, Grumio! then he shall have no odds.
PETRUCHIO: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.
GRUMIO: You are i' the right, sir: 'tis for my mistress.
PETRUCHIO: Go, take it up unto thy master's use.
GRUMIO: Villain, not for thy life: take up my mistress'
GRUMIO: gown for thy master's use!
PETRUCHIO: Why, sir, what's your conceit in that?
GRUMIO: O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for:
GRUMIO: Take up my mistress' gown to his master's use!
GRUMIO: O, fie, fie, fie!
PETRUCHIO: [Aside]  Hortensio, say thou wilt see the tailor paid.
PETRUCHIO: Go take it hence, be gone, and say no more.
HORTENSIO: Tailor, I'll pay thee for thy gown tomorrow:
HORTENSIO: Take no unkindness of his hasty words:
HORTENSIO: Away! I say, commend me to thy master.
NARRATOR: Exit Tailor
PETRUCHIO: Well, come, my Kate, we will unto your father's
PETRUCHIO: Even in these honest mean habiliments:
PETRUCHIO: Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor,
PETRUCHIO: For 'tis the mind that makes the body rich,
PETRUCHIO: And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds,
PETRUCHIO: So honour peereth in the meanest habit.
PETRUCHIO: What is the jay more precious than the lark,
PETRUCHIO: Because his fathers are more beautiful?
PETRUCHIO: Or is the adder better than the eel,
PETRUCHIO: Because his painted skin contents the eye?
PETRUCHIO: O, no, good Kate, neither art thou the worse
PETRUCHIO: For this poor furniture and mean array.
PETRUCHIO: if thou account'st it shame. lay it on me,
PETRUCHIO: And therefore frolic: we will hence forthwith,
PETRUCHIO: To feast and sport us at thy father's house.
PETRUCHIO: Go, call my men, and let us straight to him,
PETRUCHIO: And bring our horses unto Long-lane end,
PETRUCHIO: There will we mount, and thither walk on foot
PETRUCHIO: Let's see, I think 'tis now some seven o'clock,
PETRUCHIO: And well we may come there by dinner-time.
KATHARINA: I dare assure you, sir, 'tis almost two,
KATHARINA: And 'twill be supper-time ere you come there.
PETRUCHIO: It shall be seven ere I go to horse:
PETRUCHIO: Look, what I speak, or do, or think to do,
PETRUCHIO: You are still crossing it. Sirs, let't alone:
PETRUCHIO: I will not go to-day, and ere I do,
PETRUCHIO: It shall be what o'clock I say it is.
HORTENSIO: [Aside]  Why, so this gallant will command the sun.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Padua. Before BAPTISTA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter TRANIO, and the Pedant dressed like VINCENTIO
TRANIO: Sir, this is the house: please it you that I call?
Pedant: Ay, what else? and but I be deceived
Pedant: Signior Baptista may remember me,
Pedant: Near twenty years ago, in Genoa,
Pedant: Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.
TRANIO: 'Tis well, and hold your own, in any case,
TRANIO: With such austerity as 'longeth to a father.
Pedant: I warrant you.
NARRATOR: Enter BIONDELLO
Pedant: But, sir, here comes your boy,
Pedant: 'Twere good he were school'd.
TRANIO: Fear you not him. Sirrah Biondello,
TRANIO: Now do your duty throughly, I advise you:
TRANIO: Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.
BIONDELLO: Tut, fear not me.
TRANIO: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?
BIONDELLO: I told him that your father was at Venice,
BIONDELLO: And that you look'd for him this day in Padua.
TRANIO: Thou'rt a tall fellow: hold thee that to drink.
TRANIO: Here comes Baptista: set your countenance, sir.
NARRATOR: Enter BAPTISTA and LUCENTIO
TRANIO: Signior Baptista, you are happily met.
NARRATOR: To the Pedant
TRANIO: Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of:
TRANIO: I pray you stand good father to me now,
TRANIO: Give me Bianca for my patrimony.
Pedant: Soft son!
Pedant: Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua
Pedant: To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio
Pedant: Made me acquainted with a weighty cause
Pedant: Of love between your daughter and himself:
Pedant: And, for the good report I hear of you
Pedant: And for the love he beareth to your daughter
Pedant: And she to him, to stay him not too long,
Pedant: I am content, in a good father's care,
Pedant: To have him match'd, and if you please to like
Pedant: No worse than I, upon some agreement
Pedant: Me shall you find ready and willing
Pedant: With one consent to have her so bestow'd,
Pedant: For curious I cannot be with you,
Pedant: Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.
BAPTISTA: Sir, pardon me in what I have to say:
BAPTISTA: Your plainness and your shortness please me well.
BAPTISTA: Right true it is, your son Lucentio here
BAPTISTA: Doth love my daughter and she loveth him,
BAPTISTA: Or both dissemble deeply their affections:
BAPTISTA: And therefore, if you say no more than this,
BAPTISTA: That like a father you will deal with him
BAPTISTA: And pass my daughter a sufficient dower,
BAPTISTA: The match is made, and all is done:
BAPTISTA: Your son shall have my daughter with consent.
TRANIO: I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best
TRANIO: We be affied and such assurance ta'en
TRANIO: As shall with either part's agreement stand?
BAPTISTA: Not in my house, Lucentio, for, you know,
BAPTISTA: Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants:
BAPTISTA: Besides, old Gremio is hearkening still,
BAPTISTA: And happily we might be interrupted.
TRANIO: Then at my lodging, an it like you:
TRANIO: There doth my father lie, and there, this night,
TRANIO: We'll pass the business privately and well.
TRANIO: Send for your daughter by your servant here:
TRANIO: My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently.
TRANIO: The worst is this, that, at so slender warning,
TRANIO: You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.
BAPTISTA: It likes me well. Biondello, hie you home,
BAPTISTA: And bid Bianca make her ready straight,
BAPTISTA: And, if you will, tell what hath happened,
BAPTISTA: Lucentio's father is arrived in Padua,
BAPTISTA: And how she's like to be Lucentio's wife.
BIONDELLO: I pray the gods she may with all my heart!
TRANIO: Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone.
NARRATOR: Exit BIONDELLO
TRANIO: Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way?
TRANIO: Welcome! one mess is like to be your cheer:
TRANIO: Come, sir, we will better it in Pisa.
BAPTISTA: I follow you.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TRANIO, Pedant, and BAPTISTA
NARRATOR: Re-enter BIONDELLO
BIONDELLO: Cambio!
LUCENTIO: What sayest thou, Biondello?
BIONDELLO: You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?
LUCENTIO: Biondello, what of that?
BIONDELLO: Faith, nothing, but has left me here behind, to
BIONDELLO: expound the meaning or moral of his signs and tokens.
LUCENTIO: I pray thee, moralize them.
BIONDELLO: Then thus. Baptista is safe, talking with the
BIONDELLO: deceiving father of a deceitful son.
LUCENTIO: And what of him?
BIONDELLO: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.
LUCENTIO: And then?
BIONDELLO: The old priest of Saint Luke's church is at your
BIONDELLO: command at all hours.
LUCENTIO: And what of all this?
BIONDELLO: I cannot tell, expect they are busied about a
BIONDELLO: counterfeit assurance: take you assurance of her,
BIONDELLO: 'cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum:' to the
BIONDELLO: church, take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient
BIONDELLO: honest witnesses: If this be not that you look for,
BIONDELLO: I have no more to say, But bid Bianca farewell for
BIONDELLO: ever and a day.
LUCENTIO: Hearest thou, Biondello?
BIONDELLO: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench married in an
BIONDELLO: afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley to
BIONDELLO: stuff a rabbit, and so may you, sir: and so, adieu,
BIONDELLO: sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint
BIONDELLO: Luke's, to bid the priest be ready to come against
BIONDELLO: you come with your appendix.
NARRATOR: Exit
LUCENTIO: I may, and will, if she be so contented:
LUCENTIO: She will be pleased, then wherefore should I doubt?
LUCENTIO: Hap what hap may, I'll roundly go about her:
LUCENTIO: It shall go hard if Cambio go without her.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE V. A public road.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO, KATHARINA, HORTENSIO, and Servants
PETRUCHIO: Come on, i' God's name, once more toward our father's.
PETRUCHIO: Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!
KATHARINA: The moon! the sun: it is not moonlight now.
PETRUCHIO: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.
KATHARINA: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.
PETRUCHIO: Now, by my mother's son, and that's myself,
PETRUCHIO: It shall be moon, or star, or what I list,
PETRUCHIO: Or ere I journey to your father's house.
PETRUCHIO: Go on, and fetch our horses back again.
PETRUCHIO: Evermore cross'd and cross'd, nothing but cross'd!
HORTENSIO: Say as he says, or we shall never go.
KATHARINA: Forward, I pray, since we have come so far,
KATHARINA: And be it moon, or sun, or what you please:
KATHARINA: An if you please to call it a rush-candle,
KATHARINA: Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.
PETRUCHIO: I say it is the moon.
KATHARINA: I know it is the moon.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, then you lie: it is the blessed sun.
KATHARINA: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun:
KATHARINA: But sun it is not, when you say it is not,
KATHARINA: And the moon changes even as your mind.
KATHARINA: What you will have it named, even that it is,
KATHARINA: And so it shall be so for Katharina.
HORTENSIO: Petruchio, go thy ways, the field is won.
PETRUCHIO: Well, forward, forward! thus the bowl should run,
PETRUCHIO: And not unluckily against the bias.
PETRUCHIO: But, soft! company is coming here.
NARRATOR: Enter VINCENTIO
NARRATOR: To VINCENTIO
PETRUCHIO: Good morrow, gentle mistress: where away?
PETRUCHIO: Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too,
PETRUCHIO: Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman?
PETRUCHIO: Such war of white and red within her cheeks!
PETRUCHIO: What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty,
PETRUCHIO: As those two eyes become that heavenly face?
PETRUCHIO: Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee.
PETRUCHIO: Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.
HORTENSIO: A' will make the man mad, to make a woman of him.
KATHARINA: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet,
KATHARINA: Whither away, or where is thy abode?
KATHARINA: Happy the parents of so fair a child,
KATHARINA: Happier the man, whom favourable stars
KATHARINA: Allot thee for his lovely bed-fellow!
PETRUCHIO: Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad:
PETRUCHIO: This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither'd,
PETRUCHIO: And not a maiden, as thou say'st he is.
KATHARINA: Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes,
KATHARINA: That have been so bedazzled with the sun
KATHARINA: That everything I look on seemeth green:
KATHARINA: Now I perceive thou art a reverend father,
KATHARINA: Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.
PETRUCHIO: Do, good old grandsire, and withal make known
PETRUCHIO: Which way thou travellest: if along with us,
PETRUCHIO: We shall be joyful of thy company.
VINCENTIO: Fair sir, and you my merry mistress,
VINCENTIO: That with your strange encounter much amazed me,
VINCENTIO: My name is call'd Vincentio, my dwelling Pisa,
VINCENTIO: And bound I am to Padua, there to visit
VINCENTIO: A son of mine, which long I have not seen.
PETRUCHIO: What is his name?
VINCENTIO: Lucentio, gentle sir.
PETRUCHIO: Happily we met, the happier for thy son.
PETRUCHIO: And now by law, as well as reverend age,
PETRUCHIO: I may entitle thee my loving father:
PETRUCHIO: The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman,
PETRUCHIO: Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not,
PETRUCHIO: Nor be grieved: she is of good esteem,
PETRUCHIO: Her dowery wealthy, and of worthy birth,
PETRUCHIO: Beside, so qualified as may beseem
PETRUCHIO: The spouse of any noble gentleman.
PETRUCHIO: Let me embrace with old Vincentio,
PETRUCHIO: And wander we to see thy honest son,
PETRUCHIO: Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.
VINCENTIO: But is it true? or else is it your pleasure,
VINCENTIO: Like pleasant travellers, to break a jest
VINCENTIO: Upon the company you overtake?
HORTENSIO: I do assure thee, father, so it is.
PETRUCHIO: Come, go along, and see the truth hereof,
PETRUCHIO: For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but HORTENSIO
HORTENSIO: Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart.
HORTENSIO: Have to my widow! and if she be froward,
HORTENSIO: Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Padua. Before LUCENTIO'S house.
NARRATOR: GREMIO discovered. Enter behind BIONDELLO, LUCENTIO, and BIANCA
BIONDELLO: Softly and swiftly, sir, for the priest is ready.
LUCENTIO: I fly, Biondello: but they may chance to need thee
LUCENTIO: at home, therefore leave us.
BIONDELLO: Nay, faith, I'll see the church o' your back, and
BIONDELLO: then come back to my master's as soon as I can.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCENTIO, BIANCA, and BIONDELLO
GREMIO: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.
NARRATOR: Enter PETRUCHIO, KATHARINA, VINCENTIO, GRUMIO, with Attendants
PETRUCHIO: Sir, here's the door, this is Lucentio's house:
PETRUCHIO: My father's bears more toward the market-place,
PETRUCHIO: Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.
VINCENTIO: You shall not choose but drink before you go:
VINCENTIO: I think I shall command your welcome here,
VINCENTIO: And, by all likelihood, some cheer is toward.
NARRATOR: Knocks
GREMIO: They're busy within, you were best knock louder.
NARRATOR: Pedant looks out of the window
Pedant: What's he that knocks as he would beat down the gate?
VINCENTIO: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?
Pedant: He's within, sir, but not to be spoken withal.
VINCENTIO: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two, to
VINCENTIO: make merry withal?
Pedant: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself: he shall
Pedant: need none, so long as I live.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, I told you your son was well beloved in Padua.
PETRUCHIO: Do you hear, sir? To leave frivolous circumstances,
PETRUCHIO: I pray you, tell Signior Lucentio that his father is
PETRUCHIO: come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with him.
Pedant: Thou liest: his father is come from Padua and here
Pedant: looking out at the window.
VINCENTIO: Art thou his father?
Pedant: Ay, sir, so his mother says, if I may believe her.
PETRUCHIO: [To VINCENTIO]  Why, how now, gentleman! why, this
PETRUCHIO: is flat knavery, to take upon you another man's name.
Pedant: Lay hands on the villain: I believe a' means to
Pedant: cozen somebody in this city under my countenance.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BIONDELLO
BIONDELLO: I have seen them in the church together: God send
BIONDELLO: 'em good shipping! But who is here? mine old
BIONDELLO: master Vincentio! now we are undone and brought to nothing.
VINCENTIO: [Seeing BIONDELLO]
VINCENTIO: Come hither, crack-hemp.
BIONDELLO: Hope I may choose, sir.
VINCENTIO: Come hither, you rogue. What, have you forgot me?
BIONDELLO: Forgot you! no, sir: I could not forget you, for I
BIONDELLO: never saw you before in all my life.
VINCENTIO: What, you notorious villain, didst thou never see
VINCENTIO: thy master's father, Vincentio?
BIONDELLO: What, my old worshipful old master? yes, marry, sir:
BIONDELLO: see where he looks out of the window.
VINCENTIO: Is't so, indeed.
NARRATOR: Beats BIONDELLO
BIONDELLO: Help, help, help! here's a madman will murder me.
NARRATOR: Exit
Pedant: Help, son! help, Signior Baptista!
NARRATOR: Exit from above
PETRUCHIO: Prithee, Kate, let's stand aside and see the end of
PETRUCHIO: this controversy.
NARRATOR: They retire
NARRATOR: Re-enter Pedant below, TRANIO, BAPTISTA, and Servants
TRANIO: Sir, what are you that offer to beat my servant?
VINCENTIO: What am I, sir! nay, what are you, sir? O immortal
VINCENTIO: gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet! a velvet
VINCENTIO: hose! a scarlet cloak! and a copatain hat! O, I
VINCENTIO: am undone! I am undone! while I play the good
VINCENTIO: husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at
VINCENTIO: the university.
TRANIO: How now! what's the matter?
BAPTISTA: What, is the man lunatic?
TRANIO: Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman by your
TRANIO: habit, but your words show you a madman. Why, sir,
TRANIO: what 'cerns it you if I wear pearl and gold? I
TRANIO: thank my good father, I am able to maintain it.
VINCENTIO: Thy father! O villain! he is a sailmaker in Bergamo.
BAPTISTA: You mistake, sir, you mistake, sir. Pray, what do
BAPTISTA: you think is his name?
VINCENTIO: His name! as if I knew not his name: I have brought
VINCENTIO: him up ever since he was three years old, and his
VINCENTIO: name is Tranio.
Pedant: Away, away, mad ass! his name is Lucentio and he is
Pedant: mine only son, and heir to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.
VINCENTIO: Lucentio! O, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold
VINCENTIO: on him, I charge you, in the duke's name. O, my
VINCENTIO: son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, where is my son Lucentio?
TRANIO: Call forth an officer.
NARRATOR: Enter one with an Officer
TRANIO: Carry this mad knave to the gaol. Father Baptista,
TRANIO: I charge you see that he be forthcoming.
VINCENTIO: Carry me to the gaol!
GREMIO: Stay, officer: he shall not go to prison.
BAPTISTA: Talk not, Signior Gremio: I say he shall go to prison.
GREMIO: Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be
GREMIO: cony-catched in this business: I dare swear this
GREMIO: is the right Vincentio.
Pedant: Swear, if thou darest.
GREMIO: Nay, I dare not swear it.
TRANIO: Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.
GREMIO: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.
BAPTISTA: Away with the dotard! to the gaol with him!
VINCENTIO: Thus strangers may be hailed and abused: O
VINCENTIO: monstrous villain!
NARRATOR: Re-enter BIONDELLO, with LUCENTIO and BIANCA
BIONDELLO: O! we are spoiled and--yonder he is: deny him,
BIONDELLO: forswear him, or else we are all undone.
LUCENTIO: [Kneeling]  Pardon, sweet father.
VINCENTIO: Lives my sweet son?
NARRATOR: Exeunt BIONDELLO, TRANIO, and Pedant, as fast as may be
BIANCA: Pardon, dear father.
BAPTISTA: How hast thou offended?
BAPTISTA: Where is Lucentio?
LUCENTIO: Here's Lucentio,
LUCENTIO: Right son to the right Vincentio,
LUCENTIO: That have by marriage made thy daughter mine,
LUCENTIO: While counterfeit supposes bleared thine eyne.
GREMIO: Here's packing, with a witness to deceive us all!
VINCENTIO: Where is that damned villain Tranio,
VINCENTIO: That faced and braved me in this matter so?
BAPTISTA: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?
BIANCA: Cambio is changed into Lucentio.
LUCENTIO: Love wrought these miracles. Bianca's love
LUCENTIO: Made me exchange my state with Tranio,
LUCENTIO: While he did bear my countenance in the town,
LUCENTIO: And happily I have arrived at the last
LUCENTIO: Unto the wished haven of my bliss.
LUCENTIO: What Tranio did, myself enforced him to,
LUCENTIO: Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.
VINCENTIO: I'll slit the villain's nose, that would have sent
VINCENTIO: me to the gaol.
BAPTISTA: But do you hear, sir? have you married my daughter
BAPTISTA: without asking my good will?
VINCENTIO: Fear not, Baptista, we will content you, go to: but
VINCENTIO: I will in, to be revenged for this villany.
NARRATOR: Exit
BAPTISTA: And I, to sound the depth of this knavery.
NARRATOR: Exit
LUCENTIO: Look not pale, Bianca, thy father will not frown.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCENTIO and BIANCA
GREMIO: My cake is dough, but I'll in among the rest,
GREMIO: Out of hope of all, but my share of the feast.
NARRATOR: Exit
KATHARINA: Husband, let's follow, to see the end of this ado.
PETRUCHIO: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.
KATHARINA: What, in the midst of the street?
PETRUCHIO: What, art thou ashamed of me?
KATHARINA: No, sir, God forbid, but ashamed to kiss.
PETRUCHIO: Why, then let's home again. Come, sirrah, let's away.
KATHARINA: Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay.
PETRUCHIO: Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate:
PETRUCHIO: Better once than never, for never too late.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Padua. LUCENTIO'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter BAPTISTA, VINCENTIO, GREMIO, the Pedant,  LUCENTIO, BIANCA, PETRUCHIO, KATHARINA, HORTENSIO,  and Widow, TRANIO, BIONDELLO, and GRUMIO the Serving-men with Tranio bringing in a banquet
LUCENTIO: At last, though long, our jarring notes agree:
LUCENTIO: And time it is, when raging war is done,
LUCENTIO: To smile at scapes and perils overblown.
LUCENTIO: My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome,
LUCENTIO: While I with self-same kindness welcome thine.
LUCENTIO: Brother Petruchio, sister Katharina,
LUCENTIO: And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow,
LUCENTIO: Feast with the best, and welcome to my house:
LUCENTIO: My banquet is to close our stomachs up,
LUCENTIO: After our great good cheer. Pray you, sit down,
LUCENTIO: For now we sit to chat as well as eat.
PETRUCHIO: Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!
BAPTISTA: Padua affords this kindness, son Petruchio.
PETRUCHIO: Padua affords nothing but what is kind.
HORTENSIO: For both our sakes, I would that word were true.
PETRUCHIO: Now, for my life, Hortensio fears his widow.
Widow: Then never trust me, if I be afeard.
PETRUCHIO: You are very sensible, and yet you miss my sense:
PETRUCHIO: I mean, Hortensio is afeard of you.
Widow: He that is giddy thinks the world turns round.
PETRUCHIO: Roundly replied.
KATHARINA: Mistress, how mean you that?
Widow: Thus I conceive by him.
PETRUCHIO: Conceives by me! How likes Hortensio that?
HORTENSIO: My widow says, thus she conceives her tale.
PETRUCHIO: Very well mended. Kiss him for that, good widow.
KATHARINA: 'He that is giddy thinks the world turns round:'
KATHARINA: I pray you, tell me what you meant by that.
Widow: Your husband, being troubled with a shrew,
Widow: Measures my husband's sorrow by his woe:
Widow: And now you know my meaning,
KATHARINA: A very mean meaning.
Widow: Right, I mean you.
KATHARINA: And I am mean indeed, respecting you.
PETRUCHIO: To her, Kate!
HORTENSIO: To her, widow!
PETRUCHIO: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.
HORTENSIO: That's my office.
PETRUCHIO: Spoke like an officer, ha' to thee, lad!
NARRATOR: Drinks to HORTENSIO
BAPTISTA: How likes Gremio these quick-witted folks?
GREMIO: Believe me, sir, they butt together well.
BIANCA: Head, and butt! an hasty-witted body
BIANCA: Would say your head and butt were head and horn.
VINCENTIO: Ay, mistress bride, hath that awaken'd you?
BIANCA: Ay, but not frighted me, therefore I'll sleep again.
PETRUCHIO: Nay, that you shall not: since you have begun,
PETRUCHIO: Have at you for a bitter jest or two!
BIANCA: Am I your bird? I mean to shift my bush,
BIANCA: And then pursue me as you draw your bow.
BIANCA: You are welcome all.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BIANCA, KATHARINA, and Widow
PETRUCHIO: She hath prevented me. Here, Signior Tranio.
PETRUCHIO: This bird you aim'd at, though you hit her not,
PETRUCHIO: Therefore a health to all that shot and miss'd.
TRANIO: O, sir, Lucentio slipp'd me like his greyhound,
TRANIO: Which runs himself and catches for his master.
PETRUCHIO: A good swift simile, but something currish.
TRANIO: 'Tis well, sir, that you hunted for yourself:
TRANIO: 'Tis thought your deer does hold you at a bay.
BAPTISTA: O ho, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.
LUCENTIO: I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.
HORTENSIO: Confess, confess, hath he not hit you here?
PETRUCHIO: A' has a little gall'd me, I confess,
PETRUCHIO: And, as the jest did glance away from me,
PETRUCHIO: 'Tis ten to one it maim'd you two outright.
BAPTISTA: Now, in good sadness, son Petruchio,
BAPTISTA: I think thou hast the veriest shrew of all.
PETRUCHIO: Well, I say no: and therefore for assurance
PETRUCHIO: Let's each one send unto his wife,
PETRUCHIO: And he whose wife is most obedient
PETRUCHIO: To come at first when he doth send for her,
PETRUCHIO: Shall win the wager which we will propose.
HORTENSIO: Content. What is the wager?
LUCENTIO: Twenty crowns.
PETRUCHIO: Twenty crowns!
PETRUCHIO: I'll venture so much of my hawk or hound,
PETRUCHIO: But twenty times so much upon my wife.
LUCENTIO: A hundred then.
HORTENSIO: Content.
PETRUCHIO: A match! 'tis done.
HORTENSIO: Who shall begin?
LUCENTIO: That will I.
LUCENTIO: Go, Biondello, bid your mistress come to me.
BIONDELLO: I go.
NARRATOR: Exit
BAPTISTA: Son, I'll be your half, Bianca comes.
LUCENTIO: I'll have no halves, I'll bear it all myself.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BIONDELLO
LUCENTIO: How now! what news?
BIONDELLO: Sir, my mistress sends you word
BIONDELLO: That she is busy and she cannot come.
PETRUCHIO: How! she is busy and she cannot come!
PETRUCHIO: Is that an answer?
GREMIO: Ay, and a kind one too:
GREMIO: Pray God, sir, your wife send you not a worse.
PETRUCHIO: I hope better.
HORTENSIO: Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife
HORTENSIO: To come to me forthwith.
NARRATOR: Exit BIONDELLO
PETRUCHIO: O, ho! entreat her!
PETRUCHIO: Nay, then she must needs come.
HORTENSIO: I am afraid, sir,
HORTENSIO: Do what you can, yours will not be entreated.
NARRATOR: Re-enter BIONDELLO
HORTENSIO: Now, where's my wife?
BIONDELLO: She says you have some goodly jest in hand:
BIONDELLO: She will not come: she bids you come to her.
PETRUCHIO: Worse and worse, she will not come! O vile,
PETRUCHIO: Intolerable, not to be endured!
PETRUCHIO: Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress,
PETRUCHIO: Say, I command her to come to me.
