PROSPERO: And promise you calm seas, auspicious gales
PROSPERO: And sail so expeditious that shall catch
PROSPERO: Your royal fleet far off.
NARRATOR: Aside to ARIEL
PROSPERO: My Ariel, chick,
PROSPERO: That is thy charge: then to the elements
PROSPERO: Be free, and fare thou well! Please you, draw near.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
PROSPERO: EPILOGUE
PROSPERO: SPOKEN BY PROSPERO
PROSPERO: Now my charms are all o'erthrown,
PROSPERO: And what strength I have's mine own,
PROSPERO: Which is most faint: now, 'tis true,
PROSPERO: I must be here confined by you,
PROSPERO: Or sent to Naples. Let me not,
PROSPERO: Since I have my dukedom got
PROSPERO: And pardon'd the deceiver, dwell
PROSPERO: In this bare island by your spell,
PROSPERO: But release me from my bands
PROSPERO: With the help of your good hands:
PROSPERO: Gentle breath of yours my sails
PROSPERO: Must fill, or else my project fails,
PROSPERO: Which was to please. Now I want
PROSPERO: Spirits to enforce, art to enchant,
PROSPERO: And my ending is despair,
PROSPERO: Unless I be relieved by prayer,
PROSPERO: Which pierces so that it assaults
PROSPERO: Mercy itself and frees all faults.
PROSPERO: As you from crimes would pardon'd be,
PROSPERO: Let your indulgence set me free.
''' PLAY: Timon of Athens '''
PROSPERO: ACT I
PROSPERO: SCENE I. Athens. A hall in Timon's house.
NARRATOR: Enter Poet, Painter, Jeweller, Merchant, and others, at several doors
Poet: Good day, sir.
Painter: I am glad you're well.
Poet: I have not seen you long: how goes the world?
Painter: It wears, sir, as it grows.
Poet: Ay, that's well known:
Poet: But what particular rarity? what strange,
Poet: Which manifold record not matches? See,
Poet: Magic of bounty! all these spirits thy power
Poet: Hath conjured to attend. I know the merchant.
Painter: I know them both, th' other's a jeweller.
Merchant: O, 'tis a worthy lord.
Jeweller: Nay, that's most fix'd.
Merchant: A most incomparable man, breathed, as it were,
Merchant: To an untirable and continuate goodness:
Merchant: He passes.
Merchant: Jeweller:	I have a jewel here--
Merchant: O, pray, let's see't: for the Lord Timon, sir?
Merchant: Jeweller:	If he will touch the estimate: but, for that--
Poet: [Reciting to himself]  'When we for recompense have
Poet: praised the vile,
Poet: It stains the glory in that happy verse
Poet: Which aptly sings the good.'
Merchant: 'Tis a good form.
NARRATOR: Looking at the jewel
Jeweller: And rich: here is a water, look ye.
Painter: You are rapt, sir, in some work, some dedication
Painter: To the great lord.
Poet: A thing slipp'd idly from me.
Poet: Our poesy is as a gum, which oozes
Poet: From whence 'tis nourish'd: the fire i' the flint
Poet: Shows not till it be struck, our gentle flame
Poet: Provokes itself and like the current flies
Poet: Each bound it chafes. What have you there?
Painter: A picture, sir. When comes your book forth?
Poet: Upon the heels of my presentment, sir.
Poet: Let's see your piece.
Painter: 'Tis a good piece.
Poet: So 'tis: this comes off well and excellent.
Painter: Indifferent.
Poet: Admirable: how this grace
Poet: Speaks his own standing! what a mental power
Poet: This eye shoots forth! how big imagination
Poet: Moves in this lip! to the dumbness of the gesture
Poet: One might interpret.
Painter: It is a pretty mocking of the life.
Painter: Here is a touch, is't good?
Poet: I will say of it,
Poet: It tutors nature: artificial strife
Poet: Lives in these touches, livelier than life.
NARRATOR: Enter certain Senators, and pass over
Painter: How this lord is follow'd!
Poet: The senators of Athens: happy man!
Painter: Look, more!
Poet: You see this confluence, this great flood
Poet: of visitors.
Poet: I have, in this rough work, shaped out a man,
Poet: Whom this beneath world doth embrace and hug
Poet: With amplest entertainment: my free drift
Poet: Halts not particularly, but moves itself
Poet: In a wide sea of wax: no levell'd malice
Poet: Infects one comma in the course I hold,
Poet: But flies an eagle flight, bold and forth on,
Poet: Leaving no tract behind.
Painter: How shall I understand you?
Poet: I will unbolt to you.
Poet: You see how all conditions, how all minds,
Poet: As well of glib and slippery creatures as
Poet: Of grave and austere quality, tender down
Poet: Their services to Lord Timon: his large fortune
Poet: Upon his good and gracious nature hanging
Poet: Subdues and properties to his love and tendance
Poet: All sorts of hearts, yea, from the glass-faced flatterer
Poet: To Apemantus, that few things loves better
Poet: Than to abhor himself: even he drops down
Poet: The knee before him, and returns in peace
Poet: Most rich in Timon's nod.
Painter: I saw them speak together.
Poet: Sir, I have upon a high and pleasant hill
Poet: Feign'd Fortune to be throned: the base o' the mount
Poet: Is rank'd with all deserts, all kind of natures,
Poet: That labour on the bosom of this sphere
Poet: To propagate their states: amongst them all,
Poet: Whose eyes are on this sovereign lady fix'd,
Poet: One do I personate of Lord Timon's frame,
Poet: Whom Fortune with her ivory hand wafts to her,
Poet: Whose present grace to present slaves and servants
Poet: Translates his rivals.
Painter: 'Tis conceived to scope.
Painter: This throne, this Fortune, and this hill, methinks,
Painter: With one man beckon'd from the rest below,
Painter: Bowing his head against the sleepy mount
Painter: To climb his happiness, would be well express'd
Painter: In our condition.
Poet: Nay, sir, but hear me on.
Poet: All those which were his fellows but of late,
Poet: Some better than his value, on the moment
Poet: Follow his strides, his lobbies fill with tendance,
Poet: Rain sacrificial whisperings in his ear,
Poet: Make sacred even his stirrup, and through him
Poet: Drink the free air.
Painter: Ay, marry, what of these?
Poet: When Fortune in her shift and change of mood
Poet: Spurns down her late beloved, all his dependants
Poet: Which labour'd after him to the mountain's top
Poet: Even on their knees and hands, let him slip down,
Poet: Not one accompanying his declining foot.
Painter: 'Tis common:
Painter: A thousand moral paintings I can show
Painter: That shall demonstrate these quick blows of Fortune's
Painter: More pregnantly than words. Yet you do well
Painter: To show Lord Timon that mean eyes have seen
Painter: The foot above the head.
Painter: Trumpets sound. Enter TIMON, addressing himself  courteously to every suitor, a Messenger from  VENTIDIUS talking with him, LUCILIUS and other servants following
TIMON: Imprison'd is he, say you?
Messenger: Ay, my good lord: five talents is his debt,
Messenger: His means most short, his creditors most strait:
Messenger: Your honourable letter he desires
Messenger: To those have shut him up, which failing,
Messenger: Periods his comfort.
TIMON: Noble Ventidius! Well,
TIMON: I am not of that feather to shake off
TIMON: My friend when he must need me. I do know him
TIMON: A gentleman that well deserves a help:
TIMON: Which he shall have: I'll pay the debt,
TIMON: and free him.
Messenger: Your lordship ever binds him.
TIMON: Commend me to him: I will send his ransom,
TIMON: And being enfranchised, bid him come to me.
TIMON: 'Tis not enough to help the feeble up,

Messenger: All happiness to your honour!

NARRATOR: Enter an old Athenian

TIMON: Freely, good father.

TIMON: I have so: what of him?
Old Athenian: Most noble Timon, call the man before thee.
TIMON: Attends he here, or no? Lucilius!
LUCILIUS: Here, at your lordship's service.

Old Athenian: By night frequents my house. I am a man
Old Athenian: That from my first have been inclined to thrift,
Old Athenian: And my estate deserves an heir more raised
Old Athenian: Than one which holds a trencher.

Old Athenian: Join with me to forbid him her resort,
Old Athenian: Myself have spoke in vain.

Old Athenian: Therefore he will be, Timon:
Old Athenian: His honesty rewards him in itself,

TIMON: Does she love him?

Old Athenian: Our own precedent passions do instruct us
Old Athenian: What levity's in youth.

TIMON: This gentleman of mine hath served me long:
TIMON: To build his fortune I will strain a little,

TIMON: What you bestow, in him I'll counterpoise,
TIMON: And make him weigh with her.
Old Athenian: Most noble lord,

APEMANTUS: he's but a filthy piece of work.

APEMANTUS: No, I eat not lords.
TIMON: An thou shouldst, thou 'ldst anger ladies.
APEMANTUS: O, they eat lords, so they come by great bellies.
TIMON: That's a lascivious apprehension.
APEMANTUS: So thou apprehendest it: take it for thy labour.

APEMANTUS: Not so well as plain-dealing, which will not cost a
APEMANTUS: man a doit.
TIMON: What dost thou think 'tis worth?
APEMANTUS: Not worth my thinking. How now, poet!
Poet: How now, philosopher!
APEMANTUS: Thou liest.
Poet: Art not one?
APEMANTUS: Yes.
Poet: Then I lie not.
APEMANTUS: Art not a poet?
Poet: Yes.
APEMANTUS: Then thou liest: look in thy last work, where thou
APEMANTUS: hast feigned him a worthy fellow.

APEMANTUS: labour: he that loves to be flattered is worthy o'
APEMANTUS: the flatterer. Heavens, that I were a lord!

APEMANTUS: E'en as Apemantus does now, hate a lord with my heart.
TIMON: What, thyself?
APEMANTUS: Ay.
TIMON: Wherefore?
APEMANTUS: That I had no angry wit to be a lord.
APEMANTUS: Art not thou a merchant?
Merchant: Ay, Apemantus.
APEMANTUS: Traffic confound thee, if the gods will not!
Merchant: If traffic do it, the gods do it.
APEMANTUS: Traffic's thy god, and thy god confound thee!

TIMON: Ladies, there is an idle banquet attends you:
TIMON: Please you to dispose yourselves.
All Ladies: Most thankfully, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Cupid and Ladies
TIMON: Flavius.
FLAVIUS: My lord?
TIMON: The little casket bring me hither.
FLAVIUS: Yes, my lord. More jewels yet!
FLAVIUS: There is no crossing him in 's humour,
NARRATOR: Aside
FLAVIUS: Else I should tell him,--well, i' faith I should,
FLAVIUS: When all's spent, he 'ld be cross'd then, an he could.
FLAVIUS: 'Tis pity bounty had not eyes behind,
FLAVIUS: That man might ne'er be wretched for his mind.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Lord: Where be our men?
Servant: Here, my lord, in readiness.
Second Lord: Our horses!
NARRATOR: Re-enter FLAVIUS, with the casket
TIMON: O my friends,
TIMON: I have one word to say to you: look you, my good lord,
TIMON: I must entreat you, honour me so much
TIMON: As to advance this jewel, accept it and wear it,
TIMON: Kind my lord.
First Lord: I am so far already in your gifts,--
All: So are we all.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
Servant: My lord, there are certain nobles of the senate
Servant: Newly alighted, and come to visit you.
TIMON: They are fairly welcome.
FLAVIUS: I beseech your honour,
FLAVIUS: Vouchsafe me a word, it does concern you near.
TIMON: Near! why then, another time I'll hear thee:
TIMON: I prithee, let's be provided to show them
TIMON: entertainment.
FLAVIUS: [Aside]  I scarce know how.
NARRATOR: Enter a Second Servant
Second Servant: May it please your honour, Lord Lucius,
Second Servant: Out of his free love, hath presented to you
Second Servant: Four milk-white horses, trapp'd in silver.
TIMON: I shall accept them fairly, let the presents
TIMON: Be worthily entertain'd.
NARRATOR: Enter a third Servant
TIMON: How now! what news?
Third Servant: Please you, my lord, that honourable
Third Servant: gentleman, Lord Lucullus, entreats your company
Third Servant: to-morrow to hunt with him, and has sent your honour
Third Servant: two brace of greyhounds.
TIMON: I'll hunt with him, and let them be received,
TIMON: Not without fair reward.
FLAVIUS: [Aside]                What will this come to?
FLAVIUS: He commands us to provide, and give great gifts,
FLAVIUS: And all out of an empty coffer:
FLAVIUS: Nor will he know his purse, or yield me this,
FLAVIUS: To show him what a beggar his heart is,
FLAVIUS: Being of no power to make his wishes good:
FLAVIUS: His promises fly so beyond his state
FLAVIUS: That what he speaks is all in debt, he owes
FLAVIUS: For every word: he is so kind that he now
FLAVIUS: Pays interest for 't, his land's put to their books.
FLAVIUS: Well, would I were gently put out of office
FLAVIUS: Before I were forced out!
FLAVIUS: Happier is he that has no friend to feed
FLAVIUS: Than such that do e'en enemies exceed.
FLAVIUS: I bleed inwardly for my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
TIMON: You do yourselves
TIMON: Much wrong, you bate too much of your own merits:
TIMON: Here, my lord, a trifle of our love.
Second Lord: With more than common thanks I will receive it.
Third Lord: O, he's the very soul of bounty!
TIMON: And now I remember, my lord, you gave
TIMON: Good words the other day of a bay courser
TIMON: I rode on: it is yours, because you liked it.
Second Lord: O, I beseech you, pardon me, my lord, in that.
TIMON: You may take my word, my lord, I know, no man
TIMON: Can justly praise but what he does affect:
TIMON: I weigh my friend's affection with mine own,
TIMON: I'll tell you true. I'll call to you.
All Lords: O, none so welcome.
TIMON: I take all and your several visitations
TIMON: So kind to heart, 'tis not enough to give,
TIMON: Methinks, I could deal kingdoms to my friends,
TIMON: And ne'er be weary. Alcibiades,
TIMON: Thou art a soldier, therefore seldom rich,
TIMON: It comes in charity to thee: for all thy living
TIMON: Is 'mongst the dead, and all the lands thou hast
TIMON: Lie in a pitch'd field.
ALCIBIADES: Ay, defiled land, my lord.
First Lord: We are so virtuously bound--
TIMON: And so
TIMON: Am I to you.
Second Lord: So infinitely endear'd--
TIMON: All to you. Lights, more lights!
First Lord: The best of happiness,
First Lord: Honour and fortunes, keep with you, Lord Timon!
TIMON: Ready for his friends.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but APEMANTUS and TIMON
APEMANTUS: What a coil's here!
APEMANTUS: Serving of becks and jutting-out of bums!
APEMANTUS: I doubt whether their legs be worth the sums
APEMANTUS: That are given for 'em. Friendship's full of dregs:
APEMANTUS: Methinks, false hearts should never have sound legs,
APEMANTUS: Thus honest fools lay out their wealth on court'sies.
TIMON: Now, Apemantus, if thou wert not sullen, I would be
TIMON: good to thee.
APEMANTUS: No, I'll nothing: for if I should be bribed too,
APEMANTUS: there would be none left to rail upon thee, and then
APEMANTUS: thou wouldst sin the faster. Thou givest so long,
APEMANTUS: Timon, I fear me thou wilt give away thyself in
APEMANTUS: paper shortly: what need these feasts, pomps and
APEMANTUS: vain-glories?
TIMON: Nay, an you begin to rail on society once, I am
TIMON: sworn not to give regard to you. Farewell, and come
TIMON: with better music.
NARRATOR: Exit
APEMANTUS: So:
APEMANTUS: Thou wilt not hear me now, thou shalt not then:
APEMANTUS: I'll lock thy heaven from thee.
APEMANTUS: O, that men's ears should be
APEMANTUS: To counsel deaf, but not to flattery!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A Senator's house.
NARRATOR: Enter Senator, with papers in his hand
Senator: And late, five thousand: to Varro and to Isidore
Senator: He owes nine thousand, besides my former sum,
Senator: Which makes it five and twenty. Still in motion
Senator: Of raging waste? It cannot hold, it will not.
Senator: If I want gold, steal but a beggar's dog,
Senator: And give it Timon, why, the dog coins gold.
Senator: If I would sell my horse, and buy twenty more
Senator: Better than he, why, give my horse to Timon,
Senator: Ask nothing, give it him, it foals me, straight,
Senator: And able horses. No porter at his gate,
Senator: But rather one that smiles and still invites
Senator: All that pass by. It cannot hold: no reason
Senator: Can found his state in safety. Caphis, ho!
Senator: Caphis, I say!
NARRATOR: Enter CAPHIS
CAPHIS: Here, sir, what is your pleasure?
Senator: Get on your cloak, and haste you to Lord Timon,
Senator: Importune him for my moneys, be not ceased
Senator: With slight denial, nor then silenced when--
Senator: 'Commend me to your master'--and the cap
Senator: Plays in the right hand, thus: but tell him,
Senator: My uses cry to me, I must serve my turn
Senator: Out of mine own, his days and times are past
Senator: And my reliances on his fracted dates
Senator: Have smit my credit: I love and honour him,
Senator: But must not break my back to heal his finger,
Senator: Immediate are my needs, and my relief
Senator: Must not be toss'd and turn'd to me in words,
Senator: But find supply immediate. Get you gone:
Senator: Put on a most importunate aspect,
Senator: A visage of demand, for, I do fear,
Senator: When every feather sticks in his own wing,
Senator: Lord Timon will be left a naked gull,
Senator: Which flashes now a phoenix. Get you gone.
CAPHIS: I go, sir.
Senator: 'I go, sir!'--Take the bonds along with you,
Senator: And have the dates in contempt.
CAPHIS: I will, sir.
Senator: Go.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. A hall in Timon's house.
NARRATOR: Enter FLAVIUS, with many bills in his hand
FLAVIUS: No care, no stop! so senseless of expense,
FLAVIUS: That he will neither know how to maintain it,
FLAVIUS: Nor cease his flow of riot: takes no account
FLAVIUS: How things go from him, nor resumes no care
FLAVIUS: Of what is to continue: never mind
FLAVIUS: Was to be so unwise, to be so kind.
FLAVIUS: What shall be done? he will not hear, till feel:
FLAVIUS: I must be round with him, now he comes from hunting.
FLAVIUS: Fie, fie, fie, fie!
NARRATOR: Enter CAPHIS, and the Servants of Isidore and Varro
CAPHIS: Good even, Varro: what,
CAPHIS: You come for money?
CAPHIS: Varro's Servant	Is't not your business too?
CAPHIS: It is: and yours too, Isidore?
CAPHIS: Isidore's Servant	It is so.
CAPHIS: Would we were all discharged!
CAPHIS: Varro's Servant	I fear it.
CAPHIS: Here comes the lord.
CAPHIS: Enter TIMON, ALCIBIADES, and Lords,  and c
TIMON: So soon as dinner's done, we'll forth again,
TIMON: My Alcibiades. With me? what is your will?
CAPHIS: My lord, here is a note of certain dues.
TIMON: Dues! Whence are you?
CAPHIS: Of Athens here, my lord.
TIMON: Go to my steward.
CAPHIS: Please it your lordship, he hath put me off
CAPHIS: To the succession of new days this month:
CAPHIS: My master is awaked by great occasion
CAPHIS: To call upon his own, and humbly prays you
CAPHIS: That with your other noble parts you'll suit
CAPHIS: In giving him his right.
TIMON: Mine honest friend,
TIMON: I prithee, but repair to me next morning.
CAPHIS: Nay, good my lord,--
TIMON: Contain thyself, good friend.
TIMON: Varro's Servant	One Varro's servant, my good lord,--
TIMON: Isidore's Servant	From Isidore,
TIMON: He humbly prays your speedy payment.
CAPHIS: If you did know, my lord, my master's wants--
CAPHIS: Varro's Servant	'Twas due on forfeiture, my lord, six weeks And past.
CAPHIS: Isidore's Servant	         Your steward puts me off, my lord,
CAPHIS: And I am sent expressly to your lordship.
TIMON: Give me breath.
TIMON: I do beseech you, good my lords, keep on,
TIMON: I'll wait upon you instantly.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ALCIBIADES and Lords
NARRATOR: To FLAVIUS
TIMON: Come hither: pray you,
TIMON: How goes the world, that I am thus encounter'd
TIMON: With clamourous demands of date-broke bonds,
TIMON: And the detention of long-since-due debts,
TIMON: Against my honour?
FLAVIUS: Please you, gentlemen,
FLAVIUS: The time is unagreeable to this business:
FLAVIUS: Your importunacy cease till after dinner,
FLAVIUS: That I may make his lordship understand
FLAVIUS: Wherefore you are not paid.
TIMON: Do so, my friends. See them well entertain'd.
NARRATOR: Exit
FLAVIUS: Pray, draw near.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter APEMANTUS and Fool
CAPHIS: Stay, stay, here comes the fool with Apemantus:
CAPHIS: let's ha' some sport with 'em.
CAPHIS: Varro's Servant	Hang him, he'll abuse us.
CAPHIS: Isidore's Servant	A plague upon him, dog!
CAPHIS: Varro's Servant	How dost, fool?
APEMANTUS: Dost dialogue with thy shadow?
APEMANTUS: Varro's Servant	I speak not to thee.
APEMANTUS: No,'tis to thyself.
NARRATOR: To the Fool
APEMANTUS: Come away.
APEMANTUS: Isidore's Servant	There's the fool hangs on your back already.
APEMANTUS: No, thou stand'st single, thou'rt not on him yet.
CAPHIS: Where's the fool now?
APEMANTUS: He last asked the question. Poor rogues, and
APEMANTUS: usurers' men! bawds between gold and want!
All Servants: What are we, Apemantus?
APEMANTUS: Asses.
All Servants: Why?
APEMANTUS: That you ask me what you are, and do not know
APEMANTUS: yourselves. Speak to 'em, fool.
Fool: How do you, gentlemen?
All Servants: Gramercies, good fool: how does your mistress?
Fool: She's e'en setting on water to scald such chickens
Fool: as you are. Would we could see you at Corinth!
APEMANTUS: Good! gramercy.
NARRATOR: Enter Page
Fool: Look you, here comes my mistress' page.
Page: [To the Fool]  Why, how now, captain! what do you
Page: in this wise company? How dost thou, Apemantus?
APEMANTUS: Would I had a rod in my mouth, that I might answer
APEMANTUS: thee profitably.
Page: Prithee, Apemantus, read me the superscription of
Page: these letters: I know not which is which.
APEMANTUS: Canst not read?
Page: No.
APEMANTUS: There will little learning die then, that day thou
APEMANTUS: art hanged. This is to Lord Timon, this to
APEMANTUS: Alcibiades. Go, thou wast born a bastard, and thou't
APEMANTUS: die a bawd.
Page: Thou wast whelped a dog, and thou shalt famish a
Page: dog's death. Answer not, I am gone.
NARRATOR: Exit
APEMANTUS: E'en so thou outrunnest grace. Fool, I will go with
APEMANTUS: you to Lord Timon's.
Fool: Will you leave me there?
APEMANTUS: If Timon stay at home. You three serve three usurers?
All Servants: Ay, would they served us!
APEMANTUS: So would I,--as good a trick as ever hangman served thief.
Fool: Are you three usurers' men?
All Servants: Ay, fool.
Fool: I think no usurer but has a fool to his servant: my
Fool: mistress is one, and I am her fool. When men come
Fool: to borrow of your masters, they approach sadly, and
Fool: go away merry, but they enter my mistress' house
Fool: merrily, and go away sadly: the reason of this?
Fool: Varro's Servant	I could render one.
APEMANTUS: Do it then, that we may account thee a whoremaster
APEMANTUS: and a knave, which not-withstanding, thou shalt be
APEMANTUS: no less esteemed.
APEMANTUS: Varro's Servant	What is a whoremaster, fool?
Fool: A fool in good clothes, and something like thee.
Fool: 'Tis a spirit: sometime't appears like a lord,
Fool: sometime like a lawyer, sometime like a philosopher,
Fool: with two stones moe than's artificial one: he is
Fool: very often like a knight, and, generally, in all
Fool: shapes that man goes up and down in from fourscore
Fool: to thirteen, this spirit walks in.
Fool: Varro's Servant	Thou art not altogether a fool.
Fool: Nor thou altogether a wise man: as much foolery as
Fool: I have, so much wit thou lackest.
APEMANTUS: That answer might have become Apemantus.
All Servants: Aside, aside, here comes Lord Timon.
NARRATOR: Re-enter TIMON and FLAVIUS
APEMANTUS: Come with me, fool, come.
Fool: I do not always follow lover, elder brother and
Fool: woman, sometime the philosopher.
NARRATOR: Exeunt APEMANTUS and Fool
FLAVIUS: Pray you, walk near: I'll speak with you anon.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Servants
TIMON: You make me marvel: wherefore ere this time
TIMON: Had you not fully laid my state before me,
TIMON: That I might so have rated my expense,
TIMON: As I had leave of means?
FLAVIUS: You would not hear me,
FLAVIUS: At many leisures I proposed.
TIMON: Go to:
TIMON: Perchance some single vantages you took.
TIMON: When my indispos ition put you back:
TIMON: And that unaptness made your minister,
TIMON: Thus to excuse yourself.
FLAVIUS: O my good lord,
FLAVIUS: At many times I brought in my accounts,
FLAVIUS: Laid them before you, you would throw them off,
FLAVIUS: And say, you found them in mine honesty.
FLAVIUS: When, for some trifling present, you have bid me
FLAVIUS: Return so much, I have shook my head and wept,
FLAVIUS: Yea, 'gainst the authority of manners, pray'd you
FLAVIUS: To hold your hand more close: I did endure
FLAVIUS: Not seldom, nor no slight cheques, when I have
FLAVIUS: Prompted you in the ebb of your estate
FLAVIUS: And your great flow of debts. My loved lord,
FLAVIUS: Though you hear now, too late--yet now's a time--
FLAVIUS: The greatest of your having lacks a half
FLAVIUS: To pay your present debts.
TIMON: Let all my land be sold.
FLAVIUS: 'Tis all engaged, some forfeited and gone,
FLAVIUS: And what remains will hardly stop the mouth
FLAVIUS: Of present dues: the future comes apace:
FLAVIUS: What shall defend the interim? and at length
FLAVIUS: How goes our reckoning?
TIMON: To Lacedaemon did my land extend.
FLAVIUS: O my good lord, the world is but a word:
FLAVIUS: Were it all yours to give it in a breath,
FLAVIUS: How quickly were it gone!
TIMON: You tell me true.
FLAVIUS: If you suspect my husbandry or falsehood,
FLAVIUS: Call me before the exactest auditors
FLAVIUS: And set me on the proof. So the gods bless me,
FLAVIUS: When all our offices have been oppress'd
FLAVIUS: With riotous feeders, when our vaults have wept
FLAVIUS: With drunken spilth of wine, when every room
FLAVIUS: Hath blazed with lights and bray'd with minstrelsy,
FLAVIUS: I have retired me to a wasteful cock,
FLAVIUS: And set mine eyes at flow.
TIMON: Prithee, no more.
FLAVIUS: Heavens, have I said, the bounty of this lord!
FLAVIUS: How many prodigal bits have slaves and peasants
FLAVIUS: This night englutted! Who is not Timon's?
FLAVIUS: What heart, head, sword, force, means, but is
FLAVIUS: Lord Timon's?
FLAVIUS: Great Timon, noble, worthy, royal Timon!
FLAVIUS: Ah, when the means are gone that buy this praise,
FLAVIUS: The breath is gone whereof this praise is made:
FLAVIUS: Feast-won, fast-lost, one cloud of winter showers,
FLAVIUS: These flies are couch'd.
TIMON: Come, sermon me no further:
TIMON: No villanous bounty yet hath pass'd my heart,
TIMON: Unwisely, not ignobly, have I given.
TIMON: Why dost thou weep? Canst thou the conscience lack,
TIMON: To think I shall lack friends? Secure thy heart,
TIMON: If I would broach the vessels of my love,
TIMON: And try the argument of hearts by borrowing,
TIMON: Men and men's fortunes could I frankly use
TIMON: As I can bid thee speak.
FLAVIUS: Assurance bless your thoughts!
TIMON: And, in some sort, these wants of mine are crown'd,
TIMON: That I account them blessings, for by these
TIMON: Shall I try friends: you shall perceive how you
TIMON: Mistake my fortunes, I am wealthy in my friends.
TIMON: Within there! Flaminius! Servilius!
NARRATOR: Enter FLAMINIUS, SERVILIUS, and other Servants
Servants: My lord? my lord?
TIMON: I will dispatch you severally, you to Lord Lucius,
TIMON: to Lord Lucullus you: I hunted with his honour
TIMON: to-day: you, to Sempronius: commend me to their
TIMON: loves, and, I am proud, say, that my occasions have
TIMON: found time to use 'em toward a supply of money: let
TIMON: the request be fifty talents.
FLAMINIUS: As you have said, my lord.
FLAVIUS: [Aside]  Lord Lucius and Lucullus? hum!
TIMON: Go you, sir, to the senators--
TIMON: Of whom, even to the state's best health, I have
TIMON: Deserved this hearing--bid 'em send o' the instant
TIMON: A thousand talents to me.
FLAVIUS: I have been bold--
FLAVIUS: For that I knew it the most general way--
FLAVIUS: To them to use your signet and your name,
FLAVIUS: But they do shake their heads, and I am here
FLAVIUS: No richer in return.
TIMON: Is't true? can't be?
FLAVIUS: They answer, in a joint and corporate voice,
FLAVIUS: That now they are at fall, want treasure, cannot
FLAVIUS: Do what they would, are sorry--you are honourable,--
FLAVIUS: But yet they could have wish'd--they know not--
FLAVIUS: Something hath been amiss--a noble nature
FLAVIUS: May catch a wrench--would all were well--'tis pity,--
FLAVIUS: And so, intending other serious matters,
FLAVIUS: After distasteful looks and these hard fractions,
FLAVIUS: With certain half-caps and cold-moving nods
FLAVIUS: They froze me into silence.
TIMON: You gods, reward them!
TIMON: Prithee, man, look cheerly. These old fellows
TIMON: Have their ingratitude in them hereditary:
TIMON: Their blood is caked, 'tis cold, it seldom flows,
TIMON: 'Tis lack of kindly warmth they are not kind,
TIMON: And nature, as it grows again toward earth,
TIMON: Is fashion'd for the journey, dull and heavy.
NARRATOR: To a Servant
TIMON: Go to Ventidius.
NARRATOR: To FLAVIUS
TIMON: Prithee, be not sad,
TIMON: Thou art true and honest, ingeniously I speak.
TIMON: No blame belongs to thee.
NARRATOR: To Servant
TIMON: Ventidius lately
TIMON: Buried his father, by whose death he's stepp'd
TIMON: Into a great estate: when he was poor,
TIMON: Imprison'd and in scarcity of friends,
TIMON: I clear'd him with five talents: greet him from me,
TIMON: Bid him suppose some good necessity
TIMON: Touches his friend, which craves to be remember'd
TIMON: With those five talents.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
NARRATOR: To FLAVIUS
TIMON: That had, give't these fellows
TIMON: To whom 'tis instant due. Ne'er speak, or think,
TIMON: That Timon's fortunes 'mong his friends can sink.
FLAVIUS: I would I could not think it: that thought is
FLAVIUS: bounty's foe,
FLAVIUS: Being free itself, it thinks all others so.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A room in Lucullus' house.
NARRATOR: FLAMINIUS waiting. Enter a Servant to him
Servant: I have told my lord of you, he is coming down to you.
FLAMINIUS: I thank you, sir.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCULLUS
Servant: Here's my lord.
LUCULLUS: [Aside]  One of Lord Timon's men? a gift, I
LUCULLUS: warrant. Why, this hits right, I dreamt of a silver
LUCULLUS: basin and ewer to-night. Flaminius, honest
LUCULLUS: Flaminius, you are very respectively welcome, sir.
LUCULLUS: Fill me some wine.
NARRATOR: Exit Servants
LUCULLUS: And how does that honourable, complete, free-hearted
LUCULLUS: gentleman of Athens, thy very bountiful good lord
LUCULLUS: and master?
FLAMINIUS: His health is well sir.
LUCULLUS: I am right glad that his health is well, sir: and
LUCULLUS: what hast thou there under thy cloak, pretty Flaminius?
FLAMINIUS: 'Faith, nothing but an empty box, sir, which, in my
FLAMINIUS: lord's behalf, I come to entreat your honour to
FLAMINIUS: supply, who, having great and instant occasion to
FLAMINIUS: use fifty talents, hath sent to your lordship to
FLAMINIUS: furnish him, nothing doubting your present
FLAMINIUS: assistance therein.
LUCULLUS: La, la, la, la! 'nothing doubting,' says he? Alas,
LUCULLUS: good lord! a noble gentleman 'tis, if he would not
LUCULLUS: keep so good a house. Many a time and often I ha'
LUCULLUS: dined with him, and told him on't, and come again to
LUCULLUS: supper to him, of purpose to have him spend less,
LUCULLUS: and yet he would embrace no counsel, take no warning
LUCULLUS: by my coming. Every man has his fault, and honesty
LUCULLUS: is his: I ha' told him on't, but I could ne'er get
LUCULLUS: him from't.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Servant, with wine
Servant: Please your lordship, here is the wine.
LUCULLUS: Flaminius, I have noted thee always wise. Here's to thee.
FLAMINIUS: Your lordship speaks your pleasure.
LUCULLUS: I have observed thee always for a towardly prompt
LUCULLUS: spirit--give thee thy due--and one that knows what
LUCULLUS: belongs to reason, and canst use the time well, if
LUCULLUS: the time use thee well: good parts in thee.
NARRATOR: To Servant
LUCULLUS: Get you gone, sirrah.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
LUCULLUS: Draw nearer, honest Flaminius. Thy lord's a
LUCULLUS: bountiful gentleman: but thou art wise, and thou
LUCULLUS: knowest well enough, although thou comest to me,
LUCULLUS: that this is no time to lend money, especially upon
LUCULLUS: bare friendship, without security. Here's three
LUCULLUS: solidares for thee: good boy, wink at me, and say
LUCULLUS: thou sawest me not. Fare thee well.
FLAMINIUS: Is't possible the world should so much differ,
FLAMINIUS: And we alive that lived? Fly, damned baseness,
FLAMINIUS: To him that worships thee!
NARRATOR: Throwing the money back
LUCULLUS: Ha! now I see thou art a fool, and fit for thy master.
NARRATOR: Exit
FLAMINIUS: May these add to the number that may scald thee!
FLAMINIUS: Let moulten coin be thy damnation,
FLAMINIUS: Thou disease of a friend, and not himself!
FLAMINIUS: Has friendship such a faint and milky heart,
FLAMINIUS: It turns in less than two nights? O you gods,
FLAMINIUS: I feel master's passion! this slave,
FLAMINIUS: Unto his honour, has my lord's meat in him:
FLAMINIUS: Why should it thrive and turn to nutriment,
FLAMINIUS: When he is turn'd to poison?
FLAMINIUS: O, may diseases only work upon't!
FLAMINIUS: And, when he's sick to death, let not that part of nature
FLAMINIUS: Which my lord paid for, be of any power
FLAMINIUS: To expel sickness, but prolong his hour!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCILIUS, with three Strangers
LUCILIUS: Who, the Lord Timon? he is my very good friend, and
LUCILIUS: an honourable gentleman.
First Stranger: We know him for no less, though we are but strangers
First Stranger: to him. But I can tell you one thing, my lord, and

Second Stranger: so many talents, nay, urged extremely for't and

SERVILIUS: See, by good hap, yonder's my lord,

LUCILIUS: him, thinkest thou? And what has he sent now?

SERVILIUS: with so many talents.
LUCILIUS: I know his lordship is but merry with me,
LUCILIUS: He cannot want fifty five hundred talents.
SERVILIUS: But in the mean time he wants less, my lord.
SERVILIUS: If his occasion were not virtuous,
SERVILIUS: I should not urge it half so faithfully.
LUCILIUS: Dost thou speak seriously, Servilius?
SERVILIUS: Upon my soul,'tis true, sir.
LUCILIUS: What a wicked beast was I to disfurnish myself
LUCILIUS: against such a good time, when I might ha' shown
LUCILIUS: myself honourable! how unluckily it happened, that I
LUCILIUS: should purchase the day before for a little part,
LUCILIUS: and undo a great deal of honoured! Servilius, now,
LUCILIUS: before the gods, I am not able to do,--the more
LUCILIUS: beast, I say:--I was sending to use Lord Timon
LUCILIUS: myself, these gentlemen can witness! but I would
LUCILIUS: not, for the wealth of Athens, I had done't now.
LUCILIUS: Commend me bountifully to his good lordship, and I
LUCILIUS: hope his honour will conceive the fairest of me,
LUCILIUS: because I have no power to be kind: and tell him
LUCILIUS: this from me, I count it one of my greatest
LUCILIUS: afflictions, say, that I cannot pleasure such an
LUCILIUS: honourable gentleman. Good Servilius, will you
LUCILIUS: befriend me so far, as to use mine own words to him?
SERVILIUS: Yes, sir, I shall.
LUCILIUS: I'll look you out a good turn, Servilius.
NARRATOR: Exit SERVILIUS
LUCILIUS: True as you said, Timon is shrunk indeed,
LUCILIUS: And he that's once denied will hardly speed.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Stranger: Do you observe this, Hostilius?
Second Stranger: Ay, too well.
First Stranger: Why, this is the world's soul, and just of the
First Stranger: same piece
First Stranger: Is every flatterer's spirit. Who can call him
First Stranger: His friend that dips in the same dish? for, in
First Stranger: My knowing, Timon has been this lord's father,
First Stranger: And kept his credit with his purse,
First Stranger: Supported his estate, nay, Timon's money
First Stranger: Has paid his men their wages: he ne'er drinks,
First Stranger: But Timon's silver treads upon his lip,
First Stranger: And yet--O, see the monstrousness of man
First Stranger: When he looks out in an ungrateful shape!--
First Stranger: He does deny him, in respect of his,
First Stranger: What charitable men afford to beggars.
Third Stranger: Religion groans at it.
First Stranger: For mine own part,
First Stranger: I never tasted Timon in my life,
First Stranger: Nor came any of his bounties over me,
First Stranger: To mark me for his friend, yet, I protest,
First Stranger: For his right noble mind, illustrious virtue
First Stranger: And honourable carriage,
First Stranger: Had his necessity made use of me,
First Stranger: I would have put my wealth into donation,
First Stranger: And the best half should have return'd to him,
First Stranger: So much I love his heart: but, I perceive,
First Stranger: Men must learn now with pity to dispense,
First Stranger: For policy sits above conscience.

SEMPRONIUS: But his occasion might have woo'd me first,

SEMPRONIUS: That e'er received gift from him:
SEMPRONIUS: And does he think so backwardly of me now,
SEMPRONIUS: That I'll requite its last? No:
SEMPRONIUS: So it may prove an argument of laughter
SEMPRONIUS: To the rest, and 'mongst lords I be thought a fool.
SEMPRONIUS: I'ld rather than the worth of thrice the sum,

SEMPRONIUS: I'd such a courage to do him good. But now return,

Servant: Excellent! Your lordship's a goodly villain. The
Servant: devil knew not what he did when he made man
Servant: politic, he crossed himself by 't: and I cannot
Servant: think but, in the end, the villainies of man will
Servant: set him clear. How fairly this lord strives to
Servant: appear foul! takes virtuous copies to be wicked,
Servant: like those that under hot ardent zeal would set
Servant: whole realms on fire: Of such a nature is his
Servant: politic love.
Servant: This was my lord's best hope, now all are fled,

Servant: Doors, that were ne'er acquainted with their wards

Servant: Now to guard sure their master.
Servant: And this is all a liberal course allows,
Servant: Who cannot keep his wealth must keep his house.

NARRATOR: SCENE V. The same. The senate-house. The Senate sitting.
First Senator: My lord, you have my voice to it, the fault's
First Senator: Bloody, 'tis necessary he should die:
First Senator: Nothing emboldens sin so much as mercy.
Second Senator: Most true, the law shall bruise him.
NARRATOR: Enter ALCIBIADES, with Attendants
ALCIBIADES: Honour, health, and compassion to the senate!
First Senator: Now, captain?
ALCIBIADES: I am an humble suitor to your virtues,
ALCIBIADES: For pity is the virtue of the law,
ALCIBIADES: And none but tyrants use it cruelly.
ALCIBIADES: It pleases time and fortune to lie heavy
ALCIBIADES: Upon a friend of mine, who, in hot blood,
ALCIBIADES: Hath stepp'd into the law, which is past depth
ALCIBIADES: To those that, without heed, do plunge into 't.
ALCIBIADES: He is a man, setting his fate aside,
ALCIBIADES: Of comely virtues:
ALCIBIADES: Nor did he soil the fact with cowardice--
ALCIBIADES: An honour in him which buys out his fault--
ALCIBIADES: But with a noble fury and fair spirit,
ALCIBIADES: Seeing his reputation touch'd to death,
ALCIBIADES: He did oppose his foe:
ALCIBIADES: And with such sober and unnoted passion
ALCIBIADES: He did behave his anger, ere 'twas spent,
ALCIBIADES: As if he had but proved an argument.
First Senator: You undergo too strict a paradox,
First Senator: Striving to make an ugly deed look fair:
First Senator: Your words have took such pains as if they labour'd
First Senator: To bring manslaughter into form and set quarrelling
First Senator: Upon the head of valour, which indeed
First Senator: Is valour misbegot and came into the world
First Senator: When sects and factions were newly born:
First Senator: He's truly valiant that can wisely suffer
First Senator: The worst that man can breathe, and make his wrongs
First Senator: His outsides, to wear them like his raiment,
First Senator: carelessly,
First Senator: And ne'er prefer his injuries to his heart,
First Senator: To bring it into danger.
First Senator: If wrongs be evils and enforce us kill,
First Senator: What folly 'tis to hazard life for ill!
ALCIBIADES: My lord,--
First Senator: You cannot make gross sins look clear:
First Senator: To revenge is no valour, but to bear.
ALCIBIADES: My lords, then, under favour, pardon me,
ALCIBIADES: If I speak like a captain.
ALCIBIADES: Why do fond men expose themselves to battle,
ALCIBIADES: And not endure all threats? sleep upon't,
ALCIBIADES: And let the foes quietly cut their throats,
ALCIBIADES: Without repugnancy? If there be
ALCIBIADES: Such valour in the bearing, what make we
ALCIBIADES: Abroad? why then, women are more valiant
ALCIBIADES: That stay at home, if bearing carry it,
ALCIBIADES: And the ass more captain than the lion, the felon
ALCIBIADES: Loaden with irons wiser than the judge,
ALCIBIADES: If wisdom be in suffering. O my lords,
ALCIBIADES: As you are great, be pitifully good:
ALCIBIADES: Who cannot condemn rashness in cold blood?
ALCIBIADES: To kill, I grant, is sin's extremest gust,
ALCIBIADES: But, in defence, by mercy, 'tis most just.
ALCIBIADES: To be in anger is impiety,
ALCIBIADES: But who is man that is not angry?
ALCIBIADES: Weigh but the crime with this.
Second Senator: You breathe in vain.
ALCIBIADES: In vain! his service done
ALCIBIADES: At Lacedaemon and Byzantium
ALCIBIADES: Were a sufficient briber for his life.
First Senator: What's that?
ALCIBIADES: I say, my lords, he has done fair service,
ALCIBIADES: And slain in fight many of your enemies:
ALCIBIADES: How full of valour did he bear himself
ALCIBIADES: In the last conflict, and made plenteous wounds!
Second Senator: He has made too much plenty with 'em,
Second Senator: He's a sworn rioter: he has a sin that often
Second Senator: Drowns him, and takes his valour prisoner:
Second Senator: If there were no foes, that were enough
Second Senator: To overcome him: in that beastly fury
Second Senator: He has been known to commit outrages,
Second Senator: And cherish factions: 'tis inferr'd to us,
Second Senator: His days are foul and his drink dangerous.
First Senator: He dies.
ALCIBIADES: Hard fate! he might have died in war.
ALCIBIADES: My lords, if not for any parts in him--
ALCIBIADES: Though his right arm might purchase his own time
ALCIBIADES: And be in debt to none--yet, more to move you,
ALCIBIADES: Take my deserts to his, and join 'em both:
ALCIBIADES: And, for I know your reverend ages love
ALCIBIADES: Security, I'll pawn my victories, all
ALCIBIADES: My honours to you, upon his good returns.
ALCIBIADES: If by this crime he owes the law his life,
ALCIBIADES: Why, let the war receive 't in valiant gore
ALCIBIADES: For law is strict, and war is nothing more.
First Senator: We are for law: he dies, urge it no more,
First Senator: On height of our displeasure: friend or brother,
First Senator: He forfeits his own blood that spills another.
ALCIBIADES: Must it be so? it must not be. My lords,
ALCIBIADES: I do beseech you, know me.
Second Senator: How!
ALCIBIADES: Call me to your remembrances.
Third Senator: What!
ALCIBIADES: I cannot think but your age has forgot me,
ALCIBIADES: It could not else be, I should prove so base,
ALCIBIADES: To sue, and be denied such common grace:
ALCIBIADES: My wounds ache at you.
First Senator: Do you dare our anger?
First Senator: 'Tis in few words, but spacious in effect,
First Senator: We banish thee for ever.
ALCIBIADES: Banish me!
ALCIBIADES: Banish your dotage, banish usury,
ALCIBIADES: That makes the senate ugly.
First Senator: If, after two days' shine, Athens contain thee,
First Senator: Attend our weightier judgment. And, not to swell
First Senator: our spirit,
First Senator: He shall be executed presently.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Senators
ALCIBIADES: Now the gods keep you old enough, that you may live
ALCIBIADES: Only in bone, that none may look on you!
ALCIBIADES: I'm worse than mad: I have kept back their foes,
ALCIBIADES: While they have told their money and let out
ALCIBIADES: Their coin upon large interest, I myself
ALCIBIADES: Rich only in large hurts. All those for this?
ALCIBIADES: Is this the balsam that the usuring senate
ALCIBIADES: Pours into captains' wounds? Banishment!
ALCIBIADES: It comes not ill, I hate not to be banish'd,
ALCIBIADES: It is a cause worthy my spleen and fury,
ALCIBIADES: That I may strike at Athens. I'll cheer up
ALCIBIADES: My discontented troops, and lay for hearts.
ALCIBIADES: 'Tis honour with most lands to be at odds,
ALCIBIADES: Soldiers should brook as little wrongs as gods.

NARRATOR: SCENE VI. The same. A banqueting-room in Timon's house.
NARRATOR: Music. Tables set out: Servants attending.  Enter divers Lords, Senators and others, at several doors

TIMON: Each man to his stool, with that spur as he would to

TIMON: the meat cool ere we can agree upon the first place:

TIMON: You great benefactors, sprinkle our society with
TIMON: thankfulness. For your own gifts, make yourselves

TIMON: godheads to borrow of men, men would forsake the
TIMON: gods. Make the meat be beloved more than the man
TIMON: that gives it. Let no assembly of twenty be without
TIMON: a score of villains: if there sit twelve women at
TIMON: the table, let a dozen of them be--as they are. The
TIMON: rest of your fees, O gods--the senators of Athens,
TIMON: together with the common lag of people--what is
TIMON: amiss in them, you gods, make suitable for
TIMON: destruction. For these my present friends, as they
TIMON: are to me nothing, so in nothing bless them, and to
TIMON: nothing are they welcome.
TIMON: Uncover, dogs, and lap.
NARRATOR: The dishes are uncovered and seen to be full of warm water
Some Speak: What does his lordship mean?
Some Others: I know not.
TIMON: May you a better feast never behold,
TIMON: You knot of mouth-friends I smoke and lukewarm water
TIMON: Is your perfection. This is Timon's last,
TIMON: Who, stuck and spangled with your flatteries,
TIMON: Washes it off, and sprinkles in your faces
TIMON: Your reeking villany.
NARRATOR: Throwing the water in their faces
TIMON: Live loathed and long,
TIMON: Most smiling, smooth, detested parasites,
TIMON: Courteous destroyers, affable wolves, meek bears,
TIMON: You fools of fortune, trencher-friends, time's flies,
TIMON: Cap and knee slaves, vapours, and minute-jacks!
TIMON: Of man and beast the infinite malady
TIMON: Crust you quite o'er! What, dost thou go?
TIMON: Soft! take thy physic first--thou too--and thou,--
TIMON: Stay, I will lend thee money, borrow none.
NARRATOR: Throws the dishes at them, and drives them out
TIMON: What, all in motion? Henceforth be no feast,
TIMON: Whereat a villain's not a welcome guest.
TIMON: Burn, house! sink, Athens! henceforth hated be
TIMON: Of Timon man and all humanity!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter the Lords, Senators,  and c
First Lord: How now, my lords!
Second Lord: Know you the quality of Lord Timon's fury?
Third Lord: Push! did you see my cap?
Fourth Lord: I have lost my gown.
First Lord: He's but a mad lord, and nought but humour sways him.
First Lord: He gave me a jewel th' other day, and now he has
First Lord: beat it out of my hat: did you see my jewel?
Third Lord: Did you see my cap?
Second Lord: Here 'tis.
Fourth Lord: Here lies my gown.
First Lord: Let's make no stay.
Second Lord: Lord Timon's mad.
Third Lord: I feel 't upon my bones.
Fourth Lord: One day he gives us diamonds, next day stones.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Without the walls of Athens.
NARRATOR: Enter TIMON
TIMON: Let me look back upon thee. O thou wall,
TIMON: That girdlest in those wolves, dive in the earth,
TIMON: And fence not Athens! Matrons, turn incontinent!
TIMON: Obedience fail in children! slaves and fools,
TIMON: Pluck the grave wrinkled senate from the bench,
TIMON: And minister in their steads! to general filths
TIMON: Convert o' the instant, green virginity,
TIMON: Do 't in your parents' eyes! bankrupts, hold fast,
TIMON: Rather than render back, out with your knives,
TIMON: And cut your trusters' throats! bound servants, steal!
TIMON: Large-handed robbers your grave masters are,
TIMON: And pill by law. Maid, to thy master's bed,
TIMON: Thy mistress is o' the brothel! Son of sixteen,
TIMON: pluck the lined crutch from thy old limping sire,
TIMON: With it beat out his brains! Piety, and fear,
TIMON: Religion to the gods, peace, justice, truth,
TIMON: Domestic awe, night-rest, and neighbourhood,
TIMON: Instruction, manners, mysteries, and trades,
TIMON: Degrees, observances, customs, and laws,
TIMON: Decline to your confounding contraries,
TIMON: And let confusion live! Plagues, incident to men,
TIMON: Your potent and infectious fevers heap
TIMON: On Athens, ripe for stroke! Thou cold sciatica,
TIMON: Cripple our senators, that their limbs may halt
TIMON: As lamely as their manners. Lust and liberty
TIMON: Creep in the minds and marrows of our youth,
TIMON: That 'gainst the stream of virtue they may strive,
TIMON: And drown themselves in riot! Itches, blains,
TIMON: Sow all the Athenian bosoms, and their crop
TIMON: Be general leprosy! Breath infect breath,
TIMON: at their society, as their friendship, may
TIMON: merely poison! Nothing I'll bear from thee,
TIMON: But nakedness, thou detestable town!
TIMON: Take thou that too, with multiplying bans!
TIMON: Timon will to the woods, where he shall find
TIMON: The unkindest beast more kinder than mankind.
TIMON: The gods confound--hear me, you good gods all--
TIMON: The Athenians both within and out that wall!
TIMON: And grant, as Timon grows, his hate may grow
TIMON: To the whole race of mankind, high and low! Amen.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Athens. A room in Timon's house.
NARRATOR: Enter FLAVIUS, with two or three Servants
First Servant: Hear you, master steward, where's our master?
First Servant: Are we undone? cast off? nothing remaining?
FLAVIUS: Alack, my fellows, what should I say to you?
FLAVIUS: Let me be recorded by the righteous gods,
FLAVIUS: I am as poor as you.
First Servant: Such a house broke!
First Servant: So noble a master fall'n! All gone! and not
First Servant: One friend to take his fortune by the arm,
First Servant: And go along with him!
Second Servant: As we do turn our backs
Second Servant: From our companion thrown into his grave,
Second Servant: So his familiars to his buried fortunes
Second Servant: Slink all away, leave their false vows with him,
Second Servant: Like empty purses pick'd, and his poor self,
Second Servant: A dedicated beggar to the air,
Second Servant: With his disease of all-shunn'd poverty,
Second Servant: Walks, like contempt, alone. More of our fellows.
NARRATOR: Enter other Servants
FLAVIUS: All broken implements of a ruin'd house.
Third Servant: Yet do our hearts wear Timon's livery,
Third Servant: That see I by our faces, we are fellows still,
Third Servant: Serving alike in sorrow: leak'd is our bark,
Third Servant: And we, poor mates, stand on the dying deck,
Third Servant: Hearing the surges threat: we must all part
Third Servant: Into this sea of air.
FLAVIUS: Good fellows all,
FLAVIUS: The latest of my wealth I'll share amongst you.
FLAVIUS: Wherever we shall meet, for Timon's sake,
FLAVIUS: Let's yet be fellows, let's shake our heads, and say,
FLAVIUS: As 'twere a knell unto our master's fortunes,
FLAVIUS: 'We have seen better days.' Let each take some,
FLAVIUS: Nay, put out all your hands. Not one word more:
FLAVIUS: Thus part we rich in sorrow, parting poor.
NARRATOR: Servants embrace, and part several ways
FLAVIUS: O, the fierce wretchedness that glory brings us!
FLAVIUS: Who would not wish to be from wealth exempt,
FLAVIUS: Since riches point to misery and contempt?
FLAVIUS: Who would be so mock'd with glory? or to live
FLAVIUS: But in a dream of friendship?
FLAVIUS: To have his pomp and all what state compounds
FLAVIUS: But only painted, like his varnish'd friends?
FLAVIUS: Poor honest lord, brought low by his own heart,
FLAVIUS: Undone by goodness! Strange, unusual blood,
FLAVIUS: When man's worst sin is, he does too much good!
FLAVIUS: Who, then, dares to be half so kind again?
FLAVIUS: For bounty, that makes gods, does still mar men.
FLAVIUS: My dearest lord, bless'd, to be most accursed,
FLAVIUS: Rich, only to be wretched, thy great fortunes
FLAVIUS: Are made thy chief afflictions. Alas, kind lord!
FLAVIUS: He's flung in rage from this ingrateful seat
FLAVIUS: Of monstrous friends, nor has he with him to
FLAVIUS: Supply his life, or that which can command it.
FLAVIUS: I'll follow and inquire him out:
FLAVIUS: I'll ever serve his mind with my best will,
FLAVIUS: Whilst I have gold, I'll be his steward still.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Woods and cave, near the seashore.
NARRATOR: Enter TIMON, from the cave
FLAVIUS: O blessed breeding sun, draw from the earth
FLAVIUS: Rotten humidity, below thy sister's orb
FLAVIUS: Infect the air! Twinn'd brothers of one womb,
FLAVIUS: Whose procreation, residence, and birth,
FLAVIUS: Scarce is dividant, touch them with several fortunes,
FLAVIUS: The greater scorns the lesser: not nature,
FLAVIUS: To whom all sores lay siege, can bear great fortune,
FLAVIUS: But by contempt of nature.
FLAVIUS: Raise me this beggar, and deny 't that lord,
FLAVIUS: The senator shall bear contempt hereditary,
FLAVIUS: The beggar native honour.
FLAVIUS: It is the pasture lards the rother's sides,
FLAVIUS: The want that makes him lean. Who dares, who dares,
FLAVIUS: In purity of manhood stand upright,
FLAVIUS: And say 'This man's a flatterer?' if one be,
FLAVIUS: So are they all, for every grise of fortune
FLAVIUS: Is smooth'd by that below: the learned pate
FLAVIUS: Ducks to the golden fool: all is oblique,
FLAVIUS: There's nothing level in our cursed natures,
FLAVIUS: But direct villany. Therefore, be abhorr'd
FLAVIUS: All feasts, societies, and throngs of men!
FLAVIUS: His semblable, yea, himself, Timon disdains:
FLAVIUS: Destruction fang mankind! Earth, yield me roots!
NARRATOR: Digging
FLAVIUS: Who seeks for better of thee, sauce his palate
FLAVIUS: With thy most operant poison! What is here?
FLAVIUS: Gold? yellow, glittering, precious gold? No, gods,
FLAVIUS: I am no idle votarist: roots, you clear heavens!
FLAVIUS: Thus much of this will make black white, foul fair,
FLAVIUS: Wrong right, base noble, old young, coward valiant.
FLAVIUS: Ha, you gods! why this? what this, you gods? Why, this
FLAVIUS: Will lug your priests and servants from your sides,
FLAVIUS: Pluck stout men's pillows from below their heads:
FLAVIUS: This yellow slave
FLAVIUS: Will knit and break religions, bless the accursed,
FLAVIUS: Make the hoar leprosy adored, place thieves
FLAVIUS: And give them title, knee and approbation
FLAVIUS: With senators on the bench: this is it
FLAVIUS: That makes the wappen'd widow wed again,
FLAVIUS: She, whom the spital-house and ulcerous sores
FLAVIUS: Would cast the gorge at, this embalms and spices
FLAVIUS: To the April day again. Come, damned earth,
FLAVIUS: Thou common whore of mankind, that put'st odds
FLAVIUS: Among the route of nations, I will make thee
FLAVIUS: Do thy right nature.
NARRATOR: March afar off
FLAVIUS: Ha! a drum ? Thou'rt quick,
FLAVIUS: But yet I'll bury thee: thou'lt go, strong thief,
FLAVIUS: When gouty keepers of thee cannot stand.
FLAVIUS: Nay, stay thou out for earnest.
NARRATOR: Keeping some gold
NARRATOR: Enter ALCIBIADES, with drum and fife, in warlike manner, PHRYNIA and TIMANDRA
ALCIBIADES: What art thou there? speak.
TIMON: A beast, as thou art. The canker gnaw thy heart,
TIMON: For showing me again the eyes of man!
ALCIBIADES: What is thy name? Is man so hateful to thee,
ALCIBIADES: That art thyself a man?
TIMON: I am Misanthropos, and hate mankind.
TIMON: For thy part, I do wish thou wert a dog,
TIMON: That I might love thee something.
ALCIBIADES: I know thee well,
ALCIBIADES: But in thy fortunes am unlearn'd and strange.
TIMON: I know thee too, and more than that I know thee,
TIMON: I not desire to know. Follow thy drum,
TIMON: With man's blood paint the ground, gules, gules:
TIMON: Religious canons, civil laws are cruel,
TIMON: Then what should war be? This fell whore of thine
TIMON: Hath in her more destruction than thy sword,
TIMON: For all her cherubim look.
PHRYNIA: Thy lips rot off!
TIMON: I will not kiss thee, then the rot returns
TIMON: To thine own lips again.
ALCIBIADES: How came the noble Timon to this change?
TIMON: As the moon does, by wanting light to give:
TIMON: But then renew I could not, like the moon,
TIMON: There were no suns to borrow of.
ALCIBIADES: Noble Timon,
ALCIBIADES: What friendship may I do thee?
TIMON: None, but to
TIMON: Maintain my opinion.
ALCIBIADES: What is it, Timon?
TIMON: Promise me friendship, but perform none: if thou
TIMON: wilt not promise, the gods plague thee, for thou art
TIMON: a man! if thou dost perform, confound thee, for
TIMON: thou art a man!
ALCIBIADES: I have heard in some sort of thy miseries.
TIMON: Thou saw'st them, when I had prosperity.
ALCIBIADES: I see them now, then was a blessed time.
TIMON: As thine is now, held with a brace of harlots.
TIMANDRA: Is this the Athenian minion, whom the world
TIMANDRA: Voiced so regardfully?
TIMON: Art thou Timandra?
TIMANDRA: Yes.
TIMON: Be a whore still: they love thee not that use thee,
TIMON: Give them diseases, leaving with thee their lust.
TIMON: Make use of thy salt hours: season the slaves
TIMON: For tubs and baths, bring down rose-cheeked youth
TIMON: To the tub-fast and the diet.
TIMANDRA: Hang thee, monster!
ALCIBIADES: Pardon him, sweet Timandra, for his wits
ALCIBIADES: Are drown'd and lost in his calamities.
ALCIBIADES: I have but little gold of late, brave Timon,
ALCIBIADES: The want whereof doth daily make revolt
ALCIBIADES: In my penurious band: I have heard, and grieved,
ALCIBIADES: How cursed Athens, mindless of thy worth,
ALCIBIADES: Forgetting thy great deeds, when neighbour states,
ALCIBIADES: But for thy sword and fortune, trod upon them,--
TIMON: I prithee, beat thy drum, and get thee gone.
ALCIBIADES: I am thy friend, and pity thee, dear Timon.
TIMON: How dost thou pity him whom thou dost trouble?
TIMON: I had rather be alone.
ALCIBIADES: Why, fare thee well:
ALCIBIADES: Here is some gold for thee.
TIMON: Keep it, I cannot eat it.
ALCIBIADES: When I have laid proud Athens on a heap,--
TIMON: Warr'st thou 'gainst Athens?
ALCIBIADES: Ay, Timon, and have cause.
TIMON: The gods confound them all in thy conquest,
TIMON: And thee after, when thou hast conquer'd!
ALCIBIADES: Why me, Timon?
TIMON: That, by killing of villains,
TIMON: Thou wast born to conquer my country.
TIMON: Put up thy gold: go on,--here's gold,--go on,
TIMON: Be as a planetary plague, when Jove
TIMON: Will o'er some high-viced city hang his poison
TIMON: In the sick air: let not thy sword skip one:
TIMON: Pity not honour'd age for his white beard,
TIMON: He is an usurer: strike me the counterfeit matron,
TIMON: It is her habit only that is honest,
TIMON: Herself's a bawd: let not the virgin's cheek
TIMON: Make soft thy trenchant sword, for those milk-paps,
TIMON: That through the window-bars bore at men's eyes,
TIMON: Are not within the leaf of pity writ,
TIMON: But set them down horrible traitors: spare not the babe,
TIMON: Whose dimpled smiles from fools exhaust their mercy,
TIMON: Think it a bastard, whom the oracle
TIMON: Hath doubtfully pronounced thy throat shall cut,
TIMON: And mince it sans remorse: swear against objects,
TIMON: Put armour on thine ears and on thine eyes,
TIMON: Whose proof, nor yells of mothers, maids, nor babes,
TIMON: Nor sight of priests in holy vestments bleeding,
TIMON: Shall pierce a jot. There's gold to pay soldiers:
TIMON: Make large confusion, and, thy fury spent,
TIMON: Confounded be thyself! Speak not, be gone.
ALCIBIADES: Hast thou gold yet? I'll take the gold thou
ALCIBIADES: givest me,
ALCIBIADES: Not all thy counsel.
TIMON: Dost thou, or dost thou not, heaven's curse
TIMON: upon thee!
TIMANDRA: Give us some gold, good Timon: hast thou more?
TIMON: Enough to make a whore forswear her trade,
TIMON: And to make whores, a bawd. Hold up, you sluts,
TIMON: Your aprons mountant: you are not oathable,
TIMON: Although, I know, you 'll swear, terribly swear
TIMON: Into strong shudders and to heavenly agues
TIMON: The immortal gods that hear you,--spare your oaths,
TIMON: I'll trust to your conditions: be whores still,
TIMON: And he whose pious breath seeks to convert you,
TIMON: Be strong in whore, allure him, burn him up,
TIMON: Let your close fire predominate his smoke,
TIMON: And be no turncoats: yet may your pains, six months,
TIMON: Be quite contrary: and thatch your poor thin roofs
TIMON: With burthens of the dead,--some that were hang'd,
TIMON: No matter:--wear them, betray with them: whore still,
TIMON: Paint till a horse may mire upon your face,
TIMON: A pox of wrinkles!
TIMANDRA: Well, more gold: what then?
TIMANDRA: Believe't, that we'll do any thing for gold.
TIMON: Consumptions sow
TIMON: In hollow bones of man, strike their sharp shins,
TIMON: And mar men's spurring. Crack the lawyer's voice,
TIMON: That he may never more false title plead,
TIMON: Nor sound his quillets shrilly: hoar the flamen,
TIMON: That scolds against the quality of flesh,
TIMON: And not believes himself: down with the nose,
TIMON: Down with it flat, take the bridge quite away
TIMON: Of him that, his particular to foresee,
TIMON: Smells from the general weal: make curl'd-pate
TIMON: ruffians bald,
TIMON: And let the unscarr'd braggarts of the war
TIMON: Derive some pain from you: plague all,
TIMON: That your activity may defeat and quell
TIMON: The source of all erection. There's more gold:
TIMON: Do you damn others, and let this damn you,
TIMON: And ditches grave you all!
TIMANDRA: More counsel with more money, bounteous Timon.
TIMON: More whore, more mischief first, I have given you earnest.
ALCIBIADES: Strike up the drum towards Athens! Farewell, Timon:
ALCIBIADES: If I thrive well, I'll visit thee again.
TIMON: If I hope well, I'll never see thee more.
ALCIBIADES: I never did thee harm.
TIMON: Yes, thou spokest well of me.
ALCIBIADES: Call'st thou that harm?
TIMON: Men daily find it. Get thee away, and take
TIMON: Thy beagles with thee.
ALCIBIADES: We but offend him. Strike!
NARRATOR: Drum beats. Exeunt ALCIBIADES, PHRYNIA, and TIMANDRA
TIMON: That nature, being sick of man's unkindness,
TIMON: Should yet be hungry! Common mother, thou,
NARRATOR: Digging
TIMON: Whose womb unmeasurable, and infinite breast,
TIMON: Teems, and feeds all, whose self-same mettle,
TIMON: Whereof thy proud child, arrogant man, is puff'd,
TIMON: Engenders the black toad and adder blue,
TIMON: The gilded newt and eyeless venom'd worm,
TIMON: With all the abhorred births below crisp heaven
TIMON: Whereon Hyperion's quickening fire doth shine,
TIMON: Yield him, who all thy human sons doth hate,
TIMON: From forth thy plenteous bosom, one poor root!
TIMON: Ensear thy fertile and conceptious womb,
TIMON: Let it no more bring out ingrateful man!
TIMON: Go great with tigers, dragons, wolves, and bears,
TIMON: Teem with new monsters, whom thy upward face
TIMON: Hath to the marbled mansion all above
TIMON: Never presented!--O, a root,--dear thanks!--
TIMON: Dry up thy marrows, vines, and plough-torn leas,
TIMON: Whereof ungrateful man, with liquorish draughts
TIMON: And morsels unctuous, greases his pure mind,
TIMON: That from it all consideration slips!
NARRATOR: Enter APEMANTUS
TIMON: More man? plague, plague!
APEMANTUS: I was directed hither: men report
APEMANTUS: Thou dost affect my manners, and dost use them.
TIMON: 'Tis, then, because thou dost not keep a dog,
TIMON: Whom I would imitate: consumption catch thee!
APEMANTUS: This is in thee a nature but infected,
APEMANTUS: A poor unmanly melancholy sprung
APEMANTUS: From change of fortune. Why this spade? this place?
APEMANTUS: This slave-like habit? and these looks of care?
APEMANTUS: Thy flatterers yet wear silk, drink wine, lie soft,
APEMANTUS: Hug their diseased perfumes, and have forgot
APEMANTUS: That ever Timon was. Shame not these woods,
APEMANTUS: By putting on the cunning of a carper.
APEMANTUS: Be thou a flatterer now, and seek to thrive
APEMANTUS: By that which has undone thee: hinge thy knee,
APEMANTUS: And let his very breath, whom thou'lt observe,
APEMANTUS: Blow off thy cap, praise his most vicious strain,
APEMANTUS: And call it excellent: thou wast told thus,
APEMANTUS: Thou gavest thine ears like tapsters that bid welcome
APEMANTUS: To knaves and all approachers: 'tis most just
APEMANTUS: That thou turn rascal, hadst thou wealth again,
APEMANTUS: Rascals should have 't. Do not assume my likeness.
TIMON: Were I like thee, I'ld throw away myself.
APEMANTUS: Thou hast cast away thyself, being like thyself,
APEMANTUS: A madman so long, now a fool. What, think'st
APEMANTUS: That the bleak air, thy boisterous chamberlain,
APEMANTUS: Will put thy shirt on warm? will these moss'd trees,
APEMANTUS: That have outlived the eagle, page thy heels,
APEMANTUS: And skip where thou point'st out? will the
APEMANTUS: cold brook,
APEMANTUS: Candied with ice, caudle thy morning taste,
APEMANTUS: To cure thy o'er-night's surfeit? Call the creatures
APEMANTUS: Whose naked natures live in an the spite
APEMANTUS: Of wreakful heaven, whose bare unhoused trunks,
APEMANTUS: To the conflicting elements exposed,
APEMANTUS: Answer mere nature, bid them flatter thee,
APEMANTUS: O, thou shalt find--
TIMON: A fool of thee: depart.
APEMANTUS: I love thee better now than e'er I did.
TIMON: I hate thee worse.
APEMANTUS: Why?
TIMON: Thou flatter'st misery.
APEMANTUS: I flatter not, but say thou art a caitiff.
TIMON: Why dost thou seek me out?
APEMANTUS: To vex thee.
TIMON: Always a villain's office or a fool's.
TIMON: Dost please thyself in't?
APEMANTUS: Ay.
TIMON: What! a knave too?
APEMANTUS: If thou didst put this sour-cold habit on
APEMANTUS: To castigate thy pride, 'twere well: but thou
APEMANTUS: Dost it enforcedly, thou'ldst courtier be again,
APEMANTUS: Wert thou not beggar. Willing misery
APEMANTUS: Outlives encertain pomp, is crown'd before:
APEMANTUS: The one is filling still, never complete,
APEMANTUS: The other, at high wish: best state, contentless,
APEMANTUS: Hath a distracted and most wretched being,
APEMANTUS: Worse than the worst, content.
APEMANTUS: Thou shouldst desire to die, being miserable.
TIMON: Not by his breath that is more miserable.
TIMON: Thou art a slave, whom Fortune's tender arm
TIMON: With favour never clasp'd, but bred a dog.
TIMON: Hadst thou, like us from our first swath, proceeded
TIMON: The sweet degrees that this brief world affords
TIMON: To such as may the passive drugs of it
TIMON: Freely command, thou wouldst have plunged thyself
TIMON: In general riot, melted down thy youth
TIMON: In different beds of lust, and never learn'd
TIMON: The icy precepts of respect, but follow'd
TIMON: The sugar'd game before thee. But myself,
TIMON: Who had the world as my confectionary,
TIMON: The mouths, the tongues, the eyes and hearts of men
TIMON: At duty, more than I could frame employment,
TIMON: That numberless upon me stuck as leaves
TIMON: Do on the oak, hive with one winter's brush
TIMON: Fell from their boughs and left me open, bare
TIMON: For every storm that blows: I, to bear this,
TIMON: That never knew but better, is some burden:
TIMON: Thy nature did commence in sufferance, time
TIMON: Hath made thee hard in't. Why shouldst thou hate men?
TIMON: They never flatter'd thee: what hast thou given?
TIMON: If thou wilt curse, thy father, that poor rag,
TIMON: Must be thy subject, who in spite put stuff
TIMON: To some she beggar and compounded thee
TIMON: Poor rogue hereditary. Hence, be gone!
TIMON: If thou hadst not been born the worst of men,
TIMON: Thou hadst been a knave and flatterer.
APEMANTUS: Art thou proud yet?
TIMON: Ay, that I am not thee.
APEMANTUS: I, that I was
APEMANTUS: No prodigal.
TIMON: I, that I am one now:
TIMON: Were all the wealth I have shut up in thee,
TIMON: I'ld give thee leave to hang it. Get thee gone.
TIMON: That the whole life of Athens were in this!
TIMON: Thus would I eat it.
NARRATOR: Eating a root
APEMANTUS: Here, I will mend thy feast.
NARRATOR: Offering him a root
TIMON: First mend my company, take away thyself.
APEMANTUS: So I shall mend mine own, by the lack of thine.
TIMON: 'Tis not well mended so, it is but botch'd,
TIMON: if not, I would it were.
APEMANTUS: What wouldst thou have to Athens?
TIMON: Thee thither in a whirlwind. If thou wilt,
TIMON: Tell them there I have gold, look, so I have.
APEMANTUS: Here is no use for gold.
TIMON: The best and truest,
TIMON: For here it sleeps, and does no hired harm.
APEMANTUS: Where liest o' nights, Timon?
TIMON: Under that's above me.
TIMON: Where feed'st thou o' days, Apemantus?
APEMANTUS: Where my stomach finds meat, or, rather, where I eat
APEMANTUS: it.
TIMON: Would poison were obedient and knew my mind!
APEMANTUS: Where wouldst thou send it?
TIMON: To sauce thy dishes.
APEMANTUS: The middle of humanity thou never knewest, but the
APEMANTUS: extremity of both ends: when thou wast in thy gilt
APEMANTUS: and thy perfume, they mocked thee for too much
APEMANTUS: curiosity, in thy rags thou knowest none, but art
APEMANTUS: despised for the contrary. There's a medlar for
APEMANTUS: thee, eat it.
TIMON: On what I hate I feed not.
APEMANTUS: Dost hate a medlar?
TIMON: Ay, though it look like thee.
APEMANTUS: An thou hadst hated meddlers sooner, thou shouldst
APEMANTUS: have loved thyself better now. What man didst thou
APEMANTUS: ever know unthrift that was beloved after his means?
TIMON: Who, without those means thou talkest of, didst thou
TIMON: ever know beloved?
APEMANTUS: Myself.
TIMON: I understand thee, thou hadst some means to keep a
TIMON: dog.
APEMANTUS: What things in the world canst thou nearest compare
APEMANTUS: to thy flatterers?
TIMON: Women nearest, but men, men are the things
TIMON: themselves. What wouldst thou do with the world,
TIMON: Apemantus, if it lay in thy power?
APEMANTUS: Give it the beasts, to be rid of the men.
TIMON: Wouldst thou have thyself fall in the confusion of
TIMON: men, and remain a beast with the beasts?
APEMANTUS: Ay, Timon.
TIMON: A beastly ambition, which the gods grant thee t'
TIMON: attain to! If thou wert the lion, the fox would
TIMON: beguile thee, if thou wert the lamb, the fox would
TIMON: eat three: if thou wert the fox, the lion would
TIMON: suspect thee, when peradventure thou wert accused by
TIMON: the ass: if thou wert the ass, thy dulness would
TIMON: torment thee, and still thou livedst but as a
TIMON: breakfast to the wolf: if thou wert the wolf, thy
TIMON: greediness would afflict thee, and oft thou shouldst
TIMON: hazard thy life for thy dinner: wert thou the
TIMON: unicorn, pride and wrath would confound thee and
TIMON: make thine own self the conquest of thy fury: wert
TIMON: thou a bear, thou wouldst be killed by the horse:
TIMON: wert thou a horse, thou wouldst be seized by the
TIMON: leopard: wert thou a leopard, thou wert german to
TIMON: the lion and the spots of thy kindred were jurors on
TIMON: thy life: all thy safety were remotion and thy
TIMON: defence absence. What beast couldst thou be, that
TIMON: were not subject to a beast? and what a beast art
TIMON: thou already, that seest not thy loss in
TIMON: transformation!
APEMANTUS: If thou couldst please me with speaking to me, thou
APEMANTUS: mightst have hit upon it here: the commonwealth of
APEMANTUS: Athens is become a forest of beasts.
TIMON: How has the ass broke the wall, that thou art out of the city?
APEMANTUS: Yonder comes a poet and a painter: the plague of
APEMANTUS: company light upon thee! I will fear to catch it
APEMANTUS: and give way: when I know not what else to do, I'll
APEMANTUS: see thee again.
TIMON: When there is nothing living but thee, thou shalt be
TIMON: welcome. I had rather be a beggar's dog than Apemantus.
APEMANTUS: Thou art the cap of all the fools alive.
TIMON: Would thou wert clean enough to spit upon!
APEMANTUS: A plague on thee! thou art too bad to curse.
TIMON: All villains that do stand by thee are pure.
APEMANTUS: There is no leprosy but what thou speak'st.
TIMON: If I name thee.
TIMON: I'll beat thee, but I should infect my hands.
APEMANTUS: I would my tongue could rot them off!
TIMON: Away, thou issue of a mangy dog!
TIMON: Choler does kill me that thou art alive,
TIMON: I swound to see thee.
APEMANTUS: Would thou wouldst burst!
TIMON: Away,
TIMON: Thou tedious rogue! I am sorry I shall lose
TIMON: A stone by thee.
NARRATOR: Throws a stone at him
APEMANTUS: Beast!
TIMON: Slave!
APEMANTUS: Toad!
TIMON: Rogue, rogue, rogue!
TIMON: I am sick of this false world, and will love nought
TIMON: But even the mere necessities upon 't.
TIMON: Then, Timon, presently prepare thy grave,
TIMON: Lie where the light foam the sea may beat
TIMON: Thy grave-stone daily: make thine epitaph,
TIMON: That death in me at others' lives may laugh.
NARRATOR: To the gold
TIMON: O thou sweet king-killer, and dear divorce
TIMON: 'Twixt natural son and sire! thou bright defiler
TIMON: Of Hymen's purest bed! thou valiant Mars!
TIMON: Thou ever young, fresh, loved and delicate wooer,
TIMON: Whose blush doth thaw the consecrated snow
TIMON: That lies on Dian's lap! thou visible god,
TIMON: That solder'st close impossibilities,
TIMON: And makest them kiss! that speak'st with
TIMON: every tongue,
TIMON: To every purpose! O thou touch of hearts!
TIMON: Think, thy slave man rebels, and by thy virtue
TIMON: Set them into confounding odds, that beasts
TIMON: May have the world in empire!
APEMANTUS: Would 'twere so!
APEMANTUS: But not till I am dead. I'll say thou'st gold:
APEMANTUS: Thou wilt be throng'd to shortly.
TIMON: Throng'd to!
APEMANTUS: Ay.
TIMON: Thy back, I prithee.
APEMANTUS: Live, and love thy misery.
TIMON: Long live so, and so die.
NARRATOR: Exit APEMANTUS
TIMON: I am quit.
TIMON: Moe things like men! Eat, Timon, and abhor them.
NARRATOR: Enter Banditti
First Bandit: Where should he have this gold? It is some poor
First Bandit: fragment, some slender sort of his remainder: the
First Bandit: mere want of gold, and the falling-from of his
First Bandit: friends, drove him into this melancholy.
Second Bandit: It is noised he hath a mass of treasure.
Third Bandit: Let us make the assay upon him: if he care not
Third Bandit: for't, he will supply us easily, if he covetously
Third Bandit: reserve it, how shall's get it?
Second Bandit: True, for he bears it not about him, 'tis hid.
First Bandit: Is not this he?
Banditti: Where?
Second Bandit: 'Tis his description.
Third Bandit: He, I know him.
Banditti: Save thee, Timon.
TIMON: Now, thieves?
Banditti: Soldiers, not thieves.
TIMON: Both too, and women's sons.
Banditti: We are not thieves, but men that much do want.
TIMON: Your greatest want is, you want much of meat.
TIMON: Why should you want? Behold, the earth hath roots,
TIMON: Within this mile break forth a hundred springs,
TIMON: The oaks bear mast, the briers scarlet hips,
TIMON: The bounteous housewife, nature, on each bush
TIMON: Lays her full mess before you. Want! why want?
First Bandit: We cannot live on grass, on berries, water,
First Bandit: As beasts and birds and fishes.
TIMON: Nor on the beasts themselves, the birds, and fishes,
TIMON: You must eat men. Yet thanks I must you con
TIMON: That you are thieves profess'd, that you work not
TIMON: In holier shapes: for there is boundless theft
TIMON: In limited professions. Rascal thieves,
TIMON: Here's gold. Go, suck the subtle blood o' the grape,
TIMON: Till the high fever seethe your blood to froth,
TIMON: And so 'scape hanging: trust not the physician,
TIMON: His antidotes are poison, and he slays
TIMON: Moe than you rob: take wealth and lives together,
TIMON: Do villany, do, since you protest to do't,
TIMON: Like workmen. I'll example you with thievery.
TIMON: The sun's a thief, and with his great attraction
TIMON: Robs the vast sea: the moon's an arrant thief,
TIMON: And her pale fire she snatches from the sun:
TIMON: The sea's a thief, whose liquid surge resolves
TIMON: The moon into salt tears: the earth's a thief,
TIMON: That feeds and breeds by a composture stolen
TIMON: From general excrement: each thing's a thief:
TIMON: The laws, your curb and whip, in their rough power
TIMON: Have uncheque'd theft. Love not yourselves: away,
TIMON: Rob one another. There's more gold. Cut throats:
TIMON: All that you meet are thieves: to Athens go,
TIMON: Break open shops, nothing can you steal,
TIMON: But thieves do lose it: steal no less for this
TIMON: I give you, and gold confound you howsoe'er! Amen.
Third Bandit: Has almost charmed me from my profession, by
Third Bandit: persuading me to it.
First Bandit: 'Tis in the malice of mankind that he thus advises
First Bandit: us, not to have us thrive in our mystery.
Second Bandit: I'll believe him as an enemy, and give over my trade.
First Bandit: Let us first see peace in Athens: there is no time
First Bandit: so miserable but a man may be true.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Banditti
NARRATOR: Enter FLAVIUS
FLAVIUS: O you gods!
FLAVIUS: Is yond despised and ruinous man my lord?
FLAVIUS: Full of decay and failing? O monument
FLAVIUS: And wonder of good deeds evilly bestow'd!
FLAVIUS: What an alteration of honour
FLAVIUS: Has desperate want made!
FLAVIUS: What viler thing upon the earth than friends
FLAVIUS: Who can bring noblest minds to basest ends!
FLAVIUS: How rarely does it meet with this time's guise,
FLAVIUS: When man was wish'd to love his enemies!
FLAVIUS: Grant I may ever love, and rather woo
FLAVIUS: Those that would mischief me than those that do!
FLAVIUS: Has caught me in his eye: I will present
FLAVIUS: My honest grief unto him, and, as my lord,
FLAVIUS: Still serve him with my life. My dearest master!
TIMON: Away! what art thou?
FLAVIUS: Have you forgot me, sir?
TIMON: Why dost ask that? I have forgot all men,
TIMON: Then, if thou grant'st thou'rt a man, I have forgot thee.
FLAVIUS: An honest poor servant of yours.
TIMON: Then I know thee not:
TIMON: I never had honest man about me, I, all
TIMON: I kept were knaves, to serve in meat to villains.
FLAVIUS: The gods are witness,
FLAVIUS: Ne'er did poor steward wear a truer grief
FLAVIUS: For his undone lord than mine eyes for you.
TIMON: What, dost thou weep? Come nearer. Then I
TIMON: love thee,
TIMON: Because thou art a woman, and disclaim'st
TIMON: Flinty mankind, whose eyes do never give
TIMON: But thorough lust and laughter. Pity's sleeping:
TIMON: Strange times, that weep with laughing, not with weeping!
FLAVIUS: I beg of you to know me, good my lord,
FLAVIUS: To accept my grief and whilst this poor wealth lasts
FLAVIUS: To entertain me as your steward still.
TIMON: Had I a steward
TIMON: So true, so just, and now so comfortable?
TIMON: It almost turns my dangerous nature mild.
TIMON: Let me behold thy face. Surely, this man
TIMON: Was born of woman.
TIMON: Forgive my general and exceptless rashness,
TIMON: You perpetual-sober gods! I do proclaim
TIMON: One honest man--mistake me not--but one,
TIMON: No more, I pray,--and he's a steward.
TIMON: How fain would I have hated all mankind!
TIMON: And thou redeem'st thyself: but all, save thee,
TIMON: I fell with curses.
TIMON: Methinks thou art more honest now than wise,
TIMON: For, by oppressing and betraying me,
TIMON: Thou mightst have sooner got another service:
TIMON: For many so arrive at second masters,
TIMON: Upon their first lord's neck. But tell me true--
TIMON: For I must ever doubt, though ne'er so sure--
TIMON: Is not thy kindness subtle, covetous,
TIMON: If not a usuring kindness, and, as rich men deal gifts,
TIMON: Expecting in return twenty for one?
FLAVIUS: No, my most worthy master, in whose breast
FLAVIUS: Doubt and suspect, alas, are placed too late:
FLAVIUS: You should have fear'd false times when you did feast:
FLAVIUS: Suspect still comes where an estate is least.
FLAVIUS: That which I show, heaven knows, is merely love,
FLAVIUS: Duty and zeal to your unmatched mind,
FLAVIUS: Care of your food and living, and, believe it,
FLAVIUS: My most honour'd lord,
FLAVIUS: For any benefit that points to me,
FLAVIUS: Either in hope or present, I'ld exchange
FLAVIUS: For this one wish, that you had power and wealth
FLAVIUS: To requite me, by making rich yourself.
TIMON: Look thee, 'tis so! Thou singly honest man,
TIMON: Here, take: the gods out of my misery
