TIMON: Have sent thee treasure. Go, live rich and happy,
TIMON: But thus condition'd: thou shalt build from men,
TIMON: Hate all, curse all, show charity to none,
TIMON: But let the famish'd flesh slide from the bone,
TIMON: Ere thou relieve the beggar, give to dogs
TIMON: What thou deny'st to men, let prisons swallow 'em,
TIMON: Debts wither 'em to nothing, be men like
TIMON: blasted woods,
TIMON: And may diseases lick up their false bloods!
TIMON: And so farewell and thrive.
FLAVIUS: O, let me stay,
FLAVIUS: And comfort you, my master.
TIMON: If thou hatest curses,
TIMON: Stay not, fly, whilst thou art blest and free:
TIMON: Ne'er see thou man, and let me ne'er see thee.
NARRATOR: Exit FLAVIUS. TIMON retires to his cave
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The woods. Before Timon's cave.
NARRATOR: Enter Poet and Painter, TIMON watching them from his cave
Painter: As I took note of the place, it cannot be far where
Painter: he abides.
Poet: What's to be thought of him? does the rumour hold
Poet: for true, that he's so full of gold?
Painter: Certain: Alcibiades reports it, Phrynia and
Painter: Timandra had gold of him: he likewise enriched poor
Painter: straggling soldiers with great quantity: 'tis said
Painter: he gave unto his steward a mighty sum.
Poet: Then this breaking of his has been but a try for his friends.
Painter: Nothing else: you shall see him a palm in Athens
Painter: again, and flourish with the highest. Therefore
Painter: 'tis not amiss we tender our loves to him, in this
Painter: supposed distress of his: it will show honestly in
Painter: us, and is very likely to load our purposes with
Painter: what they travail for, if it be a just true report
Painter: that goes of his having.
Poet: What have you now to present unto him?
Painter: Nothing at this time but my visitation: only I will
Painter: promise him an excellent piece.
Poet: I must serve him so too, tell him of an intent
Poet: that's coming toward him.
Painter: Good as the best. Promising is the very air o' the
Painter: time: it opens the eyes of expectation:
Painter: performance is ever the duller for his act, and,
Painter: but in the plainer and simpler kind of people, the
Painter: deed of saying is quite out of use. To promise is
Painter: most courtly and fashionable: performance is a kind
Painter: of will or testament which argues a great sickness
Painter: in his judgment that makes it.
NARRATOR: TIMON comes from his cave, behind
TIMON: [Aside]  Excellent workman! thou canst not paint a
TIMON: man so bad as is thyself.
Poet: I am thinking what I shall say I have provided for
Poet: him: it must be a personating of himself, a satire
Poet: against the softness of prosperity, with a discovery
Poet: of the infinite flatteries that follow youth and opulency.
TIMON: [Aside]  Must thou needs stand for a villain in
TIMON: thine own work? wilt thou whip thine own faults in
TIMON: other men? Do so, I have gold for thee.
Poet: Nay, let's seek him:
Poet: Then do we sin against our own estate,
Poet: When we may profit meet, and come too late.
Painter: True,
Painter: When the day serves, before black-corner'd night,
Painter: Find what thou want'st by free and offer'd light. Come.
TIMON: [Aside]  I'll meet you at the turn. What a
TIMON: god's gold,
TIMON: That he is worshipp'd in a baser temple
TIMON: Than where swine feed!
TIMON: 'Tis thou that rigg'st the bark and plough'st the foam,
TIMON: Settlest admired reverence in a slave:
TIMON: To thee be worship! and thy saints for aye
TIMON: Be crown'd with plagues that thee alone obey!
TIMON: Fit I meet them.
NARRATOR: Coming forward
Poet: Hail, worthy Timon!
Painter: Our late noble master!
TIMON: Have I once lived to see two honest men?
Poet: Sir,
Poet: Having often of your open bounty tasted,
Poet: Hearing you were retired, your friends fall'n off,
Poet: Whose thankless natures--O abhorred spirits!--
Poet: Not all the whips of heaven are large enough:
Poet: What! to you,
Poet: Whose star-like nobleness gave life and influence
Poet: To their whole being! I am rapt and cannot cover
Poet: The monstrous bulk of this ingratitude
Poet: With any size of words.
TIMON: Let it go naked, men may see't the better:
TIMON: You that are honest, by being what you are,
TIMON: Make them best seen and known.
Painter: He and myself
Painter: Have travail'd in the great shower of your gifts,
Painter: And sweetly felt it.
TIMON: Ay, you are honest men.
Painter: We are hither come to offer you our service.
TIMON: Most honest men! Why, how shall I requite you?
TIMON: Can you eat roots, and drink cold water? no.
Both: What we can do, we'll do, to do you service.
TIMON: Ye're honest men: ye've heard that I have gold,
TIMON: I am sure you have: speak truth, ye're honest men.
Painter: So it is said, my noble lord, but therefore
Painter: Came not my friend nor I.
TIMON: Good honest men! Thou draw'st a counterfeit
TIMON: Best in all Athens: thou'rt, indeed, the best,
TIMON: Thou counterfeit'st most lively.
Painter: So, so, my lord.
TIMON: E'en so, sir, as I say. And, for thy fiction,
TIMON: Why, thy verse swells with stuff so fine and smooth
TIMON: That thou art even natural in thine art.
TIMON: But, for all this, my honest-natured friends,
TIMON: I must needs say you have a little fault:
TIMON: Marry, 'tis not monstrous in you, neither wish I
TIMON: You take much pains to mend.
Both: Beseech your honour
Both: To make it known to us.
TIMON: You'll take it ill.
Both: Most thankfully, my lord.
TIMON: Will you, indeed?
Both: Doubt it not, worthy lord.
TIMON: There's never a one of you but trusts a knave,
TIMON: That mightily deceives you.
Both: Do we, my lord?
TIMON: Ay, and you hear him cog, see him dissemble,
TIMON: Know his gross patchery, love him, feed him,
TIMON: Keep in your bosom: yet remain assured
TIMON: That he's a made-up villain.
Painter: I know none such, my lord.
Poet: Nor I.
TIMON: Look you, I love you well, I'll give you gold,
TIMON: Rid me these villains from your companies:
TIMON: Hang them or stab them, drown them in a draught,
TIMON: Confound them by some course, and come to me,
TIMON: I'll give you gold enough.
Both: Name them, my lord, let's know them.
TIMON: You that way and you this, but two in company,
TIMON: Each man apart, all single and alone,
TIMON: Yet an arch-villain keeps him company.
TIMON: If where thou art two villains shall not be,
TIMON: Come not near him. If thou wouldst not reside
TIMON: But where one villain is, then him abandon.
TIMON: Hence, pack! there's gold, you came for gold, ye slaves:
NARRATOR: To Painter
TIMON: You have work'd for me, there's payment for you: hence!
NARRATOR: To Poet
TIMON: You are an alchemist, make gold of that.
TIMON: Out, rascal dogs!
NARRATOR: Beats them out, and then retires to his cave
NARRATOR: Enter FLAVIUS and two Senators
FLAVIUS: It is in vain that you would speak with Timon,
FLAVIUS: For he is set so only to himself
FLAVIUS: That nothing but himself which looks like man
FLAVIUS: Is friendly with him.
First Senator: Bring us to his cave:
First Senator: It is our part and promise to the Athenians
First Senator: To speak with Timon.
Second Senator: At all times alike
Second Senator: Men are not still the same: 'twas time and griefs
Second Senator: That framed him thus: time, with his fairer hand,
Second Senator: Offering the fortunes of his former days,
Second Senator: The former man may make him. Bring us to him,
Second Senator: And chance it as it may.
FLAVIUS: Here is his cave.
FLAVIUS: Peace and content be here! Lord Timon! Timon!
FLAVIUS: Look out, and speak to friends: the Athenians,
FLAVIUS: By two of their most reverend senate, greet thee:
FLAVIUS: Speak to them, noble Timon.
NARRATOR: TIMON comes from his cave
TIMON: Thou sun, that comfort'st, burn! Speak, and
TIMON: be hang'd:
TIMON: For each true word, a blister! and each false
TIMON: Be as cauterizing to the root o' the tongue,
TIMON: Consuming it with speaking!
First Senator: Worthy Timon,--
TIMON: Of none but such as you, and you of Timon.
First Senator: The senators of Athens greet thee, Timon.
TIMON: I thank them, and would send them back the plague,
TIMON: Could I but catch it for them.
First Senator: O, forget
First Senator: What we are sorry for ourselves in thee.
First Senator: The senators with one consent of love
First Senator: Entreat thee back to Athens, who have thought
First Senator: On special dignities, which vacant lie
First Senator: For thy best use and wearing.
Second Senator: They confess
Second Senator: Toward thee forgetfulness too general, gross:
Second Senator: Which now the public body, which doth seldom
Second Senator: Play the recanter, feeling in itself
Second Senator: A lack of Timon's aid, hath sense withal
Second Senator: Of its own fail, restraining aid to Timon,
Second Senator: And send forth us, to make their sorrow'd render,
Second Senator: Together with a recompense more fruitful
Second Senator: Than their offence can weigh down by the dram,
Second Senator: Ay, even such heaps and sums of love and wealth
Second Senator: As shall to thee blot out what wrongs were theirs
Second Senator: And write in thee the figures of their love,
Second Senator: Ever to read them thine.
TIMON: You witch me in it,
TIMON: Surprise me to the very brink of tears:
TIMON: Lend me a fool's heart and a woman's eyes,
TIMON: And I'll beweep these comforts, worthy senators.
First Senator: Therefore, so please thee to return with us
First Senator: And of our Athens, thine and ours, to take
First Senator: The captainship, thou shalt be met with thanks,
First Senator: Allow'd with absolute power and thy good name
First Senator: Live with authority: so soon we shall drive back
First Senator: Of Alcibiades the approaches wild,
First Senator: Who, like a boar too savage, doth root up
First Senator: His country's peace.
Second Senator: And shakes his threatening sword
Second Senator: Against the walls of Athens.
First Senator: Therefore, Timon,--
TIMON: Well, sir, I will, therefore, I will, sir, thus:
TIMON: If Alcibiades kill my countrymen,
TIMON: Let Alcibiades know this of Timon,
TIMON: That Timon cares not. But if be sack fair Athens,
TIMON: And take our goodly aged men by the beards,
TIMON: Giving our holy virgins to the stain
TIMON: Of contumelious, beastly, mad-brain'd war,
TIMON: Then let him know, and tell him Timon speaks it,
TIMON: In pity of our aged and our youth,
TIMON: I cannot choose but tell him, that I care not,
TIMON: And let him take't at worst, for their knives care not,
TIMON: While you have throats to answer: for myself,
TIMON: There's not a whittle in the unruly camp
TIMON: But I do prize it at my love before
TIMON: The reverend'st throat in Athens. So I leave you
TIMON: To the protection of the prosperous gods,
TIMON: As thieves to keepers.
FLAVIUS: Stay not, all's in vain.
TIMON: Why, I was writing of my epitaph,
TIMON: it will be seen to-morrow: my long sickness
TIMON: Of health and living now begins to mend,
TIMON: And nothing brings me all things. Go, live still,
TIMON: Be Alcibiades your plague, you his,
TIMON: And last so long enough!
First Senator: We speak in vain.
TIMON: But yet I love my country, and am not
TIMON: One that rejoices in the common wreck,
TIMON: As common bruit doth put it.
First Senator: That's well spoke.
TIMON: Commend me to my loving countrymen,--
First Senator: These words become your lips as they pass
First Senator: thorough them.
Second Senator: And enter in our ears like great triumphers
Second Senator: In their applauding gates.
TIMON: Commend me to them,
TIMON: And tell them that, to ease them of their griefs,
TIMON: Their fears of hostile strokes, their aches, losses,
TIMON: Their pangs of love, with other incident throes
TIMON: That nature's fragile vessel doth sustain
TIMON: In life's uncertain voyage, I will some kindness do them:
TIMON: I'll teach them to prevent wild Alcibiades' wrath.
First Senator: I like this well, he will return again.
TIMON: I have a tree, which grows here in my close,
TIMON: That mine own use invites me to cut down,
TIMON: And shortly must I fell it: tell my friends,
TIMON: Tell Athens, in the sequence of degree
TIMON: From high to low throughout, that whoso please
TIMON: To stop affliction, let him take his haste,
TIMON: Come hither, ere my tree hath felt the axe,
TIMON: And hang himself. I pray you, do my greeting.
FLAVIUS: Trouble him no further, thus you still shall find him.
TIMON: Come not to me again: but say to Athens,
TIMON: Timon hath made his everlasting mansion
TIMON: Upon the beached verge of the salt flood,
TIMON: Who once a day with his embossed froth
TIMON: The turbulent surge shall cover: thither come,
TIMON: And let my grave-stone be your oracle.
TIMON: Lips, let sour words go by and language end:
TIMON: What is amiss plague and infection mend!
TIMON: Graves only be men's works and death their gain!
TIMON: Sun, hide thy beams! Timon hath done his reign.
NARRATOR: Retires to his cave
First Senator: His discontents are unremoveably
First Senator: Coupled to nature.
Second Senator: Our hope in him is dead: let us return,
Second Senator: And strain what other means is left unto us
Second Senator: In our dear peril.
First Senator: It requires swift foot.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Before the walls of Athens.
NARRATOR: Enter two Senators and a Messenger
First Senator: Thou hast painfully discover'd: are his files
First Senator: As full as thy report?
Messenger: have spoke the least:
Messenger: Besides, his expedition promises
Messenger: Present approach.
Second Senator: We stand much hazard, if they bring not Timon.
Messenger: I met a courier, one mine ancient friend,
Messenger: Whom, though in general part we were opposed,
Messenger: Yet our old love made a particular force,
Messenger: And made us speak like friends: this man was riding
Messenger: From Alcibiades to Timon's cave,
Messenger: With letters of entreaty, which imported
Messenger: His fellowship i' the cause against your city,
Messenger: In part for his sake moved.
First Senator: Here come our brothers.
NARRATOR: Enter the Senators from TIMON
Third Senator: No talk of Timon, nothing of him expect.
Third Senator: The enemies' drum is heard, and fearful scouring
Third Senator: Doth choke the air with dust: in, and prepare:
Third Senator: Ours is the fall, I fear, our foes the snare.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The woods. Timon's cave, and a rude tomb seen.
NARRATOR: Enter a Soldier, seeking TIMON
Soldier: By all description this should be the place.
Soldier: Who's here? speak, ho! No answer! What is this?
Soldier: Timon is dead, who hath outstretch'd his span:
Soldier: Some beast rear'd this, there does not live a man.
Soldier: Dead, sure, and this his grave. What's on this tomb
Soldier: I cannot read, the character I'll take with wax:
Soldier: Our captain hath in every figure skill,
Soldier: An aged interpreter, though young in days:
Soldier: Before proud Athens he's set down by this,
Soldier: Whose fall the mark of his ambition is.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Before the walls of Athens.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound. Enter ALCIBIADES with his powers
ALCIBIADES: Sound to this coward and lascivious town
ALCIBIADES: Our terrible approach.
NARRATOR: A parley sounded
NARRATOR: Enter Senators on the walls
ALCIBIADES: Till now you have gone on and fill'd the time
ALCIBIADES: With all licentious measure, making your wills
ALCIBIADES: The scope of justice, till now myself and such
ALCIBIADES: As slept within the shadow of your power
ALCIBIADES: Hav e wander'd with our traversed arms and breathed
ALCIBIADES: Our sufferance vainly: now the time is flush,
ALCIBIADES: When crouching marrow in the bearer strong
ALCIBIADES: Cries of itself 'No more:' now breathless wrong
ALCIBIADES: Shall sit and pant in your great chairs of ease,
ALCIBIADES: And pursy insolence shall break his wind
ALCIBIADES: With fear and horrid flight.
First Senator: Noble and young,
First Senator: When thy first griefs were but a mere conceit,
First Senator: Ere thou hadst power or we had cause of fear,
First Senator: We sent to thee, to give thy rages balm,
First Senator: To wipe out our ingratitude with loves
First Senator: Above their quantity.
Second Senator: So did we woo
Second Senator: Transformed Timon to our city's love
Second Senator: By humble message and by promised means:
Second Senator: We were not all unkind, nor all deserve
Second Senator: The common stroke of war.
First Senator: These walls of ours
First Senator: Were not erected by their hands from whom
First Senator: You have received your griefs, nor are they such
First Senator: That these great towers, trophies and schools
First Senator: should fall
First Senator: For private faults in them.
Second Senator: Nor are they living
Second Senator: Who were the motives that you first went out,
Second Senator: Shame that they wanted cunning, in excess
Second Senator: Hath broke their hearts. March, noble lord,
Second Senator: Into our city with thy banners spread:
Second Senator: By decimation, and a tithed death--
Second Senator: If thy revenges hunger for that food
Second Senator: Which nature loathes--take thou the destined tenth,
Second Senator: And by the hazard of the spotted die
Second Senator: Let die the spotted.
First Senator: All have not offended,
First Senator: For those that were, it is not square to take
First Senator: On those that are, revenges: crimes, like lands,
First Senator: Are not inherited. Then, dear countryman,
First Senator: Bring in thy ranks, but leave without thy rage:
First Senator: Spare thy Athenian cradle and those kin
First Senator: Which in the bluster of thy wrath must fall
First Senator: With those that have offended: like a shepherd,
First Senator: Approach the fold and cull the infected forth,
First Senator: But kill not all together.
Second Senator: What thou wilt,
Second Senator: Thou rather shalt enforce it with thy smile
Second Senator: Than hew to't with thy sword.
First Senator: Set but thy foot
First Senator: Against our rampired gates, and they shall ope,
First Senator: So thou wilt send thy gentle heart before,
First Senator: To say thou'lt enter friendly.
Second Senator: Throw thy glove,
Second Senator: Or any token of thine honour else,
Second Senator: That thou wilt use the wars as thy redress
Second Senator: And not as our confusion, all thy powers
Second Senator: Shall make their harbour in our town, till we
Second Senator: Have seal'd thy full desire.
ALCIBIADES: Then there's my glove,
ALCIBIADES: Descend, and open your uncharged ports:
ALCIBIADES: Those enemies of Timon's and mine own
ALCIBIADES: Whom you yourselves shall set out for reproof
ALCIBIADES: Fall and no more: and, to atone your fears
ALCIBIADES: With my more noble meaning, not a man
ALCIBIADES: Shall pass his quarter, or offend the stream
ALCIBIADES: Of regular justice in your city's bounds,
ALCIBIADES: But shall be render'd to your public laws
ALCIBIADES: At heaviest answer.
Both: 'Tis most nobly spoken.
ALCIBIADES: Descend, and keep your words.
NARRATOR: The Senators descend, and open the gates
NARRATOR: Enter Soldier
Soldier: My noble general, Timon is dead,
Soldier: Entomb'd upon the very hem o' the sea,
Soldier: And on his grave-stone this insculpture, which
Soldier: With wax I brought away, whose soft impression
Soldier: Interprets for my poor ignorance.
ALCIBIADES: [Reads the epitaph]  'Here lies a
ALCIBIADES: wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft:
ALCIBIADES: Seek not my name: a plague consume you wicked
ALCIBIADES: caitiffs left!
ALCIBIADES: Here lie I, Timon, who, alive, all living men did hate:
ALCIBIADES: Pass by and curse thy fill, but pass and stay
ALCIBIADES: not here thy gait.'
ALCIBIADES: These well express in thee thy latter spirits:
ALCIBIADES: Though thou abhorr'dst in us our human griefs,
ALCIBIADES: Scorn'dst our brain's flow and those our
ALCIBIADES: droplets which
ALCIBIADES: From niggard nature fall, yet rich conceit
ALCIBIADES: Taught thee to make vast Neptune weep for aye
ALCIBIADES: On thy low grave, on faults forgiven. Dead
ALCIBIADES: Is noble Timon: of whose memory
ALCIBIADES: Hereafter more. Bring me into your city,
ALCIBIADES: And I will use the olive with my sword,
ALCIBIADES: Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each
ALCIBIADES: Prescribe to other as each other's leech.
ALCIBIADES: Let our drums strike.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Titus Andronicus '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. Before the Capitol.
NARRATOR: The Tomb of the ANDRONICI appearing, the Tribunes  and Senators aloft. Enter, below, from one side,  SATURNINUS and his Followers, and, from the other side, BASSIANUS and his Followers, with drum and colours
SATURNINUS: Noble patricians, patrons of my right,
SATURNINUS: Defend the justice of my cause with arms,
SATURNINUS: And, countrymen, my loving followers,
SATURNINUS: Plead my successive title with your swords:
SATURNINUS: I am his first-born son, that was the last
SATURNINUS: That wore the imperial diadem of Rome,
SATURNINUS: Then let my father's honours live in me,
SATURNINUS: Nor wrong mine age with this indignity.
BASSIANUS: Romans, friends, followers, favorers of my right,
BASSIANUS: If ever Bassianus, Caesar's son,
BASSIANUS: Were gracious in the eyes of royal Rome,
BASSIANUS: Keep then this passage to the Capitol
BASSIANUS: And suffer not dishonour to approach
BASSIANUS: The imperial seat, to virtue consecrate,
BASSIANUS: To justice, continence and nobility,
BASSIANUS: But let desert in pure election shine,
BASSIANUS: And, Romans, fight for freedom in your choice.
NARRATOR: Enter MARCUS ANDRONICUS, aloft, with the crown
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Princes, that strive by factions and by friends
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Ambitiously for rule and empery,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Know that the people of Rome, for whom we stand
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: A special party, have, by common voice,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: In election for the Roman empery,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Chosen Andronicus, surnamed Pius
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: For many good and great deserts to Rome:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: A nobler man, a braver warrior,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lives not this day within the city walls:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: He by the senate is accit'd home
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: From weary wars against the barbarous Goths,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That, with his sons, a terror to our foes,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Hath yoked a nation strong, train'd up in arms.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Ten years are spent since first he undertook
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This cause of Rome and chastised with arms
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Our enemies' pride: five times he hath return'd
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Bleeding to Rome, bearing his valiant sons
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: In coffins from the field,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And now at last, laden with horror's spoils,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Returns the good Andronicus to Rome,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Renowned Titus, flourishing in arms.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Let us entreat, by honour of his name,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Whom worthily you would have now succeed.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And in the Capitol and senate's right,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Whom you pretend to honour and adore,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That you withdraw you and abate your strength,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Dismiss your followers and, as suitors should,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Plead your deserts in peace and humbleness.
SATURNINUS: How fair the tribune speaks to calm my thoughts!
BASSIANUS: Marcus Andronicus, so I do ally
BASSIANUS: In thy uprightness and integrity,
BASSIANUS: And so I love and honour thee and thine,
BASSIANUS: Thy noble brother Titus and his sons,
BASSIANUS: And her to whom my thoughts are humbled all,
BASSIANUS: Gracious Lavinia, Rome's rich ornament,
BASSIANUS: That I will here dismiss my loving friends,
BASSIANUS: And to my fortunes and the people's favor
BASSIANUS: Commit my cause in balance to be weigh'd.
NARRATOR: Exeunt the followers of BASSIANUS
SATURNINUS: Friends, that have been thus forward in my right,
SATURNINUS: I thank you all and here dismiss you all,
SATURNINUS: And to the love and favor of my country
SATURNINUS: Commit myself, my person and the cause.
NARRATOR: Exeunt the followers of SATURNINUS
SATURNINUS: Rome, be as just and gracious unto me
SATURNINUS: As I am confident and kind to thee.
SATURNINUS: Open the gates, and let me in.
BASSIANUS: Tribunes, and me, a poor competitor.
NARRATOR: Flourish. SATURNINUS and BASSIANUS go up into the Capitol
NARRATOR: Enter a Captain
Captain: Romans, make way: the good Andronicus.
Captain: Patron of virtue, Rome's best champion,
Captain: Successful in the battles that he fights,
Captain: With honour and with fortune is return'd
Captain: From where he circumscribed with his sword,
Captain: And brought to yoke, the enemies of Rome.
Captain: Drums and trumpets sounded. Enter MARTIUS and  MUTIUS, After them, two Men bearing a coffin  covered with black, then LUCIUS and QUINTUS. After  them, TITUS ANDRONICUS, and then TAMORA, with  ALARBUS, DEMETRIUS, CHIRON, AARON, and other Goths,  prisoners, Soldiers and people following. The Bearers set down the coffin, and TITUS speaks
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hail, Rome, victorious in thy mourning weeds!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lo, as the bark, that hath discharged her fraught,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Returns with precious jading to the bay
TITUS ANDRONICUS: From whence at first she weigh'd her anchorage,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Cometh Andronicus, bound with laurel boughs,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To re-salute his country with his tears,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tears of true joy for his return to Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou great defender of this Capitol,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Stand gracious to the rites that we intend!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Romans, of five and twenty valiant sons,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Half of the number that King Priam had,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Behold the poor remains, alive and dead!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: These that survive let Rome reward with love,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: These that I bring unto their latest home,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: With burial amongst their ancestors:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here Goths have given me leave to sheathe my sword.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Titus, unkind and careless of thine own,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why suffer'st thou thy sons, unburied yet,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To hover on the dreadful shore of Styx?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Make way to lay them by their brethren.
NARRATOR: The tomb is opened
TITUS ANDRONICUS: There greet in silence, as the dead are wont,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And sleep in peace, slain in your country's wars!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O sacred receptacle of my joys,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sweet cell of virtue and nobility,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How many sons of mine hast thou in store,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That thou wilt never render to me more!
LUCIUS: Give us the proudest prisoner of the Goths,
LUCIUS: That we may hew his limbs, and on a pile
LUCIUS: Ad manes fratrum sacrifice his flesh,
LUCIUS: Before this earthy prison of their bones,
LUCIUS: That so the shadows be not unappeased,
LUCIUS: Nor we disturb'd with prodigies on earth.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I give him you, the noblest that survives,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The eldest son of this distressed queen.
TAMORA: Stay, Roman brethren! Gracious conqueror,
TAMORA: Victorious Titus, rue the tears I shed,
TAMORA: A mother's tears in passion for her son:
TAMORA: And if thy sons were ever dear to thee,
TAMORA: O, think my son to be as dear to me!
TAMORA: Sufficeth not that we are brought to Rome,
TAMORA: To beautify thy triumphs and return,
TAMORA: Captive to thee and to thy Roman yoke,
TAMORA: But must my sons be slaughter'd in the streets,
TAMORA: For valiant doings in their country's cause?
TAMORA: O, if to fight for king and commonweal
TAMORA: Were piety in thine, it is in these.
TAMORA: Andronicus, stain not thy tomb with blood:
TAMORA: Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods?
TAMORA: Draw near them then in being merciful:
TAMORA: Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge:
TAMORA: Thrice noble Titus, spare my first-born son.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Patient yourself, madam, and pardon me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: These are their brethren, whom you Goths beheld
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Alive and dead, and for their brethren slain
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Religiously they ask a sacrifice:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To this your son is mark'd, and die he must,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To appease their groaning shadows that are gone.
LUCIUS: Away with him! and make a fire straight,
LUCIUS: And with our swords, upon a pile of wood,
LUCIUS: Let's hew his limbs till they be clean consumed.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCIUS, QUINTUS, MARTIUS, and MUTIUS, with ALARBUS
TAMORA: O cruel, irreligious piety!
CHIRON: Was ever Scythia half so barbarous?
DEMETRIUS: Oppose not Scythia to ambitious Rome.
DEMETRIUS: Alarbus goes to rest, and we survive
DEMETRIUS: To tremble under Titus' threatening looks.
DEMETRIUS: Then, madam, stand resolved, but hope withal
DEMETRIUS: The self-same gods that arm'd the Queen of Troy
DEMETRIUS: With opportunity of sharp revenge
DEMETRIUS: Upon the Thracian tyrant in his tent,
DEMETRIUS: May favor Tamora, the Queen of Goths--
DEMETRIUS: When Goths were Goths and Tamora was queen--
DEMETRIUS: To quit the bloody wrongs upon her foes.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS, QUINTUS, MARTIUS and MUTIUS, with their swords bloody
LUCIUS: See, lord and father, how we have perform'd
LUCIUS: Our Roman rites: Alarbus' limbs are lopp'd,
LUCIUS: And entrails feed the sacrificing fire,
LUCIUS: Whose smoke, like incense, doth perfume the sky.
LUCIUS: Remaineth nought, but to inter our brethren,
LUCIUS: And with loud 'larums welcome them to Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Let it be so, and let Andronicus
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Make this his latest farewell to their souls.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sounded, and the coffin laid in the tomb
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In peace and honour rest you here, my sons,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rome's readiest champions, repose you here in rest,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Secure from worldly chances and mishaps!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here lurks no treason, here no envy swells,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here grow no damned grudges, here are no storms,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No noise, but silence and eternal sleep:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In peace and honour rest you here, my sons!
NARRATOR: Enter LAVINIA
LAVINIA: In peace and honour live Lord Titus long,
LAVINIA: My noble lord and father, live in fame!
LAVINIA: Lo, at this tomb my tributary tears
LAVINIA: I render, for my brethren's obsequies,
LAVINIA: And at thy feet I kneel, with tears of joy,
LAVINIA: Shed on the earth, for thy return to Rome:
LAVINIA: O, bless me here with thy victorious hand,
LAVINIA: Whose fortunes Rome's best citizens applaud!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Kind Rome, that hast thus lovingly reserved
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The cordial of mine age to glad my heart!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lavinia, live, outlive thy father's days,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And fame's eternal date, for virtue's praise!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Enter, below, MARCUS ANDRONICUS and Tribunes, re-enter SATURNINUS and BASSIANUS, attended
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Long live Lord Titus, my beloved brother,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Gracious triumpher in the eyes of Rome!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thanks, gentle tribune, noble brother Marcus.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And welcome, nephews, from successful wars,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: You that survive, and you that sleep in fame!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Fair lords, your fortunes are alike in all,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That in your country's service drew your swords:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But safer triumph is this funeral pomp,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That hath aspired to Solon's happiness
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And triumphs over chance in honour's bed.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Titus Andronicus, the people of Rome,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Whose friend in justice thou hast ever been,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Send thee by me, their tribune and their trust,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This palliament of white and spotless hue,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And name thee in election for the empire,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: With these our late-deceased emperor's sons:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Be candidatus then, and put it on,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And help to set a head on headless Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A better head her glorious body fits
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Than his that shakes for age and feebleness:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What should I don this robe, and trouble you?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Be chosen with proclamations to-day,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To-morrow yield up rule, resign my life,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And set abroad new business for you all?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rome, I have been thy soldier forty years,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And led my country's strength successfully,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And buried one and twenty valiant sons,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Knighted in field, slain manfully in arms,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In right and service of their noble country
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Give me a staff of honour for mine age,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But not a sceptre to control the world:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Upright he held it, lords, that held it last.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Titus, thou shalt obtain and ask the empery.
SATURNINUS: Proud and ambitious tribune, canst thou tell?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Patience, Prince Saturninus.
SATURNINUS: Romans, do me right:
SATURNINUS: Patricians, draw your swords: and sheathe them not
SATURNINUS: Till Saturninus be Rome's emperor.
SATURNINUS: Andronicus, would thou wert shipp'd to hell,
SATURNINUS: Rather than rob me of the people's hearts!
LUCIUS: Proud Saturnine, interrupter of the good
LUCIUS: That noble-minded Titus means to thee!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Content thee, prince, I will restore to thee
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The people's hearts, and wean them from themselves.
BASSIANUS: Andronicus, I do not flatter thee,
BASSIANUS: But honour thee, and will do till I die:
BASSIANUS: My faction if thou strengthen with thy friends,
BASSIANUS: I will most thankful be, and thanks to men
BASSIANUS: Of noble minds is honourable meed.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: People of Rome, and people's tribunes here,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I ask your voices and your suffrages:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will you bestow them friendly on Andronicus?
Tribunes: To gratify the good Andronicus,
Tribunes: And gratulate his safe return to Rome,
Tribunes: The people will accept whom he admits.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tribunes, I thank you: and this suit I make,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That you create your emperor's eldest son,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lord Saturnine, whose virtues will, I hope,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Reflect on Rome as Titan's rays on earth,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And ripen justice in this commonweal:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then, if you will elect by my advice,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Crown him and say 'Long live our emperor!'
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: With voices and applause of every sort,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Patricians and plebeians, we create
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lord Saturninus Rome's great emperor,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And say 'Long live our Emperor Saturnine!'
NARRATOR: A long flourish till they come down
SATURNINUS: Titus Andronicus, for thy favors done
SATURNINUS: To us in our election this day,
SATURNINUS: I give thee thanks in part of thy deserts,
SATURNINUS: And will with deeds requite thy gentleness:
SATURNINUS: And, for an onset, Titus, to advance
SATURNINUS: Thy name and honourable family,
SATURNINUS: Lavinia will I make my empress,
SATURNINUS: Rome's royal mistress, mistress of my heart,
SATURNINUS: And in the sacred Pantheon her espouse:
SATURNINUS: Tell me, Andronicus, doth this motion please thee?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: It doth, my worthy lord, and in this match
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I hold me highly honour'd of your grace:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And here in sight of Rome to Saturnine,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: King and commander of our commonweal,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The wide world's emperor, do I consecrate
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My sword, my chariot and my prisoners,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Presents well worthy Rome's imperial lord:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Receive them then, the tribute that I owe,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Mine honour's ensigns humbled at thy feet.
SATURNINUS: Thanks, noble Titus, father of my life!
SATURNINUS: How proud I am of thee and of thy gifts
SATURNINUS: Rome shall record, and when I do forget
SATURNINUS: The least of these unspeakable deserts,
SATURNINUS: Romans, forget your fealty to me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: [To TAMORA]  Now, madam, are you prisoner to
TITUS ANDRONICUS: an emperor,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To him that, for your honour and your state,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will use you nobly and your followers.
SATURNINUS: A goodly lady, trust me, of the hue
SATURNINUS: That I would choose, were I to choose anew.
SATURNINUS: Clear up, fair queen, that cloudy countenance:
SATURNINUS: Though chance of war hath wrought this change of cheer,
SATURNINUS: Thou comest not to be made a scorn in Rome:
SATURNINUS: Princely shall be thy usage every way.
SATURNINUS: Rest on my word, and let not discontent
SATURNINUS: Daunt all your hopes: madam, he comforts you
SATURNINUS: Can make you greater than the Queen of Goths.
SATURNINUS: Lavinia, you are not displeased with this?
LAVINIA: Not I, my lord, sith true nobility
LAVINIA: Warrants these words in princely courtesy.
SATURNINUS: Thanks, sweet Lavinia. Romans, let us go,
SATURNINUS: Ransomless here we set our prisoners free:
SATURNINUS: Proclaim our honours, lords, with trump and drum.
NARRATOR: Flourish. SATURNINUS courts TAMORA in dumb show
BASSIANUS: Lord Titus, by your leave, this maid is mine.
NARRATOR: Seizing LAVINIA
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How, sir! are you in earnest then, my lord?
BASSIANUS: Ay, noble Titus, and resolved withal
BASSIANUS: To do myself this reason and this right.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: 'Suum cuique' is our Roman justice:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This prince in justice seizeth but his own.
LUCIUS: And that he will, and shall, if Lucius live.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Traitors, avaunt! Where is the emperor's guard?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Treason, my lord! Lavinia is surprised!
SATURNINUS: Surprised! by whom?
BASSIANUS: By him that justly may
BASSIANUS: Bear his betroth'd from all the world away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt BASSIANUS and MARCUS with LAVINIA
MUTIUS: Brothers, help to convey her hence away,
MUTIUS: And with my sword I'll keep this door safe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCIUS, QUINTUS, and MARTIUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Follow, my lord, and I'll soon bring her back.
MUTIUS: My lord, you pass not here.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What, villain boy!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Barr'st me my way in Rome?
NARRATOR: Stabbing MUTIUS
MUTIUS: Help, Lucius, help!
NARRATOR: Dies
NARRATOR: During the fray, SATURNINUS, TAMORA, DEMETRIUS, CHIRON and AARON go out and re-enter, above
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS
LUCIUS: My lord, you are unjust, and, more than so,
LUCIUS: In wrongful quarrel you have slain your son.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Nor thou, nor he, are any sons of mine,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My sons would never so dishonour me:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Traitor, restore Lavinia to the emperor.
LUCIUS: Dead, if you will, but not to be his wife,
LUCIUS: That is another's lawful promised love.
NARRATOR: Exit
SATURNINUS: No, Titus, no, the emperor needs her not,
SATURNINUS: Nor her, nor thee, nor any of thy stock:
SATURNINUS: I'll trust, by leisure, him that mocks me once,
SATURNINUS: Thee never, nor thy traitorous haughty sons,
SATURNINUS: Confederates all thus to dishonour me.
SATURNINUS: Was there none else in Rome to make a stale,
SATURNINUS: But Saturnine? Full well, Andronicus,
SATURNINUS: Agree these deeds with that proud brag of thine,
SATURNINUS: That said'st I begg'd the empire at thy hands.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O monstrous! what reproachful words are these?
SATURNINUS: But go thy ways, go, give that changing piece
SATURNINUS: To him that flourish'd for her with his sword
SATURNINUS: A valiant son-in-law thou shalt enjoy,
SATURNINUS: One fit to bandy with thy lawless sons,
SATURNINUS: To ruffle in the commonwealth of Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: These words are razors to my wounded heart.
SATURNINUS: And therefore, lovely Tamora, queen of Goths,
SATURNINUS: That like the stately Phoebe 'mongst her nymphs
SATURNINUS: Dost overshine the gallant'st dames of Rome,
SATURNINUS: If thou be pleased with this my sudden choice,
SATURNINUS: Behold, I choose thee, Tamora, for my bride,
SATURNINUS: And will create thee empress of Rome,
SATURNINUS: Speak, Queen of Goths, dost thou applaud my choice?
SATURNINUS: And here I swear by all the Roman gods,
SATURNINUS: Sith priest and holy water are so near
SATURNINUS: And tapers burn so bright and every thing
SATURNINUS: In readiness for Hymenaeus stand,
SATURNINUS: I will not re-salute the streets of Rome,
SATURNINUS: Or climb my palace, till from forth this place
SATURNINUS: I lead espoused my bride along with me.
TAMORA: And here, in sight of heaven, to Rome I swear,
TAMORA: If Saturnine advance the Queen of Goths,
TAMORA: She will a handmaid be to his desires,
TAMORA: A loving nurse, a mother to his youth.
SATURNINUS: Ascend, fair queen, Pantheon. Lords, accompany
SATURNINUS: Your noble emperor and his lovely bride,
SATURNINUS: Sent by the heavens for Prince Saturnine,
SATURNINUS: Whose wisdom hath her fortune conquered:
SATURNINUS: There shall we consummate our spousal rites.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but TITUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I am not bid to wait upon this bride.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Titus, when wert thou wont to walk alone,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Dishonour'd thus, and challenged of wrongs?
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARCUS, LUCIUS, QUINTUS, and MARTIUS
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O Titus, see, O, see what thou hast done!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: In a bad quarrel slain a virtuous son.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No, foolish tribune, no, no son of mine,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Nor thou, nor these, confederates in the deed
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That hath dishonour'd all our family,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Unworthy brother, and unworthy sons!
LUCIUS: But let us give him burial, as becomes,
LUCIUS: Give Mutius burial with our brethren.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Traitors, away! he rests not in this tomb:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This monument five hundred years hath stood,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Which I have sumptuously re-edified:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here none but soldiers and Rome's servitors
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Repose in fame, none basely slain in brawls:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Bury him where you can, he comes not here.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My lord, this is impiety in you:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My nephew Mutius' deeds do plead for him
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: He must be buried with his brethren.
MARTIUS: And shall, or him we will accompany.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'And shall!' what villain was it that spake
TITUS ANDRONICUS: that word?
QUINTUS: He that would vouch it in any place but here.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What, would you bury him in my despite?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: No, noble Titus, but entreat of thee
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To pardon Mutius and to bury him.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Marcus, even thou hast struck upon my crest,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, with these boys, mine honour thou hast wounded:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My foes I do repute you every one,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: So, trouble me no more, but get you gone.
MARTIUS: He is not with himself, let us withdraw.
QUINTUS: Not I, till Mutius' bones be buried.
NARRATOR: MARCUS and the Sons of TITUS kneel
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Brother, for in that name doth nature plead,--
QUINTUS: Father, and in that name doth nature speak,--
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Speak thou no more, if all the rest will speed.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Renowned Titus, more than half my soul,--
LUCIUS: Dear father, soul and substance of us all,--
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Suffer thy brother Marcus to inter
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: His noble nephew here in virtue's nest,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That died in honour and Lavinia's cause.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Thou art a Roman, be not barbarous:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The Greeks upon advice did bury Ajax
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That slew himself, and wise Laertes' son
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Did graciously plead for his funerals:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Let not young Mutius, then, that was thy joy
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Be barr'd his entrance here.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rise, Marcus, rise.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The dismall'st day is this that e'er I saw,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To be dishonour'd by my sons in Rome!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Well, bury him, and bury me the next.
NARRATOR: MUTIUS is put into the tomb
LUCIUS: There lie thy bones, sweet Mutius, with thy friends,
LUCIUS: Till we with trophies do adorn thy tomb.
All: [Kneeling]  No man shed tears for noble Mutius,
All: He lives in fame that died in virtue's cause.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My lord, to step out of these dreary dumps,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: How comes it that the subtle Queen of Goths
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Is of a sudden thus advanced in Rome?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I know not, Marcus, but I know it is,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Whether by device or no, the heavens can tell:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is she not then beholding to the man
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That brought her for this high good turn so far?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Yes, and will nobly him remunerate.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Flourish. Re-enter, from one side, SATURNINUS  attended, TAMORA, DEMETRIUS, CHIRON and AARON, from the other, BASSIANUS, LAVINIA, and others
SATURNINUS: So, Bassianus, you have play'd your prize:
SATURNINUS: God give you joy, sir, of your gallant bride!
BASSIANUS: And you of yours, my lord! I say no more,
BASSIANUS: Nor wish no less, and so, I take my leave.
SATURNINUS: Traitor, if Rome have law or we have power,
SATURNINUS: Thou and thy faction shall repent this rape.
BASSIANUS: Rape, call you it, my lord, to seize my own,
BASSIANUS: My truth-betrothed love and now my wife?
BASSIANUS: But let the laws of Rome determine all,
BASSIANUS: Meanwhile I am possess'd of that is mine.
SATURNINUS: 'Tis good, sir: you are very short with us,
SATURNINUS: But, if we live, we'll be as sharp with you.
BASSIANUS: My lord, what I have done, as best I may,
BASSIANUS: Answer I must and shall do with my life.
BASSIANUS: Only thus much I give your grace to know:
BASSIANUS: By all the duties that I owe to Rome,
BASSIANUS: This noble gentleman, Lord Titus here,
BASSIANUS: Is in opinion and in honour wrong'd,
BASSIANUS: That in the rescue of Lavinia
BASSIANUS: With his own hand did slay his youngest son,
BASSIANUS: In zeal to you and highly moved to wrath
BASSIANUS: To be controll'd in that he frankly gave:
BASSIANUS: Receive him, then, to favor, Saturnine,
BASSIANUS: That hath express'd himself in all his deeds
BASSIANUS: A father and a friend to thee and Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Prince Bassianus, leave to plead my deeds:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Tis thou and those that have dishonour'd me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rome and the righteous heavens be my judge,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How I have loved and honour'd Saturnine!
TAMORA: My worthy lord, if ever Tamora
TAMORA: Were gracious in those princely eyes of thine,
TAMORA: Then hear me speak in indifferently for all,
TAMORA: And at my suit, sweet, pardon what is past.
SATURNINUS: What, madam! be dishonour'd openly,
SATURNINUS: And basely put it up without revenge?
TAMORA: Not so, my lord, the gods of Rome forfend
TAMORA: I should be author to dishonour you!
TAMORA: But on mine honour dare I undertake
TAMORA: For good Lord Titus' innocence in all,
TAMORA: Whose fury not dissembled speaks his griefs:
TAMORA: Then, at my suit, look graciously on him,
TAMORA: Lose not so noble a friend on vain suppose,
TAMORA: Nor with sour looks afflict his gentle heart.
NARRATOR: Aside to SATURNINUS
TAMORA: be won at last,
TAMORA: Dissemble all your griefs and discontents:
TAMORA: You are but newly planted in your throne,
TAMORA: Lest, then, the people, and patricians too,
TAMORA: Upon a just survey, take Titus' part,
TAMORA: And so supplant you for ingratitude,
TAMORA: Which Rome reputes to be a heinous sin,
TAMORA: Yield at entreats, and then let me alone:
TAMORA: I'll find a day to massacre them all
TAMORA: And raze their faction and their family,
TAMORA: The cruel father and his traitorous sons,
TAMORA: To whom I sued for my dear son's life,
TAMORA: And make them know what 'tis to let a queen
TAMORA: Kneel in the streets and beg for grace in vain.
NARRATOR: Aloud
TAMORA: Come, come, sweet emperor, come, Andronicus,
TAMORA: Take up this good old man, and cheer the heart
TAMORA: That dies in tempest of thy angry frown.
SATURNINUS: Rise, Titus, rise, my empress hath prevail'd.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I thank your majesty, and her, my lord:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: These words, these looks, infuse new life in me.
TAMORA: Titus, I am incorporate in Rome,
TAMORA: A Roman now adopted happily,
TAMORA: And must advise the emperor for his good.
TAMORA: This day all quarrels die, Andronicus,
TAMORA: And let it be mine honour, good my lord,
TAMORA: That I have reconciled your friends and you.
TAMORA: For you, Prince Bassianus, I have pass'd
TAMORA: My word and promise to the emperor,
TAMORA: That you will be more mild and tractable.
TAMORA: And fear not lords, and you, Lavinia,
TAMORA: By my advice, all humbled on your knees,
TAMORA: You shall ask pardon of his majesty.
LUCIUS: We do, and vow to heaven and to his highness,
LUCIUS: That what we did was mildly as we might,
LUCIUS: Tendering our sister's honour and our own.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That, on mine honour, here I do protest.
SATURNINUS: Away, and talk not, trouble us no more.
TAMORA: Nay, nay, sweet emperor, we must all be friends:
TAMORA: The tribune and his nephews kneel for grace,
TAMORA: I will not be denied: sweet heart, look back.
SATURNINUS: Marcus, for thy sake and thy brother's here,
SATURNINUS: And at my lovely Tamora's entreats,
SATURNINUS: I do remit these young men's heinous faults: Stand up.
SATURNINUS: Lavinia, though you left me like a churl,
SATURNINUS: I found a friend, and sure as death I swore
SATURNINUS: I would not part a bachelor from the priest.
SATURNINUS: Come, if the emperor's court can feast two brides,
SATURNINUS: You are my guest, Lavinia, and your friends.
SATURNINUS: This day shall be a love-day, Tamora.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To-morrow, an it please your majesty
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To hunt the panther and the hart with me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: With horn and hound we'll give your grace bonjour.
SATURNINUS: Be it so, Titus, and gramercy too.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. Before the Palace.
NARRATOR: Enter AARON
AARON: Now climbeth Tamora Olympus' top,
AARON: Safe out of fortune's shot, and sits aloft,
AARON: Secure of thunder's crack or lightning flash,
AARON: Advanced above pale envy's threatening reach.
AARON: As when the golden sun salutes the morn,
AARON: And, having gilt the ocean with his beams,
AARON: Gallops the zodiac in his glistering coach,
AARON: And overlooks the highest-peering hills,
AARON: So Tamora:
AARON: Upon her wit doth earthly honour wait,
AARON: And virtue stoops and trembles at her frown.
AARON: Then, Aaron, arm thy heart, and fit thy thoughts,
AARON: To mount aloft with thy imperial mistress,
AARON: And mount her pitch, whom thou in triumph long
AARON: Hast prisoner held, fetter'd in amorous chains
AARON: And faster bound to Aaron's charming eyes
AARON: Than is Prometheus tied to Caucasus.
AARON: Away with slavish weeds and servile thoughts!
AARON: I will be bright, and shine in pearl and gold,
AARON: To wait upon this new-made empress.
AARON: To wait, said I? to wanton with this queen,
AARON: This goddess, this Semiramis, this nymph,
AARON: This siren, that will charm Rome's Saturnine,
AARON: And see his shipwreck and his commonweal's.
AARON: Holloa! what storm is this?
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS and CHIRON, braving
DEMETRIUS: Chiron, thy years want wit, thy wit wants edge,
DEMETRIUS: And manners, to intrude where I am graced,
DEMETRIUS: And may, for aught thou know'st, affected be.
CHIRON: Demetrius, thou dost over-ween in all,
CHIRON: And so in this, to bear me down with braves.
CHIRON: 'Tis not the difference of a year or two
CHIRON: Makes me less gracious or thee more fortunate:
CHIRON: I am as able and as fit as thou
CHIRON: To serve, and to deserve my mistress' grace,
CHIRON: And that my sword upon thee shall approve,
CHIRON: And plead my passions for Lavinia's love.
AARON: [Aside]  Clubs, clubs! these lovers will not keep
AARON: the peace.
DEMETRIUS: Why, boy, although our mother, unadvised,
DEMETRIUS: Gave you a dancing-rapier by your side,
DEMETRIUS: Are you so desperate grown, to threat your friends?
DEMETRIUS: Go to, have your lath glued within your sheath
DEMETRIUS: Till you know better how to handle it.
CHIRON: Meanwhile, sir, with the little skill I have,
CHIRON: Full well shalt thou perceive how much I dare.
DEMETRIUS: Ay, boy, grow ye so brave?
NARRATOR: They draw
AARON: [Coming forward]  Why, how now, lords!
AARON: So near the emperor's palace dare you draw,
AARON: And maintain such a quarrel openly?
AARON: Full well I wot the ground of all this grudge:
AARON: I would not for a million of gold
AARON: The cause were known to them it most concerns,
AARON: Nor would your noble mother for much more
AARON: Be so dishonour'd in the court of Rome.
AARON: For shame, put up.
DEMETRIUS: Not I, till I have sheathed
DEMETRIUS: My rapier in his bosom and withal
DEMETRIUS: Thrust these reproachful speeches down his throat
DEMETRIUS: That he hath breathed in my dishonour here.
CHIRON: For that I am prepared and full resolved.
CHIRON: Foul-spoken coward, that thunder'st with thy tongue,
CHIRON: And with thy weapon nothing darest perform!
AARON: Away, I say!
AARON: Now, by the gods that warlike Goths adore,
AARON: This petty brabble will undo us all.
AARON: Why, lords, and think you not how dangerous
AARON: It is to jet upon a prince's right?
AARON: What, is Lavinia then become so loose,
AARON: Or Bassianus so degenerate,
AARON: That for her love such quarrels may be broach'd
AARON: Without controlment, justice, or revenge?
AARON: Young lords, beware! and should the empress know
AARON: This discord's ground, the music would not please.
CHIRON: I care not, I, knew she and all the world:
CHIRON: I love Lavinia more than all the world.
DEMETRIUS: Youngling, learn thou to make some meaner choice:
DEMETRIUS: Lavinia is thine elder brother's hope.
AARON: Why, are ye mad? or know ye not, in Rome
AARON: How furious and impatient they be,
AARON: And cannot brook competitors in love?
AARON: I tell you, lords, you do but plot your deaths
AARON: By this device.
CHIRON: Aaron, a thousand deaths
CHIRON: Would I propose to achieve her whom I love.
AARON: To achieve her! how?
DEMETRIUS: Why makest thou it so strange?
DEMETRIUS: She is a woman, therefore may be woo'd,
DEMETRIUS: She is a woman, therefore may be won,
DEMETRIUS: She is Lavinia, therefore must be loved.
DEMETRIUS: What, man! more water glideth by the mill
DEMETRIUS: Than wots the miller of, and easy it is
DEMETRIUS: Of a cut loaf to steal a shive, we know:
DEMETRIUS: Though Bassianus be the emperor's brother.
DEMETRIUS: Better than he have worn Vulcan's badge.
AARON: [Aside]  Ay, and as good as Saturninus may.
DEMETRIUS: Then why should he despair that knows to court it
DEMETRIUS: With words, fair looks and liberality?
DEMETRIUS: What, hast not thou full often struck a doe,
DEMETRIUS: And borne her cleanly by the keeper's nose?
AARON: Why, then, it seems, some certain snatch or so
AARON: Would serve your turns.
CHIRON: Ay, so the turn were served.
DEMETRIUS: Aaron, thou hast hit it.
AARON: Would you had hit it too!
AARON: Then should not we be tired with this ado.
AARON: Why, hark ye, hark ye! and are you such fools
AARON: To square for this? would it offend you, then
AARON: That both should speed?
CHIRON: Faith, not me.
DEMETRIUS: Nor me, so I were one.
AARON: For shame, be friends, and join for that you jar:
AARON: 'Tis policy and stratagem must do
AARON: That you affect, and so must you resolve,
AARON: That what you cannot as you would achieve,
AARON: You must perforce accomplish as you may.
AARON: Take this of me: Lucrece was not more chaste
AARON: Than this Lavinia, Bassianus' love.
AARON: A speedier course than lingering languishment
AARON: Must we pursue, and I have found the path.
AARON: My lords, a solemn hunting is in hand,
AARON: There will the lovely Roman ladies troop:
AARON: The forest walks are wide and spacious,
AARON: And many unfrequented plots there are
AARON: Fitted by kind for rape and villany:
AARON: Single you thither then this dainty doe,
AARON: And strike her home by force, if not by words:
AARON: This way, or not at all, stand you in hope.
AARON: Come, come, our empress, with her sacred wit
AARON: To villany and vengeance consecrate,
AARON: Will we acquaint with all that we intend,
AARON: And she shall file our engines with advice,
AARON: That will not suffer you to square yourselves,
AARON: But to your wishes' height advance you both.
AARON: The emperor's court is like the house of Fame,
AARON: The palace full of tongues, of eyes, and ears:
AARON: The woods are ruthless, dreadful, deaf, and dull,
AARON: There speak, and strike, brave boys, and take
AARON: your turns,
AARON: There serve your lusts, shadow'd from heaven's eye,
AARON: And revel in Lavinia's treasury.
CHIRON: Thy counsel, lad, smells of no cowardice,
DEMETRIUS: Sit fas aut nefas, till I find the stream
DEMETRIUS: To cool this heat, a charm to calm these fits.
DEMETRIUS: Per Styga, per manes vehor.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A forest near Rome. Horns and cry of hounds heard.
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS ANDRONICUS, with Hunters,  and c., MARCUS, LUCIUS, QUINTUS, and MARTIUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The hunt is up, the morn is bright and grey,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The fields are fragrant and the woods are green:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Uncouple here and let us make a bay
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And wake the emperor and his lovely bride
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And rouse the prince and ring a hunter's peal,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That all the court may echo with the noise.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sons, let it be your charge, as it is ours,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To attend the emperor's person carefully:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I have been troubled in my sleep this night,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But dawning day new comfort hath inspired.
NARRATOR: A cry of hounds and horns, winded in a peal. Enter  SATURNINUS, TAMORA, BASSIANUS, LAVINIA, DEMETRIUS, CHIRON, and Attendants
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Many good morrows to your majesty,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Madam, to you as many and as good:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I promised your grace a hunter's peal.
SATURNINUS: And you have rung it lustily, my lord,
SATURNINUS: Somewhat too early for new-married ladies.
BASSIANUS: Lavinia, how say you?
LAVINIA: I say, no,
LAVINIA: I have been broad awake two hours and more.
SATURNINUS: Come on, then, horse and chariots let us have,
SATURNINUS: And to our sport.
NARRATOR: To TAMORA
SATURNINUS: Madam, now shall ye see
SATURNINUS: Our Roman hunting.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: I have dogs, my lord,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Will rouse the proudest panther in the chase,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And climb the highest promontory top.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And I have horse will follow where the game
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Makes way, and run like swallows o'er the plain.
DEMETRIUS: Chiron, we hunt not, we, with horse nor hound,
DEMETRIUS: But hope to pluck a dainty doe to ground.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A lonely part of the forest.
NARRATOR: Enter AARON, with a bag of gold
AARON: He that had wit would think that I had none,
AARON: To bury so much gold under a tree,
AARON: And never after to inherit it.
AARON: Let him that thinks of me so abjectly
AARON: Know that this gold must coin a stratagem,
AARON: Which, cunningly effected, will beget
AARON: A very excellent piece of villany:
AARON: And so repose, sweet gold, for their unrest
NARRATOR: Hides the gold
AARON: That have their alms out of the empress' chest.
NARRATOR: Enter TAMORA
TAMORA: My lovely Aaron, wherefore look'st thou sad,
TAMORA: When every thing doth make a gleeful boast?
TAMORA: The birds chant melody on every bush,
TAMORA: The snake lies rolled in the cheerful sun,
TAMORA: The green leaves quiver with the cooling wind
TAMORA: And make a chequer'd shadow on the ground:
TAMORA: Under their sweet shade, Aaron, let us sit,
TAMORA: And, whilst the babbling echo mocks the hounds,
TAMORA: Replying shrilly to the well-tuned horns,
TAMORA: As if a double hunt were heard at once,
TAMORA: Let us sit down and mark their yelping noise,
TAMORA: And, after conflict such as was supposed
TAMORA: The wandering prince and Dido once enjoy'd,
TAMORA: When with a happy storm they were surprised
TAMORA: And curtain'd with a counsel-keeping cave,
TAMORA: We may, each wreathed in the other's arms,
TAMORA: Our pastimes done, possess a golden slumber,
TAMORA: Whiles hounds and horns and sweet melodious birds
TAMORA: Be unto us as is a nurse's song
TAMORA: Of lullaby to bring her babe asleep.
AARON: Madam, though Venus govern your desires,
AARON: Saturn is dominator over mine:
AARON: What signifies my deadly-standing eye,
AARON: My silence and my cloudy melancholy,
AARON: My fleece of woolly hair that now uncurls
AARON: Even as an adder when she doth unroll
AARON: To do some fatal execution?
AARON: No, madam, these are no venereal signs:
AARON: Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand,
AARON: Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.
AARON: Hark Tamora, the empress of my soul,
AARON: Which never hopes more heaven than rests in thee,
AARON: This is the day of doom for Bassianus:
AARON: His Philomel must lose her tongue to-day,
AARON: Thy sons make pillage of her chastity
AARON: And wash their hands in Bassianus' blood.
AARON: Seest thou this letter? take it up, I pray thee,
AARON: And give the king this fatal plotted scroll.
AARON: Now question me no more, we are espied,
AARON: Here comes a parcel of our hopeful booty,
AARON: Which dreads not yet their lives' destruction.
TAMORA: Ah, my sweet Moor, sweeter to me than life!
AARON: No more, great empress, Bassianus comes:
AARON: Be cross with him, and I'll go fetch thy sons
AARON: To back thy quarrels, whatsoe'er they be.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter BASSIANUS and LAVINIA
BASSIANUS: Who have we here? Rome's royal empress,
BASSIANUS: Unfurnish'd of her well-beseeming troop?
BASSIANUS: Or is it Dian, habited like her,
BASSIANUS: Who hath abandoned her holy groves
BASSIANUS: To see the general hunting in this forest?
TAMORA: Saucy controller of our private steps!
TAMORA: Had I the power that some say Dian had,
TAMORA: Thy temples should be planted presently
TAMORA: With horns, as was Actaeon's, and the hounds
TAMORA: Should drive upon thy new-transformed limbs,
TAMORA: Unmannerly intruder as thou art!
LAVINIA: Under your patience, gentle empress,
LAVINIA: 'Tis thought you have a goodly gift in horning,
LAVINIA: And to be doubted that your Moor and you
LAVINIA: Are singled forth to try experiments:
LAVINIA: Jove shield your husband from his hounds to-day!
LAVINIA: 'Tis pity they should take him for a stag.
BASSIANUS: Believe me, queen, your swarth Cimmerian
BASSIANUS: Doth make your honour of his body's hue,
BASSIANUS: Spotted, detested, and abominable.
BASSIANUS: Why are you sequester'd from all your train,
BASSIANUS: Dismounted from your snow-white goodly steed.
BASSIANUS: And wander'd hither to an obscure plot,
BASSIANUS: Accompanied but with a barbarous Moor,
BASSIANUS: If foul desire had not conducted you?
LAVINIA: And, being intercepted in your sport,
LAVINIA: Great reason that my noble lord be rated
LAVINIA: For sauciness. I pray you, let us hence,
LAVINIA: And let her joy her raven-colour'd love,
LAVINIA: This valley fits the purpose passing well.
BASSIANUS: The king my brother shall have note of this.
LAVINIA: Ay, for these slips have made him noted long:
LAVINIA: Good king, to be so mightily abused!
TAMORA: Why have I patience to endure all this?
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS and CHIRON
DEMETRIUS: How now, dear sovereign, and our gracious mother!
DEMETRIUS: Why doth your highness look so pale and wan?
TAMORA: Have I not reason, think you, to look pale?
TAMORA: These two have 'ticed me hither to this place:
TAMORA: A barren detested vale, you see it is,
TAMORA: The trees, though summer, yet forlorn and lean,
TAMORA: O'ercome with moss and baleful mistletoe:
TAMORA: Here never shines the sun, here nothing breeds,
TAMORA: Unless the nightly owl or fatal raven:
TAMORA: And when they show'd me this abhorred pit,
TAMORA: They told me, here, at dead time of the night,
TAMORA: A thousand fiends, a thousand hissing snakes,
TAMORA: Ten thousand swelling toads, as many urchins,
TAMORA: Would make such fearful and confused cries
TAMORA: As any mortal body hearing it
TAMORA: Should straight fall mad, or else die suddenly.
TAMORA: No sooner had they told this hellish tale,
TAMORA: But straight they told me they would bind me here
TAMORA: Unto the body of a dismal yew,
TAMORA: And leave me to this miserable death:
TAMORA: And then they call'd me foul adulteress,
TAMORA: Lascivious Goth, and all the bitterest terms
TAMORA: That ever ear did hear to such effect:
TAMORA: And, had you not by wondrous fortune come,
TAMORA: This vengeance on me had they executed.
TAMORA: Revenge it, as you love your mother's life,
TAMORA: Or be ye not henceforth call'd my children.
DEMETRIUS: This is a witness that I am thy son.
NARRATOR: Stabs BASSIANUS
CHIRON: And this for me, struck home to show my strength.
NARRATOR: Also stabs BASSIANUS, who dies
LAVINIA: Ay, come, Semiramis, nay, barbarous Tamora,
LAVINIA: For no name fits thy nature but thy own!
TAMORA: Give me thy poniard, you shall know, my boys
TAMORA: Your mother's hand shall right your mother's wrong.
DEMETRIUS: Stay, madam, here is more belongs to her,
DEMETRIUS: First thrash the corn, then after burn the straw:
DEMETRIUS: This minion stood upon her chastity,
DEMETRIUS: Upon her nuptial vow, her loyalty,
DEMETRIUS: And with that painted hope braves your mightiness:
DEMETRIUS: And shall she carry this unto her grave?
CHIRON: An if she do, I would I were an eunuch.
CHIRON: Drag hence her husband to some secret hole,
CHIRON: And make his dead trunk pillow to our lust.
TAMORA: But when ye have the honey ye desire,
TAMORA: Let not this wasp outlive, us both to sting.
CHIRON: I warrant you, madam, we wil l make that sure.
CHIRON: Come, mistress, now perforce we will enjoy
CHIRON: That nice-preserved honesty of yours.
LAVINIA: O Tamora! thou bear'st a woman's face,--
TAMORA: I will not hear her speak, away with her!
LAVINIA: Sweet lords, entreat her hear me but a word.
DEMETRIUS: Listen, fair madam: let it be your glory
DEMETRIUS: To see her tears, but be your heart to them
DEMETRIUS: As unrelenting flint to drops of rain.
LAVINIA: When did the tiger's young ones teach the dam?
LAVINIA: O, do not learn her wrath, she taught it thee,
LAVINIA: The milk thou suck'dst from her did turn to marble,
LAVINIA: Even at thy teat thou hadst thy tyranny.
LAVINIA: Yet every mother breeds not sons alike:
NARRATOR: To CHIRON
LAVINIA: Do thou entreat her show a woman pity.
CHIRON: What, wouldst thou have me prove myself a bastard?
LAVINIA: 'Tis true, the raven doth not hatch a lark:
LAVINIA: Yet have I heard,--O, could I find it now!--
LAVINIA: The lion moved with pity did endure
LAVINIA: To have his princely paws pared all away:
LAVINIA: Some say that ravens foster forlorn children,
LAVINIA: The whilst their own birds famish in their nests:
LAVINIA: O, be to me, though thy hard heart say no,
LAVINIA: Nothing so kind, but something pitiful!
TAMORA: I know not what it means, away with her!
LAVINIA: O, let me teach thee! for my father's sake,
LAVINIA: That gave thee life, when well he might have
LAVINIA: slain thee,
LAVINIA: Be not obdurate, open thy deaf ears.
TAMORA: Hadst thou in person ne'er offended me,
TAMORA: Even for his sake am I pitiless.
TAMORA: Remember, boys, I pour'd forth tears in vain,
TAMORA: To save your brother from the sacrifice,
TAMORA: But fierce Andronicus would not relent,
TAMORA: Therefore, away with her, and use her as you will,
TAMORA: The worse to her, the better loved of me.
LAVINIA: O Tamora, be call'd a gentle queen,
LAVINIA: And with thine own hands kill me in this place!
LAVINIA: For 'tis not life that I have begg'd so long,
LAVINIA: Poor I was slain when Bassianus died.
TAMORA: What begg'st thou, then? fond woman, let me go.
LAVINIA: 'Tis present death I beg, and one thing more
LAVINIA: That womanhood denies my tongue to tell:
LAVINIA: O, keep me from their worse than killing lust,
LAVINIA: And tumble me into some loathsome pit,
LAVINIA: Where never man's eye may behold my body:
LAVINIA: Do this, and be a charitable murderer.
TAMORA: So should I rob my sweet sons of their fee:
TAMORA: No, let them satisfy their lust on thee.
DEMETRIUS: Away! for thou hast stay'd us here too long.
LAVINIA: No grace? no womanhood? Ah, beastly creature!
LAVINIA: The blot and enemy to our general name!
LAVINIA: Confusion fall--
CHIRON: Nay, then I'll stop your mouth. Bring thou her husband:
CHIRON: This is the hole where Aaron bid us hide him.
CHIRON: DEMETRIUS throws the body of BASSIANUS into the  pit, then exeunt DEMETRIUS and CHIRON, dragging off LAVINIA
TAMORA: Farewell, my sons: see that you make her sure.
TAMORA: Ne'er let my heart know merry cheer indeed,
TAMORA: Till all the Andronici be made away.
TAMORA: Now will I hence to seek my lovely Moor,
TAMORA: And let my spleenful sons this trull deflow'r.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter AARON, with QUINTUS and MARTIUS
AARON: Come on, my lords, the better foot before:
AARON: Straight will I bring you to the loathsome pit
AARON: Where I espied the panther fast asleep.
QUINTUS: My sight is very dull, whate'er it bodes.
MARTIUS: And mine, I promise you, were't not for shame,
MARTIUS: Well could I leave our sport to sleep awhile.
NARRATOR: Falls into the pit
QUINTUS: What art thou fall'n? What subtle hole is this,
QUINTUS: Whose mouth is cover'd with rude-growing briers,
QUINTUS: Upon whose leaves are drops of new-shed blood
QUINTUS: As fresh as morning dew distill'd on flowers?
QUINTUS: A very fatal place it seems to me.
QUINTUS: Speak, brother, hast thou hurt thee with the fall?
MARTIUS: O brother, with the dismall'st object hurt
MARTIUS: That ever eye with sight made heart lament!
AARON: [Aside]  Now will I fetch the king to find them here,
AARON: That he thereby may give a likely guess
AARON: How these were they that made away his brother.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARTIUS: Why dost not comfort me, and help me out
MARTIUS: From this unhallowed and blood-stained hole?
QUINTUS: I am surprised with an uncouth fear,
QUINTUS: A chilling sweat o'er-runs my trembling joints:
QUINTUS: My heart suspects more than mine eye can see.
MARTIUS: To prove thou hast a true-divining heart,
MARTIUS: Aaron and thou look down into this den,
MARTIUS: And see a fearful sight of blood and death.
QUINTUS: Aaron is gone, and my compassionate heart
QUINTUS: Will not permit mine eyes once to behold
QUINTUS: The thing whereat it trembles by surmise,
QUINTUS: O, tell me how it is, for ne'er till now
QUINTUS: Was I a child to fear I know not what.
MARTIUS: Lord Bassianus lies embrewed here,
MARTIUS: All on a heap, like to a slaughter'd lamb,
MARTIUS: In this detested, dark, blood-drinking pit.
QUINTUS: If it be dark, how dost thou know 'tis he?
MARTIUS: Upon his bloody finger he doth wear
MARTIUS: A precious ring, that lightens all the hole,
MARTIUS: Which, like a taper in some monument,
MARTIUS: Doth shine upon the dead man's earthy cheeks,
MARTIUS: And shows the ragged entrails of the pit:
MARTIUS: So pale did shine the moon on Pyramus
MARTIUS: When he by night lay bathed in maiden blood.
MARTIUS: O brother, help me with thy fainting hand--
MARTIUS: If fear hath made thee faint, as me it hath--
MARTIUS: Out of this fell devouring receptacle,
MARTIUS: As hateful as Cocytus' misty mouth.
QUINTUS: Reach me thy hand, that I may help thee out,
QUINTUS: Or, wanting strength to do thee so much good,
QUINTUS: I may be pluck'd into the swallowing womb
QUINTUS: Of this deep pit, poor Bassianus' grave.
QUINTUS: I have no strength to pluck thee to the brink.
MARTIUS: Nor I no strength to climb without thy help.
QUINTUS: Thy hand once more, I will not loose again,
QUINTUS: Till thou art here aloft, or I below:
QUINTUS: Thou canst not come to me: I come to thee.
NARRATOR: Falls in
NARRATOR: Enter SATURNINUS with AARON
SATURNINUS: Along with me: I'll see what hole is here,
SATURNINUS: And what he is that now is leap'd into it.
SATURNINUS: Say who art thou that lately didst descend
SATURNINUS: Into this gaping hollow of the earth?
MARTIUS: The unhappy son of old Andronicus:
MARTIUS: Brought hither in a most unlucky hour,
MARTIUS: To find thy brother Bassianus dead.
SATURNINUS: My brother dead! I know thou dost but jest:
SATURNINUS: He and his lady both are at the lodge
SATURNINUS: Upon the north side of this pleasant chase,
SATURNINUS: 'Tis not an hour since I left him there.
MARTIUS: We know not where you left him all alive,
MARTIUS: But, out, alas! here have we found him dead.
MARTIUS: Re-enter TAMORA, with Attendants, TITUS ANDRONICUS, and Lucius
TAMORA: Where is my lord the king?
SATURNINUS: Here, Tamora, though grieved with killing grief.
TAMORA: Where is thy brother Bassianus?
SATURNINUS: Now to the bottom dost thou search my wound:
SATURNINUS: Poor Bassianus here lies murdered.
TAMORA: Then all too late I bring this fatal writ,
TAMORA: The complot of this timeless tragedy,
TAMORA: And wonder greatly that man's face can fold
TAMORA: In pleasing smiles such murderous tyranny.
NARRATOR: She giveth SATURNINUS a letter
SATURNINUS: [Reads]  'An if we miss to meet him handsomely--
SATURNINUS: Sweet huntsman, Bassianus 'tis we mean--
SATURNINUS: Do thou so much as dig the grave for him:
SATURNINUS: Thou know'st our meaning. Look for thy reward
SATURNINUS: Among the nettles at the elder-tree
SATURNINUS: Which overshades the mouth of that same pit
SATURNINUS: Where we decreed to bury Bassianus.
SATURNINUS: Do this, and purchase us thy lasting friends.'
SATURNINUS: O Tamora! was ever heard the like?
SATURNINUS: This is the pit, and this the elder-tree.
SATURNINUS: Look, sirs, if you can find the huntsman out
SATURNINUS: That should have murdered Bassianus here.
AARON: My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.
SATURNINUS: [To TITUS]  Two of thy whelps, fell curs of
SATURNINUS: bloody kind,
SATURNINUS: Have here bereft my brother of his life.
SATURNINUS: Sirs, drag them from the pit unto the prison:
SATURNINUS: There let them bide until we have devised
SATURNINUS: Some never-heard-of torturing pain for them.
TAMORA: What, are they in this pit? O wondrous thing!
TAMORA: How easily murder is discovered!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: High emperor, upon my feeble knee
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I beg this boon, with tears not lightly shed,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That this fell fault of my accursed sons,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Accursed if the fault be proved in them,--
SATURNINUS: If it be proved! you see it is apparent.
SATURNINUS: Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
TAMORA: Andronicus himself did take it up.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I did, my lord: yet let me be their bail,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For, by my father's reverend tomb, I vow
TITUS ANDRONICUS: They shall be ready at your highness' will
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To answer their suspicion with their lives.
SATURNINUS: Thou shalt not bail them: see thou follow me.
SATURNINUS: Some bring the murder'd body, some the murderers:
SATURNINUS: Let them not speak a word, the guilt is plain,
SATURNINUS: For, by my soul, were there worse end than death,
SATURNINUS: That end upon them should be executed.
TAMORA: Andronicus, I will entreat the king,
TAMORA: Fear not thy sons, they shall do well enough.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, Lucius, come, stay not to talk with them.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Another part of the forest.
NARRATOR: Enter DEMETRIUS and CHIRON with LAVINIA, ravished, her hands cut off, and her tongue cut out
DEMETRIUS: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak,
DEMETRIUS: Who 'twas that cut thy tongue and ravish'd thee.
CHIRON: Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so,
CHIRON: An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
DEMETRIUS: See, how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.
CHIRON: Go home, call for sweet water, wash thy hands.
DEMETRIUS: She hath no tongue to call, nor hands to wash,
DEMETRIUS: And so let's leave her to her silent walks.
CHIRON: An 'twere my case, I should go hang myself.
DEMETRIUS: If thou hadst hands to help thee knit the cord.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DEMETRIUS and CHIRON
NARRATOR: Enter MARCUS
MARCUS: Who is this? my niece, that flies away so fast!
MARCUS: Cousin, a word, where is your husband?
MARCUS: If I do dream, would all my wealth would wake me!
MARCUS: If I do wake, some planet strike me down,
MARCUS: That I may slumber in eternal sleep!
MARCUS: Speak, gentle niece, what stern ungentle hands
MARCUS: Have lopp'd and hew'd and made thy body bare
MARCUS: Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments,
MARCUS: Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in,
MARCUS: And might not gain so great a happiness
MARCUS: As have thy love? Why dost not speak to me?
MARCUS: Alas, a crimson river of warm blood,
MARCUS: Like to a bubbling fountain stirr'd with wind,
MARCUS: Doth rise and fall between thy rosed lips,
MARCUS: Coming and going with thy honey breath.
MARCUS: But, sure, some Tereus hath deflowered thee,
MARCUS: And, lest thou shouldst detect him, cut thy tongue.
MARCUS: Ah, now thou turn'st away thy face for shame!
MARCUS: And, notwithstanding all this loss of blood,
MARCUS: As from a conduit with three issuing spouts,
MARCUS: Yet do thy cheeks look red as Titan's face
MARCUS: Blushing to be encountered with a cloud.
MARCUS: Shall I speak for thee? shall I say 'tis so?
MARCUS: O, that I knew thy heart, and knew the beast,
MARCUS: That I might rail at him, to ease my mind!
MARCUS: Sorrow concealed, like an oven stopp'd,
MARCUS: Doth burn the heart to cinders where it is.
MARCUS: Fair Philomela, she but lost her tongue,
MARCUS: And in a tedious sampler sew'd her mind:
MARCUS: But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee,
MARCUS: A craftier Tereus, cousin, hast thou met,
MARCUS: And he hath cut those pretty fingers off,
MARCUS: That could have better sew'd than Philomel.
MARCUS: O, had the monster seen those lily hands
MARCUS: Tremble, like aspen-leaves, upon a lute,
MARCUS: And make the silken strings delight to kiss them,
MARCUS: He would not then have touch'd them for his life!
MARCUS: Or, had he heard the heavenly harmony
MARCUS: Which that sweet tongue hath made,
MARCUS: He would have dropp'd his knife, and fell asleep
MARCUS: As Cerberus at the Thracian poet's feet.
MARCUS: Come, let us go, and make thy father blind,
MARCUS: For such a sight will blind a father's eye:
MARCUS: One hour's storm will drown the fragrant meads,
MARCUS: What will whole months of tears thy father's eyes?
MARCUS: Do not draw back, for we will mourn with thee
MARCUS: O, could our mourning ease thy misery!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter Judges, Senators and Tribunes, with MARTIUS  and QUINTUS, bound, passing on to the place of execution, TITUS going before, pleading
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hear me, grave fathers! noble tribunes, stay!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In dangerous wars, whilst you securely slept,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For all my blood in Rome's great quarrel shed,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For all the frosty nights that I have watch'd,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And for these bitter tears, which now you see
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Filling the aged wrinkles in my cheeks,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Be pitiful to my condemned sons,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Whose souls are not corrupted as 'tis thought.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For two and twenty sons I never wept,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Because they died in honour's lofty bed.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lieth down, the Judges,  and c., pass by him, and Exeunt
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For these, these, tribunes, in the dust I write
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My heart's deep languor and my soul's sad tears:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Let my tears stanch the earth's dry appetite,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My sons' sweet blood will make it shame and blush.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O earth, I will befriend thee more with rain,
