TITUS ANDRONICUS: That shall distil from these two ancient urns,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Than youthful April shall with all his showers:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In summer's drought I'll drop upon thee still,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In winter with warm tears I'll melt the snow
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And keep eternal spring-time on thy face,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: So thou refuse to drink my dear sons' blood.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS, with his sword drawn
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O reverend tribunes! O gentle, aged men!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Unbind my sons, reverse the doom of death,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And let me say, that never wept before,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My tears are now prevailing orators.
LUCIUS: O noble father, you lament in vain:
LUCIUS: The tribunes hear you not, no man is by,
LUCIUS: And you recount your sorrows to a stone.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, Lucius, for thy brothers let me plead.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Grave tribunes, once more I entreat of you,--
LUCIUS: My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speak.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, tis no matter, man, if they did hear,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: They would not mark me, or if they did mark,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: They would not pity me, yet plead I must,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Therefore I tell my sorrows to the stones,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Who, though they cannot answer my distress,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Yet in some sort they are better than the tribunes,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For that they will not intercept my tale:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When I do weep, they humbly at my feet
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Receive my tears and seem to weep with me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, were they but attired in grave weeds,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rome could afford no tribune like to these.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A stone is soft as wax,--tribunes more hard than stones,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A stone is silent, and offendeth not,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And tribunes with their tongues doom men to death.
NARRATOR: Rises
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But wherefore stand'st thou with thy weapon drawn?
LUCIUS: To rescue my two brothers from their death:
LUCIUS: For which attempt the judges have pronounced
LUCIUS: My everlasting doom of banishment.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O happy man! they have befriended thee.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But me and mine: how happy art thou, then,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: From these devourers to be banished!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But who comes with our brother Marcus here?
NARRATOR: Enter MARCUS and LAVINIA
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Titus, prepare thy aged eyes to weep,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Or, if not so, thy noble heart to break:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: I bring consuming sorrow to thine age.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will it consume me? let me see it, then.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This was thy daughter.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, Marcus, so she is.
LUCIUS: Ay me, this object kills me!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Faint-hearted boy, arise, and look upon her.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Speak, Lavinia, what accursed hand
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hath made thee handless in thy father's sight?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What fool hath added water to the sea,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or brought a faggot to bright-burning Troy?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My grief was at the height before thou camest,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And now like Nilus, it disdaineth bounds.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Give me a sword, I'll chop off my hands too,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For they have fought for Rome, and all in vain,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And they have nursed this woe, in feeding life,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In bootless prayer have they been held up,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And they have served me to effectless use:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Now all the service I require of them
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is that the one will help to cut the other.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Tis well, Lavinia, that thou hast no hands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For hands, to do Rome service, are but vain.
LUCIUS: Speak, gentle sister, who hath martyr'd thee?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, that delightful engine of her thoughts
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That blabb'd them with such pleasing eloquence,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Is torn from forth that pretty hollow cage,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Where, like a sweet melodious bird, it sung
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Sweet varied notes, enchanting every ear!
LUCIUS: O, say thou for her, who hath done this deed?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, thus I found her, straying in the park,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That hath received some unrecuring wound.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: It was my deer, and he that wounded her
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hath hurt me more than had he killed me dead:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For now I stand as one upon a rock
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Environed with a wilderness of sea,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Expecting ever when some envious surge
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will in his brinish bowels swallow him.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This way to death my wretched sons are gone,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here stands my other son, a banished man,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And here my brother, weeping at my woes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But that which gives my soul the greatest spurn,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Had I but seen thy picture in this plight,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: It would have madded me: what shall I do
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Now I behold thy lively body so?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou hast no hands, to wipe away thy tears:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Nor tongue, to tell me who hath martyr'd thee:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thy husband he is dead: and for his death
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thy brothers are condemn'd, and dead by this.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Look, Marcus! ah, son Lucius, look on her!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When I did name her brothers, then fresh tears
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Stood on her cheeks, as doth the honey-dew
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Upon a gather'd lily almost wither'd.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Perchance she weeps because they kill'd her husband,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Perchance because she knows them innocent.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: If they did kill thy husband, then be joyful
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Because the law hath ta'en revenge on them.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No, no, they would not do so foul a deed,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Witness the sorrow that their sister makes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss thy lips.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or make some sign how I may do thee ease:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Shall thy good uncle, and thy brother Lucius,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And thou, and I, sit round about some fountain,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Looking all downwards to behold our cheeks
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How they are stain'd, as meadows, yet not dry,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: With miry slime left on them by a flood?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And in the fountain shall we gaze so long
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Till the fresh taste be taken from that clearness,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And made a brine-pit with our bitter tears?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or shall we cut away our hands, like thine?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or shall we bite our tongues, and in dumb shows
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Pass the remainder of our hateful days?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What shall we do? let us, that have our tongues,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Plot some deuce of further misery,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To make us wonder'd at in time to come.
LUCIUS: Sweet father, cease your tears, for, at your grief,
LUCIUS: See how my wretched sister sobs and weeps.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Patience, dear niece. Good Titus, dry thine eyes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, Marcus, Marcus! brother, well I wot
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thy napkin cannot drink a tear of mine,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For thou, poor man, hast drown'd it with thine own.
LUCIUS: Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe thy cheeks.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Mark, Marcus, mark! I understand her signs:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Had she a tongue to speak, now would she say
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That to her brother which I said to thee:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: His napkin, with his true tears all bewet,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Can do no service on her sorrowful cheeks.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, what a sympathy of woe is this,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As far from help as Limbo is from bliss!
NARRATOR: Enter AARON
AARON: Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor
AARON: Sends thee this word,--that, if thou love thy sons,
AARON: Let Marcus, Lucius, or thyself, old Titus,
AARON: Or any one of you, chop off your hand,
AARON: And send it to the king: he for the same
AARON: Will send thee hither both thy sons alive,
AARON: And that shall be the ransom for their fault.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O gracious emperor! O gentle Aaron!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Did ever raven sing so like a lark,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That gives sweet tidings of the sun's uprise?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: With all my heart, I'll send the emperor My hand:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good Aaron, wilt thou help to chop it off?
LUCIUS: Stay, father! for that noble hand of thine,
LUCIUS: That hath thrown down so many enemies,
LUCIUS: Shall not be sent: my hand will serve the turn:
LUCIUS: My youth can better spare my blood than you,
LUCIUS: And therefore mine shall save my brothers' lives.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Which of your hands hath not defended Rome,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And rear'd aloft the bloody battle-axe,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Writing destruction on the enemy's castle?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, none of both but are of high desert:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My hand hath been but idle, let it serve
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To ransom my two nephews from their death,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Then have I kept it to a worthy end.
AARON: Nay, come, agree whose hand shall go along,
AARON: For fear they die before their pardon come.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My hand shall go.
LUCIUS: By heaven, it shall not go!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirs, strive no more: such wither'd herbs as these
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Are meet for plucking up, and therefore mine.
LUCIUS: Sweet father, if I shall be thought thy son,
LUCIUS: Let me redeem my brothers both from death.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And, for our father's sake and mother's care,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now let me show a brother's love to thee.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Agree between you, I will spare my hand.
LUCIUS: Then I'll go fetch an axe.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But I will use the axe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt LUCIUS and MARCUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come hither, Aaron, I'll deceive them both:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lend me thy hand, and I will give thee mine.
AARON: [Aside]  If that be call'd deceit, I will be honest,
AARON: And never, whilst I live, deceive men so:
AARON: But I'll deceive you in another sort,
AARON: And that you'll say, ere half an hour pass.
NARRATOR: Cuts off TITUS's hand
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCIUS and MARCUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Now stay your strife: what shall be is dispatch'd.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tell him it was a hand that warded him
TITUS ANDRONICUS: From thousand dangers, bid him bury it
TITUS ANDRONICUS: More hath it merited, that let it have.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As for my sons, say I account of them
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As jewels purchased at an easy price,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And yet dear too, because I bought mine own.
AARON: I go, Andronicus: and for thy hand
AARON: Look by and by to have thy sons with thee.
NARRATOR: Aside
AARON: Their heads, I mean. O, how this villany
AARON: Doth fat me with the very thoughts of it!
AARON: Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace.
AARON: Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
NARRATOR: Exit
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And bow this feeble ruin to the earth:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: If any power pities wretched tears,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To that I call!
NARRATOR: To LAVINIA
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What, wilt thou kneel with me?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Do, then, dear heart, for heaven shall hear our prayers,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or with our sighs we'll breathe the welkin dim,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And stain the sun with fog, as sometime clouds
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When they do hug him in their melting bosoms.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O brother, speak with possibilities,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And do not break into these deep extremes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is not my sorrow deep, having no bottom?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then be my passions bottomless with them.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But yet let reason govern thy lament.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: If there were reason for these miseries,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then into limits could I bind my woes:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When heaven doth weep, doth not the earth o'erflow?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: If the winds rage, doth not the sea wax mad,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Threatening the welkin with his big-swoln face?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And wilt thou have a reason for this coil?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I am the sea, hark, how her sighs do blow!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: She is the weeping welkin, I the earth:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then must my sea be moved with her sighs,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then must my earth with her continual tears
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Become a deluge, overflow'd and drown'd,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For why my bowels cannot hide her woes,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But like a drunkard must I vomit them.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then give me leave, for losers will have leave
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To ease their stomachs with their bitter tongues.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger, with two heads and a hand
Messenger: Worthy Andronicus, ill art thou repaid
Messenger: For that good hand thou sent'st the emperor.
Messenger: Here are the heads of thy two noble sons,
Messenger: And here's thy hand, in scorn to thee sent back,
Messenger: Thy griefs their sports, thy resolution mock'd,
Messenger: That woe is me to think upon thy woes
Messenger: More than remembrance of my father's death.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now let hot AEtna cool in Sicily,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And be my heart an ever-burning hell!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: These miseries are more than may be borne.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To weep with them that weep doth ease some deal,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But sorrow flouted at is double death.
LUCIUS: Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound,
LUCIUS: And yet detested life not shrink thereat!
LUCIUS: That ever death should let life bear his name,
LUCIUS: Where life hath no more interest but to breathe!
NARRATOR: LAVINIA kisses TITUS
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Alas, poor heart, that kiss is comfortless
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: As frozen water to a starved snake.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When will this fearful slumber have an end?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now, farewell, flattery: die, Andronicus,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Thou dost not slumber: see, thy two sons' heads,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Thy warlike hand, thy mangled daughter here:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Thy other banish'd son, with this dear sight
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Struck pale and bloodless, and thy brother, I,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Even like a stony image, cold and numb.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, now no more will I control thy griefs:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Rend off thy silver hair, thy other hand
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Gnawing with thy teeth, and be this dismal sight
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The closing up of our most wretched eyes,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now is a time to storm, why art thou still?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ha, ha, ha!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Why dost thou laugh? it fits not with this hour.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, I have not another tear to shed:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Besides, this sorrow is an enemy,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And would usurp upon my watery eyes
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And make them blind with tributary tears:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then which way shall I find Revenge's cave?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For these two heads do seem to speak to me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And threat me I shall never come to bliss
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Till all these mischiefs be return'd again
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Even in their throats that have committed them.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, let me see what task I have to do.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You heavy people, circle me about,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That I may turn me to each one of you,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And swear unto my soul to right your wrongs.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The vow is made. Come, brother, take a head,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And in this hand the other I will bear.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lavinia, thou shalt be employ'd: these arms!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Bear thou my hand, sweet wench, between thy teeth.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As for thee, boy, go get thee from my sight,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou art an exile, and thou must not stay:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hie to the Goths, and raise an army there:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, if you love me, as I think you do,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Let's kiss and part, for we have much to do.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TITUS, MARCUS, and LAVINIA
LUCIUS: Farewell Andronicus, my noble father,
LUCIUS: The wofull'st man that ever lived in Rome:
LUCIUS: Farewell, proud Rome, till Lucius come again,
LUCIUS: He leaves his pledges dearer than his life:
LUCIUS: Farewell, Lavinia, my noble sister,
LUCIUS: O, would thou wert as thou tofore hast been!
LUCIUS: But now nor Lucius nor Lavinia lives
LUCIUS: But in oblivion and hateful griefs.
LUCIUS: If Lucius live, he will requite your wrongs,
LUCIUS: And make proud Saturnine and his empress
LUCIUS: Beg at the gates, like Tarquin and his queen.
LUCIUS: Now will I to the Goths, and raise a power,
LUCIUS: To be revenged on Rome and Saturnine.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A room in Titus's house. A banquet set out.
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS, MARCUS, LAVINIA and Young LUCIUS, a boy
TITUS ANDRONICUS: So, so, now sit: and look you eat no more
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Than will preserve just so much strength in us
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As will revenge these bitter woes of ours.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Marcus, unknit that sorrow-wreathen knot:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And cannot passionate our tenfold grief
TITUS ANDRONICUS: With folded arms. This poor right hand of mine
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is left to tyrannize upon my breast,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Who, when my heart, all mad with misery,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Beats in this hollow prison of my flesh,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then thus I thump it down.
NARRATOR: To LAVINIA
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: When thy poor heart beats with outrageous beating,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou canst not strike it thus to make it still.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Wound it with sighing, girl, kill it with groans,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or get some little knife between thy teeth,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And just against thy heart make thou a hole,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That all the tears that thy poor eyes let fall
TITUS ANDRONICUS: May run into that sink, and soaking in
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Drown the lamenting fool in sea-salt tears.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Fie, brother, fie! teach her not thus to lay
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Such violent hands upon her tender life.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How now! has sorrow made thee dote already?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but I.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What violent hands can she lay on her life?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, wherefore dost thou urge the name of hands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To bid AEneas tell the tale twice o'er,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How Troy was burnt and he made miserable?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, handle not the theme, to talk of hands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lest we remember still that we have none.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Fie, fie, how franticly I square my talk,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As if we should forget we had no hands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: If Marcus did not name the word of hands!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, let's fall to, and, gentle girl, eat this:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here is no drink! Hark, Marcus, what she says,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I can interpret all her martyr'd signs,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: She says she drinks no other drink but tears,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Brew'd with her sorrow, mesh'd upon her cheeks:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Speechless complainer, I will learn thy thought,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: In thy dumb action will I be as perfect
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As begging hermits in their holy prayers:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But I of these will wrest an alphabet
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And by still practise learn to know thy meaning.
Young LUCIUS: Good grandsire, leave these bitter deep laments:
Young LUCIUS: Make my aunt merry with some pleasing tale.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Alas, the tender boy, in passion moved,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Doth weep to see his grandsire's heaviness.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Peace, tender sapling, thou art made of tears,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And tears will quickly melt thy life away.
NARRATOR: MARCUS strikes the dish with a knife
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What dost thou strike at, Marcus, with thy knife?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: At that that I have kill'd, my lord, a fly.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Out on thee, murderer! thou kill'st my heart,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Mine eyes are cloy'd with view of tyranny:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A deed of death done on the innocent
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Becomes not Titus' brother: get thee gone:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I see thou art not for my company.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Alas, my lord, I have but kill'd a fly.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But how, if that fly had a father and mother?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How would he hang his slender gilded wings,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And buzz lamenting doings in the air!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Poor harmless fly,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That, with his pretty buzzing melody,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Came here to make us merry! and thou hast
TITUS ANDRONICUS: kill'd him.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Pardon me, sir, it was a black ill-favor'd fly,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Like to the empress' Moor, therefore I kill'd him.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, O, O,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then pardon me for reprehending thee,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For thou hast done a charitable deed.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Give me thy knife, I will insult on him,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Flattering myself, as if it were the Moor
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come hither purposely to poison me.--
TITUS ANDRONICUS: There's for thyself, and that's for Tamora.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, sirrah!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Yet, I think, we are not brought so low,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But that between us we can kill a fly
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That comes in likeness of a coal-black Moor.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Alas, poor man! grief has so wrought on him,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: He takes false shadows for true substances.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, take away. Lavinia, go with me:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I'll to thy closet, and go read with thee
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sad stories chanced in the times of old.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, boy, and go with me: thy sight is young,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Rome. Titus's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter young LUCIUS, and LAVINIA running after him,  and the boy flies from her, with books under his arm. Then enter TITUS and MARCUS
Young LUCIUS: Help, grandsire, help! my aunt Lavinia
Young LUCIUS: Follows me every where, I know not why:
Young LUCIUS: Good uncle Marcus, see how swift she comes.
Young LUCIUS: Alas, sweet aunt, I know not what you mean.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Stand by me, Lucius, do not fear thine aunt.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: She loves thee, boy, too well to do thee harm.
Young LUCIUS: Ay, when my father was in Rome she did.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: What means my niece Lavinia by these signs?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Fear her not, Lucius: somewhat doth she mean:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: See, Lucius, see how much she makes of thee:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Somewhither would she have thee go with her.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, boy, Cornelia never with more care
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Read to her sons than she hath read to thee
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sweet poetry and Tully's Orator.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Canst thou not guess wherefore she plies thee thus?
Young LUCIUS: My lord, I know not, I, nor can I guess,
Young LUCIUS: Unless some fit or frenzy do possess her:
Young LUCIUS: For I have heard my grandsire say full oft,
Young LUCIUS: Extremity of griefs would make men mad,
Young LUCIUS: And I have read that Hecuba of Troy
Young LUCIUS: Ran mad through sorrow: that made me to fear,
Young LUCIUS: Although, my lord, I know my noble aunt
Young LUCIUS: Loves me as dear as e'er my mother did,
Young LUCIUS: And would not, but in fury, fright my youth:
Young LUCIUS: Which made me down to throw my books, and fly--
Young LUCIUS: Causeless, perhaps. But pardon me, sweet aunt:
Young LUCIUS: And, madam, if my uncle Marcus go,
Young LUCIUS: I will most willingly attend your ladyship.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lucius, I will.
NARRATOR: LAVINIA turns over with her stumps the books which LUCIUS has let fall
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How now, Lavinia! Marcus, what means this?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Some book there is that she desires to see.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Which is it, girl, of these? Open them, boy.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But thou art deeper read, and better skill'd
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, and take choice of all my library,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And so beguile thy sorrow, till the heavens
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Reveal the damn'd contriver of this deed.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why lifts she up her arms in sequence thus?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: I think she means that there was more than one
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Confederate in the fact: ay, more there was,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Or else to heaven she heaves them for revenge.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lucius, what book is that she tosseth so?
Young LUCIUS: Grandsire, 'tis Ovid's Metamorphoses,
Young LUCIUS: My mother gave it me.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: For love of her that's gone,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Perhaps she cull'd it from among the rest.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Soft! see how busily she turns the leaves!
NARRATOR: Helping her
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What would she find? Lavinia, shall I read?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This is the tragic tale of Philomel,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And treats of Tereus' treason and his rape:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And rape, I fear, was root of thine annoy.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: See, brother, see, note how she quotes the leaves.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lavinia, wert thou thus surprised, sweet girl,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ravish'd and wrong'd, as Philomela was,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Forced in the ruthless, vast, and gloomy woods? See, see!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ay, such a place there is, where we did hunt--
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, had we never, never hunted there!--
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Pattern'd by that the poet here describes,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: By nature made for murders and for rapes.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, why should nature build so foul a den,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Unless the gods delight in tragedies?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Give signs, sweet girl, for here are none
TITUS ANDRONICUS: but friends,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What Roman lord it was durst do the deed:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or slunk not Saturnine, as Tarquin erst,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That left the camp to sin in Lucrece' bed?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Sit down, sweet niece: brother, sit down by me.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Apollo, Pallas, Jove, or Mercury,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Inspire me, that I may this treason find!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My lord, look here: look here, Lavinia:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This sandy plot is plain, guide, if thou canst
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This after me, when I have writ my name
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Without the help of any hand at all.
NARRATOR: He writes his name with his staff, and guides it with feet and mouth
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Cursed be that heart that forced us to this shift!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Write thou good niece, and here display, at last,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: What God will have discover'd for revenge,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Heaven guide thy pen to print thy sorrows plain,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That we may know the traitors and the truth!
NARRATOR: She takes the staff in her mouth, and guides it with her stumps, and writes
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, do ye read, my lord, what she hath writ?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.'
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: What, what! the lustful sons of Tamora
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Performers of this heinous, bloody deed?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Magni Dominator poli,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tam lentus audis scelera? tam lentus vides?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, calm thee, gentle lord, although I know
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: There is enough written upon this earth
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To stir a mutiny in the mildest thoughts
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And arm the minds of infants to exclaims.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My lord, kneel down with me, Lavinia, kneel,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And kneel, sweet boy, the Roman Hector's hope,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And swear with me, as, with the woful fere
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And father of that chaste dishonour'd dame,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lord Junius Brutus sware for Lucrece' rape,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That we will prosecute by good advice
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Mortal revenge upon these traitorous Goths,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And see their blood, or die with this reproach.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Tis sure enough, an you knew how.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But if you hunt these bear-whelps, then beware:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The dam will wake, and, if she wind you once,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: She's with the lion deeply still in league,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And lulls him whilst she playeth on her back,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And when he sleeps will she do what she list.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You are a young huntsman, Marcus, let it alone,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, come, I will go get a leaf of brass,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And with a gad of steel will write these words,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And lay it by: the angry northern wind
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will blow these sands, like Sibyl's leaves, abroad,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And where's your lesson, then? Boy, what say you?
Young LUCIUS: I say, my lord, that if I were a man,
Young LUCIUS: Their mother's bed-chamber should not be safe
Young LUCIUS: For these bad bondmen to the yoke of Rome.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Ay, that's my boy! thy father hath full oft
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: For his ungrateful country done the like.
Young LUCIUS: And, uncle, so will I, an if I live.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, go with me into mine armoury,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lucius, I'll fit thee, and withal, my boy,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Shalt carry from me to the empress' sons
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Presents that I intend to send them both:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, come, thou'lt do thy message, wilt thou not?
Young LUCIUS: Ay, with my dagger in their bosoms, grandsire.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No, boy, not so, I'll teach thee another course.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lavinia, come. Marcus, look to my house:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lucius and I'll go brave it at the court:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ay, marry, will we, sir, and we'll be waited on.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TITUS, LAVINIA, and Young LUCIUS
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O heavens, can you hear a good man groan,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And not relent, or not compassion him?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Marcus, attend him in his ecstasy,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That hath more scars of sorrow in his heart
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Than foemen's marks upon his batter'd shield,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But yet so just that he will not revenge.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Revenge, ye heavens, for old Andronicus!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. A room in the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter, from one side, AARON, DEMETRIUS, and  CHIRON, from the other side, Young LUCIUS, and an  Attendant, with a bundle of weapons, and verses writ upon them
CHIRON: Demetrius, here's the son of Lucius,
CHIRON: He hath some message to deliver us.
AARON: Ay, some mad message from his mad grandfather.
Young LUCIUS: My lords, with all the humbleness I may,
Young LUCIUS: I greet your honours from Andronicus.
NARRATOR: Aside
Young LUCIUS: And pray the Roman gods confound you both!
DEMETRIUS: Gramercy, lovely Lucius: what's the news?
Young LUCIUS: [Aside]  That you are both decipher'd, that's the news,
Young LUCIUS: For villains mark'd with rape.--May it please you,
Young LUCIUS: My grandsire, well advised, hath sent by me
Young LUCIUS: The goodliest weapons of his armoury
Young LUCIUS: To gratify your honourable youth,
Young LUCIUS: The hope of Rome, for so he bade me say,
Young LUCIUS: And so I do, and with his gifts present
Young LUCIUS: Your lordships, that, whenever you have need,
Young LUCIUS: You may be armed and appointed well:
Young LUCIUS: And so I leave you both:
NARRATOR: Aside
Young LUCIUS: like bloody villains.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Young LUCIUS, and Attendant
DEMETRIUS: What's here? A scroll, and written round about?
DEMETRIUS: Let's see,
NARRATOR: Reads
DEMETRIUS: 'Integer vitae, scelerisque purus,
DEMETRIUS: Non eget Mauri jaculis, nec arcu.'
CHIRON: O, 'tis a verse in Horace, I know it well:
CHIRON: I read it in the grammar long ago.
AARON: Ay, just, a verse in Horace, right, you have it.
NARRATOR: Aside
AARON: Now, what a thing it is to be an ass!
AARON: Here's no sound jest! the old man hath found their guilt,
AARON: And sends them weapons wrapped about with lines,
AARON: That wound, beyond their feeling, to the quick.
AARON: But were our witty empress well afoot,
AARON: She would applaud Andronicus' conceit:
AARON: But let her rest in her unrest awhile.
AARON: And now, young lords, was't not a happy star
AARON: Led us to Rome, strangers, and more than so,
AARON: Captives, to be advanced to this height?
AARON: It did me good, before the palace gate
AARON: To brave the tribune in his brother's hearing.
DEMETRIUS: But me more good, to see so great a lord
DEMETRIUS: Basely insinuate and send us gifts.
AARON: Had he not reason, Lord Demetrius?
AARON: Did you not use his daughter very friendly?
DEMETRIUS: I would we had a thousand Roman dames
DEMETRIUS: At such a bay, by turn to serve our lust.
CHIRON: A charitable wish and full of love.
AARON: Here lacks but your mother for to say amen.
CHIRON: And that would she for twenty thousand more.
DEMETRIUS: Come, let us go, and pray to all the gods
DEMETRIUS: For our beloved mother in her pains.
AARON: [Aside]  Pray to the devils, the gods have given us over.
NARRATOR: Trumpets sound within
DEMETRIUS: Why do the emperor's trumpets flourish thus?
CHIRON: Belike, for joy the emperor hath a son.
DEMETRIUS: Soft! who comes here?
NARRATOR: Enter a Nurse, with a blackamoor Child in her arms
Nurse: Good morr ow, lords:
Nurse: O, tell me, did you see Aaron the Moor?
AARON: Well, more or less, or ne'er a whit at all,
AARON: Here Aaron is, and what with Aaron now?
Nurse: O gentle Aaron, we are all undone!
Nurse: Now help, or woe betide thee evermore!
AARON: Why, what a caterwauling dost thou keep!
AARON: What dost thou wrap and fumble in thine arms?
Nurse: O, that which I would hide from heaven's eye,
Nurse: Our empress' shame, and stately Rome's disgrace!
Nurse: She is deliver'd, lords, she is deliver'd.
AARON: To whom?
Nurse: I mean, she is brought a-bed.
AARON: Well, God give her good rest! What hath he sent her?
Nurse: A devil.
AARON: Why, then she is the devil's dam, a joyful issue.
Nurse: A joyless, dismal, black, and sorrowful issue:
Nurse: Here is the babe, as loathsome as a toad
Nurse: Amongst the fairest breeders of our clime:
Nurse: The empress sends it thee, thy stamp, thy seal,
Nurse: And bids thee christen it with thy dagger's point.
AARON: 'Zounds, ye whore! is black so base a hue?
AARON: Sweet blowse, you are a beauteous blossom, sure.
DEMETRIUS: Villain, what hast thou done?
AARON: That which thou canst not undo.
CHIRON: Thou hast undone our mother.
AARON: Villain, I have done thy mother.
DEMETRIUS: And therein, hellish dog, thou hast undone.
DEMETRIUS: Woe to her chance, and damn'd her loathed choice!
DEMETRIUS: Accursed the offspring of so foul a fiend!
CHIRON: It shall not live.
AARON: It shall not die.
Nurse: Aaron, it must, the mother wills it so.
AARON: What, must it, nurse? then let no man but I
AARON: Do execution on my flesh and blood.
DEMETRIUS: I'll broach the tadpole on my rapier's point:
DEMETRIUS: Nurse, give it me, my sword shall soon dispatch it.
AARON: Sooner this sword shall plough thy bowels up.
NARRATOR: Takes the Child from the Nurse, and draws
AARON: Stay, murderous villains! will you kill your brother?
AARON: Now, by the burning tapers of the sky,
AARON: That shone so brightly when this boy was got,
AARON: He dies upon my scimitar's sharp point
AARON: That touches this my first-born son and heir!
AARON: I tell you, younglings, not Enceladus,
AARON: With all his threatening band of Typhon's brood,
AARON: Nor great Alcides, nor the god of war,
AARON: Shall seize this prey out of his father's hands.
AARON: What, what, ye sanguine, shallow-hearted boys!
AARON: Ye white-limed walls! ye alehouse painted signs!
AARON: Coal-black is better than another hue,
AARON: In that it scorns to bear another hue,
AARON: For all the water in the ocean
AARON: Can never turn the swan's black legs to white,
AARON: Although she lave them hourly in the flood.
AARON: Tell the empress from me, I am of age
AARON: To keep mine own, excuse it how she can.
DEMETRIUS: Wilt thou betray thy noble mistress thus?
AARON: My mistress is my mistress, this myself,
AARON: The vigour and the picture of my youth:
AARON: This before all the world do I prefer,
AARON: This maugre all the world will I keep safe,
AARON: Or some of you shall smoke for it in Rome.
DEMETRIUS: By this our mother is forever shamed.
CHIRON: Rome will despise her for this foul escape.
Nurse: The emperor, in his rage, will doom her death.
CHIRON: I blush to think upon this ignomy.
AARON: Why, there's the privilege your beauty bears:
AARON: Fie, treacherous hue, that will betray with blushing
AARON: The close enacts and counsels of the heart!
AARON: Here's a young lad framed of another leer:
AARON: Look, how the black slave smiles upon the father,
AARON: As who should say 'Old lad, I am thine own.'
AARON: He is your brother, lords, sensibly fed
AARON: Of that self-blood that first gave life to you,
AARON: And from that womb where you imprison'd were
AARON: He is enfranchised and come to light:
AARON: Nay, he is your brother by the surer side,
AARON: Although my seal be stamped in his face.
Nurse: Aaron, what shall I say unto the empress?
DEMETRIUS: Advise thee, Aaron, what is to be done,
DEMETRIUS: And we will all subscribe to thy advice:
DEMETRIUS: Save thou the child, so we may all be safe.
AARON: Then sit we down, and let us all consult.
AARON: My son and I will have the wind of you:
AARON: Keep there: now talk at pleasure of your safety.
NARRATOR: They sit
DEMETRIUS: How many women saw this child of his?
AARON: Why, so, brave lords! when we join in league,
AARON: I am a lamb: but if you brave the Moor,
AARON: The chafed boar, the mountain lioness,
AARON: The ocean swells not so as Aaron storms.
AARON: But say, again, how many saw the child?
Nurse: Cornelia the midwife and myself,
Nurse: And no one else but the deliver'd empress.
AARON: The empress, the midwife, and yourself:
AARON: Two may keep counsel when the third's away:
AARON: Go to the empress, tell her this I said.
NARRATOR: He kills the nurse
AARON: Weke, weke! so cries a pig prepared to the spit.
DEMETRIUS: What mean'st thou, Aaron? wherefore didst thou this?
AARON: O Lord, sir, 'tis a deed of policy:
AARON: Shall she live to betray this guilt of ours,
AARON: A long-tongued babbling gossip? no, lords, no:
AARON: And now be it known to you my full intent.
AARON: Not far, one Muli lives, my countryman,
AARON: His wife but yesternight was brought to bed,
AARON: His child is like to her, fair as you are:
AARON: Go pack with him, and give the mother gold,
AARON: And tell them both the circumstance of all,
AARON: And how by this their child shall be advanced,
AARON: And be received for the emperor's heir,
AARON: And substituted in the place of mine,
AARON: To calm this tempest whirling in the court,
AARON: And let the emperor dandle him for his own.
AARON: Hark ye, lords, ye see I have given her physic,
NARRATOR: Pointing to the nurse
AARON: And you must needs bestow her funeral,
AARON: The fields are near, and you are gallant grooms:
AARON: This done, see that you take no longer days,
AARON: But send the midwife presently to me.
AARON: The midwife and the nurse well made away,
AARON: Then let the ladies tattle what they please.
CHIRON: Aaron, I see thou wilt not trust the air
CHIRON: With secrets.
DEMETRIUS: For this care of Tamora,
DEMETRIUS: Herself and hers are highly bound to thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DEMETRIUS and CHIRON bearing off the Nurse's body
AARON: Now to the Goths, as swift as swallow flies,
AARON: There to dispose this treasure in mine arms,
AARON: And secretly to greet the empress' friends.
AARON: Come on, you thick lipp'd slave, I'll bear you hence,
AARON: For it is you that puts us to our shifts:
AARON: I'll make you feed on berries and on roots,
AARON: And feed on curds and whey, and suck the goat,
AARON: And cabin in a cave, and bring you up
AARON: To be a warrior, and command a camp.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. A public place.
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS, bearing arrows with letters at the  ends of them, with him, MARCUS, Young LUCIUS,  PUBLIUS, SEMPRONIUS, CAIUS, and other Gentlemen, with bows
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, Marcus, come, kinsmen, this is the way.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sir boy, now let me see your archery,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Look ye draw home enough, and 'tis there straight.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Terras Astraea reliquit:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Be you remember'd, Marcus, she's gone, she's fled.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirs, take you to your tools. You, cousins, shall
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Go sound the ocean, and cast your nets,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Happily you may catch her in the sea,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Yet there's as little justice as at land:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No, Publius and Sempronius, you must do it,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Tis you must dig with mattock and with spade,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And pierce the inmost centre of the earth:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then, when you come to Pluto's region,

TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tell him, it is for justice and for aid,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And that it comes from old Andronicus,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Shaken with sorrows in ungrateful Rome.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ah, Rome! Well, well, I made thee miserable
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What time I threw the people's suffrages
TITUS ANDRONICUS: On him that thus doth tyrannize o'er me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Go, get you gone, and pray be careful all,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And leave you not a man-of-war unsearch'd:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This wicked emperor may have shipp'd her hence,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, kinsmen, then we may go pipe for justice.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O Publius, is not this a heavy case,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To see thy noble uncle thus distract?
PUBLIUS: Therefore, my lord, it highly us concerns
PUBLIUS: By day and night to attend him carefully,
PUBLIUS: And feed his humour kindly as we may,
PUBLIUS: Till time beget some careful remedy.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Kinsmen, his sorrows are past remedy.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Join with the Goths, and with revengeful war
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Take wreak on Rome for this ingratitude,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And vengeance on the traitor Saturnine.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Publius, how now! how now, my masters!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What, have you met with her?

PUBLIUS: Marry, for Justice, she is so employ'd,
PUBLIUS: He thinks, with Jove in heaven, or somewhere else,
PUBLIUS: So that perforce you must needs stay a time.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: He doth me wrong to feed me with delays.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I'll dive into the burning lake below,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And pull her out of Acheron by the heels.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Marcus, we are but shrubs, no cedars we
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No big-boned men framed of the Cyclops' size,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But metal, Marcus, steel to the very back,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Yet wrung with wrongs more than our backs can bear:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, sith there's no justice in earth nor hell,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: We will solicit heaven and move the gods
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, to this gear. You are a good archer, Marcus,
NARRATOR: He gives them the arrows
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Ad Jovem,' that's for you: here, 'Ad Apollinem:'
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Ad Martem,' that's for myself:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here, boy, to Pallas: here, to Mercury:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To Saturn, Caius, not to Saturnine,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You were as good to shoot against the wind.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To it, boy! Marcus, loose when I bid.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Of my word, I have written to effect,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: There's not a god left unsolicited.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Kinsmen, shoot all your shafts into the court:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: We will afflict the emperor in his pride.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Now, masters, draw.
NARRATOR: They shoot
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O, well said, Lucius!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good boy, in Virgo's lap, give it Pallas.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My lord, I aim a mile beyond the moon,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Your letter is with Jupiter by this.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Ha, ha!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Publius, Publius, what hast thou done?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: See, see, thou hast shot off one of Taurus' horns.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This was the sport, my lord: when Publius shot,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The Bull, being gall'd, gave Aries such a knock
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That down fell both the Ram's horns in the court,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And who should find them but the empress' villain?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: She laugh'd, and told the Moor he should not choose
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But give them to his master for a present.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, there it goes: God give his lordship joy!
NARRATOR: Enter a Clown, with a basket, and two pigeons in it
TITUS ANDRONICUS: News, news from heaven! Marcus, the post is come.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirrah, what tidings? have you any letters?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Shall I have justice? what says Jupiter?
Clown: O, the gibbet-maker! he says that he hath taken
Clown: them down again, for the man must not be hanged till
Clown: the next week.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But what says Jupiter, I ask thee?
Clown: Alas, sir, I know not Jupiter, I never drank with him
Clown: in all my life.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, villain, art not thou the carrier?
Clown: Ay, of my pigeons, sir, nothing else.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, didst thou not come from heaven?
Clown: From heaven! alas, sir, I never came there     God
Clown: forbid I should be so bold to press to heaven in my
Clown: young days. Why, I am going with my pigeons to the
Clown: tribunal plebs, to take up a matter of brawl
Clown: betwixt my uncle and one of the emperial's men.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Why, sir, that is as fit as can be to serve for
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: your oration, and let him deliver the pigeons to
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: the emperor from you.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tell me, can you deliver an oration to the emperor
TITUS ANDRONICUS: with a grace?
Clown: Nay, truly, sir, I could never say grace in all my life.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirrah, come hither: make no more ado,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But give your pigeons to the emperor:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: By me thou shalt have justice at his hands.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hold, hold, meanwhile here's money for thy charges.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Give me pen and ink. Sirrah, can you with a grace
TITUS ANDRONICUS: deliver a supplication?
Clown: Ay, sir.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Then here is a supplication for you. And when you
TITUS ANDRONICUS: come to him, at the first approach you must kneel,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: then kiss his foot, then deliver up your pigeons, and
TITUS ANDRONICUS: then look for your reward. I'll be at hand, sir, see
TITUS ANDRONICUS: you do it bravely.
Clown: I warrant you, sir, let me alone.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirrah, hast thou a knife? come, let me see it.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here, Marcus, fold it in the oration,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For thou hast made it like an humble suppliant.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And when thou hast given it the emperor,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Knock at my door, and tell me what he says.
Clown: God be with you, sir, I will.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, Marcus, let us go. Publius, follow me.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same. Before the palace.
NARRATOR: Enter SATURNINUS, TAMORA, DEMETRIUS, CHIRON,  Lords, and others, SATURNINUS with the arrows in his hand that TITUS shot
SATURNINUS: Why, lords, what wrongs are these! was ever seen
SATURNINUS: An emperor in Rome thus overborne,
SATURNINUS: Troubled, confronted thus, and, for the extent
SATURNINUS: Of egal justice, used in such contempt?
SATURNINUS: My lords, you know, as know the mightful gods,
SATURNINUS: However these disturbers of our peace
SATURNINUS: Buz in the people's ears, there nought hath pass'd,
SATURNINUS: But even with law, against the willful sons
SATURNINUS: Of old Andronicus. And what an if
SATURNINUS: His sorrows have so overwhelm'd his wits,
SATURNINUS: Shall we be thus afflicted in his wreaks,
SATURNINUS: His fits, his frenzy, and his bitterness?
SATURNINUS: And now he writes to heaven for his redress:
SATURNINUS: See, here's to Jove, and this to Mercury,
SATURNINUS: This to Apollo, this to the god of war,
SATURNINUS: Sweet scrolls to fly about the streets of Rome!
SATURNINUS: What's this but libelling against the senate,
SATURNINUS: And blazoning our injustice every where?
SATURNINUS: A goodly humour, is it not, my lords?
SATURNINUS: As who would say, in Rome no justice were.
SATURNINUS: But if I live, his feigned ecstasies
SATURNINUS: Shall be no shelter to these outrages:
SATURNINUS: But he and his shall know that justice lives
SATURNINUS: In Saturninus' health, whom, if she sleep,
SATURNINUS: He'll so awake as she in fury shall
SATURNINUS: Cut off the proud'st conspirator that lives.
TAMORA: My gracious lord, my lovely Saturnine,
TAMORA: Lord of my life, commander of my thoughts,
TAMORA: Calm thee, and bear the faults of Titus' age,
TAMORA: The effects of sorrow for his valiant sons,
TAMORA: Whose loss hath pierced him deep and scarr'd his heart,
TAMORA: And rather comfort his distressed plight
TAMORA: Than prosecute the meanest or the best
TAMORA: For these contempts.
NARRATOR: Aside
TAMORA: Why, thus it shall become
TAMORA: High-witted Tamora to gloze with all:
TAMORA: But, Titus, I have touched thee to the quick,
TAMORA: Thy life-blood out: if Aaron now be wise,
TAMORA: Then is all safe, the anchor's in the port.
NARRATOR: Enter Clown
TAMORA: How now, good fellow! wouldst thou speak with us?
Clown: Yea, forsooth, an your mistership be emperial.
TAMORA: Empress I am, but yonder sits the emperor.
Clown: 'Tis he. God and Saint Stephen give you good den:
Clown: I have brought you a letter and a couple of pigeons here.
NARRATOR: SATURNINUS reads the letter
SATURNINUS: Go, take him away, and hang him presently.
Clown: How much money must I have?
TAMORA: Come, sirrah, you must be hanged.
Clown: Hanged! by'r lady, then I have brought up a neck to
Clown: a fair end.
NARRATOR: Exit, guarded
SATURNINUS: Despiteful and intolerable wrongs!
SATURNINUS: Shall I endure this monstrous villany?
SATURNINUS: I know from whence this same device proceeds:
SATURNINUS: May this be borne?--as if his traitorous sons,
SATURNINUS: That died by law for murder of our brother,
SATURNINUS: Have by my means been butcher'd wrongfully!
SATURNINUS: Go, drag the villain hither by the hair,
SATURNINUS: Nor age nor honour shall shape privilege:
SATURNINUS: For this proud mock I'll be thy slaughterman,
SATURNINUS: Sly frantic wretch, that holp'st to make me great,
SATURNINUS: In hope thyself should govern Rome and me.
NARRATOR: Enter AEMILIUS
SATURNINUS: What news with thee, AEmilius?
AEMILIUS: Arm, arm, my lord,--Rome never had more cause.
AEMILIUS: The Goths have gather'd head, and with a power
AEMILIUS: high-resolved men, bent to the spoil,
AEMILIUS: They hither march amain, under conduct
AEMILIUS: Of Lucius, son to old Andronicus,
AEMILIUS: Who threats, in course of this revenge, to do
AEMILIUS: As much as ever Coriolanus did.
SATURNINUS: Is warlike Lucius general of the Goths?
SATURNINUS: These tidings nip me, and I hang the head
SATURNINUS: As flowers with frost or grass beat down with storms:
SATURNINUS: Ay, now begin our sorrows to approach:
SATURNINUS: 'Tis he the common people love so much,
SATURNINUS: Myself hath often over-heard them say,
SATURNINUS: When I have walked like a private man,
SATURNINUS: That Lucius' banishment was wrongfully,
SATURNINUS: And they have wish'd that Lucius were their emperor.
TAMORA: Why should you fear? is not your city strong?
SATURNINUS: Ay, but the citizens favor Lucius,
SATURNINUS: And will revolt from me to succor him.
TAMORA: King, be thy thoughts imperious, like thy name.
TAMORA: Is the sun dimm'd, that gnats do fly in it?
TAMORA: The eagle suffers little birds to sing,
TAMORA: And is not careful what they mean thereby,
TAMORA: Knowing that with the shadow of his wings
TAMORA: He can at pleasure stint their melody:
TAMORA: Even so mayst thou the giddy men of Rome.
TAMORA: Then cheer thy spirit : for know, thou emperor,
TAMORA: I will enchant the old Andronicus
TAMORA: With words more sweet, and yet more dangerous,
TAMORA: Than baits to fish, or honey-stalks to sheep,
TAMORA: When as the one is wounded with the bait,
TAMORA: The other rotted with delicious feed.
SATURNINUS: But he will not entreat his son for us.
TAMORA: If Tamora entreat him, then he will:
TAMORA: For I can smooth and fill his aged ear
TAMORA: With golden promises, that, were his heart
TAMORA: Almost impregnable, his old ears deaf,
TAMORA: Yet should both ear and heart obey my tongue.
NARRATOR: To AEmilius
TAMORA: Go thou before, be our ambassador:
TAMORA: Say that the emperor requests a parley
TAMORA: Of warlike Lucius, and appoint the meeting
TAMORA: Even at his father's house, the old Andronicus.
SATURNINUS: AEmilius, do this message honourably:
SATURNINUS: And if he stand on hostage for his safety,
SATURNINUS: Bid him demand what pledge will please him best.
AEMILIUS: Your bidding shall I do effectually.
NARRATOR: Exit
TAMORA: Now will I to that old Andronicus,
TAMORA: And temper him with all the art I have,
TAMORA: To pluck proud Lucius from the warlike Goths.
TAMORA: And now, sweet emperor, be blithe again,
TAMORA: And bury all thy fear in my devices.
SATURNINUS: Then go successantly, and plead to him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Plains near Rome.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS with an army of Goths, with drum and colours
LUCIUS: Approved warriors, and my faithful friends,
LUCIUS: I have received letters from great Rome,
LUCIUS: Which signify what hate they bear their emperor
LUCIUS: And how desirous of our sight they are.
LUCIUS: Therefore, great lords, be, as your titles witness,
LUCIUS: Imperious and impatient of your wrongs,
LUCIUS: And wherein Rome hath done you any scath,
LUCIUS: Let him make treble satisfaction.
First Goth: Brave slip, sprung from the great Andronicus,
First Goth: Whose name was once our terror, now our comfort,
First Goth: Whose high exploits and honourable deeds
First Goth: Ingrateful Rome requites with foul contempt,
First Goth: Be bold in us: we'll follow where thou lead'st,
First Goth: Like stinging bees in hottest summer's day
First Goth: Led by their master to the flowered fields,
First Goth: And be avenged on cursed Tamora.
All the Goths: And as he saith, so say we all with him.
LUCIUS: I humbly thank him, and I thank you all.
LUCIUS: But who comes here, led by a lusty Goth?
NARRATOR: Enter a Goth, leading AARON with his Child in his arms
Second Goth: Renowned Lucius, from our troops I stray'd
Second Goth: To gaze upon a ruinous monastery,
Second Goth: And, as I earnestly did fix mine eye
Second Goth: Upon the wasted building, suddenly
Second Goth: I heard a child cry underneath a wall.
Second Goth: I made unto the noise, when soon I heard
Second Goth: The crying babe controll'd with this discourse:
Second Goth: 'Peace, tawny slave, half me and half thy dam!
Second Goth: Did not thy hue bewray whose brat thou art,
Second Goth: Had nature lent thee but thy mother's look,
Second Goth: Villain, thou mightst have been an emperor:
Second Goth: But where the bull and cow are both milk-white,
Second Goth: They never do beget a coal-black calf.
Second Goth: Peace, villain, peace!'--even thus he rates
Second Goth: the babe,--
Second Goth: 'For I must bear thee to a trusty Goth,
Second Goth: Who, when he knows thou art the empress' babe,
Second Goth: Will hold thee dearly for thy mother's sake.'
Second Goth: With this, my weapon drawn, I rush'd upon him,
Second Goth: Surprised him suddenly, and brought him hither,
Second Goth: To use as you think needful of the man.
LUCIUS: O worthy Goth, this is the incarnate devil
LUCIUS: That robb'd Andronicus of his good hand,
LUCIUS: This is the pearl that pleased your empress' eye,
LUCIUS: And here's the base fruit of his burning lust.
LUCIUS: Say, wall-eyed slave, whither wouldst thou convey
LUCIUS: This growing image of thy fiend-like face?
LUCIUS: Why dost not speak? what, deaf? not a word?
LUCIUS: A halter, soldiers! hang him on this tree.
LUCIUS: And by his side his fruit of bastardy.
AARON: Touch not the boy, he is of royal blood.
LUCIUS: Too like the sire for ever being good.
LUCIUS: First hang the child, that he may see it sprawl,
LUCIUS: A sight to vex the father's soul withal.
LUCIUS: Get me a ladder.
NARRATOR: A ladder brought, which AARON is made to ascend
AARON: Lucius, save the child,
AARON: And bear it from me to the empress.
AARON: If thou do this, I'll show thee wondrous things,
AARON: That highly may advantage thee to hear:
AARON: If thou wilt not, befall what may befall,
AARON: I'll speak no more but 'Vengeance rot you all!'
LUCIUS: Say on: an if it please me which thou speak'st
LUCIUS: Thy child shall live, and I will see it nourish'd.
AARON: An if it please thee! why, assure thee, Lucius,
AARON: 'Twill vex thy soul to hear what I shall speak,
AARON: For I must talk of murders, rapes and massacres,
AARON: Acts of black night, abominable deeds,
AARON: Complots of mischief, treason, villanies
AARON: Ruthful to hear, yet piteously perform'd:
AARON: And this shall all be buried by my death,
AARON: Unless thou swear to me my child shall live.
LUCIUS: Tell on thy mind, I say thy child shall live.
AARON: Swear that he shall, and then I will begin.
LUCIUS: Who should I swear by? thou believest no god:
LUCIUS: That granted, how canst thou believe an oath?
AARON: What if I do not? as, indeed, I do not,
AARON: Yet, for I know thou art religious
AARON: And hast a thing within thee called conscience,
AARON: With twenty popish tricks and ceremonies,
AARON: Which I have seen thee careful to observe,
AARON: Therefore I urge thy oath, for that I know
AARON: An idiot holds his bauble for a god
AARON: And keeps the oath which by that god he swears,
AARON: To that I'll urge him: therefore thou shalt vow
AARON: By that same god, what god soe'er it be,
AARON: That thou adorest and hast in reverence,
AARON: To save my boy, to nourish and bring him up,
AARON: Or else I will discover nought to thee.
LUCIUS: Even by my god I swear to thee I will.
AARON: First know thou, I begot him on the empress.
LUCIUS: O most insatiate and luxurious woman!
AARON: Tut, Lucius, this was but a deed of charity
AARON: To that which thou shalt hear of me anon.
AARON: 'Twas her two sons that murder'd Bassianus,
AARON: They cut thy sister's tongue and ravish'd her
AARON: And cut her hands and trimm'd her as thou saw'st.
LUCIUS: O detestable villain! call'st thou that trimming?
AARON: Why, she was wash'd and cut and trimm'd, and 'twas
AARON: Trim sport for them that had the doing of it.
LUCIUS: O barbarous, beastly villains, like thyself!
AARON: Indeed, I was their tutor to instruct them:
AARON: That codding spirit had they from their mother,
AARON: As sure a card as ever won the set,
AARON: That bloody mind, I think, they learn'd of me,
AARON: As true a dog as ever fought at head.
AARON: Well, let my deeds be witness of my worth.
AARON: I train'd thy brethren to that guileful hole
AARON: Where the dead corpse of Bassianus lay:
AARON: I wrote the letter that thy father found
AARON: And hid the gold within the letter mention'd,
AARON: Confederate with the queen and her two sons:
AARON: And what not done, that thou hast cause to rue,
AARON: Wherein I had no stroke of mischief in it?
AARON: I play'd the cheater for thy father's hand,
AARON: And, when I had it, drew myself apart
AARON: And almost broke my heart with extreme laughter:
AARON: I pry'd me through the crevice of a wall
AARON: When, for his hand, he had his two sons' heads,
AARON: Beheld his tears, and laugh'd so heartily,
AARON: That both mine eyes were rainy like to his :
AARON: And when I told the empress of this sport,
AARON: She swooned almost at my pleasing tale,
AARON: And for my tidings gave me twenty kisses.
First Goth: What, canst thou say all this, and never blush?
AARON: Ay, like a black dog, as the saying is.
LUCIUS: Art thou not sorry for these heinous deeds?
AARON: Ay, that I had not done a thousand more.
AARON: Even now I curse the day--and yet, I think,
AARON: Few come within the compass of my curse,--
AARON: Wherein I did not some notorious ill,
AARON: As kill a man, or else devise his death,
AARON: Ravish a maid, or plot the way to do it,
AARON: Accuse some innocent and forswear myself,
AARON: Set deadly enmity between two friends,
AARON: Make poor men's cattle break their necks,
AARON: Set fire on barns and hay-stacks in the night,
AARON: And bid the owners quench them with their tears.
AARON: Oft have I digg'd up dead men from their graves,
AARON: And set them upright at their dear friends' doors,
AARON: Even when their sorrows almost were forgot,
AARON: And on their skins, as on the bark of trees,
AARON: Have with my knife carved in Roman letters,
AARON: 'Let not your sorrow die, though I am dead.'
AARON: Tut, I have done a thousand dreadful things
AARON: As willingly as one would kill a fly,
AARON: And nothing grieves me heartily indeed
AARON: But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
LUCIUS: Bring down the devil, for he must not die
LUCIUS: So sweet a death as hanging presently.
AARON: If there be devils, would I were a devil,
AARON: To live and burn in everlasting fire,
AARON: So I might have your company in hell,
AARON: But to torment you with my bitter tongue!
LUCIUS: Sirs, stop his mouth, and let him speak no more.
NARRATOR: Enter a Goth
Third Goth: My lord, there is a messenger from Rome
Third Goth: Desires to be admitted to your presence.
LUCIUS: Let him come near.
NARRATOR: Enter AEMILIUS
LUCIUS: Welcome, AEmilius	what's the news from Rome?
AEMILIUS: Lord Lucius, and you princes of the Goths,
AEMILIUS: The Roman emperor greets you all by me,
AEMILIUS: And, for he understands you are in arms,
AEMILIUS: He craves a parley at your father's house,
AEMILIUS: Willing you to demand your hostages,
AEMILIUS: And they shall be immediately deliver'd.
First Goth: What says our general?
LUCIUS: AEmilius, let the emperor give his pledges
LUCIUS: Unto my father and my uncle Marcus,
LUCIUS: And we will come. March away.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Rome. Before TITUS's house.
NARRATOR: Enter TAMORA, DEMETRIUS, and CHIRON, disguised
TAMORA: Thus, in this strange and sad habiliment,
TAMORA: I will encounter with Andronicus,
TAMORA: And say I am Revenge, sent from below
TAMORA: To join with him and right his heinous wrongs.
TAMORA: Knock at his study, where, they say, he keeps,
TAMORA: To ruminate strange plots of dire revenge,
TAMORA: Tell him Revenge is come to join with him,
TAMORA: And work confusion on his enemies.
NARRATOR: They knock
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS, above
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Who doth molest my contemplation?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is it your trick to make me ope the door,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: That so my sad decrees may fly away,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And all my study be to no effect?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You are deceived: for what I mean to do
TITUS ANDRONICUS: See here in bloody lines I have set down,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And what is written shall be executed.
TAMORA: Titus, I am come to talk with thee.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: No, not a word, how can I grace my talk,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Wanting a hand to give it action?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou hast the odds of me, therefore no more.
TAMORA: If thou didst know me, thou wouldest talk with me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I am not mad, I know thee well enough:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Witness this wretched stump, witness these crimson lines,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Witness these trenches made by grief and care,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Witness the tiring day and heavy night,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Witness all sorrow, that I know thee well
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For our proud empress, mighty Tamora:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Is not thy coming for my other hand?
TAMORA: Know, thou sad man, I am not Tamora,
TAMORA: She is thy enemy, and I thy friend:
TAMORA: I am Revenge: sent from the infernal kingdom,
TAMORA: To ease the gnawing vulture of thy mind,
TAMORA: By working wreakful vengeance on thy foes.
TAMORA: Come down, and welcome me to this world's light,
TAMORA: Confer with me of murder and of death:
TAMORA: There's not a hollow cave or lurking-place,
TAMORA: No vast obscurity or misty vale,
TAMORA: Where bloody murder or detested rape
TAMORA: Can couch for fear, but I will find them out,
TAMORA: And in their ears tell them my dreadful name,
TAMORA: Revenge, which makes the foul offender quake.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Art thou Revenge? and art thou sent to me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To be a torment to mine enemies?
TAMORA: I am, therefore come down, and welcome me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Do me some service, ere I come to thee.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Lo, by thy side where Rape and Murder stands,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Now give me some surance that thou art Revenge,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Stab them, or tear them on thy chariot-wheels,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And then I'll come and be thy waggoner,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And whirl along with thee about the globe.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Provide thee two proper palfreys, black as jet,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To hale thy vengeful waggon swift away,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And find out murderers in their guilty caves:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And when thy car is loaden with their heads,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I will dismount, and by the waggon-wheel
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Trot, like a servile footman, all day long,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Even from Hyperion's rising in the east
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Until his very downfall in the sea:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And day by day I'll do this heavy task,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: So thou destroy Rapine and Murder there.
TAMORA: These are my ministers, and come with me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Are these thy ministers? what are they call'd?
TAMORA: Rapine and Murder, therefore called so,
TAMORA: Cause they take vengeance of such kind of men.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good Lord, how like the empress' sons they are!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And you, the empress! but we worldly men
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Have miserable, mad, mistaking eyes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O sweet Revenge, now do I come to thee,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, if one arm's embracement will content thee,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I will embrace thee in it by and by.
NARRATOR: Exit above
TAMORA: This closing with him fits his lunacy
TAMORA: Whate'er I forge to feed his brain-sick fits,
TAMORA: Do you uphold and maintain in your speeches,
TAMORA: For now he firmly takes me for Revenge,
TAMORA: And, being credulous in this mad thought,
TAMORA: I'll make him send for Lucius his son,
TAMORA: And, whilst I at a banquet hold him sure,
TAMORA: I'll find some cunning practise out of hand,
TAMORA: To scatter and disperse the giddy Goths,
TAMORA: Or, at the least, make them his enemies.
TAMORA: See, here he comes, and I must ply my theme.
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS below
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Long have I been forlorn, and all for thee:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Welcome, dread Fury, to my woful house:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Rapine and Murder, you are welcome too.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: How like the empress and her sons you are!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Well are you fitted, had you but a Moor:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Could not all hell afford you such a devil?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For well I wot the empress never wags
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But in her company there is a Moor,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, would you represent our queen aright,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: It were convenient you had such a devil:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But welcome, as you are. What shall we do?
TAMORA: What wouldst thou have us do, Andronicus?
DEMETRIUS: Show me a murderer, I'll deal with him.
CHIRON: Show me a villain that hath done a rape,
CHIRON: And I am sent to be revenged on him.
TAMORA: Show me a thousand that have done thee wrong,
TAMORA: And I will be revenged on them all.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Look round about the wicked streets of Rome,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And when thou find'st a man that's like thyself.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good Murder, stab him, he's a murderer.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Go thou with him, and when it is thy hap
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To find another that is like to thee,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Good Rapine, stab him, he's a ravisher.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Go thou with them, and in the emperor's court
TITUS ANDRONICUS: There is a queen, attended by a Moor,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Well mayst thou know her by thy own proportion,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: for up and down she doth resemble thee:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I pray thee, do on them some violent death,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: They have been violent to me and mine.
TAMORA: Well hast thou lesson'd us, this shall we do.
TAMORA: But would it please thee, good Andronicus,
TAMORA: To send for Lucius, thy thrice-valiant son,
TAMORA: Who leads towards Rome a band of warlike Goths,
TAMORA: And bid him come and banquet at thy house,
TAMORA: When he is here, even at thy solemn feast,
TAMORA: I will bring in the empress and her sons,
TAMORA: The emperor himself and all thy foes,
TAMORA: And at thy mercy shalt they stoop and kneel,
TAMORA: And on them shalt thou ease thy angry heart.
TAMORA: What says Andronicus to this device?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Marcus, my brother! 'tis sad Titus calls.
NARRATOR: Enter MARCUS
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Go, gentle Marcus, to thy nephew Lucius,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Thou shalt inquire him out among the Goths:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Bid him repair to me, and bring with him
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Some of the chiefest princes of the Goths,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Bid him encamp his soldiers where they are:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tell him the emperor and the empress too
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Feast at my house, and he shall feast with them.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This do thou for my love, and so let him,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: As he regards his aged father's life.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This will I do, and soon return again.
NARRATOR: Exit
TAMORA: Now will I hence about thy business,
TAMORA: And take my ministers along with me.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Nay, nay, let Rape and Murder stay with me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Or else I'll call my brother back again,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And cleave to no revenge but Lucius.
TAMORA: [Aside to her sons]  What say you, boys? will you
TAMORA: bide with him,
TAMORA: Whiles I go tell my lord the emperor
TAMORA: How I have govern'd our determined jest?
TAMORA: Yield to his humour, smooth and speak him fair,
TAMORA: And tarry with him till I turn again.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: [Aside]  I know them all, though they suppose me mad,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And will o'erreach them in their own devices:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A pair of cursed hell-hounds and their dam!
DEMETRIUS: Madam, depart at pleasure, leave us here.
TAMORA: Farewell, Andronicus: Revenge now goes
TAMORA: To lay a complot to betray thy foes.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I know thou dost, and, sweet Revenge, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit TAMORA
CHIRON: Tell us, old man, how shall we be employ'd?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Tut, I have work enough for you to do.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Publius, come hither, Caius, and Valentine!
NARRATOR: Enter PUBLIUS and others
PUBLIUS: What is your will?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Know you these two?
PUBLIUS: The empress' sons, I take them, Chiron and Demetrius.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Fie, Publius, fie! thou art too much deceived,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The one is Murder, Rape is the other's name,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And therefore bind them, gentle Publius.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Caius and Valentine, lay hands on them.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Oft have you heard me wish for such an hour,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And now I find it, therefore bind them sure,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And stop their mouths, if they begin to cry.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: PUBLIUS,  and c. lay hold on CHIRON and DEMETRIUS
CHIRON: Villains, forbear! we are the empress' sons.
PUBLIUS: And therefore do we what we are commanded.
PUBLIUS: Stop close their mouths, let them not speak a word.
PUBLIUS: Is he sure bound? look that you bind them fast.
PUBLIUS: Re-enter TITUS, with LAVINIA, he bearing a knife, and she a basin
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, come, Lavinia, look, thy foes are bound.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Sirs, stop their mouths, let them not speak to me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: But let them hear what fearful words I utter.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: O villains, Chiron and Demetrius!
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Here stands the spring whom you have stain'd with mud,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This goodly summer with your winter mix'd.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You kill'd her husband, and for that vile fault
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Two of her brothers were condemn'd to death,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My hand cut off and made a merry jest,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Both her sweet hands, her tongue, and that more dear
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Than hands or tongue, her spotless chastity,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Inhuman traitors, you constrain'd and forced.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: What would you say, if I should let you speak?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Villains, for shame you could not beg for grace.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hark, wretches! how I mean to martyr you.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This one hand yet is left to cut your throats,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Whilst that Lavinia 'tween her stumps doth hold
TITUS ANDRONICUS: The basin that receives your guilty blood.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: You know your mother means to feast with me,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And calls herself Revenge, and thinks me mad:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Hark, villains! I will grind your bones to dust
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And with your blood and it I'll make a paste,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And of the paste a coffin I will rear
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And make two pasties of your shameful heads,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And bid that strumpet, your unhallow'd dam,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Like to the earth swallow her own increase.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: This is the feast that I have bid her to,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And this the banquet she shall surfeit on,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For worse than Philomel you used my daughter,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And worse than Progne I will be revenged:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And now prepare your throats. Lavinia, come,
NARRATOR: He cuts their throats
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Receive the blood: and when that they are dead,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Let me go grind their bones to powder small
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And with this hateful liquor temper it,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And in that paste let their vile heads be baked.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Come, come, be every one officious
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To make this banquet, which I wish may prove
TITUS ANDRONICUS: More stern and bloody than the Centaurs' feast.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: So, now bring them in, for I'll play the cook,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And see them ready 'gainst their mother comes.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, bearing the dead bodies
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Court of TITUS's house. A banquet set out.
NARRATOR: Enter LUCIUS, MARCUS, and Goths, with AARON prisoner
LUCIUS: Uncle Marcus, since it is my father's mind
LUCIUS: That I repair to Rome, I am content.
First Goth: And ours with thine, befall what fortune will.
LUCIUS: Good uncle, take you in this barbarous Moor,
LUCIUS: This ravenous tiger, this accursed devil,
LUCIUS: Let him receive no sustenance, fetter him
LUCIUS: Till he be brought unto the empress' face,
LUCIUS: For testimony of her foul proceedings:
LUCIUS: And see the ambush of our friends be strong,
LUCIUS: I fear the emperor means no good to us.
AARON: Some devil whisper curses in mine ear,
AARON: And prompt me, that my tongue may utter forth
AARON: The venomous malice of my swelling heart!
LUCIUS: Away, inhuman dog! unhallow'd slave!
LUCIUS: Sirs, help our uncle to convey him in.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Goths, with AARON. Flourish within
LUCIUS: The trumpets show the emperor is at hand.
NARRATOR: Enter SATURNINUS and TAMORA, with AEMILIUS, Tribunes, Senators, and others
SATURNINUS: What, hath the firmament more suns than one?
LUCIUS: What boots it thee to call thyself a sun?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Rome's emperor, and nephew, break the parle,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: These quarrels must be quietly debated.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The feast is ready, which the careful Titus
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Hath ordain'd to an honourable end,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: For peace, for love, for league, and good to Rome:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Please you, therefore, draw nigh, and take your places.
SATURNINUS: Marcus, we will.
NARRATOR: Hautboys sound. The Company sit down at table
NARRATOR: Enter TITUS dressed like a Cook, LAVINIA veiled,  Young LUCIUS, and others. TITUS places the dishes on the table
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Welcome, my gracious lord, welcome, dread queen,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Welcome, ye warlike Goths, welcome, Lucius,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And welcome, all: although the cheer be poor,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Twill fill your stomachs, please you eat of it.
SATURNINUS: Why art thou thus attired, Andronicus?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Because I would be sure to have all well,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To entertain your highness and your empress.
TAMORA: We are beholding to you, good Andronicus.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: An if your highness knew my heart, you were.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: My lord the emperor, resolve me this:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Was it well done of rash Virginius
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To slay his daughter with his own right hand,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Because she was enforced, stain'd, and deflower'd?
SATURNINUS: It was, Andronicus.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Your reason, mighty lord?
SATURNINUS: Because the girl should not survive her shame,
SATURNINUS: And by her presence still renew his sorrows.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A reason mighty, strong, and effectual,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: A pattern, precedent, and lively warrant,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: For me, most wretched, to perform the like.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Die, die, Lavinia, and thy shame with thee,
NARRATOR: Kills LAVINIA
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And, with thy shame, thy father's sorrow die!
SATURNINUS: What hast thou done, unnatural and unkind?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Kill'd her, for whom my tears have made me blind.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: I am as woful as Virginius was,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And have a thousand times more cause than he
TITUS ANDRONICUS: To do this outrage: and it now is done.
SATURNINUS: What, was she ravish'd? tell who did the deed.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Will't please you eat? will't please your
TITUS ANDRONICUS: highness feed?
TAMORA: Why hast thou slain thine only daughter thus?
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Not I, 'twas Chiron and Demetrius:
TITUS ANDRONICUS: They ravish'd her, and cut away her tongue,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: And they, 'twas they, that did her all this wrong.
SATURNINUS: Go fetch them hither to us presently.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Why, there they are both, baked in that pie,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Whereof their mother daintily hath fed,
TITUS ANDRONICUS: Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
TITUS ANDRONICUS: 'Tis true, 'tis true, witness my knife's sharp point.
NARRATOR: Kills TAMORA
SATURNINUS: Die, frantic wretch, for this accursed deed!
NARRATOR: Kills TITUS
LUCIUS: Can the son's eye behold his father bleed?
LUCIUS: There's meed for meed, death for a deadly deed!
NARRATOR: Kills SATURNINUS. A great tumult. LUCIUS, MARCUS, and others go up into the balcony
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: You sad-faced men, people and sons of Rome,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: By uproar sever'd, like a flight of fowl
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Scatter'd by winds and high tempestuous gusts,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O, let me teach you how to knit again
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: This scatter'd corn  into one mutual sheaf,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: These broken limbs again into one body,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And she whom mighty kingdoms court'sy to,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Like a forlorn and desperate castaway,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Do shameful execution on herself.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But if my frosty signs and chaps of age,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Grave witnesses of true experience,
