MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Cannot induce you to attend my words,
NARRATOR: To LUCIUS
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Speak, Rome's dear friend, as erst our ancestor,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: When with his solemn tongue he did discourse
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To love-sick Dido's sad attending ear
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The story of that baleful burning night
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: When subtle Greeks surprised King Priam's Troy,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Tell us what Sinon hath bewitch'd our ears,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Or who hath brought the fatal engine in
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: That gives our Troy, our Rome, the civil wound.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: My heart is not compact of flint nor steel,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Nor can I utter all our bitter grief,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: But floods of tears will drown my oratory,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And break my utterance, even in the time
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: When it should move you to attend me most,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lending your kind commiseration.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Here is a captain, let him tell the tale,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Your hearts will throb and weep to hear him speak.
LUCIUS: Then, noble auditory, be it known to you,
LUCIUS: That cursed Chiron and Demetrius
LUCIUS: Were they that murdered our emperor's brother,
LUCIUS: And they it were that ravished our sister:
LUCIUS: For their fell faults our brothers were beheaded,
LUCIUS: Our father's tears despised, and basely cozen'd
LUCIUS: Of that true hand that fought Rome's quarrel out,
LUCIUS: And sent her enemies unto the grave.
LUCIUS: Lastly, myself unkindly banished,
LUCIUS: The gates shut on me, and turn'd weeping out,
LUCIUS: To beg relief among Rome's enemies:
LUCIUS: Who drown'd their enmity in my true tears.
LUCIUS: And oped their arms to embrace me as a friend.
LUCIUS: I am the turned forth, be it known to you,
LUCIUS: That have preserved her welfare in my blood,
LUCIUS: And from her bosom took the enemy's point,
LUCIUS: Sheathing the steel in my adventurous body.
LUCIUS: Alas, you know I am no vaunter, I,
LUCIUS: My scars can witness, dumb although they are,
LUCIUS: That my report is just and full of truth.
LUCIUS: But, soft! methinks I do digress too much,
LUCIUS: Citing my worthless praise: O, pardon me,
LUCIUS: For when no friends are by, men praise themselves.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now is my turn to speak. Behold this child:
NARRATOR: Pointing to the Child in the arms of an Attendant
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Of this was Tamora delivered,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The issue of an irreligious Moor,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Chief architect and plotter of these woes:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The villain is alive in Titus' house,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And as he is, to witness this is true.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now judge what cause had Titus to revenge
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: These wrongs, unspeakable, past patience,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Or more than any living man could bear.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Now you have heard the truth, what say you, Romans?
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Have we done aught amiss,--show us wherein,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And, from the place where you behold us now,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: The poor remainder of Andronici
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Will, hand in hand, all headlong cast us down.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And on the ragged stones beat forth our brains,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And make a mutual closure of our house.
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Speak, Romans, speak, and if you say we shall,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Lo, hand in hand, Lucius and I will fall.
AEMILIUS: Come, come, thou reverend man of Rome,
AEMILIUS: And bring our emperor gently in thy hand,
AEMILIUS: Lucius our emperor, for well I know
AEMILIUS: The common voice do cry it shall be so.
All: Lucius, all hail, Rome's royal emperor!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Go, go into old Titus' sorrowful house,
NARRATOR: To Attendants
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: And hither hale that misbelieving Moor,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: To be adjudged some direful slaughtering death,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: As punishment for his most wicked life.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Attendants
NARRATOR: LUCIUS, MARCUS, and the others descend
All: Lucius, all hail, Rome's gracious governor!
LUCIUS: Thanks, gentle Romans: may I govern so,
LUCIUS: To heal Rome's harms, and wipe away her woe!
LUCIUS: But, gentle people, give me aim awhile,
LUCIUS: For nature puts me to a heavy task:
LUCIUS: Stand all aloof: but, uncle, draw you near,
LUCIUS: To shed obsequious tears upon this trunk.
LUCIUS: O, take this warm kiss on thy pale cold lips,
NARRATOR: Kissing TITUS
LUCIUS: These sorrowful drops upon thy blood-stain'd face,
LUCIUS: The last true duties of thy noble son!
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Tear for tear, and loving kiss for kiss,
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Thy brother Marcus tenders on thy lips:
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: O were the sum of these that I should pay
MARCUS ANDRONICUS: Countless and infinite, yet would I pay them!
LUCIUS: Come hither, boy, come, come, and learn of us
LUCIUS: To melt in showers: thy grandsire loved thee well:
LUCIUS: Many a time he danced thee on his knee,
LUCIUS: Sung thee asleep, his loving breast thy pillow:
LUCIUS: Many a matter hath he told to thee,
LUCIUS: Meet and agreeing with thine infancy,
LUCIUS: In that respect, then, like a loving child,
LUCIUS: Shed yet some small drops from thy tender spring,
LUCIUS: Because kind nature doth require it so:
LUCIUS: Friends should associate friends in grief and woe:
LUCIUS: Bid him farewell, commit him to the grave,
LUCIUS: Do him that kindness, and take leave of him.
Young LUCIUS: O grandsire, grandsire! even with all my heart
Young LUCIUS: Would I were dead, so you did live again!
Young LUCIUS: O Lord, I cannot speak to him for weeping,
Young LUCIUS: My tears will choke me, if I ope my mouth.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Attendants with AARON
AEMILIUS: You sad Andronici, have done with woes:
AEMILIUS: Give sentence on this execrable wretch,
AEMILIUS: That hath been breeder of these dire events.
LUCIUS: Set him breast-deep in earth, and famish him,
LUCIUS: There let him stand, and rave, and cry for food,
LUCIUS: If any one relieves or pities him,
LUCIUS: For the offence he dies. This is our doom:
LUCIUS: Some stay to see him fasten'd in the earth.
AARON: O, why should wrath be mute, and fury dumb?
AARON: I am no baby, I, that with base prayers
AARON: I should repent the evils I have done:
AARON: Ten thousand worse than ever yet I did
AARON: Would I perform, if I might have my will,
AARON: If one good deed in all my life I did,
AARON: I do repent it from my very soul.
LUCIUS: Some loving friends convey the emperor hence,
LUCIUS: And give him burial in his father's grave:
LUCIUS: My father and Lavinia shall forthwith
LUCIUS: Be closed in our household's monument.
LUCIUS: As for that heinous tiger, Tamora,
LUCIUS: No funeral rite, nor man m mourning weeds,
LUCIUS: No mournful bell shall ring her burial,
LUCIUS: But throw her forth to beasts and birds of prey:
LUCIUS: Her life was beast-like, and devoid of pity,
LUCIUS: And, being so, shall have like want of pity.
LUCIUS: See justice done on Aaron, that damn'd Moor,
LUCIUS: By whom our heavy haps had their beginning:
LUCIUS: Then, afterwards, to order well the state,
LUCIUS: That like events may ne'er it ruinate.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
''' PLAY: Troilus and Cressida '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: PROLOGUE
LUCIUS: In Troy, there lies the scene. From isles of Greece
LUCIUS: The princes orgulous, their high blood chafed,
LUCIUS: Have to the port of Athens sent their ships,
LUCIUS: Fraught with the ministers and instruments
LUCIUS: Of cruel war: sixty and nine, that wore
LUCIUS: Their crownets regal, from the Athenian bay
LUCIUS: Put forth toward Phrygia, and their vow is made
LUCIUS: To ransack Troy, within whose strong immures
LUCIUS: The ravish'd Helen, Menelaus' queen,
LUCIUS: With wanton Paris sleeps, and that's the quarrel.
LUCIUS: To Tenedos they come,
LUCIUS: And the deep-drawing barks do there disgorge
LUCIUS: Their warlike fraughtage: now on Dardan plains
LUCIUS: The fresh and yet unbruised Greeks do pitch
LUCIUS: Their brave pavilions: Priam's six-gated city,
LUCIUS: Dardan, and Tymbria, Helias, Chetas, Troien,
LUCIUS: And Antenorides, with massy staples
LUCIUS: And corresponsive and fulfilling bolts,
LUCIUS: Sperr up the sons of Troy.
LUCIUS: Now expectation, tickling skittish spirits,
LUCIUS: On one and other side, Trojan and Greek,
LUCIUS: Sets all on hazard: and hither am I come
LUCIUS: A prologue arm'd, but not in confidence
LUCIUS: Of author's pen or actor's voice, but suited
LUCIUS: In like conditions as our argument,
LUCIUS: To tell you, fair beholders, that our play
LUCIUS: Leaps o'er the vaunt and firstlings of those broils,
LUCIUS: Beginning in the middle, starting thence away
LUCIUS: To what may be digested in a play.
LUCIUS: Like or find fault, do as your pleasures are:
LUCIUS: Now good or bad, 'tis but the chance of war.
LUCIUS: SCENE I. Troy. Before Priam's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS armed, and PANDARUS
TROILUS: Call here my varlet, I'll unarm again:
TROILUS: Why should I war without the walls of Troy,
TROILUS: That find such cruel battle here within?
TROILUS: Each Trojan that is master of his heart,
TROILUS: Let him to field, Troilus, alas! hath none.
PANDARUS: Will this gear ne'er be mended?
TROILUS: The Greeks are strong and skilful to their strength,
TROILUS: Fierce to their skill and to their fierceness valiant,
TROILUS: But I am weaker than a woman's tear,
TROILUS: Tamer than sleep, fonder than ignorance,
TROILUS: Less valiant than the virgin in the night
TROILUS: And skilless as unpractised infancy.
PANDARUS: Well, I have told you enough of this: for my part,
PANDARUS: I'll not meddle nor make no further. He that will
PANDARUS: have a cake out of the wheat must needs tarry the grinding.
TROILUS: Have I not tarried?
PANDARUS: Ay, the grinding, but you must tarry
PANDARUS: the bolting.
TROILUS: Have I not tarried?
PANDARUS: Ay, the bolting, but you must tarry the leavening.
TROILUS: Still have I tarried.
PANDARUS: Ay, to the leavening, but here's yet in the word
PANDARUS: 'hereafter' the kneading, the making of the cake, the
PANDARUS: heating of the oven and the baking, nay, you must
PANDARUS: stay the cooling too, or you may chance to burn your lips.
TROILUS: Patience herself, what goddess e'er she be,
TROILUS: Doth lesser blench at sufferance than I do.
TROILUS: At Priam's royal table do I sit,
TROILUS: And when fair Cressid comes into my thoughts,--
TROILUS: So, traitor! 'When she comes!' When is she thence?
PANDARUS: Well, she looked yesternight fairer than ever I saw
PANDARUS: her look, or any woman else.
TROILUS: I was about to tell thee:--when my heart,
TROILUS: As wedged with a sigh, would rive in twain,
TROILUS: Lest Hector or my father should perceive me,
TROILUS: I have, as when the sun doth light a storm,
TROILUS: Buried this sigh in wrinkle of a smile:
TROILUS: But sorrow, that is couch'd in seeming gladness,
TROILUS: Is like that mirth fate turns to sudden sadness.
PANDARUS: An her hair were not somewhat darker than Helen's--
PANDARUS: well, go to--there were no more comparison between
PANDARUS: the women: but, for my part, she is my kinswoman, I
PANDARUS: would not, as they term it, praise her: but I would
PANDARUS: somebody had heard her talk yesterday, as I did. I
PANDARUS: will not dispraise your sister Cassandra's wit, but--
TROILUS: O Pandarus! I tell thee, Pandarus,--
TROILUS: When I do tell thee, there my hopes lie drown'd,
TROILUS: Reply not in how many fathoms deep
TROILUS: They lie indrench'd. I tell thee I am mad
TROILUS: In Cressid's love: thou answer'st 'she is fair,'
TROILUS: Pour'st in the open ulcer of my heart
TROILUS: Her eyes, her hair, her cheek, her gait, her voice,
TROILUS: Handlest in thy discourse, O, that her hand,
TROILUS: In whose comparison all whites are ink,
TROILUS: Writing their own reproach, to whose soft seizure
TROILUS: The cygnet's down is harsh and spirit of sense
TROILUS: Hard as the palm of ploughman: this thou tell'st me,
TROILUS: As true thou tell'st me, when I say I love her,
TROILUS: But, saying thus, instead of oil and balm,
TROILUS: Thou lay'st in every gash that love hath given me
TROILUS: The knife that made it.
PANDARUS: I speak no more than truth.
TROILUS: Thou dost not speak so much.
PANDARUS: Faith, I'll not meddle in't. Let her be as she is:
PANDARUS: if she be fair, 'tis the better for her, an she be
PANDARUS: not, she has the mends in her own hands.
TROILUS: Good Pandarus, how now, Pandarus!
PANDARUS: I have had my labour for my travail, ill-thought on of
PANDARUS: her and ill-thought on of you, gone between and
PANDARUS: between, but small thanks for my labour.
TROILUS: What, art thou angry, Pandarus? what, with me?
PANDARUS: Because she's kin to me, therefore she's not so fair
PANDARUS: as Helen: an she were not kin to me, she would be as
PANDARUS: fair on Friday as Helen is on Sunday. But what care
PANDARUS: I? I care not an she were a black-a-moor, 'tis all one to me.
TROILUS: Say I she is not fair?
PANDARUS: I do not care whether you do or no. She's a fool to
PANDARUS: stay behind her father, let her to the Greeks, and so
PANDARUS: I'll tell her the next time I see her: for my part,
PANDARUS: I'll meddle nor make no more i' the matter.
TROILUS: Pandarus,--
PANDARUS: Not I.
TROILUS: Sweet Pandarus,--
PANDARUS: Pray you, speak no more to me: I will leave all as I
PANDARUS: found it, and there an end.
NARRATOR: Exit PANDARUS. An alarum
TROILUS: Peace, you ungracious clamours! peace, rude sounds!
TROILUS: Fools on both sides! Helen must needs be fair,
TROILUS: When with your blood you daily paint her thus.
TROILUS: I cannot fight upon this argument,
TROILUS: It is too starved a subject for my sword.
TROILUS: But Pandarus,--O gods, how do you plague me!
TROILUS: I cannot come to Cressid but by Pandar,
TROILUS: And he's as tetchy to be woo'd to woo.
TROILUS: As she is stubborn-chaste against all suit.
TROILUS: Tell me, Apollo, for thy Daphne's love,
TROILUS: What Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we?
TROILUS: Her bed is India, there she lies, a pearl:
TROILUS: Between our Ilium and where she resides,
TROILUS: Let it be call'd the wild and wandering flood,
TROILUS: Ourself the merchant, and this sailing Pandar
TROILUS: Our doubtful hope, our convoy and our bark.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Enter AENEAS
AENEAS: How now, Prince Troilus! wherefore not afield?
TROILUS: Because not there: this woman's answer sorts,
TROILUS: For womanish it is to be from thence.
TROILUS: What news, AEneas, from the field to-day?
AENEAS: That Paris is returned home and hurt.
TROILUS: By whom, AEneas?
AENEAS: Troilus, by Menelaus.
TROILUS: Let Paris bleed, 'tis but a scar to scorn,
TROILUS: Paris is gored with Menelaus' horn.
NARRATOR: Alarum
AENEAS: Hark, what good sport is out of town to-day!
TROILUS: Better at home, if 'would I might' were 'may.'
TROILUS: But to the sport abroad: are you bound thither?
AENEAS: In all swift haste.
TROILUS: Come, go we then together.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The Same. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter CRESSIDA and ALEXANDER
CRESSIDA: Who were those went by?
ALEXANDER: Queen Hecuba and Helen.
CRESSIDA: And whither go they?
ALEXANDER: Up to the eastern tower,
ALEXANDER: Whose height commands as subject all the vale,
ALEXANDER: To see the battle. Hector, whose patience
ALEXANDER: Is, as a virtue, fix'd, to-day was moved:
ALEXANDER: He chid Andromache and struck his armourer,
ALEXANDER: And, like as there were husbandry in war,
ALEXANDER: Before the sun rose he was harness'd light,
ALEXANDER: And to the field goes he, where every flower
ALEXANDER: Did, as a prophet, weep what it foresaw
ALEXANDER: In Hector's wrath.
CRESSIDA: What was his cause of anger?
ALEXANDER: The noise goes, this: there is among the Greeks
ALEXANDER: A lord of Trojan blood, nephew to Hector,
ALEXANDER: They call him Ajax.
CRESSIDA: Good, and what of him?
ALEXANDER: They say he is a very man per se,
ALEXANDER: And stands alone.
CRESSIDA: So do all men, unless they are drunk, sick, or have no legs.
ALEXANDER: This man, lady, hath robbed many beasts of their
ALEXANDER: particular additions, he is as valiant as the lion,
ALEXANDER: churlish as the bear, slow as the elephant: a man
ALEXANDER: into whom nature hath so crowded humours that his
ALEXANDER: valour is crushed into folly, his folly sauced with
ALEXANDER: discretion: there is no man hath a virtue that he
ALEXANDER: hath not a glimpse of, nor any man an attaint but he
ALEXANDER: carries some stain of it: he is melancholy without
ALEXANDER: cause, and merry against the hair: he hath the
ALEXANDER: joints of every thing, but everything so out of joint
ALEXANDER: that he is a gouty Briareus, many hands and no use,
ALEXANDER: or purblind Argus, all eyes and no sight.
CRESSIDA: But how should this man, that makes
CRESSIDA: me smile, make Hector angry?
ALEXANDER: They say he yesterday coped Hector in the battle and
ALEXANDER: struck him down, the disdain and shame whereof hath
ALEXANDER: ever since kept Hector fasting and waking.
CRESSIDA: Who comes here?
ALEXANDER: Madam, your uncle Pandarus.
NARRATOR: Enter PANDARUS
CRESSIDA: Hector's a gallant man.
ALEXANDER: As may be in the world, lady.
PANDARUS: What's that? what's that?
CRESSIDA: Good morrow, uncle Pandarus.
PANDARUS: Good morrow, cousin Cressid: what do you talk of?
PANDARUS: Good morrow, Alexander. How do you, cousin? When
PANDARUS: were you at Ilium?
CRESSIDA: This morning, uncle.
PANDARUS: What were you talking of when I came? Was Hector
PANDARUS: armed and gone ere ye came to Ilium? Helen was not
PANDARUS: up, was she?
CRESSIDA: Hector was gone, but Helen was not up.
PANDARUS: Even so: Hector was stirring early.
CRESSIDA: That were we talking of, and of his anger.
PANDARUS: Was he angry?
CRESSIDA: So he says here.
PANDARUS: True, he was so: I know the cause too: he'll lay
PANDARUS: about him to-day, I can tell them that: and there's
PANDARUS: Troilus will not come far behind him: let them take
PANDARUS: heed of Troilus, I can tell them that too.
CRESSIDA: What, is he angry too?
PANDARUS: Who, Troilus? Troilus is the better man of the two.
CRESSIDA: O Jupiter! there's no comparison.
PANDARUS: What, not between Troilus and Hector? Do you know a
PANDARUS: man if you see him?
CRESSIDA: Ay, if I ever saw him before and knew him.
PANDARUS: Well, I say Troilus is Troilus.
CRESSIDA: Then you say as I say, for, I am sure, he is not Hector.
PANDARUS: No, nor Hector is not Troilus in some degrees.
CRESSIDA: 'Tis just to each of them, he is himself.
PANDARUS: Himself! Alas, poor Troilus! I would he were.
CRESSIDA: So he is.
PANDARUS: Condition, I had gone barefoot to India.
CRESSIDA: He is not Hector.
PANDARUS: Himself! no, he's not himself: would a' were
PANDARUS: himself! Well, the gods are above, time must friend
PANDARUS: or end: well, Troilus, well: I would my heart were
PANDARUS: in her body. No, Hector is not a better man than Troilus.
CRESSIDA: Excuse me.
PANDARUS: He is elder.
CRESSIDA: Pardon me, pardon me.
PANDARUS: Th' other's not come to't, you shall tell me another
PANDARUS: tale, when th' other's come to't. Hector shall not
PANDARUS: have his wit this year.
CRESSIDA: He shall not need it, if he have his own.
PANDARUS: Nor his qualities.
CRESSIDA: No matter.
PANDARUS: Nor his beauty.
CRESSIDA: 'Twould not become him, his own's better.
PANDARUS: You have no judgment, niece: Helen
PANDARUS: herself swore th' other day, that Troilus, for
PANDARUS: a brown favour--for so 'tis, I must confess,--
PANDARUS: not brown neither,--
CRESSIDA: No, but brown.
PANDARUS: 'Faith, to say truth, brown and not brown.
CRESSIDA: To say the truth, true and not true.
PANDARUS: She praised his complexion above Paris.
CRESSIDA: Why, Paris hath colour enough.
PANDARUS: So he has.
CRESSIDA: Then Troilus should have too much: if she praised
CRESSIDA: him above, his complexion is higher than his, he
CRESSIDA: having colour enough, and the other higher, is too
CRESSIDA: flaming a praise for a good complexion. I had as
CRESSIDA: lief Helen's golden tongue had commended Troilus for
CRESSIDA: a copper nose.
PANDARUS: I swear to you. I think Helen loves him better than Paris.
CRESSIDA: Then she's a merry Greek indeed.
PANDARUS: Nay, I am sure she does. She came to him th' other
PANDARUS: day into the compassed window,--and, you know, he
PANDARUS: has not past three or four hairs on his chin,--
CRESSIDA: Indeed, a tapster's arithmetic may soon bring his
CRESSIDA: particulars therein to a total.
PANDARUS: Why, he is very young: and yet will he, within
PANDARUS: three pound, lift as much as his brother Hector.
CRESSIDA: Is he so young a man and so old a lifter?
PANDARUS: But to prove to you that Helen loves him: she came
PANDARUS: and puts me her white hand to his cloven chin--
CRESSIDA: Juno have mercy! how came it cloven?
PANDARUS: Why, you know 'tis dimpled: I think his smiling
PANDARUS: becomes him better than any man in all Phrygia.
CRESSIDA: O, he smiles valiantly.
PANDARUS: Does he not?
CRESSIDA: O yes, an 'twere a cloud in autumn.
PANDARUS: Why, go to, then: but to prove to you that Helen
PANDARUS: loves Troilus,--
CRESSIDA: Troilus will stand to the proof, if you'll
CRESSIDA: prove it so.
PANDARUS: Troilus! why, he esteems her no more than I esteem
PANDARUS: an addle egg.
CRESSIDA: If you love an addle egg as well as you love an idle
CRESSIDA: head, you would eat chickens i' the shell.
PANDARUS: I cannot choose but laugh, to think how she tickled
PANDARUS: his chin: indeed, she has a marvellous white hand, I
PANDARUS: must needs confess,--
CRESSIDA: Without the rack.
PANDARUS: And she takes upon her to spy a white hair on his chin.
CRESSIDA: Alas, poor chin! many a wart is richer.
PANDARUS: But there was such laughing! Queen Hecuba laughed
PANDARUS: that her eyes ran o'er.
CRESSIDA: With mill-stones.
PANDARUS: And Cassandra laughed.
CRESSIDA: But there was more temperate fire under the pot of
CRESSIDA: her eyes: did her eyes run o'er too?
PANDARUS: And Hector laughed.
CRESSIDA: At what was all this laughing?
PANDARUS: Marry, at the white hair that Helen spied on Troilus' chin.
CRESSIDA: An't had been a green hair, I should have laughed
CRESSIDA: too.
PANDARUS: They laughed not so much at the hair as at his pretty answer.
CRESSIDA: What was his answer?
PANDARUS: Quoth she, 'Here's but two and fifty hairs on your
PANDARUS: chin, and one of them is white.
CRESSIDA: This is her question.
PANDARUS: That's true, make no question of that. 'Two and
PANDARUS: fifty hairs' quoth he, 'and one white: that white
PANDARUS: hair is my father, and all the rest are his sons.'
PANDARUS: 'Jupiter!' quoth she, 'which of these hairs is Paris,
PANDARUS: my husband? 'The forked one,' quoth he, 'pluck't
PANDARUS: out, and give it him.' But there was such laughing!
PANDARUS: and Helen so blushed, an Paris so chafed, and all the
PANDARUS: rest so laughed, that it passed.
CRESSIDA: So let it now, for it has been while going by.
PANDARUS: Well, cousin. I told you a thing yesterday, think on't.
CRESSIDA: So I do.
PANDARUS: I'll be sworn 'tis true, he will weep you, an 'twere
PANDARUS: a man born in April.
CRESSIDA: And I'll spring up in his tears, an 'twere a nettle
CRESSIDA: against May.
NARRATOR: A retreat sounded
PANDARUS: Hark! they are coming from the field: shall we
PANDARUS: stand up here, and see them as they pass toward
PANDARUS: Ilium? good niece, do, sweet niece Cressida.
CRESSIDA: At your pleasure.
PANDARUS: Here, here, here's an excellent place, here we may
PANDARUS: see most bravely: I'll tell you them all by their
PANDARUS: names as they pass by, but mark Troilus above the rest.
CRESSIDA: Speak not so loud.
NARRATOR: AENEAS passes
PANDARUS: That's AEneas: is not that a brave man? he's one of
PANDARUS: the flowers of Troy, I can tell you: but mark
PANDARUS: Troilus, you shall see anon.
NARRATOR: ANTENOR passes
CRESSIDA: Who's that?
PANDARUS: That's Antenor: he has a shrewd wit, I can tell you,
PANDARUS: and he's a man good enough, he's one o' the soundest
PANDARUS: judgments in whosoever, and a proper man of person.
PANDARUS: When comes Troilus? I'll show you Troilus anon: if
PANDARUS: he see me, you shall see him nod at me.
CRESSIDA: Will he give you the nod?
PANDARUS: You shall see.
CRESSIDA: If he do, the rich shall have more.
NARRATOR: HECTOR passes
PANDARUS: That's Hector, that, that, look you, that, there's a
PANDARUS: fellow! Go thy way, Hector! There's a brave man,
PANDARUS: niece. O brave Hector! Look how he looks! there's
PANDARUS: a countenance! is't not a brave man?
CRESSIDA: O, a brave man!
PANDARUS: Is a' not? it does a man's heart good. Look you
PANDARUS: what hacks are on his helmet! look you yonder, do
PANDARUS: you see? look you there: there's no jesting,
PANDARUS: there's laying on, take't off who will, as they say:
PANDARUS: there be hacks!
CRESSIDA: Be those with swords?
PANDARUS: Swords! any thing, he cares not, an the devil come
PANDARUS: to him, it's all one: by God's lid, it does one's
PANDARUS: heart good. Yonder comes Paris, yonder comes Paris.
NARRATOR: PARIS passes
PANDARUS: Look ye yonder, niece, is't not a gallant man too,
PANDARUS: is't not? Why, this is brave now. Who said he came
PANDARUS: hurt home to-day? he's not hurt: why, this will do
PANDARUS: Helen's heart good now, ha! Would I could see
PANDARUS: Troilus now! You shall see Troilus anon.
NARRATOR: HELENUS passes
CRESSIDA: Who's that?
PANDARUS: That's Helenus. I marvel where Troilus is. That's
PANDARUS: Helenus. I think he went not forth to-day. That's Helenus.
CRESSIDA: Can Helenus fight, uncle?
PANDARUS: Helenus? no. Yes, he'll fight indifferent well. I
PANDARUS: marvel where Troilus is. Hark! do you not hear the
PANDARUS: people cry 'Troilus'? Helenus is a priest.
CRESSIDA: What sneaking fellow comes yonder?
NARRATOR: TROILUS passes
PANDARUS: Where? yonder? that's Deiphobus. 'Tis Troilus!
PANDARUS: there's a man, niece! Hem! Brave Troilus! the
PANDARUS: prince of chivalry!
CRESSIDA: Peace, for shame, peace!
PANDARUS: Mark him, note him. O brave Troilus! Look well upon
PANDARUS: him, niece: look you how his sword is bloodied, and
PANDARUS: his helm more hacked than Hector's, and how he looks,
PANDARUS: and how he goes! O admirable youth! he ne'er saw
PANDARUS: three and twenty. Go thy way, Troilus, go thy way!
PANDARUS: Had I a sister were a grace, or a daughter a goddess,
PANDARUS: he should take his choice. O admirable man! Paris?
PANDARUS: Paris is dirt to him, and, I warrant, Helen, to
PANDARUS: change, would give an eye to boot.
CRESSIDA: Here come more.
NARRATOR: Forces pass
PANDARUS: Asses, fools, dolts! chaff and bran, chaff and bran!
PANDARUS: porridge after meat! I could live and die i' the
PANDARUS: eyes of Troilus. Ne'er look, ne'er look: the eagles
PANDARUS: are gone: crows and daws, crows and daws! I had
PANDARUS: rather be such a man as Troilus than Agamemnon and
PANDARUS: all Greece.
CRESSIDA: There is among the Greeks Achilles, a better man than Troilus.
PANDARUS: Achilles! a drayman, a porter, a very camel.
CRESSIDA: Well, well.
PANDARUS: 'Well, well!' why, have you any discretion? have
PANDARUS: you any eyes? Do you know what a man is? Is not
PANDARUS: birth, beauty, good shape, discourse, manhood,
PANDARUS: learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, liberality,
PANDARUS: and such like, the spice and salt that season a man?
CRESSIDA: Ay, a minced man: and then to be baked with no date
CRESSIDA: in the pie, for then the man's date's out.
PANDARUS: You are such a woman! one knows not at what ward you
PANDARUS: lie.
CRESSIDA: Upon my back, to defend my belly, upon my wit, to
CRESSIDA: defend my wiles, upon my secrecy, to defend mine
CRESSIDA: honesty, my mask, to defend my beauty, and you, to
CRESSIDA: defend all these: and at all these wards I lie, at a
CRESSIDA: thousand watches.
PANDARUS: Say one of your watches.
CRESSIDA: Nay, I'll watch you for that, and that's one of the
CRESSIDA: chiefest of them too: if I cannot ward what I would
CRESSIDA: not have hit, I can watch you for telling how I took
CRESSIDA: the blow, unless it swell past hiding, and then it's
CRESSIDA: past watching.
PANDARUS: You are such another!
NARRATOR: Enter Troilus's Boy
Boy: Sir, my lord would instantly speak with you.
PANDARUS: Where?
Boy: At your own house, there he unarms him.
PANDARUS: Good boy, tell him I come.
NARRATOR: Exit boy
PANDARUS: I doubt he be hurt. Fare ye well, good niece.
CRESSIDA: Adieu, uncle.
PANDARUS: I'll be with you, niece, by and by.
CRESSIDA: To bring, uncle?
PANDARUS: Ay, a token from Troilus.
CRESSIDA: By the same token, you are a bawd.
NARRATOR: Exit PANDARUS
CRESSIDA: Words, vows, gifts, tears, and love's full sacrifice,
CRESSIDA: He offers in another's enterprise,
CRESSIDA: But more in Troilus thousand fold I see
CRESSIDA: Than in the glass of Pandar's praise may be,
CRESSIDA: Yet hold I off. Women are angels, wooing:
CRESSIDA: Things won are done, joy's soul lies in the doing.
CRESSIDA: That she beloved knows nought that knows not this:
CRESSIDA: Men prize the thing ungain'd more than it is:
CRESSIDA: That she was never yet that ever knew
CRESSIDA: Love got so sweet as when desire did sue.
CRESSIDA: Therefore this maxim out of love I teach:
CRESSIDA: Achievement is command, ungain'd, beseech:
CRESSIDA: Then though my heart's content firm love doth bear,
CRESSIDA: Nothing of that shall from mine eyes appear.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Grecian camp. Before Agamemnon's tent.
NARRATOR: Sennet. Enter AGAMEMNON, NESTOR, ULYSSES, MENELAUS, and others
AGAMEMNON: Princes,
AGAMEMNON: What grief hath set the jaundice on your cheeks?
AGAMEMNON: The ample proposition that hope makes
AGAMEMNON: In all designs begun on earth below
AGAMEMNON: Fails in the promised largeness: cheques and disasters
AGAMEMNON: Grow in the veins of actions highest rear'd,
AGAMEMNON: As knots, by the conflux of meeting sap,
AGAMEMNON: Infect the sound pine and divert his grain
AGAMEMNON: Tortive and errant from his course of growth.
AGAMEMNON: Nor, princes, is it matter new to us
AGAMEMNON: That we come short of our suppose so far
AGAMEMNON: That after seven years' siege yet Troy walls stand,
AGAMEMNON: Sith every action that hath gone before,
AGAMEMNON: Whereof we have record, trial did draw
AGAMEMNON: Bias and thwart, not answering the aim,
AGAMEMNON: And that unbodied figure of the thought
AGAMEMNON: That gave't surmised shape. Why then, you princes,
AGAMEMNON: Do you with cheeks abash'd behold our works,
AGAMEMNON: And call them shames? which are indeed nought else
AGAMEMNON: But the protractive trials of great Jove
AGAMEMNON: To find persistive constancy in men:
AGAMEMNON: The fineness of which metal is not found
AGAMEMNON: In fortune's love, for then the bold and coward,
AGAMEMNON: The wise and fool, the artist and unread,
AGAMEMNON: The hard and soft seem all affined and kin:
AGAMEMNON: But, in the wind and tempest of her frown,
AGAMEMNON: Distinction, with a broad and powerful fan,
AGAMEMNON: Puffing at all, winnows the light away,
AGAMEMNON: And what hath mass or matter, by itself
AGAMEMNON: Lies rich in virtue and unmingled.
NESTOR: With due observance of thy godlike seat,
NESTOR: Great Agamemnon, Nestor shall apply
NESTOR: Thy latest words. In the reproof of chance
NESTOR: Lies the true proof of men: the sea being smooth,
NESTOR: How many shallow bauble boats dare sail
NESTOR: Upon her patient breast, making their way
NESTOR: With those of nobler bulk!
NESTOR: But let the ruffian Boreas once enrage
NESTOR: The gentle Thetis, and anon behold
NESTOR: The strong-ribb'd bark through liquid mountains cut,
NESTOR: Bounding between the two moist elements,
NESTOR: Like Perseus' horse: where's then the saucy boat
NESTOR: Whose weak untimber'd sides but even now
NESTOR: Co-rivall'd greatness? Either to harbour fled,
NESTOR: Or made a toast for Neptune. Even so
NESTOR: Doth valour's show and valour's worth divide
NESTOR: In storms of fortune, for in her ray and brightness
NESTOR: The herd hath more annoyance by the breeze
NESTOR: Than by the tiger, but when the splitting wind
NESTOR: Makes flexible the knees of knotted oaks,
NESTOR: And flies fled under shade, why, then the thing of courage
NESTOR: As roused with rage with rage doth sympathize,
NESTOR: And with an accent tuned in selfsame key
NESTOR: Retorts to chiding fortune.
ULYSSES: Agamemnon,
ULYSSES: Thou great commander, nerve and bone of Greece,
ULYSSES: Heart of our numbers, soul and only spirit.
ULYSSES: In whom the tempers and the minds of all
ULYSSES: Should be shut up, hear what Ulysses speaks.
ULYSSES: Besides the applause and approbation To which,
NARRATOR: To AGAMEMNON
ULYSSES: most mighty for thy place and sway,
NARRATOR: To NESTOR
ULYSSES: And thou most reverend for thy stretch'd-out life
ULYSSES: I give to both your speeches, which were such
ULYSSES: As Agamemnon and the hand of Greece
ULYSSES: Should hold up high in brass, and such again
ULYSSES: As venerable Nestor, hatch'd in silver,
ULYSSES: Should with a bond of air, strong as the axle-tree
ULYSSES: On which heaven rides, knit all the Greekish ears
ULYSSES: To his experienced tongue, yet let it please both,
ULYSSES: Thou great, and wise, to hear Ulysses speak.
AGAMEMNON: Speak, prince of Ithaca, and be't of less expect
AGAMEMNON: That matter needless, of importless burden,
AGAMEMNON: Divide thy lips, than we are confident,
AGAMEMNON: When rank Thersites opes his mastic jaws,
AGAMEMNON: We shall hear music, wit and oracle.
ULYSSES: Troy, yet upon his basis, had been down,
ULYSSES: And the great Hector's sword had lack'd a master,
ULYSSES: But for these instances.
ULYSSES: The specialty of rule hath been neglected:
ULYSSES: And, look, how many Grecian tents do stand
ULYSSES: Hollow upon this plain, so many hollow factions.
ULYSSES: When that the general is not like the hive
ULYSSES: To whom the foragers shall all repair,
ULYSSES: What honey is expected? Degree being vizarded,
ULYSSES: The unworthiest shows as fairly in the mask.
ULYSSES: The heavens themselves, the planets and this centre
ULYSSES: Observe degree, priority and place,
ULYSSES: Insisture, course, proportion, season, form,
ULYSSES: Office and custom, in all line of order,
ULYSSES: And therefore is the glorious planet Sol
ULYSSES: In noble eminence enthroned and sphered
ULYSSES: Amidst the other, whose medicinable eye
ULYSSES: Corrects the ill aspects of planets evil,
ULYSSES: And posts, like the commandment of a king,
ULYSSES: Sans cheque to good and bad: but when the planets
ULYSSES: In evil mixture to disorder wander,
ULYSSES: What plagues and what portents! what mutiny!
ULYSSES: What raging of the sea! shaking of earth!
ULYSSES: Commotion in the winds! frights, changes, horrors,
ULYSSES: Divert and crack, rend and deracinate
ULYSSES: The unity and married calm of states
ULYSSES: Quite from their fixure! O, when degree is shaked,
ULYSSES: Which is the ladder to all high designs,
ULYSSES: Then enterprise is sick! How could communities,
ULYSSES: Degrees in schools and brotherhoods in cities,
ULYSSES: Peaceful commerce from dividable shores,
ULYSSES: The primogenitive and due of birth,
ULYSSES: Prerogative of age, crowns, sceptres, laurels,
ULYSSES: But by degree, stand in authentic place?
ULYSSES: Take but degree away, untune that string,
ULYSSES: And, hark, what discord follows! each thing meets
ULYSSES: In mere oppugnancy: the bounded waters
ULYSSES: Should lift their bosoms higher than the shores
ULYSSES: And make a sop of all this solid globe:
ULYSSES: Strength should be lord of imbecility,
ULYSSES: And the rude son should strike his father dead:
ULYSSES: Force should be right, or rather, right and wrong,
ULYSSES: Between whose endless jar justice resides,
ULYSSES: Should lose their names, and so should justice too.
ULYSSES: Then every thing includes itself in power,
ULYSSES: Power into will, will into appetite,
ULYSSES: And appetite, an universal wolf,
ULYSSES: So doubly seconded with will and power,
ULYSSES: Must make perforce an universal prey,
ULYSSES: And last eat up himself. Great Agamemnon,
ULYSSES: This chaos, when degree is suffocate,
ULYSSES: Follows the choking.
ULYSSES: And this neglection of degree it is
ULYSSES: That by a pace goes backward, with a purpose
ULYSSES: It hath to climb. The general's disdain'd
ULYSSES: By him one step below, he by the next,
ULYSSES: That next by him beneath, so every step,
ULYSSES: Exampled by the first pace that is sick
ULYSSES: Of his superior, grows to an envious fever
ULYSSES: Of pale and bloodless emulation:
ULYSSES: And 'tis this fever that keeps Troy on foot,
ULYSSES: Not her own sinews. To end a tale of length,
ULYSSES: Troy in our weakness stands, not in her strength.
NESTOR: Most wisely hath Ulysses here discover'd
NESTOR: The fever whereof all our power is sick.
AGAMEMNON: The nature of the sickness found, Ulysses,
AGAMEMNON: What is the remedy?
ULYSSES: The great Achilles, whom opinion crowns
ULYSSES: The sinew and the forehand of our host,
ULYSSES: Having his ear full of his airy fame,
ULYSSES: Grows dainty of his worth, and in his tent
ULYSSES: Lies mocking our designs: with him Patroclus
ULYSSES: Upon a lazy bed the livelong day
ULYSSES: Breaks scurril jests,
ULYSSES: And with ridiculous and awkward action,
ULYSSES: Which, slanderer, he imitation calls,
ULYSSES: He pageants us. Sometime, great Agamemnon,
ULYSSES: Thy topless deputation he puts on,
ULYSSES: And, like a strutting player, whose conceit
ULYSSES: Lies in his hamstring, and doth think it rich
ULYSSES: To hear the wooden dialogue and sound
ULYSSES: 'Twixt his stretch'd footing and the scaffoldage,--
ULYSSES: Such to-be-pitied and o'er-wrested seeming
ULYSSES: He acts thy greatness in: and when he speaks,
ULYSSES: 'Tis like a chime a-mending, with terms unsquared,
ULYSSES: Which, from the tongue of roaring Typhon dropp'd
ULYSSES: Would seem hyperboles. At this fusty stuff
ULYSSES: The large Achilles, on his press'd bed lolling,
ULYSSES: From his deep chest laughs out a loud applause,
ULYSSES: Cries 'Excellent! 'tis Agamemnon just.
ULYSSES: Now play me Nestor, hem, and stroke thy beard,
ULYSSES: As he being drest to some oration.'
ULYSSES: That's done, as near as the extremest ends
ULYSSES: Of parallels, as like as Vulcan and his wife:
ULYSSES: Yet god Achilles still cries 'Excellent!
ULYSSES: 'Tis Nestor right. Now play him me, Patroclus,
ULYSSES: Arming to answer in a night alarm.'
ULYSSES: And then, forsooth, the faint defects of age
ULYSSES: Must be the scene of mirth, to cough and spit,
ULYSSES: And, with a palsy-fumbling on his gorget,
ULYSSES: Shake in and out the rivet: and at this sport
ULYSSES: Sir Valour dies, cries 'O, enough, Patroclus,
ULYSSES: Or give me ribs of steel! I shall split all
ULYSSES: In pleasure of my spleen.' And in this fashion,
ULYSSES: All our abilities, gifts, natures, shapes,
ULYSSES: Severals and generals of grace exact,
ULYSSES: Achievements, plots, orders, preventions,
ULYSSES: Excitements to the field, or speech for truce,
ULYSSES: Success or loss, what is or is not, serves
ULYSSES: As stuff for these two to make paradoxes.
NESTOR: And in the imitation of these twain--
NESTOR: Who, as Ulysses says, opinion crowns
NESTOR: With an imperial voice--many are infect.
NESTOR: Ajax is grown self-will'd, and bears his head
NESTOR: In such a rein, in full as proud a place
NESTOR: As broad Achilles, keeps his tent like him,
NESTOR: Makes factious feasts, rails on our state of war,
NESTOR: Bold as an oracle, and sets Thersites,
NESTOR: A slave whose gall coins slanders like a mint,
NESTOR: To match us in comparisons with dirt,
NESTOR: To weaken and discredit our exposure,
NESTOR: How rank soever rounded in with danger.
ULYSSES: They tax our policy, and call it cowardice,
ULYSSES: Count wisdom as no member of the war,
ULYSSES: Forestall prescience, and esteem no act
ULYSSES: But that of hand: the still and mental parts,
ULYSSES: That do contrive how many hands shall strike,
ULYSSES: When fitness calls them on, and know by measure
ULYSSES: Of their observant toil the enemies' weight,--
ULYSSES: Why, this hath not a finger's dignity:
ULYSSES: They call this bed-work, mappery, closet-war,
ULYSSES: So that the ram that batters down the wall,
ULYSSES: For the great swing and rudeness of his poise,
ULYSSES: They place before his hand that made the engine,
ULYSSES: Or those that with the fineness of their souls
ULYSSES: By reason guide his execution.
NESTOR: Let this be granted, and Achilles' horse
NESTOR: Makes many Thetis' sons.
NARRATOR: A tucket
AGAMEMNON: What trumpet? look, Menelaus.
MENELAUS: From Troy.
NARRATOR: Enter AENEAS
AGAMEMNON: What would you 'fore our tent?
AENEAS: Is this great Agamemnon's tent, I pray you?
AGAMEMNON: Even this.
AENEAS: May one, that is a herald and a prince,
AENEAS: Do a fair message to his kingly ears?
AGAMEMNON: With surety stronger than Achilles' arm
AGAMEMNON: 'Fore all the Greekish heads, which with one voice
AGAMEMNON: Call Agamemnon head and general.
AENEAS: Fair leave and large security. How may
AENEAS: A stranger to those most imperial looks
AENEAS: Know them from eyes of other mortals?
AGAMEMNON: How!
AENEAS: Ay,
AENEAS: I ask, that I might waken reverence,
AENEAS: And bid the cheek be ready with a blush
AENEAS: Modest as morning when she coldly eyes
AENEAS: The youthful Phoebus:
AENEAS: Which is that god in office, guiding men?
AENEAS: Which is the high and mighty Agamemnon?
AGAMEMNON: This Trojan scorns us, or the men of Troy
AGAMEMNON: Are ceremonious courtiers.
AENEAS: Courtiers as free, as debonair, unarm'd,
AENEAS: As bending angels, that's their fame in peace:
AENEAS: But when they would seem soldiers, they have galls,
AENEAS: Good arms, strong joints, true swords, and,
AENEAS: Jove's accord,
AENEAS: Nothing so full of heart. But peace, AEneas,
AENEAS: Peace, Trojan, lay thy finger on thy lips!
AENEAS: The worthiness of praise distains his worth,
AENEAS: If that the praised himself bring the praise forth:
AENEAS: But what the repining enemy commends,
AENEAS: That breath fame blows, that praise, sole sure,
AENEAS: transcends.
AGAMEMNON: Sir, you of Troy, call you yourself AEneas?
AENEAS: Ay, Greek, that is my name.
AGAMEMNON: What's your affair I pray you?
AENEAS: Sir, pardon, 'tis for Agamemnon's ears.
AGAMEMNON: He hears naught privately that comes from Troy.
AENEAS: Nor I from Troy come not to whisper him:
AENEAS: I bring a trumpet to awake his ear,
AENEAS: To set his sense on the attentive bent,
AENEAS: And then to speak.
AGAMEMNON: Speak frankly as the wind,
AGAMEMNON: It is not Agamemnon's sleeping hour:
AGAMEMNON: That thou shalt know. Trojan, he is awake,
AGAMEMNON: He tells thee so himself.
AENEAS: Trumpet, blow loud,
AENEAS: Send thy brass voice through all these lazy tents,
AENEAS: And every Greek of mettle, let him know,
AENEAS: What Troy means fairly shall be spoke aloud.
NARRATOR: Trumpet sounds
AENEAS: We have, great Agamemnon, here in Troy
AENEAS: A prince call'd Hector,--Priam is his father,--
AENEAS: Who in this dull and long-continued truce
AENEAS: Is rusty grown: he bade me take a trumpet,
AENEAS: And to this purpose speak. Kings, princes, lords!
AENEAS: If there be one among the fair'st of Greece
AENEAS: That holds his honour higher than his ease,
AENEAS: That seeks his praise more than he fears his peril,
AENEAS: That knows his valour, and knows not his fear,
AENEAS: That loves his mistress more than in confession,
AENEAS: With truant vows to her own lips he loves,
AENEAS: And dare avow her beauty and her worth
AENEAS: In other arms than hers,--to him this challenge.
AENEAS: Hector, in view of Trojans and of Greeks,
AENEAS: Shall make it good, or do his best to do it,
AENEAS: He hath a lady, wiser, fairer, truer,
AENEAS: Than ever Greek did compass in his arms,
AENEAS: And will to-morrow with his trumpet call
AENEAS: Midway between your tents and walls of Troy,
AENEAS: To rouse a Grecian that is true in love:
AENEAS: If any come, Hector shall honour him,
AENEAS: If none, he'll say in Troy when he retires,
AENEAS: The Grecian dames are sunburnt and not worth
AENEAS: The splinter of a lance. Even so much.
AGAMEMNON: This shall be told our lovers, Lord AEneas,
AGAMEMNON: If none of them have soul in such a kind,
AGAMEMNON: We left them all at home: but we are soldiers,
AGAMEMNON: And may that soldier a mere recreant prove,
AGAMEMNON: That means not, hath not, or is not in love!
AGAMEMNON: If then one is, or hath, or means to be,
AGAMEMNON: That one meets Hector, if none else, I am he.
NESTOR: Tell him of Nestor, one that was a man
NESTOR: When Hector's grandsire suck'd: he is old now,
NESTOR: But if there be not in our Grecian host
NESTOR: One noble man that hath one spark of fire,
NESTOR: To answer for his love, tell him from me
NESTOR: I'll hide my silver beard in a gold beaver
NESTOR: And in my vantbrace put this wither'd brawn,
NESTOR: And meeting him will tell him that my lady
NESTOR: Was fairer than his grandam and as chaste
NESTOR: As may be in the world: his youth in flood,
NESTOR: I'll prove this truth with my three drops of blood.
AENEAS: Now heavens forbid such scarcity of youth!
ULYSSES: Amen.
AGAMEMNON: Fair Lord AEneas, let me touch your hand,
AGAMEMNON: To our pavilion shall I lead you, sir.
AGAMEMNON: Achilles shall have word of this intent,
AGAMEMNON: So shall each lord of Greece, from tent to tent:
AGAMEMNON: Yourself shall feast with us before you go
AGAMEMNON: And find the welcome of a noble foe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all but ULYSSES and NESTOR
ULYSSES: Nestor!
NESTOR: What says Ulysses?
ULYSSES: I have a young conception in my brain,
ULYSSES: Be you my time to bring it to some shape.
NESTOR: What is't?
ULYSSES: This 'tis:
ULYSSES: Blunt wedges rive hard knots: the seeded pride
ULYSSES: That hath to this maturity blown up
ULYSSES: In rank Achilles must or now be cropp'd,
ULYSSES: Or, shedding, breed a nursery of like evil,
ULYSSES: To overbulk us all.
NESTOR: Well, and how?
ULYSSES: This challenge that the gallant Hector sends,
ULYSSES: However it is spread in general name,
ULYSSES: Relates in purpose only to Achilles.
NESTOR: The purpose is perspicuous even as substance,
NESTOR: Whose grossness little characters sum up:
NESTOR: And, in the publication, make no strain,
NESTOR: But that Achilles, were his brain as barren
NESTOR: As banks of Libya,--though, Apollo knows,
NESTOR: 'Tis dry enough,--will, with great speed of judgment,
NESTOR: Ay, with celerity, find Hector's purpose
NESTOR: Pointing on him.
ULYSSES: And wake him to the answer, think you?
NESTOR: Yes, 'tis most meet: whom may you else oppose,
NESTOR: That can from Hector bring his honour off,
NESTOR: If not Achilles? Though't be a sportful combat,
NESTOR: Yet in the trial much opinion dwells,
NESTOR: For here the Trojans taste our dear'st repute
NESTOR: With their finest palate: and trust to me, Ulysses,
NESTOR: Our imputation shall be oddly poised
NESTOR: In this wild action, for the success,
NESTOR: Although particular, shall give a scantling
NESTOR: Of good or bad unto the general,
NESTOR: And in such indexes, although small pricks
NESTOR: To their subsequent volumes, there is seen
NESTOR: The baby figure of the giant mass
NESTOR: Of things to come at large. It is supposed
NESTOR: He that meets Hector issues from our choice
NESTOR: And choice, being mutual act of all our souls,
NESTOR: Makes merit her election, and doth boil,
NESTOR: As 'twere from us all, a man distill'd
NESTOR: Out of our virtues, who miscarrying,
NESTOR: What heart receives from hence the conquering part,
NESTOR: To steel a strong opinion to themselves?
NESTOR: Which entertain'd, limbs are his instruments,
NESTOR: In no less working than are swords and bows
NESTOR: Directive by the limbs.
ULYSSES: Give pardon to my speech:
ULYSSES: Therefore 'tis meet Achilles meet not Hector.
ULYSSES: Let us, like merchants, show our foulest wares,
ULYSSES: And think, perchance, they'll sell, if not,
ULYSSES: The lustre of the better yet to show,
ULYSSES: Shall show the better. Do not consent
ULYSSES: That ever Hector and Achilles meet,
ULYSSES: For both our honour and our shame in this
ULYSSES: Are dogg'd with two strange followers.
NESTOR: I see them not with my old eyes: what are they?
ULYSSES: What glory our Achilles shares from Hector,
ULYSSES: Were he not proud, we all should share with him:
ULYSSES: But he already is too insolent,
ULYSSES: A nd we were better parch in Afric sun
ULYSSES: Than in the pride and salt scorn of his eyes,
ULYSSES: Should he 'scape Hector fair: if he were foil'd,
ULYSSES: Why then, we did our main opinion crush
ULYSSES: In taint of our best man. No, make a lottery,
ULYSSES: And, by device, let blockish Ajax draw
ULYSSES: The sort to fight with Hector: among ourselves
ULYSSES: Give him allowance for the better man,
ULYSSES: For that will physic the great Myrmidon
ULYSSES: Who broils in loud applause, and make him fall
ULYSSES: His crest that prouder than blue Iris bends.
ULYSSES: If the dull brainless Ajax come safe off,
ULYSSES: We'll dress him up in voices: if he fail,
ULYSSES: Yet go we under our opinion still
ULYSSES: That we have better men. But, hit or miss,
ULYSSES: Our project's life this shape of sense assumes:
ULYSSES: Ajax employ'd plucks down Achilles' plumes.
NESTOR: Ulysses,
NESTOR: Now I begin to relish thy advice,
NESTOR: And I will give a taste of it forthwith
NESTOR: To Agamemnon: go we to him straight.
NESTOR: Two curs shall tame each other: pride alone
NESTOR: Must tarre the mastiffs on, as 'twere their bone.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A part of the Grecian camp.
NARRATOR: Enter AJAX and THERSITES
AJAX: Thersites!
THERSITES: Agamemnon, how if he had boils? full, all over,
THERSITES: generally?
AJAX: Thersites!
THERSITES: And those boils did run? say so: did not the
THERSITES: general run then? were not that a botchy core?
AJAX: Dog!
THERSITES: Then would come some matter from him, I see none now.
AJAX: Thou bitch-wolf's son, canst thou not hear?
NARRATOR: Beating him
AJAX: Feel, then.
THERSITES: The plague of Greece upon thee, thou mongrel
THERSITES: beef-witted lord!
AJAX: Speak then, thou vinewedst leaven, speak: I will
AJAX: beat thee into handsomeness.
THERSITES: I shall sooner rail thee into wit and holiness: but,
THERSITES: I think, thy horse will sooner con an oration than
THERSITES: thou learn a prayer without book. Thou canst strike,
THERSITES: canst thou? a red murrain o' thy jade's tricks!
AJAX: Toadstool, learn me the proclamation.
THERSITES: Dost thou think I have no sense, thou strikest me thus?
AJAX: The proclamation!
THERSITES: Thou art proclaimed a fool, I think.
AJAX: Do not, porpentine, do not: my fingers itch.
THERSITES: I would thou didst itch from head to foot and I had
THERSITES: the scratching of thee, I would make thee the
THERSITES: loathsomest scab in Greece. When thou art forth in
THERSITES: the incursions, thou strikest as slow as another.
AJAX: I say, the proclamation!
THERSITES: Thou grumblest and railest every hour on Achilles,
THERSITES: and thou art as full of envy at his greatness as
THERSITES: Cerberus is at Proserpine's beauty, ay, that thou
THERSITES: barkest at him.
AJAX: Mistress Thersites!
THERSITES: Thou shouldest strike him.
AJAX: Cobloaf!
THERSITES: He would pun thee into shivers with his fist, as a
THERSITES: sailor breaks a biscuit.
AJAX: [Beating him]  You whoreson cur!
THERSITES: Do, do.
AJAX: Thou stool for a witch!
THERSITES: Ay, do, do, thou sodden-witted lord! thou hast no
THERSITES: more brain than I have in mine elbows, an assinego
THERSITES: may tutor thee: thou scurvy-valiant ass! thou art
THERSITES: here but to thrash Trojans, and thou art bought and
THERSITES: sold among those of any wit, like a barbarian slave.
THERSITES: If thou use to beat me, I will begin at thy heel, and
THERSITES: tell what thou art by inches, thou thing of no
THERSITES: bowels, thou!
AJAX: You dog!
THERSITES: You scurvy lord!
AJAX: [Beating him]  You cur!
THERSITES: Mars his idiot! do, rudeness, do, camel, do, do.
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES and PATROCLUS
ACHILLES: Why, how now, Ajax! wherefore do you thus? How now,
ACHILLES: Thersites! what's the matter, man?
THERSITES: You see him there, do you?
ACHILLES: Ay, what's the matter?
THERSITES: Nay, look upon him.
ACHILLES: So I do: what's the matter?
THERSITES: Nay, but regard him well.
ACHILLES: 'Well!' why, I do so.
THERSITES: But yet you look not well upon him, for whosoever you
THERSITES: take him to be, he is Ajax.
ACHILLES: I know that, fool.
THERSITES: Ay, but that fool knows not himself.
AJAX: Therefore I beat thee.
THERSITES: Lo, lo, lo, lo, what modicums of wit he utters! his
THERSITES: evasions have ears thus long. I have bobbed his
THERSITES: brain more than he has beat my bones: I will buy
THERSITES: nine sparrows for a penny, and his pia mater is not
THERSITES: worth the nineth part of a sparrow. This lord,
THERSITES: Achilles, Ajax, who wears his wit in his belly and
THERSITES: his guts in his head, I'll tell you what I say of
THERSITES: him.
ACHILLES: What?
THERSITES: I say, this Ajax--
NARRATOR: Ajax offers to beat him
ACHILLES: Nay, good Ajax.
THERSITES: Has not so much wit--
ACHILLES: Nay, I must hold you.
THERSITES: As will stop the eye of Helen's needle, for whom he
THERSITES: comes to fight.
ACHILLES: Peace, fool!
THERSITES: I would have peace and quietness, but the fool will
THERSITES: not: he there: that he: look you there.
AJAX: O thou damned cur! I shall--
ACHILLES: Will you set your wit to a fool's?
THERSITES: No, I warrant you, for a fools will shame it.
PATROCLUS: Good words, Thersites.
ACHILLES: What's the quarrel?
AJAX: I bade the vile owl go learn me the tenor of the
AJAX: proclamation, and he rails upon me.
THERSITES: I serve thee not.
AJAX: Well, go to, go to.
THERSITES: I serve here voluntarily.
ACHILLES: Your last service was sufferance, 'twas not
ACHILLES: voluntary: no man is beaten voluntary: Ajax was
ACHILLES: here the voluntary, and you as under an impress.
THERSITES: E'en so, a great deal of your wit, too, lies in your
THERSITES: sinews, or else there be liars. Hector have a great
THERSITES: catch, if he knock out either of your brains: a'
THERSITES: were as good crack a fusty nut with no kernel.
ACHILLES: What, with me too, Thersites?
THERSITES: There's Ulysses and old Nestor, whose wit was mouldy
THERSITES: ere your grandsires had nails on their toes, yoke you
THERSITES: like draught-oxen and make you plough up the wars.
ACHILLES: What, what?
THERSITES: Yes, good sooth: to, Achilles! to, Ajax! to!
AJAX: I shall cut out your tongue.
THERSITES: 'Tis no matter! I shall speak as much as thou
THERSITES: afterwards.
PATROCLUS: No more words, Thersites, peace!
THERSITES: I will hold my peace when Achilles' brach bids me, shall I?
ACHILLES: There's for you, Patroclus.
THERSITES: I will see you hanged, like clotpoles, ere I come
THERSITES: any more to your tents: I will keep where there is
THERSITES: wit stirring and leave the faction of fools.
NARRATOR: Exit
PATROCLUS: A good riddance.
ACHILLES: Marry, this, sir, is proclaim'd through all our host:
ACHILLES: That Hector, by the fifth hour of the sun,
ACHILLES: Will with a trumpet 'twixt our tents and Troy
ACHILLES: To-morrow morning call some knight to arms
ACHILLES: That hath a stomach, and such a one that dare
ACHILLES: Maintain--I know not what: 'tis trash. Farewell.
AJAX: Farewell. Who shall answer him?
ACHILLES: I know not: 'tis put to lottery, otherwise
ACHILLES: He knew his man.
AJAX: O, meaning you. I will go learn more of it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. Troy. A room in Priam's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter PRIAM, HECTOR, TROILUS, PARIS, and HELENUS
PRIAM: After so many hours, lives, speeches spent,
PRIAM: Thus once again says Nestor from the Greeks:
PRIAM: 'Deliver Helen, and all damage else--
PRIAM: As honour, loss of time, travail, expense,
PRIAM: Wounds, friends, and what else dear that is consumed
PRIAM: In hot digestion of this cormorant war--
PRIAM: Shall be struck off.' Hector, what say you to't?
HECTOR: Though no man lesser fears the Greeks than I
HECTOR: As far as toucheth my particular,
HECTOR: Yet, dread Priam,
HECTOR: There is no lady of more softer bowels,
HECTOR: More spongy to suck in the sense of fear,
HECTOR: More ready to cry out 'Who knows what follows?'
HECTOR: Than Hector is: the wound of peace is surety,
HECTOR: Surety secure, but modest doubt is call'd
HECTOR: The beacon of the wise, the tent that searches
HECTOR: To the bottom of the worst. Let Helen go:
HECTOR: Since the first sword was drawn about this question,
HECTOR: Every tithe soul, 'mongst many thousand dismes,
HECTOR: Hath been as dear as Helen, I mean, of ours:
HECTOR: If we have lost so many tenths of ours,
HECTOR: To guard a thing not ours nor worth to us,
HECTOR: Had it our name, the value of one ten,
HECTOR: What merit's in that reason which denies
HECTOR: The yielding of her up?
TROILUS: Fie, fie, my brother!
TROILUS: Weigh you the worth and honour of a king
TROILUS: So great as our dread father in a scale
TROILUS: Of common ounces? will you with counters sum
TROILUS: The past proportion of his infinite?
TROILUS: And buckle in a waist most fathomless
TROILUS: With spans and inches so diminutive
TROILUS: As fears and reasons? fie, for godly shame!
HELENUS: No marvel, though you bite so sharp at reasons,
HELENUS: You are so empty of them. Should not our father
HELENUS: Bear the great sway of his affairs with reasons,
HELENUS: Because your speech hath none that tells him so?
TROILUS: You are for dreams and slumbers, brother priest,
TROILUS: You fur your gloves with reason. Here are
TROILUS: your reasons:
TROILUS: You know an enemy intends you harm,
TROILUS: You know a sword employ'd is perilous,
TROILUS: And reason flies the object of all harm:
TROILUS: Who marvels then, when Helenus beholds
TROILUS: A Grecian and his sword, if he do set
TROILUS: The very wings of reason to his heels
TROILUS: And fly like chidden Mercury from Jove,
TROILUS: Or like a star disorb'd? Nay, if we talk of reason,
TROILUS: Let's shut our gates and sleep: manhood and honour
TROILUS: Should have hare-hearts, would they but fat
TROILUS: their thoughts
TROILUS: With this cramm'd reason: reason and respect
TROILUS: Make livers pale and lustihood deject.
HECTOR: Brother, she is not worth what she doth cost
HECTOR: The holding.
TROILUS: What is aught, but as 'tis valued?
HECTOR: But value dwells not in particular will,
HECTOR: It holds his estimate and dignity
HECTOR: As well wherein 'tis precious of itself
HECTOR: As in the prizer: 'tis mad idolatry
HECTOR: To make the service greater than the god
HECTOR: And the will dotes that is attributive
HECTOR: To what infectiously itself affects,
HECTOR: Without some image of the affected merit.
TROILUS: I take to-day a wife, and my election
TROILUS: Is led on in the conduct of my will,
TROILUS: My will enkindled by mine eyes and ears,
TROILUS: Two traded pilots 'twixt the dangerous shores
TROILUS: Of will and judgment: how may I avoid,
TROILUS: Although my will distaste what it elected,
TROILUS: The wife I chose? there can be no evasion
TROILUS: To blench from this and to stand firm by honour:
TROILUS: We turn not back the silks upon the merchant,
TROILUS: When we have soil'd them, nor the remainder viands
TROILUS: We do not throw in unrespective sieve,
TROILUS: Because we now are full. It was thought meet
TROILUS: Paris should do some vengeance on the Greeks:
TROILUS: Your breath of full consent bellied his sails,
TROILUS: The seas and winds, old wranglers, took a truce
TROILUS: And did him service: he touch'd the ports desired,
TROILUS: And for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive,
TROILUS: He brought a Grecian queen, whose youth and freshness
TROILUS: Wrinkles Apollo's, and makes stale the morning.
TROILUS: Why keep we her? the Grecians keep our aunt:
TROILUS: Is she worth keeping? why, she is a pearl,
TROILUS: Whose price hath launch'd above a thousand ships,
TROILUS: And turn'd crown'd kings to merchants.
TROILUS: If you'll avouch 'twas wisdom Paris went--
TROILUS: As you must needs, for you all cried 'Go, go,'--
TROILUS: If you'll confess he brought home noble prize--
TROILUS: As you must needs, for you all clapp'd your hands
TROILUS: And cried 'Inestimable!'--why do you now
TROILUS: The issue of your proper wisdoms rate,
TROILUS: And do a deed that fortune never did,
TROILUS: Beggar the estimation which you prized
TROILUS: Richer than sea and land? O, theft most base,
TROILUS: That we have stol'n what we do fear to keep!
TROILUS: But, thieves, unworthy of a thing so stol'n,
TROILUS: That in their country did them that disgrace,
TROILUS: We fear to warrant in our native place!
CASSANDRA: [Within]  Cry, Trojans, cry!
PRIAM: What noise? what shriek is this?
TROILUS: 'Tis our mad sister, I do know her voice.
CASSANDRA: [Within]  Cry, Trojans!
HECTOR: It is Cassandra.
NARRATOR: Enter CASSANDRA, raving
CASSANDRA: Cry, Trojans, cry! lend me ten thousand eyes,
CASSANDRA: And I will fill them with prophetic tears.
HECTOR: Peace, sister, peace!
CASSANDRA: Virgins and boys, mid-age and wrinkled eld,
CASSANDRA: Soft infancy, that nothing canst but cry,
CASSANDRA: Add to my clamours! let us pay betimes
CASSANDRA: A moiety of that mass of moan to come.
CASSANDRA: Cry, Trojans, cry! practise your eyes with tears!
CASSANDRA: Troy must not be, nor goodly Ilion stand,
CASSANDRA: Our firebrand brother, Paris, burns us all.
CASSANDRA: Cry, Trojans, cry! a Helen and a woe:
CASSANDRA: Cry, cry! Troy burns, or else let Helen go.
NARRATOR: Exit
HECTOR: Now, youthful Troilus, do not these high strains
HECTOR: Of divination in our sister work
HECTOR: Some touches of remorse? or is your blood
HECTOR: So madly hot that no discourse of reason,
HECTOR: Nor fear of bad success in a bad cause,
HECTOR: Can qualify the same?
TROILUS: Why, brother Hector,
TROILUS: We may not think the justness of each act
TROILUS: Such and no other than event doth form it,
TROILUS: Nor once deject the courage of our minds,
TROILUS: Because Cassandra's mad: her brain-sick raptures
TROILUS: Cannot distaste the goodness of a quarrel
TROILUS: Which hath our several honours all engaged
TROILUS: To make it gracious. For my private part,
TROILUS: I am no more touch'd than all Priam's sons:
TROILUS: And Jove forbid there should be done amongst us
TROILUS: Such things as might offend the weakest spleen
TROILUS: To fight for and maintain!
PARIS: Else might the world convince of levity
PARIS: As well my undertakings as your counsels:
PARIS: But I attest the gods, your full consent
PARIS: Gave wings to my propension and cut off
PARIS: All fears attending on so dire a project.
PARIS: For what, alas, can these my single arms?
PARIS: What Propugnation is in one man's valour,
PARIS: To stand the push and enmity of those
PARIS: This quarrel would excite? Yet, I protest,
PARIS: Were I alone to pass the difficulties
PARIS: And had as ample power as I have will,
PARIS: Paris should ne'er retract what he hath done,
PARIS: Nor faint in the pursuit.
PRIAM: Paris, you speak
PRIAM: Like one besotted on your sweet delights:
PRIAM: You have the honey still, but these the gall,
PRIAM: So to be valiant is no praise at all.
PARIS: Sir, I propose not merely to myself
PARIS: The pleasures such a beauty brings with it,
PARIS: But I would have the soil of her fair rape
PARIS: Wiped off, in honourable keeping her.
PARIS: What treason were it to the ransack'd queen,
PARIS: Disgrace to your great worths and shame to me,
PARIS: Now to deliver her possession up
PARIS: On terms of base compulsion! Can it be
PARIS: That so degenerate a strain as this
PARIS: Should once set footing in your generous bosoms?
PARIS: There's not the meanest spirit on our party
PARIS: Without a heart to dare or sword to draw
PARIS: When Helen is defended, nor none so noble
PARIS: Whose life were ill bestow'd or death unfamed
PARIS: Where Helen is the subject, then, I say,
PARIS: Well may we fight for her whom, we know well,
PARIS: The world's large spaces cannot parallel.
HECTOR: Paris and Troilus, you have both said well,
HECTOR: And on the cause and question now in hand
HECTOR: Have glozed, but superficially: not much
HECTOR: Unlike young men, whom Aristotle thought
HECTOR: Unfit to hear moral philosophy:
HECTOR: The reasons you allege do more conduce
HECTOR: To the hot passion of distemper'd blood
HECTOR: Than to make up a free determination
HECTOR: 'Twixt right and wrong, for pleasure and revenge
HECTOR: Have ears more deaf than adders to the voice
HECTOR: Of any true decision. Nature craves
HECTOR: All dues be render'd to their owners: now,
HECTOR: What nearer debt in all humanity
HECTOR: Than wife is to the husband? If this law
HECTOR: Of nature be corrupted through affection,
HECTOR: And that great minds, of partial indulgence
HECTOR: To their benumbed wills, resist the same,
HECTOR: There is a law in each well-order'd nation
HECTOR: To curb those raging appetites that are
HECTOR: Most disobedient and refractory.
HECTOR: If Helen then be wife to Sparta's king,
HECTOR: As it is known she is, these moral laws
HECTOR: Of nature and of nations speak aloud
HECTOR: To have her back return'd: thus to persist
HECTOR: In doing wrong extenuates not wrong,
HECTOR: But makes it much more heavy. Hector's opinion
HECTOR: Is this in way of truth, yet ne'ertheless,
HECTOR: My spritely brethren, I propend to you
HECTOR: In resolution to keep Helen still,
HECTOR: For 'tis a cause that hath no mean dependance
HECTOR: Upon our joint and several dignities.
TROILUS: Why, there you touch'd the life of our design:
TROILUS: Were it not glory that we more affected
TROILUS: Than the performance of our heaving spleens,
TROILUS: I would not wish a drop of Trojan blood
TROILUS: Spent more in her defence. But, worthy Hector,
TROILUS: She is a theme of honour and renown,
TROILUS: A spur to valiant and magnanimous deeds,
TROILUS: Whose present courage may beat down our foes,
TROILUS: And fame in time to come canonize us,
TROILUS: For, I presume, brave Hector would not lose
TROILUS: So rich advantage of a promised glory
TROILUS: As smiles upon the forehead of this action
TROILUS: For the wide world's revenue.
HECTOR: I am yours,
HECTOR: You valiant offspring of great Priamus.
HECTOR: I have a roisting challenge sent amongst
HECTOR: The dun and factious nobles of the Greeks
HECTOR: Will strike amazement to their drowsy spirits:
HECTOR: I was advertised their great general slept,
HECTOR: Whilst emulation in the army crept:
HECTOR: This, I presume, will wake him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Grecian camp. Before Achilles' tent.
NARRATOR: Enter THERSITES, solus
THERSITES: How now, Thersites! what lost in the labyrinth of
THERSITES: thy fury! Shall the elephant Ajax carry it thus? He
THERSITES: beats me, and I rail at him: O, worthy satisfaction!
THERSITES: would it were otherwise, that I could beat him,
THERSITES: whilst he railed at me. 'Sfoot, I'll learn to
THERSITES: conjure and raise devils, but I'll see some issue of
THERSITES: my spiteful execrations. Then there's Achilles, a
THERSITES: rare enginer! If Troy be not taken till these two
THERSITES: undermine it, the walls will stand till they fall of
THERSITES: themselves. O thou great thunder-darter of Olympus,
THERSITES: forget that thou art Jove, the king of gods and,
THERSITES: Mercury, lose all the serpentine craft of thy
THERSITES: caduceus, if ye take not that little, little less
THERSITES: than little wit from them that they have! which
THERSITES: short-armed ignorance itself knows is so abundant
THERSITES: scarce, it will not in circumvention deliver a fly
THERSITES: from a spider, without drawing their massy irons and
THERSITES: cutting the web. After this, the vengeance on the
THERSITES: whole camp! or rather, the bone-ache! for that,
THERSITES: methinks, is the curse dependent on those that war
THERSITES: for a placket. I have said my prayers and devil Envy
THERSITES: say Amen. What ho! my Lord Achilles!
NARRATOR: Enter PATROCLUS
PATROCLUS: Who's there? Thersites! Good Thersites, come in and rail.
THERSITES: If I could have remembered a gilt counterfeit, thou
THERSITES: wouldst not have slipped out of my contemplation: but
THERSITES: it is no matter, thyself upon thyself! The common
THERSITES: curse of mankind, folly and ignorance, be thine in
THERSITES: great revenue! heaven bless thee from a tutor, and
THERSITES: discipline come not near thee! Let thy blood be thy
THERSITES: direction till thy death! then if she that lays thee
THERSITES: out says thou art a fair corse, I'll be sworn and
THERSITES: sworn upon't she never shrouded any but lazars.
THERSITES: Amen. Where's Achilles?
PATROCLUS: What, art thou devout? wast thou in prayer?
THERSITES: Ay: the heavens hear me!
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES
ACHILLES: Who's there?
PATROCLUS: Thersites, my lord.
ACHILLES: Where, where? Art thou come? why, my cheese, my
ACHILLES: digestion, why hast thou not served thyself in to
ACHILLES: my table so many meals? Come, what's Agamemnon?
THERSITES: Thy commander, Achilles. Then tell me, Patroclus,
THERSITES: what's Achilles?
PATROCLUS: Thy lord, Thersites: then tell me, I pray thee,
PATROCLUS: what's thyself?
THERSITES: Thy knower, Patroclus: then tell me, Patroclus,
THERSITES: what art thou?
PATROCLUS: Thou mayst tell that knowest.
ACHILLES: O, tell, tell.
THERSITES: I'll decline the whole question. Agamemnon commands
THERSITES: Achilles, Achilles is my lord, I am Patroclus'
THERSITES: knower, and Patroclus is a fool.
PATROCLUS: You rascal!
THERSITES: Peace, fool! I have not done.
ACHILLES: He is a privileged man. Proceed, Thersites.
THERSITES: Agamemnon is a fool, Achilles is a fool, Thersites
THERSITES: is a fool, and, as aforesaid, Patroclus is a fool.
ACHILLES: Derive this, come.
THERSITES: Agamemnon is a fool to offer to command Achilles,
THERSITES: Achilles is a fool to be commanded of Agamemnon,
THERSITES: Thersites is a fool to serve such a fool, and
THERSITES: Patroclus is a fool positive.
PATROCLUS: Why am I a fool?
THERSITES: Make that demand of the prover. It suffices me thou
THERSITES: art. Look you, who comes here?
ACHILLES: Patroclus, I'll speak with nobody.
ACHILLES: Come in with me, Thersites.
NARRATOR: Exit
THERSITES: Here is such patchery, such juggling and such
THERSITES: knavery! all the argument is a cuckold and a
THERSITES: whore, a good quarrel to draw emulous factions
THERSITES: and bleed to death upon. Now, the dry serpigo on
THERSITES: the subject! and war and lechery confound all!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter AGAMEMNON, ULYSSES, NESTOR, DIOMEDES, and AJAX
AGAMEMNON: Where is Achilles?
PATROCLUS: Within his tent, but ill disposed, my lord.
AGAMEMNON: Let it be known to him that we are here.
AGAMEMNON: He shent our messengers, and we lay by
AGAMEMNON: Our appertainments, visiting of him:
AGAMEMNON: Let him be told so, lest perchance he think
AGAMEMNON: We dare not move the question of our place,
AGAMEMNON: Or know not what we are.
PATROCLUS: I shall say so to him.
NARRATOR: Exit
ULYSSES: We saw him at the opening of his tent:
ULYSSES: He is not sick.
AJAX: Yes, lion-sick, sick of proud heart: you may call it
AJAX: melancholy, if you will favour the man, but, by my
AJAX: head, 'tis pride: but why, why? let him show us the
AJAX: cause. A word, my lord.
NARRATOR: Takes AGAMEMNON aside
NESTOR: What moves Ajax thus to bay at him?
ULYSSES: Achilles hath inveigled his fool from him.
NESTOR: Who, Thersites?
ULYSSES: He.
NESTOR: Then will Ajax lack matter, if he have lost his argument.
ULYSSES: No, you see, he is his argument that has his
ULYSSES: argument, Achilles.
NESTOR: All the better, their fraction is more our wish than
NESTOR: their faction: but it was a strong composure a fool
NESTOR: could disunite.
ULYSSES: The amity that wisdom knits not, folly may easily
ULYSSES: untie. Here comes Patroclus.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PATROCLUS
NESTOR: No Achilles with him.
ULYSSES: The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy:
ULYSSES: his legs are legs for necessity, not for flexure.
PATROCLUS: Achilles bids me say, he is much sorry,
PATROCLUS: If any thing more than your sport and pleasure
PATROCLUS: Did move your greatness and this noble state
PATROCLUS: To call upon him, he hopes it is no other
PATROCLUS: But for your health and your digestion sake,
PATROCLUS: And after-dinner's breath.
AGAMEMNON: Hear you, Patroclus:
AGAMEMNON: We are too well acquainted with these answers:
AGAMEMNON: But his evasion, wing'd thus swift with scorn,
AGAMEMNON: Cannot outfly our apprehensions.
AGAMEMNON: Much attribute he hath, and much the reason
AGAMEMNON: Why we ascribe it to him, yet all his virtues,
AGAMEMNON: Not virtuously on his own part beheld,
AGAMEMNON: Do in our eyes begin to lose their gloss,
AGAMEMNON: Yea, like fair fruit in an unwholesome dish,
AGAMEMNON: Are like to rot untasted. Go and tell him,
AGAMEMNON: We come to speak with him, and you shall not sin,
AGAMEMNON: If you do say we think him over-proud
AGAMEMNON: And under-honest, in self-assumption greater
AGAMEMNON: Than in the note of judgment, and worthier
AGAMEMNON: than himself
AGAMEMNON: Here tend the savage strangeness he puts on,
AGAMEMNON: Disguise the holy strength of their command,
AGAMEMNON: And underwrite in an observing kind
AGAMEMNON: His humorous predominance, yea, watch
AGAMEMNON: His pettish lunes, his ebbs, his flows, as if
AGAMEMNON: The passage and whole carriage of this action
AGAMEMNON: Rode on his tide. Go tell him this, and add,
AGAMEMNON: That if he overhold his price so much,
AGAMEMNON: We'll none of him, but let him, like an engine
AGAMEMNON: Not portable, lie under this report:
AGAMEMNON: 'Bring action hither, this cannot go to war:
AGAMEMNON: A stirring dwarf we do allowance give
AGAMEMNON: Before a sleeping giant.' Tell him so.
PATROCLUS: I shall, and bring his answer presently.
NARRATOR: Exit
AGAMEMNON: In second voice we'll not be satisfied,
AGAMEMNON: We come to speak with him. Ulysses, enter you.
NARRATOR: Exit ULYSSES
AJAX: What is he more than another?
AGAMEMNON: No more than what he thinks he is.
AJAX: Is he so much? Do you not think he thinks himself a
AJAX: better man than I am?
AGAMEMNON: No question.
AJAX: Will you subscribe his thought, and say he is?
AGAMEMNON: No, noble Ajax, you are as strong, as valiant, as
AGAMEMNON: wise, no less noble, much more gentle, and altogether
AGAMEMNON: more tractable.
AJAX: Why should a man be proud? How doth pride grow? I
AJAX: know not what pride is.
AGAMEMNON: Your mind is the clearer, Ajax, and your virtues the
AGAMEMNON: fairer. He that is proud eats up himself: pride is
AGAMEMNON: his own glass, his own trumpet, his own chronicle,
AGAMEMNON: and whatever praises itself but in the deed, devours
AGAMEMNON: the deed in the praise.
AJAX: I do hate a proud man, as I hate the engendering of toads.
NESTOR: Yet he loves himself: is't not strange?
NARRATOR: Aside
NARRATOR: Re-enter ULYSSES
ULYSSES: Achilles will not to the field to-morrow.
AGAMEMNON: What's his excuse?
ULYSSES: He doth rely on none,
ULYSSES: But carries on the stream of his dispose
ULYSSES: Without observance or respect of any,
ULYSSES: In will peculiar and in self-admission.
AGAMEMNON: Why will he not upon our fair request
AGAMEMNON: Untent his person and share the air with us?
ULYSSES: Things small as nothing, for request's sake only,
ULYSSES: He makes important: possess'd he is with greatness,
ULYSSES: And speaks not to himself but with a pride
ULYSSES: That quarrels at self-breath: imagined worth
ULYSSES: Holds in his blood such swoln and hot discourse
ULYSSES: That 'twixt his mental and his active parts
ULYSSES: Kingdom'd Achilles in commotion rages
ULYSSES: And batters down himself: what should I say?
ULYSSES: He is so plaguy proud that the death-tokens of it
ULYSSES: Cry 'No recovery.'
AGAMEMNON: Let Ajax go to him.
AGAMEMNON: Dear lord, go you and greet him in his tent:
AGAMEMNON: 'Tis said he holds you well, and will be led
AGAMEMNON: At your request a little from himself.
ULYSSES: O Agamemnon, let it not be so!
ULYSSES: We'll consecrate the steps that Ajax makes
ULYSSES: When they go from Achilles: shall the proud lord
ULYSSES: That bastes his arrogance with his own seam
ULYSSES: And never suffers matter of the world
ULYSSES: Enter his thoughts, save such as do revolve
ULYSSES: And ruminate himself, shall he be worshipp'd
ULYSSES: Of that we hold an idol more than he?
ULYSSES: No, this thrice worthy and right valiant lord
ULYSSES: Must not so stale his palm, nobly acquired,
ULYSSES: Nor, by my will, assubjugate his merit,
ULYSSES: As amply titled as Achilles is,
ULYSSES: By going to Achilles:
ULYSSES: That were to enlard his fat already pride
ULYSSES: And add more coals to Cancer when he burns
ULYSSES: With entertaining great Hyperion.
ULYSSES: This lord go to him! Jupiter forbid,
ULYSSES: And say in thunder 'Achilles go to him.'
NESTOR: [Aside to DIOMEDES]  O, this is well, he rubs the
NESTOR: vein of him.
DIOMEDES: [Aside to NESTOR]  And how his silence drinks up
DIOMEDES: this applause!
AJAX: If I go to him, with my armed fist I'll pash him o'er the face.
AGAMEMNON: O, no, you shall not go.
AJAX: An a' be proud with me, I'll pheeze his pride:
AJAX: Let me go to him.
ULYSSES: Not for the worth that hangs upon our quarrel.
AJAX: A paltry, insolent fellow!
NESTOR: How he describes himself!
AJAX: Can he not be sociable?
ULYSSES: The raven chides blackness.
AJAX: I'll let his humours blood.
AGAMEMNON: He will be the physician that should be the patient.
AJAX: An all men were o' my mind,--
ULYSSES: Wit would be out of fashion.
AJAX: A' should not bear it so, a' should eat swords first:
AJAX: shall pride carry it?
NESTOR: An 'twould, you'ld carry half.
ULYSSES: A' would have ten shares.
AJAX: I will knead him, I'll make him supple.
NESTOR: He's not yet through warm: force him with praises:
NESTOR: pour in, pour in, his ambition is dry.
ULYSSES: [To AGAMEMNON]  My lord, you feed too much on this dislike.
NESTOR: Our noble general, do not do so.
DIOMEDES: You must prepare to fight without Achilles.
ULYSSES: Why, 'tis this naming of him does him harm.
ULYSSES: Here is a man--but 'tis before his face,
ULYSSES: I will be silent.
NESTOR: Wherefore should you so?
NESTOR: He is not emulous, as Achilles is.
ULYSSES: Know the whole world, he is as valiant.
AJAX: A whoreson dog, that shall pelter thus with us!
AJAX: Would he were a Trojan!
NESTOR: What a vice were it in Ajax now,--
ULYSSES: If he were proud,--
DIOMEDES: Or covetous of praise,--
ULYSSES: Ay, or surly borne,--
DIOMEDES: Or strange, or self-affected!
ULYSSES: Thank the heavens, lord, thou art of sweet composure,
ULYSSES: Praise him that got thee, she that gave thee suck:
ULYSSES: Famed be thy tutor, and thy parts of nature
ULYSSES: Thrice famed, beyond all erudition:
ULYSSES: But he that disciplined thy arms to fight,
ULYSSES: Let Mars divide eternity in twain,
ULYSSES: And give him half: and, for thy vigour,
ULYSSES: Bull-bearing Milo his addition yield
ULYSSES: To sinewy Ajax. I will not praise thy wisdom,
ULYSSES: Which, like a bourn, a pale, a shore, confines
ULYSSES: Thy spacious and dilated parts: here's Nestor,
ULYSSES: Instructed by the antiquary times,
ULYSSES: He must, he is, he cannot but be wise:
ULYSSES: Put pardon, father Nestor, were your days
ULYSSES: As green as Ajax' and your brain so temper'd,
ULYSSES: You should not have the eminence of him,
ULYSSES: But be as Ajax.
AJAX: Shall I call you father?
NESTOR: Ay, my good son.
DIOMEDES: Be ruled by him, Lord Ajax.
ULYSSES: There is no tarrying here, the hart Achilles
ULYSSES: Keeps thicket. Please it our great general
ULYSSES: To call together all his state of war,
ULYSSES: Fresh kings are come to Troy: to-morrow
ULYSSES: We must with all our main of power stand fast:
ULYSSES: And here's a lord,--come knights from east to west,
ULYSSES: And cull their flower, Ajax shall cope the best.
AGAMEMNON: Go we to council. Let Achilles sleep:
AGAMEMNON: Light boats sail swift, though greater hulks draw deep.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
