NARRATOR: SCENE I. Troy. Priam's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant and PANDARUS
PANDARUS: Friend, you! pray you, a word: do not you follow
PANDARUS: the young Lord Paris?
Servant: Ay, sir, when he goes before me.
PANDARUS: You depend upon him, I mean?
Servant: Sir, I do depend upon the lord.
PANDARUS: You depend upon a noble gentleman, I must needs
PANDARUS: praise him.
Servant: The lord be praised!
PANDARUS: You know me, do you not?
Servant: Faith, sir, superficially.
PANDARUS: Friend, know me better, I am the Lord Pandarus.
Servant: I hope I shall know your honour better.
PANDARUS: I do desire it.
Servant: You are in the state of grace.
PANDARUS: Grace! not so, friend: honour and lordship are my titles.
NARRATOR: Music within
PANDARUS: What music is this?
Servant: I do but partly know, sir: it is music in parts.
PANDARUS: Know you the musicians?
Servant: Wholly, sir.
PANDARUS: Who play they to?
Servant: To the hearers, sir.
PANDARUS: At whose pleasure, friend
Servant: At mine, sir, and theirs that love music.
PANDARUS: Command, I mean, friend.
Servant: Who shall I command, sir?
PANDARUS: Friend, we understand not one another: I am too
PANDARUS: courtly and thou art too cunning. At whose request
PANDARUS: do these men play?
Servant: That's to 't indeed, sir: marry, sir, at the request
Servant: of Paris my lord, who's there in person, with him,
Servant: the mortal Venus, the heart-blood of beauty, love's
Servant: invisible soul,--
PANDARUS: Who, my cousin Cressida?
Servant: No, sir, Helen: could you not find out that by her
Servant: attributes?
PANDARUS: It should seem, fellow, that thou hast not seen the
PANDARUS: Lady Cressida. I come to speak with Paris from the
PANDARUS: Prince Troilus: I will make a complimental assault
PANDARUS: upon him, for my business seethes.
Servant: Sodden business! there's a stewed phrase indeed!
NARRATOR: Enter PARIS and HELEN, attended
PANDARUS: Fair be to you, my lord, and to all this fair
PANDARUS: company! fair desires, in all fair measure,
PANDARUS: fairly guide them! especially to you, fair queen!
PANDARUS: fair thoughts be your fair pillow!
HELEN: Dear lord, you are full of fair words.
PANDARUS: You speak your fair pleasure, sweet queen. Fair
PANDARUS: prince, here is good broken music.
PARIS: You have broke it, cousin: and, by my life, you
PARIS: shall make it whole again, you shall piece it out
PARIS: with a piece of your performance. Nell, he is full
PARIS: of harmony.
PANDARUS: Truly, lady, no.
HELEN: O, sir,--
PANDARUS: Rude, in sooth, in good sooth, very rude.
PARIS: Well said, my lord! well, you say so in fits.
PANDARUS: I have business to my lord, dear queen. My lord,
PANDARUS: will you vouchsafe me a word?
HELEN: Nay, this shall not hedge us out: we'll hear you
HELEN: sing, certainly.
PANDARUS: Well, sweet queen. you are pleasant with me. But,
PANDARUS: marry, thus, my lord: my dear lord and most esteemed
PANDARUS: friend, your brother Troilus,--
HELEN: My Lord Pandarus, honey-sweet lord,--
PANDARUS: Go to, sweet queen, to go:--commends himself most
PANDARUS: affectionately to you,--
HELEN: You shall not bob us out of our melody: if you do,
HELEN: our melancholy upon your head!
PANDARUS: Sweet queen, sweet queen! that's a sweet queen, i' faith.
HELEN: And to make a sweet lady sad is a sour offence.
PANDARUS: Nay, that shall not serve your turn, that shall not,
PANDARUS: in truth, la. Nay, I care not for such words, no,
PANDARUS: no. And, my lord, he desires you, that if the king
PANDARUS: call for him at supper, you will make his excuse.
HELEN: My Lord Pandarus,--
PANDARUS: What says my sweet queen, my very very sweet queen?
PARIS: What exploit's in hand? where sups he to-night?
HELEN: Nay, but, my lord,--
PANDARUS: What says my sweet queen? My cousin will fall out
PANDARUS: with you. You must not know where he sups.
PARIS: I'll lay my life, with my disposer Cressida.
PANDARUS: No, no, no such matter, you are wide: come, your
PANDARUS: disposer is sick.
PARIS: Well, I'll make excuse.
PANDARUS: Ay, good my lord. Why should you say Cressida? no,
PANDARUS: your poor disposer's sick.
PARIS: I spy.
PANDARUS: You spy! what do you spy? Come, give me an
PANDARUS: instrument. Now, sweet queen.
HELEN: Why, this is kindly done.
PANDARUS: My niece is horribly in love with a thing you have,
PANDARUS: sweet queen.
HELEN: She shall have it, my lord, if it be not my lord Paris.
PANDARUS: He! no, she'll none of him, they two are twain.
HELEN: Falling in, after falling out, may make them three.
PANDARUS: Come, come, I'll hear no more of this, I'll sing
PANDARUS: you a song now.
HELEN: Ay, ay, prithee now. By my troth, sweet lord, thou
HELEN: hast a fine forehead.
PANDARUS: Ay, you may, you may.
HELEN: Let thy song be love: this love will undo us all.
HELEN: O Cupid, Cupid, Cupid!
PANDARUS: Love! ay, that it shall, i' faith.
PARIS: Ay, good now, love, love, nothing but love.
PANDARUS: In good troth, it begins so.
NARRATOR: Sings
PANDARUS: Love, love, nothing but love, still more!
PANDARUS: For, O, love's bow
PANDARUS: Shoots buck and doe:
PANDARUS: The shaft confounds,
PANDARUS: Not that it wounds,
PANDARUS: But tickles still the sore.
PANDARUS: These lovers cry Oh! oh! they die!
PANDARUS: Yet that which seems the wound to kill,
PANDARUS: Doth turn oh! oh! to ha! ha! he!
PANDARUS: So dying love lives still:
PANDARUS: Oh! oh! a while, but ha! ha! ha!
PANDARUS: Oh! oh! groans out for ha! ha! ha!
PANDARUS: Heigh-ho!
HELEN: In love, i' faith, to the very tip of the nose.
PARIS: He eats nothing but doves, love, and that breeds hot
PARIS: blood, and hot blood begets hot thoughts, and hot
PARIS: thoughts beget hot deeds, and hot deeds is love.
PANDARUS: Is this the generation of love? hot blood, hot
PANDARUS: thoughts, and hot deeds? Why, they are vipers:
PANDARUS: is love a generation of vipers? Sweet lord, who's
PANDARUS: a-field to-day?
PARIS: Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the
PARIS: gallantry of Troy: I  would fain have armed to-day,
PARIS: but my Nell would not have it so. How chance my
PARIS: brother Troilus went not?
HELEN: He hangs the lip at something: you know all, Lord Pandarus.
PANDARUS: Not I, honey-sweet queen. I long to hear how they
PANDARUS: sped to-day. You'll remember your brother's excuse?
PARIS: To a hair.
PANDARUS: Farewell, sweet queen.
HELEN: Commend me to your niece.
PANDARUS: I will, sweet queen.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: A retreat sounded
PARIS: They're come from field: let us to Priam's hall,
PARIS: To greet the warriors. Sweet Helen, I must woo you
PARIS: To help unarm our Hector: his stubborn buckles,
PARIS: With these your white enchanting fingers touch'd,
PARIS: Shall more obey than to the edge of steel
PARIS: Or force of Greekish sinews, you shall do more
PARIS: Than all the island kings,--disarm great Hector.
HELEN: 'Twill make us proud to be his servant, Paris,
HELEN: Yea, what he shall receive of us in duty
HELEN: Gives us more palm in beauty than we have,
HELEN: Yea, overshines ourself.
PARIS: Sweet, above thought I love thee.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. Pandarus' orchard.
NARRATOR: Enter PANDARUS and Troilus's Boy, meeting
PANDARUS: How now! where's thy master? at my cousin
PANDARUS: Cressida's?
Boy: No, sir, he stays for you to conduct him thither.
PANDARUS: O, here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS
PANDARUS: How now, how now!
TROILUS: Sirrah, walk off.
NARRATOR: Exit Boy
PANDARUS: Have you seen my cousin?
TROILUS: No, Pandarus: I stalk about her door,
TROILUS: Like a strange soul upon the Stygian banks
TROILUS: Staying for waftage. O, be thou my Charon,
TROILUS: And give me swift transportance to those fields
TROILUS: Where I may wallow in the lily-beds
TROILUS: Proposed for the deserver! O gentle Pandarus,
TROILUS: From Cupid's shoulder pluck his painted wings
TROILUS: And fly with me to Cressid!
PANDARUS: Walk here i' the orchard, I'll bring her straight.
NARRATOR: Exit
TROILUS: I am giddy, expectation whirls me round.
TROILUS: The imaginary relish is so sweet
TROILUS: That it enchants my sense: what will it be,
TROILUS: When that the watery palate tastes indeed
TROILUS: Love's thrice repured nectar? death, I fear me,
TROILUS: Swooning destruction, or some joy too fine,
TROILUS: Too subtle-potent, tuned too sharp in sweetness,
TROILUS: For the capacity of my ruder powers:
TROILUS: I fear it much, and I do fear besides,
TROILUS: That I shall lose distinction in my joys,
TROILUS: As doth a battle, when they charge on heaps
TROILUS: The enemy flying.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PANDARUS
PANDARUS: She's making her ready, she'll come straight: you
PANDARUS: must be witty now. She does so blush, and fetches
PANDARUS: her wind so short, as if she were frayed with a
PANDARUS: sprite: I'll fetch her. It is the prettiest
PANDARUS: villain: she fetches her breath as short as a
PANDARUS: new-ta'en sparrow.
NARRATOR: Exit
TROILUS: Even such a passion doth embrace my bosom:
TROILUS: My heart beats thicker than a feverous pulse,
TROILUS: And all my powers do their bestowing lose,
TROILUS: Like vassalage at unawares encountering
TROILUS: The eye of majesty.
NARRATOR: Re-enter PANDARUS with CRESSIDA
PANDARUS: Come, come, what need you blush? shame's a baby.
PANDARUS: Here she is now: swear the oaths now to her that
PANDARUS: you have sworn to me. What, are you gone again?
PANDARUS: you must be watched ere you be made tame, must you?
PANDARUS: Come your ways, come your ways, an you draw backward,
PANDARUS: we'll put you i' the fills. Why do you not speak to
PANDARUS: her? Come, draw this curtain, and let's see your
PANDARUS: picture. Alas the day, how loath you are to offend
PANDARUS: daylight! an 'twere dark, you'ld close sooner.
PANDARUS: So, so, rub on, and kiss the mistress. How now!
PANDARUS: a kiss in fee-farm! build there, carpenter, the air
PANDARUS: is sweet. Nay, you shall fight your hearts out ere
PANDARUS: I part you. The falcon as the tercel, for all the
PANDARUS: ducks i' the river: go to, go to.
TROILUS: You have bereft me of all words, lady.
PANDARUS: Words pay no debts, give her deeds: but she'll
PANDARUS: bereave you o' the deeds too, if she call your
PANDARUS: activity in question. What, billing again? Here's
PANDARUS: 'In witness whereof the parties interchangeably'--
PANDARUS: Come in, come in: I'll go get a fire.
NARRATOR: Exit
CRESSIDA: Will you walk in, my lord?
TROILUS: O Cressida, how often have I wished me thus!
CRESSIDA: Wished, my lord! The gods grant,--O my lord!
TROILUS: What should they grant? what makes this pretty
TROILUS: abruption? What too curious dreg espies my sweet
TROILUS: lady in the fountain of our love?
CRESSIDA: More dregs than water, if my fears have eyes.
TROILUS: Fears make devils of cherubims, they never see truly.
CRESSIDA: Blind fear, that seeing reason leads, finds safer
CRESSIDA: footing than blind reason stumbling without fear: to
CRESSIDA: fear the worst oft cures the worse.
TROILUS: O, let my lady apprehend no fear: in all Cupid's
TROILUS: pageant there is presented no monster.
CRESSIDA: Nor nothing monstrous neither?
TROILUS: Nothing, but our undertakings, when we vow to weep
TROILUS: seas, live in fire, eat rocks, tame tigers, thinking
TROILUS: it harder for our mistress to devise imposition
TROILUS: enough than for us to undergo any difficulty imposed.
TROILUS: This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that the will
TROILUS: is infinite and the execution confined, that the
TROILUS: desire is boundless and the act a slave to limit.
CRESSIDA: They say all lovers swear more performance than they
CRESSIDA: are able and yet reserve an ability that they never
CRESSIDA: perform, vowing more than the perfection of ten and
CRESSIDA: discharging less than the tenth part of one. They
CRESSIDA: that have the voice of lions and the act of hares,
CRESSIDA: are they not monsters?
TROILUS: Are there such? such are not we: praise us as we
TROILUS: are tasted, allow us as we prove, our head shall go
TROILUS: bare till merit crown it: no perfection in reversion
TROILUS: shall have a praise in present: we will not name
TROILUS: desert before his birth, and, being born, his addition
TROILUS: shall be humble. Few words to fair faith: Troilus
TROILUS: shall be such to Cressid as what envy can say worst
TROILUS: shall be a mock for his truth, and what truth can
TROILUS: speak truest not truer than Troilus.
CRESSIDA: Will you walk in, my lord?
NARRATOR: Re-enter PANDARUS
PANDARUS: What, blushing still? have you not done talking yet?
CRESSIDA: Well, uncle, what folly I commit, I dedicate to you.
PANDARUS: I thank you for that: if my lord get a boy of you,
PANDARUS: you'll give him me. Be true to my lord: if he
PANDARUS: flinch, chide me for it.
TROILUS: You know now your hostages, your uncle's word and my
TROILUS: firm faith.
PANDARUS: Nay, I'll give my word for her too: our kindred,
PANDARUS: though they be long ere they are wooed, they are
PANDARUS: constant being won: they are burs, I can tell you,
PANDARUS: they'll stick where they are thrown.
CRESSIDA: Boldness comes to me now, and brings me heart.
CRESSIDA: Prince Troilus, I have loved you night and day
CRESSIDA: For many weary months.
TROILUS: Why was my Cressid then so hard to win?
CRESSIDA: Hard to seem won: but I was won, my lord,
CRESSIDA: With the first glance that ever--pardon me--
CRESSIDA: If I confess much, you will play the tyrant.
CRESSIDA: I love you now, but not, till now, so much
CRESSIDA: But I might master it: in faith, I lie,
CRESSIDA: My thoughts were like unbridled children, grown
CRESSIDA: Too headstrong for their mother. See, we fools!
CRESSIDA: Why have I blabb'd? who shall be true to us,
CRESSIDA: When we are so unsecret to ourselves?
CRESSIDA: But, though I loved you well, I woo'd you not,
CRESSIDA: And yet, good faith, I wish'd myself a man,
CRESSIDA: Or that we women had men's privilege
CRESSIDA: Of speaking first. Sweet, bid me hold my tongue,
CRESSIDA: For in this rapture I shall surely speak
CRESSIDA: The thing I shall repent. See, see, your silence,
CRESSIDA: Cunning in dumbness, from my weakness draws
CRESSIDA: My very soul of counsel! stop my mouth.
TROILUS: And shall, albeit sweet music issues thence.
PANDARUS: Pretty, i' faith.
CRESSIDA: My lord, I do beseech you, pardon me,
CRESSIDA: 'Twas not my purpose, thus to beg a kiss:
CRESSIDA: I am ashamed. O heavens! what have I done?
CRESSIDA: For this time will I take my leave, my lord.
TROILUS: Your leave, sweet Cressid!
PANDARUS: Leave! an you take leave till to-morrow morning,--
CRESSIDA: Pray you, content you.
TROILUS: What offends you, lady?
CRESSIDA: Sir, mine own company.
TROILUS: You cannot shun Yourself.
CRESSIDA: Let me go and try:
CRESSIDA: I have a kind of self resides with you,
CRESSIDA: But an unkind self, that itself will leave,
CRESSIDA: To be another's fool. I would be gone:
CRESSIDA: Where is my wit? I know not what I speak.
TROILUS: Well know they what they speak that speak so wisely.
CRESSIDA: Perchance, my lord, I show more craft than love,
CRESSIDA: And fell so roundly to a large confession,
CRESSIDA: To angle for your thoughts: but you are wise,
CRESSIDA: Or else you love not, for to be wise and love
CRESSIDA: Exceeds man's might, that dwells with gods above.
TROILUS: O that I thought it could be in a woman--
TROILUS: As, if it can, I will presume in you--
TROILUS: To feed for aye her ramp and flames of love,
TROILUS: To keep her constancy in plight and youth,
TROILUS: Outliving beauty's outward, with a mind
TROILUS: That doth renew swifter than blood decays!
TROILUS: Or that persuasion could but thus convince me,
TROILUS: That my integrity and truth to you
TROILUS: Might be affronted with the match and weight
TROILUS: Of such a winnow'd purity in love,
TROILUS: How were I then uplifted! but, alas!
TROILUS: I am as true as truth's simplicity
TROILUS: And simpler than the infancy of truth.
CRESSIDA: In that I'll war with you.
TROILUS: O virtuous fight,
TROILUS: When right with right wars who shall be most right!
TROILUS: True swains in love shall in the world to come
TROILUS: Approve their truths by Troilus: when their rhymes,
TROILUS: Full of protest, of oath and big compare,
TROILUS: Want similes, truth tired with iteration,
TROILUS: As true as steel, as plantage to the moon,
TROILUS: As sun to day, as turtle to her mate,
TROILUS: As iron to adamant, as earth to the centre,
TROILUS: Yet, after all comparisons of truth,
TROILUS: As truth's authentic author to be cited,
TROILUS: 'As true as Troilus' shall crown up the verse,
TROILUS: And sanctify the numbers.
CRESSIDA: Prophet may you be!
CRESSIDA: If I be false, or swerve a hair from truth,
CRESSIDA: When time is old and hath forgot itself,
CRESSIDA: When waterdrops have worn the stones of Troy,
CRESSIDA: And blind oblivion swallow'd cities up,
CRESSIDA: And mighty states characterless are grated
CRESSIDA: To dusty nothing, yet let memory,
CRESSIDA: From false to false, among false maids in love,
CRESSIDA: Upbraid my falsehood! when they've said 'as false
CRESSIDA: As air, as water, wind, or sandy earth,
CRESSIDA: As fox to lamb, as wolf to heifer's calf,
CRESSIDA: Pard to the hind, or stepdame to her son,'
CRESSIDA: 'Yea,' let them say, to stick the heart of falsehood,
CRESSIDA: 'As false as Cressid.'
PANDARUS: Go to, a bargain made: seal it, seal it, I'll be the
PANDARUS: witness. Here I hold your hand, here my cousin's.
PANDARUS: If ever you prove false one to another, since I have
PANDARUS: taken such pains to bring you together, let all
PANDARUS: pitiful goers-between be called to the world's end
PANDARUS: after my name, call them all Pandars, let all
PANDARUS: constant men be Troiluses, all false women Cressids,
PANDARUS: and all brokers-between Pandars! say, amen.
TROILUS: Amen.
CRESSIDA: Amen.
PANDARUS: Amen. Whereupon I will show you a chamber with a
PANDARUS: bed, which bed, because it shall not speak of your
PANDARUS: pretty encounters, press it to death: away!
PANDARUS: And Cupid grant all tongue-tied maidens here
PANDARUS: Bed, chamber, Pandar to provide this gear!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The Grecian camp. Before Achilles' tent.
NARRATOR: Enter AGAMEMNON, ULYSSES, DIOMEDES, NESTOR, AJAX, MENELAUS, and CALCHAS
CALCHAS: Now, princes, for the service I have done you,
CALCHAS: The advantage of the time prompts me aloud
CALCHAS: To call for recompense. Appear it to your mind
CALCHAS: That, through the sight I bear in things to love,
CALCHAS: I have abandon'd Troy, left my possession,
CALCHAS: Incurr'd a traitor's name, exposed myself,
CALCHAS: From certain and possess'd conveniences,
CALCHAS: To doubtful fortunes, sequestering from me all
CALCHAS: That time, acquaintance, custom and condition
CALCHAS: Made tame and most familiar to my nature,
CALCHAS: And here, to do you service, am become
CALCHAS: As new into the world, strange, unacquainted:
CALCHAS: I do beseech you, as in way of taste,
CALCHAS: To give me now a little benefit,
CALCHAS: Out of those many register'd in promise,
CALCHAS: Which, you say, live to come in my behalf.
AGAMEMNON: What wouldst thou of us, Trojan? make demand.
CALCHAS: You have a Trojan prisoner, call'd Antenor,
CALCHAS: Yesterday took: Troy holds him very dear.
CALCHAS: Oft have you--often have you thanks therefore--
CALCHAS: Desired my Cressid in right great exchange,
CALCHAS: Whom Troy hath still denied: but this Antenor,
CALCHAS: I know, is such a wrest in their affairs
CALCHAS: That their negotiations all must slack,
CALCHAS: Wanting his manage, and they will almost
CALCHAS: Give us a prince of blood, a son of Priam,
CALCHAS: In change of him: let him be sent, great princes,
CALCHAS: And he shall buy my daughter, and her presence
CALCHAS: Shall quite strike off all service I have done,
CALCHAS: In most accepted pain.
AGAMEMNON: Let Diomedes bear him,
AGAMEMNON: And bring us Cressid hither: Calchas shall have
AGAMEMNON: What he requests of us. Good Diomed,
AGAMEMNON: Furnish you fairly for this interchange:
AGAMEMNON: Withal bring word if Hector will to-morrow
AGAMEMNON: Be answer'd in his challenge: Ajax is ready.
DIOMEDES: This shall I undertake, and 'tis a burden
DIOMEDES: Which I am proud to bear.
NARRATOR: Exeunt DIOMEDES and CALCHAS
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES and PATROCLUS, before their tent
ULYSSES: Achilles stands i' the entrance of his tent:
ULYSSES: Please it our general to pass strangely by him,
ULYSSES: As if he were forgot, and, princes all,
ULYSSES: Lay negligent and loose regard upon him:
ULYSSES: I will come last. 'Tis like he'll question me
ULYSSES: Why such unplausive eyes are bent on him:
ULYSSES: If so, I have derision medicinable,
ULYSSES: To use between your strangeness and his pride,
ULYSSES: Which his own will shall have desire to drink:
ULYSSES: It may be good: pride hath no other glass
ULYSSES: To show itself but pride, for supple knees
ULYSSES: Feed arrogance and are the proud man's fees.
AGAMEMNON: We'll execute your purpose, and put on
AGAMEMNON: A form of strangeness as we pass along:
AGAMEMNON: So do each lord, and either greet him not,
AGAMEMNON: Or else disdainfully, which shall shake him more
AGAMEMNON: Than if not look'd on. I will lead the way.
ACHILLES: What, comes the general to speak with me?
ACHILLES: You know my mind, I'll fight no more 'gainst Troy.
AGAMEMNON: What says Achilles? would he aught with us?
NESTOR: Would you, my lord, aught with the general?
ACHILLES: No.
NESTOR: Nothing, my lord.
AGAMEMNON: The better.
NARRATOR: Exeunt AGAMEMNON and NESTOR
ACHILLES: Good day, good day.
MENELAUS: How do you? how do you?
NARRATOR: Exit
ACHILLES: What, does the cuckold scorn me?
AJAX: How now, Patroclus!
ACHILLES: Good morrow, Ajax.
AJAX: Ha?
ACHILLES: Good morrow.
AJAX: Ay, and good next day too.
NARRATOR: Exit
ACHILLES: What mean these fellows? Know they not Achilles?
PATROCLUS: They pass by strangely: they were used to bend
PATROCLUS: To send their smiles before them to Achilles,
PATROCLUS: To come as humbly as they used to creep
PATROCLUS: To holy altars.
ACHILLES: What, am I poor of late?
ACHILLES: 'Tis certain, greatness, once fall'n out with fortune,
ACHILLES: Must fall out with men too: what the declined is
ACHILLES: He shall as soon read in the eyes of others
ACHILLES: As feel in his own fall, for men, like butterflies,
ACHILLES: Show not their mealy wings but to the summer,
ACHILLES: And not a man, for being simply man,
ACHILLES: Hath any honour, but honour for those honours
ACHILLES: That are without him, as place, riches, favour,
ACHILLES: Prizes of accident as oft as merit:
ACHILLES: Which when they fall, as being slippery standers,
ACHILLES: The love that lean'd on them as slippery too,
ACHILLES: Do one pluck down another and together
ACHILLES: Die in the fall. But 'tis not so with me:
ACHILLES: Fortune and I are friends: I do enjoy
ACHILLES: At ample point all that I did possess,
ACHILLES: Save these men's looks, who do, methinks, find out
ACHILLES: Something not worth in me such rich beholding
ACHILLES: As they have often given. Here is Ulysses,
ACHILLES: I'll interrupt his reading.
ACHILLES: How now Ulysses!
ULYSSES: Now, great Thetis' son!
ACHILLES: What are you reading?
ULYSSES: A strange fellow here
ULYSSES: Writes me: 'That man, how dearly ever parted,
ULYSSES: How much in having, or without or in,
ULYSSES: Cannot make boast to have that which he hath,
ULYSSES: Nor feels not what he owes, but by reflection,
ULYSSES: As when his virtues shining upon others
ULYSSES: Heat them and they retort that heat again
ULYSSES: To the first giver.'
ACHILLES: This is not strange, Ulysses.
ACHILLES: The beauty that is borne here in the face
ACHILLES: The bearer knows not, but commends itself
ACHILLES: To others' eyes, nor doth the eye itself,
ACHILLES: That most pure spirit of sense, behold itself,
ACHILLES: Not going from itself, but eye to eye opposed
ACHILLES: Salutes each other with each other's form,
ACHILLES: For speculation turns not to itself,
ACHILLES: Till it hath travell'd and is mirror'd there
ACHILLES: Where it may see itself. This is not strange at all.
ULYSSES: I do not strain at the position,--
ULYSSES: It is familiar,--but at the author's drift,
ULYSSES: Who, in his circumstance, expressly proves
ULYSSES: That no man is the lord of any thing,
ULYSSES: Though in and of him there be much consisting,
ULYSSES: Till he communicate his parts to others:
ULYSSES: Nor doth he of himself know them for aught
ULYSSES: Till he behold them form'd in the applause
ULYSSES: Where they're extended, who, like an arch,
ULYSSES: reverberates
ULYSSES: The voice again, or, like a gate of steel
ULYSSES: Fronting the sun, receives and renders back
ULYSSES: His figure and his heat.  I was much wrapt in this,
ULYSSES: And apprehended here immediately
ULYSSES: The unknown Ajax.
ULYSSES: Heavens, what a man is there! a very horse,
ULYSSES: That has he knows not what. Nature, what things there are
ULYSSES: Most abject in regard and dear in use!
ULYSSES: What things again most dear in the esteem
ULYSSES: And poor in worth! Now shall we see to-morrow--
ULYSSES: An act that very chance doth throw upon him--
ULYSSES: Ajax renown'd. O heavens, what some men do,
ULYSSES: While some men leave to do!
ULYSSES: How some men creep in skittish fortune's hall,
ULYSSES: Whiles others play the idiots in her eyes!
ULYSSES: How one man eats into another's pride,
ULYSSES: While pride is fasting in his wantonness!
ULYSSES: To see these Grecian lords!--why, even already
ULYSSES: They clap the lubber Ajax on the shoulder,
ULYSSES: As if his foot were on brave Hector's breast
ULYSSES: And great Troy shrieking.
ACHILLES: I do believe it, for they pass'd by me
ACHILLES: As misers do by beggars, neither gave to me
ACHILLES: Good word nor look: what, are my deeds forgot?
ULYSSES: Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back,
ULYSSES: Wherein he puts alms for oblivion,
ULYSSES: A great-sized monster of ingratitudes:
ULYSSES: Those scraps are good deeds past, which are devour'd
ULYSSES: As fast as they are made, forgot as soon
ULYSSES: As done: perseverance, dear my lord,
ULYSSES: Keeps honour bright: to have done is to hang
ULYSSES: Quite out of fashion, like a rusty mail
ULYSSES: In monumental mockery. Take the instant way,
ULYSSES: For honour travels in a strait so narrow,
ULYSSES: Where one but goes abreast: keep then the path,
ULYSSES: For emulation hath a thousand sons
ULYSSES: That one by one pursue: if you give way,
ULYSSES: Or hedge aside from the direct forthright,
ULYSSES: Like to an enter'd tide, they all rush by
ULYSSES: And leave you hindmost,
ULYSSES: Or like a gallant horse fall'n in first rank,
ULYSSES: Lie there for pavement to the abject rear,
ULYSSES: O'er-run and trampled on: then what they do in present,
ULYSSES: Though less than yours in past, must o'ertop yours,
ULYSSES: For time is like a fashionable host
ULYSSES: That slightly shakes his parting guest by the hand,
ULYSSES: And with his arms outstretch'd, as he would fly,
ULYSSES: Grasps in the comer: welcome ever smiles,
ULYSSES: And farewell goes out sighing. O, let not
ULYSSES: virtue seek
ULYSSES: Remuneration for the thing it was,
ULYSSES: For beauty, wit,
ULYSSES: High birth, vigour of bone, desert in service,
ULYSSES: Love, friendship, charity, are subjects all
ULYSSES: To envious and calumniating time.
ULYSSES: One touch of nature makes the whole world kin,
ULYSSES: That all with one consent praise new-born gawds,
ULYSSES: Though they are made and moulded of things past,
ULYSSES: And give to dust that is a little gilt
ULYSSES: More laud than gilt o'er-dusted.
ULYSSES: The present eye praises the present object.
ULYSSES: Then marvel not, thou great and complete man,
ULYSSES: That all the Greeks begin to worship Ajax,
ULYSSES: Since things in motion sooner catch the eye
ULYSSES: Than what not stirs. The cry went once on thee,
ULYSSES: And still it might, and yet it may again,
ULYSSES: If thou wouldst not entomb thyself alive
ULYSSES: And case thy reputation in thy tent,
ULYSSES: Whose glorious deeds, but in these fields of late,
ULYSSES: Made emulous missions 'mongst the gods themselves
ULYSSES: And drave great Mars to faction.
ACHILLES: Of this my privacy
ACHILLES: I have strong reasons.
ULYSSES: But 'gainst your privacy
ULYSSES: The reasons are more potent and heroical:
ULYSSES: 'Tis known, Achilles, that you are in love
ULYSSES: With one of Priam's daughters.
ACHILLES: Ha! known!
ULYSSES: Is that a wonder?
ULYSSES: The providence that's in a watchful state
ULYSSES: Knows almost every grain of Plutus' gold,
ULYSSES: Finds bottom in the uncomprehensive deeps,
ULYSSES: Keeps place with thought and almost, like the gods,
ULYSSES: Does thoughts unveil in their dumb cradles.
ULYSSES: There is a mystery--with whom relation
ULYSSES: Durst never meddle--in the soul of state,
ULYSSES: Which hath an operation more divine
ULYSSES: Than breath or pen can give expressure to:
ULYSSES: All the commerce that you have had with Troy
ULYSSES: As perfectly is ours as yours, my lord,
ULYSSES: And better would it fit Achilles much
ULYSSES: To throw down Hector than Polyxena:
ULYSSES: But it must grieve young Pyrrhus now at home,
ULYSSES: When fame shall in our islands sound her trump,
ULYSSES: And all the Greekish girls shall tripping sing,
ULYSSES: 'Great Hector's sister did Achilles win,
ULYSSES: But our great Ajax bravely beat down him.'
ULYSSES: Farewell, my lord: I as your lover speak,
ULYSSES: The fool slides o'er the ice that you should break.
NARRATOR: Exit
PATROCLUS: To this effect, Achilles, have I moved you:
PATROCLUS: A woman impudent and mannish grown
PATROCLUS: Is not more loathed than an effeminate man
PATROCLUS: In time of action. I stand condemn'd for this,
PATROCLUS: They think my little stomach to the war
PATROCLUS: And your great love to me restrains you thus:
PATROCLUS: Sweet, rouse yourself, and the weak wanton Cupid
PATROCLUS: Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold,
PATROCLUS: And, like a dew-drop from the lion's mane,
PATROCLUS: Be shook to air.
ACHILLES: Shall Ajax fight with Hector?
PATROCLUS: Ay, and perhaps receive much honour by him.
ACHILLES: I see my reputation is at stake
ACHILLES: My fame is shrewdly gored.
PATROCLUS: O, then, beware,
PATROCLUS: Those wounds heal ill that men do give themselves:
PATROCLUS: Omission to do what is necessary
PATROCLUS: Seals a commission to a blank of danger,
PATROCLUS: And danger, like an ague, subtly taints
PATROCLUS: Even then when we sit idly in the sun.
ACHILLES: Go call Thersites hither, sweet Patroclus:
ACHILLES: I'll send the fool to Ajax and desire him
ACHILLES: To invite the Trojan lords after the combat
ACHILLES: To see us here unarm'd: I have a woman's longing,
ACHILLES: An appetite that I am sick withal,
ACHILLES: To see great Hector in his weeds of peace,
ACHILLES: To talk with him and to behold his visage,
ACHILLES: Even to my full of view.
NARRATOR: Enter THERSITES
ACHILLES: A labour saved!
THERSITES: A wonder!
ACHILLES: What?
THERSITES: Ajax goes up and down the field, asking for himself.
ACHILLES: How so?
THERSITES: He must fight singly to-morrow with Hector, and is so
THERSITES: prophetically proud of an heroical cudgelling that he
THERSITES: raves in saying nothing.
ACHILLES: How can that be?
THERSITES: Why, he stalks up and down like a peacock,--a stride
THERSITES: and a stand: ruminates like an hostess that hath no
THERSITES: arithmetic but her brain to set down her reckoning:
THERSITES: bites his lip with a politic regard, as who should
THERSITES: say 'There were wit in this head, an 'twould out,'
THERSITES: and so there is, but it lies as coldly in him as fire
THERSITES: in a flint, which will not show without knocking.
THERSITES: The man's undone forever, for if Hector break not his
THERSITES: neck i' the combat, he'll break 't himself in
THERSITES: vain-glory. He knows not me: I said 'Good morrow,
THERSITES: Ajax,' and he replies 'Thanks, Agamemnon.' What think
THERSITES: you of this man that takes me for the general? He's
THERSITES: grown a very land-fish, language-less, a monster.
THERSITES: A plague of opinion! a man may wear it on both
THERSITES: sides, like a leather jerkin.
ACHILLES: Thou must be my ambassador to him, Thersites.
THERSITES: Who, I? why, he'll answer nobody, he professes not
THERSITES: answering: speaking is for beggars, he wears his
THERSITES: tongue in's arms. I will put on his presence: let
THERSITES: Patroclus make demands to me, you shall see the
THERSITES: pageant of Ajax.
ACHILLES: To him, Patroclus, tell him I humbly desire the
ACHILLES: valiant Ajax to invite the most valorous Hector
ACHILLES: to come unarmed to my tent, and to procure
ACHILLES: safe-conduct for his person of the magnanimous
ACHILLES: and most illustrious six-or-seven-times-honoured
ACHILLES: captain-general of the Grecian army, Agamemnon,
ACHILLES: et cetera. Do this.
PATROCLUS: Jove bless great Ajax!
THERSITES: Hum!
PATROCLUS: I come from the worthy Achilles,--
THERSITES: Ha!
PATROCLUS: Who most humbly desires you to invite Hector to his tent,--
THERSITES: Hum!
PATROCLUS: And to procure safe-conduct from Agamemnon.
THERSITES: Agamemnon!
PATROCLUS: Ay, my lord.
THERSITES: Ha!
PATROCLUS: What say you to't?
THERSITES: God b' wi' you, with all my heart.
PATROCLUS: Your answer, sir.
THERSITES: If to-morrow be a fair day, by eleven o'clock it will
THERSITES: go one way or other: howsoever, he shall pay for me
THERSITES: ere he has me.
PATROCLUS: Your answer, sir.
THERSITES: Fare you well, with all my heart.
ACHILLES: Why, but he is not in this tune, is he?
THERSITES: No, but he's out o' tune thus. What music will be in
THERSITES: him when Hector has knocked out his brains, I know
THERSITES: not, but, I am sure, none, unless the fiddler Apollo
THERSITES: get his sinews to make catlings on.
ACHILLES: Come, thou shalt bear a letter to him straight.
THERSITES: Let me bear another to his horse, for that's the more
THERSITES: capable creature.
ACHILLES: My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirr'd,
ACHILLES: And I myself see not the bottom of it.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ACHILLES and PATROCLUS
THERSITES: Would the fountain of your mind were clear again,
THERSITES: that I might water an ass at it! I had rather be a
THERSITES: tick in a sheep than such a valiant ignorance.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Troy. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter, from one side, AENEAS, and Servant with a  torch, from the other, PARIS, DEIPHOBUS, ANTENOR, DIOMEDES, and others, with torches
PARIS: See, ho! who is that there?
DEIPHOBUS: It is the Lord AEneas.
AENEAS: Is the prince there in person?
AENEAS: Had I so good occasion to lie long
AENEAS: As you, prince Paris, nothing but heavenly business
AENEAS: Should rob my bed-mate of my company.
DIOMEDES: That's my mind too. Good morrow, Lord AEneas.
PARIS: A valiant Greek, AEneas,--take his hand,--
PARIS: Witness the process of your speech, wherein
PARIS: You told how Diomed, a whole week by days,
PARIS: Did haunt you in the field.
AENEAS: Health to you, valiant sir,
AENEAS: During all question of the gentle truce,
AENEAS: But when I meet you arm'd, as black defiance
AENEAS: As heart can think or courage execute.
DIOMEDES: The one and other Diomed embraces.
DIOMEDES: Our bloods are now in calm, and, so long, health!
DIOMEDES: But when contention and occasion meet,
DIOMEDES: By Jove, I'll play the hunter for thy life
DIOMEDES: With all my force, pursuit and policy.
AENEAS: And thou shalt hunt a lion, that will fly
AENEAS: With his face backward. In humane gentleness,
AENEAS: Welcome to Troy! now, by Anchises' life,
AENEAS: Welcome, indeed! By Venus' hand I swear,
AENEAS: No man alive can love in such a sort
AENEAS: The thing he means to kill more excellently.
DIOMEDES: We sympathize: Jove, let AEneas live,
DIOMEDES: If to my sword his fate be not the glory,
DIOMEDES: A thousand complete courses of the sun!
DIOMEDES: But, in mine emulous honour, let him die,
DIOMEDES: With every joint a wound, and that to-morrow!
AENEAS: We know each other well.
DIOMEDES: We do, and long to know each other worse.
PARIS: This is the most despiteful gentle greeting,
PARIS: The noblest hateful love, that e'er I heard of.
PARIS: What business, lord, so early?
AENEAS: I was sent for to the king, but why, I know not.
PARIS: His purpose meets you: 'twas to bring this Greek
PARIS: To Calchas' house, and there to render him,
PARIS: For the enfreed Antenor, the fair Cressid:
PARIS: Let's have your company, or, if you please,
PARIS: Haste there before us: I constantly do think--
PARIS: Or rather, call my thought a certain knowledge--
PARIS: My brother Troilus lodges there to-night:
PARIS: Rouse him and give him note of our approach.
PARIS: With the whole quality wherefore: I fear
PARIS: We shall be much unwelcome.
AENEAS: That I assure you:
AENEAS: Troilus had rather Troy were borne to Greece
AENEAS: Than Cressid borne from Troy.
PARIS: There is no help,
PARIS: The bitter disposition of the time
PARIS: Will have it so. On, lord, we'll follow you.
AENEAS: Good morrow, all.
NARRATOR: Exit with Servant
PARIS: And tell me, noble Diomed, faith, tell me true,
PARIS: Even in the soul of sound good-fellowship,
PARIS: Who, in your thoughts, merits fair Helen best,
PARIS: Myself or Menelaus?
DIOMEDES: Both alike:
DIOMEDES: He merits well to have her, that doth seek her,
DIOMEDES: Not making any scruple of her soilure,
DIOMEDES: With such a hell of pain and world of charge,
DIOMEDES: And you as well to keep her, that defend her,
DIOMEDES: Not palating the taste of her dishonour,
DIOMEDES: With such a costly loss of wealth and friends:
DIOMEDES: He, like a puling cuckold, would drink up
DIOMEDES: The lees and dregs of a flat tamed piece,
DIOMEDES: You, like a lecher, out of whorish loins
DIOMEDES: Are pleased to breed out your inheritors:
DIOMEDES: Both merits poised, each weighs nor less nor more,
DIOMEDES: But he as he, the heavier for a whore.
PARIS: You are too bitter to your countrywoman.
DIOMEDES: She's bitter to her country: hear me, Paris:
DIOMEDES: For every false drop in her bawdy veins
DIOMEDES: A Grecian's life hath sunk, for every scruple
DIOMEDES: Of her contaminated carrion weight,
DIOMEDES: A Trojan hath been slain: since she could speak,
DIOMEDES: She hath not given so many good words breath
DIOMEDES: As for her Greeks and Trojans suffer'd death.
PARIS: Fair Diomed, you do as chapmen do,
PARIS: Dispraise the thing that you desire to buy:
PARIS: But we in silence hold this virtue well,
PARIS: We'll but commend what we intend to sell.
PARIS: Here lies our way.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. Court of Pandarus' house.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS and CRESSIDA
TROILUS: Dear, trouble not yourself: the morn is cold.
CRESSIDA: Then, sweet my lord, I'll call mine uncle down,
CRESSIDA: He shall unbolt the gates.
TROILUS: Trouble him not,
TROILUS: To bed, to bed: sleep kill those pretty eyes,
TROILUS: And give as soft attachment to thy senses
TROILUS: As infants' empty of all thought!
CRESSIDA: Good morrow, then.
TROILUS: I prithee now, to bed.
CRESSIDA: Are you a-weary of me?
TROILUS: O Cressida! but that the busy day,
TROILUS: Waked by the lark, hath roused the ribald crows,
TROILUS: And dreaming night will hide our joys no longer,
TROILUS: I would not from thee.
CRESSIDA: Night hath been too brief.
TROILUS: Beshrew the witch! with venomous wights she stays
TROILUS: As tediously as hell, but flies the grasps of love
TROILUS: With wings more momentary-swift than thought.
TROILUS: You will catch cold, and curse me.
CRESSIDA: Prithee, tarry:
CRESSIDA: You men will never tarry.
CRESSIDA: O foolish Cressid! I might have still held off,
CRESSIDA: And then you would have tarried. Hark!
CRESSIDA: there's one up.
PANDARUS: [Within]  What, 's all the doors open here?
TROILUS: It is your uncle.
CRESSIDA: A pestilence on him! now will he be mocking:
CRESSIDA: I shall have such a life!
NARRATOR: Enter PANDARUS
PANDARUS: How now, how now! how go maidenheads? Here, you
PANDARUS: maid! where's my cousin Cressid?
CRESSIDA: Go hang yourself, you naughty mocking uncle!
CRESSIDA: You bring me to do, and then you flout me too.
PANDARUS: To do what? to do what? let her say
PANDARUS: what: what have I brought you to do?
CRESSIDA: Come, come, beshrew your heart! you'll ne'er be good,
CRESSIDA: Nor suffer others.
PANDARUS: Ha! ha! Alas, poor wretch! ah, poor capocchia!
PANDARUS: hast not slept to-night? would he not, a naughty
PANDARUS: man, let it sleep? a bugbear take him!
CRESSIDA: Did not I tell you? Would he were knock'd i' the head!
NARRATOR: Knocking within
CRESSIDA: Who's that at door? good uncle, go and see.
CRESSIDA: My lord, come you again into my chamber:
CRESSIDA: You smile and mock me, as if I meant naughtily.
TROILUS: Ha, ha!
CRESSIDA: Come, you are deceived, I think of no such thing.
NARRATOR: Knocking within
CRESSIDA: How earnestly they knock! Pray you, come in:
CRESSIDA: I would not for half Troy have you seen here.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TROILUS and CRESSIDA
PANDARUS: Who's there? what's the matter? will you beat
PANDARUS: down the door? How now! what's the matter?
NARRATOR: Enter AENEAS
AENEAS: Good morrow, lord, good morrow.
PANDARUS: Who's there? my Lord AEneas! By my troth,
PANDARUS: I knew you not: what news with you so early?
AENEAS: Is not Prince Troilus here?
PANDARUS: Here! what should he do here?
AENEAS: Come, he is here, my lord, do not deny him:
AENEAS: It doth import him much to speak with me.
PANDARUS: Is he here, say you? 'tis more than I know, I'll
PANDARUS: be sworn: for my own part, I came in late. What
PANDARUS: should he do here?
AENEAS: Who!--nay, then: come, come, you'll do him wrong
AENEAS: ere you're ware: you'll be so true to him, to be
AENEAS: false to him: do not you know of him, but yet go
AENEAS: fetch him hither, go.
NARRATOR: Re-enter TROILUS
TROILUS: How now! what's the matter?
AENEAS: My lord, I scarce have leisure to salute you,
AENEAS: My matter is so rash: there is at hand
AENEAS: Paris your brother, and Deiphobus,
AENEAS: The Grecian Diomed, and our Antenor
AENEAS: Deliver'd to us, and for him forthwith,
AENEAS: Ere the first sacrifice, within this hour,
AENEAS: We must give up to Diomedes' hand
AENEAS: The Lady Cressida.
TROILUS: Is it so concluded?
AENEAS: By Priam and the general state of Troy:
AENEAS: They are at hand and ready to effect it.
TROILUS: How my achievements mock me!
TROILUS: I will go meet them: and, my Lord AEneas,
TROILUS: We met by chance, you did not find me here.
AENEAS: Good, good, my lord, the secrets of nature
AENEAS: Have not more gift in taciturnity.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TROILUS and AENEAS
PANDARUS: Is't possible? no sooner got but lost? The devil
PANDARUS: take Antenor! the young prince will go mad: a
PANDARUS: plague upon Antenor! I would they had broke 's neck!
NARRATOR: Re-enter CRESSIDA
CRESSIDA: How now! what's the matter? who was here?
PANDARUS: Ah, ah!
CRESSIDA: Why sigh you so profoundly? where's my lord? gone!
CRESSIDA: Tell me, sweet uncle, what's the matter?
PANDARUS: Would I were as deep under the earth as I am above!
CRESSIDA: O the gods! what's the matter?
PANDARUS: Prithee, get thee in: would thou hadst ne'er been
PANDARUS: born! I knew thou wouldst be his death. O, poor
PANDARUS: gentleman! A plague upon Antenor!
CRESSIDA: Good uncle, I beseech you, on my knees! beseech you,
CRESSIDA: what's the matter?
PANDARUS: Thou must be gone, wench, thou must be gone, thou
PANDARUS: art changed for Antenor: thou must to thy father,
PANDARUS: and be gone from Troilus: 'twill be his death,
PANDARUS: 'twill be his bane, he cannot bear it.
CRESSIDA: O you immortal gods! I will not go.
PANDARUS: Thou must.
CRESSIDA: I will not, uncle: I have forgot my father,
CRESSIDA: I know no touch of consanguinity,
CRESSIDA: No kin no love, no blood, no soul so near me
CRESSIDA: As the sweet Troilus. O you gods divine!
CRESSIDA: Make Cressid's name the very crown of falsehood,
CRESSIDA: If ever she leave Troilus! Time, force, and death,
CRESSIDA: Do to this body what extremes you can,
CRESSIDA: But the strong base and building of my love
CRESSIDA: Is as the very centre of the earth,
CRESSIDA: Drawing all things to it. I'll go in and weep,--
PANDARUS: Do, do.
CRESSIDA: Tear my bright hair and scratch my praised cheeks,
CRESSIDA: Crack my clear voice with sobs and break my heart
CRESSIDA: With sounding Troilus. I will not go from Troy.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. Street before Pandarus' house.
NARRATOR: Enter PARIS, TROILUS, AENEAS, DEIPHOBUS, ANTENOR, and DIOMEDES
PARIS: It is great morning, and the hour prefix'd
PARIS: Of her delivery to this valiant Greek
PARIS: Comes fast upon. Good my brother Troilus,
PARIS: Tell you the lady what she is to do,
PARIS: And haste her to the purpose.
TROILUS: Walk into her house,
TROILUS: I'll bring her to the Grecian presently:
TROILUS: And to his hand when I deliver her,
TROILUS: Think it an altar, and thy brother Troilus
TROILUS: A priest there offering to it his own heart.
NARRATOR: Exit
PARIS: I know what 'tis to love,
PARIS: And would, as I shall pity, I could help!
PARIS: Please you walk in, my lords.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. The same. Pandarus' house.
NARRATOR: Enter PANDARUS and CRESSIDA
PANDARUS: Be moderate, be moderate.
CRESSIDA: Why tell you me of moderation?
CRESSIDA: The grief is fine, full, perfect, that I taste,
CRESSIDA: And violenteth in a sense as strong
CRESSIDA: As that which causeth it: how can I moderate it?
CRESSIDA: If I could temporize with my affection,
CRESSIDA: Or brew it to a weak and colder palate,
CRESSIDA: The like allayment could I give my grief.
CRESSIDA: My love admits no qualifying dross,
CRESSIDA: No more my grief, in such a precious loss.
PANDARUS: Here, here, here he comes.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS
PANDARUS: Ah, sweet ducks!
CRESSIDA: O Troilus! Troilus!
NARRATOR: Embracing him
PANDARUS: What a pair of spectacles is here!
PANDARUS: Let me embrace too. 'O heart,' as the goodly saying is,
PANDARUS: '--O heart, heavy heart,
PANDARUS: Why sigh'st thou without breaking?
PANDARUS: where he answers again,
PANDARUS: 'Because thou canst not ease thy smart
PANDARUS: By friendship nor by speaking.'
PANDARUS: There was never a truer rhyme. Let us cast away
PANDARUS: nothing, for we may live to have need of such a
PANDARUS: verse: we see it, we see it. How now, lambs?
TROILUS: Cressid, I love thee in so strain'd a purity,
TROILUS: That the bless'd gods, as angry with my fancy,
TROILUS: More bright in zeal than the devotion which
TROILUS: Cold lips blow to their deities, take thee from me.
CRESSIDA: Have the gods envy?
PANDARUS: Ay, ay, ay, ay, 'tis too plain a case.
CRESSIDA: And is it true that I must go from Troy?
TROILUS: A hateful truth.
CRESSIDA: What, and from Troilus too?
TROILUS: From Troy and Troilus.
CRESSIDA: Is it possible?
TROILUS: And suddenly, where injury of chance
TROILUS: Puts back leave-taking, justles roughly by
TROILUS: All time of pause, rudely beguiles our lips
TROILUS: Of all rejoindure, forcibly prevents
TROILUS: Our lock'd embrasures, strangles our dear vows
TROILUS: Even in the birth of our own labouring breath:
TROILUS: We two, that with so many thousand sighs
TROILUS: Did buy each other, must poorly sell ourselves
TROILUS: With the rude brevity and discharge of one.
TROILUS: Injurious time now with a robber's haste
TROILUS: Crams his rich thievery up, he knows not how:
TROILUS: As many farewells as be stars in heaven,
TROILUS: With distinct breath and consign'd kisses to them,
TROILUS: He fumbles up into a lose adieu,
TROILUS: And scants us with a single famish'd kiss,
TROILUS: Distasted with the salt of broken tears.
AENEAS: [Within]  My lord, is the lady ready?
TROILUS: Hark! you are call'd: some say the Genius so
TROILUS: Cries 'come' to him that instantly must die.
TROILUS: Bid them have patience, she shall come anon.
PANDARUS: Where are my tears? rain, to lay this wind, or
PANDARUS: my heart will be blown up by the root.
NARRATOR: Exit
CRESSIDA: I must then to the Grecians?
TROILUS: No remedy.
CRESSIDA: A woful Cressid 'mongst the merry Greeks!
CRESSIDA: When shall we see again?
TROILUS: Hear me, my love: be thou but true of heart,--
CRESSIDA: I true! how now! what wicked deem is this?
TROILUS: Nay, we must use expostulation kindly,
TROILUS: For it is parting from us:
TROILUS: I speak not 'be thou true,' as fearing thee,
TROILUS: For I will throw my glove to Death himself,
TROILUS: That there's no maculation in thy heart:
TROILUS: But 'be thou true,' say I, to fashion in
TROILUS: My sequent protestation, be thou true,
TROILUS: And I will see thee.
CRESSIDA: O, you shall be exposed, my lord, to dangers
CRESSIDA: As infinite as imminent! but I'll be true.
TROILUS: And I'll grow friend with danger. Wear this sleeve.
CRESSIDA: And you this glove. When shall I see you?
TROILUS: I will corrupt the Grecian sentinels,
TROILUS: To give thee nightly visitation.
TROILUS: But yet be true.
CRESSIDA: O heavens! 'be true' again!
TROILUS: Hear while I speak it, love:
TROILUS: The Grecian youths are full of quality,
TROILUS: They're loving, well composed with gifts of nature,
TROILUS: Flowing and swelling o'er with arts and exercise:
TROILUS: How novelty may move, and parts with person,
TROILUS: Alas, a kind of godly jealousy--
TROILUS: Which, I beseech you, call a virtuous sin--
TROILUS: Makes me afeard.
CRESSIDA: O heavens! you love me not.
TROILUS: Die I a villain, then!
TROILUS: In this I do not call your faith in question
TROILUS: So mainly as my merit: I cannot sing,
TROILUS: Nor heel the high lavolt, nor sweeten talk,
TROILUS: Nor play at subtle games, fair virtues all,
TROILUS: To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant:
TROILUS: But I can tell that in each grace of these
TROILUS: There lurks a still and dumb-discoursive devil
TROILUS: That tempts most cunningly: but be not tempted.
CRESSIDA: Do you think I will?
TROILUS: No.
TROILUS: But something may be done that we will not:
TROILUS: And sometimes we are devils to ourselves,
TROILUS: When we will tempt the frailty of our powers,
TROILUS: Presuming on their changeful potency.
AENEAS: [Within]  Nay, good my lord,--
TROILUS: Come, kiss, and let us part.
PARIS: [Within]  Brother Troilus!
TROILUS: Good brother, come you hither,
TROILUS: And bring AEneas and the Grecian with you.
CRESSIDA: My lord, will you be true?
TROILUS: Who, I? alas, it is my vice, my fault:
TROILUS: Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion,
TROILUS: I with great truth catch mere simplicity,
TROILUS: Whilst some with cunning gild their copper crowns,
TROILUS: With truth and plainness I do wear mine bare.
TROILUS: Fear not my truth: the moral of my wit
TROILUS: Is 'plain and true,' there's all the reach of it.
NARRATOR: Enter AENEAS, PARIS, ANTENOR, DEIPHOBUS, and DIOMEDES
TROILUS: Welcome, Sir Diomed! here is the lady
TROILUS: Which for Antenor we deliver you:
TROILUS: At the port, lord, I'll give her to thy hand,
TROILUS: And by the way possess thee what she is.
TROILUS: Entreat her fair, and, by my soul, fair Greek,
TROILUS: If e'er thou stand at mercy of my sword,
TROILUS: Name Cressida and thy life shall be as safe
TROILUS: As Priam is in Ilion.
DIOMEDES: Fair Lady Cressid,
DIOMEDES: So please you, save the thanks this prince expects:
DIOMEDES: The lustre in your eye, heaven in your cheek,
DIOMEDES: Pleads your fair usage, and to Diomed
DIOMEDES: You shall be mistress, and command him wholly.
TROILUS: Grecian, thou dost not use me courteously,
TROILUS: To shame the zeal of my petition to thee
TROILUS: In praising her: I tell thee, lord of Greece,
TROILUS: She is as far high-soaring o'er thy praises
TROILUS: As thou unworthy to be call'd her servant.
TROILUS: I charge thee use her well, even for my charge,
TROILUS: For, by the dreadful Pluto, if thou dost not,
TROILUS: Though the great bulk Achilles be thy guard,
TROILUS: I'll cut thy throat.
DIOMEDES: O, be not moved, Prince Troilus:
DIOMEDES: Let me be privileged by my place and message,
DIOMEDES: To be a speaker free, when I am hence
DIOMEDES: I'll answer to my lust: and know you, lord,
DIOMEDES: I'll nothing do on charge: to her own worth
DIOMEDES: She shall be prized, but that you say 'be't so,'
DIOMEDES: I'll speak it in my spirit and honour, 'no.'
TROILUS: Come, to the port. I'll tell thee, Diomed,
TROILUS: This brave shall oft make thee to hide thy head.
TROILUS: Lady, give me your hand, and, as we walk,
TROILUS: To our own selves bend we our needful talk.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TROILUS, CRESSIDA, and DIOMEDES
NARRATOR: Trumpet within
PARIS: Hark! Hector's trumpet.
AENEAS: How have we spent this morning!
AENEAS: The prince must think me tardy and remiss,
AENEAS: That sore to ride before him to the field.
PARIS: 'Tis Troilus' fault: come, come, to field with him.
DEIPHOBUS: Let us make ready straight.
AENEAS: Yea, with a bridegroom's fresh alacrity,
AENEAS: Let us address to tend on Hector's heels:
AENEAS: The glory of our Troy doth this day lie
AENEAS: On his fair worth and single chivalry.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. The Grecian camp. Lists set out.
NARRATOR: Enter AJAX, armed, AGAMEMNON, ACHILLES, PATROCLUS, MENELAUS, ULYSSES, NESTOR, and others
AGAMEMNON: Here art thou in appointment fresh and fair,
AGAMEMNON: Anticipating time with starting courage.
AGAMEMNON: Give with thy trumpet a loud note to Troy,
AGAMEMNON: Thou dreadful Ajax, that the appalled air
AGAMEMNON: May pierce the head of the great combatant
AGAMEMNON: And hale him hither.
AJAX: Thou, trumpet, there's my purse.
AJAX: Now crack thy lungs, and split thy brazen pipe:
AJAX: Blow, villain, till thy sphered bias cheek
AJAX: Outswell the colic of puff'd Aquilon:
AJAX: Come, stretch thy chest and let thy eyes spout blood,
AJAX: Thou blow'st for Hector.
NARRATOR: Trumpet sounds
ULYSSES: No trumpet answers.
ACHILLES: 'Tis but early days.
AGAMEMNON: Is not yond Diomed, with Calchas' daughter?
ULYSSES: 'Tis he, I ken the manner of his gait,
ULYSSES: He rises on the toe: that spirit of his
ULYSSES: In aspiration lifts him from the earth.
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES, with CRESSIDA
AGAMEMNON: Is this the Lady Cressid?
DIOMEDES: Even she.
AGAMEMNON: Most dearly welcome to the Greeks, sweet lady.
NESTOR: Our general doth salute you with a kiss.
ULYSSES: Yet is the kindness but particular,
ULYSSES: 'Twere better she were kiss'd in general.
NESTOR: And very courtly counsel: I'll begin.
NESTOR: So much for Nestor.
ACHILLES: I'll take what winter from your lips, fair lady:
ACHILLES: Achilles bids you welcome.
MENELAUS: I had good argument for kissing once.
PATROCLUS: But that's no argument for kissing now,
PATROCLUS: For this popp'd Paris in his hardiment,
PATROCLUS: And parted thus you and your argument.
ULYSSES: O deadly gall, and theme of all our scorns!
ULYSSES: For which we lose our heads to gild his horns.
PATROCLUS: The first was Menelaus' kiss, this, mine:
PATROCLUS: Patroclus kisses you.
MENELAUS: O, this is trim!
PATROCLUS: Paris and I kiss evermore for him.
MENELAUS: I'll have my kiss, sir. Lady, by your leave.
CRESSIDA: In kissing, do you render or receive?
PATROCLUS: Both take and give.
CRESSIDA: I'll make my match to live,
CRESSIDA: The kiss you take is better than you give,
CRESSIDA: Therefore no kiss.
MENELAUS: I'll give you boot, I'll give you three for one.
CRESSIDA: You're an odd man, give even or give none.
MENELAUS: An odd man, lady! every man is odd.
CRESSIDA: No, Paris is not, for you know 'tis true,
CRESSIDA: That you are odd, and he is even with you.
MENELAUS: You fillip me o' the head.
CRESSIDA: No, I'll be sworn.
ULYSSES: It were no match, your nail against his horn.
ULYSSES: May I, sweet lady, beg a kiss of you?
CRESSIDA: You may.
ULYSSES: I do desire it.
CRESSIDA: Why, beg, then.
ULYSSES: Why then for Venus' sake, give me a kiss,
ULYSSES: When Helen is a maid again, and his.
CRESSIDA: I am your debtor, claim it when 'tis due.
ULYSSES: Never's my day, and then a kiss of you.
DIOMEDES: Lady, a word: I'll bring you to your father.
NARRATOR: Exit with CRESSIDA
NESTOR: A woman of quick sense.
ULYSSES: Fie, fie upon her!
ULYSSES: There's language in her eye, her cheek, her lip,
ULYSSES: Nay, her foot speaks, her wanton spirits look out
ULYSSES: At every joint and motive of her body.
ULYSSES: O, these encounterers, so glib of tongue,
ULYSSES: That give accosting welcome ere it comes,
ULYSSES: And wide unclasp the tables of their thoughts
ULYSSES: To every ticklish reader! set them down
ULYSSES: For sluttish spoils of opportunity
ULYSSES: And daughters of the game.
NARRATOR: Trumpet within
ALL: The Trojans' trumpet.
AGAMEMNON: Yonder comes the troop.
AGAMEMNON: Enter HECTOR, armed, AENEAS, TROILUS, and other Trojans, with Attendants
AENEAS: Hail, all you state of Greece! what shall be done
AENEAS: To him that victory commands? or do you purpose
AENEAS: A victor shall be known? will you the knights
AENEAS: Shall to the edge of all extremity
AENEAS: Pursue each other, or shall be divided
AENEAS: By any voice or order of the field?
AENEAS: Hector bade ask.
AGAMEMNON: Which way would Hector have it?
AENEAS: He cares not, he'll obey conditions.
ACHILLES: 'Tis done like Hector, but securely done,
ACHILLES: A little proudly, and great deal misprizing
ACHILLES: The knight opposed.
AENEAS: If not Achilles, sir,
AENEAS: What is your name?
ACHILLES: If not Achilles, nothing.
AENEAS: Therefore Achilles: but, whate'er, know this:
AENEAS: In the extremity of great and little,
AENEAS: Valour and pride excel themselves in Hector,
AENEAS: The one almost as infinite as all,
AENEAS: The other blank as nothing. Weigh him well,
AENEAS: And that which looks like pride is courtesy.
AENEAS: This Ajax is half made of Hector's blood:
AENEAS: In love whereof, half Hector stays at home,
AENEAS: Half heart, half hand, half Hector comes to seek
AENEAS: This blended knight, half Trojan and half Greek.
ACHILLES: A maiden battle, then? O, I perceive you.
NARRATOR: Re-enter DIOMEDES
AGAMEMNON: Here is Sir Diomed. Go, gentle knight,
AGAMEMNON: Stand by our Ajax: as you and Lord AEneas
AGAMEMNON: Consent upon the order of their fight,
AGAMEMNON: So be it, either to the uttermost,
AGAMEMNON: Or else a breath: the combatants being kin
AGAMEMNON: Half stints their strife before their strokes begin.
NARRATOR: AJAX and HECTOR enter the lists
ULYSSES: They are opposed already.
AGAMEMNON: What Trojan is that same that looks so heavy?
ULYSSES: The youngest son of Priam, a true knight,
ULYSSES: Not yet mature, yet matchless, firm of word,
ULYSSES: Speaking in deeds and deedless in his tongue,
ULYSSES: Not soon provoked nor being provoked soon calm'd:
ULYSSES: His heart and hand both open and both free,
ULYSSES: For what he has he gives, what thinks he shows,
ULYSSES: Yet gives he not till judgment guide his bounty,
ULYSSES: Nor dignifies an impure thought with breath,
ULYSSES: Manly as Hector, but more dangerous,
ULYSSES: For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes
ULYSSES: To tender objects, but he in heat of action
ULYSSES: Is more vindicative than jealous love:
ULYSSES: They call him Troilus, and on him erect
ULYSSES: A second hope, as fairly built as Hector.
ULYSSES: Thus says AEneas, one that knows the youth
ULYSSES: Even to his inches, and with private soul
ULYSSES: Did in great Ilion thus translate him to me.
NARRATOR: Alarum. Hector and Ajax fight
AGAMEMNON: They are in action.
NESTOR: Now, Ajax, hold thine own!
TROILUS: Hector, thou sleep'st,
TROILUS: Awake thee!
AGAMEMNON: His blows are well disposed: there, Ajax!
DIOMEDES: You must no more.
NARRATOR: Trumpets cease
AENEAS: Princes, enough, so please you.
AJAX: I am not warm yet, let us fight again.
DIOMEDES: As Hector pleases.
HECTOR: Why, then will I no more:
HECTOR: Thou art, great lord, my father's sister's son,
HECTOR: A cousin-german to great Priam's seed,
HECTOR: The obligation of our blood forbids
HECTOR: A gory emulation 'twixt us twain:
HECTOR: Were thy commixtion Greek and Trojan so
HECTOR: That thou couldst say 'This hand is Grecian all,
HECTOR: And this is Trojan, the sinews of this leg
HECTOR: All Greek, and this all Troy, my mother's blood
HECTOR: Runs on the dexter cheek, and this sinister
HECTOR: Bounds in my father's,' by Jove multipotent,
HECTOR: Thou shouldst not bear from me a Greekish member
HECTOR: Wherein my sword had not impressure made
HECTOR: Of our rank feud: but the just gods gainsay
HECTOR: That any drop thou borrow'dst from thy mother,
HECTOR: My sacred aunt, should by my mortal sword
HECTOR: Be drain'd! Let me embrace thee, Ajax:
HECTOR: By him that thunders, thou hast lusty arms,
HECTOR: Hector would have them fall upon him thus:
HECTOR: Cousin, all honour to thee!
AJAX: I thank thee, Hector
AJAX: Thou art too gentle and too free a man:
AJAX: I came to kill thee, cousin, and bear hence
AJAX: A great addition earned in thy death.
HECTOR: Not Neoptolemus so mirable,
HECTOR: On whose bright crest Fame with her loud'st Oyes
HECTOR: Cries 'This is he,' could promise to himself
HECTOR: A thought of added honour torn from Hector.
AENEAS: There is expectance here from both the sides,
AENEAS: What further you will do.
HECTOR: We'll answer it,
HECTOR: The issue is embracement: Ajax, farewell.
AJAX: If I might in entreaties find success--
AJAX: As seld I have the chance--I would desire
AJAX: My famous cousin to our Grecian tents.
DIOMEDES: 'Tis Agamemnon's wish, and great Achilles
DIOMEDES: Doth long to see unarm'd the valiant Hector.
HECTOR: AEneas, call my brother Troilus to me,
HECTOR: And signify this loving interview
HECTOR: To the expecters of our Trojan part,
HECTOR: Desire them home. Give me thy hand, my cousin,
HECTOR: I will go eat with thee and see your knights.
AJAX: Great Agamemnon comes to meet us here.
HECTOR: The worthiest of them tell me name by name,
HECTOR: But for Achilles, mine own searching eyes
HECTOR: Shall find him by his large and portly size.
AGAMEMNON: Worthy of arms! as welcome as to one
AGAMEMNON: That would be rid of such an enemy,
AGAMEMNON: But that's no welcome: understand more clear,
AGAMEMNON: What's past and what's to come is strew'd with husks
AGAMEMNON: And formless ruin of oblivion,
AGAMEMNON: But in this extant moment, faith and troth,
AGAMEMNON: Strain'd purely from all hollow bias-drawing,
AGAMEMNON: Bids thee, with most divine integrity,
AGAMEMNON: From heart of very heart, great Hector, welcome.
HECTOR: I thank thee, most imperious Agamemnon.
AGAMEMNON: [To TROILUS]  My well-famed lord of Troy, no
AGAMEMNON: less to you.
MENELAUS: Let me confirm my princely brother's greeting:
MENELAUS: You brace of warlike brothers, welcome hither.
HECTOR: Who must we answer?
AENEAS: The noble Menelaus.
HECTOR: O, you, my lord? by Mars his gauntlet, thanks!
HECTOR: Mock not, that I affect the untraded oath,
HECTOR: Your quondam wife swears still by Venus' glove:
HECTOR: She's well, but bade me not commend her to you.
MENELAUS: Name her not now, sir, she's a deadly theme.
HECTOR: O, pardon, I offend.
NESTOR: I have, thou gallant Trojan, seen thee oft
NESTOR: Labouring for destiny make cruel way
NESTOR: Through ranks of Greekish youth, and I have seen thee,
NESTOR: As hot as Perseus, spur thy Phrygian steed,
NESTOR: Despising many forfeits and subduements,
NESTOR: When thou hast hung thy advanced sword i' the air,
NESTOR: Not letting it decline on the declined,
NESTOR: That I have said to some my standers by
NESTOR: 'Lo, Jupiter is yonder, dealing life!'
NESTOR: And I have seen thee pause and take thy breath,
NESTOR: When that a ring of Greeks have hemm'd thee in,
NESTOR: Like an Olympian wrestling: this have I seen,
NESTOR: But this thy countenance, still lock'd in steel,
NESTOR: I never saw till now. I knew thy grandsire,
NESTOR: And once fought with him: he was a soldier good,
NESTOR: But, by great Mars, the captain of us all,
NESTOR: Never saw like thee. Let an old man embrace thee,
NESTOR: And, worthy warrior, welcome to our tents.
AENEAS: 'Tis the old Nestor.
HECTOR: Let me embrace thee, good old chronicle,
HECTOR: That hast so long walk'd hand in hand with time:
HECTOR: Most reverend Nestor, I am glad to clasp thee.
NESTOR: I would my arms could match thee in contention,
NESTOR: As they contend with thee in courtesy.
HECTOR: I would they could.
NESTOR: Ha!
NESTOR: By this white beard, I'ld fight with thee to-morrow.
NESTOR: Well, welcome, welcome! I have seen the time.
ULYSSES: I wonder now how yonder city stands
ULYSSES: When we have here her base and pillar by us.
HECTOR: I know your favour, Lord Ulysses, well.
HECTOR: Ah, sir, there's many a Greek and Trojan dead,
HECTOR: Since first I saw yourself and Diomed
HECTOR: In Ilion, on your Greekish embassy.
ULYSSES: Sir, I foretold you then what would ensue:
ULYSSES: My prophecy is but half his journey yet,
ULYSSES: For yonder walls, that pertly front your town,
ULYSSES: Yond towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds,
ULYSSES: Must kiss their own feet.
HECTOR: I must not believe you:
HECTOR: There they stand yet, and modestly I think,
HECTOR: The fall of every Phrygian stone will cost
HECTOR: A drop of Grecian blood: the end crowns all,
HECTOR: And that old common arbitrator, Time,
HECTOR: Will one day end it.
ULYSSES: So to him we leave it.
ULYSSES: Most gentle and most valiant Hector, welcome:
ULYSSES: After the general, I beseech you next
ULYSSES: To feast with me and see me at my tent.
ACHILLES: I shall forestall thee, Lord Ulysses, thou!
ACHILLES: Now, Hector, I have fed mine eyes on thee,
ACHILLES: I have with exact view perused thee, Hector,
ACHILLES: And quoted joint by joint.
HECTOR: Is this Achilles?
ACHILLES: I am Achilles.
HECTOR: Stand fair, I pray thee: let me look on thee.
ACHILLES: Behold thy fill.
HECTOR: Nay, I have done already.
ACHILLES: Thou art too brief: I will the second time,
ACHILLES: As I would buy thee, view thee limb by limb.
HECTOR: O, like a book of sport thou'lt read me o'er,
HECTOR: But there's more in me than thou understand'st.
HECTOR: Why dost thou so oppress me with thine eye?
ACHILLES: Tell me, you heavens, in which part of his body
ACHILLES: Shall I destroy him? whether there, or there, or there?
ACHILLES: That I may give the local wound a name
ACHILLES: And make distinct the very breach whereout
ACHILLES: Hector's great spirit flew: answer me, heavens!
HECTOR: It would discredit the blest gods, proud man,
HECTOR: To answer such a question: stand again:
HECTOR: Think'st thou to catch my life so pleasantly
HECTOR: As to prenominate in nice conjecture
HECTOR: Where thou wilt hit me dead?
ACHILLES: I tell thee, yea.
HECTOR: Wert thou an oracle to tell me so,
HECTOR: I'd not believe thee. Henceforth guard thee well,
HECTOR: For I'll not kill thee there, nor there, nor there,
HECTOR: But, by the forge that stithied Mars his helm,
HECTOR: I'll kill thee every where, yea, o'er and o'er.
HECTOR: You wisest Grecians, pardon me this brag,
HECTOR: His insolence draws folly from my lips,
HECTOR: But I'll endeavour deeds to match these words,
HECTOR: Or may I never--
AJAX: Do not chafe thee, cousin:
AJAX: And you, Achilles, let these threats alone,
AJAX: Till accident or purpose bring you to't:
AJAX: You may have every day enough of Hector
AJAX: If you have stomach, the general state, I fear,
AJAX: Can scarce entreat you to be odd with him.
HECTOR: I pray you, let us see you in the field:
HECTOR: We have had pelting wars, since you refused
HECTOR: The Grecians' cause.
ACHILLES: Dost thou entreat me, Hector?
ACHILLES: To-morrow do I meet thee, fell as death,
ACHILLES: To-night all friends.
HECTOR: Thy hand upon that match.
AGAMEMNON: First, all you peers of Greece, go to my tent,
AGAMEMNON: There in the full convive we: afterwards,
AGAMEMNON: As Hector's leisure and your bounties shall
AGAMEMNON: Concur together, severally entreat him.
AGAMEMNON: Beat loud the tabourines, let the trumpets blow,
AGAMEMNON: That this great soldier may his welcome know.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all except TROILUS and ULYSSES
TROILUS: My Lord Ulysses, tell me, I beseech you,
TROILUS: In what place of the field doth Calchas keep?
ULYSSES: At Menelaus' tent, most princely Troilus:
ULYSSES: There Diomed doth feast with him to-night,
ULYSSES: Who neither looks upon the heaven nor earth,
ULYSSES: But gives all gaze and bent of amorous view
ULYSSES: On the fair Cressid.
TROILUS: Shall sweet lord, be bound to you so much,
TROILUS: After we part from Agamemnon's tent,
TROILUS: To bring me thither?
ULYSSES: You shall command me, sir.
ULYSSES: As gentle tell me, of what honour was
ULYSSES: This Cressida in Troy? Had she no lover there
ULYSSES: That wails her absence?
TROILUS: O, sir, to such as boasting show their scars
TROILUS: A mock is due. Will you walk on, my lord?
TROILUS: She was beloved, she loved, she is, and doth:
TROILUS: But still sweet love is food for fortune's tooth.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The Grecian camp. Before Achilles' tent.
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES and PATROCLUS
ACHILLES: I'll heat his blood with Greekish wine to-night,
ACHILLES: Which with my scimitar I'll cool to-morrow.
ACHILLES: Patroclus, let us feast him to the height.
PATROCLUS: Here comes Thersites.
NARRATOR: Enter THERSITES
ACHILLES: How now, thou core of envy!
ACHILLES: Thou crusty batch of nature, what's the news?
THERSITES: Why, thou picture of what thou seemest, and idol
THERSITES: of idiot worshippers, here's a letter for thee.
ACHILLES: From whence, fragment?
THERSITES: Why, thou full dish of fool, from Troy.
PATROCLUS: Who keeps the tent now?
THERSITES: The surgeon's box, or the patient's wound.
PATROCLUS: Well said, adversity! and what need these tricks?
THERSITES: Prithee, be silent, boy, I profit not by thy talk:
THERSITES: thou art thought to be Achilles' male varlet.
PATROCLUS: Male varlet, you rogue! what's that?
THERSITES: Why, his masculine whore. Now, the rotten diseases
THERSITES: of the south, the guts-griping, ruptures, catarrhs,
THERSITES: loads o' gravel i' the back, lethargies, cold
THERSITES: palsies, raw eyes, dirt-rotten livers, wheezing
THERSITES: lungs, bladders full of imposthume, sciaticas,
THERSITES: limekilns i' the palm, incurable bone-ache, and the
THERSITES: rivelled fee-simple of the tetter, take and take
THERSITES: again such preposterous discoveries!
PATROCLUS: Why thou damnable box of envy, thou, what meanest
PATROCLUS: thou to curse thus?
THERSITES: Do I curse thee?
PATROCLUS: Why no, you ruinous butt, you whoreson
PATROCLUS: indistinguishable cur, no.
THERSITES: No! why art thou then exasperate, thou idle
THERSITES: immaterial skein of sleave-silk, thou green sarcenet
THERSITES: flap for a sore eye, thou tassel of a prodigal's
THERSITES: purse, thou? Ah, how the poor world is pestered
THERSITES: with such waterflies, diminutives of nature!
PATROCLUS: Out, gall!
THERSITES: Finch-egg!
ACHILLES: My sweet Patroclus, I am thwarted quite
ACHILLES: From my great purpose in to-morrow's battle.
ACHILLES: Here is a letter from Queen Hecuba,
ACHILLES: A token from her daughter, my fair love,
ACHILLES: Both taxing me and gaging me to keep
ACHILLES: An oath that I have sworn. I will not break it:
ACHILLES: Fall Greeks, fail fame, honour or go or stay,
ACHILLES: My major vow lies here, this I'll obey.
ACHILLES: Come, come, Thersites, help to trim my tent:
ACHILLES: This night in banqueting must all be spent.
ACHILLES: Away, Patroclus!
NARRATOR: Exeunt ACHILLES and PATROCLUS
THERSITES: With too much blood and too little brain, these two
THERSITES: may run mad, but, if with too much brain and too
THERSITES: little blood they do, I'll be a curer of madmen.
THERSITES: Here's Agamemnon, an honest fellow enough and one
THERSITES: that loves quails, but he has not so much brain as
THERSITES: earwax: and the goodly transformation of Jupiter
THERSITES: there, his brother, the bull,--the primitive statue,
THERSITES: and oblique memorial of cuckolds, a thrifty
THERSITES: shoeing-horn in a chain, hanging at his brother's
THERSITES: leg,--to what form but that he is, should wit larded
THERSITES: with malice and malice forced with wit turn him to?
THERSITES: To an ass, were nothing, he is both ass and ox: to
THERSITES: an ox, were nothing, he is both ox and ass. To be a
THERSITES: dog, a mule, a cat, a fitchew, a toad, a lizard, an
THERSITES: owl, a puttock, or a herring without a roe, I would
THERSITES: not care, but to be Menelaus, I would conspire
THERSITES: against destiny. Ask me not, what I would be, if I
THERSITES: were not Thersites, for I care not to be the louse
THERSITES: of a lazar, so I were not Menelaus! Hey-day!
THERSITES: spirits and fires!
NARRATOR: Enter HECTOR, TROILUS, AJAX, AGAMEMNON, ULYSSES, NESTOR, MENELAUS, and DIOMEDES, with lights
AGAMEMNON: We go wrong, we go wrong.
AJAX: No, yonder 'tis,
AJAX: There, where we see the lights.
HECTOR: I trouble you.
AJAX: No, not a whit.
ULYSSES: Here comes himself to guide you.
NARRATOR: Re-enter ACHILLES
ACHILLES: Welcome, brave Hector, welcome, princes all.
AGAMEMNON: So now, fair prince of Troy, I bid good night.
AGAMEMNON: Ajax commands the guard to tend on you.
HECTOR: Thanks and good night to the Greeks' general.
MENELAUS: Good night, my lord.
HECTOR: Good night, sweet lord Menelaus.
THERSITES: Sweet draught: 'sweet' quoth 'a! sweet sink,
THERSITES: sweet sewer.
ACHILLES: Good night and welcome, both at once, to those
ACHILLES: That go or tarry.
AGAMEMNON: Good night.
NARRATOR: Exeunt AGAMEMNON and MENELAUS
ACHILLES: Old Nestor tarries, and you too, Diomed,
ACHILLES: Keep Hector company an hour or two.
DIOMEDES: I cannot, lord, I have important business,
DIOMEDES: The tide whereof is now. Good night, great Hector.
HECTOR: Give me your hand.
ULYSSES: [Aside to TROILUS]  Follow his torch, he goes to
ULYSSES: Calchas' tent:
ULYSSES: I'll keep you company.
TROILUS: Sweet sir, you honour me.
HECTOR: And so, good night.
HECTOR: Exit DIOMEDES, ULYSSES and TROILUS following
ACHILLES: Come, come, enter my tent.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ACHILLES, HECTOR, AJAX, and NESTOR
THERSITES: That same Diomed's a false-hearted rogue, a most
THERSITES: unjust knave, I will no more trust him when he leers
THERSITES: than I will a serpent when he hisses: he will spend
THERSITES: his mouth, and promise, like Brabbler the hound:
THERSITES: but when he performs, astronomers foretell it, it
THERSITES: is prodigious, there will come some change, the sun
THERSITES: borrows of the moon, when Diomed keeps his
THERSITES: word. I will rather leave to see Hector, than
THERSITES: not to dog him: they say he keeps a Trojan
THERSITES: drab, and uses the traitor Calchas' tent: I'll
THERSITES: after. Nothing but lechery! all incontinent varlets!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. Before Calchas' tent.
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES
DIOMEDES: What, are you up here, ho? speak.
CALCHAS: [Within]  Who calls?
DIOMEDES: Calchas, I think. Where's your daughter?
CALCHAS: [Within]  She comes to you.
CALCHAS: Enter TROILUS and ULYSSES, at a distance, after them, THERSITES
ULYSSES: Stand where the torch may not discover us.
NARRATOR: Enter CRESSIDA
TROILUS: Cressid comes forth to him.
DIOMEDES: How now, my charge!
CRESSIDA: Now, my sweet guardian! Hark, a word with you.
NARRATOR: Whispers
TROILUS: Yea, so familiar!
ULYSSES: She will sing any man at first sight.
THERSITES: And any man may sing her, if he can take her cliff,
THERSITES: she's noted.
DIOMEDES: Will you remember?
CRESSIDA: Remember! yes.
DIOMEDES: Nay, but do, then,
DIOMEDES: And let your mind be coupled with your words.
TROILUS: What should she remember?
ULYSSES: List.
CRESSIDA: Sweet honey Greek, tempt me no more to folly.
THERSITES: Roguery!
DIOMEDES: Nay, then,--
CRESSIDA: I'll tell you what,--
DIOMEDES: Foh, foh! come, tell a pin: you are forsworn.
CRESSIDA: In faith, I cannot: what would you have me do?
THERSITES: A juggling trick,--to be secretly open.
DIOMEDES: What did you swear you would bestow on me?
CRESSIDA: I prithee, do not hold me to mine oath,
CRESSIDA: Bid me do any thing but that, sweet Greek.
DIOMEDES: Good night.
TROILUS: Hold, patience!
ULYSSES: How now, Trojan!
CRESSIDA: Diomed,--
DIOMEDES: No, no, good night: I'll be your fool no more.
TROILUS: Thy better must.
CRESSIDA: Hark, one word in your ear.
TROILUS: O plague and madness!
ULYSSES: You are moved, prince, let us depart, I pray you,
ULYSSES: Lest your displeasure should enlarge itself
ULYSSES: To wrathful terms: this place is dangerous,
ULYSSES: The time right deadly, I beseech you, go.
TROILUS: Behold, I pray you!
ULYSSES: Nay, good my lord, go off:
ULYSSES: You flow to great distraction, come, my lord.
TROILUS: I pray thee, stay.
ULYSSES: You have not patience, come.
TROILUS: I pray you, stay, by hell and all hell's torments
TROILUS: I will not speak a word!
DIOMEDES: And so, good night.
CRESSIDA: Nay, but you part in anger.
TROILUS: Doth that grieve thee?
TROILUS: O wither'd truth!
ULYSSES: Why, how now, lord!
TROILUS: By Jove,
TROILUS: I will be patient.
CRESSIDA: Guardian!--why, Greek!
DIOMEDES: Foh, foh! adieu, you palter.
CRESSIDA: In faith, I do not: come hither once again.
ULYSSES: You shake, my lord, at something: will you go?
ULYSSES: You will break out.
TROILUS: She strokes his cheek!
ULYSSES: Come, come.
TROILUS: Nay, stay, by Jove, I will not speak a word:
TROILUS: There is between my will and all offences
TROILUS: A guard of patience: stay a little while.
THERSITES: How the devil Luxury, with his fat rump and
THERSITES: potato-finger, tickles these together! Fry, lechery, fry!
DIOMEDES: But will you, then?
CRESSIDA: In faith, I will, la, never trust me else.
DIOMEDES: Give me some token for the surety of it.
CRESSIDA: I'll fetch you one.
NARRATOR: Exit
ULYSSES: You have sworn patience.
TROILUS: Fear me not, sweet lord,
TROILUS: I will not be myself, nor have cognition
TROILUS: Of what I feel: I am all patience.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CRESSIDA
THERSITES: Now the pledge, now, now, now!
CRESSIDA: Here, Diomed, keep this sleeve.
TROILUS: O beauty! where is thy faith?
ULYSSES: My lord,--
TROILUS: I will be patient, outwardly I will.
CRESSIDA: You look upon that sleeve, behold it well.
CRESSIDA: He loved me--O false wench!--Give't me again.
DIOMEDES: Whose was't?
CRESSIDA: It is no matter, now I have't again.
CRESSIDA: I will not meet with you to-morrow night:
CRESSIDA: I prithee, Diomed, visit me no more.
THERSITES: Now she sharpens: well said, whetstone!
DIOMEDES: I shall have it.
CRESSIDA: What, this?
DIOMEDES: Ay, that.
CRESSIDA: O, all you gods! O pretty, pretty pledge!
CRESSIDA: Thy master now lies thinking in his bed
CRESSIDA: Of thee and me, and sighs, and takes my glove,
CRESSIDA: And gives memorial dainty kisses to it,
CRESSIDA: As I kiss thee. Nay, do not snatch it from me,
CRESSIDA: He that takes that doth take my heart withal.
DIOMEDES: I had your heart before, this follows it.
TROILUS: I did swear patience.
CRESSIDA: You shall not have it, Diomed, faith, you shall not,
CRESSIDA: I'll give you something else.
DIOMEDES: I will have this: whose was it?
CRESSIDA: It is no matter.
DIOMEDES: Come, tell me whose it was.
CRESSIDA: 'Twas one's that loved me better than you will.
CRESSIDA: But, now you have it, take it.
DIOMEDES: Whose was it?
CRESSIDA: By all Diana's waiting-women yond,
CRESSIDA: And by herself, I will not tell you whose.
DIOMEDES: To-morrow will I wear it on my helm,
DIOMEDES: And grieve his spirit that dares not challenge it.
TROILUS: Wert thou the devil, and worest it on thy horn,
TROILUS: It should be challenged.
CRESSIDA: Well, well, 'tis done, 'tis past: and yet it is not,
CRESSIDA: I will not keep my word.
DIOMEDES: Why, then, farewell,
DIOMEDES: Thou never shalt mock Diomed again.
CRESSIDA: You shall not go: one cannot speak a word,
CRESSIDA: But it straight starts you.
DIOMEDES: I do not like this fooling.
THERSITES: Nor I, by Pluto: but that that likes not you pleases me best.
DIOMEDES: What, shall I come? the hour?
CRESSIDA: Ay, come:--O Jove!--do come:--I shall be plagued.
DIOMEDES: Farewell till then.
CRESSIDA: Good night: I prithee, come.
NARRATOR: Exit DIOMEDES
