CRESSIDA: Troilus, farewell! one eye yet looks on thee
CRESSIDA: But with my heart the other eye doth see.
CRESSIDA: Ah, poor our sex! this fault in us I find,
CRESSIDA: The error of our eye directs our mind:
CRESSIDA: What error leads must err, O, then conclude
CRESSIDA: Minds sway'd by eyes are full of turpitude.
NARRATOR: Exit
THERSITES: A proof of strength she could not publish more,
THERSITES: Unless she said ' My mind is now turn'd whore.'
ULYSSES: All's done, my lord.
TROILUS: It is.
ULYSSES: Why stay we, then?
TROILUS: To make a recordation to my soul
TROILUS: Of every syllable that here was spoke.
TROILUS: But if I tell how these two did co-act,
TROILUS: Shall I not lie in publishing a truth?
TROILUS: Sith yet there is a credence in my heart,
TROILUS: An esperance so obstinately strong,
TROILUS: That doth invert the attest of eyes and ears,
TROILUS: As if those organs had deceptious functions,
TROILUS: Created only to calumniate.
TROILUS: Was Cressid here?
ULYSSES: I cannot conjure, Trojan.
TROILUS: She was not, sure.
ULYSSES: Most sure she was.
TROILUS: Why, my negation hath no taste of madness.
ULYSSES: Nor mine, my lord: Cressid was here but now.
TROILUS: Let it not be believed for womanhood!
TROILUS: Think, we had mothers, do not give advantage
TROILUS: To stubborn critics, apt, without a theme,
TROILUS: For depravation, to square the general sex
TROILUS: By Cressid's rule: rather think this not Cressid.
ULYSSES: What hath she done, prince, that can soil our mothers?
TROILUS: Nothing at all, unless that this were she.
THERSITES: Will he swagger himself out on's own eyes?
TROILUS: This she? no, this is Diomed's Cressida:
TROILUS: If beauty have a soul, this is not she,
TROILUS: If souls guide vows, if vows be sanctimonies,
TROILUS: If sanctimony be the gods' delight,
TROILUS: If there be rule in unity itself,
TROILUS: This is not she. O madness of discourse,
TROILUS: That cause sets up with and against itself!
TROILUS: Bi-fold authority! where reason can revolt
TROILUS: Without perdition, and loss assume all reason
TROILUS: Without revolt: this is, and is not, Cressid.
TROILUS: Within my soul there doth conduce a fight
TROILUS: Of this strange nature that a thing inseparate
TROILUS: Divides more wider than the sky and earth,
TROILUS: And yet the spacious breadth of this division
TROILUS: Admits no orifex for a point as subtle
TROILUS: As Ariachne's broken woof to enter.
TROILUS: Instance, O instance! strong as Pluto's gates,
TROILUS: Cressid is mine, tied with the bonds of heaven:
TROILUS: Instance, O instance! strong as heaven itself,
TROILUS: The bonds of heaven are slipp'd, dissolved, and loosed,
TROILUS: And with another knot, five-finger-tied,
TROILUS: The fractions of her faith, orts of her love,
TROILUS: The fragments, scraps, the bits and greasy relics
TROILUS: Of her o'er-eaten faith, are bound to Diomed.
ULYSSES: May worthy Troilus be half attach'd
ULYSSES: With that which here his passion doth express?
TROILUS: Ay, Greek, and that shall be divulged well
TROILUS: In characters as red as Mars his heart
TROILUS: Inflamed with Venus: never did young man fancy
TROILUS: With so eternal and so fix'd a soul.
TROILUS: Hark, Greek: as much as I do Cressid love,
TROILUS: So much by weight hate I her Diomed:
TROILUS: That sleeve is mine that he'll bear on his helm,
TROILUS: Were it a casque composed by Vulcan's skill,
TROILUS: My sword should bite it: not the dreadful spout
TROILUS: Which shipmen do the hurricano call,
TROILUS: Constringed in mass by the almighty sun,
TROILUS: Shall dizzy with more clamour Neptune's ear
TROILUS: In his descent than shall my prompted sword
TROILUS: Falling on Diomed.
THERSITES: He'll tickle it for his concupy.
TROILUS: O Cressid! O false Cressid! false, false, false!
TROILUS: Let all untruths stand by thy stained name,
TROILUS: And they'll seem glorious.
ULYSSES: O, contain yourself
ULYSSES: Your passion draws ears hither.
NARRATOR: Enter AENEAS
AENEAS: I have been seeking you this hour, my lord:
AENEAS: Hector, by this, is arming him in Troy,
AENEAS: Ajax, your guard, stays to conduct you home.
TROILUS: Have with you, prince. My courteous lord, adieu.
TROILUS: Farewell, revolted fair! and, Diomed,
TROILUS: Stand fast, and wear a castle on thy head!
ULYSSES: I'll bring you to the gates.
TROILUS: Accept distracted thanks.
NARRATOR: Exeunt TROILUS, AENEAS, and ULYSSES
THERSITES: Would I could meet that rogue Diomed! I would
THERSITES: croak like a raven, I would bode, I would bode.
THERSITES: Patroclus will give me any thing for the
THERSITES: intelligence of this whore: the parrot will not
THERSITES: do more for an almond than he for a commodious drab.
THERSITES: Lechery, lechery, still, wars and lechery, nothing
THERSITES: else holds fashion: a burning devil take them!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Troy. Before Priam's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter HECTOR and ANDROMACHE
ANDROMACHE: When was my lord so much ungently temper'd,
ANDROMACHE: To stop his ears against admonishment?
ANDROMACHE: Unarm, unarm, and do not fight to-day.
HECTOR: You train me to offend you, get you in:
HECTOR: By all the everlasting gods, I'll go!
ANDROMACHE: My dreams will, sure, prove ominous to the day.
HECTOR: No more, I say.
NARRATOR: Enter CASSANDRA
CASSANDRA: Where is my brother Hector?
ANDROMACHE: Here, sister, arm'd, and bloody in intent.
ANDROMACHE: Consort with me in loud and dear petition,
ANDROMACHE: Pursue we him on knees, for I have dream'd
ANDROMACHE: Of bloody turbulence, and this whole night
ANDROMACHE: Hath nothing been but shapes and forms of slaughter.
CASSANDRA: O, 'tis true.
HECTOR: Ho! bid my trumpet sound!
CASSANDRA: No notes of sally, for the heavens, sweet brother.
HECTOR: Be gone, I say: the gods have heard me swear.
CASSANDRA: The gods are deaf to hot and peevish vows:
CASSANDRA: They are polluted offerings, more abhorr'd
CASSANDRA: Than spotted livers in the sacrifice.
ANDROMACHE: O, be persuaded! do not count it holy
ANDROMACHE: To hurt by being just: it is as lawful,
ANDROMACHE: For we would give much, to use violent thefts,
ANDROMACHE: And rob in the behalf of charity.
CASSANDRA: It is the purpose that makes strong the vow,
CASSANDRA: But vows to every purpose must not hold:
CASSANDRA: Unarm, sweet Hector.
HECTOR: Hold you still, I say,
HECTOR: Mine honour keeps the weather of my fate:
HECTOR: Lie every man holds dear, but the brave man
HECTOR: Holds honour far more precious-dear than life.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS
HECTOR: How now, young man! mean'st thou to fight to-day?
ANDROMACHE: Cassandra, call my father to persuade.
NARRATOR: Exit CASSANDRA
HECTOR: No, faith, young Troilus, doff thy harness, youth,
HECTOR: I am to-day i' the vein of chivalry:
HECTOR: Let grow thy sinews till their knots be strong,
HECTOR: And tempt not yet the brushes of the war.
HECTOR: Unarm thee, go, and doubt thou not, brave boy,
HECTOR: I'll stand to-day for thee and me and Troy.
TROILUS: Brother, you have a vice of mercy in you,
TROILUS: Which better fits a lion than a man.
HECTOR: What vice is that, good Troilus? chide me for it.
TROILUS: When many times the captive Grecian falls,
TROILUS: Even in the fan and wind of your fair sword,
TROILUS: You bid them rise, and live.
HECTOR: O,'tis fair play.
TROILUS: Fool's play, by heaven, Hector.
HECTOR: How now! how now!
TROILUS: For the love of all the gods,
TROILUS: Let's leave the hermit pity with our mothers,
TROILUS: And when we have our armours buckled on,
TROILUS: The venom'd vengeance ride upon our swords,
TROILUS: Spur them to ruthful work, rein them from ruth.
HECTOR: Fie, savage, fie!
TROILUS: Hector, then 'tis wars.
HECTOR: Troilus, I would not have you fight to-day.
TROILUS: Who should withhold me?
TROILUS: Not fate, obedience, nor the hand of Mars
TROILUS: Beckoning with fiery truncheon my retire,
TROILUS: Not Priamus and Hecuba on knees,
TROILUS: Their eyes o'ergalled with recourse of tears,
TROILUS: Not you, my brother, with your true sword drawn,
TROILUS: Opposed to  hinder me, should stop my way,
TROILUS: But by my ruin.
NARRATOR: Re-enter CASSANDRA, with PRIAM
CASSANDRA: Lay hold upon him, Priam, hold him fast:
CASSANDRA: He is thy crutch, now if thou lose thy stay,
CASSANDRA: Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee,
CASSANDRA: Fall all together.
PRIAM: Come, Hector, come, go back:
PRIAM: Thy wife hath dream'd, thy mother hath had visions,
PRIAM: Cassandra doth foresee, and I myself
PRIAM: Am like a prophet suddenly enrapt
PRIAM: To tell thee that this day is ominous:
PRIAM: Therefore, come back.
HECTOR: AEneas is a-field,
HECTOR: And I do stand engaged to many Greeks,
HECTOR: Even in the faith of valour, to appear
HECTOR: This morning to them.
PRIAM: Ay, but thou shalt not go.
HECTOR: I must not break my faith.
HECTOR: You know me dutiful, therefore, dear sir,
HECTOR: Let me not shame respect, but give me leave
HECTOR: To take that course by your consent and voice,
HECTOR: Which you do here forbid me, royal Priam.
CASSANDRA: O Priam, yield not to him!
ANDROMACHE: Do not, dear father.
HECTOR: Andromache, I am offended with you:
HECTOR: Upon the love you bear me, get you in.
NARRATOR: Exit ANDROMACHE
TROILUS: This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl
TROILUS: Makes all these bodements.
CASSANDRA: O, farewell, dear Hector!
CASSANDRA: Look, how thou diest! look, how thy eye turns pale!
CASSANDRA: Look, how thy wounds do bleed at many vents!
CASSANDRA: Hark, how Troy roars! how Hecuba cries out!
CASSANDRA: How poor Andromache shrills her dolours forth!
CASSANDRA: Behold, distraction, frenzy and amazement,
CASSANDRA: Like witless antics, one another meet,
CASSANDRA: And all cry, Hector! Hector's dead! O Hector!
TROILUS: Away! away!
CASSANDRA: Farewell: yet, soft! Hector! take my leave:
CASSANDRA: Thou dost thyself and all our Troy deceive.
NARRATOR: Exit
HECTOR: You are amazed, my liege, at her exclaim:
HECTOR: Go in and cheer the town: we'll forth and fight,
HECTOR: Do deeds worth praise and tell you them at night.
PRIAM: Farewell: the gods with safety stand about thee!
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally PRIAM and HECTOR. Alarums
TROILUS: They are at it, hark! Proud Diomed, believe,
TROILUS: I come to lose my arm, or win my sleeve.
NARRATOR: Enter PANDARUS
PANDARUS: Do you hear, my lord? do you hear?
TROILUS: What now?
PANDARUS: Here's a letter come from yond poor girl.
TROILUS: Let me read.
PANDARUS: A whoreson tisick, a whoreson rascally tisick so
PANDARUS: troubles me, and the foolish fortune of this girl,
PANDARUS: and what one thing, what another, that I shall
PANDARUS: leave you one o' these days: and I have a rheum
PANDARUS: in mine eyes too, and such an ache in my bones
PANDARUS: that, unless a man were cursed, I cannot tell what
PANDARUS: to think on't. What says she there?
TROILUS: Words, words, mere words, no matter from the heart:
TROILUS: The effect doth operate another way.
NARRATOR: Tearing the letter
TROILUS: Go, wind, to wind, there turn and change together.
TROILUS: My love with words and errors still she feeds,
TROILUS: But edifies another with her deeds.
NARRATOR: Exeunt severally
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Plains between Troy and the Grecian camp.
NARRATOR: Alarums: excursions. Enter THERSITES
THERSITES: Now they are clapper-clawing one another, I'll go
THERSITES: look on. That dissembling abominable varlets Diomed,
THERSITES: has got that same scurvy doting foolish young knave's
THERSITES: sleeve of Troy there in his helm: I would fain see
THERSITES: them meet, that that same young Trojan ass, that
THERSITES: loves the whore there, might send that Greekish
THERSITES: whore-masterly villain, with the sleeve, back to the
THERSITES: dissembling luxurious drab, of a sleeveless errand.
THERSITES: O' the t'other side, the policy of those crafty
THERSITES: swearing rascals, that stale old mouse-eaten dry
THERSITES: cheese, Nestor, and that same dog-fox, Ulysses, is
THERSITES: not proved worthy a blackberry: they set me up, in
THERSITES: policy, that mongrel cur, Ajax, against that dog of
THERSITES: as bad a kind, Achilles: and now is the cur Ajax
THERSITES: prouder than the cur Achilles, and will not arm
THERSITES: to-day, whereupon the Grecians begin to proclaim
THERSITES: barbarism, and policy grows into an ill opinion.
THERSITES: Soft! here comes sleeve, and t'other.
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES, TROILUS following
TROILUS: Fly not, for shouldst thou take the river Styx,
TROILUS: I would swim after.
DIOMEDES: Thou dost miscall retire:
DIOMEDES: I do not fly, but advantageous care
DIOMEDES: Withdrew me from the odds of multitude:
DIOMEDES: Have at thee!
THERSITES: Hold thy whore, Grecian!--now for thy whore,
THERSITES: Trojan!--now the sleeve, now the sleeve!
NARRATOR: Exeunt TROILUS and DIOMEDES, fighting
NARRATOR: Enter HECTOR
HECTOR: What art thou, Greek? art thou for Hector's match?
HECTOR: Art thou of blood and honour?
THERSITES: No, no, I am a rascal, a scurvy railing knave:
THERSITES: a very filthy rogue.
HECTOR: I do believe thee: live.
NARRATOR: Exit
THERSITES: God-a-mercy, that thou wilt believe me, but a
THERSITES: plague break thy neck for frightening me! What's
THERSITES: become of the wenching rogues? I think they have
THERSITES: swallowed one another: I would laugh at that
THERSITES: miracle: yet, in a sort, lechery eats itself.
THERSITES: I'll seek them.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES and a Servant
DIOMEDES: Go, go, my servant, take thou Troilus' horse,
DIOMEDES: Present the fair steed to my lady Cressid:
DIOMEDES: Fellow, commend my service to her beauty,
DIOMEDES: Tell her I have chastised the amorous Trojan,
DIOMEDES: And am her knight by proof.
Servant: I go, my lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter AGAMEMNON
AGAMEMNON: Renew, renew! The fierce Polydamas
AGAMEMNON: Hath beat down Menon: bastard Margarelon
AGAMEMNON: Hath Doreus prisoner,
AGAMEMNON: And stands colossus-wise, waving his beam,
AGAMEMNON: Upon the pashed corses of the kings
AGAMEMNON: Epistrophus and Cedius: Polyxenes is slain,
AGAMEMNON: Amphimachus and Thoas deadly hurt,
AGAMEMNON: Patroclus ta'en or slain, and Palamedes
AGAMEMNON: Sore hurt and bruised: the dreadful Sagittary
AGAMEMNON: Appals our numbers: haste we, Diomed,
AGAMEMNON: To reinforcement, or we perish all.
NARRATOR: Enter NESTOR
NESTOR: Go, bear Patroclus' body to Achilles,
NESTOR: And bid the snail-paced Ajax arm for shame.
NESTOR: There is a thousand Hectors in the field:
NESTOR: Now here he fights on Galathe his horse,
NESTOR: And there lacks work, anon he's there afoot,
NESTOR: And there they fly or die, like scaled sculls
NESTOR: Before the belching whale, then is he yonder,
NESTOR: And there the strawy Greeks, ripe for his edge,
NESTOR: Fall down before him, like the mower's swath:
NESTOR: Here, there, and every where, he leaves and takes,
NESTOR: Dexterity so obeying appetite
NESTOR: That what he will he does, and does so much
NESTOR: That proof is call'd impossibility.
NARRATOR: Enter ULYSSES
ULYSSES: O, courage, courage, princes! great Achilles
ULYSSES: Is arming, weeping, cursing, vowing vengeance:
ULYSSES: Patroclus' wounds have roused his drowsy blood,
ULYSSES: Together with his mangled Myrmidons,
ULYSSES: That noseless, handless, hack'd and chipp'd, come to him,
ULYSSES: Crying on Hector. Ajax hath lost a friend
ULYSSES: And foams at mouth, and he is arm'd and at it,
ULYSSES: Roaring for Troilus, who hath done to-day
ULYSSES: Mad and fantastic execution,
ULYSSES: Engaging and redeeming of himself
ULYSSES: With such a careless force and forceless care
ULYSSES: As if that luck, in very spite of cunning,
ULYSSES: Bade him win all.
NARRATOR: Enter AJAX
AJAX: Troilus! thou coward Troilus!
NARRATOR: Exit
DIOMEDES: Ay, there, there.
NESTOR: So, so, we draw together.
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES
ACHILLES: Where is this Hector?
ACHILLES: Come, come, thou boy-queller, show thy face,
ACHILLES: Know what it is to meet Achilles angry:
ACHILLES: Hector? where's Hector? I will none but Hector.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter AJAX
AJAX: Troilus, thou coward Troilus, show thy head!
NARRATOR: Enter DIOMEDES
DIOMEDES: Troilus, I say! where's Troilus?
AJAX: What wouldst thou?
DIOMEDES: I would correct him.
AJAX: Were I the general, thou shouldst have my office
AJAX: Ere that correction. Troilus, I say! what, Troilus!
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS
TROILUS: O traitor Diomed! turn thy false face, thou traitor,
TROILUS: And pay thy life thou owest me for my horse!
DIOMEDES: Ha, art thou there?
AJAX: I'll fight with him alone: stand, Diomed.
DIOMEDES: He is my prize, I will not look upon.
TROILUS: Come, both you cogging Greeks, have at you both!
NARRATOR: Exeunt, fighting
NARRATOR: Enter HECTOR
HECTOR: Yea, Troilus? O, well fought, my youngest brother!
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES
ACHILLES: Now do I see thee, ha! have at thee, Hector!
HECTOR: Pause, if thou wilt.
ACHILLES: I do disdain thy courtesy, proud Trojan:
ACHILLES: Be happy that my arms are out of use:
ACHILLES: My rest and negligence befriends thee now,
ACHILLES: But thou anon shalt hear of me again,
ACHILLES: Till when, go seek thy fortune.
NARRATOR: Exit
HECTOR: Fare thee well:
HECTOR: I would have been much more a fresher man,
HECTOR: Had I expected thee. How now, my brother!
NARRATOR: Re-enter TROILUS
TROILUS: Ajax hath ta'en AEneas: shall it be?
TROILUS: No, by the flame of yonder glorious heaven,
TROILUS: He shall not carry him: I'll be ta'en too,
TROILUS: Or bring him off: fate, hear me what I say!
TROILUS: I reck not though I end my life to-day.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter one in sumptuous armour
HECTOR: Stand, stand, thou Greek, thou art a goodly mark:
HECTOR: No? wilt thou not? I like thy armour well,
HECTOR: I'll frush it and unlock the rivets all,
HECTOR: But I'll be master of it: wilt thou not,
HECTOR: beast, abide?
HECTOR: Why, then fly on, I'll hunt thee for thy hide.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES, with Myrmidons
ACHILLES: Come here about me, you my Myrmidons,
ACHILLES: Mark what I say. Attend me where I wheel:
ACHILLES: Strike not a stroke, but keep yourselves in breath:
ACHILLES: And when I have the bloody Hector found,
ACHILLES: Empale him with your weapons round about,
ACHILLES: In fellest manner execute your aims.
ACHILLES: Follow me, sirs, and my proceedings eye:
ACHILLES: It is decreed Hector the great must die.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: Enter MENELAUS and PARIS, fighting: then THERSITES
THERSITES: The cuckold and the cuckold-maker are at it. Now,
THERSITES: bull! now, dog! 'Loo, Paris, 'loo! now my double-
THERSITES: henned sparrow! 'loo, Paris, 'loo! The bull has the
THERSITES: game: ware horns, ho!
NARRATOR: Exeunt PARIS and MENELAUS
NARRATOR: Enter MARGARELON
MARGARELON: Turn, slave, and fight.
THERSITES: What art thou?
MARGARELON: A bastard son of Priam's.
THERSITES: I am a bastard too, I love bastards: I am a bastard
THERSITES: begot, bastard instructed, bastard in mind, bastard
THERSITES: in valour, in every thing illegitimate. One bear will
THERSITES: not bite another, and wherefore should one bastard?
THERSITES: Take heed, the quarrel's most ominous to us: if the
THERSITES: son of a whore fight for a whore, he tempts judgment:
THERSITES: farewell, bastard.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARGARELON: The devil take thee, coward!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter HECTOR
HECTOR: Most putrefied core, so fair without,
HECTOR: Thy goodly armour thus hath cost thy life.
HECTOR: Now is my day's work done, I'll take good breath:
HECTOR: Rest, sword, thou hast thy fill of blood and death.
NARRATOR: Puts off his helmet and hangs his shield behind him
NARRATOR: Enter ACHILLES and Myrmidons
ACHILLES: Look, Hector, how the sun begins to set,
ACHILLES: How ugly night comes breathing at his heels:
ACHILLES: Even with the vail and darking of the sun,
ACHILLES: To close the day up, Hector's life is done.
HECTOR: I am unarm'd, forego this vantage, Greek.
ACHILLES: Strike, fellows, strike, this is the man I seek.
NARRATOR: HECTOR falls
ACHILLES: So, Ilion, fall thou next! now, Troy, sink down!
ACHILLES: Here lies thy heart, thy sinews, and thy bone.
ACHILLES: On, Myrmidons, and cry you all amain,
ACHILLES: 'Achilles hath the mighty Hector slain.'
NARRATOR: A retreat sounded
ACHILLES: Hark! a retire upon our Grecian part.
MYRMIDONS: The Trojan trumpets sound the like, my lord.
ACHILLES: The dragon wing of night o'erspreads the earth,
ACHILLES: And, stickler-like, the armies separates.
ACHILLES: My half-supp'd sword, that frankly would have fed,
ACHILLES: Pleased with this dainty bait, thus goes to bed.
NARRATOR: Sheathes his sword
ACHILLES: Come, tie his body to my horse's tail,
ACHILLES: Along the field I will the Trojan trail.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IX. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter AGAMEMNON, AJAX, MENELAUS, NESTOR, DIOMEDES, and others, marching. Shouts within
AGAMEMNON: Hark! hark! what shout is that?
NESTOR: Peace, drums!
NARRATOR: Within
NESTOR: Achilles! Achilles! Hector's slain! Achilles.
DIOMEDES: The bruit is, Hector's slain, and by Achilles.
AJAX: If it be so, yet bragless let it be,
AJAX: Great Hector was a man as good as he.
AGAMEMNON: March patiently along: let one be sent
AGAMEMNON: To pray Achilles see us at our tent.
AGAMEMNON: If in his death the gods have us befriended,
AGAMEMNON: Great Troy is ours, and our sharp wars are ended.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, marching
NARRATOR: SCENE X. Another part of the plains.
NARRATOR: Enter AENEAS and Trojans
AENEAS: Stand, ho! yet are we masters of the field:
AENEAS: Never go home, here starve we out the night.
NARRATOR: Enter TROILUS
TROILUS: Hector is slain.
ALL: Hector! the gods forbid!
TROILUS: He's dead, and at the murderer's horse's tail,
TROILUS: In beastly sort, dragg'd through the shameful field.
TROILUS: Frown on, you heavens, effect your rage with speed!
TROILUS: Sit, gods, upon your thrones, and smile at Troy!
TROILUS: I say, at once let your brief plagues be mercy,
TROILUS: And linger not our sure destructions on!
AENEAS: My lord, you do discomfort all the host!
TROILUS: You understand me not that tell me so:
TROILUS: I do not speak of flight, of fear, of death,
TROILUS: But dare all imminence that gods and men
TROILUS: Address their dangers in. Hector is gone:
TROILUS: Who shall tell Priam so, or Hecuba?
TROILUS: Let him that will a screech-owl aye be call'd,
TROILUS: Go in to Troy, and say there, Hector's dead:
TROILUS: There is a word will Priam turn to stone,
TROILUS: Make wells and Niobes of the maids and wives,
TROILUS: Cold statues of the youth, and, in a word,
TROILUS: Scare Troy out of itself. But, march away:
TROILUS: Hector is dead, there is no more to say.
TROILUS: Stay yet. You vile abominable tents,
TROILUS: Thus proudly pight upon our Phrygian plains,
TROILUS: Let Titan rise as early as he dare,
TROILUS: I'll through and through you! and, thou great-sized coward,
TROILUS: No space of earth shall sunder our two hates:
TROILUS: I'll haunt thee like a wicked conscience still,
TROILUS: That mouldeth goblins swift as frenzy's thoughts.
TROILUS: Strike a free march to Troy! with comfort go:
TROILUS: Hope of revenge shall hide our inward woe.
NARRATOR: Exeunt AENEAS and Trojans
NARRATOR: As TROILUS is going out, enter, from the other side, PANDARUS
PANDARUS: But hear you, hear you!
TROILUS: Hence, broker-lackey! ignomy and shame
TROILUS: Pursue thy life, and live aye with thy name!
NARRATOR: Exit
PANDARUS: A goodly medicine for my aching bones! O world!
PANDARUS: world! world! thus is the poor agent despised!
PANDARUS: O traitors and bawds, how earnestly are you set
PANDARUS: a-work, and how ill requited! why should our
PANDARUS: endeavour be so loved and the performance so loathed?
PANDARUS: what verse for it? what instance for it? Let me see:
PANDARUS: Full merrily the humble-bee doth sing,
PANDARUS: Till he hath lost his honey and his sting,
PANDARUS: And being once subdued in armed tail,
PANDARUS: Sweet honey and sweet notes together fail.
PANDARUS: Good traders in the flesh, set this in your
PANDARUS: painted cloths.
PANDARUS: As many as be here of pander's hall,
PANDARUS: Your eyes, half out, weep out at Pandar's fall,
PANDARUS: Or if you cannot weep, yet give some groans,
PANDARUS: Though not for me, yet for your aching bones.
PANDARUS: Brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade,
PANDARUS: Some two months hence my will shall here be made:
PANDARUS: It should be now, but that my fear is this,
PANDARUS: Some galled goose of Winchester would hiss:
PANDARUS: Till then I'll sweat and seek about for eases,
PANDARUS: And at that time bequeathe you my diseases.
NARRATOR: Exit
''' PLAY: Twelfth Night '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. DUKE ORSINO's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE ORSINO, CURIO, and other Lords, Musicians attending
DUKE ORSINO: If music be the food of love, play on,
DUKE ORSINO: Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting,
DUKE ORSINO: The appetite may sicken, and so die.
DUKE ORSINO: That strain again! it had a dying fall:
DUKE ORSINO: O, it came o'er my ear like the sweet sound,
DUKE ORSINO: That breathes upon a bank of violets,
DUKE ORSINO: Stealing and giving odour! Enough, no more:
DUKE ORSINO: 'Tis not so sweet now as it was before.
DUKE ORSINO: O spirit of love! how quick and fresh art thou,
DUKE ORSINO: That, notwithstanding thy capacity
DUKE ORSINO: Receiveth as the sea, nought enters there,
DUKE ORSINO: Of what validity and pitch soe'er,
DUKE ORSINO: But falls into abatement and low price,
DUKE ORSINO: Even in a minute: so full of shapes is fancy
DUKE ORSINO: That it alone is high fantastical.
CURIO: Will you go hunt, my lord?
DUKE ORSINO: What, Curio?
CURIO: The hart.
DUKE ORSINO: Why, so I do, the noblest that I have:
DUKE ORSINO: O, when mine eyes did see Olivia first,
DUKE ORSINO: Methought she purged the air of pestilence!
DUKE ORSINO: That instant was I turn'd into a hart,
DUKE ORSINO: And my desires, like fell and cruel hounds,
DUKE ORSINO: E'er since pursue me.
NARRATOR: Enter VALENTINE
DUKE ORSINO: How now! what news from her?
VALENTINE: So please my lord, I might not be admitted,
VALENTINE: But from her handmaid do return this answer:
VALENTINE: The element itself, till seven years' heat,
VALENTINE: Shall not behold her face at ample view,
VALENTINE: But, like a cloistress, she will veiled walk
VALENTINE: And water once a day her chamber round
VALENTINE: With eye-offending brine: all this to season
VALENTINE: A brother's dead love, which she would keep fresh
VALENTINE: And lasting in her sad remembrance.
DUKE ORSINO: O, she that hath a heart of that fine frame
DUKE ORSINO: To pay this debt of love but to a brother,
DUKE ORSINO: How will she love, when the rich golden shaft
DUKE ORSINO: Hath kill'd the flock of all affections else
DUKE ORSINO: That live in her, when liver, brain and heart,
DUKE ORSINO: These sovereign thrones, are all supplied, and fill'd
DUKE ORSINO: Her sweet perfections with one self king!
DUKE ORSINO: Away before me to sweet beds of flowers:
DUKE ORSINO: Love-thoughts lie rich when canopied with bowers.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The sea-coast.
NARRATOR: Enter VIOLA, a Captain, and Sailors
VIOLA: What country, friends, is this?
Captain: This is Illyria, lady.
VIOLA: And what should I do in Illyria?
VIOLA: My brother he is in Elysium.
VIOLA: Perchance he is not drown'd: what think you, sailors?
Captain: It is perchance that you yourself were saved.
VIOLA: O my poor brother! and so perchance may he be.
Captain: True, madam: and, to comfort you with chance,
Captain: Assure yourself, after our ship did split,
Captain: When you and those poor number saved with you
Captain: Hung on our driving boat, I saw your brother,
Captain: Most provident in peril, bind himself,
Captain: Courage and hope both teaching him the practise,
Captain: To a strong mast that lived upon the sea,
Captain: Where, like Arion on the dolphin's back,
Captain: I saw him hold acquaintance with the waves
Captain: So long as I could see.
VIOLA: For saying so, there's gold:
VIOLA: Mine own escape unfoldeth to my hope,
VIOLA: Whereto thy speech serves for authority,
VIOLA: The like of him. Know'st thou this country?
Captain: Ay, madam, well, for I was bred and born
Captain: Not three hours' travel from this very place.
VIOLA: Who governs here?
Captain: A noble duke, in nature as in name.
VIOLA: What is the name?
Captain: Orsino.
VIOLA: Orsino! I have heard my father name him:
VIOLA: He was a bachelor then.
Captain: And so is now, or was so very late,
Captain: For but a month ago I went from hence,
Captain: And then 'twas fresh in murmur,--as, you know,
Captain: What great ones do the less will prattle of,--
Captain: That he did seek the love of fair Olivia.
VIOLA: What's she?
Captain: A virtuous maid, the daughter of a count
Captain: That died some twelvemonth since, then leaving her
Captain: In the protection of his son, her brother,
Captain: Who shortly also died: for whose dear love,
Captain: They say, she hath abjured the company
Captain: And sight of men.
VIOLA: O that I served that lady
VIOLA: And might not be delivered to the world,
VIOLA: Till I had made mine own occasion mellow,
VIOLA: What my estate is!
Captain: That were hard to compass,
Captain: Because she will admit no kind of suit,
Captain: No, not the duke's.
VIOLA: There is a fair behavior in thee, captain,
VIOLA: And though that nature with a beauteous wall
VIOLA: Doth oft close in pollution, yet of thee
VIOLA: I will believe thou hast a mind that suits
VIOLA: With this thy fair and outward character.
VIOLA: I prithee, and I'll pay thee bounteously,
VIOLA: Conceal me what I am, and be my aid
VIOLA: For such disguise as haply shall become
VIOLA: The form of my intent. I'll serve this duke:
VIOLA: Thou shall present me as an eunuch to him:
VIOLA: It may be worth thy pains, for I can sing
VIOLA: And speak to him in many sorts of music
VIOLA: That will allow me very worth his service.
VIOLA: What else may hap to time I will commit,
VIOLA: Only shape thou thy silence to my wit.
Captain: Be you his eunuch, and your mute I'll be:
Captain: When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not see.
VIOLA: I thank thee: lead me on.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. OLIVIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH and MARIA
SIR TOBY BELCH: What a plague means my niece, to take the death of
SIR TOBY BELCH: her brother thus? I am sure care's an enemy to life.
MARIA: By my troth, Sir Toby, you must come in earlier o'
MARIA: nights: your cousin, my lady, takes great
MARIA: exceptions to your ill hours.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Why, let her except, before excepted.
MARIA: Ay, but you must confine yourself within the modest
MARIA: limits of order.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Confine! I'll confine myself no finer than I am:
SIR TOBY BELCH: these clothes are good enough to drink in, and so be
SIR TOBY BELCH: these boots too: an they be not, let them hang
SIR TOBY BELCH: themselves in their own straps.
MARIA: That quaffing and drinking will undo you: I heard
MARIA: my lady talk of it yesterday, and of a foolish
MARIA: knight that you brought in one night here to be her wooer.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Who, Sir Andrew Aguecheek?
MARIA: Ay, he.
SIR TOBY BELCH: He's as tall a man as any's in Illyria.
MARIA: What's that to the purpose?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Why, he has three thousand ducats a year.
MARIA: Ay, but he'll have but a year in all these ducats:
MARIA: he's a very fool and a prodigal.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Fie, that you'll say so! he plays o' the
SIR TOBY BELCH: viol-de-gamboys, and speaks three or four languages
SIR TOBY BELCH: word for word without book, and hath all the good
SIR TOBY BELCH: gifts of nature.
MARIA: He hath indeed, almost natural: for besides that
MARIA: he's a fool, he's a great quarreller: and but that
MARIA: he hath the gift of a coward to allay the gust he
MARIA: hath in quarrelling, 'tis thought among the prudent
MARIA: he would quickly have the gift of a grave.
SIR TOBY BELCH: By this hand, they are scoundrels and subtractors
SIR TOBY BELCH: that say so of him. Who are they?
MARIA: They that add, moreover, he's drunk nightly in your company.
SIR TOBY BELCH: With drinking healths to my niece: I'll drink to
SIR TOBY BELCH: her as long as there is a passage in my throat and
SIR TOBY BELCH: drink in Illyria: he's a coward and a coystrill
SIR TOBY BELCH: that will not drink to my niece till his brains turn
SIR TOBY BELCH: o' the toe like a parish-top. What, wench!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Castiliano vulgo! for here comes Sir Andrew Agueface.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR ANDREW
SIR ANDREW: Sir Toby Belch! how now, Sir Toby Belch!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Sweet Sir Andrew!
SIR ANDREW: Bless you, fair shrew.
MARIA: And you too, sir.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Accost, Sir Andrew, accost.
SIR ANDREW: What's that?
SIR TOBY BELCH: My niece's chambermaid.
SIR ANDREW: Good Mistress Accost, I desire better acquaintance.
MARIA: My name is Mary, sir.
SIR ANDREW: Good Mistress Mary Accost,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: You mistake, knight, 'accost' is front her, board
SIR TOBY BELCH: her, woo her, assail her.
SIR ANDREW: By my troth, I would not undertake her in this
SIR ANDREW: company. Is that the meaning of 'accost'?
MARIA: Fare you well, gentlemen.
SIR TOBY BELCH: An thou let part so, Sir Andrew, would thou mightst
SIR TOBY BELCH: never draw sword again.
SIR ANDREW: An you part so, mistress, I would I might never
SIR ANDREW: draw sword again. Fair lady, do you think you have
SIR ANDREW: fools in hand?
MARIA: Sir, I have not you by the hand.
SIR ANDREW: Marry, but you shall have, and here's my hand.
MARIA: Now, sir, 'thought is free:' I pray you, bring
MARIA: your hand to the buttery-bar and let it drink.
SIR ANDREW: Wherefore, sweet-heart? what's your metaphor?
MARIA: It's dry, sir.
SIR ANDREW: Why, I think so: I am not such an ass but I can
SIR ANDREW: keep my hand dry. But what's your jest?
MARIA: A dry jest, sir.
SIR ANDREW: Are you full of them?
MARIA: Ay, sir, I have them at my fingers' ends: marry,
MARIA: now I let go your hand, I am barren.
NARRATOR: Exit
SIR TOBY BELCH: O knight thou lackest a cup of canary: when did I
SIR TOBY BELCH: see thee so put down?
SIR ANDREW: Never in your life, I think, unless you see canary
SIR ANDREW: put me down. Methinks sometimes I have no more wit
SIR ANDREW: than a Christian or an ordinary man has: but I am a
SIR ANDREW: great eater of beef and I believe that does harm to my wit.
SIR TOBY BELCH: No question.
SIR ANDREW: An I thought that, I'ld forswear it. I'll ride home
SIR ANDREW: to-morrow, Sir Toby.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Pourquoi, my dear knight?
SIR ANDREW: What is 'Pourquoi'? do or not do? I would I had
SIR ANDREW: bestowed that time in the tongues that I have in
SIR ANDREW: fencing, dancing and bear-baiting: O, had I but
SIR ANDREW: followed the arts!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Then hadst thou had an excellent head of hair.
SIR ANDREW: Why, would that have mended my hair?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Past question, for thou seest it will not curl by nature.
SIR ANDREW: But it becomes me well enough, does't not?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Excellent, it hangs like flax on a distaff, and I
SIR TOBY BELCH: hope to see a housewife take thee between her legs
SIR TOBY BELCH: and spin it off.
SIR ANDREW: Faith, I'll home to-morrow, Sir Toby: your niece
SIR ANDREW: will not be seen, or if she be, it's four to one
SIR ANDREW: she'll none of me: the count himself here hard by woos her.
SIR TOBY BELCH: She'll none o' the count: she'll not match above
SIR TOBY BELCH: her degree, neither in estate, years, nor wit, I
SIR TOBY BELCH: have heard her swear't. Tut, there's life in't,
SIR TOBY BELCH: man.
SIR ANDREW: I'll stay a month longer. I am a fellow o' the
SIR ANDREW: strangest mind i' the world, I delight in masques
SIR ANDREW: and revels sometimes altogether.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Art thou good at these kickshawses, knight?
SIR ANDREW: As any man in Illyria, whatsoever he be, under the
SIR ANDREW: degree of my betters, and yet I will not compare
SIR ANDREW: with an old man.
SIR TOBY BELCH: What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?
SIR ANDREW: Faith, I can cut a caper.
SIR TOBY BELCH: And I can cut the mutton to't.
SIR ANDREW: And I think I have the back-trick simply as strong
SIR ANDREW: as any man in Illyria.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Wherefore are these things hid? wherefore have
SIR TOBY BELCH: these gifts a curtain before 'em? are they like to
SIR TOBY BELCH: take dust, like Mistress Mall's picture? why dost
SIR TOBY BELCH: thou not go to church in a galliard and come home in
SIR TOBY BELCH: a coranto? My very walk should be a jig, I would not
SIR TOBY BELCH: so much as make water but in a sink-a-pace. What
SIR TOBY BELCH: dost thou mean? Is it a world to hide virtues in?
SIR TOBY BELCH: I did think, by the excellent constitution of thy
SIR TOBY BELCH: leg, it was formed under the star of a galliard.
SIR ANDREW: Ay, 'tis strong, and it does indifferent well in a
SIR ANDREW: flame-coloured stock. Shall we set about some revels?
SIR TOBY BELCH: What shall we do else? were we not born under Taurus?
SIR ANDREW: Taurus! That's sides and heart.
SIR TOBY BELCH: No, sir, it is legs and thighs. Let me see the
SIR TOBY BELCH: caper, ha! higher: ha, ha! excellent!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. DUKE ORSINO's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter VALENTINE and VIOLA in man's attire
VALENTINE: If the duke continue these favours towards you,
VALENTINE: Cesario, you are like to be much advanced: he hath
VALENTINE: known you but three days, and already you are no stranger.
VIOLA: You either fear his humour or my negligence, that
VIOLA: you call in question the continuance of his love:
VIOLA: is he inconstant, sir, in his favours?
VALENTINE: No, believe me.
VIOLA: I thank you. Here comes the count.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE ORSINO, CURIO, and Attendants
DUKE ORSINO: Who saw Cesario, ho?
VIOLA: On your attendance, my lord, here.
DUKE ORSINO: Stand you a while aloof, Cesario,
DUKE ORSINO: Thou know'st no less but all, I have unclasp'd
DUKE ORSINO: To thee the book even of my secret soul:
DUKE ORSINO: Therefore, good youth, address thy gait unto her,
DUKE ORSINO: Be not denied access, stand at her doors,
DUKE ORSINO: And tell them, there thy fixed foot shall grow
DUKE ORSINO: Till thou have audience.
VIOLA: Sure, my noble lord,
VIOLA: If she be so abandon'd to her sorrow
VIOLA: As it is spoke, she never will admit me.
DUKE ORSINO: Be clamorous and leap all civil bounds
DUKE ORSINO: Rather than make unprofited return.
VIOLA: Say I do speak with her, my lord, what then?
DUKE ORSINO: O, then unfold the passion of my love,
DUKE ORSINO: Surprise her with discourse of my dear faith:
DUKE ORSINO: It shall become thee well to act my woes,
DUKE ORSINO: She will attend it better in thy youth
DUKE ORSINO: Than in a nuncio's of more grave aspect.
VIOLA: I think not so, my lord.
DUKE ORSINO: Dear lad, believe it,
DUKE ORSINO: For they shall yet belie thy happy years,
DUKE ORSINO: That say thou art a man: Diana's lip
DUKE ORSINO: Is not more smooth and rubious, thy small pipe
DUKE ORSINO: Is as the maiden's organ, shrill and sound,
DUKE ORSINO: And all is semblative a woman's part.
DUKE ORSINO: I know thy constellation is right apt
DUKE ORSINO: For this affair. Some four or five attend him,
DUKE ORSINO: All, if you will, for I myself am best
DUKE ORSINO: When least in company. Prosper well in this,
DUKE ORSINO: And thou shalt live as freely as thy lord,
DUKE ORSINO: To call his fortunes thine.
VIOLA: I'll do my best
VIOLA: To woo your lady:
NARRATOR: Aside
VIOLA: yet, a barful strife!
VIOLA: Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. OLIVIA'S house.
NARRATOR: Enter MARIA and Clown
MARIA: Nay, either tell me where thou hast been, or I will
MARIA: not open my lips so wide as a bristle may enter in
MARIA: way of thy excuse: my lady will hang thee for thy absence.
Clown: Let her hang me: he that is well hanged in this
Clown: world needs to fear no colours.
MARIA: Make that good.
Clown: He shall see none to fear.
MARIA: A good lenten answer: I can tell thee where that
MARIA: saying was born, of 'I fear no colours.'
Clown: Where, good Mistress Mary?
MARIA: In the wars, and that may you be bold to say in your foolery.
Clown: Well, God give them wisdom that have it, and those
Clown: that are fools, let them use their talents.
MARIA: Yet you will be hanged for being so long absent, or,
MARIA: to be turned away, is not that as good as a hanging to you?
Clown: Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage, and,
Clown: for turning away, let summer bear it out.
MARIA: You are resolute, then?
Clown: Not so, neither, but I am resolved on two points.
MARIA: That if one break, the other will hold, or, if both
MARIA: break, your gaskins fall.
Clown: Apt, in good faith, very apt. Well, go thy way, if
Clown: Sir Toby would leave drinking, thou wert as witty a
Clown: piece of Eve's flesh as any in Illyria.
MARIA: Peace, you rogue, no more o' that. Here comes my
MARIA: lady: make your excuse wisely, you were best.
NARRATOR: Exit
Clown: Wit, an't be thy will, put me into good fooling!
Clown: Those wits, that think they have thee, do very oft
Clown: prove fools, and I, that am sure I lack thee, may
Clown: pass for a wise man: for what says Quinapalus?
Clown: 'Better a witty fool, than a foolish wit.'
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA with MALVOLIO
Clown: God bless thee, lady!
OLIVIA: Take the fool away.
Clown: Do you not hear, fellows? Take away the lady.
OLIVIA: Go to, you're a dry fool, I'll no more of you:
OLIVIA: besides, you grow dishonest.
Clown: Two faults, madonna, that drink and good counsel
Clown: will amend: for give the dry fool drink, then is
Clown: the fool not dry: bid the dishonest man mend
Clown: himself, if he mend, he is no longer dishonest, if
Clown: he cannot, let the botcher mend him. Any thing
Clown: that's mended is but patched: virtue that
Clown: transgresses is but patched with sin, and sin that
Clown: amends is but patched with virtue. If that this
Clown: simple syllogism will serve, so, if it will not,
Clown: what remedy? As there is no true cuckold but
Clown: calamity, so beauty's a flower. The lady bade take
Clown: away the fool, therefore, I say again, take her away.
OLIVIA: Sir, I bade them take away you.
Clown: Misprision in the highest degree! Lady, cucullus non
Clown: facit monachum, that's as much to say as I wear not
Clown: motley in my brain. Good madonna, give me leave to
Clown: prove you a fool.
OLIVIA: Can you do it?
Clown: Dexterously, good madonna.
OLIVIA: Make your proof.
Clown: I must catechise you for it, madonna: good my mouse
Clown: of virtue, answer me.
OLIVIA: Well, sir, for want of other idleness, I'll bide your proof.
Clown: Good madonna, why mournest thou?
OLIVIA: Good fool, for my brother's death.
Clown: I think his soul is in hell, madonna.
OLIVIA: I know his soul is in heaven, fool.
Clown: The more fool, madonna, to mourn for your brother's
Clown: soul being in heaven. Take away the fool, gentlemen.
OLIVIA: What think you of this fool, Malvolio? doth he not mend?
MALVOLIO: Yes, and shall do till the pangs of death shake him:
MALVOLIO: infirmity, that decays the wise, doth ever make the
MALVOLIO: better fool.
Clown: God send you, sir, a speedy infirmity, for the
Clown: better increasing your folly! Sir Toby will be
Clown: sworn that I am no fox, but he will not pass his
Clown: word for two pence that you are no fool.
OLIVIA: How say you to that, Malvolio?
MALVOLIO: I marvel your ladyship takes delight in such a
MALVOLIO: barren rascal: I saw him put down the other day
MALVOLIO: with an ordinary fool that has no more brain
MALVOLIO: than a stone. Look you now, he's out of his guard
MALVOLIO: already, unless you laugh and minister occasion to
MALVOLIO: him, he is gagged. I protest, I take these wise men,
MALVOLIO: that crow so at these set kind of fools, no better
MALVOLIO: than the fools' zanies.
OLIVIA: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste
OLIVIA: with a distempered appetite. To be generous,
OLIVIA: guiltless and of free disposition, is to take those
OLIVIA: things for bird-bolts that you deem cannon-bullets:
OLIVIA: there is no slander in an allowed fool, though he do
OLIVIA: nothing but rail, nor no railing in a known discreet
OLIVIA: man, though he do nothing but reprove.
Clown: Now Mercury endue thee with leasing, for thou
Clown: speakest well of fools!
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARIA
MARIA: Madam, there is at the gate a young gentleman much
MARIA: desires to speak with you.
OLIVIA: From the Count Orsino, is it?
MARIA: I know not, madam: 'tis a fair young man, and well attended.
OLIVIA: Who of my people hold him in delay?
MARIA: Sir Toby, madam, your kinsman.
OLIVIA: Fetch him off, I pray you, he speaks nothing but
OLIVIA: madman: fie on him!
NARRATOR: Exit MARIA
OLIVIA: Go you, Malvolio: if it be a suit from the count, I
OLIVIA: am sick, or not at home, what you will, to dismiss it.
NARRATOR: Exit MALVOLIO
OLIVIA: Now you see, sir, how your fooling grows old, and
OLIVIA: people dislike it.
Clown: Thou hast spoke for us, madonna, as if thy eldest
Clown: son should be a fool, whose skull Jove cram with
Clown: brains! for,--here he comes,--one of thy kin has a
Clown: most weak pia mater.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH
OLIVIA: By mine honour, half drunk. What is he at the gate, cousin?
SIR TOBY BELCH: A gentleman.
OLIVIA: A gentleman! what gentleman?
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'Tis a gentle man here--a plague o' these
SIR TOBY BELCH: pickle-herring! How now, sot!
Clown: Good Sir Toby!
OLIVIA: Cousin, cousin, how have you come so early by this lethargy?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Lechery! I defy lechery. There's one at the gate.
OLIVIA: Ay, marry, what is he?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Let him be the devil, an he will, I care not: give
SIR TOBY BELCH: me faith, say I. Well, it's all one.
NARRATOR: Exit
OLIVIA: What's a drunken man like, fool?
Clown: Like a drowned man, a fool and a mad man: one
Clown: draught above heat makes him a fool, the second mads
Clown: him, and a third drowns him.
OLIVIA: Go thou and seek the crowner, and let him sit o' my
OLIVIA: coz, for he's in the third degree of drink, he's
OLIVIA: drowned: go, look after him.
Clown: He is but mad yet, madonna, and the fool shall look
Clown: to the madman.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter MALVOLIO
MALVOLIO: Madam, yond young fellow swears he will speak with
MALVOLIO: you. I told him you were sick, he takes on him to
MALVOLIO: understand so much, and therefore comes to speak
MALVOLIO: with you. I told him you were asleep, he seems to
MALVOLIO: have a foreknowledge of that too, and therefore
MALVOLIO: comes to speak with you. What is to be said to him,
MALVOLIO: lady? he's fortified against any denial.
OLIVIA: Tell him he shall not speak with me.
MALVOLIO: Has been told so, and he says, he'll stand at your
MALVOLIO: door like a sheriff's post, and be the supporter to
MALVOLIO: a bench, but he'll speak with you.
OLIVIA: What kind o' man is he?
MALVOLIO: Why, of mankind.
OLIVIA: What manner of man?
MALVOLIO: Of very ill manner, he'll speak with you, will you or no.
OLIVIA: Of what personage and years is he?
MALVOLIO: Not yet old enough for a man, nor young enough for
MALVOLIO: a boy, as a squash is before 'tis a peascod, or a
MALVOLIO: cooling when 'tis almost an apple: 'tis with him
MALVOLIO: in standing water, between boy and man. He is very
MALVOLIO: well-favoured and he speaks very shrewishly, one
MALVOLIO: would think his mother's milk were scarce out of him.
OLIVIA: Let him approach: call in my gentlewoman.
MALVOLIO: Gentlewoman, my lady calls.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARIA
OLIVIA: Give me my veil: come, throw it o'er my face.
OLIVIA: We'll once more hear Orsino's embassy.
NARRATOR: Enter VIOLA, and Attendants
VIOLA: The honourable lady of the house, which is she?
OLIVIA: Speak to me, I shall answer for her.
OLIVIA: Your will?
VIOLA: Most radiant, exquisite and unmatchable beauty,--I
VIOLA: pray you, tell me if this be the lady of the house,
VIOLA: for I never saw her: I would be loath to cast away
VIOLA: my speech, for besides that it is excellently well
VIOLA: penned, I have taken great pains to con it. Good
VIOLA: beauties, let me sustain no scorn, I am very
VIOLA: comptible, even to the least sinister usage.
OLIVIA: Whence came you, sir?
VIOLA: I can say little more than I have studied, and that
VIOLA: question's out of my part. Good gentle one, give me
VIOLA: modest assurance if you be the lady of the house,
VIOLA: that I may proceed in my speech.
OLIVIA: Are you a comedian?
VIOLA: No, my profound heart: and yet, by the very fangs
VIOLA: of malice I swear, I am not that I play. Are you
VIOLA: the lady of the house?
OLIVIA: If I do not usurp myself, I am.
VIOLA: Most certain, if you are she, you do usurp
VIOLA: yourself, for what is yours to bestow is not yours
VIOLA: to reserve. But this is from my commission: I will
VIOLA: on with my speech in your praise, and then show you
VIOLA: the heart of my message.
OLIVIA: Come to what is important in't: I forgive you the praise.
VIOLA: Alas, I took great pains to study it, and 'tis poetical.
OLIVIA: It is the more like to be feigned: I pray you,
OLIVIA: keep it in. I heard you were saucy at my gates,
OLIVIA: and allowed your approach rather to wonder at you
OLIVIA: than to hear you. If you be not mad, be gone, if
OLIVIA: you have reason, be brief: 'tis not that time of
OLIVIA: moon with me to make one in so skipping a dialogue.
MARIA: Will you hoist sail, sir? here lies your way.
VIOLA: No, good swabber, I am to hull here a little
VIOLA: longer. Some mollification for your giant, sweet
VIOLA: lady. Tell me your mind: I am a messenger.
OLIVIA: Sure, you have some hideous matter to deliver, when
OLIVIA: the courtesy of it is so fearful. Speak your office.
VIOLA: It alone concerns your ear. I bring no overture of
VIOLA: war, no taxation of homage: I hold the olive in my
VIOLA: hand, my words are as fun of peace as matter.
OLIVIA: Yet you began rudely. What are you? what would you?
VIOLA: The rudeness that hath appeared in me have I
VIOLA: learned from my entertainment. What I am, and what I
VIOLA: would, are as secret as maidenhead, to your ears,
VIOLA: divinity, to any other's, profanation.
OLIVIA: Give us the place alone: we will hear this divinity.
NARRATOR: Exeunt MARIA and Attendants
OLIVIA: Now, sir, what is your text?
VIOLA: Most sweet lady,--
OLIVIA: A comfortable doctrine, and much may be said of it.
OLIVIA: Where lies your text?
VIOLA: In Orsino's bosom.
OLIVIA: In his bosom! In what chapter of his bosom?
VIOLA: To answer by the method, in the first of his heart.
OLIVIA: O, I have read it: it is heresy. Have you no more to say?
VIOLA: Good madam, let me see your face.
OLIVIA: Have you any commission from your lord to negotiate
OLIVIA: with my face? You are now out of your text: but
OLIVIA: we will draw the curtain and show you the picture.
OLIVIA: Look you, sir, such a one I was this present: is't
OLIVIA: not well done?
NARRATOR: Unveiling
VIOLA: Excellently done, if God did all.
OLIVIA: 'Tis in grain, sir, 'twill endure wind and weather.
VIOLA: 'Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white
VIOLA: Nature's own sweet and cunning hand laid on:
VIOLA: Lady, you are the cruell'st she alive,
VIOLA: If you will lead these graces to the grave
VIOLA: And leave the world no copy.
OLIVIA: O, sir, I will not be so hard-hearted, I will give
OLIVIA: out divers schedules of my beauty: it shall be
OLIVIA: inventoried, and every particle and utensil
OLIVIA: labelled to my will: as, item, two lips,
OLIVIA: indifferent red, item, two grey eyes, with lids to
OLIVIA: them, item, one neck, one chin, and so forth. Were
OLIVIA: you sent hither to praise me?
VIOLA: I see you what you are, you are too proud,
VIOLA: But, if you were the devil, you are fair.
VIOLA: My lord and master loves you: O, such love
VIOLA: Could be but recompensed, though you were crown'd
VIOLA: The nonpareil of beauty!
OLIVIA: How does he love me?
VIOLA: With adorations, fertile tears,
VIOLA: With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.
OLIVIA: Your lord does know my mind, I cannot love him:
OLIVIA: Yet I suppose him virtuous, know him noble,
OLIVIA: Of great estate, of fresh and stainless youth,
OLIVIA: In voices well divulged, free, learn'd and valiant,
OLIVIA: And in dimension and the shape of nature
OLIVIA: A gracious person: but yet I cannot love him,
OLIVIA: He might have took his answer long ago.
VIOLA: If I did love you in my master's flame,
VIOLA: With such a suffering, such a deadly life,
VIOLA: In your denial I would find no sense,
VIOLA: I would not understand it.
OLIVIA: Why, what would you?
VIOLA: Make me a willow cabin at your gate,
VIOLA: And call upon my soul within the house,
VIOLA: Write loyal cantons of contemned love
VIOLA: And sing them loud even in the dead of night,
VIOLA: Halloo your name to the reverberate hills
VIOLA: And make the babbling gossip of the air
VIOLA: Cry out 'Olivia!' O, You should not rest
VIOLA: Between the elements of air and earth,
VIOLA: But you should pity me!
OLIVIA: You might do much.
OLIVIA: What is your parentage?
VIOLA: Above my fortunes, yet my state is well:
VIOLA: I am a gentleman.
OLIVIA: Get you to your lord,
OLIVIA: I cannot love him: let him send no more,
OLIVIA: Unless, perchance, you come to me again,
OLIVIA: To tell me how he takes it. Fare you well:
OLIVIA: I thank you for your pains: spend this for me.
VIOLA: I am no fee'd post, lady, keep your purse:
VIOLA: My master, not myself, lacks recompense.
VIOLA: Love make his heart of flint that you shall love,
VIOLA: And let your fervor, like my master's, be
VIOLA: Placed in contempt! Farewell, fair cruelty.
NARRATOR: Exit
OLIVIA: 'What is your parentage?'
OLIVIA: 'Above my fortunes, yet my state is well:
OLIVIA: I am a gentleman.' I'll be sworn thou art,
OLIVIA: Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbs, actions and spirit,
OLIVIA: Do give thee five-fold blazon: not too fast:
OLIVIA: soft, soft!
OLIVIA: Unless the master were the man. How now!
OLIVIA: Even so quickly may one catch the plague?
OLIVIA: Methinks I feel this youth's perfections
OLIVIA: With an invisible and subtle stealth
OLIVIA: To creep in at mine eyes. Well, let it be.
OLIVIA: What ho, Malvolio!
NARRATOR: Re-enter MALVOLIO
MALVOLIO: Here, madam, at your service.
OLIVIA: Run after that same peevish messenger,
OLIVIA: The county's man: he left this ring behind him,
OLIVIA: Would I or not: tell him I'll none of it.
OLIVIA: Desire him not to flatter with his lord,
OLIVIA: Nor hold him up with hopes, I am not for him:
OLIVIA: If that the youth will come this way to-morrow,
OLIVIA: I'll give him reasons for't: hie thee, Malvolio.
MALVOLIO: Madam, I will.
NARRATOR: Exit
OLIVIA: I do I know not what, and fear to find
OLIVIA: Mine eye too great a flatterer for my mind.
OLIVIA: Fate, show thy force: ourselves we do not owe,
OLIVIA: What is decreed must be, and be this so.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: ACT II
NARRATOR: SCENE I. The sea-coast.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO and SEBASTIAN
ANTONIO: Will you stay no longer? nor will you not that I go with you?
SEBASTIAN: By your patience, no. My stars shine darkly over
SEBASTIAN: me: the malignancy of my fate might perhaps
SEBASTIAN: distemper yours, therefore I shall crave of you your
SEBASTIAN: leave that I may bear my evils alone: it were a bad
SEBASTIAN: recompense for your love, to lay any of them on you.
SEBASTIAN: ANTONIO: Let me yet know of you whither you are bound.
SEBASTIAN: No, sooth, sir: my determinate voyage is mere
SEBASTIAN: extravagancy. But I perceive in you so excellent a
SEBASTIAN: touch of modesty, that you will not extort from me
SEBASTIAN: what I am willing to keep in, therefore it charges
SEBASTIAN: me in manners the rather to express myself. You
SEBASTIAN: must know of me then, Antonio, my name is Sebastian,
SEBASTIAN: which I called Roderigo. My father was that
SEBASTIAN: Sebastian of Messaline, whom I know you have heard
SEBASTIAN: of. He left behind him myself and a sister, both
SEBASTIAN: born in an hour: if the heavens had been pleased,
SEBASTIAN: would we had so ended! but you, sir, altered that,
SEBASTIAN: for some hour before you took me from the breach of
SEBASTIAN: the sea was my sister drowned.
ANTONIO: Alas the day!
SEBASTIAN: A lady, sir, though it was said she much resembled
SEBASTIAN: me, was yet of many accounted beautiful: but,
SEBASTIAN: though I could not with such estimable wonder
SEBASTIAN: overfar believe that, yet thus far I will boldly
SEBASTIAN: publish her, she bore a mind that envy could not but
SEBASTIAN: call fair. She is drowned already, sir, with salt
SEBASTIAN: water, though I seem to drown her remembrance again with more.
ANTONIO: Pardon me, sir, your bad entertainment.
SEBASTIAN: O good Antonio, forgive me your trouble.
ANTONIO: If you will not murder me for my love, let me be
ANTONIO: your servant.
SEBASTIAN: If you will not undo what you have done, that is,
SEBASTIAN: kill him whom you have recovered, desire it not.
SEBASTIAN: Fare ye well at once: my bosom is full of kindness,
SEBASTIAN: and I am yet so near the manners of my mother, that
SEBASTIAN: upon the least occasion more mine eyes will tell
SEBASTIAN: tales of me. I am bound to the Count Orsino's court: farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
ANTONIO: The gentleness of all the gods go with thee!
ANTONIO: I have many enemies in Orsino's court,
ANTONIO: Else would I very shortly see thee there.
ANTONIO: But, come what may, I do adore thee so,
ANTONIO: That danger shall seem sport, and I will go.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter VIOLA, MALVOLIO following
MALVOLIO: Were not you even now with the Countess Olivia?
VIOLA: Even now, sir, on a moderate pace I have since
VIOLA: arrived but hither.
MALVOLIO: She returns this ring to you, sir: you might have
MALVOLIO: saved me my pains, to have taken it away yourself.
MALVOLIO: She adds, moreover, that you should put your lord
MALVOLIO: into a desperate assurance she will none of him:
MALVOLIO: and one thing more, that you be never so hardy to
MALVOLIO: come again in his affairs, unless it be to report
MALVOLIO: your lord's taking of this. Receive it so.
VIOLA: She took the ring of me: I'll none of it.
MALVOLIO: Come, sir, you peevishly threw it to her, and her
MALVOLIO: will is, it should be so returned: if it be worth
MALVOLIO: stooping for, there it lies in your eye, if not, be
MALVOLIO: it his that finds it.
NARRATOR: Exit
VIOLA: I left no ring with her: what means this lady?
VIOLA: Fortune forbid my outside have not charm'd her!
VIOLA: She made good view of me, indeed, so much,
VIOLA: That sure methought her eyes had lost her tongue,
VIOLA: For she did speak in starts distractedly.
VIOLA: She loves me, sure, the cunning of her passion
VIOLA: Invites me in this churlish messenger.
VIOLA: None of my lord's ring! why, he sent her none.
VIOLA: I am the man: if it be so, as 'tis,
VIOLA: Poor lady, she were better love a dream.
VIOLA: Disguise, I see, thou art a wickedness,
VIOLA: Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
VIOLA: How easy is it for the proper-false
VIOLA: In women's waxen hearts to set their forms!
VIOLA: Alas, our frailty is the cause, not we!
VIOLA: For such as we are made of, such we be.
VIOLA: How will this fadge? my master loves her dearly,
VIOLA: And I, poor monster, fond as much on him,
VIOLA: And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me.
VIOLA: What will become of this? As I am man,
VIOLA: My state is desperate for my master's love,
VIOLA: As I am woman,--now alas the day!--
VIOLA: What thriftless sighs shall poor Olivia breathe!
VIOLA: O time! thou must untangle this, not I,
VIOLA: It is too hard a knot for me to untie!
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. OLIVIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH and SIR ANDREW
SIR TOBY BELCH: Approach, Sir Andrew: not to be abed after
SIR TOBY BELCH: midnight is to be up betimes, and 'diluculo
SIR TOBY BELCH: surgere,' thou know'st,--
SIR ANDREW: Nay, my troth, I know not: but I know, to be up
SIR ANDREW: late is to be up late.
SIR TOBY BELCH: A false conclusion: I hate it as an unfilled can.
SIR TOBY BELCH: To be up after midnight and to go to bed then, is
SIR TOBY BELCH: early: so that to go to bed after midnight is to go
SIR TOBY BELCH: to bed betimes. Does not our life consist of the
SIR TOBY BELCH: four elements?
SIR ANDREW: Faith, so they say, but I think it rather consists
SIR ANDREW: of eating and drinking.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Thou'rt a scholar, let us therefore eat and drink.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Marian, I say! a stoup of wine!
NARRATOR: Enter Clown
SIR ANDREW: Here comes the fool, i' faith.
Clown: How now, my hearts! did you never see the picture
Clown: of 'we three'?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Welcome, ass. Now let's have a catch.
SIR ANDREW: By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast. I
SIR ANDREW: had rather than forty shillings I had such a leg,
SIR ANDREW: and so sweet a breath to sing, as the fool has. In
SIR ANDREW: sooth, thou wast in very gracious fooling last
SIR ANDREW: night, when thou spokest of Pigrogromitus, of the
SIR ANDREW: Vapians passing the equinoctial of Queubus: 'twas
SIR ANDREW: very good, i' faith. I sent thee sixpence for thy
SIR ANDREW: leman: hadst it?
Clown: I did impeticos thy gratillity, for Malvolio's nose
Clown: is no whipstock: my lady has a white hand, and the
Clown: Myrmidons are no bottle-ale houses.
SIR ANDREW: Excellent! why, this is the best fooling, when all
SIR ANDREW: is done. Now, a song.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come on, there is sixpence for you: let's have a song.
SIR ANDREW: There's a testril of me too: if one knight give a--
Clown: Would you have a love-song, or a song of good life?
SIR TOBY BELCH: A love-song, a love-song.
SIR ANDREW: Ay, ay: I care not for good life.
Clown: [Sings]
Clown: O mistress mine, where are you roaming?
Clown: O, stay and hear, your true love's coming,
Clown: That can sing both high and low:
Clown: Trip no further, pretty sweeting,
Clown: Journeys end in lovers meeting,
Clown: Every wise man's son doth know.
SIR ANDREW: Excellent good, i' faith.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Good, good.
Clown: [Sings]
Clown: What is love? 'tis not hereafter,
Clown: Present mirth hath present laughter,
Clown: What's to come is still unsure:
Clown: In delay there lies no plenty,
Clown: Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty,
Clown: Youth's a stuff will not endure.
SIR ANDREW: A mellifluous voice, as I am true knight.
SIR TOBY BELCH: A contagious breath.
SIR ANDREW: Very sweet and contagious, i' faith.
SIR TOBY BELCH: To hear by the nose, it is dulcet in contagion.
SIR TOBY BELCH: But shall we make the welkin dance indeed? shall we
SIR TOBY BELCH: rouse the night-owl in a catch that will draw three
SIR TOBY BELCH: souls out of one weaver? shall we do that?
SIR ANDREW: An you love me, let's do't: I am dog at a catch.
Clown: By'r lady, sir, and some dogs will catch well.
SIR ANDREW: Most certain. Let our catch be, 'Thou knave.'
Clown: 'Hold thy peace, thou knave,' knight? I shall be
Clown: constrained in't to call thee knave, knight.
SIR ANDREW: 'Tis not the first time I have constrained one to
SIR ANDREW: call me knave. Begin, fool: it begins 'Hold thy peace.'
Clown: I shall never begin if I hold my peace.
SIR ANDREW: Good, i' faith. Come, begin.
NARRATOR: Catch sung
NARRATOR: Enter MARIA
MARIA: What a caterwauling do you keep here! If my lady
MARIA: have not called up her steward Malvolio and bid him
MARIA: turn you out of doors, never trust me.
SIR TOBY BELCH: My lady's a Cataian, we are politicians, Malvolio's
SIR TOBY BELCH: a Peg-a-Ramsey, and 'Three merry men be we.' Am not
SIR TOBY BELCH: I consanguineous? am I not of her blood?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Tillyvally. Lady!
NARRATOR: Sings
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'There dwelt a man in Babylon, lady, lady!'
Clown: Beshrew me, the knight's in admirable fooling.
SIR ANDREW: Ay, he does well enough if he be disposed, and so do
SIR ANDREW: I too: he does it with a better grace, but I do it
SIR ANDREW: more natural.
SIR TOBY BELCH: [Sings]  'O, the twelfth day of December,'--
MARIA: For the love o' God, peace!
NARRATOR: Enter MALVOLIO
MALVOLIO: My masters, are you mad? or what are you? Have ye
MALVOLIO: no wit, manners, nor honesty, but to gabble like
MALVOLIO: tinkers at this time of night? Do ye make an
MALVOLIO: alehouse of my lady's house, that ye squeak out your
MALVOLIO: coziers' catches without any mitigation or remorse
MALVOLIO: of voice? Is there no respect of place, persons, nor
MALVOLIO: time in you?
SIR TOBY BELCH: We did keep time, sir, in our catches. Sneck up!
MALVOLIO: Sir Toby, I must be round with you. My lady bade me
MALVOLIO: tell you, that, though she harbours you as her
MALVOLIO: kinsman, she's nothing allied to your disorders. If
MALVOLIO: you can separate yourself and your misdemeanors, you
MALVOLIO: are welcome to the house, if not, an it would please
MALVOLIO: you to take leave of her, she is very willing to bid
MALVOLIO: you farewell.
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'Farewell, dear heart, since I must needs be gone.'
MARIA: Nay, good Sir Toby.
Clown: 'His eyes do show his days are almost done.'
MALVOLIO: Is't even so?
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'But I will never die.'
Clown: Sir Toby, there you lie.
MALVOLIO: This is much credit to you.
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'Shall I bid him go?'
Clown: 'What an if you do?'
SIR TOBY BELCH: 'Shall I bid him go, and spare not?'
Clown: 'O no, no, no, no, you dare not.'
SIR TOBY BELCH: Out o' tune, sir: ye lie. Art any more than a
SIR TOBY BELCH: steward? Dost thou think, because thou art
SIR TOBY BELCH: virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?
Clown: Yes, by Saint Anne, and ginger shall be hot i' the
Clown: mouth too.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Thou'rt i' the right. Go, sir, rub your chain with
SIR TOBY BELCH: crumbs. A stoup of wine, Maria!
MALVOLIO: Mistress Mary, if you prized my lady's favour at any
MALVOLIO: thing more than contempt, you would not give means
MALVOLIO: for this uncivil rule: she shall know of it, by this hand.
NARRATOR: Exit
MARIA: Go shake your ears.
SIR ANDREW: 'Twere as good a deed as to drink when a man's
SIR ANDREW: a-hungry, to challenge him the field, and then to
SIR ANDREW: break promise with him and make a fool of him.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Do't, knight: I'll write thee a challenge: or I'll
SIR TOBY BELCH: deliver thy indignation to him by word of mouth.
MARIA: Sweet Sir Toby, be patient for tonight: since the
MARIA: youth of the count's was today with thy lady, she is
MARIA: much out of quiet. For Monsieur Malvolio, let me
MARIA: alone with him: if I do not gull him into a
MARIA: nayword, and make him a common recreation, do not
MARIA: think I have wit enough to lie straight in my bed:
MARIA: I know I can do it.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Possess us, possess us, tell us something of him.
MARIA: Marry, sir, sometimes he is a kind of puritan.
SIR ANDREW: O, if I thought that I'ld beat him like a dog!
SIR TOBY BELCH: What, for being a puritan? thy exquisite reason,
SIR TOBY BELCH: dear knight?
SIR ANDREW: I have no exquisite reason for't, but I have reason
SIR ANDREW: good enough.
MARIA: The devil a puritan that he is, or any thing
MARIA: constantly, but a time-pleaser, an affectioned ass,
MARIA: that cons state without book and utters it by great
MARIA: swarths: the best persuaded of himself, so
MARIA: crammed, as he thinks, with excellencies, that it is
MARIA: his grounds of faith that all that look on him love
MARIA: him, and on that vice in him will my revenge find
MARIA: notable cause to work.
SIR TOBY BELCH: What wilt thou do?
MARIA: I will drop in his way some obscure epistles of
MARIA: love, wherein, by the colour of his beard, the shape
MARIA: of his leg, the manner of his gait, the expressure
MARIA: of his eye, forehead, and complexion, he shall find
MARIA: himself most feelingly personated. I can write very
MARIA: like my lady your niece: on a forgotten matter we
MARIA: can hardly make distinction of our hands.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Excellent! I smell a device.
SIR ANDREW: I have't in my nose too.
SIR TOBY BELCH: He shall think, by the letters that thou wilt drop,
SIR TOBY BELCH: that they come from my niece, and that she's in
SIR TOBY BELCH: love with him.
MARIA: My purpose is, indeed, a horse of that colour.
SIR ANDREW: And your horse now would make him an ass.
MARIA: Ass, I doubt not.
SIR ANDREW: O, 'twill be admirable!
MARIA: Sport royal, I warrant you: I know my physic will
MARIA: work with him. I will plant you two, and let the
MARIA: fool make a third, where he shall find the letter:
MARIA: observe his construction of it. For this night, to
MARIA: bed, and dream on the event. Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
SIR TOBY BELCH: Good night, Penthesilea.
SIR ANDREW: Before me, she's a good wench.
SIR TOBY BELCH: She's a beagle, true-bred, and one that adores me:
SIR TOBY BELCH: what o' that?
SIR ANDREW: I was adored once too.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Let's to bed, knight. Thou hadst need send for
SIR TOBY BELCH: more money.
SIR ANDREW: If I cannot recover your niece, I am a foul way out.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Send for money, knight: if thou hast her not i'
SIR TOBY BELCH: the end, call me cut.
SIR ANDREW: If I do not, never trust me, take it how you will.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come, come, I'll go burn some sack, 'tis too late
SIR TOBY BELCH: to go to bed now: come, knight, come, knight.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. DUKE ORSINO's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE ORSINO, VIOLA, CURIO, and others
DUKE ORSINO: Give me some music. Now, good morrow, friends.
DUKE ORSINO: Now, good Cesario, but that piece of song,
DUKE ORSINO: That old and antique song we heard last night:
DUKE ORSINO: Methought it did relieve my passion much,
DUKE ORSINO: More than light airs and recollected terms
DUKE ORSINO: Of these most brisk and giddy-paced times:
DUKE ORSINO: Come, but one verse.
CURIO: He is not here, so please your lordship that should sing it.
DUKE ORSINO: Who was it?
CURIO: Feste, the jester, my lord, a fool that the lady
CURIO: Olivia's father took much delight in. He is about the house.
DUKE ORSINO: Seek him out, and play the tune the while.
NARRATOR: Exit CURIO. Music plays
DUKE ORSINO: Come hither, boy: if ever thou shalt love,
DUKE ORSINO: In the sweet pangs of it remember me,
DUKE ORSINO: For such as I am all true lovers are,
DUKE ORSINO: Unstaid and skittish in all motions else,
DUKE ORSINO: Save in the constant image of the creature
DUKE ORSINO: That is beloved. How dost thou like this tune?
VIOLA: It gives a very echo to the seat
VIOLA: Where Love is throned.
DUKE ORSINO: Thou dost speak masterly:
DUKE ORSINO: My life upon't, young though thou art, thine eye
DUKE ORSINO: Hath stay'd upon some favour that it loves:
DUKE ORSINO: Hath it not, boy?
VIOLA: A little, by your favour.
DUKE ORSINO: What kind of woman is't?
VIOLA: Of your complexion.
DUKE ORSINO: She is not worth thee, then. What years, i' faith?
VIOLA: About your years, my lord.
DUKE ORSINO: Too old by heaven: let still the woman take
DUKE ORSINO: An elder than herself: so wears she to him,
DUKE ORSINO: So sways she level in her husband's heart:
DUKE ORSINO: For, boy, however we do praise ourselves,
DUKE ORSINO: Our fancies are more giddy and unfirm,
DUKE ORSINO: More longing, wavering, sooner lost and worn,
DUKE ORSINO: Than women's are.
VIOLA: I think it well, my lord.
DUKE ORSINO: Then let thy love be younger than thyself,
DUKE ORSINO: Or thy affection cannot hold the bent,
DUKE ORSINO: For women are as roses, whose fair flower
DUKE ORSINO: Being once display'd, doth fall that very hour.
VIOLA: And so they are: alas, that they are so,
VIOLA: To die, even when they to perfection grow!
NARRATOR: Re-enter CURIO and Clown
DUKE ORSINO: O, fellow, come, the song we had last night.
DUKE ORSINO: Mark it, Cesario, it is old and plain,
DUKE ORSINO: The spinsters and the knitters in the sun
DUKE ORSINO: And the free maids that weave their thread with bones
DUKE ORSINO: Do use to chant it: it is silly sooth,
DUKE ORSINO: And dallies with the innocence of love,
DUKE ORSINO: Like the old age.
Clown: Are you ready, sir?
DUKE ORSINO: Ay, prithee, sing.
NARRATOR: Music
DUKE ORSINO: SONG.
Clown: Come away, come away, death,
Clown: And in sad cypress let me be laid,
Clown: Fly away, fly away breath,
Clown: I am slain by a fair cruel maid.
Clown: My shroud of white, stuck all with yew,
Clown: O, prepare it!
Clown: My part of death, no one so true
Clown: Did share it.
Clown: Not a flower, not a flower sweet
Clown: On my black coffin let there be strown,
Clown: Not a friend, not a friend greet
Clown: My poor corpse, where my bones shall be thrown:
Clown: A thousand thousand sighs to save,
Clown: Lay me, O, where
Clown: Sad true lover never find my grave,
Clown: To weep there!
DUKE ORSINO: There's for thy pains.
Clown: No pains, sir: I take pleasure in singing, sir.
DUKE ORSINO: I'll pay thy pleasure then.
Clown: Truly, sir, and pleasure will be paid, one time or another.
DUKE ORSINO: Give me now leave to leave thee.
Clown: Now, the melancholy god protect thee, and the
Clown: tailor make thy doublet of changeable taffeta, for
Clown: thy mind is a very opal. I would have men of such
Clown: constancy put to sea, that their business might be
Clown: every thing and their intent every where, for that's
Clown: it that always makes a good voyage of nothing. Farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
DUKE ORSINO: Let all the rest give place.
NARRATOR: CURIO and Attendants retire
DUKE ORSINO: Once more, Cesario,
DUKE ORSINO: Get thee to yond same sovereign cruelty:
DUKE ORSINO: Tell her, my love, more noble than the world,
DUKE ORSINO: Prizes not quantity of dirty lands,
DUKE ORSINO: The parts that fortune hath bestow'd upon her,
DUKE ORSINO: Tell her, I hold as giddily as fortune,
DUKE ORSINO: But 'tis that miracle and queen of gems
DUKE ORSINO: That nature pranks her in attracts my soul.
VIOLA: But if she cannot love you, sir?
DUKE ORSINO: I cannot be so answer'd.
VIOLA: Sooth, but you must.
VIOLA: Say that some lady, as perhaps there is,
VIOLA: Hath for your love a great a pang of heart
VIOLA: As you have for Olivia: you cannot love her,
VIOLA: You tell her so, must she not then be answer'd?
DUKE ORSINO: There is no woman's sides
DUKE ORSINO: Can bide the beating of so strong a passion
DUKE ORSINO: As love doth give my heart, no woman's heart
DUKE ORSINO: So big, to hold so much, they lack retention
DUKE ORSINO: Alas, their love may be call'd appetite,
DUKE ORSINO: No motion of the liver, but the palate,
DUKE ORSINO: That suffer surfeit, cloyment and revolt,
DUKE ORSINO: But mine is all as hungry as the sea,
DUKE ORSINO: And can digest as much: make no compare
DUKE ORSINO: Between that love a woman can bear me
DUKE ORSINO: And that I owe Olivia.
VIOLA: Ay, but I know--
DUKE ORSINO: What dost thou know?
VIOLA: Too well what love women to men may owe:
VIOLA: In faith, they are as true of heart as we.
VIOLA: My father had a daughter loved a man,
VIOLA: As it might be, perhaps, were I a woman,
VIOLA: I should your lordship.
DUKE ORSINO: And what's her history?
VIOLA: A blank, my lord. She never told her love,
VIOLA: But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud,
VIOLA: Feed on her damask cheek: she pined in thought,
VIOLA: And with a green and yellow melancholy
VIOLA: She sat like patience on a monument,
VIOLA: Smiling at grief. Was not this love indeed?
VIOLA: We men may say more, swear more: but indeed
VIOLA: Our shows are more than will, for still we prove
VIOLA: Much in our vows, but little in our love.
DUKE ORSINO: But died thy sister of her love, my boy?
VIOLA: I am all the daughters of my father's house,
VIOLA: And all the brothers too: and yet I know not.
VIOLA: Sir, shall I to this lady?
DUKE ORSINO: Ay, that's the theme.
DUKE ORSINO: To her in haste, give her this jewel, say,
DUKE ORSINO: My love can give no place, bide no denay.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. OLIVIA's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH, SIR ANDREW, and FABIAN
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come thy ways, Signior Fabian.
FABIAN: Nay, I'll come: if I lose a scruple of this sport,
FABIAN: let me be boiled to death with melancholy.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Wouldst thou not be glad to have the niggardly
SIR TOBY BELCH: rascally sheep-biter come by some notable shame?
FABIAN: I would exult, man: you know, he brought me out o'
FABIAN: favour with my lady about a bear-baiting here.
SIR TOBY BELCH: To anger him we'll have the bear again, and we will
SIR TOBY BELCH: fool him black and blue: shall we not, Sir Andrew?
SIR ANDREW: An we do not, it is pity of our lives.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Here comes the little villain.
NARRATOR: Enter MARIA
SIR TOBY BELCH: How now, my metal of India!
MARIA: Get ye all three into the box-tree: Malvolio's
MARIA: coming down this walk: he has been yonder i' the
MARIA: sun practising behavior to his own shadow this half
MARIA: hour: observe him, for the love of mockery, for I
MARIA: know this letter will make a contemplative idiot of
MARIA: him. Close, in the name of jesting! Lie thou there,
NARRATOR: Throws down a letter
MARIA: for here comes the trout that must be caught with tickling.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Enter MALVOLIO
MALVOLIO: 'Tis but fortune, all is fortune. Maria once told
MALVOLIO: me she did affect me: and I have heard herself come
MALVOLIO: thus near, that, should she fancy, it should be one
MALVOLIO: of my complexion. Besides, she uses me with a more
MALVOLIO: exalted respect than any one else that follows her.
MALVOLIO: What should I think on't?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Here's an overweening rogue!
FABIAN: O, peace! Contemplation makes a rare turkey-cock
FABIAN: of him: how he jets under his advanced plumes!
SIR ANDREW: 'Slight, I could so beat the rogue!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Peace, I say.
MALVOLIO: To be Count Malvolio!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Ah, rogue!
SIR ANDREW: Pistol him, pistol him.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Peace, peace!
MALVOLIO: There is example for't, the lady of the Strachy
MALVOLIO: married the yeoman of the wardrobe.
SIR ANDREW: Fie on him, Jezebel!
FABIAN: O, peace! now he's deeply in: look how
FABIAN: imagination blows him.
MALVOLIO: Having been three months married to her, sitting in
MALVOLIO: my state,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: O, for a stone-bow, to hit him in the eye!
MALVOLIO: Calling my officers about me, in my branched velvet
MALVOLIO: gown, having come from a day-bed, where I have left
MALVOLIO: Olivia sleeping,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: Fire and brimstone!
FABIAN: O, peace, peace!
MALVOLIO: And then to have the humour of state, and after a
MALVOLIO: demure travel of regard, telling them I know my
MALVOLIO: place as I would they should do theirs, to for my
MALVOLIO: kinsman Toby,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: Bolts and shackles!
FABIAN: O peace, peace, peace! now, now.
MALVOLIO: Seven of my people, with an obedient start, make
MALVOLIO: out for him: I frown the while, and perchance wind
MALVOLIO: up watch, or play with my--some rich jewel. Toby
MALVOLIO: approaches, courtesies there to me,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: Shall this fellow live?
FABIAN: Though our silence be drawn from us with cars, yet peace.
MALVOLIO: I extend my hand to him thus, quenching my familiar
MALVOLIO: smile with an austere regard of control,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: And does not Toby take you a blow o' the lips then?
MALVOLIO: Saying, 'Cousin Toby, my fortunes having cast me on
MALVOLIO: your niece give me this prerogative of speech,'--
SIR TOBY BELCH: What, what?
MALVOLIO: 'You must amend your drunkenness.'
SIR TOBY BELCH: Out, scab!
FABIAN: Nay, patience, or we break the sinews of our plot.
MALVOLIO: 'Besides, you waste the treasure of your time with
MALVOLIO: a foolish knight,'--
SIR ANDREW: That's me, I warrant you.
MALVOLIO: 'One Sir Andrew,'--
SIR ANDREW: I knew 'twas I, for many do call me fool.
MALVOLIO: What employment have we here?
NARRATOR: Taking up the letter
FABIAN: Now is the woodcock near the gin.
SIR TOBY BELCH: O, peace! and the spirit of humour intimate reading
SIR TOBY BELCH: aloud to him!
MALVOLIO: By my life, this is my lady's hand these be her
MALVOLIO: very C's, her U's and her T's and thus makes she her
MALVOLIO: great P's. It is, in contempt of question, her hand.
SIR ANDREW: Her C's, her U's and her T's: why that?
