MALVOLIO: [Reads]  'To the unknown beloved, this, and my good
MALVOLIO: wishes:'--her very phrases! By your leave, wax.
MALVOLIO: Soft! and the impressure her Lucrece, with which she
MALVOLIO: uses to seal: 'tis my lady. To whom should this be?
FABIAN: This wins him, liver and all.
MALVOLIO: [Reads]
MALVOLIO: Jove knows I love: But who?
MALVOLIO: Lips, do not move,
MALVOLIO: No man must know.
MALVOLIO: 'No man must know.' What follows? the numbers
MALVOLIO: altered! 'No man must know:' if this should be
MALVOLIO: thee, Malvolio?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Marry, hang thee, brock!
MALVOLIO: [Reads]
MALVOLIO: I may command where I adore,
MALVOLIO: But silence, like a Lucrece knife,
MALVOLIO: With bloodless stroke my heart doth gore:
MALVOLIO: M, O, A, I, doth sway my life.
FABIAN: A fustian riddle!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Excellent wench, say I.
MALVOLIO: 'M, O, A, I, doth sway my life.' Nay, but first, let
MALVOLIO: me see, let me see, let me see.
FABIAN: What dish o' poison has she dressed him!
SIR TOBY BELCH: And with what wing the staniel cheques at it!
MALVOLIO: 'I may command where I adore.' Why, she may command
MALVOLIO: me: I serve her, she is my lady. Why, this is
MALVOLIO: evident to any formal capacity, there is no
MALVOLIO: obstruction in this: and the end,--what should
MALVOLIO: that alphabetical position portend? If I could make
MALVOLIO: that resemble something in me,--Softly! M, O, A,
MALVOLIO: I,--
SIR TOBY BELCH: O, ay, make up that: he is now at a cold scent.
FABIAN: Sowter will cry upon't for all this, though it be as
FABIAN: rank as a fox.
MALVOLIO: M,--Malvolio, M,--why, that begins my name.
FABIAN: Did not I say he would work it out? the cur is
FABIAN: excellent at faults.
MALVOLIO: M,--but then there is no consonancy in the sequel,
MALVOLIO: that suffers under probation A should follow but O does.
FABIAN: And O shall end, I hope.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Ay, or I'll cudgel him, and make him cry O!
MALVOLIO: And then I comes behind.
FABIAN: Ay, an you had any eye behind you, you might see
FABIAN: more detraction at your heels than fortunes before
FABIAN: you.
MALVOLIO: M, O, A, I, this simulation is not as the former: and
MALVOLIO: yet, to crush this a little, it would bow to me, for
MALVOLIO: every one of these letters are in my name. Soft!
MALVOLIO: here follows prose.
NARRATOR: Reads
MALVOLIO: 'If this fall into thy hand, revolve. In my stars I
MALVOLIO: am above thee, but be not afraid of greatness: some
MALVOLIO: are born great, some achieve greatness, and some
MALVOLIO: have greatness thrust upon 'em. Thy Fates open
MALVOLIO: their hands, let thy blood and spirit embrace them,
MALVOLIO: and, to inure thyself to what thou art like to be,
MALVOLIO: cast thy humble slough and appear fresh. Be
MALVOLIO: opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants, let
MALVOLIO: thy tongue tang arguments of state, put thyself into
MALVOLIO: the trick of singularity: she thus advises thee
MALVOLIO: that sighs for thee. Remember who commended thy
MALVOLIO: yellow stockings, and wished to see thee ever
MALVOLIO: cross-gartered: I say, remember. Go to, thou art
MALVOLIO: made, if thou desirest to be so, if not, let me see
MALVOLIO: thee a steward still, the fellow of servants, and
MALVOLIO: not worthy to touch Fortune's fingers. Farewell.
MALVOLIO: She that would alter services with thee,
MALVOLIO: THE FORTUNATE-UNHAPPY.'
MALVOLIO: Daylight and champaign discovers not more: this is
MALVOLIO: open. I will be proud, I will read politic authors,
MALVOLIO: I will baffle Sir Toby, I will wash off gross
MALVOLIO: acquaintance, I will be point-devise the very man.
MALVOLIO: I do not now fool myself, to let imagination jade
MALVOLIO: me, for every reason excites to this, that my lady
MALVOLIO: loves me. She did commend my yellow stockings of
MALVOLIO: late, she did praise my leg being cross-gartered,
MALVOLIO: and in this she manifests herself to my love, and
MALVOLIO: with a kind of injunction drives me to these habits
MALVOLIO: of her liking. I thank my stars I am happy. I will
MALVOLIO: be strange, stout, in yellow stockings, and
MALVOLIO: cross-gartered, even with the swiftness of putting
MALVOLIO: on. Jove and my stars be praised! Here is yet a
MALVOLIO: postscript.
NARRATOR: Reads
MALVOLIO: 'Thou canst not choose but know who I am. If thou
MALVOLIO: entertainest my love, let it appear in thy smiling,
MALVOLIO: thy smiles become thee well, therefore in my
MALVOLIO: presence still smile, dear my sweet, I prithee.'
MALVOLIO: Jove, I thank thee: I will smile, I will do
MALVOLIO: everything that thou wilt have me.
NARRATOR: Exit
FABIAN: I will not give my part of this sport for a pension
FABIAN: of thousands to be paid from the Sophy.
SIR TOBY BELCH: I could marry this wench for this device.
SIR ANDREW: So could I too.
SIR TOBY BELCH: And ask no other dowry with her but such another jest.
SIR ANDREW: Nor I neither.
FABIAN: Here comes my noble gull-catcher.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARIA
SIR TOBY BELCH: Wilt thou set thy foot o' my neck?
SIR ANDREW: Or o' mine either?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Shall I play my freedom at traytrip, and become thy
SIR TOBY BELCH: bond-slave?
SIR ANDREW: I' faith, or I either?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Why, thou hast put him in such a dream, that when
SIR TOBY BELCH: the image of it leaves him he must run mad.
MARIA: Nay, but say true, does it work upon him?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Like aqua-vitae with a midwife.
MARIA: If you will then see the fruits of the sport, mark
MARIA: his first approach before my lady: he will come to
MARIA: her in yellow stockings, and 'tis a colour she
MARIA: abhors, and cross-gartered, a fashion she detests,
MARIA: and he will smile upon her, which will now be so
MARIA: unsuitable to her disposition, being addicted to a
MARIA: melancholy as she is, that it cannot but turn him
MARIA: into a notable contempt. If you will see it, follow
MARIA: me.
SIR TOBY BELCH: To the gates of Tartar, thou most excellent devil of wit!
SIR ANDREW: I'll make one too.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT III
NARRATOR: SCENE I. OLIVIA's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter VIOLA, and Clown with a tabour
VIOLA: Save thee, friend, and thy music: dost thou live by
VIOLA: thy tabour?
Clown: No, sir, I live by the church.
VIOLA: Art thou a churchman?
Clown: No such matter, sir: I do live by the church, for
Clown: I do live at my house, and my house doth stand by
Clown: the church.
VIOLA: So thou mayst say, the king lies by a beggar, if a
VIOLA: beggar dwell near him, or, the church stands by thy
VIOLA: tabour, if thy tabour stand by the church.
Clown: You have said, sir. To see this age! A sentence is
Clown: but a cheveril glove to a good wit: how quickly the
Clown: wrong side may be turned outward!
VIOLA: Nay, that's certain, they that dally nicely with
VIOLA: words may quickly make them wanton.
Clown: I would, therefore, my sister had had no name, sir.
VIOLA: Why, man?
Clown: Why, sir, her name's a word, and to dally with that
Clown: word might make my sister wanton. But indeed words
Clown: are very rascals since bonds disgraced them.
VIOLA: Thy reason, man?
Clown: Troth, sir, I can yield you none without words, and
Clown: words are grown so false, I am loath to prove
Clown: reason with them.
VIOLA: I warrant thou art a merry fellow and carest for nothing.
Clown: Not so, sir, I do care for something, but in my
Clown: conscience, sir, I do not care for you: if that be
Clown: to care for nothing, sir, I would it would make you invisible.
VIOLA: Art not thou the Lady Olivia's fool?
Clown: No, indeed, sir, the Lady Olivia has no folly: she
Clown: will keep no fool, sir, till she be married, and
Clown: fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to
Clown: herrings, the husband's the bigger: I am indeed not
Clown: her fool, but her corrupter of words.
VIOLA: I saw thee late at the Count Orsino's.
Clown: Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun,
Clown: it shines every where. I would be sorry, sir, but
Clown: the fool should be as oft with your master as with
Clown: my mistress: I think I saw your wisdom there.
VIOLA: Nay, an thou pass upon me, I'll no more with thee.
VIOLA: Hold, there's expenses for thee.
Clown: Now Jove, in his next commodity of hair, send thee a beard!
VIOLA: By my troth, I'll tell thee, I am almost sick for
VIOLA: one,
NARRATOR: Aside
VIOLA: though I would not have it grow on my chin. Is thy
VIOLA: lady within?
Clown: Would not a pair of these have bred, sir?
VIOLA: Yes, being kept together and put to use.
Clown: I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia, sir, to bring
Clown: a Cressida to this Troilus.
VIOLA: I understand you, sir, 'tis well begged.
Clown: The matter, I hope, is not great, sir, begging but
Clown: a beggar: Cressida was a beggar. My lady is
Clown: within, sir. I will construe to them whence you
Clown: come, who you are and what you would are out of my
Clown: welkin, I might say 'element,' but the word is over-worn.
NARRATOR: Exit
VIOLA: This fellow is wise enough to play the fool,
VIOLA: And to do that well craves a kind of wit:
VIOLA: He must observe their mood on whom he jests,
VIOLA: The quality of persons, and the time,
VIOLA: And, like the haggard, cheque at every feather
VIOLA: That comes before his eye. This is a practise
VIOLA: As full of labour as a wise man's art
VIOLA: For folly that he wisely shows is fit,
VIOLA: But wise men, folly-fall'n, quite taint their wit.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH, and SIR ANDREW
SIR TOBY BELCH: Save you, gentleman.
VIOLA: And you, sir.
SIR ANDREW: Dieu vous garde, monsieur.
VIOLA: Et vous aussi, votre serviteur.
SIR ANDREW: I hope, sir, you are, and I am yours.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Will you encounter the house? my niece is desirous
SIR TOBY BELCH: you should enter, if your trade be to her.
VIOLA: I am bound to your niece, sir, I mean, she is the
VIOLA: list of my voyage.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Taste your legs, sir, put them to motion.
VIOLA: My legs do better understand me, sir, than I
VIOLA: understand what you mean by bidding me taste my legs.
SIR TOBY BELCH: I mean, to go, sir, to enter.
VIOLA: I will answer you with gait and entrance. But we
VIOLA: are prevented.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA and MARIA
VIOLA: Most excellent accomplished lady, the heavens rain
VIOLA: odours on you!
SIR ANDREW: That youth's a rare courtier: 'Rain odours,' well.
VIOLA: My matter hath no voice, to your own most pregnant
VIOLA: and vouchsafed ear.
SIR ANDREW: 'Odours,' 'pregnant' and 'vouchsafed:' I'll get 'em
SIR ANDREW: all three all ready.
OLIVIA: Let the garden door be shut, and leave me to my hearing.
NARRATOR: Exeunt SIR TOBY BELCH, SIR ANDREW, and MARIA
OLIVIA: Give me your hand, sir.
VIOLA: My duty, madam, and most humble service.
OLIVIA: What is your name?
VIOLA: Cesario is your servant's name, fair princess.
OLIVIA: My servant, sir! 'Twas never merry world
OLIVIA: Since lowly feigning was call'd compliment:
OLIVIA: You're servant to the Count Orsino, youth.
VIOLA: And he is yours, and his must needs be yours:
VIOLA: Your servant's servant is your servant, madam.
OLIVIA: For him, I think not on him: for his thoughts,
OLIVIA: Would they were blanks, rather than fill'd with me!
VIOLA: Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts
VIOLA: On his behalf.
OLIVIA: O, by your leave, I pray you,
OLIVIA: I bade you never speak again of him:
OLIVIA: But, would you undertake another suit,
OLIVIA: I had rather hear you to solicit that
OLIVIA: Than music from the spheres.
VIOLA: Dear lady,--
OLIVIA: Give me leave, beseech you. I did send,
OLIVIA: After the last enchantment you did here,
OLIVIA: A ring in chase of you: so did I abuse
OLIVIA: Myself, my servant and, I fear me, you:
OLIVIA: Under your hard construction must I sit,
OLIVIA: To force that on you, in a shameful cunning,
OLIVIA: Which you knew none of yours: what might you think?
OLIVIA: Have you not set mine honour at the stake
OLIVIA: And baited it with all the unmuzzled thoughts
OLIVIA: That tyrannous heart can think? To one of your receiving
OLIVIA: Enough is shown: a cypress, not a bosom,
OLIVIA: Hideth my heart. So, let me hear you speak.
VIOLA: I pity you.
OLIVIA: That's a degree to love.
VIOLA: No, not a grize, for 'tis a vulgar proof,
VIOLA: That very oft we pity enemies.
OLIVIA: Why, then, methinks 'tis time to smile again.
OLIVIA: O, world, how apt the poor are to be proud!
OLIVIA: If one should be a prey, how much the better
OLIVIA: To fall before the lion than the wolf!
NARRATOR: Clock strikes
OLIVIA: The clock upbraids me with the waste of time.
OLIVIA: Be not afraid, good youth, I will not have you:
OLIVIA: And yet, when wit and youth is come to harvest,
OLIVIA: Your were is alike to reap a proper man:
OLIVIA: There lies your way, due west.
VIOLA: Then westward-ho! Grace and good disposition
VIOLA: Attend your ladyship!
VIOLA: You'll nothing, madam, to my lord by me?
OLIVIA: Stay:
OLIVIA: I prithee, tell me what thou thinkest of me.
VIOLA: That you do think you are not what you are.
OLIVIA: If I think so, I think the same of you.
VIOLA: Then think you right: I am not what I am.
OLIVIA: I would you were as I would have you be!
VIOLA: Would it be better, madam, than I am?
VIOLA: I wish it might, for now I am your fool.
OLIVIA: O, what a deal of scorn looks beautiful
OLIVIA: In the contempt and anger of his lip!
OLIVIA: A murderous guilt shows not itself more soon
OLIVIA: Than love that would seem hid: love's night is noon.
OLIVIA: Cesario, by the roses of the spring,
OLIVIA: By maidhood, honour, truth and every thing,
OLIVIA: I love thee so, that, maugre all thy pride,
OLIVIA: Nor wit nor reason can my passion hide.
OLIVIA: Do not extort thy reasons from this clause,
OLIVIA: For that I woo, thou therefore hast no cause,
OLIVIA: But rather reason thus with reason fetter,
OLIVIA: Love sought is good, but given unsought better.
VIOLA: By innocence I swear, and by my youth
VIOLA: I have one heart, one bosom and one truth,
VIOLA: And that no woman has, nor never none
VIOLA: Shall mistress be of it, save I alone.
VIOLA: And so adieu, good madam: never more
VIOLA: Will I my master's tears to you deplore.
OLIVIA: Yet come again, for thou perhaps mayst move
OLIVIA: That heart, which now abhors, to like his love.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. OLIVIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH, SIR ANDREW, and FABIAN
SIR ANDREW: No, faith, I'll not stay a jot longer.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Thy reason, dear venom, give thy reason.
FABIAN: You must needs yield your reason, Sir Andrew.
SIR ANDREW: Marry, I saw your niece do more favours to the
SIR ANDREW: count's serving-man than ever she bestowed upon me,
SIR ANDREW: I saw't i' the orchard.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Did she see thee the while, old boy? tell me that.
SIR ANDREW: As plain as I see you now.
FABIAN: This was a great argument of love in her toward you.
SIR ANDREW: 'Slight, will you make an ass o' me?
FABIAN: I will prove it legitimate, sir, upon the oaths of
FABIAN: judgment and reason.
SIR TOBY BELCH: And they have been grand-jury-men since before Noah
SIR TOBY BELCH: was a sailor.
FABIAN: She did show favour to the youth in your sight only
FABIAN: to exasperate you, to awake your dormouse valour, to
FABIAN: put fire in your heart and brimstone in your liver.
FABIAN: You should then have accosted her, and with some
FABIAN: excellent jests, fire-new from the mint, you should
FABIAN: have banged the youth into dumbness. This was
FABIAN: looked for at your hand, and this was balked: the
FABIAN: double gilt of this opportunity you let time wash
FABIAN: off, and you are now sailed into the north of my
FABIAN: lady's opinion, where you will hang like an icicle

SIR ANDREW: An't be any way, it must be with valour, for policy
SIR ANDREW: I hate: I had as lief be a Brownist as a
SIR ANDREW: politician.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Why, then, build me thy fortunes upon the basis of
SIR TOBY BELCH: valour. Challenge me the count's youth to fight
SIR TOBY BELCH: with him, hurt him in eleven places: my niece shall
SIR TOBY BELCH: take note of it, and assure thyself, there is no
SIR TOBY BELCH: love-broker in the world can more prevail in man's

SIR ANDREW: Will either of you bear me a challenge to him?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Go, write it in a martial hand, be curst and brief,
SIR TOBY BELCH: it is no matter how witty, so it be eloquent and fun
SIR TOBY BELCH: of invention: taunt him with the licence of ink:
SIR TOBY BELCH: if thou thou'st him some thrice, it shall not be
SIR TOBY BELCH: amiss, and as many lies as will lie in thy sheet of
SIR TOBY BELCH: paper, although the sheet were big enough for the
SIR TOBY BELCH: bed of Ware in England, set 'em down: go, about it.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Let there be gall enough in thy ink, though thou
SIR TOBY BELCH: write with a goose-pen, no matter: about it.
SIR ANDREW: Where shall I find you?
SIR TOBY BELCH: We'll call thee at the cubiculo: go.
NARRATOR: Exit SIR ANDREW

SIR TOBY BELCH: I have been dear to him, lad, some two thousand
SIR TOBY BELCH: strong, or so.
FABIAN: We shall have a rare letter from him: but you'll
FABIAN: not deliver't?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Never trust me, then, and by all means stir on the
SIR TOBY BELCH: youth to an answer. I think oxen and wainropes
SIR TOBY BELCH: cannot hale them together. For Andrew, if he were

SIR TOBY BELCH: will clog the foot of a flea, I'll eat the rest of
SIR TOBY BELCH: the anatomy.
FABIAN: And his opposite, the youth, bears in his visage no
FABIAN: great presage of cruelty.
NARRATOR: Enter MARIA
SIR TOBY BELCH: Look, where the youngest wren of nine comes.
MARIA: If you desire the spleen, and will laugh yourself
MARIA: into stitches, follow me. Yond gull Malvolio is
MARIA: turned heathen, a very renegado, for there is no
MARIA: Christian, that means to be saved by believing
MARIA: rightly, can ever believe such impossible passages
MARIA: of grossness. He's in yellow stockings.
SIR TOBY BELCH: And cross-gartered?
MARIA: Most villanously, like a pedant that keeps a school
MARIA: i' the church. I have dogged him, like his
MARIA: murderer. He does obey every point of the letter
MARIA: that I dropped to betray him: he does smile his
MARIA: face into more lines than is in the new map with the
MARIA: augmentation of the Indies: you have not seen such

MARIA: at him. I know my lady will strike him: if she do,

NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. A street.
NARRATOR: Enter SEBASTIAN and ANTONIO
SEBASTIAN: I would not by my will have troubled you,
SEBASTIAN: But, since you make your pleasure of your pains,
SEBASTIAN: I will no further chide you.
ANTONIO: I could not stay behind you: my desire,
ANTONIO: More sharp than filed steel, did spur me forth,
ANTONIO: And not all love to see you, though so much
ANTONIO: As might have drawn one to a longer voyage,
ANTONIO: But jealousy what might befall your travel,
ANTONIO: Being skilless in these parts, which to a stranger,
ANTONIO: Unguided and unfriended, often prove
ANTONIO: Rough and unhospitable: my willing love,
ANTONIO: The rather by these arguments of fear,
ANTONIO: Set forth in your pursuit.
SEBASTIAN: My kind Antonio,
SEBASTIAN: I can no other answer make but thanks,
SEBASTIAN: And thanks, and ever [         ] oft good turns
SEBASTIAN: Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay:
SEBASTIAN: But, were my worth as is my conscience firm,
SEBASTIAN: You should find better dealing. What's to do?
SEBASTIAN: Shall we go see the reliques of this town?
ANTONIO: To-morrow, sir: best first go see your lodging.
SEBASTIAN: I am not weary, and 'tis long to night:
SEBASTIAN: I pray you, let us satisfy our eyes
SEBASTIAN: With the memorials and the things of fame
SEBASTIAN: That do renown this city.
ANTONIO: Would you'ld pardon me,
ANTONIO: I do not without danger walk these streets:
ANTONIO: Once, in a sea-fight, 'gainst the count his galleys
ANTONIO: I did some service, of such note indeed,
ANTONIO: That were I ta'en here it would scarce be answer'd.
SEBASTIAN: Belike you slew great number of his people.
ANTONIO: The offence is not of such a bloody nature,
ANTONIO: Albeit the quality of the time and quarrel
ANTONIO: Might well have given us bloody argument.
ANTONIO: It might have since been answer'd in repaying
ANTONIO: What we took from them, which, for traffic's sake,
ANTONIO: Most of our city did: only myself stood out,
ANTONIO: For which, if I be lapsed in this place,
ANTONIO: I shall pay dear.
SEBASTIAN: Do not then walk too open.
ANTONIO: It doth not fit me. Hold, sir, here's my purse.
ANTONIO: In the south suburbs, at the Elephant,
ANTONIO: Is best to lodge: I will bespeak our diet,
ANTONIO: Whiles you beguile the time and feed your knowledge
ANTONIO: With viewing of the town: there shall you have me.
SEBASTIAN: Why I your purse?
ANTONIO: Haply your eye shall light upon some toy
ANTONIO: You have desire to purchase, and your store,
ANTONIO: I think, is not for idle markets, sir.
SEBASTIAN: I'll be your purse-bearer and leave you
SEBASTIAN: For an hour.
ANTONIO: To the Elephant.
SEBASTIAN: I do remember.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. OLIVIA's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA and MARIA
OLIVIA: I have sent after him: he says he'll come,
OLIVIA: How shall I feast him? what bestow of him?
OLIVIA: For youth is bought more oft than begg'd or borrow'd.
OLIVIA: I speak too loud.
OLIVIA: Where is Malvolio? he is sad and civil,
OLIVIA: And suits well for a servant with my fortunes:
OLIVIA: Where is Malvolio?
MARIA: He's coming, madam, but in very strange manner. He
MARIA: is, sure, possessed, madam.

MARIA: No. madam, he does nothing but smile: your
MARIA: ladyship were best to have some guard about you, if
MARIA: he come, for, sure, the man is tainted in's wits.

NARRATOR: Exit MARIA
OLIVIA: I am as mad as he,
OLIVIA: If sad and merry madness equal be.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MARIA, with MALVOLIO
OLIVIA: How now, Malvolio!
MALVOLIO: Sweet lady, ho, ho.
OLIVIA: Smilest thou?
OLIVIA: I sent for thee upon a sad occasion.
MALVOLIO: Sad, lady! I could be sad: this does make some
MALVOLIO: obstruction in the blood, this cross-gartering, but
MALVOLIO: what of that? if it please the eye of one, it is
MALVOLIO: with me as the very true sonnet is, 'Please one, and
MALVOLIO: please all.'
OLIVIA: Why, how dost thou, man? what is the matter with thee?

MALVOLIO: did come to his hands, and commands shall be
MALVOLIO: executed: I think we do know the sweet Roman hand.

MALVOLIO: To bed! ay, sweet-heart, and I'll come to thee.

OLIVIA: thy hand so oft?
MARIA: How do you, Malvolio?
MALVOLIO: At your request! yes, nightingales answer daws.

OLIVIA: What meanest thou by that, Malvolio?
MALVOLIO: 'Some are born great,'--
OLIVIA: Ha!
MALVOLIO: 'Some achieve greatness,'--
OLIVIA: What sayest thou?
MALVOLIO: 'And some have greatness thrust upon them.'
OLIVIA: Heaven restore thee!
MALVOLIO: 'Remember who commended thy yellow stocking s,'--
OLIVIA: Thy yellow stockings!
MALVOLIO: 'And wished to see thee cross-gartered.'
OLIVIA: Cross-gartered!
MALVOLIO: 'Go to thou art made, if thou desirest to be so,'--
OLIVIA: Am I made?
MALVOLIO: 'If not, let me see thee a servant still.'
OLIVIA: Why, this is very midsummer madness.

NARRATOR: Exit Servant

NARRATOR: Exeunt OLIVIA and MARIA

MALVOLIO: the letter: she sends him on purpose, that I may
MALVOLIO: appear stubborn to him, for she incites me to that

MALVOLIO: 'be opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants,
MALVOLIO: let thy tongue tang with arguments of state, put
MALVOLIO: thyself into the trick of singularity,' and
MALVOLIO: consequently sets down the manner how, as, a sad
MALVOLIO: face, a reverend carriage, a slow tongue, in the
MALVOLIO: habit of some sir of note, and so forth. I have
MALVOLIO: limed her, but it is Jove's doing, and Jove make me
MALVOLIO: thankful! And when she went away now, 'Let this
MALVOLIO: fellow be looked to:' fellow! not Malvolio, nor
MALVOLIO: after my degree, but fellow. Why, every thing
MALVOLIO: adheres together, that no dram of a scruple, no
MALVOLIO: scruple of a scruple, no obstacle, no incredulous

MALVOLIO: that can be can come between me and the full
MALVOLIO: prospect of my hopes. Well, Jove, not I, is the
MALVOLIO: doer of this, and he is to be thanked.

SIR TOBY BELCH: will, for his honour's sake, have one bout with you,
SIR TOBY BELCH: he cannot by the duello avoid it: but he has
SIR TOBY BELCH: promised me, as he is a gentleman and a soldier, he
SIR TOBY BELCH: will not hurt you. Come on, to't.
SIR ANDREW: Pray God, he keep his oath!
VIOLA: I do assure you, 'tis against my will.
NARRATOR: They draw
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO
ANTONIO: Put up your sword. If this young gentleman
ANTONIO: Have done offence, I take the fault on me:
ANTONIO: If you offend him, I for him defy you.
SIR TOBY BELCH: You, sir! why, what are you?
ANTONIO: One, sir, that for his love dares yet do more
ANTONIO: Than you have heard him brag to you he will.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Nay, if you be an undertaker, I am for you.
NARRATOR: They draw
NARRATOR: Enter Officers
FABIAN: O good Sir Toby, hold! here come the officers.
SIR TOBY BELCH: I'll be with you anon.
VIOLA: Pray, sir, put your sword up, if you please.
SIR ANDREW: Marry, will I, sir, and, for that I promised you,
SIR ANDREW: I'll be as good as my word: he will bear you easily
SIR ANDREW: and reins well.
First Officer: This is the man, do thy office.
Second Officer: Antonio, I arrest thee at the suit of Count Orsino.
ANTONIO: You do mistake me, sir.
First Officer: No, sir, no jot, I know your favour well,
First Officer: Though now you have no sea-cap on your head.
First Officer: Take him away: he knows I know him well.
ANTONIO: I must obey.
NARRATOR: To VIOLA
ANTONIO: This comes with seeking you:
ANTONIO: But there's no remedy, I shall answer it.
ANTONIO: What will you do, now my necessity
ANTONIO: Makes me to ask you for my purse? It grieves me
ANTONIO: Much more for what I cannot do for you
ANTONIO: Than what befalls myself. You stand amazed,
ANTONIO: But be of comfort.
Second Officer: Come, sir, away.
ANTONIO: I must entreat of you some of that money.
VIOLA: What money, sir?
VIOLA: For the fair kindness you have show'd me here,
VIOLA: And, part, being prompted by your present trouble,
VIOLA: Out of my lean and low ability
VIOLA: I'll lend you something: my having is not much,
VIOLA: I'll make division of my present with you:
VIOLA: Hold, there's half my coffer.
ANTONIO: Will you deny me now?
ANTONIO: Is't possible that my deserts to you
ANTONIO: Can lack persuasion? Do not tempt my misery,
ANTONIO: Lest that it make me so unsound a man
ANTONIO: As to upbraid you with those kindnesses
ANTONIO: That I have done for you.
VIOLA: I know of none,
VIOLA: Nor know I you by voice or any feature:
VIOLA: I hate ingratitude more in a man
VIOLA: Than lying, vainness, babbling, drunkenness,
VIOLA: Or any taint of vice whose strong corruption
VIOLA: Inhabits our frail blood.
ANTONIO: O heavens themselves!
Second Officer: Come, sir, I pray you, go.
ANTONIO: Let me speak a little. This youth that you see here
ANTONIO: I snatch'd one half out of the jaws of death,
ANTONIO: Relieved him with such sanctity of love,
ANTONIO: And to his image, which methought did promise
ANTONIO: Most venerable worth, did I devotion.
First Officer: What's that to us? The time goes by: away!
ANTONIO: But O how vile an idol proves this god
ANTONIO: Thou hast, Sebastian, done good feature shame.
ANTONIO: In nature there's no blemish but the mind,
ANTONIO: None can be call'd deform'd but the unkind:
ANTONIO: Virtue is beauty, but the beauteous evil
ANTONIO: Are empty trunks o'erflourish'd by the devil.
First Officer: The man grows mad: away with him! Come, come, sir.
ANTONIO: Lead me on.
NARRATOR: Exit with Officers
VIOLA: Methinks his words do from such passion fly,
VIOLA: That he believes himself: so do not I.
VIOLA: Prove true, imagination, O, prove true,
VIOLA: That I, dear brother, be now ta'en for you!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come hither, knight, come hither, Fabian: we'll
SIR TOBY BELCH: whisper o'er a couplet or two of most sage saws.
VIOLA: He named Sebastian: I my brother know
VIOLA: Yet living in my glass, even such and so
VIOLA: In favour was my brother, and he went
VIOLA: Still in this fashion, colour, ornament,
VIOLA: For him I imitate: O, if it prove,
VIOLA: Tempests are kind and salt waves fresh in love.
NARRATOR: Exit
SIR TOBY BELCH: A very dishonest paltry boy, and more a coward than
SIR TOBY BELCH: a hare: his dishonesty appears in leaving his
SIR TOBY BELCH: friend here in necessity and denying him, and for
SIR TOBY BELCH: his cowardship, ask Fabian.
FABIAN: A coward, a most devout coward, religious in it.
SIR ANDREW: 'Slid, I'll after him again and beat him.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Do, cuff him soundly, but never draw thy sword.
SIR ANDREW: An I do not,--
FABIAN: Come, let's see the event.
SIR TOBY BELCH: I dare lay any money 'twill be nothing yet.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before OLIVIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter SEBASTIAN and Clown
Clown: Will you make me believe that I am not sent for you?
SEBASTIAN: Go to, go to, thou art a foolish fellow:
SEBASTIAN: Let me be clear of thee.
Clown: Well held out, i' faith! No, I do not know you, nor
Clown: I am not sent to you by my lady, to bid you come
Clown: speak with her, nor your name is not Master Cesario,
Clown: nor this is not my nose neither. Nothing that is so is so.
SEBASTIAN: I prithee, vent thy folly somewhere else: Thou
SEBASTIAN: know'st not me.
Clown: Vent my folly! he has heard that word of some
Clown: great man and now applies it to a fool. Vent my
Clown: folly! I am afraid this great lubber, the world,
Clown: will prove a cockney. I prithee now, ungird thy
Clown: strangeness and tell me what I shall vent to my
Clown: lady: shall I vent to her that thou art coming?
SEBASTIAN: I prithee, foolish Greek, depart from me: There's
SEBASTIAN: money for thee: if you tarry longer, I shall give
SEBASTIAN: worse payment.
Clown: By my troth, thou hast an open hand. These wise men
Clown: that give fools money get themselves a good
Clown: report--after fourteen years' purchase.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR ANDREW, SIR TOBY BELCH, and FABIAN
SIR ANDREW: Now, sir, have I met you again? there's for you.
SEBASTIAN: Why, there's for thee, and there, and there. Are all
SEBASTIAN: the people mad?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Hold, sir, or I'll throw your dagger o'er the house.
Clown: This will I tell my lady straight: I would not be
Clown: in some of your coats for two pence.
NARRATOR: Exit
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come on, sir, hold.
SIR ANDREW: Nay, let him alone: I'll go another way to work
SIR ANDREW: with him, I'll have an action of battery against
SIR ANDREW: him, if there be any law in Illyria: though I
SIR ANDREW: struck him first, yet it's no matter for that.
SEBASTIAN: Let go thy hand.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Come, sir, I will not let you go. Come, my young
SIR TOBY BELCH: soldier, put up your iron: you are well fleshed, come on.
SEBASTIAN: I will be free from thee. What wouldst thou now? If
SEBASTIAN: thou darest tempt me further, draw thy sword.
SIR TOBY BELCH: What, what? Nay, then I must have an ounce or two
SIR TOBY BELCH: of this malapert blood from you.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA
OLIVIA: Hold, Toby, on thy life I charge thee, hold!
SIR TOBY BELCH: Madam!
OLIVIA: Will it be ever thus? Ungracious wretch,
OLIVIA: Fit for the mountains and the barbarous caves,
OLIVIA: Where manners ne'er were preach'd! out of my sight!
OLIVIA: Be not offended, dear Cesario.
OLIVIA: Rudesby, be gone!
NARRATOR: Exeunt SIR TOBY BELCH, SIR ANDREW, and FABIAN
OLIVIA: I prithee, gentle friend,
OLIVIA: Let thy fair wisdom, not thy passion, sway
OLIVIA: In this uncivil and thou unjust extent
OLIVIA: Against thy peace. Go with me to my house,
OLIVIA: And hear thou there how many fruitless pranks
OLIVIA: This ruffian hath botch'd up, that thou thereby
OLIVIA: Mayst smile at this: thou shalt not choose but go:
OLIVIA: Do not deny. Beshrew his soul for me,
OLIVIA: He started one poor heart of mine in thee.
SEBASTIAN: What relish is in this? how runs the stream?
SEBASTIAN: Or I am mad, or else this is a dream:
SEBASTIAN: Let fancy still my sense in Lethe steep,
SEBASTIAN: If it be thus to dream, still let me sleep!
OLIVIA: Nay, come, I prithee, would thou'ldst be ruled by me!
SEBASTIAN: Madam, I will.
OLIVIA: O, say so, and so be!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. OLIVIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter MARIA and Clown
MARIA: Nay, I prithee, put on this gown and this beard,
MARIA: make him believe thou art Sir Topas the curate: do
MARIA: it quickly, I'll call Sir Toby the whilst.
NARRATOR: Exit
Clown: Well, I'll put it on, and I will dissemble myself
Clown: in't, and I would I were the first that ever
Clown: dissembled in such a gown. I am not tall enough to
Clown: become the function well, nor lean enough to be
Clown: thought a good student, but to be said an honest man
Clown: and a good housekeeper goes as fairly as to say a
Clown: careful man and a great scholar. The competitors enter.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH and MARIA
SIR TOBY BELCH: Jove bless thee, master Parson.
Clown: Bonos dies, Sir Toby: for, as the old hermit of
Clown: Prague, that never saw pen and ink, very wittily
Clown: said to a niece of King Gorboduc, 'That that is is,'
Clown: so I, being Master Parson, am Master Parson, for,
Clown: what is 'that' but 'that,' and 'is' but 'is'?
SIR TOBY BELCH: To him, Sir Topas.
Clown: What, ho, I say! peace in this prison!
SIR TOBY BELCH: The knave counterfeits well, a good knave.
MALVOLIO: [Within]  Who calls there?
Clown: Sir Topas the curate, who comes to visit Malvolio
Clown: the lunatic.
MALVOLIO: Sir Topas, Sir Topas, good Sir Topas, go to my lady.
Clown: Out, hyperbolical fiend! how vexest thou this man!
Clown: talkest thou nothing but of ladies?
SIR TOBY BELCH: Well said, Master Parson.
MALVOLIO: Sir Topas, never was man thus wronged: good Sir
MALVOLIO: Topas, do not think I am mad: they have laid me
MALVOLIO: here in hideous darkness.
Clown: Fie, thou dishonest Satan! I call thee by the most
Clown: modest terms, for I am one of those gentle ones
Clown: that will use the devil himself with courtesy:
Clown: sayest thou that house is dark?
MALVOLIO: As hell, Sir Topas.
Clown: Why it hath bay windows transparent as barricadoes,
Clown: and the clearstores toward the south north are as
Clown: lustrous as ebony, and yet complainest thou of
Clown: obstruction?
MALVOLIO: I am not mad, Sir Topas: I say to you, this house is dark.
Clown: Madman, thou errest: I say, there is no darkness
Clown: but ignorance, in which thou art more puzzled than
Clown: the Egyptians in their fog.
MALVOLIO: I say, this house is as dark as ignorance, though
MALVOLIO: ignorance were as dark as hell, and I say, there
MALVOLIO: was never man thus abused. I am no more mad than you
MALVOLIO: are: make the trial of it in any constant question.
Clown: What is the opinion of Pythagoras concerning wild fowl?
MALVOLIO: That the soul of our grandam might haply inhabit a bird.
Clown: What thinkest thou of his opinion?
MALVOLIO: I think nobly of the soul, and no way approve his opinion.
Clown: Fare thee well. Remain thou still in darkness:
Clown: thou shalt hold the opinion of Pythagoras ere I will
Clown: allow of thy wits, and fear to kill a woodcock, lest
Clown: thou dispossess the soul of thy grandam. Fare thee well.
MALVOLIO: Sir Topas, Sir Topas!
SIR TOBY BELCH: My most exquisite Sir Topas!
Clown: Nay, I am for all waters.
MARIA: Thou mightst have done this without thy beard and
MARIA: gown: he sees thee not.
SIR TOBY BELCH: To him in thine own voice, and bring me word how
SIR TOBY BELCH: thou findest him: I would we were well rid of this
SIR TOBY BELCH: knavery. If he may be conveniently delivered, I
SIR TOBY BELCH: would he were, for I am now so far in offence with
SIR TOBY BELCH: my niece that I cannot pursue with any safety this
SIR TOBY BELCH: sport to the upshot. Come by and by to my chamber.
NARRATOR: Exeunt SIR TOBY BELCH and MARIA
Clown: [Singing]
Clown: 'Hey, Robin, jolly Robin,
Clown: Tell me how thy lady does.'
MALVOLIO: Fool!
Clown: 'My lady is unkind, perdy.'
MALVOLIO: Fool!
Clown: 'Alas, why is she so?'
MALVOLIO: Fool, I say!
Clown: 'She loves another'--Who calls, ha?
MALVOLIO: Good fool, as ever thou wilt deserve well at my
MALVOLIO: hand, help me to a candle, and pen, ink and paper:
MALVOLIO: as I am a gentleman, I will live to be thankful to
MALVOLIO: thee for't.
Clown: Master Malvolio?
MALVOLIO: Ay, good fool.
Clown: Alas, sir, how fell you besides your five wits?
MALVOLIO: Fool, there was never a man so notoriously abused: I
MALVOLIO: am as well in my wits, fool, as thou art.
Clown: But as well? then you are mad indeed, if you be no
Clown: better in your wits than a fool.
MALVOLIO: They have here propertied me, keep me in darkness,
MALVOLIO: send ministers to me, asses, and do all they can to
MALVOLIO: face me out of my wits.
Clown: Advise you what you say, the minister is here.
Clown: Malvolio, Malvolio, thy wits the heavens restore!
Clown: endeavour thyself to sleep, and leave thy vain
Clown: bibble babble.
MALVOLIO: Sir Topas!
Clown: Maintain no words with him, good fellow. Who, I,
Clown: sir? not I, sir. God be wi' you, good Sir Topas.
Clown: Merry, amen. I will, sir, I will.
MALVOLIO: Fool, fool, fool, I say!
Clown: Alas, sir, be patient. What say you sir? I am
Clown: shent for speaking to you.
MALVOLIO: Good fool, help me to some light and some paper: I
MALVOLIO: tell thee, I am as well in my wits as any man in Illyria.
Clown: Well-a-day that you were, sir
MALVOLIO: By this hand, I am. Good fool, some ink, paper and
MALVOLIO: light, and convey what I will set down to my lady:
MALVOLIO: it shall advantage thee more than ever the bearing
MALVOLIO: of letter did.
Clown: I will help you to't. But tell me true, are you
Clown: not mad indeed? or do you but counterfeit?
MALVOLIO: Believe me, I am not, I tell thee true.
Clown: Nay, I'll ne'er believe a madman till I see his
Clown: brains. I will fetch you light and paper and ink.
MALVOLIO: Fool, I'll requite it in the highest degree: I
MALVOLIO: prithee, be gone.
Clown: [Singing]
Clown: I am gone, sir,
Clown: And anon, sir,
Clown: I'll be with you again,
Clown: In a trice,
Clown: Like to the old Vice,
Clown: Your need to sustain,
Clown: Who, with dagger of lath,
Clown: In his rage and his wrath,
Clown: Cries, ah, ha! to the devil:
Clown: Like a mad lad,
Clown: Pare thy nails, dad,
Clown: Adieu, good man devil.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE III. OLIVIA's garden.
NARRATOR: Enter SEBASTIAN
SEBASTIAN: This is the air, that is the glorious sun,
SEBASTIAN: This pearl she gave me, I do feel't and see't,
SEBASTIAN: And though 'tis wonder that enwraps me thus,
SEBASTIAN: Yet 'tis not madness. Where's Antonio, then?
SEBASTIAN: I could not find him at the Elephant:
SEBASTIAN: Yet there he was, and there I found this credit,
SEBASTIAN: That he did range the town to seek me out.
SEBASTIAN: His counsel now might do me golden service,
SEBASTIAN: For though my soul disputes well with my sense,
SEBASTIAN: That this may be some error, but no madness,
SEBASTIAN: Yet doth this accident and flood of fortune
SEBASTIAN: So far exceed all instance, all discourse,
SEBASTIAN: That I am ready to distrust mine eyes
SEBASTIAN: And wrangle with my reason that persuades me
SEBASTIAN: To any other trust but that I am mad
SEBASTIAN: Or else the lady's mad, yet, if 'twere so,
SEBASTIAN: She could not sway her house, command her followers,
SEBASTIAN: Take and give back affairs and their dispatch
SEBASTIAN: With such a smooth, discreet and stable bearing
SEBASTIAN: As I perceive she does: there's something in't
SEBASTIAN: That is deceiveable. But here the lady comes.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA and Priest
OLIVIA: Blame not this haste of mine. If you mean well,
OLIVIA: Now go with me and with this holy man
OLIVIA: Into the chantry by: there, before him,
OLIVIA: And underneath that consecrated roof,
OLIVIA: Plight me the full assurance of your faith,
OLIVIA: That my most jealous and too doubtful soul
OLIVIA: May live at peace. He shall conceal it
OLIVIA: Whiles you are willing it shall come to note,
OLIVIA: What time we will our celebration keep
OLIVIA: According to my birth. What do you say?
SEBASTIAN: I'll follow this good man, and go with you,
SEBASTIAN: And, having sworn truth, ever will be true.
OLIVIA: Then lead the way, good father, and heavens so shine,
OLIVIA: That they may fairly note this act of mine!
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Before OLIVIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter Clown and FABIAN
FABIAN: Now, as thou lovest me, let me see his letter.
Clown: Good Master Fabian, grant me another request.
FABIAN: Any thing.
Clown: Do not desire to see this letter.
FABIAN: This is, to give a dog, and in recompense desire my
FABIAN: dog again.
NARRATOR: Enter DUKE ORSINO, VIOLA, CURIO, and Lords
DUKE ORSINO: Belong you to the Lady Olivia, friends?
Clown: Ay, sir, we are some of her trappings.
DUKE ORSINO: I know thee well, how dost thou, my good fellow?
Clown: Truly, sir, the better for my foes and the worse
Clown: for my friends.
DUKE ORSINO: Just the contrary, the better for thy friends.
Clown: No, sir, the worse.
DUKE ORSINO: How can that be?
Clown: Marry, sir, they praise me and make an ass of me,
Clown: now my foes tell me plainly I am an ass: so that by
Clown: my foes, sir I profit in the knowledge of myself,
Clown: and by my friends, I am abused: so that,
Clown: conclusions to be as kisses, if your four negatives
Clown: make your two affirmatives why then, the worse for
Clown: my friends and the better for my foes.
DUKE ORSINO: Why, this is excellent.
Clown: By my troth, sir, no, though it please you to be
Clown: one of my friends.
DUKE ORSINO: Thou shalt not be the worse for me: there's gold.
Clown: But that it would be double-dealing, sir, I would
Clown: you could make it another.
DUKE ORSINO: O, you give me ill counsel.
Clown: Put your grace in your pocket, sir, for this once,
Clown: and let your flesh and blood obey it.
DUKE ORSINO: Well, I will be so much a sinner, to be a
DUKE ORSINO: double-dealer: there's another.
Clown: Primo, secundo, tertio, is a good play, and the old
Clown: saying is, the third pays for all: the triplex,
Clown: sir, is a good tripping measure, or the bells of
Clown: Saint Bennet, sir, may put you in mind, one, two, three.
DUKE ORSINO: You can fool no more money out of me at this throw:
DUKE ORSINO: if you will let your lady know I am here to speak
DUKE ORSINO: with her, and bring her along with you, it may awake
DUKE ORSINO: my bounty further.
Clown: Marry, sir, lullaby to your bounty till I come
Clown: again. I go, sir, but I would not have you to think
Clown: that my desire of having is the sin of covetousness:
Clown: but, as you say, sir, let your bounty take a nap, I
Clown: will awake it anon.
NARRATOR: Exit
VIOLA: Here comes the man, sir, that did rescue me.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO and Officers
DUKE ORSINO: That face of his I do remember well,
DUKE ORSINO: Yet, when I saw it last, it was besmear'd
DUKE ORSINO: As black as Vulcan in the smoke of war:
DUKE ORSINO: A bawbling vessel was he captain of,
DUKE ORSINO: For shallow draught and bulk unprizable,
DUKE ORSINO: With which such scathful grapple did he make
DUKE ORSINO: With the most noble bottom of our fleet,
DUKE ORSINO: That very envy and the tongue of loss
DUKE ORSINO: Cried fame and honour on him. What's the matter?
First Officer: Orsino, this is that Antonio
First Officer: That took the Phoenix and her fraught from Candy,
First Officer: And this is he that did the Tiger board,
First Officer: When your young nephew Titus lost his leg:
First Officer: Here in the streets, desperate of shame and state,
First Officer: In private brabble did we apprehend him.
VIOLA: He did me kindness, sir, drew on my side,
VIOLA: But in conclusion put strange speech upon me:
VIOLA: I know not what 'twas but distraction.
DUKE ORSINO: Notable pirate! thou salt-water thief!
DUKE ORSINO: What foolish boldness brought thee to their mercies,
DUKE ORSINO: Whom thou, in terms so bloody and so dear,
DUKE ORSINO: Hast made thine enemies?
ANTONIO: Orsino, noble sir,
ANTONIO: Be pleased that I shake off these names you give me:
ANTONIO: Antonio never yet was thief or pirate,
ANTONIO: Though I confess, on base and ground enough,
ANTONIO: Orsino's enemy. A witchcraft drew me hither:
ANTONIO: That most ingrateful boy there by your side,
ANTONIO: From the rude sea's enraged and foamy mouth
ANTONIO: Did I redeem, a wreck past hope he was:
ANTONIO: His life I gave him and did thereto add
ANTONIO: My love, without retention or restraint,
ANTONIO: All his in dedication, for his sake
ANTONIO: Did I expose myself, pure for his love,
ANTONIO: Into the danger of this adverse town,
ANTONIO: Drew to defend him when he was beset:
ANTONIO: Where being apprehended, his false cunning,
ANTONIO: Not meaning to partake with me in danger,
ANTONIO: Taught him to face me out of his acquaintance,
ANTONIO: And grew a twenty years removed thing
ANTONIO: While one would wink, denied me mine own purse,
ANTONIO: Which I had recommended to his use
ANTONIO: Not half an hour before.
VIOLA: How can this be?
DUKE ORSINO: When came he to this town?
ANTONIO: To-day, my lord, and for three months before,
ANTONIO: No interim, not a minute's vacancy,
ANTONIO: Both day and night did we keep company.
NARRATOR: Enter OLIVIA and Attendants
DUKE ORSINO: Here comes the countess: now heaven walks on earth.
DUKE ORSINO: But for thee, fellow, fellow, thy words are madness:
DUKE ORSINO: Three months this youth hath tended upon me,
DUKE ORSINO: But more of that anon. Take him aside.
OLIVIA: What would my lord, but that he may not have,
OLIVIA: Wherein Olivia may seem serviceable?
OLIVIA: Cesario, you do not keep promise with me.
VIOLA: Madam!
DUKE ORSINO: Gracious Olivia,--
OLIVIA: What do you say, Cesario? Good my lord,--
VIOLA: My lord would speak, my duty hushes me.
OLIVIA: If it be aught to the old tune, my lord,
OLIVIA: It is as fat and fulsome to mine ear
OLIVIA: As howling after music.
DUKE ORSINO: Still so cruel?
OLIVIA: Still so constant, lord.
DUKE ORSINO: What, to perverseness? you uncivil lady,
DUKE ORSINO: To whose ingrate and unauspicious altars
DUKE ORSINO: My soul the faithfull'st offerings hath breathed out
DUKE ORSINO: That e'er devotion tender'd! What shall I do?
OLIVIA: Even what it please my lord, that shall become him.
DUKE ORSINO: Why should I not, had I the heart to do it,
DUKE ORSINO: Like to the Egyptian thief at point of death,
DUKE ORSINO: Kill what I love?--a savage jealousy
DUKE ORSINO: That sometimes savours nobly. But hear me this:
DUKE ORSINO: Since you to non-regardance cast my faith,
DUKE ORSINO: And that I partly know the instrument
DUKE ORSINO: That screws me from my true place in your favour,
DUKE ORSINO: Live you the marble-breasted tyrant still,
DUKE ORSINO: But this your minion, whom I know you love,
DUKE ORSINO: And whom, by heaven I swear, I tender dearly,
DUKE ORSINO: Him will I tear out of that cruel eye,
DUKE ORSINO: Where he sits crowned in his master's spite.
DUKE ORSINO: Come, boy, with me, my thoughts are ripe in mischief:
DUKE ORSINO: I'll sacrifice the lamb that I do love,
DUKE ORSINO: To spite a raven's heart within a dove.
VIOLA: And I, most jocund, apt and willingly,
VIOLA: To do you rest, a thousand deaths would die.
OLIVIA: Where goes Cesario?
VIOLA: After him I love
VIOLA: More than I love these eyes, more than my life,
VIOLA: More, by all mores, than e'er I shall love wife.
VIOLA: If I do feign, you witnesses above
VIOLA: Punish my life for tainting of my love!
OLIVIA: Ay me, detested! how am I beguiled!
VIOLA: Who does beguile you? who does do you wrong?
OLIVIA: Hast thou forgot thyself? is it so long?
OLIVIA: Call forth the holy father.
DUKE ORSINO: Come, away!
OLIVIA: Whither, my lord? Cesario, husband, stay.
DUKE ORSINO: Husband!
OLIVIA: Ay, husband: can he that deny?
DUKE ORSINO: Her husband, sirrah!
VIOLA: No, my lord, not I.
OLIVIA: Alas, it is the baseness of thy fear
OLIVIA: That makes thee strangle thy propriety:
OLIVIA: Fear not, Cesario, take thy fortunes up,
OLIVIA: Be that thou know'st thou art, and then thou art
OLIVIA: As great as that thou fear'st.
NARRATOR: Enter Priest
OLIVIA: O, welcome, father!
OLIVIA: Father, I charge thee, by thy reverence,
OLIVIA: Here to unfold, though lately we intended
OLIVIA: To keep in darkness what occasion now
OLIVIA: Reveals before 'tis ripe, what thou dost know
OLIVIA: Hath newly pass'd between this youth and me.
Priest: A contract of eternal bond of love,
Priest: Confirm'd by mutual joinder of your hands,
Priest: Attested by the holy close of lips,
Priest: Strengthen'd by interchangement of your rings,
Priest: And all the ceremony of this compact
Priest: Seal'd in my function, by my testimony:
Priest: Since when, my watch hath told me, toward my grave
Priest: I have travell'd but two hours.
DUKE ORSINO: O thou dissembling cub! what wilt thou be
DUKE ORSINO: When time hath sow'd a grizzle on thy case?
DUKE ORSINO: Or will not else thy craft so quickly grow,
DUKE ORSINO: That thine own trip shall be thine overthrow?
DUKE ORSINO: Farewell, and take her, but direct thy feet
DUKE ORSINO: Where thou and I henceforth may never meet.
VIOLA: My lord, I do protest--
OLIVIA: O, do not swear!
OLIVIA: Hold little faith, though thou hast too much fear.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR ANDREW
SIR ANDREW: For the love of God, a surgeon! Send one presently
SIR ANDREW: to Sir Toby.
OLIVIA: What's the matter?
SIR ANDREW: He has broke my head across and has given Sir Toby
SIR ANDREW: a bloody coxcomb too: for the love of God, your
SIR ANDREW: help! I had rather than forty pound I were at home.
OLIVIA: Who has done this, Sir Andrew?
SIR ANDREW: The count's gentleman, one Cesario: we took him for
SIR ANDREW: a coward, but he's the very devil incardinate.
DUKE ORSINO: My gentleman, Cesario?
SIR ANDREW: 'Od's lifelings, here he is! You broke my head for
SIR ANDREW: nothing, and that that I did, I was set on to do't
SIR ANDREW: by Sir Toby.
VIOLA: Why do you speak to me? I never hurt you:
VIOLA: You drew your sword upon me without cause,
VIOLA: But I bespoke you fair, and hurt you not.
SIR ANDREW: If a bloody coxcomb be a hurt, you have hurt me: I
SIR ANDREW: think you set nothing by a bloody coxcomb.
NARRATOR: Enter SIR TOBY BELCH and Clown
SIR ANDREW: Here comes Sir Toby halting, you shall hear more:
SIR ANDREW: but if he had not been in drink, he would have
SIR ANDREW: tickled you othergates than he did.
DUKE ORSINO: How now, gentleman! how is't with you?
SIR TOBY BELCH: That's all one: has hurt me, and there's the end
SIR TOBY BELCH: on't. Sot, didst see Dick surgeon, sot?
Clown: O, he's drunk, Sir Toby, an hour agone, his eyes
Clown: were set at eight i' the morning.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Then he's a rogue, and a passy measures panyn: I
SIR TOBY BELCH: hate a drunken rogue.
OLIVIA: Away with him! Who hath made this havoc with them?
SIR ANDREW: I'll help you, Sir Toby, because well be dressed together.
SIR TOBY BELCH: Will you help? an ass-head and a coxcomb and a
SIR TOBY BELCH: knave, a thin-faced knave, a gull!
OLIVIA: Get him to bed, and let his hurt be look'd to.
NARRATOR: Exeunt Clown, FABIAN, SIR TOBY BELCH, and SIR ANDREW
NARRATOR: Enter SEBASTIAN
SEBASTIAN: I am sorry, madam, I have hurt your kinsman:
SEBASTIAN: But, had it been the brother of my blood,
SEBASTIAN: I must have done no less with wit and safety.
SEBASTIAN: You throw a strange regard upon me, and by that
SEBASTIAN: I do perceive it hath offended you:
SEBASTIAN: Pardon me, sweet one, even for the vows
SEBASTIAN: We made each other but so late ago.
DUKE ORSINO: One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons,
DUKE ORSINO: A natural perspective, that is and is not!
SEBASTIAN: Antonio, O my dear Antonio!
SEBASTIAN: How have the hours rack'd and tortured me,
SEBASTIAN: Since I have lost thee!
ANTONIO: Sebastian are you?
SEBASTIAN: Fear'st thou that, Antonio?
ANTONIO: How have you made division of yourself?
ANTONIO: An apple, cleft in two, is not more twin
ANTONIO: Than these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?
OLIVIA: Most wonderful!
SEBASTIAN: Do I stand there? I never had a brother,
SEBASTIAN: Nor can there be that deity in my nature,
SEBASTIAN: Of here and every where. I had a sister,
SEBASTIAN: Whom the blind waves and surges have devour'd.
SEBASTIAN: Of charity, what kin are you to me?
SEBASTIAN: What countryman? what name? what parentage?
VIOLA: Of Messaline: Sebastian was my father,
VIOLA: Such a Sebastian was my brother too,
VIOLA: So went he suited to his watery tomb:
VIOLA: If spirits can assume both form and suit
VIOLA: You come to fright us.
SEBASTIAN: A spirit I am indeed,
SEBASTIAN: But am in that dimension grossly clad
SEBASTIAN: Which from the womb I did participate.
SEBASTIAN: Were you a woman, as the rest goes even,
SEBASTIAN: I should my tears let fall upon your cheek,
SEBASTIAN: And say 'Thrice-welcome, drowned Viola!'
VIOLA: My father had a mole upon his brow.
SEBASTIAN: And so had mine.
VIOLA: And died that day when Viola from her birth
VIOLA: Had number'd thirteen years.
SEBASTIAN: O, that record is lively in my soul!
SEBASTIAN: He finished indeed his mortal act
SEBASTIAN: That day that made my sister thirteen years.
VIOLA: If nothing lets to make us happy both
VIOLA: But this my masculine usurp'd attire,
VIOLA: Do not embrace me till each circumstance
VIOLA: Of place, time, fortune, do cohere and jump
VIOLA: That I am Viola: which to confirm,
VIOLA: I'll bring you to a captain in this town,
VIOLA: Where lie my maiden weeds, by whose gentle help
VIOLA: I was preserved to serve this noble count.
VIOLA: All the occurrence of my fortune since
VIOLA: Hath been between this lady and this lord.
SEBASTIAN: [To OLIVIA]  So comes it, lady, you have been mistook:
SEBASTIAN: But nature to her bias drew in that.
SEBASTIAN: You would have been contracted to a maid,
SEBASTIAN: Nor are you therein, by my life, deceived,
SEBASTIAN: You are betroth'd both to a maid and man.
DUKE ORSINO: Be not amazed, right noble is his blood.
DUKE ORSINO: If this be so, as yet the glass seems true,
DUKE ORSINO: I shall have share in this most happy wreck.
NARRATOR: To VIOLA
DUKE ORSINO: Boy, thou hast said to me a thousand times
DUKE ORSINO: Thou never shouldst love woman like to me.
VIOLA: And all those sayings will I overswear,
VIOLA: And those swearings keep as true in soul
VIOLA: As doth that orbed continent the fire
VIOLA: That severs day from night.
DUKE ORSINO: Give me thy hand,
DUKE ORSINO: And let me see thee in thy woman's weeds.
VIOLA: The captain that did bring me first on shore
VIOLA: Hath my maid's garments: he upon some action
VIOLA: Is now in durance, at Malvolio's suit,
VIOLA: A gentleman, and follower of my lady's.
OLIVIA: He shall enlarge him: fetch Malvolio hither:
OLIVIA: And yet, alas, now I remember me,
OLIVIA: They say, poor gentleman, he's much distract.
NARRATOR: Re-enter Clown with a letter, and FABIAN
OLIVIA: A most extracting frenzy of mine own
OLIVIA: From my remembrance clearly banish'd his.
OLIVIA: How does he, sirrah?
Clown: Truly, madam, he holds Belzebub at the staves's end as
Clown: well as a man in his case may do: has here writ a
Clown: letter to you, I should have given't you to-day
Clown: morning, but as a madman's epistles are no gospels,
Clown: so it skills not much when they are delivered.
OLIVIA: Open't, and read it.
Clown: Look then to be well edified when the fool delivers
Clown: the madman.
NARRATOR: Reads
Clown: 'By the Lord, madam,'--
OLIVIA: How now! art thou mad?
Clown: No, madam, I do but read madness: an your ladyship
Clown: will have it as it ought to be, you must allow Vox.
OLIVIA: Prithee, read i' thy right wits.
Clown: So I do, madonna, but to read his right wits is to
Clown: read thus: therefore perpend, my princess, and give ear.
OLIVIA: Read it you, sirrah.
NARRATOR: To FABIAN
FABIAN: [Reads]  'By the Lord, madam, you wrong me, and the
FABIAN: world shall know it: though you have put me into
FABIAN: darkness and given your drunken cousin rule over
FABIAN: me, yet have I the benefit of my senses as well as
FABIAN: your ladyship. I have your own letter that induced
FABIAN: me to the semblance I put on, with the which I doubt
FABIAN: not but to do myself much right, or you much shame.
FABIAN: Think of me as you please. I leave my duty a little
FABIAN: unthought of and speak out of my injury.
FABIAN: THE MADLY-USED MALVOLIO.'
OLIVIA: Did he write this?
Clown: Ay, madam.
DUKE ORSINO: This savours not much of distraction.
OLIVIA: See him deliver'd, Fabian, bring him hither.
NARRATOR: Exit FABIAN
OLIVIA: My lord so please you, these things further
OLIVIA: thought on,
OLIVIA: To think me as well a sister as a wife,
OLIVIA: One day shall crown the alliance on't, so please you,
OLIVIA: Here at my house and at my proper cost.
DUKE ORSINO: Madam, I am most apt to embrace your offer.
NARRATOR: To VIOLA
DUKE ORSINO: Your master quits you, and for your service done him,
DUKE ORSINO: So much against the mettle of your sex,
DUKE ORSINO: So far beneath your soft and tender breeding,
DUKE ORSINO: And since you call'd me master for so long,
DUKE ORSINO: Here is my hand: you shall from this time be
DUKE ORSINO: Your master's mistress.
OLIVIA: A sister! you are she.
NARRATOR: Re-enter FABIAN, with MALVOLIO
DUKE ORSINO: Is this the madman?
OLIVIA: Ay, my lord, this same.
OLIVIA: How now, Malvolio!
MALVOLIO: Madam, you have done me wrong,
MALVOLIO: Notorious wrong.
OLIVIA: Have I, Malvolio? no.
MALVOLIO: Lady, you have. Pray you, peruse that letter.
MALVOLIO: You must not now deny it is your hand:
MALVOLIO: Write from it, if you can, in hand or phrase,
MALVOLIO: Or say 'tis not your seal, nor your invention:
MALVOLIO: You can say none of this: well, grant it then
MALVOLIO: And tell me, in the modesty of honour,
MALVOLIO: Why you have given me such clear lights of favour,
MALVOLIO: Bade me come smiling and cross-garter'd to you,
MALVOLIO: To put on yellow stockings and to frown
MALVOLIO: Upon Sir Toby and the lighter people,
MALVOLIO: And, acting this in an obedient hope,
MALVOLIO: Why have you suffer'd me to be imprison'd,
MALVOLIO: Kept in a dark house, visited by the priest,
MALVOLIO: And made the most notorious geck and gull
MALVOLIO: That e'er invention play'd on? tell me why.
OLIVIA: Alas, Malvolio, this is not my writing,
OLIVIA: Though, I confess, much like the character
OLIVIA: But out of question 'tis Maria's hand.
OLIVIA: And now I do bethink me, it was she
OLIVIA: First told me thou wast mad, then camest in smiling,
OLIVIA: And in such forms which here were presupposed
OLIVIA: Upon thee in the letter. Prithee, be content:
OLIVIA: This practise hath most shrewdly pass'd upon thee,
OLIVIA: But when we know the grounds and authors of it,
OLIVIA: Thou shalt be both the plaintiff and the judge
OLIVIA: Of thine own cause.
FABIAN: Good madam, hear me speak,
FABIAN: And let no quarrel nor no brawl to come
FABIAN: Taint the condition of this present hour,
FABIAN: Which I have wonder'd at. In hope it shall not,
FABIAN: Most freely I confess, myself and Toby
FABIAN: Set this device against Malvolio here,
FABIAN: Upon some stubborn and uncourteous parts
FABIAN: We had conceived against him: Maria writ
FABIAN: The letter at Sir Toby's great importance,
FABIAN: In recompense whereof he hath married her.
FABIAN: How with a sportful malice it was follow'd,
FABIAN: May rather pluck on laughter than revenge,
FABIAN: If that the injuries be justly weigh'd
FABIAN: That have on both sides pass'd.
OLIVIA: Alas, poor fool, how have they baffled thee!
Clown: Why, 'some are born great, some achieve greatness,
Clown: and some have greatness thrown upon them.' I was
Clown: one, sir, in this interlude, one Sir Topas, sir, but
Clown: that's all one. 'By the Lord, fool, I am not mad.'
Clown: But do you remember? 'Madam, why laugh you at such
Clown: a barren rascal? an you smile not, he's gagged:'
Clown: and thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges.
MALVOLIO: I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you.
NARRATOR: Exit
OLIVIA: He hath been most notoriously abused.
DUKE ORSINO: Pursue him and entreat him to a peace:
DUKE ORSINO: He hath not told us of the captain yet:
DUKE ORSINO: When that is known and golden time convents,
DUKE ORSINO: A solemn combination shall be made
DUKE ORSINO: Of our dear souls. Meantime, sweet sister,
DUKE ORSINO: We will not part from hence. Cesario, come,
DUKE ORSINO: For so you shall be, while you are a man,
DUKE ORSINO: But when in other habits you are seen,
DUKE ORSINO: Orsino's mistress and his fancy's queen.
NARRATOR: Exeunt all, except Clown
Clown: [Sings]
Clown: When that I was and a little tiny boy,
Clown: With hey, ho, the wind and the rain,
Clown: A foolish thing was but a toy,
Clown: For the rain it raineth every day.
Clown: But when I came to man's estate,
Clown: With hey, ho,  and c.
Clown: 'Gainst knaves and thieves men shut their gate,
Clown: For the rain,  and c.
Clown: But when I came, alas! to wive,
Clown: With hey, ho,  and c.
Clown: By swaggering could I never thrive,
Clown: For the rain,  and c.
Clown: But when I came unto my beds,
Clown: With hey, ho,  and c.
Clown: With toss-pots still had drunken heads,
Clown: For the rain,  and c.
Clown: A great while ago the world begun,
Clown: With hey, ho,  and c.
Clown: But that's all one, our play is done,
Clown: And we'll strive to please you every day.
NARRATOR: Exit
''' PLAY: Two Gentlemen of Verona '''
NARRATOR: ACT I
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Verona. An open place.
NARRATOR: Enter VALENTINE and PROTEUS
VALENTINE: Cease to persuade, my loving Proteus:
VALENTINE: Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits.
VALENTINE: Were't not affection chains thy tender days
VALENTINE: To the sweet glances of thy honour'd love,
VALENTINE: I rather would entreat thy company
VALENTINE: To see the wonders of the world abroad,
VALENTINE: Than, living dully sluggardized at home,
VALENTINE: Wear out thy youth with shapeless idleness.
VALENTINE: But since thou lovest, love still and thrive therein,
VALENTINE: Even as I would when I to love begin.
PROTEUS: Wilt thou be gone? Sweet Valentine, adieu!
PROTEUS: Think on thy Proteus, when thou haply seest
PROTEUS: Some rare note-worthy object in thy travel:
PROTEUS: Wish me partaker in thy happiness
PROTEUS: When thou dost meet good hap, and in thy danger,
PROTEUS: If ever danger do environ thee,
PROTEUS: Commend thy grievance to my holy prayers,
PROTEUS: For I will be thy beadsman, Valentine.
VALENTINE: And on a love-book pray for my success?
PROTEUS: Upon some book I love I'll pray for thee.
VALENTINE: That's on some shallow story of deep love:
VALENTINE: How young Leander cross'd the Hellespont.
PROTEUS: That's a deep story of a deeper love:
PROTEUS: For he was more than over shoes in love.
VALENTINE: 'Tis true, for you are over boots in love,
VALENTINE: And yet you never swum the Hellespont.
PROTEUS: Over the boots? nay, give me not the boots.
VALENTINE: No, I will not, for it boots thee not.
PROTEUS: What?
VALENTINE: To be in love, where scorn is bought with groans,
VALENTINE: Coy looks with heart-sore sighs, one fading moment's mirth
VALENTINE: With twenty watchful, weary, tedious nights:
VALENTINE: If haply won, perhaps a hapless gain,
VALENTINE: If lost, why then a grievous labour won,
VALENTINE: However, but a folly bought with wit,
VALENTINE: Or else a wit by folly vanquished.
PROTEUS: So, by your circumstance, you call me fool.
VALENTINE: So, by your circumstance, I fear you'll prove.
PROTEUS: 'Tis love you cavil at: I am not Love.
VALENTINE: Love is your master, for he masters you:
VALENTINE: And he that is so yoked by a fool,
VALENTINE: Methinks, should not be chronicled for wise.
PROTEUS: Yet writers say, as in the sweetest bud
PROTEUS: The eating canker dwells, so eating love
PROTEUS: Inhabits in the finest wits of all.
VALENTINE: And writers say, as the most forward bud
VALENTINE: Is eaten by the canker ere it blow,
VALENTINE: Even so by love the young and tender wit
VALENTINE: Is turn'd to folly, blasting in the bud,
VALENTINE: Losing his verdure even in the prime
VALENTINE: And all the fair effects of future hopes.
VALENTINE: But wherefore waste I time to counsel thee,
VALENTINE: That art a votary to fond desire?
VALENTINE: Once more adieu! my father at the road
VALENTINE: Expects my coming, there to see me shipp'd.
PROTEUS: And thither will I bring thee, Valentine.
VALENTINE: Sweet Proteus, no, now let us take our leave.
VALENTINE: To Milan let me hear from thee by letters
VALENTINE: Of thy success in love, and what news else
VALENTINE: Betideth here in absence of thy friend,
VALENTINE: And likewise will visit thee with mine.
PROTEUS: All happiness bechance to thee in Milan!
VALENTINE: As much to you at home! and so, farewell.
NARRATOR: Exit
PROTEUS: He after honour hunts, I after love:
PROTEUS: He leaves his friends to dignify them more,
PROTEUS: I leave myself, my friends and all, for love.
PROTEUS: Thou, Julia, thou hast metamorphosed me,
PROTEUS: Made me neglect my studies, lose my time,
PROTEUS: War with good counsel, set the world at nought,
PROTEUS: Made wit with musing weak, heart sick with thought.
NARRATOR: Enter SPEED
SPEED: Sir Proteus, save you! Saw you my master?
PROTEUS: But now he parted hence, to embark for Milan.
SPEED: Twenty to one then he is shipp'd already,
SPEED: And I have play'd the sheep in losing him.
PROTEUS: Indeed, a sheep doth very often stray,
PROTEUS: An if the shepherd be a while away.
SPEED: You conclude that my master is a shepherd, then,
SPEED: and I a sheep?
PROTEUS: I do.
SPEED: Why then, my horns are his horns, whether I wake or sleep.
PROTEUS: A silly answer and fitting well a sheep.
SPEED: This proves me still a sheep.
PROTEUS: True, and thy master a shepherd.
SPEED: Nay, that I can deny by a circumstance.
PROTEUS: It shall go hard but I'll prove it by another.
SPEED: The shepherd seeks the sheep, and not the sheep the
SPEED: shepherd, but I seek my master, and my master seeks
SPEED: not me: therefore I am no sheep.
PROTEUS: The sheep for fodder follow the shepherd, the
PROTEUS: shepherd for food follows not the sheep: thou for
PROTEUS: wages followest thy master, thy master for wages
PROTEUS: follows not thee: therefore thou art a sheep.
SPEED: Such another proof will make me cry 'baa.'
PROTEUS: But, dost thou hear? gavest thou my letter to Julia?
SPEED: Ay sir: I, a lost mutton, gave your letter to her,
SPEED: a laced mutton, and she, a laced mutton, gave me, a
SPEED: lost mutton, nothing for my labour.
PROTEUS: Here's too small a pasture for such store of muttons.
SPEED: If the ground be overcharged, you were best stick her.
PROTEUS: Nay: in that you are astray, 'twere best pound you.
SPEED: Nay, sir, less than a pound shall serve me for
SPEED: carrying your letter.
PROTEUS: You mistake, I mean the pound,--a pinfold.
SPEED: From a pound to a pin? fold it over and over,
SPEED: 'Tis threefold too little for carrying a letter to
SPEED: your lover.
PROTEUS: But what said she?
SPEED: [First nodding]  Ay.
PROTEUS: Nod--Ay--why, that's noddy.
SPEED: You mistook, sir, I say, she did nod: and you ask
SPEED: me if she did nod, and I say, 'Ay.'
PROTEUS: And that set together is noddy.
SPEED: Now you have taken the pains to set it together,
SPEED: take it for your pains.
PROTEUS: No, no, you shall have it for bearing the letter.
SPEED: Well, I perceive I must be fain to bear with you.
PROTEUS: Why sir, how do you bear with me?
SPEED: Marry, sir, the letter, very orderly, having nothing
SPEED: but the word 'noddy' for my pains.
PROTEUS: Beshrew me, but you have a quick wit.
SPEED: And yet it cannot overtake your slow purse.
PROTEUS: Come come, open the matter in brief: what said she?
SPEED: Open your purse, that the money and the matter may
SPEED: be both at once delivered.
PROTEUS: Well, sir, here is for your pains. What said she?
SPEED: Truly, sir, I think you'll hardly win her.
PROTEUS: Why, couldst thou perceive so much from her?
SPEED: Sir, I could perceive nothing at all from her, no,
SPEED: not so much as a ducat for delivering your letter:
SPEED: and being so hard to me that brought your mind, I
SPEED: fear she'll prove as hard to you in telling your
SPEED: mind. Give her no token but stones, for she's as
SPEED: hard as steel.
PROTEUS: What said she? nothing?
SPEED: No, not so much as 'Take this for thy pains.' To
SPEED: testify your bounty, I thank you, you have testerned
SPEED: me, in requital whereof, henceforth carry your
SPEED: letters yourself: and so, sir, I'll commend you to my master.
PROTEUS: Go, go, be gone, to save your ship from wreck,
PROTEUS: Which cannot perish having thee aboard,
PROTEUS: Being destined to a drier death on shore.
NARRATOR: Exit SPEED
PROTEUS: I must go send some better messenger:
PROTEUS: I fear my Julia would not deign my lines,
PROTEUS: Receiving them from such a worthless post.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The same. Garden of JULIA's house.
NARRATOR: Enter JULlA and LUCETTA
JULIA: But say, Lucetta, now we are alone,
JULIA: Wouldst thou then counsel me to fall in love?
LUCETTA: Ay, madam, so you stumble not unheedfully.
JULIA: Of all the fair resort of gentlemen
JULIA: That every day with parle encounter me,
JULIA: In thy opinion which is worthiest love?
LUCETTA: Please you repeat their names, I'll show my mind
LUCETTA: According to my shallow simple skill.
JULIA: What think'st thou of the fair Sir Eglamour?
LUCETTA: As of a knight well-spoken, neat and fine,
LUCETTA: But, were I you, he never should be mine.
JULIA: What think'st thou of the rich Mercatio?
LUCETTA: Well of his wealth, but of himself, so so.
JULIA: What think'st thou of the gentle Proteus?
LUCETTA: Lord, Lord! to see what folly reigns in us!
JULIA: How now! what means this passion at his name?
LUCETTA: Pardon, dear madam: 'tis a passing shame
LUCETTA: That I, unworthy body as I am,
LUCETTA: Should censure thus on lovely gentlemen.
JULIA: Why not on Proteus, as of all the rest?
LUCETTA: Then thus: of many good I think him best.
JULIA: Your reason?
LUCETTA: I have no other, but a woman's reason,
LUCETTA: I think him so because I think him so.
JULIA: And wouldst thou have me cast my love on him?
LUCETTA: Ay, if you thought your love not cast away.
JULIA: Why he, of all the rest, hath never moved me.
LUCETTA: Yet he, of all the rest, I think, best loves ye.
JULIA: His little speaking shows his love but small.
LUCETTA: Fire that's closest kept burns most of all.
JULIA: They do not love that do not show their love.
LUCETTA: O, they love least that let men know their love.
JULIA: I would I knew his mind.
LUCETTA: Peruse this paper, madam.
JULIA: 'To Julia.' Say, from whom?
LUCETTA: That the contents will show.
JULIA: Say, say, who gave it thee?
LUCETTA: Valentine's page, and sent, I think, from Proteus.
LUCETTA: He would have given it you, but I, being in the way,
LUCETTA: Did in your name receive it: pardon the
LUCETTA: fault I pray.
JULIA: Now, by my modesty, a goodly broker!
JULIA: Dare you presume to harbour wanton lines?
JULIA: To whisper and conspire against my youth?
JULIA: Now, trust me, 'tis an office of great worth
JULIA: And you an officer fit for the place.
JULIA: Or else return no more into my sight.
LUCETTA: To plead for love deserves more fee than hate.
JULIA: Will ye be gone?
LUCETTA: That you may ruminate.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIA: And yet I would I had o'erlooked the letter:
JULIA: It were a shame to call her back again
JULIA: And pray her to a fault for which I chid her.
JULIA: What a fool is she, that knows I am a maid,
JULIA: And would not force the letter to my view!
JULIA: Since maids, in modesty, say 'no' to that
JULIA: Which they would have the profferer construe 'ay.'
JULIA: Fie, fie, how wayward is this foolish love
JULIA: That, like a testy babe, will scratch the nurse
JULIA: And presently all humbled kiss the rod!
JULIA: How churlishly I chid Lucetta hence,
JULIA: When willingly I would have had her here!
JULIA: How angerly I taught my brow to frown,
JULIA: When inward joy enforced my heart to smile!
JULIA: My penance is to call Lucetta back
JULIA: And ask remission for my folly past.
JULIA: What ho! Lucetta!
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCETTA
LUCETTA: What would your ladyship?
JULIA: Is't near dinner-time?
LUCETTA: I would it were,
LUCETTA: That you might kill your stomach on your meat
LUCETTA: And not upon your maid.
JULIA: What is't that you took up so gingerly?
LUCETTA: Nothing.
JULIA: Why didst thou stoop, then?
LUCETTA: To take a paper up that I let fall.
JULIA: And is that paper nothing?
LUCETTA: Nothing concerning me.
JULIA: Then let it lie for those that it concerns.
LUCETTA: Madam, it will not lie where it concerns
LUCETTA: Unless it have a false interpeter.
JULIA: Some love of yours hath writ to you in rhyme.
LUCETTA: That I might sing it, madam, to a tune.
LUCETTA: Give me a note: your ladyship can set.
JULIA: As little by such toys as may be possible.
JULIA: Best sing it to the tune of 'Light o' love.'
LUCETTA: It is too heavy for so light a tune.
JULIA: Heavy! belike it hath some burden then?
LUCETTA: Ay, and melodious were it, would you sing it.
JULIA: And why not you?
LUCETTA: I cannot reach so high.
JULIA: Let's see your song. How now, minion!
LUCETTA: Keep tune there still, so you will sing it out:
LUCETTA: And yet methinks I do not like this tune.
JULIA: You do not?
LUCETTA: No, madam, it is too sharp.
JULIA: You, minion, are too saucy.
LUCETTA: Nay, now you are too flat
LUCETTA: And mar the concord with too harsh a descant:
LUCETTA: There wanteth but a mean to fill your song.
JULIA: The mean is drown'd with your unruly bass.
LUCETTA: Indeed, I bid the base for Proteus.
JULIA: This babble shall not henceforth trouble me.
JULIA: Here is a coil with protestation!
NARRATOR: Tears the letter
JULIA: Go get you gone, and let the papers lie:
JULIA: You would be fingering them, to anger me.
LUCETTA: She makes it strange, but she would be best pleased
LUCETTA: To be so anger'd with another letter.
NARRATOR: Exit
JULIA: Nay, would I were so anger'd with the same!
JULIA: O hateful hands, to tear such loving words!
JULIA: Injurious wasps, to feed on such sweet honey
JULIA: And kill the bees that yield it with your stings!
JULIA: I'll kiss each several paper for amends.
JULIA: Look, here is writ 'kind Julia.' Unkind Julia!
JULIA: As in revenge of thy ingratitude,
JULIA: I throw thy name against the bruising stones,
JULIA: Trampling contemptuously on thy disdain.
JULIA: And here is writ 'love-wounded Proteus.'
JULIA: Poor wounded name! my bosom as a bed
JULIA: Shall lodge thee till thy wound be thoroughly heal'd,
JULIA: And thus I search it with a sovereign kiss.
JULIA: But twice or thrice was 'Proteus' written down.
JULIA: Be calm, good wind, blow not a word away
JULIA: Till I have found each letter in the letter,
JULIA: Except mine own name: that some whirlwind bear
JULIA: Unto a ragged fearful-hanging rock
JULIA: And throw it thence into the raging sea!
JULIA: Lo, here in one line is his name twice writ,
JULIA: 'Poor forlorn Proteus, passionate Proteus,
JULIA: To the sweet Julia:' that I'll tear away.
JULIA: And yet I will not, sith so prettily
JULIA: He couples it to his complaining names.
JULIA: Thus will I fold them one on another:
JULIA: Now kiss, embrace, contend, do what you will.
NARRATOR: Re-enter LUCETTA
LUCETTA: Madam,
LUCETTA: Dinner is ready, and your father stays.
JULIA: Well, let us go.
LUCETTA: What, shall these papers lie like tell-tales here?
JULIA: If you respect them, best to take them up.
LUCETTA: Nay, I was taken up for laying them down:
LUCETTA: Yet here they shall not lie, for catching cold.
JULIA: I see you have a month's mind to them.
LUCETTA: Ay, madam, you may say what sights you see,
LUCETTA: I see things too, although you judge I wink.
JULIA: Come, come, will't please you go?
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE III. The same. ANTONIO's house.
NARRATOR: Enter ANTONIO and PANTHINO
ANTONIO: Tell me, Panthino, what sad talk was that
ANTONIO: Wherewith my brother held you in the cloister?
PANTHINO: 'Twas of his nephew Proteus, your son.
ANTONIO: Why, what of him?
PANTHINO: He wonder'd that your lordship
PANTHINO: Would suffer him to spend his youth at home,
PANTHINO: While other men, of slender reputation,
PANTHINO: Put forth their sons to seek preferment out:
PANTHINO: Some to the wars, to try their fortune there,
PANTHINO: Some to discover islands far away,
PANTHINO: Some to the studious universities.
PANTHINO: For any or for all these exercises,
PANTHINO: He said that Proteus your son was meet,
PANTHINO: And did request me to importune you
PANTHINO: To let him spend his time no more at home,
PANTHINO: Which would be great impeachment to his age,
PANTHINO: In having known no travel in his youth.
ANTONIO: Nor need'st thou much importune me to that
ANTONIO: Whereon this month I have been hammering.
ANTONIO: I have consider'd well his loss of time
ANTONIO: And how he cannot be a perfect man,
ANTONIO: Not being tried and tutor'd in the world:
ANTONIO: Experience is by industry achieved
ANTONIO: And perfected by the swift course of time.
ANTONIO: Then tell me, whither were I best to send him?
PANTHINO: I think your lordship is not ignorant
PANTHINO: How his companion, youthful Valentine,
PANTHINO: Attends the emperor in his royal court.
ANTONIO: I know it well.
PANTHINO: 'Twere good, I think, your lordship sent him thither:
PANTHINO: There shall he practise tilts and tournaments,
PANTHINO: Hear sweet discourse, converse with noblemen.
PANTHINO: And be in eye of every exercise
PANTHINO: Worthy his youth and nobleness of birth.
ANTONIO: I like thy counsel, well hast thou advised:
ANTONIO: And that thou mayst perceive how well I like it,
ANTONIO: The execution of it shall make known.
ANTONIO: Even with the speediest expedition
ANTONIO: I will dispatch him to the emperor's court.
PANTHINO: To-morrow, may it please you, Don Alphonso,
PANTHINO: With other gentlemen of good esteem,
PANTHINO: Are journeying to salute the emperor
PANTHINO: And to commend their service to his will.
ANTONIO: Good company, with them shall Proteus go:
ANTONIO: And, in good time! now will we break with him.
NARRATOR: Enter PROTEUS
PROTEUS: Sweet love! sweet lines! sweet life!
PROTEUS: Here is her hand, the agent of her heart,
PROTEUS: Here is her oath for love, her honour's pawn.
PROTEUS: O, that our fathers would applaud our loves,
PROTEUS: To seal our happiness with their consents!
PROTEUS: O heavenly Julia!
ANTONIO: How now! what letter are you reading there?
PROTEUS: May't please your lordship, 'tis a word or two
PROTEUS: Of commendations sent from Valentine,
PROTEUS: Deliver'd by a friend that came from him.
ANTONIO: Lend me the letter, let me see what news.
PROTEUS: There is no news, my lord, but that he writes
PROTEUS: How happily he lives, how well beloved
PROTEUS: And daily graced by the emperor,
PROTEUS: Wishing me with him, partner of his fortune.
ANTONIO: And how stand you affected to his wish?
PROTEUS: As one relying on your lordship's will
PROTEUS: And not depending on his friendly wish.
ANTONIO: My will is something sorted with his wish.
ANTONIO: Muse not that I thus suddenly proceed,
ANTONIO: For what I will, I will, and there an end.
ANTONIO: I am resolved that thou shalt spend some time
ANTONIO: With Valentinus in the emperor's court:
ANTONIO: What maintenance he from his friends receives,
ANTONIO: Like exhibition thou shalt have from me.
ANTONIO: To-morrow be in readiness to go:
ANTONIO: Excuse it not, for I am peremptory.
PROTEUS: My lord, I cannot be so soon provided:
PROTEUS: Please you, deliberate a day or two.
ANTONIO: Look, what thou want'st shall be sent after thee:
ANTONIO: No more of stay! to-morrow thou must go.
ANTONIO: Come on, Panthino: you shall be employ'd
ANTONIO: To hasten on his expedition.
NARRATOR: Exeunt ANTONIO and PANTHINO
PROTEUS: Thus have I shunn'd the fire for fear of burning,
PROTEUS: And drench'd me in the sea, where I am drown'd.
PROTEUS: I fear'd to show my father Julia's letter,
PROTEUS: Lest he should take exceptions to my love,
