MACBETH: By the worst means, the worst. For mine own good,
MACBETH: All causes shall give way: I am in blood
MACBETH: Stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more,
MACBETH: Returning were as tedious as go o'er:
MACBETH: Strange things I have in head, that will to hand,
MACBETH: Which must be acted ere they may be scann'd.
LADY MACBETH: You lack the season of all natures, sleep.
MACBETH: Come, we'll to sleep. My strange and self-abuse
MACBETH: Is the initiate fear that wants hard use:
MACBETH: We are yet but young in deed.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE V. A Heath.
NARRATOR: Thunder. Enter the three Witches meeting HECATE
First Witch: Why, how now, Hecate! you look angerly.
HECATE: Have I not reason, beldams as you are,
HECATE: Saucy and overbold? How did you dare
HECATE: To trade and traffic with Macbeth
HECATE: In riddles and affairs of death,
HECATE: And I, the mistress of your charms,
HECATE: The close contriver of all harms,
HECATE: Was never call'd to bear my part,
HECATE: Or show the glory of our art?
HECATE: And, which is worse, all you have done
HECATE: Hath been but for a wayward son,
HECATE: Spiteful and wrathful, who, as others do,
HECATE: Loves for his own ends, not for you.
HECATE: But make amends now: get you gone,
HECATE: And at the pit of Acheron
HECATE: Meet me i' the morning: thither he
HECATE: Will come to know his destiny:
HECATE: Your vessels and your spells provide,
HECATE: Your charms and every thing beside.
HECATE: I am for the air, this night I'll spend
HECATE: Unto a dismal and a fatal end:
HECATE: Great business must be wrought ere noon:
HECATE: Upon the corner of the moon
HECATE: There hangs a vaporous drop profound,
HECATE: I'll catch it ere it come to ground:
HECATE: And that distill'd by magic sleights
HECATE: Shall raise such artificial sprites
HECATE: As by the strength of their illusion
HECATE: Shall draw him on to his confusion:
HECATE: He shall spurn fate, scorn death, and bear
HECATE: He hopes 'bove wisdom, grace and fear:
HECATE: And you all know, security
HECATE: Is mortals' chiefest enemy.
HECATE: Music and a song within: 'Come away, come away,'  and c
HECATE: Hark! I am call'd, my little spirit, see,
HECATE: Sits in a foggy cloud, and stays for me.
NARRATOR: Exit
First Witch: Come, let's make haste, she'll soon be back again.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Forres. The palace.
NARRATOR: Enter LENNOX and another Lord
LENNOX: My former speeches have but hit your thoughts,
LENNOX: Which can interpret further: only, I say,
LENNOX: Things have been strangely borne. The
LENNOX: gracious Duncan
LENNOX: Was pitied of Macbeth: marry, he was dead:
LENNOX: And the right-valiant Banquo walk'd too late,
LENNOX: Whom, you may say, if't please you, Fleance kill'd,
LENNOX: For Fleance fled: men must not walk too late.
LENNOX: Who cannot want the thought how monstrous
LENNOX: It was for Malcolm and for Donalbain
LENNOX: To kill their gracious father? damned fact!
LENNOX: How it did grieve Macbeth! did he not straight
LENNOX: In pious rage the two delinquents tear,
LENNOX: That were the slaves of drink and thralls of sleep?
LENNOX: Was not that nobly done? Ay, and wisely too,
LENNOX: For 'twould have anger'd any heart alive
LENNOX: To hear the men deny't. So that, I say,
LENNOX: He has borne all things well: and I do think
LENNOX: That had he Duncan's sons under his key--
LENNOX: As, an't please heaven, he shall not--they
LENNOX: should find
LENNOX: What 'twere to kill a father, so should Fleance.
LENNOX: But, peace! for from broad words and 'cause he fail'd
LENNOX: His presence at the tyrant's feast, I hear
LENNOX: Macduff lives in disgrace: sir, can you tell
LENNOX: Where he bestows himself?
Lord: The son of Duncan,
Lord: From whom this tyrant holds the due of birth
Lord: Lives in the English court, and is received
Lord: Of the most pious Edward with such grace
Lord: That the malevolence of fortune nothing
Lord: Takes from his high respect: thither Macduff
Lord: Is gone to pray the holy king, upon his aid
Lord: To wake Northumberland and warlike Siward:
Lord: That, by the help of these--with Him above
Lord: To ratify the work--we may again
Lord: Give to our tables meat, sleep to our nights,
Lord: Free from our feasts and banquets bloody knives,
Lord: Do faithful homage and receive free honours:
Lord: All which we pine for now: and this report
Lord: Hath so exasperate the king that he
Lord: Prepares for some attempt of war.
LENNOX: Sent he to Macduff?
Lord: He did: and with an absolute 'Sir, not I,'
Lord: The cloudy messenger turns me his back,
Lord: And hums, as who should say 'You'll rue the time
Lord: That clogs me with this answer.'
LENNOX: And that well might
LENNOX: Advise him to a caution, to hold what distance
LENNOX: His wisdom can provide. Some holy angel
LENNOX: Fly to the court of England and unfold
LENNOX: His message ere he come, that a swift blessing
LENNOX: May soon return to this our suffering country
LENNOX: Under a hand accursed!
Lord: I'll send my prayers with him.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT IV
NARRATOR: SCENE I. A cavern. In the middle, a boiling cauldron.
NARRATOR: Thunder. Enter the three Witches
First Witch: Thrice the brinded cat hath mew'd.
Second Witch: Thrice and once the hedge-pig whined.
Third Witch: Harpier cries 'Tis time, 'tis time.
First Witch: Round about the cauldron go,
First Witch: In the poison'd entrails throw.
First Witch: Toad, that under cold stone
First Witch: Days and nights has thirty-one
First Witch: Swelter'd venom sleeping got,
First Witch: Boil thou first i' the charmed pot.
ALL: Double, double toil and trouble,
ALL: Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
Second Witch: Fillet of a fenny snake,
Second Witch: In the cauldron boil and bake,
Second Witch: Eye of newt and toe of frog,
Second Witch: Wool of bat and tongue of dog,
Second Witch: Adder's fork and blind-worm's sting,
Second Witch: Lizard's leg and owlet's wing,
Second Witch: For a charm of powerful trouble,
Second Witch: Like a hell-broth boil and bubble.

ALL: Fire burn and cauldron bubble.

Third Witch: Witches' mummy, maw and gulf

Third Witch: Finger of birth-strangled babe

Third Witch: Add thereto a tiger's chaudron,
Third Witch: For the ingredients of our cauldron.
ALL: Double, double toil and trouble,
ALL: Fire burn and cauldron bubble.
Second Witch: Cool it with a baboon's blood,
Second Witch: Then the charm is firm and good.

HECATE: Music and a song: 'Black spirits,'  and c

MACBETH: But no more sights!--Where are these gentlemen?
MACBETH: Come, bring me where they are.

NARRATOR: SCENE II. Fife. Macduff's castle.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY MACDUFF, her Son, and ROSS
LADY MACDUFF: What had he done, to make him fly the land?
ROSS: You must have patience, madam.
LADY MACDUFF: He had none:
LADY MACDUFF: His flight was madness: when our actions do not,
LADY MACDUFF: Our fears do make us traitors.
ROSS: You know not
ROSS: Whether it was his wisdom or his fear.
LADY MACDUFF: Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes,
LADY MACDUFF: His mansion and his titles in a place
LADY MACDUFF: From whence himself does fly? He loves us not,
LADY MACDUFF: He wants the natural touch: for the poor wren,
LADY MACDUFF: The most diminutive of birds, will fight,
LADY MACDUFF: Her young ones in her nest, against the owl.
LADY MACDUFF: All is the fear and nothing is the love,
LADY MACDUFF: As little is the wisdom, where the flight
LADY MACDUFF: So runs against all reason.
ROSS: My dearest coz,
ROSS: I pray you, school yourself: but for your husband,
ROSS: He is noble, wise, judicious, and best knows
ROSS: The fits o' the season. I dare not speak
ROSS: much further,
ROSS: But cruel are the times, when we are traitors
ROSS: And do not know ourselves, when we hold rumour
ROSS: From what we fear, yet know not what we fear,
ROSS: But float upon a wild and violent sea
ROSS: Each way and move. I take my leave of you:
ROSS: Shall not be long but I'll be here again:
ROSS: Things at the worst will cease, or else climb upward
ROSS: To what they were before. My pretty cousin,
ROSS: Blessing upon you!
LADY MACDUFF: Father'd he is, and yet he's fatherless.
ROSS: I am so much a fool, should I stay longer,
ROSS: It would be my disgrace and your discomfort:
ROSS: I take my leave at once.
NARRATOR: Exit
LADY MACDUFF: Sirrah, your father's dead,
LADY MACDUFF: And what will you do now? How will you live?
Son: As birds do, mother.
LADY MACDUFF: What, with worms and flies?
Son: With what I get, I mean, and so do they.
LADY MACDUFF: Poor bird! thou'ldst never fear the net nor lime,
LADY MACDUFF: The pitfall nor the gin.
Son: Why should I, mother? Poor birds they are not set for.
Son: My father is not dead, for all your saying.
LADY MACDUFF: Yes, he is dead, how wilt thou do for a father?
Son: Nay, how will you do for a husband?
LADY MACDUFF: Why, I can buy me twenty at any market.
Son: Then you'll buy 'em to sell again.
LADY MACDUFF: Thou speak'st with all thy wit: and yet, i' faith,
LADY MACDUFF: With wit enough for thee.
Son: Was my father a traitor, mother?
LADY MACDUFF: Ay, that he was.
Son: What is a traitor?
LADY MACDUFF: Why, one that swears and lies.
Son: And be all traitors that do so?
LADY MACDUFF: Every one that does so is a traitor, and must be hanged.
Son: And must they all be hanged that swear and lie?
LADY MACDUFF: Every one.
Son: Who must hang them?
LADY MACDUFF: Why,  the honest men.
Son: Then the liars and swearers are fools,
Son: for there are liars and swearers enow to beat
Son: the honest men and hang up them.
LADY MACDUFF: Now, God help thee, poor monkey!
LADY MACDUFF: But how wilt thou do for a father?
Son: If he were dead, you'ld weep for
Son: him: if you would not, it were a good sign
Son: that I should quickly have a new father.
LADY MACDUFF: Poor prattler, how thou talk'st!
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
Messenger: Bless you, fair dame! I am not to you known,
Messenger: Though in your state of honour I am perfect.
Messenger: I doubt some danger does approach you nearly:
Messenger: If you will take a homely man's advice,
Messenger: Be not found here, hence, with your little ones.
Messenger: To fright you thus, methinks, I am too savage,
Messenger: To do worse to you were fell cruelty,

Messenger: I dare abide no longer.

First Murderer: What, you egg!
NARRATOR: Stabbing him

NARRATOR: SCENE III. England. Before the King's palace.
NARRATOR: Enter MALCOLM and MACDUFF
MALCOLM: Let us seek out some desolate shade, and there
MALCOLM: Weep our sad bosoms empty.
MACDUFF: Let us rather
MACDUFF: Hold fast the mortal sword, and like good men
MACDUFF: Bestride our down-fall'n birthdom: each new morn
MACDUFF: New widows howl, new orphans cry, new sorrows
MACDUFF: Strike heaven on the face, that it resounds
MACDUFF: As if it felt with Scotland and yell'd out
MACDUFF: Like syllable of dolour.
MALCOLM: What I believe I'll wail,
MALCOLM: What know believe, and what I can redress,
MALCOLM: As I shall find the time to friend, I will.
MALCOLM: What you have spoke, it may be so perchance.
MALCOLM: This tyrant, whose sole name blisters our tongues,
MALCOLM: Was once thought honest: you have loved him well.
MALCOLM: He hath not touch'd you yet. I am young,
MALCOLM: but something
MALCOLM: You may deserve of him through me, and wisdom
MALCOLM: To offer up a weak poor innocent lamb
MALCOLM: To appease an angry god.
MACDUFF: I am not treacherous.
MALCOLM: But Macbeth is.
MALCOLM: A good and virtuous nature may recoil
MALCOLM: In an imperial charge. But I shall crave
MALCOLM: your pardon,
MALCOLM: That which you are my thoughts cannot transpose:
MALCOLM: Angels are bright still, though the brightest fell,
MALCOLM: Though all things foul would wear the brows of grace,
MALCOLM: Yet grace must still look so.
MACDUFF: I have lost my hopes.
MALCOLM: Perchance even there where I did find my doubts.
MALCOLM: Why in that rawness left you wife and child,
MALCOLM: Those precious motives, those strong knots of love,
MALCOLM: Without leave-taking? I pray you,
MALCOLM: Let not my jealousies be your dishonours,
MALCOLM: But mine own safeties. You may be rightly just,
MALCOLM: Whatever I shall think.
MACDUFF: Bleed, bleed, poor country!
MACDUFF: Great tyranny! lay thou thy basis sure,
MACDUFF: For goodness dare not cheque thee: wear thou
MACDUFF: thy wrongs,
MACDUFF: The title is affeer'd! Fare thee well, lord:
MACDUFF: I would not be the villain that thou think'st
MACDUFF: For the whole space that's in the tyrant's grasp,
MACDUFF: And the rich East to boot.
MALCOLM: Be not offended:
MALCOLM: I speak not as in absolute fear of you.
MALCOLM: I think our country sinks beneath the yoke,
MALCOLM: It weeps, it bleeds, and each new day a gash
MALCOLM: Is added to her wounds: I think withal
MALCOLM: There would be hands uplifted in my right,
MALCOLM: And here from gracious England have I offer
MALCOLM: Of goodly thousands: but, for all this,
MALCOLM: When I shall tread upon the tyrant's head,
MALCOLM: Or wear it on my sword, yet my poor country
MALCOLM: Shall have more vices than it had before,
MALCOLM: More suffer and more sundry ways than ever,
MALCOLM: By him that shall succeed.
MACDUFF: What should he be?
MALCOLM: It is myself I mean: in whom I know
MALCOLM: All the particulars of vice so grafted
MALCOLM: That, when they shall be open'd, black Macbeth
MALCOLM: Will seem as pure as snow, and the poor state
MALCOLM: Esteem him as a lamb, being compared
MALCOLM: With my confineless harms.
MACDUFF: Not in the legions
MACDUFF: Of horrid hell can come a devil more damn'd
MACDUFF: In evils to top Macbeth.
MALCOLM: I grant him bloody,
MALCOLM: Luxurious, avaricious, false, deceitful,
MALCOLM: Sudden, malicious, smacking of every sin
MALCOLM: That has a name: but there's no bottom, none,
MALCOLM: In my voluptuousness: your wives, your daughters,
MALCOLM: Your matrons and your maids, could not fill up
MALCOLM: The cistern of my lust, and my desire
MALCOLM: All continent impediments would o'erbear
MALCOLM: That did oppose my will: better Macbeth
MALCOLM: Than such an one to reign.
MACDUFF: Boundless intemperance
MACDUFF: In nature is a tyranny, it hath been
MACDUFF: The untimely emptying of the happy throne
MACDUFF: And fall of many kings. But fear not yet
MACDUFF: To take upon you what is yours: you may
MACDUFF: Convey your pleasures in a spacious plenty,
MACDUFF: And yet seem cold, the time you may so hoodwink.
MACDUFF: We have willing dames enough: there cannot be
MACDUFF: That vulture in you, to devour so many
MACDUFF: As will to greatness dedicate themselves,
MACDUFF: Finding it so inclined.
MALCOLM: With this there grows
MALCOLM: In my most ill-composed affection such
MALCOLM: A stanchless avarice that, were I king,
MALCOLM: I should cut off the nobles for their lands,
MALCOLM: Desire his jewels and this other's house:
MALCOLM: And my more-having would be as a sauce
MALCOLM: To make me hunger more, that I should forge
MALCOLM: Quarrels unjust against the good and loyal,
MALCOLM: Destroying them for wealth.
MACDUFF: This avarice
MACDUFF: Sticks deeper, grows with more pernicious root
MACDUFF: Than summer-seeming lust, and it hath been
MACDUFF: The sword of our slain kings: yet do not fear,
MACDUFF: Scotland hath foisons to fill up your will.
MACDUFF: Of your mere own: all these are portable,
MACDUFF: With other graces weigh'd.
MALCOLM: But I have none: the king-becoming graces,
MALCOLM: As justice, verity, temperance, stableness,
MALCOLM: Bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness,
MALCOLM: Devotion, patience, courage, fortitude,
MALCOLM: I have no relish of them, but abound
MALCOLM: In the division of each several crime,
MALCOLM: Acting it many ways. Nay, had I power, I should
MALCOLM: Pour the sweet milk of concord into hell,
MALCOLM: Uproar the universal peace, confound
MALCOLM: All unity on earth.
MACDUFF: O Scotland, Scotland!
MALCOLM: If such a one be fit to govern, speak:
MALCOLM: I am as I have spoken.
MACDUFF: Fit to govern!
MACDUFF: No, not to live. O nation miserable,
MACDUFF: With an untitled tyrant bloody-scepter'd,
MACDUFF: When shalt thou see thy wholesome days again,
MACDUFF: Since that the truest issue of thy throne
MACDUFF: By his own interdiction stands accursed,
MACDUFF: And does blaspheme his breed? Thy royal father
MACDUFF: Was a most sainted king: the queen that bore thee,
MACDUFF: Oftener upon her knees than on her feet,
MACDUFF: Died every day she lived. Fare thee well!
MACDUFF: These evils thou repeat'st upon thyself
MACDUFF: Have banish'd me from Scotland. O my breast,
MACDUFF: Thy hope ends here!
MALCOLM: Macduff, this noble passion,
MALCOLM: Child of integrity, hath from my soul
MALCOLM: Wiped the black scruples, reconciled my thoughts
MALCOLM: To thy good truth and honour. Devilish Macbeth
MALCOLM: By many of these trains hath sought to win me
MALCOLM: Into his power, and modest wisdom plucks me
MALCOLM: From over-credulous haste: but God above
MALCOLM: Deal between thee and me! for even now
MALCOLM: I put myself to thy direction, and
MALCOLM: Unspeak mine own detraction, here abjure
MALCOLM: The taints and blames I laid upon myself,
MALCOLM: For strangers to my nature. I am yet
MALCOLM: Unknown to woman, never was forsworn,
MALCOLM: Scarcely have coveted what was mine own,
MALCOLM: At no time broke my faith, would not betray
MALCOLM: The devil to his fellow and delight
MALCOLM: No less in truth than life: my first false speaking
MALCOLM: Was this upon myself: what I am truly,
MALCOLM: Is thine and my poor country's to command:
MALCOLM: Whither indeed, before thy here-approach,
MALCOLM: Old Siward, with ten thousand warlike men,
MALCOLM: Already at a point, was setting forth.
MALCOLM: Now we'll together, and the chance of goodness
MALCOLM: Be like our warranted quarrel! Why are you silent?
MACDUFF: Such welcome and unwelcome things at once
MACDUFF: 'Tis hard to reconcile.
NARRATOR: Enter a Doctor
MALCOLM: Well, more anon.--Comes the king forth, I pray you?
Doctor: Ay, sir, there are a crew of wretched souls
Doctor: That stay his cure: their malady convinces
Doctor: The great assay of art, but at his touch--
Doctor: Such sanctity hath heaven given his hand--
Doctor: They presently amend.
MALCOLM: I thank you, doctor.
NARRATOR: Exit Doctor
MACDUFF: What's the disease he means?
MALCOLM: 'Tis call'd the evil:
MALCOLM: A most miraculous work in this good king,
MALCOLM: Which often, since my here-remain in England,
MALCOLM: I have seen him do. How he solicits heaven,
MALCOLM: Himself best knows: but strangely-visited people,
MALCOLM: All swoln and ulcerous, pitiful to the eye,
MALCOLM: The mere despair of surgery, he cures,
MALCOLM: Hanging a golden stamp about their necks,
MALCOLM: Put on with holy prayers: and 'tis spoken,
MALCOLM: To the succeeding royalty he leaves
MALCOLM: The healing benediction. With this strange virtue,
MALCOLM: He hath a heavenly gift of prophecy,
MALCOLM: And sundry blessings hang about his throne,
MALCOLM: That speak him full of grace.
NARRATOR: Enter ROSS
MACDUFF: See, who comes here?
MALCOLM: My countryman, but yet I know him not.
MACDUFF: My ever-gentle cousin, welcome hither.
MALCOLM: I know him now. Good God, betimes remove
MALCOLM: The means that makes us strangers!
ROSS: Sir, amen.
MACDUFF: Stands Scotland where it did?
ROSS: Alas, poor country!
ROSS: Almost afraid to know itself. It cannot
ROSS: Be call'd our mother, but our grave, where nothing,
ROSS: But who knows nothing, is once seen to smile,
ROSS: Where sighs and groans and shrieks that rend the air
ROSS: Are made, not mark'd, where violent sorrow seems
ROSS: A modern ecstasy, the dead man's knell
ROSS: Is there scarce ask'd for who, and good men's lives
ROSS: Expire before the flowers in their caps,
ROSS: Dying or ere they sicken.
MACDUFF: O, relation
MACDUFF: Too nice, and yet too true!
MALCOLM: What's the newest grief?
ROSS: That of an hour's age doth hiss the speaker:
ROSS: Each minute teems a new one.
MACDUFF: How does my wife?
ROSS: Why, well.
MACDUFF: And all my children?
ROSS: Well too.
MACDUFF: The tyrant has not batter'd at their peace?
ROSS: No, they were well at peace when I did leave 'em.
MACDUFF: But not a niggard of your speech: how goes't?
ROSS: When I came hither to transport the tidings,
ROSS: Which I have heavily borne, there ran a rumour
ROSS: Of many worthy fellows that were out,
ROSS: Which was to my belief witness'd the rather,
ROSS: For that I saw the tyrant's power a-foot:
ROSS: Now is the time of help, your eye in Scotland
ROSS: Would create soldiers, make our women fight,
ROSS: To doff their dire distresses.
MALCOLM: Be't their comfort
MALCOLM: We are coming thither: gracious England hath
MALCOLM: Lent us good Siward and ten thousand men,
MALCOLM: An older and a better soldier none
MALCOLM: That Christendom gives out.
ROSS: Would I could answer
ROSS: This comfort with the like! But I have words
ROSS: That would be howl'd out in the desert air,
ROSS: Where hearing should not latch them.
MACDUFF: What concern they?
MACDUFF: The general cause? or is it a fee-grief
MACDUFF: Due to some single breast?
ROSS: No mind that's honest
ROSS: But in it shares some woe, though the main part
ROSS: Pertains to you alone.
MACDUFF: If it be mine,
MACDUFF: Keep it not from me, quickly let me have it.
ROSS: Let not your ears despise my tongue for ever,
ROSS: Which shall possess them with the heaviest sound
ROSS: That ever yet they heard.
MACDUFF: Hum! I guess at it.
ROSS: Your castle is surprised, your wife and babes
ROSS: Savagely slaughter'd: to relate the manner,
ROSS: Were, on the quarry of these murder'd deer,
ROSS: To add the death of you.
MALCOLM: Merciful heaven!
MALCOLM: What, man! ne'er pull your hat upon your brows,
MALCOLM: Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak
MALCOLM: Whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break.
MACDUFF: My children too?
ROSS: Wife, children, servants, all
ROSS: That could be found.
MACDUFF: And I must be from thence!
MACDUFF: My wife kill'd too?
ROSS: I have said.
MALCOLM: Be comforted:
MALCOLM: Let's make us medicines of our great revenge,
MALCOLM: To cure this deadly grief.
MACDUFF: He has no children. All my pretty ones?
MACDUFF: Did you say all? O hell-kite! All?
MACDUFF: What, all my pretty chickens and their dam
MACDUFF: At one fell swoop?
MALCOLM: Dispute it like a man.
MACDUFF: I shall do so,
MACDUFF: But I must also feel it as a man:
MACDUFF: I cannot but remember such things were,
MACDUFF: That were most precious to me. Did heaven look on,
MACDUFF: And would not take their part? Sinful Macduff,
MACDUFF: They were all struck for thee! naught that I am,
MACDUFF: Not for their own demerits, but for mine,
MACDUFF: Fell slaughter on their souls. Heaven rest them now!
MALCOLM: Be this the whetstone of your sword: let grief
MALCOLM: Convert to anger, blunt not the heart, enrage it.
MACDUFF: O, I could play the woman with mine eyes
MACDUFF: And braggart with my tongue! But, gentle heavens,
MACDUFF: Cut short all intermission, front to front
MACDUFF: Bring thou this fiend of Scotland and myself,
MACDUFF: Within my sword's length set him, if he 'scape,
MACDUFF: Heaven forgive him too!
MALCOLM: This tune goes manly.
MALCOLM: Come, go we to the king, our power is ready,
MALCOLM: Our lack is nothing but our leave, Macbeth
MALCOLM: Is ripe for shaking, and the powers above
MALCOLM: Put on their instruments. Receive what cheer you may:
MALCOLM: The night is long that never finds the day.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: ACT V
NARRATOR: SCENE I. Dunsinane. Ante-room in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter a Doctor of Physic and a Waiting-Gentlewoman
Doctor: I have two nights watched with you, but can perceive
Doctor: no truth in your report. When was it she last walked?
Gentlewoman: Since his majesty went into the field, I have seen
Gentlewoman: her rise from her bed, throw her night-gown upon
Gentlewoman: her, unlock her closet, take forth paper, fold it,
Gentlewoman: write upon't, read it, afterwards seal it, and again
Gentlewoman: return to bed, yet all this while in a most fast sleep.
Doctor: A great perturbation in nature, to receive at once
Doctor: the benefit of sleep, and do the effects of
Doctor: watching! In this slumbery agitation, besides her
Doctor: walking and other actual performances, what, at any
Doctor: time, have you heard her say?
Gentlewoman: That, sir, which I will not report after her.
Doctor: You may to me: and 'tis most meet you should.
Gentlewoman: Neither to you nor any one, having no witness to
Gentlewoman: confirm my speech.
NARRATOR: Enter LADY MACBETH, with a taper
Gentlewoman: Lo you, here she comes! This is her very guise,
Gentlewoman: and, upon my life, fast asleep. Observe her, stand close.
Doctor: How came she by that light?
Gentlewoman: Why, it stood by her: she has light by her
Gentlewoman: continually, 'tis her command.
Doctor: You see, her eyes are open.
Gentlewoman: Ay, but their sense is shut.
Doctor: What is it she does now? Look, how she rubs her hands.
Gentlewoman: It is an accustomed action with her, to seem thus
Gentlewoman: washing her hands: I have known her continue in
Gentlewoman: this a quarter of an hour.
LADY MACBETH: Yet here's a spot.
Doctor: Hark! she speaks: I will set down what comes from
Doctor: her, to satisfy my remembrance the more strongly.
LADY MACBETH: Out, damned spot! out, I say!--One: two: why,
LADY MACBETH: then, 'tis time to do't.--Hell is murky!--Fie, my
LADY MACBETH: lord, fie! a soldier, and afeard? What need we
LADY MACBETH: fear who knows it, when none can call our power to
LADY MACBETH: account?--Yet who would have thought the old man
LADY MACBETH: to have had so much blood in him.
Doctor: Do you mark that?
LADY MACBETH: The thane of Fife had a wife: where is she now?--
LADY MACBETH: What, will these hands ne'er be clean?--No more o'
LADY MACBETH: that, my lord, no more o' that: you mar all with
LADY MACBETH: this starting.
Doctor: Go to, go to, you have known what you should not.
Gentlewoman: She has spoke what she should not, I am sure of
Gentlewoman: that: heaven knows what she has known.
LADY MACBETH: Here's the smell of the blood still: all the
LADY MACBETH: perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little
LADY MACBETH: hand. Oh, oh, oh!
Doctor: What a sigh is there! The heart is sorely charged.
Gentlewoman: I would not have such a heart in my bosom for the
Gentlewoman: dignity of the whole body.
Doctor: Well, well, well,--
Gentlewoman: Pray God it be, sir.
Doctor: This disease is beyond my practise: yet I have known
Doctor: those which have walked in their sleep who have died
Doctor: holily in their beds.
LADY MACBETH: Wash your hands, put on your nightgown, look not so
LADY MACBETH: pale.--I tell you yet again, Banquo's buried, he
LADY MACBETH: cannot come out on's grave.
Doctor: Even so?
LADY MACBETH: To bed, to bed! there's knocking at the gate:
LADY MACBETH: come, come, come, come, give me your hand. What's
LADY MACBETH: done cannot be undone.--To bed, to bed, to bed!
NARRATOR: Exit
Doctor: Will she go now to bed?
Gentlewoman: Directly.
Doctor: Foul whisperings are abroad: unnatural deeds
Doctor: Do breed unnatural troubles: infected minds
Doctor: To their deaf pillows will discharge their secrets:
Doctor: More needs she the divine than the physician.
Doctor: God, God forgive us all! Look after her,
Doctor: Remove from her the means of all annoyance,
Doctor: And still keep eyes upon her. So, good night:
Doctor: My mind she has mated, and amazed my sight.
Doctor: I think, but dare not speak.
Gentlewoman: Good night, good doctor.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE II. The country near Dunsinane.
NARRATOR: Drum and colours. Enter MENTEITH, CAITHNESS, ANGUS, LENNOX, and Soldiers
MENTEITH: The English power is near, led on by Malcolm,
MENTEITH: His uncle Siward and the good Macduff:
MENTEITH: Revenges burn in them, for their dear causes
MENTEITH: Would to the bleeding and the grim alarm
MENTEITH: Excite the mortified man.
ANGUS: Near Birnam wood
ANGUS: Shall we well meet them, that way are they coming.
CAITHNESS: Who knows if Donalbain be with his brother?
LENNOX: For certain, sir, he is not: I have a file
LENNOX: Of all the gentry: there is Siward's son,
LENNOX: And many unrough youths that even now
LENNOX: Protest their first of manhood.
MENTEITH: What does the tyrant?
CAITHNESS: Great Dunsinane he strongly fortifies:
CAITHNESS: Some say he's mad, others that lesser hate him
CAITHNESS: Do call it valiant fury: but, for certain,
CAITHNESS: He cannot buckle his distemper'd cause
CAITHNESS: Within the belt of rule.
ANGUS: Now does he feel
ANGUS: His secret murders sticking on his hands,
ANGUS: Now minutely revolts upbraid his faith-breach,
ANGUS: Those he commands move only in command,
ANGUS: Nothing in love: now does he feel his title
ANGUS: Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe
ANGUS: Upon a dwarfish thief.
MENTEITH: Who then shall blame
MENTEITH: His pester'd senses to recoil and start,
MENTEITH: When all that is within him does condemn
MENTEITH: Itself for being there?
CAITHNESS: Well, march we on,
CAITHNESS: To give obedience where 'tis truly owed:
CAITHNESS: Meet we the medicine of the sickly weal,
CAITHNESS: And with him pour we in our country's purge
CAITHNESS: Each drop of us.
LENNOX: Or so much as it needs,
LENNOX: To dew the sovereign flower and drown the weeds.
LENNOX: Make we our march towards Birnam.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, marching
NARRATOR: SCENE III. Dunsinane. A room in the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter MACBETH, Doctor, and Attendants
MACBETH: Bring me no more reports, let them fly all:
MACBETH: Till Birnam wood remove to Dunsinane,
MACBETH: I cannot taint with fear. What's the boy Malcolm?
MACBETH: Was he not born of woman? The spirits that know
MACBETH: All mortal consequences have pronounced me thus:
MACBETH: 'Fear not, Macbeth, no man that's born of woman
MACBETH: Shall e'er have power upon thee.' Then fly,
MACBETH: false thanes,
MACBETH: And mingle with the English epicures:
MACBETH: The mind I sway by and the heart I bear
MACBETH: Shall never sag with doubt nor shake with fear.
NARRATOR: Enter a Servant
MACBETH: The devil damn thee black, thou cream-faced loon!
MACBETH: Where got'st thou that goose look?
Servant: There is ten thousand--
MACBETH: Geese, villain!
Servant: Soldiers, sir.
MACBETH: Go prick thy face, and over-red thy fear,
MACBETH: Thou lily-liver'd boy. What soldiers, patch?
MACBETH: Death of thy soul! those linen cheeks of thine
MACBETH: Are counsellors to fear. What soldiers, whey-face?
Servant: The English force, so please you.
MACBETH: Take thy face hence.
NARRATOR: Exit Servant
MACBETH: Seyton!--I am sick at heart,
MACBETH: When I behold--Seyton, I say!--This push
MACBETH: Will cheer me ever, or disseat me now.
MACBETH: I have lived long enough: my way of life
MACBETH: Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf,
MACBETH: And that which should accompany old age,
MACBETH: As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends,
MACBETH: I must not look to have, but, in their stead,
MACBETH: Curses, not loud but deep, mouth-honour, breath,
MACBETH: Which the poor heart would fain deny, and dare not. Seyton!
NARRATOR: Enter SEYTON
SEYTON: What is your gracious pleasure?
MACBETH: What news more?
SEYTON: All is confirm'd, my lord, which was reported.
MACBETH: I'll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack'd.
MACBETH: Give me my armour.
SEYTON: 'Tis not needed yet.
MACBETH: I'll put it on.
MACBETH: Send out more horses, skirr the country round,
MACBETH: Hang those that talk of fear. Give me mine armour.
MACBETH: How does your patient, doctor?
Doctor: Not so sick, my lord,
Doctor: As she is troubled with thick coming fancies,
Doctor: That keep her from her rest.
MACBETH: Cure her of that.
MACBETH: Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased,
MACBETH: Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow,
MACBETH: Raze out the written troubles of the brain
MACBETH: And with some sweet oblivious antidote
MACBETH: Cleanse the stuff'd bosom of that perilous stuff
MACBETH: Which weighs upon the heart?
Doctor: Therein the patient
Doctor: Must minister to himself.
MACBETH: Throw physic to the dogs, I'll none of it.
MACBETH: Come, put mine armour on, give me my staff.
MACBETH: Seyton, send out. Doctor, the thanes fly from me.
MACBETH: Come, sir, dispatch. If thou couldst, doctor, cast
MACBETH: The water of my land, find her disease,
MACBETH: And purge it to a sound and pristine health,
MACBETH: I would applaud thee to the very echo,
MACBETH: That should applaud again.--Pull't off, I say.--
MACBETH: What rhubarb, cyme, or what purgative drug,
MACBETH: Would scour these English hence? Hear'st thou of them?
Doctor: Ay, my good lord, your royal preparation
Doctor: Makes us hear something.
MACBETH: Bring it after me.
MACBETH: I will not be afraid of death and bane,
MACBETH: Till Birnam forest come to Dunsinane.
Doctor: [Aside]  Were I from Dunsinane away and clear,
Doctor: Profit again should hardly draw me here.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE IV. Country near Birnam wood.
NARRATOR: Drum and colours. Enter MALCOLM, SIWARD and YOUNG  SIWARD, MACDUFF, MENTEITH, CAITHNESS, ANGUS, LENNOX, ROSS, and Soldiers, marching
MALCOLM: Cousins, I hope the days are near at hand
MALCOLM: That chambers will be safe.
MENTEITH: We doubt it nothing.
SIWARD: What wood is this before us?
MENTEITH: The wood of Birnam.
MALCOLM: Let every soldier hew him down a bough
MALCOLM: And bear't before him: thereby shall we shadow
MALCOLM: The numbers of our host and make discovery
MALCOLM: Err in report of us.
Soldiers: It shall be done.
SIWARD: We learn no other but the confident tyrant
SIWARD: Keeps still in Dunsinane, and will endure
SIWARD: Our setting down before 't.
MALCOLM: 'Tis his main hope:
MALCOLM: For where there is advantage to be given,
MALCOLM: Both more and less have given him the revolt,
MALCOLM: And none serve with him but constrained things
MALCOLM: Whose hearts are absent too.
MACDUFF: Let our just censures
MACDUFF: Attend the true event, and put we on
MACDUFF: Industrious soldiership.
SIWARD: The time approaches
SIWARD: That will with due decision make us know
SIWARD: What we shall say we have and what we owe.
SIWARD: Thoughts speculative their unsure hopes relate,
SIWARD: But certain issue strokes must arbitrate:
SIWARD: Towards which advance the war.
NARRATOR: Exeunt, marching
NARRATOR: SCENE V. Dunsinane. Within the castle.
NARRATOR: Enter MACBETH, SEYTON, and Soldiers, with drum and colours
MACBETH: Hang out our banners on the outward walls,
MACBETH: The cry is still 'They come:' our castle's strength
MACBETH: Will laugh a siege to scorn: here let them lie
MACBETH: Till famine and the ague eat them up:
MACBETH: Were they not forced with those that should be ours,
MACBETH: We might have met them dareful, beard to beard,
MACBETH: And beat them backward home.
NARRATOR: A cry of women within
MACBETH: What is that noise?
SEYTON: It is the cry of women, my good lord.
NARRATOR: Exit
MACBETH: I have almost forgot the taste of fears,
MACBETH: The time has been, my senses would have cool'd
MACBETH: To hear a night-shriek, and my fell of hair
MACBETH: Would at a dismal treatise rouse and stir
MACBETH: As life were in't: I have supp'd full with horrors,
MACBETH: Direness, familiar to my slaughterous thoughts
MACBETH: Cannot once start me.
NARRATOR: Re-enter SEYTON
MACBETH: Wherefore was that cry?
SEYTON: The queen, my lord, is dead.
MACBETH: She should have died hereafter,
MACBETH: There would have been a time for such a word.
MACBETH: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow,
MACBETH: Creeps in this petty pace from day to day
MACBETH: To the last syllable of recorded time,
MACBETH: And all our yesterdays have lighted fools
MACBETH: The way to dusty death. Out, out, brief candle!
MACBETH: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player
MACBETH: That struts and frets his hour upon the stage
MACBETH: And then is heard no more: it is a tale
MACBETH: Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury,
MACBETH: Signifying nothing.
NARRATOR: Enter a Messenger
MACBETH: Thou comest to use thy tongue, thy story quickly.
Messenger: Gracious my lord,
Messenger: I should report that which I say I saw,
Messenger: But know not how to do it.
MACBETH: Well, say, sir.
Messenger: As I did stand my watch upon the hill,
Messenger: I look'd toward Birnam, and anon, methought,
Messenger: The wood began to move.
MACBETH: Liar and slave!
Messenger: Let me endure your wrath, if't be not so:
Messenger: Within this three mile may you see it coming,
Messenger: I say, a moving grove.
MACBETH: If thou speak'st false,
MACBETH: Upon the next tree shalt thou hang alive,
MACBETH: Till famine cling thee: if thy speech be sooth,
MACBETH: I care not if thou dost for me as much.
MACBETH: I pull in resolution, and begin
MACBETH: To doubt the equivocation of the fiend
MACBETH: That lies like truth: 'Fear not, till Birnam wood
MACBETH: Do come to Dunsinane:'  and now a wood
MACBETH: Comes toward Dunsinane. Arm, arm, and out!
MACBETH: If this which he avouches does appear,
MACBETH: There is nor flying hence nor tarrying here.
MACBETH: I gin to be aweary of the sun,
MACBETH: And wish the estate o' the world were now undone.
MACBETH: Ring the alarum-bell! Blow, wind! come, wrack!
MACBETH: At least we'll die with harness on our back.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VI. Dunsinane. Before the castle.
NARRATOR: Drum and colours. Enter MALCOLM, SIWARD, MACDUFF, and their Army, with boughs
MALCOLM: Now near enough: your leafy screens throw down.
MALCOLM: And show like those you are. You, worthy uncle,
MALCOLM: Shall, with my cousin, your right-noble son,
MALCOLM: Lead our first battle: worthy Macduff and we
MALCOLM: Shall take upon 's what else remains to do,
MALCOLM: According to our order.
SIWARD: Fare you well.
SIWARD: Do we but find the tyrant's power to-night,
SIWARD: Let us be beaten, if we cannot fight.
MACDUFF: Make all our trumpets speak, give them all breath,
MACDUFF: Those clamorous harbingers of blood and death.
NARRATOR: Exeunt
NARRATOR: SCENE VII. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter MACBETH
MACBETH: They have tied me to a stake, I cannot fly,
MACBETH: But, bear-like, I must fight the course. What's he
MACBETH: That was not born of woman? Such a one
MACBETH: Am I to fear, or none.
NARRATOR: Enter YOUNG SIWARD
YOUNG SIWARD: What is thy name?
MACBETH: Thou'lt be afraid to hear it.
YOUNG SIWARD: No, though thou call'st thyself a hotter name
YOUNG SIWARD: Than any is in hell.
MACBETH: My name's Macbeth.
YOUNG SIWARD: The devil himself could not pronounce a title
YOUNG SIWARD: More hateful to mine ear.
MACBETH: No, nor more fearful.
YOUNG SIWARD: Thou liest, abhorred tyrant, with my sword
YOUNG SIWARD: I'll prove the lie thou speak'st.
NARRATOR: They fight and YOUNG SIWARD is slain
MACBETH: Thou wast born of woman
MACBETH: But swords I smile at, weapons laugh to scorn,
MACBETH: Brandish'd by man that's of a woman born.
NARRATOR: Exit
NARRATOR: Alarums. Enter MACDUFF
MACDUFF: That way the noise is. Tyrant, show thy face!
MACDUFF: If thou be'st slain and with no stroke of mine,
MACDUFF: My wife and children's ghosts will haunt me still.
MACDUFF: I cannot strike at wretched kerns, whose arms
MACDUFF: Are hired to bear their staves: either thou, Macbeth,
MACDUFF: Or else my sword with an unbatter'd edge
MACDUFF: I sheathe again undeeded. There thou shouldst be,
MACDUFF: By this great clatter, one of greatest note
MACDUFF: Seems bruited. Let me find him, fortune!
MACDUFF: And more I beg not.
NARRATOR: Exit. Alarums
NARRATOR: Enter MALCOLM and SIWARD
SIWARD: This way, my lord, the castle's gently render'd:
SIWARD: The tyrant's people on both sides do fight,
SIWARD: The noble thanes do bravely in the war,
SIWARD: The day almost itself professes yours,
SIWARD: And little is to do.
MALCOLM: We have met with foes
MALCOLM: That strike beside us.
SIWARD: Enter, sir, the castle.
NARRATOR: Exeunt. Alarums
NARRATOR: SCENE VIII. Another part of the field.
NARRATOR: Enter MACBETH
MACBETH: Why should I play the Roman fool, and die
MACBETH: On mine own sword? whiles I see lives, the gashes
MACBETH: Do better upon them.
NARRATOR: Enter MACDUFF
MACDUFF: Turn, hell-hound, turn!
MACBETH: Of all men else I have avoided thee:
MACBETH: But get thee back, my soul is too much charged
MACBETH: With blood of thine already.
MACDUFF: I have no words:
MACDUFF: My voice is in my sword: thou bloodier villain
MACDUFF: Than terms can give thee out!
NARRATOR: They fight
MACBETH: Thou losest labour:
MACBETH: As easy mayst thou the intrenchant air
MACBETH: With thy keen sword impress as make me bleed:
MACBETH: Let fall thy blade on vulnerable crests,
MACBETH: I bear a charmed life, which must not yield,
MACBETH: To one of woman born.
MACDUFF: Despair thy charm,
MACDUFF: And let the angel whom thou still hast served
MACDUFF: Tell thee, Macduff was from his mother's womb
MACDUFF: Untimely ripp'd.
MACBETH: Accursed be that tongue that tells me so,
MACBETH: For it hath cow'd my better part of man!
MACBETH: And be these juggling fiends no more believed,
MACBETH: That palter with us in a double sense,
MACBETH: That keep the word of promise to our ear,
MACBETH: And break it to our hope. I'll not fight with thee.
MACDUFF: Then yield thee, coward,
MACDUFF: And live to be the show and gaze o' the time:
MACDUFF: We'll have thee, as our rarer monsters are,
MACDUFF: Painted on a pole, and underwrit,
MACDUFF: 'Here may you see the tyrant.'
MACBETH: I will not yield,
MACBETH: To kiss the ground before young Malcolm's feet,
MACBETH: And to be baited with the rabble's curse.
MACBETH: Though Birnam wood be come to Dunsinane,
MACBETH: And thou opposed, being of no woman born,
MACBETH: Yet I will try the last. Before my body
MACBETH: I throw my warlike shield. Lay on, Macduff,
MACBETH: And damn'd be him that first cries, 'Hold, enough!'
NARRATOR: Exeunt, fighting. Alarums
NARRATOR: Retreat. Flourish. Enter, with drum and colours, MALCOLM, SIWARD, ROSS, the other Thanes, and Soldiers
MALCOLM: I would the friends we miss were safe arrived.
SIWARD: Some must go off: and yet, by these I see,
SIWARD: So great a day as this is cheaply bought.
MALCOLM: Macduff is missing, and your noble son.
ROSS: Your son, my lord, has paid a soldier's debt:
ROSS: He only lived but till he was a man,
ROSS: The which no sooner had his prowess confirm'd
ROSS: In the unshrinking station where he fought,
ROSS: But like a man he died.
SIWARD: Then he is dead?
ROSS: Ay, and brought off the field: your cause of sorrow
ROSS: Must not be measured by his worth, for then
ROSS: It hath no end.
SIWARD: Had he his hurts before?
ROSS: Ay, on the front.
SIWARD: Why then, God's soldier be he!
SIWARD: Had I as many sons as I have hairs,
SIWARD: I would not wish them to a fairer death:
SIWARD: And so, his knell is knoll'd.
MALCOLM: He's worth more sorrow,
MALCOLM: And that I'll spend for him.
SIWARD: He's worth no more
SIWARD: They say he parted well, and paid his score:
SIWARD: And so, God be with him! Here comes newer comfort.
NARRATOR: Re-enter MACDUFF, with MACBETH's head
MACDUFF: Hail, king! for so thou art: behold, where stands
MACDUFF: The usurper's cursed head: the time is free:
MACDUFF: I see thee compass'd with thy kingdom's pearl,
MACDUFF: That speak my salutation in their minds,
MACDUFF: Whose voices I desire aloud with mine:
MACDUFF: Hail, King of Scotland!
ALL: Hail, King of Scotland!
NARRATOR: Flourish
MALCOLM: We shall not spend a large expense of time
MALCOLM: Before we reckon with your several loves,
MALCOLM: And make us even with you. My thanes and kinsmen,
MALCOLM: Henceforth be earls, the first that ever Scotland
MALCOLM: In such an honour named. What's more to do,
MALCOLM: Which would be planted newly with the time,
MALCOLM: As calling home our exiled friends abroad
MALCOLM: That fled the snares of watchful tyranny,
MALCOLM: Producing forth the cruel ministers
MALCOLM: Of this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen,
MALCOLM: Who, as 'tis thought, by self and violent hands
MALCOLM: Took off her life, this, and what needful else
MALCOLM: That calls upon us, by the grace of Grace,
MALCOLM: We will perform in measure, time and place:
MALCOLM: So, thanks to all at once and to each one,
MALCOLM: Whom we invite to see us crown'd at Scone.
NARRATOR: Flourish. Exeunt
